## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

Containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated carefully with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes:

The first, of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each of the Fathers on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers commented on the text of each book of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.

This is an edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially the fact that this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, gathered from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

# Dedication Letter

## To His Eminence and Most Reverend Lord, Lord Dominico Passioneo, Cardinal-Priest of the Holy Roman Church, holder of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, Librarian of the Apostolic See, and Secretary for Briefs to the Supreme Pontiff

The letters of the Roman pontiffs to the Frankish kings Pippin and Charlemagne concerning the great increases that accrued to the dominion of the Apostolic See through them, and the letters of Rudolph, King of the Romans, concerning imperial majesty and the principal affairs of the Roman Empire, are at last brought to light, Your Most Eminent Lord Cardinal, through your advocacy and patronage.

Those letters, which the father of the Ecclesiastical Annals had sought for so long and so fruitlessly, Gretser published after his death. But what did he publish? Letters carelessly transcribed, arbitrarily emended, improperly embellished—in a word, different from the Viennese autograph, or from that genuine codex which, borrowing its name from its author, Charlemagne, is now called the Carolingian Code.

For this reason Lambecius committed them to the press after rejecting them and partially correcting them, although he did not publish them, having died in the midst of his labor. I believe that, thirdly, after they had been copied from the autograph and completed in every respect, they were prepared for Your Felicity by Gentilotus, who had detected that Lambecius’s work was insufficiently exact.

For when a diplomatic mission to the Emperor had been assigned to you, after you had already gloriously discharged other offices for the Holy See, and after Gentilotus had died, you, Most Eminent Cardinal, who elsewhere had bound princes and all learned men to yourself by the distinguished gifts of your lofty spirit, won the Emperor’s favor at Vienna.

Therefore, using the intimacy of every order at that august see, you were able not only to learn all the circumstances of the Carolingian Code, but also to obtain, with skill and efficiency, the labors of Lambecius and Gentilotus—something truly great and extraordinary.

You brought back with you from Vienna to Rome the letters of Rudolph, collected by Abbot Seyfrid of Zwettl, unknown to Lambecius and rashly called into doubt by others, after you yourself had discovered them in the archive of the monastery of Zwettl and had copied them with the greatest fidelity.

You would have published both codices—the Carolingian according to the true reading of the Viennese autograph, and the unpublished Rudolphine, an outstanding monument of your love for the Roman Church—as soon as you had been summoned to Rome, as the reward for your distinguished achievements, had you not been compelled, by the continual occupations of your ministry, to postpone the desires of your great mind until this day.

For you know very well that the origin, growth, and perpetuity of the dominion of the Church, and the definite character and fixed limits of the Roman Empire, revolve around these two pillars. You know that the opinions and errors of others will be brought here, as to a Lydian stone, for testing. And finally you know that you will place beyond all danger the supreme dominion of the Roman Church, and therefore of the successors of blessed Peter, over Rome and over all their other territories from the very beginning—something Baronio could not do.

For this reason you did not disdain to employ me as a companion in the labor, wishing me to render, together with you, such and so great a service to the Holy See.

Supported by the protection of your admirable mind, and further equipped with an abundance of documents from your celebrated library, I entered with great eagerness, through the barbarism of the language and subject matter, the hidden chambers of pontiffs and kings. From them I drew forth the naked truth, from the very place where the learned writers of our age, relying on Gretser’s defective edition, did not hesitate to draw so many things from their own interpretation.

How great an addition this will bring, Most Eminent Cardinal, to your distinguished praises! Certainly that illustrious opinion of you was not deceptive when France, Belgium, and Holland looked upon you with admiration, although you had not yet been entrusted with any public office of the Holy See; when the doctors of the Sorbonne and the most distinguished men of the Congregation of Saint Maur, especially Mabillon and Montfaucon, admired your flourishing age; and when those same men, together with other eminent persons, handed down to posterity that age adorned with the praises it deserved.

Your distinguished achievements in the various and prolonged offices undertaken for the Holy See have won you a glory that will never die among human beings. But now, at last, to have asserted the rights of the Holy See, and the gifts that great princes bestowed upon blessed Peter and his successors as the reward for their souls, by a singular and irresistible method, will also open for you a blessed path to immortal glory in heaven—the only glory truly worth seeking.

This, after a long succession of years, is what I pray for you. Under your auspices, whatever, according to the limited reach of my mind, I have added to these monuments of yours, now comes to light,

**To Your Eminence,**

Your most humble, obedient, and devoted servant and client,

**Cajetanus Cennius**

[Col. 0011]

# Preface

[Col. 0011A]

## I

When the most celebrated jurist Janus Vincentius Gravina had followed the majesty of the Roman Empire down to Augustulus, he added these few words at the end of his work *(On the Roman Empire, single book, chapter 50)*:

> “As for its transformation under Charlemagne and its mixture with the Germanic kingdom, if life and opportunity are granted me, I shall discuss it in a treatment of its own.”

Both life and opportunity seem to have failed him, for nothing written by him has been found concerning imperial majesty, which revived in Charlemagne after 325 years.

What he could not do, the German jurists accomplished most fully. With Struvius and Monzambano, or Pufendorf, lighting the way, they publish new volumes day by day concerning the public law of the Roman-German Empire.

The foundations on which they rely are supplied by Goldast and Lunig. What sort of foundations these are must be heard from one of them, namely Peter Ludewig *(Manuscript Diplomatic Remains, vol. I, preface, §§ 33 and 39)*, an unimpeachable witness to the truth in this matter.

Speaking of false and suspect diplomas, this author says:

> “Would that the volumes of Goldast and Lunig, amid such a great and useful apparatus of diplomas, could escape this stigma!”

And of each separately:

> “He [Lunig] is concerned rather to cram everything in indiscriminately and without selection.”

Of Goldast:

> “Nearly half is fabricated and false … In him one rightly misses selection and the art of distinguishing the true from the false. Hence the diplomas praised by him are of suspect reliability.”

For this reason Baronio, Pagius, and all the learned—including Muratori himself—reject as especially rotten offspring those works: namely, the Royal Law or constitution of Hadrian, by which so many things utterly contrary to all credibility are granted to Charlemagne in the year 774 *(Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, vol. I, p. 16; Lunig, Italian Diplomatic Code, vol. I, p. 1)*;

the decree of Leo VIII, a false pope, by which he, together with the Senate of the Roman People, grants incredible things to Otto I in 963 *(Lunig, ibid., p. 3; Ecclesiastical Spicilegium, continuation 11, p. 66)*;

two senatorial decrees by which the same authorities permit Otto the election of the Roman pontiff and the investiture of bishops, and restore all temporal possessions donated to the Holy See by kings and emperors—despite the protest of all history *(Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, vol. I, pp. 221 ff.; Lunig, Italian Diplomatic Code, p. 6; Ecclesiastical Spicilegium, part I, p. 139)*;

and the constitution of Otto III, by which the patrimony of the Church is constituted from certain cities, while the Donation of Constantine is said to have been confirmed by Charlemagne and is declared to be spurious *(Goldast, ibid., p. 226; Lunig, ibid., p. 7; Ecclesiastical Spicilegium, p. 140)*.

[Col. 0012A]

## II

Upon foundations so weak—or rather upon their ruins, since it is evident to everyone that they have been utterly demolished—the defenders of public law rely.

First, they posit that the Roman Empire was acquired by Charlemagne, then recovered anew by Otto the Great, and finally joined by perpetual right to the German kingdom in such a way that it transferred its own name to that kingdom *(Struvius, Syntagma of the Public Law of the Roman-German Empire, § 3, p. 4)*.

After this they divide the Empire, thus conceived, into several periods:

1. From Otto the Great to Henry IV, King of Germany. During this time, they maintain that Otto and his successors, following the Carolingian practice, exercised supreme imperial authority over the pontiffs, the Senate of the Roman People, and the patrimony of the Holy See, without contradiction from the Roman pontiffs.

2. They extend the second period to the death of Frederick II in the year 1250.

3. From that point, they say, began the disastrous interregnum of Germany, lasting twenty-three years. From its beginning to the Golden Bull of Charles IV—more than a hundred years, down to 1356—they extend the third period.

They depict the second and third periods as disastrous for the Empire. They say that the supreme Empire was weakened by Saint Gregory VII, but maintain that it was not until the age of Charles V that the pope began to be recognized at Rome as lord of Rome and of Roman territory. They also assert that, during the interregnum, the electoral college began, together with the power of the princes of Germany, and that the authority of the Emperor in both secular and ecclesiastical matters was increasingly weakened.

In the following periods they discuss the majesty of the German Empire, strengthened both by the Golden Bull and by other written laws. Since these have no relevance to my subject, I shall willingly and deliberately pass them over.

It is otherwise with the first three periods. Because they rest on the suppositions just mentioned and on many others of lesser importance, they impose a false character upon the revived Western Empire, in opposition to the testimony of Roman pontiffs, kings, and emperors.

I shall have to weigh these suppositions fairly against an Italian writer of great reputation who, to the very great detriment of Italian youth, embraces almost the whole of a position based on suppositions that he himself admits and rejects. Moreover, together with the German jurists, he calls into doubt or accuses of falsity certain monuments by which the true character of the Empire and the dominion of the Holy See are placed beyond all danger.

[Col. 0013A]

## III

The immense abundance of books and treatises of this kind, by which we are almost overwhelmed after the publication of the six large volumes of *Italian Antiquities* and the twelve smaller volumes of the *Annals of Italy*, clearly shows how pleasing this has been to them. Those works were also translated into their own language so that their contents might be more widely accessible and easier for anyone to understand.

There has likewise been some such work, addressed to that same Italian writer, against the dominion of the Apostolic See, drawn from those published volumes.

If I wished to restrain such license, I should be beating water.

I see that my only task is to expose the entirely false opinion concerning the dominion of the Holy See, an opinion arising from a misconceived understanding of the nature of the Empire—or, better said, of the imperial dignity established in the West, or restored there by the holy pontiff Leo III—setting aside the labors of so many otherwise learned and acute writers.

In this way, at least, I shall serve the interests of Italian youth, so that it may not follow another’s error, or, if it is proceeding along byways, may be brought back to the straight path.

I shall accomplish this by producing monuments that are in no way doubtful, from which it will be clear that the holy pontiff neither transferred nor renewed the Empire—which continued, of course, in the East—nor that it was the right or intention of the pontificate to extinguish it. This is proved by the successors of Leo, who did not in the least reject the Eastern Empire.

Rather, Leo established—or restored—the imperial dignity so that he might provide for himself, his successors, and the territories of the Holy See against the audacity of its subjects.

For who can believe that he wished to destroy the supreme power of the Roman pontiffs who had preceded him and who would follow him? Who could suppose that so great a crime was perpetrated by a pontiff celebrated for the glory of his holiness: namely, that he would take from the Prince of the Apostles what King Pippin had once considered it a religious duty to offer, namely, to grant it to the Emperor of the East, and what both Pippin himself and his son Charles had defended for Saint Peter against the Lombard invaders with the strongest armies?

[Col. 0013D]

## IV

Therefore Saint Leo III restored not the Empire but the Emperor in the West.

The unimpeachable witness to this is Louis II, in his famous letter to Basil, Emperor of the East *(Baronius, 871, no. 51; Duchesne, Frankish Writers, vol. III, p. 555)*. In it he also declares the true nature of the dignity that had been restored:

> “Charles the Great,” he says, “our great-grandfather, anointed with such an unction by the supreme pontiff, was the first of our race and family, through the abundance of piety in him, both to be called Emperor and to become the Lord’s anointed.”

And, rejecting the Greek custom by which they wished him to be called Emperor of the Franks, he reveals the purpose of this renewed dignity:

> “For we assumed this name and dignity from the Romans, among whom, plainly, the summit of such exalted rank and title first shone forth. We have undertaken to govern by divine appointment their people and city, and to defend and exalt the mother of all the Churches of God.”

For this reason, you will find that Thegan and the other writers of the Carolingian age speak not of the Empire but of the kingdoms of the Emperor Charles.

Indeed, Charles himself, both in the division of the kingdoms among his sons and in his testament of the year 811, makes dispositions concerning his kingdoms, never concerning the Empire.

When he summoned the nobles of the kingdom—both ecclesiastical and lay—to Aachen and chose Louis, King of Aquitaine, as his successor, he asked them in these words *(Thegan, chapter 6)*:

> “Whether it pleased them that he should hand over his name—that is, the Empire—to his son Louis.”

The son, having thus been designated Emperor, returned to Aquitaine,

> “and the Lord Emperor held his kingdom and his name honorably, as was fitting.”

After Charles’s death, Louis *(ibid., chapter 8)*

> “came to the palace at Aachen and received all the kingdoms that God had entrusted to his father, without any contradiction.”

From all these territories he received embassies, including those of the Beneventans *(ibid., chapter 11 and following)*, and from the kingdom of Italy he received King Bernard himself, whom he sent back to Italy after he had sworn an oath of loyalty.

During the first two years of his reign, you will find him called king and prince. But in the year 816 Stephen IV, the successor of Leo, traveling to France *(ibid., chapter 18)*,

> “consecrated him in the presence of the clergy and all the people, anointed him as Emperor, and placed upon his head a golden crown of marvelous beauty, adorned with the most precious gems, which he had brought with him. And he called Queen Irmingard Augusta.”

From this point, when the name “king” had fallen into disuse, Louis began to be called Emperor.

[Col. 0014C]

## V

Although these things are true—indeed, unquestionably most true—the Italian annalist nevertheless throws out one of his false opinions concerning the year 806 and attempts to support it, as his own witness, by saying that Charles did nothing concerning the city and its duchy in that division because they were reserved for the person who would later be designated Emperor of the Romans.

And in the year 813, when the name Emperor was granted to Louis with the consent of the Frankish nobles, he says that one may rightly infer that Charles would not have done this without consulting Leo the pontiff.

He immediately adds:

> “Certainly he [Charles] did not report to the Franks that he had received the dominion of the City, nor the majesty of the title and rank of Emperor,”

as his vernacular sentence sounds when rendered into Latin.

So deeply was this false opinion concerning the dominion of the City seated in his mind!

Both claims are false. In the division of the kingdoms, where he distributed among his sons everything that belonged to his own jurisdiction, Charles did not dare assign Rome and its duchy—things belonging to pontifical dominion—to any one of them. Instead, he imposed upon all equally the duty of defending them, a duty that belonged to the patriciate and later to imperial majesty:

> “Above all,” he says, “we command that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as our grandfather Charles, our father of blessed memory King Pippin, and we ourselves have undertaken it afterward, so that with God’s help they may strive to defend it against its enemies and ensure that it possesses its own justice, insofar as this concerns them and reason requires.”

Louis the Pious gave nearly the same command to his own sons.

From this first point another conclusion follows, which the annalist extracts by conjecture. I shall hold all these matters in my own hands by the authority of the monuments that I shall produce.

For the present, we hear Louis II telling Basil that he did not rule the City but governed and defended it. These two functions were so necessary to attaining the imperial title that, even apart from the Carolingians themselves, it is certain and established that, if they failed in this duty, others received that dignity.

[Col. 0015A]

## VI

Indeed, the learned know that, in the succession of the Augusti, between Charles the Fat and Arnulf, the last of the Carolingians, and Guido, Duke of Spoleto, inaugurated by Stephen V, and Lambert, his son, crowned by Formosus *(from the year 891 onward)*, imperial majesty shone for approximately six years.

The same is true of Louis III, King of Burgundy, and Berengar, Duke of Friuli, crowned by Benedict IV and John X.

But what must especially be noted is this: when, after Berengar’s death, imperial majesty was silent for thirty-eight years, while the Tusculan counts occupied a tyranny at Rome, Agapetus II summoned Otto, King of Germany, against another Berengar, whose overwhelming power was gravely troubling the affairs and persons of the Church.

Although Otto had deserved extremely well of the Church, it was not permitted by those same tyrants that he be rewarded with the imperial diadem.

Perhaps ten years later, Octavian, Count of Tusculum, ascended the papal throne. Then John XII—for Octavian wished to be called by that name—summoned Otto once again and, after entering into several agreements concerning matters that will be explained more suitably elsewhere, crowned him, in a solemn rite in the Vatican basilica, the first Emperor from among the kings of Germany.

Afterward, unlike what had happened with the kingdoms of France, the name of Empire became attached to Germany itself.

The jurists call this the Roman-German Empire. That matter, as I said, does not concern my purpose. For it occurred after the Golden Bull, which closes the third of the periods mentioned above; and I am certain and resolved not to go beyond those periods except insofar as history permits.

Therefore, whether the Empire is mentioned by ancient writers—a thing that will rarely be found among the Franks—or whether the distinguished title of Emperor is mentioned, imperial majesty must always be understood as having been established or restored by Leo III.

Nothing is weaker, nothing farther removed from all truth, than the foundation laid by Struvius and others concerning an Empire acquired by Charlemagne and recovered again by Otto I. I trust that this will be made perfectly clear by the monuments.

[Col. 0015D]

## VII

There are altogether seven such monuments, already often published in print:

1. The Carolingian Code, or the ninety-nine letters collected by Charlemagne, which the Roman pontiffs sent to France over a period of fifty-two years, from 739 to 791.

2. Ten letters of Leo III written to Emperor Charles, which are reported by Hermann Conringius as having been received.

3. The diploma of Louis the Pious.

4–5. The diplomas of Otto I and Otto II, and of Saint Henry.

6. The donation, or charter, of Countess Matilda.

7. The diploma of Rudolph the Great, ancestor of the Most August House of Austria.

To these already published materials one extraordinary unpublished item is added: namely, the Rudolphine Codex, containing nearly all of Rudolph’s 126 letters, with a diploma of the prince-electors of the Empire appended at the end, by which the aforesaid Rudolph is confirmed, although with some differences from the published versions.

Since this monument of inestimable value sheds considerable light on the principal provisions of the Golden Bull, through those three periods devised by Struvius—from the first year of Otto the Great, 962, or over 394 years, down to 1356—we shall hold the German Empire within its certain limits, without any supposition, and shall understand its true character as perceived in the preceding monuments and confirmed more and more.

From the Rudolphine Codex we shall discover that the dominion of the Apostolic See, after so many and such prolonged invasions by Rudolph’s predecessors, was restored to its former condition.

Since all its origin and growth, apart from the Matildine donation, are revealed by the Carolingian Code, which preceded the establishment of imperial dignity in the year 800, it follows that, on the authority of both codices, the same dominion and the same rights belonged to the Holy See both in the time of the Frankish kings and under the Augusti, whether Carolingian or German.

Furthermore, the same codices provide entirely certain evidence for three diplomas that are called into doubt without justification, because neither is the character of the imperial majesty established or restored by Leo III properly understood, nor are the various titles or components of the dominion distinguished, nor, finally, is the discipline of pontifical ordering recognized as having been different at different times.

Something must now be said about each of these monuments.

## § I. On the Carolingian Code

[Col. 0016C]

## VIII

The Carolingian Code rightly leads the way, since everything else depends upon it.

Concerning its first edition, Lambecius speaks accurately when he says *(Commentary on the Imperial Library of Vienna, book I, p. 62)* concerning Tengnagel, prefect of that august library:

> “Posterity owes to his goodness the volume of letters that the Roman pontiffs Gregory III, Stephen III [II], Zachary I, Paul I, Stephen IV [III], Hadrian I, and the antipope Constantine sent to the leaders and kings of the Franks, Charles Martel, Pippin, and Charlemagne. The volume had once been collected through the study and care of Charlemagne himself; in the year 1613 it was published in quarto at Ingolstadt by the Reverend Father Jacob Gretser.
>
> “The very ancient manuscript codex, written on parchment, and thus far the only one in the world from which those letters were taken, is still preserved in the Imperial Library among the Latin historical codices, number 198. As is most clearly evident from its script and other circumstances, it was unquestionably written in the very age of the Emperor Charlemagne.
>
> “That Gretser’s edition was produced from this codex of the Imperial Library is attested by Gretser himself at the end of his preface to the reader in these words: ‘I add one thing,’ and so forth.”

In another place *(ibid., book I, p. 322)* he says of the same codex:

> “Moreover, through what various changes of fortune, and at what time and by what means that same outstanding codex finally came into the august Imperial Library at Vienna, is entirely unknown to me.
>
> “The distinguished Sebastian Tengnagel, the third prefect of the august Imperial Library before me, was the first to arrange for the letters of the supreme pontiffs to be copied from it, and he sent them for publication to the Reverend Father Jacob Gretser of the Society of Jesus, the most celebrated theologian. Through Gretser’s care they were later printed at Ingolstadt by Andreas Angelmarius in quarto in the year 1613.
>
> “Although I do not deny that both men deserve their due praise for this, it must nevertheless be stated that it would be worthwhile for that first edition to be carefully collated in full with the authentic codex mentioned above.
>
> “For it is clear that the man who copied it arrogated to himself excessive license in correcting and altering certain passages, even from the first page itself. There, not only was the word *memorialis* transformed by an incorrect emendation into *memorabilis*, but the heading of the first letter was altered and mutilated at will.
>
> “In the authentic codex it reads as follows:

> ‘Letter of Pope Gregory sent to Charles, Mayor of the Palace, for the defense of the Holy Church of God.’

> “But in the printed edition it reads:

> ‘Letter of Gregory III, pontiff, to Charles Martel.’”

[Col. 0017A]

## IX

This correct judgment of the learned man concerning Gretser’s edition gave the Italian Medieval Chorographer an opportunity *(Italian Writers, vol. X, p. 37)* to express a less equitable opinion about it:

> “Pagius, following Lambecius, indeed warns us, under the year 767, no. 2, that Gretser’s copyist altered certain things when he transcribed the codex from the authentic exemplar of the Imperial Library.
>
> “We hope that he did not alter the proper names of regions and cities. But we too observe several things—especially in the letters of Hadrian—that are entirely contrary to historical and genealogical truth. These could not have been altered by an inexperienced copyist; rather, they must certainly have been added by Gretser himself in order to support the document of Louis and other suspect documents.”

A little farther on he says:

> “For Pagius testifies, under the year 755, no. 6, that among writers there is disagreement about what the donation of Pippin contained and which cities it included. That is, it has not yet been sufficiently established whether the regions and cities promised were all actually handed over, and, if they were handed over, under what right—whether with full independence, as it is called—while the clauses inserted in the donations still stand in the Baronian copies:

> ‘Saving over those same duchies our dominion in all things—namely, our royal or imperial dominion—and their subjection to our side,’

> together with other restrictions, as in the Sigonian exemplar.”

What confidence in the man!

He calls Tengnagel, the prefect of the august library, Gretser’s copyist, and calls him inexperienced. He brands Gretser himself, with the utmost injustice, as a forger. He attributes to the complete donation the clause appended to the duchies of Tuscany and Spoleto, although that clause clearly proves that the remaining provinces and cities were granted to the Holy See with supreme right.

Who could tolerate such an offensive and false manner of writing?

Nevertheless, Muratori, holding such a writer in the highest esteem, embraces these entirely false opinions with open arms and repeatedly thrusts them upon his readers in his *Annals*.

From this the reader may judge how necessary an edition of the pure and uncorrupted Viennese codex is.

But let us proceed to the other editions of the Code; it will be more appropriate to speak of ours later.

[Col. 0018A]

## X

Twenty-eight years after this first edition, the Code again saw the light at Paris through Sebastian Cramoisy in the year 1641, under the care of François Duchesne, son of André *(Frankish Writers, vol. III, p. 700)*. Labbe used this edition in his *Collection of Councils*, as did others.

Since it contains nothing new but reproduces Gretser’s edition altogether, it must be regarded as one and the same edition.

The same is true of the most recent edition, produced with the finest Parisian type by the Benedictine Fathers in a new edition of Duchesne’s works in 1744, although a new order of the letters was devised, for they were arranged according to the chronology of Cointius and Pagius.

For this reason the two letters of Gregory III were published separately, as the order of the dates required *(vol. IV, p. 92 ff.)*. In the same way, the single letter of Saint Zachary was published there *(ibid., p. 96)*, and this too was mutilated, since the twenty-seven responses to the corresponding questions of the Franks were omitted as irrelevant.

All the remaining letters—except numbers 96 and 97, which were omitted for the same reason—were published in the following volume *(vol. V, pp. 485 ff.)*.

But what of it? The editors did not succeed in establishing the chronology of all the letters, whether true or false. Consequently, the last letters in this edition, those lacking a chronology, were placed after the others.

Thus the two letters of Paul *(Codex 43, 16)* were relegated to the end and said to have been issued in an uncertain year. And many more of Hadrian’s letters, divided into three groups, were all left uncertain.

Three are said to have been composed between the years 774 and 781 *(Codex 57, 61, 62)*. Eleven others *(Codex 67, 79, 72, 74, 77, 82, 83, 84, 87, 89, 93)*, in which Charles is called fellow godfather (*compater*), are said to have been written after the year 781. Finally, two *(Codex 70, 81)* are assigned hesitantly to the year 782.

Apart from this inversion—which would not be objectionable if the edition were more accurate—I do not see how this new edition differs from Gretser’s.

What is more, in the most recent edition of Gretser’s works, Lambecius’s warning having been treated as though it were of no account, and without attention to the injustice done to Gretser by the *Chorographer of Italy*, the Carolingian Code was once again sent to the press according to the original edition.

## XI.

Lambecius alone, who recognized the necessity of a new edition [Col. 0018D], undertook for the greatest public benefit the task of revising the Vienna Codex, and brought to light the papal letters contained in it, which differed greatly from those previously published. But since he wished this Codex to be the first of the minor works belonging to the great work he had conceived and entitled *Syntagma Germanicarum rerum*, and since—such are the vicissitudes of mortals—he died when its edition had scarcely been completed, this noble beginning of an unfinished work did not appear publicly. What other minor works ought to have followed the Carolingian Codex remains uncertain.

Why, however, so small a part of so great a work was not permitted to be brought into the light of day, we can easily understand if we examine the beginning and end of the printed Codex. For at the beginning the author sets out everything contained in this epistolary Codex, as he calls it [Col. 0019A], and, recounting its vicissitudes, says:

> “A parchment volume which formerly belonged first to the private library of Charlemagne himself, and afterward to Willibert, archbishop of Rouen; but which is now preserved as an authentic manuscript in the most august Imperial Library at Vienna.”

Immediately afterward he adds:

> “Peter Lambecius of Hamburg reviewed and collated this entire work with the utmost fidelity and diligence, and illustrated it with an accurate chronology and the necessary annotations appended at the end.”

The final page, numbered 208, bears the words: “End of the Carolingian Epistolary Codex.” At the foot of the following leaf, however, the beginning of the word *PE-* is indicated—namely, Peter Lambecius’s chronology and annotations, which he had promised at the beginning. Yet one may infer from the silence of Daniel Nessel, who succeeded Lambecius, that these were nowhere to be found; for, drawn on by the desire to continue the great work, he left none of Lambecius’s papers unexamined [Col. 0019B]. In the same way, Johann Benedict Gentilot, Nessel’s successor in the Imperial Library, makes no mention either of the chronology or of the annotations. This omission, if I am not mistaken, was the principal reason why Nessel suppressed the epistolary Codex.

## XII.

Gentilot, however, had another and more compelling reason for not allowing Lambecius’s edition to appear publicly. When he compared it with the Codex, he saw that the published text lacked all the barbarisms and defects which, more than anything else, might have commended it to confidence in the Codex. The venerable Baronius had given this warning when publishing a document [Col. 0019C] with all its blemishes:

> “Though it is covered with solecisms and barbarisms and disfigured by superimposed corruptions of antiquity, accept it as it is; for the curiosity that seeks knowledge makes every roughness pleasant.”

Moreover, Gentilot detected Tengnagel’s excessive liberty when Tengnagel copied the Codex for transmission to Gretser. He warns the reader of this in the preface to his own manuscript recension, of which more will be said shortly:

> “Tengnagel corrected nearly all the scribal errors, whose number in the manuscript is incredible, with his own hand—but with excessive freedom. He not only wrote the true reading in the margin, but everywhere erased, inserted, restored, and interpolated whatever I cannot approve, although he did this with the intention of sparing Jacob Gretser, to whom he later gave the volume for publication, the labor of correction” [Col. 0019D].

To this must be added Gretser’s own candid confession in his preface:

> “I would have you know, my reader, that I have not been excessively scrupulous about ancient orthography; for the world does not collapse if one reads *inlustris*, and so forth, or, as current usage now has it, *illustris*, and so forth.”

How serious a loss this represents for ancient manuscripts, those skilled in diplomatic studies will judge.

Therefore Gentilot, setting Lambecius’s edition aside, compared the Codex with the Gretserian edition with the utmost care and indicated every variant reading, even the smallest. He carefully restored the abbreviations themselves—for example, DI, DO, DUM, and DM—which Tengnagel had expanded as *Domini*, *Domino*, and *Dominum*, and which Lambecius had expanded as *Dei*, *Deo*, and *Deum*. These abbreviations, after all, establish the age of the Codex as earlier than the ninth century, as Godfrey, a Benedictine abbot, recognized above all others and demonstrated with many examples (*Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. I) [Col. 0020A].

Moreover, whatever Tengnagel had corrected, erased, or restored, Gentilot reduced again to the reading of the Codex, always warning the reader of the fact; and whatever Tengnagel had inserted, he rejected. Lambecius, on the contrary, often employs Tengnagel’s corrections, although, as we have seen, he had condemned them. Whatever the truth about this inconsistency of Lambecius, once the labors of these three directors of the Imperial Library have been brought forward, the Vienna Carolingian Codex itself will certainly be reproduced without any doubt.

## XIII.

[Col. 0020B] Such and so extensive an apparatus for a new edition of the Codex—an apparatus available only to the directors of the Imperial Library—was possessed for use in his exceptionally select and immense collection of books by a man celebrated among all the learned of Europe, wielding the greatest authority among princes and, more importantly, enjoying the highest favor with the Emperor: in a word, Dominicus Passioneus, then apostolic *apocrisiarius*, or nuncio, at Vienna in Austria, and now most eminent cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

How a man so richly adorned with such honors, celebrated throughout Europe and especially in Rome for his distinguished services at home and abroad on behalf of the Apostolic See, acquired such treasures will not be unwelcome to the republic of letters to learn briefly.

From his youth he had been highly commended by the testimony of Gronovius, Montfaucon, Mabillon, Fontanini, and the foremost scholars of his age [Col. 0020C]. As a private individual he visited the more celebrated academies of Europe. Although he did not yet hold any public office, he remained at The Hague in 1708 and for the three following years, at the command of Clement XI, to assist the Holy See while peace was being negotiated among the princes of Europe.

Then, when public peace was concluded at Utrecht in 1712 and among the Swiss in 1714, where negotiations were being conducted, he was always and everywhere present in the performance of his apostolic ministry. At those public assemblies, both through his natural courtesy and through his remarkable skill in conducting affairs, he vigorously defended the rights of the Holy See and won great esteem among princes.

His influence was greatly increased when, after being sent by Innocent XIII as *apocrisiarius* to the Swiss republic [Col. 0020D], he defended the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical immunity for a long time and with great perseverance (*Addit. ad Diacon.*, vol. II, pp. 727 ff.), thereby acquiring the highest authority among all ranks of society.

Thus, in 1730, when he went to Vienna distinguished by the same office of *apocrisiarius*, or apostolic nuncio, everyone strove eagerly to win the favor of so renowned a man, especially lovers of learning. They understood that he deserved the highest regard not only because of certain fruits of his intellect that had been published, but also because of the encomia bestowed upon him by the leading scholars of Europe.

When they perceived that he possessed great favor and authority with the Emperor, thereafter they granted him willingly and gladly whatever he desired or requested.

## XIV.

[Col. 0021A] The highly esteemed apostolic nuncio had only one concern: to obtain Lambecius’s edition, however imperfect, and the latest recension of the Carolingian Codex prepared by Gentilot.

As a fair-minded judge of that Codex, he knew that all the rights of the Holy See were confirmed by it, and especially that the diplomas of Louis the Pious, the Ottos, and Henry I were supported by it. The *Chorographer of Medieval Italy* also recognized this, as we have seen. He would therefore have undertaken any difficult task in order to secure so powerful a support for the Holy See.

Gentilot had already died, and John Baptist Garellius, chief physician and imperial councillor, had succeeded him as director of the Imperial Library. Garellius had been Gentilot’s closest friend and easily surpassed his predecessors in favor and in assistance to the advancement of the studies of others [Col. 0021B].

Passioneus could not have found a more favorable opportunity to obtain both Lambecius’s edition and Gentilot’s manuscript recension, copied with the greatest fidelity. How highly these works were valued even at Vienna, where in the Imperial Library the extreme antiquity of the Codex was esteemed more highly than the contents themselves, is shown by the fact that they were granted to this one eminent man, always with the obedience and reverence of all—and especially, in naming him, of me—as a gift of the greatest value.

As for Lambecius’s edition, since Gretser’s edition had long been published and circulated everywhere, and since Lambecius’s edition constituted only a small part of a larger work, there is less reason for wonder. But that Passioneus alone obtained Gentilot’s unpublished recension, a work of such time and labor, is extraordinary and most worthy of admiration [Col. 0021C]. This must certainly be attributed only to the renown of his learning, his greatest authority among all men, and the Emperor’s highest favor.

## XV.

Although, according to Gentilot himself (*Preface*), very few copies of the aforementioned edition existed, one nevertheless came into the hands of Apostolo Zeno, whose influence and friendship among all learned men during his lifetime are known to everyone.

From this copy, variant readings hastily and less accurately excerpted by another hand were published by Muratori in the new Gretserian edition (*Scriptores Italici*, vol. III, part II, pp. 73 ff.).

On this subject the author himself must be heard, for he both testifies to the rarity of Lambecius’s edition and admits that he issued it as though it had been examined with the greatest accuracy, although he himself had not investigated it [Col. 0021D]:

> “The republic of letters eagerly awaited the work of Lambecius, a man certainly most diligent. Yet I confess that I do not know what intervened to prevent this very edition of his from appearing publicly. Perhaps his death, interrupting his plans at an unfortunate moment, deprived lovers of learning of the hope they had conceived. I have also been informed that no copies were released to the public, except for a few that happily escaped from confinement and are now held by their possessors as treasures. One of these eventually came into the hands of the most distinguished Apostolo Zeno, a most diligent hunter of antiquities and rare books.
>
> “Because of his zeal for the advancement of learning, he himself gave it to Dominico Vandelli, now public professor of mathematics at the Gymnasium of Modena, whom I have praised more than once [Col. 0022A]. After comparing Lambecius’s edition with the earlier ones, Vandelli collected all the variant readings and most courteously conveyed them to me.
>
> “The reader, therefore, will here have the Gretserian text of the Carolingian Codex, together with the emendations supplied by Lambecius. In this way everyone will understand that I have, in a certain sense, presented both editions.”

Whether these claims suit an incomplete and less accurate edition such as Muratori’s can be gathered from the few examples I shall add.

## XVI.

First, I wish it to be noted that Lambecius (*Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, book II, p. 322), before thinking about his own edition, had warned that the word *memorialis* had been transformed into *memorabilis* by Tengnagel [Col. 0022B]. Ducange himself had inserted this warning into his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under “*Memoriales membranae*,” in these words:

> “In the inscription of the manuscript Carolingian Codex in Lambecius, book II of the *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, chapter 5: ‘which preserve memory and rescue from oblivion.’”

Indeed, the substantive *memoriale* is used in the same sense by Paul I (*Carolingian Codex*, letter 41, formerly 16), who, intending to praise Pippin, begins:

> “While we turn over the histories of the divine Scriptures in our memorial book…”

Likewise, in the manuscript of Vienna, Gentilot reads (*Carolingian Codex*, letter 98, formerly 82): *Regalem memorialem*. In the edition of the Codex the reading is plainly given in capital letters: *MEMORIALIBUS MEMBRANIS*. Muratori, however, follows Tengnagel’s correction, *memorabilibus*, together with Gretser [Col. 0022C].

Furthermore, Gretser—if I am not mistaken, misled by the printer’s error of repeated particles and *iam*—omitted in letter 4 these words of great importance, from which it is clear that the donations of the Frankish kings did not establish the dominion of the Apostolic See but enlarged it:

> “and now, because no increase has been made for us.”

These words are not missing from Lambecius’s edition. Nevertheless, Muratori imitates Gretser. Do not suppose that this was done deliberately; for the same words occur in letter 6, yet neither Gretser nor Muratori omits them there.

I pass over other omissions by Gretser (*Carolingian Codex*, letters 31, 42, 50, and 77), which are also found in Muratori; for Lambecius himself did not see most of them. The form *Dominus*, restored by Lambecius in place of *Domnus* in accordance with the Codex, is not noted in the first seven letters [Col. 0022D].

I do not enumerate the minor omissions occurring here and there down to the end, lest I weary the reader. Nevertheless, I do not hesitate to affirm that Muratori falsely promises to publish Lambecius’s edition. For he presents several letters—especially the sixth and the ninety-seventh, which resemble others—as mutilated, with their variant readings turned upside down and disregarded. He also inserted his own observations among the variants; I shall discuss them more suitably in the notes.

I will not pass over one of them here. Correcting a solecism in letter 59, he says:

> “Unless you wish to attribute this solecism to the papal copyist.”

This is indeed worthy of admiration. Elsewhere, however (*Antiquities of Italy*, vol. IV, dissertation 43), he uses a letter of Hadrian to demonstrate the ignorance of that age in Rome itself.

These observations are sufficient to show [Col. 0023A] that the matter of the Carolingian Codex remains unresolved, since no edition of it is faithful.

## XVII.

Since I see Lambecius’s diligence disapproved by Gentilot, I cannot refrain from exposing Lambecius’s own mistake concerning the Carolingian Codex. From this everyone may infer what sort of chronology and annotations he would have added to his edition had he survived.

In the *Commentaries on the Imperial Library* cited above (book II, p. 221), beside the words of the title *seu etiam de Imperio*—“or also concerning the Empire”—he had appended this note:

> “Namely, the Eastern, or Constantinopolitan, Empire. But, regrettably, the letters of the Constantinopolitan emperors mentioned here are not extant in this Codex. It therefore seems that the entire body of letters was divided into two volumes. The first, which still exists in the most august Imperial Library and is the very one now under discussion, contained the letters of the supreme pontiffs; the other, which I believe was lost through the passage of time, contained the letters of the Constantinopolitan emperors.”

[Col. 0023B] For my part, if I may say so without offending so great a man, I am convinced that the title indicates only papal letters. These letters deal both with the Apostolic See and with the Empire, as I shall appropriately point out in the notes.

Although some letters were written to Charles at Constantinople, there are not so many of them that they would have had to be placed separately in another Codex. Moreover, the few in question are clearly identifiable.

Accordingly, those words of the title refer to the pontiffs who wrote to the princes and kings of the Franks concerning the supreme Apostolic See of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, or also concerning the Empire, as the title states [Col. 0023C]. It will not easily be possible to find examples in which the preposition *de* is used in place of *ab*, although much barbarism still prevailed both in Italy and in France.

As for the diligence of Lambecius that Gentilot criticized, Gentilot’s recension will make it clear how many of Tengnagel’s corrections Lambecius adopted and how frequently he added corrections of his own.

## XVIII.

From what has been presented thus far it is evident that a new edition of this Codex is altogether necessary: first, so that Tengnagel’s license may be restrained; second, so that Lambecius’s work may be examined in its entirety; and finally, so that Gentilot’s truly extraordinary labor—by which the Vienna Codex was shown both as it had been and as Tengnagel had made it [Col. 0023D]—may be commended to the republic of letters.

For this reason I decided to use the Gretserian edition as my text, while appending the variant readings of the three directors of the Imperial Library.

> **Note:** “We insert only the principal variant readings within brackets in the text or display them in the notes; the remainder, which concern merely the addition, omission, or alteration of a single letter in certain words, we deliberately omit as entirely superfluous. EDITOR.” [Col. 0023D; 0024D]

If I were to publish the letters in their pure form as they appear in the Codex, which I could do with Gentilot’s assistance, I would present the reader with excessive labor merely to make known the contribution of each of the three distinguished men, and I would deprive Lambecius and Gentilot of the praise they deserve, which would be entirely unjust.

Moreover, whatever liberty Gretser allowed himself in orthography would be counted as a fault in Tengnagel, if Gretser’s policy can properly be called a fault, since diplomatic scholarship had not yet become a cherished discipline [Col. 0024A].

The most eminent Passioneus approved this decision of mine. He had been planning this edition for many years, but, hindered by the many and varied duties of his ministry, he finally entrusted its preparation to me for the greatest public benefit.

Overcome by such commanding instructions, aided by the abundance of books supplied by that same most eminent cardinal from his exceptionally select and immense library—where, astonishingly, nothing is lacking and nothing superfluous is found for any learned European who comes there—and furnished by him with the necessary information, as though guided by the hand through the inaccessible regions of this field, I completed a work for which, whatever its quality, the strength of my intellect would have been wholly inadequate.

This was especially true of two of the monuments that I am about to publish: the Carolingian Codex [Col. 0024B], which leads the way, and the Rudolphine Codex, which I shall discuss in its proper place.

## XIX.

Those who labor not only by reading but also by writing, so that they may entrust the fruits of their minds to posterity, will judge how useful this latest edition, prepared in the manner described above, will be.

Above all, it will silence those who, following the *Chorographer of Medieval Italy*, suppose that Gretser added to the text what seemed useful for defending the diplomas of Louis the Pious and others.

Since this Carolingian Codex makes clear what territory belonged to the Holy See before the donations of the Frankish kings and what increases it received from the generosity of those kings, I applied all the strength and energy of my industry—following the example of the Maurist Fathers, who arranged the letters chronologically, although I do not approve their having done so through the labor of another [Col. 0024C]—in order to ascertain, if not the exact date of each letter, at least its definite order.

I also supplied each letter with its own synopsis, as accurate as possible, so that the letters, thus equipped, might be of great use to the reader.

Muratori, whose diligence in publishing the labors of others was what it was, would undoubtedly have attempted to arrange them in another fashion rather than preserving the entirely useless order in which they stand in the Codex.

Indeed, he moved the letter of Saint Zachary and the two letters of the false pope Constantine from their places and arranged them in his own order. He also disturbed their sequence by inserting between the letters of each pontiff the life of each one, drawn from Fr. Amalric Augier and from Frodoard.

But false opinions, which he had commended in his writings [Col. 0024C] (*Italian Writers*, vol. III, part II, where the Carolingian Codex appears, deliberately postponed until the great collection was nearly complete), persuaded him that it was in his own interest to publish those letters without order and without chronological support, just as they had been transmitted in the Codex [Col. 0024D].

Thus, by arbitrarily putting forward the crafty Pope Hadrian, Charles as a false promiser, and the Holy See as deceived, he could insinuate and plausibly demonstrate to people ill-disposed toward the Apostolic See and ignorant of ecclesiastical affairs precisely what he so vehemently strove to establish—as indeed he did.

## XX.

[Col. 0025A] But if anyone should wish to inspect the Vienna Codex itself, not merely reproduced completely in its individual letters but disarranged as it stands in the Imperial Library, I do not see what good that would do through me. Nothing is easier than to restore that confused order. For immediately after the preface I place before all eyes an expanded table which presents both the ancient and the new order of the letters.

Moreover, in this epistolary Codex three matters seemed to me especially worthy of attention: one against the defenders of a collection of the canons of the Holy See before the middle of the eighth century, who unsuccessfully maintain it upon Sirmond’s discovery; another against those who, failing to perceive in the Carolingian Codex the complete freedom in the consecration of Roman pontiffs attested from Gregory III throughout the eighth century [Col. 0025B], and failing to understand that it continued after the imperial dignity had been established by the Apostolic See, distort the discipline by conjecture and reasoning and pronounce the diploma of Louis the Pious spurious; and finally a third against those same persons, who, thinking only of temporal matters, do not observe that the principal reason for first creating patricians and then emperors was to protect the Catholic faith and the Holy See from the impiety of the Greeks or any other machination of the wicked—a point very clear in the letters of the Codex—and who do not speak with due dignity of the Roman pontiffs distinguished for holiness or of the most pious Frankish kings and emperors [Col. 0025C].

I shall treat each matter more suitably in the notices prefixed to the letters of each pontiff and in the dissertations preceding the other documents, to which I refer the reader. Thus far concerning the Carolingian Codex, which is presented in the first volume of this work. I now come to the other documents of the second volume.

### § II. Ten Letters of Saint Leo III

## XXI.

The ninety-nine letters of the Carolingian Codex, written almost all by Roman pontiffs to the princes and kings of the Franks, are followed by ten others which the supreme pontiff Leo III sent to Charlemagne, whom he himself had made emperor. Concerning this same imperial dignity—both while it remained among the Carolingians and when it was transferred by apostolic authority to the Germans—and concerning the considerable difference between the two [Col. 0025D], one should consult the dissertation which will precede these Leonine letters.

There it will be seen that imperial majesty, far greater than royal majesty, exercised jurisdiction in the city itself, provided that it acted at the request or with the counsel of the Roman pontiff. Nevertheless, from these few letters it will become clear that this new majesty was devised by the supreme pontiff for the defense of the orthodox faith, the Holy See, and the Roman pontiff, just as Stephen II had devised the patriciate. For Leo addresses Charles Augustus no differently than Hadrian had addressed King Charles, so that the difference of majesty is evident only in one and the same patron and defender of the Catholic religion and of the Holy See. The import of the letters does not differ at all from that of the many letters contained in the Carolingian Codex; indeed, the agreement between them is so great that, once the necessary difference in address and conclusion is removed, in both places one finds the same spiritual and temporal power of the pontiffs, and in both the patronage and defense of Charles.

That, evidently, was the character or nature which Leo III gave to this established dignity; and the Romans recognized that alone, according to the testimony of the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 376), when they celebrated Charles, crowned with the imperial crown, with praises or acclamations [Col. 0026B]:

> “Then all the faithful Romans, seeing the great defense and love which he had shown toward the holy Roman Church and its vicar, unanimously cried out in a loud voice, by the will of God and of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven: ‘To Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, life and victory!’”

## XXII.

From these same letters the donation of Corsica, which is less clear in the Carolingian Codex, is vindicated for Charles so plainly that Conring himself, to whom we owe them, supplies this weighty testimony (letter 4, formerly 6), although he was most hostile to the Holy See:

> “That this island was given to the popes by Charles is also related by Anastasius in the *Life of Hadrian*. Leo of Ostia lists it among Pippin’s gifts. Yet because Anastasius, when he enumerates Pippin’s gifts by name in the *Life of Stephen*, does not mention Corsica, while this Pope Leo too appeals to the gift of Charles alone, it is probable that that Leo of Ostia was both mistaken and misled others. In this age Corsica was exposed to continual Saracen raids, indeed was in their power; and therefore it is not surprising that Leo’s petition had no effect. Yet today the Genoese are believed to possess it through papal favor.”

But Conring is mistaken when he thinks that Leo’s petition had no effect [Col. 0026C]. For in the time of Sergius II, who ascended Peter’s see in 844, thirty-six years after the date of this Leonine letter, Count Adelbert administered that island for the Holy See. We learn the fact from a fragment of the life of the same pontiff, now printed in the edition of Anastasius compiled by Giovanni Vignoli from various codices (vol. III, nos. 40 ff.), such as Holstenius had copied after finding it in the Farnese parchments, while the famous Farnese Library was still at Rome [Col. 0026D].

Since I possess another, far more accurate copy, made at Parma, to which the same library had been transferred, by the most diligent prelate Francesco Bianchini, I trust that the reader will welcome hearing, from Bianchini’s papers, the portion of the history relevant here. It runs as follows:

## XXIII.

> “In the time of this aforesaid pontiff, while these things were taking place, Adelvertus, a vigorous count, who was margrave and guardian of the island of Corsica, having learned of the danger to the commonwealth, sent a letter to Rome reporting that a multitude of Saracens, numbering up to eleven thousand, were hastening to come with seventy-three ships, in which there were five hundred horses; and that they said they were hastening to Rome and were striving to free the treasures of the churches of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and, if possible, to bring the bodies of the apostles themselves within Rome, lest that most impious race of pagans should exult over so great a calamity of ours [Col. 0027A]. This letter was sent on the tenth day of August.
>
> “They received it lightly and almost with contempt because of the changeable and ineffectual authority of the aforesaid men [Sergius II and his brother Benedict], although so unexpected a matter was thought by everyone incapable of occurring. Yet the more prudent Romans, after taking counsel, sent envoys and letters to the subject cities and their neighboring places, together with the letter which Adelvertus had sent, so that all might hasten in hostile array to guard the maritime shores. Disobeying this command, they would not come, except for very few men from certain cities, who came under the pretext of inquiry.
>
> “[Col. 0027B] After a period of twelve days had passed, on the twenty-third day of August, Monday, indiction IX, those most impious Saracens reached the Roman shore near the city called Ostia, etc.”

Baronius, on the authority of the *Annals of Fulda*, and Pagius, on that of the Metz annals and others, relate the plundering of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the year 846. Hermannus Contractus agrees with those annalists for the same year. Thus this history is certain; and if the supplementary material which I have adduced from the Farnese parchments is added, Conring’s observation will prove slight and erroneous, and nothing will be more certain than the dominion of the Holy See over that island, as also over Rome and its duchy, whose cities are summoned to arms by the Roman nobles.

## XXIV.

[Col. 0027C] Thus Leo III, in the letter whose elucidation led me to recount a history unknown to Conring, wrote to Charles that he was taking every care together with Pippin, the same Charles’s son and king of Italy,

> “that our shores and yours may be made safe from the attack of the pagans and our enemies.”

That is, he preserved the distinction between the maritime coast of the Roman duchy, which was within the jurisdiction of the Holy See, and the coast of the duchy of Tuscany, which belonged to Charles and was to be defended by the king of Italy. The latter is to be understood as beginning from the city or territory of Populonium, where the maritime coast of the Holy See ended. This is confirmed by another letter as well (letter 3, formerly 8), where the discussion concerns the coast of the Holy See alone:

> “Ever since your serenity exhorted us concerning their [the Saracens’] arrival, we have always had our rear areas and our shores organized, and we still have guards.”

[Col. 0027D] This corresponds wonderfully to the action of the Roman nobles in the age of Sergius II. For they summoned the subject cities,

> “so that all might hasten in hostile array to guard the maritime shores.”

[Col. 0028A] The Leonine letters addressed to Charles as emperor concern not only the ancient dominion of the Holy See, prior to the donations of the Frankish kings, without any discrepancy from the letters of the Carolingian Codex addressed to Charles when he was king; they also speak very clearly (letter 5) of the remaining dominions perpetually granted by the generosity of Pippin and Charles to the Prince of the Apostles, and through him to the Roman pontiffs. But on this subject, and on matters of greater importance, more fully and suitably in Dissertation 1.

### § III. On the Diploma of Louis the Pious

## XXV.

In third place follows a recapitulation of the aforesaid epistolary history, namely the diploma of Louis the Pious, issued in the eighty-seventh year after the beginnings of apostolic dominion. In it all the titles of that dominion and all the rights of the Holy See are set out so clearly that it is very surprising that learned men have entirely failed to grasp its purport. Why? Did it not seem interpolated to Baluze, Mabillon, and Le Blanc? Do not Pagius and Muratori, together with Goldast and Molinaeus, boldly declare it fictitious, just like the Donation of Constantine?

This headlong and audacious judgment of theirs is the reason why this diploma, so often published, is issued again by me. Nor is this in order to secure it greater credibility from some ancient codex, though I certainly could do so. For I have before me a most excellent parchment codex, whose writer identifies himself at the top of the first page:

> “Here begin the deeds of the poor scholar Albinus.”

He also states his condition in a brief narrative of those same deeds:

> “For a long time I was the rival and helper of Riccardo of Orvieto, afterward bishop, then very poor, and my uterine brother—by the same father, a full brother.”

Regarding him, the records of the monastery of Saxi Vivi in Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 1468), state:

> “Richard, a native of Gaeta, not so called by surname, was chosen for the Church of Orvieto on the same day of Saint Benedict on which his predecessor had died, after two years had elapsed, in 1177.”

At the end of the aforementioned narrative he also marks the date of the written codex:

> “But when I became a man, I was called, by the deserts of my sins, to the Roman Church; and from that time I was careful, whenever and wherever I could, to attach in this same fascicle what I had learned or found from books of antiquities to belong by right to blessed Peter, or what I myself heard and saw from the time of Lucius III, who ordained me, though unworthy, deacon in the second and priest in the fourth year of his pontificate [1184].”

Since this author preceded Cencius Camerarius by some years and, drawing the ancient documents from the same sources with the greatest fidelity, as their very great agreement with the autographs and copies preserved in Hadrian’s Mole demonstrates, this diploma together with the two following ones displays in this new edition the value of antiquity.

My purpose, however, is otherwise directed. I have resolved to expose the error both of those who have dared to accuse this diploma, on which others depend, of falsity or interpolation, and especially of those who admit that neither defect is found in the diploma of Louis, but maintain that it is a new document of donation. Accordingly, they do not hesitate to alter its reading in order to draw an ancient document to their own opinion—an outrage scarcely tolerable in one who has even greeted diplomatic scholarship at its threshold. For Louis did not give the Holy See even an ell of land; rather, at the urgent request first of Pope Stephen IV and then of Saint Paschal I, he confirmed all its rights and the preceding donations.

## XXVI

Indeed, from at least the year 728, Rome and the people of its duchy, having withdrawn from the impious Greeks and established a holy commonwealth, began to be subject to the Roman Pontiff even in temporal matters. Therefore, in the year 817, Saint Paschal I presided over that commonwealth, as his predecessors—Gregory II and III, Saint Zacharias, Stephen II, Saint Paul I, Stephen III, Saint Adrian, Saint Leo III, and Stephen IV—had done, whatever form of principality he employed.

Yet Paschal—or rather his predecessor Stephen IV—having more than once observed the fickleness of the Romans, desired his principality to be fortified by imperial authority so that he might govern more effectively, an idea that had not occurred to his predecessors. Accordingly, Louis confirms “to the lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors in perpetuity, just as you have held and administered it in your power and jurisdiction from your predecessors down to the present, the city of Rome with its duchy.” He then enumerates the individual cities of the duchy, without any of the places contained in the donations—which he confirms separately—being omitted.

What could be clearer than this? Conversely, what could be said or imagined more absurd than the bold emendation of those who order that one should read *to our predecessors*, contrary to the evidence of all the manuscripts? For it is certain that Pippin granted only the Exarchate and the Pentapolis. As for Charles, even if it were not established which individual provinces and cities he had granted, Louis would have been called “our predecessor,” not “our predecessors.”

Moreover, below Louis confirms “the patrimonies belonging to your power and jurisdiction, such as the Beneventan and Salernitan patrimonies, the patrimony of Lower and Upper Calabria, and the Neapolitan patrimony, and wherever in the territories of the kingdom and empire entrusted to us by God your patrimonies are known to exist.” Yet Greek emperors, patricians, and others had offered these patrimonies to the Holy See. Thus, whether they wish it or not, they must acknowledge that the Ludovician diploma is nothing other than a confirmation of all the rights of the Holy See.

## XXVII

One donation of Sicily, so that I may omit nothing that could be objected, inserted into the donation of Charles the Great, seems to contain some obscure element. For that Charles possessed rights in Corsica and in the neighboring island of Sardinia, and granted both to the Holy See, is clearly shown by the boundaries of the kingdoms established by Charles among his sons. This is especially and plainly evident concerning Corsica from the letters of Saint Leo III.

But concerning Sicily the only evidence available is that, when Louis confirmed all the patrimonies, he passed over the Sicilian one in silence. Yet it is otherwise established and beyond doubt that the three and a half talents of gold which the East paid to the Roman Church had been transformed by the Greeks into the two great patrimonies of Calabria and Sicily, which are recorded as having been invaded by the iconoclasts.

Therefore, when Louis confirmed the Calabrian patrimony—which, like the Sicilian, was under Greek control—but remained silent about the Sicilian, he provided sufficient light to dispel the obscurities surrounding the Carolingian donation. In addition, since after the Greeks were expelled that island came into the hands of the Saracens and remained in that condition both in 962, when Otto the Great issued his diploma, and in 1014, when Saint Henry asserted the island for the Holy See in a new diploma, each emperor confirmed the Sicilian patrimony subject to the condition: “the patrimony of Sicily, if God should deliver it into our hands.”

Thus, whether it is called Sicily or the patrimony of Sicily, the Holy See possessed an ancient right in the island; and nowhere will any document be found that can be brought against this Ludovician diploma and the later ones so as to cast doubt upon Charles’s donation. On the contrary, history contributes considerable illumination to the diploma. See the dissertation prefixed to the letters of Leo III (no. 12 and following).

## § IV. On the Diploma of Otto I

### XXVIII

The diploma of Otto I, the first of the German emperors, is presented in fourth place. Its original is preserved in the archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, where there is also one of the many authentic copies which Innocent IV ordered to be made and authenticated in 1245 at the Second Council of Lyon. All the editions derive from it; the most exact is found in the work of the most eminent Antonelli, then prefect of that archive (*Dom. della sancta sede*, etc., part VII, p. 201).

This diploma possesses a notable feature: although it is separated from the Ludovician diploma by 145 years—for it was issued in 962, when the affairs of the Church and of Italy were in the worst condition—the rights of the Holy See are nevertheless confirmed in it with only a slight and necessary difference, just as in the Ludovician diploma.

This is clear evidence that no addition had been made to ecclesiastical territory by the successors of Charles the Great, but that each of them, following Louis’s example, confirmed the various titles of dominion contained in Louis’s diploma. For Otto’s diploma, insofar as the inexperience of the registrars of a youthful pontiff and of that most unfortunate age permitted, is almost a reproduction of the Ludovician diploma as regards the dominion of the Church.

Since authentic documents of the donations employed in Louis’s time were preserved in the archives, and had then been used with discernment and selection, the same documents are found inserted into Otto’s diploma. There is no doubt that this was done so that Otto might be presented with a diploma to confirm, one more ample and more advantageous to the Holy See. Nevertheless, some superfluous and occasionally contradictory elements are found in it; yet these do not alter the substance of the diploma when they are carefully considered. Each point will be examined in Dissertation III.

### XXIX

Here I think one matter must by no means be passed over. At the Roman Council of 877, John VIII, in Labbe (*Councils*, vol. IX, p. 295), praises Charles the Great in the highest terms because he not only restored to the Apostolic See cities taken from it by others, but also “from a portion of his kingdom granted other considerable [cities].”

By contrast, when praising Louis the Pious, he does not mention cities and territories granted by him; rather, he says that Louis confirmed his father’s generosity and pursued the Holy See “with more abundant benefits and lavish benefactions.” These statements lend credibility to Otto’s diploma, in which not even Louis’s name appears, although he seems to have had to be named somewhere, as will be made clear in the dissertation. Still less is any donation of his, whether promised or voluntary, indicated.

In this respect Otto’s diploma differs from the Ludovician diploma. For Otto, following the example of Charles the Great—whence he too acquired the surname “the Great”—both confirmed donations made by others and granted from his own kingdom, namely from the Duchy of Spoleto, seven cities to be possessed by the Holy See in full right, just as all the others:

> “From our own kingdom,” he says, “we grant cities and towns with their fisheries, namely Rieti, Amiternum, Forconium, Norcia, Balva, and Marsi, and elsewhere the city of Interamna.”

The last was, of course, a city of Umbria, situated near the Roman duchy and not far from Narnia.

### XXX

The great difference in the discipline governing the consecration of pontiffs cannot be compared with the matters mentioned above. The complete freedom enjoyed by the Roman clergy and people from the time of Gregory III had already ceased under Sergius II. The elected pontiff was not consecrated without imperial confirmation, with the emperor’s envoys present.

Although this discipline was abolished for a time, it necessarily had to be restored by apostolic authority. For in 827, when the constitution of Eugenius II and the Emperor Lothair confirmed the rite of canonical election after removing the abuses that had crept into it, no mention was made of consecration.

Sergius II later wished consecration to be subject to imperial confirmation. Thus, under the emperors Lothair and his son Louis, the decree of election came to be sent, according to ancient custom, to the imperial court; nor was the pontiff consecrated unless he had been confirmed by the emperor and in the presence of the emperor’s envoys.

The Holy See shook off this yoke after Louis’s death, so that it is certain and well established that the nine successors of John VIII were freely consecrated. Yet circumstances compelled the Holy See, at the Roman Council held by John IX in 898—or, according to another reckoning, in 904 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 502)—to submit voluntarily once again to a yoke which it had always rightly rejected. It is not certain, however, that this was put into effect, since first the counts of Tusculum, who had gained control of affairs, and later the Ottos, arrogated the election itself to themselves with the utmost wickedness.

Nevertheless, before Otto I interfered in the election, he embraced this new subjection of the Holy See to imperial authority as a just and proper law in his diploma, issued at the very act of his coronation:

> “With our power, and that of our son and our descendants, preserved in all things, according to what is contained in the pact, constitution, and binding promise of Pope Eugenius and his successors, namely, that all the clergy [lacuna] and that he who is elected to this holy and apostolic government shall be consecrated pontiff with no one’s consent, before such [a declaration is made] in the presence of our envoys, etc.”

Compare this discipline with the Ludovician one. It will become clear how rashly it is said that both diplomas were fabricated in the eleventh century.

## § V. On the Diploma of Saint Henry

### XXXI

Just as no diplomas are produced between Louis and Otto because they presented nothing new, so among Otto and Henry there are no diplomas of either Otto II or Otto III included in the number. For no diploma of Otto II appears to survive other than his father’s diploma, issued in both their names and properly read in 967, when he received the imperial diadem from John XIII while his father was still alive.

The same conclusion concerning Otto III is encouraged by the diplomas he issued at Rome, when, after being crowned by Gregory V, his kinsman and a man whom he had promoted to the pontificate, he was made advocate of the Church of Saint Peter, as Ditmar says (*Book IV*). For he would have acquired no right in the City unless he had assumed the imperial crown, to which, among other rites, the reading of the diploma was attached, as will be made clear in its proper place in the dissertations.

The matter is different with the diploma of Saint Henry, which the *Chorographer of Medieval Italy* (*Italian Writers*, vol. X, no. 99) would have treated as worthless on the basis of an excessively hasty judgment, as though “Otto’s charter had been received and confirmed by the most pious Henry in good and holy faith.”

The diploma itself refutes this insult. After confirming the ancient dominion of the Holy See, it speaks of the donations as follows:

> “Which the lords Pippin, Charles, Louis, Otto, and likewise his son Otto, our predecessors, granted to blessed Peter . . .”
