It must be carefully observed that Louis is not passed over in silence, as happened imprudently under Otto; but the designation “most excellent emperors” is omitted, since neither Pippin nor Otto, the son of Otto I, was deemed worthy of that honor. This point was not attended to in Otto’s diploma, where Pippin is consequently given the title “emperor” in an obvious falsehood.

Below, however, whether they are mentioned together without Pippin’s name, or Charles alone is named, the Augustan title is never omitted. This is not to receive and confirm Otto’s charter in good and holy faith, correct its defects, and warn all his successors where they must begin the confirmation of all the rights of the Apostolic See.

### XXXII

Indeed, nothing was more customary for Henry’s Augustan successors than the confirmation of the rights of the Holy See from the time of Louis. On this matter, see Dissertation IV, prefixed to this diploma.

Accordingly, the foresight of Henry—or of Benedict VIII—should rather be praised. Although he governed the Catholic Church in an age that was scarcely more fortunate, he did not imitate the imprudence, or perhaps the ignorance, of John XII. Instead, he clearly expressed the name of Louis, or saw to it that Henry expressed it.

The diploma of Henry is exceedingly similar to Otto’s diploma, just as Otto’s is to the Ludovician one: it confirms all the territories and rights of the Holy See. It also presents, together with Otto, a discipline governing the consecration of the pontiff quite different from that set out in Louis’s diploma; for the same discipline prevailed under both emperors.

When it comes to Henry’s own donation, however, he distinguishes so clearly between what he grants beyond the Alps and what he grants in the Duchy of Spoleto, and separates so plainly what he offers by way of donation from what he offers by way of exchange, that he completely rejects the characterization of the document as something accepted and confirmed in “good and holy faith.”

For this reason, when Nicholas III wished Rudolph to confirm the territories and rights of the Holy See after the most disastrous periods of invasion, he did not send him one of three diplomas, however similar they might be. Instead, he sent each one separately, carefully copied by Conrad, Rudolph’s envoy, from the archive of the Roman Church, as can be seen in Raynaldus (1278, no. 58 and following).

For the same reason, I considered it a matter of conscience not to place each of them before the reader’s eyes, carefully collated from the outstanding Albinian codex mentioned above with the authentic copy of the Ludovician diploma and with the originals of Otto and Henry preserved in the apostolic archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, in opposition to the recent license taken in writing about each of them.

## § VI. On the Charter of Countess Matilda

### XXXIII

After Henry’s diploma, the celebrated donation of Matilda claims its place. I see that both ancient and recent writers have treated it with insufficient accuracy. Some assign the private property of the great countess to an improper location, so that it appears even today to be possessed by the Apostolic See—nothing could be more false. Others restrict it to a few estates and thereby make blessed Peter, appointed heir of all the property, inferior in status to the monasteries and churches into which that most pious princess poured her largesses.

This donation is the most celebrated monument in all the records of pontiffs, emperors, kings, and others for approximately two hundred years, from the end of the eleventh century to the beginning of the fourteenth. Since it is called by various names—land, house, allodium, estate, county, or donation—different opinions have arisen concerning it.

Opinions? Rather, one hallucination has arisen from another. Therefore it was necessary to discuss this donation more fully than the preceding ones, after investigating a considerable portion of history before Matilda’s gift and an equally important portion after it, when, during the residence of the Holy See at Avignon, the very name of the donation fell into disuse.

I did this willingly and gladly. As I traversed periods wrapped in dense darkness, I encountered the footsteps of highly learned men who had strayed from the straight path. This circumstance added astonishing energy to my efforts and, in a certain sense, impelled me to continue along a road on which not a few others had begun their journey, but, led astray by false opinions, had failed to reach the destination they had set for themselves.

### XXXIV

I observed especially that two successors of Saint Henry, Conrad the Salian and Henry II, after attaining the imperial dignity through coronation at the hands of a pontiff, did not imitate the generosity of either Otto or Henry. Rather, after confirming the ancient rights of the Holy See, they added nothing new from their own resources.

All the other Augusti, excepting Lothair II, when they were about to obtain the imperial crown, confirmed those same rights with the most ample promises and strongest oaths; yet immediately afterward, as perjurers, they mixed everything with invasions. Nor did the Apostolic See return to its primitive rights before Rudolph, elected King of the Romans in 1273.

Consequently, from the time of Henry IV, King of Germany, for nearly two centuries the rights of the Holy See appear among writers in an extremely confused state, with the ownership of places uncertain. Within this period I investigated the vicissitudes of Matilda’s estates—their acquisition must be traced back further—both before and after the donation made to the Holy See.

Among all the pontiffs I found none other than Honorius and Innocent II who entered into full possession of the donation, excepting the four cities of Parma, Reggio, Modena, and Mantua; each of them invested the other with the same property. The others, and especially Innocent III, scarcely recovered any part of it or claimed it for the Holy See through public instruments of investiture when it was held by others.

Later, after the donation had been celebrated in charters and finally displaced from its proper position and established by insufficiently learned—or pitifully ingenious—writers within the ancient dominion of the Holy See, it fell into oblivion.

For greater concern came upon the Roman pontiffs from the invading emperors over the rights of Sicily, which were of greater importance. These rights had returned to the Holy See through the valor of the Normans. The pontiffs had to labor not only to assert them for the Holy See, but also to obtain declarations in public imperial charters that they were separate from the German Empire. This was finally accomplished by Frederick II and by the princes of the Empire.

A summary of at least the principal points of this history, so varied and so necessary to our subject, will be found in Dissertation V.

### XXXV

The ancient rights of the Holy See in Parma and especially in Piacenza are asserted against the opinion of those who wrongly place these cities in the Exarchate.

But who could be persuaded that Modena, Reggio, Parma, Piacenza, and Bobbio were once included in the ancient Exarchate and subject to the jurisdiction of the exarchs during the time of Pippin, when a large part of the Lombard kingdom was still in existence? Moreover, both Pippin and Charles enumerate individually the cities of the Exarchate granted by them, and their donation does not extend beyond the territory of Bologna.

The city of Bobbio alone is mentioned in the Carolingian Codex (letters 51 and 54; alternatively 54 and 51) among the places given by the Frankish kings. But it should be carefully noted that it is listed once and again after Cesena.

Anastasius likewise reports (section 252) that Fulrad, abbot and counselor of King Pippin, after receiving the keys and hostages of each city, proceeded to the fortress of Saint Marinus, Vobio, and Urbino.

What? Did that abbot, having taken possession of the fortress of Saint Marinus, hasten with extraordinary speed to the town of Insubria, situated approximately two hundred thousand paces away, and then return to Urbino with equal speed? Was the name not perhaps Sarsina, or some neighboring town?

Besides, why should Bobbio alone be listed as a city—if indeed that town in the Cottian Alps was a city, since it had no bishop until the time of Benedict VIII and the Emperor Henry—while the other more celebrated cities were omitted? For they are named both by Anastasius and in the division of the kingdoms of Charles the Great; in both places, however, they are assigned to the kingdom of Italy.

The rights of the Holy See in Parma, therefore, must not be traced so far back, since all history protests against that claim. At most, the older right in Parma could be traced to Matilda’s donation; in Piacenza, it could be traced only to the beginning of the fourteenth century, when the Holy See was residing in Provence, on which occasion Parma also began to obey the Roman Pontiff.

### XXXVI

I see that this unquestionably false opinion arose because no distinction of periods was observed: whether in the time of the Roman commonwealth or according to the ecclesiastical provincial arrangement, all the bishops of Aemilia and Flaminia were suffragans of the archbishop of Ravenna. These two provinces are found in ancient sources under the single name of Aemilia.

Even in the age of Gregory, more than 150 years before Pippin’s donation, when part of Aemilia obeyed the Lombards and part the Greeks, the same pontiff, confirming the privileges of Mariniana, says among other things, in Ughelli (*Sacred Italy*, vol. II, p. 339):

> “By this confirmation we confirm the appointments and consecrations of the bishops of all the God-beloved cities of the entire province of Aemilia, namely Sassina, Cesena, Foripopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Forcornelio, Bologna, Modena, Reggio, Parma, Piacenza, Brescello, Vicohabentia, Adria, Comacchio, and Ficolo.”

More importantly, in 1125, after the death of Henry V, the invader of Matilda’s donation, Honorius II—who later took possession of that donation—restored an ancient privilege to Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, which his predecessors had lost through pride (ibid., p. 365). He uses these formal words:

> “By the text of the present privilege we confirm the bishoprics of the province of Aemilia, namely Parma, Piacenza, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, Ferrara, Adria, Comacchio, Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Cesena, and Ficocle.”

What then? He immediately adds:

> “Moreover, we confirm to you the Exarchate of Ravenna, which belongs by right to the Roman Church.”

And a little farther on:

> “We also entrust to your religious person the care of the monastery of Pomposa, without prejudice to the rights of our Church.”

It is therefore clear that Honorius, following the example of Gregory the Great, took account of the ancient ecclesiastical province when he subjected all the bishops of Aemilia to the archbishop. He separated from it, however, the civil province subject to the Holy See, namely the Exarchate, which ancient monuments show was called at various times Flaminia and Romandiola.

### XXXVII

What confirms the matter still more is that, shortly afterward, after taking possession of Matilda’s estates, Honorius invested Duke Albert with them. Those estates, however, were situated in that part of Aemilia which obeyed the Lombards and, after the Lombards had been expelled, belonged to the kingdom of Italy, which was also customarily called the Lombard kingdom, while retaining its ancient name.

Accordingly, that part of Aemilia which the Lombards added to their kingdom as soon as they came into Italy, and which they later reclaimed after having lost it for a time, must be distinguished from the Exarchate, which Aistulf brought under his authority in 752 after expelling Eutychius, the last of the exarchs.

This is the Exarchate that was donated to the Holy See by Pippin, king of the Franks, two years later and subsequently confirmed by his son Charles. Hadrian calls it Aemilia (Carolingian Codex, letters 51, 52, and 54; alternatively 54, 52, and 51). He also gives the people of Ravenna the title “peoples of Aemilia,” and conversely calls them “Ravennates.” It cannot extend beyond the territory of Bologna, as all history resists that conclusion and especially the letters of the Carolingian Codex, which deserve complete credence.

Whether, following Hadrian’s example, Stephen IV gave Ravenna itself the name Aemilia, or whether some neighboring city was so called—for, as Jordanes says (*On the Gothic Wars*, chapter 19), the city itself anciently gloried in three names, Ravenna, Classis, and Caesarea, since it was large and divided into three parts—we do not learn from any ancient monument.

Certainly, in his diploma of 817, Louis the Pious, and afterward all the Augusti, kings, and princes, when listing the individual cities of the Exarchate in their diplomas, add Aemilia to Ravenna. That the matter concerns a city, not a province, is made clear by the words that follow the enumeration:

> “With all the boundaries, territories, and islands belonging on land and sea to the aforesaid cities.”

Everything will be explained in Dissertation V.

### XXXVIII

But lest I perhaps appear to some to have discussed other territories of the Holy See uselessly and rashly, they should understand that the donation of Matilda, having been displaced from its proper position, could not otherwise have been restored to its true place, as I said at the outset.

Florentius and others, however, having been deceived, confidently regard as Matilda’s donation the greater part of the Trans-Tiberine Roman Duchy, or Roman Tuscany, and Lombard Tuscany, to which the name “patrimony” was given. Others, following Trithemius and Crantzius, think that it was the March of Ancona. Nor are there lacking those who attach the donation to the Duchy of Spoleto.

Finally, others interpret royal Tuscany—which in Matilda’s time was called the March of Tuscany—and Ferrara as belonging to this donation.

Yet none of the recent writers, following the traces of the ancients, has discovered that the countess’s donation was wholly contained in that part of Aemilia first invaded by the Lombards.

For this reason I considered it necessary to restore the Trans-Tiberine Roman Duchy to the more ancient territory of the Holy See, and Lombard Tuscany to the donation of Charles the Great. I also had to show that the March of Ancona, which was for the most part the Maritime Pentapolis, must be attributed to Pippin.

It was necessary to demonstrate that the Duchy of Spoleto, first offered to the Holy See by Charles the Great, who retained supreme authority there; then granted by Otto to the Holy See for full use; and finally partly given and partly transferred in exchange by Saint Henry to Benedict VIII and his successors in perpetuity, had no connection whatsoever with Matilda’s donation.

Finally, it was necessary to show that the March of Tuscany, granted by imperial favor to Matilda’s father, and Ferrara, retained by her through papal favor, returned by right to their respective original lords when she died without an heir.

Once the falsity of these opinions had been exposed, Matilda’s donation had to be assigned a definite location, for the greater part south of the Po, in the dioceses of Mantua, Reggio, Modena, and Parma, on the testimony of ancient writers and documents that cannot be called into doubt.

## § VII. On the Rudolphine Codex

### XXXIX

The unpublished Rudolphine Codex is the seventh monument, and not one of slight value. It contains 126 letters. If the nineteen belonging to others are removed, ninety-seven remain, written by Rudolph, King of the Romans—almost as many as are contained in the Carolingian Codex.

There is, however, this difference between the two: the latter received its name from its collector, Charles the Great, whereas the name “Rudolphine” was given to the codex by its author himself. I am now bringing it to light for the first time.

It appears to have remained unknown even to learned men, as can be gathered from the account given by Johann Wilhelm Goebel in his notes on Conring (*On the Boundaries of the German Empire*, vol. I, p. 305). Speaking of Aventinus, in whose work the letters of Rudolph are mentioned, he says:

> “It is nevertheless very doubtful whether Aventinus is speaking of those diplomas whose copies have been produced by the patrons of the Roman See. They have persuaded themselves, from Lambecius’s diary of the sacred journey of the Emperor Leopold to Celle, that those diplomas lie hidden in the imperial archive. But Lambecius merely reports that in a certain catalogue of documents compiled by Abbot Seyfrid of Zwettl, mention is made of the diplomas of Rudolph I; nothing is said there, however, about their contents. Since the abbot himself, in his dedication of the genealogy of the House of Austria, does not mention what the 120 letters of Rudolph—which he affirms that he saw—contained . . . . . The same Seyfrid also mentions another codex, and says that he found in it the confirmation of Rudolph’s donation by the princes of the Empire; but nothing is added to indicate whether it was a codex of authentic documents. Nor, despite all the diligence he expended, could Lambecius find any of the codices that had belonged to the Abbot of Zwettl. It is especially uncertain whether the codex containing 149 letters of Rudolph, which Lambecius mentions in his catalogue of books to be published by him, was the one of which Seyfrid speaks, and whether it contained original documents.”

Thus this author doubted, denied, and passed judgment on a matter unknown to him and in no way investigated.

### XL

It was otherwise with the most eminent Cardinal Passionei, to whom, as I have said, we owe the Carolingian Codex complete in every respect. It was enough for him that Lambecius had mentioned Seyfrid’s codices once and again. With no less concern, and perhaps with greater inconvenience, than he had undertaken in obtaining copies of the Carolingian Codex, he secured that codex of Seyfrid which contains the diploma of the princes of the Empire.

While serving as apostolic nuncio in Vienna, as we have seen, he traveled more than once to the Austrian Cistercian monastery of Zwettl—called Clara Vallis by us—near the Bohemian border. He was determined to obtain the codex, unknown to the most diligent Lambecius, wherever it might be concealed.

As always, his undertaking succeeded according to his wishes. He therefore ordered a copy to be made with the utmost fidelity and compared most carefully with Seyfrid’s transcript. Then, after serving as nuncio until the beginning of 1738, when he was summoned by Clement XII and appointed prefect of the apostolic diplomas, he brought the Rudolphine copy to Rome together with the copies of the Carolingian Codex, intending eventually to publish it if he found sufficient leisure.

But in June of that same year he was lawfully enrolled in the sacred college of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. Thereafter he was continually occupied by many serious duties of his office and deprived the Holy See and the republic of letters, for longer than was fitting, of both such singular and useful works.

For this reason he preferred, through whatever assistance I could provide—as I had said concerning the Carolingian Codex—to put an end to the delay rather than endure any longer the great desire, so long frustrated, of publishing these codices himself. The time was especially opportune, since so many false opinions concerning the Empire and the pontifical power, which they call temporal, were spreading throughout Italy itself through the publication of vast and numerous volumes. Neither the Holy See nor the republic of letters could receive an edition of monuments capable of eliminating such opinions, especially the Rudolphine Codex of which we are speaking.

### XLI

Indeed, in these letters Rudolph is seen to use no other title than “King of the Romans,” and he often urgently requests from the pontiff—the only person who could grant it—that he be advanced to the Empire.

The same is true in the Golden Bull, than which nothing is held more sacred among the Germans. From beginning to end its wording is consistent: “the King of the Romans to be advanced to emperor” or “to Caesar,” or “the future emperor” or “Caesar,” as in the edition of Limnaeus, which I use (chapter 1, nos. 1, 2, 19, 21, and 23; chapter 2, nos. 1, 3, 4, and 8; chapter 7, no. 2; chapter 18; chapters 20 and 28). Thus the King of the Romans and the emperor are clearly distinguished, so that it is entirely evident that two dignities are being discussed.

Thus, in chapter 2, sections 8 and 9, concerning the privileges of the electors:

> “He shall confirm and approve them without delay or contradiction by his letters and seals, and shall renew all the foregoing for them after he has been crowned with the imperial insignia . . . . First he shall do so in his royal name, and afterward he shall renew it under the imperial title.”

And in chapter 26, concerning the Aachen and Milanese crowns, to be worn by a Caesar who has been crowned:

> “And this shall take place only before the emperor who has already been crowned with the imperial insignia.”

Since Rudolph never attained the crown, the codex accordingly presents him with no dignity other than the royal one.

Here we see the true nature of imperial dignity, which Leo III established in Charles the Great. The boundaries of the German Empire are also clearly designated in the same codex. Romandiola, which Rudolph imprudently held, is called the outermost part of the Empire; and its rights are asserted in Lombardy and Tuscany. Thus the boundaries of the territory of the Holy See are clearly distinguished from those of the emperors.

All these matters are explained more fully in Dissertation IV, concerning the three books of Rudolph’s letters contained in this codex.

### XLII

Here it will also be possible to see that some have spoken boldly, and others ignorantly, about the first petitions. Struvius will serve as an example of all ( *Syntagm. J. P.* c. X, §32), who says concerning a privilege to be obtained solely from the Apostolic See:

> “Although it is true,” he says, “that from the time of Frederick III the emperors sought from the pope an indult concerning the first petitions, earlier emperors nevertheless appealed to an established custom, nor did they ever seek an indult from the pontiff.”

For it will be demonstrated that Charles IV was the very first to use that privilege. As for the Augusti or kings who presented first petitions to churches, Struvius himself knows of none earlier than Rudolph. Yet, thinking that he was producing two letters of the same Rudolph, he cites statements falsely attributed to Rudolph. From the first of these ( *Paralip. ad Ursperg.* a. 1286, p. 362), he quotes the following:

> “Since, by an ancient and approved custom, brought down to us by the deified emperors and kings, every church established in our Roman Empire to which the collation of ecclesiastical benefices belongs is bound to admit our first royal petitions concerning the collation of a single benefice.”

Four letters are preserved in the Codex (Book I, letters 14 ff.), and in the first of them something similar is read:

> “Since, at the beginning of our elevation, every church established in the Roman Empire is bound, according to the ancient and approved custom of the Holy Empire, to admit our first petitions concerning the provision of one person, we present to you our first petitions.”

Likewise, in the third letter (ibid., letter 16):

> “Since, therefore, an ancient and approved custom has conferred upon our predecessors, the deified emperors and kings, the right that individual persons in individual cathedral and other collegiate churches should be received as canons and brothers in response to royal first petitions.”

Struvius derives the other letter from Chiffletius, concerning Besançon; Thomassinus also cites it (*De Benef.* II, 1, c. 54, no. 7), and Goldast (*Const. Imp.* vol. III, p. 446) employs the same formula. But both he himself and the Annalist of Ursperg assign it to the year 1286, which is enough to show that the formula is spurious. For it conflicts with “at the beginning of our elevation,” that is, with the end of the year 1273.

Moreover, Rudolph does not say “by a custom brought down to us,” nor “in our Roman Empire,” nor “our first petitions.” The formula, therefore, composed according to someone’s own ingenuity, is improperly attributed to Rudolph.

### XLIII

Everyone can see that this formula was derived from the letters of Rudolph cited above. For this reason, a similar Codex, if I am not mistaken, in the Vienna Library was also accessible to others. Indeed, in our own age the Reverend Father Hansizius ( *Germania sacra* vol. I, p. 416; vol. II, p. 379 ff.) found there [lacuna] a codex exceedingly similar to ours, as is shown by the eleven letters published by him. These are found in the Codex (Book I, letter 38; Book II, letters 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 22, 29, 33): nine from Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, to Rudolph; one from Rudolph to him (letter 12), in which he replies; and another (letter 33), in which he announces to the Roman pontiff his victory over Ottokar, king of Bohemia.

From all these I have extracted variant readings whenever they seemed to me to be of some importance. What I particularly observed is that both in the Codex of Zwettl, which I am bringing into the light of publication, and in the imperial Codex used by Hansizius, the same method of writing is maintained: names of places and persons are almost always indicated by the letter N; there is no subscription at the end; no chronological order is observed; and very few letters bear an inscription.

Summaries precede the individual letters, but without any doubt they were supplied by the copyist of the Codex from the original. For the name “Emperor” is sometimes attached to Rudolph, in accordance with the ignorance or false opinion of later times. This opinion certainly did not prevail before the year 1356, when the Golden Bull was issued, about which we have recently spoken. Consequently, throughout that entire period, which Struvius divides into three sections, attention must be paid to the sense of the letters apart from their summaries.

I did not wish to omit these matters, as was only fair, lest anything be lacking in the reliability of the Codex. For the same reason I also restored to Gregory X a letter that at first sight appears interpolated (Book I, letter 39), although I have not entirely dismissed every doubt about its questionable reliability.

### XLIV

If this Rudolphine Codex had come into Gretser’s hands, that most learned man would not have devoted so much labor to editing certain letters which, he says, he had seen in an ancient Codex—letters sent between the years 1245 and 1273 by the kings of the Romans Henry, William, Richard, and Alfonso to the pontiffs (*In fin. Car. Cod.*).

For, apart from the fact that he ought to have abandoned such an arduous undertaking in the face of unavoidable errors, these letters had ultimately been corrupted by the princes whom he improperly calls caesars—and whom, in light of the Golden Bull, he would more correctly have called future caesars, provided that they had received the imperial insignia from the Roman pontiff.

Today we also make use of those letters whose editing Gretser abandoned. For after his death Rainaldus inserted them into his *Annals*, from a manuscript of excellent quality. From them we learn two things of no small importance: first, that the origin of the seven princely Electors lay in no papal or imperial constitution; and second, that the election of the king of the Romans customarily derived its authority from the approval of the Roman pontiff.

But these matters will be treated in the dissertation. Here it is useful to observe that the very darkness of the fatal Interregnum—as the German jurists call it—provides some light for the Rudolphine Codex. The latter, together with the Golden Bull, so clearly reveals the true character of the Empire that nothing further seems necessary to refute so many false opinions. Yet the diploma of that same Rudolph, which I present last, places the matter beyond all doubt.

## § VIII. On the Diplomas of Rudolph

### XLV

The edition of this diploma contains nothing new. It could therefore have been passed over, unless it were necessary both to strengthen the points made above and to restrain the excessive license of certain writers.

Three editions above all others are commended as being based on the original, which is preserved in the archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian: that of Raynaldus (1279, no. 1 ff.); that of Zacagni, after his learned historical dissertation on the dominion of the Holy See (*Append. Actor. vet.*, p. 97 ff., Frankfurt edition); and that of the Most Eminent Cardinal Antonelli, then prefect of the same archive (*Parm. et Plac.*, part 7, at the end).

I have already explained why I recently prepared this latest edition from the same original. My first reason was that a diploma embracing all the acts performed at Lyon in 1274 by Rudolph’s chancellor and other legates; at Lausanne the following year by Rudolph himself before Pope Gregory X and the cardinals; and at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the Minorite Conrad, and at Viterbo before Nicholas III by Gotefridus, provost of Solignac, in 1278—such a diploma, solemnly confirmed by the princes of Germany—might be placed before everyone’s eyes.

My second reason was that, after the other reliable monuments, this equally reliable document might be set against the Conringian sarcasm imitated by writers from Italy itself (*De fin. Imper. Germ.* vol. I, p. 285). Conringius says:

> “The pope and his adherents all boast of this donation of Rudolph. Various donations were made to the pope by Charlemagne and others, which we examined above. They say that this Rudolph of Habsburg often gave them all the property of the caesars in completely free possession, so that he reserved no right for himself.”

The ignorance of this audacious man must be proclaimed! Rudolph makes no donation; he merely renews the ancient donations. What right, then, could he reserve to himself in donations belonging to others?

When the most pious king Rudolph confirmed all the ancient rights of the Holy See, the pontiffs ceased from their long-standing invasions and received the Exarchate and the Pentapolis—by far the oldest and most important of all the donations—back into the Roman Church by right of restoration. What is there for them to boast about as a donation?

### XLVI

Not even Lunigius dares to say such things. For he places the following summary at the head of one of the Rudolphine diplomas (*Cod. Ital. Dipl.* vol. II, p. 733):

> “The repeated confirmation by Rudolph I, king of the Romans, of all privileges granted by the Roman emperors to the Apostolic See, as well as of the donations made to it concerning certain provinces and cities. Given at Vienna in the year of the Lord 1278, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our reign.”

Yet in that diploma, which Raynaldus cites from the archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian (1278, no. 45), the following formula appears:

> “To recognize, ratify, approve, renew, grant, and nevertheless to donate anew.”

But who among the learned does not know that Rudolph fully followed the instruction, or form, prescribed for him by Nicholas III? (ibid., no. 62). The pontiff expressed the matter in these words:

> “To remove every scruple, insofar as it can be done better and understood more effectively, we grant, confer, and donate anew.”

Stephen IV and Paschal I likewise wished Rome, together with its duchy, patrimonies, and other rights, to be included in the diploma of Louis the Pious, so that they might rest upon a stronger protection. Yet it will not be found that Louis donated anything to the Holy See.

Are the excellent policies of the pontiffs, then, to be perversely understood so that everything may be filled with false opinions? Let history be consulted. But history? Rather, let Rudolph himself be heard (Codex, Book II, letter 37):

> “We generously approve, with willing applause and free assent, everything and each individual matter which the Holy Mother Church is known to have hitherto requested from us, both through envoys and through special letters; and in these and in all other matters we have resolved to conform calmly to the Apostolic will.”

Thus he replies to the pontifical letter of Nicholas III (Raynaldus 1277, no. 54), sent immediately after he ascended the Chair of Peter:

> “We ask and request that the petition so often pressed upon royal excellence concerning the lands of that same Church, and especially concerning the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, be fulfilled without further delay with prompt and effective execution.”

I shall summarize briefly what is explained more fully throughout the work. Whatever the Apostolic See possesses under the title of donation, excepting the ancient patrimonies, it attributes to Pepin and Charles, kings of the Franks; to that same Charles, after he had assumed the imperial crown; to Otto the Great; and to Henry and Matilda.

From the other Augusti it owes only confirmation of the donations and of all the rights, although that confirmation, since it was necessary for obtaining the imperial diadem, was many times illusory. This cannot in any way be said of the confirmation by Rudolph, king of the Romans.

### XLVII

I say, “king of the Romans,” for this is indeed remarkable: Rudolph, distinguished only by royal dignity, confirmed by diploma the territories and rights of the Holy See. It had long been customary, however, for a king of the Romans, once confirmed by the Roman pontiff, almost always to obtain the imperial crown; for that reason the future emperor was called the king of the Romans.

The oaths of those same kings, in which they promised above all to strengthen and defend the goods of the Church by diploma, are readily found. Yet before Rudolph’s diploma no other document of the same kind appears.

It must nevertheless be observed that the following formula is contained in diplomas of his cited by Raynaldus (1274, no. 9; 1275, no. 39):

> “After we have reached Rome to receive the anointing, coronation, or imperial diadem, and have received it, we shall renew all the matters stated above, each and every one of them, or shall enact them anew.”

But the formula that deserves attention above all is the one Rudolph added, following the instruction of Nicholas III, to the diploma by which the preceding matters are confirmed—the diploma that holds the highest place among the monuments published by us:

> “After we have received it, within eight days we shall renew all the matters stated above, each and every one of them, and shall enact them anew, fully and completely.”

For this contains a custom that must be examined in its proper place: the delivery of the diploma within eight days after receiving the imperial diadem. This custom subsequently prevailed, as is shown by the book of the Sacred Rites, cited by Clement V in 1311 and by Innocent VI in 1355 (*Bullar. Vat.* vol. I, pp. 248 ff., 350 ff.). It is stated still more explicitly in the letter of Henry VII to Clement V, cited by Raynaldus (1310, no. 7):

> “Concerning all the matters mentioned above, within eight days we shall issue four open letters containing the text of this document.”

For this reason, in the published Ceremonial one finds a most extensive oath covering everything in general. But concerning the diploma once customarily read during the act of coronation, as is attested by the panegyrist of Berengar, there is complete silence.

So much for the monuments, each of which will be examined at greater length in the dissertations, and by which all the rights of Saint Peter and the Holy See will be vindicated, these monuments shining before us as a torch.

### XLVIII

I shall now add a few points from the Codex of Albinus, mentioned above (no. XXIV). That brief collection from the paper volumes of the Lateran Library, which the *Book of Censuses* of Cencius presents, is found in the Codex of Albinus—which is older than Cencius—in fuller and much more accurate form.

It belongs to the age of Gregory VII, as is clear from the penultimate monument contained there. For its collector speaks of it as follows:

> “From a synod held in Dalmatia by the legates of Pope Gregory VII, namely by Gebizo, then abbot of the monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius, but now bishop of Cesena, and also by Folcuinus, bishop of Fossombrone. This synod is preserved in the archive of the Sacred Lateran Palace. In the name of the Lord, etc. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, indiction 14, etc.”

Gebizo, for he was sent as legate to Dalmatia in 1075, became bishop of Cesena eight years later, namely in 1083, and shortly afterward a cardinal.

In this very ancient collection, therefore, which contains documents from earlier times, the following is recorded above all:

> “Likewise, in a certain paper volume kept in the cartulary near the Palatium, it is read that Pope Benedict leased the city and county of Sovana, together with its castles and villages and all their appurtenances; and the city and county of Roselle, together with its villages and castles and their appurtenances, and with jurisdiction, court, every payment, and its revenue. Each city pays sixty solidi. Likewise, in another volume of the same cartulary, it is read that Pope Boniface VII leased the castle of Petra Pertusa, etc.”

If chronological order were preserved, I would suppose that this was Benedict III or IV, at the end of the ninth century. For Benedict V and VI of the following century, while the counts of Tusculum held power, could not dispose of these cities.

But let us suppose that Benedict VIII, or even Benedict IX, leased these cities at the beginning of the eleventh century. The Lombard cities of Tuscia, therefore—the last cities granted by Charlemagne to Hadrian and his successors—were at that time fully under the right of the Holy See.

Accordingly, we shall see an Italian annalist speaking about them without having investigated the matter. Are not the three islands—Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily—which are listed immediately after Roselle in the same donation by Louis, his son, likewise unjustly called into question?

### XLIX

But, leaving Sicily aside, since it will be more appropriately discussed below, the ancient censuses in Sardinia are recorded in the Codex cited above:

> “The Judge of Cagliari: two pounds of silver as census. The Archbishop of Cagliari: six pounds of silver. The Bishop of Dolia: two pounds. The Bishop of Sulcis: two pounds. The Bishop of Barbaria: two pounds. The Church of Saint Saturninus: two pounds. The Judge of Arborea: two pounds. The Archbishop of Arborea: six pounds. The Bishop of San Pietro di Terralba: two pounds. The Bishop of Usellus: two pounds. The Bishop of San Giusto: two pounds. The Judge of Torres: two pounds. The Archbishop of Torres: six pounds. The Bishop of Ploaghe: two pounds. The Bishop of Ampurias: two pounds. The Bishop of Sorres: two pounds. The Bishop of Chisarpo: two pounds. The Bishop of Castro: two pounds. The Bishop of Osana: two pounds. The Bishop of Bosa: two pounds. The Abbot of Saccargia: two pounds. The Abbot of Planu: two pounds. The Abbot of Tergu: two pounds. The Prior of Salvenero: one pound. The total of all these amounts is fifty-nine pounds of silver.”

You see that the Judicate of Gallura is missing here; you will find it, namely, in Cencius. But the Albinian Codex presents censuses older than those of Cencius. Therefore, those imposed later are enumerated separately, and no mention is made of the Judge of Gallura:

> “In Arborea, the Church of Saint Thomas, with all its goods, pays three bezants as census every year. The Church of S…… called Cania: two small solidi each year.”

This appendix concerning the Judicate of Arborea appears in Cencius together with the other censuses. Who, then, does not see from this that Sardinia belonged by right to the Holy See?

The same is established concerning Corsica, and even more clearly, from the Codex of Albinus. Immediately after Sardinia it states:

> “Concerning Corsica: Pope Innocent granted Corsica to Genoa for an annual census of one pound of gold. And thereafter he made a privilege for it.”

In Muratori (*Ant. Ital.* vol. V, col. 894), who boasts that he published Cencius’s book, but issued an entirely different version filled with additions, the passage reads as follows:

> “The consuls of Genoa [pay] one pound of gold for half of Corsica, which Pope Innocent granted to them; and both the consuls and the people must swear fidelity to the Roman pontiff whenever they are required to do so, as is contained in their privilege.”

### L

Nor did the Genoese attribute their possession of Corsica only to Innocent II; they also attributed it to five other pontiffs who succeeded Innocent, namely Alexander III, Clement III, Celestine III, Innocent III, and Honorius III—the last of these attesting to it in Raynaldus (1217, no. 98 ff.):

> “Following the example of Innocent himself and of our predecessors of blessed memory, Alexander, Clement, Celestine, and Innocent … Moreover, following the example of those same predecessors, we grant to the city of Genoa half of the island of Corsica, on the condition that the Genoese people swear fidelity to us and our successors whenever they are required to do so, and pay us and our successors one pound of gold each year as a pension.”

It will not be useless to have mentioned these matters in advance.

## PREFACE OF GRETSER

[Col. 0045A]

Be favorable, friendly reader. If you are Catholic, I bring you a good omen; if you are a reformer, you may perhaps think that a great evil is being brought to you. In any event, here is a list indicating how many letters of each pontiff are contained in this volume:

- Gregory III: 2.
- Stephen III: 8.
- Zacharias: 1.
- Paul I: 32, although one of these was written to Pepin jointly in the name of the senate and people of Rome.
- Stephen IV: 5.
- Hadrian I: 49, although one of these was sent to Charlemagne jointly in the name of the clergy.
- Constantine the antipope: 2.

Their total would make a full hundred if one more letter had been added.

Of these, perhaps seven, or not many more, are already known, partly from volume IX of the *Annals* of the Most Illustrious Baronius, and partly from the eighth *Century* of the Magdeburg Centuriators, chapter 9. I considered it wrong to omit them, out of reverence for Charlemagne. For who would separate writings which so great a monarch wished to have joined together in one volume?

Nevertheless, the chronological order has not been observed with complete accuracy in this collection. The letter of Pope Zacharias is inserted among the letters of Stephen III, although it is certain that Zacharias preceded Stephen. The two letters of Constantine, the false pontiff, ought also to occupy a place between Paul and Stephen IV, since Constantine invaded the Apostolic See after Paul’s death; nevertheless, they have been relegated to the end of the book.

He is called a neophyte because, although he was a layman and entirely without clerical consecration, he was raised by certain turbulent men, with criminal audacity and little success, to this highest summit of Apostolic office. For scarcely a year and a month had he sat upon so lofty a watchtower when—behold!—there came his downfall and precipitous descent to the lowest depths. On this matter Baronius may be read, volume IX, under the year of the Redeemer 768.

But to come to the letters of Pope Paul: the Centuriators, while reviewing the writings of this pontiff (*Century* VIII, chapter 10), write—or rather, slanderously claim—as follows:

> “The papal compilers of the volumes of the Councils seem deliberately to have omitted the letters of Stephen II and Paul, Stephen III, Constantine, and Hadrian, so that the arts and frauds of the pontiffs in deceiving the Franks and unjustly seizing the property of the Empire might not be exposed.”

This foul accusation is sufficiently and completely refuted, in place of all others and in the name of all, by the Most Illustrious Baronius, in that mournful lament which he composed under the year of Christ 767 because he had been unable to obtain the letters of this pontiff Paul. I say nothing of his similar lament over the missing letters of Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne, whose omission led him to think that his *Annals* lacked their most splendid ornament.

Hear, reader, the words of that outstanding cardinal himself, and judge whether the papal writers deliberately suppressed such letters:

> “We would have set before you a richer table concerning the deeds of Paul, if we had been able to find the letters that he wrote to Pepin, king of the Franks, and to others. We have seen only their contents briefly summarized and listed by Panvinio in his *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, and he testifies that the letters are preserved in their entirety in the Vatican Library. But although we searched for them for a long time, we were entirely unable to find them, so that we suppose they were removed from there either by theft or in some other manner.
>
> “Nevertheless, there is nothing that can bring his reliability into suspicion, since the reformers likewise recount the contents of the same letters, equal in number. Wearied by their length and multiplicity—and still more by their truth—they published not the letters in full but only their summaries. If these had not been heaped together but arranged according to the individual years in which they were sent, they would not have brought boredom or nausea to readers but the greatest pleasure. For from them an epistolary history, superior to all others in truth and sincerity, unknown until now, could have been admirably composed.
>
> “You too will not deny this when you have read the summaries that we place before you here, so that we may not send you away entirely hungry when we are not permitted to receive you at the sumptuous table we would have wished to provide. From these summaries also let the reader understand and acknowledge, even unwillingly, how well and admirably he serves ecclesiastical antiquities who does not reproduce fragments or summaries of letters but publishes the letters themselves in full, so that they may perish no longer. By depositing them in an archive and consecrating them to immortality, he preserves them intact for posterity.”

After this, Baronius likewise lists twenty-nine summaries, or outlines, of Paul’s letters from Onuphrius. The Centuriators did the same, although they give summaries of only twenty-seven letters; in addition, they mention three others to Charles and Carloman, as well as a letter to the entire army of the kingdom of the Franks.

The reader will find all of these in this edition. The Centuriators certainly deserve the greatest criticism. Although, as they openly write, they had received thirty-one manuscript letters of this pontiff, they inserted not even one into their *Centuries*, although they did not hesitate to reproduce the letters of certain other pontiffs, and indeed rather lengthy ones.

Perhaps they feared that readers, from reading so many letters sent by the pontiffs to Pepin and to other Frankish rulers, would understand too clearly how highly the Apostolic See had been esteemed by the greatest princes, and would begin to curse Luther and his followers for their diabolical insults against the Roman pontiffs.

What was denied to the eminent Baronius has been offered to us—not by good fortune but by divine providence: namely, thirty-two letters of Pope Paul, though I wish they were more accurately corrected.

The parchment Codex that we used is indeed ancient and written in a sufficiently ancient script, but it is exceedingly corrupt, so that perhaps it would be less labor to clean out the Augean stable than to remove all the errors of this exemplar. Let whoever finds a better Codex correct them.

Meanwhile, we have judged it preferable for the letters of Pope Paul to be brought into the light in whatever condition, rather than to remain longer hidden in darkness and fall into oblivion. I wish the same to be understood concerning the letters of Pope Hadrian.

So that the reader may know which letter corresponds to which summary in Baronius and the Centuriators, we have noted this for each letter, as we have also done for Hadrian’s letters. The Most Illustrious Cardinal Baronius greatly desired the latter, as appears from his statement in volume IX of the *Annals*, under the year of the Redeemer 795, no. 1, where, concerning the acts of Hadrian, he added:

> “These great matters ought to have been narrated for you in a fuller and more luminous style, not in an iron one, and one covered with rust, mutilated and shortened by excessive brevity rather than explained, and handed down to posterity. The damage was compounded by the fact that, although the Vatican Library possessed forty-four letters of that same pontiff Hadrian, from which history could have been enriched, once they had been lost only their summaries remained—briefly extracted summaries whose draught increases the reader’s thirst, making him long for the source, not without hope that, if anyone possesses them in good faith, he may someday bring them into the light, so that each may be restored to its proper place.”

Behold: what that great man eagerly desired, we now provide. We publish even more than forty-four letters of this eminent pontiff, which the Centuriators also seem to have seen. For in *Century* VIII, chapter 10, they write:

> “We have received forty-four manuscript letters of Hadrian to Charlemagne, whose contents we considered it worthwhile to indicate.”

They then give summaries, as Baronius later did; but the order of the letters differs from that found in the manuscript Codex which we followed. This will be understood from the number of the outlines that we have assigned to the individual letters from Baronius and the Centuriators, as I already noted.

I observe, however, that the makers of the *Centuries* did not conduct themselves with sufficient good faith either in reciting or in composing these outlines. Baronius says that he copied them from Onuphrius Panvinius’s history of the pontiffs, preserved in the Vatican Library. Whence did the Centuriators obtain them? They themselves are silent. But the matter speaks for itself.

Either they saw that same Codex of Onuphrius—for what was inaccessible to these plunderers and their subordinate helpers and agents in the library?—so great is the similarity and agreement between the two sets of summaries, even in their wording; or, if they had obtained the complete letters, as they certainly seem to have done, they found those summaries prefixed to the letters in an ancient exemplar, as Onuphrius perhaps had found them, and, according to their usual practice, inserted certain slanders.

Among these are the following.

In the summary of Hadrian’s second letter:

> “He asserts the invocation of the saints and the primacy of the Roman Church.”

In the summary of the fourth:

> “He wrongly cites the saying, ‘He who perseveres to the end will be saved.’ He is entirely in favor of the invocation of the saints and the primacy.”

In the summary of the sixteenth:

> “He teaches the invocation of the saints. He boasts that he burned very many ships of the Greeks, etc.”

In the summary of the twentieth:

> “Most abundant blessings, or rather flatteries, etc.”

In the summary of the forty-third:

> “He is entirely in favor of the primacy. He heaps together many sayings of Scripture that have nothing to do with the subject.”

Finally, in the summary of the letter to Egila:

> “He abuses the testimonies of Sacred Scripture.”

All these things the fabricators of the *Centuries* fashioned out of their own slanderous hearts, contrary to the mind of the person who first composed these outlines.

The same kind of thing is found in the passage with which they contaminated the summary of the sixth letter of Pope Paul:

> “He asks him to send his legate to him, through whom he might disclose to him the plans and ambushes of the Greeks.”

These sectarians evidently could not rest until they had made Paul into a traitor, substituting the offensive word “betray” for “disclose,” which the author of the summary had used. But enough about the Centuriators.

I also wish you to know, my reader, that I have not been excessively particular about the orthography of antiquity, because, as the saying goes, “the shattered world does not collapse” whether one reads:

> *inlustris, inluster, inlicite, inliciter, inretitus, inportabilis, inmensus, assumtus* or *adsumtus, temptatio, adcresco, obtimates, obtimus, amminiculum, ammoneo, jocundus, jocunditas, dicio, suboles, conloqui, conlocutio, conroboro, conlaudo, obmisi, cotidie, isdem*;

or, as current usage now prefers:

> *illustris, illicite, irretitus, importabilis, immensus, assumptus, tentatio, accresco, optimates, optimus, adminiculum, admoneo, jucundus, jucunditas, ditio, soboles, colloqui, collocutio, corroboro, collaudo, omisi, quotidie, idem.*

There is likewise no reason for anyone to condemn the pontiffs because grammatical rules are violated in places and their style of expression is unpolished. For these letters were written in times when the Latin language in Italy was rushing toward ruin because of the immigration of so many foreign peoples.

But—to use the words of Arnobius, Book I *Against the Nations*—“what harm, I ask, or what impediment to understanding does it make whether something is uttered smoothly or with bristling roughness? Whether what ought to be inflected is sharpened, or what ought to be sharpened is inflected? Or why is what is said any less true if one errs in number, case, preposition, participle, or conjunction?

“When matters are being discussed that have been removed from display and ostentation, one must consider what is said, not with what charm it is said; nor what pleases the ears, but what benefits it brings to those who hear. Otherwise we shall have to cast out from our uses certain kinds of fruits because they grow with thorns and other refuse—things that can neither nourish us nor prevent us from enjoying what nature intended to come first and to be most beneficial to us.”

Whoever seeks elegance and beauty of expression should turn not to this work but to the letters of M. Tullius, Pliny, Muretus, and similar authors.

For a much more complete understanding of these letters, the reading of Anastasius the Librarian’s *History of the Pontiffs* will be useful, especially where he discusses those pontiffs whose monuments are seen in this volume. For he employs almost the same style of expression and either touches upon or explains at greater length many matters that are likewise touched upon or treated more fully in these letters.

I shall add one thing and make my words brief. You owe these letters, candid reader, to the noble and most learned Lord Sebastian Tengnagel, Doctor of Both Laws, prefect of the Imperial Library at Vienna, who courteously sent them to me for publication. By this kindness he has bound to himself with the closest tie all lovers of ecclesiastical history and antiquity.

Farewell, my reader. If you desire to safeguard your salvation, do not depart from the Apostolic See; or, if you have departed, return as soon as possible.

## Inscription of the Codex

[Note: [Col. 0051] The anchored note within the following ornament can be viewed by double-clicking on the note icon which follows the ornament icon.]

[Note: [Col. 0051A] Inscription of a venerably ancient parchment codex, but one very badly handled by the copyists. GRETSER.—The Carolingian Epistolary, containing ninety-nine letters of the Roman pontiffs Gregory III, Zachary, Stephen III—or, according to others, II—Paul I, Stephen IV—or, according to others, III—Hadrian I, and the antipope Constantine, addressed to the Frankish princes and kings Charles Martel, Pippin, and Charlemagne. In the year of Christ 791, through the care and under the direction of Charlemagne himself, these letters were diligently collected, lest they should perish through age and neglect, and were reduced into a single parchment volume. The volume formerly belonged first to Charlemagne’s private library and subsequently to Willibert, archbishop of Rouen; it is now preserved as an authentic manuscript in the most august Imperial Library at Vienna. Peter Lambecius of Hamburg reviewed and collated the entire work with the utmost fidelity and diligence, and furnished it with an accurate chronology and the necessary annotations.

LAMBECIUS.—Description of the manuscript of the Carolingian Codex and its collation with the text of the Gretserian edition. It is a parchment manuscript of ninety-eight folios, whose writing and nearly square form plainly belong altogether to the Carolingian age. It formerly belonged, as the distinguished Lambecius judged, to Willibert, archbishop of Rouen; his name is inscribed on a strip of parchment, a finger’s breadth wide, pasted onto the front board, in the following form: “THE BOOK OF WILLIBERT, ARCHBISHOP.” It contains a collection of ninety-nine letters, which the Roman pontiffs Gregory III, Stephen III, Zachary I, Paul I, Stephen IV, Hadrian I, and the antipope Constantine sent to the Frankish princes and kings Charles Martel, Pippin, and Charlemagne. It was assembled through the study and care of Charlemagne, as the illuminated inscription displayed above explains more fully.]

REIGNING FOREVER IS OUR LORD AND SAVIOR JESUS CHRIST. IN THE YEAR 791 OF THE INCARNATION OF THAT SAME LORD OUR GOD. CHARLES, MOST EXCELLENT AND ELECTED BY GOD KING OF THE FRANKS AND LANGOBARDS AND PATRICIAN OF THE ROMANS, IN THE MOST FORTUNATE TWENTY-THIRD YEAR OF HIS REIGN, INSPIRED BY DIVINE WILL, JUST AS HE EXCELS IN WISDOM AND PRUDENCE ABOVE ALL WHO CAME BEFORE HIM, SO IN THIS WORK HE SET HIS MOST USEFUL INTELLIGENCE TO WORK, DETERMINING TO RESTORE AND REWRITE ANEW, IN MEMORABLE [Note: [Col. 0051B] Read memorialibus, as Lambecius has already observed; Cangius uses this passage in the Glossary to explain what memorial parchments are. GENT.] PARCHMENTS, WITH THE GREATEST EFFORT, ALL THE LETTERS WHICH ARE KNOWN TO HAVE BEEN DIRECTED FROM THE APOSTOLIC SEE, THAT IS, FROM THE BLESSED PETER, PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, OR EVEN FROM THE EMPIRE TO THEM, DURING THE TIME OF HIS GRANDFATHER, THE LORD CHARLES OF BLESSED MEMORY, AND OF HIS GLORIOUS FATHER PIPPIN, AS WELL AS DURING HIS OWN TIME, BECAUSE HE HAD SEEN THAT, THROUGH EXTREME AGE AND NEGLECT, THEY HAD ALREADY BEEN PARTLY RUINED AND DELETED.

BEGINNING, THEREFORE, AS WE HAVE SAID ABOVE, WITH THE PRINCIPALITY OF THE AFORESAID PRINCE CHARLES, HIS GRANDFATHER, AND CONTINUING TO THE PRESENT TIME, HE WROTE OUT EVERYTHING IN SUCH A WAY THAT NONE OF THE TESTIMONY OF HOLY CHURCH WHICH MIGHT BENEFIT HIS SUCCESSORS WOULD APPEAR TO BE ENTIRELY LACKING, AS IT IS WRITTEN: “THE WISE MAN WILL SEEK OUT THE WISDOM OF ALL THE ANCIENTS,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0051C] Thus far the inscription of the ancient codex, which, candid reader, we wished to set before you at the very entrance, so that you might first learn the antiquity and importance of this work. Its antiquity is what you see in the table now placed before you. Its importance is threefold: it derives from the authors of the letters, from the princes to whom the letters were sent, and from the collector. The authors are the supreme pontiffs; those to whom the letters were sent are supreme kings; and the collector was the most powerful and victorious king, one whom, after Constantine the Great, the West scarcely had an equal to, and certainly no superior. Observe also that when, by Charlemagne’s command, these letters of the pontiffs were brought together into one volume, Pope Hadrian was still alive. For the year of the Lord 791 was the twentieth year of Hadrian’s pontificate, and he died in the same year as our Redeemer, 795. During this period it is credible that Hadrian sent several letters to Charlemagne. Hadrian was succeeded by Leo III, who was most closely and amicably associated with Charlemagne; who would deny that he sent that prince letters just as frequently as Hadrian? Illyricus insolently attacks Leo in his Catalogue, as though he were ignorant and barbarous. “I possess,” says Illyricus, “several of his letters to Charles, utterly crude and barbarous.” So speaks that most elegant Slav; if one wished to gather into a single bundle the solecisms and barbarisms found in his books, one could easily produce a codex equal in thickness, if not to a lexicon, at least to a thick volume. Three letters of Leo III are extant in volume III of the new edition of the Councils, p. 445. But since the Catalogue of Witnesses was published in 1562 and the Eighth Century in 1564, and since in that Century Illyricus writes: “There is no doubt that Leo III wrote at least several letters to Charles and to others, but they have been suppressed by the papists,” Illyricus is certainly rendered highly suspect of falsehood. For if he possessed some letters of Leo, as he says in the Catalogue, why did he not insert at least some of them in the Eighth Century, especially unpublished ones and ones unseen by others, when he did not shrink from stitching the letters of certain other pontiffs into his cento? Why did he not at least provide summaries of them, as he did with the letters of the pontiffs Paul and Hadrian? What need was there to say that there was no doubt that Leo had sent several letters to Charles, if he had some letters of Leo to Charles? Was Illyricus so forgetful that, while patching together the Eighth Century with his rhapsodies, he no longer remembered that these letters were still in his possession? Furthermore, against Illyricus’s insults to Leo III I set the deeds of that same pontiff, which Anastasius committed to writing, and the judgment of Charlemagne, who honored Leo no less than Hadrian—something he certainly would not have done if Leo had been the sort of man whom the worst of artists, Illyricus, depicts him as being. But now let us hear the letters of the pontiffs themselves, among which Leo’s letters too would be heard, if not all of them, at least some, unless either the long passage of time or Illyricus’s injustice has begrudged them to us.

GRETSER.—Thus far the inscription, accurately reproduced as it lies in the Codex, including the copyist’s errors, which are incredibly numerous in it. Tengnagel corrected nearly everything with his own hand, but with excessive license: not merely writing the true reading in the margin, but frequently erasing, inserting, restoring, and repeating passages. I cannot approve this, although he did it intending to relieve Jacob Gretser, to whom he later gave the volume for publication, of the labor of correction. It was published through the efforts of the aforementioned Gretser at Ingolstadt, from the printing house of Andreas Angermarius, in 1613, quarto. But Lambecius, not content with that edition, commissioned a new one at Vienna, in folio, from the Cosmorovian press. He began with that outstanding volume of letters the great Collection of German Affairs, whose appearance caused both him and his successor Nesselius to whet the appetite of the learned.]

[Col. 0053]

## Letters of the Roman Pontiffs

### Prefatory Notice on the Letters of Saint Gregory III to Charles, the Subking

#### I

It is absolutely certain that, in this troubled situation, only two letters were sent by Gregory III to Charles Martel. First, the holy pontiff himself says repeatedly that he is writing to Charles the subking. Then his grandson Charlemagne confirms this by having precisely these two letters included in the codex—Charlemagne, I mean, who, beginning “with the principality of the aforesaid prince Charles, his grandfather” (as the title runs), “and continuing to the present time” (791), wrote out everything “in such a way that none of the testimony of Holy Church which might benefit his successors would appear to be entirely lacking.” For this reason he also wished to include the decretal letter of Saint Zachary (letter 3, elsewhere 5), two letters concerning the errors of the Spaniards (69, 70; elsewhere 95, 96), and another concerning the Felician heresy (82, elsewhere 97), because the former had been sent at Pippin’s request and the latter at his own request; nor did he omit the two letters of the antipope Constantine (43, 44; elsewhere 98, 99), which had been written to his father Pippin.

Nevertheless, Pagius, followed by not a few others, maintains that another letter was sent by Gregory, outstanding both in arrangement and content, in which they boast that the consulship was conferred upon Charles. They rely, of course, on the First Continuation of Fredegarius, which they interpret according to their own judgment; but they inflict a conspicuous injustice on Charles by supposing that he passed over the finest of all the letters he had arranged. I freely admit that some letters are missing from the codex, since they are mentioned elsewhere, because they contained “no testimony of Holy Church which might be of any benefit.” Nevertheless, when I observe that a sufficiently full account is supplied of one letter which had been almost destroyed (after letter 20, elsewhere 21), although it is a copy of another (letter 18, elsewhere 15), and that two copies of the same letter are also produced (letter 33, elsewhere 30 and 33), and further see that some letters believed to have perished through Langobardic intrigue survive, while others are passed over in silence and events are even reported contrary to the facts, with the truth of events entrusted to the fidelity of messengers or legates, I have no doubt in asserting this: if a letter of such importance as the one introduced by conjecture had been sent, or if it survived, either it would itself be extant or some sort of mention of it would be made. But a sober and sound examination of the matter will expose these empty conjectures.

#### II

Ruinartius also produced, from a manuscript codex, in his recension of the Works of Saint Gregory of Tours, the passage from the Continuation of Fredegarius which Baronius, Cointius, and others quote in different ways. This is the same passage that has been used by more recent writers to cast such profound darkness over papal history. The words of the continuation (no. 110) are as follows:

> “For at that time blessed Pope Gregory, from the Roman See of Saint Peter the Apostle, sent twice to the aforesaid prince a legation bearing the keys of the venerable tomb with the chains of Saint Peter, together with great and countless gifts—something never before heard or seen in any age. This was done so that he might withdraw from the emperor’s side and confirm the Roman consulship upon the aforesaid prince Charles. The prince therefore received that legation with extraordinary and magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and sent Grimoald, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sigibert, a recluse of the basilica of Saint Denis the Martyr, to Rome, to the thresholds of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, with his envoys and companions, together with great rewards.”

Ruinartius embraces Pagius’s false opinions concerning Cointius, which Pagius himself also notes (740, no. 4 and following). Nevertheless, he admits only two letters: “He wrote,” he says, “two letters to Charles on the same occasion, which have come down to us.”

#### III

As for the passage in that continuation, Aimoinus notes that the reading is:

> “He would free the Church from the tyranny of the Langobards . . . . He would withdraw from the Langobard side, and the aforesaid prince Charles would confirm the Roman consulship. (Variant: So that the aforesaid prince Charles would depart from the Langobard territories in order to render aid to the Romans.)”

Pagius admits that all the editions vary. Ruinartius further reports that in the manuscript Codex Broherianus one reads: “Roman consultation.” But what I especially wish to be noted is that both Ruinartius, in defending this as a variant reading, and Pagius, in asserting that the continuation’s reading is corrupt, use as their witness the Annalist of Metz, who otherwise lived 160 years after that age and perhaps borrowed his material from the same source.

Whatever the truth may be, his words deserve to be heard:

> “The aforesaid bishop Gregory also sent him a letter by decree of the Roman princes, because the Roman people, having abandoned the rule of the emperor, had wished to entrust themselves to his protection and invincible clemency.”

If the Romans, having rejected the rule of the Eastern emperors, had decided to seek patronage and protection from that Frankish prince in whose hands supreme power lay, and whose might was celebrated in everyone’s conversation, then—even if this new letter were admitted—no support for a consulship could be derived from it. Who does not see that these words most clearly describe a decree, or consultation, of the Romans, with no mention whatever of a consulship?

Although Ruinartius supports his reading by the judgment of this Annalist, against the alleged consulship—for the Annalist nevertheless mentions Gregory’s letter, of which the Continuator of Fredegarius gives not even the slightest indication—he departs from him and decides that no more than two letters were sent by Gregory which still exist today. Nor can I easily understand why Pagius, proceeding along the same path as his contemporary Ruinartius—and indeed unsuccessfully, for he brought many companions along with him into error—disagreed with that learned man about the number of letters. For the errors which he and others eagerly embraced are to be attributed not to this new letter, but to the Continuation of Fredegarius; it is there that a single legation is said to have been something never before seen in that kingdom.

#### IV

Whatever the truth may be, from the recently cited passage of the Continuation of Fredegarius Pagius and other writers of no inferior reputation plainly extract three principal arguments that are false. These are: the keys of Saint Peter’s confession sent to the kingdom; the agreement made with Charles that he should withdraw from the emperor’s side; and the Roman consulship conferred upon him.

As to the first, Pagius and those who follow him read in Gregory’s first letter, “we sent [them] to the kingdom”; but Pagius and all the others are hallucinating. The true reading of the Viennese codex is *ad rogum*, a word very common in that age for a petition, as I shall show in the notes. The codex itself uses no other expression in another passage (letter 91, elsewhere 88), where it says that, after the death of Arichis his father, the Beneventans requested Grimoald as duke: “we sent a petition so that we might receive him as duke without fail.”

On this matter Pagius’s interpretation is laughable: he reads *roba* carelessly or sleepily (year 788, no. 1). I shall quote his very words, lest I be accused of disguising the truth:

> “A *roba* was formerly a looser garment used by kings, bishops, and others, as can be seen in Ducange’s Glossary.”

I pass over the fact that Ducange gives no example of *roba* that is not taken from a period after the year 1000. For him *roga* and *rogus* have the same meaning; and he adduces letter 88 of the Carolingian Codex itself as evidence for the matter, though he does not do so for *roba*.

But if Pagius’s opinion is laughable, what shall we say of Muratorius’s scarcely fair inclination toward the dominion of the Holy See? He published the Carolingian Codex from Lambecius’s recension (Italian Affairs, volume III, part 2, p. 73), and in Gregory III’s letter he read *rogum* instead of *regnum*; nevertheless, both in his Italian Annals and elsewhere, he stubbornly maintained *regnum*. This is to deceive the common people through confidence in one’s name, not to write history honestly.

#### V

The second argument is that Charles should “withdraw from the emperor’s side.” As though he had ever known the emperors of the East, rather than being joined by friendship and treaty to Liutprand, king of the Langobards and the bitterest enemy of the emperors.

I shall use as my witness Paul the Deacon, who was well acquainted with the affairs of his own people:

> “Charles, prince of the Franks, sent his son Pippin to Liutprand, so that, according to custom, he might receive his hair. When he cut his hair, he became his father.”

This happened in 735. Two years later, about a year before Gregory’s letter, Charles “sent envoys with gifts to King Liutprand and asked him for assistance against the Saracens. Liutprand, without delay, hastened to his aid with the entire Langobard army. When the Saracen people learned this, they fled from those regions. Liutprand, however, returned to Italy with his entire army” (Deacon, book VI, chapters 53, 55).

Considering this, Baronius excuses Charles for not taking up arms against the Langobards (740, no. 25):

> “He would have been bound to be present with his army, unless Liutprand had fought against the Roman Church, as he had done.”

Therefore, with Pagius’s indulgence, that codex which the continuator of Aimoinus used, and which is also supported by the one used by the Annalist of Metz, must be preferred to the edition published by Ruinartius and to the similarly corrupted editions. The reading should be: “he would withdraw from the Langobard side.”

#### VI

The third argument, concerning the consulship allegedly conferred, surpasses the others in its frivolity. Indeed, that shadowy dignity of the ancient republic, which in the age of Augustus and his successors seems to have continued more for arranging time by years than for conducting affairs—and from which the designation “post-consulship” was devised as a chronological aid in the fourth century of the Church—this dignity, I say, in the eighth century merely indicated the nobility of one’s lineage.

It was therefore hardly of such importance that it should serve as an embellishment for a Frankish prince celebrated for the glory of his achievements, and most closely joined by treaty and friendship with the Langobard king.

Various examples confirming this are supplied by the writers of the Lives of the pontiffs, frequently praised under the name of Anastasius. First, scarcely had Rome and its duchy defected from the impiety of the Greeks when, at the council of Gregory III in 731, a treaty was concluded for the sacred images, “with noble consuls and the rest of the Christian peoples standing by.”

Next, under that same pontiff, several consuls captured in battle were living among the Langobards. Liutprand restored them to Saint Zachary in 742—that is, three years after the legation sent to Charles:

> “He restored Leo, Sergius, Victor, and Agnellus, the consuls, to the aforesaid most blessed man.”

(Anastasius, section 210.)

Finally, Hadrian, then a boy and later pontiff, had been educated during those same years by his kinsman “Theodatus, formerly consul and duke.” When he came into power, he prepared a legation to King Charles and repeatedly referred to the envoys, or messengers (Carolingian Codex, letters 67 and 80, elsewhere 79 and 74), as “Theodore, our most eminent consul and duke, and our nephew.” Under that same pontiff (Anastasius, section 333), “Leoninus, consul and duke,” died.

#### VII

From what has been said it is clear how unstable is the foundation on which the opinions of learned men rest concerning the corrupted passage of the Continuator of Fredegarius. The manuscripts of Anastasius—the Regal, the Mazarin, and both Thuane manuscripts—certainly illuminate it, together with the history of that period, of which I have touched briefly elsewhere while discussing other matters. These manuscripts can be read in the royal and Roman editions.

They report Gregory III’s legation while Liutprand was encamped near Rome, in the following explicit words:

> “When he came to Rome, he pitched his tents in the Field of Nero; and after ravaging Campania, he shaved and clothed many noble Romans in the Langobard manner. For this reason the man of God, oppressed on every side by grief, took the sacred keys from the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle and sent them by sea, through his messengers, to Charles, a most sagacious man who then ruled the kingdom of the Franks, in the region of France, through Anastasius, a most holy man and bishop, and also through Sergius the presbyter, to ask the aforesaid most excellent Charles to free them from so great an oppression of the Langobards.”

Whether he commended to these illustrious envoys, orally, a Roman consultation, or rather ordered them earnestly to ask that Charles give aid to the Romans—ancient editions of the continuator of Aimoinus read “a Roman consultation”—I leave the reader to judge.

I myself see that both this passage of the manuscripts of Anastasius and both letters of Gregory III are abundant witnesses to the aid requested; but that consulship, or consultation, is mentioned only in the corrupted Codex of Fredegarius and among more recent writers, who go astray throughout this matter, as has been demonstrated. Therefore, even if I admit *consultum*, I would prefer it to be understood as the supine of the verb *consulo*—“to consult”—rather than as a decree of the Romans.

#### VIII

The Continuator of Fredegarius asserts that the pontifical envoys were received by Charles with great honors, that precious gifts were given to them to carry to Rome, and that another noble legation was prepared for the pontiff. Gregory’s first letter confirms that those gifts were presented to the basilica of Saint Peter.

But the same continuator is silent about the prince’s promise to bring aid to the Romans; nor do the pontiff’s letters clearly show either that he promised such aid or that he brought it. We must therefore either regret that the occasion for sending envoys to a prince bound by treaty and friendship to the enemies of the Holy See was wholly unsuitable, or admit that Charles honored a new legation—one never before seen in France—with such distinction because he saw that it would bring him a great increase of glory among his own people, not because he had any desire whatsoever to desert Liutprand in order to oblige the pontiff.

It is certainly clear that Charles lent a favorable ear to Liutprand’s envoys, whom Liutprand sent to Charles after discovering the pontiff’s plan. For Charles allowed Liutprand and his son to wage war against the Holy See, a fact which Gregory reproaches him for in letter 1:

> “As we see, while you have granted those same kings permission to make incursions, their false suggestion has found more acceptance with you than our truth.”

This is something quite different from bringing aid to the afflicted affairs of the Church.

Nevertheless, Charlemagne lists Charles among the princes of his lineage who undertook the defense of the Holy See (Charter of the Division of the Kingdoms). For he was deceived by these two letters of Gregory, who hoped for assistance.
