Besides, in order to attract his sons to love of the Holy See, Gregory’s twofold testimony to the assistance requested from France was sufficient, even though no aid came from there.

#### IX

Everyone consistently asserts that no assistance was brought to the Holy See by Charles Martel. But, abusing history, they offer false reasons for this fact. They say that Charles was then ill and later died; for this reason he was unable to provide the aid he had contemplated, although aid was eventually brought by Pippin, Charles’s son.

In this way they disregard the twelve-year interval between Charles’s death and the aid brought by Pippin, along with the many and great events that occurred in the meantime. To establish this, they rely only on the authority of the writer of the Life of Stephen II in Anastasius, who plainly lies—as often happens in that book when events very far removed in time are recounted or external material is drawn from elsewhere. By contrast, when contemporary or domestic affairs are described with the aid of the archives, everyone knows that no monuments of antiquity have come down to us more reliable than those faithfully recorded there.

The passage in the Life of Stephen II is as follows (section 235):

> “Just as his predecessors, the lords of blessed memory, Pope Gregory, another Gregory, and the lord Zachary, the most blessed pontiffs, sent to Charles, the king of the Franks of most excellent memory, asking that he come to their aid because of the oppressions and invasions which they too suffered in this province of the Romans from the impious Langobard people.”

The final statement is true: all those pontiffs were subjected to Langobard ferocity. But it is false that Gregory II contemplated anything from France; the Continuator of Fredegarius himself admits this when he calls Gregory III’s legation a new and previously unheard-of event. It is false that Zachary sought assistance from there, as will soon become clear. Finally, it is false that Charles Martel was king of the Franks; all the gentile writers call him mayor of the palace, while Gregory III calls him subking.

#### X

Nevertheless, these falsehoods so delight Pagius that he does not hesitate to assert (year 726, no. 14; 740, no. 4 and following) that Gregory II “either secretly fled to Charles Martel or certainly implored his assistance without sending any legation.” Elsewhere, against Peter de Marca, he maintains the same position even more vehemently and at greater length.

He makes this claim for Charles Martel after assigning him the patriciate—which for him is one and the same thing as the consulship, and for that reason he clings to it stubbornly in the Continuation of Fredegarius—despite the protests of Gregory III’s letters.

The reason why he and other learned men make the matter appear plausible is supplied by two writers of that age, Paul the Deacon and the frequently cited Continuator of Fredegarius. The latter, in his brief account of Charles’s illness and death in 741, inserts two legations and passes over whatever subsequently occurred between the pontiff and Charles. He therefore gave later writers an opening to refer to that same year events which demonstrably took place over several years and whose sequence is established by other evidence.

Paul the Deacon similarly, not only conflating events that occurred over many years into one account but also placing earlier events afterward, confused the order of time, as the distinguished Blancus observed. Thus he placed the rebellion of Trasamund, duke of Spoleto—which is highly relevant here—before the illness of Liutprand and the association of Hildebrand in the kingdom, although all these events go back to the year 736.

This gave later writers freedom to arrange the history according to their own judgment. Thus Cointius postpones the request for Langobard aid by Charles against the Saracens to the year 739, contrary to the authority of the Continuator of Fredegarius, who says, “in the second month of that year.” For, while Ruinartius and Pagius applaud him, he interprets this as “in the second year afterward.”

Pagius, for his part, extending the events carefully recorded by Anastasius through chronological calculations and correcting the indictions, brings both accounts closer to the year 741, thereby establishing that Charles, prevented by death, could not have helped the pontiff. For this reason the four-year chronology of the history must be established; the date of Gregory’s letters depends upon it, and once that date is recognized, the opinions—or hallucinations—of later writers will be exposed.

#### XI

The Annalist of Fulda, who is preferable to the other authorities used by more recent writers because of his antiquity and authority, summarizes the deeds of Charles Martel in the years 738 and following with remarkable brevity:

> “738. Charles entered the region of Provence and compelled the Moorish duke, who had previously invited the Saracens by treachery, to flee.  
> 739. Charles subjected the whole of Provence and all its coastal places to his rule.  
> 740. Peace and quiet were restored for a time to the Frankish kingdom through Charles: the Goths were defeated, the Saxons and Frisians subdued, the Saracens expelled, and the Provençals received back.  
> 741. Charles, in the twenty-eighth year of his dukedom, died at Paris and was buried at Saint Denis.”

The events of the final year are narrated at greater length in the appendix to Fredegarius. Charles is said to have fallen ill at Vermeria; to have divided the office of mayor of the palace among his sons after consulting his leading men; to have afterward gone to Quierzy; and to have died after new signs had appeared in the sky.

More importantly, inserted between his illness and the division of the administration of the kingdoms is everything that passed between the Roman pontiff and Charles.

Whether this is correct we shall now hear from Anastasius, where Gregory’s deeds are described with the chronology carefully preserved, in such agreement with Gregory’s letters that nothing more illustrious could be desired for confirming the history of those times. This is especially so since the distinguished Zacagnus published other letters of Gregory from an excellent Vatican Codex, which shed much clearer light on the events.

For in them there is mention of the four cities invaded by Liutprand at the end of the expedition of 739, whose beginning Gregory III discusses in both letters to Charles. There is also such clear mention of the Langobard affairs of the preceding year, of the assistance vainly expected from France, and of the gifts sent by Charles to Saint Peter through his envoys, that there can be no doubt that the year 738 is intended.

But let us hear the deeds of Gregory III from Anastasius.

#### XII

The writer of the Life of Zachary, describing the end of the expedition of 739 (section 207), says:

> “Since the aforesaid Trasamund had not been restored by his predecessor, the lord Gregory, of blessed memory, nor by Stephen, formerly patrician and duke, nor by the entire Roman army, a siege was undertaken on his behalf by the same king, and four cities were taken from the Roman duchy—namely Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera. Thus the same king returned to his palace during the month of August, in the seventh indiction.”

After this Gregory, taught by experience not only that assistance from Charles was a vain hope, but also that, with Charles’s consent, the Langobards had inflicted greater damage on the commonwealth, turned elsewhere.

He therefore made a treaty with the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento and, having joined their forces, planned to recover the cities through mutual assistance. The first of the allies, Trasamund, after recovering all his possessions, “entered Spoleto during the month of December, in the eighth indiction,” as the Regal, Mazarin, and Thuane Codices correctly read—not “in the same indiction,” as the common text has, since the eighth indiction began with the month of September.

In the following year, 740, the agreements required that battle be undertaken for the Holy Commonwealth, so that the four cities taken on account of Trasamund might be recovered. But the duke of Spoleto, seriously considering the retention of what he had recovered,

> “was unwilling to fulfill,” the same writer continues, “what he had promised to the aforesaid pontiff, to the patrician, and to the Romans jointly, concerning the recovery of the four cities which had perished on his account, and of the others which he had promised in the articles.”

Accordingly, the pontiff, seeing that his hopes were also frustrated here—hopes which he had maintained for almost an entire year—prepared a legation in October to Liutprand and his son Hilprand, his associate in the kingdom, so that by prayers he might obtain what he could not obtain by arms, on account of the treaty-breaking duke.

Everything is clear from the letters published by the distinguished Zacagnus, which it is worthwhile to reproduce in full.

#### XIII

> “Gregory to all the bishops in Langobard Tuscany.
>
> “Your Fraternal Holiness remembers that, at the time of your ordination, you promised by written document and by the bond of an oath to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that in circumstances affecting his Holy Church you would strive with all your strength.
>
> “Therefore, because we have sent the present men, Anastasius, our beloved son and presbyter, and Adeodatus, our regional subdeacon, our faithful servants, to entreat and, with God’s favor, obtain the restoration by our sons Liutprand and Hilprand of the four fortresses which were taken from blessed Peter in the preceding year, behold, dearest brothers, an acceptable time in which, according to your written promise, you may bear the fruit of a good work to blessed Peter.
>
> “By whose authority we exhort you in the Lord to hasten to them with our aforesaid sons, so that, inspired by God, they may restore those same fortresses to their protectors, the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.
>
> “For if—which we do not believe—you delay undertaking the journey for God’s sake, I, although weak because of bodily illness, shall undertake the arduous journey, and I shall see to it that your negligence does not become a matter of obligation for you under the knot of the agreement.
>
> “Given on the Ides of October, in the ninth indiction.”

The matter having failed, Gregory died the following year, on 27 November; four days later Saint Zachary succeeded him.

#### XIV

As soon as this most holy man had attained the highest office, he approached the king by a legation and by his own presence. With the help of the Roman army, he prevailed against the treaty-breaking duke, recovered the four cities, visited each one himself, and took possession of them. He then returned to Rome and decided that solemn thanksgiving should be offered to God for so many benefits.

All these events occurred, according to the testimony of the aforementioned author of the Life of Saint Zachary, in the tenth indiction—that is, between September of the year 741 and September of the following year. Everyone follows his authority in agreement.

They depart from the truth in only one matter: they refer the writer’s words, “which he himself had taken two years earlier by the siege undertaken on behalf of the aforesaid Trasamund, duke of Spoleto” (section 210), to the year 740, although they refer to the month of August of the year 739, which the same writer clearly identifies by the seventh indiction, still current in that month.

Although several months exceeded the two-year period when Liutprand restored the cities at the beginning of the year 742, the author rightly said “two years earlier,” since the period had been completed. For, when he is reckoning by indictions and discussing events that occurred during the tenth indiction, by “two years” he means the eighth and ninth indictions, which had elapsed after the invasion of the cities at the end of the seventh.

By contrast, if the year 740 were understood at the end of the eighth indiction, two years would not only not yet have elapsed at the time of the restoration; they would not even have elapsed when the pontiff, having completed the long journey, taken possession of the four cities, and returned to Rome, had carried out all the other events assigned to the tenth indiction.

### XV

These events took place at Rome and in its duchy in the year 738 and thereafter. Nor should attention be paid to those who, in order to defend their opinions, alter and correct ancient records with the utmost license, extend the chronology of events, and assert incredible things as certain. Gregory therefore wrote the first letter to Charles at the beginning of the Lombard invasion, in the year 739; the second shortly after the Lombards, on account of Thrasamund—who, fearing their anger, had withdrawn within the walls of the city—plundered the basilica of Saint Peter. Both letters were written before the four cities were recovered at the end of the war, neither of which they mention.¹

The letters themselves reveal their date. In the first, Gregory complains of the devastation of the Roman duchy and asks Charles, “after the return of those kings to their own territory,” to send a trustworthy envoy to Rome who could see with his own eyes what damage had been inflicted. In the second, he grieves that Peter’s basilica had been plundered, including the very gifts that, as we have seen, Charles had sent through his envoys in the preceding year. From this point for nearly fourteen years, until Stephen II more opportunely and more effectively implored the aid of the Franks, we learn from no ancient record or history that the popes turned to them. Yet Gregory III survived for two years, and Charles Martel for nearly as long. Saint Zachary governed the apostolic see for ten years and several months and vigorously defended its rights. When he found an appropriate opportunity to restore the hopes of his predecessor, he gave an abundant reply in the year 748 to numerous matters concerning corrupted discipline, but said not a word about the government of the holy commonwealth. Finally, during the first period of his pontificate, Stephen II sought no assistance from the Franks, despite the greatest hardships.

### XVI

Indeed, the same Stephen, harassed beyond measure by Aistulf, wearied the impious Copronymus with letters, imploring him to aid the afflicted city. He also sent again to Constantinople, taking advantage of the opportunity created by the envoys who, through his efforts, were seeking to recover the affairs of the Exarchate from the Lombard king. He sent his own envoy with letters “beseeching imperial clemency that, in accordance with what he had repeatedly written to him, he should come by every means with an army to defend these regions of Italy and free this city of Rome, or the whole province of Italy, from the bites of the son of iniquity,” as Anastasius relates (section 232).

So far were the Roman pontiffs from placing any hope in the Frankish princes before the year 753, or from seeking dominion over Rome and its duchy—a dominion offered to them by the people and already remaining with them for twenty-five years. But when every hope of Greek assistance had to be abandoned, especially as Eastern impiety grew stronger day by day, Stephen at last sought and obtained Frankish aid, first by letters and then by his personal presence.

Nor was this accomplished through a symbolic offering of the kingdom, or by presenting the consulship, or by any other argument that has occurred to more recent writers. Rather, it was through the true dignity of the patriciate, that is, of the protection and defense of the Roman Church. The character of such a patriciate can be found throughout the letters of this Codex, for which no more complete witness can be desired. It is likewise clear from the same evidence that no such patriciate had previously been granted to the Frankish princes. The first two letters under discussion are addressed by Gregory III to Charles as “sub-king”; Zachary’s single letter (letter 3, formerly 5) is addressed to Pippin, mayor of the palace; and Stephen II’s first letter (letter 4, formerly 10) is addressed to Pippin the king, a dignity he had acquired through Zachary’s authority two years earlier. All the remaining letters of Stephen never omit the title of patrician, since they were written after his return from Francia. The same is true of all the others entered in the Codex, whether addressed to Pippin or to his sons Charles and Carloman: Stephen had designated them both kings and patricians while he was in Francia in the year 753 and thereafter.

### XVII

I must now show why Marca, Pagius, and others are so eager to assert something plainly false. They apparently failed to understand that the Roman pontiffs, by the will of the Romans, the senate, and the people, ruled as princes of the holy commonwealth in Rome and its duchy for the twenty-five years between the defection of Italy from the impious Greeks and Stephen II’s departure for Francia.

For this reason, they suppose that Rome and its duchy rested on a title of donation, like the Exarchate; and because they find no such donation in any ancient record, they fill everything with questions. But just as they went far from the truth when discussing the patriciate of Charles Martel, so, by conjecturing and reasoning about the dominion of the City, they go entirely astray. Hence there is not merely one opinion about the time, manner, and nature of pontifical rule, but one general delusion.

To expose the falsity of these opinions, one should proceed by a concise route. Those otherwise most learned men should surely be asked: Why, in Pippin’s time—when everyone agrees that he granted the Exarchate and Pentapolis alone to the holy see—did Paul seek aid against the Greeks threatening the Exarchate and Rome (letter 25, formerly 34)? Why does Stephen, duke of Naples, promise that he will bring aid to the same pontiff if the Lord Emperor should send his soldiers against Rome (Neapolitan Chronicle, in Pratilli, volume III, p. 32)? Why does Paul himself equally call Senigallia, our city in the Pentapolis granted by Pippin, and our Castrum Valentis in Roman Campania (letter 39, formerly 14)? Why, when speaking generally of the cities of the Roman duchy, does the same pontiff always call them “ours” (letter 38, formerly 24; 40, formerly 26)? Why do Carolingian diplomas say: “Just as you have held and administered the Roman city with its duchy in your power and dominion from your predecessors until now” (this can be seen in all the diplomas, both published and manuscript, although some have timidly and others imprudently restored *nostris*, “by our predecessors”)?

It is preferable, however, to disclose the traces of pontifical rule during the same twenty-five-year period that preceded Pippin’s donation.

### XVIII

We have already seen the Roman defection from the Greeks at its very beginning. In the year 728, Gregory II recovered Sutrium after it had been invaded by Liutprand, “by sending many successive letters and admonitions to the king,” and finally “by giving many gifts.” For “the king of the Lombards restored it and donated it to the holy apostles Peter and Paul.”

At approximately the same time, “the duke Exhilaratus, deceived by diabolical instigation, held the regions of Campania with his son Adrian (this part of the Roman duchy comprised seven cities: Signia, Anagnia, Ferentinum, Alatrium, Patricum, Frusino, and Tibur), misleading the people so that they might obey the emperor and kill the pontiff” (section 184). The same events are described more fully in the Neapolitan Chronicle, in the work of the distinguished Pratilli (volume III, p. 30), as follows:

> “The duke, at the instigation of the Emperor Leo, went against the lord pope and the Romans and fought with them. The battle lasted from morning until the third hour. The duke Exhilaratus, with Adrian his son and his followers, fought for a long time with the greatest strength and courage, although he could not withstand the fortune of war because of the multitude of his enemies. He was left dead, as was Adrian; some of the others were killed, some captured, and others put to flight. Theodore was elected in the duchy . . . . . Alphanus, the secretary of the lord emperor, came to Naples and ordered that the lord pope should not be obeyed and that the money belonging to his revenues should not be sent to him.”

This was evidently the Neapolitan patrimony, also called the Campanian patrimony in the register of the letters of Saint Gregory the Great, and administered by a subdeacon.

### XIX

It is appropriate to recall here, in passing, the testimony of Theophanes (*Chronographia*, p. 273), concerning the patrimonies of Calabria and Sicily that Leo the Isaurian converted into public property:

> “He ordered the patrimonies called those of the holy apostles and coryphaei, who are venerated in Old Rome—namely, three and a half talents of gold, that is, thirty-five thousand gold pieces each year (Aleman, *De Lateranensibus Parietibus*, chapter 15, p. 64), assigned and paid to their churches from ancient times—to be transferred to the public treasury.”

Such a crime either belongs to the same period, when Duke Theodore was ordered to invade the revenues of the Neapolitan or Campanian patrimony belonging to the Roman Church, or occurred only a short time before or afterward.

These were the primordial rights which Charles the Great and all the Carolingian successors, as well as the Ottos and Saint Henry, tried in vain to vindicate for Saint Peter and his successors. At last, when the Saracens drove out the Greeks and the Normans drove out the Saracens, they returned to the Church during the eleventh century.

I now return to the traces of pontifical rule.

### XX

We have already seen the certain defection of the Romans under Gregory II, and we know with equal certainty of his rule, since the Neapolitan duke and the secretary of the impious Leo urged the people to obey him rather than the pontiff.

But another extremely certain trace is supplied by the action of King Liutprand and the exarch Eutychius. After taking counsel together, they decided “that, once the armies had been assembled, the king should subjugate the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, and the exarch should subjugate Rome,” as Anastasius relates.

Rome therefore obeyed Gregory II and the Romans. Liutprand, being of sounder judgment and about to withdraw with his army from the vicinity of Rome, thought it necessary to consult his allied prince and “begged the pontiff to receive the aforesaid exarch into an agreement of peace, which was done” (section 186 and following).

While the exarch remained at Rome, a certain Petasius plotted a rebellion in Roman Tuscany, which was part of the duchy. The pontiff joined his forces with those of the exarch, suppressed the rebellion, and sent the severed head of Petasius to Constantinople. “Even then the emperor did not grant the Romans his full favor”; he had expelled Saint Germanus from the patriarchal see and, after publishing edicts, was behaving ever more violently against the sacred images.

When Gregory II died—the man whom we have seen acting as prince at the will of the Romans, and as administrator, so to speak, of the remnants of the empire—Gregory III succeeded him and established the holy commonwealth. He therefore did not act alone in challenging Leo and his son Constantine, the associate of the empire; rather, “the entire community of this province of Italy likewise sent petitions unanimously to those same princes for the restoration of the images” (section 193).

### XXI

In Gregory III I see clearer signs of princely rule. The embassy and letters to Charles Martel of which we have spoken designate him as supreme prince. When he recovered the city of Gallese from the Lombards, he “ordered it to be joined to the structure of the holy commonwealth and to the body of the Roman army beloved by Christ” (section 203).

It would therefore depart from the truth both to call the Roman defection into doubt from its very beginnings in Greek impiety and to assert absolute dominion for Gregory III, at least.

The case of Zachary is different, as we shall soon see. Over time, the people had grown accustomed to offering obedience and reverence to the most excellent of all citizens and at the same time the supreme priest. With regard to pontifical rule, what occurred was analogous to what is known to have occurred with Octavian’s imperial authority in this same city.

The sole distinction between pontifical rule and the dominion of Augustus was that Augustus, desiring imperial power, gradually subjected the peoples through pretense; whereas the Roman pontiffs, always nurturing hope that the Eastern peoples would be converted, governed the highest affairs for many years more to accommodate the people than from a desire to rule. In the meantime, those same peoples, attracted by the gentleness of pontifical rule, honored the pontiff alone as prince.

### XXII

Foreign princes, too, clearly revered pontifical power, especially the Franks. For Charles Martel, as the Continuator of Fredegar says, “received the embassy itself with marvelous and magnificent honor.” And Pippin, the son of Charles, aspiring to the kingship, ascended the throne on the advice and authority of Zachary, as all history teaches.

These actions, however much they may be attributed to the majesty of the priesthood, brought great growth to princely authority. For the Romans, the great honor shown to the pontiff by those princes made the subjection they had voluntarily chosen more agreeable to them and gradually produced the power of a royal priesthood. Its traces are evident in Saint Zachary, through whose authority the Carolingian line came to rule.

When Liutprand restored the four cities that had been taken from him, he did not, as formerly at the time of Gregory II, restore Sutrium to the holy apostles “Peter and Paul”; rather, he “restored it to that same holy man together with its inhabitants.” He did the same, as we have seen, with the noble consuls captured in battle (section 210).

This distinction is certainly significant. He did not restore those cities and captives to both princes of the apostles, as Sutrium had been restored; nor to Saint Peter, to whom the patrimonies seized in the earlier invasion were restored on the same occasion; nor to “the holy commonwealth,” to which Gregory, Zachary’s predecessor, openly declared that Gallese had been returned. Rather, he restored them to the pontiff alone. This designates something more than the primacy of the Church and clearly shows that the pontiff himself was the prince of the holy commonwealth.

The same writer, in Anastasius (section 216), makes the matter clear. When the exarch Eutychius of Ravenna—which still obeyed the empire—through the agency of Zachary, came to an agreement with the Lombard king concerning the restoration of Cesena, the king “restored two parts of the territory of the fortress of Cesena to the commonwealth. But he retained the third part of the same fortress under pretext, an agreement having been made that, until the Kalends of June, when his envoys returned from the royal city, he would restore to the commonwealth both the fortress and the third part that he was holding as security.”

### XXIII

Here I think it must be observed that those who deny that the empire is signified by the term “commonwealth” are just as mistaken as those who interpret “holy commonwealth”—that is, Rome and its duchy—as the sacred Roman Empire, under a new name unsuitable to that period.

For before the Exarchate and Pentapolis themselves were added to the holy commonwealth through Pippin’s donation, it is clear from the recently cited passage in Anastasius that this part of the imperial dominion was designated by the bare term “commonwealth.” Likewise, shortly beforehand, the same author had called the Roman duchy simply “the commonwealth” (section 212):

> “And the length of the journey would have extended around the boundaries of the commonwealth, as far as the city of Blera, through the territory of the city of Sutrium.”

We shall also see at various points in this Carolingian Codex that, after the addition of the Exarchate and Pentapolis, the ecclesiastical dominion is absolutely called “the commonwealth.” Nowhere, however, will it be found that the term “Roman commonwealth” or “holy commonwealth”—the proper name of the ecclesiastical dominion—is attributed to the empire.

The inquiry into the name is therefore entirely useless. Used absolutely, it designates any principality; with the addition of “Roman” or “holy,” it defines only an ecclesiastical or pontifical principality.

The manner of action, however, deserves serious consideration. There were two restitutions of property by one and the same Lombard king, at the request of one and the same Zachary. Nevertheless, the possessions that belonged in much greater measure to the holy commonwealth were restored intact to the pontiff; the duke of Clusium and three other distinguished men were sent to serve him and to place him in possession of the individual cities; and the noble captives were returned to him.

By contrast, the possessions belonging to the empire were restored only in part. A third of them was retained as security for a fixed period, until an agreement could be reached through envoys with the emperor concerning their complete restoration.

Who, then, cannot see from this that the pontiff was regarded as the prince of the ecclesiastical dominion, while the Exarchate was administered by Eutychius on behalf of Constantine Copronymus?

### XXIV

I am certainly not unaware that Pope Hadrian testified in his letters to Constantine and Irene (Second Council of Nicaea, session 2) that, following the example of both Gregorys, “Zachary, Stephen, Paul, and likewise Stephen, our holy pontiff predecessors, repeatedly implored the grandfather and father of your most serene tranquility for the establishment of the sacred images.”

I also know that Copronymus, although impious in every respect, after hearing what Zachary had courageously done on behalf of the Exarchate, once Artavasdus had been defeated and he had recovered the imperial seat, “sent a written donation to that most holy and blessed pope of the holy Roman Church, granting him perpetual right to possess two estates, called Nymphae and Normiae, which belonged to the public domain” (Anastasius, section 220).

I therefore do not hesitate to affirm that the two Gregorys, Zachary, and the two pontiffs named Stephen, whom Hadrian mentions, never before the year 753 entirely abandoned the hope that the Greeks might come to their senses and, in accordance with the will of the people, recover the city and its duchy, which they had so often attempted to regain by war, but always in vain.

Meanwhile, both by the consent of the people and by the testimony of foreign princes, the pontiffs—especially Zachary—ruled in the City and its duchy. Since they did so for at least twenty-five years, and since no Carolingian prince is ever found to have altered the title of this rule in any respect, it must necessarily be admitted that the pontiffs were true princes of the holy commonwealth, their authority having been gradually confirmed by successful events. For this had been ordained from heaven.

### XXV

All these matters had necessarily to be set forth before the two letters of Gregory III, since more recent scholars have abused them in an extraordinary manner in order to defend false opinions. They were certainly aware that, throughout the entire period preceding Pippin’s donation, no other document was available from which they could derive pontifical dominion as a benefit granted by the kings of Francia.

They therefore had to use these letters alone as support for their assertion. What, then, did they do? The keys of the Confession, customarily sent to princes as a token of devotion, were transformed into a symbol of the kingdom. The embassy—which the letters themselves clearly indicate had preceded them—was made to include a “Roman resolution”; the resolution itself was changed into a consulship, and the consulship into a patriciate.

Since the letters themselves show that the pontiff truly sought aid from Francia but did not obtain it, it seemed necessary to compress the entire embassy, the letters, and the dealings between Gregory and Charles into the greatest difficulties of a few months in the year 741, so that Charles’s illness, followed by his death in October, might appear to have prevented the aid.

All this is false, as has been amply demonstrated.

I would be inclined to extend some indulgence to the distinguished Frenchmen Peter de Marca, Cointius, Ruinart, and Pagius, if, in view of the great merits of the Frankish kings toward the Roman Church, they had not added this supposed intention—frustrated by the king’s subsequent death—in opposition to history.

But what better reply can be made to our most recent writers, who openly foster false opinions and burden them with endless commentary, than the very letters of the Carolingian Codex that they misuse?

### XXVI

Indeed, these same letters mention more than once the preceding year and state that the Lombards learned that aid had been sought from Francia. They therefore cannot be joined to the embassy, nor can the failure to provide aid rightly be attributed to Charles’s death.

They are addressed to Charles as sub-king, just as Zachary’s later letters are addressed to Pippin as mayor of the palace, and Stephen II’s to Pippin as king. Yet none of the later letters fails to mention the patriciate after Stephen had certainly conferred that dignity upon the Frankish king.

Therefore, the patrician dignity, derived from an interpretation of the bronze consulship, is mere nonsense.¹⁸

Finally, the same letters make clear that the keys of Saint Peter were sent in the manner of a supplicatory petition, so that the requested aid might be obtained more quickly and effectively. Thus the notion of a kingdom at Rome—an always detested and ill-omened term—has been foolishly invented, especially by Muratori, who, publishing the variant readings of the Carolingian Codex from Lambecius’s recension (*Italian Historical Matters*, volume III, part 2), reads and prints *rogam* instead of *regnum*.

Everything will become clear from the letters that follow.

---

## I. Letter of Pope Gregory III to Charles Martel

¹⁹

[**Lambecius:** “Letter of Pope Gregory to Charles, mayor of the palace, sent for the defense of the holy Church of God.”]

### LETTER OF GREGORY III

[**Grets:** He began his pontificate in the year of Christ 731 and died in 741. It appears in Baronius, volume IV, under the year 740, no. 20, and in the Magdeburg Centuries, century 8, chapter 10.]

### PONTIFF

[**Cenn:** The Magdeburg writers were the first of all to publish both letters of Gregory in *Century 8*, chapter 10, but in reverse order. Baronius later did the same, assigning the second to the year 739, no. 6, and the first to 740, no. 20. Zacagnus followed him in manuscript Codex no. 22, 24. They are all wrong. Pagius correctly restored the order under the year 740, no. 13. But Cointius, whom all more recent scholars follow, assigns both letters to the year 741. In fact, both belong to the year 739, to which Baronius assigned the second. See the Admonition.]

### TO CHARLES MARTEL

*(Year of the Lord 739, Carolingian Codex I, chronicle 1.)*

### Argument

The Roman defection from the impious Greeks having been confirmed, the Lombards, their perpetual enemies, became more insolent. Gregory III tries to incite Charles Martel against them through a distinguished embassy. Once informed of the situation, they—under the pretext of the rebellion of the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento—afflict the Romans with the permission of their friend and ally, the prince. The pontiff writes to Charles through Anchard, an eyewitness of the plunder and slaughter, and demands the assistance that Charles had promised through his envoys. He entrusts Anchard with certain matters to be related privately. Hoping to obtain aid without delay, he sends the keys of Saint Peter’s Confession as though they were a supplicatory petition.

### Gregory, Pope, to the most excellent lord and son Charles, sub-king

[**Cenn:** Zachary below calls him “mayor of the palace.” Both designations are correct, for under the first dynasty of the Frankish kings the mayors of the palace were called sub-kings because supreme power lay in their hands, as Du Cange proves with many examples in his *Glossary*.]

We are overwhelmed by the greatest tribulation, and tears do not cease from our eyes day or night, when we see daily and everywhere the holy Church of God abandoned by her own sons, in whom there had been hope of her vindication. Therefore, confined by grief, we remain in sighing and mourning, while we see that what little remained last year for the relief and sustenance of Christ’s poor and for the provision of the lamps in the territories of Ravenna is now being consumed by sword and fire by Liutprand and Hilprand, the Lombard kings.

[**Note:** This makes clear that the Lombards inflicted damage upon the people of Ravenna in 738, and it most fully supplies the otherwise exceedingly meager account of Paul the Deacon’s history on this occasion.]

[**Note:** Hildebrand had been called by his father Liutprand into partnership in the kingdom in the year 736. So Horatius Blancus in his notes on Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 55; and Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, volume I, from documents concerning Countess Matilda preserved in the Lucchese archive.]

They have likewise sent and continue to send numerous armies into these Roman territories against us, and they have destroyed all Saint Peter’s estate-houses (*salae*).

[**Note:** For *salas*, Baronius wrongly reads *scalas*. *Salae* were houses situated on the estates or lands of the Church, inhabited by tenants, like rural houses today. The name was also extended to larger buildings, as Du Cange notes, although he did not see this passage of the letter. This is clear evidence that the letter was given before the invasion of the four cities at the end of the war, in August of the year 739, in the seventh indiction, as all the published and manuscript copies of Anastasius have it. He certainly would not have passed over this in silence.]

They have taken away the livestock that remained. Though we have made you, most excellent son, our refuge, no consolation has yet come to us. Rather, as we see, while permission has been granted by you to those same kings to make incursions, their false report has found greater acceptance with you than our truth. We fear that this may be reckoned to you as sin, since now, wherever those kings are staying, they utter these words to our reproach:

> “Let Charles come, in whom you have placed your refuge, and let the armies of the Franks come; if they can, let them help you and rescue you from our hand.”

Oh, what an incurable grief is held in our breast because of these reproaches, when such and so great sons do not try to defend their spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and her special people!

Powerful is that prince of the apostles himself, by the authority granted to him by the Lord, to defend his house and his special people and to take vengeance on their enemies; but he is testing the minds of the faithful sons.

[**Lambecius:** “through the authority granted to him by the Lord, to defend his house.” **Gentilotus:** *operam do sibi concessam potestatem suam defendere domum*—a materially uncertain reading, apparently “I render service … the authority granted to him to defend his house.”]

Do not believe, son, the deceitful reports and persuasions of those same kings. They suggest everything falsely to you, writing of supposed plots, as though their dukes had committed some offense.

[**Lambecius and Gentilotus add:** “against them.”]

That is, the duke of Spoleto and the duke of Benevento. But it is all lies. For—may the truth satisfy you (*tibi*; Lambecius and Gentilotus: *te*), son—they persecute those dukes for no other reason than that, in the preceding year, they refused to attack us from their own territories and, as those kings had done, to destroy the possessions of the holy apostles and plunder the special people.

[**Note:** From this it is inferred that incursions and plundering were certainly carried out in the Roman duchy in the year 758.]

Thus the dukes themselves say:

> “We do not wage war against the holy Church of God and its special people, since we have a pact with them and have received faith from that Church.”

Therefore their sword rages against them.

For the aforesaid dukes were and are prepared, according to the ancient custom, to obey them. But those kings, retaining their anger for the reason stated above and seeking through a contrived opportunity to destroy and invade both them and us, persecute both parties and make false reports to your goodness. Their aim is to degrade those most noble dukes, to appoint their own wicked dukes there, and every day, with still greater force and from every direction, to attack the Church of God, scatter the possessions of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and take the special people captive.

[**Note:** In fact, Liutprand appointed Hilderic duke of Spoleto; later Thrasamund, after recovering his duchy with Roman assistance, killed him, as Paul the Deacon relates (book VI, chapter 55). This occurred in December of the year 739 according to Anastasius in his life of Zachary. Let the followers of Pagius therefore see whether this letter can be postponed to the year 741.]

Nevertheless, so that the truth of the matter may be made known to you, most Christian son, order that, after the return of those kings to their own territories, you send your most faithful envoy, one who cannot be corrupted by rewards, so that he may see with his own eyes our persecution, the humiliation of God’s Church, the desolation of her possessions, and the tears of the exiles, and report everything to your goodness.

[**Note:** Although it is true that, by full spring, or May, kings were then accustomed to set out for war and return home in October, as Muratori shows (*Italian Antiquities*, vol. II, dissertation 26), Anastasius nevertheless teaches that the Lombards were accustomed to leave this place earlier, namely in August. It will also become clear below (letter 8, formerly IV) that Aistulf besieged the city on the Kalends of January. Thus, among the Lombards, both the beginning and the end of fighting were uncertain. What was certain to the Romans from the experience of so many years was that in summer those peoples brought incursions or battles to an end.]

But we exhort your goodness before the Lord and his terrible judgment, most Christian son, that for the sake of the Lord and the salvation of your soul you come to the aid of the Church of Saint Peter and its special people; that you repel those same kings with the greatest speed and drive them away from us; and that you order them to return to their own territories.

Do not despise my supplication, nor close your ears to my petition. In this way, may the prince of the apostles himself not close the heavenly kingdoms to you.

[**Note:** Compare letter XV. “I adjure you by almighty God and by his prince of the apostles,” and frequently elsewhere, as we shall see. It was customary for the Roman pontiffs to join the two together in order to move pious kings more effectively. For Pippin and Charles were especially influenced by fear of God and love of Peter. Gregory accomplishes this in vain with the mayor of the palace.]

I adjure you by the living and true Lord and by the most sacred keys of the Confession of blessed Peter,

[**Note:** The true reading of the Viennese Codex is *ad rogam*, as Lambecius noted, or, better, *ad rog[um]*, as Gentilotus reads it; this brings an end to the long scholarly dispute. Both words signify prayers or supplication in Du Cange. But he gives no other example of *roga* besides letter 91, formerly 88, of this Codex. *Rogus*, by contrast, occurs in many formulas of petitions, and frequently in the *Rule of the Master*: *rogus Dei*. The matter concerning *roga* is therefore uncertain, especially since Gentilotus reads *rogum* in the same letter 88, the unique example cited by Du Cange. It is clear, however, that the word is frequent in Anastasius and is used for both pontifical and imperial distributions. Thus Deusdedit, Boniface V, Severinus, and John IV granted the clergy the full *roga* (sections 117, 118, 123, 124), and Leo III greatly increased the *roga* in the presbytery. Certain factions, speaking of an imperial distribution, say in section 121, “with the army: Your *roga*, they say, which the lord emperor assigned to you by his representative.” I do not ask why the Magdeburg writers, and later Baronius, read *ad regnum*; the cause of the error is unimportant when the error itself is obvious. I am surprised that Augustine’s interpretation was neglected in sermon 22 on the saints, where Peter himself is called “the key to the kingdom,” so that, unless the corruption had already intervened, no kingdom other than the heavenly one should have been understood. Whether *roga*, which Tengnagel read once and Lambecius twice, carries the meaning of *rogus* does not concern me. I am greatly distressed that Muratori, in 1734, published this Codex according to Lambecius’s recension; nevertheless, in his Italian Annals, under the years 741 and 789, he obstinately maintains *ad regnum* and burdens it with commentary, thereby attempting to cast doubt on the certain dominion of the Roman pontiffs by means of a plainly false argument.]

which we have sent to you as a supplicatory petition, so that you may not *proponas* (“put forward”; Lambecius: *praeponas*, “put before”) the friendship of the Lombard kings over the love of the prince of the apostles, but that we may more quickly and with the greatest haste receive, after God, your consolation for our defense, so that your faith and good name may be proclaimed among all peoples.

Thus may we also deserve to say with the prophet:

> “May the Lord answer you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.”

The bearer of this letter, your faithful Anchard, will relate orally to your benevolent excellence everything that he has seen with his own eyes and that we have charged him to report.

And we ask your goodness, with God as witness and judge, to soothe our pains with the utmost speed and that you will swiftly send us joyful tidings (Lambecius: *mittas*, “may you send”), so that, made glad in spirit, day and night we may pour out prayers before the sacred Confessions of the holy princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, for you and your faithful.

---

## II. The Second Letter of Gregory, Sent to Charles

²³

### Likewise for the defense of the holy Church

*(Year of the Lord 739, Carolingian Codex II, chronicle 2.)*

### Argument

As the Lombards’ fury increased, the basilica of Saint Peter, then outside the walls, was plundered and the city besieged. Gregory again asks Charles for aid, using words more generous than his actions. He also entrusts many matters to the bearer to relate privately and modestly hints at something resembling distrust.

[**Grets:** It appears in the Magdeburg Centuries, century 8, chapter 10.]

### Gregory, Pope, to the most excellent lord and son Charles, sub-king
[Col. 0068A] Because of our excessive anguish of heart and tears, we have deemed it necessary to write to Your Excellence for a second time, confident that you are a loving son of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us; and that, out of reverence for him, you obey our commands for the defense of God’s Church and of the peculiar people whom we cannot any longer [Lamb.: omits “of the nation”] endure to suffer the persecution and oppression of the Lombard nation. For they have taken away all the lamps [Grets.: adds “for the honor”] of that prince of the apostles, and everything offered by your parents and by you [Note: [Col. 0068C] If, therefore, we accept the testimony of the Continuator of Fredegar—our sole authority in this matter—that Gregory’s envoys obtained precious gifts, new and previously unheard-of, and that these are now said to have been removed from the basilica of the prince of the apostles, what confidence can be placed in Ruinart when he maintains that these two letters were written on the same occasion? What confidence can be placed in Pagi, who, according to his usual practice, determines the matter thus (year 741, no. 8), when discussing the death of Gregory III on 28 November 741: “Some months before, Gregory had sent two embassies to Charles, mayor of the palace, in France, and had given him two letters”? On the contrary, if, following Anastasius, the letters are assigned to the year 739, and the embassy to the preceding period, nothing clearer could be desired. But enough has been said about this in the Admonition. The gifts of the parents are also praised here, although no gifts from the mayors of the palace are found; hence the parents of Charles seem to be called kings of the Franks. For we read in Anastasius (section 85), in the Life of Hormisdas: “At that time a kingdom with precious gems came from Chlodovechus, Christian king of the Franks, as a gift to blessed Peter the apostle.” Sigebert likewise bears witness to this under the year 510: “The king himself sent to Saint Peter at Rome a golden crown with gems, which is commonly called a kingdom.” CENN.]; and because, after the Lord, we have fled to you for refuge, for that reason the Lombards themselves hold us in contempt and oppress us. Hence the church of Saint Peter has been stripped bare and reduced to extreme desolation; [Note: [Col. 0068D] Baron rightly confirms this plundering by supplementing Anastasius’s history concerning the affairs of the Lombards in that year (739, no. 6), on the basis of the testimony of this letter. ID.] nevertheless, we have set forth all our griefs more fully to the present bearer, [Col. 0068B] your faithful servant, 24 [Note: [Col. 0068D] The silence regarding his name persuades me to believe that he was the same Anchard; thus the plundering of the basilica occurred a few days later, before his departure. The brevity of the letters, which touch only lightly upon the principal matters, and the fact that more was entrusted to him secretly in both letters, point to the same conclusion.] which (quae; Centur.: quos, “them”) he ought to lay before Your Excellence.

But you, son, may stand with that same prince of the apostles, here and in the life to come, before our almighty God, according as you have resolved and contended with all speed for his Church and our defense, so that all nations may recognize your faith, purity, and love toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward us, his peculiar people, whom you zealously protect and defend. For by this you will be able to acquire immortal [Lamb., Gent.: “memorial”] and eternal life.

## 25. ADMONITION ON THE LETTER OF SAINT ZACHARY

[Col. 0069]

[Col. 0069A] I. As I said when discussing Gregory’s letters, Zachary supplied many arguments concerning the majesty of the papacy. Nothing of that kind is found in the following decretal letter; everything concerns the direct power of the pontiff. Unless, moreover, from the letters of that same Gregory already cited we possessed unequivocal testimony that aid from the Franks had been implored, as far as indirect authority is concerned, it would seem that the Holy See had no dealings at all with the Franks: such profound silence about the matter is found in this letter! Indeed, there are many indications of the complete abandonment of the hope which we have seen Gregory alone place in the Franks.

For at the end of that same year, in which the pontiff had once and again attempted the disposition of Charles Martel, so that he might turn the fury of the Lombards away from the apostolic see, he closed a letter to Boniface concerning the churches of Germany and France—reluctantly, I suppose—in these words: “Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, while our most devout lord Augustus Leo was reigning, in the twenty-third year of his reign, and also in the twentieth year of Constantine the Great, his son and emperor, indiction 8” (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1475). Similarly, his successor Zachary adds the years of the impious Copronymus to almost all his letters. And, something I especially wish to note, the following dating is attached to the Roman council which he held in 743: “This council was held in the second year of the emperor Artabasdus, and likewise in the thirty-second year of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, indiction 12, successfully.”

II. I would indeed be doing violence to the truth if, from these chronological formulas, I inferred any right of the Lombards over the holy commonwealth which the pontiff at that time governed—whether before the imperial dignity had been raised in the West, or over the rule of the eastern emperors, as some less accurately do. For the addition of the date is more properly attributed to the notaries’ custom than used as a firm basis for determining anything about the commonwealth.

Nevertheless, apart from the years of the emperors, which it was customary to add, we see years counted according to Artabasdus, who, after overthrowing the impious Constantine, seized the empire, and according to Liutprand, king of the Lombards, who had restored four cities and several estates to Zachary and had rendered good service to the holy [Col. 0069C] commonwealth. The years of the latter were counted because Italy seemed to be recovering breath through him; those of the former because it was believed that an end would be brought to impiety.

By contrast, nowhere in any monument are the years of the patriciate of Charles Martel recorded, although necessity required that one flee to him when hardship pressed. What do I mean by “years”? There is not even any mention of his patriciate anywhere, except in the sense in which the Franks used that dignity, as though it were superior to a dukedom (Du Cange, s.v. “Patricii”). Thus Gregory II called Charles Martel “Patrician” in 724, before the impiety of the Greeks had begun (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1447). Yet this matter certainly ought not to have been omitted if he had been patrician of the Romans, as modern scholars, together with the Franks, maintain.

For from 738, when Charles was approached by the embassy, almost three years elapsed until his death—an interval which cannot, with any justification, be compressed into the few months of the year 741, as has been demonstrated. In addition, Zachary’s ten years extend across the whole period; throughout that interval there exist Gregory III’s letters to Boniface and to the bishops of Lombardy, as well as several letters of Zachary and many other documents, especially the correspondence of Boniface and the Franks with Zachary. Yet no merits of Charles Martel are mentioned anywhere; on the contrary, very many injuries inflicted upon the churches of the Franks are recounted, and these plainly conflict with what is asserted about him.

III. And indeed, even if I agree with Baronius and the other defenders of Charles in freeing him from that disastrous stigma which they say had crept into Boniface’s letters, should I deny credence to the words of Hincmar (letter 6, chapter 19) and of Boniface himself, an eyewitness? [Col. 0070A] He informs Zachary (Codex of Boniface, letter 132, and Labbe, cited above, p. 1495) that he had been summoned by Carloman, one of Martel’s two sons, so that, after a synod had been convened, he might remedy the great wound inflicted upon the churches of his province: “He promised,” he says, “that he wished to correct and amend something concerning ecclesiastical religion, which had already for a long time—that is, for no less than sixty or seventy years—been trampled upon and dissipated.”

A little farther on, while describing the wretched condition of the churches which he says they had suffered through Charles’s actions, he continues: “But now, for the most part, episcopal sees in the cities have been handed over to greedy laymen for possession, or to adulterous clerics, fornicators, and publicans for secular enjoyment.”

The German and Liptine synods, held on this matter in 742 and the following year, as well as the synod of Soissons in the other part of the kingdom, which was governed by Pippin, Carloman’s brother, confirm Boniface’s report. Above all, however, its truth will be clear from the many particulars of corrupted discipline contained in the following letter.

IV. Zachary sent that letter to Pippin, the bishops, abbots, and other Franks at the end of 747 or the beginning of the following year, after Carloman, renouncing his earthly principate, had come to Rome and assumed the monastic habit at the monastery of Monte Cassino. We derive this chronology from other letters of the same pontiff.

This letter is dated “on the Nones of January, while our most devout lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the twenty-eighth year, the sixth year of his reign, indiction 15,” and was addressed to Boniface so that he might ensure that the aforementioned letter to Pippin and the others be read in synod.

Since some discrepancy appears among these three chronological indicators, this is why Cointius assigns the date to 748, while Sirmond and Pagi assign it to 747. I think Cointius’s view is preferable and should be followed, although the indiction and the sixth year of the reign indicate 747. For Carloman came to Rome in March, as Pagi observes (year 747, no. 1), or rather in June, as the distinguished Mansius argues in the same place, [Col. 0070C] and indeed in the year 747, as all the ancient authors consistently report.

Since Zachary’s letter is addressed to a single person, “Pippin, mayor of the palace in the region of the Franks,” it is clear from this that Carloman had renounced the dignity which had been divided between the two brothers before the letter to Pippin and the others was issued—the letter which preceded the other one to Boniface.

If anyone wishes to maintain that both letters were dated at the beginning of 747, or on the Nones of January, he must demonstrate that the Continuator of Fredegar and all the chroniclers cited by Baronius and Pagi were lying—a very difficult task. Therefore, I think, with Cointius, that the date of the letters must be placed in 748. So much for the chronology, which forms only a small part of the letter.

V. It must be seriously observed that, over a period of nearly six years, the two sons of Martel could scarcely, through the efforts of the most holy man Boniface, restore even a little the discipline which had been brought low. For that reason, without detracting in any way from Martel’s praises, we must accept as certain that this prince consistently favored the preaching of that same Boniface in the regions of Germany under both Gregories.

This is shown by the records of Mundeburdium and of protection, by which Charles, at the beginning of Boniface’s mission, ordered that Boniface, the apostle of Germany, be received everywhere in the Frankish kingdom; and by the letters which Gregory II testifies that he gave “to our son Charles, the patrician,” in 747, so that he would not allow Boniface’s preaching to be disturbed by a certain bishop (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1446 and following).

Gregory III’s letters, likewise, near the end of 739, are abundant witnesses to the continued zeal and labor of Charles, so that the entire Frankish kingdom might embrace the faith of Christ. Thus the pontiff congratulates Boniface: “For what you have already made known concerning the peoples of Germany, whom our God in his mercy has freed from the power of the pagans, and whom he has deigned, through your effort and that of Charles, prince of the Franks, to gather—one hundred thousand souls—into the bosom of Mother Church.”” [Col. 0071A]

But history as a whole teaches that he would bring no assistance to the Roman Church, however much he was asked by embassy and repeated letters, contrary to the conjectures and arguments of modern writers, which in matters of fact are exceedingly weak. For he was prevented by his treaty with the Lombards and by his perpetual wars at home and abroad from lending an attentive ear to the petitioning pontiff.

Indeed, to the wounds which those same wars had already inflicted upon the Gallican Church, he added a new and more grievous wound by corrupting discipline. Six years after his death, when it required the greatest cure, this was at last disclosed to the apostolic see.

VI. A timely remedy was indeed supplied. For Zachary replied individually, on the authority of the canons, to the consultation of the Franks, which had been formulated in twenty-seven chapters.

This was a new and previously unheard-of example at the Holy See, where it had been customary to consult the archives, or library, when questions of this kind were referred to it. He used the Breviary of Cresconius, a collection of canons in the Dionysian version—not the Dionysian collection itself. This Breviary had arisen from that collection and was the source and origin of Adrian’s codex and, ultimately, of the Canon, as the Codex of Canons of the Roman Church was called.”

Leo IV teaches us what kind of canon, or Codex of Canons, this was and how it was used (Labbe, Councils, vol. VIII, p. 32) in these clear words:

“Concerning the booklets and commentaries of others, it is not fitting for anyone to judge while abandoning the canons of the holy councils or the rules of the Decretals—that is, those which are held among us together with them in the canon and which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments: those of the apostles, the Nicene, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Gangran, Antiochene, Laodicean, Chalcedonian, Sardican, Carthaginian, and African councils; and together with them the rules of the Roman bishops Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, and Simplicius. These alone are those by whom bishops judge and by whom bishops and clerics together are judged.”

VII. I do not claim that Zachary, who preceded Leo IV by almost one hundred years, used a canon of this kind. I do not hesitate to affirm that Zachary’s use of a collection is being attributed to one which only in the ninth century had developed into the Codex of Canons which we have just described.

This is not the time or place to reject Sirmond’s opinion. He held the canons of John II, inserted into letters of the year 534, to be genuine and carried all scholars along with him, so that the use of the Dionysian collection has everywhere been attributed to the Holy See from the very beginning of that collection. I will merely expose the falsity of the claim: namely, that before approximately the eighth century, when Zachary presided over the Church, the Holy See upheld only the Nicene and Sardican canons, openly rejected the Constantinopolitan canons, and, if it used any of the Chalcedonian canons, used only those three which had been enacted before the departure of the legates at the end of session 6, although these too are found among the others in action 15, in the fourth, third, and twenty-third positions.

Pelagius II speaks very clearly about these matters in his letter to the Istrians (Labbe, Councils, vol. V, pp. 615, 629 and following):

“In the conclusion of the sixth session,” he says, “the standard of the canons is already anticipated, when the prince says there to the venerable bishops: ‘There are certain chapters which we have reserved for you in honor of your reverence.’ … From this anticipation of the sixth action it is shown that, by right, the constitutions of the canons are contained only in the seventh. … Although, if we look carefully, we find the rules of the canons placed not, as is thought, in the seventh, but woven into the sixth action.”

If Natalis had observed this (section V, dissertation 15, article 4), he would not have attributed the twentieth Chalcedonian canon to Gelasius; he would have discovered that it was the third among those proposed by Marcian and approved by the council at the end of the sixth action.

VIII. As for the Constantinopolitan canons, Saint Gregory, successor of Pelagius II, writes to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch in the following sense (book VI, letter 31):

“The canons of the council of Constantinople indeed condemn the Eudoxians, but they do not say who their author Eudoxius was. The Roman Church, however, neither possesses nor accepts those canons or the acts of that synod up to the present time. Yet it accepted that synod in the matter which was defined there against Macedonius. As for the other heresies mentioned there, it rejects them because they had already been condemned by other fathers.”

And when, in his synodical letter to the patriarchs of the East (book I, letter 24), he says that he venerates four councils like the four books of the Gospels, he immediately adds the extent to which they condemned heresies. He did this lest anyone perhaps suppose that he embraced the acts of the councils insofar as they had enacted canons favorable to the ambition of the bishops of Constantinople, while the legates of the Holy See were absent.

Think of this as having been done by Gregory’s successors almost to the end of the seventh century, when it began to be considered irreligious to reject anything from the ecumenical councils. This is established by the *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs (chapter 2, title 9). For the formula, or profession, of the Roman pontiff, issued after the death of Constantine Pogonatus, that is, after the year 685, plainly teaches that whatever had been enacted in general councils was accepted by the Roman See:

“Likewise, to preserve inviolate, without altering even a single point, the holy universal councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, the First of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the Second of Constantinople, which was held in the time of the pious emperor Justinian of blessed memory; and together with them, with equal honor and veneration, to preserve inwardly and fully the holy Sixth Council, which recently assembled under Constantine, the pious prince of blessed memory, and Agatho, my apostolic predecessor.”

[Col. 0072C] IX. The causes of the reversal need not be sought far away. At that time there was such profound ignorance in the City itself that, apart from the doctrines of the faith, which could not be unknown, even false things were not sufficiently distinguished from true ones.

The acts of Marcellinus, Sylvester, Xystus, and Polychronius provide examples. Concerning these, P. Constantius rightly, if I am not mistaken, says (Preface to the *Pontifical Letters*, vol. I, p. 99):

“These little works do not display the taste, mind, or style of a Roman man, even one moderately imbued with the learning of ecclesiastical discipline, but rather of some Gothic neophyte who, in order to show his devotion to the apostolic see, did not consider it a religious offense to tell a lie.”

The bishop Theodore of Canterbury, who flourished near the end of the seventh century, nevertheless valued this sort of miscellany so highly that he did not hesitate to transfer some of it into his *Penitential*. For this reason Natalis, relying on Bede’s authority when commending Theodore (section VII, chapter 4, article 10), adds that certain things alien to the Gospel [Col. 0072D] and to tradition are found in the *Penitential*.

Yet works of this kind themselves bear the stamp of the Holy See. Thus Saint Gregory III, when composing his own book of penance, wished to give the reader the following warning in the preface (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1476):

“We have endeavored to select and gather together this little book of penance for the use of our fellow priests from many flowers of allegories, from the treatises and published sermons of great men, from the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons—that is, of Isidore, Augustine, Gregory, Bede, Gelasius, Innocent, Theodore, Cassian, Egbert, and others.”

Therefore Morinus rightly observes (On Penance, book VII, chapter 1, no. 17) that it is not at all surprising:

“if the penitential book of Theodore, archbishop, a man most learned in his age and, because of the authority of the supreme pontiff by whom he had been consecrated and sent to England, most highly esteemed by all, spread throughout almost the whole of the West in a short time, and if many other bishops imitated it, not merely approving his penitential, but also composing other, more convenient and fuller works after its model.”

31 X. How true this observation is is abundantly demonstrated by the venerable Bede’s book *On Remedies for Sins*, by the *Penitential* of Egbert, bishop of York, written somewhat later, and by several others in Gaul, as well as by the ancient Roman work preserved by Canisius and by the book of Gregory III which I recently mentioned. All of these overflow with Greek canons and are sometimes contaminated with spurious material.

Here, then, is the definite period of the collection of canons which the Holy See embraced. When it saw that the Greek canons were known everywhere and possessed a great harvest of them in the Breviary of Cresconius—canons arranged especially by subject, providing the scribal offices with a labor-saving compendium and presenting something highly acceptable to the pontiffs—it perceived that episcopal consultations could be answered with very little effort. From that time onward, the library codices began to be consulted only rarely.

Would that this method of writing had spread less widely, or had been less attractive to dull minds! For what scholar is unaware that those eighty chapters attributed for a long time to Pope Adrian—chapters containing many things contrary to ecclesiastical discipline and not a few things inconsistent with good morals—were not his?

It was finally discovered through the labors of Baluze who had compiled them, for he brought forth the true author from the best manuscripts (Preface to *Antiquities of Augustus*, dialogue):

“Here begin the chapters collected from various councils or decrees of the Roman pontiffs and offered by Angilram, bishop of Metz, to Pope Adrian”; specifically, “on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, indiction 9,” that is, in the year 785, as the printed copies have it.

Peter de Marca thinks that the wares of Isidore Mercator, which utterly overturned discipline, flowed from this collection (On the Harmony of the Church and the Empire, book VII, chapter 20). Others, however, believe that those works preceded the chapters and do not venture to determine anything certain about their date.

These matters do not belong here. I therefore return to the collection of canons which I maintain Zachary was the first of all the pontiffs to use.

XI. I may seem to be presenting a contradiction: a moment ago I said that Gregory III had used such a collection, while now I maintain that Zachary, who succeeded Gregory, preceded all the others.

But it is one thing to approve a collection and transfer something from it into one’s own booklets; it is another to decide matters of discipline on the authority of those canons, which Zachary did in this letter sent to France, in a new and previously unheard-of example, as I said.

Stephen II followed him in the replies given in 754, while he was in France (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1650 and following). Both used the collection contrary to the custom of their predecessors, although with some difference between them.

As regards the councils, both Zachary and Stephen follow the method of enumeration used by Cresconius, listing separately each individual chapter of each council. In citing decretal letters, however, although both differ from Cresconius, Zachary, when he cites the decrees of Innocent 14 and 20 (chapter 20 and following), seems to follow Dionysius.

Stephen, on the other hand, cites the chapters of the Decretals according to the number of each individual letter, just as was done with the councils. He does not, like Zachary, enumerate the decrees of each pontiff; instead, he carefully numbers the chapters of each letter, also stating the name of the person to whom each letter was written.

This seems to have happened because Cresconius’s Breviary, consisting of three hundred chapters, indicated under each individual chapter a greater or smaller number of canons and titles of decretal letters issued at different times. Nothing was better adapted to resolving each question; yet the canons and titles of the Decretals indicated there had to be obtained from elsewhere.

Thus Zachary seems to have taken his canons and decrees from the Dionysian collection, since Cresconius had used it; whereas Stephen merely excerpted the canons from that source.

XII. Although these testimonies are very clear concerning the presence of the Dionysian version at the Holy See, the ancient right of the Holy Roman Church must not be confined within the limits of that collection, as Justellus and especially Natalis so vigorously contend, eagerly embracing those spurious canons of John II’s letters under Sirmond’s leadership.

For, quite apart from the fact that none of John’s successors used the Dionysian version, Gregory III used in the aforementioned *Penitential* the version of Saint Isidore of Seville—the very version which Mercator employed. Saint Zachary, who was the first recipient of the Dionysian version, exceeded the limits of the collection itself in his letter to the Franks. In the Roman council, moreover (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1549), he adhered to Gregory II’s decree concerning degrees of kinship, and it is evident that his successors did the same, ranging widely beyond the collection through the decrees of all the pontiffs, of which Dionysius collected only a very small part.

Therefore, unless one wishes to oppose the truth, one must admit that, before the establishment of its own collection, which was called the Canon, the Holy See bound itself to no other collection, although, under the guidance of Cresconius’s Breviary, it consulted whatever was in the sacred library whenever an occasion arose, and therefore used the Dionysian collection above all.

After Zachary’s time, however, ecclesiastical judgments and other matters pertaining to discipline and morals unquestionably began to be confined within fixed limits, until the Canon itself appeared.

XIII. Indeed, Stephen III decreed as follows in the Roman council of 769:

“Let no more than the fifty chapters which the Holy Catholic Roman Church accepts be received from the canons of the apostles brought forth through Saint Clement.”

Thus the Holy See had already become accustomed to those fifty selected by Dionysius and Cresconius, since Zachary had begun to use them twenty-two years earlier.

Later, Adrian, Stephen’s successor, transmitted to Charlemagne a concise exposition of the canons—not only of those fifty, but of all the Eastern councils contained in the collection apart from the general councils—so that Charlemagne might use them to reform discipline in Gaul.

For this reason the Holy See no longer rejected those collected canons. Concerning this concise transmission of the canons—which Pagi, Labbe, and Basnage declare to be mutilated and which they do not think should be attributed to Adrian—I must briefly make several observations demonstrating that it is complete and vindicating it for Adrian against their hasty opinion.

XIV. First, the apostolic canons appear to number forty-five, because the twenty-first combines three into one—21, 22, and 23; the twenty-fifth combines two—27 and 28; the thirty-fourth likewise combines two—37 and 38; and finally the thirty-seventh combines three—41, 42, and 43—so that they appear to be one too many.

But the forty-fifth, divided into two, must be restored to unity; thus we shall have the full fifty.

The Neocaesarean canons appear to number fifteen because the second is divided into two. Similarly, when the Laodicean canon 35 is joined with the following canon, they produce fifty-nine Laodicean canons.

The Antiochene canons likewise amount to twenty-five, provided that the tenth and eleventh are separated, although they have been combined into one.

The matter is more complicated in the African canons. For after canon 49 comes 60, and 99 is joined with the following canon; the numbering thus reaches 105, although there ought to be only one hundred African canons, preceded by thirty-three Carthaginian canons according to Cresconius’s Breviary.

This clearly demonstrates that Adrian used Cresconius, as does the division of the thirty-three Carthaginian canons from the one hundred African canons. Dionysius numbers all of these together, as African canons, in a continuous sequence up to 133, whereas each Greek council has its own separate series.

Nevertheless, not one of the ten canons which appear to be missing is actually absent from Cresconius’s Breviary.

XV. The nineteenth concerns the visitation of provinces, a matter peculiar to Africa; canon 49 concerns manumissions performed in the Church with the emperor’s permission; canon 51 concerns the destruction of the remains of idols; and canon 75 begins two councils, one against the Donatists and the other against the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius.

These four canons, which are numbered 52, 82, 84, and 108 by Dionysius, are omitted by Cresconius as useless. Adrian therefore omits them as well, differing from him only in this respect: he continues the sequence of numbers, numbering 34 where he omits the aforementioned canons so that the series may not appear defective, and numbers the five final chapters which Cresconius does not list.

By adding to these nine chapters the hundredth, which Cresconius created by dividing 99 into two parts, as can be seen in chapter 287 of the Breviary (*Bibliotheca veterum iuris canonici*, vol. I, p. 108, appendix), that gap of ten numbers will be filled.

It should also be noted, with Labbe (Councils, vol. II, p. 1669), that in Vatican manuscript no. 4929 the following words are read under the hundredth chapter:

“This chapter of Aurelius, with the subscriptions of the bishops, is not found in the apostolic canon at Rome.”

These words wonderfully confirm that Adrian, like Zachary, used Cresconius’s collection, or Breviary, and not the Dionysian collection. The Dionysian version is used only because Cresconius derived his index from it, and the anonymous author who added the complete canons extracted them from the same source.

XVI. What shall I say about their double error, when elsewhere they declare Adrian’s codex to be mutilated, merely because at the beginning of the Carthaginian canons they read:

“Then, after the twenty canons of the Nicene council had likewise been recited, as they are found described above, by common decree they established the thirty-three chapters which follow”?

Is this a proper way to judge the monuments of antiquity?
