This is a summary—that is, a summary of the material preceding the one hundred chapters recited in the African council from various synods, material which is found in Labbe. The Sixth Council of Carthage, divided into ten chapters, occupies the place of a preface in Justellus both in the Dionysian collection and in the African codex, without any division into a greater or smaller number of chapters, although the first action of the African council really is involved.

Justellus reports almost the same words in the passages cited, words which Adrian copied; both the Dionysian collection and the African codex, which Adrian followed, read:

“The statutes of the Nicene council were likewise recited in twenty chapters, just as they are found written above. Then the things promulgated in the African councils are known to have been inserted in the present acts.”

Therefore, that mention of the Nicene canons refers to the African synods, not to Adrian’s codex, which is consequently unjustly called mutilated in this chapter.

For why should the Nicene canons be brought into this discussion if Adrian also omitted the Chalcedonian canons from it and gave Charlemagne, in a single codex, the six ecumenical councils, of which he wished these Greek rules to serve as an appendix together with the African canons copied, altered, and corrected by him, as they now stand?

Does the preface not explain the matter sufficiently clearly? Indeed, he thought that the bishops should be warned in these words:

“But in all these matters we must follow whatever we see not to differ from the Nicene council and from the holy and apostolic Roman Church.”

XVII. These final points demonstrate how ineptly the Dionysian collection is attributed to the Holy See from the beginning of the sixth century, when Adrian speaks with such caution of those same rules or canons, already accepted everywhere, which had also been used by his predecessors Zachary and Stephen II.

In particular, the fifty apostolic canons had been approved by Stephen III in the Lateran Council. Nevertheless, Adrian corrected some of them on the basis of his supreme authority, as is evident.

For example, apostolic canon 27 grants readers and singers permission to marry. Adrian, however, wrote: “Only readers are permitted to contract marriage.”

Apostolic canon 46 absolutely forbids bishops, presbyters, and deacons to approve the baptism of heretics. Adrian explains: “A bishop or presbyter who accepts the baptism of heretics who do not baptize in the name of the Trinity must be condemned.”

Ancyran canon 9 permits deacons to marry if, at the time of their ordination, they have declared that they are unable to remain continent. Adrian corrects this: “Incontinent deacons must be deposed.”

Neocaesarean canon 4 attributes an unfulfilled desire to divine grace. Adrian, on the contrary, says: “Let it not be imputed to divine grace if the desired lust is not consummated.”

Antiochene canon 10 permits chorepiscopi to ordain readers, subdeacons, and exorcists. Adrian says: “Chorepiscopi cannot confer the lower orders up to the subdiaconate.”

Regarding canon 12 of the same council, which concerns bishops and clerics who, after a judgment has been repeated, appeal again to the emperor and are to be rejected, Adrian rightly and in accordance with the rules of the Church says: “If condemned clerics appeal to the emperor, they are never to be restored.”

The fifteenth canon of the same council, plainly contrary to the apostolic see, is entirely omitted, with only its number being inserted.

Here I bring my examination of the end of Adrian’s codex to a close. For the points presented up to now expose the error of those who wish to make someone else the author of the *Compendium*, while maintaining that Adrian gave Charlemagne the canons in full—as though such corrections and variations could have been made by anyone other than the pontiff.

### XVIII

With regard to the fifteenth canon, I must not pass over in silence why Adrian omitted it altogether. It is plainly opposed to appeals to the Holy See, against which no part of the Western Church—not even Africa—had resisted since the Sardican canons were acknowledged, already from the fifth century of the Church.

Now this very canon, of which Adrian says not a word, together with the fourth canon of that same thirty-sixth council and two Apostolic Canons, was fraudulently appended to a letter of John II in the case of Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez. Sirmondus published it from various manuscripts inconsistently presenting these materials, especially from one manuscript at Rheims, and did so with such success that Justellus, on the authority of Cassiodorus and of this letter, wishes the Dionysian Collection to have been received from its very origin by the Apostolic See [Col. 0076C] (Preface to *Codex Universalis Ecclesiae*, p. 19).

He then continues:

> “This, therefore, is the first and most ancient collection of the decretal letters of the pontiffs, which was called the *Book of Decrees* by Pope Zacharias, in his letter to Pippin, etc.”

Finally, from the decretal letters and canons—citing the edition made by Wendelstinus at Mainz in 1525 and another at Paris—he concludes:

> “This is itself the book of canons which Pope Adrian I presented at Rome to King Charles the Great in the year 805 (although at that time the pontiff was Leo III, who had succeeded Adrian ten years earlier), for the use of the Churches of the West . . . . These are the canons and decrees by which the Roman Church made use in ecclesiastical judgments, as Pope Leo IV testifies, since he reviews the councils themselves and the decrees of the pontiffs contained in this Roman book.”

Thus, relying upon the very weak support of the unknown supposition published by the most learned Sirmondus, the equally learned Christophorus Justellus drew Natalis along with him, as well as lesser men; and in a word he founded the right of the Apostolic See [Col. 0076D] upon this exceedingly slight foundation, while the others applauded.

### XIX

I have already said that a controversy of this kind is suited neither to the place nor to the time. I undertook only to demolish its foundation, and I think I have accomplished that. In any event, Justellus rests with little discernment upon the authority of Cassiodorus in order to attribute the Dionysian Collection to the Holy See for use in judgments.

For Cassiodorus—far from ascribing that character to the Collection—was on intimate terms with Dionysius. Moved perhaps by his virtues and example, and perhaps even by his advice, he founded a monastery on his own estate near Squillace, a town in farther Calabria, and himself embraced the monastic life. On that occasion he had the Dionysian Collection transcribed and urged his monks to read it. To make this more effective, he also testified that it was commonly read at Rome.

I shall produce his very words, lest I seem to disguise the truth (*On Divine Readings*, chapter 23):

> “At the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed the ecclesiastical canons from Greek exemplars in his customary manner, for he was clear and eloquent, and set them forth with great brilliance of expression; today the Roman Church embraces them with the greatest esteem. You also ought to read them continually, lest you appear culpably ignorant of such salutary ecclesiastical rules.”

Here Cassiodorus is known to have described a dogmatic, or moral, book for forming Christian minds according to the Catholic discipline as it was then understood. Dionysius, however, had proposed another purpose for himself: namely, to instruct the bishop of Salona in the ecclesiastical rules, both those decreed in councils and those which were held in esteem among some people though less certain, as he himself testifies in his preface.

Neither Dionysius nor Cassiodorus asserts—or can assert—that the Apostolic See made use of these rules or canons, which it did not begin to embrace until two centuries later. The ancient right is therefore falsely established upon that Collection.

### XX

It must also not be passed over that Cassiodorus speaks only of the canons. For it is clear that the decretal letters were collected later by Dionysius in order to oblige Julian, a cardinal priest, whose greatest concern was to investigate matters relating to ecclesiastical discipline, as Dionysius himself testifies.

But what sort of collection is this, made by private authority and not at all drawn from the shelves of the sacred library? The principal letters of Saint Leo written to bishops and rulers in the year 449, during that great upheaval throughout the East on account of the heresy of Eutyches, are absent from it. Among them are the two celebrated letters to Flavian: the eighth and the tenth, the most famous of all, concerning which the council under Gelasius decreed not long before Dionysius’s arrival at Rome:

> “If anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it in every respect with reverence, let him be anathema.”

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1263.)

I say nothing about the decretal letters of Siricius, Innocent, and Gelasius—of whom the collector knows only the ninth—which are absent from the Collection. I cannot remain silent about this one point: everything belonging to the establishment of the dogmas of the faith, to the authority of the Roman pontiff, to the governance of the universal Church, and to the most important matters of discipline is absent from the Collection, as will be plain to anyone who examines it carefully.

For that reason, I can scarcely believe that those most learned men, Justellus and the others, understood the character and purpose of the Collections. Cresconius speaks clearly of their character in addressing Liberinus, bishop, when he says that Ferrandus, whom he follows,

> “is shown, in the same work, to have separated out, so to speak, the study of the unlearned, of whom there is a very great multitude . . . . so that those able and willing to learn might have the maze of doubt removed from them, and their complete instruction might depend not upon the difficulty of the writer but upon the reader’s own laziness . . . . and might learn by a sound examination whether he ought to govern his mind with severity or with leniency.”

(*Bibliotheca Veterum*, vol. I, p. 456.)

### XXI

From these things it is not obscurely apparent that all collections down to the eighth century of the Church—for Cresconius was writing at the end of the seventh—whether they were general collections of canons or contained only penitential material, had the public good in view. Their purpose, therefore, was the instruction of the clergy and of all the faithful.

We have a most authoritative witness to this in Martin of Braga, who gives the following preface to his Collection, among other things:

> “Because some things in the canons may appear obscure to simpler people, it seemed appropriate that I should restore, with every care and in simpler and more corrected form, both what the translators had expressed obscurely and what the scribes had altered. I observed first that those matters relating to bishops or the whole clergy should be written together in one section; similarly, those relating to the laity should be gathered together in one place, so that anyone wishing to know about a particular chapter might find it more quickly.”

(Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 1381.)

This, assuredly, is why no collection of canons will be found to have been presented to the Holy See. It did not need such streams, since the very sources were available to it in the sacred library. It will be found that in every case it consulted them through its archivists, provided that—leaving aside the disputes of more recent writers—the councils, papal letters, and other ancient documents that have been printed are carefully consulted.

Christophorus Justellus and the many others who followed him, however learned in law, appear not to have considered this. They proposed only to attach their own Code of Canons prematurely to the Holy See, thereby establishing its ancient right and showing how greatly the new right differed from it.

### XXII

Would that the barbarism spread far and wide throughout Italy had not also dulled Roman intellects! Otherwise, if I am not mistaken, the archivists would not have proposed to Zacharias that abbreviated route which Gregory III had also pointed out and which Stephen and his successors afterward did not hesitate to tread.

The ancient custom of consulting the library would certainly not gradually have fallen into disuse, so that within the space of one century the Canon, or Code of Canons, praised by Leo IV—as I said above—would have been almost the sole resource in episcopal cases and matters pertaining to discipline. More regrettably still, toward the end of the ninth century John VIII, in an excessively broad constitution, sanctioned—as Anastasius reports (*Preface to the Second Council of Nicaea*)—that all canons and decrees should be accepted that were in no way opposed to the faith, morals, or institutions of the Holy See.

I shall reproduce the very words of the librarian addressing the pontiff:

> “By the decision of your Apostolate, the Church receives not only those fifty canons alone, but also all the canons of the others, as belonging to the Holy Spirit, to the trumpets, and indeed to all approved Fathers and holy councils; it admits their rules and institutions, but only those which neither deviate from right faith nor from good morals, and which do not even in the slightest conflict with the decrees of the Roman See.”

Although these spurious wares were never introduced into the Canon by the Apostolic See, the permission to use them inflicted a profound wound upon discipline, which festered during the iron tenth century and did not scar over until after prolonged remedies.

It also gave Peter de Marca and Natalis an opportunity to debate, without risk, so many matters concerning ancient and modern law.

The source of all these things is this letter of Zacharias, which I shall now place before everyone’s eyes.

### XXIII

From the brief notes attached to it, readers will find more material relevant to what I thought should be stated in advance. I shall add two points. The first will make clear that the use of the Collection supplied material opposed to the decrees of the Apostolic See; the second will show still more clearly the falsity of Sirmondus’s opinion.

First, therefore, the Franks ask in chapter 11:

> “Which clerics ought also to abstain from their wives?”

Zacharias replies, on the authority of African Canon 37:

> “Bishops, priests, and deacons must practice continence; the others are not to be compelled.”

This conflicts with the decree of Saint Gregory, who toward the end of the sixth century had imposed continence even upon subdeacons throughout the West. Here are his words in his reply to Venantius, bishop of Luna (book IV, letters 16–17):

> “The subdeacons also, whom a similar fault binds, once irrevocably deposed from their office, shall receive communion among the laity.”

Likewise, to the metropolitan of Milan:

> “Similarly, we decree that the three subdeacons whom your Fraternity has reported to have fallen shall always be vacant and deprived of their office; nothing other than sacred communion among the laity is to be offered to them.”

Thomassinus reconciles this contradiction (*Benefices*, book XI, chapter 63, no. 10) by saying that after 150 years Gregory’s decree was still wavering and had not been observed consistently. But, with due respect to him, it was not the decree that wavered; rather, the introduction of a Collection of this sort supplied decrees contrary to it.

And unless he too had placed faith in Sirmondus, he would have perceived that Zacharias was advancing a novelty contrary to the Apostolic See, because he was the first to abandon the path trodden by his predecessors.

I see the same situation with Apostolic Canon 27, substituted for Consultation 18:

> “Which clerics ought to take wives?”

For this is contrary to the discipline of the Roman Church.

### XXIV

The second point from which the supposition becomes clear that the canons in question were appended to the letter of John II is the answer to Consultation 2:

> “Concerning bishops, priests, and deacons who have been condemned.”

This agrees with the case of Contumeliosus. Zacharias, however, replies with only one Apostolic Canon, number 29, omitting the others.

If John, in the year 534, before barbarism invaded Italy, was not afraid to add two Apostolic Canons and two Antiochene Canons, including the latter one—number 15, against appeals to the Holy See—why would Zacharias, when barbarism had already spread everywhere, not have cited either this canon or some other one from the same source in the same case, especially since he was consulting the Dionysian Collection under the guidance of Cresconius?

The reason is plainly that, both in the very similar case of Contumeliosus and in this consultation, the Antiochene canons were irrelevant and suited only to the machinations of an impostor. His homeland and date must be sought in the provinces of Rheims and Mainz after the deposition of Louis the Pious; for several other bishops hostile to appeals will appear together with Hincmar.

But more about these matters elsewhere. Let Zacharias himself now be heard, proving one by one what has been said thus far.

## III. ANOTHER LETTER OF POPE ZACHARIAS SENT TO LORD PIPPIN

[Note: The pontiff was created in the year of salvation 741 and died in 752. — Grets.]

It is entitled under the name of the mayor of the palace because he had not yet been elevated to royal dignity. Together with its chapters, which had been submitted for consultation to the aforesaid Lord Pippin [Lamb., Gent.: “from the aforesaid Lord Pippin”] and to the priests in the regions of France concerning how an answer should be given, the aforesaid pontiff wrote it.

[Annals of the Lord’s Year 748, *Code of Canons*, vol. V, chronicle 3.]

### ARGUMENT

He replies point by point to the consultation of Prince Pippin and to the twenty-seven questions of the Franks, which revealed the ruined discipline of that Church and the ignorance of its bishops and clergy. He does so by a new example, using the canons of the Dionysian translation according to the *Breviary* of Cresconius, without entirely abandoning the ancient custom of the Holy See, which avoided collections of canons.

[Note: The date of this letter should be fixed, with Cointius, in the year 748, unless it was perhaps sent toward the end of 747. For Pagii’s contrary opinion—that it was sent in January 747—collapses because of the very inscription addressed to Pippin, in whose hands supreme power lay. For in that same year, 747, Caroloman had become a monk through Zacharias’s agency, as the Fulda Annals report. Baronius assigns it to the year 744 and there, at note 3, wrongly attacks Cointius. Mansius, from documents, conjectures that Caroloman departed from Francia after 6 June. — Cenn.]

To the most excellent and most Christian Lord Pippin, mayor of the palace, or to all our beloved bishops of the churches and religious abbots, and to all princes fearing the Lord established in the region of the Franks: Zacharias, bishop of the holy, catholic, and apostolic Roman Church of God, sends greeting in the Lord. May grace and peace be granted to you from God the almighty Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, his only Son, and from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: It appears in Baronius, vol. IX, under the year 744, and in *Centuries*, book VIII, chapter 10. — Id.]

We rejoice with great joy in the Lord, learning through the report of our most exalted and God-preserved son, the aforesaid Pippin, of the good conduct of all of you and of your unanimity and cooperation in arrangements that are good and pleasing to God. Thus [Lamb. adds *ut*: “so that”] you preserve, as is fitting, the Churches of God and the venerable places situated throughout your entire province, together with their bishops, priests, and religious abbots, in holy habit and priestly conduct [Lamb.: *conversetis*, “conduct yourselves”], while they devote themselves to prayers and persist in supplications to implore divine power and the victory to be granted from heaven to your defenders against pagan [Lamb., Gent.: feminine *paganas*] and unbelieving nations.

[Note: The Saxons are meant, repeatedly attacked in war; the pontiff knew this well from the letters of Saint Boniface (the *Boniface Codices*) and from Caroloman’s own spoken testimony. They were indeed pagans and unbelievers.]

For when you approach the Lord in true confession and with a simple heart, just as Moses, that friend of God, fought by praying (Exodus 17), and as Joshua son of Nun [Baronius and the *Centuries*: “and Jonathan”] conquered by fighting the Lord’s battles with the people of Israel, so you too ought to act, my dearest ones, so that you may assist your people by praying and by adhering to good works, turning away from worldly cares and business.

For it is written: “Be still and see, for the Lord is gracious” (Psalm 45). And again: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33).

It is fitting that princes, secular men, and warriors should take care and concern for resisting the cunning of enemies and defending the province. But it belongs to bishops, priests, and servants of God to devote themselves to salutary counsels and prayers, so that, while you pray and they fight, the province may remain safe by God’s favor and may become for you a source of salvation, praise, and everlasting reward.

By this, your episcopal office will appear in holiness, and the rule of our beloved son Pippin will be approved through the obedience of his subjects and good order [Gent. reads *approbabitur*, “will be approved,” for the text’s *approbabit*, “will approve”].

Accordingly, since our aforesaid son Pippin, after consultation with you, has asked us to give an answer concerning all the chapters of which he has informed us, we have written below, as far as we are able with the Lord’s assistance, what has been handed down by the holy Fathers and sanctioned by the authority of the sacred canons.

[Note: “Placed as watchmen by God, so that, demonstrating the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and sanction what must be observed,” said Celestine to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne (letter 11). So now Zacharias speaks to all the bishops of France. The supreme authority of Peter’s successors is prescribed by no collections of canons or decrees; although he uses them for the sake of brevity, he also appropriately adds from himself what France required at that time, as we shall see.]

We have also communicated in our responses what, under divine inspiration, we have been able to decree by apostolic authority.

### First Chapter

“How the metropolitan bishop ought to be honored by chorepiscopi and parochial priests.”

In the thirty-fifth chapter of the canon of the holy Apostles it is written:

> “The bishops of each nation ought to know who among them is accounted first, whom they should regard as head, and they should undertake nothing beyond his knowledge. He is to administer only the individual matters which belong to his own parish and the villages subject to it [Lamb. adds *sunt*, ‘are’]; Lamb. and Gent. instead read *quam illa sola singula* (‘while each is to administer only those individual matters’). Nor is he himself to do anything without the knowledge of all.” Thus there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, chapter 9 of the canon of the Council of Antioch contains the following:

> “In every region, the bishops ought to know that the metropolitan bishop has the care of the entire province. For this reason all who appear to have business converge from every direction upon the metropolis [Lamb., Gent.: *concurrere debent*, “ought to converge”]. Therefore it has seemed good that he should excel in honor, and that the other bishops should undertake nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, except only those matters belonging to their own diocese and to the estates subject to them.
>
> “Each bishop is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence due to each person and exercise oversight over every estate under his authority. He is also to ordain priests and deacons and to determine each matter by his own judgment. But he must not attempt anything further apart from the metropolitan bishop. Nor is the metropolitan to undertake anything without the counsel of the other priests.”

[Note: Gent. reads: “the aforesaid metropolitan bishop. Nor is the metropolitan to undertake anything”; and he notes that the word “anything” was inserted by another hand and in more recent ink.]

Likewise, in chapter 32 of the *Book of Decrees* of blessed Pope Leo it is contained:

> “Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the several provinces, whose care has been entrusted to your Fraternity by delegation from us, retain unimpaired the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they may depart from the rules established neither through negligence nor presumption, whether in habit or in the conduct of holiness.”

[Note: These words—“whether in habit or in the conduct of holiness”—are not read in Leo’s letter 84, chapter 2. In what he decrees shortly afterward, it should be noted that monasticism was still uniform in the eighth century and was distinguished from the clergy by its way of life (Holstenius, preface to the *Codex Regius*, chapter 3), although at the same time the order of Saint Benedict was being spread throughout the Frankish kingdom through the work of Saint Boniface. It should also be noted that parish priests established in the suburbs were called cardinal priests, formerly a common designation for bishops, priests, and deacons attached to a particular church. From this shared terminology some people, with insufficient knowledge, derive a similarity of office with the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church.]

We also add, by apostolic authority, that a bishop should use clothing suited to his dignity. Likewise, cardinal priests, and those [Lamb., Gent.: *et si*, “and if”] who wish to live according to the monastic life, should discharge the duty of preaching to the people subject to them, clothed in more distinguished garments, while preserving their inward purpose in the secrecy of their hearts, so that God, who sees in secret, may reward them openly.

For it is written: “Be contrite over what you say in your hearts, and upon your beds” (Psalm 4). Honor does not commend us through clothing, but through the splendor of our souls.

Monks, however, should wear woolen clothing continually, according to the norm and rule of monastic discipline and the tradition of the holy and approved Fathers. For if, having renounced the things of the world, they have devoted themselves wholly to God, they ought to abstain from all permitted things [Lamb., Gent.: “forbidden things”], so that, insofar as they have endured labor in their bodies, they may deserve to receive from God an equal reward.

A divine command was given to the Apostles: not to have two tunics (Matthew 10). Christ said “tunics,” plainly woolen ones, not linen. Therefore whoever obeys the Lord’s command and adheres to good works will possess eternal life.

Likewise, concerning those called chorepiscopi, the tenth chapter of the canon of the Council of Antioch decrees:

[Note: Thomassinus discusses the chorepiscopi at great length (*Benefices*, part I, book II, chapter 1). The pontiff’s response to this first chapter is especially appropriate: concerning the superiority of the metropolitan over the other bishops, he speaks on the authority of the canons and decrees, and he clarifies the duties of the chorepiscopi; thus he mocks the arrogance of the chorepiscopi. Since they were nothing more than rural vicars of the bishops, they nevertheless desired to be equal to them in dignity; hence they ask how they ought to honor metropolitans. In the course of time their insolence increased to such an extent that Leo III and Charles the Great found it necessary to abolish this order of the hierarchy in France. See *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 119; book VII, chapters 187, 325, 328. They had presumed to ordain even priests and deacons (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, pp. 1169 ff.). They are discussed again below, chapter 4.]

> “Those who in villages or estates are called chorepiscopi, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decreed that they recognize their proper limits and govern the churches subject to them, remaining content with their administration and care. They may also ordain readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, and these promotions are sufficient for them.
>
> “But they may not dare to ordain either a priest or a deacon apart from the bishop of the city, to whom they themselves, together with the estate, are subject. If anyone attempts to transgress these statutes, he shall be deposed and deprived of the honor he held. The chorepiscopus is to be ordained by the bishop of the city to whom he is subject.”

### Second Chapter

“Concerning condemned bishops, priests, and deacons, who ought not to usurp their former office.”

[Note: Saint Cyprian says that fallen bishops may indeed be admitted to penance, but must be prohibited from ordaining clergy and from priestly honor (letter 68). Saint Basil (canon 51): the canons issued a general rule ordering one punishment for those who have fallen, namely removal from ministry. Jerome (*Against Jovinian*, book I): one who fathers children while in the episcopate cannot be a bishop, and so forth. In addition, Siricius to Himerius, chapter 7; Saint Innocent to Victricius, chapter 9, to Exsuperius, chapter 1; and Leo the Great’s letter to Rusticus, chapter 2, would have supplied material more suited to the circumstances, if he had not preferred to proceed by this new route.]

From the twenty-ninth chapter of the *Book of Canons of the Holy Apostles* it is stated:

> “If any bishop or deacon who has been justly deposed for certain crimes dares to touch again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be utterly cut off from the Church.”

### Third Chapter

“Concerning presumptuous priests” [Grets.: *superbientibus*, “growing arrogant”], from chapter 11 of the Council of Carthage:

> “If any priest, puffed up against his bishop, creates a schism, let him be anathema.”

The bishops all said:

[Note: Lamb. has: “the anathema was pronounced.” After the words “the bishops all said,” Gentilotus states that the manuscript has in the margin, in perhaps the same or at least a very ancient hand: “let him be anathema.”]

> “If any priest has been corrected by his superior, he ought certainly to complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his own bishop. But if he does not do this and, puffed up with pride—which God forbid—withdraws from communion with his bishop, and, separating himself, offers sacrifice to God with some others [Lamb. adds: ‘creating a schism’], let him be regarded as anathema and lose his position. If he has a just complaint against the bishop, it must be investigated.”

### Fourth Chapter

“Concerning rural priests and the obedience they ought to show to bishops and cardinal priests,” from chapter 13 of the Council of Neocaesarea:

> “Priests in the countryside and in the church of the city, when the bishop or the city’s own priests are present, may not offer, give the sanctified bread, or present the chalice. If these men are absent and the priests are summoned to give the prayer, they alone shall be permitted to give it.
>
> “The chorepiscopi also seem to be [Lamb., Gent.: plural *videntur esse*, ‘seem to be’] according to the example and form of the seventy, so that, on account of the zeal they show toward the poor, they may be honored for what they have ministered.”

[Note: Lambecius reads: “but as fellow ministers,” as in the Dionysian version. Since Tengnagelius and Gentilotus make no alteration, this should be retained as it stands in the manuscript.]

### Fifth Chapter

“Concerning monks—that is, female servants of God—about whom it was asked whether they may publicly read lessons at the solemn celebrations of Mass or on Holy Saturday, and sing at Mass, or sing the Alleluia or the responsory.”

Concerning these matters, chapter 23 of the *Book of Decrees* of blessed Pope Gelasius has established:

[Note: The number is erroneous: in Dionysius, who included this single passage in his Collection, it is chapter 26. Coustantus referred to this (*Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 85), although he attributes the question to Boniface of Mainz. Certainly, by this authority of Zacharias, the decree attributed to Soter concerning monks—then an unfamiliar designation and likewise attributed to Boniface I, both in the *Liber Pontificalis*—is overturned. Zacharias says that he knows nothing more ancient than Laodicean Canon 44: “Women ought not to enter the altar.” See further in the cited work. The Frankish question, however, is one thing; the pontiff’s response is another.]

> “It is forbidden for women to minister at the sacred altars or to presume to undertake anything belonging to the offices assigned to men.”
>
> “Nevertheless, we have heard with indignation that divine matters have fallen into such contempt [Gent.: Tengnagelius corrected this by placing ‘such contempt of divine matters’ under erasure, leaving only ‘such contempt’] that women are said to minister at the sacred altars and to perform, despite their sex, everything assigned exclusively to the service of men [Lamb. adds: ‘is assigned’]. The guilt of all the offenses that we have individually touched upon, however, rests upon those priests who either commit such acts or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor their wicked excesses.”

### Sixth Chapter

“Concerning widows, whether they can save their souls in their own dwellings.”

Likewise, chapter 21 of the same book contains the following:

[Note: Here too the question and the answer differ. Nicholas I came closer to the point (*Response* 87 to the Bulgarians), saying that widows should not be compelled to enter a monastery. He continues: “It should be known that some virtues are such that without them we cannot enter into life, while others are required only of the one who makes the vow.”]

> “Widows are not to be forced” [Tengnagelius has this reading, supplying the words “by pontiffs,” which are absent from the manuscript. Lamb. reads: “not to be veiled, and . . .”; Gent.: “violently”] “by pontiffs; and if, after having professed continence, they trample it underfoot by changing their purpose, they themselves must render an account to God for their own actions.”
>
> “For concerning widows being veiled without any blessing, we have above undertaken to discuss the matter more fully. If they have of their own will professed the chastity of their first marriage and then trampled it underfoot with an unstable mind, it will be their concern by what satisfaction they ought to appease God. For just as, according to the Apostle, if she perhaps could not remain continent, she was not in any way forbidden to marry, so, once she had given God the pledge of chastity after deliberation [Lamb., Gent., Bar.: ‘having deliberated with herself’], she ought to have kept it. We, however, must impose no snare upon such women; we should merely set before them exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their own intention may render its account to God.”

### Seventh Chapter

“Concerning a layman who drives away his wife,” from chapter 48 of the canon of the holy Apostles:

[Note: There was also Agathenian Council Canon 25, which was especially relevant. There was furthermore Innocent’s letter to Exsuperius, which is also found in the Dionysian Collection and which, among other things, cites the Gospel words: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” Also African Canon 102, or Milevitan Council II, chapter 17, unless it was preferred to adhere to the Greek rules.]

> “If any layman, driving away his own wife, marries another, or one divorced by another, let him be deprived of communion.”

### Eighth Chapter

“Concerning priests and deacons who withdraw themselves from ecclesiastical ministry and hold assemblies separately,” promulgated from chapter 5 of the Council of Antioch:

> “If any priest or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, establishes an altar, and gathers people separately, and does not submit to the bishop who admonishes him, nor consent or obey him when summoned once and again, let him be condemned in every way and receive no further remedy, because he cannot recover his dignity [Lamb. and Gent. add: ‘his own’]. If he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him be suppressed by external authorities as a seditious person.”

### Ninth Chapter

“Concerning clerics and monks who do not remain in their chosen state,” as was asked, chapter 7 of the Council of Chalcedon decrees:

> “Those who have once been enrolled in the clergy, or have chosen the life of monks, we decree shall neither enter military service nor attain any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not repent, so as not to have to return [the printed wording is corrupt or at least syntactically uncertain] to what they first chose for God, shall be anathematized.”

[Lamb.: *cum manere debeant*, “when they ought to remain”; Tengnagelius corrects *commonere debeant* by reading *quominus redire* and supplies the omitted *ad id*.]

### Tenth Chapter

“Concerning clerics who are in ptochia [hospitals], monasteries, and martyria.”

[Note: Xenodochia, or hospitals, are institutions for poor and elderly people, such as the distinguished Hospital of Saint Michael at the Ripetta, built through the generosity of Innocent XII. The *Liber Pontificalis* also relates that Pelagius II converted his own house into a ptochium.]

From chapter 9 of the Council of Chalcedon [Lamb.: 8] it has been decreed as follows:

> “Clerics who are placed in charge of ptochia, or who are ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, shall remain under the authority of the bishops in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers. They shall not, through contumacy, withdraw from their own bishop.
>
> “Those who dare to overturn this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop shall be subject to the corrections of the canons if they are clerics; but if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.”

[Inherited source boundary: the supplied text ends here.]

## Chapter Eleven: That Clerics Also Ought to Abstain from Their Wives

This is contained in chapter 37 of the African Council:

> “Moreover, since continence was reported to be lacking in certain clerics, even in relation to their own wives, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should also abstain from their wives, in accordance with their own regulations; and that, unless they do so, they should be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the matter is to be observed according to the custom of each church.”

**Note:** In my admonition concerning this letter I said that this canon conflicts with the tradition and decrees of the Apostolic See. Consult that discussion (p. 39). To what I said about Gregory, add these few words of Saint Leo to Anastasius of Thessalonica (Epistle 84, chapter 4):

> “For the exhibition of perfect purity of continence, even marriage with women is not permitted to subdeacons, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none (1 Corinthians 7), and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried. But if this ought to be observed in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more ought it to be observed in the first, second, or third?”

## Chapter Twelve: Concerning Those Who Dismiss Their Wives or Husbands So That They May Remain in That State

This is contained in chapter 69 of the aforementioned African Council:

> “It was decided that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may join themselves to another; but they are to remain in that state, or be reconciled to one another. If they disregard this, they are to be reduced to penance.”

### 49. Chapter Thirteen

It was asked what should be done if a monk should become a cleric. The following is contained in chapter 17 of a decree of blessed Pope Innocent:

> “Concerning monks who remain for a long time in monasteries and afterward attain the clerical order: they must not depart from their original purpose. For either, as he was in the monastery and as he observed it for a long time, he ought not to lose what he has in a better rank; or, if he was corrupted [Lambinus and Gentianus: ‘corrected’], was afterward baptized, and, while dwelling in a monastery, wished to approach the clerical order, he can in no way have a wife, because, having already been corrupted, he cannot be blessed together with a bride. This same rule is observed with clerics, especially since the ancient rule requires that anyone who, after being corrupted, was baptized and wished to become a cleric should promise that he would never marry.”

**Note:** Siricius, in his letter to Himerius (chapter 13), had decreed that monks commended for the gravity of their conduct and for the holiness of their life and faith should be promoted to clerical offices. The question here is what should be done with them after such promotion. The answer would then be complete if the first chapter of Zosimus’s decrees had been added; there he establishes that monks may reach the episcopal summit through the grades of exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and presbyter (To Hesychius, chapter 1). From this Coustant derives a further argument against the constitution attributed to Silvester, by which the porter is hastily included among the grades.

## Chapter Fourteen: That Presbyters or Deacons Who Have Fallen into Some Crime Cannot Obtain the Remedy of Penance through the Imposition of Hands

In chapter 16 of a decree of blessed Pope Leo it is decreed as follows:

> “It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated to presbyteral honor or to the rank of deacon should receive, for some crime of theirs, the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands. This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: ‘If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?’ Therefore, for such fallen persons to obtain the mercy of God, a secret withdrawal is to be sought, where their satisfaction may be worthy and also fruitful.”

**Note:** In the same letter (chapter 14), Siricius had used the example of the entire clergy to remove laymen from clerical honor:

> “Just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever be permitted to attain clerical honor.”

Before Leo, the Fifth Council of Carthage had likewise established the same rule concerning presbyters and deacons in canon 11. Since this canon is absent from the African Code, Cresconius was unaware of it, although Zacharias uses him as his guide. For this discipline of the clergy, originally general, later restricted to deacons and presbyters alone, see Coustant (cited work, p. 636).

### 50. Chapter Fifteen

This chapter concerns the question of laymen who build churches on their own properties: who ought to govern or administer them?

> “It was established by the holy Fathers, and is contained in the apostolic precepts, as follows. In accordance with the petitioner’s request, if an oratory or basilica of whatever legal status has been constructed on any estate, through the devotion of its founder in honor of any saint, and if the oratory or basilica has been founded within the parish of a particular bishop, then, after a legitimate donation has first been received—that is, after such-and-such has been provided [Lambinus and Baronius: ‘with such-and-such having been provided’] and the municipal records have been produced—the aforesaid oratory is to be solemnly consecrated through public Masses. No baptistery is to be constructed in that place, even in future times, nor is a presbyter to be established there as its cardinal priest. But if the founder should wish Masses to be celebrated there, he must know that a presbyter is to be requested from the bishop, so that no other priest may in any way celebrate anything of this kind unless he has been appointed by the bishop.”

**Note:** This chapter departs from the Collection and follows the decrees of its predecessors. Saint Gregory the Great speaks clearly on this matter to Benenatus, bishop of Fundi (Book 7, Letter 85), to Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum (Book 8, Letter 63), and to Passivus, bishop of Firmum (Book 11, Letter 20). Holstenius produces two letters of Pelagius I, nearly fifty years earlier, from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit (Roman Collection, part 1, pp. 234 ff.), containing the same formulas. In Zacharias’s time, however, the Book of the Roman Pontiffs’ *Liber Diurnus* supplied the formula (Garnerius, chapter 5, title 3 and following); but the decrees of the holy Fathers cited here were not available from the *Liber Diurnus*. Several of them are found in Gratian (Distinction 1, “On Consecration”), although some spurious passages are mixed in with authentic ones, and learned readers can easily separate them.

Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, volume 2 (preliminary commentary, p. XIX), extracts five requirements altogether from Gregory’s letters:

1. No body should be buried there—a point Zacharias omits as irrelevant.
2. A sufficient endowment should be assigned.
3. No baptistery should be established there.
4. No presbyter should be incardinated there.
5. No public Masses should be celebrated there; instead, a presbyter should be requested from the bishop for the celebration of Mass.

The same requirements are listed here, except for the first.

## Chapter Sixteen: Concerning Clerics Who Abandon Their Own Churches, and What Should Be Done with Them

This is contained in chapter 15 of the canon of the holy Apostles:

> “If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the number of the clerics leaves his own parish and goes to another, and if a presbyter, entirely disregarding the knowledge of his bishop [Lambinus: ‘entirely disregarding it, except with…’], dwells in another parish, we do not permit him to minister thereafter, especially if, when summoned by his bishop, he refuses to return and persists in his restlessness. Nevertheless, he may communicate there as a layman.”

**Note:** The answer ought to have been sought at home. For their predecessors, together with other bishops, had decreed at the Council of Arles in 314 (canon 21):

> “Concerning presbyters or deacons who are accustomed to leave the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves to other places, it was decided that they should minister in the places to which they were assigned. If, however, after abandoning their own places, they wish to transfer themselves elsewhere, they are to be deposed.”

The Second Council of Arles decided likewise (canon 23). See also the Nicene canons 15 and 16, and the decree of Gelasius, chapter 23.

### 51. Chapter Seventeen

Likewise, concerning bishops who receive the clerics of another bishop, so that they may be excommunicated, chapter 16 of the same council contains the following:

> “If it is established that the bishop with whom the aforesaid person is staying treats the cessation decreed against them as worthless and perhaps receives them as clerics, let him, as a teacher of disorder, be deprived of communion.”

**Note:** The aforementioned Nicene canons and the decree of Gelasius (Epistle 9, chapter 23) also apply here.

## Chapter Eighteen: Which Clerics May Take Wives

Chapter 27 of the canons of the holy Apostles decrees:

> “But concerning the unmarried men who have been advanced to the clergy, we command that, if they wish, they may take wives; but only readers and singers…”

**Note:** This canon is contrary to the discipline of the Roman Church, both because it does not recognize singers among the grades of orders and because it was not unaware that the customs of the churches in the West varied with respect to the marriages of the minor clergy. In Gaul especially, the Council of Agde states (canon 39):

> “Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and those below them, who have no permission to marry, must also avoid banquets celebrating the marriages of others.”

See Thomassin (Book 1, part 2, chapter 62), who concludes from this that marriage was forbidden even to minor clerics after ordination. Moreover, the Council of Chalcedon (canon 14) did not establish a universal discipline, and, according to the Dionysian version, had psalmists rather than singers—a designation less suitable to the Roman Church:

> “Since in certain provinces permission has been granted for readers and psalmists to marry…”

## Chapter Nineteen: That No Presbyter or Deacon Be Received without Letters of Recommendation

The same canon of the holy Apostles [Lambinus adds: “chapter 34”] contains the following:

> “No foreign bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to be received without letters of recommendation. When they bring written documents, these are to be examined carefully, and they are to be received only if they have proved to be preachers of piety. If not, they are to be supplied with none of the necessities, and are in no way to be admitted to communion, because much wrongdoing arises from surreptitious entry.”

**Note:** Canons 41 and 42 of Laodicea and canon 7 of Antioch are too brief; for that reason canon 34 of the Apostles is inserted, although it is less suited to the question. Canon 13 of Chalcedon also embraces the entire clergy. A more suitable canon for the questions of the Franks was canon 52 of Agde:

> “Let no one extend communion to a presbyter, deacon, or cleric traveling without letters from his bishop.”

They were not asking about bishops, who could not leave their churches without a *formata* from their metropolitan:

> “Let no bishop sail without a *formata* from the primate” (African Code, canon 56).

They were asking about presbyters and deacons, who had to receive *formatae* from their own bishop (African canon 106), although the Council of Antioch (canon 8) also grants this faculty to chorepiscopi. In Gaul, by the privilege of Zosimus (Epistle 1, chapter 1), it belonged to the metropolitan of Arles to grant *formatae* to those departing “from any part of Gaul and in any ecclesiastical grade.”

In Zacharias’s time, however, the condition of the Gallican Church was almost nonexistent: its metropolises had fallen into disuse, and its entire discipline had been ruined.

### 52. Chapter Twenty: Concerning Veiled Virgins Who Go Astray, and What Should Be Done with Them

In the Book of the Decrees of blessed Pope Innocent, chapter 14 [Lambinus: 19], it is asserted:

> “Those who spiritually marry Christ and are veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly corrupt themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world. For if this rule is observed among human beings—namely, that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is regarded as an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance unless one of the two has died—how much more must it be observed in the case of a woman who had previously joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward passed over to a human marriage?”

**Note:** Saint Leo, in his letter to Rusticus (chapter 15), says:

> “There can be no doubt that a great crime has been committed where both a profession has been abandoned and a consecration violated. For if human agreements cannot be broken with impunity, what will await those who have violated the covenants of the divine sacrament?”

He offers no remedy, however, as Innocent does. See also Saint Basil, canon 18.

## Chapter Twenty-One: Likewise Concerning Unveiled Virgins Who Go Astray

The same matter is contained in chapter 20 of the same book:

> “Those who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed that they would remain in the virginal calling—if they should happen to marry, even though they have not been veiled, they must perform penance for some time, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if a good-faith contract among human beings is ordinarily dissolved for no reason whatsoever, how much more must this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle Paul said that women who departed from their commitment to widowhood incurred condemnation because they had repudiated their first faith, how much more so virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?”

> “Therefore, dearest brothers, if these matters are observed by all the priests of God with full vigilance, ambition will cease, iniquity will be trampled underfoot after being overcome, truth will blaze with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will of the heart. The Apostle’s command will be fulfilled, that we should remain of one mind and one judgment in Christ, claiming nothing for ourselves through contention or empty glory, but pleasing not human beings but our God and Savior.”

**Note:** Innocent, who was writing to Victricius, says, “Dearest brother”; but Zacharias, addressing several people and making Innocent’s words his own, says, “Dearest brothers.” It is worth noting that the Second Council of Tours, held in 567, expressed both chapters (canon 20) from the decision of Pope Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen. Gaul was unfamiliar with the Dionysian Collection and then adds:

> “Which priest would dare to act against decrees of this kind, which have proceeded from the Apostolic See?”

Thus they revered, as was right, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

## Chapter Twenty-Two: Concerning Those Who Have Married Two Brothers or Those Who Have Taken Two Sisters as Wives

The Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 2, contains the following:

> “If a woman has married two brothers, she is to be excluded until death. Nevertheless, at the end of her life, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, let her obtain the fruit of penance while she remains alive.”

**Note:** Baronius and Centuriator also have this reading; in the council itself it is: “Let her obtain the fruit of penance.” Lambinus reads, “Let her obtain it in life,” and adds: “But if the woman or the man should die in such marriages, penance will be difficult while life remains.”

But we, with divine grace assisting us, confirming the matter much more strongly in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors and antecedent pontiffs, say that, for as long as human generations recognize one another, they must not be joined in marriage according to the rite and norm of Christianity and the religion of the Romans. Nor may anyone, in reckless daring, take as his wife a spiritual mother—that is, a godmother—or a spiritual daughter, God forbid. For this is an impious and pernicious sin before God and his angels. It is so grave that none of the holy Fathers, nor any assertion of the sacred synods [Lambinus: “by any assertions…”], nor even any imperial law, records anyone as having been judged for it. Fearing the terrible judgment of God, they have kept silent rather than pronounce a sentence.

**Note:** In so important a matter he relies, apart from the Greek regulations, on the support of apostolic authority. He approves and explains the decrees of Gregory II and Gregory III. Gregory II, for a time and in order to remove fear—the matter concerned Germans who had recently been converted—addressed Boniface in a letter as follows:

> “We say that, indeed, they ought not to enter into such a union so long as they recognize themselves to be related by affinity. But because moderation is more pleasing, especially among so barbarous a people, than strict severity, it should be permitted that they join together after the fourth generation.”

Gregory III, by contrast, had decreed in his decretal letter to the same Boniface, chapter 5:

> “We have decreed that each person must observe his own lineage up to the seventh generation.”

Zacharias had confirmed this latter decree five years earlier in a Roman council, in the year 743. Regarding Gregory II’s letter, he says:

> “Nor must this be kept silent: it has long been widely reported in the regions of Germany that, although we have not found it written in the archive of our holy Church, we learned from people of the German regions themselves that blessed Pope Gregory, of good memory, when by divine grace he enlightened them unto the religion of Christianity, had granted them permission to join together in the fourth generation. Although, as has been said, we have not found this written, when they were still inexperienced and were being invited to the faith, we do not hesitate to believe it.”

Here he speaks with the greatest authority, confirming also the degrees of affinity and kinship that he himself had listed in the aforementioned council after Gregory III.

## Chapter Twenty-Three: Concerning Those Who Have Committed Homicide Voluntarily

This is contained in chapter 21 of the Council of Ancyra:

> “Those who have committed voluntary homicide must submit themselves to penance; but they are to attain perfection toward the end of their life.”

### 54. Chapter Twenty-Four

Likewise, concerning those who have committed homicide involuntarily, chapter 22 of the same canon [Baronius: 25] contains the following:

> “Concerning homicides committed involuntarily: the earlier decision ordered them to attain perfection after seven years of penance; the second requires them to complete a period of five years.”

## Chapter Twenty-Five: Concerning Those Who Have Adulterous Wives, or Who Are Proven to Be Adulterers Themselves

The Council of Ancyra, chapter 19, contains the following:

> “If a man’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain perfection through seven years of penance, according to the former grades.”

**Note:** In a nearly identical case, Innocent, responding to Exsuperius (chapter 4), had said that they should be deprived of communion:

> “When the crime of women has been exposed, communion is denied to them. But when the offense of men remains hidden, someone is not easily excluded on the basis of suspicions. He will certainly be removed if his disgrace is exposed. Since the case is therefore equal, sometimes, when proof is lacking, the administration of punishment comes to rest.”

If I am not mistaken, this too ought to be inserted here, unless the earlier discipline supplied by the Greek regulations—or rather, a discipline more suitable to the time—had been preferred.

## Chapter Twenty-Six: Concerning Monks and Virgins Who Do Not Preserve Their Chosen Calling

In the Book of the Decrees of blessed Pope Siricius, chapter 6, it is contained:

> “Moreover, you report that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their chosen sanctity, have sunk into such great wantonness that at first they secretly, or under the pretext of monasteries, joined themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious pollution; afterward, driven into the sheer abyss of despair in their conscience, they freely procreated children from their unlawful embraces. Both the public laws and ecclesiastical rights condemn this. We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of the elect [Lambinus: ‘of the churches’], so that, confined in prison-workhouses, they may, by continually lamenting so great a crime, be refined by the purifying fire of repentance, and so that, at least at death, mercy alone may regard them and indulgence may come to their aid through the grace of communion.”

**Note:** The response of Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, letter 14, undoubtedly bears more directly on the question of the Franks:

> “The monastic calling,” he says, “which someone has undertaken by his own judgment or will cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God, one must also repay. Therefore, whoever, having abandoned the profession of singleness, has fallen into military service or marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage may be honorable, nevertheless abandoning the choice of better things is a transgression.”

More recently, the Sixth Council of Toledo decided as follows (canon 6):

> “Whoever, whether man or woman, has once voluntarily assumed the religious habit, or if a man has been dedicated to the church choir, or a woman has been assigned to a monastery of maidens, must in either sex be compelled to return unwillingly to the chosen calling from which he or she has defected. The man is to be tonsured, and the girl is to be restored to the monastery. But if, by any protection, they wish to remain deserters, they are to be regarded by priestly judgment as exiles from the company of Christians, so that no common conversation may be held with them.”

One of these chapters, however, is absent from the Dionysian Collection followed by Zacharias.

### 55. Chapter Twenty-Seven: Concerning Women Who Have Undertaken the Vocation of Virginity Not under Compulsion but of Their Own Will, and Who Commit an Offense by Marrying Even Though They Have Not Yet Been Consecrated

This is contained in chapter 28 of the Decrees of blessed Pope Leo [Lambinus: 27]:

> “Girls who, compelled not by the authority of their parents but by their own spontaneous judgment, have undertaken the calling and habit of virginity, if afterward they choose marriage, are transgressors—even if the grace of consecration has not yet come to them, although they would certainly not have been deprived of that gift had they remained in their chosen calling.”

**Note:** I cited the other part of this chapter, which is Letter 15 to Rusticus, in note a, column 89. Here I shall add the first passage from the canons addressed to the Gauls, which Sirmond and Labbe attribute to Innocent, but which P. Coustant thinks should be attributed to Siricius. It is useful to seek outside the Collection material that bears strongly on the subject:

> “A girl who has not yet been veiled, but has proposed to remain so, although she is not veiled in Christ, nevertheless, because she proposed it and has not been veiled in marriage, is said to have contracted a clandestine marriage: because, with love hastening toward the blindness of lust, she has not observed the commandment of heavenly marriage.”

The passage above, chapter 21, also bears on this matter.

Therefore, dearest and most beloved brothers, we have commanded that the matters appended above—so far as, with God’s mercy, we have been able—be supplied and completed for the knowledge of your episcopate, for your preaching, and for the edification of the people entrusted to you by God. Among the other chapters, we have briefly touched upon and extracted the sanctions both of the holy Apostles and of the blessed Fathers, as well as the decrees of the already-mentioned and most approved blessed pontiffs, according to the meaning contained in each chapter.

We exhort your exceedingly prudent holiness and the guidance of your leaders to observe these apostolic commands with the greatest constancy, without turning aside from any moderation to the right or the left, but walking along the royal road. For we have given these instructions to you, dearest ones, so that neither we may be judged before God for our silence, nor you be compelled to render an account before him for your neglect, as it is written in the Lord’s command:

> “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15).

Therefore, offering no excuse, see to the salvation of all rational souls, running in the contest so that your ministry may not be reproached, but so that you may receive the prize of victory from the palm [Lambinus: “may receive”], according to the saying of the distinguished Apostle. By adhering to good works, may you have laid up for yourselves the crown of righteousness in the heavenly dwelling, which the just Judge, the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, will repay you on that day. He lives in unity with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# 57. Admonition on the Letters of Stephen II

When Zacharias died, on 24 March 752, two pontiffs were elected within twelve days, and both were named Stephen. The first, however, died after three days, before he had been consecrated, and is listed among the pontiffs neither by Anastasius the Librarian nor by any of the ancients. Panvinio, whom Cardinal Baronius follows, nevertheless includes him among the others. Hence Stephen II, also called III—our Stephen—is so designated, although scarcely even the name of that three-day elect has come down to us.

Stephen II therefore ascended the chair of Peter at a time when there were many reasons for seeking assistance according to the example of Gregory III, and when it was especially opportune to seek it from Francia, since this had been interrupted for so long. For Pippin, the son of Charles Martel, had no bond of friendship or alliance with Aistulf, king of the Lombards. He was, however, bound by very many benefits to the Holy See, especially because it was through the authority of that See that he, the first of the Carolingian line, had begun to reign in the preceding year.

Moreover, Caroloman, Pippin’s brother, having received the monastic habit at Rome through the hands of Saint Zacharias, withdrew to Cassinum, where, under the discipline of Abbot Optatus, he devoted himself to heavenly matters. To this was added the fervent zeal of Boniface of Mainz to establish and strengthen the discipline of the Apostolic See in Gaul and to consolidate religion in certain parts of the Frankish kingdom. Hence there arose at Rome a close relationship with the Franks and a substantial exchange of envoys and letters in both directions.

## II

Nevertheless, Stephen, who had been brought up in the Lateran patriarchium and knew everything thoroughly, had especially before his eyes the recent example of Zacharias. Aistulf was disturbing the beginning of Stephen’s pontificate and threatening slaughter and devastation. Stephen therefore mollified him with many gifts and, through his legates—Paul, his own brother, whom he later had as his successor in the pontificate, and Ambrose the *primicerius*—entered into a treaty of peace with him for forty years.

Four months later, when Aistulf had broken the treaty and imposed a very heavy tribute upon the inhabitants of the Roman province, which they call the capitation tax, Stephen undertook a new embassy to that king, scarcely unlike a tyrant, sending the venerable abbots Optatus of Cassinum and Atto of Saint Vincent at the Volturno, together with new and lavish gifts, in an attempt to curb his audacity.

When this did not succeed according to his wishes, it happened shortly afterward that the emperor of Constantinople, having sent John the Silentarius and requested the pope’s assistance, attempted through peaceful means to recover the exarchate and the Pentapolis from the hands of the Lombards. But that most savage king treated both the pope’s pleas and the emperor’s entirely just requests with contempt. Stephen then seized the opportunity and sent his own envoys, together with the Silentarius, to Constantinople.

They carried letters from the pope full of expressions of obedience. In them he both described the unresolved matter concerning the exarchate and humbly begged the emperor to come with an army to liberate Rome and all Italy. This was done at the beginning of the year 753, as ancient and modern writers consistently report.

A very weighty proof is supplied by the fact that the Roman pontiffs Zacharias and Stephen, instructed by the useless example of Gregory III, did not even think of requesting assistance from Francia. Although for twenty-five years they had been rulers of the Holy Roman commonwealth, and were regarded as the true princes of the Roman province by the Lombard kings themselves, they had not abandoned all hope of repentance on the part of the Greek emperors. They were ready to restore to them the commonwealth, preserved through so many troubles, provided only that they would bring aid to Rome and Italy, endangered by Aistulf’s recent efforts.

## III

But, as Providence willed, the impious Copronymus was so sluggish that neither Aistulf’s contempt, though he had been occupying the exarchate since 751—when he captured Ravenna and, after expelling Eutychius, the last of the exarchs, began to rule there—nor the pope’s services and pleas moved him.

When matters stood thus, what remained for Stephen except to implore divine clemency? He repeatedly did so by visiting the sacred temples barefoot, while the whole people went sprinkled with ashes. I therefore think that this was what brought it about, together with the sacred prince of the *Annals* (Baronius, 756, no. 7), that he obtained the support of King Pippin so promptly and firmly, through whom the Holy See received a great increase. For, following in the footsteps of his predecessor Gregory III, he turned to the Franks.

He adopted this plan at a particularly opportune time, both for the reasons already mentioned and because the piety of the new King Pippin toward God was supreme, as was his love for the prince of the Apostles, Peter. The *Book of the Pontiffs* reports that he sent a letter to the king by a certain pilgrim (section 253), although no one has ever seen it. The matter of these first letters is therefore very doubtful.

Certainly, not long afterward, Droctegang, the king’s envoy, arrived in Rome, and through him Stephen sent two letters to Francia (Caroline Code, letters 4 and 5, also numbered 10 and 11). From these it is clear that the pope had begun the undertaking successfully.

## IV

The beginning of so important a matter appears to have taken place orally. For Droctegang did not carry letters, but words of greeting; and the pope himself openly testifies that he acted in the same manner:

> “Through him, placing the response in the mouth of your most sublime goodness, we sent it back.”

In the second set of letters he begs the dukes of the Franks to be fellow workers and helpers in the cause of Saint Peter, earnestly commending perseverance both to the king and to the dukes.

This both confirms that the undertaking had begun and suggests that the pilgrim—whoever he may have been—was entrusted not with letters, as Anastasius believed, which would have been a dangerous plan, but with spoken words. Bishop Rodigang and Duke Autchar, the king’s other envoys, confirm this. They arrived shortly afterward to escort the pope to Francia. Yet the letters contain no indication of what took place, as reported by Anastasius, Paul the Deacon, and the celebrated *Annals*.

Whatever the case may be, all these events had occurred before the middle of October of the aforementioned year 753, which I have embraced in a very brief narrative. Thus, in a period of approximately nine months, the loyalty of Copronymus was tested to the limit; the undertaking was begun very successfully, both by letters and by the secret conversations of the envoys among Romans and Franks; and finally the pope set out so that, by his personal presence and without an interpreter, an affair of such importance might be completed.

We learn this abundantly not by conjecturing, or by bending a consulship into another consulship and that into a patriciate, but from the pope’s own letters preserved in the Caroline Code, which agree remarkably with the whole history. The two letters mentioned above—4 and 5, also numbered 10 and 11—are the beginning of this great undertaking; the remaining six constitute its completion.

## V

The order of these letters is so certain from the matters they contain that the carelessness of the person who corrupted it in the Code can easily be corrected. Accordingly, all enumerate them by common agreement in the sequence 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, also 7, 9, 4, 6, 3, 8.

There is likewise almost no disagreement about the time at which each was written, except concerning the last, which is the eleventh—or eighth in the Code. Baronius, Cointius, Pagius, and others assign it to the year 756, whereas Muratorius, followed by Mansi (notes to the year 756, no. 2), assign it to the year 757.

The former, gathering together many observations of more recent writers, and the latter, relying on the catalogue prefixed to the Farfa Chronicle and on two documents from the archive of Lucca, are both moved by the beginning of the king’s desire, which they establish, on the authority of those monuments, in the year 757 or in December of the preceding year. Stephen, they think, could not speak of Pippin’s election in that letter in the year 756.

It is of no concern to us to linger over such chronological subtleties, which accomplish nothing; for that reason we do not depart from the ancient chronology. What must be considered above all, however, is the history contained in those letters, since it overturns all the conjectures and arguments of more recent writers.

### VI

First of all, the headings of the letters must be considered. The first letter of Stephen begins: “To his most excellent son, King Pippin”; and in another, sent at the same time, namely in the year 753, Pippin is called “the most excellent king,” in a letter addressed to the dukes of the Franks. Why, then, fifteen years earlier, did Gregory III in his letters to Pippin’s father call Charles once and again “sub-king”? Why did Zachary address his letter in the year 747: “To the most excellent and most Christian Pippin, mayor of the palace”?

Louis II explains the cause of so great a change in his celebrated letter to Basil (Baronius, 871, nos. 54, 59), which has often been published:

> “The princes of the Franks were first called kings and afterward emperors—those, that is, who have been anointed for this purpose with holy oil by the Roman pontiff . . . . . From that holy see our family received the seed and source of its authority, first to rule and afterward to exercise imperial power.”

This is even more clearly shown by the manuscript of Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, at whose end a writer contemporary with the time of Pippin recorded the age of the codex. Mabillon valued this testimony so highly (*De re diplomatica*, p. 354, plate 22) that he included it among the ancient monuments. There one reads the following, relevant to our subject:

> “That aforesaid lord, the most flourishing King Pippin, the pious one, was elevated to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier [751] by the authority and command of the lord Pope Zachary, of holy memory, by the anointing of holy chrism through the hands of the priests of Gaul, and by the election of all the Franks.”

There are some who find little of apostolic authority in the deposition of Childeric III, the last Merovingian king—although indolent and useless—and in the elevation of the Carolingians; they argue about the legality of the matter by appeal to civil law. But whether they wish it or not, the ancients approved the event and committed its memory to the records of the annals, so that no oblivion might ever erase it. This is sufficient for explaining the new and previously unheard-of titles of Stephen II’s earlier letters.

### VII

All the remaining letters, both those of Stephen and those of his pontifical successors, add to the title of king another distinguished title, “patrician of the Romans.” Although recent scholars torment themselves uselessly over this title, it cannot be found in any papal letter before the end of the year 754, when that same pontiff had returned from Francia to Rome.

From that point onward, however, we see not only Pippin but also his sons Charles and Carloman continually called patricians in the headings of the letters. The reason is clear from the consistent testimony of ancient and modern writers (Baronius, 754, no. 2, and the same, no. 5 and following; 755, no. 3). For on the fifth day before the Kalends of Sextilis—that is, on 28 July of that year—Stephen II again anointed Pippin and his two sons as kings in the monastery of Saint-Denis, and also designated them patricians of the Romans.

Pippin and Carloman retained this dignity until the final day of their lives, for it was perpetual. Charles, however, who later began to be called “the Great,” after obtaining the higher dignity of Augustus at the end of the eighth century, did not abandon the earlier title of patrician, which by its nature was falling into disuse, except in name and not in reality. But since these matters exceed the limits of the *Carolingian Book*, they do not belong here.

So much concerning the dignity of patrician, which all the letters of the aforementioned *Book* display in their headings from the end of the year 754 onward. Now a matter of greater importance must be considered: namely, what took place between the pontiff and the kings, both in Francia and in Italy, up to the year 757, when Stephen died on 24 April. Without knowing these matters, the true meaning of the letters cannot be grasped.

### VIII

Although the pontiff had departed from Rome on 14 October of the year 753, he did not obtain permission from Aistulf before 15 November to continue his journey from Ticinum toward Francia. For Aistulf could be moved neither by the pontiff’s pleas nor by the skill and services of King Pippin’s envoys to purchase willingly the great disadvantage which he foresaw for himself. Indeed, after reluctantly allowing him to depart, he dared to pursue him with ambushes until he had crossed the borders of Italy.

Then, in order to frustrate all the pontiff’s plans, he ordered Optatus, abbot of Cassino, to prepare a delegation of monks to Pippin, whose leader was to be Carloman, the brother of the Frankish king. Through this delegation he hoped to turn the king’s ears and mind away from the pontiff.

What a crafty scheme! Optatus himself, shortly before having served as the pontiff’s envoy, had been harshly received by Aistulf and ordered to return to his monastery; he had not even been able to return to Rome as the bearer of an unsuccessful mission. Moreover, the recent restoration of the monastery of Cassino by Petronax, whom Optatus had succeeded, was still remembered.
