This recalled the former savagery of the Lombards, who had destroyed the monastery from its foundations so completely that only after 135 years did a few monks begin to inhabit it again.

What if the same people, under the command of their most audacious king, had seized the opportunity to renew its destruction? What more need be said? At the urging of the endangered monastery and of the abbot’s orders, Carloman hastened with his companions to his brother the king, exaggerated the dangers that threatened, and tried every means to separate him from friendship with the pontiff.

But he could not resist the divine will. The king was firmly and deliberately resolved to place the cause of Saint Peter above all else. Therefore, in order to protect the monks’ safety, he settled them by the pontiff’s authority in the monastery of Saint-Denis. From there Carloman departed to heaven in the following year; his companions did not return to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Cassino until the year 756, after Aistulf’s death, as is clear from Stephen’s last letter (*Carolingian Book* 11, formerly 8). Meanwhile, the principal matter which had brought the pontiff there was being discussed more freely.

### IX

At Ponthion, in the royal palace where the pontiff had first been received with the highest honor on 6 January 754, everything was investigated: both the matters whose narration had been entrusted to the envoys and those whose treatment the pontiff had reserved for himself.

Afterward, at Quierzy, an agreement was drawn up in a charter, to which not only Pippin but also his sons Charles and Carloman—already designated kings and patricians of the Romans—as well as the palace officials, subscribed. This is established by Anastasius, by the letters of the *Carolingian Book*, and by all the Frankish writers.

The matter concerned the donation to Saint Peter and his successors of the exarchate and the Pentapolis—provinces which Aistulf, three years earlier, had taken from the Greeks, or rather from the Roman pontiff, under whose protection they had placed themselves, out of hostility toward Greek impiety—and their recovery from Lombard control by force of arms.

As for Rome and its duchy, the pontiff was so far from treating with the king merely about their donation that he conceived a substantial hope of recovering, with the king’s help, the city of Narni, which had long before been invaded by the duke of Spoleto. For when the king first came into Italy with his army, that duke, terrified, restored the city he had invaded.

But when, not long afterward, as the Franks were withdrawing from Italy, the treaty-breaking Aistulf refused to hand over the exarchate and the Pentapolis, but also invaded territories belonging to papal rule, and even besieged Rome itself at the beginning of the year 755, Stephen, urging Pippin toward a new expedition, clearly and distinctly informed him both that the exarchate and Pentapolis had not been handed over at all and that cities belonging to the ancient papal dominion had been taken away (*Carolingian Book*, letters 8 and 9, formerly 4 and 6).

He conveyed the same message at the same time and in the same words to the Frankish nobles:

> “We have been able to obtain nothing corresponding to what he established and confirmed by the bond of an oath, especially since no enlargement has been made for us; rather, after the devastation of our entire province, etc.”

And below:

> “For they have also taken away the city of Narni, which your Christianity granted to blessed Peter, and have seized some of our cities.”

### X

I especially wish to note here those matters which, because Gretser omitted them in letter 8, formerly 4, are likewise missing in Muratori. Muratori, adding various readings from Lambecius’s edition in a work that was not his own and was rather inaccurate (*Italian Antiquities*, vol. III, part II), omitted not a few things worthy of notice; these will be indicated in their proper places.

In the following letter, however, neither Gretser nor Muratori omitted the matters I have just cited. What, then, can those few words mean—“no enlargement has been made for us”—after the account that Aistulf had handed over absolutely nothing of the exarchate and Pentapolis, and before the territory proper of the Roman See is mentioned?

Do they not agree with the universally known inscription at Ravenna:

> “The pious Pippin, first, opened the way for enlarging the Church”?

Do not those who deny that the Roman province—that is, Rome and its duchy—was under papal rule before Pippin’s donation depart far from the truth? Let them rather dispute whether the pontiff governed the state as its first citizen or as its prince; that is the only question that can be raised. But they dare uselessly to call into doubt matters brighter than daylight itself.

Indeed, if the perjured king had given nothing at all to blessed Peter, as we read in the aforesaid letters; if he “did not allow even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to be restored to blessed Peter and the holy Church of God, or to the Roman commonwealth,” as the pontiff complained in the two preceding letters (*Carolingian Book* 6 and 7, formerly 7 and 9), what, then, do those other words of the same pontiff mean (*Carolingian Book*, letter 7, formerly 9):

> “Plunderings and depredations, or devastations, in the cities and places of blessed Peter”?

And what do the other words we have just heard mean:

> “They have seized some of our cities”?

It would take too long to pursue here all the matters that claim a more suitable place in the notes. These few points, however, seemed worthy of being offered here as a preliminary indication, since they presuppose that possession of even a single palm’s breadth of land had already been established by the pontiff. They overturn the opinions of Cointius, Pagius, and other writers, both from Francia and from Italy, who derive the beginnings of papal rule from Pippin’s donation and—something wholly incredible—define the exarchate and Pentapolis as the territory of the holy See. Others assign the rule of Rome and the Roman duchy to different years, all to a distant period, and all falsely, thereby distorting its character.

### XI

When Saint Leo III, moved both by the example of his predecessors Paul I, Stephen III, and Hadrian—who, as will be clear below from the letters of this *Book*, had scarcely, or rather hardly at all, been able to restrain the audacity of the archbishops of Ravenna with the aid of the Frankish kings—and compelled also by the recklessness of certain Romans, changed Charles’s dignity of patrician into that of Augustus, and consequently delegated, or if you prefer, granted to him authority in Rome and throughout the ecclesiastical territory, the authors mentioned above, relying on ambiguous testimonies of the ancients and on their own commentaries, turn the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs into imperial authority, and imperial authority that had been delegated or granted—except for Pagius, who judges the matter correctly—into papal authority.

These matters, however, will have to be discussed in connection with the letters of Leo III, which will follow immediately after the letters of the *Carolingian Book*.

For now, I address those passages which place the supreme power of the holy See so clearly before our eyes that they defeat all the efforts of those writers. This is especially evident from the last letter of Stephen II (*Carolingian Book* 11, formerly 8), which alone remains to be examined; for what needed to be said in advance concerning the first six letters has already been stated. The letter written in the name of blessed Peter (*Carolingian Book* 10, formerly 3), in the year 755, expresses the same judgment as the two preceding letters of that year.

But in the final letter, sent in the following year, 756, and concerning the confirmation of Pippin’s earlier donation—which was defended with a new expedition—and the sharp rejection of the Greeks’ demands, as well as the formal establishment of possession of nearly all the cities of the exarchate and Pentapolis, the language is so lucid and precise that an attempt to oppose it could be called bold, or even shameless.

### XII

After Copronymus heard that the Lombards had been defeated by the Frankish king, and that all the cities and places which four years earlier had belonged to the Greeks and had been held by the exarchs, however uncertain the loyalty of the inhabitants, had been given by the victorious king to the Roman pontiff, Copronymus remained at Constantinople awaiting the outcome of the mission entrusted to George, the *protosēcretis*, and John the *Silentiary*. He had no army prepared, as was proper, but only envoys entrusted with so great a matter. He was bolder than his father in impiety and, above all, utterly sluggish in the necessary use of arms.

The envoys first came to Rome, where they heard from the pontiff about Pippin’s new expedition. The pontiff allowed them to depart for the king, accompanied by an apostolic envoy. They reached Marseille by sea with great speed and learned that the Frankish army already held Lombardy.

Not knowing what course to take, they attempted to detain the apostolic envoy there, but this did not succeed according to their wish; for he was determined to continue where he had begun to go. One of them, taking the opportunity, went ahead of him and caught up with Pippin near Ticinum. He approached him with pleas and promises of gifts:

> “that he should grant Ravenna, or the other cities and fortresses of the same exarchate, to imperial rule.”

The king’s answer destroyed every hope. Above all, he affirmed under oath:

> “that he had repeatedly entered the struggle through no man’s favor, except for love of blessed Peter and the forgiveness of sins,”

and he asserted also:

> “that no abundance of treasure could persuade him to take away what he had once offered to blessed Peter.”

The whole matter is narrated more fully by Anastasius, who cannot be regarded as a more trustworthy witness in this affair. He wrote what the pontiff himself had learned by questioning the king, and what had doubtless been committed to writing.

### XIII

Indeed, not many days afterward, when the Frankish king had heard the Greek emperor’s envoy, he defeated Aistulf a second time and forced him, shut up within the walls of Ticinum, to send envoys. With them his counselor, Abbot Fulrad, undertook possession of the individual cities on behalf of the holy See. This took place in the final months of the year 755, perhaps even at the beginning of the following year; for the pontiff did not thank Pippin for the work completed by Fulrad until the year 756 was somewhat advanced (*Carolingian Book*, letter 11, formerly 8). He added that the new Lombard king, Desiderius, had promised to return certain cities whose possession it had not been possible to enter under Aistulf.

On the same occasion he writes concerning the other imperial envoy:

> “As for how you spoke with the *Silentiary*, or how your Goodness released him, together with a copy of the letter which you gave him, inform us, so that we may know how to act in common agreement, as was established between us and Fulrad, beloved of God.”

From this it is clear that the pontiff was at that time unaware of the king’s conversation with the envoy, of the permission granted to the latter to depart, and of the answer given to him for transmission to Copronymus; none of these matters is even found in Anastasius.

The matter is different concerning Fulrad’s taking possession of the cities included in Pippin’s donation. For it is not the donation itself, as is falsely believed, that Anastasius narrates; he merely lists the cities whose keys and hostages came to Rome. Concerning the complete donation, with the subscriptions of King Pippin and his sons, he says:

> “This document is preserved to this day in the archive of our holy church.”

Since knowledge of all these matters is necessary for grasping the meaning of this letter, I shall reproduce here Anastasius’s passage from the celebrated Farnese codex, written at approximately the same period and accurately described by the illustrious Blanchini, with the form of the script itself preserved (Anastasius, vol. II, p. LVII). In the *Life of Stephen II*, therefore, sections 252 and following, the following matters are narrated with great care:

### XIV

> “And, after again confirming the inner agreement that had arisen between the parties during the past eighth indiction, he restored the aforesaid cities themselves, adding also the fortress called Comiaclum. Of all these cities that had been received, he issued in writing a donation to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church, and to all the pontiffs of the apostolic See in perpetuity, to be possessed; it is preserved to this day in the archive of our holy church.
>
> “To receive these cities, that most Christian king of the Franks sent his counselor, namely the venerable abbot and presbyter Fulrad, and released him. Immediately his Excellency returned happily to Francia with his armies.
>
> “The aforesaid venerable abbot and presbyter Fulrad, joining the territories of Ravenna to the envoys of the aforementioned King Aistulf, and entering each of the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia, received them and took hostages from each one. He brought them with him to Rome, together with the principal men and the keys of the city gates.
>
> “He placed the keys of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the donation concerning them issued by their king, at the confession of blessed Peter. He handed them over to that apostle of God, to his most holy vicar the pope, and to all his successor pontiffs, to be possessed and administered forever:
>
> “namely Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Conca, Fano, Cesena, Sinigaglia, Jesi, Forlì, Forum Olivi, with the fortress of Sussubium, Montefeltro, Acerra, Montelucati, Serra, the Castle of San Marino, Vobio, Urbino, Gallis, Luciolis, Gubbio, and Comiaclum; and also the city of Narni, which for a succession of years had been seized from the Romans by the duchy of Spoleto.”

### XV

From this we see that among the cities of Emilia, or of the exarchate, Faenza, Imola, Ferrara, Bologna, Gabellum, and Adria are absent. Among those of the Pentapolis are Ancona, Osimo, Numana, Fossombrone, and the territory of Valva. We therefore understand that the complete donation of Pippin is not described by this author.

This is all the more evident because in the letter of Stephen II under discussion, after the death of Aistulf, who had violated part of the agreements, and concerning his successor Desiderius, then friendly to the Romans, Stephen says:

> “He promised that he would restore to blessed Peter the remaining cities: Faenza, Imola, and Ferrara with their territories; likewise Saltora and all the territories; and also the cities of Osimo, Ancona, and Humana with their territories. Later, through Duke Garinus and Grimoald, he promised that the city of Bologna with its boundaries would be restored to us.”

The letters of Stephen’s successors will teach us that Desiderius did not keep his promises, and that the Roman pontiffs did not possess the entire exarchate and Pentapolis until the time of Charles the Great, who restored both his father’s donation and his own.

Meanwhile, we can see with what accuracy Anastasius lists the cities whose secure possession began in the year 756, or even in the following year, as some assert on the authority of the *Annals of Fulda*. This difference of one year does not alter the substance of the matter.

The substance is plainly this: the holy See should, through Pippin’s action, possess in their entirety “the remaining cities, which were joined and constituted under the authority of a single dominion, their boundaries, territories, and also places and woodland-pastures”—places whose possession Fulrad had by no means entered. Thus the entire exarchate and the Pentapolis, which the Lombards had subjected to their power five years earlier and which had long since come under a single protection, should be subjected [to the holy See]. This is what Stephen requests in his final letter.

### XVI

I pass over many matters contained in Stephen’s letters, especially the last ones, since they will have to be treated in the notes, as they do not concern the territory of the holy See or the papal principate, which alone I have set before myself in these preliminary discussions concerning each pontiff’s letters.

But I cannot and must not pass over the fact that neither in Anastasius nor in any of Stephen’s letters is anything found to have been given by the Frankish king beyond the exarchate and Pentapolis. Nevertheless, a second expedition seems to have been undertaken to vindicate Rome and its duchy for the holy See, since Rome was surrounded by a siege and the unrestrained Lombard people were ravaging far and wide throughout the Roman province.

At that time the Lombards, terrified—for they could not even defend their own kingdom against the very powerful Frankish arms—ceased harassing the Roman province and promised under oath to restore what they had acquired by war against the Greeks. The duke of Spoleto, also rightly fearing for himself, voluntarily returned to the Romans Narni, which he had seized.

This is why in these letters we frequently hear that Pippin redeemed the Roman province, but nowhere do we find that it was donated or restored to blessed Peter and his successors. Nevertheless, after Paul was elevated to the supreme pontificate following the death of his brother Stephen in the year 757, King Pippin immediately reminded the Romans to remain faithful to their own prince. This is attested by “the entire senate and the whole general body of the people of the Roman city preserved by God,” in these clear words (*Carolingian Book*, letter 15, formerly 36):

> “In your honey-sweet writings, your Excellency has taken care, through your saving foresight, to admonish us that we ought to remain steadfast and faithful toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the holy Church of God, and toward your most blessed and fellow-angelic spiritual father, appointed by God, our lord Paul, supreme pontiff and universal pope.”

Accordingly, the same Romans profess:

> “We, most excellent of kings, remain steadfast and faithful servants of the holy Church of God and of the aforesaid most blessed—thrice blessed—and fellow-angelic spiritual Father, your lord, our lord Paul, supreme pontiff and universal pope.”

Therefore the pontiff had been, and then was, the ruler of Rome and its duchy.

### XVII

If another argument of far greater force is desired, it must be sought in Stephen’s fifth letter (*Carolingian Book* 8, formerly 4), sent to the king and all the Franks at the time when the city was under siege, in the year 755, when “no enlargement had been made” and not “a space of one palm’s breadth” had been added to the ancient territory.

There the “senate and general body of the people” are defined in these terms:

> “Pope Stephen, and all the bishops, priests, deacons, or dukes, chartularies, counts, tribunes, and the whole people and army of the Romans.”

Only those who resent papal rule in Rome and its duchy can fail to understand that these palace offices designate a principate.

But enough concerning Stephen’s letters. I shall preface those addressed to Paul, which are much more numerous and closely connected with these, after the reading of Stephen’s letters and the notes attached to them has revealed more than what I have mentioned here. I am convinced that the opinions—or rather, the hallucinations—of those who derive the rule of Rome and its duchy from the Frankish kings will be completely rejected.

From this follow the questions concerning the nature of papal rule: whether, while the Church possessed only a useful dominion, supreme right remained with the Augusti; and whether kings or Augusti granted Rome to blessed Peter and his successors. Books from beyond the Alps are full of these matters, which have no foundation, with a recent Italian writer of the annals supporting them.

But truth, simple and single, has never been subject to the opinions of men, even of those distinguished by every kind of learning.

### IV

**Note:** Neither Baronius nor the Centuriators knew this letter and the following one, dated in the year 753, or letter 7 of the *Carolingian Book*, dated at the end of the year 754. Pagius is correct concerning their date (753, no. 3; 755, no. 1). CENN.

## Another Letter of the Same Pope, Sent Through Abbot Droctegangus

In it are contained expressions of thanks and exceedingly abundant blessings.

*(A.D. 753, Carolingian Book X, chronology 4.)*

### Argument

He courteously replies to the secret embassy of Pippin, king of the Franks by apostolic authority. Through Abbot Droctegangus, who carried oral messages back and forth, he secretly discusses the king’s undertaking of the defense of the Church and the pontiff’s future journey to Francia. He desires that the king’s reply likewise be sent secretly.

**To the most excellent lord, his son, King Pippin,**

**Note:** After the Merovingians had been rejected because of their negligence, Pippin was designated by apostolic authority as the first Carolingian king by Saint Zachary in the year 751 (Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 354, plate 22). In the following year he was anointed by Saint Boniface (*Annals of Fulda*, 751). Pagius discusses this matter at length, examining other opinions from no. 1 onward, and agrees with Baronius that the embassy of the nobles of Francia, who wished to be released from their oath by religious sanction, cannot be removed from the year 751.

Although, therefore, according to various opinions he was inaugurated in March or May of the following year, after Zachary had already died—as the authors cited by Pagius maintain (752, no. 1 and following)—the authority of the holy See, resting on the letters of Louis II and on the authority of all the annals, must nevertheless be referred back to the year 751.

Stephen, pope.

The present Abbot Droctegangus, having been presented at the sacred thresholds of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and before our sight, conveyed to your Excellence, preserved and most dearly loved by God, the words of greeting and good health entrusted to him [or something similar]. We have joyfully offered innumerable thanks to almighty God, and, although sinners and unworthy, have asked his divine mercy that, in accordance with his goodness, he protect you, most excellent son, and that he confirm your kingdom far more fully and perfectly in his fear and in apostolic love, so that you may enjoy the present life happily for a long time and may deserve to become a participant in eternal blessedness, as the fruit of apostolic love.

**Note:** Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXII, no. 70) thinks that this Droctegangus, the king’s envoy or legate, was abbot of Jumièges, not of Gorze, as Cointius held. He too relates the history: namely, that the pontiff sent a trustworthy man in the clothing of a pilgrim to indicate to the king, either by letter or by an oral message, the pontiff’s desire to go to Francia in order to confer with him about the needs of the Church. Immediately afterward, in remembrance of the recent favor, the king sent Abbot Droctegangus, and not long afterward Bishop Rodigangus of Metz and Duke Autcharius, to accompany the pontiff on his journey there.

The letter was sent and the secret plans were entrusted before the arrival of the bishop of Metz and his companion. The fact that Pippin sent other envoys without waiting for these men is proved by the pontiff’s departure from Rome on 14 October (Anastasius, *Life of Stephen II*). For in that same year, before the pontiff turned toward the Frankish king, he had first sought aid at Constantinople; then he had sent Abbot Optatus of Cassino and Atto of Volturno as envoys to Aistulf (*Chronicle of Volturno*, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. I, part II). Only when hope had failed him both of a sounder judgment on one side and of aid on the other did he flee there, as the whole history bears witness.

For the present Droctegangus, your faithful envoy, according to what he said to us, we have sent back a reply appropriate to your most exalted goodness, placing it in his mouth; and order that he be believed in everything, because in all that you commanded, with Christ’s cooperation, we have given you salutary instructions. But fulfill the Lord’s saying, as it is written:

> “For the one who perseveres to the end [Gent. adds: here] will be saved.”

**Note:** From this the secret plans are evident, which are explained more clearly in the following letter. The discussion concerned the defense of the Church against the Lombards.

For from this you will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. We ask this of you, son: when you order your envoys to be sent back to us, command that this religious man John be sent with them and with their reply. He is your faithful servant and brings back answers prudently.

Farewell.

## V

### Another General Letter of the Same Pope

In it are contained expressions of thanks and exceedingly abundant blessings.

*(A.D. 753, Carolingian Book XI, chronology 5.)*

### Argument

On the same occasion he urges the dukes of the Franks to undertake, together with the king, the cause of Saint Peter, in accordance with what had been arranged through Droctegangus. He promises heavenly reward through the patronage of Peter himself, prince of the apostles, if they persevere to the end in the fear of God and in love of Peter, by whom they were wonderfully moved together with the king. He declares that Peter, by the power granted to him by God, wipes away sins here and opens the door of the heavenly kingdom.

**Note:** Garnerius, in the appendix to the *Book of the Diurnal*, places certain prefatory cautions before the inscription of the papal letters, of which the fifth expresses the opinion of those who believe that pontiffs placed their own name after that of the persons to whom they wrote when those persons were superior, but before it when they were inferior. He argues that this is false, producing examples from the fifth through the ninth century. This example, however, is decisive. CENN.

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our glorious men and sons, all the dukes of the nation of the Franks.

The holy mother Church rejoices gladly in the advancement of her faithful sons. Therefore, although absent in body but present in spirit, we embrace your glorious prudence and love, most exalted sons, as though we were physically present, and greet you in the Lord with the kiss of peace, saying:

> “Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart” (Psalm 124).

Because we are confident that you fear God and love your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and that with the full devotion of your minds you will cooperate with and assist our entreaty for the accomplishment of his benefit, know for certain that, through the struggle which you undertake for his holy Church, your spiritual mother, your sins will be forgiven by that same prince of the apostles, and that, in return for the course of your labor, you will receive a hundredfold from the hand of God and possess eternal life.

**Note:** The promise of the same eternal reward and the accompanying prayers were appropriate for the Frankish dukes. For Einhard, in the *Life of Charles* (chapter 6), speaks as follows concerning Pippin’s Italian expedition:

> “This war was undertaken only after great difficulty, when his father, Pope Stephen, had first begged for it; for certain of the Frankish nobles, with whom he was accustomed to consult, resisted his will so strongly that they openly declared that they would abandon their king and return home. Nevertheless, the war against King Aistulf was undertaken and completed very quickly.”

Therefore we beseech and adjure your most wise charity, by God, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the future day of judgment, on which we shall all render an account for our deeds before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, that no opportunity be allowed to intervene and that you not fail to assist our son, Pippin, preserved by God and most excellent king, in accomplishing the benefit of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, just as we have sent word through the present Droctegangus, religious abbot, and his companions.

**Note:** The leader of envoys or messengers was sometimes accustomed to be named, as we shall see done below; but that companions also came with Droctegangus is clear from the preceding letter, since the pontiff asked that John be sent with the reply.

Thus, when you join your efforts with ours and our prayer has been fulfilled, the same prince of the apostles, whose cause is at issue, will grant that your sins be wiped away; and, possessing the power granted to him by God, as the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, he will open the door for you and lead you into eternal life.

But pay attention, sons, and work with the greatest diligence to share in what we have desired, knowing that whoever turns aside in another direction will be excluded from the inheritance of eternal blessedness. For it is written:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10);

and:

> “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8).

Farewell.

## VI

### Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord Pippin the King, and [or] to Charles and Carloman

For the defense of the holy Church of God, because Aistulf had made void the pact which he had made with them and had not kept his oath, as he had promised the same kings, etc.

*(A.D. 754, Carolingian Book VII, chronology 6.)*

### Argument

After his return from Francia, he sorrowfully announces to Pippin and his three royal sons that what he had predicted has occurred: Aistulf, forgetful of the oath which Pippin had compelled him to swear at Ticinum, has treated the donation made by them as worthless. He asks them to vindicate that grant with the utmost determination, just as through the miracle of Saint Peter, their protector, they had won a notable victory over the Lombards. None of their ancestors had received the honor of kingship, the defense of the holy See, or the dignity of patrician. Fulrad and his companions will tell them what hardships the holy See was enduring.

To the most excellent lords, sons, King Pippin and our spiritual godfather, [Col. 0103C] and likewise Kings Charles and Carloman, and both patricians of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0103C] A summary of all that had been done in Francia, and of which I touched upon the substance in the admonition, is reported by the annalist of Fulda under the year 753; indeed, he also reports what was accomplished in the following year. For he says: “Pope Stephen of Rome, seeking assistance against Haistulf, king of the Lombards, came to Pippin in Francia; received by him with honor, at Paris he anointed his two sons, Carloman and Charles, as kings.” This anointing, however, certainly did not take place before 28 July 754, as the annalists and other authors cited by Pagius (no. 9) attest. Before this anointing, Stephen had received both sons of Pippin from the sacred font, as the same Pagius teaches (755, no. 2); for that reason he calls Pippin their godfather both in this letter and in those that follow. Moreover, he had appointed both father and sons patricians, or defenders, of the Roman Church, as all the letters of this Codex testify; Frankish authors of that age exaggerate only their royal dignity. Eginhard, *Life of Charles*, chapter 3: “Pippin, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, was made king from prefect of the palace.” The Frankish Annals, in Canisius’s edition revised by Basnage, volume II, part II, page 49: “In 754 the apostolic Stephen confirmed Pippin as king by holy anointing, and with him joined his two sons, Lord Charles and Carloman, as kings.” Hilduin, *Areopagitica*, [Col. 0104C] in Baronius (754, no. 3ff.), and Pagius there with his authorities. And the monk of Angoulême appears ignorant of such a very certain patriciate when he says: “Then they chose that lord Charles as patrician of the Romans. Then they raised him up as emperor.” Hence it is clear that later writers beat the air when they heap together such great and incredible claims about this patriciate: [Col. 0104D] it was nothing other than the defense of the Roman Church, which we see expressed most clearly in these letters and in the account of Charles’s division of the kingdoms among his sons, which Louis the Pious copied. The very comparison used by the writer of Adrian’s *Life* in Anastasius, when Charles was received at Rome—“As is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician”—I say, this very comparison of the king with a patrician makes clear that royal dignity among the Franks is being considered, not the patriciate, which it was not the pontiff’s or the Romans’ prerogative to confer, but the emperor’s. CENN.], Pope Stephen.

Since the name of your kingdom has shone most brightly among the other nations in sincere faith toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you must earnestly strive that, precisely in the matter by which all Christians declare you more glorious than the other nations in the service of blessed Peter, you may please the almighty Lord, who grants salvation to kings, more perfectly in defense of his holy Church, so that you may have as your helper in all things the faith which you cultivate toward that same prince of the apostles.

Indeed, most excellent sons, we had wished to prolong our address further, but because our heart is wholly [Lamb., “excessively”] crushed by grief and our spirit is wearied on account of the many tribulations inflicted upon us by the wicked Haistulf, king of the Lombards, we have therefore turned away from the prolixity of many speeches and have endeavored to make known to your most excellent Christianity the one thing that is necessary: that you, protected by God [Lamb., protector], our spiritual godfather, and you, sweetest sons, for the reward of your souls, should act as follows.

Inasmuch as our merciful and very compassionate God has deigned to grant you victories from heaven [Lamb. adds *est* (“has”)], [Col. 0104B] you have striven, as far as you could, to exact the justice of blessed Peter, and your goodness confirmed by a deed of donation that it was to be restored [Note: [Col. 0104D] The principal act accomplished in Francia was the donation of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis by a charter of Pippin, to which his sons subscribed, confirmed at the royal estate of Carisiacum, today Quierzy. To make it effective, the king undertook an Italian expedition against the Lombards; yet, when the pontiff returned to Rome and they to Francia, everything that had been negotiated and done vanished. ID.].

Now, just as we first declared to your Christianity the wickedness of that impious king, behold, his lie and evil perversity, and his perjury, have already been exposed. For the ancient enemy of the human race, the devil, invaded his treacherous heart, and he appeared to attempt to invalidate what had been affirmed under the bond of an oath. He did not allow even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to be returned to blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, or the Roman commonwealth. From that day on which we were separated from one another, he tried to afflict us and to hold the holy Church of God in great disgrace to an extent that human tongues cannot describe; indeed, even the stones themselves, if one may say so, would weep over our tribulation with a great wailing. He appeared to afflict us so severely that our infirmity seemed to have been renewed in us once again.

For I grieve exceedingly, most excellent sons, that, refusing to hear the words of our misfortune, you chose to believe the lie rather than the truth, mocking and deriding yourselves. Thus we returned without having obtained the justice of blessed Peter to our own fold and to the people entrusted to us. [Col. 0105A]

Finally, all Christians firmly believed that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, had now received his justice through your most powerful arm, when he displayed so great and radiant a miracle in your fortunate times, and when the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0105C] See Baronius, year 755, no. 24ff.] deigned, through the intercessions of his prince of the apostles, to grant you such an immense victory for the defense of his holy Church [Note: [Col. 0105C] In the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar, in Pagius (754, no. 8), we read: “When the Franks saw this, they did not think that they could free themselves by their own assistance or strength, but invoked God and sought the help of the blessed apostle Peter.” Thus, in the first notable victory they won over the Lombards, they learned to place the fear of God and love of the prince of the apostles, which the pontiff impressed upon the king and commanders, above human strength. The author of Stephen’s *Life* in Anastasius is another witness to the same matter, as are the aforementioned Frankish Annals in Canisius: “They entered battle, and with the Lord’s help and the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, King Pippin emerged victorious with the Franks.” A cause begun under such favorable auspices greatly increased the Franks’ love for the prince of the apostles, so that Pippin placed gifts, treasures, and all earthly things behind the cause of blessed Peter. As for Charles, his son, Eginhard relates in the *Life of Charles*, chapter 27, that “through him the Church of the holy apostle Peter was not only safe and defended, but also adorned and enriched with his resources above all churches.”]. Yet, as good sons, believing that same wicked king concerning what he had promised under the bond of an oath, you confirmed by your own will, through a deed of donation, that the cities and places were to be restored to blessed Peter, the holy Church of God, and the commonwealth. But he, forgetting the Christian faith and God, who ordained that he be born, appeared to invalidate [Col. 0105B] what had been confirmed by an oath [ausus est: “he dared to”].

Therefore [his] iniquity has descended upon his own head (Psalm 7); for the snare which he dug has been exposed, and in it, because of his command [Lamb., lie] and perjury, he has fallen.

I adjure you, most excellent sons protected by God, by the Lord our God, and by his holy, glorious, ever-virgin mother Mary, our Lady, and by all the powers of heaven, and by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who anointed you as kings [Note: [Col. 0105D] P. Coustant rightly observes in his preface, no. 14, why pontiffs of old were called Peter’s vicars: “It is proper and peculiar to the Roman pontiffs to be called vicars of blessed Peter, whose see and authority they inherit. Hence it has become customary for them to attribute to this apostle the exercise of the powers entrusted to them, namely judgments, the granting of privileges, and so forth.” He confirms this with the examples he cites. Stephen intended this when he attributed to Peter what he himself had done. CENN.], so that you may grieve on behalf of the holy Church of God and strive to restore and hand over to the holy Church of God everything which you ordered to be offered to that same protector of yours, our lord blessed Peter, in accordance with the donation [Note: [Col. 0105D] See this donation in Baronius, the place cited, nos. 26 and 27. ID.]. Do not now believe either the judgment of that most wicked king or his deceptive [*seductuosa*; *seductoria*, “deceptive”] words and commands of mockery [Col. 0105C] [Lamb., “lies”]. For behold, his lie has been exposed, so that he can no longer possess any power to be believed. Rather, once you have recognized his wicked character and wicked will, let his snares be frustrated [Lamb., let them defraud], and hasten to restore and hand over to blessed Peter what you once promised him and confirmed by your donation, signed with your hand [vestra], for the reward of your soul.

In the end, the blessed apostle Paul says: “It is better not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfill” [Note: [Col. 0106C] This saying belongs to Ecclesiastes, chapter 5. Why, then, is it attributed to Saint Paul? Because the pontiff considered the sense. There is, however, a corresponding passage in 1 Timothy 5, where widows who have broken their first faith are said to incur condemnation. ID.]. For we have entrusted all the causes of the holy Church of God to your protection, and you will render an account to God and blessed Peter on the day of the terrifying judgment of how you have contended for the cause of that same prince of the apostles and for the restoration of his cities and places [Note: [Col. 0106C] Nothing occurs more frequently in these letters and in other monuments of that age than *restore* and *return* when the Exarchate and the Pentapolis are under discussion, although neither of these provinces had obeyed the holy see. Consider that this was done for two reasons: first, because the Lombards had invaded them and they needed to be restored; second, because Pippin had donated them to blessed Peter, and therefore they had to be returned to him, just as, for example, letters are commonly said to be returned to the person for whom they were written, although he has not yet received them. ID.].

This good work has finally been reserved for you, after many ages have passed, so that through you the Church may be exalted and the prince of the apostles may receive his justice. None of your ancestors deserved such a radiant gift; rather, God chose and foreknew you before eternal times, as it is written: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans 8:19). You have been called: strive with the utmost haste to do justice to that prince of the apostles himself, because it is written: “Faith is justified by works” (James 2:24) [Note: [Col. 0106D] There it is said that faith without works is dead, and much is set forth concerning justification by works. ID.].

As for all our tribulations, which we have endured and which we are again suffering, with God’s help your son and counselor Fulradus, together with his companions [Note: [Col. 0106D] Just as Stephen had used Bishop Rodigang of Metz and Duke Autchar as companions on the royal mission when he set out for Francia toward the end of 753, so in the following year he returned from Ticinum to Rome accompanied by Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Quentin and his companions. The Fulda Annals and the manuscript Codex of Anastasius belonging to the Queen of Sweden name among the companions Jerome, Pippin’s brother. Concerning him Mabillon writes (*Annals of the Benedictines*, book XXI, no. 61): “Besides Carloman and Pippin, whom Charles had by Rotrude, and Grifo, whom he had by the wife Sonechilde, he also had sons Bernard, Jerome, and Remigius, whom most consider born of an illegitimate union.” Georgius proves that Fulrad was Jerome’s son from Theodulf of Orléans, book II, chapter 7 (*Notes on Baronius*, volume XII, page 598). These men are carrying letters to Pippin and reporting what they saw with their own eyes.], will recount them to you [Lamb., let them recount them]. Act concerning the cause of blessed Peter in such a way that, both in this life, with the Lord’s favor, you may be victorious, and in the future, through the intercession of that prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, you may possess eternal joys. Farewell, most excellent sons.

## VII. Another copy of the letter of the same pope to Lord Pippin, Charles, and Carloman the Beloved [Al., “the Direct”]

In it is contained the account that Haistulf [Lamb., Haistulphus] had invalidated the pact and oath which he had promised these same kings, with repeated adjurations, concerning the justice of Saint Peter, while again requesting that he obtain assistance against that same king.

*(A.D. 754, Codex Carolinus IX, chronicle 7.)*

[Col. 0107A]

### Argument

Shortly after the preceding letter, Haistulf’s audacity grew beyond all bounds. Therefore, in a letter sent in much the same sense by Bishop Wilharius to the same three kings and the patricians of the Romans, he begs Pippin to return to Italy to complete the work. He declares that he undertook the arduous journey to Francia for Peter’s cause; that the treacherous Aistulf, in addition to laying waste to the entire ecclesiastical domain, had sacrilegiously plotted against the pontiff himself; and that it was in their interest to vindicate the donation confirmed by their own hand.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] This is the first of this pontiff’s letters known to the Magdeburg Centuriators and Cardinal Baronius. It does not, however, belong to the year 755, under which Baronius recites it (no. 2), but, with Cointius and Pagius, must be assigned to the close of the preceding year: its content is the same as that of the preceding letter, and it was sent shortly after the departure of the envoys, when Lombard savagery made itself manifest. [Col. 0108D]]

To the most excellent lords, sons King Pippin and our spiritual godfather, and likewise Kings Charles and Carloman, and both patricians of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

The prophetic assertion of the prudent and most wise Solomon is reported as follows: “A good name is above mercy.” A good name, indeed, is to preserve and fulfill by one’s deeds, with an unblemished heart and pure conscience, the faith that one has promised. A good name is to contend with all one’s strength for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, through which the salvation of Christians also exists.

A good name among all nations went forth concerning you, if it had been fulfilled by deeds. For our merciful and greatly compassionate Redeemer and Lord is propitious to those whom he finds wholly faithful, with complete integrity of mind, and defenders of the holy Church. What reward or recompense under heaven can be considered or compared with that [*eam*; Gent., *ea*] which must be paid for the defense of God’s Church and the house of blessed Peter? For this reason that same King of kings and Lord of lords established your most excellent goodness, protected by God, as safe rulers over peoples and many nations: so that through you the holy Church of God might be exalted. He could have vindicated his holy Church and exacted the justice of his prince of the apostles in another way, had it pleased him; but because he wished to test your mind and conscience—truly from God [Lamb., “protected by God”]—spiritual godfather and sweetest sons, he ordered our misfortune to come to you. We entrusted our body and soul to great labors on a journey through such a broad [Id., “through so broad a”] and distant province, placing great confidence in your faith. By God’s command we set out there, afflicted by snow and cold, heat and flooding waters, mighty rivers, most rugged mountains, and various dangers [Note: [Col. 0108D] In the *Life of Stephen* by Anastasius he is said to have been afflicted by a serious illness and healed by a miracle. Baronius, drawing from the *Areopagitica* of Hilduin, cites the pontiff’s charter as a witness to his miracle (754, no. 3). The annalists are silent about the matter. Pagius follows Baronius (the same year, no. 5).].

[Col. 0108A] Indeed, when we were brought before your honey-sweet presence, we entrusted all the causes of the prince of the apostles to your hands, because, inspired by God, you deigned to lend an ear to our petitions. You promised blessed Peter that you would exact his justice and provide for the defense of the holy Church of God, and, as truly faithful men of God, you hastened with pure minds to fight for the defense of God’s Church.

But the almighty Lord, who crushes wars from the beginning, humbles the proud, and exalts the humble, immediately demonstrated blessed Peter’s justice to your goodness and to all Christians, and displayed such a radiant miracle as is altogether glorious to report. Those enemies of God and the holy Church who trusted in their ferocity, whose feet were swift to shed blood, attacked your small number of troops; and through the hand of blessed Peter the almighty Lord deigned to grant you such a victory that those who were innumerable were slain by a few men, and those enemies of blessed Peter were humbled to the ground. The Lord so instilled fear and trembling in them through the intercessions of blessed Peter that they came to nothing.

For it is not a human sword but the sword of God that fights. When the wicked King Haistulf saw his deception, he and his judges, destroyed by God [Lamb., *a Deo*, “by God”], mocked your prudence with flattering speeches, persuasions, and oaths, and you believed those who spoke falsehoods rather than us who asserted the truth.

Our heart has been filled with great pain and sadness, most excellent sons. Why did your goodness not wish to listen to us [Lamb., Gent., “refused”]? We truthfully declared everything to you by God’s command, and now the facts themselves have exposed it. For, just as we first declared to your Christianity, the wicked King Haistulf, after the devil entered his treacherous heart, invalidated everything he had promised under oath to restore to blessed Peter through our envoys, and he did not wish to return even a space of one palm’s breadth of land to blessed Peter.

From the day on which we were separated from your honey-sweet goodness, he appeared [Lamb., “tried”] to afflict and trouble us to an extent that no human mouth can recount. He appeared to hold the holy Church of God, our humility, and your envoys in great contempt, because his evil command and submission were even directed toward taking away our own life. Why say more? He troubled us so greatly that, if it may be said, even the stones themselves would weep for us. Yet your counselor, the presbyter and abbot Fulradus, together with his companions, can recount everything to you, if they have God before their eyes.

For he not only refused to return blessed Peter’s property as he had agreed, but also by his command he neither ceased nor ceases to commit *scameras* [Baronius and Lamb., *scamaras*], plunderings, and devastations in the cities and places of blessed Peter [Col. 0109A] [Note: [Col. 0109D] If *scamarae*, or plunderings—which is the same thing according to Du Cange—were being carried out in the cities and places of Saint Peter before the holy see received even a palm’s breadth of land from Pippin’s donation, is it not foolish to seek the donor of Rome and its duchy?]. For he has forgotten God, who made him, and has transgressed the Christian faith. How can either he or those who consented with him, who bound themselves by such great sacramental mysteries of God and refused to observe them, be trusted any longer? Truly, we foretold everything to you concerning the lie and falsehood of that impious king; and, as we said, these things are manifest to you [Lamb., Gent., “have been made manifest”], and his perjury has been exposed.

Therefore I ask and earnestly beseech you, most excellent sons protected by God, that you grieve on behalf of the holy Church of God and the cause of blessed Peter, and that what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by your donation you should hand over to him for his possession [Col. 0109B]. Remember, and always hold firmly in your hearts, what you promised to that same gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven. Let no persuasion or acceptance deceive you now. Consider how powerful an exactor that same prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, is. See everything that you promised him and pledged to offer by your donation, and hasten to hand it over, so that you may not mourn forever and remain condemned in the life to come.

For the life of this world is brief; it declines like a shadow and grows old like a garment. Seek with your whole mind and an undivided heart that eternal life which blessed Peter promised you for his cause and justice. Complete the good work that you began, and hasten to return to your protector, blessed Peter, what you confirmed by your own hand through the donation, because it is written: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill the vow” (Ecclesiastes 5).

Know, then, that, like a written bond, the prince of the apostles firmly holds your donation, and you must fulfill that written bond [Note: [Col. 0109D] No stronger or more illustrious testimony to the donation made in 754, confirmed by the hand of Pippin and his sons and brought to Rome by the pontiff himself, can be desired.], lest, when the just Judge comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, that same prince of the apostles should display that written bond at the future judgment, showing that it possesses no validity, and you should have to render a strict account with him. Rather, quickly fulfill what you promised, so that you may again possess the eternal life which you have received as promised by that prince of the apostles.

I adjure you, most excellent sons protected by God, by almighty God, who contains all things by his power, and by his holy mother, the glorious ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, and by the powers of heaven, and by the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and by the terrifying day of judgment, when we shall all stand compelled to render an account of our deeds, [Col. 0110A] when there is no clever excuse: quickly and without any hindrance return to blessed Peter the cities and places, and all the hostages and captives, which you promised him by your donation, or everything contained in that donation. For the Lord anointed you as kings through my humility and by the mediation of blessed Peter so that through you his holy Church might be exalted and the prince of the apostles might receive his justice.

We had a great desire in our heart to look upon your honey-sweet faces and rejoice in the joy of your happiness, in accordance with what the most wise Solomon says: “Through the streets and squares I sought him whom my soul loved” (Song of Songs 3). Certainly, those whom we loved, by God’s command, we found, and those whom we desired, we embraced. For this reason the blessing and grace of blessed Peter have been poured out upon you, as the Lord had arranged.

What none of your ancestors deserved to receive, you have received; and the prince of the apostles, making you his particular ones above other kings and nations, entrusted all his causes to you. You will render an account to God of how you have contended for the justice of that gatekeeper of the kingdom of kingdoms [Lamb., Gent., “of heaven”].

For all our people of the Roman commonwealth are suffering with us in great pain and with the bitterest tears, because, when we hastened to such a long and extensive province, our flesh was diminished by the exhaustion of the arduous journey. Thus we returned empty and fruitless, without accomplishing the justice. Yet we wretched men acted according to the Lord’s command and entrusted all the causes of blessed Peter to you, and this belongs to you, whether for sin or for reward.

Indeed, all nations firmly held that blessed Peter would now have received his justice through your most powerful arm, but it did not happen, and everyone was struck by great astonishment of heart over this.

But I ask your most excellent goodness to remove this reproach by your actions and to show your faith to all through your deeds, since, as it is written, faith without works is idle. With what confidence or strength can you go forth to defeat your enemies if you do not complete the justice of blessed Peter, as you promised and began [Col. 0110D]? For if you fulfill by your deeds what you began, you will always be victorious and most powerful over your enemies, you will possess the present kingdom with a good reputation for many years, and you will receive eternal life.

For so great a work [Note: [Col. 0110D] Lamb. and Gent.: “Yet in the work”; Teng corrected it to “For so great a work.”] we have sent to you the most reverend and holy brother, your fellow bishop [Col. 0111A] [Gent. adds: “our”] and faithful Wilharius [Note: [Col. 0110D] Bishop of Nomentum, who had followed Stephen to Francia with George, bishop of Ostia, the cardinal priests and deacons, and other companions (Anastasius, *Life of Stephen II*, section 241). At that time Nomentum was an episcopal city, although it was not as prominent as it had been in the Roman Republic. It is now a small town commonly called Mentana.], so that he may recount to you with his own mouth everything concerning our tribulation and the cause of blessed Peter. You must believe him in all things [Lamb., “be pleased to believe”] and bring the cause of blessed Peter to a good conclusion. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed. Farewell.

## VIII. Another letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin, Charles or Carloman, or to the entire community

A letter composed in the name of the same pope and sent through Bishop George, Abbot Warneharius, and [Al., “or”] Count Thomaricus, his envoys, concerning the desolation and devastation of the holy Church of God and the city of Rome, urgently requesting, with repeated adjurations, assistance against the Lombards.

*(A.D. 755, Codex Carolinus IV, chronicle 8.)*

[Col. 0111B]

### Argument

When affairs had been reduced almost to the last extremity, and the City had already endured the siege for fifty-five days, the pontiff, the sacred college, the dukes, counts, leading men, and all the Romans send letters full of sorrow to the dukes, counts, and leading men of Francia. They entrust several matters to be reported in person by the apostolic envoys Bishop George, Count Thomaricus, and Comita, who are sailing to Francia with Warneharius, the royal envoy.

They enumerate, in a most pitiable manner, the stations of the Lombards and Beneventans near the besieged city, their plundering, sacrilege, slaughter of monks, violation of holy virgins, and other atrocities. They report that Narnia, recently restored to the holy see by Pippin, had again been taken from it; the insults of the besiegers toward the Romans, who relied upon Frankish aid; and that Warneharius, armed day and night, had guarded the walls on every side. They earnestly beg to be rescued as quickly as possible from such oppression.

[Col. 0111C] [Note: [Col. 0111D] This is extant in Baronius, volume IX, under 755, and in the eighth century, chapter 10.]

To the most excellent lords Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, the three kings and our patricians of the Romans [Baronius: “the Roman patricians”]; and likewise to all the bishops, abbots, priests, and monks; and to the glorious dukes, counts, and the entire army of the kingdom and province of the Franks: Pope Stephen, and all the bishops, priests, deacons, dukes, charter officials (*chartularii*), counts, tribunes, and the entire people and army of the Romans, all placed in affliction [Note: [Col. 0111D] A new indication of ecclesiastical sovereignty: for Rome had dukes and counts just as Francia did. This and the sixth letter declare themselves to have been sent on the fifty-fifth day after the beginning of the siege of the City, that is, on 24 February 755. Baronius, followed by Muratori, changes the Kalends of January to those of June, contrary to the evidence of the codex; and Pagius, unless a mistake has entered the text, reverses their order, assigning to the fourth what belongs to the sixth. Pagius’s critic, Mansi, places the siege in the following year, for a reason more plausible than certain.].

How much mournful and most bitter sadness surrounds us, how much anxiety and anguish constrains us, and how many tears our streaming eyes pour forth as continuous evils increase, we believe that the very forms of all the elements [Baronius and Gent., “fragments”] declare. [Col. 0111D] For who, seeing these tribulations, would not grieve? Who, hearing these calamities that cling to us, would not howl? Therefore we speak the words of a certain good woman, the chaste Susanna: “Distress is upon us from every side, and we do not know what to do” (Daniel 13).

O most Christian men, behold, days of distress have come upon us; days of weeping and bitterness are at hand, because what we feared from the Lombards has happened. Therefore, distressed, afflicted, and surrounded on every side by their most wicked King Haistulf and his people, we beseech the Lord with the Prophet, saying: “Help us, O God our Savior, and for the honor of your name deliver us,” and so forth (Psalm 78). And again: “Take hold of arms and shield, and rise up to help us” (Psalm 34).

For behold, you know how the treaties of peace have been shattered by the aforementioned impious King Haistulf and his entire people, and how we have been unable to obtain anything according to what he established and confirmed by the bond of an oath. And now [Note: [Col. 0112D] Lamb. and Gent.: “to obtain anything, and now, because no increase has been made for us, and now …”] on the very Kalends of January his entire Lombard army gathered from the regions of Tuscia [Col. 0112B] into this Roman city and took up position near the gate of blessed Peter, the gate of blessed Pancratius, and the Porta Portuensis. Haistulf himself, with other armies, joined them from the opposite side and pitched his tents near the Salarian Gate and the other gates. He repeatedly sent word to us:

“Open the Salarian Gate for me, and I shall enter the city. Hand over your pontiff to me, and I will spare you. If not, I shall overturn the walls and kill you all with a single sword, and I shall see who can rescue you from my hands.”

But all the Beneventans likewise came together in general to this Roman city and took up position near the gate of blessed John, the gate of blessed Paul the apostle, and the other gates of this Roman city. They consumed with sword and fire all the estates outside the city, far and wide; burning all the houses, they destroyed them almost to their foundations; they set fire to 86 churches of God; and throwing the most sacred images of the saints into the fire, they destroyed them with their swords. They placed the sacred gifts—that is, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ—in their polluted vessels, which they call bellows, and, filled with an abundance of meat, they ate those same gifts. Removing the altar coverings of the churches of God and all their ornaments—something so cruel that it can scarcely even be called by its name—they used them for their own purposes. They beat the servants of God, the monks who remained in monasteries for the sake of divine worship, with terrible blows, and tore many of them to pieces. They dragged away and violated with great cruelty the holy women and recluses who, from childhood and the time of puberty, had devoted themselves to seclusion for the love of God.

[Note: Whoever has read this far clearly understands that the Lombards of that age were by no means unlike their forefathers in the age of Saint Gregory. The recent writer therefore lies in holding such holy views of those sacrilegious men because one of them—as was doubtless King Liutprand—showed himself more than once affected by some religious feeling.]

And, even in the midst of that violation, they appeared to kill some of them. They burned with fire all the cultivated estates of blessed Peter, and, as has been said, burning the houses of all the Romans, they utterly destroyed those outside the city. They carried off all the livestock, cut down the vineyards almost to their roots, and, trampling down the crops, entirely consumed them. Neither the household of our holy Church nor anyone dwelling in this Roman city retained any hope of living, because, as has been said, they consumed everything with sword and fire and killed many people. They also slaughtered the numerous household of blessed Peter and of all the Romans, both men and women, and led many others away captive.

Indeed, those impious Lombards separated innocent infants from their mothers’ breasts, polluted the mothers by force, and killed them. They committed such evils in this Roman province as, assuredly, not even pagan peoples had ever perpetrated. For even the stones themselves, if it may be said, seeing our desolation, howl together with us.

For fifty-five days they besieged this afflicted Roman city and surrounded it on every side. Day and night, with the most savage fury, they ceaselessly waged the fiercest battles against us at the walls of this Roman city, employing various engines and countless devices, so that—may the Divinity avert it—after subjecting it to his power, that same enemy Haistulf might kill everyone with a single sword. Thus, reproaching us with great fury, they declared: “Behold, you are surrounded by us. Let the Franks come now and rescue you from our hands.” They also seized the city of Narni, which you had granted to blessed Peter, and captured some of our cities. Therefore, under constraint, we were scarcely able, by the sea route, to send these present letters and a messenger to your Christianity; and we wrote them with great tears.

[Note: From this it is clear that the letters were sent during the siege. Pagius therefore has no grounds for accusing Anastasius of contradicting Stephen’s letters when he records that the siege lasted three months (A.D. 755, no. 4). The following two letters, especially the one written in the name of Peter himself, confirm the matter more and more; consult them.]

Therefore, beloved ones, I ask you—and, as though present in person, I adjure you before the living and true God and before blessed Peter, his chief of the apostles—to come to our aid with the utmost haste, lest we perish.

[Note: The following words occur in the manuscript: “When, after the Lord, we have entrusted the souls of all us Romans into your hands.” GENT.]

Do not abandon us; then may the Lord not abandon you in all your actions. Do not despise us; then may the Lord not despise you who invoke his power. Do not withdraw your assistance from us, most Christian men; then may the Lord not withdraw his assistance from you when you enter battle against your enemies. Help us with great speed, our beloved ones; come, come, and help us before the sword of our enemies reaches our heart.

[Col. 0113D] I ask you, lest we perish. Let not the nations throughout the entire world ever say: “Where is the confidence of the Romans, which, after the Lord, they placed in kings and in the people of the Franks?” Do not allow us to perish, and do not delay in giving us aid; do not separate us from your assistance. Do not become strangers to the kingdom of God, lest the Lord harden his ear against hearing your prayers and turn his face away from you on that future day of judgment, when he will sit with blessed Peter and his other apostles to judge every human rank, every human power, and the world through fire. And may it be said to you—may the Divinity avert it—“I do not know you” (Matthew 25), because you did not assist the Church of God and took no care to defend its endangered special people.

Hear us, beloved ones, hear us and help us. Behold, the time for saving us is here. Save us before we perish, most Christian men. For all the nations situated round about, which have made refuge with your most powerful Frankish people through the power of God, have been saved; and if you do not delay in extending assistance to all, you ought all the more to free the holy Church of God and its people from the attack of their enemies.

Consider, beloved ones, and ponder this most earnestly—I adjure you by the living God—for after God and his chief of the apostles, the souls of all us Romans depend upon you. And if, God forbid, it should happen that we perish, consider whose soul the guilt will touch. Indeed, believe this absolutely, most Christian men: if some disaster should befall us—may it not happen—you will have to render an account before the tribunal of God for all that has endangered us. Rather, beloved ones, act and rescue those who have taken refuge in you after God, so that, bringing forth good fruit, you may deserve to say on the day of future judgment:

“Our lord, chief of the apostles, blessed Peter, behold, we, your little clients, having finished our course and kept the faith, have rescued and defended from the hands of our persecutors the Church of God entrusted to you by heavenly clemency. Standing before you undefiled, we offer you the children whom you entrusted to us, rescued from the hands of the enemies, safe and unharmed.”

Then, both in the present life and in the future age, may you deserve to attain the joys of heavenly rewards, hearing that desirable paternal voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

For this reason we have sent our messenger, the most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop George, as well as Warneharius,

[Note: Mabillon calls him Warnerius (Annals 23, no. 14). He knows nothing else about him beyond what he learned from these letters and from Anastasius, who likewise reports that he received the name Warnerius; for so it appears in the printed editions, although manuscript codices read Warnarius and Unarius. If he had violated the law of nations, it would not have been left unmentioned in our age.]

a religious abbot and your messenger, and Thomaricus the count

[Lamb., Gent.: “and Comita.”]

our distinguished messengers, who must recount to you in a careful narrative, with their living voices, all our sufferings and every desolation that we have endured and continually endure at the hands of the Lombard people and their insolent king—things which they saw with their own eyes. You must order that they be believed in everything as though they were ourselves, and must arrange our liberation with the utmost haste. And I adjure you by the living God never again to disbelieve our afflictions or neglect to deliver us. For, God forbid, if you delay any longer to believe and neglect to rescue us, the calamity of perishing may fall upon us—may the Divinity avert it—and this will bring you great loss, sin, and condemnation in the present and eternal life, because we have entrusted to you the souls of all our Romans. Rather, as has been said, we adjure you more and more, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity, to order that our tribulations, distresses, pains, and desolations be believed without any doubt, and to command that, for God’s sake, assistance be brought to us and that you hasten exceedingly to free us from the hands of the Lombards, our enemies, so that, bringing forth abundant fruit, you may deserve, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to enjoy eternal life.

The aforesaid Warneharius, out of love for blessed Peter, putting on his cuirass, kept watch day and night along the walls of this afflicted Roman city and, for the defense and liberation of all us Romans, fought with all his strength as a good athlete of Christ.

Farewell.

## IX. The Ninth Letter of Pope Stephen to Lord King Pippin

Specifically and individually sent for the defense of the holy Church of God, as stated in the preceding letter of the same pope, desiring to obtain assistance against the Lombards; likewise sent through George and Warneharius.

[Annals of the Lord 755, Codex Carolinus VI, chronicle 9.]

### Argument

In almost the same words, the pontiff sends Pippin letters composed and written with bloody tears through the same messengers. He prays to be saved from the present calamity, lest some greater one overtake them, for which God would demand an account. He praises Warneharius’s steadfastness and immense courage in the defense of the City. He endeavors to move him by the lure of eternal reward.

[Note: On the occasion of this most unhappy crisis he sent another letter to Pippin alone through the same envoys. Baronius and the Magdeburg Centuriators seem not to have known it, unless its great similarity led them to disregard it. The Italian annalist (Italian Historical Matters, vol. III, part II, p. 73) omitted whatever he found similar and published the rest.]

To the most excellent lord and son, and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Stephen.

How great a mournful and most bitter sadness surrounds us, how great an anxiety and distress constrains us, and how many tears our streaming eyes pour forth amid ever-increasing and unceasing evils—we believe that even the very parts of all the elements [or: fragments] could relate. Who, witnessing these tribulations, would not mourn? Who, hearing of these calamities clinging to us, would not howl? Therefore we speak the words of the chaste Susanna, that good woman: “Distresses hem us in on every side, and we do not know what to do” (Daniel 13).

O excellent and most Christian sons, would that the omnipotent Lord, creator of all things, just as in former times he sent the prophet Habakkuk, carried by an angel in sudden flight, to refresh and console the foremost prophet Daniel, hidden in the lions’ den, had likewise now—if it may be said—made your excellence, preserved by God’s most merciful patience, present for even a single hour to behold the grievous and mournful distress and tribulations that we suffer so terribly from the Lombard people and their impious king.

Behold, days of distress have come upon us; days of weeping and bitterness, days of anxiety and painful groaning, are at hand, because what we feared has happened and what we dreaded has occurred. Therefore, distressed, afflicted, oppressed, and surrounded on every side by their most wicked king Haistulf and by those Lombards, with abundant tears and striking our breasts, we beseech the Lord with the prophet and say: “Help us, God our Savior, and for the honor of your name deliver us” (Psalm 78). And again: “Take up arms and shield, and rise to our help, O Lord; judge those who harm us and defeat those who attack us” (Psalm 34).

Indeed, although we seem often to have made our tribulations known to your goodness, we have nevertheless now decided, compelled by great danger, to report with mourning and groaning the perils of the evils that we have suffered and continue to suffer from that same insolent king and his Lombard people.

[Lamb., Gent.: “we have resolved.”]

Now, most Christian and excellent son and spiritual co-father, we believe that everything is known to your nobility: how the treaties of peace were shattered by the impious king Haistulf and his people, and how we were able to obtain nothing in accordance with what he had established and confirmed by the bond of an oath, especially since no increase was made to us.

[Note: If no increase was made to us, then temporal rule did not begin with Pippin. Note also that these few words, “especially since no increase was made to us,” are omitted in Letter 4, elsewhere numbered 8, in Gretser’s edition, although they are read in the manuscript. The Italian annalist, using the Lambecian edition—which does not lack them—omitted them in the variant readings; here, however, because Gretser does not pass them over in silence, he necessarily admitted them. Compare the famous inscription at Ravenna with Papirius Masson, Book II, Pagius, 755, no. 6, and other recent writers: “Pippin the Pious, first opened the way to enlarging the Church.” No credence will undoubtedly be given to the man who adds the Roman duchy to the donations.]

Rather, after the desolation of our entire province

[Note: What was this “entire province of ours”? Certainly nothing other than the Roman duchy, whose capital was Rome.]

and the many murders committed by that same people, you must also acknowledge what we say with great tears and anguish of heart, excellent son and spiritual co-father: on the very Kalends of January, the entire army of that same Haistulf, king of the Lombards, came from the regions of Tuscany into this Roman city and took up position near the gate of blessed Pancratius and the Portuensis Gate.

[Lamb. and Gent. add: “the gate of blessed Peter the apostle, and the gate of …”]

Haistulf himself, together with other armies, came up from the other side and pitched his tents near the Salarian Gate and the other gates. He sent us a message, saying: “Open the Salarian Gate for me, and I will enter the city. Hand over your pontiff to me, and I will have compassion on you. Otherwise, I will overthrow the walls and kill you all with a single sword; then let me see who can rescue you from my hands.”

But all the Beneventans likewise came together in general to this Roman city and took up position near the gate of blessed Paul the apostle and the other gates of this Roman city. They consumed with sword and fire all the estates outside the city, far and wide; burning all the houses, they destroyed them almost to their foundations; they set fire to the churches of God and, throwing the most sacred images of the saints into the fire, destroyed them with their swords. They placed the sacred gifts—that is, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ—in their polluted vessels, which they call bellows; and, filled with an abundance of meat, they ate those same gifts. Removing the altar coverings of the churches of God and all their ornaments—something too cruel even to say—they used them for their own purposes.

They beat the servants of God, the monks who remained in monasteries for the sake of divine worship, with terrible blows, and tore many of them to pieces. They dragged away and violated with great cruelty the holy women and recluses who, from childhood and the time of puberty, had devoted themselves to seclusion for the love of God; and even in the midst of that violation they appeared to kill some of them. They burned with fire all the cultivated estates of blessed Peter, and, as has been said, burning the houses of all the Romans, they utterly destroyed those outside the city. They carried off all the livestock, cut down the vineyards almost to their roots, and trampled down the crops. Neither the household of our holy Church nor anyone dwelling in this Roman city retained any hope of living, because, as has been said, they consumed everything with sword and fire and killed many. They also slaughtered the numerous household of blessed Peter and of all the Romans, both men and women, and led many others away captive.

Indeed, those impious Lombards separated innocent infants from their mothers’ breasts, polluted the mothers by force, and killed them. They committed such evils in this Roman province as, assuredly, not even pagan peoples had ever perpetrated. For even the stones themselves, if it may be said, seeing our desolation, howl together with us.

For fifty-five days they besieged this afflicted Roman city and surrounded it on every side. Day and night, with the most savage fury, they ceaselessly waged the fiercest battles against us at the walls of this Roman city, and they did not cease attacking us, so that—may the Divinity avert it—after subjecting the city to his power, that same wicked Haistulf might kill everyone with a single sword. Thus, reproaching us—

[Lamb. adds: “with great fury”]—

they declared: “Behold, you are surrounded by us, and you will not escape our hands. Let the Franks come now and rescue you from our hands.”
