They also seized the city of Narni, which your Christianity had granted to blessed Peter.

[Note: It is clear from this that the restoration of this city was also included at the end of Pippin’s donation, when the royal diploma was completed at Quierzy. Two points must nevertheless be noted: first, the city is said to have been “granted,” although it belonged by right to the Roman Church and had merely been vindicated for it; second, among the records only this one city of the Roman duchy is mentioned as restored through the action of the Frankish king to the Roman people, while nowhere is there any mention, however slight, of a donation or restoration of the rest. Therefore, whenever one of the pontiffs is found following Stephen’s example—who says that Narni, his own city, which Pippin admits he had recovered from the duke of Spoleto and asserted to the Holy See, had been granted to him—he should be judged to have been currying favor with the prince through flattering words, not to have been handing down a falsehood as truth on his own authority. Pippin and Charles, the only men to whom the Apostolic See attributes accepted donations, have no need of the glory of lying, since they have acquired everlasting fame by so many other titles.]

and captured some of our cities. Therefore, afflicted, we were scarcely able, by the greatest ingenuity and by the sea route, to send these present letters and messengers to your most excellent Christianity. We wrote them with great tears and, speaking with truth as our witness, say that through every letter we seemed to pour forth tears mixed with blood. Would that the Lord grant us that, at the hour when you read our mournful exhortation, tears full of blood might flow through every letter before your presence.

Therefore, excellent son and spiritual co-father, I ask you—and, as though present in person, prostrate on the ground and casting myself at your feet, I adjure you before the living and true God and before blessed Peter, his chief of the apostles—

[Note: Here you have another example of a practice that had become customary among the pontiffs, as I said in the note to the first letter. The same occurs in Letter 4, elsewhere numbered 8.]

—to come to our aid with excessive haste and the greatest speed, lest we perish; for, after the Lord, we have entrusted the souls of all us Romans into your hands.

Do not abandon us; then may the Lord not abandon you in all your actions and works. Do not despise us; then may the Lord not despise you who invoke his power. Do not withdraw your assistance from us, most Christian son and spiritual co-father; then may the Lord not withdraw his assistance and protection from you and your people when you enter battle against your enemies. Help us and assist us with great speed, most Christian one; then may you receive help from God almighty, who through the institution of blessed Peter anointed you king over the multitudes of peoples. Come, come, son; come and help us before the sword of our enemies reaches our heart.

I ask you, lest we perish. Let not the nations throughout the entire world say: “Where is the confidence of the Romans, which, after the Lord, they placed in kings and in the people of the Franks?”

[Lamb. and Gent. add: “and in the people.”]

Do not allow us to perish, and do not delay or defer bringing us aid. Do not separate us from your assistance; then may you not be a stranger to the kingdom of God, nor separated from your sweetest wife, the most excellent queen, our spiritual co-mother. Do not allow us any longer to remain anxious and endangered, persevering in mourning and weeping, good and most excellent son and spiritual co-father; then may mourning not overtake you on account of your sweetest and my sweetest sons, Lord Charles and Carloman,

[Note: God granted these prayers, for both survived their father and each obtained his own kingdom.]

most excellent kings and patricians.

Do not harden your ear against hearing us, and do not turn your face away from us. Let us not be confounded in our petitions, and let us not be endangered to the end. Then may the Lord not harden his ear against hearing your prayers, and may he not turn his face away from you on that future day of judgment, when he will sit with blessed Peter and your other apostles to judge every rank, every sex, every human power, and the world through fire. And may it be said to you—may the Divinity avert it—“I do not know you,” because you did not assist the Church of God and took no care to defend its endangered special people.

Hear me, son, hear me and help us. Behold, the time for saving us is here. Save us before we perish, most Christian king. For what is better, what more fitting or excellent, than to save those who are endangered and placed in distress? For it is written: “Whoever saves is like one who builds.” Therefore the foremost prophet Isaiah says: “Help the oppressed.”

All the nations situated round about, which have made refuge with your most powerful Frankish people through the power of God, have been saved. And if you do not delay in extending assistance to all the nations, and they are saved through you, you ought all the more to free the holy Church of God and its people from the attack of their enemies.

O how great a confidence was in our heart when we were permitted to behold your honey-sweet countenance and were bound and joined together in the bond of charity, expecting to remain in great peace and security. But while we hoped to see light from you, darkness burst forth, and our final circumstances became worse than the first.

Consider, son, consider, and ponder this most earnestly—I adjure you by the living God—for after God and his chief of the apostles, both our souls and the souls of all the Roman people depend upon your excellence, protected by God, and upon the Frankish people entrusted to you by God. For, as has been stated, we have entrusted our souls to your care. And if it should happen that we perish—may it not happen, and may divine clemency avert it—consider, I beg you, and, having considered it in every way, weigh whose soul the guilt will touch.

Indeed, believe this absolutely, most Christian one: if some disaster should befall us—may it not happen—you, protected by God and most beloved by us, will have to render an account for everything before the tribunal of God, together with all your judges. For, as has been stated, we have entrusted the holy Church of God and the people of our Roman commonwealth to no one else but your most loving excellence, your sweetest sons, and the entire Frankish people, by God’s command and that of blessed Peter, to be protected.

[Note: A clear definition of ecclesiastical rule apart from the donations, and likewise of the patriciate of the Frankish kings.]

Behold, we have made all our pains, anxieties, and distresses known to your goodness, protected by God. You, therefore, excellent son and spiritual co-father, act and rescue those who have taken refuge in you after the Lord, so that, bringing forth good fruit, you may deserve to say on the day of future judgment:

“My lord, chief of the apostles, blessed Peter, behold I, your little client, having finished my course and kept the faith, have rescued and defended from the hands of my persecutors the Church entrusted to you by heavenly clemency. Standing before you undefiled, I offer you the children whom you entrusted to me, rescued from the hands of the enemies, safe and unharmed.”

Then, holding the reins of the kingdom in the present life and reigning with Christ in the future age, may you deserve to attain the joys of heavenly rewards, hearing that desirable paternal voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

[Note: Commonly called the postscript.]

## Embolum

For indeed, [the printed reading is *opere*; variant: *oportuneque*, “and at an opportune time”], we have sent to your most Christian excellence our messenger, the most reverend brother and fellow bishop George, together with Warneharius, a religious abbot and your messenger, and also Thomaricus and Comita,

[Note: This passage could easily have corrected the corrupt reading in the preceding letter, “Thomaricus the count.” I do not see why Muratori, following Lambecius, read “Comita” while omitting the conjunction; for in both places they are called distinguished apostolic messengers, and there is no doubt that there were two of them. Moreover, the name Comita is better known than the other: in the Synod of Mopsuestia (Labbe, Councils, vol. V, p. 494), among the citizens of that city, we read: “Comitas said, ‘I am called Comitas, an agent of affairs and the father of this city.’” Both seem to have been Greek by origin, something by no means uncommon at Rome in that period.]

[Lamb., Gent.: “Comitam”]

likewise our distinguished messengers. They must tell you in a careful narrative, with their living voices, all our sufferings and every desolation that we have endured and continually endure at the hands of the Lombard people and their insolent king, just as they saw them with their own eyes. May your most Christian excellence order that they be believed in everything as though they were ourselves, and arrange our liberation with the utmost haste.

And I adjure you by the living and true God, son protected by God and spiritual co-father, never again to disbelieve our afflictions and in no way to neglect delivering us. For, God forbid, if you delay any longer to believe and neglect to rescue us, the calamity of perishing may fall upon us—may the Divinity avert it—and this will bring you great loss, sin, and condemnation in the present and eternal life, because we entrust to you the souls of all us Romans.

Rather, as has been stated, we adjure you more and more, excellent son protected and preserved by God and spiritual co-father, by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity, to order that our tribulations, distresses, pains, and desolations be believed without any doubt; and may you deign to bring us assistance for God’s sake and hasten exceedingly to rescue us from the hands of the Lombards, our enemies, so that, bringing forth abundant fruit, you may become victorious over all barbarian nations through the intercession of blessed Peter and possess eternal life.

The aforesaid abbot Warneharius, out of love for blessed Peter, putting on his cuirass, kept watch day and night along the walls of this afflicted Roman city and, for the defense and liberation of all us Romans, fought with all his strength as a good athlete of Christ.

## X. The Third Letter Which Pope Stephen Sent to Lord King Pippin, and to Charles or Carloman, or to the Entire Frankish People

[Note: Lambecius and Gentianus read: “to lord King Pippin, and to Charles or Carloman.”]

In the name of blessed Peter, composed after the aforesaid pope himself had already been in Francia, when for the second time he wished to obtain assistance against the Lombards.

[Annals of the Lord 755, Codex Carolinus III, chronicle 10.]

### Argument

To the two letters just presented, Stephen now adds this one, compelled by harsh necessity, in the name of the chief of the apostles, addressed to three kings and to the whole Frankish people: an account of the City brought to the extremity of misery. The Apostle promises his intercession with God if they protect his own house, the foundation of the whole Church, and his body resting there, from the savagery of the Lombards. He joins the Most Holy Virgin and all the saints in exhorting the king and the Franks to raise Rome from oppression. He declares that action must be taken quickly; that, if they obey, his patronage will never fail them; and that he counts the victories previously won as achieved through his favor. Finally, he threatens their alienation from the kingdom of God unless they undertake this most necessary work with the utmost speed.

[Note: This third letter, unknown neither to Baronius nor to the Magdeburg Centuriators, was produced by the extremity of the crisis. Fleury (Ecclesiastical History, Book XLIII, no. 17) would have translated it with less confidence, and Muratori would have embraced with less applause the learned writer’s untimely exaggeration of the character of that age with open arms (Italian Annals, 755), if either had noticed that such a prosopopoeia was suited not to the age but to the character of the pious king and all the Franks. Both, to the great injury of King Pippin and Pope Stephen, call it a fiction. As we have seen, all the Franks, and their king above all, loved the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, through whose patronage they attributed their victory over the Lombards, as the Frankish annals testify. The pontiff strongly nourished this confidence of theirs at a time when the East was raging against the Most Holy Virgin, Peter, and all the saints, their images having been trampled underfoot. For this reason all Italy had revolted from the impious emperors, Rome with its duchy had submitted to Peter’s successor, and, relying upon Frankish assistance, neither hoped for nor sought human help from anywhere else. Therefore, in the greatest distresses of that same See of Peter, when extreme remedies were necessary, the pontiff first disclosed to the royal house and to all the Franks, and then individually to Pippin, the savagery and crimes of the Lombards, together with the distress and impending destruction of the endangered City, and introduced Peter himself as the patron and avenger of his cause. Here, with the kind indulgence of both learned men, there is no place for a theological question about the Church or the souls of the faithful: bodies and possessions were in danger; the things most sacred in the Catholic religion were being trampled underfoot; everything consisted of slaughter, fear, crimes, and sacrilege. Speaking of all these matters, Peter himself is introduced so that a more immediate remedy might be obtained from the Franks, gathered together in the face of so many evils. We shall soon see that the petition succeeded. For now, Peter’s address itself must be weighed more attentively than those learned men weighed it, and its sentences must be examined according to the grammatical rules appropriate to the time, as befits the chief of the apostles.]

[Col. 0122A–B] Peter, called an apostle by Jesus Christ, Son of the living God—who, reigning with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit before all ages, in the last times was incarnate and became human for the salvation of us all, redeemed us by his precious blood according to the will of the Father’s glory, as he ordained through his holy prophets in the sacred Scriptures—and, through me, the whole catholic and apostolic Roman Church of God, head of all the churches of God, founded upon the firm rock by the blood of that same Redeemer, together with Stephen, bishop of that same nourishing Church: may grace, peace, and strength be more fully bestowed by the Lord our God upon you, most excellent men—Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, the three kings; the most holy bishops, abbots, presbyters, and all religious monks; and also the dukes, counts, all the assembled armies, and the people dwelling in Francia—for the rescue of that same holy Church of God and its Roman people entrusted to me from the hands of their persecutors.

I, Peter the apostle, when I was called by Christ, the Son of the living God, by the decree of heavenly mercy, was appointed by his power as the enlightener of the whole world, with the Lord our God himself confirming it: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). And again: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 21). And to me, his humble and insignificant servant and called apostle, he entrusted his sheep individually, saying: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” [Col. 0122C]. And again: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0122D] Who would dare mutter against these doctrines?] (Matthew 16).

Therefore, let all who, hearing my preaching, have fulfilled it believe with certainty that, by God’s command, their sins are released in this world, and that they will enter the life to come pure and without blemish. For, indeed, since [Cent.: quibus (“to whom”), instead of quia (“since”)] the illumination of the Holy Spirit has shone forth in your splendid hearts, and you have become lovers of the holy and unique Trinity through your acceptance of the word of evangelical preaching, surely in this apostolic Roman Church of God, entrusted to us, your hope of future recompense is bound up.

Therefore I, Peter, the apostle of God, who regard you as adopted sons, exhort you to defend from the hands of adversaries this Roman city and the people entrusted to me by God, and also the house where I rest according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0123C] It is a constant tradition, supported by the testimony of all antiquity, that Peter’s sacred ashes rest in the Vatican basilica. The numerous testimonies of Saint Gregory the Great provide abundant confirmation. Two testimonies of that same holy pontiff must not be passed over. The first is addressed to the Empress Constantina (Book IV, Letter 30): “When my predecessor of blessed memory wished to move the silver that was above the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle, although it was still nearly fifteen feet distant from that body, a sign of no small terror appeared to him.” The second is addressed to the Emperor Justin (Book II, Letter 33), in defense of the innocence of Bishop Leo: “So that nothing might seem to have been omitted, or any doubt remain in our heart, we made him, under strict oath and as an additional precaution, give an undertaking at the most sacred body of blessed Peter.” I pass over the older testimonies of Caius, Jerome, and Prudentius. Of the hundred and fifty years that followed Gregory the Great down to the present time, I wish only to consider the lists or professions of the Roman pontiffs and of bishops ordained by Rome in the *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs. In both places they will be found to say: “At your body, blessed Peter the apostle … over your most sacred body … above the most sacred body of blessed Peter.” These statements sufficiently and more than sufficiently prove that Saint Peter rests in the Vatican basilica. To this is added the most powerful testimony of the *Codex Carolinus*, by which the preceding evidence is confirmed.]—to rescue it from the contamination of the nations, I call upon the love of all of you and, earnestly protesting, admonish you to liberate from the hands of its persecutors the Church of God entrusted to me by divine power, because they are suffering the greatest afflictions and oppressions from the worst nation of the Lombards.

Do not hold otherwise, most beloved, but be firmly confident: through my own person—as though I were alive in the flesh and standing before you—we bind and constrain you by this exhortation with solemn adjurations [Note: [Col. 0124C] Baronius reads: “as though I were alive in the flesh and standing before you, and by this exhortation strongly constrain and bind you with adjurations”]. For, according to the promise that we received from that same Lord God and our Redeemer, we regard you, the whole people of the Franks, as specially chosen among all nations.

Thus I protest and admonish you, and, as though in a riddle, I adjure you by a firm obligation: you, most Christian kings, Pippin, Charles, and Carloman; all priests, bishops, abbots, presbyters, and all religious monks; and all judges [Col. 0123B], as well as dukes, counts, and the entire people of the Frankish kingdom. And as though I, Peter the apostle of God, were presently alive in the flesh and standing before you, believe firmly that the words of this exhortatory address [Note: [Col. 0124C] Baronius: “through the word of the exhortatory address”] are spoken to you, because although I am absent bodily, I am not absent from you spiritually; for it is written: “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward.”

Moreover, our Lady Mary, Mother of God, ever-virgin, adjuring you with us by great obligations, protests, admonishes, and commands—and likewise the thrones, dominations, and the entire army of the heavenly host [Col. 0124A], together with the martyrs and confessors of Christ and all who are pleasing to God. All these, together with us, exhorting and adjuring you, solemnly declare that you should feel concern for this Roman city, entrusted to us by the Lord God, and for the Lord’s sheep dwelling in it, and also for the holy Church of God entrusted to me by the Lord.

Defend and liberate it with the utmost haste from the hands of the Lombards who persecute it, lest, God forbid, my body—which suffered torments for the Lord Jesus Christ—and my house, where it rests by God’s command, be contaminated by them, and my chosen people be further torn apart or slaughtered by that same Lombard nation, which is guilty of so great a crime of perjury [Gent.: per jurii regi, perhaps “of perjury toward the king”] and whose members are proved transgressors of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0124B].

Therefore provide the Roman people, entrusted to me by God and your brothers in this life, with support through all your strength, the Lord cooperating. Then I, Peter, called the apostle of God, will continually provide you with reciprocal protection in this life and on the day of the future judgment; and luminous and glorious dwellings will be prepared for you [Lamb.: praeparem, “may I prepare”] in the kingdom of God, together with the rewards of eternal recompense. Promising you the unending joys of paradise, I shall grant them to you in return—provided that you swiftly defend my Roman city, my chosen people, your Roman brothers, from the hands of the wicked Lombards [Note: [Col. 0124C] At that time it could not be foreseen that the Frankish kings themselves would one day be made emperors, or that, when their dynasty failed, the imperial dignity would be transferred elsewhere, to the great detriment of the Roman Church. For the Roman pontiffs who occupied Peter’s chair in later centuries were first compelled to abandon Rome, then Italy, and to flee to the place from which the authority of the Holy See had received its greatest increase. These things, I say, could not then be foreseen. For nearly seven centuries, ninety-two predecessors of Stephen had held in Rome, even in the most difficult times, the chair that Saint Peter had cemented with his blood; and while Stephen was seated upon it, hope for a better age had arisen because of the exceptional love of the Franks for Saint Peter. Therefore, the person introduced here as speaking could speak only of what had already happened, what was then occurring, and what belonged to the authority granted to him by Christ Jesus—as he does here and in what follows.].

### 102

Run, run! I exhort and protest to you by the living and true God. Run and come to the rescue before the living fountain from which you were satisfied and reborn dries up; before the small ember remaining from the most blazing flame, from which you came to know your light, is extinguished; before your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, in which you hope to receive eternal life, is humbled, invaded, robbed by the impious [Gent., “violated”], and contaminated [Col. 0125A].

I protest to you, my most beloved adopted sons; by the grace of the Holy Spirit I protest, and, before God, the terrifying Creator of all, I most earnestly exhort and admonish you—I, Peter, the apostle of God, and with me the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God, which the Lord entrusted to me—not to allow this Roman city to perish, in which the Lord established my body, which he entrusted to me and made the foundation of faith.

Liberate it and its Roman people, your brothers, and by no means allow them to be invaded by the Lombard nation. Then may your provinces and possessions not be invaded by nations whom you do not know; then may you not be separated from my Roman people; then may you not be alienated or separated from the kingdom of God and eternal life. Whatever you ask of me, I will come to your aid [Col. 0125B] and offer you protection. Come to the assistance of my Roman people, your brothers; strive with greater perfection, and bring the matter to an end by liberating them. For no one receives a crown who has not struggled lawfully [Lamb., Gent., “unless he has struggled lawfully”]. Struggle bravely for the liberation of the holy Church of God, lest you perish forever.

I adjure you, I adjure you, as has been said, most beloved, by the living God, and I solemnly protest: do not at all permit this Roman city of mine and the people dwelling in it to be further torn apart by the Lombard nation, lest your bodies be torn and tortured [Note: [Col. 0125D] Lamb.: “so that they may not be torn”; Gent.: “if they are not torn”], and your souls be tormented in eternal and unquenchable Tartarean fire with the devil and his pestilential angels. Nor allow the sheep of the Lord’s flock entrusted to me by God—that is, the Roman people—to be further scattered, lest the Lord scatter and cast you away, as the Israelite people were scattered.

For it has been declared that, among all the nations beneath heaven, your Frankish nation has shown itself especially inclined toward me, Peter the apostle of God. Therefore I entrusted the Church that the Lord delivered to me to you through the hands of my vicar, so that you might liberate it from the hands of its enemies.

Hold this most firmly: I, God’s servant, called apostle, have aided you in all your necessities whenever you prayed, and by God’s power I have granted you victory over your enemies. Believe that I will continue to do so, if you hasten with the utmost speed to liberate this Roman city of mine. Remember also how, when the enemies of the holy Church of God began battle against you [Baronius: “when they began to attack”], I caused you, although few in number against them, to overthrow them [Idem: “to be overthrown”] [Note: [Col. 0125D] The Frankish annals testify to this. See Letter 6, elsewhere 7, column 105, note b.]. Therefore strive to fulfill this admonition of mine swiftly, so that through the grace given to me by Christ the Lord our God you may deserve to obtain my aid in greater measure.

Behold, my dearest sons, I have proclaimed and admonished you. If you obey swiftly, this will lead you to a great reward; aided by my intercession, you will overcome all your enemies in the present life, and, living to a great age, you will eat the good things of the land, and without doubt enjoy eternal life.

But if—which we do not believe—you introduce any delay or contrivance and do not swiftly fulfill this exhortation of ours to liberate this Roman city of mine and the people dwelling in it, and the holy apostolic Church of God entrusted to me by the Lord, together with its bishop, know that, by the authority of the holy and unique Trinity and through the grace of the apostolate given to me by Christ the Lord, you will be alienated, for transgressing our exhortation, from the kingdom of God and eternal life [Note: [Col. 0125D] This is an unmistakable indication that, like the two preceding letters, this letter was sent during the siege and conveyed by the same envoys by sea, contrary to the opinion of Pagius (755, note 4), who says that it was sent separately, when the Lombards were pressing the siege more fiercely. For everyone agrees on the same point: all conclude that immediate action was necessary.].

But may God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us with his precious blood and led us into the light of truth, and who also established us preachers and enlighteners of the whole world, grant you the wisdom, understanding, and resolve to act with the utmost speed, so that you may hasten to rescue this Roman city and the entire people, together with the holy Church of God entrusted to me by the Lord. May he mercifully command that, through the intercession of my prayers for you, he preserve you in the present life long-lived, safe, and victorious, as his faithful subjects, and in the age to come make you more abundantly worthy to receive the gifts of his reward, together with his saints and elect.

Farewell.

## XI. 105

### Another letter of the same man to Lord King Pippin, sent through the chaplain Folradus, Bishop George, and the sacellarius John, after the death of Aistulf [Note: [Col. 0126D] He died in the year of Christ 756.]

In it are contained abundant thanksgivings and blessings for the victory and restoration of the holy Church of God, together with a request that what remained lacking be restored.

*(A.D. 756, Codex Carolinus VIII, Chronicle 11.)*

[Col. 0126C]

### Argument

Rejoicing with delight, he offers immense thanks to Pippin. He exalts the Roman Church—the mother of all the Churches of God and the foundation of the Catholic faith—which had been mourning in the previous year and now rejoices, raised up by him as a new Moses and David. He declares that to anyone arriving in Rome from anywhere in the world he recounts its great glory. Since certain cities and places are still lacking from the complete donation, and possession of them has not been granted to the Holy See, he asks Pippin to complete it.

Aistulf, one year after the siege of the City, was struck down by a divine blow. Desiderius, who had sworn to Folradus that he would quickly return to the Holy See the remaining cities—namely Faenza, Imola, Ferrara, Osimo, Ancona, Numana, and Bologna, with their boundaries and territories—has now been raised up. The pope wishes the king to command that he keep his promises.

He commends the people of Benevento and Spoleto to Pippin. He says that the time has now come to vindicate the Catholic religion against Greek impiety. He wishes to be informed about the conference with the imperial *silentiarius*. He asks that Pippin send back Bishop George and the sacellarius John, his envoys and bearers of this letter [Col. 0127A], together with Bishop Wilhari of Nomentum. He also says that Abbot Optatus of Cassino is longing for his monks who had departed with Carloman.

[Note: [Col. 0127C] It appears in Baronius, volume IX, under the year 756, and in Centuriator 8, chapter 10.]

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

We cannot express with our tongue, most excellent son, how much we rejoice in your work and your life. For by divine power miracles have been performed in our days [Note: [Col. 0127C] Lamb.: “by the power of a miracle.” Gent.: “by miraculous power”; the manuscript lacks the word “divine”]. Through your excellence, the holy Roman Church, mother and head of all the Churches of God and foundation of the Christian faith, which had been lamenting greatly under the attacks and dangers inflicted by enemies [Note: [Col. 0127C] Centuriator likewise reads this, but Baronius: “which was lamenting greatly under the attacks of the enemies”], has now plainly been transferred into and confirmed in a great and solid joy [Col. 0127B]. The sorrowful souls of Christians have been especially restored to gladness by your most courageous protection. For this reason, in your work and our rejoicing, we gladly cry out with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2) [Note: [Col. 0127C] Eginhard (*Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 6) does not distinguish Pippin’s two victories; he speaks of his Italian expedition only for purposes of comparison. The Frankish annals cited by Canisius refer both victories to the year 755 and the following year. The Annals of Fulda also treat the two separately, under the years 754 and 756. Father Mansius, in his notes on Pagius (Baronius, volume XII, page 633), believes that he has disentangled this chronology, which had been confused partly by ancient annalists and partly by more recent writers, by relying on a Brescian chronicle published by Muratori. That chronicle places King Rachis between Aistulf and Desiderius and dates Desiderius’s accession to March of the year of the Incarnation 757, indiction 10. But the ancient charters, the chronologists emerging in our own age, and other streams from which these accounts derive must yield to the authority of this letter. Unless, with the aforesaid Father Mansius, the siege of the City is moved from the year 755 contrary to the testimony of the ancients, the other assertions cannot stand. I, together with Baronius, Cointius, Pagius, and others, date the letter to the year 756. The reasons appear from the letter itself, as will be made clear in the following notes.].

And because last year, at this same time, we were suffering terribly, wounded by the devastation and attacks of the enemy and surrounded on every side [Note: [Col. 0127D] At the same season in which Rome was besieged the previous year—namely, in March, as will be made clear below—the pope and all the Romans, rejoicing with delight, were giving thanks to God and had forgotten all the evils they had suffered [Col. 0128C]. Pippin, stirred by the three preceding letters, had come into Italy for a second time. After defeating Aistulf, and in order that he might not break his promises and oaths as in the previous year, Pippin had left Folradus in Italy. Folradus, having taken possession of the individual cities, brought their keys and hostages to Rome. The pope had begun to administer the exarchate and the Pentapolis, just as he administered Rome and its duchy. It is unnecessary to pursue this well-known history in Anastasius and the annalists. The dates of so important an event must not, however, be neglected. On 24 February, as I said, in the year 755, the papal envoys, traveling by sea together with the royal envoys, brought the aforesaid letters to Francia. After a period of six or seven months the envoys arrived there; preparations for war were made; the army returned to Italy; Aistulf was defeated; and, being besieged at Pavia, he was compelled to give hostages and restore the exarchate and Pentapolis. This final event clearly took place in September or October, according to Anastasius, who mentions that the eighth indiction had elapsed; it continued until the Kalends of September. Five months then passed—a sufficiently long period for Folradus to take possession of the individual cities in the name of the Holy See, whose legates were with him, and to make that possession firm and stable by placing their keys upon the most sacred body of Saint Peter, as well as to undertake other matters that, as we shall soon see, he completed before leaving Rome. Thus, from the beginning of the year 756, the Apostolic See began to rule the exarchate and Pentapolis, whereas for at least twenty-five years it had possessed Rome and its duchy by the will of the people.], but now, rescued from the dangers hanging over us by your most powerful aid, we rejoice with immeasurable joy. Blessing the name of the Lord with the psalmist, we say with one voice: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76). And again: “In the evening weeping will remain, but in the morning there will be joy” (Psalm 29).

For whose breast, even if made of stone, would not soften at once into praise of almighty God and love for your excellence, after learning of and recognizing so benevolent a work accomplished by your illustrious goodness [Col. 0127C]? I confess, most excellent son and spiritual co-father, that I often delight in recounting to nations gathered from every region of the world the marvelous things accomplished through you [Col. 0128A], often in admiring them together with those nations, and in continually celebrating, with extended and honeyed voice, the praises of your excellence. These things also frequently rouse me, even in the passing hours, to pour out unceasing prayers to almighty God, with an unwavering gaze, for your immense goodness and for the safety of the entire Frankish nation.

Finally, most beloved, divinely inspired, victorious, fortunate, and most powerful king through divine providence, your very life plainly testifies to all how blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, received the devotion you showed while striving on his behalf. For it is written [Lamb. adds “it is written”]: “The vows of the righteous are pleasing” (Proverbs 15).

Indeed, most excellent son, I greatly desire to offer your goodness abundant praise and, glorifying the name of the Lord for such extraordinary benevolence, to sing with joyful voice: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because, visiting his people and desiring to accomplish redemption” (Luke 1), he raised you up for us, most Christian victor [Lamb. adds “king”], in our days as a most powerful liberator [Col. 0128B]. For what else can I call you but a new Moses, and what else can I declare you but a radiant King David? For just as they liberated God’s people from the oppressions of the Philistines, so you, victor blessed by God and most powerful king, have striven through your struggle to rescue the Church of God and its afflicted people from the assaults of their enemies.

Blessed are you, illustrious son, by the Most High God, who made heaven and earth. And blessed be God, under whose protection the enemies are in your hands. May the Lord, the beauty of righteousness, bless you and protect in every way your most beloved sons, my spiritual children, Lord Charles and Carloman, established by God as kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, together with their most Christian mother, the most excellent queen and dearest wife [Col. 0129A], a faithful servant of God and our spiritual co-mother. May God enlarge your offspring, bless you forever, grant you perpetual enjoyment of the throne of the kingdom, and preserve unharmed the whole nation of the Franks that remains under your rule.

Farewell in the Lord, most gracious king. Through you the enemies of the holy Church of God have been humbled; through you the holy Church of God itself has been restored to great joy; its chosen people rejoice; and through you he is called blessed. For this reason its blessing has been more fully poured out upon you, since you have brought abundant joy to the whole world. These are great things and must be attributed to the praises of almighty God. Yet amid them we continually ask the mercy of our most merciful God to grant you the joys of his heavenly kingdom in return [Col. 0129B] [Note: [Col. 0129C] Lamb., Gent., Baronius, and Centuriator read: “to grant you the recompense of joy.”].

Therefore, with great confidence, as though I were presently standing before you and appearing in your honeyed presence, kneeling and asking, I beg you—and earnestly beseech you before the living God—to command that you remain firmly in this good work, as we certainly trust you will, until the end, for the perfect exultation of the holy Church of God, the liberation [Idem: “deliverance”] of its people, and their complete security. Deign to grant that same Church full justice, and command that an excellent and speedy conclusion be brought to the cause of your patron, blessed Peter, so that you may order the remaining cities, which had been joined under the authority of a single rule, together with their established boundaries [Lamb., Gent., “established places”], territories, and even their localities and forest lands, to be restored in their entirety to your spiritual mother, the holy Church [Col. 0129C–0130A] [Note: [Col. 0129C] The Lombard king had not yet granted possession of certain cities, which are listed below: Faenza, Imola, Ferrara, and Bologna in Emilia—Gabellum and Adria are not mentioned—and Ancona, Auximum, and Numana in the Pentapolis; the Forum Sempronii and the Valvense territory are omitted. The others should all be examined in Anastasius, to see whether he enumerates individually those whose possession was certain and preserved in the archive of the Holy See. Among later writers this is plainly called Pippin’s donation; indeed, it is also called the donation of Charlemagne in the prolegomena to volume II of the Roman Vatican edition (page LVII), but incorrectly. For the aforesaid cities are absent from it, and Pippin’s donation did not come fully into the possession of the Holy See until 774, eighteen years after this time, when Charlemagne was reigning.].

Thus the people of God whom you redeemed from the hands of their enemies may be able, aided by your assistance, to live in great security and joy. For our son, beloved of God, Folradus, your faithful servant, who has seen everything, has been satisfied [Baronius and Centuriator: “has given sufficient testimony”] that those people could in no way live outside those boundaries, territories, and possessions without the cities that had always been joined with them under the authority of a single rule [Note: [Col. 0129D] A simple examination of geographical maps makes clear the grounds on which the pope asserts that those peoples who had been attached to the dominion of the Holy See could not live peacefully without the cities and territories fraudulently retained by Aistulf. In the *Life of Stephen* by Anastasius (section 256), we read that this pontiff, who ceased to live at the beginning of the following year, obtained from King Desiderius, who had succeeded Aistulf before this letter was written, Faenza together with the fortress of Tiberiacum, or Gabellum, and the whole duchy of Ferrara intact. But concerning these matters below, in the letters of Paul. For now I wish to note that the pope repeatedly speaks of all the cities of the exarchate and Pentapolis as those “which were joined under the authority of a single rule.” It is therefore clear that the emperor, the exarch, or even the Lombard king, as invader, is being regarded as their lord. Accordingly, the phrase “restore,” which occurs frequently both here and elsewhere, must either refer to the Lombards themselves, invaders of property belonging to another, or to the donation previously made to the Holy See; it can in no way refer to that same Holy See, as some maintain, since it previously possessed no right in the exarchate and Pentapolis.].

I ask you, son, I ask you before the living God, and I strongly adjure you, spiritual co-father, to remain steadfast in this good work and not, God forbid, to favor human flatteries, counsels, or promises, or turn aside to another course. Rather, truly fearing God, command that everything you promised Saint Peter under oath be fulfilled [Col. 0130B], and, as you began, grant him full justice.

For that tyrant, the devil’s follower, Aistulf, devourer of Christian blood and destroyer of the Churches of God, was struck by a divine blow and plunged into the abyss of hell. Indeed, in the very days when he had set out to devastate this Roman city, after the cycle of a year had passed, he was struck by a divine sword, so that at the very time when, violating his faith [Lamb., “testing his faith”], he had committed various wicked crimes, he also ended his impious life [Note: [Col. 0130C] The foundation of the monastery of Nonantula for his kinsman Anselm, together with the friendship of the monks, as related in the patchwork history of the Anonymous of Salerno (*Chronicle*, chapter 7), is not sufficient to erase this testimony, especially since that writer lived more than two centuries after Stephen. Stephen, who had long endured the brutality of Aistulf, testifies to the Frankish king that divine vengeance had also arrived for so many sacrileges and crimes.].

Now, by God’s providence, through the hands of his prince, blessed Peter, the apostle, and also through your most powerful arm, with the industrious assistance of Folradus, a man beloved of God [Note: [Col. 0130C] See Baronius, year 756, note 3 and following] [Col. 0130C], your faithful servant and our beloved son [Note: [Col. 0130C] If Desiderius succeeded Aistulf through the efforts of Folradus, then the charters and chronologists on which recent writers rely must either be disregarded or interpreted differently. Rachis must therefore have left the monastery before Desiderius’s inauguration and contended with Desiderius for the kingdom from the end of the year 755 until March of the following year, when, through the efforts of Stephen II and Folradus, Rachis returned to the monastery and Desiderius began to reign. Stephen’s words seem to suggest this: “in the very days when he had set out to devastate this Roman city, after the cycle of a year.” For if Aistulf besieged the City on the Kalends of January, he must have set out toward it in December of the year 754, and in that same month of the following year he died. In the *Life of Stephen* by Anastasius, which agrees remarkably with this letter and is said to have been written by a contemporary author, immediately after the account of the cities’ possession delivered by Folradus, the author continues (section 254): “While these things were being pressed forward, the unhappy Aistulf, going hunting in a certain place, was struck by a divine blow and died. Then a certain Desiderius …” I would readily accept their view. I would say that Stephen, by the phrase “after the cycle of a year,” was indicating with them that he was not reckoning the year with complete precision. But what the pontiff says at the beginning of the letter—“when a year had elapsed, at this time, surrounded on every side”—so clearly establishes the date of the letter, and consequently of Aistulf’s fall, that the authority of the letter must take precedence over the ancient charters and chronologists by whose aid the date has been postponed. See below, column 147, note e, Letter 12.], has been appointed king over the nation of the Lombards: Desiderius, a most gentle man. In the presence of Folradus he swore that he would restore to blessed Peter the remaining cities—Faenza, Imola, and Ferrara [Note: [Col. 0131C] Lamb.: “Imulas”; Gent.: “Faenza, Imulas, and Ferrara”]—together with their boundaries, and also now [Lamb.: etiam, “also”], the forest lands and all their territories.

He also promised to restore the cities of Osimo, Ancona, and Numana with their territories, and later, through the duke Garinodus and Grimoaldus, he pledged to return to us the city of Bona [Lamb.: Bononiam, “Bologna”] with its boundaries. He professed that he would remain in peaceful quiet with that Church of God and our people, and testified that he would be faithful toward your kingdom, protected by God. He asked us to entreat your goodness to command that a great concord of peace be confirmed with him and the entire Lombard nation [Col. 0131B].

For the entire duchy of Spoleto, through the hands of blessed Peter and your most powerful arm, has established a duke for itself [Note: [Col. 0131C] In the catalogue of the *Chronicle of Farfa* there is found a Duke Albuinus, who precedes Gisulf; the date of the latter is assigned to the year 760, but there is no record of the former anywhere except here]. The Spoletans themselves, as well as the Beneventans, all wish to commend themselves through us to your excellence, preserved by God, and they press us most earnestly in making this request to your goodness.

Therefore we ask you, most excellent son and spiritual co-father, that if the aforesaid Desiderius, as he promised, fully restores the justice of the holy Church of God [Lamb. and Gent. omit suae, “his/its own”], of the Roman commonwealth, and of blessed Peter, your protector, and remains with his entire nation in peaceful quiet with the Church of God and our people, as is contained in the agreements confirmed by your goodness [“pacts”; Baronius, “parts”] [Col. 0131C], then command that you incline your God-inspired ears to what he requested.

Meanwhile we ask this all the more earnestly: command that messages be sent very quickly to King Desiderius, exhorting, admonishing, and commanding him to restore in full to his Church the remaining cities, places, boundaries, territories, patrimonies, and forest lands [Col. 0132A], and command that such a foundation and excellent conclusion be established in his case that, with the Lord’s help, the holy Church itself may remain secure until the end of the age; that full justice from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and a memorial name may remain for you forever, and likewise for the entire Frankish people protected by Christ [Note: [Col. 0131D] Greed allows no one to be grateful; what is given is never enough for a shameless hope. So Seneca says (*On Benefits*, Book II, chapter 27). Desiderius, established on the throne through the efforts of the pope and Folradus, forgot everything he had promised under oath. He did indeed restore to the Holy See the cities and places of Emilia, or the exarchate, except Bologna and Adria, as I recently said on the authority of the *Book of the Pontiffs*; but he did not wish to return even a clod of earth in the Pentapolis. Stephen, taught by experience and foreseeing this, invokes Pippin’s authority, but in vain.].

But, inspired by God, you will bring the cause of the holy Church to completion with excessive haste; for there are other canonical matters which we must complete, pertaining to the great praise of your kingdom and to the immense reward of your soul and of the entire Frankish people. We earnestly implore your exalted goodness to order, inspired by God and by his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, such arrangements concerning the Greek territories that the holy Catholic and apostolic faith may through you remain entire and unshaken forever; and that the holy Church of God, as it has been freed from others and from their pestilential malice, may likewise be freed from this danger and restored to security, and may receive all that belongs to it.

[Note: The patrimonies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, assigned to the churches from ancient times, had been ordered by the Isaurian to be entered on the public treasury-roll and paid into the public treasury, as Theophanes relates (*Chronicle*, p. 273). From them the holy see received 35,000 gold pieces annually; and when their collection in the East began to be difficult, the emperors transferred them to Calabria and Sicily. Such they were under the Isaurian, who took those same revenues from the holy see. I do not doubt that Stephen had this in view. Since he says this in the letter in which he thanks Pippin for the addition of two provinces to the dominion of the holy see, I infer that whatever revenue was received from the Roman duchy, the exarchate, and the Pentapolis accrued not to the Roman pontiff but to the Roman commonwealth. For all income had to be expended on dukes, counts, and other offices, military nobles, and the soldiers themselves, for the proper administration of affairs. Therefore the church lamps, the poor, and the pilgrims, whom the pontifical treasury supported, depended on the patrimonies of the holy see; hence it is not surprising that these patrimonies, no less than the cities, were dear both to Stephen and to his successors.]

[Note: Those who assert that the Roman pontiffs of this period were concerned only with temporal matters read these letters less attentively. When necessity presses, they also labor for temporal affairs, so as to provide tranquility for the peoples; but their chief concern is the preservation of the whole Catholic faith throughout the Church.]

Thus, for the salvation of your soul, may the unceasing provision of lamps remain in the churches of God, and may the hunger of the poor, the needy, and the pilgrims likewise be relieved [Note: Perhaps “raised up”; Lambinus reads “refreshed”], and may they attain true satisfaction.

112 But as to what you said to the Silentiarius, or how your goodness dismissed him, together with a copy of the letter which you gave him [Note: Two imperial envoys, whose names were George the Protosecretary and John the Silentiarius, went to Pippin during the second Italian war and found that he had departed with the army. George hastened from Massilia, where both had arrived, to Ticinum, and, having tried unsuccessfully to turn the king away from granting the exarchate to the prince of the apostles, he withdrew without accomplishing his mission (Anastasius, section 251). The other seems to have awaited Pippin’s return in Francia; for we know with certainty from this passage that he conferred with the king and received letters from him for Copronymus. The content of the conversation and of the letters, however, was unknown to the pontiff himself], inform us, so that we may know how to act in common agreement, as was agreed between us and the God-beloved Folradus.

Our beloved son Folradus himself carried out everything in accordance with your command, and we gave him the greatest thanks for his struggle. Returning to you, he will report to your goodness how everything was conducted. We ask you to receive with a cheerful countenance and order to be accepted in every respect our present most faithful men, namely George, our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop, and John, our regional officer and sacristan. Whatever they say to your goodness in our name, deign to believe them in all things, and order them to return to us with the matter effectively accomplished and with joyful reports.

We also beseech your goodness to order our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Wicharius to be dismissed for joining us with the utmost speed [Baronius and the Centuriators: “to migrate”]. [Note: The manuscript has an error; it must be read “Wilharius,” who was bishop of Nomentum, as I stated in the note to letter 7, alternatively 9, column 110.]

May almighty God, most excellent victorious king, protect you in all your actions by the extension of his right hand; may he grant you and your most excellent queen, your sweetest wife and our spiritual co-mother, as well as your and my sweetest sons, the prosperity of the present life and eternal joys after the passage of many years; may he cause you to rejoice with the greatest happiness and enjoy the governance of your kingdom, which God has granted you; and may you, who hold the power of the kingdom in the present life, also reign with Christ forever in the age to come, deserving to hear that divine promise: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), because you have fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith. Take up the crowns laid up for you, and receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

For this too we learn about your exalted and God-protected excellence: the devout abbot Optatus of your monastery of Saint Benedict [Note: Lambinus reads: “Optatus, the devout abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, petitioned us”; Gentilotus: “the abbot of the monastery of Veneti.”] petitioned us on behalf of his monks, who had departed with your brother [Note: Carolomannus, Pippin’s brother, before Pippin’s elevation—namely, in 747—had become a monk through the hands of Pope Zachary (Annals of Fulda; Anastasius of Ostia, book I, chapter 8). After living for some time in the monastery of Soracte, he transferred to Cassino, which Petronax had restored. Under Abbot Optatus, who succeeded Petronax in 751, he went with other monks as leader of an embassy to his brother the king, at Aistulf’s command. This occurred at the end of 753, after Stephen had departed from Ticinum for Francia in November, arriving there at the beginning of the following year; Carolomannus was to recall his brother from the Italian expedition. When the attempt proved unsuccessful, by the counsel of the pontiff and the king he remained with his companions in the monastery of Saint-Denis, where he died that same year (Baronius, 754, §§7 ff.; Pagi, same year, §3, and 755, §§7 ff.). Optatus now asks for those companions again. It may be noted incidentally that Gretserus has “your monastery of Saint Benedict”; Lambecius does not read “your,” and Gentilotus has “of the Veneti,” perhaps “of Veneti.” For how could the Cassinese monastery in any way be said to belong to King Pippin? If this is established by the same letters, then both the Beneventans and the Spoletans first sought the king’s friendship so that they might not, like Aistulf, someday be subject to his power?], so that you might order them to be released; but order them to be dealt with according to whatever your will may be. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

114 **PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE ON THIRTY-ONE LETTERS OF SAINT PAUL I**

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133C] 1. After Stephen II died on 25 April 757, Paul, a deacon and, in God’s name, elected to the apostolic see, as stated in the title of the first letter of this pontiff to Pippin (Codex Carolinus 12, alternatively 13), occupied the chair of Peter—not following any earlier example in succeeding his brother—for ten years and one month, namely from the day of his consecration, 29 May, to 28 June 767. The reason for the delayed ordination was a very brief schism, which the better part of the clergy suppressed.

It was entirely fitting that he should be succeeded by his brother, through whom the dominion of the holy see had received so great an increase. But he ought to have imitated his brother not only in dignity but also in labors. For Desiderius, king of the Lombards, did not long preserve friendship with the Romans. Moreover, the immense danger from Greece did not allow the Church to rest. For when Copronymus awoke and heard that the exarchate and the Pentapolis—provinces wrested from the hands of the Lombards—had come under the authority of the Roman Church, he did not cease harassing not only those provinces but also Roman territory and the City itself, by arms and treachery.

Therefore, continually troubled by almost domestic difficulties and by external enemies, Paul departed this life before he could bring tranquility to himself and to the peoples subject to him. All this is evident from the letters that follow shortly. Yet first it is necessary to say something in general about them, so that, once I have reviewed them individually, their varied and manifold content may not cause me difficulty.

II. Most of the letters which we have so far seen had been published in 1564 by Flacius and his fellow Centuriators, and by their greatest opponent, Cardinal Baronius, in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*: namely, both letters of Gregory III, the single letter of Zachary, and four letters of Stephen II (7, 8, 10, 11, alternatively 9, 4, 3, 8, in the Codex Carolinus). They omitted letter 9, alternatively 6, as extremely similar to the preceding one; letters 4, 5, and 6, alternatively 10, 11, and 7, were entirely unknown.

The situation is different with Paul’s thirty-one letters. The Centuriators (*Centuries* VIII, chapter 10) boast that they received that many; but they are silent about where. Although they present only their summaries, they reveal in their boldest comments that they had examined the letters in full. For example, they say that Paul “appointed Peter as intercessor for victory against the enemies, in the third and ninth letters to Pippin” (Codex Carolinus 35, 33, alternatively 43, 30), a statement that cannot at all be extracted from the summaries.

Furthermore, from letter 12, which is falsely attributed to Paul but belongs to Adrian [Codex Carolinus 60, alternatively 73], as I shall show in its proper place, they offer the following, exposing the carelessness of all recent scholars: “For enlarging the kingdom, in letter 12 to Pippin: ‘That the prince of the apostles himself may intercede for you before the majesty of the Lord our God, so that he may enlarge your kingdom still further and grant victories.’”

I pass over their other tasteless comments; these statements alone prove sufficiently that they had Paul’s complete letters in their hands. This was not the case with Baronius, who candidly admits the fact (year 767, §1) concerning Paul’s thirty-one letters:

“Of these,” he says, “we have seen only the summaries briefly outlined and listed by Panvinius in his lives of the Roman pontiffs; he testifies that they are preserved in full in the Vatican library. Yet, although we searched for them for a long time, we were entirely unable to find them, and therefore suppose that they were removed from there either by theft or in some other manner. Nevertheless, there is no reason to cast suspicion upon his reliability, since the innovators likewise reproduce the same number of summaries (Centuries VIII, p. 725), who, weary of their length and variety—and even more of their truth—published not the letters themselves in full but only their summaries.”

[Col. 0135B] III. Gretserus transferred this passage of Baronius into his preface to the *Codex Carolinus*. But because Baronius’s diligence failed to perceive the true nature of these summaries, and because Gretserus’s judgment concerning them needs clarification, I think I shall perform a useful service by explaining this part of the history.

Onuphrius Panvinius, who had rendered outstanding service to Roman history and to all secular learning, had not turned his attention to ecclesiastical matters until 1553. Then, at the urging of Cardinal Marcello Cervini, he devoted himself entirely to such studies. Within a short period of eight years he published several works on pontiffs and cardinals, but above all he labored to compose at length their lives, which we have seen Baronius praise.

He himself bears witness to this in the 1562 Venetian edition of Platina’s history of the pontiffs, published by Michele Tramezzino. In the dedicatory letter to Pius IV, which he had sent to the press the preceding year together with Platina’s history, his own notes, and additions, he says: “Until I should publish the works which I myself had already, for the most part, composed on the same subject.”

At the beginning of his addition, he tells the reader: “I have already arranged, with the most exact diligence, a book far richer in content, in which I have written at length the lives of the 116 Roman pontiffs and cardinals whose memory survives; but since the work is of great size and difficulty, it could not be completed so easily, although I had already labored over it for a long time and with great effort.”

How rightly he emphasizes the difficulty of the undertaking is shown by the fact that, overtaken by a very premature death in 1568, he had not completed so great a work. It still exists, contained in several volumes, in the Vatican Library (Codex 6104); according to the notice prefixed to the work, it was collated from the gift of P. Ciaconius on 25 September 1592, and it begins with Saint Gregory the Great.

IV. In its third volume (folio 1125), where Paul’s deeds are discussed, the following brief statement appears:

“Paul wrote several letters to the kings Pippin and Carolomannus, to the Frankish army, and to certain others; thirty-one of them are preserved in the Vatican library, and I shall append their very brief summaries.”

The summaries of the individual letters then follow, “briefly outlined and listed.” Baronius saw them when he had been appointed librarian of the holy Roman Church by Clement VIII. Thus, when he published the eighth volume of his *Annals* in 1599, in which he discusses Paul’s deeds, Panvinius’s manuscript codices had also been added to that “great store of materials” which Baronius said he had collected in the dedication of volume I to Sixtus V in 1588, “as into some well-stocked treasury, especially against the innovators of our age, in defense of the antiquity of sacred traditions and the authority of the holy Roman Catholic Church.”

Yet two matters seem to have escaped the attention of this most learned writer: the former condition of the Vatican library and the reasons for Panvinius’s recension of those summaries.

V. As for the library, Nicholas V began its construction, and Sixtus IV completed it, as Panvinius himself testifies in his life of Sixtus, the first of those appended to Platina:

“He constructed the Palatine Library, famous throughout the whole world, within the Vatican, with Platina as prefect and with books brought from every part of Europe; and he assigned fixed revenues so that the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew custodians and librarians might have monthly salaries on which they could live and so that books might be purchased. It was the most outstanding work, worthy of the supreme pontiff.”

But it is not clear that he made provision for the books to remain permanently in the library, as Sixtus V did more than a century later for the new library, which was far superior both in location and in the quantity of books assembled, and more celebrated than the old one.

For this reason Panvinius elsewhere (Vatican Codex 3924) described catalogues of the books that had been in the library since the time of Innocent VIII but were no longer found in his own age. Among such books or codices taken from the Palatine Library, I do not see Paul’s letters listed.

Indeed, from the same source I learn that Panvinius knew the letters to be in the Vatican Library both when he committed Paul’s life to writing and when he narrated Adrian’s deeds—that is, before 1561. For in that year, as we saw above, he admitted to Pius IV and informed his readers that he had completed the pontifical history for the most part.

Since this work was to extend over almost ten centuries, from the ninety-sixth pope, Gregory the Great, to the sixteenth century, in which Panvinius flourished, it cannot be said, thought, or imagined that less than two centuries constituted the greater part of the work. Nor is it permissible either to accuse so great a man of lying or to attribute to him so dull an intellect that he advanced exceedingly slowly along a long road he had undertaken.

It must therefore be regarded as certain that those pontifical letters existed in the Vatican or Palatine Library before 1561. What happened to them during the thirty years preceding 1592, when the new Vatican Library acquired Panvinius’s work, and how they perished, I leave to others to conjecture.

[Col. 0136C] VI. I shall now explain the reasons for Panvinius’s recension, which, as I said, escaped the principal historian of the Church. In 1564 that eighth *Century* appeared, in whose tenth chapter the summaries of Paul’s thirty-one letters and Adrian’s forty-four letters are read exactly as they appear in Panvinius’s history.

Not a single word appears to have been changed, except in their description—a change which everyone will say was deliberately made. For they say:

“Paul wrote several letters to Pippin, to Carolomannus, to the Frankish army, and to certain others: we received thirty-one manuscripts.”

If these words are compared with those which I quoted above from Panvinius, it will be seen that “kings” has been removed, for a reason unknown to us, and “we received” has been put in place of “are preserved in the Vatican Library.”

The same is true of Adrian’s letters. Where Panvinius (folio 1156) wrote, “Forty-four of his letters written to King Charles are preserved in the Vatican Library; it will be worthwhile to indicate their summaries,” the Magdeburg Centuriators say: “We received his forty-four manuscript letters to Charles; we have thought it worthwhile to indicate their summaries.”

Who does not see from this that perhaps some idle copyist—or certainly a false brother—secretly sent a copy of Panvinius’s labors to the authors of the *Centuries*, for them to use or abuse, provided only that the accursed hunger for gold might be satisfied?

From the great similarity and agreement on both sides Gretserus inferred that the Magdeburg Centuriators had seen the Onuphrian codex.

“For what library,” he says, “was not open to these plunderers and to their assistants and agents?”

But he is mistaken when he supposes that the Magdeburg Centuriators “customarily scattered slanders here and there.” Panvinius copied those summaries from the Vatican codex exactly as they are read in the Centuriators; and what seem to Gretserus to be slanders have no other author than Panvinius, who copied them word for word from that codex, without noticing that they sometimes contained a word readily capable of being twisted into a bad sense.

When he saw at Leipzig that the material had been committed to the press either too freely or not accurately enough, he corrected it in a second revision.

VII. This is certainly the recension of which Baronius speaks. What I find astonishing is that so great a man did not see that the summaries, as they had first been written by Panvinius, are found exactly in the Magdeburg Centuriators.

The words deleted or added at the end—not to mention those written above or inserted—and likewise several letters either added or removed in Panvinius’s codex, are so evident that they leap into the reader’s eyes of themselves.

Accordingly, anyone comparing the Magdeburg edition with Panvinius’s manuscript codex will find such evident similarity and agreement on both sides that, with me, he will be surprised that Baronius’s diligence was less exact in this matter.

I say nothing further about Gretserus’s error except that pardon should be granted to a most learned man who did not have Panvinius’s codex before his eyes but embraced Baronius’s judgment, adding only what the acuity of his intellect and his long engagement with ecclesiastical matters suggested should be said.

Therefore, the accusation of slander which Gretserus, in good faith, directed against the innovators but which fell back upon Panvinius must be interpreted as follows: the words and statements upon which Gretserus insists were spoken by those whose perverse intention makes them appear—and renders them—slanderous in everything concerning the apostolic see and in many matters concerning the Catholic religion. But in the case of a Catholic writer, who first extracted them from the codex with the utmost fidelity and then carefully corrected them so that they might not be committed to the press in that form, I think the mark of imprudence rather than slander should be applied.

VIII. To this must be added that this most learned man, still in the heat of youth and not yet accustomed to writing ecclesiastical history, not only copied those summaries or arguments of the letters which had been written carelessly in various places, but had himself sprinkled the entire pontifical history here and there with statements insufficiently guarded.

For this reason, in the Vatican manuscripts one sees the same history everywhere rendered more polished through a second revision. Nor is this surprising. When Baronius turned his mind to writing the *Annals*, he had already devoted thirty years to ecclesiastical matters, as he himself expressly states in volume I, in the dedicatory letter to Sixtus V:

“When ecclesiastical history had already been repeated by me seven times in chronological order over six lustrums.”

Panvinius, by contrast, composed that pontifical history while still a novice in ecclesiastical matters. He himself testifies to this before his addition to Platina, warning the reader in these words:

“About eight years ago, at the urging of Cardinal Marcello of Santa Croce, whom we later saw become supreme pontiff, to whose patronage I had then wholly entrusted myself, admiring the virtues of that blessed and most holy man, I turned my attention from writing secular histories to treating and explaining ecclesiastical matters, which until that time had been attempted by few, and then only lightly, or had been entirely neglected.”

X. I carefully copied those summaries, intending to place them before all readers. But because there is great discrepancy between them and the letters of the *Codex Carolinus*—for the letters are arranged in different orders, and the chronology is less than exact in both places—I decided to append each summary to its corresponding letter. I have attempted to assign them to approximately certain years, since some recent scholars have allowed them to wander far too freely; taking advantage of the uncertainty of the dates, they thought they could move them at will in support of their own opinions.

No one should think that I have done this merely to abuse my own leisure and that of the reader. A shorter course could indeed have been followed by stating that the summaries or arguments of the letters first written by Panvinius are precisely those reported by the Centuriators with complete fidelity; while those which Panvinius himself revised were first published by Baronius in his *Annals* and then transferred into the collection of the councils.

But the most learned cardinal did not hesitate occasionally to alter either a word or a meaning to some extent, nor did he always follow the corrections. Let the examples which I now excerpt from the letters of Paul according to the recension serve as evidence.

In the first letter (Codex Carolinus 12, alternatively 13), one reads: “The friendship contracted with the Franks by that same Stephen.” Baronius changed it to: “The friendship entered into with the Franks.”

In the eighth letter (Codex Carolinus 25, alternatively 34), Panvinius says: “He reports that the Greek emperor is under arms in order to recover the exarchate of Ravenna and Rome.” Baronius, partly following the first reading and partly the correction, says: “He reports that the emperor is under arms and wishes to recover the exarchate of Ravenna and Rome.”

In the eleventh letter (Codex Carolinus 24, alternatively 31), Panvinius said that a rumor was being spread “by the enemies”; Baronius, “by the friends.”

Finally, in the fifteenth letter (Codex Carolinus 13, alternatively 27), Panvinius wrote: “The fifteenth, written through Wulfardus, a fellow bishop—whom he commends to Pippin by the example of his brother Stephen—contains praises …” Baronius: “Writing, in that letter there are praises …”

120 X. As I said, these same summaries were transferred from Baronius’s *Annals* into the collection of Labbeus. But how different most of them are there from Panvinius’s versions!

Labbeus, unlike Baronius, was able to consult the edition of the *Codex Carolinus*, which appeared at Ingolstadt six years after Baronius’s death; and when he found some summaries less clear or less exact, he was able to publish fuller and clearer versions. That he did so can plainly be seen (*Councils*, volume VI, pages 1672, 1756 and following).

Indeed, while I myself was carefully examining the same letters in order to prepare fuller and more explanatory summaries, I came to the fifty-sixth letter of the *Codex Carolinus*, Adrian’s twenty-fifth, which for me is letter 71 and concerns the complete restoration of the Sabine patrimony.

In Gretserus’s edition that patrimony is called “Ravennate,” and in Lambecius’s edition also “Ravennate.” Since I had been informed by Gentilotus’s latest recension that no capital letters were used in the text of that codex, I easily discovered the cause of the corrupt reading.

For Mabillon (Supplement to the *Diplomata*, p. 70) gives a specimen of the Roman-Lombard script that was in use in Adrian’s time, taken from authentic letters of that same pontiff written on papyrus and preserved in the archive of Corbie. In that script I observed such similarity between *s* and *r* that one could easily be taken for the other. I also observed that *u* was frequently used for *b*, and finally that *i* was habitually written without a dot.

For this reason, indulgence seemed appropriate toward the person who copied Adrian’s letters from the originals when Charles wished them to be included in the *Codex*. Panvinius himself, more significantly, made the same mistake. For, reading in the synopsis *Patrimonium sancti Petri apud Ravennatenses* (“the patrimony of Saint Peter among the Ravennates”), he himself in a second revision wrote *Ravennates*. How close this is to the meaning of the letters is made clear by a simple reading of them.

Apart from the fact that the patrimony at Ravenna, so celebrated in Gregory the Great’s time, had no reason to be mentioned again now that the entire exarchate had been added to the pontifical dominion, Adrian elsewhere (letter 59, alternatively 49) clearly discusses the Sabine patrimony among the possessions that were to be restored, without mentioning the Ravennate patrimony at all.

XI. What more is there to say? After inspecting the letters, Labbeus brought the question to an end by presenting this summary:

“That the entire Sabine patrimony of Saint Peter had not been handed over, and that the king’s own envoys, Itherius and Maginarius, would testify to this if they were ordered to swear while holding his right hand.”

I am surprised that Pagius and his recent censor, P. Mansi, passed over this matter, especially since Muratori, who never misses an opportunity to weaken the pontiffs’ dominion in the exarchate, expressly noted (year 778) that “Sabine” should be read instead of “Ravennate.”

He would certainly not have done this unless compelled by the meaning of the letters; for once Pippin’s donation of the exarchate and the Pentapolis is admitted on that ground, it calls the holy see’s ownership into question and almost tears it apart. For amusement, one may consult the *Italian Annals* for the years 1017, 1026, 1034, 1198, 1239, 1240, and 1249.

What better opportunity could have been offered to him than Adrian’s reclamation of the Ravennate patrimony?

For my part, I have judged Labbeus’s summaries inferior to Panvinius’s for two reasons. First, although they may be more accurate in some respects, they do not fully contain the meaning of the letters. Second, although Panvinius’s versions are found among the Magdeburg Centuriators as they were first written, and in Baronius according to the recension made by the author, nowhere are they preserved in their genuine form, both in their first and second revisions, except in the Vatican codex. From that codex they may be said to be brought to light by me for the first time.

So much for the summaries of the letters; now for the letters themselves.

XII. They exceed the fraternal letters in number and are also richer than they in the variety of matters they contain. As regards the dominion of the apostolic see, however, they introduce nothing new, although several restorations of places and possessions are mentioned that are highly uncertain and full of obscurity.

For example, Paul testifies (letter 18, alternatively 15) that Desiderius had promised to return the cities of Imola, Bologna, Auximum, and Ancona, but later broke faith. Elsewhere (letter 20, alternatively 21), speaking of patrimonies, rights, places, boundaries, and territories, he says:

“In part, this same king of the Lombards is known to have rendered these rights to us, and he declares and altogether promises that he will render all the remaining rights to us.”

And since, in letter 21, alternatively 23, Paul thanks Pippin through Bishop George for so many benefits, it is believable that Desiderius kept his promises, but it cannot be asserted with certainty. Similar cases occur elsewhere.
