Therefore, Paul should not be said or imagined to have been more fortunate than his brother Stephen, although he held the pontificate for twice as long. For as long as he lived, he labored to vindicate the dominion of Saint Peter against the inconstancy of the same Lombard king.

At times he even feared the Greeks on behalf of the city of Rome itself (letter 25, alternatively 34); often on behalf of the exarchate and the Pentapolis (letters 26, alternatively 28; 33, alternatively 30; 36, alternatively 32; 38, alternatively 24). Since these letters, which bear witness to such matters, lack a date—except one or two—their authors arrange them at their own discretion in accordance with the differing opinions of different scholars.

Yet no damage results from this to the dominion of the apostolic see. As I said, no addition was made to it in Paul’s time. Its ancient dominion—namely, Rome and its duchy—as well as the territory enlarged by King Pippin, first in 754, when the pact or diploma of donation was issued and confirmed at Quierzy, and then in 755, when the hostages of the individual cities and their keys provided abundant testimony to Fulradus’s taking possession of the exarchate and the Pentapolis—has almost as many certain monuments as there are letters.

Paul calls the cities of the Roman province his own no less than those of the exarchate and the Pentapolis. We find this expressly done with respect to both dominions (letter 39, alternatively 14), where he complains about new Lombard attacks:

“In our city of Sinigaglia,” he says, “as they were proceeding, they devastated with iron and fire the places situated outside that same city … Likewise, making a hostile incursion into the parts of Campania, namely our fortress called Valentia,” and so forth.

XIII. As regards the authority of these letters, I believe that none of the ancient records rests upon a stronger foundation than these letters, especially those of Paul and Adrian.

We see thirty-one of them entered in the *Codex*; the same number reached the hands of the Magdeburg Centuriators from the Vatican codex; and no difference is found between the two collections except in the summaries or synopses, some of which nevertheless agree with one another. For, although drawn from the substance of each letter and not always accurately, they sometimes attain a certain similarity.

I said that thirty-one existed in both places, which at first sight appears false. For thirty-two are numbered in the *Codex*, while one fewer is found among the Magdeburg Centuriators, or in Panvinius’s Vatican codex. Someone may perhaps wonder about this.

But he must observe that the thirtieth and thirty-third letters of the *Codex Carolinus*—the latter being the ninth in the Vatican codex and our thirty-third letter—are one and the same letter, written twice. Once it had been published by Panvinius and others, and when the duplicate is removed, the number is equal: thirty-one remain in both places.

From each collection, however, one letter must be removed because it does not belong to Pope Paul: namely, the thirty-sixth letter of the *Codex Carolinus*, which the Roman senate and people sent to Pippin; and the twelfth letter of Panvinius’s codex, which, as I said above (no. 2), intruded among Paul’s letters although it must certainly be numbered among Adrian’s letters, as it is in the *Codex Carolinus* (letter 60, alternatively 73).

Thus all surprise concerning the number of letters disappears. A further source of surprise also vanishes entirely: namely, the summary of a letter not included in the *Codex*, which appears between letters 21 and 22 of the *Codex Carolinus*. It is in fact a copy of letter 15—our letter 18—as I shall say in the notes.

123 XIV. That letter 18, or 15, is by no means unimportant. Paul relates the condition of the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento before Desiderius’s election:

“They placed themselves,” he says to Pippin, “under your power, which has been preserved by God.”

He then adds the succession of both and explains how Arichis had been appointed successor to Liutprand, duke of Benevento, by Desiderius himself, in the year 758, to which the letter belongs.

Thus both dukes, under Pope Paul, again became subject to the Lombard king, and it is not known that they ever returned to Pippin. Indeed, Arichis did not even come under Charles’s authority, as Erchempertus testifies. When the Lombard kings were expelled—namely, when Desiderius was captured and taken to Francia, and his son Adelgisus escaped in flight to Constantinople in 774—Arichis, having assumed the title of prince, administered the duchy of Benevento like a king. He did so until Charles subjected the duchy to himself by an expedition undertaken against the Beneventans in 787. I shall discuss this matter in the letters of Adrian.

Erchempertus’s words concerning Arichis’s principate are as follows:

“§3. This Arichis was the first at Benevento to order himself to be called prince. Until him, those who had ruled Benevento were called dukes. For he also had himself anointed by bishops, placed a crown upon his own head, and ordered that in his charters the following formula be written at the end: ‘Written in our most sacred palace.’”

The anonymous Salernitan writer (chapter 9) clearly connects the beginning of this principate with the destruction of the Lombard kingdom—or, better put, with the overthrow of Desiderius:

“And King Charles himself,” he says, “was established as lord of all Italy. Duke Arichis alone remained at Benevento, disregarding his commands, because he carried a precious crown upon his head.”

From the year 758, when he was appointed duke by Desiderius, whose daughter he also married, until 774, when his father-in-law was overthrown, Arichis professed complete submission to the Lombard king.

For this reason Paul, fearing the Greeks, asks Pippin (letter 25, alternatively 34) to admonish Desiderius concerning the endangered Church, so that Desiderius himself might aid the Romans and command “the Beneventans and Spoletans, as well as the Tuscans,” who bordered on the ecclesiastical territory, to do the same.

### XV

These things being so, I cannot understand why neither Panvinio, nor Gretser, nor Labbe, nor Pagius (I except Baronius, who did not see the letters), nor any other learned men realized that that synopsis, or summary, of the twelfth letter among Paul’s letters cannot be assigned to the period of that pontiff. Indeed, the summary runs as follows:

> “The twelfth recounts the injury inflicted by the Beneventans. He asks that Pippin rebuke them by letter and, if they are unwilling to obey, that he agree to the expedition undertaken against them.”

But let us set aside this general negligence. All those learned men, including even Baronius (although the letters of the Carolingian Codex were not then available to him, though they ought to have been consulted), saw in the Magdeburg Centuries [Col. 0141A] (Century VIII, chapter 10) these few words excerpted from those letters:

> “And for the enlargement of the kingdom, in Letter 12 to Pippin, that the prince of the apostles himself may intercede for you before the majesty of the Lord our God, so that he may enlarge your kingdom further and grant you victories.”

These words, exactly as written, are found in Adrian’s Letter 60 (formerly 73), which in the Carolingian Codex has no summary. I do not ask how this summary found its way among Paul’s letters in the Vatican Codex; but I call the wandering item back to its proper place, and find it written in the year 777, when Charles, occupied with the Saxon war and contemplating a campaign in Spain against the Saracens, gave the duke of Benevento an opportunity to venture forth.

I do this especially to rebuke the freedom taken by those who, in order to defend their own opinions, have displaced many of these letters and thereby corrupted the entire history of that period. Yet whenever anything really had to be moved, whether because the sequence of events contained in it demanded this or because of religious scruple, they either refrained from touching it or rashly declared it lost without investigating the matter. [Col. 0141B]

### XVI

The same Pope Paul seems to affirm that some letters really were lost in the letter recently cited (Letter 18, formerly 15). For, having long and severely suffered at Desiderius’ hands, he addresses Pippin as follows:

> “Behold, we have secretly sent Your Excellency two declarations in apostolic letters, with the greatest care, and we do not know whether those letters themselves have reached you; hence we fear that they may have been intercepted by the Lombards.”

That they did arrive is clear, as I said, from their summary, which was entered into the Codex between Letters 21 and 22. Paul adds that he had issued other letters as well (Letter 17, formerly 29), at Desiderius’ request, candidly stating:

> “Therefore we drafted these letters in such a way that our envoys themselves might be able to pass through to you in Francia.”

Stephen III later imitated this example (Letter 45, formerly 46), to the great disadvantage of posterity, for Stephen did not, following Paul’s example, warn the king in another letter not to place any trust in letters fabricated in this manner. Consequently, later writers preferred to accuse the historian Anastasius, who was reporting the truth, of falsehood rather than accuse the pontifical letters of containing false material, since they found the interpretation of those letters more suited to their own opinion. [Col. 0141C]

Moreover, confidence is added to the letters of Paul’s predecessors, which were entered into this Codex by order of Charlemagne, by the copies of those letters published by Baronius from the Vatican Codices. Panvinio testifies that the individual Pauline letters were in the Vatican Library around the middle of the sixteenth century; and since an equal number existed both at Rome and in Francia, it is scarcely credible that some did not perish. If any did disappear, mention of them occurs in later letters, so that, apart from those matters always entrusted to the envoys’ discretion, nothing remains that ought to be missed.

### XVII

I must therefore attempt to extract from these letters a history of the pontificate purified both of the crafty interpretations of innovators and of the doubtful or false opinions of certain recent writers. Someone might think that this could easily be accomplished by arranging most of the wandering letters according to the correct chronological order. But who could determine the date of letters that, for the most part, are silent about important events? Who could divine what was entrusted to the ears of envoys? Who could grasp the complete meaning of letters sometimes attached to them?

It seems to me that the task can be completed by considering only two matters. The first concerns the Catholic faith and the veneration of sacred images; the second concerns the territory of the Holy See. Beginning from this point, I conclude, on the authority of these letters—which cover a ten-year history—that no addition was made to ecclesiastical territory throughout that entire period. Therefore nothing else is found in Paul’s letters besides the ancient territory of the Holy See, that is, the Roman duchy, and its enlargement through Pippin’s donation, which includes the exarchate and the Pentapolis.

Adrian testifies that Paul’s letters remain within these limits [Col. 0142A] (Letter 51, formerly 54). For, intending to remove the harassment caused by the archbishop of Ravenna after the Lombards had been expelled, he writes to Charles:

> “Just as in the time of Lord Pope Stephen, who went there to Francia and to whom the exarchate itself was handed over, so also in our time we wish to administer and govern it under our authority.”

### XVIII

From this it is also clear that the exarchate was in a better condition under Stephen than under Paul. Nevertheless, I find no city taken from Paul either by the Lombards or by the Greeks. I find only devastations and plundering carried out between the Romans and the Lombards; accordingly, it is clear that both sides demanded the return of what had been taken (Letters 29, 38, 39, and 40, formerly 17, 24, 14, and 26).

Furthermore, I find that borders, territories, and estates were never fully restored by the Lombards, who were skilled in the art of deceit (Letters 18, 20, 33, and 42, formerly 15, 21, 30, and 19). I see four cities listed among those whose hostages were neither given by Aistulf’s envoys nor whose keys were delivered to be placed at the confession of blessed Peter (Letters 17 and 18, formerly 29 and 15); nor do I find that Pope Paul took possession of those cities. From this, however, I think it may be inferred that all the others were obtained either by his predecessor Stephen from Aistulf or Desiderius, or by Paul himself from this last king of the Lombards. [Col. 0142B]

The strongest evidence for the matter comes from the Eastern emperors, who left no stone unturned in their effort to wrest from the Apostolic See the territories it had lost through impiety and negligence. They repeatedly attempted to win the Frankish king’s goodwill through frequent embassies and to detach him from friendship with the Roman pontiff by means of slanders (Letter 37 and 40, formerly 20 and 26).

Moreover, by repeatedly declaring that they would attack the exarchate and the Pentapolis, and even the city of Rome itself, and by boasting of a great military preparation, they instilled fear only in the pontiff and the Romans (Letters 25, 26, 27, 28, and 33, formerly 34, 28, 37, 42, and 30). I say “boasting,” for until Adrian’s time they merely threatened the Romans. It is clear from Adrian’s letters that only then, after entering into an alliance with the Lombards of Benevento on the pretext of restoring Adelgis to the kingdom of his ancestors, did they proceed to arms, though without success. [Col. 0142C]

### XIX

As for the Catholic faith and the veneration of sacred images, almost the entire substance of the letters of this holy pontiff consists in the defense of the Catholic faith and the tradition of the Fathers; by the latter expression he means sacred images. Although he was working for Pippin’s donation, as was just, he was concerned not with the wealth of the treasury, as some suppose, but with the salvation of the peoples, lest, upon returning to Greek rule, they be contaminated by the Greeks’ heresy. The peoples themselves, rejecting that rule, desired pontifical government (Letter 15, formerly 36).

This is why one sees this pontiff, and his successor Adrian, reclaiming patrimonies and other revenues assigned to the support of the poor and pilgrims, as well as those necessary for maintaining the lights of churches and for many other expenditures, neither few nor small, with even greater urgency than they sought to enlarge cities and places under their jurisdiction. [Col. 0142D]

His first and greatest concern was the preservation of the Catholic faith not only in the West but also in the East. This is especially attested by the great joy with which he almost exultantly sent Pippin a copy of the letter of Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, so that Pippin might rejoice with him over the orthodox faith’s vigorous defense by the Eastern bishops and might be encouraged all the more earnestly to defend it in the West (Letter 31, formerly 35).

There is also another letter, full of joy, to Charles and Carloman (Letter 30, formerly 40), in which, when the envoy returned from Francia to Rome, Paul learned from their letters that they would imitate their father in the constant and perpetual defense of the Catholic faith and the Holy Church.

These things certainly accord with the most holy character of this pontiff, which no one who has read the account written by Anastasius fails to notice; and they accord with the honor that the entire Catholic Church bestowed upon him after he exchanged mortal life for heavenly life. Even today, when we look upon the same man’s paternal house, converted into the church called Saint Sylvester in Capite—the house inhabited by Greek monks expelled by the image-breakers—we laugh at the wit of the innovators and judge several false opinions of recent writers among our own people worthy of pity more than admiration. [Col. 0143A]

### XX

Indeed, whose stomach would not be upset by opinions of this kind, which, if seriously considered, prove to have arisen from the wit of innovators? I am ashamed to repeat what everyone can read in printed works in the Italian language. I must not remain silent about one point: I am not surprised that innovators, who were unworthy to enjoy the company of the heavenly beings, abused the sincere sentiments of the holy pontiff, expressed with the simplicity characteristic of that age. But I consider it greatly astonishing that Catholic writers imitated this indignity.

It is better, however, to continue the discussion of the letters that we began. However much diligence someone may employ in denying that Paul was the ruler of Rome, he is wasting his efforts by extracting an ambiguous statement from one of the thirty-one letters.

Nearly thirty years had passed since the Holy Commonwealth—that is, Rome and its duchy—had for a legitimate religious reason shaken off the imperial yoke. Four years later, that same Commonwealth had received a major enlargement from the Frankish king, with the exarchate and the Pentapolis added to its ancient territory. Paul then ascended the chair of blessed Peter.

At that time the duke of Naples, a duchy that was especially small and was the only territory, apart from southern Calabria and the island of Sicily, still remaining to the Greeks in Italy, was Stephen,

> “who, at the beginning of his administration, ordered that money from his revenue be given to the lord pope and that everyone display the obedience owed to the Roman Church. For this reason he was greatly loved by the same lord pope, and he promised that, if the emperor should send his soldiers against Rome, the duke himself would bring him aid with his own soldiers.”

So teaches the Neapolitan Chronicle edited by the distinguished Pratillo (*History of the Lombards*, vol. III, p. 32), agreeing with the contemporary author of Paul’s deeds preserved by Anastasius.

This alliance between the duke of Naples and the pontiff deprived the Greeks of every hope of attempting anything in central Italy. Moreover, while the exarchate still stood, neither the exarch Eutychius, together with his Lombard ally, had prevailed against Rome, nor had the elated duke of Naples been able to resist the Romans. Indeed, by his own death and the captivity of his people, he gave posterity an example not to dare revive the shattered Greek cause in Italy. [Col. 0143C]

### XXI

For this reason, when Paul heard that the Greeks were preparing a fleet against Ravenna and Rome, he did indeed seek, through Pippin’s authority, assistance from the people of Spoleto and Benevento, with the Tuscans also included, in order to repel the attack. But when he explained the reasons for the Greeks’ undertaking, he did not mention the Romans’ defection from the Greeks, nor the recent addition of Ravenna and the Pentapolis to the ancient territory—events that ought undoubtedly to have moved the Greeks. Instead, he gave as the chief cause the very source from which the defection, the enlargement of the territory, and especially the friendship and alliance with the Frankish king had arisen: namely, the persecution of the Catholic faith and of sacred images (Letter 25, formerly 34).

This cause, however poorly it may sound to innovators and to those who discuss civil affairs without taking religion into account, was of the greatest importance to Pippin, since it alone made all the Greeks’ schemes appear utterly contemptible.

Now, those who are astonished that the pontiff did not say that Copronymus was angered by Rome’s usurped territory—which had defected thirty years earlier, in the time of his father Constantine—should be asked why they are not equally astonished that the pontiff is not said to have been provoked even by the invasion of the exarchate, which had been added to Roman territory only a few years earlier.

Elsewhere they also marvel that the pontiff informed Pippin of the departure from Constantinople of six patricians with a fleet, intending to go to Rome and to Francia (Letter 38, formerly 24), yet gave no indication of fear. But, to speak frankly, these are merely supports for slander. Did the pontiff not say that those patricians were undertaking their journey for an unknown reason? Did he not clearly report that they had been ordered to go first to him and then to the Frankish king? What, then, should he fear while pontifical, imperial, and royal envoys were traveling back and forth voluntarily on behalf of the great cause of the Catholic faith?

“But,” they say, “he must have feared the fleet and the accompanying Sicilians.” What follows from that? If such a military force had departed from the imperial city against the Roman city, then the Roman city that the Greeks were attempting to attack was under someone else’s jurisdiction. It is therefore clear that their iniquity had lied about its own rights. By the same arguments with which they try to deprive the pontiff of Rome, they unwillingly affirm Rome to be his.

These points, however, are minor. Other matters of greater importance are not lacking.

### XXII

Whatever Pope Paul relates about the meeting between George, the imperial secretary, and Desiderius (Letter 18, formerly 15); whatever he reports about the imperial letters of Leo and about those brought by the Venetians (Letter 26, formerly 28); finally, whatever he tells Pippin about the movement of the six patricians—all this must necessarily be treated as threats, not to say as popular rumor, by anyone who reconstructs the history of that period from reliable documents, especially from Anastasius and from the letters of this Carolingian Codex. [Col. 0144B]

For as long as Paul occupied the papal chair, much fear of the Greeks is found, but no action, except for the secret conversations of embassies arranged to travel back and forth.

What we learn with certainty is that, in that very letter concerning the six patricians, the pontiff once and again calls the cities of the Roman duchy “our cities.” Elsewhere, as stated above, he calls Senigallia, a city in the Pentapolis, “our city,” just as he calls the fortress of Valentia in Campania “our fortress” (Letter 39, formerly 14). One can see this same practice followed everywhere, whenever circumstances required it, in the letters that follow shortly.

When the order of events brings us to Adrian’s letters, it will become clear that the Greeks really did arrive, under an evil omen, at our city of Centumcellae (Letter 63, formerly 65), and that, after entering into an alliance with the Beneventan Lombards, they attempted—most importantly—to invade this Roman city of ours (Letter 57, formerly 59). [Col. 0144C]

Thus, both when Paul feared that the Greeks might arrive and when they certainly did arrive under Pope Adrian, Rome and the other cities of the Roman province were under the authority of the Roman pontiff.

Nor do those frivolous arguments have the character of history: namely, that Paul confessed in his own words that the Greeks opposed the Romans solely because of the Catholic faith, and that he did not show sufficient fear when he heard that a fleet was departing from the imperial city. In my opinion, to entertain such ideas is extremely frivolous; but what would it be to commit them to writing?

### XXIII

Since these things are so, it is not of great importance to establish the exact chronological order in which Paul’s letters were written. Nevertheless, although it is altogether impossible, for the reasons given above, to preserve a certain order, I must restrain the freedom of those who follow an order wholly at odds with the truth. [Col. 0144D]

In each of his letters Paul greets Pippin by the title “my spiritual co-father,” except in the first of them (Letter 12, formerly 13), which he wrote before his consecration. It is therefore wrongly placed as the sixth letter, which he received through Abbot Wulfard together with the *sabanus*, through which he acquired the title of co-father. I am surprised that Cointius, Pagius, and the recent editors of Duchesne failed entirely to notice this (Letter 13, formerly 27).

Three of these letters (16, 19, and 36, formerly 25, 39, and 32) contain the history of Marinus, a Roman priest. They teach that he was made cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus at the request of King Pippin, who regarded him as a man supremely faithful to both pontiff and king. Later he was accused of treachery before the Frankish king by the emperor’s envoys; the king made the pontiff responsible for the matter, and Marinus was condemned for high treason; finally, he was restored to his former honor.

But how can anyone recount this history with letters placed so perversely that the cardinal’s dignity appears to have been conferred as a reward for treachery? And, something utterly incredible, how can anyone confine it within the limits of a single year, 758?

The last of these letters mentions the severity of the preceding winter (Letter 36, formerly 32), remembered by both Greek and Latin historians. They differ only in this: some assign it to the year 763, when it began in October; others to 764, when it was most severe in January and February. The letter also concerns envoys sent at that time both by the king and by the pontiff to Constantinople, and especially the peaceful condition of Church affairs then, achieved through Pippin’s efforts. These are all unmistakable features of the year 764.

Nevertheless, they prefer to date this letter to the year 758, those most difficult times when Desiderius was pursuing the dukes of Benevento and Spoleto as rebels and inflicting on the pontiff and the Romans all the damage he could. [Col. 0145A]

### XXIV

This resulted in nine of the thirty-one letters being assigned to the year 757, eleven to 758, and one or two letters being assigned to each of the following nine years. How false this is in itself is obvious. Since most of the letters are replies to royal letters, a certain interval must reasonably be allowed for envoys to arrive and return, lest monks, dukes, bishops, and other distinguished men who served as envoys appear to have rushed back and forth day and night like couriers, using horses stationed along the route.

I say nothing about the many contradictions forced upon us by compressing so many letters into a single year. Among these are the claims that Paul endured hostilities and cultivated peace (Letters 18 and 23, formerly 15 and 30); that Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, was entangled in lawsuits at Rome while receiving letters at Ravenna from the imperial city and from the faithful Venetians, which he then sent to Rome (Letters 13 and 26, formerly 27 and 28); and, finally, that King Desiderius had concluded an alliance with the Greeks against Ravenna, while the pontiff asked Pippin to order Desiderius to aid him against the Greeks (Letters 18 and 26, formerly 15 and 28).

Even if these events did not contradict one another at all, it is incredible that they occurred during the seven months belonging to Paul in the year 757, namely from 29 May, when he was consecrated, to the end of the year. [Col. 0145C]

As for the eleven letters crowded into the following year, 758, the history of the priest Marinus, recently presented, sufficiently shows what should be thought of them.

This freedom must therefore be restrained—if not by an absolutely certain order, then at least by a more probable order that does not in any respect conflict with the truth—by placing Paul’s letters in their proper sequence. Establishing their exact chronology is of little importance. It is essential, however, to do this for the far more numerous and more important letters that Adrian sent to King Charles concerning the new and extensive enlargement of ecclesiastical territory, especially after the Lombards had been expelled. The displacement of those letters has supplied considerable support for the opinions of recent writers.

### XXV

Before I finish speaking about these letters, I wish to impress this upon the reader: from Paul’s time onward, when everyone recognized the supreme authority of the pontiff within his territory, royal envoys exercised considerable authority both in the exarchate and the Pentapolis—the provinces within which they restrict the territory of the Church—and at Rome and in its duchy.

Thus Widmar and Gerbert, abbots, together with Hugbald, a distinguished man, carefully examined the Lombard envoys before the pontiff in an assembly of people from the Pentapolis and other pontifical cities, and investigated the cause of the invasions (Letter 29, formerly 17).

In the same way, Andrew and Gunderic, royal envoys, investigated another dispute between the pontiff and the Lombards (Letter 29, formerly 17). In the same way, Andrew and Gunderic, royal envoys, investigated another dispute between the pontiff and the Lombards (Letter 39, formerly 14).

Finally, Bishop Wilchar, Dodo, and Wichard, royal envoys, were deliberately sent to Rome to examine the question of restitutions between the same pontiff and the Lombards (Letter 42, formerly 19).

What are these proceedings other than judicial assemblies closely resembling those whose one surviving record has been dug out from the age of Pious Louis and exaggerated in order to weaken pontifical authority?

I do see this distinction between the proceedings of the envoys of King Pippin and those of his grandson: a document from one of Louis’s proceedings has come to light (Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, appendix, no. 52). The proceedings of Pippin, however, and even those of his son Charles, although they were not committed to writing or have since perished, are nevertheless certain, since they are mentioned in the letters of the Carolingian Codex. [Col. 0146A]

Since it is perfectly clear that Pippin’s envoys exercised authority only with the pontiff’s consent and at the king’s request, the same must be thought of the envoys of Pious Louis and his successors, and even of the emperors themselves, some of whose proceedings are extant, held at Rome with pontiff and emperor deciding together.

As for the emperors, however, it had been established how their authority and that of the pontiffs were to cooperate in administering affairs; this will be made clear in its proper place.

In any event, the origin and character of the authority exercised by royal envoys within the pontiffs’ territory can be drawn most clearly from Paul’s letters.

### XXVI

Let the witnesses to the recently mentioned judicial proceedings be read:

> “In accordance with what we sent requesting, you appear to have sent to us the envoys whom you mentioned, so that they might stand before the king of the Lombards on behalf of various causes and rights of the Holy Church of God, and assist us with their support.”

Likewise:

> “We sent to Your Excellency a request that you agree to send one of your envoys, so that, through his presence, justice might be achieved between the parties.”

And elsewhere (Letter 34, formerly 18):

> “Immediately deign to send one of your men to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if necessity should arise, he may provide us with the assistance that we have indicated against those same enemies . . . We also beseech Your Excellency, established by God, that, when the month of March arrives, you order one of your men to be sent to us, who must remain here at Rome with us and, if necessity should demand it, himself stand before Desiderius.”

The same request is repeated elsewhere (Letter 27, formerly 37).

If, then, even when the matter concerned the defense of the territory of the Roman Church, it is established by these last letters that the king of Francia did nothing without the pontiff’s authority, whatever authority the king of Francia is found to have exercised through his envoys, whether in time of war or peace, was a delegation of the supreme pontifical authority—both in the ancient territory, the Roman province, and in the recently added territories of the exarchate and the Pentapolis.

Charles imitated Pippin, as we shall see in its proper place. As for Pippin, not even the Italian annalist dared mutter anything to the contrary.

How great a loss this caused to the periods that followed Pippin becomes clear from the true character of royal authority within the pontifical territory during the fourteen years in which Pippin survived the enlargement of ecclesiastical territory that he himself had effected.

For since Charles did not depart even by a fraction from his father’s example as long as he was king of the Franks and Lombards, he arrogated no authority to himself within the pontiffs’ territory, which he greatly enlarged. And when, in the year 800, he unwillingly received the imperial crown, Leo III—who established so great a majesty in the West—did not strip the successors of blessed Peter of the authority they had enjoyed for more than seventy years; rather, he made that authority more formidable by defending it with imperial majesty against the audacity of certain subjects.

But what the aforesaid author could not accomplish concerning the supreme authority of the pontiffs, he attempted to accomplish concerning Pippin’s donation itself. In the year 757 he substituted the Carolingian donation for the Pippinian; he accused Anastasius and Leo of Ostia of ignorance; and he defined the boundaries of the exarchate, all contrary to fact.

How large and extensive King Pippin’s donation was, we saw from the letters of Stephen II. What cities were not restored by Desiderius, king of the Lombards; what invasions were carried out by him; and what manifold and certain confession that same king made of pontifical rule, both in the Roman province and in the exarchate and Pentapolis—the following letters of Paul, for which we have necessarily prefixed these few remarks, will demonstrate most fully.

## XII. 133. Copy of a Letter

In which Paul, deacon and [Note: [Col. 0147C] Paul began his pontificate in the year of Christ 757 and died in 767. GRETS.] elected of the Holy Roman Church, announces the death of Pope Stephen, sent through Immo [Note: [Col. 0147C] MS: *Imomonem*; but [materially uncertain OCR] *y mo* has been deleted a second time. GENT.], envoy of Lord King Pippin [Note: [Col. 0147C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 1): “The first letter sets forth to King Pippin the death of his brother and his own [of his brother Stephen and his own] ordination, and states [states] that he will persevere in the friendship contracted by Stephen [by the same Stephen] with the Franks: he asks that Pippin do the same.” The Centuriators alter this first summary somewhat at its beginning and end; in other respects they agree with Panvinio. What is enclosed in brackets indicates Panvinio’s own revisions; this should also be noted in what follows. In any case, two things here are false: the “ordination,” which does not suit one merely elected, and that request that Pippin do the same (or “act,” as the Centuriators read); for no such request occurs in the letter. The pontiff does say that he prays the divine clemency that the aid and defense of the Franks may never fail him and the Roman Church. CENN.]

(Year of Our Lord 757, Carolingian Codex XIII, chronicle 12.)

[Col. 0147A]

### Summary

Before his consecration, delayed by the schism, Paul announces to Pippin the death of his brother and his own election. He says that he is detaining Immo, the royal envoy who had arrived, with the counsel of the nobles until he is consecrated. He will then send Immo back with his own apostolic envoys, so that they may renew with Pippin the friendship and alliance that had existed with his brother Stephen.

To the most excellent lord, his son, Pippin, king of the Franks [Note: Summary 1, in Baronius and the Centuriators. Gretser.], and patrician of the Romans: Paul the deacon, elected in the name of God to the apostolic see of the Holy Church.

[Col. 0147B]

With deep sighing and immense grief of heart, we inform Your Excellency, most powerful victorious king protected by God, that by God’s call the lord Stephen, of holy memory, my brother and pope, has been taken from this light to eternal rest. [Note: Stephen II died on 24 April 757. Recent writers should have taken this into account—writers who, following Muratori, have brought forward previously unknown charters and chronologies and place Aistulf’s death at the end of the preceding year and Desiderius’ accession in March of this year, and consequently place Stephen’s final letters, which concern both matters, either in March or April. Can such narrow chronological limits be sustained by those ancient charters and the Brescian chronicler? Let the reader consult Letter 51, formerly 54, of this Carolingian Codex. It will then be clear that, after Fulrad had taken possession of the cities, Stephen distributed all the affairs of the exarchate; that he was accustomed to have all the administrators and administrative orders—that is, diplomas—issued by the same Fulrad; that the judges residing at Ravenna, Philip the presbyter and the duke Eustace, had been sent there by the pontiff; and, above all, that Archbishop Sergius, who resisted the pontifical commands, had been removed from that see by Stephen’s order. Could all this have happened within a few days? Let the old charters stand, and let their authority—which overturns the whole of history—be brought back under examination. CENN.] In whose passing even the stones themselves, if it may be said, wept in lament for us. [Note: A long time before this, the *Book of the Popes’ Office* had proved very useful. Hence the frequent use in these letters of its formulas. Thus, in the announcement to the exarch (chapter 2, title 1), we read: “The lord N., our most holy pontiff, has been taken from this light, whose departure everyone truly mourned, and, if it must be said, even the stones themselves wept.” The complete freedom of both the election and the consecration in that age should nevertheless be noted. There is no mention of the emperor. The royal envoy is detained by the council of the nobles, so that he may carry to Francia reliable testimony of the friendship and alliance of the pontiff, who has attained supreme authority. Finally, after everything has been completed, pontifical envoys are to be sent to the king. Astronomus plainly reports the same concerning Stephen IV and Paschal I in his *Life of Louis the Pious*. This matter has provided recent writers with abundant material for disputes and a remarkable occasion for confusion. These matters, however, must be discussed in their proper place, when we speak of the diploma of that same Pious Louis.][Col. 0148D]

The whole multitude of the peoples elected me, unhappy as I am, to the succession of his apostolate. While these things were taking place, Immo, the envoy of Your Most Christian Excellency, arrived in Rome. After speaking with him, we and our nobles together recognized that it was appropriate for him to be detained here [L., G., *detinere*: to detain him] until, by God’s providence, we had been illumined by the sacred apostolic blessing. Then, once he had been more fully assured of our purity—or that of the entire people [Perhaps: *populi*]—and of the love that we bear toward Your Most Benevolent Excellency and the entire people of the Franks, we would release him to return to you with our apostolic envoys.

For you should know with certainty, most excellent one, our lord protected by God, that after God you are our assisting and defending king, and that we, remaining firm and steadfast unto the soul and the shedding of our blood in that faith, love, harmony of charity, and covenant of peace which the aforementioned lord of blessed memory, my brother, the most holy pontiff, confirmed with you, shall remain—and with our people shall remain—unto the end.

Therefore, with our hands continually extended toward heaven, we beseech the mercy of our Lord God for the preservation of Your Excellency’s life, for the safety of your sweetest sons, and for the well-being of the most excellent queen, that your assistance and strongest protection may always be extended over us.

May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellency safe.

## XIII. 135. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord Pippin, King, Sent through Wulfard

This letter contains thanksgiving and abundant praise for the defense of the Holy Church of God, requesting aid against the Lombards, because the Lombards, persisting in great arrogance, were not returning the rights of the Holy Church of God. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 15): “He wrote the fifteenth letter to Pippin through Wulfard, his co-bishop, whom he commends to Pippin, as Pope Stephen, Paul’s brother, had also done. This letter contains praise of Pippin and thanksgiving for the defense of the Holy Church of God. The pope requests aid against the Lombards because they were not returning the rights of the Holy Church of God. For the *sabanus* [“Aid against the Lombards because they were not returning the rights of the Holy Church of God is requested. Likewise, for the *sabanus*”] sent, in which Pippin’s daughter had been washed and received from the sacred font, he gives thanks [“the pontiff gives thanks”]. After celebrating the solemn Masses, with a large gathering of the people [“multitude”], he writes that he received it with great joy beneath the roof of the sacred body of the life-giving blessed Petronilla, which was consecrated [“had been”] for the praise and eternal memory of Pippin’s name. He adds that he is working continually so that Bishop Sergius may be restored to his church.” The substance of the letter is left almost entirely intact, while matters of little relevance to us are recounted at length. Cenn.]

(Year of Our Lord 757, Carolingian Codex XXVII, chronicle 13.)

### Summary

He receives from Wulfard, Pippin’s envoy, the *sabanus* brought together with the letters—the cloth in which Gisela, the king’s daughter, had been washed at the sacred font—during the solemn Masses, at the altar of Saint Petronilla. As though he had received the king’s daughter from that same sacred font, he henceforth calls Pippin his co-father.

Through the same Wulfard he replies that matters were as he had heard: Desiderius had not kept his promises, and Paul had received none of the things that Desiderius had announced through his envoys. He attaches his own envoy to the king’s envoys and announces what has happened thus far. He labors concerning Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, who is entangled in lawsuits in the City, so that he may be restored to his church. He commends again and again Wulcharius, bishop of Nomentum, who had gone to Francia with his brother Stephen.

To the most excellent lord, his son, and our spiritual co-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

The bearer of this letter, the most diligent Wulfardus, your most faithful servant [Note: [Col. 0149D] Gentilis reads: “the faithful envoy of your eminent sagacity”], has brought us a letter full of delight. Receiving it with immense joy and opening it for reading, we were relieved, exulting with great gladness [Col. 0149B], when we learned through it of your radiant excellence’s affection toward the holy Roman Church of the apostles, and of the support you have shown your patron, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven. For this reason we render more fervent perpetual thanks to almighty God, since in these days he has bestowed upon his holy Church so distinguished and mighty a protector from among men [Note: [Col. 0149D] Here is another quite clear definition of the patriciate conferred upon the Frankish kings. See Letter 6, alternatively 7, note, and below the preliminary commentary on Adrian’s letters. CENN.].

Meanwhile, most Christian prince and victorious king, by God’s providence, we have celebrated the twofold joys of a festival, in that we have attained the desires longed for by our hearts and have likewise been bound together in the bond of spiritual alliance. For the distinguished envoy of your fellowship has brought us the most precious gift of heavenly grace [Col. 0149C]—namely, the *sabanum* [Note: [Col. 0149D] Ducange, after citing various definitions from authors, says that *mappa*, *facitergium*, *linteum*, *linteum villosum*, *manutergium*, and so forth occur frequently in authors; beginning with Saint Gregory the Great, he enumerates a very large series of them. The reading of Panvinius, which the Centuriators and Baronius admit, seems laughable: for according to the same Ducange, *sabarium* is a *pastophorium*, that is, the vestibule of a temple. Nevertheless, this various reading, which distinguishes the Vatican examples from those entered into the codex by Carolus, is to be considered of great importance. For from this we learn with certainty that the Centuriators had Panvinius’s very arguments before them. ID.—The same word occurs in Saint Boniface, Letters 10 and 145. Here it signifies the linen cloth that served as the covering of Pippin’s newly baptized little daughter. GRETS.], in which our sweetest and most beloved spiritual daughter, washed in the most sacred bath, was received. We accepted it with great delight, while a gathered crowd of the people celebrated the solemn rites of Mass beneath the *aura* [F.: *aram*, “altar”] of your helper, the blessed Petronilla, which is now known to have been dedicated for the eternal praise and remembrance of your name [Note: [Col. 0150C] Fabrottus, in his edition of the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 259), supplements the Velserian edition from the Freherian codex, explaining the various reading that wonderfully illuminates this passage. He says that Paul “worked in the cemetery where the blessed Petronilla had formerly been laid to rest outside the Appian Gate, two miles from the city of Rome; and from there he removed her venerable and holy body, together with the marble sarcophagus in which it had been placed, engraved with these letters: ‘To Aurea Petronilla, the sweetest daughter.’ Hence there is no doubt that this inscription was recognized as having been fashioned by the hand of the blessed apostle Peter himself, out of love for his sweetest daughter. He then placed the holy body, together with the aforesaid sarcophagus, upon a new wagon and transported it to the church of the blessed apostle Peter with hymns and spiritual songs [Col. 0150D]; and his blessedness placed it in the mausoleum beside the church of the blessed apostle Andrew, which the aforementioned most blessed Pope Stephen, her brother, while he was still alive, had adorned with paintings of marvelous beauty in honor of that holy martyr of Christ, Petronilla.” See Baronius (year 69, no. 32 and following), Boldetti, *On the Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs* (book II, chapter 18, p. 551), and especially the notes on Adon (Rome edition, 1745), May 31. Wulfardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours, had been the bearer of the *sabanum*. See Pagi (757, no. 4). Mabillon, book XXI, no. 12, and book XXIII, no. 23, says that Wulfardus and Gulfardus were one and the same person. CENN.]. By means of that same *sabanum* we rejoice that we received her as though we had received her in person.

Therefore, because the grace of faith has kindled your kindly heart, so that you may cleave to us through the bond of spiritual alliance, in accordance with the promise you made to my lord and brother, the blessed Stephen, of holy memory, we render great thanks to God for your excellence, whom he protects. We continually implore divine mercy to preserve and protect you upon the throne of your kingdom in long-lasting [F.: *longaevis*] and prosperous times, and to allow you to rejoice with great joy in the full maturity of that spiritual daughter of ours, to the exaltation of his holy Church [Col. 0150B] [Note: [Col. 0150D] The holy pontiff’s prayers were not in vain. For Gisela, having professed the monastic life, became abbess of the monastery of Chelles, the glory and ornament of the Order of Saint Benedict, as Mabillon says. She also persuaded Alcuin to compose commentaries on the Gospel of John. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXIII, no. 28; book XXVI, no. 61. ID.].

And because that abundant grace of the Holy Spirit—namely, the spiritual kinship that, with God’s help, stands confirmed between us—has given us confidence, I ask and beg you, most kindly spiritual kinsman and excellent king, to order the good work of God’s Church’s redemption and of the complete restoration of blessed Peter’s justice to be brought to completion. For your distinguished goodness has sent us word, through your aforesaid envoys [F.: *affatus*], of the outcome of the causes opposed to us. We therefore inform your excellence, whom God protects, with certainty that up to now we have received nothing of what we instructed our envoys to request from your excellence [Col. 0150C]. For those faithless and malicious men, persisting in the great arrogance of their hearts, are in no way inclined to restore blessed Peter’s justice. Nevertheless, your envoys can learn how everything was done from those who report it. We are also sending our next envoy to you, bearing worthy thanks for everything; and through him we send your excellence our replies concerning all that may occur hereafter [Col. 0151A] [Note: [Col. 0151C] The fact that affairs of this kind were entrusted to envoys, so that they would not be committed to writing and exposed to the Lombards, gave different men the opportunity to invent different accounts at will. Here, however, they seem to be indicated without much obscurity. The envoys who had gone to Francia with Immo after the pope’s consecration had reported to the king that Desiderius had not kept his promises, and had asked him to warn the Lombard king not to delay any longer the restoration of the cities and places of the exarchate. He now announces that none of this has been done; and he leaves it to the envoys to explain what he himself has so far done on behalf of the Holy See, and what service or stratagem he has employed toward Desiderius—upon whom the treachery, malice, and arrogance fall—in order to wrest something from his hands. CENN.].

As for Archbishop Sergius, in accordance with what has become known to your excellence, we are unceasingly exerting ourselves to have him restored to his own church [Col. 0151D] [Note: [Col. 0151D] Below, in Letter 51, alternatively 54, Adrian tells Charles that Stephen II “then removed Archbishop Sergius, because he was attempting in a spirit of pride to act against his will.” But this was not the sole reason why Sergius remained in Rome: he was entangled in litigation because his wife, Euphemia, was still alive; it is said that, after attaining the archbishopric, he had ordained her a deaconess. Ughellus (vol. II, p. 243) falsely reports that these lawsuits continued throughout Paul’s entire pontificate. For, as we shall see shortly below, Sergius had returned to his see through the efforts of that same pontiff. Following Agnellus, Bacchinius argues that this happened under Stephen II; but these letters show that, while Paul was pope, Sergius had not yet been restored. See below, Letter 51, alternatively 54. ID.]. We ask your excellent goodness to command that our most reverend and holy brother and fellow bishop Wulcharius [Lambecius: *Wilcharius*], just as my aforesaid lord and brother, the holy Pope Stephen of blessed memory, commended him to your kindly excellence, be held commended in all respects.

Having said this, may our God, three and one, protect you with his extended right hand, together with your sweetest wife, the most excellent queen, our spiritual kinswoman, and your most beloved children, who are also mine. May he grant that you remain safe and prosperous upon the throne of your kingdom, both in the present life and in everlasting blessedness, and that you flourish abundantly [Col. 0152C] [Note: [Col. 0152C] Wilharius, whom Ughellus (*Italia Sacra*, vol. X) calls Villarius, accompanied Stephen II to Francia in the year 753. At the end of the following year he had been sent as an envoy to King Pippin by that same pontiff, who strongly commended him, as above, in Letter 7, alternatively 9. It is clear from Letter 11, alternatively 8, that he remained with the king; for in 756 the pontiff was asking that he be sent back to Rome. In the manuscript codex he was erroneously called Wicharius, a reading retained by Lambecius and Gentilotto. Here, too, Tengnagel erroneously wrote Wulcharius, but Lambecius restored Wilcharius. Certainly, if Stephen had commended a bishop of this name to the king, he was the Nomentan bishop, of whom there will also be mention below. ID.]. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## XIV. 139

**Also, a general copy of the same pope to the entire army of the God-protected kingdom of the Franks**, containing thanks and the richest blessings for their struggle, and exhorting them to persevere more earnestly in combat for the service of almighty God and his holy Church, and to encourage the spirit of Lord King Pippin to carry this through [Note: [Col. 0152D] Panvinius’s argument (Vatican Codex 31), in the final position, reads: “He also wrote a letter to the entire army of the kingdom of the Franks, in which he bestows upon them thanks and blessings for [‘blessings for’] the faithful service rendered to himself and blessed Peter, and exhorts them to persevere henceforth in the service of the Roman Church [‘having rendered it, he bestows them upon them; he exhorts them to persevere in the service of the Holy Roman Church and to fight bravely for it’].” CENN. Baronius’s summary is no. 29. The Centuriators place the summary of this letter outside the order of the others. GRETS.].

*(Year of the Lord 757, Carolingian Codex XXII, chronicle 14.)*

### Argument

He gives thanks to all the nobles and to the Frankish army for the service they rendered with the king, the new Moses and new David, in liberating the Church and asserting the Catholic faith. He calls them the Church’s special sons and promises them a reward from God. He expresses the hope that they will triumph over barbarian peoples in order to preserve the integrity of the faith and increase the Church.

Paul, servant of the servants of God, to all our beloved bishops, venerable priests, abbots, and religious monks; also to the glorious dukes and counts; and to the entire Christ-beloved assembly of the army of the God-protected kingdom of the Franks [Col. 0152A].

As we contemplate—and as though we saw blazing before our eyes—the radiant faith of your strength, beloved of Christ, and the laborious struggle you undertake, striving [variant: *studetis*, “you strive”] with all your efforts to liberate the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, which through the word of preaching has begotten you as sincere and special sons, a profound cause for wonder takes hold of us [Col. 0152B]. We do not cease to proclaim throughout the whole world these praises of your name and of your blessed offspring [L., G.: “and for this reason”]. O dearest and most beloved of us, what return shall we grant to your army? What abundance of treasures could be worthy of the many protections you have given the holy Church? Although reflection and ability of mind are constrained when we try to repay what is worthy of you, nevertheless our Lord God is a just judge in heaven, and he will repay the worthy merits of your works.

Truly, the name of your people has been raised (*elevatum*; Lambecius: *exaltatum*) above many generations and nations, and the kingdom of the Franks shines forth, flashing before the sight of the Lord, adorned with kings who are such most kindly liberators of God’s Catholic and apostolic holy Church. For the most Christian and God-protected son and spiritual kinsman, Lord Pippin, has become in all his works a new Moses and a new David [Col. 0153A] [Note: [Col. 0153C] From this it is clear that Pagi (757, no. 1) and the latest edition of Duchesne are wrong to assign this letter to this year while placing it before the one just mentioned. For if Pippin was a spiritual kinsman, he had therefore received the *sabanum* of the royal daughter Gisela. As for the names “new Moses” and “new David,” it should be noted that Alcuin addresses several letters to King David, calling Charlemagne by that name; Canisius therefore gives a very learned explanation of the matter (*Ancient Readings*, vol. II, p. 390). Basnage’s doctrine on the same subject, however, seems scarcely to agree with this letter and with other letters of the Carolingian Codex: “This David,” he says, “is Charlemagne. Learned men once doubted this because Alcuin sometimes calls Charles a namesake of the prophet David, in Letter 12. But it was customary in the ninth century to replace the names of kings and illustrious men with those of ancient kings, prophets, or even pagans. Thus Charlemagne was addressed by the name David because of David’s piety and courage. For the same reason the Italians called their king Berengar David.” Indeed, before Charles acquired that name, this Pippin was called by the Roman pontiff once here, again in Letter 34, alternatively 18, and a third time in Letter 41, alternatively 16, as will be clear below, by the distinguished names of both David and Moses. Nor was he called this because such a custom existed in the ninth century, but because he had protected the Church in the preceding period and had defended the Catholic faith against Greek impiety. CENN.], Lord Pippin, the most victorious king by God’s will, through whom God’s Church is exalted in triumph and the Catholic faith remains undefiled by the weapon of heretics [Col. 0154C].

And you, dearest ones, holy nation, royal priesthood, people of possession, whom the Lord God of Israel has blessed—rejoice and exult, because your names and those of your kings have been written in heaven, and your reward is great before God and his angels. You have acquired as a firm protector the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom our Redeemer granted the power of binding and loosing sins in heaven and on earth [Note: [Col. 0154D] As I said in the note on Letter 4, alternatively 10, and on Letter 6, alternatively 7, the love of the kings and peoples of Francia for the prince of the apostles was greatest at that time; this is why it is found everywhere in these letters. ID.].

But may almighty God, through the intercessions of that same apostle of his, bless, protect, strengthen, and fortify your community, beloved of God; may he direct your actions according to his good pleasure; grant you victory from heaven; enlarge your borders [L., G.: “your boundaries”]; subject all barbarian nations to your most excellent kings, for the complete liberation and exaltation of the holy universal Church of God and the integrity of the orthodox faith [the manuscript omits *ad*]; grant you to think those things that please him; illumine your hearts still more abundantly with love for blessed Peter and his apostolic see; and grant that, obeying his apostolic commands with faithful devotion and observing the orders of your kings, you may complete the course (*cursum*; Gentilis: *cursus*) of the present life with victory and a good reputation, and deserve to enjoy eternal joys with the citizens of heaven [Col. 0153B].

## XV. 145

**Also, a copy of the general letter of the Roman people and Senate, addressed to Lord King Pippin**, containing thanks and, concerning the letter that Lord King Pippin sent to that same people, exhortations to preserve their faith toward the holy Roman Church of God and toward Lord Paul the apostolic pope.

*(Year of the Lord 757, Carolingian Codex XXXVI, chronicle 15.)*

[Note: [Col. 0154D] No argument by Panvinius survives; therefore neither the Centuriators, who received these letters and arguments from Rome, nor Baronius says anything about it. Labbe himself, though the Carolingian Codex was not unknown to him, is silent about it. Muratori, after first asking pardon, postpones it to 763 and sets out its meaning on his own judgment in the *Annals of Italy*. Pagi rightly assigns it to this year, for the bearers of this letter and the preceding one seem to have been the same Abbot Wulfard and his companions, to whom a pontifical envoy had been attached; the letters to Pippin were issued after the *sabanum* had been received. For what reason was the Senate and People of Rome to be reminded of their duty toward the pontiff when he had already governed the Church for seven years? ID.]

### Argument

The Roman Senate and people, admonished by Pippin concerning their fidelity to the apostolic see and the pontiff, reply that they will always remain faithful subjects of the pontiff, whom they praise with deserved commendations. They exhort the king not to cease fighting for the Catholic faith and the Church, since he will obtain eternal rewards. They commend him greatly and pray that God grant him certain victories over all his adversaries.

To the most excellent and preeminent lord, the great victor Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, instituted by God: the entire Senate and the whole general assembly of the people of the city of Rome, preserved by God [Col. 0154A].

If human understanding should wish inwardly to weigh the zeal of your works, nothing, as we think, can be considered worthy of answering them or repaying them in this temporal life. Only those things should be considered as being repaid to you by the just judge, our Lord God, which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered the human heart—those things God has prepared for those who love him [Col. 0154B]. This is the worthy repayment due to you, since by your struggle the holy Church of God and the orthodox faith of Christians are known to have been defended, and the remedies of salvation for all of us have constantly been secured. And because our God has deigned, through you [Lambecius adds *per te*, “through you”], most excellent lord king, to work the redemption of his holy Church and of us all, it is fitting that we sing the wonders of his works, singing with the prophet in harmonious voice: “For your works are magnified, O God; you made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your wonders” (Psalm 103). “Who can speak of the powers of the Lord and make all his praises heard?” (Psalm 105).

For the heavens rejoice and the earth exults because our Lord God has bestowed upon his holy Church such a defender [Col. 0154C] [Note: [Col. 0154D] Here is a definition of the patriciate from the mouth of the Holy Roman Senate and People, so that learned men may no longer weary themselves seeking new arguments with which to support the empty disputes of Peter de Marca, Pagi, and others. Pippin is called “protector” by the pontiff and “defender” by the Senate and People of Rome—what he certainly was. See above, Letter 6, alternatively 7, note, and below passim, lest I press the same point to tedium. CENN.], through whom the name of the Lord is glorified with confidence in his holy court.

Therefore, receiving the letters sent by your most preeminent and most Christian kindness with great honor and affection, we accepted them and rejoiced at their reception as though we were seeing your excellence in person, since they brought us the twofold joys of a festival [Col. 0155A], when we learned of your great happiness. For nothing in this life is sweeter to us, lord king, than to rejoice in your prosperity, since your safety, after God, is our security.

Indeed, in those honey-sweet lines your providential care sought to greet us and your excellence sought to admonish us that we must remain firm and faithful toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward the holy Church of God, and toward your most blessed and angelic spiritual father, appointed by God, our lord Paul, supreme pontiff and universal pope [Note: [Col. 0155D] At the beginning of the letter they say, “to Pippin, the great victor king instituted by God”; here, however, “to our lord Paul, appointed by God.” What difference is there between one prince and the other? ID.]. We rejoiced exceedingly at this most prudent admonition of yours.

O how great a divine inspiration overflows within the innermost parts of our hearts, in us who are your faithful servants [Col. 0155B]! Truly, lord king, the Spirit of God dwells in your honey-sweet heart, and for this reason you have striven to admonish your well-wishers with such salutary counsel. We, most excellent of kings, remain firm and faithful servants of the holy Church of God and of your aforesaid three-times-blessed and angelic spiritual father, our lord Paul, supreme pontiff and universal pope [Lambecius: “of your prelate”], because he is our father and excellent shepherd, and does not cease daily to struggle for our salvation, just as his brother, the blessed Lord Pope Stephen of holy memory, cherished and healthfully governed us, as truly rational sheep entrusted to him by God, since he is gentle and in all things truly merciful. He has become an imitator of blessed Peter, whose place he holds and whose vicar he is [Col. 0155C].

We, therefore, most excellent and most Christian lord king, have firm confidence in this promise of yours. But we earnestly beseech you, and, as though prostrate in person at your royal feet, we ask—and blessed Peter himself, through us, appeals to your excellence—that you order and arrange matters, most kindly of kings and our defender after God, so that the perfect exaltation of the holy Church of God, the defense of our orthodox faith, and the defense of all of us may be secured [the reading *profligetur* is likely an OCR or textual error for *procuretur*, “may be secured”] [Col. 0155D].

We also ask this before the living God, who commanded that you be anointed king through his apostle, blessed Peter: order that the enlargement of this province, wrested by you from the hand of the nations, be completed [Note: [Col. 0155D] This expression should be noted: the enlargement of this Roman province was called above, in Letter 9, alternatively 6, its augmentation. Therefore, whether it is called enlarged or augmented, the papal territory could never be said to have been begun or established by the Frankish kings. Pippin claimed, or wrested, the Roman province—that is, the Roman duchy, which is the same thing—from the hand of the nations. These were the Lombards, who continually harassed it with arms. He did not donate it, but enlarged it by adding the exarchate and the Pentapolis. And because those provinces had not been handed over intact by the Lombard invaders, the Holy Roman Senate and People ask him to complete this enlargement, modestly reminding him of the benefit received a few years earlier from Saint Peter, when he had been made king from mayor of the palace. ID.], and remain in the good work you have begun, so that we may be able to live in great security and peace, and so that you may receive in heaven eternal reward and a recompense obtained through prayer [Col. 0156A]. For after God and blessed Peter, we place our greatest hope in the arm of your most powerful kingdom, and we trust in the mercy of our almighty God that this very hope of ours will bring us the richest fruit through your works.

Hear, lord king, the supplication of all who wish you well, and most willingly lend your ears to what we ask; may the Lord hear you in all your petitions. For you, after God, are our defender and helper. Even if all the hairs of our heads were turned into tongues, they would not suffice to offer worthy thanks for such great benefits of yours [Col. 0156B].

Nevertheless, insofar as our mind is able, we proclaim the praises of your renown among all nations. Therefore, raising our eyes and stretching our palms toward heaven, we beseech our Lord God with immeasurable prayers to cherish you with his grace; to send before your face an angel of his power as your champion, who, conquering all your adversaries, may subject them to your feet; to enlarge the boundaries of your kingdom; to grant you victory from heaven for the perpetual and everlasting security of the holy Church of God and of us; and to grant that you, the most excellent lady queen, and your illustrious sons, most excellent kings, may possess the royal height in safe and most fortunate times, and that he may grant you abundant eternal joys of reward with the saints and elect [Col. 0156C]. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## XVI. 145

**Also, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin through Langbard**, containing thanks and the richest blessings for his life and safety, and for those of his noble sons, Lords Charles and Carloman; seeking assistance with many adjurations against the Lombards; and containing, in an *embolum* [variant: *embolo*, “in the inserted section”], the decree he sent to the presbyter Marinus concerning the title of Chrysogonus and the books he transmitted to him [Note: [Col. 0156D] Panvinius’s summary (Vatican Codex 18) reads: “In the eighteenth [variant: ‘eighth’] are contained thanks and the richest blessings for his life and safety, or for those of Lord [variant: ‘the same Pippin’] Charles and Carloman, his most noble sons, together with [variant: ‘his: together with’] many adjurations against the Lombards, as he seeks assistance [variant: ‘asks for help’]. In the appended *embolum* is contained the decree he gave to the presbyter Marinus concerning the title of Chrysogonus and the books he sent to Pippin.” [“In the appended inserted section is contained the decree which the presbyter Marinus gave concerning the title of Chrysogonus, and the matter of the books he sent to Pippin is included.”] The similarity of this summary to that of the Carolingian Codex is so great that one seems to have been copied from the other. If all of them were like this, one could believe that the Magdeburg scholars owed these notices not to Panvinius but to this author, and that they had consulted this very Codex. But the different order of the letters and the variety of the other summaries, along with the other considerations presented in the preface, indicate otherwise. Yet, to tell the truth, such similarity in the two works remains astonishing. CENN.].

*(Year of the Lord 757, Carolingian Codex XXV, chronicle 16.)*

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Summary 18 in Baronius and the Centuriators. GRETS.]

### Argument

He replies to two letters received from the king. The first, brought by the royal envoy Langbard, bears witness to the king’s love for blessed Peter and his goodwill toward the pope; Paul admonishes him to complete what he promised his brother Stephen. The second, delivered to him by his own envoys returning from Francia, contains the bull granting the title of Saint Chrysogonus to the presbyter Marinus, in accordance with the king’s request. He also sends several books, both sacred and secular, and a nocturnal clock.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual kinsman, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

The bearer of this letter, Langbard, an illustrious man and faithful envoy of your excellence, has hastened to us and brought to you [Lambecius: “to us”] your excellence’s nectarous and flower-bearing report, protected by God. Examining the attached page more carefully, we understood each point of what its text said [Col. 0157A]. In those words of your sublimity we recognized the joy of your safety, desirable to us and more embraceable than all such delights of this world [L., G.: *amplectabilem*, “more worthy of embrace”; source reading *amplexabilem*]. Rejoicing with the richer happiness of our heart, we were especially relieved to learn what our heart desired. Afterwards, when our envoys returned from your God-imitating presence and brought us reports of those same joys of your prosperity [L.: “when they brought replies from you”], a twofold gladness was inserted into our heart.

For when the joy of your increased prosperity had resounded in the ears of all the priests and clergy, as well as of the nobles and the rest of the people, they too, filled with immense joy and rejoicing, exulted with us in the Lord when they learned that their own defender, after God, was safe [Col. 0157C].

Moreover, most excellent son protected by God and spiritual kinsman, we have learned by experience that you burn with ardent love for the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, and with affection for us, especially since your own letter is seen to have been written with the pen of charity. For your tongue, moved by the heart, had dipped what it poured onto the page of the parchment.

For this reason we render great thanks to your excellence, whom God protects, since divine mercy, through the intervention of its prince of the apostles, has most kindly established you, excellent king, as the defender and helper of his holy Church. May concern for your excellence persist in securing the complete redemption of this province and the exaltation of this most holy Church [Col. 0157D].

Therefore, together with the entire people entrusted to us, we implore the mercy of our Lord God to protect you with his grace; to grant you victory from heaven; to subject all barbarian nations to your feet; to cause you to deserve to govern the kingdom for many years; and, together with your sweetest wife, the most excellent queen and our spiritual kinswoman, and your and our most beloved children, Lords Charles and Carloman, most powerful kings, and the most excellent Lady Gisela, to grant you the joys of eternal life with God’s elect [Col. 0158A].

## 147

Therefore I ask and beseech you, most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, and I adjure you by almighty God and by the body of blessed Peter, whose excellent faithful servant you are [Note: [Col. 0158D] In his first letter Gregory III likewise adjured Charles Martel: “By the living God and the most sacred keys of the confession of blessed Peter,” which he had sent to the prince according to ancestral custom. See the note there. ID.]. With the greatest prayers I implore you to order [Lambecius: *lubeas*, “be willing”] that you diligently retain, stored in (*confertum*; variant *compertum*, “ascertained”), in your holy, God-inspired, honey-sweet heart what the lord and brother of us both, the most blessed Pope Stephen of holy memory, pope by God’s will, admonished and entreated you to carry out; that you remain in that charity and friendship; and that you order [Lambecius: *lubeatis*, “be willing”] everything to be fulfilled and brought into effect, as he urged you with a fearful adjuration to do [Col. 0158B].

Thus may you deserve to obtain the perfect reward and the crown of our redemption, fully stored up, from the just judge and creator of all, our Lord God, who anointed you king, and, when you have more perfectly liberated the Lord’s people, defended the holy Church of God, and preserved it unharmed for the divine majesty from the malice of those raging against it, obtain the eternal joys of blessedness with God’s saints and elect. For this reason, most kindly king, after God, we entertain great (*magna*; Lambecius: *magnam*) confidence in the hope contained in your promise, which you made to blessed Peter, together with the entire people of this province redeemed by you [Note: [Col. 0158D] All of this points to the cities and places of the exarchate and Pentapolis that had not yet been handed over by Desiderius. ID.].

All the priests and clergy of this most holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church therefore greet your common Christian devotion. The entire senatorial nobility and the gathered peoples of various kinds also greet you, wishing, together with us, to rejoice for a long time in your greatest prosperity and abundant happiness, and to exult in the Lord God our Savior. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## INSERTED SECTION (*EMBOLUM*)

[The supplied source ends here.]

148. For in another letter of his, your Excellency, protected by God, just as you certainly sent to your most benevolent father, requested that we should grant to Marino, the priest most beloved and most faithful to you [Lamb., “to us”], the title of your protector, Chrysogonus, blessed martyr of Christ, with everything belonging to it. You also requested that a warrant be sent to us [Lamb., “to you”]; accordingly, out of affection for you, [Col. 0159A] and because that same most holy and beloved priest Marinus is your faithful servant and ours, we have sent to your Excellency, by the bearer of this letter, the warrant for the aforesaid title, together with all the places and possessions belonging to it, urban and rural, written out for you and confirmed by our hand, to be delivered to you.

[Note: [Col. 0159C] Two matters of some importance are presented here. First, the creation of a cardinal at the king’s request; second, the character of a crafty and ambitious man, later also a criminal, who, by pretending to possess cardinalitial dignity, deceived both pope and king. CENN.]

We have also sent to your Excellency as many books as we were able to find, namely, an Antiphonary and a Responsary, together with Aristotle’s *Art of Grammar* [F., “Dialectic”], the books of Dionysius the Areopagite, Geometry, Orthography, Grammar, all the Greek-language authors, and also a nocturnal clock.

[Note: [Col. 0159C] In the epitaph of that famous man Pacificus, archdeacon of Verona—whose chapter archive is said to preserve ancient manuscript codices—Panvinio records the following, from which Ughellus quotes it (*Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 710): “No one before him had seen a nocturnal clock; behold, he discovered the device and first established it,” etc. Hence he is said to have been the inventor of this kind of clock. Here we possess an earlier testimony by almost fifty years. Ducange reports the same in his *Glossary*, and thinks that it was called nocturnal to distinguish it from the solar clock: the latter is the familiar iron or bronze device that strikes a little bell, whose inventor escaped the notice of Polydore Vergil and the others. Why should it not rather have resembled those instruments that, by means of enclosed light, indicate the hours upon a sphere? The Frankish and Fulda Annals mention an organ sent as a gift by Copronymus; but nowhere is anything found concerning a clock. As for the books, Amalarius says in the prologue to his book *On the Order of the Antiphonary* that Gregory IV lacked a single Antiphonary to send to Emperor Louis, who had requested it; this matter is noted by the venerable Thomasius, *Opusculum* VIII (new edition, vol. VII, pp. 64 ff.). Perhaps this happened because Paul, who had begun sending such books to Pippin, and the much more generous Adrian, who repeatedly presented the same books to Charles, in order that Roman chant might become widespread in Francia, thereby left Rome short of them—especially at a time when they were exceedingly rare. The premature use of the Roman Antiphonary in Francia should also be noted. ID.]
