### XVII. 149. The Same Pope’s Letter to Lord Pippin, King, Sent by Bishop George, the Priest Stephen, and Radpert, His Envoys

In it are contained thanks for the defense of the holy Church of God; and the aforesaid pope asks that Lord King Pippin restore to King Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0160C] The manuscript has *suospites* as one word; Tengnagel corrected it as it appears in the edition. GENT.] his hostages [Lamb., “his own”] and confirm the treaties of peace with him.

[Note: [Col. 0160C] Summary 13, in Baronius and the Centuriators. GRETS.—Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 13): “In the thirteenth [‘thirteenth’] he gives thanks for the defense of the Church and relates that peace has been established between himself and Desiderius; he asks that he restore Desiderius’s hostages, so that Desiderius himself may also recover the city of Imola [Forum Cornelii].” CENN.]

*(A.D. 758; Codex Carolinus XXIX, chronicle 17.)*

[Col. 0159B]

**SUMMARY.**—Through his envoys, Bishop George and the priest Stephen, traveling with the royal envoy Rodbert, he reports that Desiderius has come to Rome and promised to restore Imola, provided that he received back his hostages who were with the king. He asks that the king return them and make a treaty with the king of the Lombards, thereby becoming the guarantor of public tranquility. Written at Desiderius’s request.

[Col. 0159C] To the most excellent lord, son, and our spiritual compère, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

Since almighty God repeatedly bestows so abundant a mercy of his goodness upon the human race, it is greatly to be wondered what can be rendered in return to his divine power, or what praises in song human frailty can offer to his long-suffering. We, indeed, raised up by so great a benefit of his, although our merits in no way support us, shall offer melodious thanks to his power; nevertheless, in accordance with the Psalmist’s exhortation, “I will take the cup of salvation and call continually upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115), saying, “Great are you, O Lord, and great are your works” (Tobit 13). “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 2); flesh and tongue bless him, because, looking upon us, he has looked upon our lowliness and raised us to so eminent a pontifical height, not on account of merits that followed from us. 150 Therefore, since by his favor I have been appointed by the mediator between God and humankind as a watcher over souls, the apostolic care entrusted to me summons, exhorts, and wholly and unceasingly compels me to seek the salvation of God’s people with devout zeal and to proclaim peace among all nations with great firmness of heart, since those who have preferred to proclaim it fearlessly surely deserve the grace of blessedness. For it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). And again: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things!” (Romans 10).

Indeed, most excellent son and spiritual compère, because almighty God, having predestined you from your mother’s womb [Gent., “from your womb”], has therefore blessed and anointed you king and appointed you defender and liberator of his holy Church. For this reason we have hastened to commend to your benevolent Excellency, through these apostolic letters, those matters that concern the welfare of the holy Church of God.

Let your most excellent goodness know that our most excellent son, King Desiderius, when he came to the threshold of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0160D] Muratori (*Italian Annals*) rightly assigns this and the following letter to the year 758, contrary to Pagi’s opinion, who thinks they were written in the preceding year. Desiderius did not come to Rome before carrying out everything contained in the following letter. On that occasion—and indeed at Desiderius’s own request—Paul wrote this letter according to his wishes. The same envoys secretly carried it, which deprived it of all credibility and gave a detailed account of everything done by the Lombards. Among other things, it states that Duke Liutprand was expelled from Benevento; Camillus Peregrinus demonstrates that this occurred in A.D. 758 (*Chronicle of the Dukes of Benevento*, from the collection of Pratilli, vol. V, p. 50). It then identifies the very time, saying that the duke arrived “precisely in the month of February of that year.” ID.], peacefully and with great humility, spoke with us about matters beneficial to both parties, and promised us that he would restore the city of Imola [Lamb., “Imola”], [Col. 0161A] on the condition that we should send our envoys to your Excellency and that he should receive back his hostages [Note: [Col. 0161D] Do not suppose that the hostages mentioned here and in the following letter were again obtained by King Pippin. They were the ones whom Aistulf, when besieged a second time at Pavia, had been forced to surrender, as I said above (letter 11, elsewhere 8, note). Although two years earlier Stephen II, taught by experience, had entreated the same king—by urging, admonishing, and even commanding him—to press Desiderius not to break his pledged faith, nothing of hostages being given is inferred from the later letters written by his brother and successor. CENN.], whom he appears to have with you there; and that you should endeavor to confirm peace with him.

Therefore we ask you, most excellent son and spiritual compère, to order that those hostages be restored to our aforesaid son, King Desiderius, 151 to confirm the treaties of peace with him, and to live with him in great friendship, so that, with God’s approval, in your joyful days the people of God on both sides may live in great security and the quiet of peace, and that almighty God may deem you worthy to preserve for a long time upon the throne of your kingdom. For this reason we have sent these most faithful envoys of ours, namely, our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop George, and our beloved son the priest Stephen, together with Rodbert, your envoy [Note: [Col. 0161D] Rodbert was perhaps the illustrious man mentioned by Mabillon (*Benedictine Annals*, book XXII, no. 43). The two papal envoys are the more famous: George was that bishop of Ostia who had accompanied Stephen II into Francia with Wilcharius of Nomentum and others and had repeatedly undertaken embassies to the same king; Stephen, priest of the title of blessed Cecilia, succeeded Paul in the pontificate. ID.], to your prudence protected by God, so that they may recount these very matters to your Excellency.

Having said this, we ask the divine mercy to preserve you, clinging to the throne of your kingdom through ages [“long ages”] and joyful times in devout works, and to grant you eternal life. May heavenly grace keep your Excellency safe.

### XVIII. 152. The Same Pope’s Letter Sent to Lord King Pippin for the Defense of the Holy Church of God

It reports that Desiderius devastated the Pentapolis and consumed all the people’s food supplies with sword and fire; that he cast Albinus [Lamb. and Gent., “Alboin”], duke of Spoleto, into chains; that, when the duke of Benevento was shut up in the city of Otranto [L., “Otoranto”; G., “Otranto”], Desiderius appointed another duke, Argis, in Benevento; that he spoke with the imperial envoy George and invited the emperor’s army into Italy against Ravenna, and the army from Sicily against the city of Otranto; and that he declared that he would hand it over to the imperial party, along with many other matters.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Summary 26 in the Centuriators and Baronius. GRETS.—Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 26): “He sent the twenty-sixth letter through George, his fellow bishop, and the priest Stephen, together with Radbert, Pippin’s envoy [legate]. In it he complains at length about the cruelty and wickedness of the Lombards. He states that he had given his envoys letters asking for the release of King Desiderius’s hostages detained in Francia, and that he had done this so that they might pass through Lombardy [‘so that he himself might pass safely’]; otherwise he would not have asked for it. He urges and solemnly appeals to Pippin to retain them; moreover, he [‘earnestly entreats him not to release them’] should constrain Desiderius and compel him to restore all the possessions of blessed Peter, so that at the Lord’s coming he may shine like the most radiant sun. In the appended *embolum* he sends Pippin certain small gifts.” CENN.]

*(A.D. 758; Codex Carolinus XV, chronicle 18.)*

[Col. 0161C]

**SUMMARY.**—By the same envoys he secretly sends another letter, stating that he had written two copies of letters concerning the impiety and cruelty of Desiderius, because he feared that the Lombards might intercept them. He now writes again that the people of the Pentapolis have been ill-treated by the same king; that Alboin, duke of Spoleto, and Liutprand, [Col. 0162A] duke of Benevento, who had submitted themselves to Pippin, were attacked with arms as rebels; that when the latter escaped to Otranto out of fear, Argis, acceptable to Desiderius, was appointed in his place; and that Alboin, with several of his officials, was wounded and thrown into prison. The same Desiderius summoned from Naples the imperial envoy George, who had been in Francia, made a treaty with him, and planned with him to conquer Ravenna and, with the Sicilian fleet added, besiege Otranto. Later he came to Rome and, when reminded that, as he had promised in the presence of Folrad and Rodbert, the king’s envoys, he would restore Imola, Bologna, Osimo, and Ancona, refused to restore them and broke faith. Against this perjured man he protests: he says that he detained Rodbert so that he might be an eyewitness of everything; more would be reported by him and by the papal envoys; and no credence should be given to letters written according to Desiderius’s wishes. In the *embolum* there is a matter concerning gifts sent by him to Pippin and his sons, the kings.

[Col. 0162B] To the most excellent lord, son, and our spiritual compère, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

Whenever I contemplate the evident merits of your Excellency with mystical reflection and compare them in the eyes of my heart, I must be exceedingly astonished at the unblemished and extraordinary steadfastness of your mind and at the most fervent affection that you continually [Lamb., “earnestly”] display toward the love of God and of his chief apostle, since you strive to favor God more than human beings. Hence it is clear that you surpass all kings and powerful men in devout works, because, after attaining heavenly triumph, you voluntarily offered yourself, most excellent son and spiritual compère, for the liberation of God’s Church. Therefore, so that the contest of your devout activity may be brought to completion, it is frequently fitting for us, as the liberator of the holy Church of God and of its special people, to send apostolic letters.

First of all, nothing is sweeter and more desirable to us than to learn of the joys of your prosperity. Then, as quickly as possible, to make known those matters that are necessary to the holy Church of God and to us. But so that you, most excellent son and our spiritual compère, may know that we previously informed your Excellency by apostolic letters of what has been impiously and cruelly done in these regions by Desiderius, king of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0162D] Unless I am mistaken, that lost letter, whose summary appears in the Codex Carolinus after letter 21, our 20, belongs here, and is as follows: “The same pope’s letter to Lord King Pippin, in which are contained lamentations [Col. 0163B] (and ‘tribulations,’ added by Lamb. and Gent.) because King Desiderius [Col. 0163C] entered into a plan with the imperial envoy George, who had been in Francia, that the emperor should send his army into Italy against Ravenna or the Pentapolis to seize the Roman city, and that Desiderius himself, with the whole kingdom of the Lombards, should fight in his support or assistance to carry out those evils; and because they were daily making raids and plundering incursions into their territories, he requests assistance against those Lombards with many earnest appeals. For this reason it has not been written in this volume, because through excessive age it was already partly destroyed; nevertheless, other sections are not inserted in it. But just as it is read in the preceding letter, so it is also found written in this one.” Gretser notes in the margin: “This letter is therefore missing. Nor do Baronius and the Centuriators mention it in their summaries. The loss is more easily borne if it contained nothing other than the preceding letter.” Lambecius likewise notes: “This letter lacks a number, because its summary is found here, but the text itself is absent.” He does not, however, call the loss smaller than Gretser does, since it would be similar to letter 20, elsewhere 21; for he recognized no similarity between them. The case is different with the letter before us, as will be clear to the reader. I therefore think that this is the letter whose summary survives that is mentioned here. CENN.], when we observed his utterly destructive activity, we deemed it appropriate to detain here with us your most faithful envoy Rodbert, so that, having personally learned and seen what the malice of the aforesaid King Desiderius or [Lamb. adds, “of”] the Lombard people had begun to produce, he might make your eminent Excellency more fully informed. For, as we previously did, behold, we now inform your Excellency, protected by God, that the aforesaid king of the Lombards, passing through the cities of the Pentapolis that you bestowed upon blessed Peter as a great reward for your soul, consumed with sword and fire all the crops and everything that serves for human sustenance. Thus, to the great contempt of your kingdom, he laid waste the dukedoms, places, and cities of the Spoletans and Beneventans, who had placed themselves under your power protected by God; and, after capturing Albinus [L., G., “Alboin”], duke of Spoleto, together with his officials [“and the officials with him”], who had sworn an oath of fidelity to blessed Peter and to you [Note: [Col. 0163D] After recounting the death of Aistulf and the inauguration of Desiderius, Stephen II says (above, letter 11, elsewhere 8): “The Spoletans, through the hand of blessed Peter and the strongest arm of Pippin,” established as their duke Alboin, apparently in the year 756. He then adds that both the Spoletans and Beneventans commended themselves to the king, although the signs of submission are quite obscure. Here, on the other hand, the evidence of submission is less doubtful than Muratori rashly calls it a rebellion against the Lombard kingdom. Desiderius had been made king, after the royal line failed, by the authority of the king of the Franks, through the pope and the royal envoy Folrad; nor were these distinguished dukes bound by any law to submit to the new king. Therefore Paul says to Pippin, “they placed themselves under your power protected by God”; neither of them regarded this as rebellion. CENN.], he keeps him in chains, having inflicted dreadful wounds upon them.

When he approached Benevento, however, the duke of Benevento immediately fled to the city of Otranto [Note: [Col. 0164C] Camillus Peregrinus, *On the Boundaries of the Duchy of Benevento*, dissertation 7 (Pratilli, vol. V, p. 269), cites this passage of Paul’s letter and then says: “Since, therefore, the Greeks held Hydruntum, and Pope Paul in no way differs on this point from Porphyrogenitus, the Beneventan dukes certainly possessed Brindisi, the outermost city on the eastern side of this northern coast.” Hence it is clear how extensive that duchy was, reaching to the Adriatic Sea, and how small a portion of Italy remained for the Greeks. ID.], and, while he pressed him for a long time, he urged the duke to leave his own city; when the duke in no way fulfilled his wish, he appointed another duke in the same duchy of Benevento, named Argis [Note: [Col. 0164C] Desiderius supplied Arichis in place of Liutprand, duke of Benevento, who remained at Hydruntum as ruler in a city of Apulia under Greek jurisdiction. Much is available concerning him in the letters of Pope Adrian. ID.].

Immediately King Desiderius sent to Naples and summoned the imperial envoy George, who had been sent to Francia to you [Note: [Col. 0164C] I discussed George the protosecretary above, letter 11, elsewhere 8, among the notes, concerning the embassy to Francia in A.D. 755. Whether he returned the following year, 757, with gifts from Copronymus—especially organs—and whether he came to negotiate an alliance and treaty with the king, as the Frankish and Fulda Annals report, is not established by these letters. That he had been in Francia is known both from this passage and from the summary of the recently mentioned lost letter; it is also established by what follows shortly. ID.]. With him he spoke secretly and wickedly, entering into a plan with him; and he sent letters to the emperor, urging him to send his imperial armies into this province of Italy. Desiderius himself, with the whole Lombard people, declared that he would offer assistance to those imperial armies, although God was against him, so that the emperor’s army on one side and Desiderius with the whole Lombard people on the other, fighting together, might seize the city of Ravenna, and so that the emperor might accomplish his will—God forbid—in whatever manner he wished.

For he also arranged with the same imperial envoy George that a fleet of Sicilian dromons [“dromon”] [Note: [Col. 0164D] Concerning dromons—ships originally used as fast couriers, since that was once their function in public transport, and later warships—see Ducange’s learned discussion in his *Glossary*. Here the term signifies the Sicilian fleet. It should be noted that the summary of the missing letter contains nothing about the siege of Hydruntum or the Lombard king’s arrival in Rome. The letter must therefore have been sent before these events occurred; nor is it surprising that it contained no other sections, as the summary states, since what was still to happen could not be predicted. CENN.] should be sent to the city of Otranto, so that Greeks and Lombards together, besieging it, might be able to capture the city; and that it should be handed over to the emperor, together with the people and possessions contained there, while that duke and his foster-father John alone should be restored to the aforesaid king.

[Col. 0165A] After the dissolution of those same duchies, the Lombard king also came here to us in Rome [Lamb., “to Rome with the same men”]. We spoke with him and earnestly exhorted him; indeed, by the most sacred body of blessed Peter and also by your Excellency protected by God, we solemnly adjured him to restore those cities—namely, Imola [“Imola”], 156 Bologna, Osimo, and Ancona—which he had promised to restore to us in person and likewise through your envoys, namely Folrad, beloved of God, abbot and priest, and Rodbert [Note: [Col. 0165C] Pagi rightly says (A.D. 757, no. 3) that these envoys were sent by Pippin in the previous year, when Desiderius promised that he would restore the cities; their names had to be specified, for they are listed in this letter as Imola, Bologna, Osimo, and Ancona. This is highly important both for determining the sincerity of the author of the *Life of Stephen II* in Anastasius and for correctly understanding the letter before us. Folrad had been sent from Pavia by Pippin with the papal envoys at the end of A.D. 755 to take possession of the exarchate; several cities had not been handed over by Aistulf. After Aistulf was removed by divine providence, his successor Desiderius promised Folrad in A.D. 756 that he would restore them all. Above we saw them listed (letter 11, elsewhere 8): Faenza, Imola, Ferrara, Bologna, Osimo, Ancona, and Numana. We also noted there from Anastasius that Faenza and Ferrara were handed over to Stephen II by Desiderius, but not the others. Thus the four named here, which Desiderius had promised to the royal envoys Folrad and Rodbert, both show that Anastasius’s account is true and distinguish Desiderius’s promises: in A.D. 756 he promised Folrad alone that he would restore all those cities, while in A.D. 757 he promised Folrad and Rodbert the four not yet handed over, which are listed here. This also overturns the opinion of those who unjustly postpone the final letter of Stephen II to A.D. 757. It is incredible that Folrad was in Italy twice in the same year. Pagi’s opinion, assigning this letter to that same year, is rejected even more decisively, since the events related in it require a longer interval; moreover, as I stated in the preceding letter, Peregrinus dates the expulsion of Liutprand, duke of Benevento, to February of A.D. 758. ID.], to your most excellent Christian authority and, through you, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and your protector. He was obliged to restore them, but he was in no way inclined to consent; rather, playing the deceiver—as a *stropharius* [Note: [Col. 0166D] From the Greek word *strophē*, *stropharius*, also called *strophus* and *strophosus*, meaning a deceiver or impostor. Examples of *strophus* and *strophosus* are available in Ducange’s *Glossary*. I am surprised that he did not notice this passage and provide an example of *stropharius*. ID.] certainly did by employing various pretexts, he said that if he received back his hostages, whom Francia appeared to have there, [Col. 0165B] then he would live with us in peaceful concord.

Therefore we ask you, most excellent son and spiritual compère, and earnestly entreat your Excellency, inspired by God, to order that the complete liberation of the holy Church of God and of its special people be carried out, and thus to stand firmly by what you promised to blessed Peter at the great price of your soul. Deign also to constrain Desiderius, king of the Lombards, forcefully, so that he must restore to blessed Peter, your protector, the promise made before God and fulfill it in every respect. Let it be your care, most powerful king, just as you began, to rescue this holy Church of God and its special people more completely from the attacks of its enemies. 157 Thus, with God’s approval, the contest of your benevolent work may bear abundant fruit, so that on the day of the coming of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ you may shine like the most radiant sun among all kings and powerful men, and may deserve to offer to the divine Majesty, without any violent injury, that holy Church of God and its people, rescued through your aid; and then may you deserve to receive from the same Lord God, the just judge, a hundredfold reward and possess eternal life.

I adjure you, most excellent son, by almighty God and by his chief apostle, blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0166D] Here is another entreaty similar to one used by Gregory III to Charles Martel, invoking the living God and the most sacred keys. ID.], to deign to hear our prayers with a kindly gaze and a most willing spirit [Lamb., “be pleased”], so that almighty God may incline the ears of his divinity toward you in those matters for which you have entreated his power, and make you victorious over all barbarian nations. For all the peoples dwelling upon the face of the whole earth know your struggle, which you have undertaken for the defense of the holy Church of God, and they praise you as a great and distinguished king.

Nor do we cease to extend and spread your good reputation far and wide, because, after God, we place your most steadfast faith in our breast like an impregnable wall. After God’s protection, we possess great confidence of hope in you, and through the merit of your unstained promise and faith we have often obtained what we sought. For this reason we have sent our present envoys with the greatest urgency, namely, our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop George, and our beloved son the priest Stephen, to your Excellency guarded by God. When they have stood at your God-beloved feet, together with Rodbert [Ratbert], your most faithful envoy [Note: [Col. 0166D] Concerning both papal envoys, see the preceding letter. Rodbert, or Radpert, the companion of Folrad, after dismissing him, had detained him in Rome so that he might witness everything that the Lombards had begun to do and report it to the king as an eyewitness. ID.], they will inform your most Christian Excellency orally of everything that has happened and of whatever the nature of the matter requires, as well as of what is necessary for us.

For our mind longed intensely to send apostolic letters of greeting and visitation to your Excellency, in order to report the course of events [Lamb. adds, “and”], but we were completely unable to do so [Col. 0167A] because of the Lombard king’s plots threatening us on every side.

Nevertheless, behold, we have now sent your Excellency two copies of apostolic letters secretly and with the utmost care; and we do not know whether those letters have reached you. We therefore fear that they may be intercepted by the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0167C] The summary of the letter not preserved in the Codex, which I cited above, seems to indicate these two letters. I think they were written in duplicate as letters thirty and thirty-three, concerning which see below. CENN.].

For this reason we have now sent you other letters through our aforementioned envoys, as though obeying the will of the aforesaid King Desiderius by releasing his hostages [“his guests”] and confirming peace. But, good and most excellent son and spiritual compère, we drafted these letters in this fashion so that our envoys might be able to travel to Francia to you. For if we had not done so, they would have been entirely unable to cross the territories of the Lombards; but once you have received these letters, do not in any way carry out their contents [Note: [Col. 0167D] This event, imitated by Stephen III in A.D. 769 (letter 45, elsewhere 46), as I shall say there, is well worth noting. It sheds considerable light upon the obscure, ambiguous, defective, and at times even less-than-truthful style of writing that the pontiffs had to use before Adrian, so long as the Lombards remained in power. ID.]. Nor should you permit the aforesaid hostages [“guests”] to be restored to the Lombard party. Rather, we earnestly adjure you, most excellent son and spiritual compère, by the living God and by the body of blessed Peter, to order that Desiderius himself, or his Lombard people, be forcefully constrained, so that he may restore to your honey-sweet Excellency, and through you to blessed Peter, your patron, the cities that he promised; for, as has been said, we have been able to establish no firm agreement with him concerning what he initially promised.

We pray almighty God to look upon you and your kingdom with a merciful gaze from the throne of his Majesty, to surround your Excellency with his right hand [Col. 0167C] and fortify you in every respect, and to permit you to complete the course of this present life in safety and govern the power of your kingdom through many years, together with your most excellent daughter, protected by God and our spiritual commère, and your beloved sons, who are also mine. May you rejoice in their blossoming offspring, and may almighty God permit your most illustrious seed to enjoy the same height of royal power until the end of the world; and in the age to come may he grant you infinite joys with his saints and chosen ones, so that, having obtained in the present life and in future blessedness the promised crown of reward, you may deserve to reign with Christ. 159 May heavenly grace keep your Excellency safe.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] See letter 6. ID.]

**EMBOLUM.**

For the sake of a true blessing, we have sent you [Note: [Col. 0167D] I do not understand what Ducange means. He separates *apallarea* from *spatha* and argues that it is the same as *applare*, namely, a spoon, as though a spoon had been sent to Pippin among the other gifts. In Anastasius’s account of Sergius, he says that a silver *apallarea* (section 162) was a covering made of silver plates in the shape of a spoon. Consult him under *Applare*. I confess that I do not know what sort of sword this was; nevertheless, the reasoning of the enumeration of the other gifts suggests that we should read “one *apallarea* sword,” not “one *apallarea* and one sword.” In any case, this gift is especially appropriate for the defender of the Church; and it is known that later a sword said to have been taken from the body of Saint Peter began to be given to emperors at their solemn coronation. The words of the *Ceremonial of the Patricius* (book I, chapter 4) make me think that the blessing was devised in a later age: “Although it is called a blessed sword, I have not found its blessing; Pope Sixtus IV arranged certain words to be said when the sword is given.” See the words that follow there, and especially the Fourteenth Roman Order, in Mabillon (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 402). I say nothing about the other gifts found in Anastasius. ID.] one *apallarea* sword set with gems, with its belt; one ring containing a hyacinth [*hyacinthum*], a storax-colored stone; one cloak decorated with peacocks. We ask that, without taking offense, you order Lord Charles and Carloman to receive this small blessing as a great apostolic blessing: individual rings containing hyacinths [*yacinthos*].

### XIX. 160. The Same Pope’s Letter Sent to Lord King Pippin

Concerning the priest Marinus and his wicked counsel, and concerning his consecration.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Summary 4, in Baronius and the Centuriators. GRETS.—Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 4): “In the fourth [‘Fourth’] he orders that the priest Marinus be made a bishop, so that he may be diverted from his counsels [‘from counsels’] opposed to the Roman see.” CENN.]

*(A.D. 758; Codex Carolinus XXXIX, chronicle 19.)*

[Col. 0168B]

**SUMMARY.**—Pippin had informed him that Marinus, a priest created cardinal in the preceding year, while he was in Francia, had plotted with the imperial envoy George against the holy see—something that Paul himself already knew and that the emperor had disclosed to the king. He therefore asks that Pippin permit him to be ordained bishop in some Church of the Franks, lest he become worse, but rather so that he may repent of the crime he committed.

To the most excellent lord, son, and our spiritual compère, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans: Pope Paul.

Your most Christian excellence knows perfectly well how our presbyter Marinus [Lamb. adds: “who”] is staying there with you, seeking, in an evil undertaking [Col. 0168C] against the holy Church of God and the orthodox faith, with God opposed to him, to devise with a certain George, imperial secretary, counsels contrary to our see and likewise to yours; this the emperor himself also made known to your God-protected excellence by his letters. Therefore, since blessed Peter, apostle and prince of the apostles, has deigned to choose and confirm your most Christian goodness as defender of the orthodox faith, champion of his flock, and liberator of the Christian people, for this reason we adopt and earnestly beseech your distinguished goodness, excellent king and spiritual compater, that you order our most holy [Col. 0169A] brother [Note: I would not dare affirm that this was the same Wulcharius of Nomentum mentioned above, epistle 13, elsewhere 27, in the notes. There was also another Wilcharius in Francia at this time, who, having resigned the bishopric of Vienne, had fled to the monastery of Saint Maurice, or Agaunum, in 740, and was later made archbishop of Sens. Although he certainly did not occupy that see before 765—for he succeeded Lupus, who subscribed to the assembly at Attigny in that year (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1702)—there was also another Wilcharius of Sion, unless perhaps the same man is meant. Whoever he was, the pontiff entrusts his authority to him, so that, as a cardinal presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, he might exercise that office. CENN.] Wulcharius, bishop, to direct that he himself, in our place, should consecrate that same presbyter Marinus bishop, and that you arrange for him to be ordained in one of the cities established in those regions under your authority, wherever your most wise and distinguished excellence shall have judged appropriate, so that, remembering his crime, he may repent of having acted wickedly. Otherwise—God forbid—the ancient enemy of the human race might find his mind wandering and, as though raising it aloft, utterly destroy him with the utmost violence by whatever means he can. Rather, as we trust in your most benevolent excellence and in the God-given expansion of your illustrious heart, may your splendid excellence deign to lend an ear to this request of ours [Note: From epistle 36, elsewhere 32, it is clear that Pippin did not comply with the pontiff’s wish, as we shall see when we come to that letter: for although the king excelled in piety, he nevertheless did not consider treachery worthy of reward. ID.], so that he may remain secure in this matter, [Col. 0169B] and so that we may continually command prayers to the Lord God of heaven on behalf of your immense joy and well-being. Farewell.

## XX. 162. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord King Pippin, Sent through the Presbyter Peter

In it are contained the embassy of Bishop Remedius and Count Audecarius [Al., Andegarius], explaining how he received from Desiderius, formerly king, part of the rights of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and how he promised to restore the remaining rights [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 20): “He sent the twentieth letter through the presbyter Peter [he entrusted the twentieth letter to the presbyter Peter for delivery to the same king], containing certain praises of him, because he had defended the Roman Church against heretics [had defended it]. He then relates the acts of Bishop Remedius and Count Andegarius, how he received from Desiderius, formerly king [Desiderius the king], part of the rights of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and that he promised to restore the remaining rights [to restore the rest], with an adjuration [an earnest appeal] that, if Desiderius neglected these matters, Pippin should compel him, as he had promised Pope Stephen, Paul’s brother, and Paul himself.” [Col. 0170C] CENN.].

(Year of the Lord 759, Codex Carolinus XXI, chronicle 20.)

### ARGUMENT

Having learned in the preceding year the wicked character of Desiderius, Pippin sent illustrious envoys to Rome: Remigius, brother and archbishop of Rouen, [Col. 0169C] and Autharius, duke. Moved by their presence, throughout the whole month of April of this year he promised to restore everything to the holy see and asked the pontiff to inform the king of this. Paul announces these things through his envoy, the presbyter Peter, and promises to announce them through another envoy if the king, naturally untrustworthy, keeps his promises. Yet he implores the king’s faith [Col. 0170A] and constancy, so that he may vindicate the entire donation for Saint Peter, in accordance with the issued charter.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual compater, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul [Note: In the following year all editors place this letter, and rightly so, since it is said to have been given in March, in the thirteenth indiction, as Gretser printed it—a date indicating the year 760. But Lambecius’s recension has the twelfth indiction, and I do not see why Muratorius, who used this recension in his edition of the Codex Carolinus, disregarded it in the Italian Annals. ID.].

Because your excellence has rightly been approved by the heavenly judgment for your good works, this has already been openly demonstrated by the actual outcome of the deeds accomplished—namely, because, having received from above a share in divine wisdom, you are clearly shown to have more effectively earned the scepters of royal dignity through heavenly blessing. Therefore, since your distinguished excellence does not doubt that this grace was sent to you by almighty God, you strive with all your strength to please the one who bestowed it, and do not cease to contend, by divine will, for its sake and rather than for your own, in the struggle—namely, for the holy universal Church—and with the strength of exaltation. Your excellence, whose heart is protected by God, applies to this the rewards promised in heaven by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, rewards promised for the fruit of such labor. There one rejoices not in human glory among human beings but in a divine happiness among the angels, a happiness never to be lost. Rejoice and be glad, most fortunate king, because through your struggle, with God’s assent, your holy spiritual mother, the universal Church of God, rescued from the plots of her rivals and exalted, triumphs; and the orthodox faith, through your zeal and the arm of your strength, stands undefiled against the arrows of heretics.

[Col. 0170C] For this reason you have been made blessed and just in all your works, dearest son and most victorious spiritual compater, distinguished king. We make known to your exalted Christianity that recently, when your most faithful men had arrived to us—namely, the God-beloved Remedius [Note: In the Codex, “your brother” was read, as Gentilotus notes, although the word has been erased. This Remedius, or Saint Remigius, truly was Pippin’s brother, and is so called in epistle 35, elsewhere 43; in both letters, however, his dignity—that is, his position as archbishop of Rouen—is omitted, although the annalists cited by Pagius (755, no. 24) report that he obtained that see in 755, after Raginfridus had been deposed for insolence. In the Catalogue of Bishops cited by Guillelmus Bessin (Councils of Rouen, part II, p. 2), Remigius’s archbishopric began two years earlier: “Saint Remigius, or Remedius, brother of Pippin, king of the Franks, obtained the see of Rouen in 753. He was present at the assembly of Attigny in 761 and died in 771.” Little reliance should be placed on this chronology, however: it assigns the assembly of Attigny to 761, although the Frankish Annals and Regino establish that it was held in 765. Saint Remigius was in fact present and subscribed under the name Remedius, bishop of the city of Rouen. Thus his dignity at that time is certain; but since both of Paul’s letters, which were written before that year, are silent about it, I consider the matter highly doubtful. Let the learned judge. CENN.] your brother, and [Col. 0171A] Aucharius [Andegarius], most glorious duke—it was agreed between them and Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that throughout the whole coming month of April, of this thirteenth indiction [Lambecius: twelfth], he would restore to us in full all the rights of your patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: namely, all the patrimonies, rights, places, boundaries, and territories of the various cities of our Roman commonwealth. Therefore, the same king of the Lombards is known to have restored some of these rights to us [Note: In epistle 18, elsewhere 15, which was the occasion of so distinguished an embassy, four cities were being reclaimed. Here, however, the patrimonies, boundaries, and territories of cities belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction are mentioned without naming those cities. Perhaps the apostolic envoy privately received what is omitted in the letter, to be reported later. ID.], and he professes and altogether promises that he will restore all the rest to us. For this reason the aforesaid Desiderius, king of the Lombards, earnestly implored us to make this known to your God-protected excellence through our apostolic report. And behold, just as we have made this known, after God, to you, our distinguished, most exalted, and God-protected Christian ruler and liberator, through these apostolic lines, so we are sending to your God-inspired and exalted sublimity our present beloved son, the presbyter Peter. We ask that you receive him with your customary benevolent regard and deign to send him back to us with an effective and favorable report concerning the perfect and complete restitution of the various rights belonging to the causes of your patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. If, however, the aforesaid King Desiderius or his Lombard people remain in the promise they profess and make, and if everything has been restored by them to us according to the agreement and the terms of the pacts, then we shall make known to your excellence, which is to be preserved by God, the merit you have thereby earned [Lambecius: “the matter”].

Therefore, beseeching, we ask and earnestly implore—and indeed we adjure you, most excellent and most Christian king, most beloved son and spiritual compater—by almighty God and blessed Peter, who anointed you king, to order that you complete and fulfill more perfectly all that pertains to the exaltation and fuller liberation of the holy Church of God and of this province redeemed by you, just as you promised to blessed Peter and to our predecessor, the pontiff of holy memory, our most blessed brother, Pope Stephen [Note: This is a very clear indication that he was reclaiming the cities that were missing from the complete donation, whose original document was kept in the archive of the holy see. ID.]. Thus may you receive from the hand of almighty God the promised and reserved crown of reward [Col. 0171D]. We pray thereafter for the mercy of our almighty God, that he may surround you with his grace, together with your most sweet spouse, the most excellent queen, our daughter and spiritual commater, and your most beloved children—that is, the exalted kings—and grant you to possess the summit of the present kingdom and the triumph of victory, and to enjoy eternal joys in the heavenly kingdoms with the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XXI. 166. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord Pippin, Glorious King, Sent through Bishop George

It contains expressions of thanks for the liberation of the holy Church of God and, in an added passage, he asks that he might be worthy to receive from the sacred baptismal font the son who had then been born to him [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 19): “He sent the nineteenth letter to Pippin through Bishop George, containing expressions of thanks for the safety [defense] [Col. 0172D] of the holy Church of God. In the added passage he asks to be worthy to receive from the sacred baptismal font Pippin’s son, who had then been born to him.” ID.].

(Year of the Lord 759, Codex Carolinus XXIII, chronicle 21.)

[Col. 0172B]

### ARGUMENT

He sends Bishop George as his envoy to Pippin, placing in his mouth what he should report. The entire letter is concerned with praise of the king and thanksgiving for so many and such great benefits bestowed upon the Church. Nothing in it is especially clear except the added passage, in which he expresses the wish to receive from the sacred font Pippin’s recently born son.

To the most excellent son, our spiritual compater, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul [Note: That the letter cannot be removed from this year is shown by the Frankish Annals; Pagius (year 759, no. 14) uses the testimonies of the annalist of Metz and the chronicler of Saint Gall to establish this chronology. Both these sources and the aforementioned Annals consistently report that a son was born to Pippin, who was named after his father and died in the third year afterward; it is of this son that the pontiff speaks in the added passage. CENN.].

An epistolary communication [perhaps: “report”] always refreshes the mind by its own force and in a certain way becomes material for charity. Since, therefore, the sincere love of spiritual sons eagerly sustains paternal affection, it is fitting for us with the greatest eagerness to fulfill what the desire of a pure conscience demands. Although the scarcity of messengers, because of the length of the journey, hinders us from discharging the duties of paternal charity, whenever an appropriate need arises we nevertheless do not cease to visit your most excellent Christianity through letters sent back and forth, and, embracing you with customary honor [Lambecius adds: “and greeting you”] [Note: “to visit” also seems to belong here. GRETSER.], to make it possible, insofar as we can, to behold in writing those whom we cannot see present with our bodily eyes. Thus, with God illuminating it [Lambecius: “your excellence, illuminated by God”], opinion has everywhere spread and proclaimed the merits of your excellence, so that they are all laudably demonstrated by the deeds you have performed. Therefore, insofar as the testimony of our mouth is able, by bearing witness to your extended praise, we have judged it appropriate to return thanks to your distinguished excellence and to send there the most holy and most reverend brother [Col. 0173A] George [Note: Namely, the bishop of Ostia, equally well regarded by the pontiff and the king of the Franks. He had come to know him five years earlier in the retinue of Stephen II, and in the preceding year had received him as an envoy (epistle 17, elsewhere 29, note 4). CENN.] and our fellow bishop, to your illustrious and God-pleasing presence. To him we have entrusted, so that he may report individually to your God-protected sublimity and excellence, the needs of all the interests of your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and of this province redeemed by you [Note: Here is the principal reason why the bishop of Ostia, who had undertaken that journey against Desiderius in the preceding year, and not unsuccessfully, is sent as envoy again, after the Lombard had restored some things to the holy see and had promised in April to return everything else. It was a secret commission, and could be entrusted only to a man of grave and exceptional fidelity. For the Lombard had employed his customary art of deception, and it was unsafe to commit his deceptions to writing, lest intercepted letters should harm what had been restored. In the preceding letter he had promised to report the merit of the matter if Desiderius kept his promises. The opposite occurred, and, as Codex Lambecianus and Gentilotus read it, he judged that the merit of the matter should be explained orally by his envoy. ID.].

But we ask and earnestly implore you, son preserved by God, spiritual compater, most benevolent king, and our liberator after God, that you order this same envoy of ours to be received with your customary benevolent and congratulatory regard; and that, in response to our requests, which concern the exaltation of the holy Church of God and especially the reward of your soul and your eternal memory, you deign to lend the ears of your benevolence, moved by God, and to provide a suitable and speedy result in every matter. For, most exalted of kings, most beloved son and spiritual compater, almighty God willed you to be present, through the hands of blessed Peter, as liberator of his holy Church, so that through your customary protection the complete safety and redemption of his holy Church of God and of this province might advance. We pray to our Lord God that, in his mercy, he may so direct your actions that he may order the years of your present life with prosperity, so that, enjoying the governance of the kingdom’s victories, you may carry it out for a long life, and that, with your most sweet spouse, the most excellent queen and our spiritual commater, and your distinguished children—that is, the kings—almighty God may grant both of you to rejoice forever with his saints and elect in the rewards of eternal promise. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

+

Meanwhile, most exalted of kings, it has been brought to our knowledge that, by God’s will, almighty God has granted from your womb a new king, for the exaltation of his holy Church. We have been raised up with the greatest joy by his birth; therefore we earnestly ask you to grant us the honor of receiving this great son of yours from the most sacred bath of baptism [Lambecius omits “from” and “great”]. Thus may the grace of the Holy Spirit be doubled among us [Note: Lambecius: “May the grace of the Holy Spirit come to be in our midst,” etc.] and the joy of a twofold celebration arise for us.

## XXII. 169. Letter of the Same Pope to Lords Charles and Carloman, Kings

It contains expressions of thanks and the most abundant blessings [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex after 27): “Three letters were written to Charles and Carloman, namely 22, 28, and 30, elsewhere 41, 42, and 40. All three are mentioned together in this very brief argument: ‘He also wrote three letters to Charles and Carloman, in which he exhorts them to follow in the footsteps of their ancestors, to show faith toward God and [showing faith toward God and] blessed Peter, and to defend and exalt the Roman Church.’ CENN.].

(Year of the Lord 760, Codex Carolinus XLI, chronicle 22.)

[Col. 0174A]

### ARGUMENT

He replies to Charles and Carloman through the abbots Droctegangus and Wulfhardus, who had brought their excuses for sending no gifts, saying that he desired no gifts other than their safety, the defense of the catholic faith, and the exaltation of the Church.

To the most excellent lords, Charles and Carloman, sons and kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, [Col. 0174B] Pope Paul.

Receiving the report of your excellence brought by the bearers of this letter, namely the religious abbots Droctegangus and Wulfhardus [Note: It is clear from the following letter that these men were royal envoys. None of the three letters sent to them expressly presents the young kings’ own envoys; rather, since their requests were conveyed to Paul either by their father’s or by the pontiff’s envoys, it is clear that the pontiff customarily sent his replies through those same royal legates. ID.], we have been greatly relieved by the wished-for news of your safety. We desire that the Lord, in his mercy, protect and direct your life and actions and bring you to full maturity. Through the same lines you have made known to us that you feel the greatest embarrassment because meanwhile you have been unable to send us the convenience of gifts through these bearers [the manuscript omits “not”]. But what is it, sweetest and most beloved sons, most victorious kings, that makes you eager to gladden us with your gifts? For we desire no gifts other than diligently to learn of the prosperity of your safety and to rejoice in your progress. This is our wealth: the gladness of your exultation, which we eagerly embrace [F., “the joy of your exultation”]. This is the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and the integrity of your protection is the defense of the orthodox faith. For the Lord chose you above all kings and appointed you liberators of his holy catholic and apostolic Church, and deigned to anoint you kings through the hands of blessed Peter.

But may almighty God, through whom kings reign, bring you to full maturity and grant that you and your distinguished offspring may possess the throne of the kingdom through long-lasting [Note: Perhaps “long-enduring,” and perhaps this should likewise be read elsewhere. GRETSER.] and prosperous ages, for the exaltation of his holy [Col. 0175A] Church and the broadest defense of the orthodox Christian faith [Note: As in the preceding letters to Pippin, so also in these to the young kings, two matters must be carefully considered: namely, the proper definition of the patriciate conferred on the Frankish kings by the apostolic see, against the opinions of Peter de Marca, Pagius, and others; and the protection and defense of the Church and of the catholic faith. Also, the successors of the prince of the apostles devoted themselves no less diligently to vindicating the Church than to asserting the catholic faith. CENN.]. May he grant you victories from heaven, subjecting all barbarian nations to your God-imitating footsteps, and deign to bestow the joys of eternal life, so that, just as you reign in the present life, you may be worthy to reign with Christ in the age to come. And may all the people say: Amen, so be it, so be it (Psalm 105). Farewell.

## XXIII. 171. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord King Pippin

It asks about his health and safety and at the same time about his envoys, who had been sent to the royal city [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 5): “In the fifth [letter] he congratulates Pippin on his safety and indicates that his envoys have not yet returned from Constantinople.” ID.].

(Year of the Lord 760, Codex Carolinus XXXVIII, chronicle 23.)

[Col. 0175B]

### ARGUMENT

In this courteous letter he says that through the royal envoys Droctegangus and Wulfhardus he had written another letter, wishing to learn about the Aquitanian expedition; he had so far received no reply, though he had learned from pilgrims that Pippin had returned safely. Therefore he says that he is joyful, and that he would be still more joyful to receive a royal letter, which he eagerly desires. There is no new information about his own envoys at Constantinople.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual compater, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul [Note: Summary 5 in Baronius and Centuriator Gretser.].

After sending our letters and greetings through Droctegangus and Wulkardus [Lambecius: Wulfhardus], your God-beloved and most faithful envoys, we earnestly implored [Note: Lambecius: “We seemed earnestly to implore.” Tengnagel: “We seemed earnestly to implore.” Gentilotus deleted *visi*—“seemed”—by removing the line and wrote *deprecati* instead.] your distinguished excellence [Col. 0175C] to consent to make us more certain and more joyful concerning your extensive safety and concerning the journey on which you departed, how the Lord had dealt with you. When, after so much time had elapsed, we received no sequence of reply from you concerning this matter [Note: *Agnovimus* is absent from the manuscript but was supplied by another ancient hand. GENT.], our spirit was exceedingly worn down. But through pilgrims arriving from various regions at the thresholds of the apostles, we learned that you, most distinguished son and spiritual compater, had returned safely to your own places, with God’s assent. Therefore our spirit was relieved with great joy.

172 For this reason, having sent these present apostolic lines of ours as a visitation, we earnestly ask that your exalted excellence deign as soon as possible to make us joyful by informing us of the abundant safety of your well-being. Tell us, most Christian son and spiritual compater, how matters stand with you, with our most excellent daughter and spiritual commater, and with your distinguished [Lambecius adds: “your”] sons, so that our spirit may exult with the greatest joy, since we burn with an intense desire constantly to learn of your safety and to rejoice in your happiness; for your safety is the exaltation of your holy mother, the Church, and your prosperity is proved to be our joy.

Therefore, most distinguished son and spiritual compater, good and excellent king, behold, until now we have been unable to learn any truth concerning our envoys who departed from the royal city [Lambecius: “because they departed from the royal city,”], or what was being done with them; and for that reason we have been entirely unable to tell you anything about them. But when we have been able to learn the truth of the matter, we shall immediately send a reply to your distinguished excellence [Note: Anastasius, in the Life of Paul (section 258), says: “This pontiff often sent his envoys with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition to Constantine and Leo Augustus, for the restoration and confirmation to their former veneration of the most sacred images of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, and of the blessed apostles, all the holy prophets, martyrs, [Col. 0176D] and confessors.” Hadrian likewise testifies to this in his letters to Constantine and Irene (Second Council of Nicaea, act 2). Some light will be shed on this matter below (epistle 37, elsewhere 20). In sum, although in vain, Paul labored with the greatest zeal to restore in the East the ancient tradition of the Church concerning sacred images (Baronius, 757, no. 4); and this is the subject of the frequent commendation of the Frankish kings for the defense of the orthodox faith. This was the principal concern of the envoys sent from Francia or Rome to Constantinople, although in the East the loss of the exarchate and, in Rome, of the duchy, were also generating schemes and wars, which eventually broke out when Frankish friendship had been vainly sought through gifts and services. For the Franks and Romans, equally defenders of the catholic faith and tradition, rejected Greek dissimulation and deceit. CENN.].

After these matters, we ask the God of heaven to grant you, together with your most excellent queen, our daughter and spiritual commater, the most Christian queen, your sweetest spouse, and your most beloved children and our sons, those same distinguished kings and patricians of the Romans, both longevity in the present life and the enjoyment of the government of the kingdom, and to make you participants in the heavenly kingdom; and may he permit us always to rejoice in your abundant safety. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XXIV. 173. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord King Pippin

It contains blessings, and the aforesaid pope asks that Lord King Pippin send his envoys to the region of Rome, inform him of his health and safety, and report how he had fared on the journey, how the Lord had delivered his enemies into his hands and humbled them beneath his feet [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex): “In the eleventh [letter] he asks to be informed how Pippin is, since an unfavorable rumor about his health had been spread by his enemies [the eleventh asks him about his health because his enemies had spread some rumor about his well-being].” CENN.].

(Year of the Lord 760, Codex Carolinus XXXI, chronicle 24.)

[Col. 0177A]

### ARGUMENT

Again concerning the same matter: because an adverse rumor among the populace had spread something about that expedition, he awaits the royal envoys with their letters all the more ardently.

To the most excellent and our spiritual compater, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, [Col. 0177B] Pope Paul [Note: Cointius and Pagius (year 760, no. 2) rightly assign this letter to this year. Since it was written after the preceding letter, there can be no doubt that it belongs toward the end of the year. CENN.].

Whenever the spiritual endeavors of God’s faithful are reported, the minds of those who hear are immediately set on fire with love of God and his commandments, and are moved to proclaim most fully, for God’s praise, their merits of heavenly contemplation [Note: Lambecius and Gentilotus: “they are aroused to the contemplation of heavenly consideration”; hence, “it is altogether fitting, most powerful of kings, to consider your piety,” etc.], and to entrust them to testimonies of Scripture that are to endure forever. Through your cooperation and assistance [the text may mean “are kindled,” or something similar], the exaltation of the Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith [Note: Read *procuratur*, “is secured.” GRETSER. In the Theodosian Code (book VI, title 30, law 10), Gothofred interprets *profligationem debitorum* as “the collection of debts.” Likewise, in book VIII, title 8, law 9, one finds *necessitatem profligandam*, “a necessity to be dealt with”; and in the commentary on book XI, title 22, law 4, *profligandae seu exigendae pensitationis solemnitas*, “the solemnity of a payment to be dealt with or exacted.” Whether something similar is signified here by *profligatur*, the learned may judge. Certainly Lambecius and Gentilotus read it thus in the manuscript, and I do not see why Gretser corrects it to *procuratur*. Ducange cites the same passages of the Theodosian Code in his Glossary and adds nothing further. CENN.] are advanced. For this you are recognized as blessed and praiseworthy in all things among kings before God and human beings, most Christian king, and the name of your goodness shines, written in the sight of the divine power. For since this period of time has elapsed, during which we have neither been granted a report of your safety [Col. 0177C] nor been able fully to learn what was happening around you or how you completed the journey on which you departed [Note: This Aquitanian expedition is called a “journey” both here and in the preceding letter. The Frankish Annals likewise, speaking of the same expedition—which lasted nine years—usually have “making a journey” and “completing a journey.” CENN.], the affection of our desire has been intensely stirred by anxiety to learn this, especially since unfavorable reports concerning those regions have been brought to us both by our enemies and by yours. Therefore a great desire clings to us: to learn the joys of your safety, to rejoice in your successful undertakings, and, conversely, to learn of the crushing of your enemies. For this reason we ask that you order your messengers to make us certain, as we desire, of your prosperity and joy, since your safety is our prosperity and your exaltation is undoubtedly our joy and immense security. For this we beseech the divine power of God, that he, our protector, together with his angels, may deign to guard and govern your distinguished Christianity, so that in the heavenly kingdoms, with the saints and elect who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, you may receive abundant reward. We indeed desire that your God-protected excellence may make us more certain [Note: Lambecius and Gentilotus: “sending [letters], may your God-protected excellence command us to know what is being done,” etc.] of what appears to be happening to you or to your Christian people, and how our God has humbled your enemies and ours; and, as we have said, order your messengers to make us certain, as we desire, of your prosperity and joy. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XXV. 175. Another Letter of the Same Pope to Lord King Pippin

In it he asks for assistance against the Greeks [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 8): “In the eighth [letter] he reports that the Greek emperor is under arms and wishes to recover the exarchate of Ravenna and Rome [the eighth reports that the Greek emperor is under arms in order to recover the exarchate of Ravenna and Rome], and asks him for assistance and defense against the Greeks [and implores assistance from him against the Greeks].” CENN.].

(Year of the Lord 761, Codex Carolinus XXXIV, chronicle 25.)

### ARGUMENT

Bishop Wulcharius and the royal envoys Felix and Ratbertus had come to Rome. After they returned to Francia, the pontiff was informed that the Greeks were preparing to move against Rome and Ravenna. Therefore he asks Pippin to send an envoy to Desiderius, who, if necessary, should order the people of Benevento, Spoleto, and Tuscany to bring aid to the Church, for it was a religious war. He likewise asks him to send another envoy who would remain in Rome and press Desiderius concerning this same matter.

[Note: [Col. 0178D] Summary 8, Baronius, and the Centuriators. GRETS.]

To the most excellent lord, son, and our spiritual compadre, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

[Note: Pagius, following Cointius, assigns this letter to the year 758. Muratorius suspects that it may belong to 762, or rather to the preceding year. In this he is not mistaken (Annals, 762), although he is more concerned with the argument than with the chronology, in order to prove against Leo of Ostia that the duchies of Benevento and Spoleto at that time did not belong to the jurisdiction of the Holy See—a point that no one denies him. For the rest, the sequence of events contained in the preceding letters clearly demonstrates that this letter must be placed in the year 761. The year 760 is wholly assigned by the Annals and by the two letters of our codex recently mentioned to the king’s silence and his Aquitanian expedition. But the two preceding years are covered by causes whose effects we find in this letter, as both the Annals and the letters explain. For in 758 Desiderius had entered into plans hostile to the papal territory with George, the imperial envoy; and in 759, fearing the king of the Franks, he partly restored and partly promised to restore, before the king’s distinguished envoys, what he had seized from the Holy See. Nor is he recorded thereafter as having inflicted any trouble on the pope before the year 764 (below, Letter 38, or 24), although, as regards the restitutions, he did not keep his promises. CENN.]

[Col. 0179A] We make known to your lofty Christian devotion, preserved by God, through these apostolic writings, that now, after your envoys who recently came to us had departed—namely, Wulcharius [Lamb., Wilcharius], our most holy brother and fellow bishop, Felix the religious man, and Ratbert, an illustrious man—

[Note: This embassy seems to have been arranged by Pippin in order to comply with the pope’s request, since he had once and again asked to be informed through reliable messengers about the Aquitanian expedition and the king’s safety. For Paul was not accustomed to conceal the reasons for embassies when matters of importance were involved. The leader of the envoys seems to have been that bishop of Nomentum mentioned more than once above. Wilicarius, who appears in the letters of Hadrian, was the archbishop of Sens, the successor of Lupus, who attended the assembly at Attigny (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1701). I say “seems” to have been the bishop of Nomentum because in the same assembly there is also recorded a Williharius, bishop from the monastery of Saint Maurice; this similarity of names is the cause of the uncertainty. Nevertheless, the fact that he is everywhere called “our brother and fellow bishop”—as is also done of George of Ostia in Letter 8, or 4; 9, or 6; 11, or 8; 18, or 15, and elsewhere—strongly suggests that the same person is meant everywhere. For the other Wilcharius, the archbishop of Gaul, is always called such by Hadrian. ID.]

a messenger sent by the faithful of the Holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, has joined us, reporting to us what they always customarily report truthfully: that the most impious Greeks, enemies of the Holy Church of God and assailants of the orthodox faith, acting in opposition to God, desire to invade us and the territory of Ravenna and to undertake a military movement against us.

[Note: If the city of Rome obeyed the Greek emperors, as they claim, why then do the Greeks threaten war equally against the Romans and the people of Ravenna? ID.]

Therefore, since after God and blessed Peter we have hope nowhere except in your most noble excellence, we earnestly beseech you, most excellent son and spiritual compadre, to command, for the sake of God and out of reverence for blessed Peter, that you provide for the safety of this province redeemed by you, and that you deign immediately to send an envoy of yours to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if necessity should arise, he may provide us with the aid that has been requested against the incursion of those same enemies. Command also the Beneventans, Spoletans, and Tuscans, who dwell near us, to come to our assistance.

[Note: Here we have abundant evidence of at least an outward appearance of peace between Desiderius and the Romans. According to Pagius, Cointius, Muratorius, and all the others who trusted the edition of Gretser, which assigns Letter 20, or 21, to the year 760 under indiction 13, this peace could have begun only after the reconciliation with the Church before Remigius, Pippin’s brother, and Authari, the duke and royal envoys, in March of that same year. But for me, using the recension of Lambecius and reading indiction 12, that peace became evident in March of the year 759; and this is sufficient to remove the letter from the year 758, contrary to Cointius and Pagius. As for Muratorius, if Paul asks Pippin to instruct Desiderius to order auxiliaries to the Spoletans and Beneventans as well as to the Tuscans, then those dukes, although they may have preferred to submit to Pippin, were already obeying Desiderius, just as their ancestors had obeyed the earlier kings of Italy; and thus all Italy seemed to be breathing again. His statement that those duchies were at that time in no way subject to the Holy See is beside the point. For confusing the Carolingian donation with Pippin’s donation in the year 757 produced an entirely unnecessary argument. What learned person does not know that the Spoletans and Tuscans did not come under the dominion of the Holy See before 774, and the Beneventans before 787? As for Tuscia, which they call Lombard Tuscia, there is no doubt. Concerning those duchies, however, the matter is uncertain, as I shall note in the letters of Hadrian. ID.]

and we beseech your excellence, established by God, to command that, when this coming month of March arrives,

[Note: From this it is clear that the letter was written at the beginning of the year 761. ID.]

you send us an envoy of yours who is to remain here in Rome with us and who, if necessity should require it, is himself to press King Desiderius concerning the same matter, so that he may send us the aforesaid assistance.

[Col. 0179C] For, as your excellence has been fully informed, those most impious Greeks persecute us for no other reason than the holy and orthodox faith and the pious tradition of the venerable Fathers, which they desire to destroy and trample underfoot.

[Note: Everyone knows that this was the sole cause of the Greek persecution, which began in the time of Gregory II, except Muratorius, who, thinking only of temporal dominion, mocks this as the chief cause. ID.]

For this reason may your benevolent excellence carefully arrange that the madness of those same enemies be brought to nothing, and that this province, redeemed by your struggle and granted by you to blessed Peter for the remedy of your soul,

[Note: It is probably the exarchate and the Pentapolis that are meant; for the Roman province in no way belongs to Pippin’s donation. Moreover, unless the Spoletans and Beneventans had followed the Greeks, there would have been no danger to the Roman province. ID.]

may remain more perfectly under your customary protection from the plots of our rivals. May abundant reward be recorded for you in heaven, together with praise for your name and the exaltation of your entire people, just as has already happened and may now be proclaimed much more widely throughout the whole world. Through the intercession of blessed Peter, may the Lord grant you from heaven the triumph of victory over all peoples, so that, when the assailants of the holy orthodox faith have been confounded by your aid, peace, joy, and observance of the Christian faith may be proclaimed in all the churches, and so that, deservedly, God may bestow heavenly joys upon you for this. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XXVI. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to the Lord King Pippin, for the Defense of the Holy Church of God

In it are contained very abundant praises, and [variant: “in” added] in an additional section it is requested that the aforesaid lord King Pippin send his command to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that, if necessity should require it, he provide assistance both to Ravenna and to the other maritime cities, in order to fight against the attacks of the enemies.

[Note: Argument of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 14): “In the fourteenth letter he sends the treacherous letters of Sergius, bishop of Ravenna, and requests assistance.” ID.]

*(A.D. 761, Carolingian Codex XXVIII, chronicle 26.)*

### Argument

After letters had been sent by Sergius, the archbishop of Ravenna, Paul received two letters addressed to Sergius: one from Leo the imperial official and one from faithful Venetians, concerning the plans of the Greeks. He sends both to Pippin, urgently requesting an order to Desiderius that he provide assistance, if necessary, for the protection of the maritime cities of Ravenna and the Pentapolis.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual compadre, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

[Note: Summary of Centuriator 14: “He sends the treacherous letters of Sergius, bishop of Ravenna, and requests assistance.” The wording is highly ambiguous; someone might suppose that Sergius himself wrote treacherous letters. This is not so, as this letter shows. GRETS.]

To your lofty Christian devotion, preserved by God, excellent son and spiritual compadre, just as we promptly make known to our liberator after God whatever is arising or being done in these parts, so through these apostolic words of our reports we inform the sweet and God-appointed summit of your royal power that, after the dispatch of our letters,

[Note: Muratorius correctly assigns this letter to the year 761, contrary to the opinion of Cointius and Pagius, who assign it without justification to the year 757, against the historical evidence. It should be noted that he dated the preceding letter after the departure of the envoys, whereas this one was written after the dispatch of the letters; thus the two letters are separated by only a short interval, and both were written at the beginning of the year. CENN.]

we received words from our most holy brother Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, which Leo, the imperial official, appears to have sent to his holiness and to the province of Ravenna. And behold, we have sent below, within this apostolic letter of ours, a copy of those words to your illustrious excellence, so that, recognizing in them the cunning of the persuasion attached to them,

[Note: That imperial official was therefore persuading Sergius to defect from the pope. What the emperor had failed to obtain by gifts, prayers, or feigned friendship, he was attempting to achieve by treachery. But Sergius, restored to his see by Pope Paul, reveals the Greek schemes to him out of gratitude. ID.]

your radiant excellence may more zealously undertake the defense of the Holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith, so that you may deserve to receive from the Lord our God the crown of reward reserved for you in the heavenly kingdoms. Meanwhile, we wish you to remain forever prosperous and safe in the Lord throughout the ages. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

### Additional Section

Finally, we have sent you below, within this writing of ours, a copy of the letter secretly sent by certain faithful Venetians to our most holy brother Sergius, the archbishop, together with copies of the letters that the same most holy man sent to us. We ask, as though we were personally present, and earnestly beseech and adjure your most excellent Christian devotion by Almighty God, that you command your order to be sent with all speed to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if necessity should require it, he may provide assistance both to Ravenna and to the maritime cities of the Pentapolis, in order to fight against the attack of the enemies.

[Note: A new proof of the archbishop Sergius’s loyalty toward the pope. The attached copies of both letters undoubtedly indicated the movement of the Greeks, as is clear from the preceding material. In the Chronicle of the Dukes of Naples, edited by Pratilli, vol. III, p. 32, we read that Duke Stephen, who succeeded Theodore in the year 759, promised the pope “that if it should happen that the Lord Emperor sent his soldiers against Rome, he, the duke, would bring him assistance with his own soldiers.” This confirms the meaning of the same letter: namely, that Rome as well as the exarchate was being sought by the Greeks, although the letters sent from Sergius to Rome speak only of the exarchate and the Pentapolis. ID.]

## XXVII. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to the Lord King Pippin

In it are contained expressions of thanks for the exaltation of the Holy Church of God, and a request that he send his envoy to Rome.

[Note: Argument of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 6): “In the sixth letter he gives thanks for the exaltation of the Roman Church, and indicates that, after God, his confidence rests in the arm of the most powerful king Pippin; and he asks that he send him his legate, through whom he may reveal to him the plans and plots of the Greeks.” ID.]

*(A.D. 761, Carolingian Codex XXXVII, chronicle 27.)*

### Argument

He addresses extraordinary praises to Pippin for having undertaken the defense of the Catholic faith and the Church. He again asks him to appoint an envoy who will remain in Rome, against the impious Greeks, who were constantly plotting to destroy the orthodox faith and the Church. Peter, first defender, the pope’s envoy.

[Note: Summary of Baronius and Centuriator, Gretser.]

To the most excellent son and our spiritual compadre, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

While those things that are done through our efforts can be erased by no forgetfulness, how much more should those deeds performed for the praise of the Redeemer, our Lord God, and of his most holy Church and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, not be consigned to oblivion either by the passage of time or by changing circumstances, but should always remain publicly declared for the glory of heavenly power and as a pious example to his faithful?

[Note: In the manuscript another hand, even an ancient one, corrected the reading to “are handed down.” Tengnagel ultimately established “are consigned” as the reading. ID.]

Know, most excellent son and spiritual compadre, good orthodox king, that your lofty and pious work shines brightly in heaven before the angels of God, filled with glory, and remains laudably proclaimed among all nations throughout the whole world, because through your aid, after God, and through your excellent struggle, your holy spiritual mother, the Church of God, has plainly been rescued from the plots of her enemies, and the orthodox faith of Christians has been defended against its assailants. Therefore rejoice and be glad in the Lord, most benevolent king, because the name of your excellence shines, written in the book of life, before the sight of God.

Meanwhile, since such a great capacity of desire weighs upon our heart, we thought it appropriate to make ourselves joyful and certain regarding your prosperity by sending our reports from the Holy Church of God and by discharging our obligation to your excellence,

[Note: “Obligation,” or “bond,” as below in Letter 41. GRETS.]

since nothing in this life is sweeter or more pleasant to us than to rejoice in the Lord over your prosperity, in which, as we have often written, your safety, the exaltation of the Holy Church of God, and the true defense of the faith consist.
