Therefore, although we are separated from you by the distance of bodily presence, we desire nevertheless to be spiritually joined to you through our reports by mutual affection.

[Note: From this entire introduction, which displays such an outpouring of praise for Pippin, we infer that no reply from him had reached Rome. Nor is this surprising: Waifer’s insolence, for he had forgotten his oath and was laying waste to everything by fire and sword, had recalled Pippin to Aquitaine, as the Frankish Annals of Fulda and all the others cited by Pagius teach (761, no. 5 and following). CENN.]

Accordingly, we earnestly beseech your excellence, as we requested through our earlier letters,

[Note: I know of no earlier letters here other than those recently praised, which I rightly stated were assigned by Muratorius to the year 761. In both cases the subject is a royal envoy who is to remain in Rome; nor do the reasons for his residence conflict with one another. In the former letter the matter concerns soliciting assistance from Desiderius against the Greeks; here it concerns reporting to King Pippin what has occurred against the Greeks. In both cases Paul adds this as a kind of consequence to the principal reason given: that through the envoy he may also report the merit of the matter. ID.]

that you command your most faithful envoy to be sent here to us in Rome, where he is to remain with us on account of the plots of the enemies, and through whom we may report to your excellence the substance of the matter, as the outcome of events requires. For this reason we have now sent to your excellence, preserved by God, the present Peter, first defender of our Holy Church and our most faithful envoy, whom we have instructed to explain to your benevolence everything concerning apostolic affairs.

[Note: The fear of the Greeks, who were said to be preparing arms against the Romans and Ravennates, was not the only source of danger. There were also other matters involving Desiderius himself, who was still retaining possessions belonging to the Holy See. These, I suppose, were secretly entrusted to the first of the defenders. ID.]

We ask that you receive him with a joyful spirit and accept him in every respect for the love of your patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Deign to lend a gracious ear to our prayers and command that he be sent back to us with results and joyful messages. With humble entreaty we ask you, good orthodox king, that after God you be our firm protector and defender, steadfastly remaining in the good work you have begun and in the pious work of redeeming the Holy Church of God.

For your excellent Christian devotion knows very well how great and of what kind is the impious malice of the heretical Greeks, who eagerly meditate and plot how, in opposition to God, they may humble and trample underfoot the Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and destroy the holy orthodox faith and the tradition of the holy Fathers.

[Note: Muratorius observes that the same thought is expressed in slightly different words in Letter 25, or 34. The holy pontiff cared deeply about the affairs of the Church; but he also knew that it was especially his duty to secure the Catholic faith and the veneration of the sacred images. For this reason the Romans and Ravennates had defected from the Greeks, and for the same reason the Greeks pursued both groups, as Paul testifies more than once. See Letter 25, note. ID.]

But you, good and most powerful king, as a true orthodox ruler, deign to resist those same impious heretics manfully, and, with your customary aid protected by God and suitably arranged, defend the Holy Church of God and the orthodox faith of Christians. For after God great confidence rests in your excellence and in the arm of your most powerful kingdom. We believe that, with God’s cooperation, this hope of ours, remaining firm, will reach the desired outcome, so that deservedly the just Lord our God may grant you reward in the present and future life, through the intercession of the blessed prince of the apostles, for whose love you contend in his causes.

Then, made joyful by your pious purpose, may we be able to sing together with the Prophet in harmonious voice:

“Save, O Lord, the most Christian King Pippin, whom you commanded to be anointed with holy oil by the hand of your apostle, and hear him on whatever day he calls upon you.”

Together with these prayers, we also ask his piety that he grant your excellence, and your queen, our spiritual co-mother protected by God, the power of the kingdom to possess in health through a long old age, and likewise your beloved sons, the lords Charles and Carloman, lofty kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, and the most noble lady Gisela; granting you also the blessedness of eternal life to enjoy in the heavenly kingdoms. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XXVIII. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to the Lords Charles and Carloman, Kings

In it are contained [variant: “is contained”] matters concerning the defense of the Holy Church of God.

[Note: Argument of Panvinio (Vatican Codex after 27). See above, Letter 22, or 41; for it comprises three letters sent to Charles and Carloman at different times, without regard to chronology. ID.]

*(A.D. 761, Carolingian Codex XLII, chronicle 28.)*

### Argument

On the same occasion, he sends exhortations through Peter, first of the defenders, who is setting out for Charles and Carloman: since they are worthy of the highest praise, they should not cease, following the example of their father, to protect both the Catholic faith and the Church.

To the most noble and excellent sons, Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Long ago, when Almighty God saw the lamentation of his Israelite people and the impious oppression inflicted upon them by the Egyptians, he took pity on them and sent his servant Moses. Through him he performed signs and wonders, rescued that same people of his, and, through him, instructing them in the law

[variant in Lambecius and Gretser: “establishing”],

led them to the rest they desired.

Joshua was also joined to him in order to wage the wars of the Lord

[variants: “he joins Joshua”; “he attaches Joshua”],

and God granted them other worshipers of his divine name as helpers. Yet in all these men his divine majesty was not so well pleased as in King David:

[Note: Lambecius and Gentilotti add: “And as the same most merciful God of ours bears witness through the Prophet in what he says: ‘I have found David, my servant,’ and so forth.”]

“my servant according to my heart; with holy oil I anointed him,” and to him and his offspring he gloriously granted the kingdom to possess forever.

Thus, most excellent and noble sons, kings appointed by God, the same Lord our God has been pleased with your most Christian excellence. Sanctifying you in your mother’s womb, he raised you to so great a royal dignity, sending his apostle, blessed Peter, through his vicar.

[Note: Nothing is more frequent in these letters than the claim that this anointing was performed through Saint Peter. Here the statement is more explicit, for it is said to have been carried out by the pontiff, heir to Peter’s power. The Roman pontiff was long called Peter’s vicar; the ancients often assigned this designation specifically to him, whereas the more general title “vicar of Christ” was also customarily applied to abbots. See Coustant, preface, no. 13 and following. CENN.]

Anointing you and your most excellent father with holy oil, he filled you with heavenly blessings, and entrusted to you the exaltation and manly defense of his Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and of the orthodox faith of Christians.

This, most excellent sons, you have resolved [variant: “endeavored”] to accomplish with all your strength, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit and aided by heavenly protection. Through your aid and struggle, that same Holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, rejoices, having been freed from the plots of its enemies. In the Lord Jesus Christ and in the sight of the Divine Majesty, your pious works shine forth, and your names have been recorded in the heavenly kingdoms together with those of the kings David and Solomon and the other worshipers of God.

Meanwhile, since we recognize that we have been relieved by so great a benefit of yours, love urges us, most Christian and dearest sons, diligently to learn of your prosperity and to rejoice in the Lord. Therefore, with paternal affection, as a visit and greeting, through these apostolic writings of ours we discharge our bond by sending to your excellence the present Peter, first of the defenders of our Holy Church and our faithful envoy.

[Note: This custom continues even today: namely, of entrusting several pontifical letters, called briefs, to one messenger for delivery to different princes. Another reason also applies here, as I said in Letter 21, or 41, note: a private embassy to the royal youths was not being arranged. ID.]

May he convey on our behalf the desired greeting. We ask that you receive him kindly and that through him you make us certain and joyful regarding your safety. We earnestly ask your excellence, dearest sons, that, following the pious footsteps of your Christian parents, you become imitators of your great-grandfathers

[Gentilotti: “of your grandfather also, and of your great-grandfather”],

as well as of your most excellent and God-appointed great king, your father, and of your most distinguished mother, the queen preserved by God, who are shown to have been faithful to God and blessed Peter above all kings.

[Note: From this the story attached to Charles Martel is disproved—the story that he was condemned to eternal punishments—which is discussed by Baronius and Pagius (741, no. 16 and following). For the holy pontiff would not have commanded the royal youths to follow their grandfather’s footsteps if he were said to have been condemned to eternal punishment. Gentilotti notes that the manuscript also contains the name “grandfather,” which is missing from the printed editions; that it was omitted through Tengnagel’s carelessness is clear from the very sense of the letter. As for Pippin of Herstal and Charles Martel—whom everyone reports to have seized the property of churches—Paul says that only their Christianity is to be imitated. He presents the example of their parents because they were faithful both to God and to blessed Peter. ID.]

Their merits shine in the heavenly kingdoms. Therefore we ask the most merciful patience of our God that, protecting you with his grace, he grant you royal scepters to enjoy through long and prosperous times, enlarging the boundaries of your kingdom, granting you victories from heaven, casting all your adversaries beneath your feet, and granting you possession of the heavenly kingdom for infinite ages just as of the earthly one. Farewell.

## XXIX. Copy of a Letter of the Same Pope Addressed to the Lord King Pippin through the Abbots Witmar and Gerbert and through Hugbald

In it are contained praises of thanksgiving for the exaltation of the Holy Church of God, together with a request that he should always continue to contend for that cause.

[Note: Argument of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 24): “In the twenty-fourth letter Paul replies to two letters of Pippin. One [the other] Pippin had sent through Peter, first defender; the other through the abbots Witmar and Gerbert and the illustrious man Hugbald. It has the same subject as the preceding letter, except that it adds certain matters concerning the Lombards: namely, that they have restored some of the rights belonging to Peter [the Longobards: “some of the rights belonging to Saint Peter”], but not others, and are now attempting [variant: “were attempting”] to seize again those that they had previously restored. Therefore he asks Pippin for assistance against them.” The letter that he calls “the preceding one” is Carolingian Codex 18, our Letter 34, which Pagius and Cointius rightly assign to the year 763, as I shall show below; but I do not see what similarity it has with this one. ID.]

*(A.D. 761, Carolingian Codex XVII, chronicle 29.)*

### Argument

Having received two letters—one brought by Peter, first of the defenders, on his return, and the other subsequently by the royal envoys, the abbots Widmar and Gerbert and the illustrious man Hugbald—he gives thanks for the letters sent to him as requested. Meanwhile, he reports that they had negotiated with the Lombards concerning the affairs of the Church, but that, apart from the restoration of certain livestock, nothing had been accomplished concerning the boundaries of his cities and the invaded patrimonies. He says that he will learn everything from the mouths of his own envoys, for he himself was sending his envoys with the royal envoys to Desiderius on behalf of those same patrimonies, and he did not know what the outcome would be.

[Col. 0186C] To the most excellent son and our spiritual compadre, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

[Note: Summary 24 of Baronius and Centuriator, Gretser.]

Since such a very great affection of love toward your excellence, inspired by God

[Lambecius: “established by God”],

continually abides within us, therefore, just as thirsty earth longs for a rain-bearing flood, so we too desire to learn news of your prosperity and to rejoice in your progress,

[Note: Cointius and Pagius wrongly defer this letter to the year 766, while assigning the two preceding letters to the year 758. The same envoy who had brought those letters to Francia had returned to Rome with royal letters after Pippin’s return from the Aquitanian expedition. Nor do I see how the pope could be speaking of any other “progress.” Muratorius thinks it was written in the year 759; but the Aquitanian war did not begin before 760. CENN.]

for this is the devotion of our heart: to rejoice when your safety is our security.

Meanwhile, we received with great affection the contents of the two letters sent by your excellence: one first through Peter, first defender, our envoy, and the other through your present most faithful envoys, namely the abbots Widmar

[Lambecius: Witmar]

and Gerbert, and the illustrious man Hugbald.

[Note: Of these royal envoys, Witmar—whom Mabillon notes was called Guitmar, abbot of Centula (Benedictine Annals, book XXIII, no. 3)—signed the assembly at Attigny in the year 765; the other abbot is unknown. Hugbert, unless I am mistaken, is the Hucbert sent by Charles to Stephen III after Pippin’s death, concerning whom Hadrian writes below, Letter 93, or 71. ID.]

As we examined the pages of both letters, we immediately learned clearly everything written in them, and straightaway returned immense praises to our Lord, who had granted us cause to rejoice in your safety.

Finally, in your reports the customary steadfastness of your mind, illumined by God, brought us the confidence of hope, since you have earnestly made known and diligently demonstrated by your works that you will contend with all your strength for the exaltation of the Holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith, and that you will remain in the pledge of faith which you made to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to our predecessor, your lord and most blessed brother, Pope Stephen.

Therefore, since we are firmly joined in the bond of our charity, it appears that, in accordance with what we requested when we sent our petition, you have sent your aforesaid envoys to us, so that they might press the king of the Lombards concerning the various causes and rights of the Holy Church of God and might stand by us in our assistance.

[Note: To Peter, first of the defenders, besides the apostolic letters in which he again requested an envoy who would assist the Romans against the Greeks, he had secretly entrusted all the apostolic affairs. From this it may be inferred that both matters were carried out by Pippin. Nothing more plausible can be gathered from the other letters of this pontiff. ID.]

For this we return innumerable thanks to you, because you continually strive to act as a benevolent king and lover of your spiritual mother, the Holy Church of God, most Christian son and spiritual compadre. The Lord will surely be for you a worthy recompense both in the present and in the future.

We therefore, most excellent son and spiritual compadre protected by God, remain steadfast in our affection for your charity. No circumstance of affairs or times can separate us from your charity, because you truly stand as our defender and helper after God.

Finally, in the presence of your aforesaid envoys, who were standing with us together with the envoys of the Lombards, as well as with men from the Pentapolis and from each of our individual cities, a verification was made before them concerning certain rights held between the two parties—namely, concerning livestock

[Note: Cangius demonstrates in his Glossary, with many examples from charters and Lombard law, that at that time peculia meant nothing other than livestock. Thus, these should be understood as having been restored mutually. But the pope states that the boundaries of the cities and the patrimonies, of which the preceding material gives evidence, were still being retained by the Lombards. Indeed, he testifies that they had again invaded what had been restored two years earlier (Letter 20, or 21). Hence see how correctly Muratorius thinks that this letter was written in the year 759, since he himself assigned the aforementioned Letter 21 to the year 760. CENN.]

restored between the parties.

For concerning the boundaries of our cities and the patrimonies of blessed Peter, which were being retained and had been invaded by those same Lombards, we have received nothing up to the present time

[Lambecius and Gretser add: “we have received nothing”];

indeed, they have again invaded even those things that they had first restored.

Therefore it was agreed that our envoys and the envoys of each of our individual cities should proceed with your envoys to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, in the presence of those men and of the aforesaid king, verification might be made concerning those same boundaries and patrimonies, and that everything might be restored to us according to the agreement. We do not know what will result from this; nevertheless, through your aforesaid envoys you can learn the substance of the matter.

[Col. 0188B] Therefore we ask your excellence, protected by God, to order matters in such a way that we may receive full justice in every respect, so that the same blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for whose lamps are being restored you are contending, may be your firmest helper and best rewarder. For let your most excellent Christian piety know for certain that, if the aforesaid boundaries and patrimonies of our cities, invaded by those same Lombards, are not restored to us, they will plot to invade again even those things which they first restored.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] These, that is, had not yet been invaded a second time; for “they invaded” and “they will invade” at the same time are contradictory. The matter is otherwise if we understand that part of them was invaded again and that another part is going to be invaded again. ID.]

[Page 188] Therefore we earnestly ask your Christian piety, in accordance with your customary disposition,

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Lambinus: “that you may order these very things to be restored to us, as you are accustomed to accommodate yourself to our petitions, so that your …” The words “so that you may thus accommodate yourself to us as usual,” and everything following them, have been struck through as though deleted. GENT.]

that the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and the welfare of this province redeemed by you with God’s power, may advance; and when your envoys have more clearly reported to us everything that they had been instructed by your excellence to undertake, we have given them an answer on each point and informed them about everything they ought to report to your excellence, and we have urged them to make our petitions known to your ears.

With these matters thus set forth, we beseech the clemency of our almighty God that he may grant to you the support of his grace, and allow you to enjoy this present temporal kingdom for a long old age with bodily prosperity and the salvation of your soul.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Lambinus: “and the present temporal kingdom in a long old age.” — “The present temporal kingdom for a long old age.” Tengnagel corrected the text as it stands in the edition. ID.]

May you enjoy this together with your most sweet consort, your most excellent queen, daughter and spiritual co-mother, and your most distinguished children; and may he also grant you possession of the heavenly joys of infinite rewards. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## XXX. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORDS CHARLES AND CARLOMANN, KINGS

In it are contained thanksgivings, remarks concerning the letters sent by them, and an exhortation that they should always contend, together with their father, for the defense of the holy Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex, after 27): “This argument should also be repeated for Letter 22, otherwise 41.” CENN.]

(Year of the Lord 761; Codex Carolinus 60; chronicle 30.)

### ARGUMENT

To Charles and Carlomann, who had replied through the same chief chamberlain that they would defend the catholic faith and the Church to the end of their lives, he gives the fullest thanks, again urging them always to follow in their father’s footsteps.

To the lords Charles and Carlomann, most excellent sons, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Paul the pope.

How brightly you adorn the summit of royal glory with the radiance of honor is plainly evident to everyone, since, clearly, although born of illustrious stock, you appear also to be distinguished by pious deeds and worthy character. Thus you possess one grace of this divine gift by birth, and enjoy another through your actions. Nor is it surprising that your nobility shines with such emblems of glory, since it is written: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Psalm III).

For we glorify and praise the clemency of our God, who has bestowed upon you so great a grace of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he had predestined you before you came forth from your mother’s womb, for “those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also glorified” (Romans VIII).

Truly the Lord has magnified his mercy toward you and, anointing you as kings through his apostle, blessed Peter, has appointed you defenders of his holy Church and of the orthodox faith,

[Note: [Col. 0189D] I explained above (Letter 28, otherwise 42), with the pope himself as interpreter, how such an anointing performed by Peter is to be understood. Here, moreover, we have a very clear definition of “patrician,” a term that occurs very frequently in these letters. Pippin and his sons Charles and Carlomann had been declared kings of the Franks by Stephen II through sacred anointing and had at the same time been made patricians of the Romans—that is, defenders of the holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith. The patriciate does not refer in the least to another category of authority belonging to the Roman pontiff. We have the richest witnesses to the matter in the pontiffs themselves, whose letters are contained in this Codex Carolinus. Accordingly, all the empty labors of scholars must safely be rejected, and their opinions can be charged with falsehood. CENN.]

so that, in this good work, you may become participants with your most Christian father; for a worthy reward will be granted to you with him in the heavenly kingdoms, and you will be counted with the entire company of the saints.

Meanwhile Peter, the first among the defenders, our envoy, has returned to us and brought the letters that you sent. When they were reread, our heart was filled with great joy. Through them you have made known to us, most excellent and most distinguished sons, that you will always remain in love for blessed Peter, your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and for us; and that you will contend manfully for the defense of that holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith. Indeed, good and most excellent kings, we must place complete confidence in your steadfastness of this kind, since, after God, we have great hope in you.

But may the almighty Lord, who is rich in mercies, bring you to full maturity, granting you the strength of his arm, making you victorious over all barbarian nations, enlarging the boundaries of your kingdom, and allowing descendants from your illustrious stock to sit upon the royal throne of your power until the end of the age,

[Col. 0190B] for the eternal exaltation of his holy universal Church and the defense of the orthodox faith.

But I ask you, most excellent sons, to become imitators of your most Christian father and, following his footsteps that please God, strive to complete the good work that you have begun, just as he has demonstrated it to all nations by all his deeds. Contend bravely together with him, so that the fullest exaltation of the holy Church of God may be secured, when blessed Peter has received his just possessions through your assistance.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Everyone understands how closely this corresponds with the preceding letter; some passages are even expressed in exactly the same words. Neither letter mentions apostolic envoys, for both appear to have been delivered by royal envoys. ID.]

As a result, with blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, interceding, may you receive before God and his angels a worthy recompense of heavenly rewards, and may the memory of your name remain laudable, proclaimed for ever and ever.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Lambinus: “may it remain in praiseworthy form.”]

And may almighty God, who established all things from nothing by the word of his power, direct your endeavors according to his good pleasure, making you cling to his divine commandments, granting you the prudence and diligence by which you may be able to govern the summit of the kingdom, and subject the nations of hostile peoples beneath your feet. Just as he has granted you royal dignity in the present life, so may he also bestow upon you the joys of heavenly rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] After the word “joys,” the manuscript adds: “Farewell.” GENT.]

## XXXI. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN

Concerning a certain monk sent by Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria.

[Note: Lambinus: “from Cosmas.”]

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 7): “In the seventh [‘Seventh’] he commends to him a monk sent by Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria.” CENN.]

(Year of the Lord 761; Codex Carolinus 35; chronicle 31.)

### ARGUMENT

After the departure of the envoys, a letter came to Rome from Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, by an African ship, concerning the vindication of the orthodox faith against Greek impiety. The pope sends it because it will be welcome to the great defender of the catholic religion.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope.

Because the grace of the Holy Spirit has gone before and the love of God has inflamed the heart of your kindly and outstanding excellence, it is certainly clear, most distinguished king preserved by God, that you cling to pious endeavors. When we see such an abundance of grace accumulated in you, we and all Christians have been given full grounds for confidence in you, since we see that you will act with the whole exertion of your mind in matters relating to the worship of God and the observance of the true orthodox faith.

[Col. 0191B] Meanwhile, most exalted son and spiritual co-father, if anything reaches us, we will gladly make it known to you as an orthodox king and defender of the Christian faith. We inform you that, after your envoys had departed, a ship from the regions of Africa arrived to us. In it came a certain monk, sent with letters by Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 0191B] Lambinus: “Cosmas.”]

[Note: [Col. 0191B] In the famous letter of Hadrian to Charles, which appears at the end of the Second Council of Nicaea (Labbe, Councils, vol. VII, p. 919), we read the following relevant passage: “This Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, together with the other principal patriarchs—namely Cosmas of Alexandria and another Theodore of Antioch—formerly sent to our predecessor of sacred memory, Paul the pope, their own synodical letter concerning the true faith. In it they carefully set forth how they, together with our holy catholic and apostolic universal Roman Church, the other orthodox bishops of the East, and the Christian people, understood the matter of the most sacred images, and how, fervent in faith, they existed with a sincere devotion of mind in the veneration of those same holy images.”

Baronius too, in discussing the council of Stephen III below (year 769, no. 10), cites this passage and does not omit what Stephen, successor to Paul, decreed in the Roman council, using the authority of that synodical letter, as Hadrian testifies. Moreover, the sacred annalist, from Theophanes, gives the date of the rejection of the Monothelite heresy by this same Cosmas together with his associates (year 742, no. 2). Pagi confirms this matter (same year, no. 5) in the very words of Theophanes, since Baronius had used the corrupt edition of the Miscella in place of Theophanes. The words are: “In that same year (743), Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, together with the city itself, which at that time was held by Cyrus, who had lived under Heraclius, renounced the Monothelite depravity and, recognizing the error, returned to the orthodox Church.” Therefore the name Cosmas belongs not to the monk who carried the letter, but to the patriarch. CENN.]

We have sent you a copy of these letters from the Eastern prelates and other nations concerning the integrity of the faith, so that your radiant excellence may examine it.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] I do not insist that this was precisely the synodical letter of the three patriarchs, which the Alexandrian patriarch gave to Paul through a certain monk, since below (Letter 44, otherwise 49) it will be clear that a letter was sent to Paul by the patriarch of Jerusalem. Yet I do not see why it should have been delayed for so long. For the distinguished Mansius, in his notes on Pagi (year 760, no. 1), asserts that in approximately that same year a synod was held at Jerusalem to vindicate the veneration of the holy images. Saint John, bishop of Gothia, who had returned from a pilgrimage to the holy places, urged that it be held (Acts of the Saints, June 26, p. 191).

This is why I have judged that the letter assigned by Pagi and others to the year 758 should be brought here, especially since I see the pope confessing that he received it after the departure of your envoys—the same envoys whom we saw in the preceding letter depart without any papal envoy accompanying them. ID.]

Thus you may recognize the matters that are sent to us for the integrity of the faith by Eastern prelates and other nations, and your heart may rejoice in the devotion toward God’s commandments that they appear to possess. Since your mind is intent upon the study of pious reflection, we believe that you will greatly rejoice if we make known to you those matters that pertain to the integrity of the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0192C] What I said in the preceding discussion I emphasize again: the principal concern of the Roman pontiffs was to vindicate the orthodox faith and the tradition of the Fathers, that is, the veneration of sacred images. Next, they held dear the Roman Church—namely, Christ’s poor and the lamps of the sacred buildings—and for this reason they assert the patrimonies so forcefully. Finally, they also took concern for the Donation, so that they might preserve peoples from the stain of heresy and from the frequent hardships of war, and prevent what had once been offered to blessed Peter from perishing contrary to justice and right. Those who think that this final point was the principal one, and affirm this in their writings, have either not seriously read these letters or interpret them according to their own wishes. ID.]

May that holy orthodox faith, which you honor with reverence, support you in the present life for a long time with victory, and grant you the joys of eternity to possess with the saints. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## XXXII. 193. COPY OF THE CHARTER MADE BY PAUL, OF HOLY MEMORY, PONTIFF OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH AND UNIVERSAL POPE

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 2): “Secondly, he grants Pippin the monastery of Silvester with three others nearby, which had been granted to Zacharias by Carlomann the monk.” ID.]

(Year of the Lord 762; Codex Carolinus 12; chronicle 32.)

### ARGUMENT

He grants Pippin by apostolic letter—what they call a bull—the monastery of Saint Silvester on Mount Soracte, together with three monasteries subject to it, annulling the earlier letters of Saint Zacharias by which they had been granted to Carlomann, if they should be found anywhere. The subject monasteries are those of Saints Stephen, Andrew, and Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Summary 2 in Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.]

Paul, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most excellent son Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, and [or] to the venerable monastery of blessed Silvester, confessor and pontiff of Christ, and to the entire congregation of monks, indeed [or: and] also to all who in the future shall remain there forever.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] It is known that older letters of this kind are also found. We call them “bulls,” deriving the name from the *bulla*, or leaden seal, customarily appended to them. It should nevertheless be observed in passing that the famous Musellian Museum’s collection of such seals begins with Paul I, for which this supplies an indisputable testimony. Yet distinguished men such as Gorius, in his work on Doni, and Baldinus, in his notes on Anastasius (vol. IV, p. 29), have also brought to light one or two from the preceding century belonging to Saints Deusdedit and Honorius I.

I would not dare to decide the matter. Nevertheless, I would like the very origin of the bulls that prevails in our own age to be seriously considered. For this precious monument of antiquity supplies the formulas of the Roman pontiffs’ Book of the Daily Offices, chapter 7, in Garner’s edition; there, indeed, no example of a privilege or charter is found with its opening formula. The examples published elsewhere, such as two of Stephen II in Labbe (Councils, vol. VI, pp. 1646ff.), which display such an opening, consequently acquire greater credibility here. CENN.]

With salutary foresight, we believe that whatever the usefulness of venerable places requires should be entrusted to those persons in whom the grace of divine illumination has been diffused and who strive with all their strength to accomplish what is shown to pertain to the praise of our Redeemer and to the fullest restoration of holy places.

And since it is established that your lofty excellence has asked of us for the monastery of blessed Silvester, pontiff and confessor, situated on Mount Serapt [Lambinus: Serapte],

[Note: [Col. 0193C] Soracte. See Baronius, year 747, no. 9. GRETS.]

also for the three monasteries subject to it—namely, those of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, blessed Andrew the apostle, and Victor—

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The same Mabillon (ibid.) relates from the same chronicle that Carlomann built at the foot of the mountain, in a place called Amariano, a monastery in honor of Saint Stephen, where he lived with several brothers; likewise, at the foot of Mount Grifianelli near Castrum Babianum, he founded another in honor of Saint Andrew, having acquired many estates and assigned them to it. Later he withdrew into Samnium, to the monastery at Cassino. Mabillon, or any other writer whom I have seen, says nothing about the third monastery of Saint Victor. Yet Mabillon himself cites the passage from Paul’s letter as evidence, in which the three monasteries subject to Soracte are clearly named; this occurs again below. ID.]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The frequently cited Annals of the Franks, under the year 746, state: “Then Carlomann went to Rome, where he was tonsured, and built a monastery on Soracte in honor of Saint Silvester. After remaining there for some time, he proceeded from there as far as Saint Benedict at Cassino, and there became a monk.”

Pagi reports the matter in nearly the same words from the Tilian annalist (year 747, no. 5). Basnage, however, observes that the annals edited by Quercetanus had proceeded from the manuscript codex of Tilius and from the Annals of the Franks. Thus we learn from these alone that the monastery was founded by Carlomann, since later writers merely borrowed whatever they say about its foundation. Baronius (year 747, nos. 8ff.), on the authority of Einhard and also using the testimony of Aimoin, who followed Einhard, asserts the same matter. Mabillon (Annals, book 22, no. 12) read in a certain tenth-century chronicle of a monk of Soracte that a monastery had already been built in the same place where Silvester is said to have hidden during the persecution of Maxentius. CENN.]

with all their properties and possessions, places and various resources, and everything generally belonging to them, in their entirety—for behold, assenting to the will of your lofty excellence through this charter, we grant to you in full stability, from the present fifteenth indiction and forever, our monastery of blessed Silvester, together with the other monasteries subject to it, namely those of blessed Stephen and of the blessed Andrew and Victor, with everything generally and completely belonging to them,

[Note: [Col. 0194C] This charter, or rather charter-document, as it was then understood, and what we call a bull today, was issued after the Kalends of September in the year 761. It cannot be removed from the year 762, since the fifteenth indiction continued until September of that year. Accordingly, everyone unanimously assigns it to this year. ID.]

for the support of pilgrims and the sustenance of our brothers, the poor of Christ, and the monks who now and in the future live a spiritual life there.

[Note: [Col. 0194D] Muratorius discusses this matter at length (Italian Antiquities, dissertation 37). In the formulas of the Book of the Daily Offices of the Roman pontiffs, nothing similar is found concerning the poor and pilgrims. Only the charters of a hospice and a diaconia display anything comparable (chapter 7, titles 13–16). ID.]

We grant and bestow them upon you with firm and permanent stability, and through you upon the aforesaid venerable monastery, so that this apostolic charter of our written decree may remain there perpetually. Thus, under God’s guidance, the things known to pertain to the praise of our Redeemer and to the better condition of the aforesaid venerable monasteries may in every respect advance through your diligence, for the eternal memory of your excellence and the greatest reward of recompense. Thus we decree.

[Col. 0193C] Therefore, if at any time that charter which was issued by our predecessor of holy memory, the most blessed lord Pope Zacharias, concerning the same monastery to Carlomann, our brother,

[Note: [Col. 0194D] There can be no doubt that a similar charter or bull was made for Carlomann by the pontiff, whether because he was the monastery’s founder or because he alone had founded and endowed the buildings attached to it. Such is the nature of sacred places that their bishops seek the authority of the bishop in whose diocese they are situated. Yet no privilege or diploma of this kind is found anywhere. ID.]

or any other document of protection concerning the monasteries mentioned above, is found anywhere, it shall have no force, since its claim is empty and void. Meanwhile, by this apostolic censure, by an appeal to divine judgment, and by the prohibition of anathema, we decree that the things we recognize as having been established for the praise of God—namely, the support of pilgrims, as stated, and the lasting stability of the entire congregation of monks residing there—shall remain forever inviolate.

## XXXIII. 196. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN FOR THE DEFENSE OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF GOD

It contains thanksgivings and abundant blessings for the observance [or: observation] of the integrity of the orthodox faith.

[Note: [Col. 0194D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 9): “In the ninth he states that he will speak with Desiderius at Ravenna and prepare what is necessary for defense against the Greeks.” ID.]

(Year of the Lord 762; Codex Carolinus 30; chronicle 23.)

### ARGUMENT

Pippin had admonished him to cultivate the friendship of Desiderius, but at the time he had made no reply. He now responds that he will do so, provided that Desiderius keeps what he had promised to Pippin and to the Church. Meanwhile, he had agreed with him that they should both be at Ravenna in order to settle certain matters concerning the Church and to discuss how to resist the Greeks, who were continually devising ways to recover that city. He will write later about what decision has been reached.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope.

Since the holy spiritual mother and your particular universal Church of God is known to have been relieved by so great a benefit of your most exalted excellence and by the generous assistance you have supplied, what human language could suffice to render thanks for the merits of this benevolent action of yours? Although human understanding cannot repay it, nevertheless he who is powerful—the almighty and invisible Lord our God, by whose ordering your royal power stands confirmed—through the intercession of the sacred prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, will repay you with a worthy recompense in the present life and in future blessedness.

This is especially so since you appear to be both a most valiant defender of the holy orthodox faith and of the pious tradition of the venerable Fathers, most excellent son and spiritual co-father. Because of those very things that you reverently honor and strive to defend, you will always have the orthodox faith as your helper,

[Page 197] and surely heavenly victory will be granted to you against the ranks of your adversaries.

[Col. 0195B] Meanwhile, because we burn with great affection toward your excellent dignity, protected by God, we have diligently endeavored to discharge toward your highness the duty of visitation and greeting, distinguished son and spiritual co-father. In the meantime, we wish your excellence to remember that you recently sent us word that we should strive to live in peaceful friendship with Desiderius, king of the Lombards. If that most excellent man remains in the true love and faith that he promised to your excellence and to the holy Roman Church of God, then we too shall remain with him in firm charity and stable peace,

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Pagi incorrectly assigned this letter to the year 757, when there was not yet any fear of the Greeks. Muratorius more carefully suspects that it belongs to the year 761. I myself think it should be assigned here. For in the letter (29, otherwise 17) that I assigned to the preceding year, we heard that papal envoys had gone with royal envoys to Desiderius to deal with certain matters concerning the Holy See. The pope then said that those same royal envoys would report to Pippin what had been done with the Lombard king. Perhaps Desiderius had spoken courteously and favorably toward the Holy See with the royal envoys and had agreed to a future meeting with the pope, which is mentioned below. Pippin therefore advises the pope to cultivate the friendship of the Lombards and to maintain peace with him. The pope replies that he will do so if Desiderius keeps his promises. CENN.]

observing the teaching of the Lord’s commandment: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

[Col. 0195C] We therefore make this known to your most Christian and distinguished excellence: an agreement has been reached between us and that same king of the Lombards that we should both endeavor to appear together in the city of Ravenna (*Ravennantium* [*Ravennatium*]), in order to complete certain useful measures for the spiritual mother of your holy Church, our own Church, and to discuss the wickedness of the Greeks, who daily threaten to enter that city of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Here are two matters that are clear from this letter and others assigned to the same year: namely, fear of the Greeks concerning the exarchate, and matters relating to the Holy See. He says that he and the king will act together at Ravenna by agreement concerning both matters. It is not established from the letters in the manuscript codex that they actually met there. ID.]

When we have appeared there together, we shall make known to your most excellent excellence, protected by God, whatever we have said or whatever the circumstances require. Finally, we pray the divine clemency that, for the perfect exaltation of the holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith,

[Page 198] for everlasting and prosperous times,

[Note: [Col. 0196D] “For long ages.” GRETS.]

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Cangius observes in the Glossary of Lipsius that in the Theotisc Glossary *aevum* is understood as “eternal”; he notes that the Roman pontiffs Paul and his successors use it in this sense more than once, as do royal charters in Doublet’s History of Saint-Denis. Thus *aevus*, *longaevus*, and *aeternus* have the same meaning, and Gretser’s correction is superfluous. CENN.]

he may deign to preserve and protect your most excellent Christian piety upon the throne of royal power, together with your most sweet consort, the most excellent queen, our spiritual co-mother, and your beloved children, granting you possession of the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## XXXIV. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD [PIPPIN] THE KING FOR THE DEFENSE OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF GOD

And concerning the conference with King Desiderius in the city of Ravenna.

(Year of the Lord 762; Codex Carolinus 33; chronicle 33.)

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope.

[Col. 0196B] Since the holy spiritual mother and your particular universal Church of God is known to have been relieved by so great a benefit of your most exalted excellence and by the generous assistance you have supplied, what human language could suffice to render thanks for the merits of this good action of yours? Although human understanding cannot repay it, nevertheless he who is powerful, the almighty and invisible Lord our God, by whose ordering your royal power stands confirmed, will, through the intercession of the sacred prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, repay you with a worthy recompense in the present life and in future blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0196B] Lambinus omits *qui* (“who”). Lambinus adds *et futura* (“and future”).]

This is especially so since you appear to be a most valiant defender of his orthodox faith and of the pious tradition of the venerable Fathers, most excellent son and spiritual co-father. Because of the orthodox faith itself, which you reverently honor and strive to defend, you will always have it as your helper, and surely heavenly victory will be granted to you against the ranks of your adversaries.

Meanwhile, because we burn with great love toward your excellent dignity, protected by God, we have diligently endeavored to discharge toward your highness the duty of visitation and greeting, distinguished son and spiritual co-father. In the meantime, we wish your excellence to remember that you recently sent us word that we should strive to live in peaceful friendship with Desiderius, king of the Lombards. If that most excellent man remains in the true love and faith that he promised to your excellence and to the holy Roman Church of God, then we too shall remain with him in firm charity and stable peace, observing the teaching of the Lord’s commandment: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

We therefore make this known to your most Christian and distinguished excellence: an agreement has been reached between us and that same king of the Lombards that we should both endeavor to appear together in the city of Ravenna, in order to complete certain useful measures for the spiritual mother of your holy Church, our own Church, and to discuss the wickedness of the Greeks, who daily threaten to enter Ravenna itself.

When we have appeared there together, we shall make known to your most excellent excellence, protected by God, whatever we have discussed or whatever the circumstances require. Finally, we pray the divine clemency that, for the perfect exaltation of the holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith, it may deign to preserve and protect your most excellent Christian piety, throughout everlasting and prosperous times, upon the throne of royal power, together with your most sweet consort, the most excellent queen, our spiritual co-mother, and your beloved children, granting you also possession of the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## XXXV. 200. ANOTHER LETTER ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN THROUGH HARIBERT, THE ABBOT, AND DODO, THE COUNT

It contains abundant blessings and praises of thanksgiving for the firm and unchangeable word of promise and for his great perseverance in accomplishing apostolic affairs.

[Note: [Col. 0197C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 23): “In the twenty-third, through John the subdeacon and the abbot, together with Peter the first defender, Pope Paul sent Pippin abundant thanksgivings concerning his firm and unchangeable word of promise and his great perseverance in apostolic affairs, with an admonition that he should continue in this way. Paul compares Pippin to David.” CENN.]

(Year of the Lord 763; Codex Carolinus 18; chronicle 34.)

[Col. 0197C]

### ARGUMENT

He responds with the fullest praise, through the royal envoys Haribert the abbot and Dodo the count, to Pippin’s letter in which Pippin testified to his firmness and constancy toward the orthodox faith and the Church. The king had entrusted them with several matters to report privately, and the pope likewise gave them a private response on each matter, adding his own envoys John the subdeacon and the abbot, together with Peter the first defender.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual co-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope.

I cannot express in words, nor can the abundance of language fully embrace, how greatly, most excellent and truly Christian and orthodox of all kings, the innermost affection of our heart rejoices in your merits and pious endeavors. For, through the protection of your struggle and your laborious effort, your holy Catholic and universal apostolic mother, the Church of God, and the orthodox faith of Christians stand rescued from the attacks of their rivals; and for this reason praises are continually rendered by the entire Christian people to our Redeemer, the Lord God, because of the support of such a great benefit supplied by you.

Therefore, most Christian son and spiritual fellow-father, the minds of all the faithful rightly regard you as sharing in the heavenly kingdoms with that illustrious and distinguished king David and eminent prophet. For your Christianity is recognized to have equaled him not only in the insignia of honor but also in deeds, as the accomplishment itself clearly demonstrates. Indeed, when the ark of the Lord had been rescued from the foreign peoples [allophylos] [Note: *Allophylos* is a Greek word meaning “foreigner.” Cang. notes that Sulpicius Severus frequently, and the Septuagint, interpret *allophylos* as “Philistines.” Calmet likewise observes that in the Old Testament it is understood of the Philistines. The title of Psalm 55 in Thomas. (vol. II, p. 101) reads: “David in the inscription of the psalm: When the foreign peoples seized him in Gath.” CENN.], he rejoiced exultantly with hymns and spiritual songs and with the melody of the psaltery. You likewise strive, rejoicing and exulting, to offer to our almighty Lord God the holy Roman Church, redeeming it as the foundation and head of all Christians, together with the entire people subject to it [Note: An excellent comparison—whether one considers the Lombards, who continually harass and invade the Roman Church, or the Greeks, who attack the Catholic faith itself and the tradition of the Fathers. For what David did—rescuing the Lord’s ark from the Philistines and restoring it to God’s people—Pippin likewise accomplished by defending the holy see, the head and foundation of the Catholic faith, and the Catholic faith itself against the Greeks and Lombards. No one fails to see that both peoples were *allophylos*, or foreigners, in accordance with Paul’s statement. (Psalm 59, according to the Old Latin version, which is used in the basilica of Saint Peter.) ID.], whose perfection in so pious a work your kindness longs to bring about, believing that for it you will obtain for yourself the reward of recompense already stored up in the heavenly citadels.

For the exceptionally diligent men who hastened to you—namely, Haribert the abbot and Dodo the count, your excellency’s most faithful envoys [Note: Abbot of Morbach, or Murbach according to Mabillon, Murbach according to Pagius (763, no. 6), Morbach in Alsace; he is found serving as an envoy in these letters only on this occasion. I shall discuss Dodo below, at epistle 45, or 46, when he was sent to Rome by Carloman—unless he was perhaps another man. ID.]—brought us honey-sweet and most desirable words sent by your illustrious Christianity. In them you earnestly endeavored to assure us of your firm and unchangeable word of promise and of the steadfastness of the great perseverance which you appear to exercise in completing apostolic causes. We, for our part, firmly and with complete confidence in your benevolent purpose, believe that you will remain constant to the end and will accomplish more perfectly what you promised to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to our predecessor and most blessed brother, Pope Stephen [Note: A general reference to Pippin’s donation made at Quierzy in 754, which Stephen II indicated in his last letters to Pippin (epistle 11, otherwise 8), in 756, that he had not received in its entirety after Folrad had taken possession of the cities. ID.].

Meanwhile, those same letters of yours also stated that you had preferred not to disclose in writing what you wished us to learn from your representatives who were present; rather, having informed your aforesaid envoys of every aspect of the matters, you instructed them regarding what ought to be made known to our ears. They acted accordingly, just as you had commanded. We, in turn, fully instructed them concerning everything they had told us, explaining how they should report on our condition to your royal power, established by God [Note: In the preface to the letter he touched upon both matters: namely, the assertion of the Catholic faith against the Greeks and the liberation of the Church from the harassment and invasions of the Lombards; these two matters constitute the substance of nearly all the letters. The matters entrusted secretly were to be conveyed back and forth. They seem to concern the Lombards alone, whose friendship was necessary against the Greeks and therefore had to be preserved, but without detriment to the Church. Lest intercepted letters perhaps reveal what Pippin was planning against their obstinacy, the business is conducted secretly through faithful envoys on both sides. CENN.]. We have also sent our present envoys—John the subdeacon and abbot, and Peter, first defender—together with them to your royal presence [Grets., “summits”]. We ask that you receive them with your customary kindness and order them to be believed in everything concerning whatever they recount to you from our instructions, so that the complete liberation and exaltation of the holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith may advance, and so that you may deservedly attain in heaven the crown of the reward stored up for you.

May almighty God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly, who encloses the whole world in the span of his hand, and in whose hand rests all authority over kingdoms, protect you by his grace and grant you victories from heaven. May he subject all hostile nations to your royal majesty and cause you to possess the governance of the kingdom through peaceful and prosperous ages, together with your most excellent daughter and our spiritual fellow-mother, the most kindly queen, your sweetest wife; with your most beloved children, Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings; and with the most noble and excellent Gisela, our spiritual daughter. May he grant you possession of eternal life throughout endless ages. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

### XXXVI. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN, concerning Simeon, or the monk [Lamb., “monks”], of Remigius, bishop [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 3): “In the third [‘Third’] he gives thanks to Pippin for his defense against plotters and promises that he will arrange for Carloman’s monks to learn psalmody.” ID.]

*(A.D. 763, Codex Car. XLIII, chronicle 35.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—After Georgius, first cantor, had died, Simeon, second cantor, who had taught the monks of Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, the art of singing, was summoned from Francia to Rome to assume the office of first cantor. Pippin warned Paul that his brother had taken this badly; but Paul replies that he would repair what he had necessarily done, for he would hand Remigius’s monks over to the first cantor himself to be thoroughly instructed.

To the lord most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Since the love of charity which we bear toward your distinguished excellency, enlightened by God, grows more vigorously in our heart, it is therefore our concern, most excellent of kings, to obey your excellent will with all our efforts. This is especially so because, strengthened by the extensive protection of your excellency and, after God, seemingly rescued from the savagery of plotters [Note: Although this letter, like many others, was written in an uncertain year and the authors assign it to no particularly plausible time, I think it must be referred to this year or the following one. The Church is said to have been liberated from the plots of the Greeks, which were discussed above and are treated in the following letter. Since it matters little to investigate its date, I have decided to put an end to the excessive silence concerning this year. ID.], whenever the words of your reports are brought to us, we accept them with willing hearts and immediately strive to put into effect whatever their text expresses.

Accordingly, when we received the words of your excellency, protected by God, and at once reread them [Lamb., “left them”], we gladly fulfilled everything contained in them. For we found written there that we ought to entrust the monks of your brother, the beloved Remigius [Note: See the note to epistle 20, otherwise 21. ID.], to Simeon, prior of the school of cantors, so that he might instruct them in the melody of psalmody [another reading: “the melody of psalmody”], which they had been unable to learn from him during the time when he was in your territories and under your administration. On this account, you assert that your brother became very sad because he had not had his monks completely instructed by him.

Indeed, most kindly king, we satisfy your Christianity by saying that, if Georgius, who presided over that school, had not departed this life, we would in no way have attempted to withdraw that same Simeon from the service of your brother [Lamb., “remove him”]. But when the aforesaid Georgius died, and Simeon, as his successor [Note: Cardinal Baronius (1057, no. 22), from the Vatican Codex, writes concerning the cantors as follows: “There are twenty-one subdeacons in all: seven regional subdeacons, who sing the epistles and lessons at the stations; seven palace subdeacons, who perform the same service in the Lateran church; and seven others called the school of cantors, who sing only when the supreme pontiff customarily celebrates.” I note in passing the difference between this codex and that little work which was so highly valued by Mabillon (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 567), and before him by Panvinio and Raspon, and which is attributed to a certain John the deacon. But I shall discuss this below in the warning concerning the letters of the antipope Constantine. Cardinal Thomasius should also be heard (*Preface on the antiquity of the Book of the Mass*, vol. V, p. IX): “The principal cantors of this school were seven subdeacons (see Cardinal Baronius, 1057), of whom the first was called the first cantor, or prior of the school; the second, the second cantor; then came the third and fourth of the school, the latter of whom was also called the chief *paraphonista*.” The ancient Roman orders I and III, in Mabillon (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, pp. 7 and 55), teach that the three subdeacons who preceded the chief *paraphonista* held the principal offices of the school or college of cantors. After defining the fourth office, they add: “The chief *paraphonista*, that is, the fourth of the school, who always announces the cantors to the pontiff.” They continue: “That fourth of the school, arriving in the presbytery … after he has said, with bowed head, to the first, second, or third of the school, ‘Lord, command,’ the first of the school immediately begins the antiphon for the Introit.” Hence it is clear why Simeon, second cantor, was summoned to Rome after the death of Georgius, the first cantor: he had become first of that illustrious college, whose principal and more honorable ranks after the first were the second and third. Moreover, as Paul himself testifies, if the first, or first cantor, or prior, failed, the second by right became first, and consequently the third attained the rank of second cantor. If I am not mistaken, the same advancement applied equally to the remaining four. CENN.], occupied his place, we summoned him to us for the instruction of the school. For far be it from us to do anything in any way that might be burdensome to you or to your faithful people. Rather, as stated above, remaining steadfast in our love for your charity, we strive most willingly, as far as our ability permits, to obey your will.

For this reason we have entrusted the aforesaid monks of your brother to the frequently mentioned Simeon, and, having placed them properly, we have ordered them with diligent care to be instructed in that same melody of psalmody. Out of our very great affection for your excellency and the most noble affection of your brother [Lamb., “most noble”], we have arranged for the ecclesiastical melodies of instruction to continue under effective supervision until they are thoroughly trained [Note: In the Capitularies of Aachen, chapter 80 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 986), also transmitted in *Capitularies*, book 1, chapter 80, Charlemagne instituted the following: “The monks are to perform the Roman chant fully and in due order in the nocturnal and gradual office, according to what our father, King Pippin of blessed memory, strove to establish when he removed the Gallican chant, for the sake of the unity of the apostolic see and the peaceful concord of the holy Church of God.” Ducange, under “Roman Chant,” correctly places the date when Roman chant was brought into Gaul in the year 753, under Stephen II, on the authority of Walafrid Strabo (*On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 25). Later, however, he destroys this position by relying on this Pauline letter, asserting that Paul, at the request of Remigius, had carried out before Stephen II’s arrival in Gaul what is contained in the letter, adding immediately: “Moreover, Paul preceded Stephen.” In this matter the very learned man is seriously mistaken, as is clear. He gives a full and learned account of the entire history of Roman chant in Gaul. Consult him. ID.], out of our great love for your excellency and for your most noble brother [Lamb., “most noble”]. We wish your excellency henceforth to remain well in the Lord through peaceful and prosperous ages, to enjoy the scepter of the kingdom, and, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to obtain triumphal victories over your enemies. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

### XXXVII. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN, containing thanksgivings, concerning his own health and that of Charles [Lamb. adds “and Carloman”], and concerning Marinus the priest and Ravenna, and how evil counsels are being devised against it [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 10): “In the tenth [‘Tenth’] he clears himself of the charge made against him—as though Pippin had said that he was unable to provide aid to the Romans in any distress—and grants him authority concerning Marinus to establish whatever he wishes; and he asks for assistance in defending the people of Ravenna.” ID.]

*(A.D. 764, Codex Car. XXXII, chronicle 36.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—A courteous royal letter receives an equally courteous reply. The affairs of the Church, of Paul himself, and of the people entrusted to him are safe through the grace and action of almighty God. He refutes those who had slandered him by falsely claiming that he had said assistance from the Franks would be lacking. He will always avoid Pippin’s adversaries and adhere to his friends. Concerning the envoys, both royal and papal, who had gone to Constantinople, he knows nothing because of the bitter severity of winter. He rejoices that Marinus has been restored to his former dignity as cardinal priest, but says that he has had no correspondence with him and leaves him entirely to the king’s judgment. He sends letters received from Ravenna, where affairs were not peaceful because of rivals who left no stone unturned in their effort to recover what they had lost. Finally, he urges Pippin to complete the work he has begun and to liberate the Church from plots.

To the lord most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Your excellency’s letters, sent by the bearer of this letter and filled with every sweetness and affection, arrived. We accepted them with great reverence and, rereading them, recognized more clearly everything contained in them. Among other things, most excellent son [L. and Gent., “excellent good son”], your lofty kindness made known to us how, by the favoring mercy of our God, you are healthy, safe, and unharmed, together with your most excellent children, our spiritual sons Charles and Carloman, great kings, and the lady Bertrada, the sweetest queen, our spiritual fellow-mother [Grets., “your wife and our spiritual fellow-mother”], and also the most noble Gisela, our daughter. Having learned this, we offered great and innumerable praises to our Lord God, arbiter of heaven and King of kings, because, in accordance with what we desire and ardently long for, we have been permitted to learn of your safety. For this we earnestly implore the Lord our God to grant that for many years we may rejoice in your complete well-being; your safety is our exultation, and your prosperity is undoubtedly our joy.

It was also written in your royal letters that you wished us to inform you whether the safety or integrity of the holy Church of God, of our lowliness [Col. 0202C], or of the people entrusted to us had been overthrown [Lamb., “whether the people entrusted …”] [Note: I have given several examples elsewhere (epistle 24, otherwise 31, note), leaving the learned to interpret the word for themselves. I do the same here, although I do not see how any of the examples cited there applies to this matter, nor is it difficult to understand what Paul means here. CENN.]. For concerning this also we render great and countless thanks to almighty God and to your excellency, because, as is truly fitting for one who is most Christian and a genuine worshiper of God, your excellency does not shrink from visiting the Church of God and the people; yet this is not due to our merits but proceeds from divine mercy, since everything concerning the holy Church of God, our lowliness, and the people entrusted to us is prosperous. For this reason we shall ask the God of heaven, the giver of every good thing, to reward you for this pre-eminent and pious work and for the great kindness and concern which you are known to have for the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God and for its particular people [Grets., “special people”].

Your letters of report also stated that your envoys had informed you that certain wicked men and liars had spread throughout these regions the claim that, if some necessity should befall us, you would be unwilling to provide us with any assistance [Note: In the Lambecian and Gentilotian manuscripts *valuissetis*—“you would have been able”—is correctly read. Pippin was detained by the Aquitanian war from the year 760, as is explained more fully below: “Recognizing that, by God’s favor, there is no impediment from any quarter preventing you from providing defense and assistance to the holy Church of God,” and so forth. CENN.]. Concerning this wicked statement we have never had, nor do we now have, any hesitation, because, by divine mercy, after God we place great hope and confidence in you. We recognize that, with God’s favor, no impediment from any quarter will prevent you from granting defense and assistance to the holy Church of God and its particular people, in accordance with what you promised and pledged to the blessed apostle Peter through our predecessor of blessed memory, the lord and our brother, for the remedy of your soul and the forgiveness of your sins. We believe that this promise will remain firm and strong for all time, with the Lord’s assent.

But concerning what your most Christian excellency wrote to us—namely, that if any of your adversaries [Note: There seems to be no room for doubt that Pippin wrote this after Tassilo’s defection, which the authors record as having occurred in the previous year, after the assembly at Nevers. The *Annals of the Franks* under 763 state: “King Pippin held an assembly at Nevers, and, making his fourth expedition into Aquitaine, there Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, set aside his oaths and everything he had promised; by evil cunning he withdrew from the matter, disregarded all the benefits which King Pippin, his uncle, had bestowed upon him, and, withdrawing by fraudulent devices, went to Bavaria; nor did he ever again wish to see the face of the aforesaid king.” Pagius reports the same from the *Annals of Metz*, citing other annals that confirm it. In the following letter he commends this same Tassilo to the king, moved by repentance and wishing to return to his uncle’s favor, in such a way that, by repeated entreaties, he indicates that he had wearied himself in doing so, never departing from the royal will. ID.] or despisers should come to us, we would in no way mingle with them or associate with their company. Far be it from us to do this, since your enemies are enemies of the holy Church of God and of us. Therefore truth itself bears witness that wherever we recognize your friends, we wish to welcome and embrace them as friends and faithful servants of the holy Church of God; and wherever we find your enemies, we truly reject and pursue them as enemies of the holy Church of God and our own enemies. For your friends are friends of the holy Church of God and of us, while those who plot hostility against you are plainly shown to be enemies of the holy Church of God and of us.

Concerning your envoys and ours, who hastened together to the royal city, your illustrious excellency asked us to inform you whether we had learned anything from them. Let your excellency, protected by God, know that during these days we have been able to learn nothing from them, since it is certainly not unknown to you that, because of the savage severity of this winter season [Note: Some annalists place the severe winter in this year, others in the preceding year, together with the cited *Annals of the Franks*. Pagius (763, no. 3) gives the reason from Theophanes under the twenty-third year of Constantine: “In that same year, at the beginning of October, an immense and most severe cold settled not only upon this region but also across the East, the North, and the western quarter.” Paul’s letters clearly show that he also dealt with that dreadful winter, for several of them mention it, and the very manner of his speech points to the harshness of that winter season. In the preceding year royal envoys went to Constantinople together with papal envoys concerning the veneration of the sacred images; there are many indications of this above, where the assertion of the orthodox faith and the tradition of the Fathers is under discussion. But nowhere else is there a certain statement about it apart from this passage and the following letter. Anastasius merely records Paul’s frequent embassies, without mentioning Pippin; Pagius notes that many embassies between the emperor and the king of France are recorded in the annals at this time, but he nowhere mentions that papal envoys were added to them. ID.], no one coming from those regions has announced to us how matters stand with them. Therefore, for the present, we do not know what truthful report to give you concerning them.

But concerning the priest Marinus, your most Christian excellency wrote to us that he had finally been restored to his former dignity, according to the request we sent to you. We call God to witness that we sent to you on his behalf for no other reason than because of the tears and daily lamentations which his mother does not cease to pour forth. She is deprived of sight, and for this reason we sent to you asking that you release him to us. For you had, and have, no charge against him—and neither do we—except solely his wicked malice, by which, moved by evil and perverse audacity, he presumed to act against the holy Church of God. But concerning this matter, as we wrote to your excellency in our earlier letters, let it rest within your judgment and power what you wish to decide regarding him. We have no concern about him except, as we have said, that you should dispose of him according to your will [Note: It is certain from this that Paul sent Pippin other letters concerning this matter, but they do not survive. In epistle 16, otherwise 25, in the year 757, Paul, complying with Pippin’s wishes, had made Marinus cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. The following year, upon hearing that he was a traitor, he asked that he be elected bishop in Francia lest he become worse (epistle 19, otherwise 39). Now he says that he was moved by the tears of Marinus’s mother, who had lost her sight, and therefore asks that Pippin send him back to Rome, burdened with no other crime than treachery against the holy see, while nevertheless leaving to Pippin’s judgment whatever he thinks ought to be decided concerning Marinus. He testifies that he had touched upon these three points in the earlier letters; but such letters, as I have said, do not exist in this codex. CENN.].

Your excellency also wrote to us that we should inform you whether the same Marinus had sent us letters. Concerning this, with truth as our witness, we say that he has never sent us any letters since he hastened there to your excellency. For we had no reason whatsoever to conceal this from you if it had happened.

Meanwhile, we considered it appropriate to make known to your excellency what has reached us from the faithful of the holy Church of God and from our own people, that is, from the region of Ravenna, because the rivals of the holy Church of God, of us, and of your excellency do not cease day and night to devise how, contrary to God, they might prevail and overcome us. We have also sent beneath this letter the very writings which we received from there, so that, learning the substance of the matter, you may recognize that they have in no way abandoned their wicked purpose or their customary depravity. Therefore, most Christian good son and spiritual fellow-father, order them to labor and strive with the greatest energy, so that the good work which you have begun may be completed through you, and so that the holy Church of God and its particular people may have complete liberation and remain secure from the plots of their enemies [Note: I said above, in the note to the preceding letter, that these words concerned the plots of the Greeks, but at that time I did not state against whom those plots were being prepared. They were being prepared, of course, against the holy see and its particular people, that is, the Romans. For this reason the Greeks were striving with all their strength to bring the Exarchate and the Pentapolis under their control; from there, either by treaty or by an alliance with the people of Spoleto—as once the exarch Eutychius had done—they could attack Rome. At other times they needed the assistance of the Lombards, whose power included not only the kingdom of Italy but also the widely extended duchy of Benevento. Since they knew that these men were devoted to the king of the Franks, they had not yet dared to test their loyalty; afterward they did so, as will soon become clear. ID.].

For the rest, we ask the divine mercy of our God to deign to preserve you for many years on the throne of your kingdom, together with your most excellent children, our spiritual sons Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, and also the lady Bertrada, most excellent queen, our spiritual fellow-mother and your wife, and likewise the most noble maiden Gisela, our spiritual daughter. We wish for a long time to learn the joys of your prosperity and to implore God’s immeasurable clemency for you, for the exaltation and defense of the holy Church of God and of its particular people. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

### XXXVIII.
