ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN, SENT THROUGH FLAVINUS, THE CHAPLAIN, AND JOHN, THE SUBDEACON AND ABBOT, AND PAMPHILUS, THE REGIONAL DEFENDER OF THE HOLY CHURCH, containing thanksgivings concerning these envoys, how they were honorably received together with the imperial envoys, and other matters [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 22): “He wrote the twenty-second letter to Pippin, in which he thanks Pippin because his envoys—namely John, the subdeacon, the abbot, and Pamphilus, the regional defender of the holy Roman Church—with the imperial envoys were honorably received by Pippin. He thanks Pippin for reporting everything that had taken place with the emperor of Constantinople: he praises and commends Pippin greatly, and so forth.” CENN.]

*(A.D. 764, Codex Car. XX, chronicle 37.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He replies to many points in a royal letter brought back by his envoys, John the subdeacon and Pamphilus the defender, who returned with Flavinus, the royal envoy. First, the imperial envoys were heard in the presence of the pontifical envoys, and they disputed with them concerning the Catholic faith and the tradition of the Fathers. The envoys had also reported that this matter was so important that an act of God alone could compensate for it. Next, proceeding to the imperial letters and to Pippin’s reply—for copies of both had been attached—he praises Pippin’s response to the highest degree and condemns the imperial letters as the product of a corrupt faith. Third, he approves the detention of Synesius, one of the imperial envoys, and the order that Anthimus return to Constantinople with the royal envoys. Fourth, he declares that long experience has already taught him that neither blandishments nor the treasures of the world can remove him from the promises made to blessed Peter and Stephen. Fifth, he says that he is sending through Flavinus, the royal envoy, his seal, which Pippin had requested. Sixth, he says that, after the month of May had passed, he sent his envoys, Philip the priest and Ursus, to him concerning Tassilo, his sister’s son, who wished to return to his uncle’s favor; but that Desiderius, out of suspicion, prevented them from leaving Ticinum for Francia. Finally, he demonstrates that the imperial letters are full of deceit, since the Greeks were attempting to sow distrust of the royal and pontifical envoys, by the example of Christophorus, first cantor, a man of complete integrity, who was accused of treason.

To the lord most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

Since the summit of royal power appears to be surrounded by protection and strength more through the virtue of faith than through the arms of warriors, what wonder is it, most excellent and truly orthodox of kings, if the efforts of your endeavors do not cease to press forward with increasing force in defending God’s institution and the rule of the Christian faith? For this reason, believe me, heavenly victory is granted to you, and prosperity is destined to be bestowed upon your excellence by our Redeemer.

When our envoys returned to us—those whom we had sent to your illustrious excellency, namely John, the subdeacon and abbot, and Pamphilus, the regional defender of your spiritual mother, our holy Church—together with Flagitius, your envoy and chaplain, they brought us the honorable and most desirable letters of your Christianity [Lamb., “desirable,” plural]. We received and reread them with immense joy and delight. Immediately, their affirmation, like the fragrance of sweetness affecting us and like the nourishment of salutary providence bringing healing, made us glad.

Moreover, most Christian king, most beloved son and spiritual fellow-father, your kindness made known to us how our envoys and those of the emperor [Note: Namely, Anthimus the *spatharius* and Synesius the eunuch, whom he names below. Pagius is correct concerning this letter (764, no. 4), which is otherwise quite clear. CENN.] were received by you, and how you endeavored to reply to everything they had said to your illustrious majesty. Out of love for your protector, blessed Peter, you refused to receive them or reply to them without the presence of our envoys. Our own legates also reported these same matters to us.

Although we are unable to repay with anything worthy the great abundance of your sincere heart, which you appear to possess toward your spiritual mother, the Church of God, and toward our frailty, your protector is nevertheless the Lord our God. He commanded you to reign and entrusted his holy Church to you for its defense; he is able to repay your excellence with a worthy recompense of rewards in the present and future life.

213 Thus, on receiving the letter which the imperial envoys themselves brought to you for purposes of deception and illusion, and which you directed to us, we recognized its contents. In this matter, indeed, your pious consideration and kindness brought us the joy of exultation, because it is truly clear that you acted in this way not for human favor but out of fear of God. Moreover, what our aforementioned envoys disputed and argued in your presence with the imperial envoys concerning the observance of the orthodox faith and the pious tradition of the Fathers, you made still clearer to us through that same letter of yours. At the same time, your God-illumined Excellence consented to send us a copy of the letter that you directed to the aforementioned emperor—namely, the manner of your reply and the resolution of the requests concerning those matters which he had communicated to you. You also informed us in detail how you replied to those same imperial envoys, how you sent one of them—Ant[h]i [Grets., Anthymus], namely, the spatharius—with your own envoys to the royal city, and how you retained the other, Synesius the eunuch, with you.

Having learned all that you have done for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith, we rejoiced with great joy, and these things are pleasing to us, since it is certainly beyond doubt that you acted and replied in this manner not through human counsel but under the guidance of divine providence. [Col. 0207C] For truly, lord king, most Christian son and spiritual fellow-father, the Spirit of God enlightens the pious consideration of your inmost heart; and whoever overflows with the grace of the Holy Spirit abounds in nothing except spiritual things, since the heart of your power, resting in the hand of God, unquestionably inclines toward whatever pleases him.

[Note: How earnestly the king of the Franks acted so that the Catholic faith and the veneration of the sacred images might be upheld against the Greeks is also evident from the proceedings of the Council held at Attigny in the following year. Although those proceedings have perished, a summary of them survives in the papers of Luca Holstenius transmitted to Labbe by R. P. Possinus (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 1702), concerning which we read: “The names of the bishops, or abbots, who assembled at the royal estate of Attigny in a synodal gathering for the cause of religion and the salvation of souls, and so forth.” [Col. 0208D] Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXV, no. 1), after reporting the same summary, discusses (no. 6) the relics of Saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius, brought from Rome to Francia. These likewise correspond to the veneration of the saints vindicated through the efforts of the Frankish king. — ID.]

You sent us word in that same letter, signifying that no enticements of persuasion or abundance of promises could tear you away from the love and pledge of faith which you made to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicar, predecessor, and brother of blessed memory, the lord Pope Stephen; rather, you would remain in that same charity and fidelity to your pledge until the end. [Col. 0208B] And indeed, most excellent of kings, we have learned by experience and confirmed through your deeds that you remain to the end in that pledge with firm and most steadfast constancy. We trust in you that, even if the abundance of all the treasures of the world were offered and granted before you, it would in no way be able to turn or bend your firm mind, impelled as it is by God, in another direction. For the almighty Lord chose you above all the kings of the world and took pleasure in you, so that through your struggle the holy universal Roman Church of God, head of all the Churches and bulwark of the Christian faith, might be freed from the snares of its attackers; and behold, that which the Lord determined from the foundation of the world to accomplish through you has wonderfully been brought to pass. [Col. 0208C]

Therefore, after God, we place great confidence and hope in your royal eminence: that the holy Church of God itself, and this most wretched and afflicted little province, may be more completely freed from the faithlessness of its enemies. [Note: Muratori, who always and everywhere maintains that Rome was never sought by the Greeks as belonging by right to them, appears to have read these letters rather perfunctorily. For what else was this “little province” except Rome and its duchy? It is clearly defined below as the holy Church of God and its particular people. Yet, as I stated in the note to the preceding letter, the Greeks could not gain access to Rome unless they first brought the Exarchate under their power. — ID.] For the ancient enemy of the human race does not cease to strike the hearts of enemies, so that they may hurl their customary snares. But, good orthodox king, strive by your customary protection and with God’s power to crush their wickedness, so that the holy Church of God and its own people may be more completely freed from the savagery of their enemies, and so that, deservedly surrounded by the intercession of the apostles, you may merit to attain the crown of reward laid up for you in heaven. Accordingly, in keeping with what you communicated to us, we have sent your Excellence our sign through your present envoy. [Col. 0208D]

215 Meanwhile, we also make this known to your Christian Majesty: it has now been recognized that Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, has repeatedly asked us to consent to send our envoys to your illustrious Excellence, so that matters of peace might arise between you. Accordingly, when the opportunity arose, we gladly sent our envoys—namely, our beloved son the presbyter Philip, and also our faithful Ursus—to your presence, after the month of May had passed. [Note: Just as the preceding letter was sent at the beginning of the year, when the dreadful winter was raging most fiercely, so this letter appears to have been written very late in the same year. Paul speaks of the envoys whom he had sent in the preceding month of May on Tassilo’s account, but whom Desiderius prevented from departing from Ticinum. For, as Pagius says (year 764, no. 4), Desiderius had either given his daughter in marriage to Tassilo or hoped to give her to him shortly. — CENN.]

We sent them in such a way that you were to act according to whatever your will might be. But when our envoys hastened as far as Ticinum, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, seized by an adverse suspicion, did not allow them to pass through to your Excellence, whom God preserves. Nevertheless, we transmitted to your Christian Majesty, within this present letter of ours, the same letters that we had directed to you.

We have therefore thought it fitting to communicate this also to your Christian Majesty, protected by God: after rereading the imperial letters delivered to you by the aforesaid Antispatharius [Lamb., Antinus spatharius] and Synesius the eunuch—which, out of love for blessed Peter, your patron, you graciously sent to us so that we might examine their contents—we discovered that they contained the allegation that your men and ours, who interpret the very imperial documents sent or being sent to you and to us, do not interpret them according to what is written there, but dare falsely to interpret one thing as another. The envoys who travel between the parties likewise do not convey what has been entrusted to them, but, corrupted by the reward of acceptance, deliver one thing in place of another. Here your Excellence may perceive how great is the malice of the enemies: [Col. 0209C] acting against their own souls, they utter not words of truth but wicked lies through this opportunity for deceit, so that they may believe neither their own envoys nor yours and ours.

Since you are satisfied with your men, and we likewise with ours, we are confident that none of them would ever dare to do such a thing.

May almighty God, who searches the heart and the kidneys, satisfy the honey-sweet heart of your Excellence: not one of our men, as they assert, has committed such acts. Rather, the emperor himself is vehemently angry over this and employs deceitful pretexts because we did not remain silent with him but admonished him concerning the establishment of the holy images and the integrity of the orthodox faith. For in his own documents he asserts that our beloved son Christopher, the primicerius and counselor, without our authority and as though we were ignorant, had made those representations which we had repeatedly sent to him, and had reread some things in place of others belonging to his and your envoys. In this matter we call God as witness and judge that it is not so at all.

Our counselor has never done or presumed to do anything outside our will, since he was and remains the sincere and most proven faithful man of our predecessor and brother, the lord Pope Stephen, as well as of ourselves. We are satisfied with his spotless faith and firm constancy of heart. For this reason we believe that what is falsely reported against us is counted by God not as reproach but as a crown of victory. Therefore the Lord is helper to both of us, and we shall not fear what man can do to us. [Col. 0210B] For, after God, we shall have as the shield of protection and weapons of strength your illustrious Excellence, illumined by God.

But let your Christian Majesty order your envoys to investigate the matter, and in all things satisfy yourselves. For the same emperor asserted a lie against us, namely, that we had sent that representation, rereading before them the very things that we had sent and confirmed; and you appear to possess at your side a copy of the document which we sent from ourselves to you. [Note: The emperor had attempted to make the pontiff more suspect to the king than anyone else by misusing the letters written to himself in support of restoring the veneration of the sacred images, as is related in the *Life of Paul* by Anastasius. — ID.]

217 With these matters set forth, bending our knees together with the entire people of God, we implore the Lord God, true creator of the heavenly spheres, [Note: Gentilotus appropriately observes that *coelorum* was inserted by Tengnagel, whereas in the manuscript codex one finds *tellorum* or *tellurum*, as Lambecius read it—meaning “creator of heaven and earth.” Yet in that coarse age the spheres, which frequently occur in the texts, were better understood. — ID.] to grant you long life in the present age together with great victory over your enemies, and to deem it worthy to bestow eternal joys both upon your Excellence and upon the most Christian queen, our daughter and spiritual fellow-mother, your most beloved wife, and upon your sweetest children, the excellent kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Charles and Carloman. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

XXXIX. 218 THE NEXT LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN,

in which it is reported that six patricians with three hundred ships and a Sicilian fleet are hastening from Sicily toward the regions of Rome and Francia, and concerning the restitutions owed to the holy Church of God, which Desiderius promised to make in the presence of the king’s envoys, since he fulfilled none of them as he had promised. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 17): “In the seventeenth letter to Pippin [‘the seventeenth to Pippin’], he indicates that six patricians with three hundred ships are coming from Constantinople to Rome and afterward to Francia, to Pippin. He then complains [‘that they would proceed to Pippin; he complains’] that Desiderius had not fulfilled, as he had promised, the restitutions owed to the holy Church of God, which he had promised to make in the presence of Pippin’s envoys [legates], and that, in addition [‘he had promised, but did not fulfill as he had promised; indeed’], he had inflicted many injuries upon the Romans.” — ID.]

*(Year of the Lord 764, Codex Carolinus XXIV, chronicle 38.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He appends to his letter another letter announcing that six patricians, with three hundred ships and a Sicilian fleet, are proceeding toward Rome and from there to Francia. Moreover, he reminds him that, in the presence of the king’s envoys, an agreement had been reached between himself and Desiderius concerning the mutual restoration of property; but that the crafty king was delaying the matter begun, while meanwhile evil deeds and plundering were being committed in Roman territory. He had even sent threatening letters, which he likewise appends. He asks for the king’s customary protection. He entrusts Conibert, his vassal, with much to report. He asks that two envoys be appointed who may be a source of assistance to the Romans: one to go to Ticinum and, after hearing the king, return to Francia.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope. [Note: Summary 17, in Baronius and Centuriator. — GRETS.]

[Note: Cointius and Pagius assign this letter to the year 765, a chronology which I by no means accept; they also place the seventeenth letter of the Codex, as though it were its sequel, in the following year, which cannot be proved. There is no similarity between the two except the restitutions owed to Saint Peter and the envoys, who may also be connected with other matters. Muratori likewise thought that this letter followed that one and therefore dates them to the years 758 and 759, a chronology incompatible with the history. To me the matter appears otherwise; hence, in letter 29, otherwise 17, I assigned it to the year 761, taking account of the reason given by Peter the primicerius, defender, and bearer. I remove this letter from the year in which Cointius and Pagius place it; the following letter, as I shall soon show, requires this. — CENN.]

To your Excellence, established by God, through these apostolic words of ours, good and most powerful king, excellent son and spiritual fellow-father, we earnestly strive—after God, our liberator—to make known whatever comes to our attention from various regions.

Let your Excellency know that certain most sincere faithful men of your spiritual mother, our holy Church, have informed us that six patricians, bringing with them three hundred ships and likewise a Sicilian fleet, having departed from the royal city [Constantinople], are hastening to this city of the Romans. What they intend to do, or for what purpose they are being sent, we do not know the truth. We have been informed only that they are resolved to proceed to us and enter Francia to reach your most highly praiseworthy Excellence. We have sent to your Excellence, within this present letter of ours, the letters addressed to us, so that you may examine them. [Note: The number of patricians and the size of the fleet reported to be attacking the Romans and Franks filled the pontiff with false alarm. For nowhere is it recorded that such a fleet departed from Constantinople or landed in Italy. These things may have been devised to inspire terror in the Romans, whose defection the Greeks were unable to stomach. — ID.]

We also inform your God-preserved distinguished Excellence that when it had been agreed in the presence of your envoys with Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that we should first receive in full the restitutions owed to us Romans from all the Lombard cities, and afterward in turn make full restitutions to the Lombards from all our cities, we relied upon this promise which he made in the presence of your aforesaid envoys and sent our own envoys to receive and make these restitutions.

But he employed various crafty pretexts and, contrary to what had been agreed, refused first to make in full from all his cities the restitutions we demanded, and then to receive his own in full from all our cities. Instead, he preferred to make a restitution from one city and receive one from another, one at a time, wishing thereby to cause delay so that our Roman party [Lamb., Gent., your party] might not obtain its rightful restitution. And behold, our envoys, having accomplished nothing, returned to us without result. [Note: Anyone who tried to fit this whole matter to the letters reported earlier or to those that follow would be foolish. Nothing similar is found in any of Paul’s letters. This agreement was either entrusted secretly, like many other matters, to the envoys, or it had been arranged as circumstances required. — ID.] From that time onward he has inflicted many plunderings [Gent., prayers for relief] and many unheard-of evils upon our territories.

Therefore he promptly sent us his own letters, in which, trusting in his ferocity, having no regard for God before his eyes and fearing neither blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he sent us threats and uttered empty words of abuse [Lamb., Gent., brought forth]. We have copied it below, within the text of this writing of ours, and sent it to your splendid and God-established Excellence, so that, when your lofty Excellency recognizes its contents, you may consider how great are his malice and the proud arrogance of his heart, since, rising up against blessed Peter and your royal power, he threatens to inflict evils upon us. [Note: The injuries inflicted upon ecclesiastical territory and the threatening letters foreshadow the hostilities that follow shortly afterward and that Pagius correctly places in the next letter, namely, in the year 765, no. 4. — ID.]

But after God we place our hope, as upon an impenetrable and most firm wall, in your Excellence, strengthened by God. For this reason, kneeling, we entreat you; and through us blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, likewise approaches your distinguished Excellence, asking that, inspired by almighty God, who appointed you defender and liberator of his holy Church, you command that our safety be most fully secured, and that you become, as is your custom, our helper and protector against the ferocity and arrogance of all our enemies.

Thus may you merit to obtain the richest reward from our Redeemer, the Lord God, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and, just as you have obtained an earthly kingdom, so may you merit to obtain the heavenly kingdom with God’s saints and elect throughout the endless ages.

We have instructed Conibert, your most faithful vassal, who is present here, to report everything to your royal power in a detailed account. We also earnestly ask your gracious Excellence to send us such envoys as you deem suitable, who may be found to serve as our assistance. One of them, however, should travel as far as Ticinum, so that, after he has spoken with King Desiderius, he may report to your Excellence whatever answer he gives them. Let the other two, according to your arrangement and direction, hasten to join us, so that, as stated, they may remain as our assistance. [Note: From this it is clear that the seventeenth letter of the Codex Carolinus is incorrectly regarded as this letter’s sequel. The similarity of the cases is greater with the letters that follow than with that earlier letter, which concerns the mutual return of property and the restoration of the territories and boundaries of cities. Here, by contrast, the subject is hostilities and the king’s threatening letters; there, envoys are seeking to obtain Desiderius’s aid against the Greeks, whereas here Pippin is being asked for envoys to assist the Romans against Desiderius. — CENN.]

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

XL. THE NEXT LETTER OF PAUL, BISHOP OF ROME OF BLESSED MEMORY, SENT THROUGH ANDREAS AND GUNDRICUS,

in which there are expressions of thanksgiving and requests seeking to obtain aid against the Lombards. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 27): “He sent the twenty-seventh letter through Andreas and Gundricus, Pippin’s envoys [‘he sent the twenty-seventh letter through Andreas and Gundricus, Pippin’s legates’], containing expressions of thanks together with a petition and adjuration for aid to be sent against the Lombards.” — ID.]

*(Year of the Lord 765, Codex Carolinus XIV, chronicle 39.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He replies to the letter which Andreas and Gundericus, the royal envoys, had brought. After praising the king’s constancy in vindicating the Catholic faith and the Church, he says that no credence should be given to Desiderius when he denies making new incursions. For, after being warned the previous year about the damage inflicted upon the territory of the city of Senogallia and in Campania, Desiderius had sent him threatening letters, which Paul had appended to his own letter. For this reason he had asked for royal envoys, who, upon arriving, had discovered that Desiderius was a liar. He says that he had received the altar table previously given by the king to Saint Peter and Saint Stephen, and that, having brought it into the sacred confession, he had consecrated it and celebrated the sacred rite upon it, decreeing that it should never be removed. He permits George and Peter to be detained in Francia. The envoys had reported many matters in his presence, and he had answered each of them individually so that they might report his answers in person.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope, with the greatest effort of honor and affection of love.

The letters which your illustrious Excellence sent, brought by Andreas and Gundericus, [Note: These envoys were not distinguished by any title and served only once as legates. Andreas apparently had some matter of unknown nature for which the king commended him to the pontiff; the pontiff carried it out according to the wishes of both, as he states below. — ID.] most diligent men and envoys of your Christian Majesty, we received with acceptance. Reading them with our customary gratitude [Lamb. adds “and”] and joy, we were exceedingly glad in mind and heart, since through them we learned much about your prosperity and received the desired satisfaction of our hopes, affection, and joy. We give boundless thanks to almighty God, who, as we so often ask, has granted us joy through hearing of your immense well-being.

Nothing in this life has been sweeter or more pleasing to us than to learn continually, through favorable reports, of your safety. For the joy of your prosperity has been the exultation of the holy Church of God and the abundant defense of all the orthodox. Finally, through the words sent by you, you have made us certain that in every circumstance you are prepared to be present for the assistance and defense of the holy Church of God whenever necessity arises, and that you remain firm in that faith and love with blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and with the most blessed lord and my brother of blessed memory, Stephen, the most holy pope.

You are careful, you affirm, that everything be fulfilled and inviolably preserved which you promised to that same apostle of God and confessed for the remission of your sins. Since the heart of your Excellence is in the hand of God, and since, by divine blessing and the grace of holy anointing, you are recognized as having been anointed king, most excellent and most distinguished king, through his apostle and the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, blessed Peter, we have great confidence that you will remain firm in that same charity, love, and promise which you have striven to pledge to the gatekeeper of the heavenly kingdom. Beyond doubt, both through your letters and through the envoys whom you regularly send, you will provide us with grounds for confidence.

Therefore, throughout all the days of our life, we too shall remain firm in your charity and love, and no interruption of time will be able to separate us from your affection, charity, and love, which has been joined between us. For this reason, with earnest prayers, and adjuring your Excellence before the dreadful future judgment, I beg and beseech you to remain with firm constancy according to what has proceeded from your honey-sweet mouth and been promised to blessed Peter. Reject the wicked persuasions and empty promises of the enemies of the holy Church of God and of the orthodox faith, and take care always to please God and blessed Peter, who has granted you the governance of the present kingdom. Thus may he who has deigned to bestow upon you the height of temporal royal power also grant you the heavenly kingdoms to possess forever, and may he deem it worthy to grant you immense victories over your enemies through the intercession of the prince of the apostles.

Concerning what your Excellence reported—that Aderius [Lamb., “by Desiderius”], king of the Lombards, had informed you that no wrongdoing or invasion had been inflicted by the Lombards in our territories—let your kindly Excellence believe us: this was not truthfully reported to you. For, most gracious son and our spiritual fellow-father, most Christian king, after such great devastations had been committed by those same Lombards in our territories and cities, and after we had admonished him about this, he sent us letters threatening us. Compelled by necessity, we sent them below, within our apostolic letter of the preceding year, for your Excellence to examine. [Note: Pagius thinks (year 765, no. 4) that Desiderius gave Pippin his letters before the earlier letters reached his hands, and he is not mistaken. From this it is clear that the earlier letters were written at the end of the year 764—something Pagius appears not to have noticed, since he considers both letters to have been given in the same year—while the royal envoys had set out on their journey, and that at the beginning of the following year Desiderius gave him these letters, which confirm his earlier actions and recount additional matters more fully. — CENN.]

For, by armed bands and by sword and fire, they had hostilely devastated twenty [XX; unit unspecified in the source] places outside our city of Synogallia, carrying off a very large amount of booty and killing several men there. Likewise, when they invaded the region of Campania, namely our fort called Valentis, [Note: I find no mention among geographers of the fort of Valentis in Campania or of Foriboni in Sabina (letter 71, otherwise 56). I therefore leave these places, certainly known in the Middle Ages but unexplored by scholars, without alteration. I would point out that Paul calls the city of Senogallia “ours,” and likewise calls the fort of Valentis “ours.” Let those take note who attribute to the Frankish kings the donation of the city and its duchy, as well as those who say that the jurisdiction of the Holy See began with those kings. There is no doubt that the Exarchate and Pentapolis, added to it by Pippin ten years earlier, enlarged this jurisdiction. But Rome, together with its Roman duchy, had been possessed by the Holy See, freed from Greek domination, for at least thirty-five years, without any title of donation. See the Preliminary Discourse. — ID.] they acted in such matters like pagan peoples. Until this day we have been unable to obtain justice from them for these things.

Therefore we sent to your Excellence so that you might consent to send an envoy of yours, [Note: It should be noted that in the preceding letter he requested that two envoys be sent to Rome and one to Ticinum; here he mentions only one. We must therefore not cling so rigidly to the wording of these letters that we invert their order under the appearance of arranging them. — ID.] so that, through his presence, justice might be obtained between the parties, and so that no delay in securing that justice might arise either from our side or from that of the Lombards.

For your fullest satisfaction, we therefore produced proof in the presence of your aforesaid faithful envoys, together with the envoys of the Lombard king. Your envoys were satisfied concerning such great acts of wickedness and learned that our account was true [Lamb., “your account”] and theirs false. For this reason we cannot remain silent about such great wrongs inflicted upon us by them. Rather, it is necessary for us to make everything known to your royal eminence, since, after God, you are the liberator of this province, so that through you the entire people of this province, redeemed by you, may be able to attain its justice.

Meanwhile, most distinguished and gracious king, most Christian son and spiritual fellow-father, we received the table which you formerly offered to the lord and our brother, the most blessed Pope Stephen of blessed memory, and through him to the blessed apostle Peter. With hymns and spiritual songs, solemnly giving praise to God in the Litany, we brought it inside the hall of that same prince of the apostles. Your envoys offered it in your name in the sacred confession, above the body of that same gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven. Having sanctified it with the chrism of anointing, and placing the sacred offering upon it, we offered a sacrifice of praise to almighty God for the paternal recompense of your soul [Lamb., “for eternal … recompense”] and for the stability of your kingdom. By apostolic censure, with the imposition of anathema, we decreed that no one should ever be permitted to alienate it from the Church of blessed Peter. And behold, your memorial remains shining forever in that same apostolic hall. [Note: This remarkable information concerns the table formerly given as a gift to Stephen II and only now placed above the body of Saint Peter; Paul reports that it was received by him. What later became of it is unknown. — ID.] Believe that you will obtain its recompense from the just retributor, the Lord God, and from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the heavenly kingdoms.

Concerning Georgius [Note: It will be evident below that the reading should be Georgius, not Regius. Such errors frequently occur in the Codex, as scholars know has also happened in other codices. — ID.] and Peter, you have made your wishes known, and we have entirely understood them. We leave the matter to your discretion, so that you may act regarding them as you please, whether by retaining them with you or by releasing them to us. For everything that pleases you appears altogether agreeable and favorable to us. Finally, your aforementioned envoys reported to us in detail everything that had been entrusted to them by you. We replied to each matter, informed them about everything, and released them to report it to you; we also brought the matter of the aforementioned Andreas to completion, according to his wish and your command.

May almighty God, who is rich in mercies, protect you continually with the arm of his outstretched power, and subject all adversaries and rebels [Note: I believe that this refers to the soldiers of Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, who had defected from Pippin together with their prince in the year 763. — ID.] to your royal footsteps. May he grant that you, together with the most excellent daughter and our spiritual fellow-mother, the most gracious queen, and with your beloved children Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings and patricians of the Romans, and the most noble Gisela, may possess the governance of the kingdom for a long and healthy time, and enjoy the eternal joys of reward with the saints and elect. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

XLI. 226 THE NEXT LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING PIPPIN, SENT THROUGH WULFARD AND HIS COMPANIONS,

in which there are abundant praises, and matters concerning the apostolic envoys and the Greeks residing in Francia, as well as concerning George [Centuriator, Bishop Gregory] and Peter. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 16): “He wrote the sixteenth letter to Pippin and all the Franks [‘he wrote the sixteenth letter to Pippin and all the Franks’] through Wulfard and his companions. It contains abundant praises. Also concerning the envoys [legates] to the Greek king residing in Francia, and concerning Bishop Gregory and the presbyter Peter.” — ID.]

*(Year of the Lord 764, Codex Carolinus XXVI, chronicle 40.)*

[Col. 0216C]

**ARGUMENT.**—When the apostolic envoys, Peter, regional notary, and John, custodian of Saint Peter, were returning from Francia with Wulfhard and the king’s other envoys, they brought letters attesting to the king’s steadfastness, unshaken by any blandishments or gifts in the defense of the Catholic faith and the Church. After these letters had been read publicly and everyone had exulted with joy, Paul, in his own name and in the name of all, sent a letter full of joy and love toward the king and all the Franks.

He approves that the king was detaining the apostolic envoys and the Greeks who had returned with his own envoys from Constantinople, until the synod should decide the response to two matters: the orthodox faith and the donation made to the Holy See. He says that he had already granted, through Andreas, that George the bishop and Peter the presbyter—whom the king wished to retain with him—might remain, and now grants it again at the king’s discretion, but only on the condition that he write back what should be done about George’s bishopric and the church entrusted to Peter, so that they may not remain without a pastor for too long.

He explains that he himself is retaining Wulfhard and his companion because, while Desiderius was staying at Rome the previous autumn, an agreement had been made concerning the mutual restoration of property through the envoys: the matter concerning the Beneventans and Tuscany had already been settled; that concerning the Spoletans was now being settled; and other matters would likewise be settled.

In an addition, he gives thanks for the warning sent to Desiderius concerning the restoration of the patrimonies through the Neapolitans and Caietans, and concerning the granting of permission for those chosen to come to Rome for consecration.

To the lord Pippin, most excellent son and our spiritual fellow-father, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the pope. [Note: Summary 16, in Baronius and Centuriator. — GRETS.]

The votive desires of our heart and the affection of our inmost breast, offering to Your Excellency the support of your benefactions, convey our prayers for the desirable and exceedingly beloved welfare of your exalted Christian Majesty, and likewise of our most excellent and most gracious daughter and spiritual co-parent, the best of queens, together with your and our most beloved and illustrious sons in Christ, Charles and Carloman, most excellent kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, [Col. 0217C] and also to all our most reverend brothers and dearly beloved bishops, priests, and religious abbots, as well as to all the nobles, judges—namely, dukes and counts—and to the whole people of the Frankish kingdom protected by Christ and subject to you, we send perpetual salvation. Along with us, all our most holy brothers, the bishops and priests, and the entire order of the clergy of your holy and spiritual mother, the Roman Church, together with the body of nobles, magnates, and all Romans, great and small, embrace you in the kiss of charity and, by their continual intercessions, pray with us to the divine mercy for your life and safety, for your joy, and for victories granted to you from heaven.

And truly, most excellent son—our defender and liberator after God—it is your due that we repay you the affection of our customary honor and express more fervently the words of our greeting, and that we proclaim most fully whatever concerns the immense praise of exultation [or: exaltation] of your kingdom and the salvation of your soul. [Lamb.: “to overthrow.”]

Therefore, when our envoys returned—those whom we had sent to the feet of your royal clemency, namely Peter, regional notary of our holy Church, and John, mansionarius of the confession-basilica of your patron, blessed Peter—[Note: The apostolic envoys who performed this embassy on this occasion alone should not be passed over without notice. Regional notaries occur elsewhere as well, but mansionarii are nowhere read of as having performed this office. Ducange discusses them at great length, and their various kinds. Certainly, the mansionarii of that time must in no way be compared with the mansionarii of our age. In Falcon’s Beneventan Chronicle, under the end of the year 1128, we read: “John, abbot of Saint Sophia, died on the eighth day of the month of November, and Franco, who was then mansionarius, was elected.” From this one may infer how highly this envoy would have been regarded among the Franks, since mansionarius was a dignity in the palace of the Frankish king. Hincmar, *On the Order and Offices of the Palace*, chapters 16 and 23. John, however, the pope’s envoy, was mansionarius of the confession of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and therefore preferred to other offices or dignities among the Franks, who venerated Saint Peter with the highest reverence. CENN.]

When your envoys also joined them—Wulfhard, that is, and his companions—[Note: Mabillon saw that he was also called Gulfardus (*Annals*, book XXIII, no. 23), though he did not know of this embassy. In this codex he is called Wulfhardus, and there is no doubt that he was the same abbot of Saint Martin of Tours who, in the year 756, succeeded Bishop Wicterbus in the abbatial office alone, while Andegarius assumed the episcopal dignity. Thus, before undertaking the embassies of Adrian which Mabillon examined, he had undertaken this embassy of Paul I in the year 766. More about him below. ID.]—they delivered to us letters of Your Excellency that were honorable and greatly desired. When we had read them in the assembly of my brother priests and fellow clergy, and of the entire gathering of the lay order, and when our envoys and yours had reported that these letters contained what you had instructed them to say concerning the steadfastness of your unchanging mind and the integrity of your purity, which you appear to possess for the hope of the holy Church of God and the orthodox faith, we were immediately filled with exceeding joy. Raising our eyes to heaven and extending our palms, we gave immense thanks to our almighty God and to Your Excellency, singing that angelic praise of the divine power on account of your merits: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2).

For the minds of the faithful could not believe otherwise than what we have learned by seeing accomplished in your deeds [Note: The word *earum* is absent in Lamb.]—that you, rejecting human persuasions and empty promises out of pious regard, preferred nothing to the love and struggle that you maintain for blessed Peter. Rather, counting all earthly profits as mud trampled underfoot, you have made it your concern to please him and to obey his commands with all your strength. And therefore, behold, good king, exalted son, and spiritual co-parent: you have stored up for yourself infinite treasures in the heavenly citadels, where rust does not prevail and moth cannot consume what is destined for the righteous.

Since the deeds of your exalted majesty shine so wonderfully, who could in any way doubt you, when you strive to preserve perpetually, with his right unimpaired, what you promised to blessed Peter and sought to grant for the remission of your sins, and when you entrust it, through great exhortations, to those whom you and God preserve? Therefore we and all our people must place the greatest confidence in the steadfastness of your unchanging mind in this pious purpose: that you, your offspring, and the entire Frankish kingdom will remain firm. For, just as Your Excellency has made known to us, we know whom we have believed, and we are certain.

Concerning our purity and affection, which we are known to possess toward you and toward the entire Frankish kingdom protected by God, we believe that you are already fully satisfied. For still greater assurance, calling upon the God of heaven as witness, we confess that we shall remain in that same love of charity in which you and your offspring, all your descendants, and the entire Frankish kingdom promised that you would remain toward our brother of holy memory, the most blessed Pope Stephen, and through him toward all his successors in the pontificate, to the end of the age, for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and the defense of the orthodox faith. No condition of circumstances, however powerful, will be able to separate us from that confirmation of charity.

Your Christian Majesty therefore sent us a letter informing us that our envoys, your envoys, and the Greeks who had returned from the royal city were being detained with you for the time being, until, after assembling your priests and nobles, you might determine or accomplish what answer should be given concerning the matters that had been sent to you. Indeed, we cannot expect any other answer from you in this matter than one that is recognized as pertaining to the exaltation of the holy spiritual mother of your Roman Church, the head of all the Churches of God, and to the orthodox faith.

And since what you once offered to blessed Peter, in return for eternal life, ought by no reasoning to be separated from his right and authority, we know that no persuasive rhetoric prevails with you, since you firmly retain in your heart the divine words and apostolic teachings. [Note: From this it seems certain to me that the petitions of the Greeks were reduced to two points: the cause of the orthodox faith and the donation made by Pippin to Saint Peter of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis. Since these matters were of great importance, the king of the Franks did not wish to answer before hearing the judgment of the Fathers in council.

Baronius, who was unaware of these letters, conjectures under the year 766, no. 21, that the Greeks had unfortunately brought to Francia, together with gifts, their own opinions concerning the veneration of images. Pagi, under the same year, no. 3, adduces the testimony of the annals and especially the words of Einhard concerning the synod of Gentilly, which Baronius also mentions; but he piles up much irrelevant material and says nothing about this letter, since he assigned it to the year 758.

Labbe, *Councils*, volume IV, p. 1703, correctly places that council in the year 767, adducing the following from the Chronicle of Ado: “A synod was held in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 767, and a question was debated between the Greeks and Romans concerning the Trinity—whether, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, so also it proceeds from the Son—and concerning the images of the saints, whether they ought to be fashioned or painted in churches.” He notes that Abbot Regino agrees with this. He then observes that the Romans mentioned by Ado were none other than the legates who had come from Constantinople with the Greeks.

Finally, after quoting the very words of Paul’s letter under discussion, he says: “There were plainly two chief matters in the Greek embassy: one, the recovery of the regions of Italy attributed by Pippin to the Roman Church; the other, the questions written above.” The Frankish annals likewise state: “Then Lord Pippin held a great synod between the Romans and the Greeks concerning the holy city and the images of the saints.”

Since they say that after the synod he proceeded into Aquitaine, completed that expedition, returned to his homeland, and celebrated Easter—on 19 April—in Vienne, it is clear that the council was held at the very beginning of the year 767. This agrees remarkably with the date of this letter, which was written at the end of the year 766, as I shall soon show. The matter concerning Pippin’s donation, although shrouded in silence by the annalists, is so clear in this letter that it requires no commentary. CENN.]

And behold, just as through your letters and through our envoys and yours you have given us the greatest reason for confidence, we look forward to receiving from you joyful news on this matter and to rejoicing, as is our custom, in your gracious purpose of mind.

Your exalted Christian Majesty also asked us in those same letters to permit Bishop George and the priest Peter to remain in your service. Let Your most excellent benignity recognize that we already long ago obeyed your will in this matter through Andrew, your most religious envoy, just as you requested. In the apostolic letters written and sent by us, we granted them to you, making it known that, whether it was your will that they be retained or released, you were to deal with them accordingly. Therefore, even now we leave them to your discretion: do with them as you please, whether you wish them retained or released, since they were once granted to you by us. Would that they themselves might prove agreeable in your service! Send us word, therefore, concerning what we ought to do regarding the bishopric of the aforesaid George and the Church entrusted to the aforementioned Peter, lest, if they are left unattended any longer, they fall into excessive neglect. [Note: In the preceding letter, which Pagi correctly assigned to the year 765, Paul granted the king, through Andrew, companion of Gundricus, permission to detain George, bishop of Ostia, and Peter, cardinal priest. He grants the same permission again here, asking what he thinks should be done with the churches that they have abandoned for so long. ID.]

Meanwhile, we have retained in these regions two of your envoys—Wulfhard and his companion—in accordance with your command, for the interests of our holy Church, your spiritual mother.

Moreover, Your Excellency informed us that you had sent word to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that he ought to return Saxulus, our boy, who had fled from us. But let Your Christian Majesty recognize—and I think you also believe and know this—that Desiderius, the same king of the Lombards, arrived (pervenisse; the printed reading is *conjunxisse*) in the past autumn season [Lamb., Gent.: *autumni*, “of autumn”] at the threshold of the apostles for the purpose of prayer, bringing our boy with him, and handed him over to us. [Note: This letter was therefore given in December, not long before the synod of Gentilly was held in Francia. It is therefore clear that Pippin promptly summoned the bishops and heard the judgment of the Fathers concerning the questions of the Greeks. ID.]

While speaking with that king about completing justice between the parties, it was agreed that, as your envoys and his proceeded through the various cities, the settlements should be prepared [Lamb.: *perpetratae*, “carried out”]. And behold, with God’s favor, we both carried out and mutually received our settlements in the territories of Benevento and Tuscany. As for the duchy of Spoleto, while our envoys and those of the Lombards are still present there, we have partly carried out and received the settlements. We are also striving by every means to carry out fully between the parties the remaining matters that have been left unresolved. [Note: It is clear from this passage that neither the duchies of Benevento and Spoleto nor Tuscany belonged to the Holy See at that time. It is likewise established that these territories were neighbors of the Romans, whose army had compensated for the property taken from the Holy See by taking property belonging to them. Hence the present negotiations concern mutual restitution.

Thus Paul says to Pippin above, in letter 38, no. 24: “It was agreed with Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that we should first receive in full our Roman settlements from all the Lombard cities, and afterward in turn make complete settlements for the Lombards from all our cities.” In both passages it is absolutely certain that the Roman duchy is meant. CENN.]

In the *embolin* [Lamb.: *embolo*, “in the additional paragraph”], Your Excellency, protected by God, informed us that you had admonished Desiderius, the king [Note: This is plainly a copyist’s error; one should read *regem*, “the king,” not *reges*, “kings.” ID.], to compel the Neapolitans and Caietans to restore the estates situated there at Naples belonging to your protector, blessed Peter, [Note: Two estates are found in the letters of Saint Gregory the Great: the Neapolitan and the Campanian. These are now being reclaimed.

Let me note, meanwhile, what fear the Romans could have had from the Greeks concerning the Roman duchy, or their ancient territory, while Desiderius was granting rights to the Neapolitans—whose boundaries were very narrow—through the Beneventans, who were subject to him. The Greeks had nothing else left in Italy except the duchy of Naples and the farthest Calabria.

Muratori, in several places in his *Annals*, wonders that the Romans feared for the Exarchate and Pentapolis while being scarcely affected by fear for Rome and its duchy. The reason is evidently that he either did not hold, or did not believe others to hold, the condition of Cisalpine Italy—that is, Lesser Lombardy. From the letters of Adrian below it will become clear that the pontiff also feared for the City and its duchy because of the treaty made with the Beneventans by the Greeks. ID.]

and to grant the chosen candidates permission to hasten to this apostolic see to receive episcopal consecration. Therefore we return the greatest thanks to Your Excellency for this and for everything.

After these matters, may our almighty Lord God surround you with his continual protection, rescue you from every adversity, and subject all barbarian nations to your feet. May he grant you to enjoy your present kingdom happily for many years together with your beloved wife and exalted sons, and grant you eternal life to possess with the saints. May God preserve you unharmed, most excellent son.

## XLII. Another Letter of the Same Pope Addressed to Lord Pippin the King

Giving great thanks for the defense of the holy Church of God and for the monastery situated near Mount Soracte that he granted to it. [Note: Panvinio’s summary, Vatican Codex 25: “In the twenty-fifth letter he gives thanks for the defense of the holy Church, with an exhortation to Pippin to continue bringing about the complete exaltation of the holy Roman Church. He promises at length his love for Pippin and that he wishes to do nothing without his permission. He gives thanks for the monastery situated near Mount Soracte, donated to him by Pippin.” ID.]

(Year of the Lord 767, Codex Car. XVI, chronicle 41.)

### Argument

After receiving royal letters in which the king professes his steadfastness in the defense of the Catholic faith and the Church, and donates the monastery of Soracte to him, the pontiff compares the king’s deeds, not ungenerously, with the deeds of Moses. He declares that he has often said, and professes that he says again, that his love for so pious and generous a king will never fail, just as his love for Stephen, his brother, never failed. He gives thanks for the monastery, which he says he is joining to another monastery founded by him, that of Saint Sylvester, where the saint’s sacred body rests.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-parent, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

As we turn over in our memory the histories of the divine Scriptures, weigh the merits of God’s various elect, and bring before the eyes of our mind the works inspired in you by God, we discover that in these days you have shone forth as a new Moses among the nations, most excellent son and spiritual co-parent.

Moses received commands from the divine Majesty in order to rescue the Israelite people from the oppressions of their persecutors. You also, most excellent and distinguished king, have been divinely inspired to liberate the holy universal, Catholic, and apostolic Church of God.

Through Moses, finally, the Lord delivered the commandments of the law on Mount Sinai to that Hebrew people for their observance and illumined them with the light of his glory. Through you also our Redeemer, the mediator between God and human beings, has granted peace to his Church and to the entire Christian people, redeemed by his precious blood, and has given perfect defense to its orthodox faith.

And just as Moses the lawgiver exterminated the abominations of the nations and the worship of demons, so you, most Christian of kings, rejected the schism of heretics and the authors of impious doctrine. [Note: Everyone considers this letter to be of uncertain date. It seems to me, however, that these three comparisons between Moses’ deeds and Pippin’s deeds encompass all the letters of this holy pontiff. CENN.]

For this reason you have rightly been shown to be numbered and reckoned among the faithful kings who once pleased God, anointed with the light of divine grace and the oil of sanctification. Hence it is fitting to sing the voice and praise of the Psalmist concerning Your Excellency (Psalm 88): “The Lord found you, most gracious of kings, faithful to him and keeping his commands; therefore he anointed you with holy oil. And behold, his hand shall aid you, and his arm shall strengthen you.”

Nor is it surprising that so gracious a king has been adorned with so great a divine gift, since the Spirit inspires where he wills and in whom he wills (John 3). Indeed, he inspires those who shine with pious works, as Your Excellency is known to shine.

Although your most excellent Christian Majesty has regularly declared through your letters and through the messengers who have traveled back and forth how fervently your love burns toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward our affection, nevertheless, through the letters that you have now sent by the bearer of these, you have most fully displayed to us the affection of your fatherhood. You have signified, good and most excellent son, spiritual co-parent, and our defender and liberator after God, that you will remain with firm perseverance in love for that prince of the apostles and in affection for us. We are indeed secure in your promise, expressed in an unchanging word.

For we know whom we have believed, and we are certain that everything will be accomplished according to your words, just as you affirm. What, then, can we return to Your Excellency for this? What recompense could we make for such great supports of benefaction, which your exalted excellence has deigned to bring to the holy Church of God and to the Christian faith, while our mind labors day and night to offer praises of thanksgiving?

Rather, it is something to be admired [Note: In the manuscript, after *potius est* there follows *qualitas*. It has been erased in recent ink. GENTIL.] and greatly wondered at: how can the loquacity of my mouth proclaim supports of such great benefaction? Nevertheless, “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” With my eyes frequently raised and my palms extended toward heaven, I shall continually implore divine mercy for you, so that he himself may look upon you from the throne of his majesty, cherish the height of your kingdom, grant you immense victories from heaven, deign to cast all barbarian peoples down beneath your feet, and enlarge the boundaries of your royal power.

For we call upon God, the God of truth, as witness, most excellent son and spiritual co-parent, in whose hand the heart of Your Excellency is directed [Note: Lamb. reads *corrigitur*, “is directed,” which is followed by: “as we have often revealed the purity of our heart, in our love and charity toward you, just as between you and the lord of holy memory.” Gent. reads: “It is directed. As we have often revealed the purity of our heart, in our love and charity, just as between you and the lord of holy memory.”], just as it was confirmed many times between us and our brother of holy memory, the most holy Pope Stephen, and through him with the holy Church of God. We shall remain, and shall continue to remain, obeying your wishes. Far be it from us ever to be separated from your love.

No gift of rewards, no kind of promise, and no persuasion of flatteries will be able, as we have often said, to tear us away from your affection. But I ask, and as though present I earnestly beseech, your honey-flowing Excellency, most gracious of kings, to order that the fullest exaltation of that spiritual mother of yours, the Church, be accomplished, and to remain the firmest defender of the Christian faith, so that from this point onward the memory of your name may be celebrated in the house of the Lord until the end of the world, and that through the intercession of the apostles you may be granted both the prosperities of the present life and the joys of eternal blessedness.

Meanwhile, most excellent son and spiritual co-parent, since, inspired by God, you have deigned to grant us that monastery situated beside Mount [Note: This monastery of Soracte had been granted to Carloman by Saint Zachary in the year 747. Paul granted it to Pippin after annulling every previous grant, in the year 762. It is only now that the same monastery is donated by Pippin to the pontiff. See letter 32, no. 12, note. CENN.] Seraptem [Soracte], we return great and innumerable acts of thanksgiving to Your Exalted Excellency. May the Lord be your recompense for this and grant you a worthy reward of heavenly gifts in eternal blessedness.

We have resolved to attach that monastery to our monastery for the praise of God, for the memory of you, and for eternal reward. [Note: This monastery, under the title of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, and Saint Sylvester, pope and confessor—the monastery now called Saint Sylvester in Capite—was built by the holy pontiff in his ancestral house and granted for habitation to Greek monks, so that the divine offices might be celebrated there in the Greek language.

Baronius therefore thinks that Eastern monks expelled by Constantine Copronymus poured into the City and that the holy pontiff embraced them and gathered them into this monastery. The foundation charter is preserved by the nuns of the same monastery, who were substituted for the monks. From it Baronius produced a copy, which Labbe also published. Papebrochius, in his *Historical Chronological Attempt*, thinks that the chronological marks do not agree with one another and therefore considers the charter itself spurious. In this he is mistaken, for many authentic charters are found whose chronological marks are false, regardless of how the error arose. ID.]

Since blessed Sylvester, the illuminator of the faith of Christians, whose holy body has been placed and rests in our monastery, lived there while fleeing the persecution of the pagans, we rightly judged that it should be under his authority, where his revered body itself rests. [Note: In the same parchment that contains the aforementioned charter, these words of Pope Paul are added:

“In the month of July, on the nineteenth day, we brought into this oratory the body of blessed Sylvester, bishop and confessor of Christ. In the month of August, on the seventeenth day, we brought in the body of blessed Stephen, martyr and pontiff, in the time of Constantine and Leo, emperors, and of Pippin, most excellent king of the Franks and defender of the Romans, in the fourteenth indiction.”

The definition of the patriciate found here should be noted, since it agrees with the very frequent testimonies of this codex and contradicts the excessively elaborate arguments of more recent writers. ID.]

Nevertheless, we absolutely do not wish to do anything concerning this monastery or any other matter outside your will; rather, whatever your will may be, we strive to do in all things accordingly.

Thus our spirit was made joyful, and we returned immense thanks to almighty God and to Your Excellency because, inspired by God, you deigned to hear our prayer, most gracious king, and announced that a command of your royal majesty was to be sent to our monastery, securing that holy residence now and for all time thereafter. [Note: Observe the character of the age. The monastery of Saint Gregory on Mount Caelius, a place formerly called the village of Scaurus, is especially famous even today. We read in Anastasius that the house of Saint Gregory the Great was there; Martinellus calls it his maternal house, which the holy pontiff converted into a monastery.

Although at that time dominion over the City belonged to the emperors, and Gregory stood in the closest relationship with Emperor Maurice, we do not read that the pontiff asked him to confirm his monastery, as we see Paul doing with Pippin, who had no right whatsoever in Rome. Whoever interprets such singular acts—which testify to the greatest friendship between the pontiffs and the Franks, and to the greatest mutual service—as matters of jurisdiction seems to me to be foolish. CENN.]

Therefore we ask the divine mercy that, just as you strive to confirm our monastery, which was established for the praise of God, so he may deign to confirm your kingdom above all nations. Let Your most excellent Christian Majesty know for certain that you will have as your most steadfast intercessors with the divine mercy all those martyrs who shed their blood in confession of Christ’s name and rest in that same holy monastery.

As for what you made known, namely, that you wished to assure yourself of our health, we, good and most Christian king, confess that we are healthy precisely when the health of your body and the salvation of your soul increase, with God’s help, because your welfare is our prosperity.

After these matters, may almighty God, maker and ruler of all things, cherish you by his grace, and grant you to enjoy for a long and prosperous old age the scepters of royal majesty, with great victory, together with your sweetest wife, the exalted daughter and spiritual co-parent of us, Lady Bertrada, illustrious queen, and your and our beloved sons, illustrious kings and patricians of the Romans, Lords Charles and Carloman, and also the most noble Lady Gisela. May he grant you the joys of the heavenly kingdom to possess with the saints and elect for endless ages. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellency unharmed.

## XLIII. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Sent to Lord Pippin the King through Bishop Wilharius and Dodo and Wichard

Containing expressions of thanksgiving and the steadfastness of the same pope’s faith, so that no favor or terror could in any way separate him from the king’s love or affection. [Note: Panvinio’s summary, Vatican Codex 21: “He sent the twenty-first letter to Pippin through Bishop Wilharius, Dodo, and Wulchadus. It contains expressions of thanksgiving together with exhortations that Pippin continue to fight for the defense of the Church. The pope says much about his steadfastness toward Pippin, namely that no favor or terror could separate him from Pippin’s affection. He indicates that after God, his Mother, and the blessed apostles, he has confidence in no one more than Pippin.” CENN.]

(Year of the Lord 767, Codex Car. XIX, chronicle 42.)

### Argument

When the royal envoys arrived—Bishop Wilharius, Dodo, and Wichard—they not only testified through the royal letters to Pippin’s steadfastness in defending the holy Church and the people subject to it, but also inquired whether everything had been completely restored to Saint Peter.

Accordingly, the pontiff praised him according to his custom with worthy praises and affirmed that his own friendship and that of his people toward him would be perpetual. He said that the Lombards had been deceitful and mendacious according to their custom; that the envoys had seen everything; and that, together with the answers to the matters they had related orally, they would report what they had seen. He asks the king to raise up the Church, which is in need of assistance.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-parent, Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Paul.

No human speech, I think, can suffice to offer thanks to Your illustrious and gracious Excellency for the great supports of benefaction that you have bestowed upon the holy Church of God and the Roman people. Nor can the rewards of this world worthily be repaid to you for these things. [Col. 0226B] Nevertheless, there is one alone and true God, existing in three substances [Note: A famous question concerning the three substances in Christ, the Son of God, arose in the preceding century between Benedict II and the bishops of Spain and produced the two *Apologies* of Julian, the most learned archbishop of Toledo. It is treated at great length in the councils. Natalis Alexander summarizes it. Julian broadly establishes soul, body, and divinity as the three substances. That is not the meaning here: in this passage “three substances” is taken for “three persons.” On this matter see the Council of Florence, part 2, collation 16. CENN.] [Grets.: “persons”], who is able to grant and repay Your Excellency the joys of the kingdom and the triumph of victory.

Meanwhile, as our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Wilharius, together with Dodo and Wichard, your faithful envoys, hastened to us [Note: Wilharius, as Lambecius reads him, was, I believe, that bishop of Nomentum concerning whom see letter 7, no. 9, note, and letter 25, no. 34, note. The other two bear no distinguishing title, and I do not know who they were. Unless one of them was the same Dodo who, after an interval of two years, served as Carloman’s envoy, as in letter 45, no. 46. ID.], they brought us honey-flowing and most desired letters sent by your most Christian Excellency. As soon as we looked upon them and recognized the prosperity expressed in your joy, the inner recesses of our breast overflowed with the customary joy of exultation. We continually implored our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord God, that he might allow us for a long time and diligently to rejoice in your greater happiness and in the victories granted you from heaven over your enemies.

But, most excellent son and spiritual co-parent, through those same honorable letters you gave us the most certain confidence of your customary promise: that you would contend with firm perseverance for the defense of the holy Church of God, the entire Roman people, and the whole province, in accordance with what you promised to blessed Peter and to his vicar, our predecessor, my brother of holy memory, Pope Stephen, and that you would remain faithful to that pledge.

Indeed, good, most Christian, and God-appointed king, you have given us great grounds for confidence in this. For the minds of the faithful cannot judge otherwise than what we repeatedly see accomplished by you out of regard for that promise and have learned through experience of the matter. [Note: Here we have a clear definition of the patriciate, which Pippin’s successors, even those distinguished by the imperial crown, assumed in the very act of their coronation. This is established by the oath sworn by them:

“I promise, pledge, profess, and swear to God and blessed Peter that henceforth I shall be the protector and defender of the supreme pontiff and of the holy Roman Church in all its necessities and interests.”

Therefore there is no doubt that, before Stephen II, the king made a similar oath in the year 754, at the time of his inauguration through the hands of that pontiff, with this sole difference: he had promised protection and defense to blessed Peter and to his vicar. CENN.]

But, good and most powerful of kings, behold now the opportunity; behold, the days of necessity compel, and the time of pressing obligation demands that your Christian devotion hasten to aid and assist the holy Church of God and this province liberated by you, as is your custom, as quickly as possible [Note: Hence, and from what follows immediately, it is clear that the Roman province presently needed assistance against the Lombards. But what new danger was impending, since the authors are silent, I cannot conjecture. ID.].

240 For we, after God and his holy and glorious Mother, and his most sacred apostles, have no hope elsewhere except in your illustrious excellence. For you, Christian king, are our refuge after God; you, together with God’s arm, are our firm assistance; and the security of your kingdom, strengthened by God, is our immense joy. Thus, both we and our entire people of this province—may the divine Majesty render you a fitting recompense—shall remain steadfast and immovable in charity and affection toward you and toward your kingdom of the Franks, protected by God, constant in our love. No human favor or terror will be able to separate us from the sweetness of your love or from the affection of charity; but for us life and death alike shall be found in love for you.

Since you have made known that you sent the men presently here so that, through them, you might learn whether full restitution had been made to us by the Lombard side or not [Note: Toward the end of the year 766 (ep. 40, otherwise 26), the pontiff said that such restitutions had begun to be made. Since he wrote Pippin nothing further about the matter, he now, concerned for the interests of the Holy See, asks whether those restitutions had been completed. ID.], they themselves have learned the full substance of the matter. They have recognized the crafty deceit and the customary false statement of those same rivals of yours and ours. When, by God’s favor, they return to you, they will disclose these things in your hearing. Finally, since they are reporting to us one by one all the matters they had received from you as instructions, and since we are giving them a separate answer concerning everything, we have placed in their mouths what they ought to suggest to your excellence, hoping thereby to obtain the desired result from your excellence.

May Almighty God deign to look down from the throne of his majesty upon you, your kingdom, your most beloved wife, the exalted queen—our spiritual co-mother—and your sweetest children, who are indeed your natural offspring but our spiritual sons, and also upon the entire people of the Franks. May he extend over you the right hand of his arm, grant you victories from heaven, cast all your adversaries down before your face, and bestow upon you a long old age in the present life and future blessedness to possess forever. May God preserve you unharmed, most excellent son.

## 241. NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTERS OF THE PSEUDOPONTIFF CONSTANTINE

[Col. 0227]

1. The two letters of the layman Constantine, forced into the apostolic see, were rightly rejected at the end of the Carolingian Codex. I would follow that example, were it not that the history of the pontifical ordination, against the contrary opinions of others, and the chronological sequence already begun persuade us to proceed otherwise.

As regards the ordination of the pontiff, they attribute to Constantine Pogonatus the withdrawal from the practice of confirming the election of the Roman pontiff personally or through the exarch—a practice which Justinian, following in the footsteps of Odoacer, had introduced into the royal court of Constantinople. For this reason they date the beginning of this most auspicious restoration of the former liberty from the time of John V, who ascended the chair of Peter in the year 685, when no confirmation was awaited.

Yet, with the indulgence of the defenders of this opinion, that is false. For liberty of this kind returned forty-five years later, in the time of Saint Gregory III, when, in the year 731, or rather the following year, the holy commonwealth was established, compelled to do so by Greek impiety. Before that time, the ordination followed a decree sent to Ravenna. I willingly concede that, until then, the election decree was customarily sent to Ravenna more as a matter of obedience than necessity, and more for the sake of seeking agreement than confirmation. Nevertheless, it was sent; nor did full freedom of ordination prevail until the election of Saint Zachary, who succeeded Gregory III. Then—and for as long as the power of the exarch remained in Italy, which ended under that same pontiff Zachary, and after his death—ordination was free. The election decree, or a copy of it, was not sent to the Frankish kings except so that they might thereby learn of the general harmony and unanimity. For this reason it was customarily sent only after the consecration.

II. A still clearer proof of the matter is supplied by the brevity of the interregna. Since it is universally established that these are reckoned from the day of the pontiff’s death to the ordination, or consecration, of his successor, and since every codex and catalogue expresses them by the vacancy of the see, the matter is placed beyond dispute.

Papebrochius (*Conatus historici chronologici*, no. 3, p. 199) notes that confirmation of the decree was customarily awaited for at least six weeks. After Gregory, however, matters were different: only four days separate his death from Zachary’s ordination. On the twelfth day after this, Stephen II was consecrated; and Paul, his brother, was separated from him by a one-month interregnum because of the schism which, as I said above, was quickly suppressed. The detestable ordination of Constantine followed Paul on the eighth day; nine days after Constantine’s deposition, the consecration of Stephen III took place. Only eight days separate Adrian from Stephen III, and Leo III from Adrian by two days. Thus, in equal measure, the rule of the pontiffs and the freedom of their ordination, both arising from Greek impiety, continued throughout the seventy years of the eighth century.

What happened afterward through the concession and liberality of the pontiffs I shall discuss in its proper place, after publishing the Carolingian Codex and several letters of Leo III, when I come to speak of the diploma of Louis the Pious. For now, I must briefly discuss Constantine’s invasion; from it the certain date and character of his letters will become clear.

III. In nearly all the codices of Anastasius, the see is said to have been vacant for one year and one month after Paul’s death, for Constantine occupied the pontificate for precisely that length of time. Paul was called to the heavenly homeland on 28 June 767; the invasion then began and ended in the following year, on 29 July.
