For this reason, several codices—such as the second Freherian codex in the editions of Fabrotti and Blanchini, as well as the royal papyrus codex collated by Velser—clearly read both the invasion and the vacancy of the see: “The see is vacant for one year and one month, during which Constantine, the transgressor and invader of the apostolic see, held it.” The duration is so certain that these same codices consistently state in the *Life of Stephen III*: “For the space of a year and one month he held the apostolic see after invading it . . . Within the circle of that year and one month.”

No account, however, is taken of the eight days preceding the sacrilegious ordination of the invader; indeed, not even the nine days that elapsed after his deposition and before Stephen’s consecration are included in the reckoning. This is rare, even unique, in the codices of Anastasius, which usually extend the interregna from the death of one pontiff to the day of the consecration of another. Yet the writer was so careful to designate that pseudopontificate under the name of a vacancy that, immediately after Stephen III was elected on a Sunday—on which day he could not also be consecrated—he says: “And after all things had been duly accomplished in his election, with God as author, he assumed the summit of the pontificate.” He then recounts separately what was done on each day.

I shall embrace in a concise account this history, which is extremely necessary, especially for discerning Pippin’s silence and the government of the City during that period, although it is narrated at length in the deeds of the pontiffs and in the council held for the same reason by Stephen III in the year 769, a fragment of which I published in 1735.

243 IV. While residing at the basilica of the Doctor of the Nations during the summer, Paul was seized by a severe illness and died on 28 June 767. Thus, when everyone else departed because of the disturbances that had arisen in Rome, only Stephen, a cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia, who succeeded him after a prolonged interval, remained there until the proper rites could be completed.

While Paul lay ill, impious men—Toto, formerly duke of Nepi and then living in Rome, together with his three brothers Passivus, Constantine, and Paschal, and other associates prepared for every crime—conspired to kill the holy pontiff. Christopher, the primicerius, prevented this outrage. He summoned the leading men, together with that wicked duke, to his house and bound them all by an oath not to depart from the laudable custom of the Holy See, but to elect, together with the clergy and people, a cardinal deacon or cardinal priest.

As Christopher was leaving that house, he heard that the pontiff had died. Then the perjured Toto invaded the Lateran patriarchium, forced his lay brother Constantine into it by violence and arms, immediately had him ordained a cleric, and, when Sunday came, had him consecrated in the basilica of the prince of the apostles.

Murders and ambushes followed this sacrilegious act. Christopher and his son Sergius, then the treasurer, pretending that they intended to embrace the monastic life in the monastery of the Savior near Spoleto, barely escaped death. Released after Easter of the following year, under the evil omen of the invader, Christopher deceived his guards, went with his son to the duke of Spoleto, and through him safely reached Pavia and King Desiderius. There he implored the king’s protection, obtained troops, and, with the addition of the soldiers of Spoleto, returned to Rome. Battle was joined with Toto, who was killed; the invader was deposed; and, amid the greatest joy of all, Stephen III was duly elected on the Kalends of August 768. All this was accomplished within three months. Then, during the days preceding the consecration, punishment was inflicted upon the guilty adherents of the invader’s faction.

V. At the beginning of Constantine’s invasion, he sent an earlier letter to Pippin (43, otherwise 98). From it we understand that he announced to the king of the Franks, amid other most mendacious claims, Paul’s death and, without doubt, his own sacrilegious intrusion. For, falsely claiming the unanimous consent of all in his election, he says that, with messengers already preceding him, the pontiff’s death was being reported by them. Sending his letters to Pippin through a royal envoy, he declares that it had not been possible for him to send his own messengers, but promises to dispatch two others as soon as those who had gone to Francia had returned, following the example of Stephen II and Paul, the excellent pontiffs (11, 34, 41, otherwise 8, 18, 16).

He praises the most Christian king, comparing him to Moses because, just as Moses redeemed the Israelites, so Pippin had redeemed the Romans from impiety by God’s command. He calls him the defender of the Catholic faith and of the Church; reminds him of their former friendship and alliance with the Romans; and finally promises that his goodwill toward him will be perpetual. What more? The Lives of the Saints that the king had requested from Pope Paul—everything he had been able to find—he also generously sent him.

All this was in vain, for the king maintained a profound silence. This is certainly no obscure indication that the most devout prince found such an outrage exceedingly offensive. Whether it was reported by the primicerius himself or by others remains unknown.

VI. Constantine awaited a royal response for at least three months. In his second letter (44, otherwise 99), he mentions the past month of August, the fifth indiction, when a letter addressed to Paul arrived from the patriarchs of Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Antioch, and from several metropolitans assembled in synod to defend the Catholic religion and the veneration of the holy images against the impious Copronymus.

Perhaps seizing this occasion and imitating Paul’s example (ep. 31, otherwise 35), he again attempts to beat the air. He sends a second letter to Pippin through his own envoys, Christopher the priest and Anastasius the notary, obscure men who, as is probable, had been elevated to those ranks by his sacrilegious power.

He recycles the same lies about his election by unanimous consent, miserably patching together passages of Sacred Scripture and various sayings of Stephen and Paul. He concludes nothing. He dares earnestly to request a response from the most devout king and to ask him to permit George the bishop and the cardinal priests Marinus and Peter, who had been sent to Francia by Paul, to return to Rome.

Pippin, however, maintained a profound silence, perhaps because he held the matter in contempt, or rather because he detested the letter’s dissimulation. Certainly Rome never again saw either his envoys or his letters, although he survived the invader’s deposition and the creation of Stephen III. For it is established that he died in the year 768, on 24 September, when Sergius, the son of Christopher the primicerius and then nomenclator, was hastening there as a papal envoy with letters addressed to Pippin, Charles, and Carloman. In them he and his sons were asked to send to Rome bishops distinguished for doctrine and wisdom, for a council which Stephen was planning to hold as quickly as possible concerning matters of great importance to faith and discipline.

VII. From what has been presented thus far, in addition to the freedom of ordination—which is perfectly clear—the freedom of Rome’s rule is also evident. Recent scholars fail to grasp this because, although they neither find nor can find Rome and its duchy among the donations to the Franks, they nevertheless suppose its dominion to have been of the same nature as the jurisdiction of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis.

But Christopher the primicerius, who, even before the temporal rule of the Holy See, exercised supreme authority together with the archpriest and archdeacon when the see was vacant or the pontiff absent—as all scholars know (*Diurnum Pontificale*, titles 1, 5, 6, 7, chapter 2)— When the other nobles had been broken by fear amid this great disturbance of affairs, he pretended to go with his son Sergius to the monastery at Spoleto. From there he approached the duke of Spoleto, then the king of the Lombards; gathering forces from both sides, the duke entered the City at the head of an army organized against the antipope’s forces, fought successfully, and restored the commonwealth.

All this occurred after the tenth month of the invasion. The primicerius did not escape the antipope’s ambushes until after Easter of the year 768, namely on 10 April, under the pretext of embracing monastic life.

During this long period of thirteen months, neither did the Frankish king, the patricius of the Romans, settle Rome’s affairs, nor did the impious Greeks foment the disturbances. When force had to be repelled by force, there were no soldiers or commanders on either side. Therefore, Rome was ruled by its own prince, and that prince was the pontiff. Since, throughout the entire period during which the see was vacant, the primicerius exercised the prince’s functions, he obtained assistance from other rulers of Italy. After driving the invader from the principate, he arranged for the new prince—namely, the pontiff duly ordained—to be announced to the subjects.

No one, surely, would call these doubtful signs of a principate. There are nevertheless other, more certain signs, derived from the same invasion of the see. The punishment inflicted upon the guilty is a supreme indication of power, and Anastasius supplies several examples that ought not to be neglected.

VIII. During the few days preceding the consecration of the elected pontiff Stephen, punishments were inflicted upon those criminals who had adhered to the pseudopope. The invader himself and his brother Passivus had been committed to prison before the election and were being held there.

Two further notorious criminals are mentioned: Waldipert, a priest of Lombard birth, and Gracilis the tribune, both guilty of treason. The latter, emboldened in Campania by the favor and resources of the pseudopope, had perpetrated every crime. After the latter’s fall, fearing for himself with good reason, he fortified himself at Alatri. From there he was seized by the Roman army, brought to Rome, and thrown into close custody. Later his eyes were torn out and his tongue cut off.

Waldipert’s crime was singular and especially relevant here. It should therefore be reported in the very words found in Anastasius (section 274): “The plot which he had formed with Theodicius, duke of Spoleto, and with certain Romans, to kill the aforementioned Christopher the primicerius and the other Roman nobles, and to hand over the Roman City to the Lombard people.” He too was subjected to a similar punishment.

I shall not delay over the rest, although I read that the pseudopope and Bishop Theodore, his vicedominus, likewise had their eyes torn out, while others were subjected to various other punishments. It is nevertheless worth observing that, although Anastasius reports such penalties as having been inflicted by wicked men, this seems to have been done to avert hatred from the new pontificate.

For even in the age of Alexander III this kind of punishment prevailed, as Peter Mallius relates (*Bollandists*, vol. VI, June, part II, p. 49, E): “For prefects with judicial authority, if they hang someone, five solidi; when they behead someone, likewise; when they blind someone, twelve denarii for each eye; when they amputate a limb, likewise.”

Indeed, among the duties of princes, nothing is praised more than assigning to each person his due right, as is said of David: “David also administered judgment and justice to all the people” (*Second Book of Kings*, chapter VIII, verse 15). This twofold administration of the commonwealth was never at any time separated from the principate, and such clear evidence of both functions is found in the pontificate that it cannot in any way be weakened.

IX. And indeed, there is no doubt that there was a prefect of the City of Rome when it obeyed the rule of the emperors. For, as John the Deacon relates in the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great* (book I, chapter 5), the holy man asked the emperor by letter not to confirm his election: “But the prefect of the City, his kinsman by name, anticipated his messenger, and, having seized and torn up the letters, etc.”

We know with certainty that this same office continued after Rome began to be subject to the rule of the pontiffs. Anastasius testifies to it in the *Life of Adrian* (section 298), where, discussing the crime of the chamberlain Calvulus, he relates how Adrian “ordered the aforementioned Calvulus the chamberlain and the previously named Campanians to be handed over to the prefect of the City, so that he might examine them before the entire people in the manner of murderers.”

Several further examples of this kind will be given below from Adrian’s own letters, when we reach that pontiff. Here I would have the accumulated offenses of a single letter (ep. 61, otherwise 50) considered. Anastasius, the papal envoy, Paschal and Saratinus, and also Paulinus were all criminals, each having committed a different offense deserving a different punishment.

Adrian sent Paulinus, bound, to Charles, since he belonged to Charles’s jurisdiction. He asked that the wicked Paschal and Saratinus be sent to Rome so that he himself might punish them: “while,” he says, “I shall have exacted complete justice from them.” Concerning Anastasius, he accuses Charles of violating the law of nations because he detained an envoy, and says that he must be sent back to the City: “And, questioning him with the greatest severity, we shall correct him according to the offense found in him.”

Thus the pontiff exercised in his own jurisdiction—namely, at Rome, in the duchy, and in the other regions subject to him—the so-called coercive power in the same manner as Charles exercised it in his own territory. Consequently, this principal mark of supreme rule was not lacking at Rome during the time of the pseudopope, who revealed it through his own crime and that of his associates.

X. Eccardus (*Rerum Francicarum*, book XXV, chapter 38) and his follower Muratorius (*Italian Annals*, 789) seem not to have noticed the letter of Adrian cited above. Relying instead on another letter of the same pontiff (97, otherwise 85), and for this same reason, they assert the Roman pontiff’s dominion in the provinces of the Exarchate and Pentapolis.

Waldipert, however, of whom we have just spoken, was not of this view. That wicked priest saw that the City belonged to the pontifical dominion; he therefore believed that, by murdering the Roman nobles, it could be subjected to Lombard power. They were the administrators of the commonwealth, and once they had been removed, the commonwealth would necessarily perish.

Since this matter is important, I shall make it clearer, so that the pontifical dominion may shine forth increasingly. Seven offices in particular are frequently named in these letters of the Carolingian Codex and by Anastasius: the primicerius, secundicerius, arcarius, saccellarius, nomenclator, primicerius of the defenders, and protoscriniarius.

These distinguished men are called sometimes nobles and sometimes leading men both by Anastasius (sections 274, 293) and in the Lateran Council of Stephen III. On this point Baronius (year 638, no. 9) and others are greatly mistaken when they suppose that cardinal priests and deacons are designated by the term “leading men.”

They are correctly called palatine offices in the little book attributed to John the Deacon, which was cobbled together after the middle of the fifteenth century, an age exceedingly fertile in fabrications. Although this little work is dedicated to Alexander III, the sepulchral monuments of Alexander himself and of Clement III disprove that attribution, as do the deeds of Honorius III and Alexander IV that appear in it, and, more importantly, the following clear inscription found in chapter 8:

“In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year of the Incarnation 1297, on the day of February, the altar of the chapter was consecrated in honor of God and of blessed Mary Magdalene, by order of the lord Pope Boniface VIII, by Lord Gerard of Parma, bishop of Sabina.”

It is astonishing that Panvinio (*Vatican Codex*, no. 1106), his copyist Rasponus (*On the Lateran Basilica*, book III, chapter 18), and Mabillon (*Museum Italicum*, vol. III, p. 570) did not notice this. They attach great importance to the little book and assert that it was dedicated to Alexander III. The Vallicellian codex, however, reveals its true age, for inserted in the little book is a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs ending with Pius II, who ascended the chair of Peter in the year 1458.

XI. Whatever may be the case with the other matters contained in that compilation, the item in which the Roman nobles or leading men are called palatine offices must certainly be counted among the ancient records used by the compiler.

The primicerius of the notaries, whose authority was supreme when the see was vacant or the pontiff absent, seems, once the pope had become the supreme prince of the Romans, thereafter to have become the first dignity of the palace, if I am not mistaken. In the courts of other princes we would call him the chief minister; in the pontifical court, the secretary of state.

That the primicerius of the notaries customarily exercised this office at that time is inferred from Paul’s letters (37, otherwise 20). Defending Christopher, who had been accused of bad faith, before Pippin against the emperor of the East, he says:

“He asserted that our beloved son Christopher, the primicerius and counselor, had, without our authority and as though we were unaware, made those suggestions which we had often directed to him, and had read other matters on behalf of other envoys of his and yours. In this matter we call God as witness and judge that it is not so at all. For our counselor has never done, or presumed to do, anything outside our will, since he was and remains the sincere and most proven faithful servant of our predecessor and brother, the lord Pope Stephen, as well as of us; and we are satisfied with his spotless fidelity and steadfastness of heart.”

The other leading men and the judges of the ecclesiastical territory depended upon him, as Panvinio and Rasponus rightly state, in accordance with Cassiodorus’s judgment (book IV, letter 7). Thus the other leading men obey him after Paul’s death, and the judges supply forces when the matter concerns expelling Constantine.

However great his authority may have been, he was the first administrator of the apostolic see, and his office was permanent. Concerning the dignity of the secundicerius, which was inferior only to the first; concerning the offices of the saccellarius and arcarius, corresponding to the chamberlain and treasurer of our own age; and concerning the other three offices, I shall speak more conveniently elsewhere.

## XLIV. 249. LETTER

[Note: The chronology of this and the following letter is certain. This one was sent at the beginning of July, and the other in October of the year 767. The arguments are set out at considerable length in the Magdeburg Centuriators (*Centuries*, 8, chapter 10), and somewhat differently in Baronius (year 767, no. 7), from the same Vatican codex from which the arguments of Paul’s letters were taken. CENN.]

## OF CONSTANTINE

[Note: After Pope Paul I died, this pseudopope Constantine was forced into the apostolic see by a faction. He soon sent two letters to Pippin, which are also mentioned by Baronius, year 767, no. 7, and by the Magdeburg Centuriators, *Centuries* 8, chapter 10. GRETS.]

## POPE

[Note: Saint Gregory explains this expression, which at first sight seems improper, as follows (*Register*, book VII, indiction 2, letter 111): “Just as at that time one was called a neophyte who had initially been planted in the way of life of the holy faith, so now one must be regarded as a neophyte who, suddenly planted in the religious habit, has slipped in to seek sacred honors.” Nicholas I uses this same authority, letter 10, to the clergy of Constantinople against Photius (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 367). ID.]

## NEOPHYTE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD PIPPIN, KING

Containing expressions of thanks, an account of the death of the lord Pope Paul, and a request that he may remain in the favor of the lord King Pippin, just as his predecessors had done.

*(Year of the Lord 767, Carolingian Codex XCVIII, chronology 43.)*

### Argument

As soon as the most audacious layman had been forced into the holy see, he followed the examples of the most holy pontiffs Stephen and Paul and even appropriated their statements. He announces Paul’s death and his own election, which he falsely claims was unanimous; he dares to seek the friendship of the excellent prince; he speaks of the exaltation of the Church; and he promises to send his own envoys when those who had gone to Francia have returned. He gives the letter to a royal envoy for transmission to the most devout king.

To the most excellent son, the lord Pippin, king of the Franks and patricius of the Romans, Constantine, pope.

We fully believe that by now, with messengers preceding us, it has reached your most excellent and God-appointed royal power that, after our predecessor of blessed memory, the lord Pope Paul, had been taken from this light by God’s summons, the people of the City and of the cities subject to it chose my unworthiness to rule over them as their shepherd [Note: From the mouth of this most audacious invader we learn that jurisdiction over the Roman province belonged to the Roman pontiff. He defends his election by the consent of the City and of the cities subject to it; thus, despite his lies, he confirms the political condition of Rome in that age. What follows, taken from Paul’s letters, adds nothing new. ID.]. And behold, with immense astonishment of mind I say what I absolutely did not desire and what my merits did not require: I have attained the sacred summit of the apostolate and assumed the care of a great pastoral burden [Note: See Baronius, year 767, no. 5 and following; those clouds of smoke will immediately disperse.].

Therefore, because Almighty God, through the hands of the prince of the blessed Peter and of his vicar, ordered your excellence to be chosen and raised up in these days above all kings and powerful men of the world, for the exaltation of his holy Church and the redemption of this province, as a new Moses—who, by God’s will, redeemed the people of Israel—and because this has in fact been accomplished, with God’s assent, through your assistance and struggle, I therefore make humble entreaty. As though standing bodily before your honey-flowing royal presence, I kneel and beseech your excellence to command that you wholly remember and preserve what you promised to blessed Peter, and likewise the charity and friendship that you maintained with the lord Stephen, pontiff of blessed memory, our predecessor and his brother.

May you deign, with still greater zeal, to promote the exaltation of the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, the defense of the orthodox faith, and the complete liberation of this province entrusted to you, so that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you may deserve to receive from Almighty God the crown of reward already stored up for you in the heavenly dwellings.

For after God we have no hope anywhere except in your arm, strengthened by God. For this reason we call upon the same Lord our God, to whom the secrets of the heart have been revealed, as witness that, like our pontifical predecessors, we earnestly desire to remain firm and unchanging to the end in your charity, faithful affection, and sincere friendship. We shall never, through any interruption of time, separate ourselves from your charity or from the sincere friendship of your kingdom of the Franks, protected by God.

Therefore, most Christian, God-appointed, great, most victorious, good king, and, by God’s will, our protector, while various matters press upon us, there has so far been no opportunity to send two other envoys, until your envoys [Lambard: our envoys], who were sent there to you [Gentianus: to us], return. But when they have come back, we shall immediately send our envoys into your presence. We have nevertheless placed this very message in the mouth of your envoy, to be conveyed to your kindly excellence. As for the Deeds of the Saints which you asked to have sent to you, we have transmitted to you as many as we were able to find.

May Almighty God, in whose hand the heart of your excellence is directed, grant you prosperous times, subject all hostile nations to your royal feet, and cause you, together with your most excellent and God-enlightened daughter, the lady queen, and your most distinguished sons, the kings, to possess the government of the kingdom for many years. May he grant that you become participants in eternal blessedness with his saints and all the elect throughout infinite ages. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## XLV. 252. LETTER OF CONSTANTINE, POPE AND NEOPHYTE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD PIPPIN, KING

Containing an account of how he was elected by the Roman people through violence and forced into the apostolic see; a request that he may remain in the favor of the lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had done; and, thereafter, an account of a letter from Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, and of other letters from the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch; and, in a postscript, concerning George, Marinus, and Peter.

*(Year of the Lord 767, Carolingian Codex XCIX, chronology 44.)*

[Col. 0235C]

### Argument

Unable to bear the king’s silence, he again lies that he was created by the unanimous consent of the people. He inserts passages from Sacred Scripture and praises Pippin as a champion of the Catholic faith. He relates that the letters of the Eastern patriarchs concerning the synod held in defense of the veneration of the sacred images, addressed to Paul, had first been publicly read by him from the ambo, and that he is now sending them to Pippin in Greek and Latin. He earnestly asks that George the bishop and the priests Marinus and Peter be permitted to return, for the consolation of their parents; he urgently requests a reply. Above all, he asks him to receive his envoys, Christopher the priest and Anastasius the notary.

To the most excellent son, the lord Pippin, king of the Franks and patricius of the Romans, Constantine, pope.

When I look deeply within myself and consider intensely how great must be the care imposed upon me by the pastoral office I have undertaken, for feeding the rational sheep of the Lord, I confess that an unbearable sadness has adhered to the secret recesses of my heart. For undoubtedly, in all who undertake the care of souls, advancement to such an office appears to be filled not with merit but with burden and anxiety. I am oppressed beyond measure, and, considering that I shall not be equal to the task through any merits of my works or progress in virtue, I reflect upon what divine mercy, inspiring the affection of my heart, has commanded me to do.

Then, as though awakened from a deep sleep, I find myself, amid immense astonishment and ecstasy, asked by God to undertake what I never desired, what I never even considered in my mind, and what never in any way entered the heart of my weakness. For, by an unforeseen act of violence, by the hand of an innumerable multitude of peoples agreeing together, I was carried away like a powerful blast of wind and raised to so great and terrible a summit of pontifical office.

Therefore, just as a ship is tossed by storms upon the sea, so I, unhappy and useless, am shaken by the tumult of cares, by the proclamations of the people, and by their tearful wailings. For all alike, from the greatest to the least, crying out their own griefs and sufferings, never cease to surround me on every side with conflicts of thought, seeking consolation and the administration of justice for this people liberated by you.

[Col. 0236B] Oh, how great and fearful is the anxiety of shepherds! And how can I, wretched as I am, fulfill the care of souls’ burdens? Nevertheless, when I immediately cast my thought upon the Lord, placed the confidence of my hope in his mercy, and entrusted myself, most excellent, God-protected, and most victorious king, to your customary aid and protection, I found a remedy already prepared, and my afflicted spirit breathed again for a little while. For after God, I am greatly strengthened by your royal power and by the most robust arm of your Frankish kingdom, protected as it is by God.

Amid these things, therefore, I consider how great is the mercy of our almighty God, and at once an abundant opportunity for consolation is granted to me. For he himself, descending from the Father’s bosom for the salvation of the human race, the Word made flesh, [Col. 0236C] deigned to be born of the virgin Mary, our lady, without relinquishing his divinity; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. By dying he destroyed our death, and by rising again he restored life. Therefore he did not disdain to speak and eat with sinners and tax collectors. Indeed, he received a tax collector and made him an evangelist—I mean Matthew—who spread the evangelical words throughout the world.

O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! Truly great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no number to his wisdom. He places the humble on high and raises the sorrowful to health. For this reason, considering myself like one of the tax collectors, with a groan of heart and striking my breast, I beseech his ineffable mercy [Col. 0236D] that he may grant me to carry out safely the pastoral office which he has undeservedly conferred upon me, and to offer the gains of souls to his divine majesty. For my mouth frequently speaks the praise of our redeemer; my flesh and tongue bless his holy name, who does not consider merits but has mercy on those whom he wills to pity.

Having already sent our apostolic letters on the foregoing matters, we were commanded [Grets., “unless”] to make known to your God-appointed royal eminence the departure of our predecessor, the lord Pope Paul, and how divine favor commanded that I, unworthy and useless as I am, be advanced into the order of the apostolate. Therefore, behold, now also, through repeated apostolic utterances, we have considered it fitting to render to your most excellent Christian Majesty the due affection of honor and greeting, and an effort at visitation appropriate to you.

And since our almighty and long-suffering God, sending the word of salvation through his apostle, blessed Peter, to your eminence, has raised you up and established you as the strongest liberator and defender of his holy Church and of the orthodox faith, most excellent son and great orthodox king, therefore—even though the shepherds have changed—the care of this struggle and defense nevertheless rests upon you. For this reason, as though standing presently before your honey-sweet royal presence, I beseech you, and by almighty God, who is judge of the living and the dead, before whose sight all the elements tremble and the abysses are shaken, who governs all the kingdoms of the world by the nod of his providence, who also commanded that you, most excellent and most gracious son and king, and your most beloved sons, my spiritual sons, be anointed as kings by the hands of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I firmly adjure your eminence to observe and in every respect fulfill those things which [read: quae] you made promise of to blessed Peter for the stability of your kingdom and the reward of eternal life, for the exaltation and defense of the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, and of the holy orthodox faith.

And I adjure you to remain with us in the same charity and affection in which you remained with our predecessors, the lords Stephen and Paul, most blessed pontiffs, and to persist in the same bond of friendship with my frailty—not considering our evil merits, but fulfilling the command of the divine oracle (Matthew 10): “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.” And that which Truth himself, our God, says (Luke 10): “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever despises you despises me.”

Consider, good king, that our God could have accomplished the liberation of his Church and of the orthodox faith through an angel of his power or by some other means. Yet it pleased him to do so through no one other than your eminence, because this good work had been reserved for you. Hence it is clearly made known to all that everything was predestined by God before the foundation of the world.

Was not David predestined—the one from whom Christ was born into the world according to the flesh? Though he was little among his brothers, he was taken from his father’s sheep and anointed king. And because you have been predestined by God as defender of the holy Church of God and of us, come, hear our prayers, most gentle king; may the Lord hear you on whatever day you call upon him.

Indeed, with our God as witness—he to whom the secrets of the heart are manifest—we shall remain with all our people in firm constancy in the charity and affection, and sincere fidelity, of your God-protected Frankish kingdom, even more than our aforementioned predecessor pontiffs did. And I ask before the living God that, if perhaps anyone seized by the spirit of wickedness should attempt to chatter contrary things about us to your royal eminence, no credence at all be granted him. For, as we trust in the mercy of almighty God, you will be fully satisfied concerning our purity.

Therefore, behold, we have sent these most faithful envoys of ours to your God-directed footsteps: namely, our beloved son, the presbyter Christophorus, and Anastasius, the regional notary of your spiritual mother, our holy Church. They should satisfy you concerning the fidelity which we maintain toward your royal power, and we have put this very message into their mouths to recount to your Christian Majesty in our place. We ask that, out of reverence for blessed Peter [Lamb. adds: “your patron”], you receive them kindly and in your customary manner, believe them in all things, and command that they be dismissed with joyful messages concerning your gracious purpose and immense prosperity.

Accordingly, we inform your eminence that on the twelfth day of the past month of August, in the fifth indiction, a certain religious presbyter named Constantine came to us from the holy city, bringing a synodical statement of faith [Note: [Col. 0237D] See what I said concerning Epistle 31, alternatively 35 (notes 2 and 3). I judged that epistle should indeed be removed from the year 758, relying on the conjecture of the Jerusalem council held around 760, and believed it should be placed at the end of the year 761. Nevertheless, I confess that I cannot understand why this synodical statement was not sent to Rome before August of the year 767—that is, six years after the council is said to have been held. From this, I think, it is clear how difficult a task it is to arrange almost all these letters, which lack chronological markers, while preserving their temporal sequence. CENN.] sent by Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, under the name of our predecessor, the lord Pope Paul. In it the other patriarchs—namely, the Alexandrian and the Antiochene—as well as many metropolitan bishops of the eastern regions, appeared to have agreed.

We received and embraced it with great joy, and had it reread before the people from the ambo. We sent a copy of it to your eminence in Latin and Greek, so that you might recognize the fervor concerning the holy images which has arisen among all Christians in the eastern regions.

With these matters first set forth, extending our hands toward heaven, together with all the worshipers of God and our entire people, we implore the divine clemency of our redeemer: may he protect you with the right hand of his outstretched power, enlarge the boundaries of your Frankish kingdom, strengthened by God, and grant you immense victories over your enemies; may he cast down all adversaries at your royal feet; and may he grant you to enjoy and possess the government of your kingdom through a long and prosperous old age, together with our most excellent daughter, the God-protected queen, and your most beloved sons. May he grant you to possess both your temporal and earthly kingdom and the heavenly kingdoms, together with all the saints who from the beginning of the world have pleased his divine majesty. May heavenly grace preserve your eminence unharmed.

## Supplement

Accordingly, we ask this of your eminence: command, most Christian and most gentle king, inspired by God, that our reverend and most holy brother, Bishop George, and our beloved sons, the presbyters Marinus and Peter, who were sent to your eminence by our predecessor, the lord Pope Paul, be released and sent back to us [Note: [Col. 0239A] At the end of the year 765, and again in the following year (Epistles 39 and 40, alternatively 14 and 26), Paul granted the Frankish king’s repeated request that he retain George, bishop of Ostia, and Peter, cardinal presbyter, with him. We know with certainty that both returned to Rome after Pippin’s death, because we see George present at the Lateran Council held in 769 against this invader of the Holy See, and Peter serving in 770 as Stephen III’s envoy, together with the defender Pamphilus, to the kings Charles and Carloman, Pippin’s sons (Epistle 49, alternatively 45).

As for Marinus, the cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, the same Pippin’s request tells us that he had been created as such as early as 757 (Epistle 16, alternatively 25). We subsequently learn that he plotted together with the adversaries against the Frankish king and the Holy See (Epistle 19, alternatively 39). Finally, Pippin himself restored him to his former honor in 764 at Paul’s request; and the pontiff, moved by the tears of Marinus’s desolate and bereaved mother, asked the same king to send him back to Rome (Epistle 36, alternatively 32).

But what the pseudopope means by extending a private matter concerning one person to two others, and by praising Pippin because he freed all of them from the hands of their persecutor, I do not understand. I seem to have grasped only this: that Charles was right to consign both letters, full of lies and absurdities, to the end of the codex, and that I should not have brought such filth forward. Yet the chronological order compelled me to do so. Enough and more than enough has been said about both in the admonition, insofar as historical matters are concerned.].

For their parents come to us every day with great weeping, asking that we beseech your God-appointed eminence on behalf of their release; indeed, we cannot bear their tears. Through you, good and most merciful king, they have been made safe and stand liberated from the hands of their persecutor. Therefore a great crown of reward is laid up for you in heaven, for it is written: “Whoever saves is like one who builds.”

For this reason, before the living God, we beseech you to hear our prayers in this matter and command that they be released. When they return, we shall receive them with great joy and strive to embrace them as dear ones in our inmost being. For the bishopric and churches which they appeared to hold remain disordered to this day. Therefore let your eminence arrange matters so that the aforementioned men may return to their native land, because the time has come for them to rejoice together with their parents and with us in the Lord, and so that we may rightly pour out prayers for your life and safety.

[Lamb. adds: “The end of the Carolingian epistolary codex.”]

# 259. Admonition concerning the five letters of Stephen III

### I

Although the various disturbances of the state had been quieted and their authors punished, the savage wounds inflicted upon the Church had by no means been healed. The invasion of the Apostolic See, the illicit ordinations carried out by the same man, and the impiety of the East, which had increased in a remarkable fashion, persuaded the pontiff to convene a synod in which all matters could be seriously and wisely examined.

Accordingly, intending to assemble bishops both from Italy and from the friendly Frankish kingdom, he sent a message, as Anastasius relates:

> “At the beginning of his pontificate, when that most holy prelate had assumed the summit of the pontificate, he sent to the regions of France, to the illustrious men Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, and to Sergius, then serving as secundicerius and nomenclator, beseeching and exhorting their eminence through his apostolic letters to send several bishops who were knowledgeable and exceedingly well instructed in all the divine Scriptures and in the regulations of the holy canons, to hold a council in this city of Rome.”

These first letters of Stephen are found neither in this codex nor elsewhere. From the Vatican Codex, which Panvinio testifies that he saw, Baronius cites their substance (year 772, no. 2): “At the beginning of his pontificate he wrote to Pippin, asking that learned men be sent to the Roman synod.”

Why they perished in France, and why Charles therefore could not record them, can easily be conjectured from the sequence of events which occurred on this occasion.

### II

Indeed, the pontiff’s envoy or legate, who departed from Rome after the seventh day of August in the year 768, when Stephen was consecrated, and who arrived in France in October, found that Pippin had departed this life on the preceding 24 September. Therefore he had to approach the king’s sons, who, after their father’s funeral, had each gone to his own kingdom and had already assumed the royal insignia on 9 October: Charles at Noyon, and Carloman at Soissons, as the monk of Angoulême reports.

Where the legate found them is not stated by Anastasius. This much is certain: both had proceeded to Paris, each to his own kingdom. Thus Sergius, “continuing the journey he had begun, reached his sons.”

The loss was slight, for the letters achieved their purpose: twelve bishops from France, almost all from metropolitan cities, came to Rome with Sergius in the spring of the following year, 769. Adrian attests the matter in his Treatise to King Charles concerning the veneration of the sacred images (Labbe, Councils, vol. VII, pp. 919, 923, 944, 952):

> “Our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of blessed memory, likewise presiding together with the bishops of the regions of France and Italy, and so forth.”

Through the benefit of the Verona codex, we now also possess the names of those twelve bishops and of the forty Italians who took part in the council, both in the Roman edition of 1735 and in the recent edition of Lucca, vol. I, supplement to Labbe’s Councils.

I shall say something briefly about the matters conducted during the four days of the council, especially what is necessary for our purpose—not only so that the loss of the letters may be less regretted, but also so that they may provide a torch illuminating what is to be said concerning pontifical history as it is drawn from the following letters.

### III

In the first session, therefore, with the pseudopope placed in the midst of the bishops, Christophorus, the pontiff’s primicerius, recounted the sacrilegious invasion and presented for reading the historical account which he had been ordered to prepare. Nothing was decided that day.

In the second session the pseudopope was again brought before the council. He dared to defend his invasion by the example of Stephen, duke of Naples, who had been made a bishop from the lay state. That Stephen had been created bishop in 764 at the request of the clergy and people, being a close friend of Pope Paul and of the Holy See. The council fathers treated the pseudopope harshly, struck him with blows, and expelled him from the Church.

Afterward everything was burned that had been found committed to writing concerning the sacrilegious invasion, and penance was imposed upon all who had communicated with the sacrilegious man. Divine mercy was invoked, and the sacred canons were reread. It was decreed:

> “Let no one ever presume to promote to the sacred honor of the pontificate any layman, or anyone from another order, unless he has ascended through the distinct grades and has become a cardinal deacon or cardinal presbyter.”

Gratian also reports this decree (Distinction 79, chapter 4). Finally, penance was prescribed for the invader.

In the third session the proper discipline of pontifical election was established: namely, that the cardinal presbyters and deacons, the leading men of the clergy, and the entire clergy should elect; afterward, “all the leading military men, or the whole army, and the honorable citizens, and the entire general body of the people of this Roman city should hasten to salute him as Lord of all.” Then the decree of election was to be issued.

Every form of force was prohibited. The pontifical dignity was restricted to cardinal presbyters or deacons, in accordance with the statutes of blessed Peter and his successors. The ordinations performed by the pseudopope were invalidated, with everyone restored to his former rank. It was decreed that the bishops were to be consecrated again and everything else repeated, except baptism.

In the fourth session a decision was made concerning the veneration of the sacred images. It was first decreed that the fifty Canons of the Apostles should be received. Finally, after the decrees against force and ambition had been renewed, this splendid testimony to pontifical authority was incidentally pronounced:

> “If anyone should presume to assist or introduce into this city of Rome anyone from any city, fortified town, or place from which the pontiff has previously departed, until a pontiff has been ordained in the seat of blessed Peter, let him be anathema.”

So much for the first letter of Stephen, which is missing from the codex. We now turn to the five letters entered in it.

### IV

In these letters—which the Magdeburg Centuriators also know, and of which two (Epistles 45 and 46, alternatively 46 and 44) by universal agreement belong to the year 769 itself, after the celebration of the council, while the others (Epistles 47, 48, and 49, alternatively 47, 48, and 45) were issued in the following year—nothing clearer is supplied in this codex for treating this part of the history.

All were sent to Queen Bertrada, widow, and to her sons Charles and Carloman. They deal both with other matters and with matters concerning ecclesiastical jurisdiction, but they contain contradictions. Nor can any truth be extracted from them without the preceding history, which I recently restored here from the end of the codex, where Constantine’s letters were relegated.

The chief difficulty occurs in the first letter sent to Bertrada and Charles (Epistle 45, alternatively 46). Cointius rightly believes that it was written at the request of Desiderius, who was then living in Rome, and Pagius and Zacagnus follow his opinion. The Italian Annalist and several associates oppose it in vain (year 769), out of excessive goodwill toward the Lombard kings.

The argument they bring against these learned men is that Stephen was in Rome, not at the extramural basilica of blessed Peter, when he wrote the letter, and therefore was free from all fear of the Lombard king. But the letters of his predecessor Paul (Epistle 18, alternatively 15), in which he tells Pippin of the difficulties of writing because of the Lombards, and Stephen’s last letter (Epistle 49, alternatively 45), as well as the frequent custom both of the pontiff and of the king of France to entrust more to the ears of envoys than to commit to writing, plainly demonstrate that this argument is worthless.

I shall now place before the reader’s eyes the history as it is narrated by Anastasius in the Life of Stephen III, so that he may compare it with the letter.

### V

According to the unanimous testimony of the codices, after the council mentioned above had been briefly reported, Christophorus, the primicerius, and Sergius, the secundicerius—plainly the principal offices of the Holy See—are said to have incurred Desiderius’s hatred because they vigorously pursued the restitution of what had been taken, as was their duty.

Desiderius won over Paul Afiarta, the pontiff’s chamberlain, to his side by gifts, and, under the pretext of prayer, advanced toward Rome with an army. Christophorus, rightly fearful for the city, quickly summoned troops from Perugia, Campania, and Tuscany, closed the city gates, and prepared everything for the city’s defense, especially one gate more than the others, with masonry work.

Afterward the Lombards reached the Vatican, where the pontiff, summoned by the king, went. Following a conversation about restoring what had been taken, he returned to Rome.

Meanwhile Paul plotted an ambush against Christophorus and Sergius. When they discovered this, they entered the Lateran armed, intending to seize Afiarta by force. Although the pontiff rebuked their boldness, they withdrew.

On the following day the pontiff again went to the king, who openly demanded that Christophorus and Sergius be handed over to him. When Stephen refused, the king shut him and all who had followed him inside the basilica.

Then the pontiff sent word through envoys to those leaders who were with troops at the gate of blessed Peter that each of them should either put on monastic clothing or immediately go to the basilica of Saint Peter, since there was no other hope of safety. This alarmed the soldiers and scattered almost all of them.

At night, therefore, as the two men proceeded separately and secretly toward the basilica, they were captured by the Lombard guards and handed over first to the king and then to the pontiff. The pontiff returned to Rome the next day and left them there, so that, being brought to Rome at night, they might escape the ambushes of their enemies.

The opposite happened through Afiarta’s agency. With Desiderius’s consent, they were dragged from the basilica and their eyes were put out. Christophorus died three days later from grief, while Sergius remained in the Lateran patriarchate until the pontiff’s death.

### VI

The aforementioned letter, however, states that it was not Afiarta who was sought by force in the patriarchate. Rather, “the most wicked Christophorus and his utterly evil son Sergius,” together with Dodon, the envoy of Carloman, and the conspiratorial Franks and other accomplices in the crime, wished to kill the pontiff himself. With the help of Desiderius, who happened to be in Rome at that time to carry out the rights of blessed Peter, he escaped death together with his clergy.

In other respects the letter agrees with the history just related, except for certain names of men, which strengthen the credibility of the history but diminish that of the letter.

Moreover, the letter contains this plainly false statement:

> “We have received all the rights of blessed Peter from him more fully and completely.”

This conflicts with what Stephen asserts in the following year (Epistles 47 and 49, alternatively 47 and 45). For he supplies the royal envoys with a catalogue of everything that had to be restored, to be placed before the eyes of Charles and Carloman, and says:

> “But if anyone should tell you that we have received the rights of blessed Peter, do not believe him in any way.”

And elsewhere:

> “In the presence of your envoys they pretend to render us our rights. Nothing is brought to completion, and we have been wholly unable to receive anything from them of our rights.”

Since these things are so, no one will be persuaded that the Lombards, shortly before the worst and perpetual enemies of the Holy See, suddenly became good and most friendly; or, conversely, that those men of the highest integrity, so highly regarded by Stephen’s predecessors, through whose efforts the Holy See had breathed freely, liberated from invasion and fear, and through whose efforts the pontiff himself had been elected, suddenly became “most wicked and utterly evil.”

Therefore, I rightly say that Cointius and other learned men believe that Stephen wrote this letter, after the example of Paul, at Desiderius’s request. For one will not easily find such lies in Anastasius where he is speaking of events that occurred at Rome.

### VII

The silence concerning so great a crime in Stephen’s other letters, especially in the one which he wrote to the same Bertrada and Charles (Epistle 46, alternatively 44), is another evident argument for the point at issue.

That letter speaks at length and magnificently of the Beneventan patrimony, restored through Itherius’s utmost diligence; but both it and all the others are silent concerning the other rights which Stephen names. Throughout this pontiff’s entire tenure, only that one restitution is found to have taken place.

Pagius, a most diligent investigator of such matters (year 770, no. 7), does indeed produce two testimonies which appear not insignificant. The first is from the ancient Annals, after the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar:

> “In the year 770 Queen Berta was in Lombardy at a public assembly against King Desiderius, and very many cities were restored to the portion of Saint Peter.”

The other he takes from the Petavian Annals:

> “In this year Lady Berta was in Italy on account of the daughter of King Desiderius, and very many cities of Saint Peter were restored.”

But, with Pagius’s indulgence, such late testimonies deserve only doubtful credence. There were not many cities to be restored, and none of the few that ought to have been restored was returned by Desiderius.

Indeed, after Stephen’s death, when Adrian succeeded him and Desiderius’s envoys sought his friendship by promising complete restitution, Adrian reproached them with Desiderius’s reply to his predecessor Stephen. When Stephen had sought through his envoys, Anastasius, primicerius of the defenders, and Gemmulus, subdeacon, to demand:

> “That he fulfill what he had personally promised to blessed Peter.”

For Desiderius had replied:

> “It is enough for the apostolic Stephen that I removed Christophorus and Sergius, who ruled over him; he need not trouble himself by seeking rights.”

These facts confirm more and more strongly that the letter of which we have been speaking was either written at Desiderius’s request or adapted to that meaning through the gifts of Afiarta or someone else corrupted by Desiderius—a meaning most favorable to the Lombard’s schemes, by which he sought dissensions in France and conflicts at Rome.

### VIII

Pagius apparently believed that Berta had asked this of Desiderius so that Stephen, who was opposed to the marriage with Desiderius’s daughter, might be won over.

Yet the pontiff could not be removed from asserting the divine law by any earthly benefit. The words he spoke in the letter to the brother kings, rejecting that marriage (Epistle 49, alternatively 45), are perfectly clear:

> “You have been joined in lawful marriage by the command of your father.”

And below:

> “For it is impious even to allow it to rise into your hearts to take other wives in addition to those whom you are known to have taken first.”

This is certainly true of Carloman, the younger son, for the same pontiff (ibid., 48) expresses his desire to receive his son from the sacred font and closes the letter:

> “Together with your sweetest wife and your most beloved sons.”

The matter is different in the case of Charles, the elder. Einhard lists his wives, beginning with Desiderata, daughter of King Desiderius, whom, he says, “he repudiated after a year and took Hildegard, a woman of the Suevian people and of the highest nobility, in marriage.” Other Frankish writers do the same, giving rise to a long and highly involved question among scholars.

Nevertheless, the pontiff’s testimony is older than Einhard’s and therefore has greater authority on grounds of antiquity. Moreover, unlike Einhard and the others, he was not concerned with recounting the succession or genealogy of the Frankish kings. Rather, he was giving a reason why a wife should not be taken—a reason consistent with the truth, since Charles, the elder son, had already married and, according to the consensus of the sources, had fathered a son by Himiltrude, although the same writers dispute whether that union was a lawful marriage.

Whatever reasons the pontiff may have advanced—this entirely just one and many others, which should be attributed to that rough age and to the pontiff’s integrity rather than maligned along with the sectarians—at the end of the year 770 Charles married the daughter of Desiderius.

Although Stephen survived until the Kalends of February in the year 772, when he died, and although Carloman had predeceased him by approximately two months, no envoys and no letters are found to have been sent from Rome to France. Such was Rome’s detestation of that marriage!

### IX

It will be worthwhile to indicate what occurred during that year of silence, so that the pontifical history which we are illuminating through the testimony of the Carolingian Codex may stand securely.

Desiderius, the principal author and supporter of dissensions and conflicts both in the Frankish kingdom and in the pontifical territory, is said to have undertaken nothing concerning France throughout the entire period in which his daughter was queen of the Frankish monarchy, which was subject to the sole rule of Charles.

The events after the divorce, which Desiderius was never able to digest, concern the pontificate of Adrian. Under this pontiff, Desiderius plotted to have the sons of Carloman, who were with him and their mother Gilberga, consecrated as kings of France, so as to cause trouble for Charles and divide his strength. Yet by such deceitful schemes he harmed not Charles but himself, and most grievously; for he lost both his kingdom and his freedom, as I shall show when I come to Adrian’s letters.

As for the pontifical territory, throughout that period he never ceased sowing and nurturing dissension both in the old domain and in the new territory granted by the Frankish king Pippin. Through continual machinations he sought either to turn the palace officials, in whose hands the administration of the state lay, away from the pontiff, or to remove them altogether. This filled the city itself with conflicts and punishments.

Worse things occurred in the Exarchate and the Pentapolis through Desiderius’s schemes. After Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, died in 770 and Leo was canonically elected, Michaelius, supported by Lombard protection, invaded that see “for the space of one year and more,” as Anastasius relates in the Life of Stephen III.

It is useful to recount the matter in Adrian’s own words (Epistle 93, alternatively 71), which are very clear:

> “When the aforementioned Sergius, archbishop, died, Michaelius the usurper, through his arrogance, dared to invade the church of Ravenna; and, invading that church outrageously with the aid of Desiderius, the most savage king, he held it for a long time, while it remained deprived and bereft of its proper ruler. Then Hucbald, sent by your royal eminence for other matters to our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of holy memory, was sent by that same lord Pope Stephen to Ravenna through your royal assistance, strengthened by God, so that the aforementioned Michaelius the invader might be expelled from the church of Ravenna and brought here to Rome as a violator of the sacred canons.”

### X

Thus Desiderius, who is not said to have invaded any city belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy See, nevertheless did two principal things during the pontificate of Stephen III: he never restored anything that belonged by right to the Apostolic See, and he was always the author of dissensions.

From this, the pontiff suffered the greatest difficulty in that part of his territory which Pippin had granted. For Ravenna, the capital of the Exarchate, although it had not itself suffered a hostile invasion, was exposed to the injuries and depredations of its subjects.

When Michaelius saw that Stephen had stripped him of every hope of his sacrilegious ordination, he defended his invasion for more than a year with a strong hand, having given “many gifts to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as well as treasures, the ornaments of the church itself, and other valuables,” as the author cited by Anastasius relates.

Nor did the chief city of the Exarchate alone assume the appearance of such defection. Ariminum, the principal city of the Pentapolis, for the same reason entered into an alliance with the Lombards against the pontiff, as the same author teaches:

> “Then the most wicked Mauritius gathered an army, together with the counsel of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and hastened forth. He entered Ravenna, and by force of arms chose Michaelius himself and introduced him into the episcopal residence of the church of Ravenna. They transported Leo the archdeacon, who had been elected to the rank of archbishop, to Ariminum, and there Mauritius had him held in close confinement.”

What, then, was the pontiff to do amid such a disturbance of both provinces? Should he turn to France? But from that direction an even deeper wound had been inflicted on apostolic authority: Charles had married Desiderius’s daughter against the pontiff’s will, and his mother had arranged the marriage.

Therefore help had to be expected from Peter, prince of the apostles, who, if divine will so ordained, would vindicate the provinces entrusted to him. This plainly happened after the invasion had lasted a year, and consequently toward the end of the year 771.

### XI

For Charles, seeking from the Apostolic See a declaration that the marriage was invalid, sent his envoys Hucbert and his colleagues to Rome. On this matter, see the authorities cited by Pagius (year 771, no. 2).

Thus the phrase quoted above from Adrian—“for other matters”—must be understood. He does not say “to carry out the rights,” nor does he use any other expression that would indicate concern for the affairs of the Holy See.

This most favorable beginning of hostility toward the Lombard king, whose daughter was to be repudiated, offered Stephen an opportune occasion to bring both provinces, which were clearly in revolt, back into order by removing the schism. Therefore, from those same royal envoys, who had come to request benefits, he himself voluntarily requested a benefit—which we have heard from Adrian’s own mouth—and in this way Pope Stephen, who died shortly afterward, outwitted Mauritius, duke of Ariminum, the invader Michaelius, and King Desiderius.

From what has been said thus far it may be concluded that, before the sole rule of Charles, who subdued the Lombards and removed their king and added that part of Italy to the Frankish monarchy, there was never any cessation from invasion and fear either in the Roman province or in the Exarchate and Pentapolis.

And concerning the letters of Stephen III, enough has now been said.

## XLVI. 267. Also a Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Charles and to His Exalted Mother

Concerning Christopher and his son Sergius, who, together with Dodo and the other Franks, attempted to kill Pope Stephen.

[Note: Stephen IV, elected in 768, died in 772. — Grets.]

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 5): “He also sent another letter to the same kings, in which he relates at length the ambushes set for him by Dodo, prefect of the Franks, and the benevolence of Desiderius toward him, indicating that he had been defended by Desiderius’s aid.” It should be noted that both Baronius, from the Vatican Codex, and the Magdeburg Centuriators, except for the last, give the summaries of these five letters in reverse order: what is first in our text they place fifth. Since they also give the summary of that earlier letter which I said had perished in the Admonition, the last summary for both them and us is Letter 49, otherwise 45 of the Codex, in which the pontiff urges the kings not to contract a marriage with Desiderius’s daughter. The only difference is that for them this is the sixth summary, whereas for us it is the fifth. Nothing is more useful for establishing the chronology of Stephen’s letters. — Cenn.]

*(A.D. 769, Codex Carolinus XLVI, chronicle 45.)*

[Col. 0245B]

### Summary

He informs the widowed Queen Bertrada and King Charles, through the royal envoys, that he had nearly faced mortal danger at the hands of conspirators acting with Dodo, envoy of Carloman, Christopher the primicerius, and his son Sergius. He says that he was preserved unharmed by Desiderius, who was then at Rome and had fully and completely restored all the rights of Saint Peter, as they would better understand from the envoys’ own report. Christopher and Sergius had their eyes torn out without his knowledge. He assigned responsibility for so great a crime entirely to Dodo.

To the lady Bertrada, his religious daughter, consecrated to God, or to the most excellent lord Charles, son and king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

[Col. 0245C]

With great sorrow and groaning of heart, and in the danger of tribulation and death which has now come upon us through the followers of the devil, behold, through these apostolic words of ours we endeavor to disclose more fully to the ears of your God-consecrated religiousness and of your most excellent Christian dignity that the utterly impious Christopher and his most wicked son Sergius, having entered into a conspiracy with Dodo, the envoy of your brother, King Carloman,

[Note: Until now we have heard of no envoy or ambassador who came from Francia to Rome who did not strive with the king who sent him in service and love toward the Roman pontiff and the holy see. Should this Dodo in particular—whom Pope Paul in the year 763 (Letter 34, otherwise 18) commended as a man of the highest fidelity (for there is no reason for me to suppose that he was another man)—be believed to have become involved in this sacrilegious crime? What shall I say of Christopher the primicerius and his son, through whose efforts the schism was removed and this pontiff was canonically created? “Utterly impious Christopher”? Shortly before, namely in April of this same year, he acted as accuser of the false pope with the applause of the entire council; he himself was the chief reason why all dishonor was removed from the holy see. Christopher was regarded by earlier pontiffs as a man of such great integrity that Paul proved the wickedness of the Greeks by the single fact that they had accused Christopher through their machinations (Letter 37, otherwise 20). Christopher, I say, is suddenly called “utterly impious” by the very pontiff who acknowledged that he owed his highest dignity to Christopher’s many and great dangers? And Sergius, his son, a companion in those dangers, regarded by the pontiff as no less trustworthy than by the kings of the Franks—at whose request twelve bishops had been ordered to come to the council—is suddenly judged “most wicked”? On the other hand, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, who previously had been moved by no entreaties to restore the Church’s possessions, and who was always planning new invasions, even daring by threatening letters to frighten the pontiff when he demanded back what was his, has suddenly become the best of men, protected the pontiff, and returned everything that had been taken? Who does not see that this letter was extorted from Stephen by that most cunning Desiderius, who ten years earlier had obtained a similar letter from Paul by force and fear (Letters 17 and 18, otherwise 29 and 15)? Paul, indeed, warned Pippin about the whole matter in other letters written secretly, something Stephen was then unable to do. But the truth is evident from the letters that follow, and still more clearly from his Life in Anastasius. Cointius noticed this before me. See Pagi, A.D. 770, no. 1 and following, and the Admonition prefixed to Stephen’s letters. — Cenn.]

—were plotting to kill us. Accordingly, joining forces with that same Dodo and his Franks, together with certain of their most wicked accomplices, they assembled an army against us and entered the holy patriarchate of the Lateran with weapons. They smashed the doors and pierced all the curtains of that venerable patriarchate with spears; then they entered inside, into the basilica of Lord Pope Theodore, where no one had ever dared to enter, not even with a knife, wearing cuirasses and carrying spears, where we were sitting. Thus those wicked men lay in wait to kill us.

But almighty God, seeing the uprightness of our heart—for we have never wished evil upon anyone—snatched us from their hands. And, after our most excellent son Desiderius, king of the Lombards, had come to be with us here in order to carry out various restitutions for us on behalf of blessed Peter, we were able, by that very circumstance, to flee with our clergy to your protector. Immediately we sent our priests to those same wicked men, Christopher and Sergius, so that they might repent of the wickedness they had planned to inflict upon us and hasten to us, to blessed Peter.

As soon as they heard this, they immediately joined Dodo and his Franks, formed companies, closed the city gates, resisted us forcefully, threatened us, and utterly refused to allow us to enter the city. While they persisted in the same treachery, and while all our people had learned of their wicked plot, the people immediately abandoned them; indeed, many descended over the wall and hurried to us. Others opened the city gate, came forward to meet us, and thus those wicked men, compelled and unwilling, were led to us in the church of Saint Peter.

The whole people tried to kill them, and only with difficulty were we able to snatch them from their hands. While we were preparing to bring them safely inside the city during the silence of night, so that no one who saw them might kill them, suddenly those who had always been lying in wait for them fell upon them and tore out their eyes. With God as our witness, we say that this happened without our will or counsel.

[Col. 0246B]

Therefore our heart is worn down by great sorrow. Believe us, God-consecrated daughter and most excellent son: if the protection of God, of blessed Peter the apostle, and the aid of our most excellent son, King Desiderius, had not been present, both we [Lambach: *tam*, “so”] and our clergy, together with all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own community, would by now have fallen into mortal danger.

Behold how many wicked acts and diabolical instigations the aforesaid Dodo sowed and carried out here. He ought to have remained faithfully in the service of blessed Peter and of us; instead, they lay in wait for our life [Lambach and Gentianus: “he lay in wait”], failing to act according to what his king had commanded him—namely, to remain faithfully in the service of blessed Peter and in obedience to us. We firmly believe that, when such great wickedness on his part reaches the ears of your most excellent son, King Carloman, it will in no way please him that this Dodo, together with the aforesaid most impious followers, wished to reduce the holy Church of God to such abasement and devastation.

For this reason we have made known our tribulations, anxieties, and dangers to your most religious Christian dignity, instituted by God, and to your excellence, since almighty God has certainly not abandoned those who believe in him and trust in his mercy.

[Col. 0247B]

Let your God-loving religiousness and your most Christian excellence also recognize that, in the name of the Lord, by the good will of the aforesaid most excellent and God-protected son of ours, King Desiderius, we have come to an agreement with him and have received from him all the rights of blessed Peter more fully and in their entirety. Nevertheless, through your envoys you will be fully satisfied concerning this matter as well.

[Note: Below, in Letter 47, the same pontiff makes a few statements that conflict with these: “But if anyone should tell you that we have received the rights of blessed Peter, do not believe him in any way.” And elsewhere (Letter 49, otherwise 45): “In the presence of your envoys they pretend to be restoring the rights to us.” — Cenn.]

May almighty God surround you with the right hand of his protection, grant that you may enjoy the government of the present kingdom for long and prosperous ages, and cause you to attain in manifold ways the eternal joys of heavenly rewards. May heavenly grace preserve your religiousness and your excellence unharmed.

## XLVII. 271. Also a Letter of Pope Stephen, Addressed to Lord King Charles and to His Exalted Mother

Containing expressions of thanks, praise for Itherius [Lambach: *Ittherius*] the abbot, and a request that a worthy recompense be made to him for his exertions.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 4): “He also wrote another letter to Charles and his mother, in which he gives them thanks for the defense of the Church and commends Itherius, because he diligently carried out what had been entrusted to him.” — Id.]

*(A.D. 769, Codex Carolinus XLIV, chronicle 46.)*

[Col. 0248A]

### Summary

He writes to the same persons concerning Itherius, their royal envoy, who had arrived with his companions to carry out the rights of Saint Peter. He praises Itherius at length because he immediately went to recover the Beneventan patrimony, and commends him to their generosity as a man most faithful to blessed Peter and to the kings.

To the lady Bertrada, religious daughter consecrated to God, or to the lord Charles, son and king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

[Note: The Centuriators mention this letter in Century 8, chapter 10, where they discuss this pontiff, whom they call Stephen III. Baronius also mentions it under the year 772. They likewise cite another letter of the same Stephen, written at the beginning of his pontificate, in which he asks that learned men be sent to Rome for a synod; this letter does not appear in our copy. — Grets.]

[Note: Mabillon (Annals, book XXV, no. 34) observed that Charles held his mother Bertrada in the highest honor and that there was no cause of disagreement between them except the divorce involving Desiderius’s daughter, discussed below. From this and the preceding letter it is also clear that during the three years in which Carloman lived after their father’s death, until the year 771, Bertrada adhered not to him but to Charles and in a certain sense reigned jointly with him. — Cenn.]

While holy mother Church, universal and spiritual, rejoices, relieved by the great number of benefits [text: *tantos*; Lambach and Gentianus: *tantis*] that you have bestowed in various apostolic causes and interests, no declaration of the mouth, I think, will be sufficient to express the praises of thanksgiving owed to your most holy religiousness and to your most Christian excellence. Yet although no human recompense worthy of you can be paid for so pious a work, our merciful God, who is powerful and knows how to repay good with good, will himself grant you an abundant recompense of heavenly rewards for your labors. Our sincere affection of heart toward you also does not cease diligently to offer vows of prayer to the divine Majesty on your behalf.

Accordingly, the present Itherius, a religious and most prudent man, truly a sincere and faithful servant both of ours and of yours, whom you sent with his companions and your other envoys to carry out and execute the rights of your protector, blessed Peter, joined us and immediately departed for the territory of the Beneventan duchy in order to recover the patrimony situated in that region belonging to that same protector of yours, the prince of the apostles.

[Note: We have already seen above (Letter 20, otherwise 26) that certain possessions had then been restored in the duchy of Benevento, and that Pippin had dealt with the people of Gaeta and Naples concerning the restoration of the Neapolitan patrimonies. The matter here concerns the Campanian patrimony, famous from the letters of Gregory the Great. There would not have been such concern on the pontiff’s part for another nearly unknown patrimony which, in Gregory’s time, was called the Samnite patrimony in that province. According to Peregrinius’s opinion in Dissertation VIII (Pratillus, vol. V, pp. 296 and following), the people of Benevento called themselves Samnites for a very long time. These letters, however, do not state that the Campanian patrimony returned to the holy see through Itherius’s efforts. — Id.]

That most diligent man contended in everything according to your will and ours, and, as you had commanded him, displayed the steadfastness of his labor in those apostolic interests. Therefore our heart rejoiced greatly in the contest of his defense [Lambach: *indefesso*, “unwearied”] and in his firm perseverance in action. For, in accordance with the fact that the grace of heavenly gift illuminates him with the prudence of great knowledge and adorns him with pious merits and the integrity of unaltered faith, we found in him such fidelity in your service and ours as our ardent mind had long desired to recognize in him.

Therefore we offer the greatest and countless thanks to your most religious sobriety and, as though present in person, to your most Christian excellence. Accordingly, we earnestly ask your kindness, as though speaking to you face to face, that you order the abundance of your favor, the munificence of your generosity, and worthy consolation to be granted to this religious man for his laborious exertion, which, as has been said, he has displayed in your apostolic service and ours, so that, just as a worthy reward for his work is said to have been inscribed for him in the heavenly kingdoms by almighty God through the intercession of blessed Peter, so also he may receive from you the aid of consolation.

May our almighty God, through the sacred intercessions of the princes of the apostles, surround you with his grace, and grant you in abundance the joys of prosperity in the present life and of eternal happiness. May heavenly grace preserve your religiousness and your excellence unharmed.

[Note: I wish to point out the shared authority implied here. Envoys sent by the queen mother and by her son Charles are said to have come to Rome; both were ordered to execute the rights of Saint Peter; a reward for Itherius is requested from both; finally, the letter is addressed to both and ends with a conclusion common to both. The same is true of the preceding letter. — Cenn.]

## XLVIII. 274. Also a Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord Kings Charles and Carloman
