Containing abundant blessings, expressions of thanks for the concord of their brotherhood, and a request concerning the rights of Saint Peter.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 3): “He also sent another letter to the brothers Charles and Carloman, in which he congratulates them on having been reconciled with one another after their disputes. He asks them to compel the Lombards to return what they had seized from the patrimony of Saint Peter.” — Id.]

*(A.D. 770, Codex Carolinus XLVII, chronicle 47.)*

[Col. 0249D]

### Summary

Having received letters from Charles and Carloman through Bishop Gauzibert, the religious man Fuchbert, Ansfred, and Helmgarius, their envoys, he congratulates both of them on the discord between them having been settled and their former love for each other having been reestablished. He asks them to fulfill what they had promised to blessed Peter together with their father and to ensure that the rights be fully restored. He says that they will hear many things from their envoys and that no one should be believed who says that the rights have been restored. (This proves that Letter 45, otherwise 46, was given at the request of Desiderius.)

To the most excellent lords Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

[Note: Baronius and the Centuriators mention this letter. — Grets.]

Blessed is the Lord our God, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who exists as the consoler and propitiator of all who invoke him in truth. For he, our Redeemer, hearing the prayers of those who cry out to him, turns the tribulations of the sorrowful into joy. We certainly now see the clemency of divine piety and the kindness of mercy poured out upon us and upon the entire chosen people of his holy Church, since, hearing the vows of our prayer and the lamentation of our sorrow which until now we have endured because of the division and discord that the ancient enemy, the foe of peace, had introduced among your brotherhood, he has now, by God’s favor, after that pestilential rival was confounded, deigned to turn us to great joy by allowing us to learn that you are joined together in common love and concord, truly as brothers born of the same mother.

[Note: The ancient annals and historians are extremely obscure concerning the disputes of the Frankish kings and their origin. Nevertheless, the denial of aid to Charles when he went to keep the Vascones and Aquitanians in submission, and the fact that he met his brother on the march because of this matter, seem to have been involved. See the Annals of the Franks of Angoulême and other authors in Pagi, A.D. 779, no. 5. Mabillon above all is to be heard on this matter (Annals, book XXIV, no. 28). From these letters we understand that the pontiff and the Romans knew everything and had obtained by continual prayers to God the concord of those princes, which was very necessary for the holy see against the Lombards. — Cenn.]

Therefore, most excellent sons, great and most victorious kings and, by God’s providence, our patricians of the Romans, your most faithful and diligent envoys, namely the most reverend and holy brother of ours Gauzibert, bishop,

[Note: Mabillon thinks that Gauzibert, the leader of this embassy, was bishop of Chartres (Annals, book XXIV, no. 30). Both he and others are silent concerning the rest, except that Cointius makes Fuchbert a monk.]

and the religious Fuchbert, together with Ansfred and Helmgarius, your most glorious men, brought us your honorable and exceedingly desirable words, sent by the royal power instituted by God. Through them you made known to us that disputes and litigation had arisen between you, but that, with the Lord’s consent, you now appear to have turned toward true love, concord in unity, and fraternal affection.

When we heard this, we were filled with great joy and gladness, together with all our people of this province redeemed by you. We celebrated the double joys of a festival, offering immense thanks to our almighty God and praising his victorious clemency, singing and saying with one voice, in prophetic language: “Blessed are you, Lord our God, and blessed are all your works.” For now our God rejoices in heaven, the entire chorus of angels rejoices, and on earth also the whole Christian people exults; only the devil, the enemy of peace and sower of discord, mourns when he sees that he has been defeated and overcome.

The minds of the faithful could not have expected any other outcome than what we now rejoice has taken place, if almighty God multiplies among you that peace and fraternal love which he gave to his holy apostles and strengthens it once multiplied. Therefore your unity is also celebrated by your holy spiritual mother, the Church of God, and by all her people.

[Col. 0251A]

For indeed your very letters reported that you would strive with all your strength to demand the rights of your protector, blessed Peter, and of the holy Church of God; that you had promised to remain faithful to the pledge of love which your pious father, of holy memory, Lord Pippin, made to the same prince of the apostles and to his vicars; and that you would bring about the full rights and exaltation of the holy Church of God. And indeed, most excellent sons, most Christian and mighty kings, we are entirely certain and fully satisfied that no human persuasion or lavish gift of treasures will be able to turn you aside or in any way alter that promise of yours which you pledged to blessed Peter.

[Note: This recalls the diploma of Pippin’s donation, to which both had subscribed at Quierzy in the year 754; the matter is made entirely clear shortly afterward. — Cenn.]

Nevertheless, we have now tested your steadfastness, since you have taken care to please not a corruptible and frail man,

[Note: Namely Desiderius, who left no stone unturned in attempting to separate the Frankish kings from the holy see. — Id.]

but almighty God and the prince of his apostles.

Accordingly, we earnestly ask you, as though present in person, and adjure your excellence before the living God, who commanded you to reign, to order the full rights of blessed Peter to be demanded with the utmost speed, according to the capitulary which we have sent to you through your present most faithful envoys, and to order them to be returned to blessed Peter. May you also deign to fulfill all that you promised to blessed Peter and to his vicars together with your father, of holy memory,

[Note: The Lambach manuscript reads “pious father.”]

so that, through the intercession of that same prince of the apostles, you may receive from almighty God perfect reward in the present life and in future blessedness.

[Note: Idem adds “reward.”]

After God, we place our confidence in ourselves [Idem: “in you”], and in your love and charitable affection we firmly remain and shall remain, even unto our soul and the shedding of our blood, together with all our people. Nevertheless, concerning this matter and all the aforesaid rights of blessed Peter, we have spoken more fully with your envoys, so that everything may be recounted to your royal majesty. And now, just as thirsty earth awaits rain, so we ask for your aid and the fitting fulfillment of our requests.

And see, most excellent sons, that we adjure you by the fearful day of judgment. Blessed Peter also exhorts and adjures you through us to order the rights of that same prince of the apostles to be demanded from the Lombards with the utmost speed, forcefully constraining them by the power of God, so that the prince of the apostles himself and the holy Roman Church may receive what belongs to them.

[Note: Lambach reads: “so that the Roman Church and the commonwealth may receive them.” Gentianus reads: “so that the Roman commonwealth Church may receive them,” and notes that the word “commonwealth” has been deleted by a line drawn beneath it.]

For if—which we do not believe—you neglect or delay demanding those rights, know that you will have to render a strict account of these matters before the tribunal of Christ to that same prince of the apostles.

But if anyone should tell you that we have received the rights of blessed Peter, do not believe him in any way.

[Note: Could anything be clearer? He entrusts more to the envoys in private, but publicly testifies that the rights have not been restored to Saint Peter; he says that no one is to be believed who says otherwise. — Cenn.]

May almighty God protect you with his right hand, grant you victory from heaven, send his angel before your face to go before you and cast your enemies down before your feet, enlarge the boundaries of your kingdom instituted by God, and allow you to enjoy the government of your present kingdom for a long and prosperous time. After the long duration of this life, may he also grant you heavenly kingdoms to possess for endless ages.

## XLIX. 278. Also a Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Carloman

Containing expressions of thanks and a request that he might be found worthy to receive the king’s son from the sacred baptismal font.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 2): “He wrote another letter to Carloman, asking that he be permitted to become his son’s godfather and witness at the baptism.”]

*(A.D. 770, Codex Carolinus XLVIII, chronicle 48.)*

### Summary

Abbot Beraldus and the illustrious man Aubertus, envoys of Carloman, brought this letter and reported many matters in private, to each of which he replied in the same manner. In the letter he says that he ardently desires to be allowed to receive the recently born royal son from the sacred font. He wishes every prosperity for the child, the queen his wife, and their sons.

To the most excellent lord, his son Carloman, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Pope Stephen.

[Note: A summary is given by Baronius and the Centuriators. — Grets.]

Since our almighty Creator and Lord has deigned to pour such grace of pious consideration and effective diligence into your honey-sweet royal heart for the defense and exaltation of his holy Church, most excellent son and most gracious king, therefore the illustrious memory of your most renowned name and the wisdom bestowed upon you from heaven remain celebrated throughout the whole world, and the worthy merits of your works shine in the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore you are blessed, good and most Christian king. For, having recognized the steadfastness of your faith, which you are known to possess in apostolic affairs and in the fervor of your love for us, we remain firm in our affection for you and diligently continue to pour out prayers to our Creator on account of your immense joy and the stability of your kingdom instituted by God.

Meanwhile, the religious Beraldus, abbot, and the illustrious man Audbertus came to us and brought the honorable and exceedingly desirable words of your excellence, protected by God. We received and reread them with great honor and affection and fully understood what they contained. Your most faithful envoys themselves also reported to us in detail what your God-protected excellence had entrusted to them. As to each matter, we gave your faithful men a response for them to report clearly to your majesty, inspired by God.

But because the fervor of your love burns firmly within our heart, a great longing presses upon us, most excellent of kings: namely, that the affection of spiritual kinship may arise between us through the grace of the Holy Spirit. For this reason we earnestly ask your Christianity, good king instituted by God and most excellent son, that from your illustrious and royal offspring,

[Note: The Annalist of Pépin records the birth of Pippin, the son of Carloman, in this year. Pagi, A.D. 770, no. 4.]

which the Lord has deigned to grant you for the exaltation of his holy Church, we may be able to receive your son into our arms from the font of sacred baptism, or even through the spiritual anointing of the venerable chrism. Thus, with the grace of spiritual kinship strengthened among us by God’s favor, both we and all our people may be relieved and rejoice together in the Lord with great gladness.

May almighty God, through whom kings reign and princes rule, protect you by his grace, grant you victory from heaven for the defense of his holy Church, and allow you, together with your most excellent and Christian daughter, our queen and your sweetest wife,

[Note: Gilberga, whom Carloman had married while his father Pippin was still alive. When Carloman died toward the end of the following year and Charles again united both kingdoms into one, as they had been under Pippin, his father, she fled to Italy to Desiderius with her two young sons. See the Annals of Fulda and others in Pagi, A.D. 771, no. 5. The Frankish Annals are silent concerning the sons: “But Carloman’s wife,” they say, “went with a few Franks to the regions of Italy.”]

and your most beloved children,

[Note: Pippin, therefore, was not the firstborn; Carloman had previously had another son. These are the children whom Gilberga took with her to Italy. Nothing about them is found in the Frankish writers. But in the Life of Adrian in Anastasius (section 310) we read that in the year 773, while Desiderius was being besieged by Charles at Pavia, “Adalgisus, his true son, taking with him Autcharius the Frank, and the wife and sons of the aforesaid Carloman, entered the city called Verona, because it seemed to be the strongest of all the cities of the Lombards.” Again (section 314), when Charles went to Verona, “as soon as he had arrived there, Autcharius, and the wife and sons of the aforementioned Carloman, of their own will surrendered themselves to that most gracious King Charles. His excellence received them and returned to Pavia.”

Earlier, mention had been made of Gilberga taking refuge with Desiderius together with her sons, and of the Lombard’s deceitful strategy by which he tried to sow discord between the pontiff and Charles: “In those days it happened that the wife and sons of the former King Carloman of the Franks fled to the same Lombard king with Autcharius. Desiderius strove eagerly and zealously to arrange that the sons of the aforementioned Carloman should assume the Frankish kingdom. For this very reason he attempted to lure the most holy pontiff to come to him, so that he might anoint the sons of the aforementioned Carloman as kings, wishing to introduce division into the Frankish kingdom, to separate the most blessed pontiff from the charity and love of the most excellent Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, and to subjugate Rome and all Italy to the power of his Lombard kingdom” (section 296).

There it is also related how the Lombard contrived these schemes with the assistance and cooperation of Paul Afiarta, who was serving as the pontiff’s ambassador to him. While Paul was absent from Rome, the killer of Sergius the Blind was discovered. Therefore the pontiff, fearing that the discovered crime might reach Desiderius’s ears and that, with Desiderius’s help—at whose court Paul had great influence—Paul might bring harm upon the papal jurisdiction, secretly arranged for Paul to be seized on his return. Thus Desiderius’s schemes were dispersed.

This is certainly the history which the writer of Adrian’s Life related with the greatest fidelity. Certain recent writers, led by Muratori, distort it: they exaggerate Gilberga’s flight on the grounds that Charles deprived his nephews of the kingdom, and fail entirely to observe that such a flight to the king of Italy, the perpetual enemy of the holy see—which was the chief concern of the Frankish kings—makes Gilberga’s cause worse, even though they undertake to defend her as if she had been abandoned, than Charles’s cause when he restored both kingdoms to a single monarchy, as they had been three years earlier.

But let these matters be set aside. These recent writers wander in their treatment of the ancient affairs of Francia. Comparing their own age with that ancient one, they do not hesitate to brand Charles not only with injustice but also with wickedness, and they are not restrained from such empty assertions by the silence of all the ancient writers. They ought instead to have consulted the charters concerning the division of the kingdoms, both that of Charles and that of Louis the Pious, between their sons. They would certainly have seen that, when one of the sons died first, the portion of the kingdom left to him was to be divided among the surviving brothers, with this condition added:

“But if such a son should be born to any one of these three brothers whom the people might wish to elect to succeed his father in the inheritance of the kingdom, we wish his uncles to consent to this and to permit their brother’s son to reign in the portion of the kingdom which his father, their brother, had possessed.”

—From the Pithoean edition, part II, p. 84.

Louis the Pious established the same arrangement in almost the same words, and then added:

“But if he should not have such a son, then we wish that the portion of the kingdom which he possessed be divided equally among those brothers who have survived.”

—Ibid., p. 149.

Such was the law by which Francia was then governed. While the monarchy, divided among several brothers, produced several kingdoms, when one of them died his kingdom was divided among the brothers. It was not enough for the dead king’s son to exist for succession to occur; the people’s election was necessary, and the uncle or uncles were bound to give their assent.

The situation after Carloman’s death was different. For the archbishops, bishops, counts, and leading men of the dead king, leaving Carloman’s children aside, approached Charles and acclaimed him as their king. Thus says the monk of Angoulême; thus all the Frankish annalists unanimously affirm. Einhard, in *The Life and Deeds of Charles the Great*, chapter 6, calls Carloman Charles’s partner in the kingdom: “His partner in the kingdom,” he says, “having now been removed from human affairs.”

Therefore these recent writers, speaking such things against so great and pious a king, are mistaken. While defending King Desiderius with all their strength, they obscure the truth.]

and grant you the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom to possess.

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

L. 281 **Also, a letter of the same pope, addressed to the lords King Charles and King Carloman, prohibiting and binding them by exceedingly strong adjurations from taking wives from the nation of the Lombards**

[Note: [Col. 0255C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 6). Baronius (year 772, no. 2) reproduces the summaries of the preceding letters from Panvinio’s Vatican Codex, as I myself have given them, disregarding the variant readings, since they are of little importance. The summary of this letter is absent in Baronius, since he reports it in full (year 770, no. 9 ff.). The Magdeburg Centuriators do likewise, though they do not omit the summary, which in them and in Panvinio is as follows (in the cited place): “Also another letter to Charles and Carloman, in which he earnestly strives with hands and feet to dissuade them from marrying a wife from the Lombard nation, or from giving their sister Gisla in marriage to Desiderius’s son.” They claim to reproduce the letter in full because it is full of papal contrivances. I am ashamed to read similar statements in the most recent writer (Zanetti, *History of the Lombards*, p. 670 ff.). For Muratori, whom he follows, suspects that someone else was the author of this letter and does not repeatedly use expressions that disparage the dignity of the pope. CENN.]

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Baronius, in the year 770, and the Centuriators, *Century* 8, chapter 10, reproduce this letter in full, saying that it is full of papal contrivances. But is it fraud or trickery to dissuade kings, already betrothed to others, from taking other wives contrary to their pledged faith? For this was above all the reason why Stephen opposed this marriage with the Lombard nation with such force of argument, as is clear from the letter itself, and as Baronius also rightly observed. Although the pope had other reasons as well for dissuading them from this marriage. GRETS.]

(Year of Our Lord 770, Codex Carolinus XLV, chronicle 49.)

[Col. 0255A]

**SUMMARY.**—He sends to the kings Charles and Carloman his messengers, the priest Peter and the defensor Pamphilus, with apostolic letters of exhortation, which he had previously placed at the confession of Saint Peter and had there consecrated, so that whoever acted against them would be anathema. Their substance is that he has heard that the daughter of Desiderius is to be married to one of them, although each is already joined in lawful marriage by their father’s will. To this most powerful argument he adds others: first, against the Lombard nation, against which, carried away by zeal, he perhaps inveighs more strongly than is fitting; then, examples from their ancestors, since their father, at the admonition of Stephen II, refrained from divorcing their mother and refused to give their sister Gisla as wife to the son of the Emperor Constantine; third, their promises, confirmed by oath even after their father’s death, through Sergius the nomenclator—namely, that they would remain faithful to blessed Peter and the pope and would never join his adversaries; finally, the consequences that marriage with the perpetual enemies of the Holy See would necessarily entail, namely the destruction of ecclesiastical dominion. Afterwards, in the name of Saint Peter and of the entire Roman clergy and people, he implores them not to divorce their wives in order to marry Desiderius’s daughter, nor to join Gisla to Desiderius’s son, but rather to compel that king to return to the Holy See what, though repeatedly promised, he had never restored.

To the most excellent lords, sons, Charles and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, Stephen, pope.

When we call to mind the outstanding life and worthy merits of all God’s elect, we find, assuredly, that no difference of circumstance has been able to move them away from the state of their hearts or from the steadfastness of their former pledge. Thus, although surrounded by the various persuasions and flatteries of the ancient enemy, they plainly remained unshaken in the firmness of their minds and, because of this, deserved to attain their desired joys with the triumph of victory. And indeed we must consider that if someone, beguiled by certain persuasions, should be overcome, he must immediately strive to return from the straight path that leads to eternal life, turning aside through precipitous byways, lest he thereby slip into ever deeper guilt. For it is generally certain that the same ancient enemy tries, through weakness of nature, to steal upon the minds of the faithful. Hence it was that, long ago, when the first man had been placed in paradise, through the weakness of the woman’s nature he was able, by his poisonous flatteries, to persuade him to transgress the divine command; and for this reason the destruction of dreadful death entered upon the human race. Therefore, most excellent sons, great kings, the more diligently must you resist that same effort, the more often we see him lying in wait to deceive the hearts of the faithful by his schemes.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] This opening makes it clear to a serious reader that the pope was persuaded that both kings, bound by the bond of lawful marriage, were being assailed by the devil’s suggestions so that they might take a new wife.]

[Col. 0256B] Accordingly, it has come to our knowledge—a matter that we certainly relate with great anguish of heart—that Desiderius, king of the Lombards, is evidently persuading your excellency to join his daughter in marriage to one of your brotherhood. If this is indeed so, it is a wholly diabolical instigation and appears to be not so much a marital union as an alliance in the most wicked invention. For we have learned, as the history of divine Scripture teaches us, that many have deviated from God’s commandments through an unlawful union with a foreign people [Note: [Col. 0256D] Baronius reads “of a foreign nation.” I affirm that the reading of the Codex should be retained, with *alie nationis* written for *alius*, in accordance with the linguistic usage of that age, common in these letters.], and have fallen into great crime. For what sort of folly is this, most excellent sons, great kings—indeed, can it even be said—that your glorious Frankish nation, which shines above all nations, and the exceedingly splendid and noble offspring of your royal power, should, God forbid, be polluted by the treacherous [Note: [Col. 0256D] Excessive aversion to the Lombards, who constantly harassed the Church, and excessive partiality toward the Franks impelled the pope to make this comparison; our writers despise it without taking account of the character of those times and people. CENN.] and most foul nation of the Lombards, which is in no way counted among the number of nations and from whose stock it is certain that a race of lepers arises? No one who possesses a sound mind can suspect that such renowned kings could become entangled in so detestable and abominable a contagion. For what fellowship is there between light and darkness? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? (II Cor. VI.)

Indeed, most gentle and most kindly kings, established by God, you have already, by God’s will and design, been joined in lawful marriage at the command of your father, receiving, as illustrious and noble kings, from your own homeland—that is, from the very noble nation of the Franks—most beautiful wives; and you ought to remain attached to their love.

[Note: [Col. 0257C] It is established from the preceding material that Carloman contracted marriage with Gilberga and had two sons by her. Cointius also thinks that Charles had a wife, Himiltrude, and that she was legitimate. Mabillon, however (*Annals*, book XXIV, no. 34), influenced by the authority of Einhard and others, denies that she was legitimate. He is especially moved by the fragment of Paul Warnefrid concerning the bishops of Metz (Pithou’s edition, part II, p. 91), where he says: “By his wife Hildegard he fathered four sons and five daughters; yet before his lawful marriage he had by Himiltrude, a noble girl, a son named Pippin.” Certainly Stephen regarded the wives of both kings as legitimate, without distinction. For this reason he maintains that neither of them could be joined to the daughter of Desiderius. The *Annals of Fulda* report that Bertrada, the mother of the kings, brought from Italy a daughter of Desiderius to be married to Carloman; Andreas Duchesne considers the passage corrupt, as Pagi notes (year 770, no. 7). Nevertheless, shortly above the pope said “to one of your brotherhood.” This uncertainty as to which of them she would marry increasingly confirms that he was convinced both were joined in lawful marriage by their father’s will and that there was no place for another marriage. CENN.]

And certainly you may not, after dismissing them, take other wives or mingle yourselves through kinship with a foreign nation. For none of your ancestors—neither your grandfather nor your great-grandfather, nor even your father—took a wife from another kingdom or foreign nation. And who from your most noble lineage has ever deigned to contaminate or mingle himself with the dreadful nation of the Lombards, so that you are now being persuaded, God forbid, to be polluted by that same horrible people? Therefore no one who has taken a wife from a foreign nation has remained without guilt.

[Col. 0257B] Consider, I beg you, how many powerful men, of what stature, by foreign marriages turning away from God’s commands and following the will of wives of a foreign nation, became entangled in serious transgressions and endured immeasurable dangers. For it is impious even to allow it to rise fully into your hearts to take other wives in addition to those whom it is certain you first took.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Here is another, clearer argument for the legitimacy of both marriages. Nor does Einhard’s silence concerning Himiltrude weaken the pope’s authority, nor does Warnefrid’s uncertain assertion. For messengers arriving to and fro informed the pope about these matters, and we find that they were later committed to writing.]

It is not fitting for you to commit such a crime, since you keep God’s law and rebuke others lest they do such things. Pagan nations do this. But far be this from you, who are fully Christians, a holy nation, and a royal priesthood. Remember and consider that, anointed with holy oil by the hands of the vicar of blessed Peter, you have been sanctified by heavenly blessing, and you must take care not to become entangled in such great crimes.

Remember this, most excellent sons: our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of holy memory, adjured your father, whose memory is most excellent, never to presume to divorce your lady and mother, and he, as a truly most Christian king, obeyed his saving admonitions.

[Note: [Col. 0258C] Relying on the authority of Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXIII, no. 15, and *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 503), he relates, under about the year 755, the story of a certain Angla, the wife of Theodard, who was placed in charge of the monastery of Besançon. Pippin was passionately in love with this woman and was contemplating divorcing Queen Bertrada, but, admonished by Stephen II—perhaps while he was in Francia in 754—he came to his senses. Natalis Alexander relates the same matter from the *Besançon Chronicle* (*Eighth Century*, chapter 7, article 6) in these words: “Pippin is rebuked in the *Besançon Chronicle* because he wickedly loved Angla, Theodard’s wife, and kept her as his delight. Entangled in this love, he was considering divorcing Bertrada, but was recalled to better conduct by the salutary admonitions of Stephen, Roman pontiff. Angla likewise came to her senses, frightened by a miracle, etc.”]

For you must also remember this about your excellency: that you pledged yourselves to blessed Peter and to his aforesaid vicar, or to his successors, to be friends to our friends and enemies to our enemies, just as we too are known to remain steadfast in that same pledge.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] Nothing is more frequent in the preceding letters than such conditions of mutual friendship and alliance.]

And how are you now striving to act against your own souls and wishing to make an alliance with our enemies, when that perjured Lombard nation, continually attacking the Church of God and invading this Roman province of ours, is proved to be our enemy? Therefore I also ask that you carefully recall to your memory how, when the Emperor Constantine [Copronymus] was trying to persuade your father, of holy memory, your most gentle lord, to accept your noble sister Gisla in marriage to his son, he said that you might not join yourselves to another nation, nor in any way dare to act contrary to the will of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See. Why, then, are you now attempting to act contrary to the apostolic commands and the will of the vicar of the prince of the apostles, something your father never did? Do you not know that you despise not our unworthiness but blessed Peter, whose place, though unworthy, we occupy? For it is written (Matt. X; Luke X): “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me.”

Remember, I beg you, most excellent sons, how your aforesaid lord and father seemed to say to you in faith [Baronius: “faithfully to you”], promising on behalf of your souls to God, to blessed Peter, and to his aforesaid vicar, our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of holy memory, that you must steadfastly remain faithful to the Holy Church, obedient to all the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, and constant in unblemished charity. Afterwards, it is certain that you, together with that same father of yours, repeatedly made the same promise to our predecessor, the lord Pope Paul, through messengers and written documents. After the death of your aforesaid father, of holy memory, you yourselves repeatedly pledged to us, both through your own messengers and letters, and likewise through Sergius, our most faithful nomenclator, and through our other messengers, that you would remain, by your promise, as your father had done, steadfast in your faithfulness toward the holy Church of God and toward us.

[Note: [Col. 0259C] He alludes to the first letter, which I said had been lost in the *Admonition*. Its bearer was Sergius, at that time secondary and nomenclator, as the author of Stephen’s life in Anastasius testifies (section 275), and Stephen himself agrees here. It is worthy of notice that Sergius is called “our most faithful nomenclator,” which he was when he departed as leader of the embassy to Francia in the year 768. In the following year, when he had to endure Desiderius’s savagery, he held the office of secondary; and finally, in the year 770, when this letter was given, the wretch was living with the pope in the Lateran cellarium, his eyes having been gouged out by the agency of Paul Afiarta, and soon destined to lose his life as well after the pope’s death, at the hand of that same wicked Paul. Although he was the pope’s chamberlain, Paul was a pensioner and supporter of Desiderius against the Apostolic See. If, then, the pope himself calls Sergius “most faithful” in the year 770, who will place greater trust in Saxius, Muratori, and Mansi, who assert the integrity of the history of the letters I cited first (ep. 45, elsewhere 46), than in Cointius, Pagi, and Zacagno, who maintain that they were extorted by Desiderius through force and fear? In those letters that same Sergius, now called “most faithful,” is described as utterly wicked. See the *Admonition* to the letters of Stephen III. CENN.]

But I also ask that you recall to your memory how the aforesaid lord Pope Stephen, at his departure, endeavored, in writing and under a terrible adjuration, to exhort you to remain with firm constancy in your love for the holy Church of God and in unblemished charity toward the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, and to fulfill everything in accordance with the pledge you gave to that same apostle of God. And now, where is that promise of yours?

[Note: [Col. 0259D] This letter is missing among the letters of Stephen II. [Col. 0260C] Whether it perished through a Lombard plot or was lost by some other accident cannot be determined. We see only one letter of that pontiff, who survived until the end of April in the year 757, transmitted in the Codex after possession of the Exarchate had been delivered at the beginning of the year 756. From this, however, we can establish the content of the final letter that he sent to the Frankish kings. ID.]

O how great a labor that outstanding and most blessed pontiff endured! Though so weak, he exposed himself to the danger of so long a journey; and unless the Lord had been present, his labor would have come to nothing. That journey by which our predecessor then hastened to Francia has brought us great ruin, since our enemies are now raised to a more savage height of arrogance than before. And behold, we see occurring what we feared: our joy has been turned into mourning, the later evils have become worse than the former, and from the place where we expected light to arise, darkness has burst forth.

Therefore blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted by the Lord God and to whom the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was granted, solemnly adjures your excellency through our misery. We too, together with all the bishops, priests, and other clergy, and with all the nobles and the clergy of our holy Church, including the abbots and all religious persons devoted to divine worship, as well as the magistrates and judges and the entire Roman people of this province of ours, adjure you under the threat of divine judgment, by the living and true God, who is the judge of the living and the dead, by the ineffable power of his divine majesty, and by the dreadful day of the future judgment, when all princes and powers and the entire human race must stand in trembling; and also by all the divine mysteries and the most sacred body of blessed Peter: let no one from your brotherhood presume in any way to take the daughter of the aforementioned Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as his wife.

Nor again may your most noble sister, Gisla, beloved of God, be given to the son of the aforesaid Desiderius.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] Above I said (note e on col. 256) that in the year 764 Gisla was sought by the Greek emperor for his son Leo (IV), for whom he obtained a wife from elsewhere that year: “Finally, in the eighth indiction, Constantine summoned Irene from Greece as a wife for his son Leo.” Thus Pagi, from Nicephorus’s *Breviarium* (year 769, no. 3). At the same time Desiderius was negotiating with Bertrada for Gisla’s marriage to Adalgis, but without success. For she entered a convent and later became abbess of Caen. Consult Mabillon, *Annals*, in several places, where he discusses her at length. ID.]

Nor may you in any way dare to dismiss your wives. [Note: [Col. 0260D] From notes a and b on col. 257 it is clear that both kings had wives; only now, for the third time, does the pope insist that it is wicked for either to dismiss his own. ID.]

Rather, remembering what you promised to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, resist those same enemies of ours, the Lombards, like men, compelling them firmly to return what belongs to the holy Church of God and to the Roman commonwealth. For, transgressing everything they promised you, they do not cease daily to afflict and oppress us; nor are they at all inclined to return anything to us. They are also known to invade our borders and merely pretend, in the presence of your messengers, to render us justice by means of a stratagem. For nothing is brought to completion, and we have been unable to receive from them any of our rights at all.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] How does this agree with what is read in the first letter of this pope (45, elsewhere 46)? Namely: “We have received all the rights of blessed Peter from him [Desiderius], fully and in their entirety.” Let the defenders of that letter seriously consider this. ID.]

Therefore, so that all our sufferings may be carefully reported to your ears, we have sent our messengers, namely our beloved son Peter, priest, and Pamphilus, the regional defensor of our holy Church. We have thoroughly informed them both about the tribulation threatening us and about each of the matters that must be reported to your royal highness. We ask that you deign to receive them with your customary kindness, to lend your God-inspired ears to our petition, and to command that the most ample liberation and exaltation of the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, and the defense of this province redeemed by you be accomplished, so that you may receive a perfect reward from our just Judge, God, through the intercession of his prince of the apostles, blessed Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0261A] Let the recent writers who persuade me that Charles, moved by reverence for his mother, disregarded this admonition of Stephen—indeed, this warning, fearful in so many respects—demonstrate that it reached Charles’s hands before the marriage. Papebrochius, in the *Life of Hildegard*, says that Desiderius’s daughter was sent back by Charles untouched and that, in the following year, 771, at the end of which he married Hildegard, she was returned. Could it not therefore have happened that those fruitless nuptials were dissolved without contempt for the pope’s admonition? See Pagi (year 771, no. 2).]

Accordingly, placing this present exhortation and adjuration of ours at the confession of blessed Peter, offering sacrifice and victims upon it to our God, we have sent it to you with tears from that same sacred confession. If anyone, which we do not desire, should presume to act against the tenor of this our adjuration, let him know that, by the authority of my lord blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and assigned to be burned with the devil, his most atrocious pomp, and the other impious beings in eternal fires. But whoever proves to be an observer and guardian of this exhortation of ours may deserve, illumined by heavenly blessings from the Lord our God, to become a participant in the eternal joys of reward with all God’s saints and elect.

[Note: [Col. 0262A] Some allowance must be made for that age. There is no shortage of ancient documents issued even by lay princes with clauses of this sort, though more vehement. [Col. 0262B]]

May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

289 **PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY ON THE FORTY-NINE LETTERS OF ADRIAN**

[Col. 0261]

[Col. 0261B] **1.** The two matters that chiefly had to be considered in these papal letters—the supreme freedom of the Roman pontiff’s appointment and the free dominion of the Holy See in the City and its duchy—are, unless I am mistaken, evident from what has so far been presented. They will nevertheless become even clearer from what follows.

Moreover, in Adrian’s letters there remain documents concerning the new territory, namely the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, whose possession had always been weak and precarious before the Lombard kings were expelled, but which was then supported by a strong and stable foundation and greatly enlarged by immense additions on every side.

From some of these letters (ep. 70, 78, 82, elsewhere 96, 72, 97), a clearer knowledge will also be supplied of the collection of canons that the Holy See began to use in the eighth century, a collection different from the Dionysian one, than can be obtained from the decretal letter of Zacharias (ep. 3, elsewhere 5).

Finally—and this was especially desirable—some means of resolving the nearly innumerable questions raised by the scholars of the departing and declining century, particularly against the diploma of Louis the Pious, will be provided. For that reason, before discussing the letters, I shall say something about the consecration of the Roman pontiff, dominion over the City and the Roman duchy, the enlargement of ecclesiastical territory, and the Roman collection of canons, in opposition to the principal opinions of certain recent writers—opinions produced either by blind faith in authors of great name who flourished in an earlier age, or by excessive partiality, perhaps even by arbitrary interpretation of ancient charters.

Although these several topics will be related to the same letters, indeed, it will become clear that they arose from them, since I shall employ the very statements Adrian used when instructing King Charles. I shall begin with the consecration.

**II.** The eight-day interval between pontificates sufficiently and more than sufficiently proves the canonical freedom of the Roman pontiff’s consecration. Nevertheless, through the gracious favor of the best God, Adrian’s election and consecration have come down to us, and it would be wrong to pass them over.

Scholars know how many procedures were required before Gregory III after an election so that the pontiff might be consecrated: one report of the election to the emperor, another to the exarch, another to the archbishop of Ravenna, another to the judges of Ravenna, and finally another to the apocrisiarius of Ravenna—all full of humble petitions that the canonical election might be confirmed. For there was no other way to proceed to consecration (*Liber Diurnus*, chapter 2, title 3 ff.).

Adrian’s ordination was different, as may be seen in Mabillon [Col. 0262B] (*Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part II, p. 38). For immediately after the decree of election, somewhat different from what survives in the *Liber Diurnus* and filled with solecisms for that age, the following is found: “The election is concluded. The venerable Adrian himself, at the beginning of his ordination, composed the following statement of right faith: I, Adrian, etc.,” as in the *Liber Diurnus*.

The statement is followed by a profession of faith committed to writing and by another profession, or address; these too are found in the *Liber Diurnus* with some variation. They remained in use throughout the eighth and ninth centuries and part of the following century.

This kind of free ordination became customary in the Holy See after Gregory III among the successors whom I listed in the note to the letters of the antipope Constantine; I did not omit the ordination of Leo III, about which there can be no doubt that it was of this kind. Whether anything was changed after Charles had obtained the imperial crown from Leo himself must be investigated, as I have already said, when discussion is undertaken of the diploma of Louis the Pious.

**III.** I must not pass over in silence that the document from which I extracted Adrian’s ordination is of the same character as that little work of John the Deacon, which I said had been pieced together from various fragments of antiquity. Mabillon testifies that he saw two copies of it in two very ancient codices of the once-famous monastery of Nonantula, and another in Rome.

[Col. 0262D] That, however, is not enough to remove the taint of forgery from the document. For the author, a monk—whoever he may have been—intending to add Adrian I to the catalogue of saints of his monastery, whom the people of Modena began to venerate on 8 July, made one figure out of Adrian I and Adrian III. Thus he transmitted to later generations the ancient but false tradition, as Pagi says (year 885, no. 2), that Adrian I was buried there. The Bollandists also note this (under 8 July).

Nor is any scholar today persuaded that anyone other than Adrian III was buried at Nonantula. For, having been invited to Worms by Charles the Bald in the aforesaid year 885—while Charles was considering, by papal authority, deposing certain bishops and establishing Bernard, his son by a concubine, as heir to the kingdom—Adrian died on the journey, as the Lambecian *Annals* report (*Italian Historians*, vol. II, part II, p. 95). “Thus,” say the *Annals*, “the king’s fraudulent plans were dispersed by God’s will. For the Roman pontiff, having departed from the City and crossed the river Eridanus, ended his present life; and he was buried in the monastery of Nonantula.”

In Anastasius the place itself is indicated: “On the river Scultenna (the Panaro), in a village called Viulzachara” (section 642). Muratori discovered that this village is now called San Cesario, and that nearby, in the territory of Modena, lies the village of Spilamberto, where Adrian III is said to have died:

“He ended his life in the place called Spinum Lamberti on 8 July, and was honorably carried to and buried in the church and monastery of blessed Silvester, which is called Nonantula.”

After this he proceeds to relate the deeds of Adrian I, confusing Charlemagne with Charles the Bald, and completes the history of two kings and two pontiffs.

**IV.** This kind of writing, so harmful to posterity, must rightly be condemned and wholly rejected. But if documents are inserted whose reliability can be established intact from another source, they ought to be accepted; this is what I now do in order to demonstrate the freedom of consecration during those times.

The fact that ordination, or consecration, was customarily carried out immediately after the decree of election is supported by the statement that was issued at the beginning of the ordination, as is clear from Anastasius (section 587), against John, archbishop of Ravenna:

“Nor is it surprising,” he says, “that he acted thus afterward, since he falsified the securities and statements that the archbishops of Ravenna customarily had made in the archive at the beginning of their consecration, following the practice of his predecessor Felix.”

The formulas themselves, preserved in the *Liber Diurnus*, show that the same procedure was then followed both in the election of bishops and in the ordination of pontiffs. There was, however, this difference: papal consecration was completed between the *Kyrie eleison* and the *Gloria in excelsis*; episcopal consecration was not.

Accordingly, Gratian has the following (*Cap. Quod sicut*, *On Election*, § “Super eo”):

“Since only the Roman pontiff, who is consecrated before the angelic hymn and afterward, once consecrated, himself begins and completes the solemn celebration of Mass, is able to celebrate ordinations on the day of his consecration.”

It is certain, moreover, that both the statement and the two professions that followed fell into disuse, and that in their place a formula began to be used, which Garnerius compares with the statement mentioned above (*Liber Diurnus*, p. 26). Its opening is: “I, N., deacon, or priest, or cardinal bishop-elect of the Holy Roman Church,” together with the college of the co-apostle Paul. Both features must be dated no earlier than the ninth century.

For the first election of a Roman pontiff from among the bishops took place in the year 891, contrary to the discipline of the Apostolic See, when Formosus, bishop of Porto, was forcibly removed from his own church and raised to the chair of Peter. The gruesome deposition of his corpse subsequently struck terror into the others, lest anyone from the episcopal order be elevated there.

The college of Paul, meanwhile, was introduced at about the same time, although it seems that consideration was given more to doctrine than to authority. For Paul, the chosen vessel, chosen by Christ the Lord and distinguished by the title “teacher of the nations,” was made Peter’s associate of supreme authority, but this is confirmed neither by tradition, Scripture, nor the testimonies of the Fathers.

**V.** It will not be irrelevant to compare the celebrated profession found in Ivo, Gratian, Antonius Augustinus, and Baronius—specifically the modest portion in which Paul is introduced—with the statement that was in use during the ninth century.

The statement runs as follows:

“I shall guard with all my efforts, even unto soul and blood, and with your help patiently endure the difficulties of the times, this uprightness of true faith which, through Christ the author and giver, transmitted through your successors and disciples even to my lowliness, I found in your holy Church.”

The profession, whose date Garnerius incorrectly assigns to the ninth century, gives the same passage in this form:

“But I shall guard with all my efforts, even unto blood, the uprightness of true faith which, through you, Christ the author and giver, and through your most blessed co-apostle Paul, and through your disciples and successors, has been transmitted even to my lowliness, and which I found in your holy Church.”

There are certainly other differences between the statement and the profession. The most noteworthy, however, seems to be that whereas the statement approves only six general councils, the profession also accepts the eighth, which was held at Constantinople under Adrian II in the year 869.

This circumstance vindicates for the profession a later age than for the statement existing in the aforesaid compilation, so that all doubt is removed that in the year 772, when Adrian was being consecrated Roman pontiff, he was freely ordained immediately after the decree.

**VI.** Hence the decree of Saint Zacharias’s election was not sent to the exarch; nor, after the Exarchate had been extinguished, was that of Stephen II sent to the emperor; nor was confirmation of the decree sought from Ravenna or Constantinople for Paul, Stephen’s brother, who before his ordination—delayed by the schism—was striving to secure the friendship and alliance of the Franks and sent messengers and letters to Pippin concerning his brother’s death and his own election; nor for the usurper Constantine, who, after carrying out a sacrilegious consecration, likewise wrote to Pippin; nor, finally, for Stephen III, succeeded by Adrian, or for Adrian’s successor Leo III, throughout the sixty years of the eighth century.

Stephen himself enacted in the council mentioned in the *Admonition* to his letters that the decree itself should in no way be altered. Its words are very clear:

“And thus, customarily making the decree, and all agreeing together in it, they must subscribe.”

He adds what must be given the greatest attention:

“This, therefore, we decree under the threat of divine judgment must be observed also in the other churches.”

Therefore Adrian, showing King Charles (ep. 93, elsewhere 71) that he had no role in the election of the archbishop of Ravenna, in opposition to the confused notions of certain people, says:

“They came to our Apostolic See with joy, their own bishop to be consecrated, the decree having been confirmed by the subscriptions of all hands, just as has now also been done canonically.”

Thus far concerning the consecration, from reliable documents existing in the Nonantulan compilation.

VII. From what has been said concerning the Roman pontiff’s complete freedom of administration, an equally complete freedom of rule by the Holy See in the City and its duchy is also demonstrated. For if all obedience to the exarch, so long as the exarchate existed, and afterward to the prince, ceased, then the Romans had no dependence upon the empire, and the administration of Roman territory lay with the pontiff and the Romans. Nevertheless, Adrian’s letters testify to this rule so clearly that no inferences are needed to establish the point.

We have already seen that, at the very beginning of King Pippin’s patriciate, and in the donation charter by which he granted the Exarchate and the Pentapolis—before Stephen II took possession of the cities—the pontiff complained that the Lombards had invaded certain of “our cities” in the Roman province (Ep. 8, formerly 4). [Col. 0264D] His successors likewise, whenever they speak of any of these cities, call them “ours.” Adrian’s letters provide many examples of this kind. He calls “this our Roman city” (Ep. 57, formerly 59) the seat of royal priesthood; and he calls one of the Tuscan cities of Lombardia, which Charles had donated, “our city of the fortress of Felicity” (Ep. 55, formerly 40). He vindicates “our Romans” from calumny and says that he had ordered the ships of the Greek people to be burned in the harbor of “our city of Centumcellae,” since they were hostile to the shores (Ep. 63, formerly 65). He uses precisely the same designation for possessions situated in our territories, and calls those territories “ours,” when he speaks of the Exarchate (Ep. 83, formerly 84), which places and possessions he also calls those of the Roman duchy.

Moreover, he speaks of ecclesiastical jurisdiction in the same terms in which he speaks of Charles’s very extensive jurisdiction; for he calls the regions of both dominions alike “your boundaries,” “your territories,” “our boundaries,” and “our territories” (Ep. 84, formerly 91). The conclusion is that the pontiffs ruled with equal authority in the City and its duchy [Col. 0265A], and in the Exarchate and Pentapolis. The letters we are examining provide the most abundant evidence for this. The only difference between the origins of the two jurisdictions is that the Roman jurisdiction is about twenty-five years older than the other [p. 294]. Their titles of possession also differ: Rome and its duchy came under the pontiff’s jurisdiction by the will of the peoples, whereas the Exarchate and Pentapolis came to him by donation.

VIII. Adrian clearly distinguishes the two jurisdictions by the term “patriciate.” He calls Charles the patrician of Rome, but Saint Peter the patrician of the Exarchate and Pentapolis (Ep. 97, formerly 85). I shall give the words themselves:

“The honor of your patriciate,” he says, “is inviolably preserved by us, and is also honored with still greater honor. In the same way, may the patriciate of blessed Peter, your protector, which was wholly granted in writing by our father, the lord Pippin, of holy memory, the great king, and confirmed still more by you, remain by inviolable right.”

What Adrian intends by this comparison of patriciates is self-evident. [Col. 0265B] Since Peter dwells in heaven, he could be nothing other than the protector or defender of his successor in the administration of the provinces. That Charles was such a protector at Rome and in its duchy could be demonstrated by an immense series of unimpeachable witnesses; [Col. 0265C] two examples cited by Ducange in his Glossary will suffice (under “Patricius”).

In Capitularies 1, from the year 769, and at Aachen in 789, Charles is called “king and ruler of the kingdom and of the Franks, and devoted defender of the holy Church, and helper in all things of the apostolic see.” Hugh of Flavigny, in his Chronicle, p. 223, writes:

“The king, the son of the emperor, who did not carry the sword without cause, who ought to be patrician, guardian, and defender of the Roman state, should not have allowed so great a trampling underfoot of the Church of God.”

Accordingly, in the letter just mentioned, the pontiff demands from Charles toward the patriciate of Saint Peter the same honor with which he himself treated Charles’s patriciate. He then continues:

“For just as we, always receiving your men, admonish them to remain in your service with all their strength, in true faith and purity of heart, so also you, in the same way, whenever any of our men come to you,” and so forth.

For he says that Charles must preserve toward the prince of the apostles, the guardian and defender of Pippin’s donation confirmed by Charles, the same complete faith and benevolence that he himself preserved toward Charles, the guardian and defender of the apostolic see. Paul I plainly calls Charles “the guardian of the Church” (Ep. 27, formerly 37), and I have shown in the notes to these letters that elsewhere he is repeatedly called its protector and defender.

IX. If Charles ever attempted to claim some right for himself on account of the honor of his patriciate, as had been suggested to him [p. 295] by adversaries of the apostolic see, the pontiff gently resisted and did not permit him to exceed the boundaries of the patriciate. An example appears in the same letters of Adrian (93, formerly 71). It had been suggested that the archbishop of Ravenna ought to be elected in the presence of a royal representative.

The pontiff denies this. As regards the honor of the patriciate, he says:

[Col. 0265D] “No man in the world seems to strive more zealously for the exaltation of your royal excellence than our continual apostolic prayer. And just as, with all the efforts of our heart, we have everywhere honored and do honor to you above all others, so we desire more and more that the honor of your kingdom should surpass that of all who are known to exist in the world. Nevertheless, the benevolence that we bear toward your lofty dignity has become known throughout the world, as is plainly evident to all, because day and night we do not cease to pour forth prayers in the confession of your protector, blessed Peter.”

Many other passages of this kind occur both in the letters of Adrian and in those of his predecessors. It is therefore clear that the patriciate, elsewhere called “your royal protection” (Ep. 83, formerly 84), consisted in defending the Holy See in hope of a heavenly reward—which seems insignificant to certain learned men of our own age outside Italy, who think only of earthly things—and in seeking victory in this world over its adversaries through the assistance of the prince of the holy apostles, by the pontiff’s and the Romans’ continual public prayers before his shrine. [Col. 0266A] I find that, moved by this one hope, the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles greatly extended the jurisdiction of the apostolic see far and wide; but nowhere is it recorded that they claimed or reserved any part of the dominion for themselves, except in the duchies of Spoleto and Tuscany.

X. Since Gregory III is said to have conferred this kind of patriciate upon Charles Martel, and Stephen II certainly conferred it upon Pippin and his sons in the year 754, the pontiff therefore ruled at Rome from that time onward, since he entrusted its defense to the Frankish kings. I say defense, not dominion: that right belonged to the emperors, and the very ceremony by which patricians were created by the emperor removes this kind of patriciate from Stephen II, who was the first of all to distinguish the Frankish kings by that name.

Nor must we look far for a parallel. The Carolingian Book itself supplies a clear example (Ep. 91, formerly 88), namely that of Arichis, duke of Benevento, who hoped to obtain that dignity from the emperor, although death forestalled him and left the Greeks with their deceptive expectation. The emperor therefore

[Col. 0266B] “sent his [p. 296] legates to him, namely two spatharii, into the territory of Sicily, to establish him as patrician. They brought with them garments woven with gold, together with a sword, a comb, and shears, just as the aforesaid Arichis had promised that he would be clothed and tonsured.”

Ducange collected much material concerning this dignity and its character in his Glossary, but it is irrelevant here. Pagius also assembled much material (year 740, no. 4 and following), adopting especially the opinions of Peter de Marca concerning the patriciate of the Roman Church. I pay no attention to these views, because falsehoods are mixed with truths and the truths are exaggerated.

Indeed, the ancient Frankish annals from the years 741 to 793, which are held in such high regard by everyone (Canisius, vol. II, part II, p. 40), report the following under the year 754:

“The aforesaid apostolic Stephen confirmed Pippin as king by holy anointing” (for he had been anointed by Boniface in the year 740), “and together with him he joined his two sons, the lord Charles and Carloman, as kings.”

[Col. 0266C] The Fulda Annals likewise state under the year 753:

“He was honorably received at Paris, and anointed his two sons, Carloman and Charles, as kings.”

A corresponding account appears in Anastasius (section 244):

“The most Christian Pippin, by the grace of Christ, together with his two sons, was anointed king of the Franks by that most holy pope.”

After this solemn inauguration, the Carolingian Book itself, as well as the author of Adrian’s deeds in Anastasius (sections 294, 296), bears witness that those kings were called patricians. Whether this name or dignity arose from the oath sworn by those same kings at their anointing—that they would defend the Roman Church—or from an agreement entered into with the pontiff before the anointing, there is no doubt that they thereby became patricians of the Romans. Yet nowhere are they found to have been created by any solemn ceremony.

[Col. 0266D] Therefore those who attribute anything else to this kind of patriciate beyond the defense of the Roman Church are gravely mistaken. And those who do not see the Roman pontiff as the ruler of the holy commonwealth, whose defense against Greek impiety and the invasions of the Lombards he entrusted to the kings of Francia, seem to be blind both in bodily eyes and in the mind’s vision.

XI. Not Rome alone with its duchy, but the Exarchate and Pentapolis as well, had revolted from the impious Greeks and attached themselves to the pontiff, as has been said elsewhere. Nevertheless, these provinces did not become part of the pontifical jurisdiction until after Pippin’s donation, which was the beginning of the enlargement of the apostolic territory.

That donation, as we learn from the letters of Adrian’s predecessors, had been reduced in part by Lombard invasion or occupation and did not come wholly into the possession of the Holy See until [p. 297] the year 774. In that year the Franks, after Charles had subdued the Lombards, captured their king Desiderius, and expelled his son from Italy, took possession of their affairs.

[Col. 0267A] Einhard, speaking of the conclusion of the Italian war, which Charles undertook at Adrian’s request and completed that year, writes (ch. 6):

“The end of this war was the subjugation of Italy, the deportation of King Desiderius into perpetual exile, the expulsion of his son Adalgis from Italy, and the restoration to Adrian, rector of the Roman Church, of the possessions seized from the Lombard kings.”

For when Charles came to Rome, he first confirmed the donation of his father Pippin and not only confirmed it, but

“placed it beneath the Gospel books upon the body of blessed Peter, which are kissed there,”

as Anastasius records (section 319). Adrian also reminds Charles of this (Ep. 54, formerly 51), when accusing the audacity of the archbishop of Ravenna:

“When you went to the threshold of the apostles, you confirmed these very promises by pledging them, and in person you offered that same promise to the apostle of God with your own hands.”

The same point is made frequently elsewhere, as will become clear in the notes.

What Charles added in his charter concerning the Lombard kingdom being made his own property is less certain. Charles came to Rome four times in all: three times during Adrian’s pontificate, in 774, 781, and [Col. 0267B] 787, and once during the pontificate of Leo III, in 800.

What is certain is that the Lombard cities of Tuscany belonged to his first expedition. For in the year 776 Adrian announced to Charles that Reginald, duke of Chiusi, had committed hostile acts in one of those cities, which Adrian calls “ours” (Ep. 55, formerly 60):

“Advancing in person with an army against that same city of ours, the Fortress of Felicity, he removed those same inhabitants of the Fortress.”

XII. I have no doubt that on the same occasion Charles offered to blessed Peter the royal Tuscany that begins at Luni, and the duchy of Spoleto. Adrian speaks explicitly of the duchy of Spoleto in his letter to Charles (Ep. 56, formerly 58):

“For you have also personally offered that very duchy of Spoleto to your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through my humble agency, for the reward of your soul.”

Although he speaks less openly of royal Tuscany, he nevertheless exercises some kind of right over that duchy—both when he requests the removal of the duke of Chiusi (Ep. 55, formerly 60), and when he orders the duke of Lucca to oppose his vessels to the Greek [Col. 0267C] pirates (Ep. 63, formerly 65)—a right that he is not found to exercise in the other parts of the kingdom of Italy.

For this reason, some people very foolishly reject as false the complete donation of Charles reported by Anastasius and defined by its boundaries:

“From Luni, with the island of Corsica; then to Suriano; then to Mount Bardonis; then to Berceto; then to Parma; then to Reggio; from there [p. 298] to Mantua and Mount Silicis; and also the province of Venetia and Istria.”

They do so because the term “offering,” which is ambiguous and frequently used in this Book for “donation,” seems to make no distinction between those territories offered to Saint Peter while supreme dominion was retained—such as the duchies of Tuscany and Spoleto—and those which were donated to Saint Peter and his successors together with supreme power, in order to enlarge the jurisdiction of the apostolic see.

Yet who, seeing the pontiffs equally concerned for every city of those duchies and calling none of them “ours,” would fail to perceive the difference? [Col. 0267D] The charter of Louis the Pious removes the matter from all uncertainty, although one or two of our writers have absurdly declared it fictitious:

“When the same pontiff [Adrian],” it says, “confirmed for the same Charles, by a precept of his authority, the aforesaid duchies, namely Tuscany and Spoleto, he did so in such a way that the aforesaid census should be paid each year to the church of the holy apostle Peter.”

Thus the pontiffs were entitled to demand only the census from those duchies offered to Saint Peter; no administrative authority belonged to them there.

By contrast, in Lombard Tuscany—whatever may be said of that part of Campania containing the cities donated by Charles—and in the Sabine territory, which Adrian’s letters testify to have been donated by that same Charles sooner or later (Epistles 67, 71, 72, 73, formerly 69, 56, 76, 78), supreme jurisdiction belonged to the Holy See, as it did in the Exarchate and Pentapolis. These two provinces were Pippin’s donation, confirmed by his son Charles, and were fully recovered after the Lombard [Col. 0268A] kingdom had been destroyed. All the rest constituted Charles’s own donation.

XIII. I wish the reader to bear in mind that this is confirmed piecemeal by the letters of Adrian that follow, but in full by the charter dividing Charles’s kingdom among his sons.

When the charter discusses the division of Pippin’s kingdom among his brothers, in case Pippin should predecease them, it decrees as follows:

“From the entrance into Italy by the city of Augusta, Charles shall receive Ivrea, Vercelli, Pavia, and from there, following the boundary along the river Po, as far as the borders of Reggio, together with Reggio itself, Civita Nova, and Modena, as far as the boundaries of Saint Peter.”

The Holy See still possesses no other cities there.

The division continues:

“These cities, with their suburbs, territories, and counties belonging to them, and whatever from that point appears on the left to one traveling toward Rome, from the kingdom that Pippin possessed, together with the duchy of Spoleto [p. 299], shall Charles receive as his portion, as we have said. [Col. 0268B] Whatever from the aforesaid cities or counties lies on the right of one traveling toward Rome from the aforesaid kingdom—that is, the portion remaining of the Transpadane region, together with the Tuscan duchy as far as the Southern Sea and as far as Provence—Louis shall receive by lot for the enlargement of his kingdom.”

Certainly, anyone who hears the Tuscan duchy named in this division, after seeing that the whole of it was included by boundaries in the donation, will think the passage paradoxical. The difficulty disappears if one remembers that this duchy, together with Spoleto, was offered to the prince of the apostles while supreme right was retained.

The passage properly demonstrates that the duchy, having been offered to Saint Peter, was incorporated into the donation as a manifestation of Charles’s generosity toward him; and it is rightly counted among the provinces of Louis’s kingdom, because, once the census had been paid to the Holy See, the king retained supreme right.

Let this suffice concerning the enlargement of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, which will have to be examined more fully below. I must say something about the collection of canons, since the authority of Adrian’s letters (Epistles 70, formerly 96; 78, formerly 72; and 82, formerly 97) [Col. 0268C] confirms what I observed concerning the letter of Zacharias and reveals the character of that collection itself.

XIV. When King Charles first came to Rome in the year 774—as seems to me the better judgment—I do not think Adrian regarded temporal affairs as so important that he failed to give particular thought to the restoration of the Gallican Church, although a recent writer, who ill-employed his leisure, asserts that the pontiff and the king occupied themselves exclusively with temporal affairs.

Boniface of Mainz had begun so great a work thirty years earlier; but he found the ecclesiastical provinces so disturbed that he himself accomplished little. Nor, when Adrian assumed the pontificate, had more than two of the metropolitans recovered their former dignity.

Therefore, to the friendly king, distinguished for his piety, Adrian presented two books that might assist in completing so important a task. The first gave an account of seventeen provinces, listing both the individual metropolitan sees and the episcopal sees subject to each. A copy from Vatican Codex no. [Col. 0268D] 1338 was published through the efforts of Emmanuel a Schelestrate (On the Antiquity of the Church, vol. II, p. 643), with this title:

“This codex was copied from that authentic book which the lord Adrian, apostolicus, gave to the most glorious Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, when he was at Rome.”

The other codex contained six general councils celebrated before that time, together with a compendium of the Greek canons, as the title in the edition of Labbe and others, especially the elegant Canisian edition based on Basnage’s [p. 300] recension, shows (Ancient Readings, vol. II, part I, p. 266):

“Here begins a concise transmission of the Eastern, or African, canons, which blessed Pope Adrian gave in one volume, together with the preceding councils, for the ordering of the Western churches, to Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, when he was established at Rome.”

The first codex is relevant here only insofar as it testifies to the particular concern of the pontiff and the king for the restoration of the Frankish Church [Col. 0269A] and ecclesiastical discipline. The pontiff’s concern is shown by the fact that at the same time he wrote an encyclical to “all the archbishops and bishops,”

“so that each metropolitan may have subject to him the cities that blessed Leo and his other predecessors and successors, after the Council of Chalcedon, assigned to the individual metropolitans.”

He gave this instruction to Bertherius, metropolitan of Vienne (Labbe, Councils, vol. VI, p. 1888), and throughout his life he dealt with the same matter in his correspondence with Charles.

As for Charles, the many capitularies and episcopal councils that remain perpetual monuments of religion and piety, never to be erased by any forgetfulness, show how constantly this excellent prince was concerned with ecclesiastical affairs.

I must therefore speak again of the second codex, concerning which I spoke in connection with the letter of Saint Zacharias; the letters of the aforementioned Adrian compel me to do so.

XV. [Col. 0269B] I see three canons from Greek councils cited in those letters: Chalcedon 18 and 21, and the first canon of Antioch. If one considers the Latin version, they do not differ greatly from the Dionysian collection; the situation is different if one considers the method of numbering. The Antiochene canon comes still closer to the version, although its numbering is the same as that of the preceding canons.

There can therefore be no doubt that at the Holy See each council retained its own arrangement. Consequently, no collection yet existed for use even in ecclesiastical judgments. This is certainly proved by Leo IV in the ninth century, as I said in connection with the aforementioned letter of Zacharias.

The point is confirmed by canon 8 of the African codex, cited in one of those letters (Ep. 78, formerly 72). That canon is not called “Carthaginian” according to the canon—or, as it was called, the Roman collection, which Leo IV mentions—or according to the Breviary of Cresconius, nor is it so called in Adrian’s concise transmission of the Greek canons. It is explicitly called “African.”

Since the same canon is the sixth canon of the Second Council of Carthage, anyone who carefully compares the canon cited by Adrian with African Codex 8 and Carthaginian Council 6 will discover a variant reading in the latter. Yet he will find such agreement with the African codex that not even a difference of a single letter appears. [Col. 0269C]

[p. 301] Adrian therefore had before him a collection, or codex, of the African canons. We, as later generations, possess it in Greek and Latin, twice edited by Justellus and with greater care by Labbe (Councils, vol. II, p. 1041).

To this may be added abundant confirmation from two other letters: passages from Scripture, and passages from the holy Fathers Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Amphilochius, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, Augustine, Hilary of Poitiers, Leo the Great in his sermons, Proterius’s letter to Leo concerning Easter, Fulgentius, and others whose authorities are not quoted.

XVI. Since this is so, I believe it can be shown what collection the Roman pontiffs used even in the eighth century. The sacred library, through its librarian and its archivists, supplied them with whatever was needed from time to time. [Col. 0269D]

There can be no doubt that, especially for the general councils, no other Latin version was used than the one kept in the library. For Anastasius testifies in his preface to the Seventh Council, addressed to John VIII, that everything had been rendered into Latin with the greatest care:

“By no means,” he says (Labbe, Councils, vol. VII, p. 29), “can the eighth be called or held to exist where the seventh is not possessed—not because it had not previously been translated, but because the translator, almost everywhere abandoning the idiom of either language, followed word for word so literally that it can scarcely ever be understood what is intended in that edition; and because it had become tedious to its readers, almost everyone despised it for this reason.”

A little farther on, speaking of the canons of the apostles, he uses the very words of Dionysius Exiguus in the preface to his own collection. We therefore understand that this same collection was in the library.

This explains why Adrian cites the Antiochene canon as differing little from the Dionysian version, and does the same with the two canons of Chalcedon, although such similarity with the Dionysian text is not apparent.

It would be idle to inquire whether all of them were taken from the collection of Cresconius, which followed Dionysius’s version, or whether they flowed from some other source deriving from the same origin. For we know with certainty that all the Greek canons, except those of the general councils, are to be attributed to the Dionysian collection.

One might ask why the Chalcedonian canons, which belong to a general council, should themselves reflect the Dionysian collection. On this subject the very learned Natalis Alexander was seriously and repeatedly mistaken (century V, dissertation 15, article 4). He maintains that such eminent pontiffs as Gelasius, Pelagius II, and Gregory the Great used the Chalcedonian canons, without observing that they cite only those three canons proposed by Marcianus and confirmed by the Fathers at the end of session 6 (Labbe, Councils, vol. IV, p. 609). These differ entirely from the Dionysian version, as will become clear to anyone who compares them. [Col. 0270A]

Before the eighth century, wherever I found the same canons cited, after applying the greatest diligence, I found them altogether different from those transmitted in the Dionysian collection.

XVII. [Col. 0270B] Since those same canons were later reviewed in session 15 and occupy the fourth, third, and twenty-third places among the other texts, there is no reason for wonder if, in the eighth century and afterward, they appear according to the Dionysian version.

Once the apostolic see had accepted a collection of the Greek canons, it was permissible to use the three Constantinopolitan canons and the remaining Chalcedonian canons that had been rejected by that collection.
