It was also permissible to use the three aforementioned Chalcedonian canons, which had long been well known at the same see, both from the codex of that council preserved in the library and from the aforementioned collection.

But Hincmarus, and Natalis with him, are mistaken when they refer the passage of Saint Gregory, Homily 17 on the Gospels—“the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy”—to the second Chalcedonian canon.

Gregory does not seem to be speaking here of the canons of councils, but of the authority of Sacred Scripture, which Siricius, Innocent, [Col. 0270C] and other ancient pontiffs call “the rule,” “the ecclesiastical rule,” “the apostolic Scripture,” “the apostolic traditions,” and “the apostolic canons,” as Father Coustant notes (On the Letter of Siricius 10, p. 699).

Several letters of Gregory’s Register provide evidence of this (Book VII, Ep. 111; Book IX, Epistles 40, 49, 50, 51, 53, 54, 55, 57; Book X, Ep. 32; and Book XI, Ep. 48). In each of them he speaks of the Simoniac heresy on the authority of Scripture, not of the second canon of Chalcedon.

He says that it was “condemned by apostolic detestation” from its very origin, and that it was condemned by the prince of the apostles himself, “who first pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Simon.” He teaches that it was expelled from the Church, and makes similar statements throughout.

But let us suppose that Gregory was thinking of conciliar canons. Is it not written in canon 2 of Sardica, concerning the ordination of a bishop, that “a few might be corrupted by reward and payment”? Does not canon 30 of the apostles decree:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both him and the one who ordained him be deposed”?

[Col. 0270D] I am not unaware that the Holy See rejected the apostolic canons just as it rejected the Chalcedonian canons. Nevertheless, Dionysius and Cresconius each testify in his own preface that certain pontifical constitutions secretly arose from them.

XVIII. The situation is different with the Chalcedonian canons. For not only is none of them found to have been used, secretly or openly, before the eighth century, but Anastasius the Librarian, an unimpeachable witness in such matters, speaks as follows in his letter to the deacon John (Labbe, Councils, vol. V, p. 1770):

“Lest we seem to accuse or rashly criticize so holy and venerable a synod”—the Sixth General Council—“we believe ourselves permitted to hold concerning it the opinion that we know our holy Fathers held concerning the great Council of Chalcedon. One of them, namely Saint Pope Gregory, approved it as worthy of acceptance only up to the publication of the canons.”

Indeed, after session 14, the pontifical legates, [Col. 0271A] realizing that the same things were being proposed against the Holy See as had been proposed in the rejected canons of Constantinople, withdrew. Therefore Leo the Great, while approving what had been done before session 15, rejected the rest.

When, however, from the time of Gregory III, the collection of Cresconius began to be used, and Zacharias and Stephen II attempted to restore the discipline of the Franks, which had been utterly ruined, and Stephen III decreed that the fifty apostolic canons should be accepted, Adrian consequently followed the footsteps of his predecessors, without abandoning the ancient practice of the apostolic see.

It must nevertheless be observed that either Adrian himself or one of his predecessors wished the Chalcedonian canons to be added to the council. When he gave Charles the six general councils, together with a compendium of the Greek canons, for the restoration of discipline in the churches of Francia, he presented the general councils in full, together with their canons. Therefore no canon of the general Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, or Chalcedon exists in that compendium.

This is so even though the Dionysian collection, the Cresconian collection, and the canon or collection of the apostolic see—which emerged in the ninth century—also list the canons of the general councils.

[Col. 0271B] XIX. Everyone can see two reasons for such great variation. The first is that the Holy See did not yet possess a collection of its own; the second is that the sacred library, which contained both councils and private collections and was therefore virtually equivalent to a great collection, supplied whatever was needed for the matter at hand.

The second of these reasons clearly proves the point—despite the futile efforts of those who assert the existence of some ancient Roman collection.

If the Holy See possessed its own collection, why would the pontiff not have presented together the canons of both general and local councils, so that the Church might be restored by the most convenient means possible? Why would he not at least have transmitted in full the canons of the local councils that he separated from all the others?

The reason is that in Adrian’s time the codex, collection, or canon of the apostolic see had not yet appeared.

[Col. 0271C] Accordingly, he transmitted the canons of the general councils in full; the ambition of Constantinople no longer obstructed this, as it had formerly done. But he presented the canons of the local councils—which often opposed the discipline of the Holy See—in mutilated, corrected, and abridged [p. 304] form, omitting some of them altogether.

Moreover, at the beginning of the Sardican and African canons, he anticipates all who might see that concise series with a general admonition, invoking supreme authority:

“But in all these matters we must follow whatever we see not to differ from the Council of Nicaea and from the holy and apostolic Roman Church.”

What could be more illustrious for defeating the efforts of so many learned men who, in order to establish the old and new law and defend their own positions, support falsehood with almost endless disputations?

There is, however, another document still more explicit, which the opponents use rather incautiously for their own purposes: namely, the book of the Acts of Silvester [Col. 0271D], together with its two offspring.

XX. It would be foolish to defend the Acts of Silvester, since all learned men, and Baronius above all, recognized them as spurious—although Baronius believed them to be more heavily interpolated than wholly fabricated. I agree with them. But I do not see why I should pass over in silence what status these Acts had in Adrian’s time.

The famous decree of Gelasius, already often published by learned men, especially by Fontanini in the appendix to The Antiquities of Horta (p. 317, from Vatican Codex no. 493, fol. 101), lists these Acts among the books to be received, in the following words:

“Likewise, the Acts of blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown; nevertheless, we have learned that they are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and many churches imitate them because of their ancient usage.”

Now, under Pope Adrian, who lived approximately three centuries after Gelasius, not only had nothing been changed, but the book called the Canons of the Apostles, which had been rejected as apocryphal in the same decree of Gelasius, was received by the apostolic see according to the decree of Stephen [Col. 0272A] III at the Lateran Council of 769, concerning which enough has been said above.

Accordingly, Adrian freely used those Acts both in his letter to Charlemagne (Ep. 59, formerly 49) and in another letter to Constantine and Irene (Labbe, Councils, vol. VII, p. 102), as will shortly become clear.

Meanwhile, from these supposed Acts another supposed work emerged, namely the Constitutum of Silvester, divided into twenty chapters. An excerpt from it circulated in everyone’s hands in the Penitential Books of Theodore of Canterbury and Ecgbert of York. Gregory III had used these penitential books in his own treatise On Judgments.

Another forgery of uncertain date was also derived from the same Acts. Nevertheless, Natalis Alexander and the better critics attribute it to Isidore Mercator, and maintain that it was not known at Rome before the middle of the ninth century. This was the donation, or edict, of Constantine, which Saint Leo IX and several of his successors considered genuine throughout the eleventh [p. 305] century of the Church.

[Col. 0272B] Since these two little works flowed from the same source, they necessarily expressed the same things concerning Constantine’s baptism and the rest. Hence careless writers—perhaps also writers more hostile to the Holy See—among whom is the Italian Annalist under the year 776, think that Adrian referred to this notorious donation in the aforementioned letter to Charles, even though the donation had not yet appeared.

## XXI

But if Adrian had that most foolish donation before his eyes, he must surely have read this rotten passage:

> “Behold, we grant to our aforesaid most blessed pontiff Sylvester both our palace, as has been said, and the city of Rome, and all the provinces and cities of the whole of Italy and of the western regions.”

Why, then, after comparing Charles with Constantine, does he add only this brief statement?

> “Moreover, let all the other possessions that various emperors, patricians, and other God-fearing men, for the reward of their souls and the remission of their sins, granted in the territories of Tuscia, Spoleto, or Benevento, and Corsica, together with the Sabine Patrimony, to the blessed apostle Peter and to the holy Church of God and the apostolic Roman Church, and that were seized and taken away over the course of years by the wicked nation of the Lombards, be restored in your time. We also have several donations of this kind deposited in our sacred Lateran archive.”

From this, evidently, arose those volumes of the *Carticium* that appeared at the beginning of the *Book of the Censuses of the Roman Church* in the eleventh century, when credence was being given to the Constantinian Donation. Yet in those same volumes there is absolutely no mention of that donation.

I do not deny that Adrian placed excessive confidence in the Acts of Sylvester, where he says of Constantine:

> “Through his generosity the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church of God was raised and exalted, and he deigned to grant authority in these parts of Hesperia.”

For that word “authority” seems to me to carry some smell of exaggeration. What I deny is that Adrian saw the Donation and wrote in this way relying upon it. And, I believe, everyone will agree with me who hears Adrian testify not to donations made to Sylvester and his successors, as the Donation states, but to donations made to the holy Peter and the Roman Church, without any mention of Rome, Italy, or the provinces of the West. These matters will become clearer from another letter of the same pontiff to Constantine and Irene.

## XXII

There you may see the whole story narrated: Sylvester’s concealment on Mount Soracte; Constantine’s vision in sleep; the apostles’ admonition concerning baptism; in a word, all the matters that are read in the alleged Donation, though with remarkable variation. You will nevertheless find the Acts themselves described by Adrian down to the words:

> “And that he should no longer delay the showing, made through the Holy Spirit, of the pool which he remembered them to have promised for his salvation.”

These words, along with many others, are absent from the Donation.

The Acts of Sylvester, therefore—concerning which Baronius writes learnedly [Baronius, year 315, no. 10 ff.; year 324, no. 31 ff.] and which had been accepted at the Holy See and elsewhere—are reported in their genuine form in Adrian’s letters; but they are found shamefully interpolated and adapted to the author’s own purpose in the Donation. I cannot agree with Baronius [year 324, no. 97], who admits that the Acts were somewhat corrupted and deformed by certain additions; indeed, together with the scholars of our own age, I class them among the other fabrications. Nevertheless, I defend Adrian from a false opinion, maintaining that he followed the Acts then available for use, and not the Donation, which arose in the following century and was filled with falsehoods and absurdities.

Natalis had seen this before me [Book IV, dissertation 25, articles 2 and 3]. After rejecting the Donation or edict, already universally condemned, he adds what he himself had carefully observed: namely, that the edict first saw the light in the Isidorian collection; that Hincmar was the first of all to mention it; and that afterward, among the Roman pontiffs, Leo IX adopted it, whom Peter Damian imitated in his *Synodal Disputation between the King’s Advocate and the Defender of the Roman Church*. Finally, he says, Anselm of Lucca and Ivo adopted it as well. Yet he rightly considers the profound silence concerning it maintained by the pontiffs Adrian and Nicholas I, as well as by Anastasius the Librarian and Liutprand, bishop of Cremona, preferable to the authority of those men.

Thus, after overturning the slight conjectures of Cardinal Baronius, Jean Morin, and Peter de Marca, and with the approval of the scholars of our age, Natalis ascribes that edict to Isidore Mercator.

## XXIII

But whoever its author may have been, Saint Gregory VII bears witness that the Roman pontiffs recognized its falsehood. Although he regarded Saint Leo IX’s excessive credulity with contempt, he never once employed the authority of the edict. Yet he had many opportunities to appeal to it: when he says that the kingdom of Spain had been handed over by ancient constitutions to the blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church—not to Sylvester and his successors [Book I, letter 7; Book IV, letter 28]; when he warned Orzocor, judge of Cagliari, to confer with the other judges concerning the right of Saint Peter in Sardinia [Book I, letter 41]; and when, after Corsica had been rescued from the hands of its Saracen invaders, he sent the archbishop of Pisa there to govern it [Book V, letter 4].

As for Spain, Baronius holds [year 701, no. 16] that before the invasion the kingdom had been offered to the blessed Peter by one of the pious Gothic kings. I find this nowhere. But whatever the source from which Gregory obtained his information, he demands only a census, which indicates an offering rather than a donation.

Regarding Sardinia and Corsica—of which he knew that they formed part of the Carolingian donation—he speaks of their confirmation by Louis the Pious, the Ottos, and Henry I, as though he were their lord. If at any time he followed the Acts of Sylvester, as we have seen Adrian do, or even accepted the falsehood of the Donation, which had already grown up in his own age, why did he associate Charles with Constantine, together with the other men who had deserved well of the Church?

We learn this clearly from the oath he imposed upon Henry [Book IX, after letter 4] so that Henry might obtain reconciliation:

> “Concerning the ordering of the churches, and concerning the lands or census that the emperor Constantine or Charles gave to Saint Peter—not to Sylvester—and concerning all the churches or estates that at any time have been offered to the apostolic see by men or women, etc.”

Enough, then, has been said about the Donation, which is rashly conjectured to have emerged in Adrian’s time and to have been embraced by him and his successors. Something remains to be said about the other offspring of the Acts, namely, the constitution that flowed from them long before the Donation or edict, and whose authority was great at Rome and in the English Church, as is clear from the penitential books dating from the end of the seventh century of the Church.

## XXIV

Baronius thinks that this constitution was first published in the old Cresconian collection [year 324, no. 124]. But since several codices have been given that name, including some that also contain the constitutions of Gregory II, and since he assigns no date to the collection, I do not think that any person can establish one amid such great obscurity.

We know one thing with certainty: among the regulations of the Roman bishops, the twenty chapters of this constitution occupied the first place in the Roman canon or collection mentioned by Leo IV [Labbé, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 32]. For in Vatican Codex no. 5748, entitled *The Book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio*, not merely bare titles, as in other codices, but the constitutions themselves are listed. Thus the Roman pontiffs’ decrees are described there as follows:

> “Sylvester, the thirty-fourth after Peter; with 277 bishops assembled, twenty chapters.”

Therefore, whenever and by whomever the decrees of Sylvester were added to Cresconius—which flourished at the end of the seventh century—they are nothing other than that constitution which flowed from the Acts, and they could be used throughout the eighth century just as the Acts themselves could. Yet although I see its excerpt used everywhere, nowhere do I find any one of its twenty chapters.

For this reason, I used to say that the canon which is the first Roman collection ought to be assigned to the ninth century; Leo IV testifies that it was used only in judicial proceedings, while its use in the sacred library was not abandoned in other matters, as is known to have happened frequently.

Once the Roman collection is rejected for the eighth century, there is no reason to seek it in Adrian’s letters. The same is true of the Isidorian wares, which scholars understand to have begun circulating in the ninth century, although Figlinus either does not know this or pretends not to know it. Blondel alone nearly touched the point when he said that those fabrications bore the mark of a Franco-German author.

Indeed, the sum of all those fabrications shows that they arose in the provinces of Reims and Mainz after the deposition of Louis the Pious and the penalties subsequently inflicted upon the bishops who were guilty of that and other offenses; they were then foolishly attached to the excellent collection of Saint Isidore of Seville, which we call the Spanish collection. But more on this elsewhere. We must now speak of Adrian’s letters themselves.

## XXV

There are forty-nine of them, and therefore almost as many as those we have examined up to this point. They are far superior to the earlier letters because they were all written after Charles’s first arrival in Italy and the expulsion of the Lombards from it.

Moreover, all were given after Charles had greatly enlarged the ecclesiastical territory on the occasion of that first arrival—namely, in the year 774, at the beginning of April, when the most pious king celebrated the Paschal solemnity at Rome.

Accordingly, whereas up to this point we have observed the Pippinian Donation joined to the Roman province, or to the older territory of the Holy See, but never fully possessed by it and even frequently exposed to new invasions—so that both it and the older territory, not even the city itself excepted, were almost constantly disturbed by fear—we shall henceforth see matters of an opposite kind.

The Exarchate and the Pentapolis, that is, the entire possession derived from the Pippinian Donation, although for some time disturbed by the audacity of the archbishop of Ravenna, will be clearly visible in Adrian’s letters. There too will be found Langobardic Tuscia, which, joined to the Roman territory or to the Transtiberine part of the duchy, forms the province now called the Patrimony.

The same letters testify that the Sabine territory and six cities in Campania of the duchy of Benevento were added to the Cistiberine duchy. Finally, from Adrian’s letters we shall learn that the duchy of Spoleto was made tributary to Saint Peter. There will also be some indications that the duchy of Tuscia, which they call royal Tuscia, enjoyed the same status.

Since by the eleventh century almost all these territories were already in the power of the apostolic see, apart from the duchy of Tuscia, some men have applied all their art and every resource of ingenuity lest they rest upon so ancient a foundation and consequently become inviolable. Since they cannot demolish the foundation itself, they strive to undermine it.

The arrangement of the letters supplies a mechanism especially suited to this purpose, since the perpetual silence of chronology is joined to the negligence of the compiler. Thus, by placing some letters before others and postponing others, one may reach the desired conclusion.

## XXVI

No one is unaware that the Italian Annalist has done this more than anyone else [vol. IV, years 775 ff.]. By such an artifice he demonstrated that Charles never kept his promises. Since everyone knows what end he had in view—namely, to lend support to his earlier writings—he will find few listeners, apart from sectarians and the ignorant crowd, who will readily lend an ear to his history.

It must first be observed that these letters are all divided into two groups. Some were written after the year 774, that is, after Charles’s first arrival; others after his second arrival, which took place in the year 781. Everyone transmits this by common consent, and the Annalist himself confirms it: in that year, on the Paschal solemnity, 15 April, Carloman, Charles’s son, was baptized and, after Adrian changed his name, began to be called Pippin. The pontiff lifted him from the sacred font. All the letters afterward issued bear witness to this spiritual relationship, for they always call Charles the compater (co-godparent).

Sixteen letters are counted without this title and must therefore be assigned to the preceding years. The rest, since they bear the title of godfather, must have been given after 781.

Moreover, nine of these letters [67 and following, alternatively 69; 68; 95; 96; 56; 76; 78; 70; 93] were given while Queen Hildegard was still alive; she died on the day before the Kalends of May in the year 783. For in them mention is made of the female godmother, whereas Fastrada, the new wife, is called only queen.

It is therefore clear that the Annalist’s chronological opinion is mistaken when he wants letters 50, 63, alternatively 55, 65—which lack that title—to be assigned to the year 785; letter 66, alternatively 61, to 786; and letter 65, alternatively 64, to 787. Conversely, he brings letters 67 and 73, alternatively 69, and 78, which conspicuously bear the titles of godfather and female godmother, back to the year 778.

It is much more obvious that he is hallucinating when, concerning letter 55, alternatively 60, evidently written in the year 776—a letter more certain in its date than perhaps any other in the entire codex—he insists that it was given in 780. He wants the popular rumor to be believed that the message concerned the death of Constantine, whom Adrian certainly says was still alive.

Since Leo, the son of the emperor Constantine, died in that year, and Constantine, his young son, succeeded him together with his mother Irene, the Annalist declares that the scribes made a mistake and decides that Leo should be substituted for Constantine. What confidence in the man!

## XXVII

Yet I shall not hesitate to recall that history, for the correct chronology of the letter will become obvious. In the year 775, on 14 September, Constantine Copronymus died, as Pagi reports from the Greek authors [year 775, no. 1], using the very words of Theophanes, who relates that, while preparing to wage war against the Bulgarians,

> “on 14 September, in the fourteenth indiction, having boarded a ship and been carried to the fortress of Strongylon, he suffered an ill-fated death during the voyage.”

I am astonished to see this same event assigned to the year 775 by Muratori himself, who postpones Adrian’s letter announcing it to the year 780, the year of the death of Leo Augustus.

Yet nothing is more consistent with the truth than this letter. The pontiff announces:

> “It has reached us through messengers who preceded the others that the emperor Constantine had been taken from this light by a divine summons; but because we had not learned the matter with certainty, we delayed informing your God-protected Excellence about it. Now, however, our most holy and reverend brother Stephen, bishop of the city of Naples, has informed us through these words, which he sent to us on the seventh day of the present month of February, etc.”

What could be more credible than that, in the space of almost five months, news of the death of the persecutor of the sacred images reached Rome? What could be more prudent than the pontiff’s silence, since he did not wish to put faith in rumor, but, after receiving the letters of the duke and bishop of Naples, then announced the matter to Charles?

But let us approach the matter closely; we shall detect the Annalist’s method. No report came to Rome from the court of Constantinople; therefore, according to him, those Augusti had no relations with the City, which had long since obeyed the pontiff. Instead, a messenger was sent to Naples, whose duchy had not yet shaken off Greek domination, and Stephen would not have informed the pontiff of the matter unless he had been more friendly to him than to the Augustus, as is clear from the *Neapolitan Chronicle* in Pratillus [vol. II].

But the Annalist’s claim—that the court of Constantinople had entirely forgotten the Romans and that Duke Stephen announced so great a matter to the pontiff simply because he was a bishop and a friend—does not seem acceptable. The occasion was instead exploited by the Annalist, who was planning to subject Rome to Charles, taking the opportunity to insert Charles’s dominion through a peculiar interpretation of the patriciate, not on the authority of any ancient monument, but by embracing the false opinions of Pagi and Eckard and bending them to his own purpose [year 789].

## XXVIII

He revealed this plan from the time of Charles’s arrival in Italy [years 773, 774]. He did not deny that Charles’s invincible power had brought the Lombard kingdom to an end; but by conjecture he added that several hidden wheels had made Desiderius’s ruin more rapid and easy.

He admitted that Charles had not yielded to his father Pippin in piety, but conjectured that, once he had acquired the Lombard kingdom, Charles had not been altogether displeased to retain what he had promised as well.

Finally, by conjecture he infers that letters concerning the deposition of Desiderius were exchanged between Charles and Adrian, and laments that they have not come down to us.

Such conjectures, which reveal his mind sufficiently and more than sufficiently in his arrangement of the letters, accomplish nothing. For only the third of them—the conjecture that the affair was conducted by letters sent back and forth—rests on historical evidence; and, since that evidence is preserved complete in Anastasius, it needs no conjecture.

From Adrian’s deeds we learn that envoys were sent to Francia twice with letters. First, after the pontiff saw that Desiderius, through the stratagems by which he most cunningly sought to divide the Frankish kingdom and sow discord between the pontiff and the Franks, had exposed the territory of the Holy See and Rome itself to his anger, he fortified the City for resistance and

> “sent his own messengers by sea with apostolic letters,”

seeking nothing other than immediate assistance, following the example of his predecessors.

At that time Charles was engaged in the Saxon war, which, according to the testimony of Einhard and the Annals, began in the year 772. This first embassy was arranged toward the end of Adrian’s first year.

Desiderius, moreover, fearing that invincible king, had himself sent his own envoys, announcing that he had restored everything to the Holy See. Amid these complications, Charles—who wished to avoid an Italian war at that time and at the same time desired to learn the opposing claims of the pontiff’s and Desiderius’s envoys—sent Bishop George, Abbot Wulfard, and Alcuin Deliciosus as his envoys to the pontiff.

When they returned after learning the whole matter, Adrian gave them companions:

> “his own messengers to the aforesaid most excellent king of the Franks, with apostolic letters of admonition.”

From Adrian’s deeds we learn that the pontiff gave these two letters at the end of the year 772 and the beginning of the following year.

## XXIX

I confess that I cannot understand how these two letters neither reached Francia nor remained in the Lateran archives. If they had reached Francia, Charles would undoubtedly have entered into a codex those letters which especially concerned him. And if copies of them had been preserved in the archive, Panvinio and afterward the Magdeburg Centuriators would have listed them among the other letters.

Whatever the truth of the matter, the pontiff first earnestly asked the king of the Franks

> “to come to the aid and assistance of the holy Church of God, and of the afflicted Roman province or Exarchate of Ravenna, just as his father, Pippin of holy memory, had done, and to demand from that same king Desiderius the full rights of blessed Peter and the cities that had been taken away.”

Then, pressing the same point, he asked Charles,

> “earnestly adjuring him to fulfill what he had promised to blessed Peter together with his father, King Pippin of holy memory, and to complete the redemption of the holy Church of God; and to cause everything that had been taken away by the treacherous king of the Lombards—both the cities and the remaining rights—to be restored without conflict to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.”

The general outline of this history agrees entirely with what Einhard and the other Frankish writers relate.

It is useful to bring here several details from the monk of Angoulême concerning the end of the year 772 and the beginning of the following year, since they speak of only one envoy, explain the sea voyage, and say nothing about letters:

> “From there he proceeded to winter at the villa of Theodon. There Peter, the envoy of the apostolic lord Adrian, came to him by sea as far as Arles, and from there by land, and invited the glorious king and his Franks, for the service of God and the justice of Saint Peter, against King Desiderius and the Lombards. He therefore came by sea because the roads had been closed to the Romans by the Lombards. And the exalted King Charles, having taken counsel together with the Franks concerning what he should do, promised that he would provide assistance to the Romans.”

The frequently cited *Frankish Annals* tell the story in nearly the same words, with some variation, under the year 773.

## XXX

It would be lengthy to cite as witnesses the later chroniclers and annalists who speak of this matter. I regard this as certain and established: it never occurred to any ancient writer to brand the most holy pontiff Adrian and the pious king Charles with such a mark of disgrace.

Therefore I shall have to defend both of them against the opinion of the recent Annalist—an opinion scarcely capable of being replaced by anything more credible—by which, through the inversion of Adrian’s letters, he sought to cast doubt upon the dominion of the pontiffs, begun by the will of the peoples and greatly increased by the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles.

Examples will make these points clearer. From the letter cited above [55, alternatively 60], which this author rashly postponed from the beginning of the year 776 to 780, there is, besides those by no means doubtful indications of pontifical dominion in the City, very clear evidence that Langobardic Tuscia was given to Saint Peter by Charles in 774, when he first came to Rome, and that he added it to his father’s restored donation and gave it greater validity upon the body of blessed Peter.

For, while complaining of the invasions of the duke of Chiusi in that province, the pontiff calls one of the cities of Tuscia “our city,” the City of the Fortress of Felicity.

The Annalist insists that this donation was illusory [year 788], perversely interpreting letter 89, alternatively 90, as though Adrian were asking the king in that year—namely, the fourteenth year after the donation—to have each of the cities of Tuscia delivered to him through his envoys.

The words of the letter expose the falsity of this interpretation:

> “May you deign to send your envoys so that they dare not return to you in any way unless they are first able to deliver to us in full the cities in the Beneventan territories, just as you granted them through your sacred offering to blessed Peter and to us, and unless they diligently provide us in full with the rights belonging to Populonia and Roselle.”

Adrian therefore wishes to take possession, through the royal envoys, of the cities that Charles had recently donated before his third departure from Italy in the year 787, but that had not yet been delivered to him. Through the same assistance he also wishes to obtain what was lacking for complete possession of Populonia and Roselle.

He does not ask for anything similar concerning the other cities of Tuscia. Rather, he uses as an example those already possessed for fourteen years, so that the Beneventan cities may be delivered to him to be possessed in the same manner:

> “Just as in the territories of Tuscia you offered and gave to blessed Peter the cities—namely, Suana, Tuscania, Viterbo, and Bagno del Re—and the remaining cities with their boundaries and territories, so likewise may you immediately cause the cities in the Beneventan territories to be delivered to us for possession.”

## XXXI

This is even clearer from the later letters [92, alternatively 86]. Adrian says that none of this had been accomplished by those envoys, and that he had sent his own dukes together with other royal envoys; yet he had scarcely obtained the cities with their keys, without their inhabitants:

> “For we, while allowing them to remain in their freedom, wish to govern and administer them, as we do the other cities in the territories of Tuscia through your gifts, possessing all their law.”

Thus, to cast doubt upon the pontiff’s full dominion over the cities of Tuscia—which are again brought forward as an example—is to lie.

The letters of this codex do not establish that the pontiff exercised dominion over the six cities of Campania in the same way. From only one letter [91, alternatively 88], which appears to have been given toward the end of the year 788, we learn that the prince of Capua swore an oath of fidelity to the pontiff, who reported the matter to Charles in these words:

> “We caused the Capuans to swear in the confession of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, upon the faith of that same apostle of God, and upon our faith and that of your royal power.”

Other letters of Adrian bear witness to this event, and Mabillon reports a fragment of one from the authentic Dionysian collection, on a strip of parchment [*Supplement to the Diplomas*, p. 70]. For among other things it relates there concerning the Capuans:

> “They asked that they should be subject to us and to the most blessed Peter, just as they are recognized to have been through the donation of the most excellent lord king.”

He therefore asks advice as to whether he should accept their oath. We learn that he subsequently accepted it.

From another fragment of a letter by Maginarius, one of the royal envoys [ibid., p. 96], we recognize the fickleness of Beneventan loyalty. They did not hesitate to set ambushes for the royal envoys, and

> “they release to them those cities which you donated to Saint Peter or to the apostolic lord [lacuna]; in no way do they wish to fulfill your command.”

These events had occurred not long before the oath mentioned above [letter 90, alternatively 92].

I therefore regard the donation of those cities as just as certain as that of the Tuscan cities. Yet I would not dare to assert that their subjection to the pontiff was identical in both cases.

Tuscia, conquered by Charles and entirely dependent upon him, was possessed by the pontiff immediately after the donation, despite the Annalist’s efforts against the letters cited. The situation was different with the cities of Campania. Their princes, fearing Charles while he was present, promised everything; after his departure they not only violated their promises but even dared to attack the royal envoys by ambush.

Since Charles therefore defended his donation to the apostolic see with the greatest vigor, it is an intolerable injustice to brand it as an illusory donation. As for Adrian, whose plans and agreements with Charles for removing Desiderius from the throne of his ancestors are lamented as lost, I say only this: to inflict so grave an injury upon so great a pontiff merely by conjecture is the act of a fabulist, not of a historian.

## XXXII

Before I review the letters themselves, from which what has been said above will become clearer, I must add something concerning the Sabine territory, which the Holy See certainly possessed in its entirety through Charles’s generosity after his second arrival in Italy.

The Annalist, besides the inversion of the letters through which he pursues his history rather absurdly, puts forward this dilemma:

> “Either Sabina was not at that time under the dominion of the Roman pontiff, because it was included in the duchy of Spoleto; or, if it depended upon the Roman duchy, it would become still clearer that the pontiff was then lord neither of Rome nor of his duchy.”

Both parts of the argument collapse. For the territory is found in the monuments of the ancients neither in the duchy of Spoleto nor in the Roman duchy.

In the *Deeds of Zacharias* preserved by Anastasius, it is related that Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, recovered his peoples, namely:

> “the Marsicans, the Forconians, and the Balvans or Pinnenses. Then, entering through the Sabine territory, they came to the city of Rieti. The people of Rieti immediately submitted themselves as well.”

Later it says that the king of the Lombards restored to the pontiff

> “the Sabine Patrimony, which had been taken away for nearly thirty years.”

That the people of Rieti, who bordered upon the Sabine territory, belonged to the jurisdiction of Spoleto is clear from the *Deeds of Stephen III*, where the arrival at Rome of Christopher and Sergius with troops against the antipope Constantine is discussed:

> “with the people of Rieti, the Forconians, and other Lombards of the duchy of Spoleto.”

Although they seem to be distinguished in Adrian’s deeds during Charles’s first arrival:

> “The people of Spoleto and Rieti, and certain useful persons among them, before Desiderius and his army of Lombards proceeded to Chiusi, fled for refuge to blessed Peter and surrendered themselves to the aforesaid most holy Pope Adrian.”

In our codex the Sabine territory is separated even more clearly from the Roman and Spoletan duchies. Adrian, enumerating the ancient donations [letter 59, alternatively 49], says:

> “In the territories of Tuscia, Spoleto, or Benevento, and Corsica, together with the Sabine Patrimony.”

It is worthy of notice that, just as the two duchies—Spoletan and Beneventan—the province of Tuscia, and the island of Corsica, where the patrimonies were located, are mentioned, so the Sabine territory would have been named only if, in the case of Sabina, “patrimony” and “territory” were one and the same thing.

Thus that diocese, or small province, which is still called Sabina and lies between the people of Rieti and Latium, was the patrimony or territory of the Holy See, seized at various times and restored, so to speak, by right of return only by Charles.

## XXXIII

Nothing proves this matter better than the testimony of the letters in this codex. First, Adrian declares as follows to Charles [letter 71, alternatively 56]:

> “For I call God as witness that I seek no one’s boundaries irrationally; but just as that same patrimony existed from ancient times, and you have now granted it in its entirety to blessed Peter, so we desire to receive it.”

Likewise [letter 72, alternatively 76]:

> “We have sent our requests concerning the Sabine territory, asking that you command your most faithful envoys, who have also examined the matter in part, to deliver to us what you granted in its entirety to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the reward of your soul and likewise of that of our spiritual daughter and female godmother, as well as for the sake of your most noble offspring, just as it existed in ancient times.”

It is therefore clear that “Sabine patrimony” and “Sabine territory” are interchangeable names, and that nothing more is being requested than what had formerly been possessed.

Only this seems difficult to understand: how can a grant be called an ancient right? But this too is clear from another letter [letter 73, alternatively 78]:

> “Your envoy Maginarius has now personally seen the right that blessed Peter the apostle, your protector, possesses in that territory, as it is more fully set out both in imperial donations and in the donations of those arrogant Lombard kings, which designate the territory itself together with its dependent estates. But if the treacherous former king Desiderius did not restore to us the estates in their entirety, but only as many as could be found—estates that the Holy Roman Church had held from ancient times, since no one from the Lombard territories dared to resist them—how much more ought they, being obedient in all things to your God-protected royal power, to fulfill your commands? We give thanks neither to emperors nor to kings, but only to your most triumphant Excellence, because you have newly granted it in its entirety to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.”

The estates of that territory were therefore so extensive that they seemed to constitute almost the whole patrimony of Saint Peter. Charles, however, restoring all the donations of others and adding something from his own generosity, granted the entire territory to Saint Peter.

## XXXIV

This is so certain that it cannot be called into doubt, for the total grant is expressed in precise words in another letter [letter 67, alternatively 69], which preceded those already cited:

> “The Church of blessed Peter,” Adrian says, “has shone forth through many documents concerning the gifts brought by you, both cities and various territories that you offer in their entirety to that apostle of God. Therefore, asking your royal clemency, promoted by God, we beg that, just as your most upright Excellence has granted the Sabine territory in its entirety to blessed Peter, your nourisher, for the furnishing of lamps and the support of the poor, so you may deign, with the assistance of your most excellent effort, to deliver it whole to that same apostle of God.”

The only missing point was evidence from Adrian’s letters that possession of the patrimony had actually been delivered in its entirety. Yet, apart from the fact that the unbroken silence thereafter reminds us that possession was delivered, Charles collected these letters in the year 791, while Adrian survived until 795. Hence it is useless to seek a letter recording the completion of this affair.

In the diploma of Louis the Pious, I find the pure donation of his father Charles recorded in accordance with the sense of this codex. I therefore have no doubt that the matter of the Sabine territory had been settled. He says:

> “In the same manner, the Sabine territory was granted in its entirety by our father, the emperor Charles, to the blessed apostle Peter through a deed of donation, just as it was delimited by Itherius and Maginarius, his abbots and envoys, between that same Sabine territory and the territory of Rieti.”

Since this and many other matters will become clearer from the letters that follow—for the Louisian diploma is nothing other than a concise repetition of the ancient dominion and of the great increase it received through the donations of Pippin and Charles—we must now examine individually Adrian’s letters, upon which nearly all the territories of the apostolic see rest as upon the most certain monuments.

## LI. Letter of Pope Adrian to the Lord King Charles, Sent through Abbot Gausfridus [Note: [Col. 0279D] B. and Centuriators: Ausfridus. In the margin of Baronius: Ansfridus. GRETS.]

In this letter there is contained an account of the victory of the aforesaid king and of the bishops of Pisa and Lucca, and a request that, out of his piety, he permit them to return to their own sees and churches. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 26): “In the twenty-sixth [or sixth] letter he congratulates Charles on the victory that Ausfridus, abbot of Pisa, had reported to him; he indicates how earnestly they pray for Charles. He commends Ausfridus to Charles and asks on behalf of the bishops of Pisa and Lucca [Lucchese], that out of his piety he allow them to return to their own sees and churches (or permit them to do so). CENN.]

*(Year of the Lord 774; Codex of Charles, letter 55; chronicle 50.)*

### Summary

After Charles had departed from Rome and returned to the camp near Ticinum, which had not yet been captured, Gausfridus of Pisa set out for his homeland but fell into an ambush laid by Allo, duke of Lucca. To escape it, he fled to Rome and reported to the pontiff Charles’s victories.

The pontiff sent him back to the king together with his own envoy Anastasius and congratulated Charles on his victories. He declares that from the day Charles departed Rome he, together with the clergy, monks, and the entire people, had continually implored those victories in prayer.

He asks Charles to permit the bishops of Pisa, Lucca, and Reggio to return to their sees.

Adrian, pope, to his most excellent son Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0280D] Summary 26, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.].

Having returned from your God-beloved royal presence, Gausfridus, a resident of the city of Pisa, appeared before us and reported the immense victories which our Lord God almighty and redeemer has graciously granted you through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He also assured us in every respect of your prosperity. When we heard this, our spirit, rejoicing and exulting in the Lord, was lifted up in vehement joy; and immediately, with outstretched hands toward heaven, we offered abundant praises to the King of kings and Lord of lords, earnestly beseeching his ineffable divine mercy to grant you bodily health and salvation of soul, to bestow victories over your enemies upon you in abundance, and to subject all barbarian nations to your feet.

318 And indeed, believe us, great and most Christian king, excellent and good son: have the greatest confidence, because, so long as you remain with faithful devotion in the love of that prince of the apostles according to your promise, and strive to fulfill everything for that apostle of God, both salvation and immense victory will continually be granted you by almighty God. Indeed, we call God as our witness, to whom the hidden things of all hearts lie open: from that time, from the day [Note: [Col. 0281B] Both Lambecius and Gentilotus read in the codex *from that day*, without the word *time*. Charles was still in Italy when this letter was written; Cointius and Pagius (774, no. 9) rightly assign it to that year, against Muratori (775), who, conjecturally, postpones it to the year 785, not observing that at that time Charles is repeatedly called “co-father,” because he had taken Charles’s son from the sacred font in the year 781. CENN.] on which you departed from this Roman city for those regions, every day, even at every moment and every single hour, all our priests, as well as the religious servants of God—the monks throughout all our monasteries—and likewise the rest of the people, both through the titular churches and through the deacons [Note: [Col. 0281C] *Diaconias* should doubtless be read. I have already noted that the codex is riddled with such errors; when these are added to the solecisms of that age, they make the text inelegant, though they do not alter the sense. Ancient Roman Ordines I and III, in Mabillon (*Mus. Ital.*, vol. II), and the authors cited by him in the preliminary commentary, show that there were then twenty-eight titular churches or basilicas and seven deaconries in Rome, corresponding to the ecclesiastical regions. ID.], do not cease to cry out three hundred *Kyrie eleison* in your behalf to our God with extended voices, and, bending their knees, to entreat that most merciful Lord our God to grant you from heaven, in manifold abundance, both forgiveness of sins and the greatest joy of prosperity, as well as plentiful victories.

[Note: [Col. 0281C] A type of litany. In the treatise against the Greeks published by Stevartius from the Bavarian library (*Canisius*, revised by Basnage, vol. IV, p. 66), this is listed among their bad customs: “They never sing *Christe eleison*, but sing *Kyrie eleison* very frequently in their offices,” as though they thought Christ less powerful than the Lord. Nevertheless, canon 3 of the Council of Vaison must be recalled (Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1680), where in the year 529 it was decreed: “And because both in the apostolic see and throughout all the eastern provinces and those of Italy a sweet and exceedingly salutary custom has been introduced, that *Kyrie eleison* should be said more frequently, with great devotion and compunction, it has pleased us also that this most holy custom should, with God’s favor, be introduced into all our churches, at matins, at Masses, and at vespers.” Ducange adds chapter 205 of book VI of the *Capitularies* and chapter 58 of Herard’s capitulary, which is quoted in an addition: “Let the funerals of the dead be conducted with mourning and the secret groaning of the heart. And those who do not know the psalms should sing *Kyrie eleison* there.” Hence also *Kyrie eleisare* in the same author. It is therefore clear that the custom condemned among the Greeks also prevailed in the West during the eighth century and earlier. Yet *Christe eleison* was also said, as Gregory the Great attests (*Book VII, Letter 64*), especially at daily Masses: “Which,” he says, “is in no way said by the Greeks.” Adrian, however, taking account of the common people, who did not know the psalms, ordered three hundred *Kyrie eleison* to be sung for Charles in all the churches of the City while the siege of Ticinum was being conducted by him. See below, letter 84, otherwise 91, note. ID.]

319 For Gausfridus himself reported to us that, when he returned after being released by you, Duke Allo wished to kill him [Note: [Col. 0282C] Allo is also mentioned below, letter 65. GRETS.]. Therefore, when Gausfridus wished to return once more to your presence, Allo placed scouts and ambushers along the road to kill him. When Gausfridus learned of this, he took refuge with us [Note: [Col. 0282C] Muratori says that he found mention of Allo, duke of Lucca, in the charters of the Lucchese archive after 782, and for that reason he assigns this letter to a time after that year. But, apart from the title “co-father,” which the letter lacks, the story of Gausfridus, a resident of Pisa, teaches us that Charles was in Italy. We therefore cannot be far from the truth if we suppose that Allo was in command of the Frankish soldiers stationed in Italy, and that the administration of Lucca was later entrusted to him. For Gausfridus, returning to his homeland, fell into Allo’s ambushes; turning back in order to return to the Frankish camp, he encountered further ambushes laid by that duke. He therefore entered territory adjoining that of the Church and fled to Rome. From there the pontiff sent him back to Charles with his own legate, and this letter seems to have been written on that account, since it is concerned especially with Gausfridus. What follows concerning the restoration of three bishops to their sees, though somewhat obscure, nevertheless clearly shows that they had followed the prince on his Italian expedition and were still remaining in Charles’s company. The pontiff may therefore have feared that they would follow him into Francia, to the considerable detriment of the churches entrusted to them, and arranged for each to be sent back to his own see. The victories which he calls immense and says were granted by God through the intercession of blessed Peter are none other than the defeat of the Lombards, the capture of Ticinum, the seizure of Desiderius with his wife and daughter, the acquisition of all the treasures, and the surrender of all the cities. Pagius, following the Frankish and Fulda Annals (774, no. 9), thought that this letter was written before the capture of Ticinum, thereby giving Muratori occasion to deny that Charles had achieved any victory over the Lombards. Both learned men are mistaken. CENN.], and when he sought to be released so that he might return to your presence, and was already there, we decided to send our Anastasius to your excellence. We released him to appear before you together with this same messenger of ours. We ask that, for the love of blessed Peter and at our request, you graciously receive him and deign to grant him the assistance of your protection and favor. We also earnestly beg that, through the generosity of your authority, he may possess those estates [Perhaps: those *mansi*] which you granted him.

We also earnestly ask and implore your kindness to command that those bishops—that is, of the city of Pisa, of Lucca, and of Reggio [Lambecius: “and of Reggio”]—be released to return to their own sees, churches, and peoples entrusted to them [Col. 0282B], because, good and most excellent son, it is beneficial to your soul that those bishops be restored to their own sees, that all the churches of God stand adorned with their bishops, and that all the people of God may live in great joy during your most fortunate times; may this also be reckoned to you as an eternal reward. Thus, remaining steadfast in our affection for you, 320 we confidently make every effort to ask you for those things which we know pertain to the salvation of your soul, so that our almighty God may always be pleased with your pious works and, on account of them, grant you abundant recompense in the present and future life. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord Charles the king

In it there is contained a discussion of the insolence of Leo, archbishop of the city of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0283C] Summary of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 31): “In the thirty-first [first reading: thirtieth-first] letter he again vehemently accuses Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, of having become disobedient and insolent from the time when he returned from Charles; and he asks Charles not to permit what had been offered to Peter [Saint Peter] by him and by his father Pippin to be taken away from Peter [Saint Peter].” CENN.].

*(A.D. 774, Carolingian Codex LIV, chronicle 51.)*

### ARGUMENT

After the Italian war had been concluded, Charles had returned to Francia. The pontiff then learned that messengers sent by Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had been dispatched to oppose him. For immediately after the king’s departure Leo had invaded Faenza, Forum Populi, Forlì, Cesena, Bobbio, Comacchio, the duchy of Ferrara, Imola, and Bologna, claiming that Charles had granted these places to him together with the Pentapolis. He had been unable to detach the people of the Pentapolis from the service of Saint Peter, but in Emilia, after expelling the agents of the pontiff, he had installed his own. He defends the right of the apostolic see by the example of Stephen II. He sends his chamberlain Anastasius as his messenger, who will report more in person. The archbishop must be recalled to his duty, lest the condition of the holy see, after the Lombards have been overcome, be worse than it was before. He asks that Anastasius be sent back with good news and with the case settled.

Adrian, pope [Note: [Col. 0283D] Summary 31, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.], to his most excellent son Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans:

It has come to our attention that the insolent and exceedingly arrogant Leo, 321 archbishop of the city of Ravenna, has sent his messengers to your most excellent kindness to oppose us by making false allegations. Indeed, most excellent and great king, after your excellence returned from the city of Pavia [Note: [Col. 0284C] The authorities agree that Pavia was captured in May or at the beginning of June, and that Charles returned to Francia not long afterward. All the annalists attest this under the year 774, where they also record that he suppressed the audacity of the Saxons in the same year. CENN.] to the regions of Francia, from that time onward he has stood as a rebel against blessed Peter and against us, with tyrannical and most brazen intent. He appears to retain under his authority various cities of Emilia, namely Faenza, Forum Populi, Forlì, Cesena, Bobbio, Comacchio, the duchy of Ferrara, Imola, and Bologna, asserting that these cities, together with the whole Pentapolis, had been granted to him by your excellence. He immediately sent his messenger Theophylact throughout the whole Pentapolis, announcing this very claim and wishing to separate the people of the Pentapolis from our service. But they were in no way inclined to humble themselves before him, nor did they wish to withdraw from the service of blessed Peter and from ours. Rather, they are known to have remained steadfast in our apostolic commands [Note: [Col. 0284D] The events themselves show that several months had elapsed before all this occurred. Therefore, suppose that this letter was written in November or December, but not later. Adrian, having been deprived of the greater part of his territory, immediately wished Charles to know what had happened. ID.], just as they had remained under our predecessor, Lord Pope Stephen, to whom your father, together with your illustrious excellence, entrusted that exarchate to remain under the jurisdiction of blessed Peter, in accordance with all due firmness [Note: [Col. 0284D] The diploma of the donation of Quierzy, issued by King Pippin in the year 754 and subscribed by Charles and Carloman, is being cited here. ID.].

For, as has been said, that wicked archbishop, retaining the aforementioned cities of Emilia under his power, appointed there such agents as he wished and appears to have expelled those whom we had appointed there. He also himself organized all the administrative affairs within the city of Ravenna. And behold: what we never expected has happened—the holy spiritual mother of you, the Roman Church, is seen to have fallen into great humiliation, and we too appear to have been brought into excessive diminishment and contempt, since those matters which, while the Lombards held power, we appeared able to administer and arrange authoritatively are now, in your times, being taken from our authority by the impious and perverse men who are enemies of both you and us. And behold, many of our enemies reproach us, taunting us and saying: “What benefit did it bring you that the nation of the Lombards was destroyed and subjected to the kingdom of the Franks? Behold, nothing of what was promised has yet been fulfilled; moreover, even those things previously granted to blessed Peter by the lord King Pippin of holy memory are now known to have been taken away.”

For the claim which the aforementioned most wicked archbishop advances, putting forward as his pretext that the exarchate of Ravenna should be granted to him with the same authority that Archbishop Sergius possessed, we, most excellent son, wish to administer and arrange it under our authority in our own times just as in the time of Lord Pope Stephen, who went there into Francia and to whom that exarchate itself was entrusted. Everyone can recognize from this what authority his blessedness [Lambecius, Gentilotus: “thrice-blessedness”] possessed over that same city of Ravenna and the entire exarchate; for he removed Archbishop Sergius from there when Sergius was attempting, in a spirit of pride, to act against his will [Note: [Col. 0284D] See above, letter 13, otherwise 27, note. Everyone clearly considers this remarkable history, which we owe to our Codex, preferable to the account of Agnellus, the schismatic author of the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Ravenna*. Yet Agnellus, in his account of Sergius, chapter 4, supports the reliability of this letter and should not be rejected: “He judged,” he says, “the whole Pentapolis from the borders of Pertica, and as far as Tuscany, and as far as Walami’s table; as exarch, he arranged everything just as the Romans now customarily do.” For this reason he was living at Rome under Pope Paul, when other disputes arose against him because he was married. Rubeus, Ughellus, and Bacchinius placed excessive trust in Agnellus. I readily grant that Stephen II used the archbishop’s services in administering the new territory; but that he was deposed by that same Stephen because he was claiming too much for himself is so plainly established by this letter that the opinions of later writers seem to deserve no credence. CENN.].

[Col. 0285A] Indeed, our predecessor used to distribute all the administrative affairs of that same exarchate for execution, and all the agents received instructions concerning those affairs from this Roman city. He also sent from this Roman city judges to administer justice to all who suffered violence while residing in that same city of Ravenna—namely, Philip, at that time a presbyter, and likewise Eustachius, formerly a duke. And so that your most Christian excellence may be more fully satisfied concerning this matter, may you deign to summon the aforementioned Bishop Philip; after questioning him about such matters, you can most certainly learn the truth, because everything is exactly as we have reported.

Do not, good and most excellent son, allow the holy Church of God, the Roman Church, your spiritual mother, which is the head of all the churches of God, to fall into such contempt and diminished humiliation. Rather, I ask you before almighty God to order matters in such a way and deign to place that same archbishop under our authority, so that the entire exarchate may be administered by us [Note: [Col. 0285D] The loyalty of the people of the Pentapolis was recently praised against the archbishop’s schemes; he is therefore now striving only for the exarchate. ID.], just as the aforementioned Lord Stephen, most blessed pope, appears to have administered it in the time of your father of holy memory, Lord Pippin. Thus, during your most fortunate reign, that holy universal Church of God may remain exalted; and, through the aid of the apostles blessed Peter and Paul, may you deserve in this present life to possess the government of the kingdom for a long old age with immense victories, and in the future blessedness to attain the heavenly kingdoms.

[Col. 0285C] Behold, we have sent to your royal presence our faithful chamberlain Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0285D] The similarity of his name to Anastasius, who in the preceding letter brought the citizen of Pisa, Gausfridus, back to Charles while Charles was still in Italy, although the office of chamberlain is not mentioned there, seems to indicate that he is the same man. This causes no chronological difficulty in the two letters: four or five months lie between the two missions. ID.], and we have placed in his mouth what he is to report on our behalf to your excellence. We commend him to you in every respect and ask that you order him to be trusted in all things and sent back to us with good news and with the case settled. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord Charles the king through Andrew and Anastasius

For the justice of the holy Church of God, and concerning Leo, archbishop, who hastened to the aforementioned lord king [Note: [Col. 0285D] Summary of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 30): “In the thirtieth [reading: thirtieth] letter he asks Charles to remember what he promised to the apostle Peter and how many benefits he has received from him—namely, the province of the Lombards—and that, surrounded by his aid, he may subdue all the other nations. Concerning Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, he indicates that he is pleased that Leo has gone to Charles.” CENN.].

*(A.D. 775, Carolingian Codex LIII, chronicle 52.)*

[Col. 0286A]

### ARGUMENT

The apostolic messengers, Bishop Andrew and the chamberlain Anastasius, having returned from the court, testify to Charles’s constancy in fulfilling his promises. The pontiff rejoices and gives thanks; nevertheless, he asks that Charles fulfill his donation as soon as possible, so that blessed Peter, who subjected the kingdom of the Lombards to him, may also grant him victories over barbarian nations. He does not disapprove of Charles’s having received the archbishop Leo, as he had learned from the king’s letters; but he does not praise the fact that Leo departed without the pontiff’s knowledge, although the pontiff had joined his own messenger to him.

Adrian, pope [Note: [Col. 0286D] Summary 30, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.], to his most excellent son Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans:

Our messengers, whom we recently appeared to have sent to your excellence, illumined by God—namely, our most reverend brother Bishop Andrew and Anastasius the chamberlain [Note: [Col. 0286D] In the preceding letter only Anastasius the chamberlain was sent as legate to Charles; here we see that Bishop Andrew was his colleague on the return journey from Francia. None of Adrian’s letters preserved in the codex records a joint mission of these two men. Either Bishop Andrew had been sent before or after the chamberlain, with only a short interval between them—for both had recently departed—or he left Rome together with the same chamberlain after the letters had been sent. This letter certainly followed the preceding one. CENN.], brought us the honored and honey-sweet letters of your most kindly Christian devotion. When their contents were read to our ears, we clearly learned everything contained in them. The aforementioned messengers of yours also faithfully reported to us everything entrusted to them by you, asserting most fully your benevolent purity and the great steadfastness of heart which you appear to possess toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward our humble self, according to your promise.

For this reason, filled with excessive joy, we immediately raised our hands toward heaven and offered immense thanks to our Lord God, creator of all, earnestly beseeching his divine mercy for your prosperity, that our same Lord God may strengthen this very disposition in your flower-bearing heart, so that your holy spiritual mother, our Roman Church, head of all the churches of God [Note: [Col. 0286D] We have seen that the Roman Church was defined in the same way in the preceding letter. Learned readers will find many examples of this sort, familiar to them. One authority may suffice for all: that of Saint Boniface I (Coustant, p. 1037), in a letter to the bishops of Thessaly: “Therefore it is certain that this [Roman Church] is the head of the churches spread throughout the whole world, as of its members; whoever cuts himself off from it becomes an exile from the Christian religion, since he no longer belongs to the same structure.” For this reason, in the same passage Boniface testifies that the Council of Nicaea did not dare to establish anything concerning it—namely, in canon 6, which in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, session 16 (Labbe, vol. IV, p. 812), begins with this principle: “That the Roman Church has always held primacy.” In later centuries, as ignorance gradually increased—or, better said, as the true meaning of “Church” fell into disuse—we find primacy attributed to the walls of some temple or basilica. Adrian, although unlearned and wrapped in the thick darkness of his age, rightly assigns it repeatedly to the Roman Church founded by the prince of the apostles. CENN.], may swiftly obtain abundant fruit from your promise.

[Col. 0287A] But, good, sweetest, and most excellent son, my lord, great king appointed by God, I beseech and earnestly ask you, as though I were presently standing before your eyes, with great confidence, to order swiftly the fulfillment of what you promised to offer by your donation to blessed Peter, the great reward of your soul and the stability of your kingdom protected by God—to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Thus may that same prince of the apostles exist as your protector and helper before the power of the divine majesty to a far greater degree.

For you have been fully convinced, most excellent of kings, what kind of mighty and powerful gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven, blessed Peter, has proved himself to be as a helper to your excellence; and how, through his holy intercessions, almighty God our Lord granted you victory and ordered the kingdom of the Lombards to be handed over to your power and dominion. Henceforth, have great confidence, because, surrounded by his aid, almighty God will subject the other barbarian nations to your royal feet [Note: [Col. 0287D] Charles achieved a notable victory over the Saxons this year. Yet he did not proceed against them until the end of July, as Pagius proves (775, no. 5). Since Adrian wrote this letter before that time, he mentions only the Lombard victory which Charles had achieved in the preceding year, while anticipating the Saxon victory. ID.]. For we are wholly satisfied and have great confidence in the steadfastness of your heart that you will swiftly complete everything which you promised to that apostle and prince of the apostles. We know very well what firmness and stability of integrity, with God as guide, were strengthened between us in the apostolic court [Note: [Col. 0287D] The events briefly indicated here took place in the preceding year, on Holy Saturday and Easter Day, that is, on April 2 and 3, and are narrated at length by Anastasius in the *Life of Adrian* (sections 316 and following). ID.]; we know in whom we have trusted, and we are certain.

As for what you have informed us—that the archbishop Leo has hastened to you—we, as Truth bears witness, most willingly welcome those who hasten to your royal presence, because one love, one charity, and the same affection of purity prevail between us. If the aforementioned archbishop had informed us that he wished to go to your presence, we would gladly have sent our messenger with him [Note: [Col. 0288C] Pagius is mistaken (776, no. 3) in thinking that Leo approached Charles when Charles returned to Italy in the year 776 against the duke of Friuli; for below the pontiff also conveys greetings to the queen. The archbishop had therefore gone to Francia, doubtless to secure the king’s support against the pontiff in defending his invasions, either at the end of 774 or at the beginning of this same year, 775, while his indignation was raging and he was leaving no stone unturned to suppress the invader of the exarchate. The matter did not concern the Lombards, but a bishop subject to him who had usurped tyrannical power. ID.].

Accordingly, your present messenger brought us another letter from your excellence. As we learned the crowded contents of its page [Col. 0288A], our spirit greatly rejoiced in the kindly purpose of your mind [Note: [Col. 0288D] Others may guess who this royal messenger was and what the letter contained that brought joy to the pontiff. Certainly, the letter did not concern the archbishop of Ravenna. Indeed, when the opportunity arose, the pontiff broke off his discussion of him and clearly showed that he disapproved of his journey to Francia. ID.]. We earnestly beseech our redeemer to grant that, with a long and prosperous old age, with great victory over your enemies, you may enjoy the government of the heavenly kingdom together with our most excellent daughter, protected by God, our most gracious and truly Christian queen, the most faithful lover of blessed Peter and your sweetest wife, and together with your beloved children; and that he may grant you the joys of the heavenly kingdom, to be possessed eternally with the saints. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord Charles the king

In it are contained very abundant blessings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and a discussion of the letter of John, patriarch of Grado [Note: [Col. 0288D] Summary of Panvinio (Vatican Codex 29): “In the twenty-ninth [twenty-ninth] letter are contained very abundant blessings—or rather flatteries—for the exaltation of the holy Church of God. He indicates that he is sending a letter from John, patriarch of Grado. He complains that this letter had first been opened and read by Leo, archbishop of Ravenna. He therefore accuses Leo again.” ID.].

*(A.D. 775, Carolingian Codex LII, chronicle 53.)*

[Col. 0288B]

### ARGUMENT

After waiting a long time for the royal messengers bearing good news from the royal household, he finally writes himself. For he had received, in particular, a letter from John, patriarch of Grado, dated October 27, which he forwards to Charles. He says, however, that he received it unsealed after Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had opened and read it, so that Leo might inform Duke Arichis of Benevento and the other enemies of the pope and of Charles of its contents. For after his return from Francia Leo was dominating Emilia and allowed no one seeking a charter from the holy see to approach; he had also expelled the agents of the holy see and was boasting that Bologna and especially Imola had been granted to him by Charles.

Adrian, pope [Note: [Col. 0288D] Summary 19, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.], to his most excellent son Charles, king of the Franks [Col. 0288C] and Lombards and patrician of the Romans:

Since such great love and the firm integrity of charity have, with God’s guidance, been strengthened between us, we are seized by a great desire of fervor to be assured of the immense joy of your prosperity. Therefore, with a paternal affection of sincerity, we kiss your excellence, protected by God, three times and most devotedly in the Lord. We ask you to make us more clearly joyful as soon as possible concerning the soundness of your health, that of our most excellent daughter, our sweet daughter the great queen, illumined by God, and that of your most excellent sons [Note: [Col. 0289C] Before he married Hildegard at the end of 771, Charles had fathered a son, Pippin, by Himiltrude; he had no offspring by Desiderius’s daughter, whom he returned untouched to her father. It is uncertain how many children he had so far by Hildegard. Yet that he had several sons in the year 777 is testified by the oath of the Saxons (Frankish and Fulda Annals), in which they promise “loyalty to Lord King Charles and his sons.” Pagius conjectures that there were four (783, no. 3), citing the words of Einhard, who lists six children of Hildegard: “She bore three sons—namely Charles, Pippin, and Louis—and as many daughters, Rothrude, Berta, and Gisela.” Charles, the eldest, was born in March 772; Rotrude around February 773; Adelaide in the camp at Ticinum, as Paul the Deacon reports in *On the Bishops of Metz*, that is, in 774; and Berta in 775. See the cited Pagius, who also discusses the other two, Lothair and Adelaide, who died before their mother and are not listed by Einhard, as well as Pippin, the son of Himiltrude, and Hildegard, who survived her mother by only forty days. The point is that in the present year Charles had four or five children, whose safety the pontiff desires. CENN.], since we have remained waiting until now to receive your messengers, but they have not yet reached us [Note: [Col. 0289D] It is established somewhat below that this letter was written toward the end of October and that the royal messengers had still not arrived at Rome after Charles’s departure from Italy; hence the pontiff’s intense desire for their arrival. Outwardly, he is concerned with the safety of the king and the royal family. In reality, he is troubled by the schemes of the archbishop of Ravenna, whom he knew first to have approached Charles through legates and then in person, and whom he saw usurping control of the exarchate; nor was Charles’s attitude on this matter sufficiently clear to him. ID.].

For this reason, the greatest affection of love compels us to express openly to your royal eminence the sincerity of our heart, since your safety is our joy and the benefit of your prosperity is our exultation. Therefore we inform your excellence that we have received a letter sent to us by John, patriarch of Grado. For the letter itself reached us on the twenty-seventh day of the month of October [Col. 0289B], and immediately—not taking food or drink, neither we nor the writer of this apostolic communication—we transmitted to you, in that same hour and at that same moment, the aforementioned patriarch’s letter together with these apostolic words of ours.

We were therefore made exceedingly sad, because we found the seals of that letter to have been *asifoniatae* [Lambecius: *siphoniatae*] [Note: [Col. 0290C] *Disbullare* means to remove the seal. Ducange knows the word from the translator of the acts of the Sixth Council, session 15: “And this document was unsealed.” Likewise *dissignare*, *dissigillare*. What precisely a seal called *asifoniata*, or *siphoniata* as Lambecius reads it, may have been is not very clear. ID.] and that the letter, after first being read by Leo, archbishop, had been sent to us. In this your most excellent Christian devotion can judge what kind of deceitful faith belongs to that archbishop Leo, because he presumed to open and reread that letter beforehand for no other reason than to announce everything written there—as is certainly clear to everyone—to Duke Arghis of Benevento and to the rest of our and your enemies [Note: [Col. 0290C] These secrets doubtless concern the Greeks. The first of the enemies of the holy see and of Charles, who had driven the Lombard kings out of Italy, was Duke Arichis II of Benevento. Concerning him, the *Anonymous Chronicle of Salerno*, though everywhere overflowing with fables, says (chapter 9): “Duke Arichis alone remained at Benevento, disregarding his commands because he wore upon his head a precious crown.” The second was Rodgausus of Friuli, who paid the penalty for his audacity in the following year; the third was Hildebrand, duke of Spoleto. All of them will soon occur below, in letter 57, otherwise 59. ID.]. There is no doubt that everything has now been reported by that archbishop to the aforementioned enemies.

For our part, with Truth as witness, we declare before God that we remain purely and faithfully in your love [Col. 0290A], in accordance with what was confirmed between us in person in the apostolic court [Note: [Col. 0290D] In the note to the preceding letter, col. 287, I stated that the history indicated there and here should be sought again in Anastasius, sections 316 and following. ID.].
