We carefully strive to report to you the matters that reach us concerning the present situation, because, after God and blessed Peter, our hope and confidence are nowhere else except in your excellence, protected by God. For you, sweetest and great king, illumined by God, are our defender and protector with God; through you the holy Church of God, your spiritual mother, has been exalted and rejoices with great joy. We trust that you will swiftly bring to effect everything entrusted by you to blessed Peter.

But may almighty God, in whose hand all the kingdoms of the world are held, nurture you abundantly with his grace; may he grant that you possess the reins of the kingdom in a long and prosperous old age through the intercessions of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, rejoice together with our most excellent daughter, the queen, and your most beloved children, and attain eternally, with the saints, the heavenly kingdoms of reward. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

**POSTSCRIPT. Concerning Leo the archbishop**

[Note: “Postscript” (*embolum*, also found under forms derived from the Greek *embolis* and *embolim*) is for us a postscript, or an addition to an already written letter, as Ducange observes. Its meaning is very similar to that of the postscript of the following letter. In both places the archbishop of Ravenna claimed for himself Bononia and Imola, which it is not clear were possessed by the Apostolic See before Adrian, and he exercised tyranny over the other cities. Adrian especially emphasizes that Dominicus, commended to the pope by Charles, whom he had appointed count of Gabello, was bound, taken to Ravenna, and thrown into prison, in order to stir Charles against the archbishop. Editor.]

For we make known to your most excellent Christian Majesty that, when the aforesaid archbishop Leo returned from your royal presence, he fell into great pride and tyrannical arrogance, and was in no way inclined, as before, to obey our apostolic commands. He did not permit anyone from Ravenna or Emilia to come to us to receive instructions concerning various matters, and he grew so angry with them that he threatened them, saying that if any of them dared to come to us, he would not be able to do so. But all the people of the Pentapolis, remaining obedient in our apostolic service, hastened to us, submissive as in the time of our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, and received, as usual, instructions concerning each of their cities.

As for the remaining cities of Emilia, and likewise Gabello, which had been organized there by us, he afterward expelled those whom we had appointed and keeps others of them in chains. Concerning the cities of Imola and Bononia, he speaks so profanely as to say that your Excellence did not grant those cities at all to blessed Peter and to us, but that the archbishop himself had received and been entrusted with them by you, so that they might remain under his authority. Therefore he permitted no one from those cities to come to us, but appointed there, without our authority, whatever officials he wished and keeps them under his power.

May it not please you, most excellent son, that he should hold this Apostolic See in such contempt, disregarding the promise that he made under oath to blessed Peter and his vicars, but, like a transgressor of God’s commandments, falling under the guilt of perjury. For we firmly believe, and have great confidence, that you will strive to fulfill everything that you promised would be offered to blessed Peter through your donation, for the stability of your great kingdom and for the eternal reward to be bestowed upon you.

### LV. ITEM: LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

In it are contained thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and a report concerning the lord king’s envoys, who were supposed to come to Rome in the autumn.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 33): “The thirty-third [letter] contains thanksgivings, together with a petition for the exaltation of the holy Church of God. Likewise, [it concerns] the envoys of King Charles, who were supposed to come to Rome in the autumn.” Cenn.]

*(A.D. 775, Codex Carolinus LI, chronicle 54.)*

**SUMMARY.**—Bishop Andrew had announced that his envoys from Charles would arrive in the autumn and complete his donation through them. The pope had waited for them throughout November, and had finally sent to inquire of the judges at Pavia, who now denied that the royal envoys were coming. He therefore sends the same Bishop Andrew and Abbot Pardus with instructions concerning what they are to report in person. He asks Charles to fulfill for blessed Peter what he had promised together with his father Pippin and afterward confirmed with his own hands. Concerning Archbishop Leo he reports nearly the same things as in the preceding letter; he adds that Dominicus, commended to him by Charles and appointed by him count of Gabello, had been not only prevented by Leo from carrying out his office but ordered to be taken in chains to Ravenna, where Leo keeps him under guard.

To the lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

While your holy Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Church, your spiritual mother, rejoices in such great security and gladness, the exceedingly renowned memory of your name has therefore spread throughout the whole world and remains honorably celebrated. From the Apostolic Palace also, prayers and vows, and divine sacrificial offerings, are diligently presented by us and by all the priests of God to the divine Majesty for the forgiveness of your sins.

[Note: Although Mabillon (*Annales Benedictini*, book XLII, nos. 21 and 35) and the Maurist Fathers in their additions to the *Glossary* observe that this designation was also applied to other sacred buildings, no temple or basilica suits it better than the Vatican, where the most sacred ashes of the chief of the apostles rest. Of it one may truly say, with the great Pope Nicholas III: “This is the house of God, firmly built upon the rock, in which the most sacred body of Peter himself also rests honorably; this is the divine tabernacle loved by the heavenly choirs and venerated by the whole world” (*Vatican Bullary*, vol. I, p. 202). How highly the same place was esteemed among the Franks, especially by Charlemagne, this collection of letters repeatedly shows. Cenn.]

Therefore, most excellent son, we believe that your Christian Majesty, protected by God, sent word to us through Andrew, our most reverend and most holy brother, the bishop, in reply that during this autumn season you would endeavor to send your envoys into our presence, who were to hand over to us everything according to your promise.

[Note: What he had stated less clearly in the preceding letters, he expresses here plainly. The royal envoys were to transfer to the Apostolic See possession of cities and territories not yet possessed by it. Editor.]

We waited until now, throughout September, October, and the present month of November, to receive your envoys and learn through them of your well-being. Since they had not come to us at all, we sent our apostolic letters as far as Pavia, to those judges whom you appeared to have established there,

[Note: The Frankish Annals for the year 774 state: “After King Charles had subdued and organized Italy, he left a Frankish garrison in the city of Pavia, etc.” The Annals of Metz relate the matter in nearly the same words, as cited by Pagi (774, no. 7). The monk of Angoulême likewise does so (*Pithoean edition*, part II, p. 19). In this letter Adrian shows that, besides a garrison, judges had also been appointed to administer public affairs. Editor.]

so that they might inform us of the arrival of those same envoys of yours. They replied to us that your envoys were by no means now setting out to come to us.

Therefore a great longing weighs upon our heart, and meanwhile the innermost feelings of our mind burn more ardently with love for you. Wishing therefore to become certain and joyful concerning your prosperity, we have earnestly taken care to send our present envoys to your royal presence: namely, the aforesaid Andrew, our most holy brother, the bishop, and Pardus, beloved of God, our beloved son, the abbot.

[Note: This embassy deserves attention, lest the frequent use of Bishop Andrew in embassies cause some letters to be confused, while his colleague is overlooked. Pardus, therefore, the abbot—or, in Greek, the *hegumenus*—went to Francia on this occasion as Andrew’s companion. He is mentioned again below (letter 59, formerly 50). Editor.]

They are visiting and greeting through their agency your most excellent Christian Majesty, as well as our most excellent daughter, your beloved wife, the queen, enlightened by God, and your sweet and noble children. We have placed in the mouths of these envoys of ours everything in the greatest detail, and carefully instructed them concerning what they must recount on our behalf to your Excellence, protected by God, regarding each matter.

We ask that you receive them kindly and with a cheerful face, believe the words that they deliver on our behalf, lend the ear of your kindness to them, and deign to complete and fulfill everything that your father, of holy memory, the lord King Pippin, promised to blessed Peter together with you, and that afterward you yourself, great king instituted by God, confirmed when you journeyed to the threshold of the apostles, making the same pledge; and that you then offered that promise in person to the same apostle of God with your own hands.

[Note: There is such agreement between the writer of Adrian’s Life (in Anastasius, section 319) and these letters of Adrian himself that neither can be denied credence. Here are the actual words: “After that donation had been made, and the most Christian king of the Franks had confirmed it with his own hand, he caused all the bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts to be entered into it. Having first placed it upon the altar of blessed Peter and afterward within his holy shrine, both the king of the Franks himself and his judges delivered it to blessed Peter and his vicar, the most holy Pope Adrian, promising under a terrible oath that they would preserve everything contained in that donation. Causing a copy of the donation to be written by the same Etherius, the most Christian king of the Franks placed it with his own hands inside, above the body of blessed Peter and beneath the Gospels—which are kissed there—as the firmest safeguard and for the eternal memory of his name and of the kingdom of the Franks.” This concerns the donation of Pippin, confirmed and greatly enlarged by Charles. Cenn.]

For we have great confidence in the steadfastness of your heart, and are entirely certain of the benevolent purpose of your mind.

Accordingly, we await receiving from you an abundant fruit, so that, just as you have begun the good work, you may complete it, and in your time the holy Church of God may remain exalted to a far greater degree. Thus may the almighty Lord, through the intercession of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, grant you a worthy reward and, after the long duration of this life, receive you, eternally exalted among the saints and elect, into the heavenly kingdoms.

For through you, good and most victorious king, the aforesaid holy universal Church of God, rescued from the attacks of its enemies, triumphs, as has been said, with great joy, and the orthodox faith of Christians, through your protection, remains unimpaired in its former state of veneration.

For this reason we earnestly ask that you order us to be made certain as soon as possible of your prosperity, because your safety is our security, and your joy is demonstrably our joy. Therefore, remaining steadfast in your love and in the charity of affection, we unceasingly beseech the divine clemency to protect you in many ways by its grace, granting to your Excellence, to our most excellent daughter the queen, and to your most beloved children the possession of the reins of the kingdom through long and prosperous years, prostrating all barbarian nations before your feet, enlarging the boundaries of your kingdom in many ways, and making you participants also in the joys of the heavenly kingdom. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

**POSTSCRIPT ON THE ARROGANCE OF LEO THE ARCHBISHOP**

[Note: Centuriator calls the charter an interpolation. Grets.]

[Note: Because of this rebellion and obstinacy, this Leo deserved to be placed by Illyricus in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, p. 68. That is, the more stubborn and stiff-necked a man is, the more favor he finds with Illyricus, and the greater a witness—beyond every exception—to Lutheran truth he is. And yet, if this Leo came to life again, he would detest Illyricus as a criminal innovator and bid him go to the bad gallows. Observe, moreover, that through ignorance Illyricus did not know what the “oletan canons” were in Pope Adrian; for they are not so called from a place, but from age: for *oletanum* in Adrian means nothing other than old and ancient. Cenn.]

We also make known to your Excellence, protected by God, that after Archbishop Leo returned from you, he was raised up in excessive pride and in no way wished to obey our commands as before. Rather, with a strong arm, he appears to have retained Imola and Bononia under his own authority until the present, saying that you granted those cities in no way to blessed Peter or to us, but only to Leo himself, the archbishop.

Therefore we sent there our envoy, namely Gregory the treasurer, who was to bring the judges of those cities to us and receive from their entire population oaths of loyalty to blessed Peter, to us, and to your Excellence. But that same archbishop did not permit our treasurer to go there.

Dominicus also, whom you delivered and commended to us in the Church of blessed Peter, we appointed count in the very small city of Gabello, granting him the charter of that city. But Leo did not permit him to perform that office; instead, he sent an army, took him to Ravenna in chains, and held him under guard.

As for the other cities of Emilia—namely Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara, Comacchio, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Cesena and Bobbio, or the tenth tribunate—

[Note: Fontanini, in *On the Dominion of Parma and Piacenza* (p. 23), supposes on the authority of this passage that the exarchate was accustomed to be administered by tribunes. But he is mistaken: the passage itself indicates Sassina, or the area near Sassina. Editor.]

he permitted no one from them to come to us to receive instructions concerning their affairs, although all those people were ready to join us.

As for the remaining cities of both Pentapoles, from Rimini as far as Gubbio,

[Note: This division of the Pentapolis into the maritime and inland Pentapolis should be noted. Gregory II, in his letter to Leo the Isaurian in 726 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 19), calls the exarchate together with the Pentapolis the Decapolis: “The Lombards and Sarmatians, and the others who dwell toward the north, harassed the wretched Decapolis with their incursions and occupied Ravenna itself, its metropolis”—though the name is inaccurate, for the cities of the Pentapolis alone numbered more than ten. Adrian therefore, dividing it into two parts, more correctly calls them the Pentapoles. Paul above (letter 26, formerly 28) also mentions the maritime cities but designates a single Pentapolis. Editor.]

all came to our presence in the customary manner, received from us instructions concerning the affairs of those cities, and all faithfully remain in our service and obedience. Only the archbishop persists in the arrogance of his ferocity.

But we ask you, most excellent son, before the living God, that you in no way approve of this: that what your father, of holy memory, and you yourself granted and offered to blessed Peter should, God forbid, be taken away during your reign, and that the Church of blessed Peter should be humiliated by wicked men who introduce injustice. Rather, may it always remain exalted through you.

### LVI. ITEM: LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING [CHARLES]

In it is contained an account of the death of the emperor Constantine and of Reginald, duke of Chiusi. The aforesaid pope asks that the lord king not permit him to continue in that office and retain it, because he did not cease continually to commit many evils in the fortress of Felicitas.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 21): “The twenty-first [letter] indicates that the emperor Constantine had died, adding a letter concerning this matter from Stephen, bishop of Naples. It accuses Reginald, duke of Chiusi, of not ceasing continually [or: of continually committing] many evils in the Castle of Felicitas by taking away the property of blessed Peter. It asks that he be removed from office.” Cenn.]

*(A.D. 776, Codex Carolinus LX, chronicle 55.)*

**SUMMARY.**—He had learned from advance messengers that Copronymus was dead, but had not wished to report an uncertain matter. He now appends a letter from Stephen, bishop of Naples, received on the seventh of the present February. Reginald, formerly castaldus of the Castle of Felicitas and now duke of Chiusi, was inflicting much damage upon the Church; recently he had gone with troops to the same city, the Castle of Felicitas, a possession of the Holy See, and had removed its castellans. The pope asks Charles to remove him from Tuscany as a man harmful to both himself and the Church.

To the lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

By these apostolic writings we make known to your most excellent Christian Majesty, protected by God, that word had reached us through advance messengers that the emperor Constantine had been taken from this light by a divine summons.

Because we had not learned the matter with certainty, we delayed informing your Excellence, protected by God. But now our most holy and most reverend brother Stephen, bishop of the city of Naples, has suggested that he make the same matter known to us through this letter. We received and read it on the seventh day of the present month of February and hastened at once to communicate it to your royal highness. For the great satisfaction of your sublime dignity, we have placed the same message below within this letter addressed to you.

[Note: The age and meaning of this letter have been discussed at length in the preliminary commentary (no. 26 and following). All authorities rightly and unanimously assign it to the year 776. I have placed it before the other letters dated to that year because I found it written at the beginning of February; those that follow appear to have been written later in the same year, as will soon become clear. Cenn.]

Meanwhile we also send this message to your Excellence, most sweet and beloved son, concerning that treacherous man, sower of tares, and instigator and enemy of the human race, Reginald, formerly castaldus in the Castle of Felicitas,

[Note: *Castaldus*, *castaldio*, *gastaldus*, *gastaldio*, *gastaldius*, and *gastaldeus* designate the same office instituted by the Lombards. Its holder administered a royal estate, or even a city, but his jurisdiction also extended over the common people. See Ducange under “Gastaldus,” where the matter is treated at length. Muratori (*Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 10) argues that count and gastaldus were one and the same in the duchy of Benevento, and proves by examples that cities were also sometimes entrusted to such officials elsewhere. Editor.]

who now appears to be duke in the city of Chiusi.

[Note: The same Muratori (*Italian Antiquities*, vol. I, dissertation 5) distinguishes greater and lesser dukes in Italy. He demonstrates by numerous examples that cities were assigned to the lesser dukes, while provinces were assigned to the greater. We see the same arrangement formerly in Francia: the Carolingian mayors of the palace and their predecessors were called by the name of dukes. In the same place he also employs this letter against Florentinius and Cosmas della Rena, who argue that the dukes of Lucca governed all Tuscany. He adds letter 74 in our numbering, formerly 80, which concerns Gundibrand, duke of Florence, and rightly concludes that there were several dukes in Tuscany during the eighth century. No one will doubt that the duke of Chiusi should be counted among these lesser dukes. Editor.]

He does not cease to inflict very great evils through his wicked acts of submission upon your spiritual mother, the holy Church of God, and upon us, while he strives by his wicked device to take away everything that your Excellence has offered to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, for the salvation of your soul, and desires to hold those things in his own service.

For this reason he himself hastened with an army to that same city of ours, the Castle of Felicitas,

[Note: I have already said in the preliminary commentary (no. 30) that the Lombard cities of Tuscany also had been granted by Charles to the Apostolic See. The evidence is stronger because the pope nowhere mentions the donation of Pippin, but testifies that the Castle of Felicitas was donated by Charles himself. I do not concern myself with the fact that the site of the city remains unknown to this day and has been thought to be where Tifernas, or the city of Castello, now stands (Muratori, *Annals*, 780). It is enough for me to identify a Tuscan city of the Lombards that the pope calls “ours,” as he does the other cities of the Roman duchy and exarchate, as well as of both Pentapoles. Editor.]

removed its castellans, and we by no means believe, most kind and Christian son, that your kingship, strengthened by God, made this change for the advancement of the aforesaid Duke Reginald,

[Note: What could be clearer? Adrian suspects that Charles may have granted the Castle of Felicitas to Reginald after making the donation to blessed Peter; the following passages make this evident. The pope says one thing but believes another, for he asks that Reginald be removed from the office of duke of Chiusi because, when he was the castaldus of that same city under King Desiderius, he also troubled the Apostolic See and was therefore a bad neighbor. Editor.]

together with your most excellent daughter, the queen, your sweetest children, or the entire Frankish army instituted by God, except for the support of your beloved holy Church of God, so that it might continue forever in your benevolent struggle.

Therefore we ask, and insist with very humble supplication, that your power, enlightened by God, for love of the apostle blessed Peter, in no way permit the aforesaid Reginald to remain there in the regions of Tuscany. Nor should you grant him permission to exercise that office; and may it not seem burdensome to you to grant this request confidently, because of the love by which we are joined together.

We hope to obtain it, since even in the time of Desiderius he did not cease frequently to sow quarrels and scandals. But, most excellent son, just as after God we hope in your mighty arm, together with our whole people, and day and night implore divine clemency for your safety and victories,

[Note: Lambecius has *victoriis concedendi* (“of granting victories”). Gentilotus did indeed read the word *concedendum* (“to be granted”) in the manuscript, but it was deleted by a line drawn beneath it. Editor.]

so may you hasten to arrange all the affairs of the holy Church of God, that the holy Church of God and we ourselves may continue during your most fortunate reign, and that, just as God has granted you temporal possessions, so he may grant you the heavenly ones to possess. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

### LVII. ITEM: LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

For the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and concerning Possessor and Rabigaud [Rabigandus], who, despising the Apostolic See, had gone to Hildebrand, duke of Spoleto, and from there had reached Benevento.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 24): “In the twenty-fourth [letter] he complains that he had been slighted by Possessor, the bishop, and Rabigandus, the abbot, envoys of Charles. He indicates that they had not come to Rome but had gone to Spoleto to Duke Hildebrand and from there to Benevento. He writes how greatly distressed he is on this account and asks Charles to console him by exalting the Roman Church and restoring the duchy of Spoleto.” Cenn.]

*(A.D. 776, Codex Carolinus LVIII, chronicle 56.)*

**SUMMARY.**—When the arrival of the royal envoys had been announced to him—namely, Bishop Possessor and Abbot Rabigandus—he sent a suitable escort to meet them. But they turned aside from Perugia toward Spoleto, to Hildebrand, and from there to Benevento, and did not first come to Rome according to the royal command. Charles ought to remember what he had promised to blessed Peter before his shrine: that the duchy of Spoleto itself had been offered by him to that chief of the apostles. He asks Charles to keep faith and relieve, through other envoys, the excessive anxiety with which he was afflicted.

To the lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

We are entirely confident and certain that your Excellence, protected by the Lord, will strive to remain firmly and immutably in those matters which we agreed upon when speaking together, and will endeavor to preserve, with complete openness of mind and sincere affection, the bond of charity strengthened between us.

While, by God’s favor, we ourselves diligently strive to persevere with great sincerity of mind in that same concord of mutual affection, we say before God as witness—for by him we have been bound to your honey-sweet Christian Majesty in reciprocal friendship—that we appear to have the greatest confidence in your benevolence inspired by God: namely, that all the affairs of the holy Church of God and of our province will be brought to a beneficial conclusion.

[Note: For almost two full years he had earnestly desired envoys from Francia to come to Rome, with whom he had matters of great importance to discuss, especially the complete execution of Charles’s donation. When they finally arrived and he judged himself deceived by them, he reminds Charles of the bond of friendship by which they had previously been joined together before the body of Saint Peter. Cenn.]

But, most excellent son, preserved by God, good and best of kings, through the course of this apostolic report we bring to your knowledge that, when news reached us of the arrival of your most faithful envoys—namely, Possessor, our most holy brother, the bishop, and Rabigandus, the religious abbot—our spirit was lifted in great joy.

For it is exceedingly desirable for us always to receive the envoys of your Excellence with great joy and fitting honor and through them to learn with certainty of your sublime well-being. Therefore, in the manner befitting envoys of your royal power, we immediately sent every preparation, including horses, to meet them.

[Note: We have so far read of no royal envoy who was met with such an escort. From this we learn the custom for receiving royal embassies. Editor.]

When they had reached Perugia, however, instead of proceeding by the direct route to us, as they had been sent by your God-protected highness, and as we found when rereading your honorable letter, they despised us and went to Hildebrand at Spoleto. Through our envoys they sent us word that “we are speaking only with Hildebrand, and afterward, as we have been directed, we shall come with you to the lord apostolic.”

After they had spoken with the aforesaid Hildebrand and remained with him for a considerable time, we sent them our apostolic letter, adjuring them by God almighty and by the life of our most excellent son, the lord Charles the Great, king, to strive to come to us as they had been directed, so that together we might consider what pertained to the exaltation of the holy Church of God and strive to accomplish it for the praise of your kingdom, most excellent son. Then, as is fitting for envoys of his Excellence, we would arrange for you [the envoys] to proceed to Benevento.

But they, we do not know what they were considering, immediately went from Spoleto to Benevento, leaving us in great disgrace and increasing the Spoletoans’ insolence. Thus they greatly disturbed our province, and on this account our spirit lies in deep sadness, because, though we had expected through them to receive the hoped-for news of the exaltation of our holy Church, as we find in your honorable letters and as our envoys reported to us, they have endeavored [the text is elliptical] to leave us in such affliction and diminution.

But we believe that you remember, sweetest and most beloved son, how you addressed us with your most kindly mouth when you hastened to the threshold of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul. You would not have endured so much trouble with your entire Frankish army protected by God, seeking neither gold, nor gems, nor silver, nor letters, nor men,

[variant: *fastidium* (“weariness”); Lambecius reads *fatigium* (“fatigue”).]

unless you were striving to exact the rights of blessed Peter, complete the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and increase our security. Yet now, as though we were standing in person before your honey-sweet royal eyes, we earnestly ask and implore your royal power, established by God, to order us to be consoled and gladdened swiftly through your most faithful and kindly envoys concerning the great and grievous tribulation in which your own envoys have left us.

For you also offered the duchy of Spoleto itself in person to your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, through our humble agency, for the salvation of your soul.

[Note: Tuscany of the Lombards and the duchy of Spoleto had been offered to the Apostolic See, but with this distinction: the cities of Tuscany had been granted to the pope for perpetual possession and administration under supreme jurisdiction, whereas the duchy of Spoleto, like Tuscan Tuscany—“royal Tuscany,” as it is called—had been offered while supreme jurisdiction was retained, so that only the census, or tribute customarily paid by the Lombards to their kings before their overthrow, was granted to the Apostolic See, while supreme dominion remained with the Frankish kings.

Hence Adrian never calls the cities of those duchies “ours,” whereas we recently saw him call the Castle of Felicitas “our city,” and he regularly gives that designation to other cities of both the Roman province and the exarchate, as well as to both Pentapoles. Since some have paid no attention to this distinction, they throw both supreme jurisdiction and precarious tenure into doubt, confuse the donations, and obscure the truth. Cenn.]

Therefore we earnestly ask you, most excellent son, to bring our petition concerning the aforesaid affliction and the aforementioned duchy of Spoleto swiftly to completion. Thus may you receive from our most merciful God, through the intercession of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, for whose love and reverence you have been inspired to lend an ear to our petitions, a worthy reward.

For, as we say with God as witness, we desire nothing except your exaltation and joy, since, with God’s consent, a great and indissoluble concord of charity has been strengthened between us, and we remain in the things that we have mutually affirmed and confirmed. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

### LVIII. ITEM: LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

In it is contained an account that Hildebrand and Aragis [B. and Cent.: Arogis], as well as Rodgans and Regimbald [elsewhere: Reginald], the dukes, had made plans to unite with the Greeks and Adalgis, by land and sea, to fight against Rome and Italy; and the pope, with very solemn adjurations, asks for assistance against them.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 22): “In the twenty-second [letter] he complains that Hildebrand, Arogin, Rodgaus, and likewise Reginald, the dukes, had made plans with the Greeks and Adalgis to fight against Rome and Italy by land and sea [or: to attack Rome and Italy by land and sea]. Therefore, with many adjurations, he asks Charles for help against them.” Editor.]

*(A.D. 776, Codex Carolinus LIX, chronicle 57.)*

**SUMMARY.**—When Possessor and Rabigandus were coming from Benevento through Spoleto to Rome, the pope says that Hildebrand had asked him for a safe-conduct so that he could come here to seek pardon. He sent Stephen the treasurer there, and Stephen found the envoys of Arichis of Benevento, Rodgaus of Friuli, and Regimbald of Chiusi deliberating about undertaking war together with the Greeks and Athalgis, son of Desiderius, in the following month of March: they intended to invade Rome and restore the Lombard kingdom. He asks Charles to bring aid with the utmost speed, rescue Rome from the impending danger, and triumph over their common enemies.

To the lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

We deem it fitting to remind your excellence, protected by God, that we have repeatedly informed you about Hiltibrand, duke of Spoleto, Arigis, duke of Benevento, and Rodgaus of Friuli, concerning the most savage plot which they do not cease to devise against us and against you.

[Note: Cointius, Pagius, and Muratori assign this letter, together with the preceding one, to the year 775. Since both were written in February—for below the pontiff says that March would soon arrive—the sequence of events recommends assigning both to this year. At the beginning of 774, while Charles was besieging Pavia, Adalgis, fleeing Verona, had withdrawn to Constantinople; and the people of Spoleto, freed from fear, came to the pontiff and surrendered themselves to Saint Peter. They obtained from that same pontiff the confirmation of Hiltibrand, whom they had elected as duke, as is recorded in Anastasius (section 312). The Catalogue of Farfa, the Annals of Bertin, and Sigonius likewise testify that he became duke in that year, 774. No one will be persuaded that, after approximately seven months had passed since Charles’s departure from Italy, Hiltibrand and the other dukes formed their plans against the Holy See and Charles, that the pontiff uncovered them and repeatedly reported them to Charles, and that only now did he remember the pontifical warnings—warnings which could have been very recent only if the letter belonged to February of 775. On the contrary, in 775 (letter 53, formerly 52), the pontiff had indeed reported to Charles that those dukes were enemies of both himself and Charles. Note also that, at the end of 774 (letter 51, formerly 54), he entrusted several matters to be communicated orally to Anastasius the chamberlain. Likewise, in 775, in addition to what has been committed to writing above, he entrusted many things to the confidence of Andrew the bishop and Pardo the abbot, who were to relate them to the king (letter 54, formerly 51). Those matters undoubtedly concerned the secret plans of those dukes. Hence he says that he had repeatedly made their machinations known. CENN.]

But now, while your most faithful envoys—namely our most holy brother Possessor the bishop and Rabigaudus the religious abbot—are returning from Benevento and hastening to us through the aforesaid Hiltibrand, earnestly entreating us, on account of the fault of the aforementioned Hiltibrand, to grant him pardon, and asserting that [we should send] him our letter and hostages because of his uncertainty [Note: It seems that *mitteremus*, “we should send,” or something similar, is missing. GRETS.], and that Hiltibrand should present himself before our eyes [Note: He ceases to complain about the royal envoys, whose journey to Spoleto and Benevento had alarmed him. For he perceived that their legations would put an end to the wicked plans of the others, unless the events he soon relates had intervened; namely, the addition to that wicked alliance of Raginbald, duke of Chiusi, whom shortly before—on the seventh day of the same February—he had declared to be a man of doubtful loyalty. CENN.], we accordingly sent there as far as Spoleto our own most faithful Stephen, formerly our sacellarius, in accordance with the statement of your most faithful envoys. When he had spoken with Hiltibrand, and when we had then sent our hostages there, our envoy himself, upon joining him, found him in great insolence, because he had found there the envoys of Arigis, duke of Benevento, and of Rodgaus of Friuli [Note: As I have said, the pontiff had made known, both in writing and through the words of his envoys, the machinations of the duke of Friuli and the others toward the end of the preceding year. While his envoys were conferring with the others at Spoleto against Charles and the Holy See in February, Charles suddenly attacked the duke himself with arms, and shortly after the meeting at Spoleto the duke lost both his life and his duchy. The Frankish Annals clearly record this under the year 776: “Then King Charles entered Italy, passing through the territory of Friuli; Rodgaus was killed, and Lord King Charles celebrated Easter at the city of Treviso (14 April), and after capturing the cities of Friuli and Treviso, together with the other cities that had rebelled, he placed them all under the Franks and returned to Francia again in prosperity and victory.” The Fulda Annals briefly state under 775: “Rodgaus the Lombard seeks the kingdom of Italy.” And under 776: “Charles set out against Rodgaus into Italy and killed him.” See also Baronius (in this year, no. 3) and Pagius (no. 2), who rightly decide this matter in agreement with the ancient authors. Whatever the envoys or legates of those dukes resolved was therefore useless. I would not believe that the royal envoys were unaware of Charles’s decision; rather, they went to each duke as trustworthy guardians of the secret, so that Charles’s expedition might achieve its purpose while the dukes were unaware of his arrival—and this is what happened. ID.], as well as Regnibald, duke of the city of Chiusi, 345 meeting with the aforesaid Hiltibrand at Spoleto. They were devising a destructive plan against us: namely, that, God being opposed to them, when the coming month of March arrived they should all unite with a throng of Greeks and with Athalgis, son of Desiderius, and should rush upon us to fight by land and sea. They desired to invade this city of ours, Rome, strip all the churches of God, seize the ciborium of your protector, blessed Peter, and even—may the Divinity avert it—lead us ourselves away as captives; moreover, they intended to restore the Lombard king and resist your royal power.

For this reason, most excellent king and sweetest son, I ask you, and, as though present before you with the divine mysteries, I adjure you before the living and true God and before his chief apostle, blessed Peter, that with the greatest urgency and speed you come to our aid, lest we perish. For after God we have committed the souls of all of us Romans into your hands. Do not abandon us [Note: These words and what follows clearly show that the pontiff had no knowledge whatever of Charles’s expedition; the envoys who had conveyed the matter orally to one place had turned aside elsewhere and had not yet reached Rome. ID.], nor delay in bringing comfort, so that [Note: Lambinus and Gentianus read *solatiandum, ne dicant*, “bringing comfort, lest they say”; Gretser reads *differas solatium, ne*, “delay comfort, lest.”] the nations throughout the whole world may say: “Where is the confidence which the Romans, after God, placed in the king and kingdom of the Franks?”

And so, most beloved son protected by God, you will render an account of all these things before the tribunal of God, because, as we have said, by God’s command and that of blessed Peter, we have entrusted to your most sweet eminence the protection of God’s holy Church and the people of our Roman commonwealth. Therefore hasten to the threshold of your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that all the adversaries of God’s holy Church, whether our enemies or yours, may be laid beneath the feet of your royal majesty, and so that you may bring to fulfillment the things which you offered with your own hands to that same apostle of God for the reward of your soul. Thus, offering good fruit, may you deserve on the day of the future judgment to say:

“My Lord, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, I have completed my course, keeping faith with you. I defended and freed the Church of God, commended to you by heavenly clemency, from the hands of its persecutors. Standing undefiled before you, I offer you the children whom you entrusted to me to rescue from the hands of their enemies, now safe and unharmed.”

Then may you, who in the present life hold the reins of the kingdom, also deserve to attain the joys of heavenly rewards in the age to come, reigning with Christ, and hearing that desirable paternal voice which says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## LIX. 347 Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Charles

In it the aforesaid pope asks that, when returning from Saxony, the lord king hasten to the threshold of Saint Peter, as he had promised him.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex no. 18): “In the eighteenth [letter, formerly the eighteenth] he writes much about his own love and that of the people for Charles, and asks that, as he had promised, he hasten from Saxony, on his return, to the threshold of the apostle Peter [Saint Peter]. He also commends his envoys, Possessor the bishop and Rabigandus, for their loyalty in the service of Saint Peter.” CENN.]

*(Year of Our Lord 776, Codex of Charles LXIII, chronicle 58.)*

### ARGUMENT

Possessor and Rabigaudus reached Rome with royal letters, which brought the greatest joy to all orders, for they declared that Charles would return from Saxony to Italy, perhaps even to Rome. Rejoicing at this, the pope recalls the bond by which they had been united before the confession of the chief of the apostles. He also praises the royal envoys highly and commends them to Charles as men especially faithful to the king and to the Holy See.

To the most excellent son, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

While your spiritual mother, the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, continues to expand honorably in such joyful security, vows of prayer and offerings of divine sacrifices are diligently presented by us and by all the priests of God in the apostolic palace to the divine majesty, for the pardon of your offenses [Note: Either the pontiff had learned of Charles’s victory over the duke of Friuli, which overturned the plans of the conspirators, or the royal envoys had reported that the allied dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, terrified by the unexpected turn of events, had lost heart. He expresses the singular joy of the Holy See at having been delivered from the great fear expressed in the two preceding letters. Pagius (year 775, no. 7), following Cointius, places this letter before those two letters. But both learned men seem to have been mistaken. If the envoys had turned aside from Perugia to Spoleto, then to Benevento, and, returning from Spoleto, had passed through it again before finally coming to Rome—as is clearly contained in both letters—this letter followed both of them, not the reverse. CENN.].

And so, most excellent son, your most faithful envoys who joined us—namely, our most holy brother Possessor the bishop and Rabigaudus the religious abbot—brought us the greatly desired letters of your eminence [Note: Above (letter 56, formerly 58), while accusing them of having gone elsewhere, he says that he had reread your honored letters. This must be understood as referring to letters announcing the arrival of the envoys; for it is clearly established here that they themselves brought the royal letters. ID.]. We received them with the greatest sweetness of love, and, rereading them and learning of your immense prosperity, we gave great praise to our almighty God, who had given us so kindly and Christian a king as defender of his Church. For your royal letters stated that, with the Lord’s protection, upon your return from Saxony you desired shortly to hasten either to Italy or to the threshold of your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, in order to fulfill what you had promised him [Note: The Frankish Annals record that, on returning from Saxony in 775, Charles learned that the duke of Friuli was planning rebellion and therefore began an expedition into Italy against him. He undertook it at the beginning of the following year, as has just been said. The letters delivered by the envoys, perhaps written at the end of 775, may refer to this same expedition. This is suggested by the envoys’ visit to the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento; they did not undertake these conversations spontaneously but secretly on Charles’s orders, while Charles himself was conducting the war in the duchy of Friuli. The letters themselves, retained by the envoys until their arrival at Rome, support this still more strongly, lest Charles’s Italian expedition become known, although renewed Saxon rebellions recalled Charles from Italy. ID.]. When we heard this, our heart rejoiced exceedingly together with all our people, because we greatly desire to behold your most exalted face.

Since truth satisfies you, sweetest and most beloved son, great king appointed by God, we strive to remain firm and unchanging throughout the days of our lives, together with all our people, in that same pledge by which we were joined to one another before the sacred confession of that same apostle of God. Hence the affection of your royal eminence constantly impels us to learn of your well-being. Let your conspicuous excellence know that, if any delay should arise concerning your arrival, we have a great desire to set out to meet you wherever we may be able to join you.

349 Meanwhile we report to your excellency concerning the aforementioned most faithful envoys, that, just as they came to us and as we sent word to your royal power through our letters, so, when your envoys had been presented to us, we found them faithful in the service of your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and faithful to us and to you. Therefore we ask that you order them to be received kindly [Note: In a manner erasing what he had already written against them, since he learned that they had gone to Spoleto and Benevento for the good of the Church, the pontiff, and Charles, he says that their presence has nullified the suspicions about which he had written, and sends them back to Francia with the highest commendation. ID.].

Having said this, we beseech divine clemency to protect you in many ways by its grace; to grant you, our most excellent daughter the queen, and your beloved children long and prosperous times, that you may possess the governance of the kingdom; to cast all barbarian nations beneath your feet; to enlarge the boundaries of your kingdom in many ways; and to make you participants throughout endless ages in the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed, lord son.

## LX. 350 Another Letter of Pope Adrian, Addressed to Lord King Charles

It contains thanksgiving for the life and health of the lord king, his wife, and his son [L., G., “sons”], as well as for the exaltation of God’s holy Church; and it asks that he might deserve to receive his son from the sacred baptismal font.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 35): “In the thirty-fifth [letter, formerly the thirty-fifth] there are thanksgivings and many petitions for the restoration of the patrimony of blessed Peter. He mentions the donation made in the time of Constantine [Constantine] under Pope Silvester [Saint Silvester], and those of others who, for the reward [salvation] of their souls, donated many things to blessed Peter, which had been seized by the Lombards. He says that those donations are kept in the Lateran treasury. He calls Charles the new Constantine and asks that he be permitted to receive his son from the sacred baptismal font.” ID.]

*(Year of Our Lord 777, Codex of Charles XLIX, chronicle 59.)*

### ARGUMENT

Returning from Francia, Bishop Philip and the archdeacon Megistus reported Charles’s constant love for the Holy See, and that Charles would come to Rome with Queen Hildegard so that, when Easter arrived, he might have his newly born son Pippin baptized, with the pontiff receiving him from the sacred font. But when Charles did not come, the pontiff reveals his desire to be joined to the kings by this spiritual bond. Then, concerned for the affairs of the Church, he sends to him as envoys Philip and Andrew, bishops, and his nephew Theodore the duke, together with a catalogue of the donations made by Constantine, his successors, and the patricians in the provinces of Tuscany, Spoleto, Benevento, Corsica, and Sabina, compiled from the apostolic archive. These territories had long since been invaded by the Lombards and had not yet been restored. He asks Charles to renew the happy times of Constantine by exalting the apostolic see.

To the most excellent son, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Moved by our great love, we thought it fitting first to visit with these apostolic letters your excellence, protected by God, your offspring, and our spiritual daughter the queen, as well as the bishops and priests, all the nobles, and the entire people of your illustrious Frankish nation belonging to your kingdom strengthened by God, so that they might be assured of your health and made joyful, while we most earnestly seek the fullness of your prosperity.

Therefore, when the envoys of your spiritual mother, God’s holy Church, returned to us from the presence of your kingdom protected by God—namely, our most reverend brother Philip the bishop and our most beloved son Megistus the archdeacon [Note: It is uncertain when and with what letters this group of envoys departed for Francia. It may rightly be inferred, however, that the pontiff gave Charles letters full of official greetings, sent by those envoys merely as a gesture of salutation and to confirm fellowship and friendship; the following makes this clearer. CENN.]—they reported to us the constancy of your faith and charity, which you have deigned to show toward blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and toward our humility, for the reward of your soul.

When we heard this, our heart was greatly relieved by joy, and we began to offer praise to God and to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, for the exaltation of your kingdom, of our daughter the queen, your wife, and of your offspring, and for all the Franks, faithful to blessed Peter the apostle and to you.

But concerning what you deigned to promise us through the aforementioned envoys, our most reverend brother Philip the bishop and our most beloved Megistus the archdeacon—namely, that, with the Lord’s help, you would hasten with our spiritual daughter the queen on the holy day of Easter to the threshold of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that we might receive in our arms from the sacred baptismal font the son recently born to you—we waited for your honey-sweet excellence as parched earth waits for rain. When that holy day of Easter approached and we had received no message concerning your arrival or that of your envoys, in accordance with the agreement that had existed between us [Note: For the various meanings of *placitum*, see Ducange; here it means nothing other than an agreement. Gregory of Tours (book VII, chapter 6): “I beg that the agreements which were joined between us after my father’s death be preserved.” ID.], we became very sad [Note: This entire account, and still more its preface, refutes the learned Cointius and Pagius, who assign this letter to 776, when Charles was occupied with the Italian war against the duke of Friuli. For neither the queen, nor the children, nor the nobles, nor all the Franks together with the bishops and priests were then in Charles’s camp, although Adrian says that he was visiting all of them by his letters; nor was it then possible to travel peacefully to Rome with the queen and the newly born son, especially in winter. But these words indicate otherwise. See above (letter 57, formerly 59, note). ID.].

352 Yet we earnestly ask you, most excellent and great king, that, in accordance with what was agreed between us, you order our desire concerning that sacred baptism to be fulfilled with respect to this distinguished son of yours, so that the twofold grace of the Holy Spirit may increase among us, and that the joy of a double festival may be celebrated for us.

We also beseech your excellence, most beloved son and illustrious king, for the love of God and of that key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven who deigned to grant you the throne of your father’s kingdom, that, in accordance with the promise you made, you order all that you promised to the same apostle of God to be fulfilled, for the reward of your soul and the stability of your kingdom. Thus may the Church of almighty God—that is, the Church of blessed Peter the apostle, to whom the keys [Lambinus: “through the keys”] of the kingdom of heaven were granted by the creator of all things, together with the power of loosening and binding the bonds of sins—remain increasingly holy and exalted in all things; may everything be fulfilled according to your promise; and may a reward and good reputation be recorded for you in the heavenly citadels and throughout the whole world.

And just as, in the days of blessed Silvester, Roman pontiff, the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church was raised and exalted through the generosity of the most pious Constantine the Great, emperor of holy memory, who deigned to grant it power in these regions of Hesperia, so also in these happiest times of yours and ours may God’s holy Church—that is, the Church of the apostle Peter—flourish and rejoice, and remain ever more greatly exalted, so that all the nations that hear these things may be able to say (Psalm 19): “Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you”; for behold, a new and most Christian Constantine, emperor of God, has arisen in these times, through whom God has deigned to grant to the holy Church of the chief of the apostles, blessed Peter, all these things, 353 and also all the other possessions which various emperors, patricians, and other God-fearing men, for the reward of their souls and the forgiveness of their sins, granted to the apostle Peter and to God’s holy apostolic Roman Church in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Benevento, as well as Corsica and the patrimony of Sabina, and which the wicked nation of the Lombards seized and carried away over the course of many years.

Let these possessions be restored in your times. For we have many donations kept in our sacred Lateran treasury; nevertheless, as a satisfaction to your most Christian kingdom, we have sent them to you through the men already mentioned, so that we might display them to you. Therefore we ask your distinguished excellence to order those patrimonies to be restored in their entirety to blessed Peter and to us [Note: Muratori and others are foolish to accuse Adrian of mentioning the Constantinian Donation before it existed. For Adrian borrowed the material found here from the Acts of Silvester, which, although spurious, had not yet been rejected as apocryphal books. See the Preliminary Commentary (no. 20 and following). ID.].

When the holy Church of God has received fulfillment in all things through your properly arranged disposition, may that chief of the apostles, blessed Peter, plead before the tribunal of almighty clemency for your safety and long life, and for the rejoicing of your kingdom strengthened by God.

We have sent with great urgency to your distinguished excellence our most reverend and most holy brothers Philip and Andrew, bishops [Col. 0306D], and also our duke Theodore [Note: It is scarcely credible that Bishop Philip was sent again as head of the embassy to Francia, since he had returned from there not long before with the royal letters. Yet there is no reason to introduce another man of the same name. Rather, we should regard the man with complete confidence because of the offices entrusted to him. While still a priest, he was appointed by Stephen II as judge of Ravenna with his colleague Duke Eustachius in 756 (letter 51, formerly 54), and he carried out the embassy of Paul I to Pippin in 764 (letter 37, formerly 20). Later, after becoming bishop, we see him serving Adrian once and again as an envoy. The third of the envoys deserves no less attention. He is also mentioned with these same envoys below (letter 61, formerly 73), where the pontiff calls him “our most eminent nephew,” and again, while serving on an embassy with the deacon Agatho in 781 (letter 67, formerly 69), calls him “Theodore, our most eminent consul and duke and our nephew.” This dignity of most eminent duke and consul demolishes all the learned disputes over that corrupt passage in the Continuator of Fredegar, concerning which enough has been said in the note to the letters of Gregory III (no. 6). For although those who were later called *illustres* were called *eminentissimi* among the palace offices, as Gothofredus notes (volume III, p. 271, Code of Theodosius), nevertheless, even while the designation *illustrious* was in force, *eminentissimus* was applied to a consul, as may be seen in the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs* (chapter 1, title 5, and chapter 2, title 6). Garnerius’s observation should nevertheless not be neglected: “At that time,” he says, “the consulship, which had once been the summit of dignities, had been so reduced that it was almost an empty title. It was nearly suppressed by Justinian, but although restored in some fashion by the emperors who followed, it did not recover its former splendor.” CENN.], to whom we have placed it upon their lips [Col. 0307A] that they must explain everything to your excellence protected by God in greater detail. You ought to believe them in everything and order them to be received with your customary kindness, for the love of your protector, blessed Peter the apostle. Thus, when they return to us with the matter accomplished, before the confession of that same apostle of God, together with all the bishops and priests, all the clergy, the senate, and our entire people, we may pour out prayers to the Lord for your safety and long life and for the exaltation of your kingdom, asking that he deign to preserve your excellence throughout all ages and times, for the exaltation of your spiritual mother, God’s holy Roman Church; and just as he has granted earthly joys, so may he also grant eternal heavenly ones.

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## LXI. 355 Paul the Presbyter [Note: All are from the Roman clergy. GRETS.], Venerandus the Presbyter, Faroaldus, Adalbertus, Gaudiosus, Benedict the Deacon, Josue the Deacon, Hermenfridus, Raginbertus, Autcarius [Gentianus: Autcarius], Gregorius, Agemodus, David, Gaidualdus, Ariolfus, Stephanus, Garibaldus, Gregorius, Savinus, Aldosintus, Rothbertus, Ratchis, Haribertus, Leo, Martinianus, Allo, Majo, Beaptulfus [Gentianus: Scaptulfus], Cunualdus, Leminosus, Magnus, Ursus, Autbaldus, Aldefusus, Petrus, Ansualdus, Allo, Petrus, Gratiosus, Faroaldus, Ursus, Adual[d]us.

*(Year of Our Lord 777, Codex of Charles LXXIII [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 12, among the letters of Paul I): “In the twelfth [letter, formerly the twelfth] he relates the injury inflicted by the Beneventans and asks that Pippin rebuke them by letter; and, if they refuse to obey, that he consent to the expedition undertaken against them.” The falsity of this summary will be evident from the context of the letter, where Charles’s consent is said to be requested. Adrian was not asking for consent but for an alliance in arms. CENN.], chronicle 60.)*

### ARGUMENT

Shortly after the departure of the envoys, in the month of May, he learned from the royal letters that the territories of the Franks were about to be invaded by the Saracens. He therefore devoted himself, day and night, to continual prayers together with all the Roman clergy; he reports this to Charles as a source of consolation and wishes him victory.

He states that the Beneventans, joined by treaty with the people of Gaeta and Terracina and with the patrician of Sicily residing at Gaeta, had planned to seize the Roman cities of Campania from the Holy See and subject them to that patrician. He says that he first acted through envoys, but in vain, and therefore decided to send an army there. He asks Charles to send an envoy to the Beneventans with rebukes, so that they may return to their duty; he says that he refuses to receive them even for the consecration of bishops, as enemies of the Holy See and of Charles. Finally, he begs Charles to do what he had requested through the envoys.

The royal power established by God has informed us through your letters that, God being opposed to them, the nation of the Agarenes desires to enter your territories for battle [Note: The synod at Paderborn was held for the Saxons, to establish them in the faith which they had recently embraced. The annalists call it an assembly and meeting at which Ibimalarabi came with his companions—Saracens from Catalonia—having defected from their king and imploring Charles’s protection; for this reason Charles took up arms against Spain the following year. See the Frankish and Fulda Annals and others in Pagius (777, no. 4; 778, no. 1), and Labbe (*Councils*, volume VI, p. 1823). ID.].

When we learned this, we were thereby placed in great tribulation and affliction. But may our Lord God in no way permit such things to happen, nor blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

We, dearest son and great king, incessantly beseech the clemency of our Lord God for you, together with all our priests, religious monks, the entire clergy, and our whole people, that he may subject that unmentionable nation of the Agarenes to you and cast it beneath your feet, so that they may in no way prevail against you. For just as the people of Pharaoh were drowned in the Red Sea because they did not believe in God, so now may our Lord God, through the intercessions of blessed Peter the apostle, deliver them into your hands [Note: What the pontiff predicts did not happen. For in the following year, after capturing several cities, while returning to Francia against the rebellious Saxons, Charles suffered a great defeat in the Pyrenees, at the place called the Valley of Roscida, commonly Roncesvalles, as Einhard records. See Pagius (year 778, no. 4). The Frankish and Fulda Annals are entirely silent about this matter. ID.].

Take courage and be strong, because the almighty Lord will grant victory over your enemies and ours to those in your kingdom who trust in him. And just as, unceasingly day and night before the confession of that same apostle of God, we beseech the Lord’s majesty to enlarge your kingdom, so may he cause us always to rejoice in the Lord over your safety and the exaltation of your kingdom.

A few days ago, in this month of May, when we had received your letters, we sent to your excellence, protected by God, Andrew and Philip, most holy bishops, and Theodore, our most eminent nephew, for consolation and visitation, so that we might learn the joy of your prosperity [Note: In the preceding letter he said that he was sending these envoys for the same purpose, though in somewhat different words. The only difference is that there he puts Andrew before Philip, while here he puts Philip before Andrew; I do not know why. I have no doubt, however, that they are the same men, since I see them mentioned as envoys whom he had sent in May a few days before receiving the royal letters, not as envoys whom he was sending again in the same month. Indeed, since no other royal or pontifical envoy is named, and since these men are commended below, this letter seems to have been sent to the same envoys with great urgency, so that they might carry it together with the other letter—unless perhaps Wilcharius and Dodo, mentioned in the following letter, were the bearers of this one. CENN.].

We ask you also, most beloved son, for the love of your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, kindly to order them to be received in the customary manner, so that, when they return to us with joy, the matter accomplished, and the holy Church of God, the Roman Church, exalted, you may deign to release them quickly. Then may that chief of the apostles intercede for you before the majesty of our Lord God, so that he may enlarge your kingdom still further and grant you victories [Note: The Magdeburg Centuriators reproduce these exact words from a letter which they mistakenly regarded as letter 12 among the Pauline letters. They say: “And for the enlargement of the kingdom, in letter 12 to Pippin.” They derive this from the context of the letter: “That chief apostle, etc.” (*Centuries*, 8, chapter 10). ID.]. May we also, though sinners, be able to pour out prayers before the confession of that apostle of God.

And let your Excellency, protected by God, recognize this also: because your rivals and ours, the utterly wicked Beneventans, are striving to seize several of our cities in Campania, persuading our people themselves to withdraw from our jurisdiction. They are acting together with the inhabitants of Castrum Caietanum and of Terracina, binding themselves by strong oaths [Col. 0309B] with the patrician of Sicily himself, who resides in the aforesaid Castrum Caietanum; and they are striving to usurp these Campanians from the power and jurisdiction of blessed Peter and of us and to subject them to the patrician of Sicily.

[Note: Peregrinius, writing about the boundaries of the Duchy of Benevento (Dissertation 5, in Pratilli, vol. V, p. 231), maintained, on the authority of this letter, that Terracina had been “taken from the Greeks by Charles the Great and granted to the Roman Church, and then recovered from them through the agency of Arichis, prince of Benevento.” But, with due respect to the learned man, Adrian here is dealing with Beneventans allied by treaty with the patrician of Sicily, whose seat was in Castrum Caietanum, and with the Caietani and Tarracinenses themselves, in order to invade the cities of Roman Campania; he provides no indication whatever that this city had been acquired or lost. Much greater is the error of Cointius and Pagi, who follows him (year 788, no. 1 and following). For they assign this letter to the year 788, supposing that the Campania mentioned in Adrian’s letters was the Campania of the Duchy of Benevento, several cities of which had been granted to the Holy See by Charles, who in the preceding year, 787, had brought that duchy back under his authority. In this matter Peregrinius was not deceived (in the passage cited): when quoting Adrian’s letter, upon reaching the name Campania he immediately adds “Roman.” Muratori usually follows Pagi and Cointius, unless they conflict with his own opinion; and, since he was unable to locate the passage in this letter, he assigns it to the year 791 as being of uncertain date, affirming as certain that it was written after 787, because before that year the Beneventans, and consequently the Campanians, did not obey Charles the Great. Yet Cointius, Pagi, and Muratori would seem worthy of excuse for being misled by the word Campania, since they did not realize that Adrian was speaking of the Campania about which Paul I was speaking (letter 39, formerly 14) in the year 765—unless they themselves admitted having seen the words “dearest son” in this letter. That makes them inexcusable: for every letter written after the year 781 calls Charles “godfather” (*compater*), either in the superscription or in the body of the text, as anyone can see. Therefore it must certainly be affirmed that this was written before that year. And since the same envoys are mentioned as in the preceding letter, there is no doubt that both belong to the month of May in the year 777. —The Editor.]

But when we had recognized this very thing, we sent word and admonished them through our bishops and the faithful of blessed Peter, repeatedly and at suitable times, wishing to preserve these Campanians safe for ourselves, so that no harm might befall them, and asking that they either come into our presence or send five leading men from each city [Col. 0310A] to your Excellency, founded by God. But we were unable either to direct them into your presence or to bring them into our sight, nor did they wish to come into ours. Nevertheless, we sent our most reverend brother Philip, and also Paschal, our nephew, to them, so that they might present themselves before us or hasten to come into the presence of your royal power. Even then they did not wish to comply with our admonitions.

[Note: In the preceding letter there is not even a word about the Beneventans’ plotting these things against the cities of Roman Campania. This is not surprising, first because he had entrusted more matters to the envoys to be related privately, and secondly because he hoped that they would either go to Charles, with whom they were joined by a treaty of alliance, or come to Rome to obtain pardon for their offense. Now, having abandoned all hope of their repentance, he discloses the whole matter. —The Editor.]

But when we were quite unable to prevail over their wickedness, we resolved, with God’s power and assistance, and together with your power, to send our general army there. It ought to constrain them and correct the enemies of blessed Peter and of us—and likewise of you.

[Note: The pontiff’s deliberation deserves serious attention. He wishes to compel the Beneventans by force and arms to withdraw from their alliance with the Greeks. For that reason he decided to send there the general army of the Church, that is, troops from the whole territory that then belonged to it. That entire territory, as is clear from what precedes, was the Roman province: Rome and its duchy, the Exarchate, the two Pentapoles, and Tuscia of the Lombards. He resolved to add to this general army Charles’s auxiliaries, namely those from the royal duchies of Tuscia and Spoleto. Two points clearly follow from this: first, Adrian’s complete authority in the ecclesiastical territory; second, the precarious nature of his rule in those duchies which Charles administered through his own dukes, while, under the supreme right he had retained for himself, he had subjected them to the authority of blessed Peter and the pontiff—as will become clearer below (letter 63, formerly 65). Muratori himself sensed this point (year 785). But by conjecturing that the pontiff had been granted vicarious authority over the whole kingdom of Italy, he confuses the jurisdictions and offers no support whatever for that claim. —The Editor.]

But we ask you, dearest son, before the living God, to order that the utterly wicked and God-hated Beneventans be addressed in protest through your letters and by your most faithful envoy, so that they may repent of such an unjust undertaking and not inflict such things upon our Campanians. For we do not wish to receive those utterly wicked Beneventans, or their envoys, under any circumstances; nor do we wish to admit them to the consecration of bishops, since they have become adversaries of blessed Peter, of us, and of you.

[Note: Before Benevento attained the dignity of an archbishopric under John XIII in the tenth century, the Beneventan bishop, together with the other bishops of Samnium, was also subject to the Roman pontiff. The following are listed by Labbe as formerly subject to the Roman pontiff in Samnium: “Alifanus, Beneventanus, Bovianensis, Frequentinus, Orthonensis, Samninus, Saepinas, Sulmonensis, Theatinus, Valvensis.” Whenever one of these had to be consecrated, certain members of the clergy and people customarily came to Rome with the elected bishop, as is evident from the *Book of the Daily Office* (chapter 3, title 2); for they were summoned in these words: “Seize that man with religious force and hasten to bring him to our holy see.” —Cennadius.]

Meanwhile, great king and dearest son, we ask you that, just as we sent to you through Andrew and Philip, our most holy bishops, and Theodore, our most eminent nephew, to request these things from you, so you may order that our entire petition be fulfilled.

[Note: Through the envoys mentioned above, as in the preceding letter, he had sent Charles authentic deeds of the patrimonies “in the regions of Tuscia, Spoleto, and Benevento, as well as Corsica and the Sabine patrimony.” Since all these were situated outside the ecclesiastical territory, he had then asked, and now asks again, that they be restored to the Holy See. They had been assigned to the support of the poor and pilgrims, the maintenance of the churches’ lamps, and other pious expenditures. By contrast, the revenues derived from the cities and places within the ecclesiastical territory were needed to maintain armies and for other public necessities. —The Editor.]

May the angel of almighty God go before you, make your Excellency triumphant, and grant that you return safely, with great victories and exaltation, to the summit of your own kingdom together with the entire army of the Franks, beloved of God.

## LXII. 360. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord Charles the King

In it he speaks of his own faith and constancy, and of Anastasius, his apostolic envoy, who had remained in Francia.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 32): “In the thirty-second letter he writes at considerable length to Charles about the faithfulness and constancy of his affection. He reminds him to remember the friendship and promise made in the presence of Peter—blessed Peter. He complains to him that he is detaining his envoy Anastasius in Francia. He accuses the Lombards and urges Charles to take vengeance upon them and to carry out the rights of Peter—of holy Peter—which he promised. He indicates that he sent a certain Paulinus in chains to Charles because he had spoken ill of him, and he entreats—adjures—him to do the same to his enemies.” —Cennadius.]

*(Year of the Lord 777; Codex Carolinus L, chronicle 61.)*

### Argument

When Archbishop Wilcharius and Abbot Dodo, returning from Rome to Francia, reported to Charles with how much affection and how many honors they had been received in Rome, and with what kindness they had been heard, Charles informed the pontiff of the matter. The pontiff replies that he had always acted in this way and that it was his custom to dismiss royal envoys immediately; that he did so out of love, which would be perpetual toward the excellent king, so that no credence should be given to anyone who asserted otherwise. He testifies to his joy because he had seen in the royal letter that Charles, when he came to Italy in the following month of October, would fulfill everything he had promised to blessed Peter. He did not send Abbot Pardus with the royal envoys, Bishop Possessor and Abbot Dodo, together with Bishop Andrew, according to Charles’s wish, because Pardus was ill, but sent Bishop Valentinus in his place. Finally, he grieves that the king has retained Anastasius, his apostolic envoy, because of certain imprudent statements, since the law of nations seemed to have been violated. He asks that Anastasius be sent back to him for examination and punishment according to his deserts, together with two other wicked men.

To Lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We have received the letters of your most desired Excellency, in which we rejoiced over a conversation held in your absence as much as I always desire the speaker himself to be present with me. When we reread them and learned of your immense prosperity, we rejoiced greatly, since your prosperity is proved to be our joy, and your exaltation is, after God, our security. For it was reported in the lines of your royal power that your envoys returning to you—namely, Wulcharus, our most holy brother and archbishop, and Dodo, the religious abbot—

[Note: It is not known when or why these envoys came. In the preceding note I suggested that they may perhaps have been the bearers of the letter. Certainly Archbishop Dodo had returned to Rome with Bishop Possessor in the capacity of envoy and was sent away in September, as will become clear below. A period of four months is more than sufficient for the journey there and back. —Cennadius.]

had reported to you that the matters entrusted to them by you had been received by us kindly and affectionately. But our almighty God, before whom the secrets of the heart stand revealed, knows that we strive to receive every envoy sent from your royal presence with the greatest affection and suitable honor, and that we labor to fulfill your every wish with sincere integrity of mind, and hasten to send them back to you in prosperity. Nor, so long as we live here, can any transient and fleeting resources of this world, or the blandishments of human persuasion, turn us away from love and affection for your sweet dignity or from the promises we have made to you; rather, firm and steadfast, we remain in your love.

Far be it from us, dearest and exceedingly beloved son, to attempt in any way to invalidate the things that we mutually confirmed and established before the most sacred body of your patron, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. For I too, satisfied, seem to have entreated your exalted rank:

[Note: Lambecius and Gentilotus read: “We are satisfied, and you will remain firm in our affection.” But I ask you before God, dearest son, just as formerly through our addresses . . . . .]

seem to have implored your exalted position: if anyone should prefer to utter the most wicked statements about us to your ears, wishing through deceit to commend himself to you, do not grant him any opportunity for belief,

[Note: This passage, restored by Lambecius and Gentilotus from manuscript Codex [—], seems to indicate what he had written in the year 774 about Leo, archbishop of Ravenna. By making false allegations through his envoys, Leo had attempted to win Charles over, fabricating lies against Adrian (letter 51, formerly 54), so that he might retain, with Charles’s consent, the cities of Emilia that he had invaded. —Cennadius.]

because, as we have said, we remain firm in our affection for you. Moreover, the Savior expressly declared: “By this we know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

Meanwhile, your Excellency’s letter stated that, when the coming month of October arrived, and, with God’s favor, you had come into the regions of Italy—

[Note: This letter appears to have been given at the end of August or in September.
