I assign it to the year 777 with Cointius and Pagi, because I see that matters had gone well in Saxony according to the annalists, especially the Frankish and Fulda annals, and therefore no more suitable time for Charles to undertake a journey into Italy could have occurred. He was planning a war against the Saracens of Spain, which he undertook and successfully conducted in the following year, although on his return he was attacked in the Pyrenean passes by an ambush of the Basques while he was bringing his army back with the greatest speed against the rebellious Saxons. See the preceding letter, note d. —Cennadius.]

you would hasten to bring to completion everything that you had promised to blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and to us. For a father’s joy is the progress of his sons, and natural affection rejoices in their advancement. Therefore, recognizing the perfection of your well-being, we have been made joyful; and because you are hastening to Italy for the increase and exaltation of its mother, the holy Church of God, we desire that you may accomplish this ever more fully. But may God and our Lord Jesus Christ grant that we soon rejoice in your presence and exult together with you in mutual gladness.

Regarding our envoys—namely, Andrew, our fellow bishop, and Pardus the abbot—

[Note: An abbot, that is, the ruler or superior of monks. —Grets.]

concerning whom you sent us word that we should dispatch them, returning to your royal presence with your envoys, our brother Bishop Possessor and the religious Abbot Dodo—

[Note: Gentilotus reads “to your royal footsteps” and observes that Tengnagel corrected these words to “from your royal footsteps.”]

we have accordingly arranged to fulfill your request as quickly as possible.

[Note: Gentilotus rightly and appropriately advised that the manuscript reading should be followed: “to your royal footsteps,” in accordance with the elegance of that age, and that Tengnagel had corrected—or, better, corrupted—this passage. Bishop Possessor and Abbot Dodo were returning from Rome to Francia, not in the opposite direction. —Cennadius.]

But Abbot Pardus was quite unable to set out because of the weakness of his body, and we sent Bishop Valentinus in his place.

As for what you reported to us about our envoy Anastasius—that he had spoken to you certain unbearable words which it was not appropriate for him to speak, causing you great sadness, and that for this reason you are still detaining him—

[Note: Anastasius, the chamberlain, had returned from Francia in the year 775 with Bishop Andrew, whose colleague in the embassy he had been at the end of the preceding year. At the end of that same year, 775, we find Andrew sent again as envoy, together with Abbot Pardus; no mention of anyone is found in the following year, although four letters to Charles have been transmitted. It can therefore be inferred that Anastasius was the bearer of one of these letters. For if the pontiff complains in the year 777 that his envoy is still being detained, Anastasius must have gone there some time earlier, and therefore at least in the preceding year. —Cennadius.]

our heart is deeply distressed, while the Lombards and Ravennates admit and declare that the king in no way remains in apostolic affection, since he is detaining the envoy in his possession. But it has not been known to have happened from the beginning of the world that an envoy of your protector, blessed Peter, great or small, was detained by any people. Therefore let your concern order him to be sent to us; and after questioning him most severely, we shall correct him according to the offense found in him.

As for that Lombard who traveled to you with this envoy of ours Anastasius, named Gaidifridus—

[Note: This is the inhabitant of the city of Pisa whom Adrian called Gausfridus and Gausfredus in the year 774 (letter 50, formerly 55), when he entrusted him to Anastasius, the apostolic envoy, to be brought back to Charles, who was still staying in Italy. We learn from this that he was a Lombard by birth. Charles had come to suspect him of being a deceitful man who was plotting discord between the pontiff and the Franks. It is therefore not surprising that he had begun to suspect something even concerning the apostolic envoy who had had Gaidifridus as his traveling companion; and thus, when an opportunity for a new embassy arose, with several imprudent statements added, he detained Anastasius in his possession. Adrian, however, defended Gausfridus briefly and only on the authority of his own knowledge, while complaining that Anastasius was being detained and affirming that it had never before happened that an envoy of the Holy See was detained. The essential point is that the pontiff rightly grieved that the law of nations had been violated and did not conceal that Anastasius’s case concerned him. —The Editor.]

you informed us that, while he was in our palace, he had acted fraudulently against your royal authority and had even persuaded your notary to prepare false letters by which he wished to bring us into disgrace with you—may God avert this! Nor will anyone be found who can in any way provoke us to anger against you. God, who knows the hidden things of human beings, is our witness: we have not recognized him as unfaithful to you on any count. But, to speak more briefly, if the man sent to you by your lover, blessed Peter, deserved to receive such treatment, what should be thought of the utterly wicked and exceedingly deceitful Paschal and Saratinus, who, as you yourself indicated to us through your honored letters, dared to do such things in this Roman city—things such as had never been heard of since the beginning of the world? Perhaps, after committing such acts and coming into your presence, they did not doubt that, because of the crime they had committed, they should ask you to restore them to our favor. But rather, in your presence and before our envoys, they devoted themselves to slander. And I am greatly astonished that you recognize as worthy of enjoying great favor those who uttered such unheard-of words about them before your presence.

[Note: This pair of utterly wicked men, stained by so many crimes, had deceitfully won Charles’s favor and, in his presence and that of the apostolic envoys who repeatedly traveled there, slandered another man’s reputation. The pontiff asks that they be sent back to Rome for judgment, since it was his right to punish them. I wish this to be noticed by those who assert that the administration of affairs in Rome at that time was obscure. —The Editor.]

Does your Excellency not know that if any person, from any people whatsoever, had reported hostile or empty words about your distinguished greatness, we would have inflicted a fitting punishment upon him and sent him bound to your Excellency, just as we acted in the case of Paulinus? For this reason we beseech and adjure your Excellency, dearest son, through our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, that, rising up manfully as God inspires you, you order that, as befits a pious king, you exercise royal vengeance upon them for their wretched and criminal presumption—

[Note: Lambecius reads “as a pious king”; Gentilotus, “as a pious king,” and observed that the verb *decet* (“befits”) was absent from the manuscript but had been inserted by Tengnagel, who consequently reads: “as befits a pious king.”]

[Gentilotus: “legal vengeance.”]

[Note: This passage, partly badly transcribed and partly corrupted by Tengnagel, should be read according to the versions of Lambecius and Gentilotus: “and for their wretched and criminal presumption, as a pious king—or, alternatively, a pious king—you may deign to exercise legal vengeance upon them for us.” For, as Cangius proves by the examples he cites, *jubere* (“to order”) can mean “to deign” or “to wish”; and the pontiff, wishing to exercise his right, asks Charles to deign to send those criminals to Rome, just as he himself had sent the guilty Paulinus to Francia. Princes still act in this way today, each exercising his own right over peoples subject to him. —Cennadius.]

so that the nations may learn from this that, for the love of blessed Peter, you hold great affection for us: that those who grieve with us in our sorrow may likewise rejoice with us in our joy. Or may you deign to send them to us, so that almighty God, looking down from on high, may grant you, together with our most excellent daughter the queen and your beloved children, long years of life for the proper vengeance we shall inflict upon them. And I, though a sinner, once I have obtained complete justice from them, may continue, as I do now, to pour out prayers for your safety before the sacred confession of that doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency safe.

## LXIII. 366. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord Charles the King

For the exaltation of the holy Church, and concerning the prayers of the apostolic pontiff.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex no. 19): “In the nineteenth letter he prays for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and also reports the prayers of the Romans for Charles and his people.” —Cennadius.]

*(Year of the Lord 778; Codex Carolinus LXII, chronicle 62.)*

### Argument

To Charles, who was waging war against the Saracens of Spain, he announces that he is praying continually, day and night, together with the entire clergy, for his victory. He declares his confidence that Charles will never depart from the faith, affection, and promise that he had made before blessed Peter and that they had mutually pledged to one another.

To Lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We have received with the greatest kindness the gracious letters of your sweet and God-protected Excellency, by which we have also been clearly informed, with immense affection—

[Note: He prudently conceals what his friend Charles had announced concerning the Spanish journey and the war that he was about to undertake against the Saracens. The Fulda Annals briefly state: “Charles came with his army as far as Zaragoza in Spain. He destroyed the city of Pamplona. After subduing the Basques and Navarrese, he received hostages from Ainalarabi and Abitauro, the Saracen commanders, and returned to Francia.” The Frankish Annals report that Charles celebrated “Easter in Aquitaine, in a place called Cassivogla,” or Casinogilo, as Regino and others say. These letters, therefore, were written when Charles had decided to undertake that war; perhaps he had even received the pontiff’s reply before beginning the journey, for Easter that year fell on 19 April. Petrus de Marca (*Hispania*, book III, chapter 7), and Pagi after him (year 778, no. 1 and following), derive and summarize this expedition from Einhard and the Frankish writers. Baron (year 778, no. 4) uses a spurious letter of Saint Ludger as a witness to the Spanish and Saxon wars. Henschen, in Pagi under the same year, no. 9, demonstrates how vain and worthless that letter is. —Cennadius.]

but may almighty, merciful, and compassionate God, in whose hand the heart of your Excellency is governed, good son worthy of God’s imitation, strengthen your heart and mind and extend to you the arm of his power. We, indeed, never cease, day and night, together with all the priests and the Christian people, humbly to pray at the confession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—

[Note: A clear indication that the expedition was being undertaken. It is credible that the prayers began in the preceding year, when Rome first heard of the Saracens of Spain, since the pontiff explains the prayers that were then being offered, not those that would be offered afterward. —The Editor.]

that, together with our most excellent daughter the queen and your most distinguished and noble offspring, he may make you victorious over all barbarous nations, so that all, humbled beneath your arm, may kiss the very traces of your feet, and that the Church of God may be greatly exalted by your royal power, established by God—

[Grets.: “exceedingly exalted.”]

[Note: The exaggeration is evident: Charles was born in the year after the death of his grandfather Charles Martel, namely in 742. Thus, when he confirmed his paternal diploma at Quierzy in 754, he was in his twelfth year. Nor can the beginning of his love for blessed Peter be placed any earlier than this. —The Editor.]

for we do not believe that any false power or principality could ever separate your most steadfast Excellency from the affection and love that, from your cradle, you have held for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Rather, we trust that you remain in that faith and affection, and likewise in that promise, in which we, firm and steadfast, remain until the end, with the Lord presiding and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, acting as mediator, in the promise we made face to face. Therefore may almighty, pious, and merciful God grant you, together with our most distinguished daughter the queen and your most noble offspring, to enjoy the governance of the kingdom through a long and prosperous old age, and grant you eternal life to possess.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency safe.

## LXIV. 368. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord Charles the King

It concerns the sale of slaves to the pagan people of the Saracens; and the aforesaid pope, excusing the Romans, says that they never committed such a crime, but that the Romans had been handed over by the Lombards and Greeks.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 16): “In the sixteenth letter he reports his own prayers and those of the Romans for Charles. He excuses the Romans, saying that they did not sell Christians to the Saracens, but transfers the blame to the Lombards and Greeks. He also excuses—defends—his priests, who were accused before Charles of being polluted by lust. He provides an invocation of the saints. He boasts that he burned very many Greek ships and detained the Greeks themselves in chains, and finally warns him.” —Cennadius.]

*(Year of the Lord 778; Codex Carolinus LXV, chronicle 63.)*

### Argument

He congratulates Charles on his safety and that of the entire Frankish kingdom, and says that he and all the clergy and people pray continually for his victories and for the enlargement of his kingdom. It is false that his Romans sold slaves to the Saracens; rather, the Greeks bought those slaves from the Lombards. He says that he had written to Duke Allo in vain to capture the Greeks and burn their ships, since he himself had neither vessels nor sailors sufficient for that purpose. Nevertheless, to avert that evil, he had Greek ships burned in his own harbor at Centumcellae and had detained the Greeks in prison for some time. The Roman priests were falsely accused of sexual incontinence by wicked men.

To Lord Charles, most excellent son, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We have received the lines of the renowned proclamation of your royal power, founded by God, and we have given thanks to almighty God—

[Note: As soon as Charles returned from the Spanish expedition, he informed his friend the pontiff of the matters he had successfully accomplished. The thanksgiving mentioned here refers to nothing else. The Italian annalist, often misled by old documents, unjustly thought that this letter should be assigned to the year 785. See the preliminary discussion, no. 26. —Cennadius.]

who made us certain of the safety of your kingdom, protected by God, and likewise of our spiritual daughter, the queen, your sweetest wife, and of your offspring—

[Note: Something appears to be missing concerning the prayers offered for Charles and the condition of the entire kingdom. —Grets.]

and of all the bishops, various priests, the senate, and the entire people of the Franks preserved by God. For our God, the knower and searcher of hearts and reins, knows that we remain sincerely, without any pretext, in affection for your sweet royal power. Together with our bishops, priests, clergy, senate, and entire people, we implore the mercy of almighty God that he may continually grant you victories and enlarge your kingdom—

[Note: Many institutions established by Adrian have come down to our own time and still survive in the solemn prayers of the Church; they originated around this period. In the Roman Order I, in Mabillon (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 17), concerning the Saturdays of Lent, we read: “In Adrian’s time it was instituted that prayer should be offered for King Charles; previously this was not customary.” Likewise, on Wednesday and Friday of Holy Week (ibid., pp. 19 and 23), concerning the solemn prayers: “He says the prayer for the king, and then the others in order.” From this we can easily understand what that prayer was like; in the old Gallican Missal (Thomasius, vol. VI, p. 390) it appears in this form: “Let us pray also for the most Christian kings, that God and our Lord may make all barbarous nations subject to them, for our perpetual peace.” If one reads “for the most Christian king Charles,” one has the prayer as it existed in Adrian’s time. The same applies to the ferial prayers at Lauds, “Lord, save the king,” and others that have fallen into disuse. Certainly prayers by day and by night are frequently mentioned in these letters, and Adrian appears to have been their author. —Cennadius.]

for the exaltation of your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church of God, and for the salvation of the people entrusted to us by God. For your exaltation is our joy; and we always desire and wish to learn whatever is new and prosperous concerning your kingdom protected by God and whatever is beneficial to all the Franks. For after God we have no confidence in anyone else except in your strongest arm. And just as our predecessor, Lord Pope Stephen, placed good confidence in your father, Lord King Pippin of holy memory, so we place far greater confidence in your mighty kingdom and remain assured.

We also found in your honey-sweet lines [a complaint] about the sale of slaves, as though they had been sold by our Romans to the wicked nation of the Saracens. But never, God forbid, have we fallen into such a crime, nor was it done by our will. Rather, they always sailed to the coastal territories of the Lombards, and the Greeks [reading uncertain: *nec dicendi Graeci*] bought the slaves from there; they made an alliance with those Lombards, and through those same Lombards received the slaves. [370]

[Note: These slaves, unless I am mistaken, Charles discovered in Spain. From this letter we learn that the Greeks engaged in piracy and that the Lombards, who were then subject to Charles, perpetrated this crime not from fickleness in the faith but, as Adrian says a little below, because hunger compelled them to do so. I do not see, however, why the Italian Annalist here invokes the coastlands of Liguria; for the coastlands of the Lombards ended at Lucca and its territory, and that is what is being discussed here. ID.]

We therefore sent word to Duke Allo that he should prepare several ships, seize the aforementioned Greeks, and burn their vessels; but he was unwilling to obey our orders.

[Note: The Annalist supposes that in the same year, 785, the government of Italy was entrusted to Adrian by Charles—an opinion in which he will soon be shown to be mistaken—and he argues against those who believe that the duke of Lucca was obeyed throughout all Etruria. He cites as examples Duke Regimbald of Chiusi and Gundibrand of Florence, who, according to the custom of that time, exercised administration over a single city, not over a province. As for Allo, it seems to me that he was not in charge of any city but held a military command, as I said above (ep. 50, or 55, note). For this reason the pontiff orders him to prepare a fleet against the Greek pirates, seize them, and burn their vessels.

This clearly indicates that Royal Tuscany, or the Tuscan duchy, as Charles calls it in his Testament (Pithou, part II, p. 84), together with the duchy of Spoleto, was subject to Saint Peter and the Roman pontiff in 774, when Charles first came to Rome, although he retained supreme dominion over both duchies. Therefore that donation, according to the boundaries in Anastasius, which is repeatedly declared by an author ignorant of the facts to be worthless, rests on no insecure foundation.

“But,” they say, “the pontiff exercised vicarious authority in the kingdom of Italy, with the consent of the Frankish king.” This, however, is a weak conjecture. Nowhere do we find that the pontiff took pains at Ticinum or any other city of the Italian kingdom, or exercised any authority there, however vicarious; whereas we know that he did so in the cities of Royal Tuscany and the duchy of Spoleto. See the Preliminary Commentary (no. 12 ff.) and the notes to ep. 90, or 92. CENN.]

For we possess neither ships nor sailors who could have seized them. Nevertheless, insofar as we were able, we bring forward the testimony of the Lord, because we had a great struggle over this matter, wishing to prevent the crime itself: we had the ships of the Greek nation burned in the harbor of our city of Centumcellae, and we kept the Greeks themselves in prison for a long time.

[Note: Adrian supplies three arguments for the supreme dominion of the Roman pontiff in the Roman duchy, which he attributed to the voluntary submission of the peoples and which confound so many recent disputes. First, he declares that he had neither ships nor sailors; therefore the Eastern emperors, who possessed abundant equipment of that kind, had no business with the Romans. Next, he calls Centumcellae, together with its harbor, “our city.” The beginning of pontifical dominion therefore cannot be dated from the year 800. Finally, he had ordered all the Greek ships that had entered the harbor to be burned and the men to be thrown into prison. What kind of obedience was this toward the Eastern emperors! Anyone who does not see here the pontiff’s supreme dominion has no case left to argue. ID.]

But, as we have already said, many slaves were sold by the Lombards when want and famine pressed them. Others of those same Lombards, by their own efforts, boarded the Greek ships, when they had no hope of remaining alive. [371]

As for our priests, concerning whom they dared falsely and contrary to God and to their own souls to make accusations to you, wickedness has lied to itself, and, with the Lord’s favor, there is no pollution among our priests. Nor should your Sublimity believe such things. Yet while, through the cooperation of the Lord and through the intercessions of the holy ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he graciously joined us together in the bond of charity and love, now our rivals—who have always sown weeds—are seeking, against God, to sow some malice between the parties.

But with the Lord’s help, through the intercessions of blessed Peter the apostle, they will by no means prevail, because by the power of the Lord we have such confidence in your royal eminence. For the Psalmist says (Psalm 11): “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue”—of those who suggest to us such unheard-of evils and lay crimes against our priests.

May our God deign to preserve you by the right hand of his protection, for the exaltation of the holy Roman Church of God. May heavenly grace guard your Excellence unharmed.

### LXV. The Same Pope’s Letter, Addressed to the Lord King Charles

In it is contained the account of Bishop Maurice, whose eyes the Istrians had put out.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary is missing; the date of the letter is uncertain. In the latest edition of Duchesne it is placed between the years 774 and 781. I have established above, with the Frankish Annals (Ep. 57, or 59), that the duke of Friuli, Rodgaud, was defeated by Charles in 776. The blinding of the Istrian bishop seems to have occurred in that same year. Thus the events that follow show that this letter was written either in that year or in the preceding one. Muratori assigns it to 779. ID.]

*(A.D. 778, Codex Carolinus LVII, chronicle 64.)*

**Summary.**—Bishop Maurice was blinded in Istrian territory by the Greeks residing there, on the pretext that he was planning to hand that territory over to Charles. Adrian says that he sent him to Marcarius, duke of Friuli, and asks Charles to order the restoration of the blinded bishop, since he was faithful to Charles and to the holy see and had been appointed by Charles to collect the revenues of Saint Peter there.

To the most excellent son, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans: Pope Adrian.

We believe that what happened concerning Bishop Maurice of Istria has already reached the ears of your Excellence, protected by God.

[Note: At that time there were six episcopal sees in the province of Istria. Two of them today, Trieste and Peden, belong to the Austrians; Justinopolis, Pola, Parentium, and Aemonia belong to the Venetians. In the latest edition of Ughelli (vol. V, p. 229), Maurice is believed to have been the fourth bishop of the last-mentioned see, which is today also called Civitas Nova. His memory survives on the step of the baptistery adjoining the cathedral church: “Maurice, bishop of Aemonia, built this baptistery of worthy marble …” ID.]

When the most wicked Greeks who were residing in that aforesaid Istrian territory recognized that he was faithful to blessed Peter and to us, and when, through your Excellence, the aforementioned Bishop Maurice had been appointed to collect the revenues of blessed Peter in the territory named above and to send them to us,

[Note: The matter concerns the patrimony of Istria (Gregory the Great, book IV, ep. 49); for the holy see had no right in that province. Yet Charles, in his donation, names it among the outermost boundaries of ecclesiastical dominion. ID.]

then, moved by jealousy, both those Greeks and the Istrians themselves put out his eyes.

[Note: Zanetti observes (History of the Lombards, p. 673) that someone has claimed that Istria remained subject to the Greeks until 789. Muratori (under 779), on the authority of this letter, shows that at least part of Istria had returned to Greek control; if either statement is accepted, Adrian’s account collapses. Ughelli and those who follow him, who assert that Goths and Lombards, and then Franks, succeeded one another in dominion over the province, seem to have Adrian as an unimpeachable opposing witness.

For if the Greeks and Istrians gave as the reason for their cruelty their fear that this bishop was plotting to hand the province over to the Frankish king, then it was not subject to the Franks. Yet it is hardly credible that Charles, after bringing the duchy of Friuli under his power, left Istria—which is said to have been part of it—untouched. Charles himself testifies that he ordered the bishop of Aemonia, a maritime city far removed from that duchy, to administer the affairs of the holy see, and that Istria followed the fortunes of the duchy of Friuli. Nevertheless, the Istrians may initially have perpetrated this crime either because they rejected the new dominion or because they were led astray by the Greeks residing there. ID.]

They alleged against him that he was intending, as it were, to hand over the Istrian territory itself to your exalted Excellence.

[Note: Adrian uses “Istrian territory” here three times to mean the whole province. The term *territorium* is found in the Theodosian Code in more than one place and with more than one meaning. It denotes the entire possession of any decurion in book II, *On Exactions*, as Gothofredus notes. Du Cange gives an example close to Adrian’s meaning from Siculus Flaccus: “After wars had been waged, the victorious peoples publicly and universally called all the lands from which they had expelled the defeated ‘territory.’” Below, the whole Sabine province will likewise be called a territory. See the Preliminary Commentary (no. 32 ff.). CENN.]

For this reason we ask your Excellence, protected by God, most beloved son and great king, to order that Marcarius, the duke, be sent instructions to restore the aforementioned Bishop Maurice, who was presented before your Excellence in his blinded condition,

[Note: If the blinded bishop had been brought to Charles, this must have happened during the expedition to Friuli in 776, before Charles departed from there, when the collection of Saint Peter’s revenues had scarcely been entrusted to him; that assignment was the cause of the envy from which the crime arose. ID.]

and to have him return to his bishopric, for the sake of your soul’s reward. For the aforementioned bishop hastened to us, and we sent him back to Marcarius, duke of Friuli, so that he should carry out whatever had been arranged by you.

[Note: This journey to and return from Marcarius, whom Charles had appointed in place of Rodgaud, as well as the bishop’s journey to Rome, could conveniently have taken place in 777 or been completed during the first months of the following year. I therefore judged that a letter dealing with so important a matter should not be dated later. ID.]

We also ask your Excellence that, through your fitting arrangement, this matter [Lamb., Gent.: *he himself*] be taken up, so that the salvation of the people residing there may be secured. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

### LXVI. The Same Pope’s Letter, Addressed to the Lord King Charles

In it is contained the account of the Neapolitans’ invasion of the city of Terracina together with the Greeks.

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 17): “In the seventeenth letter to Charles [the seventeenth, according to Baronius], he accuses the Neapolitans and Greeks of invading his city of Terracina on the advice of Arichis, duke of Benevento; and he asks Charles, for the love of Saint Peter, for assistance so that he may recover it and other possessions belonging to blessed Peter in the duchy of Naples. Charles is the pope’s strength and glory together with blessed Peter.” ID.]

*(A.D. 780, Codex Carolinus LXIV, chronicle 65.)*

**Summary.**—The Greeks and Beneventans, on the advice of Arichis, duke of Benevento, invaded Terracina, which he had acquired for the holy see. Adrian asks Charles to order Wulfruin to be in Rome on the Kalends of August, with the Tuscan, Spoletan, and Beneventan forces, to recover Terracina and storm the fortress of Gaeta and Naples. He had previously reached an agreement with Peter, the envoy of the Neapolitans, that they should give him fifteen noble hostages, whom he would return together with Terracina if, through their patrician of Sicily, he were permitted to recover the patrimony of Saint Peter. Arichis prevented the hostages from being given because he was awaiting Desiderius’s son from Greece, intending to act with him against Charles and the holy see.

To the most excellent son, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans: Pope Adrian.

[Note: The beginning is corrupt. GRETS.]

[Note: It is absolutely certain that this letter was written before 781. As I have often said, the title “co-father” is not given to Charles, nor “co-mother” to the queen. Moreover, the sequence of events contained in it clearly belongs approximately to this year. I therefore follow Cointius and Pagius. I condemn Muratori’s excessive freedom, by which he postpones it to 787 and in that year and the following one heaps together so many letters and digests such a mass of events that he confuses the whole history. This matter must be discussed in its proper place. CENN.]

We believe that your most victorious royal Excellence has no greater protection than that you continue, as you have begun, to contend to the end on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for the exaltation of his holy Church.

[Note: Lambinus reads: “than that we, because of this …”; Gentianus: “that, than …”]

Thus, by means of these communications of ours, we explain more fully to you, while greeting your most triumphant benevolence toward us [Lambinus: “your most triumphant benevolence toward us”], what is happening in these regions. The most wicked Neapolitans and the Greeks, hateful to God, suddenly came with the evil counsel of Arighis, duke of Benevento, and invaded the city of Terracina, which we had previously subjected to the service of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to yours and ours. Now, by their feeble counsel, those aforementioned wicked Neapolitans, together with the perverse Greeks, have invaded it again.

[Note: The Italian Annalist, and before him Cointius and Pagius, have astonishingly corrupted this history, which the pontiff narrates with great clarity. They failed to understand the date of Letter 73 of the Codex Carolinus (our 60) and wrongly postponed it to 788; consequently, being uninformed about the events narrated there, they could not grasp the true meaning of this letter.

In 777, or in the following year—which is more probable—the Romans, together with the Tuscans and Spoletans, brought war against the Beneventans, who had made an alliance with the people of Terracina against the cities of Roman Campania, and captured Terracina. Gaeta, it seems, was not attacked, although the Gaetans were allies, since the patrician of Sicily—what we would today call a viceroy—had his seat there. See ep. 60, or 73, no. 8.

In the same year the Neapolitans, joined with the Greeks and acting on Arichis’s advice, recovered that city. CENN.]

We did not wish to send anyone there without your counsel. But we ask your royal Excellence, advanced by God, to act as it is accustomed to act for the love of blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and to send us Wulfruin quickly.

[Note: This duke, distinguished in the conduct of war and known to the pontiff, is mentioned by the Frankish writers, who report that Adrian was indebted to him; no mention of him, however, occurs among either ancient or more recent writers. Unless I am mistaken, he was the same commander of auxiliaries whom Adrian said in the aforementioned epistle 60, or 73, he would attach to the general Roman army. From the capture of Terracina mentioned here we infer that he led the army there, and we thereby fill out this gap in pontifical history to some extent. ID.]

Order him to hasten to be ready here with us on the Kalends of August, and command him to come with all the Tuscans, or Spoletans,

[Note: Above, in the notes to epistles 60 and 63, or 73 and 75, I said something about the Tuscan and Spoletan duchies, which Charles offered to Saint Peter by voluntary donation, as appears in Louis’s diploma. Here is a new argument. Adrian requests auxiliaries from both sides; but because Charles had reserved supreme dominion there, he wants Charles himself to order those soldiers out and appoint a commander over them.

He also asks that the Beneventans, since they were subject to Charles as king of the Lombards, be ordered by him to aid the pontifical army, though with a major distinction. From those duchies in which the Church possessed some legal authority, he asks that all the soldiers be summoned. Of the Beneventans, however, he speaks with irritation and makes light of their assistance. CENN.]

and with those most wicked Beneventans, in your service and equally in ours, come to recover the city of Terracina. At the same time, with the Lord’s permission, let them advance to storm Gaeta,

[Note: He says that Gaeta is to be stormed, not recovered, as Terracina was. When the Roman army advanced there three years earlier, it evidently did not even attempt Gaeta, which was extremely well fortified, because the patrician was present there, as I recently said. ID.]

or Naples, recovering our patrimony situated in the territory of Naples, so that, after subjecting them in all things, they may be under your dominion and ours.

[Note: In 769, as we have seen (ep. 46, or 54, note), Stephen III praised Itherius, who had been sent to Queen Bertrada, the widowed queen, and to her son, King Charles, because he had gone into the territory of the duchy of Benevento to recover one of the two most celebrated patrimonies mentioned in the Register of Gregory the Great—namely, the Campanian patrimony, although it is uncertain whether the holy see ever recovered it.

The Neapolitan patrimony, which Adrian implies could be recovered only by conquering Naples, was distinct from the Campanian or Beneventan patrimony. Moreover, after the conquest of Naples and Gaeta, following the recovery of Terracina, great security would have come to the pontifical and Carolingian dominions. Once the Greeks had been expelled, only Lower Calabria would remain in Italy, separated from the extensive duchy of Benevento; and the duchy itself, being subject to Charles, king of Italy, would be less able to undertake innovations with the Greeks.

Adrian’s plan was therefore extremely prudent, if it could have been carried out. ID.]

[376] We did indeed make an agreement with those treacherous Neapolitans through their envoy Peter at the feast of holy Easter. We were seeking the patrimony of blessed Peter the apostle situated there in Naples and wishing to subject them to your service, so that, after giving us fifteen hostages from among their most noble sons, they would recover the city of Terracina. The agreement was that they should go to their patrician in Sicily; and if they were willing to return our patrimony, they would recover the city and the hostages.

But without your counsel we were unwilling to return either the hostages or the city itself, since we wished to seize the hostages for your service.

[Note: That useless agreement made with the Neapolitans through their envoy Peter during the Easter solemnity—which took place on 26 March—concerning the taking of hostages and returning them together with Terracina if that patrimony were restored to the holy see gave the Neapolitans and Greeks, at Arichis’s instigation, the opportunity to attack Terracina unexpectedly and recover it. Therefore the pontiff’s decision to make war on them again seems to belong to the month of May. ID.]

For their evil counsel is nothing other than this: in concert with the faithless Arighis, duke of Benevento, they make plans; and every day the most wicked patrician of Sicily sends envoys, which Arighis himself receives. The aforementioned Arighis alone prevented us from receiving hostages from the Neapolitans, because every day he awaits the son of the most wicked Desiderius, formerly [reading uncertain: *nec dicendi regis Langobardorum*], so that together with him they may attack us and you.

[Note: Arichis had long before married Adelberga, Desiderius’s daughter and Adelgis’s sister, and had children by her. It is therefore unsurprising that he was concerned to restore Adelgis to his father’s kingdom. ID.]

[Note: Either this was merely a suspicion, or the Greeks truly intended to attack ecclesiastical territory together with the Beneventans in order to avenge the injury done by the Franks. Those who maintain that the Romans were still subject to Greek jurisdiction are talking foolishly. ID.]

But we ask your Excellence, advanced by God, that no person, whoever he may be, be able to hinder you in this, for the love of blessed Peter and of us. For in no way can you allow us to be mocked by them together with you, because you are our strength and glory together with blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

We indeed consider the city of Terracina as nothing, except lest through it harm be incurred and the faithless Beneventans, as they desire, find an opportunity to withdraw from your allegiance.

[Note: Here he clearly explains the reason why he considers that the nest of the Greeks, situated too near the unfaithful ruler of the duchy of Benevento, must be removed with every effort. The Beneventans, whether willingly or unwillingly, were subject to Charles, king of the Lombards. But for Arichis, a man of hidden treachery, the proximity of the Greeks was to be feared. ID.]

For this reason we send you this information, so that through your assistance, as we have said, the Church of blessed Peter the apostle, your protector, may be exalted, and your praise and victory resound throughout the world; and so that, together with our most excellent daughter the queen and your most distinguished offspring, you may deserve to reign forever with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellence unharmed.

### LXVII. The Same Pope’s Letter, Addressed to the Lord King Charles

In it is contained the matter of the *camarado*, or beams and timber, which was needed for the construction of that church of Saint Peter, and of the holy body requested by Fulgatus [Fulradus].

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 20): “In the twentieth [letter], through the deacon Oddo, he asks Charles for beams or timber for the Church of Saint Peter [for roofing Saint Peter’s Church]. He also asks that Archbishop Wulcharius be sent to Rome. Concerning the holy body which the deacon Oddo and Abbot Julradus [Fulradus] had formerly asked him to give them, he explains how he was frightened away from sending it. He promises to send the body of the martyr Candidus if Charles asks for it. He indicates that the Beneventans and Neapolitans are accustomed to consult with the Greeks, but promises to tell what Oddo will report.” ID.]

*(A.D. 780, Codex Carolinus LXI, chronicle 66.)*

**Summary.**—When the royal envoy, the deacon Addo, arrived, Adrian heard of Charles’s steadfast goodwill toward the holy see. He asks that the timber agreed upon from the region of Spoleto be brought as soon as possible to Rome for repairing the vaulted roof of Saint Peter’s basilica, since suitable timber could not be found in ecclesiastical territory. He says that Addo himself, when he formerly came with Abbot Fulradus, had requested a holy body; Adrian had been frightened by a certain vision from disturbing the bodies of the saints. His predecessor Paul had granted to the presbyter Aciulfus the body of Saint Candidus, which was in the possession of Archbishop Wilcharius, and Adrian says that he will grant the same body to Charles. He had discussed with Addo the meetings of the Neapolitans with the Greeks and Beneventans, about which he had previously written; Addo would report these matters in person.

To the most excellent son, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans: Pope Adrian.

[Note: Summary 28, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.]

[Note: The Italian Annalist wrongly assigns this letter to 786 for the reasons often stated. Above all, the absence of the title “co-father” brings it back to the years before 781. For this reason the latest edition of Duchesne assigns it to an uncertain year between 774 and 781. Zacagnus correctly observes (Manuscript Codex no. 157) that it was written shortly after the preceding letter. Its concluding account of the Neapolitans, Beneventans, and Greeks entering into plans together proves that it cannot be separated from the preceding letter. CENN.]

Addo [Addo], the deacon beloved by God, faithful to us and to you, sent directly from your royal Excellence, reported to us many familiar matters concerning what you do for us and for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Therefore we gave thanks to almighty God and to that same apostle, praying without ceasing for your safety and abundant victory. [379]

Moreover, most beloved and excellent son, just as you sent us word,

[Note: Addo’s principal task was to bring Charles’s answer concerning the transport of beams from Spoleto for the restoration of Saint Peter’s basilica, as is clear here. The fact that Adrian’s letters on this matter are not included in the Codex seems to suggest that Charles collected only those letters that concerned the benefit of the holy see, omitting those that we would call personal. He begins the manuscript as follows: “Writing everything down in such a way that no testimony whatsoever profitable to the holy Church might appear lacking to his successors.”

Why the same was done at Rome I do not understand. Although the close relationship between Adrian and Charles might persuade us that Charles shared his collection with him, the difference in subject matter and the varying order of the letters suggest otherwise. It is therefore more credible that such minor matters were handled through the words of envoys rather than by written letters. Indeed, the pontiff does not mention having received any letter from Addo that contained a response to his own. The request for beams was therefore made orally, and a corresponding answer was brought by the royal envoy. ID.]

to fulfill our request concerning the beams for the restoration of the holy Church, we ask your Excellence, advanced by God, that on the Kalends of August they be found ready here, if possible, at the threshold of blessed Peter, your patron, so that your eternal memory may endure both here and in the future.

As for the *camarado*, which is *ypochartosa* [Lambinus: *hypochartosis*, “hypocartosis”], for renewing the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle,

[Note: Du Cange uses this passage to explain *camaradum*: “It is,” he says, “*hypocartosis*, a roof covering or coating with which walls and vaults are covered.” He also says that Adrian uses the Greek word *hypocartosis*, with the same meaning, for the wooden vault itself and the vaulted structure.

What this structure formerly looked like must be learned from the panels preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica, which are also found in Ciampini (*On Sacred Buildings*, chapter 4); a treatment of those matters does not belong here.

In any event, according to Du Cange, Adrian uses *hypocartosis* less correctly for the mere structure of beams, since in his deeds preserved by Anastasius (section 342) the true meaning is expressed in these words: “He sculpted the vault of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which had been completely destroyed and ruined, after the model of the ancient one, and renewed it from the beginning with various colors.” No mention of a roofing restoration carried out by Charles occurs in the same account. Indeed, its author nowhere mentions even the construction of the vault with Charles’s resources.

From Einhard (*Life of Charles*, chapter 27) it is clear that Charles had nothing “more important than that the city of Rome should, through his work and labor, recover its ancient authority, and that the church of Saint Peter the Apostle should, through him, be not only protected and defended but also adorned and enriched above all other churches at his expense.” ID.]

first send us one master-builder who should inspect the timber that will be needed there, so that it may be renewed as it was in ancient times. Then, by your royal preeminence’s command, let that master-builder be sent to the region of Spoleto, and let him issue instructions there concerning the timber that will be needed for the aforesaid *ypochartosis*,

that is, the *camarado*, because such timber is by no means found within our borders.

[Note: Rome cannot be supposed to have been so lacking in master-builders in Adrian’s time, when Adrian surpassed all his predecessors by restoring church roofs and undertaking many other works of that kind. I will give one example above all: the restoration of Saint Peter’s basilica by Adrian himself (in Anastasius, section 335), without summoning craftsmen from elsewhere: “He sent Januarius, his treasurer, whom he knew to be capable, and with a multitude of people he replaced fourteen beams there, and newly restored the entire roof and portico of that basilica.”

Here, however, according to the agreement reached between the pontiff and Charles, whether in writing or orally, Archbishop Wilcharius of Gaul was to supervise the work. A master-builder is requested to inspect the beams necessary for the restoration and afterward to order them cut in the duchy of Spoleto and brought to Rome.

Why was this necessary? The restoration was to be carried out with the resources of the Frankish king and therefore, as an example of the greatest fidelity worthy of imitation, Adrian placed Archbishop Wilcharius in charge of the work, since sacred places are built or restored through the generosity of rulers.

Moreover, although the duchy of Spoleto had been offered to the holy see, Charles had reserved supreme jurisdiction over it; nor was it right for anything to be taken from it unless Charles himself ordered it. Thus Charles also, as will be clear below, when he desired mosaics and marble from the palace at Ravenna (ep. 81, or 67), asked the pontiff, who held supreme jurisdiction in the exarchate, to grant them to him.

In any event, Adrian’s insistence that everything be carried out with such religious care through men loyal to Charles was an act of singular prudence. Later, when the same king claimed more for himself than was proper, on the advice of flatterers, Adrian resisted him and presented his own example for Charles to imitate (epistles 93 and 97, or 71 and 85). ID.]

and, for this purpose, our most holy brother Archbishop Wulcharius,

[Note: Pagius identifies him as the archbishop of Sens (under 782, no. 5), and Mabillon considers him to have been archbishop of that same see—a title then common to all metropolitans—in the *Benedictine Annals* (book XXIV, no. 76).

Elsewhere (book XXI, no. 55), the same annalist reports that Wilcharius, bishop of Vienne, indignant that his church had been plundered by laymen, withdrew in 740 to the monastery of Agaunum, also known as Saint Maurice. At that time a bishop named Wilicarius is also mentioned at Sion, and some believe that the two were one and the same person; Mabillon rejects this (Annals, book XXIV, no. 6), since he does not think it possible that, after resigning the church of Vienne, he later presided over Sion.

Certainly, in 765 a bishop Wilicarius from the monastery of Saint Maurice attended the assembly at Attigny; and in 769 Archbishop Wilcharius of Sens was the first of twelve bishops of France to subscribe to the Lateran council of Stephen III. The brothers Sammarthanus state in the second, enlarged edition of *Gallia Christiana* that he died in the same year in which the council was held, after previously bringing relics of the Theban martyrs from the monastery of Agaunum to the see of Sens.

I admit that it is not far from the truth to suppose that the same Wilcharius, after resigning the church of Vienne, was made archbishop of Sens before 769 and died only in the thirtieth year after his resignation. But that he was still alive in 780, when he was placed in charge of the restoration of Saint Peter’s basilica, and in the following years, when he ordained Aegila, bishop of Iliberis, and sent him to Spain, seems utterly incredible. In addition to the years during which he held the see of Vienne before his resignation, more than forty further years would have to be assigned to him, which is contrary to all probability.

I shall discuss this again below (ep. 69, or 95). CENN.]

should now make every effort to come here, while the timber itself is drying, because while it is green we dare not use it for any work whatsoever.

[Col. 0327A] The aforesaid Addo, the deacon beloved of God, had formerly come here with our brother Fulrad, beloved of God, a religious abbot and priest [Note: [Col. 0327D] How greatly the Italian Annalist is mistaken in assigning this letter to the year 786 is quite clear from this passage; for Fulrad, abbot of Dionysius, died on 16 July 784, as Mabillon has shown at length (Annals, book XXV, no. 43). See the praises of this distinguished man in Pagius (year 784, no. 8). ID.]. He asked us to give him a holy body; but we, as we sent word to you long ago, terrified by a revelation [381], do not dare in any way to disturb anything further from the bodies of the saints [Note: At the end of the sixth century there are letters of Gregory the Great to the empress Constantina, who was requesting the head of Saint Paul (Register, book IV, letter 30, indiction XII). A hundred and eighty years later, when translations of relics had become customary, especially to frustrate the impiety of the Greeks, it should not be overlooked that Adrian testifies to such matters concerning the bodies of the saints located at Rome. For Paul, Adrian’s predecessor, mentioned shortly below in this letter, “seeing that many places in the cemeteries of the saints were neglected … and already exposed to imminent ruin, immediately removed those holy bodies from the ruined cemeteries themselves” [Col. 0328B] and transferred them into the city, as Anastasius records (section 259). Moreover, he granted to Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, three bodies of holy martyrs, namely Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius; their translation to Francia is celebrated by annalists and martyrologists in the year 765, as Pagius reports from Mabillon and others (year 764, no. 1). Likewise, according to Adrian, another was transferred in the same way to Aciulfus. Adrian therefore imposed a limit upon such translations, especially terrified by the vision [Col. 0328C] which he mentions. ID.]. But if it should be your will, concerning the body of the blessed martyr Candidus, which lies with our brother Wulcharius, archbishop, if it has not been moved—if it is indeed the same body—we grant that holy body to him together with you; it is the very body that our predecessor of holy memory, the lord Pope Paul, formerly granted to the priest Aciulfus [Note: In the Gothic Missal, which, according to the testimony of the most learned men Bona, Thomasius, and Mabillon, belonged to Narbonese Gaul—formerly occupied by the Goths—and was of great use throughout Gaul, there is a Mass of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, or the Thebans, who suffered at Agaunum near Sion. Only the name of Mauritius is given; but in Ruinart (Authentic Acts, p. 242, Verona edition) the three chief men are mentioned: Mauritius, the first standard-bearer; Exsuperius, the camp commander; and Candidus, the senator—all military dignities. Candidus of Sebaste is also mentioned by Ado (11 March) and by earlier martyrologists. The history of this Roman Candidus is reported only in these letters, and is nevertheless full of obscurity; no light is shed upon it either by the other letters of this Codex or by any ancient monument. Whether Ado’s earlier visit to Rome with Fulrad, his request, and the account of the vision or revelation that terrified the pontiff were committed to writing or merely entrusted to memory is uncertain; the priest Aciulfus himself and the tradition concerning the martyr’s body handed over to him are likewise unknown. This alone we know with certainty, on Adrian’s testimony: the body of the holy martyr is kept by Archbishop Wilcharius, contrary to the view based on Panvinio’s argument; and Ado, not Fulrad, requested it, as is wrongly asserted in the argument of this Codex Carolinus. ID.], since, by means of a council and the testimony of trustworthy persons, we have discovered the place and church [Col. 0327B] from which the holy body was granted by the aforesaid lord Pope Paul to the aforesaid priest Aciulfus [Note: Adrian discovered the church and place from which the body had been removed after assembling a gathering of the faithful and hearing trustworthy persons. Thus the matter was still obscure in the city itself and even among contemporaries. ID.].

As for the Neapolitan regions, concerning the way in which they have made common cause with the most wicked Greeks, or Beneventans (Lamb., Gent., Grets.: *consiliant*), we sent you word through our apostolic letters [382], setting everything out in detail and placing it upon the lips of your most faithful envoy, namely the deacon Addo, who ought to explain it to you more clearly and in order [Note: Namely, that the Greeks, together with the Neapolitans, had received Tarracina at the counsel of the duke of Benevento; also concerning the renewal of war against them and its principal objective, as well as the other matters individually related in the preceding letter. ID.]. Thus, just as always, and now also through your royal power confirmed by God, may the holy Church triumph in exaltation and increased honor, together with our spiritual daughter the queen, or rather your most excellent offspring; and may you, shining forth from your earthly kingdom, deserve to reign forever with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

## LXVIII. 383. A LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

Containing expressions of thanks for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and concerning the territory of Sabina: how the aforesaid king had promised it to Saint Peter and was asked to order that it be handed over in its entirety [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 14): “The fourteenth [letter] contains expressions of thanks for the exaltation of the holy Church of God; and concerning the territory of Sabina [the Sabine land], he asks that, just as he had promised, he order it to be handed over in its entirety [‘in full’].” CENN.].

*(A.D. 781, Codex Carolinus LXIX, chronicle 67.)*

[Col. 0328B]

### Argument

When Charles, while he was in Rome in April, had granted the Sabine territory to the Holy See, the pontiff sent his legates, Agatho the deacon and Theodore, consul and duke, his nephew, to request possession of that territory. The victories that Charles had so far gained, he says, ought to be attributed to Saint Peter, to whom the territories and cities he had bestowed had been a pleasing offering to the supreme God, through whom he had conquered, and by whom his kingdom and royal family had been made renowned throughout the whole world.

To the lord Charles [Note: [Col. 0329C] Summary 14, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.], our most excellent son and spiritual kinsman [Note: This title always occurs in the following letters; therefore one must not listen to the Italian Annalist, who mixes these letters with those already reported. As I said in the preliminary commentary, Cointius, and with him Pagius (782, no. 4), rightly prefer this letter to the others concerning the Sabine territory [Col. 0329D]. Yet the opening of the letter itself shows that it was the first of all those that follow. For that reason it is scarcely credible that Adrian, who had received the donation of the Sabine territory in April while Charles was in Rome, should have remained silent for nearly eight months about entering into its possession. Furthermore, the journey of the envoys going back and forth for the same reason, and whatever was done by them, should not be compressed into the narrow limits of a single year, since Charles was always ordering it. Thus at least this first letter should be assigned to this year. This will become clear from what follows. CENN.] king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

The blessed King and prophet David, filled with the Holy Spirit, praying for the benevolence and worthy support of your future kingdom toward the holy Church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for its most splendid and radiant glory, sings and says (Psalm LXVII):

> “Command, O Lord, your power; confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem; kings offer you gifts.”

Enriched by these gifts, your spiritual mother, the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, protected by God through your laborious struggles, rejoices, restored from the holy temple of blessed Peter, your patron. “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought” [Lamb., “confirms … what has been wrought”] in us, as we repeatedly pray for triumph in you; and through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he daily commands his power, subjecting all barbarian nations to you, enlarging and further exalting your most splendid kingdom throughout the whole world.

And because the vessel of our tongue cannot worthily express the greatness of your exalted and most dear love toward me, we proclaim with the apostolic voice, saying (Hebrews I):

> “In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; but in these last days, through the power of the magnificent work of his only-begotten Son, he has shown great things throughout the world.”

By blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, he has granted you victories which, with the right hand of God cooperating and protecting you, the Church of blessed Peter has displayed by many proofs through the gifts you have brought: both cities and various territories, in their entirety [Note: I pointed out above (letter 64, formerly 57, note g) that Adrian likewise designates the province of Istria and the Sabine province by the name “territory.” See what was said there about the other territories. ID.], which you offer to that apostle of God [Id., “which you have offered”].

Therefore, beseeching your royal clemency, advanced by God, we ask that, just as your most upright Excellency granted the Sabine territory in its entirety to blessed Peter, your nourisher, for the furnishing of lamps and the sustenance of the poor [Note: It should be recalled that in the year 777 (letter 59, formerly 49) the pontiff spoke of the patrimonies of Tuscany, Spoleto, Benevento, Corsica, and Sabina as having already been granted to the Holy See [Col. 0330C]. The distinction among these provinces is that only Sabina is called the “Sabine patrimony,” because that province was indifferently called both a patrimony and a territory, as I said in the preliminary commentary (no. 32). Had Pagius noticed this, he would not have rearranged the letters concerning the matter in order to distinguish territory from patrimony—which, nevertheless, he did not do; rather, he completely confused the history (Annals, 781, no. 1; 782, no. 4), since he did not perceive Cointius’s error. It should also be noted that this territory imitates the patrimonies not only in name but also in condition, since it was assigned to foreigners, the poor, and the lamps. ID.], so may you deign, under the guidance of your most excellent effort, to hand it over in its entirety to that same apostle of God.

For whatever you offer to blessed Peter the apostle, doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven, you sacrifice to his invisible majesty as a most pure sacrifice and holocaust, fragrant with the odor of divine sweetness, upon the altar of your heart, for your own eternal memory, and likewise for that of our most excellent daughter and spiritual co-mother [Note: You will find the title “co-mother” continually thereafter, for as long as Queen Hildegard survived; this provides considerable assistance in establishing the chronology of the letters. ID.], the lady queen, and for your most noble and excellent children, and also for your entire genealogy beloved of Christ [385]. And for the great grace granted to you by God above all kings through blessed Peter, let there be no adversary who can persuade your honey-sweet heart to withdraw from the love of blessed Peter, your protector, or from our affection, which we desire may endure forever [Lamb. adds: “to withdraw”], so that your praise may not cease throughout the whole world from the mouths of men proclaiming and spreading abroad the victories granted to you by God.

[Col. 0330C] We have therefore sent with great urgency [Note: Lambecius and Gentilotti restore the reading of the Codex. As for what the adverb *opere* means in these letters, where it occurs more than once, Ducange perhaps did not understand it and omitted the word. Stephen II uses it with precisely the same meaning (letter 9, formerly 6), for he says, “for we have sent with urgency,” as Adrian does here. Thus this adverb seems to have been used by both for “therefore” or something similar. ID.] [Lamb., Gent.: “with urgency”] our most faithful envoys to your royal power, namely our most beloved son Agatho the deacon, and Theodore, most eminent consul and duke, our nephew [Note: In the recently cited letter 59, formerly 49, this distinguished man is mentioned (note). ID.]. In our place, as we have placed it upon his lips [Col. 0331A], they will present our requests to you more fully. We ask you, for the love of blessed Peter the prince of the apostles, to receive them kindly and with the greatest affection; and when, in matters concerning blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, they present the petitions of your royal power protected by God, may you deign to heed them. Thus, when they have returned from you and reported your prosperity to us, bringing back the result of the affairs of that apostle of God, and when our spirit has thereby been relieved, may we worthily pray with the prophet as we sing (Psalm XIX):

> “O Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.”

May almighty God perfect in you the grace he has begun, prolong your life, together with that of our most excellent daughter and spiritual co-mother, the lady queen, and your most noble offspring, through many cycles of years here [Col. 0331B], and grant that you may enjoy victories while governing the reins of government at a still higher summit [386]; and, after long years and an advanced old age [Grets., “a progressed old age”], may he receive you into the assembly of the heavenly homeland, so that there you may deserve to reign without end. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

## LXIX. 389. A LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

Concerning the territory of Sabina: how Itherius and Maginarius, the lord king’s envoys, wished to return that territory in its entirety to the possessions of Saint Peter, but were unable to do so because of wicked men [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 13): “In the thirteenth [letter] to Charles, he indicates that Ittherius [Itherius] and Monegarius wished to return the Sabine territory [land] to the possessions of Saint Peter [to Saint Peter], but were entirely unable to do so because of wicked men [‘were unable to accomplish this at all’].” CENN.].

*(A.D. 782, Codex Carolinus LXVIII, chronicle 68.)*

[Col. 0331C]

### Argument

When the royal envoys Itherius, the abbot, and Maginarius, the chaplain, came so that the Sabine territory might be handed over for possession to the Holy See, they immediately proceeded into that territory together with the pontifical envoys. But for various reasons—which, as Adrian says, those same envoys will report—they were obliged to leave the matter unresolved. The pontiff therefore asks Charles to send back with his envoy Stephen the Sacellarius one or the other of them, so that he may establish the boundaries between the parties and deliver the possession of the ancient patrimony to the Holy See.

To the lord Charles [Note: [Col. 0331C] Summary 13, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.], our most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

In order to report thanks for the benefits of your most excellent royal power, the human mind, as I think, cannot speak of the many laborious struggles that you undertake each day for your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for us [387] [Note: This passage is corrupt. GRETS.], so that, through these supports of goodness [Note: Lambecius reads: “each day, so that through these supports of goodness …”], your most protected Excellency may undoubtedly believe that you will receive worthy recompense from that apostle of God, both here and in the future [Note: The expressions of thanks in this letter refer only to the royal envoys who had come to Rome with the pontifical envoys, in accordance with the requests of the preceding letter. In the Codex Carolinus it accidentally occupies its proper position. In the Vatican Codex it is likewise placed in reverse order, as we have seen happen elsewhere. Pagius assigns it to the year 783, after the death of Queen Hildegard, because her name is absent and the sons are not mentioned; both he and Zacagnus, as well as others who followed his opinion, are therefore mistaken. For the letters reported shortly below mention both the queen and the sons. Rather, there is reason to believe that this letter was written very soon after the envoys’ departure, when only the main point was touched upon and the other matters omitted. Below (letter 71, formerly 56), the matters almost indicated here will be found more clearly and fully, after two letters concerning the errors of the Spaniards. Since those letters belong to this year, they cannot be postponed longer. CENN.].

Our most faithful envoys, yours and ours, went to the Sabine territory, namely our son Itherius, the venerable abbot, and Maginarius, the religious chaplain [Note: Itherius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, was Charles’s chancellor and undertook several embassies to the Holy See. His colleague Maginarius, who succeeded Fulrad as abbot of Dionysius after the latter’s death on 16 July 784, is mentioned below more than once in Adrian’s letters. Both are praised in a diploma of Louis the Pious, which states that, in accordance with the requests made here, the boundaries between the Reatine and Sabine territories were established by the two abbots, after the aforesaid year 784. Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, volume II, in several places. ID.]. As you had properly arranged, they wished to hand over to us in its entirety the aforesaid Sabine territory, but they were entirely unable to do so, because wicked and unjust men raised various obstacles. Nevertheless, those same faithful envoys can report all this to you in detail on our behalf.

Therefore we have sent to your royal power, protected by God, our most reverend envoy Stephen [Note: The same Stephen, when he visited Spoleto in 776, had disclosed to Adrian the wicked plans of four Italian dukes who were plotting innovations (letter 57, formerly 59); and in 784 he took part in the hearing or council concerning the case of Potho, abbot of Saint Vincent at Volturno (letter 78, formerly 72). ID.], formerly the Sacellarius, to make our request known: that, for the reward of your soul, just as you began, so you may order the aforesaid Sabine territory to be handed over in its entirety to blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven [Note: The work begun—the transfer of possession of the entire territory—is clearly indicated; this shows that Pagius, Mabillon, and others are wrong to move this letter and place it last among all those found here. ID.]. Thus may that apostle of God, especially assisting your royal excellence promoted by God, grant that you may deserve to reign with all the saints.

For love of that same apostle of God and for the reward of your soul, we ask you to order that one of the two aforesaid envoys be sent to us with our aforesaid envoy Stephen, so that, just as it was in ancient times and as your aforesaid faithful envoys have now ascertained in truth [Note: These matters are treated more fully in the aforesaid letter 71; but it should be noted that in both places it is desired that one or the other of the envoys return. Here, however, they are said to be setting out from Rome with Stephen, and one or the other is urgently requested to be sent again with him; there, neither the departure of the envoys nor the return of one with Stephen is mentioned, because those envoys were already in Francia and neither had come again. This circumstance produced another letter with exactly the same meaning. ID.], you may command that it be handed over to us in its entirety [Col. 0333A]. And establish the markers [Note: “Markers” here means boundaries. A very clear example is supplied by the Visigothic law (book X, title 3, § 3), in Ducange: “Whenever a dispute concerning boundaries has arisen, the markers which were anciently established must be sought out, that is, earth embankments or enclosures which appear to have been constructed for the boundaries of estates; also stones which are known to have been fixed in place and carved as indications of boundaries. If these markers are absent, etc.” (Glossary, s.v. *Signum* 3). It is clear from the diploma of Louis the Pious that these boundaries were established by both envoys; the parties between which they were placed are also named: “As it was defined by Itherius and Magenarius, abbots and envoys of that man, between the same Sabine territory and the Reatine territory.” This occurred after the year 784, since Maginarius was not an abbot before then, as stated above (col. 331, note f). The exact time, however, cannot be determined, because it is not recorded in the letters preserved in this Codex. CENN.], setting them between the parties, so that we may remain without any dispute or controversy, and so that your most renowned memory may thereby be magnified in the heavenly kingdoms. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

## LXX. 389. A LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN, SENT TO EGILA, BISHOP IN THE REGIONS OF SPAIN

For maintaining the orthodox faith and observing a fast on Friday and Saturday [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex after 44): “He also wrote to certain others, such as Egila, bishop in Spain, and exhorts him to maintain the orthodox faith, and to observe a fast on Friday and Saturday.” He misuses the testimonies of Holy Scripture: he cites the promise, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” as referring to Peter. This final section, beginning with the words “He misuses,” appears to have been deleted by Panvinio from the Codex. ID.].

*(A.D. 782, Codex Carolinus XCV, chronicle 69.)*

### Argument

He says that he sent very lengthy letters to Aegila, the Spanish bishop who desired to preserve the right faith, confirming the Catholic faith by the authority of the Fathers. When he discovers that these letters had not reached him, and when Charles, through Peter, bishop of Ticinus, had requested that they be sent again to his friend Aegila, he gives his envoys Bellerephonsus and John a copy of them drawn from the archive. He gives Aegila many warnings to beware of heretics. He discusses the fast on Friday and Saturday.

Adrian [Note: Baronius, immediately after Summary 44, as also Centuriator. GRETS.] bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved Egila, bishop [Note: From the superscription of this and the following letter, as well as letter 82, formerly 97 [Col. 0334C], it is clear that those are not mistaken who observe that when pontiffs wrote to certain eminent persons they placed their own name after the recipient’s, while with inferiors they placed it before. Garnerius denies this (Appendix to the *Book of the Diurnal*, p. 144). Spanish authors call this bishop Egilan and contend that he was bishop of the Illiberitan see, not far from Granada; this scarcely seems credible, since almost all Spain was groaning beneath the yoke of the Moors. CENN.].

Long ago we received with immense affection your especially profound and informed address sent to the apostolic see—which is the head of all the Churches of God—in accordance with the most ardent faith that you bear from the depths of your heart toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward us. In response to what your prudence requested, we strove to compose, from the divine fountain, in the clearest and most salutary manner, writings concerning the orthodox faith, according to the ancient rite of our holy Catholic and Apostolic Church [Grets. adds: “ancient”] [Col. 0333C], observing without blemish the venerable institution of the holy Fathers. Through the carriers of those letters we then sent them to your Holiness [390].

And since, as is reported, those apostolic letters did not reach you at all, we have sent them again, having them written in our registers and transcribing them below through the bearers of this letter, namely Bellerephonsus and John the cleric [Note: The following letter is a copy of the one mentioned here, for the original was preserved in the archive of the Holy See [Col. 0334D]. It had therefore been sent much earlier; but since its date is uncertain, I have retained the order of the Codex. ID.], just as our most faithful envoy, the most reverend and holy Peter, bishop of the Church of Ticinus [Note: Cointius and Pagius record the death of this bishop in the year 783 and therefore place the date of this letter between 781 and 783, since the title “spiritual kinsman” applied to Charles is thought to prohibit an earlier date, while the death of the bishop of Ticinus prohibits a later one. Perhaps the embassy of the bishop of Ticinus was arranged by Charles before he left Italy in 781, and the letter was sent at the same time; but there is no reason to oppose the learned men on a matter of no importance. Basnage, in Canisius (Ancient Readings, volume II, p. 286), insists that this is certain. Pagius rightly establishes the birth-year of the Felician heresy as 783 on Adrian’s authority, since Adrian attacks it in letter 82, formerly 97; he does not, however, hold with Pagius that this letter of Adrian should be assigned to that year, but postpones it to 785. I follow his opinion, as I shall explain there. ID.], that most excellent and radiant son and our spiritual kinsman, the lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sent to request on behalf of your distinguished affection. Through his royal assistance, favoring your wishes, we have striven to fulfill them completely.

But those bold and heretical men who endeavor to overthrow your orthodox faith, constraining you from every side and sowing distress and various storms, you should confront clothed in the apostolic commandment, imbued with apostolic disciplines, and filled with the salutary institutions of the holy Fathers concerning the orthodox faith. Those who refuse to embrace your preaching of the true faith, after a first and second admonition or rebuke, regard as heathens and publicans; consider their undisciplined plots worthless. The prophet bears witness, saying (Ezekiel III):

> “If, however, you warn the wicked man, and he does not turn from his wickedness and from his wicked way, he himself will die in his wickedness, but you will have saved your own soul.”

For you must imitate the commands and follow the footsteps of the blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election (II Thessalonians III):

> “Withdraw yourself from every brother who walks disorderly.”

And remain steadfast (Romans VIII):

> “For all things work together for good for those who love God.”

Indeed, if you follow the teaching of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, you will fear no evil, because its most powerful author and founder, blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, is with you to the end, as the Lord promised (Matthew, last chapter):

> “Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age.”

Let no dullness or any uncertainty rise into your most gracious and sacred mind, because (Matthew V):

> “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

And again (Hebrews XI):
