> “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms” [Note: In this entire exhortation, sufficiently clear considering the barbarism of that age, he confirms the bishop’s steadfastness against the errors of the Spaniards; he does not enumerate them individually, since he had expressed them in other letters, of which he appends a copy—namely, the following letter, which precedes this one in order. CENN.].

Moreover, your own letters reported that you were very concerned about Friday and Saturday, because we say that these two days must be devoted to fasting. Do not follow the laziness, impious perversity, madness, and empty, deceitful fables of heretical men. Rather, follow the words of our teachers and holy Fathers, as they have instructed us: namely, of the blessed Pope Sylvester and Pope Innocent [Note: Whatever may be said about the decree of Sylvester found in Eusebius’s Life, Innocent teaches us in his famous decretal letter to Decentius of Eugubium (chapter 4): “We do not deny, therefore, that one should fast on Friday; rather, we say that this should also be done on Saturday, because both days imposed grief upon the apostles, and upon those who followed Christ.” ID.], and likewise of the blessed Jerome [Note: Saint Jerome writes thus to Lucinus of Baetica (letter 28): “Concerning the Saturday about which you ask whether one should fast, and concerning whether the Eucharist should be received daily—which, they say, the Roman and Spanish Churches observe—I think I should briefly advise you that ecclesiastical traditions, especially those that do not harm the faith, should be observed as they were handed down by our ancestors, and that one people’s custom should not be overthrown by another people’s contrary practice.” See the authors in Ducange, s.v. “Saturday fasting,” where this letter too is cited, but especially Quesnel’s sixth dissertation addressed to Saint Leo, which treats the matter at great length. ID.], or of Isidore. Add their divine discourses [Col. 0335B] to our apostolic rule, and let your Holiness hold firmly and without doubt that one must fast on Saturday [Note: Lambecius and Gentilotti read: “holding that it should be celebrated in imitation”; these words were deleted with a line drawn beneath them, as Gentilotti notes.].

For if you do not wish to depart from the royal road, do not abandon the judgment of the aforesaid holy Fathers, and do not neglect to read the little works of blessed Augustine, where he recalls that his outstanding preacher and teacher, Saint Ambrose, greatly praised our holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church for the Saturday fast [392] [Note: Augustine reports Ambrose’s words in his letter to Casulanus: “When I am here [at Milan], I do not fast on Saturday; when I am at Rome, I fast on Saturday” (Augustine, letter 86), for he did not disapprove of the customs of his own Church. But Gregory the Great said (in response to Augustine, question 3): “Things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things”; for he disapproved only of those customs which seemed to the monk Augustine better than the Roman ones. Adrian here argues absolutely for the Roman custom. So too, in the following century, Nicholas instructed Hincmar and other Gallic prelates: “Especially,” he says, “since concerning the Saturday fast, in the time of Saint Sylvester, confessor of Christ, the matter was sufficiently discussed and debated, and it was definitively decreed that it should be observed everywhere, and since no one afterward dared rashly to act or even to murmur against that decree; indeed, the institution of the apostolic see and the subsequent observance of the Roman Church have always been found to have carried out that salutary ordinance.” (Nicholas I, letter 70). The reason is that both in Spain in Adrian’s time and in Gaul in Nicholas’s age, it was not good ecclesiastical custom but errors opposed to the apostolic see that were being fostered. See Baronius (year 57, no. 204 and following) and Pagius there, who, using the recently mentioned dissertation of Quesnel, argues for the Roman Church’s custom of fasting on Saturday. It is not merely upon one decree of Sylvester, drawn from his pseudepigraphal acts and to which both pontiffs adhere most closely, that this custom rests; rather, it is shown clearly to go back to the times of the apostles. CENN.].

And because, with the Holy Spirit at work, we judge that your Holiness cannot be overcome by any temptations, we shall set out in a clear written sequence the matters that we promised above [Col. 0336A].

## LXXI. 393. A LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN TO EGILA, BISHOP, OR JOHN, PRIEST

Concerning their consecration, or steadfastness, to be preached in the regions of Spain; concerning the Paschal feast; concerning the predestination of man, whether to good or to evil; concerning their defilement both in foods and in drink; concerning various errors; concerning their false priests, who take wives while a husband is still living; concerning freedom of choice; and concerning many other points that had arisen in those regions against the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0336C] Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex after 44): “The same man wrote a letter to Egila, bishop, or John [Joan.], priest, concerning consecration or steadfastness [and continence] to be preached in the regions of Spain; concerning the Paschal feast, that it be celebrated [observed] at the time when it is celebrated by the Roman Church; likewise he admonished him concerning the predestination of man, whether to good or to evil; concerning their defilement both in foods and in drink, and concerning [both in drink; concerning] various errors; concerning their false priests, who take wives while a husband is still living; concerning freedom of choice; and many other points that had arisen in those regions against the Catholic faith. At the end he admonishes them that all should be concordant, that they should know the canons, and that they should excommunicate all who do not obey salutary precepts.” ID.].

*(A.D. 782, Codex Carolinus XCVI, chronicle 70.)*

### Argument

This is a copy of the letter that had been sent to Bishop Aegila and the priest John, who were going into Spain to preach. In it, numerous errors of heretics are attacked. The Felician heresy is not mentioned, because it had not yet broken out. The Nicene ordinance concerning the day of Easter is established, against Spanish errors, by the authority of councils and papal decrees. Those who held wrong views concerning predestination, grace, and free choice, and were entangled in many other errors, are reproved. Although those errors had been extinguished with the Priscillianist heresy, care must be taken lest doctrines condemned long ago revive.

Adrian [Note: [Col. 0336D] Baronius and Centuriator Gretser mention this letter.] bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Egila, our beloved bishop, and to John, presbyter [Note: This letter, of which the preceding one is virtually an appendix—for it contains something concerning discipline that is entirely absent here—is a response to Egila’s letter sent immediately after his consecration, and precedes it by several months, perhaps even more than a year. For it ought to have been known to Charles that these letters had not reached Spain, since he asked the pontiff for a copy of them. You will sometimes find it defective, either through the negligence of the notaries or through the carelessness of the person who entered it into the Codex; at times it is even mutilated. But correction is easy, since most of this letter was taken from the same source as Letter 82, elsewhere 97, from which the passages missing from this copy may be recovered and those transcribed less accurately may be corrected, as Gretser noted.]

Having heard of your orthodox steadfastness in Christ, and that you cling so firmly to the sincere traditions of the ancient faith and communion [Col. 0337A] that the contagion of those who betray it could in no way defile your mind devoted to Christian truth, we glorified the Lord and continually praised your charity. Through the bearers of your letters—namely, Saranus the deacon and Victorinus the cleric—we received the expressions of your affection; and, having examined them more fully, we were clearly informed of their meaning. Since the primacy of the apostolic see has been divinely entrusted with a concern owed to all the churches, we learned how commendably you know the truth of the faith and how diligently you devote the service of pastoral duty to the Lord’s flock.

Our brother Wulcharius, archbishop of the province of Gaul [Note: I have already said that it is difficult to believe that this archbishop presided over the see of Sens, as Mabillon and Pagi unanimously maintain. Here again we see him in the year 782, and it is certain that he was still alive, since, although this letter is a copy of one written earlier, he is not called “of blessed memory,” as he is in Letter 82, mentioned above, which I have thought, with Basnage, should be assigned to the year 785. Accordingly, if the uncertain years during which he governed the see of Vienne are added, together with at least thirty years before he obtained the episcopate, we shall have an exceedingly aged man—forty-five years after his resignation of the bishopric of Vienne—according to the discipline long established by the canons in the East and especially in the Western provinces of Gaul and Spain (Council of Neocaesarea, canon 11; Council of Agde, canons 16 and 17; Third Council of Braga, canon 20). He would have been not merely unequal to undertaking a journey to Rome to preside over the restoration of the Vatican basilica, but even to bearing the episcopal burden. Let the learned decide whether another Wulcharius should be posited, distinct from that man of Sens who took part in the Lateran Council of 769 and was there called archbishop of Gaul and archbishop of the province of Sens. ID.], to whom we also gave permission and authority to direct you concerning your ordinations, has informed us of your work of preaching orthodox [Col. 0337B] faith and the holy Catholic Church in the regions of the province of Spain [Note: He calls all Spain, which was divided into five or six provinces, the province of Spain; below he says that it was assigned to Egila’s preaching (Letter 82, elsewhere 97) on the condition that he should neither seek nor usurp any foreign see, but offer God only the gains of souls. He appears to have acted similarly in Gaul, since he calls Wulcharius archbishop of the province of Gaul. Could Wulcharius, like Augustine formerly in England and Boniface more recently in Germany, have exercised authority extending throughout all Gaul? I believe this is what Adrian meant by the permission he requested in order to care for the Spanish church. This opinion is supported by the fact that the Gallican church had not yet been restored to its ecclesiastical provinces, as will be shown below (Letter 86, elsewhere 87), since Adrian restored the metropolitan see of Bourges in 786. It should also be noted that at the Lateran Council of 769, which Bishop Hermembert of Joigny attended, Herminarius, bishop of Bourges, subscribed. According to the brothers Sammarthani, Deodatus succeeded Herminarius when he died in 774, and Hermembert succeeded Deodatus in 783; after receiving the pallium three years later, he was made archbishop. But if Herminarius, who sat sixth among the Gallican prelates at the Lateran Council, yielding precedence to his seniors, had two successors, Wulcharius must be judged to have outlived the other members of that council by a considerable time, if he was older than the rest. If it is established that two Hermemberts, together with a third Hermembert the presbyter (Letter 93, elsewhere 71), flourished in Gaul at nearly the same time, why should two Wulchariuses not be admitted as well? ID.].

We triumph with great joy, knowing that throughout the world the Lord Sabaoth has left the seed of a pure confession: a seed that, falling not upon rocky ground, has not withered under the heat of temptation; that has not fallen beside the road, exposed to wandering enemies; that has not fallen among thorns to be choked; but, scattered by your heavenly sowing upon the good soil of pious devotion, produces fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold—mystically signifying the perfection of the Lord’s grain [Col. 0338A].

Therefore, with rejoicing hearts, we urge you more confidently to preserve your breasts wisely undefiled by every assault of pestilence, since “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24; Lambecius and Gentilotius add: “until the end”). “The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing” (Philippians 4). For “greater is he who is in us than he who is in this world,” and Scripture assures us that the kingdom of the Lord is within us.

Although great distances of place separate us, if you persevere in the unity of our faith, we are with you—provided only that, with the Lord’s help, you maintain persevering steadfastness. The Apostle says (Philippians 1): “For to you it has been granted, for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” [Col. 0338B] To strengthen holy minds for this courage, the most holy archbishop already mentioned sent your affection to us, having yielded us the authority granted to him [Gretser adds: “to us, yielding it”], out of love for the apostolic faith. You may rightly hope that those who persevere in integrity will be adorned even to the crown of the prize.

For your letters themselves reported that many in those regions, having fallen into folly and mental derangement, dare to despise the substance of our account and admonition, issued according to the institution of the venerable Council of Nicaea concerning the celebration of Easter [Note: The Council of Nicaea, after condemning the Quartodecimans, settled the controversy concerning the day on which Easter should be celebrated, as Eusebius and Theodoret explain. Moreover, it assigned to the patriarch of Alexandria the duty of determining the full moon of March each year and announcing it to the Roman pontiff, who was to send Easter letters to all the churches: “We entrust all this care,” says Leo the Great (Letter 64), “to the bishop of Alexandria, since among the Egyptians the knowledge of this calculation seemed to have been handed down from ancient times, by which the day on which the aforesaid solemnity would occur each year was reported to the apostolic see, so that the decision of this writing might generally reach the more distant churches.” Some assert that this was done by those patriarchs as long as they remained in the Catholic faith, although the controversy between the Alexandrians and the Latins contradicts this. In any case, the Roman pontiffs announced the date of Easter to the churches both before the Council of Nicaea and after the defection of the Alexandrians. A formula survives (Roman Diurnus, chapter 3, title 10), expressed in these few words: “Farewell, brothers, in the name of the Lord. Easter will be on the [day] of the [month], in the [indiction].” See more on this matter in Baronius (year 325, no. 5 and following) and the authors cited by Ducange under “Easter Letter.” The nineteen-year cycle, or golden number, established by that same synod [Col. 0339B–C], as Ambrose testifies (Letter to the bishops of Aemilia), was of great assistance to the Alexandrians in fulfilling this task. For the difference between the Latin and Alexandrian churches, see Cardinal Noris, On the Paschal Cycle of the Latins, volume II, Verona edition. It is not our purpose to introduce here the various doctrines concerning Easter. When the pontiffs ceased sending these Easter letters to the provinces is uncertain. It is nevertheless clear from this passage that Adrian followed the ancient practice. CENN.], and thereby [Col. 0339A] dare to despise it.

If, when there is a full moon—that is, on the fourteenth day of the moon [Note: Lambecius has: “if the full moon occurs on the Sabbath, and the following day is Sunday, namely the fifteenth day of the moon.”], holy Easter is not celebrated, but, the fifteenth day being passed over, the joys of the Easter festival are announced as to be celebrated on another Sunday of the following week, which is the twenty-second day of the moon—if this is considered inwardly and carefully, the reckoning for the Paschal festivals promulgated by the great and venerable Council of Nicaea, at which three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled, will without doubt remove every error and ambiguity from the hearts of those who hesitate. But while many strive to defend their own inventions, presenting themselves as clever, perceptive, and learned in worldly knowledge but ignorant of spiritual instruction, they pass over through sluggish negligence the ancient tradition of the Fathers and desire to obscure the truth with falsehood [Col. 0339B].

For in that same great Council of Nicaea, after the nineteen-year cycle had been confirmed by the Fathers, it was promulgated among other things that the solemnities of this sacred festival should not be extended beyond the twenty-first day of the moon [Note: Noris (loc. cit., p. 686) observed that until the year 457, under Pope Leo the Great, Easter on the fifteenth day of the moon remained disputed between the Latins and the Easterners. He uses the words of Victor of Aquitaine to show why the Latins deferred Easter to the twenty-second moon: “It is preferable,” he says, “to extend the Easter festival to the twenty-second day of the moon than in any way to begin the Lord’s Passion before the fourteenth moon.” Thus the error of the Spaniards was once common among the Latins. Finally, in the sixth century, they adopted in Italy especially the cycle reformed by Dionysius so as to agree exactly with the Alexandrian cycle, as Noris likewise notes (p. 724), and the orthodox retained it until the Lilian Calendar approved by Gregory XIII, which was therefore called Gregorian after the name of so great an advocate. Adrian accordingly rightly reproves the Spaniards for reviving a custom long obsolete. See the letters of Dionysius Exiguus in the apparatus to the Lucchese edition of Baronius (pp. 247 and following). CENN.].

This reckoning of Easter was also confirmed by the venerable Council of Antioch; and among its other provisions, it is recorded in the first chapter that the following was written:

> “We decree that all who have dared to dissolve the definition of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, assembled in the presence of the most devout and most venerable prince Constantine, concerning the saving solemnity of holy Easter, are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church [Note: Here you have a canon close to the Dionysian version, although it differs somewhat. This also warns us against the false opinion of those who attach that version to the holy see from its very origin. See the preliminary commentary, no. 15 and following. ID.].”

Yet if they persisted more contentiously in opposing what had been rightly established, they decreed that they should be subjected to still harsher prohibitions [Lambecius: “future”]. For the most blessed Dionysius, in the letter he composed concerning the calculation of Easter, says:

> “They decreed that, beginning on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, according to the judgment of all the Easterners, and especially according to the expertise of the Egyptians, the course of the spring equinox should follow; since they are skilled and learned in this calculation, it is expressly noted that it must be sought [Note: Lambecius adds: “They decreed that the Easter festival should be celebrated only after that day, and especially …”], on which, even if the fourteenth moon should be the day on which Easter is to be celebrated, the holy Council of Nicaea firmly established without ambiguity [Note: Lambecius adds: “that it must be sought. It is also expressly noted there that if the fourteenth moon falls on the Sabbath, Easter should be celebrated on the following Sunday, the fifteenth moon, as the holy synod also [established].”].” [Note: This is none other than Dionysius Exiguus, whose letters I recently mentioned. But the pontiff evidently thought he was an Alexandrian. This passage should be restored from his first letter, not from Adrian’s letter, as Gretser and Lambecius point out and as Lambecius carries out; for the passage is mutilated and corrupt everywhere. Dionysius writes as follows: “Since the moon does not move at an equal pace with the sun, it reaches the spring equinox after an interval of so many days. This equinox is specifically marked, according to the judgment of all the Easterners and especially of the Egyptians, who are more skilled than all others in calculation, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. In this matter, even if the fourteenth moon should fall on the Sabbath—which is evidently possible once in ninety-five years—the same holy synod firmly established without ambiguity that Easter should be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the fifteenth moon.” CENN.]

Pay attention, our beloved, also to what the blessed Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian church, sent to our predecessor, the most blessed Pope Leo, at the command of the emperor Marcian of pious memory. After much else, he says:

> “In ancient times the Lord, speaking through Moses, says (Exodus 12): ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. And you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.’” [Lambecius adds: “indicating the time of Easter.”]

A little later he adds:

> “If at any time the fourteenth moon is found on a Sunday, the festival is to be deferred to the following week, just as our ancient Fathers did, transferring the fourteenth moons that occurred on Sunday to another Sunday [Note: Proterius of Alexandria, at the command of Marcian Augustus—whom the pontiff had earnestly asked to entrust the Easter question to him for careful examination (among Leo’s letters, after Letter 63)—wrote that famous letter to Leo, which Bede mentions (On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 42) and which compelled the pontiff to accept the celebration of Easter in the year 455. Adrian extracted these few words from it for his own purpose. But because both here and in his other letter the wording is quite different, I restore it from Proterius’ own letter in Labbe (Councils, volume III, pp. 1350 and following): “Formerly the Lord indicated the time of Easter through Moses, saying: ‘Observe the month of new things,’ declaring this to be the first; and again he says: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year, and you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.’ … For in ancient times, whenever the fourteenth moon was found on Sunday, the festival was deferred to the following week, as is proved in the eighty-ninth and ninety-third years of the reign of Diocletian … Just as our Fathers did, deferring the fourteenth moons that occurred on Sunday.” CENN.]”

From this, our beloved, it is clear that the solemnity of this venerable festival may not rightly be deferred beyond the twenty-first day of the moon [Lambecius adds: “that it is lawful”], observing the number of the days of the week, while the solar course is entirely out of step with the lunar course. For in six days the Lord, creator of all, made the heavenly firmament and all its adornment, the shining waters, the plants produced by the earth, the substance of the elements, and all living creatures that creep; and on the final day he fashioned man from the soil [Note: In the manuscript codices, Lambecius and Gentilotius read: “and finally he fashioned man from the soil of the fields”; nor was there reason for Tengnagel, who did not understand that word, to introduce “day” and call it “the last,” since Friday is not the final day of the week, nor does the pontiff mention days of the week. “Fields,” therefore, which Ducange found used for a field, region, or province, as his examples prove, is used here by Adrian in a broader sense for earth in general, in accordance with the Apostle (1 Corinthians 15:47): “The first man was from the earth, earthly”; and John (3:31): “He who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth.” For God himself, when expelling Adam from paradise (Genesis 3:19, 23), says: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken … The Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight to work the earth from which he was taken.” If anyone asks why these obscure terms repeatedly occur in the Codex, I reply that they were once regarded as elegant expressions, although they made the meaning more obscure. ID.], and on the seventh day rested from all the work he had done.

Accordingly, within these seven days, beginning from the fourteenth day of the moon, which is the full moon, if Sunday should occur—which is the first and holy day—then, because one ought not to fast on it, the proper order requires Christians to celebrate holy Easter after the intervening Sunday, which is the twenty-first day of the moon and likewise the first and holy day. For if the fourteenth moon occurs on the Sabbath, the following Sunday must not be passed over, namely the fifteenth day of the moon. We venerate that Sunday, which is the first day of the Sabbaths, on which light came forth at God’s command at the beginning of the world, and on which our Savior, the true light, rose bodily from the dead.

But if eight days are passed over from the fourteenth day of the moon, when the fast is broken, so that the Easter festival is deferred to the twenty-second day of the moon, then what must be called and observed is not a week, that is, a hebdomad, but an ogdoad [Note: The nineteen-year cycle mentioned above was divided into two parts: an ogdoad, comprising eight years, and an hendecad, comprising eleven. Dionysius Exiguus discusses these in another Easter letter (Baronius’s apparatus, p. 249), as do Bucher and Petavius, and Cardinal Noris in On the Ravenna Paschal Cycle (Works, volume II, pp. 819 and following). Here the word is used less properly for eight days. By counting the days of the week from Sunday, the passage makes even clearer the corruption introduced by Tengnagel, who inserted Friday as the final day of the week. Friday is the final day of the world’s creation, that is, the sixth, but certainly not the final day of the week, whose remaining day is the seventh, when Catholics break the fast. ID.], as foolish and senseless people define it [Lambecius: “profane it”].

Reason also urges us to consider that seven weeks, not eight, intervene between the Easter festival and holy Pentecost, when our Redeemer, the Son of the living God, sent the Paraclete Spirit from the Father to his holy apostles after his glorious resurrection. For this reason we proceed along the royal road and shall not turn aside completely onto the crooked path filled with thorns and thistles. Let those who desire to devise new inventions and monuments of wickedness go along that path, so that thorns and thistles may rightly be produced for them.

Long ago, our holy pontiffs, predecessors and forebears, sent admonition and exhortation concerning this question and that heresy to those fellow bishops [Gretser: “those sharing the same regions”]. In appropriate letters they promulgated the teachings of the blessed Cyril and Theophilus [Note: The letters written by both of them concerning the Paschal cycle are found in Bucher and Petavius. Consult them if you wish to know more. ID.], as well as those of many other holy Fathers, whose enumeration would be lengthy. There is no doubt that these teachings are known to your affection. Therefore, beloved, we do not cease to urge you earnestly to beware of false brothers and to strive beyond doubt to celebrate Easter as our holy Roman Church, the head of all the churches of God, celebrates the Paschal solemnity. Thus, just as the religion of Christian faith makes us equal, it may also make us equals in our festivals.

Your affection also informed us that certain people, professing—or, according to Lambecius and Gentilotius, corrupting—themselves as Catholics while persisting in error, preach that anyone who does not eat the blood of cattle or pigs, or meat from strangled animals, is uncultivated or unlearned. We, instructed and trained in the apostolic commandments, affirm and proclaim that if anyone eats the blood of cattle or pigs, or meat from strangled animals, he is not merely alien to all learning but entirely foreign even to ordinary understanding; bound by the chain of anathema, he falls into the snares of the devil [Note: The apostles of the Third Council of Jerusalem commanded abstinence from blood and strangled animals by a positive law. Baronius (year 51, no. 24) and Binius (Labbe, Councils, volume I, p. 21; volume II, p. 430) give the reason: namely, the cause of joining or welding together, so that Christians, Jews, and gentiles living together might more easily become one people. But when the cause ceased, not everyone immediately abandoned the practice; some gradually ceased to observe it. Baronius says that it was eventually abolished, equally laudably, by the consent of the whole Western Church. Its precise date of cessation cannot be determined. Certainly, as Binius observes, the law had fallen somewhat into disuse in the time of Augustine (Against Faustus, book II, chapter 13). But Baronius cites the Second Council of Orléans, canon 20, and the Council of Worms, canon 65, as restoring that law. The Second Council of Orléans was held in 533, whereas the Council of Worms occurred after 868, under Pope Adrian II. The source and origin of the adopted law, even after the original reason had ceased, were the Greek canons disseminated throughout the West and rendered into more elegant Latin by Dionysius Exiguus near the end of the fifth century, or rather at the beginning of the sixth. For in that collection is canon 2 of Gangra, which in Dionysius’ version reads: “If anyone condemns a person who eats meat, except blood, meat sacrificed to idols, and strangled meat, with religion and faith, as though he had no hope because of such eating, let him be anathema.” Hence the Spaniards, although using another version, included in their own code (book VI, title 5) the rule: “Concerning those who condemn a person who eats meat apart from sacrificial meat and strangled meat.” Hence the Gauls composed the cited canon 20 of Orléans II. Hence Theodore and others enriched their penitential books in England. Finally, Rome, embracing the collection of Cresconius, revived during the eighth century a law long obsolete. Accordingly, in Gregory III’s Judgments, chapter 29 (Labbe, Councils, volume VI, p. 1483), the law is expressed in these words: “Let no one eat strangled meat, nor presume to eat or drink the blood of any animal; but if anyone does so, let him do penance for forty days.” Adrian also alludes to it in the brief transmission of the canons that he presented to Charles, expressing canon 2 of Gangra as follows: “If anyone curses a person who religiously eats meat, let him be anathema.” In this letter he clearly declares ignorant and alien from the other faithful those who fail to observe that law. Thus Ivo and Gratian too (Distinction 30, “If anyone eats meat”) transferred the same canon, though in different words from those of Dionysius, into their respective collections. The Gloss rightly observes: “What it says concerning blood and strangled meat is not binding today, because this was prohibited only symbolically.” In addition, the collections of that crude age introduced many other penalties into discipline, contrary to ancestral custom and accepted within the city itself. CENN.]

[Col. 0343A] But concerning what others among them say—that predestination to life or to death is in God’s power [Note: You will find all these matters also in the following letter. GRETSER.] [Lambecius adds: “and not ours”; they say: “Why do we strive to live, since it is in God’s power?”]—and what still others say: “Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, since that is in our power, as though we possessed free choice?”—they are truly unable either to give or to accept any account, being ignorant of the little works written by the blessed Fulgentius, bishop, addressed to the presbyter Eugippius against the arguments of a certain Pelagian. In them that Father, teaching much below, adds these words [Note: Basnage (Canisius, volume II, p. 286) does not think that what follows concerning predestination and free choice, taken from the blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, is sufficient to refute the other error of the Spaniards. CENN.]:

> “Those people, while reprehensibly introducing grace alone on their own behalf, have damnably trampled it underfoot in themselves. They assert that some are destined to life and others to death. Consider by what bonds of impiety they bind themselves. If I have been predestined to good, I will not need to resist evil; but if I was born for evil, doing good will profit me nothing. Thus, with the desire for praise and glory shut off on both sides, one grows sluggish through security and the other through despair. Consequently every exercise of justice will cease, prayer will stop, and action will grow weak.
>
> “But it is not so. Rather, let us pray without ceasing, because the Lord himself says: ‘Pray without ceasing, lest you enter into temptation.’ Let us nevertheless struggle against every sin not only by prayer but also by labor, because the Lord himself has testified in the present reading that each person will receive his own reward according to his labor.
>
> “We shall show, with God’s help, that these words, by which the author of that discourse attempts to attack the truth of predestination, were spoken inconsiderately and indiscriminately, and so forth.”

And later:

> “God therefore prepared the works of his mercy and justice in the eternity of his unchangeableness. Just as he was never ignorant of his future works, so he was never negligent in preparing those works. He prepared merits for people who were to be justified; he prepared rewards for those same people who were to be glorified. But for the wicked he did not prepare wicked wills or wicked works; rather, he prepared just and eternal punishments for them. This is God’s eternal predestination of future works, which, just as we recognize is always conveyed to us by apostolic teaching, so we confidently preach.
>
> “For blessed Paul clearly and frequently speaks of the predestination of those whom the Lord freely saves. He says of God: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers’ (Romans 8). And afterward: ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.’ Certainly he did not call others, but those whom he predestined he called, those he justified [Lambecius and Gentilotius add: “those he justified, those he glorified”]. Nothing uncertain wavers in God’s works, because nothing nullifies his predestination. God therefore begins the works of his predestination with calling and completes them with glorification. Yet not in all whom he called, but in those whom he calls according to his purpose; for ‘all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose’ (ibid., verse 28).”

Again, after much else:

> “Let the truth of predestination therefore be held by all the faithful. Whoever does not believe in the divine purpose within this predestination will not attain the glorious effect of that same predestination. Whoever is not predestined to glory is undoubtedly foreknown for punishment. This is recognized as having been prepared and predestined in God’s name so that through it unbelief and iniquity may be punished. For this reason the blessed apostle Jude (verse 4) says that certain people have been destined for judgment, in these words: ‘For certain ungodly people have slipped in, who were long ago designated and predestined for this judgment of our God.’ Carefully following the teaching of the Holy Spirit, he does not say that the ungodly were predestined to sin, but to judgment—that is, not to ungodliness, but to punishment. They were not predestined to commit their vicious acts of ungodliness, but to receive what they receive by the judgment of divine justice. Their deed is what they do impiously; God’s deed is what they receive justly.”

Again, after other matters:

> “Accordingly, when the author of that discourse subsequently added: ‘Rather, let us pray without ceasing, because the Lord himself says (Matthew 16): “Pray without ceasing, lest you enter into temptation”;’ and afterward: ‘Nevertheless, let us struggle against every sin not only by prayer but also by labor,’ …”

And again:

> “The Lord calls those who labor in this way, saying (Matthew 11): ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.’ But let us humbly ask God for grace, which we may continually have working with us, through which God may preserve us in labor and, when our labor is completed, lead us to our reward.”

Furthermore, beloved, concerning the various matters you have made known to us: many people, saying that they are Catholics [Lambecius and Gentilotius add: “that they are”], live a common life with Jews and unbaptized pagans, both in food and drink, and also in various errors, and say that they have incurred no defilement. There is also the prohibition that no one may take on a yoke with unbelievers; yet they bless their daughters together with another person, and thus the daughters are given over to a pagan people. Others are ordained to preside without examination by the aforesaid presbyters. Another monstrous and pernicious error has also become widespread: the pseudo-priests themselves take women in marriage while their husbands are still living. There are also the matters concerning free choice, and many others, as you have reported, which would take too long to recount.

Why should I write out for you in detail every one of these heresies? For it is long ago that they fulfilled the teaching of Priscillian [Note: Leaving this heap of errors untouched, and especially remaining silent about the Son of God, whom Felix of Urgell and Elipandus of Toledo were proclaiming with blasphemous mouths to be adopted, clearly shows that this heresy had not yet arisen. As for Priscillianism, long since defeated, he considers it pointless to initiate a new controversy and leaves everything to the care of Egila and John. CENN.].

Therefore, beloved, it is necessary for your diligence to keep watch with the greatest care. As befits the priests of the Lord, you must not be ignorant of any canons, nor do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy order will be preserved by us if the standard of the established Decretals is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with license granted to the populace? [Col. 0345C]

From this it is clear that if anyone is found liable in the matters mentioned above, he must certainly be excluded according to canonical rule from the fellowship of God’s faithful, as a corrupter of the traditions of the Fathers, and must be found under eternal condemnation.

Your affection must therefore be on guard, and the greatest diligence must be used to prevent long-extinguished scandals from being revived through such people, and to prevent some shoot of that evil from the once-cut-down doctrine from arising in the province—one that would not merely grow in its own roots but would also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its odor.

Those who wish to appear corrected [Col. 0346A] should purge themselves of every suspicion and prove by obeying you that they are ours. If any of them refuses to comply with salutary commands, whether cleric or layman, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest a destroyer of his own soul lie in wait for the salvation of another. And just as we—or the blessed [Note: The importance of Wulcharius to Adrian may be inferred from this: “blessed” and “holy” were equivalent titles. Ducange, s.v. “Blessed.” ID.] archbishop—have been sent by the holy Roman Church to preach the orthodox faith for the love of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so preach in harmony, so that, just as our shepherd is one, Christ the Son of the living God, we may all together be gathered into one sheepfold under him. And just as we are members of one head, may we become one body in Christ Jesus our Lord, attaining his desirable promise, which he bestowed upon his holy worshipers who keep his commandments and have pleased his divine majesty [Col. 0346B] from the beginning of the world. He says (Matthew 25): “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

**LXXII. 405. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE ADDRESSED TO LORD CHARLES, KING**, containing an account of the faith or steadfastness of the apostolic pontiff toward the aforesaid king [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 25): “In the twenty-fifth [Vatican: ‘twenty-fifth’] he indicates that he did not receive the patrimony of Saint Peter among the people of Ravenna in its entirety [Vatican: ‘the patrimony among the Ravennates not intact’], as the senior witnesses of the church of that city testified. He asks that the Sabine patrimony be restored intact to the holy Church; he indicates that he does not need the boundaries of anyone’s property without good reason.” ID.].

*(A.D. 782, Cod. Car. LVI, chron. 71.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He commends the case of the Sabine patrimony, investigated by Itherius and Maginarius, its ancient right having been established by unimpeachable witnesses of the Holy See. He asks that the same envoys, or one of them, be sent again, through whom the Holy See may take possession according to its ancient right; for he seeks nothing else apart from this.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual fellow-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We believe that you remember—[Note: This letter is nothing but an appendix to the preceding one (letter 68), as I noted there (note g). It has the same definite purport; but matters that were there almost merely indicated are related more fully in this one. By recalling its meaning, he shows that the two letters were not separated by a short interval. I would therefore believe that this was written toward the end of the year, when the pontiff learned that neither royal envoy had returned and again presses the request he had then made. CENN.]—most excellent and God-protected son and great king, how you arranged for your most prudent and most faithful envoys to proceed together with our envoys to receive in full our patrimony of Ravenna, which you ordered to be granted to blessed Peter, your protector, for the benefit of your soul and the forgiveness of your sins. But while our envoys and yours were proceeding there—[Note: Up to this point the two letters will seem entirely alike if you compare them. The circumstances that follow were either unknown to the pontiff at that time or were entrusted to the ears of the envoys. ID.]—there were found there most faithful and elderly witnesses, about one hundred years old, who, bearing witness upon the altar inside the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, in a place called Forobonus—[Note: In his new edition, Ughelli (Italia Sacra, vol. I, p. 155) more clearly informs us that the province of Sabina was formerly divided among three episcopal sees: Cures, Nomentum, and Foronovo. After the first two had been abolished, the ecclesiastical affairs were united in Foronovo; finally, when that see too had been abolished, the episcopal see was transferred to Malliano, now called Vescovio, a rural church under the invocation of Saint Mary Major. Malliano was raised to the status of a city by Alexander VI in 1495. Of the three sees, the first to decline was Cures; a letter of Gregory survives (book II, letter 20), from the eleventh indiction, that is, A.D. 599, as evidence of its destruction. For Gregory entrusted Gratiosus of Nomentum with the care and government of the church of Saint Anthemius, established in the territory of the Sabine Cures, and thus made the bishop of Nomentum bishop of both sees. The latter see perished toward the end of the tenth century. While it existed, both bishops of Nomentum and bishops of Sabina appear in the councils; but the latter were also called bishops of Foronovo before the seventh century, after the episcopal see of Foronovo, which is found called that of Saint Euthymius in the synod of Symmachus in A.D. 504. For that church is named after Saint Mary and Saint Euthymius, as Albertus also notes in his description of Italy (p. 104). There can therefore be no doubt that Adrian is speaking here of Foronovo, either because it was then so called after nearby Montebono, which was subject to it, or because the apostolic envoys made a mistake in the name—something scarcely credible, since they related what had happened there. CENN.]—in the presence of the holy Gospels, and in the presence of your most faithful and noble envoys, namely, only your envoys Itherius and Maginarius, without the presence of our envoys, affirming, said that your own envoys could humbly report to you as sworn witnesses how, in ancient times, blessed Peter himself and our holy Roman Church held that same patrimony. We, however, did not receive the patrimony in full, nor was it handed over to our envoys, as these witnesses affirmed and testified in the presence of the holy Gospels of Christ. [Note: It was the opinion at the Holy See that almost the entire territory of Sabina had once been the patrimony of blessed Peter, although he had never possessed it in its entirety. Those elderly witnesses had confirmed the same under oath to the king’s envoys, so that Charles’s grant of the entire territory appeared to be a restoration of an ancient right. He now demands possession of it in full, just as he had requested through his own envoy in the preceding letter 68, although certain persons—especially the people of Rieti—were resisting and insisting that their boundaries extended farther. For the pontiff does not say that he failed to receive that patrimony, but that he did not receive it in full, or in its entirety. Therefore these letters do not concern the whole territory or patrimony, as some more recent writers think, but part of it, especially the portion adjoining the people of Rieti. Among these, as he said in letter 68, note d, he wished the boundaries to be established. Louis the Pious testifies that this was done (Diploma of Louis). ID.] 

But we ask you, most excellent son and great king, and spiritual fellow-father—[Note: If the Italian annalist had noticed this title, and the one read at the end of the letter, namely “spiritual fellow-mother” for the queen, he would not have assigned the letter arbitrarily to A.D. 778 in order to advertise Charles’s promises as wholly ineffective. ID.]—that your most noble envoys take them by the right hand and make them swear and declare what they foresaw and learned concerning that same Sabine patrimony of blessed Peter. For I call God to witness that I seek no one’s boundaries irrationally; but just as that aforesaid patrimony existed from ancient times, and as you granted it in full to blessed Peter the apostle, so we desire to receive it. [Note: This seems redundant, or something is missing with which it should be connected. GRETS.] Therefore we ask your lofty royal power to order that those aforesaid most faithful envoys of yours, or one of them together with another person whom you may choose, be sent to us. [Note: In the preceding letter 68 he had asked that one of the envoys be sent together with Stephen. Since he now says “with another person,” this shows that Stephen the treasurer had already returned to Rome without a royal envoy. I do not understand why all editors have placed that letter after this one. CENN.] Thus, with justice consenting, that Sabine patrimony may be handed over to us in full, just as you began to do.

Your royal power must therefore persevere to the end, just as you granted and handed over that patrimony in full to the same apostle of God for the benefit of your soul, so that here and in the future you may deserve to receive from the Lord our God and from that keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven the reward of a good deed, together with our most excellent daughter, the lady queen, our spiritual fellow-mother, and your most noble offspring, and so that your memorial may remain forever most honorably in the church of that same apostle of God. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## LXXIII. 408. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES,

Containing a discussion of the consecration of Bishop Peter and also—[Lamb. omits *et*, “and”]—of the Sabine territory. [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 36): “In the thirty-sixth letter he strongly commends Peter to Charles and asks that he arrange for the Sabine territory to be restored in full to the Roman Church. He says that the Roman Church embraces and venerates the entire fourth Council of Chalcedon.” ID.]

*(A.D. 782, Cod. Car. LXXVI, chron. 72.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—When Peter arrived with royal letters to be ordained bishop by the pontiff, he immediately consecrates him and declares that, because of the grace of Roman consecration, he should be preferred to the others. The summary of the Council of Chalcedon brought by Peter is said to be apocryphal. The complete council is preserved at the Apostolic See, while its abridgment is rejected. He sends the letter of Saint Leo that appears before the first session of that council, in which Leo condemns the robber synod of Ephesus II, held against Flavian, and commends the faith of the emperor Theodosius. On the same occasion he expresses his anxiety about obtaining possession of the entire Sabine territory through his envoys, who had already examined the case.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual fellow-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We received the nectar-like and honey-sweet words of your royal excellence through their bearer, Peter, most reverend and most holy brother and now our fellow bishop. [Note: Not long after the preceding letter was sent, Charles’s letters arrived without the royal envoys, whose dispatch he urges even more insistently than before in order to settle the case of the Sabine patrimony. Cointius and Pagius therefore rightly assign this letter to the present year, but wrongly place it before letter 68 and the preceding letter, as will become clear below. For he testifies that the royal envoys had already investigated the case of the Sabine territory—namely, Itherius and Maginarius—and asks that the same men be sent again. CENN.] In those letters we found instructions concerning Peter’s ordination, and immediately, as is our custom, we fulfilled the commands of your benevolent will. [Note: The discipline involved deserves notice. It had already been established by the Council of Nicaea (canon 6), and confirmed by other councils whose canons the Roman pontiffs themselves had repeatedly ordered bishops to observe, that bishops were not to be ordained without a metropolitan. Moreover, under the recent discipline established both in England and in the Frankish monarchy through the work of Boniface of Mainz, metropolitans did not ordain bishops before receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See. Thus John VIII, somewhat later (letter 94), expressed wonder that he had discovered an abuse in Gaul: metropolitans presumed to perform consecrations before receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See. And rightly so, since his predecessor Nicholas had testified (Bulgarian response 73) that all the archbishops of Gaul, Germany, and other regions were accustomed not to consecrate bishops before receiving the pallium. Nevertheless, the king asks that a bishop be ordained, and the pontiff immediately consecrates him. Who would not be astonished at so ancient an example of a new discipline? At that time Wilcharius was flourishing in Gaul; he was the archbishop whose jurisdiction Adrian had extended into Spain, as we recently saw (letter 71, elsewhere 96, notes b and c). We also find that the archbishopric of Bourges was restored in A.D. 786 through the conferral of the pallium, and the matter will be explained more fully below (letter 86, elsewhere 87); the other metropolitan sees are likewise known to have been restored at different times. The situation was different, however, with episcopal sees. Bishops are found everywhere, and the bishop of Bourges himself, who received the pallium at Rome, had been consecrated in Gaul three years earlier. Adrian also says that Peter acquired pre-eminence because of his ordination at the Holy See and for that reason ought to be preferred to bishops ordained in Gaul. Thus bishops of the provinces were ordained both at Rome by the pontiff, head of the universal Church and patriarch of the West, and by metropolitans according to the canonical definitions. Leo the Great once said to the bishops of Vienne (letter 89, chapter 6): “For we do not claim for ourselves the ordinations of your provinces—something which Hilary, according to his custom, might perhaps falsely say in order to corrupt the minds of your holiness—but we claim them for you through our solicitude, so that novelty may no longer be permitted anything, nor may room any longer be given to a presumptuous person to abolish your privileges.” Nothing was more important to the pontiffs than defending the rights of metropolitans established in councils and the privileges granted to some of them by the Apostolic See. But who would dare bring a lawsuit against them if they sometimes exercised jurisdiction in other provinces by means of the authority that they share with others? Certainly neither the king of the Franks, when asking that a bishop be ordained, nor the pontiff, when immediately complying with the request, nor the bishop ordained at Rome, understood themselves to be introducing anything new into the discipline. Garnerius, *Roman Diurnal*, chapter 3, title 8. In the brief statement of Saint Boniface of Mainz, consecrated at Rome, he adds these few words: he presents such formulas so that it may be understood what difference existed in this sacrament when it was performed by an Italian, a Lombard, or someone placed outside Italy. See also Thomassin, II.II, chapter 30. ID.]

We ask you, for love of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and your patron, and out of our mutual firm affection, to esteem him more highly in every respect and to exalt him. For it is fitting that the one ordained by the Apostolic See should surpass all others in those regions in the honor established by canon law, as was the ancient custom.

No human tongue, I think, can express how much trust and glory we possess in your lofty royal power. The aforesaid Peter, most reverend and most holy brother and our fellow bishop, can make known how fervently our heart rejoices day and night in your most triumphant excellence. [Col. 0349B] And while we possess such confidence in your God-protected royal excellence, we are exceedingly expectant, as we have written to you requesting, concerning the Sabine territory. [Note: From this, Cointius, Pagius, and others were able to infer that the present letter was written after the letter that I too cited above as the first of all Adrian’s letters concerning the Sabine territory (letter 67, elsewhere 69). But what follows, concerning the investigation of the ancient right by the royal envoys and their new mission, clearly refers—if I may say so with their indulgence—to the two letters that I have just cited, which they wrongly placed afterward; this will be obvious to the reader. ID.] You granted that territory in full to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as the reward of your soul and likewise of our spiritual daughter and fellow-mother, and also of your most noble offspring. We ask that you order it to be handed over to us through your most faithful envoys, who have partly examined the case, just as it existed in ancient times, so that you may deserve to receive from that keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven a fitting reward here and in the future.

Indeed, the aforesaid Peter, our most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop, presented to us a false brief—[Note: Concerning *pyttacium*, *pittacium*, *pytatium*, *pittatiolum*, and similar forms, several examples with the same meaning are available in Ducange’s *Glossary*. Gothofredus also has many examples (on book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Distribution of Military Grain*). From this we learn that among the ancients the word meant an index, commentary, or brief inscription, of the kind also customarily attached to jars. This is the sense in which it must be understood here, as the contents show: since they were apocryphal, the document acquired the name “false brief.” It contained letters issued in the name of Theodosius II and a summary of the Council of Chalcedon. It was therefore a booklet, like others written by both Hincmars. Hincmar of Reims calls it a *pittaciolum* (in Baronius, A.D. 871, no. 88 and following), saying that it was sent to him by Hincmar of Laon. Baronius calls it a booklet, and it is not unlike the form of a letter. ID.] translated, as he says, by Paulinus on behalf of Theodosius. [Note: Gentilotus restored *impdato* from the manuscript; thus the substance of the booklet seems to have been either an accusation or an apology composed by Paulinus on behalf of the younger Theodosius. Adrian in a sense confirms this by rejecting the booklet among the apocrypha and substituting Leo’s letters, which defend Theodosius’s faith. As for Paulinus, there was a man of that name distinguished in every branch of learning and in elegance of style, especially dear to Eudocia, as Theophanes says. Theodosius exiled him to Cappadocia and ordered him killed because of a certain apple, as all the Greek writers consistently report. Pagius observed that this occurred in A.D. 448 (A.D. 446, no. 12). Consequently, the booklet mentioned here cannot conveniently be attributed to this Paulinus, who held the eminent office of master of offices; nor, despite my diligence, have I found another Paulinus who would have condemned or defended Theodosius after the emperor’s death, since he is called “the former emperor.” I see two bishops named Paulinus present at the Council of Chalcedon: one of Theodosiopolis and the other of Apamea. Since the author of the booklet is not distinguished by an episcopal title, as Verecundus is, I leave it to others to conjecture who this Paulinus was. CENN.] sent to us by your excellence. It also contained, according to its inscription—[Grets. reads *ascriptum*, “written on it”]—a summary of the Council of Chalcedon composed by a certain Bishop Verecundus; finding it to be apocryphal, we judged it false. [Note: Labbe (Councils, vol. IV, p. 94) records an observation by the Roman editors, who especially note that Marcian’s address occurs twice in identical words: “The occasion of this repetition,” they say, “may perhaps have been provided by an ancient Latin book of the Council of Chalcedon preserved in the Vatican Library. In it the first session is omitted, and in its place there is found a brief epitome of the same council, prefixed by this address of Marcian to the synod; after the epitome follows the second session and the others in order to the end.” The summary sent to Adrian by Charles must have resembled this epitome. It is inferred that the work belonged to the Eutychians because of the omission of the first session, which contains the condemnation of Dioscorus and the others together with the Ephesian synod. It is therefore rightly dismissed by the pontiff among the apocrypha, since in his age the Holy See accepted the entire Council of Chalcedon, as he himself teaches. ID.]

But your holy, catholic, and apostolic spiritual mother, the Roman Church, does not embrace and venerate merely a brief summary but the whole holy and venerable fourth Council of Chalcedon; nor does she dare abandon its holy and venerable decree and follow a summary composed by someone else, which has no agreement with the holy institution.

Because of the great love that we hold toward your God-established royal power, we have sent you from that same holy and venerable council, before its first session, a copy of the letter of Saint Leo the pontiff addressed to the clergy, nobles, and people of Constantinople after the wicked and perverse act carried out in the city of Ephesus at the Second Council against the holy and venerable Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. In it Leo condemns the most impious Dioscorus and the profane Eutyches. [Note: This letter of Leo appears in Labbe (Councils, vol. IV, p. 47, no. 22). It was written after Hilary, the cardinal deacon who later succeeded Leo in the Apostolic See, had escaped the audacity of Dioscorus of Alexandria—who had mocked the presidents of the council sent from Rome—and returned to Rome by byways and through immense dangers, reporting the disastrous outcome of the robber synod. Hilary had informed Leo of Flavian’s exile after the blows inflicted upon him at the council by Barsumas and others of the same faction, but did not know that Flavian had soon died. See Henschenius, February 18. The letter bears the inscription: “Leo the bishop and the holy synod assembled in the city send greetings in the Lord to the clergy, the honored persons, and the people residing in Constantinople, beloved sons.” Another letter to the same persons follows, written on the same day, namely October 15, 449, explaining the Catholic doctrine and the condemnation of Eutyches and Dioscorus and the others assembled in the robber synod. Several other letters concerning the same matter also survive, as well as letters concerning the election of Anatolius in place of the most holy bishop Flavian before the first session of the council. Adrian certainly knew these letters, but, in order to defend the faith of Theodosius against the booklet attributed to Paulinus, he judged that this one letter, which most explicitly commends the emperor’s faith, should be sent to Charles. ID.]

Leo exhorted and admonished the aforesaid people to remain in the faith in which they knew their most Christian ruler to remain. For that gracious and venerable man, holy Leo, a saint throughout the whole world, our most renowned and praiseworthy predecessor, was such that, if anything contrary to the faith had scandalized him regarding the emperor Theodosius, then, after the wicked and criminal act committed a second time at Ephesus, he, the eminent blessed Father and holy Leo, would never, while condemning the heretics, have praised the faith of Theodosius; rather, he would likewise have condemned him as sharing their views. [Note: All historians condemn Theodosius as a man of excessive fickleness and credulity. They all further testify that, deceived by the schemes of the eunuch Chrysaphius, he took the side of Dioscorus against Flavian. Baronius discusses this matter at length in A.D. 449 and also notes that Theodosius soon became subject to divine vengeance. Briefly describing that vengeance (A.D. 450, no. 17), he says: “He experienced a punishment tempered by God’s mercy: before his death he was granted the understanding of the crime he had committed, the search for remedies, vengeance upon its author, obedience to the Roman pontiff, and communion with him, as the letters exchanged between them show.” Nevertheless, it is nowhere established that he ever departed from the true faith; indeed, Saint Leo testifies in the letter praised by Adrian that he remained in it. ID.]

We, as we have said, do not follow apocryphal books; rather, we venerate and embrace those books that the holy catholic and apostolic Church has received. May you, firmly established in that Church together with our daughter and spiritual fellow-mother, the lady queen, and your most triumphant offspring, enjoy the kingdom for many years; and may you be able to possess eternal rewards with all the saints in everlasting life. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## LXXIV. 413. ANOTHER LETTER ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES,

Containing thanksgiving for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerning the Sabine territory: how Maginarius—[Lamb., Maginarius]—the most faithful servant of that same exalted king wished to hand over the territory in its entirety to the party of Saint Peter, but could not do so because of wicked and perverse men. [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 11): “The eleventh letter contains certain praises of Charles and thanksgiving for the exaltation of the holy Church of God. It indicates concerning the Sabine territory that Maginarius, the king’s most faithful servant, wished to hand it over to Saint Peter in its entirety, but could not do so because of wicked and perverse men.” ID.]

*(A.D. 783, Cod. Car. LXXVIII, chron. 73.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—Maginarius had arrived with royal letters full of affection toward the pope and the Holy See. He had wished to hand over the whole Sabine territory, as he had been ordered, but could not do so because of the malice of the people. Nevertheless, he had inspected the imperial grants and the restitutions made by the Lombards. Adrian says that he cares neither for imperial nor royal largesses, but attributes the receipt of the entire Sabine territory to Charles alone. For that reason he will suitably send his envoys with documents, so that the truth may emerge from them and the result may follow.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual fellow-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We undoubtedly believe that your supreme royal power, divinely preordained and protected by God, has been granted according to his heart to the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, your spiritual mother. For, surpassing all former kings and emperors who were faithful and orthodox and who held true love toward her, you offer innumerable benefits every day through your arduous struggles.

Be assured of this: in proportion as you embrace, cherish, and honorably glorify that holy Church, the head of the whole world, together with its ruler and pontiff, so blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, your protector, makes you victorious here and in the future, granting that you reign unconquered over all kings. We are utterly confident that, in proportion as your efforts exalt and make triumphant the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, your spiritual mother, so he grants you, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, the right to seek and inherit the heavenly kingdom forever. [Note: The letter itself explains why he rejoices with such great joy and pursues Charles with such praises: Charles had finally granted what the pope had asked of him once, twice, and three times in the preceding letters. One of the envoys had returned to Rome, and the king had ordered him to hand over the entire Sabine territory to the Holy See. CENN.]

When the most faithful Maginarius arrived here among us and announced to us the safety of your royal power, our spirit was greatly relieved by this news. We were filled with every joy and exultation. But although your God-promoted and most triumphant excellence had ordered him to hand over the Sabine territory to us in its entirety, just as you had granted it to blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he was unable to do so because of wicked and perverse men. [Note: The people of Rieti are chiefly indicated, as I said above (letter 71, elsewhere 56, note); they prevented the entire territory from being handed over. The following shows that others were equally opposed; I believe the people of Spoleto were among them. ID.]

For your envoy, the aforesaid Maginarius, has now personally seen the whole right that blessed Peter the apostle, our protector, possesses in that territory, both through imperial grants and through the restitutions of those arrogant Lombard kings, more clearly designating the territory together with the estates belonging to it. [Note: Ducange, citing ancient charters, shows that *massa*, *massum*, *masa*, and *masada* have the same meaning and origin as *mansa* and *mansus*: namely, a definite measure of land, or a grouping and collection of possessions and estates. In the present passage Adrian uses *masa* in the place of *massa* and interprets it as a villa or farmstead. Adrian says that the Lombards designated the entire territory on the occasion of restoring such lands or estates. Why does he mention this? Because Charles had granted the territory in its entirety, while the people of Rieti, and perhaps also those of Spoleto, were contesting its boundaries. ID.]

But if the treacherous former king Desiderius, not in full but only by estates—[Note: *Mansi*, “estates.” But *massas* seems correct, since Anastasius Bibliothecarius also uses that word. GRETS.]—restored to us, as far as could be found, those which the Holy Roman Church had held from ancient times, and no one from those parts of the Lombards dared resist, how much more should your God-protected royal power, to which we are obedient in all things, have fulfilled your commands? [Note: Using what is called an *a fortiori* argument, he establishes all the more strongly that the matter concerns boundaries: no one had opposed the restoration of the estates, not even the Lombards who possessed them. CENN.]

We give thanks neither to emperors nor to kings, but only to your most triumphant excellence, because you have recently granted it in full to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Note: Two things are made very clear here: first, that the entire Sabine territory was granted by Charles to the Holy See when he came to Rome for the second time in A.D. 781; second, that possession of the entire territory had not yet been obtained. Since this is Adrian’s final letter entered in the codex concerning the matter, and since Louis the Pious’s diploma establishes that the boundaries between the people of Rieti and that territory were set by the abbots Itherius and Maginarius, all the disputes with the neighboring peoples must have been settled after A.D. 784. Maginarius was made abbot of Saint-Denis in July A.D. 784, after the death of Fulrad, which occurred on July 16 of that year. ID.]

For this reason, at a suitable time we are sending our most faithful envoys, together with our admonitions, to your royal power, so that, investigating the matter with clear scrutiny and inspired by God, they may ensure that justice be brought to blessed Peter the apostle. Thus may your lofty, God-promoted royal eminence and your memory be named among the saints in the Church of blessed Peter, your nurturer, until the end of the age.

But just as we continually remain praying for you in his most sacred hall, may almighty, merciful, and compassionate God—in whose hand the heart of your excellence is governed—together with our most excellent daughter and spiritual fellow-mother, the lady queen, and the lord Pippin, most excellent king of the Lombards and our own spiritual son, and your other most noble offspring, strengthen your heart and mind and extend to you the arm of his power, so that he may make you victorious over all barbarian nations. May all, humbled beneath your arm, kiss the footprints of your feet, so that through your God-established royal power the Church of God may remain greatly exalted. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## LXXV [Note: Notice. The summary of this letter is absent from the manuscript codex. Therefore take the following summary from Baronius: “Charles had informed the pope through Bishop George of his struggles and labors undertaken for blessed Peter; Adrian therefore gives him the greatest thanks and commends Bishop George to him.”]

*(A.D. 783, Cod. Car. LXX, chron. 74.)*

416 [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 41): “Charles had informed the pope through Bishop George of the struggles and labors undertaken for blessed Peter. Therefore Pope Adrian gives him the greatest thanks and commends Bishop George to him in the forty-first letter.” CENN.]

**ARGUMENT.**—Bishop George, the royal envoy, reports how Charles endeavored to honor blessed Peter and his successor with many benefits; Adrian says that Peter himself will reward one who has deserved so well of both. He commends the same bishop to Charles and predicts victories over all barbarian peoples.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual fellow-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Almighty God, creator of all things, in whose hand are all the rights of kingdoms, finding your most excellent royal power to be according to his heart, granted it, for the great consolation and exaltation of your spiritual mother, the holy catholic and apostolic Church. In his apostolic capacity we ask that he grant you the rewards of eternal life.

Therefore, having received from your most triumphant excellence George, our most reverend and most holy bishop, he announced to us the many good works and benefits that you perform through your arduous struggles on behalf of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and on our behalf. If we wished to write them out more fully, no speech, I think, would suffice our mouth. But that same prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, your protector, for whose love you do all these things, may himself protect you and direct your kingdom in all triumphs.

417 But since we have found the aforesaid most reverend and most holy bishop to be faithful, and yours and ours, we ask that you commend him greatly to yourself. In accordance with the steadfast faith and affection that he bears toward you and us, may he, comforted and wholly devoted, deserve, at our request, himself to appeal to your resplendent royal power. [Grets. reads *amari*, “to be loved,” instead of *clamare*, “to appeal.”] Thus, while through our intercession he enjoys your particular and universal goodwill toward him, may he be able to pour out prayers peacefully on your behalf. And while we fervently pour out our customary prayers for you in the confession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may you be found victorious over all barbarian nations. Together with our most excellent daughter and spiritual fellow-mother, the lady queen, and your most noble offspring, may you enjoy the government of the kingdom forever and deserve to reign with all the saints in the heavenly citadels. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## LXXVI. 418. ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE TO LORD KING CHARLES,

Containing an account of the Persian plundering carried out in the regions of the Greeks and of the discord that existed among them. [Note: Panvinio’s argument (Vatican Codex 34): “In the thirty-fourth letter he reports the Persian plundering in the regions of the Greeks and the discord among them.” CENN.]

*(A.D. 783, Cod. Car. XCIII, chron. 75.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He reports the Persians’ depredations sixty miles from the city of Constantinople. He says that there was a dispute over the kingdom between an uncle and his nephew, whose scepter the uncle had usurped.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Summary 34, Baronius and the Centuriators. GRETS.]

To our most excellent lord, our son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Since your love reigns continually in our heart, and since great confidence and much glorying in your excellent royal power, promoted by God, exist for us, it is fitting that we should diligently inquire each day after the health of your exalted royal majesty, protected by God, so that, having learned according to our desire that all things are prosperous with Your Excellence, we may render the highest and worthy thanks to the holy and undivided Trinity. In this connection, by informing the ears of your royal power, we make known that from the regions of Constantinople we have learned that a people of the Persians invaded and plundered its territory and came as far as the place called Moria, sixty miles from that same city of Constantinople. Carrying off great booty, they brought it away with them. And, as we have heard and as report has it, Thius, the prince of the king of the Persians and commander of their most wicked army, was in charge. When he had returned with his wicked victory, puffed up with pride, he lied to his own nephew and was made king of the Persians by that same army. Beneath him, the Persians are said to have begun tumultuously fighting one another on behalf of the nephew and Thius. [Lambecius reads: “the Persians.”]

We, for our part, continually ask divine mercy and do not cease to pray for you day and night, so that, for the exaltation of the holy Roman Church, your spiritual mother, and for our perpetual joy, He may grant that you reign in triumph and with an illustrious name for a long age, together with our most excellent daughter and spiritual fellow-mother, the lady queen, and your most excellent offspring, and that He may preserve you safe in the present life and in eternal blessedness. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

[Note: The historical account that is reported is of almost no importance; the letter itself, together with the preceding one, could safely have been omitted, and it does not matter to know its date. Nevertheless, since in Duchesne’s new edition it is assigned an uncertain date and allowed to range over the ten years extending from 781 to 791, I have had to confine it within the two-year period extending from May 781 to May 783, when Queen Hildegard died. CENN.]

## LXXVII. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to the Lord King Charles

In it he speaks of the faith or love which Charles had promised to maintain toward blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that it might remain unshaken and indissoluble, and so that no crafty deceit might separate his mind from apostolic love. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Cod. Vat. 37): “In the thirty-seventh [the thirty-seventh], he reminds him of the faith and love which he had promised to maintain toward blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and prays that he may keep it unshaken and indissoluble [keep it inviolate], and suffer no crafty deceit to separate his mind from apostolic love. Afterwards he accuses a certain Eleutherius and Gregory, and asks that he not permit [allow] them to remain with him, but send them to Rome.” ID.]

*(A.D. 783, Codex Carolinus LXXV, chronicle 76.)*

### Summary

He attacks two men of Ravenna, Eleutherius and Gregory.
