Although they had committed many crimes, they secretly approached Charles while concealing their crimes and sowed discord between the king and the pontiff. He asks that, after being rejected and dishonored by Charles, they be sent to Rome with his envoys, since their crimes must be investigated there. Thus Pippin’s donation, confirmed by Charles, and the right of the apostolic see in the exarchate will remain unshaken.

To our most excellent lord, our son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we never cease, whenever opportunity is given, to declare from the depths of our heart to no illustrious earthly ruler other than your royal power, promoted by God, how firm and stable we hope this bond to be: faithfully joined and unanimously united, so that we do not believe that any person, however great or small, can in any way break it between the apostolic see and Your Excellence. We recognize that your radiant kingdom, flourishing in triumphs, has maintained until now and will maintain indissoluble its love for blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, your supporter, and for our affection. No crafty deceit of men must ever be able to separate you from love for the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, whom, at our request and prayer, we believe you have as helper and champion in your most renowned triumphs, advancing and leading your exalted royal triumph to trample upon all barbarian nations. Therefore, while always entreating divine mercy for you, keeping the fear of God before our eyes, and considering the divine judgment on behalf of the soul of your father of holy memory, the most excellent lord Pippin, great king, and on behalf of all the faithful Franks, we strove to correct the wicked and perverse acts of Eleutherius and Gregory, worthless, useless, and foolish men. [Note: Stephen II, who was the first of all to begin ruling in the exarchate, appointed the priest Philip and Duke Eustace as judges at Ravenna, to administer justice to all suffering violence, as Adrian testified to Charles (letter 51, formerly 54). Nearly thirty years later, a similar example here supplies some who, ignorant of pontifical rule, deceive the truth. ID.]

Because of their insolent defiance, they did not allow justice to be administered in their territories. At Ravenna they miserably oppressed the poor and the weak, engaging in the sale of human beings and selling them among pagan peoples. They greedily swallowed up, without any mercy, the bread of those people. [The passage is corrupt; perhaps “their loaves.” GRETS. Lambecius reads: “their loaves.”] Through this plague a very large part of the population, failing and collapsing, was scattered. Moreover, wickedly gathering together a mob of low-born people and a band of bloodstained men, they did not cease daily to perpetrate unspeakable murders.

Thus, while the solemn Mass was being celebrated one day in a certain church, and at that very hour a deacon was preaching the holy Gospel of Christ to the people, innocent blood was shed inside that same sanctuary by their most wicked men. They committed murder as a sacrifice of praise. Since they themselves knew that we would certainly not permit them to carry out such wicked acts and perverse operations in those lands as Christian people, they were lifted up by arrogant pride and attempted, without our knowledge, to hasten to your royal presence. They imagined that through their faithless and wicked deceit they could separate you from the faith of purity and from love for blessed Peter and for us.

Wretched and unhappy men, they did not know that those who are especially faithful to that same apostle of God are also faithful to your most blessed kingdom, and that those who appear to be his enemies are without doubt your enemies also. [Note: We saw another pair of criminals of this kind in the city of Rome (letter 61, formerly 50). The same pontiff asked that they be sent to Rome, so that they might be punished there according to their offenses. See the note on the letters of the false pope Constantine (no. 9 and following).]

Therefore, we ask and beseech your royal power, protected by God, through blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to whom the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing sins in heaven and on earth, and through the holy baptism which, by the Holy Spirit, we seem to possess in common: do not allow your radiant countenance and cheerful presence to be shown to their insolence. Do not deign to receive those wicked men with your most gracious face. Rather, treating them as enemies of blessed Peter and of yourselves, reject their proud boasting and have them come to us dishonored and humbled by your most faithful envoys, so that by their presence we may establish the truth of everything we have said. [Note: In the notes to the preceding letter (notes 9 and 10), I observed that both Charles and the pontiff exercised, each within his own jurisdiction, his proper right in punishing offenders. The same thing is clearly evident here. Sigonius’s opinion must therefore be rejected: namely, that Pippin and Charles reserved supreme jurisdiction to themselves in the exarchate, although Muratori approves it (under A.D. 783). Each author from Modena preferred to follow inclination rather than reason. CENN.]

In this way, those who commit such wicked and perverse acts may be corrected by them, and the unblemished offering brought by your father of holy memory, the lord Pippin, great king, and offered by your radiant royal hands in the shrine of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and indeed confirmed, may remain forever unshaken and undefiled. [Note: Notice the difference between the judgment which the pontiff wishes to make concerning Romans and Ravennates, despite the equality of their cases. Two Roman criminals, Paschalis and Saracinus, are recalled, and likewise two Ravennates, Eleutherius and Gregory; both pairs were burdened with many crimes and both deserved condemnation. When he speaks of the Romans, who were joined to the king of the Franks only by a bond of friendship and charity, he asks Charles to deign to send the culprits to Rome for judgment, so that all nations may know that, because of love for blessed Peter, he has great affection for us. In contrast, when speaking of the Ravennates, since the exarchate had been entrusted to the Frankish kings, he likewise asks that they be sent to Rome for judgment, so that Pippin’s donation, confirmed by Charles, may remain intact, unshaken, and undefiled. Here I appeal to the followers of Sigonius, Muratori, and others who claim supreme rights for the Franks in the exarchate and, under the title of the donation, assert Rome itself to the Roman pontiffs, so that they may understand that their opinions conflict with established facts and may eventually cease adhering to them. CENN.]

Then, before the tribunal of Christ, may your protector, blessed Peter the apostle, himself appear to you as a worthy rewarder; and just as in this earthly kingdom he guards and protects you, flourishing in triumphs together with your most excellent offspring and all the faithful Franks, so may he grant that you reign without end in the heavenly citadels with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

[Note: I said that those men had been deceived (letter 68, note) who, following Pagius, moved Adrian’s letter from its place because they observed that the queen’s name is silent in it; for the royal offspring were likewise not mentioned. In this letter, however, the royal offspring are mentioned while the queen is entirely omitted—a sure indication of its date, also recognized by Pagius. CENN.]

## LXXVIII. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to the Lord King Charles

In it he speaks of the abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent, who had been falsely accused before the lord king and taken away from there, asking that Charles receive him most mercifully with a gracious countenance and a resolute spirit, since false charges had been brought against him. [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Cod. Vat. 10): “In the tenth, he intercedes for the abbot of the venerable monastery [tenth, for the abbot of the monastery] of Saint Vincent, who had been falsely accused before Charles.” CENN.]

*(A.D. 783, Codex Carolinus LXXIX, chronicle 77.)*

### Summary

He strongly commends to Charles Abbot Potho of Saint Vincent at the Volturno, who had been accused before him on false charges. He asks Charles to comply with the wishes of the entire community and to arrange for the restoration of the man who had been unjustly deposed.

To our most excellent lord, our son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Since everyone generally recognizes, from such pure love of heart, how faithfully your royal power continually conducts itself toward blessed Peter, chief of the apostles and your supporter, and toward us, it is fitting that from the depths of our heart we should willingly suggest what concerns the salvation of your precious soul. Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we make known to Your Exalted Royal Power that the entire congregation of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ, unanimously asked us to intercede in our letters on behalf of their abbot, who had been accused before you while innocent and, indeed, had been removed from there by your radiant command and brought before your royal feet. We commend him to you in every respect, since none of his accusers will be able to make or prove him guilty of disloyalty toward your royal power, because an entirely false charge has been brought against him. [Note: In the celebrated monastery beside the river Volturno, in the territory of Benevento, there were at that time two abbots, Poto and Autpertus—a matter obscure even to Mabillon. He supposes that Potho had said something against Charles and that, after another abbot had been appointed in his place, Potho was accused before Charles (Annals, book XXIV, no. 71). From this letter and the following one we learn the history. Meanwhile, through Adrian, who relied upon the monks’ support, the calumny of several accusers is exposed. ID.]

Therefore, for love of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, we earnestly and confidently ask that you command him to be received most mercifully with a gracious countenance and a resolute spirit. It is just that a man who was able to govern so great a congregation regularly, diligently, and according to religious discipline should, at our request, be released safe and sound by your exalted presence and restored to his former position by your most merciful commands. We have learned from his entire congregation that he is altogether suitable for the office entrusted to him and faithful to you. [Note: He arranges for the man unjustly deposed to be restored. Mabillon (ibid., book XXV, no. 36), placing excessive confidence in the Volturno chronicle, which is filled with errors of chronological anticipation, assigns Potho’s death to this year and says that his case was debated in A.D. 779, when Autpertus also died, according to that chronicler. All this is false. The accusation belongs to the end of this year or the beginning of the next. The hearing of the case, and consequently Autpertus’s death, must be connected with at least A.D. 784, since Adrian mentions the new queen Fastrada, as I shall say there. ID.]

May almighty God, in whose hand all the kingdoms of the world are governed, through the intercession of Peter, chief of the apostles, always make us rejoice in your royal majesty. In this world, may you reign together with your most excellent offspring over all barbarian nations, enjoy the governance of the kingdom for a long age, and merit to reign with all the saints in the heavenly citadels. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

[Note: Summary from Baronius: “He indicates how he settled the dispute of the monks sent to him. And that Abbot Potho wished to travel to King Charles with ten monks, so that he might also clear himself there of the charges brought against him.” —Summary 40 of Baronius and the Centuriators. GRETS.]

## LXXIX

*(A.D. 784, Codex Carolinus LXXII, chronicle 78.)*

[Note: Panvinio’s summary (Cod. Vat. 40): “In the fortieth [fortieth], he indicates how he settled the dispute of the monks sent to him, and that Abbot Potho wished to travel with ten monks to King Charles, so that there also he might clear himself of the charges brought against him.” CENN.]

### Summary

King Charles entrusts the case of the same Potho to the pontiff for investigation through his envoy Possessor, archbishop. Adrian therefore summons several abbots and examines the case before Possessor. He discovers that the charge of conspiracy brought against Potho is false and absolves him after he clears himself under oath together with the other monks. He permits all of them, at their request, to travel to the king. The pontiff reports all this to Charles and also informs him that Autbertus, abbot of the same monastery of Volturno, died on the journey, and that the monk Rodigausus, the accuser, was found guilty of fornication with his niece.

To our most excellent lord, our son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Receiving through your most reverend and holy archbishop Possessor, your most faithful envoy, your exalted, God-inspired, most perceptive and distinguished letter, our spirit was greatly refreshed by it. We found in them royal triumphs and safety, and for this we gave great thanks to almighty God while beseeching divine mercy in the shrine of your supporter, the blessed apostle Peter. For your royal letters reported that your cause is ours and ours yours. In this we are confident: that by divine inspiration this truth, plainly written by you, shines forth as evident and certain to everyone.

Accordingly, since Your Exalted Royal Excellence directed that the disputes between the monks of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent and its abbots, namely Autbertus and Potho, should be examined and investigated by our judgment canonically and according to regular discipline, the aforesaid Abbot Autbertus, while traveling along the road, was overtaken by sudden death and was unable to appear before our apostolic presence. [Note: The passage is corrupt. GRETS.]

Therefore, several of the leading monks came together with the aforesaid Abbot Potho and all stood before our apostolic decree. They were seated together with the reverend and holy archbishop Possessor, Abbot Ansoaldus of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter, Abbot Aquilinus, Abbot Devaregius, and Abbot Raginbaldus of the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God, together with Abbot Gisulfus of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter, Duke Hiltibrand, Tacipertus and Prandulus, and, standing in attendance as our officials, Theophylactus the librarian, Stephen the treasurer, Campulus the notary, Duke Theodore, and many others.

[Note: Mabillon, full of uncertainty, identifies several monasteries over which the abbots named here presided. He thinks, namely, that Ansoaldus was abbot of Saint Peter at Benevento; Aquilinus of Saint Angelus of Baregio beside the river Sangro in the Abruzzi Citeriori; and Raginbaldus of Farfa. It does not concern us to investigate these names, which are for the most part uncertain. What must not be passed over is that the names relegated to the end of this letter must refer to those present at the assembly. Gretserus, thinking that they belonged to the letter which follows in the codex (letter 60, formerly 73), not only prefixed them to it as a summary but also asserted that all were of the Roman clergy: both claims are false. For the summary or argument of that letter must be taken from the twelfth among the arguments of the letters of Paul I, as I noted there; and names that are almost all Lombard, with a few Frankish ones intermingled, must be removed from the Roman clergy. CENN.]

[Note: Although Charles did not subdue the duchy of Benevento before A.D. 787, as all historians consistently assert, both the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento were subject to the king of the Lombards, as has often been said. It is therefore not surprising that the abbot of Saint Vincent was accused before Charles. The fact that the king of the Franks entrusted his case to Adrian is evidence of the goodwill and reverence with which the king treated the pontiff. CENN.]

[Note: Mabillon thinks that Possessor was archbishop of Embrun (Annals, book XXIV, no. 58). Above we saw him distinguished only by episcopal rank while acting as a royal envoy, until A.D. 777 (letter 61, formerly 50). Hearing that he now possessed archiepiscopal dignity, we understand that the metropolitan see of Embrun had been restored to its former honor. For almost all the Gallican metropolitan sees acquired their splendor through the work of Charlemagne, but gradually and not without considerable labor on the king’s part. Any bishop who subsequently attained metropolitan dignity received from the holy see the pallium together with the title of archbishop, according to the new discipline, as I shall show more fully in the note on letter 86, formerly 87. CENN.]

[Note: *Servitia* is used for the ministers themselves, as Ducange notes in Adrian’s letter and in Louis the Pious in Peter Chifflet. Among the ministers attending the deliberation or judgment, he specifically names Theophylactus the librarian, unknown to Panvinio and Rasponi (On the Latin Church, book III, chapter 16, p. 249), who at that time held the office of chancellor; Stephen the treasurer, or chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, praised above, especially in letter 68; Campulus, Adrian’s nephew and Paschal’s brother, who carried out an embassy to the Beneventans in A.D. 777 (letter 60, formerly 73). Campulus rose from notary of the holy see—that is, protonotary, as we now say—to the office of treasurer, at the time when his brother was primicerius. Both later perpetrated against Pope Leo III, Adrian’s successor, that great crime which different authors recount in different ways. Finally, he names Duke Theodore, probably also a nephew, mentioned more than once above (letters 59, formerly 49; 60, formerly 73; 67, formerly 69), and never again mentioned as duke in the codex. Such *servitia*, offices, or ministers are highly authoritative witnesses to the majesty of the pontificate. ID.]

When Rodigausus, a monk of the same monastery, had entered, he gave testimony against the same Abbot Potho, saying:

“Lord, when we had completed the course of the sixth hour and, according to custom, were singing the prophetic psalm for the safety of the king and his offspring, namely, Psalm 53, ‘Save me, O God, by your name,’ the abbot suddenly rose and refused to sing.” [Note: From this first point of the accusation, we see that a custom had become established in that famous monastery: prayers were offered for the king of the Franks after all the hours. Yet this manner of prayer does not seem to correspond to the monks’ purpose. Although Psalm 53 is entitled for prayer, what connection could the safety of Charles and his royal offspring have with David, exposed to the dangers of the treachery of the Ziphites and delivered by God’s help? Since the matter here concerns the psalm customarily sung after Sext, and since it is unclear which psalms were sung after the other hours for the same purpose, I would not dare condemn this form of prayer. The remaining two charges are much more obscure, and I leave them to the conjectures of others. To disclose my own view to some extent, I think that both charges arose from the election of Autbertus, a Frank, as abbot and from the introduction of other Frankish monks into the monastery. CENN.]

“He also testified that, while we were traveling together, the abbot began to say to me: ‘What do you think of this matter? For from that point I expected to see a sign, but I did not see one.’ Then I replied: ‘May almighty God humble his heart and bring us back safely, for our merits are not such that we should be deemed worthy to recognize such things.’ The abbot then said to me again: ‘If it were not for the monastery and the land of Benevento, I would have regarded him as nothing more than a dog.’ And he added against him: ‘As many Franks would have remained as I am able to carry on my shoulder.’” [GRETSERUS reads *vectare*, “carry,” instead of *vedare*.]

When the aforesaid Abbot Potho was questioned by us whether this was so, he replied with great protestation:

“It is true that our entire congregation undoubtedly sings psalms in the monastery for Your Excellence and likewise for your offspring. But while I was working with him, and the other boys were also present [Lambecius reads: “while he and the other slanderers were present”], after the prayer had been completed and they had prostrated themselves on the ground and begun to sing Psalm 53, ‘Save me, O God, by your name,’ I suddenly rose because of the work being carried out for the benefit of the monastery.” [Note: I am surprised that Ducange’s editors overlooked this passage, in which *opera* clearly means work on a building. What else can *esse in opera* and *fieri operam* mean? CENN.]

“As for the conversation on the journey, I said nothing at all to insult his royal excellence. I merely said that, if I had not had the monastery or that land, I would certainly have gone to such a place that I would have cared about no one.” [Note: Tengnagel corrected the text in this way. Gentilotus, however, read: “I would have regarded it as a place where I would have cared for no one.”]

“As for what he said about the Franks, I never uttered such words, nor did anything of the kind come from my mouth. But when he opposed such matters to me on every side—” [Lambecius and Gentilotus read: “when he opposed this contagion to me”; something appears to be missing. GRETS.]

When the aforementioned Rodigausus was questioned by us whether anyone else had heard these things with him, he then affirmed that he had been alone and that no one else had heard them.

Then several of the senior monks gave testimony concerning Rodigausus, saying that he had been caught in fornication with his own niece and, after having been a priest, had become a monk; therefore he was not able to bring such a charge against their abbot, since it was rejected by the sacred canons. [Note: The canons themselves are cited below and seemed relevant to the case. Mabillon (Annals, book XXIV, no. 94) concludes that Potho fell from office because Hainrad succeeded Autbertus, according to the Volturno chronicle. But what credibility can be assigned to a chronicle that dates his death to A.D. 778, before Charles’s spiritual kinship, assigns Hainrad’s succession to nearly four years, and Potho’s abbacy to two years and five months ending on April 22, 783, while it says that he died? All these claims conflict with Adrian’s letters. Since these letters are contemporary with the events, they must unquestionably be preferred to a chronicler living many centuries later. CENN.]

Three other monks were then brought in. They had come with Duke Hiltibrand and had remained with Abbot Autbertus. [Note: The three monks who had come with Hildebrand are named above: Gisulfus, abbot of Saint Peter; Tacipertus; and Prandulus of the same monastery, which was subject to the Volturno monastery and stood near the walls of Benevento, as Mabillon inferred from a privilege of Charlemagne (Annals, book XXV, no. 61). It seems more probable to me, whatever Mabillon may suspect, that the monastery of Saint Peter, whose abbot was Ansoaldus, should be understood as the Beneventan monastery. If they had remained with Autbertus, they therefore depended on the monastery of Vincent; and if they had been captured by Potho’s order while crossing the bridge of the Volturno, as the letter soon relates, they must have been neighbors of the monastery of Saint Vincent. Concerning the origins of this monastery in A.D. 707, and concerning its three founding brothers and abbots, Paldus, Tato, and Taso, the same Abbot Autbertus gives an extensive account in Ughelli (Sacred Italy, volume VI, p. 370 and following). From this account much can be learned about the loosening of discipline that illuminates this letter. ID.]

They declared against Abbot Potho:

“While we desired to travel to the most excellent king, we were seized by the guards and thrown into prison.”

The abbot mentioned above replied:

“It is true that I had guards on the bridge—not to prevent those who were going to the king from passing, but to seize those who abandon their rule and, when sin threatens, return to their vomit in the world. I ordered them to be apprehended. But when they say this, I was not there at all; I was setting out on the road to the great king.”

Then, examining the matter more closely and investigating the provisions of the sacred canons, we found the following confirmation in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 18:

“The crime of conspiracy and collusion is prohibited even by secular laws; much more should this be forbidden in the Church of God. If, therefore, any clerics or monks are found conspiring, colluding, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, they shall be completely deposed from their own rank.”

Likewise, chapter 21:

“Those who accuse a bishop, whether clerics or laypeople, should not be admitted indiscriminately and without proof to an accusation unless their reputation and standing have first been examined.” [Lambecius adds *ad*, “to.”]

Likewise, in the African Council, chapter 8, it is stated:

“Furthermore, there are very many persons of bad conduct who think that elders or bishops should indiscriminately and indiscriminately be dragged into accusation. Should such persons be admitted so easily, or not?”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“Does it therefore please your charity that a person entangled in certain crimes should have no voice to accuse an elder?”

All the bishops said:

“If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted. It is agreed.” [Note: Concerning these canons, which reject an accuser, see what I said in the preceding commentary (no. 15) to establish the discipline of the holy see in that age. ID.]

Considering all these things, and since the enemy himself has such snares that, when, God resisting him, he cannot deceive people into perpetrating wicked acts, he presently tears apart their reputations by feigning false accusations, we had a strict inquiry made over three full days to determine whether these statements were true. We found no fault in the matter concerning what had been said. Nevertheless, lest anything seem to have been omitted by us, or lest any doubt remain in your heart, we decided that the aforesaid Abbot Potho should give an oath that he had said nothing of the kind through disloyalty toward your royal power. Nor had he ever been, nor would he ever be, disloyal to that great king throughout all the days of his life.

Likewise, we ordered ten other senior monks of that venerable monastery—five of Frankish origin and five of Lombard origin—to give an oath that they had never heard from the abbot’s mouth any disloyalty toward Your Royal Excellence. [Note: It is evident from this that men of both peoples pursued monastic life in the monastery of Volturno. Nor did this begin only after Desiderius had passed away, but from the very beginnings of the friendship between the Franks and Romans, when the power of their kings began, through the Roman pontiff, to be feared and honored by the Beneventans. For scarcely had Pippin defeated Aistulf and made the donation of the exarchate to the Roman pontiffs, when Aistulf’s death soon followed; and the people of Spoleto and Benevento preferred to obey Pippin rather than Desiderius, as Stephen II testifies (letter 2, formerly 8). Therefore, under his successor Paul I, it is certain that the aforesaid Autbertus lived there. He speaks of himself as follows (Codex Regius Vaticanus 96): “Ambrose, also called Autpertus, born in the province of Gaul but instructed for the most part in divine matters within the region of Samnium at the monastery of Vincent, martyr of Christ, and not only so instructed but also entrusted to the most holy altars for offering Christ’s gifts: through the working of the blessed and inseparable Trinity, with the merits of the blessed Virgin Mary also assisting, in the times of Paul, Roman pontiff, of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and of Arochis, duke of the province in which I dwell, I composed and completed this work, which, to make it easier to understand, I called *The Mirror of Little Ones*.” CENN.]

They all asked permission to come together into your royal presence. After examining their faithfulness toward Your Royal Power, we allowed them to hasten there, while not ceasing, as usual, to pour out prayers for you in the shrine of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. May you, together with your lady queen and your offspring, flourish here through the course of many years and merit to reign without end with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellence unharmed.

[Note: In the codex there follows a list of the monks and all the others assembled, which Lambecius rightly attached to this letter. Gretserus, by contrast, placed it as a summary before letter 60, formerly 73; it must therefore be restored here. ID.]

## LXXX. 432

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Lambecius: “The following is a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to Lord King Charles, in which bishops are discussed.”]

### ON BISHOPS OR PRESBYTERS

That they should not put on military armor, but spiritual armor—that is, that they should devote themselves to fasts and prayers; also concerning the sale or enslavement of people, or other unlawful matters perpetrated by wicked men; and concerning the vision of John the monk, which appeared false or empty.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 11): “In the eleventh letter he treats of bishops and presbyters, that they should not put on military weapons but spiritual ones, that is, that they should devote themselves to fasts and prayers; and he declares vain the vision of John the monk, by which he had been warned that the faith of the Roman Church was dead.” In Panvinio, from whom Baronius and others drew their material, this is composed from the summary of letter 73 (otherwise 78) and that of the present letter, omitting what follows after “that they should devote themselves to prayers”; thus the summary is placed first and runs: “that they should devote themselves to prayers. Certain praises of Charles,” etc. Cenn.]

*(A.D. 784, Codex Carolinus LXXVII, chronicle 79.)*

[Col. 0366A]

### SUMMARY

Through Garamannus, the royal envoy, he says that he had favorably received John the monk, whom he would have subjected to canonical discipline, after the example of the monk Cyril, had his profound respect for the king not prevented him. Just as John had reported to the king that wicked men practicing seizure and other unlawful activities ought to be punished, so he had reported to him that the bishops of Gaul were carrying weapons, contrary to his judgment. He asks that the king not permit this, and commends him because he had treated the monk’s visions with contempt.

To our most excellent son and spiritual kinsman, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We received the most orthodox and nectar-like addresses of your royal excellence, promoted by God, [Col. 0366B] which, when opened, revealed your salvation, promoted by God, and your victories in triumphs, [Note: [Col. 0366C] The Fulda Annals, under the year 783, after relating the death of Hildegard, report that the Saxons were defeated by Charles, an immense multitude of them having been killed. Unless I am mistaken, this letter refers to this double victory. In Duchesne’s praised edition this letter is one of eleven that circulate for that decade, from the year 781 to the age of the codex. It was certainly written after the year 783, since it mentions Queen Fastrada, whom Charles is known to have married at the end of that year. This is also an unmistakable feature of all the letters that follow: each names the queen, and none adds the title “co-mother.” Muratori, by chance, correctly assigns this letter to the current year; but very craftily, in order to disturb the dominion of the exarchate and attribute supreme authority over ecclesiastical territory to Charles, he places it before another letter [Col. 0366D] (letter 83, otherwise 84), guided by the name of the same royal envoy; below it will become clear that the latter letter is the later one. Cenn.] or those of our most excellent daughter, the lady queen, and of your most excellent sons, 433 and finding therein the safety of our and your faithful people, together with sincerity, we offered great thanks to the clemency of almighty God.

But concerning what your royal power made known to us through its most faithful envoy, namely Garamannus, the glorious duke, [Note: [Col. 0366D] Carolomannus, Charles’s son, was born in the year 776, as Pagi establishes (under the year 783, no. 3) on the authority of Adrian and by chronological reasoning. Thus his ninth year was passing; and although in 781 he had assumed the name Pippin and had been anointed by Adrian as king of Italy, he was still a nine-year-old child and therefore unequal to administering the kingdom. Even Charles, the elder by birth, was scarcely beginning his apprenticeship under his father at this time. Hence Italy, conquered and organized in 774, as the Frankish Annals say, was administered through dukes and counts whom Charles appointed over the cities. Some such men appear in these letters, such as the dukes of Clusium and Florence. Other dukes, to whose administration no city is found to have been entrusted, seem to have commanded the Frankish soldiers who were in the kingdom of Italy. And it will indeed be established that this Garamannus performed such an office in the following year. ID.] concerning John the monk and presbyter, who, as was reported in your royal letters, had informed you about the enslavement of people and other unlawful matters perpetrated by wicked [Col. 0367A] men, so that, by God’s favor, they might be corrected or amended through your exalted royal arrangement, [Note: [Col. 0367C] Muratori incorrectly infers that Charles had instructed this duke to amend such matters, for Charles would not have dared invade another’s jurisdiction (see letter 63, otherwise 65), nor would the pontiff have remained silent about such an invasion, as we shall see occurred on another occasion (letter 93, otherwise 71). It is therefore more credible that the monk was speaking about Charles’s subjects rather than about men within ecclesiastical territory. For he wished to win his favor, so that Charles might support him before the pontiff and prevent him from suffering the punishment to which he was liable. Cenn.], just as your royal power requested of us, we received him with willing mind, habitually accommodating your wishes in all things. We know your royal excellence to be precisely such that in these matters it needs no admonition, because, with the Lord’s assistance and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, always interceding for him, it preserves unharmed and immovable the true preaching of the orthodox faith which it received from his Church, and, spontaneously brandishing it irreproachably and without stain, rejoices; indeed, it shines forth completely in all things and does not cease to correct fierce, wicked, and crafty men from unlawful acts.

[Col. 0367B] He has also frequently caused captives to return to their own people. The aforesaid John the monk told us that he had said to you 434 that every bishop should hold spiritual weapons and not earthly ones, so that, if it is true that they put on military weapons, we make known our exhortation to your royal excellence, protected by God, that it should in no way permit this to happen. Rather, whoever it wishes to be entrusted with any place—bishops as well as presbyters—should earnestly devote themselves to prayer, clothed in the helmet of orthodox faith and the weapons of salvation, so that they may exercise among the whole people the spiritual office that concerns the salvation of souls. [Note: [Col. 0367C] Lambecius and Gentilotto read in the manuscript what follows, which Tengnagel omitted: “or, preaching that they may attain eternal life and receiving their confession, let them irreproachably exercise the priestly office.” Many more passages on this subject are found in the capitularies (Capitularies, book VI, chapter 285 and following; book VII, chapters 91, 103 and following), which are also reported by Labbe (Councils, vol. VII, pp. 1162ff.). It is therefore clear that the origin of Charles’s constitutions must be sought here. The entire passage should be restored according to the manuscript reading from Lambecius and Gentilotto, concerning bishops’ weapons as described by Adrian. Tengnagel omitted two of their principal duties, namely preaching and receiving confession, unless the fault is to be attributed to the typesetter, whom the repeated word “office,” as often happens, may have confused. ID.] But let the other bishops and presbyters living in their churches, each canonically, through your strongest royal protection, be able to govern their people entrusted to them by God. [Col. 0367C]

Concerning the revelation of the same John the monk, [Col. 0368A] as his account related it, it is truly thought to be a phantasm. For they said [Lambecius and Gentilotto: “he said”] that in the beginning, in sleep, he saw the heavens opened and the right hand of God; afterward he saw another dream: a great tower, and angels descending. Among them he saw the figure of a man having eagle’s wings and existing as dead; and another figure of a man having dove-like wings, saying, “For this is the Son of God.” [Note: [Col. 0367D] Lambecius reads here: “This is the Christian faith.”] For let it be far from the hearts of the faithful that the faith of Christians should be proclaimed dead. [Note: [Col. 0367D] Who would not recognize a fanatical monk from this imagination? Similar examples are not lacking among historians. ID.]

For we testify that the figure having eagle’s wings, as we have received from the holy Fathers, is John the Evangelist, who proclaims heavenly secrets to human beings (John 1): “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. But in the figure of the dove the Holy Spirit was seen. For we have never read of a human figure clothed with the wings of a dove. Therefore, while praising exceedingly your most firm and praiseworthy faith, we recognized in this that you considered those visions themselves a phantasm, since your royal power asked us on his behalf that he not be condemned, anathematized, or scourged by us, [Note: [Col. 0367D] Charles acknowledges that the monk was liable to punishment and intercedes for him. As for the punishment of scourging, Antoninus Augustinus (on chapter 50, otherwise 46, of Ingilramnus) notes from the capitularies of the Frankish kings that this kind of punishment had slipped into canonical collections, although it did not belong to pontifical jurisdiction. Here Adrian mentions regular discipline. Saint Aurelian, chapter 41, says of it: “For any fault, if it is necessary to receive the discipline of the scourge, the lawful number must never be exceeded, namely thirty-nine.” Likewise, see Saint Benedict’s Rule on excommunication and discipline or scourging, chapters 23, 24, 28, and 30. Most especially, see chapter 10 of Saint Columbanus’s Rule, or the Penitential, on various kinds of faults, where we read the following provision relevant to our subject: “For a diabolical illusion and for the manner of a vision, some who require penance ought to chant twenty-four psalms in order, others fifteen, others twelve.” From this it is clear that Charles, when interceding for the monk so that he would not be condemned, excommunicated, or scourged, did not do so on account of the vision, which he regarded as a phantasm, but on account of some other serious fault that had driven the monk to seek Charles’s patronage, lest he suffer the punishment that was sometimes extremely severe in monasteries. I encountered the matter in the Rule of the Master (chapter 13), and shudder as I report it: “But if excommunicated brothers should become so proud that, persisting in the pride of their hearts, they refuse on the third day, at the ninth hour, to make satisfaction to the abbot, they are to be guarded and beaten with rods until death.” ID.], and that we would inflict no adversity upon him; so, accommodating your royal petition in all these matters, insofar as necessary we admonished the monk and released him unharmed to his proper place. For if your royal support had not benefited him, we would have been fully entitled to impose ecclesiastical discipline upon him canonically and, as with the monk Cyril, whom we corrected and amended, to make the monastic rule clear to him irreproachably. [Col. 0368C] [Note: [Col. 0368D] There is no doubt that “ecclesiastical discipline” here must be understood as scourging; the context of the letter demonstrates this, especially the rule mentioned here. What punishment Adrian thought should be inflicted on this monk, following the example of another whom he had corrected, is not clear, for in Saint Benedict’s Rule (chapter 24) it is left to the abbot’s judgment: “According to the measure of the fault, the measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended; and the measure of the faults should depend on the abbot’s judgment.” Discipline was imposed canonically, for one kind was regular, another secular. This is evident from the chapters of Charlemagne for monks (Labbe, Councils, vol. VII, p. 988), which, as Sirmond notes, belong to the year 789, for no. 16 reads: “Let regular discipline, not secular discipline, be imposed upon monks; that is, let them not be deprived of limbs or subjected to other mutilations except by the authority of the Rule.” These provisions are explained by canon 18 of the Council of Frankfurt: “We by no means permit abbots, for any fault committed by monks, to blind them or inflict mutilation of their limbs, unless they are subject to regular discipline.” Cenn.]

Because of your great love, he was received and admonished with great patience [Col. 0369A] and kindness, and, with divine precepts exchanged on both sides, was released in peace. May divine clemency grant that your royal excellence, together with our most excellent daughter, the lady queen, and your exalted offspring, enjoy the reins of the kingdom for many years, so that, reigning in this world over all barbarian nations, you may deserve to reign without end with all the saints in the heavenly citadels. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LXXXI

### ANOTHER LETTER, ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES

In it the matter concerns the monastery of Saint Hilary the Confessor at Calligata: he asks that no one permit it—or the hospices situated along the Alpine passes—to be seized in the reception of pilgrims. [Note: [Col. 0369C] The words “he asks that no one permit it” are absent from the manuscript. Gentilotto.] [Lambecius and Gentilotto: “to invade.”] [Note: [Col. 0369C] Baronius and Centuriator place the following after this: “That he order Gundibrandus, duke of Florence, to restore what he took from the same monastery.” Gretser.] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 38): “In the thirty-eighth [letter] he commends to Charles the envoys of the monastery of Saint Hilary at Calligata. He asks that he not permit the monastery itself, or the hospices situated along the Alpine passes, to be invaded by any person, great or small, for the reception of pilgrims; and that he order Gundibrandus, duke of Florence, to restore what he took from the same monastery.” Cenn.]

*(A.D. 784, Codex Carolinus LXXIV, chronicle 80.)*

[Col. 0369B]

### SUMMARY

He asks Charles to protect the monastery of Saint Hilary at Galiata and the hospices situated in the Alps for receiving pilgrims as guests, and not to permit anyone to invade them. He also asks him to reprimand Gundibrandus, duke of Florence, who had seized certain properties of the Curtis Sasantina belonging to that monastery, as well as others who had invaded lands belonging to the same estate, and to see that everything was restored to the monastery.

To our most excellent son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope. [Note: [Col. 0369D] Summary 38, Baronius and Centuriator. Gretser.] [Note: [Col. 0369D] I place this letter here although its date is itself uncertain, a matter otherwise of no importance, both because it was written after the year 783 and because it mentions the duke of Florence, whom in the preceding letter (Col. 366, note g), together with others, I said was in charge of one or more cities of the kingdom of Italy, contrary to the false opinion concerning Garamannus as a royal envoy. Cenn.]

[Col. 0370A] We know the kindness of your royal excellence 437, for the love of the Lord and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by whose merits and distinguished dignity the Church is enriched, and, as one who loves justice, [Note: [Col. 0369D] Lambecius and Gentilotto read: “By whom, for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, it deserved a distinguished dignity, and as one who loves justice.”] to grant assistance to each person. Therefore, we ask you, as petitioners, that, for the love of the same blessed Peter, your protector, and because of our paternal affection, just as your radiant royal power is accustomed to bring the aid of restoration to pious places, so also in the monasteries named below [Gentilotto: “holy monasteries”] of your spiritual mother, our holy Roman Church, to which the most vigorous royal authority has granted and offered [Note: [Col. 0369D] Mabillon (Annals, book XXII, no. 28) lists at least six monasteries in Tuscany in the year 748, one of which is Galactense, or Galiatense, of which Adrian speaks; he says it was founded by Abbot Hilary. It was subject to the archbishop of Ravenna, although within the boundaries of Tuscany. From 755 to 759, however, it belonged to Anscaus, bishop of Foropopulus. For when he was abbot of that monastery and had deserved well of Stephen II while the latter was traveling to France in 753, Stephen, out of gratitude, granted Anscaus the monastery for the duration of his life after acquiring control of the exarchate. When Anscaus died in 759, the monastery returned to its former jurisdiction, as is clear from the diplomas of popes and kings in Ughelli (On the Archbishops of Ravenna). It still exists today and has been possessed by the Camaldolese for about two centuries. Mabillon (Annals, book XXIII, no. 5; Ughelli, On the Archbishop of Ravenna and On the Bishops of Foropopulus, vol. II, p. 598). Vecchiazzanus adds that in 757 Paul I confirmed the abbey of Saint Hilary to Abbot Ansauco, and cites a papal diploma as evidence. Cenn.] their flourishing royal favor amid triumphs, namely the monastery of Saint Hilary, confessor of Christ, which [printed text: “who”] is a bridge [or: a place; the reading is uncertain] at Calligata, [Col. 0370B] together with the hospices situated along the Alpine passes for receiving pilgrims, [Note: [Col. 0370C] Muratori uses the serious authority of these letters (Italian Antiquities, vol. IV, dissertation 37) to prove that Italy at that time lacked taverns and lodging houses where travelers could take shelter—a conclusion easier to state than to believe. For it is one thing to provide lodging for poor pilgrims, as has been an ancient monastic custom, and another to force wealthy travelers into hospices because of the absence of lodging houses: “Pursuing hospitality in all things,” Macarius said (Rule, chapter 20), “and do not turn away your eyes or send away the poor empty-handed, lest perhaps the Lord come to you in the guest or in the poor person, see you hesitating, and despise you.” At the end of the fourth century clerics were forbidden to enter taverns (Council of Carthage III, chapter 27), unless compelled by the necessity of pilgrimage. Much earlier, they had been forbidden to do so in the East (Council of Laodicea, chapter 24). See also the Theodosian Code (book IX, title 7, law 1) and the commentary there of Gothofredus. ID.] we ask that your distinguished clemency not permit any person, great or small, to inflict any act of invasion upon it, but that, in all things, for the praise of the monks serving God and for the reception of pilgrims, it deign to preserve justice there, as it is accustomed to do. And concerning the invasion which Gundibrandus, duke of the city of Florence, [Col. 0370D] [Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus above (letter 55, otherwise 60) he mentioned Reginald, duke of the city of Clusium. Therefore there is no doubt that Charles wished to place a duke over individual cities as well. ID.] has inflicted upon the same monastery, in a certain estate of Sasantina, namely in Florentine territory, seizing from it unlawfully several properties that do not belong to him and carrying them away, you are ordered [Gretser: “may you order”] to correct this. Likewise, may your royal power, inspired by God, cause the lands that several men have unjustly taken from the same estate [Col. 0371A] to be restored. For the love of that same keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven and for our sake, receive the envoys of the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 0371B] Those who attribute to the envoys of the Franks the same authority before the acquisition of the empire that history testifies they used throughout the ninth century have either failed to understand their character or departed from the truth. Those who went back and forth during Adrian’s time were nothing other than messengers or legates, to whom important matters were sometimes entrusted at the pope’s insistence. Therefore Adrian, and this should be noted, uses the same phrase concerning the envoys of the monastery of Galiata as we have repeatedly seen him use concerning both apostolic and royal envoys. Cenn.] with the gentlest expression and the kindest cheerfulness, and let them receive, with the utmost clemency, the effect of the justice they request from you, so that, receiving a worthy reward for those monks and for the reception of pilgrims, we may be able to pray more effectively for you, for our daughter the lady queen, and for your most triumphant offspring, in the presence of the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, asking divine clemency that, while enjoying the governance of the kingdom here for ages and times, you may be found companions in the heavenly citadels with that same confessor of Christ, blessed Hilary. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LXXXII. 439

### ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES

In it the matter concerns mosaic and marble from the palace of the city of Ravenna [Ravennatis: “of Ravenna”]. The aforesaid pope says that he willingly grants to the dominion of the lord king whatever he might wish to do with it. [Note: [Col. 0371C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 12): “In the twelfth [letter] he gives King Charles, as he had requested, the mosaic and marble of the palace of Ravenna [the mosaics and marbles of the city of Ravenna], both those situated in temples and those in walls and pavements. He gives thanks for the horse sent to him and asks that horses be sent which will suit his seat, distinguished by sound bones and fullness of flesh.” ID.]

*(A.D. 784, Codex Carolinus LXVII, chronicle 81.)*

[Col. 0371B]

### SUMMARY

He grants Charles, who requested them through Arvinus, his duke and envoy, mosaics, marbles, and other materials from the palace of Ravenna. Arvinus had sent two horses to the pontiff, one of which failed on the way. Adrian gives thanks but asks for other horses that are more noble and better-fleshed.

To our most excellent son and spiritual kinsman Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope. [Note: [Col. 0371C] Summary 12, Baronius and Centuriator. Gretser.]

We received the radiant letters of your royal power through Duke Arvinus, [Note: [Col. 0371C] This same duke is elsewhere (letter 92, otherwise 86) called at one time duke and at another count; likewise, in letter 89, otherwise 90, he is distinguished solely by the title of count. Ducange shows that the princes of Armorica, and sometimes also the rulers of Normandy, were called by these titles interchangeably (see “Counts”). He also observes, on the authority of Ditmar, that among the Burgundians many were not accustomed to be called counts unless they possessed the honor of duke. It is unnecessary to inquire of what nation Arvinus was, who was variously called count and duke. This nevertheless needed to be noted, both so that no one would think that two Arvinuses served as royal envoys in these letters and so that the distinction might be maintained between the dukes of the first line of Frankish kings, when the Carolingians themselves, who later became kings, were merely dukes, and the dukes of the second line, that is, of those same Carolingians. The latter generally presided over a single city, as we have just seen the dukes of Clusium and Florence doing. The former presided over entire provinces and had counts under them who administered individual cities. And those who formerly rose to the dukedom through the rank of count now acquired the dukedom in name but the countship in reality. Therefore all could generally be called both dukes and counts. I would not dare to assert that the same was true in papal territory, for I see Adrian (letter 54, otherwise 51) appointing a count over the city of Gabellium, which he calls very small, and mentioning the duchy of Ferrara in the same place. From this it could be inferred that he placed dukes over the larger cities and counts over the smaller ones. And since he usually calls them judges, by which general name both dignities seem to have been designated at that time, I confess that the form of their administration is unknown to me. Furthermore, Stephen II, according to the same Adrian (letter 51, otherwise 54), sent a duke to administer the city of Ravenna, but wished a presbyter to be his colleague, evidently for ecclesiastical matters; Adrian calls both of them judges. Muratori (Italian Antiquities, vol. I, dissertation 5), although led astray by false opinions and therefore departing from the truth, supplies much material illuminating this part of pontifical history. I shall discuss these matters more opportunely below. Cenn.]

[Col. 0372A] in which it was reported that we would grant you the mosaics and marbles of the palace of the city of Ravenna, and the other materials placed both in pavements and in walls. We, with willing mind and pure heart, out of our great love for your excellence, have gladly carried this into effect, and grant you permission to remove from that palace both the marbles and the mosaic, as well as the other materials, [Col. 0372B] because through your arduous royal struggles the Church daily enjoys many benefits from your protector, blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. [Note: [Col. 0372C] Einhard, chapter 26, reports that these marbles were requested for adorning the basilica of wondrous beauty that Charles built at Aachen. Moreover, Muratori himself does not dare to call into question this very evident proof of pontifical dominion in the exarchate (under the year 784). For Charles would not ask the pontiff to grant these things to him unless he enjoyed supreme authority there; nor would the pontiff have freely bestowed them, as though returning thanks for so many benefits, as he clearly declares. The king would either have silently taken them away or ordered them sent to him, and the pontiff would not have sought gratitude for a gift that he recognized as belonging to the king’s jurisdiction. But what of it? Lest he seem compelled to admit the pope’s dominion, Muratori immediately adds another letter of Adrian (letter 83, otherwise 84), in which the pontiff indicates that he expelled Venetian merchants from his own territory according to Charles’s will. From this he concludes that Charles held dominion there, as though the king had sent an order to the pontiff, and the pontiff had not used the word “order” as a matter of office—as we frequently see done—in order not to appear to have sent a message to a prince who had deserved so well of the Church, not as an act of obedience but as an official directive. Has this not always been done, and is it not done today, even in letters between private persons? Yet a little below in the same letter one reads: “May you deign entirely to expel him from there through your most merciful royal command.” For Adrian asks the king to have Garamannus, one of Charles’s dukes appointed in a city of the kingdom of Italy and troublesome to ecclesiastical territory, removed from there. To state the matter more plainly, see the relevant letter. ID.] so that your abundant reward may be recorded in heaven.

We also received through the same Arvinus one useful horse sent by you; but the other that was sent with it failed during the journey and died. For this we offer you our greatest thanks in remembrance of your kindness. But in keeping with the love that we hold in our inmost [Col. 0373A] heart for your radiant kingdom, send us such very famous horses as will suit our seat, distinguished by sound bones and fullness of flesh. While they are praiseworthy in every respect, may they be able to praise your radiant name amid triumphs. [Note: [Col. 0373C] Saint Gregory the Great wrote the following to the subdeacon Peter, who was administrator of the patrimony of Sicily (book XII, letter 30, indiction 7): “You sent us one wretched horse and five good asses. I cannot sit upon that horse, because it is wretched; but I cannot sit upon those good animals, because they are asses. We ask, however, that if you intend to keep us supplied, you send us something worthy of you.” Compare the similar action of the two holy pontiffs, both born of distinguished families. In Gregory you see a pontiff who, although humble and outstanding in every virtue, nevertheless does not wish pontifical majesty to be cheapened. In Adrian, however, you see both the majesty of a pontiff and that of a prince: concerned for both, he desires not only usefulness but also splendor in outward display. Cenn.] And for such a matter, as you are accustomed to do, may you be able to receive a worthy recompense from that apostle of God, so that, reigning in this world together with the lady queen and your most noble offspring, you may deserve to attain eternal life in the heavenly citadels. May heavenly grace keep your excellence safe.

## LXXXIII. 442

### ANOTHER LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN, ADDRESSED TO THE BISHOPS RESIDING THROUGHOUT SPAIN, BUT ESPECIALLY TO ELIPANDUS AND ASCARICUS AND THEIR ADHERENTS

He rebukes them for the heresy or blasphemy by which they call the Son of God adoptive, citing many passages of the holy Fathers. He also treats of the Paschal feast, and of the blood of cattle, swine’s blood, and the blood of strangled animals [Lambecius omits “blood”], which they preach in error, saying that anyone who does not eat such things is crude and uneducated; he declares that such people are bound under the bond of anathema and are strangers to the Church. Likewise, he treats of God’s predestination: if someone were predestined to good, it would not be necessary for him to resist evil; but if he were known [or born, or predestined] for evil, exercising goodness would profit him nothing. Concerning this doctrine he corrects them through apostolic exhortations. He also rebukes them because they say that, although they live a common life with Jews and with unbaptized pagans—in food, drink, and various errors [“practice” or “pursue”]—they are not defiled at all; and he rebukes them concerning their daughters, whom they give in marriage to Gentile peoples, their sacramental rites, and women who, while their husbands are alive, take another man as husband; likewise concerning freedom of the will and many other matters too numerous to list, correcting them in accordance with the traditions of the holy Fathers. [Note: [Col. 0373D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex after 44): “The same Pope Adrian wrote a letter to all the bishops of Spain, especially to Elipandus and Velascharius [Elipandus and Ascaricus]. At the beginning of this letter he calls the Roman Church the head of all members, or of the other Churches [the head of the Churches], and says that whoever cuts himself off from it becomes an exile from the Christian religion. He then refutes the error of Elipandus or Ascaricus, who had called the Son of God adoptive, opposing to it, among other passages, Romans 8, ‘He did not spare his own Son,’ and citing Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Gregory of Nazianzus; Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium; Gregory of Nyssa; Chrysostom; Augustine; Hilary; and Pope Leo.” ID.]

*(A.D. 785, Codex Carolinus XCVII, chronicle 82.)*

[Col. 0374A]

### SUMMARY

He says that he has heard that Aegila was ordained in good faith by Willicarius, archbishop of Sens, and sent to Spain to preach, and that he was making known the errors of a certain Mingentius, his teacher. He warns the bishops to remain steadfast in the true doctrine of the apostolic see and to beware of those same false teachers. He attacks the heresy of Elipandus, Ascaricus, and others who were repeating the blasphemies of Nestorius, using many authorities from the Fathers. He also treats extensively and wisely of the proper celebration of Easter, predestination, grace, and free will, so as to fortify against an immense succession of errors those who were gaining ground in Spain as the Felician heresy was already breaking out.

Adrian, [Note: [Col. 0373D] Baronius and Centuriator mention this letter. Gretser.] pope, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 0374B] to all our most beloved orthodox bishops residing throughout Spain. [Note: [Col. 0374C] Concerning the date of the letter, I preferred to follow Basnage rather than Pagi and the others. In his historical observations on the Felician heresy (Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. III, pp. 284ff.), after investigating the matter with the greatest care, he demonstrates that the letter was not written before this year. Cenn.]

The institution of the universal Church at its birth took its beginning from the dignity of blessed Peter, in whom its government and supreme authority reside; for from his ecclesiastical discipline, as the cultivation of religion already increased throughout all the churches, it flowed forth like a spring. The decrees of the Council of Nicaea bear witness to no other principle, to such an extent that it did not dare establish anything over it, since it saw that nothing could be conferred upon it above its merit; indeed, it knew that everything had been granted to it by the Lord’s word. It is therefore certain that this Church, diffused throughout the whole world, is like the head of its members; and if anyone cuts himself off from it, he becomes an exile from the Christian religion, since he has not begun to belong to that same structure.

[Note: Adrian took this entire passage, beginning “The institution of the universal Church,” from a letter of Boniface I to all the bishops established throughout Thessaly. See it in the collection of Romanus Holstenius (part I, p. 65), where one will also find the observation that Nicholas I (letters 8 and 42) used the authority of this same letter. At the end of the second part (p. 273): “Adrian I transcribed the entire beginning of this letter in letter 97 of the Carolingian Codex, edited by Gretserus, p. 322.” Adrian is at fault in three places, unless the blame is perhaps to be assigned to the copyist. First, in line 4 he omits *de*; it should therefore read *de beati Petri*, “from blessed Peter.” Next, in line 10 he changes the gender; it should read *super eum*, namely, as Holstenius correctly has it, *super eum honorem beati Petri*, “over that dignity of blessed Peter.” For this reason P. Coustantius, in his notes on this letter (p. 1037b), remarks that in ancient manuscripts canon VI of the Council of Nicaea reads, “The Roman Church has always held primacy,” whereas Quesnel corruptly prefers, “Let it always hold primacy.” Finally, in line 14 Adrian is slightly at fault in reading, “if anyone cuts himself off from it,” whereas Boniface says, “whoever cuts himself off from it.” Moreover, as the same Holstenius observes, Nicholas teaches that the privileges of Saint Peter are called by Gelasius “the ordinances of Christ.” Let the advocates of the Dionysian collection consider whether a letter of such importance should be attributed to that collection, and whether the apostolic see should be restricted by it. —ID.]

For we have heard that certain bishops living in your regions, despising the teaching of the apostolic see, are attempting to introduce new heresies against the orthodox tradition of the faith [Lambecius adds: “and Roman,”], neglecting the judgment of the vessel of election, blessed Paul the Apostle, who says (Galatians I): “If anyone preaches to you a gospel beyond what was preached to you, let him be accursed.” Therefore, with joyful hearts, we confidently exhort your orthodoxy to keep your breasts wisely undefiled from every attack of pestilence, and likewise to strive to defend and observe to the end the doctrine of the true faith which your predecessors formerly received from our holy predecessors from our holy Catholic and apostolic see. For (Matthew X and XXIV), “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

[Note: Saint Innocent, in his decretal letter to Decentius of Gubbio, says: “Since it is manifest that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests—or let them read whether another of the apostles is found or is read to have taught in these provinces; and since they produce no such evidence because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, from which there is no doubt that they received their beginning, lest, while they pursue foreign assertions, they appear to omit the head of the institutions.” The Spaniards held this decretal in such high esteem that they transferred each of its chapters into their own book of canons (book II, title 20; book IV, titles 11, 15, 18, and 36), as may be seen in Cardinal Aguirre (vol. III of the *Collectio Maxima*), who first published that book; and in the *Antiquities of the Spanish Church*, vol. I. For that same code, unknown both to Aguirre and to other highly learned writers, was discovered by me and published in a more corrected form, opening, as it were, a brilliant path for dispersing the great darkness surrounding the ancient Spanish Church. Under its guidance we not only understand this passage in Adrian’s letter, but also learn with certainty that before the eighth century the Spaniards attributed the correct doctrine of the faith to no one except the prince of the apostles and his successors, whatever may be believed concerning the tradition that arose among them in that same century. For the authority and other documents of the Roman pontiffs teach otherwise. —CENN.]

Although, therefore, great distances of place separate us, we are with you if you persevere in the unity of our faith—provided only that, with the Lord’s help, there is steadfast perseverance, as the Apostle says (Philippians I): “For to you it has been granted for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.”

Some time ago Archbishop Wulcharius of Gaul made a request to us concerning a certain Egila, asking that we consecrate him bishop; he praised him very highly and exceedingly in the Catholic faith, in his morals, and in his conduct, so that, once consecrated, he might send him to your regions to preach.

[Note: See above, letter 70, elsewhere numbered 96, note. —ID.]

Trusting, however, in the petition of the aforesaid Archbishop Wulcharius, we granted him the customary permission to examine Egila canonically, so that, if after discussion and genuine examination he found him upright and Catholic, he might ordain him bishop; and so that Egila would neither seek nor usurp any foreign see, but offer to God only the gains of souls. Yet when he came into your regions together with the presbyter John, what is worse—as his reputation has reached our ears—that Egila does not preach rightly, but, following certain errors of his teacher Mingentius, attempts, outside Catholic discipline, to teach them, as is reported, and seems to persuade others of many additional propositions which lack ecclesiastical rule [Lambecius adds: “are”].

[Note: The name is not unknown. For Migetius, metropolitan of the province of Narbonne, took part at the Third Council of Toledo toward the end of the sixth century, when, through the efforts of King Reccared and Leander, the Arian heresy was renounced in the year 589; and others likewise took part at the Council of Toledo in 597. The name Egila too is known in Spain throughout the seventh century. I would therefore believe, with a highly probable conjecture, that this Egila was Spanish by birth, while Migetius came from Occitania, which was formerly joined to Spain. In any case, Migetius’s principal error concerning Easter was not a revival of the Quartodeciman error, as Basnage supposes (*Canisius, Ancient Readings*, vol. II, p. 286), but his teaching that the Sunday immediately following was to be omitted if the fourteenth day of the moon fell on a Saturday. Enough has been said on this matter in the cited letter 70 and its notes. —ID.]

But if this is so, let your most faithful devotion, which follows the rule and discipline of our holy Roman Church, in no way consent to believe or follow their madness. For without doubt we by no means believe ourselves ignorant of the discipline of the holy Roman Church [Lambecius reads: “you”], but rather, as we admonish you, strive to bring them back to the true and orthodox faith.

[Note: The errors which he commands them to avoid are listed both in the aforesaid letter and later in this one. See the notes to that same letter 70. —ID.]

Moreover, a grievous report has reached us from your regions: certain bishops living there, namely Elipandus and Ascaricus, together with others who agree with them, are not ashamed to confess the Son of God as adopted. No one from any heresy had previously dared to utter such a blasphemy except that faithless Nestorius, who confessed a mere man to be the Son of God.

[Note: How correctly Panvinius and the Centuriators, as well as the summary of the letter in this codex, say that the letter was directed especially to Elipandus and Ascaricus is clear from this passage. For both are attacked as leaders of the Nestorian error. Etherius and Beatus pursue this history at length in their letter to Elipandus (*Canisius, Ancient Readings*, vol. II, pp. 297ff.). See also Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXV, nos. 52ff.). The sum of the error was that Christ was an adopted Son of God, not his proper Son. —ID.]

Therefore, do not allow their serpentine poison in any way to creep into or defile your devotion, wherever it may be; but, holding fast the divine confession of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, following the tradition of their holy Catholic, apostolic, and Roman Church, and likewise embracing the doctrines of the foremost, Catholic, and approved Fathers, strive firmly, steadily, immovably, and without wavering to persevere with us, irrefragably and without hesitation, in their radiant tradition.

First of all, hold fast the confession of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, who says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI).

[Note: Adrian treated this matter most fully in the letter which precedes the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794 against Elipandus. He does not cite merely one or two passages of Scripture, but follows the introduction with a long series of passages, supported by the authority of the Fathers, who themselves interpret the Scriptures and vigorously defend the Catholic doctrine that Jesus Christ is the proper Son of God. —CENN.]

Next, hold fast the teaching of blessed Paul the Apostle, the vessel of election, the support of the faith [Note: The passage is corrupt unless *subposterium* or *suppositum* is an inversion. —GRET. —Gretser considers the passage corrupt; but *suppostorium* is in fact classed by Gregory the Great among sacred ministrations, as Cangius notes; and the continuators or annotators add that it perhaps means the bowl placed beneath a small vessel while drinking [reading uncertain]. Although the allusion may therefore seem less fitting—Peter is called keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and Paul the supporting vessel of faith—*subposturium*, *suppostorium*, and *suppositorium* have the same meaning; only through scribal carelessness did *e* intrude for *o*. —ID.], who says: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans VIII). And if those chief apostles confessed the living and proper Son of God, how do heretics, barking against the truth, presume to say that the Son of God is adopted—a statement which, when merely heard, makes every Christian groan and tremble?

Thus blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, an ancient and distinguished preacher, in his work on the divine Incarnation of the Word, agreeing with the holy First Council held at Nicaea, says among other things:

“If anyone, contrary to divine Scripture, says that one is the Son of God and another is the man from Mary according to grace [Lambecius and Gentilotius add: ‘adopted according to grace, like you,’ so that there would be two sons, one by nature the Son of God, who is from God, and one according to grace], and if anyone says that the flesh of our Lord came from above and not from the Virgin Mary, or changes, confuses, alienates, or makes passible the divinity in the flesh, or says that the flesh of the Lord God is not to be adored, as though it were merely human, rather than to be adored as the flesh of a man and God—him the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes, in agreement with the divine Apostle, who says: ‘If anyone preaches to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed’ (Galatians I).”

But blessed Gregory Nazianzen, also called the Theologian, writing to Cledonius, says among other things:

[Note: Perhaps the reading should be “within” or “between.” Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 51, in the new Paris edition. —GRET.]

“If anyone introduces two sons, one indeed from God and the Father, but the other from the mother, and not one and the same Son, let him fall away from the adoption promised to those who believe rightly. There are two natures, God and man, just as there are soul and body; but there are not two sons, nor two gods. For there are not two men here either, although Paul called what is inward and what is outward in man by those names (I Corinthians XV). If one must constantly say ‘another and another,’ according to the things from which the Savior is composed—or unless what is invisible is the same as what is visible, and what is without time the same as what is subject to time—let there not be ‘another and another’; rather, both are one.”

And further:

“If anyone says that he became perfect through works, or after baptism, or after rising from the dead, and that he was then worthy of adoption, as the pagans introduce those who are enrolled as citizens, let him be accursed.”

[Note: This entire passage of Nazianzen is almost wholly corrupt in our copy. In Billius’s edition it reads, in agreement with the Greek text: “If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, the other from the mother, and not one and the same Son, let him also fall away from that adoption of sons which was promised to those who believe rightly. Although God and man are two natures, just as soul and body are, nevertheless there are not two sons, nor gods; just as here too there are not two men, although Paul called the inward and outward part of man in this way. And, to sum up the matter briefly, the things from which the Savior is composed are indeed different—unless what cannot be seen is the same as what comes within the sight of the eyes, and what is free from time is the same as what is subject to time—but they are not two different beings; both are one through their union.” Further: “If anyone says that he became perfect through works, or after baptism, or after resurrection from the dead, and was adopted as a son, as the Greeks introduce those enrolled as citizens, let him be accursed.” —ID. Both passages, that of Athanasius and that of Nazianzen, are cited throughout the aforesaid letter preceding the Council of Frankfurt, but they differ everywhere from the version Adrian uses here. Both are mutilated: Athanasius’s at the beginning, Nazianzen’s at the end; for what follows here is lacking there. Nevertheless, the pontiff deliberately omits it there, saying: “But the explanation of this chapter is reserved for a suitable time.” —CENN.]

Therefore the eminent Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, taught us in his sermon on the holy Epiphany:

“Now, in the Holy Spirit, because of the grace of adoption—for it is impossible for you to receive the authority of adoption and cry, ‘Abba, Father,’ unless the Spirit of adoption has marked you.”

And shortly afterward:

“Unless he had suffered in the form of a servant, you would in no way have gained the glory of adoption.”

And a little later:

“Love the imperial gift; receive the dignity of adoption.”

Blessed Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, also, in his treatment of Matthew [“discussing”], says:

“If you are a peacemaker, you are crowned with the grace of adoption.”

Likewise blessed John, bishop of Constantinople, also called Chrysostom, instructing the newly baptized, writes:

“Blessed be God—let us say it again—who alone does wonders, who makes all things and transforms all things. Behold, those who were previously held captive enjoy the serenity of freedom, and those who had been wandering in exile are citizens of the Church; those who had been in the confusion of sin now stand in the lot of righteousness. For they are not merely free, but also holy; not merely holy, but also righteous; not merely righteous, but also sons; not merely sons, but heirs; not merely heirs, but brothers of Christ; not merely brothers of Christ, but co-heirs; not merely co-heirs, but members; not merely members, but a temple; not merely a temple, but instruments of the Spirit. Blessed be God, who alone does wonders. You see how many are the gifts of baptism. Yet many think that heavenly grace consists only in the remission of sins, whereas we have counted ten honors.
