For this reason we also baptize infants, so that they may not remain stained by sin, and so that they may be granted the adoption of righteousness, inheritance, brotherhood with Christ; so that all may be his members and become the dwelling place of the Spirit.”

The same writer also taught in his commentary on John the Evangelist:

“Do not become useless toward your benefactor, nor repay him with opposites—the one who gave you the fountain of blessedness. For where there is the dignity of adoption, there is the cutting away of evils and the gift of every good.”

The same writer says in the Psalms [Lambecius adds “in”]:

“This has come to pass, and it is wonderful in our eyes: we who formerly, before the Lord’s passion, were without covenant and law, have been adopted as sons of God.”

[Note: The authorities of Amphilochius, Gregory of Nyssa, and John Chrysostom are absent from the aforesaid letter. —CENN.]

Behold, our most beloved brethren, how the holy Eastern Fathers taught that adoption is among the gifts of grace, and that it has been granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to all of us who were born in sins and were reborn through baptism.

Thus blessed Augustine, that distinguished teacher, says in his sermon on the Nativity of the Lord:

“Listen, sons of light, adopted into the kingdom of God.”

And again, in his exposition of the holy Gospel according to John, he plainly taught this:

“But as many as received him, what did he grant them? Great benevolence, great mercy. He was born the only one, and he did not wish to remain alone. Many people, when they have had no children and have reached an advanced age, adopt children for themselves and by their will accomplish what they could not by nature; this is what human beings do. But if someone has an only son, he rejoices in him all the more, because he alone will possess everything and will have no one with whom he must divide the inheritance, so that he may remain poorer. God did not act in this way. He sent into this world the one and same Son whom he had begotten and through whom he had created all things, so that he would not be alone but would have adopted brothers. For we were not born from God as the Only-Begotten was, but were adopted by his grace. He, the Only-Begotten, came to abolish sin,” and so forth.

Again, in another sermon of the same book:

“Those who divide unity can in no way claim that they possess charity.”

After these words, let us examine what follows:

“John bore witness because he saw. What testimony did he bear? That he is the Son of God. Therefore the one who is the only Son of God, not an adopted son, had to baptize. Adopted sons are ministers of the Only-Begotten; the Only-Begotten has authority and adopts them into the ministry. Although a minister baptizes, he does not belong to the number of the brothers, because he lives badly and acts badly. What consoles us? This is the one who baptizes,” and so forth.

[Note: As regards the authorities of the Latin Fathers, there is a major discrepancy. A comparison of the two letters will make this clear: there the pontiff says more than Augustine does, whereas here the reverse is evident. —ID.]

The same writer says in another sermon:

“We came from the nations; but we would not have come from the nations unless God had raised up children for Abraham from stones. We became children of Abraham by imitating his faith, not by being born according to the flesh. For just as they, by degenerating, were disinherited, so we, by imitating, were adopted.”

And further, in another sermon, the same writer says:

“The Father loves the Son, and has given everything into his hand” (John III). He added, “He has given everything into his hand,” so that you might know the distinction intended here. “The Father loves the Son.” Why, then, does the Father not love John? Yet he did not give everything into his hand. Does the Father not love Paul? Yet he did not give everything into his hand. “The Father loves the Son”—but how does the Father love the Son? Not as the Lord loves the servant; as the only son, not as an adopted son.

[Note: From this point there follows a major discrepancy between the two letters. For there Gregory and Ambrose are cited instead of Hilary and Leo; and the manner of writing differs so greatly that, although the letters are separated by only nine years and present the same author, the later one, issued by the pontiff when already advanced in age, appears more elegant and forceful and seems to recall the decretals of ancient usage. The present letter, however, differing in no way from the others contained in the Codex, reveals Adrian’s private effort. If another, more extensive letter to Charlemagne on sacred images is added to it—the one found in the Second Council of Nicaea—the great concern of both Churches, Eastern and Western, becomes apparent, as befitted a pontiff distinguished for holiness of life and learning. —ID.]

Likewise the exposition of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, on Matthew says:

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. The blessedness of peacemakers is the reward of adoption, so that they may remain sons of God. For God, the parent of all, is one; nor can anyone otherwise pass into the designation of his family unless, having put away those things by which we can be offended, we live together in the peace of mutual brotherly love.”

Blessed Leo, too, that eminent pope and outstanding teacher, taught us in his sermon on the holy Epiphany (Sermon 5):

“Therefore what the distinguished men who represented all the nations obtained by worshiping the Lord, the whole world achieves among its peoples through the faith that justifies the ungodly; and those adopted receive the inheritance of God, prepared before the ages, while those who seemed legitimate lose it.”

And later in the same sermon:

“We must run along that road which the Lord himself testified that he is. Without any merits of works assisting us, he provided for us by sacrament and example, so that through the former he might advance those called into adoption to salvation, and through the latter instruct them for labor.”

Again, from a sermon of the same most blessed pontiff Leo on the passion of the Lord:

“But we, dearly beloved, who have been freed from the darkness of ignorance, have received the light of faith, and have entered by the election of adoption into the inheritance of the New Testament, let us rejoice in the festival which carnal Israel lost.”

Another sermon of the same writer on Pentecost says:

“But we, dearly beloved, adopted through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit into the blessed inheritance of both soul and body, let us celebrate this most sacred feast of the day with rational service, trusting with blessed Paul the Apostle that the Lord Jesus, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men, so that the Gospel of God might be preached through every expression of human speech and every tongue might confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

For if we were to write out for you the works of all the holy orthodox Fathers on this subject, paper and scribes would run out before the divine discourse contained in their discussions came to an end. But in all these matters, let your most faithful belief strive to bring those who are placed in error back to the faith of the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church and to offer the fruit of souls to God, so that the gain may increase especially for us and for you.

[Note: Up to this point the letter has dealt with the heresy of Elipandus and Felix of Urgell, who proclaimed the Son of God to be adopted. The remaining errors concerning Easter, predestination, and free will, together with several others, are related in nearly the same words that we saw above in letter 70, elsewhere numbered 96. —CENN.]

Likewise, this too has reached our apostolic ears: many in those regions, having fallen into folly and madness of heart, dare to disregard the successive statements and admonitions of our holy predecessors, the pontiffs, and of ourselves, concerning the celebration of Easter, in accordance with the ordinance of the venerable Council of Nicaea. They say that if the full moon—the fourteenth day of the moon—falls on a Saturday, holy Easter is not to be celebrated on the following Sunday, namely, the fifteenth day of the moon; instead, after omitting that fifteenth day, they declare that the joys of the Easter feast are to be celebrated on another Sunday of the following week, which is the twenty-second day of the moon.

If the rule concerning the Easter festivals promulgated by the great and venerable Council of Nicaea, where three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled together, is considered inwardly and carefully, all error and every ambiguity will unquestionably be removed from the hearts of those who hesitate. But while many labor to defend their own inventions as clever, perceptive, and skilled in worldly knowledge, yet ignorant of spiritual learning, they pass over the ancient tradition of the Fathers through sluggish negligence and desire to cast a shadow over the truth with falsehoods.

For in that same great Council of Nicaea, when the Fathers had confirmed the nineteen-year cycle, it was promulgated among other things that the solemnities of this sacred festival should not be extended beyond the twenty-first day of the moon. This rule concerning Easter was subsequently confirmed by the venerable Council of Antioch, where among other things, in its first chapter, the following is recorded:

“We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, assembled in the presence of the most pious and venerable prince Constantine, concerning the saving solemnity of holy Easter, are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church.”

And if they should nevertheless persist more contentiously [more correctly: “more obstinately”] against what has been properly established, that council decreed that they would be subjected to more severe prohibitions.

For blessed Dionysius too, in the letter which he issued concerning the calculation of Easter, says:

“They determined that, beginning on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, according to the judgment of all the Easterners, the course of the spring equinox should follow, and that especially the expertise of the Egyptians should be consulted, since they are knowledgeable and learned in this calculation.”

It is expressly noted that in this matter the holy Synod of Nicaea also firmly established without ambiguity that, even if the fourteenth day of the moon falls on a Saturday, Easter is to be celebrated on the following Sunday, the fifteenth day of the moon.

Pay attention, our most beloved brethren, also to what blessed Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, sent to our most blessed predecessor Pope Leo at the command of the pious emperor Marcian. After much else he says:

“Formerly the Lord, signifying this through Moses, said: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year, and you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month’” (Exodus X).

And shortly afterward he adds:

“If ever the fourteenth day of the moon has occurred on a Sunday, the festival must be postponed to the following week, just as our ancient Fathers did, transferring the fourteenth days of the moon that occurred then to another Sunday.”

Therefore, dearly beloved, it is clear that it is not lawful for the solemnity of this venerable festival to extend beyond the twenty-first day of the moon, provided that the number of days in the week is properly observed, since the course of the sun is entirely out of accord with the course of the moon.

For in six days the Lord, Creator of all, fashioned the heavenly firmament and all its adornment, the shining things of the sea and the plants produced by the earth, the substance of the elements, and all living creatures that creep; and finally he formed the man of the clay of the field [Note: In the related letter, I criticized Tengnagel’s carelessness in replacing *arva* with *feria*, whereas Lambecius and Gentilotius also read *arva* here. Therefore even *agri* should not be admitted, although *arva* also signifies “field.” In that age *arva, arvae* was declined more elegantly than *arva, arvorum*. —ID.], and on the seventh day he rested from all the work that he had made.

Accordingly, during these seven days, beginning with the fourteenth day of the moon, which is the full moon, if that day should nevertheless fall on a Sunday—which is the first and holy day, on which one ought not to fast—the order of the calculation requires that, after passing over to another Sunday, which is the first and holy day, on the twenty-first day of the moon, Christians celebrate holy Easter.

For if the following Sunday is omitted when the fourteenth day of the moon has fallen on a Saturday, namely, the fifteenth day of the moon, and that Sunday—which is the first day of the week, on which light came forth at God’s command at the beginning of the world, and on which our true Light, the Savior, rose bodily from the dead—is not venerated, then, if eight days are passed over from the fourteenth day of the moon, when the fast is ended, so that the Easter festival is postponed to the twenty-second day of the moon, it must now be called and observed not as a seventh-day period—that is, a week—but as an eight-day period, as foolish and senseless people profane it.

Reason also urges us to consider this: seven weeks, not eight, are passed over from the Easter festival to holy Pentecost, on which our Redeemer, the Son of the living God, after his glorious resurrection, sent the Paraclete Spirit from the Father to his holy apostles. For this reason let us walk along the royal road and not turn aside completely onto a crooked path filled with thorns and briars. Let those who desire to compose new inventions and monuments of wickedness proceed along that path, so that thorns and briars may rightly be produced for them.

Long ago our holy pontiffs, predecessors and forefathers, sent to those regions admonitions and exhortations concerning this question and this heresy together, publishing appropriate chapters of blessed Cyril and Theophilus, as well as of other holy Fathers too numerous to list. There is no doubt that this is known to your devotion. Nevertheless, dearest brethren, we do not cease to admonish you with special urgency: beware of false brothers, and strive to celebrate the Easter solemnity in the manner in which our holy Roman Church, the head of all the Churches of God, celebrates it—and rightly, if it holds to God’s traditions—so that, just as the religion of Christian faith makes us equal, it may also make us equal in our festivals.

We have also heard this from your regions: certain men who make promises while persisting in error preach that anyone who does not eat the blood of cattle or swine, or what has been strangled, is uncultivated or uneducated. We, instructed and educated by the apostolic precepts, firmly proclaim that if anyone eats the blood of cattle or swine, or what has been strangled, he is not only excluded from all consolation but is also utterly alien to sound understanding. Thus, bound under the sentence of anathema, they fall into the snares of the devil.

But as for what others among them say—that predestination [Col. 0383C] to life or to death lies in God’s power and not ours—they say: “Why do we strive to live, since this lies in God’s power?” Others again say: “Why do we ask God not to let us be overcome by temptation, since this lies in our power, as though by freedom of choice?” In truth, they can neither give nor accept any reason, being ignorant of the little works sent by blessed Fulgentius, bishop, to the presbyter Eugypius against the sermon of a certain Pelagian, in which the same Father, teaching many things below, adds these words:

> “But while those men reprehensibly introduce grace only on their own behalf, they have damnably trampled it down in themselves: they assert that some are destined to life and others to death. Consider by what bonds of impiety they bind themselves. If I have been predestined to good, I will not need to resist evil; but if I have been born for evil, it will profit me nothing to practice good. Thus, with the desire for praise and glory shut off on both sides, one will languish in security and the other in despair; consequently, the practice of righteousness will be idle, prayer will cease, and good work will grow weak. But it is not so. Rather, let us pray without ceasing, because the Lord himself says: ‘Pray without interruption, lest you enter into temptation.’ Nevertheless, let us struggle against every sin not only by prayer but also by labor, because the Lord himself testified in the present reading that each person will receive his own reward according to his labor. These words, spoken inconsiderately and indiscriminately, by which the author of that sermon attempts to attack the truth of predestination, we shall demonstrate, with God’s help [Col. 0384A].”

And afterward:

> “God therefore prepared works of mercy and justice in the eternity of his unchangeableness; and just as he was never ignorant of his future works, so he was never improvident in preparing those same works. He prepared merits for those who were to be justified; he prepared rewards for those same people who were to be glorified. For the wicked, however, he did not prepare evil wills or evil works, but he prepared for them just and eternal punishments. This is God’s eternal predestination of future works, which, just as we know is continually made known to us through apostolic teaching, so also we confidently proclaim. For blessed Paul clearly and frequently makes known the predestination of those whom God saves freely. He says of God: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers’ (Romans VIII). And afterward: ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified’ (ibid.). Nothing uncertain wavers in God’s works, because nothing makes his predestination void. God therefore begins the works of his predestination with calling and completes them with glorification. Yet not in all whom he calls, but in those whom he calls according to his purpose; for all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose.”

Again, after much else:

> “Let the truth of predestination therefore be held by all the faithful, because whoever does not believe in this divine plan of predestination will not attain the glorious effect of that same predestination. Whoever, however, has not been predestined to glory is undoubtedly found to have been foreknown for punishment; this punishment is therefore recognized as predestined in God’s preparation, so that unbelief and iniquity may be punished through it. For this reason blessed Judas the apostle says that certain people were predestined to judgment, in these words: ‘For certain impious men have slipped in, who were long ago marked out and predestined for this judgment of our God’ (Jude IV). But, watchfully following the teaching of the Holy Spirit, he does not say that the impious were predestined to sin, but to judgment—that is, not to impiety but to punishment. They were not predestined to commit vicious acts of impiety, but to receive what they receive through the judgment of divine justice. Their work is what they do impiously; God’s work is what they receive justly.”

Again, after other material:

> “Therefore, what the author of that sermon subsequently added, saying, ‘Rather, let us pray without ceasing, because the Lord himself says: “Pray without interruption, lest you enter into temptation,”’ and afterward, ‘Nevertheless, let us struggle against every sin not only by prayer but also by labor,’ and again, ‘Thus, while we labor, the Lord calls us, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you”’ (Matthew XI)—let us humbly ask God for grace, which we may continually have working with us, through which God may preserve us in our labor and, when the labor has been completed, bring us to our reward.”

[Col. 0385A] Moreover, beloved, we have heard from those regions various matters: that many who say they are Catholics, living a common life with Jews and unbaptized pagans, both in food and drink and in various errors, claim that they are not defiled by anything; that although it has been forbidden for anyone to bear the yoke with unbelievers, they themselves bless their daughters together with another party and thus hand them over to the pagan people; that men are ordained to preside without examination by the aforementioned presbyters; and that another huge and pernicious error has gained strength, namely, that even while their husbands are alive, women take these pseudo-priests as husbands. The same is true of free choice and many other matters, as we have heard from those regions, which would take too long to recount.

Therefore, beloved, your diligence must watch with the greatest care, and, as befits the priests of the Lord, none of you may be ignorant of the canons, nor do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy order will be preserved by us if the standard of decreed constitutions is broken at the pleasure of some, with license granted to the peoples? Hence it is established that if anyone is found liable in the matters mentioned above, then, after a first and a second admonition, if he refuses to correct himself, he shall certainly be expelled according to the rule from the fellowship of God’s faithful, as a corrupter of the traditions of the Fathers, and shall be found under eternal condemnation.

Your belovedness must therefore beware, and must prohibit with great diligence, lest through such men scandals long since extinguished be rekindled, and some seed of the same evil arise in the province from the doctrine once cut off [Col. 0385C]; lest it not only grow from its roots but also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its stench. Those who wish to appear corrected should clear themselves of every suspicion and prove by obeying you that they are ours. If any one of them refuses to comply with salutary commands—whether cleric or [458] layman—let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest a destroyer of his own soul lie in wait for the salvation of another.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] We have detected some changes, and very slight ones, in this part of the letter, which it took from an earlier one. The principal difference is this: no mention is made of Wilcharius, archbishop of Gaul. This is not because he had died—for at the beginning of the letter he is praised as still living—but because the bishops of Spain had no business with the archbishop of Gaul. The earlier letter had been sent to Egila, whom Wilcharius had ordained and instructed in correct doctrine. CENN.]

But you, beloved, embracing the orthodox faith of our holy Catholic and apostolic Church, strive to proclaim that, just as our shepherd Christ, the Son of the living God, is one, so we may all together be gathered into one of his sheepfold; and, just as we are members of one head, so may we become one body in Christ Jesus our Lord. Thus may we merit what he has bestowed upon his holy worshipers who keep his commandments, and who have pleased his divine majesty from the beginning of the world: the desirable promise in which he says, “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

## LXXXIV. 459. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Charles

In it he deals with the Venetians [Lamb., Gent., Venetics], so that they might be expelled from Ravenna or the Pentapolis, and also with Duke Garamannus, who had violently invaded or stripped the possessions [Lamb., “property and possessions”] of the Church of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 5): “In the fifth [letter] he indicates that he ordered the Venetians to be expelled from Ravenna or the Pentapolis; then that Duke Garmannus had invaded the property and possessions of the Church of Ravenna. Therefore he begs Charles, according to Peter’s custom, to expel him, so that his territories may remain untouched.”]

(AD 785, Codex Carolinus LXXXIV, chronicle 83.)

### Argument

He immediately complied with the royal wish: namely, he ordered the Venetian merchants to be expelled [Col. 0386B] from the exarchate and the Pentapolis, and furthermore instructed the archbishop of Ravenna to expel them from all places belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction and from whatever belonged by right to the Church of Ravenna. Against Duke Garamannus he petitions that he be removed from the office entrusted to him, because he had invaded the estates of the Church of Ravenna and of other pious places situated in territories under ecclesiastical jurisdiction and had treated pontifical admonitions with contempt.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual compater, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Summary 5, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.]

[Note: [Col. 0386D] That this letter should rightly be placed in the year 785, against those who let it wander after 781 at an uncertain date, is clear also from the fact that Duke Garamannus, who in the preceding year had acted as Charles’s envoy and had been appointed by Charles himself commander of his forces in Italy, was already exercising his office. Adrian asks that he be removed from office because he was extending rapacious hands into the dominion of the Holy See. CENN.]

We make known to the ears of your most merciful royal excellency that, when your royal victory in triumph sent forth an order that the Venetians should be expelled from the regions of Ravenna or the Pentapolis for purposes of trade, we immediately sent [Col. 0386C] your order into those regions, fulfilling your royal will. Moreover, we sent a command to the archbishop that, in every territory of ours and [Lamb., Gent. add “ours”] belonging by right to the holy Church of Ravenna, wherever those Venetians had strongholds and possessions, he should expel them altogether from there and thus hold the rights of his Church in his own hands.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] It is not clear what Charles feared from the Venetian merchants in the kingdom of Italy. It is certain only that he asked the pope to expel them from the whole territory of the Church, including even those who had long lived there and had acquired possessions or held other resources or property in those regions. That the pope fulfilled everything either personally or through the archbishop of Ravenna is so clear in the letters that the dominion of the Holy See cannot be denied. ID.]

But what happened concerning Duke Garamannus, who suddenly rushed upon the estates and possessions of the holy Church of Ravenna situated in our territories? He not only occupied them but also took away all the crops from the aforesaid Church, and did the same with property belonging to other pious places. We immediately endeavored to admonish him that, if he were your faithful servant, he should by no means fail to return the possessions of the pious places, since they appear to belong by right to the Church of Ravenna or to such pious places, and since they are situated in our territories. But he in no way took this into consideration, nor did he wish to return the possessions; rather, he attempts to retain them unlawfully.

Therefore, asking your royal power in triumph, we beg you, for the love of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and out of our paternal affection, not to allow him to do such things. Instead, by your most merciful royal command [Col. 0387C], may you deign to expel him entirely from there, so that our territories may remain untouched through your royal protection and so that we may enjoy, without dispute, the possession and right of the same places over whatever is known to be within those territories.

[Note: [Col. 0387C] Here is the reason why Adrian, complying as a companion and friend with the prince’s wishes, fulfilled them completely: he wanted to remove all fear of suspected persons from him. He desired, clearly, that a more immediate remedy be brought to his jurisdiction through the removal of Duke Garamannus. It should be noted that he does not use the courteous language he had used shortly before, when he said that he had carried out what the king had ordered. Instead, he requests a “most merciful royal command”—that is, a charter, diploma, or royal order—by whose supreme authority that duke might be removed. CENN.]

Thus may your royal power, together with your lady queen and your most noble offspring, merit reigning here and in the future without end, just as your victory in triumphs deserves. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Lamb reads: “that they may enjoy the rights of those possessions held by the pious places”; and Gent: “that they may enjoy the rights of those possessions belonging to the pious places.”]

## LXXXV. 461. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Charles

In it he deals with the formerly faithless people, namely the Saxons: how our Lord and Redeemer, through the arduous struggles of the aforesaid king, had brought them to the worship of God, to the rectitude of faith of his Catholic and apostolic Church, and to the sacred font of baptism; and also with litanies, fasts, and prayers for this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 44): “King Charles had reported that through arduous struggles he had brought the Saxons to the Catholic faith and to the baptismal font. For this reason he had asked Adrian that litanies be performed on one or two weekdays. The pope replies that in all his regions [the pope’s letter 44: ‘in all the regions of the West’] litanies ought to be performed on the twenty-third, twenty-sixth, and twenty-eighth of June [that is, the vigil of John the Baptist, the feast of Saints John and Paul, and the vigil of the holy apostles Peter and Paul]. He orders Charles to see that litanies are performed in all his regions on those same days. He states that at Rome they continually give thanks for Charles and pray to God—letter forty-four.” CENN.]

(AD 786, Codex Carolinus XCI, chronicle 84.)

### Argument

He received with immense joy the royal letters brought by Abbot Andrew, reporting that the Saxons had been defeated and converted to the orthodox faith [Col. 0387C]. At Charles’s request, he decreed that public prayers of thanksgiving should be offered throughout the whole ecclesiastical territory on three fixed days of the coming month of June. He allowed this interval so that on those same days the same public prayers could be proclaimed throughout the Frankish kingdom and even in the Catholic regions overseas.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual compater, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

[Col. 0388A] We have received the royal communications from your excellence, long awaited and greatly desired by us, through your most faithful bearer and envoy, namely Andrew, the religious abbot. When we opened them, we found in them news of the health, safety, and sincere prosperity of your lofty royal power, of your consort and offspring, and of all your chief and our faithful servants. For these things we rendered our customary thanks to the Redeemer of the world.

We learned there, moreover, of your royal triumphs, protected by God: how you have brought savage and hostile peoples, namely the Saxons, to the worship of God and to the rectitude of faith of his holy Catholic and apostolic Church; and how, with the Lord’s help and through the support of the intercession of Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, their necks have been brought under your power and jurisdiction [Col. 0388B]. Having subjected their nobles, and with divine inspiration and royal exertion, you have brought that entire Saxon people to the sacred font of baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0388C] There is no controversy about the date of this letter. All the ancient annals, especially those of the Franks and of Fulda, connect the conversion of the Saxons to the Catholic faith with the year 785. Therefore, at the beginning of this year, both the envoy and the letters came from Charles as messengers of such great joy. According to Mabillon (Annals, book XXV, no. 46), the royal envoy identified by Cointius was the abbot of Luxeuil. From the same author, page [or entry] (AD 786, no. 8). CENN.]

For this reason we have given even greater praise to divine clemency, because in our times and yours the peoples of the pagans, led into the true and great religion and into perfect faith, have been subjected to your royal dominion. Your power, founded by God, is indeed supported by this; for if it fulfills, with a pure heart and most willing spirit, what it promised to its protector, blessed Peter the apostle, and to us, it will subject the greatest and strongest of those peoples to your feet through its principal acts of assistance.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] Adrian appropriately reminds Charles to recall the patronage of the prince of the apostles, if a pious prince needed such a reminder. For fourteen years war had been waged against those barbarians. Although they had always been defeated, they had never been completely subdued; scarcely had the Franks gone away free from fear when, taking up arms again under their leader Widukind, they rebelled. In this year Charles not only defeated them but also brought them, together with Widukind himself, to the Catholic faith. He could not have achieved this by human strength had not Peter interceded with God and superior grace worked in the hearts of the Saxons, so that “the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God,” might shine upon them (2 Corinthians IV, 4).]

Thus, with no one pursuing them, may they be subjected to your royal powers, and may you merit offering before the tribunal of Christ, on the day of judgment, the greatest and most worthy fruit from the salvation of their souls [unus; Lamb., munus, “gift”]; and, for love of souls, may you merit acquiring infinite gains in the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0388C] As for what your royal excellency reported—that during one month or on one day we should sing praises to God for such works, namely, for the victory establishing your rule, and perform litanies on one or two weekdays—this is exceedingly pleasing to us. Therefore, writing in accordance with apostolic authority, we decreed and sent orders that the same litanies should immediately be celebrated with us in all our regions subject to the authority of your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church: namely, on the twenty-third, twenty-sixth, and twenty-eighth days of the coming month of June. These are, first, the vigil of blessed John the Baptist, the feast of Saints John and Paul, and the vigil of blessed Peter the apostle.

[Note: [Col. 0389B] In letter 50, otherwise 55, Adrian reported to Charles that during the siege of Pavia in AD 774 he had ordered Kyrie eleison to be sung three hundred times throughout the city. There he was speaking of the kind of litany that was performed without a supplication, with hands extended in all the churches. Here, however, the subject is the celebration of a three-day litany with a supplication. Mabillon provides the following account of the manner of celebrating it (in the preliminary commentary on the Roman Ordines), from an ancient Ritual of the Holy Roman Church in a Cassinese codex:

> “On the Assumption of Saint Mary, during the evening of the vigil itself, a certain bier is prepared at Saint Lawrence at the Lateran. After a panel bearing an image of Christ our Lord has been placed beneath it, at midnight the assembled people go out with the litany to Saint Mary Minor. The streets are cleaned along the route and lamps are hung from the houses. There, after the icon has been set down for a time on the steps of Saint Mary, the entire choir of men and women, humbly kneeling before it and also striking their breasts with their fists, say with one voice, in order: one hundred times Kyrie eleison, one hundred times Christe eleison, and again one hundred times Kyrie eleison. Then, with tears and prayers poured out, they go by the direct route through Saint Adrian to Saint Mary Major; after hearing the celebration of Mass, they return to the palace.”

> The account concerns the time of Otto III, or rather perhaps the end of the tenth century. Therefore it is probable that the three-day litanies instituted by Adrian were not unlike those just described, especially since two of the days were appointed to be celebrated on vigils. The commentators on Cangius’s Glossary, citing the Capitularies (vol. I, col. 256), produce a letter of Charlemagne that relates the following:

> “With the Lord’s help we performed the litany for three days, namely on the Nones of September, beginning on Monday, and on Tuesday and Wednesday, beseeching God’s mercy to grant us peace and health, victory, and a prosperous journey … And our priests decreed that those who, because of weakness, old age, or youth, were able to abstain should abstain from wine and meat … And while they were performing those litanies, they were to walk barefoot.”

> From this, if I am not mistaken, it is sufficiently clear that the litanies were celebrated with a supplication, or, as people commonly say, a procession. The only difference between the Roman and Frankish practice was that in the city some interval of rest was granted to those celebrating the litany three times, whereas in Francia the supplications were conducted throughout an uninterrupted period of three days, in the manner of the Rogations, according to the discipline then prevailing there. CENN.]

Similarly, may your royal power direct that three-day litanies be completed throughout all its regions, and also in the overseas lands where the Christian people dwell. For this reason we have appointed such a prolonged interval: because of the very distant Christian nations living beyond your royal kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0390B] Two things may certainly be inferred from this. First, the litanies proclaimed by the pontiff on the occasion of the conversion of the Saxons were celebrated on fixed days throughout the ecclesiastical territory and throughout the whole Frankish monarchy. Second, the two jurisdictions are distinguished so clearly that anyone who dares to call the dominion of the Holy See into question must be said not only to depart far from the truth but manifestly to lie.]

We have not merely planned, as you indicated to us, to celebrate one or two litanies; wishing also to pray continually for your excellency, as is our custom, we have decreed that this should be done, and that praises should be sung to the Redeemer of the world. May he cause those peoples who have been brought to the Christian faith through your royal struggle to remain forever under your support; may he drive away every disease and cast pestilence far from our borders and yours; and may you, while the people entrusted to us by God dwell in great abundance and in the joy of most sincere well-being, together with your lady queen and your most noble offspring, merit enjoying the reins of the kingdom for a longer age and reigning without end in the heavenly citadels. May your arduous struggles cause your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church, to remain ever more greatly exalted. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

[Note: [Col. 0390C] Summary from Baronius: King Charles had informed Adrian through the abbots Itherius and Magenarius that certain Saxons had relapsed into paganism and had asked what should be done with them. Pope Adrian replied that after a long penance they could be restored to the fellowship of the Church. Summary 9, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.]

## LXXXVI. 465

(AD 786, Codex Carolinus LXXX, chronicle 85.)

[Note: [Col. 0390C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 9): “King Charles had informed Adrian through the abbots Itherius and Monegarius that certain Saxons had relapsed into paganism and had asked what should be done with them. Pope Adrian replies [Adrian’s ninth letter] that after a long penance they may be received into the fellowship of the Church.” CENN.]

### Argument

When Itherius and Magenarius, abbots sent as royal envoys, asked what penance should be imposed on the Saxons who had returned to paganism, the bishop replies that prudence is necessary and that such fallen people, if they have truly converted, should be admitted.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual compater, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Receiving the envoys of your royal excellency protected by God, namely Itherius and Magenarius, religious abbots [Col. 0390D], we were questioned about the Saxons who had been Christians and had returned to paganism: what kind of penance the priests should prescribe for them.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Pagi (AD 783, no. 13) assigns this letter to AD 783 because he does not find a mention of the queen; Zacagnus follows him (manuscript no. 165). Both are mistaken, as I have said elsewhere (letter 68, note). The pontiff is concerned only with discipline regarding the apostates and mentions neither the queen, nor the royal offspring, nor any temporal matter. Moreover, another error arises from the fact, which I noted there among the notes: Magenarius, abbot of Saint-Denis, succeeded Fulrad after 16 July 784. Therefore the letter could not have been delivered in the preceding year by Magenarius and his colleague Itherius as royal envoys. It must therefore belong either to this year or the next. I place it immediately after the conversion of the Saxons, since the affinity of the subject recommends that placement. It is also highly credible that, because the conversion was carried out hastily after the example of the duke, some people, either inexperienced or too deeply attached to paganism, immediately returned to error.]

This was long ago decreed by our holy pontifical predecessors: that those who, “coming to their senses and considering their ruin, should prefer to return, are to be admitted under a lengthy satisfaction of penance” [Col. 0391A]; and again, “they are to be cleansed by the satisfaction of penance, which is to be measured not so much by length of time as by compunction of heart.”

[Note: [Col. 0391B] For the civil and ecclesiastical penalties established for such an offense, see the Theodosian Code (book II and following, “On Apostates”), and Gothofredus there; also the Council of Elvira (canons 1 and 21), with Mendoza’s commentary (chapters 16 and 21). Siricius, writing to Himerius about the same people (chapter 3), says: “If at some time they should come to their senses and turn to lamentation, they must perform penance for as long as they live.” The authority used here is that of Innocent I, from letter 2 to Victricius, chapter 8 (according to the Dionysian Collection, chapter 16), though, to speak frankly, it is not entirely appropriate. Innocent is dealing with those who come from the Montanists and Novatians and must not be rebaptized. But it is clear here, as has often been said, that the Holy See used the Cresconian collection; it is even clearer because he does not list the number of the decree but introduces the authority covertly, without naming the pontiff, so that not even Lambecius noticed it. It is evident that this decree does not suit the consultation from the words that precede it: “If by chance,” Innocent says, “some of those who came over to them from us have been rebaptized, if they come to their senses,” and so forth. The consultation concerned pagans who had been baptized and had returned to paganism. It was not permissible to rebaptize baptized pagans who returned [to the Church]. Yet it was extremely difficult to find a decree more suitable before the preceding three centuries. At that time the rigor against such fallen people was so great that reconciliation was scarcely permitted even at the end of life [Col. 0391D], which would have contributed little to the matter at hand, especially in the eighth century, when that earlier rigor had been somewhat relaxed. CENN.]

Therefore, excellent son protected by God, the priests of those regions must surround them with pastoral care and assume episcopal vigilance. They must impose penance according to their judgment, considering the offense both of those who returned to their vomit voluntarily and of those compelled to do so against their will [Col. 0391D]. Then they should pronounce a canonical decision, so that, if those people have truly returned and wish to persevere in the orthodox faith, promising that they will fulfill every episcopal instruction, they may write out a declaration [Col. 0391B] of orthodox faith, according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers, confessing one baptism. After swearing that they will preserve the Christian faith, they should be received into the bosom of the Church of orthodox faith, so that abundant reward may be credited to you in heaven. May heavenly grace preserve your excellency unharmed.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] The second decree is taken from a letter of Leo the Great, letter 79 to Nicetas of Aquileia, chapter 5 (Dionysian Collection, chapter 47). The pontiff is dealing with people compelled by force or fear to repeat baptism. This too appears to be unrelated to the matter proposed, just as the earlier example was; but Adrian had no better material available from the Cresconian collection, which follows the decrees of the Dionysian collection. ID.]

[Note: [Col. 0391D] According to the meaning of both decrees—which, apart from the repetition of baptism, otherwise applies to the matter—he decrees that penance should be imposed on these fallen people at the discretion of the bishops. ID.]

[Note: [Col. 0391D] We learn from the *Diurnus Pontificum* that a declaration, or profession, of the Catholic faith was accustomed to be made and subscribed in his own hand by bishops and even by the Roman pontiff himself; its formulas were still in use in the eighth century. I cannot confidently affirm that the word should be understood in that same sense here; I would rather believe that Adrian is speaking of a declaration nearly like the one that Leo the Great (letter 87, chapter 3) wished Donatus of Salicina to send to Rome: “We wish Donatus,” he says to the bishops of Mauritania, “of Salicina, converted from the Novatians together with his people, to preside over the Lord’s flock in such a way that he remembers to send us a written statement of his faith, by which he both condemns the error of Novatian doctrine and fully confesses Catholic truth.” He required the same from Maximus. It may also be an instruction or admonition given to envoys by Hormisdas (in Baronius, AD 515, no. 24). For other uncertain meanings of this word, see Cangius, *Glossary*. I confess that I do not know the formula which the pontiff says rests upon the ancient tradition of the Fathers. ID.]

## LXXXVII. 467. Another Letter of the Same Pope, Addressed to Lord King Charles

It contains thanksgiving for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the honor of the priestly pallium granted to Bishop Ermenbertus.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 2): “In the second [letter] he gives thanks to the king for the exaltation of the holy Church of God; he grants Bishop Ermembertus, as Charles had requested, the use of the pallium [and asserts the invocation of the saints and the primacy of the Roman Church].” ID.]

(AD 786, Codex Carolinus LXXXVII, chronicle 86.)

### Argument

He carefully examined Hermenbertus, sent by Charles to receive the pallium from the apostolic see, since he was bishop of the metropolitan church of Bourges, to determine whether he was subject to any archbishop and to prevent anything contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. He sends him back adorned with that sacred garment, while imploring royal assistance so that he may peacefully exercise metropolitan dignity.

[Col. 0392B] To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual compater, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] Summary 2, Baronius and Centuriator. GRETS.]

The most reverend and holy man, Bishop Ermenbertus, sent by your royal power [Col. 0392C] and presented to our apostolic sight, brought us the highly discerning and honorable royal communication of your lofty excellence. We received it with immense affection and gave thanks to the King of kings, in whose power are all the kingdoms of the world, who frequently makes us joyful through the renowned health of your person, because through the kingdoms of this world he permits us to seek and inherit the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0393C] Lamb reads: “on account of the kingdom of this world, the heavenly kingdom”], triumphing over the savagery of our adversaries through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0393A].

[Note: [Col. 0392C] Herminarius, bishop of the see of Bourges, as I said above (letter 70, otherwise 96, note), attended the Lateran Council in AD 769 and died in AD 774. Deodatus succeeded him until AD 783, followed by Hermenbertus, according to the brothers Sammarthani; I rely on their authority in assigning a date to this letter, so that it may no longer wander at an uncertain time. It is worth observing that in AD 743 Saint Boniface of Mainz, at a synod held among the Franks, issued, among other decrees, the provision that metropolitans should seek pallia from that see—the see of Saint Peter—as he himself testifies in a letter (Boniface Codex 105) to Saint Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury. Nevertheless, twenty-six years later, a single archbishop, Wilcharius of Sens, attended the aforesaid Lateran council adorned with the sacred pallium, an unmistakable witness of his restored metropolitan church; all the others, at least six metropolitans, including the bishop of Bourges, attended merely as bishops. Indeed, the same bishop of Bourges came to Rome forty-three years later, as you see, to obtain the restoration of his metropolitan church’s former honor. CENN.]

[Note: [Col. 0393C] Thus above (letter 84, otherwise 91) he says that Charles triumphed over the Saxons through Peter’s assistance. This seems to be the reference here, unless perhaps the subject is the Britons, subdued in this year, as the Frankish and Fuldan annals relate. ID.]

We found, moreover, in these royal communications of yours that you had asked us to grant the aforesaid Bishop Ermenbert the pallium, adorned with sacerdotal insignia, by apostolic authority, because there appears to be a metropolitan city in Aquitania called Bourges, where the aforesaid venerable man is now recognized as presiding and appears devotedly to exercise pastoral care. Accordingly, since we did not know whether he had already been canonically ordained in those provincial regions by our predecessors or by us, we took care to investigate the matter more thoroughly, lest any opportunity for usurpation be granted to priests in another’s jurisdiction. The aforesaid most holy man confessed to us that he appeared to be subject to the jurisdiction of no archbishop.

> **Note:** Here we have the richest testimony to the discipline established in the synod under the presidency of Saint Boniface, in the Frankish monarchy—or rather throughout the whole West—for the same discipline flourished in England, Africa, and almost all Spain, then groaning under the yoke of the Saracens. It also shows that the metropolitan see of Bourges had by this year not yet been restored, since the pontiff takes great care not to become an invader of another’s jurisdiction. — **ID.**

Therefore, out of the profound affection of our heart for your great royal dignity, we have granted to the aforesaid Ermenbert, constituted archbishop in the metropolitan city called Bourges by our apostolic and most sacred see and authority, the use and enjoyment of the pallium, as had long been customary, while he lives under the jurisdiction of the Church of blessed memory [something appears to be missing here], so that we ask that, through your exalted royal assistance, he may be able to administer the ministry entrusted to him worthily and canonically, receiving priestly governance with affection [Lamb., Gent.: “effect”]. Thus, while the people entrusted to him remain undisturbed and untouched by plotters, and are likewise protected by your royal majesty, may you deserve to receive a worthy recompense from blessed Peter the apostle, the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. May God, the Redeemer of all, cause you, together with your most excellent spiritual daughter, the lady queen, and your exalted offspring, to enjoy more fully the governance of an increasingly exalted kingdom through a long and prosperous old age, and likewise grant you possession of eternal life. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

> **Note:** For further discussion, see Thomassin, I, I, chapter 33, no. 12, and chapter 35, no. 1. For when Aquitania was erected into a kingdom, Bourges obtained primacy over the metropolitan sees of Bordeaux and Auch; this produced no small number of disputes, and that primacy eventually collapsed. That matter does not concern us here. What must be observed and kept in mind is only the discipline concerning the sacred pallium requested from the Apostolic See, in accordance with the synodal decree of the year 743. In the following century Hincmar of Rheims dared to reverse it, and he found not a few highly learned modern followers—or rather restorers of his audacity. — **CENN.**

### XXXVIII. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord King Charles

In this letter there is discussion of larger beams for restoring the churches, which Lord King Charles had ordered him to receive; he says that the agents themselves, through negligence, had done nothing in the matter as they had been instructed by the said king; and he also writes about tin for reroofing the church of Saint Peter.

> **Note:** Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 15) reads: “In the fifteenth [letter] he reminds [asks] Charles to send quickly the larger beams which he had promised for the restoration of the churches, and tin for roofing the church of blessed Peter. He also writes about the disputes between the Neapolitans and the Amalfitans.” — **ID.**

*(A.D. 786; Codex Carolinus LXVI, chronicle 87.)*

**Summary.** Beams repeatedly requested from him for restoring the churches of the City had still not been delivered. He asks that a royal envoy come who will both arrange for the beams to be handed over and order the counts of Italy to provide one hundred pounds of tin each; Charles had promised one thousand pounds, and Itherius an equal amount. Arichis, duke of Benevento, took up arms against the Amalfitans, who belonged to the Neapolitans; with the aid of the Neapolitans, they killed many men and led away many of their leading nobles as captives.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-parent, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

We have often sent requests to your royal power, protected by God, asking you, for the reward of your soul, to order larger beams to be sent through your royal protection for the restoration of the churches of God. We have received no result from those to whom the order was given. Consequently, the churches in which larger beams are necessary to us have partly collapsed, and we see others also collapsing; and while we await those beams, we do not know what to do, and because of this we remain in great sorrow.

> **Note:** It is established that Adrian requested larger beams only for the basilica of Saint Peter (letter 66, otherwise 61), in the year 780, before Charles came to Rome again and became his spiritual co-parent. In this letter, however, which was undoubtedly written after Hildegard’s death and Charles’s new marriage to Fastrada—that is, after 783—and before Charles’s third arrival in 787, he says that he had requested them for other churches as well. Since no such petitionary letters survive in the codex, one may infer that Charles refrained from having the so-called familiar letters reviewed unless something of importance had been inserted into them. For this reason he did not omit the celebrated letter 66 or this one, since they contain some information especially concerning the disturbances involving the Neapolitans. In the latest edition of Duchesne, I see that the letter under consideration is assigned to this year, and I do not think it should be moved from it, as what follows will soon make clear. — **CENN.**

Therefore, earnestly petitioning your most triumphant Excellency, we ask that no further delay occur, but that through your royal arrangement, protected by God, you order these larger beams to be sent to us more quickly. In no way should they dare to commit any negligence, for we are fully confident that however many churches of God have been restored from these beams, and are being restored, are restored for the everlasting memorial of you, of your lady queen, and of your most noble offspring. Therefore we ask that you order your own suitable envoy to be sent, who must compel those agents who have dared to be negligent regarding the aforementioned beams, so that he himself may strive, through your arrangement, to deliver them to us, and so that you may thereby receive the great reward, as we have said.

Moreover, we make this known to your royal power: Arichis, duke of Benevento, seeking justice from his own men, led an army against the Amalfitans of the duchy of Naples. Having surrounded them on every side, he burned all their possessions and their dwellings situated outside the walls. When they heard this, the Neapolitans sent a large number of men to their aid; they defeated them and killed a great multitude of the Beneventan duchy. As a result, they now hold many others captive, including several leading nobles. We have hastened to report to you in fuller detail what has occurred in these regions.

> **Note:** The annalist of Fulda connects Charles’s victory over the Bretons, the conspiracy discovered against him, his journey to Italy, and the armed attack upon the duchy of Benevento with this year. But, in mentioning the eclipse of the sun on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, he shows that events which occurred in the following year have been assigned to this one. For Calvisius, after consulting even the Prutenic tables, teaches us that the eclipse belonged to the following year, the eighth year of Irene and Constantine. The Frankish Annals more correctly postpone Charles’s journey until the end of the year, so that he celebrated Christmas at Florence and then came to Rome at the beginning of the following year. The annalist of Metz, cited by Pagius (A.D. 786, no. 5), uses almost the same words. Accordingly, what Adrian relates about the Beneventans against the Neapolitans does not conflict with the journey Charles was planning, and perhaps had already undertaken, when he received this letter. In the Neapolitan Chronicle (in Pratilli, volume III, p. 33), this history is narrated at considerable length, and the date of this letter is established. At the end of its account we read how, while Caesarius, son of Stephen the bishop and duke, was directing affairs, the Beneventans were defeated; and after Caesarius—using the words of the chronicle—“had gained the joy of victory and saw that Aragisus, fleeing, had escaped his hands, he forbade his men to pursue farther.” This occurred in the year 786. — **CENN.**

We also believe that your pre-eminent dignity, promoted by God, will remember the following: for love of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and for the restoration of that same Church, your Excellency promised to send us one thousand pounds of tin for the roof of his basilica. Likewise your most faithful Itherius promised, through your distinguished arrangement, to send another thousand pounds. Therefore, petitioning your royal Excellency, we ask that you order this tin to be sent to us through your good arrangement, because the church of your patron, blessed Peter, suffered greatly from water during the spring, and we have nothing with which to restore the roof of his basilica.

We earnestly ask that you order the aforesaid tin to be sent through your counts who are acting in Italy, one hundred pounds through each count, so that you may deserve to receive a worthy recompense for this from that same apostle of God.

> **Note:** From this passage we learn something about the administration of the Italian kingdom during the minority of King Pippin. On this occasion twenty counts are mentioned, who governed an equal number of cities. Above (letter 81, otherwise 67, note), we saw Arvinus called at one time duke and at another count; elsewhere, dukes are placed in charge of the cities of Clusium and Florence. Whether both titles, duke and count, were used indiscriminately, as in the case of Arvinus, or whether these offices were assigned to cities without distinction at that time, is uncertain. Adrian calls each man both a count and an agent. See above (letter 81, otherwise 67, note). — **ID.**

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

### LXXXIX. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord King Charles

This letter contains expressions of thanks and blessings for the cross which he had sent him, and concerns the territory of Populonia or Roselle, asking that Lord King Charles send suitable envoys who would hand over to him these cities, together with their suburbs, in their entirety.

> **Note:** Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 8) reads: “In the eighth [letter] he gives thanks for the cross sent and writes that he always prays for Charles and for his father of blessed memory. He asks that he send envoys who will restore to the Roman Church the territories of Populonia and Roselle, together with the portions of the duchy of Benevento.” — **ID.**

*(A.D. 787; Codex Carolinus LXXXI, chronicle 88.)*

**Summary.** He commends to Charles, who had commended himself to his prayers, that he continually does this not only for him but also for his parents and his wife Hildegard, who had died. He gives thanks for the cross sent and prays that Charles send envoys who will vindicate for the holy see, in their entirety, the Populonian and Rosellian territories not yet delivered. At the same time he asks that the cities of the duchy of Benevento be handed over intact, in accordance with the donation recently made by Charles.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-parent, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

> **Note:** At the beginning of the year 787, Charles entered the duchy of Benevento with his army and halted at Capua, while the archbishop, out of fear, withdrew to Salerno. He brought the whole duchy back under his authority by methods of peace rather than war. He took with him Grimoald, son of Arichis, and twelve others as hostages and pledges of the settlement. He celebrated Easter at Rome, which fell on 8 April, and then returned to Francia; the matter of Tassilo, through the intervention of the pontiff, was attempted rather than settled, and he subsequently led an army into Bavaria and brought Tassilo into submission. These events are narrated at length in the Frankish Annals. See also Baronius, from Regino (A.D. 787, no. 64), and Pagius, from the Annals of Metz (same year, no. 6). On this occasion Charles evidently donated Capua and the other cities of Campania, or of the duchy of Benevento, to the holy see, as this letter makes clear. Pagius incorrectly postpones the donation of Tuscany to this period; numerous arguments demonstrate that it was made in 774, when Charles first came to Rome. — **CENN.**

We received the most excellent, most brilliant, honey-sweet verses of your exalted royal wisdom, dedicated to God. When we opened them and read them one by one, we embraced their strength with exceedingly great love. Your royal power may undoubtedly believe that everything you have made known to us through them will be carried out by us in every respect. For I call upon God, whom I serve in my spirit, as witness that without interruption, day and night, I always remember you in my prayers, entreating both your royal victory in triumphs and your perpetual stability, and also remembering your parents of holy memory, together with your wife, the lady Queen Hiltibranda [Grets., Hildegard], our daughter and spiritual co-mother. Indeed, their memory shall not be abandoned forever.

> **Note:** The pious king’s request was nothing other than prayers, as the pontiff testifies, for he says that he continually prays also for the deceased Pippin and Hildegard. Therefore it is not correct to suppose, as in the latest edition of Duchesne, that the letter was written around the year 782. Muratori more correctly assigns it to the year 788, when several letters were composed, as I shall soon show. I believe that this letter was written toward the end of 787, for it is not probable that during the eight months after Charles’s departure from Rome a single letter—the one mentioned here—was written, especially since this is a reply to Carolingian verses perhaps delivered shortly after the letter in which they are mentioned. — **ID.**

When we placed the cross which you sent us in our holy church, your memory will remain in it forever.

> **Note:** In Anastasius, in the Life of Leo III (section 378), we read: “In the basilica of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which is called the Constantinian basilica, he offered a cross with hyacinth gems, which the life-giving pontiff ordered to precede him in the litany, in accordance with the request of that most pious emperor.” The same author says that Leo IV later restored this cross after it had been stolen (section 502) and returned it to its former use. He mentions no other cross offered by Charles. It is therefore clear that the church of Saint Peter had been endowed with a similar gift long before this. Charles particularly honored that church above all others, as Einhard testifies (chapter 27) in these words: “Above all the other sacred and venerable places at Rome, he honored the church of blessed Peter the apostle, in whose treasuries he amassed a great amount of money, both gold and silver, as well as gems.” — **ID.**

As for our well-being, which your royal clemency wishes to hear about, everything concerning us is prosperous, with God’s favor. We also desire to hear with certainty about your royal health and victories, because your health is ours, and this we earnestly request. Just as through our earlier words we petitioned your royal power, so may it deign to carry this out: order your envoys to come again, who must hand over to us the boundaries of Populonia and Roselle, just as they existed from ancient times.

> **Note:** The matter here concerns the restoration of the boundaries in their entirety, not of the cities. See the preliminary discussion, no. 30. Pagius, under the year 787 (no. 7 and following), postpones the donation of Tuscany and considers its possession to have begun immediately. But the Castle of Felicitas, which belonged to the holy see before Charles’s second journey to Italy, contradicts this view. See above (letter 55, otherwise 60, note). The donation of Tuscany was, in my opinion, made in 774, when Charles first came to Rome. Accordingly, the pontiff wishes the boundaries of Roselle and Populonia to be handed over to him as they had existed from ancient times. But let us suppose otherwise: if these two cities, far removed from ecclesiastical territory on the coastal side of Siena—for Grosseto is said to have arisen from the ruins of Roselle, while Massa, neighboring destroyed Populonia, received its episcopal dignity—were donated by Charles to the holy see in 787, should the same be said of the other Tuscan cities? The following passages will show that this is not so. — **ID.**

For they have not handed over part of those boundaries to us. But we ask that the donation of your royal offering remain undisturbed in its entirety. In particular, may you deign to send suitable envoys to the territories of the duchy of Benevento, who will be able, according to your donation, to hand over to us those cities in their entirety.

> **Note:** After Arichis had been brought into submission and hostages had been accepted as pledges of subjection, Charles donated six Campanian cities to the holy see: Capua, Teano, Arpino, Aquino, Arce, and Sora. The pontiff wishes to take possession of them through royal envoys. We have always seen this done whenever a new donation was made. — **ID.**

Thus you may deserve to receive from blessed Peter the apostle, the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the greatest recompense, together with our spiritual daughter, the lady queen, and your most excellent offspring.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

### XC. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord Charles

This letter concerns the arrival of Adalgis in the regions of Calabria; it asks that he not appoint Grimoald as duke in Benevento; and it discusses the cities of Benevento, Roselle, and Populonia.

> **Note:** Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 42) reads: “In the forty-second [letter] he indicates that Adalgis, son of Desiderius, has arrived in the regions of Calabria. He asks Charles to wage war against him and compel the Beneventans, together with the others, to obey. He also asks that he not appoint Grimoald as duke of Benevento, and that he return Benevento, Roselle, Populonia, and the other places to blessed Peter.” — **ID.**

*(A.D. 788; Codex Carolinus XC, chronicle 89.)*

**Summary.** When the royal envoys Roro and Betto came to inquire whether Athalgis, son of Desiderius, had entered Italy, he immediately informed Charles through Count Arvinus of what he had recently learned: namely, that Athalgis was staying in Calabria near the Beneventan frontier. He says that this had been reported to him from Gaeta and from the Pentapolis, and he appends letters received from both places. He considers it inexpedient for Grimoald to succeed his father; if the Beneventans do not keep their promises, they must be compelled by troops. Unless Charles sends an army from the Kalends of May until September, Athalgis may perhaps plot something against Charles and the holy see with the Greeks. As soon as Grimoald arrives in the duchy of Benevento, his mother Adelberga will depart with her daughters, under the pretext of prayer, for Gargano and then Tarentum, where she kept her treasures. He asks Charles to prevent his envoys from returning before they have delivered intact the cities of Campania and likewise the intact boundaries of Populonia and Roselle. Just as the holy see possessed Suana and the other Tuscan cities with their territories, so it was fair that it should possess the Campanian cities intact, together with their territories.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-parent, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope.

Your most faithful envoys, namely the chaplain Roro and Betto, came to us and, after announcing your desired royal well-being, asked us about the most wicked Athalgis, son of Desiderius, the tyrant king: whether it was true that, with God opposed to him, he had come into the regions of Italy. We did not fail recently to report to you, through your faithful envoy Count Arvinus, what we had heard about Athalgis. In consideration of your royal victory, with God as our guide, we neglect nothing in any respect, informing your radiant Excellency so that, with the Lord’s help and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, accompanying you, your distinguished royal prudence may wisely secure both your safety and ours.

For this is what was reported to us in truth concerning the aforementioned most wicked Athalgis: with God opposed to him, he is staying with the emperor’s envoys in the regions of Calabria, near the boundary of the duchy of Benevento. Bishop Campulus of the city of Gaeta informed us of this in his letter. Likewise, from the Pentapolis they informed us in writing about the arrogance of that same Athalgis. Because of our great love for you, we have sent below the letters addressed to us, both from Gaeta and from the Pentapolis. Indeed, we know that this wicked and faithless Adalgis came into these regions for no other reason than to oppose you and us. Therefore your exalted royal Excellency must strive to send firm sacred [words, perhaps “instructions”] to the Beneventan regions [the phrase appears redundant], so that through your royal assistance we may both remain undisturbed on every side.

> **Note:** Charles learned of Adalgis’s arrival in Italy from no other source than the letter of the bishop of Gaeta and the letters of the people of the Pentapolis, which Adrian sent through Count Arvinus, as can be gathered from this account. It is also inferred from what follows that through the same Arvinus he announced to Charles the death of Arichis. Cointius and Pagius (A.D. 787, no. 14) place the death of Arichis on 26 August of that year. But Baronius had already done so, presenting an epitaph (A.D. 787, no. 65), to which these words are appended: “He lived fifty-three years; he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the year 787 from the Lord’s incarnation; and by the lady Adelperga, princess, he fathered Romoald and Grimoald, Egisisus, Theorald, and Adeleisa.” This epitaph has most recently been published as the work of Paul the Deacon among the Tombs of the Lombard Princes by the distinguished Pratilli (volume III, p. 305), who restored the recently cited words to Camillo Peregrinio, against Pagius, who attributed them to Paul the Deacon. The letter mentioned in the preceding passage seems to have been none other than the one said to have been given to Count Arvinus with the messages concerning the prince’s death and Adalgis’s arrival, together with the aforementioned letters from the bishop of Gaeta and from the Pentapolis. — **CENN.**

But when we consider all these matters, dearest and most beloved, most exalted son protected by God, it seems fitting to us that, whether those Beneventans have fulfilled your will, it is in no way expedient to send Grimoald, son of Arichis, to Benevento.

> **Note:** Romoald, the firstborn, had died before his father in the same year, as Pagius notes in the passage cited. Therefore the succession belonged to Grimoald, who was a hostage at Charles’s court. But the pontiff had reasons for disapproving this succession. He had expressed them in the letter given to Arvinus, as he himself testifies below (letter 92, otherwise 86), and he now states them again—or rather recalls them to mind. — **ID.**

Nevertheless, just as the most prudent wisdom has been granted to you by our omnipotent God, so may you order that this matter be carefully considered and suitably arranged, so that whatever is expedient for you and for us may safely reach completion, and so that we may not together fall into some difficulty. But if the often-mentioned Beneventans have not fulfilled your royal will, as they promised you, then immediately strive to send an army there in such a way that it may advance for the benefit of our holy Church and of your royal Excellency. Let those regions be so arranged that the enemy finds no opportunity to cause harm, while your royal victory in triumphs always rejoices in the Lord.

> **Note:** He wants the Beneventans to be entirely under Charles’s power, and therefore uses this dilemma: either the Beneventans remain faithful to the Frankish king, in which case it is inexpedient to appoint Grimoald as their duke; or they depart from their promises, in which case they must be kept in their duty by force and arms. This is certainly very wise advice, though he nevertheless leaves the matter to Charles’s decision. — **ID.**

Indeed, after deliberating and considering these matters together with your faithful envoys, we have concluded that, if the Beneventans are unwilling to fulfill your royal will by the Kalends of May, your very strong army should be found prepared at the frontier to attack those Beneventans. Yet, after advancing together, we shall not dare to establish ourselves there because of the illnesses of the summer season. Again, if an army does not come against them from the Kalends of May through the month of September, it seems doubtful to us that perhaps, with God opposed to him, the aforesaid most wicked Adalgis may attempt, through the intrigues of the Greeks, to cause some disturbance for us and for you. The aforementioned Greek envoys are known to be with him, while others appear to be staying in Naples. Considering these matters, we have entrusted them to your strong royal judgment, protected by God, so that you may deign to arrange whatever pleases you as quickly as possible and inform us, through your royal communications, of the security and salvation of both you and us.

> **Note:** He insists that action is needed promptly and limits the preparation and military operation to five months at most. And rightly so: Adalgis, the brother of Adelberga, was living near the borders of Calabria, supported by the Greeks, and awaiting the succession of his sister’s son Grimoald in the duchy of Benevento, so that with joined forces he might invade the territory of the holy see and from there the Italian kingdom. — **ID.**

Therefore, earnestly petitioning your most exalted Excellency, we ask you not to order anyone to be trusted more than us in the matter of Grimoald, son of Arichis. For know with certainty that if you send Grimoald to Benevento, you cannot possess Italy without disturbance. Bishop Leo told us privately that Adelberga, widow of Arichis, has the following plan: once her son Grimoald has entered the Beneventan territories, she intends by stratagem to take her two daughters with her, proceed as though for the sake of prayer to Saint Michael on Gargano, and then go to Tarentum, where she has her treasures hidden, since the distance from Saint Michael to Tarentum is only eighty miles.

> **Note:** The journey undertaken by Adelberga toward the eastern borders of the duchy of Benevento, where her brother Adalgis had also landed, immediately after Grimoald had obtained his father’s duchy, demonstrates that the pontiff’s suspicion was not unfounded. — **CENN.**

But your dignity, promoted by God, should in no way suppose that we have made these disclosures out of eagerness to acquire those cities which you donated to blessed Peter the apostle and to us. We have not neglected to disclose to your royal ears what we have heard and been able to learn for the sake of the great security of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and for the victory and exaltation of your exalted royal power.
