Your royal Excellency should prudently arrange all these matters as it pleases you and seems appropriate.

Therefore, earnestly petitioning your most merciful royal goodwill, we ask, for love of your patron blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and because of our clear and special spiritual fatherly affection for you in Christ, that you deign to send your envoys instructions through honorable royal letters, so that they do not dare return to you in any way until they have been able to hand over to us in their entirety the cities in the Beneventan regions, just as through your sacred donation you granted them to blessed Peter the apostle and to us, and until they have striven to render us in full the legal possessions of Populonia and Roselle.

> **Note:** As in the preceding passage, the matter here concerns the delivery of the boundaries of Roselle and Populonia, together with the six Campanian cities mentioned above. Therefore, what I said there (column 398, note d) is not improbable: both coastal cities may have been granted to the holy see separately from the other Tuscan cities. This will become clearer from what follows. — **ID.**

For there are some of your envoys who are attempting to disregard and defile your sacred donation. But just as in the regions of Tuscany you offered and donated to blessed Peter the cities of Suana, Tuscania, Viterbo, and Bagno del Re, together with their boundaries and territories,

> **Note:** Here the Tuscan cities are listed beginning with Suana, which lies farther west than the others. Accordingly, the “other cities” must be understood as the Old City and the Castle of Felicitas, not Roselle and Populonia, which, being farther west than Suana, ought to have been listed first. On the other hand, neither of these two cities is mentioned when the delivery of the Campanian cities is discussed below using the Tuscan example. Therefore, whatever view one may hold concerning the date of the donation of Roselle and Populonia, it is necessary to conclude that the other Tuscan cities were donated, together with the Castle of Felicitas, at Charles’s first arrival in 774, contrary to the opinion of Pagius and more recent writers. — **ID.**

so now you should immediately cause the cities in the Beneventan regions to be handed over to us. Once your envoys have received your firm royal communications, let them be able to deliver them to us in their entirety without any intervening delay. Thus no one may be able to extinguish your unblemished sacrifice. By acquiring this especially profitable reward, may you deserve, together with our spiritual daughter, the lady queen, and your most noble offspring, to reign without end in the heavenly citadels.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.

### XCI. The same pope’s letter, addressed to Lord King Charles

This letter concerns the Greek envoys, together with the *dioeceta*—that is, the administrator of Sicily—who, after the return from Benevento of Atto the deacon, the lord king’s envoy, reached an agreement with the widow of Duke Arichis about how they might secretly withdraw the duchy of Benevento from the power of the aforementioned king.

> **Note:** *Dioeceta*, διοικητής, means “administrator.” — **GRETS.**

> **Note:** Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 23) reads: “In the twenty-third [letter] he indicates what advice he gave to his envoys. He also reports concerning the Greek envoys with the administrator of Sicily, who had conferred with the widow of Duke Arichis about how they might take [or by what means they might take] the duchy of Benevento from King Charles. He therefore asks Charles to arrange everything in such a way as to secure his own safety and that of the Roman Church.” — **CENN.**

*(A.D. 788; Codex Carolinus XCII, chronicle 90.)*

**Summary.** The royal envoys Atto the deacon and Goteramnus the doorkeeper arrived, and afterward Abbot Maginarius and Joseph the deacon announced the royal will to the pontiff, namely that everything should be done according to his counsel. The pontiff therefore thought that they should never separate from one another. He sent the first two ahead toward the duchy of Benevento, instructing them to wait at the town of Valva for the others, who remained in Rome, and for Liuthericus, the fifth envoy. Forgetting the instruction, they proceeded to Benevento without waiting for their companions and from there went on to Salerno to Adelberga, the widow. The remaining three went to Benevento and there heard that plans were being conducted at Salerno against Charles and the holy see. Soon Goteramnus arrived, and together with him they fled to Valva, in the territory of the duchy of Spoleto, where they awaited the royal orders. Atto, overcome by fear, took refuge at the altar in a church at Salerno. The Beneventans pretended to calm him and gave him letters to Charles filled with assurances of loyalty. The pontiff reports all this to Charles.

He then adds that certain Capuans, recently subjected to the holy see, came to Rome and reported that after Atto’s departure the Greek envoys, together with the administrator of Sicily, went to Adelberga at Salerno on 20 January. From there they were escorted to Naples and received with great honor, where they conferred with Bishop Stephen and the Neapolitans. The Beneventans appeared likely to revolt in the summer. He asks Charles to forestall them, lest they defect together and invade the cities donated to the holy see.

Domino Adrian, pope, to our most excellent son and spiritual co-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] Summary 23, Baronius and Centuriators, GRETSER.]

[Note: This letter differs little from the preceding one; for it was given in the spring, whereas the preceding appears to have been written in midwinter. Pagi praises Cointius’s diligence (year 788, no. 1 ff.), and follows his careful numbering; the latest edition of Duchesne does the same. Muratori confuses their order and, adopting the absurdity of the anonymous Salernitan, [Col. 0403B] throws the history into confusion. Cointius makes one mistake, followed by everyone else: they judged that Letter 73 of the Codex Carolinus belonged here as the sixtieth letter, understanding Roman Campania rather than Beneventan Campania. See it above, together with its notes. Once that letter has been removed, I retain the order of the present letter and the following two, an order which, as will soon be clear, cannot safely be altered. CENN.]

Your royal Excellency, promoted by God, remembers how you sent to us 482 your most faithful envoys, namely Atto, the religious deacon, and Goteramnus, the magnificent doorkeeper; and after them there came to us Maginarius, the religious abbot, and Joseph, the religious deacon, who faithfully reported to us what your most upright royal power had instructed them to accomplish, according to our apostolic counsel, in the Beneventan territories.

While the four aforesaid envoys were residing in our presence—Maginarius, the religious abbot; Atto and Joseph, the religious deacons; and Goteramnus, the magnificent doorkeeper—Liuthericus had not yet joined our apostolic presence. He had been sent to us with the aforesaid Maginarius and Joseph. We therefore gave them this counsel: that none of them should in any way separate from another, but that Atto and Goteramnus, going ahead, should await in the town of Valva both Maginarius and Joseph and Liuthericus, whom his companions were awaiting while they remained with us.

[Note: [Col. 0403C] These envoys must have arrived in Rome long beforehand. This is clearly shown both by Adrian’s manner of speaking, when he recalls the mission to Charles, and by the context of the letter. For before 20 January Atto, the last of all the envoys, had departed from Salerno; and the envoys of the Greeks had entered that city, having awaited his departure at Acropolis, a town of Lucania about thirty miles distant, so that it must be regarded as certain that Atto had departed at least the preceding day. Consequently, all the events which the letter reports cannot be compressed into nineteen days, although it is uncertain how much time must be transferred here from the preceding year. This seems less doubtful: these envoys arrived before Roro and Betto, and in the preceding letter Adrian asked that they not return to Francia before possession of the Campanian cities had been delivered to them. He did not know what adversity had befallen them and later pursues the matter in this letter. Cointius and Pagi, wishing to escape the difficulty, assigned the preceding letter to the earlier year; but they entirely failed to notice that the months of May and September mentioned there establish that letter as belonging to this year, although it was written at its beginning, before the dangers and flight of the envoys who had advanced into the Beneventan duchy reached the pope’s ears. Therefore both letters must be assigned to this year: the former to January, and this one to March, perhaps even April. ID.]

But the men who went ahead—Atto and 483 Goteramnus—did not at all follow our counsels. Completely abandoning Maginarius, Joseph, and Liuthericus, they went separately to Benevento. Maginarius, Joseph, and Liuthericus, following behind them to Benevento, were then unable to find Atto and Goteramnus at all, because they had gone on to Salerno to Adelberga, the widow of Duke Arichis.

There, while Maginarius and his companions heard from your faithful men—as they themselves reported to us—that both the widow of the aforesaid Duke Arichis and the other Beneventans continued to act treacherously, devising evil and hostile measures against your royal Excellency and our apostolate, Maginarius, Joseph, and Liuthericus took flight. Together with Goteramnus, who had come from Salerno to speak with them, they entered the territory of the duchy of Spoleto, at the aforesaid town of Valva, and remain there awaiting your royal [triumphal disposition; reading uncertain].

[Note: [Col. 0403D] Since these men were envoys, not military commanders, it is not easy to understand the pope’s great anxiety that they should not be separated from one another. That anxiety evidently depended upon secret conversations held between them and the pope before they departed from Rome. Nevertheless, the duchy, vacant of a duke; Adelberga, the widow, directing all its plans and affairs; Adalgisus, her brother, supported by the Greeks within the duchy’s borders; and the attempted succession of Adelberga’s son Grimoaldus were not unknown to the pope, since he had reported them to Charles through Arvinus and had communicated his well-founded fear to him. Whoever therefore thinks that these grave affairs were the reason for that insistence upon unity will, in my judgment, not be far from the truth. ID.]

As for Atto, when he heard, as is reported, he fled inside the church of Salerno out of fear and took hold of the altar of that church. The Beneventans, however, apparently offering persuasion and pretending to calm him, deceitfully dispatched your cleric, commending themselves as faithful in every respect.

[Note: [Col. 0404C] In this sufficiently clear account, the pope appears to place the blame upon the envoys’ journey to Salerno, contrary to his counsels. In the following letter, however, the Beneventans’ treachery will become apparent, and the envoys’ agreement would have done nothing to help. ID.]

[Col. 0404B] Moreover, because of the exceedingly tender love which we bear toward your unconquered kingdom, we cannot in any way fail to explain the whole matter more clearly to you. Men came to us from Capua, which you offered to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the redemption of your 484 soul and for perpetual remembrance, together with the other cities—namely, the priest Gregory, Saductus, Pergulfus, Audemundus, Haimo, Landemarus, Warnefridus, Sigulfus, Audualdus, and Corbulus—and reported to us that, when the deacon Atto had returned to your Excellency, the envoys of the Greeks immediately arrived: two imperial sword-bearers, together with the *diucitin* [Gretser: *dioecete*], who is called in Latin the “administrator of Sicily.”

They descended at Acropolis in Lucania and travelled by land to Salerno, to Adelberga, the widow of Duke Arichis. They arrived on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January]. There they held discussions with the Beneventans for three days. After the third day, the Beneventans escorted them to Naples. The Neapolitans, receiving them with great service, banners, and images, entered Naples with them; and up to the present they continue to deliberate with those Neapolitans and with Stephen, bishop of that Neapolitan church.

[Note: [Col. 0404C] In Mabillon (Supplement to the Diplomata, p. 70), there is a fragment of Adrian’s letter, preserved on parchment from the authentic Dionysian collection, in which he asks the advice of some magnate—whether of his own dominion or of the Frankish dominion is uncertain—whether he ought to receive the oath of fidelity from certain Capuans separately from the others. Since this fragment has a close affinity with the present letter, I have thought it useful to insert it here:

“... we bring to the attention of your most prudent ... or glory, because ... there were certain citizens of Capua, namely the priest Gregory, Saductus, Haimo, Au... Erulphus, Landemarus, Waldifridus, Andulphus, and Corbulus, from ... and our spiritual co-father, the illustrious Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards ... and patrician of the Romans ... to blessed Peter the apostle, his protector, and ... together with his most excellent consort, the queen ... and their most noble offspring, and all ... most noble Franks, asking that blessed Peter and we should have them subject to us, just as they have been recognized through the donation of the most excellent lord king ... We ask your advice whether we ought to receive them into the service of blessed Peter the apostle ... for it is better for us ... if we receive them, so that there may be dissension among them and they may be found divided ... the part, and the interest of blessed Peter the apostle and of our most excellent son the lord king make it advantageous that, when they have been divided, they may more easily ... without our and your favor. But this also was proposed to us ... that we ought to send our envoy together with a note to Adelberga, the widow of Arichis ... so that, together with all the Beneventans, they might not dare ... the Beneventans or other citizens from those regions ... or inflict any malice upon them ... We have wished to favor this counsel. Therefore we ask your royal ... prudence that you give us counsel both concerning receiving them and concerning sending our envoy with our note to the aforesaid ... Adelberga or to Benevento; and that you hasten to inform us by your letters how appropriate and correct measures may proceed from this ... with blessed Peter the apostle, your protector, interceding, the divine majesty ... for many ...” CENN.]

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Atto, the royal envoy, had undertaken the journey to Francia with the king in order to negotiate concerning Grimoaldus’s succession; for an upright man does not easily recognize men of doubtful loyalty. The pope, however, possessed greater prudence and therefore opposed Grimoaldus’s succession so vehemently. The Capuans’ report, which is fuller and clearer in the following letter, is both an abundant testimony to the pope’s foresight and a complete overthrow of Muratori’s method. Against the sequence of events, Muratori arbitrarily distorted Adrian’s letters (year 788), preferring the fabrications of the anonymous Salernitan to their authority and composing a history entirely different from the truth, so as to portray Adrian as deceived even by Charles himself. Moreover, the Chronicon Neapolitanum (in Pratilli, vol. III, p. 34) confirms the reliability of this letter and supplies the names of the imperial envoys: “Iscamus and Leo, ambassadors of the lord emperor, came to Naples and were received with great honor and joy.” ID.]

485 But your most upright royal Excellency, promoted by God and inspired by God, ought to act in such a way as to secure your own safety and ours in every respect, and to pay no attention to the empty tales of any man. Let no one be able to persuade you by gifts; let your only endeavor be for the exaltation of your spiritual mother, our holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, and for the welfare of your royal Excellency and of us.

For, as we suppose, the Beneventans will allow this springtime to pass, so that in summer, with God opposed to them, they may incur the guilt of perjury against you.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] He foretells that after the spring, when the letter was given, the Beneventans would burst into open revolt and become troublesome to the Church and to Charles’s territories unless King Charles forestalled them. For the secret discussions held over three days with the Greek envoys at Salerno, and their escorting of those envoys to Naples by the Beneventans, where secret plans were being discussed for so long, could portend nothing else. ID.]

Your royal power should therefore strive to go before them in triumph, so that it may undoubtedly trample their impending insolence beneath its feet and so that your exaltation may be proclaimed throughout the world, both because of your most prudent royal victory and because of the most sacred offering which, in those Beneventan territories, you presented with a pure heart to blessed Peter, your protector, out of your exceeding love and for perpetual remembrance.

[Note: [Col. 0406C] What could be more consistent with justice? He predicts victory for Charles and desires that possession of the six Campanian cities be handed over to the Holy See. He calls this a “most sacred offering,” a phrase offensive to the recent writer who attacks rulers: acquisitions obtained by force and arms, whether justly or unjustly, are regarded by him as full of justice, while donations made to the Roman Church are judged unjust, frivolous, and subject to a thousand objections. ID.]

Thus, when blessed Peter the apostle, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, your protector and defender, has received your sacred offering of donation intact, we may fittingly pour out prayers in his life-giving confession both for you and for our spiritual daughter, our lady the queen, and for your most noble offspring, so that, enjoying the governance of the kingdom in this world for many years, you may deserve to reign without end in the heavenly citadels.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency in safety.

## XCII. Another letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord Charles the King

In it the matter concerns Arichis, duke of Benevento, who [Lamb.: “because”], after King Charles had returned from the city of Capua, sent his envoys to the emperor, contrary to God’s will toward him, asking for aid and the dignity of the patriciate. He desired to invalidate the fidelity which he had promised, and promised that he would adopt the Greeks’ customs both in tonsure and in dress.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 1): “In the first letter he complains about Arichis, duke of Benevento: after King Charles had returned from the city of Capua, Arichis sent envoys to the Constantinopolitan emperor, asking for aid and the dignity of the patriciate, promising similarity with the Greeks both in dress and in tonsure. The priest Gregory of Capua reported these matters to Pope Adrian. Adrian made the Capuans swear to blessed Peter, to himself, and to the emperor [king]. Charles is summoned to aid for the exaltation of the Holy Church.” ID.]

(Year of the Lord 788, Codex Carolinus LXXXIII, chronicle 91.)

[Col. 0406B]

### Argument

When informed by Charles of his victory over the Bavarians, Adrian rejoices. He then proceeds to recount the Beneventan affairs. He says that the Capuans mentioned in the preceding letter had made an oath of fidelity before the confession of Saint Peter. Afterwards, one of them, Gregory, secretly informed him that in the previous year, after Charles’s departure, Arichis, through his envoys, had asked the emperor for the patriciate and the duchy of Naples, and also that he send Athalgisus, his kinsman, with forces.

The emperor sent two sword-bearers to confer the patriciate and sent Athalgisus to Treviso or Ravenna. God destroyed their plans, for when they arrived they found that Arichis was dead.

At that time the Beneventans did not wish to receive the Greeks at Salerno because Atto was there. When he had departed, the Greeks were received, and with Adelberga they held discussions for three days. Nothing, apparently, was to be done until Grimoaldus arrived; the Beneventans had asked Charles through Atto to give Grimoaldus to them as duke. When he arrived, they would accomplish what Arichis had been unable to accomplish. In the meantime, the Greeks were to remain at Naples. From there they had informed the emperor of Arichis’s death and were awaiting instructions concerning what should be done.

The four royal envoys fled to Spoleto because they had discovered a conspiracy of the Neapolitans, Sorrentines, and Amalfitans with the Beneventans for their destruction.

Domino Adrian, pope, to our most excellent son and spiritual co-father, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0407B] Baronius, same place; Summary 1. GRETSER.]

We received your sweet, most pleasing, exalted royal letters with immense affection of heart. On opening and reading them, we learned of your royal well-being and likewise of the prosperous health of our spiritual daughter, your lady the queen, and of your most noble offspring. We offered great thanks to almighty God, who, through the intercessions of blessed Peter the apostle, your protector—for whom we, though unworthy, continually pray—unceasingly grants victories everywhere and arranges everything beneficially around you, both the marches and the frontiers.

We heard with still greater joy about the subjection of the Bavarians. Just as we had foretold and desired, so also we had awaited and heard of your exalted royal victory in triumph.

[Note: [Col. 0407B] In the year 787 Charles reduced Tassilo to submission and at the beginning of the following year compelled him to enter a monastery after surrendering the duchy, according to the Frankish Annals. The Fulda annals assign both events to the year 787; the authors cited by Pagi (no. 13) likewise record both, and further record that Tassilo stood before King Charles on the fifth day before the Nones of October, as is confirmed by another chronicle. Certainly news of the victory reached Adrian very late in the year 788, as is clear from this letter. CENN.]

Indeed, we believe that you remember how, in our preceding apostolic letters, we sent you word concerning the Capuans who came to us through your royal assistance. After we had sent those letters to you, and after some days had passed, we made the aforesaid Capuans swear before the confession of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, upon the faith of that apostle of God, and upon our faith and that of your royal power.

After the oath had been completed, one of those Capuans, the priest Gregory, asked to speak with us privately, saying:

“I can no longer conceal anything, having given you such an oath.”

When we questioned him more fully, he reported to us, saying that when Lord Charles, the great king, had returned from the city of Capua in the previous year—

[Note: [Col. 0407C] Pagi, following Cointius, and the author of the latest edition of Duchesne correctly place this letter immediately after the preceding one; the reason is evident. No letter among those given by Adrian has a date so certain and clear. He says that in the preceding letters he spoke about the same Campanians of whom he now speaks; everyone unanimously, including Muratori, assigns those letters to this year. Therefore this later letter certainly does not belong to the preceding year, as Muratori argues (year 788). Moreover, the Capuans report how, after Charles had departed from the city of Capua in the previous year, Arichis began his schemes. That preceding year was universally understood to be 787, a point which even Muratori himself admits. How then can the present letter be referred to that year? This is plainly an abuse of ancient monuments, offering false opinions to the ignorant and corrupting pontifical history to the worst public disadvantage. You may observe this especially in the present year, 788, when the Italian Annalist both reverses the order of the letters and postpones the donation of the Tuscan cities to that same year.

Next, observe how correctly this letter follows the preceding one. The ten Capuans named by Adrian voluntarily came to Rome and reported that the Beneventans were of doubtful fidelity. After Atto, the royal envoy, had departed for Francia to seek Grimoaldus’s succession on their behalf, they brought the imperial envoys into Salerno. After the envoys had held secret discussions before Adelberga for three days, the Beneventans escorted them to Naples, where they were plotting what was to be done after Grimoaldus’s arrival.

This is what the pope recounts in the preceding letter; it is clarified by another letter of the same pontiff, which I have inserted below from Mabillon’s diplomata. Adrian asks whether he should admit these few men separately from the other Capuans to the oath of fidelity—a substantial testimony that they had not been deputed by the entire city, despite Muratori’s addition. In this letter Adrian recalls to Charles what he had said about the Capuans in his preceding apostolic letters. He then adds that after several days, when he had sent those letters—understand this as meaning that Adrian’s consultation had already received an answer—the Capuans had sworn the oath of fidelity before the confession of blessed Peter. Finally, he follows the whole history as it had been explained to him by one of those Capuans, beginning with Charles’s departure from the city of Capua in the previous year.

Could anything be more evident for showing at what cost to the truth this letter is not only placed before the preceding one but is also declared certainly to belong to the earlier year? I leave the examination of the remaining letters to learned readers. ID.]

Arichis, their duke, had sent envoys to the emperor, contrary to God’s will toward him, asking for aid and the dignity of the patriciate together with the duchy of Naples in its entirety. He also asked that his kinsman Athalgisus be sent to him with a strong force as assistance. He promised the emperor that he would adopt the Greeks’ customs, both in tonsure and in dress, under the emperor’s rule.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] Understand this as having been done by the Beneventan prince in April, or at the latest May, of 787. ID.]

When the emperor heard this, he sent his envoys to him—namely, two sword-bearers into the territory of Sicily, carrying with them woven-gold garments and a sword, or comb, and scissors, in order to make him patrician, just as the aforesaid Arichis had promised to be clothed and tonsured.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] This matter has been sufficiently discussed in the Preliminary Commentary, no. 10. ID.]

They also asked for Ramualdus, the son of that Arichis, as a hostage.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] I believe that Arichis had informed the emperor that Charles had taken Grimoaldus, the brother of Romualdus, with him together with other hostages. For that reason he asked for this one as a hostage, although he was older and heir to the duchy. ID.]

Concerning Athalchius, known to him [Lamb.: *cognato*, “his kinsman”], the emperor sent word to him, saying: “We are not sending him to you now whom we are sending elsewhere; rather, we are sending him with an army to Treviso or Ravenna.”

[Note: [Col. 0408D] Lambecius and Gentilotus restore this passage, which Tengnagel had corrupted. Gentilotus notes that the duplication of the sentence had been written in the margin of the manuscript codex. Both read it as follows: “But concerning Atalgisus, his kinsman, he sent word to him, saying: ‘We are not sending him to you, but we are sending him with an army to Treviso or Ravenna.’” ID.]

489 When the envoys arrived, by God’s providence and through the intercession of the apostles, they found that the plans of the wicked had been destroyed, because they found that Duke Arichis, or his son Waldon, had died.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] This was divinely accomplished, even if Adrian had not said so; anyone can easily understand it. For Romualdus, who was to become a hostage of the Greeks, died prematurely on 21 July of that same year, while he was perhaps staying in Constantinople, engaged—contrary to the divine will—in plans to subject Italy once more to Lombard tyranny and to remove the Exarchate from the Holy See. This is recorded beneath his tomb in Pratilli (vol. III, p. 304), Ughellus, and others: “He lived twenty-five years; he was buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, while his father was ruling in the thirtieth year, the tenth indiction being in progress. His father himself died one month and five days later, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.” Thus, when the sword-bearing envoys reached the territory of Sicily, they found that the secret plans had been destroyed by the deaths of both men. Athalgisus and the fleet, terrified by this unexpected event, likewise turned their journey toward Calabria, as is clear from Adrian’s letters cited above (letter 89, elsewhere 90), for he mentions another letter sent through Arvinus, which is missing from the Codex. CENN.]

While Atto, your most faithful envoy, was there at Salerno, the Beneventans were unwilling to receive the Greeks. But after the aforesaid deacon Atto had returned, they brought the Greeks by land from Greek territory and received them at Salerno. They remained there for three days, having been reconciled [Lamb.: *consiliati*, “having taken counsel”], with Athalberga, the widow of Arichis, and with the Beneventan nobles.

[Note: [Col. 0409C] Almost the same things are related in the preceding letter, since the Capuans had already touched upon the principal matters even before they were admitted to the oath of fidelity. ID.]

The Beneventans advised the aforesaid Greek envoys, saying: “We have sent our envoys to King Charles, asking him to receive our duke Grimoaldus. Moreover, through the deacon Atto, who promised this to us, we sent a *roga* [or *rogam*].

[Note: [Col. 0409C] This is the exact reading of the word *rogum*, or, as Lambecius reads it, *rogam*, which was explained in the notes to the first letter of this Codex. Pagi absurdly interprets it as *robam* (year 788, no. 1), confidently putting forward this small point: *Roba* was a looser garment formerly used by kings, bishops, and others, as may be seen in Du Cange’s Glossary. See above, in the note to the letter of Gregory III, Preliminary Discussion, no. 4.

Muratori, who not only saw Lambecius’s recension of the Carolinian Codex but also published it (Italian History, vol. III, part II, pp. 73 ff.), retained in the annals of the first-mentioned letter the corrupt reading of Tengnagel and read *regnum*; here, however, he interprets *rogam* as an expensive gift. Both interpretations are inept. In the former letter he preferred the correction of the distinguished scholar Lambecius to his own opinion, but here he gives *rogam* an entirely new meaning.

Du Cange demonstrates, with many examples from both sacred and secular history, that this word signifies a gift, honorarium, stipend, or alms. In the earlier passage he even placed “prayer” and “prayers,” on the authority of this letter. Gifts or stipends were customarily given at fixed times to soldiers and clerics; gifts are also found to have been given by supreme princes and pontiffs to nobles. But it is learned only from Muratori’s boxes that subject peoples gave a *roga* to princes. You may ask why Muratori, otherwise most learned, treated Lambecius and Du Cange with such contempt on this double occasion. I shall answer briefly: he wished to deceive us and to destroy pontifical authority. ID.]

We sent a *roga* through Atto the deacon, he promising it to us, so that we might receive him completely and consequently as duke. But for this reason it is fitting that you remain in Naples until we are able to receive that Grimoaldus as duke. What his father Arichis was completely unable to accomplish, Grimoaldus his son, once he has attained his father’s position, will entirely accomplish: he will fulfill the imperial will in every respect, with the whole dominion, just as he stood with his father, while we likewise fulfill our promises.”

[Note: [Col. 0410B] Charles, seriously reflecting upon Adrian’s great opposition and upon the many dangers impending from the Beneventans, preferred to obey the pope when the matter was entrusted to his own judgment rather than when he was asked not to grant Grimoaldus the principality. For a long time he was uncertain; but at last, fearing that the Beneventans might submit to the Greeks, with the greatest injury to the Italian kingdom and ecclesiastical territory, he allowed the prince to succeed his father, trusting rather to overcome bad men by goodness than to drive them to desperation through severity, as Pratilli correctly observes (Chronicle of the Dukes and Princes of Benevento, vol. V, p. 17). This was not done until a year after his father’s death, namely in 788, toward the end of August. See also Muratori’s notes on the anonymous Salernitan (chapters 22 and 26). At the time when this letter was given, Grimoaldus had not yet been released into the Beneventan principality. ID.]

For this reason they escorted the Greeks by land as far as Naples with great honor. The Neapolitans received the Greeks there with banners and standards, and, remaining in the city while awaiting the arrival of the aforesaid matter, did not cease to devise hostile measures with Stephen the bishop, Constantine, and the Neapolitan citizens.

[Note: [Col. 0410C] Lambecius and Gentilotus read *constantineis* in the Codex, evidently a scribal error for *consentaneis*; the latter reading must certainly be adopted. Stephen the bishop was not a citizen but the duke of Naples, especially since his son Caesarius, who held the military office of duke, had died that year: “Caesarius died a natural death, greatly to the displeasure of the duke Stephen, his father,” as recorded in the often-cited Neapolitan Chronicle in Pratilli (vol. III, p. 34).

It is not credible that this same Stephen, the duke who, before becoming bishop, had been most acceptable to Pope Paul the Roman as one who had served the Church well, as was said in the preliminary discussion of Paul’s letter (no. 20), was involved with the Greeks and Beneventans in plots against the Church while he was also most holily exercising the episcopal office. In the following letter we shall see that the matter was otherwise. ID.]

The Greeks sent word to the emperor concerning the death of Arichis and his son, and awaited from him instructions about what they ought to do.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] This new secret, revealed to the pope by Gregory, who had now become subject to the Holy See and had not disclosed it before the oath, increasingly confirms that Muratori abused these letters for his own purpose when he decided that this one certainly belonged to the preceding year. ID.]

491 But in all these matters, most excellent son protected by God, let your most diligent royal power strive to act both for the exaltation of your spiritual mother, the Holy Roman Church, and for our safety, and—while the Lord protects and blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, presides—for the security in triumph of your unconquered kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The pope’s advice is most prudent, since he rightly fears for ecclesiastical territory and the Italian kingdom, while nevertheless leaving the matter to the king’s judgment. ID.]

[Col. 0410B] Moreover, Gregory the Capuan priest himself informed us of this concerning your most faithful envoys—Maginarius, the religious abbot, or Joseph, and Count Liudericus, together with Goteramnus the doorkeeper [Lambecius: *ostiarius*]. They had returned from Benevento to Spoleto and fled from there because the Beneventans had made this plan with the Neapolitans, Sorrentines, and Amalfitans:

They would have your envoys land outside the city of Salerno, beside the sea. At night, the Beneventans would suddenly rush upon them together with the Neapolitans and kill them. Afterwards they would spread the report that the Neapolitans, thinking the Beneventans to be coming against them, had secretly killed the envoys, believing them to be Beneventans.

When your aforesaid envoys learned of this, they were compelled to flee, lamenting your royal deception. If your envoys had remained at Salerno, the Neapolitans, together with the Amalfitans and Sorrentines, would have hidden there under arms so that, with the Beneventans, they might attack and kill your envoys.

[Note: [Col. 0411C] Gretser notes that this passage is corrupt. ED.]

But we have become certain that all their wicked plans are reduced to nothing, because we recognize that your royal power possesses such abundant fidelity and such a loving affection from the depths of the heart toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward us.

[Note: [Col. 0411C] Another letter—or rather fragment of a letter—of Maginarius the abbot to Charles the Great exists in the same Mabillon (Supplement to the Diplomata, p. 96). It gives an account of everything that happened to Maginarius and the other royal envoys at Benevento and Salerno. It is mutilated and everywhere full of lacunae, but it contains much that confirms the report of this Capuan and often illuminates the events which he narrates in general terms. I have appended it; but since it is very long and not especially necessary to the main point, it may safely be omitted. CENN.]

Therefore, just as we ask the apostle of God day and night, we lay everything before you, suggesting it to you and laying it down before your radiant royal feet.

As for our well-being, concerning which you sent to inquire, with the Lord’s assistance we recognize your complete safety. We do not cease to pour out prayers for you, so that, enjoying the governance of the kingdom in this world for many years, you may deserve to reign without end in the heavenly citadels together with our lady the queen and your most noble offspring.

May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency in safety.

## XCIII. Another letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord Charles the King

In it are contained expressions of thanks, and matters concerning Roselles and Populonium, the Beneventan cities, and the plots of the Greeks.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 3): “In the third letter he gives thanks for Roselles, Populonium, and the Beneventan cities [Benevento], which Charles had given to him [which cities Charles had given to him]. He complains about their disobedience and also about the plots and wickedness of the Greeks. He asks that Charles keep an army ready and send it when necessary, as he had promised.” ID.]

(Year of the Lord 788, Codex Carolinus LXXXVI, chronicle 92.)

[Col. 0411C]

## Argument

In two letters, the first brought by Count Arvinus and the second by the royal envoys Roro and Betto, Charles replied, giving thanks to the pontiff for his prudent counsel. Here, however, the pope explains that he had opposed Grimoald’s succession in order to safeguard the interests of the king, himself, and the holy see. What the bishops of Naples and Gaeta had reported to him concerning Athalgis’s plots, he says Charles will see in the enclosures to both letters. He gives thanks that Charles had ordered Arvinus and his associates to hand over the cities of Campania and the territories of Populonia and Roselle. He says that nothing had been handed over to him except bishoprics, monasteries, and public estates, together with the keys of the cities but without their inhabitants; he wishes to administer the Campanian cities entirely, just as he administered those of Tuscany. Grimoald boasts that he enjoys the king’s favor and will have as subjects whomever he chooses; he said this at Capua in the presence of the royal envoys, and for this reason the Greeks living at Naples insulted the holy see. The pope asks Charles not to prefer Grimoald to Saint Peter. He says that Charles will hear more from the envoys whom he is sending together with the royal envoys.

To our most excellent son and spiritual godfather, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

We received the nectarous and exceedingly honey-sweet words of your royal excellence, in which, recognizing the welfare of your sincerity, of our spiritual daughter the lady queen, and of your lofty offspring, and learning that in your territories, by Christ’s favor, all things are seen to prosper, we returned great thanks to almighty God, who frequently makes us joyful through your royal triumphs.  
[Note: The Frankish annals record many wars in this year, with Charles always victorious, especially against the Avars; the pontiff seems to be referring to these. As for the title of sincerity that he gives the king, it is credible that the king, who was the pontiff’s very close friend, had disclosed to him all the reasons why he preferred Grimoald to return to his paternal principality, contrary to the pontiff’s most prudent counsel, rather than in some way compel the Beneventans to follow the Greek side. This is certainly inferred from what follows. Cennadius.]

### 494

Concerning the apostolic letters that we sent to you—first through Count Arvinus and afterward through your sister [Lambinus: Roro] and Betto—and in which we found, in your royal letters, that thanks were consequently returned to us, your royal excellence should wish to believe us completely: we never wished Grimoald, son of Arichis, to return to Benevento  
[Col. 0412C]  
[Lambinus adds: “for no other purpose”]  
except because of the schemes and ambushes of your enemies and ours; but also, as your royal excellence promised us, for the advancement and defense of God’s holy Church and for the benefit of both you and us. You, with the Lord’s help and blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, accompanying you, believe that you are undertaking all these things with the greatest strength. Without doubt, therefore, we believe that in these matters you will complete to the end the work that you have begun for the advancement of your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church; and it will remain increasingly exalted through your laborious struggles, because for such a work your royal name has been inscribed in the book of eternal life.  
[Note: These two points concerning the interests of the holy see and of Charles arose from the supreme pontiff’s official duty toward the holy see and from his greatest goodwill toward the king. In both cases the security of the Catholic faith was intended, once the Greeks had been entirely driven from Italy—something that Adrian and his predecessors desired above all. This, clearly, was the defense of God’s holy Church that we have seen commended in almost all the letters to the Frankish kings, Pippin and Charles, patricians of the Romans. By “the holy Church of God” the Roman Church is meant, which is the head and center of the universal Church; only those severed from it are ignorant of this. Cennadius.]

As for what your excellence communicated to us—that whatever we learned concerning these regions we should quickly strive to report in full to your royal excellence—Stephen, bishop of Naples, sent us, through his letters, a request that certain deaconries belonging by right to our holy Church be granted to him. In it he inserted a statement, informing us about the impious Adalgis, son of the arrogant Desiderius, and about the ambushes of the Greeks. In the same way Campulus, bishop of Gaeta, informed us of these very matters in his own letter. Because of our great love for you, therefore, we have inserted both that statement and the letter below. But let your excellence commend and arrange matters in such a way  
[Col. 0413B]  
that the armies which you assigned to us, as you informed us, remain prepared and hasten to come to our aid whenever we require it.  
[Note: It is not surprising that the bishop of Gaeta disclosed to Adrian the plans of the Greeks and the plots of Adalgis. Gaeta and Terracina belonged by right to the holy see; there is no doubt in the case of Terracina. After Stephen, duke and bishop of Naples, made peace in the preceding year with the duke of Benevento, his son Caesarius led an army to Terracina, with the same Beneventan duke offering counsel. The Neapolitan Chronicle relates the matter in these very clear words: “In the following year [787] Aragis wished to make peace with Duke Stephen, and Caesarius, at Aragis’s instigation, set out with his army for Terracina, which displeased the lord pope.” And rightly so: in 780, when the Greeks and Neapolitans invaded the same city, Adrian complained that a city which he had subdued was being taken from blessed Peter. The pontiff retained it as part of the Neapolitan patrimony that had been taken from the holy see, and promised to restore it as soon as the patrimony itself was returned. Since it was not returned, Terracina therefore remained in the power of the holy see even in 787.

Those are mistaken who think that Pagius, under the year 787, numbers Terracina and Gaeta among the other Campanian cities, as though Charles had granted them to the holy see and they were named in the constitution of Louis the Pious. Pagius says nothing about them, and the constitution mentions the Neapolitan patrimony without mentioning either city. Peregrinius too was misled by failing to establish the date of Adrian’s letters: he thinks that Letter 65, elsewhere 64, was written before Letter 60, elsewhere 73, and therefore holds that Terracina was given by Charles and afterward taken from the Greeks through the counsel of Arichis. In 777, to which Letter 60, elsewhere 73, refers, Terracina and Gaeta were under Greek rule; but in 780, to which Letter 65, elsewhere 64, refers, the Neapolitans and Greeks invaded Terracina. The pontiff plainly admits that he had subjected it to the holy see by his own forces and would have restored it if the Neapolitan patrimony had been returned. See the notes attached to both letters.

The same learned author correctly adds that both cities came sooner or later under the dominion of the holy see, which he infers from Letters 69 and 74 of John VIII. I will not insist on testimonies nearly a century later. I do not hesitate to affirm as certain that Charles the Great granted neither Terracina nor Gaeta to the holy see, as is clear from the constitution of Louis the Pious. Rather, it appears that Adrian first subjected Terracina through the papal army and then recovered it with Frankish assistance in 780 (Letter 65, elsewhere 64); on that same occasion he seems to have conquered Gaeta and added it to the maritime territory extending as far as the Liris. For this reason, in 787 Charles added the inland cities of Campania, which were necessary both for enlarging the ecclesiastical territory and for enclosing those maritime cities within its boundaries. Charles’s grant, by which the Church’s dominion extended as far as the Volturnus, provides almost certain evidence of this. There is also another, less doubtful, argument in the report of the bishop of Gaeta concerning the ambushes of Athalgis and the Greeks.

One might wonder that Stephen, bishop and duke of Naples, did the same thing, since he had been implicated in the plots of the Greeks and Beneventans against the holy see and King Charles, according to the testimony of Gregory the priest and of various Capuans. But the Capuans knew the deed; they could not have known Stephen’s words. Here we have abundant testimony to his goodwill and supreme reverence toward the holy see. Just as in 776 he had informed the pontiff of the death of the iconoclast Copronymus (Letter 55, elsewhere 60)—a matter concerning which see the Preliminary Commentary, section 27, from which great security for the orthodox faith resulted—so now he reports Athalgis’s plots against the holy see, lest it suffer any harm from them. Nor could everything contemplated by the confederates have been disclosed in detail unless Stephen himself had taken part in their counsels. Thus the report of the Capuans was reliable, and Stephen’s faith and love toward the pontiff remained unchanging. Cennadius.]

### 496

We also found in your letters a statement concerning the cities in the Beneventan territories which you offered with devoted mind to the blessed apostle Peter and to us—concerning Roselle and Populonia—and you instructed Duke Arvinus how, together with your other faithful envoys, he should carry everything out as pleases God and the blessed apostle Peter. For this reason we do not cease to implore divine mercy for your benevolent excellence.

But what happened to your envoys? They did not wish to fulfill your orders in this matter—neither concerning Roselle and Populonia nor concerning the Beneventan territories.  
[Note: So that blame might not be placed upon the royal envoys because of the obscure wording of the letter, consider what Maginarius wrote to Charles, in Mabillon: “And they also alleged . . . we had not given them security, because we would grant Grimald to them as duke . . . or those cities which you granted to Saint Peter and the lord apostolic, we would release to them . . . in no way do they wish to fulfill your order, etc.” Lambecius clarifies the passage by placing a single question mark: “But what happened to your envoys? They did not wish to . . .” Cennadius.]

Therefore we sent Duke Crescent and Adrian, together with your faithful envoys, into the Beneventan territories, accepting your royal wishes. But they did not wish to hand over anything else to them except bishoprics, monasteries, and public estates, together with the keys of the cities but without their inhabitants. The inhabitants themselves remain under their control, entering and leaving as they please. How could we possess those cities without their inhabitants if the inhabitants plotted against them?

We desire to govern and administer them, while they remain in their freedom, just as we do the other cities in the Tuscan territories granted by you, possessing all their law.  
[Note: When the pontifical envoys went to Campania to take possession, in Adrian’s name, of the six cities, the illusory possession handed over reveals the supreme pontiff’s foresight. He had so vehemently opposed Grimoald’s succession, and he did not wish to admit even those few Capuans to the oath of loyalty without outside counsel. See the Preliminary Commentary, sections 30–31. Also Letter 89, elsewhere 90, section 8, concerning the cities of Tuscany already possessed. Cennadius.]

We therefore ask your excellence to ensure that no one can obstruct your sacred wishes, and that you do not prefer Grimoald, son of Aragis, to your supporter, blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For Grimoald himself, in Capua, in the presence of your envoys, boasted, saying: “The lord king ordered that whoever wishes to be my man, whether great or small, is without doubt as much mine as he is whoever he wishes.”  
[Note: Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, likewise abused the prince’s favor, if you remember, in Letter 51, elsewhere 54; but the outcome was different in a similar case. Leo was promptly reduced to his office, and the free dominion of the holy see was vindicated. The situation in Campania was different. To prevent the submission to the Greeks of that extensive duchy, which embraced almost the whole Neapolitan kingdom, Charles prudently endured much and also concealed much. The new grant of Charles did not begin to have any settled status until the time of Louis the Pious, and indeed much later. No further memory of it occurs in this codex. Cennadius.]

When this reached our ears, the leading Greeks sitting at Naples, insulting us, angrily exclaimed: “Thanks be to God, for their promises have come to nothing.” But we regard their laughter and mockery as worthless, although the Greeks themselves reported that the apostolic envoys had already returned twice without accomplishing anything.  
[Note: Let those who during this period stubbornly defend Greek domination in the city of Rome itself, despite the whole testimony of history, consider this: Greek domination consists entirely in mocking the pontiff and the Romans, because the expansion of their power in the Campanian territories did not achieve its intended result. Cennadius.]

Behold, therefore, we are sending back men of this kind in the service of the blessed apostle Peter, together with your faithful envoys—our men [Lambinus: “and our men”] who will report everything to you more clearly. We ask you to order them to arrange matters in this cause in such a way  
[Col. 0415C]  
that your supporter, the blessed apostle Peter, may obtain the result promised by your sacred offering.  
[Note: No clearer testimony could be desired from the pontiff’s own mouth. Before 791, when this collection was compiled, full possession of the Campanian cities had not reached the Roman pontiff, although those ten Capuans, who are said to have been freely appointed by their city, had promised loyalty by oath to blessed Peter and the pontiff. Cennadius.]

Then, here and in the future, may he be your rewarder together with the lady queen and your most noble offspring. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## XCIV

*(A.D. 789, Codex Carolinus LXXI, chronicle 93.)*

### 498

[Note: Panvinio’s summary, Codex Vaticanus no. 39: “In the thirty-ninth [letter] he accuses him of falsehood and reproaches him for sending his envoys to Ravenna for the election of a new pontiff.” Cennadius.]

## Argument

He recalls that through the presbyter Hermembert he received a memorandum concerning the election of the archbishop of Ravenna. He states that Hucbert, the royal envoy, had attended Leo’s election in honor of the patriciate. He replies that after Sergius died, Michael had seized the see with Desiderius’s assistance, and that Hucbert—who was then in Rome for other reasons—had been sent there by Stephen so that, armed with royal authority, he might depose that transgressor of the canons and bring him to Rome. At the elections of John and Gratiosus, neither Pippin nor Charles had sent any envoy. The election there had always been conducted canonically by apostolic authority, as it had now been in the case of Gratiosus’s successor. No one, he says, is more solicitous for the honor of the patriciate than himself. He warns Charles not to put faith in wicked men.

To our most excellent son and spiritual godfather, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

[Note: Summary 39, Baronius and Centuriator. Grets.]

[Note: The date of this letter depends upon Gratiosus’s successor as archbishop of Ravenna. Since, according to Ughelli, Gratiosus died on 23 February 788 and John VII succeeded him in the same year, the letter should, as the matter itself suggests, be assigned to that year, not to the preceding year, as in Duchesne’s latest edition. But Agnellus rejects that John and holds that Valerius succeeded Gratiosus; Bacchinius and, after him, Muratorius therefore extend Gratiosus’s life to 794, maintaining that Valerius succeeded him. Yet the collection of the Codex Carolinus, made in 791, prevents those scholars from extending Gratiosus’s tenure to 794. Rejecting Ughelli’s chronology would leave a two-year period to be added to Gratiosus’s tenure; I would readily add it if any document were available on which to rely. What, then? Until such a document is produced from elsewhere, I do not depart from Ughelli. I therefore assign this letter to 789, or at the latest to the following year, despite Muratorius, who, although he was not unaware of the date of the Codex, makes such errors—doubtless led by the same freedom with which he did not hesitate to invert the order of the other letters to suit his purpose. Cennadius.]

Sent by your distinguished royal excellence, namely the devout presbyter Hermembert, he presented to us, amid the words of his reply, a memorandum which, as he asserted, had been written by your excellence—concerning the election of the bishops of the Church of Ravenna. It stated that when Sergius, archbishop, died, your envoys Hucbald or his counterparts had been present at the election of Leo, archbishop.

We believe that your excellence should remember this very well: when the aforementioned Sergius, archbishop, died, Michael the usurper, in his arrogance, dared to invade the Church of Ravenna; with the assistance of Desiderius, that most savage king, he violently seized the church and held it for a long time, while it remained deprived and bereft of its proper ruler. At that time Hucbald, sent by your royal excellence to our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen of holy memory, for other matters, was dispatched by that same lord Pope Stephen to Ravenna through your royal support, strengthened by God, so that he might expel the aforementioned usurper Michael from the Church of Ravenna and bring him here to Rome as a transgressor of the sacred canons.  
[Note: On this matter see the Preliminary Commentary, section 9, and the Admonition to the Letter of Stephen III, section 9 and following. Cennadius.]

For we have absolutely no memory—whether from our holy pontifical predecessors, from your father of most excellent memory, the lord Pippin, great king, or from your triumphant royal victory—of an envoy being sent to the election at Ravenna, either at the election of John, archbishop, or at that of Gratiosus, archbishop of the same see  
[Lambinus adds: “of the see”].  
[Note: Although Adrian mentions only the two most recent archbishops, the history of Ravenna must nevertheless be traced farther back. The people of Ravenna would have imitated the audacity of the patriarchs of Constantinople had the Roman pontiffs not resisted. Cardinal Noris observes that this unbridled ambition arose because Ravenna had first been the seat of Honorius and Valentinian, and then of Theodoric and other Gothic kings, and finally of the exarchs. I will pass over the celebrated autocephaly of those prelates, which arose from the causes just mentioned.

I will say only that in 708, under Justinian the Younger, Felix, archbishop, was again ordained at Rome according to the ancient custom and brought the long schism to an end, whatever may be said about his defection after his return to Ravenna. Felix was succeeded by John V, elsewhere VI, in 718; Sergius succeeded him around 752; Leo succeeded Sergius in 770, before Adrian’s pontificate; and finally, under Adrian, John VI, elsewhere VII, held the see in 777, and Gratiosus in 784. All were duly ordained at Rome, although they had not entirely forgotten the schism. For Sergius, as we read in Anastasius’s Life of Constantine, refused to make the customary guarantees in the scrinium and, through the power of the judges, displayed what he preferred. The clergy remained deeply attached to the schism.

When, a few years later, the exarchate came under the authority of the holy see through the generosity of the Frankish kings, both Sergius and Leo, as stated above, devised another kind of trouble for the Roman pontiffs; this too was suppressed. If I am not mistaken, it was through the suggestions of the schismatic clergy—Agnellus belonged to their circle and must be read with great caution—that Charles, on this occasion, became a supporter of the archbishops’ ambition without realizing it. Instead, he found in the pontiff a vigorous defender of the rights of the holy see. Cennadius.]

But when the archbishop of the city of Ravenna departed from this life, the clergy and people, assembled according to the ancient tradition of the apostolic see, sought the unimpaired doctrine, so that, gathered together in one harmony, one and the same will, and one counsel, and receiving the apostolic admonition, they might choose for themselves such a shepherd as would neither be rejected by the sacred canons nor be liable to objection under any clause outside the chapter. When, with joy, they came to our apostolic see, carrying the decree confirmed by the signatures of everyone’s hands  
[Lambinus: “by everyone’s hands”],  
they asked that their own bishop be consecrated, just as has now been done canonically.  
[Note: It is clear from this that Gratiosus’s successor was duly elected at Ravenna and came to Rome; after receiving consecration, he returned to Ravenna before Charles issued this letter. Cennadius.]

Having set all this before you, we urge your royal excellence to reject far from you, without doubt, the lying tongues that pretend to chatter against the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church. Do not in any way order that faith be placed in those wicked and deceitful men. For, as the memorandum reported, in honor of your patriciate no one in the world appears to strive more for the advancement of your royal excellence than our constant prayer.  
[Note: Here there is very clear evidence that the clergy of Ravenna had not forgotten the former ambition of their archbishops. Below, in the discussion of Letter 97, elsewhere 85, there is another reference to the patriciate. To understand its character, consult the Preliminary Commentary, section 7 and following. Cennadius.]

Just as, with all our efforts, we have honored and continue everywhere to honor you above all others in the depths of our heart, so we desire increasingly that the honor of your kingdom surpass that of all who are known to exist in the world. Nevertheless, the goodwill that we bear toward your lofty rank has resounded throughout the whole world, as is plainly evident to everyone: day and night, in the presence of your supporter, blessed Peter, we do not cease to pour out prayers that, together with the lady queen and your most exalted offspring, you may reign as victorious rulers in this world throughout the ages and times, and may reign without end in eternal life. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

## XCV. Another letter of the same pope, addressed to the lord King Charles

It concerns Constantine and Paul, his [the pope’s] dukes, who had been falsely accused before the aforementioned king by wicked men; he asks that one of them, namely Paul, whom he had sent to be presented to the king, might be received kindly.  
[Note: “Requesting” is absent from the manuscript, but Tengnagel supplied it. Gentilis.]

*(A.D. 789, Codex Carolinus LXXXIII, chronicle 94.)*

## Argument

He defends Constantine and Paul, dukes faithful to the holy see and to Charles, who had been falsely accused before the king. He wishes Charles to remember that Constantine had been commended to him in the aula of Saint Peter as an upright and faithful man. As for Paul, who wished to go to the king, he willingly sends him.

To our most excellent son and spiritual godfather, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

[Note: Summary 6, Baronius and Centuriator. Grets.]

I think it cannot be said how great our love is from the depths of our heart for your God-granted, triumphant power and royal excellence. For this reason we do not cease frequently to commend both our faithful and yours to your broad royal clemency. Therefore, when Constantine and Paul, dukes, came to be presented before our apostolic presence  
[Note: Lambinus and Gentilis read: “when they came to be presented before our apostolic presence”],  
they informed us, with profound sorrow of heart, that they had heard that they had been falsely accused before your royal power by wicked men. Since we recognize them as exceedingly faithful in the service of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and in your service and ours, we therefore freely release one of them, namely Paul, the glorious duke, to go to your most triumphant royal power.

We earnestly and insistently ask your excellence, established by God, that just as your love has embraced our assistance, so you may kindly order him to be received and deem him worthy to be kept as one commended to your royal power.

We believe that your royal excellence remembers how, in the court of your supporter, blessed Peter the apostle, you graciously commended to us the aforementioned Constantine and Romanus, affirming without doubt that they should be faithful to us and to you. We found them indeed as subjects who faithfully served you and us with complete humility, never wavering in their loyalty, but always remaining devoted to your service and ours and to our love.

When you have lent them your royal ears in all matters and have embraced the aforementioned Paul, the glorious duke, surrounded by royal protection  
[Lambinus reads: “when you have surrounded him with the support of royal protection”],  
and, by him, received the fruit of a good work and the effect of goodness, may we be able, before the body of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, to implore divine mercy for you, for our spiritual daughter, the most excellent lady queen, and for your most noble offspring, so that, enjoying the governance of the kingdom for a long age in this world, you may reign without end in eternal life with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.

[Note: These dukes were subject to Adrian and, since they are praised as faithful to the holy see and to Charles, appear to have been placed in command of soldiers. No city is mentioned as administered by them, and no civil office is recorded as entrusted to them. I confess that, despite applying as much diligence as possible after the distinguished Muratorius, I have discovered nothing new concerning these dukes, whom they call minor dukes, to whom the administration of a city or even a smaller place, a palatine office, or a military office may have been entrusted during the eighth century. I have therefore had to infer from their actions what civil or military dignity distinguished them. Although I am not entirely satisfied with the result, since the substance of the matter is unchanged whichever office is assigned to them, I preferred to offer the more probable account rather than leave their offices in complete obscurity. The main point is that both the Frankish kings and the pontiffs had offices of this kind. I have noted this elsewhere as well, Letter 8, elsewhere 4. Cennadius.]

## XCVI. Another letter of the same pope, addressed to the lord King Charles

It concerns the envoys of Offa, king of the English, who were traveling from Rome together with the envoys of the aforementioned King Charles  
[Lambinus: “who traveled to Rome”],  
and how the aforementioned pope had received those English envoys honorably; also what the aforementioned King Charles had instructed him through his legates, together with other matters.  
[Note: Panvinio’s summary, Codex Vaticanus no. 43: “In the forty-third [letter] he reports that the envoys of Offa, king of the English, were honorably received by him together with Charles’s envoys, as Charles had requested through his legates. The whole letter concerns primacy; it piles up many scriptural passages irrelevant to the matter. He writes that he was elected neither by men nor through man, but called by our Lord Jesus Christ to his Gospel and predestined. He writes that he permits the divine word to be preached to the nations.” Cennadius.]

*(A.D. 789, Codex Carolinus LXXXIX, chronicle 93.)*

## Argument

He praises Charles for having despised the fabricated story spread by ill-disposed men—namely, that Offa, king of the English, had advised Charles to depose Adrian and create another pontiff from his own people. He then says that he was appointed over the entire Christian world not by men but by Christ Jesus, and therefore announces the word of life and truth to kings and peoples. He says that he received Offa’s envoys favorably when they arrived with the royal envoys, and that he granted them what Charles had requested, so that they might give thanks to him.

To our most excellent son and spiritual godfather, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Pope Adrian.

[Note: Summary 43, Baronius and Centuriator. Grets.]

[Note: This letter is one of eleven that, in Duchesne’s latest edition, are scattered over a period of ten years, from 781 to the date of the Codex. Because the title “godfather” was considered, while the absence of “godmother” was disregarded, the date of the letter was believed to range uncertainly throughout that entire period. It should nevertheless have been narrowed to the period after Fastrada’s marriage, known to Adrian in 784, so that the letter would range over only seven years. I would not dare determine to which of those years it most properly belongs. I have placed it here, however, because it has greater affinity with what follows than with the letters reported so far. There is no subsequent mention of any city either given or to be given, but only of a donation in general, to be completed on the model of Pippin. This manner of writing begins with the present letter. Consequently, whatever happened after 788 concerning the territories of Roselle and Populonia and the six cities of Campania cannot at all be deduced from the few letters that remain. Cennadius.]

Most discerning and nectar-like communications, dispatched by your eminent royal power amid its triumphs, we have received from your own lips. When, with more than customary love, we opened them, we first learned what we had continually longed to know—namely, of your illustrious health and prosperity, and likewise that of our spiritual daughter, the lady queen, as well as of your most excellent royal offspring and all her faithful household. For, as is reported by your royal clemency, you have a great desire that we should frequently make known through our apostolic letters or through a messenger how we are disposed toward you [Lamb.: *intimaremus*, “we might make known”]. Accordingly, we ourselves are continually presented with eager desire to hear, both through your royal writing and through your distinguished messenger, of your victory and prosperity amid triumphs—and indeed of that of the aforesaid lady queen, of your most noble offspring, and likewise of the sincerity and safety of all your most faithful subjects.

You should certainly deign to believe that our apostolic prayers never cease to implore divine clemency for you, in the confession of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom. For we are completely assured that your most exalted royal benevolence never ceases, for the exaltation of its mother, the holy Roman Church, which is the head of all churches [Note: [Col. 0421B] Thus Stephen II (ep. 10, otherwise 3), speaking in Peter’s name, said: “The Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, head of all the churches of God, founded by the blood of God himself, our Redeemer, upon a firm rock.” And again (ep. 11, otherwise 8), in his own words: “The holy Roman Church, mother and head of all the churches of God, foundation of the Christian faith.” This indeed is the judgment of the Fathers: “You have Rome,” says Tertullian (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 36), “from which authority is available to us also. How blessed is that Church, upon which the apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood! Where Peter is made equal to the Lord’s passion; where Paul is crowned with an end like John’s; where the apostle John, after being plunged into boiling oil and suffering nothing, is exiled to an island!” Cyprian, ep. 55: “To Peter’s chair and to the principal Church, from which sacerdotal unity arose”; and similarly in many other letters. I omit the rest, since the matter is sufficiently well known. Yet I should like it to be observed what the true understanding of the Roman Church was before the year 1000. In later centuries, after that true understanding—or notion—had been lost, a question arose among the Roman basilicas as to which of them seemed to be the greater. It was indeed a trivial question, though we know that it was violently agitated on both sides. For it is not considered that Adrian and his predecessors, residing at the Lateran at that time, preferred the church of Saint Peter, then outside the walls, to the other churches of the city. Nor do the kings of the Franks and other princes seem to have recognized any other church as Roman than the Vatican, where the sacred body of Saint Peter rests. Hence Einhard (*Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 27) states that Charles “venerated above all other sacred and venerable places at Rome the church of blessed Peter the apostle … And through him the church of Saint Peter the apostle was not only kept safe and defended, but also adorned and enriched above all churches with his resources.” Nothing occurs more frequently throughout this entire Codex than Peter as intercessor with God for victory over barbarian peoples and for the extension of the Frankish monarchy after their defeat. The kingdom itself is said in this same Codex to have been transferred by Peter, through his successors or vicars—as they were then called—to the Carolingian line; and finally temporal and eternal goods are promised to the kings of the Franks through the patronage of the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom. These things especially offend the Magdeburg centuriators—would that they offended none of our own!—who thereby reveal how greatly learned they are in pontifical history: for he did not see that Adrian was employing the opinions of his predecessors. Indeed, almost four centuries earlier Boniface warned the bishops of Illyricum as follows: “Whoever rises up in insult against him, the inhabitant of the heavenly realms, will not be able to be of the heavenly kingdoms. ‘To you,’ he says, ‘I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ into which no one will enter without the doorkeeper’s grace” (*Against Constantius*, p. 1041). “Since it is certain,” as he says at the beginning of the letter, “that the highest affairs depend upon his deliberation.” Let the ancient prayers and supplications addressed to this great patron of the universal Church be consulted; it is not worthwhile to linger over matters clear in themselves. CENN.]; and for our apostolic paternal prosperity, to labor with the utmost effort. For it has taken up the rule of your holy-memory father, the gracious king Pippin, and, just as it began, has completed it intact to the end. Having acquired his teaching, your royal power exists in all things elevated by the support of the apostles and by our continual intercessions.

Moreover, in your royal letters it was reported that Offa, king of the English people [Note: [Col. 0422C] The deeds of Offa, king of the Mercians, and the history of his predecessors, insofar as it could be made less obscure, were reviewed from Bede by Natalis Alexander (*Ecclesiastical History*, century VII, ch. 8, § 7). But, following Polydore Vergil, and with Baronius (775, no. 10), he concludes that Offa’s vices were greater than his virtues, and that, fearing their punishment, he came to Rome and made his kingdom tributary to the Holy See. He places this in the year 775, which Pagius, under the same year (no. 10), notes to be false, and, with Alford’s annals, postpones the matter to 794. It is clear that those who, with Baronius, Natalis, and Polydore, accept this account were misled by Adrian’s letter. ID.], had sent to your royal eminence a memorandum for communication, so that certain rivals of yours and of his [Note: [Col. 0422D] In the year 787 the Council of Calchuth was celebrated by the legates of the Holy See, Gregory, bishop of Ostia, and Theophylact, bishop of Todi; Offa himself was present. The legates speak of him to Adrian in these words (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VI, p. 1862): “We reached the court of Offa, king of the Mercians. But he, with great joy, out of reverence for blessed Peter and respect for your apostolate, received both us and the sacred letters brought from the supreme See.” These statements sufficiently and abundantly show that both Charles and Offa, with the greatest good faith, exposed to Adrian the audacity of wicked men. It should also be noted that a legate sent by Charles had joined the apostolic legates, and that the council dealt with many abuses requiring correction. This, I think, gave wicked men the opportunity of fabricating in the king’s name those exceedingly audacious letters mentioned under the name of a memorandum. ID.] might report to our apostolic presence that Offa himself had suggested to you that, through his exhortation and persuasion, you ought—God forbid—to expel us from the holy See of our dignity and establish there another ruler from your own people. This was written as something utterly wicked and contrary in your eyes, and your excellence recognizes with complete certainty that it is altogether false: Offa himself never made such a suggestion to you, nor did anything else ever arise in his heart, except that our paternity, by God’s mercy, might in his time rule and govern the holy Church of God for the advancement of all Christians. In this we unquestionably place our confidence in your royal power, because toward our apostolic paternity your benevolent, unconquerable, orthodox faith [Col. 0422B] burns in the Holy Spirit [Grets.: *fervet*, “burns”]. Like a brilliant, blazing fire, it will remain pre-eminent, and the craft of the ancient enemy will in no way be able to shake it through any heresy against the Catholic and apostolic orthodox faith. Rather, like a spotless mirror and a true and shining defender of that orthodox faith and of our supreme See, it will remain most vibrantly so forever [Note: [Col. 0422D] These words seem to refer to the council mentioned above, whose first canon established orthodox faith according to the Council of Nicaea, while the remaining canons corrected many abuses that had crept in. CENN.]. Yet, concerning the aforesaid defilement of the assertion—which you confess to have been made, though it is impious even to say so—by King Offa [Col. 0423A], we had never until now heard such things, nor, now that we hear them, have we believed that he would have contemplated perpetrating them even had he been a pagan—which God forbid. How much more, then, do we regard such unheard-of and incredible cunning as impossible in one whose predecessors were kings who were always subject in obedience and faithful love to our holy predecessors, the pontiffs, and to us! [Note: [Col. 0423C] Although, on the basis of the examples of his ancestors, he entirely believes Offa to have been free from that fabrication, nevertheless, lest he seem to have passed over the matter’s extraordinary character, he touches on it in passing. About the successors of Saint Peter [Col. 0423D], he speaks with due dignity, affirming that such things could not have entered even a pagan’s mind. ID.]
