**507** Nevertheless, if God is for us, who can be against us? “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 117). And again: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; whom shall I dread?” (Ps. 26). For “every planting which the heavenly Father shall plant, no one will be able to uproot” (Matt. 15). “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). Although unworthy, we have obtained the seat of the apostles, assuming and holding the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and governing the whole Christian people entrusted to us by God [Note: [Col. 0423D] This prerogative of the successors of Saint Peter, who are heirs of his authority—and therefore have long been called those who act in Peter’s place and Peter’s vicars—is treated at length by P. Coustant (*Preface*, no. 13). The following words, borrowed from the Apostle (Gal. 1), concern supreme jurisdiction over the universal Church, which he attributes to God alone. ID.]. We were not chosen by men or through a man, but were called through Jesus Christ our Lord and predestined for his Gospel, as blessed Paul the apostle, the vessel of election, taught: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also chose; those whom he chose, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–30). And again blessed James the apostle instructs and teaches: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration; for of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth” (James 1:17) [Note: [Col. 0423D] These words could also apply to other bishops, and therefore add little force to the argument. Rather, they show Adrian’s sincere mind, formed by holy customs, and conversely the depraved and perverse character of the person who prefixed the malicious heading to this letter. ID.]. Therefore, being adamant and flint, as the prophetic word confirms, and fearing nothing, we do not cease to preach the divine word to the nations, as it is written: “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; and when you hear a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me” (Ezek. 33). Observing the commands of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, we do not cease to preach the word of truth and life to kings and peoples. For love of it, we gladly received the messengers of the aforesaid King Offa, together with your most faithful envoys whom you sent to us; and, for the sake of your illustrious excellence, we looked upon them with a suitably cheerful countenance, fulfilling their requests so that they might convey thanks to your royal power, advanced by God and victorious in triumphs, because we customarily strive to fulfill your will, just as you fulfill ours [Note: [Col. 0423D] What the king of the Mercians requested through his messengers has nowhere been discovered. Two things, however, can be learned here with certainty. First, those exceedingly audacious letters were unjustly attributed to King Offa, who was arranging an embassy to Adrian; second, Offa did not stand so high in the pontiff’s estimation that whatever he requested could be obtained from the Apostolic See without Charles’s intercession, since nothing reasonable was ordinarily denied to Charles. ID.].

When these things have been perfectly observed to the end, may the divine majesty grant you, together with the lady queen and your most noble sons, enjoyment of the governance of this world’s kingdom through ages and times, and may it grant you to rejoice forever in triumph with all the saints. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XCVII. 509. ALSO A LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES

In it he deals with the dioceses or parishes of the bishops in the regions of Italy and Tuscany, which they invaded mutually, and with the monastic habit, which they abandoned contrary to the holy canons, putting on secular clothing again and joining themselves in illicit marriage [Note: [Col. 0424C] Summary by Panvinio (Vatican Codex 27): “In the twenty-seventh [Twenty-seventh] letter he indicates that in the regions of Italy and Tuscany certain bishops invade one another’s dioceses [some bishops invade the dioceses of others] and parishes [invade them], abandon the monastic habit [monastic clothing] contrary to the holy canons, and contract marriages, being clothed in secular garments. He therefore asks Charles to correct these things, so that he may show [correct: embrace] the faith of the Catholic and Apostolic Holy Roman Church [once embrace it] and uphold it continually [maintain it without error], so that he may remain [may be able to remain happily] with all the saints.” ID.]

*(A.D. 790, Codex Carolinus XCIV, chronicle 96.)*

### ARGUMENT

It had been reported to him that the Lombard bishops, not content with their own dioceses, were invading one another’s boundaries. He asks Charles to admonish them not to despise the canons and decrees of the pontiffs. The monastic institution was being violated there: Raginald and Ragimbald gave Ermenald’s daughter, a nun, in marriage to their nephew Nazarius, and many others perpetrated the same crime on their example. He asks Charles to prohibit such crimes and to cooperate with him in eradicating them.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-father Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope [Note: [Col. 0424D] Summary 27 by Baronius and Centuriators, Gretser.]. [Note: [Col. 0424D] Pagius, followed by the latest editor, Duchesne, correctly assigns this letter to this year; but they wrongly place the following letter before it, as though it had been written in the preceding year. It will be evident below that the order is otherwise. CENN.]

If, in secular affairs, each person’s right and proper order must be preserved, how much more in ecclesiastical arrangements must no confusion be introduced, lest discord find a place there from which peace ought to proceed. This will be preserved by such reverence [Note: [Col. 0424D] Gretser reads: “peace ought to proceed.” This reading accords with the true meaning.] if nothing is attributed to power but everything to equity. For it has been reported to us that the bishops of the Lombards, invading one another, expose themselves to danger, and at the same time, outrageously violating ecclesiastical statutes, attempt to invade the territories of others; while unlawfully retaining those territories, they strive to persevere in their former error [Note: [Col. 0425C] Two canons among others clearly prohibit this: Council of Carthage I, canon 10: “Let no bishop usurp the peoples or boundaries of another bishop.” And Carthage III, canon 20: “Let no one presume upon another’s parish.” There is also the letter of Innocent to Florentinus, bishop of Tibur (in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. 8, in Coustant, p. 40). CENN.].

Formerly, while their nation remained in error, it was reserved for your royal power, protected by God, to correct it from such wicked and faithless acts [Note: [Col. 0425C] In the capitulary of Aachen, A.D. 789, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April (in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 972), it was decreed (ch. 11) that bishops should presume nothing in another’s parish, on the authority of the canons of Antioch 13 and Sardica 18. The letter of Innocent to Florentinus cited above is also relevant. Whether before that time he had separately restrained the Lombard bishops, as Adrian seems to indicate, I confess is unknown to me. ID.]. Thus, in the very respect in which you surpass the other kings in glory, may you please the omnipotent Lord, who grants salvation to kings, more perfectly; and may you deserve to have as your helper in all things the faith which you venerate and practice orthodoxly, Catholic and apostolic, through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and his vicar.

[Col. 0425B] Therefore, entreating your royal excellence, advanced by God, we ask that, rejecting their errors, each man may be able to hold and govern his own diocese under priestly direction and ecclesiastical office. Just as secular boundaries exist according to territories and are administered in court under the law of the city and its jurisdiction, so the diocese and parishes of the bishop of that same city must not be disregarded. Thus, when each bishop, through the institutions of the holy canons and of our holy pontifical predecessors, has received the rights of privileges and sanctions [Note: [Col. 0425D] Zosimus says to the bishops of Gaul (ep. 1, ch. 3): “We admonish all that each be content with his own boundaries and territories.” More appropriate to Adrian’s time, when the formulae of the *Book of Diurnal* were in use, is the bishop’s promise at his ordination (ch. 3, title 6), which among other things states: “Furthermore, I promise never to usurp the parish or rights of any other church under the jurisdiction of my episcopate.” Garnerius says that the words of Gregory II to Serenus of Friuli—“never to invade another’s rights or, with the rashness of presumption, usurp anyone’s jurisdiction”—show that this was enjoined upon bishops of the outer regions when the pallium was sent to them, just as it was enjoined upon suburbicarian bishops at their ordination that they should keep within their own boundaries. ID.], ministering in every priestly office within their parishes and dioceses, they may worthily pour forth prayers for your broad and outstanding royal victory in triumphs, established by God [Col. 0425C].

Furthermore, by bringing this matter to your royal excellence, we make known the error which, in that same nation of the Lombards, cunningly continues to reign in the shameful acts and filth of the devil [Col. 0426A]. Those who once vowed themselves to God and put on the dark garment of the monastic habit are said, after turning back again, to put on secular clothing—something impious to say—and to be joined in illicit marriage. For this reason we have repeatedly admonished them through Guntfrid and other *gasinds* [Note: [Col. 0425D] Pagius incorrectly interprets *gasinds* as chamberlains, according to their first meaning in the Glossary. Muratorius more accurately lists them among the first-order retainers, namely dukes and counts (Italian Antiquities, vol. I, dissertation 4, p. 129), although he thinks them similar to the Goths’ *gardingi*. From the history of Wamba in Duchesne (vol. I, p. 222), it appears that this office among the Goths was a rank leading to the comitatus and dukedom: Rangindo, duke of the province of Tarragona, was attached to him, and Hildigisus still held the office of *gardingus*, whereas among the Lombards—and likewise among the Frankish kings—*gasinds* belonged to the class of nobles. Muratorius speaks of the *gasinds* with due respect and cites this passage of the letter, together with other documents, to establish the point. The names Raginald, Ragimbald, and Nazarius are unknown to me, but they must have possessed considerable authority, since Adrian judged that they should be admonished through the magnates of the Italian kingdom; and he says that they had provided the Italians with a bad example to follow. ID.], sending your letters to Raginald and Raginbald, so that they might avoid such detestable fornication. But, refusing to comply, in their contumacy they joined Ermenald’s daughter, clothed in the monastic habit, to their nephew, named Nazarius, through the devil’s cunning. They refused to assent to our apostolic exhortations, fulfilled their wicked presumption, and became ministers of the devil. Many in Italy continue to be drawn into this by their example [Lamb.: *imitari exempla*, “to imitate the examples”]. We are entirely confident that, in this matter, the canonical decrees are not unknown to your royal eminence, protected by God [Note: [Col. 0426D] Many canons have been issued and many decrees of pontiffs promulgated on this subject. The Council of Chalcedon (canon 16), Siricius to Himerius (ch. 6), Innocent to Victricius (ch. 12), and Leo to Rusticus (ch. 15) are presently available and sufficiently establish the matter. In the year following this letter, Paulinus of Aquileia held a council whose canon 11 (Labbe, vol. VII, p. 1006) has great affinity with this and the following letter. It decreed that virgins who had put on the black garment and thereafter either secretly corrupted themselves or publicly married should be punished with appropriate bodily penalties by secular judgment, separated from one another, perform penance all the days of their lives, and be deprived of communion in the body and blood of Christ—unless perhaps the pontiff, having learned of their penitence, should … ID.].

The two-edged sanctions that prohibit such filthy unions strike them; and therefore we ask that, in our times and yours, such illicit wickedness be canonically corrected throughout all the Christian people entrusted to us by God, so that you may thereby show yourselves more worthy worshipers of the omnipotent Lord. Then, once the Christian people has been freed from every error, may it be able to cry out with the prophet: “O Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you” (Ps. 19). For he rejoices frequently in your strength and greatly exults in your salvation; and, embracing the faith of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church forever, affirming it without error, he will remain with all the saints. We, rejoicing in this and giving thanks to the omnipotent Lord, implore his divine clemency for you, that you may enjoy the governance of the kingdom for a long age together with the lady queen and your most excellent offspring, and may deserve to reign without end in the heavenly citadels. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

## XCVIII. 513. ALSO A LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO LORD KING CHARLES

In it he deals with the parishes of bishops, their consecration, the honor of the king’s patriciate, and other chapters [Note: [Col. 0427C] Summary by Panvinio (Vatican Codex 4): “In the fourth [Fourth] letter he indicates much about his love for him. Likewise, that he pours forth prayers for him with all his strength in the confession of blessed Peter. He congratulates Charles that, through his arduous struggles, with Saint Peter’s aid, the efforts of the enemies of the Church have been reduced to nothing. He incorrectly cites the saying, ‘He who perseveres to the end will be saved.’ [He urges him to persevere to the end.] He gives thanks that Charles had promised to do everything not for the Church’s diminution but for its exaltation. If anyone has spread lies about him, he asks Charles to send him to Rome [asks that he send him to Rome], so that he may be punished according to his perverse deserts [may be punished]. He then says much about the parishes of bishops. The whole letter concerns the invocation of the saints and primacy [he writes much about the bishops’ parishes]. CENN.].

*(A.D. 790, Codex Carolinus LXXXV, chronicle 97.)*

### ARGUMENT

He says that he replied individually to Bishop Bernard and the royal protonotary Rado, royal envoys who brought welcome letters and reported many things orally. He strives to correct the Lombard bishops canonically, so that they may cease invading the boundaries of others. The daughter of Ermenald, whom Charles had sent so that she might be punished, had not yet arrived. The stain of simony was spreading far and wide, to the great detriment of the Church’s affairs. He had never interfered in canonical elections, and wished the king likewise to refrain. He speaks briefly about the proper discipline of ordinations and the supreme authority of the Holy See. He asks that Charles return the people of Ravenna and the Pentapolis to him, as he had written in the preceding year, just as he had done for the duke of Benevento. Those who refused obedience to the pontiff fled to Charles without permission; therefore they should not be heard, but sent back to Rome for judgment. He is very concerned about the royal patriciate, and says that Charles ought likewise to be concerned about the patriciate of Saint Peter. Therefore, just as no one comes from Francia to Rome without the king’s permission, so no one from Roman territory ought to go to Francia without pontifical permission. Those arriving from either side should be admonished to remain in faith and charity toward their own prince. Likewise, royal and pontifical messengers traveling back and forth should be held in esteem and honored, since he recognizes them as especially faithful to blessed Peter and to himself.

To the most excellent son and our spiritual co-father Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope [Note: [Col. 0427D] Summary 4 by Baronius and Centuriators, Gretser.].

[Col. 0428A] As intensely as we burn with love for your kingdom, advanced and enlarged by God, so firmly do we remain in its radiant royal sweetness and steadfast constancy. If we wished to express in words how greatly our heart exults toward your royal power, triumphant in victories, no extended sequence of writing, I think, would suffice, nor could any speech explain how, as we continually await news of your immense victories and safety, day and night we implore divine clemency for your royal excellence. Thus, receiving your royal and nectar-like communications through your most faithful messengers—namely, the most reverend and holy Bishop Bernard, and also Rado, your beloved protonotary and abbot [Note: [Col. 0427D] Rado was the celebrated abbot of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Arras and, from the year 778 onward, served as archchancellor. Since he was one of the royal notaries, Hitherius, abbot of Saint Martin, entrusted the office of archchancellor to him because he was occupied with frequent embassies to Pope Adrian, as Mabillon reports (*Annals*, book XXIV, no. 87). Documents therefore occur with the subscription *in place of Rado* in the years 781, 783, and 786, in the same annalist (book XXV, nos. 20, 34, and 58). But when, in 796 (same work, book XXVI [Col. 0428C], no. 47), he places Hitherius’s death together with Alcuin’s succession to the abbacy of Saint Martin of Tours and Rado’s succession to the office of archchancellor, saying that Rado became abbot of Saint Vedast at the same time, he shows that this letter was unknown to him. For, since it was entered into Adrian’s codex by order in 791, it could not have been issued later in that year. Rado, therefore, had become abbot of Saint Vedast much earlier. He held the office of chancellor—for the title protonotary means the same thing (Ducange, under “Chancellor” and “Notary”)—together with Hitherius, although he began to hold it alone after Hitherius’s death. CENN.], we remember in our prayers your exalted memory, as well as that of our daughter, the lady queen, your most noble offspring, and all the people entrusted to you by God [Note: [Col. 0428D] This is what the copy has, but everything seems corrupt. It should read: “We found in them [a request] that in our prayers we should remember your exalted person, likewise … your most noble offspring, and all the people entrusted to you by God.” GRETS.]. Your royal excellence, advanced by God, may rest fully assured that, in the confession of blessed Peter, your protector, we continually pour forth prayers for you with all our strength and with our apostolic intercessions, so that he himself, the prince of the apostles, accompanying you everywhere, may cast the necks of all your adversaries beneath your feet [Note: [Col. 0428D] The Frankish Annals state for this year: “The king held an assembly at Worms, and the year passed without an enemy.” The Fulda Annals similarly state: “This year was quiet from the disturbances of war; the king spent it at Worms.” Einhard likewise bears witness to this in Pagius (790, nos. 3 and 6), although he wrongly assigns the preceding letter to this year after the present one, and the present letter to the preceding year. CENN.].

Since you promise that our prosperity gives you most welcome and ineffable joy, and since the condition of your spiritual mother, the Roman Church, overflows upon you [Note: [Col. 0428D] Lamb reads: “the Church, with its safety overflowing.”], if anything otherwise should occur—which God forbid—it would be difficult for us to remain without your sorrow. In these matters we are entirely certain: the soul loves the one who loves it, and affection binds us together, nor will anyone be able to sever it, since our joy exists in your prosperity, and we believe that our safety is your perpetual delight. And when the wicked and insolent men who were plotting to perpetrate evil against your mother, the holy Roman Church, were, with the Lord’s cooperation and the aid of the keeper of the keys of heaven, destroyed and reduced to nothing through your arduous struggles, we learned with certainty that, as your royal power proclaimed, she remained unharmed, exulting in happiness and rejoicing in her restoration [Note: [Col. 0429C] Adrian undoubtedly refers to the useless efforts of the Constantinopolitan fleet, with which Adalgisus had arrived—Adalgisus himself having been removed from the living, according to Theophanes, and the Greeks having been defeated. The Frankish and Fulda Annals say that these events occurred in 788; other annals, more plausibly, place them in the following year. For who could believe that Grimoald, who assumed his father’s duchy toward the end of August 788, after the Beneventans’ alliance with the Greeks had been broken, stirred up those same Beneventans against them through Charles’s favor, joined the Franks and Spoletans to himself, made preparations for war, and successfully dealt with the Greeks in so short a span of time, freeing the territory of the Church and all Italy from fear? Some might object that the death of Hildebrand, duke of Spoleto, is recorded under the year 788; yet there are those who, on the authority of the Farfa chronicle, say that he died in the following year. Thus he could have been present with his men at the battle and opened the way for Winigis, commander of the Frankish soldiers, to the duchy of Spoleto—whether he was killed or died of illness in 789. Once the Greeks had been defeated, peace was secured for Italy; for it is clear from Erchempert (no. 5) and from Anastasius under Leo III (section 371) that Hildebrand was succeeded. CENN.]. For it is written: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

Concerning all that your excellence learned through our legates and letters, and to which you partly responded through our messengers, who had announced beforehand what you had said orally, everything became clearer to us. We listened to them, as usual, kindly and affectionately, lent our ears to them, and gave each of them an appropriate and suitable reply.

For we found in your royal letters [Col. 0429B] that your excellence labors not for the diminution of the holy Roman Church and our apostolate, but rather for their exaltation and honor, and for preserving the integrity of our mystery [Grets.: *ministerii*, “ministry”]. You asked that we give no assent to a wicked mouth and its lies, since neither ambition for earthly possessions nor any human seduction will ever be able to separate you from what you promised to blessed Peter the apostle, nor from our charity and steadfast affection. For we know beyond doubt that your royal power, having always struggled not for the diminution but for the exaltation of your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church, will remain devoted and exalted to the end, its fame spread among every people. Rather, we ask your royal excellence not to give assent to a deceitful and lying man, as you report [Note: [Col. 0429D] It is easy to determine what this false report concerned. Rome and its duchy, as is clear from the preceding material (preliminary commentary, no. 7), belonged by full right to the Holy See through the will of the peoples and the frequent affirmations of the Frankish kings. The Exarchate and both Pentapoles were possessed through the generous grant of those same Frankish kings, without anyone any longer opposing it. The same was true of the cities of Tuscany, as is evident from letter 89, otherwise 90, and the matters noted there in letter 92, otherwise 86, as well as in the preliminary commentary, no. 30 and following; the same must be thought concerning the territory of Sabina, although these letters do not contain certain testimony to the initiation of that possession. The whole falsehood, therefore, concerned the cities of Campania and the boundaries of Roselle and Populonia [Col. 0430C]. Adrian was being told that Charles would not at all hand over possession of those cities. Charles, however, was receiving an insulting report about the pontiff, as though the latter had said that the king would not keep his promises—perhaps out of regard for Grimoald, whom he had found faithful—and therefore that he himself would not continue in love and benevolence toward Charles. If one may sometimes venture to conjecture, nothing else can be inferred from this letter, provided that the contents of the preceding letters are kept in mind. ID.]. If he is found to have lied about such matters against us, may you deign to send him, together with your messenger, to our apostolic presence; and if he proves to be a liar, let him be punished according to his perverse deserts [Note: [Col. 0430C] I have said more than once, especially in the note on the letters of the antipope Constantine (no. 9), concerning the coercive jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff. Here is another example of it. ID.], just as you promised to the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, blessed Peter. May you deign to persevere in this, for our promise will remain unaltered and unshaken, without any deceit.

What you report having found in our letters—that the dioceses of the Lombards, with one bishop invading another’s and unlawfully holding them, remained in their former error [Note: An evident argument that this letter was issued after the preceding one, contrary to the opinion of Pagius and others, who cite them in the wrong order. — Ed.]—we are endeavoring wholly to correct, as is pleasing to you, according to the provisions of the canons, [Col. 0430B] because those who eagerly seize another’s parishes incur the guilt of perjury; while observing the boundaries and jurisdiction of the Lombard kings [Note: In the preceding letter (col. 425, note c), I praised the bishop’s oath not to invade another’s diocese: [Col. 0430D] this obligation rests upon the authority of the canons and the decrees of the pontiffs. For understanding these words of Adrian, the *Directory of the Bishop of Lombardy* (Diurnal, chap. 3, title 8) is relevant, where, among other things, one reads: “I likewise promise to hasten with every effort so that the peace which God loves may always be preserved between the commonwealth and us—that is, between us and the Lombard people—and that in no way shall I act or do anything contrary to it, so that I may show my faith in all things to be utterly sincere.” Adrian does not disapprove, nor could he disapprove, of their loyalty. At that time Pippin’s son Charles was king of the Lombards, and Adrian wished the bishops to preserve sincere loyalty toward him; but he strongly resented their disregard of the canons. — Ed.] they fall far from observance of the canons into transgression of them, and, generating quarrels and dissensions, plunge into a mass of errors. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we have provided that, just as their decrees canonically establish—and whenever they are ordained, the ancient custom is proclaimed—the clergy and the people residing in the Church of that city chose that bishop for themselves [Note: In the *Roman Order* 8, in Mabillon (p. 88), which is of the greatest antiquity, one reads: “The clergy and the consenting people of such-and-such a city, together with its neighboring parishes, chose for themselves that particular deacon or priest to be consecrated bishop.” — Ed.]; so he may retain in his hands the parish of that same city. And if it is canonically expressed and established in their decrees and in the writings of our apostolic ordination, why should he not possess his parish in its entirety within the territory of that same city where he was ordained? [Col. 0431A] But those who, transgressing the boundaries of the ancient Fathers, attempt to fulfill their own immoderate and uninstructed will submit themselves to the judgment of the canons [Note: This matter was established by several canons from the earliest beginnings of discipline. Apostolic Canon 14, Nicaea 16, and, more explicitly, Antioch 9 decree that “each bishop shall have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern it with the respect due to each person and exercise oversight of all property under his authority; he shall ordain priests and deacons and comprehend each matter under his own judgment.” This matter, I say, was established by several canons. In Adrian’s time all these provisions had been set out in the *Order* and the *Diurnal*, to which this pontiff refers, however much he also praises the canons. — Cenn.].

### 518

As for the daughter of Ermenaldus, who, after changing her clothing, returned again behind him and entered into an unlawful marriage, and who, as you stated, was sent to our presence to be judged canonically, she did not come to us at all [Note: Here is another, still more certain, argument that this letter was written after the preceding one. In that letter he said that this nun had married; in this one he testifies that she had been sent by Charles to be punished by him. — Ed.].

We, who have pastoral care of all the Churches, do not permit the divine precepts to be disregarded concerning the defect of consecration which, in the regions of Italy and Tuscany, is produced by the simoniacal heresy. Nevertheless, it is not permitted in many places; indeed, in the Church of the city of Ravenna itself, as your envoys, according to your report, informed you, it is customarily practiced. As a result, much money is evidently alienated through such wicked giving; they are seen to have no longer any gold or silver, and the very properties of the Churches are now alienated through written emphyteuses and are seen to have been afflicted and laid waste by this wicked giving [Note: The Council of Chalcedon (canon 2), Symmachus in letter 5 to Caesarius (title 2), and Hormisdas to the bishops of Spain (letter 25, chap. 2) bear witness that this heresy was widely spread even in earlier centuries. From this we learn that during the eighth century it had established itself in Italy proper, in Tuscany, and in the exarchate, to the great detriment of the Churches; their immovable goods were granted on emphyteusis, while their movable goods were squandered. Such abuses, which increased greatly in later centuries, had to be restrained by summoning episcopal consecrations to Rome. — Ed.].

For far be it from us, once the truth concerning such men had been ascertained, to lay upon them the hands of consecration; nor would we incline our ears to hear them, even if any authority whatever had requested us to consecrate such *acanonists* [Note: The commentators on the *Glossary* observe that Sirmond, at the end of the *Supplement to the Gallican Councils*, interprets *acanonists* as those who do something contrary to the canons, without citing an example. These letters supply an especially abundant example, since Adrian calls violators of the canons and decrees *acanonists*. — Ed.]—for never have we found, nor shall we find, in any election subject to us [Lamb. adds: “subject”] such men; nor do we wish your Excellency to undertake such a matter. Rather, when someone has been canonically chosen by the clergy, the people, and the whole populace, and there is nothing that harms the sacred order [Note: Lamb reads: “Let there be no one who harms his sacred order.”], we ordain him according to the customary tradition. We receive him as one elected with the subscription of a decree confirmed by the whole people [Col. 0431C] [Note: Adrian is plainly alluding to Charles’s unjust request in the previous year (ep. 93, elsewhere 71), when he wished his envoys to be present at the election of the archbishop of Ravenna. It is worth noting how firmly canonical election stood at that time, since the pontiff undertakes to assert it so forcefully. — Cenn.]. And lest the Church appear to remain widowed of its own rector, as the canonical provisions have ordained, when he has been presented to us through our apostolic representatives, we bring the elected man forward and examine him more precisely, asking him one by one about each chapter concerning the orthodox faith and the divine books, to determine whether he possesses the necessary knowledge. After he has given us a faithful answer and declared himself clean from the other ancient chapters that priests must avoid [Note: All this is clear from the aforementioned *Roman Order* 8 in Mabillon (chap. 2, no. 5). The chapters that must especially be avoided, since they had long fallen out of use, ought not to be passed over: “The archdeacon shall inquire of him concerning four chapters according to the canons: namely, *arsenokoitia*, which concerns a male; concerning a consecrated female servant of God, who among the Franks is called a *nonnata*; concerning four-footed animals; and concerning a woman joined to another man.” — Ed.], especially from the simoniacal heresy, we solemnly ask him whether he has made any promise or payment to anyone, since that is simoniacal and contrary to the canons. And while he is questioned by us before everyone, he answers, “Far be it from me”; and we say, “You will see to it; and if they are accomplices, let the danger fall upon their heads” [Note: See these matters expressed more fully and somewhat differently in the same *Order*. — Cenn.].

Accordingly, in the same manner they answer under oath in writing that they will never accept anything for the laying on of hands [Note: This type of document is called a *cautio* in the *Diurnal* (chap. 3, title 7), and a *chirograph* by Zacharias, as Garner notes there. — Ed.].

For we do not doubt that no one is unaware of how great an authority has been granted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his most sacred see: namely, that it has the right to judge concerning all Churches, and that no one is permitted to judge its judgment. The see of blessed Peter the apostle has the right to loose those bound by the sentences of any pontiffs whatsoever, through whom the care of the universal Church converges upon the one see of Peter; and nothing ever dissents from its own head [Note: These final words are taken from Leo’s decretal letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica (letter 84, chap. 11). The other assertions—namely, the supreme power of the Roman pontiff over the universal Church, the irreformability of his judgment, and appeals to the holy see—cannot be separated from the primacy, although in later centuries they were separated and called into question. Adrian borrowed them from the common manner of speaking of his predecessors and the Fathers; they require no greater illumination than that which Catholic canonists and most learned theologians have supplied in so many written volumes. — Ed.].

Meanwhile, in those royal letters of yours we have found written, as we sent to you in the preceding year concerning the men of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, about whom we wrote that you should send them to us as you did with the duke of Benevento [Note: The letter mentioned here is one of those not included in the *Codex*, although its substance is clearly preserved in this passage. The fact that it was issued in the preceding year, and that it proposed the example of the men whom Charles had sent back to Grimoaldus, further confirms Pagius’s error in maintaining that the present letter was written in the preceding year. — Cenn.], and, as you report, they have brought back nothing evil concerning our apostolate, but rather what is good.

But you should in no way have given your consent to them, or to any man, against us. If you found such men, you should immediately have sent both the man and the case to our judgment. From the beginning and to the end, we have such confidence in your royal Excellency that, for no earthly man, you will withdraw from the love and charity of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and from our affection, as you promised. For we too shall remain to the end in the faith that we promised you.

But the Ravennans and Pentapolitans and the other men who come to us without our absolution, lifted up by arrogant pride, despise our commands when justice is to be done and do not deign to acknowledge any authority, although it was granted by you to the blessed apostle Peter and to us. Nevertheless, your aforementioned most faithful envoys saw [Col. 0433B] how those Ravennans whom they presented to you behaved toward us in their pride. We therefore ask your royal power not to undertake any innovation against the holocaust which your father, of holy memory, offered to blessed Peter and which your Excellency has further confirmed. For, as you have stated, the honor of your patriciate is irrefragably preserved by us and is even honored with still greater distinction. Likewise, may the patriciate of blessed Peter, your protector, which your father, the lord Pippin, king and great ruler of holy memory, granted in writing in its entirety and which you have further confirmed, remain by irrefragable right [Note: For a discussion both of the pontifical dominion here clearly described and of the patriciate of blessed Peter and King Charles, consult the preceding discussion (no. 7 ff.). — Ed.].

For, as your royal Excellency stated in your letters, it would not at all seem contrary to it if any of the bishops, counts, [Col. 0433C] or other men from your territories should wish to come to us, whether to fulfill our command or of their own accord. Nor is it right for our paternal authority to be displeased if any of our people should hasten to you, either to offer greetings or to seek justice; you should not therefore regard anything arising from this as harsh.

But just as your people do not come to the threshold of the apostles, nor to us, without your absolution, so also our people who wish to come to you should come with our absolution and letter [Note: Whoever does not see from the complete equality of the official position of the king’s and the pontiff’s subjects the equality of the supreme authority of both rulers—his case is hopeless. — Ed.]. For just as we always receive your people and admonish them to remain in your service in true faith and purity of heart, with all their strength, so we ask your royal prudence likewise to admonish and exhort any of our people who come to you [Col. 0434A] that, just as your father, the lord Pippin, king and great ruler of holy memory, granted them to blessed Peter and his vicar, and your Excellency later confirmed the grant, so you should command them to be admonished and exhorted that they dare in no way to raise themselves in arrogant pride when they hasten to you. Rather, let them remain subject and humble in the service of blessed Peter and obedient to our command; and exhort them, because we shall remain entirely in the service and authority of blessed Peter the apostle until the end of the age [Note: The following words, which are found in Lambecius and Gentianus, are absent from the text: “We shall never withdraw you from the service of blessed Peter and his vicar, but shall remain in that faith and purity which we promised to blessed Peter the apostle.” — Ed.]. If they are not found to be such, let them be corrected both by your Excellency and by us [Note: Earlier (ep. 92, elsewhere 86), Adrian complained that the cities of Campania had been handed over to him without their people—that is, without their subjects—in contrast with what had long before been done with the cities of Tuscany. Here, however, Adrian tells Charles that the inhabitants of the cities of the exarchate and the Pentapolis had first been subjected to the holy see by Pippin and then by Charles. What could be clearer? — Cenn.].

And we likewise ask your God-protected royal power to deign, for the love of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for love of us, to foster and commend our most faithful envoys, as well as yours, going back and forth between us; for we have found them exceedingly faithful toward our defender and protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward us. Therefore we ask that, through your royal assistance, at our request, they may stand more elevated and exalted in your splendid kingdom for love of us.

For in proportion as your divinely ordained supreme Excellency, honorable and thrice-glorifiable, embraces and loves the holy Roman Church, the head of the whole world [Lamb. adds: “Church”], together with its rector and bishop [Note: The title “rector” can also be applied to a bishop; but “rector,” “prelate,” or “bishop” denotes primacy and pontificate. It would be futile to try to extend this notion to other princes, for the excellent pontiff, thinking humbly of himself, assigns himself no other title than that by which deacons, notaries, and defenders, who were customarily sent to administer the Church’s patrimonies, were called. This letter, from beginning to end, is such a distinguished monument of pontifical principality that everyone, Muratori included, acknowledges the dominion, at least in the exarchate and the Pentapolis. Consult him on the year 789; he writes about this kind of dominion with remarkable ineptitude and far from the truth. — Ed.], so may blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, together with our most excellent lady, our spiritual daughter the queen, and your most noble offspring, grant that you may enjoy for a longer age the government of the kingdom in this world, and through his intercession may cause you to rejoice without end in the unconquered stability of victory in the life to come. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency safe.

## XCIX. 523

### ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE, ADDRESSED TO THE LORD KING CHARLES

Containing expressions of thanks or blessings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and mentioning the Sacramentary arranged by Saint Gregory, which the lord king had requested and which Adrian had sent through John, monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna [Lamb., Ravennatium] [Note: Panvinio’s summary (Vatican Codex 7): “The seventh contains expressions of thanks or blessings; and it also indicates that the Sacramentary which King Charles had requested was sent through John, monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna [Ravennatem].” — Cenn.].

*(A.D. 791; Codex Carolinus LXXXII, chronicle 98.)*

[Col. 0435A]

### ARGUMENT

When Bishop Hucbertus came to the holy threshold bearing royal letters, he said that from them he had learned Charles’s intention to exalt the holy see even without his own petitions. For this reason Adrian promises him a heavenly reward and everlasting remembrance of his name. He says that he had already sent the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory, which Charles had requested, through John, abbot of Ravenna, after obtaining it from Paulus the grammarian.

To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual kinsman, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Adrian, pope [Note: This letter too wanders through a decade in the latest edition of Duchesne, from the year 781 to 791. I, however, think that it must certainly be assigned later than some others, not merely after 783, when a messenger arrived in Rome the following year concerning the marriage to Fastrada, the new queen, but after 789. The request for the Sacramentary moves me to this conclusion.

Since it is agreed among scholars that Roman chant and liturgy prevailed in Gaul through the assistance of Pippin and Charles, as regards chant, in the year 787, as Pagius showed with Baronius’s support (no. 9), Charles brought back with him from Rome, on the authority of the monk of Angoulême, Theodore and Benedict. One was sent to Metz and the other to Soissons to teach all Gaul the chant according to the Roman rite. Charles labored greatly thereafter to abolish the Ambrosian office and to have the Gregorian rite received everywhere according to Roman custom; this was achieved only with considerable effort, as Durandus says (*Book V*, chap. 2, no. 5).

In the year 789, however, I find a provision in the Aachen Capitularies (chap. 80) that monks should perform Roman chant fully and in due order through the nocturnal or gradual office, according to what our father, King Pippin of blessed memory, had striven to establish when he removed the Gallican chant for the sake of unanimity with the apostolic see and the peaceful concord of the holy Church of God.

Again, fifteen years later—that is, in the fifth year of the emperor—I find another decree of Charles (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 1183), preserved in the *First Appendix to the Capitularies* (chap. 2), which orders that chant be learned and performed according to the order and custom of the Roman Church, and that the singers return from Metz.

These matters concern Roman chant introduced into Gaul from the year 757 (ep. 16, elsewhere 25, and 35, elsewhere 43). Charles is said to have restored it, when it had become greatly corrupted, by bringing the finest teachers from Rome in 787; they instructed the Gauls in it for nearly eighteen years.

The matter is different in the case of Roman liturgy, which Charles was the first of all to establish as something the Gauls should embrace. Indeed, Roman Mass is mentioned in Gaul only in Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 219, as Bona observes (*Liturgy*, book I, chap. 12, no. 1), and also in chapter 70, as Vezzosi notes (*Preface to Thomas*, vol. VI, no. 25, note 3).

It is clear that Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, collected the four books with their three appendices in the year 827, as he himself admits. Benedict the Levite added the following three books with a fourth appendix in 845, according to Pagius (no. 17), or in 847, according to Baronius (no. 12). Thus neither author is a particularly reliable witness in chronological matters. Ansegisus confused the certain capitularies of both Charles and Louis the Pious; and Benedict, mixing certain matters with uncertain ones, gathered materials older even than Pippin. The collection of Labbe is safer.

Since in the year 789 there is no mention whatever of the Roman liturgy (Aachen Capitularies, chap. 70 and the two following chapters), there can be no doubt that Charles began considering the introduction of that liturgy into Gaul only after that time. [Col. 0436C] Consequently, the Sacramentary sought from Rome and sent—as this letter testifies—must indicate a period subsequent to the Aachen capitulary. — Cenn.].

As the most reverend and holy Bishop Hucbertus completed his journey and reached the threshold of the blessed apostolic princes Peter and Paul, fulfilling the vows of his desire, he presented us with your splendid and eminent royal messages of triumph [Col. 0435B]. We opened and reread them with the greatest love of heart, and found in them your most vibrant and mellifluous greeting addressed to us. But what we desired and awaited even more eagerly [Note: This seems redundant. — Grets.] was the great mass of information [Note: According to Lambecius’s reading, the pontiff seems to have been without royal letters for some time; I therefore prefer to assign the letter to this year, although all the letters are said to have been included in the same codex. — Cenn.] concerning your lofty royal victory in triumph and your safety, and indeed the prosperity of all your faithful, as well as the progress and exaltation of your spiritual mother, the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church. As we looked upon all these things in your royal and mellifluous letters, our spirit was lifted up, and we gave thanks to the Redeemer of the world.

Above all, in confession of the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we do not cease frequently and humbly to beseech divine mercy for you. For toward your royal clemency we act in such a way that, whether in silence or when you make requests [Note: In the five preceding letters, after Grimoaldus’s return to Benevento, the pontiff remained completely silent both concerning the Campanian cities and concerning the territories of Rosella and Populonium. These were the two remaining matters required for the Carolingian donation to achieve its full effect. — Ed.], you do not cease striving for the progress and exaltation of your spiritual mother, the holy Roman Church, so that through your arduous struggles she may remain increasingly, irrefragably, and fittingly exalted, your worthy name may be inscribed in the heavenly book of life, and your royal memory may endure forever and ever [Note: Gentianus reads: “Strive earnestly to believe that your royal memorial will endure forever and ever.”].

Concerning the Sacramentary [Note: Ducange states that *Sacramentary* and *Book of Sacraments* are interchangeable terms for an ecclesiastical book containing the sacred liturgies for celebrating the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist. Before him, Cardinal Thomasius, in the preface to the four sacramentary codices which he edited, relies upon the testimony of the Fathers, who by antonomasia call the sacraments Christ’s body and blood. There, among many other observations reflecting his profound learning in ecclesiastical matters, he emphasizes that such books were not written merely for scholarly instruction but chiefly for the use of the Churches.

After demonstrating by many arguments that the codex he used represented the Gelasian Sacramentary, he explains why it also displays many additions made after Gregory’s time. Among other things, on Good Friday (new edition, vol. VI, p. 65), the prayer for the emperor reads: “Look favorably upon his Roman, or Frankish, empire.” Just as this clearly shows that the written codex belongs to the ninth century, so it shows that the use of the Gregorian rite among the Franks—for much evidence proves that it was written there—was adopted only very late.

Since I hear mention of the Sacramentary here for the first and last time, it seems probable to me that this letter was issued around this period, as I recently demonstrated by other arguments. Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXIII, no. 35) establishes nothing certain concerning the beginning of the Roman liturgy in Gaul; he merely notes the variety of the Gallican rite from Gregory’s replies to Augustine and from Zacharias’s letters to Boniface.

From this letter, however, if I am not mistaken, the beginning of the Carolingian undertaking is clear. In the same Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXVI, at the end), information is available about the *Book of Sacraments* used by Menardus in his edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary: it was written in the year 800 by Lantbertus, at the command of Godelgaudus, a monk and priest, for the monastery of Saint Remigius. This confirms that both the Roman liturgy and the Sacramentary sent by Adrian were gradually disseminated throughout all Gaul through the king’s efforts. — Cenn.].

As for the Sacramentary arranged long ago by our holy predecessor, the divinely inspired Pope Gregory, Paulus the grammarian requested it from us on your behalf; and according to the tradition of our holy Church we sent it through John, monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna [Note: The Ravenna monastery is indicated here; several years later Pope Paschal I gave it to Petronacius, archbishop. For, as is clear from a diploma in Ughellus (vol. II, p. 344), it stood near the palace, and there seems to have been no other monastery within the city at that time. The diploma reads: “The monastery of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, whose foundations are so called, and which lies beside the palace,” etc.

If it is permissible to conjecture amid such antiquity, the abbot of this monastery was that John whom Ughellus lists in his catalogue of archbishops between Gratiosus and Valerius, despite Bacchinius’s objection, as I stated above (ep. 93, elsewhere 71, in the note). This is neither new nor unusual, as scholars know. Abbots of monasteries near cathedrals are sometimes included in catalogues of archbishops. — Ed.], and sent it to your royal Excellency, wishing that, while we beseech this same apostle of God and your protector on behalf of your unconquered royal Excellency, he may always accompany you everywhere and make you victorious over all barbarian nations [Col. 0438A]. Together with our lady, our most excellent spiritual daughter the queen, and the noble offspring of your line, may he grant that you, reigning in this world for a long age, may reign without end with all the saints in eternal life through his intercession. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency safe.

[Col. 0437]

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS CONTAINED IN THE FIRST BOOK OF THE CAROLINE CODEX ACCORDING TO CENNIUS’S EDITION

*(The numbers in this index correspond to the bold numbers inserted in the text.)* [Note: In this index, Roman numerals refer to the column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

## A

**Acanonists**, or violators of the canons, no. 518.

**Aciulphus**, a priest, obtains from Saint Paul I the body of Saint Candidus the martyr, 381.

**Acts and Constitutum of Silvester**, remain in use throughout the eighth century, 304, 306.

**Supposititious Acts**, popular in Rome, 30.

**Precepts of the *actiones***, or diplomas, are obtained from the pontiff throughout the cities of the Pentapolis, 335.

**Adalgisus.** See **Athalgisus**.

**Adelberga**, daughter of Desiderius and sister of Athalgisus, wife of Arichis, duke of Benevento, bore him five sons, 477. She plots against Charles, 479. Her plots were about to erupt after Grimoaldus’s arrival from Gaul, 479, 483. She demands from the emperor the patriciate for her son Grimoaldus, which Arichis had been unable to obtain because death overtook him, 489.

**Adeodatus**, a subdeacon of the region, in the time of Gregory III, 9.

**Pope Adrian** gives Charles the complete collection of the Greek canons in order to restore the discipline of the Gallican Church, 33. He corrects some of those same canons, 35. He is wrongly said to have mentioned the Donation of Constantine before it arose, 305. His letters show the jurisdiction of the holy see; the contrary is maintained in vain by reversing their order, 308 ff. He establishes public prayers for the remission of sins and for Charles’s victories over barbarian nations, 318. He renews prayers for Charles when he campaigns against the Saracens of Spain in 777, 356, 366. For the Saxons defeated by Charles and converted to the faith, he orders general fasts, 462. He pours forth constant prayers for the deceased parents and Queen Hildegard, 474. He is foolishly attacked as though he cared only about temporal matters, 310 ff. He disapproves of the journey of Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, to Charles, 326. He announces the death of Constantine Copronymus, 336. He asks Charles to honor him as a spiritual kinsman, 351. He demands possession of the donation in its entirety, 345. Following the example of Stephen II, he establishes supreme dominion in the exarchate, 369. He reports that the Sabina has been received by Charles alone, 415. He sends a Roman army against the people of Terracina and Gaeta, 358. His prudence is evident in the restoration of the Church of Saint Peter at Charles’s expense, 380. He holds a hearing in the case of the abbots of Volturno, 427. Following the example of Gregory the Great, he requests distinguished horses worthy of the pontiff’s dignity, 441. He announces Athalgisus’s arrival to Charles, 477. He advises that the Beneventans, who are watching for an opportunity to defect, be restrained by arms, 478. He disapproves of Grimoaldus’s succession to the duchy of Benevento, but nevertheless leaves everything to Charles’s discretion, 479, 491, 494. He refuses Charles nothing when Charles makes reasonable requests, 508. He sends Paulinus, the accused, to Charles and wishes the same treatment to be applied to himself, so that each ruler may act against the people subject to him, 364.

**Adulterers** are to do penance for seven years, 54.

**Aegila**, an ancient name for bishops in Spain, 445. A Spanish bishop is appointed by Adrian, together with the priest John, to uphold the Catholic faith against the errors of the Spaniards, 390, 393. Ordained by Willicarius of Sens, he spreads errors in Spain, 442 ff.

**Cities of Aemilia** are enumerated, 321, 335; its inhabitants are called Ravennans, 329.

**Aeva**, “ages,” is used for “perpetual times,” 137, 170, 184, 198, 354, and frequently elsewhere.

**Paul Afiarta**, a friend of Desiderius, plots against the holy see and the pontiff, 262.

**Aimoinus’s continuator** is contrasted with the continuator of Fredegar’s continuator, 5.

**King Aistulf of the Lombards**, exercising tyranny, compels the Romans to implore the aid of the Franks, 57. Besieged at Pavia by Pippin in 755, he promises under oath to restore the exarchate, 65; he is perjured, 74; cruel toward the Romans, 80; struck by God, he dies, 190.

**Alboin**, duke of Spoleto, is badly treated by Desiderius, 154.

**Alcuin**, tutor of Charles the Great, 474.

**Alexandrian patriarch**, the determination of the date of Easter is entrusted to him by the Council of Nicaea, 395.

**Ambrosian office** falls out of use in Francia, the Gregorian office being admitted through the efforts of Charles the Great, 523.

**Ambrose**, chief notary, is sent by Stephen II as envoy to Aistulf, 57.

**Amphilochius**, bishop of Iconium, on the doctrine of the adoption of human sons, 448.

**Anastasius**, the first bishop sent by Gregory III from among the pontifical envoys to Charles Martel, 5. Anastasius the chamberlain, Adrian’s envoy to Charles the Great at the end of 774, 323; detained by the king, he is demanded back by the pontiff, 363.

**Anastasius the Librarian** dedicates the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, translated into Latin, to John VIII, 38.

**Anchard**, a faithful envoy of Charles Martel, is sent by Gregory III to the same prince, 22, 24.

**Ancona.** See **Pentapolis**.

**Holy Angels**: the sanctuary on Mount Gargano, left by Adelberga, is to be visited for political purposes by Arichis, 479.

**Angilramnus**, bishop of Metz, author of the eighty chapters attributed to Adrian, 31.

**Angla**, whom Pippin loved, is terrified by a miracle and comes to her senses, 284.

**Annals of Fulda**, concerning Charles Martel, 8.

**Annals of Metz**, concerning Gregory III’s embassy, 3.

**Ansegisus**, abbot of Fontenelle, collector of four books of capitularies with three appendices in 827; Benedict the Levite collected the remainder, 524.

**Council of Antioch**, concerning the proper celebration of Easter according to the decision of the Council of Nicaea, 452.

**Use of the Roman Antiphonary in Francia**, 148.

**An archbishop** does not exercise his office before receiving the pallium, 409.

**Vatican Archive** preserved the donations which Adrian sent to Charles the Great, 353.

**Archchancellor**, indicated by the title “protonotary,” 514.

**Arichis**, duke of Benevento, is appointed by Desiderius in 758, and his daughter Adelberga is given to him in marriage. After carrying off his father-in-law to Francia, he ceases to submit to the king of the Lombards, 123. He succeeds Liutprand, who had fled, 154. In order to restore Athalgisus, his wife’s brother, he stirs up the Neapolitans against Adrian and Charles, 376. He attacks the Amalfitans in war, but they defeat him with the assistance of the Neapolitans, 471. In 787 he is brought into order by Charles, 475. He dies the following year, when everything was prepared for conferring upon him the honor of the patriciate by the authority of the Greek emperor, etc., 488.

**Ariminum.** See **Pentapolis**.

**Artabasdus**, after overthrowing Constantine, seizes the empire, 16, 25.

**Arva**, “fields,” is inflected in place of *arvorum* and used to mean “land” in Adrian’s time, 453.

**Arvinus**, count and duke, 439, 477. Through him Adrian announces to Charles Athalgisus’s arrival in Calabria with the Greeks, 476.

**Athalgisus**, son of Desiderius, who, after his father had been taken to Francia, fled to Constantinople, is summoned by the allies to Italy, 345. He comes to Calabria in 786, 476. He dies after two years, 515.

**Doctrine of Saint Athanasius** concerning Christ, the Son of God, 446.

**Synod of Attigny**, held in 766 in accordance with King Pippin’s vow concerning the sacred images and the donation of the exarchate and the Pentapolis, in the presence of papal and Greek envoys, 229 ff.

**Atto**, abbot of Volturno, envoy of Stephen II to Aistulf, 57. Atto is one of the five envoys or representatives of Charles in 788, sent by the Beneventans to Charles with a petition, or supplicatory libellus, concerning Grimoaldus’s succession; he acts as his representative at Salerno, 482, 489.

**Doctrine of Saint Augustine** concerning Saturday fasting, 392; concerning the adoption of human beings through God’s mercy, 449.

**Hall of Saint Peter**, for his sacred confession, 224 ff., 347, 426. Also called the apostolic hall, 329, 331.

**Ausimum**, together with Ancona and Humana, was lacking from the possession acquired through Fulradus in 756, 110. It did not come under pontifical power until after 774.

**Autbertus** becomes abbot of Volturno after Pothon is slandered and deposed, 425. When he comes to the hearing in Pothon’s case, he dies unexpectedly, 427.

## B
## B

**The king’s bath.** See *Tuscia*.

**Baronius, Venerable Cardinal.** His pure method of writing concerning Saint Gregory III, 4. He published some letters of the *Codex* from the Vatican Library, but, compelled to pass over others that he had searched for in vain, 114. In treating ecclesiastical affairs, superior to Panvinio, 118; he somewhat alters Panvinio’s arguments, 119. Laws concerning the foundation of basilicas on one’s own property, 50.

**Bavarians**, or **Bajoarii**, subdued by Charles in 787, 487.

**Benedict the Levite** added three books and a fourth appendix to Ansegisus’s collection of capitularies in 845, or two years later, 524.

**Beneventans**, together with the Lombards, besiege Rome and ravage everything around it, 85. Cruel and impious, 86, 92. They implore Pippin’s pardon through Stephen II, 110. They enter into counsels contrary to the Holy See with the Greeks, 381; they are defeated by the Neapolitans after their leading men have been captured, 471. At Adelberga’s instigation they create disturbances against the Holy See and the Franks, 483. When their ambushes are discovered, Charles’s envoys save themselves by flight, 491.

**Duchy of Benevento**, transformed by Arichis into a principality, 123; subdued by Charles, 475.

**Bertrada**, queen and wife of Pippin, 206. Stephen III writes to her after Pippin’s death, and sends letters to her son Charles, 267. Desiderius attempts by cunning means to take her away from her other son, Carloman, and to win her favor and that of Charles, 268. The sharing of authority between her and Charles, 273.

**Vatican Library.** Its antiquity and development. The founder of the new library was Sixtus V, 116.

**Bourges**, metropolitan see of Aquitaine, restored through the granting of the pallium in 786, 468.

**Horatius Blancus**, annotator of Paul the Deacon, 7.

**Bobium**, or Sassina, 335.

**Boniface I (Saint).** A sentence from his letter is used by Adrian in his letter to Aegila, 443.

**Bologna and Imola** are not handed over by Aistulf to Fulrad, 108; nor by the perjured Desiderius, 111; Charles claims them for Saint Peter along with the other territories, but Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, falsely claims that they have been granted to him, 330, 334.

**Brindisi**, eastern boundary of the duchy of Benevento, 154.

**Bull**, or leaden seal: the papal letter received its name from it; its ancient example, 193.

## C

**Distinguished horses**, procured from the time of Gregory the Great for the use of the popes, 440.

**Gaeta**, conquered by papal arms, 495.

**Gaetans and Tarracinans** plan, together with the patrician of Sicily, to invade Roman Campania, 357.

**Slanders fabricated against Adrian and Charles** concerning the six cities of Campania, 516.

**Camaradum**, or wooden vault of Saint Peter’s Confession, 379.

**The six cities of Campania**—Capua, Teanum, Arpinum, Aquinum, Arces, and Sora—are granted by Charles to the Holy See in 787, 475. Adrian wishes to take possession of them through the royal envoys, 480. Documents asserting this grant, 484. Their possession is delivered by deceit, 496. It is uncertain whether they were actually possessed, 504.

**Campulus**, bishop of Gaeta, announces to Adrian Athalgis’s arrival in Calabria, 476.

**Candidus (Saint).** His body was sent to Francia, 381.

**Canon**, or collection of the canons of the Holy See, 28. The fifty Apostolic Canons are received by the Holy See at the council of Stephen III in 769, 32. The spurious ones deceived learned men through letters attributed to John III, ibid. The canons and decrees of the popes ought not to be unknown to preachers, 403. They reject a witness guilty of crime against a bishop, cleric, or monk, 430. Their observance is commended to the Spaniards, 457. They are violated by Lombard bishops through their invasion of other dioceses, 511, 517.

**Roman chant**, brought to Francia by Stephen II in 753, 205, 523.

**Four ancient chapters**, by which bishops were examined, 519.

**Capitularies of the Frankish kings**, collected by Ansegisus and Benedict, 524.

**Capua**, granted to the Holy See in 787 along with the other cities of Campania, 473. Ten of its citizens separately from the others swear an oath of fidelity to Adrian, 484, 487.

**Cardinals** were called bishops and presbyters attached to a particular church, 44 and following; they were not to be established in private oratories or basilicas, 50. In Charles’s age, only the cardinal presbyters and deacons of the Holy Roman Church attained the pontificate, 260. Paul I creates Marinus cardinal presbyter of the title of Saint Chrysogonus at King Pippin’s request, 145.

**Carisiacum.** The first donation of all is stipulated there by King Pippin and confirmed by his sons Charles and Carloman, 74.

**Carloman**, son of Charles Martel and brother of Pippin, labors, through the efforts of Saint Boniface, for the Gallican Church, 26. In 747 he assumes the monastic habit, 27, 41, 57. At Aistulf’s command and through fear of him, Optatus, abbot of Cassino, sends an envoy to his brother to turn him away from the Italian expedition, 61; Carloman dies in Francia, 113.

**Carloman**, son of Pippin and brother of Charlemagne. In 754 he is made king and patrician together with his father and brother, 73. After their father’s death, the discord that arose between the brothers is settled, 275. He had married Gilberga, just as Charles had married Hildegard, while their father was still alive, 283. For this reason both he and his brother are forbidden by Stephen III to take Desiderius’s daughter as a second wife, 281. He dies in 771, 279.

**Charles the Great**, who became emperor after the time of the *Codex Carolinus*, 61, 63. Perpetual defender of the Catholic faith and the Church; for this reason he is compared with Moses, 140. These two things Paul I demanded from him while his father was still alive, 169. He is called David on account of his piety and courage, 140. He is compared with Constantine the Great, 352. He exalted the Roman Church, as he had promised Saint Peter before his Confession, 341. He always honored Peter’s church above all others, 474, 505. He commends himself to Adrian’s prayers, 474. In 787 he brings teachers of Roman chant from Rome to Francia, 523.

So pious a prince is unjustly disparaged by an Italian annalist, 310. At the beginning of his reign, more obedient to his mother than to the pope, he marries Desiderius’s daughter; within a year, by the authority of the Holy See, he repudiates her, 264. He marries Hildegard, by whom he has sons, 327. His great love for blessed Peter and Adrian’s continual prayers subject all the barbarian nations to him; he wins a notable victory over the Lombards, 318. After a long struggle lasting many years, he conquers the Saxons and leads them to the Catholic faith, 462. He triumphs over the Saracens of Spain, 368. He overcomes the enemies of the Roman Church and defeats the duke of Friuli, 348. He defeats the Beneventans, 475, 487. When they are contemplating defection, after also taking the pope’s advice, he treats them kindly, granting them their desired duke Grimoald, 490, 494.

He comes to Rome three times during the pontificate of Adrian: in 774, when he vindicates in full his father’s donation, confirmed by himself, with the Lombard Tuscia added, 297, 521; in 781, when he grants the whole Sabine territory to Peter and his successors, 383, 415; and in 787, when he grants the six cities of the duchy of Benevento, 475 and following.

He declares the supreme authority of the pope in ecclesiastical territory by asking Adrian for the mosaics and marbles of the palace at Ravenna, 440. He demands from him that the Venetians be expelled from the Exarchate and Pentapolis, 459. He also asks whether the royal envoys ought to take part in the election of the archbishop of Ravenna, 498. Revering spiritual authority, he wishes the case of the abbots of Volturno to be judged by the pope, 427. He asks that a universal three-day fast be proclaimed for the conversion of the Saxons, 462.

Adrian, for his part, restrains Lombard bishops who violate the canons by means of Charles’s authority, 508, 510.

**Charles Martel**, mayor of Francia and under-king, 7. He is said to have been a despoiler of churches, 26, 28. Six sons of his are enumerated, 77.

**Cassiodorus.** His judgment concerning the Dionysian collection, 36.

**Castle of Felicitas**, in Lombard Tuscia, belonging by right to the Holy See from 774; an argument for the subjection of all Tuscia, 337.

**Castle of Valens**, in Roman Campania, 224.

**Defense of the Catholic faith and the Church**, one of the duties of the patriciate of Pippin, 180, 202, and of Charles, 334, and elsewhere.

**Adrian** explains the Catholic faith and discipline to Aegila, bishop of Spain, 389 and following.

**Ships of the Greeks burned at Centumcellae** by order of the pope, 370.

**Centuriators** published some letters of the *Codex Carolinus*, 114.

**Council of Chalcedon.** Its canons were not received by the Apostolic See until the seventh century was drawing to its close, 29, 303. An apocryphal summary of that council, 410.

**Handwritten document of the bishops of Lombard Tuscia**, 9.

**Office and subordination of chorepiscopi**, 43 and following.

**Christopher**, primicerius, is declared by Paul in 764 to be a completely upright and supremely trustworthy man, 216. He gives proof of his integrity in abolishing Constantine’s schism and in the election of Stephen III in 769, 243 and following. Desiderius blinds him and his son Sergius, 262, 267. In a letter of impaired reliability, Stephen III seems to declare them guilty of treason, 268.

**Christ** is called by the Spaniards the adoptive Son of God in an erroneous sense, 445 and following.

**Four cities**—Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera—invaded by the Lombards in the Roman duchy, 9.

**Cities of the Exarchate and Pentapolis**, possession of which the Holy See took through Fulrad, the royal envoy, 65 and following. Those whose possession it did not take, 66, 105. Paul calls them “our cities of the Roman republic,” 163.

**Cities of Lombard Tuscia**, granted at Charles’s first arrival, 480.

**Cities with their entire territories** are granted to Saint Peter by the Frankish kings, 384.

**Keys of Saint Peter’s Confession**, 5; sent as a supplicatory petition to Charles Martel, 22. For it is clear that the popes were accustomed to join God and blessed Peter in their petitions and appeals to the kings of Francia, 147, 157, 158, and frequently elsewhere.

**Clerics and monks** who do not remain faithful to their chosen vocation: what penalty is imposed on them, 47.

**Roman clergy**, accused of incontinence before Charles, defended by Adrian, 371.

**Clusium**, a city obedient to its duke, 337.

**Dionysian collection of canons**, first used by Saint Zachary, 28. It lacks the principal decretals, 37. There was no Roman collection in Adrian’s time, 303. The character of all the collections, 37.

**Comacchio**, a city of Emilia, invaded by Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, 321.

**Comita**, envoy of Stephen II, 89, 96. See *Papal envoys*.

**Counts and dukes** govern cities indiscriminately, 439.

**Co-fathers**: the popes greatly desired to become co-fathers of the kings of Francia. For this reason kings of the Franks are found with the titles of co-fathers and patricians of equal antiquity. Thus Stephen II received Pippin’s sons from the sacred font in 754 and later made them patricians, 73. His successor Paul I, scarcely created pope, boasts that he received Pippin’s daughter while absent, 137. Stephen III demands from Carloman that he too enjoy the same honor, 279. Finally, in 781, Adrian receives at Rome Carloman, Charles’s son, who was thereafter to be called Pippin, 309, 351, 353.

**Four general councils**, fully received by the Apostolic See toward the end of the seventh century, 30. Charles receives six general councils from Adrian at his first arrival, together with a Greek summary of their rules, 34, 299. The council of Calchuth, held in 787 by legates of the Holy See to correct many abuses among the English, 505. The council of Jerusalem, held about 760 concerning sacred images, 256.

**Confession of Saint Peter**, where continuous prayers are offered for Charles, 417. See *Hall*; *Saint Peter’s Confession*.

**Constantinopolitan fleet**, and all Greek efforts against the Roman Church, thwarted by the Beneventans under Duke Grimoald in 789, 515.

**Constantinopolitan canons**, not received by the Holy See before the end of the seventh century, 29.

**Adrian praises Constantine’s baptism** from the Acts of Sylvester, 305.

**Constantine Copronymus** grants Zachary the estates of Nymphae and Normiae, 16. He demands the Exarchate back from the Lombards, 11. Stephen II asks him for assistance, ibid. He refuses to provide aid to Rome, 58. His negligence proves useful to papal rule, 64. He dies in 776, 336.

**Constantine**, called the neophyte pseudo-pope, 240, 243.

**Constantine and Paul**, accused by slanders before Charles, are defended by Adrian, 502.

**Constitution of Constantine**, an excerpt of which survives from the eighth century, 307.

**Consulate**, of little authority at Rome in Adrian’s time, 5, 353.

**Cosmas**, patriarch of Alexandria, to Paul concerning sacred images, 192.

**Cresconius’s Breviary**, comprising 300 chapters, indicates several canons and letters in each chapter, 32. The canons and letters are taken from the Dionysian collection, 28.

**Cross**, sent as a gift by Charles in 787, placed by Adrian in the Vatican church, 474. He later sent another to Leo III, for use in processions, ibid.

**Nineteen-year cycle**, approved by the Council of Nicaea, 396.

## D

**Decrees of the popes and canons** against invaders of another’s diocese, 517.

**Decretals and canons**, not to be ignored by preachers, 403.

**Defender; helper.** See *Patrician*.

**Desiderius** is chosen king of the Lombards with Fulrad’s support, 109. Stephen II praises him for his promised restoration of all the cities lacking from Pippin’s donation, 66, 110. He breaks faith, 121, 137. Together with George, the imperial envoy, he begins plotting evil against Rome, 153. In 758 he deceitfully negotiates at Rome for the restoration of Imola and the other cities belonging to the donation, so that he may recover his hostages from Francia, 155. In 761 the Beneventans, Spoletans, and Tusci obey him, 176. He restores the movable property but retains the territories of the cities and their estates, and again invades what he had restored, 187. When he intends to give his daughter in marriage to Tassilo, he forbids the papal envoys to go to Francia, 215. His wickedness and audacity toward the pope, 219. He alternately restores and recovers what had been taken by the armies, 231. He comes to Rome under pretext of prayer, 262. He does not cease sowing discord at Rome and in the Exarchate, 265. He extorts from Stephen III letters against Dodo, Charles’s envoy, and against Christopher and Sergius, whom he had blinded and who favored him, 269. The same Stephen testifies to Charles and Carloman that Desiderius had restored nothing, 277. Adrian calls him a tyrant, 476.

**God and Peter** were customarily set before the Franks by the Roman pontiffs so that they might defend the Church more zealously, 22, 345, 367. The defeat of the Lombards is ascribed to both, 75. Arichis and his elder son Romuald die while negotiations with the Greeks are being conducted at Naples against the Holy See; an evident miracle of God, 489.

**Deacons and presbyters** are excluded from penance, 49.

**Paul the Deacon**, author of the *History of the Lombards*, 4, 7.

**A woman dismissed from her office or by her husband** is not permitted to marry, 48.

**Dioecetes**, or administrator of Sicily, together with the Neapolitans, supports the Beneventans’ schemes against the Holy See, 484.

**Dionysius Exiguus** is taken by Adrian for Saint Dionysius of Alexandria, 397, 452.

**Discipline** is restored to some extent in Francia, 27. Monastic, or regular discipline, extremely strict, 435.

**Supreme papal dominion** before the donations, 80, 84, 91, 95. After the donations and the expulsion of the Lombards, 358. It did not include Spoleto, 379. It is called the Roman republic, 345. It contained entire cities and territories, 384, 440.

**Dodo**, envoy of Charlemagne, is accused, through Desiderius’s intrigues, of treason, 268.

**Domna** is the title given to Queen Bertrada, 210; to Gisla, 337.

**Domni Pippinus, Carolus, and Carolomannus**: 237, 285, 322, 323, and frequently in the titles of letters.

**First donation**, made by Pippin in Francia and confirmed with their own hands by his sons, the kings, in 754, 81. Stephen III calls it an enlargement of Roman dominion, 85, 91; an extension of the province by the Roman Senate and People, 144; made to Peter and his vicar, 239; for the remission of sins, 228.

**Second donation of Charlemagne**, in 774, 297, 321; made to the divine Peter and his vicars for the salvation of his soul, 325, 330, 333, 341, 384. See *Charles*.

**Donation of Constantine**, a forgery that emerged in the middle of the ninth century, 304, 306. The genuine [documents] of that Constantine, the patricians, and others, 353.

**All donations** made for the salvation of the donor’s soul, 405.

**Droctegangus**, abbot and envoy of Pippin, negotiates at Rome concerning Stephen II’s journey to Francia, 69. He carries the pope’s letters to the king, 58.
