**Dromones**, warships of the Sicilians, 155. See *Fleet*.

**Eastern boundaries of the duchy of Benevento**, 154.

**Duchies of Spoleto and Tuscia**, offered by Charles to Saint Peter while supreme dominion was retained, 342.

**Dukes** belonged both to the pope and to the Frankish kings, 502.

**Dukes of cities**, 437.

**Frankish dukes** are asked by Stephen II to assist Pippin, who is bringing help to the Church, 72.

**Four dukes**—of Spoleto, Benevento, Friuli, and Clusium—join in alliance against the pope and Charles, 344.

## E

**Ecbert’s Penitential Book**, 304.

**The Church and the Catholic faith** are undertaken for defense by Pippin and his successors, 142, 334.

**Defense of the Church against Greek heresy**, always sought by the popes, 494.

**Adrian complains** that people who dissipate the Church’s goods do so through simony, 518.

**Preeminence of Saint Peter’s church**, 505.

**Canonical election**, vindicated by Adrian, 518 and following. The archbishop of Ravenna is subjected to the Holy See, 499.

**Error of Elipandus and Ascaricus**, Spanish bishops, concerning the adoptive Son of God, 445.

**Embolum**, or postscript, 329, 334.

**No blessing before the patrician**, 159.

**Bishops**, through their prayers, obtain victories for a people at war, 42. They are forbidden to handle temporal weapons, 434. One who receives deserters is excommunicated, 51.

**Oath of the bishops of Tuscia**, 9.

**Pisan, Lucanian, and Regian bishops**: Charles is asked to send them back to their churches, 319.

**The almost completely excised subject of a letter** is ordered by Charles to be entered in the *Codex* for the benefit of the Roman Church, 153.

**Letter delivered to Arvinus** concerning Beneventan affairs is missing, 494.

**Distinguished horses**, requested for papal majesty, 441.

**Ermenald’s daughter**, after abandoning the monastery, marries, 511, 518.

**Examination of bishops** before consecration in Adrian’s age, 519.

**The Exarchate** invaded by the Lombards, 11. It and Pentapolis are said to have been restored because they belonged to Saint Peter by right, 76. He calls both provinces an extension of Roman dominion belonging to the Roman Senate and People, 144. Through Desiderius’s intrigues they are inclined toward defection, 265. Their peoples are subject to the pope, 522. See *Donation*.

## F

**Fastrada**, Charles’s wife after Hildegard, 424, 431, 435.

**Faenza, Imola, and Ferrara** are promised for restoration by Desiderius, 109.

**Origin of the Felician heresy**, 383, 390.

**Cresconius follows Ferrandus’s collection**, 37.

**The duchy of Ferrara and Comacchio** are invaded by Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, 321.

**Defense of the Catholic faith and the Apostolic See**, the two duties of the patriciate, 140 and following, and frequently in the *Codex*.

**Boundaries of papal dominion and of the Frankish monarchy**, clearly named, 464.

**Flagellation** is imposed on erring monks, 435.

**Fleury** criticizes the letter written in Peter’s name for its untimely erudition, 98.

**Fulrad**, abbot, son of Jerome, Pippin’s brother, 77. He takes possession of the cities of the Exarchate and Pentapolis on behalf of the Holy See, 65. Together with his companions, he becomes an eyewitness to Lombard cruelty, 80.

**Formata**, necessary for bishops traveling from a metropolitan see, 51.

**Forobonum**, today Foronovo in the Sabine region, 223, 406.

**After the defeat of Rodgaud**, duke of Friuli, Charles substitutes Marcarius for him, 372.

**The Franks** are asked to bring aid to the Romans, 1 and following. Although negligent, they are not sought for fourteen years, 11. As soon as they come into Italy to defend the Holy See, they return victorious to Francia. From this began their great love for the prince of the apostles, 23, 76.

**A corrupt passage in Fredegar’s continuator** concerning the twofold embassy of Gregory III, 2, 7.

**Fulgentius (Saint)** to Eugyppius, against the Pelagians, concerning predestination, 445 and following.

## G

**Gabel**, a royal count, is mistreated by Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, 335.

**History of the monastery of Saint Hilary at Galliate**, 437.

**Gallican bishops**, reverers of the decrees of the popes, 52.

**Garamannus**, Charles’s duke in the kingdom of Italy, is requested by Adrian to be removed because he had invaded the goods of the Exarchate, 460.

**Garinodus**, duke, and **Grimoaldus**, envoys of Desiderius to the Holy See, 110.

**Gasindi** among the Lombards: an office resembling that of the Gothic *gardingae*, 511.

**Gausfridus**, a Lombard, falls into Allo’s ambush, 317, 319. He comes under suspicion with Charles, 363.

**George**, cardinal bishop of Ostia, accompanies Stephen II to Francia, 83. He is sent by the same pope to Pippin, 88. Again he goes with John the *regionarius* and the *sacellarius*, 112. He and Peter, cardinal presbyter, are detained by Pippin in Francia with Paul the pope’s consent; in exchange, the pope detains Wulfard and Collega at Rome, 230 and following.

**George**, primicerius of the singers, dies, 203.

**George**, *protosecretarius*, together with John the *silentiarius*, carries out the emperor’s embassy to Pippin in 755, 112. In 758, however, he makes an alliance with Desiderius to seize Ravenna and conquer Otranto, with the assistance of the Sicilians, 155.

**A dispensation for recently converted Germans**, in the fourth degree, is granted by Gregory II, 53.

**Gilberga**, Carloman’s wife, after his death takes refuge with her sons with Desiderius, 279.

**Gisila**, Pippin’s daughter, later abbess of the monastery of Chelles, 137. She is refused to Constantine Copronymus for his son, 285. Desiderius unsuccessfully asks Bertrada for her for his son Athalgis, 287.

**The Greeks** always frighten Paul I with threats, never with arms, 128. They are said to be preparing to march against Rome and Ravenna, 176. They practice piracy; Adrian burns their ships at Centumcellae, 370. Their proximity seems threatening to the duchy of Benevento, 377. They enter into counsels contrary to the Holy See with the Beneventans, 381. Their rule in Italy does not extend beyond Calabria and Naples, 497.

**Gregorian office**, received by the Gauls after the rejection of the Ambrosian, 523.

**Gregory the Great (Saint)** venerates the four synods as he venerates the four Gospels, insofar as they condemn heresies, 29. He testifies that in his age the bodies of saints were not moved, 381. He says that it dishonors papal majesty to have wretched horses or excellent little donkeys, 441.

**Gregory III** writes two letters to Charles Martel, 1. Learned men abuse the meaning of these letters for their own purposes, 17. He counts the years of the emperor, 25. He writes a penitential book entitled *Judicia*, 30.

**Gregory Nazianzen (Saint)**, concerning the two natures of Christ, 447.

**Gregory of Nyssa**, concerning the adoption of human beings as sons, 448.

**Gregory**, presbyter of Capua, reveals to Adrian the schemes of Adelberga and the Beneventans, 487, 489.

**Grimo**, abbot of the monastery of Corbie. See *Royal envoys*.

**Grimoaldus**, son of Arichis, duke of Benevento, is requested as successor by Charles after the death of his father and his elder brother Romuald; he was then a hostage with Charles, 3, 477. Charles sends him to Adrian against Adrian’s will, 489.

**Gundibrandus**, duke of the city of Florence, 437.

## H

**Haistulf**, Lombard king, besieges the city, 21. See *Aistulf*.

**Hegumenus**, or abbot, 632.

**Eleutherius and Gregory of Ravenna**, wicked men, 421.

**Hermembert**, a name frequent in Gaul, 395.

**Archbishop of Bourges**, comes to Rome for the pallium, 467. See *Royal envoys*.

**Severe winter** in 764 in the East and West, 209.

**Hilary of Poitiers (Saint)**, doctrine concerning adoption, 450.

**Monastery of Saint Hilary at Galliate**, founded by Abbot Hilarus, 437.

**Hildebrand**, duke of Spoleto, dies in 789, 515.

**Queen Hildegard**, Adrian’s co-mother, dies on the day before the Kalends of May in 783, 420.

**Hilderic**, made duke of Spoleto by the Lombards, 21.

**Peter**, founder of the Spanish Church, and his successors, 444. Before Adrian, Saint Innocent had testified to this, ibid.

**Spanish error concerning Easter**, differing from that of the Quartodecimans, 445, 451; their other errors, 457.

**Bishop of the island of Istria**, blinded, 372. Its territory did not belong by right to the Holy See, 373.

**Homicides**: communion is denied to a deliberate murderer until the end of life; to an involuntary murderer, after seven or five years of penance, 53 and following.

**Night clock**, sent to Pippin by Paul I, 148.

**Hospitals in the mountains**, for receiving pilgrims, 437.

**Hucbald**, envoy of Charlemagne, restores Michael, intruder at Ravenna, to his proper order at Stephen III’s request, 265.

**Hugbert**, bishop, comes to the threshold of Charles bearing letters, 524.

**Hypocartosis.** See *Camaradum*.

## I

**Sacred images**, violated by the Greeks, cause the Romans’ revolt, 14. Burned by the Lombards, 86, 92. Stephen II proposes that they be vindicated to Pippin, 111. Their defense, together with that of the Catholic faith, is the chief concern of the popes, 126 and frequently in the *Codex*. It is likewise the chief cause of the Greeks’ estrangement from the Holy See, 128, 177. They are vigorously defended by the patriarchs of the East, 192, 256. To establish their veneration in Francia, the bodies of Saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius are transferred there, 213. **Immo**, Pippin’s envoy to Stephen II, 134. See *Royal envoys*.

**Imola**, together with the other cities whose possession Fulrad did not deceitfully take, is promised by Desiderius for restoration to the Holy See, 150. Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, claims it for himself together with Bologna, 330.

**The Greek emperors** seek to win over the Frankish kings through envoys and letters, 126. They accuse Paul I of correspondence with Constantinople, namely, the letters he was writing in defense of the sacred images, 216.

**A statement of orthodox faith** was customarily issued by the pope himself even in the eighth century, 466.

**Innocent I (Saint)**, concerning the fast of Friday and Saturday, 391.

**Italy**: in the eighth century a small part of it obeys the emperor of the East, 127. Dukes and counts governed its cities, 472. Lombardy is commended to Charles as subject to vices, especially afflicted by the stain of simony, 511, 518.

**Itherius**, envoy of Bertrada and Charles, praised by Adrian, 272. See *Royal envoys*.

## J

**Fast of Friday and Saturday**, by the authority of the Fathers, 391; a three-day fast proclaimed for the conversion of the Saxons, 462.

**John VIII** decrees that all canons and decretals are to be accepted, 38.

**John Chrysostom (Saint)**, doctrine concerning the adoption of human beings, 448.

**Book of John the Deacon concerning the Lateran church**, spurious, 247.

**Vision of John the monk**, incredible, 434.

**Judges**, namely dukes and counts in Francia, 227; Charles establishes them at Pavia, 332.

**Julian**, cardinal presbyter concerned with discipline, promotes the Dionysian collection, 37.

**Oath of fidelity** to Saint Peter, the pope, and Charles in the Exarchate, 334.

**Justellus**, concerning the collection of canons, less accurately, 36.

**The ancient right of the Holy See** is falsely included in the Dionysian collection, 37.

## K

**Kyrie eleison**—three hundred repetitions for Charles’s victories over barbarian nations, 318.

## L

**Labbe**, after seeing the Gretser edition of the *Codex Carolinus*, published more accurate summaries of the letters, 120.

**Lombard envoy of Pippin.** See *Royal envoys*.

**Date of the Lombard expedition**, 21.

**Lombard cruelty and impiety**, 84, 86, 92. Their threatening letters and obstinacy against the Holy See, 223, 240. In difficult times they were accustomed to entrust more to oral communication than to letters, 261. They sell slaves to the Saracens, 369. They provide a bad example by returning from the monastery to the secular world, 511. Their bishops invade other dioceses, 509, 517. The duke of Friuli and his allies attempt to seize their kingdom from Charles, 345. See *Aistulf, Desiderius, Pippin, Charles*.

**Porphyry stone of the Vatican basilica.** See *Table*.

**Legates of the Holy See** celebrate the council of Calchuth, 505.

**Leo (Saint)**, his doctrine concerning the adoption of human beings as sons of God, 450.

**Leo**, archbishop of Ravenna, elected after the intrusion of Michael, is carried away to Ariminum, 266. He invades the Exarchate and attempts to win over the people of Pentapolis through his envoy Theophylact, 321. Following Sergius’s example, he causes Adrian trouble, 323. He goes to Charles, against Adrian’s wishes, 326. He intercepts the letters of the patriarch of Grado to the pope, and Adrian laments that Leo broke its seal, 328.

**Leo**, imperial Greek ruler, unsuccessfully attempts to corrupt Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, 178.

**Leo and Constantine**, impious Greek Augusti, 14.

**Agreement between the *Liber Pontificalis* and the *Codex Carolinus***, 110.

**Litanies**, in the tenth century, consisting of one hundred *Kyrie*, one hundred *Christe*, and one hundred *Kyrie*, 463.

**Letters of the *Codex Carolinus*** fabricated through fear of the Lombards, 124.

**Liuthericus.** See *Royal envoys*.

**Liutprand**, with his son Hildebrand, kings of the Lombards, 20.

**Liutprand**, duke of Benevento, flees to Otranto through fear of Desiderius, 154.

**Testimony of Louis II** concerning the Frankish kings by apostolic authority, 60.

**Lights, the poor, and pilgrims** were supported from the revenues of the estates, 111.

## M
The Magdeburg Centuriators know them from Panvinio’s Vatican manuscript, 117. Maginarius, abbot of the Dionysian monastery, successor of Fulradus. See “Royal Envoys.” Mallianum, today an episcopal see of Sabina, 406. Slaves are sold by the Lombards to the Saracens, 369. The mansionarius of the confession of Saint Peter serves as envoy, 227. Marcarius is made duke of Friuli by Charles in 776, 372. The Virgin Mary, the angels, and others are invoked by Stephen II when he implores Pippin’s aid for the defense of the City and the Church, at a time when Greek impiety was especially powerful, 75, 81. Marinus is created cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus at Pippin’s request, 148. “Guilty of treason,” 129. “Lest he fall into destruction,” Paul asks Pippin to allow Wilcarius, vicar of the Apostolic See, to create a bishop in Gaul, 160. “He is restored to his former state,” 209. Martin of Braga publishes a collection of canons useful to clergy and laity, 38. Mauritius, bishop of Istria, blinded, 372. Mauritius, duke of Rimini, disturbs the Pentapolis after entering into an alliance with Desiderius, 266. Paul consecrates the altar-table donated to Stephen II by Pippin and set up by the royal envoys in the confession of blessed Peter, 224. He celebrates Mass upon it and decrees that it shall remain there forever, 225. It is perhaps the very one whose inscription, attached to the wall of the basilica, records the division of the bones, ibid. The authority of the metropolitan in the province, 43. Michael, after the death of Sergius, seizes the see of Ravenna, 265. Migetius, an ancient name in Occitania, 445. “Imperial Envoys.” In 754, John the silentiary and George the protosecretary, 112, 160; the silentiary remains in Francia and obtains royal letters for the emperor, ibid. Ten years later, Synesius the eunuch and Anthimus. The latter is sent back; the former is detained in Francia, 213. Around 763, royal and papal envoys set out for Constantinople, 208. In 787, Ischamus and Leo come with Athalgis to Calabria, 477. The following year they go to Naples, where the Beneventan defection is directed against the Holy See and Charles, 485. Envoys of the monastery of Galliatum, 438.

### Envoys of the Roman Pontiffs

Of Gregory III to Charles Martel: Anastasius, bishop, and Sergius, priest, 5. In 739, Anchartus, 22.

Of Stephen II. In 754, Wilharius, bishop of Nomentum, 78, 83. In 755, George, cardinal-bishop of Ostia; Warnearius, abbot and royal envoy; Thomaricus; and Comita, 88, 96. In 756, the same George, bishop, and John, regionary and sacristan, 112.

Of Paul I. In 757, unnamed envoys, 134, 137, 146. In 758, Gregory, bishop, and Stephen, priest, 151. In 759, Peter, priest, 164; George, bishop, 167. In 761, Peter, first of the defenders, 181, 184. In 763, John, subdeacon and abbot, and Peter, first defender, 202. In 764, John, subdeacon and abbot, and Pamphilus, regionary defender, return from Francia with Flavinus, the royal envoy, 212. Philip, priest, and Ursus the faithful, on behalf of Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, 215. In 766, Peter, regionary notary, and John, mansionarius of the confession of Saint Peter, 227.

Of Constantine the Neophyte. In 777, Christopher, priest, and Anastasius, regionary notary, 256.

Of Stephen III. In 768, Sergius, nomenclator, 259. Anastasius, first defender, and Gemmulus, sent to Desiderius, 263. In 770, Peter, priest, and Pamphilus, regionary defender, 287.

Of Hadrian. In 774, Anastasius, 319. Andrew, bishop, and Anastasius, chamberlain, 323. In 775, Andrew, bishop, and Pardus, abbot, 332. In 776, Stephen, sacristan, goes to Beneventum, where treaties were being negotiated, 344. In 777, Philip, bishop, and Megistus, archdeacon—the date of whose embassy is uncertain, for they are mentioned here as returning. Philip and Andrew, bishops, and Theodore, Hadrian’s nephew, consul, 353, 356. Andrew and Valentinus, bishops, 362. In 781, Agatho, deacon, and Theodore, consul, 385. In 782, Stephen, formerly sacristan, 387. In 788, Crescens and Hadrian, dukes, go into the Beneventan duchy with the royal envoys concerning possession of the six cities, 496.

### Royal Envoys of the Frankish Princes

Of Charles Martel: Grimo, abbot of Corbie; Sigibert, recluse of Saint-Denis. In 732.

Of King Pippin. In 754, Folradus, priest and abbot, with companions, 77. In 755, Warnearius, abbot, 88, 97. In 756, Folradus and his companions, 108. In 757, Immo, 134; Folradus and Rodbertus, 156; Wulfardus and his companions, 137; Langbardus, 145. In 759, Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, “of the king of the Franks,” and Autharius, duke, 163. In 760, Droctegangus and Wulfardus, abbots, 169, 171. In 761, Wilcarius, bishop; Felix, a religious man; and Ratbertus, an illustrious man, 175; Vidmarus and Gerbertus, abbots, and Hugbaldus, an illustrious man, 186. In 763, Haribertus, abbot, and Dodo, count, 200. In 764, Flavinus, chaplain, 211. In 765, Andrew and Gundericus, 222, 230. In 766, Wulfardus and his companions, 228. In 767, Wilcarius, bishop; Dodo; and Wichardus, most faithful, 239.

Of Charles, Carloman, and Bertrada. In 769, Dodo, of Carloman, 267; Itherius, of Charles and Bertrada, 272. In 770, Gauzibertus, bishop; Fugbertus, a religious man; Ansfredus; and Helmgarius, of Charles and Carloman, 275; Beraldus, abbot, and Aubertus, an illustrious man, of Carloman, 278. In 773, Hucbaldus, of Charles, 265, 499.

Of Charlemagne. In 776, Possessor, bishop, and Rabigaudus, abbot, 340, 347. In 780, Ado, deacon, 378. In 782, Itherius, abbot, and Maginarius, chaplain, 387; Peter, bishop of Pavia, on behalf of Aegila, 390. In 783, Maginarius, abbot, on behalf of the transfer of the Sabine territory, 414; George, bishop, 416. In 784, Possessor, archbishop of Embrun, 426; Garamannus, duke, 433; Arvinus, duke, to obtain mosaics and marbles from Hadrian out of the palace at Ravenna, 439. In 786, Andrew, abbot of Luxeuil, 461; Itherius and Maginarius, abbots, 465. In 788, Roro, chaplain, and Betto, 476; Atto, deacon; Gotteramnus, usher; Maginarius, abbot; Joseph, deacon; and Liuthericus—the five envoys at the time of the Beneventan uprising, 481 ff. In 789, Hermembertus, priest, on behalf of the rite of electing the archbishop of Ravenna, 498; unnamed envoys with the envoys of Offa, king of the Mercians, 507. In 790, Bernardus, bishop, and Rado, abbot and protonotary, 514.

They were received with the greatest honor wherever they entered the territory of the Church, 340. They held hearings at Rome at the pope’s demand, 131. When an important matter arose, they were detained at Rome, 153. Sometimes they were sent to transfer possession of cities and so forth to the Roman pontiff, 332. At Rome and in Francia, the royal and papal envoys were to be treated with equal honor, 522. Many matters not expressed in the letters were entrusted to them for settlement, 225.

Monks who have attained clerical status must remain in their adopted state, 49. They may advance to the episcopate by stages, ibid. Deserters are punished, 54. Likewise those who abandon their adopted state, 47. The monks of Volturnum voluntarily go to Charles in order to repel accusations, 431. Remigius, Pippin’s brother, learns the Roman chant from Simeon, first of the singers, 204. Uniform monasticism in Gaul in the time of Saint Boniface of Mainz, who propagated the order of Saint Benedict, 43. The monastery of Saint Sylvester is founded by Paul I in his own house, 236. The monastery of Saint Sylvester at Soracte, together with three others subject to it, is granted to Pippin, 193. History of Galliatum, 437. Nuns are kept away from the altar and forbidden to perform the duties of men, 46. Unveiled women, if they marry, are to be admitted to penance, 52. Veiled women, or professed nuns, if they marry, are excluded from penance as long as the husband lives, 52. Women who voluntarily undertake the religious state sin if they marry before profession, 55. Moria was a place sixty miles from Constantinople, 418. Pippin is compared with Moses and David because he liberated the Church from oppression, 107. See “Charlemagne.” By the example of Moses and Joshua, bishops obtain victories through prayer, 42. Mosaics and marbles from the palace at Ravenna are granted to Charles when he requests them, 440.

## N

Narnia, a city of the Roman duchy, is restored to the Romans through fear of Pippin before the donation takes effect, 66. The same city, together with other Roman cities, is invaded by the Lombards before possession of the exarchate, 87, 93. Natalis Alexander and Peter de Marca are less than correct concerning the old and the new pontifical law, 39. The Neapolitans act deceitfully with Hadrian, on the advice of Arichis, duke of Beneventum, 376. Nestorius, blaspheming, called the Son of God a mere man, 445. The doctrine of the Council of Nicaea concerning Christ, the Son of God, 446. Concerning the proper celebration of Easter, 452. He taught that it should be postponed until the twenty-first day of the moon, not the twenty-second, in accordance with the error of the Spaniards, 454. Nicholas V founded the Vatican Library; Sixtus IV completed it, 116. A notary and chancellor are sometimes the same person, 514. Marriages with two brothers or two sisters are forbidden; the degrees of affinity are explained, 53. Constantine Copronymus gives Nymphas and Normias, estates of the Roman Church, 16.

## O

Offa, king of the Mercians in England. A fable and a short index are attached to him, 503, 506. He makes his kingdom tributary to the Holy See, 505. The military and civil offices of the pontiffs are very similar to the royal offices, 502. The seven palatine offices: the first of these is the primicerius, etc., 247. *Opere* used for *idcirco*, or something similar, 385. Optatus, abbot of Cassinum, is sent by Stephen II to Aistulf, together with Atto of Volturnum, 57, 70. He recalls his monks from Francia, 113. Constant prayers are offered for Charles and his parents who have died, 474. The laws governing the erection of oratories, or basilicas, on private land, 50. Episcopal ordinations in Rome from other dioceses in the eighth century, 408. Constantine Copronymus sends an organ as a gift to Francia, 148.

## P

The discipline concerning the pallium, established in Gaul in 743 by Saint Boniface of Mainz, continues in the age of Charlemagne, 467. Hincmarus and his more recent followers attempt, but in vain, to undermine it, 468. Panvinio testified that in his own time the letters of the Carolingian Codex existed in the Vatican Library, 115. He is the author of the arguments in the Centuriators and Baronius, 118. The readings found in Labbe are more accurately corrected, 120. Account must be taken of the same matters, 133. The same author, after devoting himself late and for a short time to the affairs of the Church, completed a work on the pontiffs and cardinals, 116, 119. Pardus, abbot. See “Envoys of the Pontiffs.” *Parochia* is customarily understood as “diocese,” 510. When Easter is to be celebrated, 452. The true doctrine of the limits of Easter and the controversy between the Latins and Alexandrians, 396. The patriciate of the Frankish kings is conferred upon Pippin by Stephen II, and upon his sons in 753, through royal anointing, 11, 60. Its true character: the defense of the Catholic faith and of the Roman Church, 73, 189, 460, 500. The patriciate is attributed to Peter in the exarchate, and to Charles in the City, 294, 521. The imperial patriciate is something quite different, 74, 295, 488. In the Codex, the Roman patrician is called “guardian,” 136; “defender,” 142; “helper,” 144; “defender and liberator of the Church,” 150; “liberator of the holy Church of God and of its special people,” 153.

The patrimonies of Calabria and Sicily are invaded by the Greeks, 13, and recovered, 111. The Campanian patrimony is sought by Stephen III, 272, and is distinct from that of Naples, 376. The Sabine patrimony is also called the territory, 384. The patrimonies of Tuscany, Spoleto, Beneventum, and Corsica, of the most ancient grant of the Greek emperors, and others, are granted for the salvation of their souls, 353. A certain Paulinus writes apocryphal material concerning Theodosius II, 410.

Paul I, before becoming pope, is sent by his brother Stephen II to Aistulf, 57. He succeeds him, 114. He is more concerned with the Catholic faith and the sacred images than with temporal rule, 126. During his pontificate no increase is made to Pippin’s donation, 125. The order of his letters is confused, 129 ff. Arguments are found in the Centuriators and Baronius, 114. He is constantly troubled by the double fear of the Lombards and the Greeks, 121. He reports the Greek schemes to the king, 178. He urgently requests a royal envoy to remain at Rome against those same Greeks, 181. He announces that six patricians are coming with a fleet, 219. He writes to Pippin at Desiderius’s request, 149. In other letters he dispels the credibility of the earlier letters, 158. He promises that he will cultivate the friendship of the Lombard king if the latter keeps faith, 197. He clears himself of accusations, 207. He grants a privilege to the monastery of Saint Sylvester, 236.

There are two Pentapolises, the inland and the maritime, 335. Their cities, together with the exarchate, are donated by Pippin from Rimini as far as Gubbio, ibid. They suffer hostile acts from Desiderius, 154. They prefer to obey the pope rather than Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, 321. They report Athalgis’s arrival to Hadrian, 476. An incursion of the Persians occurs near Constantinople, with great booty, 418. Petasius, a Roman rebel in Tuscany, 14. Saint Petronilla: her oratory in the Vatican basilica, 136.

Saint Peter forgives sins, 71; grants victories, 75; through his vicar anoints Pippin and his sons as kings, 76, 82, 94, 183, 189, 222, and elsewhere throughout. He miraculously grants Pippin victory over the Lombards, 79. He chooses the Frankish kings as his special ones, 82. Immediately after God he is invoked in the most urgent petitions, 87, 345, 367. The power of the keys, 140 and throughout the Codex. The Codex of Stephen II, besieged within the City and in the greatest straits, represents Peter himself almost as a suppliant, 98. Pippin makes a donation to Peter and his vicars as a reward for his soul, 154, 156, 201, 223, 276, 321. Charles confirms and enlarges it over the most sacred body itself, 367 and elsewhere throughout the Codex, which consistently teaches that so great a treasure rests in the Vatican basilica, 100, 361, 367. Hence it was loved and enriched by Charles above all others, 474, 505. Peter and Paul are invoked together, 223, 273, 462. The doctrine of both concerning the Son of the living God, 446. Peter de Marca is less than correct concerning the old and the new pontifical law, 39.

Philip, priest, and Eustachius, duke, are sent by Stephen II as judges to administer the exarchate, 323. Pippin, mayor of the palace of Francia, 41. He becomes king by the authority of Zacharias, 69, 73. His donation at Quierzy, 321. It is preserved intact in the archive of the Holy Church, 65. The new Moses and the new David, 140, 200, 233. Paul I presents him to Charles and Carloman as one to be imitated, as faithful to God and blessed Peter, 184, 190. In all Paul’s letters he is consistently called protector and defender of the Catholic faith and of the Church, or helper and liberator, 182, 186 ff., 220. Defender of the sacred images, 196. His love for Saint Peter and the pope, 146. He hears the envoys of the Greeks only in the presence of papal officials, 212. His constancy in defending the Holy See and the Romans, 214. His concern for the condition of the Holy See and the pope, 207. He communicates the Greek letters to Paul, 215. Paul wishes to receive Pippin’s namesake son from the sacred font, 168. He warns him not to marry Angla after dismissing Bertrada, 284. Pippin, previously called Carloman, son of Charles, is received by Hadrian from the sacred font and later anointed king of Italy, 351, 383. Hearings held at Rome by Pippin’s envoys, 131. Penitents are not to be admitted to the clergy, 49. Penitential books spread throughout Europe, 30. God, arbiter of the poles, creator of heaven and earth, 207, 217. The *Pontifical Book* attributed to Anastasius, 7, 9. The equal power of pope and king within each one’s own territory, 521. The territories of Populonia and Roselle had not yet been occupied in 787, 474 ff., 480. The possession of the exarchate and Pentapolis in 756, 107. The case of Potho, abbot of Volturnum, 387, 424 ff., 431. Predestination and free will are defended against the Spanish error, 401, 455. The prefect of the City heard criminal cases, 247, 365. Priests and deacons are subject to penalties, 47, 50 ff. The first of the singers of the Holy See, 204. The beginning of the lesser Lombard principality, 123. Priscillianism revived in Spain in the eighth century, 403. Hadrian [sends] a Gallican provincial to Charles, 299. A *ptochium*, a hospital for poor old people, 48. What are a *pyttacium* and a pseudo-*pyttacium*? 410.

## Q

The Quartodecimans were condemned by the Council of Nicaea, 395. Their error is falsely attributed to the Spaniards, 445.

## R

Ravenna fears the arms of the Greeks, 176. The people of Emilia are called Ravennates, 329. The archbishops of Ravenna, imitating the patriarchs of Constantinople, fabricate a schism, 499. Those duly elected are consecrated at Rome, 501. The Ravennates and Pentapolitans are to be judged at Rome, 520. Reginaldus, bad duke of Chiusi and a neighbor of the Church, is to be removed under Desiderius, 338, 344. Before holding the dignity of duke, he was castaldus of Castrum Felicitatis, 337. A Roman *responsale* sent to Pippin by Paul, 148. The Holy Commonwealth is wrongly called the Holy Roman Empire, 15. Rodicausus, a monk and accuser of Potho, abbot of Volturnum, is rejected by the canons because he is guilty of fornication, 429. Rodgaudus, duke of Friuli, aspires to the kingship of Italy, 345; is defeated by Charles, 347; and is deposed by him, 372. Rodigangus, bishop of Metz, and Autcharius, duke, royal envoys, lead Stephen II to Francia, 58, 69, 77. The form of litanies in the age of Charlemagne, 463. A supplication, or prayer, for obtaining Frankish aid, 3; for the succession of Grimoald in the duchy of Beneventum, 489.

Rome and its duchy belonged to pontifical jurisdiction before the donations; they are wrongly counted among the donations, 12, 68. They are liberated from the savagery of the Lombards, 147. They are said to have obeyed the Greek emperors in vain, 128, 176. The Greeks themselves acknowledge this, 210, 345. Hadrian calls the Roman Church “the Church of God,” that is, of blessed Peter, 352. The Roman pontiff is chosen by God, 507. The rite of election in 769, 260. Until the end of the ninth century, he was elected only from among cardinal priests and deacons, 291. Before consecration, the elected pope is entered in the record, 114. Before Gregory III, ordination or consecration followed confirmation by the prince, 289; from Gregory III to Leo III, consecration was free, 134, 241, 290, 292. “Vicar of Peter” occurs throughout the Codex, 183, 239. His supreme power in spiritual matters, 520; in temporal matters, 521 ff. He is prince at Rome and in its duchy, 67, 293, 370, until 728, 13. He is to return dominion to the Greeks if they should repent, 16, 58; in the exarchate from 756 onward, 261, 423, 440. His power, which they call coercive, 364 ff., 516, 520. The Senate and People of Rome call him “our lord, ordained by God,” 143. His territory is clearly distinguished from that of the Frankish kings, 463. He uses no collection of canons before Zacharias, 32, 42, 301; he extols even the least things in kings, 474. Through his efforts, reconciliations among princes are sought, 215. Romuald, the elder son of Arichis, dies before his father, 489. Ruinart knew only two letters of Gregory III, 2, 5.

## S

*Sabonum*, not *sabarium*: the linen cloth in which those baptized were received from the sacred font, 136. The Sabine territory or patrimony, 314, 384, 414 ff. The Sacramentary of Saint Gregory is sent to Francia, 523, 525. The oath of the bishops of Tuscany, 9; the oath exacted by Hadrian concerning the innocence of the monks of Volturnum, 431. The *salae* of Saint Peter, or country houses, 20. The sacred image of the Savior in processions, 463. Hadrian teaches that the bodies of the saints must not be moved, 381. Blood and strangled meat were formerly forbidden, 400, 454. The Saracens buy slaves from the Lombards, 369. In 777 they are defeated by Charles in Spain, 356. The estate of Sasantina belonging to the monastery of Galliatum, 438. In 785 the Saxons are finally conquered and converted to the faith, with their duke Widukind, through Charles’s efforts, 462. Some who return to paganism are to be admitted to penance, 465. The schism of the archbishops of Ravenna, 499. Roman-Lombard script in Hadrian’s age, 120. The *secundicerius* succeeded the first of the singers, 204. The office of the third singer, 204. The Holy See uses the collection of Cresconius, 34. Senigallia belongs to the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, 224.

Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, married and involved in lawsuits at Rome, 138; claiming too much for himself, he is deposed by Stephen II, 322. Restored, he reports Greek plots to Paul out of gratitude, 178. A sign used as a boundary-marker, 388. Sirmond, deceived concerning the Dionysian collection, deceives others, 28, 39. *Spatha apallarea*, 159. The dukes of Spoleto and Beneventum swear fidelity to Pippin, 154; both duchies are subject to the Lombards, 176; both are offered by Charles to the Holy See, 298, 341, 379.

Stephen II asks Constantinople for aid, 70. He obtains it from the Franks, 11. He goes to Francia after overcoming Lombard ambushes, 58, 61. There he recovers from a serious illness, 79. He receives Pippin’s sons from the sacred font, 73. Having obtained possession of the exarchate and Pentapolis, he sends administrators and judges there, 323. He dies, 114, 133. The order of his letters is consistent, 59.

Stephen III. In 758, Paul’s envoy to Pippin, 151. After being made pope, he decrees that the fifty Apostolic Canons are to be accepted, 32. At the request of Desiderius, who was disturbing the state of the Church, he sends fabricated letters to Bertrada and Charles, 262, 265, 291. He wishes to become godfather to Carloman, 279. He strongly disapproves of a marriage with Desiderius’s daughter, 284. Stephen, bishop and duke of Naples, faithful to the Holy See, offers Paul aid against the Greeks, 127, 179, 495. Marriage is forbidden to subdeacons, 39, 48.

## T

The oldest inns for travelers, 437. Terracina belongs to the Holy See because it was conquered by papal arms and retained for the Neapolitan patrimony, 495. It is invaded by the Neapolitans and Greeks, 375. The people of Terracina. See “Gaetani.” Territories, or provinces, and cities donated to Saint Peter, 373, 384. The penitential book of Theodore, 30, 304. The librarian Theophylactus, 427. Thius, king of the Persians, fights with his nephew, 419. Charles asks Hadrian for large beams for churches from the duchy of Spoleto, just as Charles had asked the pontiff, lord of Ravenna, for the mosaics of Ravenna, 471. Trasimundus, duke of Spoleto, is besieged at Rome, 9, 21. The Lombard cities of Tuscany belong to Saint Peter, 475, 480, 496.

## V

The faithful Venetians report the Greeks’ schemes against Ravenna to Archbishop Sergius, 179. At Hadrian’s request, Charles drives them from the exarchate and Pentapolis, 459. Verecundus, bishop, is the author of an apocryphal abridgment of the Council of Chalcedon, 410. Widows are not to be veiled, 46. A consecrated virgin abandoning her adopted state, 518. Charles rejects an incredible vision, 434. The monastery of Volturnum. See “Potho.”

## W

Waldipertus, Lombard priest, and Gracilis, tribune, are guilty of treason, 245. Several Wilcarii were contemporaries in Gaul, 395. Wilcarius, archbishop of Sens, is appointed to oversee the restoration of the Vatican basilica, 380; his jurisdiction is extended into Spain, 409. He ordains and instructs Aegila, 458. Wilharius, bishop of Nomentum, is sent as an envoy and later accompanies Stephen II when he goes to Gaul, 78, 83, 138. Winigisus succeeds Hildebrand in the duchy of Spoleto, 515.

## Z

Zacharias is first consecrated without the dispatch of a decree to the prince, 241. He recovers four cities of the Roman duchy, 10. He writes to Pippin, mayor of the palace, 27, 41. He makes him king, 15. He counts the years of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, in an unusual manner together with the imperial years, 25, 27. He is the first of all the pontiffs to use the Dionysian collection of canons, 30.

# [Volume II of Cennio’s Edition]

[Col. 0451]

## Preface Placed at the Beginning of Volume II of the Edition of Cajetan Cennio

[Col. 0451A] I. What had to be said at the beginning concerning the monuments of the entire work I have already stated. For that reason I shall not compose a new preface concerning the same matters, since that would indeed be superfluous. For if at any time, relying upon the authority of eminent men, I embraced some less correct opinion and then, after thoroughly investigating the matter, decided that it had to be abandoned, you will find that I did so once, twice, and even three times, and you will also learn why I departed from their opinion.

But I have decided to place before the materials contained in the second part of this volume a new monument: namely, the *Notice of the Provinces of the Universal Church* and the authentic *Censual Book of the Holy See*. In this way you may hold in your own hands the evidence of how far astray the more recent historians are, who have not hesitated to declare the Ludovician diploma fictitious and consequently to undermine the authority of the other materials that follow.

I shall place before your eyes the new names of provinces, almost all unknown in the time of Louis: Sclavonia, Hungary, Dalmatia beyond the sea, likewise Istria beyond the sea, Croatia, [Col. 0451B] Alemannia, Burgundy, the March, Marsia, and Lombardy; and also new names of cities and new rights of the Holy See. I consider this monument especially valuable, not because it presents a better knowledge of places and things than the later geographers, whose study, indefatigable and exceedingly diligent, has transmitted descriptions both ancient and modern of the whole world, but because it displays the barbarism and ignorance of the tenth century and the two following centuries.

It gains an additional and by no means insignificant value because it corrects more than once, and not obscurely, the medieval chorography of Italy which the anonymous author (*Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. X), often misled by the Ludovician diploma, extracted from it, by supplying certain and entirely reliable arrangements of the provinces and cities. Its author is uncertain, and its age likewise doubtful, for it circulated over nearly two hundred years. Since, however, the copyist is known and there can be no doubt about his date, we can readily determine what the arrangement of those provinces was in the eleventh century and the following one.

[Col. 0451C] II. Albinus, indeed, about whom I have spoken elsewhere (*Preface*, no. 25), clearly testifies that he drew from older codices whatever he committed to posterity: “I was careful,” he says, “whenever and wherever I could, to attach in this same little bundle what I had learned or found to belong to blessed Peter by means of books of antiquity, or what I myself had heard and seen from the time of Lucius III”—that is, the pope who began his pontificate in 1181.

The earliest of the additions made by him occurs when he speaks of Ireland. He says: “In the time of our lord Pope Eugene III, the whole of Ireland was divided into four metropolises by John, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, legate of the Apostolic See.” Thus Albinus added these few words to books of antiquity that already existed before 1145, when Eugene III became pope.

These, therefore, are the limits beyond which one must not go; but they do not provide the certain age of each monument from which he extracted his material. In this connection, one must observe that he gave his own work the title *Excerpt from Ecclesiastical History*. The work should therefore be regarded as assembled from various short writings, which Albinus collected through his diligence and commended to us, his late descendants.

I am confident that I shall make this perfectly clear when I show that the labors excerpted were not those of a single age or a single author, but that the work was composed from notices belonging to different times and to different authors—what they call *notitiae*—and that these notices more than once contradict one another. Nevertheless, the work is exceedingly useful for illuminating the ecclesiastical history of the Middle Ages, especially papal history, and necessary for defending the monuments of this volume. Therefore, in order to speak of it clearly and distinctly, I have decided that it must be divided into six parts, which I shall examine individually in a very brief discussion.

To the inelegant description of Italy placed before these materials I shall append a few notes, more to avoid seeming to have neglected the remains of that uncultivated age—for it has the character of the tenth century—than to offer the reader anything useful. It has no agreement whatsoever with the notices that follow. I begin with the first of them.

III. Emmanuel de Schelstrate published a notice similar to this one long ago, from a manuscript codex of the library of the Queen of Sweden, together with the variant readings of another codex of the same royal library, no. 1248 (*Antiquitates ecclesiasticae*, appendix, p. 649). I shall append the variant readings from both codices.

What he himself thought about it should not be overlooked: “The codex,” he says, “from which this notice was taken was written 688 years ago, as is evident from the chronicle contained at the beginning of the codex, which ends in the year 1000. . . . The notice seems, however, to have been written after Honorius and Arcadius, around the time of the Council of Chalcedon, when Leo the Great was pope. For it asserts that the province of Narbonensis belonged to Gaul, and Tingitana and the Balearic Islands to Spain; and I do not think that this continued beyond the pontificate of Leo the Great.”

Perhaps the learned man did not perceive that in listing the provinces the author adhered for the most part to the *Notice of the Empire*, and therefore described civil rather than ecclesiastical provinces. It is well known to every learned person that the ecclesiastical provinces did not conform to them. Since I see that this notice contains neither wholly civil nor wholly ecclesiastical provinces for the centuries that are to be illuminated, I willingly and deliberately leave its preparation to another person who may have a greater interest in it.

For the notices that follow conflict with this one just as much as they conflict with the description of Italy which Albinus placed in the principal position.

[Col. 0452C] IV. Immediately after it indeed follows a notice far older than both: namely, the division of Gaul into Gauls and seven provinces. Sirmond was the very first to publish it, in volume I of the Councils of Gaul; and Peter de Marca (*Dissertation on the Primacy of Lyons*) and Pagius interpreted it, each with the greatest zeal and diligence. I shall say nothing about de Schelstrate’s negligence (*Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 638), for the whole of the province of Lyons III escaped him.

The version found in Sirmond and Pagius was composed toward the end of the fourth century, before the *Notice of the Empire*. But the version now published by me for the first time from Albinus’s codex bears the script of the eleventh century. This will become clear to learned readers if they examine the episcopal suffragan sees of both Germanies.

It would be long and irrelevant to our purpose to examine individually everything contained in this notice. Our concern is to disclose the components of this provincial notice, so that, once the age of each has been recognized, anything that does not accord with the time of this codex may not be charged as a fault against Albinus but may be attributed to the ignorance of those who preceded him. For the ancient monuments that he collected were copied either without any fidelity or with additions and various alterations.

This most ancient Gallican notice is followed by a brief notice of the kingdom of Hungary, which cannot be called older than the eleventh century. No learned person is unaware that at the beginning of that same century, through the work of Saint Stephen, that kingdom acquired its own bishops.

Indeed, since I see that the bishopric of Gurk is listed, although it was established only in 1072, I would judge that the notice should more safely be assigned to the twelfth century. Attached to it is another, much older notice, from the time when Salona was the metropolis of all Dalmatia and Croatia. For in 1062 these kingdoms had two metropolises, as Pagius observed in that same year (no. 6): Split, which had long before succeeded the destroyed see of Salona, and Antivari, which later became a suffragan of Ragusa and recovered its former dignity only at a later time.

V. Next, after the two chorographical notices inserted here out of order, comes that ancient and celebrated notice of the churches of Spain, attributed to Wamba, king of the Visigoths, and hitherto supported by none of our monuments.

It exists in Labbe (*Councils*, vol. V, p. 878), with the following title: “Division of the boundaries of the dioceses and parishes of Spain made by King Wamba, from manuscripts of the Church of Toledo and the Church of Oviedo, whose title is Ithacius; in it the history of the kings of the Vandals and Alans in Galicia, and afterward of the Suevi, and finally of the Goths, is written.”

When anyone leisurely compares our unpublished version with that one, it will be clear that the cities are listed in the same order, but the metropolises are not. The last of them in Wamba’s division is Narbonensis, whereas here it is Arles—a thing which, I confess, I have never read in any notice.

Moreover, one will discover that the earlier sees of Oretum and Baetia, subject to the metropolitan of Toledo, are omitted; among the suffragans of Seville one will find Eliberi, that is, Granada; four sees are taken away from Mérida—Egeditania, Coimbra, Viseu, and Lamego—and assigned to Braga; and finally, one will notice that the Balearic Islands are missing from Tarragona.

These details remind us that much of Spain had been wrested from the hands of the Moors, and therefore that the old notice was copied at the end of the eleventh century or the beginning of the following one, and that Albinus incorporated it into his codex somewhat more than a hundred years later.

It can be gathered from the notice composed by a religious man for Celestine III, and by Milo, his abbot, in Schelstrate (*Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 747), what all the ecclesiastical provinces enumerated thus far were, and in what region or dominion they were situated in Albinus’s age. From that notice I have decided to append all the provinces, although listed in a different order, always indicating the kingdoms or principalities in which they existed at the end of the twelfth century.

I shall do the same in what follows, and indeed with greater ease. For, except for the kingdom of England, notices of the provinces reaching back to so remote an age neither occur nor could occur. It is established that the foundations of the churches that follow began to be laid, at the latest, in the eighth century.

### VI

It begins with the kingdom of Poland, converted to the faith through the preaching of Saint Adalbert at the beginning of the eleventh century. In Alemannia he establishes only three metropolises: Bremen, Magdeburg, and Salzburg; for he had counted four—Mainz, Cologne, Trier, and Tarentaise—among the seventeen provinces of Gaul, following the ancient custom. Nor were there any other metropolises in Alemannia. After listing England’s two ancient metropolises, Canterbury and York, he subjects the bishops of Scotland to no metropolitan, since they were all exempt. For until Sixtus IV the prelate of Saint Andrews had not attained the dignity of archbishop. It must not, however, be overlooked that the Scottish bishops were exempted by Celestine III in the year 1192, which demonstrates the age of the codex.

He separates Ireland from Great Britain, taking account of the establishment of metropolitan sees in the northern kingdoms. Although Urban II is said to have established the metropolitan see of Denmark, Innocent III (Register, book I, letter 419, p. 247) mentions only the privileges of Adrian IV and his successors; and he established the other two in 1148, or three years before the organization of Ireland, which the same pontiff effected through his legate.

The venerable Cardinal Baronius (1151, no. 4) saw in the Vatican Library a description of the four metropolitan sees of Ireland then first established, together with the churches subject to each one. I present it all the more willingly because from its title I see that it is precisely the same document that Albinus carefully copied into his codex. This monument therefore gains considerable credibility from the genuine records of the Roman Church, from which it was compiled.

For this reason, concerning the arrangement of the ecclesiastical provinces of Italy, which are enumerated after Ireland, it is sufficient for me to place before everyone’s eyes what it was like in the twelfth century. The same applies to the Eastern provinces, which before the end of the following century suffered destruction at the hands of the most savage enemies of the Christian name. Something will have to be said about these provinces, reduced to the last extremity, in the notes to the Rudolphine codex.

It is now time to proceed to the second part of this outstanding monument, namely, the genuine Censual Book of the Roman Church, attributed to Cencius.

### VII

When Cencius de Sabellis was chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church—for he later succeeded Innocent III under the name of Honorius III—he published the Book of Revenues with the following preface. Baronius commended it to posterity (1192, no. 19), and I shall appropriately transcribe it here:

> “Since the work concerning the revenues of the Roman Church had already been arranged at an earlier time by certain other persons, why was it necessary, and why did it become necessary, to arrange it again? I, Cencius, formerly chamberlain of Pope Clement III, of blessed memory, and now chamberlain of the lord Pope Celestine III, canon of Saint Mary Major, answer briefly and plainly.

> “When Eugenius I of blessed memory and Adrian—one must certainly read Eugenius III and Adrian IV—his papal successor, and afterward certain others had reduced to writing certain incomplete memoranda concerning the revenues, which were neither fully nor authentically written or arranged, their successors were unable, from those memoranda, to be adequately informed which churches, monasteries, hospitals, or charitable houses—for these are recognized as practically the same thing—as well as which cities, castles, villages, or private houses, or which kings and princes admitted into the jurisdiction and property of blessed Peter and of the Holy Roman Church, remained subject to a revenue, or how much they ought to pay. Consequently the same Roman Church suffered no small loss and damage.

> “When I discovered this and saw that I could easily provide a remedy for this harm, and also recognized that my own person had been educated, promoted in every respect, and created by the Holy Roman Church from its earliest beginnings, I was moved by vigilant and intense reflection. I marked down the revenues themselves, as I found them in the parchment volumes and registers of the ancient and modern Roman pontiffs, and in certain other books or reliable memoranda—not bringing all of them forward, but identifying, insofar as circumstances permitted, those originally established by the aforementioned holy Fathers for particular kingdoms, provinces, bishoprics, and places, as will be noted below.

> “I have also carefully caused the new revenues that were established in the Roman Church in my own time, or that will henceforth be established, to be depicted in this volume. By doing so I provide my successors with material by which, from now until the end of the world, they may record both those revenues and whatever new ones are established in their own times.”

I should certainly like all this to fit Cencius, just as he himself testifies about himself, and no one before this day has thought otherwise. But for a little while, one must lend an ear to Albinus, who is likewise his own witness.

### VIII

He declares that he is by birth a Gaetan, when he says that he was for a long time the brother of Richard, bishop of Orvieto and master of the liberal arts, and, after the death of his maternal uncle, who was a monk, his assistant in teaching. Since his brother Richard obtained the episcopate in 1176 or the following year, as is clear from the records in Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 1468), and since Albinus himself was summoned to Rome after that time, he therefore came there already of mature age.

He was summoned to the City, as is known to have happened at all times to men like him, because—so I judge—his tireless studies had been heralded by their reputation. Indeed, he had gathered much useful material from the Fathers and Councils in nine books. Speaking of these, he says:

> “I added certain necessary canons, which I collected with labor from various works of the Fathers, not accessible to everyone and not incorporated into Gratian’s edition.”

He composed the final two books, the tenth and eleventh, at Rome, beginning in the time of Lucius III, who was elevated to the highest dignity in 1181. The same author valued them so highly that he regarded the preceding nine as contemptible in comparison:

> “When I composed them, because my understanding was poor, I more confidently ask the readers’ pardon for these and other things ineptly stated. All the foregoing was done in an unstable age and with weak knowledge. But when I became a man, because of the merits of my sins I was summoned to the Roman Church, and from that time onward I was diligent,”

as I said at the beginning.

This is what Albinus says in the preface to his codex, whose title is: *Here Begin the Deeds of the Poor Scholar Albinus*. I shall touch briefly on Book X.

### IX

He begins with the donations, patrimonies, and estates of the Frankish kings, drawn from the *Liber Pontificalis*. Then he warns the reader:

> “What follows is taken from the volumes of the Lateran Library, and since certain proper names of patrimonies in those same volumes have been entirely or partially destroyed by excessive antiquity, so that in place of the proper name nothing could be read, either wholly or in part, a theta has been inserted, of which the poet says:
>
> ‘O theta, letter much more unhappy than all others!’”

Afterward he lists the patrimonies and estates situated in the territories of Lucca, Pisa, Carfagnana, and Rosello, as well as the other acquisitions of revenues down to Gregory VII.

He presents numerous documents, especially from the tenth century, when the counts of Tusculum are said to have usurped every right of the Holy See. Let the following document of the false pope Boniface VII, from the year 984, stand for them all:

> “Likewise, in another volume of the same cartulary, it is read that Pope Boniface VII leased the castle of Petra Pertusa, with everything belonging to it, together with its court, jurisdiction, and dues in acorns and pasture, both from the same castle and from the villages belonging to it. It is situated in the territory of Silva Candida. It pays ten gold solidi annually.”

And likewise the document of the following year:

> “Likewise, in another volume, under Pope John XV, Judge Dago and the senator Ote, and their sons Misica and Lambert, are read to have granted to blessed Peter an entire city, namely Schinesgne, in the province of the Polanians, with all its appurtenances within these boundaries: beginning on the first side at the long sea, ending at Pruzze, as far as the place called Russe; and from the end of Russe extending as far as Craccopin, and as far as the river Oder, directly to the place called Alemure; and from Alemure itself as far as the land of Milze; and from the end of Milze directly within the Oder; and thence proceeding beside the river Oder as far as the aforesaid city of Schinesgne.”

After these parchment volumes of the library, he turns to the registers of Popes Honorius I, Gregory II, Zacharias, Alexander II, and Gregory VII. Of the first three he records only leases of estates and properties. He then enumerates the revenues of the kings and princes of England, Gaul, Spain, Saxony, Hungary, Russia, Dalmatia, and Croatia under Alexander II and Gregory VII.

He next continues with charters, documents, oaths, and other ancient monuments, concluding with an excerpt from ecclesiastical history, which will follow shortly.

To sum up much in a few words: what Cencius says he collected in 1192, Albinus had already collected at least eight or ten years earlier and had included in the tenth book of his codex. At its end, after the *Notitia of the Provinces* mentioned above, he placed the Book of Revenues as it then existed and as it is now being published for the first time.

### X

Since this is so, I do not think anyone will assign to Cencius the assiduous labors of Albinus, who, although accustomed to collecting ancient monuments, nevertheless spent many years examining those pertaining to the Holy See. Cencius perhaps added something to another man’s labor. I say “perhaps”; for if the genuine Book of Revenues about which he himself writes still existed, it would differ little, or not at all, from the Albinian book.

The book that appeared some years ago through the work of Muratori (*Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. V, p. 851) seems to have been written approximately a hundred years after Cencius’s edition. For Honorius IV, who appears in it, did not ascend the chair of Peter before 1285.

Moreover, since the codex easily the most ancient of all, which Panvinio used (Vatican Codex 3924), now preserved in the archive of Castel Sant’Angelo, contains a privilege (p. 480) granted by Emperor Charles IV in 1368 and published by Lunig (*Codex Italiae Diplomaticus*, vol. II, p. 791), the Muratorian book must be regarded as much later and cannot in any way be attributed to Cencius.

This is confirmed by the enormous difference between it and the Albinian book. The type of coin is generally different; the enumeration of revenues differs most extensively; the order of the bishoprics is different; and the provinces are more than once confused.

Moreover, the practice of leasing offerings, which Muratori recorded separately together with the charters, bears the wholly false title:

> *Concerning the revenues that the lord pope receives from the Confession of blessed Peter and the Basilica of the Holy Saviour, around the year 1220.*

When this is compared with the subsequent obligations of the lessee of the offerings, although those obligations have there been altered in a pitiable manner, it is found not to correspond to them at all.

Perhaps this leasing was thought to dishonor the dignity of the Holy See. Yet even the letters of John XXII to the vicar, the bishop of Viterbo, written 106 years later (Vatican Bullarium, vol. I, p. 272), teach otherwise:

> “If, as you, brother bishop, have consulted us by your letters, you should judge it more expedient for the advantage of our treasury to lease, or to grant on contract, all the rights, rents, revenues, and casual receipts of the altar-service or alms-house of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, rather than have them collected or exacted by us . . . We wish you to inform us fully, by your sealed letters or by a public instrument, of the amount of money for which such leasing or grant on contract is to be made, to which person or persons, for how long a period, and under what security it is to be made.”

Therefore nothing ought to be altered out of reverence for venerable antiquity. For if anything conflicts with the customs of later ages, the ancient times ought rather to be lamented than corrected; the chastity and integrity of history forbid such correction.

### XI

For this reason I would not dare to assert that Albinus was the author of the earlier part of the Collection, which he transferred from the Roman *Pontifical Book* into his own codex under the number 149—namely, the excerpt taken from the parchment volumes of the Lateran Library.

For it contains features belonging to an earlier collector, showing that it was composed either while Gregory VII was still alive or immediately after his death.

In both the Albinian codex and the edition published by Muratori, it begins:

> “Pope Hadrian obtained from Charles,” etc.;

and it ends:

> “Likewise, in a certain little Lateran volume, among other things, Spicioneus, duke of Bohemia, is said to have received permission from Pope Nicholas to wear a mitre, and promised that he would give one hundred pounds of silver every year from his land under the name of a revenue.”

Before this final section, however, after several items drawn from the entire Register of Gregory VII, the following is appended:

> “From the synod held in Dalmatia by the legates of Pope Gregory VII, namely by Gebizo, then abbot of the monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius and now bishop of Cesena, and also by Folcuinus, bishop of Forlimpopoli. This synod is preserved in the archive of the sacred Lateran palace.”

This also survives, with slight differences, in Baronius (1076, no. 66).

The cabinets of the Lateran Library were therefore being examined after the year 1083. For Gebizo had not served as legate in Dalmatia before that year, nor had he received episcopal dignity from the same Gregory.

Albinus, however, must be regarded not as the author but as the mere copyist of this first collection in its pure form. Regarding the many other monuments that follow, it is not easy to decide whether he found them collected by others or collected each one himself.

This much can be affirmed with certainty: before Cencius the chamberlain published his Book of Revenues, filled with so many ancient monuments, nearly all of these had already been collected by Albinus.

### XII

Albinus also collected in the eleventh and final book of his Collection the leases, charters, and other revenues from the times of Eugenius III—not Eugenius I, as is incorrectly read in Cencius’s preface, since what Cencius narrates does not fit the age of Saint Eugenius, whether as vicar or successor of the holy martyr Martin I—and of Adrian IV.

Some of these will be found below; others are being prepared for the press, to be inserted into a work that I confidently expect to publish shortly: *On the Eminence of the Vatican Basilica*.

Above all, Albinus will present the genuine Roman Order, both concerning feast days and the coronation of the Roman pontiff. This Order, shamefully interpolated in the Book of Revenues attributed to Cencius, first deceived Panvinio and afterward Mabillon, easily the leading authority in diplomatic scholarship. Each of them too readily defended the many false rites introduced into that Order.

For the present I present the Provincial and the Book of Revenues from the tenth book, written at least eight years before Cencius. No one will persuade me that this book was not available to Cencius. Its author had indeed been summoned to Rome for no other reason than to devote his service to the interests of the Holy See; and since he was a contemporary of Cencius, it is easier to believe that Cencius invaded his labors than that he rejected the most exact of all collections of revenues, the Albinian one.

Cencius was not so great that he can be compared with Albinus in learning and diligence. Although Albinus speaks modestly of himself, he nevertheless perceived that Gratian’s work was incomplete and gathered monuments of such a kind as do not indicate a dull intellect.

If time ever brings forth Cencius’s genuine book, it will then become clear by how slight a distance I have departed from the truth. For both the printed book and the manuscripts in the codices attributed to Cencius had been preceded by another collection, that of Nicolaus Rosellius of Tarragona, of the Order of Preachers, commonly called the Cardinal of Aragon. He was born in 1314 and died in 1362, as appears in the outstanding codex—easily the first of all—now in the possession of the eminent Passionei and soon to be transferred, together with several other codices, to the Vatican Library.

The following title is prefixed to that collection:

> “The present book was arranged and caused to be written by the most reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Nicolaus, Cardinal of Aragon. He compiled it from various registers, from the books of the apostolic treasury, and also from other diverse books and chronicles, with great diligence and labor.”

Anyone who compares the books will see that not a little was derived from this collection into later codices of the Books of Revenues.

In the edition of both little works, the following distinction has been maintained: the variant readings of the Provincial, which is especially necessary for illuminating the monuments contained in this volume, are appended together with brief notes from a very similar little work written several years later. The Censual Book itself, pure and simple as it appears in the codex, is presented to the learned reader so that he may himself be its interpreter and judge.

# THE OLD PROVINCIAL, OR THE CATALOGUE OF THE PROVINCES OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH

## EXCERPT FROM ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

Italy is said to derive its name from King Italus. It is also called Ausonia, from Auson, the son of Ulysses. Italy, therefore—the homeland or region of the Romans—extends from the northwest wind toward the southeast; to the southwest it has the Tyrrhenian Sea, and to the north the Adriatic Gulf. On the west it is enclosed by the barriers of the Alps.

The Alps, rising from the Gallic Sea above the Ligurian Gulf, first separate the territory of the Narbonenses, and afterward Gaul and Raetia, until they terminate in the Gulf of Liburnia.

Italy also has eighteen provinces.

The first is called Histria.

The second is Liguria, named from legumes, because it is evidently fertile in them. Milan and Pavia are in it.

The third is Raetia I, to which Raetia II is joined, situated among the Alps.

**Note [Col. 0457D]:** It is established that in all the *Notitiae* two Raetias are found, Raetia I and Raetia II.

The fourth is the province called the Gothic Alps, named from King Gothus.

The fifth province is also called the Gothic Alps; the city of Genoa is situated in it.

**Note [Col. 0457D]:** I hear for the first time that the Cottian Alps were divided into two provinces.

The sixth province is called Tuscia, in which Rome stands.

**Note [Col. 0457D]:** Schelstratius also read this in the *Notitia* of Codex II of the Swedish Queen. But this conflicts with the *Notitia* of the Empire and with all the others. Rome is placed in Latium and Campania.

Umbria is joined to it; Perugia and Spoleto are in Umbria.

The seventh province, Campania, begins at the city and extends as far as the river Silarus. It contains the very wealthy cities of Capua and Naples.

**Note [Col. 0457D]:** Roman Campania is improperly joined with Campania Felix, which is called the Land of Labor. But something must be conceded to the ignorance of the age. When we come to the Ottonian charter of approximately the same period, we shall see that Roman Campania was unknown.

The province of Bricia is named after a certain queen of the province.

**Note [Col. 0457D]:** What an ingenious interpreter! Saint Gregory the Great, in his letters to Arichis, duke of Benevento (book X, letter 24), does not write *Britannorum*, as Labbe’s edition erroneously has, but, according to the excerpts from the history of Paul the Deacon in Pratilli (*History of the Princes of the Lombards*, vol. I, p. 6), writes the following, relevant to our subject:

> “We have also indicated that, for the churches of the blessed Peter and Paul, we need a number of beams; and therefore we instructed Sabinus, our subdeacon, to cut a number of them in the regions of the Bricci.”

Thus *Bricia* as a province is not new; but “Bricia the Queen” is new and unheard of. In any case, Bruttium forms one province with Lucania.

The eighth is Lucania, to which Bricia is joined, extending from the river Silarus to the Sicilian Strait and bordering the upper reaches of the Tyrrhenian Sea. The cities of Petulanius and Rhegium are situated in it.

The ninth province is situated in the Apennine Alps.

**Note [Col. 0458D]:** It is established that the Graian and Pennine Alps, called by the same name without distinction, were a province of Gaul, whose metropolis was Tarentaise. Pancirolus (*On the Notitia*, chapter 68) says:

> “The Pennine and Graian Alps lie beyond the Cottian Mountains, or Mount Cenis, where the Allobroges, or Savoyards, are found, as well as Tarentaise and part of the Helvetians.”

In the following *Notitia* too, this is listed last among the provinces of Italy, contrary to the *Notitia* of the Empire.

The tenth is called Emilia. It begins among the Apennine Alps and proceeds beside the waters of the Po toward Ravenna. It is adorned with the wealthy cities of Piacenza, Parma, Bologna, and the Forum of Cornelius, which is now called the fortress of Imola.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** In France.

The eleventh is called Flaminia and lies between the Apennine Alps and the Adriatic Sea. Ravenna is situated in it.

**Note [Col. 0459D]:** We shall see in its proper place that the Exarchate arose from two of these provinces and that its extent changed at different times.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** Flaminia, Aurelia, and Emilia derive their names from men so called who came to Rome.

The twelfth is Picenum. It has the Apennine Mountains to the south and the Adriatic Sea on the other side, and extends as far as Piscania.

The Apennine Alps, running through the middle of Italy, are named after the Carthaginians—that is, after Hannibal’s army, which crossed them.

The thirteenth province is called Valeria, to which Nursia is attached. Its western part is also called Etruria.

The fourteenth province is Samnium.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** The Samnites are named from the spears they were accustomed to carry; for a spear is called *senna* in Greek.

Samnium begins at Piscaria and proceeds between Campania and the Adriatic Sea. Its chief city is Benevento.

The fifteenth is Apulia.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** Apulia is named after a traitor; for there the green things are quickly betrayed by the sun’s heat.

Calabria is joined to it. It contains the wealthy cities of Luceria, Sipontum, Canusium, Brundisium, and Tarentum.

The sixteenth is Sicily, which is nourished by the Tyrrhenian or Ionian Sea.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** Sicily is named after the leader Siculus.

The seventeenth is Corsica.

**Note [Col. 0459]:** Corsica and Sardinia are named after their leaders, Corsus and Sardus, the son of Hercules.

The eighteenth is called Sardinia.

It must nevertheless be understood that ancient historians called Liguria, part of Venetia, Emilia, and Flaminia Cisalpine Gaul.

For in ancient times Brennus, who ruled near the city of Senones, came to Italy with three hundred thousand Gauls and occupied it as far as Senigallia, situated on the Adriatic Sea. There the Gauls were separated from one another.

Of these, one hundred thousand went to Delphi and perished by the swords of the Greeks. Another one hundred thousand, remaining in Greece, were first called Galatogreeks because of the whiteness of their bodies, and afterward Galatians. These, then, are the people to whom the apostle Paul writes.

Another one hundred thousand remained in Italy. Building Ticinum, Milan, Pergamum, and Brescia, they gave the name Cisalpine Gaul to the region.

Thus Gaul beyond the Alps is called Transalpine Gaul, while Gaul on this side of the Alps is called Cisalpine Gaul.

**Note [Col. 0459D]:** From this entire description you grasp the knowledge or learning of that age. It would be idle to dwell on it longer. I willingly allow the author to become his own interpreter.

Altogether there are 113 provinces.

There are eleven regions: Italy, Gaul, Africa, Spain, Illyricum, Thrace, Asia, the East, Pontus, Egypt, and Britain.

**Note [Col. 0461B]:** In Schelstratius, the number of regions and provinces is indicated at the beginning.

To this the same author adds:

> “There were formerly not eleven regions but thirteen dioceses in the Roman world, as is clear from the ancient *Notitia* of the Roman Empire, in which Illyricum is divided into three dioceses.”

But here a division not civil but ecclesiastical is being designated. For that reason Illyricum, both western and eastern, since it belongs to the sacred jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, is counted as one region. I shall speak below of that jurisdiction, which was invaded by the Iconoclasts (Dissertation I, no. 10 and following).

## II

### HERE ARE THE NAMES OF THE CITIES OF THESE REGIONS

**Note [Col. 0461C]:** The title was carelessly attached. For the cities that are enumerated correspond neither in name nor in order to the regions; moreover, almost all the eastern ones are necessarily omitted.

The first province of Lugdunensis has four cities.

The metropolitan city of the people of Lyon.

The city of the Aedui.

The city of the Lingones.

The fortress of Chalon.

The fortress of Mâcon.

**Note [Col. 0461]:** In France. The archbishop of Rouen has the following suffragans: Bayeux, Avranches, Évreux, Sées, Lisieux, and Coutances.

**Note [Col. 0461C]:** The *Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul*, first published by Sirmond, was illustrated by Pierre de Marca in his dissertation on the primacy of Lyon; Labbe also included it in his collection (*Councils*, vol. X, p. 540, no. 62 and following), as did Antoine Pagi (374, nos. 10 and following). They say that it was made by Gratian between the years 369 and 374.

From it many others proceeded, with the order changed according to the circumstances of the times. Among them is the one delivered to Charlemagne by Pope Adrian in 774 (Schelstratius, *Ancient Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, p. 643).

In this codex the earlier one appears with a considerable difference in the names, which is not indicated in the variant readings. It seemed more appropriate to append the ecclesiastical provinces of approximately Albinus’s period from another *Notitia*, since various territories were recognized in Gaul, namely Burgundy, Francia, Alemannia, and Gascony. Cities are sometimes found attached singly, in pairs, or even in larger numbers to the provinces; I shall not omit them.

The second province of Lugdunensis has seven cities.

The metropolitan city of the people of Rouen.

The city of the people of Bayeux.

The city of the people of Avranches.

The city of the people of Évreux.

The city of the Solari (*Solarum*), that is, of the Sagii (*Sajorum*).

**Note [Col. 0462C]:** Sagium, commonly called Sées, is still famous today in Lugdunensis II, or Normandy. In all the *Notitiae* it is called the city of the Sagii or Sagii; “the city of the Solari” is perhaps heard here for the first time.

The city of the people of Lisieux.

The city of Coutances.

**Note [Col. 0461]:** The same.

The third province of Lugdunensis has nine cities.

Metropolitan city of the Turones. City of the Cenomani. City of the Redones. City of the Andegavi. City of the Namnetes. City of the Coriosopites. City of the Cians, that is, of the Veneti. [Note: [Col. 0462C] The same applies to this new name of the ancient Veneti. Both names, unless I am mistaken, were bestowed on those cities in the Middle Ages; and the same should apparently be believed concerning the Diablintes under another name, for such names do not occur among the ancients and are read only in this Notitia.] City of the Ossismi. City of the Diablintes, which under another name is called something else, or is assigned to another place. [Col. 0462B] [Note: [Col. 0461] In Francia. The Archbishop of Tours has these suffragans: Le Mans, Rennes, Angers, Nantes, Quimper, Vannes, Saint-Malo, Saint-Brieuc, Tréguier, and Léon.] [Note: [Col. 0462C] This entire province is missing from Schelstratius. From the other Notitiae, especially the aforesaid one of Adrian, it is clear that these names arose after the eighth century.]

City of the Silvanectes. City of the Bellovaci. City of the Ambianenses. City of the Morini, that is, Ponticum. He adds: “Valesius confesses that he does not know from where the surname Ponticum derives.”] City of the Bononenses. [Note: [Col. 0463] In Francia. The province of Germania II contains two cities.

The metropolitan see of Cologne has as suffragans Liège, Utrecht, Münster, Meissen, and Osnabrück. [Note: [Col. 0463] In Alemania. The province of Maxima Sequanorum contains ten cities.
