[Note: [Col. 0463] In Burgundy. The Archbishop of Besançon has these suffragans: Basel, Lausanne, and Belley.] 

The province of the Graian and Pennine Alps contains two cities.

Under the metropolitan see of Tarentaise is the city of the Vallenses, that is, Octodurus. [Note: [Col. 0463C] The aforementioned Cellarius, in the same work, p. 158, reads in the Notitia: “the city of the Vallenses at Octodurus,” in accordance with the designation of the codex; elsewhere, however, it is called Octodurus, as also in the Itinerary of Antoninus.] Here end the names of the cities of the regions. [Note: [Col. 0463] In Alemannia. The Archbishop of Tarentaise has these suffragans: Sion and Aosta.] [Note: [Col. 0463C] So that I might omit nothing concerning the fidelity of the codex, I have placed this rubric here. I do not know why the author of the Notitia, or Albinus, its copyist, set it before the seven provinces of Gaul, unless perhaps he finally perceived that the cities did not correspond to the regions of the earlier Notitia. [Col. 0463D]]

[Col. 0464A] The province of Vienne contains fourteen cities.

Metropolitan city of the Viennenses. City of the Gennavenses. City of the Gtiapolitani. City of the Albenses, now Vivarium. [Note: [Col. 0463D] The same Cellarius, speaking of the Gallican Notitiae, says: “In some, Vivarium, or now Vivarium, is added; and in an ancient chronicle preserved by Valesius, ‘the city of the Albenses, which is also Vivarium.’” Hence it is clear that such surnames and additions should not be attributed to Albinus.] City of the Detenses. City of the Valentiani. City of the Tricastini. City of the Vasiones. City of the Arausici. City of the Cabellici. City of the Avennici. [Note: [Col. 0463D] Below, among the provinces of Spain, and in the Book of Revenues, this city is called Avinio. It is not worth investigating when this name was given to the city of the Avennici; attention should rather be paid to its renown, since the Roman pontiffs resided there for seventy years, from which time it began to belong to their jurisdiction. For Joanna, heir and granddaughter of Robert, king of Sicily, sold that city and all its rights to Clement V in 1346 for eighty thousand gold florins, a considerable price for those times. Thus the city became the capital of the County of Venaissin, which had long belonged to the Holy See; it was subsequently made a metropolitan see, to which three bishops are suffragan.] City of the Arelatenses. City of the Capentoratenses, now Vinclausca. [Note: [Col. 0464C] Gallic geographers know Vindausca, from whose ruins some of them think Carpentoracte arose. If the codex is to be trusted, however, the city was called Vinclausca—and indeed in the Middle Ages—so that the origin of Carpentoracte, a town known even to Pliny, must be older than that surname. No one is unaware that this is the same city as one of the three suffragans of the metropolitan see of Avignon.] City of the Massilienses. [Note: [Col. 0463] In Burgundy. L., as printed], bears this title: “In the year 1068, in the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, a council was held at Auch, a metropolitan city”; in Labbe, volume IX, p. 1195.] City of the Aquenses. Metropolitan city of the Narbonenses. City of the Tolosates, that is, Toulouse. City of the Biterrenses. City of the Agathenses. City of the Nemausenses. City of the Magalonenses. [Note: [Col. 0465B] In Sirmond’s Notitia only six cities are assigned to Narbonensis I; Agde and Maguelonne are not included. Concerning the latter, Cellarius says: “The city of the Magalonenses, as it is called in the Notitia, or Magalona, as it is separately called by Theodulf in his Paraenesis to the Judges, verse 133, lies on an island and belongs more to the geography of the Middle Ages than to ancient times, in which no mention of it is found.” Indeed, in Adrian’s Notitia, which extends into the eighth century, both Agde and Maguelonne are found in Narbonensis.] City of the Lutevenses, that is, the fortress of Loteva. Valesius thinks was Ptolemy’s Vindomagus, later called Ucecia or Ucetia; for in the Notitia he found it called the fortress of Ucecia. This differs very greatly from the Albinian version.]

Since their varied and complex history is irrelevant to our present purpose and cannot be fully explained in the notes, I leave it open to the reader to consider ancient Dalmatia; for my part, it is enough not to neglect medieval Dalmatia, as I shall do below.]

IV.

IN SPAIN.

Metropolitan city of Toledo. [Note: [Col. 0465D] The division of the provinces made by King Wamba places Oretum first among the suffragans, followed by Baetia; both are absent from the codex. Oretum, however, still a well-known town, as Garcia says, because of the notable monastery of the military Order of Calatrava, began to be called Calatrava in the time of the Saracens. Cellarius states that this is an interpretation of Tarapha, rejected by Nonius (book II, chapter 1, p. 79). Therefore it would not seem unreasonable that the name should shortly afterward be assigned to Complutum, unless, according to the common opinion of all, Alcalá de Henares is called Complutum and Oretum Calatrava; these names, of course, were attached to those cities, as to many others, during the time of the Saracen invasion. As for Baetia, a city located by Ptolemy in the territory of Oretum, there is no doubt that it is omitted from the codex for the same reason. For it is established that Innocent IV transferred it to Jaén in 1244, a city which the Moors had called Mentesa.] City of Metesa. City of Acci. City of Asti. City of Urci. City of Dongasti. [Col. 0466B] City of Ilici. City of Saetabis. City of Denia. City of Valencia. City of Segóbriga. [Note: [Col. 0466C] In Wamba’s division Valeria precedes Segóbriga. Garcia observes that the Moors destroyed it and that its see, together with that of Arcabrica, likewise laid waste, was transferred to Cuenca, a very strongly fortified castle captured and taken from the Moors by Alfonso IX, who made it a city. He says this was done on the authority of Lucius III. Mariana attributes it merely to the authority of the Roman pontiff (book XI, chapter 13). Didacus de Castejon, among the papal diplomas of Urban III, who succeeded Lucius, cites letters listing Cuenca as the last of the episcopal sees. But Urban’s successors, Celestine and Innocent III, say otherwise: “We decree that the parish of Complutum, and Cuenca, as subject to it as to a metropolitan see, with their boundaries, and likewise all the churches which it is known to have possessed by its own right from ancient times, shall belong to you; moreover, confirming the episcopal sees which you at present possess justly and canonically, namely Palencia, Segovia, Osma, and Sigüenza.” It is clear that Cuenca was also an episcopal see not long afterward, from the Notitia of Abbot Milo, which I have placed after the Albinian version. But whatever may be said about the letters of Urban III, the assertion that this was done on the authority of Lucius III is gratuitous, as Albinus’s silence shows.] City of Arcabrica. City of Complutum, that is, Calatrava. [Note: [Col. 0466D] It was not Complutum but, as I said just now, Oretum that was transformed into that famous monastery. Mariana briefly recounts the whole matter (book XI, chapter 6): Raymond, abbot of the Cistercians at Fitero on the Pisuerga, expelled the Moors from Calatrava at the urging of the monk Diego Velasquez, formerly a distinguished soldier of Alfonso, and with financial assistance from John, Archbishop of Toledo. Therefore, as a reward for his labor, the king gave the lordship of Calatrava, with the attached territory, as a perpetual gift to Blessed Mary of the Cistercian Order, and in her name to Abbot Raymond and his companions. Following the abbot’s example, the clothing was changed to garments more suitable for fighting. The Order was confirmed by Alexander III in 1164. To this narrative he adds the following epilogue: “Now, with affairs changed from their ancient condition, they are enslaved to the pleasures of courtiers and the lust of kings; thus human affairs commonly degenerate after being undertaken with a noble beginning.”] City of Segontia. City of Osma. City of Segovia. City of Palencia. These cities are suffragans of the see of Toledo, eighteen in number. [Note: [Col. 0465] The Archbishop of Toledo has these suffragans: Sigüenza, Osma, Burgos, Palencia, Sahagún, Segovia, and Cuenca.]

[Col. 0467A] Metropolitan city of Seville. City of Itálica. City of Asidona. City of Erepla. City of Málaga. City of Eliberris, that is, Granada. City of Astigi. City of Córdoba. City of Écija. City of Tucci. These cities are suffragans of the see of Seville, ten in number. [Note: [Col. 0467C] Abbot Milo correctly omits Seville as a metropolitan see, for he presents not the ancient condition but that of the provinces in his own age. The Moors were not expelled from Seville before the year 1247. On this matter see Mariana, book XIII, chapter 7. Which sees were then assigned to it is clear from the later codex of 1253, whose variant readings Schelstratius adds to the Notitia: “The Archbishop of Seville has these suffragans: Jaén, Córdoba, Cartagena, Cádiz.”]

Metropolitan city of Mérida. City of Badajoz. City of Lisbon. City of Exonoba. City of Caliabria. City of Salamanca. City of Elbora. City of Albia. City of Coria. These sees are suffragans of the metropolitan see of Mérida, nine in number. [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop of Mérida has these suffragans: Ávila, Plasencia, Salamanca, Estorga, Coria, Lisbon, León, Oviedo, and Zamora.]

Metropolitan city of Braga. City of Dumio. City of Porto. City of Coimbra. City of Viseu. City of Egitania. City of Lamego. City of Tui. City of Ourense. City of Lugo. City of Britonia. City of Astorga. City of Iria. These cities are suffragans of the metropolitan see of Braga, thirteen in number. [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop of Braga has these suffragans: Porto, Coimbra, Viseu, Lamego, Ourense, Tui, Lugo, Astorga, and Mondoñedo.] [Note: [Col. 0467C] In 1110 Callixtus II restored Braga as a metropolitan see, at the expense of Mérida, as is evident from his letters to Pelagius, the metropolitan, preserved in Labbe (Councils, volume X, p. 830). Four cities were taken from Mérida and subjected to Braga: Astorga, Lugo, Tui, Mondoñedo, Ourense, Porto, Coimbra, and the towns now bearing episcopal names—Viseu, Lamego, Egitania, and Britonia—with their parishes. About the year 1124, near the end of his pontificate, the same pontiff also transferred to Compostela the metropolitan dignity of Mérida, which groaned under the Moorish yoke. This became the source of disputes between the new metropolitan see and Braga. While Albinus flourished, those four bishoprics taken from Mérida were especially at issue. Innocent III thought he had settled the matter (Register, book II, letter 133) between Compostela, which claimed the rights of Mérida, and Braga by granting Viseu and Coimbra to the latter, but Lamego and Egitania to Compostela. This was done in 1199, when Albinus had long since died. Therefore his Notitia records only the preceding situation, taking no account of the disputes of the new metropolitan of Compostela, because he was copying a Notitia older than its creation. The case is quite different with Abbot Milo’s Notitia, as the same Innocent testifies (ibid., letter 149). “The Archbishop of Compostela,” he says, “renounced forever, in our presence and that of our brothers, his claims to the churches of Coimbra, Viseu, Tui, Ourense, Mondoñedo, Lugo, and Astorga, as well as to the churches of Saint Victor and Saint Fructuosus with all their dependencies, and to half of Braga.” I would be surprised that Milo nevertheless gives Mérida as an archbishopric belonging to Compostela, despite the authority of so many pontiffs, unless I had found it reported that Compostela was read in another royal codex, no. 1253.]

Metropolitan city of Tarragona. City of Barcelona. City of Exauria. City of Girona. City of Empúries. City of Ausona. City of Auriello. City of Híjar. City of Hictosa. City of Tortosa. City of Zaragoza. City of Oseti. City of Pamplona. City of Tarazona. City of Calahorra. City of Senona. [Note: [Col. 0468C] There can be no doubt that this city has intruded here by mistake.] City of Anca. These cities are suffragans of the metropolitan see of Tarragona, seventeen in number. [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop of Tarragona has these suffragans: Barcelona, Girona, Ausona or Vic, Lleida, Huesca, Tarazona, Calahorra, Urgell, Zaragoza, Tortosa, and Pamplona.]

Metropolitan city of Arles. City of Marseille. City of Toulon. City of Cavaillon. City of Vaison. City of Carpentras. City of Avignon. City of Orange. City of Saint-Paul; and they number eight. [Note: [Col. 0467] In Burgundy. The Archbishop of Arles has these suffragans: Marseille, Avignon, Orange, Vaison, Cavaillon, Tricastin, Carpentras, and Toulon.] [Note: [Col. 0468C] This province belongs to the twelfth century, when the counts of Barcelona had added the county of Provence to their dominion (Baluze, in the appendix to Marca Hispanica). No other province is found annexed to the provinces of Spain in the Notitia. In 1196, after the death of Alfonso, king of Aragon, Provence was separated from the county of Barcelona, with its own duke, Alfonso, the king’s second son, left in charge of it. (Pagi, 1196, no. 6.)]

V.

IN POLAND.

The metropolitan see of Gniezno has eight suffragans in Poland: Uredicilatia, Lubusz, Dachau, Liegnitz, Butivice, and Donice. [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop of Gniezno has these suffragans: Uredicilatia, Lubusz, Cuyavia, Płock, Kraków, Poznań, Mazovia, and Pomerania.] [Note: [Col. 0468C] Baronius, on the authority of Thietmar, places the beginnings of the metropolitan see of Gniezno at the end of the tenth century, but admits that the evidence seems highly suspect to him, since he sees Saint Gregory VII writing in 1074 to Bolesław, duke of Poland: “The bishops of your land, having no fixed metropolitan see and being subject to no master, wander here and there, each according to his own ordination; beyond the rules and decrees of the holy Fathers they are free and unrestrained. Moreover, since among so great a multitude of people there are so few bishops, and the parishes of each are so extensive, they are in no way able either to carry out the care of the episcopal office among their subjects or to administer it properly.” Therefore Basnage, in Canisius, volume III, p. 55 and following, rejecting the opinions of the Poles, assigns this dignity to Gniezno only after Gregory, that is, after a full century. What should be thought about these suffragan churches, consider for yourself; I prescribe nothing.]

IN ALEMANNIA.

The metropolitan see of Bremen has these suffragans: [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop, etc.] Bardowick, Solesic (Solesiucen), [Note: [Col. 0467] Soleluicen.] Ratzeburg (Raskeburgen), [Note: [Col. 0467] Kasleburgen.] Mecklenburg (Michiliburgen), [Note: [Col. 0467] Michiburgen.] Lübeck.

The metropolitan see of Magdeburg has these suffragans: [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop, etc.] Halberstadt, [Note: [Col. 0467] Hellebergen.] Brandenburg, Meissen, Merseburg, and Zeitz. [Note: [Col. 0467] Brandenburg, Meissen, Merseburg, Zeitz.]

The metropolitan see of Salzburg has these suffragans: [Note: [Col. 0467] The Archbishop, etc.] Passau, [Col. 0468B] Regensburg, Freising, Gurk, [Note: [Col. 0467] Freising, Gurk.] and Brixen. [Note: [Col. 0468D] Hansiz regards the Notitia of Abbot Milo as an older monument by which the five suffragan churches of the metropolitan of Salzburg are confirmed. Therefore Schelstratius borrowed it and included it in his work (Germania Sacra, volume II, p. 7), without rejecting even an obvious chronological inconsistency; for he says that it was composed in the time of Celestine III, in the year 1225. Although this pontiff died in 1198 and had Innocent and Honorius III as successors, the ninth year of the latter was running in the year of Christ 1225. Here, however, is a much older monument to which those same churches belong, and thus the author is consistent with himself. For shortly afterward he relates how Eberhard II, Archbishop of Salzburg, arranged for the sees of Chiemsee to be erected in 1215 and of Seckau in 1218, the first by Innocent III and the second by Honorius III (ibid., pp. 8 and 322 ff.). These two cathedrals would not have been omitted by Milo in 1225 if he had composed that Notitia at that time.]

IN THE KINGDOM OF ENGLAND. [Note: [Col. 0469] In England.]

[Col. 0469A]

The metropolitan city of Canterbury has these cities under it: [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Canterbury has these suffragans: London, Rochester or Rocester, Chichester, Exeter, Winchester, Bath, Salisbury, Worcester, Hereford, Coventry, Lincoln, Norwich, Ely, St. Davids, Llandaff, Bangor, and Saint Asaph.] London, Rochester, Chichester, Chester, Exeter, Winchester, Salisbury, Hereford, Gloucester, Bath, Nicholas [uncertain], Norwich, Ely, while in Wales there are Menevia, Bangor, Llandaff, and Saint Asaph. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Nidaros has these suffragans: Bergen, Stavanger, Hamark, Hålogaland (Hailonen), Horcaden, Suderejen, or Subtranen.]

The metropolitan see of Lund has these suffragan bishops under it: Roskilde, Odense, Schleswig, Ribe, Viborg, Aarhus, and Burgundarholm. Thus they number eight. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Lund has these suffragans: Roskilde, Odense, Schleswig, Ribe, Viborg, Aarhus, and Bornholm.]

IN THE KINGDOM OF SWEDEN. [Note: [Col. 0469] In Sweden.]

The metropolitan see of Uppsala has these suffragan bishops under it: Västerås, Strängnäs, Linköping, and Skara. Thus they number five. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Uppsala has these suffragans: Västerås, Strängnäs, Linköping, and Skara.] [Note: [Col. 0469D] Through Abbot Milo’s negligence, two kingdoms have been merged into one, and eleven Scottish prelates, all exempt, have been subjected to the metropolitan of Uppsala in the kingdom of Sweden. These will be found below at the end of the bishops belonging to the consecration of the Roman pontiff, except for the bishop of Moray, or Morayensis, as Abbot Milo calls him. [Col. 0470C]]

[Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Armagh, primate of all Ireland, has these suffragans: Connor or Duleek, Lughudun, Clonard, Conennas, Ardachadh, Raphoe, Rathlurig, Dromore, and Derry.]

The metropolitan of Dublin has these suffragans under him: the Bishop of Glendalough; the Bishop of Ferns; the Bishop of Kilkenny (Cainnig); the Bishop of Leighlin; the Bishop of Kildare. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Dublin has these suffragans: Glendalough, Ferns, Kilkenny (Cainnig), Leighlin, and Kildare.]

The metropolitan of Cashel has these suffragans under him: the Bishop of Killaloe; the Bishop of Limerick; the Bishop of the island of Gathay; the Bishop of Cellinabrach; the Bishop of Emly; the Bishop of Roscrea; the Bishop of Waterford; the Bishop of Lismore; the Bishop of Clonmacnoise; the Bishop of Cork; the Bishop of Rossailithir; and the Bishop of Ardfert. Two churches, however, [Col. 0470B] are under the same archbishop which claim that they ought to have bishops; their names are Ardinoi and Mungarath. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Cashel has these suffragans: Killaloe, Limerick, the island of Gathay, Emly, Cellinabrach, Roscrea, Waterford, Lismore, Clonmacnoise, Cork, Rossailithir, and Ardfert.] [Note: [Col. 0470C] Both this passage and what he said above concerning the division of all Ireland testify to the author’s extreme diligence; he is the interpreter of his own reliability. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Archbishop of Tuam has these suffragans: Mayo, Cellalaid, Roscommon, Kilfenora, Achonry, Conarri, and Kilmacduagh (Celinudvach).]

VI.

IN DALMATIA BEYOND THE SEA. [Note: [Col. 0470C] These two metropolitan sees, formerly famous for instability and schism, from which their patriarchal dignity arose, underwent a great change in the time of Charlemagne. In the eleventh century of the Church, the letters of Leo IX to the bishops of Venetia and Istria show that nothing better had happened to them: “By the judgment of the holy synod it was decreed that New Aquileia (Grado) should perpetually be regarded as the head and metropolitan see of all Venetia and Istria, in accordance with the most evident privileges of our predecessors. But the bishop of Friuli should be content only with the boundaries of the Lombards, according to the privilege of Gregory II and the subsequent revision of the third.” Pagius, however, observes that in 811, when Charlemagne drew up his will, the patriarchs of Aquileia were already residing at Friuli.]

The metropolitan see of Aquileia has eleven suffragans. [Note: [Col. 0469] The Patriarchate of Aquileia has these suffragans:] the Bishop of Verona, Padua, Vicenza, Como, Mantua, Treviso, Trent, Concordia, [Note: [Col. 0469] Concordia.] Ceneda, [Note: [Col. 0469] Seneda.] Feltre, [Note: [Col. 0469] Feltre.] and Belluno. [Note: [Col. 0469] The six first suffragans of Grado are added.]

IN ISTRIA BEYOND THE SEA. [Note: [Col. 0471C] Pagius, on the authority of Einhard, establishes that Charlemagne held Istria and Liburnia under his power, as well as Dalmatia except for the coastal cities. For he left these to the Greeks. This matter will be treated again more appropriately below (Dissertation I, p. 48).]

[Col. 0471A]

The metropolitan see of Grado has these suffragans. [Note: [Col. 0471] The Patriarchate of Grado has these suffragans:] Pola, [Note: [Col. 0471] Pola.] Parentium. Trieste. Comacchio. [Note: [Col. 0471C] Below, this see is correctly placed under the metropolitan of Ravenna. Thus the two Notitiae were written at different times; but nothing certain can be determined about a matter so uncertain.] the Bishop of Caput Histriae, [Note: [Col. 0471] Caput Histriae.] of Marano, [Note: [Col. 0471] Matria.] the Bishop [Note: [Col. 0471] “Bishop” is absent in both places.] of Cittanova, Castellan, Torcello, [Note: [Col. 0471] Torcello.] Aquilense, [Note: [Col. 0471] Equileia.] Caprula, and [Note: [Col. 0471] “and” is absent.] Closena. [Note: [Col. 0471] Closena, of Cittanova; this too is made subject to the see of Aquileia.]

The metropolitan see of Jadera has these bishops as suffragans, namely, the Bishop of Sinj, Ossero, Veglia, Arbe, and Nin. [Note: [Col. 0471] The Archbishop of Jadera has these suffragans.]

Metropolis of Spalatum [Note: Baronius (1062, no. 113) and Pagius (there, no. 6), commenting on the letters of Alexander II to the archbishop of the Dioclean and Antibarian Church, observe that there were two metropolitan sees in the kingdom of Dalmatia and Croatia: the Salona see, long before transferred to Spalatum, and Antibar, to which the Dioclean see had been transferred after its destruction. But in our two *Notitiae*, which extend throughout the twelfth century, Antibar is suffragan to Ragusa; and only in the later *Notitia*, in the account of the bishoprics of Catharensis in Schelstr. (p. 754), is Antibar found as the third metropolis of Sclavonia, whose suffragans differ from those listed in Alexander II’s letters. Nevertheless, I would not dare to contradict Pagius—or rather Joannes Lucius—for in the tenth century and thereafter, down to the time of Gregory VII, who transformed the duchy of Dalmatia into a kingdom, as we have seen, the arrangement of the ecclesiastical provinces must have been as Pagius observes; afterward, however, it was as these *Notitiae* display.] has [Note: The archbishopric of Spalatum has these] the following suffragans: the bishop of Trangurium [Note: Tragurium]; and [Note: “and” is absent] the bishop of Signa [Note: He adds the bishops of Scardona, Arba, Nona, Croatia, Corbavia, Tragurium.].

## In Sclavonia

The metropolitan city of Ragusa has these bishops [Note: The archbishopric of Ragusa has these] as suffragans: Stagnum; Bosnia; Tribunia; Cathara [Note: Cattaro]; Rose; Budua; Antibar; Dulcigno; Suacia; Drivastum; Polatum; Scodra [Note: Scodrona]; and Arbanum.

## In the Province of Flaminia [Note: Flaminia]

The metropolis of Ravenna [Note: That Ravenna was the metropolis of Aemilia and Flaminia is clearly shown by the *Orbis Ecclesiasticus*. For this reason it also had as suffragans the Lombard cities of Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, and Modena. It remained in this condition even in the twelfth century, as is evident from the *Notitiae*. Whatever was changed afterward, through the creation of new metropolises, is irrelevant here. It is enough to repeat what has been stated (*Cod. Car.*, vol. I, pp. 321, 329, and 335): namely, that in the age of Charlemagne Hadrian established in Aemilia the cities that are here placed in Flaminia. For the Exarchate, first granted to the Holy See by Pippin and afterward by Charles, comprised three provinces, which I shall discuss more fully in the dissertations: Aemilia, bounded by the territory of Bologna, and the two Pentapoles, one inland and the other maritime. None of these appears in these *Notitiae*, which cover the tenth century and the two following centuries. But the transformation of Aemilia into Flaminia, and of the two Pentapoles into the March, as will shortly be clear, demonstrates that the old arrangement had long since become obsolete. What confidence, then, should be placed in those learned men who, recklessly confusing the periods, maintain that the Ludovician diploma is a wholly reliable witness to that antiquity, although what it contains had been buried in oblivion? How much weight should be given to the interpretation of the Ottonian [Col. 0472D] and Henrician documents, by which these same scholars plainly show that they have not kept to their subject, since the new place-names have introduced considerable discrepancy and obscurity?] has fifteen suffragans [Note: The archbishopric of Ravenna has these suffragans]: [Col. 0471B] Piacenza [Note: absent here]; Parma; Reggio; Forlì [Note: Forlivio]; Adria; Forlimpopoli [Note: Adria and Forlimpopoli]; Ferrara [Note: also absent here]; Modena; Bologna; Faenza; Imola; Cesena [Note: Caesenatum]; Cervia; Comacchio; and [Note: “and” is absent] Sarcina [Note: Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, seized this city among the others of Aemilia in the age of Charlemagne, when its name was Bobbio or the Tenth Tribunate (*Cod. Car.*, vol. I, p. 335). It will have to be discussed in the notes to the Ludovician diploma. Here it is more than enough to warn the critics of the *Monumenta vetera* of their error in assigning obsolete names to the eleventh century.].

## In the Alps of Gothia

And this, unless I am mistaken, is the certain date of the *Notitia* that Albinus incorporated into his codex, with some additions made from time to time, none earlier than Eugene III and none later than Clement III.]; Apruniacum [Note: Aprumacen]; in Corsica [Note: “in Corsica” is absent]; and Marana.

## VII

### The Patriarchate of Antioch

The patriarchate of Antioch has under it the following metropolitans [Col. 0476A] and suffragan bishops.

The archbishops of Tarsus; Mamistra [Note: The archbishopric of Manistra]; Tylos [Note: The archbishop of Tylos, also called Elyospolis]; and Edessa [Note: The archbishop of Edessa, also called “the king of the Medes.” He adds two: Aphania and Coriza].

The bishops of Laodicea; Gabala; Valenia [Note: He makes this a suffragan of Aphania]; Antaradus; Tripoli; and Byblos.

The metropolis of Mamistra has these suffragan bishops: [lacuna].

### The Patriarchate of Jerusalem

The patriarchate of Jerusalem has under it the following suffragan bishops and the metropolises listed below: the bishop of Bethlehem; the bishop of Saint George; and the bishop of Ascalon [Note: Hebron, Lydda, and Ascalon].

The metropolis of Tyre has under it these suffragan bishops: Acre; Sidon; and Beirut [Note: Beirut, Paneas].

The metropolis of Caesarea has under it these bishops: Sebaste [Note: Sebaste, that is, the city called Samaria by another name].

The metropolis of Nazareth [Note: Nazareth] has under it the bishop of Tiberias [Note: Tiberias].

### The Patriarch of Constantinople

The patriarch of Constantinople has under him the archbishop of Crete, who has under him sixty bishops. He also has the metropolitan of Methone, who has under him [lacuna] bishops, and the metropolitan of Heraclea, who has under him [lacuna] bishops. These three metropolitans are said to have seven hundred suffragan bishops. Moreover, the same patriarch is said to have under him apostolic catholics.

[Col. 0475]

# The Genuine Book of Censuses

## Concerning the revenues of all the provinces and churches owed to the Roman Church

### First, concerning the city of Ferrara

[Col. 0475C]

The Roman Church is to receive from the city of Ferrara an annual census of fifty Luccan solidi. Half the riverbank tax, and the annual jurisdiction over the market. Also the whole *arimannia* of the parish of Cornacervina; the whole *arimannia* of Massa Fuscalia; and all its public revenue. Also the whole *arimannia* of Gabbiana; the whole *arimannia* of Lungula; the whole *arimannia* of Settepolesine; the whole court or jurisdiction of Massa; and the whole jurisdiction or property of Ciniselli and Cavalto. Also the whole *arimannia* and all the public revenue of Sadriano; the whole *arimannia* and all the public revenue of Trecenta; the whole *arimannia* of Bagnolo and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Villanova and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Maneggio and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of San Martino and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Lucarano and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Santa [Col. 0475D] Maria and all the public revenue; the whole *arimannia* and public revenue of Villa Comede; all the public revenue of Gognano; all the public revenue of Villa Marthana; the whole *arimannia* of Arquà and all the public revenue; all the public revenue of Bonisciago; all the public revenue of Agnano; the whole *arimannia* of Pontiato and its public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Filattico and its public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Ronchi and its public revenue; the whole *arimannia* of Cirpillatica; the whole *arimannia* of Bratica; the whole saltworks; all of Ficarolo; three parts of the river toll and three parts of the port of Rupta Ficaroli; the whole *arimannia* [Col. 0476C] of Trenta; the whole *arimannia* of Leone; the whole *arimannia* of Gello; the whole *arimannia* of Fabriciano; the whole *arimannia* of San Donato; and the whole *arimannia* of Flesso and Ficarolo, together with its entire county. Jurisdiction and authority over all crimes. And twice each year, namely in May and on Saint Martin’s day, a general court session.

Likewise, the church of Ficarolo owes four Luccan solidi for Villa Salaria. The church of Saint Gregory owes one morabitino.

## These are owed to the lord pope by those who purchase the Confession of Saint Peter

These are what the lord pope is to receive from those who purchase the Confession of Saint Peter, according to the terms imposed on former purchasers. First, in the treasury, every day three pounds of wax; every month one *aquaricia* of oil and one pound of frankincense. At Easter, twenty pounds of wax in addition to what is owed in the treasury. For the torch on Holy Saturday, ten pounds of wax; ten pounds for the *Agnus*; three denarii of balsam according to the Lateran weight, and three for Saint Peter. Five pounds of wax for Saint Peter for the baptismal torch. Twelve ampullae, six larger and six smaller. Six fans.

On the feast of Saint Mary, twenty pounds for the *rosta* of the Lord Savior. At the Nativity of the Lord, twenty pounds of wax in the treasury in addition to the three pounds given each day, and two pounds of frankincense. At the Purification of Saint Mary, ten pounds and four denarii for the *jungae*. At the Annunciation, likewise. At the Nativity, ten pounds of wax and four denarii for the *jungae*. By customary practice, twelve denarii are given to the acolytes on Palm Sunday for palms.

During Holy Week, the bishop of Santa Rufina has the right that he customarily possesses—namely, the chest and altar from which the signal is rung for Matins until the office is completed, and from which it is rung for Mass until the end of Mass—without prejudice to the right of the singers, which they exercise at the altar together with the bishop. On Holy Thursday, from the ringing of the signal for the morning office and for Mass until the end of the offices, likewise. On Good Friday, likewise. On Holy Saturday, from the ringing of the signal for the morning office, and from the ringing of the signal for the baptismal office, throughout the entire night and day until the end of the principal Mass at Easter, he is to have his right.

When the lord pope is not in the city, twelve papal denarii are given to the ushers each week; on Palm Sunday, two solidi; and at each feast of Saint Mary, one candle and ten denarii for making candles. To Saint Lawrence of the Palace are given each month one *aquaricia* of oil, one pound of wax, and half a pound of frankincense.

When the lord pope goes to Saint Peter for the station, he receives twenty solidi and two *aquariciae* of drink. The chaplains [Col. 0477B] with their companions have half the altar from the time the altar cloth is spread over it. The cardinals receive five Pavia solidi at the station. When the singers sing the responsory in the ambo, eighteen papal denarii.

At Easter, at the Lateran, the lord pope receives two *aquariciae* of drink. From the feast of Saint Gregory until Pentecost, twelve papal denarii are given to the lord pope each day. At the greater litanies, twenty-seven Luccan pounds for the provision of the crosses of the cardinal bishops, the couches, and the gallery.

For the lights before the altar of Saint Peter: thirteen candles, and thirteen in the body of the church by day and night. One candle is to be lit in each small chapel throughout the night until Mass is finished. At the stations: four in the large chapel, and three in the small chapel with the porticoes; twelve in the net; eighteen on the rod. Before the Veronica, one by day and night. At Saint Processus, one by day and night. At Santa Maria de Cancellis, one at night. At the Vatican, one at night. At Santa Croce, one at night. At Santa Lucia, one at night. Before the crucifix, two at night. On the rod, three; in the net, three.

On the Monday after Easter: “I am the good shepherd.” At the Ascension; at Pentecost; on the feast of Saint Peter; at the dedication of that church; at Epiphany; at the Chair; and at the greater litany, the nets are to be lit. On Saint Peter’s feast alone, the large net before the silver doors is to be lit.

When the roof is repaired and broken beams of the church of Saint Peter are replaced, two denarii are given to each master and each laborer until the work is completed. When the sandal-makers take up Saint Peter’s beams, they receive two papal solidi and four pounds of wax at the feast [lacuna].

The church of Saint Andrew receives two *aquariciae* of oil. The clerics of Saint Peter who perform the office receive three papal solidi. The cardinal who has custody of Saint Peter receives four papal denarii each day. As alms, each week, in addition to what is given to the expelled, twelve solidi of Rouen while the road is in use. Each member of the household receives two papal denarii each day.

When the prefects of Sorrento hang someone, they receive five solidi; when they behead someone, five solidi; when they blind someone, twelve denarii for each eye; when they cut off a limb, likewise twelve denarii.

Santa Rufina receives as alms one *aquaricia* of oil, ten pounds of wax, and half a pound of frankincense. The Four Saints, Saint Clement, and Saint Pancras receive as alms four papal denarii for the masters, for the cage and four ropes, when they light the net, except for the cardinals’ weekly allowances, the church of Saint Lawrence in the Palace, the clerics of Saint Peter, the singers, and the dominical allowances of the cardinal deacons.

At the stations, one pair of torches weighing two pounds is provided at Vespers, and another pair weighing two pounds at Mass. The lord pope’s household also customarily receives a blessing.

When the lord pope remains away from Rome for more than one day’s journey, no wax is given to him for the treasury. Moreover, the chalices, crosses, censers, and basins of gold or silver; the *camisiae*, amices, stoles, maniples, corporals [Col. 0478A] placed over the chalices; the German towels; and the pallia weighing more than six pounds of *affortiati*, which are offered at the altar, belong to the lord pope.

When necessary, the altar is to replace three beams in the nave each year, and is to give two papal denarii for food to the masters of Saint Peter when they work in that church. It is also to provide a good meal for the canons of Saint Peter when they have spent the entire night keeping vigil over the pallia of the Roman pontiff, patriarchs, archbishops, and certain bishops. Whenever necessary, the prior of the basilica is to prepare these pallia and, together with the cardinal deacons, attend their presentation [Note: Here you see several points of the ancient discipline that require explanation. You will find them explained by me in the book *On the Pre-eminence of the Vatican Basilica*, if it should ever be published. The same applies to what follows.].

## Revenues in the City of Rome

The monastery of Saint Paul: bread for the person of the lord pope. The canons of the Lateran likewise. The church of Saint Mark: ten papal solidi for the estate that Pope Celestine granted to it. The church of Saint Peter: twenty Luccan solidi. The church of Saint Susanna: one *scifatus* and one morabitino. Those who hold the tower at the head of the Bridge of the Jews: four [Col. 0478B] papal denarii. The church of Saint Giles, with the hospital situated beside the Leonine City: forty *affortiati* at the feast of Saint Andrew. The church of Saint Praxedes: one *scifatus*. The church of Saint Abbacirus: one morabitino. Petrus Latro: two morabitini for the castle of Ceri.

In the bishopric of Albano: the church of Saint Donatus of the coast, one morabitino. The hospital of Cantaro, one pound of wax.

In the bishopric of Porto: Petrus Latro, two morabitini for the castle of Ceri.

In the March and the duchy of Spoleto: in Senigallia; in Ancona; in Osimo; the men of Monte Saint Peter, three Luccan solidi; the church of Saint Peter in the same place, two solidi; in Numana, the church of Saint Fabian of Recanati, twelve denarii; in Fermo, the hospital of Acqua Santa, twelve Paduan [denarii] per year; in Assisi; in Camerino, the monastery of Santa Maria of Frastra [Col. 0478C], two pounds of wax; the monastery of Santa Maria of Villa Magna, one pound of wax as census and one bezant as rent for a certain piece of land; the monastery of Cliente, one pound of wax and one bezant for what it holds from the Roman Church; in Forum Sempronii; in Urbino; in Cagli, the church of Saint Gerontius, twelve *affortiati*; in Jesi, the church of Santa Maria of the Forest, twelve papal denarii; in Montefeltro, the church of Saint Anastasius, twelve silver denarii; in Nocera; in Gubbio, the monastery of Saint Emilianus, three *affortiati* solidi; the monastery of Saint Ambrose, three solidi; in Foligno; in Perugia, the church of Saint Peter on Monte Teuzi, three *affortiati* solidi; the church of Santa Maria situated on Monte Ferioli, three papal denarii and one torch each year; in Amelia; in Todi; [Col. 0478D] in Narni, the monastery of Saint Nicholas, one pound of wax; in Ascoli; in Spoleto, the church of Saint Peter beside the city, two Luccan solidi; the castle called Moriciola, obtained through the surrender of Gisler, belongs by right to Saint Peter, as is found in the Register of Pope Gregory VII; and the monastery of Saint Peter of Bovaria, five Luccan solidi; in Rieti, the monastery of the Savior; in Valva, the monastery of Bominaco, one Romanato; in Marsica, the monastery of Santa Maria of Appamia, three Provençal solidi and one pound of wax; in Chieti, the monastery of Majella, one morabitino; the monastery of Saint Stephen, one ounce of gold; in Penne.

## [THE LETTERS OF LEO III]

[Col. 0487]

### 1. DISSERTATION ON THE LETTERS OF SAINT LEO III TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES

#### § I.—Many more remain hidden than those published by Conring

[Col. 0487C]

I. Gretserus rightly complained (Carolingian Codex, preface) of the insolence of Illyricus, who calls the letters of Leo III, that most holy pontiff, completely crude and barbarous (*Catalogue of Witnesses of Truth*, p. 127). For if Flacius had taken the circumstances of that rough age into account, he would have discovered that this inelegant style of writing was attributable more to the age than to the pontiff. Moreover, what seemed distasteful to Flacius is most agreeable to us, who have become accustomed to the letters of Hadrian. Would that he had committed to posterity those letters which he rejected! For it is scarcely credible that, during the long period of eighteen years in which he enjoyed intimacy with Charles, the pontiff gave him only ten letters—those which Hermann Conring published in 1647, after Gretser’s death, having copied them from the parchment manuscripts of the Julia library of the Helmstedt Academy.

People acquired these few letters with such avidity that they had to be committed once more to the Helmstedt press in 1655, somewhat more accurately corrected. Labbe, having obtained a copy of this second edition, included these ten letters in his great collection of the Councils [2], after the three older ones also known to Gretser, which have no bearing on our subject and which, before Conring’s edition, had been seen by our forefathers as the letters of so great and long-lived a pontiff—for, succeeding Hadrian in 795, he held the pontificate for nearly twenty-one years, until 816. Labbe, however, placed a brief notice at the margin (*Councils*, vol. VII, p. 1113), through which the great rarity of both editions becomes clear:

“Conring, Hermann, published this and the following nine in 1655 at Helmstedt; but, in accordance with the customary practice of heretics, they had been befouled with the most shameful accusations and calumnies against the Catholic Church and its supreme pontiffs.”

Among such untimely witticisms, utterly unworthy of a man endowed with reason, much less of an honest man, and contributing nothing beyond the barren laughter from idle and indolent little men, two matters show that the judgment of that most learned and venerable man—Cardinal Bona (*Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 12, no. 2)—is applicable against Flacius Illyricus, who, intending to inflict harm upon the Catholic Church, published the Latin Mass:

“His own wickedness blinded him,” he says; “for, on the contrary, the doctrines of the orthodox faith and the received rites of the Church are confirmed throughout it”: namely, the confession of the supreme dominion of the pontiffs and the empire renewed by them.

II. Indeed, at the outset he admits what he cannot deny (Preface), the supreme power of the Roman pontiff: “Released by every right from the Caesars, they would also rule a good part of Italy with royal power.” Later, openly lying, he adds how Leo III was subjected to force by his own people and compelled—“especially at the demand of those same Roman citizens—to subject the pontifical see once again to imperial authority, when Charles the Great had been elected Caesar.”

For this reason he also took care that the headings and conclusions of all the letters should be printed in the Italian character, as it is called, so that they might strike the reader’s eyes at first sight: “To the most devout and most serene victor and triumphant son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus,” and likewise, “May the most devout empire of the lord be guarded by heavenly grace.” These should be compared with the letters of the Carolingian Codex which he calls Gretserian, so that the difference may be grasped.

What then? These are the words; and none of the learned, nor Conring nor the more recent writers who follow him, denies that Leo III addressed Charles with imperial majesty, omitting none of the titles proper to such dignity. Yet Leo addresses the emperor in this manner (letter 2, elsewhere 10):

“By the very key-bearer of the heavenly Kingdom, who has appointed you defenders of his interests.”

Similarly, speaking of King Pippin [3], who was about to come to Rome (letter 4, elsewhere 6), he says:

“As is fitting for the son of so great a defender of the holy Church of God.”

And in other letters he repeatedly calls the emperor “defender of the holy Church [Col. 0489A] of God,” just as his predecessor Hadrian had called that same Charles a patrician.

Moreover, he complains (letter 3, elsewhere 1) that certain people had accused him of being difficult toward the imperial envoys and of disdaining to receive subjects into his favor if they had sought imperial protection:

“Not only,” he says, “are your envoys afraid to carry your embassy to our lowliness, but others have now no longer dared to seek help from you, because, as they say, no one who has sought your clemency has subsequently been able to attain our complete favor.”

I pass over the appointments of dukes in ecclesiastical territory, the preparation of arms for the defense of the coast, and other actions indicating a supreme ruler, which will be discussed more appropriately in the notes. Was this “to subject the pontifical see once again to imperial authority”? Wretched defenders of a false opinion! They use a two-edged weapon by which, while they think they are inflicting wounds, they themselves are wounded.

[Col. 0489B]

III. What of the fact that Leo is urged by concern for Sicily and Sardinia because of the Moorish schemes against both islands (letters 8 and 9, elsewhere 3 and 2)? What of the fact that Gregory, the patrician of Sicily, although he followed the custom of the Greek emperor, maintained an exchange of letters with Charles and Leo?

“We received,” says the pontiff, “the reply of Gregory, the patrician of Sicily—that is, your Serenity’s letter, which we sent to him through our man.”

Was there a question here of the donation of that island to the holy Roman Church, which had long before been unjustly stripped of the extensive revenues of the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies, so that, through Saint Peter’s intercession, it might not be swallowed by the jaws of the Agarenes who continually coveted it, with evident and perpetual danger to the shores of the papal territory and the kingdom of Italy?

Certainly, five years earlier—or in the year 808—it is clear from these letters that the island of Corsica had obeyed papal commands (letter 4, elsewhere 6), for the same reasons, unless I am mistaken. The rights of the Holy See over it may have been lesser, since it possessed there only one patrimony, whereas from the Sicilian patrimony it should have demanded every year, by way of exchange, the extensive ancient revenues belonging to the East:

“But concerning the island of Corsica,” he says, “about which you have written to us and sent your messengers, we commit it to your judgment and disposition, and have placed it in the mouth of Count Helmgaud, so that your donation may always remain firm and stable and remain safe from the snares of enemies, through the intercession of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed chief Apostles Peter and Paul, and through your most powerful arm.” [4]

And Louis the Pious, the son of Charles, in his diploma—of which more below—lists these three islands among Charles’s donations. This circumstance persuaded several more recent scholars to believe that the Ludovician diploma had been interpolated.

IV. In view of these facts, no one at all will deny that more of Leo’s letters are missing. In particular, the oldest of those published by Conring concerns the year 806, whereas Leo had been pontiff since 795. Meanwhile, until it is granted to someone more fortunate to drag them from their hiding place, I shall devote myself to examining these ten letters, which are the greatest surviving remains of the intact papal dominion and display the beginnings of imperial majesty. [Col. 0489D]

And lest I be accused of having shown too little diligence in editing these letters—both easier to understand and much fewer in number—when I so carefully arranged the letters of the Carolingian Codex, I imposed upon myself precisely the same rules which I followed in preparing those letters.

As regards variation of readings, the Helmstedt manuscripts must be said to have supplied corrections made by one and the same reviser who examined them again, rather than variant readings. Nevertheless, our edition will possess this distinctive feature: it will place before the eyes of readers both Conring’s first and his second efforts.

But since imperial majesty was Conring’s principal aim when he published Leo’s letters, it will also be fitting that I concern myself with the same majesty established—or, if you prefer, restored—by Leo III. Therefore, beginning with that restoration itself, I shall set forth its true character not only for German jurists, but especially for the Italian annalist [Col. 0490A] who ascribes (*Italian Annals*, 800) the supreme rule of Rome and its duchy by the Greek emperors until the year 800.

Then, taking advantage of the circumstance of the woman ruling at Constantinople, he supposes that the pontiff and the Romans, with the legal authority of the Greeks transferred to Charles, subjected themselves to him, guided by no historical record and no weighty authority.

Although both the Lambecian annalist, cited by Pagius (800, no. 9), and others—all of them mistakenly—consider the absence of an Eastern emperor to have been the cause of the renewal of the Western Empire, they neither assert nor could assert that supreme dominion had hitherto belonged to the Greeks and thereafter to the Franks.

The contemporary authors give only one cause for the renewal of imperial majesty in the West: namely, the necessity of keeping in their allegiance the peoples who had long been subject to the Roman pontiff. All the other causes are arguments advanced by writers who flourished long after those times and committed to writing not what was true but what resembled the truth.

For the defense of the Catholic faith and of the Roman Church was the office of the patrician; and how excellently Charles fulfilled it is known from the letters of the Carolingian [Col. 0490B] Codex [5]. Nor was imperial majesty necessary for him to continue performing that same office. But I shall speak of these matters somewhat farther below.

For now, the deeds which Charles the patrician accomplished with distinction for the orthodox faith and the Roman Church after the age of the Carolingian Codex must be recalled to memory, so that discussion of the restoration of imperial dignity may become clearer and more useful.

### § II.—The Catholic faith and the Roman Church nobly defended by Charles the Great, patrician of the Romans, and papal dominion enlarged
### V.

Nothing is in fact more celebrated among historians, both ancient and modern, than the madness of the iconoclasts throughout the eighth century of the Church. From it arose Italy’s defection from the emperors of the East, the dominion of the Roman Church, the change in the Exarchate, the destruction of the kingdom of the Lombards, and especially the beginnings and power of the Carolingian kings, which they credited as gifts to the prince of the apostles and his successors. All this is established by the letters of Leo III’s predecessors included in the *Caroline Code*. Orthodox faith and the tradition of the Fathers—for that is how the veneration of sacred images is called in those letters—are earnestly commended to the Frankish kings. Above all, those most devout kings are urged to vindicate the image of Saint Peter, celebrated throughout the whole world.

For the Isaurian had threatened Gregory II, in blasphemous language, at the very beginning of his impiety, that he would shatter it, as is clear from his letter, translated into Latin by Fronto Ducaeus, in Baronius (726, vol. XII, p. 352) and Labbe (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 7 ff.). In his precise words: “I will send to Rome,” he said, “and shatter the image of Saint Peter; and I shall also see to it that Gregory the pope is brought back from there in chains.”

For this reason, in the first embassy arranged to Charles Martel, prince of the Franks, the keys of Peter—namely, the symbol of the power to open and close the kingdom of heaven—were sent with such success that, although Charles himself had not been permitted to do so, his son Pippin, the first Carolingian king, was made king by Peter’s authority through his vicar or successor. Pippin and his son Charlemagne were designated patricians, or defenders of Peter and his successors, and protectors of the particular people—the Romans—and of all the inhabitants of the Roman duchy; they considered nothing more ancient or holier than the defense and exaltation of the bearer of the keys of the kingdom of heaven and of his particular people, the Apostolic See.

How richly both kings performed this duty is abundantly shown by the many barbarian nations they defeated, the spread of the Catholic faith, and the great fear they struck into those impious emperors. Hence Charles was wearied by the embassies arriving from Constantinople, though generally with uncertain or fruitless results. For the more eagerly Charles fought on behalf of the sacred images, the more detestable was the impiety with which the Greeks sought to destroy them. All this is established by the documents of the *Caroline Code*.

### VI.

In that Code, written in the year 791, the principal testimony to the defense by which Charles the patrician upheld the sacred images and exalted the Apostolic See is unfortunately lacking. But the Second General Council of Nicaea preserves for us, later generations, the memory of this great matter (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 915 ff.). It is the letter of Hadrian to Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, written, as Labbe observes, in the year 794 after the Council of Frankfurt, against the opponents of the aforementioned Nicene synod.

To grasp its meaning, we must step back a little. After Constantine Copronymus died, as we said (vol. I, p. 336), in the year 776, his son Leo IV succeeded him as emperor and heir to his father’s impiety. Leo had by the empress Irene a son, Constantine, and, after Leo was carried off by an untimely death, he left his successor under his mother’s guardianship in the year 780. While these emperors possessed power, a momentary light shone after a storm of nearly sixty years.

Hadrian, who recognized this as the helmsman of Peter’s ship, sent a letter addressed to both rulers on 25 October, Indiction 9, that is, in the year 785. Baronius (785, no. 14 ff.) and Labbe (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 99 ff.) transmit it, and not without good reason. For those rulers, inclined to restore the Catholic faith, allowed a general council to be convened; it was held at Nicaea toward the end of the year 787.

When the acts of that council had been brought to Francia, it became clear that its second canon had been understood in a distorted sense and condemned at the Council of Frankfurt. On this matter, since we must not linger over lengthy questions that would divert us from our subject, one should consult Baronius’s annals, Sirmond’s observations on that council, and especially Peter de Marca (*On the Councils*, book VI, chapter 25).

As for our present concern, the Fathers of Frankfurt attacked that canon according to the aforementioned distorted interpretation, in very virulent language, in a capitulary divided into four books. These books are attributed to Charles with gross injustice because he sent them to Hadrian for refutation, and for that reason they are called the *Caroline Books*. Hadrian shows that this attribution is false in the letter mentioned above, in which he most learnedly demolishes that capitulary.

### VII.

And indeed, when he comes to the final chapter (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 960), he quotes the whole passage:

> “The final chapter is this: let the apostolic lord, our father, and the entire Roman Church together know that, in accordance with what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory, which he sent to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles: ‘We permit images of the saints to be made by anyone who wishes, both in the church and outside the church, for the love of God and his saints. We do not, however, compel those who do not wish to adore them. We do not permit anyone to break or destroy them, even if he wishes to do so. And because in this letter we unquestionably and freely profess that we follow the mind of the most holy Gregory, in accordance with the universal Catholic Church pleasing to God.’”

Then he replies to Charles as follows:

> “This sacred and venerable chapter differs greatly from all the chapters mentioned above. Therefore we have recognized that it is characteristic of your God-preserved and orthodox royal excellence in this respect: that it has fully and thoroughly confessed the right faith, namely, that it follows the most holy mind of Gregory. For your most upright and exalted royal wisdom remembers how, in that letter of the holy Pope Gregory addressed to Bishop Serenus of Marseilles, among other things he is said to have written, rebuking that same bishop: ‘For it is one thing to adore a painting, and another to learn from the history represented in a painting what ought to be adored.’”

He continues by demonstrating from various letters of that same Gregory that the veneration due to sacred images is entirely different from the adoration owed to the one triune God.

The devout prince had acted in the same way when, before the Council of Frankfurt, he received in writing the heretical opinions recorded by the bold Elipandus and had them submitted to the examination of learned men. For, having those opinions brought to Hadrian, he elicited from him that sober yet very lengthy letter to the bishops of Hispania and Galicia (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 1014), in which the guardian of the deposit of the divine Savior instructed those bishops in uncorrupted doctrine.

Although he had Alcuin with him, a most learned man under whose instruction he had been educated, nevertheless, whenever controversies of faith were at issue, he turned to the source of infallible doctrine in order to receive the dogmas of orthodox faith, whose most vigorous defender he was, as we have often seen in the first volume of this work.

### VIII.

Moreover, Hadrian used as an example that extraordinary veneration with which Charles honored the prince of the apostles above other saints in the letter mentioned above to Constantine and Irene, admonishing them to implore the protection of Peter after the example of Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. For he says:

> “With the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, accompanying you against all barbarian nations, you will rule in triumph as victorious rulers, just as our son and spiritual compater, Lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, obeying our admonitions and fulfilling our wishes in all things, has cast down beneath his feet, subdued their power, subjected them to his kingdom, and united under it all the barbarian nations of the whole western and Occident regions. Hence, because of his great love, through his laborious struggles he has continually offered many gifts for the possession of the Church of that same apostle of God: provinces as well as cities, fortresses, and other territories, indeed also patrimonies that had been held by the treacherous Lombard people, [recovered?] by a strong arm for that same apostle of God, whose rights they were known to be. Nor does he cease daily to offer gold and silver for the adornment of the lamps and the support of the poor, so that his royal memory may not be abandoned throughout all ages.”

I have considered it my duty not to omit anything from this statement, since it contains almost the very words of the diploma of Pious Louis, Charles’s son—an important proof of its authenticity:

> “All these provinces written above—Emilia, the Pentapolis, Tuscany—cities and towns, fortified places and castles, villages and territories, and likewise patrimonies…”

I would have the defenders of the false opinion of Pagius and the Italian annalist take note of this. By reversing the wording of the *Caroline Code*, they postpone the donation of Tuscany to the year 787, so that they may more easily cast doubt on the transfer of possession. For if Hadrian announced these donations to the Greek rulers in the year 785, only the cities of Campania ought to be postponed until Charles’s third arrival, that is, until the year 787.

### IX.

What more? Is this lavish generosity not attributed to the patrician of the Romans? Does it not demonstrate that Greek rule in Rome had been completely obliterated?

The patriciate, as de Marca observes (*On the Councils*, chapter 12), with Pagius approving the doctrine (740, no. 8), comprised two things: the jurisdiction that the Frankish kings exercised in the city of Rome itself by consent of the pope and the Roman people, and the defense of the Roman Church. To these must certainly be added the protection of the orthodox faith, which we have often seen to be the principal duty of the patriciate.

Nor was this unfamiliar to the Greeks, who had repeatedly attempted, though in vain, to bring both the Exarchate and Rome back under their authority. Therefore those who assert that supreme Greek dominion continued until the end of the eighth century are disguising the truth. For what confidence would the pope have had to insult rulers whom he hoped would return to the Catholic religion?

Stephen II is known to have acted otherwise (vol. I, pp. 16, 58). Through an envoy, or imperial representative, and by humble letters, he had invited Copronymus to defend the City; he was willing to renounce the dominion, provided only that the City’s defense was not neglected.

In Hadrian’s time, however, when a great defender was present in Rome, the holy commonwealth had for nearly sixty years cast off Greek rule, and very few remained who remembered any other dominion in the City besides that of the pope. Hadrian spoke from Rome to the rulers of Constantinople in keeping with his dignity and majesty.

Such, certainly, was the status of the Roman pontiff in the City and in Gaul. In the year 757, the Senate and People of Rome confessed him to be “our lord appointed by God” (vol. I, p. 143). Alcuin, Charles’s teacher, who would stand for all the Franks (letter 27, formerly 72), speaks of the supreme pontiffs in this way:

> “I have always loved, as far as I was able, the most blessed princes and shepherds of the holy Roman See.”

But we must not pass over the letter of Hadrian, prince of Rome, to the rulers Constantine and Irene, which we are examining. In it Hadrian demands back from those rulers both the sacred and civil rights that had been usurped for so many years, if they wished to embrace the Catholic faith, in these words:

### X.

> “If you strive to embrace the true and orthodox faith of the holy Catholic Roman Church, just as the patrimonies of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and your patron, were anciently offered and granted by orthodox emperors and by other Christian believers, may you deign to restore them to us in their entirety for the adornment of the lamps of that Church of God and for the support of the poor. Moreover, may the consecrations of archbishops and bishops belonging to our diocese, as ancient tradition clearly establishes, be completely and canonically restored to our holy Roman Church.”

As regards sacred rights, the consecrations of the bishops of Sicily, Calabria, Venetia, and both Illyricums were being reclaimed. The civil rights extended less widely, for they were confined to the boundaries of Calabria and Sicily. Alemannus treats both matters with great learning (*On the Lateran Walls*, chapter 15).

Hadrian demanded these rights so forcefully that nine years later, in his letters to Charles in which he refutes the *Capitulary*, or *Caroline Books*, as the innovators called them, he declared that Constantine—who had excluded his mother from sharing the empire, to his own destruction—would not emerge from heresy unless he restored those rights:

> “For some time ago, when we urged them to restore the sacred images, we likewise spoke of the diocese both of the archbishops and of the bishops of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, which they then took away together with our patrimonies, when they removed the sacred images; and they gave no answer whatsoever concerning it. From this it is shown that, having returned from error in one chapter, they remain in the same error in the other two.”

And below:

> “Therefore, if your royal excellence, protected by God, should consent, we urge you with the same force to restore the sacred images to their former state, giving thanks. But concerning the diocese of our holy Roman Church, both of archbishops and of bishops, and concerning the patrimonies, we again rebuke and admonish you that, if he refuses to restore them to our holy Roman Church, we shall decree him a heretic because of his persistence in this error. For we desire more to preserve the salvation of souls and the stability of right faith than to possess such worldly property.”

Thus Hadrian wrote in 794. At the end of the following year he died; nor, during the twenty-year pontificate of Saint Leo III, did those patrimonies return to the Church.

Meanwhile the Saracens, intent upon Sicily and having repeatedly attempted its invasion, finally invaded the island in 827 and expelled the Greeks permanently from all Italy. After they had occupied the island for more than two centuries, the Holy See recovered those ancient rights with the aid of the Normans.

### XI.

Alemannus explains why Hadrian demanded those patrimonies so forcefully, citing the words of Theophanes:

> “They are called the patrimonies of the holy princes, the apostles, who are venerated in Old Rome. Three and a half talents of gold, that is, three hundred and fifty pounds of gold, had once customarily been paid to their churches.”

These, Alemannus adds, “according to our reckoning, amount to thirty-five thousand gold pieces each year.”

Thus, when the pontiff reclaimed them, nearly two million gold pieces—intended to be spent on the support of the poor and the maintenance of the lamps—had been sacrilegiously taken by the iconoclasts from the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies. Whatever Constantine the Great and his imperial successors, patricians, and others had contributed in the East to the churches mentioned above for the relief of their souls had been transferred there to make collection easier.

But we shall speak of this again when Louis the Pious’s diploma is discussed. For now, I wish to point out seriously the reasons why the Roman pontiffs so zealously reclaimed the Church’s patrimonies, as is evident from the *Register* of Saint Gregory the Great in the case of the Sicilian patrimony, while the Church enjoyed it.

Men and women of every rank, including members of the clergy, received what was necessary for food and clothing throughout their lives (book I, letters 18, 44, 65; book V, letter 38; book VII, letter 38). Those burdened with debt and detained in prison because of poverty obtained relief, freedom, and protection for their lives (book II, Indiction 11, letter 56). The needs of the entire diocese were supported with two thousand measures of grain for food (book V, letter 4). I omit countless other lesser necessities.

In the *Pontifical Book* one can see the Church’s highly praised custom, innate from its origin, of pouring out its treasures upon the poor and providing for the beauty of the churches. The same appears in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*. Their venerable father, Baronius (175, no. 10), promising to give several examples of pontifical generosity poured out upon the poor, introduces them with that notable example of Gregory XIII, who died in his own day and, in less than thirteen years of his pontificate, distributed nearly two million gold pieces.

For this reason, besides provinces and cities, patrimonies were chiefly claimed for the Holy See in the diplomas of rulers at the urging of the pontiffs. For rulers were not free to pour out upon the poor and churches, from the public treasury, funds that had to be spent on military and civil duties, troops, public works, and other matters, both at Rome and in other cities and places under ecclesiastical rule.

### XII.

This distinct use of money was the reason why Hadrian repeatedly sought Charles’s assistance for repairing the Basilica of Saint Peter (the *Caroline Code*, letter 66, formerly 61; 87, formerly 66). It was also the reason why the Leonine City, begun by Leo III, could not have been completed by Leo IV, according to the *Pontifical Book* (section 532), unless the Emperor Lothair and his brothers had supplied considerable pounds of silver.

King Charles, by nature most generous toward the poor and churches and trained in the best disciplines, understood well the character of the Church’s patrimonies. Therefore, whether, seeing Hadrian’s constancy and the long-standing obstinacy of the Greeks—whose methods he had learned by experience—and cultivating a pretended friendship for the peace of the Italian kingdom and the Apostolic See, he granted the island of Sicily to that same Holy See before he became emperor, together with Sardinia and Corsica; or whether he did so later, after learning that Sicily could be defended from Saracen incursions more effectively through the patronage of the prince of the apostles than by arms—this remains a matter of conjecture, since no ancient document confirms such a grant.

Only from letters of Leo III do we learn that, in the year 808, the island of Corsica belonged to the Holy See through Charles’s generosity. Nine years later, we learn that Sardinia and Sicily as well were added by Pious Louis to his father’s donation.

Thus the Apostolic See nevertheless attributes its rights in that island to Charles, whether as patrician or emperor, even if it did not possess them continuously because of Greek obstinacy, followed by the Saracen invasion. I myself would prefer to attribute them to him as patrician, so that the Carolingian donation might precede Charles’s imperial dignity in its entirety; but I would not dare to assert so important a matter merely by conjecture.

I shall proceed to discuss the other matters that occurred between the Holy See and the patrician of the Romans before the restoration of so conspicuous a dignity in the West.

### XIII.

After Hadrian died on 25 December in the year 795, an embassy was immediately sent to the great defender of the Church to announce the death of his friend, the pope. Another followed, arranged by Leo himself, who was elected the next day and consecrated two days later.

The monk of Engolism (V. *Charlemagne*, in Pithoeus, p. 45) speaks of it in these words:

> “Pope Hadrian died, and as soon as Leo succeeded him, he sent envoys with gifts to the king; he also sent him the keys of the shrine (*confessio*) of Saint Peter and the banner of the city of Rome.”

Others say different things about such gifts; I have no time to weigh the lengthy disputes of more recent writers. The same monk of Engolism (ibid., p. 52) determines what should be thought of them when he describes similar gifts brought by envoys from the patriarch of Jerusalem:

> “For the sake of a blessing they brought the keys of the Lord’s tomb and of the place of Calvary, and also the keys of the city and of the Mount of Olives, together with a banner.”

The Lorsch Annals, as Cointius calls them, which Pagius, Duchesne, and others attribute to Einhard, introduce a false claim on this occasion:

> “And he asked,” they say concerning the pope, “that he send one of his nobles to Rome to bind the Roman people to his allegiance and submission by oaths.”

That would attribute too much to the patrician. Therefore the annalist, whoever he was, confuses the periods and fails to distinguish, as he should have done, the emperor from the patrician. For although the office of each was the defense of the Roman Church, the obedience of the Romans toward the two was not the same.

Basnage, with his customary learning, understood this (Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. II, p. 418). He therefore preferred to commit an anachronism by anticipating Charles’s imperial dignity rather than, through ignorance, appear uncertain about an established fact:

> “This letter,” he says concerning Alcuin’s letter 27, formerly 72, “was written to Leo III in the year 796. After Hadrian’s death, Leo, who had taken his place, sent the keys of Peter’s shrine (*confessio*) to the emperor Charles the Great and requested that some of the nobles be sent to him on an embassy, so that the Roman people might be bound to the emperor by a new oath. For this reason Angilbert was chosen, since he had already gone to Rome twice.”

### XIV.

I shall not dwell on refuting the opinions of the Italian annalist, who, in accordance with the fate implied by his name, embraced whatever seemed to weaken pontifical dominion and establish imperial dominion. The matters relevant here refute themselves.

In the year 796 he opposes Pagius, who gives no credence to those attributing dominion over the City to King Charles. He says that the sacred keys of Peter’s confession signify what had once been exhibited to Charles Martel through the keys: the kingdom of Rome.

In the year 800 he attacks Baronius, as though Baronius were using an argument contrary to his own position. For, while Baronius rejects the arguments of those who suppose that dominion over the City was transferred to King Charles through the keys of Peter’s confession and the banner, he does so by appealing to the example of the keys sent to Jerusalem for the sake of a blessing, together with a banner. Meanwhile, forgetting himself, the Italian annalist asserts that the Greeks possessed the same dominion until the aforementioned year.

Pagius had correctly interpreted the banner as signifying the defense of the city of Rome (796, no. 10), and, before the Italian annalist, had thoroughly refuted de Marca and Cointius, who prolonged Greek rule to the end of the eighth century.

These and similar inferences are dismissed by Charles’s own letter in Labbe (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 1128), which is addressed:

> “Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to Leo the pope, perpetual blessedness in Christ.”

In its opening words he acknowledges Leo as prince:

> “Having read the letters of your excellence…”

He continues with thanksgiving because the pontiff had sent him the decree of his election—not out of necessity, for he had already been consecrated, but as a matter of duty, so that the unanimity of the election might be evident without any defect—and he promised to preserve his loyalty to him forever.

After much else that reveals the mind of the most devout prince, he says that he had instructed Angilbert to convey:

> “Whatever seemed voluntary to us or necessary to you, so that by mutual discussion you may determine whatever you understand to be necessary for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, for the stability of your honor, or for the firmness of our patriciate. For just as I entered into a pact with the most blessed predecessor of your holy fatherhood, so I desire to establish with your blessedness an unbreakable covenant of the same faith and charity, so that, by divine grace, with the prayers of the saints advocating for me, the apostolic blessing may everywhere accompany me, and, by God’s gift, the most holy See of the Roman Church may always be defended by our devotion.”

### XV.

What he promised in words he confirmed by deeds. For this holy pontiff required the defense that properly belonged to the patrician of the Romans. Since this was the final act of Charles’s patriciate and the sole origin of his imperial dignity, I shall carefully relate the entire matter as it occurred.

In the fourth year of Pope Leo III, that is, in 799, on 25 April, during the Major Litanies, a monstrous crime, horrifying to relate, was perpetrated. It appears with only slight differences of wording in all the ancient writers (the *Pontifical Book* in the *Life of Leo III*, and the annals of Baronius and Pagius, 799, no. 1 ff.).

The leaders of the sacrilegious conspiracy were Paschalis and Campulus, both nephews of Hadrian and both distinguished by palatine office (the *Caroline Code*, letter 60, formerly 73): Paschalis was primicerius, and Campulus was sacellarius. The names of those who joined these leading men are passed over in silence, and the reason for the conspiracy is likewise concealed.

The essential point is that violence was inflicted upon the holy pontiff in the middle of a procession, near the monastery of Saint Sylvester in Capite, which Stephen II, the founder of the patriciate of the Frankish kings, and his brother, Saint Paul, had established in their own house. The pope’s eyes were gouged out and his tongue cut off, a form of savagery common at that time, and he was left half alive.

For this reason his followers brought him to the aforementioned monastery, where he miraculously recovered both sight and speech—a fact that those who understand only earthly things call into question—and from there to the Basilica of Saint Peter.

Then, supported by the protection of Winigisi, duke of Spoleto, who hastened there with forces to defend the holy pontiff against the impious, the pontiff fled through Spoleto to Francia. There he was received with the highest honors, as his dignity required. After spending some time at Paderborn, we learn that he returned to Rome with the king’s envoys. He was received there with great joy by his faithful subjects, and the same occurred throughout the entire ecclesiastical territory, at the end of November, as is read in the *Pontifical Book*, from which other writers derived this accurate account.

Nearly a full year later, Charles himself came to Rome, namely on 24 November in the year 800 (Baronius, 800, no. 3; Pagius, no. 8).

### XVI.

Before Charles undertook his journey toward Italy, so that so great an affair—one like which Rome had never imposed upon either his royal father or himself—might be settled wisely and justly, he informed Alcuin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, eminent in age, wisdom, and other virtues, his teacher and especially dear to him, of the Romans’ crime, and consulted him about what ought to be done in so grave a matter.

What Alcuin replied must be heard from his letters in Canisius (*Ancient Readings*, vol. II, p. 392; letter 4, formerly 11), part of which Baronius and Pagius also quote (799, nos. 6, 3):
