> “Thus far there have been three most exalted persons in the world: the apostolic sublimity, which is accustomed to govern, in the office of vicar, the See of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. What happened, however, to the one who had been ruler of that See, your venerable goodness has informed me.
>
> “The second is imperial dignity, together with the secular power of the second Rome. How impiously the ruler of that empire was deposed—Constantine, blinded at the command of his mother Irene and dead from grief—is proclaimed everywhere by common report, not by strangers but by his own people and fellow citizens.
>
> “The third is royal dignity, in which the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ has appointed you ruler of the Christian people, superior to all the aforementioned dignities in power, brighter in wisdom, and more exalted in royal dignity.”

A little farther on, coming to the matter itself, he continues:

> “The care of the head must by no means be neglected. It is less serious for the feet to suffer than for the head. Let peace be arranged with the wicked people, if this can be done; let threats be abandoned, lest, hardened, they flee, but let them be retained in hope until they can be recalled to peace by sound counsel. One must hold on to what one possesses, lest, in acquiring something smaller, what is greater be lost. Let one’s own sheepfold be preserved, lest the wolf devastate it. Let one labor among others in such a way that one suffers no loss among one’s own.”

Again, in another letter, in which Charles invited him to undertake the journey toward Rome with him (ibid., letter 7, formerly 13), Alcuin replies that he would rather live quietly at Tours, and continues in accordance with his earlier judgment:

> “Rome, which was set in motion by fraternal discord, has not ceased to retain the mixed poison of dissension, and it compels the power of your venerable dignity to hasten from the sweet seats of Germany to learn the ruin threatening this faction. We, for our part, accompany your absence with tears and your journey with continual prayers, humbly beseeching divine mercy that it may lead and bring back your people and ours safe, together with every prosperity, and rejoicing.”

### XVII.

Different writers interpret Alcuin’s earlier letters, explaining them to some extent through the later ones. Eckard’s opinion (*History of the Franks*, book XXV, chapter 11), toward which the Italian annalist inclines, is that Charles should deal gently with the Romans, lest, if he punished them, those savage citizens strip him of the patriciate and dominion over the City.

Pagius, however, thinks that Alcuin meant Charles should not lose his own possession—namely, the kingdom of Italy—while defending another’s territory. I adhere to neither view. Eckard’s opinion is manifestly false; Pagius’s, although more credible, seems excessively forced.

Alcuin is speaking of Charles’s army, which he strongly advises him not to commit against the tumultuous Romans, naturally fierce as they were, and which he hopes will return safely.

Moreover, the comparison of these three great rulers—the pope, the emperor, and the king of France—is highly significant. I admit that it indicates the pope’s supreme authority. In another letter (27, formerly 72), Alcuin speaks of this authority and says that

> “the whole multitude of Christ’s flock, although dwelling in different pastures of the earth, is subject to its shepherd.”

Here, however, we hear the pope called the ruler of the city of Rome, and Roman territory is called another’s possession. Therefore the defense of the Roman Church, whose head is Rome, must by no means be confused with dominion.

Einhard, who was not ignorant of the patrician’s office—that is, of the defender’s office—speaks of the church of Saint Peter, than which nothing was holier to Charles, in this way (chapter 28):

> “Although he valued it so highly, nevertheless, during the forty-seven years in which he had reigned, he went there only four times, solely for the fulfillment of vows and for prayer. The reasons for his final visit were not only these, but also that the Romans compelled Pope Leo, who had suffered many injuries—namely, the removal of his eyes and the cutting out of his tongue—to appeal to the king’s protection.
>
> “Therefore he came to Rome to restore the condition of the Church, which had been thrown into great confusion, and remained there throughout the winter. At that time he received the name of emperor and Augustus. At first he opposed it so strongly that he declared that, although it was the greatest feast, he would not have entered the church on that day if he could have foreseen the pontiff’s plan.”

Thus, after forty-six years, the patriciate of the Frankish kings, instituted by Stephen II in the year 754, ceased in name in the year 800, replaced by the more illustrious imperial title, to which the same duty of defense remained attached, as will soon become clear.

### XVIII.

But before this notable change, unexpected even to King Charles himself, took place, the king’s envoys had held a judicial assembly in the papal palace. This must not be passed over, since it is recorded in the *Pontifical Book* (sections 376 ff.), and no fuller witness to these events can be found in all antiquity. Labbe also transferred it into his collection (vol. VII of the *Councils*, p. 1155).

After recounting how, in the year 799, “all the Romans generally, on the eve of the blessed apostle Andrew, with the greatest joy,” received the pontiff returning from Francia, the account immediately continues:

> “And after some days, when the most faithful envoys who had come with him for the service of the pontiff were residing in the dining hall of that lord Pope Leo—namely, Hildebald and Arno, most reverend archbishops; Cunipert, Bernard, Atto, and Jesse, most reverend and holy bishops; Flaccus, the elected bishop; and also Helmgoth, Rotticarius, and Germarius, glorious counts—and when for more than a week they were investigating those most wicked criminals, Paschalis and Campulus with their followers, to discover what charge they had against the pontiff, they had nothing to say against him. Then the aforementioned envoys of the great king arrested them and sent them to Francia.”

I have already said elsewhere that similar judicial assemblies were held in the City itself under King Pippin by his legates or envoys (*Caroline Code*, vol. I, p. 131).

I have thought it worthwhile to place this distinguished fact before the Italian annalist for two reasons.

First, so that he may understand that, when he searches out one or another judicial assembly held in Rome in the time of the emperors in order to magnify their dominion, he is beating the air: similar proceedings took place in the age of the kings, when not even the kings themselves dared to inquire into such dominion.

Second, so that he may grasp with his own hands that Rome and the other cities of the Roman duchy came under Charles’s authority neither through the conquest of the City nor through the voluntary surrender of the peoples. Nor was the matter settled by secret or useful negotiations on either side. Rather, it occurred through fear of the pontiffs, who, being more accustomed to heavenly than earthly affairs, were unable to keep their subjects in obedience—and especially through the distinguished office of the patriciate, or defense, which the most devout prince, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, had exercised.

Now we must discuss the restoration of imperial majesty in the West itself, so that its true character may become clear.

### § III. — The Restoration of the Empire in the West by Saint Leo III in the Year 800
[Col. 0498C] **XIX.** All the ancient authorities agree that Charlemagne was unexpectedly and almost against his will crowned with the imperial crown. “When, at Mass, he rose from prayer before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter,” says the monk of Angoulême, “Lord Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head.” We have recently heard similar testimony from Einhard, who was Charlemagne’s secretary. Ademar and the *Liber Pontificalis* agree with both of them, and all consistently report that, after this unexpected coronation, “the whole Roman people acclaimed him: ‘Life and victory to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor of the Romans.’”

The *Liber Pontificalis* (section 376), a witness even to minor details, adds the plain reason for the acclamations of the entire people: “All the faithful Romans, seeing the great protection and affection which he had shown toward the holy Roman Church and its vicar, unanimously cried out in a loud voice, by the will of God and of blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven: ‘To Charles Augustus,’ and so forth.”

This decision of a single pontiff is exaggerated by Louis II in a letter to the emperor Basil, which others report from the anonymous Salernitan (chapter 102), as I said in the preface (vol. I, no. 4), after recounting the Roman pontiff’s coronation:

“Especially,” he says, “since emperors have often been raised up who, without any divine operation through the ministry of the pontiffs, attained the imperial dignity solely through the senate and people, neither of whom cared about any of these matters. Some, indeed, were not even acclaimed in this way, but were merely hailed by the soldiers and established in the empire; so that some of them were advanced to the scepter of the Roman Empire by women, and others by this or that means.”

It is therefore so certain that the imperial majesty originated from that crime of the Romans that there remains a permanent monument of a pontiff who had never conceived anything of the kind: a dining hall built shortly beforehand by Leo himself, where we saw that a hearing had been held in his case in the year 799. There are visible there mosaic images of Leo and Charles; the image representing Charles displays the standard, the insignia of the patriciate. Above each is also placed an inscription of this form:

> MOST HOLY OUR LORD POPE LEO; OUR LORD CHARLES, KING.

Alemannus wrongly interprets this (*On the Lateran Walls*, chapter 15) as referring to Charles after his coronation, as Pagi correctly observes (796, no. 8 and following); he himself is also mistaken in the remaining matters relating to the dining hall. It is not the place here to establish this point.

**XX.** Against testimonies of this kind, sound and unimpaired, the Lambecian annalist—an authority of uncertain date and standing—and John the Deacon, who wrote the *Lives of the Bishops of Naples* toward the end of the ninth century, are brought forward to no purpose. The latter says:

“Leo, fleeing to Charles, promised him that, if he would defend him against his enemies, he would crown him with the imperial diadem.”

This writer evidently drew the conclusion from an established fact. Similarly, the Lambecian annalist, drawing a false inference from an established fact, says that it seemed to Leo “and to all the holy Fathers who were present at that council, as well as to the rest of the Christian people, that they ought to name Charles, king of the Franks, emperor, since he held Rome.”

Nonsense. On 1 December the council was assembled, called the canonical purification of Pope Leo. At it the pontiff voluntarily cleared himself by oath of the crimes charged against him, upon the book of the four Gospels; Labbe supplies the formula of this oath (*Councils*, vol. VII, p. 1158). The coronation, however, according to the consistent testimony of contemporary writers, took place on the holy day of the Nativity of the Lord in the basilica of Saint Peter, crowded with the people who had flocked there for the solemnity and who acclaimed the pontiff’s unexpected decision.

For this reason, the two writers published to illuminate Italian affairs (*Italian Writers*, vol. I, part II) seem to me to have to be left to those who find it useful to remain ignorant of the restoration of imperial dignity, lest their writings collapse. Liutprand, too, who flourished a hundred years later, recounts the event in the wrong order, though he is far from the lying assertions of the Lambecian annalist and John the Deacon:

“After this, on the day of the Nativity of our Savior, the aforesaid king was constituted emperor Augustus of the Romans by all, and was crowned by the pope who has been named” (*Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 268).

This should not be counted as a fault in Liutprand, who was reducing to a compendium the deeds of the pontiffs obtained from elsewhere. But the *Liber Pontificalis* attributed to Anastasius—for, I insist again, no more complete witness to these matters is available—also gives the reason why the people’s acclamations followed the coronation: namely, because those acclamations, borrowed from the rite of the pontiff’s consecration, were in substance nothing other than the praises customarily spoken or sung before the confession of Saint Peter immediately after the coronation, as we shall see (*Dissertation* VI, § 5), where the rite itself will be set forth.

Meanwhile, the words of the *Liber Pontificalis* must be heard, so that the matter may become clearer:

> “To Charles, most devout Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, life and victory: before the sacred confession of the blessed apostle Peter, after invoking several saints, this was said three times, and by all he was constituted emperor of the Romans.”

**XXI.** This inauguration of the Augusti of the West, which was incorporated among the sacred ceremonies and, through various additions made from time to time, reached the degree of majesty visible in the ceremonial books before the publication of the patriciate, is an entirely new institution. From its very beginning it displays a wholly different jurisdiction and character of the renewed imperial majesty in the West. Those who maintain that it was like the Eastern institution torment themselves in vain.

Although in the East the custom had also become established of crowning the emperor through the hands of the patriarch of Constantinople, as Leo himself testifies (*Letter* 10, formerly 4), it was not the patriarch’s role to constitute the emperor, but to crown, by solemn rite, one already elected and acclaimed. [Col. 0500A] In contrast, when Charles was constituted emperor, the coronation performed by the pontiff was not a ceremony but the actual institution of the emperor. Thus, for many centuries, no successor could be called or be emperor unless he received the diadem from the Roman pontiff and before the confession of Saint Peter.

For just as kings and patricians are continually said by Leo’s predecessors to acknowledge that they received the patriciate from blessed Peter:

> “Anointing you as kings through his apostle, blessed Peter, he constituted you defenders of his holy Church and of the orthodox faith” (*Carolingian Code*, vol. I, p. 189),

so that emperors might appear to be constituted by Peter himself through his successors, Leo, the institutor of this new dignity, wished to receive the crown before the most sacred body of Peter and from his altar.

This opinion took such deep root in the minds of the princes themselves that two of them, Henry IV and Louis the Bavarian, when they could obtain the imperial crown neither by threats nor by prayers, wished to be inaugurated by pseudopontiffs in the basilica of Saint Peter, according to the form established by Leo III, at that sacred altar. From it they received “a crown not of glory but of confusion,” as Berthold says of Henry IV in Baronius (1084, no. 2).

I shall demonstrate the matter by examples, for it is of the greatest importance, in order to reject false opinions, to leave no room for doubt.

**XXII.** Eleven Augusti in all are counted before the anarchy of the tenth century, which was ended by the first German emperor, Otto the Great: namely, seven of the Carolingian line—Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Lothair I, Louis II, Charles the Bald, Charles the Fat, and Arnulf, who died in the year 899, on the third day before the Kalends of December. But between Charles the Fat and Arnulf two emperors of another line are inserted, Guy, duke of Spoleto, and his son Lambert, for approximately eight years.

Finally there were two competitors for the Augustan dignity: Louis III, son of Boso, king of Burgundy, by Irmingard, daughter of Louis II; and Berengar, duke of Friuli, son of Everard by Gisla, daughter of Louis the Pious. The latter reached the year 924, the first year of the thirty-eight-year anarchy. These facts are established by Frankish history and can almost be seen at a glance in John Adam Bettinger’s *Genealogical Exercise on the Augustan Carolingian Family*, displayed in seven tables.

Throughout that period of 124 years, no one attained the imperial dignity by any other method than the one described in Louis II’s letter to Basil: by receiving the sacred anointing and imperial diadem from the hand of the pontiff. Not even Louis the Pious was excepted; in an unprecedented example, he received the imperial crown in Francia from Stephen IV. Stephen went there immediately after his consecration, both lest Leo’s institution suffer any diminution and, above all, so that that celebrated and foundational document which modern writers call the Ludovician might be drawn up. I shall discuss it in its proper place.

**XXIII.** On this matter the highly reliable writers Einhard and Thegan recount an event which, at first sight, seems to disturb the certain character of the renewed Western Empire. For, when Charlemagne was already worn out by age, Einhard says:

“He made him his associate in the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial name; placing the diadem upon his head, he ordered him to be called emperor and Augustus.”

Thegan (chapter 6), agreeing with him, relates that Charles asked the leading men of the kingdom “whether it pleased them that he should transfer his name—that is, the name of emperor—to his son Louis.” When they consented, he went with his son to church on Sunday and, after addressing him with paternal admonition, ordered him to place the golden crown upon his own head “in remembrance of all the instructions which his father had given him.” He concludes his narrative with these words:

> “He went to Aquitaine, and the lord emperor held the kingdom and his name honorably, as was fitting.”

In the following chapters he continues by explaining how, after Charles the emperor died the next year, “Louis came from the regions of Aquitaine to the palace at Aachen and received all the kingdoms which God had granted to his father, without any opposition. This was in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814, which was the first year of his reign.”

He later received embassies from those same kingdoms, including one from Benevento and from Bernard, his brother’s son and king of Italy. Finally, in the third year of his reign, Stephen IV, the pontiff, was received at Reims by the king with the greatest honor and respect. Afterwards Louis, together with Queen Irmingard, received the imperial diadem and from then on was always called emperor.

Hence the Italian annalist, indulging in conjecture as usual, infers that Louis was made emperor by his father with Leo’s consent (813):

“For he had not received domination over Rome from the nobles of Francia together with the imperial dignity.”

I am astonished that such things should be advanced by a learned man after he had seen Thegan’s candid account, which clearly lists the Italian and Beneventan kingdoms among Charles’s realms while omitting the intervening pontifical territory. [Col. 0501B] Moreover, Einhard and Thegan unanimously and most clearly affirm that Charles, with the consent of the leading men, granted his imperial name. This was to designate, not to create, an emperor—just as, later, the king of the Romans, or future emperor, began to be elected, and unless he received the imperial diadem from the pontiff he was not emperor.

**XXIV.** Nor should Charlemagne be reproached as though, forgetful of partnership and friendship, he had injured the holy see. Louis the Pious himself, imitating his father, made his son Lothair heir of the kingdoms and associate in the empire. Thegan recounts the matter (chapter 21) in almost the same words:

> “The aforesaid emperor designated his son Lothair, so that after his death he might receive and possess all the kingdoms which God had delivered to him through his father’s hands, and might have the name and empire of his father; and for this reason the other sons were indignant.”

But what of this? What Charles was unable to do, if I am not mistaken, because of the shortness of his life, Louis did: he sent his son to Rome as associate in the empire, so that he might obtain the imperial diadem from Saint Paschal I. That this happened is attested by Lothair’s own letter, reported by Mabillon (fourth century of the Benedictines, p. 513), in which he announces his promotion to his father:

> “Before the holy altar and before the sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I received from the supreme pontiff, with your consent and will, the blessing, honor, and name of the imperial office; moreover, the diadem for my head and the sword for the defense of the Church.”

There can be no doubt that the same thing happened with Louis II. First, he too was made associate by his father, as the Bertinian annals testify in Pagi (850, no. 6), and he was sent to Rome to Leo IV to receive the crown:

> “Lothair sent his son Louis to Rome; he was honorably received by Pope Leo and was anointed emperor.”

Second, Louis II himself testifies to Basil that the Western Empire was far superior to the Eastern, because its emperors were accustomed to be anointed and crowned by the supreme pontiff, just as his predecessors—his great-great-grandfather, grandfather, father, and he himself—had been anointed and crowned.

Most relevant here is the fact that, although I have cited it elsewhere (vol. I, Preface, no. 4), he boasts that he had undertaken “to govern the Romans and the City by divine providence, and to defend and exalt the mother of all the Churches of God.” As we have often seen, this was the duty of the patrician.

**XXV.** “What distinction, then,” you will ask, “is found between the patrician and the emperor?” From the brief and truthful rather than elegant little work of Thegan, chorepiscopus of the Church of Trier, that distinction—and consequently the true character of the new imperial dignity—becomes clear, just as Walafrid Strabo defined the work.

In the year 816 (chapter 17), after announcing the death of Leo III, Thegan says:

> “Stephen succeeded him. Immediately after assuming the pontificate, he ordered all the Roman people to promise fidelity with an oath to Louis.”

There is the distinction. The Romans, who had committed the sacrilegious crime against Saint Leo III and had compelled him to take Charles the patrician, or defender, as an associate in power so that they might be kept in their duty, brought forth the imperial majesty. This was neither conceived nor done by the holy pontiff Leo in order to strip Saint Peter and his successors of their dominion—a thing unworthy not only of a pontiff but of any human being—nor would Charles, a prince of the greatest piety who had so vigorously defended the rights of the holy see, have allowed those rights to be restored or granted to himself. Rather, the purpose was to govern the peoples subject to him more easily by the addition of imperial power.

For this reason, when Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, to whom the Romans had not sworn an oath of fidelity when he became associate in the empire, was demanding it from them even in the year 844 on behalf of his son Louis II, king of Italy, Sergius II ordered the following to be conveyed through his messengers, as it appears in the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 487):

> “If you wish Lord Lothair, the great emperor, to have this oath made, I consent and permit it alone; but that this should be carried out for his son Louis, neither I nor all the Roman nobility permit.”

From the formula of the oath—an oath sworn to Arnulf, the last of the Carolingians, in the Fulda annals, reported by Marquard Freher (vol. I, p. 66)—it will become clear who held supreme power in the City:

> “I swear by all these mysteries of God that, saving my honor and law, and the fidelity owed to Lord Pope Formosus, I am and shall remain faithful every day of my life to Arnulf the emperor, and I shall never join myself with any man in disloyalty to him. I shall never provide Lambert, son of Agiltrude, or his mother herself with assistance toward secular honor, and I shall not surrender this city of Rome to Lambert himself, to his mother Agiltrude, or to their men by any device or contrivance.”

**XXVI.** You hear the Romans swear an oath to the emperor, while preserving “my honor and law.” Those who portray the Romans as a vile and powerless herd thereby show that they are ignorant of ancient times. As we saw above (no. XVI), Alcuin depicted them to Charlemagne in a very different way.

Therefore, when Einhard (chapter 38) speaks of the additions and changes to the laws made by Charles, he says:

> “After assuming the imperial name, when he noticed that many things were lacking in the laws of his people—for the Franks have two laws, very different in many places—he considered adding what was missing, reconciling what differed, and correcting what was wrong and improperly stated. But in these matters he did nothing more than add a few chapters, and those incomplete, to the laws”—namely, the Frankish and Lombard laws.

As for the Roman law, although he might have had the power to do so, he did not touch even its smallest point, even with the pontiff’s consent. For the Romans, so that no one might dare such a thing, stipulated in the very oath by which they pledged their loyalty that their law should remain inviolate under the emperors. They also placed that partnership in imperial power below the pontifical rule of legitimate domination: “Saving the power of my lord N.”

These two points seem sufficient for understanding that imperial power in Rome, unless someone abused it, was nothing other than partnership and participation in pontifical power. Pagius, speaking too modestly for so exalted a dignity, considers it to have been a delegation of power.

For that reason, those who debate to whom the dominion of the City should be assigned seem foolish to me. The supreme authority unquestionably belonged to the pontiff, as the emperors themselves—witnesses beyond all exception—demonstrate in their agreements or privileges confirming the regalian rights. They reserved supreme jurisdiction expressly to themselves only in the duchies of Tuscany and Spoleto; in all other matters they confirm everything to the pontiffs with full right. The pontiffs either possessed these territories with full right before the donations or had obtained them from the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles.

It is not known whether Charles donated the islands of Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica before or after the imperial coronation; nor is it easy to believe that he left the Roman Church without a donation for thirteen years.

With respect to the supreme pontifical authority over the persons and property of the City, the emperors became participants in its administration and defense, as Louis II says, through the imposition of the imperial diadem. Yet they were not to hold any hearing or issue any ordinance there concerning everything belonging to the pope and the Romans.

This condition, however, began only with Otto in the year 962, together with the German Empire. For it is established that the Carolingians, while they exercised royal power, held hearings in the City by virtue of the patriciate; and that, after they were made emperors, they continued to do so.

**XXVII.** Among the hearings held by kings I cited above (no. 8) the notable one conducted by royal messengers in the case of Saint Leo III in the year 799. Let us now hear from the monk of Angoulême about the hearing held by Charles, already emperor, in the same case:

> “After a few days he ordered those who had dishonored the pope in the preceding year to be brought before him. After an inquiry into them according to Roman law, they were condemned to death as guilty of treason. Nevertheless, the pope, moved by pious affection, interceded with the emperor for them; their lives and limbs were spared, but, because of the enormity of their crime, they were carried into exile.”

You see Charles, participating in the pontiff’s supreme authority, taking action against persons guilty of treason who had dared to commit a crime against the supreme prince; and at the same time you see Roman law preserved from the very origin of the restored imperial majesty.

Another celebrated hearing is reported in the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 555), held by Louis II:

> “With the most holy pontiff Leo IV, all the Roman nobles and the best—or perhaps, the leading—Franks likewise being seated in the house which the blessed memory Pope Leo III had built beside the Church of the blessed apostle Peter, he held a hearing.”

At it, an accusation of this kind was heard from Daniel, master of the soldiers:

> “Gratian, supervisor of the city of Rome, whom you believe to be faithful to you, while he was alone with me in his house, muttering excessively against the Franks, said secretly: ‘The Franks do nothing good for us and provide no assistance; rather, they violently take away what belongs to us. Why do we not call in the Greeks, make a peace treaty with them, and expel the king and people of the Franks from our kingdom and dominion?’”

The accusation was exposed as false, the accuser himself confessing the calumny. Therefore, “the most merciful emperor, unwilling to act against the institutions of the ancient Roman Augusti, ordered them to be judged according to Roman law.” In that judgment, Daniel, reproved by the words of many, openly acknowledged with his own mouth that he had made a false accusation against Gratian. He was therefore handed over to Gratian before everyone, so that Gratian might have the power to do with him whatever he wished. But when the emperor, with much humble supplication, asked Gratian for Daniel, who had been handed over to him, Gratian consented. The emperor immediately received him with full pardon, and thus he was freed from the danger of death.

**XXVIII.** I cannot understand why Pagius (855, no. 5) and other recent writers use this hearing to magnify Louis Augustus’s supreme dominion in the City. Plans, evidently, were being stirred up against the Franks because they were providing no assistance. From this, however, it is evident that the imperial majesty was exercising the office of the patriciate. The issue was the conclusion of an alliance with the Greeks in order to drive the Franks out of “our kingdom and dominion.”

There can therefore be no doubt about the Roman dominion, in which the Franks maintained military stations to serve as a defense for the Church, especially against the Saracens, who at that time were exceedingly troublesome to Italy and the Roman territory.

That this dominion was distinct from the kingdom of Italy and the duchy of Benevento, as it is today, and was administered by the pontiff and the Romans under the same right by which the Franks administered their own territory, is clear from the Constitution which Lothair, Louis’s father, had issued at the urging and with the approval of Eugene II (Holsten, *Roman Collection*, part II, p. 210).

In its seventh chapter, provision is made for harmony between the two dominions in these terms:

> “We also command that no depredations be committed on our frontier; whatever has been committed, and all other injustices, shall be corrected according to the law by both parties.”

I pass over the fact that a sentence issued according to Roman law, requiring the false accuser to be sought back from the accused with much humble supplication, does not suggest supreme dominion.

As for hearings, I see that, for the same reason—namely, to establish imperial dominion in the City—people appeal to a hearing held by imperial messengers in the Lateran palace in the year 829, under Louis the Pious and Lothair Augusti, from the Farfa archive (in Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, Appendix, no. 52).

I would gladly hear what distinction they perceive between that hearing and the others held during the reign of King Pippin: in the year 761 (*Carolingian Code*, letter 29, formerly 17), and in 765 and 767 (there, letters 39 and 42, formerly 14 and 19). Yet no one has ever thought of asserting dominion over the City for Pippin.

I wish to place the first of these before everyone’s eyes, so that it may be compared with the hearing drawn from the Farfa archive and so greatly exaggerated in the Italian annals.

**XXIX.** Paul relates that Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, was told how “finally your aforesaid messengers, standing in our presence together with the Lombard messengers, as well as with the men of the Pentapolis and of each of our cities, established in their presence proof concerning certain legal matters conducted between both parties, and so forth.”

The hearing in the Farfa archive, however, concerns invasions which the monks claimed had been committed against the monastery by the supreme pontiffs Hadrian and Leo III. The imperial messengers therefore say:

> “As we were sitting there in judgment in the Lateran palace in the presence of Lord Pope Gregory, and together with us were present Leo, bishop and librarian of the holy Roman Church, Theodore the bishop, Sirinus the primicerius, Theophylact the nomenclator, Gregory son of Mercury, Peter duke of Ravenna, Ingoald and Aceris the abbots, Alboin, Lanfrid, Emmo, and Maximus, vassals of the lord emperor, gastalds, and many others…”

There can be no denial that there was some difference between the royal and imperial messengers; nevertheless, the case was similar and the judgment similar.

To the Italian annalist (829), the argument seems so clear for the supreme imperial power in the City itself—and for acting as a tribunal in the pontifical residences—that he considers anyone who does not agree with him an enemy of truth. Pagius, more prudently, speaks of the same hearing as follows (839, no. 3):

> “Certainly, many public records and passages of the ancients cannot be rightly understood unless it is known who at this time possessed the power of judging in Rome.”

A brief answer must be made to both learned writers. The annalist evidently holds that the monastery of Farfa, situated in the duchy of Spoleto, belonged at that time to the supreme imperial jurisdiction, and therefore that its privileges and rights had to be vindicated by the emperor.

Thus, when a dispute over possessions arose between the monastery and the holy see, and the pontiff necessarily had to hear the matter, the abbot was brought from that monastery to Rome to plead his case before the pontiff, as the supreme dignity required. Two bishops sat there together with the imperial legates or messengers, one of them being chancellor of the holy see, along with the primicerius and other palace officials. These circumstances are more than sufficient to demonstrate that the imperial messengers did not sit as a tribunal; rather, according to the custom of that age, they examined ecclesiastical cases in a council or assembly, in view of the very great harmony that then existed between priesthood and empire.

To Pagius, however, it must be answered that the participation in pontifical power of which we have spoken provides sufficient light for understanding the obscure public records and passages of the ancients.

**XXX.** I must not pass over the observation of the distinguished recent historian of Lesser Lombardy, or the duchy of Benevento (Pratilli, vol. II, pp. 196 and following), concerning Louis II’s words in his letter to Basil:

> “We have undertaken to govern by divine providence that people and City, and to defend and exalt the mother of all the Churches of God.”

The distinguished writer thought that Rome with its duchy had come under the power of the Roman pontiffs through the cession of Louis the Pious. I demonstrated most clearly from the letters in the *Carolingian Code* that this is false.

Nevertheless, impelled by his love of truth, he says:

> “Louis the Pious Augustus had therefore reserved no dominion over the city of Rome for himself in that celebrated Constitution, or Diploma of Donation—which almost everyone, including Hugo Grotius, Pierre de Marca, Labbe, and other writers of Gaul and Germany, now acknowledges as true, legitimate, and certain. In it, it is read most plainly that jurisdiction over the Roman duchy passed to the pontiff, with only the right of intervention on behalf of those who appealed to him, and the defense and protection of the Church reserved to himself and his successors by those same kings, together with the rights and privileges assigned to them—namely, the patriciate or patronage.”

Then, after adducing the irresistible argument from Charlemagne’s Testament, which Louis the Pious copied word for word on this point, while both commended to their three sons “that they should undertake together the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, and so forth,” he immediately adds:

> “I have therefore thought it necessary to repeat these points so that certain frivolous arguments advanced by recent writers—by which they contend that the city of Rome was under the dominion of the Western emperors—may be dissolved; and you have ample refutations of them among the defenders of the Roman pontificate.”

All hearings that may be found must therefore be referred to this principle, and all public records must be understood in its light, if their true meaning is to be retained.

Accordingly, just as the messengers of King Charlemagne, holding a hearing in the case of Leo III, and Charles himself, after being crowned emperor, when he held a new hearing in the same case, acted only in the capacity of patrician or defender, so emperors—who acquired no new right in the City beyond the aforementioned participation in power over persons subject to the pontiff—or their messengers, when holding hearings and performing other acts of jurisdiction at Rome, offer evidence of supreme power only to those hostile to the holy see, flatterers of lay authority, and enemies of truth, who, having no real knowledge of antiquity, flatter themselves that they have illuminated it.

**XXXI.** I cannot deny that the ancient fervor which for more than 120 years had inflamed Pippin, Charlemagne, and their grandsons toward the prince of the apostles and his successors had cooled. Nor are such extensive efforts for the defense of the Church and the Romans found after the death of Louis II, although they were especially necessary, as the letters of John VIII demonstrate. He crowned Charles the Bald, brother of Lothair I and son of Louis the Pious, in the year 876, and Charles the Fat, son of Louis the German, brother of the same Lothair I, in the year 880.

But what followed? From this negligence there emerged an even stronger argument for the true character of the imperial majesty restored by Leo III. Since the Carolingians, who had almost forgotten their duty, were passed over, protection for the Church was sought elsewhere. When the princes of Italy had solemnly acclaimed Guy, duke of Spoleto, and Berengar’s rival, as king of Italy at Pavia in the year 889, Stephen V summoned him to Rome in 891 and adorned him with the imperial diadem. His son Lambert was crowned in the same manner as associate in the empire the following year by Formosus.

Only when Lambert seized tyranny and became hostile to the holy see did this dignity return, at the very end of the Carolingian line, to Arnulf, son of Carloman, who was brother of Charles the Fat. It returned only for a moment, from the year 896 to 899. This is highly convenient for our argument, since the oath sworn to Arnulf by the Romans—“saving my honor and law, and the fidelity owed to Lord Pope Formosus,” cited above (no. 25)—makes sufficiently clear what power the Carolingian Augusti possessed in the City.

Something remains to be investigated concerning Louis III, son of Boso, king of Burgundy, by Irmingard, daughter of Louis II, whom Benedict IV crowned in the year 900, and concerning Berengar, duke of Friuli, whom Count Everard fathered by Gisla, daughter of Louis the Pious.

But concerning both of them, as concerning their predecessors from the time of John VIII, I do not hesitate to affirm that they departed from the examples of their ancestors. The last of them in particular, Berengar, who was killed by his own men, brought the line of the Carolingian Augusti to an end.

**XXXII.** We learn with certainty from these same Augusti, in order to grasp fully the character of the renewed majesty, that at the very act of coronation they had publicly read the pact of confirmation, or diploma, by which all the donations and rights of the holy see were confirmed.

Each emperor did not customarily compose this document according to his own wishes. Rather, he followed the model sent from Rome by the pontiff to the person who was to be adorned with the imperial diadem. For all the donations and privileges, or diplomas, of the preceding Caesars were preserved in the archive of the holy see, as is repeatedly attested in the *Liber Pontificalis*.

John VIII testifies that this model was customarily sent, in a letter to Carloman (letter 63), who ardently desired to obtain the imperial crown, which his brother Charles the Fat eventually received:

> “We shall solemnly send legates from our side to you, together with a document containing in chapters what you must perpetually grant to your mother, the Roman Church, and to your protector, the apostle blessed Peter.”

Nor should it be thought to have been any other document than the one first made by Louis the Pious for Saint Paschal and confirmed to that same pontiff by his son Lothair; by Louis II for Leo IV; and by Charles the Bald for John himself.

For elsewhere (letter 84), John wishes to inform the emperor Charles the Fat of the Roman disasters:

> “While we were dwelling with blessed Peter—in the Leonine City, which had not yet acquired the name of the City—we had no power over the city of Rome handed over by the pious emperors to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicars.”

In these words he is plainly flattering the emperor whose aid he seeks, for no one had granted Rome to the pontiff, as has been demonstrated in the *Carolingian Code*. But Louis the Pious had included Rome together with the other rights of the Roman Church. Following that model, each of the three succeeding Augusti composed his own diploma. This was sufficient for John to claim that Rome had been handed over by the pious emperors.

In the same way, Charlemagne and Louis the Pious list Charles Martel among the princes who had deserved well of the Roman Church, because he had received embassies from Gregory III, by which he was asked, in the Church’s greatest distress, to come to its aid.

### XXXIII

That the pope was not unaware which kings or emperors were to be credited with the donations made to the Roman Church is confirmed by the council in which, in the year 877, he wished the election and coronation of Charles the Bald, which he himself had carried out in the preceding year, to be confirmed (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 295). There he praises Charles the Great with deserved commendations:

> “He increased the commonwealth by battles, enlarged it by victories, and adorned it with wisdom. Although he had exalted all the churches, this was always his resolve and always his desire—as is read in the deeds written about him—that he should restore the holy Roman Church to its ancient condition and order. Hence he raised it up with many honors and enlarged it with many gifts and acts of generosity, so much so that he restored to it cities once lost and also bestowed upon it, from a portion of his own kingdom, other territories of no small extent. But little has been said unless the great and sublime things he accomplished for the advancement of religion are also recalled, and so forth.”

Then, coming to Louis the Pious, he commends him in some thirty passages, but does not mention that any city was handed over by him:

> “His son, the late divine Louis, the greatest emperor, father of this prince chosen by God, Charles, ever Augustus, imitated his ancestral throne so closely in religion and laudably rivaled him in piety that, born in piety, he equaled and strengthened both his father’s vows concerning divine worship and the notable marks of generosity shown toward the foremost Church”—here you have the Ludovician diploma confirming everything and adding nothing—“but as a most grateful heir he enlarged them with more abundant benefits and lavish acts of beneficence.”

Yet this same John, only a few months later, after—so I said—flattering the emperor by affirming that Rome had come into the power of the Church through the generosity of the emperors, took part with Louis the Stammerer in the Second Council of Troyes in the year 878 (ibid., p. 308). There,

> “the promise of the kings was read, and the oaths that Pippin and Charles had offered to the blessed apostle Peter were read,”

because the matter concerned the excommunication of those who invaded the Church’s possessions. But the diplomas of the four successors of Charles, since they presented no donation of their own but merely confirmed ancient rights, are not mentioned at all. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that it was customary for each emperor, before receiving the diadem—that is, before becoming emperor—to issue a diploma of this kind.

### XXXIV

Indeed, if this pact of confirmation could have been omitted by any of the emperors, neither Wido nor Lambert nor Berengarius would have omitted it. They had no interest in what the Carolingians had done; moreover, they had reached that sublime height through overwhelming power and successful deeds. Nevertheless, these men themselves provide clear testimony to this praiseworthy custom.

The Council of Ravenna was held in the year 898 by John IX. Lambert was emperor at the time, and in that same year he died after falling from a horse while hunting (ibid., p. 507). The pope and the emperor issued constitutions in turn. Among the papal constitutions relevant here (chapters 6 and following) are these:

> “Let the pact which was made by your father, the lord Wido of blessed memory, and by you, most pious emperors, according to the preceding custom, now be restored and preserved inviolate. Concerning the places and possessions contained in that pact, certain unlawful decrees have been made there; we ask that these be settled in this same synod, and that the decrees improperly made be annulled. We ask that the patrimonies, or suburban estates, as well as the estates and tenant holdings, and also the cities which, contrary to justice, have been granted as though by decrees, be returned.”

That Berengarius not only issued the customary diploma but also had it publicly read during the solemnity of his coronation is attested by an anonymous panegyrist of that emperor, preserved by Leibniz (*Brunswick Historians*, vol. I, p. 255). After describing his coronation at the hands of Pope John X on Holy Easter Day in the year 915, he continues:

> … At last silence having been made,  
>   
> The reader standing high upon the steps,  
> In obedience to the prelate, reads aloud  
> The estates granted by the emperor’s gift,  
> So that all may know what gifts were given by Caesar;  
> May the plunderer henceforth fear  
> To seize the sacred lands for himself.

It therefore seems safe to affirm that the diplomas of all the Carolingians claimed this place in the public celebration of the coronation. I shall describe the rite more suitably in Dissertation VI, when the Rudolphine Codex is discussed. The matter will be shown to be otherwise with the diplomas of the emperors of Germany in the following section.

### XXXV

Of the five successors of Charles the Fat mentioned above, who succeeded him after his inglorious end at the beginning of the year 888, the principal distinction is not that each of them confirmed all the Church’s rights in his own diploma. What must be especially noted is that, while the kingdom of Italy was divided among them and torn apart by factions, whichever of them appeared the more powerful and promised that he would undertake the defense of the Church was summoned to Rome by the pope and received the imperial diadem.

If none of them asserted this dignity for himself by force of arms, but obtained it only after being drawn by the hope of papal support and seeking it eagerly, then the imperial majesty which Leo III restored in the West had to be entered upon through papal coronation; there was no other way to reach that sublime height. Goldast is therefore entirely mistaken (in his note on chapter 28 of Einhard) when he sets against the eyewitness Einhard the authority of Sigebert, who flourished almost three centuries after the renewed empire.

Sigebert’s words are:

> “The Romans, who had long since in spirit withdrawn from the empire of Constantinople, now, having received a favorable opportunity—for a woman ruled over them, having blinded her son Constantine, the emperor—by unanimous consent acclaim King Charles with imperial praises, crown him Caesar through the hands of Pope Leo, and call him Augustus.”

Some more recent writers embrace this opinion with open arms, paying insufficient attention to the fact that this man was an inveterate enemy of the holy Pope Gregory VII, as the learned annotator of the works of Saint Anselm demonstrates (on book I, letter 56, p. 557), as do Bellarmine (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*) and especially Baronius. Baronius censures him in many passages and clearly proves that he was devoted to Henry IV; he brands him as false in many respects, an impostor, and a schismatic.

It is therefore surprising that Catholic writers were not ashamed to weaken the history of the Romans by relying on such a man’s authority. I believe that the true and certain character of the renewed empire has been revealed by the monuments of antiquity. For that reason, it is enough for me to indicate the sources from which certain learned men derived their false opinions, so that those opinions may be rejected.

I now come to the transfer to the Germans of the imperial majesty thus created and established. This transfer did undergo certain changes, but it will be found and established that nothing at all was changed in its character. It is necessary first to set forth the condition or state of the City which preceded this transfer, so that what follows may be clearer.

## § IV. — On the transfer of the empire to the Germans, effected by John XII in the year 962

### XXXVI

We have seen that the Romans inserted these words into the oath which they customarily rendered to the emperor (above, no. 25):

> “Saving my honor and law, and fidelity to the lord N., pope … I will never join myself to any man … I will not hand over this city of Rome to N.”

These words attest the supreme power of the pope, of which the emperor became a participant through his coronation; but they also clearly designate the power of the Romans and their administration of the commonwealth.

Accordingly, in the monuments of that period, and especially in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, we see primates and nobles, both laymen and members of the clergy, honored with the highest distinctions. To this order belonged the famous seven who were called judges and palatine officials: the *primicerius*, *secundicerius*, *nomenclator*, *arcarius*, chief *defensor*, *sacellarius*, and *primiscrinius*. They frequently occur in the *Caroline Codex*.

As for the laymen, the *Caroline Codex* supplies the names of very eminent dukes and consuls (letters 59, 60, and 67; elsewhere 49, 73, and 69), as well as military commanders bearing the same title of honor. Above all it mentions the *superista*, whom the continuator of Liutprand (*History of the Emperors and Kings*, book VI, chapter 6) calls the first of all the primates:

> “Among the primates of the Roman city was Stephen, son of John, the *superista*.”

After him he lists ten others by name.

The *Book of the Pontiffs* likewise (§ 554) calls him “the *superista* of the Roman city.” It joins this dignity or office with the command of the troops and calls him, without distinction, the *superista* of the palace and of the Roman city:

> “The most eminent master of the soldiers, the distinguished *superista* and counselor of the Roman palace.”

From these facts it is clear that many offices were subject to the supreme Roman pontiff, just as offices in the kingdom of the Franks were subject to its kings. Thus it became customary on both sides to appoint governors of cities and commanders of troops, and to arrange embassies in more serious matters.

Nothing better demonstrates what power these Roman primates possessed and what their role was in the administration than the vacancy of the empire for thirty-eight years, from the death of Berengarius in 924 until 962, when Otto the Great received the imperial diadem from John XII. For while the Romans opposed it, none of the kings of Italy—whose succession never failed—was permitted by the popes to be raised to the imperial dignity.

### XXXVII

The overwhelming power of the Tusculan counts, which emerged toward the end of the ninth century while Arnulf was still alive, grew as the two great rivals Louis III and Berengarius contended for the kingdom of Italy, and finally erupted into open tyranny. It presents a horrifying picture of Rome itself.

I prefer to have it observed in Liutprand and Baronius (from the year 908, no. 5) rather than to explain it myself and become a narrator of that age’s indignities while bringing forward evidence of the Romans’ power. I shall touch only on the principal points that lead to the new establishment of imperial majesty according to the original restoration by Leo III. They must be set against Struvius and the defenders of his opinion, who, abusing the virtue of so great a prince, do not acknowledge, as they ought, that the emperor was created by the supreme pontiff for the defense of the holy Roman Church and the Romans, but insist that he obtained the empire for himself by arms.

The Tusculan counts, therefore, having usurped tyranny, did not hesitate to stretch their impious hands even into the sanctuary. From their own stock they were not afraid to raise to the see of the prince of the apostles men who were generally foolish and, if Liutprand is to be believed, born in vice and enslaved to vice, so that they might more securely continue to possess power. Thus, apart from the deposit of faith—which, according to the infallible oracle of the divine Savior, we know the gates of hell will not overcome—everything went to ruin.

The most famous of these were the senatrices Theodora the elder and the younger, Marozia, and Stephania. Through their agency such great indignities were perpetrated. By their schemes, those who were elected as successors of Peter exercised almost no authority in civil affairs.

In this shameful state of affairs, King Hugh of Italy married Marozia after the death of her husband, namely Guido, son of Alberic, margrave and count of Tusculum. With her he ruled the Romans from the Mausoleum of Hadrian, as her mother Theodora had previously done. Yet not for long: Alberic the Younger, son of Alberic, for a trivial reason stirred the Romans against his stepfather, the king of Italy. Hugh therefore escaped by flight and only at last purchased peace by marrying his daughter Alda to Alberic.

The son of that same Alberic, Octavian, while still a minor, invaded the pontificate in the year 956. Then, being lord of the City on two grounds, and having suffered many indignities from Berengarius, king of Italy, and his son Adelbert, he summoned Otto, king of Germany, into Italy with an army. Having found him to be the greatest defender of the Church and Italy, he created him emperor in the year 962.

### XXXVIII

Frodoard provides notable testimony concerning the expulsion of the king of Italy (under the year 933). He reports how envoys of the church of Rheims, returning from Rome with the pallium for Archbishop Artaldus,

> “announced that Pope John XI, son of Maria, who was also called Marozia, was being held in custody by his brother named Alberic, who was also keeping their mother Marozia confined and holding Rome against King Hugh.”

Concerning the counsel of Alberic and the Romans after the expulsion of the king, Blondus (*Decades*, book II) relates the following:

> “For at that time two consuls were annually appointed at Rome from the nobility, who, on the model of the ancient consulship, presided over the highest affairs. A prefect, likewise chosen from the nobility, administered justice to the people. From the common people, twelve were appointed each year; they were called *decarcones* and exercised the functions of the senate in councils and deliberations.”

That this administration of affairs continued at the beginning of the following century is attested by Ditmar, preserved by Leibniz (*Brunswick Historians*, vol. I, p. 400), in his account of the coronation of Henry I:

> “Thirteen years having passed after the completion of a thousand years from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second month and third week of the following year, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the Lord’s day and the sixth day before the Kalends of March, Henry, the illustrious king by the grace of God, proceeded surrounded by twelve senators, six with shaven beards and the others mystically wearing long beards, carrying staffs.”

Thus, when John ascended the chair of Peter, he found this form of administration established at Rome by his father and the Roman primates. Since, by divine providence, the seizure of the principate and the power of the legitimate ruler were united in one and the same man, John, his successor, accomplished with ease what Agapitus II had been unable to do ten years earlier.

For the mighty Otto, king of Germany, had also been invited by that pontiff and had come, and through repeated victories had freed Italy from the tyranny of Berengarius and his son. But when, according to the wishes of that same pontiff, he was preparing to advance into the City, Alberic and the Romans prevented him, as Flodoardus records in Pagius (952, no. 1):

> “King Otto sent an embassy to Rome concerning his reception; when this was not obtained, he returned with his wife to his own country.”

### XXXIX

The matter turned out otherwise under Pope John, as Liutprand, a reliable eyewitness authority, affirms. I shall relate the whole matter in his own words, as it occurred (*book VI, chapter 6*):

> “While Berengarius and Adelbert were reigning—or rather raging—in Italy, and, to speak more accurately, exercising tyranny, John, the supreme pontiff and universal pope, whose Church had then experienced the savagery of the aforementioned Berengarius and Adelbert, sent envoys of the holy Roman Church—namely, John, cardinal deacon, and Azo, the *scriniarius*—to Otto, then the most serene and pious king, now emperor and Caesar. In letters and by royal tokens he humbly begged that, for the love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whom he desired to be the forgivers of his sins, Otto would free him and the holy Roman Church entrusted to him from their jaws and restore them to their former safety and liberty.  
>   
> “He expelled Berengarius and Adelbert from the kingdom all the more swiftly because it is plainly evident that he had the most holy apostles Peter and Paul as his fellow soldiers. Thus the good king, gathering what had been scattered and strengthening what had been broken, restored to each what was his own. Thereafter he hastened to Rome to do likewise. There he was received with marvelous adornment and preparation, and by that same supreme pontiff and universal pope John he received the anointing of the empire. He not only restored to him what was his own, but also honored him with immense gifts of gems, gold, and silver. From that same Pope John, over the most precious body of Peter, and from all the nobles of the city, he received an oath that they would never aid Berengarius and Adelbert. After this he hastened back to his homeland.”

The Romans rendered a similar oath to Arnulf, if you remember (above, no. 25). It therefore seems impossible to doubt that the nobles used the same formula:

> “Saving the honor, law, and fidelity owed to the lord John.”

No one would dare to assert anything similar concerning the oath rendered by the pope. The supreme ruler does not swear fidelity or subjection to another ruler whom he makes a participant in his own power over subjects; rather, by oath he promises that he will not join himself to that ruler’s enemies.

Liutprand, however, affirms that even the Romans used no other oath. Writers hostile to the apostolic see abuse both oaths in a remarkable fashion: by diminishing the authority of the pontiff, they raise the imperial power beyond what is proper. The matter must therefore be examined directly, so that it may become clear how far their account is from the truth.

### XL

When Pope John was considering the transfer of imperial majesty to the Germans, he did not judge that so important a matter should be undertaken unexpectedly, as Leo III had done; the times and customs were different. Instead, through his legates, as becomes clear from what followed, he proposed two oaths to the great king. One was to be rendered to the pontiff and the other to the Roman people before he received the imperial diadem. The arrangement was that he would render the oath to the pontiff through his envoys before setting out toward Rome and would afterward repeat it personally, as can be inferred from the practice of his successors, during the solemnity of the coronation.

Likewise, ancient monuments attest that the kings of the Romans rendered another oath to the Romans once at the foot of Mount Mario and again when entering the Leonine City.

The first oath of Otto is preserved in the outstanding Albinian Codex, together with the very place where the autograph is kept:

> “The oath of the envoys of Otto, the future emperor, which is in Saxony in the monastery called Lüneburg.  
>   
> “To the lord John, pope XII, King Otto promises and swears through us, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints, that, if God permits him to come to Rome, he will exalt the holy Roman Church and that same lord John the pope, its ruler, according to his power, if he finds him alive. If not, then whoever he may be, he will not, either by his own will and consent or by his counsel or exhortation, cause him—or any of his successors—to lose his life, his limbs, or the honor he possesses.  
>   
> “[In Rome he will make no judgment or ordinance concerning anything belonging to the pope and the Romans without your counsel. And whatever of the land of Saint Peter comes into our power, I will return to you.]  
>   
> “Whoever he permits to hold the kingdom of Italy, he will make that man swear that he will be an aid to the lord pope and his successors in defending the land of Saint Peter according to his power. So may God, these holy Gospels, and these sacred sanctuaries help that same lord King Otto.”

I have supplied once and again from Gratian (*Decree*, distinction 63, chapter 33, “To You, Lord”) what certainly seems to be missing from the copy which Albinus obtained at Rome. I did so because Baronius (960, no. 4) and all other learned men—even the Italian annalist, with the sole exception of one—knowing only that version, considered it improper to remove anything from it; and also because, what is more important, Otto’s successors expressed through their envoys whatever is missing from the Albinian copy.

### XLI

To this may be added the testimony of Liutprand—or, if one prefers, that of his contemporary continuator—which is beyond all exception (*book VI, chapter 6*). He relates how Otto replied to the papal envoys, who complained that the fortress of Saint Leo on Mount Feretrano, which belonged by right to the holy see, was being besieged:

> “We have promised to return to the Church all the land of Saint Peter that is subject to our power. This is precisely why we are striving to expel Berengarius with his entire household from this fortress. For how can we return this land to him if we do not first rescue it from the hands of violent men and place it under our power?”

There can therefore be no doubt that Albinus happened upon a less accurate copy. The reason I prefer this copy to the one accepted by all learned men is Gratian’s freedom in presenting ancient monuments. Although he did not miss the substance of the matter, he took less care than he should have to reproduce it word for word.

For what necessity was there to strip Otto’s envoys of the delegated authority of their prince, so that the prince himself might seem to speak through their mouths? None of his successors will be found to have followed such an example.

Auspiciously, the oath of Otto the Saxon, the first emperor from Germany, emerged from the monastery of Saint Michael at Lüneburg in Saxony. It demonstrates that the text published by Gratian was valid and authentic. Although no learned person had ever called it into doubt, a fuller testimony nevertheless had to be supplied to German jurists, so that the true character of the empire transferred to the Germans might be preserved.

It was therefore not that the Roman empire acquired by Charles the Great was later reclaimed by Otto the Great and permanently joined to the German kingdom in such a way that it transferred its name to it, as everyone consistently teaches. Rather, it was the liberation of Italy from the tyranny of its kings and the undertaking of the defense of Roman territory, especially of the pontiff, that brought imperial dignity or majesty to both Charles and Otto.

There was, however, this difference between the two great kings: Charles was unexpectedly crowned by the hands of the pontiff and called emperor, while the Romans acclaimed him only as their patron or defender. Otto, on the other hand, did not reach that sublime height until the oath of which we are speaking had first been rendered to the pontiff, together with another oath to the Romans, about which I shall say a little shortly and discuss more fully below (Dissertation VI).

### XLII

It is certainly astonishing that Conringius failed to understand this character from the few letters of Leo III, although in publishing them repeatedly he labored only to establish the name of Augustus.

Yet Leo had testified to Charles Augustus (letter 5):

> “We await your defense and consolation … Your imperial defense resounds everywhere in many ways.”

Elsewhere (letter 8, elsewhere numbered 3) he declares that he and his priests pray to God that He may preserve and protect Charles for long years, for the exaltation and defense of the Church.

When speaking of his own dominion (letter 5), he first complains that the revenues of the Exarchate are being usurped in each city by Frankish men:

> “According to what the duke who had been appointed by us used to do … Hence those dukes are quite unable to provide us with assistance in full measure.”

Elsewhere (letter 2, elsewhere numbered 10), when the revenues of the palace at Ravenna were being invaded, he says:

> “We ask your imperial clemency to command that you so administer the donation received from God, which you offered to the apostle of God mentioned above, that it may not be diminished in any part; rather, through your laborious struggle, may it be able to remain firm, stable, and unshaken for all time.”

Again, elsewhere (letter 3, elsewhere numbered 1), concerning the same cities of the Exarchate, he says:

> “The offering which your most beloved father, the lord King Pippin, offered to the blessed apostle Peter, and which you confirmed.”

These statements dispel the imaginings of jurists who, equating the age of Charles and Otto with the times of Octavian or at least Constantine, suppose that both acquired the empire by arms.

The Roman empire was not constituted by regions and provinces. Rather, whichever king was clothed by the Roman pontiff with the imperial diadem added to his dominions, whether greater or fewer, the kingdom of Italy—or Lombardy—Tuscany, and the duchy of Spoleto. Since these territories almost encircled the land of Saint Peter, or the ecclesiastical domain, they promised the pontiff and the holy see a more effective defense.

### XLIII

The most learned Abbot Godefridus observed that the kings of Germany were not even called kings of the Romans before they possessed the kingdom of Italy (*Godefridus’s Chronicle*, vol. I, book II, chapter 1, p. 119):

> “If we examine the title ‘king of the Romans’ more precisely, it was never used by the Ottonian emperors, nor even in later times, before the actual possession of the Italian kingdom.”

Further below (ibid., chapter 3, p. 163), where he is speaking of Otto the Great, he says:

> “It must be observed that neither our earlier kings, namely Conrad and Henry, nor Otto I before receiving his coronation at Rome, and therefore before obtaining the empire, are represented with a scepter in any seals.”

After adducing many proofs, this most diligent investigator of ancient monuments (ibid., p. 166) does not hesitate to define the matter in these terms:

> “From all these things it must be firmly concluded that, before receiving his coronation at Rome, Otto I used only the title of king in most cases simply, and in some diplomas with certain additions.”

The Italian annalist likewise established this matter on the authority of diplomas and charters. Thus, throughout his annals, especially under the years 1433, 1493, and 1519, he asserts that no king of the Romans is found to have been given the name of emperor before receiving his coronation at Rome from the hand of the pontiff.

Hence, during that disputed election of the kings of Germany—namely, Philip and Otto—Innocent III, instructing the Germans in the established truth (*On the Affair of the Empire*, letters 30, 33, and 92), says:

> “Although he receives the crown of the kingdom elsewhere, the emperor nevertheless receives from the apostolic see the final imposition of hands and the crown of the empire.”

Likewise, when he presented to the Lombards the example of Lotharius II, duke of Saxony, and Conrad, brother of Frederick, duke of Swabia, both of them elected, he said:

> “The Roman pontiff crowned Lotharius, and, once crowned, he obtained the empire.”

The kings of Germany themselves were so thoroughly convinced that this was the true character of the empire renewed by Leo III that many of them, especially those of the Swabian line, concealed their hostility toward the holy see until they had obtained the crown. Henry IV and Louis the Bavarian even arranged for pseudopopes to be created, as I said above (no. 21), so that they might receive the imperial diadem from them. This is the fullest testimony of all.

### XLIV

Nor did coronation alone make the Germans resemble the Carolingians. The election itself did so, before a definite form of election was established by the counsel of the Roman pontiff after Frederick II in the thirteenth century.

When Otto III dared to deliberate on something new concerning the election of the future emperor, with Gregory V’s approval—both because he belonged to the same royal lineage and because he had risen to the highest dignity through the emperor’s efforts—Benedict VIII, as Glaber records in Baronius (1013, no. 5), issued this decree, thereby confirming the original character of the empire:

> “Let no prince rashly desire to carry the scepter of the Roman empire or to be called or be emperor unless the pope of the Roman see has chosen him as suitable to the commonwealth for the integrity of his morals and entrusted the imperial insignia to him.”

This constitution was strengthened by the holy Emperor Henry through his distinguished example, when in the following year he received the imperial crown from that same Benedict.

Ditmar, preserved by Leibniz (*Brunswick Historical Writers*, vol. I, p. 400), relates the event in these words, which are less clear in the sole Italian annalist (under the year 1014):

> “He came with his beloved wife Cunegund to the church of Saint Peter, while the pope awaited him; and before he was admitted, when the same man asked him whether he wished to be a faithful patron and defender of the Roman Church and in all things faithful to him and to his successors, he replied with a devoted profession. Then from him he received the anointing and the crown together with his wife.”

Nat. Alexander correctly interpreted this passage of Ditmar (eleventh century, chapter 9, article 1, p. 617):

> “Having first sworn fidelity and defense to the Roman Church itself, to Benedict, and to his successors, as Ditmar attests at the beginning of book seven.”

The one Italian annalist either did not perceive or did not wish to perceive that the matter concerned the promise or profession celebrated in the ceremonial books, which the Carolingians likewise used to make upon the steps of the basilica of Saint Peter.

Although this matter should more suitably be treated elsewhere, it is nevertheless necessary to set out in advance the distinction between the professions, since the most learned Mabillon, himself interpreting the words of Ditmar cited above (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 216), incorrectly asserts that the Carolingians used a formula not unlike this one.

### XLV

The formula of the profession used by the Carolingians appears in that ancient *Order* preserved by Mabillon (ibid., p. 215) and by Martène (*On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book II, chapter 9), with only slight differences, as follows:

> “The emperor’s promise. In the name of Christ, I, N., emperor, promise, pledge, and declare before God and the blessed Peter that I will be the protector and defender of this holy Roman Church in all its interests, insofar as I shall be supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability.”

The venerable Baronius had long ago included a somewhat different version in his *Sacred Annals* (800, no. 7), calling it an oath and maintaining that Charles and his successors used it, with Pagi not even opening his mouth in opposition.

I observe that Leo III (letter 2, elsewhere numbered 10) used a manner of speaking which I find that Hadrian did not employ:

> “He established you as defenders of his interests.”

These words do not greatly differ from the profession. I further observe that it is called the emperor’s promise and that the emperor made this profession, which can apply only to Charles, who was unexpectedly crowned and called emperor.

I therefore accept Baronius’s opinion and attribute this promise, or oath, to Charles the Great.

The case is different with Charles’s successors. It is certain from the letter of Lotharius cited above (no. 24), addressed to his father Louis the Pious, that they did not use the name emperor before their coronation:

> “I have received the blessing, honor, and name of the imperial office.”

All the ancient monuments agree with this, as will become clear in its proper place.

I understand that the only respect in which those successors agreed with Charles was that they made a profession or oath quite different from the oath of the Germans—at least those who were descended from Charles and may truly be called his successors with Baronius.

The last kings of the Carolingian line themselves seem to have rendered an oath of fidelity, although, owing to the lack of documents, this cannot be asserted with certainty.

### XLVI

It must be affirmed beyond all doubt that the kings of Germany did not obtain the imperial insignia unless an oath of fidelity had first been rendered. In the *Order*, or *Ceremonial*, belonging to the year 1046 (below, Dissertation VI, no. 24), it runs as follows:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, N., king of the Romans and future emperor of the Romans, promise, pledge, declare, and swear by these Gospels before God, the blessed apostle Peter, and the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, the lord N., pope, fidelity to you and to your successors who canonically enter office. From this moment I shall be the protector and defender of this holy Roman Church, of your person, and of your successors in all their interests, insofar as I shall be supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability, without fraud or evil intent. So may God and these holy Gospels of God help me.”

Whether Otto the Great and the other two Ottos—his son and grandson—issued an oath like this, apart from the one cited under “To You, Lord”; or whether Otto III’s successor, the holy Henry, was the first of all to promise fidelity, I confess that I do not know.

It is nevertheless easy to believe that, even if they did not promise it in the same words—for the title “king of the Romans” did not suit the Ottos—they promised the same thing in substance.

For when the pontiff and the Roman primates deliberated on transferring the imperial dignity to the powerful King Otto, I have already said that the matter was not handled rashly (no. 40). This is confirmed more and more by another oath which the Romans exacted from the elected emperor before he was to receive the imperial diadem and enter the Leonine City.

Nothing else could have made the king of Germany more ready to swear or the Romans more bold to demand an oath than the occasion of this transferred dignity, since for thirty-eight years they had grown unaccustomed to obeying a dual authority.

Moreover, the same Otto the Great received an oath not only from the pontiff but also from all the nobles of the city that they would never aid Berengarius and Adelbert, as Liutprand testifies. Therefore, just as the pontiff did, the nobles too must evidently have exacted an oath from King Otto.

42. XLVII. Certainly, in that very ancient Order of the year 1046, there stands the record of a twofold oath sworn to the Romans by Henry III, king of Germany; and in the record of Henry V’s coronation at Baronius (1111, no. 5) we read: “He made two oaths according to custom: one beside the little bridge, the other beside the gate of the portico, before the people.” This custom cannot be referred to Henry IV, since he was not crowned; still less can it be referred to Henry III, who, when he was at Rome, swore those two oaths elsewhere. Thus the acts commend a custom, or an older usage. I do not see where it could more suitably be traced than to the transfer of the Empire to the Germans. Therefore, although I am not ordinarily indulgent toward conjectures, I am nevertheless utterly convinced that no more certain origin of this definite practice can be found.
