Moreover, it should be observed that the promise, or profession, of the Carolingians was ordinarily made in the area above the steps of the basilica of Saint Peter; but the oath of the Germans began, during the twelfth century, to be made in the oratory of Saint Mary in the Tower. There, too, the oath previously sworn through envoys was customarily repeated. Such a place is prescribed in the old ceremonial book used by Clement V (in Raynaldus, 1311, no. 14), although the same pontiff permits the elected emperor, at his discretion, to renew the oath sworn through envoys in either place, provided that it is not omitted:

“Let him also renew before us, at the time of his approval, the oath sworn through his representatives, according to the tenor written above. And if, upon his arrival, at the steps where you and the legate will meet him, he should prefer to make the aforesaid renewal, we are content.”

From this same ancient Ceremonial we learn something that must by no means be passed over. That explicit profession of fidelity, of which enough seems to have been said, fell into disuse after Henry III; nevertheless, the formula of the oath, different from the Carolingian promise and incorporated into the coronation order, remained. Accordingly, we find from the book—namely, from the Order or Ceremonial—that Henry V and Frederick I swore the oath. If the word “to swear” was lacking in the Ceremonial book that Clement V sent from Avignon to Rome for the coronation of Henry VII, this should be understood to have happened not because the oath had fallen out of use, but because the sacrament, or oath, sworn through envoys had to be renewed by the elected emperor. Hence the oath of the patrician is also found in the Ceremonial; for its formula to be called an oath of fidelity, nothing is lacking except the explicit word “fidelity.”

XLVIII. This matter is clearly confirmed by the oath of Lothair II, sworn during the greatest difficulties in Roman affairs, as a new precedent, before the doors of the Lateran basilica. It is famous in Baronius (1133, no. 2), but I am pleased to reproduce it from the Albinian manuscript, differing by one or two words from the Vatican papers from which Baronius copied it:

“This is the oath which Lord King Lothair swore to the lord Pope Innocent, at the time of the heresy of Peter Leo’s son, before the doors of the basilica of Saint Savior, which is called Constantine’s, on the day on which he was crowned by that same Innocent, before he received the crown; Lord Censius Frangipane [Baronius: de Frajapanis] administering the oath, with his nephew Otto and the other Roman nobles who were present there.

“I, Lothair the king, promise and swear to you, lord Pope Innocent, and to your successors, security of life and limb (Baronius: ‘and of the limbs’), and protection from wrongful seizure; to defend the papacy and your honor; to maintain the regalia of Saint Peter that you possess; and, insofar as I am able, to recover what you do not possess.”

Lothair’s predecessors, Henry V and Frederick I, certainly swore a fuller oath from the Ceremonial book, as their respective records relate. Nevertheless, anyone comparing the substance of this oath will see clearly that, although the antipope Anacletus, in his haste to accomplish everything, occupied the Vatican, the Mausoleum of Hadrian, and other fortifications with very powerful armed forces, this oath differs not only from the Carolingian promise but is truly an oath of fidelity.

XLIX. When you hear that Lothair was crowned in the Lateran basilica, do not suppose that anything was taken away from the character of the restored imperial majesty. Henry VII, too, was supposed to be crowned there in the year 1312. For King Robert of Sicily, like an antipope in earlier times, had invaded the Vatican, and no law can be imposed upon harsh necessity. Indeed, Henry himself and Charles IV received the imperial diadem through legates of Clement V and Innocent VI, in an entirely new manner.

This proves ever more strongly that the coronation ought to be performed nowhere other than before the most sacred body of Peter. Since each pontiff was at Avignon, he preferred to delegate his authority rather than change the place of coronation. For the oath of fidelity was first sworn to Peter, and then to the Roman pontiff, his successor, as is clear from the formulas quoted above. Thus the defense of that Church—and consequently of the Roman pontiff and of ecclesiastical jurisdiction—was undertaken.

Accordingly, when Charles V, the last of all to receive the imperial diadem, was crowned by Clement VII at Bologna, because delay was dangerous while Germany was in turmoil and his brother Ferdinand was urgently requesting aid against the Turks, the church of Saint Petronius was transformed into a Vatican, as Jovius reports (vol. II, book XXVII, p. 224), in whose presence everything was done:

“Everything,” he says, “had been arranged in the likeness of the Vatican temple, and new names had been assigned to the chapels, so that each detail might correspond, according to the ancient custom, with the pontifical books.”

So firm and stable was the character of the renewed Western Empire established by Saint Leo III seven hundred and thirty years earlier! Most importantly, Blasius de Martinellis, master of ceremonies, who committed the entire rite observed on that occasion to posterity, reports that the confession of blessed Peter had been arranged beneath the high altar in imitation of the Vatican.

Therefore Charles swore an oath to Peter and to his successor Clement—an oath that, as we recently saw, Lothair II did not swear within the City, because he received the imperial diadem in the Lateran basilica, far from the confession. Three things, in fact, were necessary for the establishment of an emperor, according to the restoration carried out by Leo III:

1. The king designated as emperor had to profess that he would be the defender of the Roman Church and of the pontiff.
2. He had to be inaugurated before the confession of blessed Peter.
3. He had to receive the imperial insignia from the hand of the Roman pontiff.

That these same requirements had repeatedly to be added to the necessary conditions has been demonstrated with complete clarity, insofar as the institution or restoration of imperial dignity is concerned. More will have to be said when we discuss election and coronation.

L. We ought now to turn to the letters of Leo III. But something must first be added concerning the first and third of the foregoing points, so that every doubt may be removed that each of them indicates this new character of the Empire.

It is established that Euphemius, patriarch of Constantinople, was the first to demand a profession of faith from Anastasius in the year 491, before he was crowned emperor, as the Greek authors cited by Baronius teach (491, no. 7); this profession was later incorporated into the rite of the Byzantine coronation. It is obvious that the West contained nothing comparable to this profession, because it was first demanded from the Greeks, who were considered alien to the orthodox faith; afterward it was demanded from those same Greeks lest they oppose that orthodox faith. By contrast, the Western Augusti, all of them Catholics, defended the orthodox faith against those same Greeks without any public promise or oath, since the latter exclusively concerned the Roman Church and pontiff.

To come closer to our own times: at the very beginning of the persecution of the holy images, Saint Germanus, the patriarch, before inaugurating Leo, had him promise that he would in no way disturb the Church, and accepted from the emperor God as guarantor. Saint Germanus himself is a witness to this in Baronius (726, no. 7):

“The patriarch recalled to him the promises he had made before assuming the Empire, and how he had given God to him as surety that he would in no way disturb the Church in its apostolic and divinely handed-down rites.”

From these words it is clear what the profession of the Greeks was and by what ceremonies they were inaugurated. Edmund Martene (On the Ancient Rites of the Church, book II, chapter 9) presents both rites and both professions; if they are compared, the distinction between them will be unmistakable.

Therefore it must be affirmed beyond all doubt that this first point designates an entirely new character of the Empire. We have discussed the second point at length in the dissertation, and it will be still clearer when the rite of coronation is discussed. A few things must now be asserted concerning the third point.

LI. Twenty-eight emperors are counted down to Charles V; of these, only two—Henry VII and Charles IV—did not receive the imperial insignia from pontifical hands. Learned men know that this was a matter of fact, not of law. In Raynaldus (1311, no. 7 ff.; 1355, no. 3 ff.) there are letters of Clement V and Innocent VI that explain the matter very clearly.

First, concerning the law, each of them says:

“Decreeing that the anointing and the diadem of that Empire must be granted to him by our hands at the appropriate place and time,”

and assigning a definite date for this purpose. They then insert the order or rite of coronation, to be performed by the Roman pontiff alone—a rich testimony to the fact that, for five hundred years, twenty-three Augusti “were called emperors only if they had been anointed for this purpose with holy oil by the Roman pontiffs,” as Louis II informed Basil (Anonymous of Salerno, chapter 106).

Afterward they carefully prescribe what must not be omitted. Finally, they assert their right in these carefully formulated words:

“But since, as is evident from the foregoing, many observances, many solemnities, and many acts of reverence and honor due to the Roman pontiff are omitted because of our absence, we protest, and we wish, and by apostolic authority we decree, that no prejudice in law or in fact is thereby generated against the Roman Church, or against us and our successors; rather, whenever the case of a king of the Romans to be crowned emperor arises, everything must be exhibited and performed by the persons to be crowned before the Roman pontiffs, just as is more fully expressed in the form described above, which is contained in the archive of the Church and in the pontifical Ordinary.”

Everyone was so firmly convinced that the coronation had to be performed by the Roman pontiff alone that these same two kings of the Romans judged that the place could be changed rather than the person. Each of them, considering that the pontiff was residing at Avignon and delayed by countless obligations from undertaking the long journey to Italy, concluded the oath sworn through envoys to that pontiff, contrary to the custom of their predecessors, in these words:

“And when our aforesaid lord king is to be crowned emperor by you at Rome or elsewhere, he shall personally renew the said oath and the other oath customarily made, at your request, at the time of his coronation.”

EPILOGUE

LII. These matters seem sufficient to me for demonstrating the frivolity of Struvius and of those who follow him concerning the transfer of the restored Empire to the Germans.

I am not unaware that Otto the Great and his two successors named Otto attributed too much to themselves, especially when they raised to the chair of Peter those whom friendship, blood relationship, or some other cause commended to them, as the senatorial and Tusculan counts had previously done. Yet this did not harm the condition of the Empire at all; it produced envy, boldness, and seditions at Rome, which had to be suppressed by arms.

From this arose disturbances among the nobles against both powers, the pontifical and the imperial, and these made the forty years of their rule turbulent and sometimes even disastrous. My spirit shudders to recount the rebellions and massacres of Rotfred, prefect of the city, Cencius, and Crescentius, which are recorded by Baronius and Pagius (965, 974, 998).

When I recall also the unhappy periods of the Roman Church under King Henry IV, the Augusti of the same name, V and VI, and both Fredericks, while flattery, boldness, and heresy were rampant, I see oppression rather than defense of the Church, of the pontiffs, and of all sacred laws.

These things do not erase the condition of the restored Western Empire; rather, they provide writers hostile to the Apostolic See, and others insufficiently cautious—both kinds haters of the truth—with the most favorable opportunities for contradiction and wandering into error. But I would ask them: what kind of praise is it to portray the Church and pontiffs as deceived by the Augusti, and those same Augusti as perjurers?

I now come to the letters of Leo III, the restorer of imperial majesty.

[Col. 0517]

47. THE LETTERS SENT BY POPE LEO TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES BEGIN.

FIRST LETTER. HOW A CERTAIN BISHOP WAS FOUND IN EXILE.

(Year of Our Lord 806, Codex IX, chronicle 1.)

[Col. 0517C]

SUMMARY.—When Fortunatus, archbishop of Grado, had been driven from his see by the Greeks and Venetians and was living in exile in Francia, Charles obtained from the pontiff the vacant church of Pola for him, until Grado might be recovered. On this occasion the pontiff reports to Charles that the archbishop’s conduct had been less than praiseworthy both in Italy and in Francia, and wishes Charles to admonish him beneficially.

To the most pious and serene lord, victor and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

[Note: Pagius dates the letter to this year (no. 10), observing that the church of Pola belonged to the province of Grado before Istria came under Frankish control. Conringius agrees: he places in this year the beginning of the war between the Greeks and Charles in the Adriatic Sea, which was concluded in 810. The Continuator of Ughelli (Italy Sacred, vol. V, p. 476) follows both of them.]

When your imperial letter had reached us from city to city, and had been received and reread by us, we found in it that Fortunatus, the archbishop, is recognized as being in exile from the island of Grado, where he appeared to possess his own proper see, because of the persecution of the Greeks or Venetians.

[Note: Einhard, in Pagius (no. 8), relates that the Venetians and Dalmatians came into Charles’s friendship, and that a fleet sent by Nicephorus, under the command of the patrician Nicetas, was dispatched to recover Dalmatia. See the very lengthy account from Dandolo and others in Ughelli (vol. V, p. 1094).]

And that, if it seemed fitting to us, he might, on grounds of necessity, have his see at Pola, where a certain Bishop Aemilianus had long presided, and which is the diocese of the aforesaid Fortunatus; and that your imperial power, protected by God, had by no means wished to place him elsewhere without consulting our apostolic see.

[Note: A very substantial argument for the condemned royal law, or constitution of Hadrian, by which Charles acquired a right in the election of pontiffs and archbishops, and so forth, is found in Goldast (Imperial Constitutions, vol. I, p. 16) and Lunig (Italian Diplomatic Records, vol. I, p. 1). Even an emperor newly created does not arrogate anything of the kind to himself without consulting the Roman pontiff.]

As for us, after considering this matter, we made provision: just as it pleased your imperial clemency that he remain in the church of Pola, so let him remain, under precisely this condition: if, with the Lord’s assent and blessed Peter the apostle’s protection, his own see should be restored to him through your victory in triumph, then, just as he received the aforesaid church of Pola intact, with everything belonging to it, so let it again be restored to him. He must not remove anything from its property or money for his own see, nor presume in any way to give any of that property, money, or goods to anyone, so that the church itself may always remain secure and inviolable with its bishop.

[Note: The pontifical formulas of the Book of the Offices were then in especially great use; consequently, it was not necessary to consult canons and decrees concerning the alienation of church property. Consult them (Offices, chapter 3), together with Garnerius’s accompanying notes. The letters of Gregory the Great cited by him are particularly relevant here.]

It is likewise reserved in your imperial letters how, at the palace of Aachen, you made provision with us concerning the church of Aquileia, as though it were one that possessed its own see.

[Note: Aquileia at that time seemed to have been abandoned. The patriarchal see had long before been transferred from there to Grado; and after various changes, which may be seen in Ughelli, the patriarch then resided at Forum Julii, which is called the municipality of Aquileia in the acts of the synod of Forum Julii celebrated by Paulinus in 791. Thus, even in Charles’s testament of 811, it is not Aquileia the metropolis but Forum Julii that is mentioned.

What Leo and Charles deliberated concerning Aquileia in 804 may easily be inferred from these words: “as though it were one that possessed its own see.” The rights and property of Aquileia had passed to the church of Grado; meanwhile, the church of Forum Julii claimed many things for itself. The restoration of the patriarchal see of Aquileia to its former status was not even being considered.

For this reason Leo seems to have dealt with Charles concerning the restoration of the see of Aquileia at the expense of Forum Julii. Gregory II and Gregory III had each attempted precisely this, declaring Forum Julii to be the metropolis of the duchy of Forum Julii alone. Yet Leo IX, two hundred and fifty years later, demonstrates that nothing had been accomplished concerning Aquileia. He restores the decrees of both Gregorys concerning the metropolis of Forum Julii; but instead of saying anything about a restored Aquileia, he calls Grado the new Aquileia and subjects Istria and Venetia to it. See Baronius (year 729, no. 5 ff.). Conringius also refers the reader to this passage, saying that he nowhere finds what was agreed at Aachen concerning the church of Aquileia.]

For your clemency should believe us that whatever your envoys discussed there with us, or with our brothers and fellow bishops, is seen to concern entirely the salvation of your soul and of your sons. May almighty and merciful God, through the intercession of his holy Mother and of his apostles Peter and Paul, deign to preserve you for a long time in this world and, through the course of many years, grant you to attain the heavenly kingdoms with his saints. May heavenly grace guard the most pious dominion of our lord, and may it bow before him the necks of all nations.

49. ADDITION.

We have also taken care to inform your serenity concerning the aforesaid Fortunatus, so that, just as you always labor for his temporal honor, you may likewise care for his soul, in order that, through the fear you inspire, he may fulfill his ministry better.

For we have not heard of him what is fitting to hear of an archbishop, either from these regions or from the regions of Francia, where you bestowed benefices upon him.

[Note: How accurately the pontiff judged his conduct was revealed by what followed. For in the year 818, after peace had been restored with the Venetians, as Sigonius says, he returned to the church of Grado. Later, summoned by Louis the Pious on a charge against his majesty, and driven by the reproaches of conscience, he went to Constantinople (Baronius, year 821, no. 59, and Pagius there). Conringius reports the same matter more fully in his notes on this letter, from the Frankish annals attributed to Einhard.]

Nevertheless, we give thanks to God, because not everything will be unknown to you. Indeed, question your faithful servants, and everything will become known to you, since those who praise him to you do so in exchange for gifts and payments.

[Note: Ducange observes that this word is used for any gift or any payment, both here in this letter and in the charter of Athanasius III, bishop of Naples, and elsewhere, although in Ughelli it is always corruptly written “Calzarium.”]

What is more beloved to us than your most sweet soul? And God, who knows all things, is witness that we disclose all this to you for the salvation of your soul, because, out of the great love that we bear toward your serenity, we cannot remain silent.

You can question our brother Archbishop Hildibald.

[Note: In the Life of Leo III by Anastasius, Archbishop Hildewald is sent to meet Leo when he first travels to Charles; he was Archbishop of Cologne, as Hansiz (German Sacred History, vol. II) and Conringius (in the work cited) state.]

And Chancellor Ercanbald.

[Note: In the Frankish annals cited by Baronius (year 801, no. 20), Ercelbald is called a notary; Charles sent him into Liguria to prepare a fleet. It is therefore clear from both men that Fortunatus’s wicked conduct was known.]

Perhaps through them you will learn something, since we have found them faithful to your soul in every respect.

50. SECOND LETTER. HOW ENVOYS SENT TO ADMINISTER JUSTICE CAUSED DAMAGE.

(Year of Our Lord 807, Codex X, chronicle 2.)

[Col. 0520B]

SUMMARY.—Through his envoys, Bishop John and the hegumen Basil, who bring a small gift marked by relics of Saint Peter, the pontiff complains that estates and other property belonging to the palace of Ravenna, previously restored by Herminus at Charles’s command, have again been invaded. He asks that Charles not permit the donation made by Pippin and confirmed by Charles himself to be diminished in any respect.

To the most pious and serene lord, victor and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

[Note: Conringius conjectures that this letter, the first in the codex and our third, ought to be placed before the first. He assigns both, hesitantly, to the year 807. Pagius assigns them to that same year with complete confidence (no. 9 ff.).]

To this end our almighty and invisible God made your imperial power, protected by God, the guardian of his holy Church, so that everywhere it might remain more vigilant, under praiseworthy governance, for the increase of your glory, and might not permit those whom you rule externally by counsel to perish inwardly. Thus, through the fruit of your pious solicitude, you may deserve to reach the eternal joys that he will give to his saints, and may receive manifold worthy recompense for your good deeds.

We have therefore sent our present envoys, namely the most reverend Bishop John and the religious hegumen Basil, to your imperial clemency for the sake of visitation, with the blessing of blessed Peter the apostle, your patron.

[Note: Conringius is absurd, pouring out all his venom against the holy see in the most audacious notes on this letter. Here “the blessing of Saint Peter” is nothing other than a gift accompanied by relics, as the following words make clear. They were not keys, nor filings or scrapings from the chains of Saint Peter, which were customarily sent to leading men; I have nowhere found their name suppressed. Ducange, who collected much concerning the meaning of this word, passes over this passage, although it is sufficiently clear. No one would readily extract from it an argument for sectarian mockery except a sectarian.]

But we ask your serenity not to consider it an insult that we have been unable to send you anything worthy of your munificence. Nevertheless, the things of blessed Peter the apostle, however small what is offered may be, must always be received as a great blessing, since through them he will be able to bestow greater benefits upon you here and present eternal blessings before almighty God.

Since, after God and his saints, we place our trust in no one among human beings except in your imperial power, we considered it right to disclose first to your ears both our joy and the distress that we continually endure, so that the offering that your most beloved parents and you yourselves presented to blessed Peter the apostle may be acceptable and secure in his sight.

Thus you may deserve to receive worthy recompense from him, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, who appointed you defenders of his interests.

[Note: We have seen Charles, while still king, frequently called by this title of defender in the letters of Hadrian. We now hear him called by the same name by the pontiff after he has just been made emperor. Whether patrician or emperor, Charles claimed nothing for himself beyond the defense of the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See.]

May your widely renowned imperial munificence be honorably proclaimed among all the faithful people; and may we not be summoned for negligence before the tribunal of God, together with the Lord himself and our nurturer, the blessed apostle Peter, because we failed to report to your clemency the oppressions suffered by God’s people.

Your pious serenity therefore sent your envoys, so that they ought to have administered justice for us; but they caused us more damage than benefit.

[Note: Conringius is entirely mistaken in inventing another pair of envoys for himself. Those same envoys whom Charles, as defender of the Church, sent at the pontiff’s request to vindicate the rights of the holy see went to Rome. They reported that they could not decide the case on behalf of the holy see, for the reasons given by those who claimed the disputed property for themselves; and they inspected the violence done to the pontifical subjects, or collectors.]

You should question the envoys whom you sent and who came to us; they themselves can explain orally what they heard or saw being done to our people.

The present Bishop John, our envoy, can also inform your imperial power of every detail: everything that, through your pious and lawful judgment, we recovered concerning the case of the palace of Ravenna, for which you ordered that no one thereafter presume either to disturb or to bring an action in court, whether concerning the common lands or the mansi.

[Note: There were two things that the pontiff claimed as belonging to the jurisdiction of the palace of Ravenna, the revenues of which were paid into the pontifical treasury from the income of the Exarchate: common lands and mansi.

Concerning the common lands, Ducange rightly observes from Sirmondus that they were certain estates or meadows which the inhabitants used jointly, lands held in common, some of which were leased by the prince; this appears to have been the character of the lands at issue here. Certainly Ducange establishes the point on the authority of this letter.

Muratori thinks that common land means a tax customarily paid by the common people: a fine interpretation!

The mansi, also called mansi and mansae, should be understood as farms or estates, some of which belonged then, and still belong today, to princes.

But both the revenues of the common lands and those of the mansi that are mentioned had been assigned to the palace by Charles’s decision in such a way that all litigation was thereafter to cease. The matter therefore was neither settled nor clear; they had previously been subject to disputes, and the opposing party supported its case with documents so clear that, unless I am mistaken, the imperial envoys could not decide in favor of the holy see.]

Herminus, your faithful servant, restored all these to us according to your arrangement, together with the houses, vineyards, cultivated lands, and livestock; but they took everything away, and nothing of it remained to us.

Therefore we ask your imperial clemency to order that, with regard to the donation accepted from God and offered by you to the aforesaid apostle of God, action be taken in such a way that it may not be diminished in any part.

[Note: Muratori most foolishly understood the system of the Exarchate as though Pippin, retaining supreme ownership for himself, had granted the holy see only beneficial possession. See the Book of the Carolingians (letter 81, elsewhere 67); this single argument overturns the entire system.

The pontiff says that the donation must not be diminished in any part—that is, that the revenues proper to the palace, which he said shortly before that he himself received, were being occupied not by the imperial envoys but by the inhabitants of Ravenna, who claimed those estates and common lands for themselves. Thus the Pippinian donation was being diminished in some respect. Leo is working with all his might to prevent this.]

Rather, through your laborious struggle, may it remain firm, stable, unshaken, and enduring through all ages; and may we, although unequal to the task, holding the place of the same disciple by God’s mercy, be able securely and patiently to implore the clemency of almighty God, so that he may extend your strongest arm mightily against the enemies of the holy Church of God, and so that you may crush all barbarian nations beneath the foot of your strength.

[Note: P. Coustant sufficiently and more than sufficiently refutes Conringius’s foul mockery concerning the vicariate of Saint Peter, which the most holy and learned pontiffs claimed for themselves for a very long time, in his preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs (no. 43 ff.). At the same time he shows that Christ’s vicars, although more rarely—for the title was common to bishops and even to abbots—were in fact so called, beginning with Saint Cyprian. The following words of Cyprian himself seem useful against Conringius:

“Indeed, heresies have arisen nowhere else, nor have schisms been born, except from the fact that the priest of God is not obeyed, and that it is not considered that, for a time, there is one priest in the Church and one judge in Christ’s place” (letter 55, to Cornelius).]

May heavenly grace guard the most pious dominion of our Lord, and may it bow before him the necks of all nations.

53. THIRD LETTER. CONCERNING ACCUSERS.

(Year of Our Lord 807, Codex I, chronicle 3.)

[Col. 0523A]

SUMMARY.—The apostolic envoys, returning, bring two letters and a capitulary from the emperor Charles. In them Charles testified that he was favorably disposed toward the holy see; he expressed sorrow that, according to the report, none of the imperial envoys pleased the pontiff; and he complained that both those who had died and those who survived were subject to blame, so that no one could now be found willing to undertake an embassy to Rome.

Leo replies that these are slanders, and that ears should not readily be given to such whisperers. Such men, however, should be summoned to judgment either by Charles or by the pontiff. Meanwhile Charles should send a legate to investigate what benefit they had brought to the holy see, since those who had arrived for that purpose had displeased the pontiff.

Leo gently reproaches Charles by saying that none of his predecessors from Francia had deserved better than Charles himself; he openly disdains the suggestion that such a singular benefit had accrued to him against everyone’s wishes.

To the most pious and serene lord, victor and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

[Note: I am less concerned with the chronology, since I see that both Pagius and Conringius have established it in this year, perhaps toward its end, with a highly probable consideration of the contents of the letters. As for the capitulary, Ducange interprets it as a small book. But afterward, in Chapter V, section 2, he explains the meaning of the capitulary more clearly; he had done the same in connection with the Fifth Capitulary, showing that Gregory the Great also used the term, and that it means nothing other than various matters divided into brief chapters. This is also clear below: for the pontiff says that he came to the sixth chapter, which turned the joy received from the preceding five and from the two letters into sorrow.]

When our most faithful envoys, whom we sent to your imperial power, returned to us, they reported your most gracious benevolence toward blessed Peter the apostle and toward his vicar, which you bear from the inmost love of your heart. Among other things, they presented to us your honorable letters and the capitulary.

But as for the capitulary, when we had opened it after rereading the two letters, among all the other joys which those letters had poured into our heart, its first chapter so refreshed our heart that we began to say with the prophet: “Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.” But when, proceeding in order, we joined it to the sixth chapter, just as much joy and gladness as the aforementioned letter and the other chapters had brought us, so much sorrow and sadness did we afterward become filled with. For the aforesaid sixth chapter stated that you were unable to find envoys who pleased us, and your serenity is greatly saddened by this matter; [Col. 0524B] and none of those who had already been sent to us would thereafter be sent again of his own accord [Note: [Col. 0523C] Conring’s cleverness is laughable. He lays down as his foundation that envoys were customarily sent from Rome, according to Frankish royal practice, and to other lands subject to the pope, for the purpose of holding judgments, and on this basis he establishes supreme imperial jurisdiction. Muratori embraces this argument wholeheartedly, without mentioning Conring’s name, for he says in the margin that he is presenting these letters from the Labbe edition. But if Charles sent envoys into papal territory, according to royal custom, to conduct judicial proceedings by virtue of supreme jurisdiction, what difference would it have made whether they pleased or displeased the pope? If Charles was the supreme lord, [Col. 0523D] why was he so concerned with the selection of the envoys, and why was he grieved to hear that they were less acceptable to the pope? Why are the envoys themselves said to come unwillingly to Rome?], except that each of them willingly desires to fulfill his obedience to you. And not only do your envoys fear carrying your embassy to our lowliness [Note: [Col. 0523D] What could be desired that is clearer for demonstrating that the matter concerns undertaking an embassy to the pope, not erecting a tribunal at Rome and throughout the territory of the Holy See? That the cities which Pippin and Charles offered to the Holy See were handed over through royal envoys is perfectly clear from the letters of Hadrian and his predecessors in the *Codex Carolinus*; and those letters likewise testify that the rights of the Holy See were vindicated through the same envoys. Yet it is established and certain from that exceedingly rich source of documents—than which none more outstanding on this matter has survived to our time—that both things were always done at the popes’ request. It is easier to say than to prove that Charles’s envoys, according to Frankish royal custom, held judicial proceedings at Rome both before and after he assumed the title of Augustus, and that Charles’s supreme jurisdiction in the territory of the Holy See rested on that embassy of the envoys. Why do Conring and Muratori, who follow him, not produce some document by which we might unlearn what these letters teach us? The pope speaks very humbly of himself, as was characteristic of his profound humility; nevertheless, he testifies that Charles arranged embassies to him just as he arranged them to Charles. For what does “to carry an embassy to our lowliness” mean? Does it not indicate envoys, or administrators, of Charles Augustus? There certainly were other envoys who exercised judicial authority in the provinces of the Frankish monarchy—indeed, even in papal territory, for, compelled by the boldness of his subjects, the pope had granted Charles, once he had been raised to imperial power, sufficient authority that just and proper things might be done everywhere by everyone through fear of imperial majesty. But this shared authority establishes Charles as defender of the Church, not as possessing supreme jurisdiction.], but others too have now no longer dared to seek help from you, because, as they say, no one who has sought your clemency has afterward been able to attain our full favor [Note: [Col. 0524C] Several letters of Hadrian deal with this matter. More than any others, *Cod. Car.* 97, otherwise 85, should be consulted. From it there is a definite reason why the pope rebuked his subjects who went over to Charles. But in this passage the holy pontiff declares it false that those who fled to Charles lost his favor; therefore he calls reports of this kind made to Charles slanders—not because they were wholly false, but because, by plucking out whatever was odious from actions that had been just and proper, they had been so exaggerated that nothing truthful seemed to remain in them. Yet from the wickedness of such slanderers itself emerges the supreme jurisdiction which the pope exercised over peoples subject to him. For if those who fled to Charles lost the pope’s favor, then the pope did not possess merely beneficial or usufructuary lordship, but exercised the right of a prince over his subjects. Hence Hadrian complained (*Cod. Car.*, ep. 92, otherwise 86) that in Campania the keys of the cities had been handed over to him without their inhabitants, and he asked Charles that Campania too should be given to him in full right, like the other cities of his dominion. The matter is made still clearer by the example he cites of the peoples of Lombard Tuscany, whom Charles had subjected to the Holy See: “As with the other cities and districts of Tuscany, by your gifts we wish to rule and govern them, possessing all their law.”], and because you have had many faithful envoys sent here, some of whom have now died, and they themselves were slandered, while none of those who are alive now seems to be free from slander. Therefore, dearest son, what else is left for us to do except pour out prayers to the Lord for those who have lied to you in such matters? As it is written: “Pray for your enemies.” Let your serenity believe us, for whatever we know to be conducive to the salvation of your soul, we conceal in no way; and if previously we kept silent, now we do not cease to make known to your power whatever concerns good or evil. For whoever by lying and wicked schemes wishes to separate a son from his mother will receive judgment together with that keeper of the keys [Note: [Col. 0525C] Nothing is more frequently heard in the *Codex Carolinus* than this kind of title being attributed to Saint Peter. We see nearly the same thing done in almost all of Leo’s surviving letters, and there are other monuments of the Middle Ages that bear this title. It evidently rests upon the divine oracle, when the keys of the kingdom of heaven are figuratively handed over to Peter by our Savior, signifying the power to bind and loose. Accordingly, Augustine (*Sermon 22 on the Saints*) said: “Certainly worthy is he to be a stone for the foundation of peoples being built into the house of God, a pillar for their support, and a key to the kingdom.” Had later scholars taken this into consideration, when they encountered “keys to the kingdom” in Gregory III’s letter to Charles Martel (*Cod. Car.*, ep. 1)—although through scribal error “kingdom” had been written for “funeral pyre”—they would not have fallen into so many varied false opinions. For either Peter would be called “the key to the kingdom,” or the keys would symbolically be sent “to the kingdom”; in no way should this be understood of the kingdom of the Romans, a name that has always been disastrous, but of the kingdom of heaven, which is properly indicated by the keys delivered by Jesus Christ to the chief of the apostles. Certainly at that time everyone was so convinced that through Peter the entrance to the kingdom of heaven lay open, according to the divine oracle, especially to the kings and peoples of the Franks, that this alone was one reason why the Holy See emerged from barbarian servitude and was raised so magnificently. Hence the title “keeper of the keys” is heard so frequently.], the blessed apostle Peter. For in this world nothing is more precious to me than the salvation of your soul. But since we cannot write out one by one all that we carry in our heart concerning your prosperity and exaltation, [Col. 0525B] may almighty God repay us in the same measure as we desire your honor and safety. Nevertheless, since we are bound to you by great love and great faith, we cannot remain silent, so that you yourselves may keep watch over your soul, knowing that this wretched and fleeting life is soon cut short and has an end, and that all will render an account to the Lord for their idle words. Therefore, do not believe people too quickly before they have made satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0525D] He gently rebukes Charles for lending ears that were too ready to slanderers, without testing their reliability. Neither Ducange nor his commentators have understood this meaning of *satisfaction*.]. Yet if we received and honored them well for love of you, may God repay us with good and satisfy you, so that you may strive more and more in the causes of the blessed apostle Peter; and if they did not report to you how honorably we received them, what else can we say except that God forgive them [Note: [Col. 0525D] The fact that the holy pontiff calls God as witness is the strongest argument that these informers were slanderers.]? Nevertheless, if we had been nearby, with the help of the mercy of almighty God, you would have had the truth and falsehood distinguished, because we believe that God has given you such wisdom that we would not have had such reproach and confusion brought upon our face. [Col. 0525C] We believe that your serenity remembers that you sent us word on several occasions that you would not permit anyone to speak ill of us, nor give him any opportunity to do so [Note: [Col. 0526C] Several of Hadrian’s letters may be seen written in this sense. From this we know with certainty that Charles acted likewise toward Leo. It is by no means doubtful evidence that, together with the temporal dominion of the Holy See, hostility toward it and the slander arising from that hostility had their origin.]. But what, then, remains except that amid so many accusations spoken to you against us and against our faithful servants who were advancing the interests of our Holy Church, I give thanks to almighty God with tears? For no one in this life can separate us from the love which we bear toward you, except death alone, whenever it comes upon us. But why do we impose so much weariness upon your ears? Most certainly, insofar as God has deigned to grant us understanding, we think in our heart that none of our predecessors has served these regions with as much love as we have served them. Yet, as we see, our service has been acceptable to no one [Note: [Col. 0526C] See the dissertation, no. 25 and following.].

As for the accusers of your envoys, whom you sent to us so that they might come either into our presence or yours to have the matter examined, if it pleases your piety, send your envoy without them, one who will investigate everything more clearly and faithfully report to your imperial power what they have done, and how they have acted, in these regions, and what benefit your mother, the Holy Church of God, has received from it [Note: [Col. 0526C] Here is the point I recently made (*col.* 523, note c): that there was a definite procedure for holding judgments through Charles’s envoys within the territory of the Holy See itself. The supreme prince, namely the pontiff, was the one requesting it. At that time there was indeed the greatest harmony between priesthood and empire. Hence we see that Leo’s successor, Stephen, asked Louis, who succeeded Charles, without being compelled by anyone, that the Romans should promise fidelity by oath; and we know that this was afterward done by all the Carolingian emperors. But the formula they used must be considered. A similar one is found in Pagi (*Annals*, 896, no. 3), from the continuator of the *Annals of Fulda*: “I swear by all these mysteries of God that, saving the honor and law of my own person and the fidelity owed to my lord Pope Formosus, I am and shall remain faithful all the days of my life to Emperor Arnulf.” As for the city of Rome and the Romans, however, no Carolingian held judicial proceedings there, either personally or through his envoys, without the pope’s will and presence. This is revealed by Louis III, successor to Arnulf, in Florence, where he “sat in judgment together with the same supreme pontiff”; and above all by Otto I, king of the Germans, who expressly declares it in his oath: “In the city of Rome I shall make no judgment or arrangement concerning anything that belongs to you or to the Romans without your counsel” (*Distinction* 63, *To You, Lord* 33, chapter “Roman Princes,” on the law of oaths; Clementine title 9; Baronius, 960, no. 5; Muratori, vol. V of the *Annals*, p. 400).]. Nevertheless, we entrust everything to your most discerning judgment.

With these matters stated, may almighty and merciful God, through the intercession of his holy Mother, the ever-virgin Mary Mary our Lady, and of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, inspire your heart with such saving counsel that the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom may present you before God together with that very donation—the offering which your most beloved father, the lord King Pippin, offered to the blessed apostle Peter and which you confirmed—so that you may deserve to receive eternal joys. May heavenly grace guard the most pious imperial rule of our lord, and may bend beneath it the necks of all nations.

EPISTLE IV. ON BENEFITS RECEIVED.

(A.D. 808, codex VI, chronicle 4.)

SUMMARY.—He replies to two letters from Charles concerning the journey of Pippin his son, king of Italy. In the first, delivered to him by Helmengaud and Hunfrid, counts and envoys of the emperor, together with great gifts, Charles stated that Pippin would be at Rome in Mid-Lent. Leo says that, following their advice, he made every arrangement through an apostolic envoy to receive, in a manner befitting his majesty, the king, son of so great an emperor. In the second letter, brought by envoys of that same Pippin on 25 March, Charles reported that the journey had been postponed until after Easter; Leo says that he is always prepared to receive so great a guest. He calls it a calumny that the royal journey was undertaken for the sake of reconciliation: there is no disagreement between himself and the king. By unanimous agreement they are fortifying the seacoasts against pagans—he, namely, those of the ecclesiastical dominion, and Pippin those of the Italian kingdom; each needs Charles’s counsel and assistance. Concerning Corsica, given by Charles to Saint Peter, he says that he discussed with Count Helmengaud what course of action he thought should be taken.

To the most pious and most serene lord, victor and triumpher, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus: Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God. [Note: [Col. 0527B] There is no single opinion concerning the date of this letter. Pagi [Col. 0527C] and Mabillon (*Annals*, book XXVII, no. 88) think it was written in 806; Muratori, in 807; Conring, in 808. Conring moreover, rather unwisely, places it before the following letter, maintaining that both were written in the same month and on the same day. Certainly, if one considers every year of Charles’s reign, one finds that Pippin the king’s envoys arrived before Mid-Lent in every year except 805. For in that year Easter fell on 20 April, and Mid-Lent on 27 March, two days after the envoys’ arrival on the 25th of that month. Leo’s words seem to indicate that they must be assigned to that year: “They told us that he cannot come at Mid-Lent.” The pope would not speak thus if Mid-Lent had already passed. Yet this chronological reasoning conflicts with the history contained in the following letter, written in the same year. What then? Another calculation of time must be adopted, and the beginning of Lent must not be reckoned from Ash Wednesday according to the discipline of our age, but from the Monday after the first Sunday in Lent. [Col. 0527D] On this matter consult Venerable Thomassin, opusculum XXV (vol. VII, p. 187). Against Menard, he shows that the four-day fast before the first Sunday was instituted long before Gregory; nevertheless, he observes that the Lenten fast of thirty-six days began on the Monday after the first Sunday, the four days being added outside Lent to make up the full number of forty days. Thus, in 808, when Easter fell on 16 April, Mid-Lent was 26 March, after the arrival of Pippin’s envoys. They could therefore testify in person that the king would not come at Mid-Lent, as this letter shows that they did. The middle day of Lent was the fourth Sunday, bounded on either side by eighteen days of fasting. This is the name it bears in the Responsorial and Antiphonary of Saint Gregory the Great (Thomassin, vol. IV, p. 225), books with which Francia then abounded, repeatedly sent from Rome, as we have seen in the *Codex Carolinus*. There the fourth Sunday, later called Rose Sunday and Laetare Sunday, [Col. 0528B] is entitled “Sunday in [Col. 0528C] the middle of Lent.” The same is true in the Missal (Thomassin, vol. V, p. 60), where Vezzosi’s notes cite various manuscripts attesting the same view. Nor should the authority of the Astronomer in the *Life of Louis the Pious* (in Pithou, part II, p. 254) be neglected: “While he was staying there at Mid-Lent, with the joy of the day itself smiling upon him and the ecclesiastical chant of the office exhorting him and saying: ‘Rejoice, Jerusalem.’” Therefore Conring’s opinion is preferable to the others. For neither in 806, when Easter fell on 12 April, nor in 807, when it fell on 28 March, did the arrival of Pippin’s envoys precede Mid-Lent.].

By the great mercy of God the joys of the whole world have been multiplied, when we received the most beautiful little gifts of your overflowing munificence and reread the writings of your serenity, which tasted in our heart like honey preserved. For the pious and glorious zeal which your clemency shows toward the holy Church of God and our lowliness caused us at once, as was fitting, joyfully and exultantly to offer thanks to God. [Col. 0528A] For in them we found not only words of joy, but also recognized your most diligent concern for our prosperity. But for such great and boundless benefits and gifts, by which you continually enrich us, we desire that you may receive a worthy recompense from that very keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, whose office, by God’s mercy, we hold, and to whom you constantly render so great honor. [Note: [Col. 0528C] It is clear that other bishops, and even abbots of monasteries themselves, were formerly accustomed to be called vicars of Christ. But Coustant clearly shows in his preface (no. 13) that the title “vicar of Peter” was distinctive of the Roman pontiff, because in him, as Leo the Great says (*Sermon* 2, ch. 2; *Sermon* 3, ch. 4), Peter lives perpetually; see above, epistle 2, otherwise 10, col. 522, note f. It was later decreed that, just as other names formerly general, so also the vicariate of Christ should be assigned to the Roman pontiff alone.]

For we know, and faithfully know, that in all things and in everything pertaining to you, you will bring about our joy; but may the recompense of the Most High, which approves pious deeds and repays kindly acts with its accustomed mercy, itself render worthy rewards for us to your piety. After the presentation of the gifts, your most faithful envoys, Helmengaud and Hunfrid, glorious counts, informed us that our son, the lord King Pippin, [Col. 0528B] desires, through your generosity, to come to the thresholds of the Apostles at Mid-Lent and to hold a conference with us. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Born in 776, he was first called Carloman, as Pagi observes (year 783, no. 4); baptized at Rome at the age of five in 781, he was named Pippin and anointed king of Italy by Hadrian. Thus in this year he was in his thirtieth year of life and the twenty-fifth of his reign. Add that two years earlier Charles had divided the kingdoms among his three sons (in Pithou, part II, p. 81), a division today vigorously defended by Baluze against Pithou’s objections and accepted by all in agreement (Pagi, year 806, no. 6). Nevertheless, while Charles lived, each son administered his kingdom, as it were, by a precarious right. Therefore Pippin does not undertake the Roman journey without his father’s permission, and below it is clear from this very letter that he was obliged to obey his father’s commands concerning the visiting and addressing of the pontiff.]

Accordingly, our heart was raised into great joy, as those most faithful envoys themselves can report to you orally. At once we arranged everything with them concerning the journey of our aforesaid most beloved son, [Col. 0529A] and immediately sent our own envoy, who was to make every preparation [Note: [Col. 0529C] Thus Hadrian, having heard of Charles’s coming journey, says (*Cod. Car.*, ep. 58, otherwise 63): “We wish to set out to go to meet you wherever we may be able to join you.” And shortly before (ep. 56, otherwise 58), when he was about to receive royal envoys, he says: “At once, according as befits envoys of your royal power, we sent every preparation, including horses, to meet them.” Now, when he is to receive the king of Italy, he sends beforehand an apostolic envoy to arrange throughout the territory of the Holy See everything necessary everywhere for the reception of so great a king. The same would occur today on a similar occasion, and it is certain that it occurred in past centuries whenever an emperor or kings undertook a Roman journey. The only difference noted is that this preparation was entrusted to the prefect or governor of the province through which the emperor or kings were to pass. See the *Ceremonial*, section 13, ch. 1 and following.] so that he might come with joy to the thresholds of the Apostles and to our lowliness.

Then, a few days later, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the envoys of our aforesaid son, the lord King Pippin, came to us and offered us your honorable letter. On rereading it, we found concern for the welfare of your prosperity and the most diligent care which your serenity always exercises toward the tranquillity of the holy Church of God; and we found, concerning the arrival of our son, the lord Pippin, that he would not come before the holy day of Easter, namely at a suitable time. Let your clemency believe us: at whatever time he comes to us, we shall receive him with as much joy and gladness [Col. 0529B] as befits the son of so great a defender of the holy Church of God. [Note: [Col. 0529C] We have often observed in the *Codex Carolinus* that no title other than “Defender of the Holy See” is bestowed on the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles. We now hear Charles, adorned with Augustan dignity, called the same by the pontiff. For it belonged to the office both of a king while he was patrician of the Romans and of an emperor to guard, defend, and protect the Church. He possessed no other authority in papal territory except that communicated or delegated, as Pagi holds, by the pontiff himself, the supreme prince. Therefore in these letters of Leo he is plainly called only defender, except in the address and subscription, out of deference to the dignity devised by Leo himself and solemnly bestowed on him by the unprecedented act of coronation through the pope’s own hands in Saint Peter’s basilica.]

For, with the Lord’s help, we know that it will profit both him and us if we meet. Again, after the aforesaid envoys of our son, the lord King Pippin, came to us and told us that he could not come at Mid-Lent, those same envoys of yours, namely Helmengaud and Hunfrid, glorious counts, delivered to us another letter [Col. 0529D] of your serenity. It contained instructions that your most faithful envoys should first go to our son, the lord Pippin, and convey your command to him, so that he might meet us wherever it pleased both of them, [Note: [Col. 0529D] See above, col. 528, note c.] in order that what you earnestly desire may, with God’s help, come wholly to fulfillment: namely, that firm and stable peace and concord may be established between us, with God as mediator.

For we say truly that the Lord has given us a peace-making emperor, of whom the Apostle says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” [Col. 0530A] For almighty God can satisfy your heart, since we have no discord or wrongdoing whatsoever toward him; rather, we love him and desire his advancement as that of a most beloved son. But concerning those who carry tares into your presence or that of our son, the lord King Pippin—things which we do not even hold in our heart—may almighty God, the just judge, before whose sight all hidden things are revealed, himself judge between us and them. [Note: [Col. 0529D] It does not disgrace a holy man to expose calumnies, especially when the matter was manifestly false; therefore he calls God himself as witness and makes him judge of his cause.]

Concerning the churches of God, that they may have their rights, and that our and your coastlands [Note: [Col. 0530C] I should like the words “our and your coastlands” to be carefully noted here. The supreme power of each ruler is indicated. The pontiff’s, namely, since the coastlands of the ecclesiastical dominion are called ours; conversely, the coastlands of the Italian kingdom which belonged to King Pippin are called not Pippin’s but entirely yours, for Pippin held the kingdom, I say, precariously as long as Charles lived. Who does not see the difference between Pippin’s authority and papal authority, and the very great similarity between papal and imperial authority? See *Cod. Carol.*, ep. 63, otherwise 65, and below ep. 8, otherwise 3, where the pope says: “We have always kept our frontier districts and coastlands in order.”] may be made safe and defended from the assaults of pagans [Col. 0530B] and our enemies, we, insofar as the Lord grants strength, are applying ourselves together with that same aforesaid son of ours; but both he and we need your counsel and your assistance.

Concerning the island of Corsica, [Note: [Col. 0530C] No one can state in what particular year Charles gave the island to the Holy See. No one dares deny the fact. Muratori (year 807) threatens that the donation will be seen, as time proceeds, to have remained without effect. From this Conring attacks the bishop of Ostia, who added Corsica to Pippin’s donation. The Fulda annalist records that in the preceding two years (806–807) Pippin the king’s fleet went out against Moors ravaging the island; so likewise Einhard in Pagi (807, no. 5). But that the donation had been made earlier, and that the fleet was sent to protect it, we certainly learn from the recently mentioned charter dividing Charles’s kingdoms, which defines Pippin’s kingdom as extending to the southern sea and Provence. Under Pope Sergius II, who began in 844, we have from the Farnese documents—of which I have spoken more appropriately in the Preface, nos. 22 and following—“Adelvert, warden and protector of the island of Corsica” on behalf of the holy Roman Church. This more than sufficiently proves, against Muratori’s opinion and threats, that the donation was not without effect. I am indeed certain that this donation, reported from the apostolic archive into the *Liber Pontificalis* with its boundaries, should not be assigned to 774, 781, or finally 787, when Charles came to Rome to Pope Hadrian.]

concerning which you sent us word both in writing and through your envoys, we entrust the matter to your judgment and disposition. We have communicated to Count Helmengaud our view that your donation should remain always firm and stable [Col. 0530D] and safe from the snares of enemies; and, through the intercession of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and through your most mighty arm, and by the Lord’s mercy, at a suitable time and as quickly as we can, through our faithful envoy we shall make known more clearly to your imperial power every advantage of the holy Church of God. [Col. 0531A] Therefore may almighty God, who foreknows all future things, grant that you may be exalted by prosperous triumphs and, after a long life, bestow upon you everlasting joys. May heavenly grace guard the most pious imperial rule of our lord, and may bend beneath it the necks of all nations.

EPISTLE V. OF THANKSGIVING.

(A.D. 808, codex V, chronicle 5.)

SUMMARY.—Having received Charles’s letter, he recognizes that Count Helmengaud has faithfully reported what Leo had entrusted to him for Charles. He adds complaints against the envoys who had come to administer justice. He rejoices that Eardwulf, king of the Northumbrians, deposed from his throne, is living safely with Charles. He seeks advice concerning the disputes of Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, and the archbishop of York: whether they should be settled by Charles or by himself, and whether an envoy should be deputed there from either court, with apostolic letters, to summon the archbishop and his associates. In the embolismal week he disapproves of entrusting the ministry to a certain bishop, and reports to Charles the evil conduct of the archbishop of Ravenna.

To the most pious and most serene lord, victor and triumpher, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus: Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God. [Note: [Col. 0531C] The *Annals of Fulda* and other authorities in Pagi (808, no. 10) determine the date of this letter by Eardwulf’s deposition. Accordingly, all assign it to this year. Conring, as I said, rather unwisely places it before the preceding letter. But the pope plainly relates that in the embolismal week Helmengaud and Hunfrid, who were at Rome on 25 March, after being dismissed by him, were staying at Ravenna on Palm Sunday, that is, 9 April; and in the body of the letter he mentions matters that he had privately entrusted to Helmengaud to report to Charles. This sufficiently clearly teaches that it follows the preceding letter, not the reverse.].

To express in words, most merciful son, how greatly I rejoice in your work and in your life is beyond my ability. We therefore render great thanks to almighty God, because, through the heart’s experience, the savor of charity becomes sweet in the mouth. For what is written is fulfilled: “As cold water is to one who is thirsty, so is good news from a distant land.” Having received your serene and wholly consoling letter [Col. 0531C], we immediately, as was fitting, rendered thanks to almighty God, who has made your imperial power the guardian of ecclesiastical peace. For that very faith preserves you which you maintain toward the holy catholic [Col. 0532A] and apostolic Church of God, the supporter and helper in all your petitions, and which you preserve in priestly unity. And when you humbly submit your heart to our insignificance under the yoke of piety, heavenly grace brings it about that, aided by divine assistance, you bring to completion, according to your benevolent desire, everything which you wish to do concerning God from your purest will, and that you extend your strong arm against the enemies of God’s holy Church and against your own enemies.

[Note: Catholic rulers were accustomed to venerate the Roman Church, especially because the Roman Empire had proceeded from it. Thus Honorius wrote to Theodosius (Holstenius, *Roman Collection*, p. 81): “Without doubt the Church of that city must be venerated by us with particular devotion, since from it we also received Roman rule.” Justin “humbled himself, prostrate, and worshiped the most blessed Pope John” (Anastasius, § 88). Justinian, “filled with joy, humbled himself before the holy apostolic see and worshiped the most blessed Pope Agapitus” (ibid., § 96). Justinian the Younger “prostrated himself with the crown upon his head, kissing the feet of Pope Constantine” (ibid., § 173). With still greater right, every act of submission ought to have been shown toward the Roman Church and its pontiff, especially Leo III, who had restored the dignity of the Empire, by Charles. Leo testifies that Charles did so, with abundant return. Concerning the obedience of emperors and princes toward Rome and the pontiff, see Thomassinus at length (p. 11, book III, chs. 60, 62, 65).]

The God in heaven, who searches hearts and reins, knows the affection and firm charity which we bear toward your serenity, and what love and concern we have daily for your very long prosperity.

[Note: These two things—affection and charity—flourished greatly between the priesthood and the kingdom, as is evident from numerous letters in the *Carolingian Code*. These same qualities were likewise desired between the priesthood and the Empire. Therefore the pontiff invokes God as their witness.]

For after God and his saints we have no comforter except your imperial power, protected by God, from whom we always expect defense and consolation.

[Note: Here again is the duty of the patriciate and imperial dignity: the defense of the Church. Nothing occurs more frequently, I insist again, in the *Carolingian Code* of letters; the rest are merely opinions—would that they were not also inventions.]

Having reread your imperial words, we found in them that your count and our faithful servant Helmengaud reported to you, one by one, everything that he had heard from us. But if he, as well as your other envoys who come to these regions, had disclosed to you everything that we suffer daily, we believe that they would weary your ears. For we do not know whether it was your instruction that your envoys who came to administer justice [Note: [Col. 0532C] I do not know whether a clearer distinction among the envoys could be desired. Some were envoys accustomed to discharge an embassy before the pontiff, such as Helmengaudus, and those who came to Rome; others, however, were sent to administer justice, as the pontiff wished. This will become clearer below from the wicked conduct of the archbishop of Ravenna reported to Charles. The office and authority of such envoys must not be estimated too highly; they should be understood from chapter 4 of Lothar’s Constitution under Eugene II (*Roman Collection*, part II, p. 208). That constitution is only sixteen years later than the period of this letter: “We also wish,” it says, “that envoys be appointed by the apostolic lord and by us, who shall report annually to us how each duke and judge administers justice to the people, and how our constitution is observed. We therefore decree that all complaints arising through the negligence of dukes or judges shall first be reported to the apostolic lord, so that either he may immediately have them corrected through his messengers, or notify us, so that they may be corrected by an embassy sent by us.”], brought many men with them and established them in each city, so that they might take everything away by trying cases, as the duke whom we had appointed used to do, and now, according to our accustomed practice, [annue] themselves undertook to give it to us; and they made a great collection from that very people, whereby the dukes themselves are scarcely able to present us with adequate assistance.

[Note: These matters do not differ greatly from Lothar’s Constitution. The duty of the dukes and judges was to administer justice to the peoples; the envoys, however, necessarily had to press those dukes and judges, lest through inactivity they neglect their duty. Whatever they discovered to have been done negligently or wrongly, they were to report to the pontiff—if the cities belonged to the pontifical jurisdiction—not to the emperor, so that he might correct it through his own messengers if possible, or otherwise invoke the emperor’s authority and power. It should also be noted that the envoys began with the office of bishops and descended to the lower ecclesiastical orders; from there they proceeded to the dukes or counts and judges, so that they were to examine diligently not only civil but also ecclesiastical administration. See the capitulary of Louis the Pious, A.D. 828 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, pp. 1579 ff.). Thus these envoys, accused by Leo, had not arrogated to themselves the duties of the dukes, but had brought men with them who usurped those duties to the detriment of the pontifical treasury. Since this seemed to the pontiff both novel and intolerable, for his own right was being invaded, he reports it confidently and passes on to other matters.]

But it seems very burdensome to us if we weary you [Col. 0533A]; for we trust in God’s mercy that in your times the holy Church of God will remain tranquil and peaceful.

As for all the good and prosperous things which you have done, as is your custom, for our envoy whom we sent into the regions of Britain to the English people, out of love for the blessed Apostle Peter, your supporter, we give great thanks for them to your piety, because you always strive for the consolation of God’s holy Church and for the assistance of orthodox faith. But, as you informed us through your honorable letter, that King Eardulf had been expelled from his kingdom, we had already learned this through the Saxons; and for that very wickedness we sent our envoy there. Great joy and [Col. 0533B] gladness rose in our heart because your piety sent your envoys and brought him alive all the way to you. I rejoice greatly in his life, because he has always been faithful to you and used to send his envoys to us. For this reason your imperial defense resounds everywhere in many ways.

[Note: The expulsion of Eardulf and his return to the kingdom of Northumbria through the aid of Leo and Charles are related in the annals in Baronius (no. 33 ff.) and in Pagi (no. 10). Concerning the envoy whom Leo sent there as soon as he learned of the wicked deed, and concerning Charles’s envoys who brought Eardulf safely to Nijmegen, they maintain an unhelpful silence; Conring’s sarcasm rests entirely upon that silence.]

**64** Having reread the letters which Archbishop Eanbald, King Caenulf, and Wado sent to you, we found the deceitfulness which they have among themselves. We are therefore greatly saddened. For this Caenulf, the aforesaid king, has neither his own archbishop nor this same Eanbald, the archbishop, at peace. Daily, indeed, at the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, although unworthy, we pour out prayers concerning their division, asking that almighty God reconcile them, dissolve the discord which they have between them, and, just as your serenity has begun to strive with us for that peace, so may you deign to labor unceasingly so that your abundant reward may increase in heaven.

You sent word to us that, by reason of our apostolic authority, we should send a letter of exhortation to the aforesaid Archbishop Eanbald through a suitable envoy of ours, so that he ought to come with his adherents to this holy apostolic see, or to present his case in your presence.

[Note: Charles claims nothing for himself in the case of the Archbishop of York, who had attacked him in his letters; he subjects everything to pontifical authority and therefore asks for the privilege of hearing the case. It seems that the great and very long-standing controversy between the archbishops of Canterbury and York concerning primacy had flared up again. Malmesbury testifies that it was finally settled in 1072 under Pope Alexander II by subjecting York to Canterbury (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, pp. 1211 ff.). Thomassinus should also be consulted (p. 1, book I, ch. 36). From this it is clear that neither Leo nor Charles was then able to put an end to the dispute.]

We immediately dictated that letter and sent it to you. But if it pleases your serenity to send our letter through your suitable envoy to the envoy whom we likewise sent in those regions, so that, together with our aforesaid envoy, he might exhort that archbishop either to join us here in our presence, or there in yours together with his associates, this would have seemed entirely proper to us; for we have not yet received our envoy, and those men are deceitful, lest, by receiving envoys upon envoys, they should turn the matter to deceit. Nevertheless, we are preparing our envoy until you issue instructions according to your pleasure. If it pleases your imperial power that we send our envoy there, kindly signify this to us through your communication, and we shall immediately send that envoy according to your will.

May almighty and merciful God deign to preserve you under his protection for long ages and grant you possession of eternal joys with all the saints. May the most pious imperial rule of the lord be guarded by heavenly grace, and may he subject to it the necks of all nations.

[Note: The pontiff knew the bishop’s character well. Conring confirms the matter: this Bishop of Amiens, who had served as an ambassador to Constantinople in A.D. 802, later became an author of the conspiracy of the sons against Louis the Pious and consequently suffered the penalty of deposition (Thegan, nos. 36–37). Leo therefore rightly persuades Charles not to entrust embassies to him or admit him to confidential counsels. Ducange offers much concerning the *missaticum* being carried through the provinces, or embassies being discharged throughout the territories, and cites this letter as an example.]

**ADDITION**

For the sake of the great love, affection, and fidelity which we bear toward your serenity, we cannot remain silent about what we are able to recognize. Bishop Jesse, your servant, can render you another service. We do not think him suitable for carrying the *missaticum* through the provinces, nor should he be admitted to confidential counsel. But we ask your clemency to consider this matter mercifully, because we all desire to remain safe in your service. Concerning ecclesiastical cases, from which we fear detriment may come to us, and which we cannot correct in this manner, we inform you [Note: Nothing more clearly confirms the custom, established by Lothar in his constitution, of reporting wrongs to the pontiff, who, if he could not correct them, was to seek the emperor’s assistance. Thus that constitution seems to have restored an ancient custom rather than introduced something new. Conring, as usual hostile to Saint Gregory VII, speaks foolishly: it is clear from the canons that even lay rulers are excluded from ecclesiastical judgments; but who would deny that, by pontifical privilege, ecclesiastical cases may also be conducted through them? As for discipline, Thomassinus teaches that, if they act under the guidance of religion, prudence, and obedience to the canons, no action should be brought against them even without a privilege (p. 2, book II, ch. 34). Here the matter concerns the correction of corrupt conduct by admonition or rebuke.]

so that you may ask your faithful servants Helmengaud and Hunfrid, when they had departed from us and met at Ravenna, and were invited to dinner by the archbishop—that is, on Palm Sunday—what readings and what admonitions they heard recited before that meal, as is fitting during the holy Lenten season, when everyone entreats God concerning his sins so that he may deserve to amend them. But what they heard there is also a shame for us to disclose to you in writing.

**EPISTLE VI. 66 — INTERCESSIONS AND OTHER MATTERS**

*(A.D. 808, codex VIII, chronicle 6.)*

**SUMMARY.**—Charles had been angered because he believed that he had been deceived by Adulfus, the apostolic envoy and deacon, and by another envoy of the Archbishop of York, and thought that both had carried out a fraudulent embassy against King Eardulf (for both had hurried to Rome without greeting him). The pontiff first soothes him; then proves by several letters delivered to him from England that both are falsely accused of wrongdoing, and forwards those letters. He admits that both acted imprudently, ignorant of worldly astuteness; therefore, considering them worthy of pardon, he sends them back to Charles, dispatching Adulfus once more to England so that he may assist that endangered Church.

To the most pious and serene lord, victorious and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Augustus Charles, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

[Note: Although the annals attributed to Einhard relate in this year the deposition of King Eardulf, his journey to Francia, then to Rome, and his restoration to his kingdom through the envoys of Leo and Charles, I believe greater credence should be given to the Fulda annals, which do not report the king’s restoration until A.D. 809. Thus the many events will not be compressed within excessively narrow limits of time. The words of the Westminster chronicler, cited by Pagi (808, no. 10), likewise support this: “After Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians, had been driven from his kingdom, Arfwold succeeded him for two years.” Conring correctly assigns this letter to A.D. 808; for it not only is silent about the king’s restoration but also says nothing of his arrival in the City. It was delivered on the final day of the year.]

For all who claim to be faithful to us, if they have not proved faithful in this way to your imperial power, so that they can recognize the peace and affection which, by God’s mercy, you bear toward God’s holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, your mother, and toward us, have an empty hope and labor without fruit, and their works are useless—except those who, through ignorance, have erred in some respect, as a human being may. Nevertheless, we judge that even these must be corrected.

Your serenity sent word to us that, although Adulfus the deacon, the envoy of our apostolic see, had been kindly and honorably received by you in the customary manner, escorted as far as the seaport, and from there released suitably for his voyage, when he turned back and professed that he first wished to come to you, he did not wish to await your envoy, who would escort him to you. Instead, he set out as though fleeing and, while you waited several days expecting him to come to you, deceived your hope.

[Note: If you remember, Adrian (the *Carolingian Code*, letter 56, elsewhere 58), when the envoys of Charles, then king, arrived, sent men to meet them so that they might be received honorably. They nevertheless deceived him, for they decided to turn their journey elsewhere. Here an envoy of the pontiff has repaid the same treatment to Charles, now emperor. Charles too was prepared to receive the apostolic envoy honorably, and complains to Leo that he had been deceived, just as Adrian had complained to Charles. These matters may seem minor, but the parallel of events between the highest rulers deserves notice.]

And the envoy of Archbishop Eanbald, who himself sent his letters to you, asking that you receive his aforesaid legate kindly and permit him to come to you, did not strive to carry out his master’s command either.
