Therefore, let your serenity believe us, dearest and sweetest son: they did not do this through any wrongful counsel whatsoever, but ignorance of the astuteness of this world produced this foolish encounter.

We, supported by apostolic authority, do not fail to send them to your imperial power according to your will.

[Note: We find here a slight difference in the parallel case: Adrian previously sought through other envoys to remedy the deception of the former ones, whereas Charles asks that these same men be sent back to him. Nevertheless, the outcome is similar: both envoys were kindly received by Charles, and especially the pontifical envoy experienced Charles’s benevolence and assistance, as the following letter will show.]

But we ask your clemency, for the love of the blessed Apostle Peter, your supporter, in whose service we sent the aforesaid deacon Adulfus, indeed also because of what he promised us under oath—that he would strive for the advancement of God’s holy Church and of you and us, and would endeavor to sow peace in that island—that we may send him back again to those regions, and that he suffer no punishment for this, so that he may be able to say with the Prophet: “The righteous man rebukes me in mercy.”

For who will be able to deceive your wisdom, given by God, when you possess heavenly grace, as we unquestionably believe you do? But because we are human and liable to error, we ask your piety not to disdain granting this offense of theirs to the blessed Apostle Peter, so that you may deserve to receive from that keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom the reward of recompense.

As for what your serenity sent us—that they had undertaken a fraudulent embassy which they feared to show you, and that they departed so hastily in order to reach Rome before King Eardulf’s journey—we have sent you, for your satisfaction, all the letters brought to us from those regions for you to read.

[Note: Observe the pontiff’s faith and prudence: the fault to which the envoys appeared liable had to be removed. Therefore he does not send copies of the letters from England that absolved them from wrongdoing, but the letters themselves in their original form, as is clear at the end of the epistle.]

As far as, with God’s help, we have been able to ascertain, we found the aforesaid envoy of Archbishop Eanbald to be in every respect a servant of God. We therefore earnestly ask your imperial power that, since he was sent to your supporter, the blessed Apostle Peter, things may be better for him and not worse, as we fully believe they should be, although he erred through ignorance.

For we greatly fear that the people belonging to the holy Roman Church, through any occasion or conflict, may cause the undertaking of my predecessor, the lord Gregory, most blessed pope, which he established in those regions, to appear fruitless in my time, and that this may befall me at the judgment [Note: When the peoples of Germany—the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes—invaded the great island of Britain around the middle of the fifth century, they began to be called Anglo-Saxons by a composite name, although they did not lose their earlier names. After various reversals, they conquered the Britons and forced them to flee into Cambria or Wales, where whatever religion existed on the island was preserved, and established seven kingdoms, one at a time. The kingdom of the Jutes was Kent, whose capital was Dorovernum or Canterbury. The Saxons had three kingdoms: the East, South, and West Saxons. The Angles likewise had three: the East Angles, the Middle Angles or Mercians, and the Northumbrians. The monk Augustine, sent there by Gregory, found this heptarchy miserably enslaved to idolatry. The kingdom of Kent was the first of all to be converted to the Catholic faith by Augustine, in A.D. 597. East Saxony, now Essex, was converted to the faith in A.D. 604. Northumbria was recalled to the faith by Bishop Paulinus, who made York its metropolitan see, in A.D. 627; and, not to be excessively lengthy, by A.D. 661 all those kingdoms had embraced the faith of Christ. Leo rightly attributes so great an achievement to Saint Gregory the Great, who died in A.D. 604. The work he had successfully begun was later completed with ease by the divine heralds sent there. In addition, the controversy between the archbishops of Canterbury and York concerned Gregory in particular, for he himself had established (Book XII, letter 15) that York, whenever Northumbria came to the faith of Christ, should enjoy equal honor with London, which nevertheless later adhered to Canterbury, as is clear. See also Labbe (*Councils*, vol. VII, p. 1110).]

What more can we say? Just as through their foolishness we have perceived some anger in you, so may we more swiftly experience your mercy through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

With these matters stated, may almighty and merciful God guard you by his protection from every evil; and because your life is greatly necessary for every good thing, may he lead you, after many more years, to the joys of the heavenly homeland. May the most pious imperial rule of the lord be guarded by heavenly grace, and may he subject to it the necks of all nations.

We earnestly ask your clemency to order that the aforesaid letters which were sent to us from the regions of Saxony [Note: From the brief indications given in the preceding note it cannot be inferred that the island of Britain acquired the name Saxony. The kingdom of Kent, whose capital was Canterbury, did not belong to the Saxons. Likewise Northumbria, where York was located, belonged to the Angles, not to the Saxons. In the same way, King Eardulf, being of the Mercians, or Middle Angles, rejects the name Saxony. Conring must therefore be followed, since he observes that the transmarine Saxony was then called the island before the name England had yet been adopted.] be returned to us, because we retain their words as a pledge.

Concluded on the day before the Kalends of January.

**EPISTLE VII. 69 — QUESTIONS TO BE RESOLVED**

*(A.D. 809, codex VII, chronicle 7.)*

**SUMMARY.**—As Leo’s and Charles’s envoys were returning from Britain, having restored Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians, to his kingdom, pirates encountered them, plundered Adolphus, the apostolic envoy, and carried him to Britain, where he was ransomed. Charles reports the matter to the pontiff and at the same time proposes three questions. The pontiff declares himself especially anxious about his envoy and resolves the questions on the authority of Jerome.

[Col. 0538A]

To the most pious and serene lord, victorious and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Augustus Charles, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

[Note: The date of this letter, A.D. 809, is made clear by the restoration of King Eardulf; for the Fulda annals and others cited by Conring unanimously report it. See the note to the preceding epistle.]

With God’s assent, the devout Bishop Sabinus returned to us from the transmarine regions [Note: The Fulda annals say that the king was restored by the envoys of the emperor and of Pope Leo. Likewise the Frankish Annals used by Conring relate the matter more fully: “After Eardulf, king of the Northumbrians, had been restored to his kingdom and the envoys of the emperor and pontiff had returned, one of them, namely Adolphus the deacon, was captured by pirates, while the others crossed without danger; he was carried by them to Britain and ransomed by one of King Caenulf’s men, and returned to Rome.” Similarly, the Frankish Annals under Louis the Pious, attributed to Einhard and cited in Baronius and Pagi (A.D. 808, no. 33; Pagi, no. 10), first say that the matter was conducted by the legates of the Roman pontiff and the lord emperor, and then name only Adolphus and two of the emperor’s men: “with him, sent by the emperor, were two abbots, Rotfridus the notary and Nantharius, abbot of Saint Aldomar.” Therefore Mabillon (Annals, book XXVII, no. 64) does not seem deserving of approval when he attributes this honor to only the two abbots sent by Charles. I think that the Bishop Sabinus mentioned here, who returned from an embassy to the overseas regions, was another legate of the pontiff. For Adolphus had set out at the end of the preceding year, before the pontiff had examined Eardulf’s case and decided that the king should be restored. As far as can be understood, Adolphus awaited Eardulf with Sabinus, the apostolic envoy, at Charles’s court so that they might depart together—unless he had gone there with the two abbots for the same purpose, with the king later arriving with another pontifical legate.], and presented us with a letter from your serenity concerning the embassy entrusted to him and concerning the capture and ransom of Adolphus, our deacon and envoy. We remain in great sorrow about him until almighty God, through your assistance, brings him back to us.

We also found in your honorable letter three questions appended. One concerns what is written in the Gospel according to Matthew, where it is said of our Lord Jesus Christ: “And coming to Nazareth, he dwelt there,” so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazarene.” The second concerns what, at the beginning of the Gospel [Col. 0539A] according to Mark, is set down as prophetic testimony: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel, who shall prepare your way before you.” The third concerns the first epistle of the eminent teacher, the Apostle Paul, where he says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory; but, as it is written, What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him.”

[Note: These three questions are taken from Matthew 2:23; Mark 1:1–2; and 1 Corinthians 2:8–9. They correspond neither to the Vulgate nor to the Old Latin text. The same questions are explained below on the authority of Saint Jerome, although they are irrelevant to our subject, since they concern neither history nor discipline. In the preface, Venantius Thomas (vol. I) testifies that the ancient Latin version according to the Septuagint was then in everyone’s hands.]

For concerning the first question, that is, according to Matthew, blessed Jerome writes that this is found written in Isaiah, but that the evangelist used it more according to the sense than according to the precise wording. In the commentary on that evangelist, blessed Jerome wrote as follows:

> “And coming, he dwelt in the city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He shall be called a Nazarene.’ If he had set down a fixed example from the Scriptures, he would never have said ‘what was spoken through the prophets,’ but simply ‘what was spoken through the prophet.’ By saying ‘through the prophets,’ however, he shows that he took not the words from the Scriptures but the sense. For *Nazaraeus* is interpreted as ‘holy’; and all Scripture declares that the Lord would be holy. We may also say otherwise: that even in these same words, according to the Hebrew truth, it is written in Isaiah: ‘A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall ascend from his root.’”

Concerning the testimony of blessed Mark the evangelist, which he sets forth at the beginning of his Gospel, saying, “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.” And again: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

It must be understood that he wove together, into a single composition, testimonies from two prophets, namely Malachi and Isaiah, naming one and remaining silent about the other. What he says, “Behold, I send my angel,” and so forth, he took from Malachi. What he added, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” and so forth, is Isaiah’s prophecy.

Thus blessed Jerome says in his exposition of Malachi:

> “Mark the evangelist, weaving together two testimonies of Malachi and Isaiah under the speech of a single prophet, began in this way: ‘The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before you, who prepares your way.’ We read this, although in different words, in Malachi. But what follows—‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness,’ and so forth—is spoken by the prophet Isaiah.”

Again, in his commentary on Matthew, the same blessed Jerome says:

> “Since the testimony has been woven together from Isaiah and Malachi, the question arises how we should think that the example was taken from Isaiah alone; concerning this, ecclesiastical men have given a full answer.”

As for the testimony of the blessed Apostle Paul, which he offered in the Epistle to the Corinthians, saying, “What eye has not seen nor ear heard,” and so forth, it is written in the prophet Isaiah in different words but with the same meaning. For it is written there:

> “From of old they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears; eye has not seen, O God, except you, what you have prepared for those who await you.”

Let your most prudent imperial power seek it in the one-hundred-seventieth chapter, and it will find it there.

[Note: Isaiah’s prophecy was formerly divided into 181 chapters, as the cited Thomasius presents it. He likewise uses this letter of Leo to support his edition: “This corresponds sufficiently,” he says, “to our present chapters, if one number is added—for it could easily have been omitted through the copyist’s inadvertence—and 171 is read in place of 170.” In the Vulgate it is chapter 64, verse 4, the final verse of the ancient division into 171 chapters; that division begins at verse 15 of chapter 63.]

Although blessed Ambrose, in his exposition of the same Epistle, affirms that this passage, in accordance with the Apostle’s text, is written in the apocryphal *Apocalypse of Elijah*.

With these matters stated, may almighty and merciful God guard you by his protection and grant you everlasting life through the course of many years. May the most pious imperial rule of the lord be guarded by heavenly grace, and may he subject to it the necks of all nations.

**EPISTLE VIII. 72 — CONCERNING THE SLAUGHTER OF THE GREEKS BY THE MOORS**

*(A.D. 812, codex III, chronicle 8.)*

[Col. 0540C]

**SUMMARY.**—When the Moors threatened to invade Sicily, the Emperor Michael sent a fleet with a patrician and officers bearing the sword. The patrician was unable to obtain assistance from Anthimus, duke of Naples; such assistance was not denied by the Amalfitans and Gaetans. The Moors plundered the islands of Lampadusa, Pontia, and Ischia. Everything was safe within the territory of the holy see: scarcely had the movements of the Moors been reported by Charles when the frontiers and maritime shores began to be guarded by soldiers, and continual prayers were offered to God at the confession of the Church for its protection and for the granting of long life to Charles.

To the most pious and serene lord, victorious and triumphant, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Augustus Charles, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of [Col. 0540D] God.

[Note: As for the date of this letter, Muratori assigns it, together with the following two, to A.D. 813. This is ruled out chiefly by two considerations. First, Michael ceased to rule in the following year after being betrayed by Leo the Armenian and became a monk; consequently, the dispatch by Michael of Gregory the patrician with a fleet to Sicily does not accord with his subsequent deposition from the throne of Constantinople. Second, the statement that everything was safe on the part of the Church conflicts with the calamities inflicted by the Saracens in the following year; this led Conring to an uncertain conclusion, namely, that the letter was delivered either in this year or the next. But since it was delivered in September and the following letter is separated from it by only a two-month interval, the reversal of circumstances—entirely silent in this letter but fully narrated in the next—removes all doubt that the two letters were delivered in different years. See the following column, note c.]

[Col. 0541A] We know, therefore, that your imperial power, protected by God, has always been most diligently concerned with the integrity, exaltation, and preservation of its mother, the holy Church, and of her territories. For this reason we make known to your Serenity what we have recently heard and of which we are partly certain.

[Note: [Col. 0541B] The pontiff’s prudence is noteworthy: he does not claim that everything he writes is certain, but reports what he has heard as doubtful and distinguishes it from what he knows with certainty. He entrusts to the reliability of informants, as doubtful, the Saracens’ landing on the islands of the Greeks; the devastation inflicted by them on Lampadusa; the seven Greek ships sent to reconnoiter and plundered by the Saracens, whose crews were killed to the last man; and, conversely, the later complete destruction of the Moors by the Greeks. By contrast, he narrates as certain that the Saracens had decided to attack Sicily that year; the arrival of the Greek fleet; the aid denied by Anthimus and that supplied by the Gaetans and Amalfitans; and the invasions of the islands of Pontia and Ischia.]

For it is not unknown to your wisdom, given by God, that that most wicked people of the Hagarenes had resolved to come into the regions of Sicily in the present year. Now, as we have heard, they have joined together at certain Greek islands. For this reason the emperor Michael sent a patrician [Note: [Col. 0541C] In the Neapolitan Chronicle published by Pratillo (vol. III, p. 35), the name Michael is attributed to the patrician. Whether this happened through the carelessness of the writer, or whether the patrician was called by the same name as the emperor, is uncertain; for the letter gives him no name. Muratori too confidently gave him the name Gregory, but the learned man was misled by the expression “patrician of Sicily.” This would not have happened to him had he assigned this letter to the following year; for since two letters were sent in the same year, which follow shortly, and Gregory the patrician is mentioned in both, he supposed that there could be no other commander of the fleet. Thus the patrician who, as we would say today, resided in the island of Sicily in the king’s place, in charge of the remnants of the Greek Empire, is transformed into a naval prefect. Pagi likewise thinks that all these letters were written in 813, and uses them to continue the history of the Saracens; yet he dared assign no name to the patrician who was naval prefect, since he found him anonymous in Leo.]

and spatharii with a fleet, so that, with Christ’s assistance, they might fight against them. When the patrician had joined the forces in Sicily, he sent his envoys through Beneventum to Anthimus [Note: [Col. 0541D] Nothing could better illuminate this letter than the testimony of the aforesaid Neapolitan Chronicle, edited by Pratillo:

“Anthimus, who refused to obey the commands of the lord emperor, that he should go with his army against the Saracens; therefore they reached as far as Naples, devastating villages and places without any obstacle or hindrance. Anthimus, commander of the imperial army, was accused by the patrician Michael before the lord emperor of having an understanding with the Saracens, since he had been able to defend those places but left them undefended. Then a report spread that the army of the lord emperor was coming to Naples and would not turn back until it had first destroyed the houses and all the goods of Duke Anthimus. For this reason Duke Anthimus wished to flee to Rome, but could not, and out of fear died a few days later. In the year 813 Theoctistus succeeded him in the duchy.”

Indeed, if Anthimus died of grief in the year 813, all the events that caused his grief cannot possibly be assigned to that year. Moreover, if Michael at the beginning of his reign, according to Einhard as cited by Baronius and Pagius (Baronius, 812, no. 12; Pagius, same year, no. 7), confirmed peace at Aachen with Charles and at Rome with Leo through his envoys, then the events narrated in this letter must also be referred here. For Charles, scarcely having dismissed the envoys, deliberated at a council likewise convened at Aachen about preserving Italy, “because of the report that a fleet was said to be coming from Africa and Spain to devastate Italy” (Pagius, same year, no. 9).

The envoys sent by the emperor should also be noted: “Michael the bishop, Arsaphios, and Theognostus the protospatharius.” Could there not therefore have been another Michael the patrician, who led the fleet to Sicily with the spatharii and had come from Constantinople?]

the duke of Naples, [Col. 0541B] so that he might endeavor, with the whole Neapolitan duchy willing to obey him, to provide him naval assistance. But the duke, putting forward excuses, refused to go to his aid. Nevertheless, the Gaetans and Amalfitans, gathering some ships, went to his assistance. Afterwards, as we have heard, those most wicked Moors themselves entered the island called Lampadusa, situated in the regions of Sicily, with thirteen ships, and plundered it.

When seven ships from the aforementioned Greek fleet likewise went out to reconnoiter, so that they might learn the truth, the Moors, hateful to God, captured and killed them. When the Greeks who had sent them to reconnoiter waited for them, and they did not return, they went out against the Moors in full force and, through Christ’s mercy, killed all those wicked Moors, leaving not one of them alive.

Moreover, this too was reported to us: forty ships belonging to those Moors came to the island called Pontia, where monks lived, and plundered it. Afterwards, leaving it, they entered another island called greater Ischia [Note: [Col. 0542C] No authors say that the name Ischia was added to the island of Aenaria, formerly called Inarime and Pithecusa, before the beginning of the ninth century. Yet this letter speaks of no other island, although it says that it was thirty miles from Naples, when it is only six miles distant. I do not understand why it is called “greater,” unless perhaps consideration is being given to Ischia, which others call Pandataria, near Pontia (Pliny, book III, chapter 7), and which at that time also bore the name Ischia.

As for the thirty miles, I see that Conring, in his first edition of 1647, wrote “miles,” but in the revised edition of 1655, after carefully inspecting the manuscripts again, corrected this to “military,” as though the number of Moors arriving there were being indicated. And surely Leo would have said that it was not far from the city of Naples if it lay thirty thousand paces away. One might believe that the livestock and households of the Neapolitans were there, unless it were almost adjacent.

I think, in fact, that a passage of the Neapolitan Chronicle (in Pratillo, vol. III, p. 61), from the beginning of the following century, ought to be referred here. It says that “the warlike men from Isola, afflicting Neapolitan territory, were subdued at sea, and many were brought to Naples.” I therefore believe that the ancient chronicler wrote Ischia, not Isola, and that through the error of Ubaldo the copyist, or of someone else, Isola was written incorrectly. This can certainly be seen in Pagius’s Critique on Baronius (Lucca edition, year 813, no. 21). For this very letter of Leo has Isola where it should have Ischia.

As for the recent name Ischia, which they say the island received from its town, shaped like a thigh—for the Greek word for thigh is ἰσχίον, ischion—let me freely state what I think: from this letter I understand both islands to have been called Ischia, the lesser and the greater. From whom, however, the letter i was changed into l, I leave others to determine.]

not far from the Neapolitan city, thirty [military] miles away; there they found a considerable number of Neapolitan households and livestock. They remained there from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September to the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, and the Neapolitans never went out against them.

When they had plundered the entire island, filling their ships with people and with its necessities, they departed, carrying them away. The Gaetans, however, who were there after the devastation of the aforesaid island, said that they found men slain, *lacere* [probably “lying”] [Note: [Col. 0543C] In both editions of Conring and in Labbe, the reading is *lacere*; but Pagius and Du Cange (under the word *Scirpha*) correctly read *jacere*, “lying.” This sufficiently confirms that *j* before a vowel, which in medieval manuscripts is sometimes extended upward, was here, as also in *Iscja*, used for *l*. These facts frustrate the interpretations of scholars who seek to derive Ischia from a Greek name, as well as the carelessness of medieval writers who either pass over a matter that should not be neglected in silence or openly confess their ignorance.]

there, together with grain and rushes (*scirpha*), which the Moors themselves could not carry away with them. They also left there dead Moorish horses, which they had brought in their ships.

Behold, whatever we have been able to hear concerning the regions of the Greeks, we have taken care to report to your Serenity. Concerning our own territories, however, we inform your most tranquil imperial power that, through the intercession of holy Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and through your most prudent governance, everything remains safe and unharmed.

From the time when your Serenity encouraged us concerning their arrival, we have always had our rear and coastal regions [Note: [Col. 0543C] The territories of the papal domain mentioned shortly before are clearly designated here by the two expressions “rear” and “coastal.” By the latter there can be no doubt that he means the maritime coast extending from Populonia to Terracina. By “rear,” everyone can see that Leo means the territory adjoining the duchy of Naples, and even that of Benevento, as far as the river Liris, or Garigliano. For in the following year the coastal region, and in subsequent years the aforesaid inland territories, were exposed to Saracen invasions or plundering.]

properly organized and guarded. We, together with our priests, have prayed in the church of your patron, blessed Peter, and Paul [the apostle], to the mercy of Almighty God, asking that he deign to guard and defend his holy Church from the snares of her enemies [Note: [Col. 0543D] Both matters are proved by countless examples from the Old Testament: prayers poured out to God and military preparations. God’s omnipotence must not be put to the test; prayer and supplication are necessary, but action must be joined to them. Thus the holy Leo III provided his successors with an example to follow. We have seen Adrian behave in the same way in the *Codex Carolinus*.]

and that it may please him to preserve and protect you for the exaltation and defense of that Church through long courses of years, and lead you with all the saints to eternal joys through many ages. May heavenly grace guard the most pious rule of the Lord, and may it subject to him the necks of all nations. Completed on the seventh day before the Ides of September.

## LETTER IX. HOW THE SICILIANS MADE A PACT WITH THE SARACENS AND THE CAPTIVES WERE RETURNED

(Year of the Lord 813, codex II, chronicle 9.)

**ARGUMENT.**—Letters from Gregory, the patrician of Sicily, to Charles Augustus, without an address, are delivered to Leo: they were evidently to be returned, read, and sent to Francia with a seal affixed—either the originals or a copy—for they were replies to Charles’s letters, and the papal envoy had carried both sets back and forth. The pontiff sends the letters intact to Charles and, thinking that they were left without an address because the emperor Leo had not been consulted, asks that they be returned to him after they have been read. The same envoy reported that the patrician had concluded a ten-year truce with the Saracens, with captives returned on both sides; and that Michael Augustus had become a monk. Many other events had also occurred, which he recounts individually.

To the most pious and serene lord, victor and triumpher, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0543D] The chronological indications of this letter are so clear that it should not seem at all surprising if everyone agrees that it must be assigned to the year 813. The month of June, already elapsed, indicates the year 813, before September; here, however, the seventh indiction begins, since the letter was given on the eleventh day of November. Moreover, the eighth indiction is mentioned as future, since the seventh extended to September of the following year.]

Accordingly, on the third day before the Ides of November, we received a letter from Gregory, the patrician of Sicily—namely, a reply to your Serenity’s letter, which we had sent to him through one of our men. For some reason unknown to us, he did not send you a letter addressed in your name [Note: [Col. 0544C] In the year 811, after the emperor Nicephorus of the East had been killed by the Bulgars, Michael Curopalates was elevated on October 2 and crowned by the patriarch Nicephorus on October 5. After receiving the envoys sent by Charles to Nicephorus to establish peace, he added his own embassy, and peace was confirmed at Aachen in the following year, according to Einhard in the Annals as cited by Pagius (812, no. 7 and following). Yet it was a Greek peace, since Charles is called *basileus* by the envoys—a title that the Greeks not only denied Charles but always resented and rejected when applied to him.

Later writers have debated this matter through conjecture, without any ancient monument to support their arguments. They begin with the envoys of Nicephorus in 803 (Pagius, same year, no. 3) and do not hesitate to present the beginnings of peace negotiations as a peace already concluded with the clause “as you possess” (Muratori, year 803). Splendid dreams! At that time discussion of peace began. In 810, however, as may be seen in the same Pagius (no. 4), some say that after Pippin had subdued the Venetians, a certain peace was concluded with Charles, who returned Venetia to Nicephorus; others deny it.

Only in 812, with Charles retaining Istria, Liburnia, and Dalmatia except for the coastal cities, did Charles, as we have said, establish some kind of peace with Nicephorus; this is the nearly unanimous opinion of the ancients. The title of emperor or *basileus*, granted to Charles by the generosity of the envoys and regarded as full of offense, was rejected by the Greeks. For this reason the patrician of Sicily sent Charles a letter without an address through the pontiff.

See Pagius (year 824, no. 10), who shows that the Greeks then greeted both emperor and king by the name *basileus*. Thus, if any Greeks applied that title to the Franks, they meant only “kings”; nowhere are the Franks called *basileis* of the Romans.]

Nevertheless, he sent us the letter he directed to us, asking that we send you a copy of it—or, after we had read it, the letter itself, bearing our seal, to your imperial power [Col. 0544C]. 77 For your satisfaction, we neither opened it to read it nor learned what it contained [Note: [Col. 0545B] I praised above the pontiff’s complete fidelity in matters of this sort (letter 6, or 8, note). Here is another, even clearer example of the same subject. He does not wish to know at all what Charles wrote or what Gregory replied, so as not to fail in his obedience or duty toward Charles.

Yet I would point out that if the patrician of Sicily asked Leo to read the letter and send either a copy or the signed original to Francia, it contained nothing that needed to be concealed from the pontiff—especially since Sicily at that time was frequently harassed by the Saracens. Whether the matter concerned entering an alliance with the Romans to repel the Saracens, or exchanging the island for the provinces of Dalmatia, Liburnia, or others, remains entirely obscure. Only this is certain: Sicily remained subject to the emperor of the East until the year 827 (Baronius, year 827, no. 24; Pagius, same year, no. 4). I shall discuss this more suitably when treating the diploma of Louis the Pious.]

except for what our envoy conveyed to us verbally through him. It concerned those Saracen envoys with whom the patrician himself confirmed a pact for ten years. For he said to the aforesaid Saracen envoys:

“What sort of pact do you wish to make with us, when it has already been eighty-five years since you made a pact with us and it was not kept? Indeed, Constantine the patrician, who governed before me, made a firm pact with you for ten years, until the coming eighth indiction [Note: [Col. 0545C] In the year 804, then, Constantine the patrician, Gregory’s predecessor, struck a treaty with the Saracens for ten years. Note also that patricians governed Sicily for a long time, so that you may understand more clearly how far Muratori departs from the truth when he takes the patrician to be commander of the fleet rather than governor of Sicily, as I pointed out above (letter 8, or 3, note).]. But you did not keep that pact firm either. Now we do not know what sort of pact we should make with you.”

The Saracen envoys replied:

“The father of this Amir al-Mu’min [Note: [Col. 0545C] Pagius observes (year 813, no. 24) that *amir*, or *emir*, means a prefect or ruler, while *al-Mu’min* added to it denotes the prince of the faithful, or caliph, whose royal seat is Baghdad. On the authority of Elmacin he likewise notes that Leo is speaking of the death of Harun, followed in this same year, on September 25, by the killing of his brother al-Amin and the accession of another brother, al-Ma’mun, whom they count as the twenty-eighth of the caliphs. I easily understand that al-Mu’min and al-Ma’mun are one and the same person; but I do not understand how the same name can be taken for the prince, or caliph. For our present purpose, although this letter contains some falsehood, the caliph’s death, according to the notes of the same Pagius, is certain. Calvisius likewise records, from another author, the death that year of “Imin Amira” and the succession of “Maimon.” This slight discrepancy in names does not alter the matter.]

who now appears to reign among us has died; this one was left a child; the one who had been a slave became free, and the one who had been free became lord. They thought they had no king. But now, after he has subjected to himself everything that his father possessed, he wishes to preserve with firm stability the pact that we are arranging.

We do not make a guarantee to you concerning the Spaniards [Col. 0546A] [Note: [Col. 0545D] The Saracens were one and the same people. But after they invaded Africa and occupied Spain at the beginning of the eighth century, settling there and obeying their own king, while the provinces of that extensive kingdom were administered by his prefects, fourteen kingdoms later arose. Then they began to be regarded as rebellious by the Saracens subject to the caliph of Baghdad. The name “Moors” was also applied to them, so that the designation “Saracens of Spain” distinguishes them from the other Saracens. This letter is an especially authoritative witness to both facts.]

because they are not under the authority of our kingdom. But insofar as we are able to overcome them, we permit both you and us to fight them at sea. And if we are not able to do so alone, we, from our side, and you, from yours, shall drive them from the territories of the Christians.”

After this they reached an agreement and confirmed in writing a pact between them for ten years. He gave them an envoy named Theopistus, a notary, and returned to them however many of those Saracens he had captured, so that they might return the Christians whom they had plundered from their own territories [Note: [Col. 0546B] No historian records this solemn treaty, confirmed by the mutual restoration of captives; therefore this unique information must be credited to Leo the pontiff alone. Certainly history does not show that the Saracens of Africa troubled the Sicilians until the year 827. At that time, through the treachery of Euphemius the Sicilian, Sicily came under Saracen power, as both Baronius and Pagius demonstrate on the authority of the Greeks (Baronius, 827, no. 23; Pagius, same year, no. 4).

Leo of Ostia’s opinion that the Saracens arrived in Sicily in 820 is rightly refuted by Baronius. Nothing is more certain than the Sicilian invasion in 827, after the publication of the Sicilian-Arabic chronicle among the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* (vol. I, part II, p. 245). Therefore anyone who said that Sicily was held by the Greeks until the aforementioned year 827 and thereafter remained for more than two centuries in Saracen power, or that it was held either by Charlemagne or by one of his Carolingian successors, would be disguising the truth. Nevertheless, Sicily is listed in the diploma of Louis the Pious; why this was done I shall show in the dissertation on that diploma, which will follow these letters.]

After the aforesaid pact had been confirmed between them and the envoy sent by the patrician had been released, a man in chains was found hurrying with great speed to announce to the patrician that seven ships of the Moors had plundered a village at Reggio, and that two of their ships had afterward come ashore empty. For our envoy also reported this to us: he had heard from the Saracen envoys that in the past June, during the sixth indiction, they had intended to sail with another hundred ships to ravage Sardinia [Note: [Col. 0546C] This account of the African Saracens, before the ten-year truce was concluded, seems scarcely credible. Leo himself, using several witnesses, shows that he is committing a very doubtful matter to writing. The case is different with the Moors who often harassed Sardinia and Corsica through plunder and slaughter.

The Annals of Fulda and the monk of Angoulême, together with Einhard, report that Charles and his son King Pippin protected those islands with a fleet, as was stated above (letter 4, or 6, note). Since neither island belonged to the kingdom of Italy, while Corsica, on the other hand, had been given to the Holy See, as was demonstrated in that place, Sardinia too might appear to have enjoyed the same status. But no document is available to establish the matter.

Only two indications here are nearly certain: namely, that the island belonged neither to the Greeks nor to the Franks. For if Greek dominion had extended there at that time, the Franks would not have sent a fleet there to repel the Saracens; and if the island had belonged to the Franks, Charles would not have terminated the kingdom of Italy at the Tyrrhenian Sea: “together with the duchy of Tuscany, as far as the Southern Sea and as far as Provence” (in Pithoeus, part II, p. 84).

I see no other reason why Charles would have sent a fleet to defend the island than the same reason that moved him to defend Corsica: “namely, so that its grant might always remain firm and stable” (letter 4, or 6). You will say that Sardinia is not mentioned, except in this incidental report in which a prodigy is announced by the pontiff. I reply that Leo does not even mention Corsica except in passing. Yet who does not see that during eighteen years many letters were sent back and forth between Leo and Charles, all of which have perished? Indeed, we would not boast that even these ten letters had reached us if Conring, while others perhaps neglected them, had not judged them worthy of publication with their notes—which Labbe rightly defined as “defiled with the foulest accusations and slanders against the Catholic Church and its supreme pontiffs” (*Councils*, vol. VII, p. 1113).]

to make a circuit, and when they had come near Sardinia, suddenly an abyss of the sea opened and swallowed those hundred ships. Afterwards the Saracens who reported this returned to Africa in great fear and informed the families of those who had been drowned.

When our envoy had heard such things, he asked the notary who was guarding him whether the report he had heard from those Saracens was true. The notary said that it was so, and that he himself had read aloud the letter sent to the patrician by a Christian friend of his from Africa [Note: [Col. 0547C] The absence of any mention of this prodigy near Sardinia in Anastasius is the reason I commend this great event to the credibility of the informants. For a similar event, after the Saracens devastated the basilica of Saint Peter in 846, is not omitted by Anastasius (sections 495–497). It is entirely plausible that the sacrilegious men were swallowed up at sea with their booty.

John the Deacon agrees, recounting events after the plundering of the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul (in Pratillo, vol. III, p. 46): “But while they were plowing the vastness of the sea,” he says, “the Lord raised a south wind, by which they were scattered and drowned, and very few of them returned to their own homes.” An unknown writer of Cassino, followed by Leo of Ostia, also relates this matter (same work, vol. I, no. 9, p. 205).

I observe, however, that the event was reported to the patrician of Sicily by a captive friend, so that he might bring back some news from that transmarine region; whereas the pontiff reported the prodigy to Charles with the circumstances of the event, time, and persons, so as to add greater credibility to the account. Does this not suggest that it was of considerable interest to the pontiff, through that prodigy, to show that Sardinia had escaped the devastation threatened by the Saracens?

Moreover, the monk of Angoulême recounts two Saracen expeditions to Sardinia. Of the first, which must be assigned to the preceding year, he says: “That fleet which was sent to Sardinia was entirely destroyed.” Of the second, which he connects with Michael’s becoming a monk and therefore assigns to this year, he says that it was defeated in battle by the Christians of Sardinia. Thus the prodigy seems more suitable to the first expedition than to the second. But since Leo connects it with the month of June of this year, he plainly speaks of the second.]

And this happened in the month of June, when many saw in the sky that fiery sign resembling a lamp [Note: [Col. 0548C] Baronius (year 811, no. 48), on the authority of Einhard, reports that during the last three years of Charles’s life prodigies and portents appeared in heaven and on earth that foretold his death: frequent eclipses of the moon and sun, repeated trembling of the palace at Aachen where he lived, lightning, the collapse of the royal palace, fires, and many other things. Calvisius records the eclipses; historians, especially, record the other signs, including the fires. Therefore this new celestial sign mentioned by the pontiff is not inconsistent with credibility, although its conjunction with the swallowing up by the sea may seem incredible.]

The Saracen envoys themselves came in Venetian ships, and while coming they burned with fire the ships that were arriving from Spain. Behold, what we heard through our envoy we have taken care to report to your Serenity. We ask, however, that after you have reread the letter of Gregory the patrician, you do not disdain to send it back to us.

As for why the patrician did not send the letter to you himself, and why he did not write your name on the letter he sent us, your wisdom, given by God, will immediately understand, once it has read the letter, why he did not send it to you as was proper. Nevertheless, if it is not counted presumptuous in us that, out of love, we disclose to your Serenity what we think about this matter, it seems to us that he has not yet dared to send you his letter without the advice of Leo, his emperor [Note: [Col. 0548C] The certain reason why the patrician did not address the letter to the emperor Charles is the peace concluded in the preceding year with the Greek Augustus through the envoys. For the title “emperor of the Romans” was offensive at Constantinople and was never granted to Charles and his successors. New events in the East had also intervened: Michael, after abdicating the imperial power and witnessing the reversal of affairs and peoples after his defeat by the Bulgars, had become a monk, as is stated at the end of the letter. The impious Augustus Leo the Armenian had succeeded him; he revived the persecution of the sacred images and the exile and slaughter of bishops and monks. Therefore the prefects of this impious Caesar, especially the patrician of Sicily, who defended the remnants of the Eastern Empire in the West, would not have dared to do something they knew had displeased Michael, an excellent prince.]

With these matters stated beforehand, may God almighty and merciful guard you by his protection and lead you, through many years, to eternal joy. May heavenly grace guard the most pious rule of the Lord, and may it subject to him the necks of all nations. Completed on the third day before the Ides of November.

Gregory the patrician told our envoy that the emperor Michael had become a monk together with his wife and sons.

## LETTER X. CONCERNING AN EVIL COUNSEL THAT WAS TAKEN

(Year of the Lord 813, codex IV, chronicle 10.)

[Col. 0548B] **ARGUMENT.**—After receiving a new and doubtful report from Greek men concerning Michael’s defeat by the Bulgars and his retirement to a monastery together with his family, as well as concerning the acclamation and coronation of Leo the Armenian, Leo writes this new letter. Its principal matter is certain; but since the pontiff readily lent his ears to the tales of the Greeks, he reports some contradictory and fabulous things as though they were certain.

To the most pious and serene lord, victor and triumpher, son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0548D] Leo himself states at the end that this letter was given fifteen days after the preceding one, namely on November 25, saying that it was completed on the seventh day before the Kalends of December. It would therefore be pointless to investigate more carefully the date of a letter that adds nothing new and is for the most part useless.]

After we had sent your Serenity the letter of Gregory the patrician of Sicily [Col. 0549A] together with ours, one of our ships joined us, carrying several Greek men. One of them told us that, while Leo—who has now become emperor—was away fighting against the Bulgarians, Procopia, the wife of the emperor Michael, had a certain friend named Constantine, a patrician, and had urged him [her] 81 to unite himself with her in marriage. She promised him a great hidden treasure, which she said she possessed, concealed by her father, and by means of which they were to distribute money to the people, so that they might choose him as emperor for her.

Then, seduced [or: led astray] by her words, he obeyed her wicked counsel and won over many men by giving lavish gifts. After this they admitted him into the imperial palace, singing his praises [Col. 0549B]. Constantine himself then had the patriarch Nicephorus summoned to him and said that he wished to crown [or: be crowned] according to the custom of emperors.

[Note: [Col. 0549C] Although the opinion is that the coronation of emperors by the hand of a bishop originated with Marcian, Tillemont observes (Leo I, art. 1) that it is no older than Leo I, who was crowned in 457 by the patriarch Anatolius. There is no reason to deny credence to so eminent a man, who traces imperial history with unsurpassed diligence. From the year 457, therefore, the emperors of the East began to be crowned by the patriarchs of Constantinople. Yet this coronation has nothing in common with the coronation instituted by Leo III except the name. For, according to the same Tillemont, Greek authors report that Anastasius was crowned by Ariadne in 491 (In [Col. 0549D] Anastasius Dicorus, art. 2), although Theophanes and Cedrenus relate that it was done by the patriarch Euphemius. Baronius (year 491, no. 7), drawing on Theodore the Lector and Suidas, shows that Euphemius rejected the coronation of a heretical man, or at least of one whose faith was suspect, unless he first made a profession of the Catholic faith; but he says nothing about coronation by the hand of the patriarch. Nevertheless, since it is clear that someone had been crowned by a patriarch long before Leo I, and since in 525 Justin wished to be crowned a second time by Pope John I as an act of devotion, although he had been inaugurated by the patriarch seven years earlier, as Baronius records (year 525, no. 7), there can be no doubt that this rite had already been introduced. Accordingly, Leo III devised nothing new concerning the crown itself when he crowned Charlemagne; what he devised was the rite, which he wished to belong not merely to the Roman pontiff privately but to be entirely new, both in the requirement of making a profession of faith [Col. 0550C] and in the other circumstances of the new rite. See Dissertation, nos. 50 ff.]

That patriarch, however, refusing to crown him with his own hands, was killed. He blinded the wife of the emperor Leo and killed her young son. When the emperor Leo, who was then at the Bulgarian frontier preparing for battle, heard this, he began to rebuke the patricians and nobles who were with him in sorrowful words, saying:

“Good and most Christian men, why did you wish to commit such an injustice against me, in choosing me as your emperor? And behold, now they have killed both my wife and my son and have set up another emperor for themselves.”

Then, filled with great astonishment, they said to him:

“Most gracious lord, let us not make any disturbance beforehand, until we are able to enter the city.”

After taking counsel, he removed his imperial clothing and put on military dress. Taking with him five thousand armed men chosen for battle, he returned to the wall of the city [Col. 0550A] of Constantinople. With them he began outside the walls, in loud voices, to praise Constantine and say:

“Long live Constantine the Great, the emperor!” 82

When it was announced that many soldiers had deserted Leo and had come over to him, praising him, he ordered the city gates to be opened for them, so that he might give them a gratuity. But when they entered, they spared neither men nor women, nor even the children whom they were able to find. Sixteen thousand men and women, it is said, were killed.

Then the emperor Leo himself took pity on his people and asked to engage Constantine in battle, so that the blood of so many Christians might not be shed for the sake of two men. After this request, the two entered the place called the Hippodrome, and Constantine was killed by the emperor Leo [Col. 0550B]. At the same hour he killed the patrician Theodore and all who had taken part in that plot. He killed Procopia, the wife of the emperor Michael, and, cutting off her limbs, distributed them along the city wall.

When he had thus completed his vengeance and properly reorganized the city, he returned to his army at the Bulgarian frontier.

[Note: [Col. 0550C] This entire account is fictitious; nevertheless, the pontiff not only believed it but announced it to Charles as something to be believed. The true history must be sought in the Greek authors cited by Baronius (year 813, nos. 1 ff.) and by Pagius, who, after presenting the accounts of Constantine Porphyrogenitus and others, refutes the whole falsity of this letter (same place, nos. 4 ff.). The essential point is this: Leo the Armenian was asked by the patriarch Nicephorus to profess the creed before receiving the imperial crown. He refused to do so at that time, although he promised that he would after the acclamation had been confirmed and made secure. Accordingly, after being crowned by Nicephorus on the following day, 11 July, he broke the promise he had given and subjected the Eastern Empire to immense evils.]

Later one of Gregory the patrician’s men joined us and told us that they had neither killed the patriarch nor blinded the wife of the emperor Leo, and that his son had not been killed either, except that Procopia, the wife of the emperor Michael, had ordered one of her young daughters to be killed.

Having heard these things from Greek men, we have taken care to report them to your Serenity.

[Note: [Col. 0550D] None of this, either, is supported by any Greek author; it must therefore be rejected even among popular rumors. The letter, conveyed to Aachen, where Charles was wintering, reached the hands of that great prince shortly before his final illness. For, falling ill in January and dying on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, according to Einhard in his Life, or on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of that month, according to the monk of Angoulême, he died. Baronius (year 814, nos. 57 ff.), Pagius (same year, nos. 22 ff.), and Georgius in his notes on Pagius treat this matter sufficiently and more than sufficiently. Consult them.]

With these matters stated, may the almighty and merciful God guard you by his protection and, after the passage of many years, lead you to eternal joys. May heavenly grace guard the most pious rule of the lord and subject to him the necks of all nations. Completed on the seventh day before the Kalends of December.

[PRIVILEGE OF LOUIS THE PIOUS]

[Col. 0551]

## Dissertation on the Diploma of Louis the Pious

[Col. 0551A] I. Among ancient monuments, none has been brought to light more frequently than the Ludovician diploma. Baronius published it from the best Vatican manuscripts, and in our own age the most distinguished Antonellus, when he was prefect of the archive of the Mole of Hadrian, published it with the greatest accuracy from a copy of that same archive, since the original had perished.

The purpose of my undertaking requires me also to publish so precious a monument. Since I have at hand from the Albini manuscript a very old copy differing little from the copy of the Mole of Hadrian, I shall produce it together with the variant readings of that copy. I believe that a similar version of both was reported by Cencius in the Book of Censuses. For Panvinius, in whose time this genuine book still existed in the Vatican Library, speaks as follows in his catalogue of the privileges of the Holy See (Vatican Codex 3924), where he lists the Ludovician privilege (p. 45):

“Extracted from the Book of Censuses of the Roman Church, folio 110.”

Then he gives the beginning of the Diploma:

“The privilege of the emperor Louis concerning the confirmation of the royal rights to Pope Paschal.”

The wording is exactly that of the Albini manuscript, except that the name Ludowici is written with a double *w*. This form, together with others occurring in the diploma, reflects the character of the ninth century, when the monument was issued. From this it follows that Albini was more diligent in copying ancient charters, and that he transcribed the Ludovician privilege itself from the original, from an authentic codex of the Lateran archive.

The author of the codex is himself a witness to the matter, as I pointed out in the preface to the first volume (no. 25). Indeed, no greater confidence ought to be placed in anyone than in Albini and Cencius, both of whom examined the Lateran archive. Since Cencius’s genuine codex was stolen from the Vatican Library after Panvinius’s time—as I confidently assert, for no codex now existing at the Holy See corresponds to the page number cited by Panvinius—I present this illustrious monument from Albini, both because he is older than Cencius and because he wrote his codex with his own hand [Col. 0551C].

I add one point, required by historical accuracy and integrity: Albini had another ancient copy of the diploma available, and he placed its title beneath the earlier one. It reads as follows:

“And the pact of the constitution of the emperors Louis I, Otto I, and Henry I with the Roman pontiffs.”

After the privilege has been completed, the codex continues:

“From another privilege of Otto I and Henry I.”

It then records Otto’s privilege, omitting what Otto had received from the Ludovician privilege and confirmed. Finally it gives:

“From the privilege of the emperor Henry,”

from which likewise it reports only those matters that concern Henry’s donation, omitting the rest.

II. From this, unless I am mistaken, a nearly identical copy was made. Dominicus Georgius found it in Vatican Codex 1984—dating, that is, from the age of Gelasius and Callixtus II, or the beginning of the twelfth century—and published it in the new edition of Baronius’s Annals (vol. XIII, p. 627). He used it against Pagius and Muratori, who have served as auxiliaries to the sectarians [Col. 0551D] in the matter of the diploma’s authenticity. I too used it elsewhere (Orsi, *On Temporal Dominion*, Appendix), as a copy older than others I had seen. For at that time it had not yet been possible to examine the Albini codex, which still lay buried in obscurity.

When this priceless codex came into my hands, however, I studied it at length and carefully read the mutilated diplomas of Louis attached to it. In both I discovered an omission of some importance. Otto and Henry had each said in his own diploma:

“And also the patrimony of Sicily, if God should deliver it into our hands. In like manner, etc.”

But in both mutilated copies one reads:

“And also the patrimony of Sicily. In like manner, etc.”

Who does not see that this sort of omission indicates the date of the three diplomas considered together? It was made after the Norman princes had been pacified and released from anathema, when Nicholas II went there to demonstrate the rights of the Holy See in Apulia and the other provinces, held a council there, and received an oath of fidelity from those princes in 1059, as is recorded in the Book of Censuses and more clearly by Baronius (1059, nos. 3 and 70 ff.).

A similar action by Nicholas III with Rudolph, to whom he likewise sent the same three mutilated diplomas, will have to be considered in its proper place. It should not be thought that these diplomas were accidentally shortened, or that the condition “if God …” was mutilated by a copyist in both instances. Since the Normans were no longer hostile to the Apostolic See, it was necessary to show that Sicily belonged by right to the Roman Church, as it truly did because of the seizure of the patrimonies of Calabria and Sicily, which we saw in the preceding Dissertation (nos. 10 ff.) Adrian had compared to the persecution of the sacred images.

Since Louis issued his Diploma before the arrival of the Saracens and confirmed the grant of the island made by his father Charlemagne—a grant made with excellent right, for the Greeks had already possessed those patrimonies for ninety years by the greatest injustice, depriving the poor and churches of thirty million and one hundred fifty thousand gold pieces, perhaps more than the island was worth at that time, and thereby provoking divine vengeance at some future time—since, I say, Louis issued his diploma before the Saracen invasion, there was no reason for him to add the condition that necessarily had to be added in the diplomas of Otto and Henry, because the rights of the Holy See had to be vindicated by the expulsion of the Saracens.

III. In the time of Pope Nicholas, the island of Sicily had groaned under the Saracen yoke for two hundred and thirty years, and the Greeks had abandoned all hope of recovering it. Calabria, Apulia, and Capua—which later began to be called Sicily on this side of the Strait—the Normans possessed by force of arms. Saint Leo IX had unsuccessfully risked taking these territories from them by force in order to assert the right of the Holy See.

Accordingly, Nicholas approached the Normans, who had evidently been reconciled to the Holy See by divine providence. Bringing with him the diplomas of the emperors, he taught them the rights of the Roman Church more briefly and effectively than if he had demonstrated the nearly threefold sum by which those same rights had been increasingly confirmed, at the expense of the poor and churches.

That the matter succeeded according to his wish is shown by the oaths of fidelity by which Robert Guiscard obtained, by apostolic authority, the duchy of Apulia and Calabria, as well as Sicily, which was to be recovered from the power of the Saracens. These oaths are found in the Albini codex shortly after the diplomas mentioned above and in Baronius, from the Book of Censuses (1059, no. 70 ff.).

In the same Albini codex there is also, two years later, the oath rendered to Alexander II by Richard, to whom the principality of Capua was granted:

“Done in the hall of the sacred Lateran palace on the sixth day before the Nones of October, Tuesday, indiction 15, in the year 1061.”

A similar oath rendered by the same man to Gregory VII is given by Baronius (1073, no. 63) from the register of that holy pontiff in Labbe (Councils, vol. X, p. 23), with some variant readings at the end.

The following words of Robert belong to the substance of these oaths:

“And I shall swear fidelity to no one except with the fidelity owed to the Holy Roman Church,”

words omitted by Baronius because he did not find them in the Book of Censuses. They must absolutely be restored, for the Normans knew that Apulia and Calabria were Greek provinces and therefore preserved the memory that their domination had not yet been entirely erased, while nevertheless acknowledging the supreme authority of the Holy See.

Richard likewise says:

“But to King Henry, when I have been admonished by you or by your successors, I shall swear fidelity, while preserving the fidelity owed to the Holy Roman Church.”

We shall discuss these matters more suitably when the diploma of Otto is considered.

For now, it must be observed that the Norman princes could not possibly have learned all these things without examining their diplomas. Therefore, proceeding not by conjecture but by firm inference from the consequences, I have no doubt in asserting that Nicholas II was the author of the aforementioned mutilation of the diplomas, and that it was therefore carried out in 1058 or the following year.

IV. Let no one blame the pontiff for this act, as though he had craftily removed that condition. The originals of both diplomas are still carefully preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo. There the condition is plainly visible, and nothing prevents it from referring to the donation of Sicily made by Charles before the Saracen invasion and confirmed by Otto and Henry, on the understanding, however, that they were restoring to the Holy See what had been wrested from the Saracens.

Neither emperor had recovered it, and therefore the successors had to appeal to the pure and simple donation of Charles, confirmed by them. Nicholas clearly did so.

Perhaps the Italian annalist caught a glimpse of something in the year 1059. For, forgetting himself—since in the year 817 he had portrayed the Ludovician diploma as spurious, contrary to the opinion of the most learned men Baronius, Gretser, Nat. Alexander, P. de Marca, Cointius, Claude de Fleury, Gootius, Hottomannus, and Basnage, to say nothing of more recent writers, all of whom recognize the Ludovician diploma as genuine—he asserts that in these times the three diplomas came to light, with additions made according to the wishes of the Roman pontiffs.

I, however, have demonstrated from the Ottonian and Henrician diplomas that something was removed rather than added. As for the Ludovician diploma, whose value lies not in its antiquity but in its contents, I trust that I shall make clear [Col. 0553C] why those most learned men whom I have mentioned unanimously declared it to be the genuine offspring of the emperor.

Meanwhile, it will not be irrelevant to observe that the complete privilege of Louis, together with the other two, is listed among the earliest monuments of the eleventh century in the codex under the title:

“The privilege of the emperor Louis, etc.”

By contrast, the other two complete diplomas are inserted among the monuments of the twelfth century and are entitled:

“Copy of the privilege of the emperor Otto, etc.”

“Copy of the privilege of the emperor Henry, etc.”

It therefore seems possible to assert that the Ludovician diploma was copied from the original in the time of Nicholas II, just as the other two were, even though, toward the end of the twelfth century, when Albini flourished, none of the originals was still at Rome.

To propose explanations for why the others, transferred here and there, survived down to our time, while the Ludovician diploma could nowhere be found, would be mere speculation. The loss is nevertheless slight, since excellent copies exist with Albini and in the archive of the Mole of Hadrian.

The essential point is to reveal the character of the diploma. Since I see that no one else has done this, I willingly and deliberately take the task upon myself.

87 V. First, the diploma itself reveals that it is a pact of confirmation, calling itself repeatedly both a pact of confirmation and a decree of confirmation.

The chronicler of Saint Vincent on the Volturno (Duchesne, vol. III, p. 681), in the *Life of Abbot Joshua*, who attended the assembly at Aachen where this diploma was issued, calls it a pact of constitution and confirmation. The Cassinese chronicler, Leo of Ostia, uses these very words, and the learned Fontanini (Defense 1, p. 145) believed that he had introduced the new term *constitution*, which the diploma itself rejects.

For my part, to say what I think, the wording seems rather redundant than indicative of a new matter. Whether it is simply called a pact, according to the usage of that age, or a pact of constitution, it will always be an instrument requested on the basis of an agreement, that is, a stipulation, whose character is made clear by the word “confirmation.”

For throughout the whole pact not even a cubit of land will be found that Louis granted to the Roman Church. Neither Stephen IV nor Paschal I through his legate had asked this of the emperor. They wanted the ancient rights of the Church confirmed by imperial authority, as was done in the pact of confirmation mentioned above.

Accordingly, Astronomus, Louis the Pious’s contemporary and a member of his entourage, who wrote the Life of that emperor, says:

“The bearer of the embassy was Theodore the nomenclator. When the business had been completed and the requests obtained—namely, confirmation of the pact and friendship—he returned according to the custom of his predecessors.”

Moreover, the same chronicler of Volturno, as Mabillon reports (Annals, book XXVIII, no. 45), asserts that Abbot Joshua was so highly regarded by Pope Paschal that, when he received the pact of confirmation from Louis, he wished to be present among the abbots of France on behalf of the Apostolic See [Col. 0554B]. Here, as you see, he passes over in silence the word “constitution,” which Fontanini found less acceptable.

In the same place the chronicler seems to me gratuitously to testify that he found the pact of confirmation in the *Book of the Pontiffs*. In that work you will find donations reported in the fullest language, but you will not find their confirmations unless they are new confirmations joined to the donation. Thus the silence of the *Book of the Pontiffs* supports the character of this pact.

Albini—or rather Nicholas II—and Cencius place no other title before the Ludovician diploma than:

“The privilege of the emperor Louis concerning the confirmation of the royal rights to Pope Paschal.”

By contrast, they entitle the privileges of Otto and Henry:

“Concerning the royal rights granted to blessed Peter,”

because each added a new donation.

VI. If Pagius had understood this, he would not have made the mistaken assertion he did (787, no. 8), when he recognized the Ludovician diploma as genuine:

“As for the other Tuscany, which the emperors have always possessed, other places belonged to it, which the emperor Louis granted to that See in the regions of Tuscany, as we shall show in the year 817.”

This statement does not reflect the judgment of the learned and venerable cardinal but of a man suffering from the greatest delusion. For when the reader reaches the year mentioned (817, no. 7), he finds, not without astonishment, that Pagius follows Molinaeus and Goldastus:

“The donation which Gratian is said to have made to the Roman Church by Louis the Pious is no less fictitious than the one attributed to Constantine the Great, as some learned men have already recognized.”

This opinion pleased the Italian annalist so greatly that he not only embraced it with open arms but, demanding all the formal legal solemnities in this most ancient monument, argued that it was false because those solemnities were absent. He did so with such success among certain writers beyond the Alps, equally hostile to the Catholic religion and to the Holy See, that one of them, as though this diploma had been condemned by common proclamation, dedicated his writings—or rather his mockeries—against the dominion of the Apostolic See to that same annalist, and declared in several places that he owed to him whatever he brought forward in disparagement of this chief bulwark of pontifical authority.

He relegated the diploma itself, as though it were a matter deserving contempt, to the end of his little volume, having drawn it not from a copy of good standing or from any of its many editions known to scholars, but from Volaterranus’s nearly unknown *Urban Commentaries* (Geography, book III, p. 41) and composed it from his own imagination.

I shall give the title of that work, not so much because I wish to spend time refuting so many fallacies—a task that would waste labor—as to make clear how highly the support of a Catholic writer is valued among the members of his sect when it can be used to uphold the temporal dominion of the Roman Church.

VII. “Christian Wilhelm Franz Walch’s critique of the diploma which is said to have been granted by Louis the Pious, emperor Augustus, to Paschal I, Roman pontiff. Dedicated to the eminent Louis Antonio Muratori and directed against the celebrated historian of Padua, Antonio Sandini. The diploma itself is appended, with variant readings noted. Leipzig, etc.”

If one wishes merely to catch a glimpse of the writer’s intention, let these few words from his dedication suffice. He praises the Italian Annals to the skies because they are of great use in defending and upholding “the right of our most august German emperor to Italy, confirmed by the consistent practice of eighteen centuries, while the impudence of his adversaries is restrained.”

Further on he writes:

“I present to you the investigation of the Ludovician diploma, which, following the example and imitation of the great Hermann Conring among the historians of our nation, you see adorned with the title of a critique and consecrated according to ancient custom to your celebrated name. I earnestly beg and implore you to receive it with greater kindness.”

I firmly maintain that such a mark is unjustly inflicted on a Catholic writer. He is not speaking with the sectarians about all Italy, but about Italy properly so called, that is, the kingdom of Italy—or, more precisely, Lombardy. Although he failed to establish that the emperors became participants in supreme power through the Roman coronation, he wrote on that subject to the detriment of pontifical authority, as we discussed in the preceding Dissertation.

But because he considered the Ludovician diploma spurious, since he likewise failed to grasp its character, he showed himself a writer of little discernment rather than an ally of the sectarians, as the critic supposes.

Nevertheless, lest an unwary youth, deceived by a writer of such reputation, should think that the Ludovician diploma ought to be dismissed together with the edict or donation of Constantine, I have decided to examine its character more fully, preferring to sacrifice to truth rather than attack the false opinions of others. I shall begin with the very causes that gave rise to this pact of confirmation.

VIII. The Lorsch Annals, wrongly attributed to Einhard, and the Fulda Annals, in Baronius and Pagius (815, no. 1), report that “at Rome certain leading men who had conspired to kill Pope Leo were executed.”

Astronomus gives a fuller account of the matter (chapter 38), under the year mentioned:

“In this year, as the course of events proceeded, word was brought to the emperor that certain powerful Romans had entered into wicked conspiracies against Leo the Apostolic. The same Apostolic, having dragged them before him and convicted them, subjected them to capital punishment, in accordance with the Roman law that applied to such a conspiracy. The emperor, hearing this, was deeply displeased, as though the first priest of the world had dealt so severely with them. Therefore he sent Bernard, king of Italy, there, so that, after learning for himself what was true and what false rumor had spread about the matter, he might report to him through Gerold. King Bernard himself came to Rome and reported what he had seen through the aforesaid messenger. But soon afterward the envoys of that same Apostolic Leo—John, bishop of Silva Candida, and Theodore the nomenclator, as well as Sergius the duke—cleared Leo the Apostolic of the charges brought against him.”

Observe that Louis, who was not emperor, as Astronomus calls him—he wrote nearly thirty years later and prematurely granted him that title—but king, as Theganus correctly calls him, sent an inquiry at his father’s commission, taking charge of the Roman Church, to discover whether the pontiff himself had punished the guilty. Once informed of the facts, he remained satisfied.

For in such cases the pontiffs acted as the *Book of the Pontiffs* reports of Adrian [Col. 0555D]:

“The most holy bishop, at the entreaties of the judges and of the entire Roman people, ordered the aforesaid chamberlain Calvulus and the previously named Campani to be handed over to the prefect of the City, so that he might examine them before the whole people according to the custom applied to homicides. They were taken to the Elephant, the public prison, where they were examined before the entire people. Thus the Campani confessed in that examination just as they had earlier. But Calvulus, hardening his heart, scarcely admitted that everything was so; nevertheless, in that same prison he lost his life by a cruel death.”

After the aforementioned conspiracy against the holy pontiff, Leo was then afflicted with a grave illness [Col. 0556A], from which he died the following year. Astronomus therefore continues:

“When Leo the Apostolic was weighed down by this adverse illness, they attempted, without awaiting any judge, to seize and restore to themselves all the estates that they call *domocultae*, which had recently been established by that same Apostolic, as well as those which they complained had been taken from them contrary to justice.”

The Lorsch Annals contain similar statements.

What wonder, then, if Leo’s successor, Stephen IV, immediately after his consecration, set out for Francia and dealt with the pious prince concerning a pact of confirmation of all the rights of the Apostolic See, with the prince whom he himself had crowned with the imperial diadem?

IX. In fact, a death that followed shortly after his return prevented Stephen from taking the documents of all the donations from the Lateran archive, arranging them in order, and preparing a pact or diploma complete in every respect. It would have begun with the city of Rome and its duchy, which had been subjected to the Holy See twenty-five years before the first donation of the Frankish kings, and would have included even older rights. It would also have contained the regulations governing the election and consecration of the Roman pontiffs.

What Stephen could not accomplish within the span of two months and several days, his successor Paschal completed. He prepared an embassy to the prince and obtained confirmation of everything, as the writers mentioned above unanimously affirm, especially Astronomus (chapter 40) under the year 817.

Theganus, who devotes himself entirely to describing the character of the pious Augustus, is silent about this matter. He had, however, said of Stephen (chapter 18):

“As long as the most blessed pope was there, they held daily discussions concerning the welfare of the holy Church of God.”

And since Astronomus adds under the year 816:

“The Apostolic Lord, having obtained everything he had requested, returned to Rome,”

I see no remaining doubt that Stephen reached an agreement with Louis concerning the pact of confirmation, which Paschal later obtained.

Two chroniclers, from Volturno and Cassino, support this conclusion. Although they lived far removed from those times—for the Volturno chronicler reaches the year 1071 and may seem more recent than the Italian annalist, while the Cassinese chronicler reaches 1115, when Leo of Marsica, bishop of Ostia, who wrote the Chronicle, died—no learned person is unaware that chroniclers rely on ancient monuments when writing about events that occurred before their own times.

The Volturno chronicler therefore extracted the following from the acts of the Life of Abbot Joshua, who attended the assembly at Aachen:

“Then, too, he made a pact of constitution and confirmation with the most blessed Pope Paschal, strengthening it also with his own hand and the seals of his three sons, and sent it to the aforesaid pope through Theodore the nomenclator, legate of the Holy Roman Church. In it he caused ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, the librarian, the mansionary, and the doorkeeper to subscribe.”

Leo of Ostia reports the same matter in somewhat different words (book I, chapter 16):

“This Louis made a pact of constitution and confirmation with blessed Peter the apostle and his vicar, lord Paschal, after the example of his parents Pippin and Charles. Strengthening it with the seal of his own hand and those of his sons, he caused ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian, one mansionary, and one doorkeeper to subscribe to it, and sent it through Theodore the nomenclator, legate of the Holy Roman Church, to the lord Pope Paschal.”

X. To some, the testimony of the Cassinese Chronicle, or of Leo of Ostia, may seem superfluous. It is not. Pagius rashly attributes the first mention of this diploma to Leo (817, no. 7):

“Leo of Ostia, who died at the beginning of the twelfth century, was the first to mention it; therefore it had been devised not long before.”
