What confidence in the man! What, then, of Ducange, who, under the word *Signaculum*, quotes the charter of Charlemagne, the two royal decrees of Charlemagne and his son Louis, and these words from the Chronicle of Saint Vincent of Volturno (book II, p. 681):

“Strengthening it with the gift of his own hand and the seal of his three sons”?

Leo of Ostia says:

“With the seal of his own hand and of his sons.”

Therefore the first mention of the diploma must not be attributed to Leo of Ostia but to the ancient monuments of the monastery of Volturno. For, while composing the Cassinese Chronicle, he demonstrates that he had both the Volturno monument and the Ludovician diploma before his eyes.

From the former he takes the substance of the matter, but he constructs the variant readings himself from the diploma. Thus the words of the diploma:

“To you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you to your vicar, lord Paschal,”

he adapts to the wording of the Volturno monument, which he is copying:

“To blessed Peter the apostle and his vicar, lord Paschal.”

He immediately adds:

“Imitating his parents Pippin and Charles,”

because the diploma distinctly lists the donations of Pippin and Charles.

The rest is self-evident.

Leo of Ostia is mistaken, however, when he says that Louis imitated his parents. Each of them had confined himself to the boundaries of his own donation. Moreover, Pippin, the first enlarger of ecclesiastical territory, gave provinces and cities to blessed Peter and his successors, while Charles, the confirmer of his father’s donation, added his own very extensive donation.

Louis, by contrast, went far beyond the Frankish donations and granted no cities or provinces at all. For this reason, the simple account of the Volturno chronicler concerning the pact of confirmation is preferable to that of Leo of Ostia. Contrary to Pagius’s view, Leo was not the first to mention the diploma; he was the first to disturb it with his additions.

The diploma itself must now be examined.

### XI

We have already said quite enough about the title of that document. Its opening, or invocation of the Trinity, appears at first sight to be unusual; but, if considered attentively, it makes the reason for its distinctiveness clear. The very learned Mabillon ( *Dipl.* book II, chapter 3), in opposition to Papebroch’s *Propylaeum*, cites the invocations of the Carolingian age: “In the name of God and our Savior Jesus Christ”; “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ”; and “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Observing this, Godefridus (*Chron. Gotw.* volume I, book II, chapter 1, p. 117 and following) notes that the notaries’ style in these formulas varied.

More particularly, however (chapter 6, p. 231), he writes concerning the various invocations of Henry I:

> “I do not see why the invocation formula ‘In the name of God Almighty, the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ should be rejected in the Henrician diploma granted to the Roman Church and produced by the eminent Baron at the year 1014, no. 7—a formula which D. Frideric Hahn wished to condemn as suspect in *Hist. imp.*, part II, chapter 6, §10, p. 208, letter a—when nevertheless we find the same formula in several diplomas, especially Italian ones, plainly written in the style of Italian notaries.”

I think no one will dispute this observation of that most learned man with respect to the diplomas of the emperors, which were customarily drawn up at Rome—not even in the case of Charlemagne, since he issued his donation in the City. But the matter would seem to require a different judgment in the case of the invocation of the Ludovician diploma, however it may have been arranged by Stephen IV or Paschal, since it was nevertheless confirmed in Francia—unless, in Baronius (811, no. 44), one encounters the testament of Charlemagne, likewise made in Francia, with this invocation: “In the name of God Almighty, the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

The same wording is also found in Labbe (*Concil.*, volume VII, p. 1202), and especially in Bollandus (93, *Acta sanctorum*, volume II, p. 887). He presents the Life of Saint Charlemagne from two manuscripts of Einhard of excellent quality, collated with five other manuscripts and better editions. The only difference is that all the witnesses read: “In the name of the Lord God Almighty,” and so forth, as in the Ludovician apograph of Hadrian’s Mausoleum, and in the diplomas of Otto and Henry in the Albinian codex, according to their autographs.

It may therefore safely be inferred that all the privileges granted by the Carolingians to Saint Peter and his successors bore this invocation, which Otto and Henry likewise imitated—clearly following the style of the scriniarii of the Holy See, whose task it was to compose such documents from the records of the archive. Nor do I doubt that, if Pippin’s donation still existed, it would display precisely the same invocation, which all his successors adopted.

### XII

Ludovic places first in his confirmation that holy commonwealth—namely, Rome and its duchy—which, as we have seen, belonged to the Apostolic See long before the donations of the Frankish kings, through the submission of the peoples who had defected from the impious Greeks.

This was what Stephen IV had agreed upon with the emperor, wishing by imperial authority both to ward off plundering and at the same time to protect all the places belonging to the ecclesiastical territory with a strong safeguard. The emperor himself expresses the matter in explicit words:

> “Just as you have held and governed them in your power and dominion from your predecessors down to the present.”

He then lists the individual cities, both of Roman Tuscany and of Campania. For, as no learned person fails to know, the duchy was divided into two parts: the Cis-Tiberine and the Trans-Tiberine.

We have seen so clearly in the letters of the *Carolingian Codex* that these cities belonged to the Apostolic See before any donation that it would seem pointless to demonstrate the matter again here. It will be more than sufficient simply to recall what Stephen II signified to Pippin, who had returned to Francia (*Cod. Car.* letters 6 and 7, elsewhere 7 and 9): the Lombards had rendered the donation void and had not handed over “even a space of land the breadth of one palm” to the Holy See. Indeed, they had committed “plunderings and devastations, or destructions, in the cities and places of Saint Peter.”

Again urging him to undertake a new expedition (*ibid.*, letters 8 and 9, elsewhere 4 and 6), while Rome was being besieged by the Lombards, he says:

> “No increase has been made for us; rather, after the devastation of our entire province …”

What could be clearer for establishing that the Roman city and its duchy belonged to the Apostolic See before the first donation of all?

There is nevertheless still fuller testimony available. For later in the same letter the pontiff says:

> “They took away the city of Narni, which your Christianity granted to Saint Peter, and seized some of our cities.”

He thus distinguishes Narni, a city of the Roman duchy, from the others, and openly reports to Pippin that he had received it. It had formerly been seized by the duke of Spoleto (*Liber pontificalis*, section 254); but at Pippin’s first arrival, Aistulf, terrified by the king’s envoys, restored it (*ibid.*, section 249, from the Royal, Mazarin, and Thüringian codices).

### XIII

Since Pagius and others contend that this part of the papal territory was owed to royal munificence, they are not ashamed, contrary to the consistent testimony of all the manuscripts, to substitute “our predecessors” for Ludovic’s words “from your predecessors,” so that Pippin and Charlemagne appear to have handed over Rome and its duchy to Saint Peter and his successors. It will therefore be worthwhile to demonstrate the contrary—not by arguments, as I did in my elucidation of the *Carolingian Codex*, but by their own admission.

Although they argue at great length, and with little substance, about Charles Martel’s patriciate, they do not count him among Ludovic’s predecessors. They say that, having been overtaken by death in 741, he could not assist the endangered Church. They further admit that the Roman pontiffs, until the year 753, did not abandon their obedience to the Greek emperors, however impious those emperors might have been.

In the following year, during Pippin’s first expedition, they say that Narni, one of the cities of the Roman duchy, was restored through fear of the Franks. Thus, whatever lord they imagine to have ruled the Roman duchy, whose head was Rome, that territory, by their own admission, was subject to its former ruler before Pippin’s donation took effect.

Who that ruler was, Pippin himself had testified to the Romans one year after his donation (*Cod. Car.* letter 15, elsewhere 36). The Romans themselves inform us of this in the letters they deposited with the king:

> “Concerning your most blessed and co-angelic spiritual father, our lord Paul, the supreme pontiff, appointed by God …”

Accordingly, Ludovic’s predecessors, before the donation and over the course of twenty-five years, were Gregory III, Zachary, and Stephen II; after the donation, they were Paul I, Stephen III, and Hadrian. For, since they themselves admit what they cannot deny—that Pippin’s donation was confined to the Exarchate and the Pentapolis—they do not even dare to utter the names of Hadrian himself and his successor Leo III, although one of them may attempt by another route to evade their sovereignty, as I have demonstrated at length in the notes to the *Carolingian Codex*.

Why they prefer to follow Gratian, who was the first to substitute “our predecessors” for “your predecessors,” rather than the consistent testimony of the manuscripts and their own confession, is not difficult to understand: they do not know what they are saying.

### XIV

The second section of the Ludovician diploma presents Pippin’s donation itself—not the donation said to have been made at Quierzy in 754 and confirmed by Pippin’s two sons, Charles and Carloman, but the form in which Charlemagne confirmed it at Rome in 774.

The earlier document was being carefully preserved in the Lateran archive. Twenty years later, in 774, when Charlemagne came to Rome, he ordered “the promise made in Francia, in the place called Quierzy, to be read back to him; it pleased him, and all the provisions attached to it pleased his judges as well,” as stated in the *Liber pontificalis* (section 318). The most Christian king then “strengthened it with his own hand and caused all the bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts to be entered in it. First placing it upon the altar of Saint Peter, and afterward within his holy confession, both the king of the Franks and his judges, promising by oath to preserve everything contained in that donation, handed it over to Saint Peter and to his most holy vicar, Pope Hadrian.” This is how Albinus read it in his day, and all the manuscripts, both printed and unprinted, have the same account with only minor differences.

That donation, confirmed by Charles with such solemnity and sanctity—a donation which Hadrian repeatedly and rightly calls an offering and a holocaust in his letters—is nowhere else to be found in its entirety; it survives complete in only one Ludovician diploma.

The most diligent collector of ancient monuments, Francesco Blanchinus, believed that he had published it for the public good from the celebrated Farnesian Codex (*Anast.*, volume II, p. 57). As a fair-minded examiner of that precious codex, after it had been transferred to Parma with the Farnese library, he went there once and again. He obtained a specimen of its uncial script, which indicates that the codex was contemporary with Charlemagne—something neglected by Holstenius and Schelstratius while the codex was still in Rome—and copied the entire passage that I cited when discussing the letters of Stephen II, as a monument of Pippin’s donation.

### XV

Yet the very learned man was misled by the account in the *Liber pontificalis*. Although that work reports how Pippin, confirming everything that he had granted to Saint Peter and his successors by his diploma at Quierzy, strengthened the earlier document with a new diploma and added Comacchio, it nevertheless lists only the cities whose possession Pippin’s envoy Fulrad entered and whose keys he brought to Rome.

It will therefore be discovered that the *Liber pontificalis* lacks ten cities, all of which occur in the Ludovician diploma, except for Narni, a city of the Roman duchy. Fulrad had also taken possession of Narni, although the city had been separated from the donation because, after its restoration, it had returned to the jurisdiction of the Holy See. Ludovic therefore rightly lists it among the cities of the Roman duchy.

Pippin’s donation itself is recorded in the diploma so completely, precisely, and distinctly that it is astonishing that two more recent scholars were not thereby deterred from suspecting its authenticity. For although the document reports only Pippin’s donation, it does not attribute it to Pippin alone; it makes Charles a participant in it as well.

During the twenty years following Pippin’s donation and preceding Charles’s first arrival in the City, ten of those cities—whose possession the Lombards refused to surrender—are found to have been promised repeatedly but never restored. But after Charles captured Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and subdued their kingdom, he recovered the entire donation for the Holy See.

Two letters of the *Carolingian Codex* bear witness to this (51 and 53, elsewhere 54 and 52), written a few months after Charles’s departure. In them Hadrian informs the king that Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had invaded Faenza, Imola, Ferrara, Bologna, and Adria, or Gabello, where he had installed a count whom Charles had commended to him in the church of Saint Peter. It is therefore certain that all the cities of Emilia were possessed by the Roman Church.

As for the four cities of the Pentapolis, the same letters remove every doubt, since they indicate that both Pentapolises, from Rimini to Gubbio, remained faithful to the Apostolic See. Moreover, other letters show that the territory or town of Valva served as a refuge for five of Charles’s legates during the disturbance in Benevento (90, elsewhere 92).

### XVI

“You will say that I do not see Emilia named among the remaining cities in the *Carolingian Codex*, where it occurs immediately after Ravenna in the diploma.” Yet I find mention of it both in the letters just cited and elsewhere, as a province. I therefore believe that the medieval geographer was gravely mistaken when he was the first of all to dare to turn a province into a city.

Nor are you mistaken in this judgment: I too, once deceived along with others, embraced that opinion. Why should I not have done so? I saw that the Exarchate had narrower boundaries under the Lombards than it had possessed under the Roman Republic, and that the province of Emilia, divided into two parts as far as the territory of Bologna, formed part of the kingdom of Italy, while the Exarchate began beyond it.

Nevertheless, I found Emilia granted absolutely to the Apostolic See in this diploma, which so many very learned men judged genuine. What was I to do in such difficulties? A remarkable and previously unheard-of doctrine emerged from the geographer, who removed the name of the province of Emilia from the Exarchate on grounds that at first sight seemed excellent. I followed his opinion completely.

Later, however, when I seriously turned to vindicating the rights of the Holy See and admitted no opinion of men that conflicted with the certain records of the annals, I recognized that this geographer—so highly esteemed by Italian historians in many other matters—had been gravely mistaken here as well, in depriving the province of Emilia of its dignity.

That province did not cease to be a province in its own nature, as is clear from the division of the ecclesiastical provinces; rather, it began to be narrower in civil administration. In the Exarchate it retained the name of Emilia, whereas in the kingdom of Italy that distinguished royal designation absorbed the provincial one.

Moreover, when the double Pentapolis arose within the Exarchate, it narrowed Emilia still further. Thus there came to be three provinces in the Exarchate: Emilia, the Maritime Pentapolis, and the Inland Pentapolis.

### XVII

When these matters are understood, Fulrad, about to take possession of the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia, proceeded into the Exarchate, as the Farnesian Codex records, and brought to Rome “the very keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities of that same Exarchate of Ravenna.”

The cities themselves are enumerated in the codex, without distinction among the provinces of the Exarchate. But when Hadrian informed Charles of Archbishop Leo’s invasion, he said that Leo had invaded “the cities of Emilia” and had then tried to induce the people of the Pentapolis to defect. He adds that the latter remained steadfast in obedience to the Holy See:

> “Just as they existed under our predecessor, Lord Stephen the pope, to whom your father of blessed memory, together with your own illustrious excellence, handed over the Exarchate itself to remain under the jurisdiction of Saint Peter.”

Likewise, in another letter (53, elsewhere 52), he lists the provinces separately and clearly teaches that the people of Ravenna and those dwelling in the province of Emilia were distinct from the people of the Pentapolis:

> “No one from the people of Ravenna or Emilia …”

He then commends the fidelity of the people of the Pentapolis.

I am therefore ashamed to have trusted the geographer in this matter. Restoring Emilia to its former dignity, I confirm it by the authority of the diploma. Ludovic, then, confirming the donation of his grandfather Pippin, restored by his father Charles, recites that donation in its very form: Ravenna, the head and metropolis of the entire Exarchate; and Emilia, one of the provinces of the Exarchate, listing its individual cities so that no one might think of extending that province more broadly.

He then adds another province, together with the Pentapolis—which in Pippin’s time had not yet been divided into two provinces, a fact that increasingly confirms the authenticity of the donation—and in a similar manner enumerates the cities of that province. In both cases he appends the territories, towns, and boundaries belonging to them, and does so with such clarity and precision that he describes the same boundaries which the ecclesiastical territory still has today, by which Emilia is separated from the duchy of Modena.

### XVIII

The more celebrated writers of the sixteenth century extend this province of Emilia very widely, contrary to the testimony of all the ancient records and according to the boundaries of the Roman Republic. Some indulgence may perhaps be granted them, both because they considered the ecclesiastical province and because the relative obscurity of their age encouraged such a view.

The case is different with writers of our own age, for whom it was convenient to disregard the *Carolingian Codex* and the Ludovician diploma rather than, by following the traces of the earlier writers, become defenders of both monuments.

The enlargement of the Exarchate, or the cities which they add to the donations of the Frankish kings, will be discussed elsewhere. Here, however, one city must not be omitted—one which they remove from that donation. This is Bobium, today Sassina, somewhat farther south than Cesena, which the diploma lists first among all. The *Carolingian Codex* (letters 51 and 53, elsewhere 54 and 52) names it next to Cesena, while the Farnesian Codex lists it between San Marino and Urbino.

It was an ancient city of Emilia, whose bishop attended the councils of Symmachus at the end of the fifth century (Labbe, *Concilia*, volume IV, pp. 1367–1376). In the census book of the Albinian codex, the bishopric of Bobium, with three monasteries, appears between those of Forlì and Popoli. Moreover, out of the fifty villages subject to Sassina, four formed the county of Bobium, as Ughellus observes (*Italia sacra*, volume II, p. 652).

Yet, while removing this noble and ancient city of Emilia from Pippin’s donation, they substitute for it the town of Bobium in Insubria, famous for the monastery of Saint Columbanus and endowed with an episcopal see by Benedict VIII at the beginning of the eleventh century (Ditmar, in Baronius, 1014, no. 4; Ughellus, Mabillon, and several others).

Let the reader judge how rightly this city is sought outside the limits of Emilia, however broadly Emilia is understood. For my part, I see impossible claims being advanced in the heat of controversy. Fulrad, Pippin’s envoy, who entered into possession of Bobium as he did of the other cities, certainly did not travel to regions so distant.

And since I take it as certain that all the successors of Saint Peter protested in the words of Hadrian (*Cod. Car.*, letter 71, elsewhere 56):

> “For I call God as my witness that I seek no one’s boundaries irrationally,”

I confidently declare that Bobium in Insubria never belonged to the jurisdiction of the Holy See.

I admit that the other cities which they attach to the Exarchate stand differently—not because they were contained in the Pippinian or Carolingian donation, for that assertion would be as false as transferring Bobium from Insubria to Flaminia and claiming it for the Holy See without authority, but because, for another reason, they belong entirely to the territory of the Apostolic See, as I shall show in its proper place.

Meanwhile, to establish more firmly the boundaries of the ecclesiastical territory, I shall add a few points from Charles’s division of the kingdoms among his sons Ludovic, Pippin, and Charles. He gave Pippin Italy, also called Lombardy, to be divided among the brothers if he should die before them—although the same matter has been brought forward elsewhere for another purpose (volume I, p. 298 and following).

### XIX

> “From the entrance into Italy by way of the city of Aosta, let Charles receive Ivrea, Vercelli, Pavia, and from there, with the boundary running along the Po River, as far as the borders of Reggio; and Reggio itself, and the New City, and Modena, as far as the boundaries of Saint Peter. Let Charles receive these cities, with their suburbs, territories, and counties belonging to them, and whatever from that point, on the way to Rome, lies to the left, from the kingdom which Pippin possessed, together with the duchy of Spoleto, as we have said. Whatever, however, from the aforesaid cities or counties lies to the right of one traveling to Rome from that kingdom—that is, the portion of the Transpadane region which remained, together with the Tuscan duchy, as far as the southern sea and as far as the province—let Ludovic receive as an enlargement of his kingdom.”

You see that the kingdom of Italy ends at the territory of Modena, since the territory of Bologna, as today, bordered that of Modena. You also see that this division is marked by boundaries running from the entrance into Italy as far as Modena. From there, that considerable part of Italy or Lombardy extending to the left of one traveling toward Rome—where the vast dominion of the Venetian Republic now lies—together with the duchy of Spoleto, which, although offered to Saint Peter and his successors, belonged in supreme jurisdiction to the emperor, as will be made clear below, was to constitute an enlargement of Charles’s kingdom.

The other portion assigned to Ludovic is explained best by another delineation according to the boundaries of the ecclesiastical dominion, contained in Otto’s diploma. It is also assigned to Charles both in that diploma and in the *Liber pontificalis*, as follows:

> “From Luni with the island of Corsica, then to Soriano, then to Mount Bardone, then to Berceto, from there to Parma, then to Reggio, from there to Mantua, and then to Monte Silicis, together with the province of Venetia and Istria.”

This matter will again be discussed in the notes to the Ottonian diploma.

In the meantime, understand Ludovic’s Transpadane portion of the kingdom of Italy; but do not interpret the boundaries just described as the actual walls of the named cities. Rather, understand them as the outer limits of each territory. Moreover, understand the duchy of Tuscany, like that of Spoleto, as belonging to the emperor’s supreme jurisdiction, although it had been offered to the Apostolic See. Therefore it is included within this territory and added to Ludovic’s portion.

So much for the complete donation of Pippin, confirmed by his son Charlemagne at Rome in 774 before the most sacred body of the prince of the apostles. We must now come to the donations of Charlemagne himself.

### XX

This great prince, distinguished by piety toward God and by obedience, love, and generosity toward Peter, came to Rome four times in all, as is stated in the *Carolingian Codex*: in the years 774, 781, 787, and 800.

On his first arrival, besides restoring his father’s donation before the most blessed remains of the apostle, he granted Langobardian Tuscany—or rather a part of it, since formerly all of it was called Langobardian, although later writers introduced the name “Royal Tuscany” (*Cod. Car.*, volume I, pp. 297, 321). On his second arrival he granted the entire Sabine territory (*ibid.*, pp. 383, 415); on the third, six cities of the duchy of Benevento (*ibid.*, p. 475 and following).

What he granted on the fourth occasion, “for the forgiveness of sins and as a reward for his soul,” as both he and his father had always done (*ibid.*, pp. 228, 325, 330, 333, 341, 384), is not found in the *Carolingian Codex*, which had been compiled nine years earlier. Yet he seems to have donated Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily, both because Corsica is mentioned in a letter of Leo III to the emperor Charles, and because Einhard attests that Charles did not depart from the City without granting something to the Holy See. Finally, the *Carolingian Codex*, a witness to the donations beyond all exception, passes these islands over in profound silence.

It is therefore absolutely certain that before the year 791 none of them had been donated to the Holy See. Why, then, should he not have granted them in the year 800, when Saint Leo III had made him, through the imperial diadem, a partner in supreme pontifical authority?

I admit, however, that this is confirmed by no ancient monument except the Ludovician diploma. For a long time I therefore followed the opinion of Baluze, Mabillon, and Le Blanc, who regarded this privilege or diploma as interpolated in some place.

But when, on examining it more carefully, I recognized that only the donation of Sardinia and Sicily was uncertain, I decided immediately to set aside their opinion in favor of the judgment of Baronius and the other most learned men—a judgment embraced by Grotius, Hotoman, and Basnage.

The rights of the Holy See in Sicily were in fact less doubtful, as we have explained at length in the preceding dissertation. Otto the Great vindicates this right for the Holy See among the other rights, as we shall see in the following dissertation. Saint Henry not only imitates Otto but also accepts Ludovic’s diploma as valid, despite the futile efforts of those who are distressed to see their false opinions collapse.

But nothing rash should be affirmed about those islands. I therefore assert that their donation is entirely certain, while the date of the donation remains uncertain.

### XXI

As for the other donations of Charlemagne, I do not think anything need be added, lest I appear to repeat what has already been done, to the abundant material presented in the preliminary commentary on Hadrian’s letters.

One point, nevertheless, must not be passed over: the Sabine patrimony or territory is placed in the Ludovician diploma immediately after Pippin’s donation because the arrangement follows the geographical position of the regions rather than their chronological order.

In any event, the letters of the *Carolingian Codex*, all written before 781, establish that the cities of Langobardian Tuscany, together with the duchies of Tuscany and Spoleto, were the first things donated by Charles; they explicitly mention both the cities and the duchies.

The second donation, namely that of the Sabine territory, certainly did not take place before 781, when Carloman was baptized at Rome and, having been given the auspicious name of Pippin by Hadrian, acquired through his parents the title of godson.

One distinctive feature of this diploma is that the abbots Itherius and Maginarius settled every dispute between the Holy See and the people of Rieti by establishing the boundaries between them and the Sabine territory after 784. For Maginarius succeeded Fulrad as abbot of the Dionysian monastery in July of that year.

This could not have been found in the letters of the *Carolingian Codex* (67, 68, 71, 72, 73, elsewhere 70, 68, 56, 76, 78), since all of them were written before Maginarius became abbot. They were all issued while Hildegard was still alive; she died in 783.

The third donation, that of six cities of Campania, is rightly placed last. It belongs to the year 787, when Charles recalled the people of Benevento to their duty, took Grimoald away with him along with twelve other hostages, and subjected Arichis, Grimoald’s father, the duke of Benevento, and that entire region to his power.

### XXII

After completing the account of the ancestral and paternal donations, Ludovic confirms both patrimonies as belonging by right to the Holy See, although not necessarily as possessions actually held by it.

He lists the Beneventan patrimony first. Hadrian had testified to Charles (*Cod. Car.*, letter 59, elsewhere 49) that “various emperors, patricians also, and other God-fearing men, for the reward of their souls and the forgiveness of their sins, had granted [possessions] to the Apostolic See in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Benevento.”

Several years earlier, Stephen III had praised Itherius, the envoy of Bertrada and Charles, because “he immediately proceeded to the region of the duchy of Benevento, in order to recover the patrimony in those parts” (*ibid.*, letter 46, elsewhere 44).

Next he confirms the Calabrian patrimony, to which he does not add the Sicilian, because he had confirmed the whole island shortly before in Charles’s donation.

Enough has already been said about this patrimony, but it is essential to add that Stephen II, as early as 756, while thanking Pippin (*Cod. Car.*, letter 11, elsewhere 8), seriously discussed with that king the possession of the Exarchate entered into by Fulrad:

> “Inspired by God and by blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, may you order matters concerning the portion of the Greeks in such a way that the holy Catholic and Apostolic faith may through you remain whole and unshaken forever; that the Holy Church of God may be freed from others and from their poisonous malice, and may be made secure; and that it may receive everything belonging to it, so that, for the salvation of your soul, the unceasing preparation of lamps may continue for the churches of God, and the hunger of the poor, needy, and pilgrims may be relieved.”

In third place the Neapolitan patrimony is confirmed. Like the Calabrian, it was unjustly held by the Greeks, just as the Beneventan was held by the Beneventans, who at that time were more friendly toward the Greeks than toward the Holy See.

It would take too long to follow the history of this patrimony, which you may recover from the *Carolingian Codex* (p. 495). For the present it is enough to indicate that Hadrian subdued Terracina with papal troops, since he held it in place of that patrimony. Gaeta was also conquered for the same reason. After Charles later donated six cities of Campania, the enlargement of the Holy See’s dominion in that region, for the sake of a single Neapolitan patrimony, shows how significant that patrimony was.

The history of the three great patrimonies, however, does not belong here. It does make the donation of Sicily—whenever Charles made it and Ludovic confirmed it—more probable. The Italian historians especially reveal an ill-timed, not to say audacious, objection.

### XXIII

This ancient rival of papal dominion says that the diploma appeared in the eleventh century, with additions concerning Benevento, Calabria, Sicily, and other regions—regions of particular concern to the Holy See at that time, rather than regions belonging to it in earlier centuries.

This may persuade the ignorant crowd, and Walch and the members of his school (*Praef.*, p. IV), who call the Italian historian “a treasure of antiquity and of historical events, and the chief ornament of our age.” But to men distinguished by genuine learning and acquainted with papal history, it will appear that every rule prescribed to a historian has suddenly been violated.

Do not falsity, audacity, and hostility emerge from this claim? The certain monuments of the *Carolingian Codex* prove that the historian’s testimony is false. Nicholas II, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, repels an injury rashly inflicted upon him. The annals themselves, repeatedly sprinkled with matters of this kind concerning papal dominion, reveal hostility.

Still, let us grant that Sicily was inserted into the pact of confirmation, or privilege, by Stephen IV or by his successor Saint Paschal I, and incorporated into the Carolingian donation. For the donation had been made once, twice, three times, and even four times, with new regions always specified, and therefore had to be joined together in that pact of confirmation.

Were the ancient rights of the Sicilian patrimony less certain than those of Benevento, both Calabrias, and Naples? Why, then, did Stephen II, in the year 756, in the same letters in which he thanked Pippin for acquiring possession of the cities of the Exarchate, persuade that king that the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies should be claimed for the Apostolic See as its property, as I recently stated?

Why did Hadrian testify to Charles in 794 (*Concil.*, volume VIII, p. 963) that he would regard the Eastern Emperor as a heretic unless he restored the aforesaid patrimonies together with the consecrations of the bishops, as was stated above in the preceding dissertation, no. 10?

> “We again warn and admonish concerning the patrimonies: if he should refuse to restore them to our Holy Roman Church, we shall decree that he is a heretic on account of his persistence in such error.”

I shall deal with the other, lesser matters in the notes.

### XXIV

Since matters stand thus, it must be observed that the authenticity of this diploma is so powerful that the same historian who portrayed it as forged in 817 contends that in 1059 it was merely interpolated.

I believe that I have shown that the frivolity of this second opinion should likewise be rejected.

It remains for me briefly to gather the principal reasons why only the patrimonies of the two Sicilies [the wording is textually uncertain] are expressly confirmed by name, while the other patrimonies are passed over, so that the legitimate authority of the diploma may become increasingly clear.

The vast Syracusan and Panormitan patrimonies, celebrated in the letters of Gregory the Great and sometimes called simply “the patrimony of Sicily” or “the Sicilian patrimony” by ancient writers, are included in the confirmation of all Sicily. Likewise, the Sardinian patrimony is included in the confirmation of that island. Since the rights of the Roman Church were sufficiently protected by these general confirmations, those patrimonies are not mentioned separately among the others.

The situation is different with the patrimonies of both Calabrias and of Naples, which were located in regions still subject to Greek power, like Sicily.

Because the Calabrian patrimony was so remote, we have seen that it was treated in the same manner as Sicily, both by Stephen II and by Hadrian. But Pippin himself had dealt much earlier with the Neapolitan patrimony, which could be wrested from the Greeks by the Lombard king through the Beneventans subject to him.

Thus, in 766, Paul I thanked Pippin because he had ordered Desiderius “to compel the king to restore to your protector, blessed Peter, the patrimonies situated there at Naples, belonging to the Neapolitans and Gaetans” (*Cod. Car.*, letter 40, elsewhere 26).

And in 780 Hadrian reminded Charles of the Neapolitans’ bad faith (*ibid.*, letter 65, elsewhere 64), because they had refused to observe their agreements and had declined to restore “the patrimony of the blessed apostle Peter, which is situated there in Naples.”

Finally, although the Beneventan patrimony was not under Greek control, the three letters of the *Carolingian Codex* clearly show how difficult its condition still was in 788 (89 and following, elsewhere 90, 92, 88).

Accordingly, confirmation in Ludovic’s pact was necessary both for this patrimony and for those that were under Greek control, lest the rights of the Holy See—rights which the grandfather and father had tried in vain to assert—suffer any loss, since they would return to the Holy See when it seemed good to the almighty God.

We saw this finally occur during the eleventh century, when the Italian historian, having investigated antiquity not at all, did not hesitate to brand Nicholas II as an impostor, without any monument, any brief historical account, or even any condemnable witness.

## XXV

Thus far two titles, or, better put, two kinds of legal basis on which papal dominion rests, have been clearly and distinctly demonstrated. Namely, the voluntary submission of the peoples, after their revolt from the Greeks, subjected Rome and its duchy to the Roman pontiffs. Through the generosity of the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles, they acquired the remaining provinces and cities. Louis confirms all these things perpetually to Paschal and his successors, so that he may retain them in his own right, principate, and dominion.

There follows another kind of generosity or donation by the aforesaid kings, concerning which the pontiffs had reached no agreement with the kings; rather, the kings themselves, of their own will, granted these possessions to the prince of the apostles and his successors. We shall discuss donations of this kind, since they are not expressed in the diploma, when the order of events brings us to the privilege of Saint Henry, where the voluntary donations of all the predecessors of this Augustus will be discussed.

Here one feature of the Carolingian material must be considered, since it dismisses—or rather drives away—several recent questions about the kind of dominion by which the pontiffs acquired these possessions. In the year 774, therefore, when Charles first came to Rome, he not only renewed and strengthened his paternal donation, adding a considerable part of Lombard Tuscany, but also offered to Saint Peter another part of Tuscany, distinguished from the former as a duchy—recent writers have given it the name “Regalis.” It contained the cities of Luna, Pisa, Lucca, Volterra, Siena, Pistoia, Florence, Arezzo, and New Clusium, together with the duchy of Spoleto, both of them separated from Italy properly so called, that is, from Lombardy.

Adrian testifies to this matter (Codex Carolinus, ep. 56, elsewhere 58). In the year 776 he says:

> “Because you also recently offered the duchy of Spoleto itself to your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through our mediation, as a reward for your soul.”

No similar evidence for the duchy of Tuscany is supplied by the letters of the Codex Carolinus. Its condition, however, is found to be very different from that of Spoleto. For several other dukes of different cities are encountered: the duke of Clusium, the Florentine, and the Lucan (Cod. Car. ep. 55, elsewhere 60; 80, elsewhere 64; 50, elsewhere 55). These both establish the truth of the matter and frustrate the feeble efforts of those who investigate the metropolitan authority of Tuscany at that time.

Moreover, both the duchy of Spoleto, which was entrusted to one man, and Tuscany, which was administered by several dukes, were offered by Charles to Saint Peter and his successors. They are distinctive additions to Louis’s diploma, which not only declares the diploma genuine but most abundantly confirms the supreme papal dominion in the remaining territories.

## XXVI

Indeed, the concession of merely usufructuary dominion; the precept, or papal diploma, by which each duchy is restored to Charles, its donor; and the clear declaration of the supreme right reserved to Charles himself are such manifest indications of genuineness that they exclude any other proof.

Moreover, their combination—or that final clause:

> “Always preserving our dominion in every respect over these same duchies, and their subjection to our authority”—

provides two arguments that are even less open to doubt:

1. All the revenues of these duchies are confirmed to Saint Peter and his successors. These revenues had shortly before been expressly listed as tributes, payments, and offerings. Thus the copy of the Adrianean collection correctly reads *dationes*, “payments,” not *donationes*, “donations,” as the Codex reads through a scribal error.

2. These two duchies alone, throughout the ecclesiastical dominion, did not belong to the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff in Louis’s time. For the emperor, in order to accommodate the pontiff, had confirmed the remaining rights by imperial authority in such a way that they would continue in the right, principate, and dominion of the Holy See until the end of the age, as he indicates in what follows, using these and still stronger words.

This was done for no other reason than that thereafter the pontiffs might appear, by imperial authority, to exercise supreme dominion in the regions donated by the kings of the Franks, as well as in Rome and its duchy, in order to restrain the boldness of subjects. These could not be restrained from plotting against the life of the supreme ruler and invading the Church’s estates merely by the renewed majesty of the emperor, as I said above (no. 8).

Anyone who thinks otherwise departs far from the truth. The many indications of dominion that precede the kings’ donations and are clear in the Codex Carolinus demonstrate this. After the donations, when nothing more was feared from the Lombards and the Frankish patriciate provided great protection against Greek efforts, nearly as many arguments are available from the same Codex as there are letters of the Roman pontiffs. For the sake of brevity, more certain and evident evidence may be drawn from the preliminary discussion of Adrian’s letters and from letters 63, elsewhere 65; 76, elsewhere 75; 81, elsewhere 67; and 97, elsewhere 85.

## XXVII

I cannot persuade myself that the two oft-praised men failed to notice this—not to mention their followers, as many or more, whom I disregard. For the inconsistency of both men—now calling Louis’s diploma genuine, now forged, now interpolated—clearly shows that each was conscious of his own error.

But how could it be otherwise? At first glance, the only interpolation appears to be the confirmation of the three islands. Yet what follows dispels the suspicion:

> “And with the territories, maritime shores, and ports belonging to the cities and islands written above.”

And again below, where all the rights of the Holy See are gathered together:

> “Namely, concerning the provinces, towns, cities, fortified places, castles, villages, islands, territories, and patrimonies written above, as well as the payments and tributes.”

And finally, a third time, where he promises to defend the islands together with all the things mentioned above:

> “So that all these things may firmly remain in his dominion, for use, enjoyment, and disposition.”

What is more, from any city subject to the Holy See, he promises to receive persons fleeing to him either from a desire to withdraw themselves from papal rule, from an intention to foment revolution, or from fear of punishment, solely for this purpose: if their fault is slight, he will seek pardon for them; if it is serious, he will return them to their own ruler to be punished. The only exceptions are those who have suffered violence or have been oppressed by the power of other citizens and therefore require imperial intervention with the pontiff.

Nor should you think that these provisions were inserted by chance. The audacity of Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had not slipped from his mind (Cod. Car. ep. 52, elsewhere 53): in 775 Leo had gone to Charles without the pontiff’s knowledge, plotting revolution in the exarchate. Nor had Adrian’s example been erased from memory (ibid., ep. 61, elsewhere 1): Adrian had demanded that certain persons subject to him be sent back by Charles, just as two years earlier he himself had sent a subject of Charles back to Francia for the same reason. A more recent example of the same pontiff was also kept in mind (ibid., ep. 97, elsewhere 85): in 790 he had demanded from Charles the return of certain Ravennates and inhabitants of the Pentapolis who wished to withdraw from his obedience.

Moved by this example, Eccardus (*De rebus Francorum*, book XXV, chapter 38) and the Italian annalist (Annals, 789) openly admitted that at that time the Roman pontiff exercised dominion in the exarchate and the Pentapolis.

## XXVIII

I see, indeed, indications of dominion in the city of Rome no less clear than those in the exarchate. For in the letter cited (61, elsewhere 50), Adrian not only demands the return of persons subject to him but demands that they be punished. After emphasizing to Charles the enormity of their wicked crimes, he addresses him in these words:

> “That, rising up manfully, with God inspiring you, you may order legal vengeance to be exercised upon them by us, as a pious king, for their miserable and shameful presumption . . . or that you may deign to send them to us, so that almighty God, looking down from on high upon the just vengeance inflicted upon them by us, may grant you, and so forth.”

I am not surprised, however, that they acknowledge dominion in the exarchate while denying the same dominion in Rome. Some of them expect the donation of the City to have occurred in one year, others in another, and they all expect it to have occurred with an uncertain kind of dominion.

The idea has become deeply rooted in the minds of Frankish writers that the Roman pontiffs derived indirect, or temporal, power from the donations of the Frankish kings. We hold this opinion to be entirely false, since we know for certain that twenty-five years before Pippin—the first of all to enlarge the papal territory—gave the provinces of Emilia and the Pentapolis of the exarchate, Gregory III, Zachary, and for some time Stephen II exercised dominion in Rome and its duchy.

Other writers, however, both because they had absorbed the same false opinion, and because they do not see that the pontiffs just mentioned abandoned hope of converting the Greeks before the year 753, when Stephen II himself sought protection for the Holy See in Francia, and finally because they know that Pippin donated only the exarchate and that nothing else was added to Pippin’s donation until Charles’s first arrival in Rome in 774, attribute the donation of the City to Charles, in an uncertain year, with uncertain dominion and an uncertain author.

I have no need to attack again the delusions of both classes of writers, since they have been refuted by the letters of Adrian’s predecessors. I shall, however, demonstrate as briefly as possible the great difference between the dominion of the City and its duchy and the other territories of the Apostolic See, thereby making Louis’s diploma more transparent.

## XXIX

Although the supreme papal dominion over the City, and consequently over its duchy, is established by several letters of the Codex Carolinus, none proves it better than the very letter (97, elsewhere 85) in which Peter’s patriciate is compared with Charles’s patriciate. For this reason Eccardus and the Italian annalist are compelled to admit the same supreme dominion in the exarchate, as we have said.

For if Charles’s dominion in the City was nothing other than the defense of the City before he became emperor, and afterward a sharing of the same supreme power with the pontiffs, then, when he was designated patrician in Francia together with his father Pippin and his brother Carloman by Stephen II in the year 754, that same Stephen was lord in Rome, just as his predecessors Gregory III and Zachary had been. Paul I, his successor and brother, is called in letters to Pippin, king and patrician of the Romans, “Our Lord, appointed by God,” by the Roman Senate and People.

That dominion, nevertheless, was not without the participation of the Roman Senate and People, who rendered an oath of loyalty to the pontiff as supreme ruler, while Roman civil law or right remained intact. Thus the Roman pontiff was at that time indeed the supreme ruler, but by no means absolute in the administration of the republic.

Nor did Stephen IV or Saint Paschal attempt anything new against the Senate and People when they later desired their own supreme authority in the City to rest upon imperial authority. Roman pontiffs had never practiced such a thing. Rather, they wished Louis to strengthen that very authority by which their predecessors had governed, without in any way diminishing the administration of the Roman Senate and People.

The words of the diploma are so clear that they require no commentary:

> “Just as you have held and administered [the City] in your power and dominion from your predecessors until now.”

I therefore wish this to be accepted as established: Paschal’s dominion did not begin anew, but was strengthened by Augustus Louis—the dominion which for almost ninety years the Roman Senate and People, defecting from the impious Greeks, had voluntarily embraced in the person of Gregory III as the head of the holy commonwealth, and had acknowledged in the letters cited above to King Pippin, without any diminution of their own authority. The subsequent course of events, as I demonstrated openly in the preceding dissertation, showed this sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

## XXX

In the other territories acquired through the generosity of rulers, however, the Roman pontiff alone ruled as an absolute prince, without the participation of the Senate and People. For their dominion had been granted to Peter alone and to his successors.

Several letters of the Codex Carolinus, witnesses beyond all exception, explicitly convey this. Concerning the cities of the Pentapolis, Paul said:

> “Which you have conferred upon blessed Peter as a great reward for your soul” (ep. 18, elsewhere 15).

Elsewhere, concerning the entire exarchate, he says:

> “You strive to preserve perpetually, with his right unimpaired, those things which you promised to blessed Peter and endeavored to grant for the forgiveness of your sins” (ep. 40, elsewhere 26).

Likewise he says that the donation was made:

> “To blessed Peter and to his vicar, our predecessor, my lord and brother of blessed memory, Pope Stephen” (ep. 42, elsewhere 19).

Adrian addresses Charles the Great in the same sense:

> “Which [things] [are] for blessed Peter, as a great reward for your soul and for the stability of your God-protected kingdom” (ep. 52, elsewhere 53).

He accuses Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, of saying concerning the cities of Emilia:

> “That your Excellency did not at all grant those cities to blessed Peter and to us” (ep. 53, elsewhere 52).

More importantly, in the following letter he reminds him how

> “You recently offered that same promise to the same apostle of God with your own hands.”

Finally, speaking of all the patrimonies, he says:

> “Those which, through various emperors, patricians, and other God-fearing men, for the reward of their souls and the forgiveness of their sins, in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Benevento, and in Corsica, as well as in the Sabine patrimony, have been granted to blessed Peter the apostle and to the holy Church of God and the Apostolic Roman Church” (ep. 59, elsewhere 49).

I pass over many other passages that, together with these, were appropriately cited above. These few, however, demonstrate the great distinction between the donations of the kings and the dominion of the City and its duchy.

For this reason, even the Swabian emperors—the greatest of all invaders of such donations—are not found to have imitated the Romans. They left the pontiffs only the name of ruler while usurping the temporal administration of the commonwealth for so long and with such obstinate determination. So greatly did the patriciate, or defense, of the prince of the apostles prevail over the defense of the emperors!

## XXXI

The archbishops of Ravenna also dared to disturb this absolute dominion in the exarchate. What then? Adrian reports to Charles (Cod. Car. ep. 51, elsewhere 54) how Stephen II deposed Sergius, who claimed too much for himself:

> “We, most excellent son, wish in our own times to administer and order it under our authority, just as in the time of our lord Pope Stephen, who went there to Francia and to whom the exarchate itself was entrusted. Everyone can recognize from this what authority his blessedness possessed three times over in that same city of Ravenna and throughout the entire exarchate. He even removed Archbishop Sergius from it when Sergius was striving, in the spirit of pride, to act against his will.”

Leo’s obstinacy, however, was suppressed by a short life. For he died in 777, after causing Adrian scarcely three years of trouble. Thereafter no similar example of such audacity is found.

Indeed, in the year 790 the same pontiff treats the Franks subject to Charles in the same manner as the Ravennates and inhabitants of the Pentapolis subject to blessed Peter and to himself (Cod. Car. ep. 97, elsewhere 87):

> “Just as your men do not come to the threshold of the apostles or to us without your absolution, so also our men who wish to come to you should come with our absolution and letter. For just as we, always receiving your men, admonish them to remain in your service with all their strength in true faith and purity of heart, so we ask your royal prudence in the same way to exhort and admonish any of our men who come to you, so that, just as your father, the lord Pippin, king of blessed memory, granted them to blessed Peter and his vicar, and your Excellency later confirmed them, you may likewise order them to be admonished and exhorted not to dare to exalt themselves in pride when they hasten to you, but rather to remain subject and humble in the service of blessed Peter and subject to our command.

> “And exhort them that we shall never withdraw you from the service and dominion of blessed Peter and his vicar, but shall remain until the end of the age in the faith and purity which we promised to the apostle Peter.”

## XXXII

I now seem to have made clear why Louis, in confirming the dominion of the Roman pontiffs in the City and its duchy, uses that condition:

> “Just as you have held and administered [them] in your power and dominion from your predecessors until now.”

By contrast, he clearly confirms the territories granted to the See “by a deed of donation,” with every condition omitted:

> “To Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors until the end of the age, in such a way that they may retain them in their own right, principate, and dominion.”

This was of great importance for vindicating the genuineness of Louis’s diploma and revealing its character. Since almost everything I have discussed thus far is established from the ninety-nine letters of the Codex Carolinus and the ten Leonine letters edited by Conringius, I rightly called this diploma an epitome of the history of the letters, since by it all the rights of the Holy See are briefly gathered together and strengthened.

After this, the discipline governing the election and consecration of the Roman pontiff is confirmed. Concerning the predecessors of Stephen IV, this may be established both from the preliminary discussion of Adrian’s letters (no. 2 ff.) and from the note on the letters of the antipope Constantine.

The essential point is that the election and ordination—that is, the consecration—of the Roman pontiff was entirely free. This is confirmed still more strongly by the presence of King Pippin’s envoy at the consecration of Paul I (Cod. Car. ep. 12, elsewhere 13).

When he had arrived in Rome at the time when the pontiff’s election was taking place, Paul says:

> “Speaking with him, together with our nobles, we judged it appropriate that he be detained here until, by God’s providence, we had been illumined by the sacred apostolic blessing. Then, being more fully satisfied concerning our own purity and that of the entire people, and concerning the love which we bear toward your most benevolent Excellency and the whole Frankish people, we released him to return to you with our apostolic envoys.”

These envoys were to testify to the king that the pontiff would remain

> “in that faith and love, in that concord of charity and covenant of peace which the most blessed lord and brother of mine, the most holy pontiff, confirmed with you.”

## XXXIII

This discipline of electing and consecrating the pontiff, and afterward sending envoys to the king of Francia to renew the aforesaid concord between kingdom and priesthood, is so firm and constant that no example whatever opposed to it can be found.

Indeed, the usurper Constantine himself sent envoys to the king only after his detestable election and ordination (Cod. Car. ep. 43, elsewhere 98), promising that, following the example of Stephen and Paul, he would

> “remain in your charity, faithful love, and sincere friendship.”

He repeats and presses this point again and a third time in the following letter.

The embassies and letters of Stephen III and Adrian sent to the kings after their consecration do not survive. Nevertheless, the same conclusion is supplied by other letters of both pontiffs (ibid., ep. 47, 62).

Stephen says to Charles and Carloman, brothers:

> “In your love and charitable affection we remain and shall remain firmly, together with the whole people, unto our very soul and the shedding of our blood.”

And Adrian says to Charles the Great:

> “We trust that you will remain in that faith and love, and likewise in that promise, in which we too, firm and steadfast, shall remain until the end, with the Lord presiding and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, mediating, just as we promised face to face.”

The letters of King Charles preserved by Labbeus (Councils, vol. VII, p. 1128), sent through Angilbert, establish that after his consecration Leo III announced Adrian’s death and his own elevation. In them Charles declares that he wishes to renew the concord between priesthood and kingdom that had prevailed under Adrian:

> “For just as I entered into a pact with the most blessed predecessor of your holy fatherhood, so I desire to establish with your blessedness an inviolable covenant of the same faith and charity.”

Since this is so, I should gladly hear from Pagius and the Italian annalist what distinction they discern in these words of Louis’s diploma:

> “That he whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration and through the intercession of blessed Peter, shall elect by common agreement and harmony to the order of the pontificate, without any promise, shall be consecrated without any ambiguity or contradiction, according to canonical custom. And when he has been consecrated, envoys shall be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, who shall establish friendship, charity, and peace between us and them.”

Nevertheless, these two men confidently declare the diploma fictitious on the grounds that they infer this from the embassy and letters sent by Leo’s successors to Charles the Great’s son, Louis the Pious, as reported by the Astronomer in the year 816 and thereafter.

Concerning Stephen’s journey to Francia, the Astronomer says:

> “Nevertheless, he sent an embassy beforehand to satisfy the emperor concerning his ordination.”

And concerning Paschal:

> “After completing the solemn consecration, he sent envoys with an apologetic letter and very great gifts to the emperor, indicating that he had submitted to this dignity—or rather had been thrust into it—not through ambition or his own will, but through election and the acclamation of the people.”

They claim that these letters are unmistakable signs of imperial confirmation. A learned pair indeed!

## XXXIV

Yet we see that, in addition to what had been decreed in the Lateran Council of 769, lest the supreme freedom of the pontifical election and consecration suffer damage from another quarter, the words “without any promise” are inserted here.

This further confirms the integrity of the diploma. What had once been established to avert the Simoniac heresy (Council of Chalcedon, canon 2; Symmachus, to Caesar, letter 5, title 2; Hormisdas, to the bishops of Spain, letter 25, chapter 2) is found renewed through new decrees and sanctions for Italy, or the kingdom of Lombardy, Tuscany, and the exarchate, and even for the kingdom of the Franks. For at that time this plague was spreading far and wide.

Accordingly, Adrian wrote to Charles in 790 (Cod. Car. ep. 97, elsewhere 84):

> “Much money is seen to have been alienated through such wicked giving, so that, since they no longer possess gold or silver, even the property of the Churches is found to have been alienated through written emphyteuses.”

A little farther below, concerning the ordination of bishops and their examination, he says:

> “We ask and adjure you: see to it that you have made no promise or gift to anyone, because that is Simoniac and contrary to the canons.”

Charles himself, in the year 795, wished Leon to be especially admonished of this by Angilbert in a memorandum (Councils, vol. VII, p. 1129):

> “Urge him most diligently to overthrow the Simoniac heresy, which gravely defiles the holy body of the Church in many places.”

What more is needed? In that same year 816, when Stephen IV—whom Paschal imitated in the following year—announced to Augustus Louis after his consecration that his election was free from every stain, the same emperor issued a capitulary (book I, chapter 84), also reported by Labbeus (Councils, vol. VII, p. 1479), in which we read:

> “Not ignorant of the sacred canons, so that the holy Church might more freely enjoy its honor in the name of God, we have given our assent to the ecclesiastical order, namely, that bishops should be chosen from their own diocese by the election of clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, with all acceptance of persons and gifts removed, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom.”

## XXXV

Since this is so, one may read with no small astonishment the following inference, full of falsehood and audacity, in Pagius (817, no. 7), after he has quoted the passage of the diploma concerning an embassy to be sent

> “to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks”:

> “This is a pure fiction, since, while Louis the Pious was still alive, Pope Eugenius II, at the request of Lothair, his colleague in the paternal empire, established that the Roman pontiff should not be consecrated except in the presence of imperial envoys.”

No rational person could approve such a proposition:

> “The discipline governing the creation of the Roman pontiff, confirmed in Louis’s diploma in the year 817, is fictitious because in the year 825 Lothair, Louis’s son, obtained from Eugenius II the privilege that thereafter Roman pontiffs should not be consecrated unless imperial envoys were present.”

To this must be added the falsity of that privilege, recognized by Baronius, Cointius, Natalis, Papebrochius, and many Catholic authors. The Italian annalist also regards the privilege of 825 as highly suspect, although, because it suited his opinion, he embraces it with Eccardus, who altered the chronology, with open arms.

Neither Eccardus nor the annalist removes the falsity of the privilege by this chronological device. For the privilege rests on no serious authority. Its mention appears in a supplement to the history of the Lombards falsely attributed to Paul the Deacon, following the custom of such men, who borrow the name of some distinguished writer in order to lend credibility to their compilations.

After the little book on the bishops of Metz, we read:

> “In the year 825, the emperor Lothair, coming again to Italy, celebrated the mass of Saint Martin at Rome. This is the oath which he and Pope Eugenius ordered the Roman clergy and people to make:
>
> “ ‘I therefore promise to you, by almighty God, by these four sacred Gospels, by this cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the body of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that from this day forward I shall be faithful to our lords, the emperors Louis and Lothair, throughout the days of my life, according to my strength and understanding, without fraud or evil intention, while preserving the faith which I promised to the apostolic lord; and that I shall not consent that the election of a pontiff be made otherwise in this Roman See than canonically and justly, according to my strength and understanding. And he who has been elected shall not, with my consent, become consecrated pontiff before he has made, in the presence of the emperor’s envoy and the people, under oath, such an oath as the lord Pope Eugenius has voluntarily made in writing for the preservation of all things.’ ”

## XXXVI

In order to expose the delusion of Pagius and those who follow him, I think the genuine constitution of Eugenius and Lothair, issued in the atrium of the apostle Saint Peter in the year 824, should be introduced here (Roman Collection, part II, p. 207). We shall see almost the whole of it confirmed in the privileges of Otto and Henry.

As regards the election of the pontiff, therefore, the pontiff and emperor establish the following in chapter 111:

> “In the election of the Roman pontiff, no one, whether free or slave, shall presume to create any impediment. Only those Romans to whom this was anciently granted by the constitution of the holy Fathers shall elect the pontiff for themselves. If anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be consigned to exile.”

I cannot deny that the pontifical consecration once again fell under the yoke of imperial confirmation. Yet the age of this new subjection, its causes, and finally its condition are certain; and they show that it was very different from the earlier usurpation by the Goths and the emperors of the East.

The date is defined by the Bertinian Annals under the year 844 in these explicit words:

> “Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church, died, and Sergius succeeded him and was installed in the same See. After he had been ordained in the Apostolic See, Lothair sent his son Louis with Drogo, bishop of Metz, to ensure that henceforth, whenever the apostolic pontiff died, no one there should be ordained as bishop except by the emperor’s command and in the presence of his envoys. When they came to Rome, they were honorably received. After the business had been completed, the Roman pontiff consecrated Louis king by anointing him and adorned him with the belt; but he appointed Bishop Drogo as his vicar in the regions of Gaul and Germany.”

If such a privilege is no older than the year 844, then Eugenius II did not grant it to Lothair’s son Louis twenty years earlier. Rather, Sergius II granted it to Louis, Lothair’s son. The compiler, a false deacon, reversed the names and dates and fashioned from the genuine privilege the false one that we have just examined.

## XXXVII

But the compilation itself convicts the compiler, Pagius, and, in a word, all those hostile to the Apostolic See to their own ruin. For the privileges of Otto and Henry, from which they derive credibility for the false account, consistently read:

> “Such a promise as our lord and venerable spiritual father Leo is known voluntarily to have made.”

This confirms the date of the privilege still more strongly. For Leo IV, who succeeded Sergius II, although he was consecrated without the prince’s command because of fear of the Saracen invasion, nevertheless, by voluntarily making the promise, confirmed by his own example the privilege granted by his predecessor.

The *Book of the Pontiffs*, a witness beyond all exception, will testify both to the genuine and to the false privilege. Here is the entire account (section 455) of the election and consecration of Valentine, who succeeded Eugenius II in the year 827, without the presence of an imperial envoy and without any promise or oath:

> “He was elected to the see of the pontiffs by the voices of the people and the joyful voices of both Roman military bodies. Then, with fitting praises of glory and the full dignity of honor, he was escorted by them to the Lateran patriarchate and placed upon the pontifical throne. After all the Roman Senate had jubilantly kissed his feet, and after everything that had to be performed had been duly and reverently completed, great sobriety and great joy remained among the people of every sex and age. On the day of his consecration, when the serene light of day had already begun to shine, all the Romans together escorted the aforesaid bishop from the Palace to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and, with divine majesty assisting, they consecrated him supreme pontiff upon the lofty throne.”

By contrast, concerning Leo IV, the successor of Sergius II (section 497), it says:

> “Struck with fear by this danger and by what might happen in the future, they consecrated him bishop without the prince’s permission.”

And concerning Benedict III, Leo’s successor (section 558):

> “The clergy and all the nobles drew up the decree, strengthened it with their own hands, and, as ancient custom required, sent it to the invincible Augusti, Lothair and Louis.”

Thus, after Gregory III, the ancient custom of sending the decree of election to the prince was restored—in the year 847, namely, at the election of Leo IV—even though the danger threatening the City prevented them from waiting for the command and imperial envoys.

The date of this restoration, therefore, is so certain that it cannot in any way be extracted from documents of doubtful reliability.

## XXXVIII

A cause equally certain preceded this definite restoration of the former subjection: namely, the reason why Sergius allowed the Apostolic See once again to undergo a yoke long since shaken off. Louis had approved the canonical election of Gregory IV in the year 827.

For when Valentine died after a brief pontificate of forty days, Gregory IV was duly elected, yet he so steadfastly refused the supreme honor that Louis’s authority is found to have intervened before the consecration of the elected pontiff.

The Astronomer testifies to this in the *Life of Louis the Pious*:

> “Gregory, priest of the titular church of Saint Mark, was elected, his consecration being postponed until the emperor had been consulted. When the emperor gave his approval and confirmed the election of the clergy and people, Gregory was ordained in place of his predecessor.”

The annals attributed to Einhard and the Bertinian Annals confirm the same matter in different words:

> “He was not ordained before the emperor’s envoy came to Rome and examined what kind of election the people had made.”

Pagius and others use these testimonies to strengthen the supposed constitution of Eugenius and Lothair mentioned above. But since those same annals report Valentine’s election and consecration without mentioning any imperial consent, they rather demonstrate that the emperor’s authority was sought because Gregory refused the office, in order to protect a canonical and just election, than that they attribute such an unjust usurpation to the pious emperor.

Moreover, if they attempt by such devices to weaken the discipline confirmed by the same Augustus Louis in the diploma under discussion, issued in 817, I have already said (no. 35) how much weight should be assigned to this kind of argument.

In any event, the certain cause of the restored subjection was the aforesaid appeal to imperial authority; its restorer was Sergius II, at the request of Lothair, Louis’s son.

As long as his pious father lived, Lothair attempted nothing new. But after Louis died in the year 840, and Gregory IV also died at the beginning of 844, the Romans elected and ordained Sergius according to the discipline of that time without consulting the emperor. Lothair therefore sent his son Louis to the City to obtain the aforesaid privilege from the Apostolic See.

### XXXIX

I certainly would not dare to determine whether Lothar, because of the hostilities that had arisen between himself and Gregory—since Gregory had been unwilling to abandon the friendship of Lothar’s father Louis and attach himself to Lothar—or for some other secret reason, sought that privilege from the Apostolic See, adducing as an example that same Gregory, who had assumed the pontificate through imperial authority. This much I know for certain: neither Lothar, nor his son Louis, among the Carolingian Augusti [Col. 0573D], nor any of the Germans, imitated the Eastern Goths or Eastern emperors in this matter. For, throughout their lifetimes, they regarded the elections of the Roman pontiffs as valid, not by virtue of a privilege attached to imperial dignity, but by apostolic concession; this will become clear when the elections of those pontiffs are examined.

During the reigns of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, Leo III, Stephen IV, Paschal I, Eugenius II, Valentine, and Gregory IV were elected. No confirmation of an election is found except the necessary confirmation of the last of these. An irresistible proof that this confirmation was sought by the clergy and people from an emperor who had been elected accidentally and only under sheer necessity, but who refused it, is the election of Sergius II, who succeeded Gregory IV, and his consecration, carried out without any consultation of Lothar.

Another argument is supplied by Gregory himself. For, unlike Saint Gregory the Great his predecessor, or Saint Gregory VII, in whose time imperial confirmation was in force, he did not send humble letters to the Augustus [Col. 0574A] asking him to confirm his election. Rather, fully aware of the discipline that prevailed in his own age, he first testified in secret and then openly and steadfastly that he shrank from so great a burden.

After Louis II, at the command of his father Lothar, had obtained the apostolic privilege, Leo IV, Benedict III, Nicholas I, Adrian II, and John VIII were inaugurated over a period of twenty-five years, in accordance with this discipline established by papal authority.

The situation was different with the nine successors of John VIII, elected over a period of sixteen years from 882 to 898: Martin II, Adrian III, Stephen V, Formosus, Boniface VI, Stephen VI, Romanus, Theodore II, and John IX. It will be found that all of them were ordained without the prince’s command or the presence of his envoys. This demonstrates that Charles the Fat and his successors lacked that personal privilege.

### XL

Three pontiffs were elected and consecrated during the reign of Charles the Fat. The emperor took the last of them, Stephen V, badly, for reasons unknown to us, because he had been created without his knowledge [Col. 0574B]. The matter is reported by the Annals of Fulda, in Freherus (vol. I, p. 60), which at the same time show how ineffectual the Augustus’s protest was:

> “When they learned of the death of their Roman pontiff, Adrian III, the Romans appointed Stephen in his place. Therefore the emperor, angry that they had presumed to ordain anyone without consulting him, sent Liutward and certain bishops of the Roman See to depose him; but they were entirely unable to accomplish this. For the aforesaid pontiff sent to the emperor through his legates a written list of more than thirty bishops, together with all the presbyters and cardinal deacons, persons of the lower orders, and the lay nobles of the region; all of them had unanimously elected him and subscribed to his ordination.”

For the sake of brevity I shall pass over the opinions of others, especially those who attribute to Adrian III a decree providing that the former freedom of consecration should henceforth be restored. But I have no doubt in affirming that, among the Carolingians [Col. 0574C], only those two Augusti made use of this personal privilege.

Yet, since during the sixteen years following the death of John VIII and preceding the creation of John IX in 898 many evils occurred, and since the election of John himself was disturbed by the Sergian schism, that pontiff perceived that it would not be useless to conduct so important a matter with imperial authority. Accordingly, in the same year, after summoning a council, he decreed—among other serious matters—concerning the renewal of this privilege (Council, vol. IX, p. 502):

> “Because,” he says in chapter 10, “the holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, suffers very many acts of violence when a pontiff dies, and these are inflicted because the consecration of the pontiff takes place without the emperor’s knowledge and without the presence of his legates; and because the envoys sent by the emperor, in accordance with canonical rite and custom, are not present to prevent violence and scandals from occurring at his consecration: we wish this practice henceforth to be abolished. The pontiff to be appointed shall be elected by the assembled bishops and the entire clergy, at the request of the senate and people; and, having thus been elected, the man who is to be ordained with the greatest publicity by everyone, he shall be consecrated in the presence of all, with the imperial legates present. No one shall dare, at his peril, to extort from him by any novel contrivance an oath or any promises, except those required by ancient custom, lest the Church be scandalized or the honor of the emperor diminished.”

### XLI

Anyone who consults the history of those times will discover how ineffectual the restoration of this privilege was. For at the end of 899 Arnulf Augustus, the last of the Carolingians, died while John IX was still alive:

> “Around the end of that year the emperor Arnulf departed this life, on the third day before the Kalends of December, and was honorably buried at Ötting, where his father also—Carloman, brother of Charles the Fat—lies buried,”

as the Annals of Metz report. The Annals of Fulda, in Freherus, give the year 900, differing by approximately one month.

As the same year was drawing to a close, John died [Col. 0575A], and Benedict IV was elected and consecrated without an emperor. This pontiff crowned Louis III with the imperial diadem in 902.
