Louis was captured and blinded by his rival Berengar, and under that same pontiff Benedict began to lead a miserable and uncertain life.

There can therefore be no doubt that his six successors—Leo V, Christopher, Sergius III, Anastasius III, Lando, and John X—were elected and consecrated without any assent of the emperor [119]. John X crowned Berengar emperor in 916. Berengar died while that pontiff was still alive; even if he had obtained the privilege—which no one asserts—he could not have used it under those circumstances.

For what happened afterward, when Marozia and the Tusculan counts usurped control of the City and its duchy for thirty-eight years, and no longer wished to submit to either papal or imperial authority, see Liutprand.

The Venerable Cardinal Baronius, rightly deploring the depravity of the age (900, nos. 1–8), concludes as follows:

> “Thus everything at Rome, both sacred and profane, was so entangled with factions that promotion to the Apostolic See of the Roman pontiff belonged to whichever party appeared more powerful. At one time the Roman nobles, at another the princes of Etruria, used secular power to install whoever they wished and to overthrow whichever Roman pontiff they could, when he had been promoted by the opposing faction. These practices continued through nearly the entire century, until the emperors of Germany, the Ottos, intervened between the two parties, hostile to both—although they too, arrogantly, claimed for themselves alike the election of the pope and the deposition of the elected pope.”

### XLII

Everyone can see that this invasion by the princes was an indication of a corrupted discipline in that iron tenth century, rather than a continuation of a privilege granted to the Augusti by the Apostolic See.

Moreover, the privileges that follow clearly show that, once the decree of John IX is set aside as never having entered into practical use, Otto and Henry merely confirmed the discipline of the times of Eugenius II and Leo IV. Thus the only privilege mentioned is the one that Sergius II [Col. 0575C], at Louis’s request, granted to his father, the Augustus Lothar; and it is certain and established that Louis himself also used it.

That this privilege was personal even in the case of the German emperors—if any of them are found to have used it—is evident from the decree of Nicholas II at the council held at Rome in 1059 (Council, vol. IX, p. 1104), concerning the election of the Roman pontiff:

> “Let him be elected from the bosom of that Church itself, if a suitable candidate is found there; but if none is found there, let him be taken from elsewhere, subject to the due honor and reverence owed to our beloved son Henry, who is at present regarded as king and, with God’s granting, is expected to be the future emperor, just as we have already granted this right to him, and to those of his successors who shall personally obtain it from the Apostolic See.””

No document more suitable for confuting the opinions of Pagius and the Italian annalist could have been devised. They contend with equal confidence and rashness that confirmation of the papal election was an imperial right. Nicholas, however, declares in the clearest words that he granted this privilege to King Henry IV, and that those who personally obtain it from the Apostolic See will likewise use it.

That Henry did in fact use it is attested by the Vatican record of the creation of Saint Gregory VII, in Baronius (1073, no. 27). For, following the example of Gregory the Great,

> “Gregory promptly sent envoys to King Henry. Through them he disclosed to him the election that had taken place and earnestly begged him not to give his assent. If he did not do so, Gregory was certain that he would in no way tolerate with impunity the king’s more serious and manifest excesses. When the king learned the truth of the election, he gave his assent to it and sent Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the kingdom of Italy, to Rome, so that he might confirm the election by royal authority and take part in Gregory’s consecration. This was done without delay.”

### XLIII

This entirely removes that reproach from the Carolingian [Col. 0576A] and German Augusti which the two writers so often mentioned, siding with the partisans of both sides, cast upon them. It is as though they had imitated Odoacer and the Eastern emperors and appropriated to themselves something that, without the authority of the Apostolic See, is nothing but usurpation.

For it was not only the Augusti, who acquired a partnership in supreme authority over the papacy together with the imperial diadem, but even kings—who, by the constant confession of everyone, had nothing to do with the City or Roman affairs—who obtained this privilege from the supreme pontiffs.

What is more, Saint Gregory VII himself, who, while preparing to decline the pontificate, acknowledged the king’s privilege, thought it right not to follow the examples of his predecessors but to free the Holy See entirely from that subjection. Baronius says:

> “I would be lying if these things could not now be demonstrated by the experience of present events: namely, that through Gregory the investitures of churches were reclaimed from the hands of princes, the free election of Roman pontiffs restored to its former state, ecclesiastical discipline, which had completely collapsed, repaired, and countless other benefits obtained” (1085, no. 12).

And indeed, from that time onward no imperial or royal assent will be found to have been required for the ordination of Roman pontiffs. It can therefore safely be asserted that only two Augusti among the Carolingians, and King Henry among the Germans, used this privilege.

A different judgment must be made concerning the six German Augusti who preceded that king. The three Ottos, having embraced the corrupted discipline of the tenth century, must not be taken into account at all.

Saint Henry the Augustus, crowned by Benedict VIII, would never have departed from what was right and just, such was his piety. But both he and Benedict died within a short interval in 1024, and John XIX, elevated from the laity to the pontificate through the payment of money, as Glaber says in Baronius (1024, no. 4), was confirmed by no one.

Nor is it found anywhere that Benedict IX, likewise elected, was confirmed by Conrad the Salian.

Only Henry III, king and emperor of Germany, appears to have used this privilege. But since he did not obtain it through apostolic authority, I do not think that even he should be compared with the two Carolingians. Peter Damian had already held the same opinion before me (*Disputation between the Royal Advocate and the Defender of the Roman Church*, Council, vol. IX, p. 1159).

### XLIV

I shall reproduce the very words, for it is no small matter to reduce to King Henry IV alone the privilege that the Italian annalist regarded as an imperial right. The royal advocate is introduced as speaking in this manner:

> “The father of my lord the king, Henry, of pious memory, after he had been made emperor, became patrician of the Romans, from whom he received, in the election for the ordination of the pontiff, the primacy. In addition, and what is more important, Pope Nicholas granted to this lord of mine the king the privilege which he had already received by paternal right, and further confirmed it by the written instrument of a synodal decree.”

The advocate of the Roman Church also maintains that the right of the Augustus Henry rested upon the authority of the Roman people, and, venerating only the authority of the Holy See, replies:

> “We too defend this privilege for our most invincible king, and we desire that he possess it in complete and unimpaired form.”

He then demonstrates that the ordination of Alexander II took place without Henry’s knowledge because Henry was still a minor. Indeed, we recently saw that Gregory, Alexander’s successor, remembered this same privilege.

Anyone who holds a contrary view resorts to the support of corrupted discipline and, mixing usurpation with the tolerance of the pontiffs, which was in some sense necessary, assigns more than is proper to the Augusti, to the greatest detriment of papal authority.

So much for the privilege of Henry IV.

But since Otto and Henry, in their privileges, praise the constitution of Eugenius II and the spontaneous promise of Leo IV, and since the patchwork composition cited above (no. 35) arose from this, it is worthwhile, in order to determine what the true discipline of papal election and consecration ought to have been in the time of the Germans, and what should be attributed to Eugenius and to Leo, to learn the truth of the matter from historians who were for the most part nearly contemporary.

### XLV

Astronomus, in his *Life of Louis the Pious* (Pithou edition, p. 222), relates how Lothar, sent by his father to Rome,

> “was received most willingly by Pope Eugenius. When he complained about the matters that had occurred—namely, why those who had been faithful to the emperor and the Franks had been killed by an unjust death, while the survivors were left and treated as objects of ridicule; and why such great complaints were being voiced against the Roman pontiffs and judges—it was discovered that, through either the ignorance or negligence of certain pontiffs, but also through the blind and insatiable greed of the judges, the estates of many people had been unjustly confiscated. Therefore, by restoring what had been unjustly taken away, Lothar created great joy for the Roman people.”

The annals attributed to Einhard report the same matter:

> “When he had disclosed to Eugenius the matters entrusted to him—the condition of the Roman people, which had long been corrupted by the perversity of certain prelates—the pope corrected it with such benevolent agreement that all who had been grievously desolated by the seizure of their property were greatly comforted by the recovery of their possessions, which, through his arrival and by God’s favor, had been restored.”

Eugenius’s predecessors had been Saint Leo III, Stephen IV, and Saint Paschal I. Astronomus therefore more appropriately accuses the judges of greed and calls the pontiffs ignorant or negligent, whereas the annalist, whoever he may have been, calls them perverse.

Furthermore, the privileges of Otto and Henry blame the “unreasonable harshness of the pontiffs toward the people subject to them.” The constitution itself made by Eugenius and Lothar also exposes the excessive freedom taken by this annalist, as we shall see when we discuss those privileges.

But let us set aside these minor matters. The oath imposed upon the Romans by Lothar and Eugenius, as it is described in the aforementioned patchwork concerning the canonical and just election of the pontiff, is either certain or highly probable.

What is asserted there, however, through an obvious falsehood concerning a promise spontaneously made by Eugenius, reveals—with due pardon to Eccardus and the Italian annalist—the forgery of Pseudo-Warnehfrid. Otto and Henry—or rather the Apostolic Archive and the *Liber Pontificalis*—serve as witnesses. Accordingly, that spontaneous promise must be postponed to the consecration of Leo IV in 847, after the privilege granted by Sergius II three years earlier. Leo is said to have made the promise voluntarily because, owing to fear of the Saracens, neither the emperor’s command nor his envoy had been awaited; therefore that promise was not necessary.

### XLVI

We have already seen that this discipline prevailed under the Augusti Lothar and Louis; that it was vainly restored by John IX in 900 after having fallen into disuse; that it was confirmed amid the great corruption of the tenth century by Otto and Henry, though never put into practice; and finally that it was preserved only in the creation of Gregory VII, who abolished it.

Let us now return to the objection of Pagius, who declares the diploma of Louis to be a mere fabrication because it displays a discipline entirely different from that instituted nearly thirty years later. Is this not to pass judgment on matters that have been wholly unexplored [Col. 0577D]?

Every sensible person will regard his remaining objections as worthless. When he says that none of the Roman pontiffs ever mentioned Louis’s donation, and that Otto and Henry list the donations of Pippin and Charles but remain silent about Louis’s, he exposes his own ignorance, because he has failed to understand the nature of the diploma: all the rights of the Holy See are confirmed in it, without a single yard of land being added to the earlier donations.

Likewise, when he supposes that Sicily and the other islands were granted by Louis to the Apostolic See, I may say, with due respect, that he is disgracefully mistaken.

To prove the diploma false, however, it was necessary to discover in it words and formulas inconsistent with its period, just as Ludewig (*Preface to the Relics of Manuscripts of Every Age*, § 22) declared a diploma of Charlemagne concerning Frisia spurious because he saw that it contained references to:

- feudal law;
- the perpetual Augusti;
- the duchy of Saxony;
- fiefs dependent upon the empire;
- the king of Saxony;
- the council of the faithful;
- the consent of the princes of the empire;
- the signatures of the king of Bohemia;
- the margrave of Meissen;
- the landgrave of Thuringia.

For, however much diligence the makers of a fabrication may employ in imitating the character of a remote age, they must sometimes slip into the customs of their own time.

Indeed, if Pagius and the Italian annalist had raised any of these objections, I would be ashamed to fight so vehemently for the validity of the diploma.

But to the objections of Pagius—which I said should be treated with contempt rather than refuted—the aforementioned annalist adds one more, more suitable to a litigant pleading a case than to someone weighing ancient documents (year 817): namely, that the diploma did not at all proceed from the chancery of Louis, because it lacks a date, which is an indication that only an unfinished copy of it survives.

But what scholar has ever dared to assert that the autographs of the diplomas of Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis have survived to our distant posterity? Nevertheless, such great credibility is supplied to them by the *Codex Carolinus* and other historical records that the absence of the autographs is consistently judged a very slight loss.

The Chorographer of medieval Italy also serves as a reserve for Pagius and the annalist. Nevertheless, he bases whatever truth there is in his map upon this principal support, so that he would rather resemble someone who drills a hole in the ship in which he himself is sailing than the aforementioned authors, upon whose words he swears while opposing them.

### XLVII

The absence of a date—an external defect—does little harm to Louis’s diploma, since the same defect occurs in other documents that are not of such great antiquity.

The date is in fact given as the assembly at Aachen in the year 817, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, as appears at its beginning (Council, vol. VII, p. 1507) [124]:

> “In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 817, in the fourth year of the empire of the most glorious prince Louis, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, when several abbots, together with their monks, had assembled in the house of the palace at Aachen which is called Lateran, etc.”

Among them is listed Joshua, abbot of the monastery of Volturno, highly esteemed by the pontiff, as Mabillon teaches (*Annals*, book XXVIII, no. 45). He supplied the chronicler of that monastery with the documentary record, as we stated above (no. 9 and following).

What deserves greatest attention in the diploma is that subscriptions in the ancient manner are appended, of the sort said to have belonged to the donation first made by King Pippin at Quierzy.

Concerning the Pippinian donation, the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 318) reports the following in the *Life of Adrian*:

> “That promise which his father, King Pippin, of sacred memory, and the most excellent Charles himself, together with his brother Carloman and all the judges of the Franks, had made to blessed Peter and to his vicar, the lord Stephen, pope of sacred memory.”

Elsewhere it had said of the same matter (section 253):

> “He sent to blessed Peter, to the holy Roman Church, and to all the pontiffs of the Apostolic See in perpetuity, for possession, what is still preserved to this day in the archive of our holy Church.”

I do not see what differs from this in the conclusion of Louis’s diploma:

> “We sent it through Theodore, the nomenclator and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to the lord Paschal, pope.”

The subscriptions likewise belong to the emperor, his sons, bishops, abbots, counts, and palace officials. Their number alone is given both by the Volturno and Cassino chroniclers, just as they are numbered in the diploma itself.

This is the strongest indication of antiquity. It can be inferred from Anselm of Lucca—unless, perhaps, the collection attributed to him is somewhat later—who in that same year, 1073, entered upon the episcopate of Lucca, when Gregory VII entered upon the pontificate.

For he included in his collection of canons, later enlarged by Gratian, the chapter on the election of the pontiff from the privileges of Otto and Henry (book VI, chapter 35), and at the end says:

> “Both emperors subscribed, each in his own time, as did twenty-three bishops, six abbots, thirteen counts, and seventeen nobles; their names will be seen below in both privileges—ten bishops in the Ottonian privilege, thirteen in the Henrician, and likewise the others joined together by Anselm.”

Accordingly, it cannot be denied that a copy of Louis’s diploma has come down to us—yet a copy of considerable antiquity, since it was known to Anselm himself (book IV, chapter 35), just as were the two documents mentioned above. It was derived not from the autographs but from the copies of which I spoke at the beginning (no. 2 and following), and whose principal document was the complete diploma of Louis, while the other two were abridged. This is clear from the listing of the subscriptions.

[Col. 0579]

[125] **Note:** Variant readings are supplied from the copy in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo.

## PRIVILEGE OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS CONFIRMING THE REGAL RIGHTS TO POPE PASCHAL

[Col. 0579A]

In the name of God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

**Note [Col. 0579B]:** For the various invocations of the Carolingians, see what was said above (*Dissertation*, no. 11). The diplomas of Otto and Henry also display this invocation, a highly probable indication that the diplomas of Pippin and Charlemagne, which are missing, had the same form. For a copy of the preceding concessions of this kind was requested from the Apostolic Archive; it seems to have been considered improper to alter their formulas. Walchius (*Censure of Diplomas*, p. 12 and following) tries in vain to weaken the diploma on the basis of invocations customary in his own time.

I, Louis, Augustus, emperor, establish and grant by this pact of confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you to your vicar, the lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors in perpetuity, just as you have held and administered them until now, having received them from your predecessors, in your power and jurisdiction: the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, together with all its villages and mountainous territories, as well as its maritime districts, shores, and ports, or all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany; namely, Porto, Centumcellae, Ceri, Blera, Manturanum [Maturanum], Sutrium, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Horta [Orta], Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, namely the greater and lesser Pulvensis [Pulvensis and the lake], Narni [Col. 0580A], and Otricoli, together with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the cities written above.

**Note [Col. 0579C]:** The unusual beginning of the diploma confirms the same point, since Otto and Henry use the same form. Mabillon (*Benedictine Annals*, Appendix, no. 26) cites a diploma of Pippin with this subscription: “I, Pippin, and my wife Bertrada.” From this simplicity of subscription one might infer that Pippin himself, his son Charles, and therefore his grandson Louis, did not wish to use any other formula.

**Note [Col. 0579C]:** Baronius, Hardouin, Lecointe, and Sigonius, together with Cencio, rightly retain *vestris* (“your predecessors”); all the manuscripts consistently have this reading, and the sense proceeds accordingly, since Paschal had received Rome and its duchy from his own predecessors. Gratian, the Annals of Reichersberg, Baluze, Muratori, Walchius, and others read *nostris* (“our predecessors”) incorrectly, as though Pippin and Charles had given Rome to the pontiffs, which is manifestly false. See *Dissertation*, no. 12 and following.

In the same way, in the regions of Campania, [I grant] Segni, Anagni, Ferentino, Alatri, Patrica, and Frusino, together with all the boundaries of Campania; and also Tibur, together with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities [Col. 0580B].

**Note [Col. 0579D]:** A considerable part of the Roman duchy consists of the lake near Perugia. This is Lake Trasimene, famous in Roman history for Hannibal’s victory. See Cellarius (*Ancient Geography*, book II, chapter 9). Elbertus (*Medieval Etruria*) testifies that the three islands mentioned here are in the lake and inhabited; he complains that the Apostolic cosmographers and geographers make no mention of this lake. The Anonymous Chorographer (*Italian Writers*, vol. X, table, section 20) discusses it very fully.

**Note [Col. 0579D]:** Narni is one of the places which the pontiffs acknowledge as having been received from the Frankish kings (*Carolingian Code*, letters 8, 9, and elsewhere 4, 6). Stephen II complained that the Lombards had invaded it; he said to Pippin that “your Christianity granted it to blessed Peter.” The people of Spoleto had formerly invaded it (Anastasius, section 254), but Aistulf, terrified at Pippin’s first arrival, restored it. Anastasius (section 249).

**Note [Col. 0579D]:** The more distant cities of Latium, or of the Roman duchy, on this side of the Tiber are listed. The fields or districts are generally included among the Roman cities in the suburbs [Col. 0580B]. Otto mentions no city of Campania, since he understands all of them to have been expressed together under the duchy and suburbs. See the notes below on his diploma.

Moreover, the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with its cities, towns, boroughs, and castles, which the pious-memory lord King Pippin and our good-memory father, the Emperor Charles, restored by deed of donation to the blessed Apostle Peter and to your predecessors long ago: 
> **Note [Col. 0580B–D].** Here I appeal to all interpreters of diplomas and to all recent writers on pontifical history. Louis [Col. 0580C] first speaks of the apostolic dominion enlarged by Pippin and Charles, so as not to wrong his grandfather and father: “Which, he says, the pious-memory lord King Pippin and our good-memory father the Emperor Charles, etc.” Likewise below, concerning the Sabine territory: “Just as it was granted by our father the Emperor Charles.” Again, further below, concerning voluntary donations: “Which our pious-memory grandfather, the lord King Pippin, and afterward our lord and father the Emperor Charles.” And a little later, concerning Adrian’s diploma for the duchy of Spoleto: “It was agreed between the pious-memory Pope Adrian and our lord and father the Emperor Charles.” Finally, at the end, in speaking of the renewal by every pontiff after his consecration of the bond of friendship, charity, and peace: “as, he says, it was customary to do in the times of the pious-memory lord Charles, our great-grandfather, or the lord Pippin, our grandfather, or likewise Charles the Emperor, our father.” Thus Louis never calls his ancestors “predecessors,” but refers to them by name and by their title of kinship. Let Gratian, the Reichersberg annalist [Col. 0580D], Baluzius, and the other moderns now come forward, and, against Cencius and all the manuscripts, Baronius and other most learned men, confidently change *vestris* (“your”) into *nostris* (“our”), so that Rome and the duchies may assume the character of donations according to their wish. What monument do they produce? What even slightest support have they by which to sustain so novel a claim? About fifty years after this diploma, Rome itself is described by John VIII as having been granted by the pious emperors, either to flatter emperors or because Roman dominion was in truth also confirmed in imperial diplomas. But wrongly so: Louis and his successors do not grant Rome and its duchy; rather, they confirm the dominion of Rome and its duchy, as the pontiffs wished, since they rightly feared no less their subject peoples than their enemies.

namely, the city of Ravenna and Emilia [Aemilia],

> **Note [Col. 0580D].** Beginning with the donation of Pippin and Charles, he first names the whole Exarchate in its entirety, then lists its individual cities, together with all the territories belonging to those cities [Col. 0581A], which he enumerates one by one. Among them are neither Mutina, nor Parma, nor Placentia, those most celebrated cities from the time of the Republic. In the donation [Col. 0581B], Parma is named as a boundary from Tuscan Lombardy, or the royal territory, which was not far distant. In the division of the kingdoms among the sons, these same cities form part of Pippin’s kingdom. Learned men of the sixteenth century thought that these cities were in the Exarchate; in our own age, very distinguished scholars have embraced that opinion and, in learned volumes, have made it appear highly credible. I do not wish to quarrel with our countrymen; I say only this: the mention of Emilia in the Ludovician diploma indicates not a city but a province. For at that time the Exarchate was divided into two provinces: Emilia, whose cities are listed separately, and the Pentapolis, whose cities likewise are enumerated separately. Thus also in the *Codex Carolinus* the cities of the first province of the Exarchate are distinguished from those of the Pentapolis (ep. 51, 53, 54, alternatively 54, 52, 51), and they are spoken of no differently from the cities of Emilia which the archbishop of Ravenna had usurped for himself. Certainly, in this matter Muratori and the *Chorographer* are correct. Mutina, Parma, and Placentia, although cities [Col. 0581C] of Emilia whose bishops were suffragans of the metropolitan of Ravenna, do not belong to the donation of Pippin and Charles. See more in Dissertation no. 16.

Bobium [Col. 0581A],

> **Note [Col. 0581C].** That the city celebrated for the monastery of Saint Columbanus, situated in the Cottian Alps, is not mentioned here is clear from the fact that it did not enjoy episcopal dignity before the eleventh century, by authority of Benedict VIII (Ditmar, in Baronius, 1014, no. 4; Ughelli, Mabillon, etc.). Sassina, or Sarsina, must be understood as the ancient city whose bishop calls himself Bobian at the councils of Symmachus. See Dissertation no. 18.

Cesena, Forum Populi [Pompilii], Forum Livii, 127 Faventia, Imola [Imola]; Bologna, Ferrara, Comiacrum [Comiaclum], and Adria, which is also Gabelum [Gabellum], together with all the boundaries, territories, and islands on land and sea belonging to the aforesaid cities [Col. 0581C],

> **Note [Col. 0581C].** The Anonymous *Chorographer* extracts just as many cities in the Exarchate from Agnellus, Blondus, Anastasius, and Cluverius, thereby doubling the number (*Chorographical Table*, section 16). But the condition and chronology of the new names must be considered: most were castles included within the boundaries of the cities of the Exarchate; some designated places already named, as we have just seen that Bobium and Sarsina are one and the same. The diploma teaches that Adria and Gabelum are likewise one and the same city. The Exarchate, however, was donated in its entirety by Pippin and Charles as it then existed, its boundary being defined by the territory of Bologna, as is established by the aforesaid division of the kingdoms. Whoever contends that it was donated according to its earlier extent lacks documentary evidence to prove it.

and likewise the Pentapolis,

> **Note [Col. 0581D].** The variation in terminology according to the period must be noted. In the year 726, Gregory II wrote to Leo the Isaurian, who persisted in impiety, concerning the whole Exarchate as follows (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VII, p. 19): “The Lombards and Sarmatians, and the others who dwell in the north, have harassed the wretched Decapolis with raids, and have occupied the metropolis Ravenna itself; and, having expelled your magistrates, they appointed magistrates of their own.” When Pippin transferred the Exarchate to the Holy See at Quierzy in 754, there appears to have been no distinction between Emilia and the Pentapolis. The people of the Pentapolis are often praised in Paul’s letters. [Col. 0582A] Adrian, in the letters mentioned above, not only preserves that distinction but sometimes divides the Pentapolis itself into two parts (ep. 54, alternatively 51), namely the inland [Col. 0582B] and the maritime Pentapolis.

namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo [Auximum], Humana, Jesi, Fossombrone, Montefeltro, Urbino and the territory of Valva [Balneum], Cagli [Calle], Luciolis, Gubbio [Eugubium], together with all the boundaries and lands belonging to those same cities.

In the same way, the Sabine territory, just as it was granted to the blessed Apostle Peter by our father, the Emperor Charles, through a deed of donation, in its entirety, according to the definition established by the abbots Ithier and Maginarius, whom he sent, between that same Sabine territory and the territory of Rieti—

> **Note [Col. 0582B].** See the letters of the *Codex Carolinus* (59, 67, 71, 72, 73, alternatively 49, 69, 56, 76, 78) and the preliminary commentary on Adrian’s letters, no. 32 ff. From these sources the beginning of this history is available; the rest is not preserved in that Codex, and it cannot safely be determined when Abbots Ithier and Maginarius established those boundaries between the Rieti and Sabine territories. It is certain, however, that Maginarius did not attain the dignity of abbot before the year 784, when he succeeded Fulrad as abbot of Saint-Denis. Consequently, the Sabine territory was not transferred to the Holy See for possession until after that year. Since the abbot of Saint-Denis, Maginarius, died in the year 793, while Ithier survived until 796, when Alcuin succeeded him in the administration of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, it appears that the dispute over the Sabine territory came to an end between the year 791, when the letters of the *Codex Carolinus* were collected, and Maginarius’s death in 793. If this is so [Col. 0582C], we would not know of either the extraordinarily prolonged course of the case or its outcome unless this diploma existed. For Adrian’s letters make clear that the matter had been entrusted to the aforesaid abbots, but that, because difficulties arose once, twice, and three times, it could not be concluded.

Likewise, in the parts of Tuscan Lombardy, the castle of Felicitas, Orvieto, the King’s Baths, Ferento Castle, Viterbo, Orcla, 128 Marta, Tuscania, Populonia, Suana, Roselle,

> **Note [Col. 0582C].** Although these two maritime cities of the territory now belonging to Siena, like the rest, were by the donation of Charles under the jurisdiction of the Holy See, the Holy See never possessed them peacefully or wholly in the eighth century (*Codex Carolinus*, letters 88, 89, alternatively 81, 90). At the beginning of the eleventh century, in Albinus and Cencius, the following is found, with little difference: “In a certain parchment volume, which is in the cartulary beside the Palladium, it is written that Pope Benedict [VIII] leased the city and county of Suana, together with castles and villages and all their appurtenances; and the city and county of Roselle, with villages and castles and their appurtenances, jurisdiction, court, and all its payment and revenue. Each city pays sixty solidi.” Populonia and Roselle, moreover, fell away not long afterward. For at the beginning of the twelfth century the bishops of Roselle began to be called Grossetans; Rusella, once a Roman colony, had long since been destroyed (Cellarius, *Ancient Geography*, book II, chapter 9, p. 454, London edition). It was near Grosseto, just as Populonia was near Piombino (Cellarius, ibid.), as is demonstrated in both places by the conspicuous ancient ruins. The bishopric of Populonia was united with Massa. Consult Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. III, pp. 655 and 701).

and the islands Corsica,

> **Note [Col. 0582D].** The donation of this island is certain, and the donor, Charles, is likewise certain; the date, however, is uncertain. Enough has been said above concerning the other two islands; something will be added in the following diplomas. Their ancient and certain rights, especially those of Sicily, are clear. But because Louis, Stephen IV, and Paschal, following the same policy, list them among Charles’s donations, I conjecture that a genuine document must at that time have existed in the papal archive by which Charles donated the three islands. For when he saw Adrian so deeply concerned [Col. 0583B] that the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies—whose rich and ancient revenues had long ceased to be brought into the papal treasury for the support of the poor and the adornment of the churches—might be restored by Constantine and Irene, and after he had subsequently learned the whole matter from Adrian’s letter to him in the year 794 (*Councils*, vol. VII, p. 963), he may have considered subjecting Sicily, as he had done the duchy of Benevento. Meanwhile, I think that the whole island was granted to the Holy See under a condition not very different from that expressed in Otto’s diploma, if God should place that document in our hands. For it is established that Sicily remained subject to the Greeks until 827, when the Saracens invaded it. From where could that statement about Sicily have entered Otto’s diploma except from some document in the archive, from which the Ludovician diploma and several other things were supplemented? Note also that in Otto’s diploma, of which the Henrician is a copy, that conditional grant of Sicily is neither placed among Charles’s spontaneous donations nor added to his own donation. This is certain evidence that Sicily was regarded as donated by Charles, and indeed as having been the subject of an agreement with the pontiff. Why Louis passed over that condition need not be sought: he was confirming all rights to the Holy See and granting it nothing new; it would have been foolish to confirm Sicily as donated by Charles under a condition.

Sardinia and Sicily in their entirety, together with all the adjacent territories and maritime territories, shores, [Col. 0583A] and harbors belonging to the aforesaid cities and islands.

Likewise, in the parts of Campania, Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, and Capua,

> **Note [Col. 0583C].** There is no doubt that these Campanian cities were donated by Charles. This is established by the letters of the *Codex Carolinus* (ep. 88, 89, 92, alternatively 81, 90, 86). We also learn that the people of Capua rendered an oath of fidelity before the confession of blessed Peter (ep. 91, alternatively 88). And although, in taking possession of them, the same difficulties arose [Col. 0583D] as in the Sabine territory and in the two cities of Tuscany, namely Populonia and Roselle, their rights nevertheless did not lapse, since together with the others they were recovered by the pontiffs in the eleventh century with the aid of the Normans, as I shall explain below.

and the patrimonies belonging to your authority and dominion, such as the Beneventan 129 and Salernitan patrimony

> **Note [Col. 0583D].** There were two patrimonies in Campania in the time of Gregory the Great. John the Deacon, who flourished after Louis the Pious, under Pope John VIII, expressly names two patrimonies in the *Life of Gregory* (book II, no. 53), the Neapolitan and the Campanian. The same number is listed in Otto’s and Henry’s diplomas. Why, then, does Louis mention three? I have encountered the Salernitan patrimony nowhere except in this diploma. But why do I say three patrimonies? For Louis there is one patrimony, the Beneventan and Salernitan, although he designates it by two names; this creates no small difficulty for one seeking a definite explanation. Erchempertus relates (no. 14) that Siconulf was made prince of Salerno by the leading men of Benevento who had defected from Prince Radelchis; all authorities, together with Peregrine, assign this event to the year 840. There also survives a capitulary of Radelchis, prince of Benevento, from the year 851 (in Pratilli, vol. III, p. 214), by which the boundaries of both principalities were established with Siconulf, so that from then on two principalities began to be recognized. Therefore, if the Ludovician diploma had followed those events, it would be reasonable that we should learn something new from it—namely, that the patrimony of the Holy See lay in both principalities. But that diploma precedes Siconulf’s principality by nearly twenty-five years. I therefore think that Louis meant nothing more than to designate the districts of both cities in which that patrimony, divided into two parts, was situated; this was suggested to him by Stephen IV and Paschal, who were thoroughly familiar with the condition and location of that patrimony.

and the patrimony of Lower and Upper Calabria, and the Neapolitan patrimony, and wherever in the territories of the kingdom and empire entrusted to us by God your patrimonies are known to exist—

> **Note [Col. 0584C].** Consider the Tuscan, Istrian, Dalmatian, Illyrian, Ligurian, Germanician, and Gallican patrimonies, as well as any others that existed in the Gallic monarchy and did not require specific mention in order to be vindicated for the Holy See, since they lay outside Greek rule.

All these provinces, cities, and towns mentioned above, the boroughs and castles [fortresses], the villages and territories, and likewise the patrimonies, we confirm by this decree of our confirmation to your aforesaid Church, blessed Apostle Peter, and through you to your spiritual vicar, our father, the lord Paschal, supreme pontiff [Col. 0583B] and universal pope, and to his successors until the end of the age, in such a way that they may retain them in their right, principate, and dominion.

Likewise, by this decree of our confirmation, we confirm the donations which the pious-memory lord King Pippin, our grandfather, and afterward the lord and our father, the Emperor Charles, freely granted to the blessed Apostle Peter,

> **Note [Col. 0584C].** What these spontaneous donations were can be gathered from history, but they cannot be listed individually. See the Dissertation on Henry’s diploma, no. 14 ff.

and likewise the tribute and payments, or other contributions [payments], which used to be brought annually to the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscan Lombardy or from the duchy of Spoleto [Spoletan territory], as is contained in the donations set forth above. And it was found between the pious-memory Pope Adrian and the lord and our father, the Emperor Charles, when that same pontiff confirmed to him, by a precept of his 130 authority, the matters concerning the aforesaid duchies, namely Tuscany and Spoleto,

> **Note [Col. 0584C].** No clearer argument could be desired for refuting the opinions of certain persons. They debate the right granted to the Roman pontiffs in the cities and provinces of the donations—whether it was merely beneficial or supreme. Here the supreme right is defined more clearly than daylight in the other territories, with this exception concerning the duchies. These duchies too would have come under the same supreme power if Adrian had not, by his precept or diploma, granted to the donor Charles those things which already belonged to blessed Peter, as he had agreed with Charles.

in such a way that the aforesaid tribute might be paid each year to the Church of blessed Apostle Peter [Col. 0584B], while our dominion in every respect over those same duchies and their subjection to our side remain intact.

> **Note [Col. 0584D].** Concerning the remaining territories of the Holy See, whether actually possessed or belonging to it by right, it had been stated plainly that they should retain them in their right, principate, and dominion, by which supreme right is defined. Here, however, supreme dominion is declared to belong to Charles, while beneficial ownership belongs to the pontiff. Immediately, so that no suspicion of pontifical supreme dominion over all the other territories might arise, the same clause not only again declares supreme right but explains it in the clearest words. We cannot even suspect that those learned men failed to notice this; for that reason they resort to the sole remedy of supposing the document spurious. In vain: the same expressions occur in the diplomas of Otto and Henry, and it would be madness to claim that they are false.

But, as we have said, we strengthen all the things named above [Col. 0585A] on our side [your side] by this decree of our confirmation,

> **Note [Col. 0585B].** The word “agreement,” otherwise sufficiently familiar, is not without significance. In both the Ottonian and Henrician diplomas it remains unchanged, but here it is again expressed through the word “decree”; for the subject is also the confirmation of spontaneous donations, which had by no means been made by formal agreements.

so that they may remain in the right, principate, and dominion of you and your successors; so that neither by us nor by our sons or successors may your power in any part be diminished by any device or contrivance, nor may anything be taken from you or your successors out of all the aforesaid provinces, cities, towns, boroughs, castles, villages, islands, territories, and patrimonies, or from the payments and tributes. Thus neither will we take these things away nor consent to anyone wishing to take them away; rather, we promise, insofar as we can, to defend all that is written above—namely, the provinces, cities, towns, boroughs, castles, territories and patrimonies [Col. 0585B], as well as the islands, tributes, and payments of the Church of blessed Apostle Peter and of the pontiffs who shall reside forever in his most holy see—so that all these things may remain firmly held for his use, enjoyment, and disposition, in his [in no one's] dominion.

Nor do we claim for ourselves any share in these things, or any power of disposing, judging, taking away, or diminishing them, unless 131 [to the extent that] we should be asked to do so by him who at that time holds the government of this holy Church.

> **Note [Col. 0585C].** You will find this matter attested in several letters of the *Codex Carolinus*, but especially in the preliminary commentary on Adrian’s letters (no. 7 ff.). The final words are not found in the Ottonian diploma, but great changes in circumstances and times had taken place. Moreover, in the oath which began under Otto and which all his successors customarily swore, much fuller and clearer provisions appear, which did not concern the Franks. In particular, observe the following directed against those who do not hesitate to subject Rome itself to the emperors: “In the city of Rome I shall make no judgment or regulation concerning anything that belongs to you or to the Romans without your counsel” (*Distinction* 63, chapter 33).

And if any person from the aforesaid cities belonging to your Church should come to us [shall come], wishing to withdraw himself from your dominion or power, or fearing some other unjust [any] contrivance, or fleeing a fault he has committed, we shall in no way receive him otherwise than for the purpose of making a just intercession on his behalf—provided only that the fault he committed is found to be pardonable. Otherwise, once he has been apprehended, we shall return him to your power [shall return him].

> **Note [Col. 0585C].** These provisions, which are rightly omitted by Otto and Henry, to whom that reciprocal observance between priesthood and kingdom did not pertain, must be learned from the letters of the *Codex Carolinus*, especially letters 76 and 97, alternatively 75 and 85. From this it will be clear how excessively easy it is to condemn ancient documents when they conflict with one’s own opinion.

Except those who have suffered violence or oppression at the hands of powerful persons and have therefore come to us [come] so that through our intercession they may deserve to receive justice. Their condition is different and is entirely distinct from the preceding one.

And when, by divine summons, the pontiff of this most sacred see has departed from this world, no one from our kingdom—whether a Frank, a Lombard, or a person of any nation subject to our authority—shall have permission to come against the Romans, publicly or privately, or to conduct an election.

> **Note [Col. 0585D].** Stephen III, at the Lateran council in 769, decreed the following concerning the election of the Roman pontiff: “No one from the castles of Tuscany or Campania, or from other places, shall dare enter Rome, nor shall they be invited by anyone or brought into the city. Nor shall anyone from the servants of either the clergy or the soldiery be present at that election; nor shall anyone at all come with arms or clubs.” Likewise: “If anyone should presume to assist or introduce into this city of Rome anyone from any city, castle, or place before the pontiff has departed, until a pontiff has been ordained in the see of blessed Peter, let him be anathema.” You may see similar decrees concerning the Franks and other peoples subject to Louis, issued by the council of the pontiff, so that the freedom of the election might be complete. But observe the discipline carefully. In the time of Stephen III [Col. 0586B], pontifical territory did not extend beyond Latium, or ancient-law Tuscia and Roman Campania, and the Exarchate, namely Emilia and the Pentapolis, received through Pippin’s donation. Therefore Stephen decreed that no one from Tuscany and Campania, or from any other place, should be brought into Rome until the pontiff had been ordained by the Roman clergy and people, according to the canonical election and the complete freedom of consecration then in force. In the time of Louis the Pious, the Lombards having been expelled along with their kings, the Franks ruled, and their garrisons remained in the cities of the kingdom of Italy. Therefore both peoples are forbidden to obstruct the freedom of the election or to enter Rome to disturb an election which by right belonged to the Romans alone. Do you see that Louis leaves the pontifical territory untouched and extends his provision only to the Franks, Lombards, and other peoples subject to him? This is precisely what Stephen III had decreed concerning his own peoples.

And no one in the cities or territories belonging to the power of the Church of blessed Apostle Peter 132 shall presume on that account to do any harm [Col. 0586A].

> **Note [Col. 0586C].** The Astronomer, speaking in the *Life of Louis the Pious* of the final illness of Leo III, reports that the Romans, seizing the opportunity presented by Leo III’s grave illness, plundered and usurped the properties of the Church, as I said above, quoting the Astronomer’s own words (Dissertation no. 8). From this it is clear both that examples of this matter were not far to seek for Stephen IV, Leo III’s successor, and that the Ludovician diploma adheres to certain and contemporary circumstances. In the eighth year afterward, namely 824, Lothair, Louis’s son, established the following in the atrium of blessed Peter by authority of Eugene II: “Let the plunderings which have hitherto been customary in no way occur, whether while the pontiff is alive or after his death. If anyone should do this hereafter, let him know that he is to be condemned by legal sentence. Whatever has been done in the past shall be legally repaired.” The remaining provisions will occur below in the diplomas of Otto and Henry, who appear to make another’s constitution their own. You will find more in the admonition on the letters of Stephen III and in the preliminary commentary on Adrian’s letters. See also the Dissertation on the letters of Leo III.

But let the Romans, with every mark of reverence and without any disturbance, provide their pontiff with an honorable burial.

> **Note [Col. 0586D].** As soon as the pontiff was near death, he was generally abandoned in those times by almost everyone—not only so that the proper election of a successor might be held, but also so that violence and other disturbances might be prevented; no thought was given to the honor of his funeral. Stephen III explains the matter in his address to the aforesaid council: “When the lord Pope Paul had departed this life, everyone abandoned him, and I alone remained to guard the funeral so that he might be committed to burial.” For this reason Stephen IV and Paschal wished such an inconvenience to be prevented by imperial authority and ordered the matter as follows.

And let the man whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration and through the intercession of blessed Peter, have chosen by common counsel and concord, without any promise,

> **Note [Col. 0587B].** See above, Dissertation no. 34.

for the order of the pontificate, be canonically consecrated without any uncertainty or opposition [be consecrated]; and once he has been consecrated, let legates be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, who shall establish friendship, charity, and peace between us and them [him],

> **Note [Col. 0587B].** Consult the same Dissertation (no. 33). In view of the agreement of this discipline with the records of that age, judge whether Pagius and the others who accuse the diploma of falsity were mistaken, especially on this point.

as was customary in the time of the pious-memory lord Charles, our great-grandfather [grandfather],

> **Note [Col. 0587B].** Both Charlemagne, in the preface to the letters of the *Codex Carolinus*, and Louis mention Charles Martel. Charlemagne places him among the defenders of the Roman Church, whence arose the many scholarly disputes concerning the patriciate allegedly conferred upon him; I rejected those disputes in the Admonition on the letters of Gregory III. Louis, however, wants legates to have been sent to him after the pontiff’s ordination; the Continuator of Fredegar, whose account extends to the final years of Gregory, vehemently declares this false, since the legations were delayed. On this matter consult the aforementioned Admonition. Moreover, Gregory III, during whose lifetime Charles Martel died, is said to have been the last of all the pontiffs to send the decree of the election to the exarch of Ravenna as a sign of obedience. Yet the mention of Charles Martel here is not pointless: it refers to the legation that was sent to Francia long after the ordination. Since Louis defines the legations of Gregory’s successors as having the same character, we learn clearly from this, as has been demonstrated by several testimonies of the *Codex Carolinus*, that legations were sent by the pontiffs after consecration in order to confirm friendship, charity, and peace both with those kings and after the grant of imperial dignity. This practice continued until the time of Sergius II, who granted Lothair and Louis II the privilege of confirming the election, as I have demonstrated at length in the Dissertation. To those, however, who do not hesitate to swear by the words of Pagius, Muratori, the Anonymous *Chorographer*, and all their followers without investigating the matter, I advise them to place no faith in my words, but seriously to examine the documents I have cited and then judge whether the opinions of modern writers ought to be preferred to those same documents.

or of the lord Pippin, our grandfather, or even of the lord Charles, the Emperor, our father.

**133.** But so that this may be believed to be firm by all the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own people, and so that it may be preserved still more firmly by future generations and ages to come, we have strengthened this agreement of our confirmation with the seal of our own hand and with the promises and subscriptions under oath of the venerable bishops and abbots, as well as of our nobles; and we have sent it to the lord Paschal, pope, through Theodore, *nomenclator* and legate of the Holy Roman Church.

> **Note [Col. 0588B].** The diploma was produced at Aachen and was sent to Rome through an apostolic envoy. It is exceedingly difficult to find a clause of this sort in diplomas. Is it therefore spurious? No. Those who fabricate documents imitate genuine ones so closely that they deceive even wise men; and unless the style, formulas, or words reveal the fabrication, documents that are undoubtedly false are regarded as certain and authentic. Therefore Walchius, emboldened by the authority of the *Italian Annalist*, attacks the external formulas of the Ludovician diploma in vain. Whatever unusual features they contain derive from the donations of Pippin and Charles that then existed in the archive of the Roman Church.

I, Louis, by the mercy of God emperor, have subscribed; and there have subscribed his three sons, ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian [*bibliothecarius*],

> **Note [Col. 0588C].** Ducange notes in his *Glossary* that this was an office at the palace of the kings of Francia under Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and down to the time of Charles the Bald.

one *mansionarius*,

> **Note [Col. 0588C].** The same author, on the authority of Hincmar (*On the Offices of the Palace*, chapters 16 and 23), demonstrates that this too was an office of the palace of the Frankish kings; he also praises the *mansionarius* under Louis the Pious, to whose subscription Gauzlinus, the *mansionarius*, added his own.

and one usher [*ostiarius*].

> **Note [Col. 0588C].** The importance of this palatine office of usher is shown by the fact that the magnificent usher Gotramnus was sent as Charles the king and patrician’s envoy, or legate, in the year 788 (*Codex Carolinus*, p. 482).

# APPENDIX

**134. DISSERTATION ON THE DIPLOMA OF OTTO I, AUGUSTUS, AND OTTO II, KING**

**I.** Although the original of this diploma, written in golden letters, exists in the archive of the Castle of Sant’Angelo, I nevertheless ordered another copy, from the Albinian manuscript, to be published for more than one reason. First, the father of the *Annals of the Church* rightly thought it worthwhile (962, no. 2) to publish it in a duplicate copy carefully collated with the original from Vatican manuscripts, with several variant readings excerpted; Labbe and many others transferred that copy into their own works. Secondly, because the original bears no title, although that is customary in other diplomas, later editors attached different titles to it. Among them, Goldastus (*Imperial Constitutions*, vol. II, p. 44) and Lunigius (*Italian Diplomatic Code*, vol. II, p. 693, and *Continuation of the Ecclesiastical Miscellany*, p. 159) gave it a title more freely than was appropriate:

> “Pact of confirmation of the Emperor Otto I, by which he confirms the territories and cities of the Roman Church donated by his predecessors and adds several others, A.D. 962, indiction V, February 13, in the twenty-seventh year of Otto’s emperorship.”

For Rome and the other cities of the Roman Duchy had to be distinguished from the donations of the emperors, as we demonstrated at length in the preceding Dissertation, and as Otto himself admits, according to the consistent testimony of the original and all the manuscripts: “Just as you have held and administered them in your power and dominion from your predecessors until now.” Therefore Baronius correctly derived the following title from the sense of the diploma itself: “Diploma of the Emperor Otto concerning the confirmation of the rights of the Roman Church.” In the Albinian manuscript it reads: “Copy of the privilege of the Emperor Otto concerning the royal rights granted to blessed Peter.”

Finally, because when the distinguished Antonellus, while he was prefect of that archive, published a copy of the diploma from the ancient original, which was extremely difficult to read in certain places, it will be very pleasing to the reader to examine with trustworthy eyes another copy, taken scarcely a hundred years later from the same source, without omitting the variant readings of the original. For all learned men are deeply distressed that in our own distinguished age this diploma, which was always held in such great authority among the ancients, should be declared interpolated (*Italian Annals*, 1059), and indeed interpolated by the Apostolic See, so that it might assert territories belonging to others for itself by the authority of princes. Nothing can demonstrate more effectively how unjustly that allegation has been made than this illustrious document, copied with the utmost fidelity.

## II

Lest anyone wonder why the Ottonian diploma was written in golden letters, contrary to the custom long established by usage, he should call to mind the donation of Aripert, king of the Lombards, of which the *Liber Pontificalis* (section 168) speaks as follows:

> “King Aripert restored to the rightful possession of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the Church’s right and held by that people, having written the donation in golden letters.”

More closely relevant to our subject is the observation of the often-mentioned Godefridus, abbot of Göttweig (*vol.* I, *book* II, p. 82), which should be heard both concerning this diploma of Otto I [Col. 0589C] and concerning another of Otto II, likewise written on purple parchment, as Leukfeld reports (*Antiq. Boeld.*, chapter 8, § I, p. 29), as well as concerning the Henrician diploma of 1014 and others. The learned man notes that ink was the more usual liquid in writing, although he found that golden ink had been employed for the greater splendor of royal majesty; and he adds:

> “From these examples the magnificence and majesty of our Teutonic kings and emperors shine forth, in their diplomas, far more augustly and splendidly through that sacred encaustic so celebrated and renowned among the ancient emperors, especially the Greeks.”

He is supported in this by Mabillon, easily the leading authority in diplomatic studies and several years older than Godefridus. When Mabillon was staying in Rome in October 1685, Cardinal Ottoboni showed him the same generosity and kindness that I have now enjoyed for sixteen years from the most eminent Cardinal Domenico Passionei, who by nature is disposed to benefit letters and all who cultivate them. The learned man therefore relates (*It. Ital.*, part I, p. 96) how, among several ancient codices sent to him through the kindness of the aforementioned cardinal so that he might examine and use them more conveniently at home, he found in one of them a register of the privileges of the Roman Church:

> “Some of these, as he read there, had been recorded and transcribed for the perpetual preservation of their memory by Pope Innocent IV of blessed memory at the Council of Lyons, under his bull and the seals of forty prelates who were present; and to those transcripts, thus recorded, the said Lord Innocent, with the aforesaid council’s approval, decreed that perpetual faith should be given, just as to the originals.”

## III

The privileges of the two Ottos, the first and the second, and then of Henry Augustus, are said to occupy the first place among the imperial documents:

> “Written throughout in golden letters; the first of these is not sealed, although its tenor shows that it ought to have been sealed. The second, however, is sealed with an imperial golden bull, [Col. 0590A] though no date has been affixed to it; and in both are placed the subscriptions of the emperors themselves, as well as of their prelates and princes.”

For this reason the learned man, rejoicing, says that everything he had observed in his work on diplomatic studies is confirmed. Hence it is clear with what fidelity the Roman pontiffs vindicated their rights on behalf of the apostolic see. Innocent did not wish the diplomas of Pippin, Charles, and Louis—from which the privileges of Otto and Henry derived—to be copied and solemnly authenticated when only copies of them existed, but only those whose originals were available. Indeed, if there were any defects in the originals, the archival records do not conceal them.

It is astonishing that all this did not restrain the confidence of a certain person who, obstinately maintaining his opinion, did not hesitate to detract somewhat from the authenticity of such privileges. To be sure, when ancient records are found written inconsistently in so many codices, a reasonable and proper suspicion concerning them may arise. But when their original exists—and I can affirm this with certainty, since our most holy lord Clement XIII granted me, when I requested it, permission to see it with my own eyes and compare it carefully—then it is audacious to doubt them in any respect.

Indeed, if Innocent had foreseen the marvelous art of printing, he would not have taken care to produce so many authentic copies. Yet this turned out well for us. One of them is preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo together with the same original, written on purple parchment in golden letters, from which it receives the fullest authentication. That several more are carefully preserved in the Cluniac archive, in a chest surrounded by iron plates, is attested by the eyewitness, the most eminent Cardinal Domenico Passionei, who has no equal in investigating such ancient records. Mabillon himself testifies that he saw those authentic copies there (*It. Ital.*, cited above).

Thus it was very easy for Goldast, the most hostile enemy of the Holy See, and for the Italian annalist [Col. 0590C], the editor of so many ancient records (*962, 1014, 1023, 1059*), to have anything that seemed suspicious to him investigated by some careful examiner. He would then have imitated Pagius, whose opposition to the Louisian diploma he follows; Pagius, defending the Ottonian diploma against Goldast’s objections, rightly calls it “a most certain monument of antiquity” (*962*, no. 2).

## IV

The two matters that might at first sight seem capable of being raised as objections—the absence of a seal and the twenty-seventh year of the empire—disappear when examined attentively. The privilege was issued on 13 February, and on the following day the emperor departed from the City. Georgius observed this from Vatican Codex 1340, written at that time (*ad Baron.*, 962, no. 1). Concerning John XII, the codex reads:

> “In his time, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962, the emperor Otto first came to Rome with Adelaide in January, on the thirty-first day, Friday, and remained there for fifteen days; and he departed from there on 14 February, the feast of Saint Valentine, in the fifth indiction.”

What could be easier, given an interval of only a few hours, than for the seal’s necessary attachment to have been omitted through the negligence of a youthful pontiff and the remarkable inertia of the archival officials of that age? Besides, as Godefridus observes concerning Otto’s seals (*Chron. Gotw.*, vol. I, book II, chapter 3, p. 163):

> “In royal seals he generally appears beardless and still youthful in appearance, with his head either bare or at least encircled by a closed crown, holding in his hands either a royal staff or a lance and shield. In imperial seals, by contrast, he is represented with a somewhat full beard, a crown closed above, and adorned with the orb and scepter; such a form Heineccius observed in the Zyllesian seal.”

Perhaps, then, the seal had not yet been engraved. Someone who had not seen the original might conjecture this. One who has seen it will judge otherwise: the perforated parchment, at the two customary places on its lower edge, shows that the seal was lost through the custodians’ negligence.

As for the chronology, a similar date appears in a privilege for the monastery of Lorsch preserved by Freher (*Rer. Germ.*, vol. I, p. 119):

> “Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 963, in the sixth indiction, while the pious emperor Otto was reigning in the twenty-eighth year. Done happily at Pavia.”

Struvius immediately appends to this, in the new edition of Freher, the subscription of another diploma:

> “Issued on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 965, in the eighth indiction; in the thirtieth year of the reign of Lord Otto, but in the third year of his empire. Done happily at the Palace of Heresteyn, in the name of God. Amen.”

## V

The Venerable Cardinal Baronius, with the full measure of his learning (*962*, no. 12), immediately after the subscriptions and date says:

> “Thus reckoning, joining the same years from the time when he obtained the kingdom with the empire—of which this is to be counted as the first year—and considering the other elapsed years to belong properly to the reign, the diplomas of that same Otto and all the synodal acts demonstrate; and nothing is more consistent.”

Godefridus, however (*cited above*), after praising the privilege of the monastery of Lorsch from Freher’s ancient edition, adds, in order to show that it was not unique to the Roman Church, that he had observed elsewhere that the years of the reign were separated from those of the empire. [Col. 0591B] The Italian annalist also confirms this, for it cannot be otherwise, since the designation “emperor” and the empire itself did not begin until the imperial diadem had been received from the hand of the pontiff.

Apart from these two very slight matters, it will soon become clear that nothing can be objected. Therefore the chorographer (*Script. Ital.*, vol. X, preface), who treated the Louisian diploma—by whose aid he composed his map—so badly, speaks about the privileges of Otto and Henry (nos. 20, 22, 30, and 99) in the manner commonly adopted by those who wish to appear learned and take great pleasure in themselves after imposing upon the public:

> “And two diplomas,” he says, “unless these too are called into question: those of Otto I and Henry I.”

But why dwell on this? Neither the absence of the seal nor the less exact chronology alters the character of the privilege. Its original exists, and it was compiled from the Louisian diploma and the deeds of donation in the archive of the Roman Church. It contains several things not found in the Louisian diploma, while some things present there are absent from Otto’s privilege. These matters may cause difficulty for us who come later, but they can in no way diminish the document’s authenticity.

It is therefore our task to investigate why this was done, not to condemn what we do not understand or to disregard what conflicts with our own opinion. Let this suffice concerning the authenticity of the diploma; I now proceed to examine its individual provisions.

## VI

What those concerned more with courtroom procedure than with the character of ancient records seek in the Louisian diploma but miss there is not absent from Otto’s privilege. Otto I is called “emperor by the grace of God and king by divine providence,” and Otto II is included with him. This is something new in a diploma: in no Carolingian example does the son, as king of Germany—who had no connection with the Romans or their affairs—compose a diploma together with the emperor and become possessed of everything that ought to belong to the emperor alone. Such was the inertia at Rome in those days, such the forgetfulness of matters of the highest importance!

What did the king of Germany have to do with the ordination of the pontiff? Nevertheless, the presence of envoys either of the emperor or of the king’s son is stipulated in the pope’s promise made before the consecration. [Col. 0591D] What did that same king have to do with the kingdom of Italy? Yet the king’s son is made a participant in his father’s voluntary donation of six cities from that kingdom.

I say nothing about the confirmation of whatever rights belonged to the Holy See, for Charles and Carloman, the sons of King Pippin, also confirmed the donation of the Exarchate made by Pippin, as is established by several letters in the Carolingian Codex. Thus Otto, whether deliberately imitating the Carolingians or, rather, through the negligence of the librarian and archival officials who had the donations before their eyes and paid little attention to whether they were royal or imperial, produced a diploma out of keeping with ancient custom. Later writers, by calling this into question, would either unwittingly deprive Otto the Great of his glory or, by abuse, confuse imperial rights with royal rights. German jurists and some of our own have done this often enough and more than enough.

This is all the more striking because Otto, as we recently saw, without maintaining any distinction between kingship and empire, attached in several privileges some already elapsed regnal years to imperial years that were then just beginning. I am astonished that the words “we promise and undertake” have not supplied them with a new argument for spreading even thicker darkness over pontifical history.

But when they recognized, from the subsequent words “confirm and strengthen,” and also from the similarity of language in the oath made through envoys (*Dissertation* 1, no. 40), that the words “promise” and “undertake” carried greater force among the Augusti of Germany than the words “establish” and “grant” among the Carolingians, and when they noticed that Henry too had used the word “grant” in his voluntary donation, they abandoned that new argument, as I believe.

## VII

The confirmation of Rome and its duchy is made according to the Louisian diploma, although the phrase “and to his successors forever” is omitted. A title is added for Peter, the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. I think the latter was done also to suggest to the Germans the Carolingians’ love for so great a prince.

The omission of the successors is corrected below in the general collection of all the donations, where the words are added: “and to his successors until the end of the age.”

More important is the fact that Campania and its cities are passed over in silence—Campania, that famous region both in the time of Charlemagne (*Cod. Car.*, letter 60, elsewhere 73) and under his son Louis, by whom Patricum, a not insignificant town, is listed above others in the ninth century, as appears from an ancient *Notitia* (*Cod. Vat.* 1184), attributed to Leo the Wise by Schelestratius (*Ant. Eccl.*, vol. II, p. 681), and therefore belonging to the ninth century.

A small town still exists today called Pratica, where the once-famous city of Lavinium stood, as Philippus Ametus carefully notes in his maps of Latium. The chorographer of medieval Italy (*Scr. It.*, vol. X, p. 227)—and this I especially wish to note—observing that the place was not unknown even to Maginus and quoting Ortelius, says:

> “Patricum, a town of the Roman duchy in Latium.”

He rejects Holstenius’s opinion that Patricum was the place where anciently stood Linternum, in the Land of Labor; hence he says:

> “If we have Patricum in Latium, or in Roman Campania, according to the Louisian diploma, why seek it far away and outside the duchy?”

Thus, on the authority of the very ancient Louisian diploma, he establishes this city, which I do not know whether anyone found elsewhere except in Leo the Wise’s *Notitia* and in this diploma.

For my part, I find this city in no *Provinciale* or *Notitia*. It is therefore credible that it was ravaged, perhaps even destroyed, by the Saracens in that same ninth century, or abandoned by its inhabitants out of fear of them. Certainly, it is clear from the letters of John VIII that Italy suffered enormous losses, especially in the towns along the coast. The *Liber Pontificalis* (section 476) even testifies that the better-fortified towns of Ostia and Portus had been in great danger fifty years earlier. Accordingly, Gregory IV surrounded Ostia with new fortifications so that it would not be plundered by the Saracens, and he took care to fortify Portus.

## VIII

From the same letters of John, especially letters 217, 246, 277, 286, 293, and 299, we learn that a new name had already entered civil administration for Campania. We find that the suburban cities, together with all the other cities of Campania, were called by the designation “land” and “territory.”

Accordingly, the same pontiff asks Berengar to report to the emperor (letter 85) how Lambert, count of Spoleto, after gathering a multitude of people, invaded the entire territory of Saint Peter.

It seems impossible to doubt that all Roman Campania was called the territory of Saint Peter, because the other regions retained their ancient names, as is evident from the council held at Ravenna by the same pontiff in 877, in Labbe (*Councils*, vol. IX, p. 303), whose canon 17 decrees:

> “We decree that from now on no man of any nation or rank presume, in the manner of a beneficiary, whether by written instrument or in any other way, to seek, receive, or confer monasteries, courts, estates, and halls established throughout Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and Emilia, as well as throughout the Roman and Lombard Tuscany, and throughout the entire territory of the apostle Saint Peter.”

Ancient records further testify that all the provinces from Radicofani to Ceprano were later called by the name “the land.” Moreover, in his oath made through envoys to John XII, Otto embraces the entire ecclesiastical domain under the name “the land of Saint Peter” (*Dissertation* 1, no. 40, p. 36).

But in this diploma neither the name “land” nor “territory” is heard; the suburban cities and those of Campania are included under the single name “duchy.” The same was true in the time of Innocent III. Although both Tuscan regions were called a patrimony, the part on this side of the Tiber—that is, the suburban and Campanian cities—was separated from Tuscany under the single name “duchy,” as may be seen in Baluze (*Deeds*, no. 124).

For Innocent “summoned to his presence bishops, abbots, counts, barons, magistrates, and consuls of the cities from Tuscany, the Duchy, and the March,” even though at that time Campania extended more widely and was famous under the two names Campania and Maritima.

This is enough to have noted for the clarification of a diploma separated by 145 years from the Louisian diploma.

## IX

We now come to the first of all the donations of the Exarchate. It is rightly attributed to Pippin and Charles, both because both are often said in the Carolingian Codex to have made it at Quierzy, and because Charles claimed for the Holy See all the cities whose possession the Lombards had prevented him from acquiring.

Yet both are incorrectly called emperors, a matter that must doubtless be attributed to the gross ignorance of that age. Those who infer from Louis’s silence that the Louisian diploma is spurious expose their own delusion. In the Henrician diploma, since it was thought appropriate to mention even the names of the Ottos, Louis too had to be named—not because anything concerning the Exarchate belonged to his generosity, but because he confirmed the ancestral and paternal donations that Otto and Henry later likewise strengthened.

I cannot sufficiently marvel at the ingenuity of such critics. If Louis’s name had to be missing anywhere, it would more plausibly have been missing in the grant of the City and the Roman duchy, which is nowhere found to have been made by either Pippin or Charles, rather than in donations made both by agreement and voluntarily, whose authors were displayed in the charters and records of the apostolic archive.

It would indeed have been a great act of audacity to cast out the words of the original:

> “As you have held and administered them, from your predecessors until now, in your power and jurisdiction,”

and to put in their place:

> “Which Louis, our predecessor, the distinguished emperor of blessed memory, long ago bestowed by a deed of donation.”

Yet it is no lesser act of audacity to declare the Louisian diploma forged because Otto does not mention it while listing the donations of Pippin and Charles.

I am firmly convinced that Henry would not have introduced Louis’s name unless it had necessarily needed to be included, so that the German princes who preceded Henry would receive equal honor. For it was no less in Louis’s interest than in that of the Ottos to be called the defender of the Holy See’s rights in a solemn diploma. In that diploma, either the Ottos had to be passed over in silence, or Louis—who had preceded them both in confirming the Pippinian and Carolingian donation—had to be placed before them.

The word “restored” in the Louisian diploma should also be noted: it was changed to “bestowed,” because in the age of the Ottos the reasons why the former term had anciently been used were unknown. Yet the *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Stephen II, repeatedly uses the words “return” and “restore” concerning the donation that the Lombard king had dared to evade.

Although it says that Pippin protested to the imperial envoy (*section* 251)

> “that no abundance of treasure could persuade him to take away what he had once offered to blessed Peter,”

it adds shortly afterward:

> “He restored the aforesaid cities, adding also the fortress called Comiaclum.”

So true is it that ancient records have no need of grammatical critics.

## X

The Ottonian diploma differs somewhat from the Louisian in several donations of Charles alone, but in such a way that it clearly shows that archival records were used together with Louis’s diploma. If you consider the order in which the same donations are listed, you recognize a copy of the Louisian diploma; if you consider the various omissions and additions interspersed among them, you understand that they came from the archive and nowhere else.

The donation of the Sabine territory is indeed recorded in its pure form. The dispute over the boundaries, which had long delayed possession and was finally removed by the royal envoys, the abbots Itherius and Maginarius, is passed over in silence. In Louis’s time, since the matter was still recent in memory and the establishment of definite boundaries made mention of it seem necessary, it would have been considered improper not to express it. In Otto’s time, however, the long prescription of uninterrupted possession suggested that the matter should be handled otherwise.
