In the enumeration of the Lombard cities of Tuscany, there is such agreement between the two diplomas that the two seem almost one and the same. But after Rosellae, the donation of the three islands is entirely omitted by Otto, so that for a time the interpolation of the Louisian copy aroused suspicion in the minds of the most learned men and in my own.

But what of this? From the letters of Leo III, brought to light from their hiding place by Conringius, there is firm evidence for the donation of Corsica. In this very diploma, immediately afterward, follows another donation defined by boundaries, beginning at Luna together with the island of Corsica. Below it, the donation of Sicily is confirmed on the condition that God should deliver it into our hands, since it had already been groaning miserably for 135 years under the yoke of the Saracens.

Corsica and Sardinia were subject to the same fortune. Yet the greatest difference between them and Sicily was that no forgetfulness ever erased the Sicilian patrimony, whose abundant revenues were to be distributed among the poor and expended for the adornment of the churches. The revenues of Sardinia and Corsica, however, were so meager that the Holy See scarcely considered them anywhere. Thus, unless that donation defined by boundaries had been found in the archive, one should believe that Otto would not even have mentioned Corsica.

Their only common feature is that the Augusti of Germany never showed any concern for them except when, with outside assistance, they returned to the Holy See. For then, as history teaches us, they coveted them—especially Sicily and Sardinia.

## XI

Since I have mentioned Sardinia, I should add that I do not agree with those who place hasty reliance on the acts of Silvester reported in the *Liber Pontificalis*, in which Sardinia is said to have been donated to the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter.

At the beginning of the seventh century, Saint Gregory the Great says to Vitalis, the defender administering the rights of the Holy See there (*book* XI, letter 59):

> “Since the possessors of Sardinia have asked us, because they are afflicted by various burdens, that you should go to Constantinople for their relief, we grant you permission to go.”

The Roman defenders Sabinus and Vitalis, as well as Peter the notary, do not appear to differ greatly from apostolic envoys or legates (*book* II, eleventh indiction, letter 36; book IV, letter 9; book VII, letter 66; book IX, letter 10; book XI, letters 53 and 59). For the monasteries, vacant churches, bishops, and priests of the entire island are entrusted to them.

But to mutter about the Holy See’s temporal rule before the iconoclasts is to lie. The matter is found differently in the age of Charlemagne, especially after the renewal of the empire. Since the Saracens of Spain raided Sardinia and Corsica almost every year and caused those islands great hardship, in 806 and the following years Pippin, Charles’s son and king of Italy, sent Burchard, count of the stables, with a fleet to Corsica to defend it—as I believe—for the Holy See, to which we have seen that it had been donated around that time (p. 60).

The Annals of Fulda testify to this, and they agree with Einhard’s *Annals*, the Bertinian Annals, and others. Aimoinus reports their actual words (*book* IV, chapter 94); since they are of some importance, they should be heard:

> “They came out of Spain according to their custom and first reached Sardinia. There, after engaging in battle with the Sardinians and losing many of their men—for three thousand are said to have fallen there—they proceeded directly to Corsica. There, again, in a certain harbor of that island, they fought a naval battle with the fleet commanded by Burchard. They were defeated and put to flight, losing thirteen ships and many of their men.”

The Annals of Fulda and the others assign this battle to the year 807. Since the letters of Leo III belong to the following year, the donation might also have preceded it. Therefore it cannot be determined whether Pippin was defending his paternal rights or those of the Holy See.

What can safely be affirmed is that at that time the Greeks, who were struggling with great difficulty to retain Sicily—finally losing it in 827—had entirely lost their right to those two islands. Nor is it clear whether Sardinia came under Charles’s power in the same way as Corsica, since the annals speak only of Corsica.

## XII

The fact that no ancient record has yet been brought to light from its hiding place that would remove all doubt does not justify rashly accusing the Louisian diploma of falsification. For in the eleventh century the rights of the Holy See returned by restoration not only in Sicily, of which enough has been said, but also in two other islands.

The letters of Gregory VII preserved by Labbe (*Councils*, vol. X) bear witness to this. In 1076 he strongly commends the Corsicans (book V, letter 4) because, as they had informed him, they wished to return to the jurisdiction of the apostolic see. He promises assistance:

> “By the mercy of God we have in Tuscany many forces of counts and noblemen prepared for your assistance and defense, if necessary.”

He says that he is sending them the bishop of Pisa as legate, to whom they are to render fidelity,

> “after first promising fidelity to Saint Peter, to us, and to our successors,”

and finally he exhorts them to constancy in the faith.

The pontiff himself begins negotiations with the Sardinians (book I, letter 29). In a letter addressed “to Mariano of Torres, Orzocco of Arborea, likewise Orzocco of Cagliari, and Constantine of Gallura, judges of Sardinia,” while he was still at Capua in 1073, he exhorts them to their former obedience and promises that he will soon send his legate to them. Meanwhile he gives many instructions to Constantine, archbishop of Torres, whom he had consecrated at Capua.

What effect these letters had may be gathered from others issued the following year (same work, letter 41) to Orzocco, judge of Cagliari, who had written to the pontiff that he would come to Rome. From the same letters it is clear what he had commissioned Archbishop Constantine to do and what the pontiff had determined concerning the rights of the Holy See:

> “We admonish your prudence to speak with the other judges of Sardinia concerning the matter which we entrusted to you through Archbishop Constantine of Torres, whom we consecrated at Capua this year. After firmly consulting together, report to us promptly whatever you have at heart and in mind concerning it. Know that unless you give us a definite answer on this matter in the present year, we shall neither seek your responses any further nor leave the right and honor of Saint Peter unclaimed.”

## XIII

You see how firmly the holy pontiff was convinced that Sardinia belonged by right to Saint Peter. From other letters of the same pontiff, sent to the same judge in 1080 (*book* VIII, letter 10), you will quickly understand that this was regarded as certain both within and outside Italy.

He gives thanks to God that the bishop of Populonia, his legate, had been received with great honor in Sardinia and that devotion owed to him and to Saint Peter had been rendered. Then, among other matters relating to the business begun, he adds:

> “Furthermore, we do not wish your knowledge to be unaware that your land has been sought by many peoples, and that great services were promised if we permitted it to be invaded, so that they wished to leave half of the whole land for our use and retain the other part for themselves under our fidelity. Since this had repeatedly been requested of us not only by the Normans, Tuscans, and Lombards, but also by certain men from beyond the Alps, we resolved never to give assent to anyone in this matter until, by sending our legate to you, we had learned your mind. [Col. 0596A] Therefore, because through his legate you have shown that you hold devotion toward blessed Peter, if you are willing to preserve it as you ought, not only shall no one be given permission by us to enter your land by force, but if anyone should attempt it, he shall be prohibited and repelled by us both temporally and spiritually. Finally, if you persevere in the fidelity of blessed Peter, we promise without doubt that the assistance of blessed Peter will not be lacking to you, both here and in the future.”

If anyone wishes, for the sake of sectarians, to accuse the holy pontiff of falsehood because he does not sufficiently favor their opinions and conjectures, let him do so. For my part, I see that the holy pontiff dealt with these four judges, who ruled Sardinia almost as four kings, in nearly the same manner in which he had dealt four years earlier with the Corsicans, who had voluntarily subjected themselves to blessed Peter according to ancestral custom.

For this reason, I believe that not long afterward the ancient obedience of both islands was rendered to the apostolic see, before the Pisans and Genoese began, in the latter half of the following century, to contend fiercely for their possession.

## XIV

That at the beginning of the same century the supreme dominion of the Holy See was recognized in both islands is demonstrated by the unimpeachable evidence of the register of the Albinian codex, whose authority I used in the preface (no. 49). There the three judges of Sardinia, excepting the judge of Gallura, are seen to pay their annual tribute to the apostolic see:

> “The judge of Cagliari, two pounds of silver as tribute; the judge of Arborea, two pounds; and the judge of Torres, two pounds,”

in addition to the tributes of the archbishops, bishops, and churches of the whole island.

As for Corsica, Innocent II, who began his pontificate in 1130, is said to have granted that island

> “to Genoa under an annual tribute of one pound of gold.”

The two islands are discussed very differently in the register of revenues published by Muratori (*Antiq. Ital.*, vol. V, col. 851). The tribute of Corsica is prescribed to the Genoese consuls, and the tribute of the judge of Gallura in Sardinia is stated, while that of the judge of Cagliari is omitted.

But since the codex made public as the register of revenues of Cencius mentions Honorius IV, who ascended the chair of Peter in 1285, everyone can see how much weight it deserves for asserting the rights of the Holy See in the eleventh and following centuries. Even in the genuine work of Cencius, if it lies hidden somewhere, whoever possesses it will not find the ancient authenticity of the Albinian register.

For in the time of Pope Celestine III, when Cencius was engaged in compiling it for him, there was considerable disagreement among the provinces, as appears from the ecclesiastical *Notitia* of that period preserved by Schelestratius (*Ant. Eccl.*, vol. II, p. 754).

The later register of revenues nevertheless provides this advantage: we can trace, down to the age of Boniface and the migration of the Apostolic See into Provence, the continuation of the apostolic jurisdiction restored in both islands at the end of the eleventh century, however much it was disturbed by the Pisans and Genoese, whom certain emperors of Germany imitated. It will therefore be understood that the investitures of both islands to the kings of Aragon, begun by that same Boniface VIII, introduced a new character not of jurisdiction but of tribute.

If anyone wishes to inspect such records with his own eyes, he may consult Raynaldus (*1295*, no. 24; *1297*, no. 2; *1303*, no. 29; *1304*, no. 16; *1305*, no. 8; *1306*, no. 10). What has been presented seems sufficient for clarifying the Ottonian diploma, in which no mention is made of Sardinia.

## XV

At the end of the donation defined by boundaries—the donation to which Otto’s diploma owes its mention of Corsica—the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento are said to have been donated to the Holy See. But those words, unquestionably taken from the *Liber Pontificalis*, require interpretation.

That Spoleto, together with the duchy of Tuscany, was offered to the apostolic see is attested both by the Carolingian Codex (letter 56, elsewhere 58) and by the Louisian diploma, but with the qualification:

> “Always preserving over those same duchies our dominion in every respect and their subjection to our side.”

Accordingly, the donation both of Tuscany within the specified boundaries and of the separately named duchy of Spoleto is certain as far as the payment of a tribute or pension to the Holy See is concerned. The supreme dominion over both, however, belonged from the beginning to the king of Italy, before the renewal of the empire.

The case of the duchy of Benevento is different. Although a small part of it—namely Capua with five other cities—was donated by King Charles in 787, Adrian nevertheless obtained supreme right over that small portion, as was stated earlier (*Cod. Car.*, vol. I, pp. 473, 484, 487).

If, in the *Liber Pontificalis*, Spoleto was reported without any qualification and the small portion of Benevento under the general name “duchy,” this was due to the carelessness of the librarian of that period. The substance of the matter should not therefore be accused of falsification, as the often-mentioned two men do with excessive confidence; rather, it must be separated historically so that the truth may be drawn out.

The same applies to the Ottonian diploma. Through the negligence of those times, this donation in the *Liber Pontificalis* appeared to be something different from that reported in the Louisian diploma. Consequently, both were inserted with insufficient care, so that first the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento are found to have been donated absolutely; afterward, only six cities of the latter and merely its pension or tribute are found.

These statements conflict with one another. What the archival officials of John XII’s time, through their lack of care, added to the Louisian material must therefore be rejected or counted as having no authority.

The church or monastery of Saint Christina near the royal palace of Olonna in Insubria, founded by the Lombards, as Mabillon believes (*Annals*, book XXIX, no. 37; book XXXIX, no. 65), and highly commended by Glaber, seems to have been attached to these two duchies for no other reason than that it was situated outside the specified boundaries. Letters of John VIII survive addressed to its abbot Gisulf (letter 239), by which the care of another monastery is entrusted to him by apostolic authority. In the *Liber Pontificalis*, however, his name is absent.

## XVI

The confirmation that follows of the right over the six cities of Campania, modeled on the Ludovician diploma, renders the aforementioned donation of the duchy of Benevento more explicit and at the same time shows that the scriveners, through negligence, narrated one and the same matter in two different ways. The two cities added at the end—namely Gaeta and Fondi—provide still stronger confirmation that “Roman Campania” was understood as the duchy, or territory, of Rome; for otherwise Campania was known in later centuries as a broader region, divided into two parts, namely Campania and the Maritime district (Chronicle of Fossanova, 1160, 1165, 1186, 1194, 1196). In the ancient Notices published by Schelestratus (Ancient Ecclesiastical Records, vol. II, p. 760), and by Baronius (1057, no. 19 ff.), ten episcopal sees are assigned to it. Indeed, in the Provincial manuscript of Albinus, Ravello is also listed as the final bishop of Campania, from the province of Salerno:

> “In Campania: Tiburtine, Anagnine, Signine, Tarracinense, Fundan, Gaetan, Ferentan, Verulan, Alatrine, Soran, Ravellan.”

The Fundan, Gaetan, and Tarracinan sees occur in every notice. I have discussed Tarracina and Gaeta elsewhere (vol. I, p. 495): both cities, although possessed in various parts, were captured by papal arms and belong by right to the Holy See. Here we see that Fondi, situated between the two towns, was counted by Otto among the cities of Campania, while Tarracina is omitted; it was doubtless thought to be included with the other cities of the Roman duchy. Whether the beginning of the domination over these cities should be dated to the pontificate of John VIII, as the chorographer of medieval Italy thinks, or to an earlier period, it is not relevant for us to investigate. This, however, is certain and established: in neither of the two Campanias is it listed by Louis; whereas in Otto’s age papal dominion—whatever name it is given, whether Terra, Territory, or Campania—extended as far as the Liris, commonly called the Garigliano. More will be said about this in what follows.

The two matters of greater importance that are confirmed to the Holy See in the diploma—namely Naples and Sicily—require me to add something to what I said in the preceding dissertation about the same Holy See’s ancient right over the island of Sicily, because of the long-standing invasion of the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies. [Col. 0597C–D]

## XVII

We have seen throughout the first volume of this work that the pontiffs of the Roman Church diligently and vigorously demanded back all the Church’s patrimonies from the Greek invaders, since those possessions were devoted to the honor of the churches and the relief of the poor. Yet we never find those pontiffs more solicitous than regarding the two patrimonies mentioned above and the Neapolitan one. Adrian went so far as to retain Tarracina, which had been captured by force, as a pledge in order to recover that patrimony (Codex Carolinus, letter 65, otherwise 64).

From this passage of the diploma we learn that the pontiffs were concerned with asserting the Neapolitan duchy itself; we shall discover that Henry did so in the same words. But the pontiffs’ hopes were deceptive, and the promises of both Augusti were vain. It had not yet been divinely ordained that those patrimonies should return to the Apostolic See, nor had the glory of so great an achievement been destined for the emperors of Germany. The Roman pontiffs themselves had to vindicate all their rights for the Holy See with the powerful assistance of the Northmen.

This was accomplished while the Empire was vacant and while Henry IV, still a minor, was the greatest despiser of both papal and imperial authority. It began with the greater matter: namely, by granting the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies—invaded for 333 years—to the Northman princes by apostolic authority in 1059. Then, after an interval of eighty years, by permitting the Neapolitan duchy also to them, an annual tribute having been established that would equal the ancient revenues of the patrimonies.

It came about by divine providence that, just as Calabria and Sicily reached the Roman Church’s former right without the aid of any emperor, so too the Neapolitan duchy, in 1139, followed the example of Calabria and Sicily under Conrad, king of Germany and brother of Duke Frederick of Swabia, who vainly aspired to the imperial diadem. Moreover, Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, while the whole island had not yet been recovered from the hands of the Saracens, swore an oath of fealty to Nicholas II and promised the aforementioned tribute in 1059; he later renewed it to Gregory VII, Nicholas’s successor, who confirmed his investiture.

Roger, the first of the Northmen, received from Innocent II in 1139 the title of king and the investiture of the kingdom of Sicily—for henceforth the island is so called—as well as of the duchies of Apulia and Calabria and the principality of Capua. Thus both the establishment of the kingdom of the Two Sicilies, as the island and all the mainland on this side of the Strait later came to be called, extending to the boundaries of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and the general investiture and all tribute had their origin without any intervention by the emperor and without any imperial undertaking.

I indeed believe that this was divinely ordained because neither Henry IV nor anyone from his line imitated the piety of Louis, Otto, and Henry, or their service toward the Apostolic See, as their deeds sufficiently and abundantly demonstrate. [Col. 0598A–C]

## XVIII

Everything is clearly established by the oaths rendered by the aforementioned Robert to the two pontiffs. These are found in Baronius (1059, no. 70 ff.; 1080, no. 36), and I have carefully compared them with the Albinian manuscript, with which they do not differ. After the oath of fealty to the Roman Church, however, that manuscript adds these few words:

> “And I shall swear fealty to no one, except with the fealty of the Holy Roman Church preserved.”

The first oath is as follows:

> “I, Robert, by the grace of God and Saint Peter duke of Apulia and Calabria, and, with the assistance of both, future duke of Sicily, for confirmation of the grant and acknowledgment of fealty concerning all the land that I personally hold under my dominion, and which I have not yet granted to any man from beyond the Alps to hold, promise that I shall pay annually to blessed Peter, and to you, my lord Pope Nicholas, and to all your successors, or to your messengers or those of your successors, a payment of twelve denarii in Pavia currency for each yoke of oxen. The term for this payment shall always be at the end of the year, namely on the Sunday of the holy Resurrection. Under this condition of paying the due, I bind myself and all my people, whether heirs or successors, to you, my lord Pope Nicholas, and to your successors. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.”

There follows a considerably longer oath of fealty, with the additional clause indicated above; see it in Baronius.

During the lapse of twenty years, many events occurred that produced no small hostilities between the Holy See and Robert. Meanwhile Richard, prince of Capua, rendered his oath of fealty to Pope Gregory VII while he was at Capua in 1073; it is found in the same Baronius (under that year, no. 63). Robert, after greatly extending his dominion, especially in Sicily, returned to Gregory’s favor and rendered him an oath somewhat different from the one he had rendered to Nicholas II. The difference deserves notice:

> “I, Robert, by the grace of God and Saint Peter, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.”

After promising to defend the regalia of Saint Peter, he continues:

> “Excepting the part of the March of Fermo, Salerno, and Amalfi, concerning which no decision has yet been made; and I shall help you to hold the Roman papacy honorably and securely. The land of Saint Peter that you now hold, or will hold, once I know that it is under your authority, I shall neither invade nor seek to acquire.” [Col. 0599A–B]

## XIX

These conditions receive their explanation from the pontiff’s own investiture, which immediately follows in the register of Gregory VII in the Albinian manuscript and in Baronius:

> “I, Pope Gregory, invest you, Duke Robert, with the land that my predecessors, of blessed memory, Nicholas and Alexander, granted to you. As for that land which you unjustly hold—namely Salerno, Amalfi, and part of the March of Fermo—I now patiently tolerate you in it, trusting in God and in you, so that afterward you may conduct yourself in it for the honor of God and Saint Peter as it is fitting for you to act and for me to accept, without danger to your soul or mine.”

Thus Gregory openly declares the invasions, both those made in papal territory and those made in Campania, since the latter belonged to the prince of Capua, from whom Gregory had likewise received an oath of fealty. For the agreements made by the pontiffs with Robert concerned Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, provided that he expelled the Saracens from them. Regarding the principality of Capua, however, an agreement had been made with Richard, who likewise had to expel the Neapolitan dukes.

The genuine Chronicle of Cava, although full of various lacunae, published by the distinguished Pratillo (History of the Lombard Princes, vol. IV, pp. 386 ff.), speaks of both matters without ambiguity:

> “Year 1059. By the apostolic lord Nicholas, [lacuna] Guiscard occupied all Calabria, Apulia, and also Sicily, insofar as he might free it from the Saracens, [lacuna] Richard received the honor of the principality of Capua, if he expelled Landulf. Therefore the Northmen joined themselves to the apostolic lord and subdued the enemies of the Church.”

Speaking of Robert’s advances in Sicily under the year 1072, it says:

> “Guiscard, after capturing the city of Palermo, gave the whole of Sicily to Count Roger, reserving only for himself the aforesaid city with its castle, and Messina.”

Whatever either of them acquired outside the lands granted to him was an invasion. Gregory calls Robert’s acquisitions by no other name.

The same chronicle gives the reasons for the invasion of Campania in 1075:

> “Guiscard, under the pretext that Gesulfus, his kinsman, had caused him to be excommunicated by Pope Gregory, besieged Salerno after the Kalends of April, and after seven months subdued it. Guiscard, after capturing Salerno, also seized Amalfi.”

If one adds to the authority of this contemporary writer the oaths of fealty cited above, one obtains a definite date for papal dominion in both Sicilies and at the same time understands that the diplomas of the three Augusti are nothing other than splendid monuments of the ancient right that the pontiffs themselves, with the aid of others, vindicated for themselves and their successors. [Col. 0599C–D]

## XX

Something should be added concerning the city of Naples alone, with everything belonging to it, about which the diplomas of Otto and Henry speak in a very obscure manner. No part of Sicily on this side of the Strait requires new proof, since we shall speak of the kingdom of the Two Sicilies in subsequent times (Dissertation 7, § 2, no. 17).

We have already said that the principality of Capua was transferred by Gregory to Richard, but in such a way that he was to acquire the Neapolitan duchy. This did not occur before 1139, sixty-six years after that investiture. For in that year, when Innocent II had led an army against Roger and was captured by an ambush and taken to the royal camp near Benevento, “seeing himself,” as Falco says under that year, “bereft of strength and arms and utterly desolate, he yielded to the king’s prayers and requests; and, after capitularies and privileges had been confirmed by both sides, the king himself, his son the duke, and the other princes came before the apostolic lord on the seventeenth day of July, and, falling at his feet, asked for mercy and submitted themselves entirely to the pontiff’s command. Immediately, by the Gospels, they confirmed that they would render fealty to blessed Peter and to Pope Innocent and to his canonically succeeding successors, together with the other matters that had been written down. To King Roger he immediately gave the kingdom of Sicily by the standard; to his son, the duke, he granted the duchy of Apulia; and to his other son, the prince, he granted the principality of Capua.”

The papal diploma, which will be produced in its proper place, grants everything to Roger alone.

A little farther on, the same Falco continues by describing how “in those days the citizens of Naples came to Benevento, surrendering the city of Naples to the fealty of their lord the king; they brought his son the duke and submitted their necks to his fealty.”

Thus the Neapolitan dukes came to their end, as Pratillo observes in his notes on the Chronicle of Naples (vol. III, p. 80). At the same time this marked the beginning of Northman domination under a fiduciary right, as well as the beginning of that prescription of so many centuries which compelled the Italian annalist to admit that the right of the Roman pontiffs could no longer be doubted. Below, in the following dissertation (nos. 13 ff.), we shall return to this matter. [Col. 0600A–B]

## XXI

He would, I think, have judged differently concerning the ancient right if he had examined it thoroughly. But let us briefly consider what remains concerning the Ottonian diploma.

It grants seven cities, “for the remedy of our soul and of our son and our parents,” from our own kingdom. That the duchy of Spoleto belonged to the supreme right of the emperors, although its beneficial lordship had belonged to the Apostolic See since the age of King Charlemagne, is entirely unknown to no learned person.

Why, then, a little farther below, are all the provisions that Charles established by voluntary donation concerning the census and payment of that duchy copied word for word from the Ludovician diploma, while supreme dominion over it, as over the duchy of Tuscany, is reserved to him? We can hardly understand this unless we suppose that this donation, made through Otto’s generosity, was inserted by his chancellor into a diploma which the scriveners had arranged in their customary fashion, wholly unaware of it.

Certainly Otto declares that he is donating those seven cities for the remedy of his soul, a point he emphasizes again, so that the Roman pontiffs might hold them perpetually in their right, principality, and jurisdiction. But this plainly conflicts with the condition added below: “with our dominion in every respect preserved over those same duchies.”

Accordingly, in that iron age we detect no less incapacity among the scriveners of the Holy See than in Otto’s chancery. This contradiction, together with the others we have seen above, increasingly confirms the authenticity of the diploma; if its original did not survive, the very character of its composition would establish it.

Indeed, the scriveners transfer from the Pontifical Book the entire donation of the duchy of Spoleto, which is certain, although it lacks the condition that supreme dominion remains with the donor Charles. Then, when they encounter in the Ludovician diploma that very donation expressed in different words together with the aforesaid condition, they think it different from the earlier donation of the Pontifical Book and therefore list it as another donation to be confirmed by Otto. Finally, Otto’s chancellor inserts his lord’s voluntary donation, leaving the other two untouched, although the first, taken from the Pontifical Book, ought to have been rejected, while the second, presented by the Ludovician diploma, ought to have been distinguished, lest the donated cities bear the former burden together with the rest, or lest the donation appear illusory within one and the same diploma.

But if this had been done, the character of that age would have been less evident. [Col. 0600C–D]

## XXII

If the foregoing establishes the authenticity of the Ottonian diploma, the following passages condemn those who reject the Ludovician diploma as false and rashly fabricated.

I discussed the discipline governing papal consecration in the preceding dissertation. From the words “Moreover, other lesser matters,” nothing appears except a faithful transcription of Lothar’s constitution of 824, with Eugene II’s assent, occasionally expressed in somewhat different words and in a slightly different order. For chapter 3 is placed first, followed by chapter 1, and from the two a constitution is assembled which in Anselm of Lucca (book VI, chapter 35) is called the constitution of the emperors Otto I and Henry I. In reality, however, it is Lothar’s, as is clear from its fourth chapter, reproduced in full after the two passages; that chapter is absent from the constitution attributed to those Augusti, although the latter is a composition of the scriveners. Consult both documents at leisure in Holstenius (Roman Collection, part II, pp. 208 and 214).

Let it be your judgment, then, whether the diploma of Louis, containing none of these matters because they had not yet been established, should rightly be called a fabrication, in accordance with the hasty opinion of the partisans. For when I carefully consider the Ottonian diploma, which Pagi regards as a most certain monument of antiquity, and the Ludovician diploma, which he considers fabricated, the latter appears to me full of authenticity because it contains the history and discipline of its own age and carefully, without contradiction, states the donations then present in the archive.

The authenticity of the Ottonian document, on the other hand, seems to me to be indicated by its undigested and crude composition, the confusion and repetition of the donations, and the discipline governing papal election, which differs greatly from that of the Ludovician age. “Seems,” you say? Indeed, I do not hesitate to affirm as certain that to brand the Ludovician diploma with falsity—although Otto, through the work and office of the Holy See’s scriveners, transferred into his own whatever elements in it are mutually consistent and which demonstrate the diligence of the ancient scriveners—and to throw the Ottonian diploma into doubt is an act of falsehood. [Col. 0601A–C]

## XXIII

One point that I had failed to note must be added. The matters mentioned above concerning the discipline of the election and confirmation of the Roman pontiff are rather carelessly thought to begin with the words “according to which,” and so forth; in fact, they begin with the condition “with our authority preserved in all things,” and so forth, since otherwise the sentence lacks an opening.

But this had to be done by writers hostile to the Holy See, so that they might take from the pontiffs what belonged to them and attribute to princes what did not belong to them, lest their false opinions concerning papal dominion collapse and the imperial right, or a power resting upon the privilege of the Holy See, appear.

Nothing is easier than to corrupt such matters when copying diplomas. John Heumann speaks of the subject (Commentary on Diplomatic Affairs, chapter 1, § 18, p. 11), based on Mabillon’s observations (On Diplomatic Affairs, book I, chapter 11, no. 15); both Abbot Godefrid (Göttweig Chronicle, vol. I, book I, § 6) and all who wrote after so great a man confirm it:

> “Ancient diplomas adhere together in a kind of continuous sequence, with no marks of distinction inserted between them. Those who transcribed the documents added various signs, the placement of which might more properly have been left to the reader’s judgment. Charlemagne, with the assistance of Alcuin and Paul Warnefrid, did indeed arrange for books to be illuminated with punctuation; yet such signs entered charters somewhat later.”

I mention this for those who have not seen the Ottonian original. They may perhaps be persuaded that all marks of distinction are likewise absent from it and that, for this reason, the aforesaid words may safely be referred to the preceding material.

But the case is otherwise in the original of the Ottonian diploma: the variety of its punctuation distinguishes the sentences. Although the continuity of the writing does not admit of division into the chapters into which I distributed it according to the subject matter, following Baronius’s example, the passage in question is expressed as follows:

> “May they be firmly possessed. With our authority preserved in all things, and that of our son and our descendants, according to what is contained in the pact, constitution, and solemnity of the promise of Pope Eugene and his successors, likewise that all the clergy, etc.”

I confess that I cannot understand why all the manuscripts consistently read *idest* (“that is”), when the original, in very clear letters, reads *idem*, which was undoubtedly written for *item* (“likewise”); for it is well known that among the ancients *d* and *t* are frequently interchanged.

Accordingly, three matters should be referred to the prince’s authority, or to the dignity, honor, and reverence owed to him, as John IX and Nicholas II call it (Councils, vol. IX, pp. 502 and 1104): the pontiff’s promise or profession, modeled on that of Eugene II; the oath of the clergy and people concerning a canonical and lawful election; and that same papal profession, to be made before the imperial envoys, following the example of Leo IV.

I think that this promise had the following purpose: just as the king of the Romans, before becoming emperor through coronation, bound himself by an oath of fealty to the Roman pontiff, so the Roman pontiff in turn would bind himself to the emperor—a practice that in the age of Eugene II was customarily expressed under the name of a pact.

Certainly Liudprand, or his continuator (On the Deeds of Emperors and Kings, book VI, chapter 6), reports that John XII rendered such an oath to Otto:

> “He received from that same Pope John an oath over the most precious body of Peter, and from all the leading men of the city, that he would never assist Berengar and Adalbert.”

Thus, from what we saw sanctioned in Louis’s diploma—that after the pontiff’s consecration “legates should be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, who would establish friendship, affection, and peace between us and them”—we infer that Eugene II, who succeeded Paschal I, and Eugene’s successors, at the time of their promise or profession during consecration, expressed that association of friendship, affection, and peace which the legates were to convey to the emperor.

This practice began to be carried out before imperial envoys by the successors of Leo IV, as is clear from what was said above. [Col. 0601D–0602C]

## XXIV

The final part of the diploma—namely, the confirmation and the emperor’s sign, together with the subscriptions of the nobles, bishops, and counts—supports the authenticity of both diplomas.

For Otto’s association with his son was taken from no other source than the Ludovician diploma, to which Louis’s three sons subscribed. Although Otto the son does not subscribe as they did, because he had remained a child in Germany, he is nevertheless introduced together with his father as confirming the rights of the Holy See. This would certainly not have been done unless it had been observed that Louis’s sons strengthened their father’s confirmation.

Among the subscribers, however, the offices or dignities of the Frankish palace—librarian, chamberlain, and door-keeper—are not found, for the times were different and the customs of the Germans were different.

Moreover, whence should the expression “by the seal of his own hand,” occurring here in the diplomas of Otto and Henry, be thought to have arisen except from Louis’s diploma, which was undoubtedly before the scriveners and also plainly before Otto’s eyes?

The often-cited abbot of Göttweig (Chronicle, vol. I, book II, chapter 3, p. 177), than whom no more diligent investigator of the kings and Augusti of Germany will be found, adduces various subscriptions of Otto and derives from them three certain rules:

1. Otto consistently used his own hand, or the sign of his own hand, in diplomas.
2. He used the words “ring” and “seal” interchangeably.
3. He always used the terms “marked,” “sealed,” “strengthened,” “confirmed,” “sealed with a seal,” “attached,” “secured,” “protected,” and “confirmed.”

Otto should at least have observed one of these three rules in this diploma, so that he might appear to have followed his customary practice! Instead, in place of “by the sign of his own hand,” we find “by the seal of his own hand”; and, in place of “marked with a ring or seal,” and so forth, “sealed by the impression of our bull.”

Should the diploma therefore be accused of forgery? Certainly not. The reasons for its peculiarities must be sought elsewhere.

The Ludovician diploma, strengthened by the sign of the donor’s own hand and by the subscriptions of the nobles, supplied Otto and Henry with a model to follow. As for the seal, since Louis issued that diploma at the assembly of Aachen and placed before it his own subscription together with the names of his sons, bishops, abbots, counts, and palace officials who confirmed the diploma, without any mention of a seal, Otto and Henry were free to act in their own fashion in this one matter.

For this reason Otto preferred to imitate the Frankish custom rather than his own customary practice. In the *Spicilegium* of D’Achery (vol. V, pp. 407 ff.), one can see several examples of Otto using not a *bulla* but a seal; this confirms the teaching of the Göttweig chronologist.

The commentators on the *Glossary* observe that Otto the Great was the last of all to use the designation *bulla*, a point confirmed by the authority of this diploma. [Col. 0602D–0603A]

## XXV

It would certainly have been desirable that, just as this precious monument of antiquity came down to us from that iron age through so many vicissitudes of the Holy See, the bull, which was certainly attached to it, should also have survived.

For when Godefrid noted the difference between Otto’s royal and imperial seals (Göttweig Chronicle, book II, chapter 3), the observations of that most learned man would, if I am not mistaken, have gained confirmation from this bull.

Moreover, the statement that I said Mabillon had read in the Ottobonian manuscript—“It is not sealed, although from the tenor of the document it appears that it ought to have been sealed”—would likewise have been confirmed by the same bull.

For the rest, this Ottonian diploma is most carefully preserved in the Apostolic Archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian. It is wrapped in silk cloth protecting the gold writing and enclosed in a tube made of a thin sheet of metal. It is as follows:

An oblong parchment, purple-colored on the inside, with modest ornamentation along both margins, is inscribed for most of its length in golden letters that remain exceedingly bright even in our own day. The writing continues from beginning to end, with only rare punctuation dividing the discourse. There are no larger letters at the invocation, as is customary; no usual monogram at the end; and finally no verification by the chancellor appears.

Everything indicates, however, that the Ludovician exemplar was used in drafting the diplomas of Otto and Henry. The form of the script cannot usefully be sought in Otto’s other diplomas. In comparison with the specimen exhibited by Papebrochius (Bollandists, April, vol. II, p. 12), the greatest similarity is found in a diploma of Otto III issued thirty-four years later in this same city of Rome for the church of Saints Boniface and Alexius; I shall point this out more suitably elsewhere (Dissertation 6, no. 14).

Some letters have fallen away; others have suffered damage in part of their form. Albinus, however, testifies that some had already been worn away even in the twelfth century: he calls Otto *Octo*, since the two letters *c* and *t* are entirely alike below, being distinguished from one another only by a thin line in the upper part. Whether the same thing happened to the word *ditioni* (“jurisdiction”), which after Albinus’s time is always read that way in the original, is uncertain. Albinus consistently wrote *ditionem*.

I shall now place this precious monument before the reader’s eyes, both from the Albinian manuscript and from the original.

[Col. 0603C] The variant readings of the original manuscript are enclosed in brackets.

### Example of the Privilege of the Emperor Otto concerning the Regalia Granted to Blessed Peter

[Col. 0603D] The original in the Archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo bears no title. A copy is preserved there in a bull of Innocent IV, issued at Lyon at the Third Council on the third day before the Ides of July, in the third year of his pontificate, that is, 1245; it is secured by a leaden bull and the seals of forty prelates. He ordered several other similar copies to be made, some of which Mabillon testifies that he saw preserved under the strictest custody in the Cluniac Archive (Italian Journey, part I, p. 96).

In the same archive there is a copy, or transcript, of the Ottonian privilege, made by John of Amelia with three public notaries “at Assisi, in the place of the Friars Minor, in the palace of the lord pope,” in 1339, by order of Benedict XII. At that time the original was still there, and the document is described as “written in golden letters on parchment of a reddish-purple color.”

The complete agreement of the transcripts, although they were made at different times, and their agreement even more particularly with the original, gives them the greatest credibility. This is naturally consistent with the source from which both diplomas derive, namely the Ludovician diploma, whose original perished together with the ancient charters of Pepin and Charlemagne, though only with slight loss. [Col. 0604B–C]

[Col. 0603]

In the name of the Lord God almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. I, Otto [Otto], by the grace of God emperor Augustus, together with Otto [Ottone], our glorious son and king, by divine providence, pledge and promise by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and holder of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XX [XII], that just as your predecessors have held and administered them in your power and jurisdiction up to the present, so we confirm to you the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, and all its villages [and] territories, mountainous and maritime, shores and ports, or all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany.

That is: Portus, Centumcellae, Caere, Plera [Blera], Marturianum, Sutri, Nepi, [Col. 0604C] Castellum Gallise, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, namely the larger [larger one] and the smaller, Polvensim [Pulvensim], Narni, and Otricoli, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the cities written above.

[Col. 0604C] In this confirmation of the Holy See’s ancient jurisdiction, you will observe no alteration, although 145 years separate the Ottonian diploma from the Ludovician one, apart from a few words discussed in the Dissertation; the essential matters remain untouched. Among these are the beginning, similar to that of the Ludovician diploma—“I, Otto”—and the reference to earlier times, designating the pontiffs as lords of these possessions who preceded John XII, just as Louis had indicated the predecessors of Paschal.

Several cities of the Cistiberine duchy, namely of Roman Campania, which Louis had listed, are passed over in silence, perhaps because Campania extended more broadly, since it reached as far as the Liris. The Patriciate, mentioned in the Dissertation, is likewise not found; it is uncertain whether it had been destroyed by the Saracens in the tenth century.

Thus all the cities of Campania are included under the expression “the duchy,” together with the suburbs, except Gaeta and Fondi. These formerly did not belong to Roman Campania and therefore are not said to belong to the Holy See’s ancient right; they are named separately, as we shall see shortly below.]

## 158

Likewise the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with the cities, towns, settlements, and castles that the excellent emperors, our predecessors, Pepin and Charles, of pious memory, long ago conferred by a deed of donation upon blessed Peter the apostle and your predecessors: namely the city of Ravenna, Emilia [Emilia], Bobbio, Cesena, Forum Popilii, Forlì, Faenza, Imola [Imola], Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio [Comiacchio], and Adria, together with Gabellum, with all the boundaries, territories, and islands by land and sea belonging to the aforesaid cities.

[Col. 0605B] The donation of the Exarchate and Pentapolis is likewise derived from the Ludovician diploma, and is rightly attributed to Pepin and Charles. For, besides confirming his paternal donation at Quierzy, Charles later, in 774, after expelling the Lombard kings, asserted for the Roman Church the whole Exarchate, part of which had been occupied by them. Yet the two are plainly called “excellent emperors.” This is manifestly erroneous. Therefore either Louis must be substituted, as in the Henrician diploma, or we must read “emperor,” as it is read in Louis’s diploma.

Later monuments repeating such donations, from the time of Louis onward, bring Louis back into the text, although the ignorance of the Ottonian age led it to suppress both his name and those of his Carolingian successors because they had added nothing to the donations of Pepin and Charles. [Col. 0605C]

At the same time, the Pentapolis, namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Humana, Jesi, Forum Sempronii, Montefeltro, Urbino, and the territory of Balneum, Calli, Lucioli, and Gubbio, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities.

In the same way, the territory of Sabina, just as it was granted in its entirety to blessed Peter the apostle by our predecessor, the emperor Charles, through a deed of donation.

[Col. 0605C] No mention is made of the boundaries established by the abbots Maginarius and Itherius, as in the Ludovician diploma, perhaps because below the entire duchy of Spoleto is said to have been donated by that same Charles. This omission lends credibility to the Ludovician diploma, which conveys a history not fully narrated in Adrian’s letters; it also demonstrates the inadequate examination of those who seem to have scented out a fabrication for themselves.]

Likewise, in the Lombard parts of Tuscany: Castellum Felicitatis, the Old City, the King’s Baths, Ferentum, Viterbo [Ferentum, Viterbo], Orte, Marta, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, Roselle, with all their suburbs and villages, territories, maritime towns and villages, or all their boundaries.

[Col. 0605C] The three islands of Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily, which we saw inserted in Louis’s diploma among the three Carolingian donations, are omitted by Otto and Henry. And rightly so: for Corsica follows immediately in the Donation through designated boundaries, while Sicily, which was then under Saracen control, is treated below as territory to be vindicated for the Holy See. Sardinia is not mentioned. It is uncertain whether it escaped the scriveners because they were merely piling together charters and donations, or whether they then neglected its established rights. Gregory VII (book I, letter 29) attributes all the blame to the negligence of his predecessors. In the year 1073, he refers to rights that would become evident in the following centuries, especially under Pope Innocent III, when Frederick Barbarossa, Otto IV, and Frederick II attempted to assert Sardinia for themselves as a right of the Empire—a claim that is entirely false. For the kingdom of Italy ended at the southern sea, as is established by the division of Charlemagne’s kingdoms.]

159 Likewise, from Luna with the island of Corsica, then to Surianum, then to Mount Bardonis, then to Berceto, thence to Parma, then to Reggio, thence to Mantua, and to Mount Silicis, and likewise the province of Venetia and Istria [Note: [Col. 0605D] This designation by boundaries, which I discussed in the dissertation on the diploma of Louis the Pious (no. 19), is to be understood as excluding—apart from Corsica, which is included among the papal territories by the conjunction used in the list—the cities and places enumerated. It should therefore be seriously considered whether, with the better-known places named, chiefly cities (whose territories, towns, villages, and everything belonging to them are undoubtedly comprehended under the name of the city alone), the boundaries of the dominion of the Holy See have been correctly established. They are still the same today, except for those enclosing the Tuscan duchy. Those boundaries were then correct, for the Tuscan and Spoleto duchies had been offered to Saint Peter by King Charles, although the kings of Italy exercised supreme rights over them by concession and privilege of the Holy See, according to the agreements made between Hadrian and Charles, with only a tribute being paid to the Apostolic See. It is not relevant now to investigate how that tribute disappeared in the duchy of Tuscany, while the Spoletan duchy was wholly subject to the authority of the Holy See.] and likewise the whole duchy of Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0606B] That the whole duchy of Spoleto was offered or donated to the Holy See is clear from Hadrian’s letters (Cod. Car. ep. 56, elsewhere 58). The Beneventan duchy is established from no other monument than Anastasius and these two diplomas; it was doubtless inserted by the archivists from the very *Liber Pontificalis* attributed to Anastasius. [Col. 0606C]], or the Beneventan duchy, together with the church of Saint Christine, situated near Pavia beside the Po at the fourth milestone.

Likewise, in the parts of Campania, Sora [Soram], Arces, Aquino, Arpinum [Arbinum], Teanum, and Capua [Note: [Col. 0606C] Nothing more certain has been established concerning the donation of these cities on Charles’s third arrival in Rome in the year 787, as has often been stated above. For, after subjecting the Beneventan duchy, he offered those six cities to blessed Peter; their chief city, Capua, rendered an oath of fidelity to the Roman pontiff Hadrian before the confession of that same prince of the apostles (Cod. Car. ep. 91, elsewhere 88).], and likewise the patrimonies belonging to your authority and dominion, namely the Beneventan patrimony and the Neapolitan patrimony, and the patrimonies of Upper and Lower Calabria [Note: [Col. 0606C] In Louis’s diploma the Beneventan patrimony is divided into the Beneventan and Salernitan patrimonies; see what was said concerning Louis’s diploma (in the note).]—and concerning the city of Naples, with its castles, territories, boundaries, and islands belonging to it, as they appear to pertain to those same possessions—likewise the patrimony of Sicily, if God should deliver it into our hands [Note: [Col. 0606C] In the time of Saint Gregory III there were three extensive patrimonies on the island of Sicily: the Sicilian, Syracusan, and Panormitan patrimonies. In later centuries all three together were called the Sicilian patrimony. Numerous letters from the register of Gregory the Great bear witness to the earlier threefold division. The later arrangement is abundantly attested by Theophanes (*Chronographia*, p. 273), by Hadrian in his letter to Charlemagne (Concil., vol. VII, p. 963), and by Nicholas I (letter to the emperor Michael). In Otto’s time the whole of Sicily was called the patrimony of the Church, as is clear here and from Henry’s diploma, and still more from the investiture of the whole island granted by Nicholas II to the Normans; concerning this, see the dissertation (nos. 17 ff.).] In like manner, the city of Gaeta and Fundi with all their appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0606D] They belonged by right to the Holy See, as the ancient records state (*Dissert.*, no. 16). But the origin of this right is uncertain: some assign it to the age of John VIII, others to different periods.].

160 Moreover, we offer to you, blessed apostle Peter, and to your vicar, Lord Pope John, and to his successors, for the remedy of our soul, of our son’s soul, and of our parents’ souls, from our own royal domain, cities and towns with their fisheries, namely Rieti, Amiternum, [Col. 0606B] Furconium, Norcia, Balva, and Marsi, and elsewhere the city of Teramo with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0606D] A little earlier it was testified that the whole duchy of Spoleto had been donated to the Holy See. And rightly so, for Charlemagne had offered it all to Saint Peter; but Hadrian had received it back from him, with only a tribute being paid to the Holy See. Here Otto donates seven cities of that same duchy: the emperor therefore renounces his right over a considerable part of the duchy, which the Holy See acquires.].

All the aforesaid provinces, cities and civic communities, towns and castles, villages and territories, together with [Col. 0607A] the patrimonies, for the remedy of our soul, of our son, or of our parents and successors, and for the whole Frankish people, preserved and to be preserved by God [Note: [Col. 0607B] Du Cange notes in his *Glossary* that the name “Franks” extended broadly, even to the Germans. This is familiar to all scholars, since Charlemagne and his successors ruled the Frankish monarchy. Otto himself had been adopted by Henry, the German king, from his wife Mathilda, daughter of Louis the Stammerer, as William of Nangis relates in his chronicle; thus he was descended from the line of Charlemagne, though through the female line. Nevertheless, at that time the Franks were distinguished from the Germans. Hence the reading “Christians” in the Henrician text is better. But at Rome in Otto’s time the Carolingian age was believed to have been restored, and Louis’s diploma and other charters displayed nothing but Frankish liberality. Therefore that prayer, which is commonly found in the letters of the Carolingian Register for the Frankish people, seems to have been employed here.], we hereby confirm to your aforesaid church, blessed apostle Peter, and through you to your vicar, our spiritual father Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and to his successors until the end of the age, in such a way that they may retain them in their right, principate, and dominion [Note: [Col. 0607C] This clause deserves attention; I discussed it in the preceding dissertation.].

In like manner, by this pact of our delegation, we confirm the donations which Lord King Pippin, of blessed memory, and afterward Lord Charles, most excellent emperors [most excellent emperor] [Note: [Col. 0607C] In this passage Pippin is not counted among the Augusti in the autograph; instead, a distinct title is certainly assigned to each of the two, in Louis’s wording—something that had not been done above (col. 605, note a).], conferred upon blessed Peter the apostle of their own free will. We likewise confirm the census, or payment, and the other contributions that were accustomed to be brought annually into the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto, as is contained in the donations written above and as was agreed between Hadrian, of holy memory, [Col. 0607B] and Lord Charles the emperor, when that pontiff confirmed to him, concerning the duchies written above—that is, Tuscany and Spoleto—a precept of his authority: namely, that every year the aforesaid census should be paid to the account of the church of blessed Peter the apostle [Note: [Col. 0607C] What has often been said above is nowhere better demonstrated than by the enumeration, among Charles’s spontaneous donations, of the tributes or payments of the Tuscan and Spoletan duchies [Col. 0607D]. Indeed, in that obscure age of Otto, could the donation of that entire duchy and its grant by Hadrian to the king of the Franks, together with an annual payment, have been narrated so accurately unless the Apostolic archives had supplied all the documents? Would the very words of Louis’s diploma have been used unless that diploma had lain before the author of Otto’s document? A payment appropriate to the Carolingian or Louisian age is certainly little suited to Otto’s time. For the seven cities torn from the duchy of Spoleto and donated by Otto to the Holy See ought to have reduced the total tribute by something. Yet affairs could hardly have been handled better at that time, and we, living later, cannot conjecture by what method or under whose authority this diploma was compiled. Only this is absolutely certain: Otto’s diploma derives from Louis’s.]. Our dominion over those same duchies in every respect being reserved, and their subjection to our side by this confirmation of ours and of our son [Note: [Col. 0607D] I have already said in the note to Louis’s diploma that dominion and subjection are reserved only on this occasion. I now add that this singular precaution sufficiently and more than sufficiently instructs those who either do not know or pretend not to know that all the other territories were under the supreme right of the pontiffs and were confirmed as such by the Augusti. The words “by this confirmation of ours” were undoubtedly taken carelessly from what follows, for they are absent from the autograph.].

Moreover, as we have said, we strengthen all the things named above for your side by this pact of our confirmation, so that they may remain in your right, principate, and dominion; and neither by us nor by our successors, through any device or contrivance, may your authority in any part be diminished, nor may anything be taken away from you therefrom [variant: *aut da vobis*, “or by you”]—namely, from the provinces, cities, towns, settlements, castles, villages, islands, territories, and patrimonies written above, and likewise from the payments and censuses—so that neither shall we do such things nor consent to anyone wishing to do them. But rather, we declare ourselves defenders, insofar as we are able, of everything read above—that is, the provinces, cities, towns, settlements, castles, territories, patrimonies, and islands [Note: [Col. 0608C] So that no suspicion may arise that Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica are not being discussed here, one should examine the order in which they are listed once and again both in Louis’s diploma and here. In Otto’s diploma the arrangement is not very skillful. Corsica had already been mentioned in the donation by specified boundaries, and Sicily when its restoration to the Holy See was promised if it could be wrested from the hands of the Saracens; but Sardinia is not mentioned even once in the diploma. Therefore what Louis asserted concerning the three aforesaid islands is less applicable to Otto, who is silent about Sardinia and promises to recover Sicily for the Holy See only if he should wrest it from the Saracens. Yet the need to adapt to Otto’s time those elements of Louis’s diploma that were appropriate, together with the crudity of that age, forced the insertion everywhere of statements that either fit the preceding material poorly or contradict one another. This is a most compelling argument for the authenticity of both the Louisian and the Ottonian diplomas.] [islands], censuses, and payments, on behalf of the church of blessed Peter the apostle and of the pontiffs residing in his most sacred see [162], so that these things may firmly remain in his dominion for use, enjoyment, and disposition.

Our authority, and that of our son and our descendants, being reserved in all things [Note: [Col. 0608C] The sectarians incorrectly refer what follows, in Dietrich Hermann’s work [Col. 0608D] (*Introduction to Public Law*, book I, chapter 15, no. 8), to everything stated above. For what follows becomes entangled unless it is supported by that condition, “our authority being reserved.” Besides, it would say “dominion,” not “authority,” as we saw in the case of the Tuscan and Spoletan duchies. I discussed this matter in the dissertation (no. 23).], according to what is contained in the pact, constitution, and firmness of the promise of Pope Eugenius and his successors—that is, that all the clergy and the entire Roman people and nobility, on account of the various needs, and in order to curb the unreasonable harshnesses of the pontiffs toward the people subject to them, should bind themselves by oath so that the future election of the pontiffs might, insofar as each person understood it, be conducted canonically and justly [Note: [Col. 0608D] Here is the extent of imperial authority: it concerned these three matters. First, it rested upon the promise of Eugenius II and his successors. Second, by pontifical constitution, the Roman clergy and people, to whom the election exclusively belonged, were to bind themselves by oath to a canonical and just election; and, to bring this about, Eugenius appears to have thought it appropriate to invoke the fear of imperial authority. Such an oath was not new; what was new was the emperor’s power, which otherwise he possessed by apostolic authority. You will find this matter treated at greater length in the following dissertation.]. And that the man elected to this holy and apostolic government should be consecrated pontiff without anyone’s consent only after, in the presence of our envoys, or of our son, or of the whole community, he had made such a promise for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation as Lord Leo, our spiritual father, venerable and revered, is known to have made voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0609B] The third matter to which imperial authority extended consisted in this: imperial envoys were to be present at the consecration, before whom the elected pontiff was to make a promise or profession such as Leo IV, who had been consecrated without the envoys’ presence, subsequently made of his own accord. What this promise was is nowhere recorded. Its substance must therefore be inferred from this diploma and the following one.].

Moreover, we foresaw that other minor matters should be inserted into this work, namely, that at the election of pontiffs neither free man nor slave should dare to come forward in order to cause any impediment to those Romans whom the ancient custom established by the constitution of the holy fathers had admitted to this election. If anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be handed over to exile [Note: [Col. 0609C] These provisions are taken from the constitution which Lothair made with the consent of Eugenius II in the atrium of Saint Peter in the year 824, chapter 3, with the wording somewhat altered but the sense intact. Holsten, *Roman Collection*, part II, p. 208.]. Furthermore, we prohibit any of our envoys from daring to devise any pretext for obstructing the aforesaid election [163] [Note: [Col. 0609C] These few words are absent from the aforesaid constitution, nor could they have been present there: Lothair obtained the privilege that imperial envoys should attend the consecration more than twenty years later. From this it is clear how vigorously the struggle was waged for the freedom of canonical election.]. For we have also resolved to establish this in every way: that those who have once been received under the special protection of the apostolic lord or of us should justly enjoy the protection obtained. If anyone should presume to violate it against any one of those who have deserved this protection, let him know that he will incur danger to his life. We likewise confirm that they should render just obedience in all things to the apostolic lord, and to his dukes and judges [Col. 0609B] for the administration of justice [Note: [Col. 0609C] Chapter 1 of the constitution mentioned above, which suits the age of the Frankish kings better than that of the Saxon emperor, as is evident.].

For we have perceived that this provision must necessarily be attached to the foregoing institution: that envoys of the apostolic lord or of us should always be appointed, who may report annually to us or to our son how each of the dukes and judges administers justice to the people and how they observe this imperial constitution. We decree that these envoys should first bring to the attention of the apostolic lord all complaints found through the negligence of the dukes [or judges], and that he himself should choose one of two alternatives: either that those needs should immediately be remedied through the same envoys, or, if our envoy reports to us, that they should be remedied by our envoys sent by us [Col. 0610A] [Note: [Col. 0609C] Chapter 4 of the same constitution, altered somewhat like the other provisions but with the sense intact. Anyone who compares these three chapters attentively with the history of those times [Col. 0610B] will easily understand that this addition is poorly suited to Otto’s age, when the Romans were hostile to imperial power.]. So that all the faithful of the holy Church of God and our own people might believe this to be firm, we have strengthened this pact of our confirmation with the mark of our own hand and the subscriptions of our noble princes, and have ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our seal [Note: [Col. 0610B] See the dissertation (no. 24).].

+ The sign of Lord Otto, most serene emperor, and of his bishops, abbots, and counts. + The sign of Adalgag [Adaldag], archbishop of the church of Hamburg. The sign of Arbert [Hartbert], bishop of the church of Chur. The sign of Driogo, bishop of the church of Osnabrück [*Dryog. Osnabrugguensis*]. The sign of Otto, bishop of the church of Strasbourg [*Yotonis Argentenensis*]. The sign of Otwin, bishop of the church of Hildesheim [*Hiltinesemen.*]. The sign of Conrad [Cronrates], count. The sign of Ernust. The sign of Thiether [Thiesteris], Ricdag. Liupo, Harwig. Arnulf. Ingild, Burghard, Reting.

In the year 962 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction V, in February, on the thirteenth day of that month, in the twenty-seventh year indeed of the empire of Lord Otto [*Ottonis imperii*], the unconquered emperor, this pact was successfully made [Note: [Col. 0610B] This chronology would be more correct if “the twenty-seventh year of the empire” were replaced by the first year [Col. 0610C]. Baronius (year 962, no. 12) says that the preceding years are shown by diplomas and synodal acts to refer to the reign, not to the empire. All scholars unanimously affirm the same. For in fact, when Henry I, king of Germany, died in 936, his son Otto was crowned king at Aachen; thus in this year, 962, his twenty-seventh year was running. But Otto had scarcely become king of Italy in 961, and in February 962 he was crowned emperor at Rome. The often-mentioned abbot of Göttweig, however, notes that another diploma exists in Freher in which the following year is called the twenty-eighth year of the empire (*Chronicle*, vol. I, book II, chapter 3, p. 189), although in other diplomas, as he himself observes, the years of the reign are distinguished from the years of the empire. Pagius and Muratorius agree with the other scholars; only the German writers, who are certainly ignorant of the nature of the imperial dignity restored or established by the Apostolic See, hold a different opinion.].

[Col. 0609]

165. DISSERTATION ON THE DIPLOMA OF HENRY I

[Col. 0609D] Although I seem to have shown, through the diploma of the great Otto, how a prince resembling Charlemagne in so many and such great afflictions of the Apostolic See and of all Italy was summoned from Germany to Rome, crowned with the imperial diadem by the pontiff, made a partner in supreme authority, and appointed defender of the Church, nevertheless, since German jurists are not afraid to lay the foundations of so many falsehoods upon this great prince, it is worthwhile to explain somewhat more fully what I treated in very brief form at the beginning of this work (*Preface*, no. 1 ff.), before saying something about Henry’s diploma, which is almost a copy of Otto’s.

In the second year of his empire, events occurred at Rome which rightly and justly summoned the enraged prince back to the City. The annals show that on this occasion he exceeded the limits of the power entrusted to him, and with good reason; nor am I prepared to depart from the venerable Cardinal Baronius in order to defend against the integrity of history what the youthful pontiff imprudently did. The essential point is that Pope John was deposed and Leo VIII, a pseudo-pontiff, was created; the rest is irrelevant here.

This man, neither properly elevated to so great a height nor possessing any authority, issued a decree which Georgius published from Codex Vaticanus 1984 as genuine in his new edition of the Luccan annals, to be compared with the edition of Theodoric of Niem, which Goldastus transcribed (*Imperial Constitutions*, vol. I, p. 221). I shall not place before the eyes of readers either the same decree, published long before by Gratian (*Decretum*, distinction 63, chapter 23) and thence taken up by Baronius (year 964, no. 22), or the recent version appended to Baronius’s text by Georgius, since both are worthless; but I shall present that forged decree, altered at the license of impostors and filled with foolish additions, which stands in Goldastus. The aforesaid jurists use it, burdened with almost immeasurable commentaries, to insinuate the false character of the renewed empire which they call Romano-Germanic. Indeed, since I do not ordinarily stir up such filth unless compelled, I shall excerpt only the portion relevant to the matter, omitting the rest, although it is especially well suited to sustaining the imposture. It is as follows.

[Col. 0611B] II. “For that same holy man, Hadrian, convened a synod and, in the presence and with the authority of all, granted to Lord Charles, the most unconquered king of the Franks and Lombards and Roman patrician, and to his successors, the kingdom of Italy, the dignity of the patriciate, and the government of the Apostolic See; moreover, the investiture of bishoprics, as he himself might wish with discretion and reverence, except for those which Charles himself left to the supreme pontiff and to the archbishops. Therefore we, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, following the example of Hadrian, together likewise with all the clergy, the entire Roman people, and all the orders of this nourishing City, as appears in their writings, establish, confirm, and strengthen, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow, upon Lord Otto, first Augustus, the most prudent king of the Teutons, our spiritual son in Christ, and upon his successors in this kingdom of Italy forever, both the power to choose a successor and the power to appoint the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See; and likewise, through this grant, archbishops and bishops, so that they may receive investiture and consecration from him alone wherever this may be appropriate, except those whom the emperor has granted to the pontiff and the archbishops. We therefore assert that henceforth no one, of whatever rank, condition, dignity, or religious status, shall have the power to elect a king or patrician, or the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, or any bishop, or to ordain; but we assign this revered power solely to the king of the Roman Empire, who shall administer and govern it without any payment, as king and Roman patrician.”

Thus far concerning this spurious constitution. To leave nothing out, I shall append the title of the royal law attributed to Hadrian, as indicated by Goldastus (*Imperial Constitutions*, vol. I, p. 16; Lunig, *Italian Diplomatic Code*, vol. I, p. 1):

“Royal law of the empire of the Franks, or constitution of Hadrian I, supreme pontiff, and of the Roman people, by which the right to elect the Roman pontiff, as well as the archbishops and bishops, together with direct dominion over the city of Rome and its territory, was transferred to Charlemagne, Roman emperor, and his successors”—a law which they claim was enacted in the year 774, that is, twenty-six years before the renewal of the empire.

III. I shall also add the titles of the likewise supposedly fabricated senatorial decrees (Goldastus, ibid., pp. 217, 221; Lunig, *Ecclesiastical Miscellany*, continuation 11, p. 63, part I, p. 139), since they seem to me to have come from one and the same workshop and to have met with one and the same fate. The first bears this title:

“Senatorial decree of the Romans concerning the royal law by which all right and power are transferred by the pope, the Senate and People of Rome, to Otto I, emperor, and vested in him. Also concerning the election of the Roman pontiff and the investiture of bishops.”

The second is prefaced as follows:

“Roman senatorial decree concerning the restoration to the Roman Empire of all temporal possessions that had been conferred upon the Roman Church by kings and emperors.”

When the Italian annalist encountered such disgusting fabrications [Col. 0612A] in the Reichersberg chronicle, he detested them so thoroughly (year 964) that he warmly commended the diligence of Baronius, Pagius, and others who refuted these impostures.

To all these is added another constitution attributed to Otto III, who, at approximately seventeen years of age, having received the imperial diadem from his kinsman Gregory V in 996, supposedly issued it after three years. The same authors report it (Goldastus, ibid., p. 226; Lunig, *Italian Diplomatic Code*, vol. I, p. 7; and *Miscellany*, part I, p. 140). In Lunig it is entitled:

“Constitution of Otto III, Roman emperor, by which a definite patrimony consisting of certain cities is assigned to the Roman See, and the most famous donation of Constantine the Great, emperor, made to that See and confirmed by Emperor Charlemagne, is declared fictitious and spurious.”

Concerning the eight cities of the supposed patrimony—“Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Fossombrone, Cagli, Jesi, and Osimo”—and concerning all the other contents, I shall add nothing to Pagius’s observation (year 999, no. 3) [Col. 0612B]: “Nearly as many lies as words.” The jurists themselves left the constitution for others to use, since it agrees poorly with both the royal law and the constitution of the antipope Leo.

IV. Both of these, as though resting upon substructures, are employed by the jurist under discussion; the writers themselves openly admit as much. Struvius will stand for them all (*On Public Law*, chapter 1, section 3), who, adhering to the constitution of the same antipope, says:

“From this pact the rights of the Roman Empire, which the Franks had hitherto possessed, were transferred to the Germans and are to be derived from the fact that the Romans, treating the Franks as having abandoned them, transferred the rights of direct dominion, together with the Roman Empire, to Otto and his successors, the kings of Germany. Thus, through a bond never to be violated and a pact destined to endure forever, the Roman Empire was joined to the German kingdom. From this, therefore, are to be derived the origins and foundations of the public law of the Romano-German Empire of which we are speaking.”

To deny that this happened would be ignorance. For Conrad, brother of Frederick, duke of Swabia, understanding that the title of king of Italy was insufficient for him to obtain the imperial crown he so ardently desired, took every possible measure to acquire the crown of the German kingdom. He obtained it when his rival Lothair II died, in the year 1138; and none of the illustrious princes of the Alemanni attained imperial majesty without first being made king of Germany. Thus, whereas this had not been customary in the time of the Carolingians [168], after the Ottos the practice was introduced that in Germany the king of the Romans, the future emperor, was crowned, then received the diadem of the kingdom of Italy, and finally became emperor at Rome through the Roman pontiff, as has been demonstrated at length (*Dissertation* 1, nos. 43 ff.).

But the legal question must be stated differently. Not every king created king of Germany simultaneously became emperor. Witnesses to this are Henry IV, king of Germany; the aforesaid Conrad II, king of Germany; Rudolph—I shall say nothing about those elected during the fatal interregnum, as they call it—Adolphus, Albert I, Louis the Bavarian, Wenceslaus, Robert, Albert II, and Maximilian, kings of the Romans elected as future emperors, who did not reach that supreme dignity. None of them received the imperial insignia from the Roman pontiff, in accordance with the innate character of the renewed majesty.
