Nor was the Roman Empire transformed into the Romano-German Empire except by writers who followed those fabricated documents cited above, as the Rudolphine code, which overthrows such fictions, will make clear below, together with the Golden Bull of Charles IV—a more sacred monument which the same jurists constantly affirm cannot be found. In both places one finds “Roman Empire”; but “Romano-German Empire” is found neither there nor anywhere else. If they do not understand this, it weakens the majesty of the Roman Empire, which it is easy to believe neither pontiffs nor emperors ever contemplated.

V. It does not seem necessary to deny absolutely that Gregory V, to whom the imperial matter undoubtedly belonged above all, together with Otto III—whether because of their kinship or for some other cause persuading both of them—issued a constitution concerning the election of the future emperor. It did not, however, determine anything concerning the number of electors, as Blondus and Platina assert, but restricted the election to the princes of Germany.

For this reason I would not reject altogether the words of Platina, although he produced them on the authority of Blondus, where he is treating Gregory V:

“Having recognized the weakness of the empire and the instability of fortune, so that supreme power might remain longer among the Germans and might be held by the man who surpassed the others in virtue and dignity, he issued, with Otto’s consent, a decree concerning the election of the emperor in the year of Christ 1002. We see it preserved down to our own time: namely, that only the Germans should have the right to choose a prince who, called Caesar and king of the Romans, would then be regarded as emperor and Augustus if the Roman pontiff confirmed him.”

The chronology is plainly false—for Otto died at the beginning of the year 1002, and Sylvester II was then pontiff—but once it is rejected, the remainder proceeds correctly.

Setting aside the opinion that the college of Seven Electors was then established, which I shall show below cannot be admitted (*Dissertation* 6, no. 7), one should note that Otto, the son of Otto II, “alienated from marital intercourse after the death of his wife, by whom he had not begotten a male child,” as Landulf the Elder, an eleventh-century writer, relates (*Italian Writers*, vol. IV, book II, chapter 18), knew well that he would be the last of the Augusti named Otto. He also knew that there were many reasons why the imperial dignity might either return to the Franks or be conferred upon another summoned from elsewhere, as had happened thirty-four years earlier, when the imperial diadem had been placed upon his grandfather Otto the Great.

Moreover, the pontiff, whose concern for the honor of his own people was equal to that of the Augustus, is said, in his desire to perpetuate so great an honor in Germany, to have adopted a policy more consistent with the truth than any other. To this must be added the fact that it is so certain that the innovation of the election was owed to the Roman pontiff alone, as founder of that majesty, that the jurists themselves placed Hadrian’s royal law and the institution of the pseudo-pope Leo at the foundation of their Romano-German Empire [Col. 0613C].

VI. What most strongly confirms that such a constitution was made by Gregory V and Otto, as formerly by Eugenius II and Lothair, is that Henry II, king of Germany and Emperor I, is found to have been the first of all to be called king of the Romans (Gotweig Chronicle, vol. I, book II, chapter 6, p. 233) in two diplomas and in a bull of Benedict VIII.

There is no doubt that he used this title, for several diplomas of Henry IV are entitled with the name “Henry III, King of the Romans.” And the seal of Zyllesia belonging to Henry III, king of Germany and emperor II, displays the inscription: “Henry III, by the grace of God king of the Romans.” Whatever may be unusual about this, namely, that it begins the reckoning of the German kingdom, with Henry V also following the example in his diplomas, it nevertheless supports the publication of the constitution. For it shows that he already held the title of king of the Romans.

Between the two Augusti, Henry I and Henry II, stands Conrad, king of Germany II, surnamed the Salian. No diploma of his survives in the aforementioned chronicle with the title “king of the Romans.” By contrast, several diplomas of Conrad III survive, and he is the first to have “king of the Romans” on his seal. In his diplomas, reckoning both the Roman and German kingdoms, he assigns himself the title “king of the Romans II” in several documents and “III” in others.

A distinguished example survives from the autograph preserved by Johann Friedrich Falke (*Corvey Traditions*, p. 907), concerning the year 1147. Both its opening and its seal present him as the second king of the Romans; the only difference is that the opening reads: “Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, second king of the Romans,” while the seal reads: “Conrad, by the grace of God, king of the Romans II.”

Heineccius saw in the same Corvey archive this diploma, written in golden letters on purple parchment (*On German Seals*, part I, chapter 4, section 3), like the Ottonian diploma mentioned above (*Dissertation* 3, no. 25). This new form, used by none of the three Ottos and immediately adopted by Otto III’s successor, indicates that something new had been established.

Furthermore, it is inferred that Henry was elected not merely king of Germany but future emperor from his acquisition of the kingdom of Italy, after expelling the tyrant Harduin, whom the Italian princes had chosen for themselves after the death of Otto III without a male heir. Adelbold, a contemporary author of the highest reliability, gives this account above all others in the Bollandists (*July*, vol. III, p. 747 ff., nos. 20, 23):

“The king was received in each of the kingdoms of his predecessor, except Italy and Alemannia, and was unanimously acclaimed by all, etc.”

And below:

“At the same time a certain bishop-murderer named Harduin did not reign, but served the vices that reigned in him in Italy. For when they heard of the death of Emperor Otto, the Lombards, deaf, blind, and without foresight concerning the future, chose this man and, hastening toward repentance, crowned him king for themselves.”

Later, when they were about to expel him, they turned to Henry with envoys and supplications, as to the true king [Col. 0614B].

### VII

Since these matters stand thus, I say that Platina’s and Blandi’s assertion concerning the election in Germany, among the princes of that nation, of the king of the Romans who was to become emperor (provided that the pope approved him) is not altogether to be rejected. But I shall discuss these matters more opportunely elsewhere (*Dissertation* 6, no. 4 ff.). For now, however, we must speak of the diploma of the first confirmed king of the Romans and of the emperor instituted with the golden crown.

I am aware that highly learned men have debated its date. Yet neither Baronius and those who follow him, in assigning it to the year 1014—for it was customary among the Carolingians for such a diploma to be read at the solemnity of the coronation—nor Mabillon, in assigning it to 1024 because he read among the subscriptions “Richard, abbot of Fulda,” and thought that he had not attained that dignity before 1023 (*Annales*, book 53, no. 97), establishes anything certain about the date of the diploma, which specifies none. Several other diplomas of this emperor of the same kind are found; both Mabillon and the abbot of Göttweig observe this point (*Chronicon*, chap. 6, p. 243).

Mabillon, however, would, I believe, have discovered a definite date if he had not stopped at the subscription of the abbot of Fulda. More important than the others is the subscription of Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, who calls himself a subject of the Roman see. This indicates a period following the pope’s journey into Germany.

The matter is recorded by the Bishop of Ostia (*Chronicle*, book II, chap. 46), who relates in a single account the foundation, dedication, and exchange concerning the church of Bamberg:

> “This same Augustus, at his own expense and from his patrimony, built a church in Bamberg in honor of Saint George. He summoned Pope Benedict and had it consecrated by him; and, establishing an episcopal see there, he offered it in its entirety to blessed Peter, imposing an annual census of one excellent white horse, with all its ornaments and trappings, and one hundred marks of silver. Later, Pope Leo IX, receiving Benevento from Henry, son of Conrad, as an exchange, restored the aforesaid bishopric of Bamberg under his jurisdiction, retaining for himself only the horse mentioned above.”

But long before this, Pope Benedict himself, in a letter to that same Bishop Eberhard of Bamberg (*Bollandists*, July, vol. III, p. 771), had testified concerning the foundation of the bishopric, its subjection to the Holy See, and the establishment of the aforesaid census, though with some difference.

### VIII

The bishopric which Leo mentions is much later than the earlier one established by the pope together with its founder Henry, as is clear from Benedict’s own words:

> “Indeed, in such a way that at each successive indiction he shall pay to us and to our successors, under the name of a pension, one white horse with a saddle suitable for the Roman pontiff.”

The older *Book of Censuses* of Cencius, in the Albinian Codex, confirms this:

> “In the bishopric of Bamberg: one white palfrey for the saddle of the lord pope, or twelve marks of good silver.”

J. B. Sollerius demonstrates by the authority of ancient writers that this was certainly not done before the year 1019 (*ibid.*, p. 742). Baronius and Pagius had proceeded in the same way; only Janning opposed them, following the fuller chronicle of Hermann the Lame and postponing that journey to the following year.

I neither approve nor reject that chronology. Whether Benedict came to Bamberg in 1019 or the following year, I regard it as certain that on that occasion this diploma—whose date is in question—was issued. Indeed, the same pontiff says in the letter cited above:

> “We therefore came to Bamberg, where we were received by the same emperor as he was able and knew best; and he offered to the Holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, and to us, the church together with the entire integrity of the bishopric.”

What the pontiff relates as having been done, Henry explains in his diploma in such a way as to leave no room for doubt that at Bamberg he made the offering of the bishopric together with the confirmation of the other rights of the Holy See. I quote the very clear passage from the diploma:

> “Moreover, under the protection of Saint Peter, and of you and your successors, we offer the aforesaid bishopric of Bamberg. Therefore we decree that you shall receive from the bishop of that place each year, under the name of a pension, one white horse equipped with trappings.”

What prevents the date of the diploma from being placed earlier than 1020 is established by Hermann himself. The same Hermann who compelled Janning to remove Benedict’s journey from the preceding year, contrary to the observations of Baronius and Pagius, assigns the deaths of the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne to the year 1021:

> “Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, a man of great holiness, departed this life. He became renowned for many miracles, and Piligrim succeeded him. When Erkanbald, archbishop of Mainz, had also died, Aribo became archbishop.”

### IX

I consider that more credence should be given to Hermann, a contemporary, than to the later chronicler who placed Richard at the head of the monastery of Fulda in 1023, and whom Mabillon follows. Although Hermann himself testifies concerning the year 1020, saying, “I, Hermann, was committed to writing on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October,” nevertheless his fuller chronicle, preserved by Canisius (*Thesaurus*, vol. III, part II, p. 193), was either enlarged and shaped by a relative, as Canisius and Urstisius think, or received corrections and additions from learned men who used it, as Basnage maintains. If an adolescent author was mistaken about the death and succession of bishops, it would not have been difficult to correct him from obituaries and ecclesiastical catalogues.

Therefore it is not the uncertain beginning of Richard of Fulda, attached to no ancient document, that ought to prescribe a chronology for Henry’s diploma; rather, the diploma itself ought to move Richard’s beginnings back before the year 1020, or, if one prefers, to the preceding year, when it was issued at Bamberg.

Mabillon, not having thoroughly investigated the matter, failed to notice that the principal archbishops of Germany had already died when he placed Richard’s administration in 1023 and postponed the diploma to the following year. But lest anyone think that he relied on some weighty authority when he abandoned Baronius’s chronology, let us hear his own words (*Annales*, book 54, no. 28), under the year 1016:

> “After Boppo’s death, the abbacy of Fulda also became vacant. Brantho, or Brantohus, who had been deposed by Henry three years earlier, appears to have recovered it; this may be inferred from Lambert’s chronicle, in which Brantho is said to have become bishop of Halberstadt in 1023, and Richard to have succeeded him in the administration of Fulda.”

This manner of writing, to say what I think, deserves no consideration. I am therefore astonished to see this falsehood asserted in the Chronicle of Göttweig in Mabillon’s very words (chap. 6, p. 243), and to see Lunig depart from Baronius, Labbe, Goldast, and Rousset in order to follow Mabillon in his assessment of the diploma.

So much for the date, which I believe I have established. Although I can discover no other reason for its long delay than the subjection of the church of Bamberg to the Holy See, I have no doubt that Henry confirmed the rights of the Roman Church at the very solemnity of his coronation, following the custom of his predecessors. For diplomas of this kind, when they introduced nothing new, were generally praised by popes and emperors in the monuments of the annals; only the diplomas of Louis, Otto, and Henry are brought forward here because each had to be presented separately in order to establish all the rights of the Holy See.

### X

The Roman pontiffs ruled Rome and its duchy even before the two provinces of the Exarchate—Emilia and the Pentapolis—were added to their dominion by the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles. Later, under the newly invented name of the Royal Territory, Tuscia of the Lombards, or rather part of it, as well as the Sabine territory, the census or tribute of the duchy of Spoleto, and part of Lombard Tuscia—which was itself recognized under the name of a duchy—and finally Capua together with five other cities of the duchy of Benevento, became the property of the Holy See through the generosity of that same Charles.

Moreover, the patrimonies of Calabria, Sicily, Naples, Benevento, and others in various provinces, derived from the most ancient donations of the emperors of the East and of the patricians, and held by the Greeks and their Beneventan allies, belonged to the same Holy See. Since all these possessions were expressed in various charters of donation and preserved in the archive of the Roman Church, Louis, at the insistence of Stephen IV, strengthened them by his diploma so that, confirmed by imperial authority, they would be more secure. All the Carolingians renewed this confirmation on the very day of their coronation.

The same Otto the Great strengthened it, adding a donation defined by specified boundaries. This did not in fact enlarge the former dominion, but he himself voluntarily added seven cities from the duchy of Spoleto—over which the emperors possessed supreme right—as part of the kingdom of Italy, to the ancient donations. Therefore Otto II and Otto III, as well as Henry, must be considered to have confirmed this Ottonian diploma at the solemnity of their coronations, although Otto II shared in his father’s diploma.

Consequently, just as from the year 817, when the Ludovician diploma was issued, to 962, when the Ottonian diploma was issued, only Louis’s diploma is mentioned because the similar diplomas of his successors were included in it, so from the aforesaid year 962 to 1020 both Louis’s and Otto’s diplomas were mentioned.

Then Henry granted to the church of Saint Peter whatever remained of the duchy of Spoleto that pertained to the kingdom of Italy, namely, all the land which “we held as part of our kingdom between Narni, Teramo, and Spoleto.” From that time onward, Louis’s, Otto’s, and Henry’s diplomas began to be confirmed by their successors by name; the other possessions were included under the general designation of the emperors and kings who preceded them.

### XI

It must nevertheless be observed that Capua, together with the five other cities of the duchy of Benevento, was possessed by the Holy See neither in the time of Louis, nor of Otto, nor of Henry. These cities shared not only the same fate as the other patrimonies of the vast region now called Sicily this side of the Strait, but were also subject to their own prince from the year 900, who was called the prince of Capua.

Therefore, in the time of Louis, when the memory of Charles’s donation—made, that is, in the year 787 (*Codex Carolinus*, letter 88 ff.; alternatively 81, 90, 92, 88, 86)—was still recent, it was right and proper to count among Charles’s donations the fact that the Capuans had sworn an oath of fidelity to Hadrian, that possession, though not complete, had been delivered to the apostolic envoys, and that Hadrian had labored to secure their complete possession, as he had done that of the Sabine patrimony or territory. For the fickleness of peoples could not extinguish an acquired right.

In the age of Otto and Henry, those same ancient rights were confirmed. Thus, when thirty-six years later Nicholas II granted those cities to Richard, prince of the Normans, he exercised his own right just as in the other patrimonies of both Sicilies, imposing a census that did not exceed the ancient revenues.

Nor should it be omitted that a few years after Henry had confirmed the rights of the Holy See, he was summoned by those peoples to aid them against the Greeks, since the Normans had not yet prevailed. He took full charge of the principality of Capua, as though supreme authority belonged to him, as may be seen in the Bishop of Ostia (*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book II, chaps. 41 and 58). The anonymous Chronicle of Monte Cassino and the Chronicle of Cava also relate the matter in Pratilli (*History of the Princes of Lombardy*, vol. IV, pp. 71 and 432 ff.).

The account of Cava is especially as follows:

> “In the year 1022 the aforesaid Emperor Henry departed for Apulia and captured Troy, Trajanopolis, and Ascoli. Pandulf of Capua was captured and exiled to Germany. Landulf, prince of Benevento, made an agreement with the Augustus, received him in Benevento with great honor, and entertained him in lofty triumph. This occurred a few days before Holy Easter, in the month of April. Vaimar, prince of Salerno, and the consul of Naples did the same; they surrendered themselves and their possessions in homage to Henry, because they saw that their Greeks were already almost destroyed. The emperor then went to Capua and made Pandulf of Teano, nephew of the exiled Pandulf, its prince; from there he departed for Monte Cassino.”

### XII

The charter establishing Pandulf of Teano as prince, after the deposition of Pandulf IV, is preserved in P. Abbot Gattola, in the register of Peter the Deacon, and in Pratilli:

> “Given on the second day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1022, but in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry and the eighth of his empire, indiction 6. Acted at Paderborn, successfully.”

An Italian annalist uses this document to cast doubt—something that occurred to no learned person except the partisans—on Henry’s diploma in favor of the Roman Church. He therefore calls that diploma a copy and, by the following perverse argument, declares it false. I translate his words literally:

> “In the copy of the diploma by which Henry is said to have been the first among the emperors to confirm the territories of the Roman Church in 1014, we read: ‘In the regions of Campania: Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, Capua—the cities composing the principality of Capua.’ If this had been so, it is impossible to believe that the holy Emperor Henry was so forgetful of himself and so devoid of religion that he later invested Pandulf, and his son John, with Capua and its principality. Even if he had done so, the Roman pontiff would have protested; yet no trace of such a protest appears. What, then, are we to say about the copy of the diploma of 1014 reported by Baronius?”

The answer, with due respect to him, is that the autograph of the diploma—although it is not extant together with the Ottonian diploma—has been preserved in an authenticated transcript, strengthened by the hanging seals of forty bishops, in the archive of Molis Adriana. It confirms, as do the two preceding diplomas, what belonged by right to the Holy See, although it was not in its possession.

Henry contributed sufficiently to the public welfare by removing the less worthy prince from that principality and substituting another who was better and more acceptable to the people. The pontiff did not make an untimely protest because the time had not yet come to vindicate his rights. Finally, not even the Italian medieval chronicler dared to say anything of this sort about so certain a monument of antiquity. For if at one point he seemed to doubt it, he later accepted it as valid, saying that “Otto’s charter had been received in good and holy faith and confirmed by the most pious Henry.”

Therefore ancient monuments which we cannot fully comprehend should rather be left for investigation by a more fortunate mind than for something far from the truth to be either asserted about them or proposed for assertion.

### XIII

On the occasion of that charter, it was reasonable to observe that the supreme authority of the Augusti still existed in the duchy of Benevento, although the duchy was divided among several dynasties and exposed to the troubles caused by the Normans, Greeks, and Saracens.

For not many years later, when the Normans subjected those regions to their authority, the ancient right of the Roman Church returned to it by restoration, whereas imperial authority disappeared altogether. The emperors themselves stripped themselves of every right, however much the Normans, conquerors of those peoples, had left intact.

For King Henry III of Germany, the second emperor of that name, exchanged with Saint Leo IX, in the year 1052, everything that the Roman Church possessed in the regions beyond the mountains. Hermann the Lame is witness to this, and no fuller account can be found. In the penultimate year of his life he records the event as follows:

> “The emperor celebrated Christmas at Worms with the lord pope and many bishops and princes. There, when the pope, as he had begun some time earlier, had demanded and obtained from the emperor the abbey of Fulda and several other places and monasteries said to have been anciently given to Saint Peter, the emperor finally handed over to him in exchange for the lands on this side of the Alps many possessions beyond Rome that belonged to his own right. When that same pope had complained at length about the violence and injuries inflicted by the Normans, who against his will were forcibly holding the possessions of Saint Peter, the emperor also assigned him aid to drive them out from there.”

He gives this account under the year 1053, which he begins with Christmas (Canisius, vol. III, part I, p. 272 ff.).

The Chronicle of Cava agrees with him, although it names only the head of that principality:

> “Benevento was handed over into the hands of the apostolic pope by the pious Emperor Henry, which aroused the hatred and jealousy of the Normans, who wanted that city as their own kingdom.”

The Bishop of Ostia likewise mentions only Benevento, as I said above (no. 7). But when he says that this city was exchanged for the bishopric of Bamberg, he does not exclude the other places and monasteries exchanged in the same way for Fulda and other possessions.

Certainly, thereafter neither is the emperor found defending the ancient rights in those regions against the Normans, nor does the pope, conversely, seek the properties of the Apostolic See beyond the mountains. This is sufficient to refute the arguments of Sigonius and other recent writers on the matter.

### XIV

If Benevento, together with everything that remained of imperial right in the once extensive duchy of Benevento, came to the Holy See by right of exchange, then the principality of Capua returned to the same See by right of Charles’s donation. Throughout the land on this side of the Strait, and also on the island of Sicily, the rights of the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimonies—which the Normans later acquired after conquering the Greeks and Saracens—were revived when those same Normans promised by oath to pay a census or tribute.

Thus papal right in both Sicilies does not rest merely upon the prescription of so many centuries, as the Italian annalist is compelled by the force of truth to admit. Rather, it begins at a definite point—the restoration by the Roman pontiffs themselves, with the aid of the Normans, of the ancient right—together with the origin of that prescription.

I may seem to have wandered far from Henry’s diploma while discussing Benevento and the other matters belonging to imperial authority in the former duchy of Benevento, together with those possessions beyond the mountains that belonged to the Holy See and were exchanged for them. But I necessarily connected the period of that exchange with the date of the diplomas in order to shed some light on the voluntary donations of Pippin, Charles, Otto, and Henry confirmed in the same document.

Concerning Pippin’s donation, I have found only this in Aimoinus (book IV, chap. 62): that Stephen III received from that king “a certain estate called Palatiolum, situated in the district of Paris, to be held perpetually by royal charter.” The monastery of Soracte was also donated, or rather restored, to Paul I (*Codex Carolinus*, letter 41, alternatively 16); four years earlier he had granted it to the same king (*ibid.*, letter 32, alternatively 12).

Charles the Great, who, as Einhard says, “adorned and enriched the basilica of Saint Peter above all churches from his own resources” (*Life of Charlemagne*, chap. 27), bestowed much more, apart from the censuses or pensions derived from the duchies of Tuscia and Spoleto. For according to Saint Gregory VII (*Letters*, book VIII, letter 23), among his other benefactions,

> “Emperor Charles, as is read in the volume of his deeds preserved in the archive of the church of blessed Peter, collected annually in three places twelve hundred pounds for the service of the Apostolic See: at Aachen, at the Podium of Saint Mary, and at Saint Giles.”

Pagius calls this kind of tribute an alms (804, no. 8).

Otto’s generosity is clearly indicated by the half of the duchy of Spoleto granted to Saint Peter and his successors. Similarly, the grant of the remainder of that duchy, although called an exchange, is evidence of Saint Henry’s generosity. The complete exchange of all the possessions beyond the mountains, which I reported from Hermann, together with Benevento and the other imperial possessions, clearly demonstrates that Henry III’s predecessors had made substantial voluntary donations.

### XV

Louis the Pious is not counted among those predecessors, for he confirmed the donations of others but added nothing of his own. For this reason, in Henry’s diploma he is named only once, where the provinces of the Exarchate, Emilia and the Pentapolis, are concerned:

> “Lord Pippin, lord Charles, lord Louis, Otto, and likewise his son Otto, namely our predecessors.”

Louis could not be omitted here, since it was desirable to list the names of the Ottos, as I explained in the preceding dissertation (no. 9).

He is mentioned again in general terms, together with the other Augusti, when the Sabine territory and the other possessions donated by Charles and confirmed by his successors are confirmed:

> “As by the aforesaid emperors, our predecessors.”

But when the voluntary donations are enumerated, the text lists King Pippin, Charles the most excellent emperor, and the most pious Ottos. It should also be noted that the Ottos are not called emperors, because Otto II possessed only the royal title when he was included in his father’s diploma.

It is therefore evident that neither he nor his son Otto III added anything new in their own diplomas. Otherwise Henry would not have omitted it if the Roman pontiffs had acknowledged anything received from their generosity.

Likewise, when a little earlier he listed the cities of the duchy of Spoleto, he had not honored his predecessors Otto with the imperial title. On the contrary, when confirming the ancient offering of that duchy, he says:

> “As was agreed between Pope Hadrian, of holy memory, and lord Charles the emperor.”

This shows even more clearly that the honor was deliberately denied to the Ottos once and again. For Charles had certainly not yet obtained the title of Augustus in Hadrian’s time; nevertheless, that same pontiff is said to have invested Emperor Charles with the duchies of Spoleto and Tuscia, which the great Frankish king had offered to Saint Peter twenty-six years before he received the imperial diadem from Saint Leo III.

As for Louis, the objection of Antonio Pagius (1014, no. 2) and of the chorographer of medieval Italy (*Chorographical Table*, no. 20) is certainly ingenious: both contend that the name is an interpolation. The chorographer also rebukes Goldast because he did not see this.

Indeed, if we reject with our hands whatever we cannot grasp mentally from autographs, we shall find nothing contrary to our opinions, however false, and nothing obscure. But what are we then to think of later monuments that consistently preserve the passages we reject, as in the present case? Nothing is easier: whatever has once appeared to us interpolated must everywhere be erased. Is that really so? I leave this manner of writing intact for others.

### XVI

The weight of Henry’s diploma, and consequently that of the two preceding diplomas, did not escape Molinaeus, Wolf, Goldast, and others of their school. Their learning is evident from their writings, but their hostility toward the Holy See skillfully transformed the truth of events into other meanings.

Therefore it was necessary for them to declare these three diplomas—opposed as they were to their own efforts—to be of doubtful authenticity. A later age may produce ardent minds unafraid to follow in their footsteps in defending their opinions. I believe that I have answered them with arguments sufficient to restore these three ancient monuments to their integrity.

To that part of Henry’s diploma which concerns ecclesiastical discipline I think something should be added to what I discussed at length in the second dissertation (no. 32 ff.). Meanwhile, lest the Ottonian and Henrician privileges or diplomas—for there is great similarity between them—suffer any damage precisely from what most strongly confirms their integrity, it must be observed that a modest alteration of place occurs in them because they generally follow the model of the Ludovician diploma.

In the following dissertation (no. 16 ff.) it will become clear how great a variety of names is found in monuments of the tenth and following centuries. This is especially true in the duchy of Benevento, where the dominion of the Western emperors was almost always shadowy, even while the Carolingians remained in power. So many dynasties had arisen that they confined the principality of the age of Henry III within very narrow limits. In addition, Marsia, Apulia, and other smaller names had absorbed that old name.

When the Augusti began to be summoned from Germany, a great change had occurred in the names of places and in political circumstances. Therefore Sigonius and others of recent times, inquiring whether only the city of Benevento or also other places belonging to the imperial right had been exchanged, seem to me to have posed a most empty question.

For it is clear from the chronicle of Falco of Benevento that the dominion of the Holy See there was far more extensive (under the year 1113 and following). Thus greater credence should be given to Hermann, who relates that at the end of the year 1052 Henry III exchanged with the pontiff everything that belonged to imperial right, than to the chronicler of Cava, who asserts that only that city was handed over—unless, as is probable, he believed that by naming it as the head of the principality he had not thereby been silent about all the rest.

### XVII

The Continuator of Ostia (*Chronicle*, book IV, chap. 19) does not allow me to be mistaken. He presents the following document under the year 1098:

> “Anso, rector of the principality of Benevento, in fealty to the Roman Church, together with his noble brothers Dauferius, Atenulfus, John, Berardus, Peter, Alfanus, and Liuprand, sons of Lord Dacomarius, rector of Benevento, offered to Saint Benedict the church of Saint Nicholas, built above in the New Tower of the city of Benevento, which is called Pagana.”

When Peregrinius reread the counterpart of this charter or donation in the register of the same continuator (p. 283), he saw that this Anso was called prince. He therefore thought that, with the connivance of Urban II, Anso had usurped dominion over Benevento, which his successor Paschal II would not tolerate in any way, as is clear from Falco.

Apart from the constant attacks of the Normans, Benevento also suffered from internal discord under this pontiff. When he arrived there toward the end of 1112, the boldness of the citizens was somewhat restrained. Since they had resolved, without consulting the pontiff, to choose different rectors for themselves in order to ward off the depredations of the Normans, the pope, after deliberation, appointed Landulf of Greece, an energetic man, as constable in March of the year 1113.

The remedy was disastrous abroad and useless at home. The struggle with the Normans was difficult, and a revolt arose against the constable. Therefore the archbishop, whose name was also Landulf, compelled him to resign after he had scarcely completed a year in office; the archbishop was the head of the conspiracy.

Later, after the archbishop had been deposed by Paschal, the constable was restored in 1115, as Falco says:

> “In this year Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, was captured, and Landulf of Greece, who had been expelled from the city of Benevento, returned after receiving the office of constable. When all these and other matters had been settled, the apostolic pope himself proceeded to Troy on the ninth day before the Kalends of September and established a council there.”

From this brief summary of a history narrated at greater length by Falco, the principality of Benevento appears to have been reduced by the Normans to the city itself, together with the camps and castles belonging to its territory; moreover, its territory was subject to their incursions.

Yet sixty years had already passed since the exchange had been made, and only a few years afterward the pope granted all Apulia together with Calabria to Robert Guiscard, duke of the Normans. It is therefore unsurprising that the Normans, who had been reluctant to see the head of that province subject to a pontiff whom they then hated, should, after laying aside their hostilities, have desired the same possession; and that, while they held everything else by fiduciary right, and a prince of the same nation held the principality of Capua by an equal right, only the city of Benevento with its territory should be found to belong by right to the Apostolic See.

### XVIII

Even within that city alone, only very modest regalian rights belonging to the Roman pontiffs came to them, as is clear from a document belonging to this period, preserved in the Albinian Codex from the register of Paschal II and supplementing Falco’s history:

> “The property of regalian rights that remained for the curia of Benevento. These are what remained in the pope’s demesne:
>
> Four mills at Donno.
>
> Two mills at Saint Barbara.
>
> The mills at the Borgo.
>
> Towers and the gate toll of the upper gate.
>
> Gardens at the Crow Tower.
>
> The plaza of the Great Bridge, and all the stalls with the toll on fish and vegetables.
>
> The dye works of the Jews.
>
> The toll of the little bridge and the bridge.
>
> The houses around the palace.
>
> The whole alder grove, and the whole willow grove at the Leper Bridge, and the vineyards of Scullais, and the vineyard of Vardia, and the vineyards of Cirdo, and the vineyards of the prince.
>
> The island of Callarulo with its post.
>
> The Lord’s meadow, the garden, the bath, and the oven.
>
> The fish stall, and the customs office of Brudus at the Red Gate.
>
> The vineyard of Cantaro.
>
> The land of the Old Vineyard.
>
> All the churches.
>
> Half the vineyard of Cellarulo.
>
> The house of Christianus in the Borgo of the Golden Gate, the mint, and the *electa*, that is, the ban.
>
> Half the revenues from legal judgments, forfeitures, and the escheats of pilgrims and foreigners.
>
> All the escheats of the Beneventans.”

However small these regalian rights may have been, this document is powerful confirmation of possession so certain and so enduring.

Therefore it must be accepted as settled and firm that the city of Benevento, just like the Exarchate—or the provinces of Emilia and the Pentapolis—and, in a word, whatever rests upon the donations of princes, with the exception of Rome and its duchy, whose case has been shown to require a different treatment, belongs by proper right to the Roman pontiffs as successors of Saint Peter, without any admixture of the Roman princes.

If Roman rulers at any time claimed something for themselves under whatever pretext, they must be regarded as invaders of the Church’s goods, as were certain of the Augusti. For the emperors of the East and the patricians, the kings of the Franks, and the emperors of the West granted these possessions to Peter alone and to the Roman pontiffs, for the salvation of their souls, so that they might remain under their dominion and principality until the end of the age. They reserved only supreme authority in the duchy of Spoleto, from which Otto and Henry completely divested themselves, as their diplomas make clear.

I now turn to the matters that must be added concerning the discipline established by the pontiffs.

### XIX

I recognize that tracing the entire discipline governing the election and consecration of the Roman pontiffs would be a lengthy task. For this reason, in another work (*On the Superiority of the Vatican over the Basilica*), I shall explain individually what is true concerning enthronement, benediction, coronation, and several other matters found in the ceremonial book. Here I shall say only what more fully illuminates the discipline of the age of Otto and Henry.

I have discussed some of these matters elsewhere (vol. I, pp. 260 and 289 ff.) and later presented more (vol. II, p. 110 ff.). From these discussions it is clear that there was a difference between the time of Louis, when the Roman pontiff was chosen from the body of the clergy of the Roman Church—that is, from among the priests and deacons—and was consecrated, and the age of Otto, when men had already begun to be promoted to the highest office of the universal Church from outside that body, and even men distinguished by episcopal dignity were advanced there contrary to the custom of their ancestors and the statutes of the Fathers.

First, it must be added that the eighteen methods of creating a pontiff devised by Panvinio must be greatly reduced, and that the six into which the most learned Mabillon reduced them (*Preliminary Commentary on the Roman Order*, chap. 17, p. 109) must be treated differently.

Mabillon adhered too closely to Panvinio, who was more distinguished by profane than by sacred learning and flourished at a time when the critical method, though necessary, was feared and wrapped in childish coverings.

The incomparably learned writer of that same age, Cardinal Baronius, certainly speaks in these terms about the constitution of the false pope Leo VIII, which was particularly pleasing to Panvinio (*Annals*, 774, no. 13):

> “We contend that this too is an imposture, and that the decree is fictitious, similar to the earlier one—the fabricated law attributed to Hadrian—for everything that is asserted is shown to be false.”

Peter de Marca and Pagius support him with additional arguments, except that Sigebert is vindicated against Baronius’s sharp judgments directed at him, as though Sigebert himself had fabricated that synod. The reason is that in Miraeus’s edition of Sigebert, prepared according to manuscript codices, there is no mention of any synod.

Mabillon, however, with Gratian and Ivo—who were excessively credulous—supporting Panvinio’s opinion, places this new and false period of ecclesiastical discipline between Charlemagne and Pope Formosus. He also adduces Anastasius as a witness, although nothing concerning the matter is found in the *Book of the Pontiffs*. This demonstrates that Mabillon was deceived by Panvinio.

### XX

For how could such a false doctrine have been entered into the *Pontifical Book* under Hadrian I, or even under Leo III, if it is said that under Hadrian II—who was separated from Leo by nearly forty years—it was not wished to permit the legates of Louis II to attend the election of the Roman pontiff? The reason is likewise given in these explicit words: “Lest, that is, the practice of awaiting the legates of princes for the election of Roman prelates should, through such encouragement, take root.”

But if even the legates of Louis—who had obtained from Sergius II, for his father Lothair, twenty-four years earlier, a privilege which he himself also used, namely that consecration should not take place without the presence of imperial envoys—were not permitted to attend the election, as the *Pontifical Book* testifies, can it be affirmed on the authority of that same book that Hadrian granted “Charles the power of electing the pontiff and arranging the apostolic see”?

The same applies to Otto, if one looks to his privilege or diploma, of which the Henrician document is a copy; the matter is otherwise if one considers what he and his two namesake successors usurped. For, imitating the counts of Tusculum, they dared to elect Roman pontiffs not merely from outside the body of the Roman Church, but even from outside the cardinal bishops—a practice manifestly contrary to the diploma.

Henry Augustus, indeed, in keeping with his piety, would not have violated even a word of his diploma if any election of a pontiff had taken place while he was alive. Accordingly, serious attention must be paid to what he confirms with the words: “Our authority in all things remaining intact,” and so forth. The purpose was that the clergy and the whole nobility should bind themselves by oath, in accordance with the constitution of Eugenius II, that no one would be elected except “canonically and justly”; and that the decree of election should be sent to the emperor according to ancient practice. Although this is not expressed in the diploma, it is inferred from the requirement that the imperial envoys be awaited before the consecration. For this reason the *Pontifical Book*, as stated above (*Dissertation* 2, no. 37, p. 115), gives luminous testimony to the matter. Finally, the pontiff who was to be consecrated was to make, in the presence of the imperial envoys and before everyone, the same sort of profession or promise that Leo IV voluntarily offered, and of which enough—and more than enough—has been said above.

### XXI

Since certain recent scholars hold in such high esteem the privilege attributed, at the end of the little book on the bishops of Metz, to Lothair Augustus and Pope Eugenius II, I think I shall perform a useful service if I show that this compilation—which I rightly called it (*Dissertation* 2, no. 35)—introduces nothing new into pontifical discipline.

Inappropriately, it begins with the oath, or oath of fidelity, which the Romans were accustomed to render to the emperor from the very renewal of the empire, as I have demonstrated elsewhere (*Dissertation* 1, no. 25, p. 22); yet it does so without that unusual opening, awkwardly cobbled together from formulas of a later age. How suitably this has been done, you can see for yourself.

There follows, under the same oath, a promise of a canonical and just election. But I long ago published a fragment of the Lateran council held under Stephen III, seventy-four years before the pontificate of Eugenius II, in which Christopher, *primicerius* of the notaries, addressed the assembled fathers as follows:

> “Having brought forth in the same house of my lowliness the four holy Gospels of Christ, and the venerable chrism, and the other mysteries of God, we mutually gave an oath that no one would conduct the election of the pontificate apart from the others, but that we would choose as bishop the one whom divine providence should grant from the body of our holy Church, according to its counsel—that is, from among the priests and deacons—in accordance with the tradition of this apostolic see. And after giving this same oath among ourselves, we trusted in their pledge, affirming also in the same bond of the oath that we would not permit any of the country people subject to the castles of this Roman city to enter this city.”

Is this not a far more ancient oath concerning a canonical and just election? Those scholars, therefore, are contending over a practice already established, so as to appear to have conferred some new honor upon the imperial majesty.

What is new in that compilation is its final section: namely, that the pontiff was not to be consecrated without the presence of an imperial envoy, and that Eugenius II had voluntarily made the promise in writing. The falsity of this is otherwise demonstrated by Otto and Henry, since they substitute at least two imperial envoys and make the promise one voluntarily given by Leo IV—neither of which is contrary to the truth.

I admit that it is not easy to understand why the author of such a fabrication should have lied about a matter that was certain. For the substance of the discipline is one and the same. Moreover, Lothair’s definite law, which Otto and Henry each inserted almost in its entirety into his own diploma, completely removes the need for this compilation.

### XXII

I would not dare deny that Eugenius II established something new concerning the oath to be rendered by the Roman clergy and people regarding a future election according to the canons. But if such a constitution should ever emerge, recovered from its hiding place, I am certain that it will in no way present an oath of fidelity to be rendered to the emperor.

For Otto and Henry clearly show that the oath of the clergy and people consisted in this: that the election should be conducted canonically and justly. This was the characteristic of that age, expressed in capitularies and other records, as I suppose no scholar is unaware. Yet it was necessary that the clergy and people should understand that they were being bound by that oath through imperial authority.

Would that the promise voluntarily made by Leo IV for the satisfaction of all and future preservation had enjoyed the same good fortune. For, unless one wishes to introduce a new and unheard-of rite into the creation of the Roman pontiff, it was a profession—the one called the pontiff’s *indiculum* in the *Liber Diurnus* (Garnerius, ch. 2, vol. 9)—which from the tenth century onward began to be called a *professio*. It followed the decree of election, or, better put, it marked the beginning of the consecration, with a necessary delay intervening: a shorter delay when consecration, being permitted only on a Sunday, was separated from the election; a longer one when confirmation of the decree was awaited from the prince, together with the arrival of his legates.

Records from the period in question confirm both practices. In the election of Hadrian in the year 772, when the clergy and people enjoyed complete freedom, as may be seen in Mabillon (*Iter Italicum*, vol. I, part II, p. 38), ordination or consecration followed immediately after the decree:

> “The election is concluded. The venerable Hadrian himself, at the beginning of his ordination, composed the following statement of orthodox faith: ‘I …’”

By contrast, the election of Leo IV, because Sergius II had granted Lothair the privilege that the decree of election should be confirmed according to ancient practice and that legates should be sent in the new manner to attend the consecration, preceded the ordination by two months and fifteen days. It would have been delayed even longer had the danger threatening the city from the Saracens not compelled the neglect of the prince’s command, as the *Pontifical Book* testifies.

There is no doubt that in this profession Leo IV added whatever was consistent with the wording of the diplomas: “A promise for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation,” say Otto and Henry, “such as our lord and venerable spiritual father Leo is known to have made voluntarily.”

### XXIII

I should be lying if I did not indicate here the addition that appears in the profession published by Garnerius in opposition to the *indicium*, where the pontiff professes concerning the non-alienation of Church property:

> “And to preserve the Church’s possessions undiminished”  
> (and neither to alienate them nor to grant them in fief, census, or emphyteusis, in any manner or for any reason), “and to take care that they be kept undiminished.”

Although in the time of Leo IV the word *fief* had not yet come into use, in later centuries, when this profession had become customary, one little word was changed so that the matter might be expressed more significantly.

Certainly, a more suitable occasion for adding this clause “for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation” never presented itself than after the pontificate of Sergius II. His pontificate is described in a very unpolished style; see Vignolius (*Anastasius*, vol. III, under Sergius II, years 40–48), or rather the account most carefully excerpted from the Farnesian parchments by the most learned bishop Francis Blanchinius and published elsewhere by me (*G.*, 1755, p. 292).

Whatever Leo IV’s profession may have been, both diplomas prescribe that it be made before the consecration, with the imperial envoys present. Since Leo necessarily made it without the presence of the envoys, he is said to have made it voluntarily.

Rightly and properly, in those most unjust times, the decrees of Eugenius II concerning a canonical and just election and of Leo IV concerning consecration before the imperial legates were restored. For before, during that prolonged vacancy of the empire in the tenth century, the entire discipline of the Roman Church was overthrown, John IX had attempted—though in vain—to restore both matters in a Roman council (*Dissertation* 2, no. 40, p. 118). In another council held at Ravenna (*Baronius*, 904, no. 16; Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 509), he complained in chapter VII that the imperial diploma of Wido and Lambert Augustus had been violated by alienating Church property, or granting it by census or emphyteusis (*Dissertation* 1, no. 34); for this reason he urgently requested that the emperor provide some remedy.

It is therefore clear how necessary the restoration of imperial authority was in those times, lest such things be committed—provided only that the Augusti of Germany had imitated Charlemagne and his descendants, knowing that they had undertaken to govern the City by divine ordinance and to defend and exalt the Mother of all the Churches of God, as Louis II said in his letter to Basil.

### XXIV

I have already said in the preceding dissertation that what follows is taken from Lothair’s constitution, with the consent of Eugenius II, in the year 824, with only the order of the matters altered and different words occasionally employed.

One point must be added here. Pagius and other scholars, by referring the clause “our authority in all things remaining intact,” and so forth, to the preceding material, destroy with a double-edged stroke both what precedes and what follows. For if the emperors include under that clause all the rights of the apostolic see that they have confirmed, reserving only supreme lordship for themselves in the duchies of Tuscany and Spoleto, then the confirmation is deceptive.

But in the creation of the Roman pontiff, no authority remains to the emperors either to confirm the decree of election or to send legates “who would prevent violence and scandals from occurring at his consecration,” as was decreed in the council under John IX. They seem merely to attend the consecration together with the clergy and people, though it is uncertain under what right they came to Rome.

Conversely, if that clause is referred to the constitution of Eugenius II and his successors—by which the clergy and people were bound by imperial authority to swear to a canonical and just election—and to the voluntary promise or profession of Leo IV, by which he promised in the presence of the imperial envoys that he would preserve the canons and decrees of his predecessors, and especially the Church’s property, then the imperial power in the creation of the Roman pontiff is unmistakable.

The opinion of Pagius and the others is therefore overturned. In claiming for the emperors of the West the right to confirm the election, they do them serious injury by attributing to them the usurpation of Odoacer and of the emperors of the East.

For Otto and Henry testify that this imperial power, which each of them wishes to remain intact, is attributed not to the Augusti Lothair and Louis, but to Eugenius, who issued the decree concerning the election, and to Leo IV, who was the first of all the pontiffs to put into effect the constitution of Sergius II, by which Lothair and Louis had obtained that power.

Thus the emperors themselves reject the imperial right over which they dispute so much and so vehemently. They confess that, in a matter of such importance, they possess authority by the privilege of the apostolic see, and they establish that this authority shall remain intact for themselves and their successors.

I have discussed the subscriptions and the other matters belonging to the final portion of the diploma in the preceding dissertation.

## Example of the Privilege of the Emperor Henry Concerning the Regalia Granted to Blessed Peter

[Note: Variant readings enclosed in brackets are taken from the authentic document of Innocent IV.]

In the name of the Lord God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Henry, by the grace of God emperor Augustus,

[Note: Enough has already been said in the dissertations about the invocation and the consistently similar opening in the three diplomas. Concerning the title “emperor Augustus,” which he assigns to himself, it should be noted against German writers—who also count Henry, Otto’s father, among the emperors—that the diplomas of this man, carefully examined by the abbot of Gottwic, bear no title other than that of king, with no addition of “of Germany,” “of the Franks,” or “of Eastern Francia” (*Chronicle*, vol. I, book II, ch. 2, p. 151). I would not have noted this had I not encountered, among the continuators of Cangius’s *Glossary* (under “The Empire Vacant”), an addition full of ignorance and audacity. Consult it; marvel at the confidence of these men, and see what zeal can accomplish when joined to constant partisan reading. No sound-minded person will accept the charters they produce; but scholars know well that the imperial dignity was established by Leo III and attested by so many records.]

promise and declare by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and holder of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, that, just as your predecessors have held and governed them in your power and jurisdiction until now,

[Note: For nearly three hundred years the pontiffs had ruled the Roman duchy, whose head was Rome; as has often been said, that rule passed from their predecessors to their successors from hand to hand. The letters of the *Codex Carolinus* and the other ancient records already cited consistently affirm this down to the death of Charlemagne. From that time onward the diplomas of all the emperors do so as well; these three under consideration are examples, beginning with Louis the Pious. Stephen IV and Paschal I sought to strengthen by imperial authority all the rights of the Holy See, including those unjustly held by others, since they hoped that these too would eventually be vindicated for the Holy See; and it is clear that those hopes were not deceptive.]

the city of Rome with its duchy and suburbs, together with all its villages, its mountain and maritime territories, shores, and harbors, and all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany, namely Porto, Centumcellae, Caere, Pledum, Marturanum, Sutrium [Maturianum, Sutrium], Nepi, Castellum Gallise, Orte [Orce], Pollimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, namely the greater and the lesser, Pulvensis [, and the lake], Narnia, and Otricoli [Otriculum], with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the aforesaid cities.

Moreover, the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety,

[Col. 0626B] with its cities, towns, and castles, which the lords Pippin, of blessed memory, Charles, Louis, and Otto, his son—namely our predecessors—formerly conferred by deed of donation upon the blessed apostle Peter and your predecessors,

[Note: Here the beginning of the donations is clearer than daylight. The donors are expressly named, which could by no means have been done where the matter concerned the dominion of the Roman pontiffs. For it is not clear whether Gregory II or Gregory III was the first ruler, or what sort of administration existed—whether absolute, or combined with the laws of the senate and people. Therefore, by the phrase “just as you have held,” the character of the dominion is left uncertain.]

that is, the city of Ravenna and Aemilia,

[Note: I would gladly agree with those who, led by excessive love for the Holy See, extend Aemilia as far as Piacenza, where that province truly began in Roman times. It was likewise a province in the eighth century and afterward, as is clear from the records of the ancients. Among other evidence, this is luminously attested by canon 17 of the council of Ravenna in the year 877 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 302): “through Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and Aemilia, and through the Tuscany of the Romans and Lombards, and the whole territory of Saint Peter the Apostle.” But it was a very narrow province, bounded on one side by the territory of Bologna and on the other by the Pentapolis. Thus Louis, Otto, and Henry enumerate the cities of the Exarchate and Pentapolis, while passing over Piacenza, Parma, and the other places beyond Bologna in profound silence. Is it credible that Gabellum, such a small city—which Hadrian calls “very brief” (*Codex Carolinus*, letter 54, elsewhere 51)—should be listed, while none of the more celebrated cities beyond Bologna is named? Does anyone deserve belief who, seeing Parma openly excluded from the dominion of the Holy See by the boundaries specified in the donation, along with Mutina, brings against venerable antiquity the hallucinations of sixteenth-century authors? In my view, he errs as much who detracts from these diplomas as he who adds an arm’s length of land to them. See the notes on the diploma of Louis the Pious.]

Bobium [, and], Cesena, Forum Populi, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio [Comiaclum], Adria, and Gabellum, with all the boundaries, territories, and islands belonging by land and sea to the aforesaid cities.

Likewise the Pentapolis, namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo [Ausimum], Humana, Jesi, Fossombrone [F. Sempronii], Montefeltro, Urbino, and the territory of Valva [Balva], Cagli, Lucioli, and Gubbio, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities.

In the same way, the Sabine territory,

[Note: Enough has been said about this territory in the *Codex Carolinus* and in the dissertations. See also the notes on the diploma of Louis the Pious and on that of Otto.]

just as it was granted in its entirety to the blessed apostle Peter by the aforesaid emperors, our predecessors,

[Note: In the diploma of Louis the Pious: “just as it was granted by our father Charles”; in Otto’s diploma: “just as it was granted by the lord Charles, our imperial predecessor”—both correctly, since Charles alone had been the donor of the Sabine territory. Here, however, you see all the emperors named somewhat earlier indicated—Charles, Louis, and the Ottos—not because they too had been donors, but because they had confirmed the Carolingian donation. Pagius thinks Louis should be removed, since he declared Louis’s diploma a forgery. But for me, who have demonstrated that it is not merely genuine but the source of the others, Louis must certainly be retained with the other Augusti. The negligence of the Ottonian age, which produced a transcription of the Ludovician diploma while passing over its author in silence, ought to be condemned rather than summoned in defense of a false opinion.]

So too [That is, “and it is”],

[Note: This is an erroneous reading, though it occurs in an even more corrupt form in Baron’s manuscripts. It can easily be corrected from the preceding diplomas, which read: “Likewise, in the regions …”]

in the regions of Lombard Tuscany: Castellum Felicitatis, Orvieto, Bagni del Re, Ferento, Viterbo, Orte [Orthem], Marta, Pledum, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, and Roselle [Roselles], with the suburbs, villages, all the territories, and the maritime towns—in short, all the boundaries.

Likewise, from Luna [alunis], with the island of Corsica, to Surianum; then to Mount Bardone; then to Berceto; from there to Parma; then to Reggio; and from there [Reggio, from there] to Mantua, and to Mount Silicis, and to the province of Venetia and Istria [Ystria].

Moreover, the entire duchy of Spoleto, and Benevento [the Beneventan territory], together with the church of Saint Christina situated near Pavia beside the Po, four miles away.

Likewise, in the regions of Campania: Sora, Arce, Aquino, Ariminum, Teano [Arpinum, Theanum], Capua, and also the patrimonies belonging to your power and jurisdiction, namely the Beneventan and Neapolitan patrimonies, and the patrimony of Upper and Lower Calabria.

As for the city of Naples, with its castles, territories, boundaries, and islands belonging to it, according as they appear to pertain to those same places, and also the patrimony of Sicily, if God should deliver it into our hands.

In the same way, the city of Gaeta [Cajeta] and Fondi, with all their dependencies.

[Note: Up to this point it does not differ from Otto’s diploma. See what we said in the notes there.]

In addition to these things, we confirm to you the monastery of Fulda and the consecration of its abbot, as well as all the monasteries, estates, and villas that Saint Peter is known to possess beyond the Alps, except Antesna Uinni Reringa, or Uuillinbach [Vumiteringa, or Urullmbach], which have been transferred from the Church of Saint Peter to our bishop of Bamberg by deed of exchange [commutation].

[Note: Henry, who greatly loved the Church of Bamberg, raised it to an episcopal see through a privilege addressed to John XVII, relying on a council held at Frankfurt in the year 1007 (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 784). Thietmar, who attended the council, recounts the matter; what is lacking there is supplied here.]

In exchange for these, we convey, grant, and confirm to the aforesaid Church of Saint Peter all that land which we held from our kingdom between Narni, Terni, and Spoleto.

Moreover, under the protection of Saint Peter, and of you and your successors, we offer the aforesaid bishopric of Bamberg [the bishop of Bamberg]. Therefore,

[Note: See the dissertation, no. 7 and following. Baronius (year 1019, nos. 1 ff.) and Pagius place Benedict VIII’s arrival at Bamberg in that same year, 1019. Janning, relying on Hermann’s fuller chronicle, postpones the event until the following year. Whichever account is correct, the bishopric was then subject to the Holy See. Therefore, the date of the diploma cannot be 1014, for the bishop of Bamberg signs as a subject of the Roman See.]

we decree that you are annually to receive from the bishop of that place, under the name of a pension, one white horse with a saddle.

Furthermore, we offer, establish, and strengthen for you, blessed Peter, and for your vicar, our lord Benedict, and for his successors, just as was done for Pope John of blessed memory and his successors by our predecessors the Ottos [the Ottons], the cities and towns with their fisheries: Rieti, Amiternum [Amiternum], Forcona, Norcia, Valva, and Marsica; and elsewhere the city of Teramo with its dependencies.

[Note: Two points must be noted here. First, Henry subjects to his own donation in the duchy of Spoleto—or, better put, to his exchange, whose title is much more secure—the cities donated by the Ottos; consequently, the whole duchy becomes the property of the Holy See. Second, he attributes this donation without any ambiguity to his predecessors, the Ottos. From this it is easy to infer that, in the passage above concerning the Sabine territory, he did not exclude any of his predecessors—a point on which we saw Pagius use a freedom that is less tolerable when he removed Louis’s name. The matter will become clearer shortly below.]

We confirm all the provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, territories, and patrimonies mentioned above to your aforesaid Church, blessed Peter, and to your vicar Benedict and his successors, for the preservation of our kingdom and of the entire Christian people, until the end of the age, in such a way that they may hold them in their own right, principate, and jurisdiction.

[Note: The essential point is that all the diplomas consistently confirm the supreme pontifical right over all the provinces, cities, and places enumerated here, so that the Roman pontiff is declared absolute ruler both in the ancient dominion of the Holy See and in the enlargement of that dominion made by Pippin and Charles, as well as by Otto and Henry.]

In the same way, by this pact of our delegation, we confirm the donations which King Pippin, of blessed memory, and afterward the most excellent emperor, our lord Charles, and thereafter the most pious lords [the Ottos], by spontaneous free will, conferred upon blessed Peter, the apostle of Christ.

[Note: The silence concerning Louis here is not surprising, since, as has often been said, it is certain that he donated absolutely nothing to the Holy See. The confirmation of such donations is nevertheless worthy of note. For Louis used the term “decree” here for the pact, while Otto and Henry call it a “pact of delegation” for confirmation. The variety of expression is clear. It is not difficult to understand Louis’s use of “decree” for a pact, or constitution, arranged between the parties; but substituting “delegation” for “confirmation,” without changing the word “pact,” makes the idea somewhat obscure. Ducange nevertheless notes (under “Mediators”) that in charters of that age the word “delegation” designated a means of acquiring property through monasteries: “by firm delegation, into whose hand the same delegation had previously been made through our hand.” Thus the term “delegation” is not foreign to our subject. As for the spontaneous donations of the Ottos, I have found no others except the seven cities of the duchy of Spoleto; but that itself is sufficient for listing their names, with the Ludovician material rejected.]

and likewise the census or pension, or other donations [grants], which used to be brought annually into the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto, as was agreed in the donations written above and between Pope Hadrian, of holy memory, and the emperor Charles, when that pontiff confirmed for him, by a precept of his authority, the aforesaid duchies—that is, Tuscany and Spoleto—in such a way that each year the aforesaid census should be paid to the portion of the Church of Saint Peter, while our lordship over those duchies in all things and their subjection to our authority remain intact.

[Note: In the dissertations and notes on the preceding diplomas almost every clause has been explained, and those clauses most openly vindicate the rights of the Holy See. Nevertheless, I wish to point out that this formula too deserves great esteem for the elegance of its age. The expressions proceed in parallel toward “your portion,” where the matter concerns the jurisdiction of the Holy See, and toward “our portion,” where imperial dominion is at issue. See further examples in Ducange (under “Portion”: “to pay to someone’s portion”). From all this it follows that, unless the diplomas—strengthened by so many ancient records—are rashly denied, the civil rights of the apostolic see rest upon exceedingly firm foundations.]

Moreover, as we have said, we have strengthened all the things named above for your portion by this pact of our confirmation, so that they may remain in your right, principate, and jurisdiction, and so that neither by us nor by our successors, through any device or contrivance, in any part may your power be diminished or anything thereby be taken away from you.

Concerning the aforesaid provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, territories, and patrimonies, as well as the pensions and censuses, we declare that we ourselves will neither do such things nor consent to anyone who wishes to do them.

Rather, we testify that, insofar as we are able, we are defenders of everything written above—that is, the provinces, cities, towns, castles, lands, patrimonies, islands, censuses, and pensions—for the portion of the Church of the blessed apostle Peter and of the pontiffs residing there in the most holy see, so that these may firmly be held in his jurisdiction, for his use and disposition.

With our authority and that of our successors remaining intact,

[Note: What follows to the end has already been noted in connection with Otto’s diploma. The provisions concerning the discipline of the ordination of the Roman pontiff are entirely the same, insofar as they concern the Roman pontiffs themselves, even though the matter turned out otherwise on the part of the Ottos, who claimed too much for themselves. We have discussed this sufficiently for our purpose at the end of the dissertations.]

according to what is contained in the pact, constitution, and binding force of the promise of Pope Eugenius and his successors: namely, that all the clergy and the entire nobility of the Roman people, in order to restrain the various necessities and the unreasonable harshness of the pontiffs toward the people subject to them, should bind themselves by oath, so that the future election of pontiffs, insofar as each person’s understanding permitted, might be conducted canonically and justly.

And that the man who is elected to this holy apostolic government should not, with anyone’s consent, be consecrated pontiff before he has made, in the presence of our envoys or of the whole general assembly, such a promise for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation as our lord and venerable spiritual father Leo is known to have made [is known to have made voluntarily].

Furthermore, we foresaw that other minor provisions should be inserted into this work: namely, that at the election of pontiffs neither free man nor slave should presume to come for the purpose of causing any impediment to those Romans whom the ancient custom established by the constitution of the holy fathers admitted to this election.

If anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be handed over to exile.

Moreover, we prohibit any of our envoys from daring to devise any pretext for hindering the aforesaid election.

For we have also determined in every respect that those who have once been received under the special protection of our lord the apostolic pontiff or of us should make rightful use of the protection they have obtained.

If anyone should presume to violate it against any of those who have earned this protection, let him know that he will incur danger to his life.

We also confirm that they are to render just obedience in all things to the apostolic lord, as well as to his dukes and judges, for the administration of justice.

We have deemed it necessary to append this provision: that envoys of the apostolic lord, or of ourselves, should always be appointed who can report to us annually how each duke and judge [Col. 0630B] administers justice to the people and how they observe this imperial constitution. We decree that these envoys should first bring to the apostolic lord’s attention all complaints found to have arisen through the negligence of dukes or judges; and he himself shall choose one of two alternatives: either the wrongs shall immediately be corrected through those same envoys, or, upon our envoy reporting the matter to us, they shall be corrected by our envoys whom we send. 193 So that this may be believed firm by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people [your people], we have strengthened this pact of our confirmation with the subscription of our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

+ Sign of the lord Henry, most glorious emperor of the Romans, Augustus.

Sign of Erchandild, archbishop of Mainz.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] One manuscript codex of Baronius reads Erkinbald, while the other copies retain the reading of the autograph. Mabillon (Annals of the Benedictines, book LIII, no. 89 and elsewhere), however, reads Erchanbald, or Erkembald, with the Saxon Chronicle. The same chronicle testifies that he died in 1021, as printed by Mabillon (ibid., book LIV, no. 105). Indeed, it also says that Henry was then staying at Merseburg, where he celebrated Easter, and that the death of Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, was announced. Hence there is reason to wonder that Mabillon nevertheless reports these matters, since he had previously stated that Richard, abbot of Fulda, who subscribed the diploma, scarcely attained that dignity before the year 1023. Indeed, at the Council of Salegunstad, held in 1022, Aribo subscribed; he had succeeded Erchembald in the see of Mainz [Col. 0630C] (Labbe, Councils, vol. IX, p. 844).]

Sign of Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.

Sign of Bobo, archbishop of Trier.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] This man is found called Poppo in documentary records. Mabillon reports that he succeeded Megingau in 1016, two years after the date assigned to the diploma by Baronius.]

Sign of Thiederic, bishop of Metz.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] Ditmarus, who was present at the Bamberg council at the dedication of its basilica in 1012, calls him Theodoricus and relates the following about him: “Afterward a great synod was held here, at which Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, was accused by his own archbishop, and Theodoric, bishop of Metz, was reproved by the king, because he had unjustly accused this man before the pope (Sergius IV) in his own letter.” [Col. 0630D] See Baronius and Pagi, under 1011, no. 1 and following.]

I, Eberhard, bishop of the Bamberg church [Col. 0630C], subject to the Roman See, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0630D] Labbe, drawing from the Hildesheim Chronicle, reports the following about the Bamberg monastery: “The venerable monastery, the noble and special undertaking of the lord king himself, was consecrated by Eberhard, the first bishop of that see, with the consent and assembly of all the bishops of this side of the Alps, on 6 May” (1012). Mabillon calls him Henry’s chancellor. In this diploma he opportunely subscribes himself as subject to the holy See, which indicates the year 1020, as I said in the dissertation (no. 7). For that subjection lasted scarcely twenty-two years at Bamberg. We learn this from Hermann the Lame at the end of the year 1052, which he calls his fifty-third year, since he reckons the years from the Nativity of the Lord. Since he died the following year, he deserves the highest confidence. See the dissertation (no. 3 and following).]

I, Macelin, bishop of Würzburg, have subscribed.

I, Walti, bishop of Speyer, have subscribed.

## 195 Dissertation on the Charter of Countess Matilda, or on the Donation Made Once and Again to the Holy See

### Chapter One. On the Name, Nature, Location, and Changes of Matilda’s Land

[Col. 0631B]

### I

Although, after the holy emperor Henry, two Roman kings received the imperial diadem—Conrad the Salian in 1027 from John XIX, and his son Henry from Clement II in 1046—and consequently each confirmed all the rights of the holy See in his own diploma, the diplomas of the subsequent emperors show that neither of them enlarged the territories of the holy See. Only the exchange involving the city of Benevento was made by the aforesaid Henry for the Church’s transalpine rights, as we saw in the preceding dissertation (no. 13 and following), while Saint Leo IX was staying at Worms in 1053.

Two extraordinary events occurred in the eleventh century that brought the Church’s territories a very substantial increase. First, with the aid of the Northmen, the Roman pontiffs vindicated the ancient rights of the holy See in the duchy of Apulia and Calabria and in the principality of Capua, from which the kingdom of Naples later arose; and on the island of Sicily, whose possession had already been confirmed by prescription of seven centuries. Then the great countess Matilda, dying without offspring, appointed the prince of the apostles heir to all her possessions, as Donizo says:

> She submitted all her own possessions to Peter, the bearer of the keys;  
> Her heir is the doorkeeper of heaven, and Peter himself;  
> The gracious pope receives the written deed concerning everything.

Something has already been said above about the first of these two matters, and an appropriate addition will be made. But concerning the second—that is, the Matildan donation—since the opinion of different writers is found to differ in so many published books, I must now treat it seriously.

### II

That this donation was made once and again is agreed by all, both ancient and modern.
