The first was made at Canossa in 1077, after Matilda discovered that the repentance of Henry IV, king of the Romans, [Col. 0631D] had been false and began to fear him. The matter is related by Donizo, the countess’s chaplain; on his authority it is treated more fully by Cardinal Baronius (1077, no. 23) and Florentinius (*Memoirs*, book II, p. 181), and also by Peter the Deacon, continuator of Leo of Ostia—whom Baronius and others incorrectly call “the Ostiensian.” They did not realize that the Ostiensian continuation begins with chapter 34 of book III of *On the Renewal of the Church of Saint Martin*. Peter the Deacon, then, (book III, chapter 49) agrees with Donizo:

> “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1077,” he says, “Matilda, countess of Liguria and Tuscany, fearing the anger of the emperor Henry, who was hostile to her, most devoutly offered Liguria and Tuscany to Pope Gregory and the holy Roman Church. This, therefore, supplied the cause and kindling of dissension and hatred between the pontiff and the Roman Empire.”

It is certain that this first diploma was lost, as appears from the second, which the same countess drew up twenty-five years later, namely in 1102, according to its wording. This latter document is extant in Baronius (under the same year, no. 20), Leibniz (*Writers of Brunswick History*, vol. II, p. 687), Muratori (*Writers of Italian History*, vol. V, p. 384), and several others whom I omit, together with Lunig (*Italian Diplomatic Code*, vol. II, p. 701; and *Ecclesiastical Spicilegium*, continuation I, p. 163). For I have discovered that all the editions derive from that very ancient Vatican codex once belonging to Cardinal Sirleto, from which Cardinal Baronius transcribed it.

Leibniz clearly testifies to this (same work, vol. I, Introduction): “I have added,” he says, “the charter of Countess Matilda concerning the grant of her possessions to the Roman Church, which is found written in the same codex; nor do I know whether an authentic copy of it exists elsewhere.” He also admits that he used the assistance of the illustrious Lorenzo Zacagni, custodian of the Vatican Library, in checking both the charter itself and the Life of Matilda written by her chaplain Donizo.

### III

The copy of this charter that I now bring to light is unquestionably preferable to all others drawn from elsewhere. I understood that it had to be copied and published from the outstanding Albinian codex, from which I have presented other documents to my reader, for more than one reason.

First, the author of the codex, Cencio, was earlier and—if I may say so without envy—more diligent and accurate in collecting ancient documents. Next, he shows the Leibnizian recension to be faulty in many places. Finally, he makes the corrections introduced by Muratori with the aid of other diplomas unnecessary, and reveals that he himself copied it from the countess’s autograph. Therefore, as far as the diploma is concerned, no one of all the copies published before this day has produced a charter more like the Matildan charter.

Would that the substance of the charter itself were not everywhere the same! The prince of the apostles alone is appointed heir to all the possessions of the great countess; yet these possessions are not enumerated individually, as they are in many of her diplomas for various monasteries and churches, but are designated either by the general expression “all her possessions” or “her own land”:

> “To him she submitted the entire allotment of her own land,”

says the above-praised Donizo, than whom no more complete witness can be found.

This matter has been a cause of much disagreement among ancient and modern writers. Some maintain that provinces, cities, and castles were Matilda’s; others that only estates were her own property. The continuator of Leo of Ostia affirms that Liguria and Tuscany were donated to the pontiff and to the holy Roman Church, which could by no means have happened.

Dominicus Mellinus, who in 1589 published a book sufficiently learned for his time on Matilda’s affairs, and five years later a defense of the same book against D. Benedict Luchinus of Mantua, of the Benedictine Order, follows the opinion of Giovanni Villani (book IV, chapter 20) concerning certain towns purchased jointly by Beatrice and others built by Matilda, as well as concerning many of Matilda’s resources and estates—matters that leave our question wholly unresolved.

The aforementioned Luchinus (*Chronicle*, chapter 3) says that Beatrice’s dowry was established by her kinsman Henry II as Modena, Lucca, Reggio, and Parma. Felix Contelorius, a highly learned man, in his genealogy of Matilda (p. 61 and following), speaking of her marriage to Welf, son of the duke of Bavaria, cites Matilda’s letters from the Bohemian Chronicle of Cosmas of Prague, in which she promises Welf the whole kingdom of Lombardy and very many cities and towns. But the Lombard kingdom was subject to imperial jurisdiction.

### IV

From these authors we learn of Matilda’s immense wealth, whether real or fictitious, but they contribute no light concerning the possessions left to the holy See. The matter might seem otherwise with Francesco Maria Florentinius, who in 1642 published a book entitled *Memoirs of Matilda, the Great Countess of Italy*. But if one removes the documents containing the many donations, decrees, and charters of Matilda, one will find that he has gone astray. He thinks that only allodial possessions were donated (book II, p. 344).

What then? Fifty-four years later, in 1696, D. Benedict Bacchini, easily preferable to all the others, while discussing this donation in his complete history of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone (book II, p. 74), lists among the principal causes of Henry IV’s great anger against Matilda “the donation of all her territories, which Matilda made to the holy See.” Later (book III, p. 141 and following) he raises the question whether only allodial possessions, or also royal possessions, should be understood. Then, saying that it is no concern of his to investigate this, he leaves the question to those treating the subject expressly. This certainly amounts to subjecting Florentinius’s opinion to scrutiny while leaving the matter unresolved.

### V

Nevertheless, it is incredible how enthusiastically Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Ludovico Antonio Muratori, and in our own day Christian Ludwig Scheidt the Younger accepted Florentinius’s opinion. They would have acted more wisely had they abandoned it with Bacchini, as will become clear from what follows.

Leibniz writes in the very introduction to his work: “It must be noted,” he says, “that Matilda donated only those possessions that she held by proprietary right, that is, as allodial property. Therefore the duchy of Spoleto, the Tuscan march, and whatever else her ancestors had held by feudal grant from the emperors could not have been included in the donation.”

Muratori—whose letter on the two Guelf lines, the Modenese and the Brunswick line, Leibniz, as a man most friendly to him, appended to the first volume of his work—follows the same opinion everywhere, especially in volume IV of the *Annals* and elsewhere (*Italian Writers*, vol. V, p. 366).

No one, however, has treated this question more fully than Scheidt, who embraced Guelf origins in four large volumes. Discussing the Matildan donation (vol. I, pp. 448–463), he restricts it, with Leibniz and Muratori, to estates and castles alone. Then, using Muratori’s authority, he does not hesitate to remove from those castles some that belonged by right to the Roman Church:

> “The illustrious Muratori,” he says, “not without reason thinks that Henry also gave the castle of Canossa as a fief to the grandfather of Guido and Rolandino, whose investiture the Emperor Frederick I renewed by a diploma in 1185, the publication of which he promises.”

What a learned pair! Henry V held the donation in contempt and invaded Matilda’s inheritance. As for Frederick’s diploma, although it was made after the Peace of Constance, it ought to count for nothing in such a situation—not only with respect to the holy See but with respect to all Italy. I shall discuss this more fully and at a more appropriate point.

### VI

Here I cannot and ought not pass over the dissertation prepared in 1735 by Johann Friedrich Joakim of Halle in support of the claim that the Matildan donation belonged to the king-elector of Great Britain, Brunswick-Lüneburg. He did this for no other purpose than to demonstrate that it is quite wrong to distinguish feuds arising after Matilda’s time from those ancient benefices of the Matildan age.

This author first states (*Preface*, p. 1, and chapter 2, p. 29) that learned men define the countess’s land as “the Tuscan march, the duchies of Ferrara and Parma, Piacenza, Mantua, Spoleto, the Anconitan march, and Lucca.” He then says that some claim the first of these territories to have been granted, before the others, to Boniface, Beatrice’s husband and Matilda’s father, by Conrad the Salian under feudal right. Since fiefs had not yet arisen, they therefore contend that both Tuscany and the other territories of which Matilda was heir were allodial possessions.

“They were handed over to him [Boniface] by Conrad the Salian as his own property; and therefore they were allodial possessions, in which all Boniface’s descendants and all members of his family were to succeed.”

So he writes (chapter 3, §3 and following, p. 46). I pass over the rest. For I do not agree with him insofar as he wants the provinces listed above to have taken on the nature of allodial possessions because fiefs had not yet arisen. Some things, after all, were customarily given as gifts, while others were granted as benefices, or by beneficed right, with only a slight distinction between benefice and fief.

Many charters of both kinds are found in the annals, and new ones are published every day by more recent scholars. In the often-praised Albinian codex there is a “Transcript of the charter of Odo of Poli concerning all his land, which he donated as property to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church,” in [m. prop.], the fifth indiction—that is, in 1157. In the same year there is also “another transcript of the charter of the lord pope concerning the same land, which he granted to the same counts as a benefice.”

It should also be noted that two years earlier the same codex mentions a fief: “Concerning half the city of Tusculum given as a fief to Jonathan, which after his death must freely revert to the Roman Church.” Thus, whether feudal rights had arisen in the Matildan age is of little importance: these were beneficed possessions, distinguished from donations made as property.

### VII

For this reason Sigonius was correct when, after recounting Matilda’s death, he wrote concerning the year 1115 in *On the Kingdom of Italy*: “Thus Parma and Mantua came to him [Henry V]. Ferrara, which Theobald, his grandfather, had received from Pope John XIII, returned to the Roman Church.” He could not have spoken otherwise, considering the practice of that age.

Indeed, who does not know that Baronius and Pagi drew this part of their history from contemporary authors and reliable documents and incorporated it into their annals? The territories of the holy See and the kingdom of Italy are relevant to our subject.

We must seriously observe the following in the authors cited above. It will be clear (Baronius, 1110, no. 2 and following) that among the agreements made between Paschal II and Henry V before the coronation were these two provisions:

> “He would restore the patrimonies and possessions of blessed Peter, just as they had been granted by Charles, Louis, Henry, and the other emperors, free and unencumbered, and would preserve them for blessed Peter with all his strength.”

And shortly afterward:

> “After the king has fulfilled all these things, the pope would order the bishops present on the day of his coronation to release to the emperor the royal possessions that had belonged to the kingdom from the times of Charles, Louis, Henry, and the other predecessors.”

These provisions were confirmed by the oath of Henry and the princes of the Empire, and also by Peter Leo on behalf of the pontiff (same source, 1111, no. 1 and following).

Whatever the sacrilegious emperor, who had perjured himself, did on the very day of the coronation—the privileges extorted from the captive pontiff by force and fear, and later annulled in a council of bishops and cardinals—I prefer to read in Baronius rather than digress excessively from my subject by recounting these tragic events.

I wish only this to be kept in mind: neither the kingdom of Italy nor the pontifical territories, disturbed in the times of Henry IV by that great and prolonged struggle between priesthood and kingdom, could be restored to their former condition before Matilda’s death, and consequently before it became lawful for the holy See to enter upon her inheritance.

### VIII

Nor is it established that, when Matilda died in 1115, Paschal II had the opportunity to enter upon that inheritance. For Henry V invaded the entire inheritance by right of kinship (Baronius and Pagi, no. 8, 7).

Only after the death of this Augustus, in 1125, on 22 May, did Honorius II, vindicating the rights of the holy See, grant Albert, duke and marquis of Tuscany, the investiture of that inheritance. Muratori teaches this (*Estense Antiquities*, part I, chapter 30, p. 293), citing a donation made by him to the monastery of Polirone:

> “Albert, by the grace of God marquis and duke, living according to Salic law, by the cooperation of grace, and raised to the heights of this honor by the gift of blessed Peter and of the lord pope Honorius, his vicar, at the request of his wife and also for the salvation of the soul of the lady Matilda, countess, etc.”

Likewise, the successor of Honorius, Innocent II, invested Lothar II and Richenza Augusta in 1133. A document of this kind is extant in Baronius (1133, no. 3) and in Labbe (Councils, vol. X, p. 946). I shall not hesitate to transcribe it here from the Albinian codex, where it differs somewhat:

> “Pope Innocent II to Lothar, emperor Augustus, and the empress Richenza. We entrust to you and grant by dispensation of the apostolic See the allodial possession of the late Countess Matilda, which is certainly known to have been conferred by her upon blessed Peter; and in the presence of our brothers, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, princes, and barons, we invest you by the ring, namely on the condition that each year you pay one hundred pounds of silver to us and our successors, and that after your death the property return intact, without diminution or disturbance, to the right and dominion of the holy Roman Church. If it should be necessary for us or our brothers [Col. 0635C] to come into, remain in, or pass through that same land, we are to be honored in receiving, provisioning, and safe conduct, as is fitting for the apostolic See. Those who hold the castles, or who are governors of the land, shall render fidelity to blessed Peter, to us, and to our successors.”

It may be inferred from their character that both investitures were very brief. For they did not pass to successors; when the person who had received the investiture died, they reverted to the right and dominion of the holy See. Accordingly, Marquis Albert retained that land for approximately seven years, while Lothar retained it for not quite five, since he died on 3 December 1137.

### IX

From this point for nearly seventy-seven years, until 1215, while the Arnoldists were raging in the City under Conrad, king of the Romans, and later Frederick Barbarossa was invading the rights of the holy See everywhere, while the pontiffs, because of the extreme difficulty of affairs, wandered far from Rome, no investiture is found.

In the aforementioned year, however, Innocent III, who from the beginning of his pontificate had recovered the principal territories of the Church, granted Salinguerra of Ferrara part of Matilda’s inheritance. I shall append the documentary evidence reported by Raynaldus (1215, no. 40), insofar as it pertains to our subject, from the oath of the aforementioned Salinguerra:

> “All that you have granted me as a fief from the land of the late Countess Matilda of illustrious memory—namely, Medicina; two parts of Argellata; Mombarozzo with the parish of Saint Mary; Carpi; Carpineti; Besinate; Mandrina; Bibbianello; the castle of Ariano; Foscundo; Mozzole; Bondeno; Ardumi; Pignatico, with all the courts, appurtenances, rights, and honors of all the aforesaid castles and places; and all the rights, revenues, payments, jurisdictions, honors, usages, and albegaria belonging to the said territory of the aforesaid Countess Matilda of blessed memory in these places or their appurtenances, namely Sablono, Gazolo, Belegaria, Biolotorta, [Col. 0636A] Dianzano, Casale Magno, Casale Ligogno, Fregasso, Pregnano, Caviano, Runcalia, Planzo, the castle of Canossa and its court, Fontana, Campogalliano, San Martino of Riosustinolo, Padi, Correggio, Fossacanale, Miliare, Gurgatello, Fossuli, Brundium, and Soleria; and in the entire territory of Cavalcacomitis, and in the whole county of Imola, and in all that belongs to the aforesaid territory.

“In the bishoprics of Bologna, Modena, Reggio, Parma, and all the others, I shall assist in retaining and defending what it possesses, and in recovering what it does not possess; and when it has been recovered, in retaining and defending it against every mortal. I neither hold nor shall hold that same land from anyone except the Roman Church, and for it I shall pay forty marks of silver each year in the name of a census. I shall serve it at my own expense for that land: in Lombardy and Romagna with one hundred knights; in Tuscany, the Spoleto Valley, or the March with fifty.

“From Rome and southward toward Apulia, through Campania and the entire kingdom of Sicily, with twenty men, for one full month each year, whenever I am summoned, without counting the time needed to go and return; and thereafter, whenever it pleases him, at his own expense alone. I shall devoutly receive and honorably treat the legates and envoys of the apostolic See who come into the aforesaid land.”

### X

The later events showed that the pontiff had placed excessive confidence in this two-faced man; but those matters do not belong here.

Another example of the investiture of Matilda’s possessions—and, unless I am mistaken, the last of all—is found in Raynaldus (1221, no. 29 and following), from the *Book of Censuses* and another manuscript codex of the *Bullarium*. Although we shall more accurately call this investiture a restoration, since Frederick II uses the language of investing when he restored Matilda’s land to Pope Honorius:

> “Both with respect to the aforesaid castle [Gonzaga] and with respect to the other castles, namely Pegognaga and Bondeno, as well as the entire county, territory, and lands of the aforesaid countess, we invest the aforesaid chaplains in the name of the Roman Church, establish them as possessors, and order that they be led into bodily possession of the aforesaid castles by the venerable bishop of Turin, our vicar.”

It is established and certain that Frederick II survived until 1250, and that afterward the interregnum ended after twenty-three years—according to German writers—or after a period five years longer, as others more accurately believe—with Rudolph, ancestor of the Austrian imperial house.

Nicholas III wished to express clearly and distinctly in his diploma that this same Rudolph restored all the rights and possessions of the holy See after so many Swabian invasions:

> “To these belongs the whole land extending from Radicofani to Ceprano, the Anconitan March, the duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, the city of Ravenna, Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, [Col. 0636D] Adria, Gabello, Rimini, Montefeltro, the territory of Balneum, the Pentapolis, Massa Trabaria, with the adjoining lands.”

This diploma, together with the preceding ones, was confirmed by Albert, son of Rudolph, to Boniface VIII. See Raynaldus (1303, no. 9), with this addition from the papers of Cardinal Baronius:

> “Albert the emperor” [that is, the elected emperor, or king of the Romans] “by letters dated at Nuremberg in this year rendered homage to the pope and swore an oath of fidelity; he confirmed all the privileges and donations of lands made by his predecessors, and was confirmed by that same pontiff as emperor, as is found in the book of privileges of the Roman Church.”

### XI

Here I believe I must stop. For I do not see that it is enough merely to have indicated for two hundred years the rights, possession, invasions, and restorations of Matilda’s donation, since I have not determined anything concerning its nature or character. This was especially necessary because some wish the donation to include allodial possessions, while others also include royal possessions.

Matilda’s own possessions must therefore be examined thoroughly, after first setting out their location, according to the weighty testimony of Radevicus in the appendix to Otto of Freising, which Florentinius also uses (book II, p. 352). Speaking of these same possessions, Radevicus says (book II, chapter 10):

> “Those who have traveled along the banks of the Eridanus are not ignorant of the extent of these estates and of the abundant wealth of that land.”

To this must be added the countess’s own words when she renewed the diploma at Canossa: “both what I possessed on this side of the mountain and what seemed to belong to me in the transalpine regions.” She says this concerning the first diploma, by which she appointed Gregory VII heir.

Soon afterward, confirming the same matter to Paschal II, she adds: “what I possess or shall possess in the transalpine regions, whether by hereditary right or by any other right, for the reward and remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents.”

Speaking clearly of the transalpine possessions, Donizo (book I, chapter 10, and book II, chapter 4) testifies that Henry IV invaded them:

> Especially the villages and towns that the countess  
> Had possessed beyond the mountains from her mother.

For Beatrice, daughter of Frederick, duke of Lorraine, whom he had fathered by Matilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of Swabia—and therefore related by blood to Conrad the Salian and the emperors Henry III—when she married Boniface, marquis of Tuscany, is said to have obtained Lucca, Modena, Reggio, and Parma on this side of the mountains as her dowry (Luchinus, *Chronicle*, chapter 3). Yet ancient records testify that she also possessed more land beyond the mountains, although Donizo does not enumerate the villages and towns. Without doubt the principal evidence is Matilda’s own charter, or donation.

Nevertheless, it would be pointless to investigate transalpine possessions that were never held by the Roman Church. Only those on this side of the mountains—and those situated, as Radevicus says, along the banks of the Eridanus—should be sought.

### XII

First, I believe it must be seriously observed that these possessions of Matilda, called her own, are found under various names in ancient records: they were called allodial property, land, estate, territory, or county. These general names extend more broadly than may appear to those who measure that age by our customs.

Radevicus, as reported by Baronius (1159, no. 16), relates that the legates of Adrian IV proposed to Frederick Barbarossa, among other points, that “the emperor’s messengers should not be received in the palaces of bishops.” To this Frederick replied:

> “I agree, if perhaps any bishop has a palace on his own soil and not on ours. But if the bishops’ palaces are on our soil and allodial property, etc.”

He was thoroughly convinced that the entire world of lands was subject to his empire. It would be difficult to find a broader meaning of “allodial property.”

Ducange discusses the various uses of *allodium* in ancient charters with learning, but he supplies nothing similar. From almost countless examples nothing else can be gathered than that allodial possessions were estates exempt from every payment and subject to no burden.

That definition plainly does not fit the Matildan allodial property, as the documents cited make clear. Indeed, Innocent II’s own investiture, calling those possessions “allodial” once but more often calling them Matilda’s land and property, then demanding oaths of fidelity from the castle keepers and governors of the land, imposing a census, and finally granting them for a fixed period, plainly shows that the Matildan donation was more than free estates. Consequently, Radevicus’s opinion does not depart very far from the truth.

Moreover, in the passages cited from Adrian IV, Matilda’s own possessions are called by the same name as the two Tuscan lands, the Roman and the Lombard, which encompassed many cities:

> “The whole land of Countess Matilda.”  
> “The whole land extending from Acquapendente to Rome.”

The Weingarten Chronicle, as cited by Leibniz (vol. I, p. 785), likewise uses the same expression:

> “A woman of manly spirit, who, in the likeness of a most powerful prince, subjected that entire land to her dominion” (no. 9).

### XIII

What is more, the same chronicler (no. 13), following the ancient example of the imperial house, which embraced the whole Roman Empire, calls that land Matilda’s “house.” He relates that Frederick Barbarossa “granted to his uncle Welf the Tuscan march, the duchy of Spoleto, the principality of Sardinia, and the house of Countess Matilda as a benefice.”

That this notable invader of the holy See’s territories did such things is also established elsewhere; under what right need not be considered at present. Rather, attention should be paid to what follows shortly afterward in the chronicle:

> “Passing through the cities, castles, and villages throughout the whole house of Matilda, he conducts the affairs of the land in a civil manner.”

Besides these names by which Matilda’s own possessions are designated, two others are found among the ancients and must not be passed over.

Margarinus (*Cassinese Bullarium*, vol. II) preserves a constitution of Philip, brother of Henry VI, entitled:

> “Philip, by the grace of God duke of Tuscany and lord of the entire territory of Countess Matilda.”

Raynaldus (1221, no. 29), from the *Book of Censuses*, also presents the diploma of Frederick II mentioned above. Its autograph is preserved in the archive of the castle of Saint Angelo, and in it Matilda’s possessions are repeatedly called both land, territory, and county:

> “Since our serenity has given a special mandate against any and all holders, for the resignation to the holy Roman Church, our venerable mother, to whom it belongs by full right, of the county, land, and territory of the late Countess Matilda, etc.”

Therefore, whatever name the possessions belonging to Matilda by her own right may bear in the records of the eleventh century and afterward, they appear to have been substantial estates, towns, castles, and cities.

Consequently, if Paschal II had been able to enter upon that inheritance, I believe there can be no doubt that he would also have acquired the cities belonging to Matilda’s house. But since the greed and overwhelming power of Henry V, king of Germany, postponed possession throughout his lifetime, until he died without offspring on 22 May 1125, it is easy to believe that those cities, like other Lombard cities, also asserted their liberty after Matilda’s death, although while she was alive they had attempted this with unfortunate results.

Certainly, nowhere will one find that the Roman pontiffs reclaimed any city, while, on the contrary, they never ceased to assert to the holy See the land invaded by the cities, through strongly worded letters and embassies.

### XIV

Even if these things are true, that great pontiff Innocent III—greater than whom the Roman Church never had a champion of its dominions—at the beginning of his pontificate continually asserted the rights and possessions of the Holy See, as appears in the *Deeds* published by Baluze (vol. I, no. 13):

> “When, through his legates specially appointed for this purpose, he demanded from the cities holding it the land of Countess Matilda, although those cities wished to acknowledge and hold the same land from the Roman Church under certain agreements, nevertheless, because those agreements were not suitable, he did not wish to grant anything from that land except what he granted to the bishop of Mantua.”

[Col. 0638D]

For in the time of so great a pontiff, all the Lombard cities, long since administered by their own consuls and magistrates, not only defended each its own rights by arms, setting imperial majesty aside, but had also greatly increased their individual power. After Lothair II died—the man who had obtained Matilda’s land from Innocent II for as long as he lived—from the year of his death, 1137, until 1155, when Frederick Redbeard assumed the imperial crown, they had acquired strength from foreigners during eighteen years, first through the neglect of Conrad, king of Italy, and afterward through hostility toward Frederick himself. Consequently, in 1173 almost all of them, having entered into an alliance, dared to take up arms against Frederick; and, so that they might be stronger, each restored its territory according to ancient custom. This development disturbed Matilda’s inheritance, or donation, in a remarkable way.

To this must be added that Frederick himself, in the celebrated Peace of Constance in 1183, confirmed the freedom of the cities, provided that they acknowledged the emperor’s supreme lordship. Therefore Innocent III demanded back the castles, villages, and estates seized by the cities; and that these were recovered sooner or later by him is shown by the aforementioned grant made to Salinguerra and by another made to the bishop of Mantua, mentioned in the *Deeds*. Yet when he granted the Mantuan prelate a portion of Matilda’s inheritance, he openly excluded the cities from that land, or estate. For Mantua, Reggio of Modena, and Parma are those cities which Matilda possessed by right of ownership, and which must be treated separately.

Now the precise location of Matilda’s land, estate, holding, or county must be confirmed more and more firmly against those who wrongly assign foreign rights to her while unjustly withholding from her what was properly hers.

### XV

This can in no way be done better than by following the praised *Deeds of Innocent III*, which enumerate individually the territories recovered by that pontiff for the Holy See. Although, when new disturbances arose in the kingdom of Sicily, Innocent postponed the recovery of that land—and consequently all the towns and places listed in those *Deeds* are not found there—nevertheless the remaining territories that he recovered confine the Matildine estate within such narrow boundaries that they do not allow it to range across the dominions of the Holy See. The two grants of towns, castles, and estates made by Innocent to the bishop of Mantua and to Salinguerra nearly define its actual location within the territories of Parma, Modena, Reggio, and Mantua.

Indeed, when Henry VI died in 1197, the greater part of Henry’s usurpation was in Marcuald’s hands, who, enjoying the prince’s favor to the highest degree, had been appointed executor of his will (*Deeds*, no. 9). Since he was “seneschal of the Empire, duke of Ravenna and Romagna, marquis of Ancona and Molise,” he left no stone unturned in order to retain the march by fiduciary title. But in vain:

> “He offered the lord pope a large sum of money, promising an annual payment, if, after receiving his fealty, he would grant him the land. But since the lord pope would not do this, because he suspected his deceit, [Marcuald] abandoned the march and entered the kingdom. Thus the entire march, except Ascoli, was restored to the lordship and allegiance of the Church: namely Ancona, Fermo, Osimo, Camerino, Fano, Jesi, Senigallia, and Pesaro, with all their dioceses.”

[Col. 0639C]

In the same way, Conrad the Swabian, duke of Spoleto and count of Assisi,

> “tried in many ways to see whether he could find favor with the lord pope, offering him ten thousand pounds immediately, an annual payment of one hundred pounds of silver, and the service of two hundred knights throughout the patrimony of the Church from Radicofani to Ceprano.”

Moreover, he promised the oath of fealty of himself and his followers, as well as his own sons as hostages.

[Col. 0639D]

The pontiff rejected all these offers for the sake of the Italians, who detested the Germans because they had exercised tyranny and reduced them to wretched servitude:

> “Therefore the Roman Church recovered the duchy of Spoleto and the county of Assisi, namely Rieti, Spoleto, Assisi, Foligno, and Nocera, with all their dioceses. … It also recovered Perugia, Gubbio, Todi, and the city of Castel di Castello with their counties, after receiving an oath of fealty from the citizens, barons, and cattani (lesser vassals).”

### XVI

You hear that the March, formerly called the Pentapolis, one of the two extensive provinces which King Pepin of the Franks gave to the Holy See; and that the duchy of Spoleto, offered to the Holy See by Charlemagne while supreme ownership was reserved to himself; and that a considerable part of it, with full rights, was granted to the Roman Church by Otto the Great; and finally that, having been handed over by Saint Henry in exchange, it returned by restoration to Benedict VIII and to the Holy See—although its name was changed, its ancient right was in no way erased by its possessors or invaders.

The same is true of the Exarchate, to which the name of Romagna had been added, in the time of Innocent—not because the archbishop who possessed it through the favor of the invader Henry VI was deposed, as happened with Marcuald and Conrad, but because the rights of the Holy See were confirmed both in the Exarchate and in another small territory that arose there, called the land of Cavalcacomite. Its chief place was the castle formerly famous in Pepin’s donation as Sussubium, later called Brittonorium.

In addition to its ancient right, this castle acquired a new one through the donation made at Venice by Cavalcacomite himself in 1177, when Alexander III was staying there to establish peace with Frederick Redbeard, the father of Henry VI. The matter is attested by the acts of that pontiff in Baronius (1177, no. 29), and even better by Nicolaus Rosellius Aragonius, a native of Tarragona, of the Order of Preachers, commonly called Cardinal of Aragon, who was born in 1314 and lived until 1362 [Col. 0640B] (manuscript codex, fol. 98). For he had at hand genuine acts that differ somewhat from those of Baronius:

> “C., count of Brectanoro, died without children at Venice. For the remission of his sins and those of his dead relatives or parents, he donated to the Holy Roman Church as its own inheritance the castle itself of Brectonorium, which is otherwise called Subsubium (Baronius reads *Sussulianum*), and his entire land, although it had belonged to blessed Peter from ancient times.”

Accordingly, after recovering the provinces mentioned above, Innocent says (*Deeds*, no. 12):

> “He also sent messengers and legates to recover the Exarchate of Ravenna, Brittonorium, and the land of Cavalcacomite.”

But what happened?

> “The archbishop of Ravenna asserted that the Exarchate had anciently been granted by the Roman pontiffs to the Church of Ravenna, and he produced the privileges. He also claimed that Brittonorium had recently been granted by Pope Alexander while he was staying at Venice. Therefore the lord Innocent prudently deferred the matter for a time, rather than wishing to attempt anything concerning it. Nevertheless, he allowed the archbishop of Ravenna, without prejudice to the right of the Holy See, to recover Brittonorium and hold it.”

How prudent the pontiff’s policy was is made clear by the archbishop’s situation.

### XVII

Ughellus records that this archbishop, known by various names—William, Guillemot, and Otto Curianus—was the recipient of letters from Henry VI calling him “among the other prelates of the world, a special member of the Holy Empire”; in these letters the Augustus entrusted him with the highest affairs of the Empire. Henry’s death in the second year of the archbishop’s tenure, together with the outstanding achievements of the great pontiff Innocent at the very beginning of his pontificate, was undoubtedly the reason why the archbishop claimed the Exarchate and Brittonorium for himself solely by pontifical authority.

As for the Exarchate, he was right. His predecessor Walter had obtained confirmation of the Exarchate for himself from Honorius II in 1125, namely as something granted by earlier apostolic privileges. This is clear from the bull published by Ughellus (same place, p. 365), confirmed by the subscriptions of eighteen cardinals:

> “Moreover, we confirm to you the Exarchate of Ravenna, which belongs by right to the Roman Church.”

The situation was different with the special grant of Brittonorium made by Alexander at Venice, as is said, although Gerard, the archbishop of Ravenna, was exceedingly close to that pontiff. For no such privilege is established. On the contrary, the acts mentioned above show that the oath-breaking Frederick, immediately after departing from Venice, went to besiege Brittonorium; after expelling those whom Alexander had sent to take possession of the new inheritance, he invaded it:

> “He expelled them from the castle, captured that impregnable castle without conflict or battle, and compelled everyone of that place to swear obedience to himself and his son, the king” (Baronius, 1177, no. 89).

That the people of Brittonorium obeyed Henry VI, the son of Frederick, until his final day is amply proved by his will (*Deeds of Innocent III*, no. 27 [Col. 0641A]; also Baronius, 1197, no. 8), in which the following passage is relevant to our subject:

> “Concerning the Empire, we decree that the lord pope and the Roman Church confirm it to our son; and in return for this confirmation of the Empire and kingdom, we wish the whole land of our Countess Matilda to be restored to the lord pope and the Roman Church, except Medisana and Argelata with their dependencies. Moreover, we decree and wish that the whole land from Mount Paille together with Montefortino be left free to the lord pope as far as Ceprano, and that the Roman Church have Mountfiascone with all its dependencies. Furthermore, we order Marcuald, our seneschal, to receive from the lord pope and the Roman Church the duchy of Ravenna, the land of Brittonorium, and the March of Ancona, and also to acknowledge from them Medisana and Argelata with their dependencies. For all these possessions, let him swear security to him and render him fealty as to his lord.”

### XVIII

This precious document, by the favor of the most good God, came into Innocent’s hands after he had recovered the provinces mentioned above. When Henry was close to death, either moved by repentance for his former life or fearing for his infant son and his August wife because of the Sicilians—especially on account of the two-year slaughter—he drew up his will in 1197. Marcuald, however, concealed it, for reasons that are uncertain, until the year 1200. Then, after being defeated in Sicily and put to flight, having lost all his belongings, he also left the will, stored in a chest together with Henry’s golden seal, as booty for the victors.

Immediately after Henry’s death, however, as Roger records in the English annals published by Baronius (1197, no. 9),

> “A large part of Tuscany, which that emperor and his predecessors had taken from the Roman pontiffs, was restored to the lord Celestine, the supreme pontiff: namely Acquapendente, Santa Cristina, Montefiascone, Radicofani, and San Quirico with all their dependencies. Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and all the lands that had belonged to the king of Sicily were also restored to him as the proper patrimony of blessed Peter. From these lands, as stated above, he established Frederick, the son of Henry, Roman emperor, as king.”

[Col. 0641C]

For this reason, in the *Deeds*, Innocent is not said to have recovered Tuscany, as he did the other provinces, or at least to have asserted its rights for the Holy See. Rather:

> “The cities of Tuscany, which, because of the unbearable tyranny of the Germans, had nearly fallen into grievous servitude, entered into this association with one another, except for the city of Pisa, which could never be induced to join the association. They obtained from the supreme pontiff that the cities of the Church situated in Tuscany and in the duchy of Spoleto should join them in this association, always falsely subjecting themselves in all things to the dominion and command of the Holy See. They therefore appointed individual rectors from the individual cities and one prior, to whom, during his priorate, all would attend for the conduct of the association’s affairs. All of them, both rectors and others, swore that they would preserve the association for the honor and advancement of the Holy See, that they would defend in good faith the possessions, rights, and goods of the Holy Roman Church, and that they would accept no one as king or emperor except one approved by the Roman pontiff.”

### XIX

That Tuscany acquired the specific name “Roman patrimony,” formerly applied to the possessions of any church, before the thirteenth century is demonstrated both by the offer of “two hundred knights throughout the patrimony of the Church from Radicofani to Ceprano,” which Conrad the Swabian made to Innocent III, and especially by the grant made by Innocent’s successor, Honorius III, to John of Brienne, king of Jerusalem, which Raynaldus reports from the papal registers (1227, no. 5).

The misfortune of that king, stripped of all his possessions by Frederick II, moved the pontiff to assist the prince by whatever means he could. Accordingly, he granted him the administration of Tuscany:

> “We have decided to entrust to the care, government, custody, and preservation of that king the whole patrimony which the Roman Church possesses from Radicofani to Rome, except the March of Ancona, the duchy of Spoleto, Rieti, and Sabina, to hold, guard, and preserve for as long as it shall be our will and that of the Roman Church. Namely: Radicofani, Proceno, Acquapendente, Montefiascone, Marta, Valentano, the island of Martana, together with the other places that formerly were accustomed to be subject to the jurisdiction of the castellan of Montefiascone; Vetralla and Petroniano, with the revenues granted to our beloved son R., cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin; Orte, Montalto, Centumcellae, Corneto, Perugia, Orvieto, Todi, Bagnoregio, Viterbo, Narni, San Gemini, and Stroncone, with the revenues granted to our beloved son, the nobleman Peter Capocci, our kinsman and doorkeeper; Tuscania, Orte, Amelia, Nepi, Civita Castellana, and Gallese, with the revenues granted to our beloved son Giles, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Sutri; and all the other possessions that the Roman Church has or holds within the boundaries specified above, together with all their dependencies and rights.”

I wish to point out, however, that until the beginning of the fourteenth century the patrimony was enclosed within broader boundaries. For whatever belonged to cities, castles, and other places from Radicofani to Ceprano was called the patrimony. Hence in documents that same land is found without any mention of the patrimony; nevertheless, the whole land from Radicofani to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, the duchy of Spoleto, and the land of Countess Matilda are clearly and distinctly listed, as can be seen in several of Rudolf’s diplomas published by Raynaldus (1275, no. 38; and 1279, no. 1 ff.). This certainly proves abundantly that those who establish Matilda’s inheritance either in the March, or in the duchy of Spoleto, or finally in Tuscany, are mistaken.

### XX

Above all others, however, Florentinius’s error seems to me scarcely tolerable. At the end of his second book, he teaches that Henry VI had ordered in his will that Matilda’s patrimony be restored to the pontiff if the pope confirmed the Empire and the kingdom of Sicily to his son Frederick, still a child; that Celestine III did this; and that, consequently, a large part of Tuscany was restored to the Church, as Roger testifies. Yet, according to his own plan, he considers it unnecessary to investigate the extent of the patrimony restored—namely, whether the whole land from Radicofani to Ceprano that Matilda had donated to the Church, according to Aeneas Sylvius (*History of Bohemia*, ch. 21), reached that same Church at the end of the twelfth century.

Nevertheless, he thinks it important to observe that Matilda’s land, disputed for a century between pontiffs and emperors, retained the name “principate” as long as it remained in the hands of laymen; and that, when it was finally transferred to the successors of blessed Peter, it acquired the ancient name “patrimony” as a perpetual monument of such generosity.

But this is not to write history chastely and accurately; rather, it is to distort it. For, as we have just seen, Henry first ordered that the whole land of Countess Matilda be restored, except “Medisana and Argelata.” These two towns, belonging to Matilda’s rights in the territory of Bologna, together with the duchy of Ravenna, the March of Ancona, and the land of Brittonorium, he ordered later in the same will to be received by Marcuald from the pontiff as a fief.

Then he says:

> “Moreover, we decree and wish that the whole land from Mount Paille, together with Montefortino, be freely left to the lord pope as far as Ceprano.”

Therefore Roger’s testimony about a large part of Tuscany being restored to Celestine has no connection whatsoever with Matilda’s donation. For Innocent III, Celestine’s successor, after asserting the rights of the Exarchate, whose boundary was defined by the territory of Bologna, demanded from the cities holding it the land of Matilda adjoining the Exarchate, apart from what he granted to the bishop of Mantua.

Moreover, when granting part of that land to Salinguerra, he names castles, villages, and other places situated not in Tuscany but in the duchy of Modena, which had not yet been formed. I shall discuss its origin separately in the following chapter, when the cities of Matilda’s land are considered.

For now, something brief and clearer must be said about the patrimony, in order to reject Florentinius’s false opinion, which several learned men rashly follow along with the common view.

### XXI

It is clear from what was said in the preceding dissertations that Tuscany was divided into three parts from the age of the Frankish kings, and that this division continued for almost three centuries thereafter: namely, Roman, Lombard, and royal Tuscany.

I have shown sufficiently from all the diplomas that I cited that the last of these, now called Etruria, together with the duchy of Spoleto, was offered to the prince of the apostles for beneficial lordship, while supreme ownership was reserved to the emperors. I have also made clear the distinction between Etruria and Spoleto. We learned that Spoleto gradually came to the Church, whereas royal Tuscany, together with the kingdom of Italy, remained subject to the emperors.

The letters of the Carolingian charter make clear that Lombard Tuscany, with each of its cities, was donated to the Holy See by Charlemagne; the diplomas of Louis, Otto, and Henry confirm this. Finally, I have demonstrated that Roman Tuscany was part of the duchy of the venerable City and was never donated by any king or emperor to the prince of the apostles or his successors, but was strengthened by the aforementioned diplomas, together with the other dominions, for greater security—namely at the request of the Roman pontiffs, who reported that they had received Rome and its duchy through the voluntary submission of the peoples.

Recently I stated that, after the age of Saint Henry, certainly before the end of the twelfth century, these two Tuscan regions came to be called the patrimony. At first, however, this name extended more widely than it did at the beginning of the fourteenth century, when the pontiffs were residing at Avignon. This is clear from a letter of Henry VII, issued at Lausanne in 1310 to Clement V and reported by Raynaldus (1311, no. 3 ff.) from the archive of the Castle of Sant’Angelo and from manuscripts.

For then, not as previously, whatever land there was from Radicofani to Ceprano was called the patrimony; rather, the name was restricted to the two Tuscan regions mentioned above, with the cities of Perugia and Castel di Castello removed and others, belonging to other provinces, named separately:

> “The patrimony of blessed Peter in Tuscany, with the cities of Todi, Narni, Orvieto, and Rieti.”

A reference of this kind is found in apostolic letters down to the middle of the same century (*Vatican Bullary*, vol. I, pp. 272, 289, 340). For in 1326 John XXII thanked Pandulf of Savelli because he had assisted “the rector of the patrimony of blessed Peter in Tuscany.” In 1339 Benedict XII wrote to “the treasurer of the patrimony of blessed Peter in Tuscany.” And in 1350 Clement VI wished “the rector of the patrimony of blessed Peter in Tuscany” to preside over the soldiers stationed there for the security of pilgrims.

### XXII

In the time of this pontiff, as is read in Vatican Codex 2040, p. 51, published by Raynaldus (1350, no. 6), the nobles of the ecclesiastical dominion, rebellious against the pontiff, established various unlawful regimes:

> “In his time almost all the cities, lands, and castles of the patrimony of Saint Peter, the March of Ancona, and Romagna rebelled against the Holy See and against its rectors and officials in those regions. All fell into the hands of tyrants: namely, the patrimony into the hands of John of Vico, prefect of Viterbo; the March into the hands of the lords Malatesta and Galiotto of Rimini; and so forth. Romagna likewise, and so forth.”

Matthew Villani too (*Book I*, ch. 80; *Book III*, ch. 16; *Book IV*, ch. 7) mentions the patrimony once, twice, and three times: when the Romans led an army against the prefect of Vico and when the latter surrendered to the cardinal legate Giles Albornoz, with the name Tuscany omitted.

Therefore I believe that the bare name “patrimony,” in the sense in which it is used today, began to be employed in the middle of the fourteenth century, just as it had been used at the end of the twelfth century, although in the thirteenth century the land from Radicofani to Ceprano was more frequently called the patrimony, and before the aforementioned year 1350 it was called the patrimony of blessed Peter in Tuscany.

Whether its boundaries were precisely the same as those we know today, amid that great upheaval of Italy’s affairs and territories, with the Guelf and Ghibelline factions prevailing in turn, I confess that I do not know. One author of the *Chorographical Map of Medieval Italy* might have assisted anyone investigating these confused periods. Yet, unless I am mistaken, terrified by the difficulty of the events that occurred after the tenth century, he touched on them only superficially or inaccurately.

For me, the following few remarks about Matilda’s donation will be sufficient (*Chorographical Map*, no. 22). After prefacing the history of the two documents, he says:

> “Be that as it may, if the diplomas or donations of Pepin, Charles, Louis, Otto, and Henry that have been mentioned are genuine, it certainly follows, by virtue of these imperial donations, that the regions and cities possessed by Matilda had previously belonged by right to the Church, as is most clearly apparent when they are compared with one another. Therefore, once the donations of those emperors, all of whom prohibited alienation, have been presupposed, Matilda cannot properly be said to have made a donation, but rather a rightful restitution; so that, when she died without heirs, as she did, her goods would by right devolve upon the Church without any other legitimate disposition.

> “For Matilda’s goods and those of her ancestors had either come from the emperors or from the Church. If from the Church, they ought to return to the Church by right of devolution and restitution, not donation; hence it was not properly said ‘I give’ or ‘my donation,’ nor in accordance with the custom of that age. If from the emperors, let the negligent ones argue, since the inference is necessary.”

### XXIII

So deeply fixed in his mind was the idea that the March of Ancona and the duchy of Spoleto should be counted among Matilda’s rightful possessions!

I pass over how he uselessly rejects, as very ineptly written by Florentinius, what was said about Tuscany (*same place*, no. 98), while omitting what ought seriously to have been said about the Tuscan March. For that was the countess’s principal dominion. She retained it, inherited from her father Boniface, by beneficiary right—or, better, by a grant resembling the fief that later arose—until her death. In the same way, she administered the Church’s territories, which he rightly called devolved but wrongly thought had been donated, for as long as she lived and with the permission of the pontiffs.

Even if both Tuscan regions had been subject to Matilda—which nowhere will be found—neither Roman Tuscany, resting on the ancient right of the Holy See through submission, nor Lombard Tuscany, resting on the Carolingian donation and forming the better part of the present patrimony, had a worse legal position than the duchy of Spoleto and the March of Ancona.

Therefore both the author of the *Chorographical Map* and Florentinius—if they will allow me to say so—are completely mistaken. Matilda’s donation, or holding, estate, and land, must be sought not in the papal dominion but in the kingdom of Italy. For there Matilda’s private possessions had been acquired both through imperial and royal generosity and through wealth and arms, and the Holy See had been appointed their heir.

Bertholdus gives clear testimony to this in Baronius (1092, no. 1), before the Matildine document was brought to light again:

> “The impious emperor Henry, he says, had now been staying in Lombardy for two years; there he did not cease to devastate everywhere the land of Welf, duke of Italy, by plunder, sword, and fire, in order to compel that duke and his most prudent wife to abandon the allegiance of Saint Peter and adhere to him; but in vain.”

Do not suppose, when you hear “duke of Italy,” that Welf had received Lombardy, or the kingdom of Italy, from the emperor, as was customary. For several Lombard cities, allied against Henry, greatly increased Welf’s power in the following year, as the same author reports:

> “The cities of Lombardy—Milan, Cremona, Lodi, and Piacenza—also conspired against Henry for twenty years, and all of them adhered to the aforesaid duke” (in Baronius, 1093, no. 2).

Therefore there is absolutely no doubt that Matilda’s land was in Lombardy and was enclosed within nearly the same boundaries as the duchy of Modena later was, whose history will soon become clear.

### XXIV

Matilda’s jurisdiction extended over every imperial right in the kingdom of Italy. For it is evident from the records that, through the favor of the emperors, her own territory extended widely through the Tuscan March and the kingdom of Lombardy.

Wipo relates how Rainerius, marquis of Tuscany, refused to obey the emperor Conrad the Salian. For this reason, after the year 1027, Boniface is found in Rainerius’s place as marquis; Muratori concludes that he was raised to that dignity in the same year, after Rainerius had been defeated and expelled by Conrad.

Domnizo reports that in the fourth year after his Roman coronation, Henry V, returning from Rome, stayed for three days at Bibianello with Matilda:

> “To whom he gave the government of the kingdom of Liguria in place of a king.”

Nevertheless, anyone who counted the kingdom of Italy and the Tuscan March among Matilda’s private possessions would appear to be out of his mind. The same is true of those who do not distinguish the territories of the Roman Church from those same private possessions.

Even the Swabian emperors who invaded them did not unite Matilda’s dominion with the ecclesiastical territories. I cited as evidence the Weingarten chronicle, published by Leibniz, which describes Frederick Redbeard’s invasion. Florentinius too (*Memoirs of Matilda*, book II, p. 350), drawing from the archive of Lucca, cites several privileges received by Welf and recording the territories invaded by Frederick. They consistently bear the title:

> “Welf, by the grace of God duke of Spoleto, marquis of Tuscany, prince of Sardinia, lord of the countess’s estate.”

For this reason I accepted Sigonius’s opinion. He knew that Ferrara had been granted by John XIII to Tedald, Matilda’s grandfather, and says that after Tedald’s death it returned to the Church. Concerning this grant, Domnizo writes (*Book I*, ch. 2):

> “The Roman pope, whom he sincerely loved,  
> granted him that Ferrara should serve him.”

### XXV

I would not wish to be considered so sluggish as to deny that Matilda also possessed certain things by private right in the county of Ferrara, just as she possessed Argelata and Medisana in the Bolognese territory. For it has always been customary among the highest princes to retain allodial possessions in the territories of others, as no one is unaware still happens today.

Moreover, an illustrious document, or charter, of Matilda is produced by Ughellus (*Italia sacra*, vol. II, p. 170) for the monastery of Nonantola, to this effect:

> “And all the territorial possessions which I seem to possess throughout the county of Ferrara; namely, all the aforesaid possessions which I transferred by right of ownership to the aforementioned Holy Roman Church and now seem to possess from it.”

But what should I say? Should I listen to Leibniz (*Brunswick Writings*, vol. I, Introduction) and his copyist Scheid (*Origins of the Welfs*, vol. I, p. 449), who contend that Matilda donated to the Holy See “the possessions which she held by right of ownership or allodial right”? I would readily do so, were it not that both authors, relying on Muratori (*Italian Matters*, vol. V, p. 385), use as evidence for their opinion a report concerning the treasure of the Church of Canossa.

For in that report we read:

> “At last, after the treasure had been sent to Rome with the assent and will of Pope Gregory VII, who had received from her a charter of offering concerning all the estates of the aforesaid countess.”

But since the author of the report flourished long after those events—for below he says, “Finally, after the reconciliation of Pope Paschal with the emperor, and after the death of Countess Matilda, etc.”—it seems that greater credibility ought to be given to the charter or donation than to such a report.

In the charter itself we read these explicit words:

> “I give and offer all my goods, both those which I now possess and those which, God willing, I shall acquire in the future; both those which I have on this side of the mountain and those which I have or shall have in the regions beyond the mountains, whether by hereditary right or by any other right, for the reward and remedy of my soul and of my parents. Whatever these goods of mine, said above to belong to my right, together with their additions and accessions, or with their upper and lower parts, may be, as we have read above in full, from this day I give and offer to that same Church and confirm by this charter of offering that they are to be held there.”

And above she had said:

> “Whether they belonged to me by right of succession or by any other right.”

### XXVI

If Matilda donated to the monastery of Nonantola “all the territorial possessions” of the county of Ferrara, while to the Roman See she donated all goods belonging to her by whatever right, then—without offense to the author of the aforementioned report and to Muratori, Leibniz, and Scheid, who embrace his opinions with open arms—the charter or donation of which we are speaking was not a donation of estates or territorial possessions, to use Matilda’s own expression. Rather, it concerned towns, villages, and cities, which made up the land, estate, county, or holding of that great princess.

Indeed, according to Domnizo, Matilda held “villages and towns” beyond the mountains by hereditary right; while on this side of the mountains, according to the testimony of the Weingarten chronicler, she possessed “cities, castles, or villages.” Among these were the two important towns of Argelata and Medisana in the Bolognese territory, as Henry VI, the greatest of invaders, admitted near the gates of Judgment.

In part, Innocent III granted the land itself—which contained many towns, villages, and other places—to the bishop of Mantua and, in part, to Salinguerra by fiduciary right. Since I have explained all these matters at length above, I think it sufficient here to recall them to memory.

As for Carfagnana, which certainly belonged to Matilda by private right, Florentinius (*Book II*, p. 306, and Appendix, p. 73) produces a diploma issued to the countess at Pontremoli in 1110, by which the tithes of “the parish of the old castle of Garfagnana,” donated to her by Count Ugolinellus, its patron, were confirmed.

Gregory IX also, in repeated letters—as Raynaldus observes (1230, no. 19; 1234, no. 11)—threatens the Lucchese with ecclesiastical censures unless they promptly restored the castles of Carfagnana that they had invaded.

Finally, in our own age, the distinguished Joseph Garampi, Basilian, canon of the Vatican Basilica and prefect of both apostolic archives, namely the Vatican archive and that of the Castle of Sant’Angelo, published a few days ago (*Ancient Seals of Garfagnana*, p. 14 ff.) documents illuminating this matter. Above all, he published the oath of fealty sworn by the nobles and barons of Carfagnana to Cencius, chaplain and subdeacon of Pope Gregory IX and rector of that province, on 23 November 1128. It survives in the register of the book of censuses (*Secret Vatican Archive*, p. 263), together with several genuine letters from the registers of the Roman pontiffs. These remove all doubt that the towns of Carfagnana belonged to the Holy See by Matilda’s hereditary right.

### XXVII

Although several estates and holdings are listed as belonging to the apostolic see both in the most distinguished Albinian codex and in Cencius, the castles and towns of Garfagnana did not come to it except through Matilda’s donation. Indeed, those ancient estates and holdings which are listed, in a very confused manner, in the book of the Lateran library entitled *Benedictus*—it is uncertain whether Benedict VIII or Benedict IX is meant—are recorded in the following way:

> “Likewise, in another volume, at the head of which is written Pope Benedict, these patrimonies are recorded as being situated in the county of Lucca, and in the county of Cornino, and in the county of Roselle, and in the county of Pisa.”

Below this, “Garfagnana” is added in the margin. The text itself reads:

> “Estates and lands situated in: Θ Land at Dimizano. Land at Funo Agnio. Land at Timpaniano. Land at Decimo. Land at Leojana. Land at Pastrino. Estates at Vane and estates at Rojo, and estates and land at Convalli. Land and estates at Anclano. Land and estates at Lacune. Estates and land at Controni: formerly belonging to the house of Basciana or to Buliano, or to the church of Saint Peter at Cisarana, with all their appurtenances. Villa Miliana and Villa Ariana. A villa at Bargano, or Ros in Duza; at Villa Maggiore, at Bacano, at Foscana; and an estate at Castiglione. A villa at Colle, estates at Siliquano and Rojana. Estates at Caricino. Estates at Rojo. Estates at Casatico. The estate of Cesarana with the church of Saint Andrew, and the estate called Vicus, and the church of Saint Rufina with its estate; and the estate at Piscaria in its entirety. And the estate of Campaniatico. Estates and land at [Col. 0647A] Cascania, or at Corfine, or at Petroniano, in the castle of Curfiniano. An estate at Vasignano. Estates called Grisomolecio, situated between Paterno and Petronio. At Capruniana; at Vipiliano; at Ba Θ; at Ceruliana. At Gragnio. At Gragniana, Cahalia, and another Gragniana; at Icano. The estate of Faloniana with its appurtenances. An estate at Coscuniana; an estate at Θia. And the estate at Lactaria, with their entrances and exits, and with everything generally and entirely belonging to all the estates and lands written above.”

I have transcribed the passage in full, without omitting even those possessions which the copyist designated by the Greek letter Θ, since they had been effaced in the ancient charters from which he took them. This makes it clear that no castle or town whatsoever, either in Garfagnana or in the territory of Lucca, belonged to the apostolic see before Matilda’s donation. Consequently, the popes’ complaints concerning seized castles must be referred to the period following the countess’s death, namely the year 1126, when Honorius II granted this allod to Albert, margrave of Tuscany [Col. 0647B]. This is an absolutely certain indication that possession had been entered upon.

### XXVIII

“You will say, then, that Matilda’s land, or house, was not, like other dominions, a region or province separated from the rest, but that castles and possessions scattered here and there formed that body of property of which the apostolic see was appointed heir; and those who assert that the March, Spoleto, and Tuscany were included in this inheritance are not far from the truth. For Matilda’s own property is found everywhere.”

So it may indeed seem at first sight. But the *Deeds of Innocent III*, cited above, show that the matter was otherwise. For this great pontiff, after recovering the other territories of the Roman Church and vindicating the rights of the Exarchate and of Britonorium as far as the boundaries of the present duchy of Modena, immediately undertook in earnest, through legates and messengers, the recovery of Matilda’s land, as I said above (no. 14).

Although Matilda’s own property existed in the bishoprics of Ferrara, Bologna, and elsewhere, there was nevertheless a distinct “own land” in which a rector was appointed, fortifications were guarded, and the Roman pontiff or cardinals who came and remained there were honorably received. We saw above (no. 9) that this territory was identified in Salinguerra’s oath as lying “in the bishoprics of Bologna, Modena, Reggio, and Parma”; Radevico placed it beside the banks of the Eridanus; and Frederick Barbarossa surveyed “the cities, castles, or villages throughout the whole house of Matilda.”

Moreover, it is established beyond doubt that in the diplomas of the emperors and kings of the Romans down to the beginning of the fourteenth century, Matilda’s land is mentioned separately from the patrimony of Tuscany—that is, the territory from Radicofani to Ceprano—from the March of Ancona, the duchy of Spoleto, and the Exarchate. Indeed, Imola, Bologna, and Ferrara, in whose counties Matilda’s castles and estates are known to have existed, are distinguished from her own proper land, or, to speak in the manner of our age, from the principality of the great countess.

For it is not easy to believe that a woman of such exceptional power in Italy ruled in royal Tuscany and in Liguria merely by imperial favor, and also administered the city of Ferrara by papal favor, while possessing only castles, land, and towns under her own right. I shall soon show that Modena and Reggio must be counted among Matilda’s own possessions, and that Parma and Mantua too may, with very strong probability, be added to them.

Yet I do not hesitate to affirm as certain that none of these cities was ever either acquired or reclaimed by the apostolic see by that right of inheritance. The reasons are evident from what has been said. First, they asserted their freedom together with the other cities of Lombardy; then they chose their own ruler. Modena and Reggio in particular boast that they chose rulers who had served the Roman Church so well that, before Julius II, they had always seen the popes increase their honors and territories—though under a fiduciary right, which is permissible in the case of ecclesiastical property.

They afterward experienced temporary changes of fortune, not because they were said to have been donated as Matilda’s own possessions for nearly four hundred years, but because people believed that the boundaries of the Exarchate extended farther. I cannot be surprised that even in our own time outstanding men have defended this opinion. Reliable documents preserved by Raynaldus demonstrate the futility of their efforts and plainly show that they were advocates of a cause less just than they supposed. I shall demonstrate this in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II. On the cities of Parma, Reggio, Modena, and Mantua, once belonging to the jurisdiction of Countess Matilda

### I

When the matter concerned the diplomas of the emperors Otto the Great and Henry I, that famous yet obscure designation of the territories of the Holy Roman Church by boundaries was set forth. It is appropriate to bring it forward here:

> “Likewise, from Luni with the island of Corsica, then to Suriano, then to Mount Bardone, then to Berceto, thence to Parma, then to Reggio, thence [Col. 0648B] to Mantua, and to Mount Silicis, and to the province of the Venetians, and Istria.”

Elsewhere I showed that this designation of boundaries, attributed to Charlemagne, although the pious Louis does not mention it when comparing it with the boundaries of the kingdom of Italy prescribed by that same Charles for his sons, presents something obscure. I was surprised that it seemed to include Modena within the territory of the Church, while, conversely, in the division of the kingdoms it was clearly included “as far as the boundaries of Reggio, and Reggio itself, and Civitas Nova, and Modena as far as the borders of Saint Peter.”

Who, however, would dare to diminish the credibility of such ancient records merely because he does not understand their meaning? As is evident from the division of the kingdoms, Charles customarily included extensive territories of cities under the sole name of the cities themselves, passing over many of their towns and villages in silence. Therefore, it is not the city walls but the boundaries of each territory that are designated by those names.

Since it is unknown whether the territory of Reggio or that of Modena was nearer to the ecclesiastical territory, it is not for us to reject that designation. Certainly, from what was said in the preceding chapter, we conclude that within the boundaries described below—boundaries which at that time separated the duchy of Tuscany, offered to the Holy See by Charles under a useful dominion, from the Lombard kingdom—Matilda’s own possessions were contained in her age.

We learned from the same discussion that not only castles and villages, but also four cities—Reggio and Modena without any doubt, and Parma and Mantua as well, although sufficiently firm records proving ownership are lacking—must be referred to Matilda’s inheritance.

The unqualified wording of the donation charter concerning all property of whatever kind led some people to a different opinion. Yet no one, except those who imprudently reduced the donation to estates alone, removed the cities from those own possessions. They thought that the cities, being situated in ecclesiastical provinces or having been given to Beatrice in Lombardy by way of dowry and thereby passed to her daughter, were not devoid of cities. It therefore seems worthwhile to investigate which cities truly belonged to Matilda’s land or house, although, having obtained their freedom along with the other Lombard cities, they obeyed neither popes nor emperors except apparently.

### II

During that prolonged vacancy of the empire after the emperors of the Carolingian line, while the affairs of the Italian kingdom were in a very poor state, Atto—or Azzo, son of Sigefridus and Matilda’s great-grandfather—an exceedingly powerful and wealthy man, built the fortress of Canossa from its foundations in the county of Reggio Emilia.

Muratori notes that he was called by the distinguished title of count (*Antichità Italiane*, dissertation 28, *Annals*, 958), but admits that he does not know of which city he was count. The fortress of Canossa itself, situated not far from that city, readily persuades us that it belonged to Reggio.

Furthermore, after Otto the Great had obtained the imperial diadem in 962, he gave several cities to Atto, in order to express his gratitude to him for rescuing the innocent Adelaide from danger and keeping her safely in that same impregnable fortress. Domnizo bears witness to this matter (*Book I, chapter 2*):

> “With great gifts he enriches Atto, and [the printed reading *aitis* is uncertain];  
> he freely bestowed on him several counties.  
> Through him he reigned; no wonder, then, that he loved him dearly.”

That cities must be understood by “counties” is taught us above all by another record from approximately the same period, attributed to Otto III. Although Baronius, reproducing it in full, condemns it as manifestly false (1191, no. 57), and Pagi demonstrates that it was fabricated in the eleventh century by an idle person (999, no. 3), and although all scholars call it, in a word, a foul forgery and rightly dismiss it entirely, what concerns our subject is that we should attend to the character of the document rather than to its verdict:

> “Therefore, for the love of our master, Lord Pope Sylvester II, we offer and donate eight counties to Saint Peter, so that he may possess and hold them for the honor of God and Saint Peter, with his own salvation and ours, and for the advancement of his apostolate and of our empire. We grant these to him for administration: Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Fossombrone, Cagli, Jesi, and Osimo.”

Thus, whatever may be said about this forgery, cities are designated by the name “counties.” Why should the cities that Domnizo called counties not be cities? Why should Atto, who had long borne the surname of count and therefore perhaps administered the city of Reggio, not later have obtained supreme lordship over both Reggio and Modena through Otto’s generosity?

Atto was succeeded by his son Tedaldus, concerning whom the same Domnizo writes:

> “After Atto, he preserved the whole honor,  
> greatly enlarging his own lands, exceedingly rich,  
> beloved and well known to kings.  
> The Roman pope, whom he sincerely loved,  
> granted him that Ferrara should serve him.”

### III

Muratori finds both men distinguished by the title of margrave in the records (*Antichità Italiane*, dissertation 6). He therefore suspects that a march was formed from the four cities—Reggio, Modena, Parma, and Mantua—and that both men ruled it.

I am, for my part, exceedingly reluctant to indulge conjectures, for I know very well how important facts are in such matters. It is indeed clear from reliable records that Reggio and Modena were subject to both men.

Bacchinius cites one such record in his history of the monastery of Polirone:

> “Adalbert, also called Atto, by the grace of God count of Modena.”

Ughelli (vol. II, p. 269) also preserves a diploma dating from 964, issued by Otto the Great “at the intervention and request of Adalbert, the illustrious count of Reggio, or Modena.” Muratori saw both documents (*Antichità Italiane*, vol. I, dissertation 8), and adds a third, namely Tedaldus’s placitum of 1001, in which we read:

> “Tedaldus, margrave and count of this county of Reggio.”

I would not dare to affirm the same concerning the other two cities. In the case of Mantua, it is uncertain whether Otto II granted it to Theobald, Matilda’s grandfather, or whether Conrad granted it to his father Boniface, whom Conrad held in the highest esteem because of his outstanding achievements.

Parma is different, although it must be regarded as certain that these four cities, together with their territories, formed the land—or, to speak in our manner, the principality—of Countess Matilda, but not a march, a name unusual and indeed unheard-of in that region.

It would be pointless to establish Matilda’s house by the authority of placita, diplomas, and other records of this kind, since these documents are available in the new edition of her *Memoirs*. From their context, however—from the signatures of the witnesses, the various concessions, and especially the bishops meeting together with the countess—we infer that the land, house, estate, county, or whatever has been discussed at length in the preceding chapter was defined by these four cities and their territories.

As for the other castles and estates located elsewhere—for example Medicina and Argelata in the bishopric of Bologna, territorial possessions in the Ferrarese district, and estates in the territory of Imola—since they were situated within another jurisdiction, who does not see that they should be called accessions rather than her own proper land?

### IV

“You will say that the cities belonged by imperial right to the kingdom of Italy, and therefore were granted as benefices or fiefs.”

But they were also donated. Thus Otto the Great said that he donated cities and towns from his own kingdom to the prince of the apostles and to his successor, John XII; and by that same right, his successors donated Reggio and Modena to Atto, and Mantua to his successors.

Did not Henry IV acquire Mantua, which he had failed to capture after a three-year siege, through treachery, as Domnizo testifies? Did not its mistress—whom Mabillon correctly calls its mistress (*Annales Benedictini*, book LXVII, no. 3; book LXX, no. 54; book LXXII, no. 105)—after bringing the city under her control before her death, “return to the place where she had received the oath of fidelity from her subjects”?

As for Parma, documents preserved by Ughelli prove that the entire county of Parma was granted to Bishop Hugh by Conrad II, once in 1029, again in 1035, and a third time in 1036; Henry III confirmed it to Cadolaus in 1047 (*Italia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 164 ff.):

> “By perpetual donation,” Conrad says, “we generously grant to the holy church of Parma, over which Bishop Hugh presides, the entire county of Parma, both within the city and outside it throughout the surrounding territory.”

And in another diploma six years later:

> “We confirm, by this instrument of our remuneration, the entire and undivided county, both within the walls and outside them, with its definite boundaries and the limits of its ancient description, just as we previously granted it to the holy church of Parma in faithful devotion.
