Namely, as far as that bishopric extends from the Po to the Alps, and from the boundary where the division lies between the aforesaid bishopric and the bishopric of Piacenza to the boundary where the division of the aforesaid bishopric of Parma and that of Reggio lies; outside the aforesaid county of Parma, we confirm to the aforesaid bishopric the estates belonging to it, the castle of Arriano, Saxolum, the castle of Picicoli, Palazanum, and Longura, with all their appurtenances.”

Finally, he confirmed the donation in a new diploma in the following year, 1036. In precisely the same words—“the county, both within the city and outside it”—Henry III, Conrad’s son, confirmed it to Cadolaus in 1047. It is therefore gratuitously asserted that this city came to Matilda by hereditary right merely because it had supposedly been assigned to Beatrice as a dowry by Henry II, her relative, in 1037, when she married Boniface. This is the opinion of Benedict Luchini (*Chronicle*, chapter 3).

Why should we not instead recognize Boniface as margrave of Italy, together with Hermannus Contractus? For Hermannus, who was living at that time, writes under the year 1052:

> “In these days Boniface, the richest margrave of Italy, husband of the most noble Countess Beatrice, was wounded by two soldiers with poisoned arrows, died, and was honorably buried at Mantua.”

Domnizo agrees with him:

> “To whom, while their father was still alive,  
> faithful servants, prudent nobles, counts alike,  
> swore allegiance.”

### V

Counts whose county, or city together with its territory, was subject to them were obliged to obey the margrave, who ruled the province like a duke. Accordingly, in the same year, 1037, when Emperor Conrad appointed Hugh, bishop of Parma, count, he entrusted to the margrave Boniface the suppression of the Parma revolt.

Therefore, unless we wish to disguise the truth or, following Muratori, mentally invent new marches by conjecture, we must acknowledge that Boniface ruled Italy and Tuscany as margrave during the reigns of Conrad II and the emperor Henry III.

It must also be regarded as certain that Beatrice and Matilda ruled those same provinces under the same right until 1061, when Bishop and Count Cadolaus of Parma sacrilegiously invaded the apostolic see and those great conflicts between kingdom and priesthood arose which disrupted the former subjection of the cities of Italy.

From the records it is inferred that Beatrice, during that period—that is, until 1076, when she died at Pisa—ruled in Tuscany and in the province of Lombardy, or the kingdom of Italy, under fiduciary right as well as over her ancestral principality.

It is equally established that her daughter Matilda, harassed by almost continuous wars with Henry IV, extended her ancestral land more widely by right of war and, from the fourth year onward, administered in Italy whatever belonged to imperial authority on behalf of the king.

Indeed, when Henry IV—whom, since he had never been invested with the imperial diadem, the principal cities of Italy rejected—received in 1084 from the hand of the false pope Guibert “the crown of perdition,” as Baronius calls it, he fought Matilda at the Sorbarian fields with such disastrous fortune that he lost almost all Italy.

Meanwhile, several cities, having shaken off the yoke of their ancient subjection, assumed the form of republics and governed themselves through their own magistrates. Thus, ten years later, as stated above, Berthold reports in Baronius (1093, no. 2), Milan, Cremona, Lodi, and Piacenza formed an alliance, sounded the trumpet of war against Henry, and adhered to Matilda.

This fact gives us reason to suspect that the city of Parma, bordering on Matilda’s land, did not enter into the same alliance because it was itself part of that land.

### VI

What if the supreme right of Matilda in that city is also confirmed by events? Before the countess administered the kingdom of Italy—or rather its remnants—on behalf of the king, the citizens of Parma in 1104 committed a monstrous sacrilege against Bernard, cardinal and legate of the apostolic see, whom they afterward urgently requested to be given to them as bishop.

When Matilda heard of the affair, she hastened there with troops to punish the guilty for so great a crime. Yet, moved by Bernard’s pleas, she merely recalled the supporters of the Henrician schism to their duty (Baronius, years 1102, no. 24; 1106, no. 31).

Does it not follow that this city should be counted among the countess’s possessions of which she said in the donation charter:

> “both what I now possess and what, with God’s favor, I shall acquire in the future . . . whether by hereditary right or by any other right whatsoever”?

Only one consideration would stand in the way: what I said in the preceding chapter (no. 7), namely, that if the kingdom of Italy had been restored according to the agreements—as it had been in the time of Saint Henry and his predecessors.

But Henry V was far from keeping the agreements. After violating his oath, he carried Pope Paschal II and the cardinals into captivity, and by force extorted from Paschal the privilege which many have called not a privilege but a “pravilege.” Paschal, seeking to end his own captivity and that of the others and to sacrifice greater victims for the sake of public peace, granted him investitures which had previously been condemned in lay princes.

Finally, Henry invaded the papal territories even more aggressively than his father had done. Later, claiming for himself the whole inheritance of Matilda after her death, he evaded the donation she had made to the Holy See.

Therefore the pope neither ought nor could have commanded the bishops present on the day of the coronation:

> “not to interfere with or invade those same regalian rights—that is, the cities, duchies, marches, counties, mints, markets, advocacies, and estates—which clearly belonged to the kingdom,”

as the agreements recorded by Baronius stated (IV, no. 2).

Still less could he strip Matilda of her possessions, which had once belonged to the kingdom of Italy and whose heir the Holy See had been appointed.

Henry understood this very well and perhaps was already considering what he would do after the countess’s death. Returning to Germany after his coronation, he stayed with her for two days at Bibianello and, relying on her power and wealth, entrusted the administration of the kingdom of Italy to her. Accordingly, when she died four years later, he claimed for himself both what belonged to the kingdom and what belonged to Matilda’s land or house, on the pretext of kinship.

### VII

It is clear that matters remained in this condition until the time of Callixtus II, that is, until 1122. At that point an end was finally brought to the long and dreadful conflict which had afflicted the priesthood with war and schism. Among other promises, Henry made the following oath:

> “The possessions and regalian rights of blessed Peter which, from the beginning of this discord [Col. 0652A] until the present day, whether in my father’s time or even now, have been taken away, and which I possess, I restore to the same Holy Roman Church; and those which I do not possess, I shall faithfully assist in restoring.”

For the rest, see Baronius (1122, no. 5 ff.), where the matter is also preserved in the distinguished Albinian codex that I use, though with considerable differences in facts and wording.

That the Roman pontiff did not even murmur about Matilda’s inheritance while healing the more serious wounds inflicted on the Holy See is clear from the fact that only after Henry’s death did Honorius II take possession of it, in 1126—and even then of a mutilated possession. For it is reported that Honorius, Innocent II, and finally Innocent III granted to others, under proprietary right, land which at that time was devoid of any city.

Nevertheless, none of these pontiffs granted anything beyond estates, castles, and villages, because in the age of Innocent III all the Lombard cities were under their own jurisdiction. Since several of them had asserted their freedom long before the time of Honorius and Innocent II, it is highly credible that Parma and the remaining cities of Matilda’s land followed their example, although no record of the event survives.

Whatever the facts may have been, it must be held certain that Matilda possessed Parma either by right of acquisition or by some other right, just as she possessed Reggio, Modena, and Mantua by hereditary right. For that reason I have no doubt that, if first invasion and then liberty had not intervened, these four cities would have passed to the apostolic see together with the other proper possessions of the testatrix.

A placitum of Matilda, preserved by Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 171), appears to establish a matter of such importance. I shall not hesitate to quote part of it here:

### VIII

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Matilda, by the grace of God, if she is anything. When we were formerly at Monte Baroncione, and were discussing certain matters in the presence of Lord Bernard, bishop of Parma, Bonosenior, bishop of Reggio, and Manfred, venerable bishop of Mantua, men from Monticchio came complaining that certain evil and unjust customs were being imposed upon them by our officials, customs which had never previously been imposed upon their predecessors . . . .
>
> “Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that we have henceforth remitted to all the men of Monticchio all the evil and unusual customs which they had endured since the time of the blessed memory of our mother Beatrice, or which had been unjustly imposed upon them by us or by our officials . . . .
>
> “The aforementioned Lord Bernard, bishop of Parma, on his own behalf and that of his successors, in turn renounced to us and to our successors the claim that he would henceforth demand from our *arimanni* of Monticchio any other customs or services except those which his predecessors—namely, Cadolaus and Eberardus, bishops of Parma—had received from them solely in time of peace and not in time of war . . . .
>
> “Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, indiction 7, at Monte Baroncione.” [Col. 0652D]

Several indications of supreme jurisdiction are plainly revealed here. Bishops from Matilda’s house were present at the placitum, with the exception of the bishop of Modena, who is nevertheless known from other evidence to have belonged to the same house, or land.

Furthermore, officials had exercised authority in the county or territory of Parma since the time of Beatrice; Bernard, bishop of Parma, was subject to that authority; and the *arimanni*, whom Matilda wished to enjoy immunity even under her successors, claim supreme lordship for Matilda.

I admit that it is unknown to me whether the origin of this right should be traced to the battle of Sorbara or rather to the beginning of the schism. Accordingly, although the apostolic see never took possession of any of the four cities for the reasons given above, it cannot safely be denied that Parma too should be counted among Matilda’s own possessions.

Since this is so, although some may think that there is considerable obscurity in that designation by the boundaries of Otto’s diploma, nevertheless, if one considers the boundaries of the counties of Parma, Reggio, and Mantua adjoining the limits of the ecclesiastical territory, those boundaries will both separate the kingdom of Italy from the dominion of the apostolic see in Otto’s time and encompass Matilda’s land, house, county, estate, or principality.

### IX

Why no further memory of Matilda’s own possessions, whose heir Saint Peter had been appointed, appears from the beginning of the fourteenth century onward can easily be understood if one considers the long vacancy of the empire, from 1245—when Frederick II was deposed by Innocent IV at the Council of Lyon—to 1273, when Rudolf, that great ancestor of the most august Austrian house, was elected king of the Romans.

German writers call this vacancy, which was five years shorter—namely, from the death of the aforementioned Frederick in 1250 until Rudolf—the fatal interregnum.

During that long vacancy, the Lombard cities shook off every form of subjection which they had seemed to have accepted in the Peace of Constance. Individually or in groups, they began to choose their own rulers.

Following their example, the four cities of Matilda’s land likewise chose a ruler of their own, although Mantua alone anticipated the election of the new king of the Romans, for in 1269 it acclaimed Pinamonte Bonacossi. Somewhat later, when Rudolf was already king, Modena submitted voluntarily to the margrave Opizzo d’Este in 1288, and Reggio did so two years afterward.

Parma too, though its submission lasted less long, submitted to Giberto da Correggio in 1303, during the reign of Albert, son of Rudolf, as king of the Romans.

It follows that these new rulers exercised authority not only over the cities but over their counties in their entirety, because no mention of Matilda’s land occurs in diplomas after Rudolf’s time.

Albert, son of Rudolf, who appears to have been the last to confirm it to Boniface VIII (Raynaldus, 1303, no. 9), confirms the diplomas of Louis and Otto from the Book of Decrees (distinction 63), especially his father’s, in these words:

> “I acknowledge and confess that all and each of the things which were acknowledged, confessed, promised, done, sworn, confirmed, renewed, remitted, or newly donated—whether concerning the oath of fidelity or concerning anything else—by my father Rudolf, of blessed memory, king of the Romans, and also by any of his predecessors, kings or emperors of the Romans, whether at one time or at different times, I ratify, renew, and confirm; I swear that I shall inviolably observe them; and from this moment, by these present open letters of mine, sealed with my great seal, I remit, perform, and newly grant similar things.”

Neither Albert nor any of the kings or emperors of the Romans who followed him made any special mention of Matilda’s land. Nor did any Roman pontiff, following the example of his predecessors, either reclaim it after it had been invaded or grant it to anyone as a fief.

### X

Accordingly, when we have seen Roman pontiffs for nearly two hundred years so anxious and solicitous to assert the rights of Saint Peter, and the kings of Germany and their emperors at one time defending their invasion and at another voluntarily abandoning it, we cannot help wondering at the sudden appearance of such profound silence.

This is especially true since those same pontiffs, who possessed great authority and resources in the province, could have recovered Matilda’s land by force from the hands of others, just as they had recovered the other provinces.

But I ask that attention be paid to this fact: when the Roman pontiffs established their seat in the province, they were more concerned with the former kingdom of Italy, however divided among various dynasties, than with Matilda’s inheritance. This was particularly so when the empire was vacant, since they themselves exercised supreme right in that kingdom.

We shall easily understand this if we consider the final part of Clement’s *Pastoralis* (Clementines, book II, title 11), omitting the matters concerning the disputes between Emperor Henry VII and Robert, king of Sicily, as irrelevant to our subject:

> “We,” Clement V says, “both by the superiority which we undoubtedly possess over the empire and by the authority through which, when the empire is vacant, we succeed the emperor.”

These words are plainly ill-received by writers of our age, because they suppose that the majesty of the Romano-Germanic Empire still existed at that time and do not grasp the true character of the imperial dignity instituted by Leo III and established by the constant authority of all the emperors. For the Caesars never attained it at any time except through the imposition of the imperial diadem by the Roman pontiff.

At that time, in addition to sharing supreme authority over peoples subject to the Roman pontiff, they possessed Italy and Tuscany by right as the endowment of so great a dignity. Other kingdoms or territories belonging to kings raised to that supreme eminence had no connection whatsoever with that dignity.

For this reason Clement V speaks not of Germany, Burgundy, or another kingdom, but only of Italy and Tuscany—or, as they were called in his time, Lombardy and Etruria.

These provinces, which in Matilda’s age had been disfigured and alienated by King Henry IV, and which thereafter, under his successors the Swabian emperors, had been reduced by tyrannical administration to almost no stable condition and had become prey to factions, were found by Rudolf somewhat relieved through the concern of the Roman pontiffs, taking advantage of the prolonged vacancy described above. This will become clear below, when we discuss the Rudolfine codex.

### XI

The aforementioned Clement expressed his judgment not merely in words but confirmed it by his actions. For, when the empire was then vacant because of Henry’s premature death, he appointed Robert himself—Henry’s imperial rival—as vicar of the empire in those two provinces, with the provision that he should resign the vicariate once a king of the Romans had been elected.

Robert did not do so, taking advantage of the double election: five electors had chosen Louis the Bavarian, while the remaining two had chosen Frederick, duke of Austria. Thus, from 1314 until 1322, when Frederick was captured in war by Louis, while the two contended with one another for supreme power, the Sicilian king attempted with impunity to gain domination over the whole of Italy.

Afterward he had to contend with the Bavarian, whom the Ghibellines summoned into Italy in 1327 because they were unable to overcome King Robert and Bertrand, the pope’s cardinal legate and leader of the Guelfs.

Meanwhile, in the year of Frederick’s captivity mentioned above, the people of Piacenza, detesting the tyranny of Galeazzo, son of Matteo Visconti, the vicar of Milan whom Henry VII had appointed vicar of Piacenza in 1313, voluntarily surrendered and came under papal rule through the agency of Verzusius Landi (*Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. XVI, *Chronicle of Piacenza*).

Shortly afterward, it is clear from a record preserved by Raynaldus (1322, no. 13) that the people of Parma submitted to the same apostolic legate. Among other things, it reads:

> “Likewise, to confess, acknowledge, and assert in reality and in fact that the government of the city and district of Parma, while the Roman Empire is vacant—as it is now recognized to be vacant—belongs to our lord the supreme pontiff and to the Roman Church; and that they will receive and henceforth hold that government and its rulers in the name of the aforesaid lord our supreme pontiff and the aforesaid Roman Church, for as long and as often as the aforesaid empire shall be vacant, just as they would receive and hold it from the emperor if the said empire were not vacant.”

If those who extend the Exarchate of the Donation of Pepin as far as Piacenza, following the ancient ages of the Romans, had looked to this passage, they would not have attributed to the pontiff and the Roman Church what the pontiff and the Roman Church clearly show had not yet become their own right.

## XII

And all the more so because John XXII, as Raynaldus notes (1322, no. 10 and following), makes the same assertion concerning the Milanese in the apostolic letters he cites:

> “They have returned to our devotion and obedience, and to that of the Roman Church, from which they had strayed, rushing headlong through byways and errors, by adopting the sounder counsel; and they intend faithfully to obey and submit to us and to that same Church, to whom the government of the Empire belongs when the Empire is vacant—as it is now recognized to be vacant—and to comply with our wishes and commands and those of that Church.”

These, indeed, are the consequences of the Clementine constitution *Pastoralis*, against which Marsilius of Padua, the heresiarch, protested in order to flatter Louis of Bavaria. Yet I think no learned person is unaware that both Marsilius and John of Jandun, who infected Italy and especially Rome with their writings, were clients of the Bavarian.

Since at that time the Ghibellines seemed to be prevailing over the Guelfs, it became customary for the more ancient and certain rights of the Holy See to be called into question by the audacity of writers and attacked by the weapons of factions. The Marquis himself, Obizzo of Este, from whom no such thing was feared, first oppressed Ferrara and then, under the pretence of returning for a time to obedience to the Holy See, Comacchio and Adria.

Although the pontiffs then residing at Avignon were not inactive—in fact, by wielding both swords and daily acquiring new military commanders through the agency of their legates, they asserted the ancient rights of the Holy See more effectively than their predecessors—nevertheless, unless they drew the kingdom of Italy, adjoining the dominion of the Apostolic See, to their side, the legates and military commanders would have had no reason to expend their labor and military skill. For from that quarter the defense, and from that quarter the security, of the dominion of the Apostolic See under the Carolingians was expected. [Col. 0655A–B]

My witnesses will be Wido, Duke of Spoleto, the rival of Berengar, and his son Lambert, who were summoned to the imperial crown while Arnulf of the Carolingian line was passed over, because they were the most powerful kings in Italy; Berengar, who for the same reason was preferred to Louis III; and the first Augustus of the Germans, Otto the Great, whom Agapetus II would have crowned emperor—distinguished as he was by military valor in Italy—if the powerful Romans had not opposed him. Likewise, several years later, Octavian (John XII), raised to the Apostolic See from among those same powerful citizens, crowned Otto with the imperial diadem. Finally, there is Matilda, a woman of manly spirit, who, because she was formidable in Italy, was both a great protection to the Roman Church and its pontiffs and was especially honored by them; she obtained several territories of the Apostolic See as a benefice. [Col. 0655B]

## XIII

Since it was necessary to take care that the ecclesiastical dominion should suffer no harm from the faithless governors of the kingdom of Italy and Tuscany, John XII and his successors, following his example, wished the oath of those governors to be added to the oath that the elected emperors were required to swear. Henry VII promised that he would exact this oath through his messengers:

> “Whenever he sends anyone into Lombardy or Tuscany to govern his lands or rights, each time he sends him he shall make him swear that he will be your helper, according to his ability, in defending the territory of the Roman Church and the Roman Church itself” (Raynaldus, 1311, no. 7; *Bullarium Vaticanum*, vol. I, p. 248).

A prescription of this kind is later found in the *Ceremonial* of Patritius (book I, section 5, chapter 2), to be performed by the elected emperor before entering the Roman territory:

> “Whomever I entrust with the government of Italy, I shall make him swear that he will be an assistant to His Holiness in defending the territory of Saint Peter according to his ability.”

Learned men know well whether this oath could have been demanded in 1488, when Patritius, more knowledgeable about ceremonial books than about history, was prescribing it. Since Blasius de Martinellis presents the oath, couched in the same words, as one to be sworn by Charles V in 1530, in Gatticus (*Ceremonial Diaries*, vol. II, p. 102), I shall do something worthwhile, I think, by bringing here an outline of Milanese history. For, together with the ill-timed prescription in the *Ceremonial*, it demonstrates that the silence concerning Matilda’s territory arose from the changing fortunes of the kingdom of Italy, or of the Duchy of Milan. [Col. 0655C–D]

## XIV

The city of Milan, which had sworn an oath of fidelity to the Roman pontiff while the Empire was vacant, returned to the Visconti as soon as Louis of Bavaria entered Italy; it remained subject to them until the year 1395.

In that year Giovanni Galeazzo, surnamed Count of Virtue, purchased at great cost the distinguished title of duke from Wenceslaus, that most inept prince, the son of Charles IV, who had bought the title of King of the Romans for money. In the following year he received from the same prince, both for himself and for his descendants, the duchy consisting of Pavia and the other cities that he had invaded, including Piacenza and Parma—cities which otherwise had at one time been held by various parties through defection from pontifical rule and at another through treachery (Raynaldus, 1331, no. 19; 1335, no. 27).

These were the beginnings of the Duchy of Milan at the end of the fourteenth century. In the following century the Visconti were succeeded by the Sforza; when they were defeated, the duchy, at the end of that same century, came under the power of the French. Not long afterward, history records that Julius II, having entered into an alliance with Maximilian and other princes, expelled the French.

It is then recorded in the diaries of Paris, cited by Raynaldus (1512, no. 70), that Maximilian Sforza was designated Duke of Milan by the allied princes, and that Parma and Piacenza were restored to Julius, namely in the year 1512. When Julius’s death was heard of in the following year, the Sforza briefly invaded those cities; afterward, upon the election of Leo X, they restored them, partly voluntarily and partly because of the will of the Emperor Maximilian. To make this settlement more secure, it was confirmed in 1515 by agreements concluded between the Emperor and the pontiff (ibid., 1515, no. 40). [Col. 0656A–B]

When Louis XII, king of the French, died in that same year, Francis I succeeded him. He immediately brought the Duchy of Milan under his power through his commanders and also retained Parma and Piacenza for some time, the pontiff not objecting for other reasons. Then, when the pontiff formed an alliance with Charles V against the French, he recovered those cities by war in 1521, with Charles’s approval.

There survive letters of Charles to the cardinals during the pontificate of Clement VII, expressing the following:

> “We restore Parma and Piacenza, severed from the fief of the Roman Empire, to the Roman See, to be possessed by it while compelled by no legal right.”

They were written after the famous disaster of Rome in 1527, when Clement, about to escape from the Castle of Saint Angelo, promised to surrender both cities, along with several others, to Caesar. It is said that this was not done at that time; nevertheless, from the cited letters—which may be seen in Fontanini (*The Dominion of Parma and Piacenza*)—it is clear that sooner or later both cities came under Caesar’s power. [Col. 0656B–C]

After this restoration, Paul III granted both cities, which had been peacefully possessed by the Holy See, to Pier Luigi Farnese by fiduciary right in 1545. When Luigi was killed two years later, Charles—who in 1535, upon the death of Francesco Sforza without children, had been designated heir to the Duchy of Milan—invaded Piacenza, claiming that it belonged to the Duchy of Milan. Only when near death, in 1554, did he order in his will that his son Philip II should restore it to the Holy See. That this was indeed done is clear.

## XV

From the summary of this history, treated at great length by the illustrious Fontanini and others—would that they had kept every motive of partisanship far from their study—several points are clarified. [Col. 0656C–D]

First, during that exceedingly long period of years from 1395 to 1535, while the Duchy of Milan endured, Patritius and Blasius Martinelli, masters of ceremonies, depart very far from the truth when they prescribe the old oath for the King of the Romans about to receive the imperial diadem:

> “Whomever I entrust with the kingdom of Italy.”

Second, Parma and Piacenza, once cities of the Italian kingdom and in no way belonging to the Duchy of Milan, possess, besides their more ancient rights, this new title of acquisition, no weaker than the right of the dukes of Milan: Julius II in 1512, and again the legate of Leo X in 1521, asserted both cities by arms for the Holy See.

Third, after a lengthy dispute in the age of Clement VII, concerning which Conringius writes (*On the Boundaries of the Empire*, chapter 20, p. 312), these cities were restored to the Roman Church; and in the same manner Piacenza, after several years of controversy with Charles V, returned by right of restoration to the Holy See, Charles himself ordering it. In addition to this legitimate right of the Holy See, there is the nearly two-hundred-year possession, which must be preferred to that of almost any other claimant.

Finally, through the destruction of the kingdom of Italy of this kind, which tore it apart into several dominions, all mention of the territory or house of Matilda has been entirely antiquated. In its place, in the age of Julius II, the exarchate was claimed, both because it once extended as far as Piacenza and because an ecclesiastical province was rather ineptly taken for a civil one. [Col. 0657A]

Yet it is perfectly clear from the donation of Pippin what the civil territory was—or what exarchate, in the age of Pippin, had been divided from the kingdom of the Lombards—for all its cities are listed, the last of them being Bologna.

What the ecclesiastical province was and how extensive it remained down to the twelfth century is shown by the ancient provincial register of the often-cited Albinian manuscript:

> “In the province of Flaminia, the metropolitan church of Ravenna has fifteen suffragans: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Forlì, Adria, Populonia, Ferrara, Modena, Bologna, Faenza, Imola, Cesena, Cervia, Comacchio, and Sarcino.”

Toward the end of the twelfth century, the provincial register cited by Schelestratius presents this province as somewhat altered (*Ancient Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, p. 750). For Piacenza and Ferrara are listed among the suffragans of the metropolitan of Milan, as in the register of Cencius edited by Muratori. Both registers, however, present the province of Flaminia and are entirely silent about Emilia, contrary to the wishes of the defenders of a false position. [Col. 0657A–B]

## XVI

Returning to the kingdom of Italy, I should also point out that Charles IV, that great defender of the majesty of the German Empire, whose Golden Bull is so celebrated, in his diploma preserved by Raynaldus (1347, no. 5), taken from the original kept in the archives of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, swore an oath following the example of Henry VII:

> “We further promise and swear that whenever we send anyone, or anyone at all, into Lombardy and Tuscany, or either of them, to govern the lands and rights of the Empire, each time we send him or them we shall make him or them swear that he or they will be assistants to the lord pope in defending the territory of Saint Peter and of the Roman Church according to their ability.”

But Sigismund, who was the first after Charles to obtain the imperial insignia—for his brother Wenceslaus, removed in 1400 from the dignity of King of the Romans because he had purchased the votes with money, and Robert, Count Palatine, pious and merciful but foolish, did not attain the honor of imperial majesty—found Lombardy alienated by his brother and therefore did not swear a similar oath. [Col. 0657B–C]

Thus, from the beginning of the fifteenth century, no further mention is found of the kingdom of Italy, or of Lombardy and Tuscany. In place of both there arose the Duchy of Milan and the free cities of Etruria, which, at the end of that same century, developed into a duchy.

The chief of these cities was Florence, which, being wealthier and more powerful than the others, sought out neighboring and more distant territories through almost continuous wars and already ruled widely. Then, through the counsels and resources of Leo X and afterward Clement VII, pontiffs of the Medici family, that same family was elevated and governed the Grand Duchy of Etruria down to our own age with great prosperity and equal glory.

In the kingdom of Italy, besides the Duchy of Milan and the other Duchy of Parma and Piacenza mentioned above, there arose another much more ancient and no less glorious dominion, that of the Marquises of Este, which absorbed almost the whole territory of Matilda. The Roman pontiffs, remembering—if I am not mistaken—that Matilda had married Azzo of Este, and considering especially their own interests and those of the Apostolic See, were far from protesting. Rather, protected by the virtue and resources of the Este family, they preserved the ancient territories of the Roman Church and placed them in charge of the Estes, especially Ferrara, granting them to that family as a fief, just as in Matilda’s time. [Col. 0657C–D]

Before this happened, however, while the cities of Italy were in great disorder throughout the twelfth century, historians report that Ferrara obeyed various lords. Hence some more recent writers either rashly remove it from the pontifical dominion or imprudently attach it to Matilda’s donation.

Since the Albinian manuscript provides a document unquestionably older than the mutilated and corrupt one found in the census book of the chamberlain Cencius—and even older than the age of Pope Lucius III, who began to sit in Peter’s chair in 1181—I think it should be placed before everyone’s eyes, so that the pontiff’s right may be vindicated against the claim of a benefice or fief belonging to others, and the usurpation of what belongs to another may be made plain. [Col. 0657D–0658A]

## XVII

> “Concerning the revenues of all the provinces and churches owed to the Roman Church. First, concerning the city of Ferrara.
>
> “The Roman Church ought to receive from the city of Ferrara an annual census of fifty Lucchese solidi. Half of the toll of the riverbank and the district of the market each year. And the whole *arimannia* of the parish of Cornacervina. And the whole *arimannia* of the estate of Fuscalia. And the whole public revenue of the same. And the whole *arimannia* of Gabbiana. And the whole *arimannia* of Lungula. And the whole *arimannia* of Septepullesino. And the whole court, or district, of Massa. And the whole district, or property, of Ciniscelli and Cavalto. And the whole *arimannia* and the whole public revenue of Sadriano. And the whole *arimannia* and the whole public revenue of Trecenta. And the whole *arimannia* of Banniolo and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Villanova and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Maneggio and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of San Martino and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Lucarano and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Santa Maria and the whole public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* and public revenue of Villa Comede. And the whole public revenue of Gognano. And the whole public revenue of Villa Marthana. And the whole *arimannia* of Arcuada and the whole public revenue. And the whole public revenue of Bonisciago. And the whole public revenue of Agnano. And the whole *arimannia* of Pontiado and the public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Filthatico and the public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Runci and the public revenue. And the whole *arimannia* of Cirpilliatica. And the whole *arimannia* of Bratica. And the whole *Salaria*, and all of Ficarolo, and three parts of the river toll, and three parts of the port of Rupta Ficaroli. And the whole *arimannia* of Trenta. And the whole *arimannia* of Leone. And the whole *arimannia* of Gello. And the whole *arimannia* of Fabriciano. And the whole *arimannia* of San Donato. And the whole *arimannia* of Flesso. And of Firacolo and its entire county, the *balia* and district in all criminal matters. And twice every year, namely in May and on Saint Martin’s day, a general court session.”

Since this concerns censuses or tributes, I prefer, with Du Cange, to understand *placitamentum* as a type of *laudimium*, rather than to imagine that it denotes something different from tribute or census. [Col. 0658A–C]

## XVIII

In the same manuscript there is in fact a somewhat older fragment of the privilege of the people of Ferrara, from the time when agents of the Holy See administered that city before it was granted as a benefice to others. It reads as follows:

> “Excerpt from the privilege of the people of Ferrara. Once a year, if we are asked to do so, before our apostolic messenger, if the herald has proclaimed the ban, they shall guard the general court for three days; until the third hour complaints and grievances shall be written down. Afterward, for the course of a month, when they have been summoned to administer justice, if they have been called, they shall guard the court.”

There is no indication of the age of this privilege. Nevertheless, since it is placed in the manuscript immediately after the lease of the city of Palestrina made by John XIII in 970, it appears to be of similar date. Since the same pontiff granted the city, by way of benefice, to Matilda’s grandfather, the condition of that city—before it was handed over as a benefice to Tedald and after its return to the Apostolic See—is clearly apparent from both documents down almost to the end of the twelfth century, when Albinus, the writer of the manuscript, was alive and committed to writing the ancient documents he had collected.

How greatly, therefore, are those in error who, disregarding the genuine donation of Matilda, claim that Ferrara was offered by her to the Holy See! It is certainly worthy of amazement that whenever, outside the ecclesiastical dominion, there is talk of Matilda’s land or personal possessions, these consist of nothing other than estates, or at most castles, without any city. But when, according to the false opinion of others, these same possessions are placed in Lombard Tuscany, or the patrimony of Tuscany, in the Duchy of Spoleto, or in the March, then whatever cities there are in those provinces is said to belong to Matilda’s donation.

What are we to say about the recent Italian annalist, who by a circuitous route risks cutting the donation apart entirely (*Italian Historians*, vol. V, p. 366)? He makes the following observation concerning Matilda’s charter:

> “In that century, and especially in the time of Pope Gregory VII, the custom became widespread of offering not only castles but entire kingdoms to the Apostolic See, and then receiving them back from it as fiefs. Demetrius, king of the Russians, did this two years before the peace of Canossa, namely in 1075; so too did another Demetrius, duke—or king—of Croatia and Dalmatia. Bertram, count of Provence, also offered all his possessions to the same See in 1081.” [Col. 0658C–0659A]

## XIX

It was not because of a custom of the century, but because of the magnanimity of Gregory VII, that kings and princes preferred to receive the investiture of their kingdoms or principalities from blessed Peter rather than from Henry IV, the king of the Germans.

But neither Matilda’s donation nor Bertram’s offering belongs to that category. This will be perfectly clear from the letter of that holy pontiff to Demetrius, king of the Russians, and to the queen (book II, letter 74):

> “Your son,” he says, “visited the threshold of the apostles and came to us. After offering the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the fidelity that was his due, he earnestly requested that he might obtain that kingdom as a gift from Saint Peter through our hands. He asserted without hesitation that his request would be ratified and made firm by your consent if it were granted through the favor and protection of apostolic authority.”

Is this to offer principalities and kingdoms first and then receive them as fiefs?

Concerning the other Demetrius, whom the legates of Gregory himself made a king from a duke at a synod held in Dalmatia (Albinian manuscript; Cencius; book of Censius; Baronius, 1076, no. 66), the opinion of the venerable annalist will be sufficient for me:

> “The same Pope Gregory,” he says, “who deprived King Henry of his kingdom—his impiety extorting this from him unwillingly, while piety required it—raised the duke of Croatia and Dalmatia to be king. A wholly astonishing event took place: in the very year in which King Henry separated himself from the Church by schism, a barbarian king joined himself to it, made himself subject, swore fidelity, and voluntarily promised tribute, thinking that a great addition would thereby be made to his glory if, from being a free prince, he should become a subject of Saint Peter and be called his faithful servant.”

The document remains in the places cited. Since it is very long and irrelevant to reproduce in full here, I have provided a summary of it in Baronius’s brief account. [Col. 0659A–B]

By contrast, I shall place Bertram’s offering, although readily available in the registers of Gregory VII (book IX, letter 12) and in Baronius (1081, no. 33), in full before Matilda’s charter, which follows shortly from the same Albinian manuscript. I do so because the text found in the registers and in Baronius is extremely varied, as is customary with unauthenticated documents, since copyists in former ages thought they could alter ancient charters with impunity and adapt them to their own times; and because, together with Matilda’s donation, with which it agrees very closely, it exposes the recent annalist’s falsehood, to the great detriment of the public, since he heaps together dissimilar materials in order to weaken the rights of the Holy See. [Col. 0660A–B]

> “The oath of Bertram, Count of Provence.
>
> “I, Bertram, by the grace of God count of Provence, from this hour and henceforth shall be faithful to Saint Peter, to my lord Pope Gregory, to the Holy Roman Church, and to all your successors who shall enter through the better cardinals. Knowingly, I shall consent to no harm against you or against the Holy Roman Church. So help me God and these holy Gospels.
>
> “Moreover, for the remission of my sins and those of my parents, I offer, grant, and give all my honor, insofar as it belongs to me by right of my parents, to almighty God, to his holy apostles Peter and Paul, to my lord Pope Gregory VII, and to his aforementioned successors, so that henceforth they may do with me and with all my honor whatever pleases them, without any contradiction. I entirely surrender to their power all the churches that are under my authority.”

Now the charter of the great countess herself must be heard.

## CHARTER OF COUNTESS MATILDA

*[Manuscript addition: “Matilda concerning the grant of her possessions made to the Roman Church.”]* [Col. 0659C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1102, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, indiction 10, in the time of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the Lateran palace, in the chapel of the Holy Cross, in the presence of Cencius Frajapan [Frangipane], Gratian, Cencius [Cencii] Franculini, Alberic of Peter Leo, Cice, and Benincasa, his brother [variant: Peter Leo and Benincasa, his brother], and Ubertus de Tascio [variant: that same Ubertus of Tuscany], and many others.

*[Editorial note: Muratorius, in his edition, reads *domni Gregorii* once and again. The Vatican manuscript has *domini*, as Leibniz reads it; this reading deserves greater confidence because he employed the distinguished Laurentius Zacagnus to assist him in collating the manuscript. Moreover, it has been established that in monuments of the twelfth century the pontiff is called *dominus*, not *domnus*; and in our manuscript *dominus* is always read in this charter. Conversely, in the diplomas of Louis, Otto, and Henry, *domnus* is always found. This should be noted for the greater reliability of the documents.]*

I, Matilda [*Mathildis*], countess by the grace of God, for the remedy of my soul and of my parents, gave and offered to the Church of Saint Peter, through the intervention of Lord Pope Gregory VII [*per interventum domini Gregorii VII papae*; variant word order: *papae VII*], all my possessions by proprietary right [*jure proprietario*], both that which [variant: *quae*, “those which”] I then possessed and those that I was thereafter to acquire, whether by right of succession or by any other right whatsoever through which they might belong to me [*pertinerent* / *pertinent*]. [Col. 0659D–0660C]

*[Editorial note: Du Cange appropriately observes under the word *intervenire* that the expressions *per interventum* or *interventu*, which occur in grants of this kind, are used for intercession or mediation. The matter is explained more clearly below by the phrase “through the hand.” It is therefore evident that the donation was made to the Roman Church in precisely the same manner in which Pippin, Charles, Otto, and Henry made their donations to the prince of the apostles through Stephen II, Hadrian, John XII, and Benedict VIII; and in which later emperors, following the example of Louis the Pious, confirmed various grants through the pontiffs.]*

*[Editorial note: Although she donated what belonged to her own right—both what she then possessed and whatever she was thereafter to acquire by any right—the ambiguous form of expression scarcely allows us to determine whether she is using toward the Roman Church that strongest right by which owners and legitimate possessors act, so that the donation may be more secure and by which she confesses that she has divested herself after the donation, thereafter enjoying the goods as a beneficiary; or whether the Roman Church is henceforth to use the proprietary right. Muratorius (*Italian Historians*, vol. V, p. 366), following Domnizo, says that the custom had arisen “of offering not only castles but entire kingdoms to the Apostolic See, and then receiving them back from it as fiefs”; he supports this with examples. But Matilda’s donation is not of that kind, as is clear from what follows, even though the donor continued to enjoy the same possessions as long as she survived. For it was a true institution of the Church of Rome as heir, as Domnizo says more than once.]*

And both those possessions that I held on this side of the mountains [*montis* / *montium*] and those that appeared to belong to me in the regions beyond the mountains, all of them, as stated above, I gave and transferred to the Roman Church through the hand of Lord Pope Gregory VII, and I requested that a charter be made concerning them.

But because the charter nowhere appears [*nusquam* / *nunquam*], and I fear that my donation and offering may be called into question, therefore I, the aforesaid Countess Matilda, again, from the present day, give and offer to the same Roman Church through the hand of Bernard, cardinal and legate of that same Roman Church, just as at that time I gave through the hand of Lord Pope Gregory VII, all my possessions, both those that I now have and those that, with God’s favor, I shall acquire in the future, and both those that I possess on this side of the mountains and those that I have or shall have in the regions beyond the mountains, whether by hereditary right or by any other right, for the reward and remedy of my soul and of my parents. [Col. 0660D–0661A]

*[Editorial note: Concerning this Bernard, formerly abbot of Vallombrosa and admitted to the college of cardinals, and concerning his virtues and activities in the city of Parma, see Baronius (1102, no. 22 and following), and especially Ughelli, in the bishops of Parma (vol. II, pp. 168 and following).]*

*[Editorial note: The manuscript reads: “I have, and those which, with God’s favor, I shall acquire in the future by any other right whatsoever” (*habeo, quam que in posterum Deo propitio acquisitura sum alio quocumque jure*).]*

Whatever, then, these possessions of mine, spoken of above as belonging to my right, are, together with their additions and revenues, or with their upper and lower parts, as we have read above [*qualiter supra legimus* / *legavi*], in their entirety: from this day I give and offer them to the same Church, and through this present charter of offering I confirm that they are to be held there. [Col. 0661B–C]

*[Editorial note: This passage is extremely corrupt, yet everyone reads it in this form, since it derives from the recension of the Vatican manuscript. Baronius (1102, no. 20), who consulted another manuscript containing ancient documents of this kind in addition to that one, gives it as: “together with their additions and revenues, or their upper parts or lower parts, as I have bequeathed above.” Muratorius observes that *qualiter supra legitur*—“as it is read above”—was a common formula of that period and believes that it should be read here as well. The reading of our manuscript is not far removed from this emendation.]*

*[Editorial note: Here too Muratorius notes that *habendum* is a customary formula of notaries. Our manuscript confirms this observation.]*

*[Editorial note: Baronius observes that these formulas, arising from the idioms of that period, occur in diplomas of this kind but are now obsolete. Investitures of property were made by such formulas, as numerous examples in Du Cange’s *Glossary* show under *Investitura*. Among others, he cites from Miraeus (*Diplomata Belgica*, vol. I, p. 370): “And by this present charter of offering I confirm them as to be held there; moreover, by a knife, a knotted staff, a glove, and a clod of earth, and a branch of a tree.” Leibniz reads *quantonem*, as in our manuscript, and defines it as a glove; he likewise reads *guvascionem* with Miraeus and explains it as a turf. Du Cange should certainly be consulted both in the cited place and under the individual terms, since it would be too long to assemble here the many examples by which he demonstrates the matter.]*

Moreover, by means of a knife, a knotted staff, a glove, and a clod of earth [*gantonem et vascionem terrae* / *guantonem et guuasionem*], as well as a branch of a tree, I expelled myself from them, renounced them [*guarpivi* / *garpivi*], and made myself absent from them; and I left them to be held on behalf of that Church, so that from this day the party of that Church, or whoever the party of that Church shall grant them to, may do whatever it wishes with them, without any contradiction on my part or on the part of my heirs or heirs’ heirs. [Col. 0661C–0662B]

*[Editorial note: Leibniz thinks that after the aforesaid formulas of investiture one should add *tradidi*, “I handed over,” although this word is absent everywhere. What follows consists largely of synonyms. *Carpire*, which is also found in charters as *guerpire* and *verpire*, means to relinquish possession of something. Thus Leibniz, in explaining it as “I expelled,” correctly indicates that Matilda expelled herself from possession of her possessions in the very act of donation. Accordingly, the Church acquired their ownership in that same year, 1102, although they remained for Matilda to possess and use until 1115, when, at her death, they were invaded by Henry V. The Roman Church did not enter into possession of them until several years later, as stated in the dissertation.]*

*[Editorial note: This is another difficult passage. Baronius, with the aid of the other manuscript mentioned above, reads: “and I left them to be held on behalf of that Church, so that henceforth the pope, or whoever the pope shall grant them to, may do whatever he wishes.” Leibniz correctly restored *habenda*, “to be held”; but he declares *facienda* barbarous and believes that *dederit*, “shall grant,” is redundant. He says that the sense is: “so that henceforth the party of that Church may do whatever it wishes.”]*

But if anything should happen—which I do not believe will happen—if [*si*; variant *sive*] I, Countess Matilda, God forbid, or any one of my heirs or heirs’ heirs, or any opposing person, should at any time attempt to act against this charter of offering or seek by any device to invalidate it [*aut eam* / *tam*], then we shall pay to the party against whom we have brought [variant future perfect: *intulerimus*] the lawsuit [*intulimus*] a penalty [*mulctam* / *multa*] of one thousand pounds of the finest gold and four thousand pounds by weight of silver. And whatever we have claimed, we shall not be able to recover or vindicate. [Col. 0662A–C]

*[Editorial note: Leibniz reads *tam*; Muratorius correctly thinks that *aut eam* should be written. Leibniz, however, wrongly emends it further.]*

*[Editorial note: Leibniz reads *quo*. Baronius has *quod*, a reading that Leibniz himself approves.]*

But let this present charter of offering remain and persist firm for all time.

And I lifted the parchment [*pergamena* / *bergamena*] and the inkwell from the ground, handed them to Guido the notary, and asked that it be written. In it, confirming below, I offered it to be strengthened by witnesses. [Col. 0662C]

*[Editorial note: Baronius’s reading is more explicit: “I lifted the parchment with the ink from the ground and handed the page to Guido the notary.” Leibniz found the concluding words pleasing. The formula is extremely ancient, for Du Cange, under *pergamenum*, cites from the Casaurian Register an example of Louis, son of Lothar. For our purpose nothing is more relevant than a charter printed by Muratorius (*Antiquities of Este*, p. 100), in which the following words occur only seventy years before Matilda’s charter: “And I, the aforesaid Adelaida, lifted the parchment with the inkwell from the ground and handed it to Agimone, notary of the sacred palace, and asked that he write it; in which, confirming below, and having offered it to be strengthened by witnesses …”]*

Done successfully at Canossa.

Matilda, by the grace of God, whatever there is in this charter made by me, subscribed [*s-s*].

*[Editorial note: Baronius reads *subscripsi*, “I subscribed,” and likewise in what follows: “I was present and subscribed.” The appended sign *s-s* indicates nothing else.]*

I, Arderic the judge, was present and subscribed.

I, Ubald the judge, was present and subscribed.

The sign of the hand of Atto of Monte Barranzone and of Bonvicinus [*Bonvicini*] of Canossa, witnesses requested to attend.

I, Guido, notary and scribe of the sacred palace, completed and delivered this charter of offering after it had been handed over.

*[Editorial note: Leibniz and others consistently read *offersionis*, “of offering,” rather than *oblationis*.]*

[DISSERTATION ON THE RUDOLPHINE MANUSCRIPT]

## DISSERTATION ON THE RUDOLPHINE MANUSCRIPT, OR ON THE THREE BOOKS OF RUDOLF’S LETTERS

### 241 PREFACE

#### I. On the character of the imperial majesty restored in the West

I think I discussed the character of the imperial majesty restored in the West sufficiently when I was treating the letters of Leo III. Now, as I am about to speak of the letters of Rudolf, King of the Romans, it is necessary to set forth two matters in advance, without knowledge of which we can in no way grasp the meaning of those letters. They are the election and the coronation of the emperor. [Col. 0661D–0663A]

Rudolf, although he did not attain the latter, sought it so insistently from the pontiffs and testifies in so many letters that he would come with such elaborate preparation to obtain it, that he makes the importance and necessity of the matter plain.

As for the former, Boeclerus correctly says (*Commentaries on the Empire*, vol. II, p. 870) that it “began with Count Rudolf of Habsburg through the electors alone, as they are called today, without the counsel of the other princes and estates, and has continued down to the present time.”

Accordingly, this kind of election must be considered both before and after Rudolf.

As for the coronation, since it has always been the same—for one Roman pontiff could institute the emperor by the imposition of the imperial diadem, and such a solemnity had to be celebrated in the basilica of the prince of the apostles—it is not the coronation itself but the additions repeatedly made to it and the rite varied according to the circumstances of the times that must be examined.

Therefore, after I have supplied whatever is necessary concerning the business of the election and the definite origin of the seven men, or electors, of the Holy Roman Empire, I shall undertake the subject of the coronation, which is neither easy nor brief, and, if I am not mistaken, shall make it as fully explained as possible.

Moreover, I shall overthrow the false opinion of those who, failing to understand the character of this new dignity, think that it must be traced back to Octavian—or, as they believe more truly, to Constantine the Great. Then I shall say a few words about the letters themselves.

### 242 § I.—On the election of the Carolingian successors of Charlemagne

[The supplied source ends here.]

## II. As long as the Carolingian line endured—from the year 814, that is, until 887, when Charles the Fat was deposed and Arnulf, the son of Charles’s brother Carloman and therefore his nephew, was elected king of Germany—it is found that election was quite readily available among those six Augusti who succeeded Charlemagne: Louis the Pious, Lothar I, Louis II, Charles the Bald, Charles the Fat, and Arnulf.

Louis the Pious, heir to his father’s kingdoms, was elected by his father Charlemagne himself. In the same way Lothar I was elected by his father Louis the Pious, and Louis II by Lothar; and all were confirmed by the Roman pontiff. The remaining three, since they did not succeed their parents but were elected kings of Alemannia and Gaul without any designation to the imperial dignity, owed their election to the Roman Empire more to the Roman pontiffs than to their own princes or parents.

I call as witness the Roman council held in 877 for the confirmation of Charles the Bald (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 296), when John VIII addressed the bishops as follows:

> “Since we have learned that the same matter had previously been revealed by heavenly inspiration to our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Nicholas, we rightly chose and approved him together with the support and vote of all our brothers and fellow bishops.”

From the case of Arnulf, the last of these, the character of this pontifical election—restored by Leo III—is clearly discerned. For after the death of Charles the Fat, Stephen V raised not his nephew Arnulf, who had been elected king of Germany in 887 at the deposition of that same Charles, but Wido, duke of Spoleto, to the imperial dignity. The following year Formosus followed his example, choosing Lambert, Wido’s son, as associate in the empire with his father. They held the kingdom of Italy, and greater hope of defending the Apostolic See seemed to shine from either of them than from Arnulf.

But when experience showed the matter to be otherwise, Formosus, while Lambert was still alive, summoned Arnulf to his ancestral dignity. Benedict IV supplied Louis III, king of Burgundy and Provence, in place of Arnulf in 900—not because he had been born from Boso by Ermengard, daughter of Louis II, and thus descended from the Carolingian line, but because protection for the Holy See, then exceedingly necessary, was being sought.

The same reasoning that had supported Wido and his son Lambert supports the designation to the empire of Berengar, whom Count Everard had begotten by Gisla, [Col. 0664A] daughter of Louis the Pious, by John X in 916, while Berengar’s rival Louis, deprived of his sight, was still enduring a useless life. For since 888 Berengar had been the most powerful king of Italy, and no more immediate protection for the Holy See seemed capable of being found.

I therefore think it may be affirmed that no other form of election was devised as long as the Carolingian line endured.

## § II. — On the election of the three Ottos and their successors down to Frederick II

### III.

In the seventh year of Berengar’s fortunate reign—according to the sound opinion of those who date his imperial coronation from the very day of the Nativity of the Lord in 915, or alternatively from the year 921—the peoples of Italy invited Rudolph, king of Burgundy, to assume the kingdom of Italy against Berengar. They followed him, crowned with the Italian diadem, against the emperor from whom they had revolted. [Col. 0664B]

Accordingly, after two battles had been unsuccessfully fought, Berengar abandoned the kingdom that he would have had to recover through civil war. After three years he was killed at Verona by conspirators, bringing the Carolingian empire to an end in 923.

For nearly forty years thereafter the kings of Italy were Rudolph; Hugh, margrave of Provence; his son Lothar; and Berengar II together with his son Adalbert. Their tyrannical rule and profound hostility to ecclesiastical authority compelled both the princes of Italy and, above all, the Roman pontiff to restore the imperial majesty.

It happened that Octavian, son of Alberic II, who had invaded pontifical rule following the example of his father and grandmother Marozia, ascended the chair of Peter under the name John XII. From there he saw more clearly the enormous injuries inflicted upon Italy and the Holy See by the tyrants. He therefore chose Otto, king of Germany, commended by his distinguished achievements against the tyrants of Italy and unsuccessfully summoned to the imperial crown ten years earlier by his predecessor Agapetus II. [Col. 0664C]

I do not dispute the corresponding action concerning Otto II, who was crowned emperor together with his father, or concerning his son Otto III, so far as the election is concerned. But I have no doubt that the election of both was approved by the Roman pontiff before they received the imperial diadem from him, as had been the case with the earlier Carolingians.

Whoever holds otherwise follows the error of those who regard the election of the kings of Germany as the imperial election. One must, however, consider that Conrad, duke of Franconia, and Henry, duke of Saxony, were likewise elected kings of Germany, yet neither is called emperor or king of the Romans in the charters. Although each, as he led an army, preceded a line of kings of the Romans and emperors bearing the same name, he deceived ignorant writers, so that they count seven Henrys, although there were only six kings of the Romans and five emperors; and three Conrads, although there were only two kings of the Romans and only one emperor.

### IV.

The most diligent investigator of charters, Godefridus, abbot (*Chronicle of Godwic*, book II, vol. I, p. 119), declares false the charters of Conrad I exhibited by Brower and Schannat, in which he is titled “king of the Romans and Franks.” He proves his case by genuine charters and by the authority of writers of that age—Regino, Widukind, Liutprand, and others.

Likewise, he testifies that in the charters of Henry I the word “king” is always found (ibid., p. 151), without the addition “of the Franks,” “of Germany,” or “of Eastern Francia.” Concerning the three Ottos who attained the imperial diadem, he declares absolutely that the title “king of the Romans” was never used by them.

By contrast, he finds Henry II, king of Germany and the first emperor, with the title “king of the Romans” (ibid., p. 233), as was stated above (Dissertation 4, no. 6), after the words of Platina, who made Blondus’s opinion clearer. His statement is as follows:

> “For shortly after Pope Gregory had returned, he established a sanction concerning the election of the emperor which we see has been observed for more than four hundred years up to the present: that only the Germans, who are therefore called electors, may choose the prince who is then called Caesar and king of the Romans and, if he is crowned by the Roman pontiff, is to be called Emperor Augustus.”

He is mistaken, and Platina with him, in thinking that the college of seven men was instituted by Gregory; I shall demonstrate this clearly below. But later monuments make it evident that the same pontiff sanctioned the election of the future emperor with the title “king of the Romans.”

### V.

First of all there is the decree of Benedict VIII, issued before he bestowed the imperial diadem upon Henry II, king of Germany. Glaber reports it in Baronius (1113, no. 5), and it is as follows:

> “So that no prince may rashly desire to carry the scepter of the Roman Empire prematurely, or be able to be called or to be emperor, unless the pope of the Roman See has chosen him, proven in character and suitable for the commonwealth, and has entrusted the imperial insignia to him.”

This explains the condition which Blondus rightly adds: “if he is crowned by the Roman pontiff.” It follows that one thing—and that the principal thing—was lacking from the election of the king of Germany by the princes of his nation: namely, the approval of the Roman pontiff.

It seems impossible to doubt that Gregory V and Otto III established something concerning the election of the king of the Romans. For both Henry, the successor of Otto, as we recently said, and all Henry’s successors call themselves kings of the Romans in their charters before their Roman coronation, as may be seen in the aforementioned Godefridus (ibid., pp. 269, 284, 310, 326, and 344).

Moreover, in his promise, or profession, before his coronation in 1046, Henry III, king of Germany, openly presents himself as “I, N., king of the Romans,” as is clear from the Roman order, which I shall produce when discussing the coronation.

Therefore, contrary to what nearly all scholars have been persuaded of, the title “king of the Romans” should not be traced to the year 1138, when Conrad III, king of Germany, was elected and crowned at Aachen, but to the election of Henry II, who was crowned at Mainz in 1002. The scholars’ opinion seems to have arisen from Conrad’s seal, which is first found with the title “king of the Romans,” and from the fact that all his successors followed his example—something not done by Conrad’s predecessors, the kings of Germany (see Dissertation 4, no. 6).

### VI.

I think I must not pass over the fact that the frequently mentioned Godefridus, after correctly affirming that none of the three Ottos used that title (ibid., p. 119), seems to have added, less cautiously:

> “Nor was it used in later times before the actual possession of the kingdom of Italy.”

Yet it nowhere appears that Henry III and Henry V, kings of Germany who use that title in their charters, obtained the Lombard crown. Concerning Henry III alone, an Italian annalist (under the year 1046), following his customary practice, conjectures that after the meeting held at Pavia he might have received the crown at Milan from Wido, the metropolitan. But apart from the fact that history rejects conjectures, the lack of time indicates otherwise. Concerning Henry V also, Gualvanus Flamma and other later writers, comparing their own age with that earlier one, assert the same thing.

Pagius (1110, no. 2), however, objects that Landulf, Otto of Freising, and other contemporary writers say nothing of the sort. His objection is certainly confirmed by the absence of Archbishop Grossolanus.

What more need be said? Conrad, brother of Duke Frederick of Swabia, was inaugurated king of Italy by Anselm, metropolitan of Milan, in 1128, as Landulf reports in Puricellus and Pagius (under that year, no. 13)—first at Monza and then at Milan. Nevertheless, the title “king of the Romans” is not found in his charters until after the year 1138, [Col. 0666A] when he received the German crown at Aachen.

Thus it was not actual possession of the kingdom of Italy, but the German election and coronation, that established the future emperor as king of the Romans, unless the Roman pontiff refused his consent.

So much for the election of the future emperor before Rudolph the Great, progenitor of the Austrian house. I shall now discuss the same election beginning with Rudolph himself and continuing down to our own age, when the matter was reduced to the imposing college of seven men.

## § III. — On the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire

### VII.

Wearied by all the injuries that had been inflicted upon Italy and the Roman Church over a period of many years by the Augusti of the Swabian line, they finally reached the point of deciding that Frederick II should be deposed in a general council held at Lyon in 1245. This was done by the authority of Innocent IV, who presided over the council.

From this arose the great interregnum, which lasted twenty-eight years, as Rudolph’s letters testify—or twenty-three, as German writers assert, reckoning it from Frederick’s death. Among those writers it is called “the fatal interregnum.” For at that time, more than anything else, they say that

> “the senate of seven men began, excluding the other princes of Germany from the election of the king of the Romans”

(Kemmerich, *Introduction to Public Law*, book II, chapter 1, article 6).

Boecler’s authority, cited above, does not depart from this common opinion of Puffendorf and the other writers on public law. He reports that Rudolph was the very first to be elected by that senate of seven, as we have heard. This election of the king of the Romans brought the long interregnum to an end.

I entirely reject the opinion of Bessel (notes on Einhard, chapter 9), who thinks that the college was instituted either in Frederick II’s time or shortly before it, as well as the opinion of the commentators on the glossary, who postpone such an institution until the Golden Bull of Charles IV, issued in 1356. We must adhere to the writers on public law.

For the letters of Gregory X to Alfonso, king of Spain, near the end of the interregnum, in Raynaldus (1272, no. 34), warn that the matter could not have been handled otherwise:

> “Among other matters, this was mentioned: since Richard of blessed memory, elected king of the Romans, had been chosen without the electors being summoned, or at least without any notification having been made to them, one ought not to have proceeded with the dispatch of such petitions, since it appears especially to concern them, inasmuch as they claim for themselves the right to elect the king of the Romans, who is afterward to be advanced to the imperial dignity, and are said to be in peaceful possession of that right, or something equivalent to possession. From this it was also argued that they could neither be forbidden nor ought to be forbidden from freely exercising such possession, by choosing another person if they thought it expedient.”

### VIII.

If the electors defended their right by possession, rather than by any pontifical constitution—which is nowhere found—or by an imperial one—which could not have been issued during the interregnum—the older monuments must therefore be examined more attentively, so that the definite origin of that senate of seven may be established.

First of all, the contemporary author Paris must be heard. Baronius speaks of him as follows (966, no. 63):

> “If anyone removes from him the calumnies, invectives, witticisms, and blasphemies frequently directed against the Apostolic See, he would rightly call the work a golden commentary, since it is found to have been excellently composed and joined together from public records, reproduced in so many words.”

Paris, therefore, on the authority of Mallinkrot and against Gewold, shows that the kings of Germany had formerly been accustomed to be elected in an assembly of all the orders. But after Innocent IV deposed Frederick II in 1245, so that a prince more advantageous to the Church might be substituted, he entrusted the matter to seven princes selected from the whole body.

He lists them below in this order:

> “The magnates of Alemannia, though not electors of the emperors: the king of Bohemia, the duke of Lorraine, the duke of Brunswick, the duke of Swabia, the landgrave of Thuringia, the duke of Limburg, the duke of Carinthia, the duke of Saxony, and the count of Guelders.
>
> “The lay electors of the emperors: the duke of Austria, the duke of Bavaria, the duke of Saxony, and the duke of Brabant, who is also duke of Lothier.
>
> “The principal prelates: the archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop of Mainz, and the archbishop of Salzburg.
>
> “These men will be taken to an island in the Rhine, left there alone, and all the boats will be removed. There they will deliberate on the election of the emperor, and no one will come to them until they are all in agreement. The archbishop of Cologne will preside over this business, the archbishop of Mainz will be second, and the archbishop of Salzburg third.
>
> “The lord pope sent them an extremely earnest admonition, together with a supplication, that they should elect another emperor for him. He promised them his own counsel and that of the whole Church, and at the outset, in the hope of a better outcome, fifteen thousand pounds of silver.
>
> “But Frederick’s opposition forestalled and prevailed, for he was bound to them, and especially to the duke of Austria, by ties of kinship. Hence the electors paid no attention to the papal admonitions and entreaties.”

Thus writes, as Hansiz of the Society of Jesus says, the most serious historian of English affairs of that age (Germania Sacra, vol. II, p. 959).

### IX.

Antonius Pagius (996, no. 14), and after him Raynaldus (1257, no. 6), attribute to Paris another list of the princes of Germany, entirely different from the one we have reported. It was evidently the work of a writer less familiar with German affairs, who continued and revised Paris’s chronicle and, following his own judgment, inserted princes down to the year 1258.

Yet they could have known that Paris himself, by his own testimony, did not pass beyond the year 1250. He says:

> “Here end the chronicles of Brother Matthew Paris, monk of Saint Albans, which, for the benefit of posterity, out of love for God and in honor of blessed Alban, the proto-martyr of the English, he committed to writing lest the memory of recent events be destroyed by antiquity or forgetfulness:
>
> “The Sun has now completed a thousand volumes of years  
> Since the Virgin gave birth, and with two hundred and fifty  
> Annual courses besides; yet it was not seen that, in so long a time,  
> Easter fell on the sixth of April before the Kalends,  
> While the fiftieth year was traversing the world.  
> This, however, happened in the year at whose end this work stands.  
> For from the Incarnation of the Lord twenty-five groups of fifty years have passed.”

Nothing could make this chronology clearer. If Pagius had noticed it, he would have affirmed, as he did elsewhere (under the year 996, no. 15), that “the Roman pontiffs, by whom the Western Empire was renewed, preserved their right unharmed and either approved or rejected the elections.” He would therefore have asserted with certainty that in 1245 the number of electors had originated not through any constitution, but through the counsel of Innocent IV.

Not long afterward four of these were changed because they adhered to Frederick: the archbishop of Salzburg, in whose place the archbishop of Trier was substituted, and the dukes of Austria, Bavaria, and Brabant. In their place were admitted the king of Bohemia, the count palatine of the Rhine, and the margrave of Brandenburg.

This is attested by Albert, abbot of Stade (in Baronius, 996, no. 47), a contemporary author who continued his chronicle to the year 1256:

> “From the previously designated princes and by their consent, the archbishop of Trier, the archbishop of Mainz, and the archbishop of Cologne elect the emperor. The count palatine elects because he is the steward; the duke of Saxony because he is the marshal; and the margrave of Brandenburg because he is the chamberlain. The king of Bohemia, who is the cupbearer, does not elect because he is not German.”

### X.

The election of the senate of seven, arising from Innocent IV’s counsel, however, seems not at the outset to have abrogated the right granted by Gregory V and Otto III to the other German princes.

For in the Council of Lyon, after the sentence against Frederick II had been pronounced (Labbe, *Councils*, vol. XI, p. 645), the following is added:

> “Those to whom the election of the emperor in that empire belongs shall freely elect a successor.”

And in the following year Innocent IV wrote a letter expressing the same uncertain judgment (Raynaldus, 1246, no. 2):

> “To the archbishops and other noble princes of Germany who possess the power of electing the king of the Romans, afterward to be advanced to the imperial dignity.”

Moreover, when Henry, landgrave of Hesse, who had been elected, died within two years, the same pontiff, still residing at Lyon, sent various letters for the election of William, count of Holland (Raynaldus, 1247, no. 4 ff.), to the princes of Germany who were by no means included among the seven electors.

Therefore, as long as Frederick II lived, it cannot be asserted with certainty that the election had devolved upon those seven men.

The situation was different afterward. Letters of Alexander IV preserved by Raynaldus (1256, no. 3 ff.) order the archbishop of Mainz to oppose Conradin’s election, in these words:

> “You shall firmly forbid your other fellow electors, both ecclesiastical and secular, on our authority.”

In the following year, when the election had been made by a double authority, Henry Stero speaks of it in his chronicle, preserved by Canisius (vol. IV, p. 191), as follows:

> “The princes of the kingdom, after holding various assemblies for a long time to elect a king, finally fixed the definitive day of the election for the octave of Epiphany, to be celebrated at Frankfurt. When some had assembled there, the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Cologne, and Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, together with his brother Lord Henry, duke of Bavaria, united in favor of Richard, brother of the king of England.
>
> “He was subsequently elected by them and, on Ascension Day, anointed king at Aachen and firmly established upon the throne of the kingdom.
>
> “But the lord bishop of Trier, unwilling to agree to the aforesaid election, chose Lord Alfonso, king of Spain, in mid-Lent, relying upon the letters and authority of the king of Bohemia, the duke of Saxony, the margraves of Brandenburg, and many princes.”

### XI.

What Stero relates in no way conflicts with the letters of Alexander, Urban, Clement IV, and Gregory X, or with the other monuments that may be consulted in Raynaldus concerning that prolonged dispute over the double election. Richard and Alfonso each wished his own election to be ratified by the pontiff, so that they would not be prevented from attaining the imperial diadem, and they never ceased to weary the Roman pontiffs with letters and messengers.

Let two letters of Urban IV stand for all the rest (1262, no. 5 ff.; 1263, no. 43 ff.). In the first, addressing Ottocar, king of Bohemia, he says:
