> “Our venerable brother the archbishop of Mainz [writes] to you and the other princes of the kingdom of Germany, to whom belongs the election of the king of the Romans to be advanced to the imperial dignity.”

In the second, he addresses Richard more clearly:

> “Your prudent circumspection knows that our most beloved son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile and León, affirms that he was elected by the greater part of the princes possessing a vote in the election of the king of the Romans; to you, etc.”

If those four princes who possessed a vote in the election of the king of the Romans and elected Alfonso in 1257 are called the greater part of the electors, then there is no doubt that the senate of seven was by that time in existence.

Indeed, from the very year 1245, when by the pontiff’s counsel the matter was reduced to seven princes, Gregory X could not otherwise have described their peaceful possession.

The origin of the senate of seven is therefore certain: at first varied and somewhat obscure, as are the origins of other institutions, but afterward very clear, and evident in Rudolph’s election, as is established by several of his letters that I shall cite below.

Especially noteworthy among them is the letter he wrote to the king of Bohemia, Ottocar (book I, letter 31). Although Ottocar had joined the election “with the other fellow princes,” he immediately defected from Rudolph. For, as Gerard de Roo says (*History of Austria*, book I, p. 18), he held Rudolph in contempt because shortly before he had seen him as commander of the cavalry, or marshal, in his court:

> “He thought nothing of Rudolph, saying that he had shortly before been his servant.”

Although, as we have seen, the abbot of Stade denies that Ottocar belonged to the number of seven, whatever may have been the case in that writer’s age, Gregory X counts him among the electors in a letter to the archbishop of Salzburg (Raynaldus, 1274, no. 56):

> “The illustrious king of Bohemia, who asserts that he possesses a right in the election of the emperor.”

Rudolph agrees with Gregory in those letters.

### XII.

Someone might perhaps object to the diploma of the electors, in which all the rights of the Holy See are confirmed, as well as to Rudolph’s letters, preserved uncertainly in book III after letter 47. For the diploma bears these subscriptions:

> “We, the princes of the Empire: Henry, archbishop of Trier; Siffrid, archbishop of Cologne; Werner, archbishop of Mainz; Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of both Bavarias; John, duke of Saxony; Albert, duke of Saxony; John, margrave of Brandenburg; and we, Otto, margrave of Brandenburg.”

It is therefore clear that several princes of the same family subscribed, so that the electoral dignity seems to have been attributed not to persons but to houses. Hence we understand why Alfonso boasted that he had been elected by the greater part of the electors: the archbishop of Trier, the king of Bohemia, the duke of Saxony, and the margraves of Brandenburg had elected him, although an equal number seem to have elected Richard—namely, the archbishops of Mainz and Cologne, the count palatine of the Rhine, and his brother, the duke of Bavaria.

These last two must be counted as only one elector, since the dukes of Bavaria were not at that time included among the electors.

But the name of the king of Bohemia is absent from the subscriptions mentioned above. It must be observed, however, that Ottocar, king of Bohemia, Rudolph’s perpetual enemy, who had been defeated by him once and again, was finally killed in 1278 (book II, letter 32 ff.). The diploma itself was issued in the following year, when Wenceslaus, Ottocar’s eight-year-old son, had been entrusted to the guardianship of Otto of Brandenburg.

Therefore, whether we believe that Wenceslaus’s subscription is also contained in the subscriptions of the margraves of Brandenburg, or consider it entirely unnecessary, the senate of seven suffers no diminution.

The same applies to the charter, or letter (book III, letter 1), by which the electors, as they say, “together with our other fellow electors,” ratify the property, castles, lands, and possessions granted by Rudolph to his wife Anna.

### XIII.

No one is unaware that the Golden Bull of Charles IV added much dignity and majesty to this final form of election, which remains in force even in our own times (the two most recent electors, the dukes of Bavaria and Hanover, do not pertain to it). The substance, however, remains the same.

Only this difference arose beginning in the time of Maximilian: the king of the Romans began to be called “the elected emperor,” and, with that addition gradually omitted, he is commonly called “emperor.” Since the Roman coronation—which alone makes an emperor—fell into disuse after Charles V, and since several acts are judged equivalent to coronation, especially the confirmation of the Holy See and the first prayers, it has long been the case that neither pontiffs nor kings of the Romans—that is, elected emperors—establish the imperial majesty by placing the imperial diadem upon the head of the elect through the hands of Christ’s vicar before the most sacred body of the prince of the apostles, as was done in Rudolph’s time, as several of his letters will make clear.

It is not surprising, however, that coronation was once held in such high esteem. The pontiffs needed protection and defense, not only against the enemies of the Roman Church but also to keep the peoples subject to them in their obedience; enough has been said of these matters in Dissertation 1.

Through such a coronation, the emperors became partners in the supreme pontifical power within the city itself—so, at least, the pontiffs wished, whose interests were involved. For this reason Rudolph sought it so earnestly, and it seemed to him that nothing could be accomplished except that it be completed by the Roman pontiff as a work of God, to use his own words (book II, letter 1).

Since this never happened, he left no such monument of jurisdiction for posterity. By contrast, the enactments and charters of his predecessors who attained the crown are extant; to some recent writers—whom they call learned, though they might more accurately be called ignorant of these matters—they seem to provide evidence of the supreme imperial power to the detriment of pontifical authority.

Pagius comes closer to the truth when he calls this a delegation of pontifical power (823, no. 1). Several charters of the Ottos, especially Otto III, are extant by which he confirms the property and privileges of churches within the city itself. Yet acts of this kind seem never to have been more opportune. For in his time the city was agitated by factions under Crescentius, and imperial authority was necessary to suppress them.

Thus the anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Adalbert of Prague*, in Pagius (996, no. 3), speaking of his coronation, says:

> “The new emperor gives laws to the peoples; the new pope gives laws.”

### XIV.

Of the charters mentioned above, Ughellus cites one in his account of the bishops of Verona (*Sacred Italy*, vol. V, p. 750), dated the tenth day before the Kalends of June. Margarinus cites another (*Cassinese Chronicle*, vol. I), dated the eighth day before the Kalends of June. Muratorius cites another (*Italian Antiquities*, Dissertation 8, and under the year 996), dated the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Finally, the most learned Hieronymite abbot Felix Nerinius produced another among the many historical monuments he collected in his distinguished work on the Church and monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius (p. 372). Since he had published it from an ancient parchment but was not entirely satisfied with it until he discovered its autograph, he joyfully shared with me the autograph when it was found several years later.

Its final portion, which is missing from the parchment, runs as follows:

> “The sign of the lord Otto, the most invincible [place of the seal]. Heribert, chancellor, acting in place of Peter, bishop of Como and archchancellor, have reviewed this. Given on the day before the Kalends of June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 996, indiction nine; in the thirteenth year of the reign of our lord Otto III, but in the first year of his empire. Done successfully at Rome.”

To understand the character of such documents, which indicate jurisdiction, one must recall what the emperor himself had promised under oath before attaining the crown:

> “In the city of Rome,” he says, “I shall make no judgment or ordinance concerning anything that pertains to you or to the Romans without your counsel.”

Similar provisions are found in the charter, or pact, confirming the rights of the Holy See, issued while the emperors of the Carolingian line still endured:

> “Nor do we claim for ourselves any share or power over their administration, judgment, subtraction, or diminution, unless we are asked by him who at that time governs this Holy Church.”

When Leo III elevated Charles, as patron and defender of the Church, to the imperial dignity, he did not remove dominion from the prince of the apostles or from his successors—for that would have been impious. Rather, by wise counsel he decided that the peoples subject to them, especially the Romans, should be kept in obedience by such authority.

For this reason, immediately after receiving the diadem, the successors of Charles, before departing from the city, issued charters or held judicial assemblies there, always with the consent of the pontiff. Through these the jurisdiction or authority of the prince was made manifest, but without any diminution of pontifical authority.

Therefore, when the same Romans took an oath of loyalty to the new prince, they said that they did so while preserving the loyalty owed to the pontiff, as we demonstrated at length in Dissertation 1, where we also discussed to some extent the other matters relating to the coronation.

I shall now discuss the varying rite of that same coronation, so that greater light may thereby be shed upon Rudolph’s letters.

## § IV. — On the rite of the coronation of the Carolingian Augusti

### XV.

In the very first coronation, it is useless to seek evidence of any particular rite. For Einhard, who was Charlemagne’s secretary and knew everything that occurred (*Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 28), the author of the *Life of Leo III* in Anastasius (section 376), and the other contemporary writers—especially the monk of Angoulême—testify that it was performed unexpectedly:

> “When, at Mass, before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, he rose from prayer, Lord Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head.”

Nevertheless, since Louis II testifies in his famous letter to Basil, emperor of the East (Anonymous of Salerno, chapter 102), that anointing preceded the coronation:

> “Our great-grandfather Charlemagne, anointed with such an anointing by the supreme pontiff, was the first from our people and lineage, with piety abounding in him, to be called emperor and made Christ’s anointed”;

since, I say, Louis II adds anointing, it is not improbable that the anointing together with the placing of the crown constituted the whole rite of Charlemagne’s coronation.

The coronation of Louis the Pious, performed in France in a singular manner, is described by Thegan (chapter 17) in these words:

> “On the following Sunday, in the church, before the solemn celebration of Mass, in the presence of the clergy and all the people, he consecrated and anointed him as emperor, and placed upon his head a golden crown of wondrous beauty adorned with the most precious gems, which he had brought with him.”

And Lothar, son of Louis the Pious, who was crowned as his father’s associate, thus reminded his father of the event:

> “Before the sacred altar, and before the sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I received from the supreme pontiff, with your consent and will, the blessing, honor, and name of the imperial office; moreover, the diadem for my head and the sword for the defense of the Church.”

Mabillonius reports this (*Benedictine Section IV*, p. 513). I shall show that Louis II, Lothar’s son, was crowned in a similar manner by Leo IV in 850, since he himself bears witness to this and to his predecessors in the aforementioned letter to Basil.

Concerning Charles the Bald, son of Lothar and brother of Louis II, and in nearly the same words concerning Charles the Fat, son of Louis, Lothar’s brother, the Bertinian annalist in Pagius (876, no. 6; 880, no. 7) records the following:

> “On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, after offering many precious gifts to blessed Peter, he was anointed and crowned emperor, and was called emperor of the Romans.”

In the Roman council of 877, preserved in Labbe (vol. IX, p. 295), in the confirmation of Charles the Bald, mention is made not only of anointing, the crown, and the sword, but also of the scepter.

Nothing new is available concerning Wido and his son Lambert, who were inserted among the Carolingians, in the *Chronicle of Casauria*, preserved by the Continuator of Freherus, and in Pagius (892, no. 2).

### XVI

A somewhat fuller account of the rite of the coronation of Arnulf, the last of the descendants of Charlemagne, performed by Formosus, is found in the same author (896, no. 3):

> “The apostolic father, cherishing the king with paternal affection, received him before the paradise, at the place called the steps of Saint Peter, and brought him joyfully and honorably into the basilica of the blessed chief apostles; then, according to the custom of his predecessors, placing the imperial consecration upon his head, he called him Caesar Augustus.”

I would indeed regard this testimony—since it calls the basilica of the chief apostles the church of Saint Peter, and calls the emperor Caesar Augustus—as having been written in a later period, were it not that the anonymous panegyrist of Berengar, who completes the series of the Carolingians, demonstrates that the account of the continuator of Freher’s narrative is entirely true. In a very obscure poem he follows the rite, but I shall present it in the clearer and abridged form given by Pagius (915, no. 7).

Thus, then, Berengar was received and crowned:

> “Franks, Lombards, Saxons, and English, divided into schools and companies, each in his native language, proclaimed praises to him; and Peter, the brother of the pope, and the son of Theophylact, consul of the Romans, led him to Pope John, who was sitting on the steps of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, or in the atrium above the 255 steps of that basilica. After Berengar had climbed all the steps of the same basilica, John X, who was sitting on a golden throne, rose to meet the king and kissed him. After entering the basilica and after Berengar had made his profession and prayers had been poured out at the tomb of blessed Peter, Pope John gave him a most sumptuous dinner in his palace; finally, on the Sunday of the Resurrection, or Easter—the day on which Christ, God and man, rose from his tomb—he adorned him with the imperial crown. Berengar then issued a document confirming the donations of all the preceding princes.”

### XVII

The schools enumerated by the panegyrist were within the walls in Berengar’s time, but those of the first four emperors—Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Lothair, and Louis II—were outside the walls. For it is clear that the Leonine City was founded and dedicated by its founder, Leo IV, in the year 852.

Since, however, he mentions only those schools, he seems to suggest that the practice of receiving the emperor at the gate of the fortress should be traced back to the Carolingians. This practice was customary in the reception of the kings of Germany and continued down to the last Roman coronation, that of Frederick III.

But since this ceremony differs greatly from the reception customarily accorded to kings at Rome, and since it began with Charlemagne when he first came to Rome in the year 774, I shall insert it here from the *Pontifical Book* (section 314 and following):

> “He sent all the judges to meet him nearly thirty thousand paces from this Roman city, to a place called Novae, where they received him with the *bandora*. When he had approached to within nearly one mile of the Roman city, he sent all the military schools together with their patrons, and also the boys who were going to learn letters. They all carried branches of palm and olive and sang all the praises, with the acclamations of those same praises; they received him as king of the Franks. His Holiness sent venerable crosses to meet him—that is, standards—as is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician, and caused him to be received with the greatest honor.”

Later, concerning the pontiff himself, who was to receive the king:

> “He hastened with all the clergy and the Roman people to blessed Peter to receive that same king of the Franks, and in the steps of that apostolic hall he awaited him with his clergy.”

And concerning the king’s approach:

> “He proceeded until he reached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the atrium above the steps beside the doors of the church. After he had been received there, they embraced one another; then that most Christian king took the right hand of the aforesaid pontiff, and thus they entered together into the same venerable hall of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.”

### XVIII

The reception and welcome of this kind, similar examples of which we infer from the aforementioned panegyrist to have been accorded to the arriving king who was to be crowned, were followed by the coronation rite itself. I shall append it here from a most excellent Albinian manuscript.

**Here begins the Roman order for blessing the emperor when he receives the crown.**

**The emperor’s promise.** In the name of Christ, I, N., emperor, promise, pledge, and swear that before God and blessed Peter I shall be the protector and defender of this holy Roman Church in all its interests, insofar as I shall be supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability.

Then the bishop of Albano is to give the first prayer before the Silver Gate of the basilica of blessed Peter:

> God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, etc.

The bishop of Porto is to give the second prayer inside the church of Saint Peter, in the middle of the *rota*:

> Ineffable God, author of the world, creator of the human race, etc.

Then they are to go before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter. He is to prostrate himself face downward upon the ground, and the archdeacon is to recite the litany. When it has been completed, the bishop of Ostia is to anoint his right arm and the space between his shoulders with exorcised oil, and to say this prayer:

> Almighty Lord God, to whom belongs all power, etc.

The following prayer is then said:

> God the Son of God, Jesus Christ, our Lord, who [was anointed] by the Father with oil (the following word is corrupt: *exsul*), etc.

Finally, the Roman pontiff, above before the altar, places the diadem upon his head, saying:

> Receive the sign of glory in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that, having spurned the ancient enemy and the contagions of all vices, you may love judgment and justice, and live so mercifully that from our Lord Jesus Christ himself you may receive, in the company of the saints, the crown of the eternal kingdom. Who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives …

### XIX

Raynaldus (1209, no. 18) was the first of all to publish this very brief Roman order, believing it to have been written in the age of the coronation of Otto IV. Mabillon then published it in his collection (*Museum Italicum*, vol. II, Order XII, no. 88), as though it were the work of Cencius. Finally, Martène (*On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book II, chapter 9, Order VII) issued it in a fuller form than the others from an Arles manuscript, without determining its date.

Yet the single promise, or profession, beginning “I, N., emperor,” assigns the order to the Carolingians. For the first of all the kings of Germany—and the two who followed imitated him—claimed no other title for himself than that of king, neither in very many charters, as Godefridus observes (*Chronicon Godwicianum*, vol. I, p. 166), nor in the celebrated oath also reported by Gratian.

I readily acknowledge that Charlemagne, according to Einhard’s testimony in his *Life* (chapter 28), received the name of emperor and Augustus only after his coronation; this too was customary among the successors of the Carolingian line. But the profession of defending the Church “in all its interests” suits only the Carolingians. The Germans, as will be clear below, professed, together with the defense of the Church, the defense and exaltation of its ruler.

Therefore, learned editors of this order, may they forgive me: they have not attained its true age. Nor would I say that the order existed from the very beginning of the imperial dignity, since no mention is found among the authors of the rite having been observed, except in the panegyrist of Berengar. But his testimony is more than sufficient to carry this order back and remove it from the period assigned to it by those who reasoned that Cencius the chamberlain was the first to record the rite.

For shortly we shall see that, before the middle of the eleventh century, another fuller order, more appropriate to the kings of Germany, was in use. Moreover, the prayers to be said by the three cardinals are merely indicated, both in our manuscript and in every ancient order. Thus, in the age of Cencius, when it was a well-known fact that the emperor acquired the title of emperor through the coronation, either the word “prince” or “king” would have been placed in place of “emperor,” or only the first prayer, to be said by the bishop of Albano, would have been indicated.

The same will be found to be true if at some time the genuine order inserted by Cencius emerges from the *Censual Book*.

### XX

It must also be observed—and this especially vindicates that order for the Carolingians—that no mention is made of the Mass, nor is any opportunity left for someone wishing to imagine one to insert it into the same order. For as soon as the bishop of Ostia has anointed the king, the pontiff completes the rite by placing the diadem upon him.

Accordingly, the order reads: “Finally, the pontiff, etc.,” which clearly indicates the completion of the entire rite.

There is no doubt, however, that Mass was celebrated afterward, since the Sunday or solemn day chosen for the coronation required it. Theganus plainly says this of the Mass following the coronation of Louis the Pious (chapter 17): Stephen IV

> “on the following Sunday, before the solemnities of the Mass, consecrated him in the presence of the clergy and all the people, and anointed him as emperor.”

No one would dare deny that, in that Mass, besides the proper prayer of the day, another prayer for the emperor was added. This was not taken from the ceremonial books, which were not used for the sacrifice of the Mass, but from the *Book of Sacraments*, just as it would be taken today from the Missal.

It will not be out of place to insert here the Mass from the same *Book of Sacraments* (Thomasius, vol. VI, p. 202), to be compared with that which is found in the ceremonial books:

> **Prayer.** God, protector of all kingdoms, and especially of the Roman Empire, grant your servants, our kings, N., to cultivate knowingly the triumph of virtue, so that, by whose ordinance they are princes, by his gift they may always be powerful. Through …
>
> **Secret.** Receive, Lord, the prayers and offerings of your Church for the salvation of your servant N., who makes supplication; and, for the protection of faithful peoples, perform the ancient miracles of your arm, so that, once the enemies of peace have been overcome, Christian liberty may serve you in security. Through …
>
> **After communion.** God, who prepared the Roman Empire for the preaching of the Gospel of the eternal King, extend heavenly weapons to your servants, our princes, N., so that the peace of the Churches may not be disturbed by any storm of wars. Through the Lord.

In the ceremonial books the name “emperor” is found everywhere in place of “prince.” But this is not at all incompatible with the coronation rite of the Carolingians, who were called emperors before Mass.

When the coronation began to be performed during the solemnities of Mass, the name in the first prayer necessarily had to be changed. Why it was not changed in the coronation of Henry III, king of Germany, which necessarily took place during the solemnities of Mass, we shall soon see.

## § V — The Rite of the Coronation of the Kings of Germany after the Election of the King of the Romans Had Been Established

### XXI

After an interregnum lasting thirty-eight years, the imperial dignity again shone forth at Rome in the year 962, in Otto the Great. He was the first among the kings of Germany to be girded with the imperial diadem and leads the line of the Augusti of that nation; this is universally acknowledged.

But a different coronation rite and different imperial insignia are found in the ancient monuments. For when the coronation began to be performed during the solemnities of Mass, it brought new distinction to the emperor; and, in addition to the Carolingian insignia—the crown, scepter, and sword—the pontiffs added the golden orb.

Dufresnius observes (*Dissertation on the Coinage of the Later Ages*, § 19) that Stephen Baluze had caused an image of Charles the Bald to be drawn, holding in his left hand a globe surmounted by a cross. But however diligently one searches, one will find no ancient monuments confirming this.

Godefridus, often mentioned above, observes from the seals of Otto I (*Chronicon Godwicianum*, vol. I, p. 163) that the German emperors used such an orb:

> “In the royal seals he generally appears beardless and with a still youthful face, his head either bare or at least encircled by a closed crown, holding in his hands either a royal staff or a lance and shield. In contrast, in the imperial seals he is represented with a somewhat long beard, a crown closed above, and adorned with an orb and scepter, as Heineccius observed something of this kind in the Zyllesian seal.”

For this reason, when Glaber Rodulfus speaks of Benedict VIII—whom they falsely make the inventor of his orb—he says in Baronius (1013, no. 5 and following):

> “Although that imperial insignia had previously been represented in various forms, nevertheless it was ordered for the venerable Pope Benedict in a highly intelligible form. He likewise ordered that the insignia be fashioned as a golden orb, surrounded in a square by the most precious gems, and that a golden cross be inserted above it.”

### XXII

From this it is clear that the golden orb by which Godefridus saw Otto I distinguished was given a new form by Benedict VIII after the Ottos—namely, to Henry II, king of Germany and the first king of the Romans.

But that it was not from the beginning to be counted among the imperial insignia customarily delivered at the solemn coronation, we learn from the same Glaber, who reports how Benedict, when Henry

> “had come to Rome, went out according to custom to meet him with a very great multitude of men and sacred orders, and in the sight of the entire Roman populace presented him with such an insignia, namely that of the empire, etc.”

The coronation took place in the following year.

Moreover, the Roman order that I shall soon place before everyone’s eyes shows that neither Conrad the Salian, who succeeded Henry in 1027, nor Henry III, his successor, who was crowned by Clement II in 1046 and was the second emperor of that name, received the cross-bearing orb among the other insignia.

The first who appears to have received an orb among the other insignia was Frederick I Barbarossa, crowned by Adrian IV in 1155. I say “appears,” for the acts reported by Baronius (1155, no. 17) do not list it among the other objects:

> “The king approached the pontiff to be crowned, and, after the imperial insignia had been presented, received from the hands of that same pope the sword, scepter, and crown of the empire.”

Nevertheless, Gotfridus of Viterbo, priest, chaplain, and notary of Conrad III, king of Germany, and of the emperors Frederick I and Henry VI—he completed his chronicle in 1186 and dedicated it to Urban III while Frederick was still alive, and therefore had witnessed no other coronation—counts the orb among the other insignia (in Dufresnius, *On the Coinage of the Later Ages*, § 19), describing it as follows:

> This golden globe is called an orb or ball,
>
> Whence it is thought to bear the figured world.
>
> When he is crowned, the ball is given to be carried.

And, what is more, Henry IV, successor of Frederick I,

> “after he had received his crown from our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Celestine,”

as Innocent III says,

> “having withdrawn for a little while and then returning to him, asked from him investiture of the empire by the golden orb”

(*Register*, vol. I, p. 697).

So highly was that insignia regarded at that time, as representing the whole world!

For the opinion had gradually prevailed—as we shall see attested by several letters of Rudolph—that the temporal power of the emperor extended as far and as widely as the spiritual power of the Roman pontiff. This was not because the emperors believed themselves to be masters of kingdoms and territories belonging to others, but because, just as the pontiff exercises authority throughout the whole world without being bounded by limits, while all patriarchs, metropolitans, and bishops retain their own rights, so the emperor seemed to become, through the imposition of the imperial diadem, the supreme imperial prince of the whole world, without diminishing the rights of any king or prince.

Although this was not the true character of the dignity instituted by Leo III, it did not seem vain or excessive to the Roman pontiffs. Indeed, they themselves, using the comparison of the sun and the moon, designated the pontiff and the emperor as lords of the whole world.

### XXIII

As for the coronation that began to be performed during the solemnities of Mass, ancient monuments show that Henry, son of Conrad the Salian, who is called the second emperor of that name, was necessarily crowned contrary to the custom observed up to that time, during the solemnities of Mass.

For the pontiff, from whom he was to receive the imperial insignia, first had to be consecrated or blessed. Therefore, after the blessing of Clement II, Henry was crowned before the *Gloria in excelsis*, in the year 1046.

Many new and unusual things then occurred, which have come down to us in a ceremonial book written on that occasion. Onuphrius Panvinius, a diligent investigator of ancient matters, listed this ceremonial among the Roman orders he had collected, but left it unexplored (*Vatican Codex* 6112). From it Father Giovanni Battista Gatticus, abbot and canon regular of the Lateran, extracted and published it in 1753 (vol. I, p. 215), without knowing what it was.

I recognized the value of the ceremonial and inspected the Vatican manuscript myself. I found two copies (folios 102 and 121) and detected that the editor had committed not a few errors against the authority of the manuscript. I corrected what was more necessary and neglected the rest.

Would that the autograph of so valuable a monument could be found somewhere! Whatever Panvinius preserved for us, together with the other materials edited by Mabillon, I judged ought to be committed to the press again, so that it might not remain unknown to any learned person—and on an occasion more suitable than any other could not have been offered.

Hermannus Contractus, whom scholars trust as a contemporary witness, relates how, after the Council of Sutri, where Gregory VI abdicated, Henry came to Rome with his wife Agnes and Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord in the year 1046. From this point Hermannus begins the following year.

Suidger had been elected by those who had assembled at Sutri and was consecrated on the very day of the Nativity. “Immediately afterward,” he continues,

> “on that very day, he raised King Henry and his wife Agnes by the imperial blessing; and when the solemnities of Mass had been completed, the lord pope and the emperor with the empress, crowned as he was, proceeded to the Lateran palace with great glory, while all the Roman citizens marveled and each one, according to his ability, offered them honor as they passed.”

Thus the pious monk of Augia makes a certain history incredible through the compression of time. For no one could embrace even in thought that the pontiff had been consecrated contrary to tradition, the custom of the ancestors, and established practice on the Thursday into which the Nativity of the Lord fell that year—and, what surpasses all belief, that within a few hours the clergy, people, and prelates who had assembled at Sutri had gathered, elected, enthroned, and consecrated the pontiff; that everything had been prepared for so great a solemnity involving three coronations, such as had never before and never afterward taken place; and finally that the new and unusual ceremony then employed had been carried out as described.

But the ceremonial itself will expose Hermann’s error more clearly.

**THE ROMAN ORDER containing the rite observed in the year 1046 at the blessing of Clement II and the coronation of Henry II and Agnes.**

### XXIV

Here begins the Roman order for blessing the emperor when he receives the crown from the lord pope in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, at the altar of Saint Maurice the Martyr.

Early on Sunday morning, the elected emperor descends with his wife to Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, which is beside the Terebinth. There he is honorably received by the prefect of the city and the count of the Lateran palace; his wife is received by the *dativus* judge and the treasurer.

They are led through the portico, while all the city clergy, wearing copes, chasubles, dalmatics, and tunics and carrying censers, sing:

> Behold, I send my angel,

until they reach the platform of the upper court, which is at the head of the steps before the bronze doors of Saint Mary in the Tower.

There the lord pope sits in his seat, surrounded by bishops, cardinal deacons, and all the other orders of the Church. Then the elected emperor, with his wife and all his barons, clergy, and laymen, kisses the feet of the lord pope. When the queen has withdrawn to one side with the guides mentioned above, the elected emperor swears fidelity to the lord pope in this form:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, King N. of the Romans and future emperor of the Romans, promise, pledge, swear, and, by these Gospels, swear before God, blessed Peter the apostle, and the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, the lord Pope N., fidelity to you and to your successors canonically entering upon the office; and I promise that from now on I shall be the protector and defender of this holy Roman Church, of your person, and of your successors in all its interests, insofar as I shall be supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability, without fraud or evil intent. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.

### XXV

There the lord pope’s chamberlain takes the *palla* for his own possession. Then the lord pope asks him three times whether he wishes to have peace with the Church. When he has answered three times, “I do,” the lord pope says:

> And I give you peace, as Christ gave it to his disciples.

He kisses his forehead, chin—for he must be shaved—and both cheeks, and finally his mouth.

Then the lord pope rises and asks him three times whether he wishes to be a son of the Church. When he answers, “I do,” the lord pope says:

> And I receive you as a son of the Church.

He places him beneath his mantle, and the elected emperor kisses the lord pope’s breast. The pope takes him by the right hand, while his chancellor supports him with his left.

The elected emperor is led by the right hand by the lord pope’s archdeacon, and thus enters through the Bronze Gate, while the clergy of Saint Peter chant:

> Blessed is the Lord God of Israel,

until they reach the Silver Gate.

There the lord pope leaves him praying. The queen, with her guides, follows slowly until she reaches the aforementioned Silver Gate.

When the elected emperor has completed his prayer, he rises, and the bishop of Albano gives this first prayer over him:

> God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, incline the ears of your mercy to the prayers of our humility, and place the governance of your wisdom upon our prince, your servant N., so that, having drawn counsels from your fountain, he may please you and excel above all kingdoms. Through.

### XXVI

Afterward the lord pope enters the church of Saint Peter, while the clergy of that church sing the responsory:

> Peter, do you love me?

When it has been completed, the lord pope gives a blessing, then sits in the seat prepared for him on the right side of the same *rota*.

[**Note:** The arrangement of the seats is missing through the fault of the person who copied the manuscript. Both of Panvinius’s copies are defective. I would conjecture that the text should read: “of the *rota*, opposite the seat prepared for the elected [emperor] on the left side.”]

After the bishop of Albano has completed his prayer, the elected emperor enters and sits in the aforementioned seat. The cardinal archpriest and archdeacon lead him from either side and sit beside him, so that they may instruct him how he should answer the lord pope during the examination.

When the lord pope conducts the examination, the elected emperor answers in the following manner. Seven bishops sit to the pope’s right in their proper order; the German bishops sit to the right of the elected emperor; the cardinals and the other orders of the Church are seated.

The lord pope says:

> The ancient institution of the holy fathers teaches and commands that whoever is chosen to preside must first be examined with the greatest diligence and complete charity concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity, and questioned about the various matters and morals that suit and are necessary for this government, according to the apostle’s saying: “Lay hands hastily on no one.” He must also be instructed beforehand concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the Church of God once established in that office, so that those who lay hands upon him in ordination may be excusable.
>
> Therefore, by the same authority and command, we ask you, dearest son, with sincere charity: do you wish to devote all your wisdom, insofar as your nature is capable of it, to divine service?

He answers:

> With all my heart I wish to fulfill and consent to everything.

He asks:

> Do you wish to restrain your conduct from every evil and, insofar as you are able, with the Lord’s help, to change it toward every good?

**Answer:** I do.

**Question:** Do you wish to preserve sobriety with God’s help?

**Answer:** I do.

**Question:** Do you wish, insofar as human frailty permits you, to be devoted to divine affairs and free from shameful concerns?

**Answer:** I do.

**Question:** Do you wish to preserve humility and patience within yourself and incline others toward them?

**Answer:** I do.

**Question:** Do you wish, for the sake of the Lord’s name, to be approachable and merciful toward the poor, pilgrims, and all those in need?

**Answer:** I do.

Then the lord pope says:

> May the Lord grant you all these things and the other good things, preserve you, and strengthen you in every good work.

And all respond:

> Amen.

> Do you believe, according to your understanding, etc.

And it is said to him:

> May this faith be increased, etc.

[**Note:** This is to be sought from the *Pontifical*, *On the Consecration of an Elect as Bishop*. In Panvinius it is given in full. I willingly omit a matter that is by no means necessary.]

Then the lord pope goes to the sacristy and puts on the pontifical vestments as far as the dalmatic, wearing which he sits.

Meanwhile, the bishop of Porto, in the middle of the central *rota*, gives this prayer over the elected emperor:

> Ineffable God, as in the anointing of a king.

### XXVII

When the prayer has been completed, the elected emperor goes to Gregory’s choir with the aforementioned cardinal archpriest and archdeacon, whom he is to use as his instructors throughout the entire office of anointing. They clothe him in an amice, alb, and girdle, and thus lead him to the lord pope in the sacristy.

There he makes him a cleric and grants him a tunic, dalmatic, cope, miter, hose, and sandals, which he is to use at his coronation. Thus clothed, he stands before the lord pope.

When the examination has been completed, the bishop of Ostia goes out to the Silver Gate, where the queen awaits with the judges and her barons, and gives her this prayer:

> Almighty eternal God, etc.

[**Note:** Other manuscripts of the coronation of the queen read *sempiterne Deus*—“everlasting God”—instead. In Panvinius it is given in full. The same applies to the following four prayers.]

When the prayer has been completed, one of the cardinal priests, whom the prior has instructed, and likewise one of the deacons, whom the archdeacon has ordered, lead the queen to the altar of Saint Gregory. There she waits until the lord pope comes out with his procession.

When all the foregoing has been completed, the ministers clothe the lord pope in a chasuble and pallium. After the miter has been placed upon him, he proceeds, with the orders proceeding according to custom.

After this, the elected emperor goes with his aforementioned guides, followed by his wife, to the tomb of blessed Peter.

Then the *primicerius* chants the introit with the choir, followed by the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”), and becomes silent.

The lord pope ascends to the altar, gives the kiss of peace to the deacons after the confession, and incenses. After the incensation he ascends to his seat.

Meanwhile, the elected emperor and his wife prostrate themselves before the tomb of blessed Peter, and the archdeacon recites the litany. When it has been completed, the elected emperor removes only the cope, leaving on the mantle.

The bishop of Ostia anoints his right arm with exorcised oil and the space between his shoulders, and says:

> Almighty Lord God, etc., with the offering of justice, etc.

The following prayer is then said:

> God the Son of God, Jesus Christ, our Lord, etc.

After the anointing of the king, the blessing of the queen follows before the altar:

> God, who alone, etc.

The sacred anointing of oil upon the queen’s breast:

> May the grace of the Holy Spirit descend abundantly upon the breast of the queen through the ministry of our humility, etc.

### XXVIII

After this the lord pope descends from his seat and goes to the altar of Saint Maurice, followed by the elected emperor and the queen.

While the lord pope stands upon the threshold at the entrance to the altar, the elected emperor stands before him in the middle of the *rota*. The queen stands to his right. Six bishops of the Lateran palace stand around them in the *rotae* placed there; a seventh serves the lord pope in the office of the altar.

Then the first and second *oblationarii* take the crowns of the elected emperor and the queen from the altar of Saint Peter and place them upon the altar of Saint Maurice.

Then the lord pope gives a ring to the elected emperor and says:

> Receive the ring, the sign, that is, of holy faith, the firmness of the kingdom, and the increase of power. By it may you know how, with triumphal power, to drive away enemies, destroy heresies, unite subjects, and bind them to the perseverance of the catholic faith. Through.

**Prayer after the ring has been given:**

> God, to whom belongs all power and dignity, grant your servant the prosperous fulfillment of his dignity, in which, with you as his rewarder, he may remain, always possess it, and continually strive to please you. Through.

Here he girds him with the sword and says:

> Receive this sword, bestowed upon you with God’s blessing, by which, through the power of the Holy Spirit, you may be able to resist and drive out all your enemies and all the adversaries of the holy Church of God; and may you guard the kingdom entrusted to you and protect the camp of God through the help of the unconquered triumphant one, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

**Prayer after the sword:**

> God, who by your providence govern heavenly and earthly things together, be favorable to our most Christian king, so that all the strength of his enemies may be broken by the power of the spiritual sword and utterly crushed when he fights. Through.

Here he is crowned.

Then the archdeacon takes the crown from the altar of Saint Maurice and hands it to the lord pope. When the lord pope has placed it upon the head of the elected emperor, he says this prayer:

> Receive the sign of glory, etc.

[**Note:** In Panvinius it is given in full.]

**The placing of the crown upon the head of the queen:** When the lord pope places it upon her head, the seven bishops lay their hands upon her, while the lord pope says in a loud voice and the seven bishops remain silent:

> Receive the crown of royal excellence, so that, although from unworthy bishops, etc., you may deserve to enter. Who with God the Father …

Here the lord pope gives the scepter to the emperor and says:

> Receive the scepter, the insignia of royal power, namely the straight rod of the kingdom, the rod of virtue, by which you may govern yourself well, defend with royal virtue the holy Church and the Christian people entrusted to you by God from the wicked, correct the corrupt, reconcile the upright, and guide them by your assistance so that they may keep to the straight path; thus may you pass from the temporal kingdom to the eternal, with the help of him whose kingdom and empire remain without end forever and ever. Amen.

**Prayer after the scepter has been given:**

> Lord, source of all good things and God who establishes every advancement, we beseech you to grant your servant N. the ability to govern well the dignity he has acquired and to strengthen the honor bestowed upon him by you. Honor him above all the kings of the earth; enrich him with abundant blessing and establish him firmly and securely upon the throne of his kingdom. Visit him in his offspring; grant him length of life. In his days may justice always arise, so that with joy and eternal gladness he may glory in the kingdom. Through the Lord.

### XXIX

After this the lord pope returns with his ministers to the altar of blessed Peter.

Then the prefect of the city and the *primicerius* of the judges lead the emperor; the prefect of the naval district and the *secundicerius* of the judges lead the empress.

When they are standing in their appointed places, the lord pope begins:

> Glory to God in the highest.

The choir responds. Then he says this prayer:

> God of all kingdoms, etc.

When it has been completed, the archdeacon, together with the other prelates, deacons, the *primicerius*, and the subdeacons, begins these praises between the cross and the altar:

> Hear us, O Christ.

The choir with the notaries responds:

> Life to our lord C., appointed by God supreme pontiff and universal pope.

This is repeated three times.

Again the archdeacon and those standing with him say:

> Hear us, O Christ.

The choir with the notaries responds:

> Life and victory to our lord, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor.

Three times.

> Hear us, O Christ.

**Response of the choir with the notaries:**

> Life to our most excellent lady, his wife, the empress.

Three times.

Again:

> Hear us, O Christ.

**Response:**

> Life and victory to the Roman and German army.

Three times.

Again:

> Savior of the world.

**Response:**

> Help them.

> Holy Mary.

**Response:**

> You, help them.

> Saint Michael.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Gabriel.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Raphael.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Peter.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Paul.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint John.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Gregory.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Maurice.

**Response:**

> You.

> Saint Mercury.

**Response:**

> You, help them.

Three times.

> Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands.

The others respond likewise:

> Christ, etc.

> Our hope.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our victory.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our honor.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our glory.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our unconquerable wall.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our praise.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> Our triumphant one.

**Response:**

> Christ.

> To him be praise, honor, and dominion throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

### XXX

When this praise has been completed, the epistle is read, and the gradual and alleluia are sung. After these, the emperor and empress remove their crowns.

Then the Gospel is read. Afterward the emperor lays aside the sword and ascends to the lord pope’s seat, followed by the empress. He offers the lord pope bread, candles, and gold; separately, the emperor offers wine and the empress water, from which the sacrifice is to be made that day.

When these things have been completed, they return to their places.

When the preface begins, the emperor removes the cope and puts on his own mantle. When the words “The peace of the Lord” are said, he ascends to receive communion wearing his own mantle, and the empress goes with him. After receiving communion, they return to their places.

### XXXI

When the Mass has ended, the count palatine shall approach the emperor, remove his sandals and stockings, and put on him the imperial boots and the spurs of Saint Maurice. Having received their crowns, they shall follow the lord pope as he proceeds to mount his horse, being escorted as far as the horses by the guides mentioned above. When the lord pope comes to his horse, the emperor shall hold the stirrup, receive his crown, and join the procession. The empress, with her guides, shall follow the emperor; the other barons shall follow. All the clergy of the city shall perform the customary acclamations (laudes) in their respective places. The Jews likewise shall do so in their own place. Let the city be crowned; let all the bells be rung. The emperor’s chamberlains shall go ahead and follow, throwing coins so that the path of those riding may not be obstructed.

When they have reached the mounting-place, the prior of the cardinal-priests of Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls shall begin the customary acclamations (laudes), and the others shall respond. When these have ended, the emperor shall dismount and hold the stirrup for the lord pope as he dismounts, having first removed his crown. Then the lord pope shall be escorted by the emperor and the prefect of the city as far as the chamber of the greater palace, where they shall separate. The empress shall be escorted by the chief and second chief of the judges to the chamber of the empress Julia, in which she is to dine with the bishops and her other barons. The emperor’s chamberlains, together with the lord pope’s chamberlains, shall provide the presbyterial due (presbyterium) to all the orders of the sacred palace, while the pontiff and the emperor rest in the chamber.

### XXXII

This having been done, the emperor shall dine at the lord pope’s right hand, while the others sit in their appointed places. When the meal is finished, one of the deacons whom the archdeacon has instructed shall rise and read the lesson. When it has been read, the singers shall rise and sing what they customarily sing. When the singing has ended, everyone shall rise with the blessings. The lord pope shall return to his chamber; the emperor to the chamber of Julia.

The Elect, descending from Mons Gaudii and coming to the little bridge, shall swear this oath to the Romans:

> I, N., who am to become emperor, swear that I shall preserve the good customs of the Romans, and I confirm the charters of the third kind and the libelli, without fraud or malicious design.

He must swear likewise at the Colline Gate, and likewise on the steps of Saint Peter’s.

### XXXIII

I do not understand why Panvinio failed to recognize this monument of such antiquity and such reliability, which reveals its own character, nor why the editor Gatticus had no suspicion of it whatsoever. For in the entire succession of emperors you will find no three persons crowned on one and the same day—the pontiff C., the emperor, and the empress—apart from Clement II, Henry II, and Agnes.

It is enough for me to have exposed its date; I have no leisure to examine individually all the features of that venerable antiquity which I have judged should be placed before the eyes of scholars. I shall not, however, pass over those which bear most directly upon the matter.

First, the oath sworn to the Romans must necessarily be placed at the end, because when Henry came to Rome while the see was vacant, he neither swore at the little bridge nor was solemnly received, as his predecessors had been. But after the pontiff had been elected, and on the day of his blessing, which was joined with the solemnity of the coronation, Henry took at the Colline Gate—situated on the farther bank of the river near the fortress of Hadrian—the oath prescribed for the little bridge at the foot of Mons Marius. The other oath, which was to be sworn at the Gate of the Castle, he swore on the steps of Saint Peter’s.

The Orders of later times wrongly place at the end what necessarily belonged here, and take the Gate of the Castle for the Colline Gate. Canon Benedictus gives its certain location (Mus. Ital., vol. II, p. 143), describing how on Easter Monday he escorted the pontiff from the Lateran:

> “Passing,” he says, “before Saint Tryphon, beside the posterns, as far as the bridge of Hadrian, he enters by the bridge and exits through the Colline Gate before the church and castle of Hadrian; proceeding before Nero’s obelisk, he enters through the portico beside the tomb of Romulus and ascends to the Vatican.”

Benedictus is supported by the Chronicle of Fossanova and by the chronicle of Romuald (Vat. Cod. 3973), in which, after the gates of the City have been listed, the highest place is given to “the Colline Gate at the castle of Hadrian.”

But since in the Life of Leo IV, in Anastasius (section 537), the same pontiff is said to have opened a postern “where, in a marvelous manner, the castle rises above it, which is called Saint Angelo,” this is why in later Orders that postern of the Leonine City was rather ineptly taken for the City Gate called the Colline Gate throughout the eleventh and the following century.

Patritius rightly censures those writers, although he too was deceived and thought only that the name was false, paying no attention to the location. By rejecting the name Colline as belonging to the ancient city, he thus unwisely contradicts the sure documents of the Middle Ages.

Nevertheless, he correctly places the customary double oath to the Romans before the entrance of the king of the Romans into the Leonine City. Thus the account of the coronation of Henry V in Baronius (1111, no. 5), which was the first to follow the coronation of Henry III, also called Henry II as emperor—for Henry IV was not crowned by the Roman pontiff—states:

> “He took two oaths according to custom: one beside the little bridge, and the other before the gate of the Portico—which was the name then given to the Leonine City—he made before the people. Before the gate he was received by the Jews; at the gate, by Greeks singing. All the clergy of the Roman City had gathered there at the pontiff’s command.”

### XXXIV

These last details shed considerable light upon the ancient Order which we have presented. Henry and Agnes, who were staying in the Lateran palace of the pontiff, came through the Colline Gate to the church of Saint Mary in Transpadina, which at that time stood near the castle of Hadrian, not far from the postern of Leo IV, or the Gate of the Castle. There were also, at a short distance, Nero’s terebinth, the tomb of Romulus or the goal, and the other places mentioned in the Orders. That the space in their midst was an area with a basin (concha) is attested by the master of ceremonies at the coronation of Sigismund, in Raynaldus (1433, no. 14):

> “When they had reached the basin of the area of the castle of Saint Angelo, they said farewell to one another; and the pontiff withdrew to the Vatican palace, etc.”

For that area had been designated as the place for receiving the future emperor and escorting him to the basilica; in the same way, after the coronation, he rode back with the pontiff, crowned with the diadem.

Moreover, when Henry V took the customary oath, he implied that such an oath had been sworn to the Romans before Henry III, king of Germany. The coronation immediately preceding that of Henry V does not seem sufficient by itself to establish the custom. It is therefore credible that his predecessors, together with the oath of fidelity to the pontiff, also swore another oath to the Romans.

What is new here is that Henry confirms the charters of the third kind and the libelli. A charter of the third kind was a written instrument of cession of a castle or place. Mabillon gives an example (Ann. B., book LIII, no. 17, p. 114) concerning the castle of Tribucco, between the abbot of Farfa and Crescentius; Henry I ordered that charter to be annulled.

Ducange interprets the charters called libelli as precariae and prestariae, two matters whose preservation was of the greatest concern to the Romans of that time. Castles and estates received from churches by emphyteusis could easily be claimed back by those same churches through an imperial diploma. We have seen several such grants made by Otto III after he had assumed the imperial diadem. The pontiffs wisely wished that authority to be attached to the crown, for the common good of the churches, so that they might turn away the anger of the powerful and secure for the churches a firmer protection.

I should also like it to be observed that neither the prefecture of the city—except perhaps at some time through an invasion—nor any palatine offices, nor any other rights of the supreme prince came to the emperor through the imperial diadem; they remained inviolate with the pontiff.

### XXXV

This explains why the oath of fidelity customarily sworn by the king of the Romans before he was led through the bronze gate of Saint Mary in the Tower to the silver gate is expressed in this Order in the clearest terms. Thirty-three years earlier it had been presented to Benedict VIII by Saint Henry I, as Ditmarus testifies in Baronius (1014, no. 1) and in Leibniz (Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium, vol. I, p. 400):

> “Thirteen years having elapsed from the Lord’s Incarnation after the fullness of the thousand-year number, and in the second month and third week of the following year, and in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the Lord’s day and the sixth day before the Kalends of March, Henry, the illustrious king by the grace of God, surrounded by twelve senators—six shaven in the beard and the others bearded at length, proceeding mystically with staffs—came with his beloved wife Cunegunda to the church of Saint Peter, while the pope awaited him. Before he was admitted, the same pope asked him whether he wished to be a faithful patron of the Roman Church and defender of the Church, and faithful in all things to him and to his successors. He answered with a devout profession.”

If anyone dislikes the name “oath of fidelity” and prefers the more recent term “promise” or “profession,” I have no objection, provided that he holds firmly and certainly that beneath the difference of name the substance is the same.

This profession, having been entered into the ceremonial book, was presented at the silver gate to Henry V, who was the first after Henry II to receive the diadem, as the account in Baronius (1111, no. 5) testifies:

> “There, making the imperial profession from the book, he was designated emperor by the pontiff.”

Likewise, in 1155, Frederick I Barbarossa, as the records also testify,

> “proceeded to the church of Blessed Mary in the Tower, in which the pontiff was awaiting him before the altar; and, laying on hands, he publicly presented the customary profession and full security, according to what is contained in the Order.”

It ran as follows:

> “I, N., king of the Romans, by the Lord’s assent to become emperor, promise, undertake, pledge, and swear to God and blessed Peter that henceforth I shall be the protector and defender of the supreme pontiff and of the Holy Roman Church in all their necessities and interests, preserving and safeguarding its possessions, honors, and rights, insofar as I shall be supported by divine assistance, according to my knowledge and ability, in upright and pure faith. So help me God, etc.”

(Mus. It., vol. II, p. 398.)

### XXXVI

You have heard that Henry V made his profession not in the area on the steps before the bronze gate of Saint Mary in the Tower, but at the silver gate, contrary to the custom of his ancestors; and that Frederick Barbarossa made his in the church of Saint Mary in the Tower. I willingly pass over Henry’s tragic coronation.

With regard to Frederick’s profession, which he was the first of all to present in the aforesaid church, it should be observed that Durandus, who flourished under Pope Nicholas III and therefore preserves the tradition of the ancient Order—for no coronation had taken place since the beginning of the thirteenth century—speaks of the emperor as follows (Rational., book II, chapter 8, no. 6):

> “Since on the day of his ordination he is first received as a canon by the canons of Saint Peter, he serves the lord pope at Mass in the office of subdeacon, preparing the chalice and performing similar duties.”

Clement V gives the legates the same instruction at the beginning of the fourteenth century concerning the proper coronation of Henry VII:

> “When the pontiff descends to the altar to complete the mysteries of the Mass, the emperor, in the manner of a subdeacon, shall offer the chalice and the cruet.”

But since Henry II did nothing of this kind in 1046, and his successor, Henry IV, did not obtain the crown, while Henry V’s unusual coronation rejected the entire rite, and finally Lothair II, driven by necessity, hastily received the crown from Innocent II in the Lateran basilica, it follows that we must descend to Frederick Barbarossa, crowned by Adrian IV in 1155.

There is no certain reason why we should count this man as the first among the canons, except for the rite prescribed in the ancient Order in the church of Saint Mary in the Tower, which agrees almost word for word with the acts of Adrian IV:

> “Having left the king there,” say the acts, “the pontiff ascended to the altar of blessed Peter.”

But the ancient Order says:

> “Then the supreme pontiff proceeds with all his orders to the altar, and, having prayed there, ascends to the seat, while the king with his attendants and the three bishops—namely, those of Ostia, Porto, and Albano—remain in the church of Saint Mary in the Towers. There, having been received as a brother by the canons of Saint Peter, he is clothed in the imperial insignia, his pallium having been given to the lord pope’s chamberlain.”

### XXXVII

But what of this? Peter Mallius, who flourished under that same Barbarossa and belonged to the college of the canons of Saint Peter, is completely silent about a matter of no small honor, although, when speaking of the customs of the basilica, he commends to posterity the following account of the rite of anointing and the delivery of the imperial insignia (Bollandus, vol. VI, June, part II, p. 39):

> “Beside this altar”—the altar of Saint Sylvester—“directly opposite is the altar of Saint Maurice, at which altar, according to the ancient custom of the Romans, the Roman emperor is blessed and anointed by the lord cardinal bishops. At the greater altar of Saint Peter he is blessed and crowned by the lord pope, and from his most sacred altar he receives the sword through the hands of the Roman pontiff for the defense of the Church.”

Whether this custom of anointing should be traced to the coronation of Henry V, amid the great upheaval of affairs in 1111, or rather to the somewhat more favorable time of Frederick I, around whose twentieth year Mallius was writing about it, I do not know.

Certainly, in the span of one hundred and ten years between Henry II and Frederick I, only Henry V was anointed in the Vatican basilica by the bishop of Ostia. It is more probable that the rite began to be employed in 1111 and was called an ancient custom by Frederick’s contemporary writer than that it began at Frederick’s own coronation.

Nevertheless, I prefer to leave the antiquity of the rite uncertain rather than to establish it by conjecture as more than fifty years older than it really was.

The same applies to the reception of the king of the Romans among the canons. It is preferable to postpone this ceremony to the beginning of the thirteenth century, when Innocent III crowned Otto IV with the imperial diadem in 1209, rather than to attribute to Frederick I or his successor Henry VI a practice for which no ancient document provides support.

The testimonies cited above from the ancient Order praised by Clement V and from Durandus lose nothing by this postponement. It is also more reasonable to attribute this new institution to Innocent III than to Adrian IV, who crowned Frederick against the wishes of the Romans and amid warfare, or to Celestine III, who, as is reported, almost under compulsion and by an exceptional procedure raised Henry VI and his wife to the imperial dignity.

Innocent himself testifies that he added something to the ancient rite. Unless he had added the canonicate, I do not see what new element could be credited to him.

The imperial insignia—crown, sword, scepter, and orb—had already customarily been delivered at the greater altar during the solemnities of Mass, after the Epistle. Frederick I had begun to make his profession in the church of Saint Mary in the Tower. In the age of that same Frederick, Mallius, a contemporary writer, called the anointing at the altar of Saint Maurice an ancient custom. Finally, the ride of the pontiff with the crowned emperor as far as the area of the Mole of Hadrian, where the one to be crowned had been received, was older than the other rites as well.

The canonicate therefore rightly belongs to Innocent III, and with it the office of subdeacon at Mass.

### XXXVIII

Indeed, the pontiff himself took such pride in having been a canon of that basilica that, once raised to the See of Peter, he derived from that fact a special reason for serving it (Vatican Bullary, vol. I, p. 77). Thus he addressed the canons:

> “Considering that among all the churches spread throughout the world we are bound to love and honor more especially the basilica of the prince of the apostles, as being our see, just as we who once obtained with you in that very church the benefit of the canonicate have now, by divine mercy, been advanced from the position of son to that of father.”

And in his letter to the king of the Romans, preserved by Baluzius (vol. I, p. 702), in which he confirms his election:

> “Desiring to awaken more fully in you the devotion of your ancestors and to reward it more abundantly, [lacuna] you will surpass them in this respect all the more, the more you understand yourself to have been honored by us. [lacuna] Desiring, with the counsel of our brothers, to honor Your Serenity in this matter beyond what a secular prince in the world can be honored.”

These are very clear indications of the Order enlarged by Innocent III and completed in every respect. Clement V calls it the pontifical ordinary. The additions later made by the masters of ceremonies—of whom the last was Patritius Pientinus, bishop—must be said to have brought it obscurity rather than splendor.

### XXXIX

If these things are true, all the ancient manuscripts of the Roman Orders, except the one which I said above had been preserved from the time of the Carolingians and of several German predecessors of Henry II, indicate only the prayers, down to the year 1046, when the coronation first began to take place amid the solemnities of Mass.

Some of them had to be altered: for example, the prayer which the bishop of Albano recited at the Silver Gate, and the one which the pontiff chanted before the Epistle. Before receiving the diadem, the elected emperor had to be called prince, as in the manuscript which we edited above, or king, not emperor.

This is confirmed by all the diplomas and documents carefully examined by Godefridus, abbot of Godwic, Ludovico Muratori, and those other learned scholars.

From a single Vatican manuscript, no. 4737, written at the beginning of the fifteenth century, the error spread into more recent Orders. The same error was even introduced into the ancient Orders by insufficiently cautious writers.

Thus Raynaldus (1355, no. 8), writing concerning the letters of Innocent VI in which the ancient Order reviewed by Innocent III is inserted, says:

> “The formulas of these prayers are extant in an ancient pontifical Ceremonial—Vatican MS 4737, p. 90—from which it seemed appropriate to copy them.”

The editor of the Vatican Bullary follows Raynaldus in those same letters of Innocent VI; so does the compiler of the Order attributed to Jacopo Gaetano; and so do the other Orders printed by Gatticus, who published the Vatican manuscript used by Raynaldus, thereby spreading this error for the benefit, as he thought, of the reader.

If they had stopped there, the matter could have been endured. But the writer of the aforesaid manuscript did not hesitate to corrupt the formulas used by the pontiff when delivering the imperial insignia, despite the protest of history; Raynaldus and the others then introduced them into the ritual books.

In the ancient Orders, down to Innocent VI, the formula for delivering the sword is given in this form:

> “Receive the sword for the vengeance of evildoers, etc.”

But in the manuscript just mentioned the following words are inserted, which I shall enclose in parentheses:

> “Receive the sword (taken from above the body of blessed Peter the apostle by our hands, unworthy though they are, yet consecrated in the place and authority of the blessed apostles; granted to you in imperial fashion and divinely ordained by the office of our blessing for the defense of holy Mother Church) for vengeance, etc.”

### XL

I leave the interpretation of this addition in full to the learned reader, who shortly before, in section 37, was taught by Mallius the canon that the sword taken from the most sacred altar of Peter was customarily delivered by the pontiff after the imperial diadem had been received. He also knows from the most ancient Order in Mabillon (Order IX, no. 2) that it was once customary for “the archdeacon to remove the oraria from the confessio, where they had been put away the previous day.” In our own age, too, the archiepiscopal pallia are taken from that same place, because the matter concerns spiritual power.

In the same way, I leave intact that inversion of the imperial office at Mass which is supported by certain and very clear documents. The more recent Orders make the emperor not a subdeacon but a deacon. Only Charles V performed this function, at Bologna, with Blasius de Martinellis directing the ceremonies (Raynaldus, 1530, no. 31; Gatticus, vol. II, unpublished, p. 149), as is clear from the acts:

> “After the cardinal had withdrawn a little from the place of the Gospel, Caesar entered in his place at the altar, serving the pope by handing him the paten with the host, and then presenting the chalice with wine and water to the pontiff; offering and serving at the same time, he performed the office of deacon most beautifully and excellently.”

I leave these corruptions of the ancient Orders intact. But I cannot pass over the matter of the pontiff’s ride with the emperor, since it is easily the chief of all the others.

From what has been said it is clear that its terminus was always the area of the castle of Saint Angelo. The final two rides—that of Eugene IV with Sigismund in 1433 and that of Nicholas V with Frederick III in 1452—place the matter beyond all doubt.

Contemporary authors in Raynaldus (1433, no. 14), speaking of Eugene and Sigismund, say:

> “When they reached the basin of the area of the castle of Saint Angelo, they said farewell to one another, and the pontiff withdrew to the Vatican palace; the emperor proceeded to the Aelian Bridge, etc.”

Likewise, concerning Nicholas V and Frederick III, Nauclerus says in the same annalist (1452, no. 2):

> “Having mounted their horses, they proceeded together as far as the church of Saint Mary. Then the pope returned to the palace, while Caesar proceeded to the bridge of Hadrian.”

### XLI

Since these things are so, we cannot even conceive why Bishop Pientinus should have thought of transforming a rite confirmed by every Roman Order, by contemporary authors, and by the examples of twenty-seven emperors. Nevertheless, in section 5, chapter 4, commenting on the rubric “Concerning the procession of the pontiff and Caesar through the City,” he writes:

> “They will proceed directly through the Field of Flora and the Jews’ quarter to the church of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. There the pontiff, if he has a rose, gives it on horseback as a gift to the mounted emperor. Turning to the right, he returns with all his attendants through Trastevere to the palace. Caesar, however, by whatever route he prefers, carrying the rose in his hand, returns to the bridge of Hadrian.”

Fortunately, no further coronation took place at Rome after Frederick III. But the image of Rome thus transformed, displayed at Bologna—even though the roads and rites had been greatly abridged—represented the ceremony to the master of ceremonies himself as so inconvenient that he admitted it had to be interrupted for food and drink lest he lack the strength to complete it:

> “I complained to the pope that we Italians had not been as provident as the Spaniards for their prince, for whom they had arranged a refreshment; whereas we had thought of nothing for our pontiff, who had remained greatly exhausted. It was already late, nearly the twenty-first hour, and he still had to ride ceremonially with Caesar through the city for another two hours.”

Thus Blasius de Martinellis in Raynaldus (1530, no. 35).

If, after two hours of riding with Caesar, the latter had to return to the bridge of Hadrian, where he was to designate them by striking each of approximately three hundred knights three times with a naked sword; and from there proceed to the Lateran basilica to obtain that canonicate, for what purpose I do not know; while the pontiff returned through Trastevere to the palace, both with ceremonial display—let the reader judge at what hour the emperor would have rested after so many and such varied labors.

To me, this exceedingly long rite should be restored to the ancient custom, for the document itself betrays that it was written after the Roman coronation had fallen into disuse.

## § VI.—On the Three Books of Rudolf’s Letters

### XLII

I now come to Rudolf’s letters. Before them it was necessary to set down everything that has been said concerning the election of the king of the Romans and concerning his Roman coronation at the hands of the pontiff. Since Rudolf repeatedly and earnestly sought that coronation but never obtained it, he did not acquire the title of emperor.

Nauclerus (Generation 43) relates how Gregory X, after the death of Richard, to whom the Holy See had adhered, while Alfonso the Wise was still alive and desiring the crown more vehemently than before, announced to the electors that, unless they elected a king of the Romans as quickly as possible, he would proclaim him [Alfonso] by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, on 4 October 1273, Rudolf was elected with the agreement of the seven electors.

Meanwhile, in that same year Gregory had moved from Orvieto to Florence in the middle of June, then proceeded to Piacenza, his native city, and from there to Milan; around 12 October he departed for Lyons, where a council was to be held the following year. Raynaldus demonstrates from the Vatican registers that he remained in that city until 1275, on the day before the Ides of May (that year, no. 1).

He then went to Bellegarde to confer with the king of Castile, whom many were following against Rudolf. From there, in September, he proceeded to Vienna and afterward to Lausanne, where he met with Rudolf in October.

On 18 November, on the feast of the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter, he promulgated at Milan, in the basilica of Saint Ambrose, proceedings against the invaders of the Church’s possessions. He later went again to Piacenza, and on 18 December to Florence. Finally he went to Arezzo, where, at the beginning of the following year, 1276, he died on 10 January.

The first book of the letters belongs approximately to this period. The final letter of the second book bears the very clear date of 26 August 1278, on the day after Saint Bartholomew’s day, “in the morning, on the sixth day of the week.”

The third book seems to extend into the time of Martin IV, for it ends with a diploma of Rudolf, king ever Augustus, dated at Haguenau on 2 December 1283, in the second indiction and the tenth year of our reign. Since this diploma is preceded by another diploma of the princes of the empire from the year 1279, and some of the letters seem to belong to earlier years, it is impossible to define the exact period.

So much for the chronology.

### XLIII

Why these letters did not see the light before the present day—apart from some published by the author of *Austrian Piety* and several others concerning the archbishop of Salzburg, which Father Hansiz brought to light—is readily understood from their content concerning the boundaries of the empire, the Roman coronation, the first prayers, and other subjects which clearly show that the German writers had wandered far from the truth.

First, the cities of Germany, rejoicing in the election of Rudolf, king of the Romans, testify that Germany was the seat of the king of the Romans (book I, letter 6):

> “Let invincible Germany rejoice and give thanks with all her heart, rejoicing and praising,”

as one of the cities writes while promising obedience to its king.

Rudolf himself informs Gregory X (ibid., letter 12) that:

> “The princes, barons, cities, castles, and other possessions of the sacred empire throughout Alemannia unanimously obey our authority.”

That the kingdom of Italy and Tuscany—which was formerly called a kingdom and is now the grand duchy of Etruria—were included within the boundaries of the empire is clear from these letters.
