More noteworthy than the others is the letter which the Ghibelline Pisans sent to Rudolf, imploring his aid against the Guelphs (ibid., letter 20). The citizens speak as follows:

> “The laws assert, custom approves, antiquity bears witness that the region of the Tuscans serves the Roman prince under tribute, to say nothing of the rest.… Behold the province of Tuscany, which by its proximity to the pious seat of the Roman Empire, as a principal member, ought to respond more familiarly to its head.… The city of Pisa mourns, wounded by the hostile sword of its enemies and by that of the supreme pontiff and the royal majesty.”

To this Rudolf replies (ibid., letter 21) that he had sent envoys to Lyons to the pontiff, so that, with his good pleasure and consent, their final wishes might be fully satisfied concerning the matters contained in their petition.

The causes of the dispute between the pontiff and the Pisans may be found in Raynaldus (1273, no. 32 and following).

### XLIV

The damage inflicted upon the Church’s territories by the continuous invasions of the German emperors—especially those of the Swabian dynasty—is also evident from Rudolf’s letters.

It is entirely unknown to no one that the two provinces, the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, rested upon the donations of the Frankish kings Pippin and Charlemagne and were earlier than any other donations. Likewise, everyone knows that Innocent III, after recovering the other territories, “sent messengers and legates to recover the Exarchate of Ravenna, Brictonorium, and the land of Cavalcacomite,” as recorded in his *Deeds* (no. 12).

On that occasion,

> “the archbishop of Ravenna asserted that the Exarchate had anciently been granted by the Roman pontiffs to the church of Ravenna, and he produced the privileges. Brictonorium too had been newly granted by Pope Alexander while he was staying at Venice. Therefore Lord Innocent prudently refrained for the time being from attempting anything further in the matter.”

But it is clear that afterward Otto IV and Frederick II, easily the foremost invaders among all their predecessors, nearly obliterated such ancient and certain rights.

Rudolf, therefore, misled especially by the variety of names, was so firmly persuaded that both provinces—called Romandiola and the Maritime Province—were included within the boundaries of the empire that he does not hesitate to call them the glorious boundary of the empire (book I, letters 24 and following). He also entrusted their administration to Count Fürstenberg and wrote several letters on the matter. The first of these bears the following heading:

> “To the excellent and prudent men, marquises, counts, nobles, captains, magistrates of cities, elders, and all the peoples established throughout Romandiola and the Maritime Province.”

We understand that this was contrary to equity and justice. Nevertheless, even after learning the truth of the matter and after Rudolf had promised by oath that he would vindicate all the rights of the Holy See, he did not withdraw from this unjust possession until two years later.

### XLV

In 1274, during the third session of the Council of Lyons, Otto, provost of Saint Wido of Speyer and chancellor, together with Rudolf’s other ambassadors, were admitted to the consistory. After producing the mandate by which the king of the Romans granted them full power to act in the king’s name, they confirmed on 6 June all the diplomas of Louis, Otto, Henry, and all Rudolf’s predecessors, as well as the diploma of Frederick II declaring that the kingdom of Sicily was in no way subject to the empire. This is clear from the records in Raynaldus (1274, no. 5 and following).

Moreover, Rudolf himself, in his conference with the pontiff at Lausanne on 20 October of the following year—a meeting of which he boasts so greatly (book I, letter 34)—not only confirmed and ratified everything which the chancellor and the other ambassadors had done at Lyons; he also expressly named the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, which they had not done, adding:

> “I shall restore all these, to the best of my ability, and leave them in peace with all their jurisdiction, territorial authority, and honor.”

(Raynaldus, 1275, no. 37.)

Nevertheless, it is known that he did not relinquish those two provinces until two years later.

Shortly afterward Rudolf’s chancellor, also named Rudolf, without a royal mandate and even without Rudolf’s knowledge, had received an oath of fidelity from many cities of the Exarchate in the king’s name. Rudolf therefore, by letters issued to Nicholas III on 29 May 1278, declared everything done by the chancellor invalid and once again vindicated the whole Exarchate for the Holy See (Raynaldus, 1278, no. 51 and following).

Certain documents concerning the matter are preserved in the archive of the Mole of Hadrian.

You may perhaps wonder that so certain a matter was prolonged for so long. But you must recall over how many years, even in our own times, the manifest invasion of Comacchio in that same Exarchate was treated in writings filling so many volumes as a just possession.

That the same judgment ought to be made concerning Rudolf’s excessive delay in relinquishing the Exarchate is amply demonstrated by the recently cited action of the chancellor.

I shall discuss all these matters at the appropriate time in the notes to the letters—book II, letters 33 and 37—and especially in Dissertation 7, concerning Rudolf’s diplomas confirmed by the electors of the sacred Roman Empire.

### XLVI

From these facts it is clear how greatly Conring, the enlarger of the boundaries of the empire, went astray (vol. I, *On the Boundaries of the Empire*), and how imprudently Goebelius, in his very extensive notes to him, dared—against the evidence of the monuments—to extend the boundaries of the Roman Empire beyond the limit prescribed by the very Augusti who invaded those territories. Rudolph, king of the Romans, bears witness to this: having thoroughly grasped the matter, he explained with complete clarity in his letters both the invasions of his predecessors and his own deception.

Yet still greater is the audacity of those who deny that, throughout his life, Rudolph very earnestly desired to become emperor by receiving the imperial diadem from the hands of the Roman pontiff. By accepting the fable which Trithemius (*Chronicle of Hirschau*) and Godefridus Hectius (*Germania Sacra*, part II, book 11, *On the State of Religion*) report him as having used, they do not hesitate to oppose the truth. If I am not mistaken, those authors expressed the sense of the fable in their own manner, for they placed these words in Rudolph’s mouth:

> “Italy has consumed many kings of the Alemanni. I shall not go to Rome. I am a king, and I trust that I shall do no less for the welfare of the commonwealth than if I had been crowned at Rome.”

The same story is reported from Nieremberg by the author of *Austrian Piety* (book I, chapter 128) in the following form:

> “When they advised him to undertake the journey, he replied with an Aesopian fable. The lion, king of the beasts, had wished and obtained that the lesser animals should visit him while he was ill. The fox came last; but, after being warned, he refrained from entering, because he had observed many footprints of those going in and none of those returning. The former, naturally, had served as food for the sick animal; and, unless he wished to perish foolishly, the danger did not appeal to him. Rudolph said that it had happened to several emperors either that they perished on this journey or that they returned without glory. He would not, he declared, squander his majesty by following the example of either group.”

The substance is the same in both accounts, but the latter seems closer to the truth than that brief, weighty, and unfamiliar saying attributed to Rudolph—a saying contemptuous of imperial majesty, although he could not have been unaware that it could be acquired only by a Roman coronation. For he never ceased, even to the final years of his life, to commend this matter as the empire’s principal concern, both in letters and through envoys and his own ambassadors at the Holy See. He died in 1291, more than seventy years old.

I freely admit that I do not find it incredible that the great prince, who by his nature sometimes indulged in wit and playful speech, may have entertained his intimates with that fable. But I confidently deny that he ever did so seriously. Far be it from me lightly to accuse so great a king of falsehood, or to place greater trust in any writer, however distinguished, who makes an assertion about Rudolph than in Rudolph himself, who denied it by both words and deeds. It is vain, however, to establish by reasoning a matter which the chronology of Rudolph’s letters places beyond all doubt.

### XLVII

Indeed, immediately after he had been elected king of the Romans, he wrote the following letter to Gregory X. I do not know why the author of *Austrian Piety* omitted it from that manuscript; he presents it to us from the Imperial Manuscript (book I, chapter 4, p. 32):

> “Since the Roman Empire had long been vacant, the electoral princes, to whom the right of electing the king of the Romans has belonged from ancient times, having fixed the day and place and having accordingly assembled from every side, after many and varied deliberations concerning the future king, at last, following the lengthy consideration which the nature of the matter required—although they could have agreed upon several others, men marked by far more illustrious titles of virtue and distinguished by the brilliance of far greater merit—nevertheless raised us to the summit of so honorable a burden and burdensome an honor. We had sought no such elevation whatsoever, as our conscience bears witness; indeed, their demand was pressed upon us with unwelcome insistence.

> “We therefore, although with anxious spirit reflecting upon what and of what kind was the calling of this divine disposition, and although not unaware of our manifold insufficiency, feared to ascend the watchtower of so great a dignity, struck as it were by astonished trembling and amazement. Yet, trusting in him who by the lofty and ineffable counsel of his divinity disposes, varies, and alternates the conditions and state of earthly things as he wills; who multiplies strength and grants eloquence to those who stammer; and assuming the spirit of fortitude, for the praise and glory of the King of kings, out of reverence for Holy Mother Church and for the support of the Catholic faith, we submit our weak shoulders to the exercise of so arduous a solicitude and the administration of so burdensome a charge. We hope that neither the fullness of God’s favor nor that of Holy Mother Church, nor the abundance of apostolic grace, nor the clemency of your paternal favor, will be lacking to us, lest what the height of heavenly counsel had decreed should be weakened through division or rupture.

> “Having therefore cast our thoughts upon him by whose command we live, and having placed the whole anchor of our hope in you, we prostrate ourselves at the feet of Your Holiness, humbly begging and entreating you kindly to assist us in the undertaking we have assumed, by your customary benevolence and by sacrificial offerings that may aid us before the Most High. May he graciously direct our cause—or rather, the special cause of the whole commonwealth—and lead our steps in the path of his commandments.

> “Therefore, so that we may be able to pursue continually, with greater health and success, those things which are pleasing to him and agreeable to his holy Church, may it please Your Holiness, we beg, to distinguish us graciously with the diadem of imperial dignity. For we are girded with the armor of a powerful and willing spirit, ready for whatever you and our nurturing Mother Church may judge ought to be imposed upon us.”

### XLVIII

The annals teach that Rudolph’s election was not confirmed by the Roman pontiff until the following year, at the consistory of Lyon. Gregory then wrote to the elected king of the Romans in these terms (Raynaldus, from the *Register*, 1274, no. 55ff.):

> “Since manifest utility advises that the auspicious beginning of your advancement toward the summit of the same empire, already happily commenced, should not be delayed through procrastination in its prosecution but should thereafter be completed by a swift consummation, we exhort Your Serenity, and with sincere affection and counsel we advise you, to prepare and arrange yourself in such a way that, when we summon you to receive from our hands unction, consecration, and the coronation of the imperial diadem—and we intend shortly to designate a date for this, insofar as the circumstances to be considered permit—you may appear not unprepared but ready, as the solemnities of so great a matter require, and may come to the aforesaid undertakings not slowly but promptly and speedily.

> “It is expedient that you quickly send to our presence certain persons who can fully communicate to us both the designation of a date suited to your convenience and your wishes in every other respect concerning this matter.”

> “Given at Lyon, 26 September, in the third year.”

As I indicated above, the principal reason for the pontifical concern was the obstinacy of Alfonso, king of Castile. Omitting this and other causes, since they are not necessary here, I shall continue my account of the matter under discussion.

The undertaking appears to have been delayed for no great length of time, although the king of the Romans desired this one thing with the utmost intensity. For, toward the end of the year, when the pontiff was explaining the entire matter to the archbishop of Salzburg, he said:

> “Recently, therefore, when the envoys of the king of the Romans, sent for this purpose by His Magnificence, publicly and solemnly requested in his name, in the presence of ourselves and our brothers, that a date be assigned to him for the aforesaid matters, we conferred with those same brothers. After considering and discussing through deliberation those things which we thought ought to be attended to in this matter, we judged, with the counsel of our brothers, that the coming feast of All Saints should be assigned to the king of the Romans as the date on which, with the Lord’s favor, he might receive from our hands in the basilica of the prince of the apostles in the City the unction, consecration, and coronation of the imperial diadem which he had requested.”

Yet the burdens of affairs delayed the pontiff’s concern and the king’s eagerness far too greatly. Thus, when the king and the pontiff conferred at Lausanne in Switzerland on 20 October 1275, they extended the date fixed for the coronation, since it was approaching, to the feast of Pentecost, which in 1276 fell on 24 May.

### XLIX

While everything was being prepared for so great a solemnity, and the princes and cities, having received from the king of the Romans notices that they should undertake the journey, were making themselves ready to attend him with as splendid a service as possible (book I, letters 34, 35, 36, and 38), Gregory died a holy death at Arezzo.

Rudolph nevertheless did not abandon his purpose, as he himself admits in his letter to the cardinals during the vacancy of the See (ibid., letter 42):

> “We had girded ourselves and our people for the journey, so that, according to what had been arranged through your counsel, if fate had favored us, we might receive from his sacred hands the holy diadem of the empire . . . Yet, still prepared and girded for the very purpose of proceeding, we remain steadfast and immovable, hoping in the unchangeableness of Mother Church. We have merely suspended and deferred the journey for a time, until through you or the future supreme pontiff—whose good pleasure we are always prepared to obey in all things with readiness of spirit—we may be more fully informed what ought now further to be done by a devoted son of the Church.”

The cardinals received the royal letters after the pontiff had already been elected, but their reply does not survive in their manuscript. Rudolph’s congratulatory letter, however (book II, letter 1), demonstrates the continuation of his purpose. He addresses Innocent V as follows:

> “We beg you to embrace a singular son who will always obey the good pleasure of yourself and Mother Church with complete readiness of spirit, and graciously complete in us the work of God through the authority entrusted to you from above.”

This letter was written at the beginning of February. Moreover, from our manuscript there is another letter of the same king of the Romans to the same pontiff (book I, letter 28), in which he promises that, in accordance with the date established at Lausanne, he will be present at Rome on Pentecost:

> “At the next approaching feast of the Lord’s Resurrection we shall be present at Milan; from there, in accordance with the good pleasure of Your Beatitude, we shall immediately proceed to the imperial coronation.”

It follows that the letter was dated in March, since Easter in 1276 fell on 5 April. Accordingly, from the time of his election until the month just mentioned—nearly two years and six months—Rudolph had nothing more important than the Roman coronation.

Why he remained silent about undertaking the Italian journey until the final year of Nicholas III, that is, until 1280, must be sought in the action of the Apostolic See.

### L

Raynaldus learned from a manuscript of the Vallicellian Library that Rudolph had been forbidden by Innocent himself to enter Italy before the disputes with Charles, king of Sicily, had been settled. But the cardinals’ letter to Rudolph during the vacancy of the See in 1277 will explain the matter more seriously and clearly (Raynaldus, 1277, no. 48). Concerning Innocent they report:

> “Since it was altogether expedient, and since it was consequently his will, that you should not undertake the journey to come into Italy, and, if you had undertaken it, that you should by no means continue the journey before the matters mentioned above had been strengthened with suitable solidity, the venerable brother Bernard, then-elect bishop of Albi, was sent to your presence for this purpose. He was to disclose more clearly the useful and necessary reasons which not unjustly moved Innocent himself to these measures, and his will concerning them, although plainly expressed in the aforesaid letters; he was also to explain how he sincerely advised that these things should be fulfilled and how, after deliberation and consultation with his brothers, he wished them to be carried out.”

The same cardinals testify that Adrian V and John XXI followed Innocent’s example. It will become clear from several records in the annals, and from what I shall say in the notes to the letters, that Nicholas III likewise followed in the footsteps of his predecessors.

One of Rudolph’s letters deserves particular attention, in my judgment (book II, letter 37). It was written after Austria, Styria, and the other provinces had been brought under his authority. Continuing to show every obedience to the newly elected supreme pontiff, and sending him two envoys to negotiate concerning the coronation and other affairs of the empire, Rudolph begs and implores him not to disdain to direct both himself, the empire, and the envoys—namely, concerning the difficulties that obstructed the coronation, or, to use his own words, “concerning the principal matter.”

He found it difficult to bear being prevented from undertaking the Italian journey and, consequently, from attaining the imperial majesty which only the Roman pontiff could bestow by placing the imperial diadem upon the royal head. Nevertheless, he had to endure that ardent desire to undertake the journey to the Roman coronation until the final year of that pontificate.

At that point, the excuse of a bishop (book III, letter 15) bears witness that the princes and churches were again preparing to accompany Rudolph on his journey to Rome. Prevented by very serious difficulties, the bishop humbly begs:

> “May Your Royal Majesty, compassionating me in these matters, mercifully release me from the journey undertaken for your coronation, and learn to pity my incapacity.”

The arrangements concerning the treaty to be concluded between Rudolph and Charles, however, were not completed in time; consequently, the subsequent death of Nicholas again became the reason for postponing the coronation.

### LI

Indeed, on 28 March 1280 Rudolph assigned Provence to Charles, king of Sicily, according to the terms of the agreement, as is clear from the diploma preserved by Raynaldus (1280, no. 2). At its conclusion he says:

> “Nevertheless, we promise to renew all the aforesaid matters, each and every one of them, after we have received the imperial diadem, with God’s favor, for greater and perpetual firmness.”

> “Done and given at Vienna, 28 March, indiction VIII, in the year of our Lord 1280, in the seventh year of our reign.”

In turn, Charles issued his diploma concerning the maintenance of peace with the empire:

> “At Naples, in the year of our Lord 1280, on 10 May, indiction VIII, in the fourth year of our reign over Jerusalem, and the fifteenth of our reign over Sicily.”

Since Nicholas died in August, it was not until the following year that his successor, Martin IV, confirmed this peace. He also secured the allegiance of the peoples for the vicars of the king of the Romans established in Etruria, namely the bishop of Gurk and Rudolph the chancellor (Raynaldus, 1281, no. 17).

Thus those two principal disputes concerning the lordships of Provence and Etruria, which had kept Rudolph from the Italian journey, were finally removed in the sixth year. Yet it is not recorded that Rudolph nourished under this pontiff the hope conceived at the end of Nicholas’s pontificate.

Whether Martin restored to Charles the senatorial dignity of Rome, contrary to Nicholas’s constitution; whether the tragic events in Sicily in 1282, which shook Rome and all Italy; or whether other causes prevented Rudolph from pursuing the matter of the coronation is uncertain.

This much is certain: after Charles, king of Sicily, died at the beginning of 1285, and after Martin likewise died nearly three months later, on 26 March of the same year, Rudolph, as the year was drawing to a close, prepared a splendid embassy to Honorius IV, Martin’s successor, seeking the assignment of a date for receiving the imperial diadem.

The letters were dated:

> “At Lausanne, 22 November, indiction XIV, in the year of our Lord 1285, in the thirteenth year of our reign.”

Their autograph is preserved in the archive of the Mole of Hadrian; Raynaldus obtained them from there (1285, no. 22). Since they are of considerable importance for correcting the false opinions of certain writers, they must be reproduced here in full.

### LII

> “To the most holy father in Christ, lord Honorius, by divine providence most holy supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, Rudolph, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever august, with the most devoted readiness of filial obedience and reverence, sends the kisses of blessed feet.

> “Because we have greater confidence than in others in the sincere faith and pure devotion of the honorable men, Masters Leopold of Wistdingin, William of Sellofort, and Peter, provost and elect of the church of Mainz, our beloved chaplains, and of the valiant man Marquard of Hyfendal, our beloved familiar—since we have often fruitfully experienced, and daily experience, their praiseworthy and distinguished services— We therefore confidently send them, to whom we have disclosed the secrets of our heart, to the feet of Your Beatitude.

> “We grant them full authority, free power, and a special mandate to request, obtain, and accept from Your paternal providence a day to be appointed for us for receiving from your sacred hands the imperial diadem and for having placed upon us the crown of Caesarean dignity; and to swear upon our soul concerning the observance of all those things which Your reverend fatherhood may require of them concerning the matters aforesaid. We shall consider as confirmed and agreeable whatever the aforesaid men accept, arrange, or do in these matters.

> “In testimony of this, we have caused this present document to be written and have ordered it to be fortified with the seal of Our Majesty.

> “Given at Lausanne,” as above.

The reply of Honorius appears in the same Raynaldus (1286, no. 1), after six full months, namely, on 30 June in the second year—unless, perhaps, Honorius was replying to a later second letter concerning the same matter. For he says:

> “Recently, when our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz, then bishop of Basel, had been sent for this purpose by Your Magnificence, and, in the presence of ourselves and our brothers, had earnestly requested in your name that a date be assigned to you for receiving from our hands the unction, consecration, and coronation of the imperial diadem.”

Whether there was one embassy or two, the pontiff says:

> “With the counsel of those same brothers, we assign the coming feast of the Purification.”

He adds that a more convenient day may be assigned if some impediment should arise.

And so it happened, just as the pontiff had foreseen. For Rudolph not only failed to come to Rome on the fixed day in 1287, or on some more convenient day, but did not come even in the following year. Lest we imitate those who imprudently obscure the truth by treating unexplored matters as established, we must investigate the reasons why he did not undertake the journey he so greatly desired.

### LIII

The date assigned by Honorius, with the counsel of his brothers, was the feast of the Purification, that is, 2 February 1287. But this date was excessively close. Within the space of eight months the German envoys would have to return to Germany, all preparations for the royal journey would have to be made, and the king himself would have to arrive with a noble retinue during the winter.

Two months later Honorius died. His death was followed by a ten-month interregnum, from 3 April until 22 February 1288, when Nicholas IV, the first pope elected from the Order of Friars Minor, was elected.

The reason Rudolph did not begin pressing this great matter until the following year was the presence of serious impediments in Germany. In replying to the letters of the king of the Romans, Nicholas himself briefly recounts what had occurred under his predecessor and in his own time:

> “We carefully conferred concerning these matters with our brothers. At last, after considering more attentively and weighing and examining through deliberation what is required for the prosecution of so great an undertaking, we judged that, since the date fixed for your coming to the coronation had not produced the intended result because impediments had arisen, it would be expedient for royal honor that we send our envoy to you. Through him, both the progress of your intention might become more clearly known to us and, once we had fuller certainty, we might respond to Your Royal Highness more suitably and appropriately.

> “For your other envoys, contrary to the counsel which we had given them when we held a lesser office, constrained themselves excessively by the shortness of the date.”

These letters were dated 13 April; they may be read in full in Raynaldus (1289, no. 46ff.). Rudolph was then more than seventy years old and survived for scarcely more than two years and a few months. It is therefore not surprising that this final wish of his, delayed to so great an extent by the pontiff, also failed to be fulfilled.

What is rather worthy of admiration is that even in our own age there are people who place greater trust in writers of the fourteenth and later centuries than in reliable monuments, and who therefore do not hesitate to call Rudolph, who desired the imperial diadem passionately to his final breath, either a contemptuous or at least a careless opponent of the Roman coronation.

### LIV

Who, however, would despise the imperial diadem, by which imperial majesty was conferred together with that great increase of authority described above?

To preside over the empire is one thing: the king of the Romans, or future emperor, acquired that right through his election. To be adorned by the imperial diadem from the supreme pontiff is another: through it, the pontiff made him a participant in his own supreme power over temporal affairs throughout the whole world.

Nothing better reveals what the empire was in Rudolph’s time—for formerly, especially under the Carolingians, it had been something very different, as we have seen—than the negotiation conducted by Nicholas III with Rudolph, which Raynaldus reports from a manuscript of the Vatican Library belonging to Jordanus (1280, no. 28):

> “The same pontiff also negotiated with the said king concerning innovations to be made in the empire: namely, that the whole empire should be divided into four parts—the kingdom of Germany, which would be given perpetually to Rudolph’s descendants; the kingdom of Vienna, which would be given as a dowry to the wife of Charles Martel, the daughter of the said Rudolph; and, in Italy, apart from the kingdom of Sicily, two kingdoms would be created, one in Lombardy and the other in Tuscany.”

Blondus and Platina transmitted this matter to posterity in a somewhat different form.

Nor does the plan of Brother Humbert of the Romans, of the Order of Preachers, differ greatly from this. It was proposed before the celebration of the Second Council of Lyon and reported by the distinguished Father Mansi in his notes to Raynaldus (1273, no. 6) in these words:

> “That, while the empire was vacant, a vicar should be appointed; or that thereafter the king of Germany should be made king by succession rather than election; and that, if content with his Germany, he should entrust Italy to one or two kings elected with the consent of the prelates and communities. The elected kings, however, could in certain cases be deposed by the Apostolic See; or finally, that the king established in Lombardy should exercise the vicarious power of the empire in Tuscany while the empire was vacant.”

The imperial majesty instituted by Leo III, so that it might keep subject peoples in their duty, conferred far greater authority upon the king of the Romans. Through coronation, the emperor became a participant in the pontiff’s supreme power insofar as temporal matters were concerned. For wherever the pontiff’s spiritual power was believed to extend, there the emperor’s temporal power was believed to extend as well.

Hence the famous comparison of the two greater lights; hence the authority of the two men throughout the world, which occurs more than once in these letters; and hence, to use Rudolph’s own words, “the completion of the divine work” to be accomplished by one vicar of Christ.

Who is unaware that all royal power comes from God? Rudolph had acquired this power, like other kings. But all the ancient records testify that the kings of the Romans, or elected emperors, acquired imperial majesty—with that increase of authority added to royal power—solely through the favor of the Roman pontiff, by the imposition of the imperial diadem.

### LV

Among the principal evidence for this, without doubt, are the many letters in this manuscript, together with several others drawn from elsewhere, which will occur in the notes. Their authority makes the true character both of the empire and of imperial majesty so evident that the recent invention of the German jurists concerning the Roman-German Empire cannot in any way be applied to an emperor or to the Roman Empire before the Golden Bull.

Let others decide what should be said about the subsequent periods. It does not belong to my purpose to discuss the majesty of the German Empire. I shall therefore proceed to speak of several other matters contained in the Rudolphine manuscript.

Among the other letters, four occur (book I, letters 14ff.) concerning the “first prayers”—that is, the right once to nominate a person to cathedral and collegiate churches. Since this right is said to belong to emperors and kings by an ancient and approved custom, yet is attached to no privilege of the Apostolic See, it causes canonists no small difficulty.

I therefore believe I shall perform a useful service by demonstrating the origin and nature of these prayers. Great obscurity surrounds their origin, and everywhere among writers there is great confusion. Nor is the bold falsehood of sectarians absent, such as that of Vitriarius (*Jus Publicum*, book III, volume II, no. 9), to which Conringius adheres in his note to the bull of Innocent X.

He maintains that:

> “This right is of the same kind as that by which, by virtue of coronation, the emperor becomes a canon at Aachen of the collegiate church of Saint Mary and of the major church of Cologne, and at Rome of the collegiate church of Saint Peter. These rights are likewise not owed to the popes, but are rather slight remnants of the ancient Caesarean right concerning the conferral of bishoprics, abbeys, and other ecclesiastical benefices.”

These dreams of the sleepless show clearly enough that the origin of these prayers was entirely unknown to them.

Nor is there any greater success among experts in canon law. Thomassinus (*On Discipline*, book II, part 1, chapter 54, no. 7) and Chokier (*Preface to the Scholia on the First Prayers*) may stand for all such writers. Each of them cites, from an addition to the Abbot of Ursperg, a formula drawn from Rudolph’s letters. Yet neither presents it in the pure and exact form in which it is read in the letters.

But why should I resort to such remote arguments? Rudolph offers the first prayers to a bishop and an abbot. When the bishop refuses to admit them without consulting the pontiff, Rudolph says:

> “We do not believe that apostolic authority is necessary for the reception and provision of this N. in your church.”

He is angry with the abbot because:

> “Having made light of our commands and prayers,”

the abbot was unwilling to admit the cleric.

Yet to neither does Rudolph give any other reason beyond the example of other churches that followed the custom and the ancient practice.

### LVI

When Rudolph was elected king of the Romans in 1273, seventy-four years had elapsed since the election of Frederick II, who is known to have been elected as a two-year-old in 1196, while his father, Henry VI, was still alive.

Anyone who thought that the origin of such prayers must be sought at that time would therefore be completely mistaken. Frederick did not receive the German crown as a prerequisite for those prayers. Rudolph himself bears witness to this:

> “From the beginning of our elevation, every church established in the Roman Empire is bound, according to the ancient and approved custom of the Holy Empire, to admit the first fruits of our prayers concerning the provision of one person.”

Charles IV confirms the point even more clearly in a charter preserved by Marquard Freherus, dated 1350:

> “By virtue of the solemnities of our coronation to the kingship of the Romans, which have long since been completed in us by divine will, we may, in every monastery established in the empire, cause one person only to be promoted to an ecclesiastical benefice by virtue of our primary prayers.”

Finally, Wenceslaus, in 1376, delegated his authority to Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine:

> “By these presents we grant [authority] in respect of all primary prayers by reason of our coronation as king of the Romans, solemnly received today, 6 July, at Aachen, by the favor of divine clemency, throughout the city and diocese of Speyer and Worms, etc.”

It is therefore beyond all doubt that the custom whose origin we are investigating was attached to the German coronation of the king of the Romans.

Frederick, however, was not crowned with the German crown before 1215, according to the authors cited by Raynaldus (1215, no. 35). For Philip, the brother of Henry VI, had been summoned by the emperor into Italy to bring the child elected king of the Romans to Germany for his coronation. When Philip heard on the journey of his brother’s death in 1197, he returned to Germany and, having become an invader of the empire, had himself crowned at Mainz.

Against him, Otto IV, elected king of the Romans and son of Henry the Lion, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, was crowned at Aachen. At that time began the great struggle for the empire, which ended in 1209, when Otto received the crown of the empire from Innocent III, as may be seen in Baluzius (*The Register of Innocent III*, vol. I, p. 687ff.).

To seek the origin of the primary prayers in the period of this conflict—or even in the coronation of Frederick II, while Otto IV tyrannically ruled the empire and, dying only after three years, opened the way to the empire for Frederick—would be to engage in empty labor.

### LVII

This is all the more true because these prayers bear the character of what are called expectative graces. Although their beginnings may be traced to Adrian IV, whom writers commonly call their author (Thomassinus, *On Discipline*, book II, part 1, chapter 43, no. 2), their use had become established enough that Adrian’s successor, Alexander III, forbade promises of benefices in 1179 at the Third Lateran Council. This is shown by the very words of canon 8 of that ecumenical council:

> “Let no ecclesiastical offices, or even benefices or churches, be granted or promised to anyone before they are vacant, lest anyone appear to desire the death of his neighbor, in whose place and benefice he believes he will succeed.”

In view of this, Innocent III repeatedly asserted the rule, as may be seen in his register preserved by Baluzius. One of several letters, belonging to the year 1211 (Innocent III, *Letters*, book XIV, letter 161, vol. I, p. 588), may stand for all:

> “It has been reported to us through your communication that, in response to the importunate requests of many, you frequently happen to make promises concerning benefices that are not vacant. You have therefore humbly petitioned us to provide you mercifully with guidance in these matters.

> “Wishing to guard your devotion against such a burden, and observing that this is attempted contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, we declare such promises null and void. By the authority of this present letter we strictly forbid you hereafter to presume to promise anyone benefices that are not vacant, contrary to the aforesaid council.”

It is therefore incredible that, after their German coronation, Otto IV and Frederick II sought from churches benefices that would first become vacant, and consequently that these two predecessors of Rudolph offered primary prayers.

Still less should it be believed that Henry VI, crowned with the German crown in 1169, did this. He too is listed together with the two men mentioned above among the early practitioners of expectative graces. Rudolph, however, does not rely upon an isolated example; he says that this privilege was granted to “the holy emperors and kings” by custom.

### LVIII

Since this is so, and since no one whatever before Rudolph is found to have used that formula which, before this date, we reported as having been received from the Continuator of the Abbot of Ursperg [Col. 0695B], whereas today we see it repeated four times<sup>291</sup> in these letters, we must not immediately accept the practice as though it were certain and established; rather, it ought to be examined carefully, so that we may determine what status should be assigned to it.

First, then, it must be considered that neither Rudolph—who was fifty-five years old when he was elected king of the Romans—nor any of the courtiers or living men had seen that so-called practice accepted by usage. This was not because nearly sixty years had elapsed since the last coronation at Aachen—for we have seen that neither Frederick II nor Otto IV, even if the practice had been certain, was permitted to use it—but because the sole example that could be produced, the coronation of Henry VI in 1169, unless it were brought forward to accuse Rudolph of falsity, lies 105 years before his coronation. Rudolph, therefore, invokes a practice seen by no one at all, but heard of by one or another of his counselors.

Next, it must be observed that the requests appeared to both the abbot and the bishop to be something new: to the abbot, because, unless I am mistaken, the decree of the ecumenical Lateran Council cited above, together with the several letters of Innocent III asserting it, against those who importunately sought benefices that were about to become vacant, was not unknown to him; to the bishop, not only because the canons and decrees of the pontiffs were known to him, but because by virtue of his office he had to defend them, and would have committed a grave sacrilege by permitting even the slightest violation of them without consulting the Holy See, which alone could grant this privilege to laymen, however great their rank, contrary to the statutes of the canons and pontifical decrees, if it knew that this would benefit the Church at large.

Yet Rudolph employs three arguments to establish the matter: namely, that the practice is ancient and approved; that no corner of the empire is unaware of it; and that other churches of Germany obey royal requests and commands. But, with due respect, these arguments are of the same kind as those others by which he claimed the Exarchate and the Pentapolis [Col. 0695D] for himself, as I said above (no. 44), and as I shall explain more fully below (Dissertation 7, nos. 5 ff.). For the practice can be neither ancient nor approved, since it is found to have been accepted by none of his predecessors and is contrary to the Third Ecumenical Lateran Council. That elegant assertion, that no corner of the empire is unaware of it, conflicts with the whole of history, since nowhere is knowledge of such a matter found. Finally, the fact that primary petitions were admitted by other churches of Germany proves obedience to the prince more than expertise in ecclesiastical discipline.

### LIX

Would that the author of *Ancient and Modern Discipline* (Part II, book I, chapter 54, no. 7) had seen these letters in their entirety, just as he saw a fragment of Rudolph’s letter in the Abbot of Ursperg! For, according to his opinion,<sup>292</sup> he would not have conjectured that “all cathedral, abbatial, and collegiate churches had been subjected to this servitude,” nor that “commands should be mixed with petitions.” For he was not a most pious prince who wished to impose servitude upon churches and to command ecclesiastics by means of requests.

I call Rudolph himself as witness. When commending a new canon to the chapter of Liège (book III, letter 22), he says:

> “We ask Your Prudence, with all the affection of which we are capable, that, showing him suitable favor concerning that residence, out of respect for us and for your own advantage, you endeavor to send him as soon as possible to our court, where he will more fruitfully perform the services there previously mentioned for you and for the Church.”

I say nothing about his conduct toward bishops: many letters addressed to them are found in which he venerates even rebellious bishops as fathers. It is therefore beyond doubt that the newly elected king of the Romans, placing excessive trust in his counselors, was more zealous than was proper for the rights and dignity of the empire.

The outcome, however, was favorable to the primary petitions; for, once an apostolic privilege was added, they gained strength and remain in force to this day. Clement VI appears to have been the first of all the pontiffs to grant primary petitions to Charles IV, king of the Romans. For in the charter cited above he says:

> “Since, therefore, it belongs to us by both right and the ancient and approved custom hitherto observed by the deified Roman emperors and our predecessors, etc.”

Wenceslaus and the others later imitated him, claiming the petitions for themselves no longer merely by custom, but by right and ancient custom. Whatever, then, may be said about that ancient and approved custom which is reported as having been received by Rudolph alone, after the Apostolic See ratified it, it became an imperial right. Not even the Council of Trent abolished it (Session 24, chapter 19), as the Sacred Congregation declared, Gregory XIII confirming its decree. Thomassin (Part II, book I, chapter 54, no. 10 ff.) therefore argues that primary petitions rest upon an apostolic privilege, because Pius IV and Gregory XIII ratified them in the aforesaid manner. But they rest upon a much more ancient apostolic privilege.

### LX

Indeed, no one would say that Charles IV added a right to the custom on his own authority, since it is especially well established [Col. 0696C] that this prince was most highly esteemed by Clement VI, was elected through his agency, and received many benefits from him.

Nevertheless, since no apostolic privilege is found, it cannot be affirmed with certainty that, from the middle of the fourteenth century, primary petitions began to rest upon an apostolic privilege in the case of this king of the Romans, the author of the Golden Bull.

There is no doubt, however, that a full century later, namely in 1452, when Frederick III received the imperial diadem from Nicholas V, he obtained by pontifical diploma the grant of primary petitions. This was renewed for all his successors down to our own time by the Holy See after their election had been confirmed by it.

The same diploma exists in the secret Vatican archive. It was published at the beginning of our century by Cardinal Corradini, as George reports (*Life of Nicholas V*, pp. 116 and 156), and was cited by Clement XI (*Letters and Briefs*, vol. I, p. 308), in a letter to the chapter and canons of the church of Hildesheim:

> “If, then,” he says, “the same Frederick and the emperors who subsequently succeeded him, before the time of the late Emperor Leopold, recently deceased, directed primary petitions, it is clear that this occurred because all of them, after obtaining confirmation of themselves from the Roman pontiff, took care to be furnished with an apostolic grant. Since that Leopold himself lacked this grant, it came about that the bishops, prelates, and chapters of Germany—remembering that a not inconsiderable and by no means contemptible part of their liberty consisted in refusing to admit and execute primary petitions, from which he himself did not abstain—declined to accept them and put them into execution.”

Thus these petitions had rested upon an apostolic privilege for more than 120 years when the Sacred Congregation of the Council of Trent declared that they had not been abolished. Thomassin therefore traces the beginning of the Holy See’s authority from that point.

From the aforementioned year, 1452, emperors or kings of the Romans who use such a personal privilege lawfully offer primary petitions. But those who neglected to obtain it tried in vain, under pretext of ancient custom, to violate the liberty of the churches of Germany by means of those petitions, as we learn from the letters of Clement XI. For, following the example of the bishop and abbot who rejected Rudolph’s petitions, bishops and chapters, disregarding the ancient custom that was alleged, reject petitions offered without any legal right and fight with the utmost vigor for ecclesiastical rights.

### LXI

From the very beginning ecclesiastics bore this with the greatest indignation. Aeneas Sylvius, who was later elected pontiff and assumed the name Pius II, bears witness to this. For he replies as follows to Bartholomeo Medici (letter 372):

> “It is not proper for us to oppose the emperor’s primary petitions, because we have obtained them and have often defended them; and we ought to uphold the honor of the imperial majesty, because by it we have been promoted and enriched.”

Nevertheless, neither the German Concordats concluded between Nicholas V and Frederick III—which appeared contrary to the freedom of conferring benefices during the appointed months and thus contrary to primary petitions—nor the later collapse of the expectatives harmed that privilege.

Therefore the primary petitions first employed by Rudolph in the year 1274, resting more upon opinion than upon custom, and leaving only very rare traces during a period of 178 years, when they began to support and defend themselves by a definite privilege of the Apostolic See, survived all dangers and, as they proudly claim, have reached our own age unharmed.

Yet there is a great difference between those ancient petitions and petitions obtained through the favor of the Holy See. The former did not extend beyond the first year of the reign following the German coronation; the latter, which depend upon an apostolic grant, were granted to Frederick III after his imperial coronation, while to his successors they were customarily granted after the Apostolic See had confirmed the imperial election—a confirmation which, after imperial coronation fell into disuse, occurred several years after that election.

Let Joseph Augustus serve as an example. Elected king of the Romans in 1690 and succeeding his father Leopold in the empire in 1705, he died of smallpox in 1711 while the confirmation and privilege were being prepared. Speaking of this unexpected event in consistory on 17 April 1711, Clement XI says (*Consistorial Orations*, p. 117):

> “Everything was ready, so that whatever still had to be done, both with regard to the apostolic confirmation of Joseph’s election, to be completed with the advice of your fraternities, and with regard to the grant called that of primary petitions…”

Thus he would scarcely have used the apostolic privilege in the twenty-second year after his election as king of the Romans, or in the sixth year after the death of his father Leopold, had premature death not intervened.

Moreover, what of Leopold, who ruled the empire from the death of Ferdinand III, the father of Augustus, that is, from the year 1658—for an interregnum of fifteen months intervened—and never obtained the grant of the Holy See? Nevertheless, the *precistae*—as those who claim to have obtained benefices through primary petitions are called by a newly introduced term—appeared even while the apostolic grant was not in force, at the vacancy of dignities and other benefices, as though they had acquired a right to them by primary petitions. See Clement XI (*Letters and Briefs*, vol. I, part II, pp. 408, 414 ff., and 605).

Indeed, as the same pontiff testifies (*Bullarium*, pp. 104 ff.), while the empire was vacant they did not hesitate to offer petitions in the name of its vicar.

### LXII

This conduct, since it was carried out neither by ancient custom nor by virtue of an apostolic privilege, rightly compelled the churches of Germany and the supreme pontiff—who alone can grant privileges or concessions of this kind—to protest against such abuse.

It certainly caused Clement great difficulty, yet we do not read that his resolve was broken. In a letter to the bishop of Augsburg (same work, p. 409), he declared that “the man who obtained the canonry by this means was in no way its legitimate possessor, nor did he make the revenues his own.” He indicates that he was relieved of his concern in no other way than by “driving the *precista*, the holder of the canonry, from its unlawful possession” [Col. 0698A].

Likewise, after being informed by the apostolic nuncio “that a certain *precista*, as they call him, was now striving with great eagerness to have the deanery of the collegiate church of Saint Maurice assigned to him,” in the city of Münster, he earnestly asked the bishop of that city “that the petition of the aforesaid *precista* be entirely rejected” (same work, p. 549).

From this it is clear that, when primary petitions were believed to rest upon custom, although they were presented without any legal right, they inflicted no wound upon the discipline governing the conferral of benefices. For kings of the Romans, crowned with the German crown, offered their petitions only during the first year of their reign and once only to each cathedral, collegiate, or monastic church, as though by a right of patronage, for a vacant canonry or benefice, or one about to become vacant.

By contrast, the *precistae* inflicted a most serious wound upon that discipline. For according to the new practice, against which Clement XI inveighed so vehemently, whenever a canonry, dignity, or other benefice in any church first became vacant, the *precista* would suddenly appear, entirely unknown to that church. This occurred not only when the emperor’s election had not been confirmed by the Apostolic See, but even while the empire was vacant; and he would maintain that the canonry, dignity, or benefice was owed to him by right of primary petitions.

From these four letters of Rudolph, then, not only the origin of those petitions but also their proper use—especially since they are now offered by apostolic authority—is clear. So much for this matter.

### LXIII

It would remain for me now to say something about the other subjects contained in these letters, especially about the immense zeal with which Rudolph burned to take up arms for Syria—not merely to defend what remained of the Holy Land, but also to recover from the barbarians the holy city of Jerusalem and the neighboring places consecrated by the blood of Jesus Christ, which, through the negligence of Christians, had again been occupied by them.

It is painful to relate! The patriarch of Jerusalem, and everything that the forefathers had established for the administration of that new kingdom, had been reduced to Acre, or Ptolemais. [Col. 0698C] Desolation, ambushes, and fear on every side compelled those wretched and pitiful peoples to seek timely assistance from Rudolph. Other and even stronger causes invited him there, above all the ashes of his wise father Albert, long since buried at Acre.

Rudolph himself testifies to this in a letter to Gregory X (book I, letter 12), when he gives thanks for the confirmation of his election:

> “The ardor of desire within us is kindled all the more intensely for this purpose, insofar as the bones of our natural father, resting there abroad and far from their native soil for the glory of the Crucified One, are recalled each day with greater concern in our hearts. And who could prevent a son from desiring with all his heart to become an exile beside his father’s tomb, for the sake of him who, abounding in the delights of paradise, gave himself over to exile and misery?”

Yet this immense desire met the same fate as another equally powerful desire: to receive the imperial diadem in the City from the Roman pontiff. For wars breaking out within the borders of the empire delayed the necessary assistance to the Holy Land for so long that, while Rudolph was still alive, the capture of Acre and the slaughter of all the Christians, with very few crossing overseas, were heard of with the grief they deserved (book III, letter 40). But I shall discuss all these matters more appropriately in the notes.

What must be said beforehand is that the outstanding virtues of this great progenitor of the august House of Austria—his excellent character, modesty, devotion to peace, clemency, humanity, generosity, and patience—which are celebrated by the authors, are described so clearly in these letters that outside testimony is unnecessary.

### LXIV

I should indeed have wished to present an edition of this outstanding manuscript fully perfected in every respect for the republic of letters. But my meager strength did not permit me to undertake so grave and altogether unbearable a burden without assistance from elsewhere.

For, apart from the fact that almost all the letters lack the identity of their sender, their place, and their date, their negligent collector divided them into three books without any regard for order, as though their subject matter varied and their chronology were certain. In reality, the manuscript lacks both of these things, and letters in one book must therefore be referred to another, since similarities of subject and chronological confusion occur everywhere.

Wenceslaus Adalbert Czerwenka, author of the *Annals and Acts of the Habsburg-Austrian Piety*, whom for the sake of brevity I call throughout the author of *Austrian Piety*, speaks of the Rudolphine manuscript as follows (book I, chapter 4, p. 37):

> “The most reverend and most learned Lord Johann Seifrid, once the most vigilant abbot of Zwettl of the Cistercian order, certainly deserves great praise for having collected, through his care and industry, from the manuscripts of the two ancient monasteries of Heiligenkreuz and Zwettl, 149 letters written partly by Rudolph, and especially by him, partly to him, and partly concerning him, and for having divided them into three books. He would have attained the highest praise if he had indicated the persons, the year in which the letters were written, and the persons to whom they were sent. The distinguished Petrus Lambecius was preparing these same letters for the press and wished to insert them into his *Syntagma of German Affairs*, adding not only Seifrid’s annotations but also his own, together with a chronological table and variant readings from an ancient parchment manuscript of the Imperial Library, among the Latin philosophical and philological manuscripts, no. 262, in which the same letters are found. I have not yet had the opportunity to inspect it. But Lambecius himself, overtaken by death, was not permitted to bring forth this offspring of his intellect and crown his scholarly labors.”

He speaks of the same manuscript in the same sense elsewhere (book I, chapter 20, p. 118).

Hansizius, however, praises the Imperial manuscript of civil law, no. 77 (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 416). Since I carefully compared one of the letters (book II, letter 33), as printed both by the author of *Austrian Piety* (book I, chapter 13, p. 75) and by Hansizius (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 388), I discovered that both had used the Imperial manuscript.

I therefore state without hesitation that the variant readings which I have appended to certain letters were taken from the Imperial manuscript, wherever the letters that I carefully collated occur in either of the aforementioned authors. Do not suppose that I did this by chance: I thoroughly investigated the matter before adopting this plan.

### LXV

First I observed that both Lambecius, in his catalogue of books to be published, and the author of *Austrian Piety* mention 149 letters. I then saw Seifrid himself cite several letters in his *Genealogy of the House of Austria* from the manuscript of the monastery of Heiligenkreuz, where they were arranged in a different order.

For example, the first letter in our manuscript is number 53 in his; what is number 20 in the manuscript, book I, is number 59 in Seifrid; and finally what is number 29 of book I in the manuscript is number 130 in his. Moreover, in fragments of these letters I found variant readings which clearly show that the manuscript used by the author of *Austrian Piety* is different from that of Heiligenkreuz.

Is it not therefore clear that these 126 letters were collected and arranged into three books by that same Seifrid—whoever may not be persuaded by the earlier letters—because they were placed before all the others precisely because they concern his own Cistercian order? To this may be added the supposition or interpolation of a certain privilege (book III, letter 36) in favor of the monastery of Zwettl.

Furthermore, Lambecius frankly admits that, despite diligent searching, he was nowhere able to find the Seifrid manuscripts (*Preface*, vol. I, no. 39). The author of *Austrian Piety* (book I, chapter 4, pp. 33 and 37) attributes to Seifrid the celebrated manuscript of 149 letters praised by Lambecius, and thus accuses so eminent a man of falsity because Lambecius denies having found the Seifrid manuscripts anywhere.

But the Lambecian, or Imperial, manuscript, which Hansizius also used and which contains letters entirely similar to those published by the same author of *Austrian Piety*, proves otherwise. Our manuscript, however, which comes from the monastery of Zwettl itself, removes all doubt that the work should be regarded as Seifrid’s.

The Imperial manuscript of 149 letters would certainly have been more convenient. Since their sequence is continuous, it would have required less labor to restore to order those that had been disrupted by faulty arrangement. Moreover, because it either bears no titles for the letters or bears titles quite different from those in our manuscript, it would have relieved me of part of the burden I had to undertake in order to make the meaning of the letters clear and restore the integrity of their historical account.

For Seifrid, an author of the early seventeenth century, paid more attention to the concerns of his own age than to those of ancient times, as I shall point out in its proper place in the notes.

### LXVI

As far as I could, I prefixed summaries to the individual letters. I was obliged to do this when I published the letters of the Carolingian manuscript. There was certainly less need for the same procedure in the edition of the Rudolphine manuscript. Many letters that would have been of great use to Lambecius for his *Syntagma of German Affairs* are superfluous to me, since I am concerned with pontifical affairs and imperial majesty. I shall therefore leave their examination to those for whom they are of greater importance.

But the collector’s license in appending summaries to each letter had to be restrained, and his negligence corrected. I could not tolerate that Rudolph—who always calls himself king of the Romans, since he had not been crowned with the imperial diadem—should frequently be called “emperor” in those appended summaries, nor that the letters should often be given a false advance interpretation.

Since it was not possible to avoid these two serious defects by substituting the titles that the same letters bear in the old Viennese, or Imperial, manuscript, I composed brief summaries of them.

The collector’s license will become evident from one of the titles in the Imperial manuscript, which Hansizius gives in full for the letter of the archbishop of Salzburg. In our manuscript this is book II, letter 29. The title is brief and simple:

> “Letter of the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans to the supreme pontiff.”

Now hear the collector’s summary:

> “The archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans joyfully announce to the Roman supreme pontiff that Austria has been liberated from the tyranny of Ottocar the Bohemian by the emperor Rudolph, whose virtues and praises they extol magnificently.”

I, however, could not avoid interpreting the brevity and sincerity of the title, which the collector had explained rather improperly, through the following summary:

> “The archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans, after Rudolph’s first victory over Ottocar, king of Bohemia, congratulate John XXI, the new pontiff, on his election and exaggerate the tyranny and audacity that the same king had exercised against themselves and all the other bishops, whom the Council of Lyons had restored. They recount how he had obstructed the payment of tithes for the aid of the Holy Land, obedience to the commands of the Holy See, and submission to the king of the Romans confirmed by apostolic authority; how he had extorted unlawful oaths, overthrown churches by fire and plunder, and joined an alliance with the tyrannical Tartars. Then, after recounting at length Rudolph’s most fortunate advances for the liberation of Austria, they commend to him so great a king, so deserving of the commonwealth and of the churches, in gratitude.”

### LXVII

As for the variant readings that occasionally occur, I state that all of them were taken from the Imperial manuscript, although the letters printed in the author of *Austrian Piety* are said to have been excerpted by him from Seifrid’s manuscript copies.

For the thirty-third letter of book II, which the same author publishes from his own manuscript, agrees so closely with the same letter published by Hansizius from the Imperial manuscript that there can be no doubt that both editions derive from one and the same manuscript.

Moreover, from the same manuscript that he calls Seifrid’s, he places three letters before the first letter of our manuscript (book I, chapter 4, pp. 32 ff.), namely:

1. Rudolph’s letter to Gregory X;
2. Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, to the same pontiff;
3. A cardinal of the Holy Roman Church to Rudolph.

Elsewhere (book I, chapter 16, p. 94) he presents from the same manuscript a privilege granted to the monastery of Zwettl concerning salt. According to Lambecius’s testimony, that manuscript contained 149 letters.

The letters to which variant readings are appended amount to twenty-eight. So that it may not be unknown to whom they are to be credited, I should list them here.

Of book I, letters 1, 2, 3, 12, and 42 were published by the author of *Austrian Piety*. Letter 38 of the same book was published by Hansizius.

Of book II, letters 1, 3, 4, and 34 belong to the aforementioned author; letters 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 22, 24—the last of which escaped me in the preface, where I incorrectly listed number 13—and 29 belong to Hansizius; and letter 33 belongs to both.

Finally, eight letters of book III—namely letters 13, 19, 24, 25, 26, 27, 30, and 36—are all attributed to the author of *Austrian Piety*.

The two diplomas found at the end of our manuscript without any numbering are absent from the Imperial manuscript, as is evident from the same author, who presents one of them from the annals of Bzovius (*Annals*, 1283, no. 15) (book I, chapter 17, p. 102). But this matter must be discussed at the end of this volume, where we defer it.

Nor should it be omitted that the cited author (same work, pp. 103 ff.) says that he found in Seifrid’s manuscript two letters addressed to Philip III, king of France, on behalf of the monastery of Val-Dieu (*Codex*, nos. 19 and 24). He quotes them while omitting number 20 of our manuscript, since that letter was lacking in the manuscript which—despite Lambecius’s objection—he calls Seifrid’s, although many more letters are found there than in the true Seifrid manuscript, which is only now being brought to light through my efforts.

The manuscript is truly outstanding, since it contains letters copied from the original autographs themselves. This is readily inferred from the signs (*) that occur more than once, which openly reveal the customary defect of nearly all manuscripts and the copyist’s extreme fidelity, provided that the collector’s summaries are nowhere treated as part of the text.

### LXVIII

From what has been said it is clear that these Rudolphine letters exist, with only minor differences in wording, in an ancient parchment manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna. Hansizius extracted from it the letters concerning the archbishop of Salzburg, while the author of *Austrian Piety* extracted others suited to his purpose—unless perhaps he used another person’s work and did not know from where the copies had been made. For he asserts that the manuscript of 149 letters should be attributed to Seifrid, whereas Lambecius denies this.

That same manuscript Lambecius had resolved to commit to the press in his *Syntagma of German Affairs*. How beneficial this has proved for me, who am vindicating the rights and privileges of the Holy See through the best monuments, is shown by this one fact: the two matters that could easily be preferred to all the rest, and which I wished to make the central pillars of this work, will become especially welcome to all scholars through the commendation of so great a man.

Would that the Imperial manuscript itself had come into my hands, as the Carolingian manuscript did—the latter I wished to have printed at the beginning of Lambecius’s *Syntagma* as the first monument of pontifical dominion! Then the last part would answer to the first, and I could boast that I had succeeded to the labors of this most learned man, publishing for the common view all the rights and privileges of the prince of the apostles and his successors as confirmed by the great progenitor of the august House of Austria, together with the grants of his predecessors, renewed in their entirety for greater authority; and that through the imperial authority of so great a king I had demonstrated the true character of imperial majesty.

But since this did not happen as I had hoped, I have shown, by collating the twenty-eight letters mentioned above, that the Seifrid manuscript differs only very slightly from the Imperial manuscript that Lambecius intended to publish. I then cited the first of the Lambecian letters absent from the Seifrid manuscript (above, no. 47), as well as the two following letters (book I, letter 11, no. 2; book II, letter 20, no. 3), which are likewise absent from the Seifrid manuscript. From the words of Rudolph himself and of one of the electors of the Holy Roman Empire, the archbishop of Cologne, I elicited the same character. I confirmed it further by carefully collating other letters found in the Seifrid manuscript (book I, letters 12, 38, and 42; book II, letter 1) with the letters of the Imperial manuscript.

The remaining materials concerning rights and privileges require no other attestation, since their originals exist in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo. Nevertheless, I confess that it seems wholly incredible to me that only one letter (book II, letter 37) should be found as their vindicator. I have no doubt that several of the twenty-three letters absent from the Seifrid manuscript concern so important a matter.

I trust that the prefect of the Imperial Library of Vienna, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, will not permit the chief glory of Rudolph, king of the Romans, to remain hidden any longer.

Meanwhile, I have ordered these letters, prepared through my labors however inadequate, to be brought into the light of day. I consider it in the public interest to dispel so many false scholarly opinions by the authority of monuments of this kind.

The very nature of the matter shows that the Rudolphine material ought to precede the diploma of the electors of the Holy Roman Empire, which is read at the end of the letters. I shall therefore have to discuss it in the following dissertation, with which I shall complete the entire work.

---

## 303 THE THREE BOOKS OF THE LETTERS OF RUDOLPH I, AUGUSTUS CAESAR

### BOOK I

### LETTER ONE

Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, asks a religious congregation for the assistance of its prayers in establishing the auspices of his empire.

[Note: All the titles were supplied by the collector. They rarely agree with the letters. Those called “religious” are Cistercian monks, as is clear from the following letter. They were renowned for holiness. Innocent III, too, at the beginning of his pontificate, commended himself to the abbot and convent of Cîteaux and to the abbot and convent of Clairvaux (Register, book I, letter 176). His letters to the Cistercians are also preserved in Raynaldus (Register, book IX, letter 119), in which, in the ninth year of his pontificate, he commends the Roman Church, suffering great difficulties, to all the abbots assembled in the general chapter of the Cistercian order. I reproduce the pontiff’s own words, which have considerable similarity to Rudolph’s:

> “Since, placed amid so many and such great dangers, we need to be assisted by your merits and prayers, we ask and beseech you, by the mercies of our God, that, while we are tossed upon the sea’s deep, you extend to us the assistance of your charity; and, raising up the fisherman and the little boat by the oars of your prayers, entreat him who commands the sea and the winds, etc.”]

*(In the year of the Lord 1273; Imperial manuscript LIII, Rudolphine manuscript I.)*

[Col. 0701D]

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, anxious to obtain the imperial diadem and terrified by the dreadful appearance of the empire after its long vacancy, reminds the Cistercian monks of his affection and generosity and attracts them by the hope of royal patronage. He begs them to implore divine assistance for him through their prayers.

Having been divinely appointed to direct the undertakings [Col. 0703A] of the Roman Empire, while from the height of the lofty watchtower to which the hand of the Lord has virtuously raised us we turn our eyes downward toward the face of the abyss lying below, while we look all around upon the untilled field of that same empire, daily becoming overgrown through the density of rising storms [Note: The letters of the bishop of Olomouc to Gregory X and other documents in Raynaldus (1273, nos. 10 ff.) demonstrate the wretched condition of the empire in that age. Almost universal wars and rebellions were accompanied by the continual harassment of brigands. Rudolph is said to have destroyed about eighty such haunts or nests during his reign (the author of *Austrian Piety*, book I, chapter 5, p. 40). Moreover, Germany was shamefully torn apart by the crimes of clergy and people; and princes accustomed to liberty bore with resentment the imposition of an emperor upon them. The neighboring regions were no better. Hungary in particular was afflicted by schismatics and heretics, in addition to the evils of war.], we are cast down by a certain fear and trembling alike [ [Note: Variant readings are given from the Imperial manuscript.] horror] and, in view of what has been set forth, tremble with good reason in uncertain dread.

Yet, at times turning the gaze of our consideration back toward the beginnings of our original elevation, and reflecting that the hand of the Most High has brought us from so humble a dwelling to such lofty, such [“elevated and”] magnificent palaces [Note: The illustrious origin of the Austrian line is celebrated by the consistent testimony of writers. Nevertheless, the excellent prince does not deny the humility of his homeland. Nor do I see what Conringius means (*On the Limits of the German Empire*, vol. I, p. 285), when he says of Rudolph:

> “This man is the author of imperial dignity in the House of Austria. He was count of Habsburg; Habsburg, however, is a city in Switzerland and is today held by the city of Bern. From there came the Austrian family and the kings of Spain.”

For it was the great prudence, military valor, integrity of character, innate piety, and other exalted qualities of mind with which this great progenitor of the august House of Austria was endowed that caused him to be preferred to all the princes of Germany in the election of the king of the Romans.]

—in him whose wondrous power by grace makes stable what is fragile by nature, we place the hope of our confidence, confidently presuming that he will bring to a happy completion the work which is recognized to have been woven together by the ineffable dispensation of his omnipotence [Note: The recent examples of the kings of the Romans Richard and Alfonso trouble Rudolph. Both had been called kings of the Romans by Alexander IV and Urban IV and were therefore designated emperors. Yet neither of them did the Roman pontiff raise to imperial majesty by imposing the imperial diadem upon him. This meant raising an elected king of the Romans to imperial majesty, as Rudolph himself explains more clearly in the following letters.].

Since we judge the continual prayers of the righteous to be supremely necessary for this purpose, we earnestly exhort Your Devotion that, attentively and gratefully recognizing that royal highness gladly assists you in your undertakings, you commend us to the divine mercy through the assistance of your devout prayers.

### 305. LETTER II

Brother John, general abbot of the holy Cistercian Order, replies to Rudolph’s preceding letters, commending his Order to him.

*(A.D. 1273, Rudolph Codex II.)*

[Col. 0704A]

**Argument.**—Brother John, abbot of Cîteaux, replies to the royal letter, explaining that it was read in the general chapter and that all heard with joyful hearts that the hope of their ancient affection and patronage was being confirmed. Sacrifices of Masses and appointed prayers for the entire royal household have been prescribed throughout the whole Cistercian Order, whose privileges and grants he commends to royal protection.

To the most serene Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, Brother John wishes happiness in Him who grants salvation to kings.

I caused the letter of Your Royal Sublimity, which I had received with due reverence, to be read before the brothers gathered from various parts of the world [Note: [Col. 0703D] The royal letter was read in the general chapter. The first such chapter was held, as is believed, at Cîteaux in Burgundy in the year 1116, and thereafter it began to be annual. Mabillon teaches that the example of celebrating such general chapters was provided to the Benedictines by the Cistercians (Annals, book LXXII, chapter 119). At that time, namely in the eighteenth year after the foundation, there were only four monasteries, and consequently the same number of abbots could assemble. But afterward, through almost incredible growth, that Order spread everywhere to such an extent that in the fifty-third year after its foundation, that is, in 1151, it had to be decreed that no further monastery should be founded. Thomassin asserts this in the words of Matthew of Paris [Col. 0704B] (I, book III, chapter 68, no. 3): “It was decreed in the Cistercian chapter that henceforth no one should build a new abbey, because the number of abbeys of that Order had grown to five hundred.” Mabillon confirms this from another source (Annals, book LXXX, no. 9), although he testifies that it was decreed in the general chapter of 1153. Therefore, when Innocent III imposed upon the Cistercian, Clairvaux, Pontigny, La Ferté, and all the abbots of the Cistercian Order a fiftieth part of their revenues as an aid for the Holy Land (Register, in Baluze, book II, letter 268, p. 514), that contribution was doubtless imposed upon five hundred abbots. Yet it seems incredible [Col. 0704C] that five hundred abbots assembled in 1244, when Saint Louis IX came to the general chapter so that he might be adopted into the fraternity and communion of the Order’s prayers, as Thomassin interprets the words of Matthew of Paris. For he himself (II, book III, chapter 42, no. 13), in discussing the constitutions or statutes of the chapters, observes that long before it had been decreed that the abbots of Ireland, Scotland, and Sicily should come to the general chapter every fourth year; those of Norway, Greece, Livonia, and Syria every fifth year; and those of Hungary every third year. Therefore those words of Paris (p. 439)—“And behold, all the abbots, together with the entire convent, nearly five hundred in number, came out in procession to meet him in honor of the lord king”—must be understood of the total number of monks, not of the abbots alone.
