From this it is also plainly evident with what emotion this letter of Rudolph was read in the assembly of the Cistercian monks and with how many suffrages of prayers [Col. 0704D] its great progenitor, Rudolph, the elected king of the Romans, judged that the beginnings of the august House of Austria should be commended to God almighty]: and because those same letters (eadem, an obvious OCR correction of caedem), as though fulfilling a twofold office, were seeking to present to Your Excellency the suffrages of the devout prayers of our brothers devoted to you [Note: [Col. 0704D] No record has been found that other great princes, following the example of Saint Louis, sought fraternity with the Cistercians. Nevertheless, notable examples of the fraternity requested are not lacking. There is a famous document in Hansiz (Germania Sacra, vol. II, p. 329), from a manuscript chronicle of the Imperial Library, by which “the Salzburg chapter is received into fraternity by the entire Cistercian Order in the general chapter of abbots.” I shall append it here, so that the distinction may be clear between the suffrages of prayers requested by Innocent III and Rudolph and fraternity:

“Brother William of Monteacuto, called abbot of Cîteaux, and the entire convent of the abbots of the general chapter, send greeting and the salutary suffrage of prayers to the venerable and discreet provost and chapter at Salzburg. Because of the pious affection of love toward our Order, which, with the Lord inspiring you, you sincerely love [Col. 0705B] in Christ and cherish, we have decided to respond with kindly consent to your request, which was presented to us through our venerable co-abbot of Raitenhaslach. Therefore we grant you full participation, both in life and in death, in all the good works performed and to be performed throughout our entire Order, whether in Masses, prayers, or other good works. Accordingly, when your death has been announced to the general chapter, as much shall be done throughout the whole Order for each one of you as is customarily done for each one of us. Given at Cîteaux in the year of grace 1228, during the time of the general chapter.”], and because you testified that you were their particular lord, most beloved patron, and munificent provider, [Col. 0705A] your letters were not only heard and understood with greater pleasure and gratitude, but their request also deserved to be effectively and cheerfully granted.

Let Your Serenity therefore know that, for the preservation of your well-being and [in: “for”] its increase, for the most illustrious lady Anna [Note: [Col. 0705C] When Albert, count of Habsburg, died in Syria and was buried at Acre, his son Rudolph—whom some report to have followed the camp of Frederick II—returned to his homeland and married. Gerard de Roo, briefly relating the whole matter (History of Austria, book I, p. 8), says: “After his father’s death, Rudolph returned home and completed the marriage he had contracted with Anna of Hohenberg in the year 1240.” He was then twenty-two years old, for in 1218 Hedwig, daughter of Hermann, count of Kyburg, and Albert’s wife, had given birth to him on the Kalends of May.] who shares and participates in Your Magnificence, and likewise for your most illustrious offspring [Note: [Col. 0705C] Authorities differ concerning the number of Rudolph’s children. The author of Austrian Piety lists seven sons: Rudolph, who died in the twelfth year of his age; Albert, who succeeded his father after Adolphus and propagated the august House of Austria; Hartmann and Frederick, who died childless; a second Rudolph, duke of Swabia, who married Agnes, daughter of Ottocar; a second Hermann or Hartmann, who was drowned in the Rhine before he could marry Margaret, daughter of Edward, king of England; and finally Charles, who died in childhood.

Authors consistently list an equal number of daughters: Euphemia, who followed her mother’s example and embraced a more holy way of life among the nuns of the Dominican monastery at Tulln; Gutha, or Jutta or Judith, wife of Wenceslaus, son of Ottocar; Mechtild, wife of Louis, duke of Bavaria; Agnes, whom Albert, duke and elector of Saxony, married; Catherine, given in marriage to Otto, duke of Bavaria; Anna, also called Hedwig, wife of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and Clementia [Col. 0706B], given in marriage to Charles Martel, grandson through his son of the king of Sicily.

Gerard mentioned above (History of Austria, p. 16) says of them: “There are those who wish the princes to have consented more willingly to this election because the archbishop of Mainz had said, among other things, that Rudolph had six daughters of outstanding beauty and character, through whose marriages there would be great opportunities for joining the princes to one another . . . Before the king himself departed from Aachen, Mechtild, Rudolph’s daughter, was betrothed—with the support of the archbishop of Mainz—to Louis, the Count Palatine; Agnes to Albert of Saxony; and Hedwig to Otto of Brandenburg.” For some reason Henry Stero omits the last of these (in Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. IV, p. 201). All others report that these three married the three aforementioned electors in the very year of the coronation, and the remaining three in subsequent years: Catherine married Otto, son of Henry, in 1276, after his reconciliation with his brother Louis; Gutha married Wenceslaus, son of Ottocar, after his father’s death in 1278; and finally Clementia—whom Stero and Gerard pass over in silence—married the grandson of Charles, king of Sicily, in 1280, as the chronicle and History of Austria in Freher show, and as will be explained more fully below.] suffrages of Masses and other prayers have been imposed and enjoined upon all and each of the brothers throughout our entire Order. They will offer them to divine mercy all the more willingly and promptly because they recognize you as a benevolent father and ardent champion of them. Although, out of the abundance of your goodness, I commend them more closely to Your Excellency, in return for the grants, favors, and privileges bestowed upon them [Note: [Col. 0706C] Thomassin (I, book III, chapter 28, no. 12; III, book III, chapter 23, no. 5) observes that until Innocent IV the Cistercians had enjoyed no privileges. They had therefore found the bishops to whom they were subject so favorable that they had built as many as two thousand monasteries. Later, however, when that pontiff absolved them, they were no longer restrained either by the statutes of the general chapters or by the most holy laws of Bernard from seeking privileges and wealth.], I rise to offer you manifold thanks and am nevertheless prepared, with an even more willing spirit and according to the measure of my ability, to carry out in practice whatever I know to be acceptable to Your Will.

---

### LETTER III

Rudolph likewise requests prayers for himself and his consort from consecrated virgins.

*(A.D. 1273, Rudolph Codex III.)*

[Col. 0705B]

**Argument.**—In the following two letters, written for the same reason and toward the same end to nuns of different Orders, Rudolph requests their fervent prayers. He considers those prayers likely to be effective because they will be directed to Jesus Christ, the Son of the most holy Virgin, by consecrated women who are especially acceptable to her.

Having been raised by divine ordinance to the watchtower of royal dignity [Col. 0706A], while we diligently consider the burdens that weigh upon our shoulders, while on the scales of continual meditation we weigh the weakness and insufficiency of our own strength, and while we contemplate the gravity of the labor we have undertaken, we are compelled to be struck with a certain (quodam; variant quod jam, “because now”) fear and trembling, fearing both the preeminence of our rank and the abyss below, whose face we clearly behold. We fear lest the height of this terrible place perhaps often frighten us. Yet we are lifted up by confidence in divine mercy, hoping that we may pass unharmed through the narrows of this broad and storm-tossed sea, if you obtain for us the help of salvation and grace—you who have prepared for the heavenly Bridegroom a flower-filled bed amid the delights of your conscience.

For what will divine piety deny you, who (quae; variant quanquam, “although”) always deserve to have it propitious through the brightness of your virtues and the fragrance of your blessed works [Beatorum?]?  What will your praises not obtain from the radiant queen, the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0706D] The innate devotion of the House of Austria toward the most blessed Virgin, deriving from its great progenitor, has always produced notable victories over the most hostile enemies of the Catholic faith.]—you whose (quarum; variant quorum) merits make the Church shine, whose examples strengthen the world, and through whom the Christian religion advances? What will that illustrious array of the citizens above not obtain through your votive affections, since it is made favorable to you by the praises of divine glory and by the merits of an innocent life?

Behold, then: while we, like Martha, are troubled by the disturbances of many cares, awaiting timely assistance and consolation from those who, like Mary, sit listening, we have decided to appeal in humble prayers to all of you. We presume, on clear evidence, that you possess the grace of the eternal King and the favor of the heavenly court. We ask you to obtain for us and for the illustrious Anna [Note: [Col. 0706D] It may easily be inferred from this that these letters were sent to nuns of the Order of Saint Dominic. It is reported that Hedwig, Rudolph’s mother, after Albert of Habsburg died in Syria, professed among the nuns of the Order of Preachers; her example was later followed by Euphemia, Rudolph’s daughter, although it is uncertain whether this occurred before or after her father’s election as king of the Romans. It is certain that Rudolph founded the monastery at Tulln in Lower Austria and summoned thither nuns of the Order of Saint Dominic from Nuremberg, to whose Order he offered that monastery. He had vowed to build it in honor of the holy Cross before the battle with Ottocar, king of Bohemia. The foundation charter appears in the author of Austrian Piety (book I, chapter 15, p. 87): “Given at Vienna through Godfrey, protonotary of our court and provost of Passau, on the day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth indiction, after the Nativity of Christ, in the seventh year of our reign, 1280.”], our most beloved consort, queen of the Romans, the grace of divine omnipotence through your pious intercession. May His wondrous power make by grace what is fragile by nature exceedingly strong; may He support our weakness with strength and fortify it with virtue; and may He grant us from above to pursue what He has entrusted and handed over to us, so that the increase of His glory may be strengthened and the Christian people [Note: [Col. 0707C] When Leo III renewed the Western Empire, he sought the defense of the Roman Church, the supreme pontiff, and especially the orthodox faith. Likewise, by transferring that dignity to the Germans—or rather, by confirming it among the Germans—John XII is shown to have acted to preserve the majesty of Charlemagne, the first of the German emperors, as is clear from Otto I’s oath (Dissertation 1, no. 40). When the ceremony of handing over the imperial insignia began, the pontiff said during the presentation of the scepter (Dissertation 6, no. 28): “Defend with royal virtue the holy Church and the Christian people entrusted to you by God from the wicked.” From this arose the later opinion that imperial power in temporal affairs and pontifical power in spiritual affairs were unlimited—hence also the comparison of the two greater lights.] may at last sit with us in the beauty of peace and abundant rest, to be illumined by the rays of everlasting brightness.

---

### 309. LETTER IV

On the same subject as the preceding letter, and written in nearly the same words.

*(A.D. 1273, Rudolph Codex IV.)*

In the honor of that exalted dignity to which the Exalter of the humble has raised us, a burden that is almost unbearable has been fastened to our shoulders. When we consider its venerable and overwhelming magnitude, we rightly fear it. Yet just as we are submerged by consideration of our weakness [Col. 0707B], so we are in a certain measure lifted up by confidence in divine mercy, hoping that we may safely pass through the dangers of this stormy sea if you obtain for us the help of salvation—you [masculine plural qui] who have prepared for the heavenly Bridegroom a flower-filled bed amid the delights of your conscience.

For what will God’s mercy deny you, who deserve to have it propitious through the brightness of your virtues? What will your manner of life not obtain from the radiant queen, the Mother of God and glorious Lady of the angels, since through your (quorum, masculine plural) merits the Church shines, through your examples the Christian religion flourishes and advances? What will that host of the blessed not obtain through your votive affections, since it is made favorable to you both by the praises of divine glory and by the merits of an innocent life? It is presumed on clear evidence and confirmed by manifest signs that you possess the grace of the eternal King and the favor of the heavenly court.

Accordingly, through God’s mercy, we earnestly beseech all of you to weigh in pious meditation how great a cause for astonishment may arise from the fact that we, who bear the substance of dust and ashes [Col. 0707C], have been made vicars of Him who rules forever by means of the temporal sword [Note: [Col. 0707D] The argument for the opinion mentioned above is expressed more clearly here. There is no doubt concerning pontifical power: “Placed by God as watchmen,” says Celestine, “so that we may demonstrate the diligence of our vigilance, cut away what must be restrained, and establish what must be observed. Although spiritual care extends far away, it does not fail, but extends everywhere that the name of God is proclaimed.” Thus he admonished the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, in Coustant (Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, vol. I, p. 1066). We shall often hear Rudolph speaking in this sense of temporal power, although we shall never find him claiming any right for himself in another’s territory.].

Obtain for us through the pious protection of your prayers [Col. 0708A] the aid of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0708C] In the preceding letters he asked that prayers be poured out not only for himself but also for Anna, queen of the Romans. This confirms my opinion that those letters were addressed to nuns of the Order of Saint Dominic, among whom Rudolph’s mother and daughter were counted.], humbly asking that His wondrous power grant by grace that what is fragile by nature may be exceedingly strong; that He support our weakness with strength and fill it with virtue; and that He grant us so to pursue what He has entrusted to our weakness and committed to our humility that it may advance His glory, that the Christian people may prosper through us in peace and tranquility, and that at last the ray of eternal brightness may shine upon them and upon us.

---

### 310. LETTER V

Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, writes to all the estates of the Empire concerning the restoration of peace and requesting that they render him the obedience owed to him [Note: [Col. 0708C] The title is entirely appropriate. The letter itself reveals its purpose: the excellent prince, about to undertake a difficult office, after imploring divine assistance, sends an encyclical letter to all the feudatories of the Empire, as I stated in the argument, so that no one may fail in his duty.].

*(A.D. 1273, Rudolph Codex V.)*

**Argument.**—Having implored divine assistance through religious men and holy virgins, and seriously considering the restoration of the shattered affairs of the Roman Empire, Rudolph invites all the princes of that Empire, both ecclesiastical and lay, through this encyclical letter to render homage and swear the oath of fidelity.

Called to the governance of the Roman kingdom by the calling of Him who, striking down the pride of proud heights, sets devoted humility on high, we arrange in our mind and examine through wakeful meditation how, established on the lofty throne of majesty by the lofty and exalted King of kings, we may care for the restoration of the peace of the commonwealth, long since destroyed, and more cautiously safeguard those hitherto oppressed and subjected to the tyranny of tyrants from ruinous dangers.

From this we hope that, in such a struggle and contest—one that inwardly afflicts the mind and does not permit outward rest to the senses—heavenly assistance will come to us, and that we ought to advance through the increase of human favor [Note: [Col. 0708D] The distinction between an elected and a hereditary prince is well known. An elected prince needs favor and goodwill, especially that of the electors, to whom he generally leaves part of the government for that purpose; this does not occur with a hereditary prince. The king of the Romans, designated as emperor, needs both more than others, since among his electors he has men distinguished also by royal dignity. Therefore Rudolph seeks, after divine assistance, the favor of the subject peoples and princes. And rightly so, for he found Ottocar, king of Bohemia, and Henry, duke of Bavaria, among his adversaries, as will become clear below.].

This is why, since we have been placed at the summit of dignity so that the entire sacred Roman Empire, and the members which render it and us loyalty through devoted services, may fittingly contemplate our serenity with clear eyes and sincere affection [Note: [Col. 0708D] In the Golden Bull (chapter 2, § 8), the electors are called the nearer members of the Holy Empire. The remaining princes of all Germany, of Italy or Lombardy, and of Tuscany—or, as they are now called, of the duchies of Milan and Etruria—are members of the Empire. Rudolph addresses all of them in this letter.], we embrace all of you and each of you with every kindness [Col. 0708C] befitting royal serenity [Col. 0709A] [Note: [Col. 0709C] The beginning of the letter refers to the Roman kingdom. Here he calls his dignity “royal serenity.” In this codex he always dignifies himself with such an honor, never with the imperial title. Seifrid should have noticed this and used less liberally the titles that Rudolph himself rejects.], believing and confidently presuming, without any scruple of doubt, that the affection we show you through the favor of our serenity, which you will be able to experience, ought in its turn to receive from you an entirely fitting recompense through the devoted service of your fidelity [Note: [Col. 0709C] Namely, the collation or investiture of fiefs, which could and should be performed only by the king of the Romans, as was later established in the Golden Bull (chapter II, § 8). The confirmation of privileges and rights also belonged to him. All these matters are indicated in one word.].

---

### LETTER VI

A certain city congratulates Rudolph on his election, gives thanks for the remission of an offense, and commends itself to him.

*(A.D. 1273, Rudolph Codex VI.)*

**Argument.**—The city of Basel, recently besieged by Rudolph’s forces and soon afterward liberated upon receiving news of his election, replies to his letters, which were full of goodwill and hope of benefits. It expresses immense joy, thanksgiving, forgetfulness of past events, due service, and obedience. Finally, it asks him to confirm its rights and good customs [Col. 0709B].

Let invincible Germany rejoice and give thanks with its whole heart, rejoicing and praising [Note: [Col. 0709C] This does not refer to the Roman-German Empire—a name equally recent and false—but Germany is commanded to rejoice because of the election of the king of the Romans, as follows shortly below.]. After various calamities and hardships, the heavenly King, looking down from the dwelling place of heaven, has graciously deigned in our days to visit, through divine rather than human mercy, the election of a Roman prince in truth.

The nobility of this prince’s lineage and character, the distinguished virtue of his spirit, and his tireless magnanimity have been impressed by report upon the ears of those dwelling in the remotest parts of the world [Note: [Col. 0709C] Gerard de Roo (History of Austria, p. 8) reports that Rudolph, both before and after his marriage, followed Frederick II’s camp into Asia. Thus the fame of his name was celebrated even in regions beyond the sea. There is an excellent testimony concerning this highly praised prince by Siffrid in Raynaldus (1273, no. 9): “He was a just judge to rich and poor; he defended and protected churches and hospitals. When he saw soldiers preventing humble persons who wished to speak with him from approaching, he said: ‘By God, give people room to approach; for I was not elected to the Empire for the purpose of being shut away from men in a chest.’”].

Moreover, since, out of the abundance of Your Royal Majesty’s grace, you have deigned to send us, undeserving as we are, your letter, which clearly contains the sweet words of royal clemency—that is, that whatever resentment our city had harbored against you, with every scruple of any future dispute entirely set aside, you have remitted by royal kindness—we therefore rise to meet the excellence of Your Serenity, humbly bowing with every kind of thanks within our power.

We entirely and completely remit any offense that you inflicted upon all of us collectively and upon each of us individually, before the Lord called you to the summit of imperial dignity [Col. 0710A], according to the circumstances of the times, covering it over with the rust of perpetual forgetfulness [Note: [Col. 0709D] The causes of the war between Rudolph and the bishop of Basel are said to have been Breisach and Neuenburg, each claiming to belong to itself. From this followed devastation, fires, and killings. The city demonstrated by its actions that it had forgotten all these matters in the following year, as Gerard reports (History of Austria, p. 13). For when Rudolph went there, “he was received with the greatest honor by all the orders of the city. The citizens swore the oath of fidelity to him as to a Caesar, the memory of their former offenses having been abolished.”], and recalling to memory the poetic saying:

> He who was able to harm may at some time be able to help.

Therefore, with all our strength and affection, we humbly beseech the magnificence of Your Lordship to be pleased, through the munificent generosity of Your Magnificence, to continue to support us in preserving the rights of our city and the good custom that is an apt interpreter of the laws, as the letter recently sent to us by Your Serenity promises [Note: [Col. 0710C] It is known and established that the Romans too were accustomed to ask the king of the Romans to preserve their good customs. Yet there was a great difference between the Romans and the people of Basel. These people sought to obtain it through humble prayers; the Romans, on the contrary, before the king of the Romans entered the Leonine City to receive the imperial diadem from the hand of the pontiff, by which he became the associate of supreme pontifical power, required the same oath from the king once and again. The author of the Golden Bull itself, which fully declares the majesty of the Empire, likewise swore twice according to custom (Roman Ceremonial, book I, chapter 2), in these words:

“I, Charles, future king of the Romans and future emperor, swear that I shall preserve the good customs of the Romans.”

They willingly rendered this oath because they had been taught by the examples of Henry V, Frederick II, and other predecessors, who had experienced the hostility of the Romans. For they were not unaware that their ancestors had voluntarily subjected themselves to the Roman pontiff and that, consequently, the emperor acquired a share in power substantially different from that which the pontiff exercised in other territories acquired through the generosity of princes—territories in which the Romans dared claim no share.], with the special favor of your grace, as we are and intend inviolably to remain prepared faithfully to execute the commands and orders of Your Majesty, insofar as justice and equity require and insofar as our strength permits.

---

### 313. LETTER VII

Another city congratulates Rudolph on his election as king of the Romans and humbly commends itself to him.

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolph Codex VII.)*

[Col. 0710B]

**Argument.**—After Rudolph had received the crown of the German kingdom at Aachen, he sent messengers through the provinces subject to the Roman Empire to receive homage from all the cities of Germany. One of those cities, delaying its response, sent an embassy to Rudolph so that it might perform that duty with greater magnificence. It pours forth extraordinary praises of the crowned king; it gives thanks to almighty God for having freed it from the tyranny of invaders; and it humbly asks that its subjection to the ecclesiastical prince, confirmed by agreed pacts, be moderated.

Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, virtue, and strength belong to Him who sits upon the throne and lives forever and ever. He, as the evening of the world declined, has in our days adorned the monarchy of the Roman Empire, already tottering as though upon feet of clay, with a golden head, having crowned the king with honor and glory [Col. 0710C] [Note: [Col. 0710D] The safer opinion is that the coronation at Aachen took place at the beginning of 1274, rather than in the preceding year, as some believe. Stero, Gerard, and others consistently report that the scepter was absent on that occasion and that, for this reason, many refused to render homage. “Rudolph,” they say, “immediately demanded from the clerical and lay princes an oath of fidelity. When they refused because the scepter was absent, the elected king is said to have taken the sign of the cross and said: ‘Behold the sign by which we and the whole world have been redeemed. Let us use this sign in place of the scepter.’ After he had kissed the cross, all the spiritual and secular princes kissed the same cross in place of the scepter, received their fiefs, and rendered the oath of fidelity.”].

May the King of kings, rich toward all, who anointed him above all his companions, make him steadfast in the empire predestined for him, and glorious through the ages, with Solomon’s wisdom and riches—the breast of silver—with the victorious iron sword of warfare, and with the bronze proclamation of every virtue throughout the whole earth and to the ends of the world.

With confidence approaching the throne of grace, we offer to this imperial and most excellent Majesty of yours, our singular lord and the universal lord of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0711C] This accords with the opinion discussed above, which we infer from this passage to have been general among all.], our city, all our possessions, and our persons, certain that we shall find grace in timely assistance. For until now we have been possessed by alien lords, whose right was uncertain, and have lived in miserable servitude.

Therefore, let the throne of the king be established in clemency. As we are being transferred from alien possession to our own, from many lords to one, and as our temporal salvation now lies in your hand, O Lord, may the eyes of your compassion look upon us, so that we may serve our king with the greatest joy.

The reason we did not make this profession of due servitude and fidelity when requested by the messengers of Your Majesty was nothing other than our desire to present ourselves personally before Your Magnificence through the bearers of this letter. We selected them from among all our people because of their honor, so that they might perform the office of our embassy in your imperial court.

For this purpose we greatly need you, once our fidelity has been recited on our behalf, to take care, while claiming imperial jurisdiction over us, to arrange harmoniously with the venerable lord N. the commission and pact by which King N., then governor of the Empire [Note: [Col. 0711C] Above he had spoken of imperial majesty and the imperial court. Nevertheless, he never calls the king of the Romans “emperor,” but always addresses him by the royal title. For it was established that a person became emperor only through Roman coronation, even though whoever was elevated by the electors to that dignity governed the Empire.], subjected us to him, so that from this the aforesaid prince may have no claim against us; indeed, so that, for the sake of the excellence of your highness, he may be our helper in our times of need.

---

### LETTER VIII

A certain person writes to Rudolph that, through the work of the supreme pontiff and Rudolph’s wondrous elevation, the fallen condition of the Church and the Empire will be restored.

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolph Codex VIII.)*

[Col. 0711C]

**Argument.**—After allegorically describing the prolonged interregnum following Frederick II [Col. 0712A], during which tyrants, wicked in crime and irreligious, overturned all divine and human laws, the writer says that by God’s mercy Gregory X, distinguished in virtue and holiness, was established in the See of Peter. He was like the sun, while Rudolph was assigned to the wavering Empire like the moon. It was the common hope of all that, through both luminaries, its former serenity would be restored.

The wisdom of the heavenly counsel, which alone, uncreated, traverses the secret circuit of heaven, perceiving that the misfortunes of our first parent were transmitted to his descendants and provoked by the deviation of its own creation—which in a certain sense embraces the norm of transgression—generally suffers the weakness of the human race to be enveloped now in pestilence, now in disaster, now in the waves of the tempest of war. For a long time the moon, as though removed from the heavens [Note: [Col. 0711C] He reckons twenty-seven years of interregnum, during which the empire, its light having been removed, was tossed about.], condensed into the shadowy darkness of gloom, became a heavy night, full of dangers. Through it the wild beasts of the forests passed in herds, the whelps of lions roaring so as to tear the innocent. But in the midst of Egypt [Col. 0712B], amid a spirit mingled with dizziness, truth had come into oblivion; the keys of Peter had in a certain sense fallen into contempt; the liberties of the Church, twisted by furious tyranny, had been trampled underfoot [Note: [Col. 0711C] Bruno of Olomouc relates that these evils extended beyond Germany, in a letter to Gregory X, in Raynaldus (1273, no. 12). Ezelin and Manfred had divided Italy into factions and reduced it to misery. For this reason Charles of Anjou had been summoned, so that he might restore the Roman commonwealth to some sort of order.].

But the Most High, mediator between God and humanity, who is not accustomed to withhold mercy in anger, after the manifold distress of a dreadful persecution—by which the world, worn down, withered away, and by which the bond of the Christian structure was loosened, shaken by the losses of division—has now seemed to take pity on the pitiable misery of the afflicted. He has appeared to wipe away the tears of the faithful with the right hand of gracious consolation and to restrain the mournful lamentations of those who sob.

For he established upon the apostolic see a man after his own heart, like a most brilliant solar star, shining forth with the excellence of virtue, the works of holiness, and the rays of justice [Note: [Col. 0711D] After the election assemblies had been postponed for nearly three years, Gregory X was elected at Viterbo on 1 September 1271. His name was Theobald; he was a native of Piacenza and archdeacon of Liège, and was living in Syria with the Christian army. Accordingly, when he came to Rome the following year and was consecrated, he had Syria especially at heart. To send aid there, he summoned a general council at Lyons; he sought to bring tranquility to the Church and the empire and devoted himself to extinguishing the factions in Italy. All this clearly shows that the comparison with the sun is not inappropriate.].

In your wondrous elevation, too, every faithful and impartial interpreter may judge that, by divine command, the light of the lunar sphere having been restored [Note: [Col. 0712C] Just as the moon possesses no brightness except from the sun, so the king of the Romans, receiving from the pontiff a share in authority through the imposition of the imperial diadem, is rightly compared with the moon. Here, however, the comparison with the moon is used only to signify that light has been brought near to disperse the darkness of Germany.], the cloudy mist of the condition of the empire, tossed upon the waves until now, having been swept away [Note: [Col. 0712C] The principal cause of the empire’s instability may be heard from the letters of the recently praised bishop of Olomouc to Gregory: “In matters which we have learned through experience, we speak what we know and testify to what we have seen. For, according to the Apostle, perilous times have already come, in which people, loving themselves, put private advantage before the welfare of the commonwealth. Hence this plague has prevailed so greatly not only in the kingdom of Germany but everywhere, that, so far as concerns both spiritual and secular persons, they shrink from the yokes of their superiors. In the elections of kings and even of prelates, they either choose people who ought rather to be subject to them than to rule them, or they divide their votes among several candidates [Col. 0712D]—perhaps for two reasons: either so that they may extort more from several persons than from one, or so that, if one should wish to proceed against them with the rigor of justice, they may be defended by another” (in Raynaldus, 1273, no. 7). It should nevertheless be noted that this bishop adhered to the Bohemian king, Rudolph’s rival; hence, when he came to examples, he said: “An example of this kind is before your eyes and has already passed before ours, and is now present: it has passed in the election of the king of Spain and Count Richard; and it is now present in the case of the king of Spain and Count Rudolph.” This is plainly false in light of what has already been said.], [Col. 0712C] may henceforth shine more brightly and more radiantly to the joyful serenity expected by all the faithful from both luminaries [Note: [Col. 0712D] Saint Gregory VII, writing to William, king of the English (book VII, letter 25), says: “Just as, for the beauty of the world to be displayed to bodily eyes at different times, he appointed the sun and moon, lights more eminent than all the others, so, lest the creature [Col. 0713C] whom his goodness had created in this world in his own image should be drawn into erroneous and deadly dangers, he foresaw that it should be ruled through different offices by apostolic and royal dignity.” And, more than one hundred and twenty years later, Innocent III, in Baluzius (On the Affairs of the Empire, letter 32), says: “Just as in an eclipse of the moon the darkness grows darker and the obscurity of a greater gloom increases, so, when the emperor is lacking, the madness of heretics and the violence of pagans rise against Catholics and the faithful, multiplying their wickedness more treacherously and more cruelly.” From these passages it is clear that this manner of speaking, common in the Rudolphine codex, is by no means unusual.] [Col. 0713A], so that Jerusalem may be restored [Note: [Col. 0713C] I would not believe that the author of this letter is speaking allegorically here as well; for I do not see why the empire or Germany could be signified by this name. The reference, therefore, is to the true city of Jerusalem. At that time Syria was especially dear to the pontiff, the emperor, and the other princes, and especially needed military support, which was being gathered from every quarter. And, if I am not mistaken, this letter was written by some ecclesiastical man who was with the Christian army in the Holy Land; the following letter was likewise sent from there.] as it had been in ancient days, and that its deserted places may be made like gardens of delight, and its trackless wilderness like a garden.

## LETTER IX. A certain prince writes to the supreme pontiff concerning Rudolph’s election, commending Rudolph to him

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex IX.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—Prince N., exaggerating the calamities of the same interregnum and understanding that Rudolph had been divinely elected king of the Romans to punish the wicked and reward the good, earnestly begs Gregory X to support that king, so that peace may be restored, heretical depravity exterminated, and the orthodox faith extended in Syria.

The dignity of human understanding, not forgetful of its primitive origin—for all were born free in the beginning and did not know the eminence of a ruler—seemed to shake off the yoke of servitude and reject the superiority of dominion. But the unpunished license of wrongdoers, giving malicious people an incentive to offend, had scattered so many seeds of wickedness in the little plot of Mother Church that the poisonous growth of nettles and other harmful plants seemed to choke the Lord’s wheat.

Therefore Justice, looking down from heaven to reward the merits of the just and restrain the wickedness of the perverse, appointed upon earth, from the depth of its counsel, the lord Rudolph, most serene king of the Romans, as an animated law for all mortals [Note: [Col. 0713D] This manner of speaking occurs nowhere more frequently than in the Golden Bull issued eighty years later (chapter II, nos. 1, 3, 4, 5): “That they may be able to choose a good and useful man as future king of the Romans and future Caesar, and for the salvation of the Christian people. With God’s help I wish to choose a temporal head for the Christian people, that is, the king of the Romans to be advanced to Caesar. Nor shall they henceforth depart from the aforesaid city of Frankfurt unless the greater part of them has first elected a temporal head for the world, that is, the king of the Romans to be advanced to Caesar for the Christian people. The ruler, or temporal head, of the faithful.” Hence the comparison of the greater lights, first with apostolic and royal power and then with apostolic and imperial power, gave rise to the opinion that had prevailed in Rudolph’s time and in subsequent times became universal.], worthy of reverence in temporal matters. From him, as the law of right prescribes, I have received fiefs, together with my sons and the princes of the eastern regions, in a solemn and duly manifest ceremony [Note: [Col. 0714C] Fiefs, rights, and privileges were to be confirmed immediately after the assumption of the diadem of the German kingdom, according to the constitution of the Golden Bull (chapter 2, no. 8): “Without delay or contradiction he shall confirm and approve them by his letters and seals, and renew all the foregoing for them after he has been crowned with the imperial insignia.” Other princes were accustomed to receive confirmation of their fiefs at different times, as was convenient for each, depending on the greater or lesser distance of the places. Voluntary delay on the part of vassals, however, was an evident sign of disloyalty. Nevertheless, always (ibid., no. 9), “first he shall act in his royal name, and then renew it under the imperial title.”].

I humbly beseech your most pious fatherhood that, with the fullness of favor and the customary affection of benevolence, you may deign to assist my said lord, both fatherly and piously, for the good condition of the Christian people. May lost peace flourish again; may heretical depravity be extirpated; and may the planting of the orthodox faith, against the rivals of Christ’s cross, spread abroad to the glory of Christ [Note: [Col. 0714D] Nothing is more credible than that this unknown prince, who had received confirmation of his fiefs together with the eastern princes, was in Syria and sent this letter to Gregory from there.].

## LETTER X. A certain city rejoices at Rudolph’s advancement and wholly devotes itself to him

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex X.)*

[Col. 0714A]

**ARGUMENT.**—One of the many cities of the provinces of the empire, confident that it will emerge from the tyranny of its invader, renders the service owed to Rudolph. In accordance with the opinion of that age, it commends the imperial dignity and, as far as it is able, the office of the emperor.

It is no wonder that we continually give glory and honor to the Lord for your advancement, since he has bestowed upon us a pearl from his treasure. Nor does this come to us without reason as a fullness of joy, since the Lord, mercifully providing for us and assenting to our desires, has shaken off the rust and given us a vessel of the purest silver: the hope of our captivity and the redeemer of our destruction.

For before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world formed [Col. 0714B], it was predestined from the first age that you should sit upon the throne of imperial majesty, before whose tribunal natural and civil laws tremble; conscience willingly reveals what it has heard; ignorance is exposed; justice is strengthened; and iniquity is driven away. Therefore all who glory in the Christian name ought, and are able, to have recourse with fullest confidence to the clemency of your imperial majesty [Note: [Col. 0714D] Enough has been said about this opinion, common to all, in the notes to the two preceding letters, which the reader should consult.].

For the Lord has given you the power of the temporal sword, so that it may be your proper task to restrain the whole earth by the bridle of law and justice, and also of equity. For the Lord made you emperor [Note: [Col. 0714D] The earlier references to imperial eminence and imperial majesty appear to be tolerable. All learned men, and Rudolph above all, unanimously reject the title of emperor. The flattery or ignorance of this city should therefore be noted.] upon earth. We acknowledge you as our proper lord, and our city is subject to you [Note: [Col. 0714D] The writer wrongly says that this city wholly devotes itself to the king of the Romans. It acknowledges him as its legitimate lord, from whom it hopes to be restored to its former condition.], so that you may be a shield against the enemies of the faith, a defender of right, a lover of equity, an extirpator of wickedness, a pacifier of scandal, and a refuge for the powerless. For the power of Caesar does not abandon those who hope in justice; it raises up the oppressed, sustains those who have been raised up, protects widows, watches over orphans [Col. 0714C], defends the weak, cherishes the feeble, lifts up the fallen, and strengthens those who have been raised in virtue.

## LETTER XI. He receives with gratitude the congratulation offered to him

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XI.)*

[Col. 0715A]

**ARGUMENT.**—He pursues with abundant praise the congratulatory letter sent by Bishop N. and received through an envoy. He promises that he will never remove from his memory either its meaning or the envoy’s interpretation, which he had prudently fulfilled in carrying out his office; and he promises that he will always support both the bishop and the Church entrusted to him.

The pleasant words of your applauding congratulation, recently presented to our highness in a graceful and sweet eloquence, together with an unforced display of voluntary gratitude and devotion on the happy auspices of our elevation, have renewed our inmost heart with the fragrance of immense delight, by the sweetness inherent in their honeyed nature.

Indeed, such beautiful charm was present in the texture of the words praising the theme, and such an agreeable savor of adornment was added at the root to the excellent beauty of the sentences [Col. 0715B], that—even if, God forbid, no further fruit of any consequence should ever afterward spring from these little blossoms—the stream of hope nevertheless does not cease to flow from what has been said.

We graciously received your messenger, who presented the words of his mission discreetly and prudently, and judged worthy of being commended to our most tenacious memory both what the messenger himself proposed and what the letter contained. We perceive that you possess integrity of faith and purity of spirit continually directed toward advancing royal titles [Note: [Col. 0715C] In other princes, the royal title designates the summit of honor. The situation is different with the king of the Romans, whose apex is imperial majesty. It may easily be inferred from this passage that the bishop was concerned about this matter and had disclosed his desire to Rudolph, both by letter and through the envoy’s voice: namely, that the royal title should be advanced to that majesty. Rudolph therefore regarded the congratulation as especially welcome because the highest honor had not been confined merely to royal dignity; he rejects the flattery or ignorance of the preceding letter, which falsely called him emperor.].

For this we offer more abundant acts of thanks. Nevertheless, in matters concerning you and your Church [Note: [Col. 0715C] Although the congratulatory letter praised by Rudolph is not the same as the one that the author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 4, p. 34) presents as having been written by a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—for it contains nothing about advancing the royal title, and indeed speaks of the Church entrusted to the author of the letter—I shall nevertheless place it before the reader’s eyes so that the distinction between letters bearing congratulations and those presenting homage may be clear. It will also expose the deceptive variety of titles in this codex:

“Your glorious advancement, procured by divine auspices for the illumination of the whole world, long deprived of imperial light; for the protection and assistance of holy Mother Church; and for the propagation and glory of the Christian faith, had scarcely become known to me through a truthful report when it filled my heart with so sweet a joy that I can neither write it fully with my pen nor declare it completely in words. For from this I have plainly gathered that the Father of mercies, opening the eyes of his compassion over the desolation of the Christian people, wishes to put an end to the internal discord that has long raged especially within the entrails of the Roman Empire, and through the arm of your victorious power to sow throughout the world the peace that had been banished for many years. And since, in order to confirm the joy conceived over your exaltation according to the desire of our heart, I cannot personally appear because certain circumstances prevent it, I have decided to send to your highness a prudent man, trustworthy in every respect and in many ways worthy of confidence. He will in a certain manner supply my place in expressing my joy and, though absent, represent me to your lordship as presently ready for your royal commands.” [Col. 0716C]]

and in your necessities you will nevertheless find us ever ready and devoted.

## LETTER XII. Rudolph gives thanks to Gregory X, supreme pontiff, for graciously hearing his chancellor, whom he had sent as an envoy, and promises that he will always be most obedient in all things to the Roman Church

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XII.)*

[Col. 0715C]

**ARGUMENT.**—Rudolph gives the fullest thanks to Gregory X for graciously hearing his envoy Otto in the consistory at Lyons [Col. 0716A]. He promises filial obedience in all things and pledges that he will bring powerful aid to the Holy Land, where his father’s ashes rest. He ardently desires to confer with Gregory about establishing peace among Christians. He commits his dispute with the count of Savoy to the pope’s arbitration, with interpreters sent by both sides. He indicates that all the princes, barons, and others throughout Germany obey him, and that he will comply entirely with the pontiff’s commands.

Most loving father of fathers, revered above all by all the children of humanity who live under the condition of our mortality: rising to proclaim your praises, we offer abundant acts of thanks—not as many as we ought, but as many as we can—for you have graciously heard and, with your customary merciful kindness, more benevolently attended to the proposal of our sincere devotion, or rather our readiness, set forth and offered through the entirely commendable man N. [Col. 0716B] (Otto, provost of Saint Guido) in the presence of your holiness and your brothers [Note: [Col. 0716C] The embassy was arranged for the pontiff, who was residing at Lyons. Its leader was Otto, provost of Saint Guido of Speyer and chancellor, bearing a royal mandate: “Given at Rothenburg, A.D. 1274, on the day after the Sunday on which ‘Like newborn infants’ is sung,” that is, 10 April, the Tuesday after Low Sunday [Col. 0716D]. The same envoy, together with the German princes, archbishops, and bishops who were present at the council, took the customary oaths and confirmed the rights of the Holy See in Rudolph’s name “in June, on Tuesday the sixth of that month.” All the records of this matter are preserved in Raynaldus (1274, no. 10 and following).].

Therefore, persisting with an unwavering heart in our settled [*in solidati*; *insolidati*] purpose and with a pure [*pura*; *corde puro*, “with a pure heart”] and unfeigned conscience, we wish always to be found wholly ready, with all our strength, to honor God and exalt the Roman Church; to support all churches and ecclesiastical persons through the continuance of our favor; to be readily accessible to them in the administration of justice and liberal in the granting of favor, as the honor of the empire requires; to uproot from the very core, with every effort, the root of discord as it rises, for the universal peace of the world; and, in avoiding the occasion of dissension, to obey filially the decisions and commands of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0716D] An excellent prince’s fair and upright promise, which achieved its effect, as will become clear below. The Holy See never received a similar promise from the Swabian emperors, whom, bound by a terrible oath to receive the imperial diadem, it later found perjured and most bitterly hostile.].

With fervent spirit and heartfelt desire, we wish to come to the aid of that Holy Land, which, with the counsel or assistance of your goodness supporting us [Note: [Col. 0716D] Below we shall see (letter 23) that the pontiff generously gave twelve thousand marks, or thirty-six thousand gold pieces, for the holy expedition; for no one was better informed about Syrian affairs. He had been summoned from there to the chair of Peter and was likewise to cross over with Rudolph after his coronation, had not his death prevented the fulfillment of that hope.], the only-begotten Son of God preferred above all the regions of the world by manifold favor and consecrated by marking it with the sprinkling of his most holy blood [Col. 0716C]. We wish to aid it as powerfully as openly [*patienter*, “patiently,” in the manuscript], so that [*quod*; *quo*, “by which”] the people of God, afflicted and bound for many years by the enemies of Christ’s cross, may be able fearlessly to visit the Lord’s tomb for the glory of Christ [Col. 0717A].

The ardor of this desire burns more intensely in us because the bones of our natural father, resting there in exile far from his native land for the glory of the Crucified, are recalled every day with greater concern in our hearts. Who, then, could prevent a son from desiring with his inmost heart to become an exile at his father’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0717B] Rudolph’s father Albert, having set out for Syria under the auspices of Frederick II, died there and was buried at Acre, according to Gerardus (*History of Austria*, p. 7).] on behalf of him who, though abounding in the delights of paradise, gave himself over to exile and misery?

Among all our other and more ardently desired wishes, we have an unceasing desire to confer with you and discuss how the peace long lost among Christian peoples may be restored. In all the matters discussed with our chancellor through the sweetness of your honeyed piety, we offer our soul, body, honors, possessions, and everything that is ours to the pleasure of your holiness. And so that our gratitude in deed may correspond to our words, when it pleases you we wish to touch the feet of your blessedness with devoted kisses and to enjoy face-to-face the sight of your most holy person [Note: [Col. 0717C] This conference took place at Lausanne in October of the following year, as we shall see below (letter 34), and concerned the holy expedition and matters relating to the Holy See and all Italy (Raynaldus, 1274, no. 5 and following).].

Furthermore, concerning the dispute that has arisen between us [Col. 0717B] on the one side and the illustrious count of Savoy, your faithful servant, on the other, which is to be settled amicably or through justice, without tumult, we have both agreed that we shall send one suitable man, and the count another, to your court; they will have full authority to reconcile us with each other. If they are unable to agree upon a single decision, we both promise in good faith to abide by your arbitration, having firm confidence in the Lord that, since after God we wish to have no refuge or recourse except in you and the holy Roman Church, you will always hold all our affairs committed to your fatherly care as those of beloved sons [Note: [Col. 0717C] Ptolemy of Lucca reports that Rudolph, in order to assert the rights of the empire, sent his eldest son into the territories of the count of Savoy with armed forces. It is otherwise known that Louis, count of Savoy, joined Charles of Anjou when he came to Sicily. What should especially be noted is that the king of the Romans submitted his entire cause to the pontiff’s arbitration. The pontiff therefore attempted to bring that count, as well as the kings of France and Sicily, into friendship with Rudolph. Raynaldus, drawing on the Vallicellian Codex, cites the papal letters that bear witness to this matter (1274, no. 60).].

And so that you may not now be unaware of the auspices of our successful progress, let it be known to you that the princes, barons, cities, castles, and other possessions of the Holy Empire throughout Germany [Col. 0718A] unanimously obey our rule [Note: [Col. 0717C] He knew that Ottokar, king of Bohemia, Henry, duke of Bavaria [Col. 0717D], and others attached to them opposed him, but perhaps he hoped that they would not persist in their defiance. Meanwhile he announces the consent of the princes, which was necessary for his election to be confirmed and for him afterward to obtain the imperial insignia from the pontiff.].

We therefore beseech your most holy piety [Note: [Col. 0717D] The word *pietati* is absent from the Caesarean codex.] that, trusting N. in the ministry of his living voice, you may deign to make known to us your will and pleasure [Note: [Col. 0717D] The following words appear in the Caesarean codex: “Thus he has devoted himself and the whole empire to God and to the apostolic see with Caesarean reverence.”] [Note: [Col. 0717D] Gregory’s reply to this letter is preserved in Raynaldus (1274, no. 55), dated “at Lyons, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the year 111.” Among other things it says: “Although, therefore, we have not without cause delayed until now to assign you a designation, nevertheless, after deliberation with our brothers, we now, with their counsel, designate you king of the Romans. The reasons for this salutary delay—or rather, as we hope, for this deliberately chosen acceleration—will be explained to you by our beloved son, the elect of Trent [Col. 0718B], and Brother Henry of the Order of Friars Minor, messengers of your highness [Col. 0718C] …”].

## LETTER XIII. Rudolph gives thanks to a certain cardinal for having supported his cause exclusively at the Roman court

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XIII.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He gives thanks to N., a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, whom he had learned from the reports of his legates to have firmly and consistently maintained in the consistory at Lyons that, Alphonso being passed over, his own election ought to be ratified. He begs him, having laid the foundation, to ensure the completion of the lofty structure—namely, that the imperial majesty should be conferred upon him by the supreme pontiff.

It has come to us as an occasion of immense and joyful celebration that, although no cause arising from our merits had preceded and no prior acquaintance with your familiarity had prepared the way [Col. 0718B], solely, as we firmly believe, through the prompting of divine goodness, you rose to embrace us in such a way that, as we have learned from a faithful account, with a faithful hand you cast the foundation stone and laid the first step upon which the ladder of our advancement rests; and the foundations for climbing to the heights already seem to be rising more solidly [Note: [Col. 0718C] Alphonso, king of Castile, who had long before been elected king of the Romans, left no stone unturned to obtain confirmation from the pontiff. His legates were therefore present at Lyons, striving competitively with Rudolph’s legates, each by services and promises to secure for his own lord the imperial dignity through royal confirmation. Rudolph’s sworn assurances were admitted, whereas Alphonso’s legates departed without accomplishing their purpose. From this letter we learn that this cardinal was foremost among the brothers by whose counsel Rudolph was designated king of the Romans through apostolic authority. Rudolph himself testifies that this designation was only the foundation upon which imperial majesty would be raised. A more complete witness for understanding the true nature of the empire, nearly five centuries after its origin, cannot be desired.].

Therefore, excellent father, setting aside the praises by whose widely diffused proclamation your perfection has deserved to be commended in many ways, we incline inwardly toward the thanks we are able to offer you and humbly beseech your fatherhood that, through your native excellence of goodness, you strive to bring the praiseworthy beginnings you have made concerning us to a more praiseworthy middle and a most excellent conclusion [Note: [Col. 0718C] What he had called the foundation of imperial majesty shortly before, he now calls the beginning. Gregory embraces the middle and the end in the letter just praised [Col. 0718D]: “Moreover, since manifest advantage urges that the auspices of your advancement, which have happily begun toward the summit of that same empire, should not be delayed by postponement of their prosecution but completed henceforth by speedy consummation, we exhort your serenity, and with sincere affection and counsel advise you, to prepare and arrange yourself in such a way that, when we decide to summon you to receive from our hands the anointing, consecration, and coronation of the imperial diadem—and we intend shortly to assign a date for this, as far as the circumstances to be weighed permit—you may appear prepared, not unprepared, as the solemnity of so great a matter requires, and may hasten to what has been mentioned, not slowly but readily and swiftly. It is expedient that you should soon send to our presence certain persons who can fully inform us what date for this purpose would suit your convenience and, in all other respects, communicate your will to us.”].

You may securely obtain from us the fullest confidence that, in all matters which we know to be pleasing to the most pious mother, the holy Roman Church [Col. 0719A], we intend to make ourselves especially ready in accordance with your prudent counsel and to burn continually with filial reverence in fulfilling your wishes [Note: [Col. 0719D] The cardinal dignity, which was divinely instituted to be compared with the episcopate, is clearly demonstrated by the *Liber Pontificalis* in its account of Evaristus, who established the titles of Rome after the manner of dioceses or parishes, as they were called. Cyprian (letter 15, elsewhere numbered 20), recognizing presbyters and deacons as the governors of the Church of Christ, refutes the opinion of those who assert that the parishes instituted later have some similarity to the titles of the cardinals and that parish priests correspond to the office of cardinals. The example from which the institution of parishes and parish priests was derived cannot be denied. But to compare the chief clergy of the universal Church with them is the act of an unlearned writer. Rudolph honors the cardinals in the same way as the principal archbishops of Germany and displays filial reverence toward them as fathers.].

## LETTER XIV. He offers an abbot a royal request concerning the conferral of an ecclesiastical benefice upon a certain person

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XIV.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—In the next four letters, invoking ancient custom, he offers an abbot, a chapter, and a bishop royal requests concerning a vacant benefice or canonry, or one that will become vacant shortly. He urges the reluctant abbot by royal authority. In the same way, he approaches the bishop who denies that this can be done without consulting the Holy See, renewing his requests and holding out the hope of love and favor.

Since, at the beginning of our elevation, every church established in the Roman Empire is bound, according to the ancient and approved custom of the Holy Empire, to admit our first royal requests concerning the provision of one person [Note: [Col. 0719D] However carefully one investigates, one will find no example of requests of this kind earlier than Rudolph. The authors, having found one of these four formulas without the prince’s name and without any indication of date, defend a matter that is altogether uncertain. Consult the Dissertation (no. 55 and following).], we offer you our first royal requests, earnestly entreating your devotion and nevertheless commanding you by royal authority to ensure that the bearer of this letter—whose merits of probity, as well as the services of his worthy father and ancestors, have powerfully moved us to increase his honors and advance his interests, and who has also been commended to us as a man of sufficient learning—be generously provided, out of special regard for us and for the Holy Empire, with an ecclesiastical benefice within your collation, if one is vacant at present or as soon as an opportunity arises. In this way, we shall be obliged thereafter to honor you and your church with fitting honors.

## LETTER XV. He addresses the abbot a second time, but with threats [Note: [Col. 0720D] If the compiler of the letters had read this one attentively, he would not have imprinted such a mark upon an excellent prince. For who was more affectionate and, at the same time, more reverent toward all the men of the Church, especially monks, than Rudolph? “But with threats”? The letter itself shows with what moderation he tolerated the disobedient abbot in a matter he considered entirely just.] concerning the conferral of the ecclesiastical benefice for which he had previously interceded

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XV.)*

[Col. 0719C]

Although we previously sent our first royal requests concerning N., asking that, according to the ancient and approved custom, you take care generously to provide him with an ecclesiastical benefice within your collation, you have disregarded these commands and requests of ours, failing to recognize that these same royal requests bear the character of commands. As we have learned, you refused to admit them.

For this reason we have thought it appropriate to exhort and admonish your devotion once again with affection, nevertheless commanding you by royal authority to ensure that, making a virtue of necessity, you generously provide him with the said benefice if one is vacant at present or as soon as an opportunity for this arises. In this matter you should so preserve our right that, in turn, we may be induced all the more favorably to recognize the rights of you and your monastery [Col. 0720A], and may not be compelled to seek against you the goad that drives us to action.

## LETTER XVI. On the same subject as the two preceding letters

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XVI.)*
The radiant serenity of royal majesty so protects and safeguards the rights and customs of others that each person’s own rights are granted and preserved. How much more, then, is that same royal magnificence bound to defend its own rights, when it strives to preserve those of others? Since an ancient and approved custom had conferred upon our predecessors, the deified emperors and kings, the right that individual persons in the several cathedral and other collegiate churches should, at royal first petitions, be received as canons and brothers, to obtain a prebend when the opportunity arose [Note: [Col. 0720D] Although he uses the word *right* in these letters, he does not mean a right acquired through a privilege of the Holy See. Such a right the one Holy See can confer upon lay princes, and did confer in later times, as was stated in the dissertation. Rudolph himself confirms this, asserting that this matter rests solely on custom.], we, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors, send our royal first petition to you through N., asking with every insistence and affection—and at the same time commanding you by royal authority—that, considering the suitability of the person, you do not refuse, for love of us, to receive him into your college with the dignity of a canon, and that, if a prebend is now vacant, or as soon as an opportunity for it presents itself, you confer it upon him without allowing any circumstance to intervene. Act in such a way that, while you do not diminish the royal rights, it may please the royal clemency not to diminish but to increase the freedom of your church, and that we may not have to send you our letters a second time concerning the promotion of the aforesaid N.

**LETTER XVII. He commends a certain man to a bishop for admission as a canon by a royal first petition.**

*(A.D. 1274, Rud. codex XVII.)*

If you have carefully considered the splendor and dignity of the Roman Empire, which has deserved to be set before the eyes of all princes as though in a mirror—for from it those very princes derive the insignia of their principalities, enlarged by its generous gifts and endowed with the prerogative of honors [Col. 0720C]—and if, finally, you have weighed on the scales of your judgment how important a place the discerning man N. has hitherto held in our court for you and your church, and how important a place he may still hold in the future, you will certainly neither hesitate nor waver in doubt that for many reasons you are obliged to promote him.

For there is no corner of the Empire in which it is unknown that, by the ancient and approved custom of the Empire, provision of one person is owed to us and to our predecessors, the deified Roman emperors and kings, by every ecclesiastical prelate. Therefore, we do not believe that apostolic authority is required for the reception and provision of this N. in your church, since your church does not differ in the disparity of its conditions from the other churches of our kingdom that have provided, and continue unceasingly to provide, with suitable readiness for those on whose behalf we have presented our royal first petitions [Col. 0721A], nor is it supported by any privilege of exemption.

For this reason we have thought it proper to exhort your fraternity with complete affection [Note: [Col. 0721B] In the preceding letters to the abbot and canons, because of the service owed to ecclesiastical men, he added the words “at the same time commanding you by royal authority” [Col. 0721C]. But he venerates the bishop, although he is in some way subject to his jurisdiction, as a father, and makes no mention of royal authority, even though he had found him more resistant than the abbot. Indeed, the bishop had declared that he could not heed royal petitions without pontifical authority. It seems appropriate to cite here what Valsingham reports in Thomassin (II, book I, chapter 54, no. 6) concerning Louis VII, king of the French, returning from Palestine: “When,” he says, “a certain cleric brought him a papal privilege by which he was to have the first vacancy in every church of his kingdom, together with the revenues accruing in the meantime, he immediately burned the letters, saying that he would rather burn such letters than have his soul tormented in hell.” Although this example differs from royal first petitions, it nevertheless shows the liberality of the pontiffs toward princes in ecclesiastical benefices and other revenues of the Church while the holy war was being waged. Hence it would not be surprising if royal first petitions had also been granted to the emperors or kings of the Romans. Rudolph, however, defends them not by an apostolic privilege but by custom. No earlier example confirms this, as I stated in the dissertation.], so that, showing an approving response consonant with our right and with that of the Empire, you may have the aforesaid N. received by royal letters as a canon and brother, to obtain a prebend according to the order of his reception.

This will prejudice neither the church nor those already received; rather, it will preserve with us for you and for him an abundance of favor and grace, and will secure a fuller measure of benevolence. Whatever, finally, your will and intention on this matter may have been, do not fail to disclose it clearly to us through the bearer of these presents.

**LETTER XVIII. He remits services not rendered during the vacancy of the Empire.**

*(A.D. 1274, Rud. codex XVIII.)*

**SUMMARY.**—He remits to the faithful princes, or barons, P. and H., throughout the entire period of the interregnum, the payments or tribute owed to the Empire on account of fiefs, as well as other imperial goods consumed because of the wars that arose.

Our serenity judges and decrees that, just as persons and places are distinct, so too there should be a different regard for the merits of each and a different quality of recompense; and that each person’s grace and favor should be increased in proportion to the extent to which his dutiful loyalty is known to surpass that of others [Note: [Col. 0721D] Gratification above other virtues was especially conspicuous in Rudolph. A celebrated example of it is supplied by the author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 5, p. 41): “While he was staying at Mainz in this year, he ennobled James Müller, an ordinary soldier, with the rank of knight. When the princes expressed astonishment, he said: ‘When I was fighting against Baron Regensberg and, covered with many wounds and almost entirely abandoned by everyone, was in great danger, he placed me on his horse and rescued me from danger.’”].

Since, therefore, we know you, P. and H., to be so devoted and so faithful to the Holy Roman Empire, and since we have no small assurance that you are such in comparable matters, wishing likewise to bestow upon you the gift and munificence of special grace, we mercifully and generously remit to you all the services [Note: [Col. 0721D] Although *servitium*, occurring without qualification in charters of vassalage, usually means military service, the matter here is not personal service in military campaigns or at judicial assemblies—a term that also extends to the designation of palatine offices, as we have seen (*Codex Carolinus*, vol. I, p. 427)—but feudal service [Col. 0722B], as is clear from what follows. The matter therefore concerns censuses, tributes, or payments that had remained unpaid for nearly thirty years. [Col. 0722C]], which from the time of the vacancy of the Empire until our accession you were bound to render to each emperor or king, as well as whatever you received in the meantime from imperial goods on account of the wars that oppressed you. All this we grant you by royal kindness, mercifully and generously, inflicting upon you no penalty or threat of penalty whatsoever for the fault, but rather comforting you with every favor and with the richest grace of consolation and the benefit of protection.

**LETTER XIX. He gives thanks for congratulations offered to him.**

*(A.D. 1274, Rua. codex XIX.)*

**SUMMARY.**—He replies to a prince, baron, or other nobleman of Germany who promises to attend his coronation ceremony, declaring that he, in turn, will take care to do whatever contributes to the increase of that man’s honor.

Our serenity recently heard—and this has brought us a new accumulation of joy and increased the material of renewed delight—that you, whom virtue, together with the distinction of noble blood, has united to native powers and the blessedness of a more fortunate destiny as though by certain inseparable embraces, are congratulating us with an approving affection on the occasion of our elevation and advancement, and are showing yourselves ready and willing to undertake those things that may make the titles of our honor and advancement more conspicuous [Note: [Col. 0722C] Shortly after Rudolph’s election had been confirmed at Lyons, Gregory X sent him letters on 26 September, warning him to send as soon as possible men who would request the fixing of a date for the coronation, and at the same time men equipped with royal authority to be present for settling the disputes of the king of Sicily and the count of Savoy. We saw above (letter 12) that Rudolph replied to these letters. Gregory also sent letters at nearly the same time to the magnates of Germany, instructing them to accompany the king of the Romans as he came to Rome to receive the imperial insignia. I therefore suppose that this letter was written to Rudolph by one of them, although, since the matter is uncertain, I prescribe nothing to the reader. From his Vallicellian Codex (1274, no. 56 and following), Raynaldus indicates these letters and recites in full others written in the same year to the bishop of Salzburg concerning the date of the coronation, which had already been agreed upon. In them, among other things, the pontiff says: “We advised him to prepare himself in such a way that, when we summoned him to receive from our hands anointing, consecration, and coronation with the imperial diadem—and we announced that we would quickly set a date for this to him, to you, to the other princes and magnates, and to the communities of Alemannia, insofar as consideration of the circumstances allowed—he might appear prepared, as the solemnity of so great an undertaking requires.” He goes on to explain that, when the royal messengers arrived, the feast of All Saints that was to come first—that is, the feast of the year 1275—had been fixed in the consistory at Lyons for the coronation. He then urges him to accompany the king of the Romans, so that “surrounded by the glory and retinue of yourself and the other princes on the journey and at the solemnity of his coronation, you may appear glorious to all.”] [Perhaps: *more suitable*]. Therefore, reciprocally prompted, we offer ourselves to you freely and present ourselves as ready for everything that may likewise contribute to your advancement, and for all that delights your spirit. Given.

**LETTER XX. The Pisans invite Rudolph to settle the disturbances of Tuscany.**

*(A.D. 1274, Rud. codex XX.)*

[Col. 0723A]

**SUMMARY.**—An address by an envoy of the city of Pisa, in which he repeatedly begs the king of the Romans, in the name of the entire city, to come to Italy as soon as possible to calm the internal dissensions of its citizens. This would be especially welcome to many nobles driven from their homeland, and above all to the Roman pontiff.

The laws assert, custom approves, and antiquity bears witness that the region of the Tuscans, to say nothing of other matters, serves the Roman prince under tribute [Note: [Col. 0723C] The region that you hear called here, and below, a province was known in the age of Charlemagne as the Duchy of Tuscany. It had been offered, together with the Duchy of Spoleto, to the Holy See, although supreme dominion remained with Charlemagne and his successors. The same name appears in the charters of Louis, Otto, and Henry. But toward the end of the eleventh century, in the time of Boniface and his daughter Matilda, it was called the Tuscan march. Then, when nearly all the cities of Tuscany, following the example of the Lombard cities, had claimed their freedom, the ancient names fell into disuse and it was called the region or province of Tuscany; this finally acquired its modern name, the grand duchy of Etruria. Whatever name it bore, it was subject, together with the kingdom of Italy, or Lombardy, to the emperor.].

Relying, therefore, on this consideration, I speak as one for many, alone for the majority, to you, who, before the face of the prince, I am believed [Perhaps: *am sent*] to approach as intercessor for all [Note: [Col. 0723D] It too was divided into two factions, like the others. The envoy, however, who appears to speak in the name of the entire city, reveals himself in what follows as belonging to the Ghibelline faction.].

Behold the province of Tuscany, which by its proximity to the pious seat of the Roman Empire, as a principal member, ought to respond more familiarly to its head [Col. 0723B], lies torn apart by wars amid a multitude of schisms and is being torn apart by conflicts worse than civil wars [Note: [Col. 0723D] A few years earlier they had been engaged in great disputes with the Roman pontiff, and Gregory’s predecessor, Nicholas IV, had therefore removed their archbishop. The principal cause of the disputes was that they had rejected Charles, king of Sicily, first when he was serving as peacemaker and later when he had been appointed vicar of the Empire by apostolic authority; they had supported Conradin and had not hesitated to attack Charles with arms. Gregory, as can be seen from his letters in Raynaldus (1273, no. 33 and following), embraced them when they humbly returned to the Church, and then restored their archiepiscopal dignity to them [Col. 0724C]. This public reconciliation had not removed their internal hatreds, as is clear here.].

Twins clash in the womb, and at last the malice of Ishmael prevails in Jerusalem: the enemy pursues his friend, the stranger the member of his household, the Guelph the Ghibelline; sons become exiles, and those worthy of their seat are exiled into exile. The city of Pisa mourns, wounded by the hostile sword of enemies of the supreme pontiff and royal majesty [Note: [Col. 0724C] I have no doubt that the envoy is interceding for the exiled Ghibelline faction. For, holding the Guelphs in contempt, he praises his own people beyond measure—those whom Charles perhaps had sent into exile for the sake of peace.].
