The royal highness is believed to be bound to protect it and to strive more ardently to repel its oppression, in proportion as it has adhered to that same highness from the time of its forefathers with a firmer purity of faith [Note: [Col. 0724C] This perpetual adherence to the kings of the Romans proves the same point. The privileges that are emphasized—those of Henry IV and V, for example, in Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. III, pp. 365, 367, 376)—and any others that exist to strengthen the city’s loyalty demonstrate the matter still more clearly.] and it has been elevated by the privilege of a greater grace [Note: [Col. 0724C] All this is absent from the codex of the Cistercian monastery of Santa Croce, as Seifridus notes (fol. 69). Lequile uses this letter to attach an Anician origin to Rudolph. How contrary to the facts this is becomes clear from the absence there of the same words [Col. 0724D].].

Therefore let the royal highness be stirred to hasten his arrival, to be imitated [Perhaps: *invited*] by the favors of not a few Gentiles and embraced by the arms of apostolic power, lest our enemies mock us any longer because of the delay in his arrival [Note: [Col. 0724D] That is, the Guelph faction, which gloried in the expulsion of the noble citizens.].

**LETTER XXI. The emperor Rudolph replies to the Pisans.**

*(A.D. 1275, Rud. codex XXI.)*

[Col. 0723C]

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolph replies that he has sent his envoy to the pontiff together with an envoy of the Pisan commonwealth, so that, with the pontiff not dissenting, he may comply with their wishes.

We have kindly received the industrious man N., your envoy, recently sent by you to the presence of our majesty, and we have willingly heard him carefully and properly set forth, in eloquent speech, the words entrusted and committed to him by you. Since whatever may redound to the advancement and benefit of your community as a whole and in particular [Note: [Col. 0724D] We infer without difficulty that this designates the petitions of the entire city and separately those of the Ghibelline faction. But, unless I am mistaken, the letters of the Pisans to which Rudolph replies are missing. For nothing else can be extracted from the envoy’s preceding address than an invitation to the king to come to Italy.] readily accords with our disposition, we have willingly and generously inclined benevolent ears to your petition, presented to our majesty by him, and are sending our envoy together with your envoy to the court of the lord pope, so that, with his good pleasure and consent, your final wishes may receive full satisfaction concerning the matters contained in your petition.

[Note: [Col. 0724D] Charles, king of Sicily, had been appointed vicar of the Empire in Tuscany, as we have just said. Rudolph therefore, whose interest it was not to dissent from the pontiff in matters concerning Italy, communicates to Gregory—who was still residing at Lyons—through an envoy both the requests of the Pisans and his own desire to comply with them. For Gregory did not leave there before the Ides of May in 1275, in which year it is probable that these letters were written.]

For we are ready, and shall willingly show ourselves prepared for you, for whatever may, by the favor of the Apostolic See, advance your honor and advantage. Given.

**LETTER XXII. Rudolph sends an envoy to the supreme pontiff.**

*(A.D. 1275, Rud. codex XXII.)*

[Col. 0724B]

**SUMMARY.**—After the death of Otto, provost of Speyer and Rudolph’s chancellor and envoy to the pontiff, he sends another envoy, who is to conduct business before Gregory chiefly concerning the imperial coronation and other affairs both of the Empire and of Rudolph himself.

Most blessed father, very many mysteries of the interpreter of Scripture, in which filial devotion has been represented under a father’s gaze, have thus far flowed from the pen of our heart, indicating and expressing inadequately and insufficiently the affection of our inward mind, which we unfailingly bear toward the Holy Roman Church, our mother. Since, therefore, the desires of those who are absent are explained more fully and clearly by the utterance of a living voice than by the silent notation of letters [Col. 0724C], behold, we confidently send to the feet of your Beatitude the honorable man N., distinguished by great virtue, endowed with character and learning, acceptable to us through the merits of his goodness, and devoted also to you and to the Roman Church. We ask your holiness to deign to receive him with the favor that is fitting, as one whom we already believe, by the marks of praiseworthy conduct, to be a true follower and also successor of his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0725B] At the beginning of this year Raynaldus, from the Vallicellian Codex, reports a letter of Gregory X to Rudolph containing the following: “You know, dearest son, that the late Otto, provost of Speyer of blessed memory, your chancellor and procurator, possessing a lawful special mandate for this purpose, recently at the Council of Lyons, in the presence and with the consent of the princes and the other prelates and magnates of the kingdom of Alemannia who had then assembled at the council, recognized certain privileges of your predecessors, the kings of the Romans, and other privileges granted by those kings to the Roman Church, and, renewing and granting them in your name, promised under oath upon your soul that you would renew and also grant them, first as king of the Romans and afterward, once you had received the imperial diadem, as emperor. Although in other letters we may appear to have assigned you an unconditional date for receiving anointing, consecration, and coronation from our hands, nevertheless we wish the royal serenity to know that it was expressly agreed between us and our brothers, and is the intention both of us and of them, that before that date you, as king of the Romans, fully fulfill all the aforesaid matters that the aforementioned chancellor solemnly promised in your name, with the consent of the princes and magnates who had personally inspected them, when you have been requested by us through an envoy or letters.” The letters testify that a successor was given to Otto. We shall see that the remaining matters were conducted in the Lausanne conference toward the end of the year.]—that you may more graciously grant him, concerning our principal affair and that of the Empire, as well as concerning the other equally just petitions that he will present to your holiness, the result of a favorable hearing and a gracious, favorable response [Note: [Col. 0725D] This kind of letter is called a letter of credence. Very considerable matters were to be handled: the disputes of Charles, king of Sicily, and the count of Savoy; the abdication of Alfonso, king of Castile; subsidies for the preparations of the holy expedition; and other matters entrusted to the envoy, as well as others that were to be entrusted to him in turn. Among them, however, the solemnity of the future coronation claimed first place, by which the king of the Romans, assuming imperial majesty, was to be called emperor.]. Given.

**LETTER XXIII. Rudolph asks the Roman supreme pontiff to lend him three thousand marks in addition to the previous loan.**

*(A.D. 1275, Rud. codex XXIII.)*

**SUMMARY.**—Having received from Gregory twelve thousand marks as a gift for the preparations of the expedition to Syria, Rudolph asks for another three thousand as a loan, with suitable security. He also writes that he has chosen a capable commander, whom he will shortly send with troops into Etruria, as the pontiff had requested.

If we speak while preserving the reverence due to your fatherly benevolence, without stirring any spirit of displeasure in your pious heart, concerning the gratuitous subsidy of twelve thousand marks [Note: [Col. 0725D] Rudolph himself confirms that this sum of marks was delivered as a loan. The author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 7, p. 49), drawing on the Colmar Chronicle, reports that “the pontiff ordered the bishop of Basel, to whom he had entrusted the collection of tithes for the holy war in Germany, to pay twelve thousand marks to the emperor after he had crossed the mountains” [Col. 0726B]. As for the value of the mark, in Ducange’s additions one finds a charter of the year 1327 in which it reads: “That is, florins of twenty-four carats of fine gold, and sixty-five of the said florins, and no more, are to be counted in the mark of the Roman court.” Thus, if every mark had had that value, they would have amounted to a nearly incredible sum of money [Col. 0726C]. But the warfare of that period and the papal treasury make so generous a gift unlikely. The marks should therefore be understood as silver marks, of the kind Gregory expressly names in 1274 in a letter to Roger of Merlemont concerning tithes to be collected, in Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 373). According to Grimaldus of Verona, their value was three *baiocchi* and seventy-five [per mark], so that Gregory gave more than thirty-six thousand nine hundred coins as a gift, while Rudolph asks to borrow 9,225.], by which you so generously provided for us, and for which filial devotion fervently inclines itself toward the offering of the fullest thanks, it seems to us, from probable conjectures, that, when the magnitude of the undertaking has been weighed and the brevity of the time considered, that subsidy may be judged somewhat insufficient for so great and celebrated a preparation [Col. 0726A].

We therefore ask, with a countenance covered in modesty and blushes, that, lest any difficulty be raised against the aforesaid undertaking—which, after God, the apostolic right hand directs above all—you deign abundantly to add another three thousand to the aforesaid twelve thousand, by way of a loan, provided that suitable security is first received [Note: [Col. 0726C] What Gregory replied may be heard from his letters in Raynaldus (1275, no. 4): “We wish you to know that, because of the absence of our brothers and also of the merchants, we have been unable to attend to procuring a loan for you, nor did we think we should do so, lest your necessity should be disclosed, not without great danger to you, to our beloved son in Christ, the illustrious king of Castile and León, who was already very near us and was to be with us within a few days.”].

For we have already taken care to provide you with a magnanimous and experienced commander or governor, who, gathering an appropriate military force, will set his steps immediately toward that same province, so that he may preside over and benefit Tuscany, once the horrors of its ancient calamity have been put to rest [Note: [Col. 0726C] In the same letters the pontiff speaks of a duke or commander to be sent as soon as possible with troops, referring to earlier letters that are preserved in the same Raynaldus. There he says that the troops are to be sent into Lombardy, adding: “At least by the end of the present May, let there be in the regions mentioned above a good and proven commander.” Why Rudolph says that Tuscany must be fortified for him instead of Insubria is not at all easy to understand. Certainly, in replying concerning the requested loan, Gregory appears to have received these letters from Rudolph—unless perhaps, after the affairs of Insubria had been settled, he wrote again about the same matter, and the papal and Rudolphine letters no longer exist anywhere, which is almost improbable.], and so forth.

**LETTER XXIV. He sends Count of Fürstenberg to Italy as governor.**

*(A.D. 1275, Rud. codex XXIV.)*

[Col. 0726B]

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolph, believing the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, which in his time were called Romandiola and the Maritime region, to belong to the jurisdiction of the Empire, entrusts those provinces to Duke Fürstenberg, who is coming there, and commends him to the cities.

Rudolph, etc., sends greetings and benevolent good will to the excellent and prudent marquises, counts, nobles, captains of cities, magistrates, elders, and all the peoples established throughout Romandiola and the Maritime region [Note: [Col. 0726D] The first donation of Pippin, king of the Franks, by which the Holy Republic, or Rome, and its duchy, enlarged after breaking away from the impious Greeks, had been strengthened, is clearly established by the *Carolingian Code*. The Exarchate—called by Charles Augustus, son of Pippin, the Exarchate and Pentapolis—was recognized at that time under the names Romandiola and the Maritime region, although Rudolph, together with all the successors of Louis, continued to claim it for the Holy See under the twofold name of Exarchate and Pentapolis, through envoys at the consistory of Lyons and in person at Lausanne in this same year.].

Amid so many and such great waves of pressing affairs, by which the material for thought is continually poured into our heart, we are deeply troubled by a particular meditation and reflect with wakeful anxiety on how that noble region of Romandiola and the Maritime region, as the glorious borderland of the Empire [Note: [Col. 0727C] From monuments of that age it is clear that *pomoerium* is understood as *pomarium*, an orchard or garden. Rudolph takes both provinces in this sense in these letters. So firmly was he persuaded that the disguised name concealed a Swabian invasion distinct from the Exarchate!], in which the royal majesty has taken no small pleasure, because of the delightfulness of its peaceful cultivation, might bloom again in restored tranquility and, after the hostile straits of cruel and prolonged exhaustion and the exceptional storms of the tempest of war, come to rest in the harbor of desired tranquility and in the beauty of peace.

For in this region the Empire recognizes its own fosterlings [Note: [Col. 0727C] It is noteworthy that no mention is made of Boniface, archbishop of Ravenna, although some of his predecessors are found called princes of the Empire. Among them the celebrated one is Guido, son of Guido, count of Blandrata, intruded by Frederick I in 1158; from this arose schisms and violent elections for nearly twenty years, until Alexander III, with whom Frederick was reconciled. To him, as a prince of the Roman Empire, he confirmed all the ancient privileges, although he never received the pallium from the Apostolic See and always administered that church as an elected archbishop. There also survive letters of Henry VI, given in 1192, to William of Curia, who succeeded Gerard and the younger Guido after the aforementioned Guido: “To his beloved prince William, venerable father and archbishop of Ravenna, his grace and every good thing. Since among all the prelates of the world you are a special member of the sacred Empire … we earnestly request and admonish you that the noble men who from Rimini, Ravenna, Faenza, and the other cities and castles of Romandiola were expelled from their own houses by the late Emperor Frederick, who then ruled over them, etc.” Hubaldus too, whose election Innocent III confirmed, obtained a privilege from Otto IV in 1209, when he was crowned at Rome, in which we read: “Let both the present and future generations of all the faithful of our Empire know how our beloved prince Hubaldus, venerable archbishop of the holy church of Ravenna, humbly approached the presence of our majesty, etc.” See Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 371 and following) and below, the final dissertation (no. 4 and following).]. This is indeed the Empire’s delightful garden, in which it gathers the verdant and flourishing flowers of grateful subjection and plucks the pleasing fruits of devoted sweetness.

It is therefore natural that the royal highness should direct careful attention to its cultivation and protection, and apply the diligence of especially watchful care, so that it may breathe the fragrance of sincere purity through devotion and return, through complete loyalty [Col. 0727B], the awaited fruit of steadfastness.

Yet since a region is governed beneficially when it is directed by the leadership of a proper governor and administered by the diligence of a vigilant ruler, we desire that this province should rejoice in a circumspect leader. We therefore appoint the illustrious H., count of Fürstenberg, our kinsman, whom the merits of his prudence and faith render dear to us and whose proven valor makes him more distinguished, as governor of that province for you and for the whole region mentioned above. We entrust to him in full the exercise of royal authority in our name, so that under his diligent leadership it may be protected from harmful forces and established securely on the throne of what is beneficial.

Therefore, fosterlings of pure faith and sincere devotion, armed with these presents of our serenity [Perhaps: *letters*], representing us in his presence, since this count is taken from our bones and is flesh from our flesh, receive him joyfully and devotedly as an outstanding pledge of familiar affection and grace [Col. 0728A]. In all matters belonging to the office entrusted to him, reverently obey him, and take care to submit humbly with willing affection, so that the provision of august generosity—which knows how to reward the services of the faithful—may accordingly pursue the constancy of your devotion with a worthy recompense [Note: [Col. 0728C] Whether, in accordance with Rudolph’s desire, the whole province rendered obedience to this new duke amid the complete upheaval of all affairs, when the factions alternately held power, is a very uncertain matter. It cannot be doubted, however, that Rudolph, imitating his august predecessors, retained this most certain and most ancient of all donations, for all the successors of Gregory up to Nicholas III never ceased to reclaim it, as I shall say in the following dissertation.].

Know with certainty that we shall embrace with equal favor and benevolence the signs of obedience that your devotion displays toward him, as though they had been displayed specifically to us ourselves.

**LETTER XXV. By the same author, with the same subject as the preceding.**

*(A.D. 1275, Rud. codex XXV.)*

**SUMMARY.**—He appears to commend the same duke in a special manner to the magistrates and citizens of Ravenna, as one who would have his seat in that city and govern the entire region from there.

To the distinguished and prudent men, the elders, consuls, [Col. 0728B] and all the citizens of N., etc. [Note: [Col. 0728C] I suppose no one is unaware that Ravenna was the metropolis of the Exarchate both in the time of King Pippin, when it was regarded as a single province, and in the age of Charlemagne, when the Exarchate was divided into two parts and contained Emilia and the Pentapolis, so that Ravenna was named first, followed by Emilia and the Pentapolis, each with its own cities. That this arrangement continued in subsequent times down to the beginning of the eleventh century is attested by the Henrician diploma. Therefore no credence should be given to Pancirolo (*Notitia imperii Occidentis*, ch. 59), Albertus, or others who attribute that new name, Romandiola, to Charlemagne. “Romania” first began to be heard toward the end of the twelfth century, as is clear from the *Notitia* in Schelestrate (*Antiquitates Ecclesiasticae*, vol. II, p. 747), and from the Farfa Chronicle. In the following century it was called Romaniola, as is evident from these letters; and it is alternatively called Romandiola in the notice of the bishop of Cattaro in Schelestrate (ibid., pp. 761, 763), which belongs to the fourteenth century. In any event, Ravenna is found everywhere as the metropolis both of the Exarchate and of Emilia, Romania, and Romaniola. Nevertheless, I establish the ducal seat at Ravenna only with hesitation; for, as I shall explain more opportunely (*Dissertation* ult., no. 5), at that time the Exarchate was distinguished from Romandiola. Moreover, toward the end of this letter Rudolph says that we have placed him over you and over the whole surrounding region: words that do not suit the maritime city of Ravenna.]

his grace and benevolent goodwill. As we turn over the volumes of our conscience, and as we contemplate in the mirror of royal observation the cities subject to our rule, presenting to our majesty examples of pure devotion, we turn the gaze of our mind especially toward your city, which offers us the first fruits of unblemished fidelity.

Indeed, how calmly and gratefully we received it; how acceptable and productive of fertile rejoicing was the ardent fragrance of your native goodness, which shines in your hearts with the brighter spark of faith; and how, at the mere sound of a single command, you devoted yourselves to our service and received our messengers, whom we sent to you, with such solemnity and honor—we have truly been unable to express our feeling about this adequately through its effects.

These are the splendid signs of a virtue worthy of praise; these, I say, are [Col. 0729A] the sure proofs of constancy and the unfailing evidences of outstanding integrity. In these things you have hitherto rendered appropriately to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are his [Note: [Col. 0729C] Whatever city this may have been, it had placed itself under Rudolph’s authority, since he considered it to belong to imperial jurisdiction. Nor is this surprising: whenever the Ghibelline faction prevailed over the Guelphs, it rejected the legitimate dominion of the pope. Hence arose the error and confusion of writers who were insufficiently careful or hostile to the Holy See, and who take the inconstancy of peoples for a matter of right. Such writers either do not know, or pretend not to know, the nature of the possessions which princes granted in perpetuity to blessed Peter and his successors as a remedy or recompense for their souls. As though these possessions had been acquired by arms, they apply to them the same reasoning as to unjust possession or invasion, rather than the reasoning applicable to legitimate right and dominion.].

Thus, delightfully refreshed as though by an attraction of great sweetness, by the display of so welcome and spontaneous a service—by which, far from forgetting your ancestral nobility, you adapt yourselves to the royal good pleasure—we incline toward you with the fullest thanks. With an unchanging resolve, we intend on this account to exalt you and the aforesaid city, which we have indelibly received into the embrace of our household through the bond of steadfast union, with abundant favors and to enlarge you with titles of honor and beneficence, so that when the imperial power arrives—terrible to restless rebels [Note: [Col. 0729C] Meaning the Guelphs, who defended an equitable cause by adhering to the pope. But to Rudolph, who was convinced that Romandiola belonged to the empire, they appeared to be rebels. This twofold promise, however, was deceptive. For in the following year he was forbidden by Innocent V, whom his successors imitated, to descend into Italy, and was ordered, despite the opposition of the Ghibellines, to restore possession of Romandiola to the Roman pontiffs, its true and legitimate lords. [Col. 0729D]], but gentle toward you—when the terrors of war’s storm have been driven away, whose long calamity has wearied the face of the empire—you may rightly find, amid the beauty of peace and abundant repose, nothing sweeter or more delightful than the yoke of our dominion.

Furthermore, so that the splendor of the Roman [Col. 0729B] scepter may now illuminate the darkness of your region, and so that the same region may receive the flourishing increase of renewal, we have judged it appropriate to exhort the prudence of your community with the greatest urgency of entreaty that you hasten to anticipate with suitable marks of honor the noble man H., count of Fürstenberg, our dearest kinsman, whom we have appointed governor over you and the entire surrounding region, out of reverence for us and the empire; and that, in matters concerning the general and particular welfare of ourselves and the commonwealth, you attend him with gracious counsel and timely assistance, since the sender is customarily honored in the person of the one sent.

### 339. LETTER XXVI. To a certain Italian prince concerning the same matter

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXVI.)

**SUMMARY.**—He gives special commendation to a certain Italian prince—perhaps Napoleone [Col. 0730A] Torriani—who ruled in Milan, thanking him for his exceptional service to himself, the elected King of the Romans; he praises his sincere fidelity; promises to display royal generosity toward him and his people; and repeatedly commends to him the Duke of Fürstenberg, whom he has sent into Italy with his advice.

The vigor of your distinguished fidelity has shone forth in that you continually embrace the Roman Empire and boldly labor to enlarge its honor and splendor by magnificent distinctions, shining gloriously among its other tireless athletes and fearless champions.

Among all your great deeds, this appeared especially pleasing and most welcome to our royal majesty; it greatly accorded with our wishes: when you learned in advance of the arrival of our envoys, you immediately withdrew your victorious standards from the enemy whom your encircling siege had powerfully surrounded, sparing, out of reverence for our name and honor, those whom your authority could easily have subdued in triumph [Note: [Col. 0729D] I leave this episode of history to someone more fortunate, for whom it may be of greater interest. I merely point out that it is altogether incredible that Rudolph entrusted the Exarchate to this duke while Gregory X was either alive or aware of it. For Innocent V, elected toward the end of January of the following year and governing the Church for only five months, admonished Rudolph by letter to restore the Exarchate. As evidence of this I use the sacred college of cardinals during the vacancy of the see in 1277, in Raynaldus (ibid., no. 52), in a letter to the same Rudolph: “Moreover, concerning the lands of that same Church, and especially the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, which the pontiffs Innocent and John requested from your magnificence through their aforesaid messengers and letters, we repeatedly and earnestly beseech and implore you to have these matters completed at last by swift [Col. 0730B] execution.” For Rudolph had not stood by the promises made at Lausanne to Gregory X on 20 October of that year: namely, that he would assist in recovering and restoring to the Roman Church the lands invaded by his predecessors, specifically the Exarchate and the Pentapolis. Indeed, by sending a duke or governor into Romandiola, he was claiming the Exarchate and the Pentapolis for the empire. The change of name deceived him; but Gregory, not deceived by the novelty of the name, could not possibly have passed over in silence the appointment of a governor, just as his successor Innocent did not pass it over. Therefore this letter, together with the two preceding ones, must be moved to the end of this year, after 22 November, when Gregory entered Piacenza, his native city; from there, in the following month, passing through Parma and Florence, he went to Arezzo, where, after falling ill, he died on 10 January. Why the compiler placed these letters before the Lausanne conference is easy to understand. Rudolph had written in the preceding letter to Gregory that he would soon send a captain or governor. The compiler therefore, without regard to place or circumstance, immediately appended letters lacking any date-mark, which may safely be moved by anyone who has examined their meaning.].

For this, finally, we incline toward you with abundant thanks, and, commending the excellence of your fidelity with a worthy proclamation of praise, we have resolved with unchanging purpose to raise you and your people up with the lavish gifts of our beneficence and to enlarge you with fitting honors.

Moreover, since, relying upon your faithful counsel and your promise and favor, we have appointed the illustrious H., count of Fürstenberg, our dearest kinsman, governor of the region of Romaniola and the Maritime district [Note: [Col. 0730D] In the year 1273, when Gregory was traveling to Lyon, he stayed for some time in Milan during October and was received by the Torriani with great honor. Returning there in November 1275, he received Napoleone Torriani kindly out of gratitude: Napoleone showed him greater honor than two years earlier, was a powerful man, and was beloved by the people. It is said that Gregory then ceased to favor Otto Visconti, archbishop of Milan, Napoleone’s rival. For this reason it is not unlikely that Rudolph sent the duke into Italy at Napoleone’s advice. It was in Napoleone’s interest both to win Rudolph’s favor increasingly and especially to have the king of the Romans’ kinsman, a prince attached to him in those very difficult Italian circumstances.], we have decided to beseech your sincerity with the fullest affection, so that you may endeavor to assist him earnestly with fruitful counsel and timely aid. For we wish always to repay such services to you and yours with a pleasing and generous return.

### LETTER XXVII. He sends a certain religious envoy

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXVII.)

[Col. 0731A]

**SUMMARY.**—Open letters to all magistrates of the cities of Italy belonging to the jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, granting the religious N. full royal authority to arrange everything, with their counsel, for the honor of the King of the Romans and the welfare of the empire.

Rudolph, etc. To the energetic, etc., distinguished men, marquises, counts, nobles, captains, magistrates, and communities established throughout the Roman Empire, to whom these letters shall come: his grace and benevolent goodwill.

By the tenor of these presents we declare to the knowledge of your community that, having placed our fullest confidence in the prudence and fidelity of the religious and honorable N., we have judged it appropriate to send him to the transalpine regions of the empire [Note: [Col. 0731C] The regions which to us are cisalpine appeared transalpine to Rudolph, who was staying in Germany. He sends this religious man there with a royal mandate. Suppose that this occurred before Fürstenberg was designated governor of Romandiola, falsely believed to belong to the imperial jurisdiction, although Lombardy and Tuscany, which truly belonged to the empire, lay outside the boundaries assigned to Fürstenberg.], granting him a special mandate and full authority [Col. 0731B] 341 to establish, regulate, and arrange everything, with your counsel, that he may judge advantageous to imperial honor and the welfare of the empire [Note: [Col. 0731C] This deceptive appointment made Italy’s circumstances difficult, although after the Lausanne conference some hope appeared, while Gregory X was alive, that the factions disrupting the cisalpine regions might be reconciled and the greater controversies removed.].

Therefore we exhort your prudence with devoted affection that, favorably assisting him in these matters out of reverence for us and the empire, you take care to provide him, as willingly as generously, with gracious counsel and aid, and with whatever else he may need for this journey. Thus your devotion may rightly be commended by us on this account.

### LETTER XXVIII. He promises the pope that he will come to Milan for the coronation

(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolphine codex XXVIII.)

**SUMMARY.**—In these letters he gives the Roman pontiff his assurance that he will be present at Milan for the solemnity of Easter and will proceed from there to Rome to receive the imperial insignia from the pontiff’s hand.

[Col. 0731C]

To the most holy, etc. [Note: [Col. 0731D] It is easy to establish that these letters were not addressed to Gregory X if we consider that the pontiff was still staying at Lyon when Rudolph promised to be present at Milan. In 1275 Easter fell on 14 April; Gregory did not leave Lyon before 14 May of that year. Moreover, Rudolph was not unaware that the date of the coronation had been fixed as the feast of All Saints. Meanwhile, the pontiff was to confer with Alfonso in order to abolish all the discord between them, especially since a considerable part of Italy adhered to Alfonso; afterward he was to speak with Rudolph somewhere about several matters, something Rudolph himself had requested (above, letter 12) and greatly desired. Therefore this letter too must be moved from its present place and assigned to the following year, after the death of Gregory X and the election of his successor.].

That credence may be given to reports of our fortunate progress [Note: [Col. 0731D] Alfonso had already abdicated through Gregory’s efforts, and at Lausanne the pontiff had conferred with the King of the Romans. Since the date of the coronation necessarily had to be changed because the feast of All Saints was approaching, the Colmar annals testify that this was done at that conference: “The king,” they say, “had spent more than 900 marks on costly garments. The pope advised the king to come to Rome for the feast of Pentecost with two thousand soldiers, so that he might solemnly crown him Roman emperor.” Bernard the Treasurer, a contemporary author, reports the same thing (*Chronicle*, in Martène, *Monumenta*, vol. V), who ends his chronicle in this year. Raynaldus (1275, no. 26), deceived by Gregory’s letters, in which the feast of All Saints is prescribed, does not hesitate to accuse him of falsehood. [Col. 0732D] This letter, however, confirms the change of date. Rudolph promises to come at the agreed time and to be present at Milan on 5 April, the day on which Easter fell in 1276, and to receive the crown at Rome on Pentecost, 24 May. Raynaldus himself (1276, no. 24), citing the Vallicellian codex, reports that Rudolph prepared an Italian expedition in order to recover the rights of the Roman Empire, dispersed by the long interregnum, and to be adorned with the imperial insignia promised him by Gregory X; but that Innocent, through the elected bishop of Albi, Bernard, forbade him to enter Italy before his disputes with Charles, King of Sicily, had been settled.].

to receive from your sacred apostolic hands the diadem of the empire, we hereby solemnly promise and bind ourselves that we intend to extricate ourselves from all other difficulties in such a way that, at the approaching feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, we shall be present at Milan and from there, according to the pleasure of Your Beatitude [Note: [Col. 0732D] Those who say that Rudolph was not concerned about the coronation are indulging in prophecy. Innocent and his successors were responsible for the coronation’s being delayed so long that, as further causes arose, which will be explained below, it disappeared from view.], we shall immediately proceed to the imperial crown. We are sending you these open letters as testimony to this.

### LETTER XXIX. Rudolph thanks Gregory X, Roman pontiff, for confirming his election

(Year of the Lord 1275, Caesarean codex CXXX, Rudolphine codex XXIX.)

**SUMMARY.**—When Rudolph learned that Gregory had sent letters to all the princes of Germany exhorting them to accompany with honor the King of the Romans, who was coming to receive the imperial insignia, he rejoices exultantly and gives thanks for such great kindness, recalling all the former benefits. Because the imminent assembly had delayed the distinguished embassy, he sends ahead a messenger, or envoy, named Probus.

The sweetness of the immeasurable serenity poured forth by the trumpet of the apostolic office, now to be spread everywhere among all the worshipers of orthodox faith, has appeared to us especially from this circumstance, like a new light from heaven increased by fresh splendors, every shadow of darkness having been dispelled. It has now shone forth clearly because the zeal of Your Beatitude, which directs just causes and detests unjust ones, refusing to allow us any longer to be attacked by the slanderous assaults of our rivals, has publicly displayed the affection of paternal favor which it has made resplendent toward us through the instrument of pious and generous praise, mingled with the applauding sweetness of justice and equity. The work of the Most High, which his right hand has wonderfully woven in your person, has been brought manifestly into public knowledge by your sending to our princes and subjects letters of apostolic grace blossoming with every fullness of goodwill [Note: [Col. 0732D] As I said in the notes to letter 19, toward the end of the preceding year Gregory wrote to all the princes of Germany asking them to come with Rudolph to the coronation. When Rudolph learned this, he could not refrain from giving thanks to the pontiff in this most generous letter, saying that the thanks were owed to God Almighty, which he humbly declares himself unable to offer adequately.].

For these abundant gifts of your beneficence, by which we have been enriched with inexplicable joy, our tongue of flesh is insufficient for rendering the gratitude that is due; for human power cannot perfectly express in action the feeling conceived in the mind.

O wondrous clemency of paternal compassion, which has not disdained, from the earliest beginnings of our creation and birth, to offer us the breast of compassion, to extend breasts bedewed with milky fluids, fragrant [printed: *redolentia*; perhaps *reddentia*, “rendering back”] with a weighty pledge of love!

O ineffable gratitude for your favor, astonishing affection of love, which once received us, tender in the kingdom, delightfully into the arms of nurture, cherished us among the underage [printed: *impuberes*, “underage”; variant *puberes*, “mature”] and the grown [Note: [Col. 0733C] Seifridus and Lequile, in a remarkable manner, abuse these two periods in the author of the *Pietas Austriaca* (preface, p. 24). Nor should they be understood as a comparison with the other princes of Germany on the ground that Rudolph was a newcomer of recent nobility. Rather, they concern the auspices of imperial majesty in the election of the King of the Romans, which Gregory had confirmed in a solemn consistory; afterward he had been concerned that the requirements necessary for so great an undertaking should be fulfilled.].

Although our vigilant intention sighs for this, and although our ardent desire perseveres immovably in it—that, in response to the auspices so graciously and peacefully offered by you and by the blessed Roman Church, our most compassionate mother, to our progress, filial devotion may repay them with the fitting dignity—nevertheless, since, as we humbly acknowledge, the ability granted to us is insufficient for this, we are compelled to implore divine assistance, so that, from the abundance of his goodness, he may perfect by his strength what is lacking in us, namely, the pursuit of those things that are pleasing in your eyes [Note: [Col. 0733C] The candor of an excellent prince! The high and equitable esteem in which the Roman coronation was held! [Col. 0733D]].

Furthermore, since we had resolved to send our solemn envoys to the feet of Your Beatitude concerning this and other matters that weigh upon us [Col. 0733B]—[Note: [Col. 0733D] Raynaldus (1275, no. 3), citing the Colmar annals, reports that the Duke of Teck, the royal chancellor, and the elected bishop of Basel were appointed envoys to request the imperial insignia. Gregory testified to the bishop of Salzburg that they had indeed arrived, as I mentioned above (letter 19, no. 1); this letter undoubtedly preceded that one, since here Rudolph promises that he will send the same envoys.]—but have delayed dispatching them on account of the imminent solemn assembly of our court, now to be celebrated very soon [Note: [Col. 0733D] Gerardus (*History of Austria*, book I, p. 22) records two assemblies held in this year: at Nuremberg on the Ides of May, and then at Augsburg on 24 June. The same princes, Goldastus says (*Constitutions*, vol. I, p. 311), gathered in various cities. I would not have Hansiz believed, when he asserts (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, pp. 379, 381) that the princes first met at Nuremberg on Saint Martin’s Day in 1274, then at Würzburg on Pentecost, 31 May, and again in the following month, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at Augsburg, relying on the authority of the anonymous author of the Leobien Chronicle [Col. 0734C]. I accept only the two assemblies recorded by Gerardus. Concerning the Augsburg assembly, at which Bernard of Seckau, bishop and representative of King Ottokar of Bohemia, was present and delivered a very bold speech against Rudolph, highly displeasing to the princes, I shall speak below. Therefore this letter was written before the Nuremberg assembly of 31 May.], so that, after consultation with our princes who will gather there, the embassy entrusted to them might be arranged with greater solemnity and festivity.

Behold, we have confidently sent, or rather sent ahead, to the presence of Your Holiness N., surnamed Probus [Note: [Col. 0734C] In 1287, a council of bishops and an assembly of princes were held at Würzburg. In mentioning the assembly, the aforementioned Gerardus says: “While Probus, from the household of Saint Francis, bishop of Toulouse, was speaking, to his great discomfort.” The similarity and rarity of the name, together with Rudolph’s customary practice, persuade me to believe that this Franciscan, before attaining episcopal dignity, served as Rudolph’s envoy. What is certain is that the Franciscans enjoyed great esteem at that time among pontiffs and other princes. Holiness of life and true learning always raised men to honor and dignity without any recommendation from their ancestors.], a man whose conduct, rich in virtuous works, does not contradict the meaning of his surname. We most humbly beseech you that you deign willingly to hear what he brings to your ears and favorably anticipate it with gracious reception. Given.

### LETTER XXX. He asks a certain city for financial assistance for holding an imperial assembly

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXX.)

[Col. 0733C]

**SUMMARY.**—Since the long interregnum, with some seizing the possessions of others and no one paying the services owed, had reduced the imperial treasury to the greatest straits, Rudolph, who was about to hold an assembly, seeks aid from the cities of the empire.

For a long time we have lamented, with the bitterest compassion, the grave decline of the empire in its fluctuating condition, and the pressures and groans of the unhappy Christian people, so that in our prosperous age the restored flourishing of the commonwealth may advance through the salutary growth of peaceful tranquility . . . . . . . Therefore, on such-and-such a day, we have judged it appropriate to proclaim a solemn court at N. [Note: [Col. 0734D] That the first assembly at Nuremberg is being discussed is made clear by the very difficulty of the matter. The circumstances show that this letter must be placed before the preceding one. There Rudolph says that the assembly is imminent; here he says that it must be convened. It could therefore also be assigned to the preceding year.].

Its splendid celebration must suitably be provided for with royal preparation. But since we ourselves are not sufficient for the magnitude of so great a matter, for the effort of bearing so heavy a burden, or for conducting the solemnities of so costly a festival, we must call upon you and our other faithful subjects for timely assistance, and confidently burden you and them with a contribution of this kind.

Therefore we have judged it necessary to make the most urgent appeal to your prudence, with all the force of exhortation at our disposal, that, since we are perplexed by so evident a necessity, you take care to provide and assist us with so many marks, freely and with cheerful spirit, by the deadline finally specified to you by our beloved and faithful N. [Note: [Col. 0734D] It is clear from this that the opinion of the anonymous Leobien writer must be abandoned: all these circumstances require a suitable date.]. We ask you also to give credulous faith to whatever he decides to say to you in our name, just as you would to our own words.

Let there therefore arise the ever-grateful and diligently proven readiness of the faithful, adapting itself to royal good pleasure through willing and customary benevolence. In other matters, with an unchangeable disposition of mind, we have resolved to bind your hearts to us by this remedy of relief, so that it may be repaid by a reciprocal return; and you will truly rejoice that you have freely devoted so gracious a service to the uses of the Lord.

Moreover, your prudence is not unaware that it would bring an unbecoming stain upon royal dignity and would also cause harm to you if—God forbid—the lack of necessary resources compelled us to subject you and our other faithful subjects to the hardship of seizure for debt [Col. 0734C] [Note: [Col. 0734D] To provide for ecclesiastical persons against these hardships, Gregory X had decreed in the preceding year (*Second Council of Lyon*, II, ch. 28): “Although seizures for debt, which common speech calls reprisals, in which one person is burdened on behalf of another, are prohibited by civil constitution as grievous and contrary to law and natural equity, nevertheless, so that their prohibition may be feared all the more by ecclesiastical persons, since such seizures are especially forbidden in their case, etc.” In Germany especially this wicked custom had become established, as the Altach annals report in Canisius (*Ancient Readings*, vol. IV, p. 217).]. Given.

### 346. LETTER XXXI. To a prince who defected from him [Note: [Col. 0735C] It is established that at the beginning of 1274, when Rudolph received the crown of the German kingdom at Aachen, he betrothed, before leaving that city, his three daughters to three electors, on the advice of the archbishop of Mainz: namely, Matilda to Louis the Count Palatine, Agnes to Albert of Saxony, and Hedwig to Otto of Brandenburg. They say that Henry, Louis’s brother, regarded this as an insult, and that from it arose fraternal hostility and aversion toward Rudolph. This letter appears to have been written to no one else. The other lay electors were relatives; and Ottokar was neither present at nor consenting to the election, nor have any letters sent to him by Rudolph ever been found. Moreover, the royal title owed to Ottokar kept him completely away from letters of this kind.].

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXI.)

[Col. 0735A]

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolph, having tried through several letters to influence the mind of Henry, Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine, who had consented to his election but afterward became hostile to the elected king, neglected to request his feudal investiture and persisted in defiance, threatens to seek counsel and justice from his co-electors in a matter that can no longer be tolerated.

You once consented, together with your other fellow princes, by unanimous vote, to our person when solemnly electing us King of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0735D] That Henry consented to the election is so certain that Gerardus says the whole business of the election was entrusted to his brother Louis (*History of Austria*, book I, p. 15): “The princes, wishing to prevent the parties from again diverging, entrusted Louis the Count Palatine with the power of election. After he had long resisted, but saw that they were determined, on the fourth day before the Nones of October he declared Rudolph of Habsburg Caesar; the others approved, and with auspicious acclamations they repeated Rudolph’s name.”]; and afterward, as your counsel changed, you withdrew from devotion to us, turning your back upon royal majesty and neglecting to request from us your royal fiefs [Note: [Col. 0735D] Namely, in the following year at Aachen, when he believed that the right of kinship had been violated because the marriages mentioned above had been arranged without consulting him.]. Indeed, as may reasonably be inferred, you did so in arrogance and contemptuous abuse. Although repeatedly summoned by letters, and although at times you may have had free and safe opportunity to come into our presence for this purpose [printed: *suffuerit*; perhaps *defuerit*, “may have been lacking”], we do not believe that this opportunity has escaped your conscience, since you have gone off to distant places [Note: [Col. 0735D] The Golden Bull later established (ch. 2, no. 8) that fiefs and privileges were to be confirmed to the electors without delay or contradiction. In Rudolph’s time, however, this was not yet customary, as is clear from this and the following letter.].

Therefore, since we can no longer, and ought no longer, conceal your defiance without bringing disgrace upon ourselves and the empire, we wish you to know that we are immediately turning to those same fellow princes of yours, intending to ask them earnestly, in plaintive words, that concerning this case they assign to us whatever the order of law dictates [Note: [Col. 0735D] It may easily be gathered from this that the principal reason for holding the assembly was the opposition to Rudolph’s election shown by Ottokar, King of Bohemia; Henry, Duke of Bavaria; the Margrave of Baden; Eberhard, Count of Württemberg; and others in Germany.]. Given.

### 347. LETTER XXXII. Rudolph to a certain prince who adhered to the King of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0736C] Although the compiler never gives names, he clearly indicates here Henry, the brother of Louis the Count Palatine. Of the electors, no one except Henry adhered to the King of Bohemia.]

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXII.)

**SUMMARY.**—Writing again to the same man in nearly the same vein, he reproaches his obstinacy: neither letters nor repeated messengers had been able to move him to request the investiture of his fiefs from Rudolph, his lord. He says that he will report such persistence to the other princes, so that they themselves may judge this great offense.

In the zeal of fervent charity with which we sincerely embrace all and each of the princes of the holy empire, as noble members joined to their head, we have hitherto directed devoted effort and timely action toward this purpose, sparing no expense: that, through the applause of grateful devotion, you might recognize us as your king, to whom you are known to have consented by unanimous vote [Note: [Col. 0736C] You should take it as certain that Henry supported Rudolph’s election not as Duke of Bavaria but as Count Palatine of the Rhine. For both he and his brother are listed by Rudolph himself, in Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 415), among the princes present at his diploma. Louis and Henry, brothers, are listed as Counts Palatine of the Rhine and Dukes of Bavaria. At that time, as has been stated elsewhere, several members of the same house enjoyed the dignity of elector.], and as possessor of the empire [Note: [Col. 0736C] Writers ignorant of the imperial character should, following Rudolph himself, cease to call the King of the Romans emperor, since imperial majesty was not attained except through Roman coronation; therefore the King of the Romans was called the future emperor. [Col. 0736D]], and that you might seek from us investiture with your fiefs.

We remember that at different times we sent to you several suitable mediators and messengers, and that you sent them to us. We recall that first through N., and second through C., our beloved household officers, dispatched from the royal majesty to your presence, and afterward in your name, conversely, through M. and N., sent by you to us on several occasions, the aforesaid matter was discussed through various negotiations [Col. 0736B] [Note: [Col. 0736D] If I am not mistaken, the cause of such moderation and patience was more likely Rudolph’s innate gentleness, which he exaggerates, than any relationship between them.].

In the gentleness implanted in us concerning this matter, we waited in expectation that the tranquility presented by a smiling face and the offering of a fabricated proposal would give birth to the outcome which they had promised in agreeable sweetness. But, shamefully, we have been carried far from our intention. Our pleasure in the prince who was irreverently deviating from the path of our commands proved vain.

Since, while awaiting this promise, royal majesty had been so greatly inclined that our tolerance had in a certain sense lost the name and effect of true patience, and since the antidote of that patience has proved ineffective, we judge that we must have recourse to stronger remedies of healing. We cannot and ought not conceal your illness—your hardness, or rather your obstinacy—from your fellow princes, which extreme necessity truly compels us to disclose at the proper time and place, in order to seek judgment and justice for an offense of such magnitude [Note: [Col. 0736D] This letter appears to have been written after the Nuremberg assembly, since, after the minds of both Ottokar and Henry had been examined through messengers sent back and forth, Gerardus says (*ibid.*, pp. 24 ff.), serious action was being taken toward denouncing both as enemies of the empire. This is said to have occurred at the Augsburg assembly held on 24 June. Envoys were sent to Ottokar—Henry, bishop of Basel, and Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg—to demand from him, in the name of the empire, Austria, Styria, and the other provinces; so Gerardus and the author of the *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, ch. 11, p. 63) report. As for Henry, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, the initials in this letter indicate who was sent to him.].

### LETTER XXXIII. He promises the pontiff that he will carry out his reform against the exorbitant bishops of Germany

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXIII.)

[Col. 0737A]

## Argument

Rudolph promises Gregory X that he will apply every effort and all his strength so that the pope’s decree against the corrupted discipline of the bishops of Germany may be carried out, without respect of persons.

As the sparks of fervent charity continually grow—sparks which paternal affection toward a singular son draws forth as though from a furnace already burning abundantly—the benevolent fullness of your favor, with which your goodness ceaselessly embraces us, has been so widely infused into our mind through reliable report and so deeply impressed upon our innermost selves that, rising up joyfully from this to a hymn of divine praise, we are vehemently inflamed toward a free return of gratitude to the eternal Father, to his holy Church, and also to you, most blessed father. We are eagerly stirred by the dominion of both men [*potentatu*], and, laying before your most special commands all that we are and all that we can do, we offer ourselves entirely.

> **Note:** This opinion, then commonly held—namely, of spiritual, that is pontifical, power and imperial temporal power bounded by no limits—has often been discussed. On this occasion, however, Rudolph speaks of pontifical and royal power; for every king employs in his own kingdom the same temporal power as the Church’s external arm, as it is called.

Moreover, rejoicing in your praiseworthy zeal for justice as in the exquisite fragrance of spices—because you have struck with the sword of due punishment those bishops who have hitherto exceeded their bounds and turned aside into crooked paths—we promise, with paternal foresight, that if among them there should perhaps be someone, however closely related to us by blood or marriage, who has been rejected by God and who, through the mouth of his holy Church, should lift up the heel of disobedience against your commands, then, provided it pleases Your Holiness, we wish to expose the matter together with the person, in order to tame his arrogance. Given.

> **Note:** Bruno, bishop of Olomouc, as I said above (Epistle 8, no. 5), warned the pope about the corrupted discipline involved in episcopal elections. You will find that he also delivered a very extensive discourse on the utterly corrupt morals of clergy and laity in Raynaldus (1273, no. 14 ff.). But he is silent about the crimes of the bishops of which Rudolph speaks; nor have I been able by any other means to ascertain what in particular he has in mind—certainly serious offenses and ones deserving papal correction, as we learn here.

## Epistle XXXIV. He thanks a certain prince for letters sent to him and reports that he held a familiar conversation with the pope at Lausanne.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXIV.)*

### Argument

Rudolph writes to a friendly prince with whom he had maintained an exchange of letters, full of joy over the conversation held at Lausanne with Pope Gregory X, and over the appointed day on which he would receive the imperial insignia in Rome from that same pontiff’s hands.

We received the letters which you sent to our royal highness with the customary eagerness of your goodness, and in them we certainly recognized, by our understanding, the sweetness of your sincerity. Since the agreeable pleasure of receiving them, welcome and pleasing to us, has filled the depths of our heart with abundant joy, we incline toward offering you the greatest thanks for them, and we wish your desires to know that we shall shortly send our solemn envoys into your presence. They will faithfully interpret our common purposes, suitably settle matters with you, and inform you more fully and clearly about everything necessary and appropriate.

Furthermore, so that the continuing happiness of our condition may gladden your heart with a certain delightful refreshment, we wish you to learn from the savor of these words that we recently held a familiar conversation at such a place with our most holy father, the lord supreme pontiff. In that conversation we were received, heard, and more fully answered in all matters concerning the empire, embraced with ineffable devotion. At the coming feast of N. we shall now receive in Rome, from his sacred hands, the glorious imperial diadem.

Given.

> **Note:** The Colmar annals, in Raynaldus (1275, no. 36), speak as follows of this matter, which all historians unanimously affirm: “On the day before the Nones of October, Pope Gregory came to Lausanne. King Rudolph came to him on the feast of Luke, with the queen and almost all his children.” Since Rudolph admits that this conversation was recently held, these letters must certainly have been written in November, or at the beginning of the following month.

> **Note:** Namely, five months later, on the feast of Pentecost, 14 May, as the annalist cited above testifies: “That he should come to Rome for the feast of Pentecost with two thousand soldiers.” This day necessarily had to be fixed after the earlier date established at the council of Lyon had been changed, because the feast of All Saints, being only ten days distant, required a more suitable feast.

> **Note:** Here Rudolph himself states the three requirements necessary for attaining the imperial title: that the solemnity should be celebrated at Rome; that the imperial diadem should be placed upon the king of the Romans; and that this same king should receive it from the hand of the Roman pontiff.

## Epistle XXXV. Of the same subject, addressed to a certain city.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXV.)*

### Argument

With equal eagerness he informs an imperial city of the same conversation and of the coronation soon to take place at Rome; he indicates that it should send envoys there so that so great a solemnity may be properly conducted.

So that new and gracious tidings of the fortunate events of our happiness may delight your devoted ears, and so that the joys of a more fortunate auspice may shine forth, behold, we describe this clearly to you in writing: having recently been received with paternal affection by our most holy father, the lord supreme pontiff, having been kindly heard in matters concerning the empire, and indeed more kindly answered, we shall shortly receive in Rome, from his sacred hands, the sacred imperial diadem.

Since, however, we consider the presence of your envoys there altogether necessary for the celebration of the solemn rites of so great a festival, we exhort and admonish your fidelity to send, at the request of the honorable man N., your capable envoys, distinguished by authority, to the ceremonies of our said coronation. Thus, through their report, you may be more conveniently and perfectly informed about everything that must there be beneficially arranged for the good condition of the commonwealth and of the Christian faith.

Given.

> **Note:** Those who dare to represent the Roman coronation as a mere ceremony are entirely mistaken. It was necessary not only because it was the solemn culmination of the renewal of the Western Empire by Saint Leo III, but also because the prince and the envoys of the cities who gathered for so great a solemnity were instructed by the Roman pontiff concerning the proper administration of affairs and the preservation of the Catholic faith.

> **Note:** The three conditions mentioned above are repeated by Rudolph in almost the same words. There was no other way to arrive at so great a dignity; nor had any of his predecessors reached it, except Louis the Pious, who was crowned in France as an exceptional case.

## Epistle XXXVI. He thanks a certain prince for preceding him into Italy to receive the imperial crown.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXVI.)*

### Argument

He thanks one of the princes of Germany who had undertaken a journey to Italy with magnificent preparation in order to attend the coronation, promising that he would repay him suitably. He urges him to learn from the envoy whom he is sending to the pope the definite day of his arrival, so that he may not proceed farther but may complete the remainder of the journey with him.

It is not easy to express in words or letters how much your display of devotion pleased us, a devotion whose purity, as we now confidently presume, “does not change” (*quae non mutat*; perhaps *mutatur*, “is changed”) or deviate. For you left behind your famous and comfortable homes out of reverence for our honor and the sacred empire, and, entering the danger of the flames, moved with magnificent preparation into the regions of Italy in order to proceed with us to the imperial coronation. We received this with profound gratitude, and for this reason we incline toward offering you our fullest thanks. Without doubt, at the appropriate time and place, we shall cause abundant benefits of gratitude to flow toward you and yours, so that you can in no way regret having endured the burdens of labor or expense for the advancement and elevation of our name.

Therefore, with all the affection we can muster, we earnestly request and exhort your sincerity to consider and diligently seek out the routes most useful for our progress toward the imperial diadem, and not to be wearied of awaiting our presence. Stirring up all your own people, and others whom you can attract to our service by *allectitiis* (“inducements”; perhaps *allectivis*)—knowing most certainly that the man N., whom we are sending in our name to the feet of the lord pope, will state to you more explicitly the date at which your desired presence, and that of our other faithful servants, ought to bring us consolation.

Given.

> **Note:** This letter must have been given toward the end of the year, for the princes had begun their journey toward Rome in order to celebrate the great solemnity on 14 May.

> **Note:** Rudolph always speaks in this sense, for it was necessary that the title of king of the Romans should be raised to imperial majesty.

> **Note:** Gregory had urged the princes of Germany to accompany the king so that his arrival might be made more solemn; Rudolph therefore requests the same from the prince who had gone ahead.

> **Note:** The copyist correctly marks this as a collector’s error. Rudolph uses this word elsewhere as well (Book II, Epistle 3), and Du Cange shows in his Glossary that it is not a new expression.

> **Note:** After the Lausanne conversation, Gregory crossed the Alps and went to Milan. There, while residing in the city, he published on 18 November, during the dedication of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, the bull of Clement IV known as *In Coena Domini*. From there he turned aside to Piacenza, his native city, remained there for a few days, and toward the end of the year went through Florence to Arezzo. Rudolph’s envoy, arriving there, found the pontiff suffering from a terminal illness.

> **Note:** From that same envoy the prince was to hear explicitly of the arrival of the king of the Romans, whom he ought to have accompanied to the City so that he might enter it with more solemn preparation. Thus Rudolph’s arrival for the coronation was first impeded by Gregory’s repeated journeys across the Alps, which caused the earlier date of the feast of All Saints in 1275 to pass; then it was delayed by the unexpected death of that same pontiff.

## Epistle XXXVII. He attempts to reconcile the same prince with his brother.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXVII.)*

### Argument

He informs Henry, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, who was greatly angered, that, having joined himself by treaty to the king of Bohemia—long since proclaimed an enemy of the empire—he is uselessly carrying on hostile operations in the lands of his brother Louis; that Alfonso, king of Castile, whose support the enemies of the empire had relied upon, has entirely abandoned the title of king of the Romans and every hope of attaining imperial majesty; that the fraternal reconciliation which Rudolph had so long and fruitlessly sought would be advantageous to him; and finally that he must in no way negotiate a reconciliation between the king of Bohemia and Ladislaus, lest he too appear to be an enemy of the empire.

That the customary form of greeting, issuing from the benevolence of royal familiarity, has not been addressed to you—if you are willing to weigh on an even scale and with the just balance of judgment the treasures of discernment placed in the chamber of your heart—a reason by no means natural wavers [lacuna], murmuring against your actions, and is in no way surprised at the reason why what is written to others is worthily withheld from you.

Behold, illustrious prince, for the preservation of your good condition we have long interposed ourselves in good faith, and at great expense, to restore solid bonds of peace between you and your brother Louis. But you, yielding to the counsels of certain men who seek not your interests but rather their own, strive, to no great advantage of yourself and yours, if you deliberate well (to say nothing of anyone else), to destroy your brother’s territories, associating with yourself the enemy H. of the sacred empire and his other accomplices, through fires and plunder.

> **Note:** Undoubtedly N. should be read, as elsewhere, for Ottocar is meant. What is more, not only is a faithful prince of the empire violently invaded, but the empire itself is attacked in a hostile manner within its own districts.

Take heed, therefore, illustrious duke; consider, ponder and reconsider within yourself; be a diligent investigator in the dwelling-place of your heart. Reflect how the empire is bound to you, and you to the empire, each to the other; may a passing shadow not afflict you [lacuna] or ensnare you, so that what is momentary may not delight you.

But so that you may clearly understand how certain men have hitherto attempted to deceive you to the diminution of your status, holding out to you the king of Castile’s staff as though it were a reed to support you, we do not wish you to remain unaware that the said king has simply renounced, into the hands of the supreme pontiff, every right, claim, and lawsuit which he asserted belonged to him in the empire. He has wholly withdrawn, in name and in fact, from the imperial dignity which he had hitherto illicitly claimed for himself, freely resigning to us, as the true king of the Romans, whatever right in the empire he had hitherto claimed.

Therefore, with royal clemency, we advise you to restrain and curb your impulses, to make yourself and adapt yourself to royal good pleasure, and to look ahead to the outcome of all your actions in such a way that the sacred empire may always rejoice to have in you, its prince, a noble member; and that you may truly, not merely verbally, appear as a noble pillar of that empire, firmly supporting the throne of imperial majesty.

Although on other occasions we have fruitlessly offered our services so that you might be restored with your aforesaid brother to the unity of fraternal concord, nevertheless, provided that you are willing to comply at the proper time, we are not reluctant even now to apply every care and labor toward reconciling you.

Finally, since the king of Bohemia is a manifest enemy of the empire and persists under royal proscription, we firmly command you, under pain of forfeiting imperial favor, not to involve yourself in reconciling N. with that same N. in any way, because such a reconciliation plainly appears to aspire toward a conspiracy against us and the sacred empire. Otherwise, if you should in any way dare to reconcile those kings contrary to our prohibition, you would appear more clearly than daylight to favor our enemies and adversaries, and from now on we could not promote and love you as a faithful prince of the sacred empire.

Given.

> **Note:** The young king of Hungary, Ladislaus, is meant, with whom Ottocar had old and recent quarrels. At that time it seemed more expedient to foster these quarrels than to settle them. Before long we shall see Rudolph join forces with Ladislaus by treaty and take up arms together against Ottocar, winning a notable victory over him.

> **Note:** The author attempts to restrain the prince by verbal blandishments, lest he harm himself, and also seeks to soften him with the attractions of benefits, so that he may maintain his feigned anger without feeling that he has entirely fallen from royal favor.

> **Note:** Something is missing.

> **Note:** The collector’s negligence is evident. In the preceding epistle Rudolph, dealing with a friendly prince, competes with him in acts of service. Here, because of kinship, he suppresses his anger, yet abandons every mark of courtesy and does not conceal the character of one who reproaches. This letter, therefore, was not addressed to the same prince.

> **Note:** Henry is plainly indicated, the man discussed above (Epistle 31 and following). They say that he was proclaimed an enemy of the empire, together with Ottocar, at the assembly held at Augsburg on 24 June. Since, however, during the time of the Lausanne conversation Alfonso had wholly abandoned the title of king of the Romans—a matter dealt with in this letter—it seems that the matter should be understood otherwise on the testimony of the same witnesses. Indeed, after the exceedingly bold speech of Bernard, bishop of Seckau, who was Ottocar’s envoy, Henry’s envoy at that assembly is said by Gerard to have conducted himself very differently (*History of Austria*, p. 23): “Henry, provost of Ötting, who was present as envoy on behalf of the Bavarian, conducted himself more moderately, offering excuses not altogether unworthy of a prince.” Moreover, after Gregory departed from Lausanne and spent several days at Sion, as Raynaldus notes (1275, no. 43) from the papal register, he instructed the archbishop of Embrun, who was going to Germany to collect tithes, to reconcile these princes. Finally, this letter, written at nearly the same time, presses this reconciliation with particular insistence; yet we have no evidence from it that he was dealing with a man proclaimed an enemy of the empire.

> **Note:** Alfonso abandoned his false hope of the empire partly because of the adverse situation in Spain, with the Moors invading his kingdoms, partly because he was compelled by threats of censures, and partly because he was enticed by the payment of tithes, while the pontiff was at Lausanne. There Rudolph learned what he could no longer keep hidden from Henry.

> **Note:** In the *Austrian Chronicle*, under the year 1276, the quarrels and reconciliation of these brothers are reported as follows: “Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, and Henry, duke of Bavaria, brothers by blood, had been enemies of one another for two years and six months because of resentment over the election of King Rudolph, and had mutually ravaged one another’s lands by plunder and fire. With the assent of Pope Innocent V, they returned to peace.” If this is to be trusted, the reconciliation took place on 5 April 1276, since that many years and months had elapsed from Rudolph’s election. Gerard, however, assigns another cause to the quarrel: the marriage of the brother to Rudolph’s daughter; on that account the reconciliation would have followed two months later, namely in June. Certainly the two brothers were in Rudolph’s camp when he took up arms against Austria, as is clear from the royal charter published by Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 415): “Given at the camp at Passau, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, indiction IV, A.D. 1276, in the third year of our reign.” Gerard also gives other causes of the reconciliation (p. 26). For, describing how Rudolph moved his camp toward Bavaria, he says: “But Henry, seeing that he was unequal in strength, first made peace with his brother Louis, and then, at the pleas of his wife Matilda and others, obtained peace and pardon from the Emperor.”

## Epistle XXXVIII. The archbishop of Salzburg promises that he will come to the coronation.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XXXVIII.)*

### Argument

After receiving Rudolph’s letter inviting him to the coronation, he replies that he is greatly rejoicing because they have determined by unanimous vote to bring aid to Syria, whose priesthood and kingdom are in peril. He will attend the coronation if Ottocar allows him a little breathing room; otherwise he will participate in so great a solemnity through his envoys.

To the most serene lord, etc., the archbishop of Salzburg, etc.

We have been clearly informed, and have joyfully gathered from your royal letters, that your continuing service of devotion and faith has brought us the consolation [*consolati*; perhaps *consolatis*] of news filled with new and happy sweetness: namely, that the solemn day, the festal day, that desired day, has been appointed to take place at Rome by our most holy father in Christ and lord supreme pontiff. On that day Holy Mother Church will crown her dearest son, prince and protector, with the imperial diadem. Through him the broad expanse of the commonwealth, hitherto narrowed by private abuses, will rejoice, and will see itself once again enlarged according to the form of its former power under your fortunate name.

Finally, in that event kingdom and priesthood will sit together with equal purity of mind, so that they may discuss and arrange when and how the needs of the Holy Land—now, alas, close to destruction—may be succored worthily and in an orderly fashion. This is the land in which the only-begotten Son of God, having become human, assumed the miseries of human mortality so that, making us sharers in his divinity, he might also mercifully render us immortal.

Accordingly, as far as it lies within our power, we are resolved with all our strength to attend these sacred solemnities, at which heaven will distill saving dew upon the earth, and we hope there to rejoice together with the common joys of the Christian people, provided that the intolerable attack of your rival, frequent and continually increasing against us, allows us to draw breath and recover for a little while.

But if, through the sins of men increasing the burden of our affliction, we are unable to honor in person the divinely ordained solemnities of your aforesaid festival, God forbid, we shall nevertheless discharge the duties of our devotion there through solemn envoys. Thus, although we cannot adorn that celebrated day—which we cannot honor in accordance with the duty owed by our name and rank—by our own presence, we shall at least frequent it with humble acts of service.

Given.

> **Note:** Raynaldus, under the year 1274, reports Gregory’s letter to the archbishop of Salzburg, which I discussed in the notes to Epistle 29. Rudolph appears to have written to the same archbishop before the change of date made at Lausanne; indeed, the somewhat obscure wording of the letter suggests that the day of the coronation had not yet been fixed. Hansiz believes that the letter belongs to the preceding year and that the archbishop of Salzburg is speaking of the first date, namely the feast of All Saints. But the hostile actions of Ottocar mentioned below identify this year: the letter was written after the bishops had returned from the council of Lyon and before that king was proclaimed an enemy of the empire at the Augsburg assembly. At that assembly the envoys of Austria and the neighboring provinces complained of Ottocar’s tyranny, and above all Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, pursued his complaints at length concerning the burnings, plunder, and killings caused by Milota, the governor of Styria, who had recently been sent into his territories. He had previously reported this to Rudolph by letter (Book II, Epistle 15), which the collector wrongly assigned to the following year.

> **Note:** This is a correct definition of the emperor, according to the character of the empire renewed by Leo III in Charlemagne, a matter discussed at length in the first dissertation. Although all kings ought to be patrons or defenders of the Church within their own territories, the defense of the Roman Church belongs to the Roman emperor. Therefore, when kings are crowned (*Roman Pontifical*, “On the Blessing and Coronation of a King”), they swear these words: “I promise before God and his angels that henceforth I shall, to the best of my knowledge and ability, make and preserve law, justice, and peace for the Church of God and for the people subject to me, with due regard for God’s mercy, as I shall be able to determine better in the counsel of my faithful. I shall also show the pontiffs of God’s churches the due and canonical honor.” By contrast, the king of the Romans, or the emperor-elect, before receiving the imperial diadem from the pontiff’s hand (*Ceremonial*, Book I, section 5, p. 23), makes this oath: “I, N., king of the Romans, by God’s help destined to be emperor, promise, pledge, and vow, and swear to God and blessed Peter that henceforth I shall be the protector and defender of the supreme pontiff and of the holy Roman Church in all their necessities and interests, guarding and preserving their possessions, honors, rights, and law, insofar as, supported by divine assistance, I shall be able according to my knowledge and ability, in upright and pure faith.” Although this has been noted above, it is useful to repeat it in memory of Rudolph’s age. For certain writers, seizing upon the opportunity provided by the opinion of imperial power over the whole Church, seek to obscure the true character of the Roman Empire renewed by apostolic authority.

> **Note:** Here is new testimony to the opinion mentioned above.
