> **Note:** This is unmistakable evidence of the ferocity of Ottocar against those adhering to Rudolph after Rudolph’s confirmation at the Second Council of Lyon.

> **Note:** What I said above (Epistle 35, no. 2) concerning the envoys of cities is shown here to have been customary among princes as well, if some impediment prevented them from attending in person.

## Epistle XXXIX. The last letter of Gregory X, suffering from illness at Arezzo in Tuscany, to Rudolph.

> **Note:** Gregory’s letters in Raynaldus, said to have been given at Florence, are extant. In them he informs Charles, king of Sicily: “With him guiding our steps who knows, and him making the journey prosperous who is able, we arrived safely on 18 December at the place called Santa Croce in the diocese of Florence. There, having interrupted for one day the usual labor of travel, we then proceeded toward Arezzo, where we intend to celebrate the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. When the solemnities of that feast and of the following feasts requiring celebration have been performed there, we shall, God leading, continue the journey begun toward the lands of the Patrimony, as our condition permits.” Compared with the present letter, these words lend it some credibility, insofar as Gregory says that he contracted ill health while he was in remote regions in order to secure the imperial majesty for Rudolph. Yet, since the letter takes account of 15 and 16 December, and all writers consistently report that at Arezzo he deliberated about undertaking a journey to Syria with the emperor after the coronation, he was struck by severe illness and within a few days met a precious death. It is therefore scarcely credible that Rudolph, upon receiving news of the illness, sent a consolatory letter, and that the pontiff, having received it in time, replied with this letter, which smells of forgery. It seems more credible that Rudolph’s envoy, mentioned recently (Epistle 36), found Gregory suffering from his final illness and gave him letters addressed to Rudolph, which the collector corrupted. Although these letters have nowhere been seen by anyone, I do not reject them; nevertheless, I think they should be weighed carefully.

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXXIX.)*

### Argument

Gregory, suffering from a terminal illness and foreseeing his impending death, responds to Rudolph’s courteous letter. He offers him most salutary advice suited to an excellent prince and, after presenting certain proofs of his love for him, asks in return for his love toward the Church of God, which he commends to him again and again.

It is no small pleasure and satisfaction to us that the height of your imperial majesty rejoices everywhere in happy successes. For we have always loved, and continue to love, the honor of the empire and the increase of your prosperity in such a way that we consider the advantage of your magnificence especially our own.

Therefore, rejoicing with paternal affection as with a most beloved son in Christ, we admonish your sublimity, which rises above others, that however much the successes of human prosperity may smile upon you, it should in no way turn the excellence of your inward reflection away from love and fear of the heavenly Creator alike. For without doubt we are led astray by vain delight if, elevated by whatever degree of worldly eminence, we take pleasure in the events of transitory happiness.

Nevertheless, we give thanks to Your Serenity because, concerned about our illness, you offered us welcome consolation through your imperial letters. Nor is this undeserved: for, as our conscience assures us, no one who is known hitherto to have loved your happiness and glory more sincerely and faithfully can fall ill or succumb to illness at this critical time.

The very illness from which we suffer seized us in that place and at that time when, for the sake of your honor—which we have always loved with sincere affection—we left our native land and went to distant regions. Therefore, recalling this form of our affection more earnestly, we exhort your magnificence to place all these matters before the eyes of your mind in pious meditation and to repay us with a fitting return: whether God rescues us from the labor of this illness or leads us out of the prison of bodily frailty, always love and honor his Church.

As a most devout prince and most Christian emperor, strive to grant it peace and tranquility, so that whether we live or die, we may glory in your good works in its presence. Even in the present life we serve it as our duty requires; and if, trusting in God’s mercy, he should wish to summon us, we shall proceed to him with confidence.

Given.

> **Note:** Four letters of Gregory preserved in Raynaldus (1275, no. 2 ff.) should be consulted at leisure. There one may see expressions such as “royal serenity,” “royal highness,” “royal excellence,” “the throne of royal magnificence,” and similar phrases, almost at the very beginnings of your advancement. Here, however, we hear “the height of imperial majesty,” “imperial letters,” and “most Christian emperor.” I say nothing of the rest; you may judge for yourself.

> **Note:** This serious admonition of the holy pontiff, so close to death, is not unworthy of Gregory.

> **Note:** These words conflict not only with the character of the holy pontiff but also with the other intact letters of this codex.

> **Note:** These words also suit Gregory, if one understands “leaving his native land,” since the pontiff’s homeland was Piacenza. When he was elected pontiff he was living in Syria, having abandoned the archdeaconry of Le Puy and gone there with the Christian army out of zeal for the Catholic faith. Summoned from there to Rome and consecrated, he called the general council at Lyon, where, among many other matters concerning discipline and morals, the affair of the Holy Land was to be discussed; for this reason he ardently desired to return there until his final breath. He went there and celebrated the council, at which, once the other preparations for the sacred expedition had been made and Rudolph’s election confirmed, he sought through envoys and letters to remove Alfonso, his rival, from his attempt to obtain the empire, so that he might bestow imperial dignity upon Rudolph by placing the crown upon him, since Rudolph was to be the leader of that sacred expedition. For the same purpose he departed from Lyon for Bellecour, and although he was more than once attacked by the fevers to which he was subject during these various journeys, he nevertheless reached Arezzo safely, as we recently said.

> **Note:** These words are likewise fitting for the holy pontiff; for that reason I think the letter should neither be wholly rejected nor wholly accepted. When I come to Book III, Epistle 36, I shall disclose more certain indications of its being an interpolation. This in particular was why I carefully compared the letters of the imperial codex reported by Hansiz and by the author of *Pietas Austriaca*, so that the audacity of the collector—whoever he may have been—in adding titles and rashly altering the letters themselves would not lead anyone to doubt the reliability of the codex in the remaining material.

## Epistle XL. He writes to someone in the Roman Curia and clears himself of an unfavorable suspicion.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XL.)*

### Argument

Rudolph, who had always been generously received at Lausanne by Master Bernard—if I am not mistaken, treasurer of the Holy See—becomes concerned after once detecting a little cloud upon Bernard’s brow. He sends a religious man as an intermediary, together with a most courteous letter, and excuses himself, conscious that he has not offended him even in thought.

Rudolphus, etc. To the honorable and prudent man, Master Bernard [Note: Why I consider him the treasurer is evident from the office described in the letter. For either the vice-chancellor, the chamberlain, or the treasurer could perform such a function. That he was not the vice-chancellor is attested by Panvinio (*De Ecclesia Lateranensi*, book III, chapter 16) and Cohellius (*Notitia Cardinalium*, chapter 38, p. 249), for until the year 1274 Master John Lecacorvius of Piacenza held that office, and from then until 1277 Master Lanfrancus, archdeacon of Bergamo. As for the chamberlain, this should not even be considered, since that distinguished office was held by the cardinals of the Roman Church. Therefore this Bernard must have been the treasurer. The distinguished Muratori (*Scriptores Italici*, vol. VII, p. 657) persuaded himself that he had published from a manuscript in the Estense Library Bernard the treasurer’s book *On the Acquisition of the Holy Land*. He says in his preface that it was written in French and translated into Latin in the year 1320 by Brother Francis Pipino of Bologna, of the Order of Preachers; yet Pipino’s work ends in 1230, although Bernard reaches the year 1275. Edmund Martène (*Veterum Monumentorum*, vol. V, chapters 204) likewise does not concern himself with whether the work was written in French or Latin: “These things,” he says, “are taken from the history of Damietta. But concerning the departure of King John, how the Christians returned Damietta to the sultan, and several things that followed afterward, Bernard the treasurer writes as follows.” And again (chapter 297): “These things concerning the deeds of King John are taken from the history of Bernard the treasurer. I have not discovered what the outcome was—whether he did not complete the history, or whether the manuscript from which I took it was incomplete.” Whatever the truth concerning the Latin history, the similarity of the name, the age, and the office persuaded me to believe that these letters were addressed to this Bernard. Nevertheless, I would not dare assert it as certain.]

The serene graciousness of your gentle countenance, which represents the mystical disposition of your heart, has thus far been neither ignorant nor fearful in the administration and advancement of royal affairs; it has so warmly and powerfully displayed toward us its virtuous impulses that, with the sole exception of our most holy father, the lord pope [Note: From Bernard’s reply, which follows this letter, we can determine its date, namely toward the end of December. For Bernard replied after the pope had died. How much credibility, then, deserves the assertion in the preceding letter concerning Rudolph’s consolatory letter to the ailing pope?], we rightly ascribe principally to you whatever honor and glory the right hand of apostolic consolation has added to the progress of our exaltation.

For to you we have most confidently disclosed the innermost secrets of our mind, placing upon your [perhaps: your own] shoulders the weight of the whole care and burden of our anxiety. From this there proceeded a most desirable benefit, and the advancement we had hoped for emerged. Yet recently—we report this with a heavy heart—it has seemed to us, on the basis of certain notable conjectures, that the admirable serenity of your countenance toward us has probably changed, and that the gentleness of your mind has been embittered. Concerning this, the sharp sting of astonishment has rightly pierced our inmost being, perplexed by the unforeseeable novelty of the matter.

For incontaminable truth of conscience, more solemn than any deposition of witnesses, testifies that we have never attempted anything by word or deed, nor presumed anything even in thought, that ought to have produced in you a spirit of displeasure. Rather, we have always desired, and still constantly hold in mind, to be present to you and yours, when a suitable opportunity should arise, with gracious and generous assistance, and to aspire more abundantly to the overflowing outpourings of our beneficence.

Whatever may have been the beginning from which this movement of ours arose, we safely submit it to your judgment, to be freely decided according to what your prudent circumspection shall deem fitting [Note: What an excellent prince’s character! Suspicion alone draws a frank apology from his heart. Nevertheless, there is another reason why he wishes so earnestly to preserve Bernard’s goodwill inviolate, as we saw in the preceding letter (letter 23) and shall soon see confirmed.].

For this reason we earnestly request your honesty that you may receive our apology with a gentle spirit and, from the sanctuary of your mind, sweep away with the broom of right judgment whatever cloud or resentment the impression of an unfavorable suspicion may have implanted, introducing the guest of truth with greater charity.

And behold, we have therefore deemed it appropriate to send to you especially an honorable and religious man [Note: The dignity of the office and Rudolph’s concern are thereby made especially clear.], earnestly asking that you take care to place unquestioning faith in him as the truthful spokesman for our innocence in these matters. Given.

## 361. LETTER XLI. A reply to the preceding letter

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XLI.)*

**Argument.**—Bernard replies that, if he had perhaps given occasion for suspicion because he had not personally visited Rudolph at Lausanne, he had been prevented by the multitude of affairs familiar to the royal retinue, which had compelled him to remain there for a considerable time after both courts had departed. In other matters, he deserved praise rather than suspicion concerning his character; despite the hostility of slanderers, he was and would remain unchanging. He says that he will add nothing concerning the pope’s death, but will announce the election of his successor.

In the letter that your Excellency most recently sent me, my eyes recoiled from the complaint you formed concerning my change of attitude toward you, and my mind, not without profound astonishment, examined and scrutinized it with the greatest care: what could have formed the beginning of this complaint; what change, which truth certainly does not know, may have offered slight indications to someone’s perhaps disordered imagination; what sort of conjecture it may have supplied [Col. 0747A].

Without doubt, the inquiry of the investigator failed in these matters, and the judgment of the examination found nothing. For how could it have found what did not exist? If the complaint is directed to what took place at Lausanne, the arduous labors involved in conducting your affairs do not permit such an interpretation [Note: The principal matters handled there were the collection throughout Germany of the six-year tithe for the preparation of the sacred expedition. Gregory placed the archbishop of Embrun in charge of this. Raynaldus (1275, no. 43) records the oath to be sworn by the collectors, so that the tithe granted by the Apostolic See for aid to the Holy Land might everywhere be collected with complete fidelity.

Another matter of no small importance was the coronation, without which he could not be emperor; but, like the king of Castile, he gloried only in the imperial title. He himself admits how important it was in the confirmation of the rights of the Holy See: “If,” he says, “because of my business the Roman Church should be forced to incur war, I shall assist it as necessity demands in the expenses.”

What other matters required so many of Bernard’s labors Rudolph embraced in only two words: “benefit” and “advancement.” By “benefit” he included both the tithes and whatever assistance he had obtained; by “advancement,” the day of Pentecost already fixed, on which he was to be advanced to the imperial dignity at Rome and crowned with the imperial diadem by the supreme pontiff.], unless perhaps the occasion for some complaint arises from the fact that I did not personally come to your presence at the lodging where you were then staying [Note: It is hardly easy to believe that the two affairs mentioned above, together with several other lesser matters that had to be completed during the short number of days Rudolph remained at Lausanne, were the reason he failed in his duty toward so great a prince. Bernard undoubtedly possessed my own disposition: namely, he preferred leisure for letters to every other obligation.].

The Most High knows that I was prevented by the business occupying me there, which kept me at Lausanne after the departure of both courts, as your own people know. But if the complaint refers to the matters entrusted to the venerable Father N. [Note: He seems to indicate the archbishop of Embrun, who had been placed in charge of collecting the tithes after Rudolph, departing from Lausanne, had reached Sion.], and which afterward, through merchants and by the special mandate of the late lord Gregory [Note: Thus other financial assistance had been decreed for Rudolph. For several months earlier the pope had considered it unsuitable to disclose the royal need to Alfonso (letter 22); moreover, since the merchants were absent, the sum of marks that Rudolph had promised to borrow had been deferred until a more suitable opportunity. Nor are all the matters they discussed at Lausanne found committed to letters. Everyone sees that the subject here is financial. The date of the letter must also be noted: it was written after the tenth day of January, the day of Gregory’s death. This increasingly confirms that the consolatory letter supposedly addressed by Rudolph to the ailing pope is spurious, as I said above (letter 39).], I disclosed in my letters to certain of your familiars, and as to how those matters are to be directed, the very nature of the facts protects my innocence, since they deserved a proclamation of merit rather than any accusation of fickleness.

But, illustrious prince [Col. 0747B], there is no need to dwell on excuses where, with him who is the faithful witness in heaven as witness, no impulse toward accusation can even be conjectured—an impulse that some detractor, intending to harm both you and me, may have fashioned with a third tongue.

Let the concern of your royal highness therefore be at rest, because my constancy, by God’s grace—if I may speak without a charge of boasting—is known, has thus far remained unmoved and free from the disgrace of any fickleness, and, while the vital spirit sustains my limbs, will remain, with God’s help, unchanged, firm, and undefiled.

Certainly, a full discussion concerning other matters affecting you was held with N., and, as we agreed together, he is, I think, writing to you more fully [Note: In the frequently cited letter of the cardinals during the vacancy of the See, in Raynaldus (1277, no. 48), we read: “So that, with your steps placed upon a peaceful path, the business of your advancement might proceed more quietly and be conducted more securely; for this purpose, as you know, the same pontiff, Gregory X, undertook various highly useful negotiations, which he was not permitted to bring finally to completion, since it pleased the Lord to call him from this world.” These remarks must refer to the two principal affairs and to the others that I shall indicate in the following note. He says that he had agreed concerning the other lesser matters with the royal envoy at the Apostolic See. What those matters were I leave to others to determine.].

As for the calling from this world of the aforesaid father, this little letter has deliberately kept silent, because, since it is painful to remember pain, I did not think it right to reopen your wound by repeating his removal [Note: I must not pass over Raynaldus’s brief account of Gregory X’s departure to the heavenly realms (1276, no. 1): “He departed from the living,” he says, “leaving behind a tremendous longing for himself and an irreparable loss to the Holy Land, which he was about to rescue from the hands of the Saracens together with the emperor to be crowned, and with the kings of France, England, Sicily, and Aragon, and innumerable other princes.” The same annalist preserves letters of the pope that confirm this account.], but thought it should be sweetened by the holiness and justice of his successor [Note: It is clear from this that the letters were written within the ten days between Gregory’s death and the election of Innocent V.]. Given.

## 363. LETTER XLII. To the cardinals, after the death of Gregory X, urging them to elect a good pope

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XLII.)*

**Argument.**—Having received the ill-omened news while traveling to receive the imperial diadem, Rudolph halted and wrote to the sacred college of cardinals. He extols the deceased pontiff with much sincere praise, saying that his funeral should be accompanied by the tears of the whole world, and especially by Rudolph’s own, since Gregory had exalted him above all kings and loved him with paternal affection. Hoping that a successor would be elected who might complete the work begun, he begs them to elect as quickly as possible an excellent successor who, on the solemn day established by their counsel, would bestow upon him the imperial insignia. He says that he will not continue his journey without the deliberation of the cardinals or of the future pontiff.

When the distinguished gardener of the Church militant had been transferred to the heavenly dwellings—namely, the lord Gregory, of blessed memory, supreme pontiff, summoned to rest, whose presence the world seemed altogether unworthy to possess [Note: These letters were sent to the sacred college of cardinals during the brief interval of eleven days while the See was vacant, as is evident from the letters themselves]—although the angelic host of heaven now rejoices on high, and although those blessed ranks of the citizens above sing peaceful hymns to God over the arrival of so glorious a fellow citizen [Note: The devout prince’s belief was not mistaken, for the Church venerates the blessed pontiff, and his name was entered into the martyrology by order of Benedict XIV], nevertheless the multitude of the faithful on earth mourns his departure [Note: The faithful rightly mourned, for they had lost a holy man who immediately began to shine through miracles. See the authors cited by Raynaldus (1276, nos. 2 ff.).].

Let Greece, therefore, mourn, bereft of its kindly converter, for the drachma that had long been lost was found again through his office (*munere*; variant *numero*, “in its number”), and the sheep that had long wandered through the desert of indifference, joined to the Lord’s flock, is now fed by him upon saving pastures [Note: It is known that at the Second Ecumenical Council of Lyons the Greeks professed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and were received into communion with the Latin Church—“for the fourteenth time,” as they say. Michael Palaeologus, the Greek emperor, declares that he attributes this glory to Gregory alone in Labbe (vol. XI, p. 950): “Although previously,” he says, “we were proceeding along the path that sows union and had long been hastening toward this ancient enterprise, which offers the common advantage of Christians, we never undertook so great a work without anxiety. But now, since the letters of your holiness have reached us, we have applied ourselves to it much more earnestly, and, hastening with ardor of soul, have undertaken the work we so greatly desired.”

Other points of the union are made clear by the oath of the Greek prelates in the same Labbe (ibid., p. 971). Their envoy first professes the Catholic faith on behalf of all and then adds: “I likewise freely approach the obedience of the same Holy Roman Church concerning its primacy, as contained in the foregoing statement; I confess, acknowledge, accept, and willingly embrace it. I further promise and confirm, having sworn bodily, that I shall observe all the foregoing matters, both concerning the truth of the faith and concerning the primacy of the same Roman Church, and concerning the recognition, acceptance, reception, observance, and perseverance of the bishops.” See Raynaldus (1274, nos. 14 ff.) for a similar profession by the emperor himself and the entire account of the matter, confirmed by documents.].

Let the Latins utter sobbing sighs from the depths, whose conduct that same father, the father of virtue, guided into the path of righteousness and salvation. Let all the tribes of the earth likewise mourn and howl over the removal of their faithful father, but especially those who, having taken up the victorious sign of the life-giving cross, eagerly desired under that father’s secure leadership to rise powerfully against the blasphemous enemies of the Christian name [Note: A brief account of everything accomplished at that council is found in Labbe (vol. XI, p. 955 ff.). At its conclusion: “The lord pope addressed the council, recounting the three causes mentioned above for summoning it, and explaining how the affairs of the Holy Land and of the Greeks had been begun and, with the Lord’s favor, happily completed. Among other things he said that the prelates were bringing the whole world to ruin, and that he wondered why certain men of evil life and conduct were not corrected, since individuals of evil life as well as of good life and conduct had come insistently to him requesting resignation. He therefore warned them to correct themselves, because once they were corrected there would be no need to enact constitutions for their reform; otherwise, he said, he would deal harshly with them concerning the reform of their morals. Concerning the ordering of parish churches, so that they would not be deprived of the presence of their rectors and suitable men might be appointed to them, and concerning other matters, he said that he would soon, with God’s help, apply appropriate remedies. This could not be done during the council itself because of the occupation caused by many affairs.”].

Let this common lament therefore go forth over the whole earth, and let the pain of mourning reach to the ends of the world, because the passing of so great a father calls forth the tears of many, having abundantly watered some by the example of his blessedness [Note: I think that Alfonso, king of Castile and León, and Edward, king of England, are meant above other princes, since he granted them the tithes.].

Yet among all the other kings and princes of the earth, our eyes, exhausted by want and already dried up by the abundance of tears, have especially languished in compassionate grief, because that same most holy father, placing our throne above kings and kingdoms, cherished us while he lived with pious embraces and surrounded us with paternal favor [Note: See the notes appended to letter 29.].

Since human resources and abilities fail to repair this loss, it is consoled rather by the providence of the heavenly ordering and by the general equity of fate. We have therefore offered ourselves, from the strength of our spirit, a remedy for this grief—whose fading scar will scarcely ever disappear from our breast—in the hope born of unquestioning confidence: that he who did not grant his chosen servant Moses permission to lead out the people will appoint in his place another not unequal in the distinction of his merits, who will happily complete everything salutarily ordered by the aforesaid holy father in zeal for God [Note: Although Gregory undertook many highly useful negotiations which he could not complete, as the cardinals say in the following year, all of them—including even the preparations for the sacred expedition—were directed, according to the same witnesses, toward making Rudolph’s advancement proceed more quietly and securely. For Rudolph was to be the leader of the sacred expedition, crowned with the imperial diadem; that is, he was to become emperor.].

To this end, therefore, we ask you, devout fathers, fervent hinges and pillars of the universal Church, to exercise vigilance and apply your diligent care and labor, so that, once every obstacle of contention has been removed, a necessary prelate may quickly be raised up for the headless world, where divine inspiration urges you on and the burdens of equity are assumed.

Moreover, although, as Scripture says and as incontrovertible arguments make known, one generation passes away, another following after it, yet the earth stands firm forever—namely, the Church of the living God, which, in its actions and in arrangements for the things to be done, remains immovable after mature deliberation has ripened them [variant reading: *de eo et is*; Col. 0750B].

Before the hostile and clouded rumor of the death of the aforesaid most holy father had reached us, we had decently equipped and girded ourselves for the journey, so that, according to what had been arranged through your counsel, if fate had favored us, we might receive from his sacred hands the imperial diadem [Note: The Annals of Colmar, describing the pontiff’s arrival at Lausanne, say of Rudolph: “The king had spent more than 900 marks on expensive garments.” From this we learn that these were purchased not for a meeting at Lausanne, but for the solemnity of the coronation. For within only two months everything was ready for undertaking the journey toward Italy.

So that I may not pass over anything unnoticed in a matter of such importance: when, at the end of 1274, the first date for the coronation was fixed as the feast of All Saints in the following year, this was done not only after hearing the wishes of the cardinals but also after ascertaining Rudolph’s will, as Gregory says in his letter to the archbishop of Salzburg in Raynaldus (1274, no. 56): “That he should send one or more persons to our presence who, concerning the assignment of the date and whatever might suit his convenience, would fully express his wishes to us in this matter and otherwise.”

The same should be thought to have occurred when the date was necessarily changed at Lausanne to the holy day of Pentecost in 1276. It was reasonable that the desire or will of so great a prince should precede every deliberation. Thus Clement V likewise assigned the day of Pentecost in 1311 to Henry VII; nevertheless, the prince selected another, more convenient day: “After mature deliberation had been undertaken concerning this matter, he accepted the approaching feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary as the date for receiving, in the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, according to custom, such anointing and the diadem of the Empire, together with the other solemnities to be performed there, as he informed us through his solemn ambassadors and envoys and through special letters secured with his pendant royal seal.” (*Vatican Register of Clement V*, year 6, letter 754, fol. 186; Raynaldus 1311, no. 7; *Vatican Bullarium*, vol. I, p. 248.)

Therefore Rudolph’s words assigning a fixed date to the pope and cardinals must be understood in such a way that they do not exclude the king’s own preference.].

Yet although it seemed otherwise to the Most High, the creator of all, who, as we believe, will place in the Apostolic See a man after our own heart, we nevertheless remain steadfast, ready and girded for the purpose of proceeding, and hoping in the unchangeability of Mother Church. We have merely suspended and deferred the journey for a time, until through you or the future supreme pontiff—whose good pleasure we always intend to obey in all things with ready spirit—we may be more fully informed what a son devoted to the Church ought now further to do [Note: No more splendid testimony can be offered to those who deny that Rudolph seriously contemplated a Roman coronation. Until the interregnum after Gregory X—from January 10 of the year 1276 to January 21 of the same month, when his successor was elected—the king of the Romans had nothing more important than to receive the imperial insignia at Rome from the hand of the pontiff. Why, after the death of Gregory X, he ceased for several years to seek them will become clear shortly below. Meanwhile, the devout prince testifies to the sacred college of cardinals that he is suspending his journey until they or the elected pontiff decide what he should do thereafter.]. Given.

## 367. BOOK TWO

[Col. 0751]

## LETTER I. Rudolph congratulates Pope Innocent V on his election as Roman pontiff

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex I.)*

**Argument.**—Rudolph congratulates the newly elected pontiff, Innocent V, in the same vein and with almost the same words he used in the preceding letter to the sacred college of cardinals. He praises him highly, submits himself to him as a special son, and says that, according to Gregory’s determination, he will receive the imperial diadem from his hands, if God so ordains. He sends Henry, bishop of Basel, as his envoy to transact with him both the matter of the coronation and other affairs.

Let heaven rejoice, and let earth exult in the voice of festive gladness. For the solemn festivals of the Catholic faith are here; new joys of the sacred Mother Church are here after her lamentation. The Lord, who sometimes turns serenity away from His bride so that He may turn again to her in the radiance of greater joy, has not cut off His mercy from her. He illumines the face of the Church, which at the death of the late lord Gregory X, most holy and gracious supreme pontiff and our father, He had covered with the dark cloud of mournful grief, with the ray of succeeding consolation, and, raising up a new father in place of the deceased for her whom He continually multiplies with ever-new offspring, He has given her one conspicuous for the brightness of his merits and radiant with the excellence of his virtues. Through the effect of this joyful substitution, whatever stream of mourning had burst upon her cheeks because of the sudden removal of the former father may confidently be hoped to be wiped away.

And although, because of the loss of so great a father, our eyes have languished through lack and have been dried by the abundance of tears—since, besides many other glorious and praiseworthy things that he conceived and established for the good condition of the orthodox Catholic faith, he placed our throne above kings and kingdoms, cherished us while he lived with pious embraces, and enlarged us with paternal favors—nevertheless, from this very grief, whose fading scar will scarcely ever disappear from our breast, we have already offered ourselves a remedy: he who did not permit His chosen servant Moses to lead out the people has appointed in the Apostolic See a man after our own heart, who, following in the footsteps of his most holy predecessor, ought happily to complete everything that the same predecessor salutarily ordered [Note: The principal affairs requiring attention were undoubtedly the sacred expedition and the coronation of the king of the Romans. Nevertheless, the dispute between Rudolph and Charles, king of Sicily, after Gregory’s death became so important that it prevented Rudolph from continuing the journey into Italy. Indeed, Innocent, elected at Arezzo, proceeded to Rome and was consecrated there on February 22; but the king of Sicily, Charles, whose interest it was to retain the senatorial dignity, or government of the City, and the vicariate of Tuscany, rendered homage to the new pontiff a few days later, on March 2, for the kingdom of Sicily and the land on this side of the Faro, as recorded by P. Lazzari (*Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 18 ff.). The pope inserted this in his apostolic letters and added at the end:

“On the advice of our brothers, we declare that, because of what you or others have hitherto done, you have not in any respect, with the approval of the Apostolic See, acted or proceeded against the conditions contained in the instrument or letters drawn up concerning the grant to you, by authority of the Apostolic See, of the kingdom of Sicily and of the whole land this side of the Faro up to the borders of the lands of the Roman Church—excepting the city of Benevento with its territory, districts, and dependencies—by the late Anibald, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and our beloved sons Richard, cardinal of Saint Angelo, John, cardinal of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, and James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Nor have you incurred the penalties expressed in those conditions, or any one of them, nor have you in any way violated the oath you swore to fulfill and observe those conditions fully and inviolably. Nor, for as long as you henceforth hold the dominion, senatorial office, or government of the City during the entire period granted to you for this purpose by the same See, or hold the vicariate of Tuscany by grant or good pleasure of us or of our aforesaid predecessors, will you act or proceed in any way against those conditions, incur the aforesaid penalties or any of them, or thereby violate the aforesaid oath.” Enacted in our Lateran palace, March 4, in the first year of our pontificate.”

These two matters—namely, the government of the City of Rome and the vicariate of Tuscany—confirmed to Charles for a period of ten years, extending to September 1278, conflicted with Rudolph’s coronation. Therefore Innocent warned him “not to undertake the journey to come into Italy, and, if he had undertaken it, not to continue the journey,” as the cardinals say in their full account of the matter in Raynaldus (1277, no. 48). For, with Charles present in the City, the pontiff could not deny him what he had long before obtained from the Apostolic See. But fearing that the dispute might perhaps be decided by arms, he judged that it should first be settled and that the coronation should follow afterward.].

For although each generation passes away and another follows in turn, the earth nevertheless stands firm forever—namely, the Church of the living God, which, in its actions and in its arrangements for things to be done, remains immovable after mature deliberation has ripened them, as the evident course of events has shown.

Therefore, most blessed father, through whose divinely ordained creation our spirit has been wholly revived and made fruitful with unspeakable rejoicing, gather into your embrace, we ask, your special son, who will always obey your good pleasure and that of Mother Church in every matter with complete readiness of spirit. Kindly complete in us the work of God through the authority entrusted to you from above [Note: These letters seem to belong to the same period as the patent letter (book I, letter 28), in which Rudolph promised that he would be present at Milan on Holy Easter, or April 5, and would proceed from there to the City. It is not credible that they were written after Rudolph had been forbidden to advance. Whether both letters were written at the same time as this congratulatory letter, or separately, cannot readily be determined. Certainly both were written before Innocent’s warning mentioned above, for in both the matter of receiving the imperial diadem is treated according to Gregory’s deliberation.].

For we cannot help believing that the completion of so arduous a matter has been reserved by heaven for your glory, so that in your right hand it may be brought to perfection—a matter whose gracious protection has not been absent from the beginning of our advancement.

Behold, therefore, we have deemed it right to send to the feet of Your Beatitude, with the utmost confidence and humble devotion, our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Basel, devoted to you and to the Roman Church, asking that you deign to grant him, into whom we have poured the innermost secrets of our heart, a kindly hearing, and to place trusting faith in all our affairs, just as you would in us, with gracious granting of the request (*exauditione*; variant *ex auditione*, “after the hearing”) following.

## LETTER II. Rudolph writes to a cardinal after the death of Pope Gregory X and commends his envoy to him

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex II.)*

[Col. 0753B]

**Argument.**—On the same occasion he informs the sacred college of cardinals that he is sending an envoy both to the new pontiff and to them. He has appointed the bishop of Basel, who is to attend to his affairs, and commends him to them all.

Since, as it pleased the Lord, the condition of the sacred Mother Church has unexpectedly changed in these days [Note: The date of the letter appears to be shortly after the death of Blessed Gregory. This increasingly confirms that Rudolph is referring to the dispatch of the envoy whom the cardinals say arrived in Rome several months later.], our own position could not be stabilized amid so sudden a change without suffering along with it the disadvantages of that change.

Behold, we have confidently decided to send the venerable N., to whom all the secrets of our heart have been communicated, as an image of our presence to the feet of Your Apostolic Beatitude and to you [Note: We have seen that whatever was done in the matter of the coronation and in the other negotiations affecting Rudolph was done on the advice of the sacred college. Therefore the envoy is rightly dispatched to the pontiff and the cardinals, that is, to the Apostolic See.]. We earnestly ask and exhort you to take care to place trusting faith in him concerning all matters, both collectively and individually, that he will present to you in his speech, applying effectively to their completion, as we trust in your kindness, your freely given aid and assistance [Note: The distinction should be noted: the authority of the pontiff and the patronage of the cardinals are being requested.].

## LETTER III. He rejoices over the newly elected pontiff and appoints a procurator in the Roman Curia

*(A.D. 1277, Rudolphine codex III.)*
## ARGUMENT

By this royal diploma he appoints a new procurator, or legate, of his own at the Holy See, with the necessary powers. He instructs him concerning the matters to be conducted and promises rewards for their successful execution.

God, the exalt­er of the humble, looking down from on high upon our vows, foresaw as desired—indeed, as the husband suited to the Church, his holy bride—the man of her desires; and if anything, if we dare say so, was imperfect in his predecessors, he has mercifully deigned to perfect it in our most holy father, the lord pope, as though by a completed form. [Note: The compiler is doubtless mistaken in thinking that this diploma belongs to the pontificate of Innocent V; moreover, by treating it as a letter of congratulation, he again shows himself mistaken in the title. In the imperial codex the author of *Pietas Austriaca* also read the same title (book I, chapter 9, p. 56). He rightly assigns the date instead to the pontificate of Nicholas III, which began toward the end of 1277. For if Rudolph were speaking of Innocent, he would not dare to suspect anything imperfect in his predecessors. Innocent had succeeded only Gregory, whose benevolence and generosity he had praised so extensively in the preceding letters. This diploma must therefore be moved from its present place [Col. 0754D] and transferred to nearly the end of the year 1277.]

Certainly, in him our mind rests; in him we place the anchor of our hope, so that he may rule the kingdom with us, govern, order, and dispose within the empire those things that concern the salvation of both men. [Note: Truly a great service, and great reverence toward the successors of the prince of the apostles! He indicates the harmony of priesthood and kingdom by “both men,” namely, the supreme pontiff and himself, the future emperor.]

Moreover, we believe—or rather hold it as certain—that before him you must be our ever-watchful eye, our open ear, our right hand directing and governing our affairs; so that our direction and advancement in the Holy Roman Empire may, from generation to generation, redound to you and your descendants for the exaltation of name and honor. [Note: Together with a document highly useful to administrators of the greatest princes, he joins the chief concern of all affairs: namely, advancement to the empire through Roman coronation. For two years Nicholas’s predecessors, Innocent and Adrian V, and John XXI had excluded him from this for the sake of peace.]

Furthermore, before that most holy father of ours we appoint you our procurator, to offer counsel and, by persuasive appeals, to obtain everything beneficial to the Holy Roman Empire, not contrary to the wishes of His Holiness but in every respect agreeable to him. [Note: A most splendid testimony to the same harmony, a lasting monument of the great progenitor of the Austrian imperial house. This constant will of the pious prince plainly dates from his very election: “We submit our weak shoulders, hoping that the fullness of grace both of God and of the holy mother Church, as well as apostolic favor and the clemency of your paternal goodwill, will not be lacking to us.” So he said in his letters to Gregory X, as *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 4, p. 33) records; we have quoted them in full (p. 280).] For his will and his refusal will at no time differ from our own will. [Col. 0755A] Keep watch on our behalf, fulfill your ministry, perform the work of a faithful man; for the rest, await from us the crown [care] of justice.

## LETTER IV. Innocent the pontiff commends the Church of Cologne and its archbishop to the emperor Rudolph

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex IV)*

### ARGUMENT

Innocent V, bearing with the greatest indignation the distresses and injuries of Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, and of his Church, repeatedly commends both of them to the king of the Romans.

Innocent, etc. [Note: A new offense by the person who supplied the title! On his own authority he calls the king of the Romans “emperor.” In the imperial codex, which the author of *Pietas Austriaca* examined, even the name of Innocent is not expressed; for this reason he believed the letter should be attributed to John. He ought, however, to have observed that Innocent, probably a Burgundian by birth and formerly archbishop of Lyons, would more plausibly have been concerned with the archbishop and Church of Cologne than John the Portuguese, whose zeal is praised for preserving the relics of the Holy Land. Our codex removes every doubt: it restores to Innocent this letter, which had been wrongly taken from him.]

To our most beloved son in Christ, Rudolph.

We commend churches and ecclesiastical persons to you with the greater confidence because we know that you are all the more ready to show zeal toward them—thereby rendering pleasing service to God and making yourself deservedly gracious to men [most gracious]. Indeed, as we have learned, the noble G., count of Jülich, not content with having already afflicted the Church of Cologne with serious injuries and oppressions, does not hesitate still to harass that Church and our venerable brother, the bishop of Cologne, with countless hardships and various persecutions. [Note: Guille­lmus, also called Willelmus. Concerning him Trithemius writes (1277): “William, count of Jülich, besieged the royal town at Aachen with his three sons and 468 armed men,” and attempted to bring it under his control out of hatred for Rudolph; he was slain together with all his men. Thus he paid the penalty for the injuries he had inflicted upon churches and ecclesiastical persons.]

Since we trust that, through the help of your favor, that same Church—which we cherish with paternal zeal—ought to breathe again after its hardships, we affectionately ask and earnestly exhort your Highness that, out of reverence for God and for us, you hold the aforesaid archbishop and Church especially commended, assist them in their rights, and defend them with the authority divinely entrusted to you. Thus may you more abundantly merit divine favor, and may we rightly commend your devotion. [Note: Siegfried, previously provost of Mainz, had been appointed in the preceding year and succeeded Engelbert of the noble house of Walckenburg. The latter had suffered much more serious things at the hands of his fellow citizens. See Raynaldus (1264, nos. 41 ff.). In 1267, Count of Jülich, joining those same citizens, had defeated and captured the archbishop and committed him to a dreadful prison, as Trithemius says. There is no doubt that the pontiff had this in mind.]

[Note: I stated above (book I, letter 38, in the note) that all kings bind themselves by oath to defend the churches within their respective dominions. Here, however, the pontiff urges the king of the Romans to avenge the injuries of the Church of Cologne and of its archbishop-elector, as the future emperor who would obey the universal pontifical authority in temporal matters.]

## LETTER V. He congratulates the new pontiff on his pontifical dignity and submissively commends himself to him

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex V)*

[Col. 0756A]

### ARGUMENT

Rudolph, about to move his camp into Austria against Ottocar, king of Bohemia, replies in haste and congratulates the new pontiff, John XXI, to whom he promises that he will send suitable and solemn envoys at a more opportune time. Meanwhile he submits himself and all his people to the pontiff’s will; finally, he informs him of the expedition that he is about to undertake immediately against Ottocar.

Most holy father, etc. [Note: These letters seem to have been sent to Adrian V, who was elected but not consecrated pontiff for thirty-seven days, as the pontifical and royal chronology appears to indicate. Adrian was elected on 12 July and died on 18 August; after an interregnum of twenty-eight days, John XXI was elected on 15 September. Rudolph moved his camp from Alsace to Kempten on 4 August, then to Regensburg, after first subduing the duke of Bavaria, and finally to Padua, where he arrived on 26 September. Thus, when Rudolph told the pontiff that he was preparing a powerful army and was arming himself vigorously to defeat his enemies, he seems not yet to have moved his camp from Alsace, where he had received news of the newly elected pontiff in July. He must have issued this letter in the same month, before moving his camp the following month.]

The praiseworthy and glorious Son of God throughout eternal ages, blessed and blessing all who trust in him, the inscrutable ordainer of eternal and transitory things, has deigned to console holy Mother Church with the breasts of the richest consolation, anoint her with the oil of gladness, and restore her, once anointed, to a secure station. For by divinely elevating you to the summit of supreme dignity, to the highest and most holy rank of the apostolate, for the restoration of the empire and the salvation of the Holy Land marked with Christ’s precious blood, that same holy Mother Church, renewed with reviving joys and rejoicing in the exultations of promised fruitfulness, gives thanks and celebrates.

Nor is this surprising. For the God of peace and love, of immeasurable goodness, placed in her these signs when he appointed you her father and mercifully chose you beforehand as shepherd for his flock. Although the subject of this immense joy ought to move all who recognize themselves as members attached to the head, we rejoice first and foremost, and with all the greater joy, in your exaltation because we understand more clearly that, through the counsel and aid of your infinite goodness and assistance, we have been called toward the prize of the salvation we desire. [Note: Historians relate much about Adrian, formerly cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian and nephew on his brother’s side of Innocent IV—his name was Ottobono—and a Genoese by nation; he performed many deeds for the Holy See with the highest praise. Clement IV, after he had wisely and steadfastly completed his English legation, said to him: “You have labored long enough, and the Lord has honored you in your labors and, by human judgment, has now completed them,” in Raynaldus (1267, no. 34). Nevertheless, the historians provide nothing relevant to our subject. Only in the Vallicellian codex are there letters of Cardinal John Gaetani, later Nicholas III, mentioned by Raynaldus (1276, no. 26). From these it is clear that, immediately after Adrian’s election, the cardinal and Cardinal Jacobus, deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, were sent to Viterbo to settle the disputes between Charles, king of Sicily, and Rudolph. What then? In the frequently cited letter to Rudolph the cardinals bear witness to the same thing: “But,” they immediately add, “because the aforesaid pontiff Adrian survived his promotion for a very short time, the undertaking begun did not reach the object toward which the urgency of those pursuing it was directed.” Accordingly, this testimony of Rudolph diverges from Adrian’s initiatives. On the other hand, there is considerable agreement with the deeds of John XXI, whose name—Peter Julian, cardinal bishop of Tusculum—is less well known among historians, as will become clear below in note c.]

We can express this testimony of him who searches hearts and reins not so much by letters or envoys as by carrying it in our heart and mind. Therefore, without any uncertainty of deliberation or consultation, because of the great clemency that we have conceived toward your holiness, we entrust and have entrusted our own person, our wife, our children, sons and daughters, our possessions and honors, to the hands and commands of your holiness, reclining the head of our humility in the lap of your mercy. [Note: Nothing was lacking from the honor of the king of the Romans, or of the elected emperor, except the imperial diadem, which he hoped to obtain after the disputes had been settled. John the pontiff had informed him in his letters that he was devoting himself especially to this matter.]

Thus we may truly say with the wise man: “In all things I sought rest, and in the inheritance of the Lord I shall dwell.” We shall dwell securely, casting all our care upon you, because we know that you care for us. How, then, shall we turn aside from your paths or in any way depart from the road of your commandments? We subject everything to you, entrust all things to your hands, and wish to live for you and to have you as ruler in the kingdom, so that between us there may be identity of minds and inseparable union of wills. [Note: Although this most pious and excellent prince always pursued the successors of the prince of the apostles with such obedience, it must nevertheless be admitted that the pontifical letters to which he is replying compelled him to express his feelings in this manner, full of reverence and love.]

With these few words, most holy father, we have decided to express the joy of our mind through a private and familiar envoy, with some haste; thereafter, by continuous suitable and solemn envoys, we shall visit the presence of your holiness. [Note: In the aforesaid letter the cardinals relate how they had been unable to devote themselves to settling those disputes because the bishop of Basel, or whoever else possessed Rudolph’s mandate, was absent from the Roman Curia. They then say: “For this reason, following the praiseworthy paths of their predecessors in these matters, he earnestly begged and exhorted Your Magnificence in the Lord Jesus Christ to send, with all the haste you could, certain suitable men, zealous for peace and concord and bearing from Your Highness a full mandate concerning the matters mentioned above, to his presence, so that they might confirm these matters in your name. The same pontiff John also wished you to inform him when you thought those men would probably come into his presence, so that meanwhile he might arrange for the aforesaid king [Charles] to provide envoys of his own for this purpose, etc.”]

Furthermore, we wish your holiness to know that, by the favor of divine clemency, all the princes of our Roman kingdom stand favorably by us for the recovery of the possessions, rights, and goods of the empire; and with their counsel, strength, and aid we are arming ourselves vigorously to defeat the illustrious king of Bohemia, the sole contemptuous and injurious violator of our rights and those of the Holy Roman Empire, who holds many principalities. [Note: I believe he received the pontifical letters at Padua. There he could state with certainty that all the princes of our Roman kingdom were present with their counsel, strength, and aid. For, after the duke of Bavaria, Henry, had recently been subdued and was following his camp, the king of Bohemia remained as the sole enemy of the Roman Empire to be defeated.]

We hope in the mercy of him who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble that we shall successfully accomplish our purpose against him.

## LETTER VI. Rudolph replies to the king of Hungary and excuses himself for not granting his request

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex VI)*

### ARGUMENT

Ladislaus, king of Hungary, had requested for his chamberlain certain districts in lands belonging by right to the empire that had been occupied by Ottocar. Rudolph replies that, since the right to those lands is still uncertain, it would be less than suitable to grant anything in them; but, in order to win the king’s favor, he offers him whatever can be granted without injury to the law. [Col. 0757C]

Having received your royal letter, recently sent to our Highness with kindly affection, and having read and fully understood it as was fitting, we have decided to respond to your Highness concerning its contents as follows. [Note: After the death of Stephen, king of Hungary, around the Kalends of August 1272, his two minor sons succeeded him. Ladislaus, the elder, obtained the royal scepter, while Andrew received the duchy of Slavonia (below, letter 16). The king of Sicily gave Ladislaus his daughter Isabella in marriage, though it is uncertain in what year—certainly not in 1272, although Raynaldus (no. 52) refers to letters of Gregory X to him in which Gregory admonishes him to choose faithful administrators: “who,” he says, “should possess due fidelity and devotion toward your person and toward that of your illustrious consort, our beloved daughter in Christ, the queen of Hungary, born of our beloved son in Christ Charles, king of Sicily.” For, as the authors consistently report, he was still a minor.]

Although we wish to be spontaneous in all things that can please your mind and affection, and although we embrace your distinguished chamberlain N. with the open arms of gracious goodwill, as his illustrious and virtuous merits require, nevertheless, since we ourselves and our beloved princes N. and N. claim to possess rights in certain lands that the illustrious king of Bohemia is known to have occupied, it would seem no less blameworthy if we were suddenly and rashly to leap to the granting of certain districts belonging to those lands, neglecting such a declaration or determination as would establish to whom and to which parties they legally belong. [Note: This is a sure indication that the letter was written before Ottocar had been defeated; afterward there was no need for either deliberation or mature procedure.]

Therefore, your petition presented to us on behalf of the aforesaid N. is for the present frustrated in its effect. Let it not, however, disturb the royal mind with a spirit of displeasure, since, as you know, proceedings of this kind must be weighed in the scales of equitable judgment and examined with mature counsel, with the principal authority taking care that it cannot be accused of changeability and inconsistency. Nevertheless, we are so fervently disposed, with unwavering sincerity, to increase the titles of your glory that, whatever you may wish regarding this matter, we are gladly and generously prepared, in the abundant overflow of singular goodwill, to do as much as we can without injury to the law. [Note: The prince, a cultivator of justice and powerful in counsel, as Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, says (*Pietas Austriaca*, book I, chapter 4, p. 34), gives a reasonable account of the refusal and declares the uncertain outcome of war; then he wins the favor of the youthful king by goodwill and generosity.]

## LETTER VII. Rudolph promises to take vengeance for a certain crime that has been committed

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolph codex VII)*

### ARGUMENT

He instructs a prince allied to him, who was about to abandon allegiance to Ottocar, that the latter should be proclaimed an enemy of the empire by a written declaration, or defiance, as was then customary. He reports hostile actions by a certain adherent of Ottocar and condemns an outrage committed against a priest.

We have learned recently, through your report, of a horrible and pernicious deed—namely, the mutilation of a certain priest’s seminiferous organs. We lament it with bitter grief and are prepared, at our pleasure, to hasten toward the correction of the crime committed.

Regarding the defiance of the king of Bohemia, as you have written, we think it more prudent to await an appropriate opportunity—namely, when a sentence has been issued against him [perhaps: “when the sentence has been definitively issued”]—so that the process may be entirely free from accusation; then the defiance itself should be formally proclaimed. [Note: From this it is clear that the letter was written before the Diet of Augsburg, that is, before 24 June 1275.]

Furthermore, so that the rumors we have recently received may certainly not escape your notice, we report to your sincerity that N., in support of N., recently entered a certain city, N., violently with several wagons and horsemen, devastating it with fires and plunder. [Note: Concerning the hostile acts committed by Ottocar against the Church of Salzburg in this year, I shall speak below (letter 15). These letters testify that his adherents, or those with whom Ottocar had made an alliance, committed similar acts. Their principal figures were Henry, duke of Bavaria, the margrave of Baden, and Eberhard, count of Württemberg. It is unknown to me which of them is meant here. Letter XV, placed below in the codex outside its proper location, must be referred to this matter.]

## LETTER VIII. The archbishop of Salzburg accuses his suffragan, the bishop of Seckau, before Rudolph the emperor

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolph codex VIII)*

### ARGUMENT

Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, who, while raiding into Styria and Carinthia with Conrad of Freising, had been denounced by his suffragan Bernard of Seckau as inciting peoples subject to Ottocar to revolt and had been forced to save himself by flight, accuses him of undertaking a legation to the Diet of Augsburg, boasting against the empire and the Holy See, and subverting clergy and people. He asks Rudolph to punish the insolence of one man as an example to others.

My lord, know that our suffragan, the bishop of Seckau, despite our prohibition and against our will, is undertaking legations contrary to God and to you, [Note: He doubtless alludes to a legation undertaken on Ottocar’s behalf to the Diet of Augsburg. See above (book I, letter 29, in the note). The principal purpose of the legation, as the author of *Pietas Austriaca* observes (book I, chapter 11, p. 62), was to protest: “that Rudolph had been made emperor defectively and therefore should not be recognized as legitimate, capable of convoking a general diet or disposing of affairs of the empire.”] despising the devotion owed to the Roman Church, by which he is bound to you and to us.

When that same bishop recently passed through our territory, we rebuked him fraternally and in secret concerning this matter. But he rashly scorned our correction and, breaking into foolish speech against us and our venerable brother Conrad, publicly proclaimed and declared, in the presence of many distinguished men, that the two of us had come down to the lands of his lord king for no other reason than to disturb their condition treacherously in your favor. He provoked so many supporters and accomplices of his faction against us that we were obliged to withdraw from those lands by remote roads and flight, to the great disgrace of our name. [Note: Carinthia and Styria, together with Austria and the other provinces reclaimed by Rudolph as belonging by right to the empire, were held by Ottocar partly by dowry-right and partly by hereditary right. Ottocar refused to restore them and was therefore proclaimed an enemy of the empire at the Diet of Augsburg. Thus, when the archbishop of Salzburg urged their subject peoples to show allegiance to the king of the Romans, he was in no way departing from equity and justice.]

That same bishop, boasting and repeatedly vaunting himself over certain foolish words [perhaps “in Augsburg”], not only turns laymen away from and withdraws them from devotion to you, but also inflates and urges clerics and religious men to rebel not only against the empire but also against the apostolic see. [Note: See below, letter 24 and the notes attached to it. Gregory’s letters of rebuke to Ottocar, dated at Belliquadri on 22 July in the fourth year of his pontificate, are preserved in Raynaldus (1275, no. 10). In them, unless I am mistaken, the character of this bishop is touched upon: “What,” Gregory says, “did this rash attempt of yours—or rather, as we reasonably suspect, of your counselors—amount to except guilt? … For we embrace your person with the bonds of our customary affection in such a way that we believe the matters mentioned above are, until we hear from you that you said them deliberately, to be attributed to your negligence or to the malice of others.” Unless he had advised the king, through an envoy and letter, to abandon the obedience owed to Christ’s vicar, he himself was turning clergy and people away from him. Moreover, certain defamatory pamphlets against Rudolph were circulating, and the same bishop was thought to be their author. He nevertheless emphatically denied this in his letters to Rudolph, whose meaning can be inferred from Rudolph’s aforementioned letter 24 to him.]

Our counsel, then, which we join to our petition, is this: with all your strength, consider how you may show by the actual effect of punitive action against the said bishop—who alone among the suffragans and other prelates raises himself up and acts insolently, and gives others occasion to offend—how rash it is to injure the Roman majesty so atrociously and insolently. For we know that if you restrain the jaws of his rash mouth with a bridle, the hands and lips of the other foolish men who rise up against you will become quiet. [Note: Nature had given Rudolph the quality of honoring ecclesiastical men with the highest reverence. Accordingly, content merely to admonish the bishop, however guilty he might be against royal majesty, in his own name and with royal indignation, he prevailed upon him to return from the clemency he had abused to sounder counsels and to beg forgiveness in repeated letters, as will be clear below.]

## LETTER IX. The gravest complaint of the archbishop of Salzburg concerning Ottocar, king of Bohemia, after the death of Gregory X, supreme pontiff

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex IX)*

[Col. 0760B]

### ARGUMENT

After the death of Gregory X, Ottocar loosened the reins of his anger against Rudolph’s adherents and drove the archbishop of Salzburg into such great distress that he was compelled to implore royal assistance. He therefore sends an envoy to report all his misfortunes orally; in addition, he asks Rudolph about the election of the new pontiff and about his future coronation, and promises that he will remain steadfast in faith toward him through every danger.

To my serene lord, the archbishop of Salzburg sends the readiest will, with devout prayers, to do whatever pleases him. [Note: Hansiz lacks the title and salutation, though he rightly observes that this letter, as well as the following three, cannot be removed from this year. For, as we shall see shortly, they were all written before the summer of this year.]

Those who long ago raised themselves contumaciously against the holy Roman Church and the Holy Roman Empire, brandishing the horns of their rebellion, now exulting in their wicked deeds after the death of our most blessed father and lord, Pope Gregory, grow insolent so atrociously and boldly as though both dignities and powers—which, by God’s favor, we believe immortal—had been destroyed by the death of one man. [Note: This reflects the opinion of that age concerning the two great lights, that is, pontifical and imperial power, throughout the entire world.]

This is easily, though miserably [miraculously], seen in us and in our Church. We suffer persecution, endure reproaches, and await our destruction for no other reason than that we willingly render due and devoted service both to the apostolic see and to the Roman Empire, to which we recognize that we are bound by the obligations of fidelity. The bearer of this letter, who knows our countless hardships well, will recount them fully to your royal Highness. [Note: He recognizes in Rudolph not imperial majesty but royal highness, although he knows the empire as perpetual. Below he also speaks of royal glory and royal majesty and says that he will remain faithful to the Roman Empire as long as he lives.]

We have also sent him especially to behold the royal glory, so that he may inquire carefully and diligently about the creation of the supreme pontiff and about your progress—whom we desire to be more fortunate than our own condition, since we do not stand but fall—and may also report our pitiable condition to your royal majesty, so that he may bring back to us your counsel concerning the help by which, amid our hardships, whose weight and number grow heavier day by day, we may be directed in this perilous time. [Note: Through his envoy he asks two things: whether a successor to Gregory has been elected, and when Rudolph will set out for Rome for the imperial diadem. This is what is meant by the king of the Romans’ “progress,” which he wishes would prove more fortunate than his own wretched condition. He had promised to go with him the previous year (book I, letter 38), if the king of Bohemia had allowed him to breathe, unaware that a greater misfortune threatened him after Gregory’s death. Out of reverence for, or fear of, that pontiff, Ottocar would sometimes cease his violence.]

For our deliberative purpose has been immovably fixed by steadfast constancy: no weight of adversity and no storm of danger shall destroy it, but rather our fidelity toward you and the Roman Empire shall appear and shine forth more brightly. Therefore, may it please your glory, illustrious prince and lord, to console our misery—which we see has neither end nor measure—with the sound counsel of your instruction, in accordance with what the bearer of this letter will explain to your ears. [Note: Nothing is more frequent in the Carolingian codex than this sort of commission to envoys during wartime.]

## LETTER X. Another letter of the bishop of Salzburg to Rudolph, a more serious complaint against Ottocar, king of Bohemia, whose tyranny he asks to be freed from, together with his people

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex X)*

[Col. 0761C]

### ARGUMENT

As the savagery of the enemies grows stronger, the archbishop again implores help. He writes that his constancy has been tested in vain; that he and his people would rather die than defect from the empire; that he has suffered much to draw some who were defecting away from their miserable servitude; and he asks Rudolph to come as quickly as possible, to redeem those provinces and rule over them.

To his serene lord, etc., the archbishop of Salzburg sends, with prayers, diligent devotion and indefatigable fidelity. [Note: Hansiz likewise lacks the title and salutation.]

Until now, while placed amid hardships and exposed to death, dying daily for justice, I have awaited you—the lord and savior who would rescue me—impelled and repeatedly driven toward falling. I have often been solicited to become, against you, an apostate from faith and a deserter from truth; I have remained immovable, made great in faith with Moses. I renounced the sin of the Egyptian king; I denied, and deny, that I am the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. [Note: Moses, having become great through faith, denied that he was the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary pleasure of sin (Hebrews 11:24–25). The archbishop had this passage in mind; others may judge whether the application is apt.]

Indeed, trampled under the savage rages of men without any guilt of my own, abandoned and treated as a laughingstock by nearly all those dearest to me, I did not deny you as lord. Because of you I endured reproach from my acquaintances and relatives; I suffered insults and terrors. By fire and sword I lost myself and my people in order to win and save others—those who, departing from devotion to the empire, sold themselves into miserable servitude at the price of their own [precious] blood.

Therefore, may your soul live, my lord; may it live and prosper. Come, and do not delay, so that we may not see death, whose fear is near—at least for me and for those men strong in heart and faith who, out of zeal for justice and for the laws of the empire, have chosen, like new Maccabees, either to triumph with you in glorious combat or, if necessary, to rest for you in honorable death within their graves rather than, while living, await innumerable calamities every day and finally die a sordid and ignoble death. [Note: I leave to others the task of weighing this comparison with the Maccabees.]

I have drawn to myself those whom I could; I consoled the weak, strengthened the fainthearted, and have sustained many in the faith until now, so that nothing remains for you but to come, receive the kingdom, and return. What more shall I say? Whatever happens, whatever face Fortune—the force that changes human circumstances—may show, now serene and now troubled, my faith toward you and the Roman Empire will never fail. Either I shall joyfully introduce you into my province as the redeemer of the afflicted peoples, or I shall flee, never again to see the face of the persecutor. Send us envoys dispatched with joyful news.

## LETTER XI. The same archbishop of Salzburg sends his notary to Rudolph the emperor and repeatedly urges him to prepare as quickly as possible for the liberation of himself and his people

[Note: The title is absent from the imperial codex.]

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolph codex XI)*

### ARGUMENT

For the third time, pouring out more abundant prayers, he sends his notary, whom he had employed in drawing peoples over to Rudolph’s obedience, to recount everything fully. The entire matter depends upon speed, lest prolonged affliction bring despair, and despair bring defection. Everything is ready for victory; Rudolph’s name is terrifying to those who hate it and foretells triumphs. He warns him to take care for his life and to beware the plots of new friends.

Dearest lord, whatever I have hitherto arranged among those men concerning your affairs and theirs, I carried out almost entirely through the service of this man, my notary. The works of truth commend and prove how great his diligence has been. I now send him to you, so that from his own words and from the other reliable indications that he will show you, you may gather both the frequency of my efforts and the purpose of those men, and may take greater care to look after yourselves than after them (ipsis; variant ipsi), considering at what peril to their own lives they submit themselves to your favor. They fluctuate between hope and fear; and would that the despair which your delay might induce should not overwhelm the confidence of those poor afflicted people. [Col. 0762D] Whatever is neglected this summer [Note: [Col. 0762D] Here is a definite indication of the date of the three letters recounting Ottokar’s audacity and cruelty after Gregory’s death—namely, the months preceding the summer season.], [Col. 0763A] will scarcely recover thereafter. Behold: because of you they abandon everything and empty themselves of their own resources—what, then, will become of them? Be for them a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.

I hold this as certain and true: all, without exception, who will come or have come to you will enter joyfully with you and undergo the danger of death for you; nor, if it should be necessary for them to die with you, will they deny you. Thus may the torments of flesh and spirit, in which they and their dearest servants daily die within themselves, end in a single agony (finiant; variant finiat, “may end”). I believe that the matter will henceforth be easy, and that, if you wish to conquer, the means of conquering are well prepared.

**384** I see the faces and minds of those opposing you so tremulous and cast down with fear, and I see them so deprived of strength, that those who do not yet know you fear you, and those who have not yet seen you see you already; they flee from the face of the bow and shrink from the sound of your name. What will they do, and how will they fear the voice of thunder, when the eagles come upon them like flashing lightning? [Note: [Col. 0763C] It is well known that the Romans placed the eagle on the standards of their legions, on coins, in books, and on monuments—sometimes to signify the power of the Roman people, sometimes the majesty of the emperor, and sometimes the admission of the Caesars among the gods, which they call apotheosis. After the empire in the West had been renewed by apostolic authority, the first use of the eagle is found on scepters; and not even then while the Carolingians endured, but after imperial majesty had passed to the kings of Germany. Ditmarus (Annals, book III) reports that Otto II used the sign of the eagle. Henry II Augustus is likewise found to have used an eagle-bearing scepter. It began to be used on standards later, and then not of black but of golden color. Rigordus shows this when, speaking of Otto IV in the year 1215, he says: “On the opposite side, he says, Otto stood in the middle of a very dense battle line; he had raised up as his standard a gilded eagle above a dragon”—that is, an elongated cloth of the sort that standards are—“hanging from a long upright pole on a quadriga.” Thus it must be held that the sign of the eagle began only when the Saxons were governing the empire, and it should be accepted as established that down to Rudolf’s time it was not black but gilded, as Dufresnius (On the Coins of the Lower Age, § 12) and Godefridus (Godfrey’s Chronicle, book II, chapter 8, pp. 265 ff.) observe. Nor should we heed Berosus and Aventinus, who, following fables, derive the image of the black double-headed eagle from the origin of the renewed Western empire. Dufresnius’ diligence failed to discover why and when the Westerners introduced the black eagle, and he supposes that it happened with regard to its proper color. Sigismund, however, was at most the first to display the double-headed eagle on standards, as the Constantinopolitan empire was hastening toward its end, as a sign of both empires, so it is believed. Since this is so, Rudolf’s standards, mentioned more than once in this codex, displayed neither a black nor a double-headed eagle, but a simple gilded one. [Col. 0764C]]

The bearer of this letter has deserved well, and will continue to deserve still more, so that in his pious and just requests he may find grace and favor in your eyes. Be a watchful guardian and diligent protector of your life. Beware of those plots laid by the men who sometimes surround your side.
