Many are those who persecute and afflict me, but my life will fail before my faith does; nor will I turn aside from your testimonies, in which I have set law and end (finem; variant fidem, “faith”). [Note: [Col. 0764C] The archbishop uses—or abuses—passages of Scripture in order to strengthen his faith and constancy; he reveals more the candor of his spirit than the sharpness of his mind.]

**385. LETTER XII.** Rudolf replies to the bishop of Salzburg, thanking him for his singular care and vigilance toward him.

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolf codex XII.)*

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolf replies to the three preceding letters of the archbishop of Salzburg from his camp, after the assembly held at Kempten. He gives him many thanks for his sincerity and constancy in speech and action. He hints at Ottokar’s cunning; the rest, he says, he has entrusted to the bearer of the letter to explain orally. [Col. 0763C]

For the pure, complete, and undefiled ardor of your friendship, which you display toward us with the utmost readiness of mind, we do not seek external arguments in words, when the effect of the deed, outweighing the statement, makes clear to us certain proofs, and when our conscience, as witness, appeals with greater solemnity than any deposition of witnesses. For we know—indeed, we have proved it by manifest evidence—that what has been conceived in your heart toward us does not grow cold, but, the further it advances through time, the more graciously it matures.

This is certainly clearer than all clarity from what your letter sent to us contained. From its tenor we reasonably infer that, around our sides, you are performing the office of a vigilant watchman, and that you are fulfilling the duty of royal guard both beneficially and faithfully, since nothing so stormy, so turbulent, so inaccessible to the light and so dark can confront us that it is not made serene by the radiance of your luminous prudence. [Note: [Col. 0764C] We can readily understand Rudolf’s replying once to the archbishop’s three letters if we consider that the archbishop of Salzburg was so pressed by difficulties that he needed rapid assistance. Thus, just as Stephen II once wearied Pippin with letters against the Lombards, so Salzburg wearied Rudolf against the Bohemians: where necessity advises, the rules of official duty are set aside.]

For these salutary admonitions and this freely given instruction, by which you have usefully trained us, we offer our thanks and gratitude to your fatherhood. Because of these and the other sweet-flowing signs of your goodness and goodwill, and placing ourselves and all that is ours at your every nod, we have thought it proper to disclose to your desires the events of our prosperity, which we believe you are eager to hear. **386** [Note: [Col. 0764C] Hansiz briefly and correctly says of Rudolf (Germania Sacra, vol. I, p. 414): “He ruled the kingdom with the great favor of both pontiffs and princes: he won over the pontiffs by reverence and accessibility, the princes by justice and courtesy, and both by moderation and piety. Yet the king of Bohemia opposed him.” Rudolf was advancing against him with an army when he wrote this letter. The Annals of Altach give a fuller account, although they place the event in the following year and combine several events together.]

We properly celebrated our solemn court in such a place [Note: [Col. 0764D] Aventinus records that this assembly was held at Kempten in Swabia, where the army was also reviewed before the camp was moved into Bavaria; these letters lend credibility to Aventinus.], and on such a day, with a numerous company of princes seated with us and surrounded by an escort of chosen soldiers, the like of which has scarcely been seen in our time, in royal power. Several appropriate constitutions were issued, many young men were adorned with the military belt [Note: [Col. 0764D] The author of the History of Austria (book I, chapter 12, p. 73), drawing on Gerard and others, reports that among the many whom Rudolf honored with military or knightly rank were one hundred men of Zurich, all of whom fell fighting bravely in battle against Ottokar; their heraldic insignia could still be seen painted in the church of the Friars Minor at Zurich.], and all the other things that magnify a king seated on his throne and adorn a royal court were duly performed, with nothing omitted that was relevant.

Although the cunning of the king of Bohemia, seated in secret in the north, appeared [Col. 0764C] to be present, since he could not openly oppose our celebrated advances or resist such profitable and festive solemnities by a wicked attempt (in tentatione), it [quae; variant qui], through the Lord’s right hand exercising power, failed in its cunning and did not prosper. [Note: [Col. 0765C] This may refer to the archbishop of Salzburg’s other letter, in which he warned Rudolf to beware of plots.]

The rest our dear familiar servant [famulus] N., the bearer of this letter, will explain more clearly through the oracle of the living voice. [Note: [Col. 0765C] It is customary for princes, especially when they are taking up arms against an enemy with an army already assembled, to commit to writing only those matters which, if the letters should happen to be intercepted, would not disclose deliberations of any importance. Today they use ciphers, a more convenient practice. See V. Hoffmann, Lexicon.]

**387. LETTER XIII.** The same archbishop of Salzburg complains to the emperor Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0765C] We have already encountered the collector’s license in the titles. It is therefore not new here; indeed, it will not be new below (letters 14, 17, 18, and 29, and book III, letters 1 and 14) that he uses the same license, although elsewhere the context of the letters repeatedly accuses him of falsity and everywhere rebukes his audacity.] against a certain count concerning the violent occupation of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia.

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolf codex XIII.)*

**SUMMARY.**—The same archbishop relates that, while visiting his province and staying at Passau, he was informed of a sacrilege committed by Count N. in the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia. Namely, his suffragan-elect N. had been dragged from there and taken to a castle belonging to N.; and the captive had been forced, by violence and fear, to transfer it to the count. This sacrilege must be corrected by the same count, lest those lands remain longer under interdict, and lest all prelates, with so great a crime left unpunished, become exposed to such outrages. He demands this insistently in the name of all.

To his most serene lord, etc., the constant and faithful purpose of the archbishop of Salzburg to serve [Note: [Col. 0765C] It is scarcely credible that this letter is found nowhere. Yet Hansiz, a diligent investigator of all matters concerning Archbishop Frederick, saw it neither in the imperial codex nor elsewhere.].

Recently, while we were established at Passau in your province, a grievous event occurred in Carinthia, which we report to your royal majesty with heavy complaint and sorrow. Count N. of P., after having sworn and transmitted his oath to you and to the empire, sent his scouts into the venerable monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia. Entering the monastery amid the clamor and force of weapons, they dared with bloody hands to drag the captive Lord N. out of the monastery itself. They led him bound to a certain castle of N., [Col. 0765C] which the same elect held in his own possession.

When he delayed, upon their demand, to hand over our castle to them, they threw him to the ground and, placing naked swords against his neck three times, and inflicting other bodily and atrocious injuries, compelled him, under fear of imminent death, to surrender our castle to that same count. In the castle, the count removed many provisions and several other valuable possessions. [Note: [Col. 0765D] I leave investigation of this sacrilege to those whom it will concern more directly. In the Salzburg Chronicle in Canisius (Ancient Readings, vol. III, part II, p. 487), I read the following under the year 1279: “Dietrich, bishop of Gurk, died, and John, bishop of Chiemsee, succeeded him; in his place Lord Conrad of Hindperch, a canon of Passau, was appointed.” Hansiz (Germania Sacra, vol. I, p. 424) observes that nearly all chroniclers report that he was consecrated by Paul the Minorite, bishop of Tripoli and apostolic legate, in the year 1280, on 5 May. Since below there is mention of the bishop of Chiemsee as one of Rudolf’s first loyal men, I infer that this letter was written before John was transferred to the see of Gurk, namely toward the end of 1279.]

Although, during the time of persecution, [Note: [Col. 0765D] The period of the persecution of the Salzburg Church extends until Rudolf’s arrival in Austria, namely in September of the year 1276. Since in the following years the archbishop always remained attached to Rudolf at least until the beginning of spring, the nature of the letter denies that it was written at that time, because it mentions persecution and because it was written by the archbishop while he was visiting his province.] **388** the province of Salzburg was troubled by many hardships among its clergy, it has nevertheless never endured so atrocious an injury. In the grave disgrace of this deed, all the inhabitants of our territories, collectively and individually, rightly stand amazed and fear with astonishment.

Unless this recent and bloody outrage is avenged by royal power, many others will rise up who, following the example of the count mentioned above, will trample underfoot the condition of clerics and churches. We therefore beseech your royal majesty in the name of all the prelates of our province: cause the said count, who by a twofold sacrilege, with diabolical presumption, violated the holy things of the Lord in a holy place and a consecrated person, and who, disregarding the homage of due fidelity owed to us, seized our castle by both deceitful plots and open injuries, to make reparation for this offense through Lord N., count at the time when the crime was committed and still present in those regions, [Note: [Col. 0766C] I have no doubt that Meinhard, count of Tyrol, is indicated here, both because he is hinted at below by the letter M and because, after Duke Philip had been removed, Rudolf entrusted Carinthia and other provinces to Meinhard to govern; later, in 1282, he designated him duke of Carinthia.] in such a way that satisfaction may be made both for the injury to us and for that to the whole clerical order, and that other clerics and prelates, who await similar events, may not despair of your protection.

They would see this crime committed with impunity in the persons of ourselves and of the venerable bishop of Chiemsee, whose blood brother the same count is, [Note: [Col. 0766C] John, bishop of Chiemsee, is appropriately identified as Meinhard’s full brother. For Rudolf, who had appointed Meinhard to Carinthia because of his excellent service, would with greater right have delegated to him the authority to redress his brother’s injuries.] although we have perseveringly adhered to you in this way and were the first of the others.

Your piety must also oppose so great a crime, lest the lands which, by a statute of our provincial council, [Note: [Col. 0766D] He is speaking of the Salzburg synod celebrated in November 1274. In Labbeus and Harduinus it contains twenty-four constitutions; in the imperial codex, as Hansiz observes (Germania Sacra, vol. II, p. 378), there are twenty-six, since the sixth is divided into two parts and another unpublished constitution is added after the sixteenth. They also appear in Canisius (Ancient Readings, vol. IV, p. 90). The constitution cited here is number 22, which reads as follows: “By the present edict we decree that, if—which God forbid—it should happen that an archbishop or bishop among us is taken captive, or that our churches or those of any one of us are invaded so hostilely and injuriously that there is reasonable fear of the overthrow of his position, then throughout the entire province of Salzburg there shall generally be a cessation from divine services, once the captivity or persecution of this kind has become clearly known throughout the province.”] have long been held subject to ecclesiastical interdict, should remain deprived of divine services for a long time, **389** and lest the people, who still waver in uncertainty, be led into the crooked path of error and scandal, something that could easily happen.

But woe to that man through whom this scandal has come. The interdict also, because of the form of the statute which we made long ago on account of fear of the lord king of Bohemia, as Bishops N. and N. fully know, we neither dare nor can relax unless the injury is first withdrawn; and Count M., if he wishes, will be able to make full restitution. [Note: [Col. 0767C] The form of the statute, said to have been enacted long ago, follows immediately after the words cited: “Yet, out of reverence for illustrious persons adorned with the dignity of princes, we do not wish this present edict to extend to them or to their lands, unless, after being warned, they disdain to cease from such offenses and refuse to make reparation within the space of one month for what they have done.”]

For the present we are also on the road, by which we are entering Carinthia and Styria [Note: [Col. 0767C] Two foundation charters of the convent of nuns at Tulln are extant. The first was issued at Vienna “on the day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth indiction, after the Nativity of Christ 1280, in the seventh year of our reign.” The second, after an interval of nine months, “on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the ninth indiction, in the year of Christ 1281, in the eighth year of our reign.” These are cited by the author of the History of Austria (book I, chapter 15 and following, pp. 87 and 91). The archbishop of Salzburg was not present at the former, but at the latter he was the first witness of all. Thus it is increasingly confirmed that this letter was given by the archbishop toward the end of 1279 while traveling through his extensive province, a journey he did not complete before September 1280. Had Hansiz seen this letter, he would not have maintained, on the basis of an empty conjecture, that the archbishop of Salzburg was idling in Vienna in rivalry with the apostolic legate—nothing could be more incredible at that time, as the records prove.], for the advancement of your honor; and from there we shall descend into the regions of Austria.

**LETTER XIV.** The patriarch of Aquileia writes to the emperor Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0767D] See column 765, note c.] about many matters, especially about subduing the king of Bohemia.

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolf codex XIV.)*

**SUMMARY.**—Raymond della Torre, patriarch of Aquileia, replies to Rudolf’s letter, saying that he rejoices that Rudolf follows the faith and counsels of the Torriani and that he is waging war against Ottokar, king of Bohemia. He promises aid against Ottokar, who is hostile to him and to his church. He says that he will have no disagreement with N., provided that N. destroys the castle recently erected against the rights and privileges of his church. He will return immediately to his church, so that from there he may be more ready and prepared to serve Rudolf.

To the most serene lord, etc., from the patriarch of Aquileia. [Note: [Col. 0767D] Raymond della Torre, Ughello, son of Martino, while bishop of Como, “Pagani” [reading/meaning uncertain], when he was transferred to the patriarchate of Aquileia. (Italia Sacra, vol. V, pp. 300 and 94.)]

I received the royal letters, which demand and seek examples and signs of pure faith and ready devotion, with prompt honor; and, after reading them with the most affectionate feeling, I conceived such immense joy that my spirit, mind, and indeed every sense were renewed with gladness. For I have a chief and most welcome source of joy and exultation in the fact that your royal highness, trusting in the faithful faith of myself and my people, has chosen to direct your imperial proceedings according to our counsel, as though it had been offered to you as the more salutary course, and to rule [Note: [Col. 0767D] Raynaldus (1275, no. 5), on the authority of apostolic letters, states that Napoleon and Francesco della Torre, who ruled Milan, were ordered by Gregory to resist Alfonso, king of Castile, who was seeking the empire, while everywhere securing obedience to Rudolf. From this we learn that, with the patriarch supporting their counsels, he made use of them in the more serious affairs of the empire.] accordingly.

I also have a special and overflowing accumulation of joys because your imperial serenity, striving to adorn the dignity of the imperial throne with virtuous deeds befitting the glory of so great a lord, intends to humble beneath your powerful right hand your contemptuous subjects, who, like the columns and foundations of the empire, ought with all readiness to run along the path of your commands; and, as their insolent rebellion demands, to crush them beneath the hammer of deserved punishment. Thus he who, while tranquil, is despised in his commands may afterward be felt as angry in vengeance; and those whom all the faithful, individually and collectively, who render to your excellence the due debt of loyalty, know as a gentle and pious lord, may be perceived by your rivals as a corrector to their own confusion.

For the more their punishable acts increase through excess, the greater the correction that must be applied to the offenders, so that they may at least recognize their crime through the punishment that avenges it, and so that fear of punishment and vengeance may restrain others from unlawful acts.

Since, moreover, the mind of the writer is so fixed upon advancing your exaltation that the sum of my desires chiefly wishes to promote the honor and renown of your name in word and deed, I wish your magnificence to know that I shall gather together whatever I can in men and resources, so that, as soon as possible, after your successful campaign against the king of Bohemia [Col. 0768B]—who exists as an enemy to God and all justice, injurious to the rights of myself and my church [Note: [Col. 0768C] Everyone knows that the rights of the patriarchate extended to the imperial provinces held by Ottokar. In Carinthia alone, Duke Ulrich held by feudal right the towns of Tyffer, Treven, Windischgraz, and Clemau, the city of Saint Veit, Klagenfurt, and Saint George. After his death, his brother Philip invaded them, preparing a path for himself to the Aquileian mitre, which he sought in vain. At Ottokar’s command he had been forced to restore those towns to the Church of Aquileia. When Rudolf was elected king of the Romans, the same Philip, like the other princes of the other provinces, obtained from Rudolf the investiture of Carinthia. When, however, in 1276 the king brought that province and the others back under his own authority, he granted Carinthia, after it had been offered to Philip, to Count Meinhard of Tyrol for administration. Since Raymond complains of Ottokar’s injustices, there is no doubt that Philip and the dukes of the other provinces who had adhered to Rudolf enjoyed the same fortune as the archbishop of Salzburg, and consequently that the rights of the Church of Aquileia were exposed to the plunder and fires of raging Ottokar.] and dishonoring to its dignities), I shall make myself ready, to the extent of my powers, for the service of your excellence. [Note: [Col. 0768D] In none of the records I have seen have I found Raymond among the prelates who followed Rudolf’s camp.]

Moreover, the favorable invitation of your letter moved me to seek to arrange a settlement with N. Concerning this I explain my will through the present letter: at present there is no matter of disagreement or resentment between him and me, nor will any ground of discord arise from me toward him; rather, may the integrity and strength of friendship and affection flourish between us.

Nevertheless, while I was engaged in your service, he caused a certain castle to be erected to the prejudice of my church and against its public privileges and rights. Unless perhaps he chooses the path of equity and justice and desists from such an unjust and violent injury, this may become a source of ill will and nourish it beyond what is expedient. [Note: [Col. 0768D] I do not know whether this is said of Philip, duke of Carinthia, or of some neighboring prince. It does, however, shed some light on Italian history: Raymond seems to have rendered obedience to Rudolf in Lombardy while adhering to his Torriani, who were involved in war with the Visconti. Otherwise, he would have noticed the erection of his castle.]

Although I have thus far prolonged my stay in these regions in order to direct your steps and prepare your undertakings, behold, I am hastening to return immediately to my own land [Note: [Col. 0768D] The preceding statements are confirmed by this: his own land was the patriarchate of Aquileia. The see was at Udine, to which he was, as it seems to me, returning from the provinces of Germany. I leave all these matters, reached by conjecture, intact for others, neither denying nor affirming anything.], so that I may make myself more ready and prompt for your service, in accordance with the ardent desire of my heart.

**392. LETTER XV.** Concerning the captain of Styria, who in the name of Ottokar, king of Bohemia, devastated all the possessions of the Church of Salzburg; the same archbishop of Salzburg writes to Rudolf, asking him for speedy aid.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolf codex XV.)*

**SUMMARY.**—The archbishop of Salzburg informs Rudolf that in Austria, Carinthia, and Styria all who were loyal to the king of the Romans were being subjected to hostilities by Ottokar; and finally that troops had been sent into the rights and territories of the Church of Salzburg, which by plunder and slaughter had nearly destroyed everything. The enemy would agree to no other terms of peace than that the Church and the empire should abandon their fidelity. He asks for speedy help, lest what little remained be destroyed.

The indignation which the lord king of Bohemia unjustly conceived against the Church of Salzburg [Col. 0769B] [Salzburg Church] [Note: [Col. 0769C] Another letter written by the same archbishop to Gregory X sheds light on this letter; Hansiz (Germania Sacra, vol. II, p. 381) reports it immediately after the letter sent to Rudolf:

“We are compelled by great necessity to bring the multitude of our afflictions before the holy clemency of Your Apostolate. For our illustrious prince, after our return from the general council, having conceived a grave indignation against us, has so completely seized all the revenues and income of our churches that he has left most of us no more temporal resources than would suffice for eight days’ needs. Our men, possessions, and estates, entered by royal edict, serve and attend not us but him. Our cities, towns, and castles are occupied as by an enemy, and no one is exempt from this severe persecution except those who have bound themselves by oaths and other guarantees that in future they will do nothing at the command of the Roman Church or at the order of the king of the Romans that might displease that king.

“Such unlawful oaths and disgraceful alliances are extorted from both secular and regular persons. But we, who abhor such horrendous extortion, indeed such damnable conspiracy, cannot find a place of pardon with the aforesaid king; rather, we await still heavier injuries because we preserve justice. And although these dangers pressing upon us, directed toward the overthrow of our churches and our destruction, provide us with sufficient cause for fear and grief, we are tortured even more cruelly by the fact that, under pretext of this danger, we are all prevented from promoting aid for the Holy Land, preaching the saving cross, and pursuing the holy enterprise in which the state of the Christian faith is at stake.

“Therefore, holy father, may your clemency from the height of the apostolic see look upon our tribulations and deign to rescue us, the afflicted, from the hand of the one who unjustly afflicts us; and may your goodness stir up the power of our most serene lord, the king of the Romans, both to aid our redemption and to repel the injury inflicted upon him himself, which we suffer for his sake. For unless prompt assistance comes to us, our churches, placed on the brink, will be overthrown.”

This letter to Gregory ought to precede letter 38 of the first book, and the present letter should immediately follow it, since it contains fresh evidence of Ottokar’s fury.]

As we have learned by experience, he will not rest until every trace of us and of our church has been erased from the earth. For after everyone in Austria, Styria, and Carinthia who cultivated justice and obeyed the laws of the Roman empire had perished, and after our faithful devotion could neither be removed nor changed—though it had been tested by many terrors, enticed by various promises, and solicited by the aforesaid king with the greatest number of blandishments—behold, on that day the captain of Styria, in the name of the said king, invaded all the estates, markets, castles, and towns of the Church of Salzburg with an assembled army.

They captured the inhabitants, killed many, carried away movable property, and so cruelly devastated immovable property with fire and sword that now nothing of all the possessions of the aforesaid church can be seen to remain which has not been trampled underfoot by the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0770C] The Salzburg Chronicle in Canisius (Ancient Readings, vol. III, part II, p. 487), summing up the losses in a brief statement, says: “In the year 1275, the king of Bohemia invaded the Church of Salzburg as an enemy, inflicting damage publicly assessed at forty-three marks, especially through the alienation and burning of estates.” The captain mentioned was Milota Záviš, governor of Styria. The archbishop discussed this matter with great force not long afterward at the assembly held at Augsburg on 24 June, as Gerard reports (History of Austria, book I, p. 22). After hearing the complaints of the Austrians, he “speaking of the recent injury inflicted by sending the governor Milota into his territories, where he had defiled everything with iron and fire, pleaded and begged the emperor and the other princes to oppose his efforts in time.”]

Although we prostrated ourselves with devoted humility before that same king and sought the grace of peace, or at least a truce, we could accomplish nothing under any definite condition unless we wished, by violating the obligation of our faith toward the Roman Church and the sacred Roman empire, to become faithless. We therefore, being in distress out of reverence for the Emperor, implore aid and await assistance from your most fortunate majesty. With sorrow and groaning we ask that at least you come swiftly to the remnants of the said church, which have been pitifully abandoned, lest the small and meager amount of resources that has fallen from the claws of the plunderers be swallowed up again by those same men, before we are brought to complete ruin.

**394. LETTER XVI.** Rudolf writes to the nobles of the kingdom of Hungary, saying that he will shortly take vengeance upon their enemy, the king of Bohemia.

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolf codex XVI.)*

[Col. 0770B]

**SUMMARY.**—Rudolf highly praises the Hungarian nobles for their fidelity and concern toward the young King Ladislaus and Duke Andrew, whom he has adopted as sons. He intends to prove his words by his deeds, and encourages them to seek honors in the Roman kingdom, affirming that they are dear to him in the court and kingdom; he declares that he will restore the former glory of their kingdom and, with God’s favor, break the audacity of his rival Ottokar.

That the vigor of your unblemished faith and the distinction of your natural power illuminate; that a more radiant spark of purity has shone forth through the strength of your steadfast spirit—this has appeared through the clear evidence of your deeds and has become manifest through tangible proofs, while you have not ceased freely to anticipate with services the illustrious Ladislaus, king of Hungary, and Andrew, duke of Slavonia, our dearest sons, deprived by the lot of human fate of paternal comfort, whom we have taken up to be cherished in a paternal embrace and bosom as flesh from our flesh and bone, as it were, from our bones; nor have you ceased to cling to them with devoted and unremitting solicitude in the affairs of themselves and of the kingdom.

For these laudable actions of yours, in which indeed you have pleased us as though in some delightful refreshment, we pursue your zeal with the fullest expressions of gratitude and commend it with worthy praise. Wishing, therefore, to abound toward you more in deeds than in words on this account, we ask you as a special favor that, if any such prerogatives shine forth in the Roman kingdom or among us as might delight your spirit, you should confidently request them from us, trusting that you will obtain them.

For it is undoubtedly in our heart and care to restore that magnificent and famous kingdom of Hungary, through a renewed reformation, to the standards of its ancient glory, and thus, while it remains unharmed, to strike down the ferocity of its persecutor—since we intend to spare no loss whatsoever of persons or property in order to tame the arrogance of that haughty man, under victorious eagles, with the Lord of hosts as our leader—so that henceforth, with his brow lowered by his own defeat, he may learn how hard and difficult it is to kick against the goad.

[Note: This letter is clearly to be preferred to the one cited above (Epistle 6), as the facts themselves show. For Ladislaus’s chamberlain, moved by this generous display, requested that certain lands not yet wrested from the invader’s hands be granted to him as a commendation from his king.]

[Note: The error must be attributed to the collector or copyist, since elsewhere (Epistles 6 and 20) he is correctly called Ladislaus.]

[Note: The History of Austria under the year 1277 states: “Around the feast of All Saints, the king of the Romans and the king of Hungary held a conference near Hainburg, where the king of the Romans adopted that same king of Hungary as his son. And all promised to serve the Roman king. At the same time the Roman king invited that same king of Hungary to dinner at Bruck.” Gerard gives the same account (History of Austria, p. 29). But below we shall see (Epistle 31) that at that meeting, or conference, not adoption but a treaty was concluded. Therefore, when Rudolph, wishing to encourage the nobles, declares that paternal comfort will not be lacking to the royal youths, he indicates that he has already adopted them.]

[Note: Stephen, the youths’ father, retained for himself in the peace treaty with Ottocar, as reported by Raynaldus (1271, no. 30ff.), “Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, Rama, Serbia, Galicia, Lodomeria, Cumania, Bulgaria, and the whole duchy of Slavonia with their appurtenances.” But he surrendered every right “in the duchies of Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and the March.” Gregory X subsequently confirmed this treaty by apostolic authority in the following year, 1272. But when Stephen died that same year, the peace vanished. For Beda, duke and cousin of Ottocar, accused before Ladislaus of treason and killed, compelled the enraged Ottocar to break the peace. Although Gregory, invoking also the assistance of Charles, king of Sicily, tried to restrain the anger that was about to erupt, he could not suppress the movement of that fierce spirit. Accordingly, Rudolph commends the nobles’ outstanding loyalty and concern, promises to act in the place of a parent, and declares that he will honor them with benefits and very soon take up arms against the rival of the kingdom.]

[Note: See above concerning the eagle on banners (Epistle 11, no. 2).]

## Epistle XVII. The emperor Rudolph commends his firstborn son, whom he sends ahead into Austria with military forces, to a certain prince, so that he may assist him in every way.

[Note: Correct the title-maker’s error: Rudolph, king of the Romans, as Rudolph himself consistently wished.]

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XVII in the codex.)*

### Argument

Having decided to move his camp toward Eger and having sent his firstborn Albert ahead into Austria with a strong army, Rudolph asks N. to grant him passage through his territories, promising that he will not be burdensome to the places or their inhabitants. He also asks him to order the peoples subject to him to provide protection for Albert, since they are about to shake off the yoke that Ottocar had long ago imposed upon them.

Rudolph, etc. The spirit of our serenity is rightly disturbed, and we are stirred to anger all the more vehemently, and with so much greater justice, the more seriously we perceive that you and the other princes and faithful of the Holy Empire are being afflicted by the mad tyranny of the illustrious king of Bohemia, because of the purity of the faith that you bear toward the Roman Empire.

Indeed, desiring with fervent and unremitting wishes to display to you and to our other princes who are unjustly afflicted and likewise oppressed the spirit and affection of manifold love that our serenity bears toward you, through diligent and speedy assistance and powerful support, we purpose and intend to proceed with our son L. toward Eger, with the King of Kings happily directing our steps, and with rapid progress, while our firstborn son has been sent toward the regions of Austria with a multitude of armed men and a most fitting abundance of military equipment.

Since he must cross your borders without injury, loss, or damage to any person, we ask you to prepare a road and entrance for our firstborn, in keeping with the steadfast confidence that we possess in your fidelity and prudence. Make arrangements so that your faithful subjects may assist him from their fortifications—or rather, may assist themselves—and may pursue their own cause in supporting our firstborn so ardently and vigorously that, having cast off the yoke of servitude imposed upon them long ago by the aforesaid king, they may breathe freely in the peaceful pleasantness of peace.

We commit this son of ours entirely to your tested fidelity and prudent counsel, and entrust him to you as a son, to be instructed, governed, and directed in everything that concerns the liberation of his homeland.

[Note: I believe this letter was given after the army at Kempten, a city of Swabia now called Kempten in the Allgäu, had been reviewed. From this it is clear that the route of each army into Austria was Rudolph’s through Franconia toward Eger on the Bohemian frontier, and Albert’s through the county of Tyrol and the borders of Carinthia.]

[Note: None of Rudolph’s sons had a name beginning with the letter L, as I stated in its proper place (Book I, Epistle 11, no. 4). H. or R. must therefore be restored: Hermann, or another son bearing his father’s name, who was serving his apprenticeship under his vigorous father and was present in the army. For the following year, in two documents published by Hansiz (German Sacred History, vol. I, pp. 418ff.), fiefs are found to have been granted to Albert, Hermann, and Rudolph and to their male heirs by Peter, bishop of Passau.]

[Note: It is known that Philip, duke of Carinthia, received the investiture of that province at the diet of Nuremberg (Epistle 14, no. 4), although in this same year Rudolph entrusted that province, together with the other Austrian territories he had acquired, to Count Meinhard of Tyrol to administer. The army might therefore be thought to have been commended to this duke’s loyalty and prudence; but when these were later shown on this occasion to be deceptive, they became the reason for his subsequent deposition. Yet what follows cannot possibly apply to Philip.]

[Note: These words certainly concern not a man known only on one occasion, who obtained from Rudolph both the investiture of his fiefs and restoration in full—for he had been deposed by Ottocar from Carinthia and Carniola—but a man of proven fidelity, to whom Albert could be commended as to a father, such as the archbishop of Salzburg. Yet I would not dare to assert that the letter was written to him, since above (Epistle 12) I observed a difference in the language and official formulas between this letter and the letter to the archbishop.]

## Epistle XVIII. The emperor Rudolph informs a certain duke that he will march against the Bohemian, and asks him to occupy camps nearer to the enemy.

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XVIII in the codex.)*

[Note: Correct the title-maker’s error, as at column 771, note d: Rudolph, king of the Romans.]

### Argument

To secure a safer route against the king of Bohemia, Rudolph urges N. to occupy whatever enemy camps he can that are nearest to his territory. He promises him reward, praise, and honors.

How the reckless enemy of the Empire, N., is plotting the disinheritance of that same Empire through the snares of crafty deceit and the assaults of slanderous accusation is, we believe, sufficiently known to you nearby—what has already spread to distant regions.

Since we are soon to move the standards of imperial power to recover the splendid possessions of the Empire that have hitherto been occupied by that same man, with the Most High Lord of hosts as our leader, we have thought it right to exhort your sincerity—which enjoys no small measure of our confidence—with the strongest urgency of entreaty possible, so that you may not fail to turn all the concerns and suitable efforts of your spirit toward occupying the camps of the aforesaid king that are nearer to your power [perhaps, province], in order that through those same places a freer passage and easier entrance may be opened for us into his territory, and that the utter destruction of his desolation may thereby be prepared for us and ours forever.

Through this, without doubt, you and your people will be able to be anticipated by worthy praises from our magnificence and exalted to lofty honors.

[Note: Carinthia, Styria, Carniola, and the other Austrian provinces had been unsuccessfully demanded back through ambassadors before the enemy of the Empire was declared.]

[Note: He was going to travel through Bavaria. Yet he is always silent concerning its duke, Henry, and his territory. When he arrived, he restrained him by the mere display of arms. Then all Austria lay open as far as Vienna.]

## Epistle XIX. Caesar Rudolph excuses himself to the Roman pontiff for not having come at the appointed time to receive the imperial crown.

*(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolph XIX in the codex.)*

### Argument

Rudolph assures Gregory X that after the conference at Lausanne he had nothing more at heart than to make a magnificent preparation for the journey into Italy to receive the imperial coronation on the holy day of Pentecost, as had been arranged; but that for some time he was detained by serious affairs, which his legate will relate.

That zeal concerning the accomplishment of the mysteries of our father’s good pleasure continually overflows; that effect of filial devotion truly burns unceasingly in our breast, concerning the honorable service to be rendered to Mother Church. From the time when we had the good fortune to depart from your beloved presence, we spared no expense or labor in making suitable royal preparations for the journey on which we hoped to proceed, in order to receive from your sacred hands, at the time appointed for us by your kindness, the diadem of the Empire.

But the suitable sequence of successive undertakings did not favor such wishes [perhaps, did favor them]. Rather, a tangled accumulation of unforeseen circumstances that subsequently arose, intruding, detached our ready spirit for a little while from the voluntary execution of so agreeable a work.

We have therefore thought it preferable that these troublesome obstacles be explained to Your Holiness through the eloquence of a trusted interpreter rather than in writing. For this reason we send to the feet of Your Beatitude, with the greatest confidence, the religious and honorable N., a man distinguished for faith and devotion, shining with the purity of a celibate life, and acceptable to us because of the radiant merits of his probity. Into his mouth we have perfectly poured our words concerning the matters mentioned above and others. We humbly beg that you deign to place credulous faith in him concerning these matters, just as you would in us ourselves.

[Note: It must be taken as certain that he is speaking of the conference at Lausanne, specifically with Gregory X. Since after the pontiff’s death he assured the cardinals that he was already prepared to come, these letters must necessarily be dated earlier and placed before those to the cardinals (Book I, Epistle 42). They were written before 20 January 1276; therefore these appear to have been written toward the end of the preceding year, as Rudolph himself testifies when he says that he was detained not for long but for a little while from undertaking the proposed journey.]

[Note: We have already stated that the first appointed date was the feast of All Saints in 1275; but as it approached, while the king was staying with the pontiff at Lausanne, it was postponed until Pentecost of the following year. Thus the title-writer is wrong to say that Rudolph is excusing himself for not having come: Rudolph himself says, “we were preparing ourselves with royal magnificence for the journey on which we hoped to proceed.” Let the reader judge what is meant by such frequent transformations; to me, this collector or copyist seems of doubtful reliability.]

[Note: The preceding material makes clear that long before the conference at Lausanne all hostile actions by Ottocar against the archbishop and the other princes, barons, and counts who had deserted him in order to adhere to the Roman king were already underway. Yet, however serious this cause was, it did not prevent Gregory, while he was alive, from seriously undertaking those two greatest and most important matters: the Syrian expedition and Rudolph’s coronation, since, as the authorities consistently affirm, their future leaders were to be the emperor and the pontiff. Other impediments therefore arose, which the legate was to relate and which Rudolph later promised to explain to Innocent V (Book I, Epistle 38), so that he might be present in Rome on the appointed day.]

[Note: At that time Minorites very often served as ambassadors to the pontiff and to the highest princes. I should not pass over the distinguished testimony of the Council of Lyons, both concerning them and concerning the religious of the Order of Preachers. Both orders were considered especially necessary to the Church when the question concerned disapproving new religious orders: “Indeed,” say the Fathers, “we do not allow the present constitution to be extended to the Orders of Preachers and Minors, which evident usefulness arising from them for the universal Church shows to have been approved. But we permit the Orders of Carmelites and Hermits of Saint Augustine, whose institution preceded the said general council [the Lateran Council under Innocent III, canon 12], to remain in their present state until other arrangements have been made concerning them.” From whichever order this religious belonged, two points in particular deserve serious notice: first, that the holy conduct and sincerity of such men were greatly esteemed by the highest princes; and second, that the religious of both orders, before their former rigor cooled, were held in the highest regard for the benefit of Church and state. We shall see this confirmed by examples below.]

## Epistle XX. He rouses Ladislaus, king of Hungary, and Andrew, duke of Slavonia, against the king of Bohemia.

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XX in the codex.)*

### Argument

Rudolph announces to Ladislaus, king of Hungary, and his brother Andrew, duke of Slavonia, whom he has adopted as sons and joined to himself by treaty, that he will free them and their kingdom from Ottocar’s tyranny. He orders them to be of lofty and courageous spirit, for they will fight with a just and fortunate prince.

The bond of peaceful kinship, which unites us in the embraces of mutual identity, has been so fixed in our hearts, has truly grown so firmly rooted, and continually coalesces as though planted in the garden of our memory, that among the many matters whose frequent concern affects us, this above all remains fixed in our wishes: how we may rescue you and the illustrious N., whom we have taken up to be cherished in a paternal embrace and bosom as flesh from our flesh and as bone, so to speak, from our bones, from the mad tyranny of an unjust persecutor, and enlarge the boundaries of the cords of your ancestral inheritance within fitting limits.

For it is undoubtedly in our heart and care to restore that magnificent and famous kingdom of Hungary, through a renewed reformation, to the standards of its ancient glory, and thus, while it remains unharmed, to strike down the ferocity of that persecutor—since we intend to spare no loss whatsoever of persons or property in order to tame the arrogance of that haughty man, under victorious eagles, with the Lord of hosts as our leader.

Let him henceforth learn, with his brow lowered by his own defeat, how hard and difficult it is to kick against the goad.

[Note: The similarity of this letter to Epistle 16 makes me believe that both were issued at the same time. Since in both letters the royal youths are said to have been adopted, I confess that I do not understand why the author of the Austrian history, placing excessive trust in Gerard, postpones the adoption until the following year. See above, column 771, note b.]

[Note: He addresses the nobles of Hungary in nearly the same words.]

Come, therefore, prince, into whom the generous valor of your ancestors has transmitted strength and courage through an unearned inheritance: put on the virtuous man, girding yourselves with the strength of fortitude. We trust in divine clemency that prosperous success will not be lacking for you in all things, while you fight in an easy and just cause and under a fortunate prince who is zealous for justice.

[Note: It would be pointless to compare such a great prince, adorned with such great virtues, with Caesar or other pagan rulers. Yet the testimony of Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, must not be passed over in silence. He describes Gregory X’s elected king of the Romans as follows (Caesarean Codex, in the author of Austrian Piety, Book I, chapter 4, p. 34):

“And that new joys concerning the person of the elected—and likewise crowned—king may fill the sacred Roman Church, our mother, the same king is Catholic in faith, a lover of churches, a cultivator of justice, strong in counsel, shining in piety, powerful in his own strength, and joined by kinship to many powerful men; beloved of God, as we firmly believe, and gracious in human eyes, as is evident. Moreover, he is vigorous in body and fortunate in military affairs against unbelievers. Therefore we hope in Him who establishes kings and kingdoms that under his rule peaceful rest will come to the kingdom, peace to the churches, concord to the peoples, and discipline to morals, so that swords may be beaten into plowshares and the horn of his Christ may be magnificently exalted by the King of Kings.

We therefore ask you, holy father, to receive this singular son, whom you will undoubtedly find to be an intrepid champion of Mother Church and an unconquered defender of the Catholic faith. Following with the applause of benevolent approval the process concerning him, conducted with such propriety, prudence, and maturity, and completing the work through the abundant sweetness of paternal piety, deign, when it pleases Your Holiness and seems appropriate, mercifully to summon him to the diadem of imperial majesty, so that all may know and understand that the Lord has placed you as a light to the nations, and that through the judgment of your prudence a long-desired serenity may shine upon the world after the clouds.”]

## Epistle XXI. Rudolph invites a duke to command the army in military service.

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XXI in the codex.)*

[Note: Reader, judge whether the title suits the letter. The king himself, together with one of his sons, commanded the royal army, and everything had already been arranged for moving camp. Why, then, does he seek a commander for that same army?]

### Argument

He praises highly the duke who was sent ahead with part of the forces into the provinces to be recovered for the Empire, on account of his distinguished achievements. He announces to him that he will soon depart for Austria with magnificent preparations and pursue him with royal generosity.

It is sufficiently apparent and known to the royal highness how much virtue shines forth in you; clear and pleasing indications sufficiently reveal, and well-known proofs have made manifest, how you glitter with the purity of valor and fidelity.

[Note: The authorities consistently report that Meinhard, count of Tyrol, was sent ahead by Rudolph into Styria and Carinthia. When Rudolph reached Passau on 26 September, Meinhard is found in the royal camp and is said to have brought both provinces under oath. I should be lying if this letter was not addressed to that vigorous commander. Indeed Albert, Rudolph’s firstborn, whom we saw above (Epistle 17) sent ahead in the same manner into the Austrian provinces, seems to have been with Count Meinhard. Certainly, with the army entrusted to him, he had accomplished deeds worthy of Rudolph’s highest commendation.] Thirsty and eager for our glory, avoiding neither the loss of persons nor of property, you do not cease to leap forward fearlessly for the exaltation of the Empire, directing gloriously and vigorously the troops of our army entrusted to you.

For this, we commend the achievement of your steadfastness, which has pleased us in the performance of the work. We wish your desires to know that, in the near future, with God as our guide, we intend to proceed into the regions of Austria with royal power and magnificent equipment, liberally anticipating you with beneficence worthy of your merits and, according to the counsel of your industry, providing for the undertaking with a salutary conclusion [Note: Something seems to be missing here.]

[Note: In this same year, after Philip, duke of Carinthia, had been deposed, Rudolph appointed Meinhard over the provinces, as Hansiz observes (German Sacred History, vol. II, p. 365), whose words I will not omit: “When Rudolph had occupied the provinces in 1276, he entrusted them not to Philip but to Meinhard, count of Tyrol, because of the outstanding service he had rendered; Philip endured his modest station near the town of Krems until the end. He died in 1279.”]

## Epistle XXII. Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, absolves his diocesan subjects from an oath sworn to a certain prince.

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XXII in the codex.)*

### Argument

The archbishop of Salzburg absolves his provincials from the oath of fidelity by which they were bound to the king of Bohemia. With the counsel of his suffragans, he threatens to strike with anathema anyone who, on the pretext of that oath, does not adhere to Rudolph.

Frederick, by the grace of God, etc., wishes you all fullness of good together with salvation.

Since the sacredness of an oath is not a bond of iniquity but rather a confirmation of truth, prudent and provident men, among whom we count you, fully understand and readily perceive that the oaths sworn by you and others to the illustrious prince N. against the Holy Empire and your most serene lord neither hold nor bind you, because they were improperly extorted against the duke, justice, and the order of the commonwealth.

And since those same oaths cannot be observed without prejudice to your salvation and mortal danger to your souls, by the authority of Almighty God we remit and absolve you from them; indeed, we declare that you are not bound to observe them.

Moreover, with the counsel of our venerable suffragan brothers, we shall proceed by a sentence of excommunication against all and each of those who, under the pretext of oaths given in this manner, choose to wander in the deviation of their conceived error rather than be brought back to the path of manifest truth, by which the Roman Empire, with God already leading us, advances before us.

[Note: See above, Epistle 15, concerning the oaths that Ottocar extorted.]

[Note: While the archbishop was doing this, he was in safety, since he was following Rudolph’s camp. After Rudolph’s arrival in Austria, the History of Austria narrates the same matter as follows: “The ministerials received him honorably and solemnly; abandoning and rejecting the aforesaid king of Bohemia, they adhered to Rudolph and forgot the pact and oath that they had made with him, setting aside their heirs whom they had delivered to him as hostages. At the counsel and instruction of the Preaching and Minor Brothers, and of the entire clergy, who, by the authority of the pope, removed the crimes of the oaths, they all received King Rudolph as their lord.” I do not ask whether the counsel of the brothers and clergy was involved; this clear historical testimony most plainly establishes that the peoples were absolved from their oath by episcopal authority.]

[Note: Moved by the eagerness of the peoples, who desired to be freed from Ottocar’s tyranny, and with spiritual weapons added to their cause, cities and castles submitted themselves to Rudolph’s rule, except the city of Vienna, which he enclosed under siege, as Eberhard of Altaich briefly and others more fully consistently report.]

## Epistle XXIII. Rudolph writes to the king of Hungary for assistance against the Bohemian.

*(Year of the Lord 1278, Rudolph XXIII in the codex.)*

[Note: Epistle 29 should have been placed here. But since I have made it a principle not to alter the order of the codex in any way, I will not disturb even this evident inversion, especially since the letter that follows should be placed before the preceding one, and several others have wandered from their proper place, as we shall see. It should rather be noted in advance that on 19 November 1276, Elisabeth, queen of Bohemia, fell on her knees and swore allegiance to Rudolph before many princes; this matter will be related at length below (Epistle 29).]

### Argument

Rudolph, stationed at Vienna after Ottocar’s withdrawal and gathering assistance against that same rebel from every direction, while preparing himself for the final conflict, asks the king of Hungary to support him in the duchies of Austria and Styria. He informs the king that if the enemy should turn in that direction, he has resolved to pursue him from behind.

When alliances of kinship and friendship are sometimes contracted among the kings and princes of the world, a union of affection among them ought rightly to arise all the more strongly, the higher they are placed above others upon the loftier watchtowers of dignity, the more they ought to display examples of virtue to those beneath them, and the more firmly peace among the peoples grows through their unanimous wills; mutual honors are enlarged, and the rights of their kingdoms are strengthened for posterity.

Indeed, the identity of mutual connection formerly contracted happily between us has become so indestructibly rooted in our hearts, and has been so firmly established in the innermost affections of our heart, that it delights us to carry out in action whatever may please your royal spirit and whatever we may judge will increase the honors of Your Majesty. With unchanging purpose we therefore resolve to preserve this bond of fellowship indissolubly.

Hence, in reciprocal fashion, we now claim from you the obligation of the inviolable friendship contracted between us, according to what your procurator and envoy is known to have promised and to which he solemnly bound you. With all the greater affection of entreaty that we can muster, we earnestly ask Your Royal Serenity and urge you to assist us mutually in our necessities, and to extend to our faithful subjects and supporters in the duchies of Austria and Styria the effective shelter of timely protection and the support of consoling counsel and aid, according to what our beloved faithful N. and N. shall deem fit to explain to Your Royal Highness.

For we are remaining for the present in our city of Vienna, which is sufficiently near the king of Bohemia, so that if that king should perhaps direct the rash advance of his steps toward the destruction of those faithful of ours, we may pursue that king manfully from behind and strike him down while leaving those aforesaid faithful unharmed.

We therefore ask you to write back to us quickly concerning what is being considered and intended in your purpose and good pleasure regarding the matters set forth above.

[Note: The relationship contracted through adoption was discussed above (Epistles 16 and 20). Here mention is also made of the treaty that was initiated, whose conditions are given below (Epistle 31). Thus this letter, which belongs to the year 1278, should have been placed before that one.]

[Note: Before the treaty was concluded between the Roman king and the king of Hungary, agreements had been made through envoys sent back and forth, and everything had been properly completed that is customary in such great negotiations, as Rudolph clearly affirms. Therefore, the brevity of the chroniclers of Altaich and others concerning the friendship mutually contracted, when combined with the astonishing speed of events, must be interpreted in such a way that several months should be assigned to the conclusion of the treaty, and no fewer to the preparations for the new war. For the result of both matters did not appear before the end of August 1278 (Epistle 32ff.).]

[Note: Rudolph and Ladislaus fought with united armies, as this letter itself shows. For the Bohemian, encamped in Austria, frustrated Rudolph’s plans concerning the duchy of Styria.]

[Note: The king of the Romans remained in this city until the death of Queen Anna in 1281. He then left the administration of Austria and the other provinces to his firstborn Albert and departed for the Rhine.]

[Note: Although it seemed that, by virtue of the treaty entered into for protection and harm to the enemy, assistance from the allied king would not be lacking, Rudolph nevertheless wished that the same king should indicate in writing whether or not he intended to provide aid. For it was necessary to fight with the strongest and most warlike king of his age, accustomed to victories according to the Prague Chronicle, and moreover with an angry king.]

## Epistle XXIV. Rudolph accepts the excuse of a certain man, but does not wish him to be a mediator of peace between himself and the king of Bohemia.

*(Year of the Lord 1276, Rudolph XXIV in the codex.)*

### Argument

The excellent prince responds with the greatest generosity to the petition of Bernard, bishop of Seckau. He declares that he will not accept him as arbitrator of peace between himself and Ottocar unless Ottocar first repairs the immense damages inflicted upon the bishops; then he will lend an ear to proposals consistent with reason.

Your letters, most recently sent to us [Note: [Col. 0778D] Specifically those of Bernard, bishop of Seckau, an ardent partisan of Ottocar, who, acting as royal envoy at the Augsburg assembly the previous year, had rashly launched an attack against Rudolph; relying on Bohemian power, he had despised him as an enemy despises an enemy.], we received with kindly affection, since they, rendering you innocent of the leaven which the earlier version of your letters had marked out and scattered [Col. 0778C], revealed the coverings of a truly modest fleece [Note: Other letters had preceded these, by which he had turned away the allegation that he had poured forth disgraceful pamphlets against the Roman king. The manuscripts preserve neither letter [Col. 0779B]. From this reply of Rudolph, however, a fragment of which Hansiz quotes [Col. 0779C] (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 383), it is clear that Bernard pleaded his case in two letters. We can readily establish their date if we observe that on 26 September Bernard was not present with the other bishops of Passau in Rudolph’s camp, but late in November, together with the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans, sent a letter of congratulation to John XXI, announcing with rejoicing the liberation of Austria and other provinces from tyranny. Thus, first out of fear, when he saw Rudolph approaching Austria with the support of the princes and the terror of arms; then, recovering his senses after the example of Henry, duke of Bavaria, he began by letter to beg pardon—which he certainly obtained before Rudolph moved his camp out of Bavaria.].

Certainly, up to this time the royal majesty had never doubted the unwavering rectitude of your character, but had always believed that whatever art the industrious nature of a man of pure heart could have infused into you had been divinely implanted in you. Accordingly, in view of what your sincere heart, apparently incapable of receiving the rust of a scar, has now brought forth into the light—namely, the excellence of your celebrated reputation and the firmness of your constancy—which we commend with an appropriate proclamation of praise, we gladly accept your excuse and approve the claims of your striving innocence.

Let those, however, who, without your knowledge, dictated libels empty of truth, see what honor and glory they will gain from such fabrications [Note: With a magnanimity and gentleness rarely encountered, the prince accepts the bishop’s excuse and leaves the conscience of whoever authored the libels to judge the wrongdoing. Therefore Bernard, appreciative of so great a favor, wrote a third letter to the Roman king, which Hansiz reports from the imperial manuscript [ibid., same page]. Since it is lacking from our collection, it should be heard:

“My spirit revived, awakened by the joy of an unexpected exultation. As I sat in darkness and the shadow of death, light seemed to me to rise from heaven. Now that the murky mists of rancor, which the smiths of the North had introduced with their bellows, have been driven away, I rejoice that the bright radiance of your serenity has suddenly smiled upon me. I embrace and hold your letters dearer than gold and topaz; they were brought to me by the Angel of Peace. In them I acknowledge that I have received, like Noah tossed upon the waters, the olive branch extended in a dove’s beak. Finally, with the Lord’s assent, great joy has returned, just as hope returns when the cock crows. Salvation has been poured back into the sick man; health has been restored to one half-dead.

“Yet my soul is greatly troubled, because your gracious gentleness seemed to have been disturbed and angered against me. I attribute this wholly to my sins, by which I deserved anger and diminished your favor, while your anger and terrors thus passed over onto me [Col. 0780B]. Consequently, there is no one else to accuse but myself, since I plainly confess that I have sinned. But if in anything, whether deed or word, I have committed an offense by which your kindness has been provoked or your advantage diminished, I willingly submit myself to your judgment and satisfaction, so that you may weigh the balance of your examination with the even scale of discretion: thus there may be pardon for the confessor, and this offense may not thereafter be imputed to the innocent. May the South Wind come, and by the tempering of a gentler breeze cool the pot of indignation kindled by the deceitful North; and, establishing charity in the middle chamber of Solomon’s bridal chamber, may it reduce the storm of your mind to the calm plain of tranquility.”

Moreover, he confirmed by his actions what he had embraced in his letters. For, together with the other princes, he vied in relieving Rudolph’s need during the prosecution of the war against Ottocar. For records of this matter, see the same Hansiz [ibid., p. 386 ff.].]

Furthermore, concerning what among other matters you wrote to our highness—that you wished, in the conscientious manner of a mediator, to interpose your assistance for the good of concord between us and the king of Bohemia—we have judged that we should answer you as follows.

Since that same king has stretched the hand of hostile invasion against our princes, archbishops, and bishops, as though against the two pupils of our eyes [Col. 0779B], raging violently toward their continual destruction, we regard it as wholly inappropriate and unbecoming that, while he behaves so insolently and fiercely, we should become entangled in the winding course of negotiations concerning uncertain outcomes. But if he were to withdraw his hand from offenses and correct his evil deeds by restoring what he has taken, we could more readily incline toward whatever might accord with reason [Note: These words expose the deception of the title. Rudolph does not refuse to lend a willing ear to some agreement, provided that Ottocar correct his evil deeds.].

## LETTER XXV. Rudolph exhorts a kinsman to march with him against the king of Bohemia

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXV.)*

### Argument

He exhorts a prince or count related to him by blood to bring him assistance against Ottocar, king of Bohemia, promising that the royal highness will reward him and his family according to their merits with great honors, rich gifts, and his own benevolence.

Since we judge that you cannot in any way degenerate from the union of noble blood by which you are bound to us [Note: This and the following letter reveal the ignorance of writers who derive the illustrious lineage and power of this great ancestor of the Austrian imperial house from his election as Roman king. The archbishop of Cologne correctly described him, as we saw above (book I, letter 20, note), as connected, at the moment of his election, by affinity with many powerful men; he would doubtless have spoken more accurately if he had added kinship. Certainly Albert, duke of Saxony, to whom Rudolph betrothed his daughter Agnes, and Otto of Brandenburg, to whom he betrothed Hedwig, were not yet counted among his powerful relations by marriage, for these events occurred at Aachen after the coronation, in the following year. Among his powerful blood-relations, however, he had placed Henry of Fürstenberg (book I, letters 24 ff.) over the provinces which he thought belonged to imperial jurisdiction in the preceding year; he now exhorts two others to oppose their forces to the most powerful king Ottocar.], we have thought it right to exhort your sincerity, in which we place confident trust, with the greatest urgency of entreaty at our command. You should worthily consider that, by the natural pull of the cord of kinship joining us, the auspices of royal supremacy divinely assigned to us are yours, and that the perpetual growth and splendid supports of your distinguished posterity are also yours. Therefore, in this moment of impending danger, strive to stand beside us and our supporters against the power of the unjust aggressor, with as much courage as constancy, and faithfully to defeat those who attack us.

For in this cause, without doubt, your affair is being conducted just as ours is. Therefore, if with a ready spirit you undertake what is requested, the royal highness will magnify you and yours with worthy honors and enlarge your prosperity with the abundant favors of his benevolence.

## LETTER XXVI. Rudolph assigns an imperial office to a certain prince, and invites him—and through him others—to join the war

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXVI.)*

### Argument

To another prince related to him by blood, in a province exposed to the jaws of Ottocar, he assigns an office of the Empire, subject to ratification by the princes when he comes to the imperial court. Meanwhile, he commends constancy in loyalty to him and earnestly asks him to attract his uncles to the same cause by the hope of rewards.

We do not doubt that two incentives are available to you, by which you serve us and the Roman Empire with such devoted diligence that you resemble an ingenious bee. One arises from the distinction of the blood by which we are joined; the other from the natural obligation of loyalty by which you recognize that you are bound to the Empire [Note: This powerful kinsman was therefore one of the princes of the Empire.], an obligation that does not permit the scar of rupture.

Accordingly, commending with a worthy proclamation of praise the constancy of a manly man whom neither flattering words overturn nor adversity terrifies, and resolving with an unchanging mind to magnify you with worthy honors and exalt you with appropriate distinctions, as a distinguished seal placed upon our heart, we declare to your loyalty that we commit to you the office of N. until it pleases our will [Note: Why he does not confer the office absolutely is explained below. Hence it is clear under what law the Roman king, or elected emperor, was bound before the Golden Bull established anything on the matter.].

For we have confirmed by oath that we cannot alienate imperial properties at all without the counsel of the princes. But because of the merit of your probity, whose excellence has always given and still gives distinction to your loyalty, when you come into our presence we readily believe that we shall incline those princes to this: that you should deservedly be honored not only with these benefits but also with richer consolations of our benevolence.

Moreover, when the noble N. [Note: The reference seems to be to Count Meinhard of Tyrol, sent ahead into Carinthia. Since such particulars are supplied by these letters but are not found in Austrian history or other chronicles, it is not easy to determine whether the princes assembled at Kempten in the diet promised these things to Rudolph—several princes are mentioned here—or whether one of them, sent ahead with troops and accompanied by his adherents, was to attack Ottocar’s loyalists. What is certain is that Albert, Rudolph’s firstborn son, and the aforesaid count of Tyrol preceded Rudolph’s army into the provinces invaded by Ottocar.] has departed from our presence in such a way that he himself, together with his other men, is to rise powerfully against the enemies of the Roman Empire and openly to offer you the support you desire, as you will be able to learn more fully from him and his associates if you send your messengers to them, we earnestly request and exhort your sincerity not to abandon your purpose through the influence of any fear, but, keeping yourself safely guarded by prudent foresight from the snares of those lying in wait, to persevere manfully in the undertaking you have begun, with the vigor you have conceived.

You shall also draw your uncles—toward whom we likewise wish our abundance of rewards to overflow—to assist us, by whatever inducements you can effectively employ in this matter. For we have conceived the intention of overflowing so abundantly toward you and toward them with the sweetness of our benevolence, so that, forgetful of labors through its efficacy, when the abundant sweetness of rewards supervenes—[sentence incomplete in the supplied text].

## LETTER XXVII. Rudolph congratulates a certain prince on an agreement concluded and urges him against the Bohemian

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXVII.)*

### Argument

Rudolph congratulates Henry, duke of Bavaria, who had been reconciled in the public interest with his brother Louis, count palatine. He asks him to send back envoys concerning the celebration of the marriage between Otto, Henry’s son, and Rudolph’s daughter. He urges him to attack Ottocar from his side, while Rudolph will attack from the other, so that Ottocar cannot escape from between the two fires.

A great cause of rejoicing entered our heart: the spirit of swelling resentment which the uproar of a terrible storm had introduced between you and the illustrious bridegroom of our daughter has now subsided; and, through the arrangement of him who, after clouds, grants clear skies, you have been so united in the kiss of a desired reconciliation and in fraternal sweetness that this will bring you glory just as it will bring an increase of the longed-for peace to your loyal subjects [Note: We have already stated (book I, letter 37) that this reconciliation took place on 5 April of this year, as we have gathered from the Austrian Chronicle. The Austrian History speaks of it as follows:

“In the year 1276 Rudolph reached as far as Regensburg and defeated Henry, duke of Bavaria—with powerful force, for at that time Henry supported the aforesaid king of Bohemia with his money. He also lawfully joined his daughter in marriage to Otto, the son of the aforesaid duke, and the often-mentioned duke received his land from King Rudolph as a feudal holding. Thus King Rudolph, passing powerfully through Bavaria, reached Passau”—namely, on 26 September.

No one will say that these letters were issued before he entered Bavaria; for the marriage would not yet have been discussed before the matter had been put in order. It is therefore easy to believe that Henry’s reconciliation with his brother, his restoration to Rudolph’s favor, and the aforesaid betrothal occurred within a short interval. The Salzburg Chronicle, in Canisius (*Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. III, part II, p. 487), reports under the year 1278:

“Lord Henry, duke of Bavaria, works through his son-in-law, the king [*regem; regis*] of the Romans, to regain the king’s favor; he finally obtains it by surrendering the land situated between the Danube and the Enns, which he had received from the Roman king as a pledge specifically for the purpose of helping the Roman Empire against the king of Bohemia.”

Thus Henry appears not to have remained loyal, and whatever he acquired in his first restoration to favor, he lost in the second.].

Yet a cause of wonder is poured into our hearts by the fact that our messengers, sent long ago into your presence concerning the completion of the marriage, have incurred so long and protracted a delay in your court. We now ask that they finally be dispatched [Note: Rudolph betrothed his daughter Catherine to Otto, the son of Henry, after Henry’s restoration to favor, as Gerard notes (*Austrian History*, p. 25). Thus, in complaining of the envoys’ long stay, he shows himself impatient because of the delay, chiefly in view of the imminent conflict with Ottocar, rather than legitimately reproaching the matter as having been excessively postponed.].

And because our loyal subjects in Austria are shaken by the dreadful assaults of the hostile rival and are attacked by bitter threats of persecution, we ask your serenity, in which we place firm confidence, with the greatest urgency of entreaty at our command, that you strive to attack their invaders from your side with courage and power [Note: These plans were frustrated by the precipitous defection of both Upper and Lower Austria, except for Vienna. They say that both Austrias defected from Ottocar within eight days, for the people had found him harsh and merciless. Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 415) observes that Rudolph was invited by the people in ancient monuments: “The provincials, hostile to Ottocar because of his tyranny, had invited Rudolph some time before. All Austria on this side of the Danube required scarcely eight days’ effort.”].

For, trusting in the finger of God, who accompanies and directs the justice of our cause, we shall endeavor to attack and defeat them from this side through the strength of German power, so that the aforesaid invaders will be led between the hammer and the anvil to late repentance for what they have done. Thus you will be able not only to recover the ancestral boundaries taken from you, but also to extend your cords to greater territories. Therefore, if it pleases you, inform us promptly, upon seeing this letter, more explicitly what is being undertaken and approved in your intention concerning these matters.

## LETTER XXVIII. Rudolph writes to a certain person concerning the defection of the Carinthians from Ottocar, king of Bohemia

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXVIII.)*

### Argument

To Meinhard, apparently striving to draw the people of Carinthia into his obedience, he announces that N. and N. have come to him from the borders of that province, and, after asking pardon, have immediately departed to declare war on Ottocar and invade places along those same borders. He considers that this should be communicated to their loyal subjects, so that they may become more eager.

Recently N. and N. came into the presence of our majesty, and, after careful discussion with them in the form of this informative report, they simply departed from us with the assurance that, as soon as they had formally challenged the king of Bohemia, they would extend the hand of invasion against him around the borders of Carinthia and undertake vigorous military attacks; N. and N. are, as is reasonably believed, applying themselves to our service at that same frontier with heart, mind, and deed [Col. 0783B].

Tell this, therefore, and announce it to those loyal subjects whom you judge likely to rejoice in our fortunate auspices, so that, just as they are eager for our honors, they may likewise rejoice in sharing our glory, and, having driven fear far away, may trust that they are protected by the imperial arm against the attacks and snares of slanderers [Note: The interpreter of the law of Arcadius and Honorius knows five kinds of slanderers, in the title “Concerning Slanderers” (*Theodosian Code*, book IX, title 39, law 3). The fourth is: “Slanderers are those who, under the name of the treasury, attack the property of others and do not allow the innocent to remain in peace.” I think that the reference here is to slanderers of this kind.].

## LETTER XXIX. The archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans joyfully announce to the Roman pontiff that Austria has been liberated from the tyranny of Ottocar the Bohemian by the emperor Rudolph [Note: The license of the compiler of titles must again be restrained by the authority of the imperial manuscript, whose title we have reproduced.]

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXIX.)*

### Argument

After Rudolph’s first victory over Ottocar, king of Bohemia, the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans congratulate John XXI, the newly elected pontiff, on his election. They set forth the tyranny and audacity which that king had exercised against themselves and all the other bishops returning from the Council of Lyons: he had prohibited the collection of tithes for the support of the Holy Land, obedience to the commands of the Holy See, and service to the Roman king confirmed by apostolic authority. He had also extorted unlawful oaths, overturned churches by fire and plunder, and joined an alliance with the tyrants of the Tartars.
