Then, after recounting at length Rudolph’s most auspicious progress in liberating Austria, they commend to him, out of grateful affection, so great a king who had rendered such service to the commonwealth and to the churches.

“To the most holy one” [Note: John XXI succeeded the extremely brief pontificate of Adrian V on 15 September of this year, memorable for the deaths of three pontiffs.], etc., “such bishops,” etc.

With hands raised to heaven, we joyfully offer praises to our Redeemer, God’s Son Jesus Christ, and humbly bow before his supreme goodness in giving thanks as best we can. He, entreated by the prayers of his holy Church, has placed your most holy fatherhood upon an eminent watchtower, so that from on high you may shine forth and, gleaming like a radiant pearl, illuminate the minds of the Christian people.

At this same fortunate time, when by the revelation of divine grace, holy father, you were worthy to ascend to the primacy of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the Son of God, blessed forever, visited his people in the regions of Germany and raised up for us the horn of salvation. At this time the Lord exalted the horns of the righteous and broke the horns of sinners, which had been raised against the corruption of the whole Church and especially against our destruction.

And although, as we believe, many informants of this matter have appeared before your clemency, we nevertheless reveal to your fatherhood in this letter the sequence and order of the truth of what occurred [Note: I do not see why Hansiz omitted this passage. In keeping with the practice of those times, it makes use of passages from Sacred Scripture, and does so even more aptly than the preceding passages. Moreover, it is clear that information about so great an event reached the Holy See from elsewhere, but a certain sequence of events and a correct explanation of their course are supplied only by these letters.].

Recently, as we were returning to our own territories from the Council of Lyons and wished to carry out what had been beneficially decreed at that council, the illustrious Ottocar, king of Bohemia, summoned us into his presence. He expressly prohibited those who were summoned from arranging for the tithe designated for the support of the Holy Land to be collected in his territories, and from allowing any of us to preach the glory of the saving cross.

He also demanded that we provide him, by oath and by various other securities, with guarantees that neither at the command of the Apostolic See nor under the pretext of any sentence or order issued by anyone at all would we do anything contrary to his purpose. By this he was preparing insolently to resist the Apostolic See and the Roman Empire, exacting unlawful oaths through terrible fear not only from us but also from every lesser prelate in our regions.

When we refused to stain ourselves with this crime, he imposed upon us the yoke of harsh servitude. Finally, with fixed purpose, he resolved to destroy our innocence: he ordered, through specially selected executioners and tortures, that the cities and fortresses, villages and towns of our churches be overturned from their foundations by fire and plunder [Note: The sequence of so many evils is evident from the preceding letters of the same archbishop. The unlawful oaths are also established by letters 15 and 20.].

And although the accumulation of so many evils would have sufficed for our destruction, the aforesaid king nevertheless made us utterly lifeless with fear because he joined himself in a shameful alliance with the tyrants and kings of the Tartars [Note: This alliance with the barbarians is a striking new piece of information. Ottocar gave as the principal reason why he did not wish to surrender the provinces of the Empire—as the chronicles and history testify—that for many years he had defended them from those same barbarians in repeated battles. The Altaich annalist for the year 1277 may stand for all others:

“Otaker, the fifth king of the Bohemians, who had held Austria, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and the port of Naon during the vacancy of the Empire, refused to resign them, saying that he possessed those lands in good faith and by a just title, and that, in accordance with the commands and commissions of the apostolic envoys who had been in office in his time, he had defended them for twenty-four years against the attacks of the Hungarians, Cumans, and Tartars, at great expense and labor, indeed with much expenditure of his men’s blood” [Canisius, vol. IV, p. 218].

From these letters of the bishops we learn that Ottocar had joined an alliance with the Tartars, perpetual enemies of the Christian name, to the supreme disgrace of a Catholic prince and the greatest detriment of Christians and churches. Certainly these letters deserve complete credence. Nevertheless, it should be observed that in July of the preceding year Ottocar was not entangled in this wicked alliance. For Gregory’s rebuking letter in Raynaldus [1275, nos. 10 ff.], dated at Bellinzona on 22 July, in the fourth year, although it lists other matters worthy of censure, does not mention this as the greatest of all. Therefore, this disgraceful alliance must be believed to have been made recently, when he perceived that the provinces were defecting from him one after another, although the bishops, in enumerating his evil deeds, give no chronological indication.].

Hearing of these sufferings of ours and these injuries to Christ, the Christian prince and our most beloved lord, the most serene Rudolph, king of the Romans, and hearing our prayers, which he had often heard before, assembled the strength of a military army and moved his camp from the farthest borders of Germany. Passing over long distances and through various peoples, around the feast of All Saints he entered the districts of the land of Austria, fearing neither the precipitous peaks of the mountains, nor shrinking from the winter’s inclement weather, nor leaving [lacuna] amid the deep snows of the frozen region.

After he had triumphed with triumphant glory over the principalities of Austria, Styria, and so forth, he surrounded with a large army the city of Vienna, the finest among the cities of our regions, which the king of Bohemia still held under his authority. He also magnificently equipped ships with military apparatus, intending to cross the broad river Danube, so that he might seize the aforesaid king—already considering the means of flight—in the heart of Bohemia like a fugitive.

The said king of Bohemia, relying on sound but tardy counsel, asked for a truce of a few days [*trewgas*] and obtained what he requested. Within those days [*infra quos; quas*] he came to the army of our aforesaid lord [Rudolph] and, in our presence, with a broken spirit and bent knees, obtained the pardon he devoutly sought, after first surrendering hostages, cities, fortresses, and all the towns belonging to the said principalities.

For the lands of Bohemia and Moravia, after rendering homage of loyalty, he deserved to be invested [Note: The praised Altaich annalist briefly recounts the event:

“The cities and fortresses there submitted themselves to his authority, except for the city of Vienna, which he also surrounded with a siege, though he did not take it by force. Rather, by a certain arbitration which the two kings entered into, he began peacefully to possess the city of Vienna itself and the whole land of Austria beyond the Danube toward the south; while the other part beyond the Danube toward the north, or Bohemia, remained by the same arbitration with the king of Bohemia.”

The author of the Austrian History, coming closer to this letter, says:

“The king of Bohemia, in the camp of the Roman king before Vienna near the Danube, with thirty-six banners, received the aforesaid lands on bended knees before him in the presence of many spiritual and secular princes, and swore and promised to obey and faithfully stand by the Roman king. … Then for the first time Vienna and the other cities were opened to the Roman king upon the resignation of King Ottocar.”

The letter must unquestionably be preferred to these testimonies. As for what Dubravius relates about the tent arranged so that, when its sides fell away, Ottocar could be seen kneeling by the crowd, this appears to have been invented to arouse hatred against Rudolph and to provide a pretext for Ottocar’s rebellion. Neither this letter nor any ancient record reports it; and, more importantly, it is wholly alien to Rudolph’s character.].

We therefore commend this glorious prince to your holiness, most devout father, humbly and [not so humbly as] devoutly beseeching you, for God’s sake above all, to deign to receive our aforesaid lord into your special care. In these days, as clear signs have shown [Note: From this it is clear that the letter was sent shortly after 19 November, since Ottocar had obtained pardon and rendered homage to the Roman king for Bohemia and Moravia.], divine justice has triumphantly and commendably prevailed in his hands.

## LETTER XXX. Rudolph praises the king of Hungary for undertaking the war with him against the king of Bohemia

*(A.D. 1278, Rudolphine codex XXX.)*

### Argument

When Ladislaus, king of Hungary, had written back that he would bring assistance at an opportune time, Rudolph, exulting with joy, pours forth lavish praise, abundant thanks, and the most generous promises. He prepares an impressive embassy to him, intending to receive a similar one from him if he wishes.

To the illustrious and magnificent prince, the lord Lord L., etc., with the affection of paternal sweetness and greetings [Note: We stated above (letter 23) that Rudolph, while staying at Vienna, was seeking assistance against Ottocar, who had rebelled. This letter follows from that one and therefore belongs to the year 1278.].

O how celebrated, how remarkable a sign of coming joy! O how great and how extraordinary an indication of virtue has been placed in our hearts concerning a son so excellent, so lofty above the kings of the earth, who, gradually ascending to the summits of probity, strives in tender years to adorn himself prematurely with the insignia of mature conduct and to be clothed with the wife (*uxore*) of a grown man [Note: An obvious error: perhaps *virore*—“vigor”—should be read.].

Indeed, no tongue is sufficient to express, nor can the writer’s pen adequately set down, how immense and inexplicable a cause of rejoicing has been poured into our heart because you have roused your power so forcefully and magnanimously to avenge our injuries and yours, which are joined by indivisible bonds, against the common enemy of the Roman Empire and the kingdom of Hungary [Note: Gerard, mentioning the assistance requested by Rudolph, speaks of the king of Hungary as follows (*Austrian History*, p. 25):

“Already hostile to Ottocar because he held Bibersburg, Tyrnau, Pressburg, Altenburg, Cherlburg, Musenburg, and certain other places of the Hungarian kingdom near Pressburg, he promises assistance.”].

Therefore, raising the jubilation of our instrument in praise of God, we offer the royal highness the fullest thanks that we can, promising most earnestly that no adversity of any hostility will ever be able in any way to bend the unbreakable treaties made with you, so that we would not regard your cause as entirely and properly our own [Note: A great alliance was begun, and the assistance was most timely. The author of the Austrian History reports under the year 1277 how Ottocar “again assembled a large army, entered Austria, and powerfully stormed all the fortifications with new instruments and engines called *cati*. Thus a serious dispute and war arose between them. For throughout the whole winter the Austrians ravaged Moravia, while the Bohemians ravaged Austria with various acts of plunder, seizure, and burning.”].

Behold, therefore, we send our solemn envoys from our side into your presence, so that they may carefully discuss and arrange with you how we and you should proceed from this point in a manner more magnificent and more prudent. We nevertheless leave the entire matter to your decision, adapting our desires to your will. And if it should seem expedient to your royal prudence that, together with our envoys, you send to us discreet envoys of your own, we shall regard this as most welcome, receive them with the benevolence that is fitting, and send them back to you with a willing dispatch.

## LETTER XXXI. Rudolph explains to a certain person the conditions of the alliance concluded between himself and the king of Hungary

*(A.D. 1277, Rudolphine codex XXXI.)*

### Argument

Rudolph explains how he finally concluded an alliance with Ladislaus, king of Hungary. It had earlier begun through envoys sent back and forth, then been confirmed by public letters, and finally completed when the two contracting parties joined right hands in place of an oath. He especially recounts the terms of the alliance made against the king of Bohemia.

The arranger of good counsel and disposer of upright intentions has so harmoniously reconciled us with the magnificent prince Lord L. that each of us regards what affects the other’s losses and gains, advantages and disadvantages, as his own affair and considers it his particular concern.

[Note: This solemn alliance, which has been mentioned more than once above (Epistles 16, 20, 23, and 30), is explained so clearly in these letters that anything added might seem superfluous. Only the chronology needs to be established, which the compiler has strangely confused.]

Recently, when we had met and were enjoying the joyful sight of N., we, the two kings, jointly established that all the promises or arrangements begun here and there by our counsellors at various times, and finally approved by the open letters of both of us, should be regarded as ratified and acceptable and preserved forever. We gave faith to one another by a handshake, which we offered in place and stead of an oath.

[Note: Concerning this meeting, see above (Epistle 16, in the note); for the purpose of removing it from this year, the testimony of the *History of Austria* cited there is relevant. From it we learn that, in 1277, around the beginning of November, at the border of Austria and Hungary, the two kings brought to a successful conclusion their long deliberations over entering an alliance. This letter therefore ought to be placed before not only the preceding letter but also Epistle 23. The latter two, however, must be assigned to the year 1278. In the first of them aid is requested from the allied king, whereas in the second it is said to have been obtained. Rudolph himself testifies in the aforementioned Epistle 23 that assistance was not requested immediately after the alliance was concluded: “the identity of the mutual bond contracted between us long ago has happily been established.” These words certainly do not refer to the remaining two months of 1277. Moreover, as I recently stated (Epistle 30, in the note), on the authority of the *History of Austria*, both the Bohemians in Austria and the Austrians in Moravia carried on hostilities throughout the winter, that is, until the spring of 1278. There are indeed extant in Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 419) Rudolph’s documents recording gratuitous gifts from bishops, dated at Vienna in the year of the Lord 1277, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June; these were evidently made for the purpose of repairing the war against the rebellious Ottocar. But the alliances had been joined and the great armies gathered for a general engagement had not yet occurred. Since the battle was fought when August was almost over in the year 1278, the matter itself shows that all this took place in that same year. Rudolph’s letters (Epistle 33) will soon make these points clearer.]

We also added this by common agreement: in lawsuits and disputes concerning damages inflicted and injuries committed, or any other matters that we have against the illustrious king of Bohemia, each of us shall assist the other as faithfully and valiantly as possible; neither shall ever make a truce, peace, or settlement with the aforesaid king without the other’s approval and consent, nor shall he negotiate such matters. To this we bound ourselves by the pledge of the same faith.

[Note: This clause, the chief element of the alliance just concluded, increasingly confirms that Ottocar had abandoned his allegiance but had not yet declared war against Rudolph.]

Furthermore, concerning the lawful demarcation of our territorial boundaries and their observance, once demarcated, in peace and concord, we decided to arrange matters in the following way, and so forth.

## EPISTLE XXXII. Rudolph informs a certain prince of the notable victory obtained from the king of Bohemia

*(A.D. 1278, cod. Rud. XXXII.)*

[Col. 0788A]

### Argument

He announces to a princely friend the notable victory that he and his allied king of Hungary won over Ottocar, together with the slaughter of Ottocar and a great part of the Bohemian nobility. He attributes the triumph over so powerful an enemy entirely to God, by whose mercy he had been rescued from death at the height of the danger. Thanks are to be rendered to Him and to the blessed Virgin Mary.

No one knows better than you, no one has seen more clearly than you, dearest prince, how many reproaches and shameful injuries the relentless disturber of the commonwealth, Ottocar, the illustrious king of Bohemia, inflicted upon us, impelling us to raise the hand of our power in order to restrain his criminal attempts. You are not unaware of the conspiracies that the same king had formed against our safety, the arrows of ambush that he had aimed, or the snares that he had concealed.

And since you once received with us some of the snares of bitterness and bitter draughts from the torrent of so great a danger,

[Note: These words apply to no one more appropriately than to the archbishop of Salzburg, who had not been present at the great conflict. Concerning him, the Salzburg chronicle says, in Canisius: “For he himself, and Lord Peter, bishop of Passau, conspicuous for their upright devotion and shining like lamps among the other princes of the Empire, although they were tested by the enemies of the commonwealth with great cunning—those enemies soliciting their loyalty with dreadful zeal, like pimps courting them for the brothel of treachery—stood firm like immovable pillars. They preferred to endure the loss of their possessions and bodies rather than leave the Roman Empire desolate and alone, or prostitute and surrender their loyalty to profane enemies, since nothing more useful is found in human society. Although they were not present in the victorious battle, they were promoters both of the triumph and of a triumph that was not ordinary but virtually supreme.” Since Hansiz, a diligent investigator of the archbishop’s affairs, did not find this letter, and since it lacks the customary official service to the archbishop, it appears to have been written rather to a lay prince who was neighboring Bohemia and exposed to its tyranny. This letter escaped both Hansiz and the author of *Austrian Piety*, although both had seen the Imperial manuscript.]

we think it fitting that you should now also be joyfully satisfied by our triumphant victory, after learning from this letter of ours the character of what has happened.

Know, therefore, that on the Thursday immediately following the feast of the blessed apostle Bartholomew we placed our camp at a location scarcely half a German mile from the tents of the said king of Bohemia. On the morning of the following Friday,

[Note: Nothing is more certain than this chronology. In the year 1278 the feast of Saint Bartholomew fell on Wednesday, as the dominical letter B demonstrates. On the following Thursday Rudolph pitched his camp near the enemy and postponed the battle until the next day, 26 August. For he had made it his practice, whenever possible, to defer important business on Friday, in memory of the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most holy Cross. Authors especially note campaigns and battles undertaken on that day; their testimony, together with Gerard’s (*History of Austria*, p. 29), must certainly yield to Rudolph’s own statement.]

we advanced together with our beloved son, the king of Hungary,

[Note: Here, unless I am mistaken, the compiler of the letters, who elsewhere indicated one of Rudolph’s sons by the letter L. (Epistle 17, in the note), has been misled. Here he is speaking of Ladislaus, who had been adopted as a son; there he was speaking of a legitimate son.]

and joined the wedges of our battle lines to the enemy’s position. Thus, at about the sixth hour of the day, a fierce battle was joined between us.

[Note: The following letter does not indicate the hour of the battle. The distance mentioned shortly before as half a mile is there called almost a full mile, but this slight discrepancy does not alter the substance of the matter.]

In it the said king of Bohemia, defending himself valiantly like a vigorous boxer, was finally defeated and fell—not overthrown by our strength, but struck down rather when God suddenly defeated those who were attacking the commonwealth.

[Note: The author of the *History of Austria* says: “The illustrious king of Bohemia himself was captured by the enemy, dragged, struck, and thrown from his horse. Exhausted by Berchtold, steward of Emmerberg, and many other nobles, he was cast to the ground, pierced through the neck by a lance, wounded by other blows, and finally transfixed by a sword; he died on the very spot.” This agrees closely with the account given in the following letter, whatever other writers may say in narrating the established facts differently.]

In that same battle the leading nobles of the kingdom of Bohemia either fell dead by the sword or, defeated in the struggle, were intercepted by their pursuers when they turned to seek safety in flight.

But since true and certain indications make it clear to us that the victory was achieved not by our power but by the power of the Most High God, who mercifully protected our life amid so great a danger, we ascribe this glorious victory to the titles and honor of Him who, to bring an end to the distress of our lowliness, mercifully inclined the eyes of His immeasurable clemency toward us when the danger of extreme necessity threatened.

[Note: The *Annals of Altaich*, describing the event—also related by others—somewhat more fully, says: “The king of Bohemia promised a certain brave soldier that he would give him many things if, in the encounter, he killed either the king of the Romans or at least his horse. Having accepted this promise, the soldier pierced through a wedge of the strongest warriors, struck the king of the Romans with great force, and threw him to the ground, killing his horse. But the nobles who surrounded the king captured that soldier and placed the king on another horse. Behold, however, the remarkable clemency of the aforesaid king of the Romans: after the captured soldier had been brought before him, he later permitted him to depart unharmed.” Gerard relates that this soldier was called Herbot of Tullenstein, a Pole.]

Therefore, dearest prince, give thanks to the Most High and turn your heart toward the praises of the glorious Virgin Mary,

[Note: This is a new testimony, from the very origin of the Austrian house, to its devotion toward the Mother of God. The records of the annals and the testimony of people in our own time celebrate the notable victories won over the savage Turkish people through the patronage of the most holy Virgin.]

through whose protection our life, when close to death, was preserved, and the honor of the Roman Empire, which had been shamefully bent low, wonderfully revived.

## EPISTLE XXXIII. The same Rudolph reports the same victory to the Roman pontiff

*(A.D. 1278, cod. Rud. XXXIII.)*

[Col. 0789B]

### Argument

He announces to Pope Nicholas III the same notable victory, carefully discussing the Bohemian king’s perjury and the definite causes and certain origin of this final battle.

We believe that it must be reported to Your Apostolic Holiness what outcome brought to an end that dispute in which the illustrious king of Bohemia, once an indefatigable harasser of the commonwealth and a notorious persecutor of our safety and life, rashly rose against us and the Roman Empire, after having sworn to us oaths of fidelity and homage which he himself later contemptuously violated.

For on the most recent feast of Pentecost the said king, moving his camp against the territories of the Empire and subjecting them to devastation by plunder and fire, stormed certain camps and fortified towns in a hostile manner.

[Note: Pentecost fell on 5 June in this year, specifically eight days after Rudolph condemned in a letter to the pontiff the rash act of his chancellor, who without our consent, knowledge, or mandate had exacted an oath of fidelity from the cities of the Exarchate. In the same letter Rudolph instructed his departing legate, Gotifred, provost of Soli, that all the rights of the Holy See should be restored in full, expressly willing and consenting that this should add no right to us or diminish any right of the Roman Church, whether concerning possession or ownership in the cities, and so forth.]

By so many and such great damaging injuries, shameful insults, and acts of contempt he drove us to the point that, in order to defend the condition of the commonwealth—whose foundations that same king had nearly destroyed—we were compelled, even if belatedly, to draw the power of the sword entrusted to us by God.

[Note: The authority of the ancient chroniclers and annalists must undoubtedly yield to Rudolph’s authority. Consequently, whatever is said to have been done hostilely by Ottocar before that day will have been done in the manner of brigandage and may be disregarded, as Rudolph evidently regarded it. But when the defection broke out and the enemy formally challenged him, Gerard says: “When news of this matter was brought, Ottocar took the defection so badly that he said he would rather die than fail to avenge the injury. When he had read the letter, he said: ‘Since, having disregarded the sanctity of his oath, he renounces fidelity and obedience both to me and to the Roman Empire, he shall find that God, the avenger of the broken alliance and oath, will offer His aid to the defenders of the just cause against force and treachery.’” After this declaration, Rudolph’s request for assistance from the king of Hungary (Epistle 23) and his gathering forces from every side are shown by the very necessity of fighting.]

Thus, on the day after the feast of the blessed Bartholomew, my son Ludovicus,

[Note: See column 788, notes e and f.]

king of Hungary, and I placed our camp at a location scarcely one German mile from the army of the king of Bohemia.

On the morning of the following Friday, after invoking the aid of the eternal God, we advanced and, raising our war banners,

[Note: We have already stated (Epistle 11, in the note) that a golden eagle appeared on Rudolph’s standards. But the author of *Austrian Piety* (book I, chapter 5, p. 39, etc., and chapter 12, p. 69) observes that an image of the Crucified was depicted on many military banners, although he says that the enemies learned from the imperial eagle in which part of the camp Rudolph was fighting.]

reached the place where the king of Bohemia, having drawn up his battle lines, awaited the outcome of the fight.

There the soldiers of both sides, as they looked upon the standards on either flank, rushed together in a savage charge; there, with swords drawn, they contested the equality of their strength. So great was the desire of each side to triumph that everyone considered it worthy and proper to purchase victory with death and to live by dying.

There brave soldiers were trampled beneath horses’ hooves; there the earth was drenched with so much human blood that not only those fighting but even those watching the ferocity of the battle might have grown weary of life.

At last our soldiery, prevailing not by its own strength but by the power of Almighty God, drove the soldiers of the king of Bohemia into a nearby river, where almost all of them either were slain by the sword, drowned in the river, or captured and fell into the hands of the enemy. Thus flight offered protection to only a few,

[Col. 0791A]

for almost all remained with us, either captured or dead.

Although the aforesaid king saw the ranks of his soldiers scattered and realized that he had been abandoned by nearly everyone, he nevertheless refused to yield to our victorious standards. With the manner and spirit of a giant, he defended himself with remarkable courage until some of our soldiers knocked him down, mortally wounded, together with his horse.

[Note: See column 789, note a.]

Then that magnificent king lost his life together with the victory—not slain by the strength of our power, but by the right hand of the Most High God, who mercifully judged our cause.

We therefore humbly acknowledge these and other benefits from Him who bestowed them upon us, and refer them to the praise and glory of His most holy name. We shall turn our concern with more devoted readiness toward whatever we know to be pleasing to the supreme King, God’s Son Jesus Christ.

[Note: The praised author of *Austrian Piety*, in the same place, observes that the military watchword in Ottocar’s camp was “Prague,” whereas in Rudolph’s camp it was “Christ,” a sure omen of future victory.]

[Note: The same author, drawing on the Imperial manuscript, gives part of the letter in which Nicholas congratulates the king of the Romans on the aforementioned notable victory and at the same time asks him to ensure that the rights and privileges of the Apostolic See are confirmed by the prince-electors. This is known to have been done through their charter at the end of this manuscript, whose autograph is preserved in the Apostolic Archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo. Since that passage is not without importance, I wish to include it here: “So that the devotion of your loyalty, which we see so gratefully adhering to our hearts, may appear in the effect of perfect solidity and be proved to remain in all purity; and so that the prosperity of your successes—namely, victory through the defeat of your enemies, whom in these days the rod of divine judgment has delivered into your hands—may present you to us and to others as pleasing and acceptable in the grace of gentleness that adorns royal acts after triumph, and may promise us and the Church gentle auguries of a greater royal gratitude after your felicity, and gradually make us more securely confident of your sincerity, and so forth.” Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year 1278.]

## EPISTLE XXXIV. The victorious Rudolph shows mercy to the children of the defeated Ottocar

*(A.D. 1278, cod. Rud. XXXIV.)*

[Col. 0791B]

### Argument

A portion of the charter by which Rudolph, following the example of the best princes, displays his clemency toward the orphaned children of the king of Bohemia and bestows his favor and affection upon them.

Rudolph, by the grace of God ever Augustus, king of the Romans, to all forever.

The divine princes who, by God’s command, governed the earthly Empire by both arms and laws made that virtue especially their own: they considered it no less their duty to spare the defeated and compassionately pity the fallen than to conquer rebels and restrain the proud. Thus they tempered the victorious power of the commonwealth with mercy; thus they made themselves terrible to enemies and beloved by the devout.

[Note: Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book III, chapter 15, supplies much material relevant to this subject, especially toward the end, where he applies Caesar’s words to Oppius Cornelius: “Let this be a new method of conquering: that we fortify ourselves with mercy and generosity” (*To Atticus*, book IX, after Epistle 8).]

Desiring to follow in the footsteps of these princes and of our ancestors, we turn the eyes of our clemency toward the orphaned children of the once illustrious king of Bohemia, Ottocar [Ottogar],

[Note: Two children of the king of Bohemia are mentioned: Wenceslaus, an eight-year-old boy, and Agnes. Her father had already betrothed her to Rudolph’s son, the king of the Romans, in 1276, when he rendered homage to him at Vienna. The marriage is reported to have been celebrated at Iglau, when peace was established between Rudolph and Otto of Brandenburg, the son of Beatrice, Ottocar’s sister. Otto, while intending to defend the boy Wenceslaus, offered the victor something like a new battle, but after matters were quickly settled, the episode disappeared. Rudolph betrothed Wenceslaus to Gutham or Judith, whom Wenceslaus, once he had reached maturity, married at Prague with royal magnificence in 1286, having children by her (*History of Austria*, 1285; *Austrian Chronicle*, 1286, in Freher). In the same city, four years later, Rudolph’s son, the king of the Romans and duke of Swabia, who had come with Agnes to visit the kings, died in 1290, when he was scarcely twenty-one years old. *Author of Austrian Piety*, book I, chapter 22, p. 128.]

and, regarding the boys with the merciful gaze of our gentleness, we open to them the bosom of our grace and the secure refuge of our full favor, and so forth.

## EPISTLE XXXV. Privilege of the city of Brünn in Moravia

*(A.D. 1279, cod. Rud. XXXV.)*

### Argument

He confirms the liberties, customs, rights, and privileges granted and approved by Ottocar for the city of Brünn in Moravia, enlarging some of them. By perpetual enactment he strengthens the immunity of its property and persons. He decrees that the Jews shall be subject to the burdens imposed upon the citizens according to custom.

Desiring to extend the strength of the Roman Empire by piety rather than tyranny, we generously open the channels of merciful pardon to those who come to the harbor of our refuge to seek grace.

Accordingly, by a gracious act of our will, we receive our beloved and faithful citizens of Brünn—who have humbly subjected themselves and the city itself to our power—into the fullness of our favor and grace. By the tenor of these presents, we confirm to those citizens [the corrupt words *hujus dimissi*; perhaps *hinc dimissis*, “having dismissed them hence”] all and every one of the liberties, rights, privileges, and customs that, by the grant of the former illustrious king of Bohemia, Ottocar, they have held without anyone’s opposition.

[Note: Rudolph’s generosity toward Wenceslaus, Ottocar’s son, did nothing to diminish the consequences of the victory, as this letter and the following one openly show. Moravia and Bohemia came under the power of the king of the Romans. The city of Brünn makes clear that the cities of both provinces passed not to a victor but to a more loving and generous lord.]

Among these, we enlarge by this document certain favors previously granted to them. First, we decree that the toll which the said king is said to have assigned for eight continuous years to the use of that city shall remain for twelve continuous years for the city’s use, four years being added as a favor granted by the said king.

We also establish that the aforesaid citizens, while traveling through the various cities and places of the Empire for their necessities, shall not, on the pretext of damages or promises made by the king of Bohemia to anyone, be seized in their property or persons by anyone.

[Note: Such seizures by way of pledge, which were especially common in Germany, were discussed above (book I, Epistle 30, in the note).]

We also decree that the favor by which they have hitherto traveled through the lands of Bohemia and Moravia without payment of toll shall remain permanently ratified.

Furthermore, if the aforesaid citizens prove by legitimate documents that the two villages of Kuřim and Streletz were pledged to them by the king of Bohemia for three hundred and fifty marks, we add one hundred and fifty marks to that obligation, so that they shall be held by the bond of the pledge for five hundred marks.

Moreover, the plots of land that anciently belonged to the use of the city shall revert to the benefit of that city, without prejudice to anyone else.

In addition, by perpetual enactment we establish that no baron or nobleman of the land shall presume to commit any violence, whether against the property or the persons of the citizens, within the walls of the city.

It is truly close to our heart that every immunity or liberty conferred upon these citizens by the munificence of the kings of Bohemia and still preserved intact should remain strengthened by perpetual right, and that no one, by a rash act, should dare to violate it to the injury of our majesty.

Concerning the Jews also we judge as follows: the customs hitherto observed concerning the burdens of the city shall not be violated, but they shall bear those burdens together with the citizens.

[Note: The Jews of Brünn were in a favorable position if they were subject only to the burdens of the citizens. See Ducange and his commentators on this matter.]

## EPISTLE XXXVI. Rudolph informs the king of Hungary about the condition of Bohemia and Moravia

*(A.D. 1279, cod. Rud. XXXVI.)*

### Argument

To Ladislaus, king of Hungary, whom he raises to the highest praise for his vigorous assistance in the final conflict with Ottocar, he declares with every assurance that neither the alliance nor the friendship will fail as long as he lives. He says that the bishop of Olomouc and the nobles of Moravia have rendered homage to him and the Empire in the presence of religious men, who will also inform Ladislaus about the condition of Bohemia. Hence his hostages will be restored to him in exchange for the Bohemian nobles held among the Hungarians. He explains that he was unwilling to receive John and his brothers, formerly hostile to both of them, into his favor and protection, nor will he do so thereafter unless Ladislaus, moved by pity, grants them pardon. Indeed, he will avenge the injuries together with Ladislaus if that is what he prefers.

To the magnificent prince, etc.

Rudolph, etc.

[Note: The exact date of this letter will become clear below, in note e.]

The works of your probity are luminous: at the time when it was necessary, Your Royal Highness allowed us to experience the full steadfastness of your reliable alliance and the infallible truth of your unblemished faith. We have also thereby learned what we ought to expect from you in the future—so that we may distinguish you from others [perhaps: *discurramus apud alios*, “range among others”]—since the certainty of your faith has been proved to us by faithful deeds.

The vigorous courage of your youthful spirit also deserved that, when we speak at length with you about our supporters and friends, we should love you above all others and prefer you to everyone else.

[Note: To show his gratitude for the outstanding service rendered against Ottocar on 26 August of the preceding year, he addresses this splendid praise to the youthful king.]

And although our beloved former N., the illustrious husband of our daughter,

[Note: It is not easy to determine which husband of Rudolph’s daughter is meant. On the one hand, all the husbands of his daughters were still alive: Wenceslaus and Charles Martel, to whom Judith and Clementia had been betrothed, were both growing up safely. Above all, none of them seems to have had any connection with the statement that follows concerning the permanence of the alliance.]

as is said, has, alas, passed too swiftly beyond the goal of his brief life, nevertheless the foundation of our alliance and friendship entered into with you shall remain immovable as long as we live. Of this, dearest son and friend, let your certainty be firm and unquestionable.

Indeed, religious men—men ardently zealous for your honor—will clearly inform you about our progress in the kingdom of Bohemia. In their presence the venerable bishop of Olomouc

[Note: Bruno, bishop of Olomouc, who is meant here, had been wholly devoted to Ottocar. After Ottocar’s death, when Otto of Brandenburg came to defend the cause of Wenceslaus and opposed Rudolph with a new army in Moravia, Bruno conferred with the archbishop of Salzburg about finally establishing peace. Later, when two peacemakers from each side had been selected by agreement, Bruno and the margrave represented the Brandenburg side, while Count Meinhard of Tyrol and Henry, burgrave of Nuremberg, represented the cause of the king of the Romans. After the agreement was later strengthened at Iglau by a reciprocal marriage, they went to Vienna, as Hansiz reports from Orneggio (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 389). Whether all these events took place during the four months preceding the year 1279 after the aforementioned victory, or during the earlier months of that same year, I do not know. But this letter also contains references to later events and undoubtedly belongs to the year 1279, before Ladislaus’ defection to the Romans caused him to bring the greatest anxiety concerning the Christian faith upon the Roman pontiff, Rudolph, and the bishops. On this matter see Raynaldus (1279, nos. 30 ff.).]

and certain barons of Moravia rendered to us and to the Roman Empire the homage of fidelity.

Although it would have been easy for us to subject both the kingdom and the children to utter devastation, it nevertheless seemed much more salutary and pleasing to God that we should attain your purpose and ours without the perpetual destruction of so many people, and especially of children.

[Col. 0794A]

Nor should Your Royal Highness doubt that, whether the promised assignment of the children to you takes place or fails, we shall pursue your business in this matter with faithful constancy as if it were our own.

[Note: This is what he was bound to do by the alliance (Epistle 31). Moreover, the repetition of persons and events confirms what I stated earlier (Epistle 16, note 4): that Ottocar’s anger had not been restrained.]

And since certain Bohemian nobles are being held by your barons, through whom the restoration of your possessions could easily be advanced, we advise Your Serenity and earnestly beg you to undertake the liberation of four persons, whose release [lacuna] to your will and ours, as we have said.

[Note: Something is missing.]

As for Count John, he presses us greatly to forgive from our heart the injury he inflicted upon us and to receive him, since he wishes to come to us, under the protection of our favor. We have not troubled to give him any other answer than that we disdain to gather into our service those who are disloyal to the king and kingdom of Hungary.

But if Your Royal Majesty should judge it worthy of compassion to pardon the transgressions of the aforesaid John and his brothers, we earnestly ask that you take account of the innumerable injuries inflicted upon us by them in a hostile manner.

We also assure you that we shall in no way receive them without your express approval. But if you will take thought for avenging the common injury, you will experience the usefulness of our faithful and powerful assistance in this and in every other matter.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. Rudolph writes to the Roman pontiff and most generously grants whatever the Roman Church has hitherto requested from him

*(A.D. 1277, cod. Rud. XXXVII.)*

### Argument

He replies to the letter of Nicholas III, who had not yet been consecrated, renewing individually through envoys and apostolic letters the requests previously made by his predecessors: Rudolph says that he will obey as quickly as possible with filial obedience. He submits himself and the Empire to the Holy See. He asks that the pope kindly hear and direct his legates, who will deal with the coronation, the alliance with Charles, king of Sicily, and other matters. Finally, he most earnestly and repeatedly commends to him the clergy, whose extreme generosity he had recently experienced, together with all their causes.

Most Holy Father, etc. Rudolphus, etc.

The integrity of sincere devotion and the readiness of fitting affection which, long ago, took root and grew firmly in our heart toward the most holy Roman Church, our most loving mother, now most recently, in these days—

[Note: Nicholas III was elected at Viterbo on 25 November 1277 and immediately set out for Rome. Before he was consecrated—namely, on 12 December—he sent a letter to Rudolph, preserved in Raynaldus (1277, no. 54). Rudolph replied as soon as it was delivered to him, as is clear from this abrupt manner of expression. Therefore this letter too must be moved from its present place and carried back to the end of 1277. The nineteen days remaining in that year were more than sufficient for letters to be sent back and forth from Rome to Vienna and thence to the City; perhaps they arrived at the beginning of the following year, since Raynaldus (1278, no. 45) asserts that Rudolph requested the imperial insignia. To this may be added the speed of reply emphasized in the pontifical letter to the king. First, it says: “Contrary to the custom of the Church, according to which apostolic letters announcing the promotion of the Roman pontiff—especially to princes—ordinarily precede all other letters of that pontiff, we present peace to Your Royal Highness first with paternal affection, before announcing it through the written expressions composed for that purpose.” Then, indicating the need for speed more forcefully, it urges him to send envoys “with a full mandate to pursue, conclude, and likewise confirm those negotiations in your name at that same See, sending them without any delay, as the opportunity may prudently permit, and announcing beforehand by your letters when you judge that they will probably arrive at that See.”]

through which the providence of the supreme Father has provided for us and for the Christian people, according to our desire, an apostolic father—

[Note: Nothing was more important to Rudolph than his coronation. The long negotiations for establishing a firm friendship between him and Charles, king of Sicily, had been directed chiefly toward this end; for nearly two years they had kept him away from Italy, and now he heard from Nicholas that they were to be brought to a very speedy conclusion. Thus he says that the pontiff had been created according to his desire.]

—so it puts forth and grows more abundantly, so it turns the innermost parts of our mind toward every path of justice, that not only is the suspicion of evil which that same mother Church might have held against us now completely cut away, but every appearance of evil that could have been weighed by a careful conjecture based on what had actually occurred is also utterly removed from the sight of the Father, so that our filial intention, which in truth never deviated into a crooked path, may shine forth ever more clearly.

[Note: The aforementioned letter of Nicholas begins as follows: “It is customary for the union of princes, to express only a little of much, to silence the wicked tongues that seek by their whispers to sow discord between them and kindle the sparks of dissension.” It then continues at great length, recounting the anxieties of Gregory X, Innocent, and Adrian V, as well as of John XXI, concerning two matters: namely, Rudolph’s discord with the king of Sicily, and the restoration of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis. Rudolph, thinking that these provinces—invaded by the Swabian emperors and called by the name of Romandiola—were different from the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, retained them as though they were still imperial rights, even though he had confirmed them to the Holy See through his envoys at Lyons and personally at Lausanne.

[Col. 0795D] With regard to the disagreement with the king of Sicily, Nicholas bars Rudolph from Italy, following the example of his predecessors, until it has been settled through the envoys of both parties: “Meanwhile, however,” he says, “contrary to the aforesaid provision and intention of those providing for the matter, he is not to come into Italy, nor to send any military force or body of troops.” As for the second matter: “We ask and request that the petition concerning the lands of that same Church, and especially the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, so often urged upon Your Royal Excellence, be fulfilled without further delay by readiness for effective execution.”]

Behold, therefore, we freely approve, with benevolent applause and willing assent, each and every matter which the nourishing mother Church is known to have hitherto requested from us, both through envoys and through special letters, and we have resolved to conform calmly to the apostolic wishes in these matters and in all others.

[Note: In these two matters he gives a brief reply to the opinion of the title-writer, who advertises Rudolph’s service as an act of generosity. In our own age, the envoy of Charles VI exaggerated before Benedict XIII, an old-style pontiff, the restoration of Comacchio as an act of imperial munificence (Ottieri, *History*, vol. VIII, p. 131), when he received from the pontiff this serious answer: “We do not reclaim what belongs to another. If Caesar thinks Comacchio belongs to him by right, let him keep it for himself. But if, as we are entirely convinced, he knows that it belongs by right to the Church, let him consult his conscience and consider the censures to which invaders of ecclesiastical property are subject. For princes granted such things either from generosity or as a remedy for their souls; therefore the restoration of Comacchio must be regarded not as a favor but as a duty.” This is given word for word in Italian.]

We humbly beseech Your Most Clement Holiness, therefore, that you may deign, by prudent administration, to direct us and the empire entrusted to us from heaven toward the honor of the Most High and the salvation of the Christian people, and likewise to strengthen us through the benefit of apostolic grace.

[Note: I find in this matter such certain testimony of service toward the successors of the Prince of the Apostles on the part of the ancestor of the august house of Austria that I cannot refrain from calling it to my reader’s attention.]

Furthermore, we send with the greatest confidence to the feet of Your Beatitude the diligent and prudent men N. and N., so that, concerning the principal matter; concerning the friendship to be solidified between us and the illustrious N., according to your counsel, if that counsel accords with our wish; and concerning all other affairs of the Christian commonwealth which we desire to see advanced through the industry of Your Piety, they may be directed by the support of your will.

[Note: These two envoys, sent by Rudolph together with the letters, were to conduct business concerning the principal matter—that is, the coronation—the two matters mentioned above, and other imperial affairs. They had not, however, received the royal mandates which the pontiff desired, especially concerning the controversy with the king of Sicily. From the provinces’ restoration having been promptly completed, it may be inferred that Rudolph, by a diploma issued at Vienna on 19 January 1278, restored everything to the Holy See and sent his brother Conrad, a Friar Minor, to Rome to confirm everything with greater validity by royal authority. He did so in the consistory “on the fourth day of the month of May, Indiction VI, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas III.”

Meanwhile, because Rudolph’s chancellor, a namesake of the king, had exacted unlawful oaths from the cities of the Exarchate without the knowledge of the King of the Romans, Rudolph immediately sent a new diploma, dated “29 May,” and a new legate, Gotifred, provost of Sollen, to Rome. In the consistory at Viterbo, “on the day before the Kalends of July,” Gotifred declared the chancellor’s act void and again confirmed all the rights of the Holy See. Certain monuments of these matters exist in the apostolic archive of Castel Sant’Angelo and in Raynaldus (1278, nos. 45 ff.). See the final Dissertation, no. 8.

The second matter was more difficult. Charles was to be deprived of the senatorial dignity and the vicariate of Tuscany, and then genuine concord was to be established between them. Nevertheless, this too would have been settled had not the pontiff’s death intervened and postponed the matter to the following year. Everything is clear from the documents preserved in the same Raynaldus.

It is appropriate to insert here the royal letter (1278, no. 64) concerning the marriage of Rudolph’s daughter Constance to Charles Martel, the son of the king of Sicily’s son, a marriage arranged by Nicholas himself:

“Most holy father in Christ and lord, Lord Nicholas, by divine providence supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, Rudolph, by the grace of God King of the Romans, ever Augustus, with the reverence of filial obedience and the most devoted kisses of the blessed feet.

As your most devoted servant and son of the Roman Church, we possess the fullness of undoubting confidence in the undeviating uprightness of Your Holiness, by which, without respect of persons, you render to each what is his with an even balance, and in the fervor of your inward charity, by which, as a most loving father, you love with all your heart concord, union, and friendship among all Christians, and especially among the illustrious and most illustrious, such as kings and princes, among whom the danger that may arise from dissension is graver in proportion to their higher dignity.

Therefore, concerning the familiarity, confederation, and union of indissoluble friendship to be negotiated, effected, confirmed, or solidified in our name between us and the illustrious Charles, king of Sicily, through marriages and whatever obligations or other means Your Holiness may deem expedient, we have decided to entrust the matter to Your Beatitude, granting you in this matter, insofar as it lies within our power, full, free, and unrestricted authority.

Nevertheless, we appoint the honorable men Brother Conrad of the Order of Friars Minor, minister of Upper Germany, and Master Godefrid, provost of the church of Sollen, your chaplain and our protonotary, as our representatives, to inform Your Paternity in our name, whenever necessary and whenever they are requested by Your Holiness, about the circumstances of the fact and the business.

We hold as ratified and acceptable whatever Your Paternity’s providence may have done or effected concerning the good of concord, familiarity, and friendship, and its solidification under the aforesaid arrangement, or whatever it may have decided to order in our name.

As testimony and fuller evidence of this, we send these letters to Your Holiness, strengthened by the authority of the seal of our majesty.

Given in the camp at Dyax, on the Nones of September, Indiction VI, in the year of Our Lord 1278, and in the fifth year of our reign”—namely, on the tenth day after the notable victory won over Ottokar.]

For this reason, we earnestly ask that our petitions, and especially those of our clerics, who by their gratuitous and profitable services have shown themselves very pleasing and acceptable to us—

[Note: Testimony of this matter exists in Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 417), namely, Rudolph’s diploma: “Given at Vienna in the year of Our Lord 1277, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, Indiction V, in the fourth year of our reign,” that is, seven months after these letters were issued. In it he admits that, because he lacked the necessary funds to carry on the war, “our princes, moved by the urgency of our pleas, willingly consented that we should seek a tolerable subsidy both from their demesne property and from the estates of monasteries and churches subject to their jurisdiction in the regions of Austria, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and the March, so that the crisis of such great necessity, which was constraining us and the empire, might be removed through their assistance and support, worthy of grateful remembrance.” He then takes care that his successors should not follow his example to the detriment of the churches.]

—or whatever may happen to be presented to Your Holiness through the ministry of those same envoys—may be graciously and effectively heard in the sweetness of your desired favor.

## 429. BOOK THREE

[Col. 0797]

### LETTER I. The electors of the Holy Roman Empire confirm a donation made by the emperor Rudolph to the empress Anna, his first wife

[Note: In the text of the diploma I have no doubt that *annui* should be read instead of *auri*, as I confidently printed it. For it seems incredible that one hundred and fifty thousand gold pieces could be collected every year from a few castles, lands, and possessions; whereas it is easier to believe that three thousand seventy-five coins were granted to the queen annually. See the distinction between silver and gold marks in the note to Book I, Letter 23; you will recognize that the stated sum of gold marks is almost unbelievable to me.]

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex I.)*

[Col. 0797B]

**Argument.**—The electors of the Holy Roman Empire approve the grant made by Rudolph, King of the Romans, to Queen Anna, his wife, of an annual income of one thousand marks—

[Note: The title-writer’s license gains strength as it proceeds: not content with conferring upon the King of the Romans the title of emperor, he also honors the queen with the same dignity. Yet he condemns himself by calling Anna his first wife, since she died in 1281 and Rudolph did not take another wife until 1287, namely Agnes, as Peucer and Cuspinianus report in the *Swabian Annals*. The titles, therefore, were added by a later hand and must be regarded accordingly.]

—from castles, lands, and possessions to be assigned at Rudolph’s discretion, provided that their custodians promise under oath to restore those revenues to the rights of the empire when the queen dies.

The outstanding brightness of virtue and the praiseworthy presence of goodness with which our illustrious lady Anna, queen—

[Note: The electors’ title itself exposes the license mentioned above. Rudolph, then Count of Habsburg, married Anna of Hohenberg in 1240, as stated in the note to Book I, Letter 2.]

—is splendidly adorned, so refresh and delight us by the pleasure of her fragrance, and so delight and refresh us, that we willingly rise to enlarge her honor and advantage and are freely moved toward everything that may benefit her welfare.

Accordingly, we wish all of you to know that we, together with our other fellow electors—

[Note: See the penultimate Dissertation, § 3, no. 7.]

—voluntarily consent to this arrangement and grant our full and free assent, namely, that our most serene lord Rudolph may assign to that same lady, his illustrious consort, from his goods, castles, lands, and other possessions, up to one thousand marks of gold in revenue, in places convenient for her and wherever he may judge most expedient, for peaceful possession by our lady throughout her lifetime—

[Note: Unless *auri* is changed to *annui*, it is difficult to understand whether this assignment is monthly or annual. Moreover, since we have just seen how narrow the imperial treasury was, so that a gratuitous contribution had to be requested from the churches, we cannot even imagine how the new lord of the provinces—who had been awaited by those same provinces with great anxiety as a savior—could, upon his arrival, have burdened them so heavily that one hundred and fifty thousand gold pieces were exacted for the queen alone.]

—provided, however, that the custodians of these castles, lands, and possessions bind themselves by oath to restore and return these same goods faithfully to the ownership and rights of the empire as soon as our illustrious lady Anna, queen, has been taken from this world.

[Note: This precaution deserves careful notice. If this provision is enacted in this way concerning imperial rights, lest they perish through an assignment that is supposedly equitable and proper, what ought one to think concerning the goods of the Church, whose character is far more exalted, since they are sacred from their very origin and supported by the sacred canons? Nevertheless, relying either on the length of alien possession or on the silence of the pontiffs, and whether rightly or wrongly trusting in these grounds, some have not feared to call into doubt the certain dominion of the Holy See in particular places.]

### LETTER II. A certain city congratulates Rudolph on his prosperous successes

*(A.D. 1277, Rudolph Codex II.)*

**Argument.**—When word had reached the distant provinces of the empire that Rudolph had brought Austria and the other provinces back under his authority, a certain loyal city, subject to the king, congratulates him on the successful outcome, offers wishes for an even happier result, and humbly begs him not to disdain informing it of the truth of the matter by letter.

Most Excellent Lord, etc. N., city: our most ready service of devoted loyalty—

[Note: From the wording of the following letter it can easily be inferred that this one was issued at the beginning of 1277, unless perhaps at the end of the preceding year, when the successful outcome of that great expedition into Austria became known. Speaking of it, the annalist of Altaich says: “The cities and castles there submitted themselves to his rule, except the city of Vienna, which he also surrounded with a siege”; and after receiving an oath of loyalty from Ottokar, he brought all Austria under his authority.]

As much as we can, we give thanks to almighty God because, looking to the justice of the royal cause, he has willed to grant, as we have heard, that everything may proceed favorably in accordance with Your Serenity’s counsels and actions. In this matter, the credulity of our devotion and faith, readily directed toward what it desires, blooms again in joy amid the gladness it has conceived, ardently longing for the fruit of certain knowledge of the truth.

Therefore, with the most reverent devotion to Your Majestic Lordship, we humbly ask that you may wish to declare by the truth of a royal letter the progress and successes of your affairs—which may divine providence in its justice promote favorably, preserve, and lead to a better outcome—so that the joy which the ready credulity of your devoted subjects conceived upon hearing the report may be brought by the infallible truth of Your Majestic authority into the harbor of the certainty it desires. It belongs to you to command, forbid, and establish concerning us as you please; and it is and will be easy for us to receive and carry out, to the best of our ability, every command that the mandate of your fear-inspiring majesty imposes, without neglect.

### LETTER III. Of the same subject as the preceding letter

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex III.)*

**Argument.**—Another city, having heard of the notable victory over the king of Bohemia, who had dared to rebel against Rudolph, the most just prince, declares its rejoicing to him over his recent triumph and, with the greatest devotion, begs him to deign to send it a royal letter bearing the most certain news of so great a glory, for which it anxiously waits.

Most Serene Lord, etc. N., city, presents itself ready for every service—

[Note: That this is a different city and that the argument differs, contrary to the title-writer’s opinion, are shown by the different form of greeting and by the entire context of the letter. It is not important to our subject to know either city.]

It is necessary that the promise of divine truth be unshaken, and every power is crushed into nothingness that is fortified against the will of the supreme prince. For it is written that no evil thing can oppose a just king when he sits upon the throne, and that it is the Spirit of God who speaks, against whom all arrogance vainly struggles to rise.

We have heard, most just king, that certain men in the audacity of rebellion presumed to act against the royal majesty and attempted to oppose the seat of justice; Your Excellence triumphantly overcame and subdued them—

[Note: We have often said that Ottokar, king of Bohemia, and Henry, duke of Bavaria, both of whom opposed Rudolph, were reduced to order in 1276. Here, however, the matter concerns rebels, and certainly no others are indicated than Ottokar and the many who adhered to him.]

—leveling the rough obstacle, making hard things soft, and showing that hostile arrogance has no lasting horns. At this our hearts are filled with the joys they have conceived and do not cease to bloom again in royal happiness, adorned with the fresh ornaments of celebration.

For this is the chief ardor of our mind, this is the desire of our inmost heart: that Your Sublimity may be surrounded on every side by all prosperity and by continual increases. But because things declared with greater effectiveness have greater force, and the glorious assertion of the prince enters more joyfully, we most devotedly beseech the sacred royal majesty that you may wish to communicate something concerning the progress which divine providence is supplying, so that our devotion, eager for your exaltation, may be most securely nourished amid the conditions of the joyful peace you have attained.

### LETTER IV. He entrusts the defense of a devastated monastery to someone

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex IV.)*

**Argument.**—Moved by the prayers of Abbot N., who complained that many injuries had been inflicted upon his monastery by wicked men, Rudolph entrusts that monastery, its brothers, property, and persons belonging to it to N., according to the abbot’s desire, commanding him by royal authority to ensure that henceforth it be subject to no harm.

As we examine the diadem of imperial dignity and the resisting insignia of the scepter-bearing hand of strength—

[Note: I would be lying if this monastery were not of the Cistercian order. Certainly the collector of the letters does not ordinarily use such license in titles except in monasteries belonging to his own order.]

—and search the chamber of our mind, reflecting on what the anointing, the scepter, and the royal crown given to us by God signify—

[Col. 0800B]

[Note: Here an imperial diadem has been turned into a royal crown, which is followed shortly below by the royal arms. Here, plainly, Rudolph is speaking, whereas there the impostor is speaking; for imperial dignity was to be conferred at Rome by the Roman pontiff.]

—in the oil of sacred anointing with which the royal arms have been anointed, we clearly understand, gather, and discern that mercy, or compassion, is to be exercised toward the afflicted and oppressed; in the crown, preeminence; and in the scepter, the power of defending the oppressed through the strong right hand.

Therefore it is close to our heart to protect all subjects of the Roman Empire, but especially churches and ecclesiastical persons, from the assaults of every kind of evildoer, and to rise with all our strength to repress the cunning of the wicked.

Indeed, the honorable man N., abbot of the monastery N., came into our presence and lamentably complained to us that certain men, seduced by the impulses of a malignant spirit, fearing neither God nor respecting men, had inflicted many injuries upon his monastery, its people, and its possessions through robbery and plunder.

The same venerable father, therefore, fearing and drawing from past events the most pessimistic conjecture concerning the future, humbly begged our majesty that we entrust the aforesaid monastery to your devotion, together with all that belongs to it, for defense against the attacks of the wicked.

We, therefore, moved by his prayers, have deemed it appropriate by this letter to request the purity of your loyalty, while nevertheless commanding and granting you by royal authority that, in our place, you maintain, protect, and defend the aforesaid monastery and the community of its brothers, its people, their possessions, movable and immovable goods, and everything belonging to that monastery, and that from now on and hereafter you permit no one to molest them unjustly.

### LETTER V. Rudolph congratulates the king of France on the relationship contracted with him

[Note: Philip III, surnamed the Bold, was the son of Saint Louis IX and the first cousin of Charles II, the father of Charles Martel, to whom Clementia of Austria had been betrothed.]

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex V.)*

**Argument.**—Having contracted, through the marriage arranged by Nicholas III between his daughter Clementia and Charles Martel, the grandson of Charles, king of Sicily, the desired relationship with the illustrious house of France, Rudolph joyfully informs King Philip III of the matter in highly courteous letters and promises that his goodwill will be suitably useful.

Among all the insignia of august titles divinely attributed to us, and amid the many omens of wished-for happiness with which the Lord’s right hand has surrounded us, one thing has constantly pleased our mind with a truly sweet delight and has filled our innermost heart with an immense cup of joy: that between us and you, in whom ancestral vigor has transmitted its strength and spirit, a friendly marriage establishing kinship has been contracted.

[Note: Nicholas III testifies in his letter to Rudolph, preserved in Raynaldus (1279, no. 10), dated on the third day before the Nones of June, that he arranged this marriage. “Because,” he says, “the indissoluble bond of marriage, instituted by God, possesses by its institution the power of joining people together, among other matters we carefully arranged that the unity of charity between you and that same king should be joined by the bond of kinship.”

It is known that within the seven months remaining in that year, concord between the King of the Romans and the king of Sicily had been completed by the aforesaid betrothal. Hansiz infers from Hornek and from the diplomas that Rudolph’s daughter was not released by her royal father until the following year was already declining (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 390). Rudolph was then touring Styria; from there, accompanied by Rudolph the chancellor, John of Gurk, and the counts of Sayn and Wertenberg, he handed Clementia over, Nicholas III having already died.]

We therefore intend not only to preserve but also to strengthen these bonds ever more inseparably and indissolubly, in proportion as it delights us more desirably to be united with the illustrious house of France.

Accordingly, we ask that Your Royal Highness receive from the expressions of our letters the fullest evidence of our confidence: in times of need our concern will not be lacking toward you, but in everything that we know will contribute to your honor and glory, it will show itself dutifully benevolent and freely willing.

[Note: Further evidence of concord and friendship is available from other letters (Letter 19).]

### LETTER VI. Rudolph writes to a certain city, praising its loyalty

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex VI.)*

**Argument.**—He replies to a Tuscan city that had demonstrated its loyalty toward the Roman Empire, promising that he will commend it highly to the Roman pontiff, and sends it an envoy who will present certain matters in his name for execution.

Rudolphus, etc.

We have received the letters which you directed to the royal dignity with kindly affection, expressing your devotion and the faith which you bear toward the Holy Empire.

Indeed, we follow up, for the commendation it deserves, the memorable steadfastness of your integrity, by which you have honored yourselves in the affairs of the empire. We intend to attend watchfully to matters that concern the increase of your peace and advancement, and to expend, as far as we are able, our concern and efforts with our most holy Father, the lord supreme pontiff, so that he may extend over you the shelter of paternal benevolence.

[Note: Since Charles, king of Sicily, in 1278, on 16 September, renounced the vicariate of Tuscany together with the senatorial dignity of the City, as Nicholas III desired, it is not credible that among the Tuscan cities, each of which belonged by right to the empire, this one—whether it was Lucca, Pisa, or Florence is uncertain—had turned to its legitimate prince. But the letter provides no further evidence.

Nor would one perhaps depart from the truth who identified it with Pisa, since that city had previously fled to Rudolph through its envoy, even when Charles was imperial vicar, in order to obtain help against a rival faction (Book I, Letter 20). For nearly all the cities at that time were divided into factions, and not even those favoring the pontiff were exempt—especially Bologna, as has often been said. Therefore I would not dare to assert that the entire city wrote to Rudolph, but rather only the Ghibelline faction, as it had done five years earlier while Gregory X was staying at Lyons.]

Furthermore, we exhort and earnestly ask the prudence of your entire community that you may wish to place unquestioning trust in N., our beloved familiar servant, concerning the matters he presents to you in our name, and grant the benefit of appropriate execution, so that on this account we may always bind ourselves especially to you for everything that we know will be advantageous to you.

### LETTER VII. Rudolph grieves that someone passed through his land without being recognized

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex VII.)*

**Argument.**—He gently reproaches a most beloved prince because, passing rapidly through the provinces of Austria, he deprived both of them of the mutual comfort of conversation. He sends an envoy to interpret their mutual excuses.

Rudolphus, etc.

[Note: The heading of the name rules out the king of Hungary or another supreme prince, since Rudolph does not usually address supreme princes in this way. I ought not, nor do I usually, indulge conjectures concerning a matter of no importance; nevertheless, it seems to me that the letter was written to the archbishop of Salzburg. Rudolph addresses ecclesiastical princes in the plural, and the jurisdiction of Salzburg extends through the Austrian provinces; these two facts support the opinion. There is also the relationship between them, for which I do not wish to cite any witness other than Rudolph himself (Book II, Letter 12).]

Because your passage through the districts of our land was so secret and so hurried that we were not permitted to refresh ourselves with the beloved comfort of seeing and conversing with you, it has caused us no slight inward disturbance, since we are peacefully delighted to have one heart and the same soul with you.

For this reason we grieve all the more deeply, the more confidently we believe that you too desired to enjoy our superior presence in return.

Therefore, so that on both sides there may intervene a remedial benefit of friendly excuse concerning this matter, behold N., our credential envoy—

[Note: Ducange, in his *Glossary* under “Credentia,” demonstrates on the authority of documents and historians that among the Italians *credentia* was a public assembly of citizens convened to deliberate on public affairs. Hence members were called *credentiarii*, because they were admitted to a share in the secrets of the commonwealth.

From a charter of Frederick I, “according to the term which the consuls of Milan shall report to us together with the council of the credentia.” From the Genoese annals under the year 1282: “A certain new council was established at Genoa, consisting of fifteen men, and it was called the credentia.” From other Italian chronicles he shows that wise men were called “of the credentia” and senators “of the credentia.” I think that this credential envoy of Rudolph belonged to that class.]

etc.

### LETTER VIII. Rudolph enters into friendship with a certain cardinal

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex VIII.)*

**Argument.**—He wishes to attach to himself, in a closer relationship, a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church whose name was celebrated throughout Germany, as one who possessed great influence through counsel and authority at the Holy See, and with whom he had had little exchange of letters, so that henceforth it might become more frequent. He hopes shortly to speak with him in person.

To the Venerable Lord, etc. Rudolphus, etc.

So many and such great reports of your virtuous deeds have gained currency among us; the nourishing mother Church is adorned with so many and such great insignia of your praiseworthy reputation and of your ministerial counsel, and is embellished with the titles of your outstanding authority, that we are greatly delighted to enter with you into the comforts of mutual familiarity and into the harmonious sweetness of reciprocal affection [lacuna]

[Note: Something is missing.]

Although until now, separated from you by the inconvenience of distance, a rare letter of our greeting has conveyed the innermost thoughts of our mind, and although we have not often been refreshed by the conversation of your letters, nevertheless the little stream of hope we have conceived concerning your goodwill does not cease to flow; rather, it is made fruitful by continual increase.

For henceforth, when opportunity presents itself, we intend not only to visit you by letter but, with the Most High as our guide, shortly to present ourselves to you in person—

[Note: No clearer testimony of the settlement of all disputes, both old and recent, with the king of Sicily can be desired. Since the serious cause that had kept Rudolph from undertaking a journey into Italy for nearly four years had ceased, the King of the Romans assures his friendly cardinal that he will soon be present in the City, evidently in order to receive the imperial diadem from the Roman pontiff.

Raynaldus (1278, no. 45) infers from the letters of Nicholas III that Rudolph requested the imperial insignia at the beginning of that year; but since he does not produce those letters, his authority must be accepted on trust. The matter is different regarding the formula which that same Nicholas prescribed for the King of the Romans to use in a diploma (ibid., no. 63). At its end we read: “We further promise that after we have arrived at Rome to receive the anointing, coronation, and imperial diadem, and have received them, within eight days we shall renew all the aforesaid matters, each and every one, and shall perform them anew in full and complete form.” We shall see this formula expressed in its proper place in the diploma.

If this most weighty testimony of Rudolph is added, one must admit that those who do not hesitate to accuse Rudolph of lying on the basis of his elegant words are speaking foolishly.]

—so that the affection of grateful love, solidified by successive advances, may grow into abundant and fruitful branches of gracious offspring.

Behold, therefore, the honorable man, etc.

## 437. LETTER IX. Rudolph writes to a cardinal, commending himself to him and discussing the affairs of the empire
