[Note: The collector’s negligence! Was it so difficult to distinguish the title “Venerable,” used in the preceding letter, from the “Honorable” used here? The position of the king’s name after the title in one letter and before it in the other—do they indicate the same office?]

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolph Codex IX.)*

[Col. 0803B]

**Argument.**—He encourages his orator, or representative, who has received much praise from all the envoys returning from Rome, with the hope of rewards, and adds impetus to his efforts through the allurements of royal favor and goodwill, so that he may proceed honorably with his own affairs and those of the empire.

Rudolphus, etc., to the honorable and prudent man N. [Note: The public records by which Conrad the Minorite, in the king’s name, confirms the rights and privileges of the Holy See (in Raynaldus, 1278, no. 50) append the following: “Enacted at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the aforesaid papal consistory, in the presence of, etc., Master Paul of Interamna, cleric and procurator in the audience of the Roman Curia of the aforesaid lord King Rudolph.” Thus, in the year 1278, Master Paul of Interamna was the royal procurator. Before him it had been the bishop of Basel (Book II, Letter 1 ff.), namely in 1276. Yet letters of the cardinals, often mentioned, when the see was vacant, testify that in that year he had been absent from Rome, for he had hastened to Rudolph’s camp in Austria.], etc.

The increasingly frequent and trustworthy reports of our messengers returning from the Roman Curia at different times, praising your pure faith, which you maintain with unwearied devotion toward us and the Empire, have woven and spread throughout the royal court such lavish commendation that, as we attentively recall the services of your grateful devotion, we are fervently drawn toward those actions which we know will contribute equally to the increase of your honor and that of your people. We have therefore judged that your integrity should be exhorted with the fullest affection, so that, secure in the gracious privilege of our goodwill, you may not cease to pursue, with the duty of ever more praiseworthy continuance, the concerns and services of your commendable purpose toward us and our affairs [Note: In the year, apparently, 1280, the aforesaid Master Paul [Col. 0804D] exchanged life for death; consequently, he could not enjoy the benefits that Rudolph most generously promises. A new testimony to his great fidelity is supplied by the same King of the Romans when he acknowledged his death (below, Letter 38).].

### 438. LETTER X. The Citizens of Liège Complain about Certain Clerics

*(A.D. 1279, Rudolphine codex X.)*

#### Argument

The citizens of Liège, disturbed by a privilege anciently granted to the city’s clergy and renewed and clarified by Rudolph, which had recently been published by him, appeal to him in complaint on the ground that by it the laws of the city and of the entire province, enacted by Rudolph’s predecessors, were being overturned. Since the maker of a law is himself its interpreter and corrector, they seek that he should promote the public peace of the city and province by abolishing that privilege.

To their most serene lord, the citizens of Liège, etc.

Since, by the supreme ordinance of God, from whom all power proceeds, the authority of the state is recognized as having been entrusted to your clemency, so that through the strength of your greatness justice may be preserved, injuries eradicated, [Col. 0804B] the weakness of the faithful relieved, and the rebellion of the powerful suppressed, directing all things by the just balance of laws in the service of the Savior, we have come to your majesty’s clemency from the penultimate boundaries of the Roman Empire [Note: Belgium, the outermost boundary of Lower Germany, shows that the province of Liège may properly be called the penultimate boundary of the Empire. In our own age, however, the arrangement of the provinces is different—a fact that, I think, no one fails to recognize.], and, trusting especially in your grace, have judged that we must report to your royal highness, not without sorrow and disturbance of heart, that the honorable men of the city’s clergy N.—although we honor them with every veneration in our power—being impatient of the peace and quiet of our city and of our entire homeland [Note: I think no one explains the meaning of *patria* better than Arnobius, quoted by Du Cange (*Glossarium*, s.v. “Patria”). He says: “In those languages there are four hundred and six peoples belonging to homelands—not of different languages, but, as I have said, of different homelands. For example, although there is one Latin language, under that one language are the different homelands of the Bruttians, Lucanians, Apulians, etc.” In the same way, the people of Liège call their corresponding province their homeland.], recently caused a certain hitherto unheard-of privilege, which they claim had been renewed, confirmed, or even clarified for them by your magnificence, to be publicly proclaimed among us in the presence of many people, when we suspected nothing adverse from them.

Although the privilege, once received and publicly announced, disturbed the entire crowd as though stunned by the blows of unexpected thunder and the terror of lightning, we nevertheless listened to it reverently out of veneration for your auspicious name. After obtaining a copy of it and giving the matter mature consideration, we concluded that, if it is indeed to be called a privilege, the entire law of our city and homeland is almost wholly swallowed up by it, and the general constitution of our homeland, established from ancient times by your deified predecessors, is disfigured. After various consultations with the wise and discussions in common, our deliberation finally settled on this: since it belongs to the one who makes a law to interpret or amend it [Note: “Nevertheless, the author of a law ought not to remove the law except for a probable reason; otherwise he would sin against the rules of justice, which governs.” These are the words of Grotius (*On the Law of War and Peace* II, 20, 24), who elsewhere speaks more clearly of a king (II, 14, 9): “If he repeals them, he does no injury to anyone. Yet he sins if he does so without just cause.” Therefore, when the people of Liège request the abolition of the new private law of the clerics, which conflicted with the public law of the city and homeland, they provide a just reason why he may revoke it without injury to the clerics.], we have judged it appropriate to proclaim jointly and solemnly, in a definite form, before the hearing of your majesty—which we believe in this matter has been circumvented by the petitioners’ cunning.

We hope, and place our confidence in the Most High, that when the inconvenience and dangers arising from such a privilege have become clear to you, your prudent and benevolent wisdom, watching over the remedies of your faithful subjects, will relieve us from such disturbances and the burdens of the entire homeland, and, cutting away harmful innovations, will salutarily restore everything to its peaceful and ancient condition.

### LETTER XI. Rudolph Exhorts the Citizens of Mainz to Concord

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XI.)*

#### Argument

Warned by a legate of Mainz about the conflict between the citizens and the ministeriales, who had resolved to settle the matter by arms, and at the same time asked to confront the impending conflagration by the authority of the crown, Rudolph replies that prudence and moderation must be used, so that the contending parties may lay down their drawn swords. For the same purpose he has appointed Count G., so that, after exchanging counsel with him, they may extinguish the fire.

Rudolphus, etc., to the citizens of Mainz.

The hateful disturbance of discord that has arisen, taking root in your territories as the seedbed of conflict [Note: Trithemius, in Calvisius under the year 1280, says: “The man of Mainz and John, Count of Sponheim, fight a war; the count is defeated, and many distinguished men are carried away captive. They are released from captivity the following year, on December 12, through the intervention of the emperor, who attacks the Burgundian rebel, defeats him in battle, and compels him to surrender. He also captures in rebellion many cities of the Rhine that had formed an alliance, and kills or proscribes the leaders of the rebellion.” Let the authority of this writer stand as regards the chronology; the rest seems to me to agree very closely with these letters.], recently reported to our royal highness by the industrious man N., pricks us with the sharper goad of compassion insofar as we perceive more serious dangers for the whole land arising from it; and we wish willingly and generously to apply our efforts to extinguishing this fire.

It has seemed expedient to us, and we advise in good faith, that, taking precautions against the losses of so great a ruin, you, who are creatures full of eyes [Note: A form of praise! The phrase is indeed taken from John (*Revelation* 4:6, 8), and is therefore sacred: “And in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. And the four living creatures were full of eyes within and around.” Yet this comparison is somewhat flat in our own age.], should proceed in this crisis by the path of moderation.

You should direct the oath that you swore with the ministeriales [Note: From a charter of the same Rudolph, in Ludewig (*Reliquiae Manuscriptorum*, vol. IV, p. 262), we understand who the ministeriales were. “The coinage also,” he says, “which, each year, at the demand of avarice, used to be renewed to the common detriment of the inhabitants of that land, we now decree that henceforth it may in no way be renewed by any future prince of the land without the common counsel of the great ministeriales of Styria.” Du Cange’s *Glossary* supplies much material concerning the various kinds of German ministeriales. But that the Mainz ministeriales were not unlike those of Styria is clearly demonstrated by the history of these letters.] along the straight line of integrity, so that the form of the oath previously given concerning the common peace may not be touched by any injury whatsoever; rather, strive fervently to bring those same ministeriales into union in peace and concord.

Thus, while your persons and homes remain safe, the neighboring fire may be brought close to the walls. For a house situated in the midst of a conflagration, even if it is not consumed by the fire, is nevertheless weakened, its joints exhausted of strength and brought near collapse.

We therefore ask and earnestly exhort you that, springing immediately into the midst of the regions of destruction, you should endeavor, under the guidance of your innate prudence, to repair the dangers of so great a division [Note: The preceding comparison with the creatures full of eyes belongs here.]. And behold, within three days after your messenger’s departure from our presence, we propose to send the noble Count G. to your presence for this purpose, so that, with his counsel assisting, you may snatch the drawn swords from the hands of the disputants.

### 441. LETTER XII. Rudolph Writes to the Mainz Clergy about the Same Concord

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XII.)*

#### Argument

When entreated by the prayers of the Mainz clergy, who foresaw future losses, Rudolph replies in the same matter that he will gladly devote effective effort to smothering that fire, as the outcome will soon make clear.

Rudolphus, etc., to the dean and chapter of Mainz.

We certainly pity with all the more compassionate feeling the cruel distress of the tribulations and calamities by which the force of war is feared to invade your territories, insofar as we perceive more destructive dangers springing from them. Therefore, stirred by your fervent appeals [Col. 0806B] to the enduring good of concord and to the complete eradication of the seeds of conflict, we gladly intend to interpose our effective and diligent assistance [Note: The preceding letter is a faithful explanation of this one. In both, Rudolph’s excellent character is evident: according to the consistent testimony of his authors, “he directed his military strength and fortune solely toward seeking peace” (Austrian *History*, Book I, ch. 24, p. 139).], as the evident result of our work, with the Lord as author, will show you.

### LETTER XIII. Rudolph Provides for a Religious House of the Order of Penitents

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XIII.)*

#### Argument

Distressed that a religious house of women penitents was being very badly administered in both spiritual and temporal matters, Rudolph earnestly asks a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church to obtain from the supreme pontiff the removal of its administrators and to have the house entrusted to the provincial of the Friars Minor, with permission for them to enter the cloister in order to administer the Church’s sacraments.

[Col. 0806C] Since in our city N. there is a religious house of the Order of Penitents, which is said to suffer deficiency in the provision both of spiritual and temporal matters, we ourselves, sympathizing all the more urgently with that house because the weakness of its sex is more liable to fall, request and exhort your paternity with the fullest affection in our power: since the persons of the aforesaid house, through the negligence of their administrators, who now preside over them [there], might incur serious harm to their reputation and salvation, may you deign effectively to arrange with our most beloved father, the lord supreme pontiff [Note: Ptolemy of Lucca, in Raynaldus (1280, nos. 27 ff.), testifies that Nicholas III greatly loved the Friars Minor, who by the holiness of their lives had won such esteem that no one was thought more useful than they for restoring ecclesiastical affairs: “He especially loved them and was always their protector until he became pope.” And after becoming pontiff, as Jordan reports in the same place, when entrusting them to Cardinal Matthew Rosso, he said: “We give you the best thing we have; we give you the desire of our heart and the apple of our eye.” Nothing, therefore, could have happened more opportunely for Rudolph; the rest is self-evident.], that this house, released from the bonds of such useless administrators [Col. 0807A], may henceforth be entrusted to the administration of the provincial of the Friars Minor, so that in regard to it “a change at the right hand of the Most High” may be made.

Let the aforesaid provincial, either personally or through suitable friars of his order, be able to exercise over those women the office of visitation and correction, while the women themselves remain in their former Order of Penitents; and let the friars appointed for this purpose be permitted to enter the cloister of those Penitents in order to administer the ecclesiastical sacraments whenever necessary.

### LETTER XIV. Someone from the Roman Curia Commends Someone to the Emperor Rudolph [Note: The same string always goes astray. See above, Book II, Letter 13, in the note.]

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XIV.)*

#### Argument

The procurator of the King of the Romans in the city commends to him N., who had rendered excellent service in the matter of the coronation, so that, honored by him with reward and distinction, he may serve as an example for others to follow with eagerness of spirit.

To the most serene lord, etc. [Note: Master Paul of Interamna, cleric and procurator of Rudolph before the Holy See, mentioned above (Letter 9, in the note), writes this letter of recommendation for N., who was setting out for Germany.]

It is recognized as contributing to the increase of your glory if those who have deserved well receive from your highness the rewards of their merit, so that by their example others may be encouraged to advance from good to better. Since, therefore, the discerning man N. faithfully stood by us in the matter of promoting your exaltation [Note: Here is another indication of the entire controversy that existed between Rudolph and Charles, King of Sicily (see Letter 8, in the note). The “matter of the exaltation of the King of the Romans” was nothing other than the reception from the hands of the Roman pontiff of the imperial diadem and the other insignia, from which the title and authority of emperor in the City itself derived. After the death of Gregory X, at the beginning of 1276, nothing had ever been accomplished in this matter. The aforesaid controversy could never be resolved, and for that reason Rudolph was always forbidden to come into Italy until late in the year 1279, when Nicholas III brought so great a matter to an end. Hence we possess a fixed date for this and several following letters, in which mention is made of the completion of the same matter: the year 1280, before the death of Nicholas III, who died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.], and showed himself commendable by promoting your honor to the extent of his powers, I commend him most highly to your excellence, earnestly begging your magnificence on his behalf that, when he comes to you, you may kindly receive him with royal clemency and deign to treat him graciously in all things, generously granting him the effect both of due justice and of your favor, so that he himself, as well as others, prompted by a similar example, may hasten eagerly to serve your greatness.

### LETTER XV. A Certain Bishop Explains the Burdens of His Bishopric to Rudolph

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XV.)*

#### Argument

A bishop who had received many benefits from Rudolph and was therefore greatly indebted to him, deeply regretting that he could not accompany him to the solemnity of the coronation because his see was weighed down by debt and exposed to the attacks of neighboring powers, and because he himself was detained by personal difficulties, excuses himself while promising that he will not fail in service after Rudolph’s return.

To his most serene lord, N., bishop, greetings with obedience, all reverence, and honor.

I confess that, from the abundance of your royal generosity, I have freely received many favors and grants. Their efficacy has so convinced me of your benevolence that, although by the obligation of subjection I am bound to the royal majesty by fidelity, in this matter my expanded will surpasses my duty; and, in comparison with it, that duty itself, though great in itself, is almost of no importance. Therefore I offer myself, mine, and all that I am wholly to your excellence, not despairing of finding grace before God, with whom the deepest abyss of gifts and graces has established for itself the most suitable seat.

I therefore humbly ask that, with royal serenity patiently attending to what is set out here by the office of writing, you may hold me excused, spare me, and show me consideration, while nevertheless preserving your favor toward me.

Indeed, when I had newly arrived in person at the bishopric entrusted to me, on this new arrival I entered a new labyrinth of debts. I was so oppressed and importunately harassed on every side by the fury of creditors that time is scarcely sufficient for consultations, and revenues scarcely enough to restrain the gaping throats of those clamoring for payment or to suppress the destructive cries of creditors.

To these misfortunes is added the fact that the neighboring nobles violently seize, one after another, the rights of my bishopric. They not only obstruct my jurisdiction but, as far as they are able, attempt utterly to weaken it. They could cause me and the Roman Empire much trouble every day if there were no one to resist their efforts. To these matters, moreover, there contributes to my assistance by way of harm the fact that, etc.

For these and other reasons I have been so drained of money and stripped of resources that at present I am rendered immobile for carrying out my promises, bound by other insoluble obligations, while bodily illness—which is hateful to me but nevertheless becomes my tireless companion—adds to these troublesome affairs a heap of anxious disturbance and annoyance.

For these reasons, may the royal majesty, sympathizing with me in these matters, mercifully release me from the journey undertaken for your coronation [Note: This is an unmistakable indication that the princes and churches of the Empire had received messengers concerning the future Italian journey, for the completion of the greatest of all imperial matters.], and learn to pity my inability. For on your fortunate return, when you have returned wearing the triumphal crown [Note: He rightly calls it a triumphal crown, since Rudolph was to receive it from the supreme pontiff after reclaiming so many churches and provinces for freedom and liberating them from tyranny.], I shall visit you in person and shall certainly not fail to redeem the delay of the past by the expenditure of grateful service.

### 445. LETTER XVI. He Commends a Newly Elected Bishop to Counts, Barons, etc.

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XVI.)*

#### Argument

He commends to the counts and others Sigfrid, Archbishop-elect of Cologne [Note: In Levold of Northof’s *Catalogue of the Archbishops of Cologne*, printed by Meibom (*Rerum Germanicarum*, vol. II, p. 1), Sigfrid of Westerburg is said to have been elected after the death of Engelbert of Walckenburg by Gregory X at the Council of Lyon. The Sammarthani (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 694) state that Sigfrid was made archbishop from being provost of Mainz, and consecrated on Palm Sunday in 1275—at Lyon, of course, where the pontiff remained until the Ides of May of that year. Hence the date of these letters is clear: they must without doubt be placed before those occurring below (Letter 18); both, moreover, must be dated earlier and placed before the letters of Innocent V (Book II, Letter 4), which themselves wander from their proper place, as we have said in its place. As regards Sigfrid’s history, it is enough to place those three letters in this order: Letters 18 and 16 of this book, in the year 1275. The fourth letter of the second book must be placed from the [uncertain] position. Thus the sequence will proceed.], whom Gregory X had commended and entrusted to him at Lyon, asking that they permit him, not without royal protection, to proceed to a church and diocese then exceedingly troubled and hostile to their archbishops. He commends him in such a way that they should understand that harming him is equivalent to offending the royal majesty; they should render the service of fidelity both to Rudolph and to him, and, consigning their former quarrels to oblivion, cultivate peaceful relations thereafter.

Rudolphus, etc., to all counts, barons, etc.

The God of infinite mercy, looking with eyes of compassion upon the city and diocese H., which have long been afflicted [Note: It should without hesitation be read as N., as in the other passages, for the church of Cologne is meant.], has deigned, with the dangers of wars and other adversities excluded and removed [Note: He is considering the difficult times of Engelbert. In 1263, citizens of Cologne, having inflicted insults upon him, extorted by force and fear an oath in which he promised that he would never avenge the sacrilegious crime of those who had dared to thrust his sacred person into prison. In the following year Urban IV absolved him from that unjust oath, as may be seen in Raynaldus (1264, no. 41). Several years later the same citizens, relying on the rebellious support of the Count of Jülich, again seized the archbishop and committed him to prison; the rebellion did not cease until 1270, through the intervention of Albert the Great. Yet that it was not entirely extinguished at the time of the Council of Lyon, which the unfortunate Archbishop Engelbert attended and where he died, is clear from Rudolph’s letter. Indeed, as we have already seen, Sigfrid himself was exposed to the audacity of the Count of Jülich as late as 1276; it is uncertain whether the citizens adhered to him in defiance of royal authority.], to provide the aforesaid city and diocese, hitherto oppressed—not without human fault, as we believe—with a pastor who knows, wills, and is able to relieve them. In his mercy he has provided the honorable man N. [Note: Namely Sigfrid, mentioned above (Col. 0808, note f.).]

Since this man was very well known to our most holy father and, the better known he was, the more pleasing to him, he has brought us many commendations and benefits [Note: Gregory had not elected him; for a canonical election was not to be violated. Rather, he consecrated the elected man and invested him with the pallium, judging that he should be supported by Rudolph’s patronage according to established discipline. Rudolph’s oath at Lausanne, sworn near the end of this year, confirms the matter: “Therefore, wishing to abolish the abuse that some of our predecessors are known and said sometimes to have exercised in the elections of prelates, we grant and enact that elections of prelates shall be made freely and canonically, so that the man whom the entire chapter, or its greater and sounder part, shall have chosen may be placed over the widowed church, provided that nothing required by the canonical ordinances is lacking,” as may be seen in Raynaldus (1275, no. 38). Rudolph was not the first to use these words, but he confirmed for Gregory X what Otto IV and Frederick II had previously promised.].

Accordingly, instructed by the admonitions and commands of our aforesaid most holy father, and wishing to treat the aforesaid N. and his church with special grace and favor, both because of his own merit and because of the gracious intervention of our dearest father [Note: Nothing is more customary in diplomas, and certainly nothing more familiar to scholars, than *interventu*, meaning intercession, when kings and princes granted something to churches or others through the intervention of a pontifical or cardinal legate, bishop, or another. This provides increasing confirmation that the discipline of canonical election, already restored in Rudolph’s time, was in force and was later perpetuated by Nicholas V in the concordats of 1448. As for the approval or disapproval of the Holy See, it should be noted that only those cathedral and regular churches were subject to the Holy See which, in various parts of the world, were immediately subject to it or whose appeals were devolved to it, as Nicholas III teaches (*Cap. Cupientes*, in 6, *de Elect.*). Therefore Gregory X is rightly said in this letter not to have elected or approved, but to have interceded and commended.], and wishing to regard as our own any injuries that he might henceforth happen to suffer, we command you firmly and strictly, under threat of losing our favor, that you attend in all things faithfully and devotedly to that N., the elect, our most beloved prince and a member of the sacred Roman Empire, as to your bishop, so that the service of your fidelity may earn a worthy reward both before our majesty and before his paternal care.

May you, together with this father of yours, be able to remain in the pleasantness of peace and tranquility of mind, with a new source of joy arising and your tears wiped away.

### LETTER XVII. The Privilege of the City of Hall

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XVII.)*

#### Argument

Rudolph grants the Swabian city of Hall its freedom through royal munificence, on account of the constant service it has rendered to him and the Empire, so that citizens of either sex may neither pursue their cases nor be summoned to judgment outside the city of Hall.

We recognize that we have been called to the summit of supreme dignity by the supreme and first founder of all kingdoms for this reason: although we ought to be readily accessible in law, or in the administration of justice, to all placed under the protection of our rule, and generous in granting favor, we judge it worthy to bestow a broader grace and a fuller measure of favor upon those who are not torn away from the service of ourselves and the Empire by any storms of adversity.

Since, therefore, the beloved sons, the citizens of the city of Hall, have rendered and continue to render us such devoted services of fidelity [Note: Three cities in Germany are celebrated under this name. One lies in the County of Tyrol on the River Inn, scarcely two leagues from Innsbruck; another lies in Upper Saxony on the River Saale, between Torgau and Leipzig, seven leagues from the latter; and the third is in Swabia, a free city between Nördlingen and Wimpfen, four leagues from the former and eight from the latter. The last is evidently meant here, since the services rendered to Rudolph in the preceding wars and its constant fidelity to the Empire seem to indicate it.], that their prayers deserve from our majesty the grace of being heard and the fulfillment of what they desire, we, moved by their humble petitions, wish—and as a special favor grant them this freedom—and confirm it, once granted and conceded, by the protection of the authority of this royal decree: no citizen of the city of Hall, of either sex, shall be compelled to stand trial outside the city of Hall, whether a real, personal, or any other action whatsoever is brought against that person.

Moreover, if anyone has any action against any of the aforesaid citizens, let him pursue it before the judge of that city according to the order of law, etc. [Note: No learned person is unaware that among the free cities of Germany there are imperial cities and others that are Hanseatic. The city of Hall derives the beginning of its freedom from this privilege.]

No one, therefore, etc.

### LETTER XVIII. Rudolph Commends the Elect of Cologne to the Roman Pontiff

*(A.D. 1275, Rudolphine codex XVIII.)*

#### Argument

He praises Sigfrid, canonically elected Archbishop of Cologne, in many ways before the pontiff residing at Lyon, and asks that, once consecrated and invested with the sacred pallium according to custom, he send him as soon as possible to his see, which is subject to enormous calamities—unless he has decided to exalt him to some still higher position.

Among the other matters whose vigilant care concerns us, whose desirable completion continually agitates our mind, we truly believe this to be especially conducive to the peaceful condition of Holy Mother Church, to the restoration of the divided Empire, and to the aid of the Holy Land: that the churches of the kingdom of Germany, deprived of pastors, should bloom again through the appointment of new bridegrooms and be refreshed by the comfort of the provision they desire.

Among these churches, the venerable church of Cologne shines out as much more distinguished than all the others, and is assailed by storms of much more serious persecutions and driven by the calamities of more savage disturbances. It therefore needs to be raised up by the assistance of your paternal provision all the more swiftly [Note: It is known to every learned person that archbishops receive their name and office through the sacred pallium. This is the prompt provision Rudolph requests. For, as stated in the *Roman Pontifical*: “Because the fullness of pontifical office is conferred through the pallium, before someone has obtained the pallium, even if consecrated, he does not acquire the title of patriarch, primate, or archbishop; nor is he permitted to consecrate bishops, convene a council, prepare chrism, dedicate churches, or ordain clerics, even if he had possessed a pallium in another church, since he must request a new pallium.”].

Since N. [Note: See above, Letter 16, note f.], according to the praiseworthy testimony of many, has from the earliest beginnings of his youth always been surrounded by a company of virtues and distinguished by the praise of honorable conduct and life, we most piously beseech your blessedness, with the fullest affection in our power, that, since the church itself earnestly demands to be directed by his salutary governance and strengthened by his beloved presence, you may deign, in the compassion of your innate paternal clemency, to send the same elect man, speedily dispatched, to govern that church as soon as possible [Note: The decree of election in the orders found in Martène (*On the Sacred Rites*, Book I, chapter 8, article 2), which was customarily read before the consecration of the elected man, contains the particulars indicated here in general terms. The substance is nevertheless the same, with this one difference: Rudolph explains in his letter what the people and clergy had written in the decree.], unless perhaps your pious prudence should decide, on account of his manifold probity, to appoint him to govern some higher position, for which he is undoubtedly considered suitable [Note: The see of Trier cannot possibly be understood as the higher position. The archbishops of that see, like those of Mainz—both of which possessed electoral dignity—were still alive: Henry and Werner had attended the Council of Lyon with Engelbert, Sigfrid’s predecessor, and together with Sigfrid subscribed the diploma by which they confirmed Rudolph in 1279. The patriarch of Jerusalem, Thomas Agni of Lentino (below, Letter 27), was also flourishing in Syria, which was regarded as a place of equal importance to the pontiff and the King of the Romans—and rightly so, since it had been consecrated by the blood of our Savior. Does he perhaps mean that Sigfrid was to be enrolled among the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church?].

For it is confidently hoped that through him, as through an immovable column, the Empire will be supported, and that in the house of the Lord this same elect man will nevertheless sprout as a fruitful olive tree.

### 449. LETTER XIX. Rudolph Commends the Cistercian Monastery of Golden Valley to Philip, King of the French [Note: The author of the Austrian *History* cites this letter (Book I, chapter 17, p. 103) from the Imperial Codex, with minor differences, as is clear from the variant readings. A much different version, not mutilated in only one place, is found in Martène (*Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 1154). Its inscription and date conveniently occur there, for the date supplies a certain indication of the letter’s age. The inscription runs: “To the illustrious and magnificent prince, lord, by the grace of God King of the French, Rudolph, by the same grace ever August King of the Romans, greetings and increase of complete affection.” The date is as follows: “Given at Nuremberg, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the fourth indiction, in the third year of our reign, and in the year 1276 from the Incarnation of the Lord,” namely before he moved his camp into Austria. I would not wish the letter to be mutilated, lest this diminish confidence in the *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*; hence suspicion might also arise concerning this temporal note. But other letters appearing below will confirm the date of this one.]

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XIX.)*

#### Argument

Rudolph had been asked by the Cistercian monks of the monastery of Golden Valley, in the diocese of Trier, to place them under the patronage of the King of France because, situated on the outermost boundaries of the Empire, they were suffering serious troubles from unjust men. He explains the monks’ petition to that king and fully complies with their wishes.

In the lofty thrones of kings, and in the tribunals of all other powers illumined by the radiance of the Catholic faith—especially where proximity of place brings them near to one another—there ought above all to flourish a conformity of wishes and to grow stronger an inseparability of minds, so that, when loss threatens either party, they may be refreshed by the effective consolation of mutual compassion [Note: [Col. 0812C] Since no indication of a contracted relationship exists, of the kind mentioned above (Epistle 5), it is clear that this letter was improperly delayed for so long by the compiler.]. Since, therefore, we gladly offer this to your serenity and to you, as something that will be useful in your circumstances, we rightly await the same from you in reciprocal fashion, with firm hope.

Indeed, the petition presented to us by the religious men, N. and N., abbot and convent of the Cistercian monastery of the Golden Valley [Note: [Col. 0812C] In the aforementioned edition of Martène, “of the diocese of Trier” is added; by this addition the extreme boundaries of the Empire are clearly identified, as is evident from the location of the monastery of the Golden Valley. Mabillon (Annals of the Benedictine Order, book LXIII, no. 69, and book XLIX, no. 39) must be consulted especially concerning its origins. He teaches that it was founded in a very pleasant place in the county of Chiny, in the Ardennes forest, in the year 1070, by certain Calabrian monks sent to Lorraine to preach [Col. 0812D]. But in the year 1131, he says: “Adalbert, bishop of Verdun, born of the lineage of the counts of Chiny, offered the place to Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux . . . There, in our own time, the original institution of the Cistercians, renewed, offers to the whole province, indeed to France itself, a distinguished example of religious life.” Speaking of the same place below, where he observes that there are at least four places in France distinguished by the name of the Golden Valley, he says: “The third is in Luxemburg, where the monastery of the Golden Valley is most renowned for the revived fervor of the primitive Cistercian institution.” Again, when discussing it (book LXXIV, no. 100), he gives the following monument concerning the consecration of the church, which took place seven years before it passed to the Cistercians: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1124, indiction III, on the day before the Kalends of October, the church was dedicated in honor of the holy and perpetual virgin Mary in the Golden Valley by the lord Henry, venerable bishop of Verdun, at the command and request of the lord Godfrey, archbishop of Trier, in the first year of his ordination, while Henry, fourth of that name, was reigning, in the second year of the reconciliation between kingdom and priesthood. Present at the dedication of the church were Otto, count of Chiny, with his wife Adalade and their sons, namely Frederick, provost of the church of Reims, and Albert, later count after his father, together with many other nobles and free men.” Having cited this monument, he continues the history of the monastery and then says: “Most people think that regular canons existed there after the departure of the Calabrian monks, first under the provost Fulbert and then under Herbert. But it is established that in the year 1131 Cistercian monks were introduced there, whom Count Albert requested from Saint Bernard. The task was entrusted to Guido, abbot of the Three Fountains, which is the first daughter-house of Clairvaux, and from there sent a colony under the leadership of Constantine, who became the first abbot of the Golden Valley. In our own time, under the direction of Charles, a most religious abbot who is still living, the original discipline of the Cistercian institution flourished there anew.”] contained a request [Col. 0813A] that, since they were far removed from the heart of the Roman Empire and situated at its extreme boundaries, and were unable to breathe beneath the shelter of imperial protection while the insolence of wicked men raged against them, we might deign to assist them through you, so that you might effectively attend to their tranquillity and peace [affectu, “with goodwill”].

Since, therefore, we trust in your royal benevolence—that, through the sincere ardor of devotion implanted by Heaven in your heart and handed down from the lineage of your illustrious ancestors, you will apply your care and efforts to our wishes in this pious matter—we have deemed it appropriate earnestly to beseech your highness that, out of regard for divine mercy, respect for the Order, and concern for your own salvation, you deign, from royal benevolence, to grant freely, generously, and perpetually to the aforesaid abbot and convent, in accordance with the contents of the privilege which we are known to have granted them, the assistance, patronage, and relief of your gracious defense and timely protection against all persons whatsoever of the aforesaid Empire, whatever their condition, who act violently or insolently and injuriously against them, in all their possessions, men and persons, rights, and every other thing whatsoever, by whatever name they may be designated and wherever in the Empire they may be located [Col. 0813B], as well as concerning all liberties granted to them by anyone.

This will undoubtedly accrue to you as an increase of merit before God and as an enlargement of your magnificent name among men, if you maintain the said monastery and its persons in their rights, punishing their injurers, evildoers [their abettors, evil supporters], violent plunderers, and oppressors everywhere in the Empire with a fitting penalty, as your subjects [Note: [Col. 0813D] More is missing in Martène, especially the words “and situated at the extreme boundaries of the same Empire,” as well as what follows at the end after “an enlargement of your magnificent name.” Several things are also changed, such as: “We have deemed it appropriate earnestly to ask and exhort your highness [Col. 0814C] that, out of reverence for God and the Holy Roman Empire, and for your own salvation, bearing with our absence in this matter, you deign, in our place and by the authority of the aforesaid Empire, in accordance with the contents of the privileges which we are known to have granted them, to grant protection concerning their persons and all their possessions, as well as concerning all liberties granted to them by anyone, and their rights, against all persons [Col. 0814D] of whatever condition who act violently or insolently and injuriously against them, saving the right of the Empire itself, your [protection], etc. It has not been settled whether Martène, or both the imperial codices—the Caesarean and the Zwettl codex—deserve greater confidence.].”

## EPISTLE XX

Rudolph revokes and annuls all privileges already granted or to be granted contrary to the preceding epistle.

*(In the year of the Lord 1277, Rudolphine codex XX.)*

[Col. 0813C]

### ARGUMENT

Because certain privileges obtained by stealth and deceit were being displayed contrary to the aforesaid submission, Rudolph declares that those already granted, as well as those to be granted thereafter, which conflict with it, are void and possess no force.

Since we remember [Note: [Col. 0814D] This manner of expression implies some intervening lapse of time. I therefore think that the letter should be assigned, though for no certain reason, at least to the following year.] that we appealed by special letters, fortified by our royal authority, to the illustrious and magnificent prince, Lord Philip, king of the Franks, asking him to provide and furnish suitable patronage and assistance to the religious men, the abbot and convent of the monastery of the Golden Valley of the Cistercian Order, against the insolence of every kind of invader, and since we ourselves greatly desire that the abbot and convent be perpetually strengthened by the protection of that king, we have deemed it appropriate to establish by the present document that whatever has already been obtained from us, or may hereafter happen to be obtained, by anyone through the suppression of truth and the suggestion of falsehood, contrary to this our favor, shall entirely lack the force of validity. For we revoke it and declare it null, etc.

## EPISTLE XXI

Rudolph sends a legate so that peace may be made between a prince and his citizens [Note: [Col. 0814D] The time, person, and place are all obscure. The loss is slight. I assign the letter to the year 1279, since I see that it was issued after the storms of war had been quieted, while he was devoting diligent attention to the ordering of the provinces of the Empire.].

*(In the year of the Lord 1279, Rudolphine codex XXI.)*

### ARGUMENT

Fearing that discord between Prince N. and his citizens might produce more serious losses, Rudolph sends him a legate as an interpreter of peace, to whom he should lend an ear as readily as to Rudolph himself. He signifies that no service could be rendered to him greater or more acceptable than this, namely, that the prince should curb his anger by the persuasion of words.

Since we are truly solicitous, through frequent reflection, for your tranquillity and peaceful condition, we are all the more continually anxious in the depths of our heart about the stable good of concord between you and our citizens, the greater the security promised by its desired consolidation, and the more clearly we foresee the dangers of grave loss being prepared by the division arising from discord.

Indeed, since among other things suited to our wishes we desire the salutary union of concord most earnestly, behold, we send to your presence N., undoubtedly an ardent champion of your honor, for this purpose, as though he were an image of our presence, with the fullest confidence. We ask you most affectionately that, consenting to his exhortations, which he will present to you in our name, you strive effectively and finally to incline or apply your mind to complete peace, out of reverence for us and the Empire, and indeed also from the impulse of your own advantage [Col. 0814C], knowing with absolute certainty that in no case and under no circumstances could you render us a service so welcome and so pleasing. Therefore we ask you to place the fullest confidence in his words concerning everything, just as you would in ours.

## EPISTLE XXII

Rudolph commends a certain canon to the Church of Liège [Note: [Col. 0814D] We cited above (Epistle 10) the letter concerning the citizens of Liège who complained that their laws were being subverted by the privilege of the clergy. It is not improbable that this letter ought to be placed before that one. For Rudolph was not the sort of man who, while insulting the complaints of the citizens, would promise to enlarge the honors of the clergy. Moreover, if he had granted them that very extensive privilege, there would have been no reason for them to seek elsewhere [Col. 0815C] the grounds on which they demanded that the new canon be sent back to the royal court, as is clear from other letters of this kind.], and asks that they send him back to the court as soon as possible.

*(In the year of the Lord 1279, Rudolphine codex XXII.)*

### ARGUMENT

He praises the Church of Liège with distinguished commendation and presents himself as ready to protect and honor it. Then he asks that A., his courtier who has been enrolled in the college of its canons and whom he is sending to take possession, be sent back to him as soon as possible, since he will be more useful to the interests of the church in the royal court than in the choir of Liège.

That noble church, an outstanding mirror of the kingdom of Germany, is continually placed before the eyes of our benevolent favor and gracious goodwill. It so delights our spirit with its distinguished brightness and so illuminates the innermost recesses of our mind with the light of its splendor that we are especially pleased by the fragrance of its sweetness, as by the scent of a field which the Lord has blessed. Therefore, not without reason, we are ready to attend willingly to its advantages and to aspire with every promptness of spirit to the enlargement of its honors.

Indeed, although the honorable man A., who, on account of his distinguished merits, rises very high in royal favor, may, with our permission, approach your presence in order to offer, with the devotion that is fitting, the service of his first residence in your church, nevertheless, after carefully weighing the circumstances of that church’s condition and status, we judge that it is both more useful to us and far more advisable for your church that he continue to serve your church in our court rather than in the choir. We therefore ask your prudence with the greatest affection of which we are capable that, out of reverence for us and for your own advantage, treating him with suitable favor concerning this residence [Note: [Col. 0815C] That is, for the receipt of the revenues; for dispensation from residence exceeds the authority of canons, although the service of a prince, when accompanied by a common cause, constitutes a legitimate dispensation.], you take care to send him back to our court as soon as possible, where he will be established more fruitfully in the services mentioned above of yourselves and your church, knowing with absolute certainty that, because of the advantages that will thereby accrue to you, you will always find us more ready to assist you in all your affairs [Note: [Col. 0815C] Hence it is clear that the privilege of the clergy had not yet emerged, and that this canon, who was supposed to remain with Rudolph, was promptly sent back by his colleagues with the obligation, if I am not mistaken, of seeking from the king confirmation or restoration of that ancient privilege [Col. 0815D].].

## EPISTLE XXIII

Rudolph confirms the judgment of the bishop of Liège concerning the fixing of dates for duels.

*(In the year of the Lord 1279, Rudolphine codex XXIII.)*

### ARGUMENT

He ratifies throughout the entire province of Liège the decree of the bishop of Liège concerning postponing the day appointed for single combat, at the discretion of the prince of the Empire before whom the combat is to take place, and by royal authority commands everyone to observe it.

Rudolph, etc., to the distinguished noblemen, ministers, vassals, and all men subject to the episcopate of Liège.

When we recently presided solemnly as judge in our city N. on Saturday, etc., and the procurator of the venerable bishop of Liège, our most beloved prince, appeared there at his request and for the sake of justice, with the assembled crowd unanimously applauding and also approving, it was judicially decreed that any prince of the Empire possessing temporal jurisdiction, whatever his condition, before whom the contests of duels customarily take place [Note: [Col. 0815D] “May the detestable practice of duels, introduced by the devil the artificer so that, through the bloody death of bodies, he might also gain the destruction of souls, be utterly exterminated from the Christian world. The emperor, kings, dukes, princes, marquises, counts, and temporal lords by whatever other name they are called, who grant a place for single combat in their lands among Christians, shall thereby be excommunicated.” Thus the Council of Trent (session 25, on reform, chapter 19), on the day before the Nones of December in the year 1563, embracing the private decrees of pious princes and bishops, decreed against single combat and established still heavier penalties, which may be read in the cited chapter. Previously, however, such single combats were everywhere customary; and since many writers have treated this subject carefully—nearly all of whom Du Cange praises in his Glossary—it is necessary to seek from them what the laws of dueling were and what rites were observed among the various peoples [Col. 0816C]. Meanwhile, from this passage we learn that German duels were customarily fought before princes possessing jurisdiction in the Empire.], if, on the appointed or fixed day set for the champions to fight, he is unable for necessary and honorable reasons to be personally present at this duel, may, by a timely and useful change of counsel, without any injury to the parties, silently appoint another day for the combatants at his convenience and postpone the contest of the duel until a more suitable time [Note: [Col. 0816C] In a wagered duel, as they say, the fortieth day was the customary period, except in a homicide case, when the third day was announced by the lord or judge, as in the Assizes of Jerusalem, chapter 95, cited by Du Cange. This custom was observed so strictly that the privilege granted to Liège appears extraordinary.].

For this reason, approving solemnly by royal authority the aforesaid judgment, as one duly rendered, we have deemed it necessary to enjoin your whole community by a strict edict that, concerning such postponement of the combats of duels as has hitherto been made, or may hereafter be made, by the venerable A., the aforesaid bishop, you obey him humbly and attend to him with the devotion that is fitting [Col. 0816B] [Note: [Col. 0816D] There is nothing surprising in the fact that so pious a prince seriously decreed concerning such a detestable matter in order to confirm the decree of the bishop of Liège. The ordinances of Saint Louis concerning these single combats also survive; yet he prohibited them only in his own lands, not in the lands of his vassals. For customs, however blameworthy, when they have become established throughout all lands and among all peoples, are tolerated, though not approved.].

## EPISTLE XXIV

Rudolph again commends the monastery of the Golden Valley to the king of the Franks.

*(In the year of the Lord 1277, Rudolphine codex XXIV.)*

### ARGUMENT

He again commends the Cistercian monastery of the Golden Valley of Luxemburg to Philip III, king of the Franks, in accordance with the form of the earlier letters; for he had not yet heard that the king had undertaken their protection.

Although the religious men, the abbot and convent of the monastery of the Golden Valley, ought to breathe beneath the shelter of imperial power [Col. 0816C], nevertheless, since, when we are often acting at a distance, they are shaken by the hostile tyranny of wicked men, whose calumnious attacks you will be able easily to restrain [we shall be able easily to restrain], we have deemed it appropriate to entreat your serenity most earnestly that, in accordance with the contents of our letters patent, which we formerly sent to your royal highness concerning their protection [Note: [Col. 0816D] The author of *Pietas Austriaca* places this letter after the one cited above (Epistle 19), since it concerns the same matter and expresses the same judgment. Since Rudolph admits that he had previously asked the king to undertake the monks’ protection, he certainly issued this letter after discovering that the earlier ones had been ineffective. If I am not mistaken, the obstacle that prevented the king of the Franks from complying with Rudolph was that display of privileges (Epistle 20) which the same king of the Romans declared to be without force.], you deign willingly and kindly to grant them the benefit and consolation of your protection and support [Col. 0817A], so that you may thereby acquire more abundantly the favor of God and men, and so that, if opportunity presents itself, you may rightly find us more ready to assist you in your affairs.

## EPISTLE XXV

Rudolph takes the Hospitallers of the Teutonic House into his special protection [Note: [Col. 0817B] The author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 19, p. 112 and following) assigns this and the following letter, from his own codex, to the year 1285. Since there is no reason to remove them from that year, I prefer to follow him rather than determine the uncertain date of the letters according to my own judgment.].

*(In the year of the Lord 1285, Rudolphine codex XXV.)*

### ARGUMENT

He takes the Knights Hospitallers, or House of Saint Mary of the Teutons, which had been honored in spiritual matters by the Roman pontiff and in temporal matters by the emperors, and greatly increased by them, into his special protection, following in their footsteps. He confirms and renews all its privileges, liberties, and immunities, affixing his seal to the charter.

In many ways and by diverse means, the Christian people, radiant with the splendor of various virtues, have in the past caused the sacred and fortunate Roman Empire to be preferred to all the world’s principalities and to prevail over every barbarian nation, and, as the Lord of all ordains, will bring this about in the future. Indeed, the protection of the commonwealth, springing from a twofold stock and thereby strengthening its power, has allied the celibate soldiery and the earthly kingdom, the kingdom of Judah with the Levitical tribe; and, with each sword assisting the other, the priesthood strengthens and confirms the Empire, and royal authority in turn [Note: [Col. 0817C] The correct comparison would be that the Empire is strengthened and confirmed by the priesthood, and the priesthood in turn by the Empire. But Rudolph, lest he claim for himself the majesty which he ardently desired but had not yet attained, uses the less accurate comparison, proclaiming that he is a king, not an emperor, against the compiler of the letters, whose audacity he reproves.] strengthens and confirms the dignity of the priesthood. Thus the eminence of each is exalted by that of the other, and the malice of the wicked is driven beyond the boundaries of the world.

For this reason, our anchor of hope is fixed not only in our arms, armed soldiers, and commanders of wars, but also in the devout intercessions of religious men who constantly serve God as soldiers, and in other pious works; and the throne of our resplendent glory is raised higher and more securely into a watchtower [Note: [Col. 0817C] To the constant testimony of authors concerning the union of his great piety with military virtue, one should add this candid confession from his own mouth.]. It is therefore fitting that our serenity look to the advantages of those who lead a religious life, repel pressing disadvantages, and forestall future dangers.

Among all others, however, those especially deserve our favor and benevolence who devote themselves to the most pious works of hospitality and defense of the commonwealth, as well as to other works of piety. Having cast aside their possessions, renounced their own wills, and despised the torture of their bodies, they rise up against the enemy and do not fear to expose themselves as a wall for the Roman Empire and the house of Israel, nor to redden the garments of their souls in their own blood for the Catholic faith and the laws of their fathers.

Such are the venerable and most beloved in Christ master and brothers of the Hospital of the House of the Teutons of Saint Mary in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0817C] In the year 1191, when the Crusaders were besieging Ptolemais or Acre, “the citizens of Bremen and Lübeck made a hospital in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary for the use of the sick during the siege, from the sails of ships,” as Nauclerus says, cited by Pagi (1198, no. 2). From an interpolator of the Aquicinctine chronicle, he also gives there, under the year 1191, this testimony: “The Order of the Teutonic Knights begins; in the year 1191, on February 22, Pope Celestine confirmed it. Henry Walpot was made the first master of this Order” [Col. 0817D]. The confirmation by Celestine, however, belongs to the following year, as Pagi correctly states. This hospital bore the title of the House of the Teutons of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Jerusalem. Baronius reports that these knights were subject to the Rule of Saint Augustine, that no others were counted in that Order except German nobles, and that at the request of Henry VI they were given a white habit with a black cross, a type of garment that was the distinctive mark of the Templars. The Templars, who had been established by Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, more than seventy years earlier, namely in 1118, for the defense of pilgrims, resented this resemblance. Therefore Innocent III (book XIII, Epistle 125 and following), informing the master and brothers of the Hospital of the Teutons at Acre and the patriarch of Jerusalem of the complaints of the Templars, removed that similarity of dress. In any case, the Order of the Teutonic Knights has greater affinity with the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, which I shall discuss in the following epistle, than with the Templars: both orders are hospitaller and military, whereas the Templars were military alone. These three Orders flourished in Rudolph’s time [Col. 0818C]. Although the Templars had to be extinguished in 1311, twenty years after his death, because of their evil deeds, I do not find that the most pious king honored them with either patronage or any privilege. Nor am I surprised, for I find that several years earlier they had dared to withdraw themselves from the Apostolic See (Raynaldus, 1265, no. 5). What they were like in Rudolph’s time is shown by Clement V in his sentence concerning their suppression at the Council of Vienne, in Labbe (Councils, vol. XI, pp. 1557 ff.). Among other things, one may read there: “Spotted with various and diverse obscenities, perversities, blemishes, and stains of errors and crimes, not merely unspeakable but unheard-of—alas!—which, because of the sad and filthy memory of them, we now pass over in silence.” Therefore, with the approval of the whole council, he suppressed that Order and transferred to the illustrious Order of Saint John of Jerusalem “the very house of the military Order of the Temple, and all its other houses, churches, chapels, oratories, cities, castles, villages, lands, granges, and places, possessions, jurisdictions, revenues, and rights, and all its other immovable and movable or self-moving goods, with all their members, rights, and appurtenances, on both sides of the sea and in all and every part of the world.” These things they had acquired over nearly two hundred years, until, having grown rich and fat, they rebelled.].

Their holy religion, in its quest for special favor and the indulgence of many liberties and privileges, took its beginning from the benefactions of emperors and from the Apostolic See in spiritual matters; and, as a flourishing garden of the imperial court, a planting and structure of the emperors, it received no increase in temporal affairs from any prince so great as from the emperors, since, besides the king of the Romans, they have no other advocate or defender.

Therefore, following the footsteps of the Emperor N., of divine memory [Note: [Col. 0818D] Frederick II, the last emperor, is called “of divine memory” in both codices, evidently through an error for “of blessed memory,” as he is called in the following letters. After a long and altogether blameworthy delay, he undertook the holy expedition, and Rudolph is said to have proceeded with him. On his return, he went to Prussia, taking several Hospitallers with him; others also withdrew there after the loss of Syria in the year of Rudolph’s death, 1291.], and of his other predecessors [Note: [Col. 0818D] Frederick had only two predecessors: Henry VI, in whose time the Order of the Teutonic Knights began, and Otto IV.], we take under our special protection the said House, both in its head and in its members, its brothers and confraters, as well as their subjects conducting its affairs, together with all movable and immovable goods which they presently possess lawfully throughout the Roman Empire and which they may hereafter acquire by lawful title, whether they be cities, etc. We approve, confirm, and renew by the present document all privileges, liberties, immunities, and every document that has been justly and reasonably granted and bestowed by the said emperors and kings [Note: [Col. 0819C] At the very beginnings of the Order’s institution, Andrew, king of Hungary, as may be seen in Raynaldus (1224, no. 36), gave these knights the extensive land of Boza in Syria. At their request, Honorius III subjected it to the Holy See. From this we also learn that other kings were generous toward the Order.] of the Romans, strengthening the present page with the device of the pendant seal of our majesty.

## EPISTLE XXVI

Rudolph receives the brothers of the Hospital of Saint John in Jerusalem into his protection and confirms their privileges.

*(In the year of the Lord 1285, Rudolphine codex XXVI.)*

### ARGUMENT

He receives, at their petition, the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem, who fight fearlessly against the Saracens in defense of the Christian religion and Catholic faith, into his special protection, together with all their possessions, both those already acquired and those to be acquired thereafter; and he confirms and renews all the privileges, donations, and rights which they had obtained from Frederick II and his predecessors.

Although it proceeds from the generosity of royal benevolence to surround all who profess regular observance with the patronage of vigilant protection and favor, nevertheless the honorable brothers of the sacred Order of the Hospital of Saint John in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0819C] Everyone knows that the Jerusalemites, now called the Knights of Malta, are older and more fortunate than the Teutonic knights, having been established in the year 1104, and that they have flourished especially in virtue and honors. It is enough to recall that they have always been a great bulwark of the Catholic religion against the most savage Saracens [Col. 0819D]. Whoever desires more should consult William of Tyre (book XVIII, chapter 5), Jacques de Vitry (*History of Jerusalem*, chapter 64), Jacobus Bosius, and especially Sebastian Pauli of the Congregation of the Mother of God (*Codex Diplomaticus*).], who, having rejected secular warfare, fearlessly carry the standards of Christian victory against the ranks of the pagan plague, reddening the insignia of their warfare in the blood of glorious martyrdom, and, fighting bravely against barbarian nations, do not fear to surrender themselves to precious death—they ought to be cherished by the arm of royal highness all the more attentively in every respect and honored all the more exaltedly, the more fervently they are known to serve in the Lord’s camps for the defense of the Catholic faith.

Let it be known, etc. Since, therefore, we embrace with the prerogative of singular favor the aforesaid Order of the brothers of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem [Col. 0819C], whose odor of holiness, like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed, has refreshed us inwardly with the delight of its sweetness; and since the Order is known to have flourished from ancient times in conspicuous titles and to be distinguished by exceptional endowments of honors and liberties, we, desiring from the depths of our heart that the serenity of its famous name not be clouded and that the prosperity of its condition not be in any way torn apart or injuriously touched [Col. 0820A], have inclined to the devoted petitions of N.

Accordingly, we take under our special protection, in imitation of the deified emperors, our predecessors, and the aforesaid kings of the Romans, the brothers of the aforesaid Order and all their possessions and goods which they now lawfully possess or may hereafter acquire through justice; and, as regards the aforesaid privileges, as they are recorded above, together with each and every one of their articles, and all donations, indulgences, favors, liberties, and rights granted to the brothers of the aforesaid Order by Frederick, of illustrious memory, the last Roman emperor, our predecessor, before the sentence of deposition was issued against him [Note: [Col. 0819D] I wish recent writers, who subordinate truth to their own opinions, to take serious note of the form of expression Rudolph uses. He praises Frederick’s charters issued before the sentence of deposition; if any were issued afterward, he regards them as having no standing. Thus, when Frederick II was deposed by Innocent IV at the First Council of Lyon in 1245, he ceased to be emperor. Greater credence should therefore be given to Rudolph, an unimpaired and eyewitness witness, than to Dupin (*On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, dissertation 7, p. 545) and the German jurists, who everywhere disguise the truth.], and by his imperial predecessors and the kings of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0819D] Five emperors preceded Frederick II: Henry V, Lothair II, Frederick Barbarossa, Henry VI, and Otto IV. There was only one king of the Romans, Conrad III, who, because he did not receive the imperial diadem from the hand of the pontiff, did not attain imperial majesty. Why, then, you may ask, are several kings of the Romans praised here? Because those five emperors, before they were crowned by the pontiff, issued their charters for many years as kings of the Romans.] duly and prudently delivered and granted—as though all the aforesaid matters had been inserted word for word in the present document—we expressly and generously renew them by royal benevolence [Col. 0820B], and confirm them by the authority of our royal highness and by the protection of this present writing. Therefore, let no one, etc.

## EPISTLE XXVII

The patriarch of Jerusalem urges Rudolph to undertake the passage, setting forth the dangers of the Holy Land.

*(In the year of the Lord 1285, Rudolphine codex XXVII.)*

### ARGUMENT

The patriarch of Jerusalem and the officials of the Holy Land, urgently needing assistance against the sultan of Babylon, who is advancing with an immense army as far as the borders of his province, filling everything with terror and preparing countless engines for the assault of the cities, turn supplicatingly to Rudolph’s power. They set forth the dangers that threaten and, fearing the coming peril, request timely aid before the general passage.

Most excellent, etc. Brother Thomas [Note: Thomas Agni of Lentino, or Leontino, a Sicilian of the Order of Preachers, was first bishop of Bethlehem and legate of Pope Alexander IV; afterward he was made archbishop of Cosenza by Clement IV, and finally, in 1272, was appointed patriarch of Jerusalem and legate throughout the East by Gregory X. Ughelli (vol. VIII, part II, p. 216) says that he died in 1276, while others—including the distinguished Mansi (in Raynaldus, 1277, no. 18)—extend his life into the following year. See Raynaldus (1272, no. 17); Bremond’s *Bullarium*, vol. I, pp. 503, 505; Le Quien, *Oriens Christianus*, vol. III, p. 1261, no. 23.] etc., [Note: To demonstrate that Thomas survived as patriarch into July 1277, the cited Mansi produces an agreement between the Venetians and Tyrians “in the fields, in the territory of Acre, in the year 1277, indiction V, five days before the Kalends of July.” Its witnesses are “Thomas, of the Order of Preachers, patriarch of Jerusalem; Bonacursus, archbishop of Tyre; Geoffrey, bishop of Hebron; William of Beaujeu, master of the Temple; Nicholas, master of the Hospital; Conrad, master of the Germans.”] commends themselves with devoted recommendation of the Holy Land, and sends greetings in him who, for the salvation of the human race, mercifully deigned to be crucified at Jerusalem.

[Col. 0820C] The more divinely powerful Providence has gloriously exalted your majesty, and the more abundantly the omnipotence of the Son of the eternal King has endowed you, beyond the other princes of the world, with gifts of grace, the more confidently, in matters touching the cause of the Crucified One, recourse is had to the refuge of your serenity, and the more readily the opportune aid of your highness is implored for preserving the remnants of this small Christian community.

[Col. 0821A] And since, as the unquestioned belief of all firmly maintains, you are happily considering how the cause of this land may be directed, and therefore long to be informed more frequently of its condition, we announce to your magnificence in this present letter only certain matters, and those briefly, which continually agitate the inhabitants of this land, suppressing earlier events in silence, lest perhaps the length of the account offend royal ears.

Let your royal highness therefore know that the Egyptian enemy [Note: Bendocdar, whom historians call at one time the sultan of Babylonia and at another of Egypt; they say that he died on 15 April 1277 (Sanutus in Raynaldus, 1277, no. 18).], with his immense army, recently came out from the borders of Babylonia and advanced as far as the places near us. With his customary cunning, now moving toward Armenia, now toward Tripoli, and now sitting around Tyre and Acre while ranging through our other places, he is devising grave ambushes for us and the whole province. Since, with our small numbers, we rightly fear a speedy test of his strength, he threatens us by preparing more diligently the equipment necessary for attacking cities and whatever else suits the vastness of his army. [Col. 0821B]

[Col. 0821C] He recounts the Babylonian tyrant’s first movements, while it was still uncertain where his fury would end. That these letters belong to the year 1275 is made clear by their date: Sanutus and Jordanus in Raynaldus (1275, no. 51) not only assign the devastation of Armenia to that same year, but also report that aid was sent there from the West. The author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book I, chapter 23, p. 132) is far from the truth when he assigns these letters to 1291, by which time the patriarch and the tyrant had long since gone their separate ways.

But, ignorant of what the coming day will bring forth, against whom he will bend the bow of his wickedness, or what will be the outcome of the events described above, we are distressed amid the straits of dangers pressing upon us; and, as though placed beneath an enemy’s sword [variant: “beneath the sword alone”], we continually fear the assault of his rage.

Yet breathing again through the aid of your powerful right hand—for which the entire population on this side of the sea continually pours forth prayers to the Lord—we unanimously beseech your preeminence that, undertaking from your royal magnificence the cause of the aforesaid land, trodden by Christ’s feet and reddened by his most holy blood, you may deign to provide, for its protection in the meantime, with fitting and timely aid amid the dangers by which it is so greatly shaken, until it is rescued from the jaws of the enemy of Christ by the general crusade.

[Note: Although everyone knows that the sacred expedition was decreed at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274, I do not think it inappropriate to quote Gregory’s own words from a letter addressed to the archbishops and bishops of the province of York, dated at Lyons on 17 September, in the second year of his pontificate. Since it is entered in the Vatican register under “York” and in the Vallicellian codex under “Rheims,” Raynaldus (1274, no. 40) correctly calls it an encyclical to all the bishops of the Catholic world: “After the subsidy of money assigned to the Holy Land by common consent, all agreed upon this as well: that in the general crusade, whose date, with the Lord’s help, we shall quickly appoint, all Christians, joining forces against those same blasphemers, should combine their strength. The more powerful the united strength of Christians becomes, the safer will be the way to the liberation of the aforesaid land, the more readily will the opportunity arise, and the more certain will be the hope of its recovery under God’s guidance.” By these letters the patriarch, informed of this general crusade like the other bishops—and indeed more than the other bishops—and faced with the aforesaid invasion of the Babylonian tyrant, urgently requests that it be timely anticipated by Rudolph’s aid.]

May your royal majesty live and prosper for many years. To you we most devotedly commend ourselves and the cause of the aforesaid land.

### 463. LETTER XXVIII. Rudolph writes to the bishop of Trent about making an amicable settlement with the count of Tyrol

*(A.D. 1276, Rudolphine codex XXVIII.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—When Rudolph had undertaken to settle the dispute between the bishop of Trent and Meinhard, count of Tyrol and Gorizia, concerning certain castles and revenues, and had issued an award which the bishop had not observed, repeatedly claiming that he had been burdened by it, while meanwhile both parties had failed in their obedience at the very time when it was most necessary, he now intends at last to settle the matter completely. He emphasizes the disadvantages suffered by the Church and proposes a very useful opportunity, promising that he will not depart from what is equitable and right.

Rudolph, etc., to the venerable bishop of Trent, etc. [Note: Henry II, successor to Eginomus and heir to the disputes between the Church of Trent and Meinhard, count of Tyrol. See Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, pp. 605 ff. Although he handles this history very poorly, Coleti’s additions there contain excellent documents illuminating it.]

If, after considering the labors that we undertook to reconcile amicably the disputes between you and the distinguished count of Tyrol, a more agreeable result had followed, [Note: Nicolaus Coletus, making use of the work of Benedict Gentiloti, prefect of the Imperial Library at Vienna, brought forward many outstanding documents to illuminate this matter. This letter, which escaped Gentiloti’s diligence, should be inserted among them. It belongs after the award “dated at Augsburg in the year of the Lord 1275, indiction III, on 18 May, in the fifth year of our reign [read: second],” and before the amicable treaty that finally appeared in A.D. 1276, indiction IV, on 25 May.] and if both of you had looked more calmly upon the fact that in those negotiations we were occupied not with our own advantage but with yours, the Roman Empire, at this time of its necessity, would not have been deprived of your services, nor would our sincere intention, which served your interests, have suffered interpreters of hostile speech.

[Col. 0822B] And although the judgment of our mind, examined through careful deliberation, tells us nothing other than that in every respect, insofar as it was possible for us, we guarded and looked after your right, nevertheless you, as they say, complain that you have been burdened by us, allege that you have been offended, and show no consideration for our innocence, though you have more than once placed yourself in the position of defending us and served as the shield of our defense.

[Note: The necessity of the Empire began after Ottocar was declared an enemy of the Empire at the Augsburg assembly on 24 June of this year. Since the reconciliation lies nearly a full year after that date, it is not easy to determine whether this letter was given in 1275 or the following year; the agreement mentioned above shows that it was given no later than the beginning of 1276.]

[Note: In a diploma Rudolph issued on 21 July—“on the vigil of Saint Mary Magdalene, at Ulm, A.D. 1276, in the third year of our reign”—after the agreement, at the beginning, he immediately says: “A hateful dispute arose between the venerable Henry, bishop of Trent, our beloved prince, on the one side, and the illustrious Meinhard, count of Tyrol, on the other, concerning castles, fortifications, possessions, injuries, and many other articles.” From this we know the condition of the dispute. The documents of the matter do not explain why the excellent prince was badly spoken of by some for doing what was good; nevertheless, we learn clearly from this that such was indeed the case.]
