Certainly, if experience of the matter and difficult outcomes have taught you that our counsels were drawing you toward your own advantage and progress, continue even now to follow our counsel and endure with benefit, so that your Church, wounded by grave dangers, may be restored through our intervention—provided, however, that you have not subjected the free power of your own will to the wishes of others.

By God’s grace, full ability and willingness are present for us to cut away the material of discord between you both, so long as you are willing with equal purpose to submit to that truth which we have always proposed to follow. Nor shall we attend less diligently to your peace and advantage because your renewed contention has settled into something resembling an injury to us.

[Note: From another diploma of Rudolph, issued “at Vienna, on 3 November, indiction VI, A.D. 1277, in the fifth year of our reign,” it is evident that some disagreements remained. Henry’s successor, his brother Philip Bonaccoltus, was also involved in them, while Pope Nicholas IV supported the bishop’s case against Meinhard.]

### LETTER XXIX. Rudolph writes to the queen of France about renewing homage

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XXIX.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—When Count Berengarius of Provence died without a male heir, and during the interregnum it was not permissible to obtain the counties of Provence and Forcalquier from the king of the Romans by fiduciary right, as possessions belonging to the law of the Empire, Margaret, Berengarius’s eldest daughter, rendered homage through her envoy to Rudolph and promised that she would renew it to the same envoy. Rudolph sends him with full authority to demand, in the king’s name, the homage and the other agreed conditions.

Rudolph, etc., to the illustrious queen of France, etc. [Note: Margaret, the widowed queen of Raymond, eldest daughter of Berengarius, count of Provence and Forcalquier, and wife of Saint Louis IX, king of the Franks, who had married her in 1234 and, having undertaken a second crusade in 1270, died a holy death. (Surita in Raynaldus, 1270, no. 6.) Berengarius had three other daughters, all queens: Eleanor of England; Sancia, wife of Richard, elected king of the Romans; and Beatrice, wife of Charles, king of Sicily and brother of Saint Louis. He had married Beatrice, the youngest, in 1246, while he was count of Anjou; as though the right to reign had to be violated, Charles invaded his wife’s paternal counties, disregarding both her royal sisters and every consideration of imperial right. This became a seedbed of discord. Margaret defended her right above all others as long as she lived. While Saint Louis was alive, however, and especially through the intervention of the Roman pontiffs, the dispute seemed to have been quieted. It broke out more violently after his death, when Eleanor, queen of England, joined Margaret against Charles. Raynaldus (1272, no. 47) gives us from the Vallicellian codex Gregory’s futile attempt at mediation and notes that the dispute continued into the time of Nicholas III, which is certain.]

Although the industrious man N., whom the text appears defectively to describe as having been sent earlier to our presence, was to receive, in your name and that of your procurator, the counties of N. and N., then vacant to us and to the Roman Empire, as principalities with due solemnity, [Note: The futility of the papal delegation is clear from this: Gregory had appointed the bishop of Senlis and the abbot of Saint-Denis to negotiate the reconciliation. But as soon as the queen heard that the king of the Romans had been elected, even before he was confirmed by Gregory himself, she sent her own legate to him to receive investiture, in her name, of the then-vacant counties of Provence and Forcalquier, as though the matter were still open, because Charles possessed them by no lawful right.]

[Note: When Rudolph, through the agency of Nicholas III, granted these counties to Charles, king of Sicily, he spoke as follows in a diploma preserved by Raynaldus (1280, no. 2): “Although, therefore, we confirm by a special privilege the county and marquisate of Provence—understanding these two names, county and marquisate, to be synonymous and to designate one thing, not different things—and the county of Forcalquier, with all their jurisdictions, rights, and appurtenances, and everything situated within those counties which the Roman emperors, by their privileges, once granted to Lord Raymond Berengarius, count and marquis of Provence and count of Forcalquier, and to his predecessors, etc., promising that neither we nor anyone else, whether one person or several, have made any gift, confirmation, investiture, grant, contract, or anything else with the illustrious lady Margaret, queen of the Franks, or with her representatives, envoys, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons, whereby this confirmation, etc., might be weakened.”

From this it is clear that the aforesaid counties were not in fact erected into principalities, as Rudolph had intended, and that the title of marquisate, by which he had honored Provence, meant nothing other than county. Accordingly, both Charles I, king of Sicily, at the time of the invasion, and Charles II, after Rudolph’s grant, use no title other than that of count, as may be seen in the diplomas of both inserted in the bull of Clement V (*Vatican Bullarium*, vol. I, p. 242 ff.). The invader begins in 1266 as follows: “We, Charles, by the grace of God king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua, count of Anjou, Provence, and Forcalquier.” But the legitimate possessor, Charles III, in 1295 says: “Charles II, by the grace of God king of Jerusalem, king of Sicily, duke of Apulia and prince of Capua, count of Provence and Forcalquier.”]

we had decided that those principalities should be granted in your name, after receiving from him, in that same name, the oath of homage and due fidelity.

Since, however, agreements of this sort preceded the grant and receipt of those principalities, and since you would be bound personally to renew that oath of fidelity and homage to our envoy, in our name, as soon as it should happen that you were summoned to do so in this matter, behold, we are sending the honorable N. to your highness. In fulfillment of the duty of fidelity that binds you to us and to the Empire, we request you by the tenor of these presents that, in our place and in our name, you solemnly renew to him the oath of fidelity and homage owed to us concerning the matters aforesaid.

[Note: Otto, provost of Saint Guido at Speyer, confirmed at Lyons, in the consistory on 6 June 1274, in Rudolph’s name, all the privileges and rights of the Holy See (Raynaldus, 1274, no. 10). The proximity of place and similarity of name persuade me that Rudolph entrusted this office to the same Otto. In any event, Nicholas III was the author of the aforesaid grant to Charles. He prescribed to the king of the Romans the terms of the treaty to be made with the Sicilian, which Raynaldus (1279, no. 11) summarizes as follows: “That Rudolph should transfer the counties of Provence and Forcalquier to Charles and his successors by fiduciary right, while declaring that it was his intention not to diminish the rights of Margaret, queen of the Franks, and not to summon her to take the oath except through the agency of an envoy, nor to bring her to judgment; and that he should remit the injuries inflicted upon earlier kings of the Romans—namely, during the uncertainty of imperial government in the time of the interregnum—for their refusal of obedience.” Whatever was done with the queen of France is supplied by these letters.]

You are likewise to fulfill generously for us and for the same Roman Empire, in the person of the aforesaid N., the other conditions then stipulated with the said N., according to the manner in which the same provost shall deem it necessary to demand them. For we transfer to him the fullness of authority concerning all the matters aforesaid and whatever pertains to them, promising to hold as ratified and acceptable everything that the said provost shall order or arrange in all and each of these matters, as though it had been presented directly to our own person.

### LETTER XXX. Rudolph writes to an archbishop that he should judge justly

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XXX.)*

[Col. 0825A]

**ARGUMENT.**—He admonishes Archbishop N., whom, as a distinguished prince of the Empire, he had confirmed—together with his other privileges—in the right of life and death throughout his entire principality, to judge without any acceptance of persons, following the example of the supreme eternal King. He assures him that royal power and authority, if necessary, will not fail to support his just judgments.

Rudolph, etc., to N., archbishop, etc.

By the grant of your royal rights, with which our serenity long ago invested you at N. [Note: It is well established that investitures of fiefs were made in 1274 and the following year. Since Rudolph says that he had invested the archbishop long ago, it is credible that these letters were written several years later. I do not think it accidental that they should be assigned to 1280: Trithemius records that in that year the archbishop of Mainz fought successfully against Count John of Sponheim; the accompanying references to the distinguished prince and to punishment of criminals without respect of persons fit the matter as well.]

you have received full and free power to judge in civil and criminal cases within your districts and territories, according to the custom of our ancestral princes.

Since we know that you are one of the distinguished princes of the Roman Empire, we wish no one to doubt that absolute jurisdiction is attached to your principality, by which you possess the right to proceed against criminals and the power of the sword, though it is to be exercised through another person, as is fitting for your rank and honor.

[Col. 0825C] [Note: It has repeatedly been shown that the Roman pontiff, whose example ecclesiastical princes ought to follow, customarily proceeded against criminals through the prefect of the city. See the *Carolingian Code*.]

But since, according to legitimate enactments, crime removes every immunity [Note: The copyist of the letters thought *emunitas*—a new form—to mean *immunitas*. See several examples of this word in Ducange’s *Glossary*.] and abolishes every privilege, we wish and command that, with every privilege, nobility, and dignity set aside, you judge justly and cause criminals to be punished, according to the nature of their crimes, both in their property and in their persons [the bracketed word “by punishing” is supplied].

Therefore, putting on the character of a good governor, whose chief responsibility it is to cleanse the province entrusted to him of evil men, gird yourself manfully to judge without selection or distinction of persons, looking to the authority of the eternal King, who commanded, saying: “Thus shall you judge the great and the small.”

[Note: Nothing is more disgraceful or more unjust than acceptance of persons. The excellent prince keeps before his eyes the command of the Holy Spirit (Wisdom 6:8): “For God will not exempt anyone’s person, nor will he fear anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all.”]

Do not doubt that, for the execution of your just sentences once pronounced, we shall bring royal power to bear if necessary.

For it is contrary to our purpose and to Roman law that royal authority should be specially required to punish the crime of every criminal, since, according to the statutes of the deified Roman emperors, it is not crimes but the punishments of crimes that should be brought before royal ears.

### LETTER XXXI. Rudolph grants someone certain mountains for cultivation

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XXXI.)*

[Col. 0826A]

**ARGUMENT.**—He grants to Albert Lincke and his associates the working of mountains containing silver mines, on the condition that the customary rights be paid to the royal treasury.

In the course of time, what authority does not establish and written testimony does not strengthen withdraws from human memory. Bearing this in mind, our serenity has judged it worthy to record in the present letters what we have decreed concerning certain silver mines. [Note: Various laws concerning the rights of princes in this matter occur in both Codes. See Gothofredus, *Theodosian Code*, vol. III, p. 517, on metals and miners.]

Let people of the present age and the succession of future generations know that we have granted to the aforesaid Albert Lincke and his associates certain mountains, etc., to be worked and to serve their use, on condition that from those same mountains they pay us the rights that are paid by other workers of similar mountains, etc. In witness whereof, etc.

### LETTER XXXII. Rudolph commends a certain abbot to a bishop

*(A.D. 1274, Rudolphine codex XXXII.)*

[Col. 0826B]

**ARGUMENT.**—When an abbacy whose abbot was a prince of the Empire became vacant, and two persons were striving to obtain it—a circumstance that suggested to Rudolph both the death of the prince and the danger of that church—the same king of the Romans repeatedly commends to the bishop of Constance the man who was already in possession of the church, as a prudent and upright man who would bring comfort to that church.

That you might recognize, as we do, with the clear-sighted confidence of an acute mind, how many and how great are the afflictions and pressures of misery by which the sacred Roman Empire is shaken, its pillars having been shaken—the pillars by which that Empire ought to recover its strength and remain standing—these pressures are being felt in the abbey of N. [Note: In Switzerland there is the celebrated monastery of the wilderness, of the Order of Saint Benedict, called Einsiedeln, whose abbot was a prince of the Roman Empire in Rudolph’s time. Some have thought Rudolph to be the author of this princely status, but they are refuted by a diploma of Rudolph in the author of *Pietas Austriaca* (book III, chapter 13, p. 455), by which the title is confirmed to Ulrich II in A.D. 1274:

“Rudolph, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever Augustus, to all the faithful of the sacred Empire to whom the present writing shall come, his grace and every good thing. The principality of the sacred and illustrious Empire is adorned by the numerous company of renowned princes. For in the multitude of the shining cohort there gleams the prince distinguished by titles and flashing with glory.

Since, therefore, the venerable monastery of hermits of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, through the devotion to purity and sincerity of faith of those presiding over it, has deserved such an increase of grace and honor from the deified emperors and our royal predecessors that whoever is to be abbot of the aforesaid monastery should, invested by the imperial scepter through the king of the Romans with the administration of temporal affairs, shine in the company of princes, we, observing with the mirror of royal circumspection the honor of the venerable abbot Ulrich, who presides over the aforesaid monastery under the title of abbot, have aggregated him to the company of our princes and caused him to be distinguished by the royal scepter and the insignia of princely rank.

We command all the officials, knights, subjects, and dependents of the aforesaid abbey to obey and attend him as their prince, devotedly and faithfully, in all matters pertaining to the administration of temporal affairs.

Given at Zurich, on 26 January, A.D. 1274, indiction II, in the first year of our reign.”]

Two persons are striving against each other for it, and the matter presses so heavily upon everyone’s thoughts that not only do we bear the loss of so great a prince [Note: Scholars know that other abbots in Germany were princes of the Roman Empire. The reasons why I think this letter concerns Einsiedeln, and was therefore written to the bishop of Constance, are several. Among the pillars supporting the Empire must be counted the fact that the abbot was invested with fiefs in the manner of other princes, summoned to imperial assemblies—as the same author proves by the examples cited (ibid., p. 457)—and that Einsiedeln lay in Rudolph’s homeland or region. Finally, the fact that Ulrich’s predecessors had chosen the counts of Rapperswil as advocates or protectors, although supreme jurisdiction belonged to the emperors, as Abbot de Longuerue observes (*Historical and Geographical Description of France*, book III, p. 273 ff.) from the monastery chronicle—all these considerations persuaded me to believe that this letter was written to the bishop of Constance at the beginning of 1274, with the result indicated by the diploma just cited.]

[Col. 0827A] but the church itself, unless it receives speedy assistance, is bound to lose forever the hope of recovering its health.

We say this out of compassion, and with the utmost consciousness of truth we declare that N., who is now in possession of that church, knows and is able to preside over it and benefit it, and that through his care the aforesaid church can return to its former state of prosperity.

You, therefore, reverend father, most sincere of friends, having examined the justice of the aforesaid N.’s cause, should, for our sake and insofar as you can do so with God and honor, strive to advance him in consideration of our prayers, so that the aforesaid church may rejoice in a pastor as prudent and upright as we believe and know him to be from certain indications, and, casting off its sorrows, may through him and us deserve to receive at last the benefits of consolation.

### LETTER XXXIII. Rudolph sympathizes with and consoles a certain person

*(A.D. 1277, Rudolphine codex XXXIII.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He excuses a prince or count placed in difficulties by enemies of the Empire for being unable to bring him aid while he is assembling an army, and consoles him with the hope of possible relief.

The honorable man N., our beloved and trusted acquaintance, a fervent champion of your honor, has explained to us the immense pressures and varied straits of persecution with which, in these days of stormy weather, the tempestuous whirlwind has assailed you.

[Col. 0827B] We could not fail to feel inwardly the distress of compassion concerning these matters, since we await your peace and tranquility with devoted affection.

From these circumstances, therefore, we infer by a reasonably probable conjecture that on this occasion you cannot, as you wish, make yourself available for our services or contribute to our needs. [Note: I conjecture that this letter belongs to the latter part of 1277, on account of the military preparations that had to be made against Ottocar, the enemy of the Empire, who had rebelled.]

Let your sincerity know for certain, then, that we intend to work toward your relief and, insofar as we can, to deal in a good manner with your distress.

### LETTER XXXIV. Rudolph grants a certain prince the authority to mint coin

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XXXIV.)*

[Col. 0827C]

**ARGUMENT.**—A diploma granting Bishop N., a prince of the Empire, the authority to mint coin, and ordering that it be accepted throughout the Empire, provided that it is lawful.

Although we ought to extend the debt-paying hand of our munificence to all the faithful of the Roman Empire, it is nevertheless fitting that we raise up princes by a special prerogative, as excellent foundations upon which the height of the Empire rests securely, and enlarge them with worthy favors of our beneficence.

For this reason we wish all, present and future, to know that, graciously regarding the acceptable and welcome services of grateful devotion that N. has hitherto rendered to us and may continue to render, as more pleasing to us and to the sacred Empire, and greatly desiring that he and his bishopric may rejoice in the advantages they desire and prosper through continual increases, we freely and gladly assent, out of royal liberality, that the same N. may freely have lawful coin minted in the city of N.

By the present letters we grant this as we have determined, giving strict royal command to all and each of those established under the jurisdiction of the Roman Empire [Note: Nothing else need be noted concerning this and the following diploma except the distinction between two privileges granted by the king of the Romans concerning the same matter and for the same reasons. Unless I am mistaken, he wishes the coin of the prince-bishop—probably the bishop of Passau—to be accepted everywhere, throughout all places and peoples of the Roman Empire; this is an exceptional privilege. But the coin granted to a certain nobleman is confined within the limits of his jurisdiction.]

that, provided it is lawful, they do not fail reverently to accept this coin, setting aside all opposition.

### 471. LETTER XXXV. Rudolph orders that the coin which he had granted a certain nobleman authority to mint be accepted without hindrance

*(A.D. 1280, Rudolphine codex XXXV.)*

**ARGUMENT.**—He grants a certain nobleman authority to mint coin and orders that it be accepted, provided that it is lawful, in all the cities and places under his jurisdiction.

The power of august magnificence, thirsting to increase the honor of the Empire, readily adapts and inclines itself to the advancement and advantage of those who, distinguished by their nobility, shine toward the sacred Empire with the brighter light of fidelity.

[Note: I have assigned these two letters to the year 1280 because Rudolph especially honored with rewards and privileges those whose fidelity he had tested in the battles of preceding years against the enemies of the Empire.]

Indeed, since the nobleman N. has obtained by his distinguished merits before the royal majesty the right to mint perpetually, within the jurisdiction of his land, lawful coin by our permission and the fullness of royal power, we strictly entrust and command your community by royal authority that you diligently accept, in your places and cities, the same coin formed with a lawful impression, which the said nobleman has caused to be minted, as was expressed above, [Col. 0829A] permitting reciprocal commerce and allowing it to be carried on more freely once every impediment has ceased.

[Note: Here, as in the preceding diploma, he wishes the coin to be made lawful. *Lega*, as it is commonly called—and which in some places was also known as *lex*, as may be seen in Ducange’s *Glossary*—during the thirteenth century, that is, in Rudolph’s time, designates rather the value of the coin than the mixture of its metals. Whoever obtained from an emperor or king the authority to mint coin did not thereby obtain the discretion to depart from imperial or royal law. Indeed, whenever financial straits compelled an emperor or king to issue debased coin, the same debasement necessarily appeared even among those who possessed the privilege of minting it, for the sake of commerce.

An example is supplied by Frederick III in the chronicle cited by Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 494). Although it is nearly two centuries later, I will not hesitate to quote it because it bears upon our subject:

“Emperor Frederick caused a base and despised coin to be manufactured, which the people called *schinderling*. When other princes learned of this—namely, Albert, duke of Austria; John, duke of Munich; Louis, duke of Landshut; Otto, duke of Neumark; the count of Ötting in Rhaetia . . . Ulrich, bishop of Passau, also manufactured such coin, lest they should suffer loss from it. Among them Lord Sigismund, archbishop, was likewise compelled to manufacture coin of equal value, because he could not refuse the emperor’s coin in his lands.”]

472. LETTER XXXVI. Rudolph confirms a privilege of a certain monastery.

[Note: I confidently assert that this privilege is not that of Rudolph, king of the Romans. At times the compiler of this codex overstepped the limits of the headings (Book I, Letter 39), either imitating or interpolating the sentences and style of Pope Gregory. Here, by contrast, however carefully you investigate, you will find neither Rudolph’s style nor his characteristic expressions. You will also discover that the privilege itself was drawn up contrary to Rudolph’s practice.

Nothing can place the matter more clearly before our eyes than two authentic privileges granted to the same monastery, which the author of *Pietas Austriaca* (Book I, chapter 16, p. 94, and Book II, chapter 1, p. 228) presents to us: the first, Rudolph’s, from the often-cited Imperial Codex; the second, Albert’s, incorporating his father’s privilege. Learned reader, I shall set both before your eyes:

“Rudolph, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever Augustus. To all the faithful of the Roman Empire who shall inspect these present letters, his grace and every good thing. Royal serenity willingly devotes itself to the advantages of its subjects, so that others may receive from it an incentive to purer devotion and faith. Let all, both those living now and those to come, therefore know that we have deemed it fitting, out of royal kindness, to grant this favor to the honorable and religious men, the abbot and convent of Zwettl of the Cistercian order: namely, that they may freely transport two talents of salt of the larger binding, as the illustrious late Frederick, duke of Austria, is known to have granted them by his privilege, each year on the Danube without payment of the customs duty. We grant them these letters of ours as testimony in this matter. The witnesses to this are the illustrious Albert, duke of Saxony, our dearest prince; the noble men Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg; the count of Hardegg; Lettold and Henry, brothers of Kuenring; Henry, Conrad, and Siboto, brothers of Pottendorf; and many others. Given at Vienna on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1281, in the eighth year of our reign.”

Albert, Rudolph’s son, confirmed this privilege ten years later:

“We, Albert, by the grace of God duke of Austria and Styria, lord of Carniola, the March, and Port Naon, wish all to know to whom these present letters shall come that the religious man Ebro, abbot of the monastery of Zwettl of the Cistercian order, having come into our presence, exhibited to us a certain privilege of our most serene lord and dearest father Rudolph, king of the Romans, asking that it be renewed for himself and his convent by our special favor. The tenor of that privilege is in every respect as follows:

‘Rudolph, by the grace of God, etc. Given at Vienna on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the ninth indiction, A.D. 1281, in the eighth year of our reign.’

“We therefore, favorably inclined to the humble prayers of the said abbot, renew and approve the aforementioned privilege and the favors contained in it, and strengthen them by the protection of this present document, issuing these letters, confirmed by our seal, as clear testimony in the matter. Let no one therefore presume to violate this document of our renewal and approval; should anyone do otherwise, let him know that he has incurred our indignation. Given at Vienna on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, A.D. 1291.”]

(Year of the Lord 1281, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XXXVI.)

ARGUMENT.—Rudolph grants the monastery of Zwettl free transport of two talents of salt along the Danube; this privilege had formerly been granted to the same monastery by Frederick, duke of Austria.

The imperial throne is exalted and the title of Augustal honor is adorned when benevolent consideration is extended to religious institutions, and their condition and prosperity are advanced by liberal munificence. For this reason we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that while we were staying at Vienna, with the Lord happily advancing the increase of our dignity, and the duchies of Austria and Styria having been brought under our dominion by prosperous fortune, the abbot and convent of N. presented to our highness a privilege graciously granted to the said monastery by A., humbly asking that we might deign to renew that privilege by transcribing it word for word and confirming what it contained. Its tenor is as follows, etc.

Therefore, since we are bound by pious favor to devote ourselves to enlarging the status of churches and increasing the advantages of religious institutions, we have ordered the privilege itself to be inserted word for word in this present privilege, confirming by imperial grace each of the provisions contained in it. We establish and decree by imperial edict that no person, high or low, ecclesiastical or secular, shall presume rashly to molest the aforesaid abbot and convent of the named monastery concerning the matters mentioned above, contrary to the tenor of this present privilege of ours, etc.

[Note: The same author, in *Pietas Austriaca* (Book I, chapter 20, p. 119), presents this privilege, candidly admitting that he does not know the place or the person indicated in it. I, however, have no doubt that it concerns the monastery of Zwettl; but the document preserved in the Imperial Codex is one confirmed by Albert, Rudolph’s son, and its argument agrees with the heading that we have prefixed to this document attributed to Rudolph. For who does not see that “imperial throne,” “imperial grace,” and “imperial edict” are expressions unfamiliar to the Roman king throughout this entire codex? Who does not perceive that the structure of the words, from beginning to end, is wholly different from Rudolph’s style? Finally, who has not read in that initial letter the name “A.” as Albert, Rudolph’s son?

For my part, I would not wish to inflict upon Seyfrid, abbot of Zwettl, the reproach that he arrogated to himself the license to compose an allegedly imperial privilege. I would rather believe that, by the work of Rudolph II—during whose time it flourished, at the beginning of the seventeenth century—the privilege of Albert, which contained the Rudolphine privilege, was confirmed, and that it was deliberately inserted into these letters of Rudolph so that the similarity of the names might deceive posterity and thus cause what belonged to the second Rudolph to be attributed to Rudolph I. Yet the subjection of the duchies of Austria and Styria, and the other circumstances indicating Rudolph I, contradict my wishes. However the matter may stand, the privilege certainly ought not to be attributed to Rudolph I.]

LETTER XXXVII. Rudolph restores an infamous man to his former rank.

(Year of the Lord 1280, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XXXVII.)

ARGUMENT.—To a certain man condemned to proscription for a grave offense, he not only remits the punishment of the disgrace but erases the disgrace itself. He therefore decrees that the man shall be free from every mark of infamy and restores him fully to his former position, as though he had never been liable to any crime.

We pursue the noble work proper to one seated upon a throne, with clemency as our guide. If, when those who fall through the slippery follies of guilt are in need of relief, our hand swiftly makes itself ready to raise them up, and if after their offense we grant pardon to the guilty, it is because, recognizing that the disasters transmitted from our first parent to his descendants have flowed into the natural condition of transgression, we gladly bestow upon suppliants the assistance of gracious restoration.

For this reason we wish all to know that when N. had been condemned, justice so dictating, to the sentence of proscription on account of the infamy of a certain offense, [Note: The entire Roman Senate, with many of its members burdened by the infamy of the crime of sorcery and magic, sought indulgence from Valentinian the Elder. The Augustus replied to them in A.D. 371 as follows:

“Indulgence, Conscript Fathers, marks those whom it frees and does not remove the infamy of the crime; it grants pardon only for the punishment. Let this be valid in the case of one or two accused persons. He who grants indulgence to the Senate condemns the Senate.” (*Codex Theodosianus*, vol. III, p. 298.)

The learned Gothofredus discusses this law, as is his custom, preferring to indulgence a warning of security, or a summons, since infamy is joined to it. He confirms the matter by examples, including a statement of Saint Augustine from Letter 259, or 151, to Caecilianus:

“Nor did it seem that indulgence should be granted them, lest even so they should be marked by some crime; rather, only a warning was given, by which it was ordered that they be dismissed free from every form of harassment.”

Such, then, was the practice in those ancient times. But emperors renewed in the West by the Apostolic See, and even the kings of the Romans—or elected emperors—by indulgence release men both from punishment and from infamy, as is evident from this letter, whose date is uncertain and which there is no reason to remove from the order it occupies in the codex.]

considering, from the prerogative of humanity inborn in us, [Note: “Nothing is more worthy of a great and distinguished man than forgiveness and clemency,” says Cicero (*On Duties* I, chapter 25). Grotius uses these words (*On the Law of War and Peace* II, chapter 24, §3) and must be consulted at length on this subject.

Especially relevant is Seneca’s statement concerning the clemency of a ruler: “It belongs to a great spirit to endure injuries while possessing supreme power, and nothing is more glorious for a ruler than to be wronged with impunity.”

Saint John Chrysostom adds this more excellent statement: “Clemency can greatly adorn every human being, but especially those who are established in authority. For since royal power permits everything, it is noble to restrain oneself and to make divine law the guide of one’s actions, for the sake of reputation and glory.”

Rudolph rightly boasts that clemency was implanted in him by nature, since he forgave the injury done to Bernard, bishop of Seckau (Book II, Letter 24), and to the author of insolent libels by which his royal majesty had been injured. I pass over the other examples of clemency found among authors, for they are all absorbed by this single example.]

and wishing to temper the rigor of justice with the seasoning of mercy, especially since satisfaction had been made after the injury, we fully and completely restore the aforesaid N., by the favor of royal gentleness, to his former rank. By the tenor of these presents we command all that he be admitted, as before, to every civil and public act.

475. LETTER XXXVIII. Rudolph substitutes another procurator in the Roman Curia after the death of one.

(Year of the Lord 1280, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XXXVIII.)

ARGUMENT.—He laments the death of Master Paul of Terni, his representative or procurator at the Holy See, and, in the most dutiful language, wins the favor of the cardinal friend whom, after mature deliberation, he has appointed in his place. To him he entrusts the advancement of his affairs.

[Col. 0831B] Recently the bitterest cup was poured out for us by the mournful death of N., of pious memory, [Note: Master Paul of Terni, a cleric whom we saw above (Letter 9) serving Rudolph as representative or procurator before Nicholas III in the year 1278—a man of the highest prudence and fidelity, who had bound the king’s affection to himself.] and, drinking it amid tearful sobs, while we consider inwardly that his loss has inflicted upon us irreparable damage, we have recourse, after careful reflection, to the one remedy: since the hand of the Most High has pierced us with so grievous a wound and deprived us of so vigilant a promoter, we confidently entrust to you the whole mass of our affairs that require action, since you both know how and sincerely wish to advise the needs of your friends [Note: He addresses here none other than a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, evidently the one to whom he had written the previous year (Letter 8) about entering into a relationship of intimacy, as I believe.] and to come to their aid with effective remedies.

Therefore, placing the anchor of our hope chiefly in you, after God, we most devoutly beseech your fatherhood [Note: From the preceding letters it is clear that Rudolph addresses by this office either bishops or cardinals. Although in 1276 the bishop of Basel performed the same procuratorial function (Book II, Letters 1 and following), we cannot suspect that the person here is a bishop, since the letters indicate a man distinguished by counsel and authority and residing in the City, such as the aforementioned cardinal.] that you be willing to assist our affairs requiring advancement and completion with timely counsel and aid.

476. LETTER XXXIX. The king of Cyprus writes to Rudolph, asking him to report his successes.

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XXXIX.)

ARGUMENT.—The king of Cyprus, greatly wishing to learn of Rudolph’s prosperity, which would be a consolation to the unhappy condition of the Holy Land, desires to be informed by him how the undertaking concerning aid for the Holy Land is proceeding. He reports that, while writing, he is safe and well, and wishes to hear the same concerning Rudolph. He says that he will learn from the envoy whom he is sending of certain recent developments in Syria and several other matters of secrecy.

To the most excellent, etc., the king of Cyprus [Note: Hugh of Lusignan, who had succeeded his kinsman Hugh on the day of the Lord’s Nativity in 1267; the latter had died in the preceding month, according to the authors cited by Raynaldus (1267, no. 65). Since in 1276 Mary, daughter of Bohemond, prince of Antioch, transferred her right, or title, to the kingdom of Jerusalem to Charles, king of Sicily—whence the king of Cyprus entered into the greatest controversies with him, of which no mention occurs here—this letter must be referred to the preceding year, or at least to the months preceding that transfer of the title.]

Since we continually desire to hear of the wished-for successes of your magnificent state, whose prosperity would undoubtedly bring great consolation to the tearful events of the Holy Land [Note: The unhappy times of Bendocdar, the Egyptian tyrant mentioned in the following letter, are indicated here. See above (Letter 27, col. 820, note f, and 821, note a).], we implore your imperial excellence with whatever devotion we can, asking that you frequently signify to us, through your authoritative letters, the prosperous progress of the affairs taking place around us, which we desire to advance with uninterrupted increase, confidently imposing upon us your wishes and commands.

Knowing that, when these letters were composed, we were, by God’s grace, fully sound in heart, we eagerly desire to hear the same concerning your magnificence, and, if it were possible, to behold it even more eagerly with the eyes of our heart. Your imperial magnificence will be able to learn and understand through N. the condition of the aforesaid Holy Land and the developments that have now taken place [Note: Above he had called him “imperial excellence”; here the title “imperial majesty” is heard. It is uncertain whether he employs this flattery to win Rudolph’s favor, or whether he expects the letter to reach him already crowned with the imperial diadem and therefore addresses him with this honor. Either possibility does nothing to weaken the consistent testimony of all the records and of the entire codex.] and also certain matters which we have instructed him to present.

477. LETTER XL. The patriarch of Jerusalem writes to Rudolph concerning aid for the Holy Land.

(Year of the Lord 1275, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XL.)

ARGUMENT.—The patriarch of Jerusalem and the officials of the Holy Land again request aid from Rudolph. Since he is not ignorant of Syrian affairs, they implore him especially to pity the necessity and poverty of the nobles and the common people. They recount the Babylonian tyrant’s savagery against the Christians of Armenia and say that, having pitched his camp in the region of Antioch, he has spread terror far and wide, so that everyone, abandoning the weaker places, takes refuge in more strongly fortified positions, which are being equipped as far as possible to repel the enemy’s fury. They say that they can relieve the distress of others only with tears, and that they lack many kinds of fortifications needed to resist a most powerful enemy; they will perish unless timely aid arrives. They are sending an envoy, a knight who has spent a very long time in Syria, and they commend him repeatedly to Rudolph.

To the most excellent and most powerful prince, etc. Brother Thomas [Note: Contemporary authors have left the history of this period highly uncertain as regards chronology. See what we said above (Letter 27). Indeed, if the date had been attached to these two letters of the patriarch and the others, and to the preceding letter of the king of Cyprus, we would not be divided among the opinions of Sanuto, Bernard the Treasurer, and more recent writers concerning the years in which Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and Bendocdar, the impious tyrant, died—events on which the unhappy narratives of both the patriarch and the king of Cyprus depend. Nevertheless, Syrian affairs receive much light from these three monuments, which are full of authenticity.] humble pilgrim in Jerusalem, Balian, constable of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and vicar [Col. 0834A] of the kingdoms of Jerusalem and Cyprus, etc., with a humble commendation of the Holy Land, present themselves to you [Note: It may be inferred that Balian performed these offices as bailiff or governor from Sanuto’s account of Roger, count of Saint-Severina, whom Charles, king of Sicily, sent to assume possession of the kingdom (Raynaldus, 1277, no. 17). His words are worth hearing here:

“Roger, count of Saint-Severina, bailiff of the kingdom of Jerusalem, was therefore sent on behalf of King Charles, and arrived at Acre with six galleys on 7 June 1277. Immediately upon his arrival, Balian of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf, evacuated the castle and yielded it to him.”

Thus he administered the remnants of the kingdom of Jerusalem for its king, residing at Acre; it is therefore no wonder that he held precedence in the other offices. I say at Acre, in that city which was also called Ptolemais, where from 1191 onward the patriarch and the aforementioned officials remained for a hundred years in the hope of recovering Jerusalem and the whole Holy Land. For after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187, the affairs of the Christians were in a desperate state; but the modest Christian force that, at the urging of desperation, besieged Ptolemais summoned Latin reinforcements there, and in 1191, on 12 July, obtained the surrender of that barbarian stronghold. There, as I have said, they remained for a hundred years, until in 1290 the barbarians captured the city, all the Christians were either killed or driven out, and the Christians lost all Syria.

During that long interval, from 1229 to 1244, for fifteen years, the Christians possessed Jerusalem and Nazareth under the agreements made by Frederick II with the sultan al-Kamil. But would that they had not possessed them! For when those years had passed, all the Christians found there—about five thousand—were killed, and those holy places were polluted and destroyed, as reported in the *Epitome of the Sacred Wars* in Canisius (vol. IV, p. 438).]

We do not believe that your royal greatness is unaware how carefully the remnant of the Christians on this side of the sea must be fortified against hostile ambushes, with defensive works and safeguards, against the unspeakable power of the tyrant, against the poison of the dragon by which the entire region is thrown into confusion. Nor do we believe that you are unaware how the humble patriarch of Jerusalem, the religious houses [Note: Namely, the Templars, the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem, and the Teutonic House, concerning whom see above (Letter 25 and following).], and all the others, both noblemen and commoners, whatever their condition or rank, are oppressed by the burden of poverty and afflicted by the extremes of misery and want on account of the disasters of past wars, the wickedness of the times, the destruction of places, and the various calamities of peoples. With no rest granted them and no assistance supporting them amid such dangers, they are worn down.

Finally, we do not wish you to be unaware how greatly the Egyptian enemy has been lifted into arrogance by the insufficiency of the forces on our side, and how savagely he, his hands dripping with blood and his sword steeped in the blood of Christ’s faithful, has raged pitiably for twenty days throughout the kingdom of Armenia, amid the slaughter of its inhabitants, the burning of villages and cities, and the final devastation of everything he could reach in his violent assault [Note: Sanuto reports the following events for this year in Raynaldus (1275, no. 51), and this passage of the letter greatly illuminates his account:

“In the same year Bendocdar, who was called Malek Madavar, traversed the plain of Armenia and struck down more than twenty thousand people with the sword, taking captive with him boys and girls, as many as ten thousand; horses and larger and smaller animals he took up to the number of three hundred thousand.”]

There he pitilessly satisfied the rage of his long-conceived fury, and, having laid waste to that kingdom and utterly desolated it, he came into the region of Antioch [Note: You hear “the region of Antioch,” for as early as 1268 that patriarchal city—where the prince of the apostles first sat and where the name of Christians was first heard—had been destroyed by this same tyrant, together with its last Christian patriarch. Sanuto narrates its destruction in Raynaldus (1268, no. 53) as follows:

“The sultan came to Tripoli and destroyed the gardens; then he proceeded against Antioch, and on 29 May captured the city without any tumult of battle. After its capture, up to seventeen thousand persons were killed and more than one hundred thousand were taken captive, and the once-famous city became like the solitude of a desert.”

Gregory X, in his letter to Thomas, patriarch of Jerusalem and the author of this letter (Raynaldus, 1272, no. 17), maintained that the causes of this lamentable destruction were the vices of the people:

“Nor are you unaware,” he says, “how, through those enslaved to the pleasures of vices and surrendered to the servitude of the flesh, following its impulses, the eyes of the divine majesty have been so offended there that the destruction of various parts of those lands, such as Antioch and many other places, bears witness: they were exposed to the hands of enemies for overthrow, and their inhabitants were brought to destruction.”

To this I think should be added the splendid eulogy of the last Christian patriarch mentioned above, by Leander Alberti in Bosch (the *Acts of the Saints*, July, vol. IV, p. 141). He writes:

“Adorned with the sacred mitre, he fell prostrate before the altar with four brothers, commending with tears to God the end of the city and its citizens, whose wailing, dreadful howling, lamentations, and loud voices of mourners he heard because of the plunderings, wounds, rapes, and killings inflicted by the barbarians. While he was praying in this manner, behold, the most wicked men entered the church and cruelly slew him, together with the said brothers, as he lay prostrate before the sacred altar.”

Eight years earlier this region had been turned into a desert; Bendocdar had fixed his camp there, eager to glut himself on Christian blood.]

and there, [Col. 0835A] as is reported, he remains with his entire powerful army. Yet no one knows at all where his purpose is leading him, or toward what object his unrestrained will—intoxicated by past triumphs and repeatedly moistened with the spoils of the faithful—is driving him.

In view, therefore, of these and countless other dangers and fears faithfully reported through various letters and special messengers to so great a king [Note: Two points should be observed here. First, in that same year, 1275, letters and messengers were repeatedly sent to Rudolph—nothing could be more credible in such troubled circumstances. Second, the liberality, or rather the flattery, of the king of Cyprus is corrected by the patriarch, since he assigns Rudolph no title other than that of king.], by which we are shaken to the innermost depths and foundations of our hearts, our places are being fortified, since we trust that their situation and the assistance of their warriors enable them to resist the enemy’s fury. According to the resources of those undertaking the fortification, their inhabitants flee from places that can be conquered, not without grave distress and loss to their property and bodies, with their children, possessions, and household members, to safer places, abandoning their own hearths.

But since we cannot provide the necessary remedies for the misery and suffering of those from whom, and concerning whom, we are variously, frequently, urgently and insistently importuned, we are pierced by the bitterness of grief and, through lack of strength, compassion, or emotion, dissolve into tears of charity [Note: Jordanus reports in Raynaldus (1275, no. 51) that in October some auxiliary forces sent from the West arrived at Ptolemais while the general preparations were under way:

“Toward the end of October,” he says, “Lord William of Roussillon arrived at Ptolemais with forty soldiers, another sixty mounted men, and four hundred crossbowmen serving at the Church’s expense.”

The date of this letter must therefore be placed before that time, for what follows clearly shows that no aid had yet reached that place.]

Your excellence knows the strength of the inhabitants of Syria and the pitiable condition of the lands on this side of the sea; you know also the power of the Egyptians; you know furthermore the extreme poverty of the aforesaid patriarch of Jerusalem and of all the religious; you know as well how many fortifications of walls, engines, garrisons, galleys, and other instruments of war are needed to defend our Holy Land; and finally you know that we lack sufficient defenders and have neither among ourselves nor from elsewhere means sufficient for their wages. Consequently, we cannot provide ourselves or the weaker places with the necessary defenders for the aforesaid fortifications or with adequate assistance [Note: Rudolph had testified in his letters to Gregory X (Book I, Letter 12) that he was all the more inflamed toward the sacred expedition because the bones of his natural father rested there, far from their native land, for the glory of the Crucified. For this reason he desired to travel there until the final days of his life; but in 1291, while hastening to Frankfurt for the assembly that he had arranged for the same purpose, he was attacked by illness and died. Thus all these matters, which he is said in this letter to know thoroughly, were known to him before he was elected king of the Romans. These letters also support the correctness of the assertion made by Gerard and other writers that Rudolph lived in Syria with his father before the year 1240, when he married, although it seems incredible that he followed Frederick II’s army, as some claim; for in 1228, when Frederick crossed overseas, Rudolph was a ten-year-old boy. See above (Book I, Letter 2, note a, col. 705).]

Let the clemency of so great a king therefore provide, we beg, for the exposed dangers of your sons; let the right hand of your power hasten to our aid, surrounded as we are by the snares of the ravening wolf; let the blessed royal hand touch our sores and wounds, pouring into them the healing ointments of mercy before their corruption penetrates the marrow.

We especially commend to your greatness Lord Elias of Insat, the knight who bears these presents and who has long resided in that land. May your royal majesty live and prosper for many years; to it we most devoutly commend ourselves and the Holy Land.

LETTER XLI. Rudolph takes a five-year-old orphan under his protection.

(Year of the Lord 1280, Rudolphine Codex, Letter XLI.)

[Col. 0836B] ARGUMENT.—Rudolph receives under royal protection an orphan who has not yet completed his fifth year of life; by this document he announces throughout the empire that he has undertaken to defend, under royal patronage, all the child’s property, both movable and immovable. [Note: This remarkable document, the like of which I honestly confess I have nowhere found, shows a most pious prince imitating the King of kings. It is also related of him that he once rebuked attendants who were turning away humble people and those of modest fortune, using these words:

“By God, let people come to me. For I was not created for rule so that I might be shut up in a chest.” (Lipsius, *Monumenta Polonica*, chapter 7).]

To this end, the principate has been imposed upon our royal dignity and our arms have been anointed with the oil of sacred consecration, so that, with the hand of strength and outstretched arm, we may be the defenders of all who dwell under the Roman Empire.

[Note: He who nowhere makes use of any title except that of king, in so many letters, here boasts that he has received royal anointing, contrary to those who confuse the imperial dignity with the royal one and call all the kings of the Romans, indeed even the emperors of Germany, emperors—such as the compiler of these letters, who more than once calls Rudolph himself emperor, despite Rudolph’s opposition. The words of the prayer spoken at the king’s anointing should be heard from the Roman Pontifical: “Establish, O Lord, principality upon his shoulder, so that he may be a strong, just, faithful, provident, and indefatigable governor of this kingdom and of your people, etc.” Nor should you be surprised that Rudolph uses “empire” for “kingdom.” For the empire was entrusted to the king of the Romans to govern, and within it a certain kingdom was also contained among the feudal princes. The imperial anointing, however, did not designate a kingdom or empire bounded by fixed limits, but extended the emperor’s power wherever the Church of God extended, so that—without in any way diminishing the proper rights of the pontiff, kings, or other supreme princes—the emperor was said to rule temporally throughout all lands and peoples for the defense of the Catholic religion, just as the pontiff ruled spiritually.

Nothing better proves this point than the prayers instituted for such anointing (Ceremonial, section 5, chapter 3, p. 24), which I gladly insert here at the appropriate place:

“Almighty God, from whom comes all power and dignity, we beseech you with humble devotion and the most lowly prayer that you grant this servant of yours N. a prosperous exercise of imperial majesty, so that, established under your protection for the governance of your holy Church, neither present things may hinder him nor future things oppose him; but that, through the inspiration of the gift of the Holy Spirit, he may be able to govern the people subject to him with an even balance of justice, and in all his works may always fear you and continually strive to please you.

“O God, Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, who were anointed by the Father with the oil of participation above your companions, may he, through the present infusion of sacred oil, pour upon your head the blessing of the Spirit the Paraclete, and make that same blessing penetrate into the innermost parts of your heart, so that through this visible and tangible gift you may perceive invisible things, and, having administered your temporal kingdom with righteous moderation, may deserve to reign eternally with him who, without sin, lives as King of kings with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God. Amen.”

Thus, on Rudolph’s sure testimony, anyone is mistaken who maintains that Rudolph himself, or any of his predecessors or successors crowned as king of the Romans, should be regarded as emperor, unless he was constituted emperor through imperial anointing and consequently coronation by the Roman pontiff.

I would not dare deny that, after Charles V—who was the last to be crowned with the imperial crown by the Roman pontiff, in 1530, as was stated in its place—the king of the Romans, or elected emperor, is read only in the Roman Missal, on Good Friday. Nevertheless, I am compelled to extol with the highest praises Augusta Maria Theresa, firstborn daughter of Charles VI and the most glorious offspring of Rudolph, that most devout prince. Since she has not been adorned with the imperial diadem by the Roman pontiff, she nevertheless exercises, as a great imitator of her illustrious ancestor, the functions belonging to an empress in a remarkable manner, for the perpetual memory of posterity; yet she wishes to be called by no other name than queen, although in the mouths, services, and devotion of all she is proclaimed a pious, fortunate, invincible Augusta and empress.]

But although we are bound to this duty above all by the care of the government [Col. 0837A] entrusted to us, we nevertheless especially wish and ought to protect those whom the divine oracle has committed more particularly to our protection, crying out with its command: “You shall be the helper of the orphan and the fatherless.”

[Note: The reason by which he is moved to offer royal protection to an orphan need not be sought far: he himself testifies that he is moved by the divine command: “You shall be the helper of the orphan and the fatherless” (Psalm 9:35). Although in all manuscripts either “the orphan” or “the fatherless” is found, nowhere are both expressions found together, as they are read here, for a reason unknown to us and not worth investigating; the meaning, however, is the same as that explained by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius in his golden little commentary: “And you shall be a helper to the orphan deprived of human assistance.” The subject is God, whom the prophet entreats; Rudolph, however, as though this were divinely commanded to kings, and especially to the king of the Romans, clearly affirms that it was divinely commanded to him.]

Indeed, our beloved N., deprived of paternal consolation, cannot defend or assist himself, not only because of his orphaned condition but also because of the tender age of childhood, since he is not yet five years old. Therefore we receive him into our protection, asserting all his movable and immovable goods under the shield of our defense, aid, and protection. Accordingly, we command all the faithful of the Roman Empire, under pain of our displeasure, that no one dare invade the said child or his goods, or disturb them in any way. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he will be punished in such a manner that his penalty will serve as a terror to the rest.

## 482. LETTER XLII. Rudolph reproaches a certain person.

*(A.D. 1277, codex Rudolph XLII.)*

[Col. 0837B]

### Argument

After receiving a letter from N.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] Unless my judgment deceives me, these letters were written to Ottokar, king of Bohemia; for their tenor seems to single out that one man, and the concise narrative in the chronicles and histories of the eighteen months that elapsed between Ottokar’s oath of fidelity and his open rebellion persuades us, his posterity, of the same.]

who excuses himself for his treachery, directs insults against Rudolph, and removes the charge of rebellion from himself under the empty pretext of suspicion, Rudolph replies that he patiently endures from him these injuries, though he has previously suffered more serious insults at his hands; but since his embassy accomplished nothing, he has decided that he must deal with him in another way.

If your letter had proceeded from the well of an upright heart, concerning the hateful affair of treachery you would not have accused innocent hands, nor killed a faithful heart with the barb of piercing suspicion.

[Note: Ottokar, by nature violent, was unable to digest the cession of the provinces made to Rudolph on 19 November together with the oath of fidelity sworn before so many princes assembled in a tent. Historians, including Dubravius, unanimously report that he was received most indignantly and treated very badly by his wife, Queen Kunigunde. It is therefore easy to believe that he immediately broke the peace agreements and openly declared that the provinces had been taken from him by fraud, and that he began entering into alliances and assembling a new army.

Stero and the Annalist of Altach connect this with the final conflict: “At last, they say, after the aforesaid judgment had been broken for three or two years, the aforesaid king of Bohemia assembled a powerful army from his lands—namely Bohemia and Moravia—and also from other lands, namely Poland, Pomerania, Saxony, and Meissen, and encamped on the river March in a field called Marchfeld, near Cistesdarff.”

Rudolph attempted through messengers or legates to destroy these schemes from their very beginning; but in vain. From his rival and rebel came those bitter letters to which Rudolph replies. Nor should you think that these were letters of defiance, which at that time were also customarily sent to the sultan, as Ducange notes (Glossary, under “Defy”). For the Austrian Chronicle teaches that in 1278 he entered Austria “although—what is unspeakable—he had never sent letters of defiance beforehand to the king of the Romans.” In those letters, while excusing himself for the crime of rebellion, he accused Rudolph of fraud; but he did not declare war against him.]

But since it frequently happens—although I do not think this applies to you—that one suspects another of what he feels in himself, I protect myself against the assaults of such a hostile charge with the shield of patience, girded and fortified with the armor of self-control. In truth, I did not expect to suffer this from a rival, nor did I anticipate such outrageous insults from an enemy, especially since, if you recall, I had previously endured much more serious injuries from you.

[Note: Here recall the extremely bold speech of Bernard, bishop of Seckau, who acted as his legate at the Diet of Augsburg on 24 June 1275, together with the disgraceful pamphlets in which the king of the Romans was slandered, and the other deeds and words of the Bohemian against him. Marvel that an invincible and fortunate prince should dwell at length upon reproaches.]

But in order that the integrity of my blameless innocence may become publicly evident, I entrusted N. with the task of satisfying you on my behalf. Since this has not achieved the desired result, I have instructed you to proceed otherwise.

[Note: Rudolph evidently judged that the anger of his rival’s spirit could be restrained by some negotiation before recourse was had to the final remedy of arms, which subsequently proved necessary.]

## 483. LETTER XLIII. Rudolph writes against those who unjustly exact tolls.

*(A.D. 1280, codex Rudolph XLIII.)*

[Col. 0838B]

### Argument

He orders toll collectors and tax gatherers who unjustly demand tolls from travelers and oppress them with unlawful exactions to desist from their illicit practices, lest the peace established everywhere be disturbed.

The land rises against you with cries, and the groans of the poor have entered the ears of the royal highness. Although general peace has been established, you presume, according to your own will, to extort tolls from passers-by, resisting its observance with the heel of rebellion, and you do not cease to burden them with unlawful exactions.

[Note: I understand this letter to have been written when affairs were already peaceful, and therefore I date it after the year 1279. Whether it was addressed to a province or to a city I leave to others to determine; the rest is self-evident.]

Therefore we earnestly request and exhort your prudence, while nevertheless commanding you by royal authority, to restrain your hands from such unlawful conduct and turn them toward what is lawful. Otherwise, know this for certain: in order that the beauty of this peace may flourish again in its former splendor, we shall sharpen all our strength, care, and resolve.

## 484. LETTER XLIV. Rudolph commends a certain person for an ecclesiastical benefice.

*(A.D. 1280, codex Rudolph XLIV.)*

### Argument

He thanks a bishop—perhaps the bishop of Liège—for the prebend of N., his notary, or rather a prebend promised to Rudolph himself; he declares that the matter will be most pleasing to him, by which the donor may earn royal patronage for himself and his church if he fulfills his voluntary promise. He also assents that, once N. has obtained the prebend, he may either serve the church commendably by residing there or, at the donor’s command, remain in the royal court and conduct the affairs of the donor and his church.

[Note: [Col. 0839C] It is uncertain to whom this letter is written; certainly, however, to a bishop. Although Rudolph is accustomed to show reverence to the fatherhood of bishops, and therefore almost always uses “your” rather than “thy,” he nevertheless addresses the bishop of Trent, as we saw above (Letter 28), and an unknown archbishop (Letter 39) with the same form of address as this likewise unknown recipient. Was it then written to the bishop of Liège? For he recommends to the chapter of that church a canon (Letter 22) who proceeds from the royal court to take possession of his canonry, intending, in accordance with Rudolph’s wish, to return to it.]

Greatly pleased by the free offering of your devotion, because you have reverenced us and the Roman Empire with the steadfastness of pure faith, and have so commendably given the provident man N., our beloved notary—or rather, given us—in your church the hope of your provision, we rise to thank you all the more abundantly, the more we perceive that by this you are being stirred to cultivate our dominion more extensively and perfectly, and the more eagerly we desire the advancement of him whose fruitful services have rightly pleased us.

[Note: This passage agrees closely with the preceding letter, although in that letter he does not call his familiar by the title of notary, which would have removed all doubt.]

And certainly, by promoting him, you will offer our serenity a service so welcome and pleasing that we have resolved to be continually present to you and to your church in every circumstance and to support your favorable wishes. Therefore, so that you may fulfill with a mind more ready for action and pursue with more suitable goodwill the praiseworthy intention you have conceived concerning your promises, we willingly assent to your sincerity: when the said N., by the favor of divine clemency, has obtained the prebend, he may produce the desired fruit of residence in the garden of the aforesaid church like a fruitful plant, unless it should perhaps happen that, at your command, he might more usefully be occupied in our court in conducting your affairs and those of your church.

## 485. LETTER XLV. Rudolph writes concerning the rebellion of a certain person.

*(A.D. 1276, codex Rudolph XLV.)*

### Argument

He writes, apparently to Meinhard, count of Tyrol, concerning an old disagreement between him and the bishop of Trent. Rudolph says that he appointed an interpreter of peace to settle it amicably; but afterward he changed his mind when he learned that the disagreement was growing stronger. He asks him to disclose the state of the dispute and his own counsel, so that an appropriate remedy may be applied.

When N. departed from our presence, we believed that we had arranged matters between you and him in such a way that it could scarcely ever have entered our mind that he would in any way raise the heel of rebellion against you.

[Note: That Henry, bishop of Trent, was at Lausanne with Rudolph in 1275, on 20 October and the following day, is proved by his subscriptions to two royal diplomas in the appendix to the work on the supreme dominion of the Apostolic See at Comacchio. These, together with others presented by Gentilotto, are praised by Coletti (Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 608). Therefore Rudolph’s conversation concerning the settlement of this old disagreement seems to fit no one better than this bishop.]

But once we heard—indeed, with increasing amazement and even astonishment—that the matter had turned in the opposite direction, we could not fail to be disturbed by the unexpected disagreement and disturbance that had arisen. We conceived the intention of immediately sending N. to those parts, so that, repairing the damage caused by the rupture, he might bind you and that same N. inseparably in a friendly alliance.

But an adverse rumor reached our ears, by which the sending of the said N. was delayed. Therefore we are sending back to you the bearer of this letter, asking you with the greatest affection of which we are capable to announce to us immediately the state and circumstances of the matter, and to disclose your counsel, so that we may be able to lull completely to rest, by a suitable remedy, the foolishness of the resentment that has been aroused.

[Note: We have mentioned in Letter 28 what seems capable of being referred here. See the note there, letter g. To these may be added what is read in the records of the agreement of 1276, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the same Ughelli (ibid., p. 610), where Henry and Meinhard “submitted themselves to the venerable men Rudolph, imperial chancellor of the court, and Lord Henry, illustrious count of Württemberg, jointly chosen as arbiters, arbitrators, and amicable mediators, etc.” With the king of the Romans himself joining them, peace finally seemed to have been established.]

## 486. LETTER XLVI. Rudolph commends a learned man.

*(A.D. 1283, codex Rudolph XLVI.)*

### Argument

Wishing to honor his courtier, distinguished in learning and morals, according to his merits, and therefore concerned about his promotion to an episcopal see, Rudolph, because he is prevented by numerous affairs from acting personally, calls N. to share in his concern and entrusts the entire matter to him.

The customary benevolence of royal munificence distinguishes the merits of persons with such provident judgment that, as a mark of more abundant favor, it raises up and honors with richer benefits those who shine with the more splendid brilliance of learning, morals, and conduct.

[Note: I cannot refrain from inserting here a passage from the author of *Piety of Austria* (book I, chapter 4, p. 32), for the perpetual memory of the most august house of Austria:

“Although occupied with military affairs before Basel, he rewarded with a golden chain, which he wore hanging from his neck, together with an accompanying sum of money, a citizen of Strasbourg and historian who had dedicated to him a book describing the wars of the Germans with the Romans and the qualities of the commander of the war. When, on this account, he was reproached by Frederick Zoller, burgrave of Nuremberg and his nephew on his sister’s side, because he had not rather spent it on rewarding soldiers, he replied: ‘Allow learned men also to praise our deeds, and through them to be made more eager for wars. Would that I had more time for reading, and could transfer to learned men the expenses that I so often spend on useless soldiers!’”

In this matter Rudolph found imitators in all those descended from his most august house of Austria, and especially in the emperors down to our own age. It is well known that, through an innate benevolence, they were the greatest lovers of learning and of learned men; among them was Maximilian, who not only accomplished great deeds but also, in imitation of the first Roman emperor, Julius Caesar, composed commentaries on his own deeds. This, of course, was the spirit of the Augusti of former ages, whom other princes today imitate. A law of Valentinian the Elder is celebrated (Cod. Theod., book XIV, title IX, law 1; vol. V, p. 220) concerning the liberal studies of the city of Rome, distributed into twelve chapters; the last of these is pertinent: “Let similar briefs likewise be sent every year to the offices of Our Clemency, so that, once the merits and instruction of each person have been learned, we may judge whether they may at some time be necessary to us.” Learned men, therefore, are necessary to princes, if not always, at least sometimes.]

Indeed, although the prudent and honorable man N., walking agreeably and harmoniously in the royal household, has exercised—and continues unceasingly to exercise—such outstanding works of integrity around us and our affairs, spreading among us the treasure of his expertise, that we ought to raise him up by the beneficence of special favor and exalt him with appropriate honors,

[Note: I would be lying if Godefrid, provost of Solingen and Rudolph’s protonotary, were not the person whom Rudolph himself commends here for the vacant see of Passau and whom the preceding dissertation repeatedly recommends. The authors Hansiz (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 426) relate very similar things about him. Bruschius, above all, writes: “A man distinguished in learning and prudence presided, piously and faithfully, as befits a bishop. Through the recommendation of King Rudolph, so that he might receive a just reward for his loyalty and for the labors he had endured for the kingdom and the king, he was elected in 1283 by the unanimous vote of the senate of the canons of Passau.”]

yet, because the frequent and burdensome accumulation of affairs requiring action, which usually swirls around us, does not allow us to think about his promotion, we entrust the matter to your discretion, in accordance with the desires of our mind, when the suitability of time makes this possible,

[Note: The vacancy of the see of Passau seems to be indicated; it was vacant through the death of Wicard on Christmas Day in the year 1282.]

having confidence in your prudence that through you the deficiency of negligence already committed may be remedied.

[Note: Rudolph had left Austria the preceding year and had gone to the Rhine. It would therefore not be improbable that this matter was entrusted to Albert, duke of Austria, his son, although no indication of this appears in the letter; and it is consequently less safe to affirm anything certain.]

## LETTER XLVII. Rudolph approves certain chapters enacted against heresies by the Emperor Frederick.

[Note: I have nowhere been able to discover the date of this diploma. The author of *Piety of Austria*, who examined the imperial codex and must certainly have remembered it, since it is closely connected with the subject of his work, places it near the death of Gregory X (book I, chapter 7, p. 50). In my view, however, it must be removed from that date. I assigned it to the year 1280 because of another class of affairs: it is established and known that Rudolph was concerned with such matters before that year, and the circumstances of the age of Nicholas III also contributed to this judgment.

At the command of that pontiff, through his legate, King Ladislaus of Hungary “ordered all the constitutions and ecclesiastical statutes made against heretics to be observed in his kingdom by all his officials, binding himself and his successors to them,” as Raynaldus published from the papers of Baronius (1280, no. 9). As he says in the constitution itself, appended by Baronius from the Vatican manuscripts and others: “We decree that such statutes, constitutions, laws, rights, and decrees shall be inviolably observed forever in the kingdom and in all lands subject to us, by us and our successors, as well as by the dukes, counts, barons, nobles, judges, officials, and all the peoples of our kingdom and of the land subject to our jurisdiction.” Queen Elisabeth, his mother, also enacted a special sanction to the same effect for her duchies.

The statements read below in this diploma of Rudolph are not unlike these. Therefore Rudolph may have issued the diploma either moved by the instruction of Nicholas or by the example of Ladislaus; it does not seem to have been issued before this year.]

*(A.D. 1280, codex Rudolph XLVII.)*

[Col. 0841B]

### Argument

By royal authority he confirms the constitution against heresies issued by Frederick II on the day of his coronation, at the urging and with the approval of Honorius III, supreme pontiff; and he binds himself and all established within the Roman Empire to observe it.

Rudolph, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever Augustus, sends greetings to all the faithful of Christ who shall inspect the present page, together with knowledge of what is written below.

[Note: Unless the exhortation or command of the pontiff had preceded it, Rudolph would not have been Rudolph if he had crossed beyond the boundaries of the Empire before receiving the imperial diadem. Perhaps, however, he confined himself below those limits, for he entrusts the observance of his constitution to the Empire alone. Therefore “all the faithful of Christ” should be understood as those of the Empire, not of the whole world.]

Because we continually pursue with detestation the pestilential subtleties of heretical cunning, hateful to God and odious to men, which stain the sheep of the Lord’s flock with their contagion, as things carrying the gall of bitterness, and because we desire for this reason to extend fully the power of the sword divinely entrusted to us for their complete eradication,

[Note: Both codices testify that the ancient Eastern Augusti, together with the Roman pontiffs, asserted the purity of the Catholic faith through their constitutions. Although matters of this kind belong to the Roman pontiff and to councils, unless the external arm of the Church is added—the power of the prince, who by temporal penalties attached to his supreme authority eliminates these depraved practices—the most sacred laws of the pontiff and councils grow cold.

For this reason Rudolph promised Gregory X at the conference of Lausanne that he would devote every effort to eradicate this plague, confirming the promise by a royal edict for perpetual memory: “For the eradication of the error of heretical depravity, we shall give assistance and effective effort.” That document is preserved with the others in the archive of the Hadrianic fortress and was published by Raynaldus (1275, no. 38). Its date is clearly marked at the end: “1275, indiction 4, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.” But the premature death of Gregory and the brief pontificates of his three successors postponed the royal pledges until the time of Nicholas III.

Nor should you think that any letters of Nicholas III or of his successors Martin IV, Honorius IV, and Nicholas IV survive as witnesses to this action. Rather, Rudolph, as I believe, remembering his promise at Lausanne and understanding that a woman too was rising against heretical depravity, renewed the constitution of his predecessor Frederick.]

certain chapters of the constitutions issued by the lord Frederick, formerly emperor of the Romans and our predecessor, against heretics,

[Note: These too, as I said in the preceding note, must be understood as applying to the Christians of the whole Empire.
