Nevertheless, that formula—“entire, not canceled, etc.”—should not be considered without considerable astonishment, since it is complete rather than canceled. It does not accord with Rudolph’s practice.]

which we saw marked with his seal, entire, not canceled, not abolished, and not damaged in any part, we have deemed it appropriate to record here, and we decree that they be faithfully observed by all who are counted as professing Christianity. The tenor of these constitutions is as follows:

“They begin,” etc.

[Note: At the end of the *Authentic* there is a constitution of Frederick II entitled “The Constitutions of the Emperor Frederick II begin.” There are several constitutions, all ecclesiastical, though not all against heresy. Their beginning and end should be noted. Frederick begins as follows:

“On the day on which we received the diadem of the Empire from the hand of our most sacred father, the supreme pontiff, we took care, for the honor of God and of his Church, to issue certain laws, which we have ordered to be recorded on the present page and published throughout our entire Empire. Through our imperial writings we command you, ordering that each of you preserve these letters inviolably and steadfastly in his district; and these are the laws.”

The force of these imperial constitutions lies in their concluding section, which runs as follows:

“We, Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, praise, approve, and confirm these laws issued by Frederick, emperor of the Romans and our most beloved son, for the benefit of all Christians, as laws destined to endure forever. If anyone, with reckless daring and at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, should attempt in any way to violate them, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.”

From this it is clear that Frederick, although crowned with the imperial crown, did not pass beyond the limits of the Roman Empire, within which Rome itself was included, whose supreme lord was the Roman pontiff. For through the coronation that same supreme pontifical power had been communicated to him, as we demonstrated at length above. There were powerful and extensive kingdoms—those of Gaul, Spain, England, Hungary, Poland, and others—as well as principalities, to which imperial jurisdiction did not extend at all.

But from the authority of the Roman pontiff—which, bounded by no limits, extends wherever the name of Christ or the Church of God is spread, by the immutable ordinance of our Savior, the King of kings—great force is added to Frederick’s constitution. For not merely the Christians “throughout our entire Empire,” but all who are counted by the Christian name throughout the whole world, as far as the earth extends, are declared bound by that imperial constitution.

There are also other constitutions of Frederick himself against heresies, enacted at the assembly of Passau in the year 1224, on 22 February, as the learned Mansi observes in his notes on Raynaldus (1225, no. 47), citing these words from the *Abbreviated Annals*:

“Honorius also moved Frederick, emperor, who was then holding the solemn assembly of the Italian princes at Passau, to enact most sacred laws for cutting out heretical impiety; these were afterward confirmed by Innocent IV.”

It is uncertain which of these Rudolph confirms by this diploma. It is entirely clear, however, that he regards as valid those constitutions resting upon pontifical authority, and thus does nothing other than carry out what he had promised Gregory X by royal edict, as stated above (Col. 842, note f).]

Therefore we, who, principally for the protection of the Catholic faith, as the Most High bears witness, have assumed the honor and burden of royal dignity, solemnly approve all and each of the foregoing provisions, piously and prudently established for the eradication of such a wicked sect and the strengthening of the Christian faith, and by the testimony of the present document bind ourselves to their observance, likewise wishing and commanding that these same provisions be firmly and inviolably observed by all to whom the territories of the Roman Empire extend.

[Note: When he says that he has assumed the honor of royal dignity and binds the Roman Empire to observe his constitution, he is acting as his own interpreter, as I observed above (Col. 842, notes e and g). Whatever the source of the error, it must be corrected completely, and the reading should be “the territories of the Roman Empire.” For “the dominion of Roman territory” designates only pontifical authority; that Rudolph’s constitution should extend to that territory is not even to be considered, since, apart from the fact that the king of the Romans had no jurisdiction there, it would contradict the text.]

In witness whereof, etc.

[Col. 0843]

# 491. DISSERTATION ON THE DIPLOMA OF RUDOLPH, KING OF THE ROMANS, CONFIRMED BY THE ELECTORS OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE

## § I. All the rights of the Holy See are confirmed.

[Col. 0843C]

I have demonstrated through the diplomas of the distinguished princes that the territory of the Roman Church, originally confined within very narrow limits, was afterward enlarged by the greatest additions through the Frankish kings Pepin and Charles, surnamed the Great, son of Pepin, and finally through the Augusti Otto I and Saint Henry, to which the Matildine inheritance, or donation, was added.

Although no diploma of Pepin survives by which the Holy See is said to have received the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, and no diploma of Charles by which it is said to have received Tuscany and other provinces and cities, there does survive a diploma of Louis the Pious, concerning which I have made it clear that nothing more exact could be desired. In it, Rome and its duchy are distinguished from the gifts of the kings of the Franks, and, besides the donations of Pepin and Charles, all the ancient patrimonies of the Holy See and all its privileges are enumerated.

Later, the successors Otto and Henry, each wholly confirming these things by his own diploma and adding new rights, issued an example for all future emperors to follow. Would that they had followed it! Most of them, however, especially the Augusti of the Swabian line, enticed by the very bad example of Henry IV, preferred to restrict the dominion of the Apostolic See by taking away provinces and cities rather than to enlarge it through new gifts.

For this reason, in their diplomas—documents absolutely necessary for receiving the imperial insignia through the hand of the pontiff—the following unusual formula began to be heard:

“We also leave free and undisturbed for the Roman Church the possessions which the Church has recovered from our predecessors or from any others who previously held them, and we faithfully promise to assist it in retaining them. Those which it has not yet recovered, we shall assist it with all our strength to recover; and whatever comes into our hands, we shall strive to restore to it without difficulty.”

Thus it is read in the oath of Otto IV in Baluze (*Register of Innocent III*, vol. I, p. 763).

Although the invasions had begun long before the year 1209, when Otto IV was crowned, the formula began to be framed in these words only later. Not long afterward, another innovation was also found: namely, that an imperial diploma should be confirmed by the princes of the Empire. This is known to have been done under Pope Honorius in the year 1220, at the assemblies of Frankfurt (Raynaldus, 1275, no. 41).

For the promises that Frederick II had made to Innocent III concerning the kingdom of Sicily—“so that the Empire should have no union or jurisdiction whatsoever with that kingdom”—those princes confirmed by affixing their seals, for greater validity.

## II

In Rudolf’s diploma I must also note another novelty: namely, the confirmation of all the rights and privileges of the Holy See, made by the King of the Romans with royal authority, and to be confirmed within eight days after he had received the imperial diadem. This royal diploma was subsequently solemnly strengthened by the seven electoral princes, at the insistence of Nicholas III, just as Honorius III had wished this to be done by the princes of the Empire. For at that time supreme authority—the election of the King of the Romans—had not yet been reduced to that seven-member college, whose authority thereafter began to be regarded as equal to that of all the princes.

All these features, which make Rudolf’s diploma different from those of his predecessors, were the reason why I judged that this document too, although already published more than once, ought again to be committed to print. In addition, this pious and great ancestor of the august House of Austria brought the emperors’ invasions to an end by his diploma. For although Louis the Bavarian restored the ancient injuries inflicted upon the Holy See, the peoples of Italy—and among them especially the boldest writers, as well as the Italian flatterers who deserve equal condemnation—appear to have acted no less culpably than the prince himself. The history of those times, partly set out above, makes this clear.

Besides, Rudolf himself bears witness (Book II, Letter 37) that several pontiffs, the Sacred College, and all those whose interests were involved never ceased demanding that the ecclesiastical territory, overthrown by the preceding emperors, be restored:

> “What the Holy Mother Church is known to have hitherto requested from us, both through envoys and through special letters.”

And since, in his royal diploma, in accordance with the requests of Nicholas III, every individual provision of the diplomas of Louis, Otto, and Henry is wholly confirmed, without omitting the donation of Matilda, nothing more suitable can be offered as the crown of this necessary work than the diploma itself, which was confirmed by the seven-member college of electors.

Its autograph does indeed exist in the Apostolic Archive at the Mole of Hadrian. It has been published three times with the utmost fidelity: first by Odorico Raynaldo (1279, no. 1), then by Lorenzo Zacagno, keeper of the Vatican Library (*Historical Dissertation on the Dominion of the Holy See*, appendix), and finally by the most eminent Antonello. Nevertheless, other reasons have arisen why this diploma, which may be called the complement of the others, should be added to the documents published by me.

## III

The chief of these reasons is the Italian annalists, whose works, repeatedly printed in the vernacular and also circulated in German, are widely available. In them, considerable material concerning several of Rudolf’s diplomas is published with excessive freedom. Since this openly conflicts with Rudolf’s own letters, I wish to prevent the summary of such annals from suffering any damage contrary to the privileges and rights of the Apostolic See.

An example is what they assert under the year 1278 concerning the solemn cession of the Exarchate allegedly made by Rudolf. Reduced to a summary, their account runs as follows:

> “Although the Exarchate had been confirmed by a diploma to the Holy See by whatever emperors received the imperial diadem, it nevertheless remained for many centuries in the power of the kings and emperors of Italy, while the Roman pontiffs maintained profound silence. After a prolonged dispute with Nicholas III, Rudolf at last relinquished the Exarchate from his hands with the greatest reluctance. There were also additional reasons for his relinquishment: the great war threatening him with Ottocar; fear that, by alienating so great a pontiff from himself, he might cause him to support Charles, King of Sicily, against the Empire; and finally the fact that he had violated his crusading vow, so that, following the example of Frederick II, he could become subject to ecclesiastical censures.”

On these matters the annalist does not hesitate to refer the reader to Raynaldo’s annals. He immediately adds, however, these few words from the author of the Parma chronicle:

> “The Roman pontiffs always seek to squeeze something out of the commonwealth when emperors are assumed to the Empire. It is not established whether Ferrara and Comacchio acknowledged the pontiff’s supreme lordship; Bologna acknowledged it under specified agreements and reservations; certain cities came voluntarily under the pontiff’s authority, while others refused.”

Thus he pronounces these statements, most suitable for imposing upon the reader, as though from behind a curtain, without examining the annalistic records to which he imprudently refers him.

Accordingly, Raynaldo’s annals must first be set against this attractive doctrine promulgated by the Italian annalist; then we must turn to Rudolf’s case. It will be clearly and certainly established that the invasion of the Exarchate did not last even for the space of a single century; that the predecessors of Nicholas III were not negligent when the matter concerned the recovery of the chief possession contained in the donations of the kings of France; that Rudolf, having been deceived by his own people, delayed the restitution for a time, but restored the rights of the Church by no means unwillingly; and that the remaining reasons, brought forward partly by conjecture and partly from writings unworthy of consideration, are trivial and unworthy of a historian in our distinguished age.

## IV

Indeed, so that no doubt may be entertained concerning the supreme right of the Roman pontiff in the Exarchate during the time of Innocent III, near the end of the twelfth century, two very powerful arguments are available from the acts of Innocent himself (nos. 12 and 27).

First, the archbishop of Ravenna, adhering to the ancient papal privileges, both retained the Exarchate and obtained permission “to recover Brittonorium and hold it, without prejudice to the right of the Apostolic See.”

Next, Henry VI, who had conferred certain territories of the Church upon his seneschal Marquard, ordered in his testament, when near death:

> “That he receive from the lord pope and the Roman Church the duchy of Ravenna, the land of Brittonorium, and the March of Ancona, and that he also acknowledge from them Medicina and Argellata with their appurtenances. Let him swear security to him concerning all these possessions, and render him fidelity, as to his lord.”

If, then, the archbishop of Ravenna—whose predecessors, from the very time of Charlemagne, had dared to claim domination in the Exarchate by the favor and protection of the prince—and Henry, the emperor of the Swabian line and consequently the greatest invader of the Church’s territories, at the end of the twelfth century acknowledged the supreme right of the Roman pontiff, while that great pontiff Innocent vigorously vindicated the rights of the Holy See, it follows that the kings and emperors of Italy had not retained the Exarchate for several centuries while the pontiffs remained silent. Rather, the invasion lasted at most eighty years, from Innocent III to Nicholas III, under the two last emperors, Otto IV and Frederick II of the Swabian house. It persisted amid the great confusion of the Empire that German writers call the fatal interregnum; and Rudolf, deceived by it, accepted Romandiola as one of the territories of the Empire.

Indeed, it will soon become clear that the pontiffs had not remained silent even during those eighty years. Meanwhile, it should be observed that the predecessors of Nicholas III, content with the emperors’ oath, had in no way considered undertaking a new possession of the rights of the Holy See. Nicholas himself, however, entered into possession of the Exarchate by a method quite different from that of Stephen II.

Stephen received possession when Fulrad, the legate of King Pepin, laid down the keys of the individual cities upon the body of Saint Peter. Nicholas, on the other hand, obtained possession when King Rudolf annulled the oaths of fidelity which his chancellor Rudolf had unlawfully exacted from the cities of the Exarchate. This is clear from the documents in Raynaldo (1278, nos. 53 ff.):

> “And thus the said pope obtains possession.”

## V

There is nothing surprising, then—subject to the Italian annalist’s pardon—in Rudolf’s having imitated his predecessors by confirming the Exarchate and the Pentapolis through his legates and in person, while nevertheless retaining the Exarchate.

For during the time of the Swabian invasion the Exarchate had come to be called Romandiola. Moreover, the Exarchate, as a new territory within Romandiola, and the county of Romandiola are found distinguished in the older writers. Thus Ptolemy of Lucca (*Sacred Italy*, vol. XI, p. 1166) says of Rudolf:

> “At that time he also restored to the Church the county of Romandiola together with the Exarchate of Ravenna.” [Col. 0847A]

And Jordan, in Raynaldo (1278, no. 54), says of Nicholas III:

> “In the second year of his pontificate, Nicholas III demanded from Rudolf, King of Germany, the resignation of the Exarchate of Ravenna, which was a principality over six cities of Romandiola, distinguished from the county.”

We have seen that this aforesaid new principality was called a duchy in the age of Innocent III, in the testament of Henry VI. We have likewise seen that Rudolf designated the Exarchate by the names Romandiola and Maritime [territory] (Book I, Letter 24 ff.).

You will find more on this reversal of places and things in Ughelli. For my part, it is enough to have placed before the reader the difficult business of that age: the recovery from alien hands of the most ancient of all the apostolic donations of the Holy See.

Nicholas III understood this. Therefore he did not send Rudolf records of the pontiffs and kings that mentioned those new territories, but the diplomas of Louis, Otto, and Henry, in which the individual cities of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis are listed. In addition, following the example of his predecessors, he prescribed that all the places belonging to the ecclesiastical territory be clearly and distinctly enumerated in the royal diploma, which afterward had to be ratified by imperial authority.

As for whether Rudolf relinquished the Exarchate reluctantly and for the reasons supplied by the annalist, history—drawn from reliable documents in Raynaldo and reduced there to a summary—will show this, so that I do not weary the reader by repeating what has already been said.

## VI

At the council of Lyons in 1274, Rudolf’s chancellor, the provost of Speyer, confirmed all the diplomas of the preceding emperors to Gregory X. At Lausanne in the following year, Rudolf himself did the same.

In the Lausanne diploma, in Raynaldo (1275, nos. 36 ff.), dated 20 October, or the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, the following territories are listed:

> “The whole land extending from Radicofani to Ceprano, the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, the March of Ancona, the Duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, and the county of Brittonorium with the adjacent lands, expressly mentioned in many imperial privileges from the time of Louis.”

In the same diploma it is stated:

> “After we have come to Rome to receive the anointing, coronation, and imperial diadem, and have received these, we shall renew all the aforesaid things, individually and collectively, or enact them anew, and without any difficulty shall render the oaths that the Roman emperors have hitherto rendered.”

This was more than sufficient for the writers of that age to assert that Romandiola had been restored to the Holy See, as Bernard the treasurer did in his chronicle, in the same Raynaldo:

> “He came from Vienne to Lausanne, where the said King Rudolf, arriving with his wife the queen and with his sons and daughters, made an oath to the same pope and restored Romandiola, together with the Exarchate of Ravenna, to the Roman Church.”

On the same occasion Gregory, who—as the same Bernard attests—“intended to visit the Holy Land with the emperor, the King of France, and other princes, and there end his life,” and from there had been summoned to the pontificate, gave the cross to Rudolf, to the queen, and to the other nobles.

Consequently, great preparations were being made everywhere, and without doubt that expedition would have been undertaken after the imperial coronation, which was to take place in the following year. But divine counsels were otherwise. At the beginning of 1276, Gregory, returning to Rome, died at Arezzo, and no further serious thought was given to that expedition.

The imperial coronation, which had to precede it, was likewise necessarily postponed for various reasons. I find that the chief reason was not the considerable war then taking place in Austria with Ottocar, King of Bohemia, but rather the hostilities with Charles, King of Sicily, concerning which I have spoken above (*Dissertation* no. 50 ff.); here I shall add, more suitably, what bears upon the matter.

## VII

When, in 1265, Clement IV had granted Charles of Anjou the kingdom of Sicily and the entire land on this side of the Strait to be held by fiduciary right, and had thereby removed the Holy See’s perpetual anxiety concerning that kingdom, he created this new king of Sicily senator for ten years, on 16 September 1268, in order to suppress the internal disturbances of the City.

The previous year he had also entrusted Charles with the task of pacifying Etruria, which was afflicted by Ghibelline and Guelph factions, adorning him with the title of general paciarius. This is clear from the apostolic letter to the Florentines, the chief of the Guelphs:

> “We have decided to appoint the same king, who would immediately follow his army, as general paciarius in your regions until it should please us, so that, while the Empire is vacant—whose protection belongs to him—the neighboring region of our patrimony might not be torn apart by the wickedness of evil men.”

See more in Raynaldo (1267, no. 5 ff.).

Although Charles had promised under oath that he would resign that dignity as soon as the King of the Romans had been elected and confirmed by the Apostolic See, nevertheless, once Rudolf had been elected and confirmed, he did not relinquish Etruria. Hence arose hostilities between him and Rudolf, who demanded the province as belonging to the jurisdiction of the Empire.

Gregory X tried in vain to settle them (same source, 1274, no. 60). Innocent V, Adrian V, and John XXI likewise attempted the same thing unsuccessfully in 1276, the year of Gregory’s death, memorable for the funerals of three pontiffs.

During the vacancy of the Holy See, the cardinals set out the sequence of events to Rudolf through their envoy in a very long letter (same source, 1277, nos. 48 ff.). Following the example of those pontiffs, they begged him not to come into Italy with soldiers until he had settled his disputes with Charles.

Finally, scarcely had Nicholas III been elected when he addressed the King of the Romans in courteous letters, in which he enumerated all the foregoing matters individually (same source, ibid., nos. 54 ff.), and likewise warned him not to descend into Italy before reaching an agreement with Charles.

The letter was issued on 11 December. Only thirty-eight days later, the reply of the excellent prince (Rudolf’s *Code*, Book II, Letter 37) was brought by Brother Conrad of the Order of Friars Minor, the envoy and procurator of that prince, who had given him full authority to carry out everything contained in the letters of Nicholas, his predecessors, and the cardinals.

## VIII

Those letters contained two matters of great importance: first, the disputes just mentioned; second, the true and actual restoration of the Exarchate and the Pentapolis:

> “But concerning the lands of that same Church, and especially the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, so often urged upon Your Royal Excellence, we ask and request that they be fulfilled without further delay, with prompt readiness for effective execution.”

Accordingly, in Rudolf’s diploma, issued at Vienna in 1278 on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, the following appears among other provisions:

> “Furthermore, we grant and agree that the Roman Church, by itself and through others, may receive, acquire, enter upon, and seize, without any demand, authority, or mandate from us or anyone else, possession and quasi-possession of all the things contained in the aforesaid privileges.”

These were the privileges granted at Lyons in 1274 by Otto, provost of Speyer, in the council, and at Lausanne in 1275, on 20 October, by Rudolf himself.

Since the premature death of Gregory X, the very brief pontificates of three successors, and the prolonged vacancy of the Holy See lasting six months had deprived the Holy See’s petition of its effect for the space of two years and three months, Rudolf was not a man who would allow the Holy See to be evaded any longer.

Therefore, Brother Conrad, in the council on 4 May of the aforesaid year, declared that, “in order to soothe the conscience of my lord the king, and so that all the aforesaid matters might be fully secured, established, strengthened, completed, and brought to perfection,” he revoked whatever the king himself or his officials had done contrary to the aforesaid diplomas, and declared it null, so that:

> “By this no right shall accrue to my said lord the king, nor shall anything belonging to the Roman Church be diminished, either with regard to possession or with regard to ownership.”

For the rest, see Raynaldo (1278, nos. 47 ff.).

While these matters were being conducted at Rome, the chancellor of the King of the Romans—who was himself also called Rudolf and had come into Italy to recover the rights of the Empire—had been deceived by the same persuasion that had misled the King of the Romans and had demanded oaths of fidelity from the cities of the Exarchate in the king’s name.

When the king was informed of this, he not only took it very badly but also declared in royal letters that the chancellor had acted without his knowledge and against his command. His very words deserve to be heard, since they are exceedingly clear and of the highest authority.

## IX

These letters were issued at Vienna on the fourth day before the Kalends of June of the same year. In them Rudolf confirmed, individually and under oath, all the rights of the Holy See:

> “But because afterward, without our consent, knowledge, or mandate, our chancellor Rudolf is said to have received in our name an oath of fidelity from the citizens of Bologna, Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Cesena, Ravenna, Rimini, and Urbino, as well as from the citizens of other cities and places of those regions, we are sending to the presence of Your Holiness our beloved household cleric, Master Gotifred, provost of Soliensem, and protonotary of the royal court. By these present open letters we command him that whatever was done, performed, acknowledged, or otherwise undertaken by the same chancellor, or by anyone else, in the aforesaid cities, places, and lands, or by the inhabitants of those cities, lands, and places, and especially the aforesaid oaths, he shall revoke, cancel, annul, invalidate, and declare void, and render wholly ineffective; expressly willing and consenting that by this no right shall accrue to us, nor shall anything belonging to the Roman Church be diminished, either with regard to possession or with regard to ownership, in the cities, and so forth.”

Gotifred completely fulfilled the royal commands in a public instrument issued at Viterbo in the council during the following month, on the day before the Kalends of July. He also sent letters to each of the aforesaid cities, by which he released them from the oath sworn to the chancellor.

Accordingly, Cardinal Latino, Bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See sent into Emilia, took up the recovery of the rights of the Holy See in earnest, with the requested assistance of Charles, King of Sicily—for Guido da Montefeltro, the Geremei, and the Lambertazzi had thrown the province into disorder.

The zeal of Bologna toward the Holy See is praised above all others. I shall conclude this section with Raynaldo’s words, to whom the Italian annalist refers us, so that it may become clearer from where that annalist drew his material for the Italian annals.

First Raynaldo rejects Ricordano’s slander concerning Nicholas’s having neglected Syria in order to obtain Bologna (1278, no. 56); then he continues:

> “No less contrary to the truth are the reproaches which the innovators vomit forth on account of Bologna and all Flaminia having been recovered by the Church” (Century XIII, chapter 7, col. 726). “The truth of the history, however, is that Rudolf acted prudently and restored the rights of the Church to Nicholas, so that he might recover without war the rights of the Empire which Charles held in Etruria under the title of imperial legate.”

How truthfully Raynaldo makes this assertion is abundantly demonstrated by Rudolf’s letters quoted above.

## X

Indeed, four days before Rudolf ordered Gotifred to restore the Exarchate in reality, Nicholas commanded Charles to relinquish the senatorial dignity, although Charles retained that dignity, with the pope not objecting, until 16 September, in accordance with Clement IV’s privilege.

Moreover, in a manner that excludes every contrary opinion, Nicholas also deprived Charles of the vicariate of Etruria, in order to assert his own rights against Rudolf. Since this was done after the true restoration of the Exarchate, I prefer to commend Nicholas’s prudence, by which he wished the rights of the Holy See to take precedence over those of the Empire, rather than exaggerate the supposed hostility of Rudolf, who, as soon as he recognized that he had been deceived by the invasion of his predecessors, took the greatest care that the rights of the Holy See should be restored.

Since Rudolf’s royal diploma was confirmed by the princes of the Empire so that the rights of the Holy See might thereafter be safer from imperial invasions, and since it contains several new provisions from those same princes, and from those who were to be chosen from their number, especially the following:

> “We freely, fully, and anew grant, confer, and donate, so that, every cause of contention and disagreement having been removed, firm peace and complete concord may continue between the Church and the Empire,”

since, I say, it presents many new features, and since it is also a distinctive feature of this diploma that it rests solely upon royal authority, two matters must be noted.

First, at the end of the diploma we read:

> “Furthermore, we promise that after we have come to Rome to receive the anointing, coronation, and imperial diadem, and have received these, within eight days we shall renew all the aforesaid matters individually and shall fully and completely enact them anew.”

Therefore, although Rudolf never came to the City because various causes continually intervened, this royal diploma must be valued more highly than it would be if it were imperial.

Second, the condition of the City and of the entire papal territory at that time persuaded Pope Nicholas to take more careful measures for the rights of the Holy See than his predecessors had done. To make this evident, one must consider what Rome was like at that time and what was being done throughout the territory of the City and the whole ecclesiastical domain.

## XI

Among the other defections of the Roman people from their supreme ruler, the one most celebrated is that which occurred in the last year of Innocent II, namely 1143. For the minds of the laymen, infected with the heresy of Arnold of Brescia and claiming to restore the former glory of the Romans, established a senate for the civil administration of the City against papal authority.

In order to make this institution permanent, they began counting the years of the senate from its very origin, as the records show. Baronius cites one of these (1188, nos. 23 ff.) from the *Book of Censuses*: namely, the peace made by the senators with Clement III, “enacted in the forty-fourth year of the senate, indiction six, on the last day of May.”

Thirty senators had been established in the time of Innocent II. It may be inferred that the same number existed under Clement III because senators and the senatorial order frequently appear in the document by which they submitted themselves to the pope:

> “For the present, they say, we return to you the senate, the City, and the mint; nevertheless, we shall retain one-third of the mint, as is contained below. Likewise, we return the church of blessed Peter free, and so forth.”

They had done the same ten years earlier, when, believing themselves abandoned by Frederick Barbarossa and fearing that papal power might be joined with imperial power, they submitted themselves to the supreme ruler, Alexander III, as the Acts cited by Baronius attest (1178, no. 1 ff.):

> “By the counsel and deliberation of the entire Roman people it was decreed that the senators who are customarily created should render fidelity and homage to the lord pope, and that they should freely restore into the hands and power of that pontiff the church of blessed Peter and the regalian rights which they had seized.”

A certain Benedict, under Pope Celestine III, reduced those thirty to one, arrogating the senatorial dignity to himself and contending with Henry IV for the invasion of the Church’s rights. This is reported in the *Deeds of Innocent III* (no. 8), in Baluze:

> “The state of the Roman Church was in the worst condition because, from the time of Benedict Cariscum, it had lost the senate of the City; and that same Benedict, making himself senator, had taken away from it the Maritime and Sabine territories, appointing his own justiciars in them. The Emperor Henry, meanwhile, had occupied the whole kingdom of Sicily and the entire patrimony of the Church up to the gates of the City, except Campania alone, although even in Campania he was feared more than the pope.”

## XII

That same Innocent, the greatest vindicator of the ecclesiastical territory, repressed the audacity of the new senator. This is clear from the same *Deeds*:

> “Having excluded the senator’s justiciars, although the senator had sworn fidelity to him, he appointed his own justiciars; and, having elected another senator through his intermediary, both within and outside the City, he recovered the patrimony recently lost.”

Nevertheless, in order to accommodate the petitioning people, in 1208 he appointed fifty-six senators (*Deeds*, no. 141 ff.), while predicting that such a number would be created to the great detriment of the public:

> “The senators, as the lord pope had predicted, conducted themselves so badly in the administration of office that crimes were committed with impunity by anyone, both within and outside the City, while peace and justice were wholly banished. Therefore the people began to execrate them so greatly that the lord pope was obliged, at the common petition of the people, to grant them one senator.”

Whether there was one senator or several, that dignity was always a great impediment to the pontiffs’ exercising supreme authority in the City and its territory. Indeed, the factious Romans dared to advance one or another powerful prince to the rank of senator—while the Holy See and the pontiffs, during the vacancy of the Empire, were compelled to seek protection elsewhere. Such men were expected to govern the City according to their own discretion, or rather to follow the plans of the seditious citizens, instead of obeying the commands of the supreme ruler.

Such were Charles, Count of Provence and Anjou, designated perpetual senator in 1264, and Henry, brother of the King of Castile, who became senator in 1267.

When Urban IV had sought powerful aid for the endangered Church from Saint Louis, King of France, and had consequently offered him the kingdom of Sicily, the Count of Anjou, the holy king’s brother, was summoned at the king’s counsel to take possession of that kingdom. But the Romans, abusing the pope’s probity, designated that same Charles perpetual senator on their own authority.

This seemed unworthy to the pope and the cardinals: that an external prince should be entrusted with the City of Rome to the detriment of papal authority. Nevertheless, after deliberation, they did not reject the election in the midst of the greatest difficulties. Instead, after establishing certain conditions, they allowed Charles to enjoy that dignity for no more than five years, provided that he arranged for the power of creating the senator to return from the people to the pope, and that as soon as he obtained the kingdom of Sicily he should resign the dignity (Raynaldo 1264, nos. 4 ff.).

They communicated this to him in very courteous letters, for he had not yet come into Italy; he did so in the following year after overcoming Manfred’s ambushes.

Three years later, as disturbances increased in the City of Rome, the senatorial dignity was conferred by the factious upon Henry, a relative of the King of Sicily and afterward his rival, against the wishes of most of the people.

This was why Clement IV, wishing to assist the City as it struggled with continual seditions, designated Charles of Anjou himself senator for ten years in 1268, on 16 September, as stated above. Charles resigned that dignity under Pope Nicholas III in 1278, on the same day of the same month.

## XIII

Although the extremely bad condition of Rome and its territory had in some measure compelled Clement IV to yield to the audacity of the Romans, Nicholas III, so that his successors might never imitate that harmful example to supreme papal authority, issued the famous constitution *Fundamenta* (*De Electo, Electi potestate*, in Book VI), at Viterbo on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

In it he emphasizes the many injuries inflicted upon the Holy See by foreign senators, especially by Henry, brother of the King of Castile, who brought religion itself into danger and:

> “so stained the City itself, the mirror of faith, with such infamy that its most beloved daughter, compelled to depart from her mother, the Roman Church, once openly received and favored Conradin—who seemed to have sprung as a basilisk from the poisonous root of the former emperor of the Romans, Frederick, condemned by the just judgment of that Church, and who, together with his supporters, was manifestly aspiring to the extermination of the Roman mother Church—thereby making herself, as that Church’s daughter, the helper of so manifest an enemy of her mother Church, to the contempt of God, of her mother, and to the reproach of the City itself.”

He then decrees as follows:

> “With the counsel of our brothers, by this irrefragable constitution, valid in perpetuity, we enact that whenever and however often the election of a senator, or of another person by whatever name he may be called, who in any manner or under any title is to preside over the government of the City itself, shall hereafter arise, no emperor, or King of the Romans, or any other emperor or king, prince, marquis, duke, count, baron, or anyone possessing any other notable preeminence, power, authority, excellence, or dignity; nor any brother, son, or grandson of such persons, either temporarily or perpetually; nor any other person, for more than one year, under any manner, pretext, or cause, either personally or through another person to be appointed in any way, shall be nominated, elected, or otherwise appointed as senator, captain, patrician, or rector, or to the government or office of the same City, without the special permission of the Apostolic See, expressed in letters of that See specifically granting such permission.”

## XIV

I considered it a matter of conscience not to omit this portion of the constitution. It so clearly reveals both the supreme dominion of the pontiffs in the City and the authority that an emperor, prince, or other person could acquire there from that same supreme lord that it may be called a summary of everything I have discussed thus far.

Indeed, when the pontiff issued this constitution, the King of Sicily, Charles, conspicuous in the senatorial dignity, was presiding over the government of the City. Rudolf, King of the Romans, or elected emperor, was shortly to set out for Rome to receive the imperial insignia from the hand of the pontiff. Nevertheless, the pontiff enacted the foregoing provisions by virtue of his supreme authority over Rudolf and Charles.

Who, then, does not see that the words of Louis, Otto, and Henry, ratified by their successors down to Otto IV—

> “just as your predecessors have held and administered the Roman City with its duchy in your power and dominion until now”—

and also the other formula that began to be used from the time of Otto IV, “the whole land extending from Radicofani to Ceprano,” do not indicate that the dominion of the City and its duchy was granted to the pontiff by the emperors, but rather reflect the wise policy of Paschal I and his successors, so that the chief of the Church’s rights, like all the others, might rest upon imperial authority?

For how else could they have restrained the Romans, who were more inclined than other peoples to revolt? It is now clear that the sacrilegious crime committed by them against Saint Leo III was the reason why Rome and its duchy began to be confirmed in the emperors’ diplomas together with the other rights of the Holy See. It has also been abundantly demonstrated that the emperors themselves attempted, at their own peril, to restrain the audacity of the Romans.

Rudolf knew this well. Some people place in his mouth the words I quoted above (*Dissertation on Rudolf’s Letters*, Book III, no. 46), namely:

> “Many kings of the Germans have been consumed by Italy.”

I would not dare deny that he sometimes uttered these words, even though he desired a Roman coronation to his last breath.

## XV

It is scarcely credible that he overlooked the examples of his ancestors. If he knew the bloody wars fought by his predecessors in Italy, he must have understood the character of the Romans all the more clearly; the coronations so often celebrated in the City bear witness to it.

I pass over the Carolingian period, since Rudolf has no concern with it. It is certain and well established that the three Ottos suppressed seditions; and that, while present, they were treated with feigned obedience by the Romans because of fear, but, when absent, with injury and contempt.

Concerning the holy Emperor Henry, Ditmarus reports the following (*Book VII, On Princes*):

> “On the eighth day, however, a great disturbance arose between the Romans and our men on the Tiber bridge, and many fell on both sides, night finally separating them.”

Concerning his successor, Conrad the Salian, Otto of Freising, speaking in Baronius (1027, no. 1), testifies that:

> “During that very Easter week, when a disturbance arose between the emperor’s soldiers and the citizens, a serious battle was fought. After many had been slain and the Romans had fled, the emperor gained the victory.”

By contrast, a hundred years later, when Henry V sacrilegiously disturbed the joy of his coronation:

> “On the following day the Romans gathered and, attacking the enemies of the Church, forced them to flee from the Portico”—that is, from the Leonine City—“many of their men having been killed, and their horses, tents, money, and an immense quantity of equipment having been lost,”

as John, Bishop of Tusculum, writes to the Bishop of Albano in Baronius (1111, no. 13 ff.). Peter the Deacon, a contemporary of those events, agrees:

> “That same night, taking the apostolic lord with him, he fled from the Portico with the entire army in such fear that he left behind not only the baggage but also many companions in their lodgings.”

What is more, when the Romans were unwilling, it was not even permissible for the emperors to enter the City. This is known to have happened to Frederick Barbarossa, Henry VI, and Otto IV. Indeed, the last of these was forced to depart because the supply routes had been cut off.

Of the twelve German emperors who preceded Rudolf, scarcely one or two, although they approached the City with an army, failed to experience the fierce character of the Romans.

[Col. 0853B] **XVI.** To this must be added that, in Nicholas’s time, imperial authority in Italy was almost nonexistent, as is clear from the letters of Rudolph cited above. For although the peoples of this region, detesting the tyranny of Frederick II, had tried in vain to extinguish that authority, nevertheless, after Frederick had been deposed at the Council of Lyons in 1245, the emperor’s name had gradually fallen into disuse for more than thirty years, especially after the arrival of Charles of Anjou, into whom the pontiffs had transferred so much authority.

Rudolph therefore understood that the restoration of imperial authority in Italy would be no small undertaking. For this reason, both through repeated letters and through his representatives, he seriously pursued so important a matter at Rome. The recently cited papal constitution makes it plain that he would not even have obtained that ancient authority which was attached to the imperial diadem: it provides that the government of the City was not to be conferred upon the emperor, any more than upon other princes, without the pope’s special permission, nor for more than one year.

Accordingly, the Italian annalist, [Col. 0853C] and all who, by their reasoning, seem to have reached the conclusion that the cause of restoring the rights of the Church was fear—namely, fear that the pope would enlarge Charles’s authority—are far from the truth. It was not the future authority of the king of Sicily, but his present authority, together with the condition of the City and of all Italy, that ought to have inspired Rudolph with fear, if indeed he feared anything.

The restoration of Romagna, however, proceeded neither from fear nor from any of the other reasons mentioned above, but first from recognition of the error which flattery had fostered and the division of the peoples had confirmed; and then from the other reasons enumerated above, of which Charles’s power, especially in Etruria, must unquestionably have been the principal.

But, to return to the point from which I necessarily digressed: the diplomas of Rudolph, king of the Romans, confirmed by the princes of Germany, not only vigorously assert and strengthen all the rights and privileges of the Holy See, but speak of Sicily—as Louis absolutely calls it, “the Island,” and as Otto and Henry call it, “the patrimony of Sicily”—in such a way as to designate its settled condition, well known in our own age:

> “We shall be helpers,” he says, “in retaining and defending the Roman Church’s kingdom of Sicily, with everything belonging to it, both on this side of the Faro and beyond it.”

Thus Rudolph says in the diploma that he issued at Lausanne, in Raynaldus (1275, no. 38); and the princes of the Empire, or electors, confirming it, say:

> “And the kingdom of Sicily, with everything belonging to it, both on this side of the Faro and beyond it.”

It therefore seems worthwhile to me to give a brief account, as concise as possible, of this matter of such importance from its very origin, so that I may make clear something which I do not see to have been done by others: that both the origin and condition of the kingdom, and the variation in its annual payment, rest upon the most authoritative enactments of the Apostolic See.

### § II. On the kingdom of Sicily, both on this side of the Faro and beyond it

**XVII.** Baronius, and with him all learned men, condemn the audacity of Peter Leo, the antipope, against the authority of the legitimate pope Innocent II. Therefore no prudent person would say that the glory of the Sicilian kingdom rests upon foundations as weak as those laid by that detestable man in his diploma, printed by Baronius (1130, no. 52) under 27 September—however little-discerning writers may find Roger addressed there by the illustrious title of king—nine years before the certain and legitimate origin of that kingdom.

Nevertheless, lest Innocent II, its founder, should perhaps seem to have diminished anything concerning the kingdom’s condition or its tribute, I shall not hesitate to present the very words of the aforementioned antipope, who assumed the name Anacletus:

> “We grant, give, and authorize to you, and to your son Roger, and to your other sons who, according to your arrangement, are to be established as successors in the kingdom, and to their heirs, the crown of the kingdom of Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia, and of all the lands which both we and our predecessors gave and granted to your predecessors, the dukes of Apulia, namely Robert Guiscard and Robert [Col. 0854B] his son; and we grant them the kingdom itself, and the entire royal dignity and royal rights, to be held perpetually by perpetual right, and to be ruled. And we establish Sicily as the head of the kingdom.”

A little farther below he speaks thus concerning the tribute:

> “You, however, [lacuna] and your heirs shall pay the tribute—namely, six hundred schifati—which you are bound to pay each year to the Roman Church, if you are summoned to do so; but if you are not summoned, then, once summoned, you shall pay it, without taking any excuse from what has not been paid.”

Such is the document produced by Baronius from the Vatican Library. Although obscure and mutilated, it makes the condition both of the kingdom and of the tribute sufficiently clear. Namely, the island of Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and all the land granted by the Roman pontiffs to Roger’s Norman predecessors—that is, the principality of Capua, except for the city of Benevento—formed the kingdom of Sicily, whose head was Sicily itself. The tribute was six hundred schifati.

**XVIII.** Once these points have been established, the true origin of the kingdom and the ancient tribute must necessarily disclose the new name. Innocent [Col. 0854C] II, after suffering many serious injuries from Roger, which may be seen from the accounts drawn from Falco and other writers in Baronius and Pagius, finally became Roger’s prisoner.

What then occurred? I shall relate the matter in the very words of Falco (in Pratilli, *History of Lombardy*, vol. IV, p. 301), under the year 1139:

> “The pope, seeing himself deprived of strength and arms and left desolate, yielded to the king’s prayers and requests. After capitularies and privileges had been confirmed by both sides, the king himself, his son the duke, and the prince came on the seventeenth day of the month of July, while the day was still in progress, into the presence of the pope; falling at his feet, they sought mercy and submitted in every respect to the pope’s command. Immediately, by the Gospels, they confirmed that they would render fidelity to blessed Peter, to Pope Innocent, and to his canonically entering successors, and would observe the other things that had been written down. Then he immediately gave King Roger the kingdom of Sicily by the standard; to his son, the duke, he gave the duchy of Apulia; and to his other son, the prince, he granted the principality of Capua. On that day, when the aforesaid pope made peace with the king, the feast of blessed James the Apostle was celebrated, on 26 July.”

Baronius (1139, no. 12) presents the pope’s diploma, issued on the following day and transcribed from the Vatican basilica. I shall therefore bring here only what is relevant:

> “Having hope and confidence in your power,” he says to Roger, “for the honor and advantage of the holy Church of God, we grant and confirm by apostolic authority to Your Excellence the kingdom of Sicily—which, as is certainly reported in ancient histories, was unquestionably a kingdom—granted to you by that same predecessor of ours, Honorius II, with the full integrity of royal honor and the dignity belonging to kings. We likewise, with the strength of our favor, fully confirm and grant to you the duchy of Apulia, which was also conferred upon you by that same predecessor, and, in addition, the principality of Capua.”

> “The tribute, however, as established—namely, six hundred schifati—shall be paid by you and your heirs to us and our successors each year.” [Col. 0855A]

This is evidently the ancient tribute of twelve denarii for each *jugerum*, of which mention was made above (p. 149 ff.).

**XIX.** Baronius observes that Innocent, lest he seem to follow in the antipope’s footsteps, used the example of Honorius, although the latter had bestowed upon Roger only the title of duke. Whatever the circumstances may have been, Cencius Camerarius, in his *Book of Censuses* (*Antiquities of Italy*, vol. V, p. 853), accurately describes the beginning of the kingdom and the condition of the tribute as follows:

> “At the time when Robert Wiscard, the man from beyond the Alps, began the kingdom of Sicily, he swore, touching the sacred Gospels, that he and his heirs would give to Pope Nicholas and his successors twelve denarii of Pavia coin for each yoke of oxen. In the course of time, while Pope Innocent was going to Galluccio, Roger, then king of Sicily, arranged to give him annually six hundred schifati for Apulia and Calabria. Later, King William, his son, added four hundred schifati for the Marsia, which he had occupied during the time of Pope Innocent, in the time of Adrian IV, when he rendered homage and fidelity to him at Benevento.” [Col. 0855B]

This is confirmed by the brief and precise entry in the Albinian manuscript, which was being written around that time, before the aforementioned *Book of Censuses*:

> “The king of Sicily owes one thousand scifati for Apulia, Calabria, and Marsia.”

Thus the diploma of William, king of Sicily, printed by Baronius (1156, no. 6) must be corrected: it reads *Marchia* where it should read *Marsia*, and *D* where it should read *CCCC*—and this indeed on the authority of Innocent III, who, when he invested Constance and her son Frederick II with the same kingdom (Baronius 1097, no. 66; Raynaldus 1198, no. 67), addressing the latter separately, said:

> “When you, son, by the favor of the Lord, have reached legitimate age, you and your heirs shall render fidelity and liege homage to us and our successors and to the Roman Church. You have established that you will pay each year to the Roman Church, you and your heirs, a tribute of six hundred schifati for Apulia and Calabria, and four hundred for Marsia, or the equivalent in gold or silver, unless some impediment should intervene, in which case, once it has ceased, the tribute shall be paid in full.” [Col. 0855C]

If the Italian annalist had taken this into account (under the year 1156), he would not have wasted his efforts seeking which “march” was meant, which he candidly admits that he does not know. What Marsia was at that time can be gathered from the Albinian Provincial manuscript:

> “In Marsia: Reatine, Furconian, Valvense, Teatine, Pinnan, Marsican.”

Further investigation does not belong here.

**XX.** The kingdom, once thus constituted and established, remained with the Normans for only forty years. For when William II, son of William and grandson of Roger, the first king of all, died childless in 1189, it was right that his aunt Constance, wife of Henry VI, king of Germany—who two years later was crowned emperor by Celestine III—should succeed him.

But when Tancred invaded the kingdom, a great conflict arose, which occupied Innocent III and his successors for a long time. For although Innocent had invested Constance and her young son Frederick with the kingdom of Sicily, as I recently said, it is nevertheless clear that after receiving the imperial crown from Honorius III in 1220, Frederick so ill-deserved the Holy See and the Roman pontiffs that it became necessary to depose him at the Council of Lyons in 1245.

Nor did the kingdom of Sicily fare better then. For when Conrad, Frederick’s son, invaded it and then died from a draught of poison, Manfred, Frederick’s illegitimate son, claimed the kingdom of Sicily for himself in place of Conradino, Conrad’s son. To expel him, the Apostolic See first offered the kingdom to Edmund, son of Henry III, king of England; then to Saint Louis IX; and finally, when both declined it, to Charles of Anjou, Saint Louis’s brother, as was said above.

In this matter Rudolph, far from showing resentment either toward the pope or toward Charles—as he was shown consistently to have done in the matter of the vicariate of Etruria—together with the princes of the Empire, or electors, declared in their diplomas the undoubted right of the Holy See and the complete lack of connection between the kingdom of Sicily and the Empire.

Frederick II had done this before them, five years before assuming the imperial diadem, [Col. 0856A] and in the same manner all the princes of the Empire had done so at the Frankfurt assembly, nearly seven months before Frederick was crowned at Rome. Since the relevant passages from both diplomas, in Raynaldus (1215, no. 38; 1275, no. 41), are of the greatest importance, we must hear what they say.

**XXI.** Frederick, therefore, who had long before received the investiture of the kingdom of Sicily together with Constance, lest, after becoming emperor, he should enlarge the rights of the Empire to the detriment of the papal authority, sent Innocent III from Strasbourg a clear declaration of the following kind:

> “Desiring to provide both for the Roman Church and for the kingdom of Sicily, we promise, grant, and establish that, after we have attained the imperial crown, we shall immediately emancipate from paternal authority our son Henry, whom we caused to be crowned king at our command; and we shall wholly leave the kingdom of Sicily, both beyond the Faro and on this side of it, to be held from the Roman Church, just as we ourselves hold it solely from that Church. Thus from that time we shall neither possess nor call ourselves king of Sicily, but, according to your good pleasure, we shall arrange for it to be governed in the name of our son, the king, until he reaches legitimate age, by a suitable person who shall answer in every respect for the rights and services owed to the Roman Church, to which alone the lordship of that kingdom is recognized to belong.

> “Otherwise, because by divine favor we have been summoned to the summit of the Empire, someone might at some time think that the kingdom had some union with the Empire if we held both the Empire and the kingdom, which could generate some disadvantage both for the Apostolic See and for our heirs.”

In the diploma of the princes of the Empire, [Col. 0856C] which is also reported by Lunig (*Codex of Italian Diplomas*, vol. II, p. 873), the royal declaration is confirmed in these words:

> “Just as formerly, at the petitions and requests, and also at the command, of the aforementioned lord our king Frederick, in the time of the late Pope Innocent III, for the sake of peace and to avoid every scandal, we then gave our will and consent to the Holy Roman Church concerning the privileges granted by that king to it; so now we renew our same will and consent and approve it in every respect.

> “And so that this will, approval, or renewal of ours toward the Holy Roman Church may be observed by us perpetually, and that its effect may be evident as a testimony to it and to our perpetual memory, we have caused this present document to be made concerning all the privileges granted by that king to it up to the present, and those still to be granted, both concerning the Empire and concerning the kingdom of Sicily: [Col. 0856D] so that the Empire shall have no union or jurisdiction whatever with that kingdom.

> “This was enacted in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1220, dated at Frankfurt, in a solemn assembly, on 28 April.”

**XXII.** Moreover, his father Henry VI, when near death, had long before ordered Frederick, by a very pious testament—which Baronius calls such (1097, no. 8)—to acknowledge the right of the Holy See and render homage to the pope (*Deeds of Innocent III*, no. 27):

> “Our empress consort and our son Frederick shall render to the lord pope and the Roman Church all the rights which they are accustomed to receive from the kings of Sicily, and shall give security to the lord pope just as the kings of Sicily have been accustomed to give it to the supreme pontiff and the Roman Church. But if our aforesaid consort should die first, our son shall remain according to her arrangement. And if our son should die without an heir, the kingdom of Sicily shall pass to the Roman Church.”

For Henry had invaded that kingdom and, conscious of the injustice of his deed, evidently wished at the end of his life—if I am not mistaken—to follow what was fair and right. Thus, as far as the right is concerned, the two emperors themselves, who had not hesitated to invade it, provide the richest testimony.

Rudolph, however, not only followed in Frederick’s footsteps by acknowledging the rights of the Holy See and the kingdom’s complete separation from the Empire, but also recognized as legitimate its possessor, established by the Apostolic See, and promised to defend him:

> “We shall not offend,” he says in the Lausanne diploma, “the vassals of that Church, either ourselves or through another, and especially the magnificent prince, the lord Charles, illustrious king of Sicily, or his heirs; nor shall we provide publicly or secretly to those wishing to offend him any aid, counsel, or favor. Nor shall we occupy or invade the kingdom of Sicily, which King Charles himself holds from that Roman Church, or any part of it.” [Col. 0857A]

The princes of the Empire, or electors, certainly ratify and strengthen this above all else:

> “And likewise concerning the Roman City and the kingdom of Sicily, with everything belonging to it, both on this side of the Faro and beyond it.”

This designation evidently first came into use in the first year of the pontificate of Innocent III (*Register*, book I, letter 413), who adds to a letter addressed to the prelates of Sicily:

> “In the same manner, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all ecclesiastical prelates established throughout the kingdom of Sicily on this side of the Faro: so that where it says, ‘We have decided to send [him] into the kingdom of Sicily,’ it should read, ‘We have decided to send a legate to Sicily and throughout the entire kingdom.’”

[Col. 0857B] **XXIII.** For this reason, in the apostolic letters of Clement IV preserved by Dacherius (*Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 214), and in numerous manuscripts of Cardinal of Aragon and others, nothing occurs more frequently than “the kingdom of Sicily and the land that is on this side of the Faro.”

What must be especially noted is that in these same letters a tribute is imposed upon the entire kingdom, both beyond and on this side of the Faro—something that had never previously been done:

> “As a general tribute for the whole of the kingdom and land, eight thousand ounces of gold, according to the weight of that kingdom, shall be paid each year to the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church on the feast of blessed Peter, wherever the Roman pontiff may be.”

The condition was that those who failed to pay within two months after the first due date would incur excommunication; after the second due date, the kingdom and the whole land would be placed under interdict; and finally, after the third:

> “You shall forfeit the same kingdom and land entirely, and the kingdom itself and the land shall return wholly and freely to the Roman Church.”

And below:

> “Moreover, every three years you and your heirs in the said kingdom shall give to the Roman pontiff one beautiful, good, and white palfrey.”

This was observed so scrupulously that whenever the pontiff himself, for some serious reason, postponed the date of payment, he provided by a new constitution that the earlier fundamental arrangement should suffer no harm. Thus Gregory X, postponing Charles’s payment until the feast of Saint Michael (Raynaldus 1275, no. 47), says:

> “We postpone the said due date, but in such a way that by this postponement the future date for making that payment on the feast of the apostles shall in no way be altered; rather, from then onward the same payment shall be made each year on the aforesaid feast of the apostles, under the penalties established and prescribed, as is more fully contained in the conditions and agreements made between that Church and you.”

Indeed, it is entirely unknown to no one that this custom has survived down to our own age. But because there is a considerable difference in this matter between our present times and those earlier ones, I must at least touch upon the principal features of this substantial variation. For I see that some people are astonished, as though the reduction of the tribute had arisen from the laws themselves without apostolic authority; but it will soon become clear that this is false.

**XXIV.** First, this must be regarded as certain and established: the kingdom of Sicily, by whatever name it is found to be called—namely, “of Sicily and Apulia, Calabria [Col. 0858A] and Marsia,” as in the Norman period; “of Sicily on this side of the Faro and beyond it”; or “of Sicily and the land on this side of the Faro”; or finally “of Naples and Sicily,” as it is known to have been called after the Normans—was, from the year 1059 down to our own age, for seven centuries, although subject to various changes, always under the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See.

It would be lengthy to review the oaths of all the kings who rendered fidelity and homage to the Roman pontiffs. Let the homage which Charles of Anjou rendered in nearly the same words to Innocent V—who preceded John by several months—stand in place of all, passing over the two especially well-known oaths which he rendered to Clement IV and John XXI, preserved in Raynaldus (1266, no. 4; 1276, no. 39). It was recently brought to light by the learned Jesuit Father Lazzeri (*Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 9), inserted in the papal letters:

> “I, Charles, by the grace of God king of Sicily, duke of Apulia, and prince of Capua, for the honor of almighty God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and of the blessed and glorious virgin Mary, and also of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of the Roman Church, render liege homage to you, my lord, Pope Innocent V, and to your canonically entering successors, and to that Church, for the kingdom of Sicily and the entire land that is on this side of the Faro, as far as the boundaries of the lands of that same Church. That kingdom and land, except for the city of Benevento, together with its entire territory and all its districts and dependencies, the aforesaid Roman Church has granted to me and to my heirs.”

Charles rendered a similar homage to Nicholas III, with only this slight difference in the subscription:

> “Done at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the papal palace, in the year 1278, in the month of May, on the twenty-fourth day, in the sixth indiction; in the second year of my kingdom of Jerusalem, and the thirteenth of Sicily.”

For Mary, descended from the line of the kings of Jerusalem, had transferred her right and title to Charles when she married him in the preceding year. These times were followed by that disastrous upheaval known in the annals as the Sicilian Vespers, from which began the divided rule of the kingdom, subject to considerable and especially prolonged conflicts. Yet the documents show that this in no way altered the right of the Holy See or diminished the tribute; these documents, having long since been published, can be unknown to no one.

**XXV.** Indeed, Peter III, king of Aragon, who had married Constance, Manfred’s daughter, arrived with a fleet intending to invade Sicily by that right. He found the Sicilians ready to revolt for other reasons and therefore easily subjected the island to his authority. He and his successors maintained it by force of arms for ninety years.

After him, while his son James, his brother Frederick II, Peter, Frederick’s son, and Louis, Peter’s son, held Sicily beyond the Faro under the title of invasion, the Angevins—Charles II, his son Robert, and his granddaughter Joanna I—ruled legitimately on this side of the Faro.

At last Gregory XI settled the matter in 1372 [Col. 0858D] between Queen Joanna and Frederick III, Louis’s brother. From this very lengthy treaty, preserved in Raynaldus (1372, no. 5 ff.), I shall extract what demonstrates how vigorously the Apostolic See vindicated its right in the island of Sicily.

It was decreed that Sicily would henceforth be called by the newly devised name “Trinacria,” so that:

> “For this reason Frederick shall never at any time be able to style himself with the title of the kingdom of Sicily, but only with the title of Trinacria; while the queen herself, her heirs, and her successors shall be styled and called by the title of Sicily. Nevertheless, the styling of the kingdom of Sicily shall cause no prejudice to the styling of the kingdom of Trinacria, nor the reverse; rather, each kingdom, distinct in itself, shall have its own title, and neither shall be diminished by the other.”

Thus Gregory, confirming the treaty, says:

> “First, because by the duty of our office we are bound to preserve, protect, and defend the rights of the sacred Roman Church, our spouse, we have deemed it necessary to provide that the aforementioned Joanna and Frederick acknowledge that the direct lordship of the entire kingdom, both beyond and on this side of the Faro, belongs and pertains by right to us and to the Roman Church. We do not intend in any respect to derogate from this direct lordship and right which we and the Roman Church possess in the entire kingdom, both beyond and on this side of the Faro; rather, we wish and intend that they remain unharmed, and that this entire right of ours and of the Roman Church remain in the said island and its adjacent islands—which shall be called the kingdom of Trinacria—in the same form and extent as the right which we possess in the lands on this side of the Faro.”

There follows the formula of homage to be rendered to the pope and his successors, prescribed by Gregory himself. It was indeed rendered:

> “For the island of Sicily together with the adjacent islands, which is called the kingdom of Trinacria.”

See Raynaldus himself (1374, no. 20). From this treaty, however, something else, more necessary for our purpose, must be extracted.

**XXVI.** The matter of imposing the annual tribute seemed more difficult. It was not to be imposed upon the king of Trinacria—an appellation devised for the sake of concord—as an entirely unprecedented burden; nor was it to be borne wholly by the king of Sicily, a title which the pontiff wished to remain proper to Joanna and her successors, according to the prescription of the *Book of Censuses* of the Roman Church and the preceding investitures.

What, then, did the pope do? He imposed the entire burden upon Joanna and her successors:

> “In all the aforesaid matters, and in each of the other matters stated, the aforesaid Joanna and her successors in the kingdom of Sicily shall remain fully bound to the Roman Church, just as if she wholly possessed the kingdom of Sicily with the same integrity with which it had been enfeoffed to the aforesaid lord Charles.”

Then he imposed upon Frederick, king of Trinacria, a portion of the tribute, which he was to pay to Queen Joanna on the feast of the holy apostles Philip and James, that is, on the Kalends of May; thus the full tribute owed by the queen of Sicily and her successors would be considerably relieved:

> “Three thousand ounces of gold,” he says, “calculated according to the aforesaid rate of five florins for each ounce, or according to the general weight of the kingdom of Sicily for each ounce, which, when converted into gold florins according to the aforesaid weight and rate, amount to fifteen thousand florins, shall be owed by the said islands, or kingdom of Trinacria, on account of the debt owed by the queen herself to the Holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See.”

That is, eight thousand ounces, or forty thousand florins.

Therefore Urban VI, Gregory’s successor, when he transferred Joanna’s kingdom to Charles of Durazzo (Raynaldus 1381, nos. 3, 13, and 14), proceeding as though the kingdom of Trinacria did not exist and following in the footsteps of Clement IV, granted Charles:

> “The kingdom of Sicily and the entire land on this side of the Faro as far as the boundaries of the lands of the Roman Church, except for the city of Benevento, together with its entire territory and all its districts and dependencies.”

He imposed the entire tribute of:

> “Eight thousand ounces of gold according to the weight of that kingdom.”

Charles himself, in the oath of fidelity, says:

> “I promise that I shall pay each year to you and your canonically entering successors, the Roman pontiffs, and to the Roman pontiff himself and the Roman Church, as a general tribute for the whole of the kingdom and land, eight thousand ounces of gold according to the weight of that kingdom, on the feast of the holy apostle Peter in the month of June, wherever the Roman pontiff may be. [lacuna] [Col. 0859D] I also promise that at each due date I and my heirs in the said kingdom shall give to you and your canonically entering successors, the Roman pontiffs, one beautiful, good, and white palfrey, in recognition of their true lordship over the kingdom and land.”

Here it is clear from what was cited above, and from Raynaldus’s own adversaria, that *triennio*—“every three years”—must be read in place of *termino*—“at each due date”; however the manifest error crept in.

**XXVII.** What more is there to say? In Raynaldus (1458, no. 37, and 1492, no. 13) there are investitures made by Pius II and Innocent VIII to Ferdinand, Alfonso, and Ferdinand’s son, with exactly the same formulas preserved:

> “As a general tribute for the whole of the kingdom and land, eight thousand ounces of gold according to the weight of that kingdom, on the feast of the holy apostle Peter [lacuna] Moreover, every three years you and your heirs in the said kingdom shall give to us and our canonically entering successors, the Roman pontiffs, one beautiful, good, and white palfrey.”

[Col. 0860A] And, what demonstrates the matter more clearly than daylight itself, this form of oath is prescribed for Alfonso and Ferdinand:

> “I, Alfonso, duke of Calabria, firstborn son of Ferdinand, by the grace of God king of Sicily III, if, upon the death of the aforesaid King Ferdinand, it should happen that I succeed him as king in the aforesaid kingdom and land; and I, Ferdinand, prince of Capua, firstborn son of the said duke Alfonso, if, at the time of the death of the aforementioned King Ferdinand, I should survive my father, the said duke Alfonso, and it should happen by the grace of God that I succeed the aforesaid King Ferdinand in the aforesaid kingdom and land, according to the tenor of the letters granted to us concerning this matter, and become king of the aforesaid Sicily and land, rendering full liege homage and vassalage to you, my lord, the lord Innocent VIII, pope, and to the Roman Church, for the kingdom of Sicily and the entire land on this side of the Faro, and for as much as pertains to the land on this side of the Faro, as far as the boundaries of the lands of that Church, except for the city of Benevento, together with its entire territory and all its districts and dependencies, according to the ancient boundaries of the territory of those dependencies, etc.”

Thus, until the beginning of the sixteenth century, neither the pontiffs nor the kings ever changed anything concerning the tribute—since, as a matter of right, not even the pope was permitted to alter it—whether in respect of its character or its amount, either before or after Clement IV. The situation is different in the periods that followed.

**XXVIII.** In that same year, 1492, when Innocent VIII had granted both Sicilies to Alfonso and to his son Ferdinand according to the ancient custom, Alexander VI had been raised to the highest dignity upon the death of that pope. At the beginning of the sixteenth century, he divided the entire land on this side of the Faro into two parts, as may be seen in his diploma in Raynaldus (1501, no. 53 ff.), from which the history of the period may also be gathered:

> “We grant and bestow upon Louis of France, with the title of king of Naples and Jerusalem, the cities of Naples and Gaeta, and the whole Land of Labor and the province of Abruzzo, according to their just value; and to Ferdinand and Isabella, king and queen of Spain, with the title of duke and duchess of Calabria and Apulia, the duchy [lacuna] and all the provinces of Calabria and Apulia, with all their land, also according to their just value.”

When he comes to the imposition of the tribute (ibid., no. 63), he leaves intact the sum imposed by Clement IV upon the king of Sicily as the general tribute of the kingdom on this side of the Faro and beyond it. But he imposes the entire burden upon the newly established kingdom of Naples, or the land on this side of the Faro:

> “As a general tribute for the whole kingdom of Naples, four thousand ounces of gold, and as the tribute of the aforesaid duchies of Calabria and Apulia, likewise four thousand ounces of gold according to the weight of those kingdom and duchies, shall be paid each year by the said kings and queen, and their heirs in the said kingdom and duchies, to the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church, on the feast of the holy apostle Peter in the month of June, wherever the Roman pontiff may be. [lacuna] [Col. 0860D] Moreover, every three years the said king and queen, and their heirs in the said kingdom and duchies, shall each give to us and our canonically entering successors, the Roman pontiffs, one beautiful, good, and white palfrey, in recognition of their true lordship over the said kingdom and duchies.”

Alexander’s division, defended with difficulty for some time by arms between rival peoples and kings, was united after four years when Ferdinand brought the whole land on this side of the Faro under his authority.

### XXIX.

A record of the matter is supplied by the diaries of Paris de Grassis in Raynaldus (1505, no. 14). For when Franciscus de Roxas, ambassador of King Ferdinand the Catholic, presented the census-payment and the horse to Julius II, he addressed the pontiff in these words:

“Most blessed Father and most holy lord, the most serene, most powerful, and most invincible prince and lord, Lord Ferdinand, by the grace of God Catholic King of Aragon, of both Sicilies on this side and beyond the Faro, and of Jerusalem, the most devoted son of Your Holiness and of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 0861A] and my lord, and the true and legitimate king and peaceful possessor of the said kingdom of Sicily on this side of the Faro, wishing to render to God the things that are God’s, sends Your Holiness this white horse, decently adorned, and the census owed this year to Your Holiness and the Holy Roman Church for the said kingdom of Sicily on this side of the Faro, etc.”

Nevertheless, all history testifies that Ludovic had not lost the right which he had acquired from Alexander VI over the new kingdom of Naples before the year 1510.
