At that time, however, he was condemned by Julius for various reasons, chiefly on account of the rights alienated from the Roman Church which he had received; he was deprived of the kingdom, which the same pontiff granted to Ferdinand because of his outstanding merits. The Alexandrian division having likewise been annulled, he restored the land on this side of the Faro to its former condition:

“Restoring and fully reintegrating that kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem, together with all the said land on this side of the Faro as far as [Col. 0861B] the boundaries of the lands of the said Roman Church, except our city of Benevento with its territory and appurtenances, to the condition in which it existed before the aforesaid division.”

He likewise expressed the census according to the ancient formula:

“For the entire general census of the kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem, eight thousand ounces of gold . . . . In each term”—without doubt, “in each three-year period” should be read—“King Ferdinand himself, and his heirs and successors in the said kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem, shall give to us and to our canonically succeeding Roman pontiffs one beautiful and good white palfrey, in recognition of the true lordship of that kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem.”

The diploma is found in Raynaldus (1510, nos. 25 ff.) and in the *Corpo Diplomatico* (*Supplement*, vol. III, p. 20), with this difference: Raynaldus omits the formulas, since he recognized them as entirely similar to those of the preceding diplomas. In the *Corpo Diplomatico*, however, each is given separately, and in the general census just reported a double reading is admitted:

“Eight thousand ducats [another reading: ounces; but ducats must be retained].”

For Leo X was the first of all to impose “for the customary annual census seven thousand gold ducats, together with a white palfrey”; his successors followed him.

### XXX.

Julius, moreover, in keeping with the spirit of his age, speaks rather carelessly of the land or Sicily on this side of the Faro. He commonly calls it the kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem, as though that overseas kingdom, whose mere title Maria had brought to Charles of Anjou, were situated in the land on this side of the Faro. His successor Leo X held this view when he invested Charles V with both kingdoms (*Bullarium Romanum*, vol. XIV, p. 243; Lunig, *Codex Italiae Diplomaticus*, vol. IV, part II, pp. 1347 and 1354). This is shown by the wording of his letters:

“Let him expressly confess and acknowledge by his own oath the kingdom of Sicily and Jerusalem, and all their land which lies on this side of the Faro as far as the boundaries of the lands of the Roman Church, except the city of Benevento.”

It will be found that the same land was understood in the same sense by Julius III, Clement VIII, Gregory XV, Alexander VII, and [Col. 0861D] Innocent XIII, in the diplomas by which Philip II, III, and IV, as well as Charles II and VI, were invested with both Sicilies, at the places cited.

This is even clearer from the words of the royal ambassador, who, while presenting the census on the appointed day, addressed the pontiff:

“N. N., my most merciful lord, sends Your Holiness this horse, which I present in his royal name, decently adorned, and seven thousand ducats for the customary census of the kingdom of Naples, earnestly beseeching Almighty God that Your Holiness may receive it for many years, for the good of Christendom and the advancement of our holy Catholic faith—which His Royal Majesty desires and I fervently vow.”

The pontiff’s reply, according to the ancient form, makes entirely clear that nothing had been changed or withdrawn concerning the right of the Apostolic See over the kingdom of Sicily and the land on this side of the Faro:

“We willingly receive and accept this census, owed to us and to the Apostolic See for the direct lordship of our kingdom of both Sicilies, on this side and beyond the Faro. We pray the Lord to grant our most beloved son in Christ N. N. health and the most desired offspring; and upon him, his peoples, and his vassals we bestow the apostolic blessing. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

Thus, as Otterius teaches in his *History* (vol. VIII, p. 24), Innocent XIII replied to the imperial ambassador. I gladly use his authority so that matters which we receive each year with our own ears may be brought from the records of the annals before the reader’s eyes.

### XXXI.

Since this is so, it must be observed that there have been six periods of such censuses, all resting upon apostolic authority.

1. In 1059, Nicholas II imposed upon the Normans twelve denarii for each jugerum, concerning which enough has been said above.

2. In 1139, Innocent II, in place of the ancient census, imposed six hundred schifati upon Roger I, king of Sicily; Adrian IV added four hundred to William, Roger’s successor, for the Marsia. Thus one thousand schifati, or gold coins, whose value is not established, made up the entire annual census.

3. In 1265, Clement IV imposed upon Charles of Anjou eight thousand ounces of gold, or forty thousand florins, as the general census of both Sicilies.

4. In 1372, Gregory XI imposed upon the king of Trinacria, or Sicily beyond the Faro, three thousand ounces, or fifteen thousand florins, to be paid to the possessor of Sicily on this side of the Faro, who was bound to pay the full census to the Holy See.

5. In 1501, Alexander VI imposed the same census of eight thousand ounces of gold, divided into two parts, entirely upon Sicily on this side of the Faro; Julius II later restored it to its former condition.

6. Finally, in 1521, Leo X established, by apostolic authority, the annual census of our own age:

“He has obligated and does obligate the same King Charles and those who for the time being possess the kingdom of Sicily on this side of the Faro, so that, in recognition of the true and direct lordship, they shall be bound to pay every year, in perpetuity, to the Apostolic Chamber seven thousand gold ducats of the chamber on the feast of the same blessed Peter, in addition to the customary census of the white palfrey.”

Thus it appears in the clauses inserted between Leo and the ambassador of Charles V in the diploma of that same pontiff, which Raynaldus presents from the papers of Baronius (1521, II, nos. 81 ff.). Mention of this kind of “census of seven thousand gold ducats, newly imposed by reason of the new grant of the fief of the said kingdom” occurs again; and in other apostolic letters (no. 92) it is mentioned once, twice, and three times as an addition to the census of the white palfrey, while the eight thousand ounces formerly customary are buried in profound silence.

### XXXII.

The same amount was paid by Charles of Anjou as the general census of both Sicilies when Rudolph confirmed to Gregory X, and the electors of the Holy Roman Empire to Nicholas III, “the kingdom of Sicily with all things belonging to it, both on this side and beyond the Faro.”

Since a similar census—namely, thirty-five thousand gold pieces—had once been reduced by Innocent II and Adrian IV to one thousand schifati, it is not surprising that eight thousand ounces of gold were reduced, by apostolic authority, to seven thousand gold ducats. Still less should it be surprising that the entire burden was imposed upon the Land, or Sicily on this side of the Faro, or even upon the kingdom of Naples, since these three names mean the same thing.

This was indeed the arrangement in the time of the Normans. If one subtracts approximately the sixteen years of Charles of Anjou, during which it is expressly declared under that name that Sicily beyond the Faro was also subject to the census, it will become clear and certain that at other times a different census was imposed upon the possessor of Sicily on this side of the Faro. The exception is the palfrey, or white horse, which designates the direct lordship of both Sicilies exercised by the Holy See, “in recognition of the true lordship of that kingdom and land.”

It would, however, be most astonishing if the island of Sicily, which together with Calabria had been assigned by the Eastern emperors, patricians, and other faithful Christians to the Holy See in all their donations made for the salvation of their souls, and which by those same emperors had been subjected to the payment of three and a half talents, or thirty-five thousand gold pieces, and for the recovery of which the supreme pontiffs fought most fiercely, were thought to be of uncertain legal status because of a mistaken understanding of the meaning of the land on this side of the Faro.

All the reliable records, both those incorporated into the annals and those preserved in manuscript codices, teach otherwise.

This is sufficient concerning Sicily on this side and beyond the Faro, confirmed by Rudolph and by the princes, or electors, of the Empire. The diplomas will follow shortly: Rudolph’s from the original preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo; that of the electors from the Rudolphine codex which we have presented, for at its end this diploma is found together with another of Rudolph. The same document will also be given carefully collated with the original in that archive.

### I. Diploma of Rudolph, king of the Romans, with his pendant seal

[Col. 0863B]

To the most holy Father in Christ and lord, Lord Nicholas III, pope:

**[Note: Col. 0863B]** In the year 1278, on the Nones of June, Nicholas III inserted into his letters the privileges of Louis, Otto, and Henry, and sent them to Rudolph:

“Lest you suppose that through these things we are asking anything new, or anything unusual from your predecessors, the Roman emperors, and so that your conscience may be more fully reassured, concerning the manner in which certain of your predecessors, the Roman emperors, expressed these matters, and how they declared under explicit territorial distinctions that those matters belonged to the Roman Church, we send you, word for word, the texts of those emperors’ privileges, as we found them in the archives of the Roman Church, under our seal.”

He also communicated many matters to Conrad the Minorite, Rudolph’s ambassador, to be reported to the same king of the Romans for his fuller assurance.

Moreover, in another letter he prescribed the form which Rudolph was to use in the privilege. For the formula employed by Rudolph’s legates at Lyons in 1274 and by Rudolph himself at Lausanne in 1275 before Gregory X had been a cause of error, since it did not list the cities of the Exarchate by name. In accordance with the custom of that age, it described the ecclesiastical territories in this manner:

“To these belongs all the land which extends from Radicofano to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, the Duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, the county of Bertinoro, the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, Massa Trabaria with the adjacent lands, and all other things belonging to the Roman Church.”

Nicholas therefore sent the following additions to be inserted between Matilda’s land and the Pentapolis:

“The city of Ravenna and Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adria, and Gabello, Rimini, Montefeltro, the territory of Balneum, the Pentapolis.”

And after many other provisions:

“Accordingly, all the aforesaid territories, both those expressed by the proper or specific names of provinces, lands, cities, and places, and those not expressed, and every other thing belonging to the Roman Church, we freely leave, renounce, and restore to it by the will, knowledge, counsel, and consent of the princes of the Empire. Moreover, to remove every scruple, and insofar as this can be better and more effectively understood, we newly grant, confer, and donate them, so that, once every cause of contention and dissension has been removed, firm peace and complete concord may continue between the Church and the Empire.”

Finally, at the end:

“We further promise that, after we have reached Rome to receive anointing, coronation, and the imperial diadem, and have received them, within eight days we shall renew all the aforesaid matters, each and every one, and shall again carry them out fully and completely.”

Following this pontifical instruction, corroborated by the records, Rudolph issued two diplomas, which are found in Raynaldus (1279, no. 1 ff.), just as other documents of his are found there under the preceding years (1274, nos. 5 ff.; 1275, no. 38 ff.; 1278, no. 45 ff.). The document which we publish from the original in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo is the final one of all, by which all the preceding documents are confirmed.

**Rudolph, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever Augustus. For the perpetual memory of the matter.**

The supreme protection of the commonwealth, arising by divine institution from the two orders of priesthood and empire, and thereby strengthening its power, has governed the human race beneficially in the past and, with God’s favor, will govern it forever in the future. These are the two greatest gifts of God, bestowed by heavenly clemency upon all: namely, the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal excellence of power. Our Savior, Jesus Christ, mediator between God and humanity, exercised these two through himself in distinct acts and dignities in such a way that he made clear to all that both proceed from him as from one and the same source.

Acknowledging, therefore, all things from that one living and true God, from whom kings and kingdoms have received their beginnings, and recalling the countless benefits of the most holy Roman Church toward us, we are moved with our whole heart to repay and return to it whatever we can, since we see that such great and excellent gifts have been bestowed upon us and upon our predecessors, the kings of the Romans, by that Church [Col. 0864B].

**[Note: Col. 0864B]** Nothing could be more appropriate than this preface: the king of the Romans, the future emperor, attributes the dignity of his office to God, from whom all power comes, and to the successors of the prince of the apostles; he magnifies the benefits granted to himself and to his predecessors by the Holy See, declaring that these move him, in gratitude, to return thanks by confirming all earlier privileges. The records of the annals testify to the benefits received by his predecessors; those received by Rudolph himself are clear from the letters cited above. He considers especially great and singular the fact that imperial majesty had been renewed by the Holy See in the West.

Accordingly, our aforesaid predecessors, turning toward gratitude in return for the magnificence of the gifts and the somehow inexpressible generosity which they had received from the breasts of that mother Church, and paying no less attention to the fact that the same mother Church, anticipating them with the blessing of sweetness, had transferred the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans [Col. 0864C], had given them what they were, so that they might be proclaimed grateful sons through the effect of their praiseworthy acknowledgment.

**[Note: Col. 0864C]** So far was the Empire from having been transferred from Greece to the West that Greek emperors continued down to the beginning of the thirteenth century. Thereafter, for nearly sixty years, Latin emperors reigned in their place, with Baldwin, count of Flanders, leading the army. Finally, after the Greek Empire had been restored through Michael VIII Palaeologus from the year 1260 until 1453, when Mehmed II captured Constantinople, that same Greek Empire ended with Constantine XI.

For this reason Rome saw the coronation of Frederick III, the last of all, before the end of the Greek Empire. The renewal of the Empire among the Germans had taken place through Saint Leo III in the year 800, six hundred and fifty years before that end. Moreover, Innocent III approved the transfer from the schismatic Greeks to the Catholic Baldwin, as is clear from his register in Raynaldus (1205, no. 10); and Honorius III (ibid., 1217, no. 4 ff.) crowned Peter, count of Auxerre, who had hastened from Gaul to Rome, in the church of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, as the Chronicle of Fossanova reports, “with great glory and splendor,” as Greek emperor. In letters sent to the patriarch of Constantinople, he declared that he had done this without prejudice to or contempt for the patriarch or anyone else, for various reasons which he recounted.

Accordingly, Rudolph understands “imperial dignity,” or “majesty,” in this sense. The same sense should be assigned to the ancient inscription from the age of Charlemagne, *Renovatio imperii*. He rightly says that the Empire was transferred to the Germans because the Frankish monarchy in the time of Charlemagne included Germany, which was later separated from it. Thus, when Otto I, king of Germany, was designated emperor in 962, the Empire may correctly and consistently be said to have been transferred from the Franks to the Germans.

Albert, Rudolph’s son, places the matter beyond dispute in his letters to Boniface VIII. The original is preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo, and a copy in Raynaldus (1303, no. 10):

“The Roman Empire,” he says, “was transferred by the Apostolic See from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of the magnificent Charles.”

Among the other things which they confirmed, left, or even granted to the Roman Church was the whole land extending from Radicofano to Ceprano [Col. 0865B].

**[Note: Col. 0865B]** This should be understood as the city of Rome with its duchy, inserted by Louis the Pious and his successors into the privileges, with the Roman pontiff, as supreme prince, so willing it; Lombard Tuscany; and the Sabine territory from Charlemagne’s donation. In Rudolph’s time all these were called by the single name “the Land.”

They likewise confirmed the March of Ancona [Col. 0865C].

**[Note: Col. 0865C]** The maritime part of the Pentapolis turned toward the March, whenever that occurred, in which were the cities of Ancona, Firmum, Auximum, Camerinum, Fanum, Aesis, Senigallia, and Pisaurum, as well as Asculum, and Pensaunium, with all their dioceses, as stated in the acts of Innocent III preserved by Baluzius (vol. I, p. 3).

They confirmed the Duchy of Spoleto [Col. 0865C].

**[Note: Col. 0865C]** Namely, the seven cities donated by Otto I to the apostle Peter and his successors in 962, “for the remedy of our soul, and of our son and our parents,” together with all the others granted by Henry I in 1020 by way of compensation; joined together, these formerly constituted the Duchy of Spoleto. By Rudolph’s time, however, a great change had occurred. Hence the acts of Innocent III state:

“The Roman Church recovered the Duchy of Spoleto and the County of Assisi, namely Rieti, Spoleto, Assisi, Foligno, and Nocera, with all their dioceses.”

They confirmed the land of Countess Matilda [Col. 0865D].

**[Note: Col. 0865D]** Enough has been said about this in the antepenultimate dissertation; consult it.

They confirmed the county of Bertinoro [Col. 0865D].

**[Note: Col. 0865D]** Forlì was listed as an appendage in the Pippinian Donation in the *Book of the Pontiffs*. The Castle of Sussubium was also listed, as was stated elsewhere (vol. I, p. 65); yet it is not mentioned at all in the privileges of Louis and his successors. At this time, however, it was a distinct lordship, or county, which Count Cavalca, dying at Venice in the time of Alexander III, had restored to the Holy See (see the penultimate dissertation, no. 17).

They confirmed the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, Massa Trabaria with the adjacent lands, and all other goods, lands, possessions, and rights belonging to the Roman Church, expressed or contained in the many privileges of the emperors from the time of Louis [Col. 0865D].

**[Note: Col. 0865D]** In the dissertation (no. 5) I explained what the Exarchate was like, and how extensive it was, at that time. Anyone can judge the size of the contemporary Pentapolis once the March of Ancona has been subtracted. The principal point is that these various names, except for the Duchy of Spoleto and Matilda’s land, designate nothing other than the Pippinian Donation, wholly vindicated for the Holy See by Charlemagne.

They left, renounced, restored, and confirmed these territories to blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and to his successors and to the Roman Church; and, to remove every scruple, insofar as this could be done better and more effectively, they conferred, granted, and even donated them, as is contained in their privileges or letters.

**[Note: Col. 0866B]** In the privileges of Louis and his successors, to which Rudolph adheres, none of these minor territories will be found. For what reason would there have been for the special designation of Massa Trabaria if all the cities of the Pentapolis, including Urbino with all its boundaries and lands belonging to those cities, had already been named?

These new names and divisions of places were the cause why the pontiffs themselves, who resided at Avignon, were ignorant of their own rights and those of the Church. I call John XXII as witness. In 1319, in the Vatican chapter (*Vatican Bullary*, vol. I, p. 255), he indicates that the rector of the March of Ancona was in need of:

“Transcripts of the privileges concerning concessions made to the Roman Church of the province of the March of Ancona, Massa Trabaria, the land of Saint Agatha, and the city, formerly the county, of Urbino.”

In the following year he likewise ordered that the necessary documents be delivered by the same chapter to the rector of the Duchy of Spoleto:

“Since the registers concerning the jurisdiction of the Duchy of the Valley of Spoleto are said to be in your possession, and since those registers are recognized as necessary for our beloved son, the rector of the aforesaid duchy, etc.”

It is known that timber from both Massa Trabaria and the Duchy of Spoleto was regularly requested for the restoration of the basilica and other churches of the City (Codex Carolinus, letters 66 and 87, otherwise 61 and 66), and that the pontiffs had granted the chapter the right to cut it in both places. It is also clear from the letters cited that the archive of the basilica contained a book of the privileges of the Roman Church and the registers of the pontiffs. Yet no one will claim that the Pentapolis, designated by so many names, or the Duchy of Spoleto under the name “the Valley of Spoleto,” is found in the ancient privileges. No one will deny that the pontiff, among the territories of the Roman Church, was wandering amid newly introduced names.

We, later, having been raised by the Lord’s will to the summit of royal excellence, so that we might discharge no lesser debt of acknowledgment for the countless gifts received from the hands of that mother, recalled all the aforesaid matters in the presence of Gregory X, lord pope of blessed memory [Col. 0866A], and confirmed, renewed, newly granted, and donated each and every one of them to him, receiving them on behalf of the Roman Church, himself and his successors. We further strengthened them by an oath personally and bodily sworn by us.

**[Note: Col. 0866C]** Namely, in 1275 at Lausanne, he enumerates the Church’s territories in these words: “To these belongs all the land extending from Radicofano to Ceprano, the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, the March of Ancona, the Duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, and the county of Bertinoro, with the adjacent lands expressed in many imperial privileges from the time of Louis.” We have just seen them enumerated in a different order at Lyons (col. 863, note a). Therefore, by this diploma he embraces all the foregoing.

**[Note: Col. 0866D]** In the oath sworn at Lausanne:

“I shall likewise show to you, my lord Pope Gregory, and to your successors, all the obedience and honor which devoted and Catholic emperors have been accustomed to show to the Apostolic See. And if, on account of my affair, the Roman Church should have to enter into war, I shall aid it with expenses as necessity demands. I shall confirm all the aforesaid matters both by oath and by writing when I have obtained the imperial crown.”

The electors add an oath of fidelity.

But afterward, without our consent, knowledge, or command, our chancellor Rudolph is said to have received, in our name, an oath of fidelity from the citizens of Ravenna, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Urbino, and from the men of Montefeltro and Bertinoro, as well as from others of the other cities and from the inhabitants of those parts and places which belong to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church [Col. 0867A]. Seeing that this had occurred to the prejudice of the rights of that mother Church, we remit, release, and expressly renounce whatever was done, conducted, acknowledged, or sworn by that same chancellor or by anyone else in the aforesaid cities, places, and lands, or by the people of those cities, lands, and places—especially the aforesaid oaths. We revoke, cancel, annul, invalidate, and declare void and null all these acts, depriving them of every force. We expressly wish, decree, and consent that no right should thereby accrue to us or to the Empire, nor any right be lost to the Roman Church, whether concerning possession or ownership, in the aforesaid cities, lands, and places, or concerning their inhabitants, rights, and jurisdictions.

**[Note: Col. 0867C]** This matter has been discussed fully in the dissertation (no. 8 ff.).

And because royal acts ought to proceed in complete clarity, so that our royal declaration may remove every obscurity which generality frequently tends to introduce, and so that the rights of that mother Church may be fully secured by our declaration, which we decree to be perpetual, we acknowledge, confess, and declare by the present edict, for eternal memory, that the city of Ravenna and Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adria, and Gabello; Rimini, Urbino, Montefeltro, and the territory of Balneum [Col. 0867C],

**[Note: Col. 0867C]** In the form which Nicholas, following the practice of his predecessors, prescribed for Rudolph—as may be seen in Raynaldus (1278, no. 62), from the register of Nicholas III—the Pentapolis and Massa Trabaria occupy the foremost place; but Rudolph, having listed them above, omits both here.

the aforesaid provinces, cities, places, and territories, together with all the aforesaid lands, boundaries, territories, and islands by land and sea belonging in any way to the aforesaid provinces, cities, territories, and places, belong in full right and wholly—not only in spiritual matters but also in temporal matters—to blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and to you, most blessed Father, Lord Nicholas III, pope, and to your successors, the Roman pontiffs, and to the Roman Church itself; and that they exist as the full right, jurisdiction, and principate of you and of the Roman Church.

**[Note: Col. 0867C]** He appropriately declares the very plain words of Louis and his successors: “let them hold in their right, principate, and jurisdiction,” adding “in spiritual and temporal matters.” For some recent writers are not ashamed to follow certain disciples of Arnold of Brescia—or, rather, members of another sect—and delight in erring in so clear a matter.

And, to abolish every scruple of doubt for the future, and so that our devotion toward that mother Church may shine forth more clearly, we freely and fully grant, confer, and donate anew all the aforesaid matters, each and every one, both those expressed by the proper or specific names of provinces, lands, cities, and places, and those not expressed, insofar as they can be better and more effectively understood, to blessed Peter, to you, most holy Father, Lord Nicholas III, pope, and through you to your successors, the Roman pontiffs, and to the Roman Church itself [Col. 0868A], so that, every cause of contention and dissension having been removed, firm peace and complete concord may continue between the Church and the Empire.

**[Note: Col. 0867D]** Although nothing clearer or more significant concerning the rights of the Apostolic See could be desired in the Rudolphine diploma, nevertheless what was customary for Pippin, Charles, Otto, and Henry—offering provinces and cities to Peter and his successors for the remedy or reward of their souls—is nowhere heard. Pippin, enlarging the territory of the Roman Church, which had been confined within narrow boundaries, through the donation of the Exarchate; Charles, adding the provinces of Tuscany, Sabina, and Campania; and Otto and Henry, granting the Duchy of Spoleto, had excellent reason to use those words. But Rudolph, who, imitating Louis, confirms the donations of others in the broadest terms and restores territories which had been seized, adding nothing of his own, could neither use nor ought to have used the same words.

Now, so that all these matters may be observed in perpetuity by you, our aforesaid most holy Father, Lord Nicholas, supreme pontiff of the sacred Roman Church, and by your successors, and by the Roman Church itself, through us and through our successors, the kings and emperors of the Romans, and so that they may always remain firm and unshaken, we have ordered this privilege of our acknowledgment, declaration, concession, and donation, written with our knowledge and express command, to be secured with a golden seal impressed with the device of our majesty, and to be delivered to you and to the Roman Church itself for perpetual firmness and certainty.

**[Note: Col. 0868C]** The novelty resulting from the change of names is that even the absolute lordship of the City and the Roman Duchy—which is found to have been donated by no king or emperor—is asserted for the Roman pontiff. Louis and his successors, Otto and Henry, had not excluded the people’s share when they added the condition “as you and your predecessors have held and disposed of it until now in your power and jurisdiction.” But since, during the twelfth century, the expression “the Land from Radicofano to Ceprano” began to be heard, Rome, the head of that land, seems to have taken on the character of the other donations.

We further promise that, after we have reached Rome to receive anointing, coronation, and the imperial diadem, and have received them, within eight days we shall renew all the aforesaid matters, each and every one, and shall again carry them out fully and completely.

**[Note: Col. 0868D]** Rudolph’s predecessors had come with an army to their coronation, which was highly inconvenient because of the *fodrum*. Rudolph, however, was assigned a prescribed number of soldiers, as the Colmar Annals report in Raynaldus (1275, no. 36), where the matter concerns the Lausanne conference:

“The pope,” they say, “had advised the king to come to Rome for Pentecost with two thousand soldiers, so that he might solemnly crown him Roman emperor.”

The pope’s journey, undertaken because of Alfonso, and the difficulty of the matter had prolonged the Lausanne conference until the Feast of All Saints, when the ceremony was scheduled. It therefore had to be postponed until Pentecost. In the meantime, however, the pontiff died, and other reasons for delay arose, concerning which I have spoken in the dissertation. The ceremony was delayed so long that every hope of celebrating it finally disappeared.

The witnesses are these: the venerable Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg; John, bishop of Chiemsee; and Wernhard, bishop of Seckau; Giffridus, dean of the church of Saint-Omer in the diocese of Thérouanne and chaplain of the lord pope; Henry, abbot of Admont; Nicholas, archdeacon of Todi; the illustrious brothers Albert and Hartmann of Habsburg and Kyburg, counts and landgraves of Alsace, our sons; and the distinguished men Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg; Henry, margrave of Hahperch; Burchard of Hohenberg; and Henry of Fürstenberg [Col. 0868C], counts; Henry Sluzzellinus, our chaplain; Master Conrad of Herwelingen; Master Angelus, canon of Saint Valentine of Ferentino; [Col. 0869A] Henry of Loubenberg; and John of Hedingen, our household knights; and many others.

**The sign of the lord Rudolph, most invincible king of the Romans.**

**Place of the monogram.**

I, Rudolph [Col. 0869B], chancellor of the imperial court, acting in place of Lord Werner, archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Germany, have examined and authenticated this.

**[Note: Col. 0869B]** He was the successor of Otto of Speyer, who in the year 1278 exacted an oath of fidelity from the cities of the Exarchate, as though that province belonged to the Empire. Concerning him, who later attained the archbishopric of Salzburg, see Hansiz, *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 394.

These acts were performed in the year of the Lord 1279, in the seventh indiction, while the glorious Lord Rudolph was reigning as king of the Romans, in the sixth year of his reign.

Given at Vienna by the hand of Master Godfrey [Col. 0869B], provost of Solingen, our protonotary, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March.

**[Note: Col. 0869B]** In a letter to Nicholas III dated the fourth day before the Kalends of June of the same year, Rudolph says that he was sending “our beloved familiar cleric, Master Godfrey, provost of Solingen, protonotary of the royal court” [Col. 0869C], with full authority to rescind whatever the chancellor had done without the royal majesty’s knowledge. Nothing could be more appropriate for this royal diploma than the subscriptions of both men.

## II. Diploma of the Princes of the Empire concerning the Donation and Confirmation of the Privileges of the Apostolic See by Rudolph I, Emperor

**[Note: [Col. 0869C]** A new offense on the part of the compiler. Raynaldus (1279, no. 6) prefixes no title to the diploma. Zacagnus, producing it from the original in the Archives of the Castel Sant’Angelo (Historical Dissertation, Appendix, 1709), prefaces it with this title: “Diploma of the electors of the Empire, by which they approve as valid Rudolph’s preceding confirmation as King of the Romans.” I do not hesitate to affirm that this title is less consistent with the diploma; therefore, following the example of others, I too shall append a title that expresses the true meaning of the diploma: “Diploma of the princes of the Empire approving and validating all the preceding diplomas and every other document of Rudolph, King of the Romans, in support of the rights of the Holy See, and granting their will and assent to what is to be done in the future.” These words indeed restrain the compiler’s excessive license; but Rudolph himself and the princes of the Empire—or, if you prefer, the electors—by repeatedly referring to him as “King of the Romans,” make it clear that the title “emperor” was inserted by the compiler.**]

[Col. 0869B] We, the princes of the Empire—Henry, Archbishop of Trier; Siegfried, Archbishop of Cologne; Werner, Archbishop of Mainz; Louis [527], Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of both Bavarias; John, Duke of Saxony; John, Margrave of Brandenburg; and we, Otto, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Otto, Margrave of Brandenburg—[Note: [Col. 0869D] The names of the electoral princes are enclosed in parentheses, since they are missing from the original in the papal archives of the Castel Sant’Angelo, although they are printed on the nine hanging seals in the following form: “Henry, Archbishop of Trier; Siegfried, Archbishop of Cologne; Werner, Archbishop of Mainz; Louis, Count Palatine; John, Duke of Saxony; Albert, Duke of Saxony; John, Margrave of Brandenburg; Otto, Margrave of Brandenburg; Otto, Margrave of Brandenburg.” The seal of the first Otto is small and displays a human head; the second is larger and represents a standing, armed man. I have considered these details worth noting both so that the full number of subscribing electors may be known—for Duke Albert of Saxony is absent from the manuscript—and so that it may be evident that, as stated elsewhere (Dissertation on the Rudolphine Code, no. 10, p. 249), at the beginning several members of the same family could be found among the electors, without their number thereby increasing beyond seven. This is confirmed more and more by examples of this diploma: the same princes separately issued their diploma in the same sense, taking account not of the number of persons but of the family. Thus John and Albert, Dukes of Saxony, are found to have issued one diploma; and in the same way three Margraves of Brandenburg issued one under the name of Otto, both in the same apostolic archive and in Baronius (996, 43 ff.).**] to all who shall inspect this present document.

Since the Roman Mother Church has long embraced Germany with a kind of sisterly affection, she adorned it with that earthly title of dignity [Col. 0870A] which is above every name, but only in temporal matters, namely, that of those who preside over the earth [Note: [Col. 0870C] Whether one understands this as referring to the imperial dignity instituted under Charlemagne, or accepts it as having been restored under Otto I, the Holy See is proclaimed by all the princes of the Roman Empire, to the dismay of the jurists, as the creator of so great a majesty.**]: planting in it princes like choice trees and watering them with singular grace. She gave them such growth in wondrous power that, supported by the authority of that Church, like a chosen shoot, through their election they might bring forth him who would hold the reins of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0870C] When I was treating of the establishment of the illustrious College of the Seven [Dissertation on the Rudolphine Code, no. 10], I said that it owed its origin not to a constitution but to the pope’s counsel. Here is testimony to that college greater than any exception. The electors themselves testify to all who inspect their diploma that they were established by the apostolic see. More clearly still, Albert, King of the Romans, son of Rudolph, declares to Boniface VIII, according to Raynaldus (1303, no. 9): “That the promotion of a king to the imperial dignity thereafter was granted to certain ecclesiastical and secular princes by that same see, from which kings and emperors, those who have existed and those who shall exist in due time, receive the power of the temporal sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.”**]

This is that lesser luminary in the firmament of the Church militant, illuminated by the greater luminary, Christ’s vicar. This is he who draws and wields the material sword at its command, so that, aided by his protection, the shepherd of shepherds may strengthen the sheep entrusted to him by guarding them with the spiritual sword, restraining and correcting them with the temporal sword, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of believers and the good [Note: [Col. 0870D] Nothing is more frequent in this code than this comparison, used to indicate spiritual and temporal power, as though neither had any limits in the world—that is, as though both were without limits. In the *Golden Bull* as well (chapter 2, no. 5), the emperor is called “the ruler, or temporal head, of the faithful”: not because he was lord of other kingdoms and principalities, which Ahenobarbus was firmly convinced of—for not even the pope himself claims for himself the rights of the metropolitans and bishops of the Catholic world—but because the Roman emperor was thought to be the head of all kings and princes, just as the pope is bishop of all bishops. Thus, wherever the supreme power of the pope, or spiritual sword, extended, the temporal power of the emperor also extended. If you argue that this comparison is not entirely equitable, I do not object. I am merely setting forth an opinion attested by the monuments of those times.**]

Therefore, so that every cause of disagreement [528] and scandal, and even every occasion of resentment, may be removed between the Church herself and the Empire, and so that those two swords established in the house of the Lord may be joined by a proper bond and exercise themselves for the useful reform of the government of the whole world [Col. 0870B], and so that we may be found in the act of our will and work to be sons of devotion and peace—we who are bound to foster both the Church and the Empire—whatever our lord Rudolph, by the grace of God ever august King of the Romans, has acknowledged, confirmed, ratified, renewed, newly donated, declared, or granted to the most holy father and our lord, Lord Nicholas III, pope, and to his successors and to the Roman Church herself; whatever he has sworn to or undertaken [Col. 0871A] or done, whether by privileges or by any other writings of whatever tenor [Note: [Col. 0871B] From this the first part of the title which I said should be prefixed to the diploma (column 869, note a) is confirmed; the title prescribed for the others is shown to be less correct, and especially that appended by the compiler of the letters of this code is exposed as false.**] concerning the recognition, ratification, approval, renewal, confirmation, donation, concession, and deeds or acts both of other emperors and kings of the Romans who preceded that king and of the king himself, and especially concerning the fidelity [Note: [Col. 0871C] What was said concerning the oath of fidelity (Dissertation on the Rudolphine Code, no. 46 ff.) is reinforced by the unanimous testimony of the princes. It confirms ever more strongly the character of the Western Empire renewed by the supreme pontiff, especially after the Carolingian line, when Otto I assumed the imperial insignia. On this matter Albert, son of Rudolph, must again be heard, speaking thus to Boniface VIII: “With devout affection and sincere heart I profess that the kings of the Romans, who are afterward to be advanced to the imperial dignity, are especially and principally appointed by that same see for this purpose: that they may be advocates of the Holy Roman Church, of the Catholic faith, and its foremost defenders.”**], obedience, honor, and reverence to be shown by Roman emperors and kings to the Roman pontiffs and to that Church herself, and concerning the possessions, honors, and rights of that same Church, specifically concerning the whole land extending from Radicofano to Ceprano, the March of Ancona, the Duchy of Spoleto, the land of Countess Matilda, the city of Ravenna [Ravenne] and Emilia, Bobbio [Bojo], Cesena, Forlimpopoli [Foropopuli], Forlì [Forlivio], Faenza, Imola [Immola], Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adria, and Gavello, Rimini [Aremino], Urbino, Montefeltro [529], the territory of Balneum, the county of Bertinoro [Brettonorii], the Exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, Massa Trabaria [Col. 0871B], with the adjacent lands and all other things belonging to the aforesaid Church, with all boundaries, territories, and islands in sea and on land in any way pertaining to the provinces, cities, territories, and places mentioned above; and likewise concerning the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0871C] Although the city of Rome, as the head of that land which extends from Radicofano to Ceprano, appears to be included among the donations of the princes, as I said in the notes to the Rudolphine diploma, nevertheless, since it would be contrary to fairness and justice for its lordship to be confused with the others, it is named separately by the princes. The reason for this distinct mention is also clear from the present state of affairs; see the preceding dissertation, no. 13 ff.**], and the kingdom of Sicily, with everything belonging to it both on this side of the Faro and beyond it, as well as Corsica and Sardinia [Note: [Col. 0871D] Rudolph does not mention these three islands expressly in his diploma, although he renews what he had confirmed earlier. But the princes, validating whatever Rudolph had committed to writing, here refer to the celebrated edict printed by Raynaldus (1275, no. 38 ff.), issued at Lausanne on the day after the conference with Gregory X, where it reads: “We shall aid in retaining and defending the Roman Church’s kingdom of Sicily with everything belonging to it both on this side of the Faro and beyond it, and also Corsica and Sardinia, together with the other rights known to belong to it.” I have discussed these islands fully in the same dissertation.**], and the remaining lands and rights belonging to that Church—we, in the name of our principalities, approve and ratify all these things in every respect, and to each and every one of them, and to whatever else the same king has in any way done or shall hereafter do concerning them, we unanimously and harmoniously display our will [Col. 0872A], assent, and consent [Note: [Col. 0871D] This singular form of approving even Rudolph’s future diplomas and other writings in support of the rights of the Holy See is a great reproach to certain recent writers [Col. 0872B] who, after failing to investigate the matters thoroughly, preferred to reheat the opinions of the innovators, already long ago refuted by the most learned and venerable Cardinal Baronius and exposed according to the arms and resources of his age, rather than, under Baronius’s guidance, adhering to the best monuments produced by the age, vindicating with Rudolph and the princes of Germany the rights of the prince of the apostles and his successors, rights clearer than daylight.**]

And we promise that at no time shall we act against the foregoing or against any part of the foregoing. Rather, to the best of our ability, we shall ensure that all these things, individually and collectively, are inviolably observed. And so that this our will, approval, ratification, assent [the original adds: “consent”], and promise may be observed by us forever toward the same Roman pontiffs and the Church, we have caused this present document to be drawn up and have strengthened it with the protection of our seals [the original: “strengthened”].

Done and given in the year of the Lord 1279, indiction VII, during the reign of the aforesaid lord, our lord Rudolph, glorious King of the Romans, in the sixth year of his reign [530] [Note: [Col. 0872C] The illustrious college of the Seven, presenting all the princes of the Empire, together with the rights of the Holy See, vindicates Rudolph’s royal majesty once, twice, and three times—whether against the ignorance or the flattery of later writers. For it calls the year 1279 the sixth year of the reign of Rudolph, King of the Romans.**]

## III. Diploma by Which Rudolph Defends Ecclesiastical Rights by a Severe Edict

[Note: [Col. 0872C] Bzovius included this edict in his annals; from him the author of *Austrian Piety* took it (book I, chapter 17, p. 102), observing that many people at that time had tried to deprive churches of their rights. For this reason Rudolph enacted the following provision for their immunity. Raynaldus, speaking of the same constitution (1283, no. 61), says: “It should be added, it seems, to German affairs that Rudolph Caesar issued a constitution this year by which he confirmed the prerogatives granted to ecclesiastical persons.” From the [Col. 0872D] context it is clear that neither the author mentioned above nor Raynaldus understood the true meaning of this constitution.]

Rudolph, by the grace of God ever august King of the Romans, to all the faithful of the Roman Empire who shall inspect these present letters, his grace and every good thing.

Since it befits royal clemency so to bestow liberties and to grant the grace of its generosity and munificence upon those who deserve well that no prejudice thereby be inflicted upon the Empire [Note: [Col. 0872D] He therefore vindicates not merely the rights of churches and ecclesiastical persons, but especially those of the Empire—which is characteristic of a just and good prince: namely, not to lavish upon any private person those things that might inflict any harm upon the principality or upon the holy churches.**], or upon churches and the prelates of churches, in their rights, we wish it to come to the knowledge of all, present and future, that by the liberties with which, from the time of our accession, we have endowed whatever cities and places there are, we do not wish any prejudice to be generated against the Empire, the churches, or the prelates of churches, in their rights and their people [Note: [Col. 0872D] We have seen several privileges of this kind in the letters of the Rudolphine code. Among them are certain privileges confirmed to the cities of Bohemia and Moravia, which they had obtained from Ottokar. Thus Brno, a city of Moravia, enriched by him with very extensive privileges, after the notable victory won over him in 1278, together with his death, obtained from Rudolph a confirmation of those privileges, not without some increase, in that year or the following one (book II, letter 15). This constitution regulates privileges of this kind if they should harm the Empire or the churches.**]

Rather, we wish the Empire and the ecclesiastical prelates to enjoy all those rights which they used before such liberty was granted to these cities and places by us, and which they are known to have possessed in them before the time of that liberty [531] [Note: [Col. 0873A] As we have seen (book III, letter 10), the city of Liège protested against a privilege granted by Rudolph to ecclesiastical persons, but in vain. From this constitution we discover that the privileges granted to cities and places were safeguarded from causing any harm either to the rights of the Empire or to those of ecclesiastical persons. We do not, however, find that privileges granted to ecclesiastical persons were revoked or diminished because the cities and places might thereby suffer some loss.**].

As evidence of this matter, we have ordered that this present document be secured with the seal of our majesty. Given at Hagenau [in Hagen], on the fourth day before the Nones of December, indiction II [Note: [Col. 0873A] Two observations concerning this date are necessary. First, the writer of the code, who gives the day of the month in Roman numerals, records the indiction somewhat inaccurately in Arabic numerals: for in the year 1283 it was not II but XI. Second, Rudolph uses the papal indiction, as it is called, which begins on the Kalends of January, whenever that practice may have begun; for during the eleventh century it was customary to reckon it from the beginning of September, according to the old practice called Greek. Pagius (Historical Dissertation on the Hypati, part III, chapter 2, no. 13) observes that indictions beginning with the civil year on the Kalends of January are found in some places even in the sixth century, a claim that experts in diplomatics certainly will not accept. Ducange, in his *Glossary*, in order to show that the Constantinian or Caesarean indiction has always prevailed and still prevails in Germany, adduces two diplomas: one of Otto II, from the year 892, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, indiction XI; and another of Henry, from the year 1224, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, indiction XIII (Frederick II, not Henry, was emperor at that time). This proves just as much that the Constantinopolitan indiction, beginning on the Kalends of September, as that the Constantinian, beginning on the twenty-fourth of the same month, prevailed in Germany. But it should be regarded as certain that the Caesarean indiction was always customary among the Germans. At Lausanne Rudolph confirms what had been done at Lyons in the year of the Lord 1275, indiction III, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. Yet in October both the Constantinian and the Constantinopolitan indiction were running at IV. Again, in this constitution we see the eleventh indiction recorded, while the twelfth Caesarean indiction was running from the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and the Constantinopolitan from the Kalends of September themselves.**] in the year 1283, and in the tenth year of our reign.

## C
Cadolaus obtains confirmation from Henry II that the county of Parma belongs to him, 223. Coenwulf, king of the English, hostile to the archbishops of Canterbury and York, 64. Gaeta and Fondi belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy See, 147, 159. The Gaetans, together with the Amalfitans, provide assistance to the patrician Michael against the Saracens attacking Sicily, 73. Calabria and Apulia are handed over to the Normans by Nicholas II, 150. The annual revenue of Calabrita and the Sicilian patrimony is 35,000 gold pieces, 10; it is vigorously claimed by the Apostolic See, 103. Fivefold class of slanderers, 410. Calvulus, chamberlain, and Campani accused of high treason, 90. Campania Romana divided into two parts, 147. Its extent, 157. In Otto’s time confused with the Roman territory, 140. Six cities of the duchy of Benevento in Campania, donated by Charlemagne to the Holy See, 128. Campidunum, today Kempten, a city of Swabia in the Allgäu, 396. A canonry of Liège is requested by Rudolph for one of his household, 453, 484. The canonry of Saint Peter began to be conferred on the king of the Romans at the solemnity of his coronation, 272. The disagreement between the archbishop of Canterbury and the archbishop of York over primacy is settled, 64. The fortress of Canossa is founded, 221. Its church treasury is carried to Rome, 216. A captain to be sent by Rudolph into Italy, 334; sent by the king of Bohemia into the province of Salzburg, 392. A capitulary containing much under several chapters, 53. The pre-eminence of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, 324. Garfagnana belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy See by the donation of Matilda, 217. Carinthia. See Meinhard. The Carmelite order tolerated, 399. The Carolingian emperors. See Emperors. When they ceased defending the Roman Church, emperors were sought elsewhere, 28; their end, 243. The so-called Carolingian Books falsely attributed to Charlemagne, 6. Charles Martel numbered among the defenders of the Church, 132. Carloman confirms the paternal donation together with his brother, 95. Charlemagne, defender of the Roman Church before and after obtaining the imperial crown, 2, 54, 59; in matters concerning the doctrine of the faith, consults the Holy See, 7. How, on coming to Rome, he is received into the church of Saint Peter, 255; and how exceedingly generous he is toward the Roman pontiff, 8. On four visits to Rome he bestows provinces and cities on the Holy See, 100. On his final arrival he is crowned emperor Augustus, 16. False opinions concerning this coronation, 18. He designates his son Louis as emperor and heir of the kingdoms, 20. He obtains the empire not by arms but by defending the Holy See, 37. He is called by Leo III the Church’s guardian and its defender in its interests, 50 ff. For the archbishop of Grado, driven from his see, he obtains the church of Pola, 48. He divides the kingdoms among his sons, 58, 99. Thinking himself deceived by the papal legates, he is appeased by Leo III, 66. He establishes a certain peace with Michael, emperor of the East, 76. The alleged grant to him of the election of the Roman pontiff is fictitious, 181. He dies, 82. Charles the Bald is elected and confirmed at a council, 243; crowned by John VIII, 28, 254. Charles the Fat is elected, 242; crowned by John VIII, 28, 254. [Col. 0877] Charles, Rudolph’s son, dies in childhood, 306. Charles IV, author of the Golden Bull, 346; first obtains the apostolic privilege of first prayers, 392; the last to give the oath concerning the dispatch of a governor into the kingdom of Italy, 234. Charles V is crowned at Bologna by Clement VII in an exceptional manner, 43; at the coronation he performs the office of deacon contrary to ancestral custom, 274; he is designated heir of the duchy of Milan, 232. Charles of Anjou, brother of Saint Louis IX, is summoned into Italy, 315. In Tuscany he becomes peacekeeper, and afterward imperial vicar, 330, 496; he becomes senator of Rome for ten years, 502. He obtains Sicily subject to a census of eight thousand ounces of gold, 511; he takes an oath to the Roman pontiff, 512. He has disputes with Rudolph, 283, 368, 428, 496. For this reason he is barred from an Italian expedition, 283. He takes possession of the kingdom of Jerusalem through his legate, 477. He marries his daughter Isabella to Ladislaus, king of Hungary, 375. He receives the investiture of Provence from Rudolph, 284; he is again made senator of Rome by Martin IV, ibid. The Porta Castelli is the place designated for receiving the king of the Romans who is to be crowned, 268. Catherine, Rudolph’s daughter, wife of Otto, duke of Bavaria, 306, 409. Count Cavalca, Brictonorium, formerly belonging by ancient right to the Holy See, donates it again to the same see, 208. The census established for the kingdom of Sicily is different at different times, 505 ff., 513, 518; it is imposed in full on Sicily on this side of the Strait, 515. Leo X reduces it to seven thousand ducats, 517. An older census book than that of Cencio the Chamberlain, 145. Charter of donation. See Matilda. The bishops of Chiemsee, John and Conrad, 387. Chokier, concerning the first prayers, not quite correctly, 288. A chorography of medieval Italy is noted, 123, 138, 214. Christian, the last patriarch of Antioch, is slain, 478. The church of Saint Christina in Insubria belongs to the jurisdiction of the Holy See, 147. Chronology of Rudolph’s letters, 276; of Otto’s diplomas, 137; of Henry’s, 171; of Matilda’s charter, 196. Chrysostom (Saint John) commends a prince’s clemency, 474. Cistercian monks, famous for holiness, 303; the support of their prayers, or their confraternity, is sought by the greatest princes, 306. Number of their abbeys, 305. They first obtain privileges from Innocent IV, 507; their first general chapter, 303. The Leonine City is dedicated by Leo IV, 255. The cities of Lombardy, asserting their liberty, invade Matilda’s possessions, 205 ff.; four of them belong by private right to Matilda, 226. The free Etruscan cities are erected into a grand duchy, 234. The keys of the confession of Saint Peter and of the Holy Sepulchre are sent to Charlemagne as a blessing, 12. The keys of the kingdom of heaven are entrusted by the Lord to the prince of the apostles, 55; why he is called the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, 67, 139. Clement III makes peace with the Roman Senate, 500. Clement IV grants Sicily to Charles of Anjou, 496. Clement V crowns Henry VII through legates, 43, 365. By the constitution *Pastoralis* he decrees that, when the empire is vacant, the pontiff succeeds the emperor in Lombardy and Tuscany, 228. Clement VII crowns Charles V, 43. Clement XI concerns himself with the privilege of first prayers, 293. Clement XIII grants the author permission to inspect with his own eyes and carefully collate the original diplomas of the Apostolic Archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, 136. Clemency is necessary for the greatest princes, 474. Clementia, Rudolph’s daughter, is the wife of Charles Martel, grandson of Charles, king of Sicily, 306, 433. The Roman clergy and people receive the king of the Romans and lead him to the Vatican basilica at the solemnity of his coronation, 255. The Carolingian Codex was written nine years before the renewal of the empire, 100. The Farnesian Codex of the pontifical book belongs to the age of Charlemagne, 95. The Rudolphine Codex of Zwettl, 296. It contains 126 letters, of which eighteen had already been published, 299. The Colline Gate near the Castle of Saint Angelo, 268. Comacchio restored to the Holy See at the urging of Benedict XIII, 427. The diets of Nuremberg and Augsburg, 344, 355, 393; of Kempten, 386. The Third Lateran Council on the conferral of benefices, 290; the Second Council of Lyon on the sacred expedition into Syria, 462; the Second Council of Nicaea in favor of sacred images, 6; the Council of Trent on abolishing the use of duels, 454. The German Concordats, 416. Harmony between priesthood and empire, 371. The conspiracy against Saint Leo III and the punishment inflicted on the guilty, 89. Conrad I, king of Germany, disrupts the succession of the Augusti, 244. Conrad II the Salian is crowned Augustus, 169, 195, 245, 259. Conrad III did not obtain the imperial crown, 400; he calls himself the second king of the Romans, 169. Conrad, son of Frederick II, invades the kingdom of Sicily, 508; he dies after drinking poison, ibid. Conrad the Swabian restores the duchy of Spoleto and the county of Assisi to the Holy See, 207. Conrad the Franciscan, Rudolph’s legate to Nicholas III, 419, 437. Hermann Conring publishes the ten letters of Saint Leo III more than once, 1 ff., 78. He discusses the family and homeland of Rudolph, king of the Romans, 304. The Donation of Constantine is fictitious, 89. Constantine Copronymus dies; his son Leo IV succeeds him, 6. Constantine, son of Leo IV, is under the guardianship of his mother Irene, 6. The constitution of Lothar, with the consent of Eugenius II, 63, 152, is falsely attributed to Otto and Henry, 153. By what formula the imperial crown was customarily imposed, 265, 456. The imperial coronation is to be performed by one Roman pontiff, 19. It alone constitutes an emperor, 39. The rite of crowning the Carolingians, 254. The solemnity of crowning the Germans, 260. Formerly it was customarily performed before the solemn Mass, 273. The imperial coronation began to be performed by Anatolius, patriarch under Leo I, in the year 457, 81. The imperial coronation was always desired by Rudolph but never obtained, 323. Its date must be assigned by the pontiff, not without the consent of the king of the Romans, 365. The same matter was treated by Innocent III for Otto IV, 273; for Rudolph by Nicholas III, 443, to whom the number of soldiers to be taken with him is prescribed, 525. [Col. 0878] Corsica was donated to the Holy See by Charlemagne, 3, 60; when harassed by the Moors, the Franks defended it, 78. Its donation, like that of Sicily and Sardinia, took place after the year 791, 100, 128. The rights of the Holy See over that island, 144. *Credentia* and letters of credence, 435. The king of Cyprus writes to Rudolph about the unhappy condition of Syria, 476.

## D

Peter Damian on the apostolic privilege of confirming the election of the Roman pontiff, 121. Deacons. See Senators. Tithes to be collected in Germany for the crusade, 353, 362. Granted to Alfonso, king of Castile, 354. The defense of the Roman Church and of the supreme pontiff is the true cause of the renewal of the empire in the West, 37. The title “Defender” is attributed to Charlemagne after his coronation, 2, 54, 59, 62. A delegation undertaken for the acquisition of Church property, 190. Demetrius, duke of Croatia and Dalmatia, honored by Gregory VII with the title of king, subjects his possessions to the Holy See, 236. Demetrius, king of the Russians, subjects his possessions to the See of Peter, 236. After Desiderius is expelled, an end is brought to the Lombard kingdom, 96. The extent of the dominion of the Roman Church assigned to Charles by its boundaries, 99. *Diffidatio*, or declaration of war, 377. It was also customarily sent to the sultan, 482. It was not sent by Ottocarus to Rudolph, ibid. The diploma confirming the privileges of the Holy See, customary in the Carolingian period to be read at the solemnity of the coronation, 31. The Germans began to do this within eight days, 492, 500. Otto’s original diploma, written in letters of gold in the archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, 134, 136, 156; its seal has perished, 137; its authenticity, 138, 161. Ancient diplomas bear no title, 134; their character, 153. Several examples of Otto’s and Henry’s diplomas accurately copied from the originals and strengthened with the seals of forty prelates at the Council of Lyon, I, 135. After thirty years they are confirmed by Rudolph through legates, together with the Ludovician diploma, at the Second Council of Lyon, 278. Nicholas III sends excerpts from these three to Rudolph, so that he may prepare his own diploma from them, 520. The procedure for creating the Roman pontiff in the time of Louis, 131, 178, 181; in Otto’s age, 153 ff.; in Henry’s, 181. The eastern boundaries and shores of the ecclesiastical dominion, 74. The western boundaries resemble those of our own age, 98. Their various names in Rudolph’s time, 495. They were unknown even to the Roman pontiffs themselves while residing at Avignon, 520. The division of Charlemagne’s kingdoms among his sons, 99. The rule of the pontiffs in Rome and in the duchy is aristocratic, 109. In the exarchate and the other donations it is monarchical, ibid. The orders of Saints Dominic and Francis are judged useful to the Church at the Second Council of Lyon, 399. A certain Dominic, recommended by Charles to Hadrian for some government office in the territories of the Holy See, 96. All Matilda’s possessions are called “the House.” See Matilda. The Donation of Pippin is renewed by Charles, 100. The Carolingian donation was made four times, 8, 100. All donations are made for the salvation of the donor’s soul and for the forgiveness of sins, 100. Neither Louis nor Rudolph uses this formula, because they donate nothing, 524. The spontaneous donations of Pippin and his successors, 177. [Col. 0879] Drogo, bishop of Metz, is made by Sergius II apostolic vicar of Gaul and Germany, 114. The origin of the duchy of Milan, 231. Charles V is designated its heir, 232. Charles du Cange, dissertation on the coinage of the lower age, 258. Duels were permitted in the thirteenth century, 454; at the Council of Trent they were entirely abolished, ibid.

## E

Edmund, son of Henry III, king of England, is offered the kingdom of Sicily, 508. Eambald, archbishop of York, 64, 67. Eardulf, king of Northumbria, expelled and restored, 63, 66, 69. Eckard and Muratori acknowledge the supreme right of the Roman pontiff in the exarchate, 106. The property of the churches must not be alienated, 48. Edward, king of England, betroths his daughter Margaret to Hartmann, Rudolph’s son, 306. Einhard, witness to Charlemagne’s unexpected coronation, 16. The hermitage monastery of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, 468. Its abbot is a prince of the empire, ibid. The election of the Roman pontiff. See Roman pontiff. Canonical elections prevail in Germany, 445. The decree of election, 448. The character of an elective principate, 310. The origin of the electors of the Holy Roman Empire, 246, 527. Their names, 247; change, 248; the number seven becomes fixed after Frederick II, 249. Several are from the same family, 347. Rudolph’s royal diplomas confirm them, 429, 509. The Elephant, a public prison in Rome, 90. Elias of Insat, legate of the Holy Land, 480. Elizabeth, mother of Ladislaus, king of Hungary, confirms decrees against heretics in her territories, 487. The title “Most Eminent” is attributed to Roman nobles, 33. Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, suffers much from his own people, 372, 445. The morals of the bishops of Germany are corrupt, 348. Letters of the imperial codex at Zwettl missing: Rudolph’s to Gregory X concerning his election, 280; those of the archbishop of Cologne to the same pontiff, 400; of a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church to Rudolph, 319; of Bernard, bishop of Seckau, to Rudolph, 405; of Nicholas III to Rudolph after the slaughter of Ottocar, 421; of Rudolph to Nicholas III after the same slaughter, 428. Rudolph’s privilege for the monastery of Zwettl, 472. The emperor’s riding with the pontiff after the coronation has degenerated, 275. The ride of the Roman pontiff after the coronation to the Lateran palace, 267. A white horse for the census of the two Sicilies, 511. Ercambald, chancellor of Charlemagne, 49. Monastery of the hermitage. See Einsiedeln. The river Eridanus marks out Matilda’s possessions, 203. The beginnings of Este rule in the duchy of Modena, 234. Etruria and Lombardy belong to the imperial jurisdiction, 38. In Lombardy the duchy of Milan arose, 231. In Etruria there was formerly the grand duchy of Tuscany, 234, 310, 330. Eugenius II enacted something concerning the election of the Roman pontiff, 184. A privilege concerning confirmation of the election, falsely attributed to the emperor, 113, 122. Euphemia, a nun, Rudolph’s daughter, 306. [Col. 0879] Euphemius of Constantinople, the very first patriarch to require a profession of faith from the emperor Anastasius, in 491, 44. Euphemius the Sicilian treacherously subjects Sicily to the Saracens, 78. The entire exarchate is asserted to belong to the Holy See, 51. In Charlemagne’s time it was divided into three provinces: Ravenna or Emilia, and the two Pentapoles, the Maritime and the Mediterranean, 97. Their chief city was Ravenna, 337. In Rudolph’s age it had two names, Romandiola and Maritima, 278. The county of Romandiola was distinguished from the exarchate, 495 ff., 522. Hence the invasion by Rudolph’s predecessors appeared to be an imperial right, 335 ff. Once informed of the matter and having disapproved the act of his chancellor, he vigorously vindicates the rights of the Holy See, 428. Formerly the archbishops of Ravenna ruled in the exarchate by apostolic privileges, 208, 277. With what solemnity the Eastern emperor’s exarch was received at Rome, 255. The reception of kings and emperors coming to Rome, 59. Expectative graces abolished, 290.

## F

The Guelph and Ghibelline factions in Italy, 213. Ferrara: its vicissitudes and its assured subjection to the Holy See, 234. Matilda possessed much in its territory, 216. Imperial fiefs and privileges are conferred by the king of the Romans, 311. On the electors immediately after the German coronation, 346. The oath of fidelity sworn by the king of the Romans to the pontiff, 42, 262, 270; by the Romans to the emperor, 23, 28, 56; by the princes of Germany to the king of the Romans, 313. Florentinus’s notable error concerning the patrimony of the Roman Church, 197, 211. Fod na Argentaria is leased by Rudolph, 468. The established formula: “Neither cancelled nor abolished,” etc. It is found in Rudolph’s diploma, 488. The formulas for handing over the imperial insignia, 265, especially the sword, 272, 274. Fortunatus of Grado, archbishop, expelled from his see, lives in exile in France, 47; his bad reputation, 49. The orders of Saints Francis and Dominic approved, 399. The Friars Minor, or Franciscans, are especially dear to Nicholas III because of the holiness of their life, 442. A monastery of penitent women is entrusted to them, 441. See Conrad. Francisco de Roxas, ambassador of Ferdinand, the Catholic king, to Julius II, 516. The Council of Frankfurt condemns the canon of Nicholas II as wrongly understood, 6. The confraternity of the Cistercian order sought by princes, 305. Frederick I Barbarossa is the first of the emperors to become a canon of Saint Peter, 271, 272, 460. Frederick II, son of Henry VI, is elected king at the age of two by his father, 389. On the very day of his imperial coronation he issues a constitution against heresies, confirmed by Honorius III, 488; Rudolph later confirms it, 487. He is deposed at the Second Council of Lyon, 228, 508. (Hence Rudolph counts an interregnum of twenty-eight years, 460.) He restores Matilda’s land to the Holy See, 202; he becomes the greatest invader of the territories of the Holy See, 508. Frederick III obtains from Nicholas V the privilege of first prayers, 293. Frederick, Rudolph’s son, dies childless, 306. Frederick II, archbishop of Salzburg, is ordered by Gregory X to attend Rudolph’s coronation, 329. He writes to Rudolph that he will attend, 355. He accuses the bishop of Seckau, [Col. 0880] 378. Harassed by Ottocar, he asks Rudolph for help, 380, 382. He reports that Milota has been sent with troops into his province, 392. He reports to Gregory X the unhappy condition of the clergy and churches, ibid. He warns Rudolph to beware of domestic plots, 384. Rudolph commends his sincere loyalty, 385. He visits his province, 389. He absolves the peoples from the oath they had sworn to Ottocar, 402. Together with his suffragans he announces to John XXI the liberation of Austria, 411.

## G

Dominic, recommended by Charles, is appointed count in the city of Gabellum by Hadrian, 96. Garampius, canon of Saint Peter, prefect of the Vatican archives and of the Castle of Saint Angelo, 217. Garfagnana. See Carfagnana. Gatticus, abbot, collector of the Roman orders of regular canons, 20. Benedict Gentilotus, prefect of the Vienna library, supplies documents to Coleto for his edition of Ughelli, 463. All Germany swears fidelity to Rudolph, 313. Its unhappy condition after the interregnum, 315. Its princes obtain the privilege of electing the king of the Romans, 169. The German crown makes the future king of the Romans an emperor, 246. The sword is handed to the emperor from the sacred altar of the prince of the apostles according to the ancient orders, 272; according to the more recent orders, it is taken from above the body, 274. Godfrey, provost of Solingen, subscribes Rudolph’s diploma in favor of the Holy See, 526; Rudolph recommends him to the canons for the vacant church of Passau, 486. Godfrey, abbot of Godwic, proves by monuments that no one was emperor, or called himself emperor, before the Roman coronation, 39. He testifies that Otto’s and Henry’s diplomas were written in letters of gold, 135. He discusses the character of ancient diplomas, 153. He speaks less accurately concerning the title “king of the Romans,” 245. Godfrey of Viterbo on the golden apple, 259. The vicissitudes of the church of Grado, 48. Gratian is not very reliable in reporting ancient monuments, 37. Gratian the *superista*, accused before the apostolic pontiff and the emperor, 24. Gregory IV, refusing to be consecrated, is the reason why imperial authority is invoked, 116. Gregory V and Otto III issue a constitution concerning the election of the king of the Romans, 168, 245. Gregory VI renounces the pontificate at the Council of Sutri, 261. Gregory VII, Saint, restores by right of return the freedom of consecrating the Roman pontiff, 120. He compares pontifical and imperial power to the two greater lights, 316. Gregory X, Saint, is elected at Viterbo while residing in Syria with the Christian army, 315. His family, homeland, and travels, 357. Scarcely consecrated, he convokes the Second Council of Lyon, 315. He urges the princes of the empire to come to the solemnity of Rudolph’s coronation, 281, 343. He ratifies the peace between Ottocar, king of Bohemia, and Stephen, king of Hungary, 395. He prudently refuses Rudolph a pecuniary favor, 333. Leaving the Viscount behind, he adheres to the Torriani, 340. At Milan he publishes Clement IV’s bull known as *In Coena Domini*, 352. He plans to return to Syria with the Christian army, 476. He dies at Arezzo, 276, 282, 496; he is renowned for miracles, 363. His letter has been interpolated, 357. [Col. 0881] Gregory XIII is exceedingly generous toward the poor, 11. Grimoald, son of Arichis, duke of Benevento, is taken by Charlemagne as a hostage to France, 101. Guido. See Wido. William. See Willelmus. Dietrich, bishop of Gurk, dies, 387. Gutha, also called Judith, Rudolph’s daughter, marries Wenceslaus, son of Ottocar, after Ottocar’s death, 422.

## H

The distinction between a hereditary principate and an elective one, 310. The privileges of the city of Halle granted by Rudolph, 447. Hartmann, Rudolph’s son, dies childless, 306. Hedwig, Rudolph’s mother, enters a monastery, 308. Hedwig, also called Anna, Rudolph’s daughter, marries Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, 306, 346. Helmengaud, Charlemagne’s legate to Leo III, 3, 58. Henry I, king of Germany, confuses the chronology of emperors bearing the same name among historians, 244. Henry I, Saint, swears the oath of fidelity to Benedict VIII, 39. By a diploma he confirms the rights of the Holy See, 170. Henry II, also called III, swears fidelity to Clement II, 42, 262. He exchanges the transalpine rights of the Holy See for the principality of Benevento, 195. He did not assume the Italian crown, 245. Henry IV, king of the Romans, the third of that name, captures Mantua, belonging by right to Matilda, through treachery, 221; she defeats him in the fields of Sorbara, 224. Henry V, king of Germany, the third Augustus, invades Matilda’s possessions, 200. He does not assume the Italian crown, 245. The Romans are hostile to him, 312. Henry VI, son of Frederick I, makes his two-year-old son Frederick II king, 389. In his testament he orders that what was wrongly taken be restored to the Holy See, 209. He orders that the investiture of Sicily be received from that see, 510. Henry VII appoints Galeatius vicar in Piacenza, 229. He swears fidelity to the pontiff through messengers at Avignon, 42. Out of necessity he is crowned outside the Vatican basilica, 43. Henry, duke of Bavaria, adhering to Ottocar, is hostile to Rudolph, 310, 346, 352; he is brought back into order, 397; he is not proclaimed an enemy of the empire, as Ottocar was, 353. Through the efforts of the pontiff and Rudolph he is reconciled with his brother Louis, 354; he is forbidden to negotiate peace between Ottocar and the king of Hungary, ibid. He is reconciled with Rudolph, 409. Henry, brother of the king of Castile, is made senator of Rome by the factious Romans, 502. Henry, bishop of Basel, collector of tithes for the crusade, 333. Rudolph’s legate to Innocent V, 369, 437. He leaves Rome when the pontiff dies, 375. Henry, bishop of Trent, has disputes with Meinhard, count of Tyrol, 485; Rudolph appoints them arbiters of peace, ibid. Henry of Fürstenberg is sent by Rudolph as governor into Romandiola, which he believes belongs to the imperial jurisdiction, 334 ff. A council and diet are held at Würzburg, 344. Hermann, or Hartmann, another son of Rudolph, to whom Margaret, daughter of Edward, king of England, had been betrothed, is drowned in the Rhine, 306. Hermannus Contractus is noted, 261. Johann Heumann on ancient diplomas, 153. Hildewald, archbishop of Cologne, is sent to meet Leo III as he flees to the Franks, [Col. 0881] 49. Honorius II is the first to invest Duke Albert with Matilda’s possessions after the death of Henry V, the invader, 200. Honorius III crowns Emperor Frederick II, 508. Honorius IV writes to Rudolph concerning the date of the coronation, 285. The Hospitallers. See the Teutonic Order. Hugh, king of Italy, marries Marozia and rules in Rome with her, 33. He is driven out by Alberic, Marozia’s son, 34. He makes peace through the marriage of the king’s daughter Alda, ibid. Hugh of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, describes to Rudolph the unhappy condition of the Holy Land, 476. The counsel of Humbert of Romans to Nicholas III concerning the division of the Roman empire, 287. Hunfrid, Charlemagne’s legate to Leo III, 58.

## I

The insolence of Illyricus Flaccus toward the Roman pontiff, 1. Illyricus treats both matters pertaining to the consecration of the Roman pontiff, 9. The emperor in the West is renewed by Saint Leo III, 19, 31, 44. His coronation is to be performed by one Roman pontiff, 39. His office is the defense of the Holy See and the Roman pontiff, 4, 14, 251, 481, 528. There were seven Carolingian emperors, with two inserted from a foreign stock and as many added from the female line, 20.
