1. Charlemagne, crowned by Leo III in the year 800, on 25 December; died in 814, on 28 January, 17, 253.  
2. Louis the Pious, his son, crowned by Stephen IV in 816; died in 840, on 20 June, 20.  
3. Lothar, his son, crowned by Saint Paschal in 823; died in 855, on 28 September, 21, 254.  
4. Louis II, his son, crowned by Saint Leo IV in 850; died in 875, on 13 August, 28.  
5. Charles the Bald, son of Louis the Pious, crowned by John VIII in 876; died the following year, on 6 October, 28.  
6. Charles the Fat, son of Louis the German, crowned by the same pontiff in 880; deposed in 887, on 11 November; died the following year, on 12 January, 28.  
7. Wido, duke of Spoleto, rival of Berengar, crowned by Stephen V in 891; died in 894, 28.  
8. Lambert, son of Wido, crowned by Formosus in 892; died in 898, 28, 242.  
9. Arnulf, son of Carloman, brother of Charles the Fat, crowned by the same Formosus in 896; died in 899, 242.  
10. Louis III, son of Ermengard, daughter of Louis II, crowned by Benedict IV in 900; two years later blinded by Berengar, he lives a wretched life, 28.  
11. Berengar, son of Gisla, daughter of Louis the Pious, crowned by John X in 916; slain at Verona in 924, 28, 243.

See each separately under its own entry. The first six of these were elected by right of succession; the rest in the hope of defending the Church, 242. Their solemn reception, 254 ff. The solemnity of their coronation, 253. They make a profession to the pontiff, 40. By diploma they confirm the rights and privileges of the Holy See; this diploma is read at the solemnity of the coronation, 29. They receive an oath of fidelity from the Romans, 22. Through the crown they become partners in the pontiff’s supreme authority, 24, 251, 287. The beginning of the Carolingian empire was in 800, its end in 923, 243.

Twelve German emperors preceded Rudolph, king of the Romans. [Col. 0882]

1. Otto the Great, crowned by John XII in 962; died in 973, 35, 137.  
2. Otto II, crowned by John XIII in 967; died in 983, 39, 504.  
3. Otto III, crowned by Gregory V in 996; died in 1002, 168, 504.  
4. Henry, Saint, crowned by Benedict VIII in 1014; died in 1024, 40.  
5. Conrad the Salian, crowned by John XIX in 1027; died in 1039, 195.  
6. Henry II, crowned by Clement II in 1046; died in 1056, 42, 262.  
7. Henry, king of Germany, the fifth of that name, crowned by Paschal II in 1111; died in 1125, 272, 312.  
8. Lothar II, crowned by Innocent II in 1133; died in 1137, 43.  
9. Frederick I Barbarossa, crowned by Hadrian IV in 1155; died in 1190, 270.  
10. Henry, king of Germany, the sixth of that name, crowned by Celestine III in 1191; died in 1197, 260, 504.  
11. Otto IV, crowned by Innocent III in 1209; died in 1218, 372, 494, 504.  
12. Frederick II, crowned by Honorius III in 1220; deposed by Leo IV at the Second Council of Lyon in 1245, although he survived until 1250, 494.

The election of the Ottos was either carried out or approved by the Roman pontiff, 243. Saint Henry was the first of all to be elected king of the Romans by the German princes, 169, 244. At the solemnity of the coronation they swear an oath of fidelity to the Roman pontiff, 40, 262. The rites for receiving them at the castle gate, 261; the canons of Saint Peter begin to perform them, 271. The subdeacons perform their office at the coronation Mass, 274. If anyone did not attain the Roman crown, he was not called emperor, 347.

Five emperors after Rudolph, up to Charles V, are mentioned in passing.

1. Henry, king of Germany, the seventh of that name, crowned in 1312 by Clement V through cardinal legates; died in 1313, 271.  
2. Charles IV, crowned by Innocent VI through cardinal legates in 1355; died in 1378, 43.  
3. Sigismund, crowned by Eugenius IV in 1433; died in 1437, 234.  
4. Frederick III, crowned by Nicholas V in 1452; died in 1493, 243.  
5. Charles V, the last of all, crowned by Clement VII in 1530; died in 1558, 43.

There were ten elected emperors, or kings of the Romans, up to Charles V.

1. Henry, king of Germany, the fourth of that name, elected in 1053; died in 1106, 491.  
2. Conrad, king of Germany, the third of that name, elected in 1138; died in 1152, 400.  
3. Rudolph, elected in 1273; died in 1291, 276, 311.  
4. Adolf, elected in 1292; died in 1298, 306.  
5. Albert, son of Rudolph, elected in 1298; died in 1308, 203, 306, 395, 401, 472.  
6. Louis the Bavarian, elected in 1314; died in 1347, 229, 492.  
7. Wenceslaus, elected in 1376; removed in 1400, 231, 234.  
8. Robert, elected in 1400; died in 1410, 234.  
9. Albert II of Austria, elected in 1438; died the following year, 306.  
10. Maximilian I, elected in 1486; died in 1519, 481.

These ten call themselves in acts and diplomas kings of the Romans or elected emperors, 481. The election of all was confirmed by papal authority, 18. The apostolic confirmation of the king of the Romans and the privilege of first prayers are thought equivalent to the coronation, which ceased with Charles V. [Col. 0883] 251.

The Eastern emperors mentioned are Constantine Copronymus; Leo IV, his son, successor in impiety and in the empire; and Constantine, a child under the guardianship of his mother Irene, 6, 8. Their election was manifold, 18. They began to be crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople, 19, 81. A profession of faith was required of them, 44. Their succession continued for four hundred years after the renewal of the Western Empire by Leo III, 521. Michael Palaeologus restored the succession, interrupted by the Latins for nearly sixty years, for approximately two hundred years before the capture of Constantinople in 1453, ibid. Imperial temporal power exists for the defense of the Catholic faith, just as pontifical spiritual power is circumscribed by no limits, 481. Therefore, just as the pontiff is compared by Gregory VII and Innocent III to the sun, so the emperor is compared to the moon, 316. This was the common opinion in the Middle Ages, 260.

The imperial insignia of the Carolingians were the crown, sword, and scepter, 254. In addition to these three, the Germans had the orb surmounted by a cross, 258, and sometimes also a ring, 265. Imperial excellence is attributed to Rudolph by the king of Cyprus, 476. The princes of the empire begin to confirm the imperial diploma asserting the rights of the Holy See, 492. The empire was renewed in the West by Saint Leo III, 4; it was transferred to the Germans, as is said, by John XII, 32. Its seat is Germany; Lombardy and Tuscany belong to it, 277, 287.

Innocent II crowns Lothar II, 43. He invests him with the possessions of Countess Matilda, 200. He establishes the kingdom of Sicily, 506. Innocent III is the most vigorous champion of the rights of the Holy See, 494 ff. He grants Salinguerra part of Matilda’s possessions, 201. He commends himself and the Roman Church to the Cistercians, 303. Following Gregory VII’s example, he compares pontifical power to the sun and imperial power to the moon, 316. He enlarges the rite of the imperial coronation, 273. He disapproves of expectative graces, 290. He settles disputes between the Templars and Hospitallers, 457. He begins to call Sicily on this side of the Strait and Sicily beyond it by separate names, 510. He approves the transfer of the Eastern Empire from the schismatics to the Latins, 521. Innocent IV decrees at the First Council of Lyon that faith should be placed in diplomas confirming the rights of the Holy See, copied and strengthened by the seals of forty prelates, as though they were originals, 135. By his counsel the seven electors trace their origin, 247. Innocent V, pontiff for five months, accomplishes several things, 367. He commends the archbishop and church of Cologne to Rudolph, 372. Innocent VI crowns Charles IV through legates, 43. Innocent VIII grants the investiture of Sicily according to the ancient custom, 514. The interregnum after Frederick II is called disastrous by the Germans, 227, 494. Gregory VII’s investiture of Robert Guiscard, 150. The various invocations of diplomas according to local style, 92. Isabella, daughter of the king of Sicily, marries Ladislaus, king of Hungary, 375. Ischia, formerly called Aenaria, Inarime, and Pithecusa, 73. Italy, or the Italian kingdom, or Lombardy, 89. It afterward became the duchy of Milan, 231. Its kings during the vacancy of the empire after Berengar, 243. When the empire is vacant, it obeys the pontiff, 228. Roman security depends on its governors, 230. The kingdom is disturbed and its ancient rights perish, 225. Like Tuscany and other provinces, it is subject to factions, 315. Itherius and Maginarius establish the boundaries of Sabina, 101.

## J

John of Jandun. See Marsilius. Jesse, bishop of Amiens, accused, 65. John IX restores the imperial confirmation of the papal election out of necessity, 118. John XII, from the Tusculan counts, invades the pontificate, 34. He transfers the empire to the Germans, 35, 243. He swears to Otto that he will not support Otto’s rivals, 35, 41. John XXI is created successor to Hadrian V, 373, 411. He forbids Rudolph to come into Italy, 283. John, bishop of Silva Candida, legate of Leo III, 89. John of Vico, prefect of Viterbo, usurps tyranny in the patrimony, 213. John of Spanheim, hostile to the archbishop of Mainz, 467. The Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem are received by Rudolph under his protection, 457 ff. Josue, abbot of Aachen, is present at the Ludovician diploma, 87, 124. Jews and other subjects are burdened with obligations in Moravia, 423. The library of the Julia Academy, 1. The sacred and civil rights of the Holy See are asserted in equal measure, 9. The rights and privileges of the Holy See are confirmed by diploma by the Carolingians on the very day of the coronation, 29; by the Germans within eight days, 492, 500.

The oath of the Normans concerning Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, 85. The oath of Charles of Anjou concerning the kingdom of the Two Sicilies, 512. The oath of the Aragonese after the kingdom was divided into two parts, 513. The oath of the Carolingian kings to the pontiff before the coronation, 40. The oath of the kings of Germany, 36, 39, 42. The oath of the king of the Romans, 262, 270. The oath of the Roman pontiff to the emperor, 154. The oath of the electors, 523. The oath of Lothar II before the doors of the Lateran, 43. The oath of the Roman people to the emperor, 23, 28, 56, which it was impious for them to swear to a king, 23, 41. The oath of the king of the Romans to the Roman people, 42, 268. The royal oath compared with the imperial oath, 356. The oath of Robert Guiscard concerning the Two Sicilies, 149. Rudolph’s oath to Gregory X at Lausanne, 523. The oath that Ottocar extorted from his subjects, 392, 412. The German jurists are not quite correct concerning the renewal of the empire, 37.

## K
Karlus: thus always in the original charter of Otto, 158 ff. Karolus is always written in the letters of Leo III, 47 ff. Kunegundis, Ottocar’s wife, inflames his anger, 482.

## L

Labbe publishes the letters of Leo III from another edition of Conring, 1. Ladislaus, king of Hungary, succeeds his father, 375. The same man, together with his brother Andreas, duke of Slavonia, is adopted by Rudolph, 394, 403; he enters into an alliance with Rudolph, 416, 424; Rudolph invites him to enter into an alliance, 399; he is summoned to the final conflict with Ottocar, 403. Since he had both old and recent quarrels with him, 415, he defects to the Cumans and causes trouble for the Holy See, 425. He orders that all enactments against heresies be observed in his kingdom, 487.

Petrus Lambecius intended to publish Rudolph’s codex, 296.

Lambert, son of Wido, becomes co-ruler of the empire, 242.

The island of Lampadusa is invaded by the Saracens, 73.

Landulf of Greece, constable of Benevento, 179.

Lombardy, today the duchy of Milan, was subject to imperial jurisdiction, 38, 310, 340.

The end of the Lombard kingdom, 96.

In the Lateran church two emperors necessarily received their coronation: Lothar II and Henry VII, 43.

Laudes, or acclamations, at the imperial coronation, 19.

Lausanne, a city in Switzerland, where Gregory X and Rudolph confer, 321, 349, 398.

The *lega*, or law concerning the minting of coinage, 471.

Legates of the princes are excluded from the election of the Roman pontiff, 182.

Legates of the princes and cities of Germany must attend the emperor’s coronation, 350, 356.

The legate of the Holy Land, reduced to the last extremity, 480.

The laws of the Franks and Lombards supplemented by Charles, 23 ff.

The character of the supposed royal law of Hadrian, 48; its substance, 166.

A legislator amends or abolishes a law for a just reason, 439.

Leibniz published Mathilda’s charter from a Vatican codex, 196.

Leo III, successor of Hadrian, 2. Blinded in a monstrous sacrilege, he fled to Charles the patrician in France, 14. He reclaims the revenues of the palace of Ravenna as belonging to the Holy See, 51. His remarkable gentleness toward his accusers, 55, 60. He appeases Charles, who was angry with the pontifical legates who had failed in their duty, 67; he dies, 90. He renews the Western Empire in order to provide protection for the pontiff, the Roman Church, and the orthodox faith, 308.

Leo IV was the first who, with the permission of the Carolingian Augusti, had to be consecrated, 115. He voluntarily made a profession which several successors presented before the imperial envoys, 155; on this occasion something new seems to have been introduced, 184. He dedicates the Leonine City, which he had built, 255.

Leo VIII, a pseudo-pontiff, author of a fictitious constitution, 165. Baronius recognizes it as fictitious, 181.

Leo X reduced the tribute of Sicily to 7,000 ducats, 517.

Leo I, emperor of the East, is crowned by Anatolius the patriarch, 81.

Leo IV, emperor of the East, dies, leaving the child Constantine under his mother’s guardianship, 6.

Leo V, surnamed the Armenian, succeeds Michael, 80.

The citizens of Liège request that the privilege of the clergy, harmful to them, be revoked, 438. The church of Liège is praised in the highest terms by Rudolph, 453, 486. The bishop of Liège issues a law postponing the appointed day for judicial duels, 454.

The Leonine City is dedicated, 255.

Levold of Northof, on the archbishops of Cologne, 445.

Libellous writings against Rudolph, 405.

Men of learning were held in esteem by the highest princes, 486.

The coastal territories of the Holy See distinguished from the coastal territories of the kingdom of Italy, 60.

Place-names in ecclesiastical territory changed, 179.

### Lothar I Augustus

Lothar I Augustus, son of Louis the Pious, is crowned as co-ruler of his father’s empire by Saint Paschal, 21, 254. With the consent of Eugene II he issues a law concerning the administration of ecclesiastical territory, 63, 152. The same law is falsely attributed to Otto and Henry, 153, 162. He obtains the privilege of confirming the election of the pontiff, 116.

The oath of Lothar II to Innocent II, 43.

Louis the Pious is appointed heir to the kingdoms by his father and designated emperor, 20. He confirms the rights and privileges of the Holy See, 30, 87, 92. The Albinian copy of his charter, 83 ff. The conspiracy against Saint Leo III arose because of such a charter, 90. It was adulterated in some places by Gratian and others, 126. Since he added nothing to the donations of Pippin and Charles, Louis’s name is omitted from Otto’s charter, 141. Henry names him as the claimant of another’s donation, 179. The discipline observed in the pontifical election is a great proof of his sincerity, 153.

Louis II reveals the character of the renewed empire, 18.

Louis III, king of Burgundy and Provence, is crowned emperor by Benedict IV, 242.

Louis the Bavarian, elected amid discord, is summoned into Italy by the Italian Ghibellines, 229.

Louis VII, king of the Franks, burns the apostolic privilege, 327.

Louis IX, Saint Louis, is received into the brotherhood by the Cistercians, 305. He prohibits the use of judicial duels in his territories, 455. He refuses to accept the kingdom of Sicily when it is offered to him by the pontiff, 508.

Louis, duke of Bavaria and elector Palatine, takes the leading role in Rudolph’s election, 246. See *Henry, duke of Bavaria*.

Louis, count of Savoy, has disputes with Rudolph, 322.

Two great lights, symbols of pontifical and imperial power, 260, 308, 314, 318, 380.

## M

Mabillon treats the election of the Roman pontiff with Panvinius inaccurately, 181. On the monastery of Aulne, 449 ff. He testifies that the Benedictines acknowledge the Cistercians as the source of the celebration of general chapters, 305.

Mehmed II, after conquering Constantinople, brings the Eastern Empire to an end, 521.

Malatesta and Galiotto exercise tyranny in the March of Ancona, 213.

Manfred invades the kingdom of Sicily on behalf of Conradin, 508.

A *mansa*, that is, a prince’s own estate, 51.

The *mansionarius*, an office of the Frankish palace, 133.

Mantua lay within Mathilda’s principality, 222. It submits to Pinamonte Bonacossi, 227.

The bishop of Mantua obtains part of Mathilda’s territory from Innocent III, 206.

The *marca* is of two kinds, gold and silver, 333. Gregory X gives Rudolph twelve thousand silver marks for the sacred expedition, ibid. and 362. Likewise, one thousand silver marks are assigned by Rudolph to Queen Anna, 429.

Marquard, imperial seneschal under Henry VI, restores to the Holy See the March that had been invaded, 207.

Margaret, eldest daughter of Raymond Berengar, count of Provence, and wife of Saint Louis, receives from Rudolph the investiture of the counties, 464 ff.

The Virgin Mary, the Most Holy, was always venerated by the Austrian house, 308. Several victories were obtained through her patronage, 419. Her oratory in the atrium of the Vatican basilica, called “in the Tower of the King of the Romans,” was devoted to the profession and canonry, 42.

Mary, daughter of Bohemond, prince of Antioch, transfers her right to the kingdom of Jerusalem to Charles, king of Sicily, 476.

Maria Theresa Augustus, following the example of her great ancestor, calls herself queen, 481.

Marozia, a Roman senator, rules at Rome, 33.

Marsia, occupied in the time of Innocent II by William, king of Sicily, for which a tribute of 400 *schifati* was paid, 507.

Marsilius of Padua and John of Jandun, heresiarchs and clients of Louis the Bavarian, infect Italy with their writings, 230.

Martène, *Edmund’s Anecdote*, 449.

Blasius de Martinellis presents the coronation rite of Charles V as full of innovations, 231.

Mathilda’s donation charter was produced again, 195. Several editions of the same charter from the Vatican codex, 196. Various opinions concerning it, 197 ff. Her possessions on both sides of the mountains, 203. They are called *allodium*, land, houses, counties, and estates, 204. They were wrongly believed to constitute the Tuscan patrimony, 209. Their location was where the duchy of Modena later existed, 214, 219. The territories subject to the countess, belonging to the Church and the empire, 215 ff. From the beginning of the fourteenth century there is no mention of them, 228. The charter itself from the Albinian codex, 238.

The Moors, or Saracens, of Spain were not subject to the caliph, 77.

The altar of Saint Maurice in the Vatican basilica, where the emperor was anointed, 272.

Mechtildis, Rudolph’s daughter and wife of Louis, duke of Bavaria, 306, 346.

The duchy of Milan begins in the kingdom of Italy in the year 1395, 231; its vicissitudes, 232. When the empire was vacant, it obeyed the Roman pontiff, 230.

Meinhard, count of Tyrol, governor of Carinthia, 388, 401.

Michael Curopalates, emperor of the East, is betrayed and deposed by Leo the Armenian, 72.

Michael VIII Palaeologus negotiates with Gregory X concerning the union of the Greek Church, 363. He restores the Eastern Empire, 521.

Michael the patrician is sent by the emperor Michael to Sicily with a fleet against the Saracens, 73.

Milota Zawischius, commander of Styria, is sent by Ottocar with troops into the Salzburg province, 392.

*Ministeriales*: servants, or people of dependent status, 440.

Minorites. See *Order of Saint Francis*.

The envoys, or legates, of Charles the Great to Leo III were the counts Helmengaud and Hunfrid, 58. Leo III’s envoys to Charles the Great were John the bishop and Basil the hegumen, 50. John, bishop of Silva Candida, Theodore the nomenclator, and Sergius the duke were sent to Louis the Pious, 89. Imperial envoys sent to administer justice, 54, 62; they were different from the legates mentioned above, ibid.

Mainz suffers from internal dissensions, 439. The clergy of Mainz, threatened by danger, seek help from Rudolph, 441.

The Cistercian monastery of Aulne in the diocese of Trier is commended by Rudolph to Philip, king of the Franks, 449, 455. Its origin and excellent institution, 449 ff.

A devastated Cistercian monastery is entrusted by Rudolph to another’s care, 432.

The monastery of the wilderness in the diocese of Constance, 468.

The monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, 387.

The monastery of Tulln for nuns, founded by Rudolph, 308, 389.

The monastery of Zwettl obtains a privilege, 472. See *Rudolph’s Codex*.

The right to mint coinage, 470 ff.

Moravia and Bohemia obey Rudolph, 424.

Moses, having become great through faith, 382.

Muratori correctly understands the imperial majesty obtained through the Roman coronation, on the authority of the charters, 39. His inconsistency concerning the charters of Louis, Otto, and Henry, 86. Together with Eckard, he recognizes the supreme power of the pontiff in the Exarchate, 107.

The *muta*, a type of toll among the Germans, 472.

Modena and Reggio are given by Otto to Atto, Mathilda’s great-grandfather, 221. They submit to the Este family, 227.

The beginnings of the duchy of Modena, 234.

## N

Narni, a city of the Roman duchy, is invaded twice and restored to the Holy See, 93, 125.

The Neapolitan territory is claimed for the Holy See by the Roman pontiffs, 102, 148.

The kingdom of Naples is established, 515.

The duchy of Naples is claimed for the Holy See, 148, 151.

Felix Nerinius, a Hieronymite abbot, discovered Otto III’s original charter in the monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius, 252.

Nicholas II explains the rights of the Holy See to the Normans in the charters of Louis, Otto, and Henry, 85, 87. He grants Henry IV, king of the Romans, the privilege of confirming the election of the Roman pontiff, declaring that privilege personal, 119.

Nicholas III, scarcely elected, sends Rudolph letters concerning the affairs of the empire and the Exarchate, 426. Following the example of his predecessors, he forbids Rudolph to come into Italy, 283. He reconciles Rudolph’s relationship with the king of Sicily, 433. He obtains the investiture of Provence for that king, 465. He sends Rudolph an excerpt from the charters of Louis, Otto, and Henry, together with the form for expressing in charters the cities belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy See, 520.

Nicholas IV negotiates with Rudolph, through his envoy, concerning the date of the coronation, 286. Meanwhile he dies without accomplishing anything, ibid.

The monastery of Nonantola is endowed by Mathilda with her estates in the territory of Ferrara, 216.

The Normans begin to rule both Sicilies by concession of the Holy See, 85, 87, 150. The end of their rule, 508.

The mark of infamy is not removed together with the crime, 474.

## O

Octavian, son of Alberic, invades the pontificate, assuming the name John XII, 243.

The offices, or dignities, of both clergy and laity in the City, 32.

Bishop of Olomouc. See *Bruno*.

Opizo, marquis of Este, invades Ferrara, Comacchio, and Adria, 230.

Rudolph’s envoy to Innocent V, 369, and to Nicholas III, 370. He gives him very salutary exhortations concerning obedience to the Holy See, ibid. It is uncertain whether he was a bishop or a cardinal, 475.

The ancient Roman Orders present a rite of imperial coronation different from the more recent rites, 273.

The Roman order of the coronation of the Carolingian Augusti, 256.

The Roman order of the coronation of the German Augusti, 261 ff.

The *ostiarius*, an office of the Frankish palace, 133.

The *palla*, or pallium, given to the papal chamberlain for the king of the Romans who is to be crowned, 262, 271. A pallium requested for the archbishop of Rheims, 34; the archbishop’s name and office adhere to it, 448.

Panvinius treats the election of the Roman pontiff inaccurately, 181. Among the Roman Orders he collected the rite of imperial coronation, without knowing what it was, 260.

Matthew of Paris thought that the seven electors were instituted by the counsel of Innocent IV, 247. The date of his chronicle, 248.

Parma was included by some rather carelessly in the donation of Pippin and Charles, 188. It is found to have been donated by the Augusti to the bishops of Parma, 223; it is found within Mathilda’s principality, 222; at the beginning of the fourteenth century it submits to Ghiberto Correggio, 227. It voluntarily submits to Bertrand, cardinal legate of the Holy See, 229; it is acquired by Julius II by right of war, 232. Paul III grants it to Pier Luigi on a fiduciary title, ibid.

The sacrilege of the people of Parma against Bernard, cardinal legate of the Holy See, 225. Afterwards they ask and obtain that he be given to them as bishop, ibid.

Easter in the year 1250, on 27 March, seems to Matthew of Paris an extraordinary matter, 248.

Paschal I, Saint, obtains from Louis the Pious a confirmation of the donations, 90. He informs him that nothing simoniacal had occurred in his election, 112.

Paschal II. See below, *Privilege*.

Paschal and Campulus are accused of high treason, 16.

The passage, or sacred expedition, decreed at the Second Council of Lyons, 462.

Cardinal Domenico Passioneo became worthy of praise for his service to letters and learned men, 135 ff.

Homeland and language differ in this respect: a language contains several homelands, 488.

The patriarch of Aquileia, 48, 389.

The patriarch of Grado, 48.

The patriarch of Jerusalem. See *Thomas Agni*.

The two duties of the patriciate of the Holy See are the defense of the orthodox faith and of the Holy See and Roman pontiff, 8.

Patricum, an ancient town of Latium, 125, 139.

The Calabrian patrimonies were incorporated into Sicily, 3. Their revenues were to be distributed among the poor and churches, 10 ff.; for that reason they were defended with the greatest vigor, 103. The Sicilian patrimony was divided into three parts in the age of Gregory the Great, 159.

The Neapolitan, Beneventan, and Salernitan patrimonies, 102, 104, 129.

The Tuscan patrimony, 212 ff.

Augustine Patritius Pientinus, bishop and master of ceremonies, exacts an oath from the governors of the kingdom of Italy after the end of that kingdom, 231. He changes Santa Maria in Traspontina into Santa Maria in Cosmedin, 275.

Paul of Terni, Rudolph’s envoy and procurator in the City, 437, 442; he dies, 475.

The maritime part of the Pentapolis began to be called the March, 522.

Peter, Saint, chief of the apostles, the special patron of Charles the Great, 8. His sanctuaries are sent by Leo III to Charles, 50. He is recognized as the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, 55, 67, 139. He is proposed to Constantine and Irene as an example of Carolingian reverence for such a patron, 8. His image was subjected to the impiety of the Greeks, 5.

Peter III, king of Aragon, invades Sicily in order to assert the rights of his wife Constance, 512.

Peter, count of Auxerre, is crowned emperor of the East by Honorius III, 521.

Peter the Deacon, on Mathilda’s donation, 196.

Peter of Leon, the antipope, is said to have established the kingdom of Sicily, 506.

Peter, bishop of Padua, grants fiefs to Rudolph’s sons, 396.

Philip III, surnamed the Bold, king of the Franks and Rudolph’s relative, 433. Rudolph commends the monastery of Aulne to him, 449 ff.

Philip, brother of Henry VI, contests the crown of Germany, 289.

Philip, duke of Carinthia, is removed, 388, 396.

Pledges, or reprisals, are forbidden by Gregory X in ecclesiastical matters, 345.

Pippin’s donation was not held in its entirety by the Holy See until the first arrival of Charles the Great in the City, 96. The spontaneous donations of Pippin and his successors, 177.

Pippin, son of Charles the Great and king of Italy, comes to Rome, 58.

The Ghibellines of Pisa seek help from Rudolph, 277. They call the city subject to the empire, 330. Rudolph replies that he will do nothing without the pontiff, 331.

Pius—when he was Aeneas Sylvius—argues for the first petitions, 293. He grants Sicily to Alfonso according to ancestral custom, 514.

Piacenza submits to the Holy See through the efforts of Verzuzio Landi, 229; it is granted to Aloysius Farnese together with Parma, 232.

Imperial hearings are held at Rome before the pontiff, 24. Similar hearings had been held by kings, 26.

The hearing of Charles’s envoys in the case of Leo III, 16.

Platina, agreeing with Blondus concerning the constitutions of Gregory V and Otto III, is not to be rejected entirely, 168.

Leo III calls political skill “the cleverness of the age,” 67.

Benedict VIII makes the golden orb surmounted by a cross a symbol of the world, 259. Frederick I is the first of all to receive it from Hadrian IV among the imperial insignia, 260.

Populonium, a town near Piombino, destroyed and reduced to a mass, 128.

The Gate of the Castle. See *Collina*.

Preachers. See *Order of Saint Dominic*.

The prefect of the City punishes criminals, 90, 467.

John of Vico, prefect of Viterbo, usurps the patrimony, 213.

Prelates exercise the right of the sword through another, 467.

The concession of the investiture that Henry V extorted from Paschal II is called the *Privilege*, 225.

Prayers to be offered by the pontiff, without neglecting arms, 75.

The origin of the primary petitions is uncertain, 288. Their ancient formulas, 324. They were not abolished at the Council of Trent together with the other expectative provisions, 293. Apostolic privileges begin to rely upon them, 294. The new name *precista* and the practice were disapproved, 294.

A presbyter shamefully castrated, 377.

The primacy of the Roman pontiff recognized by the Greeks, 364.

Elective princes and hereditary princes differ from one another, 310. They do not commit important matters to writing, 286. They are not subject to interdict unless, after being warned, they persist in wrongdoing, 389, 401. Their supreme obedience to the Holy See, 62.

The princes of the empire confirm Frederick II’s charter prohibiting the union of the kingdom of Sicily with the empire, 509.

Privileges bring harm to religious persons, 307.

The apostolic privilege of confirming the election of the pontiff, 116 ff.

The privilege of Paschal II granted to Henry V, called “the Privilege,” 225.

Probus, a Minorite, Rudolph’s legate to Gregory X, 341.

The procession of the three crowned persons—Clement II, Henry II, and Agnes—261.

The profession of faith of the Eastern emperors, 44, entirely different from the promise or profession of the Western Augusti. See *Oath*.

The promise or profession of the Roman pontiff to the emperor, 154.

Provence is granted by Rudolph on a fiduciary title to Charles, king of Sicily, 284, 465.

Ptolemais. See *Acre*.

Rudolph undertakes the protection of the wards, 481.

## Q

In the ninth century Lent began on the Monday after the First Sunday, although four fasts preceded it, 58. Hence Laetare Sunday was called “Sunday in the middle of Lent,” ibid.

Theological questions proposed by Charles to Leo III, 69 ff.

## R

Radevicus, on the location of Mathilda’s possessions, 203.

Ravenna, the capital of the Exarchate, 337. Henry VI, the invader of the Exarchate, attests its right as belonging to the Holy See in public records, 494. Nicholas III, together with the Pentapolis, claims it for the Holy See after a lengthy occupation, 428.

The archbishop of Ravenna is accused by Leo III before Charles the Great, 65. By Henry VI, the invader of the Exarchate, it is called a special member of the empire, 208. The reasons why it received that honor from certain Augusti, 335.

The revenues of the palace of Ravenna are reclaimed by Leo III, 51.

The royal revenues of Benevento in the twelfth century, 180.

Kings of Italy coming to Rome are received honorably throughout the ecclesiastical territory, 59. After receiving the German crown, they must obtain the Roman crown in order to become emperors, 168.

The kings of Russia and Dalmatia subject their kingdoms to the Holy See, 236. They receive their investiture from the Roman pontiff, ibid.

Royal power is the Church’s external arm, 248.

The anointing of the king, 480.

The title “king of the Romans” begins with Henry I, 244; Conrad III began to place it on seals, 245. Rudolph’s letters and charters consistently display this title, 311. For he possessed imperial majesty only in intention, 319.

Reggio and Modena are given to Atto, Mathilda’s great-grandfather, 221.

The dispensation of residence is the prince’s obedience, 453.

Richiza, also called Rigetta Augustus, wife of Lothar II, 200.

Ricordanus lies boldly about the Roman pontiff, 499.

The rite of imperial coronation, carelessly pieced together by Patritius from various Roman Orders, 274.

Robert. See *Guiscard*.

Roger I, the first king of Sicily, appointed by Innocent II, 507.

Roger, count of Santa Severina, takes possession of the kingdom of Jerusalem on behalf of Charles, king of Sicily, 477.

Roger, writer of English annals, 209.

Rome and its duchy recognize the Roman pontiff as their legitimate prince, 27. Both peoples, defecting from the impious Greeks, voluntarily subject themselves to him, 93. Nevertheless, the Roman people and senate retain their own share in the administration of affairs, 108, 312. They had a great support in the kings of the Franks, 5. They are included in the charters of donation, with the pontiff’s consent, 521.

Romania, Romaniola, and Romandiola are new names for the Exarchate after the twelfth century, 337. Rudolph, recognizing only these new names, thinks Romaniola different from the Exarchate, 335.

The Roman Empire is named in all the monuments, with the sole exception of the constitution of the pseudo-pope Leo VIII, 166.

The name “Roman-Germanic” is an invention of German jurists, 167, 311.

In the age of Louis the Pious the Roman pontiff was elected and consecrated freely, 110, 181. The apostolic privilege confirming the election of Lothar and Louis II remained in force for twenty-five years, 114, 117. It was renewed by John IX but did not become established in practice, 118. Nicholas II granted it to Henry IV, king of the Romans, declaring it personal, 119. Only three princes are found to have used it: Lothar and Louis, the Augusti, and Henry IV, king of the Romans, 120. In the case of the last, Saint Gregory VII initially confirmed it and later abolished it entirely, 121.

The Roman pontiff is the absolute prince of donations, without admixture of the Senate and Roman People, 109, 181. He rules there by the same right by which Charles rules in his kingdoms, 54, 110. Conringius admits that he possesses supreme power, 2. Alcuin places his majesty above imperial and royal majesty, 14. He is recognized by Romans and Franks as the supreme prince, 9. He is hated only by the Greeks because of the veneration of the holy images, 5. Nevertheless, they recognize his primacy, 364. There is a distinction between his rule in the City and its duchy and his rule in the other provinces and cities, 312. No such distinction is found in Rudolph’s age, 525. When the empire was vacant in Lombardy and Tuscany, he exercised the emperor’s functions, 228. He alone makes the emperor by the coronation, 45. Formerly, his death was followed by plunder and abandonment of the dead body, 132.

The Roman people offer an oath of loyalty to the emperor, except for what they had promised the Roman pontiff as their own prince, 23, 28, 56. Not to the patrician, 12, nor to the king of the Romans, 23, 41. Several emperors experienced its fierce character, 504. The German Augusti customarily took an oath to it twice, 42, 269.

The bishops of Roselle began in the twelfth century to be called bishops of Grosseto, 128.

Rotfrid and other legates bring King Eardwulf back to England, 69.

Rudolph of Habsburg, Augustus, ancestor of the house of Austria, is born, 306, from a distinguished family, 304, 406. He marries Anna of Hohenberg, 306. By her he has seven sons and as many daughters, ibid. While besieging Basel he is elected king of the Romans, 276, 311. He is crowned at Aachen, taking up a crucifix in place of the scepter, 313; his election is confirmed by Gregory X, 320.

A date is assigned to him for the imperial coronation, 282, 329; at the Lausanne conference it necessarily changes, 350, 365. There Gregory X takes an oath, 523. Rudolph thanks the pontiff for inviting the princes to the coronation, 343. He excuses himself to him for postponing his journey for some time, 398. On hearing of Gregory’s death, he suspends his journey, 367. He writes to Innocent V that he will be present at Rome at the appointed time, 341; that pontiff and his successors forbid him to come into Italy because of disputes with Charles, king of Sicily, 283, 371, 427. Agreement follows, 284, and hope of coronation is revived, 426. Nicholas III designates the coronation, 436. When the pontiff dies, Rudolph consults Honorius IV about the coronation, 285, and then his successor Nicholas IV, 286. Although he desires the crown to the very end of his life, he never obtains it, for ever-new reasons, 280, 286. Therefore all his letters and charters display only the title “king of the Romans,” 386, 395, 432, 456, 480, and elsewhere passim, although at times others ignorantly call him emperor, 318, 372.

Rudolph, king of the Romans, moves his camp into Austria against Ottocar, 373, 385. He besieges Vienna and brings the king of Bohemia back into order, 413. When the latter rebels again, he gathers new forces, 406. He announces a notable victory over him, together with his death, to a friendly prince, 417, and to Nicholas III, 419.

Rudolph, king of the Romans, confirms Frederick II’s constitution against all heresies, 488. Because of his special veneration for Christ’s Passion, he undertakes contests and important affairs on Friday, 418. His great devotion to the Most Holy Virgin, 308; his singular obedience to the Apostolic See, 320, 427, to which he restores the Exarchate that he had retained, deceived by the variation of its name, 278. He reveres all ecclesiastics, 453. Thinking that the primary petitions rested on custom, he is the first to offer them, 290. He always held Syria, where he is said to have proceeded with Frederick II, close to his heart, 311, 479.

He was distinguished by many virtues: piety, 308; gentleness, 405; clemency, 474; accessibility, 480; generosity toward learned men, 486; graciousness, 328; concern for friends, 359. He was a great lover of peace, 452. The originals of all his charters for the Holy See are preserved in the archive of the Mausoleum of Hadrian, 493.

Rudolph II, son of Maximilian II, is elected emperor, 473.

Rudolph, son of Rudolph, dies in the twelfth year of his life, 306.

Another Rudolph, son of Rudolph, duke of Swabia and husband of Agnes, Ottocar’s daughter, dies at Prague, 306, 422.

Rudolph, Rudolph’s chancellor and later archbishop of Salzburg, exacts unlawful oaths in the Exarchate, 428. Rudolph declares them invalid, ibid. and 498. He subscribes Rudolph’s charter, by which, among other rights of the Holy See, the Exarchate is confirmed, 526.

## S

The count of Savoy. See *Louis*.

The Sabine patrimony, or territory, was not peacefully possessed by the Holy See before the year 784, 101; its boundaries were established, 127.

Sabinus, bishop and legate of Leo III, together with Adulf, for the restoration of Eardwulf, king of England, 69.

Sacrament. See *Oath*.

The sacrilegious crime of Hadrian’s nephews against Saint Leo III, 14; that of the people of Parma against Bernard, cardinal legate of the Holy See, 225; that of the Germans against a presbyter, 377, and against a bishop, 387.

Salinguerra of Ferrara receives from Innocent III the investiture of many towns and other possessions of Mathilda, 201.

The free transport of salt along the Danube by Rudolph’s privilege, 472.

The Cistercian chapter of Salzburg obtains a confraternity, 306.

The archbishop of Salzburg. See *Frederick II*.

The province of Salzburg is devastated by Milota, Ottocar’s captain, 293, 412.

Sanctia, daughter of Raymond Berengar, count of Provence, wife of Richard, king of the Romans, during the interregnum, 464.

A convent of nuns founded by Rudolph, 308; prayers requested from them after the election, 307.

Sanutus, on the affairs of the Holy Land, 478.

The Saracens of Spain, intending to attack Sicily, invade and devastate Lampadusa, Ponza, and Ischia, 72. Not subject to the caliph of Baghdad, they obey their own king and are called Moors, 77. On their return, after plundering the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, almost all are said to have been drowned, 79.

Sardinia was donated to the Holy See by Charles the Great, 3, 11, 24; it is omitted from Otto’s charter, 158. Together with Corsica, it is freed from Saracen attacks by the Franks, 78, 143. The rights of the Holy See over it, 144.

One thousand *schifati*, the Sicilian tribute before Charles of Anjou, 507.

The *Schinderling*, a coin of extremely low value struck by Frederick III during severe financial distress, 471.

The notaries of the Holy See are negligent in the tenth century, 147.

The Septuagint translation of Sacred Scripture prevails in the age of Charles the Great, 70.

The bishop of Seckau. See *Bernard*.

The Holy Apostolic See reclaims its sacred and civil rights from the Eastern emperors who had invaded them, 9, 11. It has detractors at the court of Charles in the age of Leo III, 55. Its temporal rule arouses envy, and this wins it rivals, 56. It has always demanded obedience from the highest princes, 62. Its territories are administered by their own dukes, 63, over whom pontifical and imperial legates keep watch, ibid.

Seifrid, abbot of Zwettl, flourished at the beginning of the seventeenth century, 198, 473.

The emperor, the king of the Romans, or any other supreme prince cannot be senator of the City without special permission of the Holy See, 503.

Twelve senators from the plebs, also called *decurions*, together with the two consuls and the prefect, administer the Roman state, 34, 270. Innocent III creates fifty senators in order to accommodate the people, 501.

Roman women senators: the two Theodoras, Marozia, and Stephania, 33.

The restoration of the Roman Senate in the time of Innocent II, 500.

Two senatorial decrees containing material consistent with the royal law and the fictitious constitutions of Leo VIII, 167.

Sergius II grants the privilege of confirming the election of the pontiff, 114.

Sergius the duke, Leo III’s legate to Louis the Pious, 89.

Francesco Sforza, duke of Milan, dying without issue, appoints Charles V his heir, 233.

Sicily belonged by ancient right to the Holy See through the donations, 158. In 1327, through the treachery of Euphemius of Sicily, it came under the power of the Saracens, 78. It returns by restoration to the Apostolic See through the aid of the Normans, without imperial intervention, 148 ff. It has no union with the empire, 492, 509. Its kingdom is established by Innocent II, 506. Innocent III begins to call it Sicily on this side and beyond the Lighthouse, 510. Its dual dominion begins on both sides of the Lighthouse, 512. The island of Sicily is then given the name Trinacria, 513. Its investiture and tribute are determined by Leo X as they remain in our own age, 517.

The Sicilian patrimony was exchanged by the Eastern Augusti for all the eastern territories, 3.

Siffrid, archbishop of Cologne, suffers much at the hands of his citizens, 372, 445, 447.

Sigebert, on the synod celebrated in the age of Otto, 182.

Otto’s royal seal is different from the seal of the same man as Augustus, 137, 156.

Sigismund Augustus, at the beginning of the fifteenth century, omits the oath concerning governors to be sent into Italy because Italy had been alienated by his brother, 234.

Many signs appear in the heavens before the death of Charles the Great, 79.

The signature of his own hand used by Louis is an example for Otto and Henry, who follow it, 155.

The simoniacal stain spreads far and wide in Italy and France in the age of Charles the Great, 112.

The pontiff and emperor are represented by the symbols of the sun and moon, 260.

The battle of Sorbara between Henry IV and Mathilda, 223.

The duchy of Spoleto was offered to the Holy See by Charles the Great, 104, 130, 146, 159. Seven of its cities are donated by Otto to the Holy See, 152, 160, 522. The remainder, together with the transmontane possessions, is exchanged by Saint Henry with the Holy See, 189 ff. In Rudolph’s age a major alteration of the names had taken place there, 522.

The spontaneous donations of Pippin and his successors, 177.

Stephania, a Roman senator, rules at Rome, 33.

Stephen II, oppressed by the Lombards, offered the archbishop of Salzburg an example of misfortune, 385.

Stephen III is freely consecrated, 111.

Stephen IV confers in France with Louis the Pious concerning the charter by which all the rights of the Holy See were to be confirmed, 90. After his consecration he informs him that his election had been properly conducted, 112.

Stephen V chooses Wido, duke of Spoleto, as emperor, passing over Arnulf, the last of the Carolingians, 242.

Stephen, king of Hungary, makes peace with Ottocar on stated conditions, 395.

Stero, on the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire, 249.

Struvius and others discuss the empire incorrectly, 167.

The subscriptions of the donations of Pippin and Charles may perhaps resemble those of Louis, 124. Three charters are examined, 155.

The Swabian Augusti are hostile to the Holy See, 321.

Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, becomes Pope Clement II, 261.

The *superista*, first among the Roman nobles, 32 ff.

Sussubium, a fortress later called Brictonorium, 208, 522.

The synod of Salzburg in the year 1274, 388.

The condition of Syria is almost nonexistent in Rudolph’s age, 295. It earnestly requests aid from the pontiff and Rudolph, 316, 321, 461, 476; it is lost by the Christians, 458.

## T
Tancredus, invading the kingdom of Sicily, becomes the principal cause of dissensions down to Innocent III, 508. Tarracina, captured by Adrian, is retained as a pledge for the patrimony of Naples, 148. The Tartars, formerly enemies, make an alliance with Ottocar against Rudolph, 412. The exaction of a toll from passersby is forbidden, 483. The Templar knights were instituted by Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, 457; they were suppressed by Clement V, their possessions being transferred to the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem, 459, 478. An artificial tent was used to mock Ottocar, whose allegiance was doubtful, 414, 482. The land of Matilda contained cities which, nevertheless, the Holy See never reclaimed, 204 ff. The unfortunate condition of the Holy Land in Rudolph’s time, 476. The testament of Henry VI reached the Holy See by divine providence, 209. The Teutonic equestrian order, renowned for the privileges granted by emperors and kings, 456; obtains Rudolph’s patronage, 457; after losing Syria, receives Prussia as its seat, 458. Two senatorial women named Theodora at Rome, 33. Theodore the nomenclator, papal legate to Louis the Pious, 89. Thomas Agni of Lentini, patriarch of Jerusalem, 448; announces Syria’s desperate condition to Rudolph and requests assistance, 461, 477. Thomassinus, concerning the first prayers, not entirely correctly, 288, 290. The venerable cardinal Thomas made a golden commentary on the Psalms, 481. One hundred men of Zurich are killed in the conflict against Ottocar, 386. Trabaria, a district in the duchy of Urbino, 522. Lake Trasimene, near Perugia, belonging to the jurisdiction of the Holy See, 125. The Leonine Triclinium displays King Charles with the insignia of the patriciate, 18; a hearing is held there concerning the sacrilegious attackers of Leo III, 16. The bishop of Trent settles his controversy with Meinhard and Rudolph, 463, 485. Paul, bishop of Tripoli, a Minorite and legate of the Holy See, 388. The convent of virgins at Tulln in Lower Austria, founded by Rudolph, 308. The archbishop of Ravenna’s insulting language before the imperial legates on Palm Sunday, 65. The Turriani enjoy Gregory X’s favor against the Visconti, 340, 390. Turrianus. See Aquileiensis. Tuscany formerly consisted of three parts: Roman Tuscany, Lombard Tuscany, and royal Tuscany, 212; Roman and Lombard Tuscany enter into an association with the royal territory, or Etruria, 210. The duchy of Tuscany, together with that of Spoleto, was offered by Charles to the Holy See, 104, 130. The counts of Tusculum dominate Rome in the tenth century, 33. Tyranny spreads widely through the territories of the Holy See while the popes reside at Avignon, 213.

## U

The Hungarians, Cumans, and Tartars are Ottocar’s long-standing enemies, 412. Stephen is succeeded as king of Hungary by Stanislaus, who is adopted by Rudolph, 375, 394. Urban VI grants Sicily to Charles according to ancient custom, 514. The continuator of the Ursperg Chronicle, concerning the first prayers, 288.

## V

The elder Valentinian promotes literary studies, 486. Valentinus, successor of Eugenius II, is freely consecrated, 115. The Vatican Basilica archive preserves the privileges of the Holy See, 522. The standard of the patriciate, an insignia, 18. Leo III sends Charles the standard of the city and the keys of the Confession, 12. The popes were long called the vicars of Peter, 52, 58. To spare the defeated is victory, 422. Vienna is besieged by Rudolph, 413. The fantasies of Vitriarius and Conringius concerning the first prayers, 288. The estates of the common people are generally held in common, 551.

## W

Christian Walchius dedicates his mockeries of the Ludovician charter to Muratori, 88; attacks it ineptly, 125. Welf, an Italian duke, husband of Matilda, 215. Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, offers the first prayers, 289; sells the kingdom of Italy to Galeazzo: the duchy of Milan begins, 231, 234. Wenceslaus, Ottocar’s son, is under guardianship, 251; marries Rudolph’s daughter, 422. Wenceslaus Adalbertus, etc., author of *Austrian Piety*, 296. Wicardus, bishop of Padua, dies, 487. Duke Wido of Spoleto and his son Lambert, as emperors, confirm the rights and privileges of the Holy See in their charters, 30. William, son of King Roger of Sicily, pays four hundred schifati annually to the Holy See for Marsica, 507. William II, the first son, the last of the Normans, dies without offspring, 508. William, archbishop of Ravenna, a prince of the Empire, 208. William, count of Jülich, hostile to the archbishop of Cologne, 372; is murdered, ibid. Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia and Calabria, swears an oath of allegiance to Nicholas II and Gregory VII in return for the investiture of Sicily, 149. He pays the Holy See a census of twelve denarii per jugerum, 507.

## Z

The seal of Zyllesia, observed by Heineccius, with a cross-bearing golden orb, 259. A Rudolphine manuscript in the monastery of Zweital, 296.

# B. Writings of the Emperor Charlemagne, or the Second Part of All His Works

## Section One

## Letters

### Letter I. To Offa, King of the Mercians, after the Conquest of the Lombards and Saxons  
*(Year 774)*

*[From the Collection of Councils by Mansi]*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends greeting, honor, and affection to the venerable man and dearest brother Offa, king of the Mercians.

Since it is fitting that powerful and famous kings should be bound together by a treaty of friendship and rejoice in one another’s mutual happiness, so that Christ may be glorified in all and by all through the bond of charity, we have judged it appropriate to send this blessing to Your Serenity.

Since, with Christ’s help—and we desire to serve him—we have subjected the most noble city of the Lombards together with all its citizens to our rule, and have successfully brought all Italy under our empire, King Desiderius of the Lombards and the Saxon dukes, whom we have bent to our commands, Withimundus and Albion, together with nearly all the inhabitants of Saxony, have received the sacrament of baptism, henceforth to serve the Lord Jesus Christ.

With this salutary message, therefore, I, Charles, the most powerful of the Christian kings of the East, desire to gladden you, Offa, the most powerful of the Christian kings of the West, and to embrace you with sincere affection.

### Letter II, or Decree Concerning the Schools of the Church of Osnabrück  
*(Year 787)*

*[From Baronius, Ecclesiastical Annals]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, emperor and Augustus, governing the Roman Empire, lord and king of the Franks and Lombards, and likewise ruler of the Saxons.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church, present and future, that, for the increase of our reward, we have granted to Bishop Uuision of Osnabrück, and to his Church—which we built as the first throughout Saxony in honor of St. Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus—a certain wood or forest within these boundaries: Farnewinchel, Rustenstheim, Angara, Osningsenethe, Dershosset, and Egesterfeldt.

With the abundant commendation of the powerful men of that region, we have granted it in perpetuity with complete rights over wild boars, deer, birds, fish, and every kind of hunting that under the customary ban is assigned to a forest, after the model of our forest at Aachen, in the Osning Forest.

If anyone should ever enter this same wood, protected by our ban, without the permission of the bishop of the aforesaid see, whether for the purpose of hunting or of doing anything else, let him know that he will incur the vengeance of both divine and royal punishment, and that, for the offense, he will have to pay us sixty solidi of our standard, which we have decreed to be owed to us for violation of the ban.

Moreover, we grant to the same bishop and his successors perpetual permission, liberty, and exemption from every royal authority, unless it should happen that the Roman emperor and the Greek king decide to arrange a marriage alliance between their sons. In that event, the bishop of that Church, with the expense supplied by the king or emperor, shall undertake both the labor and the honor of that embassy.

For this reason, we have decreed that Greek and Latin schools shall remain permanently in the same place, and we trust that there will never be a shortage of clerics skilled in both languages.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and have ordered it sealed with our ring.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth year of our empire, with Christ propitious, and the thirty-seventh year of our reign in France, and the thirty-first in Italy. Done at Aachen, in the palace, prosperously in the name of the Lord. Amen.

**Note.** This letter belongs to the number of those called “general” letters, because, with a few alterations, they were sent in one form to different recipients—to metropolitans, bishops, abbots, and others, as circumstances required.

So many peoples had burst forth from Germany across the Rhine and from Italy across the Alps that public schools had completely disappeared. The bishops therefore undertook the care of private schools for the education of clerics in the episcopal sees, just as abbots did in monasteries for the instruction of monks. Hence learning lay hidden only within the cloisters of episcopal and monastic institutions.

But because even these schools were then languishing, Charles also strove to restore them to their former splendor, sending the letters mentioned above. Since laymen did not have free access to private schools of this kind, Charles established public schools and also founded others in the royal palace itself. Abbots and bishops immediately followed the king’s example. Public schools soon resounded throughout the episcopal sees and monasteries, some intended for the instruction of monks, others for that of secular persons.

The Benedictines, who from the beginnings of their institute had professed the pursuit of letters, then wished to have schools of both kinds in their monasteries. On this subject Trithemius should be consulted in his *Chronicle of Hirsau*, where he also lists the Benedictine monasteries especially renowned for their cultivation of letters.

Concerning the zeal with which Charles was moved that learning, and especially sacred learning, should flourish in his kingdom, read the monk of St. Gall, Book I, chapter 9. These matters are taken from Pagi, under the year 787, number 11.

### Letter III. To Baugulf, Abbot of Fulda  
#### Concerning the Study of Letters  
*(Year 787)*

*[From Miraeus, Belgian Donations]*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends an affectionate greeting in the name of almighty God to Baugulf the abbot, to the entire congregation, and also to the faithful entrusted to you, our representatives.

Let it therefore be known to your devotion, pleasing to God, that we, together with our faithful, have considered it useful that the episcopal sees and monasteries entrusted to us, with Christ’s favor, for governance should, in addition to the order of the regular life and the practice of holy religion, also devote themselves to the study of letters, according to the capacity of each person who, by the Lord’s gift, is able to learn.

Thus, just as the rule of the regular life orders the propriety of conduct, so also the diligence of teaching and learning should arrange and adorn the sequence of words, so that those who desire to please God by living rightly may not neglect to please him also by speaking rightly.

For it is written: “Either you will be justified by your words, or by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). Although doing good is better than knowing, nevertheless knowing comes before doing. Therefore everyone ought to learn what he desires to fulfill, so that the soul may understand all the more abundantly what it ought to do, the more freely the tongue has run without stumbling over falsehoods in the praises of almighty God.

Since all people must avoid lies, how much more ought those to avoid them according to their ability who are shown to have been chosen for this sole purpose: that they should serve the truth in a special way?

When in these years letters were repeatedly sent to us from certain monasteries, reporting that the brothers residing there were striving on our behalf in holy and devout prayers, we learned that in many of the writings mentioned above their thoughts were sound but their expressions uncultivated. What pious devotion faithfully dictated inwardly, an uneducated tongue was unable to express outwardly without reproach because of negligence in learning.

As a result, we began to fear that, just as their prudence in writing was deficient, so also the wisdom they ought to have possessed for understanding the sacred Scriptures might be much more deficient. We know well that, although errors of words are dangerous, errors of meaning are much more dangerous.

Therefore we exhort you not merely not to neglect the study of letters, but also to learn eagerly, with the most humble and God-pleasing intention, so that you may be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures more easily and correctly.

When figures of speech, tropes, and other things of this kind are found inserted in the sacred pages, no one doubts that each reader understands them spiritually all the more quickly the more fully he has first been instructed in the discipline of letters.

Let men be chosen for this work who possess both the will and the ability to learn and the desire to instruct others. Let all this be done with the sole intention and devotion in which it is commanded by us.

For we desire you, as befits soldiers of the Church, to be devout inwardly and learned outwardly, chaste in good living and scholarly in good speech. Thus, whoever seeks to visit you because of the Lord’s name and the nobility of your holy conduct may return rejoicing and giving thanks to almighty God: just as his sight is edified by seeing you, so also he may be instructed by the wisdom he has received from your reading or singing.

Therefore do not neglect to send copies of this letter to all your suffragans and fellow bishops, and throughout all the monasteries, if you wish to have our favor.

And let no monk hold judicial office outside the monastery or attend the courts and public assemblies.

Farewell in reading.

### Letter IV

**Note.** It seemed worthwhile to publish this letter because it is worthy of reading and contains several things that, in my opinion, escape the notice of many. Although it was printed together with the *Homiliary of Paul the Deacon* at Speyer by Peter Drach the Younger in 1482 and at Cologne by Matthew Cholinus in 1557, nevertheless, because editions of this kind are rare, I thought it worthwhile to reprint here this precious monument of antiquity.

Paul the Deacon, a monk of Monte Cassino, polished this *Homiliary*, which had been prepared by Alcuin, and divided it into two volumes, as Charles testifies at the end of the letter. I believe that the testament of Ansegis, abbot of Fontenelle, refers to this work when he bequeaths to his monastery two volumes of Paul the Deacon’s *Collectanea* on the cycle of the year.

Some homilies were nevertheless inserted by later authors, namely by Hericus, a monk of Auxerre, who is known to have flourished after Paul’s death, during the reign of Charles the Bald.

#### To the Subjects  
#### Concerning the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, Monk of Monte Cassino  
*(Year 788)*

*(From Mabillon, Ancient Analecta)*

Charles, relying upon the aid of God, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to the religious readers subject to our authority.

Since divine mercy, both at home and abroad, always guards us, whether amid the events of war or in the tranquility of peace, and although human weakness cannot repay its benefits in any way, nevertheless, since our God is of immeasurable mercy, he kindly approves the wills devoted to his service.

Since it is therefore our concern that the condition of our churches should always advance toward better things, we diligently strive, through the study of letters, to restore the workshop of learning, almost obliterated by the negligence of our ancestors, and by our example we invite as many as we can to the study of the sacred books [another reading: the liberal arts].

Among these works, with God assisting us in all things, we have carefully corrected all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which had been corrupted through the incompetence of copyists.

Moreover, encouraged by the examples of our father Pippin, of venerable memory, who adorned all the churches of Gaul with the chants of the Roman tradition through his own efforts, we likewise take care, with diligent attention, to distinguish those same churches by a notable series of readings.

Finally, because we found that certain readings compiled for the night office through the fruitless labor of some men, although undertaken with a proper aim, were nevertheless inadequate—since they were presented without the names of their authors and were riddled with countless labyrinths of errors—we have not allowed the sacred offices to resound throughout our days with discordant solecisms in the divine readings. Rather, we have turned our minds to restoring the course of those readings for the better.

We have entrusted this work to Paul the Deacon, our familiar associate, to polish it: namely, by diligently going through the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, as though selecting particular flowers from their most flourishing meadows and arranging whatever was useful into a single garland.

Desiring to obey our Highness devotedly, he read through the treatises, sermons, and homilies of various Catholic Fathers, selecting the best elements, and presented to us, in two volumes covering the entire cycle of the year, readings appropriate to each feast, carefully arranged and free from errors.

After examining the text of all these with our own discernment, we have confirmed them by our authority and hand them over to your religious observance to be read in the churches of Christ.

Paul the Deacon.

May you happily enjoy Christ’s gift for many years, O great Charles, light and glory of your people, prince and ruler of the robed world, and glory of the Dardanian race.

### Letter V. To Queen Fastrada  
#### Concerning the Victory over the Avars and the Litanies  
*(Year 792)*

*[From the Collection of Councils by Mansi]*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to our beloved and greatly cherished wife, Queen Fastrada.

We have endeavored to send you affectionate greetings in the Lord through these lines, and through you to our sweetest daughters and to the other faithful who remain with you.

We inform you that, by God’s grace, we are safe and well. A messenger of our beloved son Pippin, whose name is omitted, reported to us his health and that of the apostolic lord, as well as the safety of our frontier districts situated in those regions. We were greatly delighted by this.

He also reported to us that those military divisions which we had previously ordered to proceed from Italy into the territory of the Avars and to remain in certain frontier districts entered their territory on the tenth day before the Kalends of September and engaged them in battle.

Almighty God, in his mercy, granted them victory, and they killed a multitude of those Avars, so that, as they say, a greater slaughter of the Avars had not been made for many days.

They stripped the rampart and remained there that night and on the following day until the third hour. After taking the spoils, they returned in peace. They captured one hundred and fifty of the Avars alive and kept them in reserve, awaiting our command concerning what should be done with them.

The faithful of God and of ours who carried this out were the unnamed bishop, the unnamed duke, and the unnamed counts. The duke from Istria, as was reported to us, performed well there with his men. Our vassals were the men whose names are omitted.

With the Lord’s help, we held a three-day litany: beginning on the Nones of September, which fell on a Monday, and continuing on Tuesday and Wednesday, beseeching God’s mercy that he might deign to grant us peace, health, victory, and a prosperous journey, and that in his mercy and kindness he might be our helper, counselor, and defender in all our difficulties.

Our priests ordered abstinence from wine and meat for those who, because of illness, old age, or youth, were able to abstain. Whoever wished to redeem the abstinence was permitted to drink wine during those three days. The richer and more powerful men were to give one solidus each day; those less powerful, according to their means; and whoever could give no more but wished to drink wine was at least to give one denarius.

Each person was to give alms according to his own good will and ability. Each priest was to celebrate a special Mass unless illness prevented him. Each cleric who knew the Psalms was to sing fifty of them. Meanwhile, while they were performing the litanies, they were to walk barefoot.

This is how our priests arranged matters, and we all made the same preparations and, with the Lord’s help, completed them.

Therefore we wish you, together with the unnamed persons and our other faithful, to consider how those litanies should be performed there. As for you, we leave the matter to your judgment, insofar as your illness permits.

We were surprised that neither your messenger nor a letter from you has reached us since he came from Regensburg. Therefore we wish you to inform us frequently of your health or of anything else you may wish to communicate.

Again we greet you warmly in the Lord.

### Letter VI. To Elipandus and the Other Bishops of Spain  
#### In Which Mention Is Also Made of the Three Preceding Treatises  
*(Year 794)*

*[From the seventh volume of the Collection of Councils by Mansi]*

**Note.** From the same copy by Sirmond. HARD.

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, son and defender of the holy Church of God, wishes health in Christ, the true and proper Son of God, to Elipandus, metropolitan of the city of Toledo, and to the other fellow priests of the orthodox faith and fraternal charity in the regions of Spain.

Christian piety rejoices to extend the two wings of divine and fraternal charity across the wide expanses of the earth, so that it may cherish with a mother’s affection those whom it has begotten through holy baptism.

The greatest joy of holy Mother Church is the union of her children, so that those redeemed by one may be made perfect in unity. As the same Redeemer, our Lord Jesus Christ, says: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may all be one, just as we are one” (John 17).

Therefore it is said of the holy Church in the Song of Songs: “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle array” (Song of Songs 6). The close array of an army and the unanimous strength of its warriors are usually a great terror to enemies. Thus the peaceful union of the children of holy Mother Church within the wall of the Catholic faith is exceedingly terrible to the powers of the air and wholly impenetrable to the fiery darts of wicked unbelief.

As the most truthful preacher to the nations and the Church’s strongest warrior commands: “In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6), and escape this wicked age by a free flight toward heavenly things.

For without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11). “Impossible” means what cannot be done at all by a human being. Faith is the beginning of our salvation. When it is kept undefiled and confirmed in complete soundness, the whole course of life runs happily to its end along the traces of good works.

Through faith, as the same apostle mentioned above testifies in his Letter to the Hebrews, all the saints pleased God.

This orthodox faith, therefore, handed down by the apostolic teachers and preserved by the universal Church, we profess to maintain and proclaim everywhere and in all things, according to the measure of our strength. For there is no salvation in any other faith except that which the Church has always preserved from the beginning of our salvation in peaceful unanimity.

For its sake, brothers, your good devotion—which it is fitting for you to possess in the Lord—has taken care to send letters from those regions concerning your faith: both general letters to the most holy ears of the priests and particular letters to us.

In the wording of these letters it was not sufficiently clear to us whether you intended to teach us as though by the authority of a teacher, or desired to learn from us in the humility of discipleship. Nevertheless, whether one or the other disposition was present in your minds, we judged that your request, compelled by the charity of Christian religion, should not be rejected.

We greatly desire, and pray to God from the innermost affection of our hearts, that both sides may remain firmly established in the solidity of the true faith, and that amid the tossing waves of this age, with the Holy Spirit guiding the vessel of your course [manuscript: our course], we may deserve to reach the harbor of perpetual tranquility.

To attain this tranquility, the eye of the heart must be purified by faith and the mind’s vision enlightened by the continual prayers of holy supplication, so that, every cloud of error being driven away, it may be able to contemplate the light of pure truth, lest unregulated rashness, proceeding too heedlessly into opinions of harmful falsehood, cast it down.

Let a Christian not be reluctant to ask when he is uncertain, nor ashamed to learn when he does not know. Pious humility enters into the hidden places of the wisdom of learning, and it is better to be a disciple of truth than to become a teacher of falsehood.

The former is always raised to higher things; the latter always slips toward lower things. The latter becomes a teacher of error precisely where he disdained to be a hearer of truth.

Therefore, brothers, avoiding this destructive arrogance, let us cling to the sacred understanding of the holy Fathers and Catholic teachers. Let us learn what they wrote, believe what they taught, and turn neither to the right nor to the left, but run by the royal road toward the King and Redeemer, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, in a harmonious confession of faith and truth.

“For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10), as the same apostle bears witness: “The just shall live by faith” (Romans 1). If the just lives by faith, how can one who does not possess a right faith imagine that he is living rightly?

We are not sons of unbelief destined for destruction, but sons of faith destined for the gaining of the soul. Let us follow, in charity, the venerable precepts of the holy Fathers. For it is fitting that all Christians should have one faith and one mind, just as there is one flock and one shepherd.

Those, however, who are found outside the boundaries of the ecclesiastical fold will be devoured by wolfish savagery, because they do not hear the voice of the good shepherd, who enters and leaves before his sheep in order to lead them to the pastures of eternal life.

Let us understand as spoken to us what the excellent preacher commanded his dearest children, saying: “I beseech you by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfect in one understanding and in the same knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1).

Since we possess these commands of apostolic authority, agree with us. We love you. In the Lord, we desire for you what we desire for ourselves. For the perfect charity that we have in Christ rejoices to gather, not scatter; to unite, not divide; and to preserve intact, not tear apart, the seamless tunic of our Savior.

We foresee that we must preserve this same unity in the peace of Christ which the soldiers observed during his Passion.

With these matters thus introduced, we greatly rejoice in your progress in the Lord. Yet, wounded in our hearts by fraternal love, we lament with tearful groaning the oppression you suffer among the nations.

But with much greater sadness we mourn if, through diabolical deception, you suffer inward oppression in your hearts through unbelief or through the error of any schism.

This is a continual pain in our breasts and an almost incurable wound, unless those who have grieved us gladden us through the mercy of him who heals the brokenhearted and desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

Your correction, therefore, is our joy. We desire to have you as companions in the Catholic faith and fellow workers in proclaiming the truth, so that the joy which Christ promised his disciples may dwell in us and our joy may be fulfilled in you.

For the fulfillment of this joy, compelled by fraternal charity, we ordered a synodal council of the holy Fathers to be assembled from all the Churches throughout our dominions, so that the holy unanimity of all might firmly determine what should be believed concerning the adoption of Christ’s flesh, which we have learned from your writings that you recently introduced through new assertions unheard of in the universal holy Church of God in former times.

Indeed, concerning this new invention, we sent messengers from our devotion three and four times to the most blessed pontiff of the apostolic see, wishing to know what the holy Roman Church, instructed by apostolic traditions, would choose to answer concerning this inquiry.

We also summoned from the regions of Britain certain men versed in ecclesiastical discipline, so that the truth of the Catholic faith might be investigated through the careful consideration of many and, strengthened on both sides by the most authoritative testimonies of the holy Fathers, might be held without any doubt.

For this reason we have taken care to send you, in separate treatises, what the pious unanimity and peaceful examination of the aforesaid Fathers, by ecclesiastical authority, found, established, and confirmed.

First, we set forth in the form of a single treatise what the apostolic lord, together with the holy Roman Church, the bishops residing throughout those regions, and the Catholic teachers, held.

Second, we placed in writing a treatise containing the separate responses of the ecclesiastical teachers and priests of the Churches of Christ in the nearer regions of Italy, together with Peter, archbishop of Milan, and Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli or Aquileia, men greatly venerable in the Lord, concerning what they wished to be understood or firmly believed. They too were present at our synodal assembly.

After this, the third treatise contains the orthodox faith of the holy Fathers who are bishops and of the venerable men who serve God in worthy offices in the regions of Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Britain, together with their responses to your objections, strengthened by testimonies from the holy Scriptures.

Fourth, I appended my own agreement with the unanimity of these most holy Fathers, together with their decrees and Catholic decisions, just as you yourselves requested in your letter, which you addressed specifically to me: namely, that I should not consent to the deceitful assertions of a few, but should firmly hold the faith strengthened by the testimonies of many.

I do this most certainly, by the gift of the Lord my God Jesus Christ, joining myself firmly in the profession of the true faith to this most holy multitude and its thoroughly tested authority. I do not admit myself as your companion in consenting to this new assertion, since you are few; rather, with the whole intention of my mind and the whole joyfulness of my heart, I unite myself to the apostolic see, to the ancient Catholic traditions present from the beginning of the Church’s birth, and to the traditions of the Catholic faith.

Whatever is read in the books of those who, inspired by the divine Spirit, were given by God as teachers to the whole world, I hold without doubt. I believe that this is sufficient for the salvation of my soul: what the most sacred history of evangelical truth reveals; what apostolic authority confirms in its letters; and what the eminent interpreters of sacred Scripture and the foremost teachers of the Christian faith committed to writing for perpetual memory among posterity.
