Together with these teachers and pastors of the holy Church, I also proclaim the true faith in the present age—those luminaries whom he has given us who said: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

These are the defenders of our faith; these are the rulers throughout the various sees of the city of Christ. Its rampart is the Catholic faith, its strongest wall is charity, and its defensive towers are the testimonies of the divine Scriptures.

In it are the riches of salvation: wisdom and knowledge, and the hope that guards the gates. These are opened to devout minds by four keys: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

The true and proper Son of God himself, true God and true man, Jesus Christ our Lord, presides over this city with royal power. By his grace he governs, protects, and exalts the whole structure of that city.

Whoever hastens to reach this city, with the right faith preceding him and his hands full of good works, will find its gates open and will rejoice as the King of kings, accompanied by thousands of saintly ranks, comes out to meet him.

We also give you thanks for your perseverance in prayer, by which you have said that you continually remember us. We pray that your prayers may be acceptable to the Lord our God and Savior, and that he, through his mercy, may make you worthy to be heard and may deign to recall you to the unity of his holy Church.

May he carry you back upon the shoulders of his mercy to the fold of holy Mother Church, just as, coming from heaven to seek the lost sheep, he carried the sheep he had found in triumph and glory to the seat of his Father’s majesty.

What you also graciously requested of our piety was that, in our presence, the text of your little book should be read, and that the counsel of many should examine whatever in it was found to agree with the ordinances of the true faith. We did as you asked. Having gathered from every quarter, as we said above, ecclesiastical teachers and leaders of the Christian people, and while we were all seated together in peaceful unanimity, we ordered that the same little book should be read through from beginning to end, section by section according to each sentence, and by means of questions or answers, as each person wished. But what the prelates of the Churches of Christ and the teachers of the Catholic faith understood concerning that little book, there is no need for me to repeat in this letter, since their own written statement clearly shows it to you.

In your letter, therefore, we found the following supplication written:

> We beseech you by him who for you stretched out innocent hands upon the cross, and for you shed precious blood, and for you endured death and burial; who descended into hell to free the elect; and who, rising again for you, showed you the way of returning to heaven, that is, to the heavenly fatherland, so that you yourself might sit as judge.

Behold, satisfying your petitions, I have sat as hearer and judge among the assembly of priests. We have distinguished the matters at issue and, by God’s gift, have decreed what must be firmly held concerning this inquiry. But now, by that same supplication, I earnestly entreat you again and again to remain firmly with us in peaceful unanimity and in the profession of the Catholic faith. Do not consider yourselves wiser than the universal holy Church of God. She holds the faith that the orthodox Fathers left written for us in their creeds. “Do not be wiser than it is necessary to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety.” Do not imagine that, by human reasoning and ingenuity, you can investigate the divine mysteries; rather, honor by believing what human frailty cannot discover by rash scrutiny.

[Col. 0903C] You proposed to me the example of the Emperor Constantine, whose beginning, you say, Blessed Isidore praised and whose end he lamented; and you kindly advise me to take care lest the same happen to me through one whom you have called Antiphrasius. By God’s merciful grace, I am striving to guard against this—not only against that man, but also against all who appear to teach anything contrary to the true faith. With continual devotion I beseech the Lord, and I call upon as helpers in this petition as many of the sons of holy Mother Church as I can, lest some verbose flattery or deceptive praise should mislead me and turn me aside from the way of truth. Thus I often sing with the prophet:

> “Let the righteous strike me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Psalm CXLIII).

[Col. 0903D] You, for your part, beware for yourselves—something which, out of brotherly love, you diligently urged us to do—and summon the most merciful grace of almighty God to yourselves by constant prayers, lest the cunning deceit of the ancient enemy corrupt your minds in any respect, and the devil’s service become worse within than the enemy nation’s oppression without. Await that Redeemer whom you have had as the author of your salvation. Glorify him in your heart and bear him in your body; and prepare within yourselves for him a worthy dwelling through the faith that works by love. Thus may his glorious power and ineffable mercy free and preserve you from the affliction of both kinds of servitude, namely, external and internal; may he grant you to stand glorified on the great day before the sight of his glory, with the abundant riches of your labor; and may he make you hear, together with those who practice apostolic faith, the desirable voice:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

Hope, therefore, with unwavering confidence in the truth’s promise, for the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, if you take care to join yourselves to the unanimity of the Catholic faith. Console yourselves amid the troubles of external servitude with the inward hope of faith. Lift the eyes of your minds to him who rescued you from the power of darkness and transferred you into the kingdom of his beloved Son.

Until this offense arising from the name of this adoption in Christ had wounded our hearts, we loved you with the affection of brothers. Although your bodily servitude grieved us, the uprightness of the Catholic faith nevertheless rejoiced us in you. Now, however, we are afflicted for you with a twofold sorrow: you have been deceived in heart by the devil’s fraud and oppressed in body by hostile servitude.

But return, I beg you, to the unity of holy Mother Church, so that he who through the grace of baptism freed you from the bond of original sin may rescue you from the distress of earthly servitude. You stripped off the old man; how, having again been deceived by malignant fraud, can you put him on? You have been made sons by adoption of God the Father through him who is not adopted but natural. Stand firm, through an inviolable confession of faith, in the freedom of the children of God, and do not submit to the yoke of unbelief. Drive the bonds of diabolical deception from your hearts, so that Christ God, who releases the fettered, may shake the chain of the hostile nation from your hands.

[Col. 0904C] By God’s help, we are fellow-workers in your joy if you wish to be preachers with us of the Catholic faith. The help of divine mercy will most certainly be present where the love of the whole Church is one and the confession of the true faith is one. Return to the multitude of the Christian people and to the unanimity of the priestly council. For if we do not doubt that, according to his promise, the Lord is present at the holy and devout agreement of two or three, how much more must we believe him to be present in the midst of so many most holy Fathers, so many venerable brothers, and so many sons of the devout Mother Church, when they gather peacefully in unanimity in his name—and to guide the counsels of those who are known to seek the praise of his name?

[Col. 0904D] Therefore, to strengthen your hearts in faith and truth, we have taken care to write this letter bearing our name, prompted by brotherly love. We desire that our devotion, which we have for the Catholic faith, may prosper, and that divine clemency may restore you to the Catholic faith.

Before this aforesaid scandal arose from you and caused offense, we loved you with a twofold affection, as we have said: that is, we counted you as companions in our prayers throughout all the Churches of our kingdom, making daily remembrance of you; likewise, with God’s help, we intended to free you from the service imposed by secular necessity, when the time was opportune and in accordance with the encouragement of your counsel.

But now, through this twofold affection—which we say not without grief—you have deprived yourselves of its benefits, failing to understand that you have been deceived by diabolical fraud so that it might strip you of both forms of assistance: participation in the faith and our prayers, or the support of our aid.

[Col. 0905A] See, see what a great evil you have brought upon yourselves: we have not dared to pray for you as for faithful sons of the holy Church of God, nor to help you as brothers in your greatest necessities. Therefore return to this twofold consolation and cast away from you this wicked cunning of diabolical fraud, so that you may share with us in every charity and timely assistance.

After this correction, or admonition, of apostolic authority and synodal unanimity, if you do not repent of your error, know with certainty that you will be regarded as heretics, and that we dare not have any communion with you for God’s sake. Run while you have the light, lest the darkness of anathema seize you, from which you will be unable to extricate your feet, and you will mourn that you have been entangled in eternal damnation. For holy Mother Church still calls you back to the embrace of her mercy, wishing to nourish you as sons for God. Only do not withdraw yourselves from the kindness of him who called you into the kingdom of his beloved Son.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.

We also believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Father before all ages and before all times: light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; natural, not adopted; through whom all things were created, heavenly and earthly; of one essence and one substance with the Father.

We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, giver of life to all, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

We believe that the same holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is of one substance, one power, and one essence: three persons, and each individual person in the Trinity fully God; and the three persons together one almighty God. The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Father did not begin at any time; but just as he is eternally God, so he is eternally Father, because he has always had the Son.

The Father is eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son: one almighty God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, present everywhere and wholly present everywhere; eternal, ineffable, incomprehensible God.

In this holy Trinity no person is later in time, lower in rank, or lesser in power; rather, the Son is in every respect equal to the Father, and the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son in divinity, will, operation, and glory. The Father is another only in person, the Son another in person, and the Holy Spirit another in person. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not another thing but one God in nature, power, and essence.

[Col. 0906A] We believe that, from this holy Trinity, the person of the Son alone was incarnate for the salvation of the human race, from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity might also be the Son of a human mother in humanity: perfect God in divinity, perfect man in humanity; God before all ages, man at the end of the age; the true Son of God in both substances, not putative but true, not by adoption but by natural sonship.

One person, God and man; one mediator between God and humanity. In the form of God, equal to the Father; in the form of a servant, less than the Father. In the form of God, creator; in the form of a servant, redeemer.

One and the same proper and perfect Son of God in both realities, in order to fulfill the dispensation of human salvation, suffered a true passion of the flesh, died a true death of his body, rose by a true resurrection of his flesh and a true resumption of his soul; and in the same body in which he suffered and rose, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father. In the same form in which he ascended, he will come to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

[Col. 0906B] We proclaim one holy Church of God, spread throughout the whole world, separated by place but joined in faith and charity; and true remission of sins in that same Church, whether through baptism or through repentance, by the gift of divine grace cooperating with the good will of the human being.

We also believe that all human beings will rise again and that each will be judged according to his works: the wicked will be condemned with the devil and his angels to eternal punishments, while the saints will be crowned with eternal glory with Christ and his holy angels throughout everlasting ages.

[Col. 0906C] This is the Catholic faith, and therefore ours; we also desire it to be yours, because there is one faith, one baptism, and one Lord Jesus Christ, who is true God and true man, true God and true Son of God; in both natures, one and the same mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ, who is God blessed forever.

We earnestly pray that you, dearest brothers, firmly hold this faith in common. If previously you have thought otherwise in any expression, correct yourselves and hasten with pure faith to the unity of the holy Church of God. Avoid disputes over names and innovations in language, because, according to the Apostle, no one is a heretic except through contention.

Since you are few, from where do you suppose that you could have discovered something truer than what the holy universal Church, spread throughout the whole world, holds?

Rest beneath the shelter of her wings, lest the devil’s greedy rapacity, if it finds you outside, devour you with its impious throat. Return to the devout embrace of Mother Church. Let her cherish and nourish you until you attain mature manhood and the fullness of the body of Christ.

Count us as fellow-workers in your salvation and helpers of Catholic peace. May our fellowship be in Christ Jesus our Lord, who, by faith and likewise by works, may preserve you with us incorrupt and undefiled, establish you pure and blameless before the sight of his glory, and make you together heirs of everlasting blessedness forever. Amen.

## LETTER VII. TO OFFA, KING OF THE MERCIANS (795)

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils)*

[Col. 0907A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends greetings in Christ to the venerable man and dearest brother, Offa, king of the Mercians.

First, we give thanks to almighty God for the sincerity of the Catholic faith, which we have found commendably written out in your pages. As for pilgrims who, out of love for God and for the salvation of their souls, desire to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles, let them go in peace without any disturbance. But if any are found among them who do not serve religion but pursue profit, let them pay the established tolls at suitable places.

[Col. 0907B] We also wish merchants to enjoy legitimate protection in our kingdom by our command. If they are oppressed anywhere by unjust treatment, let them appeal to us or to our judges, and we shall order full justice to be done.

Let your affection also know that we have sent some kindness from our dalmatics or cloaks to the individual episcopal sees of your kingdom and of Æthelred, as an alms for the apostolic lord Adrian, asking you to order that prayers be offered for him. We have no doubt that his blessed soul is at rest; we do this also to show our faith and affection toward our dearest friend.

Likewise, from the treasury of human goods that the Lord Jesus has granted us through his gratuitous kindness, we have sent something to the metropolitan cities. To your affection also we have decided to send one belt, one Hunnish sword, and two silk cloaks. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO POPE LEO III, SENT THROUGH ANGILBERT, ABBOT OF CENTULA (796)

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends greetings of perpetual blessedness in Christ to Pope Leo.

Having read your Excellency’s letters and heard the decretal document, we rejoiced greatly, as I confess, both at the unanimity of your election and at your humility’s obedience and your fidelity to the promise made to us.

[Col. 0907D] In all these matters we give thanks from the innermost affection of our heart to the divine goodness, because, after the grievous wound of sorrow inflicted upon our soul by the death of our dearest father and most faithful friend, God’s customary providence has deigned to grant us such consolation in you.

Therefore, as though bearing to your holiness a gift of joy in his place, through the mercy of that same God and Lord Jesus Christ, who has cared for his holy Church through the elevation of your blessedness, we commend to you the prosperity of ourselves and all our faithful, and we make known to you the peaceful unanimity of our entire kingdom in the will of God. Thus may you rejoice in the success of our devotion just as we rejoice in the successes of your holiness.

We also make known to your most holy benevolence that, when I had prepared to send gifts of affection to my sweetest father, your predecessor, so that I might show by the generosity of my gift the greatness of the charity I had for him and so that the fidelity of our most tender familiarity might be displayed to many eyes, behold, suddenly—I cannot speak of it without pain or think of it without tears—I was overwhelmed by the news of his death. Where I had prepared tokens of joy, there mourning disturbed me.

Although the Apostle forbids sorrow over the dead, charity nevertheless does not cease to draw forth tears. We do not mourn him as one dead, but remember him as living more perfectly with Christ. Although we have lost him in bodily presence, we do not think that we have lost him in spiritual assistance.

[Col. 0908B] But divine grace had foreseen a great consolation for us when it placed you, venerable man, in his position, so that there might be one who would intercede daily before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the stability of the whole Church; for the salvation of me and my faithful; indeed, for the stability of the entire kingdom given to us by God; and who would adopt us to himself as a son with paternal affection.

For the peaceful unanimity of affection we have sent Angilbert, a personal envoy of affection, to your holiness; previously, as we promised through the religious men Campolus and Anastasius, we had arranged to send him to our most blessed father, your predecessor. But, as we have said, while all the gifts were ready, his journey was suddenly delayed by the mournful news of his father’s death.

Now, made happier by the succession of your holiness, we strive to accomplish in you what we desired to do with that devout father. We have entrusted him with everything that seemed either pleasing to us or necessary for you, so that through mutual discussion you may confer about whatever you recognize as necessary for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, the stability of your honor, or the security of our patriciate.

For just as I entered into a pact with the most blessed predecessor of your holy fatherhood, so I desire to establish with your blessedness an inviolable covenant of the same faith and charity. Thus, by God’s grace and with the prayers of the saints invoked, may the apostolic blessing attend me everywhere, and, by God’s gift, may the most holy see of the Roman Church always be defended by our devotion.

[Col. 0908D] It is our responsibility, with the help of divine goodness, to defend everywhere the holy Church of Christ by arms from the incursions of pagans and the devastation of unbelievers, and to fortify her within and without through knowledge of the Catholic faith.

It is yours, most holy Father, with hands raised to God like Moses, to assist our army, so that, through your intercession, with God as guide and giver, the Christian people may everywhere and always have victory over the enemies of his holy name, and the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified throughout the world.

May the wisdom of your authority everywhere follow the canons, so that examples of complete holiness may shine clearly in your conduct before all, and the exhortation of holy admonition may be heard from your mouth. Thus may your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

[Col. 0909A] May almighty God deign to preserve the blessedness of your authority unharmed for many years, for the exaltation of his holy Church.

## LETTER IX. TO ANGILBERT, ABBOT  
*Instruction to Angilbert, who was being sent to the pope with the preceding letter* (796)

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils)*

Charles, by the grace of God king and defender of the holy Church, sends greetings to Homer, his chamberlain.

**[Note: [Col. 0909D] Charles . . . Homer.** Angilbert, abbot of Centula, whom both Alcuin in his letters and Theodulf in his unpublished verses [Sirmond published them in 1640. Labbé] likewise call Homer. Just as this Angilbert was called Homer, so Richulf, bishop of Mainz, was called Damoetas; Charles himself was called David; and at that time others called one another by other names among their intimates. **J. Sirmond.]**

By the mercy of God directing you, and bringing you safely once again to our apostolic lord the pope, admonish him carefully concerning every aspect of his life and, above all, concerning observance of the holy canons and the devout governance of the holy Church of God, according to the opportunity for discussion between you and the disposition of his mind.

Frequently impress upon him that the honor which he presently possesses belongs to only a few years, whereas the reward given to one who labors well in it lasts forever. Urge him most diligently to overthrow the simoniacal heresy, which grievously stains the holy body of the Church in many places. And convey to him whatever you remember that we have often discussed in complaint among ourselves.

[Col. 0909C] Above all, do not fail to suggest to him what my discussion with blessed Pope Adrian, his predecessor, was like concerning the construction of a monastery at Saint Paul’s, so that, if God wills, when you return you may bring me a definite answer.

May the Lord God guide you and direct his heart in all goodness, so that he may do what benefits his holy Church; so that he may be a devout Father to us and a chief intercessor on our behalf; and so that the same God and Lord Jesus Christ may make us flourish in his will and deign to lead the remainder of our life’s course to the rest of perpetual stability.

Go in prosperity, advancing in truth and returning with joy, young Homer.

## LETTER X. TO MANASSES, ABBOT (798)

*(From Labbe, New Library of Manuscripts)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, sends greetings to Manasses, abbot of the monastery of Flavigny.

Blessed be the name of the Lord forever, for, in accordance with the praiseworthy conduct of your monks, it is greatly glorified among the nations, since his praise is always on your lips.

We have therefore willingly received and mercifully granted the petition concerning the construction of a monastery at Corbiniacum, which was presented through Theodulf, bishop of Orléans and likewise [the] abbot of the monastery of Fleury [the text is corrupt here]. We command that the monks whom you send there return frequently to the monastery of Flavigny, lest at any time they forget the way of God’s commandments; there they are to strengthen their duties and return improved by your command and that of your monks.

Let them pay at all times whatever census you establish for them. From every other census owed to you, however, I make them free out of affection, just as I have made Flavigny free.

I am sending you a silver casket containing relics of the tomb of the Savior and of Saint James the apostle, the Lord’s brother. I ask and implore you to remember me and to intercede continually with the Lord for me and for our sons.

I greet you and our entire congregation. I, Rado, wrote this; I dictated it in the eighth year of the aforesaid lord King Charles, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever.

## LETTER XI. Fragment of a Letter to the Bishops (799)

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils)*

[Col. 0910B]

You must also consider this very carefully with us: what should be done concerning those priests about whom there is no approval and who always deny the charge. For this matter has very often been discussed by us, our ancestors, and our predecessors, but until now it has not been settled decisively.

Therefore we are sending our priests to consult our father, Pope Leo. Whatever we learn from him or from his representatives, we will not delay reporting to you, together with those whom we are sending.

Meanwhile, consider among yourselves more attentively what we should establish with you concerning these matters, together with the instructions of the aforesaid holy Father, so that the people’s murmuring may cease and, by satisfying them in this way, we may, with the Lord’s help, remain unharmed by both sides.

## LETTER XII. TO OFFA, KING OF THE MERCIANS  
*He sends an accused Scottish priest back to his homeland to be judged there by his bishop* (800)

*(From Mansi, Collection of Councils)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and defender of the holy Church of God, sends greetings to his beloved brother and friend, Offa, king.

This priest, a Scot, lived among us for some time in the parish of Hildebold, bishop of Cologne. But, as is reported, he was accused by a certain accuser and became subject to reproach because he had eaten meat on the days of Lent.

Our priests, however, refused to judge him because they found no full testimony from the accusers against him. Nevertheless, they did not permit him to remain longer in his customary place of residence because of the infamy, lest priestly honor be cheapened among the ignorant populace or some be encouraged by rumor to violate the holy fast.

It seemed appropriate to our priests to send him for judgment to his own bishop, in whose diocese he made his vow to God. Therefore we ask your foresight to order that, at the suitable time and when travel is possible, he be transferred to his own homeland, so that he may be judged there, from which he came.

[Col. 0911A] For there too the purity of the holy Church of God in morals, steadfastness in faith, and uprightness in conduct must be carefully observed according to canonical ordinance, so that she may be one perfect and immaculate dove, whose feathers ought to be silvered and whose hindparts should shine in the appearance of gold.

May life, health, and prosperity be granted by Christ God to you and your faithful forever.

**[Note: [Col. 0911D] Letter.** In the edition of Quercetanus, p. 1147. Here we present the same letter in a more corrected form from the manuscripts of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram. I believe that this letter concerning Septuagesima was written in the year 798, in which year Alcuin also replied to this letter of Charles in the following letter (Alcuin, Froben edition, vol. II, p. 90). The occasion for investigating this matter was provided by his disciples, “aroused by the correspondence of those times.” Therefore this letter was written during Septuagesima of that year.]**

## LETTER XIII. TO ALBINUS, ABBOT (800)

*(From the Works of Alcuin, Froben edition)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, emperor **[Note: [Col. 0912D] Emperor.** This word is absent from the manuscripts of Salzburg and Saint Emmeram; nor is it found in Goldast, who published this letter in *Constitutiones imperiales*, vol. III, p. 137. It is also omitted in the Chronicle of Centula, in Pouget, p. 624, note a. And rightly so, since this letter was sent before Charles had been declared emperor, as we said in the preceding note.]** of the Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends eternal greetings in our Lord Jesus Christ to our dearest teacher and to Abbot Albinus, whom we name with affection.

A letter sent from your religious prudence has reached us. After the praises and blessings due to almighty God, it conveyed to us and to our offspring a desirable blessing with the greatest goodwill **[Variant: “and the greatest goodwill”]**.

After this, its text proceeded to inquire why Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima are called or written in sequence according to the Sundays before Quadragesima. Taking up the matter, it sought, by traversing the fields of the arithmetical art, to make known to us fully whatever your diligence had perceived concerning it **[Variant: “had decided”]**.

But while our mind ranged here and there, we carefully considered through diligent investigation that not only within the days you prescribed, but also through individual weeks and throughout the entire cycle of the year **[Goldast: “the entire cycle”; Goldast omits “space”]**, mysteries of numbers can be discovered by those trained in mastery of this art, through intervals of hours, points, or moments.

Therefore, since it pleased your affection to consult our royal court about this matter, we do not refuse to disclose to you in orderly discourse whatever our serenity thinks concerning it **[Variant: “thought concerning it”]**.

The inquiry and consideration thus require us to ask why some abstain for six weeks, others for seven, others for eight, and some for nine **[Variant: “having considered the matter, why”; Goldast: “having considered the matter, why”]**. We shall strive to signify the reasoning of our understanding to your familiarity in these brief lines.

Those who, observing six weeks, devote themselves to abstinence, subtracting the six Sundays on which fasting is not permitted, give the tithe of the days of their body and fast for thirty-six days, as blessed Gregory, the remarkable teacher, instructs **[Goldast: “giving the tenth of their days”]**. Although two days seem to remain in this period until the holy Resurrection, the teachers of the holy Church of God have been pleased to call it Quadragesima.

As devotion increased, seven weeks were dedicated to abstinence by Pope Telesphorus, who shone as the ninth in the holy Roman Church after Peter, prince of the apostles. And by what other name could this period more properly be called than Quinquagesima, in rational sequence? **[Variants: “ought to have been called”; Goldast: “call it Quinquagesima … ought to have been called”]**

From that point onward, by a collected reckoning, those who observed eight weeks gradually called the period Sexagesima **[Variants: “eight weeks”; Goldast adds “those who strove to observe Sexagesima gradually”].**

[Col. 0912B] Similarly, those who observed nine weeks gave the period the name Septuagesima according to the aforesaid reckoning. They judged these names to be appropriate not because of the number **[Variant: “sequence of numbers”]** of weeks or days, but while preserving the pattern of the names **[Variant: “the numbers”].**

It would be as if there were now people who wished, for some just reason, to add a tenth week and, because of the number of weeks, ought to call it Decagesima **[Variant: Decimagesima]**, or by any other name; or, because of the number of days, Septuagesima or Octuagesima, proceeding along the straight path by preserving the order of the names.

Since, therefore, with the assistance of divine grace, we have written to your charity, as it seemed to us, concerning the names of Septuagesima and Sexagesima [Col. 0912C] [Al., Quadragesima], and Quinquagesima, we have now taken care, as our pen proceeds, to write to you, according to the capacity [Gold., acuity] of our understanding, concerning the observance and keeping of these weeks.

Quinquagesima is so called and observed by some so that they may offer to almighty God, by fasting, a tithe of the days, and imitate our Lord Jesus Christ, who completed a most sacred fast of forty days. From Quinquagesima to Easter there are seven weeks, making fifty days. If you subtract the eight Sundays, on which fasting may not be observed, forty-two days remain; and these two additional days—namely, Thursday and Saturday [Gold., Friday, incorrectly]—which exceed the number forty, are devoted to fasting by some, while by others they are held in veneration [Al., refreshment] because of the Lord’s Supper and Holy Saturday.

Sexagesima, as we judge, is observed by some for this reason: that they may offer to almighty God a tithe of the days of their body [Al., of their bodies], imitate our Lord Jesus Christ in the number forty by fasting in part, and be able to abstain from fasting on Sunday [Col. 0913A] or Thursday. From Sexagesima to the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection there are eight weeks. If from each week you subtract Sunday and Thursday, and also the holy day of Easter itself, only forty days remain in abstinence.

Melchiades, an African by birth, a man wholly apostolic, the thirty-fourth after Saint Peter, whom blessed Sylvester succeeded in the chair [Al., to the chair] of apostolic dignity, established that under no circumstances should any of the faithful presume to fast on Sunday or Thursday [Note: [Col. 0913D] “For why . . .” In the manuscript Codex of Saint Emmeram it is read as follows: “For why is there no fasting on Sunday, since the Savior himself has handed this down? There is no need to repeat it at length.”]. For why fasting is released on Sunday, as the Lord himself handed down, there is no need to repeat at length. We judge that Thursday was released from fasting by him because of the great mysteries contained in it. On that day the holy chrism is prepared for washing away the sins of the whole world’s first origin [Al., for washing away . . . the sin]; on that day penitents are reconciled; on that day the Redeemer of all, dining with his disciples, broke bread and likewise gave them the cup [Al., the redemption of all, dining] as a figure of his body and blood, and displayed to us a great sacrament destined for our benefit (Matthew 26:26–27) [Note: [Col. 0913D] “As a figure.” The manuscript of Saint Emmeram and Goldastus have: “In figure.” This is not to be understood in the Calvinist sense [Col. 0914D], but in the Catholic sense, as explained in the work of D. Arnauld, *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, vol. I, p. 765.]. On that same day, after many mysteries, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of his holy disciples, penetrated the heavens in a glorious ascension (Luke 24:51; Acts 1:9).

But, so that the discourse may not be prolonged, we do not fail to know that you have read much about this solemnity in the sayings of the venerable holy orthodox Fathers.

Septuagesima, finally, as we judge, is observed by some for this reason: that they may offer a tithe of the days to God [Al., to the Lord], and may release themselves from fasting on Sunday, Thursday, and also Saturday [Gold., observe, incorrectly]. From Septuagesima to Easter there are nine weeks, making sixty-four days [Gold., sixty-three]. If from each week you subtract the three days mentioned above, and also the most sacred day of Easter, thirty-six days remain in abstinence [Al., of abstinence].

They also attempt to release themselves from fasting on Saturday, on which God rested from all his works (Genesis 2:2), not merely because of Jewish superstition, nor because of the legal commandments of the Old Testament, which are a shadow of things to come, but lest they cause scandal with the Jews [Al., be scandalized; Gold., keep the Sabbath] [Col. 0913D]. The chief reason is that, as that day grows toward evening, the joy of the holy Resurrection is solemnly celebrated by the faithful.

But since each person abounds in his own judgment (Romans 14:5), whether this or something else is the case, provided faith and religion are preserved, we prejudge nothing [Al., prejudged nothing; Al., it is forbidden; Al., proclaimed nothing].

[Note: [Col. 0914D] “Concerning this matter.” We have added this clause, which was absent from the printed editions, from the manuscript Codex of Salzburg, Goldastus, the work cited, p. 138, and D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 470.]

Concerning what your letter further reported—that much could be said on this subject, but that you did not wish to exceed the limits of a letter, and especially that, since a few words should be used with a wise man, we in turn have replied briefly to a few matters.

As for your use of the words of the Queen of Sheba to Solomon concerning the blessedness of the servants who stand before us and hear the words of our wisdom: if you know this to be true, come, stand before us, listen, and together let us delight and rejoice in the Lord amid the flowering meadows, made joyful by the variety of the flowers of Scripture.

## LETTER XIV. TO FIVE BISHOPS  
### On the sevenfold grace of the Spirit (A.D. 800)

*(Mabillon, Old Historical Miscellanies.)*

Charles, by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to Hiltibald (of Cologne), Maginhart (of Rouen), Agino (of Bergamo), Gerhoh (of Eister), and Hartrich (of Toulouse), holy bishops.

We give thanks to your holiness because, when we had familiarly questioned you, you wished to give us a familiar answer; and the matters proposed to your affection at the prompting of charity have, under the same prompting of charity, been resolved for us without hesitation, according to what seemed right to you. But the order of the response given to us by your holiness must be examined, and the innermost marrow of its meaning sought out in your affection, so that both the character of our question may appear and the manner of your answer may shine forth more clearly.

For the holy Fathers who, as we read in the sequence of the Old Testament, from the beginning pleased God and preceded this final age of the world—an age made most blessed by Christ’s coming—through uprightness of conduct and the multiplicity of their merits, must without any doubt be believed both to have received and to have possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit. For who has ever pleased God while lacking the gift of the Holy Spirit?

But, as the text of your response states, we have learned that the individual gifts of the Holy Spirit were possessed individually by the saints, while all of them dwelt fully in Christ. We approve this as supported by the firm reasoning of truth; yet we by no means think that any of the holy Fathers was content with the singularity of one gift, since this can very easily be understood from the names of the graces themselves.

Wisdom and understanding are so joined by a natural bond that one cannot exist without the other in any way [Col. 0914D]. For how can someone be wise who does not understand? Or how can one understand whom it is clear does not possess wisdom? Has anyone ever been found who, deprived of wisdom or understanding, possessed counsel either for himself or gave it to another [alii]? For it is clearer than daylight that counsel belongs only to the wise.

Fortitude, if it lacks counsel, ought not to be considered fortitude, since everything done without deliberation is usually called rash rather than courageous. It is highly unbelievable that knowledge can exist in anyone without wisdom and understanding. For what can one know who is unable to understand anything [Col. 0915A]?

Whoever examines himself easily recognizes by what art piety and the fear of God are joined to one another: no one is pious unless, fearing God’s judgment, he forgives his neighbor who has sinned against him.

It is therefore no wonder that these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit were individually in the holy Fathers and were united together in Christ. For what good could be lacking in him who created all good things together with the Father? Is it a great thing if these gifts are said to have remained in Christ, in whom the whole fullness of divinity is known to dwell? Is it a great thing if you attribute to the Lord, as though as a gift, things that, when carefully considered, you will find in a servant? Can the Lord be exalted only by those gifts without which a good servant cannot exist [Col. 0915B]?

Far be it from us to say that his glory was completed by these gifts alone, since we believe that his magnificence is exalted above everything that is said or named, whether in heaven or on earth. For neither can the mind comprehend nor speech explain what and of what kind, or how great, are the things that ought to be attributed to the glory of him who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever.

But we are not surprised that these gifts were individually in the Fathers and all together in Christ, because they can be counted individually in his disciples and all together in Peter. Nevertheless, we must believe that these same gifts were in Christ in a very different manner than in the other saints.

In each of the saints, according to the variety of their wills—which human frailty does not lack—one gift or another is known to come and go, to be present or absent. But in Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, all the charisms of the Holy Spirit came to him once for all and, never again to depart, remained in him.

But why speak of patriarchs and apostles, when even now we should not doubt that many can daily be found within the bosom of holy mother Church who are enriched with either individual or several gifts of the Holy Spirit? True is he who promised that his presence would not be lacking to those who trust in him until the consummation of the age. Since he remains always with us and in us, we shall by no means lack the sevenfold-graced Holy Spirit, whom we possess by believing and doing good, as the giver of all good things.

He is governed by the spirit of wisdom who strives to learn the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity, both for his own progress and for that of others, so that through it he may resist heretics and strengthen his own people.

He possesses the spirit of understanding who, hearing the divine commandments, perceives with the understanding of his heart how necessary knowledge of them is; and, in accordance with blessed James, does not become a forgetful hearer but an active doer, striving to ensure that the commandments he has understood are kept by him with complete integrity.

He flourishes in the spirit of counsel who, in everything he plans to do, first considers whether it will please God, judging it better to reflect silently beforehand on what should be done and how than to begin anything rashly, so that repentance might not force him to abandon what he has begun.

He possesses the spirit of fortitude who strives, armed with the shield of faith and the sword of God’s word, to resist the devil and his members, namely heretics [Col. 0916A], and who arms himself with fortitude against the vices by which this mortal life is daily stained at the devil’s instigation, as against the missiles of an enemy.

For he possesses the spirit of knowledge, whoever, mindful of the Lord’s command, has the simplicity of a dove and the prudence of a serpent; whoever, distinguishing among similar things, knows how to reject evil and choose good. Evil is often found mixed with good, and without knowledge it is difficult to distinguish them.

We say that the spirit of piety is present in him who, not forgetting the Lord’s commandments, forgives his neighbor who has offended him; and who exercises proper piety not only toward others but also toward himself. For every upright person must beware lest, while he is pious by forgiving his debtor’s evil, he become impious toward himself by failing to give what is his due [Col. 0916B].

We say that he is filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord who, fearing God’s judgment, strives to do good not so much out of delight in the heavenly kingdom as because, through fear of Gehenna, he does not dare to commit evil; and who rejoices in the promise of eternal life while fearing no less the punishment of everlasting suffering, and, pierced by this spirit, turns away from evil and does good.

We believe that this Holy Spirit of sevenfold grace was in the Fathers and apostles, and that it is now breathed by divine gift into the sons of holy mother Church, who are daily reborn in Christ for the increase of his people.

But in Christ, as we said above, we are not surprised by such gifts, whose immeasurable glory the human mind cannot recount. Since we cannot explain in what manner these gifts are in him, it remains for us to offer praises to him who gives them to us:

> Christ, salvation of the world, everlasting glory of the saints,  
> Let praise and honor ever be yours in the citadel of heaven.

### Again, on the sevenfold grace of the Spirit

The spirit of wisdom was in Peter when, leaving his nets and boat, he followed the Lord. He possessed the spirit of understanding when, upon the Lord’s asking whom people said the Son of Man was, he both understood and answered that he was Christ, the Son of the living God.

The spirit of counsel was in him when, unwilling to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit to Simon who offered money, he ordered Simon himself, together with his money, to go to destruction.

He possessed the spirit of fortitude when, drawing his sword, he cut off Malchus’s ear. He possessed the spirit of knowledge when, while the other disciples in the boat were uncertain, he recognized that it was the Lord [Col. 0916D].

The spirit of piety was with him when he asked the Lord how long he ought to forgive a brother who had sinned against him. He was full of the spirit of the fear of the Lord when, astonished at the miracle of the fish, he said to the Lord: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.”

### Another treatment

The spirit of wisdom was in Andrew, and it was also in the sons of Zebedee, when, like Peter, they left their nets and boat and followed the Lord.

The spirit of understanding was in Thomas when, having touched the Lord’s wounds, he both understood and confessed that he was himself his God and Lord.

The spirit of counsel was in all the disciples [Col. 0917A] when, curious about future events, they consulted the Lord concerning the end of the world.

No one denies that the spirit of fortitude was present in all the disciples unless he maintains that they were unwilling to suffer death for Christ’s name.

The spirit of knowledge was in John, who discussed the divinity and humanity of the Savior so distinctly at the beginning of his Gospel, and who wrote with no less discernment in the Apocalypse concerning the seven thunders—what should be kept silent and what should be spoken.

The spirit of piety was in Stephen, who at the very moment of death prayed for his persecutors. The spirit of the fear of the Lord was in all the apostles, because they not only did good but also, out of love for God, did not dare to do evil.

## LETTER XV. TO GARIBALD, BISHOP OF LIÈGE  
### On the care pastors ought especially to devote to instructing the people before baptism (A.D. 800)

*(From Martène, *Ample Collection of Old Writers*.)*

[Col. 0917B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, governing the empire, and also by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to Garibald, bishop, greeting in the Lord.

We believe, therefore, that your holiness will rightly remember how often, in our assembly and council, we admonished each of you concerning preaching in the holy Church of God, that according to the authority of the holy canons each of you ought both to preach and to teach.

First of all, concerning the Catholic faith: so that whoever was unable to grasp more might at least be able to retain and recite from memory only the Lord’s Prayer and the symbol of the Catholic faith, as the apostles taught; and so that no one should presume to take someone from the sacred baptismal font before he had recited the Lord’s Prayer and the symbol in the presence of you or of your ministers of the sacred order.

As we recently discovered [Note: [Col. 0917D] This shows that in the time of Charlemagne baptism was celebrated not only at Easter and Pentecost but also at Epiphany. We have demonstrated this elsewhere from the most ancient Sacramentary of the monastery of Gellone, written in his time. See Book I, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 1, section 1.] on the day of the Lord’s manifestation, many were found among us who wished to take infants from the sacred baptismal font. We ordered that they be individually and carefully examined and asked whether they knew and retained by heart the Lord’s Prayer and the symbol, as we have said above. There were many who had no recollection of these things whatsoever. We ordered them to abstain, so that before they knew and could recite the prayer and the symbol, they should presume to take no one from the sacred baptismal font.

They were very much ashamed of this matter and wished to promise that, if permission were granted them, they could in time remove this reproach from themselves. In this matter we understood that it was not suitable for them; and, as you can find in our capitulary, we made a determination concerning the length of time each person ought to abstain from this duty, until he could be a good guarantor in this matter—namely, either he should immediately find another who knew them, or, if illness did not prevent him, he should wait from Easter until Pentecost, until he himself learned the things mentioned above.

Now we again admonish you to be mindful, as is fitting, of the priestly ministry; to hold an assembly with your priests; and carefully to seek out and examine the whole truth of the matter, so that the work of the Lord may not be neglected and no inquiry concerning it may be required of you before the presence of the holy Majesty.

## LETTER XVI. TO GARIBALD, BISHOP  
### Fasting is proclaimed for public necessities, especially famine, pestilence, and war (A.D. 800)

*(From Martène, *Ample Collection of Old Writers*.)*

[Col. 0918B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God [Note: [Col. 0918D] Thus the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Hubert at Andage, written eight hundred years ago; others, however, name Garibald as bishop of Liège.], to Bishop Ghaerbaldo, together with all those entrusted to you by almighty God and by our ordinance, greeting in the Lord.

Let it be known to your affection that, after deliberating with our faithful, both spiritual and secular, and with their agreement and common counsel, we have found it necessary, because of certain pressing needs that we shall specify below, for three three-day fasts to be generally observed by all of us, and for help to be sought from him in whom we live, are moved, and have our being. From him, whatever your faith, firm hope, or perfect charity justly and reasonably asks will undoubtedly be obtained at the proper time, for the Lord himself says: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

These fasts, as it has seemed to all of us, can suitably be carried out by the following arrangement, if the Lord grants it. The first shall take place after eleven days have passed from the feast of Saint Andrew—that is, on the third day before the Ides, the Ides of December, and the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January. All shall abstain from wine and meat on these three days and fast until the ninth hour, except those whom age or illness does not permit to do so. Such persons, according to their condition or way of life, should strive, on the advice of their teachers, to make up for what they cannot fulfill by fasting and abstinence through adequate observances [F., prayers] or suitable alms.

At the ninth hour, everyone shall devoutly gather at the nearby churches where the announcement has been made to them. If the hour and place permit, they shall proceed in a litany through some spacious place; then, entering the church while singing psalms, they shall hear Mass with complete devotion. When it has been completed, each person shall return home and satisfy the body with the prescribed foods—not according to desire, but according to necessity and sobriety.

Likewise, we admonish each person to give alms according to what the means of his property permit [Col. 0919A] and the devotion of his mind, inspired by the Lord, has suggested. Each priest shall sing Mass, and a cleric or monk of another order, or a consecrated woman who has learned the psalms, shall likewise sing Psalm 50.

We permit work to be done on these days, provided that it neither prevents them from coming to church nor compels them to eat or drink before the appointed hour [Note: [Col. 0919D] It is clear from this that it was unlawful for those fasting to drink outside the time of eating. From this one may judge how blind is the error of those who teach that liquid does not break a fast, especially if wine or another strengthening and nourishing drink is involved. Here those fasting are expressly ordered to abstain from wine even at the meal.].

The other two three-day fasts shall likewise be observed in every respect on these days: one after the Epiphany, on the seventh day before the Ides, the fourth day before the Ides, and the second day before the Ides of January; the other after Septuagesima, on the second day before the Ides of February, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, and the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

The necessities that we promised above to mention, among the others—which on this occasion we have nevertheless judged necessary to recall—are these.

We have learned through our faithful, who reported these matters to us from the various parts of our kingdom, that, contrary to customary practice and beyond what is usual, sterility appears to prevail everywhere in the land, and the danger of famine to be approaching. The unseasonableness of the weather is also highly unfavorable to the crops; pestilence is present in various places; and among the peoples settled around our borders continual wars are being waged. There are many further matters which it would take too long to enumerate now, and which can be made familiar to us by experience if we wish to remember the kinds of misfortunes we suffer each day because of our merits.

From these external things we can most certainly infer that inwardly we do not please the Lord in every respect, since we are compelled to endure so many evils outwardly. Therefore it seems entirely good to us that each of us should strive to humble his heart in truth; that wherever, whether in action or thought, he discovers that he has offended God, he should wipe it away through repentance, grieve over it with tears, and, insofar as he can with the Lord’s help, guard himself in the future from these evils by avoiding them.

The intention of the prayer undertaken beforehand ought to be this: that almighty God, who knows all things not only after they have been done but even before they are done, may pierce our hearts with repentance; make us suppliant and subject to him in true humility; turn each of us, once all error has been driven from us, to the observance of his commandments; and have mercy, whether by driving evils away from us or by granting us the good things of which we are unworthy, just as he knows that we need.

May he grant that we may deserve to be numbered among his members—that is, in the body of holy Church [Col. 0919D]—which he may deign to pacify, unite, and govern, and protect from every evil, including us who are encompassed in that unity. So that we may merit his grace, we have decreed that these fasts and prayers be universally carried out by all of you.

Read this letter again and, according to the wisdom given to you by God, have it carefully reread before everyone and delivered, so that all may understand for what necessity these things must be done. Send each of you interpreters to the individual baptismal churches, good interpreters who will transmit everything as we have said above [Col. 0920A]. Do the same throughout the individual monasteries within your diocese.

## LETTER XVII. TO PIPPIN, HIS SON, KING OF ITALY  
### On the peace of the churches of God and those who serve them (A.D. 801)

*(From Mansi, *Collection of Councils*.)*

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the empire of the Romans, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to our dearest son Pippin, glorious king, everlasting greeting in the Lord.

It has come to our ears [Al., to our clemency] that certain dukes and their young men, castaldii, vicars, centenarii, and other officials, falconers, hunters, and others living or traveling through the individual territories receive lodging dues and transport services (*mansionatica* and *paravereda*), not only from free men but also from the churches of God—namely, monasteries of men and women, hospices, and various parishes—and from the other servants of the churches of God.

They make these people work for them in their own tasks, namely in vineyards, fields, and meadows, as well as in their buildings; and they do not cease to exact from them meat dues and wine contrary to all justice. The churches of God themselves, and their servants, suffer many oppressions.

Therefore, dearest son, we have sent this letter to your affection so that you may have this matter carefully and prudently investigated and, if it is true that this has been done, strive in every way thereafter to amend and correct it, so that in our days and yours the peace of the churches of God and of those who serve them may be preserved in every respect, and so that abundant reward may continually increase for us and for you on this account.

We have also heard that in certain places some of our men and yours say that certain chapters which we ordered to be written into the law were not in fact issued by us personally for their information; and therefore they refuse to obey them, consent to them, or hold them as law.

But you know how and in what manner we spoke with you concerning those chapters. Therefore we admonish your beloved affection to make them known throughout the entire kingdom entrusted to you by God, and to order that they be obeyed and fulfilled.

Concerning bishops and priests who have been killed, as we have established, and concerning all other matters: with regard to priests, however, it seems to us that if a priest was born free, the perpetrator should pay a threefold composition according to your law; and if the priest has been wounded, the perpetrator should make compensation threefold, according to the nature of the wounds or the discipline involved.

If, however, the priest was born a slave, compensation for wounds and punishments should be paid threefold according to his birth status. The same should be done concerning deacons.

When these matters have been completed, fare ever well in the Lord, dearest son.

[Note: [Col. 0921C]

“Of great importance,” says Baluzius in his notes on the *Capitularies*, vol. II, p. 1062, “is this letter of Charles, written by a great prince and one highly skilled in both priestly and imperial law. Here you see a cleric judged by his bishop according to the canons and confined in custody because of his deserts; then, having broken—as one might say—the chains of the prison, he fled to the church of Saint Martin and abused the sanctity of the place in order to escape the punishment that had been imposed upon him by excellent judgment.

“Next you see the monks, as though they wished to advertise the religious authority of their asylum, concealing him in their hiding places and daring to undertake his defense against the bishop, even publicly heaping many insults upon him.

“This matter appeared so mad and foolish to the most wise prince that he not only chastised their stupidity in harsh words but also ordered that the cleric be returned to his bishop, and that the monks come to him so that, by appropriate satisfaction, they might wash away the branded crime. . . .

“Moreover, what happened here to Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, under the rule of Charlemagne, happened almost in the same way later to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, as Flodoard teaches, *History of Reims*, Book III, chapter 21. In listing Hincmar’s letters, he says: ‘To Ebbo, bishop and alumnus of the church of Reims, concerning a certain brother who had fled from that church and was staying with him, so that he should strive to send him back with diligent care as quickly as possible.’”

Baluzius first published this letter from an old manuscript of the Colbert Library in volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 413, and believed it was written in 803; Mabillon, however, assigned it to the preceding year.]

## LETTER XVIII. TO ALBINUS, THE MASTER, AND TO THE COMMUNITY OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARTIN (A.D. 803)

*(From the works of the blessed Alcuin, edited by Froben.)*

[Col. 0921A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, and the rest, to Albinus, venerable master, and to the entire community of the monastery of Saint Martin.

The day before your letter was brought to our presence, letters sent by Bishop Theodulf were delivered to us. They contained complaints about the dishonoring of his men, and not so much of them as of the bishop of this city, as well as about contempt for the command of our imperial authority.

We had ordered that command to be written concerning the return of a certain cleric who had escaped from the bishop’s custody and was hiding in the basilica of Saint Martin under the authority of our name. You also sent us copies of it [F., we sent you . . . copies], and we think that, as it seemed to you, we decreed nothing unjustly in them.

But when we had both letters—yours, that is, and Theodulf’s—read back to us, your letter appeared to us much harsher and composed with greater anger than Theodulf’s, and in no way sprinkled with the seasoning of charity toward him. Rather, it seemed to defend the accused, accuse the bishop, and, under a certain veil of concealed identity, maintain that the man either could or ought to be admitted to an accusation.

Yet both divine and human law have altogether established that no criminal may be granted permission to accuse another [Note: [Col. 0922D] “To no criminal.” This is found in the *Capitula of Angilram*, chapter 43, and from there in Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 187. See also Book VII, chapter 85. Baluzius.].

Although you defended and protected him for this purpose under the pretext of the command of our name, you maintained that a man who had already been accused and judged in the presence of the people of his city [Note: [Col. 0922D] “In the presence of the people.” This passage is greatly clarified by Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 370.] ought to have the right of accusation by appealing to the imperial name, on the example of the blessed apostle Paul.

Paul was accused by his own people before the rulers of Judaea, but had not yet been judged; he appealed to Caesar and was sent by those same rulers to Caesar to be judged (Acts 25:10–11). This, however, has no bearing at all on the present case.

The apostle Paul was accused by the Jews but not judged; he appealed to Caesar and was permitted to go to him. But this infamous cleric was accused and judged, sent into custody, and escaped from custody. He entered the basilica unlawfully, although he ought not to have entered it until after penance, and, as you say, he continues even now to live perversely. You say that, just as the apostle Paul appealed to Caesar, he did likewise; but he will by no means go to Caesar as Paul did.

We order that he be returned to the one before whom he was accused, by whom he was judged and sent into custody, and from whose custody he escaped; and that this man bring him to our hearing, whether he speaks the truth or falsehood. For it is not fitting that, because of such a man, any alteration should be made in our first command.

We are also very greatly surprised that it seemed to you alone that our authoritative sanction and decree should be opposed, when it is plainly evident both from ancient custom and from the constitution of the laws [kings] that right decrees ought to be valid [F., ratified], and that no one is permitted to despise their edicts or statutes.

Nor could we sufficiently wonder at this: that you preferred to obey the pleas of that wicked man rather than the commands of our authority, since it is now perfectly clear that, together with that same man, you have allowed the love of discord, through the breach of charity, to leave this place [L., as though].

For you yourselves—who are called the community of this monastery and servants of God, if only truly!—have already had your life repeatedly defamed by many people, and not without reason. At one time you said that you were monks; at another, canons; at another, neither.

Out of concern for you and to remove this evil reputation [Note: [Col. 0922D] “Master.” Alcuin, certainly?], we chose and invited for you from distant provinces a suitable master and rector, who could instruct you in the right life by words and admonitions and, because he was religious, form you by the example of good conduct.

But, alas, everything has been turned in another direction; and the devil has found you, as though you were his ministers, to sow discord among those among whom it was least fitting—namely, among the wise men and teachers of the Church, who ought to correct and chastise sinners. You compel them to break forth into the sin of envy and anger.

But, by God’s mercy, they will by no means yield to your evil suggestions.

You, however, who have proved yourselves despisers of our command—whether you are called canons or monks—know that you must appear before us at our summons, according to what our present messenger will announce to you.

And although the letter sent to us excuses you for the sedition that has occurred here, come and wash away the branded crime by making appropriate satisfaction.

## LETTER XIX. TO POPE LEO III, PUBLISHED BY SMARAGDUS THE ABBOT (A.D. 809)

*(From Mansi, *Collection of Councils*.)*

[Note: [Col. 0923A]

## Question

Einhard, in his *Annals*, records the following concerning the council held at Aachen in the year 809:

> “After returning from the Ardennes to Aachen, the emperor held a council in the month of November concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit—a question first raised by a certain monk from Jerusalem. For the purpose of settling it, Bishop Bernharius of Worms and Alahard, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, were sent to Rome to Pope Leo. The same council also discussed the condition of the churches and the conduct of those who are said to serve God in them; nevertheless, nothing was defined, because of the greatness—as it seemed—of the matters involved.” [Col. 0923B]

The other annalists and Ado in his *Chronicle* say the same, although in place of Bernharius, bishop of Worms, Ado erroneously has “the bishop of Cormaric.” For it is certain that at this time Bernharius held the bishopric of Worms, as Cointius demonstrates for this year, no. 8 and following. There he also refutes Sirmond, who considers Jesse, bishop of Amiens, to have been counted among those two legates in volume II of the *Gallican Councils*. Sirmond says that this is established by the acts of that embassy—that is, by the conference held with the pope at Rome—and by the *Life of Charlemagne*, although he admits that the name of that bishop of Amiens is corruptly written there. He understands this to be the *Life of Charlemagne* written by a monk of Angoulême, which also led Baronio astray at no. 52. For I do not discover from whom else Baronius obtained this information.

In fact, those sources contain no mention of a bishop of Amiens, except only in the heading in which Bishop Jesse is mentioned together with Bishop Bernharius and Abbot Adelhard, as can be seen in Baronius, who reproduces it. The words of that heading are:

> “The account that was given concerning the Creed of the faith, in the secretariat of blessed Peter the apostle, between the Lord Leo, most holy and fellow-evangelist pope of the City of Rome, and Bernharius and Jesse, bishops, together with Adelhard, abbot, legates of the Lord Charles, emperor, in the second indiction.”

It is evident, first, that the name Jesse was inserted in that heading by some unlearned person, as often happens, from the beginning of the papal letter to Richulf, archbishop of Mainz, which Sirmond appended to the aforesaid acts of the embassy. The opening of that letter is:

> “Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richulf, most reverend and most holy bishop. When Bernharius, venerable bishop, together with Adelhard, religious abbot, envoys of our son, our lord Charles, most serene emperor, had arrived at the thresholds of the blessed princes of the apostles…”

[Col. 0923C]

Second, it is evident that the heading is an addition by some amateur, because the second indiction had ended with the month of August of that year, whereas all the annalists testify that the synod at Aachen was assembled in November, and therefore during the third indiction. [Col. 0923D]

Through Bernharius, bishop of Worms, and Adelhard, abbot of Corbie, the legates of the Aachen synod, Emperor Charles sent a letter to Pope Leo. It was first published by Holstenius, with the following title prefixed:

> *Letter of Emperor Charles directed to Leo III, pope of the City of Rome, edited by Zmaragdus.*

In the supplement to the councils collected by Lalande, the following heading is prefixed to this letter:

> *Letter of Emperor Charlemagne directed to Leo III, pope of the City of Rome, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, edited by Zmaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in the diocese of Verdun.*

Mabillon approves this heading in volume II of the *Old Analecta*, in his notes on the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint Michael in the Verdun region*.

The letter begins as follows:

> “The question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit that has recently arisen was discussed long ago with the greatest care by the holy Fathers. But because it had lain neglected for a long time by those who were asking about it, it did not remain at rest as though it had been discussed in antiquity; rather, as something hidden, it suddenly emerged for us in these times. I do not doubt that this was faithfully inspired by God. For the present Church is battered by repeated blows of questions, so that, instructed in Catholic teachings and refined by confessions of sound faith, she may at last be able to live in the inheritance of sons and happily reign with the Lord forever.

> “But because, as I have said, this question had long lain unexamined by those who were asking about it, Almighty God willed to awaken the hearts of shepherds concerning it, so that, after the torpor of negligence had been removed, they might be able, by the arm of holy exercise, to dig through to the heavenly treasure. For the shepherds of the divine Scriptures must repeatedly plow the field with the mattock of the Lord’s word, lest the weeds and malignant seed of the wicked sower overpower the fruit of the beautiful wheat, or lest a heretical bird, flying about here and there, snatch the Catholic seed from the hearts of the little ones, or lest the dreadful growth of thorns suffocate the Lord’s shining crop.

> “Knowledge of sacred reading supplies a staff to the weak and weapons to the strong; it firmly represses the treacherous ambushes of enemies and happily promises eternal crowns to the victorious. Therefore let the torpor of negligence depart far from shepherds; let harmful inertia withdraw far from the keenness of the mind; let soft sensuality leave the limbs of the body; and let deep sleep and gentle slumber give way to rigid and profitable vigils of reading, so that the rich field of the Church, sown with the seed of teachers, may be able to return a hundredfold fruit to the Almighty. Now I shall begin concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.”

He later proves this at length from numerous passages of Holy Scripture. [Col. 0924A–C]

Baronius believes that “the question discussed or considered at the council of Aachen was not whether the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son, but whether, since those four syllables, *Filioque*, had been added to the Creed among both the Spaniards and the Gauls, this had been done correctly, so that the Creed thus enlarged should be sung in the church.” [Col. 0924D]

But the aforementioned Cointius correctly judges that the question concerned the procession itself of the Holy Spirit: namely, whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son. For all the ancient writers who mention the Aachen council assert this most clearly.

Ado, who gives a fuller account of this synod than the others, says:

> “The question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit is debated: whether, just as he proceeds from the Father, so he also proceeds from the Son.”

The monk of Angoulême, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, writes that the council was held “concerning the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son.” The Loiselian, Fulda, Bertinian, and Metz annalists, Einhard in his *Annals*, and an unknown author in the *Life of Charlemagne* testify that the council was held “concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.” None of them says anything about the aforesaid addition to the Creed, whether it was or was not to be sung in the church.

Second, the annalists—the Loiselian, Fulda, Bertinian, and Metz annalists—as well as the unknown author and the monk of Angoulême in the *Life of Charlemagne*, write that “the question was first raised by a certain monk from Jerusalem.” Einhard in his *Annals* does not disagree with them, nor does Ado. Einhard says:

> “A certain monk from Jerusalem first stirred up the question.”

Ado says:

> “This question had been raised by a monk from Jerusalem.”

Therefore the question discussed at the council of Aachen first arose at Jerusalem. Who, however, could persuade himself that the Greeks debated whether that addition, *Filioque*, should be sung in the Creed, when they did not accept it?

Third, in his letters to Pope Leo after the synod of Aachen—although they are quite lengthy, and we have just cited their beginning—Emperor Charles says not a word about whether the Creed should or should not be sung. He is entirely occupied with assembling authorities from both Testaments and from the authoritative writings of the Fathers, in order to demonstrate by the greatest number of testimonies that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but from the Father and the Son.

Therefore, at the council of Aachen, as the Ado cited above says, the question debated concerned the procession of the Holy Spirit:

> “Whether, just as he proceeds from the Father, so he also proceeds from the Son.” [Col. 0925B–C]

Finally, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, at this time, when the question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit began to be debated, composed a short treatise on the subject at Charles’s command. In his work he collected the opinions of the ancient Fathers who had written that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Their list is woven together as follows: Athanasius, Cyril, Hilary, Ambrose, Didymus, Augustine, Fulgentius, Hormisdas, Leo, Gregory, Isidore, Prosper, Vigilius, the African, Proclus, Agnellus, Cassiodorus, and Prudentius.

Consult the work itself together with Sirmond’s notes. Sirmond recognizes Vigilius of Thapsus in Africa and Agnellus of Ravenna in Italy as bishops, and attributes to Athanasius the eleven books *On the Trinity* cited by Theodulf, which circulate only in Latin under Athanasius’s works. In his own composition Theodulf has the same intention as Charles in the letters to Pope Leo mentioned above. Both produce various testimonies by which they assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Theodulf explains what he intends in the metrical preface to his work addressed to Charles:

> Following the commands of your empire, illustrious prince,  
> I, Theodulf, gladly bring these documents.  
>   
> That the gracious Spirit is declared to proceed from the Father or the Son,  
> This the trumpet of the law proclaims aloud.  
>   
> The Gospel promises this; the apostolic author declares it;  
> The devout, unanimous voice of the holy Fathers sings it.

A little later he indicates at what time this question began to be raised:

> The illustrious judgment of the holy prophets is with me,  
> Whom well the breath of this Spirit moves.  
>   
> And you too, whom that Spirit animates, will lend your hand  
> To the cause whose discussion began in your time.

Thus the question debated at the council of Aachen was whether the Holy Spirit, just as he proceeds from the Father, likewise proceeds from the Son. For the purpose of deciding this question, Bernharius, bishop of Worms, and Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, were sent to Rome. Their conference with the Roman pontiff, which Baronius reproduces in full at no. 54 and following, ought to be assigned to the following year, since the council of Aachen was convened in November.

The outcome of the dispute was this. Leo was displeased that the Creed with the addition *Filioque*, which the Roman Church had not yet inserted into it, was being sung by the Franks. Nevertheless, he did not absolutely forbid it thereafter; he asked instead that this custom be suspended in the Palace, or royal chapel, believing that the whole of Francia would afterward willingly follow the custom of the palace.

But, in order to show himself steadfastly attached to antiquity and not alienate the Greeks, he prudently arranged for two silver tablets to be affixed in the basilica of Saint Peter, at the confession of that same Saint Peter. On one the Creed was written in Greek and on the other in Latin, in both cases without the addition *Filioque*. Anastasius mentions those tablets, and Baronius reproduces his words at no. 62.
