The aforementioned Cointius writes incorrectly that the Fathers of the Council of Arles, held five years later, indicated that the Franks had consistently retained the addition *Filioque* in the Creed, because they issued this confession concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit:

> “We profess that the Holy Spirit is neither created nor begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

He further says that this had been handed down to them from the time of Clovis the Great. But if the latter were true, it would not have been passed over in silence in the acts of the conference. The former point, moreover, is irrelevant, since the only question was whether that addition should be sung at Mass.

*A. Pagani.* [Col. 0925D–0926D]

The question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit that has recently arisen was discussed long ago with the greatest care by the holy Fathers. But because it had lain neglected for a long time by those who were asking about it, it did not remain at rest as though it had been discussed in antiquity; rather, as something hidden, it suddenly emerged for us in these times. I faithfully believe—and do not doubt—that this was inspired by God.

For the present Church is battered by repeated blows of questions, so that, instructed in Catholic teachings and refined by confessions of sound faith, she may at last be able to live in the inheritance of sons and happily reign with the Lord forever.

But because, as I have said, this question had long lain unexamined by those who were asking about it, Almighty God willed to awaken the hearts of shepherds concerning it, so that, after the torpor of negligence had been removed, they might, by the arm of holy exercise, dig through to the heavenly treasure.

For the shepherds must repeatedly plow the field of the divine Scriptures with the mattock of the Lord’s word, lest the weeds and malignant seed of the wicked sower overpower the fruit of the beautiful wheat; or lest a heretical bird, flying about here and there, snatch the Catholic seed from the hearts of the little ones; or lest the dreadful growth of thorns suffocate the Lord’s shining crop.

Knowledge of sacred reading supplies a staff to the weak and weapons to the strong; it firmly represses the treacherous ambushes of enemies and happily promises eternal crowns to the victorious.

Therefore let the torpor of negligence depart far from shepherds; let harmful inertia withdraw far from the keenness of the mind; let soft sensuality leave the limbs of the body; and let deep sleep and gentle slumber give way to rigid and profitable vigils of reading, so that the rich field of the Church, sown with the seed of teachers, may be able to return a hundredfold fruit to the Almighty.

Now I shall begin concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.

That the Spirit of the Father is in the Son, and that the same Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son, Isaiah testifies, where the voice of the Father says to the Son:

> “My Spirit is in you, and my words which I have placed in your mouth shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, from now and forever.” (Isaiah 59)

Likewise it is written in Isaiah:

> “There the stags met one another, and they saw each other’s faces. They passed through; not one of them perished, and his Spirit gathered them.”

The ancient Fathers understood the stags here as the apostles, whom the Spirit of Christ gathered in Jerusalem, where they met one another and greeted one another.

Therefore, that the Spirit belongs to the Father, the Lord himself says to the apostles:

> “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” (Matthew 10)

And that the same Spirit belongs to the Son, Paul testifies, saying:

> “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.” (Romans 8)

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Galatians he says:

> “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” (Galatians 4)

Blessed Peter also says in his Epistle:

> “Receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls. Concerning this salvation the prophets inquired and searched, who prophesied of the grace destined for you, searching into what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ who was in them signified, announcing beforehand the sufferings that are in Christ and the glories that would follow.” (1 Peter 1)

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, who proceeds from the Father…” (John 15)

There he taught that the Spirit is his, because he himself is the truth, and that he is the Father’s, from whom he said that the Spirit proceeds.

That the Father gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles is written in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. For among other things it says:

> “But he who confirms us with you in Christ and who anointed us is God, who also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.” (2 Corinthians 1)

Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians:

> “For God has not called us to uncleanness but to sanctification. Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us.” (1 Thessalonians 4)

And that the Son also gave the same Holy Spirit is written in the Epistle of John:

> “By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” (1 John 4)

That the Father poured out the Holy Spirit upon the disciples is written in the Epistle to Titus:

> “But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not by works of righteousness that we had done but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.” (Titus 3)

That the Son also poured out the same Holy Spirit is written in the Acts of the Apostles. For the apostles say among other things:

> “This Jesus God raised up, of which we are all witnesses. Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Spirit, he poured out this Spirit which you see and hear.” (Acts 2)

Likewise, from Joel we learn that the pouring out of the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son is one and the same. For the voice of the Father and the Son together says:

> “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my male servants and my female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven and on earth.” (Joel 2)

That the Holy Spirit is the mouth of the Father is read in Psalm 32:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host.” (Psalm 33)

And that he is the mouth of the Son is written in Isaiah. The same prophet says concerning the Son:

> “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the Spirit of his lips he shall slay the wicked.” (Isaiah 11)

Paul, agreeing with this statement, says in the Epistle to the Thessalonians:

> “And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the Spirit of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming.” (1 Thessalonians 2)

That the Spirit proceeds from the Father, the Lord himself testifies, saying:

> “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father will glorify me.” (John 15)

Many other testimonies of this kind are found in the Gospels.

And that the same Spirit proceeds from the Son, the Book of Job, consecrated by the Lord’s mouth, bears witness. Among other things it says:

> “Hear the hearing of his voice in terror, and the sound proceeding from his mouth.” (Job 37)

Here the Son is to be understood as the mouth of the Father. The sound proceeding from his mouth is the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Son, descended upon the apostles with a sound in fire, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, where it is written:

> “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing Spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.” (Acts 2)

Blessed Gregory, explaining the aforesaid verse from the Book of Job, says among other things:

> “The only-begotten Son can be designated by the mouth of God; by the sound of the mouth, however, the same Holy Spirit can be designated. The sound proceeds from the Lord’s mouth when his consubstantial Spirit comes to us through the Son and takes upon himself the deafness of our insensibility.”

Concerning this very procession, by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, blessed Athanasius says in the book he wrote against Arius, among other things:

> “I believe that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son; and also that the Paraclete Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, belongs both to the Son and to the Father, because he also proceeds from the Son. As it is written in the Gospel, through his breathing he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them’ (John 20), and so forth.”

Cyril likewise, concerning this same procession of the Holy Spirit, writes against Nestorius, among other things:

> “Although the Spirit exists in his own substance and the distinct property of his person is understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien to him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth. Therefore he likewise proceeds from him, just as he proceeds from God the Father.”

Ambrose says among other things concerning the Holy Spirit:

> “For the Spirit is not sent as though from a place, nor does he proceed as though from a place, when he proceeds from the Son.”

Jerome likewise, concerning this same procession of the Holy Spirit, says in his exposition of the Creed:

> “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son is coeternal with the Father and the Son and equal to them in every respect. This is the Holy Trinity: that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. There is one deity and power, and one essence: the Father who begot, the Son who was begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son. These three are one God.”

Augustine likewise, in his exposition of the Catholic faith, says among other things:

> “In that holy Trinity, therefore, there is one Father, who alone essentially begot one Son from himself; and one Son, who alone was essentially born from one Father; and one Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

The same author, against the heretic Maximinus, writes:

> “You ask me: If the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit also is from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son? Behold, I answer, whether you understand or do not understand. The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father; but the one is begotten, the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he is begotten; but the other is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both.”

A little later he adds:

> “The Spirit, therefore, belongs to both by proceeding from both.”

Again, in his book *On the Trinity*, he says among other things:

> “When I had demonstrated through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, I said: If, therefore, the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 7)? Why do you think, unless it is because he customarily refers to him even what belongs to him, from whom he himself is? Hence comes what he says: ‘My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.’ If, therefore, in this passage that teaching is understood to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit there be understood also to proceed from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

> “From whom does the Son have that he is God? For if [perhaps: “he is”] God from God, he certainly has from him that the Holy Spirit should also proceed from him. Thus, that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him, just as he proceeds from the Father, he has from the Father himself.” [Col. 0929A]

Again, the same author writes:

> “The Holy Spirit does not first proceed from the Father into the Son and then proceed from the Son to sanctify the creature; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave this to the Son: that just as he proceeds from the Father, so he should also proceed from the Son.”

With the help of the supreme Creator, we have brought together these numerous testimonies from the holy Scriptures concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, so that, overcome by the statements of the divine books and pressed by a cloud of many orthodox witnesses, the enemy may be unable to resist the truth. Rather, persuaded by Catholic statements and truthful testimonies, may he return to the safest bosom of the Church, so that, educated together in the Catholic womb, he may at last deserve to receive the eternal kingdom with the sons. [Col. 0929B–C]

[Note: This letter appears among the Alcuinian letters in Quercetanus, no. 111, and in Canisius, no. 9. As the context indicates, it was sent to Pippin, king of Italy, in the very year in which he died, namely 810. It was therefore improperly inserted among the letters of Alcuin, who had died long before.]

## LETTER XX

[Note: To Nicephorus, the *logothete*, who in 802, after overthrowing the empress Irene, seized the imperial power at Constantinople. From Theophanes’ *Chronography* and other sources, in Pagius under that year, no. 2.]

### TO NICEPHORUS, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He expresses his joy at the renewed embassy for establishing peace between the two empires. (Year 810.)

*(From the works of blessed Alcuin, Froben edition.)*

Since the Lord’s help must be invoked at the beginning of every human undertaking, especially in this matter now being conducted between us with God’s assistance, the aid of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ must be sought in every way, so that we, who have been marked with his name and trust that we have been redeemed from eternal peril of death through the dispensation of his Passion, may be worthy to bring to an honorable and useful conclusion the things that we begin under his inspiration.

In his name and for his honor, we have received kindly and honorably the envoy of your fraternity whom you sent to our son of blessed memory, King Pippin—namely Arsatius, the glorious *spatarius*—who came to us with words and letters of your… [Col. 0929D]

[Note: The annalists of that period call him Arsatius, Arsasius, or Arsaphius, under the year 811.]

Although he had not been sent to us as such, we nevertheless treated him as though he had been sent to us: with attentive care we both listened to him and, since we observed that he was prudent, held conversation with him concerning what he had brought. And rightly so, since there was such an abundance of the desired and always desirable peace, not only in the letter he brought but also in the words that sounded from his mouth into our ears, that such an embassy could have pleased us and all who love God. It was indeed so steeped in the honey of charity and peace that it could convey true sweetness to the palate of the heart of every faithful person; and anyone who found such things tasteless could rightly be judged utterly foolish.

Therefore, after we learned that he had reached the borders of our kingdom, as though we already knew that his embassy was excellent and pleasing to God, we could not refrain from summoning him suitably into our presence. This was especially so because the one to whom it was clear that he had been sent—our beloved son King Pippin—had already departed from human affairs. Nor could we allow him to return empty-handed, with the great undertaking for which he had been sent left unfinished.

[Note: King Pippin had already departed this life. The annalists unanimously report that this occurred on 8 July 810.]

And not only for this reason, but also because, from the time when, in the first year of your empire, your enduring affection sent Michael, metropolitan, and *populum*, the “assiduous” abbot [Pouq.: “and Peter the Assiduous, abbot”], and Calistus, the glorious *candidatus*, in order to establish peace with us and bind and unite these two realms in the charity of Christ, we had remained suspended in long expectation, as though placed upon a watchtower, awaiting—whether through an envoy or through a letter—when we might receive in the writings of your merits an answer worthy of your fraternity.

[Note: “Michael.” The Tilian, Loiselian, and Metz Annals, and others, list the names of the legates differently: “They were sent, they say, Bishop Michael, Abbot Peter, and Calistus the *candidatus*…” The Metz annals erroneously make Calistus and Candidatus two separate persons. Calistus is called a *candidatus* because of the dignity he held. For more on this, if desired, see Canisius’s notes on this letter.]

And now, as human weakness dictates, near-despair was beginning to rise in our heart. Yet we trusted in him who never abandons those who hope in him, believing that, according to the Apostle, our labor in him would not be empty or futile, and that he would fulfill, according to the riches of his mercy, our desire—which, as we trust, we conceived through his inspiration—and bring it to effect at whatever time he should determine.

Therefore, when we heard of the arrival of the envoy of your affection, the glorious *spatarius* Arsatius, we rejoiced greatly, trusting that we would pass from uncertainty concerning these matters to the desired certainty and receive an answer regarding the things that we had entrusted to your aforesaid envoys to convey to you.

And in fact this happened. For we perceived, on our part, that we had received no small portion of the response we desired for the completion of our vows, through the favor of divine assistance and in the words and letters conveyed by the embassy of the aforesaid envoy, although those words and letters had been written and directed to our son.

Accordingly, we give thanks to Almighty God—not as we ought, but as we are able [Al.: “we gave thanks”]—because he has deigned to inspire the heart of your affection, which we have sought, with the desirable will for peace. We pray, according to the Apostle, that God, who has granted you the will for this peace, may himself grant you its accomplishment.

Therefore, without delay, casting aside all hesitation and doubt, we have prepared our envoys to be sent to your affectionate fraternity.

[Note: “We prepared our envoys,” and so forth. After releasing and dismissing Arsatius the *spatarius*, in the following year, 811, Charles sent these envoys to Constantinople to confirm the peace: namely Haido, or Hatto, bishop of Basel; Hugh, count of Tours; and Aio of Friuli, a Lombard. Herman the Contracted mentions a travel account of this embassy written by Hatto, which has either perished or is still hidden somewhere.]

[Note: We owe this letter to the industry of the distinguished scholar D. Brequigny, who extracted it together with the other letters from a manuscript in the Harleian Library; it is now published for the first time.]

## LETTER XXI

[Note: To Michael the emperor. After Nicephorus was killed in Bulgaria in 811, Michael was hailed emperor by the senate and the military orders, as Theophanes reports under the second year of Alexander 804, which corresponds to the year 811 of our era, in Pagius under that year.]

### TO MICHAEL, EMPEROR

Concerning the establishment of peace between the two empires. (Year 811.)

*(From the works of blessed Alcuin, Froben edition.)*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, by the gracious favor of God emperor and Augustus, and likewise king of the Franks and Lombards, to his beloved and honorable brother Michael, glorious emperor and Augustus: eternal salvation in our Lord Jesus Christ.

We bless the Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, and render thanks to him with our whole heart, according to the measure of our strength and the extent of our understanding. He has deigned, by the ineffable gift of his goodness, to make us so rich that in our days he has established the peace long sought and always desired between the Eastern and Western empires. He has also deigned, in accordance with the daily petitions of his holy Catholic and immaculate Church, spread throughout the whole world, not only continually to govern and protect her, but now also, in our time, to unite and pacify her.

We say this as though it had been accomplished [F.: “We therefore say this as though it had been accomplished”], because we have done whatever on our part had to be done. We do not doubt that you likewise wish to do what must be done on your part, placing our trust in him who commanded that this work now in our hands—that is, the making of peace—should be accomplished, because he is faithful and true and cooperates with everyone who does good. We trust that he will also bring to completion what has been well begun by us.

[Col. 0932A]

Burning with desire for this completion, we have sent to the glorious presence of your beloved fraternity our envoys, Amalarius, venerable bishop of Trier, and Peter, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy apostles.

[Note: “Our envoys,” and so forth. The envoys whom Emperor Charles had sent to Nicephorus in 811, whose names we gave above in note a, first arrived at Constantinople after Nicephorus’s death. Meanwhile, Michael had been raised to the throne; he received and released them, as Einhard says in his *Annals* under the year 812. Einhard’s account agrees beautifully with these letters of Charlemagne. For greater clarity concerning this event, it may be useful to transcribe it here:

> “Michael, having become emperor, received and released at Constantinople the envoys of Lord Emperor Charles who had been sent to Nicephorus. Together with them he sent his own envoys, namely Bishop Michael, Arsaphius and Theognostus, *protospatharii*, and through them confirmed the peace begun with Nicephorus. For when they came to the emperor at Aachen, they received from him in the church the written agreement of the pact and, according to their custom—that is, in the Greek language—offered him praises. In the year 813 the emperor wintered at Aachen, and at the beginning of spring—for in this letter the emperor indicated that he wished to await this season as suitable for navigation—he sent Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of the monastery of Nonantula, to Constantinople to confirm the peace with Emperor Michael.”] [Col. 0931D–0932D]

Just as your beloved fraternity’s faithful envoys, Michael, venerable metropolitan, and Arsasius and Theognastus, glorious *protospatharii*, did with us when they received from us the written agreement of the pact, confirmed by our own subscription as well as by the subscriptions of our priests and nobles, so likewise let our aforesaid envoys receive from the sacred altar, from your hand, the written agreement of your treaty, confirmed by the subscriptions of your priests, patricians, and nobles. With God prospering their journey, let them bring it to us.

For both reason required this and such was the agreement between us and your envoys: after their departure, as soon as a suitable season for navigation arrived, we would send our envoys to the glorious presence of your beloved fraternity, so that, with you granting it, they might receive the written agreement of your pact and treaty and bring it to us. [Col. 0932B–C]

Therefore we ask your beloved and glorious fraternity that, if the text of the pact which we composed and sent to you has pleased you, you deign to give our aforesaid envoys a similar document written in Greek letters [Col. 0932C] and confirmed in the manner described above. After they have come to you and, as we trust in your charity, have been received kindly by you, order them to be released without unnecessary delay, so that, with the Lord’s assistance, we may rejoice at their return and at the reply of your beloved fraternity; and may God, the giver of all good things, repay you with a worthy recompense because you have striven to be a lover and confirmer of the peace which he commanded his own people to maintain among themselves. Farewell!

## LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0933D] This letter, addressed to Odilbert, archbishop of Milan, and extracted from the Mettensian Codex by the religious man Placidus Beuvillonius of the congregation of Saint Vito, is an example of the encyclical letters which Charles the Great sent to all the bishops subject to his empire, so that he might be informed by their written responses what they thought about baptism and its rites and ceremonies. Hence Magnus, archbishop of Sens, being addressed by this letter, urged Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, to write a book on the order of baptism; Theodulf dedicated this book to that same Magnus. Alcuin’s letter, or book, on the ceremonies of baptism, addressed to Charles, the most glorious and excellent Augustus, likewise belongs to this matter. It begins as follows: “My most Christian lord emperor, you sent to your servant, in accordance with your mercy, inquiries concerning holy baptism, asking questions in due order,” etc.; these correspond most closely to the preceding letter. In his notes on Theodulf’s book mentioned above [Col. 0934D], Sirmond makes two principal observations. First, of the four copies of this book which had come into his hands, three—the Verdun, Dijon, and Vatican copies—state that the book was sent to Bishop Magnus; but the fourth, the Corbie copy, has John instead of Magnus, though Sirmond considers this erroneous. Yet, with all due respect to that excellent man, I think there is no error. Since Charles’s letter was sent to all the bishops of Gaul, it is not surprising if, among its various copies, one was addressed to Magnus, archbishop of Sens, and another to John, archbishop of Arles. His second observation is that the book on Holy Baptism addressed to Charles, which is found among Alcuin’s works, was attributed to Alcuin by a false conjecture because it lacked a title. Sirmond says that its author was in fact Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and that he learned this from the Petavian Codex. Certainly, what is read near the end of that book suits a bishop, not Alcuin.]

### XXII. TO ODILBERT, ARCHBISHOP (Year 811)

*(From Mabillon, Ancient Analecta)*

[Col. 0933A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by the Lord, great and peaceful emperor, governing the empire and, by the mercy of God, king of the Franks and Lombards, to Odilbert, archbishop: greetings in the Lord.

We would often have wished to engage in familiar conversation with you—and indeed with your other colleagues as well—about the welfare of the holy Church of God, if you had been able to do so without bodily inconvenience. But although we are not unaware that your holiness keeps watch over divine matters with complete devotion, we nevertheless cannot refrain from addressing and admonishing your devotion [Col. 0933B] through our written words, prompted by the Holy Spirit, so that you may strive with ever greater diligence and vigilant care to labor in the holy Church of God through sacred preaching and salutary teaching. Thus, through your most devoted zeal, the word of eternal life may grow, spread, and run its course, and the number of the Christian people may multiply to the praise and glory of our Savior God.

We therefore wish to learn, through your written reply or from you personally, how both you and your suffragans teach and instruct the priests of God and the people entrusted to you concerning the sacrament of baptism: namely, why the infant first becomes a catechumen, or what a catechumen is; and then, in order, everything that is done. Concerning the scrutiny: what the scrutiny is. Concerning the Creed: what its interpretation is according to the Latins. [Col. 0933C] Concerning belief: how one must believe in the Lord, the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his Son, and in the Holy Spirit; in the holy catholic Church; and in the other things that follow in that same Creed. Concerning the renunciation of Satan, all his works, and his pomps: what renunciation is, and what the works and pomps of the devil are. Why the candidate is breathed upon, and why he is exorcised. Why the catechumen receives salt. Why the nostrils are touched, the breast anointed with oil, the shoulders signed, and why the breast and shoulders are washed. Why he is clothed in white garments; why his head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil; and why he is strengthened with the Lord’s body and blood.

Strive to report all these matters to us through your writings, by careful investigation, as we have said, [Col. 0934A] and tell us whether you hold and preach them in this way, or whether you yourself observe what you preach. Farewell, and pray for us.

## LETTER XXIII. TO ATHILARD [AEDILHARD], ARCHBISHOP, AND CEOLWULF

*He commends certain exiles to them*

*(From Miraeus, Diplomatic Works)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to Athilard, archbishop [of Canterbury], and Ceolwulf, his fellow bishop: eternal blessedness.

We do not in any way think it permissible for the rights of friendship established in Christ to be broken by the distance of your land or by the vastness of the stormy sea. Rather, the farther human fellowship is separated in space, the more faithfully the covenant of affection ought to be preserved, because in one another’s presence fear or embarrassment often displays outwardly what a person does not retain within his heart.

Thus holy faith is praiseworthy in absence and venerable in presence. Therefore, trusting in the bond which we once made in your presence through pious conversation, we have sent these wretched exiles from their homeland to your compassion, asking you to deign to intercede for them with my dearest brother Offa, king, so that they may be permitted to live peacefully in their own homeland, without being oppressed by anyone’s injustice, and to serve whomever they may.

Their lord Umhrinsgstan has died. In our judgment, he would have remained faithful to his lord [Col. 0934C] if he had been permitted to remain in his homeland. But, as he used to say, in order to escape the danger of death he fled to us, always ready to clear himself of every charge of disloyalty. We kept him with us for some time, for the sake of reconciliation, not out of hostility.

If you are able to ask peace for these fellow-countrymen of his, let them remain in their homeland; but if my brother gives you a harsher answer concerning them, send them back to us unharmed. It is better to live abroad than to perish; to serve in a foreign homeland than to die in one’s own.

I trust in my brother’s goodness that, if you earnestly intercede for them, he will kindly receive them for love of us—or rather for the love of Christ, who said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). May divine mercy preserve your holiness, which intercedes for us, safe forever.

[Note: [Col. 0935] Bernard Pez published this letter in volume 5, part 1, page 73, of the *Anecdota*, from the Altach Codex, written under the direction of Abbot Hermann around the year 1260.]

## LETTER XXIV. TO FULRAD, ABBOT OF ALTACH

*He orders him to appear at the place called Starasfurt with well-armed men*

*(From Miraeus, Diplomatic Works)*

[Col. 0935A]

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, who is also, by the mercy of God, king of the Franks and Lombards, to Fulrad, abbot.

Let it be known to you that we have scheduled our general assembly for the present year in Saxony, on the eastern side of the river Rota, at the place called Starasfurt. Therefore we order you to come fully equipped, with well-armed and prepared men, to the aforesaid place on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, which is seven days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

[Col. 0935B] You are to come with your men to the aforesaid place so prepared that, wherever our command may direct, you can proceed in military fashion—that is, with weapons and provisions, as well as with all other military equipment, with food and clothing. Each mounted man is to have a shield, lance, sword, and half-sword, a bow [Col. 0936A] and quivers with arrows; and in your carts various kinds of tools, namely wedges, adzes, augers, axes, mattocks, iron spades, and the other equipment necessary for an army.

The carts are to contain food supplies for three months from the time of that assembly; weapons and clothing for half a year. We strictly order you to ensure that this is observed, so that you may proceed in good order to the aforesaid place.

Whichever road through our kingdom the proper course of your journey directs you to take, you are to presume to touch nothing except grass, wood, and water. Each of your men is to travel together with his carts and mounted men, and they are always to remain with them until they reach the aforesaid place, so that [Col. 0936B] the absence of the lord may not give his men an opportunity to do harm.

As for your goods, which you must present to us at our assembly, send them to us in May, wherever we may then be. If the proper course of your journey should make it possible for you to present them to us personally during your expedition, we would prefer that.

Take care that you show no negligence in this matter, if you wish to retain our favor.

[Col. 0935]

# APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF BLESSED CHARLES THE GREAT

## I. ODILBERT, ARCHBISHOP, REPLIES TO CHARLES THE GREAT

*(From Mabillon, Ancient Analecta)*

[Col. 0935C]

To the most Christian lord and God-preserved Charles, most invincible and most devout emperor, Odilbert, servant of the servants of God, archbishop of your holy Milanese Church and your spokesman: perpetual greetings in Christ the Lord.

Accordingly, we must without interruption give thanks to the immense mercy of our almighty God, who has placed you in so exalted a dignity of imperial rule. At the same time, with bended knees, we all implore the clemency of that same Redeemer, that he may deign to preserve your life and safety through the course of many years, for the advancement of all the churches of God and of the faithful peoples entrusted to you by God.

For we recognize and firmly hold that the salvation of us all depends upon your tranquility. You, more than all the Christian emperors who existed before you throughout the world, have shown concern for the orthodox faith, moved by devotion and divine zeal—namely Constantine, Theodosius the Great, Marcian, and Justinian. All these men, divinely inspired to free the Christian people from every stain of error, confirmed by their imperial authority only what the Lord’s priests had defined.

Surpassing them in merit and knowledge, and imitating the holy David, who presented himself as a type of our Redeemer for the salvation of the people, you are his energetic worshiper. Inflamed by divine love for the belief of the true faith, you confess concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God, above all and in every respect, that although he is the radiance of his glory, the image of his substance, and the brightness of eternal light, because of the immense love with which he loved us he emptied himself and, according to apostolic authority [Col. 0936B] and the other things that follow, presented to himself a glorious [Col. 0936C] Church without spot or wrinkle. Washing away the contagion of sin, he bestowed the sacraments of our redemption through his precious blood; and, after completing the mystery through his ascension, by which he ascended to the Father, he confirms us through apostolic tradition. The apostles preached this integrity of faith to all nations, so that the Church of Christ might not be shaken by any blasts or assaults of hostile winds, but, established upon the true and perpetual foundation, might remain firm.

Thus we too, confirmed by the spiritual instruments of the holy Fathers and strengthened by inviolate and unblemished faith concerning belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, believe and hold the true faith.

But what is fitting for a devout ruler who excels all his adversaries, unless he is always gladly diligent in good works? Your sincere piety embraces this with the greatest zeal, so that the Church of God may not languish in any part beneath the stains of wounds, nor the corruption of ignorance boil over as it increases within her. Rather, in your most fortunate times, may the hearts of God’s priests, awakened to vigilance and concern, persevere in true and upright guardianship; and may you attain eternal rewards from the Lord for the struggle of so great a labor.

Yet let none of us suppose that he can express in words or grasp in thought all the heavenly mysteries with complete clarity. Having received, therefore, the letter sent to us by your imperial piety, after reading it we sensed the fragrance of the sweetest nectar, exhaling an exceedingly rich aroma. We gave manifold thanks to our God, who deigned to inspire your hearts with concern for the condition of his Church, since, prompted by your clemency, you wish to learn from us the account of the true faith and everything that we do and teach in due order.

Although we cannot ourselves set forth a fuller answer to what your dominion requests, it is nevertheless necessary that, the poorer we recognize ourselves to be in our replies, the more devoted we become to the holy Scriptures [Col. 0937A]. Thus, although we are lesser in speaking through our own words, we may grow through the testimonies of the saints; and the labor of the most learned men—who left nothing obscure or closed in the divine Scriptures that they did not bring into true clarity, and who received the Davidic key so that they might open these things for us—may advance us toward salvation by its very gift. May the work of the saints make us, who are sluggish, more secure and ready to give answers.

We have attempted to write these things concisely, not through an abundance of words, but, in true humility, binding ourselves most submissively to your piety, we have set them down briefly. We run through the examples of the holy Fathers to signify to your most worthy presence [perhaps: “prudence”] that which, like wondrous flowers, shines forth adorned with an abundance of fragrance, surpassing gold and precious gems. We continually recognize that wisdom is widely growing with you and is always present—wisdom flowing from you like a living fountain and, like a river, pouring forth with immense sweetness to water the hearts of individuals, spreading far and wide like honey and butter [Col. 0937B] and filling the dryness of the earth with its overflowing.

Therefore we ask you to grant us the sweet gifts of your magnificent eloquence. As the rays of the sun illuminate the world, so may our knowledge shine, surrounded by the gift of your holy teaching; for what we see to be laborious for us to attain through our own inquiry, you, through God’s dispensation and the Holy Spirit abundantly flowing within your heart, are able more fully to reveal and open—the divine mysteries.

May almighty God preserve the glory of your empire unharmed for long ages. Amen.

## II. LETTER OF CHARLES THE GREAT TO OFFA, KING

[Note: [Col. 0937D] This letter is regarded as spurious. Spelman published it in volume 1 of the *Councils of England*, page 305. Although he assigned it to the year 792, on the following page he correctly noted that it appears to have been issued in the year 774, when the Lombards and Saxons were defeated by Charles, as is read in the ancient annals. The heading found in volume 7 of the *Councils* must therefore be corrected. It reads: “Letter of Charles the Great, king, to the same man. He sends the Second Council of Nicaea to Britain.” There is no mention there of the Council of Nicaea or of the controversy concerning images [Col. 0938D] (Baluzius, *Capitularia*, vol. 2, p. 1032).]

*He sends the Second Council of Nicaea to Britain*

[Col. 0937C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to the venerable man and dearest brother Offa, king of the Mercians: greetings, honor, and love.

Since it is fitting that powerful and famous kings be bound together by the covenant of friendship and rejoice in one another through mutual happiness, so that Christ may be glorified in all and by all in the bond of charity, we have decided to send this gift to your serenity.

After we had subjected the most noble Lombard city, together with all its citizens, to our rule, and had happily brought all Italy under our imperial authority, with the help of Christ, whom we desire to serve, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and the Saxon dukes whom we had bent to our command, Withimundus and Albion, together with nearly all the inhabitants of Saxony, received the sacrament of baptism, thereafter to serve the Lord Jesus Christ.

With this salutary message, therefore, I, Charles, the most powerful of the Christian kings of the East [Col. 0937D], wish to make you joyful, O Offa, most powerful of the Christian kings of the West, and to embrace you more sincerely in a special affection.

## III. LETTER TO CHARLES THE GREAT, EMPEROR

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Until now I have not been able to discover who the author of this letter was. Yet it must certainly be established that he was some bishop. For at this time the emperor Charles the Great, amid the various concerns of his kingdom, always kept matters pertaining to religion before his eyes; and, in order to stimulate bishops to investigate the holy Scriptures, he proposed to them various questions concerning the order of baptism. The author of this letter, himself also a bishop, answers these questions.]

*Concerning the rites of baptism*

*(From Martène, Anecdotal Treasury)*

This is the letter which we sent to the ears of our lord emperor.

[Col. 0938A]

It pleased your incomparable wisdom, my lord, most glorious emperor and prince of the Christian people, to question me, the least of the servants of God, concerning the mystery of holy baptism: how, understanding it, we should teach those who appear to have been entrusted to us.

Therefore, if I understand anything according to the capacity of my mind . . . I shall not refuse to answer your serenity, lest I seem to incur the charge of disobedience. I would rather be corrected by your imperial authority through rebuke than deceived by the praise of a flatterer.

We read—for the orthodox [Col. 0938B] worshipers of the catholic faith have left this written for us—that before an infant obtains cleansing from his sins through the salutary washing of the bath, he becomes a catechumen, that is, a hearer or one who is instructed. It is fitting for him to hear while he is being instructed, so that, recognizing the one God, he may worship him. Hearing also of the immortality of his soul and the eternal glory destined for the holy, but of eternal punishments for the wicked according to the measure of their merits, he is to believe that these rewards will be rendered.

The Lord Jesus first made him a catechumen when he smeared the blind man’s eyes with mud, so that afterward he might be sent to be washed at Siloam—that is, to the sacrament of baptism.

Scrutiny is an examination by which it is repeatedly investigated whether, after renouncing Satan, his works, and his pomps, the sacred words of the faith given to the mind remain firmly rooted and fixed in it.

The evil spirit is also expelled by breath from the catechumen, so that, once he has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ, the true God. He is exorcised—that is, the same evil spirit is rebuked by adjuration through the name of the eternal God—so that he may leave and withdraw, giving place [Col. 0938C] to the Holy Spirit.

For this reason we give him salt: so that, through its taste, he may perceive the seasoning of wisdom, by which his rotten and fleeting sins may be cleansed through the divine gift.

Next, the faith of the salutary and apostolic Creed is handed over to him, so that, like a house abandoned by its former inhabitant, he may be adorned with the doctrine of that faith in order to receive God as an inhabitant.

For in Greek *symbolon* means “collation” or “bringing together” in Latin. We therefore hand over to catechumens this rule of the catholic faith, handed down by the apostles to the primitive Church. The apostles themselves composed it after the Lord’s ascension, when they were commanded to teach and baptize all nations, bringing their minds together into one through the most precise words. We instruct catechumens according to the living rule of the Creed, so that they may believe in God the almighty Father.

They are to understand that God exists without any beginning and therefore is always Father and almighty, the one who created all things by the command of the Word alone.

And in Jesus Christ, his Son: that is, they should know that they must believe in the Son just as they believe in the Father. Jesus means “Savior”; Christ comes from *chrisma*, “anointing,” because of the infusion of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0938D].

He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. This means that, by God’s gift and grace, such humility was granted to us that he deigned to assume the whole human being in the Virgin’s womb, and afterward, glorified following his passion, to place him above the heavens at the right hand of God the Father.

They are to believe that this Son, at the time when Pilate was judge in Judea, truly suffered in the flesh, was [Col. 0939A] crucified, died, and was buried, while bearing the cross itself upon their foreheads. They must firmly hold that he rose from the tomb on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father—that is, in the majesty of the Father’s glory, in accordance with judicial authority—and that from there he will come on the last day to judge the living and the dead.

Let them also believe in the Holy Spirit. Indeed, just as in the Father and the Son, no catholic may doubt that he must believe in the Holy Spirit.

Concerning the holy catholic Church, they should understand that one believes that there is a Church, but not “in the Church,” since it is not God but the house of God. “Catholic” means universal.

The communion of saints: that is, let them believe that they can be held in a fellowship of faith and a communion of hope with those who have died in this faith.

The forgiveness of sins: that is, let them hold with the full affection of belief that forgiveness takes place in the baptism of Christ.

The resurrection of the flesh: understanding that the flesh which we carry in this mortal life will rise again and become immortal, let them believe it.

Let them hope to obtain eternal life if, holding these sacramental truths of the Creed, they faithfully preserve them.

The catechumen is called to renounce—that is, utterly reject—first of all the devil, who is the enemy of the human race. We must resist him firmly and with all our strength, and oppose his works and pomps.

The works of the devil are evident: they are what the Apostle called “works of the flesh.” His pomps are the empty and deadly pleasures and harmful desires of this age, together with the service of idols. After rejecting all these things, one must place all hope in God alone.

The catechumen’s nostrils and ears are touched with spittle, because we read that the spittle which proceeded from the Lord’s head signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. Thus, as long as he draws breath through his nostrils, he should strive to preserve through the grace of the Holy Spirit what has been received through spiritual ears.

The breast is also anointed with oil, so that the devil may be barred from entering by the sign of the holy cross. The shoulders are signed as well, so that he may be fortified on every side and, as though laying down the yoke of diabolical servitude, may pass [Col. 0939C] into the glorious liberty of the children of God.

Likewise, in the anointing of the breast and shoulders, the firmness of faith and perseverance in good works are signified.

Thus, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the human being, who was created in the image of the Holy Trinity, is immersed three times and renewed according to the image of that same Trinity. And just as he fell into death through the third degree of sin—that is, through consent—so, raised three times from the font, may he rise through grace to life.

Then he is clothed in white garments, signifying the joy and solemnity of regeneration, as well as the purity of angelic life and the beauty of splendor.

Next his head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that, in the mystery of baptism, he has received the diadem of royal dignity and the dignity of the priesthood, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “You are a royal and priestly race, offering yourselves to the Lord as a holy sacrifice, pleasing to God.”

He is also strengthened with the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0939] That is, he is given communion, as is clear from various ancient Rituals], so that he may become a member of that head who suffered and rose again for him [Col. 0939D].

Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, he receives the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others, having received in baptism, through grace, the gift of eternal life.

## IV. RESPONSE OF AN ANONYMOUS WRITER TO THE QUESTIONS SENT BY CHARLES THE GREAT TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 811

*(From Baluzius)*

These are the matters which our lord Augustus the emperor sent to us by his sacred letter, always for the benefit of the holy Church.

[Col. 0940A]

### Chapter I. How and in what manner each priest of God makes known, preaches, and governs the people entrusted to him by God

**Response.** We preach to and admonish the people entrusted to us according to the knowledge of our limited understanding, just as the holy Fathers—Augustine, Cyprian, Jerome, Ambrose, Gregory, Ephraem, Cassian, Cassiodorus, and the other preachers of the word of God up to the present—have left us through their examples.

First, let them believe in the ineffable, holy, and sacred Trinity, and faithfully understand its faith and doctrine. Whatever is weak in Christ’s flock we cherish with every mystical medicine; whatever is sound, with the grace of Christ favoring us, we desire to preserve with all the apostolic teaching that is like milk.

We say no more here about this, lest an overly lengthy discourse offend the holy synod.

### Chapter II. Concerning the entire holy mystery of baptism and the order in which we ought to celebrate it

**Response.** Baptism is called *baptismus* in Greek and *tinctio*—“dipping” or “immersion”—in Latin. It is called *tinctio* because there the human being darkened by Adam’s sin is immersed. These are the sacraments of the holy Church: baptism, chrism, and the body and blood of Christ. They are called sacraments because, although they are performed bodily, they signify something divinely.

The mystery of baptism is performed only under the designation of the Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For just as every word is established by three witnesses, so this sacrament is confirmed by the number three. Therefore the infant is immersed three times in the sacred font, so that the threefold immersion might mystically signify Christ’s three-day burial. The raising from the waters is an image of Christ rising from the tomb.

For this reason this most sacred mystery is celebrated only at Easter and [Col. 0940C] Pentecost—that is, at the commemoration of the Savior’s resurrection and of the Holy Spirit descending upon the apostles.

After the washing, therefore, he is anointed with royal ointment, that is, with chrism. For *chrisma* in Greek means “anointing” in Latin, and Christ receives his name from it; hence “Christians.” Just as forgiveness of sins is bestowed through baptism, so sanctification by the Holy Spirit is supplied through anointing. Ancient authority has established this, since kings and priests have been anointed with chrism ever since Aaron was anointed by Moses.

### Chapter III. Why a person becomes a catechumen, what language the term belongs to, and what it means

**Response.** *Catechumenus* is Greek; in Latin it means “hearer.” He is called a hearer because, from paganism, he is joined to the body of the Church through the ministry of God’s Word.

He is called a pagan—*gentilis*—as though “thus born,” since at that time he has not yet been imbued with that teaching. Therefore, within the embrace of the holy mother Church, the catechumen acts differently. Before approaching the sacred font, he must hear and learn the mystical sacraments of the Christian religion. Then he learns the faith of the holy Trinity, the Creed, and the other matters which the catholic law teaches Christians.

### IV. Chapter. Concerning ecclesiastical scrutiny: why scrutiny is performed, at what time, and what scrutiny is

**Response.** *Scrutiny* derives from *scrutari*, “to examine,” because the catechumens are then to be examined to see whether they now firmly hold the true faith of the Creed that has recently been handed over to them.

Much is missing here.

# WRITINGS OF THE BLESSED EMPEROR CHARLES THE GREAT

## SECTION TWO: THE CAROLINE BOOKS

### PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0941]

## BARONIUS’S DISSERTATION ON THE COUNCIL OF FRANKFURT

[Col. 0941A]

### I.

In the year 794 of the Redeemer, in the second indiction, a council was assembled at Frankfurt in Germany. Because of the large number of bishops and the presence of legates of the Apostolic See, it is found designated as a plenary council.

From Italy, Gaul, and Germany, nearly three hundred bishops assembled, since a matter of great importance demanded it. The question concerned the catholic faith, and discussion was required concerning the profound mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God: namely, whether that same Son of God, according to the humanity he assumed, should be called the adoptive Son of God or the proper Son of God.

Although the holy catholic Church of God had no uncertainty, even slight, concerning these matters—for at the ecumenical Council of Ephesus it had been most fully defined what was to be believed, when it condemned Nestorius, who introduced two sons of God, one according to divinity and another according to humanity—and although it had likewise recently condemned Felix [Col. 0941B], bishop of Urgell, who asserted that Christ according to the flesh should be called the adoptive Son of God (we have said that, repenting of his error, he recanted at Rome before Hadrian, the Roman pontiff), nevertheless this unhappy man, like a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow returning to the mud, once again took up the very error he had condemned and the heresy he had cursed at Rome.

After publicly professing the confession of the catholic faith at the altar of the prince of the apostles, he began again to defend the same error with more ardent zeal, to the great harm of faithful souls. To prevent the evil from spreading farther and the infused poison from corrupting healthy members, he had to be summoned again to a plenary judgment—especially since he was found not to be the sole advocate of so great an error, and should be called its follower rather than its author.

### II. Elipandus Perseveres Without Repentance

The archbishop of Toledo, Elipandus, primate of the sees of Spain, was the reviver of such great blasphemy. As we have seen, when he was admonished by orthodox bishops [Col. 0941C] and priests subject to him, he was so far from correcting himself, detesting the error condemned by them, and following the catholic faith in repentance that, having turned himself into a crooked bow, he did not cease to attack even the sons of the catholic Church who lived far away with arrows infected by poison. He became not merely an exceedingly fierce defender of heresy but its most devoted propagator.

Indeed, he never stopped or rested until he had recalled Felix, who had returned to the orthodox, to the camp of impiety, armed him more powerfully for battle, and sharpened him more carefully for the contest. He knew well that when someone relapses into a crime, greater assistance is usually supplied from hell, so that, in place of the one evil spirit expelled through repentance, seven demons may be brought in to assist him, as the Gospel says (Luke 11), and that these may be sent to carry out still more deadly deeds.

[Col. 0942A]

### III. Elipandus Strives to Spread His Heresy

What more can be said? All iniquity is voracious, and heresy is much more insatiable, since it burns with the fiercer heat of hell, according to the prophetic saying: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished; he has confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40).

It is as though the broadest boundaries of Spain were too narrow for sowing the weeds. He labors to fill Gaul and Germany with them, scattering the wicked seed through letters. He went so far as to attempt, if he could, to draw Charles the Great, the most Christian king and the strongest tower of orthodox faith, into his own opinion. He wrote him a letter filled with poison, but so coated with honey that it seemed to contain nothing bitter.

While informing Charles of his own position, he simultaneously asked him, after having the letter he was writing read aloud in his presence, to question theologians about what they thought concerning the matter, so that the truth might be sought—of which he presented himself as exceedingly desirous [Col. 0942B].

To this he added many other things calculated to win the mind of so great a king: namely, that he continually offered prayers to God for the king’s salvation. After these preliminaries, he pretended to offer salutary admonitions and to make the king cautious by the example of others, lest, as he said, Constantine should complete badly a work well begun and obscure the immense glory he had acquired through piety.

Mixing these and many other devices together, and trying to entice the most Christian king toward his own doctrine, he sought to make him, from a catholic, a Nestorian heretic. Elipandus’s actual letter to Charles is not extant, but Charles’s letter written in reply to him at that time shows that it contained all the things just mentioned.

### IV. Elipandus’s Devious Methods

Thus, the man who wrote privately to so great a king a letter on this subject added others, public and general, addressed to all the bishops of Gaul. Heresy knows no shame. For here was prophetically demonstrated what is written of Babylon: that she bears blasphemy written upon her forehead (Apoc. XIII, XVII). Elipandus was not ashamed or embarrassed to write letters to the bishops of Gaul concerning his heresy, although he knew that not long before it had been condemned by those same bishops in the person of their colleague Felix and together with Felix.

But what does the cunning man do? Lest the heresy he was betraying appear disfigured and infamous through its own disgrace, and thus be exposed to attack and expelled with curses and execrations, he labored to represent it as beautiful, clothing it in another’s garments like Aesop’s jackdaw, while striving to adorn it with sayings from divine Scripture and with the opinions of the holy Fathers. Yet he made it twice as deformed; for it was made evident by the judgment of all that the ornaments of the most chaste virgin, the bride of Christ, could in no way befit a prostitute.

### V. Elipandus Is Exposed as a Nestorian. Why Elipandus Spares Nestorius

But let us come to the confession—or rather the profession of perfidy—of his faith, which he wrote in the same letter, beginning with its very opening. The Fathers quote it in their synodal letter sent in reply to him, in these words:

> “We find,” they say, “written at the beginning of your little book what you set down, namely: ‘We confess and believe God, the Son of God, begotten before all ages, without beginning, from the Father, coeternal and consubstantial—not by adoption, but by generation.’ Likewise, a little farther on in the same passage we read: ‘We confess and believe that he was made from a woman, made under the law, not by nature the Son of God, but by adoption and by grace,’” and so forth.

These are Elipandus’s poisons. The Fathers, having prepared an antidote so that they could harm no one, taught that all must guard against them.

That he held these views together with Nestorius—and therefore could not in any way be excused on grounds of ignorance—is made unmistakably clear by the following evidence. In the same little book, or written letter, sent to the bishops of Gaul, when he condemns individual persons by name as heretics, he passed over Nestorius without condemning him. Yet if he had acted in good faith, he ought to have named Nestorius first and utterly cursed, detested, and anathematized him with every possible execration and detestation, thereby showing that he differed as far as possible from Nestorius’s opinion, even if he appeared to be related to it.

For this reason the Fathers rightly wrote to him:

> “Was not your heresy once refuted and condemned in Nestorius by the universal holy Church? Why, then, perhaps did you refuse to anathematize him, while in your letter you anathematized others—namely, Bonosus, Arius, Sabellius, and Manichaeus—who held wicked opinions about the Son of God?” and so forth.

They thus showed that Nestorius had held the same opinion about the Son of God made man as Elipandus himself: namely, that there were two sons of God, one according to divinity and another according to humanity and adoption.

The unfortunate Elipandus is thought to have learned, through his familiarity with the Muslims, to think in this humiliating way about Christ according to his humanity. Perhaps he persuaded himself that, if he could establish this, he would unite Muslims and Christians in a single faith.

### VI. Elipandus Acts by Fraud

The Fathers also perceived and made plain to everyone that the thrice-impious man had acted—not through ignorance but through deliberate deceit. In their letter sent in reply to him they demonstrated that the sayings of the saints quoted by him had either been corrupted by him personally or twisted into a perverse meaning wholly at variance with their genuine sense. If you read that letter, you will understand this for yourself.

Thus the holy Fathers themselves clearly demonstrated the truth concerning those sayings taken from the sacred doctors of the Church which he had cited but corrupted and distorted.

But when he produced witnesses from within his own household—when, I say, he asserted that Christ had been called the adopted Son of God according to the flesh in the liturgical books of the Church of Toledo, or by his own Toledan predecessors—the Fathers had no ready access to the manuscripts proper to that Church alone and not shared by all the others. Trusting the impostor only too readily, they consequently detested the predecessors whom Elipandus cited, just as they detested Elipandus himself: Eugenius, Ildephonsus, and Julianus, who had acquired a great name in Spain both through the holiness of their lives and through their knowledge of the sacred Scriptures.

### VII. Elipandus Slanderously Presents His Predecessors as Partners in Error. Saint Ildephonsus Is Unjustly Assailed

Lest the just be condemned together with the wicked, and lest the saints whose memory has continued to be blessed in the Catholic Church should inherit the curse of the unrighteous, these men must first of all be vindicated from so great a slander by Elipandus and from the synod’s curse.

To make the truth itself shine more clearly, we think it necessary here to reproduce what the treacherous Elipandus falsely claimed about these same predecessors in his little book sent to Gaul. The statements are repeated in the letter sent to him by the Fathers from the synod, in these words:

> “The following occurs in your same little book: ‘Likewise our predecessors Eugenius, Ildephonsus, and Julianus, bishops of the see of Toledo, stated the following in their teachings, in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper: “He who, through the passion of the adopted man, did not spare his own body.” Likewise, in the Mass of the Lord’s Ascension: “Today our Savior, after the adoption of the flesh, returned to the seat of his divinity,”’” and so forth.

Elipandus inserted these words into his little book on the faith—not because he had received them from the writings of those whom he names, but because, as he claimed, such words were customarily recited in the sacred offerings in the missal of the Church of Toledo. But whether he reported them faithfully, or—as in other matters—fraudulently, could not then be determined, since the manuscript that would have had to be examined was not at hand; from it, as in the other cases, Elipandus could have been convicted of imposture.

The Fathers therefore replied:

> “You have inserted these words from the sayings of your fathers, so that it may be clear what sort of fathers you have, and so that everyone may know from whom you were delivered into the hands of unbelievers. Because you denied that Christ the man is truly the Son of God the Father, he did not wish to be your defender, but delivered you into the hands of his enemies, that they might rule over you—those who refused to receive him.”

A little later they add, addressing the same man:

> “It is better to believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son than that of your Ildephonsus, who composed such prayers for you in the solemn celebrations of the Mass—prayers which the universal and holy Church of God does not possess, nor do we think that you are heard when you pray with them. And if your Ildephonsus called Christ ‘adopted’ in his prayers, our Gregory, the most renowned pontiff of the Roman see and teacher throughout the world, did not hesitate in his prayers always to call him ‘the only-begotten Son,’” and so forth.

The Fathers said this because they believed that, as that treacherous man asserted, such words were truly read in the sacred missals under Ildephonsus’s authority.

But who was the certain and original author of this error in Spain was stated in the preceding volume: namely, Theodiscus, a pseudo-bishop and heretic, the successor of Saint Isidore, who, after being deposed, passed over into Muslim impiety. He was a Greek by nationality and an impostor by character. As was said, in the year 636 of the Redeemer he was the first in Spain to assert that Christ, the Son of God, was the adopted Son of God the almighty Father.

### VIII. Saint Ildephonsus Is Vindicated from the Slander

Yet so far was Saint Ildephonsus from having been an advocate of this error that, on the contrary, in his writings he repeatedly destroyed such a monstrosity with frequent statements, as though with darts. It is therefore easy to expose with the greatest clarity the enormous slander brought against him by the impostor—not by doubtful witnesses or obscure testimonies, but by Ildephonsus’s own genuine writings, in which more than once, in precisely such words, he attacks the Nestorianism spread through Spain, utterly denying that the Son of God according to the flesh ought to be called an adopted son.

Let us first bring forward what he says in his book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary*, where the matter is led to a necessary conclusion. After discussing many points according to Catholic truth, he says:

> “You have heard that although God is one thing and man another, there is nevertheless not one God and another man, but my Lord Jesus Christ is one Lord, both God and man.”  
> *(Saint Ildephonsus, On the Virginity of Saint Mary, chap. 6.)*

And farther on, concerning Saint Mary:

> “Thus, in both natures, one person gives birth to one Son, so that the same one is the Son of God who is the son of man; nor is the son of man other than the Son of God.”  
> *(Ibid., chap. 11.)*

In his book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary and Her Childbearing*, recently published by the most learned theologian Feuardentius of Paris, he likewise writes in the same sense:

> “Christ was never not God from the time he became man, and, assumed in the unity of the person, he has always remained and remains true God and man. Not two, as though there were one God and another man, but one and the same God and man. For although he is one thing insofar as he is God and another insofar as he is man, in both respects he is God and man, because there was never a time when a man was conceived or born pure and without God. Rather, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit from virginal flesh and truly born as a man, immediately from that conception, through an ineffable birth, true God proceeded and was born as man.”

By teaching these things, he excludes every adoption of the Son of God according to the flesh, since the man who could have been adopted as a son was never without God.

### IX. Testimonies of Ildephonsus Against Elipandus’s Errors

These statements alone could suffice to convict the treacherous Elipandus both of slander and of impiety. Yet thanks must be given to God and to God’s most holy Virgin Mother, because her eulogist Ildephonsus repeatedly and explicitly excludes every form of adoption in the Son of God, Christ Jesus. In the same treatise he adds:

> “Accordingly, such a birth is not subject to the common law of nature; but just as he was wondrously conceived, so he was wondrously born God and man. Therefore adoption did not make him a son, as it made the other sons of God, but the nature of divinity exalted him, endowed him, and gave him the name that is above every name, so that, as man and Word, he might be wholly the Son of God. For he was never not the eternal Son of God; he remains the only-begotten Son of the one Begetter.”

After arguing the same point with the greatest care at some length, he adds these words on the authority of Saint Gregory the pope:

> “For, as he himself says in the same *Moral Works*, it is one thing for human beings who are born to receive the grace of adoption through it; it is another thing for God to have proceeded uniquely through the power of divinity from the very conception.”

Then, after further discussion, while defending the claim that the virgin Mary suffered no corruption either in conception or in childbirth, he immediately adds:

> “Otherwise, if he had been defiled by his mother, or if he had corrupted his mother’s womb as though for sin and defiled it with the stains arising from the first condemnation, he would not be the Son of God but adopted, like the others. Indeed, he would not even be adopted, and there would be no one through whom he himself could be adopted, if he were not the proper Son.”

And farther on:

> “Therefore he is not adopted, but, so to speak, the adopter of the others.”

He then adds:

> “Christ, not adopted but the proper Son of God, came in the fullness of time, sent by the Father, born of a woman, made under the law. He alone did not need the sacrament of regeneration, nor did he need to be born again, because he is the proper Son of God. In his gracious kindness he deemed us worthy, through the grace of adoption, to bestow upon us through the washing of regeneration a share in his brotherhood. Hence John says: ‘But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God’ (John I). This power he himself, begotten by the Father, possessed in himself by his own nature, and not from elsewhere, so that he might be the proper Son of God and grant the grace of adoption to whomever he wished.”

### X. Further Testimonies of Ildephonsus

These and other statements by Ildephonsus increasingly convict the heretical impostor of the slander he brought against him, and they likewise vindicate Ildephonsus from the evil reputation which the Fathers, on the basis of Elipandus’s testimony, had conceived concerning that most holy and learned man, as well as from the false opinion attributed to him. It thus becomes entirely clear that nothing could have been more foreign to so great a Father than an assertion that Christ, the Son of God according to the flesh, was adopted.

It was lamentable that the labors of this most holy man were suppressed and hidden for so long, perhaps through the deceit of the treacherous Elipandus, lest they be brought into the light. From them the son of darkness could have been refuted by the light, while he calls light darkness and darkness light.

It is nevertheless a matter for rejoicing that, amid so great a shipwreck of Spain, such distinguished monuments of a most noble intellect survived; and that they were rescued from hiding places and brought to light by a man devoted to truth and most devoted to the study of ecclesiastical antiquity—not a Spaniard, lest even the slightest suspicion of private affection for a countryman disturb anyone’s mind, but a Gaul, a professor of the University of Paris, a cultivator of integrity and piety, and a man whose illustrious name was highly honored throughout the Catholic Church: Feuardentius, whom we have mentioned.

### XI. Charlemagne Endeavors to Convene a General Synod

Having now related these matters concerning Elipandus’s letters, written before the synod was convened, let us turn to the convocation of the synod itself.

When the said letters of Elipandus had been delivered to Charlemagne, he considered nothing more urgent than to labor toward assembling a universal synod from the bishops of the entire Western world. For this purpose he repeatedly sent envoys to Adrian, the Roman pontiff, to ascertain his opinion and learn what he thought about the question proposed by Elipandus.

We shall learn how vigilant Charlemagne’s zeal was in carrying out these matters from no more faithful witness than his own letter to Elipandus, in which, among other things, we read:

> “For the fulfillment of this joy—namely, the conversion of heretics—fraternal charity compelled us to order that a synodal council of the holy Fathers be assembled from all the Churches everywhere under our rule, so that the holy unanimity of all might firmly decide what ought to be believed concerning the adoption of Christ’s flesh, which we have learned from your writings that you recently introduced through new assertions unheard of in the ancient times of the holy universal Church of God. Indeed, we have sent envoys three and four times from our devotion to the most blessed pontiff of the apostolic see, wishing to know what the holy Roman Church, instructed by apostolic traditions, would choose to answer concerning this question. We have also summoned from the regions of Britain certain men versed in ecclesiastical discipline, so that Catholic truth might be investigated through the careful consideration of many and might be held without any doubt, strengthened on every side by the most approved testimonies of the holy Fathers.”

Farther on, he records that Peter, archbishop of Milan, and Paulinus, patriarch of Forum Julii or Aquileia—as he calls him—were summoned to the synod, together with bishops from Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Britain. Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, in his little book *Sacrosyllabus*, adds that bishops from the provinces of Hesperia, Liguria, Emilia, and Austria were also summoned to the synod.

### The Option Given to the Heretics by Pope Adrian

When Pope Adrian had been moved by Charlemagne’s repeated embassies to decide concerning Elipandus’s opinion, he reconsidered and discussed the matter again and found that it was tending toward heresy. He therefore composed a public letter to the bishops of Galicia and Spain, the provinces in which the error had been disseminated. In it he argues against and refutes at length the opinion asserted concerning Christ’s adoption. Finally, in the following words, he addresses all who had strayed from the truth:

> “Before the little book is brought to its final conclusion, the disputants must be given a judicial choice: let them choose what they wish, life or death, blessing or curse. For we desire and implore the infinite mercy of the good Shepherd, the Lord, who carried the lost sheep back to the fold upon his own shoulders (Luke XV), that, abandoning the winding paths of the flesh in which evil beasts—that is, wicked spirits—dwell, they may return, with Christ drawing them onward, to the road that leads to eternal life by the steps of faith. Thus, received into the bosom of Mother Church through the lamentation of repentance, may they wash away the filth of their sins, and may their modesty, which has been disgraced, recover the former dignity of a good reputation. May they not suffer shipwreck of their honor, nor be separated from our fellowship; and thus, reconciled to communion with the Catholic faith, may divine mercy make them participants in heavenly joys.”

### Pope Adrian’s Judgment Concerning the Heretics

> “But if, because their unworthy merits demand it, the evil spirit has strangled them by the just judgment of God with so unbreakable a noose of perfidy that they cannot be released, then, by the authority of the apostolic see and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through him who entrusted that power to him as his teacher and Lord and granted him the authority to loose and bind—which we cannot say without profound sorrow—we judge that they are bound forever by the chain of anathema and must be punished with avenging retribution together with their followers. Accordingly, I define that they are alienated from the bosom of Mother Church and from our fellowship.”

### XII. The Pontiff Wishes Prayers to Be Offered for the Heretics. What Charlemagne Did at the Synod

> “If, however, any of the faithful and God-fearing should wish, by showing them the charity of kindness and out of love for Christ, to offer prayers to the Lord on their behalf [Al.: *precum*, ‘of prayers’], we not only do not forbid it, but by apostolic admonition we desire that he do so and urge him by salutary exhortation, so that almighty God—who wishes no one to perish and, because of his boundless goodness, wishes all human beings to be saved (1 Tim. II)—may recall them to the way of truth and bring them, as is fitting, to the acknowledgment of the right faith that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0947] Seek this letter of blessed Charles above, col. 897, epistle 5.]

These are the contents of Adrian’s letter, which was later read aloud at the synod under discussion.
