When the synod had assembled in the presence of King Charlemagne, he ordered the letters of Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, to be read:

> “When these had been read,” says Paulinus, “the venerable prince immediately rose from his royal seat, stood upon his platform, and spoke at length concerning the matter of the faith. He added: ‘What is your opinion? It is now entirely a year since this plague began, and, as the madness of perfidy swelled, the ulcer of unbelief boiled over more widely. A considerable error has taken root in these regions, though they lie at the farthest extremities of our kingdom; the discipline of the faith must necessarily cut it away by every means. When a lengthy postponement had been requested and granted for several days, his gentleness determined that each person should bring forth, on the appointed day, whatever he could more correctly perceive by the capacity of his intellect, and should convey to his clemency, through the vehicle of writing and with an alert mind, the offering of faith contained in his heart.’”

These are Paulinus’s words concerning Charlemagne’s command.

### XIII. The Judgment of the Italian Bishops Against the Heretics

Paulinus, producing the noble fruit of his intellect, composed a brief treatise entitled *Sacrosyllabus*, prepared against the new and resurgent heresy, and offered it to the holy synod. The synod decided that it should be sent to Spain to refute the errors that had arisen there.

The work survives intact; you may consult it. For he wrote it not only in his own name but also in the name of Peter, archbishop of Milan, and of the other bishops subject to him. At the end of the book he pronounces the following judgment against Elipandus and Felix:

> “As for Elipandus and Felix, new enemies of the Church but polluted with the age-old dregs of perfidy: unless they recover from this foolishness and wash themselves through an acknowledgment of the right faith and through the tears of repentance, we decree that they, and likewise those who, after this most salutary definition—which the plenary synod, inspired by the Holy Spirit, unanimously settled with subtle sincerity—should give assent, whether secretly or publicly, to their most false assertions, are unworthy and ungrateful and must be punished by a judgment of the same kind. In all things, however, we reserve the legal privilege of the supreme pontiff, our lord and Father, Adrian, the most blessed pope of the first see.”

But what privilege did he reserve? Clearly the privilege which, as has often been said, belonged solely to the Roman pontiff: that of condemning new heresies and the leaders of heresies. Or perhaps he means the privilege by which the Roman Church, as was demonstrated above, itself examines, approves, or rejects the acts of all councils.

### XIV. Prayers for Charlemagne. The Synodal Letter to the Heretics

Finally, Paulinus offered the following devout prayer to God for the king himself:

> “May the almighty and holy Trinity surround the Catholic and most merciful, ever-renowned lord King Charles with its grace and always protect and defend him with its right hand, through the intercessions of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, through whom we were deemed worthy to receive the author of life, and of blessed Peter, the first shepherd of the Church, and of all the saints, as well as through your prayers offered in support. May he always do what is pleasing to God, so that, relying upon heavenly arms and supported by help from heaven, he may cast down upon the earth the enemies of the name of Christ. May almighty God also subject countless barbarian nations to the dominion of his power, so that through this opportunity they may attain to knowledge of the truth and acknowledge the true and living God, their creator,” and so forth.

After Paulinus’s little book, offered in the name of the bishops, had been received and read aloud, the holy synod condemned the heresy itself. Against it, and against the little book of perfidy sent by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, in defense of his error, the synod composed a letter to the bishops of Spain. In it the Fathers refuted each of the opinions asserted by the heretics in defense of their error. The letter survives intact and concludes with an admonition to the same men that, after renouncing their error, they should follow the sound teaching of the holy Church.

Charlemagne himself also, having received—as we have said—private letters from Elipandus in defense of his error, wrote to him and to the other bishops of Spain a letter worthy of so great a prince, distinguished in piety and learning. He sent it to them together with the pontifical letters, the little book composed by Paulinus, and the synodal letter, urging everyone to abandon Elipandus’s error.

### XV. The Proceedings at the Council of Frankfurt Against the Second Nicene Synod

Some people assert that the Second Council of Nicaea was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt, and that the same council is called the seventh ecumenical synod. Whether this is so, whether it introduces any prejudice against the truth, and whether the Nicene synod suffered any injury from it must therefore be investigated more carefully and examined more thoroughly, since the matter is extremely serious and of the greatest importance.

We know that several orthodox writers, when innovators most boldly brought forward the claim that the seventh synod had been condemned at the Council of Frankfurt, took refuge in asserting that the seventh synod condemned there was not the one which the orthodox had assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia, but the one which the iconoclasts had assembled at Constantinople under Constantine Copronymus—and that they likewise called this latter council the seventh ecumenical synod.

This response of the orthodox was supported by the fact that the ancient writers who asserted that the seventh ecumenical synod had been condemned at the Council of Frankfurt named it not the Nicene but the Constantinopolitan synod, which is known to have been the council of the heretics.

### XVI. The Second Nicene Synod Was Condemned at the Council of Frankfurt

These arguments could indeed have been made with justice, and the case would have been entirely settled, if nothing else had been added. But since it is clear that the seventh synod they asserted to have been condemned was the one established in support of the veneration of the holy images, it must necessarily be referred to Nicaea, not Constantinople. The seventh synod condemned was therefore the Nicene synod, even if they erred in its name. Any impartial judge will reach this conclusion, and we do not evade such a judgment. Innocence rejoices in the truth and does not need fig leaves with which to cover shameful parts that do not exist.

Thus, far from denying that the Second Nicene Synod, also called the Seventh Ecumenical Synod, is said to have been condemned at the Council of Frankfurt, we shall even increase the number of witnesses who profess this, including witnesses of no doubtful reliability or rejectable authority. Trusting, then, in the justice of our cause, we freely and generously concede to our adversaries what they know others have utterly denied, so that they may understand that we desire nothing but the truth and that, following the custom of our holy Fathers and ancestors, we conduct the matter without disguise or deceit: affirming whatever is true and denying whatever falsehood anyone may have uttered.

As we undertake a question of such weight, we must begin by clarifying the crossroads of the divergent meanings, lest the truth, as it proceeds, be held as though in fetters by ambiguity of language. We assert first of all that it is a very different thing to say that something was condemned “in a council” and to say that it was condemned “by a council.” The former expresses an incomplete act; the latter indicates a completed one.

When something is done in a council by men who hold an evil opinion, but the agreement of those whose duty it is to ratify the statutes does not follow, then, lacking that agreement, everything decreed has no force and entirely vanishes. In such a case, the matter can be said only to have been enacted “in the council,” and it has no strength because the necessary requirements are lacking.

But it is enacted “by the council” when it is clear that everything necessary for the completion of the act has concurred and that the matter is complete.

Accordingly, as far as the matter before us is concerned, we assert with the ancient authors that the Second Nicene Synod was condemned “in” the Council of Frankfurt. But because the agreement of those whose role it was to approve the synod was lacking, we categorically deny that the Second Nicene Synod was condemned “by” the Council of Frankfurt. Whatever those men did would necessarily have been rendered wholly invalid and void. Thus it should not surprise you that the acts they then composed nowhere appear, since they were abolished and buried forever in silence: the legates of the apostolic see had not approved them, nor had Adrian, the Roman pontiff who sent them, confirmed them.

### XVII. The Nicene Synod Was Not Condemned by the Council of Frankfurt. Charlemagne Followed the Judgment of the Roman Pontiff

It is certain that the legates of the apostolic see contradicted what had been decreed there against the Second Nicene Synod; even the innovators who oppose us do not deny this (Magdeburg Centuries III, chap. 9, col. 639). Moreover, the surviving refutation and rebuttal which Pope Adrian composed against the adversaries and sent to Charlemagne clearly shows that Adrian not only did not consent but strongly opposed them.

Hincmarus also affirms that other bishops agreed with Adrian (Hincmarus, *Bishop of Rheims Against the Bishop of Laon*, chap. 20). It must therefore be considered that, by Charlemagne’s command, after the proceedings held against the Nicene Synod had been rejected and dismissed, only those acts of the same synod which had been confirmed by universal agreement against Elipandus and Felix remained intact.

Charlemagne himself knew this well, and he professes that no decrees of councils remain in force when the Roman pontiffs contradict them. This is known to have been demonstrated above with the clearest light, by the authority both of Latins and of Greeks. Thus even he—whoever he may have been who wrote the commentary against the Second Nicene Synod, which is circulated under Charlemagne’s name—does not dare deny it. Indeed, he asserts and confirms most firmly that it was the judgment of the same Council of Frankfurt that the final judgment in controversies belongs solely to the Roman pontiff. By this argument he rejects the seventh synod, claiming—for he would falsely allege—that it had not been confirmed by the Roman pontiff.

Thus the Council of Frankfurt was deprived of these proceedings. Since they received no force from the apostolic see, but were entirely refuted and condemned by it, they were also rejected by the authority of that most pious prince Charlemagne and utterly destroyed.

This must at least be affirmed for the following reason: it is certain that Charlemagne never persisted in drawing a contentious rope against Pope Adrian, so as to separate himself from Adrian’s communion. It is also thoroughly established that he never ceased to maintain communion and friendship with that pontiff. He honored Adrian not only while he was alive but also celebrated him after his death and paid him immense honor, as will be shown below in its proper place.

Thus, as we have said, it is necessary to affirm that Charlemagne entirely acquiesced in that pontiff’s judgment in these matters and, in accordance with it, condemned what had been wrongly decreed.

### XVIII. Charlemagne Always Consulted the Roman Church

Certainly, the acts of the Council of Frankfurt itself show that Charlemagne was accustomed to have recourse in ecclesiastical controversies only to the apostolic see, carefully to obtain responses from it, and to labor to carry everything out according to its instructions. This is evident from the recently produced letter of Charlemagne to Elipandus, from which the following statement concerning these matters must here be repeated:

> “We have sent envoys three and four times from our devotion to the most blessed pontiff of the apostolic see concerning this new invention, wishing to know what the holy Roman Church, instructed by apostolic traditions, would choose to answer concerning this question.”

Farther on, speaking of the responses he had received from that see and carefully preserved, he adds:

> “I am joined to the apostolic see, and to the ancient Catholic traditions that existed from the beginning of the nascent Church, with the whole intention of my mind and the whole eagerness of my heart.”

These words, worthy of so great a prince, were written in the very council. From them you may understand how clearly his own words indicate why the remaining acts of that council do not survive, and you may vindicate from slander the prince whom the innovators loudly proclaim to have been the destroyer of the Second Nicene Synod.

No one can rightly assert that he ever departed even by a finger’s breadth from the judgment of the apostolic see declared through Adrian, especially since Adrian himself testified in a letter written to him (the letter to Charlemagne concerning images) that the decrees concerning images had been established according to the ancient traditions of the Fathers under Pope Gregory II in a Roman council, and had afterward been confirmed still more firmly in another Roman council under Pope Stephen, in the presence of bishops sent from Gaul.

### XIX. The Book Sent to Adrian Against the Seventh Synod Was Not Charlemagne’s

The calumny against Charlemagne was fabricated by innovators from that book written against the Nicene Council and sent to Pope Adrian—a book which its uncertain author, who wrote its preface, asserts to be Charlemagne’s—and also from the synodal letter of the Council of Paris held under Louis on the same matter. Whether this is true remains to be investigated with the greatest care.

The occasion for the error seems to have arisen from the fact that, since Pope Adrian composed a refutation of the book and addressed it to Charlemagne, they rashly assumed that Charlemagne had been the author of the writing, since one ordinarily writes a reply to the person from whom one has received a letter.

But it cannot be denied that Charlemagne wrote letters to Adrian concerning these matters; nevertheless, he attached to them other writings that were not his own—namely, that bundle of contradictions. That these writings were not Charlemagne’s but belonged to other authors, although they had been sent by him, can easily be understood by anyone who carefully examines Adrian’s own reply to Charlemagne. This is evident at least from the single fact that, although Adrian frequently attacks the adversaries with the utmost vehemence, he never rebukes Charlemagne himself, nor does he even make the slightest complaint against him.

## XX. Charles was not the author of the writings in the Council of Nicaea

Yet neither does that book demonstrate that it had any single certain author. Rather, there were several who sharpened the pen of opposition against the Council of Nicaea. For listen to the book itself:

> “It must be added,” he says, “for the satisfaction and instruction of the unbelieving and of the Franks.”

And shortly afterward:

> “O the madness of those raging against the faith [Col. 0950D] and Christian religion, so as to assert that images in which there are figures of the Savior, of his Mother, or of the saints—by whose virtue the world subsists and the human race enjoys salvation—are not to be worshiped or venerated!”

And shortly afterward:

> “Far be it from us to yield to the madness of such wicked presumption. Let us follow the ancient traditions of the Fathers, and in no respect depart from their teaching.”

There are many other passages of this kind. You see, therefore, that the darts are not directed against Charles as the author of that book, but plainly against the many who had arranged for those writings to be sent through Charles himself to Adrian. So also, after some intervening material, Adrian says of them:

> “In this chapter those who wrote these things attempt to bring accusations and strive to contradict the truth,”

and so forth.

It is also clear to everyone who examines the context of the matter that, in that volume, one author does not proceed from beginning to end in an orderly attack upon the Council of Nicaea. Rather, the objections which each of the adversaries had undertaken to bring forward—since there were several—were heaped together and bound into one single [Col. 0951A] bundle, then given to Charles and sent by him to Adrian.

Since their objections had been distinguished according to the sequence of chapters, Adrian himself calls that book a *Capitulare*, because it contained many chapters directed against the Council of Nicaea. Hincmarus, mentioned above, a writer of approximately the same period, likewise asserts that these writings were included in the acts of the Council of Frankfurt, and that they contain the proceedings of that same council; there is therefore no reason to doubt this. For those who were afflicted with the itching desire to dissolve the statutes enacted at the said Council of Nicaea each composed separately, against that council, the objections which they had presented to the Council of Frankfurt. It is clear that the bishops were moved by these writings to condemn the Council of Nicaea because, on the basis of the false assertions of those men, they likewise declared that the Council of Nicaea ought to be condemned on the ground that it had decreed that the worship of *latria*—which is due to the one God—should be offered to images. We shall show a little below that this is entirely false. [Col. 0951B]

## XXI. The book was sent by Charles to Pope Adrian, but was the work of several authors

When Charles perceived that those men were attacking the Nicene synod, while the legates of the Apostolic See were defending it, he then, as was his custom, adopted a salutary course: he gathered together their submitted objections and sent them to Rome to Pope Adrian through the legate whom he had chosen for this task, Angilbert, abbot of Saint-Riquier.

Since several witnesses attest this, Adrian himself acknowledges it in the letter sent to Charles. Near the beginning of that letter we read:

> “Moreover, from your most merciful, exalted, and royal power we received your faithful intimate, namely Engelbert [Angilbert], abbot and minister of the chapel, who from the very beginnings of his infancy was brought up in your palace and admitted to all your counsels. Thus, just as he is received by you in every intimacy, [Col. 0951C] so also he was to be received and suitably honored by us.
>
> “Therefore, because of the exceedingly great love which we bear toward your honey-sweet royal excellence, just as you sent him with an abundance of love and extraordinary sweetness, we received him as he wished and in whatever manner he wished, listening with an accommodating ear and a benevolent mind as he related matters to us with great intimacy. And, as though your bodily excellence itself were speaking to us, we trusted him all the more openly concerning counsel for the advancement of our holy Roman Church and the exaltation of your God-protected royal power.
>
> “Among other matters, he presented to us a *capitulare* against the synod held at Nicaea for the erection of sacred images. Therefore, out of our honey-sweet royal affection for you, we gave a response to each chapter—not defending any individual (far be that from us), but holding the ancient tradition of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and following the teaching of our holy predecessors, the pontiffs, while in every way vindicating the tradition of the true faith.”

Thus Adrian prefaced his letter to Charles by describing the dispatch of the adversaries’ *capitulare* [Col. 0951D] through Angilbert. Although several men were authors of that work, Pope Adrian indicates that only its final chapter was the work of Charlemagne; he also testifies to this when responding to it at the end. We shall reproduce that chapter below.

## XXII. What the synod said about images

It is likewise clear, on the authority of the Hincmarus mentioned above, that two councils were condemned at the same Council of Frankfurt: the heretical Council of Constantinople, which ordered images to be broken, and the Second Council of Nicaea, which ordered them to be worshiped. This too can be understood from that *capitulare* sent by Charles to Adrian. The bishops’ position, according to their statements, was that Saint Gregory the pope’s opinion in his letter to Serenus had been wrongly understood: images were not to be broken, but were to be left in place, though they were not to be worshiped.

Thus, because the lies woven into that *capitulare* had not been examined carefully [Col. 0952A], the condemnation of the Seventh Synod, that is, the Second Council of Nicaea, was loudly proclaimed at the Council of Frankfurt. Since that hostile book was circulated everywhere and accepted by many without any examination of the truth, and since, once the synod had concluded, they likewise thought that its contents required no reconsideration, certain men later wrote without hesitation that the Council of Nicaea had been condemned at the Council of Frankfurt. Others afterward, deceived by their own false assertion and deriving this conclusion from its acts—namely, from the said *capitulare*—or from the acts of the Council of Paris, thought that what they falsely found asserted in those documents was true. They therefore asserted without any hesitation that the Council of Nicaea had been condemned at the Council of Frankfurt.

## XXIII. Authors who asserted that the Council of Nicaea was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt

But let us now hear the individual ancient authors who assert that the Second Council of Nicaea itself, called the Seventh Ecumenical Synod, was condemned by the Council of Frankfurt. Let us reproduce each of their words, so that amid so great a controversy the truth itself may shine forth more clearly, though it is obscured by the dense darkness of its opponents.

The oldest chronicle composed in our time, under the Emperor Louis, son of Charles, first contains the following passage. It is discussing the same Council of Frankfurt, held in that year, and the Felician heresy allegedly condemned there:

> “The synod,” he says, “which a few years earlier had been assembled at Constantinople under Irene and her son Constantine, and which they themselves had called not only the Seventh but also the Universal Synod—for it was to be held and called neither the Seventh nor the Universal—was altogether rejected by everyone as wholly superfluous.”

That is what is found there. The same words are reproduced in Aimoinus. Likewise, a chronicle written at the same time and recently published by Pithoeus has the following concerning those events in the same year:

> “The false synod of the Greeks, held concerning the worship of images, [Col. 0952C] was condemned by the bishops at that very Council of Frankfurt.”

Ado, bishop of Vienne, who wrote under Charles’s grandson, uses the same words. So does Regino, as do many other far more distinguished authors, whom we shall list below.

But first we must investigate the earliest authors themselves—namely, the bishops who attended that Council of Frankfurt—to determine how, having been influenced by the writings of their opponents, that is, by the *capitulare*, they were induced to condemn the Council of Nicaea.

## XXIV.

It is entirely certain and beyond question that those very bishops were deliberately deceived by the same adversaries, and that everything was carried through by fraud and falsehood so that the truth would find no place. Unless you yourself, reader, have touched these matters with your own hand, I do not want you to believe them. For we do not rely on testimony drawn from a distance, but on their own writings, so that the truth cannot be eluded by any evasion.

In this matter, just as I can readily say that those Fathers who attended the synod were free from deliberate fraud, so I do not excuse their negligence. How could they have preferred to believe their adversaries in so important a matter, without consulting the legitimate synodal acts, especially when the legates of the Apostolic See opposed them? And how could they, while not supposing that such men could deceive or be deceived—which is human—have failed to withhold from them complete credence in every respect in so serious a matter?

As I have long reflected upon these things, and openly confess that I am astonished, this explanation has occurred to me: in those times the affairs of the Greeks had come to smell very bad to the Franks, because the Emperor Constantine, at the urging of his mother Irene, had refused the promised marriage—long awaited by the daughter of Charlemagne. For that reason they seized every opportunity offered to disparage and insult his actions, even when those actions bore the appearance of piety. They therefore listened with no little irritation to the Council of Nicaea itself, which had been assembled and completed through the efforts of the Greeks.

We are human beings, and as long as we live this life we are sometimes compelled, against our will, to be harassed by such private emotions. Let the criticism be milder and the rebuke more tolerable than accusing them all of falsehood and fraud because they yielded to those who, by these evil arts, had attacked the same Council of Nicaea. Let all the blame fall upon those men.

## XXV. The adversaries acted by fraud against the Seventh Synod

For those adversaries—composers of lies and architects of fraud—surrounded those very bishops who came to the synod with tricks and deceptions. Under the appearance of piety they moved them to condemn the Council of Nicaea, first falsely claiming—as appears from that book called the *Capitulare*, sent to Charlemagne—that the Council of Nicaea had not been confirmed by the Roman pontiff. Without the Roman pontiff, the author there says, a council could not subsist, since every controversy concerning the faith pertains to the Roman pontiff.

But they added something plainly abominable: they claimed that the same synod had promulgated an unmistakable impiety, because it supposedly established a heresy by which, as they said, images were to be venerated by the faithful with the same honor and worship as God. The following words are found in the preface of the same *capitulare* sent to Adrian, where it discusses the proceedings of the Council of Frankfurt:

> “The question was brought forward”—they say—“concerning the new synod of the Greeks which they had held at Constantinople regarding the worship of images. In it, it was written that anyone who did not offer service or worship to the images of the saints, just as to the deifying Trinity, was to be judged anathema. Our most holy Fathers mentioned above, absolutely refusing to offer them worship and service, despised this and, agreeing together, condemned it.”

The *capitulare* also cites the acts of the same Council of Nicaea, in which it falsely claimed that Constantine, bishop of Cyprus, had pronounced anathema at that Council of Nicaea upon those who did not worship images with the worship given to the most holy Trinity. We wished to transcribe the passage here so that the matter itself might be examined more thoroughly. It reads as follows:

## XXVI.

> “What Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said unhappily, rashly, or foolishly:
>
> ‘I receive and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images. But the worship offered according to *latria*, that is, the worship of God, I reserve solely for the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity. Those who do not think in this way or glorify it I separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, subject them to anathema, and consign them to the company of those who have denied the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.’”  
> *(Second Council of Nicaea, act 3.)*

This is how the adversaries presented the passage, as though it came from the Council of Nicaea. Adrian rightly rebuked them, pointing out that neither Constantine nor the others who at that time returned with him to the Catholic Church had professed any belief other than what had been established by the same Council of Nicaea: namely, that sacred images were to be venerated, but that the worship of *latria* was in no way to be given to them, since it was due to God alone.

That Constantine’s assertion, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, had this meaning and no other is shown by the actual acts of Nicaea, which still survive intact, in these words:

> “Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:
>
> ‘Since I see that the writings now read, sent by the Eastern bishops to Tarasius, the most holy and blessed archbishop and universal patriarch, contain nothing erroneous; and since I recognize in them the same confession of faith, I, although unworthy, also agree and proclaim the same with one mind. For I receive and embrace the venerable images. But the worship offered according to *λατρεία* (*latreia*), that is, the worship of God, I reserve solely for the supersubstantial and life-giving Trinity. But those who think otherwise, and those who do not approve the glorious saints, I separate from the Catholic and Apostolic Church, subject to anathema, and consign to the company of those who stubbornly deny the incarnate economy of Christ our God.’”

Thus far runs the statement of Constantine, bishop of Constantia, according to the assertion of the Eastern letter quoted above, sent to Patriarch Tarasius. That letter makes clear that images of the Mother of God and of the saints are to be honored not as God, but—as it says—as the images of God’s friends. [Col. 0954A]

## XXVII.

The Council of Nicaea itself also contains, in its definition of the Catholic faith, a statement agreeing with all these things, confirmed by the signatures of all the Fathers, in these words:

> “We define, with all care and diligence, that the venerable and holy images, prepared suitably in the form and likeness of the venerable and life-giving cross, whether in colors, mosaic cubes, or any other appropriate material, are to be dedicated and placed in the holy churches and retained there, as well as in sacred vessels and vestments, on walls and panels, in houses and on public roads. Above all, this applies to the image of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ; then to that of our undefiled Lady, the Mother of God; of the venerable angels; and of all holy men.
>
> “Thus, through the contemplation of these painted images, all who look upon them may come to the memory, recollection, and desire of the prototypes, and may offer them greeting and an honorable veneration, but not, according to our faith, the true *latria*, which belongs solely to the divine nature.”  
> *(Second Council of Nicaea, act 7.)*

This is the holy Council of Nicaea according to the common edition, which in this respect does not differ from the edition of Anastasius, from which the same passages quoted above were taken.

You therefore have the fraud exposed: the deception concerning a falsified text and a corrupted reading, its meaning completely twisted into the opposite sense, set forth in a plenary synod for the destruction of the Ecumenical Synod. Those Fathers accepted it all too carelessly, without any examination of the legitimate reading, inspection of the Greek text, or comparison of different manuscripts—as the importance of the matter required.

## XXVIII. Other adversaries of the Seventh Synod. Jonas of Orléans, an adversary of the Seventh Synod

But what may appear worse and more astonishing is that so many and such great lies found credence not only among those Fathers who attended the Council of Frankfurt, but also among later men distinguished for their learning and highly renowned in that age. They thought and affirmed in writing that, according to the prescription of the same Council of Nicaea, images were to be venerated by us as God.

They established two classes of those who erred concerning sacred images. One class consisted of those who broke, burned, or destroyed them in any way; and on this side they condemned that Seventh Synod held at Constantinople under Copronymus. The other consisted of those who, as they thought, asserted on the authority of the decree of the Council of Nicaea that images were to be honored with the worship due to them. Into this class they cast all the teachers of the Second Council of Nicaea, and even the Roman Church, numbering it among them because it was found to profess that the same synod had been held and confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff, defended in writing, and strengthened by later councils.

You might well be utterly astonished that, simply because of their false assumption—that the Council of Nicaea had decreed that images were to be worshiped with the worship of *latria*—they included both East and West in the same sentence of condemnation merely because they accepted that synod. [Col. 0954D]

But since so obvious an error and so open a falsehood might be considered monstrous, and might perhaps fail to find credence among the ears of the faithful because of its deformity, I shall here draw up a catalogue of those who made these statements and report the opinions of each of them verbatim.

These men were distinguished for their learning and flourished under the Emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, as we shall explain in its proper place. Others likewise attended the assembly at Paris that was convened at that time for the same reason and were led by the same men into the same error, so that they declared that the Seventh Synod had taught that images ought to be worshiped as God. For this reason some of them, with great rashness and insolence, even attacked the Roman pontiff, who asserted and approved such a decree of that synod.

## XXIX.

One of them, and a prominent one, was Jonas, bishop of Orléans. For this reason he then served as an ambassador, sent to Pope Eugenius of Rome by the imperial sons of Charlemagne, Louis and Lothair, as the acts of the same Parisian assembly show.

While sharpening his pen against Claudius, the faithless iconoclast bishop of Turin, Jonas brings forward the following statements concerning the worship of images, which are relevant to our subject:

> “What you have written that the worshipers of images answered you, in order to strengthen their error, you expressed as follows:
>
> ‘We do not think that there is anything divine in the image which we worship; rather, we worship it with veneration solely for the honor of the one whose likeness it is.’
>
> “But we condemn and detest one thing in particular: since it has not escaped their knowledge that there is nothing divine in images, they deserve a more severe attack because they have offered the honor due to divinity to a weak and needy image.
>
> “It is unnecessary for me to explain one by one how far the followers and defenders of this error depart from true religion. Some Easterners who are enslaved to the same most wicked error customarily respond in the same way when we rebuke them. May the Lord, in his free mercy, grant that both these and those may at last be rescued from the same superstition and, instructed salutarily in the apostolic disciplines, be recalled to ecclesiastical tradition.”  
> *(Jonas, On the Worship of Images, book I.)*

A little farther below, addressing Claudius, who called such worshipers of images idolaters, he adds:

> “Those who, out of an excessive and indiscriminate love, make supplication before images in honor of the saints—I do not know whether they should rashly be called idolaters. It seems rather that they should be recalled from this superstition by the application of reason’s restraint, rather than be called idolaters, since they truly believe and proclaim the faith of the holy Trinity. In all the rest of your argument, however, they agree with us,”

and so forth.

This was Jonas’s position. Although he fights most vigorously against Claudius, the destroyer of images, he likewise attacks and censures those who worship them, asserting that images should be preserved in churches both for the adornment of the churches themselves and for the historical instruction of the people. He says that this is the opinion of Saint Gregory the pope, who wrote to Serenus, bishop of Marseille.

But in the remainder of that work Jonas himself argues against Claudius and confirms that the image of the holy cross ought to be worshiped, relying especially on the authority of the same Saint Gregory the pope and on the tradition of the Catholic Church. Thus he destroys everything he had built—or rather, he erects what he had wrongly destroyed. For if the image of the cross is to be worshiped, why should the image of Christ not likewise be honored?

## XXX. Walfrid and other contemporaries, adversaries of the Seventh Synod. Hincmarus, an adversary of the Seventh Synod

Walfrid Strabo, a writer of the same century, is found to have held precisely the same opinion. Establishing two classes among those who erred in these matters, he says:

> “Something must now be said about images and paintings, by which the beauty of churches is increased. Their variety should neither be honored with some immoderate worship, as certain foolish people think, nor should this beauty again be trampled upon with some contempt, as certain assertors of vanity suppose.”

And farther below:

> “It must be noted, however, that just as some venerate these same images more than is sufficient, so others, while wishing to appear more cautious in religion, reject them as forms of idolatry,”

and so forth.  
*(Walfrid, On Ecclesiastical Affairs, chapter 8.)*

When he cites the councils held against the destroyers of images, but says nothing of those previously held in support of the worship of images, it is already perfectly clear what sort of position he held. He teaches that only this much honor should be given to sacred images: that they should not be cast down and trampled underfoot. For he adds:

> “The honorable and moderate veneration of images should not be rejected altogether. For if, because we know that icons are not to be worshiped or honored, paintings are to be trampled upon and destroyed as unnecessary or harmful, then…”

and so forth; teaching that they should be preserved only for adornment and for the instruction of the people in historical truth.

Amalarius, Altigarius or Elisagarus, Threuolphus, and Adegarius belonged to the same class, as appears from the said Council of Paris under the Emperor Louis, together with others who attended that synod.

Hincmarus, bishop of Reims, must also be counted among them, when he says:

> “The Seventh Synod, called by the Greeks the Universal Synod, was a false synod concerning images, which some said ought to be broken and others said ought to be worshiped. Neither side, however, defined the matter with sound understanding or with the authority of the Apostolic See. Not long before our own time, it was held at Nicaea by a great number of bishops and sent to Rome, and the Roman pope also sent it into Francia.
>
> “Therefore, in the time of the Emperor Charlemagne, by order of the Apostolic See, a general synod was celebrated in Francia, namely at Frankfurt, after the aforesaid emperor had convened it. In accordance with the course of Scripture and the tradition of our ancestors, that false synod of the Greeks was destroyed and utterly rejected. A considerable volume concerning its destruction, which I read as a youth in the palace, was sent to Rome by the same emperor through a certain bishop.”

A little later, concerning the title “Universal Synod,” he adds:

> “By the authority of this synod, namely, the Council of Frankfurt, the veneration of images was somewhat restrained. Yet Adrian and the other pontiffs persevered in their opinion, and after Charles’s death they promoted the worship of their puppets even more forcefully, to such an extent that Louis, Charles’s son, attacked the worship of images in a book far more sharply than Charles had done.”

*(Hincmarus, Against the … Bishop, chapter 20.)*

This is what Hincmarus himself wrote, and certainly with excessive carelessness, indeed rashly. For if he had examined the legitimate acts of the Council of Nicaea, which he attacks so vehemently, he would have restrained his pen from such an insult and dealt with the matter more soberly.

## XXXI. Anastasius reproaches the Franks for not accepting the Seventh Synod

Anastasius the Librarian is referring to these men and reproaching them all in the preface which he placed before the Seventh Synod translated by him into Latin. Writing to John VIII, the Roman pontiff, he says:

> “For what the present synod, namely the Council of Nicaea, teaches concerning the worship of venerable images, this your Apostolic See, as certain writings indicate, held from ancient times; the universal Church has always venerated it and continues to venerate it to this day, with the sole exception of certain Gauls, to whom the usefulness of these things has not yet been revealed.
>
> “For they say that no work of human hands ought to be worshiped—as though the book of the Gospel were not a work of human hands, which they worship daily while kissing it; though they will surely not deny that it is more venerable than a dog, which they will not deny is not a work of human hands.
>
> “Likewise, consider the form of the holy cross, which all Christians everywhere profess that they worship. If we worship a golden, silver, or wooden cross, which is certainly not the very cross on which our salvation was accomplished, but its figure and image, why should we not worship the figure and image of the one who accomplished that salvation in the midst of the earth? He who accomplished salvation is more venerable; therefore the image of Christ accomplishing salvation is more worthy of worship than the image of the cross, which merely bears salvation.” [Col. 0956D]

These are Anastasius’s words against the adversaries of the Council of Nicaea. From this you have also learned—and you must observe this so that you are not deceived—that it was not the whole Gallican Church which was entangled in that error. Rather, as Anastasius himself says, only certain Gauls followed that perverse opinion; he was reproaching those whom we named above.

## XXXII. What the adversaries babbled about Adrian’s opinion. The manifest calumny against Adrian

Since the same men who opposed the Council of Nicaea also attacked Adrian, the Roman pontiff, whom they knew to have approved that council, we must now deal with this matter as well and refute the lies heaped upon him.

Many years after the death of Pope Adrian, those who assembled under Louis the Pious, his son, in that Parisian assembly, used the same false pretext: that the Roman pontiff had approved the Council of Nicaea, which—as they falsely claimed—had decreed that images were to be venerated like God. They directed their pen against him and, acting calumniously, did not hesitate to say that Adrian had recanted and finally come to share their opinion.

As we discuss these matters, we ask you, reader, to remain attentive, since the subject is important. Here, therefore, let us discuss that Parisian assembly only insofar as it concerns Adrian. The remaining matters will be treated more fully in their proper place and at the appropriate time.

The adversaries who assembled there, in their synodal letter to the emperors Louis and Lothair, after saying many things against Adrian’s *Apologia*, which he had written in defense of the Second Council of Nicaea, state the following:

> “Although in his objections he sometimes appears to have produced, for the sake of his defense, testimonies that are discordant, sometimes inappropriate, and sometimes even worthy of criticism, nevertheless, at the end of his *Apologia* he professed that he thought, held, proclaimed, and prescribed concerning these matters exactly as it was known that Saint Gregory had instituted.
>
> “From these words it is plainly gathered that he deviated from the straight path in this matter not so much knowingly as ignorantly. For unless, in the conclusion of his objections, he had guarded against a deviant path by binding himself to the restraints of truth—that is, to the institutions of the blessed Gregory—he could have fallen altogether into the precipice of superstition.”

These are their words concerning Adrian.

But when you, reader—whoever you are, and I do not even exclude a heretic—have read what Adrian says at the end of the said apologetic letter, you will understand how utterly false these statements are. We shall reproduce that passage shortly.

## XXXIII. The opponents of the Seventh Synod misuse the authority of Saint Gregory. The worship of holy images demonstrated from Gregory

First, let us examine what the earlier adversaries, in the *Capitulare* sent by Charles to Adrian at Rome, objected against the Seventh Synod on the basis of Saint Gregory himself. At the same time, let us observe how Adrian refutes them, so that the response to the objections later raised by the others mentioned above, after Adrian’s death, from the Parisian synod may be easier.

Those men chiefly attacked the Second Council of Nicaea on the pretext that it was contrary to the teaching of the most holy Pope Gregory. They professed that they clung to him as to the strongest anchor and boasted that they could in no way be separated from him.

Their written criticism addressed to Adrian survives in these words:

> “That it is contrary to the institutions of the blessed Gregory to worship or to break images; and because the Old and New Testaments, as well as nearly all the principal teachers of the Church, agree with blessed Gregory in not worshiping images; and Saint Gregory the pope confirms in many places that we ought not to worship anything else.”

These were the adversaries’ words.

Adrian responds to them as follows:

> “Saint Gregory, certainly, never despised sacred images, but rather observed them with the greatest constancy and venerated their figures.”

A little farther below, he proves their veneration from Gregory’s own words in his letter to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari. Discussing an image of the Mother of God and a cross which had been brought into a Jewish synagogue, and advising that they be removed from there, Gregory says:

> “With these words we exhort you that, after the image and the cross have been removed from there with the veneration appropriate to them, you must restore what was violently taken away,”

and so forth.

How, then, can anyone deny that Gregory recognized the veneration of images, when he commands that they be removed from the synagogue with veneration and carried back to their former place?

## XXXIV. That Saint Gregory was a worshiper and venerator of holy images

In addition to all this, Adrian again teaches below, after other defenses against the objections, that Saint Gregory himself taught the worship of sacred images. He says:

> “And lest anyone dare to rail against the worship promulgated by our most holy predecessors, let him know that they taught such worship as our predecessor, Saint Gregory, that eminent teacher and pope, taught in his letter, which Bishop Herulphus of the province of Gaul brought forward in the aforesaid council of the lord Pope Stephen. There, among other things, he instructed Secundinus, a servant of God enclosed in Gaul, saying:
>
> “‘We know that you do not request an image of our Savior in order to worship it in place of God or as though it were God, but for the remembrance of the Son of God, so that you may grow warm with love for him whose image you consider yourself to see. And indeed we do not prostrate ourselves before it as before the divinity, but we worship the one whom through the image we remember either as born, or as having suffered, or as seated upon the throne,’”

and so forth.  
*(Gregory, book VII, letter 53, indiction 2.)*

That is what Adrian himself says there.

Here, however, we must set down what he says at the end, where he discusses at length Saint Gregory’s opinion concerning the worship of holy images. From these words it will become clear that Adrian was so far from retreating from the decrees of the Council of Nicaea on account of Gregory’s opinion that he sought to confirm those decrees through Saint Gregory himself.

But to refute the adversaries’ calumnies completely, we can learn the sense in which Adrian understood Saint Gregory’s words, and what Charles—and Adrian himself—thought about the worship of holy images, from no source more reliably than from their own writings. For in the final chapter of the *Capitulare* sent by Charles himself to Adrian, these words are found:

## XXXV. Charles’s opinion concerning sacred images. Adrian examines Saint Gregory’s opinions

> “The final chapter is this: that the Apostolic Lord, our Father, and the entire Roman Church together may know that, according to what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory which he sent to Serenus, bishop of Marseille:
>
> “‘We permit images of the saints to be made by anyone who wishes to form them, both within the church and outside the church, for the love of God and his saints. But we do not compel those who are unwilling to worship them. If anyone wishes to break or destroy them, we do not permit it. And because we freely and without hesitation profess in this letter that we follow the mind of the most holy Gregory, pleasing to the universal Catholic Church of God.’”

Thus far runs the final chapter of his little book. The testimony of Pope Adrian himself shows that this chapter alone was Charlemagne’s, while the rest belonged to the adversaries, as he immediately adds:

«This sacred and venerable chapter differs greatly from all the chapters mentioned above. For this reason we recognized it as belonging properly to your God-preserved and orthodox royal Excellency, namely in that it fully and completely professed the orthodox faith in following the mind of the most holy Gregory [Col. 0958D]. Your most upright and exalted royal wisdom remembers how, in the letter of Saint Gregory the pope addressed to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, among other matters, the following is said. Rebuking that same bishop, he writes (Gregory, Book IX, Letter 9):

“ For it is one thing to adore a painting, and another, through the history represented by the painting, to learn what ought to be adored. What Scripture provides for readers, a picture provides for the uneducated who look at it: for in it even the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Hence, especially for the Gentiles, a picture takes the place of reading. This, since you live among the Gentiles, you ought particularly to have taken care to observe.” 

And shortly afterward:

“Since antiquity has permitted histories of the saints to be painted in venerable places, not without reason;”

and after an interval:

“Because pictures of events, which had been made for the instruction of the unlearned people, enabled those who did not know letters, by looking attentively at the history itself, to learn what had taken place.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“But let your Fraternity carefully admonish them that, from seeing the event represented, they may receive the ardor of compunction, and may humbly prostrate themselves in the worship of the almighty Holy Trinity alone” [Col. 0959A]. We likewise briefly set down above, concerning the veneration of the holy images, what he says in another letter of his addressed to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

### XXXVI.

We have likewise reported in the same way what he says in the letter addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God confined in Gaul. It runs as follows:

“The images which you asked us to send to you through your deacon Dulcitius: your request pleased us greatly, because with your whole mind you seek the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that daily bodily sight may always keep you exercised, and that, while you look at the picture, you may burn inwardly for the one whose image you desire to see.”

And shortly afterward:

“We know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as though it were God, but so that, in remembrance of the Son of God, you may grow warm in love for him whose image you desire to see. We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself, but we adore him whom through the image we remember either as born, or suffering, or seated upon the throne. And while the picture itself, like writing, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either makes our spirit rejoice over the resurrection or consoles it concerning the Passion. Therefore we have sent you, through the aforesaid deacon, our son, two curtains [or painted panels]: images of the Savior, of holy Mary the Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; also one cross and a key as a blessing, so that you may remain defended by it from the Evil One, by whose sign you believe yourself to be protected,” and so forth.

After Adrian the pontiff had cited these passages from Gregory—passages which the opponents were accustomed to bring forward—he immediately added the following:

### XXXVII. Adrian, from Saint Gregory’s teaching, teaches and accepts the veneration of images.

“And since in these matters we have recognized your God-inspired orthodox royal understanding, it is also necessary to recall and teach how Saint Gregory the pope instructed Bishop Serenus concerning the sacred images: that, from seeing the event represented, people may receive the ardor of compunction; that is, while looking upon those same sacred images, they may humbly prostrate themselves in the worship of the almighty Holy Trinity alone. In the same tenor he says to Secundinus, the enclosed servant of God: ‘For this reason you ask—not in order to worship it as God, but so that, in remembrance of the Son of God, you may grow warm in love for him whose image you desire to see.’ And: ‘We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself, but we adore him whom through the image we remember either as born, or suffering, or seated upon the throne.’ Just as he intimates to Bishop Serenus that one who looks upon the sacred images should humbly prostrate himself in the worship of the almighty Holy Trinity alone, so also he taught Secundinus, the enclosed servant of God: not to worship them as God, but, prostrating himself before those same sacred images—not as before the Divinity itself—to prostrate himself before them, and, while prostrating himself, to adore him whom through the image we remember either as born, or suffering, or seated upon the throne” [Col. 0959D].

“Now, following and embracing that same irreproachable and orthodox teaching of Saint Gregory the pope, we formerly sent to Irene and the emperor Constantine, in support of the preaching of the sacred images and their restoration, the following declaration:

‘Since throughout the entire world wherever Christianity exists, the sacred images remain and are honored by all the faithful, so that through the visible face our mind may be carried by spiritual affection toward the invisible majesty of the Divinity, in contemplation of the depicted image according to the flesh which the Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation, we adore the same Redeemer of ours who is in heaven, and, glorifying him in spirit, praise him together. For, as it is written, “God is spirit”; and therefore we spiritually adore his divinity. Far be it from us to deify the images themselves, as certain people chatter; rather, we express in every way the affection and love which we have in the love of God and his saints [Col. 0960A]. And just as we keep the books of Holy Scripture, so we keep the images themselves for the memory and veneration of holy things, preserving the purity of our faith,’ and so forth.

Whatever brief testimonies from the works of the holy Fathers we wrote there, we issued in the same meaning and tenor—as we have just stated—holding the same faith and understanding as our predecessor, Saint Gregory the pope, and preaching accordingly.

### XXXVIII.

“But they”—as our representatives, namely Peter, archpriest of our holy Roman Church, and Peter, the religious priest and venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabas, told us in person—“immediately embraced our apostolic words and ordered a council to be held. But when the heretics caused a revolt, our representatives, having been sent to the island of Sicily, returned without an answer. Then, sending after them again [Al.: at last], they caused them to ascend once more to Constantinople, and thus held this synod according to our direction [Col. 0960B]; and they restored the sacred and venerable images to their former position. And just as the teaching of Saint Gregory and ours concerning the images had stated, so they too confessed in the definition of that synod: they gave them a kiss and an honorable greeting, but by no means, according to our faith, the true worship which is due to the divine nature alone.

“Furthermore, they first anathematized and condemned, together with its followers and accomplices, that pseudo-syllogism which had been produced by the heretics under Constantine the heretic. Returning to the orthodox faith of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, they made a confession of the true faith in their written statements. Therefore we accepted that synod. For if we had not received it, and they had returned to their former vomit of error, who would have had to give an account before the terrible and dread judgment of the divine Judge for the destruction of so many thousands of Christian souls, except us alone? For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15), how much more should everyone rejoice over so many thousands of Christians who have returned from error? and who would not sing with the Psalmist, ‘Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed,’ and the rest” (Psalm 33).

### XXXIX. What Adrian did with the emperor concerning the restoration of things taken away. He presses for the restoration of the rights and property of the Roman Church. A heretic is accused who, after being admonished, did not restore the Church’s property.

“We have still not given that emperor any answer concerning the same synod, fearing that they might return to their former error. For some time ago, when we urged them to restore the sacred images, we likewise admonished them concerning the dioceses both of the archbishops and of the bishops of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church. We asked that there be restored to that same holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church the things which they then took away together with our patrimonies, when they removed the sacred images. Yet they gave no answer whatever concerning this” [Col. 0960D].

“By this it is shown that, in one matter, they have returned from error, while in two others they remain in the same error. For if the churches of Christians everywhere canonically possess their dioceses inviolate, how much more should the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church—which is the head of all the churches—by an unassailable right in every way hold and possess its diocese, namely those of the archbishops and bishops, and even its patrimonies, for the provision of lamps and the support of the poor?

“Therefore, if your God-protected royal Excellency approves, we exhort that same man with zeal for the sacred images and, giving thanks for their restoration to their former state, again rebuke and admonish him concerning the dioceses of our holy Roman Church, both those of the archbishops and those of the bishops, as well as concerning the patrimonies. And if he refuses to restore them to our holy Roman Church, we shall declare him a heretic because of his perseverance in this error [Col. 0961A]. For we desire to preserve the salvation of souls and the foundation of the true faith more than to possess the grandeur of this world [Al.: such worldly appearance].”

Here, reader, you hear that the obstinate occupation of the rights of the holy Roman Church passes into heresy, and that one who, held in such an error and admonished, does not correct what he has done wrong is to be called and condemned as a heretic. But more on this elsewhere.

### XL. The protection of Saint Peter is beneficial to kings.

Finally, Adrian turns his speech to Charlemagne himself and concludes the apologetic letter with these words:

“We are confident in your most upright God-protected Excellency, strengthened by the stability of the orthodox faith, because its most firm root is not shaken or moved at all by wicked and faithless men. Rather, we believe that in the teaching of the tradition of the true faith, which you have begun to hold and embrace from your spiritual [Al.: special] mother, the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, you will remain without hesitation, without reproach, for ever and ever.

“Therefore we trust in the power of our God: insofar as you have faith toward the Church of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and have always possessed love for its advancement and exaltation, striving everywhere with royal exertion on its behalf, so much will he graciously deign to defend and surround you with his arm in royal triumphs against hostile and unjust men [Al.: may he deign]. Thus, together with our spiritual daughter, the lady queen, and your exalted and most noble offspring, after reigning in this world for a long age, may you deserve in the future to possess life without end together with the kingdom in the citadel of heaven. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed.”

Here ends the letter. Anyone who reads it can see how the shameful calumnies concerning Adrian, written by the opponents in their brazen style, vanish: namely, the claim that he, moved by the authority of Saint Gregory and agreeing with him, cast his vote against the Seventh Synod. Rather, he used the testimonies of Saint Gregory himself in defense of that same synod [Col. 0961C].

### XLI. Adrian the pope passes over certain matters in silence.

But the reason why Adrian, in this response, did not at all touch upon those words of Charlemagne in which he had said, “We by no means compel those who do not wish to adore them,” was that circumstances at the time required him not to kindle a schism by compulsion. As we have seen, there were men whose learning seemed to stand out in that still uneducated age and who held that opinion. The most prudent pontiff saw what we quoted from Anastasius in the letter to Pope John: namely, that those about whom he was writing were not yet capable of the truth.

Yet Adrian indirectly censures those words when he praises the teaching of Saint Gregory the pope. From that teaching it could be inferred that images indeed were not to be adored as though they were gods, but were merely to be venerated because of their relation to Christ and the saints whom they represent in effigy. Therefore Adrian cautiously does not praise everything contained in the final chapter of Charlemagne’s letter, but only those things that pertain to the teaching of Saint Gregory, which he saw was accepted both by Charlemagne and by the opponents—so they professed—of the Nicene Synod. Thus Adrian speaks:

“And for this reason we recognized it as belonging properly to your God-preserved and orthodox royal Excellency, in that it fully and completely professed the true faith in following the teaching of the most holy Gregory.”

It seemed to the supreme pontiff that, for the time being, he should pass over in silence the point that they were not to be compelled to adore the sacred images which they customarily possessed. They were not yet counted among the heretics, like the iconoclasts, because they erred in this way; rather, they were tolerated so long as they might be enlightened by the light of divine grace—which happened later.

### XLII. The opponents labor in vain to prevent Gregory from being proved a worshiper of the sacred images.

Having refuted, therefore, the arguments which the opponents raised against Pope Adrian in the same Capitular Book from the writings of Pope Gregory, we must now turn to what, long after the death of that pontiff, the same opponents brought forward in the Parisian assembly which they held, again from the letters of Gregory. First, hear from the acts of the Parisian pseudo-synod mentioned above how the opponents themselves tried to draw the words of Saint Gregory into defense of their error and to twist the passage in the letter to Secundinus, which strikes at them, to their own position. The passage reads as follows (Council of Paris under Louis, p. 141):

“But because this order of words may appear so inverted and confused by those who do not understand it that, unless it is considered carefully, some less capable persons might understand it as though blessed Gregory testified that he had done what he had previously declared unlawful for all and that it was lawful for him to do it—although how absurd this is, and how unworthy it would be to think such a thing concerning so great an ecclesiastical teacher, contrary to the religion of the Church of God, no one who has come to know his statements by investigating or reading them ought to be allowed to ignore. For the justice and rectitude of the holy Church of God, and especially of the Roman Church, cannot tolerate that he should be contradictory to himself. Even if the poverty of our foolishness cannot understand this, it is better that it should presume to rise up against its own foolishness than against such great wisdom given by God. But if the power of God’s mercy deigns to illuminate our modest understanding even slightly, it will very easily be understood how this is not contradictory to itself.”

### XLIII.

“For there is no doubt that he restrained those who worshiped from the adoration of images. But in what he wrote to Secundinus—‘We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself, but we adore him whom through the image we remember as born or suffering or seated upon the throne’—our understanding is confused by the darkness of the passage, as though he had said things contrary to himself, as was stated above. But lest unnecessary ignorance, by preventing us from understanding it, torment us any longer, the meaning of that sentence is this: ‘We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself, but we adore him,’ and so forth.

“This is as though you were to say to a king seated upon a throne: ‘We, O king, prostrate ourselves before you, not as before the Divinity, but adore him whom, through your image—because you are a human being—we remember as the human Lord Jesus Christ, born or suffering or seated upon the throne, whose imitator you are as you sit upon the throne.’ Does it immediately follow from such a statement that I am compelled to adore that same king seated upon the throne? So also in the statement, ‘We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself, but we adore him,’ and so forth.

“We are invited to the adoration of images because, just as in many volumes of divine authority we find statements written with an inverted order of words, so here too we have no doubt that this was done in the sense stated above. For since it is written there, ‘We do not prostrate ourselves before them as before the Divinity itself,’ who would not notice that this was said rather to refute than to command or render that same adoration of images [Col. 0962D]? Much more, when—as was stated above—the order of the words is restored to its proper order, will it be able to correct anyone who, through excessive simplicity, has erred by supposing that the blessed teacher of the holy Church of God held an opinion contrary to himself. Moreover, even if someone who understood the passage more subtly happened to read it carelessly or inattentively, by judging himself he could very easily recall himself to a sober understanding of why he had at some point understood it otherwise.”

### XLIV.

“But if anyone—which may indeed be far from all truly wise people—prefers to follow his own understanding and condemn him rather than correct himself, there can be no doubt that he ought to be condemned by the whole Church, and especially by the holy Church of Rome. For it cannot possibly be that these two statements are not contradictory: one by which the people are forbidden to adore images, lest by doing so they appear guilty of a crime; and the other by which he is said to have done that very thing and to have taught others to do it. But far be this from so great and such a universal teacher of the Catholic Church: he who never habitually left unresolved any of the obscure questions of Scripture that seemed contradictory to one another and that came before him for explanation or discussion would not have left his own statements discordant with one another.”

Thus far in the Parisian synod spoke those wise men whom we listed above, clinging to difficult ground and sailing among shifting shoals from which they did not know how to emerge. Once they had closed the way to the truth, if it had been open to them, they would have understood clearly, in the bright light and radiant splendor of truth itself, that the obscurity of Gregory’s letter to Serenus had been illuminated by his writings to Secundinus. In the former, Saint Gregory had forbidden the worship of latria—the worship due to God alone—to be offered to sacred images; in the letter to Secundinus, however, he asserted and demonstrated by his own example a fitting veneration.

### XLV. The opponents deserve criticism.

But so that these matters may become more certain, hear what Pope Adrian writes in the same volume concerning such prostration and adoration before the sacred images, both of Saint Gregory the pope and of the most holy man Eleutherius:

“Saint Gregory the pope also established a public oratory in his monastery, had it painted with various histories, and erected sacred images there. When he entered it with blessed Eleutherius because of his stomach illness, they were both heard in prayer. And that holy man Eleutherius, who is also said to have raised a dead person, did not hesitate, while prostrating himself before those sacred images, to implore divine mercy together with Saint Gregory. They were heard together because they offered perfect faith, and those same images are venerated among us to this very day.”

This is what is said concerning Saint Eleutherius and Gregory.

You have seen, reader, that Saint Eleutherius himself, together with Gregory, actually prostrated himself before the sacred images and prayed for the recovery of Gregory’s health, so that there is no need for you to seek an interpretation of words when the deeds themselves proclaim their meaning. From this you may likewise understand how far removed it is from the opponents’ foolish assertion that Adrian, by professing that he followed the same opinion as Saint Gregory, condemned the adoration of sacred images against the Seventh Synod. Rather, from his writings he most strongly confirmed it.

It is certainly astonishing and grievous that the more distinguished men of that age and province, specifically listed above, under the two emperors Charlemagne and Louis, should have spoken so contentiously and with such utterly stubborn minds, with persistent zeal, tireless effort, and inflexible determination against the adoration of holy images and against the Seventh Synod; that they should have protested and cried out—and, if I may say so without offense, raved—against it. Having no reverence for the majesty of an ecumenical synod or for the authority of so many Roman pontiffs who fought on its behalf, and relying upon manifest falsehoods, as you have seen, and upon a misconceived interpretation of Pope Gregory’s teaching, they withdrew from the common judgment of the Catholic Church, wrote against its practice and doctrine, stirred up disturbances, hurled the darts of calumny, and added many other things wholly unworthy of their own reputation. They even forced Gregory himself—who was entirely reluctant and held the contrary opinion—to support their own error and to confess himself the author of it.

### XLVI. Gregory was a venerator of the image of the holy cross.

Moreover, those same men assert that Gregory was a worshiper of the image of the holy cross. One of the men named above, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, demonstrated this with the highest praise and glory when he acted against Claudius, bishop of Turin, and said the following [Col. 0964B]:

“Blessed Gregory, whose words no one doubts except one forgetful of his own salvation, remembers the matter in the Book of the Sacraments in this way: ‘O God, who in your mercy deigned to redeem the human race by the precious blood of your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, graciously grant that those who come to adore the life-giving cross may be freed from the bonds of their sins.’”

Jonas cites this and many other passages asserting that Gregory adored the image of the holy cross and taught others to do the same.

But Jonas, though he offers the matter well, divides it badly: while asserting that Gregory venerated the cross, he denies that Gregory likewise venerated the sacred images. Why do you divide badly what he himself joins together well? Did he not himself wish the image of the most holy Mother of God and the image of the cross to be brought together from the Jewish synagogue into the church with the same veneration, as was recently stated from his letter to Januarius? Did he not likewise join together the image of the Savior and the image of the cross, giving both to Augustine so that, protected by them, he might enter England, as Bede testifies? Why, I ask, do you wickedly divide in worship those images of the cross and of the Savior which he himself joined together in one and the same holy and devout religion?

There is nothing that can be brought forward against this. These matters are sufficient for the defense of the Council of Nicaea, Gregory, and Adrian. Now that the discourse has been led out from the thorns and thistles of controversy, let it emerge into an open and spacious field. But Charlemagne has no rest: after the disturbances of the Council of Frankfurt, recalled to military labors, he set out on an expedition against the rebellious Saxons and, by God’s favor, received their submission. This is what the frequently cited annals of the Franks report.

[Col. 0963]

## On the same synod.

[From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.]

[Col. 0963D] A capitulary concerning images—not to be broken or adored, but to be kept for ornament and remembrance—was sent to Rome from the same Council of Frankfurt, held under the auspices of Charlemagne, and divided into four books under the following title: *The Work of the Most Illustrious and Most Excellent, or Distinguished, Man*, and so forth. (See below.)

Georgius Cassander writes concerning this work in a letter addressed to Johannes Molinaeus in the year 1560, p. 1103 of his *Opera*:

“I called those four books against the synod of the Greeks held at Nicaea concerning the adoration of images remarkable, first because they were written and published under the name and authority of the most illustrious King Charles, with the agreement of the entire synod, in which the legates of the Roman pontiff were also present. Secondly, because I see that those little books have always been held in esteem and honor. This volume of Charles is preserved at Rome in the innermost Vatican library, where only distinguished and exceptional books are usually stored . . .

“Among the ancients, those who wrote about the Council of Frankfurt mention it, as does Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, a man exceedingly learned and devoted to ecclesiastical affairs, and, in the immediately preceding age, Nicholas of Cusa, on the authority of that same Hincmar. In our own age, Augustine Steuchus, bishop of Gubbio and papal librarian, also mentions it.

“In short, I read that this volume is honorably cited and praised; I do not read that it has been condemned, criticized, or even merely noted. If anyone despises the Emperor Charles, certainly he was not regarded as such by the writers of his age. Whatever he lacked in knowledge of sacred matters, he supplied through constant association with the most learned men, among whom Alcuin—called Albinus by some—was easily foremost. I am readily persuaded that these books were written especially through Alcuin’s work, since he was highly learned in sacred matters, very close to Charles, and his style agrees sufficiently. Indeed, I found an entire chapter in these books, in almost the same words, in Alcuin’s commentaries on John, so that it seems entirely to be Alcuin’s. Nevertheless, Charles, following the judgment of the whole Council of Frankfurt, wished it to be written and published under his own name out of zeal for his faith.

“This much is certain: that the synod of the Greeks held a second time at Nicaea was rejected at that famous Council of Frankfurt, insofar as it decreed that the images of the saints were to be adored, and that all the Gallic churches especially shared the same judgment, disapproving the indiscriminate adoration of images which the Greeks seemed to demand.”

[Col. 0965]

[Note: [Col. 0965C] *Frankfurt.* So called from Frankfurt, which is situated on the river Main. Adrian of Rome writes the following about it in his *Theater of Cities*:

“Frankfurt, situated on the Main, commonly called Frankfurt am Main, to distinguish it from the other Frankfurt situated on the Oder, formerly called Helenopolis after the empress Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great. Some say that this city began to be built in the year 774 by the Franks under King Charlemagne; afterward it fell into ruin and was restored by Franco, son of Marcemir IV—as Hunibald writes—duke of Franconia, and was named after him. This city is divided into two parts by the Main flowing through it, and the two parts are joined by a stone bridge” [Col. 0966C].

Concerning this city someone sings:

“ . . . which lies near the swift Main,

Bright in situation, thronged with people, and adorned with streets;

From this it draws its name: for the German inhabitant called it

Frankfurt; but let me, in Latin speech,

Call it the ford of the Franks,” and so forth.

[Col. 0966D] At the present time the city is imperial and, with two annual fairs, the most famous and distinguished marketplace in all Germany. Here the Roman kings are customarily elected by the prince-electors. The emperors have granted this city many other privileges.]

## An admonition of Francis Laurentius Surius to the reader concerning the same Council of Frankfurt.

(From Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*.)
