[Col. 0965A] Not a few writers have mentioned the council held at Frankfurt, and the heretics of our own age also boast of it greatly, as though the Second Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, which decreed that images were to be venerated piously and religiously, had been condemned there. To establish this opinion they cite Regino, abbot of Ursperg, and certain others, although in both Regino and Ursperg one can discern no obscure traces that both texts have been corrupted—or at least Ursperg must have fallen into error when, under Irene, he says that a synod was held at Constantinople. If they cite anyone else, they do so in their customary manner, that is, without good faith.

Indeed, they agree among themselves so admirably on this point that even if one wished to follow them, one would not know to whom one should chiefly give credence. But among that sort of people it has long been customary to care nothing about the faithfulness with which they handle a matter, provided they appear somehow to support their own error.

This, however, must be regarded as certain: nothing was done at the Council of Frankfurt against the Nicene Synod. Rather, the council that was condemned was the one held at Constantinople under the most impious emperor Constantine Copronymus by the iconomachists against images, which they wished to call the Seventh Ecumenical Council but attempted in vain to have recognized. This is what Ursperg says: that it was called neither the Seventh nor anything else, but was rejected by everyone as something superfluous.

Moreover, very large numbers assembled at the Council of Frankfurt—approximately three hundred bishops from Germany, Gaul, and Italy—and Adrian the pontiff did not wish his legates to be absent. This is thought to have been the reason why the Fathers who attended called it plenary.

Nor was the controversy over images the only matter debated there, nor was judgment pronounced solely against the pseudo-synod of the Constantinopolitan iconomachists. The impious doctrine of the heretic Elipandus was also condemned. He was then bishop of the see of Toledo in Spain and asserted that Christ, the Son of God, was adoptive. Of the matters now published, only this part survives; everything else that was done against the iconomachists has either been entirely lost or is still hidden somewhere [Col. 0966B].

Although we cannot assert with certainty why this happened, a probable conjecture is that it was the work of those who wrote the four books against the Second Nicene Synod, which are now seen printed under the name of Charlemagne—not without grave insult to so holy and Catholic a ruler, and through the foul fraud of our heretics who wish to be called evangelicals. Their incredible shamelessness is also evident in this: although they want by every means to prove that the Second Council of Nicaea was rejected at Frankfurt, they produce in their support the decree of the Council of Frankfurt, by which their lamentable desire to lie and invent anything whatsoever is so thoroughly exposed that it is astonishing that they ever dared to appear before any honorable man.

The decree—or rather, a portion of the decree—is as follows:

“ A question was brought forward,” it says, “concerning a new synod of the Greeks, which they held at Constantinople concerning the adoration of images.”

Here the crafty men, wishing to persuade the reader that the Nicene Synod must be understood, corrupted the decree of Frankfurt. But, by a remarkable judgment of God, so that their imposture might be exposed to everyone, they forgot to erase “Constantinople” and to substitute “Nicaea” in its place.

Now, since “Constantinople” has been left, no one is so stupid as not to understand that the synod rejected at Frankfurt was the one mentioned above, held at Constantinople by the iconomachists under Constantine Copronymus.

But let such men depart with their evil arts.

[Col. 0965]

## Mansi’s annotation on the same synod.

[Col. 0965D] Whether the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea concerning the worship of images were rejected by this council.

This was taught at that time by Alanus, *Dialogue* IV, chapters 18 and 19, and *Dialogue* V, chapters 12 and 13; Sanderus, Book II *On Images*, chapter 5, and Book VII *On the Visible Monarchy*, no. 613; Surius in the preface to this council, under the word “Council”; Vasquez, Book II *On the Adoration of Images*, disputation 7, chapter 5 and following; and Suárez, volume I, page 3, disputation 54, section 3.

This is confirmed by the authority of the Council of Sens, in the fourteenth chapter of its decrees of faith, where it says:

“Charlemagne, the most Christian king of the Franks, at the assembly of Frankfurt, suppressed the madness of that same error—iconomachy—which a certain most unhappy Felix had introduced into Gaul and Germany.”

Platina, in his *Life of Adrian*, says:

“Two years later, the distinguished bishops Theophylact and Stephen, in Adrian’s name, held a synod of the Franks and Germans, in which both the synod that the Greeks called the Seventh and the Felician heresy concerning the removal of images were abolished.”

Paulus Aemilius says nearly the same thing in Book II *On the Deeds of the Franks*, near the end. He says that the Council of Frankfurt acted against the heretics who condemned images:

“And the proper honor of the images,” he says, “was preserved.”

Blondus, *Decade* II, Book I; Sabellicus, Book and Ennead VIII; Nauclerus, Generation 27; and Gablisardus of Arles, in his *Chronology*, under the year 816, likewise bear witness.

In the passage cited above, Alanus reports that a certain heretic, Anselm Ruid, asserted that the Nicene Synod had execrated as heretical the pseudo-Seventh Council of Constantinople concerning the abolition of images, and that Adrian the pope and King Charles had done the same at Frankfurt.

The most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Baronius held that the Second Council of Nicaea had been condemned by the fathers of this council. Nearly the same had already been written before him by the most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine as well, in Book VII *On Images*, chapter 14, and elsewhere. But two considerations draw me, almost against my will, away from their opinion. The first is that, since the histories and acts of the council report that legates of the supreme pontiff Hadrian—whom Ado in his *Chronicle* [Col. 0967B] names Theophylact and Stephen—were present at this council, it cannot have happened that the entire council was unaware by what authority the true Seventh Synod of Nicaea had been convened, or what had been defined in it. For since that synod had been assembled shortly beforehand under the same pontiff, his legates could not have been ignorant of that pontiff’s authority and teaching. Therefore, even if false rumors had been spread about that Seventh Synod, as Genebrardus asserts on I know not what basis, the fathers of the Council of Frankfurt could have been instructed by the legates of the supreme pontiff and informed and taught through the writings of that Seventh Synod itself.

Indeed, since the celebration of the Council of Nicaea was a matter of the greatest renown and publicity throughout the universal Church, it is not credible that, among the bishops of all Gaul and Germany assembled here, no one could be found who had any knowledge whatsoever of the convening of the Seventh Synod of Nicaea or of its approval by the pontiff. Moreover, the error of worshiping images as gods is rather the error of pagans than of certain heretics or of those who profess the faith of Christ [Col. 0967C]. Therefore there is no reason to believe what Bellarmine and Baronius suppose: that the fathers of the Council of Frankfurt thought this, or rashly believed it merely because of false rumors—especially since at that time there was no suspicion in the Church of such an error, and the bishops of this council were pious and Catholic men. One cannot suspect that, moved by some wrongful bias against the Easterners, they attributed error to the fathers of the most holy Council of Nicaea or interpreted their opinion in the worse sense, as though they were heretics.

The second reason that compels me to withdraw from the opinion of Baronius and Bellarmine is this: the fathers of this council often profess that they proceed under obedience to the Roman pontiff; and at the end of the book *Sacrosyllabus*, while pronouncing their judgment against the heretics, they add these words: “With the privilege of the right of the supreme pontiff, our lord and father, the most blessed Pope Hadrian of the First See, reserved in every respect.” Likewise, the same fathers often profess in this council that they follow the traditions of their predecessors and do not depart from their footsteps. Moreover, Charlemagne, who took part in this council, says in a letter to the bishops of Spain that he first consulted the pontiff of the Apostolic See concerning his view of the matter discussed in that council; and shortly afterward he adds these words: “To the Apostolic See, and to the ancient and catholic traditions from the beginning of the nascent Church, I shall join myself with the whole intention of my mind and the whole eagerness of my heart.”

The fathers of the council could surely not have professed these things if they had condemned the most holy Council of Nicaea, confirmed by the Apostolic See. For, as I proved above, they could not have erred concerning the fact on the basis of false information. Therefore, if they did these things knowingly and in error, they did so with pertinacity and heresy; and thus they thought one thing about the authority of the Apostolic See and said another. Since, in my judgment, such conduct cannot be presumed of so great and distinguished an assembly of bishops, it is not probable that what the most reverend and illustrious Cardinals Bellarmine and Baronius assert actually happened: that the fathers of the council, in the presence of the legates of the supreme pontiff and of a Catholic ruler, condemned the Seventh Synod, confirmed by pontifical authority, and resisted the supreme pontiff Hadrian [Col. 0968A].

Furthermore, if the Council of Nicaea had been condemned by the authority of this synod, and thus the error of the image-breakers had in fact been approved even through faulty information, surely before our own times some adherent of that error would have tried to fortify himself and his opinion by its authority. Yet no one did so—especially since, shortly after Charlemagne, Claudius of Turin arose in that same Gaul and attempted to introduce that error into the Western Church. The authority of a Western plenary council could certainly have greatly strengthened him if it had confirmed that error by a formal definition. But neither did Claudius cite it in his own favor, nor did Jonas of Orléans, who wrote against him at the same time and refuted his foundations, answer anything from the Council of Frankfurt or write anything concerning this aspect of it [Col. 0968B].

Finally, I add that the Roman Church has never approved and received any provincial council in one part while, in another part, that same council had deviated with pertinacity and heresy. I noted above that this provincial council was received and approved by the Church insofar as it defined the adoption and sonship of Christ. Therefore it is not credible that, in this same council, the Council of Nicaea was condemned in any way. For this reason, I cannot but defend in this matter the opinion which, fortified by the authorities and arguments cited above, most strongly defends, adorns, and enhances the authority of the most holy Second Ecumenical Council of Nicaea against all image-breakers.

But you will say: What answer is to be given to the authorities of the *Caroline Books*, of Hincmar, Aimoinus, the Abbot of Ursperg, Regino, Ado, and John Aventinus, all of whom affirm that the Seventh Synod was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt?

I answer: Different people hold different opinions. Alanus, Sanderus [Col. 0968C], and Surius, in the passages cited above, say that the pseudo-Seventh Synod held at Constantinople under Copronymus was condemned by the fathers of this council. But since the historians mentioned above all write that the synod condemned here was the Seventh Synod held under Constantine and Irene in favor of the worship of images, we must without doubt concede that they understood not that pseudo-Seventh Synod but rather the true Seventh Synod. For it was this synod, not the other, that was celebrated under the empress Irene in favor of the worship of images.

Vasquez, in Book II *On Adoration*, chapter 7 of the seventh disputation, and several others concede that Hincmar and the other writers of German affairs mentioned above are speaking of the Council of Nicaea; but they say that what they report is false, and that, deceived by the false account of the pseudo-Charlemagne, they came to think this way. Accordingly, no greater credence should be given to them than to the pseudo-Caroline books.

I, however, together with the most learned Francisco Suárez, hold that this response rests upon weak conjectures and testimonies which are not self-consistent (Suárez, vol. I, disputation 54, section 3) [Col. 0968D]:

> “To begin with the preface of Eli-Phili, on which the whole preceding response principally rests, no credence can be given to it; nor is it probable that all the other historians relied upon that one source alone.
>
> “First, because the authors of the preceding opinion doubt whether, in that preface as it exists in its original form, the Council of Frankfurt is named at all; and they more probably believe that the parenthesis in which mention is made of the Council of Frankfurt was inserted by others. If this is true, neither Hincmar nor the other historians could have derived from this preface the opinion that the Council of Nicaea was condemned at Frankfurt, but at most they could have derived it from some gathering of ignorant and heretical men, by whom that book was perhaps published.
>
> “From this arises a second conjecture. For, in the judgment of all right-thinking people, that book was published by Charlemagne, but had been offered to Charlemagne, either secretly or openly, by one or more heretics. Charlemagne, however, sent it to Pope Hadrian, who expressly refuted the book in writing to Charlemagne on the subject of images. All this is extensively proved above by Alanus, and by Bellarmine in the cited Book II, chapter 15. Therefore it is not probable that Hincmar, a Catholic and learned man, attributed that act to the Council of Frankfurt solely on the authority of that book.
>
> “Third, although that book was published in Charlemagne’s time, Alanus and Surius rightly doubt whether the preface now placed before it is ancient, or whether it was recently written and attached by some heretic, or at least corrupted. For the author of the preface, whether under an invented or forged name, calls himself Eli-Phili in order to conceal himself; this immediately arouses suspicion of some deception, especially in a matter so slippery and inherently suspect. Furthermore, insofar as I can conjecture from what Alanus [Col. 0969B] reports in chapter 18, Eli-Phili himself shows that he is someone other than Charlemagne. For in that same preface he expressly attempts to show that Charlemagne was the author of those books, after first deliberating the matter with the bishops of the Council of Frankfurt. Therefore Eli-Phili, not Charlemagne, was the author of that preface; and that preface was not published in Charlemagne’s time. Consequently, nothing probable can be believed about it except that it was published by the same person by whom that book was later found again, or by whom it was printed only forty-four years ago. And it becomes even less probable that Hincmar and the other ancient historians derived their opinion from that preface.
>
> “Fourth, an objection noted by Surius is that the author of the preface says that the synod condemned by the Council of Frankfurt was held at Constantinople. For these are the words reported: ‘The question was brought forward concerning the new synod of the Greeks which they held at Constantinople concerning the worship of images.’ From this wording it can be inferred that he was speaking not of the Council of Nicaea but of the Council of Constantinople. Or at least, since he says that the matter of the worship of images was treated in that synod, and since he also says—as Bellarmine reports—that Constantinople was situated in Bithynia, it follows that this man was utterly ignorant and unworthy of credence. Or certainly it may be inferred that he believed, on the basis of some tradition or rumor, that a certain Constantinopolitan synod had been rejected at Frankfurt, but did not know what had been treated in it and added this through error.
>
> “From these points it is also clear how weak Hincmar’s testimony is if we are to believe that he testified that the Council of Frankfurt condemned the Council of Nicaea solely on the authority of the preface to the *Caroline Books*, since it is more probable that Hincmar never saw such a preface. Hence Alanus above rightly gives no credence to this testimony, nor does he believe it to be Hincmar’s, because neither does the work of Hincmar from which it is said to have been taken survive, nor has it reached us except through the report of Illyricus [Col. 0969D], a heretic to whom we give no credence; nor do we know from where he extracted that fragment, especially since Trithemius does not number it among Hincmar’s works. Moreover, those very words contain many false, contradictory, or scarcely probable statements.
>
> “First, he asserts that at a certain Seventh Synod of the Greeks some said that images ought to be broken, while others said that they ought to be worshiped. But this did not happen in one synod; it happened in different synods. Thus he appears to confuse the two synods, for he says that neither of those positions was defined there in a sound sense. Next, he says that the Council of Nicaea was held without the authority of the pope and sent to Rome.
>
> “Again, he says that the Roman pope had the Council of Nicaea sent to him and directed to France so that it might be examined or corrected there, as he indicates. This is intrinsically improbable and alien to all reliable history.
>
> “Finally, what is said there about a volume published against the Council of Nicaea and sent by the emperor to Rome through certain bishops does not agree with what Hadrian reports: that Charlemagne sent him a book through the abbot Engilbert.
>
> “Finally, concerning all the other historians, it must necessarily be admitted that some error is contained in their writings. For Aimoinus, whom the Abbot of Ursperg followed, expressly says that the synod condemned at Frankfurt had been assembled at Constantinople. Why, then, should we interpret them as speaking of Nicaea?
>
> “You will say: What of those who add, ‘under Constantine and Irene’?
>
> “Alanus replies that, in this particular, those books were corrupted by some image-breaker. But because this cannot be proved, nor can it be made sufficiently probable, I would rather say that Aimoinus was mistaken, being ignorant of the time at which the pseudo-synod of Constantinople had been assembled.
>
> “Next, Regino, whom Aventinus imitates, calls that synod a pseudo-synod of the Greeks. This is the name by which that Seventh Synod of Constantinople was called by all Catholics. For the Council of Nicaea could not be called a pseudo-synod, since it was entirely genuine; nor could it be called merely a synod of the Greeks, since it was universal and was convened by the authority of the supreme pontiff. The contrary is indicated there concerning that synod.
>
> “You will say: How, then, does Regino say that that synod was held in favor of the worship of images?
>
> “Alanus replies that it should be read ‘in favor of the non-worship of images,’ and that the particle *non* was removed either through carelessness or malice. But this is a difficult response, since it cannot be proved. I would more readily say that those authors were ignorant of what had been discussed and defined in the councils of the Greeks, just as the earlier opinion said concerning the Council of Nicaea. Nor is this without foundation, because, as far as we know, that pseudo-synod of Constantinople was never translated into Latin; and the Council of Nicaea also received a Latin version only after a long period. From the histories of those times they could scarcely have known anything certain about what had been discussed in those synods.
>
> “Alanus gives an acute response concerning Ado’s words: the words ‘in favor of the worship of images’ should not be joined with what precedes but with what follows, with a comma inserted in this way: ‘The pseudo-synod which the Greeks call the Seventh, having been entirely rejected in favor of the worship of images’—that is, it was entirely rejected in defense of the worship of images. This meaning is indeed quite consistent with the words themselves; indeed, they can scarcely be construed conveniently in any other way, since no synod was called ‘the Seventh’ because of its support for the worship of images. If this is the true meaning, perhaps Regino was deceived by Ado’s words, since they were either contemporaries or Regino was the younger. For, according to Trithemius, Regino flourished in the year 910, whereas Ado composed his history down to the year 877. Therefore Ado was either earlier or, at the very least, his equal in age. It could have happened that Regino, misunderstanding Ado’s words, was deceived by them and took from them an occasion for error, which was then followed by the Abbot of Ursperg and John Aventinus, who are unquestionably much later. The same may also be said of Aimoinus, or Anonius, if he is perhaps the man whom Trithemius reports under the name Ammonius the monk as having written about Frankish affairs in the year 900.
>
> “But if this interpretation is not accepted, it should rather be said, as concerning the others, that Ado was ignorant of what had been treated in the pseudo-synod of Constantinople and falsely believed that it had been defined there that images were to be given the full worship of *latria*, rather than that by the name ‘pseudo-synod of the Greeks’ he meant the Council of Nicaea.”

From all these considerations, therefore, it is at least clearly concluded that no firm argument can be drawn from any of the histories by which one might think that the Council of Frankfurt defined anything against the true worship of images or against the Council of Nicaea. We have likewise shown by manifest indications and arguments that, if the matter of images was discussed at the Council of Frankfurt, it could not have been ignorant either of Pope Hadrian’s opinion or of the true definition and authority of the Council of Nicaea, nor could it knowingly and deliberately have dissented from them—given the reverence which, from the surviving acts of the council, we know it showed toward the Apostolic See [Col. 0971A].

It therefore necessarily remains to be acknowledged either that the historians erred, or that their manuscripts were corrupted in some respect, or certainly that they were speaking not of the true Seventh Synod but of a falsely designated one. As for the testimony of the Caroline preface and the testimony of Hincmar, no account whatsoever should be taken of the former, because its author is unknown and suspect, and because it is not established when or where it was written, published, or discovered; moreover, it openly contains lies and false testimonies which it attributes to the Council of Nicaea. Nor should account be taken of the latter, because it is not established that the testimony is Hincmar’s, except through the report of a heretical enemy of images; and because the very things reported in that testimony are scarcely probable and do not agree with other reliable histories.

Let the complete work of Hincmar, published at Paris in 1615, be consulted: there, without any variation of reading, “at Constantinople” is found. These booklets may now be found complete in the library of the Fathers, printed at Cologne in 1618. As for the remaining authors, since we cannot deny that some error is found in their books, their authority in this matter is entirely weakened.

For this reason, someone might freely deny that anything was done concerning images at the Council of Frankfurt, either for them or against them, because the acts of that council do not survive concerning this subject, and no Catholic author reports having seen them. For what the heretics of that time circulated under this name was plainly fabricated by them. Hence they do not identify the copy from which they supposedly translated those acts, nor the place in which they had until then lain hidden and where they themselves discovered them. Nor do they transcribe the acts of the council word for word, as is done in the case of other councils, and as we possess that part of this council which concerns the adoptive sonship of Christ [Col. 0971C].

Finally, Jonas of Orléans, who flourished shortly after Charlemagne and wrote to Charles the Bald in defense of images against Claudius of Turin [Col. 0972A], mentions the Council of Frankfurt at the beginning of that work but says only that Felix’s error concerning the adoptive sonship of Christ was condemned there. He makes no mention of the matter of images having been discussed at that council. Likewise, Walafrid Strabo, in Book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 8, mentioning the error of the Greeks concerning images, says that it was condemned at the Roman council under Gregory III, and adds:

> “Finally, that very complaint of the Greeks, in the time of the emperor Louis of blessed memory, having been brought into France, was refuted by the provident care of that prince through synodal writings.”

He makes no mention of the Council of Frankfurt, although Walafrid was an author of nearly the same period. This manner of speaking, therefore, is not without a probable conjecture.

Nevertheless, since so many histories that mention the Council of Frankfurt report that something concerning images was treated there, they compel us to suspect that the matter had some foundation and that it had reached the ears of those who began to write this—namely, Ado, Aimoinus, or Regino—at least through tradition or public report [Col. 0972B]. It is therefore credible that, when Pope Hadrian sent his legates to the Council of Frankfurt, he also sent through them the acts of the Council of Nicaea, which had been completed at that same time, so that its definition might become known throughout the West.

Thus it could easily have happened that nothing further concerning images was discussed or written at the Council of Frankfurt beyond the acceptance of the Council of Nicaea and the agreement of those fathers in condemning the pseudo-synod of Constantinople. This is perhaps what Ado wished to report in brief words, according to the interpretation given above. The opinion of the others is the same, although concerning other matters or circumstances relating to that pseudo-synod of Constantinople they may have mixed in some error through ignorance of history. Later historians, as we have seen, corrected that error, partly led by reason and firm conjecture, and partly because they acquired a clearer knowledge of the Council of Nicaea.

Thus, in so uncertain a matter, the Council of Sens rightly chose the more probable opinion: that the Council of Frankfurt agreed with the Second Council of Nicaea.”

# Extracts from the Dissertation of Natalis Alexander on Images

## § I. The objection drawn from the *Caroline Books* is proposed

[Col. 0971C]

[Col. 0971D] Dallaeus, a Calvinist, and others of the same sect, together with Forbesius and other Lutheran writers, object against the Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration of sacred images the teaching of the *Caroline Books*. They attempt to prove that this teaching is entirely contrary to the decrees of the Seventh Synod and overturns its definition and all its foundations. I present here the more substantial points.

### 1.

When Charlemagne examined the passages of Scripture which the Council of Nicaea had brought forward in this matter, he repeatedly testifies that the “adoration” of images which the council established “was nowhere instituted by patriarchs, prophets, apostles, or apostolic men” (Book II, chapter 5). Throughout chapter 25 of the same book he proves that “nowhere was it instituted by the apostles, either by examples or by words, that images should be worshiped.” Book I, chapter 30, should also be consulted.

### 2.

In Book II of that work, chapter 21, the author of the book proves that God alone is to be honored and worshiped with religious worship, and from this concludes that no religious worship is to be offered to images [Col. 0972C]:

> “The terrible trumpet of all divine Scripture resounds that we must worship God alone, adore him alone, and glorify him alone. Therefore they must beware and fear in every way lest, while they strive to introduce the worship and adoration of images into the Christian religion, they appear to frustrate the singular worship and adoration of the one God. These two things are so mutually opposed that, if one stands, the other cannot stand . . . . Therefore God alone is to be worshiped, he alone adored, he alone glorified. Of him it is said through the Prophet: ‘His name alone is exalted’ (Psalm 148:12). Yet veneration is to be offered to his saints, who, having conquered the devil, reign with him. But images, with every form of cultivation and adoration excluded, whether they are in basilicas for the memory of historical events and for ornament, or whether they are not, can bring no prejudice whatsoever to the Catholic faith, since they are recognized as having absolutely no function in accomplishing the mysteries of our salvation.”

And in Book I, chapter 2, he attacks the fathers of the Council of Nicaea in these words:

> “They do not seek the grace of God in that truth of which holy Truth and true Piety said: ‘If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free’ (John 8:31–32); rather, they seek it in images fashioned by the skill of artists, which generally lead their spectators into admiration because of the memory of historical events, but always lead their worshipers into error. For it is no insignificant error when something other than the one who said, ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deuteronomy 6:13), is worshiped with religious worship.”

### 3.

“Let no quibbler,” says Dallaeus, “obtrude here the solemn distinction between *latria* and *dulia*, or between absolute and relative worship. Charlemagne removes every kind of religious worship from images—not only the adoration due to divinity, but also ‘cultivation’ and ‘observance’ (Book II, chapter 23; Book III, chapter 18), ‘veneration’ (Book II, chapter 27), and ‘honor,’ whether offered with the neck bent (chapter 30) or with the head bowed (Book I, chapter 1), or through the offering of incense and lamps (Book I, chapter 2). These terms plainly encompass every kind of religious worship, including that inferior to *latria*, and even the worship which the Roman Church today holds should be offered to images. For the Council of Trent wishes the faithful ‘to venerate and kiss images, and to uncover their heads and prostrate themselves before them’” [Col. 0973A].

### 4.

Charlemagne denies that images should receive either the veneration shown to saints who have died or the adoration shown to living persons as an act of charity and greeting—that is, civil greeting, which is far inferior to religious worship:

> “If, then, angels or human beings are not at all to be adored, while the adoration shown as an act of charity and greeting is preserved, much less are images, which lack reason and are worthy neither of greeting nor of adoration because they are without sensation, to be adored. If they are not to be adored—or rather, because they are not—they are said to commit a double lapse in this matter, either because they adore them or because, in order to do so, they falsely claim that this was handed down to them by the apostles.”

This is from Book II, chapter 25.

### 5.

The author of the *Caroline Books* does not even permit images to be compared with sacred vessels or with the books of Holy Scripture; and he is angry with the Nicene fathers, who had compared these things with one another. Yet the honor now paid to images far surpasses, by a wide interval, that accorded in the Church to sacred vessels and volumes:

> “The divine-law instruments demonstrate how greatly vessels dedicated to divine worship surpass images. Those vessels, which the Lord commanded through Moses to be placed in the tabernacle of testimony, and which the most holy David, the prophet, instituted and Solomon established and dedicated in the temple at Jerusalem, both signified the mysteries of typological meanings and performed the office of a long-standing ministry in matters pertaining to the worship of God. These images, however—with the exception of the cherubim, oxen, and lions, which were made not for worship but to signify future things—were not only never made or dedicated by any of the saints, but are everywhere rejected by the testimonies of nearly all the oracles of the divine law. These vessels too, which the holy Church possesses for the accomplishment of the mysteries of our redemption, are always necessary for the faithful and always perform a service in divine worship. In the vessels, therefore, sacrifice is offered to God, not in images . . . .
>
> “Finally, without images it is possible to receive the water of the bath and the anointing with sacred liquid, to burn incense, to illuminate sacred places with lamps, and to effect the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood; but without vessels this can never be done. For the author of our salvation, when he brought the Old Testament to an end and inaugurated the New, is reported to have taken not an image but a cup. And through the prophet the Lord does not say, ‘Be cleansed, you who carry images,’ but, ‘Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord’ (Isaiah 52:11).”

This is from Book II, chapter 29.

And in chapter 30:

> “Images cannot rightly be compared with the books of divine Scripture, since the divine Scriptures were predestined by God and, throughout the ages, graciously granted for the benefit of human salvation. They have as their authors holy and venerable men, shining with the lamps of virtues and the insignia of miracles—or certainly the Lord himself. Images, however, arose from the vanity of pagan errors, and bring mortals no benefit of salvation and no privilege of any sacrament; they merely gratify the eyes, through which, as through certain messengers, they impress the memory of historical events upon the heart . . . . Hence it is understood that not paintings but Scriptures were granted for the instruction of our faith. Anyone who possesses knowledge of the divine Scriptures can easily understand how rash and removed from reason it is to say: ‘Just as we possess the books of divine Scripture for the memory and veneration of things, so we possess images.’”

After many praises of the sacred writings, he adds:

> “None of those things which we have touched upon, or of those similar things which we have omitted for the sake of brevity, can be found by you in images, O worshiper of images, O cultor of insensible things. Since they lack all these privileges of merit, you should be pitied rather than admired for desiring to compare them with the books of divine Scripture, in which so many good things are found. You who say that you preserve the purity of your faith in images, remember to stand before them submissively with incense; let us diligently seek the Lord’s commandments in the books of divine law. You illuminate paintings with lamps; let us frequent the divine Scriptures. You be a worshiper of painted colors; let us be worshipers of and receptive to hidden meanings. You delight in painted panels; let us be delighted by divine utterances. You insist upon representations of things in which there is neither sight, hearing, taste, smell, nor touch; let us insist upon the divine law, in which are found the blamelessness of the Lord, his testimony, his justice or commandments, his fear or judgments.”

### 6.

The same author is indignant that images should be placed by the Nicene fathers on an equal footing in honor with the relics and clothing of holy martyrs and confessors. Therefore he offered images no religious veneration whatsoever, since it is universally acknowledged that the honor paid to relics is far below *latria*:

> “Antiquity did not without reason allow the bodies of the saints to be venerated and honor to be shown to their relics . . . . Let them say where we are ever commanded to worship images. The saints are believed to live with Christ in the heavenly dwellings, and their bones are at some time to rise again. But images are believed never to have lived and never to rise again . . . . To offer to images—which are believed never to have lived or to rise again, but are said to be consumed either by fire or by decay—the adoration due to God alone is either sluggishness, if it is done in some careless manner, or madness, or rather unbelief, if it is stubbornly defended.
>
> “We therefore neither deny relics, with Vigilantius and his followers, nor worship images, with Simon and his accomplices. We offer due service to relics and to the bodies of the saints; we adorn basilicas, as we please, with images of the saints and even with gold or silver; but we devote the service of adoration or worship to God alone, to whom alone it is owed, with his assistance.”

This is from Book III, chapter 24.

He much less permits images to be compared with the cross, because the ancient enemy was defeated by the banner of the cross, not by images, and we are commanded to take up the cross, not images:

> “Images therefore are not to be compared with the cross, nor worshiped, nor cultivated; they are to be left to this world, together with the other things that belong to the world.”

This is from Book II, chapter 26.

### 7.

It is clear from Book III, chapter 16, that this author does not even admit relative veneration:

> “Let those who find it so characteristic to say that the honor of the image passes to the original form say whether they have read this anywhere or by what convincing testimonies they can prove it. For our Lord and Savior does not say, ‘As long as you did this for images,’ but, ‘As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me’ (Matthew 25:40). Nor does he say, ‘Whoever receives images,’ but, ‘Whoever receives you receives me’ (Matthew 10:40).”

And in Book IV, chapter 10, he speaks as follows about the deacon Epiphanius:

> “For he said that an image, by the significance of its name, could be referred to the honor of the original form—that is, to the veneration of the saint whose name is inscribed upon it. But that this could be done cannot be approved by any clear indications of reason.”

### 8.

Does not this author openly and in the harshest terms attack what the Nicene and Roman fathers formerly did—“arrange lamps before the images of the saints and burn incense”? Does he not reproach them for this as “a madness rationally to be mocked”? Does he not describe the rite of veneration which he condemns in such a way that it appears to be the very same as that practiced by his opponents?

For, speaking of images of two beautiful women, one of whom is Mary and the other Venus, he says:

> “This one, which bears the inscription ‘Mother of God,’ is raised up, honored, and kissed.”

No one, says Dallaeus, can fail to see that these are the very things done today.

### 9.

The same point is involved in what he writes in Book IV, chapter 21. In that passage he reports that the Blessed Virgin was customarily painted riding on a donkey, carrying the child in her arms and descending into Egypt with Joseph preceding her. From this painting he argues that, if the image of the Virgin is to be worshiped, the image of the animal must likewise be worshiped, since no separation between them can be made in worship:

> “Either the worship of both must be rejected, or both must be worshiped.”

Therefore, since the latter is utterly absurd, he concludes that the former must be posited and acknowledged. Who does not understand that by this reasoning every worship of images—whether absolute or relative, whether *latria* or *dulia*—is wholly and completely overthrown, since none of these forms of worship, however slight, can be appropriate to the image of an animal?

> “Since, then, one cannot be separated from the other without contradiction, and since neither ought to be worshiped lest the image of an animal perhaps be worshiped, it remains that both should be deprived of the honor of worship. They should occupy places in basilicas or in whatever locations merely as ornaments, and provide those who look upon them with a memory of historical events” [Col. 0975C].

10. Moreover, he accuses the Nicene Fathers of imprudence and presumption in Book III, chapter 11, because they pronounced an anathema against the churches of the entire world before they had inquired, by sending legations from the churches of the individual provinces and by written letters, “whether images ought to be adored or not adored.” He calls their anathema “utterly insane” and says, “It is more tolerable to be cursed by these men than, together with them, to adore senseless things contrary to the ordinances of the divine Scriptures.” For these and other reasons, he says that this Nicene synod was so far, and beyond anything that can be said, removed from the one formerly held in the same city against the perfidy of Arius:

“While that synod,” he says, “recalls the Catholic Church from error, this one, on the contrary, leads it into error; while that one drives it away from the most perilous shipwreck of Arius, this one forces and propels it into the shipwreck of images to be adored; while that one teaches fully that the Son is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, this one judges that senseless things are to be adored, and so forth. In that synod, let them execrate the blasphemies of those who neither believe nor confess that the Son is of one essence with the Father; in this one, let them abominate the purity of those who, rejecting the adoration of paintings, profess with steadfast mind and devoted heart that they will serve God alone.”

From these statements Dallaeus concludes, in chapter 3, that there was then among Christians a novel opinion—the opinion that we now defend concerning the veneration of images—and that Catholics at that time opposed it, just as Protestants oppose it today: namely, Charlemagne and the entire clergy of the German and Gallican Churches.

## § II.—The response of those who have claimed that the Carolingian Books were the work of some heretic is refuted, and their author is shown to have been Charlemagne.

Surius, Bellarmine, and several others have thought that the Carolingian Books were wrongly attributed to the most religious emperor, and that they were written by some unknown heretic and presented to his Majesty, who sent them to Hadrian, the Roman pontiff, through Angilbert, the abbot, so that he might refute them. But the matter is not so. These books were composed and published either by Charlemagne himself or, at his command, by another in his royal name.

This is proved first from the preface to the entire work:

“Since,” he says, “by the Lord’s gift we have undertaken the government of the kingdom in the bosom of the Church, it is necessary that, with Christ’s help, we strive with all our effort for its defense and its exaltation.”

Soon afterward:

“We undertook this work,” he says, “together with the bishops who are priests, set over the Catholic flocks in the kingdom granted to us by God—not with the arrogance of pride, but with zeal for God and devotion to the truth.”

And in Book I, chapter 6, he calls Pippin “his father, the king of venerable memory”; he says that through his and his own care it came about that the Gallican and other Churches of the West agreed with the Roman Church in the order of psalmody.

Second, this is proved from the synodal letter of the council of Paris held under Louis the Pious on the same matter and addressed to the emperors Louis and Lothair:

“Moreover, when your father of holy memory had caused that same synod to be read aloud before himself and his attendants, and had properly criticized it in many places, and had marked beforehand certain chapters that were open to criticism, and had sent them through the abbot Angilbert to that same Pope Hadrian, so that they might be corrected by his judgment and authority, he himself, once again favoring those who at his prompting had inserted such superstitious and incongruous testimonies into the aforesaid work, attempted to answer, chapter by chapter, in their defense whatever he wished—but not what was appropriate.”

Third, this is proved from the response sent by Hadrian I to Charlemagne. After first testifying with how much affection he had received Abbot Angilbert, he adds:

“Among other things, he delivered to us a capitulary against the synod held at Nicaea for the erection of sacred images.”

Then he proceeds to answer each chapter. These, however, are the very chapters of the Carolingian work, with only their order changed.

Fourth, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in his book Against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 20, speaking of the seventh synod repudiated by the council of Frankfurt, adds:

“Concerning whose destruction, a not inconsiderable volume—which, as a young man, I read in the palace—was sent to Rome by certain bishops by that same emperor [namely, Charlemagne]. In the fourth book of that volume the following was written concerning the term ‘universal.’”

In this passage Hincmar describes chapter 28 of the fourth book, plainly identical with the chapter found in the Carolingian Books edited by Tilius.

Fifth, the Vatican and Tilian manuscript copies bear the name of Charles. Tilius himself, bishop of Meaux, reports that the latter bore this title:

“In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, here begins the work of the most illustrious, excellent, and distinguished man Charles, by the will of God king of the Franks, ruling, with the Lord’s assistance, Gaul, Germany, Italy, and the neighboring provinces, against the synod held in the regions of Greece, foolishly or arrogantly, for the adoration of images.”

Accordingly, Charlemagne is the author of this work; or at least, at his command, it was published by another in his person and under his name.

Nevertheless, I do not think that the four Carolingian Books of the work were sent by Charlemagne to Pope Hadrian through Angilbert, although Hincmarus seems to assert this, but only the headings or titles of the chapters.

First, the pontiff does not answer either the arguments or the reproaches contained throughout the work—although he certainly would have answered them if he had read it. Instead, he appends to each title a simple defense of the point that had been criticized and rejected.

Second, he does not answer the individual chapter headings, nor does he follow the order in which they are presented in the four books.

Third, in chapter 25 of his Apology, Hadrian refers to the final chapter of the capitulary sent to him, in which the prelates of Frankfurt speak as follows:

“So that the apostolic lord, our Father, and the entire Roman Church together may know that, according to what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory which he sent to Serenus, bishop of Marseille, we permit images of the saints to be made by anyone who wishes to form them,” and so forth.

This final chapter does not exist in the Carolingian Books. It is therefore not an empty conjecture that the Carolingian Books were written several years before the synod of Frankfurt, at Charlemagne’s command, or even with his active cooperation—namely, three years after the Second Council of Nicaea, around the year 790, as the preface to the Carolingian work itself testifies, after the acts of the seventh synod had been translated from Greek into Latin and brought into Gaul.

When the Fathers of the council of Frankfurt found those acts displeasing and decided to inform Pope Hadrian of the matter, excerpts of the chapter headings were taken from the Carolingian Books—not in the order in which they stood in the book, but in whatever order seemed suitable to the compiler. For this reason Hadrian calls it a “capitulary” at the beginning of his Apology.

In any event, it is certain that the Carolingian Books present the view of the Gallican and German Churches concerning images at that time, since they teach the same things as the synod of Frankfurt, Jonas of Orléans, Agobard, Walafrid Strabo, and the assembly held at Paris under Louis the Pious.

Now we must hear and refute Bellarmine’s arguments, by which he thought he had proved that those books were written not by Charlemagne but by some heretic.

His first argument is that Hadrian’s Apology to Charlemagne exists, in which they are refuted. From this, he says, it can be understood that they were composed by some heretic and sent by Charlemagne to the pontiff so that he might answer them.

**Response.** This argument has no force. The most prudent pontiff concealed the name of the author of these books, which he did not fail to know, and he did not wish to attribute them to Charlemagne in the parts that were open to criticism, lest he offend his mind. But he attributed them to him in the parts worthy of praise, in order to win his favor.

Although, as we have just said, the entire Carolingian work was not sent to Pope Hadrian, but only excerpts consisting of chapter headings, Hadrian, with his customary prudence, attributes the final one to Charlemagne because that one alone was worthy of approval, while he conceals the fact that the others were his:

“This sacred and venerable chapter,” he says, “differs greatly from all the chapters mentioned above. Therefore we recognized it as belonging to your God-preserved and orthodox royal Excellence, in that it fully confesses the right faith and follows the meaning of the most holy Gregory.”

Bellarmine’s second argument is this: It is clear from the historians that Gregory II, Hadrian I, and Leo III excommunicated the Greek emperors and transferred the empire to the Frankish kings because the Greek emperors were opponents of images. Therefore it is not believable that Charlemagne suffered from the same heresy and wrote in defense of the Greeks’ error against the Roman pontiff.

**Response.** The Carolingian Books attack and condemn the opponents of images in six hundred places; so far are they from defending the view of the opponents of images. It does not follow, therefore, that Charlemagne was not their author because he was not infected with that heresy. We shall speak elsewhere of the transfer of the empire.

Bellarmine’s third argument is this: Claudius of Turin, a patron of opposition to images, did not dare even to mutter during the time of Charlemagne, as Jonas, bishop of Orléans, testifies. Therefore it is the height of shamelessness to attribute books against images to Charlemagne.

**Response.** Bellarmine always assumes what is false. The Carolingian Books do not favor the opponents of images, since they do not permit images to be destroyed; indeed, they do not entirely reject their honorific adoration, but only the worship of latria, which they thought had been decreed for them by the seventh synod.

Thus, just as it would be wrongly inferred that the seventh synod was not condemned by the three hundred Fathers of the council of Frankfurt, with Charlemagne also taking part, because Charlemagne was a most religious prince and not an opponent of images, so it is wrongly inferred that the Carolingian Books were not written by his authority because he was not an opponent of images. The council of Frankfurt and the Carolingian work hold the same opinion.

Bellarmine’s fourth argument is this: At the council of Gentilly, under Pippin, the father of Charlemagne, the error of the Greeks concerning sacred images was refuted in the presence of ambassadors of the Greek emperor; and Charlemagne sent twelve prelates of the Gallican Church to the Roman council held under Stephen for the restoration of images. Therefore Charlemagne is unjustly transformed into an iconoclast.

**Response.** We grant the whole point; but it does not follow from this that Charlemagne was not the author of the Carolingian Books. These books express and defend the opinion of the Gallican prelates: images are to be preserved in churches for ornament and for the remembrance of historical events, but not to be adored. Therefore Charlemagne is not transformed into an opponent of images, even if he is said to be their author.

Bellarmine’s fifth argument is this: Charles and Hadrian were always extremely close, and after Hadrian’s death Charles placed an epitaph over him. It can scarcely be believed, therefore, that he wrote against that praised pontiff in such an acrimonious style and that he belonged to another faith and religion.

**Response.** Even if they were extremely close, does it follow that the emperor did not disagree with the pontiff concerning the worship of images? Certainly Louis the Pious was extremely close to Eugenius II, yet he disagreed with him on this very question, as is clear from the acts of the council of Paris.

Thus, just as Louis the Pious instructed the Gallican bishops Jeremiah and Jonas to incline Eugenius’ mind gently toward what they desired and to treat him with reverence and moderation, so it is likely that Charlemagne instructed Abbot Angilbert to deal with Hadrian in a reverent, not insolent, spirit and to share with him excerpts from the Carolingian Books directed against the Second Nicene Council. Hadrian received, read, and refuted them. Charlemagne therefore diminished nothing of his reverence and friendship toward the supreme pontiff.

Nor does it follow that Charlemagne and the Gallican prelates belonged to a faith and religion different from Hadrian’s because they maintained that images should be retained only for remembrance and instruction, not adored. For the truth had not yet been fully clarified and plainly perceived—to use the words of Saint Augustine in excusing Saint Cyprian and the African bishops, who held a different view from Pope Stephen I and the rest of the Church concerning the baptism of heretics—nor did they yet acknowledge a plenary council of the entire Church on this matter.

When they attacked the seventh synod, they did not think that they were dealing with an ecumenical council, but only with a national council of the Greeks. Thus the author of the Carolingian Books repeatedly declares, and complains that it arrogated to itself the name of a universal or seventh synod. He denies that it could be called ecumenical when only the Greeks had assembled for it, and when the Churches of the other provinces had neither been summoned nor consulted, according to ecclesiastical custom, through encyclical letters.

Bellarmine’s sixth argument is this: It is certain that Charlemagne was skilled in Greek and Latin, prudent, and gifted; but these books appear to be the work of a barbarous, uneducated, and frivolous man.

**Response.** Even if these books are represented as rough and unpolished, and may appear so when compared with more elegant writings, they do not appear so when compared with other compositions of the same age. They testify to the intelligence, learning, and eloquence of their author—an abundance equal to that which shone forth in the most distinguished men of that century.

But let us examine the grounds on which Cardinal Bellarmine bases his judgment. “That writer,” he says, “claims that Constantinople is a well-known city in Bithynia, although no one is unaware that it is in Thrace; and he asserts that a council for the worship of images was held in that city, although no one who has read anything is unaware that it was held at Nicaea. He also attributes certain statements concerning the Eucharist to the Nicene Fathers, although they belonged not to them but to their adversaries.”

But such lapses of a mind insufficiently attentive, or slips of memory, often occur even in highly cultivated and learned intellects. Without ignorance or stupidity, therefore, Charlemagne could have failed to know that Constantinople was a city of Thrace, not Bithynia. He could also have asserted, without the stain of disgraceful ignorance, that a council for the worship of images had been held at Constantinople, because it had first been convened at Constantinople and was later transferred to Nicaea on account of the disturbances caused by the opponents of images.

Finally, his attribution to the Nicene Fathers of statements by the iconoclasts concerning the Eucharist arose from a hasty reading of the acts of Nicaea. Since the acts of the Constantinopolitan pseudo-synod against images had been mixed together with those of the Nicene Council, it was easy for an author who read them rapidly—or perhaps merely excerpts collected by someone insufficiently careful—to suppose inadvertently that the words of the opponents of images truly belonged to the Nicene Fathers.

Bellarmine presses the point that the author of the Carolingian Books, in order to bring the Nicene Fathers into hatred, maliciously imposed upon them two notable lies concerning them. The first was that they had issued a synodal decree without the consent of the Roman pontiff; the second, that they had defined images to be adored with the worship of latria.

**I answer:** The author of the Carolingian work nowhere asserts that the synod held at Nicaea for the worship of images issued its definition without the authority of the Roman pontiff. On the contrary, he explicitly mentions the letters written by Constantine and Irene to Hadrian I concerning the convocation of the synod; he records Hadrian’s association with Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, in asserting and promoting the adoration of images; and he rebukes the presbyter John for having flatteringly praised the conspiracy of Hadrian and Tarasius in the matter of images (Book II, chapter 4), by twisting the meaning of the Davidic verse:

“Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Psalm 83:11).

Hincmarus did indeed write, in his book Against Hincmarus his Nephew, chapter 20, “that the Nicene synod defined the matter of images without the authority of the apostolic see.” But Hincmarus’ error does not pertain to Charlemagne.

Nor did the author of the Carolingian work impose upon the Nicene Council the claim that it had defined images to be adored with the worship of latria. Rather, failing to grasp its meaning, he thought that the matter stood thus, although the Nicene Fathers had expressly denied it. He thought, I say, that the synod had employed the distinction between honorific adoration and the adoration of latria as a deception, and had asserted under cover of ambiguity an error that Bishop Constantine seemed to have stated without verbal circumlocution:

“They seem,” he says, “to be introducing a concealed error to the people. For they say: ‘We do not adore images as God, nor do we offer them the worship of divine service; but while we look at and adore them, we fix the sharpness of our mind upon that place where we know those whose images they are to be present.’”

This is found in Book III, chapter 17.

## § III.—The objections drawn from the Carolingian Books are answered.

Having therefore set aside Cardinal Bellarmine’s response, and also the responses of others who lightly admit that the author of the Carolingian Books—and the entire Gallican Church at that time—opposed the veneration of images, I answer that the Carolingian Books withdraw from images only the worship of latria in itself, which is due to God alone.

The Gallican prelates and Charlemagne thought that this worship had been sanctioned for images by the Nicene Council. For the worship by which images would be honored because of the holiness residing in them, and by which Christians would place their hope in them and serve them, is the worship of latria—the worship forbidden by this command of the divine law:

“You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13).

The author of the Carolingian Books contends that only this worship is illicitly offered to images, and he thought that the Nicene Council had assigned it to them. He had been persuaded of this partly by the ambiguous term “adoration,” which that synod used, and partly by the statement of Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, as it was read in the Latin version of the acts of that synod, in these words:

“I accept and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images according to the service of adoration which I offer to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity; and those who do not think and glorify in this way I separate from the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, subject them to anathema, and consign them to the party of those who have denied the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.”

Moreover, our Gauls, and especially the emperor Charlemagne himself, were inclined to believe that Greek frivolity had fallen into the error of paying the highest adoration to images. Charlemagne was offended with Constantine, the Greek emperor, because, having rejected Charlemagne’s sister, to whom he had been betrothed, he had married Maria the Armenian. Hence there arose hostility and jealousy between the princes and between the two peoples.

Political interests therefore drew Charlemagne and the Gallican and German prelates into opposition to the synod held by the Greeks at Nicaea—for they did not regard it as ecumenical. They directed their pen against it and, being superior to the Greeks in intellectual sharpness and learning, argued against it with hostile intent. They seized upon the ambiguous term “adoration” used by the Greeks and upon the statement of Bishop Constantine as an occasion for dispute, and they mocked many of the weak proofs advanced by that synod.

They especially held up Constantine and Irene to ridicule because they called their writings “imperial letters”; because they praised themselves in their letter to Pope Hadrian with these words: “God chose us, who seek his glory in truth”; because, in a pagan manner, they had written concerning God: “We beseech your Paternity, and above all God beseeches you, who wishes no one to perish”; and because they had written incongruously and arrogantly: “Through him who reigns together with us, God.”

They laugh at the Nicene Council because it had a woman as its instructor and teacher—namely, Irene.

Against Tarasius, the patriarch, they pour out many accusations. They reproach him for the irregularity of his ordination, because he had been elevated from the lay state to the see of Constantinople; and because he did not profess the orthodox faith concerning the Holy Spirit, saying that the Spirit proceeded not from the Father and the Son but from the Father through the Son, and, with a new and absurd expression, that he was “of the same tribal origin as the Father and the Son.”

They attack more fiercely the testimony of Bishop Constantine, and then another very similar testimony of Euthymius of Sardis.

They reject many apocryphal writings whose authority the Greeks used at the Nicene Council. They criticize several expressions of the bishops that were somewhat harsh. Whatever seemed worthy of criticism—whether because of an unsuitable argument, ambiguity and uncertainty of wording, novelty of speech, or barbarism—they leave nothing untouched.

They also heap insults upon the Greeks and their synod. In a word, the entire Carolingian work breathes its author’s hostility and envy toward the Greeks. It is therefore not surprising that, under the influence of a prejudiced mind, he himself thought that the Nicene Council had sanctioned supreme adoration, or the worship of latria, for images, and attacked it all the more vehemently on that account.

That the author of the Carolingian Books attacks only this particular adoration of images is shown in many passages.

First, from Book I, chapter 2:

“But in images fashioned by the skill of craftsmen,” he says, “which for the most part lead their spectators to admiration because of the memory of historical events, but always lead their worshipers into error—for it is no slight error when something other than the one who said, ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deuteronomy 6:13), is adored with religious worship.”

He rightly denies that absolute adoration, which is due to the object of religion, can be offered to anyone other than God; but he does not deny every kind of veneration. In the course of the work he acknowledges that this veneration is due to the cross, to the saints and their relics, to the Book of the Gospels, and to sacred vessels. He would not hesitate to call this “the worship of religion”—that is, worship commanded by religion—since he admits the reality signified by the term.

And below:

“Behold, several images are seen standing. . . . In them, insofar as it depends on them, both the likeness of the image and the superscription of the name are one and the same. For example, there is an image of Paul and the superscription: ‘Saint Paul.’ Those who labor under so great an error that, according to their own will, they call them both the truth, and holy, and true, rather than, according to the tradition of the venerable Fathers, images of the saints, must be asked which image is holier or truer when all are compared; which is to be believed the holiest or the truest; and, since reason will not permit them to call them equal because of differences in materials, sizes, or workmanship, and will restrain them from admitting some to be holier than others and some the holiest, they are compelled by reason, which searches out the truth, to confess that they ought to be called neither capable of truth nor holy.”

He thought that the Greeks called images “holy” and “true” because of some internal holiness, and it is this alone that he attacks. He does not object to their being called holy in reference to the saints. And if he does not wish them to be called holy even for this reason, he is merely quarreling over the name.

Second, the same point is gathered from chapter 18 of the same book:

“Now, since they believe that they will be saved by looking at images, just as the Israelite people were healed from the bites of serpents by looking at the serpent, if some bodily affliction should happen to them, let them run to the images and look at them; and when they have not been healed by looking at them, let them return to the Lord and believe that they will receive healing from him through the intercessions of the saints, since he is the author of all health and life.”

He falsely assumes that the Nicene Council taught that hope should be placed in images, that some divine power was present in them, and that benefits could be expected or requested from them. He therefore denies that images of the saints should receive only that adoration which is offered to the object of our hope and the author of all good things—namely, the worship of latria.

For the rest, he wishes health to be expected and requested from God through the intercessions of the saints. If this may be done in every place, and especially in churches adorned with images, why not also before images?

Third, the same point is gathered from chapter 24 of the same book:

“But neither is what is written, ‘All the rich among the people shall entreat your countenance’ (Psalm 44:13), to be understood of some manufactured face, especially since manufactured faces are not to be entreated because they cannot hear. Everything that is entreated is entreated so that it may hear; and everything that hears ought not to be irrational. Therefore everything that is entreated ought not to be irrational. But if it ought not to be entreated, much less ought it to be adored, since adoration is superior to entreaty. For if manufactured faces are to be entreated and adored, as they babble, then those faces must be believed capable of hearing those who entreat and of favoring those who adore them; and if they are believed capable of hearing those who entreat and favoring those who adore them, then they must be believed to possess a life capable of sensation. But they do not possess a life capable of sensation. Therefore they are not, as they babble, to be adored or entreated.”

Through an error of fact, he attributes to the Fathers of the seventh synod the view that they had thought and decreed that supplications should be made to images. He therefore denies that supreme adoration, or at least absolute religious worship such as we offer to the saints, should be offered to images of the saints—not the veneration that is offered to sacred things on account of something else. For the author of the Carolingian Books acknowledges the Lord’s cross and its representation, the Book of the Gospels, sacred vessels, the relics of the saints, and holy places as worthy of veneration; yet it does not follow from such veneration that supplication is made to them, because they cannot hear.

Fourth, the same point is gathered from chapter 7 of Book II:

“It is not surprising if those who are deceived in great matters are deceived in small ones. Nor is their error in this more worthy of wonder: that they boast that they are righteous because they adore images, while they declare us sinners because we refuse to adore them; although, for love of them, they try to violate the purity of the divine Scriptures and think that the chief advantage of their faith lies in them, and obstinately strive to anathematize those who, rejecting these or other vanities of this kind, serve God alone and adore him in worship.”

Through the ambiguous term “adoration” he brings the Nicene Fathers into hatred, and, I might say, writes as though they had divided with images the adoration and service due to God alone; as though they had placed the chief advantage of their faith in images; and as though they had thought that the principal part of Christian righteousness lay in the adoration of images.

Fifth, the same point is gathered from chapter 13 of the same book:

“Thus, as in other matters, the assertion of those who try to support their conspicuous error in the adoration of images by claiming that Silvester, prelate of the Roman Church, is said to have brought images of the apostles to the emperor Constantine will be frustrated here as well. He brought them to him, therefore, for viewing, not for adoration. He brought them not to compel him to adore, when he was drawing him away from the worship of idols and urging him to hasten toward the adoration of God alone, but so that the emperor might recognize in the painted figures the faces of those whom he had seen in dreams. He brought them not to teach one fleeing from the worship of idols to submit to the adoration of images, and, after he had been freed from the hostile sword, to destroy him with the rigor of an internal sword, but so that through familiar things he might raise his mind to things unknown.”

Here again he denies to images only that adoration which is due to God alone and which the pagans transferred to statues and idols. But he admits that Saint Silvester could have instructed Constantine to show honor of a lower degree—or honorific adoration—to images, although this example ought not to be made into a general rule even if he had issued such an instruction. For a newly converted prince was to be fed with milk, whereas those established in the faith were to be given more solid food, according to the Apostle’s rule.

“Therefore,” he says, “even if he had ordered him to adore them—although he did not order him to do so—perhaps he would have ordered it for this reason: to summon one who was a worshiper of visible things through visible things to invisible things, not to draw us back from invisible things to visible things. Nor would it therefore be necessary for us, who have received strength to partake of solid food, to return, like infants, to the milk-food of nursing children, if milk, without deceit, were given to one who, because of the tender state of his faith, could not yet be given solid food, and if he were permitted to desire that milk in which he might grow.”

But if the author of the Carolingian Books had thought that honorific adoration of images, or their relative veneration on account of reverence and love for the saints, was illicit and forbidden by divine law, he would not have said that Silvester had offered Constantine milk-food if he had placed before him images of Saints Peter and Paul to be adored. Rather, he would have said that he had offered him deadly food and administered poison.

Sixth, the same point is gathered from chapter 21 of the same book:

“Therefore they must beware, and fear by every means, lest, while they strive to introduce the worship and adoration of images into the Christian religion, they appear to frustrate the unique worship and adoration of the one God. . . . Accordingly, if the citadel or defense of the Christian religion, and its glorious emblem, is the worship and adoration of the one God—and indeed it is—then to offer this to images or to any other things is contrary to the Christian religion. And if, as they rave, it is contrary to the Christian religion not to adore or worship them, then to adore or worship God alone, and to confess that the citadel of his worship and adoration is unique, will be contrary to the Christian religion. Therefore God alone is to be worshiped, God alone adored, and God alone glorified.”

He contends that it is contrary to the Christian religion to offer images or other things the adoration that is the glorious emblem of the one God, but not every kind of religious veneration. For in the same passage he asserts that such veneration is to be offered to the saints reigning with Christ:

“Veneration,” he says, “is also to be offered to his saints, who, having conquered the devil, reign with him, whether because they fought bravely so that the Church’s unbroken condition might reach us, or because they are known to assist that same Church through their continual entreaties and intercessions.”

He denies that images should receive a veneration equal to that offered to the saints themselves. He excludes every absolute worship and adoration of images, by which they would be honored for their own sake, but not relative veneration.

Nor do these words signify anything else:

“As for images, once every worship and adoration of them has been excluded, whether they are in basilicas for the remembrance of historical events and for ornament, or whether they are not, they can bring no prejudice against the Catholic faith.”

If, however, someone should more stubbornly contend that this author, and the Gallican and German prelates, also denied relative veneration to images of the saints, we shall say that they did not attack that veneration as illicit and inherently forbidden by divine law, but as dangerous because of the abuse of the unlearned.

This is plainly signified by these words:

“They must beware and fear by every means lest, while they strive to introduce the worship and adoration of images into the Christian religion, they appear to frustrate the unique worship and adoration of the one God.”

Seventh, the same point is gathered from chapter 16 of Book III:

“For while we reject nothing in images except adoration—for we permit images of the saints to be kept in basilicas, not for adoration, but for the remembrance of historical events and for the beauty of the walls—while they, on the other hand, place nearly all the hope of their belief in images, it follows that we venerate the saints in their bodies, or rather in the relics of their bodies, and even in their garments, according to the tradition of the ancient Fathers; whereas they, adoring walls and panels, think that they possess in this a great advantage of faith, because they are subject to the works of painters.”

He attacks only that adoration of images by which nearly all the hope of belief is placed in them. This is the worship of latria—or at least veneration offered to them for their own sake. Since the unlearned are exposed to the danger of this when images are presented to them for adoration, he thinks that all worship should be removed from them—not because it is inherently forbidden and illicit, for he acknowledges that the learned can harmlessly venerate them and honor them with relative worship, but because such a practice may provide an occasion of error to the less educated and unlearned, who are not sufficiently subtle to distinguish relative worship from absolute worship.

“For even if,” he says, “this practice of those who adore images can be avoided by the learned—those, namely, who venerate not what the images are but what they signify—it nevertheless produces scandal among the unlearned, who venerate and adore nothing in them beyond what they see.”

Eighth, this is gathered from chapter seventeen, where [Col. 0983D] he examines the opinion of Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus. “How rashly,” he says, “and, so to speak, foolishly Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, with the others agreeing, declared that he would honorably receive and embrace the images, and chattered that he would render them the service of adoration owed to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity, need not be extensively debated by us. For it is plainly evident to all who either read or hear this that he was plunged into the depths of no small error: for he admits that he renders to creatures the service owed to God the Creator alone, and, while wishing to favor paintings, he resists all the sacred Scriptures. Who, then, in his right mind has ever either uttered or agreed with anyone uttering such an absurdity—that the variety of paintings should be held in as great honor as the holy, life-giving, and all-creating Trinity? And that the same service should be offered to a painting as is offered to the Lord of all creation? . . . [lacuna] Let the bishop stand in the church [Col. 0984A] and read: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’; and then, as soon as he has taken his seat in the assembly, let him say: ‘I receive and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images, and I offer them the service of adoration owed to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity.’ Thus let him show himself unstable in divine words: professing one thing with his mouth, believing another in his heart, reading one thing in the divine pages, holding another in the cavern of his breast, resisting the divine words, and preferring his own trifles to the Lord’s commands.”
