That opinion of Constantine gave occasion for attributing to him the error which it expresses in words—or rather, for casting it back upon the whole synod, which had not corrected him—because the less accurate version of the acts of the Seventh Synod had made it harsher. Pope Hadrian, in his apologetic letter to Charlemagne in defense of the veneration of images, chapter 9, interprets Constantine’s opinion in a favorable sense, in these words: “Returning from their wicked heresy, they strove with all their strength [Col. 0984B] to satisfy the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church in their confession; and therefore they confessed that they believed such adoration to be due to the sacred images as had been established, among other matters, in the synod’s definition.” In this passage he brings forward the definition of the Second Council of Nicaea.

Hadrian indicates that these bishops, who were renouncing the heresy of the image-breakers, expressed in vigorous and emphatic language the worship which they believed should be given to images, in order to remove every suspicion from the minds of their hearers; yet their opinion was to be interpreted according to the definition of the synod in which they were participating. Nor, however harsh it may be, ought Constantine’s episcopal opinion to be held against the council, whose clear and undeniable judgment below is that the honor paid to images is inferior to latria.

The author of the Carolingian Books, however, was not equally fair toward the Second Council of Nicaea. Writing from a preconceived opinion, he attributed to the council the error which Constantine seemed to have expressed, and said that the synod’s definition had been contrived to produce a disguise [Col. 0984C] and conceal the error which the less crafty Constantine had revealed. Charlemagne and the Gallican and German bishops therefore believed that the entire Greek synod had understood images to be worshiped with the same worship offered to the most holy Trinity; that Bishop Constantine had professed this before the assembled synod without being reproved; and that the definition imposed the same error upon the common people, merely cloaked in distinctions suitable for disguising it.

Hence, after the words quoted above, Charlemagne adds concerning Constantine’s opinion: “For since he is recognized as harming himself and his associates by his perverse profession, he is, on the contrary, recognized as benefiting us, who wish to resist their trifles, since he exposes the disastrous error which they seem to be imposing upon the common people under a disguise. For they say: ‘We do not worship images as God, nor do we offer them the worship of divine service; but while we look upon and worship them, we fix the sharpness of our mind upon the place where we know those [Col. 0984D] whom the images represent to be.’ But this man, exposing their error and displaying his own thought without any obscurity, admits that he offers them the same service and the same adoration as he offers to the holy Trinity. Thus he has openly brought forth the absurdity which they secretly resist within themselves. No one can fail to perceive their cowardice, since the meaning of this profession lays it bare.”

The adoration of images which the author of the Carolingian Books attacks, therefore, is the adoration of latria which he believed the Greek synod had sanctioned.

Ninth, the same point is gathered from chapter eighteen of the same book. “Since these people,” he says, “place almost all their hope of assistance in images, they disagree in no small measure with the holy and universal Church, which fixes its hope of assistance not in the pigments of paintings, nor in the works made by craftsmen, but in God, the creator of all.” He attacks that worship of images which implies that almost all hope is placed in the pigments of paintings [Col. 0985A]. But from religious veneration, which is offered to sacred objects, it cannot be concluded, according to this author’s opinion, that we place all our hope in them—an author who asserts such veneration also for the relics of the saints, the figure of the Lord’s cross, the book of the Gospels, and sacred vessels. He therefore does not attack the honorific worship, or veneration, of images.

He does indeed deny that images are to be equated with the Lord’s cross, the sacred books, consecrated vessels, the relics of the saints, and still less with the saints themselves, thereby weakening the comparisons made by the Seventh Synod. But within the order of religious worship, below the worship of latria, there are various degrees. Some things are honored for their own sake and with absolute honor, as it is called—that is, according to the excellence proper to them—as are angels and holy human beings. Others are honored on account of something else, toward which they have an ordered relation: the relics of the saints, the Lord’s cross and its representations, the book of Sacred Scripture, sacred vessels, churches, and images. Within this category of relative worship there are also several degrees.

Therefore, although images of the saints are not to be honored as greatly as the Lord’s cross and its representations, or sacred vessels, or the book of the Gospels, or the relics of the saints—and although the author of the Carolingian Books proves this—it does not follow that he abolishes all veneration of them [Col. 0985B].

Tenth, the same point is gathered from chapter eighteen of book four. “From this example,” he says, “we clearly see the use of images becoming established, so that things which had previously been assembled for the adornment of basilicas and the commemoration of past events, as the wicked practice gradually grew, are now so exalted by many Catholics that they are worshiped, and lamps, incense, firstfruits, or certain small gifts are offered to them. What is worse—and as we read has occurred in the regions of Greece—bishops, who ought to have proclaimed that God alone is to be worshiped, that he alone is to be honored, and that he alone is to be served, themselves admit that they will serve them, and honor and worship them; and they wish to judge and anathematize as heretics those who despise them, worship God alone, and are true worshipers, simply because they despise them [Col. 0985C].

“Among the pagans, the most wicked practice of worshiping and honoring images—or rather, demons—has grown up in one and almost the same manner; and among Catholics—something we pursue not without a certain sorrow of heart—the most foolish custom of worshiping images is increasing. Things created for one purpose appear to be used for another. We do not, indeed, call the images placed in basilicas idols; but, lest they be called idols, we refuse to worship and honor them or to offer them service, since very often not the object but the reason for using the object is judged criminal: many things which can be used well are turned into wrongdoing when used badly. Thus one and the same thing is not a cause of guilt for those who use it well, but is a cause of danger for those who use it badly.

“Careful precautions must therefore be taken, and everything must be managed with the greatest diligence, lest, while some of our people try to exalt certain things beyond what order requires, the ashes of that most ancient and worm-eaten error, revived, should grow strong in them, and lest they lose within the walls of the city the victory they gained in the field” [Col. 0985D].

Charlemagne and the Gallican and German bishops therefore condemn not so much the worship of images as their fear of superstition arising from that worship. They seem to prohibit the use of honorific worship of images lest abuse arise, while the Church was being torn apart by various controversies. They admit that some people can make good use of images, but that very many abuse them; consequently, they hold that people should abstain from such worship, since the occasion of guilt must be cut away.

Eleventh, the same point is gathered from chapter twenty-six. “From this,” he says, “it is clear that they are largely in error when they assert that the images are holy and decree that they should be set up in polluted places. Their judgment becomes evident in this respect: they decide that the images should be placed on roads or in the streets of cities and villages, thereby implying that these places lack holiness, as indeed they do; for if they believed the images to be holy, they would judge that they ought to be placed in holy places” [Col. 0986A].

He plays upon an ambiguity, as though the Greeks attributed intrinsic holiness to images.

Twelfth, this is confirmed by chapter twenty-seven. “From this,” he says, “it is surely gathered that those who place almost all the firmness of their faith in images, and are not ashamed to count their worship among the instruments of good works, and who worship images sometimes beautiful and sometimes ugly, are in some way deceived. For if any image has as much more holiness and virtue as it is more beautiful, it is necessary that the uglier image should have less holiness and virtue. And if the uglier image has less, it is necessary that any extremely ugly image should have either none or very little. And if the more beautiful image is worshiped more attentively because, on account of its beauty, it has more virtue, then its holiness no longer comes from some religious cause, but from the work of the craftsman.”

And below: “They are truly deceived, and deservedly deceived, who, although God the Creator of all has judged that he alone is to be worshiped, strive to worship certain things devoid of sensation; and while they think that by worshiping images they are offering some veneration to the saints, they grant some share to the worship due to God alone. Since, therefore, God alone is to be worshiped, while martyrs and all the saints are rather to be venerated than worshiped—and we have already spoken of this in the present work, and it must be strengthened by the teaching of the distinguished doctor Jerome—when Jerome was writing against a certain heretic, Vigilantius, who said that the relics of the martyrs should in no way be venerated, he said among other things: ‘Who has ever worshiped martyrs, you madman?’ If, then, according to his opinion, martyrs are not worshiped, much less are their images to be worshiped by the faithful” [Col. 0986B].

The Gallican bishops and Charlemagne were therefore offended only by the word “worship”; they did not attack the religious veneration offered to images, although they wished it to be inferior to that offered to martyrs and their relics, indeed even to that offered to vessels sanctified by priestly consecration [Col. 0986C]. They rejected the manner of speaking more than the matter itself. Hence they did not permit images to be called holy, but only images of saints. They disagreed with the Greeks in terminology, but not so much in substance; they did not grasp their intention. They condemned the superstition which, as they thought, was joined to the religious veneration of images, not veneration considered in itself; they condemned absolute worship, by which things are honored for their own sake, not relative worship, by which they are honored on account of something else.

Since they believed that the Council of Nicaea had decreed that images were to be honored for their own sake, and that the Greeks practiced worship of them precisely insofar as they were artificial objects, they repeatedly insist that insensible things ought not to be worshiped. From this false supposition arises the foolish inference which they draw from the veneration of an image representing the Blessed Virgin carried on an ass with the child Jesus: namely, that if the whole image is honored, the image of the beast must also be worshiped. This would indeed be true [Col. 0986D] if veneration were offered to the image for its own sake and because of its material and colors. But since it is honored because of its prototype—that is, because of the Blessed Virgin—and since its honor is referred to the Blessed Virgin, the whole image is not honored, much less the animal.

The words cited from chapter twenty-one of book four reveal the false supposition: “Since, therefore, in each of these cases an image of the holy Virgin holding the child and carried upon the back of an animal is worshiped, is not the image of the animal itself worshiped along with it? For there is no way in which, in worshiping the two images—the image of the Virgin and that of the animal—any separation can be made, especially since they are made of the same material and assembled by the same artistic skill. Either the worship of both must be rejected, or both must be worshiped.”

I answer, secondly, to make clearer what we have already said in this paragraph: the dispute [Col. 0987A] between the Gallican bishops and the Greeks concerned rather the manner of worship than the matter itself. That is, our Gallicans also admitted that images should be venerated, but not in the manner sanctioned by the Council of Nicaea and practiced by the Greeks—namely, with genuflections, bowing of the head, kisses, incense, and lamps lit before them.

Although they knew that these were arbitrary signs of honor, capable of being joined either to the worship of latria, or to religious worship of a lower order, or even to merely civil veneration; and although they knew that God is worshiped in spirit and truth, and that he is to be honored only with love above all things, in which consists the service owed to God alone, nevertheless they feared that, because these rites were used in the external worship of God, especially in the unbloody sacrifice, they might become an occasion of error for the unlearned if they were also practiced in the veneration of images.

What moved them most was that the Council of Nicaea seemed to have struck with anathema those who rejected this discipline. “If anyone,” it says, “does not greet the images in the name of the Lord and his saints, let him be anathema.” Or, according to the ancient version: “If anyone does not kiss these, as having been made in the name of the Lord and his saints, let him be anathema” [Col. 0987B].

They were similarly moved by the fact that the deacon Epiphanius, in session six, with the synod applauding, had called those half-corrupt who said: “It is sufficient for images to be kept only for commemoration, and not also for greeting.”

Although this discipline had been established with the greatest sanctity by the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea in order to suppress a new heresy, the Gallican and German bishops, who had not attended the synod and had not been consulted by letter on this matter, did not think that they could be bound by it. The anathema seemed rash to them, and one that ought not to extend to those whose Church had different customs and a different discipline.

For the Gauls and Germans, disturbed by the contrary definitions of two councils—on one side, the Council of Constantinople of the image-breakers, which had expelled images from the churches; on the other, the Council of Nicaea, which had decreed honorific worship for them and had either commanded or approved that this be signified by greetings, incense, and the lighting of candles [Col. 0987C]—chose a middle way until greater light dispersed the darkness. They determined among themselves that images were neither to be destroyed nor worshiped, or rather they retained the custom established from ancient times and confirmed by Saint Gregory the Great.

This is clear from chapter twenty-three of the second book of the Carolingian Books. “Images,” he says, “whose most insolent worship gave Constantine and his mother Irene, as well as Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, the occasion for convening the synod, are both prohibited from being worshiped and prohibited from being destroyed by the blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, and so forth.” After recounting Saint Gregory’s words in his letter to Serenus, he concludes: “Behold by what teaching and instruction of the venerable pontiff we have been imbued: we do not refuse to have images in churches, but we entirely renounce their worship. Whoever destroys or worships them must recognize in every way that he is acting contrary to Gregory’s institutions” [Col. 0988A].

And in chapter thirty-one, comparing the two Greek synods—the first held at Constantinople against images, the second held at Nicaea in favor of images—he says:

“The former judged that they should be torn down and despised, with perpetual rejection from the Church; the latter strive not only to retain them, but also to venerate them with submissive worship. The former consigned them to crackling fires; the latter honor them with fragrant incense. The former even avoided looking at them; the latter do not cease embracing them. The former dug out from the walls those which had long ago been established as church ornaments; the latter illuminate with offered lamps those recently made. The former strove utterly to abominate them; the latter decree that they must be kissed. The former anathematized those who possessed them; the latter, on the contrary, anathematize those who do not worship them.

“Since these two evils are opposed to each other and both depart from the right path, it remains for us, walking according to the Apostle along the royal road, to incline neither to the right nor to the left: neither to judge with the former that they must be entirely abolished, nor to decree with the latter that they must be worshiped; but, worshiping God alone and venerating his saints, to retain them in the church, if we wish, as ornaments and memorials of past events, according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers and of the Church” [Col. 0988B].

The Gallican bishops believed that images should be venerated, but only in the manner which had prevailed from ancient times and had been approved by Saint Gregory the Great when he wrote to Serenus, bishop of Marseille: namely, that they should be honorably placed in churches. They did not accept the extension of this honor, or the addition made by the Second Council of Nicaea and originating in Greece—namely, that their veneration should be signified by greetings, kisses, incense, and lamps—until many years later. This is not surprising, since they did not regard the Second Council of Nicaea as ecumenical, but considered it merely a national council of the Greeks, as we shall see below.

[Col. 0988C] Finally, it is incredible that the Gallican bishops, from whose assembly twelve men highly skilled in Sacred Scripture and the canons, sitting with Pope Stephen IV in the Roman synod, had sanctioned the veneration of sacred images, should have departed so far from tradition as to reject every form of their worship.

Concerning this synod, Hadrian I says in his defense of the Seventh Synod to Charlemagne, chapter 5: “Our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of holy memory, presiding with the bishops of the regions of France and Italy in the basilica of the Savior, confirming and embracing the venerable council of his predecessor, together with all the presiding bishops, adhering to the testimonies of the holy Fathers, decreed that sacred images should be worshiped and venerated.” Anastasius the Librarian likewise testifies to this in his Life of Stephen IV.

# The Capitular of the Blessed Charles the Great, King of the Franks and Lombards, Patrician of the Romans, Son and Defender of the Holy Church of God, Concerning Images, Against the Decree of Constantine VII, Emperor of Constantinople, and His Mother Irene, and Against the Second Council of Nicaea, the Pseudo-Seventh Ecumenical or Universal Council; Composed and Published at the Council of Frankfurt and Sent to Pope Hadrian in the Year of Our Lord 794

Edited from the library and scholarship of Jean Tilly, bishop of Meaux.

[Col. 0989]

## Preface. Jean Tilly, Bishop of Meaux, Sends Greetings to the Christian Reader

[Col. 0989A] I would not grant this book leave to appear publicly without a preface, lest it be assailed by slanders or charged with falsity and fabrication. For, through either bad faith or negligence on the part of certain historians, the accounts that everywhere in Greece, Italy, and even Gaul treat of convened councils, and of the conflict and disturbance over images, have come down to us in large part corrupted.

I shall therefore first give a brief account of how everything took place, as the matter actually stands. Then I shall produce testimonies and proofs to establish the certainty of this work, which proceeded from so great a monarch, the architect of the Western empire, now divided and torn into two crowns, the German and the Gallic. I cannot sufficiently marvel that this work did not appear for so long, and that it remained buried in such profound oblivion.

But now receive what I have discovered: how images, which are repeatedly presented in the monuments of the canonical Scripture as rejected and detestable to God, entered the Christian commonwealth and took root there because of the abundant harvest of superstitions and abuses [Col. 0989B].

Now, after Christ had overthrown by the shame of his cross the violence and rage of the stiff-necked and rebellious Jewish nation, and after its mission had been utterly ruined and was hastening toward destruction, while the apostles were vigorously and faithfully carrying out their charge, he erected a trophy among the Greeks—a people enslaved and subjected beyond belief to idolatry.

Yet superstition was not uprooted so completely that some small roots did not remain. Then, when true religion began to cool and grow cold, they found an opportunity gradually to revive their disgrace and infamy, just as a washed sow rolls back into the mire.

First, since most people today appear to be excessively and ruinously curious, collecting from everywhere and carefully preserving, as rare and remarkable possessions, likenesses even of pagan emperors and of other famous and renowned men; and since we also preserve, among the things we value greatly, not only the features and appearance of some absent or deceased person whose memory and love we cherish, but also some small gift of his [Col. 0989C]—on this pretext some people likewise carefully retained images of Christ himself, as they said, and of the Virgin Mother, the apostles, and the others who had worked diligently to advance evangelical teaching. They did so, however, without turning them into objects of holiness or religion [Col. 0990A].

Those who wished to appear especially religious began to treat these images as objects of veneration and to make others from them. Our nature inclines us to admire and fashion images for ourselves, and to delight in them. Consider indulgent and foolish children: do they not make little images, dolls, and things of that sort—products of foolish minds lacking judgment?

How easily could the image-makers impose upon the common people and the ignorant, erecting such objects thereafter in their houses, rooms, and private prayer cells! For the good pastors of the Church would not have tolerated this. But when images began to multiply beyond measure, because it was thought that this would set an example, their display was forbidden, and they were even banned from the private and intimate houses of individuals. At that time, moreover, by decree of the Council of Elvira, convened not far from the Pyrenean mountains, all paintings were removed and erased from all churches.

With what spirit, I ask, and with what attitude would those holy Fathers have tolerated those colossal statues and enormous images [Col. 0990B]?

Others, unjust in their own judgment, were not satisfied with these precautions. They insisted that the images should be preserved or privately retained, not in order to worship or venerate them, but merely as pledges and memorials. Hence they stirred up such a crowd and such factions that some, going beyond all measure, exalted them, while others judged them to be an example of grave danger.

At that time the worth of the cause depended upon the zeal and inclination of the rulers, in whose hands supreme power lay; and one side prevailed by force. They report that the cause was first conducted and decided in favor of images at the Sixth Council of Constantinople, under the rule of Constantine and his brother Justinian, and that they then laid the foundation and began to prevail.

Yet from the acts of that synod, which have been preserved for posterity, I can establish nothing [Col. 0990C]; and I am led to believe that the papal law wished the Seventh Council to be cited—the council against which Charlemagne declared war.

Nevertheless, the monuments of antiquity assure me that Constantinople was so inflamed and so violently shaken by conflict over the worship of images that even the emperors themselves, who were deeply concerned with ecclesiastical affairs, were involved in no slight struggle and ended their lives amid such turmoil.

Philippicus Bardanes shattered the images and removed them from the sacred buildings. By this deed he incurred the greatest unpopularity, was blinded, and was driven out by Anastasius, who defended the images. Later they were restored by Theodosius, an obscure and low-born man, who was compelled by the enemies of Anastasius [Col. 0991A] to assume the empire and was inaugurated as a monk. He himself was later harassed and persecuted by Leo and offered himself for initiation into sacred orders.

This Leo fought against images with a hostile and bloody spirit. Hence he acquired the name Εἰκονομάχος—“Iconoclast,” or “Image-Fighter”—and treated their defenders with extreme severity. He deposed the patriarch Germanus and substituted another, named Anastasius; and he ordered Pope Gregory by letter to remove the images from Rome. Gregory, however, refused to obey. After deliberating with a numerous council, as they report, he stirred up all Italy to defend the images and to prepare a rebellion against the emperor.

Constantine, the emperor’s son, hated these images no less than his father had, and acted accordingly. After him, Leo neither loved nor revered them more; instead, he removed the rich diadem donated and consecrated by Maurice.

This struggle and dispute over the use and worship of images was carried to Rome and defended there in one way or another. I say this because the papal histories specifically record that Gregory, Hadrian, and Stephen defended it by councils and decrees against the Greek emperors [Col. 0991B].

At last the report spread into France and gradually grew stronger. Therefore Pepin, having observed the disagreement between the Greeks and Romans, summoned his Church at Gentilly in the year of salvation 767—some prefer Samur [Salmuniacum]—so that the matter might be decided, together with other controversies concerning the Trinity.

Constantine, the son of the last Leo, together with his mother Irene, convened the Seventh Council at Nicaea in order to win the favor and support of the Greek clergy. At that council honor was decreed and restored to images, with the approval and support, as they say, of the empress’s own superstition.

When this opinion was spreading and growing stronger in Gaul, Charlemagne, following his father’s policy, wished to have the clergy investigate the matter. In accordance with the customs received from his ancestors, he ordered a great assembly of bishops from throughout his dominions to appear at Frankfurt in the year of salvation 794 [Col. 0991C]. There also had to be examined a certain heresy which Felix, bishop of Urgell, and Eliphandus, bishop of Toledo, were defending in their writings.

Moreover, the council assembled and approved at Nicaea seemed suspect and favorable to error because its author was a child, while its authority derived from female domination and superstition; and it appeared not to have met with sufficient legitimacy, since the orders of Greece were in conflict among themselves.

Furthermore, he saw that the Christian faith had been cultivated in Gaul with the greatest holiness and integrity from the time the name of Christ was first received, without being polluted by the shameful worship of idols that had long ago been proscribed, although their worshipers still professed the Christian name. Since many provinces had only recently been converted and looked upon neighboring peoples who still clung stubbornly to the worship of idols, he feared that they might relapse into the same abomination and therefore favored the convocation of this synod.

I would scarcely believe the amusing stories of the Roman ecclesiastical historians, who, if they did not preserve the faith intact in my judgment, nevertheless retained much of its ancient sanctity, if they wished to embrace images for so trivial a reason.

Nor will what they say—that the pontiffs of that age opposed those who removed images by councils and decrees—greatly conflict with the purpose of this little book. For it appears from it that the pope’s legates were present at the assembly of Frankfurt; that images were there condemned and rejected insofar as their worship was concerned; that the Council of Nicaea had been deliberately assembled and manipulated so that images would be presented for worship; and that this little book was composed under Charlemagne’s own name in opposition to that council.

The emperor did indeed permit images as ornaments for churches and as hangings for renewing the memory of past events, but he prohibited all reverence and worship of them. Yet because this work makes such extensive mention of Pope Hadrian, I cannot be persuaded that he or the Roman Church held a different opinion, whatever those good chroniclers may boast [Col. 0992A].

Nor has it ever happened that I read his book written against the Greek emperor. I do not think that he or the other most holy Fathers wished to preserve the images so zealously that they would allow them to be worshiped in any manner. There is a great and obvious difference between frequently practicing the use of images described above and assigning to them any religious force or persuasion.

There is no doubt that the disturbances stirred up by the Greek emperors to destroy and remove images seemed bitter to the Roman pontiffs, who regarded such an opinion as rash. Yet this does not prove that their efforts greatly pleased or suited the pontiffs, since the emperors had labored to elevate the images so as to offer them divine honor. Rather, the pontiffs would have tolerated seeing them shattered into a thousand fragments.

Moreover, the heresy of Felix, already recanted by its author at the court of Charlemagne and in the presence of Pope Hadrian, had nothing to do with this controversy. It was nevertheless exposed and declared guilty of impiety for the third time at the Council of Frankfurt [Col. 0992B].

The monk Anno, Ado, bishop of Vienne, the abbot of Ursperg, and Sigebert, in their brief chronicles, report what this meant. In addition to the certain and substantial testimony left to us in a certain little book written by Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, at the command of our emperor against that heresy, they show how he himself undertook the task of writing against that worship—or, if the book was not his, that it was composed with the same purpose and religious intention which the work published under his name displays.

He did this because, as stated above, councils of Greece were being manufactured under the authority of certain emperors and the Eastern empress; and our emperor rightly and divinely opposed them.

Paulinus’s book is a powerful demonstration of how far Felix’s teaching differed from the matter of images. It now makes plain the malicious and foolish ravings of those scribblers who persisted in confusing and corrupting everything by lumping all matters together. For these reasons [Col. 0992C] I was led to arrange for it to be appended to the end of this work.

I also had at hand three books by an unknown author, who nevertheless asserts that he was present at this council and who wrote on the same subject against Felix. He nowhere attacks images. But since our volume had grown beyond a reasonable size, I did not wish to have it printed at present, especially because it did not bear the author’s name.

The mere narrative of this history, compiled and excerpted for us with the utmost fidelity from the best and most ancient authorities, would, however great the obscurity brought here and imported by the ignorance of many centuries and the malice of certain persons, sufficiently and more than sufficiently establish the reliability of our work. I wish, however, to bring forward solid arguments and unimpeachable witnesses in support of it, which I shall touch upon briefly.

First, besides the ancient copy of this book found in a certain great and most venerable church, the oldest in all Gaul, [Col. 0992D] the same work is preserved in the library of the supreme pontiff, written in the elegant and ancient characters of the Lombards, as Augustine Steuchus, prefect of that library, testifies in his recently published work concerning the Donation of Constantine against Lorenzo Valla. He transcribed the sixth chapter of that copy word for word, since he could not have borrowed or invented it from elsewhere. Indeed, the diction and style themselves sufficiently vindicate the book’s antiquity and are not inconsistent with the manner of expression of writers of that age. Certainly no one will be able to accuse it of having been produced or written in our own century.

Moreover, in another museum, also extraordinarily ancient, I found a volume that gives me firm and complete assurance that matters stood as described. Among other things, which I shall pass over, it contains the acts of this council, treating separately the individual matters that were settled and defined. This is called the second section; the first is the Felician heresy. I shall suppress the remainder, which concerns administrative and political matters, [Col. 0993A] while I bring forward these two passages, postponing them to another occasion, together with other materials of the same kind and subject that fit them more suitably. I also received as a gift a volume of the same exemplar together with our own; from the two of them I extracted that little book of Paulinus.

But now to the beginning of the acts:

“1. By God’s favor, under apostolic authority and by order of our most pious lord, King Charles, in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, all the bishops and priests of the Frankish kingdom—or of France, Italy, Aquitaine, and Provence—assembled in a synodal council. Among them the most gentle ruler himself was present at the holy gathering. At the beginning of the proceedings there arose the matter of the impious and abominable heresy of Eliphandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, and of Felix of Urgel, together with their followers, who, holding erroneous opinions, asserted adoption in the Son of God. All the most holy Fathers mentioned above rejected this and unanimously opposed it; they also decreed that this heresy should be utterly eradicated from the holy Church.

“2. The question was brought forward concerning the new synod of the Greeks, which they held at Constantinople concerning the veneration of images, [Col. 0993B] in which it was written that those who did not render service or adoration to the images of the saints in the same manner as to the divine Trinity should be judged anathema. The most holy Fathers mentioned above entirely rejected both prayer and service directed to them, and, agreeing together, condemned them.”

But now, what is more important, I shall seek testimony from the very men who falsely cited and praised the acts of this council, in order thereby to lend more convenient support to their own program and defend the worship of idols.

What John Eckius writes in his *Enchiridion* concerning the four books of Charles the Great—does it not greatly serve my cause and testify that he regarded the truth of these books as established? He wished to recall having heard of them, but never to have read them himself. I have no doubt, however, that they would have caused him disgust had they appeared publicly while he was still alive. It is clear that those volumes had reached him only by hearsay and reputation; yet it was sport for that dreamer to assert as a testimony of truth concerning the matter something of which he had no knowledge, presenting it as he wished it to be. I would not wish to expose the man as guilty of such impiety or such deceitful faith that he asserted a matter against the protest of his conscience and wished to bury it in adulterated form. What a delightful and amusing spectacle it would be if a theological doctor, conscious of such an imposture, were to devise anything of the kind!

Does not Brother Alfonso de Castro, a cobbler of compilations and patchworks against heresies—certainly a monk of broad and varied learning, educated beyond the usual lot of his order—report that Claudius, bishop of Turin, forbade his people to adore the Lord’s cross? This gives no ordinary support to my case. [Note: [Col. 0993] He confuses Claudius Clement, the Scot of Auxerre, with Claudius of Turin.] He flourished in the time of Charles the Great and was among his most intimate advisers, a man of outstanding intellectual acuity and learning and one of the foremost founders of the University of Paris. I also possess several of his works that have not yet been printed.

As for our work, the matter is now sufficiently clear. Who would dare to dispute the writings of so prudent and pious an emperor, who endured so many and such great labors in defending and extending the Catholic faith? [Col. 0993D] And whom the Church afterward deemed worthy to place in the calendar of the saints? Who, moreover, would believe that he had sunk so deeply into oblivion before God that he could have stumbled so conspicuously in a decree concerning religion? Who would be so rash, or what faction so ill-advised, as to wish to undermine and deny a work composed in accordance with the opinion and judgment of so numerous a council?

We ought therefore to follow without fear the judgment of so great a prince and embrace the deliberation and censure of so many venerable men, who, guided by the dictate of a free conscience and mind, pronounced what seemed most certainly to be from God.

Accordingly, let us turn to our subject. Today we can clearly see from where images have crept in among us and how the capricious religion of Greece—the parent and seedbed of all idolatry, which from the remotest antiquity had suckled itself upon, nourished itself with, and delighted in fashioning new patrons and forms of the gods, [Col. 0994A] with which it fornicated in conspicuous superstition and counterfeit religion until the proclamation of the one true God grew strong—after its Church began to grow wealthy in the imperial court, having been proscribed by purer doctrine, brought forth in the Christian commonwealth the first roots of the worship of images under the veil of a more imposing sanctity. Clear-sighted piety degenerated into paintings, pigments, and the foolishness of other ornaments.

The contagion of this disease also breathed upon and infected Rome itself, a city no better behaved—if I may say so with due indulgence—than that other one, not very long after its Church had become richer in possessions. I believe that this likewise occurred during the age of Charles the Great. But the powerful hearts of the Franks, who with a single overthrow had destroyed the idols, could not so easily be enticed or bound to such impious and detestable worship. In the end, however, wealth and avarice won them over to it, and the images were restored with a far more august veneration than they had ever previously received, while true religion, if I may put it so, slept for a time. [Col. 0994B]

When the Church was overwhelmed by a great scarcity of upright and learned men, certain monks and teachers, among whom letters alone had found refuge, possessed no more knowledge than was useful to them. I would not dare call it malice, lest I provoke their legitimate successors and rightful imitators. While everything above and below was being thrown into confusion by the storms of war, they obscured all learning and virtue, however well they may have conducted themselves, by perversely turning them backward—or perhaps they had lost them entirely in their own time—and perverted everything according to their own will, so as to disguise their endeavors and plunder under the appearance of religion.

Their shamelessness was equally evident in their inability to restrain hands that itched to corrupt histories. They failed to consider that Almighty God never permits there to be no survivors who, the more wickedly such men seem to be making a funeral offering for extinguished truth, or to be covering it with cosmetic disfigurement, the more diligently preserve it after receiving it into their keeping, [Col. 0994C] reserving it to be restored and proclaimed in due time by more fortunate minds.

They are also gravely mistaken in thinking that our Creator is not displeased when we measure the evangelical word by our own judgment and reasoning, insofar as it touches the majesty of his name. He expressly establishes and commands that we follow his will without straddling it in either direction. This is the path that this rabble of scoundrels could not tread.

In the calamity and misfortune of later centuries, many learned and literate men were caught and entangled. They read histories without sufficient attention to detect the contrivances of impostors, although they often fought among themselves and overturned their own positions. Their imitators, ensnared in the same errors, lied no less than those through whom they had been lured into fraud and whose mouths had been smeared shut.

It remains now to examine what we ought to think about these things, since the world has grown calloused through this practice and nearly half of its shrines have been built up with images and adorned with various paintings. [Col. 0994D] Should they be clung to tooth and nail, or should public agreement be broken and they be shattered, or committed to the flames—or what else, I ask, should be done?

We who, inspired by Christ, know God more closely and trust in him, being freed from all the minutiae and curses of the Law even more than the Jews, since we serve under the standards of our supreme Commander, find nothing placed before us—whether created, manufactured, or fashioned by any human art—that is forbidden or unavailable to us. We can receive no wound or offense from anything external; we are exposed only to injury in our inward and vital parts. May we therefore, without fraud or sacrilege, use images, statues, and paintings just as we use any other human workmanship, either for ornament, for simple architectural design, or as an indication of memorable events whose example may be fruitful and whose memory worthy of recollection, [Col. 0995A] so that if we misuse them, the whole fault may be ascribed to our own vice and not to the object itself?

I do not deny that, if I saw the people being swept across into some abuse, religion would not prevent me from immediately destroying and reducing the images to pieces, in order to provide an example and demonstration that they possess no power. But when they cause no harm or offense, and, properly understood, adorn and dignify churches, I would not rashly demolish them. Otherwise everything human would necessarily come under the same laws, and the same judgment would have to be made concerning it all, since everything may be used either well or badly.

Even so, this precaution would have to be taken: we should not admit into churches any fictitious image, fabulous panel, or tapestry depicting things that never happened. Such objects plainly retain too much barbarism and paganism. Indeed, all such things ought to be represented truthfully and according to their archetype.

As for their being dressed in washed linens, [Col. 0995B] crowned with garlands and flowers, and more elegantly adorned on feast days—and hence their number being increased, so that images differ in their rank according to their location, some more powerful here and others more feeble elsewhere, some newly carved, others eaten away and decaying with age, some blackened by smoke, and others made from this or that material, lest I irritate anyone by my words—such gyrations and follies cannot win my approval. There is no doubt that every kind of gesticulation or shadow of immodesty must be kept far away. The same sort of thing is seen even in private houses, and all of it is disgusting and putrid in those who parade themselves under the title of Christianity.

I shall now draw the conclusion in accordance with the orthodox opinion of Charles the Great and of the whole Gallican Church of his time. Just as I believe that images must not be tolerated for purposes of abuse, so I also think that they should not be removed unless abuse increases. Rather, they should be diverted to such a use that they may serve as aids to memory and as ornaments.

Therefore, concerning both kinds of use of images, the good and the bad, it seems exceedingly pleasing to me, with prudent and deliberate judgment, [Col. 0995C] to eradicate this imposture and fabrication concerning images from the world, while wishing only that what is harmful be removed. Knowing also how greatly the public interest would suffer if the outstanding work of so great a prince were devoured by bookworms and moths or taken from us by any other disaster, I have dared to bring these sacred monuments back into the light, so that they may again be crowned with triumphs throughout the world, redound greatly to the praise of the most good God, and bring honor to that most powerful and most Christian emperor.

By my efforts this work has been restored to itself and to its proper order—not, certainly, furnished as the work of so great a prince ought to have been, but as far as I was able to strive with my little strength, so that [Col. 0996A] it might return a second time into our world as the most outstanding of all the deeds he ever accomplished, through the publication of this great achievement.

I can confidently promise you, candid reader, that this book will be of benefit to you and that its reading will be pleasant and uplifting.

One further point must be stated, lest anyone seek here an occasion for doubt. There are Latin commentaries, and printed ones at that, on the seventh synod of Constantinople—though it was held at Nicaea—which we received from Irene and her son Constantine, the Byzantine emperors, whose authority was especially influential there. In those commentaries not everything is narrated in the same order in which it is described by Charles the Great.

I infer that this happened either because the acts themselves had been recorded and committed to writing in different forms in the original—something that commonly occurs in such affairs, while the substance remains intact—and were afterward translated into Latin; or because only certain principal points reached the emperor’s hands, briefly touching upon the decrees of the Greeks, [Col. 0996B] like dispatches brought in condensed pages; or, third, because he wished only to borrow the subject matter itself and the chief positions of the dispute, which he intended to overthrow against the Seventh Council of Nicaea and against all the other opposing councils celebrated in the East under the direction and auspices of earlier emperors.

Since this question, having arisen in the vastest monarchy of the whole world, produced the fiercest and most poisonous controversies and quarrels, introduced battles and the collapse and overthrow of empires, and is today breaking out afresh, producing such a storm in the Christian commonwealth and a kind of Hydra of evils throughout the world, we ought to rejoice most fervently that this controversy is presented to us as settled and determined by the counsel, labor, and majesty of that prince, than whom the Christian world has borne no more excellent or triumphant ruler. The matter also concerns the first article of the Decalogue, and the worship and adoration of Almighty God.

With prayers we ought to ask him to stir the hearts of our rulers, which are in his hand, [Col. 0996C] so that they may truly reproduce the example of that great emperor; that they may take care and make every effort to settle the disturbance and controversy in religion spreading throughout Christianity, spare the blood of the faithful, eliminate ecclesiastical impostures and corruption of doctrine, and, insofar as possible, confront human inventions that conflict with the pure word of God. May that supreme King, our Lord, in his inexhaustible mercy, soon grant them the grace and strength to accomplish this.

To him, the eternal, immortal, invisible, and only wise God, belong power and might, honor, blessing, thanksgiving, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0995]

## Testimonies of Ancient Writers

### Charles the Great

In Book I, chapter 6, Charles the Great asserts himself to be the author of this *Capitulare* in these words:

“Through the care and diligence of our illustrious and most excellent father of venerable memory, King Pippin, and through the arrival in Gaul of the most reverend and holy man Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, etc.”

He is speaking of the union of the ceremonies of the Gallican Church with those of Rome.

And in Book IV, chapter 3:

“In most places of those who boast that they offer lights and incense to images, and by whom we are thought to suffer scandal because we disdain to do this, the places dedicated to divine worship are so contemptible that, as we have learned from the reports of our envoys, both those who were sent in the time of my father, the illustrious man of venerable memory, and those who were dispatched by us to those regions [of Greece], etc.”

### Pope Hadrian I

Pope Hadrian I of Rome, in his *Capitulare of Responses* to this *Capitulare* of Charles the Great:

“To the most excellent lord, our son and spiritual fellow-countryman, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, Hadrian, pope.” [Col. 0996D]

And shortly afterward:

“Furthermore, your most gracious and exalted royal power sent to us your faithful and familiar servant, namely Engilbert, abbot and minister of the chapel, who has been raised in your palace almost from the earliest beginnings of his childhood and has been admitted to all your councils. Therefore, just as he is received by you with complete familiarity, so he was received by us and fittingly honored.

“Accordingly, because of the great love that we bear toward your honey-sweet royal excellence, we received him, as you sent him, with the greatest affection and exceptional sweetness. In accordance with his wish, and as he wished to relate it to us with great familiarity, we received him with a receptive ear and benevolent mind. It was as though your bodily excellence itself were speaking to us, and we therefore trusted his counsel with greater patience, for the advancement of our holy Roman [Col. 0997A] Church and for the exaltation of your royal power, protected by God.

“Among other matters, he presented to us your *Capitulare* against the synod held at Nicaea concerning the erection of sacred images. Therefore, out of our honey-sweet royal affection for you, we returned a response to each chapter, not defending any individual person—far be it from us—but holding to the ancient tradition of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church and following the doctrine of our holy predecessors, vindicating in every respect the tradition of the true faith.”

And in the First Chapter of the Responses:

“Tarasius did not explain this doctrine by himself, but confessed it through the teaching of the holy Fathers. Because of our great love for your most exalted royal excellence, protected by God, we briefly set down their chapters, etc.”

And in the final chapter of the Responses:

“This sacred and venerable chapter differs greatly from all the chapters mentioned above. For that reason we have recognized it as belonging peculiarly to your orthodox royal excellence, preserved by God, [Col. 0997B] etc. For your most exalted royal wisdom remembers how, in that very letter of Pope Gregory, etc.”

And at the end of the chapter:

“Therefore, if your royal excellence, protected by God, approves, we urge [the emperor of Constantinople] with the same fervor to restore the sacred images to their former position, giving thanks for the favor, etc.

“As for your most exalted royal excellence, protected by God and strengthened by the stability of orthodox faith, we are confident that its firmest root is never shaken or moved by wicked and faithless men. Rather, we believe that in the spiritual teaching of the tradition of the true faith, which it began to hold and embrace from its holy mother, the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, it will remain without hesitation and without reproach forever.

“And therefore we trust in the power of our God that, just as you have always shown faith and love toward the Church of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, and have continually striven on every side for its advancement and exaltation, so may he graciously deign to defend and shelter you with his arm in royal triumph against hostile and wicked men. Thus, together with your spiritual daughter, our lady the queen, and your most exalted and noble offspring, you may deserve to reign for a long age in this world and to possess in the citadel of heaven, in the world to come, life without end together with the kingdom. May heavenly grace preserve your excellence unharmed.”

### Synod of Paris

In its preface to the emperors Louis and Lothar:

“After your father, Charles of holy memory, had ordered this same synod [the Second Council of Nicaea] to be read before himself and his people at the Council of Frankfurt, and had rightly criticized it in many places, marking in advance certain chapters that were open to criticism, he sent them through Abbot Angilbert to that same Pope Hadrian, so that they might be corrected by his judgment and authority, etc.” [Col. 0997C]

### Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims

In his book against Hincmar, bishop of Laon, chapter 20:

“The seventh synod, called by the Greeks a universal synod, was in fact a pseudo-synod concerning images, which some said should be destroyed and others adored. Neither side, however, defining the matter with sound understanding and without the authority of the apostolic see, was held at Nicaea not long before our own time by a great number of bishops and sent to Rome; the pope of Rome then sent it on to Gaul.

“Therefore, in the time of the emperor Charles the Great, by order of the apostolic see, a general synod was celebrated in Gaul, convened by the aforesaid emperor. Following the course of Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers, that pseudo-synod of the Greeks was destroyed and utterly rejected. A substantial volume concerning its destruction, which I read as a young man in the palace, was sent to Rome by that same emperor through certain bishops. In the fourth book of that volume the following was written concerning the term ‘universal’: ‘Just as the universal Church is,’ etc.”

This appears in Book IV, chapter 28, where he immediately adds:

“By the authority of this synod the veneration of images was somewhat restrained. Nevertheless, Hadrian and the other pontiffs persisted in their opinion, and after Charles’s death they promoted the worship of their puppets with still greater vigor.” [Col. 0998A]

### Althelmus

Althelmus, a Benedictine monk of Saint-Denis near Paris, in the *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 794 (Aimoinus, Book IV, chapter 85):

“At the beginning of summer, when he also held the general assembly of his people, the king gathered at the same place (Frankfurt on the Main) a council of bishops from all the provinces of his kingdom, in order to condemn the Felician heresy. The Roman pontiff’s legates, the bishops Theophylact and Stephen, were also present at that synod, acting in the place of the one by whom they had been sent, Pope Hadrian.

“At this council the aforesaid heresy was condemned, and a book against it was composed by the common authority of the bishops, all of whom subscribed it. The synod that had been convened a few years earlier at Constantinople under Irene and her son Constantine, and which they themselves had called not only the Seventh but also the Universal Synod, was likewise rejected in its entirety by all, so that it should neither be regarded nor called the Seventh or Universal, as being superfluous.” [Col. 0998B]

### Ado, Bishop of Vienne

In his *Chronicle*, sixth age:

“A synod was again held against the aforesaid heresy at Frankfurt, with Theophylact and Stephen, bishops and legates of the apostolic see, presiding [reading: present]. Felix was again convicted and condemned with his error by the authority of the holy Fathers, and was banished into perpetual exile at Lyons. He is said to have died in that same error of his. But the pseudo-synod that the Greeks call the Seventh, held in favor of the adoration of images, was utterly rejected.”

### Strabo of Fulda

A monk of Fulda, in his *Annals*, under the year 794:

“A synod was held at Frankfurt, at which the Felician heresy was condemned for the third time before the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Italy, in the presence of the great prince Charles and of the legates of the apostolic bishop Hadrian, the bishops Theophylact and Stephen. The condemnation was confirmed by a binding stipulation. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks, held in favor of the adoration of images and falsely called the Seventh, was condemned by the bishops.” [Col. 0998C]

### The Monk of Egolisma

In his *Life of Charles the Great*:

“In the following year, the lord King Charles traveled by ship from Regensburg to the great canal between the Altmühl and the Rednitz. There the apostolic envoys were presented to him with great gifts, and he was informed that the Saxons had rebelled again.

“From there he traveled by water along the Rednitz to Mochin and celebrated Christmas at Saint Kilian’s in Würzburg, and Easter at Frankfurt. There a great synod of the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Italy was assembled in his presence. The envoys of the lord apostolic, the bishops Theophylact and Stephen, were present there. There they condemned the Felician heresy for the third time. They committed that condemnation to writing in a book on the authority of the holy Fathers, and all the priests confirmed the book by subscribing it with their own hands. [Col. 0998D] The pseudo-synod of the Greeks, which they falsely called the Seventh and which concerned images, was rejected by the pontiffs.”

### Anonymous Bishop or Abbot

An anonymous bishop or abbot, counselor of Charles the Great, in the *Annals of the Franks*, under the year 784. The portion in which he dealt with this council has perished; Regino preserved it, acknowledging that he follows that author’s *Annals* and those of the monk of Egolisma.

### Regino, Abbot of Prüm

In Book II of his *Chronicle*:

“In the year 794 of the Lord’s incarnation, the king celebrated Easter at Frankfurt and there assembled a great synod of bishops from Gaul, Germany, and Italy. The apostolic envoys, the bishops Theophilus and Stephen, were present. At this synod the Felician heresy was condemned for the third time. They committed the condemnation to writing in a book on the authority of the holy Fathers, and all the priests subscribed the book with their own hands. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks, which they had held in favor of the adoration of images, was rejected by the pontiffs.”

### The Monk of Schwarzach

In the *Chronicle* continued by the abbot of Ursperg:

“In the year of the Lord 794, while Charles was celebrating Easter at Frankfurt, a great synod of bishops was assembled from all the provinces of the kingdom. The legates of Pope Hadrian were also present in his place. At this synod the heresy of a certain bishop named Felix was condemned. He said that Christ, insofar as he is man, was the adoptive Son of God. A book against him was composed by the common authority of the bishops, and all subscribed it.

“The synod that had been convened a few years earlier at Constantinople under Irene and her son Constantine, and that they themselves had called the Seventh and Universal Synod, was rejected by all as superfluous, so that it should be called neither the Seventh nor anything else.” [Col. 0999A]

### Hermannus Contractus

Count of Veringen and a monk of Reichenau, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 794:

“When a great synod had been held at Frankfurt, the Felician heresy was likewise condemned. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks, held in favor of the adoration of images, was condemned by the bishops.” [Col. 0999B]

### Johannes Aventinus

“Charles left Regensburg in December for Sualovoltas and proceeded to the upper canal, with the ships being dragged overland. From there he was carried by ship through Rhoedonessus into the Main and reached Würzburg—the capital of ancient Franconia, distinguished by the tomb of Saint Kilian—at the end of December. From there he moved to Frankfurt and spent the remainder of the winter there.

“He ordered the bishops of Gaul, Italy, and Germany to assemble there in great numbers. The Roman pontiff’s legates, the bishops Theophylact and Stephen, were present. There the Felician and Eliphandan heresies concerning the adoption of the Son of God were condemned for the third time. All the priests subscribed; Felix and Eliphandus themselves also did so, acknowledging their error, after pardon had been granted and their rank preserved. The acts of the Greeks concerning the adoration of images were likewise annulled.”

### Augustine Steuchus Eugubinus

Librarian of the Vatican Library of the Roman pontiff, in Book II, number 60, of *On the Donation of Constantine against Lorenzo Valla*:

“There are other splendid and very ancient monuments among the Greeks and Latins, from which anyone may understand that the edict of the Donation is entirely genuine and was issued by Constantine the Great, if, turning his attention to [Col. 1000A] all the parts of this edict, he compares them with the monuments I have mentioned.

“For example, Constantine decreed that the Roman Church and the see of Peter should be the head of all the Churches, that the whole order of religion should depend upon it, that judgment in matters of faith should be awaited from it, and that it should be consulted concerning religion.

“Knowing and understanding this, the emperor Charles the Great, at the very time when Pope Hadrian brought forward the history of Sylvester in the council, wrote concerning images while Constantine and his mother Irene were ruling at Constantinople. Accepting what Constantine the Great had established, he writes in Book I, chapter 6—the book is exceedingly ancient and written in Lombard letters in the Palatine Library, and anyone who does not believe this may be given the opportunity to see it—as follows:

“‘Before the testimonies are examined,’ etc.”

He quotes the whole of Book I, chapter 6.

### Brother Bernardus Lutzenburgus

Brother Bernardus Lutzenburgus, a monk of the Order of Preachers and professor of the liberal arts and sacred literature at the University of Cologne, in Book I, chapter 14, of his *Catalogue of Heretics*:

“Charles the Great, emperor, most learned in Greek and Latin, wrote seven hundred years ago a work in four books against certain [perhaps: Greek] heretics, which is preserved at Rome in the Vatican Library.” [Col. 1000B]

### Johannes Eckius

The Swabian Johannes Eckius, in his *Enchiridion of Commonplaces against Martin Luther and Other Enemies of the Church*, published in the year of the Lord 1529, article 16:

“Charles the Great wrote four books against those who wished to abolish images. Therefore the people of Zurich ought to follow Charles, their founder and patron, together with the Catholic Church, rather than the heretic Zwingli.”

### The Bishop of Meaux

The Bishop of Meaux entered the following in his catalogue:

“The work of the most illustrious Charles the Great, by the will of God king of the Franks, ruling, with the Lord’s assistance, Gaul, Germany, Italy, and the neighboring provinces, against the synod held in the regions of Greece in favor of the adoration of images, foolishly or arrogantly conducted.

“Likewise, the little book of Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, against Felix, bishop of Urgel, and Eliphandus, bishop of Toledo.

“These works are now restored to the light for the first time. In the year of salvation 1549.” [Col. 1000C]

[Col. 0999]

## In the Name of Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ

Here begins the work of the most illustrious and most excellent, or distinguished, man Charles, by the will of God king of the Franks, ruling, with the Lord’s assistance, Gaul, Germany, Italy, and their neighboring provinces, against the synod held in the regions of Greece in favor of the adoration of images, foolishly or arrogantly conducted.

## Preface of Charles the Great
[Col. 0999D] Our mother Church, redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ the Bridegroom and washed by the regeneration of the saving flood,

[Note: [Col. 0999D] “And nourished by the saving food of the body and draught of blood.” The word *aediculo* is foreign to this passage; it disrupts both the analogy and the grammatical reference. I have written *edulio*, and now support this reading with examples. Below, Book I, chapter 17: “In which there is heavenly manna, namely food for nourishment, concerning which food David says, etc.” And Book II, chapter 27, at the end: “Nourished by the food of the Lord’s body [Col. 1000D] and the draught of his blood.” Fulgentius Placiades of Carthage, *On Ancient Speech*: “*Edulium* is derived from *edere* (‘to eat’),” etc. Philoxenus, *Glossary*: “*Edulium*, τῶν βρωσίμων [‘of edible things’].” I read τὸ βρώσιμον [‘the edible thing’], as in the Greek-Latin Glossaries. Papias Lombardus, in his *Vocabulary*.]

and nourished by the saving food of the body and draught of blood, and anointed with the ointment of nectar-like liquid, and spread in peace throughout the whole world: at one time it endures external wars, at another internal ones; sometimes it is shaken by the incursions of foreigners, sometimes struck by the tumults of its citizens. Sometimes, indeed, it is driven by the attacks of unbelievers or heretics, but sometimes disturbed by the dissensions of schismatics or arrogant men. For it is an ark containing within itself souls to be saved. The ark of that ancient father was a type of it: this Church passes through the fiercest storms of the flood of this age without danger of shipwreck, and does not know how to yield to the deadly inundations of the present age, nor to collapse under the siege of hostile [Col. 1001A] powers assailing it. Rather, he fights for it, and especially within it, who has been placed as a wall around it, as the prophet says: “The savior will be set as the wall and rampart of our strong city,” and he who has appointed watchmen upon its walls, who will not be silent forever, day or night (Isaiah 26). Resisting its adversaries, it endures tumultuous disturbances; receiving into its bosom those who hasten to the confession of the true faith, and casting out those who stubbornly resist that same confession, it remains unshaken and undefiled. With David it never ceases to sing:

“Often they have fought against me from my youth,” let Israel now say; “often they have fought against me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me” (Psalm 129).

It continually expounds, in three divisions of prayer, the mystery of the holy [Col. 1001B] Trinity. It asks that its words—namely, the melody of psalmody, which it offers without ceasing—be received by the ears of the divine majesty; it devoutly entreats that its cry be understood—namely, the affection of the heart, which is wonderfully received not by bodily ears but by the ineffable hearings of the divine majesty; and it asks that the voice of its prayer be attended to, thereby declaring that perfect prayer is that which is kindled by the affection of an ardent mind.

Although, by changing its words metaphorically, it introduces various senses of our own, it nevertheless believes that the divine nature does not distinguish things to be distinguished by parts of bodily members, but accomplishes everything by one power. He hears those things which appear to be heard by us, and sees within what we have thought or are going to think; nothing can be hidden from his ineffable [Col. 1001C] light. To perceive words with the ears, to understand a cry, and to attend to the voice of prayer—although these are repeated under a variety of expressions through that rhetorical form which rhetoricians call *metabole*—the threefold repetition nevertheless signifies one and the same thing. The same is shown in the invocation of the King and God, or Lord, when it says: “My King and my God, for to you I will pray, O Lord” (Psalms 5 and 48). By inserting singular rather than plural verbs into the invocation of three names, it demonstrates that it believes and confesses three persons and one substance in the Godhead.

For she is a holy mother; she is immaculate, illustrious, incorrupt, and fruitful. She knows neither how to lose her virginity nor how to cease bearing children. The more she is struck by the adversities of the world, the more she is enlarged by greater or more excellent virtues; and the more heavily she is pressed, the more loftily she is exalted. The prophet introduces God speaking of her through *ethopoeia* in this way: “When I called upon you, you heard me, O God of my righteousness; in tribulation you enlarged me” (Psalm 4).

Because, with the Lord granting it, we have received the governance of the kingdom in her bosom, [Col. 1002A] it is necessary that, for her defense and exaltation, we strive with all our strength, Christ assisting us, so that we may be counted by him among the good and faithful servants. This must be carefully observed not only by us, to whom the task of governing has been entrusted amid the stormy waves of this age, but also by all who have been nourished at her breasts—yet in such a way that he who is known to be her member never withdraws from her unity. For whoever is not with her is against her, and whoever does not gather with her scatters.

The cause of this matter therefore compels us to speak, a matter which we pursue not without a certain sorrow of heart, since the apostolic example teaches us to be weak with the weak and to burn with those who are scandalized. The inflated ambition of windy arrogance [Col. 1002B] and the most insolent desire for empty praise have inflamed certain persons in the eastern regions—not only kings, but also priests—to such an extent that, setting aside sound and sober doctrine and disregarding the apostolic saying, “If anyone preaches to you anything besides what was preached to you, let him be accursed, even if he be an angel” (Galatians 1), and transgressing the boundaries of their ancestors established by prophetic instruction, they attempt, through infamous and utterly foolish synods, to introduce into the Church something which neither the Savior nor the apostles are known to have introduced. While they try to exalt the pinnacle of their own praise, they heap up great guilt upon their souls; and while they wish to entrust the order of their deeds to the memory of posterity, they tear apart the bond of ecclesiastical unity.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] “A synod was indeed held several years ago in the regions of Bithynia,” etc. Either the author is historically mistaken (*ἀνιστορίζει*), or he errs in his recollection (*ἁμαρτάνει μνημονευτικῶς*). For this synod was held not in Bithynia but at Constantinople, in the palace of Hieria. Unless scribes were misled by the similarity of names, we should read “in the palace of Hieria” instead of “in Bithynia,” as follows: “a certain synod was held in the palace of Hieria.” This seems quite probable to me.]

A synod was indeed held several years ago in the regions of Bithynia, [Col. 1002C] of such heedless and undiscriminating boldness that they recklessly abolished images placed in the adornment of the Church and in remembrance of past events. What the Lord had commanded concerning idols, they carried out against all images, not knowing that an image is a genus whereas an idol is a species, and that a species cannot be referred to a genus, nor a genus to a species. For although almost every idol is an image, not every image is an idol.

An idol and an image have entirely different definitions. Images are made for adornment or to display historical events; an idol, however, is made only to entice the souls of wretched people through sacrilegious ritual and empty superstition. An image is said to be directed toward something; an idol is directed toward itself. These men were darkened by such a cloud of blindness [Col. 1002D] that, after anathematizing all who were known to possess or intended to possess images in churches, they added this to their other errors:

[Note: [Col. 1001D] “That their king Constantine had freed them from idols.” Be careful not to understand the great Constantine, the first of the emperors to renounce idols, but Constantine Caballinus, [Col. 1002D] by whose edict that synod was convened at Constantinople. At its conclusion, among the customary acclamations, one reads: “You have obscured all idolatry.” Concerning these words, Epiphanius comments in the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea: “But if—as they themselves say—the assembly of bishops and the strength of emperors freed us from idols, the human race is deceived regarding the truth. For since Jesus Christ our Lord and God freed us from the error of idols, how can they glory and boast that this was accomplished by them? O insane boasting!” Carolus Magnus undoubtedly had this passage before his eyes and referred to it. In Theophanes, in the *Miscellaneous History*, the bishops are said, after the synod had ended, “to have ordered the people to raise their hands on high, to have raised a joyful clamor, and to have proclaimed: TODAY SALVATION HAS COME TO THE WORLD—for by your deeds, O emperor, we have been freed from idols.”]

that their king Constantine had freed them from idols. They sought to attach to their own king the title of victory belonging to him who “rejoiced like a giant to run his course,” of whom it is said, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5), and who, triumphing, carried away the spoils of the world with him. Yet the prophet had foretold this not of their king but of the true conqueror, Christ:

“Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt will be shaken before him” (Isaiah 19).

By the light cloud he wished the human body to be understood—the body which Christ had assumed from the Virgin, unburdened by any stain of human intercourse—and by Egypt, the world. Through Jeremiah also he had promised long before, in almost the same words, that he would do this, saying: “I will destroy the images and bring the idols of Memphis to an end” (Ezekiel 30).

[Note: [Col. 1003D] “Moreover, another synod was held in those regions about three years ago,” etc. At Nicaea in Bithynia, by the Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus and his mother Irene, in the year of Christ 787, in the tenth indiction. The number given here is therefore false, since this synod of Frankfurt was seven full years later than that Council of Nicaea—or else the text is corrupt. What if we read: “seven years ago another synod was held in the regions of Bithynia,” etc.? In this way the generally corrupt passage would make good sense. The acts of this Council of Nicaea are extant in volume III of the *General Councils*. See below, Book IV, chapters 13 and 24.]

Moreover, another synod was held about three years ago in those regions, [Col. 1003B] by the successors of those who had conducted the earlier one, or by many who are said to have been present at the earlier synod. Although it differs from the former in its decree, it does not differ from it in error; although its business is different, it is equal in criminality; and although later in time, it is not later in guilt. Not without reason do these two seem to flow together into the filthy pool of one abyss, though they move by different channels, since they are believed to have burst forth from the fountain of one boastfulness and empty praise.

After anathematizing and abominating the earlier synod and its authors, this later one compels people to adore images which the earlier synod had not even permitted them to behold. Wherever they found any mention of images, whether in passages of Holy Scripture or in the commentaries of the holy Fathers, they twist it according to the decision of their own will [Col. 1003C] into an argument for adoration.

These two parties are joined together in possessing and adoring images by no less absurd a bond than the earlier party was joined together in confusing image and idol. The earlier party thought image and idol were one thing; the later party thought possessing and adoring were one thing. Yet these are distinct both in the nature of the matter and in the relationship of their categories: one is a condition, the other an action. Although image and idol differ greatly, they are at least joined in this respect, that one is a species and the other a genus. Possessing and adoring, however, are related neither by genus nor species nor by any such connection, since things may be adored which are not possessed, and things may be possessed which are not adored.

Thus, rejecting the restraints of moderation and neglecting the saying rightly handed down by the ancients as a proverb, “Nothing in excess,” they leave the path of the mean and walk along byways. It is as if someone, wishing to impose moderation in speaking upon a man devoted to excessive talk, should find that the man instead became so devoted to silence that he was rendered mute; and just as disordered loquacity had brought disgrace upon him, so idle silence would bring disgrace upon him no less.

Or it is as if a physician should accuse a sick man of drunkenness, and the patient, thinking that he was obeying the physician’s commands, should forbid himself not only wine but also every other liquid, so that the man who had earlier languished because he was soaked by excessive drinking would now languish, dried out by thirst, after forbidding himself every liquid. Although the causes of the illness are different, the effect of idle error is nevertheless one and the same.

Meanwhile, since neither side is held by the reins of moderation, but both rush headlong over precipices and are carried along at different speeds, they nevertheless strive, by one combined assault, to inflict a blemish upon the Bride of Christ, the Church, to whom he says in the Song of Songs: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 2).
