The one side persuades her to cast away what she properly possesses, while the other persuades her to misuse what she properly possesses. The former strive to remove her ornaments; the latter provoke her to adore those ornaments [Col. 1004B]. These two evils, as we have said, have sprung from the fountain of boasting.

While they desire human favor, wish to be called “Rabbi” by men, and place their own praises at the head of their writings, they do not heed the saying of a certain wise man: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27). Abandoning the traditions of the ancient Fathers, who decreed that images should not be worshiped but permitted them to be kept as ornaments of churches, they strive to introduce novel and unprecedented constitutions into the Church, by which they assign to her a blemish rather than an adornment.

For if introducing new constitutions into the Church is boasting, it is schism; yet schism ought not to occur in the Church. If it is schism, it is a blemish, and a blemish is denied to exist in the Bride. If, therefore, introducing new constitutions into the Church is boasting, it is unquestionably a blemish, which is denied to exist in the Bride. Hence it is understood that he is not the Bridegroom’s friend who wishes to heap up the summit of his own praise so greatly that, through the marks of error, he does not fear to blunt ecclesiastical discernment. Consequently, if a blemish does not suit the Bride, no one ought to attempt to impress one upon her; and whoever attempts to do so wrongs the Bridegroom. If, therefore, a blemish does not suit the Bride—and truly it does not—whoever attempts to impress one upon her wrongs the Bridegroom.

We, finally, content with the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, instructed in the teachings of the holy orthodox Fathers, who in their doctrines never deviated from him who is the way, the truth, and the life, and receiving the six holy and universal [Col. 1004D] synods held by the holy and venerable Fathers against the various attacks of heretics, reject every novelty of expression and every foolish invention. We not only do not accept them, but despise them as refuse, just as we despise that synod held in the regions of Bithynia on account of its most shameless tradition that images should be adored [Col. 1005A]. The text of its writing, lacking both eloquence and sense, has come down to us.

We have therefore been compelled to write against its errors, so that if it should attempt anywhere to defile either the hands of those who hold it or the ears of those who hear it, it may be driven away by the attack of our pen, armed with the authority of the divine Scriptures; and so that the inactive—or rather unarmed—enemy coming from the East may be struck down by us in the West, with God’s favor, by the sentence of the holy Fathers brought forward against it.

[Note: [Col. 1005C] “We undertook this work with the *cohibentia* of the priests.” I have corrected this to *conhibentia*, a word belonging to this period. Book III, chapter 11: “Nor did they take care to call the synod concerning the adoration of images universal without the *conhibentia* of many Catholic and God-fearing churches.” Book IV, chapter 25, interprets this as follows: “Who, without the agreement of their fellow priests established throughout the various regions of the world,” etc. Balbus of Genoa, in the *Catholicon*: “*Conhibeo* is formed from *habeo* with *con*, and retains the *n*, which is removed in *cohibeo*. *Conhibere* means ‘to close the eyes’; and because closing the eyes signifies assent, *conhibere* is used for ‘to assent’ or ‘to obey’; from this comes *conhibentia*.” Shortly afterward he says: “*Conhibentia*, that is, assent; likewise *convenientia* and *collibentia*. For example: ‘He departed without the *cohibentia*, *conniventia*, or *collibentia* of his brothers,’ that is, without their assent.” This clearly indicates that the spelling of this noun varied. I think—and it is true—that this word was corrupted by barbarous and ignorant monks already in the age of Charlemagne from the word they ought to have rendered in Latin, *collubentia* or *conlubentia*. The confusion of similar letters made the error easy.]

We undertook this work with the *conhibentia* of the priests—of the prelates of the Catholic flocks in the kingdom granted to us by God—not from the arrogance of pride but from zeal for God and devotion to truth. For just as it is holy to cling to just and honorable things, so surely it is sinful to accommodate the mind to utterly bad and disordered things [Col. 1005B]. Thus David offers God something like a pure sacrifice because he has shunned the company of the wicked, when he says: “I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and I will not sit with the impious” (Psalm 26). King Jehoshaphat of Judah was reproved by the Lord through the prophet because he had joined himself in friendship to the worst king of the Israelite nation (2 Chronicles 19).

Since, therefore, the authors of the two aforementioned synods possess neither that inexpert speech by which the Apostle calls himself unskilled in speech but not in knowledge, nor that brilliance of eloquence joined with spiritual meaning of which the Church is told, in the person of the holy preachers, in the Song of Songs: “We will make you chains of gold, studded with silver” (Song of Songs 1), we are amazed that, inflated by the wind of such vanity, they dared not only to brandish them but also attempted to number them among the six venerable synods [Col. 1005C]. In what manner neither of them can be counted as the seventh after Nicaea, but must be counted either as the third after Ariminum, with the earlier synod retained, or as the second after the earlier synod has been destroyed, we shall discuss more carefully in what follows, when the matter requires it, with the Lord’s approval.

These synods are no more to be equated with the six than the altar of the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh could have been equated with the altar which was built at the Lord’s command by the lawgiver. The fury of the Israelite sword would have destroyed its authors had not a submissive confession mingled with prayers forestalled the anger of their brothers.

Finally, taught by the prophecy of Isaiah, which says, “This is the way; walk in it; you shall not turn aside from it, neither to the right nor to the left” (Isaiah 30), and admonished by the preaching of the teacher of the nations, who instructed us to keep to the royal way, we keep images in the adornment of churches and as memorials of historical events, worship God alone, and offer his saints appropriate veneration. We neither break images with the former nor adore them with the latter, but reject the writing of that most foolish synod. It not only lacks the manner of expression by which small matters are stated modestly, middling matters temperately, and great matters grandly, but also neglects the norms of ordinary speech. We strive in every respect to become followers of our teacher—namely, the speech of the Lord.

Since, therefore, the aforementioned synod contains confused discussions both of fathers anathematizing sons and of sons anathematizing fathers, our pen, with the Lord’s favor, will set forth a mixed condemnation of both, passing over nothing unexamined, nothing untouched, and nothing buried in the caves of silence—unless, perhaps, either the difficulty of the disordered language denies our understanding access to it, or reverence restrains us from pursuing the foolishness of some childish statement [Col. 1006C].

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1005]

## CHAPTER ONE

Concerning what Constantine and Irene say in their writings: “Through the God who reigns with us.”

[Col. 1005D]

Human frailty very often exceeds the limits of its own incapacity; and the more it exalts itself beyond what it ought, the farther it withdraws from him who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth. The more it attempts, by its sublimity, to approach him who is exalted above all nations, the more decidedly it distances itself from him. But if it does not disregard the measure of its condition, and, striving to seek higher things, submits itself with a devoted mind to what is lower, it may, by bending down, climb toward him from whom it was known to descend by exalting itself; and the more it prostrates itself upon the ground, the nearer it becomes to heaven.

Since, then, our being is so far removed from God’s being, our living from his living, and our reigning from his reigning, the madness of those men is rather to be lamented than admired who, among the other things they indiscreetly usurp, even say that God reigns together with them. For he knows only “to be”; he does not know “to have been” or “to be going to be.” He does not possess that portion of eternity which we call time and divide into present, past, and future; rather, possessing the integrity of the whole of eternity in the unchangeability of his essence, for him there is only “to be.” Hence he also said to holy Moses: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III).

But our being—whose past is in memory, whose present is in perception, and whose future is in expectation—when compared with that essence, is non-being. His living experiences neither beginning, nor end, nor change in any way. Hence it is also written in the prophets: “I live, says the Lord” (Isa. XLIX); and certain holy men dared to say, “The Lord lives”—that is, he lives in that life which has neither begun, nor is disturbed by change, nor is interrupted by an end.

But our living suffers origin, decline, and change. Although the soul is immortal, it is nevertheless recognized to be changeable; and this changeability is often reckoned to it as death. Hence it was said to the first man: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. I, 2). This does not mean that, as soon as he transgressed the Lord’s commandment, he was punished with bodily death, but that through the changeability of his mind he had departed far from that holiness in which he stood near to God.

Moreover, his reigning differs from our reigning no less than his being differs from our being, and his living from our living. For just as his essence has always possessed being and living, so also it has always possessed reigning. Our reigning, however, is preceded by our being and living and succeeded by our perishing. Since these things are so, it is a great presumption for anyone to say that God reigns together with him—when even David did not dare to say this, although the Lord said of him, “I have found a man after my own heart,” and, “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Ps. LXXXIX).

Nor did Solomon say this, to whom the Lord said: “Wisdom and knowledge have been given to you; but I will give you riches, possessions, and glory, so that no king before you or after you shall have been like you” (II Par. I). He himself also speaks confidently of himself: “God taught me wisdom, and I have learned the understanding of the holy” (Prov. XXX). Nor is anyone among kings, whether among those supported by the privilege of their merits or among those whom Scripture records as having acted arrogantly, ever read to have said such a thing.

Meanwhile, the syllable *con-* in compound words, according to those who are not ignorant of the skill of literary learning, signifies almost nothing other than “together.” Thus: “Let the whole assembly of Israel be gathered together” (Lev. VIII); and, “Let them assemble for the feast day” (Dan. III)—that is, “let them be gathered together into one flock, let them come together.” And the Apostle says: “Provided that we suffer together, so that we may also be glorified together” (Rom. VIII)—that is, “co-glorified.” Likewise: “Both sat down upon the glassy edge of the spring”—that is, “sat together”; and one who sits together is called a *consessor*.

According to those who investigate the most subtle secrets of logic, “together” is said in three ways: with respect to time, nature, and kind.

With respect to time, as blessed Augustine says, things exist or appear together whenever they exist at one time, so that neither of two things is earlier than the other or follows the other, but their origin appears to be common. In this sense we must by no means be said to reign together with him, since he is eternal whereas we are temporal, he is without beginning whereas we have a beginning.

With respect to nature, things are naturally together when none of them precedes the other. For example, we must suppose that the single and the double exist together by nature; yet the double does not cause the single to exist, nor does the single produce the double. But neither can we be said to reign together with him in this sense, since by so many differences his nature is prior to ours, and in so many ways the Creator precedes the creature.

With respect to kind, things are said to be together whenever they flow from the same genus and appear to exist together by nature while being distinguished in species. Thus there is the animal. For both a terrestrial animal and an aquatic animal are called animals, but they are distinguished in species; neither is prior to the other, but all are recognized as having arisen together from “animal,” that is, from one genus.

This third mode, no less than the preceding two, resists saying that he reigns together with us, since our nature is in no way recognized as joined to his by some unity of substance, while being distinguished from it by some difference of species. Although he is everywhere through the power of his divinity, he cannot rightly be said to reign together with anyone. For it is one thing to be everywhere and another to be together with someone; one thing to reign ineffably and another to reign together with someone.

Therefore, when *conregnare* (“to reign together”), *consedere* (“to sit together”), and many similar expressions are stated absolutely, without anyone being said to sit or reign together with anyone else, they designate two or more persons reigning or sitting together. But if someone is said to reign or sit together with someone else, this signifies that he whom the other joins in reigning or sitting precedes him; while the latter becomes a participant in him who reigns or sits together with him. Thus Paul, the “Vessel of election,” says: “You have been buried together with Christ” (Rom. VI); and again: “If you have risen together with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Coloss. III). From this it is understood that the one who is buried and rises precedes, while those who are buried and rise together with him become participants in the one with whom they are buried and rise. For unless the Redeemer of the human race had been buried and had risen for us, we could in no way be buried and rise together with him.

From this evidence it is gathered that it is far from cautious to say that God reigns together with us. He does not participate with us in reigning; rather, just as he is the author of all things, so he precedes all things in being, living, and reigning.

But if some contentious person, attempting to establish the error of this word, should bring forward as testimony the things said of the only-begotten Son of God according to the form of a servant, saying, “Why should he not reign together with us, with whom, according to the Apostle, we suffer together, are buried together, are made alive together, and rise together? We are fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow participants with him in the same Jesus Christ through the Gospel, in whom God raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places. Of him the Evangelist also says, ‘While eating with them, he was taken up’ (Acts I); and again, ‘They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working together with them’ (Mark XVI)”—let him consider, once the darkness of his clouded mind has been cleared away, that this is not from Christ’s divinity but from our humanity, in which we suffer together with him, are buried together with him, and are made alive together with him.

For just as suffering, being buried, and eating—the things in which we are buried and suffer together with him, and in which he is said to eat together with us—are properly human, so reigning is properly divine. The Psalmist bears witness to this, saying: “His name alone is exalted” (Ps. CXLVIII); and again: “The kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nation” (Ps. XII); and likewise: “Your kingdom, O Lord, is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and lineage” (Ps. CXLV).

We too are said to reign, but improperly, not properly. For to reign, to be immortal, and to be truthful are natural to him; but to the others who attain these things they are attributed by the generosity of him who truly reigns and who alone is immortal and truthful. The Teacher of the Gentiles proclaims this when he says: “God is truthful, but every human being is a liar” (Rom. III); and again: “Who alone possesses immortality” (I Tim. III). This does not mean, as blessed Jerome says, that angels and the other rational creatures do not possess immortality or love truth, but that he alone is immortal and truthful by nature, whereas the others receive immortality and truth from his generosity; and that it is one thing to possess something through oneself and another to have what one possesses depend upon the power of the giver.

If, then, we can rightly be said to die and suffer together with God, who is immortal and impassible, so also God can rightly be said to reign together with us. If the former is rejected as something that cannot be said with manifest reason, the latter too must be rejected after careful inquiry.

We suffer together with Christ when, in the love of him who endured the suffering of the cross for us, we crucify our flesh—that is, the world with its vices and desires—and die to the world and die together with Christ. Thus we crucify the flesh, that is, the body, so that we may trample down its desires.

We have been buried together with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the power of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life. Thus, having been baptized, we have been buried together with him so that thereafter we may follow this life in which Christ rose. Baptism is the pledge and image of resurrection, so that, remaining now in Christ’s commandments, we may not turn back again to what has gone before.

We are made alive together with him and rise together with him if we have been planted in the likeness of his death—that is, if in baptism we lay aside all vices and are transferred into a new life, so that thereafter we do not sin. For the likeness of death produces a corresponding resurrection.

We are his fellow heirs and fellow participants, not because some possession is divided among us, but because he himself is our inheritance and possession. For the Lord says: “The Lord is your inheritance” (Deut. XVIII); and elsewhere: “The Lord is my portion and my inheritance” (Ps. XV; Eccli. XLV).

We are fellow members of the body because, although those who have believed in Christ possess different graces, they are nevertheless gathered together into one body of the Church.

Therefore he made the saints sit together with Christ in the heavenly places—not because the saints sit with him while they remain in this world and are pilgrims away from him, but because, according to the opinion of the teacher mentioned above, it is the custom of Scripture sometimes to express future events in the past tense through the figure called prolepsis. For example, concerning the Lord’s cross: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. XXII); and elsewhere concerning his passion: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII).

Or else this means, according to the spiritual sense, that the saints are in no way in the flesh while they live in the flesh, and that they have their citizenship in heaven while they walk upon earth: having ceased to be flesh and being wholly transformed into spirit, they sit in the heavenly places with Christ. For “the kingdom of God is within us,” and “where our treasure is, there also will our heart be.” We sit firmly and steadfastly with Christ—in wisdom, the Word, justice, and truth.

The apostles preached while the Lord worked together with them (Mark XVI)—that is, while he supplied them with assistance for the performance of good works. For this reason their activity had such power that, at their preaching, many thousands of people believed, and, when the powers of nature had been broken, the dead received life, the blind received sight, and the deaf received hearing.

The Lord works together with all the saints, according to the Apostle, who says: “I have become a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me according to the working of his power” (Coloss. I). But with sinners, insofar as they sin, he must in no way be believed either to work together or to reign together.

If, then, someone thinks that the Apostle’s statement, “If we endure, we shall also reign together” (II Tim. II), provides him with some support in this matter, let him recognize that this differs in three respects from what the Apostle says: person, time, and merit.

In respect of person, because it is not said that he will reign together with the saints, but that the saints will reign together with him.

In respect of time, because they are not said to have reigned together or to reign together, but to be going to reign together.

In respect of merit, because not everyone, but only the saints, will reign together with him.

For he says: “If we endure, we shall also reign together” (ibid.)—that is, if we endure in this age, we shall reign together in the future; or certainly after the judgment, when we shall behold him no longer through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face. For if we are still in this world, we still endure; if we still endure, we do not yet reign together with him. Therefore, if we are still in this world, we do not yet reign together with him.

Furthermore, if we reign together with him, then what is perfect has already come; if what is perfect has already come, then what is partial has already been abolished. But what is partial has not been abolished; therefore, we do not reign together with him.

If, then, the saints do not reign together with him so long as they are in this world, much less does he reign together with them, whose kingdom and dominion it is, and whose kingdom shall have no end. And if he does not reign together with the saints, he must in no way be said to reign together with sinners.

When the saints will reign together with him, we have learned from the Apostle John, who says: “Beloved, it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). Thus, when what we shall be appears—that is, immortal and glorious—we shall be like him.

He said “like,” not “equal.” Like, that is, not in bodily resemblance but in the inner person. Blessed Augustine says in his letter to the virgin Italica: “Who, then, would be so utterly foolish as to say that we are or will be bodily like God? This likeness is therefore in the inner person.”

We shall see him as he is when, according to his promise, he manifests himself to those who love him, existing without end. In him we shall see God infinitely, celebrating the solemnity of perpetual Sabbath, while the Lord says to us: “Be still and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLVI). None of these things will be fulfilled in the saints beforehand, until, according to the Apostle, “this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has put on incorruption.”

For if we reign together with him, then what we shall be has already appeared; if what we shall be has already appeared, then we are already like him; if we are already like him, then we already see him as he is. But we do not see him as he is; therefore, we do not yet reign together with him.

He therefore reigns in us; he does not reign together with us. He reigns, according to blessed Augustine’s opinion, in believers because he was weakened even to the cross and death. In this manner the Son properly reigns in the faith of believers. For the Father cannot be said or believed to have been incarnate, judged, or crucified. Through the form in which he is equal to the Father, he reigns in those who contemplate the truth; he does not reign together with us, since he does not participate with us in the kingdom. The kingdom is properly his, as we argued above.

For we do not yet reign together with him as long as we are clothed in the garment of this mortality. We hope, by his mercy, to do so at that time when, according to the contemplation of the truth above, in order to attain blessedness, God will be all in all, with no movement of the mind, no part of the body, and no person loving his own power resisting him.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning what Constantine and Haerena wrote in the letter addressed to the venerable Pope Adrian of the Apostolic See: “God chose us, who seek his glory in truth.”

**[Col. 1011C]**

According to the judgment of Truth, who speaks from himself, he seeks his own glory. Those who have become inflamed over the veneration of images appear to seek and embrace this glory so eagerly that they do not hesitate to despise their predecessors or parents along with their deeds.

**[Note: [Col. 1011D] “Their predecessors or parents.” Throughout these books the reading is *prodecessores*, whereas the common form is *praedecessores*. Likewise, see this book, chapters 9, 20, and 28; Book II, chapters 23 and 31; Book IV, chapters 6, 10, 13, and 22. I suppose it follows the form by which jurists use *proavus*, *propatruus*, *proavunculus*, and so forth.]**

For, having rejected and despised them, they boast that they seek the glory of God in truth. Yet they rightly despise those predecessors if they have in any way departed from that Truth which said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). He is called the way because, through the incarnation, he offers the good an example of how to live.

He is called the truth because of the judgment he exercises in truth, or because no falsehood can be found in him at all. He is called the life because of his divinity, through which he is the source of life and through which all things live. He is truly the way of those who walk rightly, leading to eternal life. The prophet discourages us from deviating from this way when he says: “Lay hold of instruction, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way” (Ps. II).

The enemy of this way, of which the same holy man says, “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous” (Ps. I), is the author of death, of whom it is added: “But the way of the ungodly shall perish” (ibid.).

For if they have departed from the truth, they have adhered to falsehood and have become liars. If they have departed from the truth, they have become liars. Therefore, according to the rule of denominatives—just as from truth comes “truthful,” from justice “just,” from piety “pious,” and from goodness “good”—so, conversely, from falsehood comes “false.”

Since liars can scarcely, or never, teach the truth, it is astonishing how these men have become so truthful and such followers of truth—men who, according to their own opinion, were taught and begotten by liars.

They do not therefore seek God’s grace in that truth of which pious Truth and true Piety said: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII). Rather, they seek it in images fashioned by the skill of craftsmen. These images often lead their spectators into admiration because of the memory of past deeds, but they always lead their worshipers into error.

For it is no small error to worship with religious devotion something other than the one who said: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone” (Deut. VI).

Truth always remains undefiled and inviolate, and is one and unchanging. These images, however, according to the craftsman’s will, appear to do many things while doing nothing. They seem to be human beings although they are not; to fight although they do not fight; to speak although they do not speak; to hear although they do not hear; to see although they do not see; to signal although they do not signal; to touch although they do not touch; and so forth.

It is therefore clear that such things are the fabrications of craftsmen, not that Truth of which it was said: “The truth will set you free” (John VIII).

It is true that images are without sense and reason; it is false that they are human beings. If someone should assert that they may be called human beings according to the logic of equivocal terms, as in the statements “Augustine was a great philosopher,” “Augustine is to be read,” “Augustine painted in the church is standing,” and “Augustine buried in that place is lying,” let him observe that although all these expressions proceed from one source, namely Augustine, only the one of whom it was said “a great philosopher” was the true Augustine. The others are one thing as a book, another as an image, and another as a buried body.

The principal difference between a painted human being and a real one is that one of them is true and the other false; they are joined nowhere except in the sharing of a name. For since the true human being is one who can be defined as an animal, rational, mortal, and capable of laughter and sensation, that one must necessarily be regarded as false who possesses none of these characteristics. And if the one who lacks all these things is not false, neither is the one who is subject to all these definitions true.

Look: many images are seen standing. Some are assembled from pigments of color, some cast in gold or silver, some shaped in wood by the sculptor’s chisel, some carved in marble, and some molded in plaster or clay. In all of them, insofar as their nature permits, the likeness of the image and the inscription of the name are the same. For example, it is an image of Paul, and the inscription reads, “Saint Paul.”

Those who suffer from such great error that they call these things, according to their own judgment, both truth and holy and true—and not rather, according to the tradition of the venerable Fathers, images of the saints—must be asked which image, when all are compared, is to be believed holier or truer, and which is to be regarded as the holiest or truest.

Since reason will not permit them to call all these images equal, given their differences in material, size, and workmanship, and since it prevents them from admitting some to be holier than others and some to be the holiest, they are compelled, according to reason’s investigation of truth, to confess that they ought to be called neither capable of truth nor holy.

For they are unequal in price, by which they are preferred to one another according to degrees of comparison, yet equal in the merit of holiness and truth, since all of them entirely lack both.

Just as a costly image admits of a costlier and a most costly image, so a holy and true image could admit of a holier and truer, a most holy and most true image—if, that is, there were a positive degree from which the comparative and superlative could arise.

Suppose that holiness is present in a painted image. Where was it before the image was made? Was it in the wood taken from the forest for use, the remainder of which is consigned to the flames? Was it in the colors, which are usually made from impure substances? Was it in the wax, which is receptive both of colors and of dirt?

If it was in the wood, why does that which is removed by the blunt striking of an axe, bitten away by the adze, and scraped by the plane perish when consumed by fire and reduced to ashes? Or why does it perish when the colors are scattered in different directions by the craftsman’s hand, or when the wax is melted drop by drop by the excessive heat of the fire—if holiness does not know how to perish?

Or, if holiness is not in the things we have just mentioned—and in fact it is not—we must ask from where it comes to the image after it has been assembled from several materials. Since it is not found to come to it either through the laying on of hands or through any canonical consecration, it must not be believed to be present in it.

If it were present, one could ask whether, as the image decayed through age, holiness would decay with it, or whether it would pass to another image made from new materials. For if it were present in it, it would come from somewhere else; and if it came from somewhere else, it would pass to another. But it does not pass to another; therefore, it must not be believed to be present in it.

Since these things are so, whoever calls these images truth and asserts that he seeks the glory of God in them has departed far from the truth.

David did not perceive the glory of God in manufactured images when he said: “His glory is above the heavens” (Ps. CXIII). Nor did the heavenly host perceive it in images when it sang: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II). Nor did the glory of the Lord appear in some image to the people of God in the vast desert when it is said: “The glory of the Lord appeared” (Exod. XV; Lev. IX; Num. XIV, XVI, XX); or again: “The glory of the Lord covered the tabernacle” (Exod. XL).

Many things could be said against the considerable delirium of this chapter, both according to the authority of the holy Scriptures and according to the investigation of truth; but what has been said briefly for the present is sufficient, and these matters should not be an obstacle to us as we hasten on to other things.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning what Constantine and Haerena call their deeds or writings “divine.”

An obsolete error of ancient paganism, driven back by Christ’s coming, appears to have left some trace in those who boast that they retain the dignity of Christian faith and religion. They boldly desire to establish new and foolish constitutions within the Church, and they do not fear, in pagan fashion, to call themselves “divine” and their deeds “divine.”

Thus it comes about that what the first parents perpetrated in the flower-bearing seat, enticed by the poisonous serpent’s promise, these men perpetrate in the Church, deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy. They too do not refuse to call themselves “divine” through the height of empty glory, and through the rapacity of greed by which they attempt to reach the summit of vain praise they strive to introduce something new into the Church.

Whoever therefore seeks what is higher than order permits, and wants to be more than he is in an extraordinary way, is cast down by him who regards the lowly and knows the lofty from afar; he begins to be less than he is.

This can be demonstrated by the example of those whose falls must be avoided. One of them, intending to establish his seat in the north, was deprived of angelic honor and companionship and assigned to the darkness of this gloom. The other, disobedient to the divine commands and wishing to be like God, was expelled from the most delightful seat, lost immortality, and was consigned to the labors and hardships of this mortality.

If their falls are to be avoided, their deeds must be shunned; if their deeds must be shunned, the practice of humility must be embraced.

If, then, their falls are to be avoided, the practice of humility must be embraced. Through it, together with the other instruments of good works, we can also become “gods,” as did the one to whom it was said: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII), and sons of God, according to what is written: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I).

For although God is called essentially the Creator of all things, according to the saying, “For God is the great Lord and the great King over all the earth” (Ps. XCV), there is another mode in which, improperly, heavenly powers and human beings are called gods. The Apostle says: “And although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father” (I Cor. VIII). The Psalmist says: “I have said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXII).

In a third way, according to sacrilegious superstition, aerial powers are called gods, as in the saying: “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCVI).

In the first sense, no one can be called God essentially except he who is ineffable, unchangeable, eternal, almighty, the supreme good, the unique summit, three in persons and one in nature, who is God above all, blessed forever.

In the second sense, angels and human beings can be called gods. This name of dignity is attained only by obeying God, embracing humility, despising arrogance, and clinging to him through good works.

The third mode has several forms. The Gentiles called demons gods; they also thought and called the stars, or various creatures of the world, gods. They believed that the inventors of certain worldly arts, the founders of cities, or those who held imperial scepters were transferred into gods after death; they called them “divine,” and their images were called gods.

Having despised the true God and rejected humility, demonic or human arrogance usurped these names for itself. A Christian ought to hate such names just as he hates their author. For whoever has rejected the author of falsehood ought to reject falsehood; and whoever rejects falsehood ought also to reject the name “liar.”

Whoever, therefore, has rejected the author of falsehood ought also to reject the name “liar.” The author of falsehood is the one of whom it was said: “From the beginning he was a liar and did not stand in the truth” (John VIII).

The name “divine” is not undeservedly a lying name, since it attempts to assert that sinners, who have been handed over according to their merits to eternal punishments, have attained divinity.

If the lovers of this name admit that it has nothing to do with divinity, let them listen to the pagans themselves, who used this name more familiarly in their writings and were accustomed to use *divos* for *dis* and *deos* for *divis* almost indifferently.

They used *divi* for *dei*, as in the following passage from Virgil:

> “You grant me to recline at the feasts of the gods,”

and again:

> “He asks, ‘What are those divine powers of the gods?’”

That is, “of the gods.”

They used *dei* for *divi*, as in the following:

> “Whether you come as a god of the boundless sea,  
> and do your divine powers alone receive the sailors?”

This was said to Octavian, whom they believed would be transferred into a god after death.

Let the ambition of the false name cease, then; let the remnant of the ancient error be abandoned; let the term of blind superstition wither away; let the arrogance of the presumptuous name be renounced; let the pagan falsehood that human beings are to be transferred into gods be driven from the faithful.

Now truth has arisen from the earth; now the sun of justice has risen for the faithful; now the one who sat in darkness has seen a great light; now light has arisen for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death. All false things have been nullified by the coming of truth.

For if the pagan opinion of false gods is false, the story that human beings are transferred into gods after death is false. But if the story that human beings are transferred into gods after death is false, the designation “divine” is vain. Therefore, if the pagan opinion of false gods is false, the name “divine” too is vain.

It is therefore plainly evident that a false thing has a false name, and that those who are disciples of truth ought not to be called by a false name.

If, indeed, some Catholics are occasionally found to have called the dead “of divine memory,” it is clear that they followed pagan usage, just as the names of days and months are often taken from pagan vanities. But these and similar expressions were admitted more by Roman ambition than by apostolic tradition.

Finally, we who are both followers of truth and redeemed by truth itself must reject pagan names just as we rejected the falsehood of pagan gods. The Apostle teaches this when he says: “What fellowship does light have with darkness? And what agreement does Christ have with Belial?” (II Cor. VI).

May we be freed, with his assent, from that agreement—he who rescued us from darkness and the shadow of death and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning what Constantine and Haerena wrote in their letter to the venerable Pope Adrian of the city of Rome: “We ask your fatherhood, and God especially asks it, who wishes no human being to perish.”

Whoever presumptuously dares to say that God reigns together with him, and arrogantly and in pagan fashion to call his own deeds divine, will undoubtedly also dare to say that God, whose is the kingdom and dominion, must ask someone—so that, while arrogating rash eminence to himself, he may attempt to detract something from the authority of the divine majesty. Nor is it surprising that he presumes to exalt his own affairs, when with unlearned words he strives to abase divine things.

For God is read to have created the light by commanding, separated the waters from the waters, set a firmament as a boundary between them so that they would not again be confused, made the earth fertile with many kinds of seed, and adorned heaven with the splendid radiance of shining stars,

> [Note: [Col. 1015] “And [he filled] the waters with creatures that swim, and the air with creatures that fly.” Thus Lindenbruch corrected the passage, since the printed editions read *natalibus*, which here is a meaningless word.]

and filled the waters with creatures that swim and the air with creatures that fly, and accomplished the creation either of the human being or of all things—in contrast to which these men say, “We ask your paternity, and above all God asks, who wishes no human being to perish.”

Of Moses it is written that he did what the Lord had commanded (Exod. XL); and the same author writes: “At the command of the Lord the children of Israel broke camp, and at the command of the Lord they pitched it” (Num. IX). Yet this man says that “God above all asks,” although he is immutable, ineffable, and eternal, and created and governs the nature of all visible and invisible things by command—now begins to ask.

This word, however, belongs not to power but to supplication, not to authority but to necessity, not to one who commands but to one who entreats. Since there is no neediness in God, and asking belongs to one who entreats, while entreating belongs to one in need, whoever says that God asks someone undoubtedly attributes neediness to him. If neediness is present in him, necessity is present as well. If necessity is present, omnipotence is absent. But omnipotence belongs to him; therefore neediness is absent.

For it is written of him: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. CXIII). If they happen to say that the word “ask” can appropriately be applied to him because of the person of the Son, who, according to the Apostle, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II), let them hear him say: “Lazarus, come out” (John XI); and again, “Take up your pallet and go” (John V, XI); and again, “Talitha cumi [Little girl, arise]” (Mark V); and once more, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke VII); and other words of this kind. These are the words not of one who asks but of one who commands, not of one who petitions but of one who orders. We read that the apostles also possessed the power of this command in his name.

For the shepherd of the Church, after healing Aeneas, says: “In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, arise and walk” (Acts III). Behold: in the name of Jesus Peter commands, while they say that Jesus ought to ask. A servant, by command in the name of the Lord, grants health to a sick man, while they say that he ought to ask the priest. This must be attributed not to prudence but to the height of madness.

If they wish, perhaps, to use for the defense of their error what Truth itself says—“I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John XIV)—and also, “Father, glorify your name” (John XII), let them consider that he did not say this according to his divinity, in which he remains of one substance with the Father and equal to the Father, of which he says, “I and the Father are one” (John X), but according to his humanity, by which “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I), and of which he says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

Although, in the form of a servant, he is less than the Father, in the form of God he is undoubtedly believed to be equal to him. Hence the Apostle says, “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II)—that is, it was not for him like robbery, as though he were seeking what belonged to another. For just as he is coeternal with the Father, so also he is coequal with him. The same Apostle confesses him to be true man and true God when he says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

If, according to their stupidity, it is necessary for him to ask someone, he is subordinate to someone. And if he is subordinate to someone, he is not “over all.” But he is over all; therefore it is not necessary for him to ask anyone.

Let the authors of this statement hear—let them hear—what blessed Ambrose said concerning this word against certain enemies of the faith:

> “But it has been read that he asked. Learn the distinction: he asks as the Son of Man; he commands as the Son of God. Do you not attribute to the Son of God what even the devil attributed, while you detract from him with greater sacrilege? The devil says, ‘If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.’ He says, ‘Command’; you say, ‘Entreat.’ He believes that, when the Son of God commands, the nature of the elements and of things is changed into its opposite; you believe that, unless the Son of God asks, not even his will is fulfilled.”

Thus, armed with the dagger of faith’s armor, this warrior of the Church fought against the enemies of the faith. Whoever fears being numbered among them should flee the madness of such a statement.

Meanwhile, let the holy Evangelist say what the Lord did for the disciples when they were afraid and the little boat was already being covered by the waves. “Then,” he says, “he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about” (Matt. VIII; Mark IV; Luke VIII).

Let him also say what the centurion said to the Lord when the latter was intending to go to his house and heal the boy: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my boy will be healed” (Matt. VIII).

O disastrous utterance! O accursed error! O pride that produces swelling rather than strength, inflation rather than power! The centurion believes that the one who would be mocked, scourged, suffer, taste death, and descend to the underworld can heal the boy by a mere word of command; and you say that he who sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, must ask someone! It is therefore not necessary for him to ask who is believed to possess authority over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things.

## CHAPTER V. That it is no small sacrilege to understand the Holy Scriptures otherwise than they ought to be understood, and to adapt them to meanings that they do not contain—as happened in the erroneous synod held in Bithynia during the reign of Constantine, with his mother Haerena acting as intermediary and Tharasius, bishop of Constantinople, presiding

From the oracle of the sacred law we have learned that, when the rock was struck, streams flowed forth for the thirsty people; and by apostolic teaching we are instructed that this same rock must be understood as Christ.

Since he is the rock whose streams irrigate parched hearts; the river whose current gladdens the city of God; the fountain of life from which everlasting life flows to believers; and the heavenly bread that removes the hunger of eternal famine from the hearts of the faithful—whoever receives his spiritual drinks and spiritual foods in a manner other than that in which he gives them, and strives to interpret the divine Scriptures according to another meaning rather than the one in which they were handed down by the Holy Spirit, is shown to be alien from his pastures.

“For the words of the Lord,” says the Prophet, “are pure words, silver tested in the fire” (Ps. XII). The man who strives to join them to the mixture of an alien meaning undoubtedly seeks to corrupt their purity with adulterous defilement. For whoever, out of a desire for arrogance and empty praise, draws the testimony of the divine Scriptures into the defense of his own error—what else does he do but shamefully seize the purity of divine speech for adultery? And he drags silver tested in the fire of the divine Spirit into the pollution of other metals, that is, of foreign meanings.

Of such people the Lord complains through the Prophet: “I gave them silver and gold, and they made Baal” (Hos. II)—that is, they turned the dignity of spiritual understanding and the beauty of eloquence into the monstrosity of depraved meanings and empty glory.

Since the lawgiver says, “In the right hand of the Lord is a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII), it is astonishing how great is the dullness of those who are neither soothed by its brightness nor terrified by its heat. For just as it illuminates by the splendor of its brightness those who approach it with a pure understanding and devoted mind, so, conversely, it burns by the greatness of its heat those who approach it rashly in order to usurp it for themselves.

Thus those who cling to it with humble minds and consecrated understandings have their steps secured in the course of the present life by the illumination of that lamp; but those who seek it with foreign and presumptuous meanings are consumed by the burning of eternal fire. This was prefigured in the four sons of Aaron.

When Eleazar and Ithamar, offering the sanctuary’s fire to the Lord according to Moses’ institution, attained the dignity of the priestly office, Nadab and Abihu, attempting to offer foreign fire to the Lord, were punished with the most fearful and atrocious kind of death. Whoever wishes to avoid their danger ought to flee their example.

Whom, then—whom do those who seize upon rightly spoken words and interpret them wrongly imitate in this deed, except the one who attempts to interpret what was said of a simple and righteous man as referring to the Mediator between God and humanity, when he says:

> “For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone’” (Matt. IV).

So that the argument of his temptation might be stronger, he drew upon an example from the divine writings, by which the drink of his temptation might be swallowed more readily if it possessed the seasoning of the Holy Scriptures.

> [Note: For unless he is to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures and followed in easy temptations. The passage is corrupt and wholly divergent in meaning. I restore it as the sense requires: “For if he is to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures, and followed in deceptive temptations; and if he is to be followed in deceptive temptations, then he is to be embraced in the rest of his conduct; but he is not to be embraced in the rest of his conduct; therefore he is not to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures.” Nothing could be truer; and this confirms what is read in Book III, chapter 12: “And having rejected deceptive byways.”]

For if he is to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures and followed in deceptive temptations; and if he is to be followed in deceptive temptations, then he is to be embraced in the rest of his conduct. But he is not to be embraced in the rest of his conduct; therefore he is not to be imitated in interpreting the Scriptures.

Blessed Jerome says: “The devil interprets the Scriptures badly.” Heretics and schismatics, who are certainly his followers, understand the divine Scriptures badly, interpret them worse, and observe them worst of all.

Catholics, however, instructed in the examples of Truth, both resist the temptations of the ancient enemy and oppose the machinations of heretics. Receiving the manna of the divine word with a pure and sound understanding, they are nourished by its sweet food. For the manna collected improperly does not boil forth worms in them—that is, it does not pierce the hidden places of their conscience and the innermost recesses of their understanding with the goads of pride.

Having therefore examined what Constantine and Haerena wrote either arrogantly or ignorantly to Adrian, the venerable pope of the city of Rome, or having summarized as briefly as possible how the Holy Scriptures ought to be understood, interpreted, and adapted—not according to each person’s own whim and private meaning, but according to sound and sober doctrine—we shall now, with the Lord’s favor, proceed in due order through the testimonies collected from the Holy Scriptures and the treatises of the holy Fathers, which were appropriated disorderly and improperly by those known to have sat in the aforementioned synod.

We shall set out only in summary what judgment the holy Fathers established concerning these matters, and how the venerable men expressed the things that those men’s madness heaped together in order to support their error. After these matters have been listed in the present two first books, the sequence of the following two books, with the Lord’s favor, will examine what constitution they produced in their own poorly instructed judgment and against the teaching of the holy Fathers concerning the excessive worship of images.

In the following chapter we shall first explain how the holy Roman Church, held in the highest veneration among the other Churches, ought to be consulted concerning matters of faith.

## CHAPTER VI. That the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, preferred above the other Churches, must be consulted whenever a question arises concerning matters of faith

Before we enter the forest of the testimonies that the Easterners absurdly censured in their synod, we have judged it worthwhile to explain how the holy Roman Church has been preferred by the Lord above the other Churches and ought to be consulted by the faithful.

This is especially so because testimonies must be taken only from those Scriptures that it receives among the canonical books, and the doctrines of no teachers other than those accepted by Gelasius or by the other pontiffs of that holy see ought to be embraced. Nor should what they have said be understood in one way and another according to anyone’s whim, but soundly and soberly.

For blessed Augustine, when he was laying down which writings ought to be received and how they ought to be understood, says:

> “The most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures will therefore be the one who first reads all the canonical Scriptures and has them familiar to him—if not yet in understanding, at least in reading. For he will read the others more securely, instructed in the faith of the truth, lest they seize an unsteady mind and, deceiving it with dangerous falsehoods and phantasms, establish some prejudice against sound understanding. But in the canonical Scriptures let him follow above all the authority of the Catholic Churches. Among these, let those especially be followed that have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive letters.”

Since here he generally prefers the apostolic sees to all the sees established throughout the world, that Church must all the more be preferred above every other which has itself been preferred above the other apostolic sees.

Therefore, just as the apostles stand above the other disciples, and Peter above all the apostles, so without doubt the apostolic sees are surpassed by the Roman see. For this Church was preferred above the other Churches not by synodal decrees but by the authority of the Lord himself, who says:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Not inappropriately, the fellowship of blessed Paul, the teacher of the nations, was added to him, so that the authority of that holy Church might be completely strengthened: one chosen from a fisherman to fish for souls, the other from a persecutor to fortify the Church; so that in the one the true confession of the Son of God might appear, and in the other the sacred preaching of the divine Word.

The same Son of God granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to one and the key for opening the words of the Law to the other. To both, however, he granted the power of signs. One approached him by the cross, the other by the sword; and, leaving the faithful a pledge of their bodily burden, by the radiance of their example, the beauty of their word, and their holy blood, they dedicated the aforementioned Roman Church to him.

Founded upon the most solid rock, that Church could be made to fall neither by descending rain, nor by coming rivers, nor by blowing winds. Thus fortified with the spiritual weapons of holy faith, nourished by saving streams from the fountain of light and the source of goodness, she resists the dreadful and savage monsters of heresies and supplies the Catholic Churches throughout the world with the honey-sweet cups of preaching.

For when blessed Jerome, a man learned in the divine laws and skilled in many languages, was staying in the fields of Bethlehem and was consulted by blessed Pope Damasus, who was stationed at Rome, concerning difficult questions, Jerome in turn is known to have consulted him concerning matters of faith. In the humblest of letters he asks whether certain *hypostases* should be mentioned or kept silent, and with whom he ought to communicate in the Eastern regions.

A remarkable matter, worthy of the highest praise! He asks the man by whom he is asked; he consults the man by whom he is consulted. Although he knows himself to be a teacher in interpreting the divine Scriptures, he is not ashamed to be the disciple of the venerable pontiff in matters of faith. To the man to whom he explains the knots of questions concerning the sacred law, he earnestly asks whether he ought to say *hypostasis* and with whom he should communicate in the East.

From this it is understood that holy and learned men, shining throughout the various parts of the world with the lamp of preaching and knowledge, not only did not withdraw from the holy Roman Church, but also, in a time of need, sought help from her for the strengthening of the faith.

As we have said above and demonstrated by examples, all Catholic Churches ought regularly to observe this practice: after Christ, they should seek help from her for the fortification of the faith. She has no spot or wrinkle, tramples upon the monstrous heads of heresies, and strengthens the minds of the faithful in the faith.

Although many have withdrawn from communion with this holy and venerable Church, the Church of our region has never withdrawn from it. Instructed by its apostolic teaching, and receiving from him from whom every good gift and every perfect endowment comes (James I), it has always accepted venerable spiritual gifts.

Since, from the earliest times of the faith, it had persevered with that Church in the unity of sacred religion, and since it differed from it only slightly in the celebration of offices—a difference that is nevertheless not against the faith—through the care and industry of our father of revered memory, the most illustrious and excellent man, King Pippin, and through the arrival in Gaul of the most reverend and holy man Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, it was also joined to that Church in the order of psalmody.

Thus the order of psalmody would not be different among those whose fervor of belief was the same; and those who were united by the sacred reading of one holy law would also be united by the venerable tradition of one melody [or: melodic form]. The varied celebration of the offices would not separate those whom the pious devotion of one faith had joined together.

We too, when God granted us the kingdom of Italy, did this, desiring to exalt the dignity of the holy Roman Church and striving to obey the salutary exhortations of the most reverend Pope Adrian. Thus many Churches of that region, which once refused to receive the tradition of the apostolic see in psalmody, now embrace it with complete diligence; and just as they had clung to that faith as a gift, so they also cling to it in the order of psalmody.

Not only all the provinces of Gaul, Germany, and Italy, but also the Saxons and certain peoples of the northern regions, converted through us, with God’s favor, to the beginnings of the true faith, are known to do this. They take care to follow the see of blessed Peter in all things, just as they desire to reach the place where he, the keeper of the keys, stands.

May he enable us to attain that blessedness and preserve us in the fellowship and unity of the holy Church—the one who deigned to found his Church in Peter. Through the intercession of the one whose chair we follow, may we be made participants in the kingdom of heaven, of which he was made the key-bearer.

## CHAPTER VII. That the statement “God created humanity in his image and likeness” (Gen. I) does not concern the worship of images

In this testimony, which they placed in their synod inconsequently—or rather, beyond all consequence—in order to establish the error of worshiping images, we need not labor greatly with our own ingenuity, since so many indications show that it is foreign to their assertion. For where there is no plausibility, no great dispute arises in discerning the matter.

Since no person in whom the acuity of sound judgment is vigorous believes that this statement pertains to the object to which they strive to apply it, but a spiritual saying must be examined by spiritual inquiry, it remains for us to record, with concise judgment, what the writings of the holy Fathers have said about it. Thus what they negligently appropriated, but venerable men filled with the Holy Spirit expressed spiritually, may be carefully received through the reader’s diligence.

Blessed Ambrose says:

> “At the beginning of the world itself I hear that there are the Father and the Son, and I see one work. I hear one speaking; I recognize another making. Yet I also read of one image and one likeness of the Father and the Son. This likeness is not one of difference but of unity.
>
> “For a human being cannot be in the image of God except through the image of God. The image of God, therefore, must be considered from the nobility of the inner person. First, just as God, being one, is always and everywhere wholly present, giving life to, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle confirms when he says that in him we live, move, and have our being—so the soul is wholly vigorous throughout its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it.
>
> “It is not greater in the larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller members, but wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the largest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God that the soul possesses in itself. The soul also bears a certain image of the holy Trinity: first, because just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and knows.
>
> “There is also another trinity in it, by which it was created in the image of its Creator, the perfect and supreme Trinity that exists in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although it is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses three faculties in itself: understanding, will, and memory. The same is designated, although in different words, in the Gospel when it says: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind’ (Deut. VI)—that is, with all your understanding, all your will, and all your memory.
>
> “Just as the Son is generated from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so from understanding the will is generated, and from these two together memory proceeds, as any wise person can easily understand.
>
> “The soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three, so far as its blessedness is concerned, be complete without the other two. And just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet there are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so the soul is understanding, the soul is will, and the soul is memory, yet there are not three souls in one body but one soul possessing three faculties.
>
> “In these three our inner person wonderfully bears his image in our nature.
>
> “Likeness, however, must be discerned in conduct. Just as God the Creator, who created humanity in his likeness, is love, goodness, justice, patience, gentleness, purity, mercy, and the other marks of the virtues that are read of him, so the human being was created to possess love, to be good, just, patient, gentle, pure, and merciful. The more each person possesses these virtues in himself, the nearer he is to God and the greater likeness of his Creator he bears.”

Blessed Augustine likewise explained that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God:

> “Since divine Scripture mentions the outer and inner person, distinguishes them so clearly, and the Apostle says, ‘Although our outer person is being corrupted, the inner person is renewed day by day,’ it may be asked whether one of these was made in the image and likeness of God.
>
> “For it would be foolish to ask this; if anyone doubts which of them it is, he should say that it is rather the one who is being renewed than the one who is being corrupted. But whether both were made so is a great question.
>
> “For if the outer person is Adam and the inner person is Christ, both are rightly understood. Yet since Adam, although made good by God, did not remain so, and by loving carnal things became carnal, it may not absurdly be thought that his fall consisted precisely in losing the image and likeness of God. Thus he himself is renewed, and he himself is also the inner person.
>
> “How, then, is he both outer and inner—outer according to the body and inner according to the soul? The inner person is the resurrection and renewal that now takes place through the death of the former life, that is, sin, and through the regeneration of the new life, that is, righteousness. The same writer calls these two persons by such names that he recalls one as the old person whom we ought to strip off, and the other as the new person whom we ought to put on.
>
> “Again, he calls the former the image of the earthly person, because he is formed according to the sin of the first person, Adam; and the latter the image of the heavenly person, because he is formed according to the righteousness of the second person, Christ.
>
> “The outer person, which is now being corrupted, will be renewed in the future resurrection when it has paid the debt of death owed by nature, according to the law that was given in paradise through the commandment.
>
> “That the body too can be said to have been made in the likeness of God is easily understood by anyone who carefully considers the statement, ‘And God made all things very good’ (Gen. I). No one doubts that he himself is supremely good.
>
> “Things can be said to be like God in many ways. Some were made according to virtue and wisdom, since in him there is uncreated virtue and wisdom; others insofar as they merely live, since he lives supremely and primarily; others insofar as they exist, since he is supremely and primarily being.
>
> “Therefore things that merely exist but neither live nor know are not perfectly but only slightly like him, because they too are good in their proper order, while he is good above all, from whom they receive their goodness.
>
> “All things that live but do not know participate somewhat more fully in likeness, for whatever lives also exists, whereas not everything that exists also lives.
>
> “Things that know, however, are so close to that likeness that among creatures nothing is nearer. Whatever participates in wisdom both lives and exists; but whatever lives must exist, whereas it need not know.
>
> “Since, therefore, the human being can participate in wisdom according to the inner person, according to that inner person he is in the image in such a way that no intervening nature is formed between him and God. For this reason nothing is more closely joined to God: he knows, lives, and exists. No creature is better than this.
>
> “If the outer person is understood as possessing the life by which we perceive through the five most familiar senses, which we share with animals—for this life too can be corrupted by sensory afflictions inflicted through persecutions—it is not without reason that the human being himself is said to participate in the likeness of God, not only because he lives, as is also evident in beasts, but even more because he turns toward the mind that governs him and which wisdom illuminates, something impossible in beasts, which lack reason.
>
> “The human body too, because among the bodies of earthly animals it alone is not stretched prone upon its belly but is visible and raised upright for looking toward heaven, which is the principle of visible things, may rightly be considered more made in the image and likeness of God in this respect than the bodies of other animals. Yet although it is known to live not by its own power but through the presence of the soul, it is good not only because it exists and insofar as it exists, but also because it is so constituted as to be more suited for contemplating heaven.
>
> “Nevertheless, since a human being without life is not rightly called a human being, it may perhaps be more correct to understand the outer person as both together, not the body alone nor merely the life that operates through bodily sensation.
>
> “Nor is it an unintelligent distinction to say that the image and likeness of God—who is also called the Son—is one thing, while another is what we understand when we say that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God.
>
> “There are also those who rightly understand the two expressions ‘in the image’ and ‘in the likeness’ as referring to two things. They argue that, if there were one thing, one name would have sufficed. They wish the mind to have been made ‘in the image,’ since it is formed by the truth itself without any intervening substance. This mind is also called spirit—not the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, but the human spirit.
>
> “For the Apostle distinguishes these in this way: ‘No one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being; and no one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God’ (1 Cor. II). He likewise says of the human spirit: ‘May he preserve your spirit, soul, and body.’ This spirit too was made by God, just like the rest of creation.
>
> “For it is written in Proverbs in this manner: ‘Know that the Lord knows the hearts of human beings, and he himself who formed the spirit of all knows all things.’
>
> “Therefore this spirit is understood without doubt to have been made ‘in the image’ of God, since it possesses the understanding of truth and clings to the truth without any intervening creature. They wish the other aspects of the human being to have been made ‘in the likeness,’ because every image is similar, but not everything that is similar is properly an image, although it may perhaps be called one by an abuse of language.
>
> “In such matters, however, care must be taken not to assert anything too strongly, while preserving this salutary principle: since every body is extended through spatial dimensions, no one should believe that anything of this kind is the substance of God. For a thing that is smaller in a part than in the whole is not fitting for the dignity of the soul—how much less for the majesty of God?”

Behold how subtly and beneficially these holy men explained that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God: the image in the soul, in which there are understanding, will, and memory; the likeness in conduct, that is, in love, justice, goodness, and holiness—all of which are incorporeal.

How far those who apply this testimony to images formed by the hands of craftsmen are removed from the meaning and teaching of these men is not for our eloquence to discuss but for the reader’s judgment to decide, so that his own understanding, rather than our pen, may warn him how great is their folly in this matter.

Whoever therefore believes that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God in the same way that an image is formed by an artisan in the image of a human being shows that he believes in something corporeal in God—something which it is impious to believe.

For if the fact that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God applies to images made by hand, then the human being was made in the image of God according to corporeal form. And if the human being was made in the image of God according to corporeal form, then God is corporeal. But God is incorporeal. Therefore the fact that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God does not apply to images made by hand.

## CHAPTER VIII. What is the difference between image and likeness, or equality
Because, with God’s help, we have explained—imbued with the sound and sober teaching of the holy Fathers—how the statement that God created man in his own image and likeness is to be understood [Col. 1025D] (Gen. I), it is now worthwhile briefly to explain what difference there is between image and likeness, or also equality. Thus those who, on account of their desire to adore images, are carried headlong through the open fields of empty assertions may recognize the difference between these three things—which they regard as almost entirely one and the same—and perceive the magnitude of their error; and all diligent readers may advance toward certain gains in understanding.

These three must therefore be distinguished, because everything that is an image is a likeness, though not everything that is a likeness is an image; and although an image is never without likeness, a likeness often exists without an image. Moreover, both likeness and image are generally known to lack equality, although equality can sometimes be joined both to image and to likeness. Although these three belong to one category, which is called relation, they nevertheless possess among themselves certain properties that the others lack.

For it is proper to an image that it is always expressed from something else; whereas it is proper to likeness and equality that, remaining in their own substance, they are judged by this name not because they have been expressed from something else, but because they have been made like or equal to other things. An image does not admit of “more” or “less,” but likeness and equality do. For one is said to be more similar or less similar, more equal or less equal; one cannot similarly be said to be more of an image or less of an image.

There is also a subtle opposition in the conversion of these terms, which in Greek is called *antistrophe*. It would take too long to pursue all of this; nevertheless, so that the difference among these three names may become clearer, the words of blessed Augustine should be brought forward. He says:

“Where there is an image, there is not necessarily likeness, nor necessarily equality; where there is equality, there is necessarily likeness, but not necessarily an image; where there is likeness, there is not necessarily an image, nor necessarily equality. Thus in a mirror there is an image, because it has been expressed from that which it reflects; there is also necessarily likeness, but not equality, because many things that are present in the object from which it has been expressed are absent from the image.

“Where there is equality, there is necessarily also likeness, but not necessarily an image—as in two equal eggs: because equality is present, likeness is present. For whatever is present in one is also present in the other; yet there is no image, because neither has been expressed from the other.

“Where there is likeness, there is not necessarily an image, nor necessarily equality. Every egg, insofar as it is an egg, is like every other egg; but although a partridge’s egg, insofar as it is an egg, is like a hen’s egg, it is nevertheless not its image, because it has not been expressed from it; nor is it equal, because it is smaller and belongs to another kind of animal.

“But when it is said ‘not necessarily,’ this clearly means that it can sometimes be so. There can therefore be an image in which there is also equality: thus in parents and children there would be image, equality, and likeness if the interval of time did not intervene. For the likeness of the child has been expressed from the parent, so that it is rightly called an image; and it may be so great that it may rightly also be called equality, except that the parent precedes in time. From this it is understood that equality can sometimes possess not only likeness but also image, as is clear in the example just given.

“There can also sometimes be likeness and equality without an image, as we said of equal eggs. There can be likeness and image without equality, as we showed in the mirror. There can also be likeness where both equality and image are present, as we mentioned in the case of children, except for the time by which parents precede them.”

Having briefly set forth these rules concerning their difference, let us proceed in the proper order to the matters begun, so that the testimonies of divine law improperly appropriated by them may be correctly expounded by us according to the teaching of the venerable Fathers. Thus their flight may be exposed, with the wings they arrogantly attached to themselves broken, while the understanding of diligent readers who desire to use these matters well may rise to higher things.

## CHAPTER IX. How the statement that Abraham adored the people of the land, the sons of Heth (Gen.
