XXIII), is to be understood, and likewise the statement that Moses is read to have adored Jethro; examples by which those who hold synods on behalf of the adoration of images seek to support their error; and the fact that neither Jacob adored Pharaoh nor Daniel King Nebuchadnezzar, as they claim

Those who burn with zeal for the adoration of images make particular and habitual use of the example that Abraham is read to have adored the sons of Heth, and Moses Jethro, the priest of Midian. Their adoration is as far removed from the adoration of a painted image as a painted man himself is removed from the nature of a real man. For just as a real man is distinguished from a painted one, a rational being from an irrational one, a sensible being from an insensible one, and an animate being from an inanimate one in their definitions, so without doubt the adoration of the former is distinguished from the adoration of the latter.

For it is one thing to greet a human being by an act of salutation and a service of human courtesy, and another to adore a picture composed of pigments of various colors—without movement, voice, or any of the other senses—by some unknown form of worship. We are taught by the examples of almost all the holy Scriptures that we should love the brotherhood, show affection toward our neighbors, and embrace the degree of humility by which, when greeting one another, we adore one another. But we are restrained rather than instructed to adore images, salute them, or worship certain senseless vanities, in almost every passage of divine Scripture.

For, to pass over the others, the most sacred shepherd upon whom the holy Church has been founded as upon the firmest rock does not say, “Love images,” but “Love the brotherhood” (I Pet. II); nor does he say, “Be subject to paintings,” but “to every human creature” (Rom. XIII; I Pet. II). And he instructs us to sanctify the Lord Christ not by images but in our hearts.

It is utterly foolish and entirely contrary to reason to use as an argument for the adoration of images the fact that Abraham is read to have adored the people of the land and Moses the priest of Midian, when holy men often, through the humility by which they pleased God, adored human beings as a form of greeting; often humbly avoided being adored by others; and often, raised upright by the strictness of their holiness, refused to adore the proud. They never even attempted to adore images in the slightest.

For in the fact that Abraham and Moses are read to have adored humble men who were useful to their interests, while Mordecai is found to have refused to adore the arrogant Haman, who thirsted for the destruction of God’s people, this is clearly shown: holy men are companions of the humble through that same humility, either to urge them toward better things or not to lose the gifts of that supreme virtue; but against the wickedness of the perverse they stand firmly, either to avoid association with evil people or to compel them to recover their senses.

Thus, when John in the Apocalypse is restrained by the angel from adoring him, the same angel saying, “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant” (Apoc. XIX and XXII); and when Peter, the shepherd of the Church, gently avoided the centurion’s adoration, saying, “Arise, brother; I also am a man just as you are” (Acts X); and when Paul, the chosen vessel, with Barnabas rejected the adoration of the Lycaonians by vigorous resistance—it is undoubtedly forbidden that the adoration which befits God alone—who alone is to be adored and alone worshiped—be rendered to any created being, except in the case of salutation, by which humility is demonstrated.

Let blessed Augustine therefore tell us—let him tell us, most holy Augustine—what he thought about this adoration of Abraham or Moses. He says:

“Here also an example of humility is suggested: Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or despise the counsel of his foreign father-in-law, although it is reasonably asked whether Jethro himself, since he was not an Israelite, should be counted among men who worshiped the true God and were religiously wise, just as it is asked concerning Job, who was not from that people; indeed, it is considered more credible that he was. For the words have been placed ambiguously: whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law, or whether Moses himself adored him.

“Even if the adoration had been expressly stated, it would seem to have been honor rendered to his father-in-law in the manner in which honor is customarily shown to human beings for the sake of respect by their fathers, just as it is written concerning Abraham that he adored the sons of Heth.”

Nor should we pass over in silence the claim that Jacob adored Pharaoh, or Daniel King Nebuchadnezzar. This is found nowhere either in the Hebrew text or in our Latin books, which were translated by blessed Jerome from the Hebrew truth. Jacob is not recorded to have been in Pharaoh’s presence more than once; and Scripture narrates the matter in this way:

“After these things Joseph brought his father before the king and set him before him. He blessed him, and, when asked by him, ‘How many are the days of the years of your life?’ Jacob answered: ‘The days of the pilgrimage and of my life are one hundred and thirty years; they are few and evil, and they have not reached the days of my fathers in which they were pilgrims.’ And after blessing the king, he went out.”

In these words he is shown not to have adored Pharaoh but to have blessed him. Even if he had done so, however, he would not have done it so that an example of the adoration of images might be drawn from it, but so that the humility of the holy patriarch, who feared God and honored the king, might be demonstrated.

Since matters stand thus, I think they suppose that divine Scripture uses that very familiar manner of speech of theirs which some call *acyrology*, so that it has put “to bless” in place of “to adore.” This manner of speaking is so characteristic of them that they themselves use “to possess,” “to salute,” “to kiss,” and “to venerate” in place of “to adore,” accept these usages when employed by others, and, so to speak, have converted almost all words of this kind into “to adore.”

But holy Scripture rejects this manner of speech, as it rejects other errors. It always uses pure, proper, fixed, and precise words or statements, as the Prophet testifies when he says, “The law of the Lord is blameless.” If it has put “to bless” in place of “to adore,” it uses improper expressions. If it uses improper expressions, it is blameworthy. But it is blameless. Therefore it has not put “to bless” in place of “to adore.”

Speak, then; speak, holy Daniel; speak, man of desires; speak, investigator of mysteries; speak, examiner of the Scriptures; speak, prophet who is shown to have proclaimed the Redeemer of the world more clearly than the others. For you not only write that he will come—which you share with the others—but teach at what time he will come, arrange the kings in order, count the years, and announce the clearest signs. Tell us whether you adored Nebuchadnezzar, as they chatter.

“I do not read,” I say, “that I did this in my book.” Even if I had done so, their assertion would in no way be supported by it. I resolved in my heart not to defile myself with his table or with the wine of his drink, and they say that I adored him. I spoke to the man who fell on his face, adored me, ordered sacrifices and incense to be offered to me, confessed God as the God of gods, the Lord of kings, and the revealer of mysteries who can disclose secrets, and who addressed me with flattering words, adoring not me but rather him in me because of the greatness of the signs, since I am his dwelling place. I asked him to exercise mercy continually toward the people of Israel, or to appoint my fellow captives Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael over the administration of the province of Babylon. I did not adore him with flattery.

Even if I had adored him, I would not have adored some insensible thing. Remaining subject through the duty of humility to a higher power, and knowing that there is no authority except from God, I would have greeted and adored a rational human being. For since I once enjoyed such a blameless way of life that, when opportunities were sought from the king’s side by which I might be accused by the envious, I was accused only concerning the laws of my God, and was thrown into the lions’ den, and now am accused of having adored one whom I did not adore, and am said by false witnesses to have done what I did not do, it remains for me to cry out with David: “False witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. XXVII).

Since, therefore, on account of their love for images they accuse both the patriarch Jacob and the prophet Daniel, and strive to turn the meaning of the divine Scriptures toward foreign interpretations, while spurning their predecessors or fathers contrary to the command of the law, it remains only that they be content with these things and, if they do not wish to correct their error, be fortified by their protection, as they themselves believe.

Let them glory in images; but let us glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to us and we to the world.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the statement attributed to John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners, who, rashly seeking to establish the adoration of images, is said to have said: “Jacob erected a pillar to God, and therefore blessed it” (Gen. XXXV)

It is a considerable sign of stupidity to offer as an argument for the adoration of images the example that Jacob erected a stone as a pillar, as John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners is read to have proposed in that same synod which was convened on behalf of the adoration of images. For that stone is not believed to have been an image or likeness of anything that had previously happened.

If it had been expressed in likeness to some past event in memory of that event, and if the holy patriarch had erected it for adoration, it might perhaps have offered some support to those who did not fear to incur the peril of so great an error. But it is one thing for a patriarch to do something as a prefiguration of future events, and another for a painter to paint something in memory of past deeds; one thing to be filled with the Holy Spirit, and another to be trained in the art of painting; one thing for this man to act by reliance upon a heavenly gift, and another for that man to act through acquired technical skill; one thing for Jacob to erect a stone as a pillar, and another for a painter to set an image upon a wall; one thing to pour oil upon it according to a typological figure, and another to command its adoration according to a vain assertion.

It is useless—indeed, more than useless—to offer as an example for establishing anything an act which, by every argumentative byway, appears to differ entirely from that matter.

Did Jacob erect that stone to be adored? Or did he paint in it an image of anything? Since images have almost no other function than to bring a remembrance to minds through their appearance, the stone erected by the patriarch is believed to have possessed three notable functions worthy of the highest honor.

First, it supported the neck of Israel and served as a pillow for the patriarch, who lacked pillows; it bore the head of the man who saw not only a ladder extending from earth all the way to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it, but also the Lord himself promising him good things.

Second, it was erected as a sign and pillar so that the holy patriarch might remember that holy place. When he returned, rejoicing in the affection of his children and wives and enriched with great possessions, he would render his vows to the Lord who had granted him all these things.

Third, it bore the type of our Mediator, who was made the cornerstone and is wonderful in our eyes; who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions; whom Daniel calls the stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it—namely, begotten from a virginal womb without intercourse and human seed.

David also calls him a rock, saying, “The Lord is my rock, my strength, and my Savior” (Ps. XXXVII). Concerning him it is also written in the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a supreme, angular, tested, chosen, precious stone, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. XXIV).

He is called angular because he joins together in himself two walls coming from opposite directions—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision, or also the two Testaments—in the supreme, tested, chosen, and precious stone, and unites them in the one assembly of the holy Church, of which he is the head.

Concerning him the paternal voice also says through the prophet Zechariah: “Behold, I shall bring my son, the Orient: for the stone which I have placed before Jesus has seven eyes in it” (Zech. III). In these seven eyes the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, which proceeds from the Father and the Son, is clearly shown. Through the prophet Isaiah he is named as follows: “The Spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI).

Concerning this angular stone the rock of the Church says: “As newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow toward salvation, if indeed you have tasted how sweet the Lord is; approaching him, a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God” (I Pet. II). And shortly afterward:

“To you therefore there is honor who believe; but to those who do not believe, the stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to those who stumble at the word and do not believe, for which they were appointed” (ibid.).

By this testimony it is shown that he is both an honor of strength to believers and a stumbling-block of hardness to unbelievers. This too was foretold in the same sense through the righteous Simeon. For he says: “This one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke II)—for the fall of unbelievers, that is, and the resurrection of believers. He is also called fire, either because he illuminates those who believe in him with the radiance of eternal light, or because he will roast unbelievers with the heat of eternal fire.

The anointing of this stone was proclaimed somewhat earlier in David’s prophetic utterances and must now also be set forth according to the testimony of the aforementioned shepherd of the Church, who says: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and power” (Acts X). Since the Holy Spirit is often indicated in the divine Scriptures under the name of oil, the apostle John is witness, saying: “His anointing teaches us about everything” (I John II).

If they have been touched by the anointing of this unspeakable nectar in order to establish the adoration of images, they certainly ought not to convene synods or appropriate the holy Scriptures to foreign meanings.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the statement attributed to the aforementioned John: “He wrestled with him in the form of a man, and he called him Israel, which is interpreted: ‘A mind seeing God’”

Nor is the statement free from criticism that the same John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners is reported, among his other ravings concerning Jacob, to have said: “He wrestled with him in the form of a man, and he called him Israel, which is interpreted, ‘A mind seeing God.’” This statement is far removed from the subject under discussion, and in the interpretation of the name he omits a more customary interpretation and presents something almost unheard of.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] In the interpretation of the name he omits a more customary one and makes something almost unheard-of resound. The corrector, removing *τῷ*—“the more customary”—substituted *visitation* from his own conjecture, though I cannot determine what he intended by it. “The more customary,” with *interpretation* understood by *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*—that is, supplied from the common construction. [Col. 1032D] What follows supports this: “Having passed over the more customary interpretations, he brought forward something almost unheard-of.” The more customary interpretation is the one he places last: “Prince with God.”]

For while some interpret that name as “A man seeing God,” and others as “Strong with God,” and some, more truthfully, as “Prince with God,” I do not know whether anyone among those whose interpretations are admitted into the canon is found to have interpreted it as “A mind seeing God.” Therefore not only is he to be criticized for passing over the more customary interpretations and presenting something almost unheard-of, but also the entire synod, which assented to him while he was dreaming in many respects. It not only failed to oppose what he said but also entered his statements in its official record.

Since the holy Church, according to the institution of the holy Fathers, accepts everything that is irreprehensible and rejects everything that is reprehensible, it also rejects this synod of theirs, which is plainly reprehensible. If it does not reject what is reprehensible, neither does it accept what is irreprehensible. But it accepts what is irreprehensible. Therefore, because this synod is open to criticism, it must not accept it at all.

The holy and universal Church accepts those synods which, for various causes of faith or religion, were celebrated in different places or at different times by learned and Catholic men and are in no way shown to have deviated from sound and sober doctrine.

Moreover, the wrestling of so great a patriarch with the angel is said to have prefigured not the adoration of images but the Lord’s Passion in that same people. That people prevailed over him by wrestling, because it crucified him; it received blessing from him in those who believed in him; and in those who refused to believe in him it remained lame. Blessed Augustine says:

“That Jacob desired to be blessed by the angel over whom he prevailed by wrestling is a great prophecy concerning Christ. For by that very fact it gives warning that something mystical is intended, since every human being desires to be blessed by one greater. How, then, did this man desire to be blessed by one whom he overcame in wrestling? Jacob prevailed over Christ—or rather appeared to prevail—through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified. Yet he is blessed by him in those Israelites who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said: ‘For I also am an Israelite, of the descendants of Abraham and the tribe of Benjamin’ (Rom. XI). Thus one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed: lame in the breadth of the thigh, as in the multitude of his descendants, concerning whom it is said, ‘They have limped from their paths’ (Ps. XVIII); but blessed in those concerning whom it is said, ‘A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace’ (Rom. XI).”

## CHAPTER XII. That the statement which they make in their synod—that Jacob, receiving from his sons Joseph’s robe, which had been soaked through, kissed it with tears and placed it upon his own eyes (Gen. XXXVII)—does not concern the adoration of images and is not found in our books translated from the Hebrew truth

[Col. 1032D]

It is not surprising that they accuse Jacob of having kissed Joseph’s tunic and placed it upon his eyes, when they also accuse him of having adored Pharaoh. For it often happens that one who has begun to be deceived once is deceived repeatedly; and one who has once departed from the road and neglected to follow the guide of his journey’s path is led abundantly by error through steep and impassable places.

Joseph’s tunic is not related to have been kissed by the father or placed upon his eyes either in the Hebrew books or in the Latin books translated from the Hebrew truth [Col. 1033A]. Even if it were reported to have happened, the adoration of images would in no way, however faintly, be suggested by the act. For to adore is one thing and to kiss another, though they perversely regard these as one and the same; and it is one thing to adore a painted image, another for a fatherly affection and grief to compel a man to place upon his tear-wet eyes the garment of a son believed to have died; one thing to submit one’s neck to a likeness, another to give an intimate kiss to the garment of a beloved son, loved above the others.

The holy patriarch was so distressed by the storm of his troubled spirit that he not only kissed or placed upon his eyes the garment of the son whom he believed to have been taken away by a cruel death, but also, putting consolation aside, lamented grievously in funeral words, magnifying his misfortune and declaring that he too would descend to the underworld after him.

How, then, should blessed Jacob be believed not to have kissed or placed Joseph’s tunic upon his eyes, but merely to have seen and recognized it? Holy Scripture recalls this in the following order. It says:

“They took his tunic and dipped it in the blood of the goat they had killed, sending someone to carry it to their father and say: ‘We found this; see whether it is your son’s tunic or not.’ When the father recognized it, he said: ‘It is my son’s tunic. A most savage beast has eaten him; a beast has devoured Joseph’” (Gen. XXXVII).

Finally, we must briefly explain what this tunic of that holy man, by which they sought to establish the adoration of images, prefigured through typological mysteries and indicated through silent signs, so that their vain assertion may be deprived of support and the reader’s spirit refreshed.

Joseph—whose name is interpreted as “increase,” and who was called “Savior of the world” by the Egyptians—bore the type of him who both saved the human race by his death and nourished the world with spiritual grain. He caused the seed of his faith to grow to such an increase that it filled the whole world and, through that same faith, joined earthly things to heavenly things.

His garment was dyed with the blood of a goat because, according to the Apostle, he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and, on account of sin, condemned sin; or because, becoming a sacrifice for sins, he carried our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having been freed from evil, we might live in righteousness. By his wound we have been healed, we who were wandering like sheep.

His garment is also the holy Church, which is the body of Christ, as Paul testifies when he says: “I rejoice in my sufferings, because I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Col. I). This garment is variegated or many-colored because the holy Church is gathered from the diversity of peoples and languages, as the Psalmist teaches when he says: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLV).

The same garment, which is described as reaching to the ankles, also commonly signifies the perfection of holy men, who are certainly members of Christ and who carry the garment of the good work they have received all the way to the ankles—that is, to the end.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the ignorant and disorderly statement: “If you accuse me because I adore the wood of the cross as God, why do you not accuse Jacob, who adored the top of Joseph’s staff? But it is clear that he did not adore while looking at the wood; rather, through the wood he adored Joseph, just as we adore Christ through the cross.”

[Col. 1034A]

The claim that Jacob also adored the top of Joseph’s staff must not be passed over, since they congratulate themselves on possessing in this matter a great example on behalf of the adoration of images. In the Latin books one does not read, “He adored the top of Joseph’s staff” (Gen. XLVII), but in some books, “He adored upon the head of the staff” (Heb. XI). In the Hebrew truth, to which faith must especially be given, there is no mention of a staff at all, even faintly; it merely says, “Israel adored God, turning toward the head of the bed.”

As blessed Augustine says, the old man was lying down there and had arranged it so that he could pray upon it without difficulty whenever he wished. Since, as we said above, some Latin books have, “He adored upon the top of the staff,” it is necessary to explain from the teaching of that learned doctor how the passage is to be understood. He says—for this is what the Latin books contain:

“And he adored upon the head of his staff. Some, correcting the text, have: ‘He adored upon the head of his staff,’ or ‘at the head of his staff,’ or ‘upon the top’ or ‘above the top.’ For the Greek word deceives them: it is written with the same letters whether it means ‘his’ or ‘his own,’ but the accents differ, and those who know these things do not disregard them in manuscripts. They are effective for making an important distinction, although it could also have one additional letter if it were *suae*—‘his own’—and not *αὐτοῦ* but *ἑαυτοῦ*.

“Therefore it is rightly asked what the statement means. It would easily be understood that the old man, who carried a staff in the manner customary for that age, as he bent himself to adore God did so upon the top of his own staff, which he carried in such a way that, bending his head over it, he adored God.

“What, then, is meant by ‘He adored upon the top of his staff,’ that is, the staff of his son Joseph? Perhaps he had taken the staff from him when that same son required an oath of him; and while he held it after the son had spoken the words of the oath, before it had yet been returned, he immediately adored God. For he was not ashamed to carry for a little while the emblem of his son’s authority, in which a figure of a great future event was being prefigured.”

Let them speak, then; let them say what they will answer to these things—those who, for the sake of the adoration of images, do not fear to accuse so great a patriarch and seek with mad intent to alter the holy Scriptures.

Behold, the Hebrew truth cries out that the same patriarch adored God at the head of his bed. Behold, the library of the Latins declares that he adored either upon the head of the staff, or at the head, or on the top, or above the top. Behold, the most learned man Augustine, inspired by the breath of divine grace and investigating with careful diligence, proclaims that he adored God either at the top of his own staff or at the top of his son’s staff—not the same staff, and not the same son.

Let them say which translator of the holy law translated the passage as “he adored the top of his son’s staff,” and as adoring the son upon that staff. Let them say which most diligent investigator of the holy law interpreted it as his having adored his son’s staff—or the son himself—rather than God. When they cannot find such a person, let them recognize that their understanding of the divine Scriptures is corrupting and contradictory, rather than investigative.

Now, since almost the entire sequence of divine law is mutilated or altered by them on account of the adoration of images, it will be necessary to hand down a new writing of the law after Moses; to discover a new restoration of the law after Ezra; to seek a new translation of the law after the Seventy Interpreters, Theodotion, Symmachus, and Aquila, or even blessed Jerome; and to search out a new exposition after the apostles and apostolic men filled with the Holy Spirit—one so opposed to the divine Scriptures that it can bind all who reject the adoration of images with the chain of anathema.

What difference there is between the cross of Christ and images painted by the art of painters; by what greater mystery the cross surpasses images; and how the human race was redeemed not through images but through the cross of Christ—matters which they regard as equal or equivalent—we shall explain in their proper place below, with the Lord’s favor.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the statement that Jacob blessed Pharaoh (Gen. XLVII) does not concern the adoration of images, as they claim
What has been said above is that the patriarch Jacob, so often mentioned, is read as having blessed Pharaoh, not worshiped him. But now, because in another reading of that same most foolish synod the blessing is in a certain way offered as a substitute for worship, this must be dealt with briefly. For the writing of that folly is so enshrouded in the darkness of ignorance that neither what follows seems to fit what precedes, nor what precedes what follows; and, as folly is accompanied by falsehood, it always follows what is fugitive, always what is perishable, and always what is slipping away. Solomon says: “He who relies on lies feeds on the winds, and himself pursues flying birds” (Prov. X).

Therefore, in order to establish the worship of images, on which their minds are fixed in love and which is the entire aim of their holiness, they strive to turn many words or meanings belonging to something else into arguments for worship. Thus, when they say that this same holy man blessed Pharaoh, they do not think that it refers to the same kind of blessing ordinarily offered by exiles to citizens, subjects to superiors, poorer people to richer people, and especially by old men to those who provide them with certain benefits; rather, they apply it to I know not what picture of images to be worshiped—a thing plainly so useless that it is less able to declare by speech the efficacy of its usefulness.

For they say: “Jacob blessed Pharaoh, but he did not bless him as God; we worship an image, but we do not worship it as God.” O inappropriate comparison! O dull conjecture! O most foolish statement!

You compare the blessing that the holy patriarch offered to a king who, above all others, bestowed a distinguished authority upon his beloved son; who granted him, together with all his offspring, a fertile tract of land for habitation; who gave him the choice not merely of a portion of some province, but of the land of his entire empire—you compare this blessing with the worship that you offer to images, which can provide their worshipers with nothing except the memory of the thing whose images they are.

Jacob therefore blessed Pharaoh, not as God, whom every creature blesses and praises; nor as a picture, which the craftsman’s hand constructs; but as a human being, to whom honor is to be shown on account of the exalted authority granted by God. I repeat: he blessed him, not as an insensible image, but as a rational human being; not as something assembled by the painter’s skill, but as one created in the image and likeness of God; not as one standing immovably upon walls, but as one who could grant favorable things to him or his offspring.

And, so to speak, Israel blessed a king who was anointed with the nectar of that same Spirit; and Israel would later say through the Apostle, “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII), and ought to pray not only for the one who enriched him and his offspring with worldly abundance, but also for those who slandered and persecuted him.

Such a blessing, therefore, which was certainly celebrated as a recompense for good, does not accord with the worship of images, since images can bring no recompense corresponding to the merits either of those who worship them or of those who refuse to worship them.

## CHAPTER XV. How absurdly those act who, in order to confirm images, bring forward the example of the divine Law, saying that Moses made the mercy seat, two golden cherubim, and the ark of the covenant at the Lord’s command

[Col. 1036C]

It is read that holy Moses, at the Lord’s command, made the mercy seat, the ark of the covenant, and two golden cherubim, and also carved stone tablets. Yet he was not commanded to worship them; nor is it believed that he made them for the memory of certain past events, but rather for the most sacred prefiguration of future mysteries.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Since matters stand thus, the extent of their absurdity and madness, namely, those who, etc. The printed editions read: “how great is their absurdity.” This is very poor, and the parallel passage below, ch. 17, refutes it: “To pursue how great their absurdity and madness are would be nearly endless.” And also Book II, final chapter: “How great is the arrogance and recklessness of anathematizing parents.”]

Since matters stand thus, neither an iron voice could express, nor the judgment of our understanding investigate, how great is the absurdity and madness of those who, endeavoring to equate images with these most sacred and supremely honorable things, fashioned by the lawgiver at the Lord’s command, strive to establish the worship of images by these examples—especially since those objects overflow with the secrets of the most sacred meanings, whereas these images possess little usefulness apart from recalling the thing whose images they are.

Since, then, the ark of the Lord’s covenant was made and overlaid with gold by the lawgiver from setim wood at the Lord’s command, and since within it were likewise the tablets of the covenant, the manna, and Aaron’s staff; and since the mercy seat was golden, in the form of a tablet, placed above the ark, commanded to be made of the same length and width and of such dimensions that the ark might be covered by that same mercy seat; and since two golden, beaten cherubim were to be placed upon the mercy seat itself, one on each side, facing one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat and their wings overshadowing it; and since from there God spoke to Moses—from the mercy seat, that is, from between the cherubim—who is so dull and foolish as to attempt, by comparing these things with such fearful and distinguished mysteries, to support the outrageous practice not merely of possessing images but of worshiping them?

For while these images indicate nothing other than, at times, the sequence of events that have taken place, and at other times falsely represent the error of events that have not taken place, that ark always shines with holy and exalted mysteries and glows with sacramental meanings.

According to some, the ark of the covenant signifies our Lord and Savior, in whom alone we have a covenant of peace with the Father. After his resurrection, when he ascended into heaven, he placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh that he had assumed from the Virgin. In him are the two tablets of the Law—that is, the two Testaments. In him is Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed, because he himself is king and priest: king, because it is written of him, “The Lord will send forth the rod of his power from Zion, and he will rule in the midst of his enemies” (Ps. CX); priest, because it is written of him, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CX and Heb. V). In him is the manna, namely, the food of heavenly nourishment, concerning which the outstanding prophet David says, “He gave them bread from heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVIII and IV Esd. I). As he himself also says in the Gospel, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI).

The mercy seat is placed above him, because mercy—the mercy of that same Mediator—surpasses the legal or evangelical commands founded upon him. Through this mercy we are saved not by the works of the Law that we have done, nor by willing or running, but by his compassion. Of him it is also said in the Father’s voice, “My truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted” (Ps. LXXXIX); and through the prophet he says, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI); and to him the Psalmist says, “Your mercies are many, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII); and, according to the Apostle, he is “the propitiation for our sins” (1 John II).

In him are the two cherubim, namely, the fullness of knowledge displayed in the two Testaments through his revelation. They face one another because the Law and the Gospel have great harmony between them, as the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). The cherubim have their faces turned toward the mercy seat because the two Testaments entirely commend the hope that must always be placed in God’s mercy.

God speaks from above the mercy seat—that is, from between the cherubim—because the same Son is the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made (John I). Since he is of one substance with the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel, “I and the Father are one” (John X), and, as he says to Philip, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV), the voice of God the Father is always heard in him from between the two Testaments.

According to most teachers of the divine Law who treat these matters morally, gold signifies wisdom, and the ark signifies the secret of God. The Law, the manna, and Aaron’s staff were commanded to be placed in the ark. The staff signifies power; the manna signifies grace, because there is no power to fulfill the commandments except together with grace. Yet because the Law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone who is making progress, the mercy seat is placed above it: for this is necessary so that God may be merciful. It is placed above because “mercy exalts itself above judgment.”

The two cherubim overshadow the mercy seat with their wings—that is, they honor it by veiling it—for these are ministries; and they face one another because they are harmonious. The two Testaments are represented there, and their faces are turned toward the mercy seat because they strongly commend God’s mercy, in which alone there is hope. Hence God promised that he would speak with Moses from between the cherubim, from above the mercy seat.

Moreover, if rational creation is signified by the multitude of knowledge—for this is the interpretation given to the cherubim—by those two living beings, there are two of them so that they may commend the fellowship of charity. They overshadow the mercy seat with their wings because they attribute their wings, that is, their virtues, to God and not to themselves: they honor God by the virtues with which they excel. Their faces are turned only toward the mercy seat because, for anyone making progress toward the abundance of knowledge, hope exists only in God’s mercy.

Since, as we said above, the tablets through which the two Testaments are signified were not given amid terror, the roar of fires, the shaking of clouds, or the blaring of trumpets—as were the first tablets, which are read to have been given by the Lord and broken by Moses—and since, when those earlier tablets were given to Moses, the people said, “Speak to us yourself, and do not let God speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. XX), it is clearly indicated that the first tablets signified the Old Testament, in which there was terror, whereas the later tablets signified the New Testament, in which there is love.

The fact that the first tablets were the work of God, while the second were the work of a human being, and that the former are said to have been written by the finger of God, whereas the latter are reported to have been written by a human being, makes this perfectly clear: the Old Testament was signified in the former, as we have said, because God commanded there but the human being did not act. The Law was given in the Old Testament to convict transgressors. Hence the outstanding preacher says, “The Law entered in so that sin might abound” (Rom. V).

The Law was not fulfilled through fear, since it is fulfilled only through love. It is therefore called the work of God because God established the Law and God wrote it; it is not the work of a human being, because the human being did not obey God, and the Law instead made him guilty.

In the second tablets, however, the human being makes and writes the tablets with God’s assistance, because the love of the New Testament fulfills the Law. Hence the Mediator of God and human beings came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. The same outstanding preacher also says, “The fulfillment of the Law is love, and faith that works through love” (Rom. XIII).

Thus, in the New Testament, what was difficult in the Old became easy for the human being who possesses faith working through love, while the finger of God—that is, the Spirit of God—writes it inwardly upon the heart, not outwardly upon stone. Hence the Apostle says, “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Cor. III), because the love of God, by which the commandment is truly fulfilled, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

This, then, is what is signified by the Law first given: the Old Testament, which is wholly the work of God and the writing of the finger of God. The Apostle says of it, “Thus the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Rom. VII). The holy and good Law is therefore the work of God, in which the human being does nothing, because he does not obey but is instead burdened with guilt by the Law as it threatens and condemns.

“For sin,” he says, “so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (ibid.). But the human being is blessed when he fulfills this holy, just, and good commandment. It is also his work, but through the grace of God.

This interpretation suits the older translation, in which the second tablets are remembered as having been written by the lawgiver. In the Hebrew text, however, both the first and the second tablets are written by God. This signifies that both the Old and the New Testament were written by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who is called the finger of God. In the former, the spirit of slavery is received in fear, because God imposes the yoke of the Law upon the human being, and the human being is unable to bear it. In the latter, where the tablets are made by a human being but written by God, the human being receives the spirit of adoption through obedience.

Let us therefore always behold these distinguished things—the ark, that is, and what is in it, the mercy seat, and the cherubim—with spiritual perception, and seek them with the entire concentration of our minds. Let us not seek them in painted tablets or upon walls, but look upon them with the eye of the mind in the innermost chambers of our hearts. According to the Apostle, we behold the glory of God with unveiled face and are transformed into that same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord, not walking in craftiness or adulterating the word of God, but in the manifestation of truth. Let us no longer seek the truth through images and paintings, but, with his help, let us reach by hope, faith, and charity that same truth which is Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the practice of worshiping images cannot be established from this either, as they most foolishly and irrationally claim, on the ground that it is written in the Law: “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, to complete work in gold and silver, and I have given him Ooliab Achisama” (Exod. XXXI)

The Law, as the Apostle says, is spiritual (Rom. VII). It has been given to us by God in the dark journey of the present age, to direct the steps of our minds, so that, when the vision of the mind has been illuminated by its radiance, it may behold the secrets of its mystical meanings. “The commandment of the Lord is clear,” says the prophet, “giving light to the eyes” (Ps. XIX); and again, “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. CXIX).

Of this, therefore, a certain wise man says: “The commandment of the Law is a lamp, and the light of life, and reproof and discipline.” Isaiah also says, “By night my spirit keeps watch for you, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI).

Since everyone who does not understand this light correctly is deprived of it, those are believed to be utterly deprived of it who, on account of I know not what worship of images, strive violently to bend it to their own interpretations and endeavor in some way to make it support their error, although they attempt to produce from it testimonies that, while not relevant to the matter, nevertheless have some appearance of support.

Because, then, Bezalel was chosen by the Lord to make work in gold and silver and was filled with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, they bring this forward as testimony to fortify their error, as though the things made through him at the Lord’s command, and redolent of typical figures of mysteries, ought to be worshiped.

Bezalel, therefore, is interpreted as “in the shadow of God”; Uri is said to mean “fire”; and Hur is understood as “light.” Whose type, then, did this Bezalel bear—he who, as we have said, is interpreted as “in the shadow of God”—if not that of the one to whom the Church continually cries, “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVII), and, “I will hope under the shadow of your wings, until iniquity passes away” (Ps. LVII), and of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs, “I sat down under the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song II)?

He is called the son of Uri, son of Hur, because he is indescribable splendor, God from God, light from light. Of him the prophet Habakkuk says, “His splendor will be like light” (Hab. III). For God, as Moses says, is “a consuming fire” (Deut. IV and IX), which the Apostle Paul also affirms in the same words in his Letter to the Hebrews (Heb. XII). The Lord himself likewise says through the prophet Zechariah, “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls because of the multitude of people and animals, and I will be for it a wall of fire all around” (Zech. II).

Although he is of one substance with the Father, he speaks to Moses in fire, and in the Gospel he says to his disciples, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). Were not the breasts of those people inflamed by that fire who said, “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

This Bezalel, then, is called by name because the Father says to him through the prophet Isaiah, “I have called you by your name; you are mine” (Isa. XLIII). Of him it is said through Moses, “Behold, I will send an angel before you, to guard you on the way and to bring you into the place that I have prepared. Pay attention to him and listen to his voice; do not think him contemptible, for he will not forgive you when you sin, and my name is in him” (Exod. XXIII).

Nor is the lineage of this Bezalel, who was called by name, passed over in silence. Scripture says: “The son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah.” For this is the one of whom it was previously foretold in the voice of Israel, “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up for the prey, my son” (Gen. XLIX)—that is, you ascended the cross to plunder hell; you rested and lay down like a lion, that is, in the tomb; “and like a lioness, who will question him?” because through the power of the Father he rose from the dead on the third day.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] “And like a lioness, who raised him?” because through the power of the Father he rose from the dead on the third day. This passage is disjointed and ἀνόητα [nonsensical]. I read and punctuate it from the original: “A lioness, who will raise him?” because, etc.]

Hear the Apostle saying that he rose through the power of the Father: “God raised him on the third day and granted that he should become manifest, not to all the people” (Acts X).

Tell me, I beg you, holy John—you who, reclining upon the breast of the Mediator of God and human beings, drank luminous draughts from the fountain of eternal light and daily offer the nectar of ambrosial liquor to the minds of Christ’s people—if you know from whom this Bezalel is descended, whose type that ancient Bezalel of the Law once bore.

“I saw,” I said, “in the right hand of him who was seated upon the throne a book written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, ‘Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?’ And no one was able, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book or look at it. And I wept greatly because no one was found worthy to open the book or see it. And one of the elders said to me, ‘Do not weep; behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered so as to open the book and break its seven seals’” (Rev. V).

Since this Bezalel, whom we have said bore the figure of Christ, is adorned with such great distinctions of virtue—chosen by God, called by name, filled with the Holy Spirit, and described as to whose son he was and from what stock he came—it is futile to bring him forward as an example in order to establish the worship of images. He is believed to have been superior to all painters and to all craftsmen who form images.

If paintings or images made by any kind of craftsman are to be compared with his works, then those painters or craftsmen who make images must likewise be compared with him. And if those painters or craftsmen who make images must be compared with him, then the craftsmen themselves, or the images made by them, must also bear a distinguished prefiguration of future things. But neither painters nor craftsmen of any kind, nor their works, bear any such prefiguration of future things. Therefore paintings or images made by any kind of craftsman are not to be compared with his works.

Since this new Bezalel, namely, the Redeemer of the human race, possessed the spirit of wisdom, knowledge, and understanding—for he is of one substance with the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son—the prophet Isaiah bears witness. He says:

“A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

The same Lord says through the same prophet, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. LXI).

This, then, is what he makes from gold and silver: he makes it in the ornaments of the tabernacle, when he establishes holy men—shining with gold, that is, with inner understanding; gleaming with silver, that is, adorned with divine utterances; and, so to speak, having gold in their hearts, according to the saying, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” and silver in the confession of the mouth, according to the saying, “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X)—in the tabernacle of God, namely, the holy Church, as they pass toward the eternal homeland.

These two things, gold and silver—that is, faith and confession—the Apostle sought when he said, “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. X): “For if you confess the Lord Jesus Christ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”

Moses likewise sought these things for the adornment of the tabernacle when he said, “Take from yourselves an offering for the Lord: everyone whose heart is willing shall offer firstfruits to the Lord, gold, silver, and the rest” (Exod. XXXV).

Although he is the wisdom of God the Father, he is recognized as dwelling in holy people overflowing with spiritual understanding. Scripture says, “The wisdom of God is above precious stones; its dwelling is in golden vessels.” Of this wisdom Solomon says elsewhere:

“Blessed is the man who finds wisdom and abounds in prudence. Its acquisition is better than trading in silver and better than pure gold; its fruits are more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired can compare with it” (Prov. III).

Since the brightness of divine utterances is understood in silver, this must be confirmed by the testimony of the Psalmist, who says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, purified of the earth sevenfold” (Ps. XII).

To this Bezalel, for carrying out the work, Achisamach is given as a helper. Whom does this Achisamach, who gives assistance to Christ, signify, if not the holy apostles and apostolic men? By preaching, study, and the example of good works, they cause human beings to shine with virtues within the bosom of the Church and lead them to the eternal homeland; thus they are helpers of Christ.

Of these was the man who said: “We are God’s helpers; you are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. III).

Since all these things, therefore, are full of allegorical meanings and were expressed by the lawgiver in figurative forms, it is not merely the height of madness but of insanity to attempt to compare them with images that every craftsman produced according to the capacity of his own ingenuity—or rather, according to the limits of his ability—in whatever form he wished.

## CHAPTER XVII. That those who say, “If, according to the lawful tradition of Moses, the people are commanded to place hyacinthine purple in the fringes, at the edges of their garments, as a reminder and safeguard of the commandments, much more ought we, through a likeness produced in painting, to see the outcome of the holy men’s way of life and imitate their faith according to apostolic tradition,” do not think correctly

[Col. 1042D]

This entire chapter must be considered clause by clause, and each individual part must be answered, because although it tends toward the purpose of a single error, it is nevertheless constructed piecemeal from many errors.

First, it must be examined why they said “purple hyacinth-colored” in this chapter, since purple is one color and hyacinth another; and [Note: Just as one cannot properly say “red whiteness” and “white redness,” as if someone were to say “silver gold” or “golden silver.” In these expressions there is no reciprocity, or, as the author says, “reciprocally derived expression.” We have restored the passage, as it seems to us, to its proper form: “one can properly say ‘reddening whiteness’ and ‘whitening redness,’ as if someone were to say ‘silver gold,’ etc.”] just as one cannot properly say “red whiteness” and “whitening redness,” as if someone were to say “silver gold” or “golden silver,” so neither can one properly say “purple hyacinth,” so that, with the order reversed, one could say “purple hyacinth-colored,” since such a reciprocal derivation cannot remain sound by the force of any meaning.

For, as we have already said, hyacinth is one color and purple another. The Law itself, given by the Lord through Moses, is witness to this: it designates these four separately—hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and also fine linen—for making the high priest’s vestments and for the other things that were to be offered in preparation of the sanctuary. Our predecessors said that these four materials signified the figure of the four elements from which the world, or the human body, is constituted, and they taught that each one indicated virtues in a tropological sense. Thus they relate hyacinth to the air, as the color itself also indicates; scarlet to fire; purple they assign to water, because it takes its dye from water; and fine linen to earth, because it arises from the earth.

Finally, it must also be examined that they try to support the use of images by the example of hyacinth-colored tassels, especially since the sequence of the ancient Law commands those tassels to be placed on the edges of garments as a mystery, whereas it nowhere commands images to be placed in sanctuaries for worship, whether in the Old or in the New Testament. Nor can the insanity of so great an error be established by this example: what was granted through the Lawgiver for the purpose of indicating signs that suggested a hidden meaning cannot be made to agree with such delirium, when the things commanded and rightly performed are themselves good.

After the Lord had delivered the commandments of the Law through Moses, he added at the end: “You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes” (Deut. VI). When we fulfill these spiritually in our conduct, we hold them immovably in our hands; and when we meditate on them day and night, we carry them placed before our eyes. He also commanded hyacinth-colored tassels to be made at the four corners of cloaks, either to distinguish the people of Israel, so that they might be a sign on the garment just as circumcision was a sign on the body; or so that we, who are spiritual Israel, might have righteousness and holy conduct as our clothing. The edge of this garment should be adorned with hyacinth-colored tassels, so that our life might be instructed by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures.

This, then, was the good use of the tassels, rightly granted by the Lawgiver either to that carnal Israel or to us, the spiritual Israel. But by those people it was abused rather than properly used. Concerning them Truth says in the Gospel: “For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their tassels” (Matt. XIII). Whose example, I ask, do these people follow, if not that of the Pharisees? While the Pharisees wish to be called Rabbi by men and seek the first greetings in the marketplace and the first seats in assemblies, and while, through their desire for empty praise, they wish their words and deeds to be entrusted to the memory of posterity, these people, through inept and useless synods, both worship images that had rightly been placed by some as ornaments in basilicas and compel others to worship them.

The former magnify their tassels through empty glory; the latter likewise worship images through boastfulness. The former enlarge the tassels, which had been properly instituted, by magnifying them improperly; the latter exalt images, which had been properly established, by worshiping them improperly. The former think they obey Moses’ commands by magnifying the tassels; the latter think they please all the saints by worshiping images. Thus, although they pursue different things and follow different objects in different ways, they are recognized as tending toward the madness appointed by one and the same error. Nor is this without reason, since the causes and effectiveness of these actions are nothing other than the glory of boastful praise or arrogance.

Therefore, in order that the error of this most vain chapter, which we have proposed to examine clause by clause, may be exposed more clearly, its text must be repeated in order. For they chatter:

“If, according to the legitimate tradition of Moses, the people are commanded to place purple hyacinth-colored tassels at the edges, at the extremities of their garments, for the remembrance and preservation of the commandments, much more ought we, through a likeness in painting, to see the conclusion of the conduct of holy men.”

Their phrase “much more,” which belongs with “is commanded,” so that the sense would be, “if it is commanded to the people, much more is it commanded to us,” cannot possess even the slightest meaning, since this error is not only not commanded “much more,” but does not appear to be commanded anywhere either equally or to a lesser degree.

As for their claim that “through a likeness in painting one may see the conclusion of the conduct of holy men,” it would be almost endless to pursue how absurd and insane this is. In images the virtue of holy conduct cannot be seen; only the materials from which the images themselves have been formed can be seen. Can the virtues and distinguished merits that belonged to those men—namely, to their subject, the mind—be seen in these images as in a kind of subject, when there is no soul in them that could underlie the virtues? Rather, their subject—that is, their material body—consists, in a sense, of colors; and virtues can be neither predicated of nor present in them as a subject.

Can we therefore discern wisdom and eloquence in these images, qualities that many of those men possessed? Can we behold prudence in them, through which they possessed knowledge of the true faith and understanding of the divine writings, and through which prudent people understand the threefold kind of understanding found in the divine books?

The first kind is that by which certain passages are understood historically, with their enigmatic or allegorical figures set aside, as with the Decalogue of the Law. The second is that by which certain passages in Scripture are understood mystically, both according to the truth of the events narrated and according to the figure of allegorical meanings. Thus, the rock from which the Lawgiver drew water was historically a rock and poured forth water, but allegorically it bore the figure of Christ, who, although he is the stone founded as the foundation of Zion, satisfies the minds of believers with the honey-sweet drink of spiritual life. The third kind is understood only spiritually, as with the Song of Songs, in which nothing is to be understood historically, but everything spiritually.

Can justice be observed in these images, the justice by which the saints feared God, revered religion, took care to benefit everyone and harm no one, embraced the bonds of brotherly love, undertook the dangers of others, or even brought aid to the distressed, repaid kindnesses received, and strove to preserve equity in judgments?

Can we discern their courage in the colors used by painters, the courage by which, being magnanimous, they endured adversities calmly, yielded to them patiently, and firmly resisted enticements? Through it they escaped the biting riches and the desire for glory; through it they were neither broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity. Clothed in its armor, they became strong for labor, prepared their minds for danger against the wicked, and yielded to no hardship.

Or is their temperance visible in these images, the temperance by which they moderated the desires of the flesh and restrained their appetite? Since none of the things we have mentioned can be seen in these images, it is extreme presumption to say that in a likeness produced by painting one can see the conclusion of the conduct of the saints.

The same most vain chapter continues: “and to imitate their faith according to apostolic tradition.” Can their faith, which according to the Apostle works through love, be imitated in images? Just as the conclusion of the saints’ conduct cannot be seen in them, so neither can their faith be imitated, because what is lacking in those images can neither be seen in them nor imitated through them.

Everything that lacks life lacks sensation; everything that lacks sensation lacks faith; therefore everything that lacks life lacks faith. Hope, faith, and charity, according to the nature of their substance, are invisible and incorporeal qualities. Even in a true human being who possesses them they cannot be seen, unless perhaps they are demonstrated through works; for their seat, like that of the other virtues, is in the soul, which is certainly invisible.

If they cannot be seen even in a true human being who possesses them, they can much less be seen in a painted figure, which lacks not only these qualities, as we have said, but also life. And if they cannot be seen in such figures, then they can much less be imitated through them. Hence it is understood that the faith of those people is vain when they claim that they will imitate the faith of the saints through images.

Now, since they say “according to apostolic tradition,” let them say where it was handed down by the apostles, either by example or by word, that through images one should see the conclusion of the saints’ conduct and imitate their faith.

The Apostle demonstrates the conclusion of the saints’ conduct in this way when he says: “All the saints died according to faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth.” He also says: “Through faith the saints conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, extinguished the force of fire, recovered from weakness, became strong in battle,” and so forth.

The same Apostle shows most clearly what we ought to imitate when he says: “Be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children” (Eph. V); and in another place: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. II). Hence it is perfectly clear that this is the apostolic tradition: that the conclusion of the saints’ conduct is to be seen not in paintings but in virtues, and that their faith is to be imitated not through the pigments of images but in good works.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### That the hope of those who place their salvation in images is vain, when they say: “Just as the Israelite people were saved by looking at the bronze serpent, so we shall be saved by looking at the likenesses of the saints.”

The hope of those who place their salvation in images is rejected by the Apostle, who teaches that hope rests not on the things that are seen but on the things that are not seen. For he says: “Hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII).

Since the bronze serpent, made by Moses at the Lord’s command and placed on high, was not set up to be worshiped but to resist temporarily the poisonous bites of the fiery serpents, those people are deceived by the mockery of false hope when they suppose that they will be healed by looking at images made by human hands, just as the Israelite people were healed by looking at that bronze serpent from the deadly attacks of the fiery serpents. This is especially absurd since the Lord commanded Moses that the serpent be made, whereas there is no passage of Scripture instituting that images should be made.

What that serpent signified, by looking at which those wounded by serpents were healed, we have learned from the teaching of our Redeemer himself, who said: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John III). When we gaze upon him attentively with the inner eyes of our mind, we overcome the deadly bites of the temptations of evil spirits and escape the dangers of eternal death.

Moreover, just as in the words of the divine Law those things that were properly spoken by the Holy Spirit in the Law, the Prophets, the Gospel, or the Apostles are often misunderstood wickedly by schismatics because of a perverse intention, so also many things instituted or done by the Fathers for the benefit of others are believed, after the long passage of time, to have been treated improperly and changed into something perverse by later generations. This is the case with the phylacteries and tassels, mentioned above, and also with the bronze serpent, which, as we have said, was necessary for a time in order to benefit those wounded by serpents. From it there later arose the most insolent practice of worshiping high places.

When the righteous king Hezekiah saw that incense was being burned to it and that certain forms of worship were being offered, and that a great part of the people was endangered, he did not delay in breaking it. He knew that it had been made by the Lawgiver for the people’s benefit, but he saw that the people were honoring it with empty cult and superstitious religion.

The praise of that most holy king Hezekiah, because he removed vain superstitions and broke the same serpent, is recorded in the divine writings as follows:

“Hezekiah did what was good in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. He destroyed the high places, smashed the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made. For until that time the children of Israel had burned incense to it, and they called it Nehushtan. He trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel; and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps; he kept his commandments, which the Lord had commanded Moses. And the Lord was with him, and in everything to which he proceeded he acted wisely” (II Kings XVIII).

The blessed Jerome also condemned these and similar superstitions, which some people think they practice out of love for God, such as those who light lamps before images out of love for the saints and worship them. While explaining the Gospel passage concerning the tassels and phylacteries of the Pharisees, he criticized them in these words:

“This,” he says, “superstitious little women among us still practice today with small Gospels, with the wood of the cross, and with things of this sort. They do indeed have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: they strain out the gnat and swallow the camel.”

Now, since these people believe that they will be saved by looking at images, just as the Israelite people were healed from the bites of serpents by looking at the serpent, if some bodily illness should perhaps befall them, let them run to the images and look at them. Then, when they have not been healed at all by looking at them, let them return to the Lord and believe that they will receive healing from him through the intercessions of the saints, since he is the author of all health and life.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That it is extremely presumptuous to say: “Just as the tablets and the two cherubim were given to the Jews, so the cross and images of the saints were given to us Christians, for writing and worship.”

We are often compelled in this work to say that neither the tablets nor the two cherubim, nor any other things of this kind, are believed to have been made in the Old Testament for worship. These people, abandoning the path of moderation and correctness, exalt all those things beyond what order requires by proclaiming that they were given for worship; but they lower them beyond what the matter warrants by attempting to equate them with images.

When they say, “Just as the tablets and the two cherubim were given to the Jews, so the cross and images of the saints were given to us Christians for worship and for writing,” what else are they doing except exalting images and diminishing the realities belonging to Christians?

They say that those who were under the Law had two cherubim made by Moses, from between which God spoke, whereas we who are under grace have crosses made by any craftsmen. They say that those who followed the shadow of the Law had the tablets of the covenant containing the Decalogue of the Law, whereas we who follow the truth, which is Christ, have works produced by any craftsmen. They say that those who received the spirit of slavery in fear had the things that Moses made at the Lord’s direction, whereas we who have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, “Abba, Father,” have images made by any painter, instructed only by worldly artistic skill.

We, who do not follow the letter that kills but the Spirit that gives life; who are not carnal but spiritual Israel; who, rejecting visible things, contemplate invisible things—we rejoice that we have received from the Lord not merely mysteries greater than images, which are entirely without mystery, but signs of mystery greater and more exalted than the tablets themselves or the two cherubim.

For the tablets and the two cherubim were examples of things to come. The Jews possessed them in a carnal manner, and the realities covered by typical figures were prefigurations of things to come. We possess spiritually, in truth, the things that were prefigured by those examples and carnal prefigurations. Therefore, as the body surpasses the shadow, truth surpasses the image, and the reality surpasses the figure, so the New Testament surpasses the Old.

The Old Testament was dedicated by Moses when the whole commandment of the Law had been read to the entire people. He took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you” (Exod. XXIV).

The New Testament, however, was dedicated by the Redeemer of the world, our Lord Jesus Christ. On the night when he was betrayed, he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body, which will be given for you; do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise, after he had eaten, he took the cup, saying: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins” (I Cor. XI).

In the Old Testament, the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctified them for the cleansing of the flesh. In the New Testament, the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanses our consciences from dead works so that we may serve the living and true God.

In the Old Testament, a lamb was slaughtered by each family, and Passover was celebrated with its flesh. In the New Testament, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John I), the true spotless Lamb, was also offered to God as a sacrifice. The Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

In the Old Testament, the kingdom of the Canaanite nation and an abundance of bodily goods were promised. In the New Testament, eternal life and the kingdom of heaven are granted. In the Old Testament, a land flowing with milk and honey was promised. In the New Testament, a heavenly homeland is promised, in which we receive what “no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.”

In the Old Testament, the beginnings of the new moons were celebrated. In the New Testament, the new creation is received in Christ, as Paul, the vessel of election, testifies when he says: “If anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (II Cor. V).

In the Old Testament, the rest and repose of the Sabbath were celebrated. In the New Testament, Sabbath rest is found in Christ, who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

In the Old Testament, sacrifices of flesh and blood were offered through slaughtered animals. In the New Testament, the sacrifice of the flesh and blood of Christ is offered, which was represented by those animals.

In the Old Testament, the heavy yoke of the Law placed upon their necks made them servants. In the New Testament, the easy yoke of Christ and his light burden make them sons through the spirit of adoption.

Since these things stand thus, it is perverse—indeed, more than perverse—to give inferior things to the superior by reversing the order, and superior things to the inferior, and to magnify the use of images to such an extent that the realities belonging to Christians are in some way diminished.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That Tarasius is known to have raved no less than all the others, and almost more than all, when he says: “Just as the ancients had the cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat, so let us have images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God, and of his saints overshadowing the altar.”

It is not inconsistent that Tarasius, who, as is reported, was extraordinarily advanced from popular life to the priestly summit, from military dress to religious dress, from the circus to the altar, from the turmoil of the law courts to preaching, and from the clamor of weapons to the performance of sacred mysteries, should compel the minds of the peoples subject to him to return from spiritual things to carnal things, from invisible things to visible things, from truth to image, from body to shadow, from the life-giving Spirit to the letter that kills, and from the spirit of adoption to the spirit of fear.

Thus, since he himself, rejecting things that perhaps were not unlawful in lay life, rushed to the rank of the priestly summit—which was unlawful for him because of his sudden change—the peoples subject to him too may, through his preaching, rush from the lawful observances of spiritual mysteries to the unlawful observances of bodily things.

Since he urges people to despise better things and use worse ones, and since the ancients had cherubim made through Moses, from between which God spoke, overshadowing the mercy seat, he therefore urges the faithful to have images, made by any craftsmen, overshadowing the altar.

Let him make an ark not of acacia wood but of willow; let it not be covered with gold but with lead; let it have not golden rings but bronze ones; and let its carrying poles be not of acacia wood but of beech. Let it contain not tablets bearing the ten words of the Law but eleven, signifying the transgression of the Law. Let it contain not Aaron’s rod but the staff of any one of his predecessors whom he anathematizes, or by whom he has been anathematized. Let there be in it an urn containing not manna but seeds of any plant.

Let him also make a lampstand of the purest lead, and a table of the bread of the Presence that is not called holy. Let him write a book of the Law commanding anyone to lay hands quickly upon anyone else, and counting it proper to promote neophytes to the episcopate; a book that also teaches that likenesses of the things in heaven and on earth should be made, honored, and worshiped.

Having briefly passed over these matters, on account of which Tarasius does not preach correctly—because he did not, as reported, ascend correctly to the height of the priesthood, and because he said, “Let us have images in place of the cherubim”—after briefly setting forth certain expressions by the same figure of speech, which some call *astismos*, let us now, with the Lord’s help, explain how the mercy seat within the holy church is overshadowed by two cherubim. We shall compare spiritual things with spiritual things, whether according to the arrangement of the tabernacle established by Moses in the wilderness or according to the construction of the temple built by Solomon in Jerusalem, lest we seem to detract from the holy Scriptures in the eyes of the ignorant because we do not worship images.

First, it must be asked why Moses, when he made the tabernacle, made two golden cherubim and placed them upon the mercy seat that was above the ark, whereas Solomon added two others, much larger, and, placing them in the temple, set the ark in the midst beneath their wings, together with the mercy seat and the earlier cherubim. Thus there were two cherubim in the tabernacle but four in the temple.

Both groups therefore belong to one and the same signification, except that Solomon—whose name is interpreted as “peaceful” and who bore the figure of Christ—raised the size of the two cherubim to a greater or broader extent. This action signified that after the Lord’s incarnation the Church would be more widely exalted through the gathering of diverse nations and joined to the citizens above.
