Those citizens praise the Creator for the gift of blessedness granted to them in such a way that they rejoice, in a certain sense, over our deliverance and introduction into that same blessedness.

For “cherubim,” as the prophet Ezekiel most clearly demonstrates, is the name of an angelic rank. In the singular it is *cherub*, and in the plural *cherubim*. Therefore, not inappropriately, the cherubim made in the sanctuary are understood as the ministries of the Gospel. Standing before their Creator in heaven, they rejoice in their perpetual blessedness.

They extend their wings toward one another over the ark when they refer every good they have received to the praise of the Lord and Savior. They extend their other wings toward the walls of the sanctuary when, seeing holy human beings also included in their fellowship, they rejoice and touch them, as it were, with the tips of their wings. They rejoice that those people have become their companions and followers in the purity of this life.

They touch two walls equally with their wings because they have with them in the heavenly court the faithful of both peoples, Jews and Gentiles. This does not mean that in that homeland there is a local distinction between the two peoples, but that the celebration of inner blessedness becomes greater through the fellowship of united brotherhood. Thus the cherubim extend their wings toward both walls of the sanctuary, because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they also arouse the righteous of both peoples, by the vision of their glory, to praise the Creator.

The heavenly hosts do not rejoice only in the happiness of those righteous human beings whom they already have with them within. They also continually care for us, who are still placed outside and cry to the Lord from the depths. Concerning the cherubim it is also well written in the Book of Chronicles: “They stood upright on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the exterior house” (II Chron. III).

The cherubim stood upright on their feet because they are believed never to have strayed in any way from the path of truth on which they were placed as soon as they were created. Their faces were turned toward the exterior house because they desire that we, rescued from the hardship of this pilgrimage, should attain fellowship with them.

Thus they stood upright on their feet, with their wings extended toward the golden walls of the sanctuary, and their faces turned toward the exterior house. In this way the angels perpetually preserve their innocence: they rejoice with the blessedness of holy souls in heaven, while they do not cease to offer assistance to the elect whom they see still journeying on earth, until they introduce them also into the heavenly homeland.

As we already explained in the preceding chapter, the two cherubim may also signify the two Testaments. They were therefore made in the sanctuary because, in the counsel of divine providence—which is inaccessible and incomprehensible to us—it was determined before the ages when, how, and through which authors sacred Scripture would be composed.

They were made of olive wood either because the divine books were written through men enlightened by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who is merciful; or because they impart the light of knowledge with the assistance of the flame of God’s charity, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

They were ten cubits high because they proclaim that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue of the Law, and because they show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the denarius of the heavenly kingdom.

They have two wings because the Testaments declare that, through adversity and prosperity alike, they have always pressed toward and reached heavenly things with tireless purpose, and because they demonstrate that their authors must do the same.

One wing of a cherub was five cubits and the other wing was five cubits, because amid every changing condition of transient things the saints extend all the senses of their bodies in the service of their Creator. They keep their eyes always directed toward the Lord; they desire to hear the voice of his praise and to proclaim all his wonders; they hold his words sweeter in their throats than honey and the honeycomb; they run after the fragrance of his ointments; and, as long as breath remains in them and the Spirit of God is in their nostrils, they do not speak iniquity with their lips or utter folly with their tongue.

Thus, proceeding with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, they attain the heavenly denarius that the supreme master of the household promised to the workers in his vineyard.

Since the work in the two cherubim was one, this indicated that the writers of both instruments served God with one and the same purity of conduct and devotion of charity, and that they proclaim God with one harmonious voice and faith. Whatever the New Testament narrates concerning the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the calling of the Gentiles, the expulsion of the Jews, and the manifold tribulation of the Church, the Old Testament, if rightly understood, truthfully foretold as destined to happen.

Both Testaments also proclaim with harmonious truth the coming of Antichrist, the end of the final age, the ordeal of judgment, the eternal glory of the good, and the punishment of the rejected.

The inner wings of the cherubim touched one another over the ark because the Testaments agree in their equal testimony concerning the Lord. Likewise, one cherub touched one wall with its outer wings and the other touched the other wall, because the Old Testament was written specifically for the ancient people of God, whereas the New Testament was written for us, who came to the faith after the Lord’s incarnation. We are rightly compared with the second wall, that is, the northern one, because after the figure and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth.

Although the primitive Church blossomed especially from the Jews, and although all Israel is believed to be saved at the end of the age, nevertheless most of the faithful of the present time are gathered from the Gentiles to receive the sacraments of the Gospel. To them also this was divinely granted: with the eyes of their hearts opened, they clearly recognize that the letter of the Old Testament is filled with the mysteries of evangelical grace.

The cherubim had their faces turned toward the exterior house because we, who still stand outside, have been saved not in reality but in hope.

The divine books were composed because their authors, now reigning with the Lord and praising him in heaven, care for our salvation [Note: “And they intercede with his mercy on behalf of our errors.” The corrector is mistaken in looking for an error in *erratibus* and replacing it with *erratis*. This usage was also current. Balbus the monk, in the *Catholicus*: “To err, that is, to deviate; hence the verbal nouns *erratus*, -us, and *erratum*, -i; both mean an offense.”] and intercede with his mercy on behalf of our errors.

The cherubim are surrounded with gold because the authority of the Testaments is confirmed by the splendid works of their writers, and because the knowledge of the divine Scriptures has been manifested throughout the world—or because of the inward glory of the heavenly hosts. As we have said, each cherub signifies both the angels and the Testaments.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### That John the presbyter did not think correctly when, in order to establish the worship of images, he said: “And Jesus Nave set up twelve stones as a memorial of God.”

In the same synod that was held for the veneration of images—and whose errors we have undertaken briefly to examine—no testimony drawn from the divine writings can be shown to pertain to this matter. Nor can the statement brought forward by John the presbyter and legate of the Orientals be shown to pertain to it: “Jesus son of Nun set up twelve stones as a memorial of God.”

If the reason for these stones is sought historically—why they were taken from the riverbed and placed at Gilgal—it is disclosed by that same Joshua. He taught that they were not intended to instruct Israel’s descendants in the worship of images, but warned that they ought to remember the river miraculously dried up, and that they should convey to posterity this voiceless message, proclaiming:

> “We whom you see were once inhabitants of the flowing element; now we are exiles from the dry land. We who for so many ages were natives of the Jordan, taken out of its depths, are now strangers upon the earth. For when, before the face of the Lord’s ark—indeed, before the face of the God of Jacob—while the ranks of the priests resounded and the assembled people marveled with great rejoicing, that river suffered a new division, sending its lower part away in flight beneath the watery waves and raising its upper part into the air; and while the astonished people saw the liquid mountains lifted on high and the river grant the Israelites an unprecedented passage along its dry bed, we were taken from our ancient dwelling places, carried on the shoulders of the Israelites, and placed here; here we shall remain for a long time.”

[Note: “And here we shall remain for a long time.” Perhaps one should read *subdiu permansuri*, “we shall remain for a considerable time.”]

But if it is asked what these stones prefigured figurally, the answer is disclosed by the teaching of the new Joshua—namely, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who grants us habitation in our eternal homeland. In order to establish the sacrament of baptism, through which one reaches the eternal homeland, he chose twelve apostles and said to them: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). They bear perpetual testimony to the posterity of the holy Church, while they summon it to the heavenly kingdom through the most sacred sacrament of baptism.

Therefore, through the other twelve stones likewise placed in the bed of the Jordan, the figure of the holy patriarchs and prophets is clearly set forth. While they did not openly preach the sacrament of baptism, because they stood beneath the shadow of the Law, but indicated it through certain mystical and veiled figures, they were, as it were, overwhelmed by the river’s waves. For although they are not seen to have instituted baptism openly, they are nevertheless not believed to have been without its mystery.

In place of these fathers, sons were born to the holy Church—namely, the apostles, whom he appointed princes over all the earth, who remember the Lord’s name in every generation and lineage. Thus, through both the former and the latter, may the Church, filled with sacred gifts and instructed in the doctrines, never cease to seek the Lord—not through the cosmetics of images or any superstitious things, but through faith and works.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That there is not, as they claim, an equal worship: the worship offered by the prophet Nathan to King David is not equal to the worship of images

[Col. 1053D]

That the worship which the prophet Nathan offered to David, both prophet and most holy king (2 Samuel 12), is not equal to the worship that some offer to images does not need to be established by many proofs, since it has been demonstrated by the clearest indications. A matter so open and so plain does not require our argument. Yet, lest we seem to have passed over it in silence, we ought to treat it briefly and succinctly.

The prophet Nathan, I say, worshiped King David not as an image assembled from painted colors, but as an authority exalted by God to the summit of kingship. He had been filled with the gift of that heavenly grace by which the one who was to say the following would himself be filled:

> “Be subject to every higher authority. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist will incur judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. For it is God’s servant for your good; but if you do evil, be afraid. For it does not bear the sword without reason. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also for conscience’ sake. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this purpose. Give everyone what is owed: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue is due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due. Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Romans 13).

The same “Vessel of Election” likewise instructed his disciple Titus through the Holy Spirit:

> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, to be ready for every good work, to slander no one, to avoid quarrels, to be gentle, showing all meekness toward everyone” (Titus 3).

Thus the prophet worshiped the king: one filled with the Holy Spirit, one filled with the Holy Spirit; trusting in the gift of prophecy, one trusting in the gift of prophecy; radiant with the marks of his merits, one radiant with the marks of his merits. He did not worship in him some senseless object with the cult of superstitious vanity, but a man found according to the Lord’s heart, a man anointed with the sacred oil, a man raised above all others in the praises of God [Note: “A man exalted above all others in the praises of God.” Perhaps *exercitatum*, “trained,” would be more correct], a man who prophesied more excellently than all others concerning Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection from the dead, and ascension into heaven; a man who not only prophesied that the Son of God would come, but also bore his type; a man who not only bore his type, but also supplied, according to the form of a servant, the genealogy of his human descent.

He honored him with affection, with the service of humility, with the duty owed to one in authority, and with dutiful worship. If he had not honored him by submitting to him and obeying his commands, he would have appeared to oppose that Spirit who was to speak through the pastor of the Church:

> “Be subject, for the Lord’s sake, to every human institution” (1 Peter 2),

whether “to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for this very purpose: to punish evildoers and praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people, living as free persons—not using freedom as a cloak for wickedness, but as servants of God. Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king.”

Since, therefore, kings are to be honored according to so many indications and such great apostolic teaching, it is utterly absurd to wish to equate the worship foolishly offered to images with the worship offered by the prophet to the most holy king. For the prophet, when he greeted David, worshiped God’s servant, so to speak, the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, and the minister of the divine incarnation; whereas these people worship in images nothing other than the materials from which the images are made [OCR: *fiant adorent*, “are made and are worshiped,” is evidently intended].

For if the worship offered by the prophet to David is equal to the worship offered to images, then David himself is equal to images. And if he is equal to images, he must be believed to have lacked not only the distinction of so many merits but also human reason itself. Yet he did not lack either the distinction of so many merits or human reason. Therefore the worship offered to him by the prophet is not equal to the worship offered to images.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### That nothing made by human hands is to be understood by what is written, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord,” or, “Your countenance, O Lord, I shall seek,” as they claim

[Col. 1055B]

What the Psalmist says, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4), has nothing to do with the faces of images made by human hands. Nor does the statement, “Your countenance, O Lord, I shall seek,” as it appears in the reading of that most vain synod which was held for the veneration of images. Its text is nothing more than material in which folly exercised its full extent.

For if this countenance, whose light the prophet sings has been marked upon us and which he declares he will seek, is to be understood as the countenance of images made by human hands, it must be diligently asked what sort of light they possess, or how that light has been marked upon us, or where the same prophet sought such a countenance.

That holy man sought God in his heart, not in faces made by human hands, when he said: “With my whole heart I have sought you, O God; do not reject me from your commandments” (Psalm 119). The countenance of God, therefore, is the knowledge of God—that is, the Son, through whom we arrive at knowledge of the Divinity.

He is also the image of God, as the Apostle says: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1). He is called the image because he is from him. For, according to the same Apostle, he is “the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Hebrews 1). He is called radiance because, since the Father is light, the Son proceeds inseparably from him like radiance from light. He is called figure because, by taking the form of a servant and displaying in himself the image and likeness of the Father through the similarity of his works and virtues, he represented the Father.

He is also the face of God, because through him the Father manifested himself to human beings, as the same Lord Jesus Christ says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

David therefore promised that he would seek this countenance, not images made by human hands, when he said: “Your countenance, O Lord, I shall seek.” He prayed for this brightness of divine knowledge when he said: “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances” (Psalm 115). He longed to reach this knowledge through the Law, not through images, when he said: “Open my eyes, and I shall behold the wonders of your law” (Psalm 115).

He urged us to seek this manifestation of the divine majesty, not the composition of any painting, when he said: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually” (Psalm 105). In another psalm he clearly shows what benefit those who seek the Lord will obtain, saying: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm 34).

And as though we were asking him how we ought to seek the Lord, he added: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” He taught that the Lord is to be sought through the fear of the Lord, not through the worship of images. He instructed the one who desires life and wishes to see good days not to worship images, but to restrain his lips from deceit and his tongue from evil.

He did not teach us to venerate a painting. Rather, he earnestly urged us to turn away from evil, to do good, to seek peace, and to pursue it everywhere.

The light of the Lord’s countenance that has been marked upon us is therefore not to be understood as residing in material images, which, just as they lack every other dignity, also lack light. It is to be understood in the standard of the cross, which, when we receive the sacrament of baptism, is impressed upon our foreheads through the sacred anointing; through it access is opened for the Holy Spirit, who is ineffable light and who also appeared in fire over the disciples, to come to us.

In the impression of the cross there is the light of God’s countenance—that is, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son—because he is always recognized as shining in those who do not allow their innocence or holiness to be violated by wicked deeds. Therefore, so that we may not violate his dwelling place within us, the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were marked for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4).

Since they say that “the light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4) refers to an imaginary face, let them say what the statement written in the same passage refers to: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’” These two clauses are so closely joined to one another in sense and wording that one can scarcely be understood without the other.

This is a figure of speech called by rhetoricians *πεῦσις* (*peusis*), that is, “questioning,” to which an answer is immediately appended without introducing different persons. Some also call it a soliloquy: when each person answers himself concerning what he has asked himself. Thus, as though those who ask, “Who will show us good things?” were being reproached, they answer themselves: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord.”

The sense is this: Many who still think carnally say what not even a few ought to have said: “Who will show us good things?”—namely, those things that the Church always proclaims: that a resurrection is to come, in which all the righteous will receive eternal rewards.

What we do not yet see at all is promised to us; we desire what we cannot attain here. In reply to them, the benefit that is already possessed in the present age is indicated: “The light of your countenance,” he says, “has been marked upon us, O Lord.” For through the standard of the cross and the light of the Holy Spirit we have been so protected that the deceitful plotting and monstrous cunning of the ancient enemy cannot overcome those whom, by the persuasion of the first human being, he once held captive.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That what is written, “All the rich among the people will entreat your countenance,” does not refer to any image made by human hands, as they assert

[Col. 1057A]

Nor is what is written, “All the rich among the people will entreat your countenance” (Psalm 45), to be understood of some face made by human hands—especially since faces made by human hands are not to be entreated, because they cannot hear. Everything that entreats does so in order to be heard, and whatever hears ought not to be irrational. Therefore, whatever entreats ought not to be irrational; and if it ought not to entreat, much less ought it to be worshiped, since worship surpasses entreaty.

For if faces made by human hands are to be entreated and worshiped, as they babble, then they must be believed capable of hearing those who entreat them and of favoring those who worship them. And if they are believed capable of hearing those who entreat them and favoring those who worship them, they must be believed to possess life capable of sensation.

But they do not possess life capable of sensation. Therefore, contrary to their babbling, they are neither to be worshiped nor entreated.

The meaning of these two members, which are called clauses—namely, “All the rich among the people will entreat your countenance” (ibid.)—is spoken by the prophet not of God, whose image and countenance is the Son, but of the Church, which is the body of Christ.

Earlier he had said, through *energeia*:

> “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. For the king has desired your beauty, because he is your Lord; and the daughters of Tyre will worship him with gifts” (ibid.).

Remaining in the same *energeia*, he added concerning the one whose beauty he had said the king desired:

> “All the rich among the people will entreat your countenance.”

The countenance of the Church, therefore, is instruction in spiritual doctrine. It is said to be entreated by the rich because many have renounced all the pomp and riches of the world for its sake, asking how they might reach it and through it fly to the eternal homeland. These are the daughters of Tyre who worship with gifts; these are the rich among the people who entreat its countenance.

There is one Church whose countenance is entreated, and by whom it is entreated: one mother with her children, one bride, one queen, all belonging to Christ, their one head, who is the eternal and immortal bridegroom. His friend addressed these same rich among the people as follows:

> “Command the rich of this world not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment” (1 Timothy 6).

These people are continually exhorted by holy preaching to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may grasp true life by worshiping with gifts.

The rich among the people therefore entreat the countenance of this queen when they run to her and make alms in her bosom, lest they be outside her fellowship. It was the countenance of this queen, not the cosmetics of images, that those who came to her with gifts entreated, placing what they carried at the feet of the apostles. It was the desire for this queen’s countenance, not for any painting, that inflamed them; and in their gifts they entreated her, not some senseless image.

Of them it is written:

> “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and none of them claimed that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common” (Acts 2).

The bridegroom wished to adorn the countenance of this queen—not the colors of some panel—with the resources of the rich when he said:

> “Sell what you possess and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Luke 12);

or when he said:

> “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11).

Since the rich ought not to come to this same queen in hypocrisy with false gifts, as though they were about to entreat her countenance, the Truth itself forbids it, saying:

> “Beware of practicing your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6).

But because it delights her that her countenance should always become brighter and more radiant in public, he clearly shows this when he says:

> “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

In all these passages, what is unmistakably shown is not the worship, entreaty, or glory of images, but either of the bridegroom, who is the head, or of the bride, who is the body.

How entirely devoid of these meanings and of the marks of these ornaments are those who refer “all the rich among the people will entreat your countenance” (Psalm 45) to the faces of images made by human hands is not for us to judge, but is left to the reader’s discretion.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### The inappropriate and delirious statement of Leo, bishop of Phocaea, who, having turned to the worship of images, applies to himself the Psalmist’s verse: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness”

[Col. 1058C]

Since scarcely any testimony from the divine writings was appropriately brought forward in the frequently mentioned synod, it is likewise clear that this passage was not appropriately brought forward by Leo, bishop of Phocaea. If he had produced anything seasoned with wit or relevant to the matter, he would have appeared unlike the others and would have stood opposed to everyone’s opinions. But by confessing that he had wept uselessly because he had not worshiped images, and that he rejoiced because he had turned, even more foolishly, to their worship, he showed himself most clearly to be as delirious as the rest of their company.

For, as he himself stated, he had sadness without loss, joy without gain, a flow of tears without destruction, laughable laughter without acquisition, anger without accusations, and reconciliations without honors—like a child eager to perform some childish amusement. If his nurse restrains him, he wails, his words interrupted by sobs; but if permission to perform these acts is granted him by his nurse, he rejoices, shouting in half-formed utterances. Thus, when restrained, he has empty tears, and when permitted to act, equally empty laughter, since there was no cause for weeping in the prohibition and no cause for laughter in the permission.

For this verse, which he applied to himself in vain in this context—“You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Psalm 30)—was spoken by the prophet in the person of the whole Church through *ethopoeia*. While the Church is engaged in the mortality and hardships of this age, it is said to mourn; but when it reaches eternal recompense, it will then be girded with gladness.

Thus the same most holy prophet said a little earlier in the same psalm: “In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning gladness” (ibid.). By evening he wished this present age of ours to be understood, in which the ends of the ages had arrived, or the day of the final judgment; by morning, the time of the resurrection and the rewards of the saints.

Isaiah the prophet likewise promises this to the saints in the following words:

> “The holy ones will possess double things in their land” (Isaiah 61),

that is, after the resurrection they will enjoy the delight of soul and body in the eternal homeland. He adds:

> “Everlasting joy will be upon my elect, when I grant their works in truth.”

Then our sackcloth will be torn, and we will be girded with gladness, when, according to the Apostle, “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality,” and the saying written in Scripture has come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15); or when, with Christ our life appearing, we too appear with him in glory in these members that we now put to death upon the earth.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### That the worship of images is not concerned with what the Psalmist sang: “Everyone spoke vain things to his neighbor, deceitful lips in his mouth,” and so forth

[Col. 1059C]

Everything without benefit is useless; everything useless is vain. Therefore everything without benefit is vain; and everything that is without service lacks benefit; and everything that lacks benefit is not free from vanity. Therefore everything that is without service is not free from vanity.

For where there is no usefulness, there is no profit; where there is no profit, there is complete vanity. Therefore where there is no usefulness, there is complete vanity.

In the worship of images, then, where there is no benefit, no profit, and no usefulness, one must believe that there is complete vanity. Those who hold assemblies and convene councils to establish and defend this practice, and who institute their absolute worship, undoubtedly speak vain things, each to his neighbor.

Nor are they separated from vanity in this respect: they attempt to bend the testimony of the divine writings violently to their own meanings. Thus they understand in one sense the verse of the Psalmist which he, inspired by the divine Spirit, sang in another sense, while they, puffed up with the arrogance of vanity, understand it differently.

If, therefore, we ask of whom the prophet said, “Everyone spoke vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and a double heart they spoke evil” (Psalm 12), let us reread the text of the holy Gospels. We will find that the Pharisees and Sadducees, as well as the other crowds of the Jews, continually tested the Lord and entered into vain conspiracies against him.

Since they obstinately refused to believe in Christ, they did not cease to speak vainly. Of them it is also written in another psalm:

> “They sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent their bow—a bitter thing—to shoot the blameless in secret. Suddenly they will shoot at him and will not fear” (Psalm 64).

To sharpen the tongue and to have deceitful lips are one and the same thing, since both are expressed by one manner of speech in which sometimes what contains is indicated by what is contained, or what is contained by what contains.

Again, in another psalm it is written of these same people:

> “Their throat is an open tomb; they acted deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Psalm 14).

By “an open tomb,” therefore, he meant their lying mouths, since by speaking destructive evil against the Lord they desired to inflict death upon him. It was called open because of their manifest wickedness, which produced stench rather than fragrance.

This is a comparison of dissimilar things through the trope called *parabole* by grammarians.

“Everyone,” he says, “spoke vain things to his neighbor” (Psalm 12). This, then, is the vanity surpassing every vanity; this is the deceit more tenacious than every deceit: that the Redeemer of the world is not believed and that he is crucified by wicked human beings—not for their salvation, though for the salvation of others, but for their condemnation.

This verse can also be understood of heretics or schismatics. Since they are imbued with the cunning of worldly wisdom and are more ready for vain investigations and superfluous disputes than for believing, they speak vain things, each to his neighbor. Because they think wrongly about Christ or the Church, they never cease inviting their neighbors—that is, other heretics—to the same error, so that they may demolish the Church, which is Christ’s vineyard, with greater violence.

Of them it is said in the Song of Songs:

> “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2).

For our vineyard has blossomed. When heresies, or their followers—the disciples of heresies and of heretics—are caught in their errors by holy and catholic men, the Lord’s vineyard, that is, the Church, continually abounds more and more in sacred gifts, so that it may forever offer cups of nectarous fragrance to its cultivator, who shed his blood for it.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### That what is written, “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Psalm 12), does not concern their forebears, as they claim

[Col. 1060D]

The verse that the Psalmist spoke concerning the deceitful lips and boastful tongues of the faithless Jews—who plotted to seize and kill the world’s Savior by deceit—they attribute in their synod to their own forebears.

Although those forebears displayed a certain rashness in removing images from the adornments of the churches, the others displayed not merely a greater and incomparably greater rashness, but also cruelty, in crucifying the Lord.

These people had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, when they entirely rejected images. Those others, pretending to have zeal for the Law, possessed the zeal of envy and the most treacherous wickedness when they fastened the Lord to the cross. These people indiscriminately damaged the ornaments of the churches; those others maliciously destroyed themselves by despising the Lord.

The most treacherous crowd of Jews therefore possessed deceitful lips and a boastful tongue when they said:

> “We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9).

Did they not have a boastful—and, so to speak, an overbearing—tongue when they said:

> “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19)?

Did they not have a boastful tongue when they said:

> “We know this man, and we know where he is from; but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from” (John 7)?

Did they not have a boastful tongue when they said:

> “Do not write him king; we have no king except Caesar” (John 19)?

From this it is plainly evident that those who are goaded by a disgraceful love of images do not blush to attach to their own forebears, because of the abolition of images, what the prophet spoke concerning the faithless Jews. With the same darts by which the prophet is known to have pierced the enemies of the Church, indeed of Christ, they pierce their own fellow citizens.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### That what is written, “The enemy’s swords have failed completely, and you have destroyed their cities” (Psalm 9), was not fulfilled in their forebears, as they claim

Nor was the prophecy of this verse fulfilled, as they assert, in their predecessors or forebears because they rejected images. Although they imprudently stripped places dedicated to divine worship of their ornaments, they nevertheless remained far removed from the wickedness of the ancient enemy, concerning whom this prophecy speaks.

The wickedness that befell the human race through his persuasion is less than the wickedness of the one who was both its author and the craftsman of his deceit. Just as he is subtler by nature, so he is more cunning in intelligence; and since bodily weakness does not burden him, the wickedness of his crafty perversity sharpens him.

The swords of this enemy have therefore failed completely, because his most wicked temptations fail entirely as soon as they are brought against Christ, who is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes, the end without end. When we reach him, we have nothing further to seek.

For this reason the prophet calls blessed the one who dashes the little ones—that is, irrational thoughts—against the Rock, namely Christ, who is the cornerstone (Psalm 137). Or, as some wish, “The enemies’ swords have failed completely” refers to the time when the sword with which the ancient enemy rages will be destroyed at the consummation of the age by the sword of almighty God. Concerning this the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword” (Psalm 7). And through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says:

> “As I live, says the Lord, I will sharpen my sword like lightning and repay vengeance upon my enemies.”

*Framea* is a Hebrew word by which the sword of the ancient enemy is signified in this passage.

“Enemy,” therefore, is not a nominative plural here, as many suppose, but a singular genitive: “The enemy’s swords have failed.” This is the figure called *prolepsis*, that is, anticipation or presumption, by which things that ought to follow are placed beforehand.

The same figure is found at the beginning of the prophet Ezekiel, when he says, “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year” (Ezekiel 1). It also occurs in the Psalm where it says, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 87).

The cities that were destroyed, therefore, are not, as they suppose, the predecessors or forebears of these people, overthrown because of the abolition of images. Rather, the Psalmist says that unbelieving peoples—or heaps of evil works, which the devil inhabits as the walls of his city—were destroyed by the manifestation of Christ.

[Note: Rather, through Moses, Deuteronomy 32:41.]

An empty and vain love of images has therefore invaded the hearts of those who, in order to establish their worship, believe that what was prophesied concerning the ancient enemy or the unbelieving Jews was spoken of their own forebears or predecessors.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### How what is written, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house,” is to be understood; they understand this beauty as images
The house of God is, according to allegory, the Church; according to anagoge, the heavenly homeland; and according to tropology, the human soul. Therefore, in most passages of Holy Scripture, when “the house of God” is read, one must understand not walls or some material building, but the spiritual and ineffable dwelling of God. The mind of those who do not consider the beauty of the Lord’s house to be its virtues, but material images, is utterly starved of these hidden meanings [Col. 1062C].

Had that eminent prophet seen certain images—or at least beautiful walls or the most precious furnishings of buildings—when he said, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. XXVI)? Is one to believe that the place where the Lord’s glory dwells is located anywhere among things made by human hands?

Holy Church therefore possesses the beauty that the Prophet loved, namely, spiritual virtues. It has gold, that is, faith or inward understanding; it has silver, that is, confession or the beauty of speech; it has silver columns, that is, holy men adorned with rational patience and beautiful eloquence. These columns have silver bases when they are set upon the stability of the word of God handed down to us through the prophets and apostles [Col. 1062D]. They also have a gilded capital, because the golden head is faith in Christ, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “For the head of every man is Christ” (I Cor. XI).

It also possesses, in place of imperishable wood, knowledge that came through the Wood, or the incorruption of chastity, which knows no old age. In place of fine linen it has virginity; in place of scarlet, the glory of confession; in place of purple, the radiance of charity; in place of hyacinth, the hope of the kingdom of heaven. Its priests are clothed in these materials, according to David’s words: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXII). Paul also exhorts them in these words: “Clothe yourselves with the bowels of mercy” [Col. 1063A] (Col. III).

Its priests also have other, nobler garments, which the same Vessel of Election describes when he says, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII).

It also has a library, that is, holy men instructed in the teachings of divine law. Of them the Prophet says, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord; blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek them with their whole heart” (Ps. CXIX). Again, he calls blessed those who keep his commandments in memory so as to do them.

It has ten spacious courts, since it is expanded in the breadth of spiritual understanding not in one word of the law alone, nor in two or three, but throughout the entire Decalogue of the law. Or this may refer to the fact that it produces the fruit of the Spirit, namely, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, modesty, faith, and self-control, together with the charity added to them, which is greater than all [Col. 1063B].

It also has an altar, that is, the firmness of faith, upon which it offers to God the sacrifices of prayers and the victims of mercy. Upon it, with the knife of self-control, it sacrifices pride as a bull, slaughters anger as a ram, and offers up extravagance and every form of lust as goats and kids. From these it separates for the priests the right arm, the breast, and the jaws, that is, good works and works of the right hand, in which nothing sinister is found.

It also has a lampstand of light, either because the Lord is its light, or because holy men—whose lamps are burning and whose loins are girded, as they await their Lord when he returns from the wedding—pour into it, as bearers of light, the teachings of their preaching [Col. 1063C].

This lampstand of lamps is placed toward the south so that it faces north, that is, so that holy men may always watch attentively and carefully the devil’s schemes and look with fearful minds toward the place from which temptation is to come. For the Prophet also says that he saw a boiling cauldron or pot, with its face turned toward the north. Elsewhere it is said, “For from the north evil shall be opened upon the whole land” (Jer. I). The Apostle Peter likewise says, “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V).

It also has a table of the Presence, bearing twelve loaves, placed on the northern side and facing south—that is, the twelve apostles, whom it is commanded to set forth daily and without ceasing toward the south, because it continually awaits the Lord’s coming [Col. 1063D]. For, says the Prophet, “The Lord will come from the south” (Hab. III).

It has an altar of incense, because from the firmness of its faith the smoke of holy prayers continually rises before the Lord, and every day, with David, it cries, “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXLI). Or this is because, according to the Apostle, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II).

It has the mercy seat, the ark, and the two cherubim, concerning which we argued above in a certain chapter.

It also has a high priest, of whom the Apostle Paul says, “But Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hand, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. IX) [Col. 1064A]. To him the Psalmist also says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CX).

He is clothed in a linen robe, when his saints, who cleave to him, are clothed with the lamp of chastity. He also has a jeweled shoulder-piece, because his chosen ones shine with the radiance of their works; when people see their works, they glorify their Father who is in heaven. He has upon his breast the breastpiece, called the rational, distinguished by four rows of stones, by which the evangelical word is signified: arranged in a fourfold order, it sets forth for us the truth of faith and the manifestation of the Trinity.

He also has upon his forehead a gleaming golden plate, called the petal [Col. 1064B], that is, divinity, because he is of one substance with the Father. For just as nothing among metals compares with gold, so among creatures nothing can compare with the Creator.

This high priest also has coverings in his inner parts, because the mystery of his incarnation is difficult to investigate, as John testifies when he says, “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark I; Luke III).

Around the hem of his garment he also has bells, placed at the edge of that same garment, so that they may always sound. For holy preachers, who are in fact his garment, cannot remain silent about the final times and the end of the world, but continually warn us about what is to come, mindful of what is said through a certain wise man: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccles. VII) [Col. 1064C].

This house of God, that is, the Church, whose beauty we briefly enumerate, also has the Holy of Holies. In the present age it has, in place of the holy things, holy conduct; in place of the Holy of Holies, into which one enters only once, it has passage to heaven, when, having despised visible things, one passes over to invisible things. Of these the Apostle says, “Beloved, it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

This, then, was the beauty of the heavenly homeland that the most holy man loved—not the cosmetics of images and colors, not the likenesses of material paintings. Because of this beauty, not because of material figures, he was dissolved, as it were, by an unbearable longing when he said, “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, for I shall enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. XLII) [Col. 1064D].

Of this house, not of these visible walls, the Apostle said, “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by hand, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V).

Isaiah likewise contemplated this beauty as something to be regarded, not the work of painters, when he said, “Look upon Zion, the city of your solemn assembly; your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a rich habitation, a tabernacle that shall never be moved” (Isa. XXXIII).

Of this house David says, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. [Col. 1065A] LXXXIV).

Were the holy Fathers—leaving aside the others—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, or the entire company of anchorites and hermits, who possessed neither the beauty of basilicas nor painted images, but dedicated their souls to God in little huts—for that reason not holy? Did they therefore not love the beauty of the Lord’s house, or did they not long with ardent hearts to contemplate the place where God’s glory dwells, because they neither possessed nor worshiped images?

For within themselves, like all the other holy souls, they possessed the temple of God and the place where his glory dwells, as the Vessel of Election says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III).

Moreover, many flowers of ambrosian fragrance could have been gathered from the golden meadows of the divine Scriptures, by which the beauty of Holy Church might be displayed according to tropology, allegory, and anagoge, if we were not restrained by the reins of the brevity to which we are devoted [Col. 1065B]. Let these few examples, therefore, offered in place of many, suffice. The diligent reader will take care to investigate the rest that has not been presented here, and will see that the beauty of the house of God shines not in material images but in spiritual virtues.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the Psalmist did not say, as they claim, on account of images made by human hands, “As we have heard, so we have seen” (Ps. XLVIII).

Since they rejoice that they have seen images made by human hands, they have adapted to themselves the Psalmist’s verse, saying, “As we have heard, so we have seen.” Let them say—let them, I ask, say—where they had previously heard what they now see in images. Let them say which patriarch, prophet, or apostle brought to their hearing what now lies before their eyes. Let them say who foretold this privilege to them: that they would not only see images but worship them. Having obtained this promised blessing, let them rightly say, “As we have heard, so we have seen.”

But we, who by God’s help understand the prophecy of the Psalms spiritually, as far as our powers allow, believe that this verse was not spoken about images made by human hands, but was prophesied concerning more important and eminent mysteries. Just as in the Law we heard about Christ’s coming, so in the Gospel we see it; just as we learned from the prophets about his incarnation, so now we behold it in the sequence of the New Testament; just as in the hagiographical books and throughout all the sacred writings we saw his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven prefigured through typological mysteries, so now we see all these things accomplished in the holy Gospels [Col. 1066A].

When, moreover, with his consent, we come to the eternal homeland and see there the happiness concerning which we heard amid the anguish of this mortality, we too shall say, “As we have heard, so we have seen”: that is, as mortal beings we heard, but now as immortals we see; as corruptible beings we heard, but now as incorruptible beings we see; as we heard in our sorrowful pilgrimage, so now we see in the most blessed land of the living. What we heard while suffering the stormiest tempests of the world, we now see while enjoying the sweetest security of paradise; and what we heard while fearing the most perilous shipwreck, we now see when we have reached the safest harbor, long desired by us.

At this point we thought that the first book should be brought to a close. Since we have mentioned a harbor, let us bring it also into harbor here, so that, wearied by our former voyage, we may walk for a while in the harbor, recover our strength, and, with the Lord’s help, spread our sails for the voyage of the second book.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1065]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1065C]

Having treated in the preceding book, as briefly as possible, certain verses of the divine Law which, as we have often stated, those against whom this work of ours is directed [Col. 1065D] are known to have brought forward in support of the material of their vanity, and having also dealt with certain chapters included in that same book which could appropriately be offered for their correction, it is necessary now, in this present second book, to undertake, with the Lord’s favor, both a sober and sound treatment of the remaining verses of the divine Law and an exposition, according to their proper meanings, of certain sayings of the holy Fathers that they have likewise misappropriated.

In this book there will also be inserted certain chapters that will block the passage of their error into the minds of the faithful. By such error they strive to equate things lacking in holiness or authority with the most sacred things instituted by the Lord himself. Thus, opposing their utterly empty fables [Col. 1066C] in these two volumes with the saving weapons of the two Testaments, we may proceed more freely to the third, at whose beginning the foundation of our faith will be laid. Since it will contain the confession of the holy and one Trinity, the number of the third book will also be completed and adorned by that most sacred number, which is to be adorned by the mystery of holy faith [Col. 1066D].

For we place the hope of all our discussion and of our other activities not in the ingenious arguments of worldly arts, but in him who, present bodily, also says, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X), and who once said through the Prophet, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXXI).

For this reason we have divided the progress of our discussion by a certain ordered manner of proceeding and by intervals between the books, lest disordered length should make the path of an undifferentiated journey tedious. Nor did we wish to present anything confused or undigested, lest the disordered mass of the work should offer the reader a kind of rustic tumult through its confused shouting [Col. 1067A]. For travelers do not refuse to walk about at suitable times, and cultivators of fields, vineyards, and gardens customarily establish boundaries by intervals across the countryside or by measurements of the fields.

## CHAPTER I. That it was not written on behalf of those who reject the worship of images, as those who worship them claim, when the Psalm says, “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places.”

It is no small madness that these people understand as referring to those who reject the worship of images things that were long ago foretold concerning those who overthrew the city of Jerusalem and burned the Lord’s temple. For it is one thing to remove from the temple the bronze sea, the two cherubim, the vessels, and the other ornaments; another [Col. 1067B] not to worship images made by human hands. It is one thing to consign the beauty of the temple to the flames that destroy a city; another to avoid the worship of images. It is one thing cruelly to destroy the Holy of Holies; another prudently to forbid the bending of one’s neck before paintings.

Finally, whoever wishes to know concerning whom the Psalmist said, “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places” (Ps. XLVII), is instructed not only by the histories in the Books of Kings and by Roman records, which recount the past destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the temple, but also by the prophecy of David himself, that distinguished prophet. Through the figure called prolepsis, he sang of the future disasters of that city and the overthrow of that most sacred temple as though they were past, saying: “O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem like a place for guarding fruit,” and so forth (Ps. LXXIX).

In the Psalm containing the verse with which we are now concerned, he says: “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places, and all who hate you have gloried. They set up their signs as signs in the midst of your court, and they did not understand, as though on a road, above, as though in a forest of trees. With axes they cut down its doors; with the double axe and the hatchet they struck them down. They burned your sanctuary with fire; they defiled the dwelling-place of your name upon the earth” (Ps. LXXIII) [Col. 1067C]. In another Psalm he expresses the same thing more clearly: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it.”

But lest anyone be troubled because he did not say, “How greatly the enemies have acted wickedly,” but [Col. 1067D] “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly,” let him observe that this was spoken through a figure of speech called syllepsis. Through it, a plurality may be represented by one, as in the Gospel: “And the robbers who were crucified with him reviled him” (Matt. XXVII); or, “For those who sought the child’s life have died” (Matt. II). Conversely, one may be represented by many, as it is read in Exodus: “Pray to the Lord, that he may take away from us the serpent” (Num. XXI); and in the Psalm: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, and the frog destroyed them” (Ps. LXXVIII).

If anyone examines this more subtly according to mystical understanding, he may not inappropriately perceive the holy Church and understand as acting wickedly within it the heretics who continually strive to attack it with perverse doctrines. Nevertheless, none of those who [Col. 1068A] possess a sound and sober understanding will interpret it as referring to those who reject the worship of images. Therefore, to the extent that those people are deprived of sound sense when they assert that this verse was spoken about such persons, to that same extent those who do not worship images remain firm in the strength of their understanding.

## CHAPTER II. That this too has no bearing on the matter, as they claim, namely what is written: “For there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.”

This verse too has been inserted incompetently into the reading of the same synod, since it is neither our voice—we who worship the Father in spirit and truth—nor the voice of those who attempt to worship God and his saints in images. For we have a great prophet, Jesus Christ our Lord, of whom it is said through Moses, “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet; you shall hear him” [Col. 1068B] (Deut. XVIII; Acts III and VII). According to the Apostle, we also have him as an advocate with the Father (I John II); every day we behold him with spiritual eyes and are diligently instructed by his prophecies.

Rather, this is the lament of the Jews mourning the destruction, dispersal, disasters, and deaths of their nation, as well as the ruin of the temple, the abolition of the ceremonies, and their withdrawal from prophecy and the knowledge of God. They say, “For there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us” (Ps. LXXIV). This too was foretold through the prophet Hosea, who says, “For the children of Israel shall sit for many days without king and without prince, without sacrifice and without altar, without ephod and without seraphim” (Hos. III) [Col. 1068C].

He subsequently added a prophecy of their conversion to the faith, which we believe will take place near the end of the world: “Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the last days.”

## CHAPTER III. How one should understand, “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing”: a passage which, like the others, they understand differently from what was said.

In the sacred writings, the city of God is sometimes understood figuratively as the human soul inhabited by God, as Scripture says, “I will dwell in them,” and again, “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom” (Ps. V). Sometimes it means the Church of the present age, which the rush of the river makes glad [Col. 1068D] and to which the Prophet says, “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me” (Ps. CXXXVI).

Most often it means the heavenly Jerusalem, understood as constructed from the ranks of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and the other faithful. Of it the Apostle says, “But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal. IV). To it the Lord also promises through the prophet Isaiah, “The sun shall no longer set for you, and your moon shall not diminish forever” (Isa. LX). John likewise says in the Apocalypse that he saw it descending from heaven, adorned with its jewels (Rev. XXI). Almost innumerable things could be said concerning its blessedness, but the style of this brief work cannot arrange them all [Col. 1069A].

In this city the images of the wicked will be reduced to nothing, because their appearance will not be able to appear before the divine presence. But just as they polluted the image of the Lord in themselves during the course of the present life, so their image will not appear in the heavenly Jerusalem. They will be consigned to everlasting fire. Of them the Psalmist says elsewhere: “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLIX). For although he possessed such great honor that he had been created according to the image and likeness of God, through lack of understanding he descended into such a depth of vices that he was deservedly compared with irrational animals.

The images of the wicked are therefore reduced to nothing when, withdrawing himself from them, Truth itself alienates them from its light [Col. 1069B]; they cannot retain the likeness whose blessedness they are known to remain wholly without.

Because of their deceitfulness, therefore, he had earlier said that evils were imposed upon them, since God, the just judge, repays each person according to his works. He had also said that they were cast down when they were exalted, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. He had said that they suddenly failed and perished because of their iniquity, like the dream of one awakening.

For just as, through certain illusions, human hearts are deceived in dreams, and people rejoice that they have suddenly obtained whatever they desired—when someone acquires the kingdom he longed for, or is raised to the office he desired, or, poverty having been driven away, is suddenly enriched, or enjoys the marriage he wished for, or, though infirm, rejoices that he has recovered his lost limbs [Col. 1069C], or a criminal rejoices that he has become honored, or an ignoble person that he has become noble, or a foolish person supposes himself wise—and then, on awakening, suddenly loses what he had acquired while asleep and, with his eyes opened, grieves that he no longer sees what he had rejoiced to see with them closed, so the happiness of the wicked appears in a certain way like a dream, because after a short time it will no longer be seen.

Just as those who awaken lose what they had suddenly acquired in sleep, so the dying lose what they appeared to possess. For the former are deprived in an instant of the illusory joy they obtained while lying down, and the latter cannot long retain the world’s empty—and, so to speak, smoky—joys.

Because of their wickedness, the Prophet, as though inflamed by a kind of severity, added: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Ps. LXXIII) [Col. 1069D]. Thus the faces of those who have polluted the beauty of your likeness in themselves by evil works will not be seen in your city, where there is eternal happiness, supreme blessedness, and perpetual joy.

In its palaces reigns the King whose kingdom shall have no end. Its benches shine with the senate of the patriarchs; its court glows with the companies of the prophets; its walls are adorned by the numerous army of martyrs; its gates are beautified by apostolic assemblies; its streets overflow with virgin choirs; its dwellings are filled with the legions of confessors. It has no need of the sun, because the Lord is its light, and throughout all its streets “Alleluia” is sung.

## CHAPTER IV. How one should understand what the Psalmist sang, “Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have embraced one another” (Ps. LXXXV): a verse which John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners, with the participation of the venerable Pope Adrian and Patriarch Tarasius, rashly and flatteringly declares to have been fulfilled.

[Col. 1070A]

David, the most eloquent of prophets, elegantly sings that mercy and truth met each other, and that justice and peace embraced one another. This is clearly fulfilled when, after the Lord’s incarnation, the two Testaments were brought together into a single framework of union.

For although they appear in some respects to differ from one another, they are nevertheless known to converge at one crossroads in Christ, who is our peace and who made both one. In the New Testament there is mercy, through which the human race is liberated by grace; in the Old there is truth, in which the proclamation of the Law and the prophets is contained [Col. 1070B].

These two are said to have met one another not to exercise opposition, but to fulfill the grace of the promised perfection. What was divided in time is shown to have become one. And so that David, the hymn-singing prophet, might clearly express the very nature of the covenant, he repeated the same idea with a variety of names, indicating that two things—namely, justice and peace—had immediately entered into mutual harmony through a kind of loving embrace.

This verse is also clearly spoken according to somatopoeia—that is, the attribution of a body—in which incorporeal things are given bodies; and according to metaphor, that is, the transference of things and words, by which transference is often made from animate things to animate, from inanimate things to inanimate, and from inanimate things to animate [Col. 1070C]. These two figures of speech differ in this respect: one gives bodies to incorporeal things, while the other attributes limbs and movements to corporeal things, and limbs, movements, and forms to incorporeal things.

John the presbyter, with the participation of the venerable Pope Adrian and Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, rashly and flatteringly brought forward this verse. Although that presbyter was lower in honor than the bishops seated at the same synod, he is not, nevertheless, read to have been inferior in error. Though they surpassed him in the eminence of their rank, he surpassed them in his long-winded insolence; and he, a subordinate, could not be overcome by his superiors in shameless loquacity, just as he was surpassed by his superiors in pontifical dignity [Col. 1070D].

He is especially believed to have committed a double fault in this matter: either because, with the superstitious intention of establishing the worship of images, he attempted to turn humanward words uttered by the Holy Spirit and filled with the mysteries’ hidden meanings; or because, blinded by the same perverse intention, he fell miserably into the vice of flattery.

That distinguished prophet feared this vice of flattery when he said, “Let the righteous rebuke me in mercy and correct me, but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. CXLI). Hence another Scripture also rightly says, “It is better to be rebuked by the righteous than praised by the sinner” [Col. 1071A]. And again: “Those who call you happy lead you into error.” For flatterers praise in order to entice, not to summon people to eternal happiness, which needs no good thing.

## CHAPTER V. That the worship of images does not concern, as they claim, what is written: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy” (Ps. XCXIX).

By this verse of the Psalmist, the error that has so taken root in certain hearts on account of the worship of images that they convene synods to establish it and strive to appropriate testimonies from the Holy Scriptures to fortify it believes that it can defend itself, since it hears that the Lord’s footstool is to be worshiped.

It thinks that it has protected the top of its body with this helmet, so that it may not feel the blows of the flashing sword; it supposes that it has armored the rest of its body with this breastplate, so that it may not suffer the loss of its stability from the strikes of darts; it believes that it has obtained protection in this shield, by which it need not fear the wounding flights of missiles.

But either by falling down it will grow weary, or by hiding it will flee, stripped of these defenses, just as it has made vain and useless use of them. It will feel so keenly the force of the spiritual sword brought against it by holy men that it will not believe that even the slightest strength remains in it [Col. 1071B].

Because the Prophet commands that the Lord’s footstool be worshiped, must the worship of images therefore be established? What likeness is there between the Lord’s footstool and material images? What fellowship is there between the ineffable works of God [Col. 1071C] and images fashioned by any human artisans? What partnership is there between so excellent and glorious a mystery and senseless figures produced by human ingenuity? Or where was it instituted that images should be worshiped, as it was instituted that the Lord’s footstool should be worshiped?

David did not say, “Worship the images of certain saints,” as he said, “Worship the Lord’s footstool.” Nor did the Lord say, “The works of human hands are my seat, and images are their footstool.” Rather, he said, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI; Acts VII).

Hear, then, most foolish—or rather, most insane—error; hear, incomparable madness; hear, ridiculous sluggishness, as blessed Ambrose teaches what the Lord’s footstool is and how it is to be worshiped.

For he says:

“They worshiped the Lord, the apostles, because they bore witness to the faith and received the teaching of faith. The angels also worshiped him, of whom it is written: ‘And let all his angels worship him.’ They worship not only his divinity but also his footstool, because it is holy.”

And shortly afterward:

“But lest an example already set forth should perhaps escape some people, let us consider in what way what the Prophet says, ‘And worship his footstool,’ appears to pertain to the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. We must not judge of a footstool according to human usage. For God is not corporeal, nor is he finite, so that we should suppose a footstool placed beneath his feet like a support. Nor do we read that anything [Col. 1072A] besides God is to be worshiped, since it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. VI). How, then, would the Prophet, who was nourished under the Law and instructed in the Law, command something contrary to the Law?

“This is therefore no ordinary question, and for that reason let us consider more carefully what the footstool is. For elsewhere we read, ‘Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet’ (Isa. LXVI). Yet we are not to worship the earth, because it is God’s creature. Let us nevertheless see whether the Prophet means that earth to be worshiped which the Lord Jesus assumed in taking flesh.

“Thus, by the footstool earth is understood, and by earth the flesh of Christ, which we also worship today in the mysteries, and which the apostles worshiped in the Lord Jesus, as we said above. For Christ is not divided, but one; nor, when he is worshiped as the Son of God [Col. 1072B], is he denied to have been born of a virgin.

“Since, therefore, the mystery of the incarnation is to be worshiped, and the incarnation is the work of the Holy Spirit, as it is written, ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God’ (Luke I), Saint Augustine, the most diligent investigator, also asserted that this footstool of the Lord’s feet should be understood as the Lord’s body, which he took from the Virgin Mary, on account of the nature of the humanity that he deigned to assume.

“This body is so subjected and united to that Power that it is established as higher than all creatures, as the Apostle says: ‘What is weak in God is stronger than men’ (I Cor. I). Elsewhere the Apostle says of the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus [Col. 1072C]: ‘For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth’ (Phil. II).

“Therefore, in this verse, by the magnificence of the Lord’s feet is understood the stability of his divinity, which always remains in the omnipotent glory of its nature, like the tireless firmness of feet.

“According to tropology, the feet of the Lord may also signify the final times, when the Lord deigned to become incarnate. Hence the evangelist John says, ‘Little children, it is the last hour’ (I John II). The Apostle Paul likewise says, ‘When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law’ (Gal. IV).

“It should certainly be noted that he did not say, ‘because it is holy,’ but ‘because he is holy’ (Ps. XCIX), [Col. 1072D] namely so that the Lord’s body might not be separated from the divinity, while the distinct property of each nature is preserved, but might be referred to one person. Hence the Gospel says, ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John I).”

Let what has briefly been stated about the Lord’s footstool suffice for now. Let us proceed to the remaining matters.

## CHAPTER VI. That the worship of images cannot be established from what they suppose is written, “Worship in his holy mountain.”

Nor can the worship of images be established in this passage either, as they themselves admit, on the basis of what is sung through the same holy prophet: “Worship on his holy mountain” (Ps. [Col. 1073A] 99). For the same holy man, in harmonious song, plainly commands that the Lord be worshiped not as the mountain, but on the holy mountain. And even if he were commanding that the mountain be worshiped, sound minds would understand this not as worship of images but of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is higher than all mountains, whose height and power surpass the heights and powers of all the saints. Of him the prophet Isaiah says:

“And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow toward it, and many peoples shall go” (Isa. 2).

Let it therefore be said, “Worship on his holy mountain” (Ps. 99), because the prophet plainly commands that one worship not the mountain here, but the Lord on the holy mountain. This can doubtless be referred to Mount Zion, which is the Church, the mountain of mountains and the Holy of Holies, whose inhabitant is Christ himself. Hence he rightly commands that the holy Lord be worshiped on the holy mountain, since, just as his praise does not belong on a wicked mouth, so the ugliness of a place cannot be appropriate to his worship.

We therefore worship on his holy mountain, not images or certain superstitious objects, but the same Lord who is the head of that mountain and who, in order to acquire that mountain, deigned not only to be born but also to die. Of him the prophet says: “He brought them to the mountain of his sanctification, this mountain which his right hand acquired” (Ps. 78). And of him the Lawgiver says:

“Bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the habitation you have prepared for yourself, which you have prepared, O Lord; your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have prepared, O Lord, who reign forever and unto the age of the age and beyond” (Exod. 15).

## CHAPTER VII. That the words “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Ps. 125) were not spoken, as they boast, on behalf of those who worship images

It is not surprising if those who are mistaken in great matters are mistaken in small ones; nor is their error in this further matter surprising: they boast that they are righteous because they worship images, while they declare us sinners because we refuse to worship them, even though out of love for those images they attempt to violate the purity of the divine Scriptures, consider their chief advantage in faith to consist in these things, and obstinately strive to anathematize those who, rejecting these and other vanities of the same kind, serve God alone and worship him.

How, then, that the text of this verse does not pertain to the very matter for which they have produced it, how it is seen to resist their interpretation, and by how many indications it differs from their opinion, is evident not only to simple readers but even to the uneducated. For, setting aside enigmatic or allegorical coverings, it openly demonstrates that the Lord does not permit the righteous to be scourged by the wicked for long, lest, subjected to prolonged punishments, they fall into the disaster of despair. Rather, if for a time he chastens some with adversities for their testing, he again raises them up by the duration of an extended period of prosperity interrupted by those trials, so that their innocence may remain unshaken.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the words “The Lord will bring those who turn aside to bondage with those who work iniquity” (Ps. 125) were not spoken through the prophet on behalf of those who reject the worship of images, as they foolishly rave

We have wished to place this verse separately in our work for the following reason: although it occurs with the preceding verse in the text of a single psalm, it differs from it in meaning; and although they have produced it to establish one and the same error, it is nevertheless clear that it was placed in a different location in the reading of the frequently mentioned synod.

“Those who turn aside to bondage” are therefore not to be understood as those who reject the superstitious worship of images, [Col. 1074B] but as those who, ensnared in the restraints of the ancient enemy, incline toward iniquity; and the more greatly they are known to sin, the more tightly, of course, they are bound by diabolical coils. Hence a certain wise man says: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5). The holy prophet Isaiah likewise speaks of this bondage: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with a cart-rope!” (Isa. 5).

The Lord will therefore bring those who turn aside to this bondage with those who work iniquity, because, plainly, with those with whom they sin in this world, they will be condemned in the future. They will go to the fire prepared for the author of crimes and for his angels, whose bonds they neglected to break in this world.

May he make us free from whose bondage he redeemed us into freedom, and who showed a great light of his splendor to us sitting in darkness; or, while we dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, himself arose as the true light.
