May that same one render us exempt from his most severe condemnation, who made us followers of his most radiant faith, hope, and love.

## CHAPTER IX. That the worship of images cannot be confirmed, as those who eagerly pursue their worship dream, by the fact that Solomon is said to have made oxen and lions in the Temple

Solomon is read to have made oxen and lions in the Temple. By their construction, we who know according to the Apostle that the Law is spiritual are instructed in certain hidden mysteries; but those who love the worship of images attempt to strengthen the vanity of their senselessness. We are thoroughly taught by mystical meanings; they are confirmed in the magnitude of their error. Warned by the shadow, we investigate the truth; deceived by a deed rightly performed, they derive authority for a deed that ought not to be performed.

Why, then, did you make them, offspring of David, king of Israel, wisest of the wise? “I made them,” I say, “not so that they should be worshiped, but so that they might signify certain mysteries; not so that they might favor error, but so that they might reveal the secrets of the mysteries; not so that they might be a stumbling block to blind minds, but so that they might suggest something great to those who subtly investigate subtle things.”

If he ought therefore to be angry because, from things rightly done by me, the wicked derive a wicked example, then no less ought one to be angry with the Lawgiver, who raised up in the desert a thing necessary for the sight of many, which the perverse will of human beings afterward used perversely.

We therefore do not in any way reject the images fashioned in basilicas for the remembrance of past events and for ornament, since we know that they were made through Moses and Solomon, although in typological figures. But we restrain their excessively insolent, or rather excessively superstitious, worship. I have nowhere found it instituted by the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, or apostolic men.

[Note: [Col. 1075] “Nor have I found it instituted anywhere by apostolic men.” The corrector had *reperimus* (“we have found”); I prefer *repererimus* (“we have found,” with the appropriate tense).]

But, to return to the matter at hand, Solomon made oxen and lions in the Temple because Christ established apostles and their successors in the Church. According to the judgment of blessed Gregory, they are “companions of those who act well through humility against the vices of those who transgress, and raised up through zeal for justice, so that the gentleness of the ox may support the former, and the fierceness of the lion goad the latter.”

Both qualities can be gathered from the example of the Church’s shepherd: he soothed Cornelius, who practiced humility, with gentle words, but rose up vehemently against Ananias and Sapphira, who acted deceitfully. Holy men therefore sometimes possess the gentleness of oxen and sometimes the fierceness of lions, for they hold both the rod with which they rule the strong forcefully and the staff with which they support the weaknesses of the infirm.

## CHAPTER X. How the words written in the Song of Songs are to be understood: “Show me your face, and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet to me and your face is beautiful” (Song 2)—a passage which they most shamelessly have produced in reference to the viewing of images

[Col. 1075C]

The face of the Church, whom Christ addresses with a pleasing variety of names, calling her now a dove, now beautiful, now his beloved, and whom he commands to rise—that is, to believe—to hasten, to increase in good works, and to come, that is, to approach eternal reward, is not bodily but spiritual. For the other things written about her in the same Song of Songs are also to be understood not carnally but spiritually.

For if this verse can be applied to some bodily object, as those dream who have produced it in reference to the viewing of images, then everything written about the members of Christ’s bride, the Church, must likewise be believed bodily. And if all these things pertain not to visible members but to invisible virtues, then her face also must be understood as an invisible virtue rather than as the face of some image seen by the eyes.

The face of the Church, therefore, is knowledge of her virtues. Because of the beauty of this loveliness she is loved by the bridegroom, to whom the prophet rightly says: “For the king has desired your beauty.” Christ therefore urges the Church to show him her face—that is, always to contemplate him in faith and works—so that she may be able to say with Elijah: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (3 Kings 17), and may not belong to those of whom the prophet declares: “They turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jer. 2).

He also urges her to let her voice sound in his ears, because he is ready to hear his saints, as the Psalmist testifies: “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations” (Ps. 34). He says that her voice is sweet and her face beautiful because the prayers of the saints are always pleasing to God, as is the gracious presence of those who have received from Christ’s light the power to remain in the beauty of righteousness.

Granted, let this verse be capable of being applied to the viewing of images: “Show me your face” (Song 2), or “Your face is beautiful.” What, then, will they say about the voice, which the prophet both sings as sweet and urges to be made heard by him? Images, of course, if they do not have a soul, enjoy a voice much less; and if they do not enjoy a voice, they enjoy the sweetness of a voice much less still. If, therefore, they have no soul, they cannot possess the sweetness of a voice.

Thus it is plainly evident that, just as in the other arguments of this matter their irrelevant statements are frustrated, so they are frustrated in this passage as well—especially since it cannot rightly be said of their images, “Show me your face,” nor of their voice, which they entirely lack, “Let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.”

## CHAPTER XI. How the words written through the prophet Isaiah are to be understood: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19)—a passage which they foolishly and with insufficient learning attempt to refer to the worship of images

[Col. 1076C]

Josephus relates that this prophecy was fulfilled in Onias the priest, who went down as an exile into Egypt surrounded by numerous bands of Jews and constructed an altar and temple there. We, however, who hold and believe with devout minds that the things prophesied concerning Christ’s coming and the calling of the nations are not future but past, do not think that this prophecy was fulfilled through the priest Onias, but through Christ the Lord, mediator of God and human beings.

He established faith in this world, which is often designated by the name “Egypt.” In the solidity of that faith, the faithful offer to the Lord sacrifices of prayer and libations of the merits of the saints. Near its boundary he placed an inscription, that is, the Gospel or apostolic teaching, by which the minds of the faithful are formed for the performance of good works.

When the prophet adds, “And it shall be for a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19), he wished the mystery of the Lord’s passion to be understood as the sign and testimony. Then those who have believed, when Egyptians rush against Egyptians, when a man fights against his brother, and when city fights against city—that is, when the time of persecution has come—will implore the Lord’s mercy. Immediately the Savior will come, that is, Jesus—for this is what the name sounds like in our language [Col. 1077A]—and the Lord will be known by the Egyptians. These will be either the persecutors who have been overcome or the believers who have been delivered by his present aid.

Since this, then, is the meaning of the prophetic utterance, and this is the interpretation of the inscription and altar, who would produce it to establish the worship of images except one blinded by the darkness of his own senselessness? Who would dare attempt to use a prophetic utterance rightly spoken by the Holy Spirit to establish his own error, except one whom the magnitude of his error has made everywhere its follower?

How, then, could the worship of images derive even the slightest support from these words of the holy prophet, when it is clear that they were spoken not so that they might be fulfilled historically in some altar or inscription, but so that they might be possessed spiritually by the faithful in the faith of Christ and in the Gospel?

Even if they had been spoken historically of a physical altar or inscription, the worship of images could not for that reason be established, since the prophet plainly foretold that the altar and inscription would not be worshiped but would merely exist. For “it will be” is one thing, and “it will be worshiped” another; the altar of the Lord is one thing, and anyone’s image another; an inscription near the boundaries is one thing, and a likeness in any material another.

He did not say: “There will be a time when no one except a worshiper of images will please God.” Nor did he say: “Such a great worship of images will grow up that whoever does not worship them or honor them with incense, lamps, or certain offerings will be worthy of anathema.” Rather, he said: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and an inscription to the Lord near its boundary; and it shall be for a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt”—as though he were plainly saying: “There shall be faith in the world and the preaching of the Gospel, through which the manifestation of the Lord’s passion and of our redemption will be made known.”

## CHAPTER XII. The testimony of the holy Gospel, “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Matt. 5; Mark 4; Luke 11), produced most absurdly and recklessly by those who worship images against those who refuse to worship them

O inconsistent and laughable matter! In the reading of that same vanity, certain things are written—I do not know with what understanding—about us who reject the worship of images, drawn from what the Lord instituted when he sent his disciples to preach: that they should have great confidence in preaching and should not, terrified by the fear of persecutors, hide themselves and become like a lamp under a bushel, but, setting aside all fear, should reveal themselves with every mark of freedom and preach on the rooftops what they had heard in private rooms.

Let them therefore place their lamp—that is, the worship of images—at the summit of their faith by worshiping it. But if there is any splendor of knowledge in us, let us place it in Christ, who is the source of light, so that, dwelling with us in the house of the holy Church, we may be able to display the splendor both of word and of example.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning their claim, made to confirm their error, that blessed Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, brought images of the apostles to the emperor Constantine, although he is not read to have ordered him to worship them

[Col. 1078A]

In this special work of ours on images, we are often compelled to admit that we prohibit them from being worshiped, not from being possessed; nor should one flee from their presence when they are placed in basilicas as ornaments and memorials of past events. What must be condemned is their excessively insolent, or rather excessively superstitious, worship.

Therefore, as in the other cases, the argument of those who attempt to support their error concerning the worship of images by the claim that Silvester, bishop of the Roman Church, is said to have brought images of the apostles to the emperor Constantine will also be frustrated.

He brought them to him for viewing, not for worshiping. He brought them not to compel Constantine to worship them—since he was urging him to withdraw from the worship of idols and hasten to the worship of God alone—but so that the emperor might recognize in painted colors the faces of those whom he had seen in dreams.

He brought them not to train a man fleeing the worship of idols to surrender to the worship of images, and, after freeing him from the hostile sword, to kill him with the severity of an internal sword, but so that through familiar things he might raise his mind to unfamiliar things; so that those whom he could not yet perceive with the eye of the mind, since he had not yet been cleansed of the stains of paganism, he might perceive through spiritual wonders—namely, their images fashioned in bodily materials.

Even if he had ordered him to worship them—although he did not order him to do so—he might perhaps have ordered it for this reason: to lead a worshiper of visible things through visible things to invisible things, not to lead us back from invisible things to visible things. Nor, because we have received strength to take solid food, should we return to the milk-food of infants, if unadulterated milk is given to one who, because of the tenderness of faith, could not yet receive solid food, so that he might grow by it.

Hence the Apostle also gave the newly founded Church, coming from circumcision and paganism, the food of spiritual milk and vegetables—that is, teachings easier to understand and commandments lighter to fulfill—so that carnal minds, nourished as though in the tenderness of infancy, might be made capable of receiving the food of spiritual mysteries.

The book of the Acts of blessed Silvester, in which it is written that images were brought to the emperor Constantine, can therefore be resisted on this point: although it is read by many Catholics, it is nevertheless not considered fully adequate for affirming the matters under dispute. This is demonstrated more clearly in the book of blessed Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, entitled *Decretal Concerning Books to Be Received or Not to Be Received* (Dist. 15, ch. 3).

[Note: [Col. 1077D] “To the milk-food of suckling infants.” We corrected *lactantium* to *lactentium*, in accordance with the usage and customary practice of the Latin language. Concerning this there are school verses among the ancient grammarians:

> “With *lacteo*, I suck milk; with *lacto*, I provide milk to the newborn.  
> While the infant suckles, the diligent nurse gives it milk.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. That the statement of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, is not to be understood in the way those who attempt to apply it to the worship of images think it should be understood

The statement of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, which they have inconsistently produced, like the other testimonies of divine Scripture, to establish their error, is plainly shown to be entirely foreign to this matter. It contains not even the slightest mention of the worship of any images. Rather, in comparison with the matter under discussion, he acknowledged that images could be restored in the same material and element, saying:

“Just as the form that is painted on wood, once obliterated by external stains, must again be restored and joined to that whose form it is, so that the image may be renewed in the same material and element—for through its form the material itself, where it is painted, is not cast down but is configured in that same form.”

Let them say, then, what support this statement provides them; let them say where it considers images worthy of worship. Since they cannot assert this, it remains for it to be understood by sound minds in the way it was spoken by the venerable man.

## CHAPTER XV. That those who seek to establish the worship of images make improper use, in support of their error, of a statement of blessed Ambrose, bishop of the city of Milan, which they falsely claim comes from Book Three, Chapter Nine

Those who do not fear to accuse the oracles of the divine Law and the prophets will very easily dare to accuse the statements of holy preachers. Nor will they fear, in order to stabilize the material of their error, to do violence to the teachings of the younger, when they do not hesitate to inflict injury on the teachings—or rather on the elders—of the earlier generation.

They are therefore said to have disturbed the statement of blessed Ambrose, priest of the Church of Milan, in its order, meaning, and wording, so that it might favor their error.

They disturbed its order, namely because it is found written not in Book Three, Chapter Nine, as they dream, but in Book Nine.

They disturbed its meaning, because when he said, “Do we divide Christ when we worship both his divinity and his flesh?” they said:

[Note: [Col. 1079D] “Do we not, whenever we worship both his deity and his flesh, divide Christ?” From the seventh act of the pseudo-Seventh Synod of Nicaea and from the *Capitulary* of Pope Hadrian, we have restored *deitatem et carnem* (“deity and flesh”). Ambrose calls these *divinitatem et carnem* (“divinity and flesh”) the divine and human nature of Christ, that is, θεότητα καὶ ἀνθρωπειότητα (*theotēta kai anthrōpeiotēta*), if the latter word could be accepted; for this the Fathers, Hebraizing with the apostles, customarily say σάρκα (*sarka*, “flesh”), although the Latins did not refuse to translate it as “humanity.” The Nicene Synod appears to have rendered Ambrose’s words in Greek as θεότητα καὶ σάρκα (*theotēta kai sarka*, “deity and flesh”)—I say “appears,” since we possess only a Latin version. The emperor censured this as a corruption. I think the fault belongs to the translator, who translated that synod from Greek into Latin.]

“Do we not, when we worship both his deity and his flesh, divide Christ?”

This little particle *ne*, a subordinating conjunction, introduces such a great loss through alteration of the meaning into this statement that it compels it entirely to confess what the original strives to deny.

They altered the wording because, in the following clause, where he wrote *veneramur* (“we venerate”), they are found to have written *adoramus* (“we worship”). To make the meaning of our argument clearer, let us set out point by point how this statement was spoken by an illustrious man, adorned with the high style of eloquence and spiritual meaning, and how they falsified it.

For, in order to affirm one person of the Lord and true man within the properties of the two natures, he said:

“Do we divide Christ when we worship both his divinity and his flesh? Do we divide him when in him we venerate the image of God and the cross?”

But they, attempting through this statement to establish the worship of images, said:

“Do we not, whenever we worship both his deity and his flesh, divide Christ? Or, when in him we worship both the image of God and the cross, do we divide him?”

Thus, by the image of God—which is Christ—and by his cross—which in this passage is placed on account of the mortality of his flesh—they obstinately seek to introduce the worship of images.

## CHAPTER XVI. That blessed Augustine did not speak of material images when he said, “What is the image of God except the countenance of God in which the people of God have been marked?”

“No one has ever seen God,” says the apostle John, “except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 4; 1). And the same supreme Majesty said to Moses: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33).

If he is invisible—or rather, because he is invisible—it is necessary that he be incorporeal; and if he is incorporeal, it is necessary that he cannot be depicted bodily. Therefore, if he is invisible and incorporeal, he cannot at all be depicted in bodily materials.

We must therefore inquire more carefully what the image of God is, and what his countenance is in which the people of God have been marked. Let us therefore question the outstanding preacher; perhaps, taught by him, we shall be able to know what the image of God is.

Speak, chosen vessel; speak, teacher of the nations: what is the image of God?

“Giving thanks,” I say, “to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1).

I have spoken of the image; I shall also speak of the figure. “In these last days God has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages, who is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his truth” (Heb. 1).

Behold: through the teaching of the apostle Paul we have learned that Christ is the image of God, while they urge us to understand this of material images. He says that the same Son, who is of one substance with the Father, is the image of God, the radiance of his glory, and the figure of his substance; they say that figures prepared by the skill of craftsmen are the image of God.

O accursed error! O shameless madness! O reckless senselessness, boiling over with such love of images that you are not ashamed to compare material figures with what has been said of the only-begotten Son of God!

Let the most holy Augustine also say what the image of God is, since they accuse him of having said that it is material. For he says:

“In God the condition of time is absent; for it cannot rightly be thought that God generated the Son in time, through whom he created time. It follows, moreover, that he is not only his image, because he is from him, and his likeness, because he is the image, but also so great an equality that not even an interval of time is an impediment.”

You too, most holy Ambrose, make clear what you are known to have thought concerning this image. Defend blessed Augustine, who, by God’s favor through you, was converted to the rudiments of the faith, and whom you now see unhappily accused by the worshipers of images. Give him support, so that he may be stripped of the burden of so great a crime—he who was once stripped by you of the error of heretical doctrine.

“The prophets,” I say, “say that Christ, who is the image of the invisible Father and the figure of his substance, is himself the splendor of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness.”

In this way, therefore, together with the prophets and apostles, I shall provide protection for my Augustine—or rather, for the worshiper of God.

See how much is said: “splendor,” because the brightness of the Father’s light is in the Son; “spotless mirror,” because the Father is in the Son; “image of goodness,” because not a body in a body but the whole virtue is seen in the Son.

“Image” teaches us that we are unlike; “character” signifies that something has been expressed; “splendor” signifies the eternal.

The image, therefore, is not a bodily face, not composed with pigments, not made of wax, but simple, from God, proceeding from the Father, expressed from the fountain. Through this image the Lord showed the Father to Philip, saying:

“Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also; and how can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

For he saw the Father in the image who saw him in the Son (John 14).

See what kind of image he calls it: this image is truth; this image is righteousness; this image is the power of God. It is not mute, because it is the Word; it is not insensible, because it is wisdom; it is not empty, because it is power; it is not void, because it is life; it is not dead, because it is resurrection.

You see, therefore, that when he is called the image, he signifies that the Father exists, whose image the Son is, since no one can himself be his own image.

Since we have established through the statements of the holy Fathers that the image of God is not material images, as they chatter, but the Son of God, it remains for us briefly to explain how we have been marked in him.

We have been marked in him when, according to the Apostle, we were baptized into his death, anointed with the liquid of the sacred oil, and received the distinction of the Christian name, in accordance with what is said to him in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1). The divine oracle once proclaimed through the prophet Isaiah is fulfilled: “Those who serve me shall be called by a new name” (Isa. 62).

We are therefore marked in him who, according to the Apostle, marked us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. In that pledge of the Spirit we have also been marked for the day of redemption. We have been marked by the Holy Spirit of God, so that both our spirit and our soul may be impressed with the seal of God, and so that we may receive again the image according to which we were created in the beginning.

Through sin we have neither wholly lost that image nor preserved it wholly undefiled within us. For if we had entirely lost it, it would certainly not be said: “Although a human being walks in an image, yet he is troubled in vain” (Ps. 39). And if we had preserved it wholly undefiled, the Apostle would certainly not say: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12), nor: “We are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3).

## CHAPTER XVII. That the life and preaching of Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, from whom they draw testimonies to establish their error, are unknown to us

What we ought to observe in this matter is thoroughly taught by the admonitions of the Apostle.

[Note: [Col. 1081D] Rather, John.]

He says: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God”; and again: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the mind” (1 John 4, at the beginning).

Since, as we have said above, both the life and the preaching of Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, are unknown to us, the testimonies brought forward from his little works to confirm doubtful matters are seen to be less than adequate. Therefore, his teaching is neither to be preferred by us with distinguished praise nor to be excessively condemned. Rather, setting aside his doctrine together with the doctrines of the other men whom we do not know, it remains for us to be content, after the prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic Scriptures, with the doctrines of illustrious Latin teachers whose life and preaching are known to us, or of Greeks who were Catholics and whose works were likewise translated into our language by Catholics.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the testimony which they have produced from the Sixth Synod does not pertain to the worship of images

The actual text of the testimony from the Sixth Synod, which they are said to have criticized in that same heap of trifles written in favor of the worship of images, is as follows:

“In certain venerable paintings of an image, a lamb is represented as being pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner; this was left as a sign of grace, truly showing beforehand for us through the Law the Lamb, Christ our Lord.”

Although they have not produced it in the form in which it appears in that synod, it is nevertheless clear that even as they have used it, it does not contain any mention whatsoever of the worship of images. Rather, since it possesses almost none of the force of sound Latin, is tepid in meaning, inelegant in wording, and in part stripped of rational structure, it is nevertheless shown to offer no support at all to their error.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the statement of John, bishop of Constantinople, which they adduce as testimony for the worship of images, is shown not to pertain to what they think it does

[Col. 1082D]

But neither the judgment of John, bishop of Constantinople, although it has been mutilated by them—as have the other judgments of the holy Fathers that we find corrupted by them in the writing of that synod—is believed to offer any support to their error. For in it there is mention not of those images that are accustomed to be in basilicas, but of those which the emperors of the Romans, with pagan and superstitious ritual, ostentatiously caused to be worshiped out of arrogant desire for their own favor [Col. 1083A]. Such sacrilegious impiety, moreover, we find to have belonged to none of the ancient kings; nor do we read that any nation anywhere existed so subjected to such cruelty and to the service of so many idols.

It was therefore an act of great—indeed, truly great—cruelty and strength that was once represented by the prophet Daniel in his interpretation of the four-part statue, which was a prophecy of the four strongest kingdoms of the world. After the golden head, which signified the kingdom of the Assyrians or Chaldaeans; the silver breast, which represented the kingdom of the Medes and Persians; and the bronze thighs, by which the kingdom of the Macedonians was shown, it was represented in the iron legs. And just as iron crushes and subdues everything, so [Col. 1083B] this kingdom subdued almost all the others.

The same kingdom is also described by the aforementioned prophet in the vision of the four beasts: after the lion, by which the Babylonian kingdom was represented, and the bear, by which the succession of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians was signified, and the leopard, by which the Macedonian kingdom was represented, in the fourth place—just as in the statue it was represented by the iron legs—there is described among the beasts a certain terrifying and most dreadful beast with iron teeth. To speak of it now would take too long. In it there were not, as in the other beasts, only individual signs, but all the indications of cruelty that had existed in those above. It is said to have devoured the nations that it destroyed and to have trampled underfoot those whom it subjected to tribute. It served the worship of demons to such an extent that, joining to its own idols the idols of certain nations that it had conquered, it unhappily worshiped them as well [Col. 1083C].

Therefore it is utterly vain and wholly contrary to reason to take examples within the holy Church from something that Catholics are believed to have rejected entirely because of the stain of paganism—unless, perhaps, it should be granted in this matter that error may be supported by error, that a vain thing may serve as an example for another equally vain thing, and that something crooked may be thought capable of receiving support from something that is not straight.

The text of John’s judgment—if indeed it belongs to that same John—is recorded in the reading of that most foolish synod in the following form:

“[The opening words are corrupt: ‘Does not him who is clothed [suffer] insults?’] Do you not know that if someone insults the image of the emperor, he principally brings an insult upon the emperor himself, upon his dignity [Col. 1083D]? Do you not know that if someone removes an image made of wood or paint, he is judged not as having dared against a lifeless element, but as one who has committed an outrage against the emperor by separating [reading uncertain] an image that bears the emperor in equal measure, and so brings an insult upon the emperor?”

And again, the same statement, attributed to the same Father in a sermon on the Thursday of Easter week:

“All things have been made for the glory of God. In our use of them, the clouds serve humanity in providing rain, the earth in its abundance of fruits, and the sea in its service to sailors, without envy; they serve humanity, and still more the image of God. For when the imperial countenance and images are brought into cities, and judges and crowds go out to meet them with praises, they do not honor the panel or the writings upon the poured wax, but the figure of the emperor. So too one honors not the earthly form of creation, but reveres that same heavenly figure” [Col. 1084A].

Although this statement lacks the adornment of polished expressions and the learning of elaborate language, and although it is thought to wander far from the matter to which it has been applied, it neither provides comfort to their assertion nor, as is clear, causes any harm to ours, nor does it inculcate any disagreement with the principles of the Christian religion. In particular, it seems to say this so that we do not stain the character of the divine image in us by evil works, and so that by sinning and polluting the image and likeness of him in whose image and likeness we were created, we do not inflict an insult upon him: whoever insults the emperor’s image is believed to insult not the image but the emperor himself.

But when he said that the clouds, [Col. 1084B] earth, or sea serve the image of the Lord, he did not say this of a manufactured and irrational image—if indeed the person whom they identify, or any Catholic, said it—but either of Christ, who is the image of God, before whom every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is bent; or of the human being, who, having been created in the image of God, has been placed above almost all visible creatures.

If, however, some contentious person should think that the statement was made about senseless images, let him explain by what agreement, in what manner, or through what familiarity the clouds, earth, and sea serve images; and he will immediately be seen to possess a large part of the support for his assertion.

If, then, the populace—partly driven by unrestrained revelry of joy, partly attracted by the novelty of secular pomp, partly desirous of the inflation of empty honor, partly enslaved by the vice of flattery, and partly terrified by fear of public execution—honors the images of emperors with vain and pernicious praises, what has that to do with us, who glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to us and we to the world? Our citizenship is in heaven; with the Apostle we say, “For us, for whom Christ has been crucified, what have we to do with the marketplace?” (1 Cor. VI). We ought rather to resist such a great error than assent to it. We must not only refuse to derive from it any example for worshiping images, but must utterly execrate it, together with its followers.

## CHAPTER XX

That the statement of Blessed Cyril in his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew does not concern the worship of images, as they assert

[Col. 1084D]

They also say that blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, declared:

“For faith is depicted: the Word who exists in the form of God, just as he was offered to God for the redemption of our life, was made man according to us and in our likeness.”

Although this seems to possess only a partial meaning, whether because of the translator’s incompetence or through the fault of the copyist, no worship of images is in any way implied there. Nor is there even any mention there—let alone an affirmation—of this error of theirs, although they say that shortly afterward he stated:

“The parables signifying by their power fulfill for us the function of images, having a vision that is incomparably brought both before the eyes and conveyed to the touch of the hands in their traces upon the mind” [Col. 1085A].

Since this book is not available among us—it is said to have been composed by that learned author in the Greek language—we must therefore seek the meaning of this chapter by conjecture amid its disordered and improper expressions, as though someone were searching for coins in dusty wrappings or in dirty coverings of any kind of material.

For, as we conjecture, the text of this chapter seems to signify that, while Christ, the Word existing in the form of God, clothed himself in the likeness of our flesh and became man, and was offered to God for the redemption of our life, he showed us in himself the true image of the Father and the vision of that same Father, in accordance with the saying, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV). And in the imaginative forms of parables he signified the secrets of the mysteries to our senses, just as in images something of the things of which they are images is somehow displayed [Col. 1085B].

This is said, indeed, in view of the ambiguity of the conjecture. But once the winding paths of uncertainty have been excluded, it is clear that no worship of images is indicated here.

## CHAPTER XXI

That it is not contrary to the Christian religion, as they claim, not to honor and not to worship images

The instruments of the Christian religion are indeed great. Although they depend upon the solidity of faith and upon love of God and neighbor, to enumerate them individually would take far too long. Among them, however, the worship and adoration of images have absolutely no place, since they are established by no testimony of antiquity [Col. 1085C] and supported by no example, but are rejected by the language of almost all the divine Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 1085D] “To worship the Lord alone.” Lindenbruch corrected this to “to worship God,” and rightly so. The error arose from an abbreviation in the writing. Thus below, in chapter 26, where the common text reads [Col. 1086D] “the true interpreter between the Lord and human beings,” we have corrected it to “between God and human beings.” Nor have we applied a remedy to this fault only once elsewhere.]

For the terrifying trumpet of all divine Scripture resounds that we must worship God alone, adore him alone, and glorify him alone. They must therefore beware, and fear in every way, lest, while they strive to introduce the worship and adoration of images into the Christian religion, they should appear to frustrate the singular worship and adoration of the one God.

These two are so mutually opposed that if one stands, the other cannot stand. For if the singular worship owed to the one and only God remains unshaken—and it truly will remain unshaken—the worship of images will in every way be nullified. And if the worship of images is not overthrown, the worship owed to the one and only God will not be singular.

Accordingly, if the citadel, or defense, and glorious emblem of the Christian religion is the worship and adoration of the one God—and indeed it is—then to offer this worship to images or to any other things is contrary to the Christian religion. And if, as they rave, it is contrary to the Christian religion not to adore or honor these images, then to adore or honor God alone, and to confess that the citadel of his worship and adoration is singular, will be contrary to the Christian religion.

God alone, therefore, must be honored, adored, and glorified. Of him it is said through the prophet, “His name alone is exalted” (Ps. CXLVIII). Veneration must also be shown to his saints, who, having triumphed over the devil, reign with him—whether because they fought bravely so that the Church’s sound condition might reach us unharmed, or because they are known to assist the same Church through continual prayers and intercessions. But images, with every form of worship and adoration excluded, whether they are in basilicas for the remembrance of past events and for adornment, or whether they are not there at all, can bring no prejudice to the Catholic faith, since they are known to have absolutely no function in carrying out the mysteries of our salvation.

## CHAPTER XXII

That those who erect images so as not to forget the saints or the Lord himself do not possess a sound memory

“For me,” says the Prophet, “it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. LXXIII). Since he is spirit, in accordance with the saying, “The Lord God is spirit” (John IV), and must be worshiped in spirit and truth, one can cleave to him not carnally but spiritually; nor can one be joined to him through bodily senses, but only through the gaze of a rational soul.

Therefore, as the most holy Augustine says:

“We are most salutarily warned to turn away from this world, which is plainly corporeal and sensible, and to turn with complete eagerness toward God—that is, toward the truth which is grasped by the intellect and the inner mind, which always remains and is of such a kind that it has no image of falsehood from which it could not be distinguished.”

To contemplate Christ, then, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, or to behold the virtues that have flowed from him into his saints, we need not the bodily sight that we share with irrational animals, but the spiritual sight which the Prophet asked the Lord to grant him when he said: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXIX).

It was this spiritual hearing, not bodily ears, that the Lord sought when he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI; Mark IV; Luke XIV). When he says to the prophet Isaiah, “Blind the heart of this people, and burden their ears, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart” (Isa. VI), he commands the people of Israel to be deprived of these senses as a punishment for unbelief, not to be disabled in their bodily members.

Since these things are so, those who demonstrate that the power of the soul called memory has been so impaired in them that, unless the aid of images supports it, they are compelled to withdraw from the practice of serving God and from venerating his saints confess that they are overwhelmed by great blindness [Col. 1086D]. Nor do they consider themselves capable of raising the eye of the mind above bodily creation to draw in eternal light unless they are supported by the assistance of bodily creation.

But lest they attempt to defend the wall of their error with these fortifications, on the grounds that we too allow images to be kept for the remembrance of past events, their firmness will be shaken by such battering rams and such powerful assaults of truth that one thing is to possess them from fear of forgetfulness, [Col. 1087A] and another from love of adornment; one thing from choice, another from necessity; one thing to see them so that someone may not be able to forget God and his saints, another to look at them so that he may be able to remember past events.

It is one thing to see objects that do no harm if they are not seen, and another to see objects that cause harm unless they are seen—since a human being can be saved without looking at images, but cannot be saved at all without knowledge of God.

Since the human mind ought to cling so closely to him in whose image it was created that, with no creature interposed, it may be formed by the truth itself, which is Christ, it is utterly foolish to claim that the mind must be reminded by material images lest it suffer forgetfulness of him. This is plainly a defect of weakness, not an indication of freedom.

That Christ’s descent into hell, his ascent into heaven, and the fruit of our hope are to be sought not in visible things but only in the heart, the Apostle Paul testifies when he says:

“Hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII).

And again:

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who has ascended into heaven?’—that is, to bring Christ down—or, ‘Who has descended into the abyss?’—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart’; that is, the word of faith that we preach. For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. X).

Many things relevant and necessary to this matter could have been said in this chapter, if the brevity to which we are devoted had permitted it.

## CHAPTER XXIII

That instituting the worship or destruction of images is contrary to the judgment of blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome

The images whose most insolent worship prompted Constantine, his mother Irene, and Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, to convene the synod—their error having supplied the subject of the present discussion—are both forbidden to be worshiped [Col. 1087D] and forbidden to be destroyed by blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome. He did not wander far from the matter in words, nor did he wrap his speech in obscure ambiguities; rather, in precise and pure language, he instructed Bishop Serenus of Marseille by letter concerning what should be observed and what should be maintained in this matter.

For while these people are said to condemn their predecessors or ancestors because they destroyed the images, and while those predecessors are believed to have detested and condemned these people because they intended to worship them, the aforementioned bishop places himself between the opposing lines of these divergent errors, holding the middle course at the crossroads of a single folly [Note: [Col. 1087D] The aforementioned writer inserts “antestis.” The corrector did not rightly amend it to “antistes,” since throughout this entire work it is consistently written in that form. Hugh of Pisa, in his Vocabulary, says: “Antestor is everywhere written with te, not ti; hence antestis.”], [Col. 1088A] and supplies weapons to both parties as they clash with one another. With the point of his episcopal sword he strikes both those who worship the images together with those who destroyed them, and those who destroyed them together with those who worship them.

Rejecting those who worship on one side and those who destroy on the other, he claims the Church for our party, which follows the middle path of the right road. He allows images to be kept as ornaments and for the remembrance of past events, but sets aside and despises those who worship them on one side and those who destroy them on the other.

Thus the same venerable pope is said both to have praised Serenus because he forbade worship and to have reproved him because he destroyed the images:

“It had been reported to us,” he says, “that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you were breaking the images of the saints under the pretext that they ought not to be worshiped. Indeed, we greatly praised you for forbidding their worship, but we reproved you for having broken them” [Col. 1088B].

And shortly afterward:

“What was placed in the churches not for worship but solely for the instruction of the minds of the uneducated ought not, therefore, to have been broken. And since antiquity admitted, not without reason, that histories of the saints should be painted in holy places, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could have both healthfully obtained what you intended and gathered, rather than scattered, the flock entrusted to you.”

For that venerable prelate believed that the minds of the populace had been disturbed by the destruction of the images, and therefore, fearing the scandalization of the weak, he offered this instruction. Accordingly, in what follows he teaches Serenus how he may permit images to be kept in churches while avoiding their worship in every way.

He says:

“Various sons of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of holy Scripture that it is not lawful to worship anything made by hand, since it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.’ Then it must be added: ‘Because you saw that the painted images which had been made for the edification of the uneducated people, so that those who did not know letters might learn what had been said by directing their attention to the history itself, had passed into worship, you were moved to order that those images be broken.’

“And they must be told: ‘If you wish to have them for the instruction for which images were made in ancient times, permit them in every way both to be displayed and to be kept in the churches. Make clear that it was not the sight of the history itself, which was revealed through the testimony of the painting, that displeased you, but the worship that had been improperly offered to the paintings.

“And by soothing their minds with these words, call them back to concord with you. If anyone wishes to make images, do not prohibit him in the least; but avoid worshiping images in every way” [Col. 1088D].

Behold the teaching and authority by which the venerable pontiff instructed us: we do not refuse to have images in churches, but we utterly reject their worship. Whoever either destroys or worships them should recognize that he is in every way acting contrary to this bishop’s ordinances.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Although nothing besides God alone ought to be worshiped, honoring a human being through the duty of charity and greeting is one thing, and manufactured images are another

[Col. 1089A]

God must be believed to have loved the human race so greatly that, at the very beginning of its creation, he made it not casually but in his own image and likeness, placed it above the other creatures, and, after it had been transferred through sin from the happiness of the flower-bearing seat to the sorrows of this mortality, never ceased to instruct it through astonishing miracles and the radiant oracles of the prophets throughout the successive moments of time.

And when the angels, who had departed from him through sin, had been condemned to everlasting punishment, he did not disdain to assume humanity in order to join it again to the heavenly citizens, for whose fellowship he had created it. The Apostle says [Col. 1089B]: “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. II).

From this it is understood that it is one thing—indeed, something entirely different—to honor a human being by way of greeting, since he possesses the distinction of so many merits, and another thing to honor images, which lack all these qualities. It is one thing to show humility toward a human being, who is God’s work, and another toward an image, which is the work of an artisan. It is one thing to honor through the duty of humility that nature which is worshiped by angels and archangels in the King of heaven, and another to honor that which serves the uses not only of human beings but also of the other animals.

Therefore, just as God’s works surpass human works, the maker surpasses what is made, rational beings surpass irrational beings, perceptible beings surpass imperceptible beings, and living beings surpass nonliving things, so the worship that, as we have said, is offered to human beings as a duty of humility and greeting surpasses the worship that is superstitiously and unnecessarily offered to images [Col. 1089C].

God commanded us to love human beings, not images. He sent his Son into the world for the sake of human beings, not for the sake of images. He wished to be called Father by human beings, not by images. And in the Gospel the Lord does not say, “Do not scandalize one of these images,” but, “one of these little ones,” because “their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Nor does the Apostle exhort us to honor images, but to “outdo one another in showing honor” (1 Pet. II).

That the craftsman is better than his work, and the maker than what is made, the Book of Wisdom testifies, for it says:

“No human being can fashion a god like himself. For since he is mortal, with wicked hands he fashions a dead thing” (Wis. XV) [Col. 1089D].

The person himself is better than the things he worships, since he lived, although he was mortal, whereas those things never lived. Blessed Augustine likewise says:

“I nevertheless confess that those who think the works of human beings are gods are sunk more deeply than those who think the works of God are gods.”

This was said about idols and their worshipers.

But those who, within the holy Church, proclaim that God alone is to be adored and worshiped, and who convene synods so that images may be worshiped, should beware lest they disturb domestic peace by civil war within and stain the prosperity of our affairs with this error as with a kind of civil war.

They will be able to avoid this very easily if they remain within the boundaries of prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teaching, and, excluding novel expressions, content themselves solely with the institutions of the holy Fathers.

## CHAPTER XXV

That nowhere, whether in apostolic examples or words, as they chatter, was it instituted that images should be worshiped

The rule of ecclesiastical instruction is sometimes commended to us through the words of the prophets, the apostles, or the Lord himself; sometimes it is shown through examples; sometimes through oracles expressed obscurely, sometimes plainly; sometimes it is taught through figurative language, sometimes through simple expressions. Throughout all these forms, while the worship of every other thing is forbidden, the worship of God alone is instituted, apart from the worship by which we honor one another in greeting.

Since those who burn with love for images admit that this worship was handed down by the apostles to be offered to images, they must necessarily say by which examples of theirs it was instituted and by what testimonies its promulgation is established [Col. 1090B].

Or did Peter institute that images should be worshiped, when he gently restrained Cornelius from worshiping him? Or John, who, when he wished to worship an angel, was told not to do so but to worship God? Or Paul, who was horrified when the Lycaonians sought superstitiously to offer this worship to him? Or Barnabas, who likewise refused it together with Paul?

Since the angel and the apostles forbid themselves to be worshiped, who is so foolish and so insane as to dare say that they instituted the worship of images? This is especially so since, even if angels or human beings ought to be worshiped, angels, human beings, and images are respectively of different merit and definition.

If, then, angels or human beings, as the present example demonstrates, are not to be worshiped, apart from the worship offered as a duty of charity and greeting, then images, which lack reason and are unworthy of either greeting or worship because they are senseless, are much less to be worshiped.

If they are not to be worshiped—and indeed because they are not—they are said to commit a double offense in this matter: either because they worship them, or because they falsely claim that the apostles handed down the practice so that they might do so.

Finally, the Apostle Paul—that evangelical innkeeper who received the human race, having departed from the vision of its heavenly homeland, having fallen into the sorrows of this defection, and having been wounded by evil spirits, from the guardian of all things, to be healed through the gentle and severe words of preaching—was entrusted by the Redeemer with the money of the twofold knowledge, that is, of the two Testaments. And if, in giving counsel for the instruction of the redeemed people, he spent anything beyond what was required, he promises to repay it.

Yet neither in the matters concerning which he freely gives commands, nor in those concerning which he gives supererogatory counsel, as he is said to have done concerning virgins, is he found anywhere to have instituted or commanded anything of the sort concerning the worship of images, as they imagine [Col. 1090D].

When that same teacher of the nations wrote to his disciples Timothy and Titus, instructing them concerning the ordering of the episcopate, presbyterate, and diaconate, and concerning the whole of ecclesiastical discipline, as well as spiritual conduct and the avoidance of heretics, he did not institute the worship of images because he knew it to be alien to the Christian religion. And in the other letters that he wrote to the whole world, teaching what should be avoided and what should be followed, he entirely disregarded this matter, which he believed neither to constitute an error if rejected nor a virtue if established [Col. 1091A].

Those who rave that not worshiping images is a crime, but that worshiping them was instituted by the apostles among the first sacraments of the faith, should consider that the same “Vessel of Election” does not even enumerate despising images among crimes, when he says:

“Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, shamelessness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, of which I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V).

Nor does he enumerate worshiping images among the spiritual fruits, when he says:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (ibid.) [Col. 1091B].

Nor, in the same elegance of expression with which he derives his thoughts through certain rivulets from the rhetorical stream, dividing them into members, clauses, and appropriate circuits, beginning with anaphora and proceeding through σχέσεις ἐνομάτων—“relations of names”—and setting opposites against opposites through the argumentative method that philosophers call argument from contraries, adorning his discourse with the most beautiful antitheses, is he known to have made even the slightest mention of this worship among the other virtues that he enumerates when he announces the acceptable time of this life, namely, the time suited to repentance, and the days of salvation, that is, days suited to good works [Col. 1091C].

He says:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation. We give no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything we show ourselves to be ministers of God: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distress, in beatings, in imprisonments, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known, as dying—and behold, we live; as chastised and not put to death; as sorrowful and yet always rejoicing; as needy and yet enriching many; as having nothing and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. VI) [Col. 1091D].

In this catalogue of virtues, as we have said, that outstanding preacher would have inserted the worship of images if he had judged it to be their companion and beneficial to the Church. He delayed enumerating it precisely because he perceived that it was of no use.

## CHAPTER XXVI

That it is a grave error to attempt to equate manufactured images with the ark of the Lord’s testament, as they attempted to do in their synod

It is an act of great absurdity, indeed of great recklessness, to attempt to equate images with the ark of the Lord’s testament, since they are known to differ from it by the indications of so many mysteries; and to assimilate a thing that was established at the command of the Lord’s voice to things that are made according to the will of any artisan [Col. 1092A].

The ark was made at the Lord’s command; these images are made with the assistance of artistic skill. The ark was made by the holy man Moses; these by any craftsman. The ark was made by the lawgiver; these by a painter. The ark overflowed with mysteries; these possess only the cosmetic coloring of paints. The ark was present to inspire astonishment through miracles and signified certain mystical and hidden things concerning the future; these, devoid both of present miracles and of the signification of future things, merely introduce a remembrance of the objects of which they are images.

The typological prefigurations of the ark, and of the things contained within it, have been shown in the preceding book. Now it remains briefly to explain how far it differs from handmade images.

Those, therefore, who strive to equate material images [Col. 1092B] made by any craftsmen with the ark of the Lord’s testament—which was made at the Lord’s command and through Moses’ obedience—should find, if they can, an artisan who can be compared with Moses in merit: one who was exposed to the currents of the river, whose safety was entrusted to God alone amid the watery streams; one who was rescued from them and restored to his mother, and who was commanded to be lavishly nourished by those who had been ordered to kill him.

Let them find an artisan who was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt; who saw branches of a tree burning without being consumed; who marveled at fragile material enduring a wondrous fire without suffering even the slightest loss, because no fuel was supplied to it—or rather, who heard a voice proceed from it, calling him by name and giving him mystical commands, the hope of liberating his people and of attaining the paternal promise.

Let them find one who was astonished to see [Col. 1092C] the stiffness of his staff transformed into the winding form of a serpent, by whose agency the Nile-dwellers were struck by ten miraculous plagues; who could become the leader of Egyptians enriched with their wealth and of people crossing the sea on dry feet; who turned bitter waters into a sweet taste and compelled barren rock, by a blow of his staff, to pour forth flowing water.

Let them find one who, by extending his hands, compelled hostile tumult to be overcome and allowed his own people to win the victory; who, amid terrifying blasts of trumpets, flashes of lightning, the shadow of the densest cloud, and the blazing heaps of crackling fire, climbed the mountain in fear and trembling, received the law, and, as the true interpreter between God and human beings, made known to the peoples the commands promulgated by the Lord for them to observe.

Let them find one who made the tabernacle according to the model [Col. 1092D] shown to him on the mountain, and when he entered it, the glory of the Lord covered it; who was the gentlest of all who dwelt on earth; to whom God spoke face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend; who, until the sun had risen and set fourteen times, went entirely without food or drink, and whose face could scarcely be looked upon because of its excessive brightness.

Let them find one who triumphed wondrously over two kings; who, after the passage of forty years, suffered neither dimness of sight nor loosening of his teeth; who could make from any material an image so overflowing with mysteries and abounding in sacred signs that dreadful oracles were heard upon its surface.

Before its presence [Col. 1093A] hostile armies were shaken with terror; through its midst rivers provided a dry path for travelers; and the walls of an ancient city, utterly overthrown in an instant, opened an entrance from every side to the armies of warriors. It was called the footstool of our God’s feet.

At its arrival, the territory of the enemies was struck by terrifying scourges; untamed cows, contrary to their nature, leaving their calves behind them, drew it in a new cart toward the land of Israel. At its return, the native inhabitants were terrified by astonishing miracles, before the illustrious prophet and robed king was not ashamed to dance with great exultation and to bring it into its appointed place amid musical harmonies and the sweet-sounding melodies of hymns.

Only when such an image has shone with so many prerogatives of signs, both its own and its maker’s [Col. 1093B], could it rightly be equated with the ark of the Lord’s testament.

Since, therefore, they have not been able to find either an artisan of such merit or a work of such glory, it remains for them to place the lawgiver above the people of our age in every way, and the ark of the Lord’s testament above manufactured images. Let them not attempt to equate such worthless things, so devoid of mysteries, with something so sublime and abounding in so many marks of mystery.

For if, as they rave, images can be likened to the ark of the Lord’s testament, there must necessarily be something about them that can be likened to the mercy seat; there must necessarily be dreadful oracles issued from them. But no such oracles issue from them. Therefore, contrary to their folly, images cannot be likened to the ark of the Lord’s testament.

## CHAPTER XXVII

That it is a grave and enormous absurdity to wish to equate the often-mentioned images with the Lord’s body and blood, as is read in the same vanity written on their behalf

[Col. 1093C]

When the Lord says in the Gospel, “True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John IV), we marvel at the madness of those who have burned with such foolish zeal for worshiping images that, although it is evident that they are neither spirit nor truth, they presume not only to worship them but even to equate them with the Lord’s body and blood, saying:

“Just as the Lord’s body and blood pass from the fruits of the earth into the sacred mystery, so images, assembled through the skill of craftsmen, pass into the veneration of those persons in whose likeness they are assembled.”

[Col. 1093D] The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, which was granted to us by that same mediator between God and humanity for the remembrance of his passion and our salvation, is fashioned through the hand of the priest and the invocation of the divine name. Images, by contrast, require no laying on of hands or mystery of consecration. They are known to be formed and assembled either by those trained in the practice of painting and skilled in preparing colors, or by those who, possessing a demonstrated knowledge of carpentry, sculpture, or some other art and understanding the properties of the material, shape faces.

Indeed, for the consecration of these [or: “for their consecration”; the manuscript reading *norum* is uncertain], the mitred priest, mingling the supplications of the assembled people with his own prayers, recalls with inward groaning the Lord’s passion, [Col. 1094A] his resurrection from the dead, and also his most glorious ascension into heaven; and he asks that these things be carried by the hands of an angel to God’s sublime altar and placed before the sight of his majesty. The painter, however, seeking suitable places for carrying out his work, looks only for beauty of color and the completion of his task in forming these images.

Thus, the person who attempts to equate images with the Lord’s body and blood stands very, very far from the path of truth, reason, and discernment. For Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, is read to have offered, as a type of the Lord’s body and blood, not some image but bread and wine. Likewise, in the words of Moses, as a prefiguration of our Redeemer—whose flesh we receive for the remission of sins, and by the sprinkling of whose blood we escape the assault of the destroying angel—the lamb is commanded to be eaten by households, while the practice of venerating or worshiping images is altogether rejected.

The Psalmist also sang, in sweet-sounding melody, both of the bread of angels—namely Christ—to be eaten by human beings, and that the makers of images would become like the images they make. For the very author of the human race, who for our salvation did not disdain to assume flesh for our sake, when he was establishing both the conclusion of the Old Testament and the life-giving beginning of the New Testament as the day of his most holy passion drew near, and, joining together in himself as the cornerstone two opposing walls and, according to the Apostle, making both one, took bread, blessed it, and broke it, and gave this saving command to his disciples: [Col. 1094C]

“Take and eat,” he said; “this is my body.” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the cup and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Take and drink; for this is the cup of my blood, of the New and eternal Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins. Whenever you do these things, you will do them in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians XI).

Since the Church holds, more clearly than light, the teaching of this most evident and sacred mystery as life-giving both through the mystical figures of the Old Testament and through the institution of the New, the most insolent practice of worshiping images must not be equated with it. That practice is not only never commanded; it is forbidden in the text of the Old Testament and not only not permitted but also censured in the sequence of the New Testament.

[Col. 1094D] For he who said, “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John VI), and, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid.), did not say, “My image is truly life, and the painting inscribed with my name is truly salvation, and whoever paints my likeness and worships my handmade image remains in me, and I in him.”

And he who said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (ibid.), did not say, “Unless you paint my image and worship my likeness constructed by the painter’s art, you will not have life in yourselves.”

Therefore, he who said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of it, he will not die, but will have eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day” (John VI); and again, “Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me” (ibid.); and again, “This is the true bread of God that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. Whoever eats of it remains forever, and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world. Whoever believes in me will never hunger or thirst” (ibid.)—of an image he is nowhere read to have said anything of the kind.

For, as we have already said, he established the remembrance of his most holy passion not in the works of craftsmen or of worldly arts but in the consecration of his body and blood; nor did he decree that his faith and confession should be made in paintings, but in mouth and heart, as Scripture says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X).

[Col. 1095B] When he says, “If you remain in me and my words remain in you” (John XV), he shows most clearly that images are not to remain in us, nor we in images; rather, he indicates that we must remain in him through faith, and that his words must necessarily remain in us through devotion to reading and completion in action.

The Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, seeing that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood was not to be equated with every sacrament but was to be preferred to nearly all, says: “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians XI).

Since he shows that those who approach to receive these things must be tested with such diligent care, and strikes those who gather negligently and unworthily to receive them with so severe a weapon of punishment, he says nothing similar about those who refuse to worship images. On the contrary, concerning those who misuse images he says: “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible humanity” (Romans I), and so forth.

The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood therefore differs by much—indeed, by more than the mind’s eye can comprehend—from images painted by the art of painters. The former is effected invisibly by the operation of God’s Spirit, while the latter are made visibly by the craftsman’s hand; the former is consecrated by a priest through invocation of the divine name, while the latter are painted by a painter through training in human art; the former is carried by angelic hands to God’s sublime altar, while the latter, constructed by human hands through art, are placed upon a wall for the gaze of those who admire them; through the former sins are remitted, while through the latter, if they are heedlessly misused, sins are added; the former, in its power, neither increases nor diminishes in any way, while the latter, according to the craftsman’s skill, both increase in beauty and are, in a certain sense, diminished; the former is confirmed by new antiquity and ancient newness, while the latter are often corrupted by decaying age; the former is life and refreshment for souls, while the latter are merely food for the eyes; the former leads through eating to entrance into the heavenly kingdom, while the latter convey through sight the memory of events; the former could not be removed from the Church even during persecutions, while the color of the latter is sometimes washed away by the filth of dripping moisture.

[Col. 1095D] And since no one is saved without receiving the former, while without observing the latter all who possess the right faith are saved, it is clear that no one of sound understanding should equate them with so great a mystery.

Therefore, those who strive to bind absolutely everyone who does not worship images with the bond of anathema must be asked what they think about the apostles, whom no sequence of catholic Scripture teaches ever to have worshiped images. Yet no believer doubts that not only they but also their followers entered the heavenly kingdoms.

And what do they think about the martyrs, who immediately passed from the baptismal font into the heavenly kingdoms by the hands of executioners, without worshiping images? And what do they think about infants, who, cleansed of original guilt through the bath of regeneration, and not yet capable through their bodily senses of doing anything of this kind, were deemed worthy to enter the heavenly kingdoms almost before they could seek the power of earthly steps?

If, according to their utterly false opinion, all who do not worship images perish, then infants washed in the water of baptism and nourished by eating the Lord’s body and drinking his blood—who were not yet able to worship images and thus departed from this age—perish. And if they perish, the word of Truth is made void, the word that says: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew XVIII; Mark X).

But the word of Truth, which promises the kingdom of heaven to infants, is not made void. Therefore, not all who do not worship images perish.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How greatly the mystery of the Lord’s cross differs from images, with which those same men contend that it should be equated

[Col. 1096C]

It is worthwhile briefly to disclose by how many prerogatives of excellence and marks of power the mystery of the Lord’s cross surpasses handmade images, with which those men rashly desire to equate it, although our exposition cannot fully explain the matter.

By this standard, not by images, the ancient enemy was defeated; by these weapons, not by the pigments of colors, the devil was conquered; through it, not through paintings, the bars of hell were broken; through it, not through them, the human race was redeemed. On the cross, not in images, the price of the world hung.

It therefore served as the instrument of a servile punishment, not some image; it is the emblem of our king, not some painting, that the legions of our army continually behold; it is the sign of our commander, not an arrangement of colors, that our cohorts follow into battle.

Thus it is not some material image but the mystery of the Lord’s cross that is the standard we must follow on the battlefield of combat, so that we may fight more powerfully; it is the weapon by which we can defend our freedom; it is the fortification by which we can avoid the assaults of hostile attackers.

For it is the helmet by which the blow of the devil’s sword is shaken off; it is the shield placed against his missiles and arrows; it is the breastplate by which the fiery impact of his darts or spears is rendered ineffective. It is the defense by which we overcome the winding labyrinths and crafty devices of his deceit, so that he cannot conquer those whom he has tempted—those whom he once held captive through the persuasion of the first human being.

[Col. 1097A] Through the wood of the cross, not through images, the crime of that ancient offense is washed away—the offense contracted in the first parent through eating from the tree. On the hook of the cross, not in some painting, the author of crimes was caught, when, constrained by reason rather than domination and by justice rather than power, he was compelled to disgorge the prey that he had long been known to hold after swallowing it.

Thus it was not through material images made by craftsmen but through the mystery of the cross—which is considered a stumbling block by the Jews and foolishness by the Gentiles—that the proud and inflated wisdom of the world collapsed. And it was not through some painting but through the cross that it became evident how much wiser than human beings is what is foolish in God, and how much stronger than human beings is what is weak in God.

Let us therefore question the teacher of the nations; let us question the distinguished preacher. Let him tell us whether he glories in images or in the cross of Christ.

“Far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Galatians VI).

Let him also say whether, in order to live for God, he was crucified to images or to the cross.

“I,” he says, “through the law died to the law, so that I might live for God; I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians II).

Let him also say whether, in understanding the pigments of colors, the forms of images, or the qualities of materials, we ought to have the eyes of our hearts enlightened, or whether they should be enlightened so that we may understand the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross.

“So that you may comprehend,” he says, “with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Ephesians III).

In explaining the words of so great a preacher, therefore, we must neither rashly display our own interpretations nor steal those of others. Instead, let us set forth the interpretations that we find laid down by blessed Augustine in his books *On Christian Doctrine*.

The breadth, then, is the transverse wood upon which the hands are extended. The height is that part which begins at the transverse wood and rises above it, where the head was. The length is that part which begins at the transverse wood and extends down to the ground. The depth is what is hidden, fixed into the earth. From this wood of the cross is described the whole life of the saints, who take up their cross and put to death their members that are upon the earth and follow Christ.

As the outer person is corrupted, so the inner person is renewed day by day; and, rejoicing in hope of eternal rest, they devote themselves cheerfully to good works. The breadth of the cross, in the transverse wood where the hands are fastened, signifies this cheerfulness.
