For through the hands work is understood; through breadth, the joy of the one who works, because sadness produces narrowness.

Moreover, through the height of the cross, to which the head is attached, is signified the expectation of eternal reward from God’s sublime justice, so that good works may be understood to be performed not for the sake of God’s earthly and temporal benefits but rather for the sake of what faith, working through love, hopes for from above.

Now through the length, by which the whole body is extended, endurance itself is signified, so that we may remain patient; hence those who endure are called patient. Through the depth, that is, the part of the wood fixed in the hidden earth and from which everything that projects upward arises, the inscrutable judgments of God are indicated. By his hidden will one person is called to share in such great grace in one way, and another in another way.

But why do we linger so long over apostolic words? Why do we wander so extensively through the broad fields of his meaning? Let us come to the Lord, sit with Mary at his feet, and hear the word from his mouth; let us hear him in his own person, whom until now we have heard speaking through the Apostle.

We have heard what the teacher of the nations said about the cross; let us hear what the Creator of the nations says. We have heard the distinguished preacher; let us hear the Creator of all things.

“If anyone wishes to come after me,” he says, “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew XVI; Luke IX).

O marvelous command, O saving exhortation, O life-giving thunder! You spoke, O fountain of light; you spoke, O source of goodness: that, laying aside the old person with his works, we should deny ourselves, each take up his own cross, and be crucified to the world, while the world is crucified to us, so that through bodily sufferings and through the putting to death of our members that are upon the earth, we may live for you—or rather, that you may live in us.

And you exalted the mystery of the cross so greatly that through it you emptied principalities and powers and all the world’s vainglory; and in the name of the cross, which must be carried daily by those who follow you, you signified the ardor of your love and the fruits of the other virtues.

Tell us also what command you establish concerning images, which some attempt to equate with the sacred cross.

“Give back,” I say, “to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matthew XXII; Luke XII).

If, then, we must take up the cross and follow you, who by triumphing through the cross joined earthly things to heavenly things, and if we must return Caesar’s image to Caesar, images must not be equated with the cross, worshiped, or venerated. They must be left to this world along with the other things that belong to the world. You alone must be worshiped, you alone followed, you alone venerated, you who forever reign in unity of substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How presumptuously and ignorantly Tarasius and his followers do not fear to equate them with the sacred vessels

[Col. 1098D]

Everyone is easily deceived in small matters who is very easily deceived in great ones; nor is it surprising if the person who cannot avoid immense and easily avoidable blows from spears inevitably endures the strikes of the small and almost invisible darts of error.

Why, then, should it be surprising if Tarasius and the synod over which he presided attempt to equate images with the sacred vessels, when they also endeavor to equate them with the ark of the Lord’s testament and with everything known to have been in it or around it, as well as with the mystery of the Lord’s cross and with the most evident and most suitable sacrament of our salvation, the body and blood of the Lord?

His error in equating them with these sacred vessels could indeed have been regarded with great astonishment, had it not been preceded by so great an error.

The divine-law writings demonstrate how greatly vessels dedicated to divine worship surpass images. Those vessels, established at the Lord’s command through Moses in the tabernacle of the testimony, and established and dedicated in the temple at Jerusalem through Solomon by the institution of the most holy David among the prophets, both signified the mysteries of typological meanings and fulfilled the duty of continual service in matters pertaining to the worship of God.

These images, however—with the exception of the cherubim, and the oxen and lions, which were made not for worship but to signify future things—are not only not known to have been made or dedicated by any of the saints but are everywhere rejected by the testimonies of nearly all the divine-law oracles.

[Col. 1099B] The vessels that the Church possesses for carrying out the mysteries of our redemption are always necessary for the faithful and always serviceable in divine worship. Sacrifice to God is offered in the vessels, not in images; incense, lamps, and other things suited to divine worship are dedicated in the vessels, not in images.

Even if certain images are present on them, they are not there in order to be worshiped, nor because without them the gift of the sacred mysteries could somehow become less valuable, but so that the character of the materials may be made more beautiful by their impressions.

Indeed, without images one can receive the water of the bath and the anointing of sacred liquid, burn incense, illuminate holy places with lamps, and accomplish the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood; without vessels, however, none of these things can ever be done.

For our author of salvation, when he was bringing the Old Testament to its completion and establishing the beginning of the New, is said to have taken not an image but a cup. And through the prophet the Lord does not say, “Purify yourselves, you who carry images,” but, “Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah LII).

The Babylonian king, therefore, is not rebuked because of any injury to an image. Rather, because he had judged that the vessels devoted to divine worship—which his grandfather had brought from Judea and placed in the shrines of his idols—should, during banquets, be removed from the shrines and used for human purposes, out of a sense of religious devotion and reverence, he was struck with the fearful astonishment of a portent and heard what was to come upon him; and amid the hostile ranks he experienced the loss both of his life and of his kingdom.

Anyone who knows the prophets understands what we are saying.

## CHAPTER XXX. Against those who say: “Just as we possess the books of divine Scripture, so we possess images for the sake of remembrance and veneration, while observing the purity of our faith”

If this error, by which they attempt to equate images with the books of divine Scripture, is compared with their other errors, then, although it is itself greatly excessive, when compared with those errors by which they have attempted to equate images with the ark of the Lord, with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and with the mystery of the cross, it is undoubtedly less serious—especially since images cannot properly be equated either with those things or with these.

For the books of divine Scripture were predestined before the ages by the highest, mysterious, and foreknowing judgment of God alone, and were granted through the ages, in merciful manifestation, for the benefit of human salvation. They have as their authors holy and venerable men, shining with the lamps of virtues and the marks of miracles—or, in any case, the Lord himself, who granted for our salvation the mystery of his body and blood and the sacrament of the cross.

Images, however, have been produced from the vanity of pagan authors, and bring mortals no manifestation of salvation and no prerogative of any sacrament. They merely gratify the eyes, through which, as through certain messengers, they commit the memory of past events to the heart.

For at the time when Moses was dwelling with the people of God in the wilderness, and, at the Lord’s command, was handing down to the people the teaching of the sacred law and the most holy rites of the ceremonies, instructing the human race in the knowledge of divine worship, a certain Cecrops, king of the Athenians, enticed by demonic poison, stirred the untutored minds of the pagans to the worship of images and idols and of vain gods.

At the very time when the people of God received the commandments of life, he prepared there, to ensnare souls, cups of everlasting death and seeds of prolonged error. Concerning him Sedulius wrote:

> Those whom deadly evil [afflicts], those [whose minds are] given over to vain cares …

The Attic doctrine of Cecrops’ poison spreads. Therefore the use of images, which has grown out of pagan traditions, neither ought nor is able to be equated with the books of sacred law, because in the books, not in images, we learn the instruction of spiritual teaching. For the apostle Paul does not say, “Whatever has been painted has been painted for our instruction,” but says, “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. XV), so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope in God. Nor does he say, “Every painting,” but, “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for refutation, for instruction, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (II Tim. III).

[Col. 1100C]

Finally, on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the lamb and the crossing of the Red Sea, the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai and gave Moses the law—not painted, but written—and on stone tablets he gave not images but letters, which are said to be indications of things or signs of words. Moses likewise taught the origin of the world not by painting but by writing. Everything that he learned through the spirit of prophecy, whether about past events—the things he proclaimed concerning the beginning of the world, the creation of humanity, the Flood, or the successive histories of the other patriarchs—or concerning events occurring in his own time, such as the things he learned were being done through Balaam or Balak or through others who were absent from him—or concerning future events, which he understood after being inspired by the breath of the Holy Spirit, such as what he is read to have said about the transgression of the Jewish people, their captivity, and even the coming of Christ—he recorded in five books and, by the Lord’s command, handed down to future ages, not by painting but by writing. It is not written of him, “He received paintings,” but, “Moses received the book and recited the words of the book in the hearing of the people” (Deut. XXXI).

[Col. 1100D]

Hence the Apostle also writes, “When every commandment of the law had been read by Moses to all the people” (Hebr. IX); and shortly afterward, “He sprinkled both the book itself and all the people” (ibid.), so that we may know that the lawgiver used not painted images but saving Scriptures.

[Col. 1101A]

Joshua likewise, the successor of that same Moses, who crossed the Jordan with the people of God on dry foot and, after overthrowing the kings of the Canaanite nation, divided the promised land by lot among the children of Israel, and who bore the type of the mediator between God and human beings—the one who, when the rites of the old law had passed away, leads the people of God through baptism to the promised land and, after overthrowing the tyrannies of vices and aerial powers, grants the faithful all the possessions of the heavenly homeland—committed everything that happened in his own time, to himself and to the people over whom he presided, to the memory of posterity by writing rather than by painting.

[Col. 1101B]

Samuel too, a man of great holiness and excellence, who was granted to his mother by divine gift after her great persistence in prayer, who from his very cradle served in prophetic ministry in the tabernacle of the Lord, and who became a model in the anointing of kings, recorded the histories of Judges, Ruth, and also Kings down to David, not in images but in letters. After him, the events accomplished in David’s time were written down, as were the histories of the other kings, either by the kings themselves or by the prophets who lived at that time, and these were handed down as far as Jeremiah. Collecting all the histories of the kings into one work, Jeremiah published the whole of the *Malachim*—that is, “Kings”—for our memory, not through painting but through writing.

The individual prophets who possess books likewise established their prophecies, destined to benefit future ages, not in paintings but in writings.

[Col. 1101C]

Thus Daniel understood in books, not in colored figures, the number of years during which the people of God were to be held in Babylonian captivity. For he says, “I, Daniel, understood in the books the number of the years concerning which the word of the Lord came” (Dan. IX).

David also, the most holy of the prophets, who sang more abundantly and more clearly than the other Fathers about Christ’s incarnation, birth, passion, death, resurrection, glory, and kingdom—just as he was placed before the other Fathers in the genealogy of the same Lord according to his humanity, so that the same Lord might be called the Son of David—is read to have spoken in the person of Christ as follows: “In the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XL). He does not say “painted,” but “written”; nor “in the head of walls” or “tablets,” but “in the head of a book.”

[Col. 1101D]

In the head, therefore, of the book of Genesis, which is certainly the head of all the books, it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). “In the beginning” means “in the Son,” for when the Jews asked who he was, he answered, “I am the beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (John VIII).

The “beginning” may also be understood in the first verse of the Psalter, which begins with Christ’s incarnation and, through the eighth type of definition—which dialecticians call κατὰ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου, that is, “by the privation of the contrary” to what is being defined—shows that Christ did not go into the council of the impious (Ps. I), meaning that he did not possess the detestable thoughts that the human race claims especially for itself; that he did not stand in the way of sinners (ibid.), meaning that he wholly avoided the actions of a vicious way of life, but, coming into the world, passed through the world’s vices with an undefiled manner of life; and that he did not sit in the seat of pestilence, meaning that he did not embrace abominable doctrines that spread the poisons of pestilential teaching, but healed the wounds of the world by salutary preaching.

[Col. 1102A]

It declares that he was entirely free from the three ways in which human errors are known to arise: thought, deed, and speech. It states that he was not impious, one who had sinned against God, since he certainly did not sin against God, having always done the will of the Father; nor a sinner, one who had offended against himself, since he said, “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV); nor pestilent, one who had ever despoiled or harmed his neighbor, since he came for this purpose: “to save what had perished” (Luke XIX).

[Col. 1102B]

Among grammarians this figure is called ὑπόζευξις, “subordination,” because individual words are suitably joined to their respective clauses; and, because several expressions end in a similar manner—as in “he went away,” “he stood,” “he sat”—it is called ὁμοιοτέλευτον, “similar ending.”

This psalm, therefore, which is the head of the book and at whose head Christ is written, appropriately has no title: either because nothing ought to be placed before our head, which is Christ, who is the Word and the beginning; or because this psalm occupies the place of the titles of the other psalms and, so to speak, of their preface. For although the other psalms say many things about Christ, none speaks so clearly about his manner of life on earth.

[Col. 1102C]

After defining him as blessed through the eighth type of definition, by the things he did not do, it immediately proceeded no less to the second type of definition, which writers on the arts call ἐννοηματική, that is, “notional.” Through the things he did, as through certain signs leading him into recognition, it specifically indicated not what he is but what he did, saying, “But his delight was in the law of the Lord,” and what follows (Ps. I).

But since, captivated a little too long by the sweetness of the head of the book, we have wandered away from our subject, we must return to our purpose. Let us now come to the Gospels and see whether the evangelists, or the Lord himself, made mention of images or of Scriptures.

[Col. 1102D]

The Evangelist says, “As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet” (Luke IV). He says “written,” not “painted,” and “in a book,” not “on some material.” The same Lord and our Redeemer, while he was destroying the devices of the ancient enemy, is reported, in many places of his preaching, to have brought forward examples from the Scriptures, not from paintings.

When a woman caught in the crime of adultery had been brought before him, with a crowd standing around her, and the Pharisees were full of the deceit of that syllogism—one which teachers of secular literature call ἄφυκτος, that is, “inescapable”—he avoided its horns, so that he would be neither cruel and consenting to bloodshed, as one who by the severity of legal rigor commanded the adulteress to be stoned, nor a transgressor of the law and supporter of sinners, as one who commanded that she be dismissed unharmed contrary to the sentence of the law; but, being just and gentle, he struck them, as a heavenly philosopher, with the weapon of a most serious proposition.

[Col. 1103A]

When they feared to hear their own crimes and went away one after another, he is reported to have written with his finger on the ground, not painted. Thus, just as the law was once written by his finger on stone to signify the hardness of the hearts of the Jews, so by that same finger the evangelical law was written on the ground of the hearts of the Gentiles, which receive the seeds of the divine Word and daily produce fruits worthy of their Creator. In this way the stone tablets signified the rigor of the Old Testament and the hardness of the Israelite people, while the earth written upon by the Lord’s finger signified the tender hearts of the Gentiles, prepared to believe and bear fruit, or the gentleness of the New Testament.

[Col. 1103B]

Finally, the Apostles—of whom it was said through the prophet, “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace and proclaim salvation” (Isa. LII)—who went forth weeping as they cast their seed, scattering the seeds of the divine Word through many temporal tribulations, and who will come with rejoicing to that universal judgment, carrying their sheaves, namely the peoples converted through their preaching to the teachings of the faith, are read to have sent letters to various regions of the world, not images.

They did not recall the human race from the worship of idols to the purity of the true faith through paintings, but through the Scriptures, by which the Redeemer opened their understanding—not so that they might understand paintings, but the Scriptures. For it is written, “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV).

[Col. 1103C]

The Gospel also says, “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name” (John XXI).

John too, drawing nectar-like streams from the secret of the Lord’s breast and offering heavenly drink to thirsty hearts, when he had been exiled to the island of Patmos by the imperial commands and received the taste of the Lord’s cup previously promised to him, and, filled with heavenly mysteries, heard or saw certain secrets revealed by the Lord, was commanded to write them in a book, not to paint them.

He also admonished the seven churches—one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit—not by painting but by writing. For a voice from above, like thunder, said to him, “What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches” (Apoc. I).

[Col. 1103D]

Hence it is understood that Scriptures, not paintings, were granted for the instruction of our faith.

Anyone who possesses knowledge of the divine Scriptures can easily understand how rash and how far removed from reason it is to say: “Just as we have books of divine Scripture for the memory and veneration of them, so we have images.”

In the Scriptures are found weapons with which to fight against adversities, by which vices are restrained, virtues raised up, and the desire of gluttony suppressed through vigils and compunction of heart; by which fornication is curbed through contrition of heart and bodily affliction, persistence in prayer, exercise in labor, fear of punishments, or love of the eternal homeland; by which envy is overcome through love of brotherly affection and desire for the heavenly kingdom, which only the harmonious attain; by which anger is broken through the weight of the most patient moderation, the sharpness of reason, and the gift of equanimity; by which greed is trampled down through almsgiving and hope of eternal reward; by which sadness is driven away through fraternal conversation, constant reading, and prayers; by which arrogance is excluded through fear of losing the virtues, without which they cannot be possessed, and the onset of vain glory, the enemy of the virtues, is shut out; and in which pride is crushed by fear of the devil’s fall and by the example of Christ’s humility.

[Col. 1104A]

In them are found the instruments of the fruit of righteousness: love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, and self-control.

In them is found a remedy by which neither the wise, glorying in their wisdom, nor the strong, trusting in their strength, are endangered, and by which the simple or weak are not cast down by their inability; by which excessive joy does not exalt the joyful, nor excessive anguish of spirit afflict the sorrowful; by which wealth does not make the rich arrogant, nor poverty break the poor.

[Col. 1104B]

In them is found the rule by which the leaders are instructed how they ought to act toward their subjects and subjects toward their leaders; how marriages ought to be cherished; how secular counsels ought to be considered with prudent deliberation; how the homeland ought to be defended; how enemies ought to be driven away; how the administration of foreign and domestic affairs ought to be conducted; and, to embrace everything briefly, in them are contained the perpetual nourishment of the soul, the teaching of the present life, the wisdom that is the adornment of life, and the instructions for perpetual life.

For it is a treasure lacking no good thing and overflowing with every good. Whoever approaches it devoutly rejoices that whatever he faithfully seeks he has happily acquired.

[Col. 1104C]

If love of worldly wisdom and of a secular school delights anyone, let him approach the armories of divine law, which precedes the wise of the world both in the loftiness of its merits and in time; let him rejoice that there he may discover the depths of the liberal studies that he knows, and find those that he does not know.

There he will find the beauty of correct expression, the etymologies of names, varieties of figures, and intricate turns of metaphor. Concerning these blessed Augustine says: “Let the educated know that our authors used all the modes of expression that grammarians call by the Greek name *tropes*.” Those who know these *tropes*, that is, modes of expression, recognize them in the sacred Writings, and their knowledge assists them to some extent in understanding them. There he will also find histories and meters, all of which properly belong to the art of grammar.

[Col. 1104D]

But perhaps someone will say, “There I do not find the scansion of meters or the precise measurements of their temporal quantities.” Let him recognize that many meters and many rhythms exist in the divine Scriptures, but that the translation of a language does not permit foreign speech to retain the same intervals of time that are found in the original, even though it possesses the same meanings and the same particular properties of things. For if someone repays a debt of gold to us, it makes little difference if it is not the same coin as what he received, provided that it is of the same weight and brilliance.

[Col. 1105A]

For, as we learned from blessed Jerome, most skilled in the Hebrew language, some passages of divine Scripture proceed according to the strict rules of art in the Hebrew dactyl and spondee, some in the anapest, and others in the iamb.

There too he will find brilliance and abundance of eloquence, the kinds and states of causes; introductions by which hearers are made favorable, teachable, or attentive; clear and concise narratives, and also long explanations, which are disclosed only when the Holy Spirit opens them; conclusions by which the nature of things is shown; arguments by which the minds of hearers are stirred to carry out what is said.

[Col. 1105B]

There he will find laws or maxims; lofty matters expressed loftily, small matters humbly, and moderate matters in a measured manner. There he will find prosopopoeia, ethopoeia, and all the figures of speech handed down by rhetoricians, as well as many others narrower than these, which he will rejoice to have grasped—figures to which neither the school of grammarians nor that of rhetoricians could attain.

There too he will find introductions, which usefully lead the reader toward the investigation of things; categories, which excel in investigating things through the usefulness of the predicaments; definitions or forms of syllogisms, which affirm through subtle inquiry matters that are in doubt; and topics, which, being sources of meanings and origins of expressions, provide arguments to everyone alike—grammarians, poets, orators, and philosophers—and which adhere continually not only to scholarly speech but also to ordinary and tumultuous speech.

[Col. 1105C]

For although speech is tumultuous and ordinary, if it is brought forward for any of life’s practical purposes, it will come to the topics. Through them, as through certain disciplines, it will find local rules by which it either cannot or ought not to wander. In them too it will discover a boundary that is difficult to cross without loss of meaning.

And, to say everything briefly, all speech will unquestionably remain undefined unless it comes to the topics.

There is also *Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*—“On Interpretation”—whose intricate paths and ragged byways contain the depth of the discovery of meanings and the affirmation of doubtful matters, and from which arises the forest of syllogisms and other arguments. All of this properly belongs to the art of dialectic.

[Col. 1105D]

There, through the art of arithmetic, he will find in numbers hidden meanings and profound depths, since, as the same Scripture says, “God made all things by measure, number, and weight” (I Esdr. VIII). There too he will find not only the consonances of music and the instruments used by many of the holy Fathers, but also their inventor.

He will also find the locations and dimensions of lands, which properly belong to the art of geometry. Likewise, anyone who studies diligently will recognize that he has found there the courses and positions of certain stars, the variations of times, the cycles of months, years, and hours, and even the day and the reason for the creation of the stars—all of which properly belong to the art of astronomy.

[Col. 1106A]

But someone may perhaps say, “The names of the disciplines as primary categories are not found there, nor the parts of each discipline individually, nor the members of each part one by one.” To this we must briefly reply: everything that the writers on the arts have placed in the little plots of their gardens can be found in parts throughout the broadest meadows of the sacred Scriptures. I say that they are found in the power of their meanings, not in the public declaration of their words; in the depths of their roots, not in the falling of their leaves.

For this is how the liberal arts are perceived by diligent students in the depth of the divine Scriptures: just as wines are contemplated in vines, crops in seeds, leaves in roots, fruits in branches, and the greatness of trees in their kernels.

[Col. 1106B]

Divine Scripture is plainly truthful, firm, chaste, an instrument of heavenly instruction, and an eternal proclamation shining with the purest eloquence. It is the light of mortals, as the prophet says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, O Lord, and a light for my paths” (Ps. CXIX). It is living and does not know death, as the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Hebr. IV). It dispels darkness, as Solomon bears witness, saying: “The commandment of the law is a lamp, and the light of life, reproof, and discipline” (Prov. VI). Through Isaiah it is said of it: “By night my spirit watches for you, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI).

[Col. 1106C]

For it always commands what gives life, forbids what is harmful, removes earthly things, and commends heavenly things.

It is, I say, a fountain springing from an ethereal bank: the more abundantly it is drawn, the less it is exhausted, and the more widely it is channeled, the more it increases in meaning. It is a purse of money from which neither what is given is lost nor constant use in giving brings diminution; rather, the more is cast out from it through the devotion of giving, the more it is filled.

None of the things we have touched upon, nor of those similar things that we have omitted for the sake of brevity, can be found by you in images, O worshiper of images, O cultist of senseless things. Since images lack all these prerogatives of merit, you should be pitied rather than admired for desiring to equate them with the books of divine Scripture, in which so many good things are found.

[Col. 1106D]

You who say that you preserve the purity of your faith in images, remember to stand before them as a suppliant with incense; let us diligently seek the Lord’s commandments in the books of divine law. You illuminate paintings with lamps; let us frequent the divine Scriptures. You be a worshiper of painted colors; let us be worshipers and apprehenders of hidden meanings. You delight in painted panels; let us be delighted by divine conversations. You devote yourself to figures of things in which there is neither sight, hearing, taste, smell, nor touch; let us devote ourselves to the divine law, which is blameless, in which are found the Lord’s testimony, ordinances or commandments, fear or judgments.

[Col. 1107A]

The Psalmist beautifully expressed these one by one through the seventh type of definition, which dialecticians call κατὰ μεταφοράν, that is, “by transference,” because it shows what a thing is by a brief proclamation. He expressed them under the perfection of the number six, which according to the discipline of arithmetic is considered perfect because, measured by its parts and with those parts again reduced to one whole, it returns to itself without any loss or increase. He says:

“The law of the Lord is blameless, restoring souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones. The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XIX).

All these things are adorned with the perfection of the number six because, although they may appear in some way to differ from one another, each nevertheless pertains to the perfection of the law by which holy men are made perfect. Just as the sixth number is not completed when one is subtracted from it, so, if anything is taken away, the integrity of perfection is mutilated.

[Col. 1107B]

The law is blameless because it consists in perfect truth. Through the Savior it was not condemned but rather shown to be fulfilled: “I have not come,” he says, “to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. II).

And so that we might know that the Gospel too is the law of the Lord, and that the law consists in the two Testaments, namely the New and the Old, he added, “Restoring souls” (Ps. XIX). For the page of the Old Testament possesses the rigor of blameless severity, while the New possesses the summons and gentleness by which those who have gone astray are corrected and the conversion of souls to Christ’s grace takes place.

The testimony of the Lord is therefore faithful, because whatever God promises is fulfilled in the fullest truth.

[Col. 1107C]

This testimony gives wisdom to the little ones—not to the proud or those who vaunt themselves with swollen arrogance, but to the little ones of whom the Apostle says, “Do not become children in your understanding, but be little ones in wickedness” (I Cor. XIV).

The Father gives testimony, the Son gives testimony, and the Holy Spirit also gives testimony; and just as they are of one essence and nature, so too they are exalted in giving testimony. Concerning the Father it is read in the Gospel that he bore witness to the Son. Concerning the Son, the Apostle writes to Timothy: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate” (I Tim. VI). Concerning the Holy Spirit the same Apostle says: “For the Spirit himself also bears witness to our spirit” (Ps. XIX).

The ordinances of the Lord are rightly called right because he is known to have done nothing other than what he taught, nor is one thing in his mouth and another in his work.

[Col. 1107D]

They gladden hearts because they charm the minds of the righteous with the bestowal of eternal rewards. The one who trusted in the reception of those rewards said, “From now on a crown of righteousness has been laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (II Tim. IV).

The commandment of the Lord is rightly called lucid, either because it proceeds from the Father of lights or, by metonymy, because it makes people luminous. It also enlightens the eyes—not the bodily eyes, which living creatures are known to possess in common with us, but the inner eyes, which are spiritually illumined by the radiance of the divine gift.

[Col. 1108A]

“The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever”: love mixed with dread is present, and in ordinary usage this is called reverence. Whoever is known both to fear and to love his judge is therefore engaged in every holiness.

There is this difference between the fear of the Lord and human dread: human dread changes with time. Of it, if I am not mistaken, it was said, “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV). But the fear of the Lord is not changed from its proper state by any temporal alteration; it perseveres in the same condition through the sincerity of a good conscience.

[Col. 1108B]

The judgments of God, which the prophet describes as both true and justified in themselves, are his commandments, written in the Old and New Testaments, because they truly proceed from judgment. They are “true,” by metonymy, and “justified,” because they make those who observe them truthful and justified.

There is nevertheless this difference between God’s judgment and his judgments: “judgment” in the singular is that universal examination, whereas “his judgments” in the plural are the sacraments found in the two Testaments, not in images or paintings. The same Psalmist expressed them through the figure that in Greek is called αὔξησις, that is, “increase,” because it gradually grows toward higher things, saying: “More desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XIX).

[Col. 1108C]

For just as precious stones are valued above gold, so honey and the honeycomb are plainly preferred in sweetness to gold and precious stones.

Through this same figure the Psalmist sings that his protector, and also the one who exalts his head, is the Lord, saying, “But you, O Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who exalts my head” (Ps. III). The Apostle likewise says, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. VIII). Through the increase of the names, the greatness of the matter gradually grows.

[Col. 1108D]

A figure closely related to this is called in Greek κλίμαξ and in Latin *gradatio*, “gradation,” when, after certain steps have been set down either in praise or in blame, the expression continually increases. Yet it differs greatly from it in this respect: αὔξησις produces increase without any repetition of the names of things, whereas κλίμαξ repeats in the following clause, in every way, the final word placed in the first clause; thus, like a chain, one thing is always linked to another. An example is the Apostle’s statement: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint” (Rom. V). Likewise: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII).

But if you, lover—or rather worshiper—of images should perhaps mutter with inward resentment, saying, “Why wander so far through figures of speech?”, understand that these are more pleasing to us than your images or painted panels, and that this is why we have wandered so far among them.

[Col. 1109A]

Recognize that we, or the other lovers of the Scriptures, find these sweet things and these refreshments in the Scriptures or in the figures of the Scriptures. You, however, and your associates will find them nowhere in figures or in the panels in which you say that you preserve the purity of your heart.

## CHAPTER XXXI

That those who anathematize their parents act against the command of the Lord’s voice; and that, if according to their opinion their predecessors were heretics, these people were born, taught, and consecrated by heretics; also concerning the non-judgment of those who have departed from the world; or how far the error of these people differs from the error of their parents, since the former judged that images should be broken, while these judge that they should be worshiped.

Finally, those who presume to equate them with the Lord’s body and blood are so inflamed by love for them that they do not hesitate even to anathematize their parents, who are known to have rejected them, thus joining error to error. For they both offer those images an incongruous [Col. 1109B] and disorderly worship, and impose an ill-timed curse upon their parents—whether those from whom they were propagated through the material of the flesh, or those through whose consecration, the sacrament of baptism, and other spiritual gifts they received these things. For if, according to their madness, all who lack the worship of images are heretics, it follows that their ancestors, who did not worship them, were heretics. If they were heretics, they had no power either to perform consecrations or to lay on hands; and if they did not possess this power, those who think they received it from them possess neither consecration nor the laying on of hands.

Likewise, if their predecessors, as they claim, deserved to be bound by an anathema, they did not possess the power of binding and loosing. If they did not possess it, everything they did in the Church must be annulled; and if everything must be rejected, their ranks and ordinations must be rejected. Therefore, if their predecessors deserved to be bound by an anathema, the ranks and ordinations of these men must be annulled. For we read that the power of binding and loosing was granted by the Lord not to schismatics and those bound by the chain of anathema, but to worthy and catholic men.

Meanwhile, that honor must be shown to parents is taught not only by the legal, prophetic, and apostolic admonition, but also by the Gospel admonition, when the Lord says: “Honor your father and your mother” (Matt. XV). He who, both through the page of the Old Testament and through the presence of his own body, bestowed this saving command also proclaimed it through the mouth of Moses, saying: “Blessed is the one who honors his father and his mother” [Col. 1109D] (Exod. XX; Deut. V); and, conversely: “Cursed is the one who does not honor his father and his mother” (Exod. XXI; Matt. XV; Mark VII). Hence one must weigh and earnestly consider how great is the arrogance, how great the recklessness and, so to speak, the crime of anathematizing parents, if the one who is proved not to honor them is subject to a curse.

For when the Law says, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Lev. XVIII), and the Apostle says, “Children, obey your parents” (Eph. VI), these men seem to resist both commands, since they strive neither to conceal their parents’ shame nor to show them honor. The sacred canons, therefore, excluding every pretext for despising parents, seem to have issued this decree:

“Whoever of the sons withdraws from his parents under the pretext of divine worship and does not render them their due reverence, let him be anathema.”

But if those who do not show them their due reverence are anathematized, by what bond of condemnation do you suppose those who anathematize them are bound?

For it is a most salutary practice, handed down to the Churches by the holy Fathers, to pray to the Lord for the spirits of the departed. Embracing this practice together with the entire holy catholic and universal Church, we ask the Lord’s most merciful compassion not only for the spirits of our parents, but also for those of faithful friends who have gone before us in the peace of the Lord. Those who strive not to assist the spirits of their departed parents through prayers, but to bind them by the chain of anathema, appear to oppose this venerable and ecclesiastical ordinance to no small degree; and although they are commanded, on the testimony of apostolic teaching, to pray even for their enemies, they resist doing this for their own parents.

We ask pardon for our own people, according to ecclesiastical custom, through the persistence of prayers and almsgiving; they desire punishment for theirs through the assemblies of empty councils. We seek rest for our own through the solemn celebration of Masses; they heap insults upon theirs through disorderly councils. We commemorate our own in prayer; they cast anathema upon theirs, with a kind of renunciation. We pray that the spirits of our own may obtain rest in Abraham’s bosom; they wish the souls of theirs to be condemned with Arius, Sabellius, Dioscorus, Nestorius, and Eutyches. We [Col. 1110C] ask that our parents be placed among the ranks of the blessed; they wish the souls of their own parents to be condemned among the obstinate crowds of heretics.

Since these things are so, it is clear that in this matter they commit a twofold offense: both they deprive their parents of honor, against the command of the Lord’s voice, and, contrary to the Apostle’s judgment, they rashly attempt to pass judgment upon those who have departed from this world.

That judgment must not, therefore, be rashly passed upon those who have already departed from this world, or upon matters that belong to God alone—this is the blessed Paul’s teaching:

“None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; or whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ both died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God. Let us therefore judge no longer; but judge this rather: not to place a stumbling block or an occasion of scandal before your brother” (Rom. XIV).

Concerning this matter, Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, is said to have written thus to the emperor Anastasius:

“Let Your Serenity know that care must be taken lest there be any stumbling block in the Church, while we attempt to judge those who have already passed away concerning matters that we cannot accomplish.”

Since, therefore, parents must not be dishonored by their children, nor the dead rashly judged by the living, as is brought forth from the pages of the divine Scriptures, we must now carefully observe with the eye of the mind how greatly the error of the children differs from the error of their parents in the abolition or veneration of the images mentioned above, since the error of both sides does not cease to oppose itself to the other.

The former judged that the images ought to be torn down and despised, with perpetual rejection from the Church; the latter strive not only to possess them, but also to venerate them with submissive worship. The former committed them to crackling fires; the latter honor them with fragrant incense. The former even fled from seeing them; the latter do not cease to embrace them. The former dug out from the walls those images that had been established there by the ancients for the adornment of the church; the latter go around newly made images with offered [Col. 1111B] lights. The former endeavored utterly to abominate them; the latter decree that they must altogether be kissed. The former anathematized those who possessed them; the latter, conversely, anathematize those who do not worship them.

Since these two evils are opposed to each other and both have departed from the straight path, it remains for us, walking according to the Apostle along the royal road, to incline neither to the right nor to the left: neither, with the former, to judge that they must be completely abolished, nor, with the latter, to decree that they must be worshiped. Rather, worshiping God alone and venerating his saints according to the ancient tradition of the Fathers and the Church, let us, if we wish, retain them in the church for adornment and as reminders of past events. Let us reject with justice severity on the one side and flattery on the other; with prudence, cunning on the one side and dullness on the other; with temperance, lust on the one side and insensibility on the other; with fortitude, cowardice on the one side and rashness on the other. Together with the holy Fathers, who allowed them to exist only as adornment of the church, let us set aside those who worship them on one side and those who abominate them on the other, and let us hold to the way of the Lord’s commandments, so that, with his help, we may be able to reach him who is the way, the truth, and the life.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1111]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1111B]

It is clear that the style of this work—whether in the preceding books, which have already been arranged by God’s assent; or in the present book, whose opening we are now undertaking; or also in that which, with the Lord’s assistance, we shall arrange later—keeps watch against the madness of those who, although at different times and with different intentions, are accustomed to convene synods either to reject images from the Church or to decree that they be worshiped.

And since the writing of that madness, which they vainly desire to be known by the name of the Seventh Synod, appears to be composed of the errors of its own opinions as though of limbs, and to be supported by the clauses of testimonies from the divine law improperly applied to it as though by wings, we have wished in the preceding books to remove from it the support of the wings by which it thinks itself vainly upheld; in the books that follow, however, we shall deprive it of the framework of those empty limbs by which it supposes that it can stand, so that the preceding books may strip from it the oars of its wings, while the following books sever its limbs piece by piece; the preceding books may deprive it of flight, and the following of its ability to walk.

Thus, when the wings of spiritual understanding and divine speech on which it was thought to ride monstrously have been cut away, and when its own opinions, by which it was violently compelled to wander abroad in other matters, have been restored to it, and when it has been struck by the strong and unconquerable fist of the catholic faith, it may appear to all to have been enervated—lacking both a sufficient mass of empty and irrational assertions, and suitable meanings and testimonies of divine writings—although it is not believed by everyone to have been properly arranged. For while it attempts to raise the reputation of its own authors to the heights of glory, it does not fear to disturb the prosperity of domestic affairs through civil conflict; and while it incites citizens to the forbidden worship of certain things, it frightens the domestic weapons of the citizens against itself and, alas, compels the darts whose purpose should have been both to defend liberty and to resist the hostile mass to be hurled against the natives. [Col. 1112B]

We have therefore resolved to weaken it—not with crafty quibbles, not with forensic eloquence, not with the rhetorical ornaments of speech wandering far from the matter, not with the charm of a seductive cothurnus, nor with the knotty arguments of clever execution—but with the scope of pure and simple speech, woven with the tenacious sinews of the divine utterances and colored by the eloquence of sound and sober teaching. Such speech, free from boastful display, is more a lover of the advancement of the holy Church than a pursuer of its own or our own windy praise.

Since, therefore, in the text of the present book, whose undertaking we now plainly see before us, we shall examine the opinions of those who in their synod set down certain matters differently from the way they were handed down by the holy Fathers, and shall in a manner dispute concerning the faith, order demands that we first lay the foundation of our faith—namely, that of which the Apostle says: “For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. III).

As soon as we have expressed the sincerity of this venerable faith, just as we believe it in our heart, and have fortified the beginnings of the work to come with the firmness of so great a foundation, our structure may rise more freely and be built more straightly and solidly; and wherever theirs has risen less correctly or less firmly, it may more easily be cast down.

Since, therefore, we must first fortify and strengthen our own position, and afterward engage in battle against what opposes us and resist what is set against us, we are taught this not only by the lessons of sacred Scripture, but are also admonished by the principles of the eloquence of the Roman author [i.e., Cicero], who says:

“One must argue in such a way that one first strengthens one’s own case, and afterward breaks down the opposing case.”

## CHAPTER ONE. The confession of the catholic faith that we received from the holy Fathers, hold, and believe with a pure heart.

[Col. 1113A]

We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible. We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created: true God, the only-begotten and true Son of God, not made or adopted, but begotten and of one substance with the Father, and in every respect so equal to God the Father that he cannot be inferior either in time, rank, or power. We confess that he who was begotten is as great as he who begot him.

When we say that the Son was begotten by the Father, we do not ascribe any time to the divine and ineffable generation; nor do we say that the Father ever began, or the Son. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be co-eternal. The Father is called Father because of the Son, and he who was always Father always had a Son.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father. I added “proceeding from the Father and the Son,” at the wish and command of Charles, below, in chapters 3 and 8, and of Pope Hadrian in the Capitulary.]

We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance. There is absolutely no rank within the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher; rather, the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection. Thus, apart from the names that indicate the distinctiveness of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most appropriately be understood of all three.

And just as, refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons as distinct according to their proper characteristics. We do not say that the Father is himself his own Son, that the Son is himself his own Father, or that the Holy Spirit is himself either the Father or the Son; rather, the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

For we confess not merely names, but also the distinct properties of the names—that is, the persons—or, as the Greeks express it, ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), that is, subsistences. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit; nor, conversely, does the Son or the Holy Spirit assume the name and person of the Father. The Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always the Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance but distinct in persons and names.

The Son of God himself, who possesses eternity without beginning together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we declare to have assumed, at the end of the ages, a complete human being of our nature from Mary ever-virgin. The Word became flesh by assuming a human being, not by changing the Godhead. Nor, as certain men most wickedly suppose, do we say that the Holy Spirit served as the seed; rather, he acted through the power and might of the Creator.

Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two perfect and complete substances: that of the Godhead and that of humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses in Christ only a mere human being, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less from human nature, and that the human being assumed—whether in flesh, soul, or consciousness—was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. We confess him to be like us in every respect except for the stain of sin, which is not natural.

We likewise abominate the blasphemy of those who, in a novel sense, try to assert that, from the time when he assumed flesh, everything that belonged to the Godhead passed into the human being, and again that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God. Thus, through this confusion, both substances—the Godhead and the humanity—would appear to have been emptied of their proper fullness and changed from their own state into something else, although no heresy had ever before dared to say this. Such men confess both an imperfect God in the Son and an imperfect human being, so that they are not believed to hold either a true God or a true human being.

We, however, say that the Son of God assumed our passible nature in such a way that the Godhead remained impassible. For the Son suffered—not apparently but truly—all that Scripture testifies: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind. He suffered them according to that which was capable of suffering—that is, not according to the substance that assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed.

For the Son of God himself, according to his Godhead, is impassible like the Father, incomprehensible like the Father, invisible like the Father, and unchangeable like the Father. And although the proper person of the Son—that is, the Word of God—assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, through that indwelling, the Godhead of the Word suffered nothing according to its substance, so that the entire Trinity must be confessed as impassible.

The Son of God therefore died according to the Scriptures, in accordance with that which could die; he rose on the third day and ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of God the Father, while the nature of the flesh in which he was born and suffered remains—the same flesh in which he also rose again. For the substance of humanity was not emptied of its fullness, but glorified, and will remain eternally with the Godhead.

Having received from the Father authority over all things in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, rewarding the righteous and punishing sinners. We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say that we shall be restored in the same reality of limbs in which we now exist, and that whatever we become once after the resurrection, we shall remain forever. There is one life for the saints, but rewards differ according to labor; conversely, punishments also exist for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

We hold one baptism, which is to be celebrated for infants with the same words of the sacrament as for adults. If a person falls after baptism, we believe that he can be saved through repentance. We accept the New and Old Testaments in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy catholic Church.

We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him, anathematizing those who say that souls, as though a part of God, belong to the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously or dwelt in heaven before they were sent into bodies.

We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings, and that God’s commandments can be fulfilled not by individuals but collectively by everyone; and we condemn those who condemn first marriages with Manichaeus or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.

We anathematize also those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the human being he assumed, he could not do everything he wished. We likewise condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that there will be no distinction of merits in the future, and that we shall possess there the virtues whose possession we neglected here.

We confess free will in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We declare both those who, with Manichaeus, say that a human being cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a human being cannot sin, to be in error; for each removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a human being can always both sin and not sin, so that we always confess ourselves to possess free will.

This is the true integrity of the faith of catholic tradition, which we believe and confess with a sincere heart, and which we have set forth in this work in the words of blessed Jerome. This is the true faith; this confession we preserve and hold. Whoever guards it firmly and undefiledly will have everlasting salvation.

## CHAPTER TWO. That Tarasius attempted to heal error with error, and fell from one sickness into another, since, having suddenly been converted from a layman and promoted to the episcopate, he tries to remedy in the worship of images what he committed in his sudden reception of consecration.

[Col. 1115C]

It is an old custom of experienced physicians to persist in treating the disorders of one illness with frequent medicines, while taking care not to provide assistance to the evil of another disease, since certain remedies weaken the strength of one illness but, when applied, supply nourishment to the strength of another. It is also the practice of cultivators of the spiritual vineyard to tear out the roots of certain vices in such a way that the roots of others do not recover through any increase, since the harmful planting of certain vices grows through the destruction of other vices; thus, while supplying support to one disease, it harms the field of the mind, which, unable by itself to cause harm, languishes after being uprooted by its own strength.

Tarasius is said to resist these excellent practices of both experienced physicians and spiritual cultivators to no small degree. Through something wholly forbidden and entirely unprofitable, he attempts to remedy something wholly forbidden and thoroughly harmful.

It is as though someone wishing to wash away something muddy with an impure substance should nevertheless attempt to wash it with muddy water: the more eagerly he seeks to cleanse it, the more he stains it with those same impurities. In the same way, Tarasius, having suddenly been promoted, as is reported, from the lay state to the episcopate, while attempting to remedy the sudden assumption of so great a rank through the worship of images, added one unlawful thing to another. The more he thought to heal one error with another error, the more he entangled himself in greater bonds of error.

For if an inappropriate ordination can be established by an inappropriate worship of images, unlawful things will easily be capable of being confirmed by unlawful things; and if unlawful things can be confirmed by unlawful things, every impurity could very easily be washed away by certain impurities.

But impurities cannot be washed away by impurities. Therefore an inappropriate ordination cannot in any way be established by an inappropriate worship of images.

And if the rule of ecclesiastical ordination handed down by the holy Fathers must be preserved undefiled—and indeed, because it must be preserved, it must not be corrupted at all—then, if it must not be corrupted at all, it must not be corrupted even for some useful purpose. And if it must in no way be corrupted for some useful purpose, then it must be corrupted even less for an useless one, since both worshiping images and entering the pontifical chair without the proper sequence of ranks are useless.

But why pursue these matters? Let us approach the Apostle; let us come to the Chosen Vessel; let us question the distinguished preacher; let him proclaim to us what he thinks concerning the ordination of a bishop. Without doubt he will answer:

“Do not lay hands quickly on anyone” (1 Tim. V).

And again:

“Not a novice, lest, being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. III);

that is, lest, while thinking that he has acquired not so much a ministry of humility as the administration of secular power, he be cast down through the arrogance of pride, as the devil was.

Hence such an ordination is extremely dangerous, since it is thought to incur the devil’s judgment. And his teaching is greatly to be feared, by which he decrees that images must be worshiped, when the ruin of so atrocious an example is feared in him. For it has been forbidden that a layman should fulfill the ministry of the priesthood, since he is believed neither to have held its office nor to have recognized its discipline; nor can he teach those things that it is clear he had never previously learned.

Concerning such an ordination, therefore, this is the judgment of blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome:

“Some men, inflated by a desire for honor, are tonsured after the death of bishops and suddenly become priests from laymen, shamelessly seizing the leadership of a religious way of life, although they have not yet learned to be soldiers. What do we think these men will provide for their subjects, when, before they have reached the threshold of discipleship, they do not fear to occupy the place of a teacher?

“Therefore, even if someone’s merit is blameless, it is necessary that he first be exercised in ecclesiastical duties through the distinct ranks. Let him see what he is to imitate, learn what he is to teach, and be formed for the position he is to hold, so that afterward the one chosen to show the way to those who err may not himself have to err.

“Let him therefore be polished for a long time through religious meditation, so that he may please; and let the lamp placed upon the lampstand shine in such a way that, when the opposing force of the winds rushes upon it, it does not extinguish the flame of learning it has kindled, but increases it. For since it is written, ‘Let a person first be tested, and then let him serve,’ the one who is appointed as the people’s intercessor must be tested all the more beforehand, lest bad priests become the cause of the people’s ruin.

“There is therefore no excuse against this, no defense can exist, because it is plainly known to all how great is the holy diligence of the distinguished teacher in this matter, by which he forbids a novice to approach the sacred orders. Just as at that time a novice was called one who had been planted in the practice of the holy faith at its beginning, so now a novice must be regarded as one who, suddenly planted in the religious habit, has insinuated himself into the pursuit of sacred honors.

“One rank must therefore be approached through another rank. The one who seeks the highest summits of office by abrupt ascent, setting aside the intervening ranks, does not rightly desire a sacred rank. And since the same Apostle teaches his disciple, among the other regulations of the sacred order, that hands must not be laid upon anyone too quickly, what could be quicker or more precipitate than for the beginning to arise from the summit, so that a man begins to be a bishop before he has been a teacher?”

While the aforementioned Tarasius strove, as they say, for the priestly summit against this norm of ecclesiastical institution, he is known to have disturbed rather than governed the peoples. Nor is it surprising if one does not preach correctly who did not correctly attain the office of preaching.

Many testimonies of the holy Fathers could have been set down concerning his disorderly consecration, but they have been omitted for the sake of brevity. It is sufficient to have stated these few things concerning the matter.

## CHAPTER THREE. Whether Tarasius thinks correctly when, contrary to the truest rule of the holy faith, he professes in the reading of his belief that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father and the Son, but from the Father through the Son.

Oblivion has by no means removed from our memory [Col. 1117C] what we promised at the beginning of this work: that we would leave nothing unexamined and pass over in silence nothing found worthy of criticism in that same synod, which was conducted in support of the veneration of images—except, perhaps, what either the difficulty of disordered speech prevented our understanding from grasping, or what the ineptitude of a childish statement made our discussion disdain to pursue, out of reverence. It does not therefore follow that our discussion should be suspended because Tarasius confessed in his profession of faith that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone—as did certain people who, although they were silent in some fashion about his proceeding from the Son, nevertheless believed absolutely that he proceeds from the Father and the Son—nor from the Father and the Son, as the whole Church universally confesses and believes him to proceed, but from the Father through the Son [Col. 1117D].

Unless that profession contains the purity and sincerity of heart that believes him not to be a creature but the Creator, neither lesser than the Father and the Son but equal and consubstantial with them, and proceeding from both, a pernicious poison may arise from it. The definition of every matter should therefore be such that, once all obscurities and ambiguities have been dispelled, its judgment proceeds by a straight course toward demonstrating the matter in question. And if the definition of other matters ought to be so clear and lucid that it plainly demonstrates what is to be demonstrated, much more must the definition of faith be clear and lucid and free from every ambiguity or crookedness. If anything in it is crooked or ambiguous, or covered by some cloud of words, it brings great loss to the speaker or hearer.

It is rightly believed and customarily confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, not from the Father through the Son. For he does not proceed through the Son as through a creature made through him, nor as though later in time, lesser in power, or of another substance; rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son as coeternal, consubstantial, coequal, and existing with them in one glory, power, and divinity. The preposition *from* (*ex*) has one force, and *through* (*per*) another. Thus the Son of God, born from a human being, is believed to have been born not through a human being—that is, not through sexual intercourse or human agency—but by assuming flesh from a virgin. And therefore [Col. 1118B] it may be asked whether it can rightly be said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, lest, when this preposition is incautiously inserted into the profession of so great a mystery, it offer anyone a cup of the poisonous error of the Arians, who blasphemously assert that the Holy Spirit is a creature and was created through the Son, just like all other created things. They likewise administered baptism to their unfortunate converts not according to the evangelical faith—“in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII)—but “in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.”

That the Holy Spirit is not a creature but the Creator is demonstrated by the following testimonies. David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Psalm XXXIII). Solomon says: “He himself created them through the Holy Spirit” (Ecclesiasticus I). David likewise says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm CIV). And in the Book of Job it is written: “The divine Spirit,” he says, “created me” (Job XXXIII). In the Book of Judith: “Every creature of yours,” she says, “will serve you, because you spoke and they were made; you sent forth your Spirit, and he built them” (Judith XVI).

The Holy Spirit is shown to possess such great power and might that, with his cooperation, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ—which is our redemption—was formed in the Virgin’s womb, as the Evangelist says: “Do not be afraid, Joseph, to take Mary your wife; for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew I). Likewise: “She was found to have conceived from the Holy Spirit” (Luke II). This does not mean that the Holy Spirit is to be called the Father of our Savior, so that two fathers may be believed to exist; rather, it means that the same Holy Spirit is believed to be the cooperator of the Father and the Son and to be of one power with them, as the Lord affirms: “Go,” he said to the disciples, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII).

For just as the Lord sent the apostles to preach, so the Holy Spirit is also shown to act in the same way. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, while Peter was considering the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: “Behold, men are looking for you. Rise, go down with them without hesitation, because I have sent them to you” (Acts X). And again: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts XIII). And again: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Acts XX).

The Holy Spirit also created all things together with the Father and the Son, as has been shown, and these testimonies prove that he is God of one essence with them. David says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.” It is therefore clearer than light that all the prophets announce or speak only through the Holy Spirit, as the Lord testifies when he says: “When that Holy Spirit comes whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and announce to you the things to come” (John XV). Again, the Lord says through the prophet: “They refused to hear my words, which I commanded through my Spirit by the mouth of the earlier prophets, says the Lord.”

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: “The Holy Spirit testifies to us, and this is the covenant that I shall establish with them after those days, says the Lord” (Hebrews X). In the Acts of the Apostles we also read that the shepherd of the Church said to Ananias: “Why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts IV). And, showing that he is God, he adds shortly afterward: “You have not lied to human beings but to God.”

Paul, the chosen vessel, writes to the Corinthians: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians XII). By these apostolic words the Holy Spirit is declared to be the same God and the same Lord. The same Lord says in the Gospel: “The Spirit is God” (John IV). Paul likewise writes to the Corinthians: “The Lord is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians III). And to the Ephesians: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians IV). Again, to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians VI). Showing that he is God dwelling in human bodies, he adds: “Therefore glorify and bear God in your body.”

Since these testimonies prove him both Creator and God, and since the whole Catholic Church believes that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, it must be asked whether it is necessary to profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son, rather than from the Father and the Son, since such a profession is not found to have been made by the holy Fathers in either the Nicene or the Chalcedonian Creed.

He appeared over the apostles in fire through the Son; he was given to human beings through the Son, since the Holy Spirit could be received by all only through the Son. But to profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son is foreign to synodal confession, because the Holy Spirit does not need the assistance of another in order to proceed from the Father or to proceed through anyone, since he is the third person in the same holy Trinity and is of one power and essence with the Father and the Son.

Although he is God in himself, in relation to us he is a gift, distributing the gifts of grace to each person as he wills. He also grants prophecies to whomever he wills and forgives sins to whomever he wills, for sins are not forgiven without him. He is therefore properly called Love, either because by nature he unites those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he effects in us that we remain in God and he in us. Hence among the gifts of God nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit. He is also Grace, which is called grace because it is given freely, not on account of our merits but by the divine will.

Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name Wisdom, although universally the Holy Spirit himself and the Father are also Wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name Love, although universally the Father and the Son are also Love.

He is the Spirit of the Father, as the Lord testifies when he says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Mark XIII). He is also the Spirit of the Son, as Paul testifies when he says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans VIII). Therefore he is called the Spirit of both, because, proceeding from the Father and the Son, he is proved to be of one substance and nature with them.

If he were called unbegotten, two fathers would be confessed; if begotten, two sons would improperly be asserted. But because he is neither Father nor Son, he is therefore called neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeding from both. The Father alone is not from another and is therefore alone called *unbegotten*—not indeed in Scripture, but in the customary language of those who dispute and speak about so great a matter as they are able, for the benefit of those present or those to come. The Son alone is born from the Father and is therefore alone called *begotten*. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son and is therefore alone called the Spirit of both.

He proceeds from both, not by being born, so that he could be called anyone’s son. He would be called the Son of the Father and the Son if both had begotten him—which is abhorrent to the understanding of all the faithful. He is therefore not begotten from both, but proceeds from both as the Spirit of both.

Our Lord Jesus Christ taught the disciples that he proceeds from the Father, saying: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me” (John XV). Again, the same Lord Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings, after his resurrection, wishing to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him just as from the Father, breathed upon his disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). If he did not proceed from him, he would certainly not have given him to the disciples by breathing upon them.

There is therefore one Spirit of the Father and the Son, one Spirit, as we stated above, of both.
