If anyone asks how the Son proceeds from the Father by being born, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds without being born; or why they are not both sons, since both proceed from the Father; or why the Holy Spirit is not also called unbegotten, like the Father; or how he proceeds from both; or why the Son says, “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V), as though the Son had previously existed without life and received it when the Father granted it; or how the Father was never without the Son and yet the Father begot the Son; or how the Son was never without the Spirit and yet said, “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI); or how the Son is not from himself but from the Father and yet is not later than the one from whom he is; or how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and yet is not preceded by those from whom he proceeds—let that person know that these matters and others like them are inscrutable and incomprehensible to the understanding of human weakness.

For who could consider these things? Who could comprehend them? If we cannot grasp the mysteries of Christ’s human birth, how shall we grasp the mysteries of the divine nature? Yet because in that coeternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable, and inseparable Trinity it is exceedingly difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let it suffice to believe this, firmly hold this, and confess this with the whole heart: that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither created nor begotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son.

This must be understood in such a way that, in the confession of faith, all opinions and all novelties of language are avoided, and the confession of the faithful is strengthened by those words and judgments that the holy and universal synods established in the Creed.

## CHAPTER IV. Whether Theodorus, bishop of Jerusalem, holds a correct view when, although he says that he believes the Father to be altogether without beginning and everlasting, he has professed the Son—by some obscure verbal circumlocution—to acknowledge no other beginning than the Father and to have his subsistence from him

In the preceding chapter we explained that, in the confession of holy faith, a clear and lucid definition must be made; and now we necessarily pursue the same matter. Unless speech proceeds by a straight course toward demonstrating the truth of the matter, setting aside all circumlocutions on every side, hearers will doubt the integrity of the faith of the one who utters it, and he will appear to approach heretical perversity, if not in intention, at least in wording.

Therefore care must be taken lest, in the profession of faith of Theodorus the bishop—who says that the Father is without beginning, and that the Son acknowledges no other beginning than the Father and has his subsistence from him—the Father is suspected of preceding the Son either in time, although the Son is coeternal with him; or in substance, although the Son is consubstantial with him; or in honor, although the Son is equal to him.

Even if the aforesaid man believes this correctly and catholicly, it has nevertheless been stated so ambiguously that a suspicion about his faith may arise in the reader. This is often caused not by weak belief but by difficulty of expression. Since, therefore, it is not clearly evident from this profession whether his faith should be approved or rejected—and since our intention preferred that it be approved rather than rejected—it remains for us briefly to set forth what we have received, believed, and hold from the holy Fathers concerning this matter.

For this is what must be feared in such a profession: that, when the Father is called without beginning and the Son is said to acknowledge no other beginning than the Father, the Father may be suspected of being older than the Son because he begot him, and the Son later than the Father because he was begotten. Yet nothing in the holy Trinity is earlier or later, since nothing there begins in time in order to be completed later in time.

For just as the three persons are consubstantial with one another, so also they are coeternal. The generation of the Son from the Father is understood to be without time, and likewise the procession of the Holy Spirit from both is without time.

The Father is the Son’s beginning—not by creating him, but by begetting him; not by proceeding through time, but by ineffably begetting an ineffable Son, without whom he never was, and who is ineffably coeternal with him. The Son is a beginning, not for the Father, but for the things created by him. The Holy Spirit is also a beginning for all things created by him, since he cannot in any way be separated from the name of Creator.

The Father and the Son are a beginning for the Holy Spirit—not by begetting him, since he is not the Son, nor by creating him, since he is not a creature, but by giving him, since he proceeds from both. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are likewise one beginning for all things created by them as the one and only Creator.

Although the Father is a beginning, the Son a beginning, and the Holy Spirit a beginning, there are not three beginnings but one beginning, one divinity, one substance, and one omnipotence.

These points, which we have briefly touched upon, must be confirmed by the words of the outstanding preacher Augustine. He says:

“Therefore the Father is called relatively Father, and relatively he is also called Beginning, and whatever else the Father may be called in relation to the Son; but he is called Beginning in relation to all things that are from him. Likewise the Son is called relatively Son, and relatively he is called Word and Image; and in all these names he is referred to the Father, whereas the Father is called none of these things.

“The Son is also called Beginning. For when it was said to him, ‘Who are you?’ he replied, ‘The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you.’ But was he the Father’s beginning? He wished to show himself to be the beginning of creation, when he said that he was the Beginning, just as the Father is the beginning of creation, since all things are from him.

“For the Creator is also called relatively to creation, just as lord is called relatively to servant. And therefore, when we say that the Father is Beginning and the Son is Beginning, we are not speaking of two beginnings of creation, because the Father and the Son together are one beginning in relation to creation, just as they are one Creator and one God.

“If whatever remains in itself and begets or works something is the beginning of the thing it begets or works, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is also rightly called Beginning, because we do not separate him from the name of Creator; and it is written of him that he works, and certainly he works while remaining in himself. He is not himself changed or turned into any of the things he works, and observe what he works.

“‘To each,’ says the Apostle, ‘is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit,’ and so forth.”

The same writer adds shortly afterward:

“Indeed, if we are questioned individually about the Holy Spirit, we answer most truly that he is God and is together with the Father and the Son one God. God is therefore called one beginning in relation to creation, not two or three beginnings. But in relation to one another in the Trinity, if that which begets is a beginning in relation to that which it begets, the Father is a beginning in relation to the Son, because he begot him. But whether the Father is also a beginning in relation to the Holy Spirit, since it is said, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ is no small question. For if this is so, he is a beginning not only in relation to the thing which he begets or makes, but also in relation to that which he gives. Here too becomes clear the point that often troubles many: why the Holy Spirit is not also a Son, although he too proceeds from the Father, as is read in the Gospel. For he proceeds not as one born, but as one given; and therefore he is not called Son, because he was neither born as the Only-begotten was, nor made so as to be born through grace as we are. For what is born from the Father is referred to the Father alone when it is called Son, and therefore he is the Son of the Father and not ours; but what is given is referred both to the one who gave it and to those to whom he gave it. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son, who gave him, but also our Holy Spirit, who have received him; just as salvation is called the Lord’s because he gives salvation, while the same salvation is also ours who receive it.”

[Note: [Col. 1123D] “And therefore [he is] the Spirit of the Father and ours.” Following Lindenbruch’s emendation, we restore the negative particle that had been lost: “and not ours.” The Son is called the Son of the Father alone, not also our son, but truly our brother. The Holy Spirit, however, is called not only the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son, by whom he is given, but also our Holy Spirit, to whom he is given.]

The same writer adds shortly afterward:

“For if, then, what is given has as its beginning the one by whom it is given, because it did not receive from elsewhere that which proceeds from him, we must confess that the Father and the Son are the beginning of the Holy Spirit—not two beginnings, but as the Father and the Son are one God; and, relatively to creation, one Creator and one Lord. So, relatively to the Holy Spirit, they are one beginning; and, relatively to creation, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one beginning, just as they are one Creator and one Lord.”

## CHAPTER V. That Tarasius was wrong to call the Holy Spirit a fellow-tribesman of the Father and the Son, when it would have sufficed to call him coeternal, consubstantial, and of the same essence and nature

Tarasius is also said to have declared in his profession of faith that the Holy Spirit is a fellow-tribesman of the Father and the Son [Col. 1123C].

[Note: [Col. 1124D] “A statement utterly absurd both when made and not at all to be torn away from the confession of the Catholic faith.” I emend *vellendum* to *convellendum*, that is, “to be rejected, set aside, eliminated.” Below, chapter 17: “Thus to tear the people of Christ away from the breasts of Mother Church.”]

—a statement both utterly absurd and entirely to be torn away from the confession of the Catholic faith, rejected and repudiated in every way, not only by those who are acquainted with the discipline of literary learning, but also by those who use only ordinary language.

It is readily apparent that just as those who are of one blood are called blood-relations, those who share one lot are called companions, those who are of one age are called contemporaries—also called coevals—and those who have one form are called conformable, so those who belong to one tribe are called fellow-tribesmen. For this preposition in compounds has the force of showing that distinct things are joined together. Thus, when we call two or more people fellow-tribesmen, we clearly show that they belong to one tribe.

A tribe is a multitude of people that either derives its origin from one stock, as the twelve tribes are known to have proceeded from Jacob, or performs one service, as at the beginning of the Roman city the Roman people were divided by the founder of that city into three orders—namely, senators, soldiers, and plebeians. Hence the etymology of this name has survived to the present day, and those who preside over them are called tribunes.

But in God, who is the highest good, the single summit and unique pinnacle of all things, one in substance and three in persons, the name “fellow-tribesman” can in no way be found, since a fellow-tribesman can be found nowhere except where a tribe is also found.

The Holy Spirit is not a fellow-tribesman of the Father and the Son but consubstantial with them. If he is a fellow-tribesman, he is joined to them only by tribal or kinship association—which it is profane to say. If, as it is not only absurd but impious to believe, he is joined to them merely by tribal or kinship association, he is not consubstantial with them. But he is consubstantial with the Father and the Son; therefore he must not be believed or called their fellow-tribesman.

In the confession of so great a mystery, it would have sufficed to reject novelties of expression and to say that the Holy Spirit is coessential, coeternal, coequal with the Father and the Son, and of one power and glory with them, so that among the three persons the unity of substance, power, and glory of the supreme God may be believed and confessed by Catholics—he who is God over all, blessed forever.

Let anyone who thinks this name ought rightly to be used of the holy Trinity, and who wishes to support it with arguments, read the thirteenth book of blessed Hilary and the fifteenth book of most holy Augustine, where they discuss the same holy and ineffable Trinity with the greatest subtlety and thunder forth with strength. When he finds that this name has nowhere been applied to the holy Trinity, let him not presume to apply it to that Trinity, since, if it in any way suited the confession of holy faith, it could not have escaped such extensive forests of discussion. Nor would it have been foreign to men so eloquent and so learned in the skill of Latin expression to use it in debate, if it were free from error.

Let him also read the brief works on faith of the other Catholic Fathers. When he does not find this name mentioned in so sublime and illustrious a matter, let him recognize that he has encountered it elsewhere without need. For if it is found somewhere outside these discussions in a confession of holy faith, it must be attributed either to ineloquence arising from lack of learning or to the idiomatic character of another language, which often loses its force when transferred into another language.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the fact that Basil, bishop of Ancyra, inserted in his profession of faith, after confessing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the kissing and veneration of images and relics, saying that he had faith in sharing sanctification with them, while entirely passing over the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life to come

[Col. 1124D]

The remission of sins, which Basil, bishop of Ancyra, omitted from his confession of faith, must be counted among the greatest gifts of ecclesiastical dignity. The Prophet places it before us with outstanding praise when he calls those blessed to whom it is granted: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm XXXII).

The voice of the Word, the voice of Wisdom, the friend of the Bridegroom, proclaimed this amid the first thunderclaps of the evangelical trumpet, as it is written: “And he came into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins” (Luke III).

The mediator of God and human beings, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, consecrated it by the mercy with which he had come to redeem the world, both forgiving the sins of certain people before his Passion and offering himself to God the Father as a sacrifice in order to wash away the sins of the whole world. And so that the Church might be able to attain it perpetually, he granted her the ineffable gift of the Spirit, the unconquerable sign of his character, and the saving sacrament of holy baptism.

The apostles are said to have placed it in the statement of faith that they established among themselves, as a kind of rule of belief and preaching, when they were about to depart from one another. After confessing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they did not delay to place it there, in the brief statement of that word of which the prophet says, “The Lord will make a brief word upon the earth” (Isaiah X; Romans IX), because they clearly perceived that without it the sincerity of faith could not be complete.

The brevity of the Creed did not restrain them from confessing it, since the integrity of holy faith required it and the sublimity of so great a gift demanded reverence. It is effected through the Holy Spirit, by whom sins are forgiven, or through the blood of Christ, which is received by us in the sacrament and was poured out for us for the remission of sins. It is also effected through the water of baptism, in which the ancient and worn-out wound of original transgression is washed away.

Hence the Apostle says that three bear witness—spirit, blood, and water—and that the three are one (1 John V), because through the Holy Spirit, the blood of Christ, and the water of baptism we arrive at one destination, namely, the remission of sins.

One of the teachers, when explaining brilliantly what the new song is, counted this among the other novelties he said had been completed in Christ’s incarnation, saying:

“New is the Son of God becoming human; new is that the same one is delivered by human beings to death; new is that he rises on the third day; new is that he ascends to heaven with his body; new is that the remission of sins is given to human beings.”

He therefore called the giving of remission of sins to human beings new, because, just as it is given in the New Testament, it was not given in the Old. The page of the Old Instrument does not wash away sins but displays them.

The resurrection of the flesh—which Christians are to believe and confess, whereas the Sadducees do not believe it—which the aforesaid bishop also passed over in his profession of faith is demonstrated in the Old Instrument, when Job, a man more evangelical than legal, says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God; whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (Job XIX).

It is also demonstrated by Daniel, that most holy man and investigator of the secrets of God, who says: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life and others to reproach, that they may see forever” (Daniel XII).

And when Truth itself descended to earth for the salvation of the human race, it was commended in full: he taught it in the holy oracles of his preaching and demonstrated it by the saving example of his resurrection.

If someone says that, in this passage, Job spoke only of his own resurrection and not of the general resurrection of all human beings, let him hear Job affirming the general resurrection of all in another place, saying:

“A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its branches will grow. If its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and produce a crown as when it was first planted. But when a human being has died, stripped bare and consumed, where, I ask, is he? As when waters withdraw from the sea and a river, emptied, dries up, so a human being, when he sleeps, will not rise again until heaven is worn away; he will not awaken or rise from his sleep” (Job XIV).

[Note: [Col. 1125D] “Does a tree have hope of growing green again, while a human being has no hope of rising?” We have restored *revirescendi* (“of growing green again”), so that the comparison may be consistent. This is a meditation full of consolation, strengthening those who trust in a most certain hope; the Fathers customarily compare the springtime, when trees begin to grow green again, with our resurrection of the flesh.]

This whole passage must therefore be understood as follows: “Does a tree have hope of growing green again, while a human being has no hope of rising? Does a human being, when he sleeps, not rise, just as when the waters withdraw from the sea and a river, emptied, dries up? Will he not awaken, nor rise from his sleep, until heaven is worn away?” By these words he demonstrates not merely his own resurrection but the general resurrection of the whole human race.

The apostles also delivered this teaching to all nations when they went out to them—although the nations were diverse, they were imbued with one faith, though with different languages, and were to receive not different institutions. To prevent it from being dissolved by forgetfulness or frustrated through the passing of time by heretical perversity, they placed it in the Creed and located it in that authoritative statement of faith in which the integrity of the whole faith is embraced with admirable brevity.

One of them, who subdued the savage hearts of the nations through the teaching of his sacred writing, foretold that it would occur “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye,” among the other things he proclaimed concerning it (1 Corinthians XV).

The life of the age to come, which the same Basil is clearly judged to have negligently passed over, is promised to us by the Lord himself and proclaimed in nearly all the oracles of the holy Scriptures. Without it the resurrection of the flesh is of no value, and the whole aim of our religion labors to attain it.

From this it may be understood that he was not moderately deranged when, in his profession of faith, he silently passed over matters filled with such great mysteries—indeed, truly filled with mysteries, without which Christian belief cannot stand—and in their place put forward matters that were unnecessary and worthy of laughter.

He is therefore not censured merely because he delayed to profess these things, provided that he believed them in his heart, since matters are often omitted in speech either for the sake of brevity or on some particular occasion even though they are firmly held in belief. Rather, he is censured because he inserted in their place something that he read had been inserted by none of the holy Fathers in a profession of faith.

A soldier who once fought, or who is going to fight, is not reproached merely because he does not fight for a time; he is reproached if, having slipped into flight, he disgraces his nobility and weakens the strength of his comrades by his useless example.

For after the aforesaid bishop had confessed the veneration and kissing of images among the first foundations of his faith, he said: “that he had faith in sharing sanctification with them.”

Nor was he undeserving of sharing inanimate things, which lack not only sanctification but also life, since after confessing the holy and unique Trinity he said that he had faith in such songs of mourning, while negligently passing over those matters that must be counted among the first gifts of the Christian religion—namely, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life of the age to come.

Finally, suppose that venerating images is something useful. What is taken away from the Christian religion if, among the first professions of faith, a profession of that matter too is not made? There are many things handed down to the faithful among the other traditions of ecclesiastical institution; even if their profession is omitted from the confession of faith, nothing is thereby taken away from holy religion.

Or how does it prejudice the integrity of faith if the veneration of images is omitted, when it is believed to have been prohibited by the holy Fathers rather than instituted by them? The omission of the veneration of images—which was prohibited rather than instituted—does not prejudice the purity of holy faith in the way that the omission of the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life of the age to come prejudices it. These are proclaimed throughout the entire sequence of the holy Scriptures and, as we stated above, are held together by the apostles in the Creed with admirable brevity.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the fact that Theodosius, bishop of Amorium, negligently passed over the faith of the holy and unique Trinity, but spoke incautiously and unusually about images: “I confess, promise, accept, kiss, and venerate images”; and shortly afterward: “Whoever does not diligently instruct all the people beloved by Christ to adore and venerate the holy and honorable images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, let him be anathema.”

We rightly showed in the preceding chapter that Basil, bishop of Ancyra, deserved censure because, having cast the foundation of his faith, he neglected to build upon it the truly necessary things in so excellent a mystery, and instead tried to build in their place [Col. 1127D] things that must be utterly rejected from every structure of religion. In the present case, however, we judge that Theodosius, bishop of Amorium, deserves to be censured more justly and appropriately: he laid no foundation of his faith at all in the aforementioned synod, but began senselessly and irrationally to construct only empty things, excluded from reason. For in Basil’s building, if what rose up meaninglessly were demolished, at least what had been well founded would remain; but in this man’s, if everything empty and frivolous were removed, nothing would remain. If, then, Basil is rightly rebuked for inserting the worship of images into the confession of the holy and only Trinity, this man deserves rebuke far more rightly, because, setting aside the confession of that sublime and ineffable mystery, he dreamed only of some frivolous matter concerning the worship of images [Col. 1128A].

For he began as follows:

> “I confess and promise, and I receive, and I kiss, and I adore the images.”

O remarkable confession of a bishop! O beautiful utterance of a priest! O praiseworthy devotion of a prelate! He is silent about the confession of the most exalted majesty and resounds with a confession of the most outrageous vanity. He withdraws his foot from the confession of the one who said, “Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X; Luke XII), and thrusts himself with all his steps into the confession of images. He is silent about what he ought both to confess himself and to urge others to confess, and he has confessed what he ought neither to confess nor to strive to make others confess it. Though he ought to set up a wall for the house of Israel and stand in battle on the day of the Lord, he himself, alas, [Col. 1128B] voluntarily slips away toward the disgrace of surrender. For the one who ought, through the zeal of preaching, to restrain other minds from perverse confession and ridiculous error himself first becomes for them a road to error, through the example of a perverse confession.

As for his anathematizing all who do not instruct the whole people beloved by Christ to adore and venerate the images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of time, let the prudent reader observe how absurdly and how recklessly he acts—especially since the anathema that he rashly presumes to impose upon others he irreverently turns against himself and his own people, and the weapon with which he attempts to pierce a party outside his own error he deflects toward his own destruction and that of his fellow citizens. The worship of images does not free his own people from the bond of the anathema that he attempted to fasten only upon outsiders.

For he anathematizes [Col. 1128C] those who do not instruct the whole people beloved by Christ to adore images. But, to say nothing of others, do all those among the people entrusted to them instruct the whole people beloved by Christ to adore images, when they have neither the office of instructing nor the rank of preaching? Does he himself instruct the whole people beloved by Christ? For nearly the entire world is filled with the people of Christ, since God has ceased to be known only in Judea: “the sound” of the apostles “has gone out into all the earth,” and all the earth has been filled with the glory of the Lord. All nations come and worship in the sight of the Lord, according to the prophecy of Malachi, who speaks in the word of the Lord:

> “From the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every [Col. 1128D] place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to me” (Mal. II).

And the shepherd of the Church, to whom the whole world, shown in the figure of a vessel filled with various kinds of animals, is revealed as filled with different nations that must be called to the grace of God, says:

> “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

For if, according to his ravings, all who do not instruct the whole people beloved by Christ are worthy of anathema, neither he himself, nor his fellow bishops who are said to have been present at the same synod, nor the peoples subject to them will be able to escape the bond of the anathema. For even if they instruct the peoples of two or three provinces, or certainly of many, they do not instruct the whole people beloved by Christ, since the Catholic Church—which is indeed the people beloved by Christ—is spread throughout the world’s very extensive and vast regions and, by the Lord’s favor, has been extended even among inaccessible and unknown nations.

[Col. 1129A] Either, therefore, he will demonstrate that he instructs the whole Church of Christ—from east to west and from north to south—together with his own people, in the worship of images, or, according to the judgment of his own vanity, he will be subject to anathema along with his associates and subjects. For even if they could instruct the whole people, they could not possess images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of time, so that they might instruct the entire people in their worship. Their multitude is so great that the Prophet, speaking in the person of the Son to the Father, says of them [Col. 1129B]:

> “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominion has been greatly strengthened. I shall number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXIX).

Even if this was spoken hyperbolically, the hosts of those who pleased God from the beginning are so numerous that no one could paint or number them except the one in whose book their names are written. If that bishop wishes to avoid the loss threatened by the anathema he himself pronounced, he must possess and adore images of all the saints who, throughout the various regions of the world, pleased God from the beginning. And if he cannot possess them because of their multitude—indeed, because he cannot—then let him submit his neck to the anathema he himself pronounced.

## CHAPTER VIII. That almost everyone’s faith is thrown into doubt, since some confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, while others confessed that he proceeds neither from the Father nor from the Son

[Col. 1129C] That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son has been shown above, insofar as concerns the brevity of the style to which, with the Lord’s approval, we devote ourselves. Since nearly everyone in the aforementioned synod either completely kept silent about this or expressed himself ambiguously, we, as human beings subject to human weakness in our thoughts and ignorant of things we have neither heard nor read, neither bear witness to the faith of those who passed over this matter in silence, nor to that of those who expressed themselves ambiguously. Nor do we therefore reject their belief because they kept silent about this or expressed themselves ambiguously. We do not know how they hold the matter.

Yet, lest by our silence [Col. 1129D] we appear to assent to passing over this question without examination, and because it is not plainly evident what they intend, we fear to condemn it and reserve it for the judgment of him whom hidden things do not deceive. We know, in the end, that those are not far from error who, if they are distant from it because they think rightly about this matter, nevertheless draw near to it because they have failed rightly to confess what they think rightly. For what is rightly believed in the heart for justification ought rightly to be confessed with the mouth for salvation.

## CHAPTER IX. That if some error has perhaps remained unexamined in the statements concerning the faith issued by the aforementioned bishops, it will have remained so because of the difficulty and monstrosity of their language, which is often so covered with ignorance that it is not at all clear what it wishes to signify or what meaning should be understood in it

Although there are many kinds of expression, which grammarians and rhetoricians have taught in abundance and variety, the sequence of all speeches or utterances is nevertheless divided according to a fourfold classification. [Col. 1130A] Every speech is either wise and eloquent, wise and not eloquent, eloquent and not wise, or neither wise nor eloquent.

A speech is wise and eloquent, like very many books of Holy Scripture; and, to say nothing of the others, such is the book of the prophet Isaiah. Its speech is wise, since the Holy Spirit dictated it, and eloquent, since it was delivered by an illustrious and cultivated man.

A speech is wise but not eloquent, as some are found even in Holy Scripture: wise, that is, in the sublimity of their meanings, proclaimed through the nectar of the divine breath, but ineloquent either because of the simplicity of the holy men by whom they were delivered, who preferred to employ the beauty of meaning rather than the elegance of words, or because of the speech customary among the native peoples among whom holy men, bearers of the divine word, are known to have been born or to have lived. Thus Jerome says of blessed Jeremiah that the simplicity of his speech came to him from Anathoth, the place where he was born.

[Col. 1130B] A speech is eloquent but not wise, as are the writings of the pagans. Although such writing is attractive through its learning in the human arts, it is nevertheless foolish because it lacks both knowledge of the true God and saving exhortation. The speech of certain heretics is also eloquent but not wise: although polished by the industry of human minds, it is entirely stripped of the truth of wisdom and the instruction of the virtues.

Of the eloquent but not wise, the prophet Isaiah says [Col. 1130C]:

> “You will not see the insolent people, the people of profound speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of their tongue, in which there is no wisdom” (Isa. XXXIII).

A speech is neither eloquent nor wise, like that of many who rashly undertake to teach whatever they please before they have been nourished by the banquets of the most sacred meanings and instructed in the ornaments of eloquence. Such also is the writing of this synod, whose errors we are attempting to examine: in its statements there is no adornment of meaning, nor is any little stream drawn from the river of eloquence.

Every writing is either cultivated and clear, cultivated and unclear, uncultivated and clear, or neither cultivated nor clear. This writing is foreign to the first two categories and entirely bound up with the latter two, because it is raised neither by cultivated language nor by the high style of eloquence, nor woven together with the clarity of pure expression—which in another kind of writing advances understanding through its purity.

It is not cultivated and unclear, because it is not wrapped in long periods, adorned with the various intricacies of topics, or chained by the slippery conclusions that deliberately arise from dialectical art. All these things are cultivated, since they are polished by the sophist’s roller; and they are unclear because, being far removed from the understanding of simple readers, they present themselves only to the minds of the highly learned [Col. 1130D].

A writing is either clear, when, lacking learned ornament, it is open to all readers and hearers; or it is arranged without order or grace, mutilated by solecisms, corrupted by barbarisms, covered over by the other clouds of faults, lacking lucid expression, and stripped of the order by which meanings are woven together. Such a writing is neither cultivated nor clear.

[Col. 1131A] Therefore, if some error has perhaps remained unexamined in the statements issued concerning the faith, it will defend itself against us with these weapons, because it has hidden itself in such wrappings of disordered language. It could not be detected by us for that reason, since it came before us clothed in the difficulty of its language as though in a kind of cloak.

## CHAPTER X. That the saying in the statement of faith of Theodore the bishop—“God is wonderful in his saints”—was expressed ridiculously and childishly, followed immediately by “He has made all my desires wonderful among his saints who are on the earth,” as though this verse followed the preceding one

The fact that Theodore the bishop [Col. 1131B] joined these two verses of the Psalmist into one by inserting the adverb “immediately,” as though one followed the other without any interval or intervening verses, deserves our criticism not because it causes some prejudice to the faith, but because it exposes him to ridicule and supplies those who criticize him with material for mockery.

The verse that he says immediately follows the first not only does not follow it at once, but is known to precede it by almost fifty psalms, to which it is later appended. This shows that such writing is not fit to instruct in great matters without error when it stumbles in small matters without force. Nor can it possess the power to affirm doubtful things and teach unknown things when it lacks the ability to relate things that are not doubtful and to present things that are known.

[Col. 1131C] How, then, can the teaching of that synod be received when its writing is censured in so many places? Or how can it attain a place of honor alongside the other synodal writings composed or received by the holy Fathers, when it avoids fellowship with their meanings and words? Those writings are censured in no respect and are therefore received in every respect; but this one, because it is censured in many respects, is not undeservedly rejected in almost every respect.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Greeks attempted uselessly and recklessly to anathematize the Catholic Church in their synod because it does not adore images, although they ought first to have investigated carefully what the Church in each region wished to believe concerning this matter

[Col. 1131D] The preaching of the ecclesiastical trumpet resounds that a sinful brother must first be rebuked privately. If he refuses to listen, he must be admonished separately in the presence of brothers, either in the hope of correction or so that they may serve as witnesses. If he scorns even them, the matter must then be made known to many, so that they may hold him in abhorrence, and so that the one who could not be saved by shame may at least be saved by reproach. If he does not yield even to the admonition of many, he must be shunned in the manner of a pagan or a publican.

The Church of those men appears to oppose this preaching in no small degree, since, before addressing the Churches throughout the world in the ecclesiastical manner by consulting and investigating through letters, it presumptuously—or rather recklessly—attempts to anathematize them.

[Col. 1132A] It ought to have sent an embassy of inquiry to the Churches of the neighboring provinces, asking whether images ought to be adored or not adored. Then, according to the saying of a certain wise man, by acting on the basis of counsel and following what should be followed while avoiding what should be avoided, it would not later have had cause for regret. Whatever the greater number of Churches wished to hold, in accordance with apostolic teaching, it too should have held; and if it attempted to resist ancient institutions supported by the agreement of many and wished, in obstinate spirit, to sever itself from the universality of the ecclesiastical body, it should have been condemned to detestation.

For what madness, what insanity is it for the Church of one region, attempting to establish a matter that was decreed neither by the apostles nor by their successors, to try to anathematize the Churches of the entire world, forcing them either to oppose apostolic institutions or to be subject to the utterly vain anathema pronounced by those men?

[Col. 1132B] But since their utterly insane anathema brings harm upon them rather than upon us, as the Apostle says, “Nor will the slanderers inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI), even if it could somehow injure us, it would be more tolerable for us to endure it than to resist the admonitions of the apostles or of the other holy Fathers. With Susanna we say:

> “It is better to fall into the hands of men than to abandon the law of our God” (Dan. XIII).

And we are fully taught by the words of the shepherd of the Church that it is necessary to obey God rather than men (Acts V).

For just as it is more tolerable for any citizen, or for anyone enjoying the fellowship of a ruler, to endure insults inflicted by certain seditious men who act against the ruler and the citizens than to conspire with them in sedition, so it is certainly more tolerable for us to be cursed by those who do not fear even to curse their own parents than to adore with them senseless things contrary to the institutions of Holy Scripture.

For an execration without reason, anger without power, and condemnation without authority harm those against whom they are directed not at all, but afflict their authors with all the greater vexation and reveal them to be more sluggish and impatient [Col. 1132C]. Unless the ancient destruction and the age-old plague—the leader of death and root of evils, which expelled both the angels from the fellowship of the heavenly citizens and human beings from the dignity of the flower-bearing seat—had inflamed them with the goads of its wickedness, they would neither have cared to call a synod assembled for the worship of images universal without the agreement of many Catholic and God-fearing Churches, nor dared so insolently to anathematize so many great Churches, which are indeed the body of Christ, nor attempted to establish the worship and adoration of senseless things contrary to the institution of the divine words.

For the Apostle says [Col. 1132D]:

> “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’” (1 Cor. XII).

Therefore care must be taken lest, while they thoughtlessly and recklessly attempt to anathematize the Church, which is the body of Christ, they seem to inflict an injury upon him who is its head.

Christ therefore joined the Church to himself with such great love that he remains inseparably superior to it, as the head to the body, while it remains forever joined to him, as the body to the head. Thus no injury or honor can be shown to the body that is not referred to the head.

For Christ referred the persecution inflicted by the Jews upon the Church to himself when he said to the ravenous wolf Saul—not yet Paul—who in the morning was devouring prey in the devastation of the Church and in the evening was about to divide the spoils through salutary preaching and the sending of letters:

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

[Col. 1133A] He did not mean that Saul was persecuting Christ, who reigns in the heavenly citadels, but the Church, which was already springing up and floating amid the terrifying waves of this age.

Christ therefore continues even now to suffer persecution in his body, which is the Church—not bodily, as he once did for the salvation of the world, but through a certain pious compassion by which he continually has mercy upon the members who belong to him, that is, the faithful who remain in the unity of the holy Church. One of these was the man who said:

> “I rejoice in my sufferings, because I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Col. I).

[Col. 1133B] David prefigured this suffering, which Christ endures in his saints, when he said:

> “I will still play, and I will appear more contemptible” (2 Sam. VI).

For when Christ humbled himself even unto death and reached the mystery of the cross, and was despised by the synagogue, which from that time remained barren, he showed in the bloody sweat that the sufferings of his members were to come. He also testified that the honor shown to the Church was honor shown to himself when he said:

> “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. X).

And:

> “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV).

If, therefore, those about whom we are speaking had embraced humility, the guardian of virtues and teacher of good things, they would neither have attempted with such shamelessness to anathematize the body of Christ, which is the Church, nor have assembled a synod for so useless and unserviceable a matter out of a desire for their own—or rather, vain—glory.

## CHAPTER XII. That for the most part they cast aside gentleness and patience by failing to restrain their mouths and by speaking disorderly words

[Col. 1133C]

Once the synod had been assembled, if they had acted in it according to ecclesiastical custom, treating matters that were necessary and beneficial to the faithful, they would have avoided every novelty of speech and every disorderly babbling of words. Holding to the path of moderation, they would have disagreed neither with apostolic teachings nor with the institutions of the ancient synods. Adorned with the beauties of patience and gentleness, they would never have contradicted the prophetic saying by calling good evil and evil good, by making bitter sweet and sweet bitter.

They would have prudently established what had necessarily to be established, carefully said what had to be said, and, rejecting the superfluous and extraordinary anathema, would have taught useful matters while condemning ambiguous or certainly useless matters to silence. Then the Churches of our region and of the other regions of the world would have obeyed their decrees.

[Col. 1133D] But since it is impossible both to assent to their decrees and to obey the ancient institutions of the Fathers, because the two are mutually opposed—and because their institutions differ from those of the holy Fathers as light differs from darkness, life from death, sight from blindness, uprightness from wickedness, purity from impurity, and health from sickness—we reject the worse and are content with the better. We disdain deceptive byways and desire to keep to the certain and royal path.

[Col. 1134A] Where, I ask, is that outstanding virtue, gentleness? And you, most powerful patience, hostile to furies and to every slight provocation—where have you gone? Where had you withdrawn when you saw so many priests carrying out such reckless and perverse decrees, when you perceived them imposing so many bonds of anathema upon the Churches?

Why did you not at least find lodging among two or three of them? Why did you reject them all? Why did you present your absence to everyone? Why did you not restrain them with the reins of your moderation from so many trifles? Why did you not curb them with the reins of your diligence from so many ravings?

For, with vainglory or the desire for empty praise goading them on and driving its servant—namely, lack of restraint of the mouth—to fight against us, and since our ranks rightly reject all these things along with the other fuel of evils, we withdrew from them and finally could not lodge among them, because we discovered that they had been seized by the tumult of such errors.

[Col. 1134B] For light has no fellowship with darkness, nor does Christ have any communion with Belial, since, according to the judgment of a certain wise man, the Spirit of God—who is certainly the commander of our army—will flee from deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins.

He who practices pride dwelt neither in our midst nor we in his. For, according to the words of Jesus son of Sirach:

> “Pride is hateful before God and men, and there is no health for the assembly of the proud; the shrub of sin will take root in them” (Ecclus. XIII).

In their synod, therefore, lack of restraint of the mouth, the disciple of pride, flourished to the extent that modesty or prudence ought to have flourished. What ought not even to have had the least role in such an action, alas, held the chief place; and what ought to have held the chief place did not even have the least role in their assembly.

[Col. 1134C] It was at your prompting, then, O lack of restraint of the mouth, that you who prevent human steps from being directed upon the earth of the living acted. The Prophet says:

> “The man of many words shall not be directed upon the earth” (Ps. CXXXIX).

And of you, from whom the sin of one’s years is not absent, it is said:

> “You will not escape sin through much speaking, but if you spare your lips, you will be wise” (Prov. X).

Through you the soul is wounded, according to the saying of the wise man:

> “Whoever uses many words wounds his soul” (Ecclus. XX).

You compel people not only to answer before they hear, but even to anathematize the holy Church before it addresses your followers, according to the saying:

> “Whoever answers before he hears—it is folly and disgrace for him” (Prov. XVIII).

[Col. 1134D] Under your pressure they so utterly rejected our fellowship that our association could not leave even the slightest trace in their minds. To follow us is the adornment of life; to reject us is the error of madness. And, according to the voice of our teacher Wisdom:

> “Our departures are departures of life” (Ecclus. XXIV).

For if the lawgiver had not followed our admonitions and kept the steps of his mind bound by the restraints of our moderation, Scripture would not say:

> “Now Moses was the gentlest of all the men who were upon the earth.”

Nor would he have enjoyed divine conversations so many times, nor been instructed, at the Lord’s revelation, in so many hidden mysteries. Nor would the Lord of all things have said of him:

> “Not so with my servant Moses, to whom I speak face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Num. XII).

[Col. 1135A] The virtue of patience and gentleness is therefore said to have been utterly cast aside by those who wickedly and extraordinarily attempted to assemble a synod for the anathematizing of the Catholic Church, and who, with insane boldness, tried to curse her who has been blessed with perpetual blessing. We, however, must approach and retain her forever in every way with the arm of faith, the hand of love, and the embrace of the heart.

For the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord is sweet and gentle; therefore he establishes a law for those who offend on the way. He guides the gentle in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways” (Ps. XXIV).

From this it is understood that whoever desires to follow the gentle Lord must not despise gentleness; rather, in order to be taught the ways of the Lord, he ought to embrace it.

[Col. 1135B] It is likewise written in Proverbs:

> “A gentle man is a physician of the heart, but a discerning heart is a moth to the bones” (Prov. XVI).

And there:

> “The gentle man with humility is better than one who divides the spoils with the insolent.”

It is also read in Ecclesiasticus:

> “Son, accomplish your works in gentleness, and you will be loved by every person” (Ecclus. XIII).

And again, in the same book:

> “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand, and speak with wisdom a true answer” (Ecclus. V).

Jesus son of Sirach, the appointed teacher, likewise thunders:

> “Son, preserve your soul in gentleness, and give it honor according to its dignity” (Ecclus. X).

[Col. 1135C] The teacher of the nations writes to the Ephesians:

> “I beseech you, I who am bound in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV).

And the apostle James says:

> “Let whoever among you is wise and understanding show by his good conduct his works in gentleness and prudence” (Jas. III).

Those who, because of the worship of images, dared to impose an anathema upon the Church certainly resisted all these commandments. The Church is entirely free from their unjust curse, just as she is continually softened by the anointing of joy from Christ, who redeemed her—an anointing that is unfading and eternal.

Concerning prudence, patience, and restraint of the mouth, it is also written:

> “Whoever refrains from uttering a harsh word benefits himself; a patient man is a wise man.”

[Col. 1135D] What word can be harsher than an anathema? If they had taken care to refrain from uttering it recklessly, they would not have strayed far from the way.

Or what patience or prudence could have been more useful to them in this matter than to consult, through their writings, the Church established throughout the various regions of the world, and to prudently and patiently enact what the consent of all had decided?

For it is said through a certain wise man:

> “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. IV).

In this saying, while the eyelids metonymically signify foreseeing counsel and the steps signify the actions themselves, he clearly suggests to us that prudent and wise deliberations should always precede the exercise of our actions, so that the eye of the mind may first foresee the matters in which action will afterward extend itself.

[Col. 1136A] Concerning the excessive speaking in which they indulged in their synod, the Psalmist sings that he restrained himself with these words:

> “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue’; I placed a guard over my mouth” (Ps. XXXIX).

And, so that he might rightly be able to restrain himself, he strives to implore the Lord with these prayers:

> “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a door of protection around my lips, so that you may not incline my heart toward words of wickedness” (Ps. CXLI).

If, therefore, we were to enumerate all that was accomplished through patience and gentleness by the holy Fathers, whether in the Old Testament or in the New, and, on the other hand, were to undertake to relate what was perpetrated through pride or lack of restraint of the mouth by various wicked people, the text of not merely one chapter, but not even one book, could contain all the testimonies by which this vice is condemned.

[Col. 1136B] Now, however, having shown in part what they did and what they ought to have done, and having discussed in part their trifles, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to other matters necessary to this work.

## CHAPTER XIII. That a woman ought not to teach in a synod, as Haerena is said to have done in their synod
Since in nearly every respect that synod which was assembled for the worship of images contradicts the salutary ordinances of the divine Scriptures, in this matter too it appears to contradict them quite seriously, since it is reported to have had a woman as its instructress or teacher. This is prohibited not only by the teachings of divine law but also by the law of nature itself. For the weakness of her sex and the fickleness of her mind do not permit her to hold the rank of teacher or ruler over men; rather, as a weaker vessel, more easily subject to deception and restrained by masculine authority, she is compelled to remain subordinate. Hence divine laws have decreed that certain vows of women may be annulled by a man’s decision, and human laws have established that unmarried women, even when advanced in age, must remain under guardianship because of this very instability of mind.

For we know that a woman is ordinarily granted to a man for the sake of offspring, for the sake of assistance, and for the sake of avoiding incontinence; but we have nowhere at all read that she is granted for the sake of teaching. For the sake of offspring, as it is written in Genesis: “And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply” (Gen. I). This is marriage, which must be considered neither a sin, according to Pelagius, nor equal to virginity, according to Jovinian; rather, virginity is to be preferred to it because of the holiness of purity and the integrity of the body, as the Apostle says: “The married woman considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband; but the virgin considers the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII).

Nevertheless, although that other state is inferior to virginity, it must not be rejected or altogether disregarded, but sought with gratitude by those to whom it belongs, since it is not something extraordinary in relation to itself and is second in relation to virginity. For it is the seedbed of virginity: just as a grape comes from nowhere other than the vine, so virginity is generated from nowhere other than marriage. And although virginity is the hundredfold fruit, it nevertheless has beneath it the thirtyfold fruit, that is, marriage; between them stands the sixtyfold fruit, which is appropriately understood of widows. [Col. 1137A]

For the sake of assistance, therefore, the woman was granted to the man, as the Lord says: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself” (Gen. II). For the sake of avoiding incontinence, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Let the one who is incontinent marry”; and again: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. VII).

Let us therefore question the Apostle. Let the distinguished preacher speak; let the chosen vessel speak: does he permit women to teach, or to exercise authority over men? For he says to Timothy: “Let a woman learn in silence with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to remain in silence” (1 Tim. II). And as though he were asked why he had forbidden her both to teach and to exercise authority over a man, he says: “Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression.” Thus we may understand that the Apostle did not grant her the dignity either of teaching or of ruling over a man because she is said to have been created not to teach the man but to assist him, nor to preside over him but to be subject to him, or because she is weaker in mind and more easily exposed to temptation. For, as the Apostle says, “man was not created for woman, but woman for man” (1 Cor. XI).

If someone should perhaps try to defend the presumption of so great an error by this argument—that the same Apostle, when speaking about the conduct and continence of older women, says “teaching what is good” (1 Tim. V)—let him consider that he permitted them to teach not some madness, nor some tradition resisting the sacred institutions of the Fathers, nor certainly the worship of some senseless thing, but prudence and examples of upright living. Nor did he permit them to do this in church, or in an assembly, or in a synod, but privately, on the basis of the experience of advanced age and after the incentives to vice had been expelled through maturity of years. Nor did he permit all women to do it, but only those who had a testimony of good works: those who receive strangers, wash the feet of the saints, minister to those suffering tribulation, and have followed every good work—women whose walk, movements, expression, speech, and silence all display a certain dignity of sacred continence. [Col. 1137C]

For it is one thing for a housewife to instruct her household through words and examples; it is another for her to take part in teaching something useless to bishops, to the entire ecclesiastical order, or even to a public synod, when the former seeks to attain the improvement both of her household and of herself in common, whereas the latter seeks in an assembly only the empty praise and the mere ambition of arrogance.

Just as Christ is the head of man, so surely man is the head of woman. Therefore, if a woman is to preside over men, she is already their head; and if she is their head, they will necessarily be the head of Christ. But no one can be the head of Christ except the Father, according to the Apostle, who says, “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. XI), and of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold” (Song V). A woman therefore must not make herself the head of men by placing herself above them, lest, while the inferior sex raises itself beyond what its order requires and prefers itself to the superior sex, the head—which ought to preside over the other members—seek the lowest place, and the feet—which hold the lowest places among the preeminent members—be raised above the others to the higher places. Thus the order of nature would be disfigured by laws that had been altered, or rather perverted.

For if someone, attempting to oppose these most sacred apostolic institutions, should try to assert that women ought to teach men, preside over men, and establish synods, on the grounds that, according to the proclamation of the evangelical trumpet, women frequently ministered to the Mediator of God and human beings—sitting at his feet, hearing the word from his mouth, diligently attending to his frequent ministry, bathing his feet with their tears, wiping them with their hair, anointing his body with the marvelous fluid of perfumes, and not delaying to follow him as he went to his passion; and that after his resurrection they returned to his tomb and were the first to learn the glorious mystery of his most sacred resurrection and announce it to the disciples—let him observe that it is one thing to sit at the Lord’s feet and do the other things mentioned above, and another to establish synods, teach men in assemblies, hand down perverse constitutions, and desire to be placed above men.

For those women, bearing the type of the holy Church, ministered to the Lord and clung to his most sacred conversations. But these women, if there are any such, follow the example of Athaliah, who, while she sought with an improper desire to rule over men, nearly destroyed the entire royal seed and ultimately ended her most impious life by a worthy death, through the destruction of her wicked head.

A woman is therefore regarded as the announcer of the resurrection of our Lord and Savior for this reason: because, since a woman had been his pathway from heaven to earth when he came, she should also be his messenger from earth to heaven when he returned; and the virgin Mary, who gave birth to him as he came into the world, should be the Mary healed by the Lord who announced him to the disciples as he departed.

The Mediator of God and human beings is not said to have been born from a woman in order to prefer the female sex to men, but in order to redeem both sexes, which had fallen into sin, through the mystery of his incarnation: man, because he deigned to become a man for our salvation, according to the prophetic saying, “Behold, a man will come; Rising is his name” (Zech. VI), of whom it is written, “Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God through mighty works and wonders, which God did through him” (Acts II); and woman, because he deigned to be born from a woman without any contamination from the male sex. Thus, as he is the true creator of both sexes, so he remains their true restorer.

## CHAPTER XIV. Against those who say, “As God’s fellow workers, we directed that you be assembled,” or, “God assembled you, wishing to establish his own counsel.”

In the first book of this work, in the first part of the book, when the error of those who say that God reigns together with them was being discussed, some argument was offered by which this error too—by which they boast arrogantly that they are God’s fellow workers—can be refuted. For they rave that God reigns together with them and that they are God’s fellow workers, not humbly, not content with the examples of holy kings, and not instructed by the teachings of the sacred Scriptures, but perversely and raised up by the pride of arrogance. And while they seek to usurp for themselves what does not belong to them, it is to be feared that they may lose what does belong to them, because whoever covets what is unlawful is accustomed to lose what has been acquired.

But since, as we have said above, this error was partly discussed earlier, let us now turn our argument to the claim for which they say that those known to have been assembled in that synod were gathered: namely, that through them the Lord might establish his own counsel.

For they say, “God assembled you, wishing to establish his own counsel,” as though it were not written, “He who lives forever created all things together,” and as though some new will that had not previously arisen were now arising in God. Concerning this it is written through the prophet: “He established them forever and for ages of ages; he set forth a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. CXLVIII). Or it is as though God, needing the assistance of someone, gathers others for the purpose of determining through the deliberation of many what he ought to do.

“Counsel” (*consilium*) is derived from “consulting,” by which something is decided through continual consideration, whether it is to be done or not done. There is a type of case that orators call deliberative, in which it is discussed, concerning whatever matters of life, what ought or ought not to be done. In this type there are persuasion and dissuasion—that is, discussion of what is to be sought and avoided, done and not done. In persuasion, moreover, two things are especially powerful: hope and fear.

Since God is therefore omnipotent, he needs no one. Consequently, he is not moved by another’s persuasion to carry out what he does not will, nor is he turned away by anyone’s dissuasion from what he wills to do; nor is he urged by some fear to do things that he wills to do; nor does he establish the deliberation of his counsel with another. If he needed any of these things, he would suffer necessity and would not be omnipotent. But he is omnipotent; therefore he has no need. Hence it is rash to say, “God assembled you, wishing to establish his own counsel.”

For the Counsel of God is the Son, who was not established by the Father through some deliberation, but was begotten before the ages by an ineffable birth. Believers hold that the Father begot him and that he never existed without him. He is the wisdom of God the Father, coeternal with him, and he says: “Before the hills I was brought forth; while he had not yet made the earth, when he was preparing the heavens, I was present with him; while he enclosed the sea with its boundary and set a law for the waters, I was with him” (Prov. VIII). [Col. 1139D]

He also displays his exalted nature in these words: “I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. XXIV); and again: “Alone I encircled the circuit of heaven, and I walked upon the waves of the sea; among every nation and every people I held primacy”; and again: “I spread my branches like a terebinth. I caused the morning star to rise in heaven. I love all who love me. For my issues are issues of life.”

The Psalmist spoke of this Counsel: “The counsel of the Lord remains forever, the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation” (Ps. XXXV). He is called “Counsel” because the mystery of his incarnation was granted for the salvation of the human race. This counsel is dissolved by no age but remains forever, because the Lord’s triumphant death eternally destroyed the diabolical ruin.

The thoughts of his heart indicate the predestination of his inward judgment, in which are stored all things that have existed or that will come to pass in succeeding ages. Human counsels are often frustrated; the Lord’s counsel, however, remains forever. Mortal man understands perishable things, but the eternal Lord never establishes anything worthy of blame.

Therefore, this counsel which they say the Lord established through them is not believed to have been established by the Lord, because it is known to contradict the Lord’s commandments. For both in the pages of the Old Testament and in those of the New, God established that he alone should be worshiped or honored, whereas they, with the most absurd deliberation, decide that certain senseless things ought to be worshiped or honored.

God is not changeable, so that he might now permit what he had previously forbidden. Rather, what he established before the ages in his counsel—that is, in the Son—he permits to remain always stable, as Isaiah testifies, speaking in the person of God the Father: “All my counsel shall stand, and I shall accomplish everything that I have thought” (Isa. XLVI). This counsel, that is, the Son, is also called a testament; hence Jeremiah says: “If my testament were not in custody day and night, I would not have established the ordinances of heaven and earth.” Of this testament it is said: “And it shall be a testament of peace in Jerusalem.”

How, then, would God gather them, as they dream, in order to establish his own counsel through them—he in whom there is such knowledge that neither some things of the past nor some things of the future exist for him, but all things are present? No opinion can reach his substance as it is; no definition can encompass it, because he is more than anything that can be said or conceived.

He is a simple spiritual nature, inaccessible light, invisible, inestimable, infinite, perfect, needing nothing, eternal, immortal; all things live to him, and from him all things have received their beginning. He is to be revered, loved, and feared. Outside him nothing exists; indeed, in him are all things that exist, whether above or below, highest or lowest. He is omnipotent, holding all things, truly rich in all things, because there is no place where he is not and no place is absent from him—except the hearts of the impious, where, although he is present by his power, he is not present by grace.

That he is everywhere is demonstrated by these testimonies of divine law. The Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the light and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

In Isaiah too it is written: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the earth is full of the glory of your majesty” (Isa. VI). Through Jeremiah also he says: “I am God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar. If a man is hidden in secret places, I shall see him. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jer. XXIII).

The Book of Wisdom also says: “For the holy spirit of wisdom, and he did not free the accursed from his lips, because God is witness of his inward parts and a true examiner of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue, because the spirit of the Lord fills the world” (Wis. I).

In Ecclesiasticus too it is written: “For God is great in wisdom and strong in power, seeing all without interruption. In his goodness he created the one who did not exist; in his justice he condemned the one who had sinned; in his mercy, indeed in great mercy, he restored the one who had perished” (Ecclus. XVII).

Of him it is said through the Prophet: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills; confession and magnificence are his work, and his justice remains forever” (Ps. CV). And again: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXV); and to him the same Prophet says: “And you, Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and rich in mercy and truthful” (Ps. LXXXVI).

Is it appropriate to believe that he whom the dominions worship, whom the powers tremble before, whom the rejoicing host of angels praises with heavenly hymns, whom the cherubim and seraphim—lofty powers filled with knowledge of him and burning with love for him—cannot comprehend in their understanding, whom no one knows except the Son, who is of one substance with him, should need another’s counsel? And for that reason should call others together in order to establish his counsel through them?

O most foolish statement! O senseless speech! O words opposed to all divine words! If those to whom they were spoken defend them, they approach madness; if they do not defend them, they must be attributed to ignorance and cowardice.

One can cling to God by persisting in good works, as the one who said, “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. CXLVII), desired. But no one can give him counsel, for he is the author and source of every good and, as we have often said, needs no one. “Great,” says the Prophet, “is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.”

Tell us, holy Isaiah; tell us, most noble of prophets; tell us, evangelical rather than merely prophetic narrator of the Lord’s incarnation and the calling of the nations: can anyone know the mind of the Lord, or become his counselor? “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him in knowledge and showed him the way of understanding?” (Isa. XL).

The same prophet also says: “Do you not know, or have you not heard? The eternal God, the Lord, who created the ends of the earth, does not grow faint or weary, and there is no searching out of his wisdom” (ibid.).

Let the teacher of the nations also say what he thinks about this matter. For he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI). Since his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable, he must in no way be believed to need another’s counsel in deliberating about matters. For just as he surpasses all in nature, so also he surpasses all in wisdom; and just as no one can be made equal to him by nature, so nothing can be added to his knowledge by counsel.

Counsel is sought from one who is either a partner by nature or a partner in understanding. But God has no equal and no partner, as Moses says: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, marvelous in majesty, doing wonders?” (Exod. XV).

Of him the Psalmist also says: “For who among the clouds shall be compared with the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God? God who is glorified in the council of the saints, great and fearful above all who surround him. Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, Lord, and your truth surrounds you” (Ps. LXXXIX).

## CHAPTER XV. Against those who say: “If, when imperial likenesses and images are sent into cities and provinces, the peoples go out to meet them with candles and incense—not honoring a panel smeared with wax, but the emperor—how much more ought images of our God and Savior, of his undefiled mother, and of all the saints to be painted in the churches of Christ?”

Whoever desires to acquire skill in any craft through diligent study applies himself to learning that craft by following the instruction of skilled, not unskilled, craftsmen. He does not attempt to usurp the teaching of those whom he sees to be less learned and contemptible in their own art, lest, while he desires through persistent labor to gain renown from the art he has acquired, he should lose both his labor and his work in vain and become an object of mockery to others.

This principle is firmly observed by students of the liberal arts, by physicians, by smelters and sculptors of metals, by workers who cut wood and stone, and by cultivators of fields. Only those neglect to observe it who, in order to establish the worship of images, seek examples from wicked practices and impudently attempt to support such a useless and perverse matter sometimes by good things, but more often by perverse things.

They are like a drunken man who, soaked with excessive wine, uses words now barbarous and now Latin, with trembling limbs, stumbling steps, and dulled senses; who delights now in the heat of fires, now in the chill of frost; who takes pleasure now in lying senseless, now in playing feebly; and who, having no fixed direction anywhere, never ceases to bring forth a mind wavering this way and that and deprived of reason. So these people constantly attempt to shore up their error: now by improperly applying testimonies of the divine Scriptures, now by the ravings of their own assertions, now by examples of evil things, now by examples of certain evil deeds and actions. [Col. 1142C]

For what madness or insanity is it to introduce as an example for the worship of images the fact that images of emperors are worshiped in cities and streets, and to prepare to establish one unlawful thing by means of another unlawful thing?

The teacher of the nations does not urge you to become imitators of emperors, but his imitators—indeed, imitators of Christ—when he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. XI). And in order to separate the imperial insignia and the revelry of the crowd from the minds of Christ’s worshipers, he says: “For us, for whom Christ was crucified, what have we to do with the marketplace?” (1 Cor. VI).

Now, since they desire to take examples from forensic or public actions and introduce them into the holy Church, why do they not appropriate theatrical and mimed follies, or even the cruelties unhappily enacted in theaters and arenas through gladiatorial games? Why does not the clergy, together with the bishop, pursue the people like a secutor pursuing a retiarius? Why does the whole Church, which guards Christ’s Church, not follow all the pagan—or rather, wretched—examples of the circus?

But far be it from Catholic religion that Christian gravity should now imitate and preserve the perverse actions once practiced by insolent paganism. “For our citizenship,” says the Apostle, “is in heaven” (Phil. III). Therefore whoever desires to journey toward the place where Christ our head has gone before must not become a follower of forensic or public actions, but of Christ himself, our head, or of his members, namely the apostles and apostolic men.

Perverse examples must be avoided by Catholics just as the seduction of evil people and the association of the unjust must be avoided. The Lord says: “You shall not listen to a vain report; you shall not consent with the unjust to become an unjust witness; you shall not join the many in evil.” A Christian, following the example of the Psalmist, ought to hate those who hate the Lord and waste away over his enemies (Ps. CXXXIX).

Nor did Tobias, a man of proven character and dear to God, urge his son to follow perverse examples when he said: “See, my son, that you do not follow the path of the wicked, and let not the multitude of sinners persuade you, for their wages are death. But if you practice truth, God will look favorably upon your works, and with all who practice righteousness you will inherit eternal life” (Tob. IV).
