Therefore whoever, seeing images of emperors worshiped by crowds of people, decides on the basis of this example to worship images in basilicas is shown to be resisting this command of the holy man in no minor way. Nor will he be able to say with David: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who do iniquity I shall not enter. I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and with the impious I shall not sit. I shall wash my hands among the innocent, and I shall surround your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXVI).

But if the defender of this error should perhaps say that it is not a sin to worship images of emperors, let him consider how great a glory was bestowed upon the three young men who refused to do this: an angel was sent from heaven into the blazing furnace, driving away the flame of the devouring fire and granting them saving dew. Let him consider also with what a great miracle the Babylonian prince testified that he had seen among them one like the Son of God—not for his own glory, but for theirs and to refute his own obstinacy.

Let them also hear blessed Jerome speaking as follows in the commentary that he composed on the Book of Daniel:

> “For behold,” he says, “our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the furnace of burning fire and to deliver us from your hands, O king. From the very thing by which he had thought he would terrify the boys, he now sees in them the source of courage. Nor do they delay long, but promise themselves immediate help, saying: ‘Behold, our God whom we worship is able to deliver us both from the fire with which you threaten us and from your hands.’ But if he does not wish to do so: appropriately, after saying ‘he is able to deliver us,’ he did not add the contrary, ‘if he cannot,’ but ‘if he does not wish to,’ so that, if they perish, it may be attributed not to God’s inability but to his will. Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, and that we do not adore the golden statue which you have erected. Whether we choose to read ‘statue,’ as Symmachus does, or ‘golden image,’ as the others have translated it, worshipers of God ought not to adore it. Therefore let the judges and rulers of the world who worship statues and images of emperors understand that they are doing what the three young men refused to do and thereby pleased God. And the distinction of wording should be noted: they say that gods are worshiped and an image is adored; neither is fitting for the servants of God.”

Behold, we are instructed by the teaching of a holy man that images of emperors ought by no means to be worshiped. Who, then, is so perverse as not only to decide to worship them, but also to derive from their worship examples of perversity for the worship of other images as well?

And if mortal men, puffed up by the insolence of vanity, exalted by worldly pomp, eager for honors, and full of ostentation, limited by place and content with a particular location because they could not be everywhere, ordered their images to be worshiped by people because they themselves could not be worshiped everywhere, why is it necessary to worship God in an image—God who is unlimited, who is wholly everywhere, everywhere marvelous, who is not contained by place and not confined by location? As Solomon says, “Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him” (2 Chron. VI); the world does not contain him, but he contains the world.

Since his power, glory, and might are so great, he is not to be sought in images but in pure and holy hearts. He is not to be worshiped in a painted panel, but in his holy court, as the Prophet says: “Worship the Lord in his holy court” (Ps. XXIX). He is not found through a painting in appointed places, but through works by pious minds. Elijah did not seek him in a place, in a painting, or on panels, but knew him to be present everywhere to the one who had made himself present through the diligence of good works, when he said: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings XVII).

To desire, then, to worship in panels the God who is without place and omnipotent, just as the Gentiles worshiped their local or mortal kings, is profane and close to unbelief. For we read that no nation committed this crime except the Babylonians and Romans, or those nations that were conquered by them, neighboring them, or took examples from them. Thus, just as these two kingdoms are known to have surpassed the other kingdoms of the world in ferocity and strength, so they are also believed to have been more inclined to cultivate idols and worship images.

There was therefore great agreement, great similarity, great cruelty, and also great strength between these two most powerful kingdoms—strength, indeed, by which each in its own time ruled over the other kingdoms of the world. For just as Babylon excelled in the East, so Rome excelled in the West: Babylon when the world was reaching maturity, Rome when the world was already growing old.

For, as histories relate, the Roman empire received the entire inheritance and accumulated greatness of the Babylonian kingdom. Between these two kingdoms, as between an old father who had ceased to be able and a young son who had not yet acquired the strength to rule, two kingdoms are said to have existed in the place of a guardian—namely, the Persian and Macedonian kingdoms. But when the heir, that is, the Roman empire, grew to maturity, the power that had held the place of guardian withdrew, and the adolescent son received the inheritance that the aged father had lost. It would take too long to pursue the correspondences and agreements between these two kingdoms.

To say nothing of the rest, there is no small correspondence between them in this matter: both decided that their kings should be worshiped in statues or images throughout fields and streets, and both inflicted various punishments on those unwilling to do so.

This evil, along with the other evils that were frustrated by Christ’s coming, ought to be entirely frustrated, and examples ought not merely to be taken from it for other practices; the thing itself must be eradicated from the roots by Christ’s worshipers, lest, according to the Apostle, “some root of bitterness spring up again and defile many” (Heb. XII).

Since we are instructed by apostolic teachings not to give the evil one any occasion, why should we give the Gentiles such an occasion by worshiping images of mortal kings and taking examples from them? They could say to us:

“We worship the statues or images of those whom we either believe to be gods by true religion or, instructed by the traditions of the ancients, know not to be gods. But you, for whom this is an abomination, why do you venerate images of men—painted in wax or cast in metal—under the reverence of kings, even with public worship? And, as you yourselves proclaim, why do you give to men the honor that is due to God alone? If this is unlawful and contrary to the law, why do you do it, Christians? Or why do your priests not prohibit it? Thus you may knowingly undertake under the pretext of office what you ascribe as sacrilege to us who are ignorant of it.”

When such and similar arguments had been brought against our people by pagan philosophers in the earliest times of the faith, our people are said to have replied as follows:

“We neither ought to approve nor are able to approve what you say, because, according to the clear words of God, we are not permitted to worship either the elements, angels, or any powers of heaven, earth, or air. For this is a special designation of divine service and is higher than every earthly veneration or reverence. But just as the first impulse toward this evil was given by human beings, so now custom scarcely recalls them from error.”

Nevertheless, although divine worship is not detected in this careless service, since the pleasure produced by the likeness of beloved faces brings greater delight than those to whom the honor is offered may perhaps demand, or than those offering it ought to perform, Christians who are more reverent and stricter abhor this custom. From what has been reported in this way, it does not appear that they then decided to worship images of kings, although the minds of those converted from paganism were still crude and not yet solid enough to receive solid food.

Now, since they say that, following the example of imperial images, the image of God, or of Mary the holy Mother of God, or of all the saints ought to be worshiped, how absurd and useless this is is immediately evident; it has also been shown in part both in this chapter and elsewhere.

For no one except almighty God can possess or retain the images or names of all the saints, as the Prophet says: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominion is exceedingly strengthened. I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXIX). And the Lord said to Abraham: “If the stars of heaven can be counted because of their multitude, then your seed too can be counted” (Gen. XV).

It is clear to everyone that all believers are the seed of Abraham. For he is the father of the nations, in whose seed—that is, in Christ—all nations will be blessed. According to the Apostle, he was called God’s friend not on account of circumcision but on account of faith; and it was not observance of the law but the belief of faith that was reckoned to him as righteousness.

## CHAPTER XVI. Against those who say that the honor given to an image passes to the original form.

This is an extremely common and familiar claim among those who are fervent in the worship of images: they believe and assert that the honor given to an image can pass to the very form of which it is the image. But how, or even whether, this can happen cannot be understood by any reasoning, nor is it approved by testimonies of the divine utterances.

Did the saints who, on account of their merits, were able to ascend to the heavenly kingdoms—and whose images they decide to worship with misguided devotion—seek superstitious or superfluous honors? Did they permit themselves to be worshiped?

Some of them desired to be despised in order to merit the Lord’s grace. Among them was the one who said: “I have chosen to be despised in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. LXXXIV). Others preferred to be scourged rather than venerated; witness the one who said: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for Christ.”

The teacher of the nations does not describe them as seekers of honors, but as burning with spiritual strength, fortified against adversity, refined by the fire of tribulation, and made stronger through worldly afflictions. He recalls that some of them were tortured, such as Achiam; some were stoned, such as Zechariah and Stephen; some were sawn apart, such as Isaiah, whose name is expressed in the plural through the rhetorical figure of syllepsis; some died by the killing of the sword, as many prophets are known to have done; some wandered about in sheepskins and in goatskins, such as Elijah and John; some were afflicted or in want, and the world was not worthy of them, as may be believed generally of nearly all the saints (Heb. XI). These examples show that they burned not with a desire for honors but with a desire for virtues.

For if, while they lived in mortal bodies, they had pursued honors out of ambition, they would not now enjoy such great glory in heaven. Since the Lord has bestowed on them perpetual honor, they have no need of transient honors.

The honor rightly shown to the bodies, relics, or basilicas of the saints remains acceptable both to almighty God and to his saints; but honor that is inappropriate and indecent remains acceptable neither to God nor to his saints.

This is why blessed Joseph, after his prophecy, solemnly required his bones to be carried with the children of Israel when they came to the promised land, lest, [Col. 1147A] while the Egyptians remembered him—or the administration by which he had governed Egypt during its great famine—they should offer his bones a useless veneration. He was firmly devoted to God the Creator and wholly estranged from the Egyptians’ empty superstition; and he showed his holiness all the more expressly by having served God humbly and rightly while alive, and by refusing after his death to have inappropriate service offered to his ashes.

Since holy men, entirely acceptable to God, avoided the empty services of human beings—as Paul and Barnabas are known to have avoided the superstitious services of the Lycaonians, and Peter rejected Cornelius’s devout veneration, while the angel in the Apocalypse forbade John to worship him—who could believe that they delight in the worship of images, or are charmed by the services rendered to paintings? And how could honor shown to them through paintings reach them, when those paintings are neither made from their bodies nor from their clothing, but are prepared by artists according to each person’s capacity for invention? [Col. 1147B]

Those who reign with Christ in heaven are not flattered by the works of painters, nor do those who have deserved to be inscribed by Christ in the book of life seek to be painted by craftsmen on panels or walls. Let those for whom it is so characteristic to say this—that the honor shown to an image passes to its original form—say where they have read it, or by what testimonies they can prove it.

For our Lord and Savior did not say, “Whenever you did this for images,” but, “Whenever you did this for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV); nor did he say, “Whoever receives images,” but, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. X). The Apostle did not say, [Col. 1147C] “Let us love images,” but, “Let us love one another, because love is from God” (Rom. XIII and I Pet. I). Nor did he prescribe that the burdens of images, but that our burdens should be borne by one another, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI).

Since images are usually made according to the skill of the artists—sometimes beautiful, sometimes ugly, occasionally attractive, sometimes even repulsive; some very similar to those whose images they are, others dissimilar; some shining with novelty, others fading with age—it must be asked which of them are more worthy of honor: those known to be more costly, or those known to be cheaper. For if the more costly possess greater honor, then the work or the quality of the materials in them receives veneration, not the fervor of devotion. But if the cheaper ones—those less like the persons they are intended to represent—are more highly honored, it is unjust that those which excel neither in workmanship nor in material, and are not even recognized as resembling the persons, should be venerated more abundantly and more fervently. [Col. 1147D]

We reject nothing in images except their worship; indeed, we permit images of the saints in basilicas, not for worship, but for recalling the deeds that were accomplished and for beautifying the walls. Since they place almost all the hope of their belief in images, it remains that we should venerate the saints in their bodies—or rather in the relics of their bodies—and also in their clothing, according to the tradition of the ancient Fathers. They, however, worshipping walls and panels, imagine that they possess a great gain of faith because they are subject to the works of painters. For even if learned people can avoid what they practice in worshipping images—namely, venerating not what the images are, but what they signify—they nevertheless cause scandal to the unlearned, who venerate and worship in them nothing other than what they see.

Therefore care must be taken lest they incur the evangelical sentence, since they drive so many little ones into scandal. If the person who scandalizes one of the little ones is subject to a most fearful sentence, he will be struck by a far more deadly severity who either drives almost the whole Church of Christ to worship images, or subjects those who reject the worship of images to an anathema. It is necessary to avoid both errors with great caution, lest, when someone strikes against either side more forcefully than order permits, he be unable to escape the loss of his salvation. [Col. 1148B]

## CHAPTER XVII

How Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, spoke unhappily, rashly, or foolishly: “I receive and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images according to the service of worship that I render to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity; and I separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and subject to anathema those who do not think and glorify in this way; and I consign to that party those who have denied the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.”

It does not require much discussion on our part to show how rashly and, so to speak, foolishly Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, with the others agreeing with him, said that he would receive and honorably embrace [Col. 1148C] images, and babbled that he would render to them the service of worship owed to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity. For it is plainly evident to all who read or hear this that he is immersed in abysses of no slight error: he admits that he offers to creatures the service owed only to the Creator, and, while wishing to favor paintings, he resists all the sacred Scriptures.

Who of sound mind, then, has ever said or agreed with anyone saying such an absurdity—that the variety of paintings should be held in as great an honor as the holy, life-giving, and all-creating Trinity, and that the same service should be offered to a painting as is offered to the Lord of all creation? Or who would endure hearing him, more sickening than speaking? Or what ears would strive not rather to reject the guilt of so great a crime than to receive it?

For it is perverse that any senseless things should receive such a service of worship as is offered to almighty God, who has no equal, of whom it is said through Solomon: “Lord, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below” (II Chron. VI). With what face, then—not to mention everything else—does he hear this one sentence of the divine law, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI), and, despising it, not only serve creatures but strive to equate their service with the service owed to God?

Let the bishop stand in the church and read, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,” and then, as soon as he has sat down in the assembly, let him say: “I receive and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images, and I offer to them the service of worship owed to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity.” Thus he demonstrates himself unstable in divine words: professing one thing with his mouth, believing another in his heart, reading one thing in the divine books, holding another in the inner chamber of his breast, overriding the divine words, and setting his own trifles above the Lord’s commandments. [Col. 1149A]

Although he is recognized as harming himself and his associates through his perverse profession, he is, on the contrary, recognized as benefiting us who wish to resist their trifles, since he exposes the unhappy error that they appear to inject into the peoples while concealing it.

They say: “We do not worship images as God, nor do we offer them the worship due to God; but when we look at and worship them, we fix the focus of our mind upon the place where we know that those whose images they are exist.” But this man, exposing their error and revealing his own thought without any concealment, admits that he offers them the same service as he offers the holy Trinity, and the same worship. Thus he has made openly manifest the absurdity that they secretly retain within themselves. Their negligence can be hidden from no one, since the judgment of this profession reveals it.

Since he endeavors to separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and subject to anathema all who disagree with his error, and to admit those who refused to believe in the saving incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ, it is clear to all readers how great his folly is. Immersed in the abyss of his own negligence, while dragging others to himself so that they may suffer such things with him, he strives to abuse with insults and reproachful words those whom he sees avoiding so great a danger. [Col. 1149C]

For what insanity or madness is it to attempt to tear Christ’s people away from the breasts of Mother Church because they refuse to offer to things without sense the service owed to God alone? What perversity is it to judge as equal those who stubbornly refuse to believe in the life-giving incarnation of Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and human beings, and those who, despising the service of all creatures according to the command of the divine law, desire to serve God alone, to whom all things are subject?

It is one thing not to believe in the redemption of the world, another to wish to serve God alone; one thing to despise the world’s salvation, another to reject the worship of images; one thing to resist saving admonitions, another to oppose empty and superstitious services.

The same Lord and Savior, having both forbidden the worship of images through the book of the Old Testament and judged, through his bodily presence, that the image of Caesar should be rendered to Caesar rather than worshipped, supplied such commandments concerning belief in him when he said: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life” (John VI); and again: “I am the door and the life; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out, and will find pasture” (John X); and again: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III).

The Truth says this; the salvation of the world bears witness to this; the Redeemer of the human race proclaims this. Who could be so dull and sluggish as to judge the person who contradicts these most authoritative admonitions equal to the person who, despising the divine utterances, refuses to worship senseless things? [Col. 1150A]

Granted that worshipping images is a virtue and a good work: can it possibly be equated with faith? Yet one must persist in all good works, though no good work can lead anyone to perfect salvation unless it is placed upon the foundation of faith and supported by its protection.

Abraham, after all, was justified not by works but by faith; Moses was made great by faith; the saints conquered kingdoms through faith; and all the saints died according to faith. The Prophet says, “All his works are in faith” (Ps. XXXIII); and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Your faith has saved you” (Mark X). Likewise he says: “Truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will do not only this to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and cast yourself into the sea,’ it will happen; and everything that you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matt. XXI). [Col. 1150B]

From this it is understood that faith surpasses the other virtues. Although hope and love are joined to it, one reaches them through faith. Nor should the person who sins in other works be judged by the same condemnation as the person who sins in faith. For although no one can be saved without faith by worshipping images, there are innumerable hosts in the heavenly homeland who, whether through martyrdom, innocence, or a solitary way of life, although they neither possessed nor worshipped images at all, have nevertheless, through observance of the faith, been joined to the heavenly assemblies and enjoy everlasting joys. [Col. 1150C]

## CHAPTER XVIII

How Euthymius, bishop of Sardis, does not differ greatly from the error of the aforementioned Constantine in saying: “With my whole heart I receive the venerable images with the honor that is fitting and with worship worthy of embrace. I judge, declare, and announce as heretics those who think or teach otherwise or contrary to the holy images, considering them alien to the Catholic Church.”

Since Euthymius, bishop of Sardis, is almost equal to Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, in his confession, there is no doubt that they have equal faith and will obtain equal recompense, unless correction precedes in either of them. For each of them confesses with his whole heart that he receives images with the highest honor and worship worthy of embrace.

O foolish confession of bishops! O insane proclamation of prelates! The Catholic Church, rejoicing in the voice of its prelates that it has received the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, says to the Lord: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple”; but these men say: “We receive and worship images.”

The assembly of believers prays that the apostles or apostolic men should receive Christ, who is our peace and who made both one, saying: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people”; but these men say: “We receive images with worship worthy of embrace.”

Since these men fix almost all their hope of assistance upon images, they dissent in no small degree from the holy and universal [Col. 1151A] Church, which fixes its hope of assistance not in the pigments of a painting, nor in the manufactured works of artisans, but in God, the creator of all things. It has as helpers the apostles and apostolic men, who daily intercede with the Lord for it and, having received the rain of holy preaching as a gift of the Holy Spirit from the heavenly dwellings, pour it down—as is fitting, from the higher places in the Church—upon faithful peoples or rulers, according to the prophecy of Joel:

“And it shall be in that day: the mountains shall drip with sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk” (Joel III).

Ezekiel also proclaims this in these words: “But your mountains, Israel, shall produce grapes, and your fruit, which you shall eat, shall be your people.” Although Christ the Lord may be understood as that grape and fruit, since he proceeded from the mountains of Israel, taking humanity from the patriarchs, the sweetness of preaching joined together from the Old and New Testaments may also be understood. It is spread through the minds of humble believers, softens the hearts of unbelievers toward believing and bearing fruit, and gladdens the understanding of rulers with the reward of eternal hope. It urges them to be clothed in righteousness and to sing a hymn to God together with the peoples subject to them. Thus the prophetic word is fulfilled:

“Your fields will be filled with abundance; the boundaries of the wilderness will grow rich, and the hills will gird themselves with rejoicing. The rams of the sheep have been clothed, and the valleys will abound in grain; for they too will cry out and sing a hymn” (Ps. LXV).

He lifts his eyes to them when he says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come” (Ps. CXXI). For he does not say, “I lifted up my eyes to senseless things, that I might obtain assistance from them,” but, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains”—namely, to those mountains upon which Christ’s Church was founded, as the Prophet says: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVII). [Col. 1151C]

When these mountains see God’s people delivered from Egyptian slavery and ascending to the promised land—that is, when the faithful despise the grievous slavery of this world and fly away to the eternal homeland—they rejoice, as the same most holy Prophet says: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the sheep” (Ps. CXIV).

Whoever, therefore, after rejecting the worship of creatures along with all other vanities, offers service to God alone and lifts the eyes of his mind, having driven away the sleep of unbelief, toward these mountains will not be afraid when the aerial powers or their followers, the proud, descend into the deadly depths of Erebus. With all such people he will sing with the greatest rejoicing:

“Therefore we will not fear, though the earth be shaken and the mountains be transferred into the heart of the sea. Its waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by its strength” (Ps. XLVI). [Col. 1151D]

Since the ancient enemy—whose satellites are often designated in the sacred writings by the name “mountains”—is unquestionably the enemy of those mountains, namely, the evil spirits of whom the prophet Nahum says, “The mountains were shaken by him, and the hills trembled” (Nahum I), and of whom the Apostle says, “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains” (I Cor. XIII), the persuader of every evil and, conversely, the dissuader from every good, persuaded human beings to worship creatures in order to turn them away from the Creator. Through his wicked persuasion it came about that the worship of creatures took root and, under something like a pretext of religion and reverence for the saints, occupies a great place among those who confess that they receive and worship images with their whole heart.

Although the error of both men is almost equal, as we have said, they are recognized as differing in one respect: Constantine judges those who refuse to offer creatures the service owed to God alone to be unbelieving and without faith, whereas Euthymius condemns them not as unbelievers but as heretics. Yet they are, as Sedulius says of certain people:

“Both equal in error, although pursuing different things.”

They falsely describe the holy Catholic Church, because of the madness of one error, as partly unbelieving and partly heretical. For if all of us Christians generally—who, rejecting the worship of creatures, wish to offer the service owed to God alone to him alone, to whom alone it is rightly owed—are judged heretics by these men because we do not serve images, then undoubtedly those who served creatures, whether before or after the Redeemer’s coming, will be judged wholly Catholic by them. And if those people are judged unbelieving—and truly unbelieving—because they worshipped creatures instead of the Creator, then we, who reject vanities and serve the one and only God, while giving his saints the service that is consequent and fitting, will be considered and judged Catholic and faithful.

## CHAPTER XIX

The useless, foolish, and laughable statement of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is refuted, namely what he said: “It is written in our divine Scriptures.”

Often ignorance is both culpable and innocent. Culpable ignorance frequently strives to cause harm, whereas innocent ignorance seeks to harm no one. Although neither kind is subject to sin in every case, both are nevertheless liable to criticism. Culpable ignorance is subject to sin because it is driven by a disgraceful intention to cause harm, and to criticism either because sin is not free from criticism or because whatever it says or does, it does foolishly and without learning. Innocent ignorance, although free from sin in that it harms no one, is nevertheless not free from criticism, because everything ignorant is unlearned, and everything unlearned falls under criticism.

Accordingly, the very ridiculous statement of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia—“It is written in our divine Scriptures”—is shown to yield either to the same criticism that is subject to sin or to the same criticism that rests upon ignorance. It is either subject to the sin by which their leaders, although human beings no different from other mortals, say that God reigns together with them and call themselves divine and their deeds or sayings divine, and by which they similarly call their Scriptures divine; or it succumbs to criticism because, ignorant of eloquence and unaware of elegance in speech, when he should have said, “in our books containing the divine Scriptures,” or something of that kind, he is reported to have said, awkwardly and ridiculously, “in our divine Scriptures.” [Col. 1153A]

This, as we have said, is madness if they uttered it through the pride of arrogance by which they presume both that God reigns together with them and that they themselves are divine. If, wishing to say one thing, they said another, and if they possess so little force of intelligence that they can scarcely express in precise and appropriate words what they conceive in their hearts, it is negligence. Thus, in either direction, they are carried along deviant paths: either lifted up by pride, or believed to be bound by the dark restraints of ignorance.

Who of sound mind has ever said such a thing? Who of sane understanding has ever uttered it? What heedlessness or madness is it for a mortal human being, subject to sufferings, to say, “It is written in our divine Scriptures”? If they are ours, how are they divine? And if they are divine, how are they ours?

That which derives from a human being is human; that which derives from God is divine. Our Scriptures are indeed human, while God’s Scriptures are divine. Yet reason permits us to say of the books of the holy law, “our books”; but of the divine Scriptures we can rightly and appropriately say, according to reason, only “the divine Scriptures.”

Granted that this statement could have stood rationally—although it cannot—so that it would not be recognized as having flowed from the fountain of boastfulness or believed to have issued from the abyss of ignorance, they could nevertheless be criticized in every way because, being uselessly spoken concerning a useless matter, it is shown to have been uttered for the purpose of establishing the worship of images. [Col. 1153C]

[Note: [Col. 1153] Nor can simplicity somehow oppose it. The corrector substituted “support” for “oppose.” Yet the verb “oppose” is also used above in this sense, Book II.]

Nor can simplicity somehow oppose it, since simplicity usually adheres to whatever is right, whereas it is evident that this statement was produced neither by a pure nor a right intention, but by a perverse one. For if it were recognized that he had proceeded from holy rusticity—which sometimes benefits only the person who possesses it—simply and innocently, and not in order to assert something illicit, God, who searches the heart and the kidneys and who often considers intentions rather than acts, would undoubtedly forgive him.

For just as an evil intention is often counted as an act even when it does not accomplish anything evil in deed, so a good intention is always accepted in place of a good deed. To illustrate this with examples: Balaam’s evil intention, by which he wished to curse God’s people, was not free from guilt, although he did not attain what he desired; and David’s good intention, by which he wished to build a temple for the Lord, although it was not fulfilled in deed, was nevertheless praised by divine oracles.

## CHAPTER XX

How John the presbyter, when Theodosius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew, was reciting the words of John Chrysostom and saying, “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians,” said: “Who is this angel except the one of whom it is written: ‘For the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians who were encamped around Jerusalem in one night’?”

The abbot Theodosius of the monastery of Saint Andrew reports that John Chrysostom said in the often-mentioned most worthless synod, which was conducted in support of the worship of images: “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians.” Since those who are reported to have been present at that synod strive to distort the words of patriarchs, prophets, and other saints and illustrious men in order to establish the worship of images, and finally lie that those patriarchs did certain things that they did not do, it is not surprising if they also falsely accuse John Chrysostom of having said such things.

Would that man, so eloquent and learned, have said, “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians,” when he knew that the immortal nature of angels in no way requires paintings in order to be seen by human beings? For by nature they are spirits and by office angels; in order to be seen by human beings, they are believed to assume bodies from the most lucid ether, not from the works of painters. Therefore it cannot be believed that such a statement was uttered by John, a most eloquent man: it is neither polished in language, nor clear in meaning, nor supported by any reasoning. [Col. 1154B]

It contains the fault that grammarians call *amphibolia*, that is, ambiguity of expression. For when it is said, “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a line of barbarians,” it does not clearly appear whether he saw an angel in an image who was pursuing a multitude of barbarians elsewhere, or whether an angel seen elsewhere was pursuing a multitude of barbarians in an image.

Even if the statement were free from this fault, it would still be apparent from other indications that it does not belong to so great a man. Since John was not of the same period, it would be extremely ridiculous, and rather entirely false, for him to say, “I saw an angel pursuing barbarians,” if—as I believe—he meant that he had seen in a painting the same story depicted by an artist, namely, that an angel had previously struck down the ranks of the barbarians.

Many eloquent and most articulate men, in the vast fields of their discussions, make mention of paintings and images, as they do of other matters, wherever order and reason require it. When those who burn with zeal for their worship read and discover such statements, they strive to distort everything toward the worship of images, so that they may make their unarmed assertion armed against us who, by the Lord’s favor, are true worshippers, worshipping the Father in spirit and in truth. Because they find that the most eloquent men made some mention of images, they act as though commandments were immediately given concerning everything mentioned in treatises.

John the presbyter, therefore, when the aforementioned abbot Theodosius falsely claimed that John, bishop of Constantinople, had said, “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians,” is reported to have immediately added and said: “Who is this angel except the one of whom it is written: ‘For the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians who were encamped around Jerusalem in one night’?”

In many passages of that empty reading which they composed concerning this matter, he is found to have spoken many notable things carelessly. In nearly all of them he is noted to have spoken incautiously; and the swifter he is in speech, the more sluggish he is evidently in understanding, as Solomon says: “If you see a man swift in his words, know that the fool has more hope than he” (Prov. XXIX). [Col. 1155A]

When he is reported to have said of a painting, “Who is this angel except the one of whom it is written: ‘For the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians,’” and so forth, how incautious and deranged he appears! For it was not the painted angel who struck the Assyrians, but the one who was sent for this purpose.

As for what he said, “who were encamped around Jerusalem,” as though this were how it was written, he is revealed here, as in the other matters, to be unlearned, since it is found nowhere written in this order of words. Although Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, captured almost all the fortified cities of Judah, as Scripture says, “And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of the reign of Hezekiah that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them” (IV Kings XVIII), he nevertheless did not reach Jerusalem, nor did he pitch camp around the city in order to strike the wall with siege engines. Rather, from Lachish he sent the Rabshakeh to Jerusalem; he is read to have stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field.

The same is testified in the same words by the book of the *Words of Days*, which is called [Hebrew title omitted in the source] in Hebrew and “Things Omitted” (*Paraleipomenōn*, Παραλειπομένων) in Greek, and which is the chronicle of the divine law: “Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, sent his servants to Jerusalem. He himself was besieging Lachish with his entire army” (II Chron. XXXII). [Col. 1155C]

What the aforementioned John, according to his custom, is recognized as having appropriated—as though it were written there, “who were encamped around Jerusalem”—is found in none of the authentic books of the holy law.

To make this clearer, the actual words of the holy law, as they appear in the books, must be set out in order. Thus it is read in the Book of Kings:

“And it came to pass in that night that the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. When he arose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead; and he departed and went away. And Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, returned and remained in Nineveh” (IV Kings XIX).

The book of the most holy and eloquent prophet Isaiah sets out this history in the following manner:

“But the angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. They arose in the morning, and behold, all were corpses of the dead. He went out and departed, and Sennacherib returned;” and so forth (Isa. XXXVII).

The book of the *Words of Days*, which, as we have said, is the chronicle of the whole divine law, nevertheless explains in detail the histories of the kings drawn from the Book of Kings, which were omitted from it, and narrates this history in the following manner:

“And the Lord sent an angel, who struck every mighty man and warrior and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria; and he returned with shame to his own land” (II Chron. XXXII).

In these examples, what John appropriated is found nowhere.

## CHAPTER XXI

How there is no authority for, and no mention in any of the authentic books of, what they say: that through the image of a certain Polemon someone was restrained from committing adultery; and how they strive to equate this with the miracle performed through the fringe of the Lord’s garment, which the woman touched and thereby received the health she desired.

[Col. 1156A]

Among the other ravings which they are detected to have heaped together in the reading of that same most empty synod in order to support their error, this is especially characteristic of them: they assert that, through the image of some Polemon, a certain man was restrained from committing adultery. Although this event—if indeed it is to be believed to have happened—is found in none of the authentic books of either the Old or the New Testament, nor has it been cited by any of those teachers [Col. 1156B] who are received by the holy Roman, catholic, and apostolic Church, nevertheless they produce it to bolster their error, as though it were some thoroughly established miracle, and do not hesitate to compare it with the miracle performed through the fringe of the Lord’s garment.

Yet if this happened, as they assert, it neither ought nor can be compared with the Lord’s saving deeds. For as great as the distance is between some unknown Polemon and the Mediator of God and human beings, so great is the distance between the deeds of the aforementioned Polemon and his image and the most holy miracles of the Lord and Savior. Acts that are utterly and exceedingly dissimilar in power cannot have equal standing. “Who,” says the Prophet, “will be likened to the Lord among the clouds? [Col. 1156C] Or who will be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXIX [89]).

Of him it is also said in the *Song of Songs*: “His head is the finest gold” (Song of Songs V), because, just as the nature of no metal can be equated with gold, so no creature can be equated with the Creator of all, who is indeed Christ’s head. Of him the bride also says in the same *Song of Songs*: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song of Songs II). For just as an apple tree, beautiful to behold and exceedingly sweet in fragrance, stands above the trees of the forest, so our Redeemer—who is the fragrance of life unto life, and whom the Church daily follows in the fragrance of perfumes—stands above all the assemblies of the saints. They are called “sons” for this reason: they are known to cling not to the world into which they were born, but to Christ, into whom they were born again [Col. 1156D].

In the *Apocalypse* also, the twenty-four elders are read to have cast their crowns before the Lamb, because all the virtues of the saints and all their victories, by which they shone with his assistance, are seen to be lesser when compared with his virtues and victory. A rivulet, when compared with the perennial spring from which it flows, is likewise declared to be smaller; and a worthless vine-shoot is altogether believed to be inferior when compared with living roots or even fruit-bearing branches.

Granted, then: it happened, and it may be believed, that the power of the image of Polemon restrained someone from the crime of adultery. Does it follow that all images are to be adored? Because the tongue of a dumb beast, uttering human speech, restrained the perverse [Col. 1157A] intention of a certain diviner who was attempting to curse the blessed people, and allowed an irrational animal to avert terrifying angelic blows from a rational human being, are animals therefore to be adored? Or because a childish crowd, provoking the man of God with empty insults, was struck down by the wounding ferocity of savage beasts, is the fury of bears therefore to be adored?

For often, through a chance occurrence, things that happen in one way or another inhibit those who wish to perpetrate harmful deeds; but reason does not therefore permit the things through which this happens to be adored. If, therefore, what they say about Polemon and his image—by whose assistance they wish to support their error—truly happened, images are nevertheless not to be adored. As the examples we briefly presented above [Col. 1157B] show, not all things through which some benefits are brought to mortals are to be adored.

If, however, what they say truly happened—which we too judge not to have happened—and they do not produce it with fully rational authority, since they approve no authentic evidence that it actually occurred, then the worship of utterly senseless things is not thereby to be established. Nor is a thing that ought rationally and truly to be done ever recorded as having been instituted by lies or examples of lies. For just as truth is never known to assent to lies, so lies are always believed to oppose truth. These two are seen to confront one another in such a way that they are always believed to resist each other.

Just as no one can nourish fuel with streams of water, or, conversely, enlarge streams of water [Col. 1157C] with fiery fuel, so no one can establish truth by lies, as they seek to do.

Having briefly and in part demonstrated that the event involving Polemon’s image—if indeed it happened, as they themselves admit—neither ought nor can be compared with the event involving the Lord’s fringe; and having shown either that it is altogether uncertain whether what they say happened actually happened, or that even if it did happen, the worship of images cannot thereby be established, and also that truth cannot be approved or instituted by lies, it is now worthwhile to explain briefly what the fringe of the Lord’s garment, which they strive to equate with the image of Polemon, signifies in types and hidden mysteries.

For the fringe of the Lord’s garment is the faith of the Incarnation, by touching which the Gentile world [Col. 1157D] lost the sickness of idolatrous impurity. Just as the fringe is a very small part in comparison with the body or the whole garment, so the Incarnation of the Redeemer, compared with the divine and ineffable generation by which he was begotten from the Father before the ages, appears to be small. Concerning that generation Isaiah says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII)—with “no one” understood. His human generation, however, the evangelist recounts in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. I).

Therefore, when the woman touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment from behind, she received the desired healing which the skill of physicians had denied her for a long period. This happened because, after the Lord’s passion and resurrection, or his ascension into heaven, the Gentile world [Col. 1158A] received the healing of faith—which neither the preaching of the patriarchs nor that of the prophets had been able to impart to it—by touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment, that is, by believing the mystery of his Incarnation.

Although scarcely a small crowd of disciples believed at the Lord’s own preaching, nevertheless, at the preaching of the apostles such a multitude was kindled by the swift ardor of faith that five thousand people are said to have believed on one day and three thousand on another. The Truth himself promised this to his disciples, saying: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV).

Some think that this can also be understood in the miracle performed by the Lord through Peter. For while the Lord is read to have healed the sick by the command of his word or by touch, Peter is read to have healed the sick merely by the touch of his [Col. 1158B] shadow.

As the Lord was going to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, he freed the woman from the flow of blood by the touch of the fringe. This signifies that, while he was hastening toward the synagogue—which descended, of course, from the stock of the patriarchs and prophets—in order to awaken it from the sleep of unbelief, he healed the Gentile world from the most insolent worship of demons through knowledge of his faith. The good which the synagogue, entangled in the guilt of unbelief, neglected to receive, the Gentile world merited to receive through the devotion of faith.

The Lord testifies that he came to liberate the synagogue when he says in his bodily presence: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). He also restrained the disciples from going into the roads of the Gentiles and from entering the cities of the Samaritans. And long ago, allegorically, through Solomon [Col. 1158C] in the *Song of Songs*, he promises that he will descend to the garden of the Israelite people, saying: “I went down to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley” (Song of Songs VI).

For when, through the assumption of flesh, he descended to the garden of the Jewish people, in which the law displayed the sharpest austerity in its shell while concealing incomparable sweetness in its kernel, he visited the lowly works of the Gentile valley and made it his own through the integrity of faith.

Moreover, the fact that the woman healed on the way is followed by the Lord to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and that his daughter, released from the bonds of death, is raised, shows that the synagogue will one day shake off the sleep of its unbelief, rise through faith in Christ, and live for him forever. For as soon as “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered” (according to the Apostle; Rom. X), all Israel will be saved by casting off the blindness [Col. 1158D] that came upon it in part through its disbelief in the Mediator of God and human beings, and by believing in him who was formerly announced to it through the patriarchs and prophets by the thunderous utterances of the sacred oracles.

Since the image of Polemon is entirely without these and similar mysteries signified by the event involving the Lord’s fringe, it is not to be held in honor in the same way as the fringe of the Lord’s garment, nor ought it to be compared with it, since it cannot be equated with it in the radiance of so many mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXII

That the judges who were present at the aforementioned synod attempted insolently and incongruously to exalt the art of painting, saying: “For the painter’s art is pious, and some foolishly disparage it unjustly; for the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously.”

[Col. 1159A]

If a pestilential humor besieges the citadel of the body—that is, the head—it easily spreads to the other members. Nor is it surprising if, after spreading to the feet, it grievously harms them, since it is established that it has already injured the head, which stands above all the members.

Therefore, the madness of worshiping images, which infiltrated the minds of Constantine and his mother Helena, and also of Tharasius, bishop of Constantinople, and of the other priests of that party, should not be considered insignificant if it descended so far as to invade the minds of judges and common people. For, as the preceding example has shown [Col. 1159B], when the head is invaded by the insolence of some matter, the other things that are shown to be subject to the head are easily invaded as well.

“The whole head is sick,” says the Prophet, “and the whole heart is faint; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no soundness in them” (Isa. I). For when kings and priests, who ought to be examples of right living to the peoples subject to them, neglect the pursuit of right living and right action, the inner health of the peoples subject to them is in a certain sense called into doubt.

Since, therefore, the minds of so many priests in that synod were covered with errors, how could the error of the judges not cling to their minds? Or who will lead the sheep back from error if the shepherds themselves hold the leadership of wandering?

For priests who are known to lead the peoples subject to them into error are rebuked by the prophet Jeremiah [Col. 1159C] with such reproaches as these: “Therefore, thus says the Lord to the shepherds who rule my people: You have scattered my sheep, and driven them away, and have not visited them” (Jer. XXIII). Immediately afterward, how great God’s care for the people is, and how, once the negligent have been removed, more diligent rulers are given to God’s people, is added:

“Behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your pursuits, and I will raise up for them shepherds who will feed them; and they will no longer fear or be terrified, says the Lord” (ibid.).

The prophet Ezekiel likewise writes about such men—something we pursue with no small anguish of heart—who enjoy ecclesiastical stipends and are believed, through their erroneous and heedless examples, to lead the people into error, as those are reported to have done who burned with the empty worship of images and joined the people [Col. 1159D] subject to them to themselves in their profession of error:

“And therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: You devour my sheep, and clothe yourselves with their wool; you slaughter what is fat, and scatter my sheep. You did not strengthen the weak, nor heal what was sick, nor bind up what was broken, nor bring back what had strayed, nor seek what had perished; and you oppressed the strong with toil. And my sheep were scattered because there were no shepherds, and they became food for all the beasts of the field. My sheep were scattered over every mountain and every high hill, and over the face of the whole earth my sheep were scattered, and there was no one to rescue or call them back” (Ezek. XXXIV).

Therefore, in this utterly empty [Col. 1160A] profession, the wickedness of the judges is not as great as the perversity of the priests. In the former, cowardice is detected; in the latter, immense madness overflows. This is especially so since the former profess that they will worship images and offer them the service owed to the holy Trinity, while the latter professed that the art of painters is pious, that it ought not to be mocked, and that the Father commends a painter who acts piously, saying:

“For the painter’s art is pious, and some foolishly disparage it unjustly; for the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously.”

In the professions of both groups it is clearly shown that the priests surpassed the judges in error by as much as they surpass them in the eminence of honor according to the sublimity of their ranks. Nor could laymen equal bishops in their absurd profession, just as they cannot equal them in [Col. 1160B] sitting upon the priestly chair.

Yet since nothing that can rightly be praised is found in either group, while in both there is something that can deservedly be condemned, and since the error of the bishops—who confessed that they would worship images and offer them the service owed to God alone—has been partly exposed, it remains for our pen’s attack to expose the error of the judges as well, by which they assert that the art of painting is pious.

For they say that the art of painting is pious, as though it did not share, together with the other worldly arts, in either piety or impiety. What greater piety does the art of painters possess than the art of smiths, sculptors, founders, engravers, stonecutters, carpenters, tillers of the soil, or other craftsmen? All the arts we have mentioned, which can be attained only through learning, and [Col. 1160C] can be practiced piously or impiously by those who exercise them. Piety or impiety does not fall upon the arts themselves, but upon the people who pursue them—people who are often either confined by the most insolent tumult of vices or adorned by the saving assemblies of virtues.

If, therefore, the art of painters is said to be pious for the reason that through it the deeds of pious people and certain pious actions are often painted, then it will also be said to be impious because through it many impieties are often depicted: the slaughter of human beings, the atrocities of wars, the cruelties of criminals, the savagery of beasts, the attacks of wild animals, and other things like these.

And if it is by no means believed to be impious for the reason that the things we have listed are presented to human eyes through outlines or various lines [Col. 1160D], then neither will it be pious because through it the deeds of good people are represented.

Just as iron is not called impious because human beings are killed with it, nor pious because certain instruments are made from it by which the clashes of flashing swords are beaten back, and by which physicians care for human health, so the art of painters is not impious because cruel things are painted through it, nor pious because certain merciful things are painted.

As for their complaint that some foolish people unjustly disparage it, no one of sound mind doubts that in this matter too, as in the others, they are following madness. No sane person disparages either images or the art of painting; rather, [Col. 1161A] he abhors the madness of those who worship images and offer them an inappropriate service.

Wine is not criticized because it produces drunkenness, since it is often poured out as a sacrifice to God. Nor are forests condemned because they provide shelter for thieves, since they often supply many things useful for human purposes. Nor is fire blamed because it sometimes devours houses or other things suited to human needs with destructive greed, since it supports human life in many ways.

As for their statement, “For the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously,” it is neither for them to prove why or where it is written that the Father commends a painter, nor for us to believe it, since praise of painters is found in none of the volumes of the divine oracles.

Let them therefore find anywhere in the divine Scriptures [Col. 1161B] a passage in which, according to their own assertion, the painter is praised because he is intent on composing images; then we shall find how we can answer them. For almighty God generally approves or disapproves not works but the devotion behind works, not actions but the intentions of actions, not things but the causes of things, and not merely who performs something but with what frame of mind he performs it.

## CHAPTER XXIII

That the statement of John, priest and legate of the Easterners, is useless and full of falsehood: “Painters do not contradict the Scriptures, but whatever Scripture says, they demonstrate, insofar as they are in agreement with the Scriptures.”

If all the ravings of John, priest and legate of the Easterners, which he uttered in that same synod—whose inept [Col. 1161C] reading our pen is engaged in criticizing—had to be gathered together and examined by us one by one, the forest of such an argument would require volumes of great size.

But we, partly out of a desire for brevity, to which we are wholly devoted, and partly by preserving the order of his own reading, have placed in our discussion what must be examined—not each item separately, but some things here and there in sequence, as each person spoke or as they are found arranged in the same book. Thus we are compelled to compress everything into the limits of a very brief discussion, and we treat nearly everything not separately but in scattered fashion, as the order dictated.

Meanwhile, it is worthwhile to examine carefully how, as he himself declared, painters [Col. 1161D] are not at all believed to contradict the Scriptures, or how they demonstrate whatever Scripture says, or how they agree with the Scriptures.

Although it is not clear which Scriptures he meant when he said this, nevertheless we must believe that he was speaking of the sacred Scriptures, which we customarily call “the Scriptures,” as in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV).

**S R.** In the meantime, since the art of painting arose for the purpose of conveying to those who look upon it the memory of things truly done and moving minds from falsehood toward the recollection of truth, it sometimes, conversely, moves the senses from truth toward the consideration of falsehood. It presents to the eyes not only things that are, were, or can be, but also things that neither are, were, [Col. 1162A] nor can be.

For falsehood concerns either things that are not but can come to be, or things that neither are nor can come to be. Philosophers have conducted a very acute or subtle discussion of these matters in the *Peri hermeneias*, but to insert it into this work would take too long.

Since he says that painters do not contradict the Scriptures, while painters depict many things about which the divine Scriptures are silent and which human beings—not only the learned but also the unlearned—demonstrate to be utterly false, who would not admit that his statement is most ridiculous, or rather most false?

Are they not known to contradict the divine Scriptures when they make the abyss have the form of a human being and pour forth an abundance of floods? Is it not beyond doubt that they contradict the divine Scriptures when they depict the earth in human [Col. 1162B] form, now dry and barren, now overflowing with fruits? Is it not manifest that they contradict the divine Scriptures when they depict rivers in the forms of human beings either pouring out water from jars or flowing one into another?

When they make the sun, moon, and the other ornaments of heaven have human forms and heads encircled with rays, do they not contradict the holy Scriptures in every way? When they assign to the twelve winds individual forms according to the character of their powers; or when, according to the character of the seasons, they give each month a figure bearing something distinctive—some naked, some half-naked, and some clothed in different garments; or when they depict the four seasons of the year, each with a different form, whether spring green with flowers, or summer scorched by heat or laden with grain, or autumn [Col. 1162C] burdened with the lips of the vintage or with clusters of grapes, or winter alternately chilled by frost, warming itself by fires, providing food for animals, or catching birds stiffened by excessive cold—are they not known to contradict the divine Scriptures, in which these things are by no means contained?

How, then, are the holy Scriptures not contradicted by painters who often follow the utterly empty fables of poets? For they sometimes invent events truly done as other and different unbelievable tales. They also invent things that neither happened nor could have happened, but which are either understood mystically by philosophers, worshiped vainly by pagans, or rejected truthfully by Catholics. Although all these things are found in the writings of pagans [Col. 1162D], they are entirely alien to the divine Scriptures.

Is it not alien to the divine writings that the three-headed Chimera is said by them to have been killed by Bellerophon, when Bellerophon did not overthrow a beast, as they falsely claim, but, as many understand, made a mountain habitable? Is it not alien to the divine writings that Erichthonius is said to be the lame Vulcan’s son by Earth, and that he is said to smelt iron on Mount Aetna, whose furnace is said to be Mount Vesuvius in Campania, which is reputed to burn with perpetual fires?

Are not the following alien to the divine Scriptures: that Scylla is represented as girded with canine heads; that Phyllis is said to have been changed into a tree through love for a certain young man; and that the other Scylla, because she cut from her father [Col. 1163A] Nisus the purple lock of hair, is said to have been transformed, together with her father; and that Itys, because of the rape committed by his father against his mother or maternal aunt and the murder of his mother or maternal aunt perpetrated against him, is said to have been changed into birds together with his parents or maternal aunt? Or that the Sirens are represented partly as virgins and partly as birds? Or that Ixion, joining with the Cloud through Juno’s deception, is said to have fathered the Centaurs? Or that Neptune, armed with a trident, is represented as ruling the sea’s waves?

Is it not alien to the divine Scriptures that Perseus is said to have killed the three Gorgon sisters with Minerva’s assistance; or that he is represented flying backward with wings; or that Pegasus, a winged horse, is said to have been born from his blood and is depicted as having broken open a spring for the Muses with his hoof?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Prometheus is said to have fashioned human beings from [Col. 1163B] mud, lifeless; that the same Prometheus is said to have been lifted by Minerva into the sky, among the edges of the sevenfold shield; and that, after seeing all the heavenly things, he is said to have applied a reed to Phoebus’ wheels, stolen fire, and restored life to the body by applying it to the little chest of the human being he had fashioned?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Tantalus is said to have been placed in the underworld in a certain pool, where deceitful water teased his lips with the temptations of gluttony, while fruits, turning to ashes at every attempted touch, appeared hanging above him at face level, and he is said to have seemed rich yet to have become poor?

Is it not alien to the divine Scriptures when Phineus is represented as blind, with the Harpies painted as snatching away his food and defiling his meals with excrement, while Zetes and Calais, the sons of the north wind [Col. 1163C], are falsely represented as having driven them from his sight?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures when Admetus, king of Greece, is depicted as having obtained the assistance of Apollo and Hercules so that, according to the agreement with his father-in-law, he might enjoy Alcestis as his wife, after yoking a lion and a boar together to a chariot? Or when Hercules is depicted as having killed Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that a certain hunter, Actaeon, because he saw Diana bathing, is represented as having been changed into a stag, unrecognized by his own dogs and devoured by their bites?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Berecynthia is depicted as having loved the most beautiful boy Atys and, inflamed by the empty madness of jealousy [Col. 1163D], having castrated him and made him half-male?

Is it not contrary to the divine Scriptures that Orpheus is depicted as having loved the nymph Eurydice and, having won her through the sound of his lyre, taken her as his wife; that she, unable to endure the pursuit of the shepherd Aristaeus, fled, fell upon a serpent, and died; that her husband followed her down to the underworld and received the command not to look back at her; and that, after looking back, he is represented as having lost her again?

Is it not alien to the divine Scriptures that Venus is depicted as having slept with Mars, being discovered by the Sun, betrayed to Vulcan, and bound by him together with Mars in adamantine chains?

These and similar stories—which are tedious for us to recount, but familiar to the poets or philosophers of the pagans for singing pleasant tales [Col. 1164A] or treating mysteries, and familiar to painters for representing—are, as we have said, entirely alien to the divine writings.

To say nothing of the rest: if a painter chooses to depict two heads on one body, or one head on two bodies, or the head of one animal with the remaining members of another—such as a Hippocentaur with an entirely equine body and a human head, or a Minotaur half-bull and half-man—does he not thereby contradict the Scriptures?

What does it mean to say, “Painters do not contradict the Scriptures,” as though painters could not depict certain things that are believed to oppose the sacred writings?

For in the sacred writings nothing vicious, nothing unfitting, nothing impure, and nothing false is found—except, perhaps, where holy Scripture records [Col. 1164B] that wicked people said or did such things. In paintings, however, learned painters depict many false things, many vicious things, many irrational things, many unfitting things, and, to pass over the individual examples, nearly everything possible or impossible.

By these proofs John, priest and legate of the Easterners, is shown to have raved in this matter as in the others.

As for the same priest’s assertion that painters demonstrate whatever Scripture says, the prudent reader should observe how false and useless it is. Do painters demonstrate all the precepts of the divine law given by the Lord through Moses, such as: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI), and the other statements of this kind, in which nothing is expressed that can be painted?

Can painting, according to his folly, demonstrate all the words of the prophets [Col. 1164C], which contain teachings, exhortations, rebukes, contemplations, threats, and other things like these, and in which we frequently find, “Thus says the Lord,” or “The Lord has sworn,” or similar expressions—things that are written by writers rather than by painters?

Can painters demonstrate each individual word of the Lord himself and of the apostles?

Painters can, in a certain way, recall to memory histories of things that happened. But things that are perceived only by the senses and expressed in words can be grasped not by painters but by writers, and can be demonstrated through the reports of others. It is therefore absurd to say: “Painters do not contradict the Scriptures, [Col. 1164D] but whatever Scripture says, they demonstrate.”

As for his assertion, “They are in agreement with the Scriptures,” how foolish and absurd it is can be established by many proofs. What agreement can they have with the sacred Scriptures, since the Scriptures are truthful while painters generally invent falsehoods? Of the Scriptures it is said, “The words of the Lord are pure words” (Ps. XI [12]), while painters sometimes invent impure and incestuous things. The Scriptures always recommend what is honorable and wholesome, while painters often depict what is dishonorable and absurd. The Scriptures always labor for human salvation, while painters generally labor for vanity. The Scriptures always exhort people toward heavenly gifts, while painters frequently depict earthly and perishable things.

For as great as the agreement is between what always rests upon truth and what generally pursues truth but often pursues falsehood [Col. 1165A], so great is the agreement between the divine Scriptures, which always preserve pure and fixed rules, and painters, who, in the manner of mortals, have many variations.

## CHAPTER XXIV

That images are not to be equated with the relics of holy martyrs and confessors, as they attempt to do in their erroneous synod, because relics are either from the body, or from things that were in the body, or from things that were around the body of a saint; whereas images are believed neither to have been nor to be in the body or around the body of those to whom they are attributed.

Accordingly, just as images are in no way to be equated with sacred things—whether those consecrated by the lawgiver, or by God and the mediator between God and human beings, or even those consecrated daily by priests through the invocation of the divine name and taken up into the mystery of our redemption—so too they are not to be regarded as equal to the relics of holy martyrs or confessors, which among the faithful are held in honor out of love for them. Those who have become inflamed with devotion to images strive to equate them with all sacred things and mysteries, full of insolence and absurdity; they likewise strive to equate them with the relics of the holy martyrs.

When, therefore, they attempt to place on the same level as the bodies of the saints—or at least their bodily relics—as well as their garments and similar objects that the saints used while living in the flesh, paintings, engravings, sculptures, or cast objects fashioned by whatever artisans, they are shown to inflict no small injury upon the saints. For the garments of the saints and similar objects are to be venerated especially because they are believed either to have been on those very saints’ bodies or to have been around their bodies, and to have received from them the sanctification on account of which they are venerated. The bodies of the saints, moreover, and even their bodily relics, although they now decay after being reduced to dust, are believed to rise again in glory at the end of the world and to reign eternally with Christ.

Images, however, which those people vainly endeavor to equate with the things just mentioned, cannot in any way be equated with them, because they are neither what the bodies of the saints are nor were they ever in or around their most sacred bodies. Rather, according to the capacity of each person’s skill or according to the tools of craftsmanship, they are made sometimes beautiful, sometimes deformed, and very often even from impure materials. Hence it is clear that those who strive to equate them with the relics of the saints are not making a minor error.

Thus antiquity did not without reason permit the bodies of the saints to be venerated and honor to be shown to their relics. Abraham, the father of the nations, a man full of faith, supreme in devotion, outstanding in obedience, and zealous in the commandments of the Lord, is read to have buried his wife not in just any place but in a field deliberately purchased; and his bones, not in any random place but in a most beautiful cave, in whose interior the first-formed man had been buried, are likewise read to have been laid to rest by his sons according to his command.

Isaac too, born from an aged womb and led forth to be offered to God as a sacrifice in the figure of our Redeemer, a man distinguished for holiness and chastity, is believed to have been buried by his sons beside his father according to his own command.

Jacob likewise, a man of great patience, abundantly strengthened by divine oracles and encouraged by repeated promises, when he wished both to escape the scarcity of famine and to see the beloved child whom he had believed dead, descended with his illustrious offspring to the regions of the Nile. He did not permit himself to be buried there, but ordered that his body be carried back to the land promised to himself and to his fathers, to be buried beside the bones of his father and grandfather. And because he was the fourth to be buried in that same cave, in whose interior Adam had been buried, beside his grandfather and father, he gave the place the name Arbee, that is, “four” (Gen. L).

Joseph too, who through typological mysteries deserved to be called the Savior of the world by the Gentiles, and who shone forth among his brothers in wondrous holiness, commanded the children of Israel to carry his bones to the promised land. The lawgiver did not delay carrying this out precisely because he knew that it was in no way contrary to faith.

When the holy man whose body had come from Judah to Bethel to rebuke the wickedness of the Israelite king was killed by a lion because, through disobedience, he had eaten the city’s forbidden food, he is nevertheless read to have been guarded by that same lion. Once the guilt of disobedience had been expiated by the bitterness of death, the savage beast did not presume to touch the holy body of the prophet whom it had brutally dared to kill.

The prophet of Bethel, therefore, if he had not known that veneration was to be shown to holy bones, would never have ordered himself to be buried beside the bones of the holy man, saying: “Bury me beside the bones of the prophet” (III Kings XIII).

The holy man Josiah—named by name before his birth, destroyer of idols, and zealous observer of the ancestral laws—when he was burning the bones of very many people in order to defile the profane altar, would by no means have ordered the bones of the two prophets to be preserved untouched if he had not known that veneration was to be shown to holy bones.

Behold, then, by these examples, to say nothing of the rest, it has been shown that veneration ought to be offered to the ashes of the saints. Let them say where we are ever commanded to adore images.

To honor the bodies of the saints is therefore a great gain for faith, especially since the saints themselves are believed to live with Christ in the heavenly dwellings, and their bones are believed one day to rise again. To images, therefore, which are not believed ever to have lived or to be destined to rise again, but are said to be consumed either by fire or by decay, to offer the adoration owed to God alone is either an act of sluggishness, if done casually, or madness—or rather unbelief—if defended obstinately.

Thus, neither denying relics with Vigilantius and his followers, nor adoring images with Simon and his accomplices, we offer fitting service both to relics and to the bodies of the saints; we adorn basilicas, as we please, with images of the saints and even with gold and silver; and, with God’s help, we render the service of adoration or worship to God alone, to whom alone it is due.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### That images are not therefore to be adored because, as they say, certain signs are thought to have been displayed through them, since not all things through which or in which miracles appear are nevertheless adored
