They also commonly use this argument to establish their error: they claim that certain miracles were performed through certain images. Yet no page of either the Old or the New Testament demonstrates this. Even if it could be proved that such things had ever been seen or heard, it would nevertheless be necessary to doubt whether they had perhaps merely appeared or been heard through the most winding labyrinths of the crooked serpent, who, being most hideous and covered with the darkness of his wickedness, transforms himself into an angel of light, daring to call himself light.

For many signs and many miracles are performed through fallen angels, or even through their followers. Since they are spiritual powers—or, as I might say, spiritual wickednesses—they both give prophecies to wretched people and perform many wonders through their agents. Such are those who will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” To them the eternal Judge will say: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII).

Since signs are often performed at the devil’s prompting, therefore the most blessed Gregory, bishop of the holy Roman Church, said: “Do not, my brothers, love signs which can be held in common with the reprobate.”

The most holy Augustine likewise testifies in these words that miracles are performed by demons, resembling the miracles performed through the holy servants of God. He says:

> “One ought not to be disturbed when miracles are often performed through magical arts that resemble the miracles performed through the holy servants of God. Thus it is written in Exodus that Pharaoh’s magicians performed certain things in a manner similar to Moses.”

These things, therefore, ought not to surprise us, since everything that occurs visibly may also, not absurdly, be believed capable of being performed through the lower powers of the air. The difference is that when the saints perform such things in the name of God, the Lord of all things, the inferior creature is commanded by higher powers; but when evil people perform similar things through magical arts, they are handed over to their own devices when they are heard by demons.

They are indeed worthy to be deceived by such an answer, so that what they seem to obtain as a benefit may become a punishment for them. For the lower powers display certain miracles to them as though privately, in order to keep them subjected to themselves; nevertheless, by divine permission, each receives according to the merits of his soul.

Therefore, if the signs and miracles that they say appeared in images did not appear—as no authoritative history transmits any such account—then the claim is a lie, and no servant of truth ought to employ a lie, since, as Truth itself says, “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI). But if they did appear, and appeared through certain phantasmal shadows to entice minds, it is most dangerous, lest the ancient enemy, by displaying certain marvels through the craft of his cunning, should deceitfully persuade people to undertake unlawful acts.

If, however, the signs appeared truly—although this is proved by no certain documentary reading—and if the matter is not subject either to their falsehood or, in this respect, to the enemy’s fraudulent machinations, but is proved to have occurred through God’s working, to whom all things are possible and nothing is impossible, then we must carefully observe this: although many wondrous things may be accomplished at God’s command through certain creatures, or even in certain creatures, not everything through which or in which they are done is consequently believed to be worthy of adoration.

For almighty God performed many signs that he displayed to mortals through visible and tangible things in order to soften the hardness of visible and mortal human beings by means of visible things. He did not do this in order to establish the adoration of any particular things, since he commanded that he alone be adored and worshiped.

Was it therefore because the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush in the fire that bushes are to be adored? He did not appear in the bush in order to declare the substance of bushes worthy of adoration, but in order through its thorns to signify the sins for which the law had come. Since a bush has no root armed with thorns, but becomes dense with thorns above, it clearly signifies that sins do not exist by nature. The bush was not consumed by the fire in order to indicate that sins were not to be destroyed by the law, but merely revealed. For the law only reveals sins, whereas grace, which was given through Christ, healed the sins that the law had revealed.

Since the Lord appeared in fire, he did not therefore decree that fire should be adored, but wished to appear in a nature that always strives to rise upward. Since he deigned to appear on a mountain, it is not believed that he established the worship of mountains. Rather, it was rationally fitting that the King of heaven should appear in something that always seeks the heights, and not in a low place but in a high one, so that he might both show himself to be Most High and clearly demonstrate that his followers would ascend to the heights.

Was it therefore because the lawgiver escaped the anger of the terrible Judge and the destruction of death through circumcision performed with a very sharp stone that stones are to be adored? The lawgiver rightly saw an angel so hostile to him because, while dwelling in the land of Midian, he had neglected to circumcise his son. Although he was the messenger of the God of Abraham, he did not bear in his son the sign of Abraham’s faith, in which he knew that the Jews gloried. He was circumcised with a stone not so that the adoration of stones might thereby be established, but so that it might be shown that through Christ, who is the cornerstone, sins must be cut away and the dangers of death escaped.

Was it therefore because the staff is repeatedly read to have been changed into a serpent and repeatedly restored to the stiffness of a staff—signifying through typological figures that Christ returned from life to death and from death to life—or because the same staff, which we have said bore the figure of Christ, divided the waters of the Red Sea, that is, the waters of baptism, and provided the people of God on their journey to the promised land, namely, the heavenly kingdoms, with a passage, that staffs are to be adored?

Was it therefore because the bitter waters are read to have been sweetened by wood—signifying, not without reason, that the law was sweetened by the wood of Christ, and that the minds of the peoples were to be satisfied with spiritual sweetness—that woods are to be adored?

Was it therefore because the sight of the bronze serpent, which prefigured Christ’s death on the wood, saved the people from the bites of serpents—that is, from the deadly persuasions of unclean spirits—that either bronze or serpents are to be adored?

Was it therefore because struck rock produced streams of water in the parched fields and freed the thirsty people from the dryness of thirst—the rock bearing the figure of Christ, who is the stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it, who drives the thirst of unbelief from the minds of the faithful through the streams of evangelical preaching, and who daily cries out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII)—that stones or water are to be adored?

Was it therefore because Aaron’s staff, signifying the birth of the blessed Virgin, having trampled underfoot the natural law and made fruitful without any watering by human action, blossomed, put forth leaves, and produced almonds, that staffs are to be adored?

Was it therefore because, in the case of holy Jerobaal, the dry threshing floor appeared with a wet fleece, or the wet threshing floor with a dry fleece—a miracle clearly signifying the whole Gentile world, untouched by heavenly dew, and Israel alone, the wet fleece, moistened by the rain of the divine word, and afterward, because of the guilt of unbelief, that same people made arid by the dryness of its infidelity, while the Gentile world was drenched with the dew of sacred faith—that either threshing floors or fleeces are to be adored?

Was it therefore because Samson killed a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey, and, when the molar of that same jawbone was pulled out, was satisfied with streams of water—the jawbone bearing the type of our Mediator, who by his death conquered the powers of the air and watered with spiritual streams the parched hearts of the faithful, who are indeed his members—that jawbones or molars are to be adored?

Was it therefore because Elijah is read to have divided the Jordan with his cloak, through which the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was figured and through which the Jordan, that is, the water of baptism, is entered, that cloaks are to be adored?

Was it therefore because Naaman the Syrian was cleansed of the contagion of leprosy in a river bath, through whom the Gentile world was signified as cleansed by Christ’s baptism from the contagion of idols, that rivers are to be adored?

Was it therefore because the coming of the Holy Spirit to the holy man Elisha was delayed until a minstrel was summoned, but when the minstrel had been summoned the Holy Spirit poured himself into his inmost being—a signifying of the Jewish people, who now do not receive the coming of the Holy Spirit because they do not receive in faith the incarnation of the Redeemer, but who, as soon as they accept it near the end of the world, will be adorned with the breath of the Holy Spirit and the gifts of all the charisms—that a minstrel is to be adored?

Was it therefore because the hem of the Lord’s garment, by whose touch a woman received healing, and which, as we have already explained above, signifies belief in the Lord’s incarnation through which the Gentile world was healed, that hems are to be adored? Or because the sick were healed by Peter’s shadow, that shadows are to be adored?

No, therefore, as we stated above, are all things through which or in which certain miracles have been displayed by God’s ordinance to be adored in any way.

If the things in which miracles appeared are not to be adored, then images are even less to be adored, since no authoritative reading demonstrates that any miracles appeared in or through them.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### That Bishop Theodore of Myra acted ridiculously and childishly when, in order to establish the adoration of images, he reported at that same synod the dreams of his archdeacon

Since nearly everything in that vain teaching, which they eagerly seek to have designated as the Seventh Synod, resembles the images of dreams and certain phantastic shadows, and since there is scarcely anything there that does not smell either of the vanity of a dream or of the dullness of some other delirium, and everything tasted by the inner palate yields a certain tasteless and insipid flavor, Bishop Theodore of Myra is nevertheless read to have reported there, in a particularly deluded act, the dreams of his archdeacon. He wished to establish by dream-deceptions the error that he had been unable to support either by the authority of the divine Scriptures or by any teaching or example of the holy Fathers. He thus supplied, not undeservedly, a fitting and almost equal support for stabilizing so frivolous and foolish a matter.

Although the use of dreams is neither to be wholly approved, since it is often produced by the deceptions of demons, nor wholly condemned, since certain mysteries are sometimes revealed through it, it is nevertheless never found suitable for establishing doubtful matters or affirming things that have come into dispute.

For who could ever affirm a doubtful matter by means of his own dream, when he cannot prove by the testimony of any witness whether he saw what he claims to have seen in the manner in which he saw it?

To strengthen a doubtful matter that has come into question, therefore, one must seek not the deceptive vanity of dreams, not the most bitter insolence of apocryphal writings, not the falsehood of frivolous and useless words, but the authoritative testimony of the divine books or of the Catholic Fathers.

For just as useful things adorned with the secrets of mysteries are revealed through angels when they are indicated by dreams, so, conversely, when harmful things devoid of every benefit are displayed through dreams, they are believed to be displayed by demons.

Therefore, if the dream that he reported at the synod was shown to his archdeacon by an angel in order to establish the adoration of images, then it is beneficial to adore images; and if it is beneficial to adore images, then it is beneficial to adore other things lacking sense.

But it is harmful to adore things lacking sense. Therefore, the dream which he reported at the synod was not shown to his archdeacon by an angel in order to establish the adoration of images.

For it is plainly evident that, since it was not shown to him by an angel, it was brought to him by the instigating spirit who is always intent upon vanities and harmful things.

To make this clearer, the argument must be established by reason. If the instigating spirit did not bring it to him, then unquestionably it must be believed that an angel brought it. And if it must be believed that an angel brought it, then angels are shown to consent to forbidden things.

But angels do not consent to forbidden or harmful things, or to things opposed to divine admonitions. Therefore, the instigating spirit must be believed to have brought it to him.

Since it has been proved that it was not presented to him by a holy angel—for spirits who continually remain in praise of their Creator and are entirely free from sin wholly reject impure things subject to wrongdoing—it remains either that he must admit that it was presented to him through the deception of a most wicked spirit, or that he must openly confess that he lied. Neither alternative is fitting for servants of God.

Every Catholic must resist unclean spirits, as the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James IV). And falsehood must be despised, as Scripture says: “Do not wish to lie with every lie, for the constant practice of it is not good” (Ecclus. VII).

Meanwhile, spirits must be tested, according to the Apostle’s teaching, to see whether they are from God; and according to the word of Truth, they are known by their fruits. From the fruit by which that spirit seeks to support the adoration of images, it is most clearly detected that the spirit who brought the dream is not from God.

But lest we seem to assert this solely by our own arguments, let us return to the divine Scriptures and question the lawgiver. Let him say whether dreams are to be accepted; let him say how we ought to act toward dreamers.

Speak, I ask you, holy Moses; speak, gentlest of men; speak, noble man and zealous examiner of God’s secrets; speak, most merciful man and most faithful interpreter of the ineffable God. You received on the mountain a law opposed to sins and hostile to vices, and you brought to the sinful people a face made glorious and a countenance intolerable, so that just as the law you carried was opposed to sins, so your face would be terrifying to those who looked upon it. Speak, illustrious man, who, bearing the type of the true Redeemer, stood as mediator between God and human beings. Give the command: are all dreams to be believed? Say whether agreement is to be given to every kind of suggestion.

“If there arises in your midst a prophet or a dreamer who says that he has seen a dream, and he foretells some sign or wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Come, let us follow other gods whom you do not know,’ do not heed the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, to make known whether you love him with all your heart or not” (Deut. XIII).

Behold, by the authority of the lawgiver we are thoroughly taught that the words of dreamers are not to be heeded, even when they come to pass.

Let Wisdom now say what it thinks about dreams. For it says: “Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities and innumerable words; but you should fear God” (Eccles. V).

The Egyptians too are believed to have been troubled by dreams, as Scripture says: “For the dreams that troubled them” (Wis. XVIII). These things signified that they should not be unaware of why they were suffering evils.

It is evident from the authorities of the divine law that dreams and omens are vain, and that the more a person fears them, the more his heart deceives him.

Therefore we judged it necessary to condemn in every way what the aforementioned bishop did: he, who ought to have fought against dreamers and other vanities with the weapons of the divine law, reported at the synod the dreams of his archdeacon in order to strengthen an useless cause.

This is found to be something to be disregarded not only in the oracles of the divine law but also in the writings of the Gentiles themselves. For the philosopher Cato says:

> “Do not heed dreams; for what the human mind hopes for when awake,  
> it sees that very thing in sleep.”

If someone should perhaps attempt to reproach us because we have inserted the words of Gentiles into our work, let him first read the books of the most blessed and learned men Jerome and Augustine. As soon as he finds in their works not only certain words of philosophers but also words of Gentile poets, he will recognize that we have as teachers and authors those whose footsteps we follow, with whom we neither refuse to be blamed nor blush to be criticized.

To go further back, the chosen vessel himself inserted something from Gentile words into his writings, as in the passage: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (Titus I).

Moreover, when we discuss the observance—or rather the vanities—of dreams, we do not testify that their use should be rejected altogether. Certain most sacred mysteries were shown in dreams, or rather in visions, to patriarchs and prophets; and the three Magi, warned in a dream not to return to the savage tyrant, went back to their own homes by another route. It is also read that an angel appeared in a dream to the holy man Joseph and showed him the secrets of mysteries announced by the prophets many centuries earlier.

Yet lest anyone, on the basis of these and similar examples, should rashly seek the use of dreams, or presume to follow or believe them, recite them in assemblies, or, like Theodore, affirm through them matters that have come into dispute, for this reason, as we stated a little above, their use has been prohibited by the holy Scriptures.

We also read that certain secrets were shown through dreams to unbelieving and profane kings—not revealed to them through any privilege of their own merits, but so that the holy men who showed them these things through the revelation of the Holy Spirit might be exalted in honor and might benefit their fellow captives.

Although common usage has admitted that visions and dreams are often spoken of interchangeably, some say that dreams and visions differ in this respect: dreams are those things that are often deceptive. They therefore sometimes arise from revelation, but much more often either from thought, temptation, or certain similar causes.

Visions, however, are said to be more truthful revelations, of which there are three kinds: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual.

The bodily kind is what occurs through the body. The spiritual kind occurs when we store in memory the images of things that we see. The intellectual kind occurs when we distinguish by the intellect those things that we see bodily and retain imaginatively in memory. By the intellect, therefore, we distinguish that one thing is a body and another is the likeness of a body.

Beasts, cattle, and birds have no such intellect at all. They too see through the body, and their spirits are shaped imaginatively by the things they see. Thus cattle recognize their stalls, and birds return to their nests; but they neither understand themselves nor the things they see with their eyes.

Finally, this bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision. Thus, when we turn our eyes away from things we have seen, we retain in memory the images of things we no longer see.

Spiritual vision, however, cannot exist without bodily vision. Thus we remember people who are absent, and in darkness we imaginatively see things that we do not see.

Intellectual vision requires neither bodily nor spiritual vision. Through the intellect we see neither a body nor the image of a body. Through it, rather, we see justice, charity, God himself, and the human mind itself, which possesses no body and no bodily solidity.

Here should be inserted the discussion of the five kinds of vision according to Theodosius Macrobius.

Since there are so many and such varied kinds of dreams and visions, arising from different sources, one must carefully ensure that, when someone recognizes that he has seen something in a dream, he does not immediately hold fast to it and bring it forward at a synod as some kind of authoritative testimony for deciding doubtful matters. Otherwise, while attempting to strengthen vanity with vanities, he may himself—God forbid—fall into vanity.

## CHAPTER XXVII
### That, since God is not in a place, they spoke very foolishly when they said: “We venerate and adore [images] as the place of God.”

They also say that images are to be venerated and adored as the place of God. If by this they mean the temple of God, which is often called the place of God in an improper sense, they are gravely mistaken. For sacrifices are offered in the Lord’s temple, not in images; the solemn offices of the Mass are celebrated in the temple, not in paintings; in the temple the people, standing and offering to God the libations of their prayers, are heard—not on painted panels. “The Lord is in his holy temple,” says David (Ps. X), not “in his holy image”; nor is he in paintings, but “his seat is in heaven” (Ps. X). Nor does he say, “His eyes look upon the proud or those who seek empty praise,” but, “look upon the poor”: that is, upon the poor of whom Truth itself says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V). And again the same most holy prophet says, “In his temple”—not in images—“all shall speak glory” (Ps. XXVIII); and again, “Adore the Lord,” not in paintings, but “in his holy court” (ibid.). As great as the difference between a temple, which can contain many people, and an image, which, apart from the remembrance of the sight it conveys to those who behold it, is suited to no functions, so great, as many indications make clear, is the difference between the veneration or adoration of images and the veneration shown to God’s temple.

But if by the place of God they mean the soul of a righteous person—which may more properly be called God’s place, since the Lord dwells there by sanctifying it and sanctifies it by dwelling there—they are also most gravely mistaken in this. For God gave the law for the salvation of souls, not for the salvation of images; the Redeemer of the world descended to earth to free souls, not images. It was on account of human beings, who are often figuratively denoted by the name of souls, not on account of images fashioned by artists, that he said to the Father: “Those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which you have given me, because you loved me” (John XVII). Therefore, although God is believed first to have given human beings the natural law, and, when that had been corrupted by human beings, afterwards the written law, and, when that too had been violated, to have presented himself to be seen in bodily presence, and although before the law, under the law, and under grace he is always believed to have provided for human salvation, he is never believed anywhere to have bestowed anything of this kind upon images. Accordingly, the veneration to be shown to human beings for the sake of charity is in no way to be equated with the veneration of images.

Let this brief statement suffice concerning the place of God—whether the temple, which is improperly so called, or the soul of a righteous person, which is more fittingly called God’s place—with neither of which images are in any way to be equated according to their madness. But to discuss the place of God who is not local, who is not contained by a place, who contains all things and is not a place, to whom none of the six parts of place applies, who has nothing prior or posterior, right or left, above or below, belongs to a subtler understanding.

Although the order of the ten categories discussed by philosophers seems to be predicated of him—so that, with respect to his οὐσία (ousia, essence), which is ineffable, he is called Lord God, one God, strong God, mighty God; with respect to his quantity, which is immeasurable, “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy” (I Chron. XVI); with respect to his quality, which is beyond narration, “the good creator of all things” (II Macc. I); with respect to relation, “the Lord of all” and “Father of those who believe in him” (Eph. IV); with respect to position, “you who sit upon the cherubim” (Ps. LXXIX); with respect to time, “and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI); with respect to place, “the Lord has prepared his throne in heaven” (Ps. CII); with respect to habit, “the deep is his garment” (Ps. CIII); with respect to acting, “he raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung-heap” (Ps. CXII); and with respect to being acted upon, “you have made me labour in your sins” (Isa. XLIII)—yet all these and similar expressions are shown to be spoken of God in a human manner, though nothing worthy can be said of him by mortals. For he is a substance not easy for anyone to investigate, and therefore ineffable because unsearchable. He is great without quantity, good without quality, Lord of all without relation, and so forth—matters that require fuller discussion.

But, to say something about the place of God, we should set down the words of Saint Augustine, who proved that God is not in a place by the chain of a single five-part syllogism. He says: “God is not somewhere. For whatever is somewhere is contained in a place; whatever is contained in a place is a body; but God is not a body; therefore he is not somewhere.” Thereafter, in another syllogism, he proved both that God is not a place and that all things are in him. He says: “And yet, because he is and is not in a place, all things are rather in him than he somewhere; yet they are not in him in such a way that he himself is a place. For a place is space occupied by a body in length, breadth, and height; but God is not anything of that kind. Therefore all things are in him, and he is not a place.” Thereafter, in a short and most fitting clause, he asserted that the temple of God is improperly called God’s place, but that the human soul can better be so called: “Yet the temple of God is called the place of God improperly,” he says, “not because he is contained in it, but because he is present to it; and nothing is understood to be better than a pure soul.”

Since, then, they say that images are to be venerated as the place of God, it is inappropriate whether they mean the temple of God or the soul of a righteous person. But if in that expression they conceive something local about God, their understanding greatly departs from the truth. As for us, being ignorant of their thoughts and not knowing with what intention or in what sense they said this, we examine only what we have learned from the evidence of the written words.

## CHAPTER XXVIII
### That the saying, “Whoever fears God honors, indeed adores and venerates, as the Son of God, Christ our God, and his sign of the cross, and the figure of his saints,” is useless, insane, and full of error.

There is also in this statement something utterly insane and wholly devoid of caution: “Whoever fears God honors, worships, or venerates him altogether in the same way as the Son of God, as well as his sign of the cross and the image of his saints.” How greatly the mystery of the Lord’s cross differs from this—the Apostle teaches that we have enlightened eyes in order to understand what is the height, length, breadth, and depth of Christ’s cross—has been shown, with the Lord’s help, in the earlier parts of this work. And how greatly the worship and veneration owed to God alone differ from the worship and veneration which they insist must be offered to images, we have discussed in this third book, examining, insofar as the Lord has deigned to help us, the words of Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, or of Euthymius, bishop of Sardis. Now, with the Lord’s aid, let us briefly discuss how far the fear of the Lord differs from the worship of images.

For they say: “Whoever fears God worships images altogether in the same way as the Son of God.” Are all the patriarchs and prophets, then, to be thought not to have feared God because they rejected the worship of images? Or are the Apostles to be said not to have possessed the fear of God because nowhere are they read to have celebrated the worship of images? Or are the multitudes of the holy martyrs, anchorites, and, generally, all ecclesiastical men, whom we know to have served devotedly in God’s service, to be thought not to have possessed the fear of the Lord because nowhere are they read or shown to have celebrated the worship of images?

For the most holy prophet David did not say that he would teach the worship of images, but the fear of God, when, calling all believers “sons” in the person of Christ, he invited them to come to him with gentle exhortations, saying: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33). Nor does he anywhere attest the worship of images, but rather the holy fear of the Lord, when he says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm 18). Nor does he call blessed anyone who worships images, but the one who fears God, saying: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments” (Psalm 111); and again: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Psalm 127).

For he does not say, as they most absurdly rave, “Whoever fears the Lord worships images”; rather, he says: “Whoever fears the Lord will greatly delight in his commandments.” Hence it is perfectly clear that the fear of the Lord consists not in the worship of images, but in the will and diligent observance of God’s commandments.

Nor does that same holy man testify that the eyes of the Lord are upon those who worship images, but upon those who fear him, when he says: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm 32). Nor does he say, “Worship images, for those who worship them lack nothing”; rather, he says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Psalm 33). Nor does he testify that the beginning of wisdom is the worship of images, but the fear of the Lord, saying: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 1).

This command concerning the fear of the Lord is likewise read as having been instituted through Moses: “Follow the Lord your God,” he says, “and fear him, and keep his commandments, and listen to his voice, and cling to him” (Deuteronomy 13). Among these saving commandments, the worship of images is nowhere read to have been instituted. Since, therefore, the worship of images is found to be forbidden in the divine utterances, it must in no way be equated with the fear of the Lord, which is commended in so many declarations of the divine law.

The order of the argument therefore requires that we briefly arrange the flowers commanding the fear of the Lord, which we have plucked with tireless hand through the immense fields of divine law, so that the reader’s spirit may be delighted by them and that anyone who tries to equate them with the worship of senseless objects may be compelled to assume shame and reverence.

In Proverbs it is said: “The fear of the Lord adds days, but the years of the wicked will be shortened” (Proverbs 10). Again in Proverbs: “The fear of the Lord is the refuge of the righteous, but destruction is for those who do evil” (ibid.). Again in Proverbs: “The fear of the Lord is life to a man, but whoever is without fear will remain in a place unvisited by knowledge” (Proverbs 19). Again in Proverbs: “The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom, and humility precedes glory” (Proverbs 15). Again in Proverbs: “Let your heart not envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord all day long” (Proverbs 23). Again in Proverbs: “Blessed is the man who fears always, but whoever is hard-hearted will fall into evil” (Proverbs 28).

Again in Ecclesiasticus: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; it is formed with the faithful in the womb, created with chosen seed, and recognized with the righteous and discerning” (Ecclesiasticus 1). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “The fear of the Lord will acknowledge knowledge; chastity will preserve holiness and will be justified; it will give the heart gladness and joy” (Ecclesiasticus 1). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “It will go well with the one who fears the Lord, and he will be blessed in the days of his consummation. The fullness of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and the fullness of its fruits has filled his whole house from generation to generation, as have the receptacles of its treasures. The crown of wisdom is to fear the Lord; both are gifts of God” (Ecclesiasticus 1).

Again in Ecclesiasticus: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin, for whoever is without fear cannot be justified” (ibid.). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not be incredulous toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a double heart” (ibid.). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “Those who fear the Lord will not be incredulous toward his word, and those who love him will keep his way. Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts, and in his sight they will sanctify their souls. Those who fear the Lord will keep his commandments and will have patience until his visitation. The fear of the Lord is not to despise a righteous poor man, nor to magnify a sinful rich man” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Again in Ecclesiasticus: “All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and in it is the fear of God” (Ecclesiasticus 19). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “There is no diminution in the fear of the Lord; the fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing” (Ecclesiasticus 40). Again in Ecclesiasticus: “If you do not hold fast to the fear of the Lord with diligence, your house will quickly be overthrown” (Ecclesiasticus 27). Again in Ecclesiastes: “The end of every matter: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12).

Again in Proverbs: “The fear of the Lord hates evil, as well as insult, pride, and the ways of the wicked” (Proverbs 8).

This fear, then, which these testimonies show not to be an indication of the worship of images but an increase of good works, must be held by the faithful. There is also another fear, of which it is said: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4). This is because the former fear drives a person toward every exercise of good works, whereas the fear which love casts out neither tolerates nor permits vigils, fasts, or other practices of this kind, nor does it endure venerable martyrdoms for Christ’s name.

For just as there are two kinds of temptation—one by which a person is deceived, as in the saying, “God tempts no one; he himself is no tempter of evils” (James 1); and another by which a person is tested through divine examination, as in, “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deuteronomy 13), or, “God tested Abraham” (Genesis 22)—as many passages in Holy Scripture are found, through careful investigation, to follow this distinction, so likewise there are two fears: one which love casts out, and another which is the beginning of good works, which love nourishes.

For if the beginning of the fear of the Lord is the worship of images, as they chatter, then it follows that all the saints, who are certainly believed to have feared God, worshiped images. And if all the saints who are truly believed to have feared God worshiped images, then it follows that they transgressed the Creator’s commands, by which he prohibited the worship of creatures and established that he alone should be worshiped. But they must not be thought to have transgressed the Creator’s commands by worshiping creatures. Therefore, the beginning of the fear of the Lord is not, as they chatter, the worship of images.

This proof establishes that the beginning of the fear of the Lord lies not in the worship of senseless objects, but in the observance of the Lord’s commandments. For the one who truly fears God is the person who, rejecting all vanities, shows by faith and works that he will serve him alone.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
The utterly insane and irrational statement of John the presbyter, in which he says that, when the emperor is not present, his image is honored and not dishonored, just as even now the image of Jesus Christ, ruler of all, who is not visibly apparent to us—for he is invisible to our bodily eyes—is to be honored because God is everywhere present; so the Father thought also of the emperor.

[Col. 1178A]

The matter of their general claim—that either all of them said, or agreed with those who said, that, following the example of imperial images, which bands of people go out to meet in the cities with candles and incense, the image of the Savior and likewise of all the saints ought also to be worshiped—has already been discussed above. It has also been demonstrated, in the words of blessed Jerome, that the images of judges and emperors, from which they attempt to derive their examples, ought not to be worshiped.

Now, however, we must examine John’s words in particular. In this affair he is found to have spoken more frequently than the others and to have raved no less than they did. Although he follows the general error of them all, he nevertheless attempts to add something distinctive to that error. And, as I think, he took care to associate his own absurdities more and more with their general nonsense because he did not believe that all their vanities were sufficient to heap upon so great an error.

As though, then, God were local in the same way as an emperor, and, while he is in one place, could not be in another, he endeavors to establish that God’s image should be worshiped like the emperor’s image. But all reason utterly forbids this. God is never absent from anywhere. If he is absent from somewhere, he is local; if he is local, he neither contains all things nor fills all things. But he completes and fills all things. Therefore, he is absent nowhere. Since this is so, he is not to be worshiped or sought in material images, but must always be held in the purest heart.

For if it is perverse to worship the emperor’s image, then it is also profane to liken the image of one who is local to the image of God, who is nonlocal. It is therefore plainly profane and perverse to attempt to reinforce one illicit thing by means of another illicit thing and, unable to control the reins of his mind or tongue, to run weakly—alas!—toward worse things, as though down steps of error.

But when he says, “The Father judged that Christ’s image should be honored just as the emperor’s image,” we must ask where, when, why, or how the Father judged this, or what “judged” means here. Did the Father judge this when it had been commanded by someone else, or when it was done by others?

Since we are not examining the errors contained in their words—for that would be immense and difficult to carry out, especially since scarcely any order of words there conveys a meaning to the reader—but are merely passing judgment on their meanings or propositions, it remains for us to consider not what they say, particularly since what has been said scarcely has any meaning, but what they intend to say.

By saying that the Father judged Christ’s image worthy of honor just as the emperor’s image, he intends this meaning: “The Father commanded that Christ’s image be worshiped like the emperor.” But where, when, why, or how this happened is utterly unknown to every Catholic.

For the Father commanded not that his image, but that Christ himself should be honored and heard, when at the waters of the Jordan the Holy Trinity appeared wondrously in the unity of substance: the Father in the voice with which he thundered, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3); the Son in the body; and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.

Suppose the Father had commanded that Christ’s image be honored like the emperor. Would it not have been more fitting to decree that the emperor be honored like Christ’s image, so that Christ’s image would occupy the higher position in such a comparison? The Father, therefore, is nowhere read to have commanded that Christ’s image be made, worshiped, or honored, since he established that he alone should be worshiped and served.

That emperors and kings are to be honored by their subjects can be demonstrated by certain examples from Holy Scripture. For if they were not to be honored, the holy man David would never, after God had departed from Saul, have called Saul “the Lord’s anointed” (1 Samuel 26; 2 Samuel 1). That man was not ignorant that the office of royal authority was a divine dispensation. Therefore, he honored Saul while he still held that dignity, lest he appear to injure God, who had decreed that honor be shown to such offices. So long as a person holds that dignity, he must be honored, if not for his own sake, then for the sake of the office.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Be subject to the higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13). And in another place: “Fear God; honor the king” (1 Peter 2).

A fuller discussion could arise from this reasoning, but since some of it has already been discussed in the earlier parts of this work, we must now pass over it and move on to other matters.

## CHAPTER XXX  
On the fact that they inserted into their statements certain apocryphal and ridiculous fables.

If someone building a wooden house wishes to adorn its walls with marble panels or to decorate them with fragments of many-colored glass, but sees that these materials cannot by nature adhere to wood, he sets aside the metals that cannot by nature adhere to wood and again tries to complete the work with wood. Or if someone wishes to make a vessel of tin but lacks a supply of the same material, he does not seek materials of other precious metals that cannot adhere to tin; rather, he seeks more tin to complete the work he has begun.

In the same way, when they tried in their synod to enlarge the instrument of their error—namely, the writing composed in support of the worship of images—and realized that the divine Scriptures could not adhere to it, they turned their pen to dictating certain apocryphal and laughable fables. When they saw that the testimonies of the divine law, applied incompetently to the same undertaking, could not adhere to it, they fitted to it statements that could not differ from it in either meaning or wording.

For just as the most precious emerald set into a ring of iron, or a strip of gold-woven cloth sewn onto a covering of goats’ hair, is wholly incongruous, so the testimonies of the divine utterances, applied to their work, are utterly unsuitable to it.

A doubtful matter that has become the subject of controversy should not be supported by the fables of apocryphal writings, but by the declarations of the divine law, or by the salutary admonitions and lucid teachings of those teachers who are accepted by the catholic and apostolic Church.

But perhaps some extremely insistent defender of this error will say: “They did not insert statements from apocryphal books into their work in order to confirm the matter under discussion; rather, they inserted them as insults, to mock the madness of certain heretics.” Our writing can easily reply to him.

When they say that an image of Polemon—something reported by no authentic reading—restrained someone from crime, are they insulting anyone? In that same reading, then, there are some things which they put forward to affirm the matter at issue. There are also many things which, although they may have inserted them as insults, are so confused, so disordered, so extravagantly expressed, and so jumbled together that it can scarcely be discerned, and scarcely reach the reader’s mind, whether the words being spoken belong to those who are insulting or to those who are professing belief in what is said.

Even if learned people understand the matter in the way described, it is said to produce scandal among some unlearned people—and not without reason—for it is so concealed by incompetence that it can scarcely be understood.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
The error-filled ravings concerning a certain recluse who is said to have sworn to a demon and then invalidated that same oath, whose abbot is recognized to have raved no little, saying that it would be more advantageous for him to enter all the brothels in the city than to deny the worship of the image of the Lord or of his holy mother.

[Col. 1180C]

We are often compelled in this work to say that examples should by no means be taken from harmful actions. We repeat this so frequently because we find that they repeatedly did this in order to affirm their error. For just as examples of good actions appropriately provide support for good actions, so they seek support for erroneous actions from the erroneous actions of others.

To establish the error at issue, they produce the example of a certain recluse. If he acted as they assert, he is known to have committed a threefold offense in this matter: either because he willingly obeyed the demon’s address, or because, at the demon’s instigation, he bound himself by an oath, or because he invalidated that oath. These three acts must not merely not be brought forward as an example; they must be utterly rejected by every Catholic, since they are forbidden by many testimonies of the divine law.

Associations and seductions not only of demons but also of evil men are prohibited by many precepts of the divine utterances. For it is written in Exodus: “You shall not listen to a vain report”; and in Proverbs: “My son, let wicked men not deceive you.” If the seductions of evil men are to be avoided, much more must the words and assent of wicked spirits be avoided, since they are enemies of humanity and always hostile to us. We must therefore always be as suspicious of their deception and as ready to resist their wickedness as we know them to be of subtler nature and intelligence.

In swearing to the demon, he also acted contrary to the divine words by which oaths are prohibited. For it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not accustom your mouth to oaths, for many are the dangers connected with them. Just as a servant is not freed from a bruise through constant questioning, so everyone who swears and continually invokes the name will not be cleansed from sin. A man who swears excessively will be filled with iniquity, and punishment will not depart from his house” (Ecclesiasticus 23).

The Truth himself also says in the Gospel: “But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matthew 5).

Moreover, since he is said to have perjured himself before that same demon, he is also revealed to have acted absurdly in this respect. For the Lord says through Moses: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, and you shall not profane the holy name of your God: I am the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19). And in the prophet Zechariah it is written: “Do not love a false oath, for all these things I hate, says the Lord almighty” (Zechariah 8).

Since this same recluse committed these three acts contrary to the divine words, his abbot offered him no correction whatsoever. Instead, he showed him a worse path of sin, saying: “It is more advantageous for you to enter all the brothels in the city than to deny the worship of the image of the Lord or of his holy mother.”

O incomparable absurdity! O destructive evil! O madness to be preferred to many other forms of madness! He says it is more advantageous to commit an act forbidden by both the Law and the Gospel than to abstain from something which is established by neither the Law nor the Gospel. He says it is more advantageous to commit a crime than to abstain from crime. He says it is more advantageous to plunge oneself willingly into deep filth than to keep one’s foot unhindered upon the path of the straight road. He says it is more advantageous to violate the temple of God than to reject the worship of senseless things. He says it is more advantageous to take Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute than to reject the worship of any work of an artisan.

Let him say, if he can find it anywhere, that the Lord said, “Do not deny the worship of an image,” just as it is perfectly clear that he said, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20). Let him say, if he can find it anywhere, that the Lord said, “If you see an image and do not worship it, you have sinned,” just as it is most plainly established that he said, “If you look at a woman in order to desire her, you have already committed adultery with her in your heart” (Matthew 5).

When he finds none of these things, let him recognize that he has gravely erred by allowing so disgraceful an act to avoid something fruitless. For while the Lord is understood, both through the Law, to command the girding of the loins over the breasts—that is, the cutting away of lusts in the heart—and through the Gospel, to gird the loins and hold lamps, joining good works to chastity, and while the books of the divine utterances give commandments concerning chastity, nowhere is anything of this kind found to have been commanded concerning the worship of images.

Thus, when the recluse’s abbot—who ought certainly to have provided him with guidance toward salvation—loosed the reins of sin for him, and when the man who ought to have drawn him back from the snare of error into which he had sworn to the demon himself fell with him into the abyss of error, declaring that he ought more advantageously to commit a most serious crime, he undoubtedly fulfilled the Gospel saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew 15).

Whoever therefore wishes to support his assertion by such an example demonstrates not that his madness is moderate, but that it is stronger than all the others.

Since, then, the persistence of their absurdity, the continual flow of their nonsense, and even the heap of their ravings find no pauses in the volume whose errors we are discussing, let them at least find rest in the interval between these books, which lies between the end of one and the beginning of another. Thus, just as their error is examined through continuous discussion, so the continuity of the books may in some way be divided by an interval.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1181]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1181D]

With the Lord’s help, three books of this discussion have now been completed. In them, certain testimonies of the divine law have been restored, briefly but according to their proper meanings and in accordance with the teaching of the holy Fathers; the confession of our faith, although written in pedestrian language, has nevertheless been set down with the sincere firmness of apostolic tradition; and the madness of those who, attempting to introduce new institutions into the Church, judge that senseless objects ought to be worshiped has in some measure been examined.

Reason now compels us to proceed to a fourth book, in which whatever chapters concerning their vanities remain are to be examined, with the Lord’s help.

For, avoiding a tumultuous and disordered manner of speaking, we arranged the number of the books; and, pursuing brevity, we extended the discussion of this work to no more than four books. Avoiding both the excessive length of a few books and the excessive shortening of many, we fixed the course of our discussion at this number, which we have found to be wholly consecrated by the testimonies of the divine utterances.

The number four is commonly approved by natural philosophers in their laborious investigation of the elements and of the whole structure of the world, and even of the human body—matters about which it would now take too long to speak—and it is shown to be most sacred by the divine writings, which testify that many things consecrated and pertaining to mystery have been confined within this same number.

For four rivers flow forth from the one spring of paradise; four Gospels proceed from the source of light and the origin of goodness; and four virtues—namely prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—are described as governing human life by the most honorable rules.

The ark, too, was made of squared timber, in which the life of the human race and of all living creatures was preserved amid waters that destroyed everything. Even now the ark of the holy Church, which floats upon the stormy waves of the temptations of this age and contains both the elect and the reprobate, is strengthened by squared timbers—that is, by holy men adorned with the virtue of patience. Their life stands firm in whichever direction it is turned, because they are not cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity.

Following in their footsteps, avoiding novelties of expression, rejecting the worship of senseless things, offering the service of worship to God alone, and bestowing upon his saints the honor appropriate to them, we hope that in our patience we shall possess our souls.

## CHAPTER I  
The utterly false and laughable statement of John the presbyter, who is known to have raved no less than the others in the worship of images. For he says: “Whoever worships an image and says, ‘This is Christ, the Son of God,’ does not sin.”

John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners has provided us with abundant material for discussion in this work. Among the other absurdities of his profession, he neither avoided being deceived in this matter under discussion, nor feared to deceive, nor was ashamed to lie or to encourage others to lie.

He did not avoid being deceived when, setting aside the path of the holy Scriptures, which enjoin the worship and adoration of the one and only God, he wandered through precipitous and crooked ways and diverted the step of his mind toward the worship of senseless things. He did not fear to deceive when, through many assertions—or rather, through vanities—he persuaded others to abandon the straight path which he himself had neglected and to wander with him through impassable places. Nor was he ashamed to lie and to exhort others to lie, since he asserted that committing an illicit act and uttering a lie were not sins.

For he says: “Whoever worships an image and says that this is Christ, the Son of God, does not sin.”

This vanity can be resisted by a very simple argument. If saying what is not the case is not a lie, then saying what is the case cannot be truth. Consequently, if lying is not a vice, neither is speaking the truth a virtue; and if speaking and pursuing the truth is a virtue, then undoubtedly lying and following falsehood is a vice.

Therefore, when someone says that a painting is Christ, the Son of God, he lies; when he lies, he acts wrongly; and when he acts wrongly, he sins. Thus, when he says that a painting is Christ, the Son of God, he sins.

For no painting whatsoever assumed humanity for the sake of our salvation, nor allowed itself to be scourged and crucified for us. No image whatsoever, having escaped the power of death and despoiled the depths of Erebus, rose from the tomb. Nor did any work of an earthly artisan ascend bodily into heaven and sit at the right hand of God the almighty Father, while the Apostles, instructed by saving admonitions and sent throughout all the crossroads of the world to preach, bore witness to it.

All these things were accomplished not by any painting, but by Christ, who is the only Son of God the Father, ineffably begotten by the Father before the ages, sent to earth at the end of the ages for the salvation of humanity. He is the one anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions; he is the one who, according to the Apostle, reconciled all things through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth; and before him every knee bows, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

Consequently, if anyone worships an image and says, “This is Christ, the Son of God,” he not only sins but also acts wickedly in his madness, attempting to apply the most exalted name of so great a reality—if indeed it is permissible to call it a reality, rather than the origin or cause of all realities—to something so base and abject, something lacking not only in mysteries but also in life.

For just as no image can be equal to Christ in nature, so it cannot be equal to him in name. If someone should perhaps think that the reasoning concerning equivocal names can be applied here, let him know that the statement we are now examining is far removed from the reasoning concerning equivocal names.

It is one thing to say “a painted man and a real man,” or “a painted lion, a real lion, and a heavenly lion,” and another to acknowledge an image as Christ, the Son of God. In the former case there is merely a similarity of names; here there is the complete meaning of an explicit profession. For the logic of equivocal names has a commonality only in the name itself. As soon as it reaches definition, the definition most clearly reveals what the commonality of the name had concealed by the mere sound of the word.

As we have said, it is one thing—entirely different—to call a painting by the name of the thing of which it is an image, merely according to the logic of equivocal names; it is another thing to worship a senseless object and to profess and say, with a complete statement, “This is Christ, the Son of God.”

For if, as he admitted, uttering such a lie is not a sin, then committing any illicit act is no sin; and if committing any illicit act is no sin, then the force of the holy Scriptures, which certainly command abstention from illicit acts, must be thought to have collapsed.

But the force of the holy Scriptures, which command abstention from all illicit acts, must not be thought to have collapsed. Therefore, uttering such a lie is a sin.

Since almost every lie uttered with the intention of deceiving is a sin, this particular lie is all the more a sin, because it endeavors to give so base a thing the name of so great a reality. And how could anyone attempt to make a senseless object bear the confession which the shepherd of the Church made to the same Redeemer, and which every holy catholic and universal Church makes to him daily—the confession through which it is saved and receives the pledge of its salvation?

Just as the other vices, so also the vice of lying is prohibited by the teachings of the divine Scriptures. Therefore, whoever obeys John’s instructions—worshiping images and calling those same images Christ, the Son of God—not only practices wicked futility but also shows himself to be undisciplined.

If this crime is committed, as he asserted, what is said through the voice of the Lord in Jeremiah’s prophecy will be fulfilled: “Falsehood and not faith has prevailed over the earth, because evils have gone forth from the wicked, and they have not known me.”

Paul, that outstanding preacher, also urges us in these words to put away lying and speak the truth. For he says in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4). Again, the same Apostle says to the Colossians: “Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3).

The apostle John also says: “Every lie is not from the truth” (1 John 2). Hence it is plainly evident that, if a painting is not Christ, the Son of God, as he urges one to admit, then what is said is a lie; and if what is said is a lie, then, according to the Apostle’s words, it is not from the truth.

Since such a profession is a lie, it is undoubtedly not from that same truth which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14).

The worship of adoration must be offered to God alone, and the confession of the Son of God to him alone who is truly his Son, coessential with him and not adopted.

If, however, the particle “here” (hic) in the same place is used as an adverb of place rather than as a pronoun, the statement can in some fashion stand, since God is everywhere.

## CHAPTER II  
On John’s incorrect statement: “Through the image that appears through colors, his power is worshiped and glorified, and we shall call to mind his presence on earth.”

This same John the presbyter, mentioned so often, did not hesitate to add this folly also through his frivolous arguments, saying that through an image which appears by means of colors the Lord’s power is worshiped—as though the Lord were in need of anything, and as though through some object he caused his power, which has no need of anything, to be worshiped.

When, under the name of heaven or light, he created the first of all creatures, the angelic nature—which is believed to have worshiped and praised God’s power from the very beginning of its creation—because human beings did not yet exist, nor indeed any materials from which images could be painted, are we therefore to believe that they neither worshiped nor praised the Lord’s power? Scripture says: “When all the stars were created, all my angels praised me together.” Here it is clearly shown that God’s power has always been praised and worshiped not through an image which appears by means of colors, but through his ineffable power.

After the creation of human beings, while the art of painting had not yet developed in the world, was the Lord’s power never worshiped by any of the saints? Indeed, neither righteous Abel, nor Enoch, nor Noah, nor any of the saints who are said to have lived in that age, is believed to have worshiped the Lord’s power through an image or through colors, since in the still-primitive world there was not yet any knowledge of certain worldly arts.

Since there are many regions of the world in which human beings are unfamiliar with the art of painting, are we to believe that there the Lord’s power is not worshiped? The Lord’s power is therefore worshiped not through an image which appears by means of colors, as he dreams, but through his ineffable power, by which the whole structure of the world is recognized to have been created.

His power is also worshiped not through certain materials, but through his Word—namely, his Son, whom he ineffably begot before the ages, and through whom and in whom he created all things. He is the right hand and power of the Father. Just as the creation of all creatures is established as having been accomplished through this power, so also perpetual worship is celebrated to him by angels and human beings. For just as he is the cause of all creation, so he is also the most just and fitting cause of worship.

Therefore the holy and universal Church confesses that we mortal human beings worship God—not through images made from colors, as the aforementioned John is evidently nauseated by the thought of, nor through ethereal powers, but through Christ the Lord. As it celebrates the mysteries of our redemption, it declares that it is worthy, just, right, and salutary that we should always and everywhere give thanks to him, through whom angels praise the ineffable majesty of the Father, dominions worship, powers tremble, and the heavens and the host of heaven are known to sing a hymn of glory with sweet-sounding melody and humble confession.

His power, therefore, is worshiped not through a color-bearing image of him, but through his most sacred and life-giving incarnation. His might is worshiped not through a painting, but through his works: through those deeds by which he deigned to take the form of a servant, to be born of a virgin, to restore hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, walking to the lame, health to lepers and to others burdened by the afflictions of disease, life to the dead, and light to the blind; to strip the underworld, destroy the dominion of death, rise from the grave, and ascend into heaven.

These are the instruments through which Catholics worship the Lord’s power; these are the defenses by which the faith of the Church is protected; this is the confession from which anyone who dissents is endangered, but which anyone who retains in his heart obtains everlasting salvation. This is the perpetual memorial by which the minds of the faithful always behold Christ with their inward eyes. To the full knowledge of these things one comes not through painting, but through faith, hope, and love.

Since, then, the same John, as I suppose, obscured by the cloud of his ignorance, said one thing while wishing to say another, is what has been said against his words sufficient? Nevertheless, we must turn the foot of this discussion toward what he intended to say, so that both what he asserted unwillingly and what he tried to say deliberately may be shaken by the fist of this work, armed with rational weapons. In this way the reader may recognize that, through argument, we have both understood what ought to be said though it was obscured by inappropriate words, and crushed what was plainly expressed for understanding. [Col. 1187A]

When he says, “Through an image which appears by means of colors the Lord’s power is worshiped,” we infer that he wished to say: “When an image assembled with colored pigments is seen, the Lord’s power is worshiped.” He almost made this clear in what follows, when he says: “And we shall come to remember his presence on earth.”

We can very easily object to this proposition that neither by the reading of the holy Scriptures nor by the examples of the Fathers has it been established that God ought to be sought in manufactured objects. David says: “In my heart, not in images, I have hidden your words; with my whole heart I have sought you, O God; do not reject me from your commandments” (Psalm 118). Moses says: “Place the words of the Lord in your hearts.” And the Lord says through the prophet: “Turn to me with your whole heart” (Joel 2). Conversely, he says of the reprobate: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29).

From this it is understood that God is to be sought not in visible things, not in manufactured objects, but in the heart; and that he is to be seen not with bodily eyes, but only with the eye of the mind.

For what madness is it to say: “Through an image which appears by means of colors his power is worshiped, and we shall come to remember his presence on earth”? Wretched is the memory which, in order to remember Christ—who ought never to depart from the breast of a righteous person—needs an imaginary vision. Nor can such a person have Christ’s presence within himself in any other way than by seeing an image of him painted on a wall or on some material object. Such a memory, fostered by images, does not arise from love in the heart but from the necessity of sight. For it is not inward love that kindles this person to remember Christ; rather, it is necessity that leads him, through vision, to recall to mind even hated things as soon as he sees them painted, however imperfectly.

Therefore, those who are so constrained by this necessity that, unless they see paintings, they can scarcely remember Christ are to be feared—unless, perhaps, they have lost the common light of this world while still alive because of some bodily affliction, or have by some accident been deprived of paintings, which cannot always be possessed, and so utterly forget Christ, who ought always to be before their eyes.

## CHAPTER III. On what they say: that one must not be scandalized because lamps and fragrant incense are made before images of the saints

Finally, since the same synod whose reading we have undertaken to impress upon the reader recommends many things to which no sane person will dare give assent, tries to dissuade people from many things from which no sound-minded person will attempt to withdraw his practical support, condemns many things which are entirely worthy of praise, and conversely praises many things which are wholly worthy of condemnation, it also warns that no one should be scandalized because lamps are arranged and incense burned before images—as though those people were not themselves scandalized who light lamps before objects devoid of light and offer fragrant incense to things devoid of smell.

Those are the ones who are scandalized: they offer, and urge others to offer, to senseless objects the things that ought to be offered worthily to God. Yet they claim that we ought to be scandalized by them, because they fear that their madness will be reasonably mocked by us; and while they think that we regard them as deserving of criticism, they boast that they are displaying zeal for our salvation.

They fear, then, that we will suffer scandal in this matter, and they think that they are earnestly engaged in good works. But this scandal on our part will harm us to exactly the degree that the presentation of that insolent service benefits them. For it is surely demanded by the order of things that the images mentioned above be compelled to bestow upon them a return for the service rendered, corresponding to the sense of honor which they are known to perceive, although they are entirely without sensation.

Perhaps, however, wishing to invalidate this assertion of ours, they will say: “Why do you mock those who arrange lamps and burn incense before images devoid of sensation, when we likewise arrange lamps and burn incense in basilicas, which are equally devoid of sensation?”

A ready answer may be given to them. It is one thing for places dedicated to divine worship to be illuminated by lamps, and for the smoke of prayers and incense to be offered to God in those same places; it is another thing to offer light to an image that has eyes but sees nothing, and to burn incense before one that has nostrils but smells nothing.

It is one thing to venerate places dedicated to divine worship, and another to offer lamps and incense to paintings adorned with whatever colors. It is one thing solemnly to venerate a house of the Lord’s majesty, built by the faithful and dedicated by a bishop; it is quite another—indeed, utterly different—to kiss images produced by various painters and irrationally presented with gifts.

“For my house,” says the Lord, “shall be called a house of prayer” (Isaiah 56). Elsewhere he says: “Gifts will be accepted upon my altar, and my house of prayer will be honored” (Isaiah 60).

That place is to be exalted with many honors where faithful peoples gather from every direction, where their supplications are heard through God’s mercy, where the mysteries of our salvation are celebrated, and where a sacrifice of praise is offered to God; where, for the offering of sacrifices to God, brought by faithful peoples through the hands of priests, an angelic gathering takes place; where the harmonious chorus of psalm-singers frequently resounds with sweet melody; where the waves of divine reading sound forth, watering hearts made dry.

Finally, in many of those places where people glory in offering lamps and incense to images—and where we, because we refuse to do so, are thought to suffer scandal—the places dedicated to divine worship are so neglected that, as we have learned from reports brought by our envoys, both those sent in the time of my father, the most illustrious man of revered memory, and those whom we ourselves have dispatched to those regions, many basilicas in their lands lack not only lamps and incense but even roofs.

Yet in the kingdom granted to us by God, basilicas, with the help of him who deigns to preserve them, abound in gold and silver, gems and pearls, and other most beautiful furnishings. We who refuse to arrange lamps and burn incense before images adorn the places dedicated to divine worship with precious objects.

## CHAPTER IV. On what they say: that the person who rejects images is guilty of the same crime as Nebuchadnezzar, who brought out the bones of the kings of Judah from their tombs, tore out the eyes of the Jewish king after killing his sons, and removed the cherubim from the Temple

[Col. 1189A]

As we have often said, breaking images contemptuously, or worshiping them by offering lamps and incense, is sanctioned by no genuinely authoritative reading, nor is it shown by the example of any saint to be something that ought to be done. This is especially so since some holy Fathers prohibited both breaking them and worshiping them—and rightly so, because it is wholly contrary to caution for those who convene synods to do either of these things: either to abolish them unnecessarily or to worship them inappropriately.

Those who reject them therefore say that they are guilty of the same crime as Nebuchadnezzar, who, when the sins of the Israelite people had grown strong and the anger of a dreadful judgment pressed upon him, destroyed the kingdom of Judah, overthrew the walls of the once-holy city, and, after demolishing all the beauty of the Temple, also cast down the cherubim.

But if this were so, the crime could not fall upon us, since we permit images to remain among the ornaments of the Church while rejecting their worship in every way. Rather, it would fall upon their predecessors or ancestors, who broke the images formerly used as basilica ornaments and decreed that they should be completely abolished.

The judgment in this matter therefore appears to hang so precariously over them that whatever they produce from it as the more troublesome and detestable charge seems inevitably to condemn either themselves or their predecessors. Since they reject their ancestors on account of the abolition of the images, while boasting that they themselves possess a great preeminence of merit on account of their worship of them, neither can be equated in praise with the builders of that venerable Temple, nor can the ancestors of the others be equated in guilt with its destroyers.

For just as there is a difference between the temple of the Most High God, built in the time of the prophets by illustrious men, and certain images made by whatever craftsmen, so without doubt there is a difference between the destroyers of that Temple and those who despise images.

But while by true reasoning we criticize both those who decree that images must be worshiped inappropriately and their ancestors, who rejected them altogether without due caution, it remains for us to demonstrate that the destroyers of the Lord’s Temple were entangled in far greater—and much greater—crimes than those who despise images.

The Prophet was not lamenting the abolition of images of the sort whose worship they glory in; rather, by prophetic inspiration he looked far into the future toward the destruction of the Temple, which had not yet been founded, and of the city that surpassed other cities, and lamented it in song as though it had already occurred, saying:

“Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Why has your anger raged against the sheep of your flock? Remember your congregation, which you established from the beginning” (Psalm 73).

He calls the destroyer of that same most sacred Temple an enemy, not one who despises images, when he continues:

“How greatly has the enemy acted wickedly in your sanctuaries, and all who hate you have gloried” (ibid.).

He does not lament signs placed in paintings, but rather hostile standards—namely, the banners of the Chaldean or Roman armies—set up in the Lord’s court, saying:

“In the midst of your court they set up their signs, and they did not recognize the signs, as though they were placed in the way above the summit” (ibid.).

He does not lament that the doors of painters, or of certain craftsmen, or even the materials of painted panels, were cast down with axes and adzes; rather, he laments that the most sacred doors of the Lord’s Temple, in which the Holy of Holies was located, were cut down by hostile forces, saying:

“As in a forest of trees, they cut down its doors with axes; with a double-edged axe and an adze they demolished them” (ibid.).

He does not pursue with anguish the burning or defilement of certain images, but rather the Lord’s sanctuary, saying:

“They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling-place of your name on earth” (ibid.).

Nor, when he sang similar things with mournful melody in another psalm, did he pray that the Lord’s anger be poured out upon those who despise images; he prayed against the destroyers of the city or Temple, and against the devastators of the entire Israelite people, saying:

“How long, O Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire forever? Pour out your anger upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name, because they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place” (Psalm 78).

He does not speak of those who despise paintings, but under the name of the Edomites he speaks of all the nations hostile to the Israelite people:

“Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations’” (Psalm 136).

Nor does he threaten those who despise the worship of images, but under the name of the daughter of Babylon he threatens the Chaldean or Roman people:

“Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the repayment you gave us; blessed is the one who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rock” (Psalm 136).

Nothing of this sort is found anywhere concerning those who despise images.

Many similar statements are found in the oracles of the prophets concerning the destroyers of the Lord’s Temple or of the city of Jerusalem, but we omit them for the sake of brevity. The Lord and our Redeemer, too, is read to have wept over the future ruin of that Temple and city.
