Although all these things, overshadowed by mystical figures, can be understood as referring to the destroyers of the Church or of the soul—those who continually strive to overthrow the virtues of the soul, like walls by whose protection one fights against vices, and the faith established in the breast, like a temple in which pure sacrifices are offered to God, while also attempting to cast down pure thoughts and certain exercises of good works like a people—nevertheless, historically they are understood to have been spoken about the destruction of the aforementioned Temple.

From this it is perfectly clear that although their ancestors were in some measure incautious in removing images from the ornaments of the basilicas, they are in no way to be equated with the destroyers of that most sacred and revered Temple. In the former there was levity; in the latter, atrocity. In the former, ignorance; in the latter, wickedness. The former, thinking that they were rendering service to God, removed the images from the ornaments of the basilicas; the latter, provoking against themselves the God who was angry with his people, cruelly destroyed his house.

Putting both groups aside, then, with God’s help, we adorn the places dedicated to divine worship and offer the service of worship to God alone.

## CHAPTER V. That the letter which they foolishly attribute to Saint Simeon, sent to the emperor Justinian, differs greatly from the divine Scriptures and from the teachings of the holy Fathers, both in what it says to the aforementioned emperor—“For these things, remembering them, we report them to your divine ears”—and in that it forbade the same emperor to show mercy

The disgraceful cunning of heretics often records certain things that persuade people toward error in written documents and labels them with the names of certain reputable and approved men, so that they may more easily offer an intoxicating cup, coated with honey, for the ignorant to drink.

It is therefore to be feared that the letter which they attribute to a certain Saint Simeon, from which they produce testimonies to establish their error, may not contain the words of a holy man but rather those of some crafty contrivance. Indeed, we and other orthodox people doubt it for this reason: its speech in certain places contradicts the teachings of the holy Scriptures. We do not dare to take its reading as testimony for confirming doubtful matters when we know that it opposes the institutions of divine law.

We do not remember having read anything more of its text anywhere except what we found marked out by them in their book. Although it lacks elegance of thought and wording and gives off the scent of some tasteless and rustic composition, we nevertheless wish to reproduce it as we found it in their book.

They say that the aforementioned Saint Simeon—whose life and preaching remain unknown to us—wrote the following to the emperor Justinian on behalf of certain Samaritans who had inflicted injury upon images:

“For these things, remembering them, we report them to your divine ears.”

And again:

“I do not have what he says, those who presume such things, unless one act of humanity has been done among them; therefore we beseech your victorious power not to show mercy to those who have presumed this, nor to spare them, nor to accept any entreaty or reply on their behalf.”

And shortly afterward:

“But I adjure you, Lord, by Emmanuel, the exalted God, not to delay, nor to be slow even for a little, in carrying out vengeance.”

And again:

“Those whom he will receive, their kinships being darkness for condemnation; he awaits them to consume them with unquenchable and dark fire; and let the holy and almighty Spirit of Jesus Christ our Lord, who proceeds from the Father, anathematize them in the lower regions of the abyss, to destroy them in infinite destruction.”

And shortly afterward:

“In him who reigns together with your piety.”

In these most foolish words, which flee not only the elegance of language but even ordinary meaning, and which, compounded of barbarisms and solecisms, produce some obscure sound, the following matters are entirely reprehensible: that it calls the ears of the emperor Justinian—himself equally mortal and subject to suffering, and subject to all human changes—“divine”; that it forbids him to use mercy; that it makes him eager to repay evil with evil; and that it neglects to act patiently and gently in the same matter.

The writer, who ought to have labored to rescue the condemned and restrain the king’s anger, instead inflamed that anger more and more and urged him cruelly to wrath. He did not follow the example of the one who wishes no one to perish. He ought to have kept watch for the salvation of souls, yet he pronounced an anathema and curses, and said that God reigned together with the emperor.

Since these words are censurable in so many respects, they prove less suitable for strengthening the worship of images. For one who is seen to stumble on level ground can hardly run safely over precipices; nor can one who is unable to keep to the road on open highways serve as a guide through ambiguous byways; and the one who is found to possess no knowledge of the ordinary use of letters is rejected by the most subtle mastery of the liberal disciplines.

Since in the earlier parts of this work we have already argued at length and in full against the ravings of those who still make use of such nonsense, on the basis that he called the emperor’s ears divine and declared that God reigned together with him, the order of the discussion now requires us to proceed with the remaining matters under consideration, fortifying the steps of our argument with testimonies from the divine writings, as the Lord grants us opportunity.

When he is found to have forbidden the emperor to use mercy, what else does he do except visibly resist all the holy Scriptures that commend the practice of mercy? It is therefore extremely dangerous to follow the instructions of writings that appear to oppose the divine Scriptures.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6). And again: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5). The teacher of the nations says: “Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 6). The Psalmist says that “the Lord loves mercy” (Psalm 32), and that “the whole earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 118). The same Lord says through the prophet: “For I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6).

Since mercy is commended by such authoritative commands, and the prophet testifies that he will sing of it forever—“I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, forever”—and since the Lord is said to love it, whoever forbids its exercise and despises its possession is convicted both of not loving God and of wholly opposing his most excellent commands.

Therefore the Truth himself answered the lawyer who said that the one who showed mercy was his neighbor: “Go, and you do likewise” (Luke 10). This instruction shows that not only are we commanded to love human beings, who share our nature, but also angels, who, although they possess another nature, are nevertheless believed to be our neighbors insofar as they exercise mercy toward us. They too are to be loved by the one who commanded love of God and neighbor.

In being so ready to repay evil with evil, he plainly contradicted the divine commands. He ought neither to have been so severe in exercising vengeance nor to have urged the emperor to exercise it, since his office was not to carry out vengeance or command it to be carried out, but to love works of mercy and proclaim to others that they should be loved.

For the Lord says in Exodus: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or wandering donkey, lead it back to him” (Exodus 23). He did not obey this command in any way when he failed to recall the aforementioned Samaritans from error, if indeed they are believed to have erred; instead, by petitioning the emperor, he stirred his mind to demand that they perish in the same error.

Those whom he saw fallen beneath the burden of sins he not only failed to raise up, but permitted to perish cruelly beneath that same burden. The Lord says: “If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him” (ibid.).

The Book of Proverbs likewise says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head, and God will repay you” (Proverbs 25). For if he had filled with the food of spiritual nourishment and the drink of salvation those whom he knew to be enemies because of their sins, he would have heaped coals of fire upon their heads—that is, upon their minds—coals that would consume the rust of their sins and kindle them to love of God and neighbor.

The pursuit of vengeance, the rejection of mercy, and the preservation of anger—all of which the letter placed above is said to have urged upon the aforementioned emperor—are restrained by the teachings of the ecclesiastical books:

“Whoever does not avenge himself will find vengeance from God, and he will preserve that person’s sins. Forgive your neighbor’s offense, and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. A human being harbors anger against another human being and seeks healing from God; he shows no mercy to a person like himself and yet pleads for his own sins. If he himself retains anger and asks God for pardon, who will plead for his offenses?” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

The oracle of the prophet Isaiah likewise forbids repaying evil with evil in these words:

“Hear the word of the Lord, you who fear his name. Say: ‘You are our brothers,’ to those who hate you and abominate you, so that the name of the Lord may be magnified and he may appear to them in their joy, while they are put to shame.”

The Lord also commanded in the Gospel, concerning enemies and those who act wickedly, not that anger should be aroused, vengeance exercised, or curses heaped up, but established that love should be shown toward them in these most sacred words:

“Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you; bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5).

If those who hate and persecute us—who are, after all, the image of God—are, according to the truthful command, to be loved rather than cursed and condemned, then those who are said to have inflicted injury upon paintings are much less to be cursed or punished.

The chosen vessel likewise warns in these words that evil must be repaid to no one. In his Letter to the Romans he says:

“Do not become wise in your own estimation; repay no one evil for evil; provide what is good not only before God but also before all human beings. If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, be at peace with all people. Do not defend yourselves, but give place to anger. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans 12).

If, then, according to the teaching of the excellent preacher, we must not defend ourselves, what madness—or what folly—is it that we should strive, in accordance with the exhortation of the same letter sent to Justinian, to defend injuries done to insensible objects, and that we should surrender the works of mercy, which we must not abandon even on account of accusations against ourselves, because of insults directed against paintings that cannot feel them?

The writer of that letter therefore did not follow the example of the holy man Stephen, the first martyr. Stephen, while being cruelly battered on every side by a hail of stones thrown at him, knelt and prayed for his persecutors. This writer, however, unable to endure injuries to images—injuries which the images themselves could not feel—requested under solemn attestation that the perpetrators of those injuries be swiftly and mercilessly killed, and took care to consign their souls, bound by the chain of anathema, to everlasting punishment.

Meanwhile, the writer of that letter neglected to act patiently and gently in this matter and refused to fulfill the preaching of the one who writes to the Thessalonians:

“Be patient with everyone. See that no one repays evil to anyone with evil, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all” (1 Thessalonians 5).

He also scorned the command of the one who says:

“The gentle person with humility is better than one who divides the spoil with the insolent” (Proverbs 16).

When he ought to have restrained the king’s anger in rescuing the wretched, Solomon says:

“Rescue those who are being led to death, and redeem those being dragged to execution; do not spare. If you say, ‘I did not know this person,’ know that the Lord examines human hearts; he who formed the spirit of everyone knows all things, and he will repay each according to his works” (Proverbs 24).

Yet, in the opposite direction, he stirred the emperor’s mind through his letter toward slaughter and cruelty.

Since those who suffer injury must be rescued, the Book of Ecclesiasticus demonstrates this. It says:

“Rescue the one who suffers injury from the hand of the arrogant, and do not let it trouble your soul. In judging orphans, be merciful as a father, and act on behalf of their mother; then you will be like an obedient son of the Most High, and he will show you mercy more than a mother” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

The prophet Isaiah likewise speaks about this matter:

“Seek judgment, rescue the one who suffers injury, judge the orphan, justify the widow, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord. Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow; though they be like crimson, I will make them white as wool. Rescue the plundered from the hand of the one who injures him” (Isaiah 1).

Therefore, if anyone wishes to become like a son of the Most High God by devoting himself to good works, and desires to receive mercy from God and be cleansed from the filth of sins, he ought to follow these salutary commands rather than the utterly cruel perversity of that letter.

Moreover, by provoking the emperor’s anger, he acted cruelly in this respect also and entirely contradicted the sacred writings here, as in the other matters.

It is said by a certain wise man:

“Every blessed soul is simple; but the passionate or angry person does not act honorably.”

And again:

“Do not befriend an angry man; do not associate with a wrathful companion, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Proverbs 22).

Since the wise man forbids learning these ways, it is much more forbidden to teach them and to urge them under solemn attestation.

The Book of Ecclesiasticus likewise thunders concerning this matter:

“An angry person kindles strife, and a sinful man troubles his friends and introduces slander among those who are at peace” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

Ecclesiastes also gives these commands:

“Do not hasten in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7).

The teacher of the nations therefore writes to the Ephesians:

“Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4).

Again, the same writer says:

“Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice” (ibid.).

And again:

“But now put away all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and abusive speech” (Colossians 3).

All these matters, if they are examined more clearly, will be found almost entirely in the text of the aforementioned letter.

Let the most just man and beloved of God, the apostle James, say whether, in accordance with the exhortation of this letter, anyone ought to be quick to anger; let him declare whether this letter should be accepted, since it decreed that the emperor cited should become angry. For he says:

> “You know, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak and also slow to anger; for the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James II).

Let Truth itself also say what its members ought to follow in this matter. Say, I mean, holy Matthew, what you poured forth from the everlasting fountain of paradise, drawing from it with the life-giving streams of your river. For the perennial fountain, the fountain of life, the fountain of light, says:

> “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew V).

When, then, anger—which is numbered among the chief vices—is declared accursed by so many examples of the divine law and by so many pronouncements of the divine words, it is readily understood that these writings are not suitable for strengthening the matters under dispute, since by them the emperor is commanded, under solemn testimony and humble entreaty, to undertake and carry out this deed.

The author of that letter ought rather to have exhorted those whom he saw in danger to repentance. If they had perhaps despised repentance, he could have approached the emperor with humble prayers, asking him to compel them to convert. Perhaps, compelled, they would have pursued the good of their salvation which, of their own accord, they had despised, since almighty God wishes no one to perish, as Paul attests when he says:

> “For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy II).

If he had been intent on winning souls, he ought rather to have summoned those whom he saw to have gone astray to repentance than to incite the ruler’s mind to shed blood. For the power of repentance is not to be placed below the other virtues, but is to be ranked with the very best of them, since, like a kind of medicine, it binds together what has been broken, heals what is sick, restores what has been lost, and very often brings sinners back after their fall to their former condition.

The Psalmist commends this when he says:

> “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities. I said: ‘I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm XXXII).

Isaiah commanded that it be practiced, saying:

> “Remember these things and groan; repent, you who have gone astray; turn back with your whole heart.”

It is also affirmed by the prophetic declarations of Jeremiah, who says:

> “Turn back, returning daughters, and I will heal your wounds” (Jeremiah III).

In another passage he likewise says:

> “Let each person now turn away from his evil way, and make your pursuits better.”

Joel too thunders with the voice of the Lord, saying:

> “Turn to me with all your heart and with all your soul, with fasting and weeping and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and patient, long-suffering and greatly merciful, patient in his kindnesses” (Joel II).

The book of Ecclesiasticus also says:

> “If we do not repent, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord according to his greatness, and his mercy is with him” (Ecclesiasticus II).

Indeed, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Repent and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away” (Acts II).

The shepherd of the Church likewise says in his second letter:

> “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some consider it, but he waits for you also, not wishing anyone to perish, but waiting for all to return to the place of repentance” (2 Peter III).

Therefore, to the extent that this virtue excels in saving—yet he neglected to preach it to those who had gone astray—to that same extent, without doubt, this cruelty excels among the other wickednesses in harming, because he both prevented the ruler from showing mercy and impelled him by grave adjurations to become angry and exercise vengeance.

If, then, according to the Lord’s pronouncement, it is a grave crime to scandalize one of the little ones, how grave do you think it is to incite not a little one but a king, who is certainly the head of the peoples, to cause scandal?

Moreover, in the fact that the writer of the aforementioned letter, among the other acts of cruelty which he exercised against those whom he saw going astray, used curses, he is found to have gone seriously astray and to have contradicted the sacred utterances. The chosen vessel says:

> “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans XII);

and elsewhere:

> “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God.”

The Rock of the Church also prohibits the use of curses in these words. For he says in his first letter:

> “Therefore, all of you be harmonious, united in spirit, sympathetic, loving the brotherhood, merciful, humble, not repaying evil for evil or curse for curse, but, on the contrary, blessing, because you were called for this purpose: that you may inherit a blessing” (1 Peter III).

[Col. 1197A]

But let no one think that we are judging anyone or attacking someone whose merit we do not know. Let him understand that we are not examining anyone’s life or merit, but are merely diligently winnowing with the winnowing-fan of the divine utterances the words that have been improperly brought forward to nourish error, although they are everywhere intertwined with the sinews of errors.

Nor are we examining other words of that same Simeon, which, as we said above, we do not remember ever having read. We examine only those things whose meaning we perceive from the letters that report them. And although we do not know whether, as they themselves confess, these are the words of that same Simeon or the words of someone else written under his name, we nevertheless know that, once every ambiguity has been set aside, they are alien to the meaning of the sacred Scriptures and deservedly must be rejected by every ecclesiastical doctrine.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That they call the Samaritans worse than all heretics, and those who destroy images worse than the Samaritans, although, according to their own view, their ancestors were worse than all heretics, since they destroyed images

It was not enough for them to reject their predecessors or ancestors with fearful anathemas and tear them apart with various insults, unless they also declared them to have been worse than all heretics. The more atrocious the injuries with which they strive to curse them, the more strongly they contradict the divine admonitions.

For they say that the Samaritans are worse than all heretics, and they place above them in guilt those who destroy images. It is established that their ancestors destroyed images; and according to their own view, those who destroy images are worse than the Samaritans, while the Samaritans, as they say, are worse than all heretics. Therefore, according to their own confession, their ancestors were worse than all heretics, since it is established that they destroyed images.

For if, as they themselves assert, they were either descended through the flesh from those worse than all heretics, or educated in their scriptural doctrines, or consecrated by the laying on of hands to perform the mysteries of the Christian religion, it is astonishing that they should consider themselves superior to the other Catholics in issuing constitutions and establishing the traditions of the Church, and should boast that they possess so great a prerogative of authority, when neither the practice of their own deeds or teachings nor the examples of their ancestors prove that they possess it.

For if these people are to be preferred to all Catholics because of the adoration of images, then it will not be the followers of the virtues but the adorers of images who hold the more eminent place in the Church. And if the adorers of images are to hold the more eminent place within the holy Church, then it is errors, not virtues, that must be employed. But virtues, not errors, must be employed; therefore these people are not to be preferred to all Catholics because of the adoration of images.

The Samaritans, whom they call worse than all heretics, are not heretics of the Christians but of the Jews. Nor do they confess that they hold the New Testament, but the Old. Yet while the Jews believe in the resurrection of bodies and accept the prophets and the Hagiographa, the Samaritans reject the resurrection and, except for the five books of the Law, set aside all the Scriptures of both the Old and the New Testament.

They are remnants of the nations whom Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, sent to guard the land of Israel after he had transferred the ten tribes of Israel to the Medes. When lions and other savage beasts, or certain harmful circumstances, were devastating them in the land of Israel, they sent a delegation to the king, declaring that they could not remain in that region unless they observed the lawful worship of the God of the land. Some Levites are said to have been sent to them, by whom they were taught the ceremonies of the Law.

After accepting some of these and appropriating many elements of heresy, their barbarous paganism became so inflated with the swelling of its pride that, setting aside the Jews—who are believed to have sprung from the stock of Jacob—they boasted that they alone were the children of Jacob. Thus, driven by arrogance, they were compelled to reject fellowship with the Jews just as with the other nations.

A Samaritan woman was descended from this stock. When she conversed with the Lord at the well, she asserted with empty boasting and great stubbornness that her father Jacob, who had given her the well, was not surpassed by the Redeemer of the world, and she said that her ancestors had worshiped not in Jerusalem but on the mountain. Together with her water jar and her unbelief, she laid aside this stubbornness and accepted the saving admonitions.

If we briefly explain what she signified through symbolic mysteries, our account will not be out of place. She represented the whole human race, which, when the world was already growing old, came to the Lord. He sat at the well in the sixth age of the world. The well signifies, through its dark depth, the earthly labor and error of this world. He sat there, I mean, wearied by the humility of the flesh assumed for us, signifying the weakness of that same flesh, although, in another interpretation, his sitting demonstrates the dignity of his teaching and instruction.

He thirsted, desiring not merely to drink water but to draw in the faith of the nations. Hence, when the disciples urged him to eat, he said that he had food of which they knew nothing. He thirsted, therefore, for the faith of the Gentiles, so that he might do the Father’s will in it and complete his work.

He therefore promised to give her living water, namely the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive. He said that she had had five husbands—that is, that she had made use of the five bodily senses—and that the sense she would finally have, by which she would believe in Christ and with whom she could enter into a lawful marriage, was not her own. For after five carnal responses she names Christ in a sixth response.

Her first response was:

> “Since you are a Jew, how can you ask me for a drink?”

Her second:

> “Lord, you have no vessel, and the well is deep.”

Her third:

> “Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw.”

Her fourth:

> “I have no husband.”

Her fifth:

> “I see that you are a prophet: our fathers worshiped on this mountain” (John IV).

This response is carnal. For a material place on earth had been given to the carnal, where they might pray—not so that they might worship either the place or anything placed in it, but so that in that place they might worship the Lord. The Lord said that spiritual people would worship in spirit and truth, not in images, not in paintings, and not in objects devoid of sensation.

After he had spoken these things, the woman’s sixth response confessed that Christ was the teacher of all these matters. For she says:

> “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

But she is still in error, because she does not see that the one whose coming she hopes for has already come. This error is driven out, as though by an adulterer, by the Lord’s merciful words:

> “I am he who is speaking with you.”

When she heard this, she said nothing, but left her water jar—that is, her desire for and love of this world, from whose dark depth and earthly way of life human beings draw pleasure, and, having tasted it, burn again with desire for it, as it is said: “Whoever drinks of that water will thirst again.”

She went into the city, because she preached to the world what she had believed: believing with the heart for righteousness and confessing with the mouth for salvation.

Since, therefore, we have digressed somewhat from the matter before us, let us return to our subject. Although the Samaritans are Gentiles and appear falsely to maintain Judaism, they are not known to rage against the Church more fiercely than the other unbelievers. Yet these people, thinking that they are Christian heretics and judging them worse than all heretics, show them a certain clemency, since they teach that their own ancestors must be preferred to them in wickedness. For the one who has anyone else who can be preferred to him in guilt is not the worst of all.

## CHAPTER VII  
### That the more examples they draw from heretics and from those who reject or despise images, the more they dishonor their own ancestors with insults and injuries, although they undoubtedly confess that their ancestors were their followers in this respect

It is a very ancient custom not only of philosophers but also of orators, when they wish to establish something, to draw an argument for proving it either from the very matter under discussion, or from other matters, or certainly from outside sources.

Although these people, because of their lack of skill, disdain to follow such men in other respects, in this matter they strive above all to follow them. For when they decide to condemn their predecessors or ancestors on account of the abolition of images, they take arguments either from the matter itself, or from elsewhere, or from outside sources; and they do not fear to tear them apart with insults, curse them with anathemas, and dishonor them with utterly insane words.

Moreover, the more examples of certain heretics they bring forward as testimony—heretics whose followers they confess their ancestors to have been—the more severely they reject those ancestors with curses, and the more clearly they demonstrate that they contradict the divine admonitions which decree that honor must be shown to parents.

The Lord says:

> “Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you” (Exodus XX).

This command is so authoritative that it was written on the tablets by the finger of the Lord, and it is called the first commandment by the Apostle. For he says:

> “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians VI),

namely, the promise in which he immediately added:

> “so that you may live long upon the earth and it may be well with you.”

It must certainly be observed how great is the condemnation of those who tear their parents apart with insults or curse them with anathemas, since those who honor them according to the command of the Lord possess such great merit and such a great promise. For just as the excellent promise greatly soothes those who obey this command, so the fearful condemnation ought greatly to terrify those who resist the same command of the Lord.

It is also written in Leviticus:

> “Let each person fear his father and his mother” (Leviticus XIX).

In Ecclesiasticus too, concerning the honoring of parents, it is written:

> “Whoever honors his father will live a longer life; whoever obeys his father refreshes his mother, and will serve those who gave him birth as though they were the Lord, in deed and word and with all patience; and his blessing remains at the end” (Ecclesiasticus III).

Again, in Ecclesiasticus:

> “My son, support your father’s old age, and do not grieve him during his life. If he fails in understanding, forgive him, and do not despise him when you are in your strength. This is not glory for you, but shame.”

The teacher of the nations also says:

> “Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord” (Ephesians VI).

If, then, it pleases God to honor or obey parents, it displeases him in every way to heap insults and curses upon them. And if that does not displease him, neither does the former please him.

It is therefore grave and fearful not to honor one’s parents; but it is most grave and most fearful to abominate or anathematize them. The Lord says:

> “Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death” (Exodus XXI).

And again:

> “Cursed is the person who does not honor his father or his mother”; and all the people shall say, “Amen, amen” (Deuteronomy XXVII).

It is also written in Proverbs:

> “Whoever curses his father and mother, his lamp will be extinguished in the midst of darkness” (Proverbs XX).

And there:

> “Whoever rejects his father and mother and considers himself not to be sinning is a companion of an ungodly man” (Proverbs XXVIII).

Therefore it must be understood that those who do not fear to heap curses upon their ancestors for the sake of objects devoid of sensation are not guilty of ordinary madness. While they wish to favor images, they do not fear to dishonor their parents or to contradict the divine utterances.

In saying these things, we are not favoring their ancestors, whom we have found to have acted absurdly in this matter also. Rather, by the testimonies of the divine law we demonstrate how great is the presumption of these people in daring such things.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### That, according to the statement of the deacon Demetrius, their ancestors acted carelessly and disorderly, burning two books plated with silver because they contained something concerning images, and cutting out two leaves of another book

Since neither party possessed moderation, these people are not restrained by the reins of reason, nor should their predecessors be thought to have been restrained by them. Rather, both groups are shown to be driven uncontrolled over steep and impassable paths, followers of forbidden and fruitless practices. As has often already been said, these people judged that images ought to be worshiped humbly, while their ancestors judged that they ought to be broken impatiently.

As Demetrius, their deacon, says:

> “Among other things, they acted carelessly and disorderly: they burned two books plated with silver because some mention of images was contained in them, and they cut out two leaves of another book,”

as though mention of images could not be made in any other way unless they were immediately judged worthy of worship.

For although no one who examines books to be received judges that images should be worshiped even slightly, mention of them is nevertheless made in many books in one way or another. If all books in which mention of them occurs are to be burned, very many instruments of Scripture will surely perish.

First, each matter must be tested and then judged. This can be established by many examples from both divine and secular laws, and it can also be supported by the teachings of the rhetoricians themselves. They placed deliberative rhetoric first, demonstrative rhetoric second, and judicial rhetoric third, so that whatever deliberation found either to be rejected or pursued, demonstration might show to be either praiseworthy or blameworthy, and judicial judgment might assign either punishments or rewards. Otherwise, if these two latter genres were not preceded by the judicial one, and the examination of deliberation were placed first with the matters reversed, while the order of demonstration was neglected, any matter might be judged otherwise than is just.

Moderation or restraint must therefore be maintained in all things, and the philosophical maxim must be remembered:

> “Nothing in excess.”

This moderation must always be tempered by the partnership of testing. For the Apostle does not say:

> “Burn everything without moderation and without testing.”

Rather, he says:

> “Test everything, and retain what is good” (1 Thessalonians V).

## CHAPTER IX  
### That, seeing images on silver tablets in the same book, Leontius of Secreta boasted that he had discovered an extremely sharp and ingenious advantage for his error

In that book, in which two leaves had been cut out because of a certain mention of images at their earlier synod—the synod held for abolishing images—there were certain images on silver tablets, as images are accustomed to be found on vessels or on many other objects.

As soon as Leontius of Secreta saw these at their second synod, which had been convened to authorize the worship of images, he thought that he had discovered a great advantage for his error. He judged those people to have been conspicuously foolish who, in the same book where the images were found, had cut out two leaves because of a mention of images.

Thus, over the passage of time and through different events and unequal procedures, the same book was judged by the former group to deserve mutilation because of the mention of images, while by the latter it was ordered to be worshiped because of the images displayed on the tablets. By the former it unjustly suffered the loss of its leaves; by the latter it was exalted through unlawful worship. When the former removed what it had and ought to have had, it improperly lost it; when the latter presented what it neither had nor ought to have had, it irrationally acquired it.

It neither lost its leaves because of any actual offenses, nor found worship because of any distinguished merits. Insofar as it deserved to lose what it rightly possessed, so it deserved to acquire what was forbidden.

Are all books in which histories have been inserted among the writings through the art of painting, whether in gold, silver, or any colors, to be burned or cut up by the former because they contain images, or to be revered and worshiped by the latter?

Are garments of silk or of any other material, cloaks suited to human use or dedicated to divine worship, decorated with various figures and colored with different dyes, to be burned by the former or worshiped by the latter because they contain images?

Are metals or pieces of wood fashioned for various uses, and decorated with images by sculpting or engraving, therefore to be burned or broken by the former, or worshiped by the latter?

Unhappy mind, which is always in a frenzy either to curse images or, conversely, to worship them.

Unhappy understanding, which is always eager either to reject things that can be possessed without offense, or to worship things that cannot be worshiped without offense.

Unhappy custom, which rejects the straight path of moderation and, unable to maintain a fixed rule, always wavers and turns now this way, now that: at one moment disorderly rejecting what should by no means be rejected; at another, disastrously worshiping what absolutely ought not to be worshiped; at one moment casting down what should not be cast down beyond what order requires; at another, raising what should not be excessively exalted beyond what order demands.

Neglecting necessary matters and pursuing unnecessary ones, it convenes synods either for the abolition of images or for their worship—neither of which is appropriate—as though images could prejudice the Christian religion either by being possessed or by not being worshiped. Yet images take nothing away when they are not possessed, nor add anything when they are possessed. When rejected, they introduce a certain careless frivolity; when worshiped, they imprint guilt.

## CHAPTER X  
### That no reading of the Gospel states that Jesus sent an image to Abgar, as they claim

[Col. 1202D]

The Gospel is good news, and truly good news, because those who receive it are called sons of God. It is a fourfold river proceeding from one ineffable fountain of Paradise, remarkably divided into four streams and beneficially sent forth to water arid hearts.

It is the way that leads to life; it is the light that leads back from the darkness of vices and directs the steps of mortals toward heavenly things along an unobstructed path. It is the fortification of a flourishing city, in which standing firmly provides the greatest advantage of life, while departing from it brings the most dangerous loss.

These are the streams of truth, which neither know how to deceive nor can be deceived. Although their immense rivers contain many notable accounts of the Lord’s deeds, there is no account that the same Lord received a letter from a certain king Abgar and sent him a reply.

Since these two letters are entirely foreign to the reading of the holy Gospel, and since the blessed Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, as well as other equally Catholic and orthodox men, has assigned them wholly among the apocryphal writings, they must not be brought forward as testimony. Like the other apocryphal writings, they are inadequate for proving or disproving the matters under dispute.

Their text was not recorded by the evangelists in the Gospel books. It was rightly assigned by Catholics among the apocrypha, and it was brought forward by these people at the synod to support the error of worshiping images. Yet it does not even slightly favor their own followers, especially since it is not read there that Abgar asked the Lord for an image in order to worship it, nor is it stated that the Lord of all sent Abgar an image to be worshiped.

If those who try to support their error by reading these letters wish to assert that one was received from the Lord and the other sent by him, saying that not everything written in the Gospel that the Lord said or did is recorded there, and if they use the testimony of John, who says:

> “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book” (John XX),

they should understand that this can be taken to refer to miracles, not letters; to signs, not ordinances.

That these letters themselves are remote from the reading of the Gospel, that they have been assigned by Catholics among the apocrypha, and that their reading contains no evidence for the worship of images, is clear. We reject the worship of images, and, while reading them among the apocrypha, we test everything and retain what is good.

## CHAPTER XI  
### That those books of the deeds of the fathers whose authors are unknown are not wholly suitable for giving testimony or affirming matters that have come into dispute

The apostolic preaching admonishes us to test everything and retain what is good. This can most especially be understood concerning the diversity of doctrines.

For we have not been permitted to taste every action or even every matter, as though, tasting everything beforehand, we might retain only what is good and reject every evil. That cannot be done without the commission of certain unlawful acts. Rather, we were commanded to test and to taste all doctrines with a spiritual palate, retaining only those which, having been delivered by thoroughly approved men, refresh the mind with inward satisfaction, and rejecting all the rest together with their authors.

Since this rule must be observed in nearly all writings of this kind, it must also be strictly maintained in books that preserve the deeds of certain holy fathers. Their number is great, their accounts varied, and their preaching diverse. Moreover, believers often doubt their sayings all the more because their authors are unknown. Therefore, not all of them should be brought forward as testimony to affirm uncertain matters, since not all are furnished with the title of their authors, nor arranged in the style of strong and eloquent men.

Accordingly, instructed by the teachings of the venerable Pope Gelasius and the other fathers, we are to receive with all honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and the others—which were either composed by the blessed Jerome, translated from Greek into Latin, or arranged in the style of teachers whose other works are accepted by the holy Catholic and apostolic Church. But the rest, whose authors are unknown, are to be assigned among the apocryphal writings.

Since these people strive to approve the worship of images—at one time by improperly applying passages of the divine utterances, at another by the sayings of certain unknown teachers, and at another by the trivial tales of apocryphal writings—they ought to recognize that they have undertaken an impossible task. The testimonies of the divine utterances can neither be forcibly appropriated to foreign meanings nor ought they to be. Nor should the preaching of unknown persons, whose spirits have not yet been tested to determine whether they are from God, be brought forward as testimony. Nor can apocryphal writings provide firmness through frivolous, doubtful, and undecided matters.

For if anyone’s words are not to be corrupted by the disguise of falsehood, much less are the divine utterances, which are pure words, silver tested by fire, to be appropriated to matters other than the order of the text allows.

And just as, in human affairs, lowly or unknown persons are not admitted to prove matters under dispute, much less should the testimony of unknown teachers or apocryphal writings be admitted in matters of such importance, which require the instruction of heavenly teaching.

The Scriptures that are to be brought forward as testimony within the holy Church to affirm uncertain matters must be tested, scrutinized through careful examination, and strengthened by the testimonies of the holy fathers. For in the Gospel the wicked servant is rebuked by the Lord because he did not give the money to the money-changers. Therefore it is fitting for us to give the money to the money-changers, lest we be rebuked together with that servant. We give it to the money-changers whenever we submit various writings of the holy fathers to examination for discernment.

The money-changers examine money in four ways: whether the gold has been tested; whether it is pure and inwardly uncorrupted by any disguise of falsehood; whether it bears the inscription of a king rather than a tyrant; and whether it has the full and equal weight.

All these things are investigated by the money-changers—namely, by holy and most eloquent men—through the testing of heavenly fire in the money of the great householder, that is, in the teachings of our Redeemer.

Thus, in the coin of each writing, it is asked whether it is the most thoroughly tested gold, with which the Lord’s ark may be adorned and the work of the entire sanctuary may shine forth, so that the brilliance of spiritual understanding may appear in it, by which the divine law may be understood and the beauty of the whole Church may gleam.

It is asked whether it is pure and inwardly uncorrupted by any disguise of falsehood, lest some perverse doctrine of heresy, concealed beneath the brilliance of eloquence and mingled, as it were, with spiritual meanings, lie hidden within. Thus, while someone thinks that he is receiving a coin of the divine word, he may instead receive the deadly poison of a venomous doctrine.

It is asked whether the inscription upon it is that of a king or of a tyrant. For learned men carefully investigate such writings to determine whether they pertain to the salvation of the soul and contain saving admonitions from our King, who is called Savior or Saving One, lest, when these are set aside, they contain certain harmful machinations of the ancient enemy.

The one who said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew XXVIII), joined earthly things to heavenly things through humility. May no one instead follow him who, wishing through tyranny to be arrogantly like the Most High, fell unhappily to the lower regions by the most just judgment of God.

Such money-changers also ask whether the coin of so great a householder possesses the full and equal weight; that is, whether a given doctrine agrees with the prophetic and apostolic doctrines, lest, disagreeing with them in some way, it proclaim either superfluous things or something incomplete.

For the offerings of gold and silver that the people presented for the work of the tabernacle were accepted by the lawgiver after being weighed according to the weight of the sanctuary.

From this it is understood that those writings, doctrines, and works are to be truly received within the holy Church by the true lawgiver—the mediator between God and human beings—which have not departed in meaning or practice from the weight of the sanctuary, that is, from the standard of the ancient fathers.

When all these matters have been individually examined with prudent scrutiny and discovered with the utmost care, whether in the books entitled *The Deeds of the Fathers* or throughout the various doctrines, the doctrines or testimonies of those books may confidently be brought forward to confirm uncertain matters. Such money cannot be rejected by anyone, since it has been approved through the careful examination of such money-changers.

## CHAPTER XII  
### That Dionysius, priest of the Church of Ascalon, is said to have reported at the same synod that a certain monk lit a lamp before an image of holy Mary ever-virgin and, returning after the third, fifth, or even sixth month, found it unextinguished

[Col. 1205D]

Finally, in the reading of that same synod it is recorded that Dionysius, priest of the Church of Ascalon, reported at the often-mentioned synod that a certain monk had prepared a lamp before an image of blessed Mary, the Mother of God, and had found it still burning after the fourth, fifth, and even sixth month.

Since this report, like the other things reported there, was introduced for no other reason than to establish the worship of images, that worship of images cannot thereby acquire any validity—especially since there is complete uncertainty about the faith of the man who reported it, about whether the event actually occurred, about the time when it occurred, about the place where it occurred, and about the manner in which it occurred. For while it is entirely unknown whether what that priest reported truly happened, even if it were proved to have happened in reality, one would have to investigate more carefully in what manner it was said to have occurred, since miracles are sometimes performed through reprobates, sometimes through aerial powers, but most often through the saints or through angelic ministries.

If, then, it was accomplished by some extremely devious contrivance of the ancient enemy, not only can no worship of images be established from it, but it must also be rejected forever along with its author and all his deceptions. If, however, it was accomplished through angelic arrangements, as many signs ordinarily are, even then no worship of an irrational object can arise from it. For it is more credible that this miracle—if indeed it occurred—was performed by reverence for the holy place rather than by the presence of any image.

Basilicas are more venerable than an image, and places devoted to divine worship are more worthy of reverence than any paintings, as the Lord himself attests when he declared that the altar is greater than the offering placed upon it, and that the temple is greater than the gold within it, because gold and offerings are consecrated to the temple and the altar.

We read that blessed Gregory said that, when an extraordinarily violent flood overwhelmed a certain basilica, the waters rose as far as the windows but, by the resisting power of the Lord, were entirely unable to enter inside; and that the lamps which had earlier been extinguished by the guardians of the basilica were later found lit by those same guardians. This miracle, it is reported, was performed not by the reverence due to any image but by reverence for the holy place.

If, therefore, it were established that the miracle which the priest of the Church of Ascalon reported as having appeared in connection with an image had appeared on account of that same image, images would not for that reason have to be worshiped, since not everything through which or in which miracles have appeared is believed to be worthy of worship. For if everything in which or through which some miracles have appeared is to be worshiped, scarcely anything will remain that is not worshiped, since divine miracles have appeared in almost all creatures in so many and such great ways. It would be idle to linger over these matters here, since, with the Lord’s assent, we have discussed them to some extent in the earlier parts of this work.

## CHAPTER XIII. That this synod cannot in any way be compared with the Council of Nicaea, although it was held in the same place, as the priest John is said to have declared flatteringly; for it is known to differ from it not only in other matters but also in the creed

Although this synod was held in Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, it cannot at all be compared—despite their boastfulness and the flattery of the priest John—with the holy Council of Nicaea. For although it disagrees with that council on many points, it does not even agree with it entirely in the creed.

In its profession of faith this synod contains various new and unusual words that were by no means recorded in the creed of the holy Council of Nicaea. We have discussed these, insofar as we were able, at the beginning of the third book of this work, with the Lord’s help. It also contains, after its confession of the holy Trinity, a confession of the images that are to be worshiped. We have nowhere found such a confession inserted either in the utterances of the prophets, in the thunderings of the Gospels, in the teachings of the apostles, in the reports of the earlier holy synods, or in the doctrines of any orthodox fathers.

This synod is very far—far beyond what can be said—from the other, especially since the former recalls the catholic Church from error, whereas this one, on the contrary, leads it into error; the former drives it away from the extremely dangerous shipwreck of Arius, whereas this one thrusts it into the shipwreck of the worship of images; the former teaches most fully that the Son is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, whereas this one judges it right to worship senseless objects; the former affirms that, according to his divinity, the Son is equal to the Father, whereas this one foolishly declares any paintings to be equal to the ark of the Lord’s testament, to the Lord’s cross, to the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and to the other most sacred things.

The former most healthfully believes that one substance of the divine majesty is to be worshiped in three equal, coessential, coeternal persons; this one shamelessly says that images are to be worshiped in the service of the holy Trinity. In the former, the errors of Arian doctrine are condemned; in this one, the elders of these people are nevertheless rejected. In the former, the blasphemies of those who stubbornly neither believe nor confess that the Son is coessential with the Father are cursed; in this one, the purity of those who, rejecting the worship of paintings, declare with resolute mind and devout heart that they will serve God alone is condemned.

In the former, after the confession of the holy Trinity, the bishops fully teach the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life of the age to come; in this one, after the confession of that same holy and unique Trinity, the worship of images is improperly established. In the former, the offering of sacrifice to God for faithful departed persons is not prohibited; in this one, anathemas are imposed upon deceased predecessors or parents by their sons or successors.

And, to say nothing of the other matters that would take too long to list, there were 318 bishops at the former, while at this one, as they themselves assert, there were 306. Therefore this synod is not undeservedly separated from the former by the number twelve—whether because that number contains two perfect numbers, or because, in the number three, which it has four times, and in the number four, which it has three times, it demonstrates the mystery of the holy Trinity in the four Gospels and the source of the four Gospels, namely the same holy Trinity; or because that number twelve demonstrates in this way every discipline that recognizes and distinguishes creature from Creator and leads upward, a discipline entirely lacking from that synod.

God is the Creator, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, as the Apostle says: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11). Therefore the Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Creation, however, is partly invisible, as the soul, and partly visible, as the body. The invisible is assigned the number three; therefore we are commanded to love God in three ways: with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Deut. 6; Lev. 19). The number four is assigned to the body because of its most evident nature, namely, hot and cold, moist and dry.

Thus the number seven is assigned to the whole of creation. When knowledge of the holy Trinity is added to it, the number ten is completed; in it is the whole discipline of wisdom that pertains to instructing human beings: to distinguish the Creator from creation, to worship him as ruler, and to acknowledge creation as subject.

When the two pre-eminent commandments—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—are added to this discipline, the number twelve is completed. For even if the five books of the Law, through which one comes to knowledge of God and to love of God and neighbor, are added to the aforementioned number seven, in which we said that human nature is shown to be partly visible and partly invisible, the number twelve is nevertheless completed.

If the four books of the Gospels are added to it, the sequence extends to the number sixteen, since that same number twelve, multiplied by its parts, reaches the number sixteen. For the six which it contains twice, the two which it contains six times, the three which it contains four times, the four which it contains three times, and the one which it contains twelve times together produce the number sixteen.

Thus, through the five parts in which the figure of the five books is represented, the seven in which visible and invisible creation is demonstrated, and the four in which the holy Gospels are signified, the number sixteen is reached. In it are displayed both the ten commandments of the Decalogue and the sixfold sum of all perfection, which was given in the New Testament through the Mediator between God and human beings. Thus, through the twelve apostles, the four Gospels, and the sixteen most noble prophets whose books are thunders, minds may be raised to the worship and adoration of the one God alone, with all the vanities of mortals rejected.

Since there are twelve patriarchs, twelve Minor Prophets, and also twelve apostles, as well as many other things of this kind that diligent readers can investigate in the divine Scriptures, there are also many things belonging to natural philosophy arranged according to the same number.

[Note: Col. 1207D: “And many more things of this kind which [*quae*] are in the divine writings,” etc. The editor changes *plures* (“many [persons/things]”) to *plura* (“many things”), a change that was unnecessary if he had substituted *qui* for *quae*.]

There are twelve signs in the zodiacal circle, which surround it like certain ranks of gems. There are twelve winds, blowing around the world in groups of three through the four regions of heaven.

[Note: Col. 1207D: “There are twelve winds blowing around the world, bounded by the four regions of heaven.” I read: “in threes.” Col. 1208D: “There are twelve winds, four of them principal and the rest lateral. They blow in groups from the four regions of the world: three from the east, three from the west, three from the south, and three from the north.” This is what Charles says: that they blow in threes.] There are twelve months, by which the year is completed. There are twelve hours, by which the day is completed. There are many other things of this kind, which learned men investigate according to their knowledge of secular literature and understand spiritually according to ecclesiastical teaching.

If someone should perhaps try to attack this work because we have offered examples from natural philosophy—that is, from matters belonging to mathematics—let him read blessed Jerome and either attack us together with him, or, since we follow his teaching and that of the other Fathers, recognize that we are not ignorant of literature.

For the same teacher says, while discussing the priestly vestment:

> “They explain the breastplate placed in the middle as the earth, which, although it contains all things within itself like a point, is nevertheless enclosed by all the elements. By the twelve stones they interpret either the zodiacal circle or the twelve months; they assign one season to each verse and allot three months to each. Let no one think the interpretation pagan. For if they have dishonored the heavenly bodies and God’s arrangement with the names of idols, God’s providence is not for that reason to be denied; it proceeds, is carried forward, and governs all things according to a fixed law. In Job we read the names Arcturus, Orion, and Mazuroth—that is, the zodiacal circle—and the other names of the stars, not because these are the names used among the Hebrews, but because we cannot understand what is said except through customary expressions.”

This number is also consecrated by many mysteries, which, for the sake of brevity, we cannot individually unfold. From this we may understand why this synod had twelve fewer bishops than the holy Council of Nicaea: because, through the most sacred preaching or authority of the twelve apostles—by whom that council is clearly fortified—this synod is clearly alien in many respects; and because the former, supplied with them as with impregnable towers, rises toward higher things, whereas this one, lacking them, runs downward toward worse things, mutilated.

The former is adorned with these twelve gems on which the names of the twelve tribes are written—that is, the knowledge of the ancient fathers or examples of virtue—whereas this one is plainly recognized as entirely lacking them. Through those twelve gates of that most beautiful city, namely, the mysteries of the most sacred constitutions, entrance is gained; such gates are by no means found in this synod.

We have therefore been unable to find any agreement of merit between the former synod and this one, except merely an agreement of name: the former is called Nicaea because it was held in Nicaea, the metropolitan city of Bithynia, for the advancement of the Church; and this one, because it was held there, is nevertheless called Nicaea, although it was conducted with a different purpose and a different merit.

For agreement of names is not always believed to possess the same force. Many names of holy and illustrious men are found to have been given to any number of ignoble persons, since a name does not confer equality of merit; rather, equality of merit increases the dignity of a name.

Since they seek to exalt this synod with the great insignia of merit because it too was held in the same place where the holy synod had previously been held, let them understand that the merit of a place is not always one and the same, just as the merit of a name is not. For human beings were made not for places, but places for human beings, like all other earthly creatures; the situation of places does not confer benefits on them, but eminence of merit does. Nor does the holiness of any place have much force if there is impurity of conduct and merit in the people who occupy it.

In the same places, both evil things can be done by the wicked and good things by the upright. In the city that was once the metropolis of Egypt, said to have been founded by the Titans—that is, by Giants—and called Thanis by them, Moses performed many great and astonishing miracles through invocation of the divine name. The magicians of Pharaoh also performed many acts of magic through the most insolent exercises of aerial powers. In the suburbs of that same Tanis, memorable wonders were performed by the holy men Moses and Aaron, while ominous fabrications were produced by worshipers of demons through various wicked consecrations and invocations.

Thus the common possession of the place, unable to prejudice either party, provided a shared dwelling both for those doing pious things and for those committing shameful ones.

The city of Luza in Samaria, which received from the holy patriarch Jacob the name Bethel—that is, “house of God”—was the place where the patriarch saw a ladder touching the earth and reaching to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it. Later it contained golden calves as a stumbling block for the house of Israel, which the most wicked of kings, Jeroboam, established there for worship.

The place of which the holy man said, “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28), and which, marveling greatly, he declared to be terrible, with nothing there except the house of God and the gate of heaven, later became the house of an idol and a cause of danger to the Israelite people.

Neither the consecration of the stone erected by the patriarch, nor the anointing with sacred oil, nor the invocation of the revered name restrained the wickedness of the impious king Jeroboam from perverse action. He did not fear to pollute with idols the place that he knew had been admired by so great a patriarch.

From this it may be understood that a perverse doctrine concerning the worship of images could easily have been established in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, where the holy synod had previously been held. For if idols could be placed at Bethel by the most wicked king Jeroboam, where Jacob had declared the house of God and the gate of heaven to be, and if the consecration of so great a patriarch later proved unable to give that place any protection, then in these times the city of Bithynia cannot in this matter derive any defense from the ancient Fathers.

It is evident that places can be sanctified by holy people and polluted by sinners, as people undergo the most varied changes, inclining now one way, now another, according to their character.

We read that the house of God at Shiloh was consecrated by the priests Eleazar and Phinehas through the placement of the ark of the Lord’s testament, or of the tabernacle, and through continual offerings of sacrifices, but was later defiled by the perpetration of wicked deeds by Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priests.

We also read of Salem, once a most illustrious city, later called Jebus or Solyma, and now, by derivation, Jerusalem. It was first founded and inhabited after the Flood by the holy man Shem, who was later, as they say, called Melchizedek; afterward it was conquered by the accursed nation of the Jebusites and possessed by them for a long time, down to David.

We also read of the most sacred and venerable temple of the Lord, planned by David, the holiest of prophets, and dedicated by Solomon; frequented by angelic guards, illumined by divine oracles, and prepared by perpetual observance of the most sacred ceremonies. Because of the distinction of so many spiritual gifts, it had been venerated by the ancient fathers. Yet it was later polluted by the filth of idols and by every other outrage through the worst kings of the same line.

There, where the Lord had established his sanctuary and the place of his glorious habitation, King Manasseh erected altars to the twelve signs and to the whole army of heaven. Even after its restoration and after the prophecy of Haggai or Zechariah, we read that the same house was profaned by the Greek kings. The reverence of the place did not restrain the people of those ages from committing unlawful deeds, because the savagery of demonic allurements had infected their minds.

The crowds of Jews, who lacked the insignia of merit and imagined that they could protect themselves merely by the fortress of the temple, are rebuked by the Lord through Jeremiah in these words:

> “Do not trust in lying words, saying: ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is here,’ and so forth” (Jer. 7).

If we come, then, to the times of the New Testament, we shall likewise find that holy places were profaned by wicked people. For idols are said to have been placed by the pagans on the rock of the cross, at the place of the resurrection, and even in the cave of Bethlehem, where the Lord cried as an infant.

Blessed Jerome says:

> “From the time of Hadrian until the reign of Constantine, for approximately 180 years, a statue of Jupiter was worshiped by the pagans at the place of the resurrection, and a marble statue of Venus was placed on the rock of the cross. The authors of the persecution imagined that they would take away our faith in the resurrection and the cross if they polluted the holy places with idols. Bethlehem, now ours, and the city’s most august site [the transmitted wording is uncertain], of which the Psalmist sings, ‘Truth has sprung from the earth,’ was shaded by a grove of Tammuz, that is, of Adonis; and in the cave where Christ once cried as an infant, the lover of Venus was mourned.”

If a grove of Adonis could pollute the place of Christ’s birth, what wonder is it if a crowd gathered in a perverse assembly could usurp the place of a holy synod in order to establish unlawful practices?

If a statue of Venus placed by the pagans defiled the place of Mount Calvary, which Christ trod on his glorious path as he went toward the triumph of the cross, what wonder is it if a foolish multitude of priests later sought to use the place where an illustrious company of the holy Fathers had once assembled to strengthen the catholic faith, in order to strengthen new constitutions opposed to the Church?

And if a statue of Jupiter profaned the place of the resurrection, which Christ consecrated by rising again and displaying angelic hosts to mortals, what wonder is it if the worship of images was established by various madmen in that same city of Bithynia, in which Christ had earlier been proclaimed by venerable bishops to be of one substance with the Father?

By these examples it can be demonstrated that, contrary to their boastfulness, a certain force belonging to places cannot always remain constant. For human beings are changeable and are not always held bound by the rigidity of one and the same character. Judas, once an apostle, afterward became an apostate; Paul, once Saul and a persecutor, later became the teacher and preacher of the Gentiles. Places once devoted to divine worship have later been profaned by pagans; and, after profanations have often been driven out, places once considered impure have subsequently been devoted to divine worship.

Moreover, both these people and their predecessors seek with insolent eagerness to hold a synod and to associate it with the six venerable synods that were held by holy men at different times for various benefits of the Church, though not with a different faith, and to have it recognized as the seventh synod.

Although both the former and the present group are believed to have greedily pursued this matter, neither has been able to bring it to the desired result. Wishing to abolish what their predecessors had carelessly and disproportionately done, and to establish what they themselves had nevertheless done foolishly and stupidly, they introduced the example of a certain man.

A man who wished to associate a seventh coin with six gold coins, when he tried to add a gold coin, is said to have accepted a bronze coin in place of the gold. These men, having rejected that one, boast that they have associated a gold coin with the gold coins. If they carefully consider the matter, however, when they tried to insert gold in place of bronze, they are believed to have inserted tin; and they attempt to complete the number seven of synods, which their predecessors wished to complete with a bronze synod, by adding a tin synod.

But when the bronze coin has been rejected from the mystery of the number seven and the tin coin likewise removed, only the six will remain—those illuminated both by the perfection of the number and by the radiance of catholic learning. In them pure gold shines through purity of faith, and glory reigns through the perfection of the number.

For in the number six, which is indeed perfect, they appear to possess the perfection of ecclesiastical preaching. In three, which is its half, the confession of the holy Trinity is declared; in two, which is its third, the two Testaments—or the two talents, namely, the gift of understanding and action—are signified as having been granted by the holy and unique Trinity. In one, which is its sixth, either the condition of the old man, who was formed on the sixth day, or the assumption of the new man, whom the Son assumed for the salvation of the world in the sixth age of the world, is most clearly demonstrated.

Thus, in these six most sacred synods, the mystery of the holy Trinity is preached; the harmony of the two Testaments, or the gift of understanding and action, is maintained; the faith in the Lord’s incarnation for human salvation is fully taught; and, because none of these things is lacking in them, they are fortified by the perfection of the number six.

Since they desire with such ardent eagerness to associate their synod with the ancient synods, it can indeed be associated with a certain ancient synod of Ariminum. For just as in that synod the confession of the **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “consubstantiality”) is rejected, so in this one those who worship and adore God alone and are true worshipers are condemned. And just as in that synod the most pernicious doctrine of different substances within the Trinity was established, so in this one the worship and adoration of different things, which are owed to God alone, is approved.

Let the first synod in such a sequence, then, be the synod of Ariminum; the second, that which was held by the predecessors of these men for abolishing the adornments of basilicas; and the third, this synod, which was held by these men in the city of Nicaea on behalf of the worship and adoration of images.

This arrangement is to be understood as follows: the first is a bronze coin, the second a tin coin, and the third a lead coin. For although there is a great distance in time between them, they nevertheless share an agreement in certain errors.

But if, through their pride and ostentation, the second is rejected, let us also give them assistance in removing it from this sequence. Let the first be, as we have said, the synod of Ariminum; let this synod held by these men be the second. Let the first, as we have said, be the bronze coin; and, since that one is despised, let the second—the synod of these men, which occupies the place of the lead coin—be counted.

When these have been set aside, let us be content with only the six holy universal synods and local councils that disagree with them neither in faith nor in preaching. Let us prepare ourselves, with complete integrity of faith and increase of good works, for the terrifying arrival of the dreadful examination and the last day—a day that will be celebrated at his glorious return, of whom the angels said to the apostles:

> “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1).

## CHAPTER XIV. On what Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, says: “Let those rejoice and exult and presume who, making, loving, and venerating the true image of Christ, offer it for the salvation of soul and body; this image he himself, the perfecter of sacrifice and God, receiving our entire substance from us, according to the time of his voluntary Passion, gave manifestly to his disciples as a sign and memorial”

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, made an unprofitable statement, covered by the cloud of ignorance and wrapped in the folds of absurdity. He is also censured for saying: “Let those rejoice and exult and be presumed who make, love, and venerate the true image of Christ and offer it for the salvation of soul and body,” and so forth.

What “let them rejoice and exult” means in this passage is easy to understand. But what is meant by the added expression “and be presumed” gives the reader no indication whatever of a meaning, since it is alien both to the rules of sense and entirely foreign to the integrity of Latin expression. For if he wished to speak of presumption, this third expression cannot be joined in meaning with the two preceding ones—unless perhaps he meant that those rejoice and exult who presume to worship an unlawful thing prohibited by the holy Fathers, and who are driven by such powerful impulses of presumption that, in worshiping senseless objects, they appear to oppose all authoritative Scriptures.

O foolish statement of a bishop, worthy of laughter! It does not clearly show what he called the true image of Christ. If he called true the image made by craftsmen from different materials, he spoke most absurdly and improperly, especially since it is plainly evident that no mortal can form a true image of Christ.

When it is called true, it is greatly removed from the image fashioned by craftsmen. For as far as truth differs from falsehood, so far does the true image of Christ differ from the image that a skilled or unskilled craftsman’s hand forms according to the capacity of its ingenuity.

If, however, he wished to speak of the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, which the faithful receive daily in the sacrament—and he almost disclosed this amid the accumulation of his own nonsense when he said, “which he himself, the perfecter of sacrifice and God, receiving our entire substance from us, according to the time of his voluntary Passion, gave manifestly to his disciples as a sign and memorial”—then he was also seriously mistaken in this.

For he did not offer an image or some prefiguration, but himself, to God the Father as a sacrifice for us. Once he had been prefigured under the shadow of the Law in the sacrifice of a lamb and in certain other things, he truly accomplished what had been prophesied about him in the oracles of the prophets and was offered to God the Father as a saving victim.

He did not give us, now that we have passed beyond the shadows of the Law, some imaginary sign, but the sacrament of his own blood and body. The mystery of the Lord’s blood and body must not now be called an image, but the truth; not a shadow, but the body; not an example of future things, but that which was prefigured by the examples.
