According to the Song of Songs, the day has already dawned and the shadows have been removed (Song 2). Christ, the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes, has already come. He has fulfilled the Law. The people sitting in the region and shadow of death have already seen a great light. The veil of Moses’ face has already fallen away, and the veil of the temple has been torn, revealing to us hidden and unknown things.

The true Melchizedek—namely, Christ, the righteous king and king of peace—has given us not the victims of animals but the sacrament of his body and blood.

He did not say, “This is the image of my body and blood,” but: “This is my body, which will be handed over for you”; and: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26).

Since, as we have said, neither the work of craftsmen can be called the true image of Christ, nor can the mystery of his body and blood—which is known to have been accomplished in reality, not in figure—be called an image, Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, is rightly censured either for one of these things or for both. By so many indications and such weighty evidence, he is shown to have uttered such an absurdity.

The same bishop also said of Christ: “Which he himself, the perfecter of sacrifice and God, receiving our entire substance from us.” He is rightly censured for this, since the human race is called a mass of perdition on account of original sin. The same bishop therefore spoke carelessly when he said that Christ had taken our entire substance from us.

For although Christ assumed the whole of human nature—namely, flesh with its senses and a soul with its reason—without divinity being changed into humanity or humanity into divinity, but with the proper character of both natures remaining intact, and although God the Word assumed a human being in the unity of person, he did not assume the original sin of humanity. It is therefore absurd to say that he assumed our entire substance from us.

For this reason he did not assume our entire substance from us: he is not to be believed to have assumed the guilt of original sin, by which the whole human race is held bound before baptism.

The mass of that ancient sin with which we are born is so great that, if it is divided carefully into its parts, all criminal sins can be found in it. There is pride, because the human being preferred to exist under his own power rather than under God’s; sacrilege, because he did not believe God; homicide, because he cast himself into death; spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; theft, because the forbidden food was appropriated; and avarice, because he desired more than ought to have been sufficient for him.

The human race is so entangled in all these things that even one born from a lawful marriage says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 51).

Christ, therefore, the power of God and the wisdom of God, assumed human nature, not the mass of sin.

But, to return to the matter from which we digressed, we are somewhat uncertain about the profession attributed to this same bishop, who is said to have declared that Christ assumed our entire substance from us. For either great lack of learning compelled him to make this profession, or an enormous error drove him to utter it.

Since we wish to regard him as both learned and orthodox, desiring that no one should perish, as the Lord himself desires, if one of these qualities is lacking in him—and in truth it is lacking—we would prefer to attribute what he said to ignorance rather than to schism.

## CHAPTER XV. On what Epiphanius the deacon said, wishing to establish the worship of images: “For here, raising a title of the Lord, and touching the fringes of the title herself, just as the holy Gospel is indeed approached, because she obtained healing between it and the image of the Lord, a certain herb sprouted which, as it approaches the foot of the title, cures all infirmities”

We have often already said in this work—and it is also plainly evident—that nearly all the statements which they advanced in their synod concerning the veneration of images have been, in some fashion, interpolated with such dense darkness of slothfulness that, being devoid of eloquence and meaning, they scarcely allow their sense to reach the minds of readers. Since the utterly foolish structure of those texts by no means expresses in clear speech what they wish to say, nevertheless amid that same cloud of words there are certain intelligible indications—namely, mentions of names or of very familiar things—just as the little flames of certain torches glimmer through dense darkness. Thus, through the names of things and through well-known realities, the reader’s mind may perceive what they wish to express.

For, unless I am mistaken, in the statement he put forward the deacon Epiphanius attempted to express that the woman healed from the flow of blood by touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment erected a title or image in honor of that same Lord, and again touched the fringes of that image; and that beneath the image a certain plant sprang up which, if it gradually grew and touched the foot of the erected image with its top, would heal every illness. In this deed, however—if indeed it is believed to have happened—no veneration of images is commended.

If, then, that woman, through the weakness proper to her sex and a certain lightness of mind, after receiving the benefit of health, erected an image because she was always seeking the Lord’s presence, being unaware that he can be present everywhere, who is so foolish, having received the gifts of the sacred faith and knowing that he is not absent anywhere, that he would therefore erect an image and venerate it in order to possess his presence?

And if, while the world had not yet been freed from the worship of idols, she imitated, as best she could, the sight of statues of certain dead men erected in cities either to preserve their memory or for worship, who of sound mind would approve her actions and, believing that the Lord is not in things made by hand but in heaven, or rather everywhere, take care to do such things?

Or if perhaps she possessed zeal for God according to a superstitious rite, but not according to knowledge, what Catholic, strengthened in the faith, would take an example from her actions in this matter and do similar things?

Or if perhaps, at the beginning of her conversion, when she was not yet able to eat solid food, she used tender food so that, gradually gaining strength for the reception of solid food, she might grow—namely, so that through something visible and tangible she might approach the worship of the invisible and ineffable God—who, becoming an imitator of her in this deed and spurning the strength of solid food, would wish to be reduced again to the food of infancy?

Therefore, in the miracle which is said to have occurred in the plant—if indeed it is believed to have happened—and which, as he himself confessed, heals every illness, their assertion cannot in any way be supported. For it is said to have happened not so that plants or images might be venerated, but so that the minds of unbelievers, rejecting the vanities of idols, might be converted to the beginnings of the true faith, since, according to the Apostle, signs are believed to have been given not for believers but for unbelievers. The Catholic Church, in order to grow toward faith, had to be nourished by miracles; and, so that its new planting might become strong, it had to be fostered by continual irrigations.

## CHAPTER XVI. The useless statement of the deacon Epiphanius is refuted: “Many things which are consecrated among us do not receive consecration through prayer”; and shortly afterward: “Nor, as things venerated, are we honored and magnified to the greatest extent; for he himself says that the sign of the life-giving cross, without prayer, is sacred among us and is to be venerated, and we are satisfied to receive its sign as sanctification, by which, when made by us, we perform worship toward him with a certain sanctification upon the forehead; and from the sign made in the air by the finger we hope that demons are driven away. Likewise, through the name of its designation, we lead an image back to the honor of the first form, and, kissing it and honoring it honorably, we receive sanctification. For we also kiss and embrace the various sacred vessels we possess, and hope for a certain sanctification.”**

“If you see,” says Scripture, “a man swift in his words, know that a fool has more hope than he”; and, “In much speaking sin will not be absent.” According to this judgment of sacred Scripture, the deacon Epiphanius—who is said to have been swift in words and to have used much speaking in that same synod—both showed that a fool has more hope than he, and accumulated every kind of error through his excessive speech. For although in the preceding chapter we discussed his absurdities to some extent, in this chapter we must likewise discuss them somewhat.

We had indeed resolved to examine in their professions not their words but their statements, and to sift not their grammar but their meanings, since it is futile to seek a grammatical order in them, especially because no statement in the lengthy text of the same reading can stand by means of it. But where there are occasional verbal errors, not yet polished by the file of learning, it is easy to dispute the errors of meaning. Where, then, in the long sequence of a reading there is neither purity of meaning nor integrity of language, it is difficult to dispute each point individually, because the order of discussion extends without limit.

For if each verbal error were discussed while we ought to investigate hidden matters and examine carefully what pertains to ecclesiastical affairs, the many rules of grammatical art learned in the schools would seem to be handed down. But since the progress of our journey in this work is greatly hindered—whether because, owing to the difficulty of their speech, it is hard to discover what some of their statements mean; or because their utterances are infected with barbarisms, solecisms, and other faults, which we are compelled to insert into our discussions because the subject requires it; or because, amid their corrupted words, their meanings are likewise corrupted, and we omit criticisms of their words for the sake of avoiding prolixity while we impress only the sequence of their meanings, doing so laboriously since one depends upon the other and one is inserted into the other—it remains that, with the Lord’s assent, setting aside the criticism occasioned by their verbal faults, we continue the journey we began and have largely completed, shaking apart the disordered conglomerations of their meanings with the blows of spiritual combat.

For the aforementioned deacon Epiphanius, whose statement we had begun to examine, says: “Many things which are consecrated among us do not receive consecration through prayer.” Since this statement, as it stands, has no complete meaning, we infer that he intended to say: “There are many things consecrated among us which are not at all consecrated through the priest’s prayer or the laying on of hands.”

If this is so, it is not sufficiently clear how it can be true. For whatever is consecrated in the Church—whether ecclesiastical orders, the dedication of temples to be consecrated, or other constitutions of this kind—is accomplished through priestly consecrations according to ecclesiastical custom. Indeed, even the nobility of the Christian faith itself, through which one advances to the other degrees, is entered at the very beginnings of infancy through the laying on of priests’ hands and prayers to God.

But if he wished to speak of places, vessels, or any utensils devoted to divine worship, his statement can be shown to be futile, since among the things we have enumerated there is scarcely anything that is not consecrated through the prayers and consecrations of priests. The Church also customarily uses exorcisms and the sprinkling of salt and water, and the consecrations or institutions of all these are known to have been handed down from the earliest beginnings of the Church by the bishops of the churches and are recorded in priestly books.

Since, therefore, the deacon introduced this point in order to associate images—whose veneration they are utterly eager to strengthen, although there is no ecclesiastical institution concerning their consecration—with vessels or other things devoted to divine worship, attempting to establish that, just as these are consecrated without prayers, so images too are consecrated without prayers, his effort can be shown to be void. The consecration of the former is recorded in priestly books and is solemnly celebrated by priests as an ancient tradition; but nowhere among the things accepted by the Church is there any institution concerning the consecration—or the veneration—of images.

When he says, “Nor, as things venerated, are we honored and magnified to the greatest extent; for he himself says that the sign of the life-giving cross, without prayer, is sacred among us and is to be venerated,” I think he intended to say that the sign of the venerable cross, which we honorably make upon ourselves without any prayer or consecration by priests, is nevertheless considered sacred.

In this statement, as in the others, he displays no small degree of madness, since the sign of the cross requires no other consecration than that which was effected through the Mediator between God and human beings.

What he added—“And we are satisfied to receive sanctification from its sign, by which, when it is made by us in worship toward him, we receive a certain sanctification upon the forehead; and from the sign made in the air by the finger we hope that demons are driven away”—belongs to the point introduced above.

It is manifest from clear indications that the sign of the cross contains a great mystery in itself and that images are not to be compared with it; this has also been demonstrated in the earlier parts of this work, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it. For while images, as we said above, are consecrated by no prayer or laying on of hands, the sign of the cross, wherever it is introduced, is made with invocation of the divine name. And while images neither possess nor can or ought to possess any consecration, the sign of the cross has been so sanctified by the Redeemer of the world that it not only does not need any consecration, but, when introduced with invocation of the divine name, consecrates and blesses everything else.

Furthermore, when he says, “Likewise, through the name of its designation, we lead an image back to the honor of the first form, and, kissing it and honoring it honorably, we receive sanctification,” how absurd and contrary to reason this is is perfectly clear. He said that an image can be led, through the designation of its name, to the honor of the first form—that is, to the veneration of the saint whose name is written above it. That this can happen cannot be demonstrated by any evident indication of reason.

If the mere inscription of a name leads images to the honor of the same saints whose names are written upon them, then every object upon which the name of a saint is written ascends to the honor of that saint. Thus stones, pieces of wood, garments, or certain animals upon which the names of particular saints have been written pass into the honor of those saints whose names have been written upon them.

But if written names cannot lead the things we have enumerated to the honor of those whose names they bear, neither can inscriptions of names lead images to the honor of the saints. If the former is rejected after prudent consideration, the latter must also be discarded after careful investigation.

Let two images of beautiful women, for example, be brought before someone who venerates images. Since they bear no inscriptions, he despises them, casts them away, and allows them to lie wherever they happen to fall. Someone then says to him: “One of them is an image of Saint Mary and must not be cast away; the other is of Venus and must be rejected altogether.” He turns to the painter and asks him—which, since they are alike in every respect, is the image of Saint Mary and which is that of Venus? The painter gives one an inscription identifying it as Saint Mary and the other an inscription identifying it as Venus. Because the first bears the inscription of the Mother of God, it is erected, honored, and kissed; because the second bears the inscription of Venus, the mother of Aeneas, a certain exile, it is cast down, reviled, and accursed. Both have the same form, the same colors, and are made from the same materials; they differ only in their inscriptions.

Let the deacon Epiphanius tell me, I ask, who said that through the inscription of a name images can be led to the honor of the first form: where was the holiness of the first image before it was inscribed? Or where did the reproach of the other exist before it was inscribed?

An inscription, therefore, which is customarily placed upon images, according to the practice of letters—whose power is so great that they speak silently and sometimes explain without a voice the words of absent persons, and sometimes those of present persons—can convey information. But it cannot bestow sanctification upon the images on which it is placed.

Sanctification is granted to rational creatures through the display of good works and the privileges of merits. But it comes to irrational and senseless things, such as vessels devoted to divine worship and similar objects, not through any inscription, but through priestly consecration and invocation of the divine name.

Accordingly, it is demonstrated by evident reason that no sanctification can adhere to images through any inscription. For the image that receives the inscription of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, and that once lay contemptibly cast aside but is now honorably adorned, can benefit its worshipers when erected and venerated just as much as it could harm its detractors while lying despised; and it can harm those who despise it just as much as it could help them if it were erected.

When he says, “And, kissing it and honoring it honorably, we shall receive sanctification,” this would amount to saying: “We kiss it and honor it honorably, wishing to receive sanctification from it”—a sanctification which it neither possesses nor is able to impart to us.

It can give sight to the blind as much as it itself sees; odor to one deprived of the sense of smell, when it too lacks that sense; hearing to the deaf, when it does not hear; speech to the mute, when it does not speak; touch in the hands to the powerless, when it can grasp nothing; walking to the lame, which it entirely lacks; life to the dead, when it does not live. To the same extent, then, it can impart sanctification to us, when it entirely lacks sanctification itself.

There is no need to linger longer over the short clause that remains, since almost all of it appears to have been connected in parts with the preceding clauses. For he says: “For we also kiss and embrace the various sacred vessels we possess, and hope for a certain sanctification.”

Sanctification does not come to human beings through vessels, but to vessels through human beings by the invocation of the divine name and the celebration of the sacred mysteries. Nor are images to be equated with vessels, since sacrifice is offered to God in vessels, not in images. For if, as we have said, sanctification is not at all imparted to human beings by vessels that have indeed been sanctified, it will be imparted much less by images, which can neither sanctify nor be sanctified.

## CHAPTER XVII. The most ridiculous statement of Epiphanius is refuted: “He spoke from his own belly.”

What is written in that same synod—that the aforementioned Epiphanius said of someone, “He spoke from his own belly”—although it brings no prejudice to matters pertaining to the faith and neither contributes nor detracts anything from the issue under discussion, has nevertheless not been passed over by us. It sounds unlearned and foolish, and no new ecclesiastical constitutions ought to be derived from such a writing, which can be criticized in so many ways.

For everything that is irreprehensible is received by the holy Catholic Church; but what is criticized on many grounds is rejected from ecclesiastical doctrine. Nor should the judgment concerning the veneration of images be observed in a reading full of criticisms and such absurdities.

They said, then, that someone spoke “from his own belly.” This statement is rejected not only by learned ears but also by unlearned ones, and is dismissed as a kind of old-womanish delirium. For what the mind conceives is brought forth from the heart through the tongue as interpreter. From the belly are administered those things which, once sent into the privy, are expelled. And just as the heart—which both in divine writings and in ordinary speech is often used for the mind or understanding—cannot digest food or contain collections of bodily fluids, so the belly cannot conceive thoughts and bring them forth through words.

Each bodily member therefore has its own function, so that the five senses are distributed among the parts of the five members, except for touch, which, although it is thought to have its seat in the hands, is spread through the other members as well.

According to the observations of philosophers, fear is in the heart, joy in the spleen, pleasure in the liver. In the three ventricles of the brain, the following are shown to reside: in the front one, which is toward the face, sensation; in the rear one, which is toward the neck, movement; and in the one between the two, memory. The lungs have the function of breathing, modulating the voice, and drawing in the breath. But the belly, which is known to have the shape of a sea, is clearly devoted only to the digestion of food and the collection of bodily fluids.

If they wish to support the error of this statement by such arguments—that the mention of the belly frequently occurs in sacred writings, as in “My belly is troubled” (Lam. I; Hab. III; Eccl. XI), or “My belly pains me” (Ecclus. XXXVII), and other expressions of this kind—they should observe that the word for this member is never used for speech, but metaphorically for various other things signified by the belly. To discuss these matters now would take too long.

The former expression, wherever it occurs, is tropological; the latter is acyrological. Through the former, truth is allegorically overshadowed; through the latter, the purity of meaning is mutilated. The former shines with mysteries; the latter is foul with absurdities.

But if they wished to speak of Pythons, whom the Seventy translated as “ventriloquists,” concerning whom it is written in Deuteronomy: “There shall not be found among you one who passes his son or his daughter through fire, one who practices divination, interprets omens, observes auguries, practices soothsaying, uses enchantments, a sorcerer, a ventriloquist, one who observes portents, or one who consults the dead” (Deut. XVIII), this too is not free from criticism.

For when they say that a certain man spoke from his own belly, as a Python, not even in the belly of the Python does a human being speak; rather, an evil spirit speaks. This happens only in such a way that, while the same Python—who is called a ventriloquist—speaks through his mouth in human fashion, the voices of unclean spirits are heard from his belly and answers are given. It is evident that there are many such ventriloquists among the Assyrian or Egyptian peoples, among whom magical arts abound.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Against those who say: “Those who called the image of idols similar to images of demons should accuse Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Samuel, and David, because they themselves offered pagan and alien sacrifices to God.”

As far as this chapter sounds, and as we have learned from their other statements, they are attempting to establish the following: since sacrifices of slaughtered animals were once offered by pagans to demons, yet this did not prevent holy men under the Old Law from offering to God victims consisting of slaughtered animals, neither should it be considered a reason to refrain from venerating images within the holy Church merely because idols were worshiped by the nations.

But just as in their other assertions concerning this matter their objections are uselessly and ineffectively brought forward, so this objection too, improperly introduced, will be defeated by the opposition of a prudent argument.

It is evident that in former times sacrifices of slaughtered animals were offered both to the almighty God by holy men and to demons by pagan priests. It is also evident that in ancient times images of wicked men were placed in shrines at the instigation of demons, while images of certain saints were kept by Catholics in basilicas to preserve the memory of their deeds and to adorn buildings.

Therefore, just as the practice of sacrificing slaughtered animals is read to have been observed by the fathers before the Law and was handed down by the Lord through Moses in the Law, let them say where the practice of venerating images was instituted—whether before the Law by the patriarchs, in the Law by the lawgiver, in the New Testament by the Lord and Savior, or by the apostles or apostolic men. And since the celebration of sacrifices has such an authoritative tradition, let them say what authority the veneration of images possesses.

Since they cannot say this, let them blush at having brought forward a useless matter, and let them come to their senses and recognize that they have attempted in vain to associate the veneration of images with the offering of holy sacrifices.

How, then, can it be believed that images were made by Catholics for veneration, when even the images of the pagans themselves are not said to have been originally made for veneration?

The use of images arose when, out of longing for deceased men—whether brave men, kings, founders of certain cities, or inventors of various arts—those who had loved them made images or likenesses of them, so that the grief of their descendants or loved ones might find some relief in contemplating the images. But gradually, as demons persuaded them into this error, it infiltrated later generations to such an extent that those whom their predecessors had judged should be painted solely for the sake of remembering their names were considered gods and worshiped by their successors; and the latter reckoned that demons had enticed wretched, deluded people to sacrifice to them.

We can see from this example that the use of images likewise becomes established. Things that had initially been assembled for the adornment of basilicas and for preserving the memory of past deeds are now, as the wicked practice gradually grew, exalted by many Catholics to such an extent that they are venerated, and lamps, incense, first fruits, or certain small gifts are offered to them. What is worse, as we read happened in the regions of Greece, bishops who ought to have proclaimed that God alone should be worshiped, that he alone should be revered, and that he alone should be served, admit that they themselves will serve the images, and worship and venerate them. They even judge those who despise them and worship God alone—those who are true worshipers—to be heretics because of their contempt for the images, and seek to anathematize them.

Thus, in one and nearly the same manner, as we have said, the most wicked practice of venerating and worshiping images—or rather demons—has grown among the pagans, while among Catholics the utterly foolish custom of venerating images is increasing. Things made for one purpose appear to be used for another.

We do not call the images placed in basilicas idols. But, lest they be called idols, we refuse to venerate or worship them or to render them service, because often it is not the thing but the reason for the thing that is reckoned as a crime. Many things that can be used well are turned into wickedness when used badly. Thus one and the same thing is not a cause of guilt for those who use it well, but becomes a cause of danger for those who use it badly.

Therefore, we must carefully guard against this and take the greatest pains to ensure that, while some of our people seek to exalt certain things beyond what order requires, the revived ashes of that ancient and decayed error do not grow strong in them, and that they do not lose within the walls of the city the victory they gained in the field. Otherwise, the deceitful illusion of civil war may unexpectedly subdue those whom the open assault of an external enemy could not subdue.

Since they chatter that the holy fathers—Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Samuel, and David—ought to be accused, we do not wish to accuse them but to praise them, as Ecclesiasticus says:

“Let us praise illustrious men and our fathers in their generations. The Lord has bestowed great glory through his magnificence: men who from of old ruled in their dominions, great in virtue and endowed with wisdom, distinguished in the dignity of prophets, governing the people in their time, and uttering most holy words in the strength of wisdom,” and so forth (Ecclus. XLIV).

Who, then, has so profane a mind that he would dare accuse Abel, who was called righteous by the Lord himself? His blood is read to have cried from the earth to the Lord. He is the model and standard of all the righteous; he was the first to go before the saints who would suffer persecution; and he was the first to lay the foundations of the city of God, which the rush of the river makes glad.

Or who would presume to accuse Noah, a righteous man? The Lord testifies that Noah found grace before him. After Adam, Noah became the second father of the human race and the renewer of the world. As a figure of Christ, who would govern the Church filled with many nations amid the terrible storms of worldly waves, Noah was the pilot of the ark filled with various living creatures amid the crashing of roaring waters. He is adorned with so many marks of merit that he alone, together with Daniel and Job, is said to be delivered on the day of judgment, as Ezekiel testifies:

“If I send pestilence upon that land and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to cut off from it man and beast, and Noah, Daniel, and Job are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter, but they themselves shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness” (Ezek. XIV).

In these three saints the entire multitude of the saints is signified: through Noah, the governors of the Church; through Daniel, virgins and the continent; through Job, married people and penitents.

Or who would desire to accuse Abraham the patriarch? He is the first path of believers and the aged father of blessed offspring. It was not observance of the Law but the faith of his belief that was reckoned to him as righteousness. Seeing the Trinity in figure and venerating unity in mystery, he was deemed worthy to hear the secrets of divine judgment and the astonishing miracle of offspring to be received from an aged wife. He figuratively perceived the future tribulations at the end of the world through the faith of which he himself was the example, when, toward the end of the day, an exceedingly great and dark terror fell upon him.

Or who would presume to accuse Moses, the lawgiver? It is written that he was the meekest of all who dwelt upon the earth. Standing as mediator between God and human beings in a figure of Christ, he liberated the people from Egyptian slavery through terrible signs and wonders after conquering the most wicked enemy.

Or Samuel, who, consecrated to the Lord from his very cradle, served in the Lord’s army until extreme old age?

Or David, who is said to have been found a man according to the Lord’s heart, and who was so distinguished in the merits of the saints that he prophesied openly to all concerning Christ and was called his father according to the form of a servant?

If we were to set forth their praises and mysteries individually, the days would run out before the words. For they were not offering pagan sacrifices to God, but sacrifices full of mysteries. The Athenians were not yet being called pagans from their villages when sacrifices were already being offered to God by them; indeed, so to speak, the city of Athens had not yet been founded, nor had Cecrops handed down to the pagans the institutions for offering sacrifices, the erection of altars, and the names of demons, when Abel, Noah, and Abraham had already offered sacrifices to God.

The saints offered sacrifices—whether before the Law or under the Law—sacrifices overshadowed by figurative mysteries. In the New Testament these mysteries were completed through the mediator of God and human beings, after the shadowy prefigurations had been removed, and were handed down to the Church, which, with his help, will remain content with them until the end.

Why, then, did the ancient fathers visibly sacrifice and offer carnal sacrifices to God? Let the reader learn from the words of blessed Augustine. He says:

“Those too are spiritual sacred rites, whose images the carnal people ought to celebrate, so that the prefiguration of the new people might be accomplished through the servitude of the old. The distinction between these two peoples may also be observed in each one of us, since each person must live as the old human being from his mother’s womb until he reaches youthful age, when it is no longer necessary to think in a carnal manner, but he can turn by his will toward spiritual things and be inwardly regenerated. What therefore occurs in one properly educated human being through the order of nature and discipline is beautifully accomplished, by proportion, in the whole human race through divine providence.”

## CHAPTER XIX. Against those who say: “If Saint Epiphanius was a destroyer and rejecter of images, how did his disciples paint images on the island of Cyprus, in the temple which they named after that same father, since many things are painted which are not venerated, and bad disciples often arise from good teachers?”

Those concerning whom we are speaking congratulate themselves on having found in this matter great weapons and instruments for defending their error, because, they say, on the island of Cyprus a basilica was painted by the disciples of a certain holy man, Epiphanius—as though nothing could be painted without immediately becoming something that ought to be venerated.

Since the practice of possessing or not possessing images does not prejudice the purity of the Catholic faith, it is clear that Epiphanius himself, or any other holy man, was neither a destroyer nor a venerator of images; and that his disciples, or any Catholic men, did not paint basilicas with colored pigments for the purpose of venerating the paintings, but so that beauty might be imparted to the walls and the memory of past deeds might be brought before those who looked upon them.

For the fact that the disciples of Epiphanius are said to have painted a basilica on the island of Cyprus does not mean that images will therefore be venerated, since not everything that is painted is immediately venerated. If each painted object had to be venerated, very few creatures would remain that were not venerated.

We see images fashioned in metals by casting or engraving; in precious stones and gems through the marvelous art of the sculptor; in marble and other stones through the skill of quarrymen or sculptors; in wood by the carver’s knife; in mosaic pavements through pieces of various colors assembled by an artisan; and in silk, wool, and linen garments of many colors through the work of embroiderers and tapestry-makers.

Since the disciples of the holy man Epiphanius painted a basilica in Cyprus, must all these things therefore be venerated? Or because they adorned a place dedicated to divine worship with various materials, must the faithful run to each of the materials we mentioned on behalf of the images applied to them, bending their knees, bowing their necks, sighing repeatedly, and reverently raising their eyes, often half closed?

It does not follow, therefore, that images should be venerated because they are said to have painted a basilica.

Another reasonable objection can also be made to their argument. Just as their assertion could not be supported by their other objections, so it cannot be established by the basilica painted by the disciples of Epiphanius—especially since, even if the agreement of the disciples of that holy man had judged that the paintings they themselves had placed upon the walls should be venerated, their judgment would possess no authority. For often disciples who have been well educated by good teachers later neglect their teachers’ instruction and become perverse.

If this is sought out through careful investigation, it will be confirmed by examples from the sacred writings.

The holy man Elisha’s disciple, endowed with a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, was so seized by love of money that, after receiving a gift from a foreigner and spurning his teacher, he was defiled by a deadly disease. Neither prophetic admonition, nor his teacher’s instruction, nor the display of terrible signs, nor living in the company of so great a prophet restrained him from such a plague—that is, from greed. Rather, the greed that invaded him branded him with leprosy together with the Syrian’s payment.

Judas too, of whom it is written through the Prophet, “The man of my peace, who ate my bread, has greatly increased his treachery against me” (Ps. XLI), and to whom it was once said, “But you, a man of one mind, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food” (Ps. LV), neglected the instruction of a good teacher—and truly a good one, who said of himself, “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. XX), and of whom David says, “You are good, Lord; teach me your goodness”; of whom Jeremiah also says, “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. III).

Judas was seized by a frenzy of greed that was especially capable—or rather, especially rapacious—so that he did not hesitate to betray his teacher. Neither heavenly words, nor the overflowing of the fountain of life, nor the display of signs, nor the fellowship of the apostles, nor the dignity of the apostolic name restrained him from committing so great a crime. Once he recognized the wickedness of his crime, he ended an unworthy life by a deserved death. Concerning him Sedulius says:

Then the apostolic man became a vile apostate. Nicholas too, a disciple of the apostles and, together with blessed Stephen, consecrated to the ministry of the diaconate as one of the seven, later disregarding the teachings of his good teachers and the fellowship of his good fellow deacons, became the founder of a heresy. Although, as a disciple of the apostles, he ought by example and word to have established the practice of good works, he reversed the proper order and himself established the crime of a wicked heresy, concerning which it is written in the Apocalypse: “But this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (Rev. II).

If, then, the bad disciple of a good prophet is rejected because of avarice; if the disciple of the good teacher—namely, our Lord and Savior—who became a thief and traitor is abhorred; and if the bad disciple of the holy apostles is condemned because of the impious doctrine he himself established, what wonder is it if the bad disciples of the good teacher Epiphanius are made so by instituting the adoration of paintings? In saying this, we do not judge them reprobates, since we do not know their life and conduct; but, having introduced the conditional clause, we assert that they are mistaken in this matter if they have judged that paintings ought to be adored.

Let us consider, then, Novatian, the presbyter of the bishop Cyprian, who founded the Novatian heresy and, following his own judgment, rejected the admonitions of his holy teacher. We also know that Arius was instructed by a Catholic teacher and afterward sowed the seeds of a destructive doctrine. Why should I speak of each one individually? It is established that nearly all the founders of heresies were disciples of Catholics, since no one could give a heresy his own name unless he had devised it according to his own judgment. From these examples it is gathered that the holiness of the teacher profited the disciples of holy Epiphanius nothing, if they are believed to have strayed from the ecclesiastical constitutions after rejecting the instruction of their good teacher.

## CHAPTER XX

That they attempted, in a flattering manner, to equate their emperor—or his mother—with the apostles, saying: “Just as formerly Jesus, the ruler and perfecter of our salvation, sent forth his own apostles clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit, so now he has raised up our own gracious and apostle-like faithful emperors, made wise by the same Spirit and possessing the power suitable for our perfection.”

We find, by the Lord’s truthful word, that the apostles will sit with the Lord to judge: “You who have followed me,” he says, “in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII). The Lord himself testifies that he chose them from the world so that they would not be of the world, but would bear abundant fruit: “I chose you,” he says, “from the world, so that you would not be of the world; and I chose you so that you might bear abundant fruit, and your fruit might remain forever” (John XV).

It is clear that they are the salt of the earth (Matt. V)—that is, the seasoning of the people, by which whatever is tasteless is seasoned and what lacks flavor is given savor. They are the light of the world, for by the radiance of the true light, namely Christ, they illumined the darkness of the world—the darkness, that is, of unbelief—through the words of their preaching. To them the Lord gives on earth, through his breathing upon them, and from heaven, through fire and the division of tongues, the Holy Spirit, to signify love of God and neighbor. To them is given the power of loosing and binding, of forgiving and retaining sins, of raising the dead, casting out demons, healing the sick, and performing other works of this kind; and authority is conferred upon them to teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Holy Trinity.

They were commanded to rejoice because the book of heavenly eternal life contains their names. To them it was said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear” (Luke X), because, according to the most truthful testimony of that same Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, many prophets and kings desired to see what they saw and to hear what they heard. For although the distinguished assemblies of all the patriarchs and prophets knew through the instruction of the prophetic Spirit that the Redeemer of the world would come for the salvation of the world, and in some manner beheld him with the eye of inward contemplation, nevertheless they yearned to see bodily the one whom they knew would come bodily.

Although they excel in so many marks of merit and possess such an abundance of blessedness, those whose errors we are examining strive in vain to assimilate their emperors to them. For it is plainly evident that the apostles were set above the prophets. If, as those men dream, their emperors are like the apostles, then they are preferred to the prophets, who, although they knew that Christ would come bodily, did not see him bodily. If they are preferred to the prophets, then they saw the Redeemer of the world bodily. But it is most evident that they did not see the Redeemer of the world bodily. Therefore their emperors are not preferred to the prophets, nor are they, as those men say, like the apostles.

How, then, can they be likened to the apostles, when they are not only not equal to them in comparable merits or endowed with a similar splendor of holiness, but even appear in many respects to oppose their most sacred preaching? Or how can they be like those whose followers they neglect to be?

The apostles pursued heavenly things that would endure forever; these men pursue all manner of earthly and perishable things. The apostles, scorning the world, preferred to cling to the Lord; these men, clinging to the world’s pageants and its smoky pleasures, frequently despise the Lord’s commands. The apostles suffered persecution for righteousness; these men frequently persecute because of unrighteousness. The apostles were handed over in councils and flogged in synagogues; these men are proclaimed in the cities subject to them and praised by the peoples. The apostles’ letters, carrying the commerce of eternal life, were taken throughout provinces and regions to be read; the images and likenesses of these men, expressing a certain pagan and obsolete error, are carried through villages and cities to be adored.

The apostles were called blessed by the Lord when people hated them, persecuted them, and spoke every evil against them falsely; these men consider themselves blessed when they appear to see that people love them, obey them, and praise them. To the apostles it is said: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” (Matt. V); to these men it is said: “Laughter is mixed with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. XIV). When the world rejoiced, the apostles were sorrowful, intending to rejoice when the world was again sorrowful; these men rejoice when the world rejoices and will be sorrowful when the world is sorrowful.

As the apostles went into the world, whose passing form they proclaimed, they mourned its wicked deeds, sowing the seeds of eternal fruit. These men, established in the world and rejoicing in the world’s prosperity, embrace the prosperity of the present life. The apostles will come to judgment in exultation, secure in their eternal reward, carrying the sheaves of those converted through their preaching; these men will come with great trembling to render an account of their deeds.

But why do we linger any longer? Why do we wander further afield? Why do we gather a few flowers from immense forests, when we cannot gather even a thousandth part of them? The distance between the apostles and emperors is as great as that between saints and sinners; and since the apostles excel all the saints of the New Testament, they are believed to excel sinners by far more.

O flattery, why do you presume so much? O oil of rancor, overflowing with stench rather than with the radiance of gentleness or nectar! You are sold by priests, smeared by bishops upon the heads of certain readers; and what the Prophet dreaded having applied to himself—“Let not the oil of sinners fatten my head,” he says (Ps. CXL)—the assembly of bishops puts upon the heads of emperors. What the virgins of the Gospel said must be bought from the sellers, this, alas, the faithful—and especially the rulers of the peoples—buy from the bishops.

When, therefore, they confess that these same emperors have been made wise by the same Spirit—that is, by the Holy Spirit—and made capable in power for their perfection, it is evident that all the faithful who are truly Christians possess the Holy Spirit, since the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. VIII). The gift of the Holy Spirit is poured out after baptism through the laying on of hands and is distributed to each according to the difference of merits through purity of life, as the vessel of election says: “Grace has been given to each according to the measure” (Eph. IV).

Although it is written elsewhere, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III), nevertheless he imparts the Spirit by measure to each of the faithful. As for the statement, “God does not give the Spirit by measure,” it should be understood of the Son alone, who is consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not given to him by measure, since, in Paul’s words, “the whole fullness of divinity is believed to dwell bodily in him” (Col. II). But when it is said that the Spirit is given by measure and distributed individually to each as he wills, this is without ambiguity understood to have been said of the faithful.

Yet although it is established that every Catholic possesses the Holy Spirit, as we recalled above and illustrated with examples, we do not dare say or affirm that any person of our age has received the Holy Spirit according to the measure of apostolic grace.

## CHAPTER XXI

Concerning what they said: “For prophecy says: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son’ (Isa. VII). Now, seeing this prophecy in an image—namely, a virgin carrying in her arms the one she bore—how can we endure not adoring and kissing it? Who would dare, with an undisciplined mind, resist? Let us therefore make ourselves worthy of such a kiss of adoration, so that, approaching unworthily, we may not suffer the punishment of Uzzah.”

The prophecy that proclaims that a virgin would conceive and bear a son is no longer to be sought among uncertainties and ambiguities, but retained in the breast; nor are its hidden mysteries to be investigated in paintings, but in the divine Scriptures and in their interpreters—namely, the apostles and their successors—and contemplated by faith rather than by the eyes.

For the most noble prophet Isaiah, giving us the flavor of the Gospel rather than of prophecy, did not say, “Unless you paint and adore images, you will not remain,” but said, “If you do not believe, you will not remain” (Isa. VII). It is therefore clear that whoever wishes to remain steadfast in the divine commandments through the integrity of faith and to attain eternal reward ought to possess the means by which he may come to these things not on walls, not on panels, not in paintings, nor in any visible objects, but in the heart through faith, in the mouth through confession, and in conduct through the exhibition of good works.

He must believe that the virgin who brought forth the Savior of the world is present not in the works of worldly craftsmen, but in the work of the eternal and ineffable craftsman—that is, in the heavenly dwellings. Therefore, whoever desires to adore her must fix the gaze of his mind not upon pigments of color, not upon material workmanship, not upon any workshop, but upon that place where she is known to reign with Christ.

When they say, “Now, seeing this prophecy in an image—namely, a virgin carrying in her arms the one she bore—how can we endure not adoring and kissing it? Who would dare, with an undisciplined mind, resist?” we, following nearly the same words in sound but not in meaning, reply: Seeing this painting on a panel or wall—a painted virgin carrying a child in her arms—how can we presume to adore a senseless object and kiss the work of any craftsman? Who with an undisciplined mind would dare commit such a deed as to offer to creatures the adoration owed to the Creator, and, while wishing to favor paintings, resist the sacred Scriptures?

Granted that an image of the holy Mother of God is to be adored: how can we know which image is hers, or by what signs it can be distinguished from other images? For there is no difference among them except the skill of the craftsmen, the things from which their works are made, and the qualities of their materials.

When, therefore, we see a certain beautiful woman depicted holding a child in her arms, if the inscription has not yet been made, or if one once made has by some accident been destroyed, by what skill can we discern whether she is Sarah holding Isaac, or Rebecca carrying Jacob, or Bathsheba tossing Solomon, or Elizabeth carrying John, or any woman holding her little child? And, to turn to pagan stories, which are often found depicted, how can we know whether it is Venus holding Aeneas, or Alcmena carrying Hercules, or Andromache bearing Astyanax?

If one is adored in place of another, it is madness; but if one is adored who ought by no means to be adored, it is insanity. Both must be avoided.

The same blessed virgin is also painted as having descended into Egypt, riding upon a donkey and carrying the child in her arms, with Joseph going before her, and as having returned from Egypt to the land of Israel. This story is inserted in many kinds of materials: not always in basilicas, but sometimes on eating or drinking vessels, and sometimes on silk garments, though most often on coverlets. Are all these things, then, to be adored?

When, therefore, in any of these objects an image of the holy virgin holding the child and seated upon the back of a four-footed animal is adored, is not the image of the animal itself adored along with her? For in adoring the two images—the image of the virgin and that of the animal—it is in no way possible to make a separation between them, especially since they are of one material and joined together by the same artistic skill. Either the adoration of both must be rejected, or both must be adored.

But perhaps some thorny-minded person will say: “This argument about adoring the animal is futile. When we adore a person seated on a chair or leaning upon a staff as a form of greeting, we are not thereby shown to adore the chair or the staff with him; once the person has been greeted, they are believed to remain ungreeted.”

Such a thorn must be shattered in this way: the definition of a human being is one thing, and that of a staff or chair another. A human being is defined in this manner: “A human being is a rational, mortal, laughable animal,” and so forth. A chair or staff, however, is not defined in the same way; they are things lacking strength, sensation, and life, prepared according to the skill or intention of the craftsman for the functions for which they are necessary, and so forth. Here it is plainly evident that greeting a rational human being with adoration is one thing, while leaving a chair or staff ungreeted as senseless objects is another.

But in the definition of the image of the virgin and of the four-footed animal, since both are without sensation or life, made from one material, formed by one and the same craftsman, and so mutually joined that they cannot be separated from one another without dividing the material in which they are set, there is almost no difference in their definition. Since there is such equality, such association, and such unity of material between them, either the adoration of both must be accepted or that of both rejected.

Since one cannot be separated from the other without division, and since both ought not to be adored lest the image of the animal happen to be adored, it remains that both should be deprived of the honor of adoration. They should occupy places merely as ornaments in basilicas or in whatever locations, and provide those who look upon them with a memory of the events represented. For since the adoration of images tends by so many byways toward such great errors, no evident reason shows that it can stand within the holy Church.

They therefore encourage one another to become worthy of kissing or adoring senseless objects, saying: “Let us make ourselves worthy of such a kiss of adoration, so that, approaching unworthily, we may not suffer the punishment of Uzzah.”

Let us, then, make ourselves worthy of adoring the divine majesty—or rather, let us be made worthy by him from whom come both the willing and the accomplishing—and, as true worshipers, let us adore the Lord not according to their vanity in some image, but in spirit and truth, as Truth himself says: “True worshipers will adore the Father in spirit and truth” (John IV).

As for their warning that they should make themselves worthy of the kisses and adorations of images so that they might not suffer the punishment of Uzzah, let them beware lest, because of that presumption by which Uzzah thought the ark of the Lord would fall without his support, while these men likewise think that divine worship would be frustrated without the support of images, they incur the sentence of that destructive punishment.

The ark did not need his support to prevent it from falling; nor does the Church need the support of images in order to stand more firmly. Just as the ark, while God suffered no want, moved onward without any falling of its own and without the support of Uzzah, so the Church, under the Lord’s governance, remains undefiled without any shipwreck, leaving aside the assistance of images.

What, then, does it mean to wish to place one’s hand beneath the ark of the Lord’s covenant, which was governed by the Lord so that it would not fall, except to wish to admit the adoration of images into the Catholic religion, which is certainly governed by the Lord so that it will not stumble along the journey of this life?

Or to whom can Uzzah be compared—he who, without the counsel of priests and fellow Levites, presumptuously wished to provide a new support for the ark of the Lord—except to those who, without the teaching of the holy Fathers and the agreement of their fellow priests established throughout the various parts of the world, strive with a certain arrogance and haughty intention to introduce a new adoration of images into the Christian religion?

He therefore lost his life who proudly desired to support the ark of God. For whoever believes that God, who is wholly everywhere and wondrous everywhere, needs some object in which he may be adored, and adores him in visible things, must beware lest he lose his life when he boldly resists his life-giving commands.

This Levite is therefore rightly called Uzzah, a name interpreted as “strong.” For unless all presumptuous people believed themselves strong in mind, they would never convene synods in which a new decree concerning the adoration of images might be established.

## CHAPTER XXII

Concerning the fact that they do not even spare themselves when they inflict injury upon their parents, saying: “Instead of true wheat they sowed weeds in the ecclesiastical fields; they mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a turbulent drink; being Arabian wolves, they mocked the wearing of sheep’s clothing; passing by the truth, they embraced falsehood; they cast the eggs of asps and, according to the prophet, wove spiders’ webs; and whoever hopes to eat their eggs will find, when he breaks the tail, a basilisk filled with poison and deadly breath.”

Their intemperate madness is condemned in this delirium just as in their other statements, because they said that their elders had sown weeds instead of wheat in the ecclesiastical fields, mixed wine with water, and given their neighbors a turbulent drink. This is especially blameworthy because, in nearly everything in which those elders are believed to have done wrong in this matter, these men are reported not only to have failed to correct those things but to have done even worse.

Thus, according to the poet who says:

> “Instead of the tender violet, instead of the purple narcissus,  
> let the thistle and the hawthorn rise with sharp thorns.”

(Virg. *Eclogue* V)

Instead of wheat, weeds rose up for the elders of these men; but for these men, while the weeds had not yet been uprooted, the thorny hawthorn rose instead of wheat. For, neglecting the wheat of prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic preaching—in which it is judged that places dedicated to divine worship should be adorned, and the worship and adoration of God alone is commended—they are shown to have received the destructive doctrine of mad weeds and thorny hawthorn, whether by abolishing ornaments from basilicas or by adoring those same ornaments.

Those who ought to have nourished the minds of the faithful with the fullness of that satisfaction which never causes weariness, through the grain of the divine word, strive instead to infect them with a doctrine that, producing great disgust, nourishes madness and thrusts in the prickles of error.

They declared that their elders had mixed water with wine and offered their neighbors a turbulent drink. With good reason it can be objected to them that their elders made the wine of sacred discourse, which they ought to have used, tasteless by mixing it with water when they decreed that ornaments should be abolished from basilicas. These men, however, sharpened the drink of that same wine, already adulterated by their predecessors with water, into poison when they professed that they would adore images and offer them service, and attempted to condemn with anathemas those who rejected their adoration.

Then neither group is ashamed to offer a turbulent drink to its neighbors, since they do not hesitate to corrupt their preaching—which they ought to adorn with sacred discourse and examples of good works—with empty and extraordinary decrees. They do not fear to display it to their contemporaries in life and conduct and to commit it to the memory of posterity in writing.

As for their assertion that wolves are concealed beneath sheep’s skins and that, rejecting the truth, they embraced falsehood, they will see the same thing happening in themselves if they pay careful attention. Those men, pretending to possess great holiness and as though inflamed by zeal for it, cast images out of the churches, since they had not been placed by the ancients for adoration. These men, inflamed as though by love of excessive holiness, decree that the images must be adored. They do not think the gifts of the Catholic faith sufficient for themselves unless they offer them the service of adoration.

Yet both act from a desire for empty praise. What else do they do but hide wolves beneath sheep’s skins? While outwardly pretending either zeal or devotion to holiness, inwardly they show that they possess the wolfish rage by which they strive to excel others and gnaw them with the teeth of anathemas.

Thus, passing by the truth, both embrace falsehood. While arrogantly and proudly they are eager to establish whatever is new, and, guided by no humility, do not follow the examples of the ancient Fathers, they depart from that truth which neither knows how to deceive nor to be deceived, and cling to the falsehood of which it is written: “From the beginning he was a liar and did not stand in the truth” (John VIII).

What, then, is it to pass by the truth except to oppose through boastfulness the commands of Christ, who is the author of humility? What is it to follow falsehood except to pursue, by being enticed into new and unlawful decrees and by resisting ancient and salutary traditions, the examples of him who is the author of pride?

Both do this when, puffed up by the wind of pride, they seize upon the error either of breaking or of adoring images.

Moreover, when they assert that their elders produced the eggs of asps and wove a spider’s web, they inflict no slight insults upon themselves in this matter. For their eggs they are, since they have either been propagated from them through the substance of the flesh, or imbued with them through various studies, or certainly consecrated by them through the laying on of hands in ecclesiastical orders. They are their web because they have been woven by them either bodily through descent or spiritually through teaching.

They therefore rightly call themselves the eggs of asps and the web of spiders, because they stop their own ears so that they will not hear with their inner ear the words of Scripture, which establish the worship and adoration of the one and only God. They do not fear to begin, through preaching, and weave through practice, the web of new and useless decrees for capturing or enticing souls.

According to their own statement, whoever desires to be their egg will find a basilisk within, because whoever wishes to follow their preaching finds in them the breath of a deadly tradition. While he wishes to find some remedy with which to soothe his hunger through preaching, he discovers the loss of his inner salvation and is destined to lose his life.

For this reason we have thought little of sparing them in our disputation, because we find that they have in no way spared themselves in their own disputation. Having received from them the material for reproach, we hurl their own darts at them.

We do all this not without love, but because we seek their conversion from error, in the hope that perhaps at some time they may cease to follow the monstrosities of their error and desire to hold fast forever to the way that leads to life.

## CHAPTER XXIII

The useless and uninstructed interpretation of those who, wishing to affirm that adoration and kissing are one and the same, said: “The holy leaders of our doctrine and their successors, the distinguished [the phrase *egregium patrum nostrorum* is grammatically uncertain], and these are to be adored, namely kissed; for the two are the same thing. In common ancient Greek usage, moreover, ‘to kiss’ and ‘to embrace’ are denoted, and by some extension of the will [kissing] signifies love, just as *fero* and *offero* [‘I carry’ and ‘I offer’], *firmo* and *confirmo* [‘I strengthen’ and ‘I confirm’], *participo* and *adoro* [‘I share’ and ‘I adore’]. This demonstrates a kiss and an extension of friendship: for what anyone loves, he also adores, and what he adores he certainly loves.”

In the distinction between kissing and adoration—two things which they think are one—we need not labor at excessive length, since these two names differ from one another as much as the things of which they are the names differ; and necessarily they have a great distinction from each other, since the things themselves often have a great separation, especially because sometimes what is adored is not kissed, and [Col. 1234A] what is kissed is not adored. God is adored, but is not kissed; the saints who departed from this world with the triumphs of their merits are venerated, but they ought neither to be adored with divine worship nor can they be kissed. Conversely, spouses, children, and also servants are kissed, yet are not adored.

For it is clear that kissing and adoration are the names of two things. How, then, can there be such unity of the names in meaning when there is such diversity of the things in understanding? Or why should words not differ in meaning when the origins of words can differ in actual usage? Things were not created for the sake of names, but names for the sake of things; nor should we believe that things are fitted to names, but rather that names are fitted to things. For we read that the animals were brought by the Lord to the first-formed man so that he might see what he should call them; the father of the human race gave names to things created by God. He did not see things brought to him, created by himself, to which he might impose names.

Finally, the philosopher Plato established that names are natural, and tried to prove this from the fact that they are, in a certain way, equipment and instruments for expressing perceptions. But natural equipment is natural, just as the eyes are instruments for seeing, and sight is a natural thing; therefore the eyes too must necessarily be natural. Likewise, speech is the equipment and instrument of natural things—that is, of thoughts—and therefore it too is natural.

Aristotle, however, says that speech is not according to nature but according to convention, and consequently that speech is not natural equipment. When he says that it is not an instrument, he does not mean that perceptions are not expressed through this instrument; he means only that speech is a thing established by convention, through which we demonstrate our own thoughts. The same philosopher, whose authority should especially be followed on this point, says in his book *On Interpretation*:

> “A name is a significant spoken sound according to convention, without time.”

That is, a name is a spoken sound. But some spoken sounds signify, while others signify nothing; a name, however, signifies that of which it is the name. A name, therefore, is a significant spoken sound.

Among significant spoken sounds, some are natural and others are not natural. A naturally significant sound is one that naturally displays pain [Col. 1234D] or joy, such as interjections. Non-natural significant sounds, however, are those which we say are according to convention. Those are according to convention which human beings have established for themselves, as was shown in the preceding example taken from Genesis. To pursue each of these points individually would take a very long time.

Meanwhile, it is clear that kissing and adoration—or kissing and adoring—are two things that are often very far apart from one another. According to the teachers of secular literature, everything expressed in conversation and argument is constituted from three things: things, concepts, and spoken sounds. Things are what we apprehend through the mind’s reason and distinguish by understanding, such as adoring, kissing, or anything of this kind. A concept is a certain power of the mind by which we learn the things themselves and distinguish how they differ [Col. 1235A] from one another. Spoken sounds are what we use to signify what we grasp in understanding: for what is adoring we say *adoration*; for what is kissing we say *kiss*.

There is something else that signifies spoken sounds: these are letters. For the writing of letters is the signification of spoken sounds. Since, therefore, there are four things—thing, concept, spoken sound, and letter—the concept apprehends the thing; spoken sounds designate the concept; and letters signify the spoken sounds.

Hence the aforementioned Aristotle says in his *On Interpretation*:

> “Those which are in speech are signs of the passions in the soul; and those which are written are signs of those which are in speech; and just as letters are not the same for everyone, so neither are spoken sounds the same…”

[Note: [Col. 1235D] “But those of which these are the primary signs are the same passions of the soul for all; and those of which these are likenesses are the same things also.” The Greek manuscript of Aristotle’s *On Interpretation* has *περὶ ἑρμηνείας*. Carolus writes *periherminiis* barbarously and incompetently, though in accordance with the usage of his age, which Balbus also noted in the *Catholicus*, writing: “Some, however, less understanding, use this as though it were a compound name, namely *haec perihermenia*.” He presents this passage as follows: [Col. 1236D] *Ὧν μέντοι ταῦτα πρώτως, ταὐτὰ πᾶσι παθήματα τῆς ψυχῆς· καὶ ὧν ταῦτα ὁμοιώματα, πράγματα ἤδη ταὐτά* (“But those of which these are the primary signs are the same passions of the soul for all; and those of which these are likenesses are the same things also”). From this the corruption of this passage is evident; we have corrected it as follows: “But those of which these are the primary signs are the same passions of the soul for all; and those of which these are likenesses are the same things also.” Nor is the text otherwise in the works of Severinus Boethius.]

> “But those of which these are the primary signs are the same passions of the soul for all, and those of which these are likenesses are the same things also.”

The concept, as the very learned Boethius explains, signifies a certain passion of the soul:

> “For, as the same Boethius says, unless someone undergoes in the reasoning of the soul a certain likeness of the thing which he understands, there is no understanding. When I see a circle or a square, I conceive its form in my mind, and its likeness is formed for me in the reasoning of the soul; and the soul undergoes the likeness of the understood thing. Thus it comes about that understanding is both a likeness of the thing and a passion of the soul.”

Of these four things, two are natural and two are according to human convention. Spoken sounds and letters are according to convention, whereas concepts and things are natural. This is demonstrated by the fact that different peoples use different spoken sounds and letters, because they themselves composed the spoken sounds they would use and the letters with which they would write. No one established concepts and things; they exist naturally.

For what is a horse among the Romans is not a stag among barbarians; rather, among different peoples the same nature of things exists. Therefore barbarians do not think that what we understand as a horse is a dog; instead, among the most diverse peoples the same relationship of substances and concepts has been established. Thus two of these—spoken sounds and letters—are according to human convention, while two—things and concepts—are according to nature. By these arguments it is shown that adoration and kissing are not one thing merely because these two names have a certain resemblance among the Greeks.

For the most part, therefore, two or more names have one signification as synonyms; yet often one name, as a homonym, signifies two or more things. Nevertheless, the order of things is not thereby confused or in some way mutilated if human beings give them names in very different ways according to convention.

Meanwhile, they add a third thing to these two, saying that adoring, kissing, and embracing are all one [Col. 1236A]. But just as those two are separated from each other, so this third is plainly separated from the other two, since, as we mentioned above, some things are adored but are not immediately kissed; some are kissed but are not immediately adored; and many things are embraced which are neither adored nor kissed.

Anyone may, by some accident, embrace a piece of wood, a stone, or any other thing to which it would be superfluous to offer a kiss, yet he does not adore it. Someone may also kiss one of his superiors whom, restrained by reverence, he scarcely dares approach, yet he does not embrace him. The more these three are seen to differ from one another in meaning, the more their examples, which they have brought forward to prove that they are one, are recognized to differ from reason; for those examples themselves have very great [Col. 1236B] differences among them, and these examples have no agreement with reason.

For they say:

> “[The opening syntax is corrupt:] ‘And each of the holy leaders of our doctrine and their successors, the eminent [men] of our fathers, and these are to be adored—that is, kissed, for the two are the same; but the common usage of ancient Greek designates kissing and embracing, and signifies some extension of the will in love, just as *fero* and *offero*, *firmo* and *confirmo*, *participo* and *adoro*, which demonstrates a kiss and an extension of friendship.’”

O interpretation that confuses meanings rather than arranging them, breaking words rather than expressing them! O acumen blunter than any pestle! O leaden sword that blunts its edge before cutting the thing against which it is employed! O sword that displays the pounding of a hammer rather than the cutting of a blade, breaking materials rather than cutting them! O argument capable of affirming nothing except that its authors are mad, offering no firmness to the matter proposed, but merely revealing that its bearers are senseless!

From the fact that *fero* and *offero* are related, it attempts to assert that adoring, kissing, and embracing are one thing. It does so while ignorant of the powers of prefixes, which often corrupt other parts of speech, are often corrupted by other parts, often both corrupt and are corrupted, and sometimes neither corrupt nor are corrupted; prefixes sometimes increase, sometimes diminish, and sometimes alter their meanings. While it seeks to establish certain empty claims, it attempts to prove them by equally empty assertions.

Who, then, is unaware that *offero*, *affero*, *infero*, *confero*, *aufero*, *defero*, *refero*, *suffero*, *differo*, [Col. 1236D] *profero*, *praefero*, *perfero*, and any others similar to these, although they derive from the verb *fero*, differ greatly from one another in meaning because different prefixes have been applied and partly altered? Or who does not know that *participo* and *adoro* have almost no agreement of meaning?

For *firmo* and *confirmo*, although they are related in meaning, nevertheless seem wholly foreign to the thing to which they are applied. If we were to discuss each of these individually in the manner taught in grammarians’ schools, this single matter would scarcely fit within the text of one book.

Nor should we pass over the fact that they tried to complete their utterly foolish argument with a frivolous and empty conclusion, almost as though by a convertible syllogism, saying:

> “What someone loves, he adores; and what he adores, he certainly loves.”

They did not understand that these two propositions cannot be mutually converted precisely because they are unequal, and because *to love* can extend more widely than *to adore*. Someone loves his wife or child, yet does not adore her or him. He loves a servant, a maidservant, a horse, a dog, a hawk, and other things of this kind, yet does not adore them.

Therefore, just as it is true when he says that what someone adores he loves, it cannot likewise be true when he says that what someone loves he adores. This conversion cannot rationally stand, since one of the two extends more widely, as we have said, and there is not such a precise correspondence between them that they should be thought mutually convertible.

Thus one may say, in converted order, that what is neighable is a horse and that what is a horse is neighable. But one cannot rightly say that what someone loves he adores and that what he adores he loves. For even among the same topics from which these arguments proceed—in the same argumentation called that of consequents, in which one thing inevitably follows from a proposed thing—many propositions can be converted, as in what we said about the neighable and the horse, while some cannot be converted at all.

These can be converted: if something is laughable, it necessarily follows that it is human; and if something is human, it is necessarily laughable; and other examples of this kind. But these cannot be converted: if it is day, it is light—for if it is day, it follows that it is light; if someone is satisfied, it follows that he is thought to have eaten; if someone is drunk, it is necessarily evident that he has been drinking; if someone is learned, it follows that he is said to have learned; if someone adores, it follows that he loves what he adores.

But one cannot say, in the reverse order, that if it is light, it is necessarily day; or that if someone has eaten, it follows that he is satisfied, since many things are luminous though it is not day, and eating often does not yet reach satiety. Nor can one say that if someone has drunk, he is drunk; that if he has learned, he is learned; or that if he loves, he adores, since drinking does not always reach drunkenness, study does not always reach mastery, and love does not always reach adoration.
