Let these propositions therefore be set out individually according to the experience of dialecticians, so that it may more easily appear how far these two things differ from one another and how this conversion cannot stand. For there are four propositions related to one another in a certain way.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] Philosophers customarily write these propositions for examination in a square diagram. According to Aristotle’s teaching:]

[Col. 1238D]

**Universal affirmative:** Everything that someone loves, he adores.

**Contraries** — *ἐναντίαι*

**Universal negative:** Nothing that someone loves does he adore.

**Subalternates** — *ὑπάλληλαι*

**Contradictories across the diagonal** — *ἀντιφατικαί*

**Subalternates** — *ὑπάλληλαι*

**Particular affirmative:** Something that someone loves, he adores.

**Subcontraries** — *ὑπεναντίαι*

**Particular negative:** Something that someone loves, he does not adore.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] These are the propositions which philosophers customarily write for examination in a square diagram. The first two are: “Everything that someone loves, he adores,” and “Nothing that someone loves does he adore.” The other two are: “Something that someone loves, he adores,” and “Something that someone loves, he does not adore.” The first two are called the universal affirmation and the universal negation; the other two, the particular affirmation and the particular negation. The two upper propositions are altogether contrary to one another, while the two lower propositions are mutually subcontrary. The universal and particular affirmations are likewise called subalternates, as are the universal and particular negations.]

Let two angular lines of inquiry, as it were, then be drawn: one from this universal affirmation, “Everything that someone loves, he adores,” to this particular negation, “Something that someone loves, he does not adore”; the other from this particular affirmation, “Something that someone loves, he adores,” to this universal negation, “Nothing that someone loves does he adore.” Let them be contrary or opposed to one another.

Since these pairs are in conflict, and since neither pair—that is, the universal affirmation and the particular negation, or the particular affirmation and the universal negation—can both be true, one will be false and the other true. Thus the true proposition will eliminate the false, and if one is true, the other immediately departs from truth. The Platonic philosopher Apuleius of Madaura says this; he discussed the principles of this sort of syllogistic reasoning most subtly in his book entitled *On the Interpretation of Apuleius*:

> “When either universal proposition is confirmed, it certainly confirms its particular; when refuted, it does not thereby weaken it. The particular, conversely, when refuted, certainly weakens its universal; when proved, it certainly confirms it.”

[Note: [Col. 1238D] In the editions of the jurists Sichardus and Colvius, Apuleius reads: “When proved, it does not thereby establish it.” The reading which the meaning supports is: “When proved, it certainly confirms it.”]

Thus in this argument the two upper universals—“Everything that someone loves, he adores,” and “Nothing that someone loves does he adore”—are false, since, as was said above, someone loves many things which he does not adore, and adores some of the things which he loves. The two lower particulars—“Something that someone loves, he adores,” and “Something that someone loves, he does not adore”—are both true.

For someone loves God according to the statement, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Leviticus 19), and adores him; from this most holy love the nourishment of all virtues proceeds. Someone loves his neighbor and adores him in the duty of greeting, and thus the proposition “Something that someone loves, he adores” is shown to be true. This too is shown to be true: “Something that someone loves, he does not adore,” according to the examples already given of a spouse, child, horse, dog, hawk, and the other things mentioned above, each of which is loved but is not adored.

The universals and the lower particulars, placed alternately, are opposed to one another. For if this universal affirmation, “Everything that someone loves, he adores,” is false, this particular negation, “Something that someone loves, he does not adore,” is true; and if this particular negation is false, the universal affirmation is true. Again, if this universal negation, “Nothing that someone loves does he adore,” is false, this particular affirmation, “Something that someone loves, he adores,” is true; and if the latter is not true, neither is the former false.

The two lower propositions are altogether true; therefore the two upper propositions must be held to be completely false.

Finally, concerning the conversion of such propositions, on which we too have argued somewhat above, the aforementioned philosopher says:

> “Propositions are called convertible when a universal negative proposition and, alternatively, a particular affirmative proposition can always exchange the roles of their parts—the subject and the predicate—while the condition of truth or falsity remains. For just as this proposition is true, ‘No wise person is impious,’ so, if the roles of the parts are exchanged, it will be true: ‘No impious person is wise.’ Likewise, just as ‘No human being is an animal’ is false, so, if it is converted, ‘No animal is a human being’ will also be false. In the same way, the particular affirmative is convertible: ‘Some grammarian is a human being,’ and conversely, ‘Some human being is a grammarian.’ The other two propositions cannot always do this, although they are sometimes converted; nevertheless, they are not for that reason called convertible. Therefore each proposition must be examined through all its significations to see whether it also agrees when converted. These are not countless, but only five: either the property of something is declared, or its genus, or its difference, or its end, or its accident.”

To refute their statement, then, and to strengthen our own assertion, many arguments of this kind could have been employed, and what has been employed could have been discussed at greater length. But for the sake of brevity these and similar matters are omitted. We have therefore undertaken, with the Lord’s help, to invalidate their assertion by arguments arising from the disciplined art of dialectic, because we have discovered that they wished to reinforce their ravings by some sort of conversion, as though by a syllogistic argument.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On what they said arrogantly and ignorantly: “Likewise, we joined those who came from the East in the same metropolitan city of Nicaea, and, with all of us presiding, we made Christ the head.”

[Col. 1239D]

The exceedingly arrogant, or rather absurd, statement of those who boasted that they had made Christ their own head—saying, “With all of us presiding, we made Christ the head”—is rightly censured. The same Lord who is the head of the Church took the Church to himself as his body; he was not chosen by that same Church to be its head. For he himself testifies to the apostles, saying, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15).

If, according to their folly, Christ was made head by them, then he was certainly chosen by them; and if he was chosen by them, the Lord’s foregoing statement is weakened. But that statement of the Lord is not weakened; therefore, according to their vanity, Christ was not made head by them.

Hence care must be taken lest these men are in fact excluded from his election, since they boast that they made him their head. For, as we conjecture, if they had been chosen by him, they would seek not their own glory but his, and would preach the adoration not of senseless things but of the one God.

For, according to the statement of the Truth, a tree is known by its fruits, and in the nature of things the efficient causes are often known from their effects. When someone sees smoke, he does not doubt that fire is beneath it; when he sees the footprint of some animal, he knows that the animal has passed by; when he sees a good work, he does not doubt that it comes from God, who is the author of all good things; and when he sees something evil, he believes that it has been carried out through the schemes of the ancient enemy.

In saying this we do not rashly pass judgment on their election, since things often well established are found to have been corrupted. But we affirm this completely: they were not chosen so that through them new constitutions might grow up in ecclesiastical affairs, and so that they might boast that they had made Christ, who is the life of all who believe in him, their head.

Granted that they were chosen by him and appointed by him to the priesthood: why do they not follow him in humility? Why do they seek their own glory rather than his, when he testified that he sought not his own glory but the glory of the one who sent him? Why do they neglect to lay aside their arrogance? Why do they improperly seek lofty things? Why do they disturb the prosperity of the Church by a kind of civil war?

If they were willing to be content with the teachings and examples of the ancient Fathers, they would neither violate domestic peace by erroneous constitutions nor turn against themselves the weapons of their associates, who were to fight alongside them against their enemies.

This useless statement, by which they imagine that they made Christ their head, although it does not detract from the faith, is nevertheless not free from criticism. For we do not believe that they were capable of such monstrous insanity that they intended to say that the Lord himself was made by them. No faithful ears can bear to hear that. But because, wishing to signify one thing, they signified another, we have chosen both to examine what they actually said and not to leave unexamined what we suppose they intended to say.

They wished, unless we are mistaken, to say: “While we, who are members of Christ, presided, we placed all the firmness of our work and hope in him, who is our head, and resolved to follow him”—or something of this sort which may be conjectured. But, with the force of their ignorance taking away what they wished to say, they said that they had made Christ their head, and they say that they made the one of whom the evangelist John says, “All things were made through him” (John 1).

In the creed of the synodical constitution it is said of him: “Born, not made” (Nicene Creed), while the Apostle says: “Who was made for him from the seed of David” (Romans 1). This is resolved as follows: insofar as he is God, all things were made through him; insofar as he is human, he too was made. Solomon says, “Wisdom built herself a house” [Col. 1241A] (Ecclesiastes 2)—that is, the wisdom of God the Father, without whom the Father never existed. This wisdom was not made by him but born, namely the Son, who is of one substance with the Father. He built for himself in the Virgin’s womb a body which he called a temple, saying, “Destroy this temple,” and so forth (John 2).

But lest this statement appear to conflict with the statement, “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1), it must be observed that the works of the Trinity are inseparable: what the Father does, the Son does, and the Holy Spirit does; and just as they are of one majesty, one substance, and one will, so also they are of one operation.

The whole Trinity acted in the Lord’s incarnation, but only the person of the Son assumed flesh. For if the body—which we think may also be called a house—was made through the agency of the Holy Spirit, it may be asked why it is referred to the person of Christ. The work of the Son is the work of the Father, because the power of both is one; similarly, the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of the Son of God, because of the unity of nature and will.

For whether the Father acts, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is the Trinity that acts; and whatever the three have done is the operation of the one God.

The Church may also be understood as Christ’s house: he built it with his own blood and adorned it with the jewels of virtues and the most splendid ornaments of teachings. But these men, not content with this, while seeking to add something new to its beauty, are recognized as imposing ugliness upon it rather than beauty.

## CHAPTER XXV. Against those who say that Epiphanius composed eighty chapters on heresies, and who claim that, if he had known the adoration of images to be a heresy, he would have counted it among the heresies.

[Col. 1241C]

The adorers or worshipers of images thought that they had found a great defense in this matter: a certain Epiphanius distinguished the varieties of heresies in eighty chapters, and, if he had known the adoration of images to be a heresy, he would have counted the adorers of those same images among the heretics.

With these weapons they tried to punish us, who are content with the worship and adoration of God alone; with these darts they attempted to pierce us; with these spears they tried to overcome us; with these swords they believed themselves to be the invaders of our liberty. As though by an argument taken from a genus through a certain reflexion, they said:

“If the one who discussed all heresies in general had known this to be a heresy, he would have inserted it among the other heresies in his discussion. But he did not place it among the heresies he arranged; therefore it is not to be considered a heresy.”

We, on the contrary, thought that we should answer them and, with the Lord’s approval, defeat them with the instruments of their own weapons. We shall not hesitate to turn against them and direct the same spears which they sent at us, saying:

“If that same Epiphanius had known those who reject the adoration of images to be heretics, he would undoubtedly have counted them among the heretics in his general discussion of heresies. But he did not count them among the heretics; therefore it must be believed that he did not believe them to be heretics.”

That Epiphanius not only rejected the adoration of images but also did not wish them to be kept in churches is made clear by the following evidence. In a letter sent by him to Bishop John, translated from Greek into Latin by Jerome, we read:

> “I heard that some were murmuring against me when we were travelling together to the holy place called Bethel, so that I might celebrate the customary ecclesiastical assembly there with you. I had come [Note: [Col. 1241] “To the estate called Anablatha.” This is how it is read in Jerome, in the Council of Paris, and in the *Itineraries*. The corrector changed it to *Anabaltum*.] to the estate called Anablatha. As I passed by, I saw a burning lamp and asked what place it was; I learned that it was a church. I entered to pray and found there a veil hanging at the doors of that church, dyed and painted, bearing an image as though of Christ or of some saint—for I do not remember clearly whose image it was.
>
> “When I saw this, that an image of a human being was hanging in the church of Christ contrary to the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it apart and advised the custodians of the place to wrap a poor dead man in it and carry him away. They, murmuring in opposition, said: ‘If he intended to tear it, it was right that he should give another veil and replace it.’
>
> “When I heard this, I promised that I would give one and send it immediately. There was, however, a brief delay while I looked for the best veil to send in its place. I thought that I ought to send one from Cyprus. Now I have sent what I was able to find, and I ask you to order the presbyter of that place to receive from the bearer the veil sent by us, and thereafter to command that such veils as offend against our religion not be hung in the church of Christ.
>
> “For it is fitting that your Honesty should have this greater concern and scrupulousness, which is worthy of the Church of Christ and of the people entrusted to you.”

This is the statement concerning this matter which we have found in Epiphanius; whether it is to be praised or blamed is left to the reader’s judgment.

Let us now turn to blessed Augustine. Let the most wise man be questioned; let the outstanding teacher be consulted; let him say whether any heresy makes use of the adoration of images. That venerable man composed a book on eighty-nine heresies, among which two approved the adoration of images—namely, the Simonians and the Carpocratians.

To make this clearer, let the statements of the aforementioned teacher be set out individually, exactly as they appear in that book. He says:

> “The Simonians derive from Simon Magus, who, after being baptized by Philip the deacon, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, wished to buy with money from the holy apostles the power that the Holy Spirit might also be given through the laying on of his hands. He had deceived many by magical tricks.
>
> “He taught a detestable shamefulness, namely, the indiscriminate use of women, and he also said that God had not made the world. He denied the resurrection of the flesh and asserted that he was Christ; he also wished to be believed to be Jupiter, and Minerva to be a certain prostitute named Selene, whom he had made his partner in crimes. He supplied his disciples with images of himself and of that prostitute for adoration, and at Rome he had them publicly established as statues of gods. In that city blessed Peter the Apostle destroyed him by the true power of almighty God.
>
> “For he had said that on Mount Sinai he had given the law of Moses in the person of the Father; during the time of Tiberius he had appeared in appearance in the person of the Son; and afterward he had come upon the apostles as the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. But he said that Christ had neither come nor suffered anything at the hands of the Jews.”

Just as the heresy that arose from that same Simon, which is called Simony, is wholly rejected by the faithful, so the use of images for adoration must also be entirely rejected.

There is another heresy that includes this error, which the aforementioned teacher described as follows:

> “The Carpocratians began with Carpocrates, who taught every shameful act and every invention of sin, and that the principalities and powers to which such things are pleasing could not otherwise be escaped and passed through, so that one might reach the heaven above.
>
> “He is also said to have thought that Jesus was merely a human being, born of both sexes, but that he had received such a soul that he knew the things above and announced them. He rejected the resurrection of the body together with the law. He denied that the world was made by God, saying that it was made by certain powers.
>
> “A certain woman named Marcellina is reported to have been an associate of his sect. She worshiped images of Jesus, Paul, Homer, and Pythagoras, adoring them and placing incense before them.”

For if someone who supports this error should say, “Blessed Augustine counted the adoration of images among the heresies because certain pagans—that is, Simon and Selene, and also Homer and Pythagoras—adored images,” let him observe that they are also said to have adored images of Jesus and Paul, and that this very practice was counted among the heresies by the aforementioned man.

For if that outstanding man had known that images made of the Lord, the apostles, or any of the saints were to be adored, he would never have counted the adoration of images of Jesus and Paul among the heresies.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Against those who call images holy and consecrated, and command that they be placed on roads or in public squares, which are often polluted.

[Col. 1243D]

Those of whom we are speaking join together in this matter two things that contradict each other, since they very often call the aforementioned images holy and venerable while asserting that they ought to be placed on roads or in public squares, which are often polluted.

For just as light does not agree with darkness, or heat with cold, so holiness does not agree with contamination, nor purity with impurity. It is therefore clear that they are largely in error when they assert both that the images are holy and that they should be set up in contaminated places.

Their judgment becomes evident in a certain way when they decide that the images should be placed on roads or in the squares of cities and villages: it shows that these places lack holiness, as indeed they do. If they believed the images to be holy, they would judge that they should be placed in holy places.

Everything holy is clean; nothing unclean is clean; therefore nothing unclean is holy. If, according to their judgment, they seek places contaminated by impurity, they do not reject the uncleanness that is contrary to holiness. If they do not reject uncleanness, they can in no way be called holy.

If, therefore, they seek places contaminated by impurity, the images can in no way be called holy.

To pass over the other examples by which it can be taught that each thing should be applied not to an unsuitable but rather to a suitable thing, let us bring forward even the precepts of the foremost teachers of eloquence. They judged that this must be thoroughly observed in eloquence: that the thing, place, time, and person be considered, so that weighty matters are not spoken to trivial people, modest matters to immodest people, wanton matters to serious people, indecent matters to chaste people, incestuous matters to the pure, ridiculous matters to the sorrowful, or profane matters to the religious. Everything in the art of eloquence should be so appropriate that nothing unsuitable or contradictory remains, but each thing is moderated according to the character of the place and time.

If orators are commanded to observe this in the art of eloquence, we must observe it much more in the practices of our religion, so that each thing pertaining to religion is observed and maintained as reason or order requires.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the worshipers of images can be deceived by badly painted images; or, an inquiry to be made of those who think that nearly the whole privilege of the Christian faith consists in the adoration or worship of images: what should be done by the poor, who entirely lack the craftsmen by whom images are made?

[Col. 1244C] Every art’s system includes various exercises. Painting, however, is an art; therefore the system of painting includes various exercises, and those who practice it, and are called painters, understand it—some more, some less. Some produce more beautiful works in it, others uglier; some compose beautiful images, others misshapen ones. From this it is plainly inferred that those who place almost the whole firmness of their faith in images, and are not ashamed to count the worship of them among the instruments of good works, and worship images sometimes beautiful and sometimes ugly, are in some way deceived.

For if any image possesses more holiness and power in proportion as it is more beautiful, it follows that the uglier one possesses less holiness and power; and if the uglier one possesses less, it follows that any extremely ugly image possesses either nothing or very little. If the more beautiful image is therefore worshiped more attentively because, on account of its beauty, it is thought to possess greater power, then its sanctity no longer comes from any religious devotion, but from the craftsman’s workmanship. And if an image that is less beautiful, or one that possesses no beauty at all, is worshiped, its worshipers are greatly deceived, since they undertake to worship things devoid of beauty.

If, then, it follows that all images—beautiful, less beautiful, and entirely without beauty—must be worshiped equally, justice, which assigns to each thing its due, must necessarily be removed from these matters. For when they worship beautiful images, they are deceived by the accident that they think they are worshiping something holy; but when they worship misshapen paintings, [Col. 1245A] they are deliberately deceived, since they worship misshapen things as holy things. Whether, therefore, they worship them accidentally or deliberately, they are deceived.

They are truly and deservedly deceived who, although God, the Creator of all things, has judged that he alone should be worshiped, nevertheless strive to worship certain things devoid of sense. While they think that by worshiping images they offer a certain reverence to the saints, they grant a kind of association with the worship owed to God alone.

Because, then, God alone is to be worshiped, while martyrs and all the saints are rather to be venerated than worshiped, we have already stated this in the present work, and it is confirmed by the teaching of the eminent doctor Jerome. When he was writing against a certain heretic, Vigilantius, who entirely denied that the relics of the martyrs should be venerated, he said, among other things: “Who has ever worshiped martyrs, you madman?” If, then, according to his judgment, martyrs are not worshiped, much less should their images be worshiped by the faithful.

As for what is read in the Book of Kings—that Saul worshiped Samuel, who had been raised by the Pythoness (1 Kings 28)—it can be understood that it was not Samuel’s soul that had been raised, but that some deceptive image of diabolical trickery appeared to King Saul. This is evident either from the fact that it allowed itself to be worshiped, which a holy man certainly would not have permitted, or because it said to the wicked king, “Tomorrow you shall be with me,” although that king of monstrous wickedness was destined, when he died, to be not with the prophet but with the devil, who drags with him in the future to eternal punishments those whom he entices in this world to commit evil deeds.

Thus the savage king, hearing of the form in which the apparition had been raised, [Col. 1245C] understood that it was Samuel; he reported what he had understood, and because he had not understood correctly, contrary to Scripture he worshiped someone other than the Lord. Thinking that it was Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception. For this is what he strives for: to be worshiped as God.

If Samuel had truly appeared to him, that righteous man would certainly not have permitted himself to be worshiped, since he had proclaimed that the Lord alone was to be worshiped. And how could the man of God, who was with Abraham in the place of refreshment, say to a man deserving the pestilence of hellfire, “Tomorrow you shall be with me”?

By these two indications the incautious Satan revealed the subtlety of his deception: he allowed himself to be worshiped under Samuel’s appearance and name—something which, I think, Samuel would not have permitted—and he falsely claimed that a man weighed down by sins would be with the most righteous Samuel, despite the great difference between sinners and the righteous.

This interpretation can seem plausible if Samuel’s name is left aside, because Saul was destined to be with the devil: he passed over to the one whom he worshiped. Nevertheless, blessed Augustine and other doctors hold different opinions about this matter, and the book of Ecclesiasticus reports it to Samuel’s praise, because he prophesied after his death.

Now those who think that almost the whole prerogative of Christian faith consists in the worship or veneration of images should be asked whether they therefore allow the poor to suffer loss of faith because, oppressed by lack of means, they do not possess the resources with which to acquire a painting.

If any poor person is to be deprived of good merits because he lacks the possessions by which he might obtain images, while the wealthy person is therefore to receive the prerogative of greater merit because he abounds in the means by which paintings may be purchased; and if the one is to receive punishments or rewards for his possessions rather than for his merits, while the other is to be judged for his poverty rather than for his works, then the worship of images will climb to a position of great authority in the Christian religion, and justice—which examines each person’s merits, not his possessions—will lose much of its force.

Since none of these propositions can be approved by any consistent relation among things, it remains that the worship of images must be understood to hold no primacy in the Christian religion. [Col. 1246B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

That they call their synod universal in vain, although it is evident that it was not assembled by the universal Church

Among the other ravings said either to have been enacted or written in that same synod, this too is no less a piece of delirium than the rest: they call that synod universal, although it possesses neither the unshaken purity of universal faith nor an authority demonstrated by the acts of all the churches.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] “For just as the Church is universal.” Hincmarus transferred the words found at the end of the chapter to its beginning, as follows: “In the fourth book of this volume these things are written concerning the name ‘universal.’ Universality is named from one, because what is propagated from one is repeatedly turned toward one. For a multitude of units, gathered by being turned into one, becomes a universality. For just as the Church is universal, etc.” He did not read this passage in that order in his book, but, to adapt it to his purpose, he transcribed this passage according to *kath’ hysteron proteron* (καθ` ὕστερον πρότερον), “the latter [put] first,” placing what came later first.]

For just as the Church is universal—the Greek expression for which is *catholic*—so undoubtedly everything that does not depart from its unity can be called catholic. Every Christian doctrine, or any ecclesiastical constitution or tradition, must be such as to accord with the universal Church. The heretics observed this not at all. Scattered through various parts of the world and confined to certain regions, they established various assemblies by which they separated both themselves and many others [Hincmarus: *plurimos*, “very many”] from participation in ecclesiastical unity.

When, therefore, the bishops of two or three provinces meet together and, fortified by the institution of the ancient canons, establish (*statuunt*; variant: *instituunt*) some preaching or doctrine that nevertheless does not differ from the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, what they do is catholic and may perhaps be called universal. For although it was not carried out by the bishops of the whole world, it does not differ from the faith and tradition of all; and we know that this has frequently happened in various parts of the world when certain necessities arose. Many councils have indeed been held, by whose decrees the holy Church is fortified and strengthened.

But if the bishops of two or three provinces meet together and, wishing to establish something new, form a private assembly because they do not agree with the Church of the whole world but dissent from it in some respect, what they do is not catholic and therefore cannot be called universal.

Everything ecclesiastical is catholic, and everything catholic is universal; but everything universal is free from profane novelties of expression. Therefore everything ecclesiastical is free from profane novelties of expression. For [variant: “And”] if this synod had been free from novelties of expression and had been content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, it could have been called universal. But it was not content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers; therefore it cannot be called universal.

Universality is named from one, because what is propagated from one is repeatedly turned toward one. For a multitude of units, gathered by being turned into one, becomes a universality. We would plainly not hesitate to profess that same synod to be universal, unless we perceived that it disagreed with the doctrines of the universal Church.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 1248A]

[Note: [Col. 1247B] “Let the apostolic lord know.” This chapter is absent from the commonly circulated Paris and Cologne editions. It is also missing from the *Capitulary of Pope Adrian* in the edition of the councils by Laurentius Surius, a Carthusian monk. Severinus Binius, in his notes on the same Capitulary, volume 3 of the *Councils*, says that he presents a complete copy sent from Gaul to Gregory XIII, the Supreme Pontiff. But where in Gaul was this place? Which library? Of what country was the person who sent it? Where in the world did he come from? These are matters, Binius, which it would have been right and proper for you to note, if you wished to find credibility among all Christians alike. In the meantime, whom will you buy who will believe you? Indeed, the sentence read here—“But we by no means compel those who are unwilling to worship them”—is rejected by Charles throughout these four books and directly contradicts the words of Pope Gregory, whose judgment he says he follows. Look and weep. Gregory writes to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles: “We certainly praised you for having zeal lest anything made by human hands should be worshiped, but we judge that you ought not to have broken those same images.” And in the same letter: “Because you forbade them to be worshiped, we praise you entirely; but we condemn your having broken them.” And later in the same place: “If anyone wishes to make images, do not forbid it in the least; but avoid worshiping images by every means.” From these words it shines more clearly than the midday sun that either this chapter is spurious and was fabricated by Roman flatterers, or that the sound sentence was corrupted by corrupt editors and ought to be restored to: “We by no means connive (*nequaquam connibemus*) at it, even if they wish to do so”—that is, we in no way permit those who wish to worship them to do so; we neither consent nor grant permission. In a word, “we by no means connive” means “we prohibit and forbid worship.” Concerning the meaning of this verb, see what we noted above in the preface.]

Let the apostolic lord, our Father, know—and the entire Roman Church together—that, in accordance with what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory which he addressed to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles:

“We permit anyone who wishes to make images of the saints to make them, both in the church and outside the church, for the love of God and his saints; but we by no means compel those who are unwilling to worship them. Nor do we permit anyone who wishes to break or destroy them to do so.”

And because in this letter we freely and without hesitation profess that the universal catholic Church, pleasing to God, follows the teaching of the most holy Gregory.

[Col. 1247] HERE ENDS HAPPILY.

# APPENDIX TO THE CAPITULARY OF THE BLESSED CHARLES THE GREAT ON IMAGES

[Col. 1247]

## LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN TO THE BLESSED KING CHARLES ON IMAGES

In which those who attacked the Second Synod of Nicaea are refuted

(From Mansi, *Larger Collection of the Councils*)

[Col. 1247C] To our most excellent son and our spiritual kinsman, Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans: Adrian, pope.

Our Lord and Redeemer, who in his provident counsel is the author of all things, deigned to descend from heaven, from the bosom of the Father . . . . It is clear to those who know the Gospel that by the Lord’s voice the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the care of the whole Church were entrusted to holy Peter, chief of all the apostles. For it is said to him: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21). It is said to him: “Behold, Satan has sought to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22). It is said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Behold, the care and primacy of the whole Church are entrusted to him. And he is recognized as having left his vicars, the bishops, to exercise his office and care for the Church. For he also received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and the power of binding and loosing was granted to him.

Therefore we confidently trust that, if your aforesaid royal excellence, protected by God, continues faithfully to remain in love and affection toward his holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church and toward us, as it has begun, until the end, he will not only cleanse and rescue it from every stain of sin, but will also grant it immense victories in this world over all barbarian peoples who oppose it, through his assistance, and will moreover grant it the kingdom of heaven without end.

Furthermore, we received from your most gracious and exalted royal power your faithful familiar, namely Engilbert, abbot and minister of the chapel, who was brought up in your palace from the earliest beginnings of childhood and admitted to all your counsels. Thus, just as he is received by you in complete familiarity, he might likewise be received and suitably honored by us.

Accordingly, because of the immense love that we bear toward your honey-sweet royal excellence, just as you sent him to us with an abundance of the sweetness of extraordinary affection, we received him as he wished and in the manner he wished. As he related matters to us with great familiarity, we received him with a receptive ear and kindly mind; and, as though your bodily excellence itself were speaking to us, we more patiently entrusted him with our counsel, for the advancement of our holy Roman Church and the exaltation of your royal power, protected by God.

Among other things, he presented to us a capitulary against the synod held at Nicaea for the erection of sacred images. Accordingly, out of our honey-sweet royal affection for you, we have supplied a response to each chapter—not defending any particular person, God forbid, but holding to the customary (*solitam*; printed *olitanam*) tradition of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church and following the teaching of our holy pontifical predecessors, while in every way vindicating the tradition of the true faith.

## IN THE THIRD SESSION

In the first chapter, the following was brought forward, namely the statement: “And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father through the Son.”

### Refutation

Tarasius does not hold the correct view, since, in the reading expressing his belief, he professes that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father and the Son, according to the faith of the Nicene Creed, but from the Father through the Son.

[Col. 1249C]

### Response

Tarasius did not explain this doctrine on his own, but confessed it according to the teaching of the holy Fathers. For the sake of your immense love—which [variant: *quem*, “which”] we bear toward your most exalted royal excellence, protected by God—we briefly set down their passages—namely, those of Saint Athanasius on the Lord’s manifestation in the flesh (*In the sermon on the human nature assumed by the only-begotten Word*), among other things:

“For this reason he breathes upon the faces of the apostles, saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20), so that we may understand that the Spirit given to the disciples comes from the fullness of the Godhead. For, he says, ‘In Christ—that is, in his flesh—dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily’ (Colossians 2), just as the evangelist John also says: ‘From his fullness we have all received’ (John 1).

“The Holy Spirit appeared in bodily form like a dove (Luke 3), descending upon him and remaining over him. In us, the first-fruits and pledge of the Godhead dwell; in Christ, however, there is the fullness of the Godhead. And lest anyone suppose that he received as though he himself did not possess it—for he himself sent it down from above, as God, and he himself received it below, as man. Therefore it descended from him to himself, from his divinity into his humanity.”

And after much more:

“It is manifest that the Father made all things through him; therefore through him he raises him, through him sanctifies him, through him exalts him, and through him gives him life.”

Likewise, from the same Saint Athanasius, *On Virginity*, among other things:

“And in the Holy Spirit, who exists in the Father and the Son, who is sent forth by the Father and given through the Son.”

Likewise, from Book 7 of Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*, after much else:

“The faith of Gregory, martyr and bishop of Neocaesarea:

‘One God, the Father of the living Word, of subsisting Wisdom, and of his own Power and Image; perfect begetter of the Perfect One, Father of the only-begotten Son.

‘One Lord, alone from the one God, image and likeness of the Godhead, Word accomplishing all things, Wisdom comprehending all things, and Power by which the whole creation could come into being.

‘The true Son of the true, invisible from the invisible, incorruptible from the incorruptible, immortal from the immortal, everlasting from the everlasting.

‘One Holy Spirit, having his substance from God, who appeared through the Son, the image of the perfect Son, the perfect cause of living things, the holiness that grants sanctification, through whom God is known above all and in all,’”

and so forth.

This historian not only records this faith of Saint Gregory; the great preacher Saint Gregory of Nyssa also explained it wonderfully and magnificently in a Greek sermon, describing how, by whom, and in what manner these things were arranged, shown, and revealed to that same Saint Gregory.

Likewise, from Saint Hilary, Book 8 of *On the Faith* (*On the Trinity*, Book 8), among other things:

“Since the Holy Spirit, who is also the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God, is demonstrated to be one substance, I ask, therefore, how they are not one in nature. The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, is sent by the Son, and receives from the Son; but everything that the Father has, the Son also has. Therefore he who receives from him is the Spirit of God, but he is likewise the Spirit of Christ.”

And shortly afterward:

“For the Spirit of God is in us, but the Spirit of Christ is also in us; and when the Spirit of Christ is present, the Spirit of God is present. Thus, since what belongs to God also belongs to Christ, and what belongs to Christ belongs to God, Christ cannot be anything different from what God is. Christ, therefore, is God; Christ is one with God. Hence the Gospel saying: ‘I and the Father are one,’ etc.” (John 10.)

Likewise, from the letter of Saint Basil to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium (*On the Holy Spirit*, Book 1, chapter 18), among other things:

“One and the same is the Holy Spirit, who is spoken of in unity, joined by the one Son to the one Father, and through him completing the highly praiseworthy and blessed Trinity.”

And shortly afterward:

“Indeed, there is one knowledge of God, from one Spirit, through one Son, in one Father.”

And again:

“Natural goodness, together with natural sanctification and royal dignity, passes from the Father through the Only-Begotten into the Spirit,” etc.

Likewise, from Saint Ambrose, Book 1, chapter 3, *On the Holy Spirit*, among other things:

“But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore there is unity of operation and unity of proclamation, which cannot be separated. If in this passage the Spirit is separated from the operation of the Father and the Son, because it is said, ‘From God are all things,’ and, ‘Through the Son are all things,’ then in that other passage too, because the Apostle said of Christ, ‘who is over all, God blessed forever’ (Romans 9), he would have placed Christ not only above all creatures but also above the Father—which is impious to say. But far be it from us. The Father is not among all things, nor among some class of his creatures. Every creature is beneath; above is the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The creature serves; these reign. The creature is subject; these rule,” etc.

Likewise, from Saint Gregory the Theologian, *On the Second Epiphany* (*Oration on the Holy Lights*), among other things:

“For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. By saying ‘from whom,’ ‘through whom,’ and ‘in whom,’ we do not divide the nature; nor will the syllables of the prepositions, having been changed, change the truth of the nature. Rather, each term indicates the particular property of the one nature. This is made perfectly clear by the fact that the same distinction is again brought together into one, if anyone reads without passing over it what the Apostle wrote when he said: ‘For from him, and through him, and in him are all things’ (Romans 11), and added: ‘To him be glory forever and ever’ (ibid.).”

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s sermon *On the Ascension of the Lord*, among much else:

“On earth, visibly and near to those who were near, he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing upon their faces; and from that love which is in heaven he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven. Receive the Holy Spirit on earth, and you love your brother; receive him from heaven, and you love God, because even on earth what you received is from heaven. On earth Christ gave him, but the one who gave him is from heaven. For he gave him who descended from heaven,” etc.

From the same Saint Augustine, *On Pentecost*, among other things:

“Let foolish people cease flattering themselves and saying to us: ‘What will we receive when we come over to you, since you already admit that we have Christ’s baptism?’ Let us answer them: ‘You have Christ’s baptism; come, so that you may also have Christ’s Spirit.’ Fear what is written: ‘Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him’ (Romans 8). You have put on Christ in the form of the sacrament; put him on by imitating the example.”

And from the same Saint Augustine, Book 4, chapter 10, *On the Trinity*, among other things:

“Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed also from the Son; for it is not without reason that the same Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. Nor do I see what else he wished to signify when, breathing upon them, he said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20). For that bodily breath, proceeding from the body and touching the body with a bodily sensation, was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration, through an appropriate sign, that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son. For what madman would say that the Spirit whom he gave by breathing was one Spirit, and that the Spirit whom he sent after his ascension was another? There is one Spirit: the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, the Holy Spirit who works all things in all,” etc. (1 Corinthians 12.)

Likewise, from the same Saint Augustine, Book 15, chapter 26, *On the Trinity*, among other things:

“That he proceeds from both is taught as follows: the Son himself says, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15). And when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20), so that he might also show that the Spirit proceeds from himself. And he is the power that went out from him, as we read in the Gospel, and healed them all.” [Col. 1251C] (Luke 6.)

And shortly afterward:

“By this the Lord Jesus signified that he gave the Holy Spirit twice: once on earth, because of love of neighbor, and again from heaven, because of love of God.”

Likewise, from the sentence of Saint Cyril, in the ninth anathema, among other things:

“If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as by an alien power, by which he could work against unclean spirits and perform divine signs through him, and does not rather say that the Spirit through whom he worked signs was his own, let him be anathema,” etc.

Likewise, from the letter of the same Saint Cyril to John of Antioch, among other things:

“Do not move the eternal boundaries which your fathers established” (Deuteronomy 16). For they themselves were not speaking, but the Spirit of God and of the Father, who indeed proceeds from him but is not alien to the Son according to the account of his essence. The sayings of the saints who handed down the mysteries confirm this for us as well.

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they had come toward Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16). The venerable Paul also writes: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him,” etc. (Romans 8.)

Likewise, from Saint Cyril’s *On the Worship of the Spirit*, Book 1, among other things:

“Just as he is the Spirit of God and the Father, so also of the Son substantially, proceeding from both—that is, from the Father through the Son—and the rest.”

Likewise, from the same Saint Cyril’s *Acclamatory Book to the Emperor Theodosius*, among other things:

“Therefore, even if the Father is said to give life wherever he gives life, he accomplishes this entirely through the Son [in] the Holy Spirit,” etc.

Likewise, from the encyclical or synodical letter of Saint Leo the pope addressed to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople (Letter 12), among other things:

“Therefore, even when the doors were shut, he entered to the disciples (John 20), and by his breath gave the Holy Spirit; and, having bestowed the light of understanding, he disclosed the hidden things of the holy Scriptures,” and the rest.

Likewise, from a sermon of the same Saint Leo, eminent doctor, *On Pentecost*, among other things:

“All, therefore, dearly beloved, who had believed in the Lord Jesus had the Holy Spirit poured into them; and the apostles had already received the power of forgiving sins when, after his resurrection, the Lord breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained,’ etc.” (John 20.)

Hence the excellent preacher and honey-sweet doctor, Saint Gregory the pope, also says in Homily 26 on the Holy Gospel, among other things:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father” (John 15). If being sent were understood solely as incarnation, the Holy Spirit would certainly in no way be said to be sent, since he was not incarnate. But his being sent is itself his procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as the Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds, so the Son is not improperly said to be sent because he is begotten.

“When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20). We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding in heaven.”

Likewise, from the same Saint Gregory the pope, Book 27 on Job, among other things:

“Of him John says: ‘All things were made through him’ (John 1). He is also called ‘mouth,’ as though by the name of mouth the Word were plainly indicated, just as we too are accustomed to say ‘tongue’ for ‘words,’ when, for example, we speak of the Greek or Latin tongue and mean Greek or Latin words. We therefore rightly understand the mouth of the Lord to be him through whom he speaks all things to us. Hence the prophet says: ‘For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things,’” etc. (Isaiah 58.)

The holy catholic and apostolic Church, receiving from that same Saint Gregory the pope the order of the Masses, solemnities, and prayers, has also given us many prayers in which it teaches us humbly to ask that the Holy Spirit be poured into us, enlightened, and strengthened through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise, from Saint Sophronius, whose orthodox doctrines are venerated in the holy Sixth Synod, among many other things:

“For the Father made all things through the only-begotten Son in the Holy Spirit, which he holds together with wise providence, as God presiding over his works,” etc.

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### CHAPTER II

### Refutation

Whether Archbishop Theodore of Jerusalem holds the correct view when, while declaring that he believes the Father to be entirely without beginning and everlasting, he nevertheless professes, in some obscure complexity of words, that the Son acknowledges no other beginning than the Father and has his subsistence from him.

[Col. 1252D]

### Response

This Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, together with the other eminent patriarchs—Cosmas of Alexandria and another Theodore of Antioch—previously sent to our predecessor, the late Pope Paul of holy memory, their own synodical letter concerning the true faith. In it they took care to make known, through a subtle exposition, how they and the other orthodox bishops of the East, together with the Christian people, think in accord with our holy catholic, apostolic, and universal Roman Church concerning the most sacred images, and how, fervent in faith, they are devoted to the veneration of those same holy images with sincere affection of mind.

Our predecessor, the late most holy lord Pope Stephen, had this synodical letter translated into Latin and, receiving and rereading it in his council—which he himself held, together with various bishops, in the regions of France or Italy, in defense of sacred images—approved it both because of the various testimonies of the Frankish Fathers [Col. 1253A] [Roman edition: “holy Fathers”] and because of the Creed, where they made this statement:

“If anyone holds another rule of faith, or another creed or doctrine, besides what was handed down by the holy, great, and universal six synods and confirmed by those holy Fathers who assembled in them; and if he does not worship the image or figure of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor confess his humanization, as one who descended and was incarnate for the human race, we anathematize such a person as impious and judge him alien and foreign to the holy catholic and apostolic Church,”

and the other matters, which would take too long to recount.

Therefore the aforesaid Archbishop Theodore made his profession in this manner, following the teaching of the holy Fathers—namely, that of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, from Book 1 *Against the Arian Heresy*, among other things:

“He was born in such a way that we may show that he always existed; and thus in him there is not the exception of being unbegotten, but the eternity of birth, because birth has an author and divinity is not without eternity,” etc.

Likewise, from the same Saint Hilary, Book 11 *On the Faith*, among other things:

“We rightly understand and believe the matter; for by the very wording of our statements we confess that he was born, but we do not thereby proclaim that he was not born. For ‘not born’ and ‘to be born’ are not the same: the latter is from another, whereas the former is from no one. It is one thing always to be eternal without an author, and another thing to be coeternal with the Father, that is, with the author. Where the Father is the author, there too is birth. But where the author is eternal, there too is the eternity of birth. For just as birth is from an author, so from an eternal author comes eternal birth,” etc.

Likewise, from Saint Gregory, who is also called the Theologian, in his sermon *On the Epiphany* (*Oration on the Holy Lights*, around the middle), among other things:

“The Father, then, is Father without beginning; for there is nothing else from which he is Father. The Son is Son, but not without beginning, for he is from the Father. But if you consider temporal beginning, he too is without beginning. For he is the Creator of times and does not himself take his beginning from time. The Holy Spirit is truly the Holy Spirit, proceeding indeed from the Father, but he is not himself the Son; for he is not begotten but proceeds,” etc.

Likewise, from the same Saint Gregory the Theologian’s sermon *On the Nativity of the Lord*, later in the sermon, etc.:

“This is the very Word of God, who is before the ages, invisible, incomprehensible, and incorporeal; who is beginning from beginning, light from light, the source of life and immortality, the true and exact image of God’s substance, the seal of truth, the image of the invisible God the Father,” etc.

Likewise, from the same Saint Gregory the Theologian, *On the Second Peaceful Oration* (*Oration 2 on Peace*, around the middle):

“But I introduce the beginning of the Godhead as without time, undivided, and immeasurable; and I honor the one who is the beginning, and what comes from the beginning, and how,” etc.

Likewise, from the same Saint Gregory the Theologian’s *Apologetic Oration*, later in the sermon (*Oration on Dogma and Constitution*, around the middle), etc.:

“For whose Son will he be, if his origin is not referred to the Father? Let the one be he who begot, and this one he who was begotten from him. For the origin is the Father—not the origin of some small or unworthy thing, but of divinity and goodness. The Father is [the text reads *enim*, “for,” in place of *origo est*, “is origin”] understood and perceived as origin in the Son and in the Holy Spirit: in the Son as the Word, and in the Spirit as the one proceeding from him,” etc.

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book 1, later in the work, etc.:

“For when Scripture says, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’ (Genesis 1), we understand by the name of God the Father [the text reads *autem*, “however,” for *Patrem*, “the Father”] and by the name of beginning the Son, who is the beginning not for the Father but, through himself, for the spiritual creature created first and above all, and consequently also for every creature. When Scripture says, ‘And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters’ (ibid.), we recognize that the Trinity has been fully mentioned,” etc.

Also from the same holy Augustine, from Book 38 on the Gospel of John, among other things:

“For the Son is the Father’s Son, and the Father is certainly the Son’s Father. But the Son is called God from God; the Son is called Light from Light. The Father is called Light, but not Light from Light; the Father is called God, but not God from God. If, therefore, God from God and Light from Light is a principle, how much more easily is it understood that the principle is Light from which comes Light, and God from whom comes God? It therefore seems absurd, dearest brethren, that we should call the Son a principle and not call the Father a principle. But what shall we do? Will there then be two principles? We must beware of saying this. How, then, are the Father a principle and the Son a principle, and yet not two principles? How do we call the Father God and the Son God, and nevertheless say that there are not two gods? For it is impious to say ‘two gods.’ It is impious, indeed, to say ‘three gods.’” [Col. 1254B]

And shortly afterward:

“In that which is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, there is no basis for saying ‘three,’ unless we also say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, one Almighty: therefore, one principle, etc.”

Also from the same author, Book 6, chapter 2, *On the Holy Trinity*, among other things:

“How, then, God from God, Light from Light? For both together are not God from God, but the Son alone is from God, namely, from the Father; nor are both together Light from Light, but the Son alone is from the Light, the Father, etc.”

Also from the synodical letter of the holy Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, which was presented at the holy Sixth Synod (Session 11), among other things:

“I therefore believe, blessed fathers, as I believed from the beginning, in one God, the almighty Father, wholly without beginning and everlasting, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who was born eternally and impassibly from God the Father himself, acknowledging no other principle than the Father; nor does he possess his very subsistence from anywhere else than from the Father: Light from Light, consubstantial, true God from true God, co-everlasting [Roman Edition: ‘everlasting’]. And in one Holy Spirit, who proceeds eternally from God the Father, and who must himself be acknowledged as Light and God, etc.”

## In the Sixth Session

### Chapter III

**Reprehension.** That the same Tarasius improperly called the Holy Spirit “of the same tribe” as the Father and the Son, when it would have been sufficient to call him co-eternal, consubstantial, and of the same essence and nature.

**Note:** [Col. 1253D] At this point the numbering of the chapters does not correspond, but is interrupted. Certainly, from the response itself it is apparent that another reprehension preceded this one, to which this response replies; the words found below in chapter 61 reply to the reprehension set forth here. The words of Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, also continue up to the end of chapter 5. Apparently eleven chapters are missing here.

**Response.** The holy Sophronius himself also says:

“And because he swore falsely. For it was necessary that the liar should swear falsely to him. From the choice of evils, it was better to choose the more useful things, etc.”

Also from the blessed Augustine’s preface to Psalm 31, among other things:

“We must not put any works before faith—that is, no one should be said to have acted well before faith. For the very works that are said to precede faith, although they may appear praiseworthy to human beings, are empty; and they seem to me to be like great strength and a very swift race off the road. Let no one, therefore, reckon his good works before faith, etc.”

## In the Fourth Session

### Chapter XV

**Reprehension.** That the passage in the Psalm, “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly against your holy places” (Psalm 73), was not written because of those who reject the worship of images, as those who worship them claim.

[Col. 1255A] **Response.** They truly said this concerning heretics, as the blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the same Psalm:

“How maliciously the enemy has acted against your holy places—that is, against the things that were your holy things: the temple, the priesthood, and all those sacraments that existed at that time, etc.”

Likewise, now the enemy’s greater evils, maliciously committed against the holy Catholic and apostolic Church and against the [olitan] and orthodox tradition concerning sacred images, have been cast down and reduced to nothing.

Also from the holy Gregory of Nazianzus, who is also called the Theologian, in his sermon on the philosopher Iron (*Oration in Praise of Iron*, approximately halfway through), among other things:

“For how could they not boast? How could they not pollute the holy temple by all kinds of invasions? And in all evils the impious and unjust man was indeed the leader, though he did not even bear the name of Christianity, etc.”

## In the Fifth Session

[Col. 1255B] ### Chapter XV

**Reprehension.** That the letter which they say was sent by the holy Simeon Stylites to the emperor Justinian [Justin] greatly differs from the divine Scriptures and the teachings of the holy Fathers, in what it says to the aforesaid emperor: “For these things we make remembrance and report to your divine ears”; and likewise in what it says about the same emperor’s forbidding the exercise of mercy.

**Response.** Did the holy Ambrose sin when, writing to the emperor Gratian a book on the orthodox faith, he called him “holy emperor”? And what did this man say that was beyond bounds when, writing to the most Christian emperor Justinian [Justin] out of zeal for his faith, he spoke of “divine ears”? He called them divine ears because the emperor hears through divine discourses and faithfully and orthodoxly observes them; thus he is rightly shown to possess divine ears—that is, divine hearing.

But concerning the alleged prohibition of mercy, the matter is not so. Rather, that holy man asked that the punishment not be delayed even for a little while, but that a fitting vengeance be carried out. For, as they said above, he was not without mercy; indeed, he appeared to possess so great a love for the images of the saints that he hurled anathemas against those impious men.

We firmly believe that your God-inspired excellence knows this, since Saint Gregory, in his *Dialogues*, mentions the blessed Boniface and relates how, in his account, with sorrow, by his word, he hurled to death the wretched man who came with a monkey and struck cymbals.

Hence, shortly afterward, Saint Gregory (*Book 1, chapter 9*) says:

“The anger of the righteous must therefore be feared all the more, since it is certain that he is present in their hearts who is not powerless to inflict whatever vengeance he wishes.”

Also the same holy Gregory, in his exposition of blessed Job (*Book 34, chapter 10*), where he was discussing the strong preachers of the holy Church, added:

“Thus the Lord says to the prophet concerning good teachers: ‘They shall devour and subject them to the stones of the sling’ (Zechariah 9). The holy teachers who instruct others in virtue devour their enemies when they change them within their own body through the power of conversion. Strong men emerge from that Church, by whose stony blows the hearts of the wicked are beaten. Thus the most monstrous Goliath dies by a stone from a sling (1 Samuel 17), because the devil’s height is overcome by the cornerstone of the holy Church.”

## In the Same Session

### Chapter XVII

**Reprehension.** Concerning their saying that all heretics are worse than the Samaritans, and that those who destroy images are worse than the Samaritans, although, according to their own opinion, the parents of the latter were worse than all heretics, since both groups destroyed images.

**Response.** In these matters also the blessed Gregory the Theologian, that honey-voiced teacher, says in his sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, among other things:

“You are offended by the flesh; so were the Jews. If you also call him a Samaritan—and, to pass over the rest—you do not believe in his divinity; neither did the demons. O you, more faithless than the Jews and worse than the demons, etc.”

Also from an edict of the emperor Justinian, among other things:

“Nor yet Theodore of Mopsuestia, who surpassed both the Jews and the Hellenes [that is, Greeks, M.; that is, gentiles and pagans, H.] in his impiety, etc.”

Also from Pope Gregory’s exposition of blessed Job, Book 14, among other things:

“Just as it is not good for one who eats much honey, so the one who is a scrutinizer of majesty is overwhelmed by glory (Proverbs 25).”

And below:

“The glory of the invisible Creator, when investigated with moderation, lifts us up; when examined beyond our strength, it presses us down. Hence, the more heretics desire to be filled with sublime understanding, the more they are emptied. For the more they seek, with immoderate ears, the knowledge of heavenly understanding, the more they lose.

“But those who are truly humble and truly learned in the holy Church know how to understand some of the heavenly secrets when they have been considered, and to venerate others that they do not understand: so that they reverently hold what they understand, and humbly await what they do not yet understand. The outstanding preacher rightly restrains this presumptuous boldness when he says: ‘Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety’” (Romans 12).

Therefore their predecessors, exalting themselves by claiming to know more than they ought and attempting to impose novelty, became worse than heretics and were reduced to nothing.

## In the Same Session

### Chapter XVIII

**Reprehension.** That no Gospel reading records that Jesus sent an image to Abgar, as they claim.

**Response.** Our predecessor, the lord Stephen of holy memory, once a most holy pope, presiding at the aforesaid council, asserted this himself among many truthful testimonies and taught as follows:

“But neither should we pass over what we have often learned through the report of the faithful who come from the regions of the East. Although the Gospel is silent on these matters, their credibility in the faith is by no means incredible in every respect, especially since the evangelist himself affirms concerning Christ: ‘Jesus did many other signs, which are not written in this book’ (John 20).

“Finally, it is reported by those who affirm it (Eusebius, Book 1, chapter 13) that the Redeemer of the human race, as the day of his Passion approached, responded to a certain king of the city of Edessa who desired to see him bodily and summoned him to escape the persecutions of the Jews, so that, having heard reports of his miracles and healings, he might bestow them upon him and his people:

“‘If you desire to see my face bodily, behold, I send you an image of my countenance transformed upon a cloth. Through it you may cool the fervor of your desire, and you may by no means think that what you have heard about me is impossible. Nevertheless, after I have completed the things written about me, I shall send you one of my disciples, who will bestow healings upon you and your people and lead you to the height of faith, etc.’”

Also from the synodical letter of the three patriarchs—Cosmas of Alexandria, Theodore of Antioch, and Theodore of Jerusalem—which was reread at the aforesaid council and faithfully honored and reverently received by all. After many testimonies of the holy Fathers, Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, says:

“It remains for me to tell of Abgar of Edessa and of other things, or things similar to these, concerning the holy Fathers, which you know better. Persevere, most holy Father; persevere in the same good faith, strengthened upon the rock of faith, just as the God-speaking voice addressed the apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it’ (Matthew 16). Truly, they shall not prevail against it forever and ever.

“I make this known to you, most holy lord: I, the humble Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, and those who are with us—Cosmas, patriarch of Alexandria, and Theodore, patriarch of Antioch—we understand and believe the same thing, as is also evident to your holiness, etc.”

## In the Same Session

### Chapter XIX

**Reprehension.** That the passage, “For there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us” (Psalm 73), does not apply to this matter, as they claim.

**Response.** They themselves spoke this psalmically concerning those heretics who, boasting in the false council under Constantine, once a heretical emperor, claimed to know and understand something while in fact knowing nothing of the sort.

They compared them with the Jews, concerning whom the blessed Augustine explained the same Psalm, saying:

“Behold these Jews, who say that they are still not recognized.”

And shortly afterward:

“You no longer see your signs; there is no longer a prophet, and you say, ‘And he will still not recognize us,’ because you still do not recognize yourselves. ‘There is no longer a prophet, and he will still not recognize us’: how long, O God, has the enemy reproached you?”

The same was true of those heretics: so long as their leader, namely Constantine the heresiarch, was reproached, they did not understand; and therefore they were reduced to nothing.

## In the Sixth Session

### Chapter XX

**Reprehension.** How the passage written in the *Song of Songs* is to be understood: “Show me your face; let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (Song of Songs 2). They brought forward this chapter most shamelessly as referring to the vision of images.

**Response.** They brought it forward correctly, because the vision of sacred images pertains to the beautiful form of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ according to the flesh, and of his holy mother and the saints.

Various works of the holy Fathers have explained the *Song of Songs* in the person of Christ and the Church. If they wish to know how the passage should be understood, we offer the exposition of Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, who says among many other things:

“‘Show me your face, and let me hear your voice.’ That is: Do not speak to me through the Law and the Prophets, but reveal yourself wholly to me. Moses too, seized by such a desire, confidently said to God: ‘Show me yourself, so that I may see you’ (Exodus 35).

“But at that time he said to Moses: ‘No one shall see my face and live.’ Yet, wishing to show himself to his bride, he became incarnate and manifested himself to her clothed in a body, through the mode of his power, through endurance and innocence, granting her the sight of piety.

“He therefore showed her his face when he was conceived in the virgin Mother of God (Matthew 5), and made her hear his voice when he taught the disciples on the Mount of Olives, and again when through them he sent the doctrines of preaching throughout the whole world.

“‘For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful’ (Song of Songs 2). His voice is truly sweet when he says: ‘Come, you blessed of my Father,’ etc. (Matthew 25).

“‘Your voice is sweet’—that is, the voice that made the blind see when he said: ‘Let it be done for you according to your faith’ (Matthew 9).

“‘Your voice is sweet’—that is, when he says: ‘Come to me, all you who labor,’ etc. (Matthew 11).

“‘Your voice is sweet’ when he says to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and walk’ (Mark 2).

“His voice is sweet when he says: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven’ (Matthew 9).

“‘Your voice is sweet’ when he says: ‘Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you; go in peace’ (Luke 7).

“And there are many other things which it would be tedious to write out in order.”

## In the Sixth Session, in the First Volume

### Chapter XXI

**Reprehension.** That the passage, “God created man according to his image and likeness,” does not concern the worship of images.

**Response.** If they understand the words “God created man according to his image and according to his likeness” (Genesis 1) in this way—that Tarasius, the patriarch, explained them because of the worship of images—they appear to possess no understanding whatsoever of the meaning of the text and have been unable to understand it.

For when the patriarch Tarasius opposed the council of the heretics and reproached them because, in their darkness, they had dared to speak against the establishment of sacred images, he said:

“When God the Creator sees the work fashioned by his own hands perishing, etc.”

For this reason he said this in the following sense: because the earth-born man is honored [as] the image of God, etc.

And shortly afterward:

“Their making of images and their exceedingly violent boasting in an empty deliberation, sewing together their minds with various speeches, lead them to judge the Church of God as being in error, etc.”

For God created man according to his image and likeness. The blessed Augustine, in Book 5, concerning what is read as having been done on the sixth day in Genesis, says among other things:

“Now pay attention: man has been placed in his punishment, and how great is the value of the remains of God’s image that have remained in him. Through sin he has worn away that image, and it is restored by grace—the image that had been made dull through lust.

“For just as a coin, if it is rubbed against the ground, loses the image of the emperor, so the mind of a human being, if it is rubbed by earthly lusts, loses the image of God.

“But Christ the moneyer came, so that he might strike the coins anew. And how does he strike the coins anew? By forgiving sins through grace. And he will show you that God seeks his image.

“For when he was asked about the tribute of Caesar, ‘Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?’ (Matthew 22; Mark 12), they were testing him, so that if he said, ‘It must not be paid,’ they might accuse him before the tax collectors: ‘Behold, he teaches that we should not pay tribute.’ But if he said, ‘It must be paid,’ they would say: ‘Behold, he has cursed Jerusalem; he has made it tributary.’

“What, then, did he say, and what did he admonish? ‘Why do you test me, hypocrites? Bring me a coin.’ And they offered him one. And he said: ‘Whose image and inscription does it have?’ They answered: ‘Caesar’s.’ Then he said: ‘Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (ibid.). That is: if Caesar seeks his image in a coin, does God not seek his image in a human being? etc.”

Also from the holy Severian, bishop of Gabala, in the homily preached on the Sabbath, *According to the Image and Likeness* (Genesis 8), among other things:

“And just as we, when the emperor is not present, honor the emperor’s image, so also creation, not seeing the invisible one according to whose image it was made, honored the image, etc.”

## In the Fourth Session

### Chapter XXII

**Reprehension.** How the passage, “Abraham worshiped the people of the land, the sons of Heth” (Genesis 23), is to be understood, or the passage in which Moses is read to have worshiped Jethro. Those who hold councils on behalf of the worship of images seek to support their error by these examples, and also by claiming that neither Jacob worshiped Pharaoh nor Daniel worshiped King Nebuchadnezzar, as they say, anywhere in Scripture.

**Response.** The blessed Augustine taught us in Psalm 46, saying:

“Our Lord God spreads among us in many different ways the faith in which we live, through his books, the holy Scriptures. He varies the sacraments of words, but commends one faith. For one and the same matter is said in many ways so that the manner of speaking may be varied to avoid weariness, while one faith is held because of harmony, etc.”

Also from the same blessed Augustine, concerning Abraham’s son who was led to sacrifice, among other things:

“Those two servants who were dismissed and not brought to the place of sacrifice signified the Jews; that she-ass signified I know not what of the Jews. Do not be surprised that one matter can so often be signified in many ways, etc.”

## In the Same Session

### Chapter XXIII

**Reprehension.** That the matter does not concern the worship of images, and that it is not found in our codices translated from the Hebrew truth, although they say in their synod:

“Jacob, receiving from his sons Joseph’s long robe, which had been stained, kissed it with tears and placed it before his own eyes.”

**Response.** From the third sermon of Saint Gregory the Theologian on peace (*Oration 2 on Peace*), among other things:

“Friendly peace, a good praised by all but preserved by few: where have you left us for so long, and when will you return to us?
