I embrace you when present, and I shall call upon you when departing with many lamentations and tears, by which neither Jacob—[obscure syntax]—that patriarch Joseph, sold by his brothers (Genesis 36) and, as he supposed, carried off by a wild beast; [Note: [Col. 1259D] The passage is obscure.] nor David, [concerning] his friend Jonathan, nor later [concerning] his son Absalom. One of them was torn by paternal affections. The beast seized him, and he cried out: ‘Joseph, the worst and most savage beast!’ And he kissed the boy’s stained garment as though it were the boy’s flesh, etc.”

Hence statements of this kind are also found in the works of many Fathers concerning various histories.

For in the third book of Saint Ambrose to the emperor Gratian (*chapter 3*), among other things, we find:

“Nor should you draw this as a prejudice, because Gabriel does not die, Raphael does not die, Uriel does not die.”

Behold, Uriel is by no means found written in our codices, which have been translated from the Hebrew truth.

Also, in the second book of the same Saint Ambrose *On the Holy Spirit* (*chapter 7*), among other things:

“Ezra taught us, saying, in the third book.”

Likewise, the third book of Ezra has not been received in our codices translated from the Hebrew truth, except only two books.

Moreover, the outstanding holy Pope Gregory says in his letter sent to the patrician Theoctista (*Book 9, Letter 39*), among other things:

“We know how great was the virtue of the forerunner of our Redeemer, who through sacred Scripture is called not only greater than a prophet but also an angel. Nevertheless, as the history of his death testifies, after his death his body was burned by his persecutors.”

Yet we read in the holy Gospel (Matthew 14) that the body of that same Saint John the Baptist was buried by his disciples; and blessed Gregory says, according to the historical account, that the body of that same Saint John the Baptist was burned.

And therefore, as we have said, the sayings of the saints are by no means rejected, for who could ever comprehend the whole of sacred divine Scripture?

## In the Same Session

### Chapter XXIV

**Reprehension.** Concerning their ignorant and disorderly statement:

“If you accuse me because I worship the wood of the cross as God, why do you not accuse Jacob for worshiping the top of Joseph’s staff?”

But it is evident that he did not worship because he saw the wood, but through the wood he worshiped Joseph, just as we worship Christ through the cross.

**Response.** The blessed Augustine faithfully and beautifully explained that very staff—that is, scepter—as a type of the cross in Psalm 37, saying among other things:

“Indeed, let us now rejoice that this is happening in the name of Christ. Now, holding the scepter, they are subjected to the wood of the cross. Now what was foretold is taking place: ‘All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him’ (Psalm 71). Now the sign of the cross is more precious upon the foreheads of kings than the jewel of a diadem.”

## In the Same Session

And it was repeated in the seventh session.

### Chapter XXV

**Reprehension.** That the passage “Jacob blessed Pharaoh” does not concern the worship of images, as they claim.

**Response.** Holy Scripture always teaches us to bless: “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12). Again, we are taught: “Bless all the works of the Lord, O Lord” (Daniel 3). And once more, prostrate in prayer spiritually before the Holy of Holies, we say in the Psalms:

“May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

Therefore, if we wished to write out the blessings of divine Scripture, the paper would run out before, as we think, the speech did.

[Col. 1260A] Nevertheless, we add to you one testimony of Saint Augustine concerning Jacob himself wrestling with the angel, where among other things he says:

“I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Psalm 66).

The faithful know what they receive when the Lord first blesses us through the flesh, because they are blessed through the flesh; they know that they would not have been blessed unless that crucified flesh had been given for the life of the world.

## In the Fifth Session

### Chapter XXVI

**Reprehension.** That the hope of those who place their salvation in images is vain, when they say:

“Just as the Israelite people were saved by looking upon the bronze serpent, so we shall be saved by looking upon images of the saints.”

**Response.** This has already been explained in the sacred councils mentioned above by my most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, and the most holy Fathers also said this.

For the satisfaction of unbelievers and for Frankish direction, a further explanation should be added concerning what God commanded his servant Moses:

“In the Book of Numbers it is written concerning the plague that had fallen upon them: ‘Make a serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever has been bitten and looks upon it shall live.’ Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and whenever those who had been bitten looked upon it, they were healed” (Numbers 21).

O the madness of those raging against Christian faith and religion, who claim that images should not be worshiped or venerated, although they contain representations of the Savior, his mother, and the saints, through whose power the world endures and the human race possesses salvation!

We believe that the Israelite people were delivered from the calamity inflicted upon them by looking upon the bronze serpent; yet when we look upon and venerate the images of Christ our God and of the saints, do we doubt that we shall be saved? Far be it from us to yield to the insanity of such impious presumption. Let us follow the ancient traditions of the Fathers and in no way depart from their teaching.

For if we hold to these things as our predecessors and fathers did, we can obtain their full favor.

Also from the blessed Augustine, concerning the manifestation of God, the staff, the hand made colorful, and the water turned into blood:

“Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life (John 3). That is: whoever has been bitten by the serpents of sins should look upon Christ, and he will have healing through the remission of sins.”

Also from the homily of the same holy Augustine on the Gospel of John concerning the same sermon (*Tractate 12*), among other things:

“In the meantime, brothers, so that we may be healed from sin, let us look upon Christ crucified. For, he says, just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness”—up to the point where he says—“but may have eternal life.”

And shortly afterward:

“Here he says: ‘So that he may have eternal life.’ This is the difference between the figure or image and the thing itself: the figure bestowed temporal life, but the reality of which it was the figure bestowed eternal life, and so forth.”

Also from the third book of the same holy Augustine *On the Trinity* (*chapter 10*), among other things:

“For just as the anointing of the stone signified Christ in the flesh, in which he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, so Moses’ staff changed into a serpent signified Christ himself, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

“Therefore he says: ‘Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life’ (John 3).

“Just as those who looked upon the serpent lifted up in the wilderness did not perish from the bites of the serpents, so our old man was crucified with him. For by the serpent death is understood—the death that came through the serpent in paradise—according to a mode of expression in which the cause is used to indicate the effect.

“Thus the staff becoming a serpent signifies Christ becoming subject to death, and the serpent again becoming a staff signifies Christ in resurrection, whole together with his body, which is the Church, etc.”

Also from Saint Severian, bishop of Gabala, in his sermon on the holy cross, among other things:

“Do you think it would not have been just to say: ‘If any one of you has been bitten, let him look upward into heaven toward God, and he shall be saved’? But, so that he might leave heaven also out of consideration, could he not have said: ‘If anyone has been bitten, let him look upon the lamp of light, and he shall be saved’? Or: ‘Let him look upon the table of the showbread of the holy loaves, and he shall be saved’? Or upon the altar, or the veil, or the ark, or the image of the cherubim, or the mercy seat?

“But the great lawgiver brought none of these things into the discussion; he set up only the image of the cross, and that through the accursed serpent.

“Tell me, as a faithful servant: Do you do what you forbid? Do you build what you renounce? You say, ‘You shall not make a graven image,’ and you fashion a cast serpent?

“But I gave that law in order to cut away the materials of impiety and to rescue this people from every form of idolatrous worship. Now, however, I cast the serpent so that I may prefigure, through an image, the dispensation of the Savior and make clear beforehand the course of the apostles, etc.”

## In the Fifth Session

And it was found in the fourth session.

[Col. 1261B]

### Chapter XXVII

**Reprehension.** The ill-timed and delirious statement of Leo, bishop of Phocaea, who, having turned to the worship of images, applies to himself the Psalmist’s verse, saying:

“You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness” (Psalm 19).

**Response.** Every Christian may pray with the Psalmist so that, when he has come from darkness into light through the grace of Christ, he may rightly say:

“You have turned my mourning into joy for me” (ibid.).

For when he was rescued from heresy, then his sackcloth was torn. When he recognized the truth of the true faith, then he was surrounded with joy by the orthodox of the holy Catholic Church.

Concerning this very matter, Saint Augustine likewise says in his exposition of the same Psalm, near the beginning:

“You have torn apart the lamentation [or veil] of my sins, the sadness of my mortality, and you have girded me with the first robe, immortal joy.”

And again:

“So that not my humility, but my glory, may weep no longer but sing to you: because you have now exalted me from humility, and I shall not be pierced by the consciousness of sin, the fear of death, the fear of judgment, and so forth.”

## In the Sixth Session, at the End of the First Volume

### Chapter XXVIII

**Reprehension.** That the passage sung by the Psalmist does not apply to those who reject the worship of images:

“They have spoken vain things, each one to his neighbor, lips deceitful in the heart; and they have spoken evil from the heart” (Psalm 11).

**Response.** It is not as though they rejected what the Psalmist sang: “They have spoken vain things,” etc. Rather, while rejecting the delirious utterances of the heretics in their perverted appearance, they sang with the Psalmist concerning them:

“They have spoken vain things, each one to his neighbor,”

and what follows.

From the blessed Augustine’s exposition of the same Psalm, among other things:

“There is one truth by which holy souls are enlightened. But since there are many souls, many truths can be spoken of in them, just as many images appear in mirrors from one face.”

And shortly afterward:

“Proud hypocrites are signified, placing their hope in their own speech in order to deceive human beings, but not subject to God.”

## In the Second Session

### Chapter XXIX

**Reprehension.** How the passage sung by the Psalmist is to be understood:

“Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced one another” (Psalm 84).

They rashly or flatteringly say through John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners that this was fulfilled in the participation of the blessed Pope Hadrian and Tarasius.

**Response.** It was rightly said, because God had mercy on the Church of Constantinople, and it encountered the truth of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, which always upheld justice, as it is written:

“Seat of justice, house of faith, court of modesty.”

When the Church of Constantinople confessed and embraced this justice, faith, and modesty, and turned away from error, it made peace, because the see of Constantinople alone resisted the [olitan] orthodox faith.

For the sees of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem always maintained the ancient tradition with us, namely the orthodox faith, as is shown by their synodical letters preserved among us in defense of the establishment of the sacred images.

From the blessed Augustine’s exposition of the same Psalm, among other things:

“Because justice and peace kiss one another, they do not quarrel. Why do you quarrel with justice? Behold, justice says to you: ‘Do not rage,’ and you do not listen; ‘Do not commit adultery,’ and you do not want to listen; ‘Do not do to another what you do not wish to suffer yourself’; ‘Do not say to another what you do not wish said to you.’

“You are an enemy of my friend, peace says to you. ‘Why do you seek me? I am a friend of justice. Whoever I find to be an enemy of my friend, I do not approach.’

“Do you therefore wish to come to peace? Practice justice. For this reason another Psalm says to you: ‘Turn away from evil and do good’ (Psalm 36)—that is, love justice. And when you have turned away from evil and done good, seek peace and pursue it, etc.”

## In the Fourth Session

### Chapter XXX

**Reprehension.** That the passage, “Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Psalm 98), does not concern the worship of images, as they claim.

**Response.** The blessed Augustine, in his exposition of the same Psalm, says approximately halfway through, among other things:

“I fear not worshiping the footstool of my Lord’s feet, because the Psalm says to me: ‘Worship the footstool of his feet’ (ibid.).”

And shortly afterward:

“I turn to Christ, because I seek him here, and I discover how earth may be worshiped without impiety, how the footstool of his feet may be worshiped without impiety.

“For he received earth from earth, because the flesh is from earth, and he received flesh from the flesh of Mary. And because he walked here in that very flesh and gave us that flesh to eat for salvation—yet no one eats that flesh unless he has first worshiped it—the manner has been found by which the Lord’s footstool may be worshiped. And not only do we avoid sin by worshiping it; we sin by failing to worship it.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, whenever you bend and prostrate yourself before any earth, do not regard it as earth, but regard the Holy One whose footstool is what you worship; for his sake you worship it.

“For this reason he added here also: ‘Worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy’ (ibid.). Who is holy, in whose honor you worship his footstool? etc.”

## In the Same Session

[Col. 1262D] ### Chapter XXXI

**Reprehension.** That the worship of images cannot be established from the passage, as they think:

“Worship on his holy mountain” (ibid.).

Responsio. In the exposition of the same psalm by blessed Augustine (toward the end), among other things:

> “Heretics do not worship on this mountain, because this mountain has filled the whole face of the earth. They clung to a part and lost the whole. If they acknowledge the Catholic Church, they will worship on this mountain with us. For that stone which was cut from the mountain without hands—we now see how much it has grown, how many regions of the earth it has occupied, and to what peoples it has reached.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We see all the kingdoms of the earth shattered by that stone (Daniel 2). What were all the kingdoms of the earth? The kingdoms of idols, the kingdoms of demons—they have been shattered. Saturn reigned over many people; where is his kingdom? Mercury reigned over many people; where is his kingdom? It has been shattered, and those over whom he reigned have been brought into the kingdom of Christ.” [Col. 1263A]

And shortly afterward:

> “That stone, therefore, was born from the mountain without hands; it grew, and as it grew it shattered all the kingdoms of the earth. It became a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth. This is the Catholic Church, in communion with which you rejoice. But those who do not communicate with it, who worship and praise God apart from that mountain, are not heard unto eternal life, etc.”

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XXXII.—Rebuke

That it is not on account of those who despise the worship of images, as they deliriously claim, that the prophet says: “The Lord will lead those who turn aside to their obligation with the workers of iniquity” (Psalm 124).

**Response.** They spoke about heretics, as blessed Augustine explained in the same psalm (toward the end), among other things:

> “That is, those whose deeds they imitated, because they loved their present pleasures and did not believe in the punishments to come.”

And shortly afterward: [Col. 1263B]

> “Therefore, because Christ, the Son of God, is peace, he came to gather his own and separate them from the wicked. Which wicked? Those who hate Jerusalem, who hate peace, who wish to climb over unity, who do not believe in peace, etc.”

## IN THE FIFTH ACTION.

### CAP. XXXIII.—Rebuke

The testimony of the holy Gospel was brought forward most absurdly and rashly by those who worship images against those who disdain to worship them: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Luke 11).

**Response.** They said very forcefully and beautifully against those who despise images that the lamp is placed under a bushel, because the lamp is our faith, namely that of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. Concerning this faith, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, testifies in his exposition of the holy Gospel according to Luke (Book 7, chapter 11), among other things, saying:

> “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand (Luke 11). Therefore, because in what precedes he preferred the Church to the Synagogue, he urges us to transfer our faith rather to the Church. For the lamp is faith, according to what is written: ‘Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet’ (Psalm 118). For the word of God is our faith; the word of God is light (John 1); faith is a lamp.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let no one, therefore, place faith under the Law. For the Law is within a measure, whereas grace is beyond measure. The Law casts a shadow; grace makes clear. Therefore let no one confine his faith within the measure of the Law, but let him transfer it to the Church, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit shines forth—the grace which that chief of priests illumines with the radiance of the heavenly Divinity, lest the shadow of the Law extinguish it.”

Likewise, from Saint John Chrysostom’s *Interpretation of the Gospel according to Matthew* (Homily 15, after the middle), among other things:

> “For I myself, he says, have kindled the light; but that it should continue burning is to be accomplished by your promptness—not for your sake alone, but also so that those who are to come may rejoice in its brightness and be led to virtue, etc.” [Col. 1263C–D]

## IN THE FOURTH ACTION.

### CAP. XXXIV.—Rebuke

That the statement of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, should not be understood in the way those who try to apply it to the worship of images think it should be understood.

**Response.** Many statements of blessed Athanasius are reported in the same synod, but in this chapter they did not write down which particular statement they had cited. Therefore, just as the statements of that same holy Athanasius are written, among other things, in the sacred councils of our aforementioned, most holy pontiffs and predecessors, we faithfully present them.

Antiochus’s question to Saint Athanasius concerning images:

> “Since the Law says through the prophet, ‘You shall not worship statues and likenesses,’ how do you make images and worship them?”

He replied:

> “We faithful do not worship images as gods—far from it, pagans!—but only with the affection and love of our soul toward the appearance of the face shown in the image. Hence, when its face has been erased [or: effaced], we often burn it as mere, ordinary wood, the thing that had previously been an image. For just as Jacob, approaching death, worshiped the top of Joseph’s staff, honoring not the staff but the one who held it (Genesis 47, according to the Septuagint), so we faithful worship images in no other way than because of our desire for the one represented by the likeness.”

And many other similar statements, as follows.

## IN THE SIXTH ACTION.

### CAP. XXXV.—Rebuke

That the testimony they produced from the sixth synod does not pertain to the worship of images.

**Response.** They produced the testimony from the holy sixth synod in order to show clearly that, by the time the holy sixth synod was held, sacred images and painted histories had been venerated from ancient times. [Col. 1264B] Hence that same holy sixth synod, faithfully establishing the orthodox position through its canons, decreed as follows:

> “In some paintings of venerable images, the lamb indicated by the finger of the Forerunner is depicted; it was left as a sign of grace.”

And shortly afterward (Canon 81):

> “We decree that, in accordance with the human form, he should henceforth be represented in images instead of the former lamb, etc.”

Thus blessed Augustine also explained Psalm 93:

> “If, however, you do not worship these earthly things in Christ, although a certain likeness taken from them has been given to signify the saints, whatever creature the likeness has been drawn from, understand that it is the likeness of a creature, and worship the Creator of the creature, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH ACTION.

### CAP. XXXVI.—Rebuke

That it was never instituted by the apostles, either by examples or words, as they chatter, that images should be worshiped.

**Response.** Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who was also bishop of Athens, was greatly praised by Saint Gregory the pope, who confirmed that he was an ancient Father and teacher. He lived in the times of the apostles and is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 17). Hence, in the sacred councils of our aforementioned, most holy pontiffs and predecessors, his truthful testimonies in favor of the veneration of sacred images were confirmed. Among other things:

> “We embrace these words from the letter of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Athens, which was addressed to Saint John the Evangelist.”

And below:

> “What is astonishing if Christ is true and the wicked cast his disciples out of the cities? Judging themselves worthy, they criminally withdraw and forbid the sacred things? In truth and manifestly, images are visible things of invisible things. Nor, in the ages to come, will the regard of God be blameworthy on account of his justice [alternate reading: ‘God will be the author of just separations from himself, but of those who separate themselves from God’]” (*On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 1).

[Col. 1264D] Likewise, from the same author’s *On the Celestial Host*:

> “For the aforementioned incorporeal ranks are represented in various colors and compositions [alternate reading: ‘he transmitted the ranks through material forms and various colors’], so that silently, through the most sacred images [alternate reading: ‘through sacred images proportioned to our capacity’], we may pass with devout mind to simple and incorporeal realities. Indeed, it is impossible for our mind to reach that incorporeal vision and imitation of the heavenly host unless, through the elements, we are able to reach the most beautiful image from the visible to the invisible, and cause visible and fragrant images, through rational instruction, to shine before the invisible, etc. [alternate reading: ‘unless it uses a material guidance proportionate to itself, possessing visible forms and perceptible fragrances, as images of invisible beauty and intellectual diffusion.’]”

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XXXVII.—Rebuke

That the statement of blessed Cyril in his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew does not pertain to the worship of images, as some assert.

**Response.** Saint Cyril of Alexandria and Saint Gregory of Nyssa spoke in the same vein, in the history of Abraham, in favor of the veneration of sacred images. For in the sacred councils of our aforementioned, most holy pontiffs, the following is reported from a sermon of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria:

> “Just as someone who sees a pleasing image that has been painted will admire the figure of the king and what appears in it, so, recognizing its inscription and seeing it at the same time, he will take delight, as though he were looking upon the king himself, etc.”

## IN THE SIXTH ACTION.

### CAP. XXXVIII.—Rebuke

That it is a matter of great presumption and enormous absurdity to wish to equate the images so often mentioned with the body and blood of the Lord.

[Col. 1265B] **Response.** They did not equate them, but spoke rather in accordance with Scripture. For no trumpet-bearing spirit—whether of the holy apostles or of our worthy Fathers—ever said that the image of his body was our bloodless offering, made in memory of the passion of Christ our God and of his entire dispensation; nor did they receive this as something commanded or confessed by the Lord. Rather, they hear him speaking in the Gospel:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 6).

And there are many other passages from the Lord’s teaching and from blessed Paul the apostle (1 Corinthians 11), which we did not wish to write out, because they are written in order in the same synod. For the heretics known as the Iconoclasts, in their false council, senselessly equated venerable images with the body and blood of the Lord, as they say.

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XXXIX.—Rebuke

That Tarasius, with his associates, does not fear to equate them presumptuously and ignorantly with the sacred vessels.

**Response.** On this matter Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, said in the synod:

> “Since we also possess various sacred vessels, we kiss and embrace them, and hope to receive a kind of sanctification from them.”

This was said because the heretics, barking in their false council, deliriously claimed that it was not the sacred prayer that sanctified the offering, so that by this means it might be transferred from the common to the holy, but that it remained common and dishonored, just as the painter had made it.

We, however, faithfully and truthfully say and affirm that it has been and is the custom of our holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church that, when sacred images or histories are painted, they are first anointed with sacred chrism and then venerated by the faithful. We act after the pattern of what the Lord said to Moses:

> “You shall make an oil of anointing, a holy ointment, compounded by the work of a perfumer, and with it you shall anoint the tent of testimony, the ark of the covenant, the table with its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altars of incense and burnt offering, and all the furnishings belonging to their worship. You shall sanctify all these things, and they shall be most holy; whoever touches them shall be sanctified” (Exodus 30). [Col. 1265C–D]

## IN THE SIXTH ACTION

In the second volume, Epiphanius reads.

### CAP. XL.—Rebuke

That the words “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Psalm 11) do not concern their forebears, as they claim.

**Response.** They spoke well and prophetically when they sang with the Psalmist, as blessed Augustine explained in the same psalm, saying:

> “‘May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, etc.’ (ibid.). He said ‘all’; who should think himself excluded? As the Apostle says: ‘Upon every human soul that works evil, upon the Jew first and also upon the Greek.’ And ‘the proud tongue’ (Romans 2).” [Col. 1266A]

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XLI.—Rebuke

That what is written—“The enemies’ swords have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities”—was not fulfilled in their forebears, as they claim.

**Response.** They always spoke this verse prophetically, singing it with the prophet. Hence blessed Augustine also explained it in the same psalm, saying (after the beginning):

> “‘The enemies’ swords have failed utterly’: not ‘enemies’ in the plural, but ‘this enemy’ in the singular. And whose enemy, if not the devil’s, swords have failed? These are understood as the various opinions of error.”

And shortly afterward:

> “‘And you have destroyed the cities.’ These cities are those in which the devil reigns, where deceitful and fraudulent counsels occupy the place of curiae, and so forth.”

Therefore this was fulfilled in those heretics when they rashly removed the sacred images after violating them. [Col. 1266B]

## IN THE FOURTH ACTION.

### CAP. XLII.—Rebuke

How the statement “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Psalm 72) is to be understood—a passage which, like the others, they understand differently from what was said.

**Response.** It is understood of the rich of this world who exist in error, and in other ways as well. Saint John Chrysostom himself, in his oration *That the Old and New Testaments Have One Lawgiver*, where he shows that he loves the painting of sacred images, explained it as follows:

> “I too loved the image infused into wax, filled with piety. For I saw in an image an angel pursuing a multitude of barbarians, and David truly saying: ‘Lord, in your city you will reduce their images to nothing’ (Psalm 72).”

Behold, the Father has shown most clearly how it should be understood. [Col. 1266C]

Likewise, from Saint Athanasius’s interpretation of the psalms, among other things:

> “For the city of the Lord is Jerusalem above; their image, however, is earthly. What he says means this: ‘Because,’ he says, ‘they have put on an earthly image and not a heavenly one, therefore they will be reduced to nothing. For at that time they will hear: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25), since they have not put on that same image of the Lord, etc.’”

Likewise, from blessed Augustine’s exposition of the same psalm (toward the middle), among other things:

> “You who do not have these things, do not desire them; you who have them, do not presume upon them. Behold, I have told you: I do not say, ‘You are condemned because you possess them,’ but, ‘You are condemned if you presume upon such things, if you become puffed up by such things, if on account of such things you consider yourselves great, if on account of such things you do not recognize the poor, if on account of an outstanding vanity you forget the common condition of the human race.’ Then God must repay you at the last, and in his city reduce the image of such people to nothing.” [Col. 1266D]

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XLIII.—Rebuke

That it was not said, as they boast, on account of those who worship images: “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Psalm 124).

**Response.** They rightly spoke with the prophet, because the rod of sinners means the heretics and the lot of the righteous means the orthodox, just as Saint Augustine explained in the same psalm, saying:

> “For a time the rod of sinners is felt over the lot of the righteous, but it is not left there; it will not last forever. The time will come when Christ, appearing in his glory, will gather all nations before him and divide them as a shepherd divides the goats from the sheep. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left, etc.” (Matthew 25).

## IN THE FOURTH ACTION.

[Col. 1267A]

### CAP. XLIV.—Rebuke

Concerning the matter in which John the presbyter, when Theodosius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew, was reciting the words of John Chrysostom—“I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians”—said: “Who is this angel, if not the one of whom it is written that the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians in a single night (2 Kings 19), who were encamped around Jerusalem?”

**Response.** We already wrote above why Saint John Chrysostom brought forward that sight, but the origin of that varied multitude was passed over. Therefore John the presbyter spoke according to his own judgment, supposing, on the basis of divine Scripture, that it referred to the time when the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians in a single night, who were encamped around Jerusalem. Whether this was so or not, he did not confirm at all; rather, he mentioned it in the form of a question. [Col. 1267B]

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XLV.—Rebuke

The statement of John the presbyter of the Easterners is utterly foolish and devoid of reason, when he says that, although the emperor is not present, his image is honored and therefore is not dishonored, so that now also, although Jesus Christ, ruler of all, does not appear visibly to us—for he is invisible to our bodily eyes, yet, as God, he is everywhere present—his image should be honored, just as in the case of the emperor, as the Father judged.

**Response.** John the presbyter of the Easterners did not say this on his own authority, but from the book of Saint Anastasius, bishop of Theopolis, which was read in the same synod. Therefore he said:

> “The Father showed that, although the emperor is not present, his image is honored; it is not dishonored.”

The rest follows as above.

## IN THE FOURTH ACTION.

### CAP. XLVI.—Rebuke

Concerning the matter in which John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners, rashly attempting to establish the worship of images, is reported to have said: “Jacob erected a monument to God, and thereby blessed him.” [Col. 1267C]

**Response.** He said this by way of analogy, because when Jacob awoke, he erected a stone monument in the place where God had spoken to him, pouring libations over it and pouring oil upon it, and calling the name of the place Bethel (Genesis 35). Therefore it appears to have several analogous interpretations.

From blessed Augustine’s book *On the Treatise concerning Esau and Jacob*:

> “Your Holiness understands—for one thing, namely the Church, is signified in many ways.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Because one thing is signified in many ways, which evidently is none of these things, yet figuratively is all of them, etc.”

## IN THE SAME ACTION.

### CAP. XLVII.—Rebuke

How absurdly those act who, to confirm images, produce the example of the divine Law, saying that Moses made the mercy seat, the two golden cherubim, and the ark of the covenant at the Lord’s command. [Col. 1267D]

**Response.** We have already written above, with the utmost moderation, how our most holy pontiffs and predecessors placed the example of the divine Law in their sacred councils to confirm images. Hence Saint Gregory the Theologian, in his sermon on Easter (Oration 2 on Easter, before the middle), says among other things:

> “And the one who spoke before that time to Moses, when he was then giving the Law concerning these things, said: ‘See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain’ (Exodus 25), showing through a kind of shadowy representation that visible things are an image of invisible things. I am persuaded that none of these things was ordered without cause, irrationally, or as something creeping upon the ground, nor was anything ordered that would be unworthy either of God’s ordinances or of Moses’ ministry, etc.”

[Col. 1268A] Likewise, from blessed Augustine’s book on Exodus, among other things:

> “We believe that these things were made as we read that they were made, and yet, through apostolic teaching, we recognize that the things themselves were shadows of things to come. Therefore we think that what was made should be investigated spiritually [the transmitted text also permits ‘specifically’], while we cannot deny that it was made, etc.”

### CAP. XLVIII.—Rebuke

That it is no small sacrilege to understand the holy Scriptures otherwise than they should be understood and to apply them to meanings that they do not contain, as happened in the erroneous synod held at Nicaea under Constantine, with his mother Irene acting as regent, and with Tarasius, a newly made bishop of Constantinople, presiding.

**Response.** The following rebukes were not drawn from the synod but from the meaning of blessed Augustine’s book *On What Appeared to Moses*, toward the end of that book, where it is explained as follows:

> “All things, therefore, are signs and mysteries of the future people concerning our Lord Jesus Christ. And if there are other mysteries in the ancient books, whether we understand them or do not understand them, they seek someone who desires them, not someone who rebukes them. Let us therefore ask, seek, and knock, so that it may be opened to us. Those things were mysteries announcing the future; we see them present in the Church.”

### CAP. XLIX.—Rebuke

What the difference is between an image and a likeness, or equality.

**Response.** Who among the faithful thinks that he does not know at some time what an image, likeness, or equality is? In the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, however, grace is given to the humble. The faithful disdain to preserve the distinctions of mathematicians’ external technical discipline, as blessed Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Faith* (chapter 3), where, among other things, he states:

> “We must say what is written: ‘See that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and according to the elements of this world, and not according to God’ (Colossians 2). For they place all the force of their poisons in dialectical disputation, which is defined by the opinion of philosophers as having not the power to establish but the ambition to destroy. Yet it did not please God to save his people through dialectic. For the kingdom of God consists in the simplicity of faith, not in verbal contention.” [Col. 1268B–C]

### CAP. L.—Rebuke

That worshiping or breaking images is contrary to the institutions of blessed Gregory; and because the Old and New Testaments and nearly all the principal teachers of the Church agree with blessed Gregory that images should not be worshiped and that we should worship nothing besides almighty God, Saint Gregory the pope confirms this in many places.

**Response.** He never despised sacred images, but rather observed them most steadfastly and venerated their representations. As for the claim that nearly all the principal teachers of the Church agree with blessed Gregory, it was irrational to write this, because Saint Gregory was obedient and consenting to his predecessors, the Fathers, and the principal teachers of the holy Catholic Church. For they did not know blessed Gregory while they were in this world, except for the one who foreknew and predestined them, etc.

We shall therefore present a letter of that same Saint Gregory (Book 7, letter 7) addressed to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, showing how he venerated his holy predecessors. Among other things, he writes:

> “Furthermore, concerning the person of the heretic Eudoxius, whose error I found nothing about in the Latin language, I rejoice greatly that your Blessedness has most generously satisfied me. You brought forward the testimonies of the exceptionally strong men Basil, Gregory, and Epiphanius, and we clearly recognize that the one against whom our heroes hurled so many darts has been defeated, etc.”

Concerning the veneration of sacred images, just as Saint Gregory taught in his other letters, so also in his letter to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Book 7, indiction 2, letter 5), which begins as follows:

> “The Jews who came here from your city complained to us that their synagogue, which is situated at Caralis [Cagliari], was seized by Peter—who, by God’s will, had been brought from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith—with the assistance of certain undisciplined men, on the day following his baptism, that is, on Sunday, during the very feast of Easter, with grave scandal and without your consent. They also complained that he had placed there an image of the Mother of God and of our Lord, a venerable cross, and the white garment in which he had been clothed when he rose from the font.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Considering the intention of your will in this matter, and especially your judgment, we exhort you in these words: after removing from that place the image and the cross with the veneration that is due to them, you should restore what was taken away by force.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, lest the aforementioned Peter, or the others who offered him assistance or consent in this disorderly perversity, reply that they did this out of zeal for the faith, so that by this means necessity might be imposed upon them to convert, they must be admonished. They should know that such moderation must rather be used toward them, so that a willingness not to resist may be drawn from them, and not so that they may be compelled against their will, because it is written: ‘I will sacrifice to you willingly,’ etc.” (Psalm 53). [Col. 1269A–B]

Behold, Saint Gregory did not dare to contradict such a faith concerning sacred images; rather, he confirmed it when he said: “They must not be compelled against their will.”

### CAP. LI.—Rebuke

That those who anathematize their forebears act contrary to the command of the Lord’s word; and if, according to their opinion, their predecessors were heretics, then these people were born, taught, and consecrated by heretics. This also concerns the principle that those who have departed from the world should not be judged, and the extent to which their error differs from the error of their forebears, since the former judged that images should be broken whereas the latter judged that they should be worshiped.

**Response.** Those who wrote this from such a viewpoint ought to have attended to the prophet Ezekiel, whose voice resounds greatly, saying:

> “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘this proverb shall no longer be used by you as a proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is, so also is the soul of the son mine. The soul that sins shall die.’”

And below:

> “When the wicked person turns away from the wickedness he has committed and does judgment and righteousness, he has saved his own soul.”

And after much more:

> “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way and live. Turn back from your most evil ways; why should you die, house of Israel? Therefore you, son of man, say to the children of your people: ‘The righteousness of the righteous will not save him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns away from his wickedness,’ etc.” (Ezekiel 18 and 33).

For, as Saint Gregory recalls in his *Dialogues* (Book 3, chapter 31), what harm did his father, the Arian Livigild, king of the Visigoths, do to King Hermenegild when he turned from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith? We firmly believe that he did him no harm at all. Rather, when that Arian father caused him to be killed for the true and orthodox faith, he became a steadfast confessor and martyr of God, while his Arian father was led into eternal fire for his Arian faith. What could he have done to harm his faithful son in any respect? [Col. 1269C–D]

The holy Catholic and Apostolic Church rejoices whenever it sees its enemies—namely, heretics—return to it in a true confession, the Lord saying:

> “There will be joy over one sinner, etc.” (Luke 15).

And if there is joy over one, how much more over the return of many thousands of people? Who would dare ultimately to resist the faithful?

Likewise, from Saint Augustine on Psalm 84, among other things (after the beginning):

> “The sins of parents do not belong to their children when the parents commit them after their children have already been born. For the children who have been born already belong to themselves, and the parents belong to themselves. Therefore, if those who have been born follow the evil ways of their parents, they must bear their parents’ merits. But if they change and do not imitate their evil parents, they begin to possess their own merit, not the merit of their parents. So far does your father’s sin not harm you if you change that it does not even harm your father himself if he changes, etc.” [Col. 1270A]

### CAP. LII.—Rebuke

That the Greeks attempted uselessly and rashly to anathematize the Catholic Church in their synod because it did not worship images, when they ought first to have investigated thoroughly what each part of the Church wished to hold concerning this matter.

**Response.** They did not anathematize the Catholic Church; rather, after returning to it, they anathematized that false council together with its heretical associates, who had shamelessly and rashly not only removed the sacred images established in the holy Church from ancient times but had also burned them. Therefore, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, after returning from that heresy, they anathematized it, particularly despising it. [Col. 1270B]

Likewise, from the letter of Saint Gregory addressed to Eusebius, archbishop of Thessalonica (Book 7, indiction 2, letter 8):

> “We urge you not to cease examining this matter with every vigilance and fraternal diligence; and if your investigation finds them innocent of this depravity, let it remove the scandal that has settled in the minds of their children by providing satisfaction, and let them specifically anathematize Severus and Nestorius among all the heresies, etc.”

So also these people acted, returning from their own heresy.

### CAP. LIII.—Rebuke

That a woman ought not to teach in a synod, as Irene is reported to have done in their synod.

**Response.** At the very beginnings of Christianity, when the emperor Constantine was being converted to the faith, his mother, Helena Augusta, came to him in the city of Rome with twelve scribes and Pharisees, as well as Jewish teachers and leaders. She and her son, Constantine Augustus, decided to hold a council of Jews with Christians. In that council Saint Pope Sylvester presided with many most holy bishops. Enlarging the standing of the Christian faith through both sacred Scripture and miracles, with the Lord’s protection, they were victorious.

Moreover, the eminent teacher Saint Pope Leo sent his letters to Pulcheria Augusta concerning the sacred Fourth Council. Hence she herself sat in the holy Fourth Synod together with the most faithful Emperor Marcian.

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s book on what is said to have been made on the sixth day in Genesis, among other things:

> “The earth brought forth grass for fodder and fruit-bearing trees; human beings in the Church bring forth works of mercy. After those works, which were also offered to the Lord while he was in the flesh, they were performed not only by men, as by Zacchaeus, but also by women who ministered to him from their own substance, etc.” [Col. 1270C]

[Col. 1270D] ### CAP. LIV.—Rebuke

That images should not for this reason be worshiped—because through them, as they claim, certain signs appear to have been demonstrated—since not everything through which or in which miracles appear is nevertheless worshiped.

**Response.** We have already written above, in favor of the worship of images, how they explained the matter in their definition, showing that a kiss and an honorable greeting should be given to them, but by no means, according to our true faith, the worship that is due to the divine nature alone.

From Saint Augustine on Psalm 76 (after the middle), among other things:

> “You alone are truly the great God, working wonders in the body and alone working them in the soul.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Moses also did them, but not alone; Elijah also did them; Elisha did them; the apostles also did them—but none of them alone. When they acted, you acted with them; when you acted, they were not with you. For they were not with you when you acted, at the time when you also made them. You are the God who alone works wonders, etc.” [Col. 1271A]

### CAP. LV.—Rebuke

Concerning the fact that they inserted into their statements apocryphal tales and nonsensical fables worthy of every kind of ridicule.

**Response.** They brought forward, for the ridicule and reproach of the heretics who made that false council, the apocryphal nonsense that those heretics had deliriously invented, showing them what sort of error they were attempting to introduce into the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. Therefore those who returned from that heresy sang with the prophet concerning those heretics:

> “The enemies’ swords have failed utterly, etc.” (Psalm 9).

And many other passages.

Likewise, from Saint Gregory the Theologian’s sermon on the Epiphany, *The Oration on the Holy Lights*, among other things:

> “Let us approach the light and ourselves also become light by participation in the eternal light.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Do the delirious inventions of the pagans possess anything like this in their mysteries—their dark rites, inventions of demons, or the insane fantasies of a deranged mind, confirmed by time and commended by fables? For the things they worship as though they were true, they again teach to be fabricated and composed through fables. But if they were true, they would certainly not be fabulous, since truth and fiction are opposed to one another in every respect. Yet they do everything like children truly playing in the streets and mocking one another. There is no assertion there of manly understanding or perfect reason, nothing they can bring forward against the worshipers of the Word of God,”

and many other similar statements. [Col. 1271B]

### CAP. LVI.—Rebuke

Concerning the fact that the more examples they draw from heretics and from those who scorn or despise images, the more they dishonor their forebears with greater insults and injuries, although they undoubtedly acknowledge that their forebears were followers of those people in this respect.

Responsion. Behold, they repeatedly bring forward the same single point in this chapter: that they despised their parents and dishonored them by wronging them. And therefore we too, as we wrote above, briefly add concerning this matter [Col. 1271C] that neither good parents can benefit evil children, nor good children can bring aid to evil parents, but each person will render an account to God for himself. Much more worthy of praise, however, are those who do not follow their parents into the most savage error, but return to the true orthodox faith of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church. From the book of Saint Augustine on prophecy (*Treatise on the Sheep*, near the end), where God speaks to the sheep, among other things:

> “Therefore, whoever has passed from the heretics to the Catholic Church will not bear this reproach of the nations, nor carry the curse of dissension, because they remain in the root of unity, in the planting of charity: ‘They shall not bear the curse, and they shall know that I am the Lord their God, and they are my people, the house of Israel,’ says the Lord God (Ezek. XXXIV).”

### CHAPTER LVII.—Reproach

That it is not contrary to the Christian religion, as they say, neither to honor nor to adore images.

[Col. 1271D] Responsion. From the book of Blessed Augustine, his treatment of Solomon’s Proverbs, among other things:

> “You find a man extending his hand in alms to the poor, yet not thinking there of God, but wishing to please human beings. A woolen garment may be seen, but it does not have the inner linen garment. You find another saying to you: ‘It is enough for me to worship God and adore God in my conscience; what need have I either to go into a church or visibly to mingle with Christians?’ He wants to have the linen garment without the tunic; he does not know, nor does this woman commend, such works. Spiritual things must indeed be spoken and taught without carnal things; but those who receive them ought to hold fast to spiritual things and not perform carnal works carnally, etc.”

### CHAPTER LVIII.—Reproach

That it is no small error to attempt to place manufactured images on a level with the ark of the Lord’s testament, as they attempted to do in their synod.

Responsion. Also from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Esau and Jacob, among other things:

> “Two Testaments are spoken of [Col. 1272A] in the Law, one Old and the other New. The Old had temporal promises but spiritual meanings. Let your charity pay attention. If the land of promise was promised to the Jews, the land of promise signifies something spiritually. If the city of peace, Jerusalem, was promised to the Jews, the name of the city Jerusalem signifies something.”

And many other similar passages. Hence, as we wrote above from the same book of Saint Augustine, one thing is signified in many ways: evidently it is none of these things, but figuratively it is all of them, etc.

### CHAPTER LIX.—Reproach

That images should not be equated with the relics of holy martyrs and confessors, as they strive to do in their erroneous synod, since relics are either from the body, or from things that were in the body, or from things that were around the body of a certain saint; whereas they believe that images neither were nor will be in the body or around the body of those to whom they are attributed.

Responsion. In the aforementioned holy councils of my predecessors, the most holy pontiffs, these testimonies were presented [Col. 1272B], namely that of Saint Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, on how the bodies or relics of the saints ought to be venerated, chapter 40:

> “The bodies of the holy, and especially the relics of the blessed, are to be honored with the utmost sincerity as though they were the members of Christ; and the basilicas called by their name are to be approached with the most devoted affection and the most faithful reverence, as places dedicated to divine worship. If anyone acts against this judgment, let him not be considered a Christian, but an Eunomian.”

Likewise, from the petition of the clergy and monks of the holy Church of Antioch against the heretic Severus at the holy Fifth Synod:

> “For he did not even spare the holy altars, tearing apart the most sacred vestments and certain vessels, and pouring out and distributing the rest with those who agreed with him” (At the synod under Menas, act 1).

> “For he dared, most blessed ones, to seize the golden and silver doves that hung above the most sacred fonts and altars as figures of the Holy Spirit, together with the relics, saying: ‘It is not necessary to name the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove,’ etc.” [Col. 1272C]

### CHAPTER LX.—Reproach

That this synod—which ought not even to be called a synod—cannot in any way be compared with the Nicene Synod, although it was conducted in the same place, as the priest John is said to have flatteringly declared; especially since it is known to differ from it not only in other matters but also in the Creed.

Responsion. Above we have already written that the divine doctrines of this synod are irreproachable, as the remarkable works of the principal holy Fathers clearly demonstrate. For if anyone says that he differs from the Creed of the aforesaid synod, he appears to differ from the Creed of the six holy synods, since these men spoke not from themselves but through the constitutions of the holy doctrines. From the book of the holy Sixth Synod, among other things (act 17):

> “Indeed, this pious and orthodox Creed of divine grace would have sufficed for the perfect knowledge and confirmation of the orthodox faith. But since the inventor of wickedness has not ceased from the beginning, finding in the serpent a co-worker for himself and through him bringing poisonous death upon human nature, so now also, finding instruments suited to his own will, etc.” [Col. 1272D]

Also from the book of Saint Augustine on prophecy (in the cited passage), where he speaks to the sheep, among other things:

> “You pushed with your sides and shoulders, and struck with your horns, and pressed down everything that was failing, until you scattered them outside; and I will save my sheep. As detestable as their iniquity and cruelty are, so praiseworthy is the mercy of our shepherd and our God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “‘And your glory is over all the earth.’ The Bridegroom is in heaven, the bride is on earth. He is above all the heavens; she is over all the earth. O heretic, do you believe what you do not see in heaven, while denying what you see on earth? Let these things be spoken, let them be spoken and heard, so that he may save his sheep. ‘And I will save my sheep,’ he says, ‘and they shall no longer be for devastation; and I will judge between sheep and sheep, and I will raise up over them one shepherd,’ and the rest.” [Col. 1273A]

### CHAPTER I.—Reproach

Against those who say: “Just as we possess the books of the divine Scriptures, so we possess images for the memory of veneration, while preserving the purity of our faith.”

Responsion. From Saint Gregory the Pope’s letter addressed to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles (Book IX, letter 9), among other things:

> “Tell me, brother: from what priest have you ever heard that what you did was right? Even if there were nothing else, that alone ought to have restrained you, lest, despising the other brothers, you should think yourself alone to be holy and wise. For it is one thing to adore a painting, and another to learn through the history represented in a painting what ought to be adored. For what Scripture provides to readers, painting provides to the uneducated who look at it: in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Hence, especially among the nations, painting serves in place of reading—a matter that you, who live among the nations, ought to have considered very carefully.”

And shortly afterward:

> “And because antiquity has admitted, not without reason, that histories of the saints should be painted in venerable places.” [Col. 1273B]

And again:

> “Because the paintings of images had been made for the edification of the unlearned people, so that those who did not know letters, attending to the history itself, might learn what had been done, etc.”

[Note: [Col. 1273] At this point, some material appears to be missing before the words of Sophronius.]

Likewise, Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, who explained the matter in this way in his holy synodical letter, which was presented and wonderfully received at the holy Sixth Council, speaking of the Holy Spirit:

> “Truly coeternal with the Father and the Son, consubstantial and of the same tribe, of the same essence and nature. Likewise, the Trinity of the Godhead is consubstantial, to be co-honored and seated together, of the same nature and kindred, and of the same tribe, to be recapitulated into one Godhead and joined into one common dominion, without personal confusion and without substantial division. Therefore we believe in the Trinity in unity, and in unity we glorify the Trinity,” and the rest.

Also from the letter of Saint Athanasius addressed to Epictetus, among other things:

> “But those who are thought to believe correctly according to all that was said by the holy Fathers, and who wish to alter things under the pretext of investigation, do nothing other than what is written: ‘They make their neighbor drink foolishness’; but they oppose nothing for any useful purpose, except that they may overthrow the simple, etc.” [Col. 1273C]

Also from Saint Augustine’s seventh book on the Trinity (chapter 6), among other things:

> “Let us speak of three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—in the same way that certain people are called three friends, or three relatives, or three neighbors: they are so in relation to one another, not because each of them is related to himself. Therefore, each one of them is the friend, relative, or neighbor of the other two, because these names have a relational meaning, etc.”

Also from that same Saint Augustine’s eighth book on the Trinity (at the beginning), among other things:

> “There is such equality in that Trinity that not only is the Father not greater than the Son with respect to divinity, but the Father and the Son together are not something greater than the Holy Spirit; nor is any single person of the three something less than the Trinity itself.” [Col. 1273D]

These things have been said; and if they are repeated by frequent reading, they become more familiar. Yet some measure must also be observed, and God must be entreated with the most devoted piety, etc.

## IN THE FIRST SESSION

### CHAPTER IV.—Reproach

That Basil the archbishop, in his confession of faith, after confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, inserted the kissing and adoration of images and relics, saying that he believed that sanctification was shared through them; but that he entirely omitted the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the future life.

Responsion. Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the first book of *On the Faith* (chapter 2), which he sent to the emperor Gratian [Col. 1274A], dogmatically teaching orthodox doctrine concerning the Father and the Son, says among other things:

> “For the fullness of divinity is in the Father, and the fullness of divinity is in the Son.”

And he said nothing about the Holy Spirit because he explained only the Father and the Son. Basil, having rejected and anathematized the heresy he had held, and making a confession concerning the true religion of the orthodox faith, reverently embraced and accepted the sacred images and the relics of the saints, concerning which he had formerly been in error. For he had no error concerning the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, or the future life, nor did he contradict the orthodox faith of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church in this matter, as did those wretched and unhappy heretics who, taking the occasion of images and the relics of the saints, attempted to disparage them, despising and rejecting the sacred images themselves and the relics of the saints.

But woe to them, because, turning aside from the straight path and walking along an erroneous road full of thorns, they have fallen into the pit which they themselves made, and they will burn eternally. For if we wished to explain the veneration of the relics of the saints through the works of divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, who would be able to write, or produce enough sheets? We briefly recall a few things from among many, from Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, in his interpretation of Psalm 115, among other things:

> “Formerly it was said to priests and Nazirites: ‘Everyone who touches a dead person shall be unclean,’ and he was to wash his garments. But now whoever touches the bones of martyrs receives some participation in sanctification from the body, while grace is present. ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,’ etc.” (Ps. CXV.) [Col. 1274B]

Also from Saint John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, in his sermon on the Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans (sermon 32), among other things:

> “For this reason I also love Rome. Moreover, I have still another way of praising it, for its greatness, antiquity, appearance, population, power, and successes in war. But leaving all such matters aside [Col. 1274C], I bless it for this reason: because, while he was alive, Paul wrote to them and loved them so greatly; he spoke to them in person, ended his temporal life there, and they possess his holy body there. For this reason the city is more honored than on account of anything else. And just as a great and strong body has two shining eyes, so are the bodies of these holy men, Peter and Paul. The sky is not brighter when the sun sends forth its rays than the two lamps of the city of Rome have shone throughout the world. From there, then, Paul will be snatched away; from there, Peter. Consider and tremble: what insignia Rome will see when Paul suddenly rises from his place of rest together with Peter and goes to meet Christ! What gift does Rome send to Christ? What two crowns does the city contain? What golden chains does it encircle? What fountains does it possess? For this I admire the city—not for the abundance of gold, not for the columns, not for any other spectacle, but for the outstanding summits of the universal Church. Who will grant me to be drenched with Paul’s body, to cling to his sacred tomb, and to see the holy dust of that body in which he imitated Christ, in which he bore the marks of Christ, and in which he spread preaching everywhere? The dust of that body through which he hastened everywhere? The dust of that mouth through which Christ was proclaimed and the light shone forth, etc.” [Col. 1274D]

Also from Saint Augustine’s sermon on the feast of the holy apostles, among other things:

> “For this most blessed Peter was a fisherman, to whom not a steward, I do not say, but the lowest kitchen servant gave orders; now the emperor, prostrate on his knees, adores him, etc.”

Also from that same Saint Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 44 (after the middle), among other things:

> “‘The daughters of kings delighted you in your honor’ (Ps. XLIV), because they did not seek the honor of their fathers but sought your honor. Let the temple of Romulus in Rome be shown to me with as much honor as I can show there the memorial of Peter. In Peter, who is honored except the one who died for us, etc.” [Col. 1275A]

Also from Saint Gregory the Pope’s letter addressed to Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica (Book IX, letter 69), among other things:

> “But if Theodore the lector wishes to come here to the apostles to pray to the saints, let your Fraternity send him without any delay.”

And there are many other such testimonies, which we foresee would take too long to write out in order.

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### CHAPTER V.—Reproach

That Theodosius, bishop of Amorium, negligently remained silent concerning the faith of the holy and undivided Trinity, but spoke carelessly and extraordinarily about images:

> “I confess and promise, and I accept, kiss, and adore the images.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Whoever does not diligently instruct all the people beloved by Christ to adore and venerate the sacred and venerable images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, let him be anathema.” [Col. 1275B]

Responsion. We think that the aforesaid Theodosius, burning with zeal for the faith, confessed such a statement as they explained in their definition. For we also find our predecessors—namely, the most blessed pontiffs Gregory and Gregory, Zachary and Stephen, Paul and again Stephen—burning in the Holy Spirit for the erection of sacred images and possessing zeal for the right faith.

For this reason Lord Gregory, the younger Pope Gregory II, presiding together with seventy-nine most holy bishops before the confession of Blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and strengthening the testimonies of many holy Fathers, decreed in their council that sacred images should be venerated and adored.

Moreover, our predecessor, the lord Stephen, Pope of holy memory, likewise presiding with bishops from the regions of France and Italy in the basilica of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, called Constantiniana [Col. 1275C], confirmed and embraced the venerable council of his predecessor; and he too, together with all the presiding bishops, adhering more and more to the testimonies of the holy Fathers, decreed that sacred images should be adored and venerated. Hence Blessed Paul the Apostle also teaches, saying:

> “Hold fast to the traditions which you received” (2 Thess. II).

And again:

> “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema,” etc. (Gal. I).

## IN THE THIRD SESSION

[Col. 1275D]

### CHAPTER VI.—Reproach

The ridiculous and childish statement in the confession of faith of Theodore the archbishop:

> “Wonderful is God in his saints” (Ps. LXVII).

And immediately afterward:

> “To his saints who are on earth he has made all my desires wonderful among them” (Ps. XV),

as though this verse followed the former one.

Responsion. By this they attempt to slander gratuitously, because when the holy Church rises at matins to sing praises to God, it first says:

> “O Lord, open my lips” (Ps. L),

and afterward:

> “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord” (Ps. XCIV);

thus it begins:

> “Blessed is the man” (Ps. I).

Similarly, the Apostle Paul, faithfully running through the names of the prophets in order, remembered Jephthah, then David, and afterward Samuel. We also find many works of the saints bearing witness first from the New Testament and afterward from the Old Testament; yet no one among the faithful dares to make such things objects of ridicule.

Also Saint John Chrysostom, in his interpretation of the Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews (homily 7), teaching among other things, says:

> “‘The Lord shall not see, nor shall the God of Jacob understand’ (Ps. XCIII). And again: ‘Our lips are our own; who is our lord?’ (Ps. XI). And again: ‘Why has the wicked provoked God?’ (Ps. IX). And again: ‘The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires,’ etc.” (Ps. XIII). [Col. 1276A]

Also that same Saint John Chrysostom, in his interpretation of the Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans (homily 7):

> “For this reason Matthew, beginning the Gospel, mentions both of these first, and then presents their ancestors in order, saying: ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ’ (Matt. I). He did not endure saying ‘after Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,’ but before Abraham he mentioned David; and what is remarkable is that he placed David before Abraham, saying: ‘Son of David, son of Abraham,’ and then began to speak in order, etc.”

## IN THE FIRST SESSION

### CHAPTER VII.—Reproach

Against those who say: “With God cooperating, we directed ourselves to assemble you,” or, “God assembled you, wishing to establish his own council.”

[Note: [Col. 1275D] This is found in the Council of Ephesus, first session.]

Responsion. At the end of the Gospel of Saint Mark:

> “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI). [Col. 1276B]

Also from Saint Cyril’s sermon on the holy Mother of God, among other things:

> “Glory to you from us, holy mystical Trinity, which summoned these men and all of us to this assembly concerning Mary, the Mother of God, etc.”

Also from the holy synod, session eighteen, after the subscriptions of the bishops and the emperor, the most pious emperor Constantine said:

> “We call upon God as witness.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Since, therefore, it pleased God to grant the time, we invited you to assemble, so that we might examine the holy Scriptures of God and expel from our undefiled Christian faith every novelty of speech or assertion that has recently been added by certain people who hold perverse opinions, etc.”

## IN THE THIRD SESSION

### CHAPTER VIII.—Reproach

Against those who say [Col. 1276C] that the honor paid to an image passes to the prototype.

Responsion. Whoever wishes to contradict this will contradict the exposition of Saint Basil (*On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 75), whom we believe no faithful person would dare to oppose against his orthodox faith. For he himself explained this point in his most sacred letter, which he sent to Amphilochius, among other things.

Also Saint Severian, bishop of Gabala, otherwise called Gavalensis, in a homily in which he demonstrated that the Scriptures were explained by the Lord, among other things:

> “If you insult the imperial garment, do you injure the one who wears it? Do you not know that if anyone insults the image of the emperor, he brings injury upon the dignity of the prototype? Do you not know that if anyone tears down an image from wood [reading uncertain], he is not judged as though he had dared to act against inanimate material, but as one who, stretching out his hands against the emperor, defiles material without the emperor’s soul, separated from the emperor? For if an image is struck in any way, its injury reaches the emperor, etc.”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

[Col. 1276D]

### CHAPTER IX.—Reproach

That Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, spoke unhappily, rashly, or foolishly:

> “I accept and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images, and I offer to them the worship that is according to service, which I offer to the substantial and life-giving Trinity. Those who do not think or glorify in this way I separate from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, submit to anathema, and consign to the party of those who denied the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.” [Col. 1277A]

Responsion. Returning from their wicked heresy, they attempted with all their strength to satisfy the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church in their confession. Therefore they confessed that they believed such worship to be due to the sacred images as was established in the definition of the synod, among other things (act 7) [Col. 1277A]:

> “That the venerable and holy images which are appropriately made from colors, metal, and other material should be restored in the holy churches of God, on sacred vessels, on vestments, walls, panels, houses, and roads: namely, images of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, of our undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God, of the precious angels, and of all the holy and righteous men. For the more frequently they are seen through their pictorial representation, the more those who look upon them rise to the memory and love of the [prototypes], the original forms; and they offer them a kiss and an honorable greeting, not at all according to our true faith’s worship, which is due to the divine nature alone, but in the same manner as to the sign of the precious and life-giving cross, the holy Gospels, and the other sacred objects that are adorned, etc.”

## IN THE SECOND SESSION

[Col. 1277B]

### CHAPTER X.—Reproach

That Euthymius, bishop of Sardis, did not differ greatly from the error of the aforementioned Constantine in saying:

> “With my whole heart I accept the venerable images, with fitting honor and an embracing worship. Those who think or teach otherwise or contrary to the holy images I declare to be strangers to the Catholic Church, and I proclaim them heretics.”

Responsion. Behold, as we said above, according to the definition of the synod they confess that they make a pure confession of the Catholic Church in saying that he accepts the venerable images with his whole heart and embraces them with fitting honor and worship, as was said above in the definition of the synod:

> “Not at all according to our true faith’s worship, which is due to the divine nature alone, but in the same manner as to the sign of the precious and life-giving cross, the holy Gospels, and the other sacred objects that are adorned.”

And therefore he said, “with fitting honor”; and he promised that he would proclaim those opposed to the Catholic Church to be heretics.

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

[Col. 1277C]

### CHAPTER XI.—Reproach

That there is no authority for, nor is it found in any authentic book, what they say: that a certain woman was restrained from committing adultery by means of an image of a certain Polemon. They strive to equate this with the miracle that occurred through the fringe of the Lord’s garment, when the woman who touched it received the healing she desired.

Responsion. In this chapter those who wrote these things endeavor to accuse and strive to contradict the truth. They cannot prove that those men would dare to equate the miracle of Polemon with the fringe of the Lord’s garment.

In the synod, however, the testimony concerning the miracle of the image of Polemon was presented from the sermons of the holy Gregory the Theologian, where he deliberately wrote the verse. Basil of Ancyra, as well as Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Nicephorus, bishop of Dyrrachium, each replied separately.

Basil the bishop replied:

> “Saint Gregory, the eloquent Father, considered the image of Polemon remarkable.” [Col. 1277D]

And the patriarch said:

> “For chastity was accomplished through it. For if the prostitute had not seen the image of Polemon, she would never have withdrawn from adultery.”

At the same time Bishop Nicephorus also replied:

> “The image is remarkable and exceedingly worthy, because it was able to rescue a woman from the performance of an abominable disgrace.”

After this another lector read in the following manner from Blessed Antipater, bishop of Bostra, in his sermon on the woman with the flow of blood, where, after a lengthy explanation, the saint says:

> “Having received the gift, she erected a memorial to Christ, spending her wealth on the poor, and offering her remaining wealth to Christ.”

After this, the patriarch again replied separately concerning the miracle of the woman with the flow of blood:

> “Just as she offers to Christ the image which bears his title, so the woman with the flow of blood offered a memorial.”

Similarly Bishop Basil replied:

> “He commands that it be said precisely, and he broadly accepts those who make images. Nevertheless, your God-inspired and truthful excellence can have the synod itself read in the fourth session, to determine whether it is so or not.” [Col. 1278A]

## IN THE SIXTH SESSION, third volume

### CHAPTER XII.—Reproach

That it does not pertain to the adoration of images—as they foolishly and irrationally suppose—that which was written by the lawgiver:

> “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding to complete the work in gold and silver; and I have given him as a companion Oholiab, son of Ahisamach,” etc. (Exod. XXXI).

Responsion. In support of these most firm examples, our predecessor, the most holy lord Pope Gregory II the Younger, said the following in his holy council—which was also accepted and venerated in another council of our predecessor, Pope Stephen, conducted together with the priests of the regions of France and Italy [Col. 1278B]—while the most holy and blessed lord Pope Gregory himself presided:
