> “If conversion to salvation could come to those who think contrary things and seek to invalidate the ancient traditions of the Fathers, the things we have already stated above from the testimonies of the Fathers and the sacred documents would certainly suffice. But because we see—and say this with grief—that many people, with confused minds, are disturbing the decrees of the Church, therefore, most beloved brothers, our discourse is extended, and we desire to say something further from ancient documents to restrain the madness of error; perhaps the restless may recover their senses.

> “For in the book of Exodus we read as follows: ‘The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, that they take first fruits for me; from every person who offers willingly, you shall receive them. These are the things that you shall receive,’ and the rest in order, including the two cherubim that shall be upon the ark of the testimony, ‘everything that I shall command you for the children of Israel’ (Exod. XXV).”

He also produced another testimony from the Third Book of Kings, so that the babblers might be silent before God’s command. When Solomon had constructed the temple:

> “Among other things, he made in the sanctuary two cherubim of olive wood.”

And below:

> “He carved upon them figures of cherubim, palm trees, and very prominent relief work, and overlaid them with gold; and he covered with gold both the cherubim and the palm trees,” and the rest (3 Kings VI).

> “Behold, dearest brothers, let us consider what Moses did at God’s command, and what the wisest Solomon constructed by divine order, etc.”

How much more ought we with pure heart and mind to honor and adore our God Christ, sculpted and represented, and his holy ever-virgin Mother Mary, as well as the apostles and all the saints of God, through their sacred likenesses and images, and to petition that God may be propitiated toward us and our sins forgiven?

We make and adore images for no other reason than the Word of God incarnate for us. But if everything made by human hands must be rejected, then neither the ark of the covenant nor its golden and engraved cherubim ought to have been accepted, since they were made by Bezalel and Oholiab according to God’s command. If, however, those things were accepted, then these images too are appropriately accepted, because they are made according to God. Hence they also perform many miracles, just as the ark does.

For the ark and the cherubim, like these images, were without a soul, manufactured, and carved. But just as God worked through those things there and was glorified, so these too are made in a similar manner, distinguished by colors according to the visions and revelations of the prophets.

And lest anyone dare to bark against the worship proclaimed by our predecessors, the most holy bishops, let him know that they taught such worship as our predecessor, Saint Gregory, the outstanding teacher and pope, taught in his letter, which Bishop Herulphus of the city of the province of Gaul [of Langres] presented at the aforementioned council of Pope Stephen. There, among other things, he taught Secundinus, a servant of God enclosed in Gaul, saying:

> “We know that you do not request an image of our Savior in order to honor it as God or as though it were God, but for the remembrance of the Son of God, so that you may grow warm in love for him whose image you consider yourself to see. We do not prostrate ourselves before it as before the Divinity, but we adore the one whom through the image we remember as having been born, having suffered, or sitting on the throne. And while that painting itself, like Scripture, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either makes our spirit rejoice over the resurrection or soothes it concerning the Passion.

> “Therefore we have sent you through our aforesaid son, the deacon, two *surtaria* [variant: *surcaria*. H.] containing an image of the Savior, of the holy Mother of God Mary, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul; also one cross and a key as a blessing from the most holy body of Peter, chief of the apostles, so that through him you may be defended from the Evil One, by whose holy wood you believe yourself fortified, etc.” [Col. 1279A]

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

### CHAPTER XIII.—Reproach

That Theodosius, bishop of Myra, acted ridiculously and childishly when, in order to establish the adoration of images, he reported the dreams of his archdeacon in the same synod. [Col. 1279B]

Responsion. Who doubts that both in the Old and in the New Testament future events were revealed to many people through dreams? But, to recall one excellent example from among many, we offer the testimony of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who says among other things in his exposition of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius (Book VII, letter 53):

> “On the third night, when my body had been exhausted by fasts, while I was not sleeping but in a state of astonishment, a certain third person appeared to me who was like the blessed Apostle Paul, whose face the painting had taught me, etc.”

This testimony was presented by Sergius, the most holy former archbishop of the Church of Ravenna, through his deacon John, at the aforementioned council of my predecessor, the lord Stephen of holy memory, in defense of the veneration of sacred images.

Also from Saint Gregory the Theologian, in the epitaph for his brother Caesarius (*Funeral Oration in Praise of Caesarius*, near the end), among other things:

> “Then I shall see my Caesarius, never departing, never returning, never lamented, never pitied, but splendid, glorious, exalted, such as you appeared to me in the vision. Beloved of your brothers to me, etc.” [Col. 1279C]

Saint Gregory the Pope also mentions in his *Dialogues* certain most blessed men and religious women, as well as girls, who saw the holy Mother of God Mary, the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, and the holy martyrs at the time of their death. How did they recognize them, unless through a painting, just as Blessed Ambrose said, as we wrote above?

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### CHAPTER XIV.—Reproach

A delirious statement full of error concerning a certain recluse, whom they say swore an oath to a demon and then invalidated that very oath. His abbot is recognized as having raved considerably, saying that it would be more advantageous for him to enter all the brothels in the city than to deny the adoration of the image of the Lord or of his holy Mother. [Col. 1279D]

Responsion. This testimony was presented from the book of the eminent doctor Saint Sophronius, and, as we suppose, no one among orthodox Christians would dare to reject his divinely inspired doctrines or any work of his exposition.

Also from Saint John Chrysostom, in his account of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, among other things:

> “For he ought not to forbid the veneration of sacred images.”

Also in the letter of Saint Gregory the Pope addressed to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Book VII, indiction 2, letter 5), as we have already written above, demonstrating these things to you.

## IN THE SECOND SESSION

### CHAPTER II.—Reproach

The useless, senseless, and laughable statement of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is censured in that he said:

> “It is written in our divine Scriptures.”

[Col. 1280A] **Response.** Divine Scripture appears to be proclaimed by the faithful for the salvation of human beings. Therefore, we suppose that he said: “Desiring faithfully to possess glory and beauty from them themselves, in our divine Scriptures, and wishing at the same time to speak as one taught by that same sacred Scripture, just as it is written in the little works of the holy Fathers, etc.” Saint Augustine, in his treatise on the Proverb of Solomon, among other things: “They too have our sacraments; they have our Scriptures; they have our Amen and Alleluia; many of them have our creed, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

### Chapter III — Reproach

The statement is condemned as useless, foolish, and full of error: “Whoever fears God altogether honors, adores, and venerates him, just as he does the Son of God, Christ our Lord, his sign of the cross, and the image of his saints.”

**Response.** From the book of blessed Augustine on the son of Abraham led to sacrifice, among other things: “You were not moved without reason when I said this: ‘The cross has horns.’ [Col. 1280B] For two pieces of wood are joined together in such a way as to produce the form of a cross. Thus, just as in many places we see two horns formed in the image of the cross, into which the hands may be fixed, so I see the crucified Lord as a ram clinging to the horns, etc.”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### Chapter IV — Reproach

Concerning the fact that the same John did not speak correctly when he said: “Through the image, which appears by means of colors, his power is adored and glorified, and we shall come to remember his presence on earth.”

**Response.** Likewise, from the letter of Pope Saint Gregory, addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion (Book VII, Letter 13), among other things: “You asked that an image of the one whom you worship be sent to you through your deacon Dulcitius. Your request greatly pleased us, because with your whole intention you seek in your heart the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that daily bodily vision may always restore what you long for; and while you look upon the painting, [Col. 1280C] you may burn in spirit toward the one whose image you consider yourself to see, etc.”

## IN THE FIFTH SESSION

### Chapter V — Reproach

Concerning their statement: “He is guilty of the same crime who despises images as Nabuchodonosor was, who brought out the bones of the kings of Judah from their tombs, tore out the eyes of the king of Judah after killing his sons, and removed the cherubim from the temple.”

**Response.** Above, in the letter of Pope Saint Gregory, we have already set forth how images are not to be despised but venerated. Hence our predecessors, the aforementioned most holy pontiffs, frequently gave this ruling in sacred councils: “If anyone refuses to venerate the holy images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his mother, and of all the saints according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, let him be anathema.”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

[Col. 1280D] ### Chapter VI — Reproach

Concerning the fact that, according to the statement of the deacon Demetrius, their parents acted carelessly and disorderly, burning two silver-covered books because they contained something concerning images, and cutting out two leaves from another book.

**Response.** This is shown to be a characteristic deed of heretics, just as they raved in their false syllogism under a certain heretical Emperor Constantine.

From a letter of Saint Cyril to Successus, bishop of Neocaesarea, near the end, among other things: “Having failed against these rebukes, they contrived something bitter and worthy of heretical impiety. For, corrupting the letter, removing some things and adding others, they published it so that it might be thought that that memorable man held views similar to Nestorius and those who were with him, etc.”

Likewise, from the holy Sixth Synod, in its third session, among other things: “The discourse of Menna, of holy memory, archbishop of Constantinople, to Vigilius, the most blessed Roman pope, concerning the fact that Christ has one will. The legates of the Apostolic See of Rome rose and cried out: ‘Most pious lord, the present book of the Fifth Synod has been falsified, etc.’” [Col. 1281A]

Likewise, it is reported in that holy Sixth Synod itself (Session 8, after the middle): “The holy Sixth Synod said: ‘Behold, you have also destroyed this testimony of the holy Father. It is not fitting for the orthodox to mutilate in this way the words of the holy Fathers and strip them bare; this is rather characteristic of heretics.’ The heretic Macarius said: ‘I have already said that, seeking to establish my position, I stripped them bare in this way.’ The holy Synod cried out: ‘He has plainly shown himself to be a heretic, etc.’”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### Chapter VII — Reproach

Concerning the fact that, seeing images on the silver panels in the same book, Leontius the secretary boasted that he had discovered the oldest and most ingenious advantage of his error.

**Response.** Likewise, from the same holy Sixth Council, [Col. 1281B] among other things (Session 8, after the middle): “The most pious emperor Constantine and the holy Synod said: ‘Let Macarius explain why he cut away these necessary things from the testimony of the holy and approved Father.’ The heretic Macarius said: ‘I stripped the testimonies that I removed according to my own intention.’” And shortly afterward: “The holy Synod said (at the place cited): ‘Behold, most gracious lord, he has also cut away this testimony. For when the testimonies are reread by order of your authority, they will show that it has been obscured by his stripping away, etc.’”

## IN THE EMPEROR’S LETTER

### Chapter VIII — Reproach

Concerning the fact that Constantine and Irene wrote in their letter to the venerable pope of the city of Rome: “We beseech your fatherhood, and above all God beseeches you, who does not wish any human being to perish.”

**Response.** In the holy Gospel the Lord says: [Col. 1281C] “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren, etc.” (Luke 22).

Likewise, in the Letter of blessed Paul the Apostle, among other things: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (1 Cor. 5).

Likewise, from Saint John Chrysostom’s sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, among other things: “Learn that peace was made not by our entreaty—we who had offended him—but at the request of the one who had been justly angered against us. ‘For on behalf of Christ,’ says the Apostle, ‘we act as ambassadors, as though God were entreating through us’ (ibid.). What does this mean? Does he himself entreat who suffered the injury? Indeed he does, he says. For God is compassionate, and as a merciful father he himself entreats. And see who has come as mediator, who has come as reconciler: not an angel, not an archangel, but the Son himself of the one who entreats, etc.” [Col. 1281D]

Likewise, from the same Saint John Chrysostom’s interpretation of the Letter to the Romans (Homily 5, near the end), among other things: “What follows from this? He sent no longer prophets, no longer angels, no longer patriarchs, but the Son himself. And he was killed; and when he came, he did not even then extinguish his love, but kindled it more greatly, and remains entreating.” And below: “Paul cries out, saying: ‘For on behalf of Christ we act as ambassadors, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God’ (ibid.).” And shortly afterward: “Let us consider how often we have insulted him after thousands of benefits, yet he has persisted in entreating; how often we have transgressed against him, yet he himself does not neglect us, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

### Chapter IX — Reproach

Concerning the fact that the aforementioned John said: “He wrestled with him in human form [Col. 1282A] and called him Israel, which is interpreted as ‘a mind seeing God.’”

**Response.** From the book of Saint Gregory the Theologian on the divinity (Oration 2, *On Theology*, after the middle), among other things: “For Jacob saw a lofty ladder.” And shortly afterward: “And as though with a human being, he wrestled with God.” And later: “The struggle received a transfer of its name, and he was renamed Israel instead of Jacob, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint Augustine on Jacob’s wrestling with the angel, among other things: “He held him, therefore, and wrestled, wishing to embrace Jacob as though in a bodily form; he said: ‘Release me bodily, because behold, it is already morning, so that you may be enlightened spiritually, etc.’” (Gen. 32).

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### Chapter X — Reproach

That those who say the following do not think correctly: “If, according to the lawful tradition of Moses, the people are commanded to place purple-blue [Col. 1282B] tassels on the edges at the extremities of their garments, for the remembrance and preservation of the commandments, much more ought we, through an analogous image, to see the outcome of the conduct of holy men and, imitating their faith according to apostolic tradition, etc.” (Heb. 13).

**Response.** We believe that you are not unaware of what Pope Saint Gregory said in his letter, as we set forth above (Book IX, Letter 9), and that antiquity did not without reason permit the histories of the saints to be painted in venerable places. Moreover, when he again expounded the distinction of sacred discourse while treating the prophet Ezekiel, he added (Homily 10, at the beginning): “Sacred Scripture is our food and drink.” And shortly afterward: “In obscure matters, which cannot be understood unless they are explained, it is food, because whatever is explained so that it may be understood is, as it were, chewed so that it may be swallowed. In clearer matters, however, it is drink. For we swallow drink without chewing. Thus we drink the clearer commandments, because we are able to understand them even without explanation, etc.”

Hence it has also been expounded by my predecessors, the most holy pontiffs, in their sacred councils, when they promulgated many things concerning the ancient histories: “If those things have been accepted, these images also are appropriately accepted, since they are made according to God. Hence they also work, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

### Chapter XI — Reproach

That the priest John did not think correctly when, in order to establish the adoration of images, he said: “Jesus son of Nave set up twelve stones in memory of God” (Joshua 4).

**Response.** It is written in the Book of Joshua: “Joshua tore his garments and fell facedown upon the ground before the ark of the Lord until evening, he and all Israel, and they put dust upon their heads” (Josh. 7). And shortly afterward: “And the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Rise; why are you lying facedown upon the ground? Israel has sinned and transgressed my covenant’” (ibid.). And again shortly afterward: “Rise, sanctify the people, and say to them: ‘Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow,’ etc.” (ibid.).

Behold, Joshua, prostrate before the ark of the covenant, was heard. Therefore the honey-voiced teacher, Pope Saint Gregory, in his letter mentioned above (Book VII, Letter 53), addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion in Gaul, warned among other things, saying: “We do not prostrate ourselves before it as though before the Divinity itself, but we adore the one whom we remember as having been born, suffered, or seated upon a throne through the image, etc.”

### Chapter XII — Reproach

That the adoration of the prophet Nathan toward King David is not, as they say, equal to the adoration of images.

**Response.** From Saint Gregory’s book on Job (Book IV, chapter 1), among other things: “Thus, when only the history is perceived in sacred discourse, nothing other than the face is seen; but if we are joined to it through continual use, we penetrate its mind, as it were through the familiarity of conversation. For while we gather one thing from another, we easily recognize in its words that one thing is what they signify inwardly and another what they sound like. Everyone is rendered that much more a stranger to its meaning the more he is bound to its surface alone, etc.” [Col. 1283A]

Likewise, in the same book he says: “What is understood by David, whose name is interpreted as ‘strong of hand’ or ‘desirable,’ except our Redeemer? What is signified by his gift except the Church?” And shortly afterward: “The inquiry into the Lord’s divinity is a hidden fountain; the manifestation of his incarnation, however, is an open fountain. What, moreover, is signified by Jerusalem, which is interpreted as ‘vision of peace,’ except the same holy Church? For in her the heart of the world contemplates the Lord, of whom it is written: ‘For he is our peace, who made both one, etc.’” [Col. 1283B] (Eph. 2).

### Chapter XIII — Reproach

That the statement of John of Constantinople, which they adduce as testimony for the adoration of images, is evidently not concerned with what they think.

**Response.** Many statements of Saint John of Constantinople are cited in the frequently mentioned synod, but they remained silent about the one among them that does not concern what they supposed. For in the councils of our holy predecessors, the pontiffs, the following statement of Saint John Chrysostom is reported, among other things: “Everything serves you, human being, and even more so the image; for when imperial faces and images enter a city, the judges and senate meet them with praise and fear—not honoring the panel or the writing formed in wax, but the emperor’s face. So also, let us venerate the heavenly face, honoring not the appearance of earthly things among human beings of the world, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

[Col. 1283C] ### Chapter XIV — Reproach

That the judges who were present at the aforementioned synod attempted insolently and inappropriately to exalt the painter’s art, saying: “For the painter’s art is pious, and some foolishly disparage it unjustly. The Father himself commends the painter who acts piously.”

**Response.** The blessed Asterius is held holy throughout the East. When he had delivered a discourse on the deeds of Saint Euphemia, he praised her martyrdom just as he had seen it more clearly depicted in due order. Therefore they likewise praised the painting against the heretics, saying that they foolishly disparaged it.

From Saint Gregory the Theologian’s sermon on blessed Gregory of Nyssa (Oration to Saint Gregory of Nyssa, at the beginning), among other things: “Do you think these things are sufficient, or that a discourse will briefly describe the man for us? If necessary, just as diligent painters repeatedly combine colors, so that I may add to your discourse a perfected form and describe for you what is most pure and manifest, etc.” [Col. 1283D]

Likewise, from Saint John Chrysostom’s sermon on the Lord’s Supper, among other things: “For just as painters customarily shade a panel with certain outlines before painting it, and then complete it through the variety of colors, so also Christ did this. On the table he depicts the Passover in figures and shows the Passover of truth, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s book on the Proverb of Solomon, among other things: “‘Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians’ (2 Cor. 6). He opened his mouth attentively and set forth the order of his tongue, praising the creature as creature, the Creator as Creator, angels as angels, heavenly things as heavenly things, earthly things as earthly things, etc.”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### Chapter XV — Reproach

The statement of the priest John and legate of the Easterners is useless and full of falsehood [Col. 1284A]: “Painters do not contradict the Scriptures; rather, whatever Scripture says, they show, so that they may agree with the Scriptures.”

**Response.** Above, we have already set forth many times how Saint Gregory, the eminent teacher and pope, taught in his sacred letter addressed to Serenus, bishop of Massilia, among other things (Book IX, Letter 9): “And then it must be added that paintings of images were made for the instruction of the unlearned people, so that those who did not know letters might learn what had been said by directing their attention to the history itself, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint John Chrysostom’s interpretation of Psalm 50, whose beginning is: “Painters imitate nature by their art, and, mixing colors with colors, they paint visible images of bodies.” And shortly afterward: “They depict an emperor sitting and a barbarian subject, a sharp sword, flowing rivers, fields adorned with various colors, and all things that are seen, imitating them through art; they present to those who see them a marvelous history, etc.” [Col. 1284B]

## IN THE FIFTH SESSION  
### And it was found in the fourth

### Chapter XVI — Reproach

The statement of the priest John is utterly false and worthy of every ridicule; he is recognized as having raved no less than the others concerning the adoration of images. For he says: “Whoever adores an image and says, ‘This is Christ, the Son of God,’ does not sin.”

**Response.** From Saint Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 86, after the beginning, among other things: “For nearly all bodies suffer limitation; they cannot be everywhere or always. But the divinity, which is present everywhere, can be compared from every side by means of a likeness, and the whole can be in likenesses, because none of those likenesses is in its proper substance. Is Christ a door in the way that we see doors made by a craftsman? Certainly not, and yet he said: ‘I am the door’ (John 10). Or is he a shepherd in the way that we see those shepherds who are set over flocks, etc.”

## ACCORDING TO THE MEANING

### Chapter XVII — Reproach

That the books called the *Lives of the Fathers*, whose authors are unknown, are not entirely suitable for providing testimonies or confirming the matters that have come into dispute.

**Response.** Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s book on Questions in the Gospel according to Luke (Gospel Questions, Book II, Question 42), among other things: “His vessels in the house are the bodily senses, by which many who use them to investigate the truth that is grasped by the intellect have gone completely astray, etc.”

For the *Lives of the Fathers* are not read in the Church without credible authors. Those bearing orthodox titles are both accepted and read. Indeed, the sacred canons have judged the passions of the holy martyrs especially suitable to be read in church when their yearly feast days are celebrated. [Col. 1284D]

### Chapter XVIII — Reproach

That those who erect images so as not to forget the saints, or indeed the Lord himself, do not possess a good memory.

**Response.** From Saint Jerome’s commentary on the evangelist Matthew, among other things: “Such people, while wishing to criticize another’s lack of knowledge, display their own. For although a thin fluid and liquid food, once it has been cooked and digested in the veins and limbs, descends through the hidden passages of the body—which the Greeks call *poroi* (πόροι)—to the lower parts and goes into the privy, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s interpretation of Psalm 98, before the middle, among other things: “The city that is Jerusalem was called Zion; it received its name through a certain interpretation, because Zion means ‘watchtower,’ that is, vision and contemplation. For to watch means to look out, to behold, or to direct one’s attention so that one may see. Every soul is Zion if it directs its attention toward seeing the light that ought to be seen. For if it turns its attention toward itself, it is darkened; if it directs it toward that light, it is illumined. Since it is clear, however, that Zion is the city of God, what is the city of God except the holy Church? etc.” [Col. 1285A]

## QUESTION

### Chapter XIX

“Let them inform us, as knowing men, where in the Old or New Testament, or in the six synodal councils, it is commanded that images be made or that images already made be adored.”

## RESPONSE

We shall indeed make it known below, as we have already done, that in both the Old and New Testaments, and in the six synodal councils, sacred images have always been made for veneration, and those that were made were given titles among the holy of holies. Rather, they ought to have told us in which of those six synodal councils sacred images were condemned. Indeed, it has often been shown that in the First Holy Council Pope Saint Sylvester and Constantine, the most Christian emperor, venerated sacred images and openly, faithfully, and wonderfully displayed them before everyone in the name of Christianity. From that time until now, the holy churches of the holy pontiffs—namely, Sylvester, Mark, and Julius—of remarkable size have been painted among us, both in mosaic and in other histories adorned with sacred images.

Likewise, in the Second Holy Council, the most elegant Pope Saint Damasus built his own church, which Pope Saint Gregory mentions in the *Dialogues* and which is called by the name of its founder, Damasus. From that time until now, we have likewise possessed it painted with sacred histories and images.

Again, concerning the Third Holy Council, Pope Saint Celestine adorned his own cemetery with paintings. But more notably, his successor, blessed Pope Sixtus, built the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, known as the Greater, which is also called “at the Manger.” In the same way, he adorned it with sacred images, both in golden metalwork and in various histories.

At his request, Augustus Valentinian made a golden image with twelve gates and the Savior, adorned with precious gems, and placed it as a votive offering of thanksgiving above the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle. From that time until now it has been venerated among us by all the faithful.

Likewise, concerning the Fourth Holy Council, the distinguished and wondrous preacher, Pope Saint Leo, also built churches and adorned them by painting them in mosaic and with various histories and images. Most notably, in the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle he constructed the great arch there and painted in mosaic our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and the twenty-four elders; he adorned them with verses bearing his name. From that time until now they have been faithfully venerated by us.

Concerning the Fifth Holy Council, the most holy Pope Vigilius built a basilica in the Lateran patriarchate and adorned it most beautifully with paintings, both histories and sacred images. Still more, his most holy successors, the lords Pelagius and John, built from the foundations a church of the apostles of remarkable size, painting various histories in mosaic and in diverse colors together with sacred images; from that time until now they have been venerated by us.

Saint Gregory the pope also made a beautiful oratory in his monastery and had it painted with various histories; he also erected sacred images there. When he entered it together with blessed Eleutherius because of his stomach ailment, they were heard together in prayer (Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 33). That holy man Eleutherius, whom they say also raised a dead person, did not hesitate to prostrate himself before those sacred images and, together with Saint Gregory, to implore divine mercy. Because they brought perfect faith, they were heard together, and those images have been venerated among us down to the present.

The church of the Arians, which Saint Gregory himself mentions in his *Dialogues* (Book III, chapter 30), also pleased Saint Gregory, so that it should be dedicated in the Catholic faith after the relics of the blessed martyrs Sebastian and Agatha had been brought there; and this was done. After the miracle that occurred in that same church, blessed Gregory himself had it painted with various histories, both in mosaic and in colors, and erected venerable images there; from that time until now they have been venerated.

If we should wish to recount in order how many churches our predecessors, the pontiffs, have built up to the present, erecting sacred images wonderfully in them, painting various histories, and also venerating them, we may confidently say in apostolic fashion that time would fail us to enumerate them and to explain their buildings with sacred images and histories.

In the Sixth Holy Council, they not only did not dare to despise them, but, venerating those same sacred images, they decreed (Canon 82) that Christ our God, the Lamb, should henceforth be represented according to his human form in images, in place of the former lamb.

Therefore Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, taught concerning this matter in the third book *On the Faith* (chapter 7), among other things: “Let us therefore preserve the precepts of our elders, and let us not dare to violate, with crude recklessness, the ancestral seals. No elders, authorities, angels, or archangels dared to open the sealed prophetic book (Rev. 5); the prerogative of explaining it was reserved to Christ alone. Who among us would dare to unseal the priestly book, sealed by confessors and already consecrated by the martyrdom of many? Those who were compelled to unseal it nevertheless afterward sealed it again, condemning the fraud. Those who did not dare to allow it to be violated became confessors and martyrs. How can we deny the faith of those whose victory we proclaim? Let no one fear, let no one be afraid, etc.”

If the heretics had not attacked the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, it would not have been necessary for the six holy synodal councils to be held. Likewise, if the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church had not been attacked on account of sacred images by the heretical emperors Leo and Constantine, my most holy predecessors would never have held councils, nor would we afterward have agreed that they should be held, except for the sake of the many thousands of souls who, remaining in heresy and daily falling into it, were endangered in the devil’s snare.

As it was defined in the Fourth Holy Council, those speaking for the true faith said: “We ought to defend with all appropriate devotion what has been handed down to us by our ancestors, and preserve inviolate in our own times the dignity of the proper veneration belonging to blessed Peter the Apostle, so that the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, to whom antiquity granted the primacy of the priesthood over all, may have the place and authority to judge concerning the faith and concerning priests.”

Therefore our predecessor, the most holy Pope Gregory the Younger, writing to the heretical emperors Leo and Constantine, said: “For the sacred images, if it should happen, we offer everything—even our own bodies. For we never accept novelty, nor do we in any way depart from our ancestral religion. For the divine voice threatens us with what must be guarded against in every way: ‘If someone gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul, he has gained nothing’” (Matt. 16). [Col. 1286D]

Likewise, in another letter of his, reasonably rebuking them on behalf of those sacred images, he said, among other things (as Pope Gelasius says in Letter 10 to the emperor Anastasius): “For it is reported that a certain most learned and venerable Father said that there are two things by which this world is principally governed: namely, the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these, the burden of the priests is so much heavier because they will also render an account before the divine tribunal for the kings themselves. Therefore no one will be able to make us cross the boundaries of our fathers or impose novelties of speech upon us; rather, remaining in the orthodox faith that we have received and embracing the ancient tradition, we undoubtedly venerate and uphold the councils of our most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, concerning sacred images, accepting from that point onward no contrary argument whatsoever and rendering no account for it. [Col. 1287A]

“For Saint Gregory, the honey-voiced teacher, while treating in his homily on the prophet Ezekiel the understanding of sacred discourse as it grows through the progress of time (Homily 16, after the middle), added: ‘Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied’ (Dan. 12).

“The holy Fathers whom we know through sacred Scripture were saved before the Law through knowledge of the one God, possessing perfect obedience to a simple way of life and, often seeing angels, already touching something of contemplation. When the Law was given, the holy Fathers were also instructed in the Ten Commandments, so that through knowledge of the one God they might also exercise themselves in the works of the Law. When grace came through the New Testament, every faithful people recognized that the one God is a Trinity and completed the power of the Decalogue in acknowledgment of him. [Col. 1287B]

“Therefore we must understand that the knowledge of spiritual Fathers also grew through the progress of time. Moses was instructed more than Abraham, the prophets more than Moses, and the apostles more than the prophets in the knowledge of almighty God. I am mistaken if I do not affirm these very things by testimonies of Scripture. ‘Many shall pass through,’ he says, ‘and knowledge shall be multiplied’ (ibid.).

“But let us show, if we can, these same things that we have said concerning Abraham, Moses, the prophets, and the apostles from the words of that same Scripture. Who does not know that Abraham spoke with God? Yet the Lord says to Moses: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and I did not reveal my name Adonai to them’ (Exod. 3 and 6). Behold, more had been made known to Moses than to Abraham, since to Moses he reveals concerning himself what he said he had not revealed to Abraham.

“But let us see whether the prophets were able to grasp more divine knowledge than Moses. Behold, the Psalmist says: ‘How I have loved your law, O Lord; all day long it is my meditation’ (Ps. 118); and he adds: ‘I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation’ (ibid.). And again: ‘I have understood more than the elders’ (ibid.). Thus, by recalling that he meditates on the law and testifying that he has understood more than all who teach him and more than the elders, he makes clear that he had received more divine knowledge than Moses.

“How shall we show that the holy apostles were taught more than the prophets? Certainly the Truth says: ‘Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see, and did not see it’ (Luke 10). They therefore knew more of divine knowledge than the prophets, because what the prophets had heard only in spirit, the apostles also saw bodily. Thus was fulfilled the statement of Daniel that we mentioned: ‘Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied’ (Dan. 12). For the nearer the world is led toward its end, the more generously the entrance to eternal knowledge is opened to us, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint Gregory’s work on Job (Book IV, chapter 10), among other things: “For the holy teachers who instruct others in virtue devour enemies when they transform them within their own body by the power of conversion. They subject them to the stones of the sling, because when they train strong men in the holy Church, through them they break the hard breasts of arrogant adversaries. For what is signified by the sling except the holy Church? When the sling is whirled around, stones emerge from it with which the breasts of adversaries are struck. So, when the holy Church is driven through the revolving course of time amid the circuit of tribulations, strong men emerge from it, by whose blows, as though by stones, the hearts of the wicked may be battered.” [Col. 1287D]

## IN THE SEVENTH SESSION

### Chapter XX — Reproach

How greatly, in reason, the mystery of the Lord’s cross differs from images, which they nevertheless strive to make equal to it.

**Response.** From Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in his book *On the Incarnation* (chapter 7), among other things: [Col. 1288A] “When we adore both his divinity and his flesh, do we divide Christ? When in him we venerate the image of God and the cross, do we divide him? The Apostle, certainly, who said of him: ‘Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God’ (2 Cor. 13), himself said: ‘For Christ is not divided, etc.’” (1 Cor. 1).

Likewise, from the same Saint Ambrose’s Book I *On the Faith* (chapter 4), among other things: “The Apostle says ‘image,’ and Arius says that it is unlike him? Why is it an image if it does not possess likeness? In paintings people do not want things to be unlike one another, yet Arius insists that the Father is unlike the Son.” And shortly afterward: “The prophets say: ‘For he is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness, etc.’” (Wis. 7).

Likewise, from the letter of Pope Saint Gregory sent to Leontius, former consul (Book VII, Letter 34), among other things: “For we have received the oil of the holy cross and the wood of aloe: one, so that by touch it might bless; the other, so that by burning it might give off a good fragrance. It was therefore fitting that a good man should send those things that could appease the Lord’s anger toward us.” [Col. 1288B]

And shortly afterward: “Moreover, we have sent you the blessing of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and the key of his most holy tomb, in which a blessing from his chains has been inserted, so that what bound his neck for martyrdom might free yours from all sins.”

## AT THE END OF THE BOOK

### Chapter XXI — Reproach

Concerning the fact that Constantine and Irene say in their writings: “Through him, the God who reigns together with us.”

**Response.** From the Proverbs of Solomon, among other things: “Counsel and equity are mine; prudence is mine; strength is mine. Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just. Through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice. I love those who love me” (Prov. 8). And after much else: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency, etc.”

## IN THE FOURTH SESSION

[Col. 1288C] ### Chapter XXII — Reproach

Concerning the fact that they do not correctly understand what was said: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,” as though he had spoken of adoration in an absolute sense and said that service belongs to him alone.

Response. From the fifth book of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, *On the Faith*, among other passages:

> “When we read, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Matt. XVI), do they think that Christ is not to be worshiped and that Christ is not to be served? If the Canaanite woman, who worshiped him, deserved to obtain what she asked, and if the apostle Paul, who professes in the opening of his writings that he is Christ’s servant (Rom. I; Gal. I), deserved to be an apostle—not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ—let them say what they think ought to be followed: whether, with Arius, they prefer to share in perfidy, so that by denying Christ to be the sole and true God they may show that they judge him neither to be worshiped nor to be served; or whether they prefer to share in fellowship with Paul, who, by serving and also worshiping Christ, certainly did not deny in word and affection that he is the sole true God, whom he confessed through devout service. But if someone should say, ‘The Son also worships God the Father, because it is written, “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know”’ (John IV), let him consider when, in whose presence, and with what disposition he speaks, etc.”

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### CHAPTER XXIII.—Reproach

That, since God is not localized, they spoke rather unlearnedly when they said: “We venerate and worship [it] as the place of God.”

**Response.** From the blessed Augustine’s explanation of Psalm 86, after the beginning, among other passages:

> “The Apostle says, ‘No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus’ (1 Cor. III). How then are the prophets and apostles foundations? And how is Christ Jesus the foundation, beyond which there is nothing further? How are we to understand it, unless, just as he is plainly called ‘Holy of holies’ (Dan. IX), so figuratively he is the foundation of foundations? If you consider the sacraments, Christ is the Holy of holies; if you consider the flock placed under authority, Christ is the shepherd of shepherds; if you consider a building, Christ is the foundation of foundations.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But the divinity, which is present everywhere, can be approached by likeness from every direction, and everything can exist in likenesses, because none of these things exists in its proper reality, etc.”

Likewise, from the same holy Augustine’s second book *On the Trinity*, chapter 17, among other passages:

> “For what does the Lord’s saying mean: ‘Behold, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock’ (Exod. XXXIII)? What earthly place is beside the Lord, unless that is beside him which touches him spiritually? For what place is not beside the Lord, who ‘reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly’? etc.” (Wis. VIII.)

Likewise, from Saint John Chrysostom’s sermon on the holy apostle Paul, where he says, “I do not do the good I want” (Rom. VII), and because Jacob became a figure of Christ, among other passages:

> “He came into the midst of the rivers, and when he saw the dream he said: ‘There is nothing else but the house of God’ (Gen. XXVIII). For you did not see a building, but a ladder. But because he knew that the ladder was a figure of the Church, he said: ‘This is the house of God; this is the Church.’ And that this house of God is the Church, Paul says when writing to Timothy: ‘I hope to come to you soon. But if I am delayed, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God,’ etc.” (1 Tim. III.)

## IN THE SAME SESSION

### CHAPTER XXV.—Reproach

That the fact that Solomon is said to have made oxen and lions in the Temple can in any way establish the worship of images, as those who pant after their worship claim; or likewise what is written in Ezekiel: “Faces and cherubim as far as the chamber” (Ezek. XLI).

**Response.** We have already written out these chapters many times, explaining how our most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, established them in their sacred councils when citing them in defense of the veneration of images. It is plainly evident that their apostolic judgment must be observed and venerated among us.

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s book on Psalm 84, among other passages:

> “In the Old Testament the New Testament was prefigured; this expression of truth had prefigured certain things. In that figure, according to a certain foretelling of things to come, the land was given to that people—the land which was called the land of promise, etc.”

Likewise, from Saint Augustine’s book *Questions on the Gospel according to Luke*, book II, question 41, among other passages:

> “What does the Lord mean when he says: ‘Whoever is on the housetop, with his vessels in the house, must not come down to take them’ (Luke XVII)? He is on the housetop who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually as if in the free air.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, the vessels of this spiritual man are now left in the house, because, rising above the body in mind and placed, as it were, on the housetop through the gaze of understanding, he enjoys the clarity of wisdom as though beneath the most open heaven, etc.”

### CHAPTER XXVI.—Reproach

The final chapter is this, so that our lord the apostolic father, and the entire Roman Church together, may know that, in accordance with what is contained in the letter of the most blessed Gregory (Book VII, Letter 9), which he sent to Serenus, bishop of Massilia:

> “We permit images of the saints to be made by anyone who wishes to make them, both in the church and outside the church, for the love of God and his saints. But we by no means compel those who do not wish to worship them to do so. To break or destroy them, even if someone wishes to do so, we do not permit.”

And because in this letter we freely and without hesitation profess that the universal Catholic Church, pleasing to God, follows the mind of the most holy Gregory.

**Response.** This sacred and venerable chapter differs greatly from all the chapters cited above. For this reason we recognized it as belonging particularly to your God-protected and orthodox royal excellence, inasmuch as it fully and completely professed the sound faith by following the most holy Gregory’s teaching.

For your exceedingly upright and exalted royal wisdom remembers how, in that very letter of Pope Saint Gregory addressed to Serenus, bishop of Massilia (at the place cited), it is said to contain the following, among other passages, when he rebukes that bishop:

> “For it is one thing to worship a picture, and another to learn from the history of the picture what is to be worshiped. For what writing provides to readers, a picture provides to uneducated people who look at it: because in it even those who do not know letters see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Hence, especially for the peoples among whom you live, a picture serves in place of reading; this you ought to have considered very carefully.”

And shortly afterward:

> “And because antiquity has admitted, not without reason, that the histories of the saints should be depicted in venerable places.”

And after an interval:

> “Because pictures of images had been made for the edification of the uneducated people, so that those who did not know letters, by attending to the history itself, might learn what had taken place.”

Again, shortly afterward:

> “But let your Fraternity diligently admonish them that, from seeing the event represented, they may receive the ardor of compunction and humbly prostrate themselves in worship of the almighty holy Trinity alone.”

Similarly, regarding another letter of his, addressed to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 2), in defense of the veneration of sacred images, we wrote briefly above. We likewise made known what is found in the letter addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God enclosed in Gaul (Book V), where it is said:

> “For we have sent the images which you asked us to send to you through your deacon Dulcitius. Your request pleased us greatly, because with your whole intention you seek him whose image you desire to have before your eyes: so that daily bodily sight may always keep you exercised, and while you look upon the picture, you may burn in spirit for him whose image you desire to see.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to honor it as though it were God, but so that, in remembrance of the Son of God, you may grow warm in love for him whose image you desire to see. And indeed, we do not prostrate ourselves before the images themselves as though before the Divinity, but we worship him whom, through the image, we remember either as born, or as having suffered, or as sitting upon the throne. And while the picture itself, as though it were writing, recalls us to the memory of the Son of God, it either makes our spirit rejoice over the resurrection or soothes it concerning the Passion. Therefore we have sent you, through our aforesaid son the deacon, two curtains containing [In the Roman edition, *continentes* is absent] images of our Savior, of holy Mary the Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with a cross and a key as a blessing, so that you may remain defended from the Evil One by that very sign by which you believe yourself protected, etc.”

And since in these matters your God-inspired, royal, and orthodox understanding is evident, it is also necessary to recall and teach how Pope Saint Gregory instructed Bishop Serenus concerning sacred images: that, by seeing the event represented, people should receive the ardor of compunction; that is, while looking upon those same sacred images, they should humbly prostrate themselves in worship of the almighty holy Trinity alone.

In the same manner he says to Secundinus, the servant of God enclosed in Gaul (Book VII, Letter 53):

> “For this is why you ask: not to honor it as though it were God, but so that, in remembrance of the Son of God, you may grow warm in love for him whose image you desire to see. And indeed, we do not prostrate ourselves before the images themselves as though before the Divinity, but we worship him whom, through the image, we remember either as born, or as having suffered, or as sitting upon the throne.”

Just as he indicates to Bishop Serenus that one who looks upon the sacred images should humbly prostrate himself in worship of the almighty holy Trinity alone, so also he taught Secundinus, the servant of God enclosed in Gaul, not to honor them as though they were God, but, while prostrating himself before those same sacred images, not to prostrate himself before them as though before the Divinity, but, through that prostration, to worship him whom we remember through the image either as born, or as having suffered, or as sitting upon the throne.

Accordingly, following and embracing this same irreproachable and orthodox understanding of Pope Saint Gregory, long ago we issued a proclamation to the emperors Irene and Constantine in support of the preaching and restoration of sacred images, saying:

> “Because throughout the whole world, wherever Christianity exists, those sacred images remain and are honored by all the faithful, so that through the visible face our mind may be carried by spiritual affection toward the invisible majesty of the Divinity, in contemplation of the image represented according to the flesh, which the Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation. We worship our same Redeemer, who is in heaven, and, glorifying him in spirit, praise him together, since, as it is written, ‘God is spirit’ (Rom. IV); and for this reason we worship his divinity spiritually. Far be it from us to deify the images themselves, as certain people chatter; rather, we express in every way the affection and love that we have for God and his saints. Thus, just as we possess the books of divine Scripture, we also possess the images for the sake of remembrance and veneration, while preserving the purity of our faith,” and so forth.

Whatever brief testimonies from the works of the holy Fathers we wrote there, we issued and preached in the same understanding and tenor as we have just stated, holding the same understanding of the faith as our predecessor, Pope Saint Gregory.

But, as our envoys—namely, Peter, archpresbyter of our holy Roman Church, and Peter, a devout priest and venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabbas—told us orally, immediately after embracing our apostolic words, they ordered a council to be held. But, after a revolt was stirred up by heretics on the island of Sicily, our envoys returned without an answer. Then, after them, they sent again to Constantinople and had them ascend once more. Thus they held this synod according to our arrangement and restored the sacred and venerable images to their former status.

And just as Saint Gregory’s teaching and our own concerning images were contained therein—[Note: [Col. 1291] Here, and throughout this entire letter, many passages appear to be corrupt, which are lacking in manuscript codices]—so they too, in that same synod, confessed the definition and rendered to them a kiss and an honorable salutation, but by no means, according to our faith, the true worship that befits the divine nature alone.

Moreover, they anathematized that pseudo-syllogism which had been produced by the heretics under Constantine the heretical emperor, and condemned it together with its followers and accomplices. Having returned to the orthodox faith of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, they made a confession of the true faith in their written statements.

For this reason we accepted that synod. For if we had not received it, and they had returned to their former vomit of error, who would have had to give an account before the terrible and fearful tribunal of the divine Judge for the destruction of so many thousands of Christian souls, except us alone? For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke XV), how much more should everyone rejoice over so many thousands of Christians who have returned from error, and sing with the Psalmist: “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed,” and the rest (Ps. XXXIII).

As for us, we have not yet given any reply to that emperor concerning the same synod, fearing that they might return to their error. For formerly, when we exhorted them to restore the sacred images, we likewise reminded them concerning the dioceses both of the archbishops and of the bishops of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, and asked them to restore to that holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church what they had then taken away together with our patrimonies, when they removed the sacred images. They gave no answer whatever concerning this. Thus it is shown that, although they returned from error in one matter, in two others they remain in the same error.

For if the canonical churches of Christians everywhere possess their dioceses intact [For *canonici*, H.], how much more ought the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church—which is the head of all the churches of God—in every way to hold and possess by unquestionable right its diocese, namely those of the archbishops and bishops, and indeed also its patrimonies, for the maintenance of the lamps and the nourishment of the poor?

Therefore, if your God-protected royal excellence gives its consent, we urge the matter with the same zeal concerning the restoration of the sacred images to their former status, giving thanks. But concerning the dioceses of our holy Roman Church, both those of the archbishops and those of the bishops, and concerning the patrimonies, we again rebuke and admonish him: if he does not wish to restore them to our holy Roman Church, we shall declare him a heretic on account of his persistence in this error.

For we desire the salvation of souls and the stability of the true faith far more than the possession of such worldly property. We are confident, moreover, that your exceedingly upright, God-protected excellence, strengthened by the stability of orthodox faith, has a most firm root which is never shaken or moved by wicked and unbelieving men. Rather, in that spiritual doctrine which began to hold and embrace the tradition of the true faith of its holy spiritual mother, the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, we believe that it will remain without reproach, unfaltering, forever and ever.

Therefore we trust in the power of our God: because, insofar as you bear faith and love toward the Church of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, may you always strive with royal zeal for its advancement and exaltation, contending on every side; and may he graciously deign to defend and surround you with his arm in royal triumphs against adversaries and wicked men, so that, together with our spiritual daughter, your lady the queen, and your most exalted and noble offspring, you may reign in this world for a long age and may deserve to possess in the citadel of heaven, without end, life together with the kingdom.

May heavenly grace preserve your excellence in safety.

[Col. 1293]

[Note: [Col. 1293C] This assembly, or, as Baronius calls it, this conference, was held on the Kalends of November in the year 825, as Baronius correctly judged, and not in the year 824, as it is read here. For the bishops of Gaul, assembled at that conference, say in their letter to Louis Augustus: “We had read back to us the letter which the envoys of the Greeks brought to you in the previous year.” It is certain, however, that the letters of the Eastern emperors Michael and Theophilus were delivered to Louis Augustus in the year 824 (Pagi, under the year of Christ 825, no. 1).]

[Note: [Col. 1293C] I judged that the acts of the pseudo-synod, which were published in the year of the Lord 1596 by an uncertain and unnamed author, without any mention of the place where they had been found or from which they had been received, as spurious and illegitimate—or at least as suspect in respect of their authenticity—should by no means be inserted into this edition. The most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Robert Bellarmine published a refutation of them in six chapters, in an appendix to his treatise *On the Worship of Images*. Since that work is elaborated with the greatest care in every respect, I judged that it ought to be presented here to the reader in its entirety. SEV. BIN.]

# THE PARISIAN ASSEMBLY ON IMAGES

Held at Paris, in the palace, on the Kalends of November in the year of Christ 824, in the first year of Pope Eugene II and the eleventh of Louis the Pious Augustus.

## PROLEGOMENA

(From Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*)

# REFUTATION OF THE PAMPHLET FALSELY ENTITLED “THE PARISIAN SYNOD,” PUBLISHED BY THE REVEREND CARDINAL BELLARMINE

[Col. 1293A]

In the year 1596 a pamphlet appeared at Frankfurt with this title: “The Parisian Synod concerning Images, transcribed from a most ancient manuscript and now published for the first time.” But in the present year, when a friend showed me this pamphlet, I immediately noticed that it was neither truly a synod nor a writing worthy of publication. Therefore, lest the title should perhaps deceive the unwary, I thought I would do something worthwhile by refuting the pamphlet as briefly as possible.

## CHAPTER I

In the first place, the fact that no Parisian synod at all is contained in this pamphlet may be demonstrated by the absence of any decrees, any canons, any subscription of bishops, or any mention of a synod. The pamphlet itself also openly exposes the emptiness of its title. For we read on page 126:

> “We did not assemble a synod, but, just as we requested permission from you and received authorization to act, we endeavored, together with our associates, your sons, to consider, insofar as we were able at intervals despite being hindered by the many different occupations of the kingdom, what we could communicate to your benevolence concerning so great a necessity.”

And, so that the meaning of these words may be understood, we shall set out the argument of the entire pamphlet.

Michael Balbus, the Greek emperor, wrote a fairly long Latin letter to the emperor Louis the Pious. In it, among many other things, he stated that the Church had been divided into two parties because of the images of Christ and the saints, since some argued that they should be worshiped and others that they should not be worshiped. At the same time, he asked Louis to work in the West so that, once the superstitious worship of images had been removed, the Church might recover peace and unity.

After receiving this letter, Louis obtained permission from the supreme pontiff [Col. 1293C] to summon several learned men who would carefully collect the testimonies of the ancient Fathers concerning the worship of images. Having done this, he ordered a letter to be written which he intended to send to the emperor Michael in the name of the supreme pontiff, with the pontiff’s own consent, since the letter was first to be shown to him. Finally, he sent both the aforesaid letter and another letter written in his own name to the pontiff himself, who was called Eugene, through two bishops.

Thus, five things are contained in the recently published pamphlet:

First, the letter of Michael Balbus to Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne.

Second, testimonies collected from the ancient Fathers, by which it is demonstrated that images should neither be broken, as the iconoclasts wished, nor worshiped, as the Second Council of Nicaea had decreed.

Third, a letter written in the name of the supreme pontiff by Frankish scholars to the emperor Michael, in which it is taught that images should neither be dishonored nor worshiped.

Fourth, a letter from the emperor Louis to Eugene, the second pontiff of that name, in which he urges him to send a legation to Greece and reconcile the Church.

Fifth, a letter from the same Louis to the bishops Jeremiah and Jonah, whom he sends to Rome to the supreme pontiff, instructing them how they ought to conduct themselves prudently with the pontiff so as to draw him over to their own opinion.

From these facts it will readily be understood that those who adorned this pamphlet with the impressive name of “the Parisian synod” intended to deceive. They attempted to aid the cause of the iconoclasts and to inflict some injury upon the Catholic faith [Col. 1294B]; but, with God’s help, we shall soon make them regret that they have wasted their oil and labor.

## CHAPTER II

To come, then, to the letter of Michael, which occupies the first part of the pamphlet: it certainly appears full of religious zeal, so that if someone did not know from another source who this Michael was, he might suppose that he had been one of the best and most Christian princes.

But there exist the public annals of John Zonaras, George Cedrenus, and others who committed the deeds of the Greek emperors to writing. From these sources it can be learned that Michael was Balbus not merely in name but also in reality: he was an impious and utterly wicked man, since he was more devoted to Hebrew superstition than to the Christian religion; he denied the resurrection of the flesh and for that reason ridiculed the prophets and apostles who had preached it; he said that fornication was lawful and so despised sacred celibacy that he chose as his wife a nun already consecrated to God; he rejected the seventh ecumenical council, which had also been approved by the supreme pontiff Adrian; he considered sacred images unworthy of any honor; he strongly favored the iconoclasts and proposed Constantine Copronymus, the leader of the iconoclasts, as the model he should imitate above all others; and he punished Saint Euthymius, Saint Methodius, and other pious defenders of the truth with exile, imprisonment, or death.

[Col. 1295A] This, then, is that Michael who, clothed in sheep’s wool while in reality being a ravenous wolf, pretends, as though inflamed by zeal for the faith, to desire nothing other than the reform and peace of the Church.

But just as in that very letter he deplores the death of the emperor Leo, whom he himself immediately succeeded, saying that Leo had been miserably killed by certain wicked men who had formed a conspiracy, although it is sufficiently clear from the authors cited above that this same Michael was the leader of the conspiracy, so also he appears piously to lament that the Church is divided because of disputes about the worship of images, although he himself was chiefly responsible for the dispute and division. He had rejected the general council that had removed those disputes and had worked to spread iconoclasm; and, not content with Eastern dissensions, he also endeavored to sow and spread dissension in the West.

As for what he censures the Catholics for at the end of his letter—namely, that they despise the life-giving cross, worship images as if they were gods, offer sacrifices to them, wish to be received from the sacred font by them through some unknown artifice, and receive sacred communion from them, and finally display other superstitions or absurdities of this kind in the worship of sacred images—these are mere slanders and fabrications. Nor will anyone be surprised that a Greek emperor could write such lies in his letter to Latins living far away, if he considers how gross and incredible are the lies that the heretics of our own time invent about Catholics living nearby.

But from the genuinely legitimate and ecumenical Second Council of Nicaea, held at that very time, it can be made clearer than daylight—whether Michael Balbus wishes it or not—that these are the inventions and frauds of heretics. For that council, to which all Catholics assented, taught that sacred images are indeed owed their own veneration, but no greater veneration than the life-giving cross; that no sacrifice should in any way be offered to them; and that they should not be worshiped with the worship of *latria*, which belongs properly to God. Let the synod be read, and the fabrication will immediately vanish.

Since this is so, either the Franks who served as counselors to the emperor Louis believed Michael’s letters or they did not. If they believed them, they were deceived and misled; if they did not believe them, they abused those letters in order to influence the supreme pontiff to rescind the acts of his predecessors and himself disapprove and condemn the Council of Nicaea, which Adrian had approved.

But whether they were deceived or wished to deceive, there was no reason to expose this error or crime of theirs to the world, especially since our ancestors did not without cause willingly allow pamphlets of this kind—which could bring no benefit but very great harm—to remain concealed.

## CHAPTER III

I now come to those testimonies which the few men summoned by the emperor Louis say they collected from the records of antiquity. Those men appear to have erred in many ways. First of all, even before making their collection, they rather boldly presumed to form a judgment for themselves concerning the apostolic writings; and they rashly passed judgment not only on the pontiff but also on the general council approved by the pontiff.

In this matter they far surpassed the error of that author who published a book under the name of Charlemagne against the worship of sacred images. He disapproved the Second Council of Nicaea—as the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt also did—because he thought that it had been celebrated without the consent of the Apostolic See.

But these counselors of the emperor Louis, whose writings we are examining, admit that the council in support of the worship of images—that is, the Second Council of Nicaea—was convened, approved, and confirmed by Adrian, the supreme pontiff. Nevertheless, they do not hesitate to examine, judge, and criticize both that council itself and Adrian’s letter to the emperor Constantine in defense of the worship of images, and again the defense of that same council which Adrian sent to Charles.

These are their words on page 19:

> “First, we had the letter of the lord Pope Adrian, which he sent to the emperor Constantine and his mother Helena, at their request, in the regions overseas, in support of the restoration of images, read aloud in our presence. As far as our small understanding could discern, just as he rightly rebuked those who in those regions had rashly presumed to break and completely abolish the images of the saints, so he is known to have acted indiscreetly in ordering them to be worshiped superstitiously; and for this very reason he ordered a synod to be assembled.”

And below, on page 21, speaking of Adrian’s defense of the Council of Nicaea, they say:

> “He attempted to respond point by point in their defense to what he wished, but not to what he taught, etc.”

Thus they were not ashamed to judge their own judge and the judge of the whole world, to feed the shepherd of all Christ’s sheep, and to teach the teacher of all—a presumption greater than which none can be imagined.

## CHAPTER IV

But perhaps they discovered some new and hidden testimonies, relying upon which they did not fear to resist the apostolic prelate to his face. On the contrary, they collected the best-known and most commonplace testimonies, which have nothing to do with the matter, without any reason or order.

To examine a few examples: they first take a testimony from Saint Augustine’s book *On Heresies*, where we read that Simon Magus ordered his own image and that of his little prostitute Helena to be worshiped by his disciples. They say that this was the first origin of the worship of images.

As though, if the issue concerns false worship, the Hebrews had not worshiped golden calves before Simon’s time, and the pagans images of dead men! But the Catholic Church does not learn the worship of sacred things from its enemies; and if from that testimony it were permissible to conclude that images of Christ and the saints should not be venerated, by the same reasoning it would be permissible to conclude that Christ himself is not worthy of any honor. For the reason that it was impious to worship the images of Simon and Helena was that Simon and Helena were utterly unworthy of being worshiped.

But the testimonies they extracted from Augustine’s Letter 56 to Dioscorus are plainly ridiculous—ridiculous, I say, if they are applied to the matter under discussion. For what Saint Augustine discusses are images that flow from bodies and enter the mind, so that through them we may see or think of something. These men produce those passages to prove that images of Christ and the saints, whether painted or sculpted, should in no way be worshiped. How well these things fit the present dispute is for the reader to judge.

What of the fact that they again cite many testimonies which Pope Adrian placed in that exceptionally learned letter of his in defense of images, even though they themselves fight against images?

[Col. 1296D] As for what they say, and try to prove by several testimonies, namely that custom, the passage of years, or any authority of antiquity should not be preferred to truth: this would correctly be said if it could be proved that the worship which the Catholic Church offers to images arose from manifest error rather than from certain truth.

But when a matter is disputed, they cannot themselves deny that custom has great force and that antiquity is to be venerated. Why, then, did they labor so greatly in unfolding the monuments of antiquity, if no probable argument can be drawn from antiquity? Do they not see that by this very action they fight against their own words and in reality destroy what they tried to establish by words? Certainly, if it were worthwhile to bring forward the testimonies of Saint Augustine, Saint Basil, and the other ancient Fathers by which they themselves prove ecclesiastical doctrines from antiquity or from the custom of the Church, there would be no end.

[Col. 1297A] But what surpasses all astonishment is this: they produce many testimonies in favor of the adoration of the cross, and when they wish to explain why the sign or wood of the cross should be worshiped while images of Christ should not be worshiped, they say that the reason is that Christ was suspended on the cross, not in an image, and that he redeemed us through the cross, not through an image.

If I wished to refute this, would I not appear to the readers to be excessively slow-witted? Certainly Christ was not suspended on the sign of the cross that we paint on a wall, a panel, or bronze; nor was he suspended on those wooden crosses that are commonly seen and worshiped in churches. He was suspended on that one cross of which these signs of ours—which we paint or erect—are images.

Therefore, if the opponents allow the image of the cross to be worshiped, why should it not be permissible to worship the image of the crucified one? And if we rightly worship an image of the cross because we were redeemed by Christ through the cross, what reason can be invented why the image of Christ, who properly redeemed us, may not rightly be honored?

“But,” they say, “it is not lawful to worship anything made by hand.” What, then? Is the wood or sign of the cross not made by hand? What are the Gospel codex and the sacred vessels, which in their opinion are worthy of veneration, other than works of human hands? And yet it is true that nothing made by hand is to be honored with that kind of worship by which God himself is honored—God who was not made at all but is the maker of all things.

Therefore, these collectors could have omitted most of the testimonies they brought forward, since they prove nothing other than that God alone is to be worshiped with the worship of *latria*, which belongs to him alone, and that images are not to be worshiped in such a way that sacrifices are offered to them. Neither do we deny this, nor did the holy Council of Nicaea deny it.

And, reader, so that you may see how powerful truth is, even those who attack it often defend it, whether unwillingly or unwittingly. This happened with our collectors. For among the other testimonies they collected, they included several to prove that images should not be broken or dishonored.

But in those same testimonies there is not only what they want—namely, that images should not be dishonored—but also what they do not want: that they should be treated with honor. Sometimes those collectors noticed this and boldly corrupted the text; sometimes they noticed it and, unwittingly, left the testimony against themselves in their own pamphlet.

An example of the former is found in action 6 of the seventh synod, where Saint Gregory is cited. In Letter 5 of Book VII, addressed to Januarius, he sharply rebukes certain people who, as an insult, carried an image of the blessed Virgin and the Lord’s cross to the synagogue of the Jews, and he commands Januarius, the bishop, to bring the image and the cross, after removing them from that place, back into the church with the veneration due to them.

Here the good collectors simply deleted or omitted the word “image,” lest they should appear to maintain, contrary to their doctrine, that not only the cross but also the image of the blessed Virgin ought to be venerated—unless perhaps the word “images” was omitted through a scribal error.

Now, shortly afterward, in action 6 of that same synod, they ascribe the following words from Pope Gregory’s synodical letter:

> “We make and worship images for no other reason than the Word of God incarnate for us,” etc.

Do you hear, collector, the word “worship”—and yet this testimony was produced by you yourself? But we have clearer evidence.

A little farther below, these words are placed from Saint Basil’s book to Amphilochius, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 17:

> “The honor given to the image passes to the original form,” etc.

There you have once again the honor of the image. But let us come to the clearest evidence.

Shortly afterward they bring forward these further words from a letter of the same great Basil to the emperor Julian:

> “I believe in one God, the almighty Father—God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit: one God. These three I worship and glorify. I also confess [Col. 1298A] the dispensation of the Son made flesh, and Mary the holy Mother of God, who bore him according to the flesh. I likewise accept the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs, and their intercession before God, which through them renders the most merciful God propitious to me. For this reason I honor and worship representations of their images; this has been handed down especially by the holy apostles and has not been prohibited. Rather, I wish their histories to be depicted in all our churches,” etc.

What are we to hear? Saint Basil the Great is summoned as a witness by the adversary—and truly he is a witness beyond all exception. Yet he openly affirms that he honors and worships images of the apostles, prophets, and martyrs. He affirms this while setting forth his confession of faith and speaking not about doubtful or probable matters, but about things most certain and well established.
