He adds that this was handed down by the apostles and received and observed by the whole Church. What, I ask, can be answered? The most authoritative writer speaks plainly, and his testimony is produced by the [Col. 1298B] adversaries themselves. Nor are there lacking other similar testimonies in the same little book—those of Athanasius, Germanus, Leontius, and others—which the adversaries imprudently bring forward against themselves and on our behalf, that is, in support of the veneration of sacred images. But I am concerned with brevity, and I do not willingly waste time refuting such absurdities.

## CHAPTER V

There follows the third part, namely, the letter of Pope Eugenius to the emperors Michael and his son Theophilus. The same collectors appear to have composed this letter; for Eugenius wrote no such letter, but—as we said above—it was written so that it might be sent in the pontiff’s name if he approved it. In this matter we are compelled to question the collectors’ prudence. With what boldness did they dare prescribe to the Roman pontiff what he ought himself to write? And with what confidence could they hope that the Roman pontiff would write to the Greek emperor things contrary to what his predecessors had written more than once?

[Col. 1298C] But let us examine, if you please, somewhat more carefully whether that letter is worthy of the supreme pontiff. I pass over the fact that in this little book the letter lacks its beginning—a fault that seems attributable not to its original author, but to the person who only now, after so many centuries, has brought this little book to light. I also say nothing of the fact that the letter is exceedingly obscure, barbarous, and unlearned because of its excessive verbosity; let this be attributed to the times. Finally, I remain silent about the fact that, while attempting to remove the contradiction that seemed to exist in Gregory’s words, it becomes all the more entangled the more it tries to disentangle itself. But there are three matters I cannot silently pass over.

First, this letter makes the supreme pontiff an exceptionally foolish flatterer of the emperor, when it says:

> “O prince revered by the world, with the whole holy Church of God which, by the Lord’s arranging and entrusting, you govern.”

And below:

> “For the uniting of the Church which, by the ordering of the Lord God, you rule.”

What flattery could be more shameful? Michael Balbus, after murdering the legitimate emperor, although he himself had already been condemned to death for his crimes, [Col. 1298D] tyrannically seized the empire; and the supreme pontiff will assert that, by God’s arranging, entrusting, and ordering, this same Balbus assumed the reins not only of the empire but also of the Church. And if the Church of God was entrusted by God himself to the emperor to govern, what do bishops do in the Church? What does the supreme pontiff himself do?

> “The emperor,” says Saint Ambrose, “is in the Church, not above the Church; a son of the Church, not its ruler; a sheep, not a shepherd.”

And Saint John Chrysostom said to his deacon:

> “If he who is crowned with the diadem should unworthily approach to receive the sacred mysteries, restrain and rebuke him; you have greater authority than he.”

Next, in the same letter this argument is repeated more than once:

> “If no painted or fashioned image had ever existed, nothing would be lost from the faith, hope, and charity by which one reaches the eternal kingdom.”

And yet it was on account of images that dissension and division arose in the Church, [Col. 1299A] peace was disturbed, and charity violated. Those who write that letter in the name of the supreme pontiff failed to notice that this argument entails—if, indeed, it entails anything, as we shall shortly see—that images ought to be removed altogether, which they themselves do not wish. Yet the argument has no force.

Even though nothing would be lost from faith, hope, and charity if no painted or fashioned image existed, nevertheless, once a painted or fashioned image does exist, the person who denies that it ought to be venerated sins against the faith, because the honor shown to the image passes to the prototype, which the faith teaches to be worthy of veneration—and the adversary does not deny this. The point can also be clarified by an analogy. If some book of divine Scripture, such as the Epistle to Philemon, did not exist, nothing would be lost from faith, hope, and charity. Yet because it does now exist, whoever denied that it ought to be regarded with veneration would sin against the faith; and if dissensions arose on that account, the Epistle should not be rejected, but the ignorance of those who dissented should be exposed and instructed.

[Col. 1299B] Finally, in that same letter Constantine and his mother Irene are reproved because, by their edict, they ordered that sacred images be held in honor according to the decree of the general council. Such a reproof could not have been written by the supreme pontiff unless he were completely insane. For what is this? Pope Adrian praises Constantine and Irene to the skies because they favor the religious veneration of sacred images, while Adrian’s successor Eugenius would reprove those same emperors for the same reason? And what greater folly could be imagined than for the supreme pontiff to say that he resented an emperor’s observing and defending the decrees of general councils approved by the Apostolic See?

But although the collectors were not very prudent, the bishop of the Apostolic See was not inconsistent. He remained [Col. 1299C] steadfast in what his predecessors had established only after the mature [Col. 1300A] deliberation of long consideration. For Eugenius did not send that letter; and shortly afterward Adrian II arranged for the eighth ecumenical synod to be held at Constantinople, at which the seventh synod was again approved concerning the veneration of images. Finally, Anastasius the Roman Librarian, in the preface to the Seventh Synod addressed to Pope John VIII, who succeeded Adrian II immediately, writes that all the Roman pontiffs held the same opinion:

> “What the present synod teaches concerning the veneration of the holy images, this too your Apostolic See, as certain writings indicate, held from ancient times; and the universal Church has always venerated them and continues to venerate them to this day, with the sole exception of certain Gauls, to whom, certainly, the truth of these matters has not yet been revealed.”

## CHAPTER VI

There remains the final part, namely, the letter of the emperor Louis to Pope Eugenius, and another letter of the same Louis to the bishops Jeremiah and Jonah. In these [Col. 1300B] nothing presents itself for observation except that certain statements in them seem to bear the scent of the deceits of recent heretics. Hence I am led to suspect that perhaps either this entire little book was fabricated or—what is more credible—corrupted and enlarged in order to bring the Roman Church into disrepute.

But whether the book is genuine, fabricated, partly authentic and partly forged, one thing is certain: it is not a book worthy of having one’s time consumed in reading it. Its false title, barbarous diction, silly arguments, perverse arrangement, and frequent repetition of the same testimonies could easily have persuaded the printer—if he had been concerned with the common good rather than his own profit—to refrain from publishing such a work.

*(Baronius writes more about this same pseudo-Synod of Paris in the years 824 and 825.)*

# THE COUNCIL OF PARIS, TO THE MOST EXCELLENT, VICTORIOUS, AND GOD-BELOVED AUGUST LORDS, THE EMPERORS HLUDOWICUS AND HLUDHARIUS

[Col. 1299]

[Col. 1299C] We, your servants and most faithful spokesmen, recall to the memory of your Highness how, on the recent Kalends of November, we assembled at the city of Paris in accordance with the command of your greatness, and how we dealt with the matter entrusted to us by your piety, namely, the question of images.

But so that it might become clearer to us for what reason your piety—burning most ardently with love for God and his holy Church—was first moved to investigate [Col. 1299D] this matter, we judged it necessary to learn the beginning of the affair. Therefore, we first had the letter of the lord Pope Adrian read before us, which he had formerly sent across the sea to the emperor Constantine and his mother Irene, at their request, in favor of erecting images. As far as our small understanding could discern, just as he rightly reproved those who in those regions had presumptuously dared to shatter and utterly destroy images of the saints, so he is known to have acted indiscreetly in ordering that they be worshiped superstitiously. On their account, moreover, he ordered a synod to be assembled and, by his authority, decreed under oath that they should be erected, worshiped, and called holy, although it is lawful to erect them but impious to worship them. In the same letter he also inserted certain testimonies of the holy Fathers which, as far as we can understand, are wholly inappropriate and have no relevance to the matter under discussion.

From the text of this letter the emperor, clergy, [Col. 1300C] and people together took their authority and held a synod. Just as those who, in the other synod held under Constantine, the grandfather of the aforesaid Constantine, decreed that images of the saints were to be utterly rejected, greatly went astray, so these men also erred considerably when they decreed not only that such images should be venerated, worshiped, and called holy, but even professed that they obtained sanctity from them. To demonstrate the truth of what they were striving to establish, [Col. 1300D] they forcibly took certain testimonies from the sacred Scriptures and sayings of the holy Fathers to confirm their superstitious error and incompetently applied them to their own work, since they are reported to have quoted or understood them neither in the sense in which they were spoken nor in the meaning in which they were expounded by the holy Fathers.

When your father, of holy memory, had the same synod read aloud before himself and his people, and had rightly reproved it in many places, marking beforehand certain chapters that were open to criticism, he sent these through Abbot Angilbert to the same Pope Adrian, so that they might be corrected by his judgment and authority. Yet Adrian, again favoring those who at his prompting had inserted such superstitious and incongruous testimonies into the aforesaid work, attempted to answer each chapter in their defense, responding not to what was proper but to whatever he chose. For some of the things he set against their objections are such that, apart from [Col. 1301A] pontifical authority, they conflict both with truth and with authority. Although in those objections he sometimes endeavored, for the sake of defending them, to bring forward testimonies that were inappropriate, sometimes unsuitable, and sometimes even worthy of reproach, nevertheless, at the end of the same defense he professed that he thought, held, taught, and commanded concerning the matters under discussion what was known to have been established by blessed Pope Gregory. From these words it is clearly gathered that, in this affair, he deviated from the straight path less knowingly than ignorantly. For unless, in concluding his objections, he had been bound by the restraints of truth—namely, the institutions of blessed Gregory—and had thus guarded against a crooked path, he could have fallen headlong into the abyss of superstition.

Having observed and understood these matters according to the measure of our ability, and wishing everything to become still clearer to us, we had the letter read again which the Greek envoys brought to you in the previous year. The venerable Bishop Freculfus carefully and prudently [Col. 1301B] informed our humble selves orally how he and his companion Adegarius had dealt with this matter with the apostolic lord and with his venerable bishops and ministers. Once we had learned everything from his prudent account—how, partly through ignorance of the truth and partly through the practice of a very bad custom, the plague of this superstition had taken root in those regions—and had examined both what preceded and what followed with the greatest care, we understood, as far as the matter was clear to us, by what zeal your holy devotion had been moved to consider these things.

For we do not fail to understand that your spirit could be afflicted with great sorrow when you saw those who, endowed with the highest authority and therefore bound to correct all who deviate, departing in any way from the right path. You were kindled by that zeal of which blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:29). When you saw two men placed in danger and turning aside from the royal road—one, on the left, falling precipitously toward the shattering of images, the other, on the right, inclining toward the superstitious worship of those same [Col. 1301C] images—you wished, in an attitude of piety, to place yourself between them and apply salutary medicine to the disease of both sides.

But since the greatest obstacle for you was that the party which ought to correct the errors and oppose this superstition by its authority was itself striving not merely to resist that superstition but even, through an incautious defense, to support it against divine authority and the sayings of the holy Fathers, the Lord opened for you a door according to your desired purpose. He granted you permission from that same authority to seek the truth familiarly, together with your own people, concerning so great a matter. Thus, since you had the will to give counsel but lacked the authority to inquire, you might seek the truth by the authority of the one whose authority appeared to be deviating from truth itself, so that, when the truth was disclosed through your holy desire and vigilant efforts and set openly before all, that same authority, willingly or unwillingly, might yield and submit to the truth.

But since the [Col. 1301D] salvation of our brothers must not be neglected and eminent authority must not easily be reproved, it seemed best to our lowliness that every word of your serenity should be directed specifically, with the authority of apostolic letters, against those for whose sake you were first stirred to investigate these matters. Whatever is found worthy of reproach in either party should rather be referred to their persons—men who may freely be admonished and whose offense, if it arises on behalf of the truth, can more easily be endured.

We therefore believe that, by reproving the former and sympathizing with them, while soothing, praising, and preferring the latter, raising their authority with great praises and rendering due praise to the holy Roman Church, yet bringing the truth forward from the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures and the sentences of the holy Fathers and explaining it truthfully and soberly, your most holy devotion will be able, as it desires, to provide for both sides. [Col. 1302A] For in this way the opponent, subtly bound by the bonds of truth—now through gentle speech, now through honor, now through demonstrating the truth according to reason—will not dare to teach anything other than what the truth contains, nor be able to hold anything other than what the truth contains, nor be able to attempt anything other than what he has handed on to others as something to be held according to the proof of truth.

In this way, then, it seemed to our mediocrity that you could most advantageously benefit the salvation of both parties and prepare for yourselves a great reward from the Lord on account of this matter. We are confident that, although they may perhaps wish in some respect to claim a superstitious custom for themselves, nevertheless no one will dare command anything from that See in any direction other than as authority and truth require. He will fear your power, the authority of the See, and the testimonies of truth. Therefore, when your holy devotion has carried out these things in this manner, even if—which we do not wish—either one side or the other should wish to deviate in some respect and disdain to hear your most salutary admonition, which is entirely [Col. 1302B] pronounced on the authority of truth, the Lord will still make no smaller recompense to you, because, in the words of blessed Elijah the prophet, you will have striven to do everything that was yours to do (1 Kings 19).

Finally, as stated above, we your servants assembled together and conferred familiarly, according to the measure of our understanding, about the matters entrusted to us. We gathered testimonies from divine authority and sentences of the holy Fathers, as the shortness of time permitted; we had them read before us; and whatever in them we judged necessary and suitable to the matter under discussion, we diligently collected into one body. We have presumed to send it to your imperial power through the venerable men Halitgarius and Amalarius, so that your wisdom, bestowed upon you by God, may select from it whatever it judges necessary and worthy in relation to this matter.

We therefore humbly beseech your most abundant piety not to attribute to us whatever may be found [Col. 1302C] there to be deficient, inappropriate, or [uncertain/illegible]. For we truly confess that, impeded by the shortness of time, we collected neither as much as we wished nor as much as we were able. Rather, desiring with all our strength to obey your sacred commands, as is fitting and necessary, we gathered briefly whatever came to hand within the limited time and devoted ourselves to this work until your most discerning examination. For some of our number, coming from far away, had no time to investigate; others could not truthfully know the reason for which they had been ordered to come to this assembly until they arrived. Moduinus, detained by the illness from which he has suffered for a very long time, was unable to come.

Your Excellence therefore knows most fully that what necessity urges one to investigate through all the books of the Catholics requires an extended period of time for reading. If sufficient time had been granted to us, with the Lord’s assistance we could have [Col. 1302D] collected such an abundance of material as might richly supply this work. Nevertheless, we judge that in what has been collected the substance of the matter under discussion has been distinctly set forth in accordance with divine authority and the sentences of the holy Fathers—namely, that every faithful person who reads it through can perceive that images of the saints are not to be shattered through foolish presumption, abolished as an insult to the saints, and utterly despised; nor are they to be venerated or worshiped with superstitious assertion. Rather, once such superstition has been removed, they are to be kept according to true religion for the sake of memory and love, in remembrance of those whose images are to be retained, as blessed Gregory has declared with sufficient Catholic clarity.

Since, therefore, we do not doubt that due reverential honor ought rightly to be paid to those who sit in the holy See of the blessed Apostle Peter, and since some of us have seen their superstitious veneration of images while all of us have learned of it through the reports of others, we wished first to set down judgments against those [Col. 1303A] who presumptuously dared to shatter images, so that these men, encouraged by this, might correct the errors of the others more forcefully together with you and more readily bend their minds to recognize their own superstition and accept the testimonies of truth.

As it seems to us, and as we stated above, the substance of your correction can everywhere be directed against those from whom the letter we reread is known to have been sent to you, since its text demonstrated that both parties deserved reproof: both the party that venerated images with an improper and superstitious worship and the party that ordered those same images to be overturned and destroyed in the lower regions. We therefore believe that, although the same emperor acted in other matters according to the authority of truth, as it is contained in his writings, nevertheless by this action he scandalized certain weak persons in those regions and also disturbed certain people in our city of Rome.

[Col. 1303B] May the Lord Jesus Christ preserve your serene dominion—humble, beloved of God, and necessary to the Christian religion—for the exaltation and peace of his holy Church, sheltering it by the right hand of his mercy and preserving it forever by his happy protection; and after the course of this life may he deem you worthy to share the company of the citizens above.

# CHAPTER I

We judged it fitting and necessary first to collect the judgments of the holy Fathers against those who presume indiscriminately to remove images not only from buildings but also from sacred vessels.

From Book VII, chapter 15, of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “Since we have mentioned this city, it seems just to recall also what took place there and what we judged worthy of inclusion in history. The Gospels relate that a woman suffering from an issue of blood was healed by the Savior. It is known that she was a citizen [Col. 1303C] of this city, and her house is still pointed out there. Before the entrance to her house there is shown a certain stone base placed in a prominent position, on which an image of the woman, as though kneeling and simply extending her hands, appears to have been cast in bronze. Beside it stands another statue, likewise cast in bronze, in the form of a man, clothed and surrounded by a robe, extending his right hand toward the woman. At the foot of this statue, from the base, a plant of novel appearance grows. Once it has sprouted, it usually grows as far as the fringe of the bronze garment; when the plant’s tip reaches it, it acquires power to drive away all diseases and illnesses, so that, whatever the bodily sickness may be, it is removed by drinking a little of the moistened medicinal herb. But it possesses no power at all if it is plucked before, as it grows, it has touched the top of the bronze fringe.
>
> “They said that this statue had been fashioned in the likeness of Jesus’ appearance. It remained down to our own times, as we ourselves saw with our eyes; [Col. 1303D] and it is not surprising if those from the nations who believed, in gratitude for the benefits they had received from the Savior, appeared to offer such a thing as a gift. For even now we see images of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the Savior himself being made and painted on boards; and we have also seen ancient images of them preserved by certain people. This seems to have been observed indiscriminately as a pagan custom, for it is their practice to honor those whom they judge worthy of honor in this way. To preserve the insignia of former times for the memory of posterity is a sign of their honor and of the affection of those who preserve them.”

In the *Acts of Pope Silvester* we read that “the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared to the emperor Constantine in a vision [Col. 1304A] and said to him:

> “‘Because you have put an end to your crimes and shuddered at the shedding of innocent blood, we have been sent by Christ, their Lord, to give you counsel for recovering your health. Hear, therefore, our instructions and do everything we indicate to you. Bishop Silvester of the city of Rome, fleeing your persecutions, is sheltering with his clergy in caves in the mountain of Syraptis. When you bring him to you, he will show you a pool of piety; when you have plunged into it three times, this illness of leprosy will entirely leave you. When this has been done, repay your Savior in return by ordering all the churches throughout the Roman world to be restored. For your part, purify yourself in this respect: abandoning the superstition of idols, worship and serve the one Lord, who alone is true, and attain to his will.’
>
> “Then, rising from sleep, he immediately summoned those who were guarding the palace and, in accordance with the substance of his dream, sent them to Mount Syraptis, where Saint Silvester, together with his clergy, had taken refuge from persecution on the estate of a certain Christian and was occupied with readings and prayers. When Silvester saw [Col. 1304B] that he had been surrounded by soldiers, he believed that he was being summoned to the crown of martyrdom. Turning to the clergy who were with him, he said: ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.’
>
> “He therefore set out as instructed and reached the king. When his arrival was announced, he entered with three priests and two deacons and said: ‘Peace and victory from heaven be granted to you.’ When the king had received him with cheerful spirit and a most gracious expression, Silvester explained everything that had happened to him, everything that had been said, and everything that had been reported, in accordance with the account given above. At the end of his narration the king asked who these gods Peter and Paul were who had visited him, and why they had revealed their hiding place for the sake of his salvation.
>
> “Silvester replied: ‘The Lord chose these men for himself as worthy servants of Christ and apostles, sent by him to summon the nations, so that believers might obtain salvation.’
>
> “While the pope was saying these and similar things to Augustus, Augustus began to ask whether he had any image [Col. 1304C] in which these men were represented, so that from the painting he might learn that they were the ones whom the revelation had shown him. Then Saint Silvester ordered a deacon to bring out an image of the apostles. When the emperor looked at it, he began with a great cry to say that these were the very men he had seen, and that the bishop should no longer delay showing him the pool which he remembered these men had promised for his healing.”

[Col. 1304C] John Chrysostom, in his homily on the superscription of Psalm 50:

> “Painters imitate nature by their art; mixing colors with colors, they depict visible images of bodies. They represent human beings, animals, and trees; kings, commoners, and barbarians; battles and conflicts; torrents of blood, spears, breastplates, and shields; a royal throne and an emperor seated upon it; a barbarian subjected to him; a sharp sword; flowing rivers; fields adorned with various flowers. By imitating through art everything that can be seen, they offer viewers a marvelous history.”

[Col. 1304D] Paulinus, Book IX.  
[Note: [Col. 1303D] *On the Birthday of Saint Felix of Nola*.]

> Now I would have you see the paintings, ranged in a long array  
> Along the painted porticoes, and tire your neck a little  
> As you read through everything with your face tilted upward.  
> Whoever sees these things, recognizing truths in empty images,  
> With an image that is not empty, he feeds his mind with faith.  
> For the painting faithfully preserves in sequence  
> Everything that the elder Moses wrote in five volumes,  
> Everything that the Lord did, marked with the name Jesus.

And shortly afterward:

> Perhaps someone may ask for what reason of acting ...  
> But let this be our purpose: to paint the holy  
> Houses rarely with likenesses of living creatures? [The printed *gerendi / Sed sit* construction and the place of *Raro*, “rarely,” are uncertain.]  
> Receive this, and I shall try briefly to explain the reasons.  
> No one is unaware of the company drawn here  
> By the glory of Saint Felix; but among them there is a larger crowd:  
> Rustic people, not empty of faith, though unlearned in reading.  
> Long accustomed to serving profane rites,  
> At last, when the belly, hitherto a stranger, is converted to Christ,  
> And when he marvels at the works of the saints revealed in Christ,  
> See how many come from every countryside,  
> And how piously they wander, deceived in their uneducated minds.  
> They have left their distant homes and disdained disasters;  
> Not cold, but fervent in faith, they now throng here  
> And extend their vigilant rejoicing through the whole night.  
> Joy banishes sleep, and torches drive away the darkness.

And a little later:

> While the painting beguiles their hunger to read holy histories,  
> The noble worth of chaste deeds steals in.  
> Sobriety, introduced by pious examples, is drunk with open mouth;  
> Forgetfulness of excessive wine takes possession of them.  
> And while they pass the day at greater length, drinking vessels  
> Become fewer, because, as time is spent upon miracles,  
> Only a few hours remain for those who feast.

[Col. 1305B] And below:

> From Genesis, I pray, gather this meaning of prayer:  
> Let me not remain earthly Adam, but let me be born  
> From virgin earth and, the old man cast away, be formed as a new image.

Blessed Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, among other passages, where he begins his discourse on Abraham:

> “I saw,” he says, “an image of the Passion, and I did not pass by the sight without tears, bringing the history before the eyes through the work of art,” etc.

The same author, in his interpretation of the *Song of Songs*:

> “Whoever,” he says, “looks upon an image does not prefer contemplation of the mere application of color, in the painted panel completed through the same art; rather, he looks only toward the depicted scene, which the artist has displayed through colors.”

Augustine, in Book XVI of *The City of God*:

> “Certain men are said to have eyes without necks, placed upon their shoulders, and other such supposed kinds of human beings, which are reportedly shown on the seafront at Carthage, drawn from a book as though from a more curious history.”

The same author continues shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, either those things, along with the other matters written about certain peoples, are altogether nonexistent; or, if they do exist, those beings are not human. It is entirely clear that just as useful and true recollections are sometimes brought back to memory through painting, producing remorse, so harmful and false images continually impose themselves upon human minds by deceiving them.”

Again, Augustine, in the book *On the Ten Strings*, says among other things:

> “How do I wrong the Lord himself? You corrupt yourself. And how do I wrong the Lord by corrupting myself? In what way does someone wrong you who might perhaps wish to stone your painted panel, on which there is your image, uselessly placed in your house for your vain honor, neither sensing, speaking, nor seeing? If someone stones it, does he not insult you?”

In Book X, chapter 30, of the *Tripartite History*:

> “For when Saint Paul came to Athens and saw the city filled with idols, he did not destroy the altars honored by them, but by reason he reproved their ignorance and displayed the claims of truth.”

Again, in Book VI of the same work:

> “I will not omit to relate what also occurred under Julian. For it was indeed a sign of Christ’s power and a judgment of the Lord’s wrath against the ruler. When he learned that in Caesarea Philippi, a city of Phoenicia which they called Paneas, there was a notable image of Christ that the woman freed from the issue of blood had erected, he removed it and placed his own statue there. When violent fire fell from heaven, the statue was split around the chest, so that its head, together with its neck, was thrown down on one side and fixed in the earth, while the remaining part continued to stand and retained the marks of the lightning. At that time the pagans dragged away and shattered the statue of Christ. Later, however, Christians gathered it up and stored it in the church, where it is preserved to this day.”

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 1306A]

What distinction should be maintained concerning the preservation of images of the saints and paintings of historical scenes is made clear by the following statements of the most holy, eminent, and admirable blessed Pope Gregory, the most learned man of the whole Catholic Church.

He writes to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles:

> “I have learned,” he says, “that it came to us some time ago that, when your Fraternity saw certain worshipers of images, you broke and threw out those same images from the churches. And indeed we praised you for having zeal lest anything made by human hands should be worshiped; but we judge that you ought not to have broken those same images. For this reason painting is used in churches: so that those who do not know letters may at least read by seeing on the walls what they are unable to read in books. Therefore your Fraternity ought both to preserve them and to prohibit the people from worshiping them, so that those who do not know letters might have a means by which to acquire knowledge of the history, and the people might not [Col. 1306B] sin at all in worshiping the painting.”

Also, in another letter to the same man:

> “It had indeed been reported to us that, inflamed by ill-considered zeal, you were smashing images of the saints under the pretext that they ought not to be worshiped. We entirely praised you for forbidding their worship, but we reproved you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: what priest has ever been heard to have done what you did? If nothing else, ought not this consideration to have restrained you—that, having despised the other brethren, you alone should believe yourself holy and wise?
>
> “For it is one thing to worship a picture, and another to learn from the picture’s subject what ought to be worshiped. What Scripture provides for readers, a picture provides for the uneducated who look at it, since in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow, and in it those who do not know letters read. Therefore, especially for the Gentiles, a picture serves in place of reading. You, who live among the Gentiles, ought to have paid the greatest attention to this, lest, while imprudently inflamed by proper zeal, you should generate scandal in fierce minds.
>
> “Therefore that which had been placed in churches not for worship but solely to instruct the minds of the unlearned ought not to have been broken. And since antiquity, not without reason, permitted histories of the saints to be painted in venerable places, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could undoubtedly have achieved what you intended beneficially and could have gathered rather than scattered the flock entrusted to you, so that the name of pastor might properly stand out in you instead of the guilt of one who disperses.
>
> “But while you have carried out this movement of your mind with such extreme imprudence, you are said to have scandalized your children so greatly that the greater part of them withdrew from communion with you. When, then, will you bring wandering sheep to the Lord’s fold, when you cannot keep those whom you already have? Therefore we exhort you to take care, even now, to restrain yourself from this presumption and to hasten, with paternal gentleness, every effort and every diligence, to call back to yourself the minds of those whom you recognize as separated from your unity.
>
> “For the various children of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of Holy Scripture that it is not lawful to worship anything made by human hands, since it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. VI; Matt. IV). Then it must be added that you had seen the pictures of the images—which had been made for the instruction of the unlearned people, so that those who did not know letters might learn by contemplating the history itself what had been said—transferred into worship. For this reason you were moved to order that those images be broken. And they must be told that, if they wish to have in the churches images for the instruction for which images were anciently made, you should permit them by every means both to be displayed and to remain.
>
> “Judge, however, that it was not the very sight of the history, which was revealed through the testimony of the picture, that displeased you, but the worship improperly offered to the pictures. By soothing their minds with these words, call them back to your concord. And if anyone wishes to make images, do not prohibit him in the least; but avoid worshiping images by every means. Let your fraternity carefully admonish them of this, so that from contemplating the event represented they may receive the ardor of compunction and humbly prostrate themselves in worship of the one almighty Holy Trinity.”

Also, in another letter to Bishop Januarius:

> “Jews coming here from your city complained to us that their synagogue, which is situated at Taralis, etc., had been seized on the following day after his baptism—that is, on the very feast of the Lord’s Pascha—with grave scandal and without your consent, by Peter, who, by the Lord’s will, had been led from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith, after he had associated with himself certain undisciplined men. He had placed there an image of the mother of our Lord, a venerable cross, and the white cloak in which he had been clothed when he rose from the font.”

And a little later:

> “Considering the intention, or rather the judgment, of your will in this matter, we exhort you with these sentiments: after the image and the cross have been removed from that place—for they deserve veneration—you ought to restore what was violently taken away.”

Also, to Secundinus, a servant of God confined in seclusion:

> “The images which you asked us to send you through your deacon Dulcidius … your request greatly pleased us, because with your whole attention you seek the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that daily bodily sight may arouse you; while you look upon the picture, may you burn inwardly with desire for the one whose image you contemplate.
>
> “We do nothing improper if, through visible things, we signify invisible things. Thus, when someone ardently desires to see another—or, loving his betrothed, longs to see her—and she goes to the bath or proceeds to church, he quickly prepares himself on the road so that he may depart gladdened by seeing her.
>
> “We know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to honor it as though it were God, but for remembrance of the Son of God, so that you may grow warm in love for him whose image you contemplate. We ourselves do not prostrate before the image as before divinity; rather, we worship the one whom, through the image, we remember either as born, or as having suffered, or as seated upon the throne. And while the picture itself, as though it were writing, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either gladdens our spirit concerning the resurrection or consoles it concerning the Passion.
>
> “Therefore, through the aforementioned deacon, our son, we have sent you two curtains, an image of the Savior, and images of Saint Mary the Mother of God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and one cross with a nail as a blessing, so that you may be defended from the evil one, believing yourself fortified by its holy wood.”

## CHAPTER III

We believe that these brief statements against those who overthrow the images of the saints out of abhorrence are sufficient. Now, against those who honor and worship them with an improper cult, call them holy, and confess that through them they attain holiness—as we find inserted in that synod of the Greeks—we have appended the statements of the holy Fathers. But we judged it necessary first to set forth how the practice of worshiping images originally arose.

Thus the blessed Augustine writes in his book *On Various Heresies*:

> “The Simonians derive their name from Simon Magus, who, after being baptized by the deacon Philip, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, attempted to purchase with money from the holy apostles the power to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. By magical deceptions he had misled many. He taught the detestable shamefulness of using women indiscriminately and said that God had not made the world; he also denied the resurrection of the flesh and asserted that he was Christ. He also wished to be regarded as Jupiter. As Minerva he presented a certain prostitute, Helen, whom he had made his partner in crimes, and he provided his disciples with images of himself and of Helen to worship. At Rome he had publicly established these images as likenesses of gods; in that city the apostle Peter extinguished them by the true power of almighty God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “A certain Marcellina is believed to have belonged to the sect of Carpocrates. She worshiped images of men, and of Paul, Homer, and Pythagoras, offering them worship and incense.”

The same author, in his letter to Dioscorus, among other things:

> “Epicurus is shown to have once fashioned many images of himself and to have handed them over to his followers. Democritus too is rightly reproved: although he thought differently from Epicurus, he believed that through images one could attain interior worship.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Epicurus says that images, which he calls emanations from the things themselves—things which he supposes to be formed from atoms—flow away and enter the mind, being subtler than those images that reach the eyes. For he also says that this is the cause of seeing: certain images extend outward and encompass the whole world.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Why did he not see that it is neither necessary nor possible for an incorporeal mind to think through the arrival and contact of bodily images? In this respect, certainly, both are equally refuted by the evidence of the eyes.”

The same author, in Book VIII of *The City of God*:

> “Hermes the Egyptian, whom they call Trismegistus, thought and wrote as follows: ‘Since, therefore, our ancestors, being unbelieving and failing to attend to the worship and religion of the divine, discovered an art by which they might make gods, they joined to this discovery a power corresponding to the nature of the world. Since they could not make souls, they summoned the souls of demons or angels and placed them in holy images and divine mysteries, so that through them the idols might possess powers both for doing good and for doing evil.’”

The same author, in his letter to Marcellinus:

> “When the Roman army first began to love, carry, and seize privately and publicly standards, painted panels, embossed vessels, images, and other objects, then that praiseworthy glory and safety of the state began to perish.”

The same author, in Book VII of *The City of God*:

> “Let everyone strive to worship the one true Lord—that is, the Creator of every soul and body. He does not sin because the one whom he worships ought not to be worshiped, but because he worships what ought to be worshiped in a manner in which it ought not to be worshiped. Whoever worships such things—that is, shameful and criminal things—and not the true Lord, the maker of soul and body, but a creature, even if that creature is not vicious—whether it is soul, body, or soul and body together—sins twice against the Lord: both because he worships in place of him one who is not he, and because he worships him through things by which even he ought not to be worshiped.”

And a little later:

> “Hence, when all ambiguity has been removed, it is evident that wicked demons and utterly unclean spirits have been invited by this entire civic theology to visit foolish images and to possess them, and through them to possess foolish hearts.”

## CHAPTER IV

These statements concerning the origins of the worship of images have now been given. We must next briefly explain what our teachers thought about the improper cult of superstition.

Origen, in Homily 8 on the beginning of the Decalogue, among other things:

> “I think that this should be understood in the following way. If, for example, someone makes from any metal—gold, silver—or from wood or stone the figure of a quadruped, or of some serpent or bird, and sets it up to be worshiped, he has made not an idol but a likeness. Likewise, if he sets up paintings for this purpose, he must nevertheless be said to have made a likeness.”

And below:

> “The word of God, which embraces all things, at once rejects and repudiates this. It not only forbids an idol to be made, but also forbids the likeness of everything that is on earth, in the waters, and in heaven. It adds and says: ‘You shall not worship them or serve them’ (Exod. XX). To serve is one thing, and to worship is another. A person can sometimes worship even unwillingly, as when certain flatterers of kings see them devoted to such pursuits; they pretend to worship idols, although in their hearts they are certain that an idol is nothing. But to serve is to devote oneself with the whole disposition, affection, and zeal. The divine word therefore cuts off both: you must neither serve with affection nor worship through outward form.”

Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Daniel:

> “Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and that we do not worship the golden statue which you have set up.” Whether we prefer to read “statue,” as Symmachus has it, or “golden image,” as the other translators render it, worshipers of God ought not to worship it. Therefore, let the judges and rulers of the world understand that, when they worship statues and images of emperors, they are doing what the three young men refused to do and thereby pleased God. The precise distinction should be noted: they say that gods are served and an image is worshiped, but neither is fitting for the servants of God.

The same Origen, in Homily 6 on the song sung by Moses:

> “Although the apostle John says, ‘Little children, we do not yet know what we shall be. But when it has been revealed to us concerning God,’ that is, when he says, ‘we shall be like him’ (1 John III), this likeness nevertheless refers not to nature but to grace. For example, if we say that a picture is like the one whose image is represented in the picture, it may be called like him with respect to grace, but with respect to substance it is very unlike him. The one is the form of flesh and a living body; the other is an application of colors and wax spread upon lifeless boards.”

Isidore, from the book *Etymologies*:

> “A picture is an image expressing the appearance of something which, when seen, recalls the mind to remembrance. It is called *pictura* as though from *fictura*, ‘a fabrication.’ For it is a fabricated image, not the truth; hence it is also called ‘painted over,’ that is, coated with a certain pigment, possessing nothing of faith or truth. Accordingly, there are some pictures that exceed bodies in the accuracy of their coloring and, while attempting to increase credibility, advance into falsehood.”

The same author shortly afterward:

> “The Egyptians invented painting: first, by tracing around a human shadow with lines; then, at the beginning, by using single colors, afterward different colors. Thus, little by little, the art itself expanded and discovered the distinctions of light and shadow and of colors, etc.”

Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel:

> “‘And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jeconiah son of Saphan standing among them, stood before the paintings, and each had a censer in his hand, and a cloud of smoke rose from the incense.’ When he says that seventy men from the elders of the house of Israel held censers in their hands, he shows that there were many other good men who did not do this, although perhaps they were held by other sins. He names Jeconiah son of Saphan as standing in their midst, as the leader of their crime and sacrilege. Having abandoned the worship of God, they worshiped idols; in the temple, which belonged to God, they did not worship God but the paintings on the walls.”

Firmianus Lactantius, in Book I of *On False Religion*, among other things, says:

> “What need is there to worship things outside the human being, things of which you are deprived? Virtue ought to be worshiped, not the image of virtue; and it should be worshiped not by some sacrifice, incense, or solemn prayer, but by the will and purpose alone. For no religion or veneration other than that of the one God is to be maintained. Why, then, O most wise man, is there any need to spend such great sums either on making or worshiping images? The human breast is a firmer and incorruptible temple. Let it rather be adorned; let it be filled with those true divine powers. For these false consecrations necessarily produce the following result: those who worship virtues in this way—that is, who pursue the shadows and images of virtues—cannot possess the virtues themselves, which are real, and so forth.”

Augustine, in his book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*:

> “Christians, being poor, as they are called foolish, worship one God in mystery, from whom all things are. They venerate nothing that has been created by him; for they know that he alone is sufficient and abundant for their salvation.”

The same author shortly afterward:

> “It therefore does not seem right to us that what a human being has made should be worshiped. The maker is judged worthy of worship by the thing made, not the thing made by the maker.”

Firmianus Lactantius, *On False Religion*, Book II:

> “The foolish sin in two ways. First, they prefer the elements—that is, the works of God—to God. Second, they worship the forms of the elements themselves, represented in human shape.”

The same author in the same book:

> “Let us worship nothing else and serve nothing else except the one name of our sole Maker and Father.”

The same author in the same book:

> “God is therefore above, not below; he is not in the lowest place, but in the highest religion, in which he ought to be believed.”

And below:

> “Nothing heavenly can exist in something made from earth. For whatever is represented must necessarily be false, and what falsely imitates truth through paint and imitation can never receive the name of truth.”

The same author in the same book:

> “So that you may understand that nothing visible to mortal eyes ought to be worshiped.”

Augustine, on Psalm 113:

> “Do not therefore lay hands upon the names, wishing to make a false god—or rather, a false human being—from that metal which the true God made, so that you may venerate him in place of the true God. Anyone who received such a being as a friend in place of a true human being would be insane. For the likeness of form and the structure that imitates the limbs both lead and, through a kind of weak affection, carry away the weak hearts of mortals.”

Fulgentius, in the book *On Faith to Donatus*:

> “Because God himself, commanding that he alone be served and ordering himself to be worshiped by the faithful, expressly forbade anyone to dare worship or serve a creature, he therefore speaks at the end of that first commandment concerning all things that he created: ‘You shall not worship them or serve them’ (Exod. XX).”

And shortly afterward:

> “True religion consists in the service of the one God.”

The same author shortly afterward:

> “Thus true faith worships one God, the Son together with the Father. It knows that God is to be served by all creatures in such a way that it also knows that the service belonging to God must not be rendered to a creature.”

Augustine, in his letter to Maximus the grammarian:

> “You will learn from the Catholic Christians, whose Church has also been established in your town, that no dead person is worshiped and that nothing made and created by God is worshiped, but only God himself, who made and created all things.”

Augustine, in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*:

> “God, as I suppose, made the soul immortal, unless perhaps you think otherwise. Therefore, you would wish [lacuna] such things to be made, I should say; but just as the immortal God made something immortal in his own likeness, so we, having been made immortal by God, ought to make something immortal in our likeness. You would be right if you painted on a panel the thing that you believe to be immortal in yourself. But now in it you represent the likeness of the body, which is certainly mortal. How, then, am I like God, since I can make nothing immortal as he can? Just as the image of your body cannot possess the power that your body truly possesses, so it is not surprising if the soul does not possess as great a power as the one in whose likeness it was made, and so forth.”

If, then, it is asserted that an image of a human body does not possess as much power as the body itself is truly said to possess, for what reason do certain people, deserving of reproach, presume to think that images can support them—those who, in that synod of the Greeks, declared that the mediation of images was necessary to them?

Augustine, Book VIII of *The City of God*:

> “Therefore a human being deservedly falls away from the one who made him when he places above himself what he himself has made. Hermes himself shows that dead human beings were worshiped with divine honor, such as Aesculapius and Mercury, whom he calls his grandfather, and others. Taking this opportunity, demons sought to become intercessors with the good gods, whom we call holy angels, archangels, or powers. In this way the wise men of the Gentiles attempted to conceal their divinities beneath a cloudy veil.”

Ambrose, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans:

> “Is anyone so insane, or so forgetful of his salvation, as to claim the honor due to a king for a count? If anyone were found even discussing such a thing, he would rightly be condemned as guilty of treason. Yet these people do not consider themselves guilty when they offer to a creature the honor due to the name of God and, having abandoned the Lord, worship fellow servants, as though there were something that they could reserve for the Lord more than this.
>
> “We approach a king through tribunes or counts because the king is a human being and does not know to whom he should entrust the state. But to win the favor of God, from whom nothing is hidden—for he knows the merits of all—no intercession is needed, but only a devout mind.”

Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*, among other things, says:

> “For the apprehension of truth, nothing is more obstructive than a life devoted to lust and the false images of sensible things which, impressed upon us through the body by this sensible world, generate various opinions and errors. No error could have existed in religion if the soul, instead of its God, had not worshiped a soul, or a body, or its own phantasms, which are nothing other than fabricated images drawn from the form of the body through bodily sensation.”

The same author in the same work:

> “Let the worship of human works not be our religion. Their makers are better than the things they make, yet we ought not to worship the makers either. Let our religion not consist in our phantasms. A genuine human being is better than anything that can be fabricated at will, and yet we ought not to worship the soul itself, although it is a real soul, when it imagines falsely. A real piece of straw is better than a light formed in empty thought according to the will of one who merely conjectures; yet it would be madness to believe that the straw which we perceive and touch ought to be worshiped.”

The same author, in Book X of *The City of God*:

> “Many things have ultimately been appropriated from divine worship for the honors offered to human beings, whether through excessive humility or through destructive flattery. Nevertheless, those to whom such honors were offered were regarded as human beings, who are said to be worthy of service and veneration; if much more is added, they are said to be worthy of worship. But who has judged that sacrifice should be offered except to one whom he has known, believed, or imagined to be a god?”

Augustine, in Book 84 of *Questions*:

> “The soul, occupied with lesser things which it makes bodily through the body, adheres less closely to supreme wisdom itself. How far those who worship such works have departed from the truth can be gathered from this: if they worshiped the bodies of the animals themselves, which have been made far more excellently and of which those works are imitations, what could we call more wretched than they?”

## CHAPTER V

By what reasoning or authority are images of the saints to be worshiped, and incense, as is reported, to be offered to them, when angels themselves and holy human beings have refused to be worshiped while alive?

Accordingly, the blessed Augustine says in Book XI of *The City of God*:

> “Some indeed thought that honor was to be offered to angels, either by worship or by sacrifice—honor that is owed to God—and they were forbidden to do this by the angels’ own admonition and commanded to offer it to the one to whom alone they knew it was lawful. The holy angels, and already the holy human beings of God, imitated this. For Paul and Barnabas, after a miracle of healing in Lycaonia, were thought to be gods, and the Lycaonians wished to sacrifice victims to them. They humbly prevented this and announced to them the God in whom they should believe.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, whatever mortal power, however great the virtue by which it is distinguished, loves us as itself and wants us to be subject to it so that we may be blessed, just as it is blessed by being subject to him. If it does not worship God, it is wretched because it is deprived of God. But if it worships God, it does not want to be worshiped in place of God. For it supports the divine judgment and favors the power of love, since it is written: ‘Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone.’ To say nothing now of the other matters pertaining to the service of religion by which God is worshiped, there is certainly no human being who would dare say that sacrifice is owed to anyone except God.”

The same author, on Psalm 96, among other things:

> “Consider holy human beings, who are like angels. When you find some holy human being, a servant of God, if you wish to honor and worship him in place of God, he forbids you; he does not wish to claim God’s honor for himself or to be God for you, but to be with you under God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “So the holy angels also seek the glory of the one whom they love. They strive to seize and inflame all those whom they love for his worship, prayer, and contemplation. They proclaim him, not themselves, because they are angels and, being soldiers, know no glory except that of their commander.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let no one say: ‘I fear that the angel will become angry with me if I do not worship him as my god.’ He becomes angry with you precisely when you wish to worship him. For he is good and loves God. Just as demons become angry if they are not worshiped, so angels are indignant if they are worshiped in place of God.”

In Book X of *The City of God*:

> “We therefore ought not to fear that we shall offend mortal and blessed beings subject to the one God by failing to sacrifice to them. For they know that sacrifice is owed only to the one true God, to whom they themselves adhere and through whom they are blessed. Without doubt, therefore, they do not wish sacrifice to be offered to them either through any symbolic figure or through the thing itself signified by the sacraments. This arrogance belongs to demons, the proud and wretched; the piety of those subject to God is entirely different.”

The same author in the same work:

> “We do not build temples for our martyrs as for gods, but memorials as for dead human beings whose souls live with the living God. Nor do we erect altars there on which to sacrifice to the martyrs, but to the one God, both theirs and ours. At that sacrifice, the martyrs are named in their place, turn, and order as human beings of God who conquered the world by confessing him. They are not invoked by the priest who sacrifices; for he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices in their memory, because he is God’s priest and not theirs. The sacrifice itself is the body of Christ, which is not offered to them, because they too are that body.”

Augustine, in his evangelical sermon concerning the power he gave to demons to enter the swine:

> “Do not bow down to angels, thinking that sacrifice ought to be offered to them—not even to good and holy angels. They do not want this when you do it, and they do not love you when you do it. They love you when you worship with them the one whom they worship.”

The same author, in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*:

> “Any other human being, however wise and perfect, or indeed any soul endowed with reason and supremely blessed, is to be loved and imitated only, and the honor appropriate to his merit and rank is to be offered to him. For ‘you shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

Origen, in his *Epistle to the Romans*:

> “Although human beings could recognize God, turning away from his worship they turned aside to worship the images of human beings and animals. To state the matter briefly, gathering everything into one definition: to worship anyone other than the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the crime of impiety.”

Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*:

> “Therefore, let the worship of ethereal and heavenly bodies not be our religion, but the worship of the one through whose contemplation they are blessed. We are not blessed merely by seeing an angel, but by seeing the truth through which we also love the angels. We do not envy them because they are more ready and enjoy the truth without any intervening troubles; rather, we love them all the more because we too have been commanded to hope for such a state from the common Lord. Therefore, we honor them with love, not with servitude, and we do not establish temples for them. They do not want to be honored in this way by us, because, when we are good, they know that we ourselves are temples of the supreme God.”

The same author, in Book VIII of *The City of God*:

> “Certainly we do not establish temples, priesthoods, sacred rites, or sacrifices for the martyrs, because it is not they but their God who is our God. We honor their memorials as those of holy human beings of God who contended for the truth even to the death of their bodies, so that true religion might become known and false and fabricated religions might be refuted—even if some who previously held such views restrained them through fear.
>
> “But who has ever heard a faithful person standing at an altar, already constructed for the honor and worship of God over the sacred body of a martyr, say in his prayers: ‘I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian’? Rather, sacrifice is offered at their memorials to the God who made them both human beings and martyrs and joined them, together with his holy angels, to heavenly honor. By that celebration we give thanks to the true God for their victories, and, invoking him for assistance, we exhort ourselves through the renewal of their memory to imitate such crowns and palms.
>
> “Whatever religious observances, therefore, are offered at the places of the martyrs are ornaments of their memorials, not sacred rites or sacrifices offered to the dead as gods.”

Jerome, to the presbyter Riparius:

> “After receiving your letter, to fail to answer would be arrogance; to answer would be rashness. For you ask about matters whose utterance and hearing alike constitute sacrilege. You say that Vigilantius—who bears this name by ironic contrast, for ‘Dormitantius’ [‘Sleepy One’] would be more appropriate—has once again opened his foul mouth and uttered the most disgusting stench against the relics of the holy martyrs, calling us, who have received them, ‘ash-worshipers’ and idolaters because we venerate the bones of dead human beings.
>
> “O wretched man, deserving of lamentation with every fountain of tears! When he says such things, he does not understand that he is a Samaritan and a Jew, who regard the bodies of the dead as unclean and even suspect that vessels in the same house are polluted, following the letter that kills rather than the life-giving Spirit.
>
> “We do not worship—not only the relics of martyrs, but not even the sun or the moon, not angels, not archangels, not seraphim, not cherubim, nor any name that is named, either in this age or in the age to come—in order that we may not serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. We honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may worship the one whose martyrs they are. We honor servants so that the honor of the servants may redound to the Lord, because ‘whoever receives you receives me.’”

The same author, against Vigilantius:

> “Who, you madman, has ever worshiped martyrs? Who has considered a human being to be God? When Paul and Barnabas were thought by the Lycaonians to be Jupiter and Mercury, and they wished to sacrifice victims to them (Acts XIV), did they not tear their garments and declare that they were human beings? This was not because they were not better than the long-dead Jupiter and Mercury, but because, under the error of paganism, the honor owed to God was being offered to them. We read the same concerning Peter: when Cornelius wished to worship him, Peter raised him up with his hand and said, ‘Rise, for I too am a human being’ (Acts X).”

Augustine, in Book 3 of *The Solution of Questions*:

> “Therefore, just as impious pride—whether of human beings or demons—commands or desires that divine honors be offered to it, so pious humility—whether of human beings or holy angels—refuses the honors offered to it and shows to whom they are owed.”

In Book XIX of *The City of God*, Augustine says:

> “But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshiped forbids sacrifice and worship to be offered to the holy heavenly angels and powers of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this mortal pilgrimage of ours, thundering in his law: ‘Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed.’”

## CHAPTER VI

Against those who wish to defend the superstition of images by the number of years, preferring to follow custom rather than the authority of truth.

Augustine, in his book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*:

> “The irrational multitude began to worship as gods either visible shadows, demons, or images of the dead. It imagines that, because this practice has been handed down through ancient custom, the truth of reason can be defended on its behalf, although the rational basis of truth does not come from custom or antiquity but from God. God is not proved by antiquity but by eternity. Therefore faith is not something that began at a particular time but is without beginning. For our beginning is to believe in God; what is believed is eternal.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What the pagans worship is after God and is a work after the craftsman. The pagans worship works; we worship the craftsman. They worship the creature; we worship the Creator. Human beings, having been made, began to venerate their Creator, because this is both fitting and demanded by the matter itself.”

The prophet Jeremiah says:

> “They went after the Baals, which they learned from their fathers.”

Accordingly, Jerome says:

> “Therefore one must not follow the error of parents or ancestors, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches.”

Augustine, on Psalm 113:

> “They seem to themselves to possess a purer religion when they say: ‘I do not worship an image or a demon; I contemplate a bodily likeness as the sign of that thing which I ought to worship.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “They dare to answer: ‘We do not worship the bodies themselves, but the divinities that preside over them and govern them.’”

If, then, as the foregoing teachings of the holy Fathers make clear, holy angels and holy men are not to be served or worshiped—for they themselves also reject this—but are to be honored through love alone, not through servitude; and if temples, sacred rites, and sacrifices are to be established for the holy martyrs not to them but to God alone; especially since they are to be honored for imitation, not worshiped as an act of religion—by what reasoning are worship, incense, lights, and the other things enumerated in the letter of the Greeks to be offered to them on the basis of ancient authority?

Therefore, with all superstition set aside, it is fitting that the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church maintain this distinction concerning images of the saints, as the outstanding teacher, the blessed Pope Gregory, taught and left for us to maintain and follow in his writings.

## CHAPTER VII

So that scandals might not arise for weaker brethren from superstition or from any other cause, holy men took the greatest care to avoid this through prudent consideration, and by their words and deeds they clearly show us that it must be avoided in every way.

Thus the blessed Augustine, in Book IV of *The City of God*:

> “Our ancestors separated superstition from religion.”

The same author, in Book X of the same work:

> “We read that the deadly bites of serpents were healed as a most just punishment for sins by a bronze serpent raised up on wood and looked upon, so that relief might be given to the afflicted people and death might be destroyed by death, or so that the likeness of crucified death might be signified. That serpent, which had been preserved as a memorial of the event, was later worshiped by the erring people as an idol. King Hezekiah, serving God with religious authority, crushed it with great praise for his piety.”

We read that the most holy and learned man, the blessed Epiphanius, inflamed by divine zeal, did something similar in a letter that he wrote to John, bishop of Constantinople, and that the blessed Jerome translated from Greek into Latin:

“I heard,” he says, “that some were murmuring against me when we were traveling together to the holy place called Bethel, so that I might celebrate the collection with you according to ecclesiastical custom. When I had come to the village called Anablatha, I saw, as I was passing by, a burning lamp. I asked what place it was and learned that it was a church. I entered to pray and found hanging in the doorway of that very church a veil, dyed and painted, bearing an image resembling Christ or some saint. I do not remember clearly [Col. 1315A] whose image it was. When, therefore, I saw an image of a human being hanging in the church of Christ contrary to the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it apart. I further advised the custodians of the place to wrap a poor dead man in it and carry him out, and I told them, when they murmured against me, that if he wished to tear it, it was right that he should give another veil in exchange. When I heard this, I promised that I would provide one and send it immediately. There was, however, a slight delay while I looked for the best veil to send in its place, for I thought that one would have to be sent from Cyprus. Now I have sent what I was able to find, and I ask you to order the presbyter of that place to receive from the reader the veil sent by us, and thereafter to instruct that such veils as are contrary to our religion not be hung in the church of Christ.”

For the blessed apostle Paul also wrote in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, in order to avoid giving offense to weaker brothers: “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge, and that an idol is nothing [Col. 1315B].” The blessed Ambrose explains this as follows:

“These men,” he says, “were puffed up by knowledge: against the salvation of their uninstructed brothers, they ate meat sacrificed to idols, knowing that it was permissible to eat meat and that an idol was nothing, and therefore that the one eating was not defiled. They were, however, an offense to their brothers, because they did not keep charity before their eyes; for it was more important to abstain from meat than to give offense to a brother.”

And shortly afterward:

“For this reason, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I cause my brother to stumble. He teaches that charity must be pursued so earnestly that permitted things are to be treated as forbidden, lest they harm a brother. For what great evil it is not to sin through forbidden things, yet to offend through things that have been permitted: thus the law is observed in forbidden matters but not kept in permitted ones, when people eat without due consideration.”

Where the blessed Apostle says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient.” The blessed Augustine explains this as follows:

“Something, then, can be lawful and yet not expedient. [Col. 1315C] What is not lawful cannot be expedient; and consequently not everything lawful is expedient, whereas everything unlawful is not expedient. There are indeed lawful things that are not expedient, as we have learned from the testimony of the Apostle (1 Cor. 6 and 10). But it is difficult to define by some universal rule what difference there is between what is unlawful and therefore not expedient, and what is lawful but nevertheless not expedient.”

And below:

“Therefore, since we cannot doubt that the Apostle spoke truly, and we dare not say that some sins are lawful, it remains for us to say that something may be not expedient and yet, if it is lawful, not be a sin—although, since it is not expedient, it certainly ought not to be done.”

And shortly afterward:

“Thus, if we can, let us strive to distinguish by some definite boundary between what is lawful but not expedient, and what is unlawful and therefore not expedient. It seems to me that those things are lawful but not expedient which are permitted by the justice that stands before God, yet must be avoided because of the offense of human beings, lest they be hindered from salvation. Those things, however, are unlawful and therefore not expedient [Col. 1315D] which justice itself avoids in such a way that they ought not to be done, even if they are not praised by those to whose knowledge they have been made known.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“A thing is expedient when it is permitted not only by the justice that stands before God, but also causes no impediment to human beings’ salvation. What is lawful is not expedient when something is permitted, yet the exercise of that power can create an impediment to salvation.”

These passages are inserted so that those who raise images for the sake of remembrance and affection may take care lest something done by them perhaps devoutly and lawfully become an occasion of scandal to the weak. Thus they may satisfy their own devotion without forgetting the salvation of the weak or defiling the weak conscience of their brothers by providing an occasion for superstition.

## CHAPTER VIII [Col. 1316A]

Since there are those who think that they have support for the adoration of images in the claim that Jacob adored his son Joseph, or certainly adored the top of his staff, we have considered it necessary to append how this was explained by the blessed Jerome and the blessed Augustine.

The blessed Jerome writes in his *Book of Hebrew Questions*:

“After his son had sworn to him, he says, and he was confident concerning the request he had made, he adored God at the head of his bed. The holy man, devoted to God and weighed down by old age, had a bed placed there so that, even while lying down, his posture would be ready for prayer without any difficulty.”

Augustine, in his *Book of Questions on Genesis*, chapter 62:

“What the Latin manuscripts have—‘and he adored over the head of his staff’—some, correcting the text, read as ‘he adored over the head of his staff,’ or ‘at the head of his staff,’ whether ‘on the top’ or ‘over the top.’ For the Greek word deceives them: it is written with the same letters whether it means ‘his’ (Latin *eius*) or ‘his own’ (Latin *suae*), [Col. 1316B] but the accents are different, and those who know these things do not disregard them in manuscripts. They are important for making a major distinction, although, if the meaning were ‘his own,’ the word could also contain one additional letter, so that it would not be αὐτοῦ but ἑαυτοῦ. Hence it is rightly asked what this statement means.

“It would easily be understood that the old man, who carried a staff in the manner customary for that age, as he bent down to adore the Lord, did so over the top of his own staff, which he carried in such a way that, by inclining his head over it, he adored God.

“What, then, does ‘he adored over the top of his staff’ mean? It may mean the staff of his son Joseph. Perhaps Joseph had taken it from him when that son swore to him; and while he held it after the words of the oath, before it had yet been returned, he immediately adored God. For he was not ashamed to carry for a little while the emblem of his son’s authority, since it signified a great future event.

“Nevertheless, it is said that in Hebrew the question has a very easy solution: there, they say, it is written, ‘Israel adored at the head of the bed,’ on which the old man was lying. He had it positioned so that, without difficulty, he could adore whenever he wished.”

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1316C]

A response must be made to those who think that they are supported by the statement in the Book of Kings that the prophet Nathan adored David.

Concerning this adoration, the blessed Gregory speaks as follows in Book X of his *Commentaries on Job*:

“Thus the law of God is almost said to be manifold, because, although charity is one and the same, when it has fully possessed the mind it kindles it in many different ways toward innumerable works. We briefly express its diversity if, by touching upon its goodness in each of the elect, we enumerate it.

“Through Abel, charity offered chosen gifts to God and endured the sword of his brother without resistance. Through Enoch, it taught him to live spiritually among human beings and also bodily withdrew him from human beings to the higher life.”

And a little later:

“Through Nathan, charity rose against the sinful king with the authority of free reproof, and, when the king was without guilt, humbly prostrated itself in petition. It is clear [Col. 1316D] that this adoration was of such a kind as ours when, in greeting persons more honorable than ourselves, we prostrate ourselves out of humility and are said to have adored them, although we offer them no worship belonging to God. In the same way, there can be no doubt that Jacob adored his brother Esau.”

## CHAPTER X

Something must also be said against those who profess to adore images because they call them sacred and equate them with sacred vessels.

Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 113:

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, but God made silver and gold; ‘the work,’ he says, ‘of human hands.’ They venerate what they themselves have made from gold and silver. Yet we too have many instruments and vessels made from such material or metal for use in celebrating the sacraments. Because they have been consecrated by that very ministry, they are called holy, and they are used in honor of the one whom they serve for our salvation.
