“Are these instruments or vessels, then, anything other than the work of human hands? [Col. 1317A] Yet do they have mouths and not speak? Do they have eyes and not see? Do we implore them, because through them we implore God? The greatest cause of insane impiety is that, in the affections of wretched people, a form resembling a living being—which objects to being implored—has greater power than the obvious fact that it is not alive and therefore ought to be despised by the living.”

## CHAPTER XI

Something must also be said against those who call upon the two cherubim as testimony in favor of the adoration of images, although they were fashioned as a sign of a mystery.

Hence the blessed Augustine says, among other things, in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*:

“Wretched is the soul’s bondage when it takes signs for realities [Col. 1317B] and is unable to raise the eye of the mind above bodily creation to drink in eternal light. Yet this bondage stood far apart from the custom of the other nations in the Jewish people, since they were so subjected to temporal things that one God was commended to them in everything.

“Although, in ignorance of what they referred to, they observed the signs of spiritual realities as though they were the realities themselves, they nevertheless had this implanted in them: that through such bondage they were pleasing the one God of all, whom they did not see. The Apostle writes that this guardianship was like that of children under a pedagogue.

“Therefore those who stubbornly clung to such signs could not endure the Lord’s rejection of them when the time of their revelation had come. Their rulers and people consequently devised accusations because he had healed on the Sabbath. Bound to those signs as though they were realities, they did not believe that the one who did not observe them as the Jews observed them was God or had come from God.

“Those who believed in him and followed him, from whom the first Church of Jerusalem was formed, showed clearly how beneficial it had been to be guarded in that manner under a pedagogue: the signs imposed temporarily upon servants bound the minds of those who observed them to the worship of the one God who made heaven and earth.

“If, then, to follow a sign usefully established for the reality it was established to signify is a carnal bondage [Col. 1317C], how much more is it bondage to take signs established for useless things as though they were realities? If you refer them to the things signified by them and bind your mind to worship those things, you will nevertheless not be free from a servile and carnal burden and veil.

“Therefore Christian liberty freed those whom it found under useful signs by interpreting the signs to which they were subject, as though they had been found nearby, and lifting them up to the realities of which the signs are signs. From these people the churches of the holy Israelites were formed.

“But those whom it found under useless signs it freed not only from the servile activity performed under such signs but also from the signs themselves. It removed them all, so that the nations might be converted from the corruption of the multitude of idols of the gods—which Scripture often and expressly calls fornication—to the worship of the one God. They were no longer to serve under even useful signs, but rather to exercise the mind in their spiritual understanding.

“He serves under a sign who performs or venerates [Col. 1317D] a thing signifying something without knowing what it signifies. But whoever performs or venerates a useful sign established by God, understanding its power and meaning, does not venerate what is seen and passes away, but rather that to which all such things must be referred. Such a person is spiritual and free, even during the time of bondage when those signs ought not yet to be revealed to carnal minds, under whose yoke they must be subdued.

“Such were the patriarchs and prophets, and all those in the people of Israel through whom the Holy Spirit supplied us with the aids and consolations of the Scriptures themselves.

“In the present age, after the resurrection of our Lord [Col. 1318A] had shone forth as the clearest judgment of our liberty, we are not burdened with the performance of even those signs that we already understand. Instead, the Lord and apostolic discipline have handed down a few signs in place of many, easy to perform, majestic in understanding, and most pure in observance, such as the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the Lord’s body and blood.

“Each person, when receiving these, recognizes, having been instructed, to what they refer, so that he may venerate them not with carnal bondage but with spiritual liberty.

“Just as following the letter and taking signs for the realities they signify is the weakness of bondage, so interpreting signs uselessly is the error of one who wanders badly. But whoever does not understand what a sign signifies, yet understands that it is a sign, is not himself oppressed by bondage. It is better to be burdened by signs that are unknown but useful than, by interpreting them uselessly, to place the neck freed from the yoke of bondage into the snares of error.”

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning the worship that is owed to God, which the Greeks call *latria*; concerning the religion and worship that the Greeks call by the single word *threskeia*; and concerning the fact that what is manufactured ought not to be worshiped or adored.

Augustine, in Book X of *The City of God*:

“This is the worship owed to divinity [Col. 1318B]—or, if it must be expressed more precisely, to deity—for which, since I do not find a sufficiently suitable Latin word to signify it in one term, I indicate what I wish to say with the Greek word wherever necessary.

“Our people have translated *latria*, wherever it occurs in the holy Scriptures, as ‘service.’ But the service owed to human beings—the service according to which the Apostle commanded servants to be subject to their masters—is usually called by another name in Greek. According to the usage of those who composed the divine utterances for us, *latria* either always, or very frequently, or almost always denotes the service that belongs to the worship of God.

“Accordingly, if one simply speaks of ‘worship,’ it does not seem to be owed to God alone. We are said to worship human beings also, whom we frequent either in honorable remembrance or in their presence; and not only those to whom we subject ourselves in religious humility, but certain things subject to us are also said to be worshiped.

“For from this word come the terms ‘farmers,’ ‘tenants,’ and ‘inhabitants.’ [Col. 1318C] The gods themselves are called *caelicolae*—‘inhabitants of heaven’—for no other reason than that they inhabit heaven, not indeed by venerating it but by dwelling in it as tenants of heaven. They are not called tenants in the same way as those who, because of agriculture, owe service to their native soil under the lordship of its possessor, but in the sense expressed by a great author of Latin eloquence:

> There was an ancient city, and Tyrian settlers held it.  
> —Virgil

“He called them settlers from inhabiting, not from agriculture. Hence cities founded by larger cities or by groups of peoples are also called colonies. Accordingly, it is entirely true that worship, in the proper sense of this word, is owed to God alone.”

Again, in Augustine’s *Book of Expressions on Genesis*, concerning the stone that Jacob set up, he says:

“When Jacob set up [Col. 1318D] the stone that he had placed at his head, establishing it as a monument and pouring oil over it, he did not do anything resembling idolatry. Neither then nor afterward did he regularly adore the stone or sacrifice to it. Rather, it was a sign established in the clearest prophecy, one pertaining to anointing, from which the name ‘Christ’ derives from *chrisma*.”

A little later:

“Jacob took a stone and established it as a monument. It must be carefully observed how they established such monuments as testimony to each matter—not in order to worship them as gods, but in order that they might signify something.”

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 1319A]

Against those who, on the authority of that same synod of the Greeks, professed to adore images, just as they honor the life-giving cross with due honor as a trophy of virtue, we have considered it necessary to insert a few passages, so that they may be convicted of being unable to use this as support for their superstition.

Concerning the cross, the *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IX, chapter IX, concerning Constantine, relates:

“He was already at that time a supporter of the Christian religion and a worshiper of the true God, though he had not yet received, as is customary among us for those being initiated, the signs of the Lord’s passion. As he traveled anxiously, turning many thoughts over in his mind concerning the necessity of the impending war, and often raising his eyes toward heaven while praying there for divine assistance, he saw during sleep, in the eastern part of the sky, the sign of the cross shining with fiery brilliance.

“When he had been terrified by so great a vision and disturbed by the strange sight, he saw angels standing before him and saying: ‘Constantine, conquer by this.’ Then, restored to joy and already confident of victory, he marked on his forehead the sign of the cross that he had seen in heaven. Thus invited from heaven to faith, he seems to me no inferior to the one to whom a voice from heaven was likewise spoken: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? I am Jesus the Nazarene’ (Acts 9)—except that the former was still persecuting, whereas Constantine was invited while pursuing his course. [Col. 1319B]

“From that time he transformed the sign that had been shown to him in heaven onto military standards and adapted what they call the Labarum to the form of the Lord’s cross. Thus equipped with the arms and standards of religion, he set out against the weapons of the impious. It is also reported that he held in his right hand a sign of the cross fashioned from gold.”

Again, in the *Tripartite History*, Book I, chapter 4:

“While he was occupied with these anxieties, he saw in sleep the sign of the cross splendidly placed in the sky. As he marveled at the vision, angels appeared and said: ‘O Constantine, conquer by this.’ It is also reported that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and commanded him to make a similar figure and to have this assistance in battles, by which he might obtain the rights of victory.

“Eusebius Pamphili reports that he himself had heard the emperor say under oath that, when the sun was already declining after midday, [Col. 1319C] he and the soldiers who were then with him saw the sign of the cross made of light and an inscription declaring: ‘By this conquer.’ For, as he was traveling somewhere with his army, on the road where the miracle was shown to him, night overtook him while he was considering what it might mean. Then Christ appeared to him in sleep with the sign he had seen in heaven and ordered him to make an image of that sign, which would serve as assistance in the clashes of battle.”

The same work, chapter 5, records:

“This military standard was more precious than the others because it was customary for the emperor to precede them and to be adored by the soldiers. For this reason I think Constantine, the most noble glory of the Roman Empire, changed it into the sign of the cross, so that through frequent sight of it and attention to it they might become unaccustomed to their former practice of subjection and might consider as God alone the one whom the emperor worshiped and under whose leadership and assistance they used their arms against their enemies.

“This sign was always placed before all the ranks, and he commanded that it be present especially for the armies laboring in battle. He therefore appointed designated standard-bearers to care for it. Their task was to carry it on their shoulders in turn [Col. 1319D] and to pass through all the lines with it.

“For it is reported that once, when someone carrying this sign suddenly became frightened as the enemy attacked and gave it to another to carry, then withdrew from the battle and evaded the missiles, he was suddenly struck and died. But the man who received the sacred trophy remained unharmed while many were hurling missiles at him. For, by the wondrous direction of divine power, the enemy arrows lodged in the sign, while the standard-bearer immediately escaped from danger.

“It is said that no one other than the minister of this sign, as is customary, ever died wounded in battle or suffered the disaster of captivity.”

Again, in the same work, Book II, chapter 18:

“It is also said that a dead man rose again through contact with the cross. Concerning this wood the Sibyl said among the pagans:

> O thrice-blessed wood on which God was stretched.”

Again, in the same work, chapter 9:

[Col. 1320A]

“I also heard that Probianus, a man serving in the palace among the physicians, was afflicted with the painful disease of gout and was there freed from his sufferings. A holy and wondrous vision appeared to him.

“Although he had once been a pagan and afterward became a Christian, he followed the doctrine to some extent; but he was unwilling to adore the most sacred cross, the source of complete salvation. Divine power appeared to him while he held this opinion and showed him the sign of the cross that had been placed on the altar of that church. It made clear and manifest that, from the time Christ was crucified, none of the things done for the benefit of the human race had been accomplished in any manner apart from the power of the cross that must be adored—not by holy angels nor by devout human beings.”

The same work, Book II, chapter 46, records:

“At that time many bishops shone forth, including Donatus of the court of Epirus. Although the provincials testify to many miracles performed by him, the greatest was what he did concerning a dragon. It lay near a bridge on the public road, feeding by seizing and devouring sheep, goats, horses, cattle, and human beings.

“Donatus came to the beast without a sword or any kind of missile. When it raised its head as though it were about to devour the man, [Col. 1320B] he traced the sign of the cross in the air with his finger before its face and spat into its mouth. The beast immediately received the spittle in its mouth and died.”

John Chrysostom, in Homily 11, *On the Cross and the Thief*:

“Today our Lord hung upon the cross, and we celebrate our joy with an extraordinary festival, so that we may learn that the cross is the substance of all spiritual rejoicing. Formerly, the name of the cross signified punishment; now it is called glory. Formerly it bore the horror of condemnation; now it is the sign of salvation.

“For the cross is the cause of every blessedness: it freed us from the blindness of error; it brought us from darkness into light; it joined those who had been driven away to tranquility; it united those alienated from God; it brought those who were far off near; it showed travelers to be citizens; it is the cutting away of discord; it is the foundation of peace; it is the abundant distribution of all good things.”

And shortly afterward in the same homily:

[Col. 1320C]

“I also want you to understand in another way that he did not leave his cross on earth but carried it with him to heaven. ‘But,’ you say, ‘how is this demonstrated?’ For this reason I heard that, when he comes, he will come with it and manifest his presence with it according to his glory. Therefore he called it the glorious cross.”

Again, shortly afterward in the same homily:

“Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Luke 21). You have seen the glory of the sign, that is, of the cross. The light of the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not receive its radiance, but that sign will shine and gleam. Just as a royal procession precedes an emperor, and soldiers customarily carry the standards upon their shoulders at the head of the army, thereby declaring his arrival, so, when the Lord comes from heaven, the assembly of angels and the multitude of archangels will carry that sign upon their exalted shoulders and announce his royal arrival.

“For the cross of Christ alone dissolves darkness, dispersed the kingdom of demons, and removed all terror of the wicked. The cross provided holiness; the cross became the sun of righteousness for us, so that, enlightened by his mercy, we may glorify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

Again, John Chrysostom, in Homily 13, *On the Lord’s Cross*: [Col. 1320D]

“And if you desire to know, beloved, the power of the cross and how much I can say in its praise, listen:

> The cross is the hope of Christians,  
> the cross is the resurrection of the dead,  
> the cross is the guide of the blind,  
> the cross is the way of the despairing,  
> the cross is the staff of the lame,  
> the cross is the consolation of the poor,  
> the cross is the restraint of the rich,  
> the cross is the destruction of the proud,  
> the cross is the punishment of those who live badly,  
> the cross is triumph over demons,  
> the cross is the defeat of the devil,  
> the cross is the pedagogue of the young,  
> the cross is the support of the needy,  
> the cross is the hope of the despairing,  
> the cross is the pilot of those at sea,  
> the cross is the harbor of those in danger,  
> the cross is the wall of the besieged,  
> the cross is the father of orphans,  
> the cross is the defender of widows,  
> the cross is the counselor of the just,  
> the cross is the rest of the afflicted,  
> the cross is the guardian of little ones,  
> the cross is the head of men,  
> the cross is the end of the aged, [Col. 1321A]  
> the cross is the light of those sitting in darkness,  
> the cross is the magnificence of kings,  
> the cross is an everlasting shield,  
> the cross is the wisdom of the senseless,  
> the cross is the liberty of servants,  
> the cross is the philosophy of emperors,  
> the cross is the law of the impious,  
> the cross is the foretelling of the prophets,  
> the cross is the proclamation of the apostles,  
> the cross is the glorying of martyrs,  
> the cross is the abstinence of monks,  
> the cross is the chastity of virgins,  
> the cross is the joy of priests,  
> the cross is the foundation of the Church,  
> the cross is the safeguard of the world,  
> the cross is the destruction of temples,  
> the cross is the rejection of idols,  
> the cross is the stumbling-block of the Jews,  
> the cross is the destruction of the impious,  
> the cross is the strength of the weak,  
> the cross is the physician of the sick,  
> the cross is the cleansing of lepers,  
> the cross is the rest of the paralyzed,  
> the cross is the bread of the hungry,  
> the cross is the fountain of the thirsty,  
> the cross is the protection of the naked.

“When I say ‘the naked,’ do not understand bodily nakedness, but nakedness through the punishment of unbelief. When he believes in Christ, he will be found clothed.”

Again, Augustine, in Book XXII of *The City of God*:

[Col. 1321B]

“In Carthage, Innocentia, a most devout woman from one of the leading families of that city, had cancer in her breast. As they say, every treatment for this disease must be abandoned. She had learned this from an experienced physician and had turned to God alone in prayer.

“As Easter approached, she was warned in a dream that, in the women’s section, she should mark the place for herself wherever the first baptized woman she encountered should meet her. She made the sign of Christ’s cross, and health immediately followed.”

Sedulius, in Book IV of the *Paschal Poem*:

> He himself was the peace of the cross;  
> displaying violent strength in his own limbs,  
> he clothed punishment in honor  
> and made the penalty a sign, rather, of salvation.  
>   
> And lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross is to be worshiped,  
> which bore the Lord, exulting by a mighty design,  
> it gathers the four regions of the four-cornered world:  
>   
> From the head of its author the shining East gleams forth;  
> from the western star the sacred feet descend;  
> the right hand holds the North,  
> the left raises the central axis. [Col. 1321C]  
>   
> All nature lives from the limbs of its Creator,  
> and Christ rules the whole world, embraced on every side by the cross.

Again, Paulinus, in Book VIII of the *Natalia of Felix*:

> The sign and confession of the unconquered cross protect us;  
> armed by God, we fortify the mind.  
> We do not seek weapons for the body,  
> and although we may seem unarmed in our limbs,  
> we nevertheless bear weapons with which, even in peaceful calm,  
> we battle in spirit against incorporeal enemies.

Again, the same author, in Book X:

> Returning home, I brought with me  
> a small but greatly saving fragment  
> taken from the wood of the eternal cross.  
> I carried it in my hand and held it out from afar  
> against the hostile flames,  
> retaining it as a shield before my breast  
> to cover me and drive back the enemy  
> repulsed by the opposing shield-boss.  
>   
> Believe it, but do not ascribe it to me;  
> render thanks to Christ  
> and offer due praises to the Almighty.  
> For our salvation rests upon the cross and name of Christ. [Col. 1321D]  
> From it our faith, resting on this cross amid danger,  
> profited, and the flame recognized our salvation.  
>   
> It was not my voice or my right hand that terrified the fire,  
> but the power of the cross.  
> At the very place from which it had risen,  
> it forced the flame enclosed within the prescribed boundary  
> to remain there and be extinguished,  
> with its roar dying away,  
> and the storm that had arisen from the ashes  
> to return to ashes.  
>   
> How great is the power of the cross,  
> that nature abandons itself!  
> The fire that devours all wood is consumed by the wood of the cross.  
> Many hands, repeatedly sprinkling those fires  
> with abundant water from vessels,  
> sought to overcome them.  
>   
> But although they sought to offset the flames  
> with streams from exhausted springs,  
> nevertheless, with greater force,  
> the fire defeated all the water  
> scattered by weary hands.  
> We extinguish fire with wood;  
> the small fragment overcame the flame  
> where water could not.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1322A]

Against those who invoke the sign of the holy cross as testimony, arguing that it is lawful for them to adore images just as they adore the wood of the holy cross.

Those who worship images are accustomed to oppose the veneration, adoration, or exaltation of the holy cross in defense of their position, asking why images should not be adored in the same way as crosses.

First, they must be answered that Christ chose to be suspended not in an image but on a cross when he wished to redeem the human race. Therefore holy Mother Church, throughout the world, among the countless mysteries of the cross that the holy Fathers have enumerated in many ways far and wide throughout the whole world, has decreed that all Catholics may lawfully venerate crosses, wherever they see them, by bowing if they wish, solely out of love for Christ’s passion. Moreover, on the holy day when the Lord’s passion is specially celebrated throughout the world, the entire order of priests and the whole people, prostrated with complete devotion, may adore the cross.

Then there is also this specific point [Col. 1322B] to be set against those who exhibit illicit worship to images—not against those who lawfully possess them: the aforementioned universal Church has decreed that the sign of the holy cross be used in consecrating the sacred fonts and in marking or blessing those who are to be baptized or have been baptized. After renouncing Satan, his pomp, and his works, it has taught all worshipers of the Catholic faith to fortify their foreheads and breasts with this sign in unwavering faith against all the snares of the devil, and it has sought to arm the right hands of all the faithful with an unconquerable sword.

Tell me, I ask: against ecclesiastical law, what comparable act has the Catholic Church throughout the whole world sanctified concerning images for the image-worshiper? And although these matters are great, what shall we say about the consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ? From the moment both begin to be consecrated in the sacred solemnities of the Mass almost without interruption until the end, they are blessed with the sign of the cross. There is no one so wise or so foolish as to presume that this consecration can in any way be completed in a manner pleasing to God unless he always strives to consecrate it with that same sign of the holy cross.

What, moreover, shall we say of the whole human race, [Col. 1322C] and almost of all the works and daily actions of the human race, embracing everything that it habitually does by day, by night, in the morning, in the evening—or, better perhaps, at every time? What is there among all these things that it would wish to begin, perform, or complete without the sign of that same cross, if it can pertain to its salvation either in this age or in the age to come?

## CHAPTER XV

These things I have said to you thus far, whoever you are, indiscriminate worshiper of images. And these things also I say to you—[the source reading is uncertain]—whoever you are, excessive destroyer: take care, when you hear them, not to think that permission is being granted to your rashness, so that whenever you see painted or sculpted likenesses of the saints—not because of illicit worship but because of a discerning and therefore lawful disposition of mind—you may destroy or mock them with derision.

Therefore both parties must be admonished, so that neither, [Col. 1322D] like Bardesanes, the superstitious lover of new inventions, but each as a truly Catholic person, may carefully preserve the mother of virtues, discernment, in all things; may possess zeal for God not according to the folly of the unintelligent but according to the virtue of the wise in the Lord; and may neither the one by loving nor the other by despising leap beyond what is proper to the right or the left and lose the way of rectitude.

But because many are so obstinate that they cannot be bent by reason at all, such people must rightly be shaken by sacred authority, so that, at least when broken, they may seek medicine.

### Letter of the blessed Pope Gregory to Serenus, Bishop of Massilia
“Your letter’s opening so displayed priestly goodwill in itself that our joy over your brotherhood became greater, but its ending so disagreed with its beginnings that the letter seemed to have come not from one mind but from several. And” [Col. 1323A] “a little later in the same letter it is written:

‘It had indeed been reported to us that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you were breaking the images of the saints under the pretext, as it were, that they ought not to be adored; and, because you had forbidden them to be adored, we praised you greatly, but we censured you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: from what priest have you ever heard of such a deed as the one you committed? If nothing else, should not even that have restrained you? Do you alone, despising the other brothers, believe yourself holy and wise? For it is one thing to adore a painting, and another to learn from the history represented in the painting what is worthy of adoration. What Scripture provides for readers, painting provides for the uneducated who look at it, because in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Thus, especially for the nations, painting serves in place of reading—a matter which you, who live among the nations, ought to have considered most carefully, lest, while incautiously inflamed by righteous zeal, you generate scandal in savage minds. Therefore that which had been placed there, not for adoration but solely for instructing [Col. 1323B] the minds of the unlearned, ought not to have been broken; and since antiquity allowed the history of the saints to be painted in venerable places, it did not do so without reason.’

And a little later he continues:

‘For various children of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of Holy Scripture that it is not permissible to adore anything made by hand, since it is written: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6). Then it must be added that the painted images which had been made for the instruction of the unskilled people were intended so that those who did not know letters, by attending to the depicted history, might learn what had happened.’

And again:

‘If you wish to have in the churches the images which were made in ancient times for this instruction, you should permit them in every way both to be displayed and to remain, and you should judge that it was not the very sight of the history revealed by the testimony of the painting that displeased you, but the adoration improperly offered to the paintings. By these words soothing their minds, recall them to concord with you; and if anyone wishes to make images, let him not be forbidden in the least. But avoid adoring [Col. 1323C] images in every way. Let your Fraternity carefully admonish them, however, so that from seeing the event represented they may receive the ardor of compunction and humbly prostrate themselves in adoration of the omnipotent Holy Trinity alone.’”

Also, a letter of Pope Gregory to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion.

“I received the letter of your Love, which tasted to my mind as though seasoned with the honey of affection, etc.” After some intervening material he says:

“For the images which you asked us to send to you through your deacon Dulcidius … your request greatly pleased us, because with your whole attention you seek him whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that the daily sight may always renew your fervor, and, when you see the painting, you may burn inwardly toward him whose image you contemplate. We do nothing unreasonable if, through visible things, we represent invisible things by visible means. Thus, when someone ardently desires to see another, or lovingly longs to see his bride, whom he is trying to visit, if he happens to think that she is going to the bath or proceeding to church, he prepares himself for the road, so that he may depart joyful from the sight.

“For we know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as God, but so that, in remembering the Son of God, you may grow warm with love for him whose image you contemplate. We do not prostrate ourselves before the images as though before divinity itself; rather, we adore him whom, through the image, we remember as having been born, suffered, or sitting upon the throne. And while the painting itself, like Scripture, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either makes our spirit rejoice over the resurrection or moves it with sorrow over the passion.

“Therefore, through the aforesaid deacon, our son, we have sent you two cloths bearing images of the Savior, holy Mary the Mother of God, and the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with a cross with a nail, [Col. 1323D] as a blessing, so that, defended by it against the Evil One, you may believe yourself fortified by the holy wood of the cross, etc.”

Also, a letter of Pope Gregory to Bishop Januarius.

“The Jews who came here from your city complained to us that Peter, who, by the Lord’s will, had been led from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith, having taken certain undisciplined men as his associates, occupied their synagogue, which is situated at Carati, on the day following his baptism—that is, on the very Sunday feast of Easter—with grave scandal and without your consent, and placed there an image of the Mother of God, of our Lord, a venerable cross, and the white garment in which he had been clothed when he rose from the font, etc.” A little later he says:

“Considering the intention of your will in this matter, and especially your judgment, we exhort you with earnest appeals that, after removing from that place both the image and the cross with the reverence that is fitting, you restore what was taken by force, etc.”

Also, a letter of Pope Gregory to Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople.

[Col. 1324B]

“What offering, and of what kind, could have so holily gladdened my spirit as the venerable report concerning you, and the most holy, God-beloved, and grateful announcement concerning your praiseworthy name, etc.” Then, after some intervening material, he added:

“But when you began to preside over the conflict, just as God himself showed you by commanding you to lead the armies of Christ, and [to display] the glorious and certainly renowned sign of the kingdom—the life-giving cross, I mean, the great triumph over death of his greatness—when I had inscribed the circuit of the four-part world, distinguishing the regions by what had been written, so also [I inscribed] the holy image of the Lady of all, the holy Mother of God, whose face the wealthy of the people entreat. For she, being holy, as seems right to the fathers, has granted such rewards because she was piously honored by you. For the honor paid to the image passes to the original form, according to the great Basil; and, as Chrysostom says: ‘I too have loved the painting poured over with wax, filled with piety.’” [Col. 1324C]

And a little later in the same letter:

“For if the prophetic arrangements have not reached their fulfillment, let not the subjects be written for display, which are not yet holy. That is, unless the Lord has been incarnate, let his holy image, which depicts him according to the flesh, not be portrayed; nor unless he was born at Bethlehem of the ever-glorious Virgin and Mother of God, and the Magi offered gifts, and an angel appeared to the shepherds, and the heavenly host rendered praise to the one who had been born; unless he was extended as an infant in his mother’s arms, he who bears all things and was nourished by milk, he who gives food to all flesh (Ps. 136). Let none of this be depicted unless he raised the dead, restored the paralytics, granted cleansing to lepers, opened the eyes of the blind, drove out demons, opened the ears of the deaf, and accomplished all the miracles which he gloriously performed as God.

“Let them not be written unless he willingly accepted the passion, despoiled hell, and, rising, ascended into heaven—he who is to judge the living and the dead. Let them not be [Col. 1324D] written or represented, since these things are recounted both by letters and by the colors of writing and history. For if all these things happened, and ‘great is the mystery of piety,’ would that it had been possible for heaven and earth, the sea, and all living creatures to proclaim them both through voices and through letters and histories.

“The depiction of nonexistent things is called idolatrous writing: it is a deranged production of things that did not exist in reality. And shall there be even one concession by the Church of Christ to idols? Far be it! For we have not worshiped calves, nor cast a calf at Horeb, nor regarded the world as God, nor again bowed down before a carved image and been consecrated to Baal-peor, nor ever sacrificed our sons or daughters to demons. These things are not ours, they are not ours. Let no one accuse us, since the people of Christ, up to this day, have served or venerated nothing that exists or has been made, except the life-giving Trinity, whose name is above every name. Far be it!

“If someone, moved in the Jewish manner to slander, thinks that what was once profaned amid the acclamations of idol worship, and that the worship of idols, should be attributed to our Church because of the venerable divine images directed toward better things, let him hear, like a Jew, nothing other than a barking dog that casts away its own vessels far from it. Would that Israel were such as to offer God prayer through visible things, through which he might remember the Maker, rather than hold a calf and flies upon the tablets of the covenant. Would that he loved the holy altar, and not the calves of Samaria. It would be good and just for him to embrace the divine rock sprinkled with dew, and not Baal. Would that he looked more toward Moses’ staff, and toward the golden urn, the ark, the mercy seat, the lamina of the ephod, the table, the inner and outer tabernacle—all of which were made for the glory of God and, although made by hand, were called rather the Holy of Holies—and toward the carved cherubim, concerning whose remembrance the Apostle says: ‘the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat’ [Col. 1325B] (Heb. 9). From these we learn through Scripture that the divine glory was made manifest. If he attended to these things, he would never bow down to idols.

“For every work done in the name of the Lord has been called precious and holy, etc.”

Also, Pope Gregory in his Synodical Letter.

“If conversion came to the aid of those who hold contrary opinions and seek to invalidate the ancient traditions of the fathers, the things we have already stated above from the testimonies of the fathers and the sacred documents would certainly suffice. But because we see—and say this with sorrow—that many, with disturbed minds, are disturbing the Church’s ordinances, therefore, dearest brothers, our discourse is extended, and we wish to say something further from ancient documents to restrain the madness of error; perhaps the restless may come to their senses.

“For in the Book of Exodus we read as follows. ‘The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, that they take for me firstfruits from every man who offers freely; you shall receive them. These are the things which you shall receive,’ and so forth in order, up [Col. 1325C] to the two cherubim which shall be above the ark of the testimony; ‘and everything that I shall command you, you shall tell the children of Israel’ (Exod. 25). And again: When Solomon had built the temple at God’s command, among other things he made in the inner sanctuary two cherubim of olive wood; and below: ‘He carved in them figures of cherubim, palm trees, and very prominent reliefs, and overlaid them with gold, and covered with gold both the cherubim and the palm trees, etc.’ (3 Kings 6).

“Behold, dearest brothers, let us consider what Moses accomplished at God’s command, and what Solomon, most wise, constructed by divine order, and so forth. How much more ought we, with pure-hearted zeal, to honor and adore our Lord Christ himself, and his ever-virgin Mother Mary, the apostles also and all the saints of God, through their sacred likenesses and images, and ask them to intercede for us and obtain the remission of our sins.

“We make and adore images for no other reason than the Word of God incarnate for our sake. But if everything made by hand must be rejected, neither the ark of the covenant, [Col. 1325D] nor its golden and embossed cherubim, which were made by Bezalel and Oholiab according to God’s command, ought to have been accepted. If those things were made as likenesses of invisible realities, then these too, in like manner, are made according to the visions and revelations of the prophets, distinguished by colors, etc.”

John Chrysostom, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper:

“Everything has been made for the glory of God; yet, for our use, the clouds serve the ministry of rain, the earth serves the abundance of grain, and the sea serves abundant commerce. Without envy, all things serve humanity, and especially the image of the Lord. For when imperial faces and images are brought into cities, and magistrates and peoples go out to meet them with praises, they do not honor the tablet or the inscription poured in wax, but the figure of the emperor. So too creation does not honor an earthly appearance, but reveres that same heavenly figure.”

Also, the blessed John Chrysostom, on the parable of the seed: [Col. 1326A]

“If you insult an imperial garment, do you not insult the one who wears it? Do you not know that if someone insults the image of the emperor, he principally brings an insult against the emperor himself and his dignity? Do you not know that if someone damages an image made of wood or color, he is not judged to have dared to act against a lifeless material, but, as one who has dismembered the image of the emperor, bearing an equal insult against the emperor, he brings that insult before the emperor himself?”

Saint Basil, from his book to Amphilochius, On the Holy Spirit, chapter 17:

“Because the emperor is spoken of, and the emperor’s image, there are not two emperors. For strength is not divided, nor glory partitioned. Just as the authority and power held over us are one, so too the glorification offered by us is one and not many, because the honor paid to the image passes to the original form.”

Also, Saint Basil in the letter sent to the Emperor Julian:

“In accordance with the divinely given [Col. 1326B] hereditary inheritance, I confess and promise the undefiled faith of Christians handed down to us. I believe in one God, the almighty Father: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit—one God. These three I adore and glorify. I also confess the dispensation of the incarnate Son and holy Mary, the Mother of God, who according to the flesh bore him. I also accept the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs, and prayer to God which, through them—that is, through their mediation—makes the most merciful God propitious to me and obtains for me the remission of my crimes. For this reason I honor and adore their images, a practice handed down especially by the holy apostles and not forbidden, but represented in all our churches through depictions of their history.”

Also, the same author in his sermon on the forty saints:

“For writers of the triumphs and victories of wars, and often painters, signify them: some adorning them in words, others marking them out upon tablets; and both have trained many [Col. 1326C] people to courage. For what the narrative of history demonstrates through hearing, the silent instruction recorded in writing demonstrates through imitation.”

Also, Saint Athanasius. Antiochus’s question to the saint concerning images:

“How can the Law and the prophets say, ‘Do not adore statues and likenesses’? Why, then, do you make images and adore them?”

Athanasius’s answer:

“We do not adore images as gods, we the faithful, like the pagans—far be it! Rather, through affection and the love of our soul, we look upon images in which the appearance of a face is represented. Hence, when the face has often been erased, we burn what was formerly an image as mere, common wood. For just as Jacob, approaching death, adored the top of Joseph’s staff—not honoring the staff, but the one who held it—so the faithful do not adore images for any other reason, nor because of desire for the represented likeness.”

Also, the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in his sermon on the evangelist Matthew:

“For faith is depicted [Col. 1326D]: the Word who exists in the form of God, just as, for the redemption of our life, he was offered to God clothed in our likeness and made human.”

And the same author, a little later:

“The parables signifying virtue fulfill for us the work of images: in a certain way they bring the matter before the eyes and into the touch of the hands, possessing in their traces, in minds, an invisible vision.”

Also, Saint Cyril:

“Just as someone who looks with pleasure upon a depicted image admires the figure of the king, and, recognizing that what appears in it is also his representation, takes delight in viewing it, so that he may look upon the king himself, etc.”

Also, Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus:

“For emperors, by virtue of possessing images, are not two emperors, but one emperor together with his image.”

Also, Saint Stephen, bishop of Bostra, to certain people, concerning images [Col. 1327A] of the saints:

“We have confidence concerning images of the saints, because every work done in the name of God is good and holy. For an image is one thing, and an idol—that is, a little statue—is another. When God formed Adam, that is, created him, he said: ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness’ (Gen. 1), and he made man in the image of God. What then? Because man is the image of God, is this idolatry—that is, the worship of idols—and impiety? By no means. If Adam were the image of demons, he would have been rejected and unacceptable; but because he is the image of God, he is honorable and acceptable.

“Every image made in the name of the Lord, whether of angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, or righteous people, is holy. For it is not the wood that is adored, but the one who is commemorated in the wood and honored as he is contemplated. We honor and greet all judges, even if they are sinners. What then? Should we not adore the holy servants of God, and, for their remembrance, establish and erect images so that they may not be forgotten?

“But you will say [Col. 1327B] that God himself commanded us not to adore things made by hand. Tell me, then, O Jew: what on earth is not made by hand after God’s creation? What, then? Was the ark of God, made and constructed from acacia wood, not made by hand? And were the altar, the mercy seat, the urn containing manna, the table, the lampstand, and the inner and outer tabernacle—not works of human hands, which Solomon made? And why are they called the Holy of Holies, although they exist as things made by hand? Were the cherubim with their six wings around the mercy seat not statues and images of angels made by human hands? And how are they not rejected? Because images of angels were made at God’s command, they are holy, even though they were statues.

“God prohibited and condemned the idols of the nations because they were images of demons. But we make images in memory of the saints: of Abraham, Moses, Elijah, Isaiah, Zechariah, and the remaining prophets, apostles, [Col. 1327C] and holy martyrs who were killed for God’s sake, so that everyone who sees them in an image may remember them and glorify God who glorified them. Honor, adoration, and commendation are fitting for them according to their righteousness, so that all who see them may hasten to become imitators of their deeds.

“For what is adoration except honor alone? We sinners also adore and greet one another according to honor and love. But we adore and glorify our God in another way, and tremble before him. An image is the likeness of the one represented in it. But let the impious, who do not do good and do not remember the saints, neither prohibit nor scandalize those who do good, honor the saints and servants of God, and remember them. For they will receive the reward of good works; but the impious, according to what they have devised, will receive the desolation of dishonor, like those who neglect what is just and depart from the Lord.

“For [Col. 1327D] the saints are represented and honored in images for the sake of remembrance—indeed, they are adored as servants of God—so that they may entreat and implore the divinity on our behalf. For it is right to remember our teachers and to give thanks.”

Also, Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, in the letter which he wrote to Saint John the Evangelist, says among other things:

“What is surprising if they drive Christ and, as he says, his disciples out of the cities, judging themselves worthy of this, and impiously exclude them from the sacred places, while those who depart from the truth are visibly images of invisible things? Nor will the contemplation of God be blameworthy in the ages to come because of his justice.”

Also, from the same author, On the Heavenly Militia, and below:

“For the aforesaid incorporeal ranks are represented in various colors and diverse compositions, so that, through these most sacred images, we may silently pass with devout minds to the simple [Col. 1328A] and incorporeal realities. For it is impossible for our mind to reach those incorporeal beings, to imitate and contemplate the heavenly army, unless, through the visible beauty of the elements, we are able to attain the invisible and most beautiful form, and unless visible and fragrant images, through rational tradition, shine forth as invisible realities, etc.”

In the definition of the holy Sixth Ecumenical Council, chapter 82:

“In certain paintings of venerable images, the lamb pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner is represented. It was left as a sign of grace, prefiguring for us, through the Law, the true Lamb, Christ our God, who took away the sins of the world.”

And a little later:

“According to the human form, we decree that he now be represented in images in place of the former lamb, considering through him the height of the humility of the Word of God, and being led by hand to the remembrance of his deeds in the flesh, his passion, his saving death, and the redemption of the world which came about thereafter, etc.”

[Col. 1328B] Hence the blessed Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 92:

“But if you do not adore these earthly things in Christ, although a certain likeness has been given from them, wherever a likeness has been drawn from any creature to signify the saints, understand that it is the likeness of a creature, and adore the Maker of the creature, etc.”

Also, Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, On the Incarnation of the Lord, whose beginning is: “We have sufficiently indicated these matters, taking a few points from many.” And afterward:

“Just as the form written upon wood, when it has been erased by external filth, must again be recovered and united with the one whose form it is, so that the image may be renewed in the same material and element. For through its form, the material itself upon which it is represented is not cast away, but is configured in that same material.”

Also, the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, to the Emperor Gratian, from Book 3, chapter 9:

“When we adore both his divinity and his flesh, do we divide Christ? Or when in him we adore the image of God and [Col. 1328C] the cross, do we divide him? Far be it!”

Also, the blessed Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, among other passages, where he begins his discourse on Abraham:

“I saw an image of the passion, and I did not pass beyond the sight without tears, bringing the history into representation through the work of art, etc.”

Also, the same author in his exposition of the Song of Songs:

“Just as written teaching is a kind of material, so entirely, in the various dyes which complete the imitation of a living being, the person who looks at the image completed by the same art through colors does not prefer the dyes to contemplation, but merely observes the depicted vision which the artist has displayed through colors.”

Leontius, bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus, in the fifth sermon written in defense of Christians against the Jews, and concerning images of the saints:

“Now let us give an answer concerning venerable and painted images, so that the mouths of those who speak iniquity may be stopped. For this tradition too is legal. [Col. 1328D] Hear God saying to Moses: ‘Construct two golden cherubim, carved, overshadowing the mercy seat’ (Exod. 25). And again, concerning the temple which God showed to Ezekiel: ‘You shall make,’ he said, ‘figures of palms, lions, men, and cherubim, from its pavement to the roof chamber’ (Ezek. 40; 3 Kings 6).

“This is certainly a fearful saying: the one who commanded Israel not to make any carved image, nor an image nor likeness of the things in heaven and on earth, himself commanded Moses to make carved animals and cherubim. Therefore Solomon, receiving the pattern from the Law, made the temple full of bronze and carved and cast figures of lions, oxen, palms, and men, and was not reproved by God.

“If you wish to reproach me on account of images, reproach God, who commanded these things to be made, so that they might be in remembrance of him among us.”

The Jew said: “But those likenesses were not adored as gods; they served only as memorials.”

The Christian said: “You have spoken well. Neither are the likenesses, images, and representations of the saints adored by us as gods. For if they adored images of wood as God, they ought certainly to adore every other piece of wood as well. But if they adored the wood as God, they would not burn the image after its likeness had been completely erased.” [Col. 1329A]

And again:

“I adore two pieces of wood joined together as a cross because of Christ who was crucified upon it; but when they have been separated from one another, I throw them away and burn them. Just as one who receives and kisses the emperor’s decree does not honor mud, paper, or lead, but offers greeting and veneration to the emperor, so Christian children, when adoring the sign of the cross, do not venerate the nature of the wood, but the sign and figure of Christ. Seeing him through it, through him who was crucified upon it, we kiss and adore, etc.”

And a little later:

“Just as we adore the cross as Christ’s staff, just as we adore his holy tomb as his seat and bed, just as we adore his house, manger, Bethlehem, and his other holy dwellings, and just as we honor his friends, his apostles, holy martyrs, and the other [Col. 1329B] saints, so we represent Christ’s passion in churches, houses, streets, images, curtains, bedrooms, garments, and every place, so that by looking at these things continually we may remember and not forget, as you have forgotten the Lord your God.

“And just as you, when adoring the book of the Law, do not adore the nature of the skins and ink, but the words of God contained in it, so I, when adoring the image of Christ, do not adore the nature of the wood or colors—far be it! Rather, while holding lifeless matter in the form of Christ, through it I hope to hold and adore Christ.”

And below it continues:

“For we often kiss even our own children, who have grown into fathers, and who are sinners, and we are not condemned for this. We do not kiss them as gods, but through the kiss we show the love of our nature which we bear toward them. As I have often said, the mind searches in every kiss and in every act of adoration, etc.

“So, O man, however many of the Christian people kiss the signs of the cross and the images, they do not offer veneration to the wood or stones themselves, or to gold, or to a corrupted image, or to relics; through these things they offer glory, a kiss, and veneration to God the Creator, who is the creator both of them and of all things.” [Col. 1329C]

And below:

“For whoever loves his friend or king, and especially a benefactor, when he sees his son, or holds his staff, seat, crown, house, or servant, kisses and honors him; through these he honors the benefactor, and especially God. When you see Christians adoring the cross, understand that they offer adoration to Christ who was crucified, and not to the wood. For if they venerated the nature of the wood, they would certainly adore trees and groves as well, just as you, Israel, once adored them, saying to a tree and to wood: ‘You are my god, and you gave me birth’ (Jer. 2).

“Therefore we do not say to the cross, nor to the figures of the saints, ‘You are our gods.’ For they are not our gods, but likenesses and images of Christ and his saints, placed for remembrance, honor, and the adornment of the churches and of those who adore. [Col. 1329D] Whoever honors a martyr honors God; whoever honors his mother offers honor to God himself; and whoever honors an apostle honors the one who sent him (Matt. 10), etc.”

Also, the blessed Augustine, concerning what appeared to Moses—the staff, the colored hand, and the water turned into blood—and after some intervening material added:

“Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. That is, whoever has been struck by the serpents of sins should look upon Christ, and will have healing in the forgiveness of sins.”

Also, the same Saint Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, in a homily on the same passage, among other things:

“Meanwhile, brothers, so that we may be healed from sin, let us look upon Christ crucified, because ‘just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up’ (John 3). For this is the difference between a figure [Col. 1330A] or image and the reality itself: the figure granted temporal life, while the reality of which it was the figure granted eternal life, etc.”

Also, Saint Augustine, from Book 3 of On the Holy Trinity, among other things:

“For just as the anointing of the stone signifies Christ in the flesh, in which he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, so Moses’ staff changed into a serpent signifies Christ made obedient unto death, concerning which he says, ‘As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness’ (Ps. 72).”

And afterward:

“If, while looking upon that serpent lifted up in the wilderness, they did not perish from the bites of serpents, our old man was crucified on the cross with him. By the serpent, however, death is understood—the death caused by the serpent in paradise—according to a manner of speaking in which the agent stands for what is effected. Thus, when the staff is shown in the serpent, Christ is shown in death; and when the serpent is again shown in the staff, Christ is shown in the resurrection, wholly in his body, which is the Church, etc.”

Also, the blessed Augustine, in the Book of Exodus, among other things:

[Col. 1330B] “We believe that the events happened in the manner in which we read that they happened; nevertheless, through apostolic teaching we recognize that the events themselves were shadows of things to come. Therefore we think that what happened must be investigated spiritually, yet we cannot deny that it happened, etc.”

Also, the same author on Psalm 71:

“Rather, let us now rejoice that we come in the name of Christ; now, while kings hold the scepter, they are subjected to the wood of the cross; now what was foretold is fulfilled: ‘All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him’ (Ps. 71). For now the sign of the cross is more precious on the foreheads of kings than the jewel of the diadem.”

Also, Augustine, concerning Abraham’s son led to sacrifice, among other things:

“You were not moved without reason when I said this: the cross has horns. For the two pieces of wood are joined together in such a way as to produce the form of a cross. Thus, as we see the image of the cross in many places, so that two horns are formed upon which the hands may be fastened, I see the ram hanging upon the horns, and the Lord crucified, etc.”

Also, Saint Severian of Gabala, from a sermon on the holy [Col. 1330C] cross, among other things:

“Do you think it would not have been right to say: If one of you has been bitten, let him look upward into heaven, toward God, and he will be saved? Yet, in order to prevent him from merely directing his attention to heaven, could he not have said: If someone has been bitten, let him look at the lamp of light, and he will be saved? Or: Let him look at the table of the presentation of the holy loaves, and he will be saved? Or at the altar, the veil, the ark, the image of the cherubim, or the mercy seat? But the great lawgiver introduced none of these into the discussion; he fixed only the image of the cross, and this through the accursed serpent.

“Tell me, as a faithful servant: you forbid what you do; you build what you renounce. You say, ‘You shall not make a carved or cast image’ (Exod. 20), yet you carve a serpent? But I established that former commandment in order to cut away the materials of impiety and rescue this people from every form of idol worship. Now I fashion the serpent in order to prefigure the image of the Savior, etc.”

Also, Saint Augustine to Dulcidius, in Question [Col. 1330D] 6, concerning the image of Samuel:

“For in Scripture images are accustomed to be called by the names of the things whose images they are. Thus all things painted or fashioned from some material—metal, wood, or whatever is suitable for such works—which also appear in dreams, and nearly all images, are accustomed to be called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“For who would hesitate to call a painted man a man? Indeed, when we look at the portrait of any individual, we readily use the person’s proper name, as when, looking at a tablet or wall, we say: ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome.’ Yet they are nothing other than painted images.

“Thus, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures made of metal at God’s command above the ark of the covenant, to signify a great reality, are nevertheless called cherubim. Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, ‘I saw [Col. 1331A] an image of Augustine or Simplicianus,’ but ‘I saw Augustine or Simplicianus,’ even though, at the time when he saw such a thing, we did not know it. It is therefore perfectly clear that it is not the people themselves but their images that are seen.

“Pharaoh likewise said that in his dream he had seen ears of grain and cattle, not images of ears of grain and cattle. If, then, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen (1 Kings 28), etc.”

# Authorities concerning signs, images, and veneration

## Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II

“A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance that it presents to the senses, causes something else to come to mind from itself. Thus, when we see a footprint, we think that the animal whose footprint it is has passed by; and when we see smoke, we know that fire is present. Some signs, therefore, are natural and others are given. Given signs are those divinely contained in the Holy Scriptures and indicated to us by the people who wrote them,” and so forth. [Col. 1331B] “Before all else, therefore, one must be turned through the fear of God toward knowing his will—what he commands us to seek and what to avoid.”

And below: “That which exists by human institution is partly superstitious and partly not. Whatever has been instituted by human beings for making and worshiping idols, or for worshiping a creature as God, is superstitious.”

And a little later in the same book it follows: “Nevertheless, all signs seek a certain likeness in signifying, so that the signs themselves may, so far as possible, resemble the things signified. But because one thing can resemble another in many ways, signs of this kind do not have an established meaning among human beings unless agreement is added. In pictures, statues, and other imitative works of this kind—especially those of skilled craftsmen—no one who sees the likenesses fails to recognize the things that they resemble. This whole class is to be numbered among superfluous human institutions, except when it matters which of them is made, for what reason, where, when, and by whose authority,” and so forth.

## Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III

[Col. 1331C] “But anyone who either uses or venerates a useful sign divinely instituted, and understands its force and signification, does not venerate the visible and passing thing, but rather that to which all such things are to be referred. Such a person is spiritual and free even in a time of servitude, when those signs ought not yet to be disclosed to carnal minds, which must be subdued under their yoke. Such spiritual people were the patriarchs and prophets and all those among the people of Israel through whom the Holy Spirit supplied us with the help and consolation of the Scriptures,” and so forth.

## Saint Athanasius, Fourth Discourse against the Arians

“The Ariomaniacs, as has been said, judging once for all that they become transgressors—.”

And after the other material: “This may also be considered more attentively from the example of an emperor’s image. In the emperor’s image are his likeness and form, and in the emperor is the likeness that is in the image. For the form that is the emperor’s likeness in the image is unchanged, so that [Col. 1331D] whoever looks at the image sees the emperor in it; and, conversely, whoever has seen the emperor recognizes that this is the one who is in the image. Because the likeness does not change, whoever wishes to see the emperor together with the image may say (the printed transition into the image’s speech is compressed): ‘I and the emperor are one, for I am in him and he in me. What you behold in me you see in him, and what you have seen in him you also see in me.’ Whoever salutes the image salutes the emperor in it, for the image is his form and appearance,” and so forth.

## Saint Athanasius, bishop of Theopolis, to Symeon, bishop of Bostra

“If, fathers, according to the saying it is necessary—as you assert—to ask questions, and moreover to ask the elders.”

And a little later: “For just as, when the emperor is absent, his image is adored in his stead, so when he himself is present it is superfluous to leave the original form and adore the image. Is it then necessary to dishonor the image because the one for whose sake it is adored takes precedence through his presence?”

And again: [Col. 1332A] “Just as one who insults the emperor’s image will suffer a just penalty as one dishonoring the emperor himself, so too, although the image is nothing other than wood together with colors mixed and tempered with wax, anyone who dishonors a person’s sign refers the insult to the person whose sign it is,” and so forth.

## The *Tripartite History*, book VI

Sozomen says in chapter 1: “I shall not pass over in silence what happened under Julian. It was both a sign of Christ’s power and an indication of God’s wrath against the ruler. For when Julian learned that in Caesarea Philippi, a city of Phoenicia which they called Paneas, there was a notable statue of Christ, erected by the woman who had been freed from her flow of blood, he removed it and set up his own statue there. A violent fire fell from heaven upon his statue and split it at the chest. The head and neck were cast down together as one part and driven into the ground; the remaining part has stood until the present and has retained the mark [Col. 1332B] of the lightning. The pagans dragged away and broke Christ’s statue at that time, but afterward Christians gathered its pieces and stored them in a church, where it has been preserved until now.”

The same author says in chapter 42: “Thus, as Eusebius reports, this statue is known to be a remedy for every suffering and illness. Beside it grows a certain herb whose kind no physician in our country, however experienced, has recognized. It seems to me that, with the Lord’s coming, no miracle and no benefit ought to be judged incredible,” and so forth.

## The *History of the English*, book I, chapter 25

The chapter begins: “Strengthened by the encouragement of the blessed Father Gregory, Augustine, Christ’s fellow servant, returned with those who accompanied him to the work of preaching the word and reached Britain. At that time Ethelbert was the most powerful king in Kent.”

And a little later in the same account it follows: “After some days the king came to the island and, sitting in the open air, ordered Augustine and his companions to come there for a conference with him. Following an old augury, he had taken care that they should not enter any [Col. 1332C] house to meet him, lest, if they possessed some art of sorcery, they should overcome and deceive him by their coming. But they, endowed with divine rather than demonic power, approached bearing a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord and Savior painted on a panel. They sang litanies and entreated the Lord for their own eternal salvation and that of those for whose sake and to whom they had come.”

It also follows: “It is related that, as they approached the city in their customary manner with the holy cross and the image of the great king, our Lord Jesus Christ, they chanted this litany with one voice: ‘We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and anger may be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned,’” and so forth.

## The blessed Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, to John, bishop of Synada

[Col. 1332D] After receiving a letter of the blessed Pope Gregory, Germanus says among other things: “I received the letter of Your Holiness in which the bishop of Natholia was discussed. We now inform you that, even before we received Your Holiness’s letter, when that same God-beloved bishop joined us here in conversation, we questioned him about the opinion that had been reported to us concerning him. He gave us this answer. It is appropriate to relate everything individually to Your Holiness: ‘Because I heard divine Scripture say, “You shall not make for yourself any likeness of the things in heaven above or on earth below so as to adore them” (Exod. 20), I said on that basis that adoration is not owed to things made by hand. Yet we regard Christ’s holy martyrs, who are the true pearls of faith, as worthy of every honor, and we invoke their intercessions.’ We answered him that the Christian faith refers veneration and adoration to the one and only God, as it is written: ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. 6). Our glorification [Col. 1333A] and service are offered to him alone.”

And a little later: “In the saints who are in heaven, and in the invisible and incorporeal powers, the holy Trinity is praised and glorified under one dominion and divinity, just as one God is confessed by us; and apart from him there is none who rules in his power forever.”

And a little later: “We do not transfer the veneration of divine dominion to fellow servants. When we adore the likeness of emperors or princes on earth, we do not appear to offer adoration to it as to God. Nor have we received the making of images, formed with wax and colors, as a transference of divine veneration. We do not represent the invisible deity by an image, likeness, guise, or any form whatever; not even the orders in which the angels exist can in any way be perceived or investigated. But because the only-begotten Son, who is in the Father’s bosom, recalled his own creature from the death of judgment and, by the good will [Col. 1333B] of the Father and the Holy Spirit, deigned to become man—being, as the Apostle says, made like us in all things apart from sin (Phil. 2)—we represent in an image his human face and his human likeness according to the flesh, and not his incomprehensible or invisible deity,” and so forth.

“In the same way, we display the likeness according to the flesh of his undefiled mother, the holy Mother of God, because, being a woman by nature and not made of substance alien to ours, she conceived in her womb and bore incarnate the invisible God who holds all things in his hand. We therefore venerate and magnify her properly and truly as the mother of the true God. We admire and call blessed Christ’s holy martyrs, apostles, and prophets, and in remembrance of their courage we portray their likenesses in images. We do not regard them as “sounds of the divine nature” (the printed *sonos*, “sounds,” is obscure), nor [Col. 1333C] do we bestow upon them the honor and adoration owed to the deity’s glory and power. Rather, through these things we manifest the love that we have for them and represent what we truly believe through hearing. For the saints of God themselves reserved service, glorification, and adoration for the one and only God; summoning and teaching everyone to do the same, they shed their blood and received the crown for confessing the truth. This is the principle governing the painting of images: we do not transfer to handmade images the adoration offered in spirit and truth to the invisible deity. Instead, in this way we show the love that we rightly have for the beloved servants of our God, and in their honor God, who glorified them, is glorified,” and so forth.

## On the meanings of adoration, from the seventh session

“Adoration is understood in many ways. There is an adoration according to honor, love, and fear, in the way that rulers and their authority are adored.

“There is another kind, properly the adoration of fear, as Jacob adored Esau (Gen. 33).

[Col. 1333D] “Again there is an adoration according to gratitude, as when Abraham, on account of the field that he received from the sons of Seth for the burial of his wife Sarah, adored them (Gen. 23).

“Again there is an adoration made in the belief that some protection will be obtained from persons of higher rank, as Jacob adored Pharaoh (Gen. 47).

“There is a true and most certain adoration which is owed only to almighty and divine majesty, as Scripture says: ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. 6). It is not lawful to transfer this adoration to any creature or to change it into adoration of things made by hand,” and so forth.

## Augustine, *On the Holy Trinity*

Speaking of the Holy Spirit, Augustine says among other things: “The Holy Spirit is altogether equal to the Father and the Son, and consubstantial and coeternal in the unity of the Trinity. [Col. 1334A] It is especially clear that the Holy Spirit is not a creature in the passage where we are commanded to serve the Creator and not the creature. This is not the manner in which we are commanded to serve one another through charity, which in Greek is *douleuein* (δουλεύειν), but the manner of service given only to God, which in Greek is *latreuein* (λατρεύειν). Hence those who offer to images the service owed to God are called idolaters. It is of this service that it was said: ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. 6). This is expressed more distinctly in the Greek Scripture, for it has *latreuseis* (λατρεύσεις), “you shall serve [God].”

“Now, if we are forbidden to serve a creature with such service, since it was said, ‘You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,’ and if this is why the Apostle condemns those who worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, then the Holy Spirit, to whom all the saints offer such service, is certainly not a creature. The Apostle says: ‘For we are the circumcision, serving the Spirit of God’ (Phil. 3), which in Greek is *latreuontes* (λατρεύοντες), “serving [God].” [Col. 1334B] Many Latin manuscripts also read, ‘we who serve the Spirit of God.’ For Greek *latria* is called ‘service’ in Latin, and, so far as true religion is concerned, it is owed to the one and only God,” and so forth.

## Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*

“God made the soul immortal, I think—unless perhaps it seems otherwise to you. Therefore, would you wish human beings to make things like those that God made?”

“I certainly would not have said that. But just as he, being immortal, made something immortal in his likeness, so what we, who were made immortal by God, make in our likeness ought to be immortal.”

“You would speak correctly if, in painting a panel in your image, you painted that which you believe to be immortal in you. As it is, however, you express in it the likeness of a body, which is certainly mortal.”

“How, then, am I like God, when I cannot make anything immortal as he can?”

“Just as the image of your body cannot have the power that your body has, so it is not surprising that the soul does not possess [Col. 1334C] power as great as the one in whose likeness it was made,” and so forth.

## Isidore, bishop, on painting

[*Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 16; source note at Col. 1333D.]

“A picture is an image that expresses the appearance of some thing and, when seen, brings the mind back to its remembrance.”

Again: “The Egyptians invented painting. At first they traced the outline of a person’s shadow with lines. Thus, in the beginning painting was of this kind; in its second stage it used individual colors, and afterward various colors. In this way the art itself gradually became differentiated and discovered light and shade and the differences of colors. Hence painters even now first draw certain shadows and the lines of the future image, and then complete them with colors, preserving the order in which the art was invented.”

Again: “Colors are so called because they are perfected by the heat (*calor*) of fire or the sun, or because in the beginning they were strained (*colabantur*) so that they might attain the greatest fineness,” and so forth.

## Augustine, *On the Teacher*

“Concerning the things that are understood, we consult the inner truth by reason. What can be said to demonstrate that we learn anything through words beyond the sound itself that strikes the ears? [Col. 1334D] For everything we perceive, we perceive either by the bodily senses or by the mind. The former things we call sensible and the latter intelligible—or, to speak in the manner of our authors, the former carnal and the latter spiritual.

“When we are questioned about sensible things, we answer if the things we perceive are at hand. Thus, when someone asks us, as we look at the new moon, what it is like or where it is, the questioner, if he does not see it, believes our words—and often does not believe them. But he does not learn in any way unless he himself sees what is being described; at that point he learns from the things themselves and his senses, not from words. The same words sound to one who sees as sounded before to one who did not see.

“When, however, we are asked not about things that we presently perceive, but about things we once perceived, we speak no longer of the things themselves but of the images impressed by them and entrusted to memory. I do not know how we can call what we say true when we behold false images, except that we report not that we now see and perceive those things, but that we saw and perceived them. [Col. 1335A] Thus we carry those images in the inner chambers of memory as certain records of things that have passed. Contemplating them in the mind, we do not lie when we speak, in good conscience; but these records are ours. If the hearer perceived the things and was present, he does not learn from my words but recognizes them by the images that he too carried away with him. If he did not perceive them, who does not understand that he believes words rather than learns?

“But when the subject is what we behold with the mind—that is, with intellect and reason—we speak of things that we contemplate as present in that inner light of truth by which the person called the inner man is illuminated and rejoices,” and so forth.

# Chapter XVI. How the destruction of images first arose in the Eastern churches

*[From the Second Council of Nicaea, act 5; compare Theophanes in the *Miscellany*, John of Damascus, *On Heresies*, and Zonaras, *Annals*, volume III. Source note at Col. 1335D.]*

There was a certain tyrant named Seleman, an Agarene by race.
