When he died, Humarus succeeded him [Col. 1335B] in the kingdom, and Humarus was in turn succeeded by Ezidus, a very frivolous and foolish man. In his time there was at Berias [variant: Tiberias] a sorcerer and diviner named Serantapicus [variant: Sarantapechy], a teacher of the wicked Hebrews and an enemy of God’s Church. When he discovered the frivolity of Ezidus the *protosymbolus* (“chief counsellor”), he approached him and began to divine and foretell certain things for him. Having thereby won his favor, not long afterward he began to say to him:

“I wish to disclose to Your Benignity how, if you listen to me, length of life may be added to you and you may continue in this principate for thirty years, provided that you fulfill my words.”

That foolish tyrant, his mind darkened by the desire for long life, said: “Whatever you command me, I stand ready to accomplish. If I obtain what you have promised, I shall repay you with the greatest honors.”

The sorcerer and diviner answered him: “Order a general letter to be written at once, directing that every painted image be erased in all Christian churches, whether on walls, on sacred vessels, or on altar cloths, [Col. 1335C] and not only these but also the images displayed in the public squares of cities.”

When that faithless tyrant heard this, he commanded every prefecture in every place to abolish the images in churches and the other likenesses, and thus he “adorned” the churches of God (printed *exornavit*, used ironically in this account of their stripping). From that time destroyers of images began to appear. But the tyrant himself died in the following year, and the images were restored with honor to their former condition, and so forth.

*[Some material is missing here.]*

# Letter in the name of Emperor Louis to the Roman pontiff

*[Lacuna.]*

Since, therefore, through the love of God—which, by his gift, has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us—it is undoubtedly known to the universal Church that everything done within that holy Church of God for the attainment of everlasting salvation must be done so cautiously through the grace of that same Holy [Col. 1335D] Spirit that the special privilege of charity may be preserved: the privilege which the Lord himself, author and giver of every good, when he was about to depart bodily from the world, deigned both to give and to leave to his faithful as the highest and greatest gift, saying, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). The Apostle’s words must likewise be considered with the greatest attention: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12).

It is therefore very necessary that whoever desires to reach that homeland into which discord never could and never can enter should earnestly strive both to maintain with everyone that peace of charity which pleases God and to recall to true concord all who are at variance with that peace.

[Col. 1336A] For it is certain that, just as anyone who could preserve that charity—the charity of brotherhood pleasing to God—but refused to do so could not reach the palace of charity, so anyone who knew others to be divided against that unity of love, and could recall them to the path of so great a blessedness but did not strive to do so with all his strength, closes the gate of that blessedness against himself with the strongest bars. By God’s entirely just judgment he likewise places an obstacle in his own path, preventing himself from walking it, if, according to the measure of his condition, he does not strive manfully, to the extent that he can resist, to keep all who are of one mind in God from falling into the abyss of discord.

These principles were not discovered by human argument. Divine authority teaches them, has spread them throughout the whole world, and has made them universally known. They ought to prevail so that wherever people are at variance they may be recalled to concord, while those who are in concord may be protected by everyone able to do so, lest they fall into discord.

[Col. 1336B] With this summary preface, the course of this discourse now requires the words that follow to explain clearly why these things have been set forth.

As the Holy Spirit has revealed to the entire ecclesiastical order, among the other evidences of piety, faith, hope, and charity are preeminent, as the Apostle bears witness. These virtues in turn are preserved inviolate, by God their author, through prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Those four virtues, when applied to sober human conduct, are possessed and employed through reason, discernment, honor, and usefulness. No one who lacks the latter can possess the former perfectly, nor, having rejected the latter, can anyone ever use the former rightly.

Although some matters exceed human reason—as do some things that can be reached by faith alone and are therefore called ineffable or incomprehensible—divine authority in the sacred books and in the decrees of the holy catholic Fathers, through God’s revelation, sufficiently discloses how those matters are to be held and confessed. [Col. 1336C] For this reason almost everyone desires, wishes, and asks that, with divine authority always and everywhere preserved and given precedence, reason should go before, accompany, or follow in every question about which certainty is desired. No merely human invention should first be set against someone before he is instructed by useful reasoning and fully informed concerning the matter about which he desires certainty.

One must therefore take the greatest care never to forbid reason to a rational person who desires and requests it, except only where, as mentioned above, so great and ineffable a sublimity confronts us that the humility of all human reasoning rightly bows beneath it.

Because we are brothers redeemed at one price, namely Christ’s blood, and because by his mercy—through which we are what we are—we have been permitted to know this, we must admit with every affection of mind, as stated above, the need of our brothers, that is, of the whole empire of the Eastern Romans, into the innermost depths [Col. 1336D] of our hearts. We have learned that their inviolable charity has been cruelly, and as many think irrationally, torn apart for no occasion of dispute other than this: some of them, together with Michael and Theophilus the emperors, our most beloved brothers, do not wish to have images of the saints; others among the same holy people, on the contrary, wish not only to have but also to adore them.

Their conflict has reached such a point that those who do not wish to have images do not permit those who wish to have them to do so, while those who wish to have images compel the unwilling even to adore them. Pulling in contrary directions against one another, each party has collected or heaped up, whether from human argument and reason or from divine authority and the writings of the holy Fathers, many testimonies that seem to it suitable to its will: one side thinks that by them it can vindicate and maintain its opinion, and the other side thinks the same of its own. [Col. 1337A]

It is fitting—truly fitting and just—that, with the power of the Holy Spirit going before him, the first arbiter among human beings to come forward in the Lord’s name to correct such matters and lead those people back to the way of truth under most holy governance should be the man whom almighty God has deigned to place in the apostolic see and to give as the apostles’ vicar to his holy Church. For this reason that same holy Church of God throughout the world has decreed for him, above all other pontiffs, a special name: he alone, not through his own abuse of the title but by the authority of such great apostles, is called, styled, and regarded by all as universal pope.

And since, as all know, the Apostle John says, “It is the last hour” (1 John 2), and Paul says, “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10), the time presses and the day of judgment approaches without any long delay. No one can doubt that, among the other devices of his ruin, the devil especially strives to tear apart the holy Church of God’s mutual charity on the last day, to split its unanimity on any occasion, and to corrupt the inward bonds of love, so that the dreadful day may find it not in the peace mentioned above but divided and mangled. [Col. 1337B]

Nor is it hidden that the unhappy author of unhappiness, the most wretched of all the wretched, does not care by what occasion—bodily, spiritual, worldly, or ecclesiastical—he can accomplish this, provided that by some device he can rupture the mutual unity in love which pleases God. Although the entire ecclesiastical order rightly ought to oppose him, no one under these circumstances is bound by a greater obligation than the man who, through the apostles’ authority and out of reverence for them, has merited the privilege of so great an honor in the apostolic see throughout the world. Yet he is not rightly called universal if he does not struggle with all the strength he possesses for the state of the universal [Col. 1337C] Church.

Lord Father, most holy pontiff venerated and revered by the whole world, we have endeavored to set these things first so as to disclose the devotion of our mind in so grave a matter.

From this point, if Your Nurturing Holiness, whom God preserve, so chooses, we shall take care to add, by way of admonition rather than merely reporting,how our common embassy might be directed to correct that holy Church of God. God forbid that we should presume to impose a limit upon the higher and more sublime advance of your holy, God-given wisdom. Rather, lest we hide in silence what the omnipotent mercy of almighty God has deigned to bestow on us in this matter for your service and our salvation, we have placed our thoughts, as befits a son, in the bosom of your paternal judgment. We trust in the Lord that he will deign to inspire in you what is pleasing and acceptable to him.

We did not, however, assemble a synod. Instead, as we requested of you and received permission to act, we considered the matter together with our intimates, your sons, during such intervals as we could find while occupied by the many and varied cares of the kingdom. [Col. 1337D] We sought to determine what we might report to Your Nurturing Holiness about so great a need and how that people, whom God is to preserve through your orthodox holiness, might be recalled to true concord, joined together by true peace, and made pleasing to the Lord of all both in this age and in the age to come. Whatever salutary counsel we were able to find by the Lord’s inspiration, we have sent to Your Paternity through the present bearers, your sons and our brothers, communicating some things orally and others in writing.

# Letter in the name of the Roman pontiff to Michael and Theophilus, emperors of the Greeks

*[Lacuna.]*

I ask and entreat throughout the whole world—to use the words [Col. 1338A] of my blessed predecessor, my lord Pope Gregory—my brothers and my lords: insofar as you are sinners, you are my brothers; insofar as you are righteous, you are my lords. Insofar as I speak from myself, I humbly beseech you; insofar as I speak from so great an authority, I solemnly admonish you. Let no one despise me here on my own account, for even if I appear wholly unworthy to issue the invitation, great indeed is the power of the charity, peace, and unity to which, by the lofty authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, whose place I hold, I presume to invite you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For when Paul says with truthful voice, “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, because without it no one will see God” (Heb. 12), what could be happier than to see God, desiring him in this age and enjoying him in the next? Conversely, what could be unhappier than to fail to merit the sight of God, either by blessed desire in this age or by more blessed enjoyment in the next?

Testimonies to this assertion and truth are so numerous throughout the whole world that no tongue could recount them at the present time. No mortal can foreknow when his own end—or, a greater matter, the fall and end of the whole world—must come. [Col. 1338B] Consequently, as everyone knows, a great necessity presses me not to dare delay any longer the payment of what I owe as a duty, lest perhaps, by withholding so great a debt of charity, I appear guilty concerning all of you before the eternal Judge. The source reads *deferre*, “to postpone”; a variant has *differre*, likewise “to defer.”

Therefore I ask and admonish you—first, Michael and Theophilus, sons of the Church of the most high God, glorious emperors of the Romans exalted on high by God, together with the entire catholic and most noble senate and the people entrusted to you by God for governance—to hear patiently what we have judged it necessary to admonish, exhort, and explain for your salvation by the authority of blessed Peter, to whom our Lord and God Jesus Christ deigned to entrust the keys of the kingdom of heaven, saying, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16). Prepare your God-pleasing mind, not to despise these things, but to obey and preserve them. The transmitted wording *primo me* is difficult here; Baronius reads *primi mei*, which could yield “my foremost sons.”

[Col. 1338C] We exhort you to obey us because we are prepared to arrange and confirm under three principal headings everything that we shall say to you concerning this cause: reason, authority, and counsel. We shall construct an argument; confirm that argument by authority insofar as it is reasonable, discerning, honorable, and useful; understand that authority in a salutary way according to the truth and rectitude of the catholic faith; and, finally, give and confirm God-pleasing counsel about what must be maintained in these matters for the salvation of the universal Church.

Although divine authority, as is fitting, excels all else, we nevertheless wish first to satisfy everyone by reasoning, so as to soothe and unite minds pulling in contrary directions. Thus, once united, they may more readily receive divine authority according to the sound understanding of the catholic faith, and then embrace definite counsel from us more gladly and preserve what they have embraced in the future. [Col. 1338D]

Among all the members of this holy Western Church, which glories that by the Lord’s gift it took its beginning in faith, hope, and charity through the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the Church has been protected by the Holy Spirit through those same apostles and by their intercession and defense, and has been preserved unstained by every heresy until the present. It not only did not turn aside toward any deviation of error, but rather, through the apostles’ orthodox successors, recalled toward rectitude throughout the world all who in any way strayed from the straight path of faith.

The witness to this is not some single corner but the whole world. Whenever persecutions of such a kind have been stirred throughout the world that they were thought to threaten the faith of the universal Church, the universal Church has always been accustomed—either in the presence of the pontiff of this holy see or at least with his consent conveyed by word or letter—to correct the matter in order to find the truth of the catholic faith and, once found, to establish it for preservation. [Col. 1339A] The printed text has *perceptiones* (“perceptions”) where the variant *persecutiones* (“persecutions”) supplies the sense.

Likewise, in matters concerning the preservation of that Church’s unstained condition in human actions, the Roman see has been accustomed, under the guidance of reason supported not by deceitful or sophistical duplicity but by truth, and illuminated alike by discernment, honor, and usefulness, to cut away not only harmful and injurious things but also superfluous and unnecessary ones. As stated above, it has been accustomed through discussion and ordinance to sanction those things that pertain to the salvation of the whole Church and which, moreover, it rightly ought not to avoid.

It has acted in this way not only in causes of faith, or, as already stated, concerning the condition of the human race and the course of rectitude, but also concerning every dissension in the holy Church of God [Col. 1339B] that appeared to disturb the peace which the Lord left to the apostles, and through the apostles to us all, in place of his presence, saying, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). Wherever it could reach by any exercise of piety, the apostolic vicars of this holy see have always endeavored to recall people to peaceful concord—soothing some, but, if the matter required it, teaching and preaching to others with the lofty and venerable authority that was fitting.

Although we are whatever we may be, yet undertaking their office by authority, strengthened alike by charity and by that same authority, we have learned that we cannot decline the duty of summoning to peace—through the mediation of those very apostles [Col. 1339C]—the dissension that has arisen between the ever God-beloved Roman and Greek Churches, a dissension that has long divided that Church more harshly than could in any way be compatible with its salvation. This is especially so because the subject of this most wretched dissension is one without which, as many think, the Church can undoubtedly be saved through faith, hope, and charity, both in this age and in the age to come. Their view and judgment is as follows:

“What could have harmed faith, hope, and charity if no image had ever been painted or fashioned anywhere throughout the world?”

And although our sons who say this do not doubt that they can demonstrate their position reasonably [*dubitabant*: “they did not doubt”], it would nevertheless have been better if that practice had never existed, without whose veneration the universal holy Church of God could have remained safe in perfect faith, hope, and charity, than that, on its account, she should incur the undeniable—indeed, most certain—evil of discord. Unless this evil is corrected, no one can ever reach the Lord, who is peace, in everlasting fellowship with all who possess the peace pleasing to him while this dissension continues.

And although their devotion constantly demands that they subsequently be allowed to explain by reasoning how they think discreetly and reasonably [Col. 1339D] about these images, they do not doubt that it is salutary for every person who wishes to undertake this with just moderation. Nevertheless, in comparison with so great an evil, they count the whole matter of images as nothing, if that peace which leads to eternal life—who is the way, the truth, and the life—is not led to that same way and truth.

Therefore the entire company of priests, as well as the whole senate of the Frankish people or empire, and the universal Church throughout Gaul, together with the other provinces subject to that empire preserved by God, upon hearing the report that the dissension among their brethren is to be destroyed, irrevocably demand that, first of all, through the authority of this holy see, preserved by God and, as they confidently believe—and we all trust through the merits of the apostles—to be preserved until the end of the age, we hasten to seek this above all: since, by God’s ordinance, these two principal kingdoms throughout the world are bound to one another by a mutual charity pleasing to God [Col. 1340A], may that dart of the devil be dispersed from the Church, and may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, be fully restored among that blessed people.

For with one voice and one heart they cry out to heaven that the judgment of almighty God will inevitably fall upon us if, by the authority of the supreme apostles throughout the world, through whose teaching and counsel the whole world bows, we do not strive to lead your discord back to true concord. They also ask what they are to do about the loss of so great a consolation before God, if, after the unchangeable protection of this holy see, they lose in those especially beloved brethren the consolation that they will have nowhere else in the universal Church. For if they do not preserve true faith and the full ardor of charity with them, what will they have neglected at the Lord’s judgment, when they have so gravely neglected charity and what has most certainly been confirmed in the Lord’s name?

But, sparing you the fatigue of a lengthy reading, and sparing your dignity [*fastigio*, perhaps “weariness” (*fastidio*)] in reading [Col. 1340B], we omit the many things that, under the pressure of such charity, they lamented—indeed, mourned—in tears concerning the mutual love pleasing to God, things that would be difficult to gather into one account. Let us return to unfolding [Col. 1340C] the sequence that they themselves promised to set forth concerning the justification of images. For they say:

“Therefore, most holy and most blessed pontiff, we ask that we may be permitted to recount the course of life of our ancient fathers in this matter, while also inserting and adding, as the order of reason requires, the disposition of their minds in this particular question—why they held one position or another. May it not weary you if, in order to display the reason of truth and the truth of reason, our speech extends somewhat further, provided that the line of truth, drawn inflexibly from our ancient fathers down to us, is preserved.

This line begins with blessed Dionysius, who, after Saint Clement, the successor of blessed Peter the Apostle, was the first of his successors in the apostolate to be sent into Gaul as its first preacher with twelve companions. After some time he was crowned with martyrdom together with his companions, who had been dispersed here and there throughout that kingdom for the sake of preaching.

Although there are many others—some martyrs, others confessors—whose merits before God, although they shine through daily miracles, may nevertheless be less familiar to you because of the distance of the lands, we shall pass over them. We consider it necessary, however, to recall Saint Hilary, an ancient teacher of the Church, and blessed Martin, venerated throughout the world, whom we do not doubt are very well known to you. Instructed by the teaching of their lives, we have undertaken to hold and preserve these practices in this way.

But since neither among us nor among our forebears, for as long as any present generation can remember, has any such question ever been raised or debated, the following custom has always been retained from those ancient times throughout the Church of this kingdom: no one has prohibited anyone who wished to paint or fashion an image, even if he acted as though he were commanding by the authority of that same holy Church of God [Col. 1340D]. Hence the same custom is observed among us to this day: since no authority commands this, no one should command it; and likewise, since no authority prohibits it, no one should prohibit it.

Since, for the reason already stated, the matter cannot be otherwise unless an account is given of it, perhaps the reasoning may appropriately begin as follows. If no image had been painted or fashioned anywhere throughout the world, would that harm anything belonging to the faith, hope, or charity of the holy Church of God?

Again, if images were painted or fashioned in the manner in which they are found especially in certain churches or the palaces of princes—not for any other worship of the Catholic faith or religion, but merely, for those who understand, as a pious memorial or ornament of those places, and for those who do not understand, as instruction in that same piety—and if they were likewise painted or fashioned in the other dwellings suited to such images and expressing the same meaning, what could they ever or anywhere have harmed the virtues mentioned above?

Since the matter stands thus [Col. 1341A], what remains except that those who do not wish to have them should not do so, while nevertheless not contradicting those who wish to possess or make them in the sense stated above? Similarly, those who wish to have them should not compel unwilling people to possess or make them. Thus, by God’s ordinance, both sides remain unharmed: the person who wishes to have them can undoubtedly remain safe by guarding against illicit worship, and the person who does not wish to have them can remain safe by guarding against illicit contempt.

Thus, imitating the custom of our ancestors regarding images or paintings, we do not doubt that, whether commanding or prohibiting, possessing or not possessing, venerating or not venerating them, we have hitherto passed through this matter unharmed with the Lord’s help, and that, under his governance, we shall continue to do so.

Therefore all who wish to possess them must be admonished not to offer them any illicit worship by loving them, praying to them in any manner, or embracing them beyond what is proper. Likewise, those who do not wish to possess them [*nec illi*, “nor should those”], if they happen to see them [Col. 1341B], must not presume to despise, insult, or mutilate them with any disgraceful or abusive detestation.

From this it can undoubtedly be gathered what reason could compel anyone, at whatever risk, to possess what he may plainly possess without any risk. The sum of the whole matter, therefore, is this: those who wish to have images painted or fashioned in suitable places, whether as a personal memorial or for sound instruction, may have them without any illicit worship. Those who do not wish to have them should not, without any illicit contempt, despise images that are thus possessed or have been possessed.

There would certainly be many more things that could be said or written here by reasoning, entirely consistent with these points, if either the brevity of the time allowed it or some necessity had demanded that they be written down in order to confirm them.”

## Authority

[Col. 1341C]

“For the satisfaction of the brethren mentioned above and of the Church of the kingdom referred to earlier, these matters have been set forth separately in an appropriate account or sequence, since otherwise it could not have been done. Anyone who wishes to satisfy his mind through reasoning as to why that Church has wished, from ancient times, to conduct itself in this matter with such moderation concerning the possession or non-possession of images may do so all the more briefly, because by reading he can learn the collected meaning of their position at one time rather than in scattered passages.

This reasoning now teaches, as was indicated above, that we should return to the authority of the holy Fathers who wrote something on this subject and left it to us in writing, and see whether that authority ought to affirm the reasoning already given by agreeing with it, or not.

It seems to us, therefore, that although many Fathers insert relevant observations on this subject in their other works, which they diligently composed under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit concerning the state of the holy Church of God, the first place in this examination should rightly be given [Col. 1341D] to those who are found to have written about this matter specifically and solely in order to resolve this question.

Among these, blessed Pope Gregory, pontiff of this holy Church of God, is the first to come before us. He wrote specifically to Serenus, bishop of Massilia, as is contained in the letter addressed to him and preserved in the archives of our holy Church of God. Gregory had heard that Serenus, inflamed—as it seemed to him—by zeal against what he considered the superfluous worship of images, had removed, broken, and entirely cast outside his church all the images that he had received there, so that by this act he might restrain the people from illicit veneration or adoration.

We judged that nothing could be done more appropriately in this matter than to place that letter first in this work of ours, which, trusting in the merits of the blessed apostles, we have undertaken with faithful intent and composed and ordered chiefly out of love for the true peace of the holy Church, believing that through them we may obtain the grace to bring this most necessary ecclesiastical work to its God-pleasing completion.

For he writes as follows:

[Col. 1342A]

> ‘I have recently learned,’ he says, ‘that your Fraternity, seeing certain worshipers of images, broke and cast out those same images from the churches. We praised your zeal, certainly, in preventing anything made by human hands from being worshiped; but we judge that you ought not to have broken those images. For this reason paintings are displayed in churches: so that those who do not know letters may at least read by seeing on the walls what they are unable to read in books. Your Fraternity, therefore, ought both to preserve them and to prohibit the people from worshiping them, so that those ignorant of letters might have a means of acquiring knowledge of the history, while the people would not sin at all in worshiping the painting.’

### The Same to the Same

> ‘It had indeed been reported to us,’ he says, ‘that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you were breaking the images of the saints [Col. 1342B] under the pretext that they ought not to be worshiped. Because you forbade their worship, we praised you entirely; but we reproved you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: have you ever heard that any priest did what you have done? Even if nothing else restrained you, should not this have done so—that, despising the other brethren, you alone should think yourself holy and wise?
>
> ‘It is one thing to worship a painting, and another to learn from the subject represented in the painting what ought to be worshiped. For what writing provides to readers, a painting provides to the uneducated who look at it, since in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow, and in it those who do not know letters read. For this reason, a painting serves the nations especially in place of reading—something that you, who live among the nations, ought to have considered very carefully, lest, while inflamed by proper zeal but without caution, you generate scandal in fierce minds.
>
> ‘Therefore what had been placed in the churches not for worship but solely for the instruction of the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken. And since antiquity has permitted images of the saints’ histories to be painted in venerable places not without [Col. 1342C] good reason, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could undoubtedly have attained what you intended beneficially and gathered rather than scattered the assembled flock, so that the name of shepherd might rightly be honored in you instead of the blame of a scatterer resting upon you.
>
> ‘But while you recklessly carried out this movement of your mind, you are said to have scandalized your sons so greatly that the greater part of them withdrew from your communion. When, then, will you bring wandering sheep to the Lord’s fold, when you cannot retain those whom you have? Therefore we exhort you to take care, even now, to restrain yourself from this presumption, and to hasten with paternal gentleness, using every effort and every diligence, to recall to yourself the minds of those whom you know to have been separated from your unity.
>
> ‘The various sons of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of Scripture that it is not permissible to worship anything made by human hands, since it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. VI). Then it must be added that, because you saw the painted images [Col. 1342D] that had been made for the edification of the uneducated people—so that those who did not know letters might learn what had happened by contemplating the history itself—being turned into worship, you were moved to order those images to be broken.
>
> ‘They must also be told that, if they wish to have in their churches images made for the instruction for which images were anciently made, you should permit them in every way both to be offered and to be kept. But make clear that it was not the sight of the history itself, disclosed through the testimony of the painting, that displeased you, but the worship improperly offered to the paintings.
>
> ‘By soothing their minds with these words, recall them to concord; and if anyone wishes to make images, do not prohibit him. But avoid worshiping images in every way. Let your Fraternity carefully admonish them, however, so that from seeing the event represented they may receive the ardor of compunction and humbly prostrate themselves in worship before the one almighty Holy Trinity.’

### The Same to Januarius, Bishop

[Col. 1343A]

> ‘The Jews,’ he says, ‘coming here from your city, have complained to us that Peter, who by God’s will was led from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith, accompanied by certain undisciplined men, seized their synagogue at Caralis on the day after his baptism—that is, on the very Sunday feast of Easter—with grave scandal and without your permission, and installed there an image of the Mother of God, of our Lord, and a venerable cross, together with the white garment in which he had been clothed when he arose from the font, and so forth.’

And shortly afterward he says:

> ‘Considering the intention of your will in this matter, and especially your judgment, we exhort you with this concern: you ought to restore what was taken by force, after removing from that place the image and the cross with the veneration that is proper to them.’

### The Same to Secundinus, Servant of God and Recluse

> ‘The images,’ he says, ‘which you asked us to send to you through your deacon Dulcidius [Col. 1343B] . . . your request has greatly pleased us, because with your whole intention you seek him whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that daily bodily sight may kindle your devotion, and, when you see the painting, you may burn inwardly for the one whose image you contemplate.
>
> ‘We do nothing unreasonable if, through visible things, we demonstrate invisible things. Thus a person who ardently desires to see someone else, or who lovingly desires to see a bride whom he is trying to see, if the opportunity arises to go to the baths or proceed to a church, prepares himself eagerly on the way so that he may depart rejoicing from the sight.
>
> ‘We know that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as God, but in remembrance of the Son of God, so that you may grow warm in love for the one whose image you contemplate. We do not, in fact, prostrate ourselves before the image as though before the divinity; rather, we worship the one whom, through the image, we remember as having been born, suffered, or seated upon the throne.
>
> ‘And while the painting itself, like writing, recalls the Son of God to our memory [Col. 1343C], it either makes our spirit rejoice over the resurrection or soothes it concerning the Passion. Therefore we have sent you, through our aforementioned son the deacon, two *systerias* [perhaps “panels” or “diptychs”], an image of the Savior and of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the apostles Peter and Paul, together with one key-shaped cross as a blessing, so that you may be defended from the evil one, believing yourself protected by its holy wood.’

Thus far the letter of Gregory.

But since this order of words can appear so inverted and confused to those who do not understand it that, unless it is considered carefully, some less capable people might understand it as though blessed Gregory testified that he had done what he had first declared unlawful for everyone and that it was lawful for him to do so, no one who has come to know his statements by examining or reading them may be permitted to remain ignorant of how absurd and unworthy of so great a teacher of the Church it would be to understand him as acting contrary to the religion of the holy Church of God.

For the justice and rectitude of the holy, and especially of the Roman, Church [Col. 1343D] cannot tolerate the claim that he was contradictory to himself. Even if the poverty of our ignorance is unable to understand this, it is better that it should presume to rise against our ignorance than against such great wisdom given by God.

And if God’s merciful goodness deigns to illuminate even slightly the little understanding we possess, it is very easy to see how the statements are not contradictory. There is no doubt that he restrained those who worshiped from worshiping images. But in what he wrote to Secundinus—“We do not, in fact, prostrate ourselves before the image as though before the divinity; rather, we worship the one whom, through the image, we remember as having been born, suffered, or seated upon the throne”—where, as stated above, he appears to have spoken contradictorily, the darkness of our understanding confuses us.

To prevent unnecessary ignorance from troubling us longer, the meaning of that sentence is as follows: “We do not prostrate ourselves before the image as though before the divinity, but we worship the one,” and so forth.

[Col. 1344A]

It is as though you were to say to a king seated on his throne: “We do not, O king, prostrate ourselves before you as before the divinity, but we worship the one whom, through your image—for you are a human being—we remember as the human Lord Jesus Christ, born, suffering, or seated upon the throne, whose imitator you are as you sit upon the throne.” Does such a statement immediately imply that I am compelled to worship that same king while he sits upon his throne?

So likewise, when it is said, “We do not prostrate ourselves before the image as though before the divinity, but we worship the one,” and so forth, we are not invited to worship images. For just as we find sentences written in many volumes of divine authority with their word order inverted, so here too we do not doubt that the statement has been made with the meaning given above.

[Col. 1344B]

Since it is written, “We do not prostrate ourselves before the image as though before the divinity,” who would not observe that the statement rejects rather than commands or practices the worship of images? How much more, then, will restoring the order of the words to its proper sequence, as was done above, correct anyone who, through excessive simplicity, has gone astray by supposing that the blessed teacher of the holy Church of God held an opinion contrary to himself?

Moreover, even if someone with subtler understanding happened to read this carelessly or inattentively, he could easily judge himself and recall himself to sound understanding by considering why he had at some point interpreted it otherwise. But if anyone—which may be far from all sound and wise people—should prefer to follow his own interpretation and condemn Gregory rather than correct himself, there can be no doubt that he deserves to be condemned by the whole Church, and especially by the holy Roman Church of God.

For it is utterly impossible that these two statements should not be contradictory: one prohibits the people from worshiping images [Col. 1344C], lest they appear guilty of a crime by doing so; the other is said to testify that Gregory himself did this and taught others to do it. But far be this from so great and such a universal teacher of the Catholic Church: he was accustomed never to leave unresolved any obscure questions of Scripture that appeared contradictory to him and that came before him for explanation or interpretation. He would not have left his own statements in discord with one another.

Having briefly set forth these points to avoid such rashness, we must now see whether any Catholic Father, even if no special necessity of writing on this subject rested upon him, has something in his other works that appears to agree with this Father’s position concerning images.

For behold, blessed Ambrose, an ancient and reputable teacher of the Church of God, says the following while treating Paul’s Epistle to the Romans:

> “By what reasoning or by what authority should images of angels or of other saints [Col. 1344D] be worshiped, when the holy angels themselves and holy human beings did not wish to be worshiped while alive?”

## Counsel

Accordingly, as we proposed, we have inserted authority in second place—not as much as could have been drawn from the Church’s abundant treasury, but as much as the brevity proper to a letter permitted—in order to admonish and exhort you, venerable princes of the world, together with the entire holy Church of God that, by the Lord’s dispensation and commission, you govern. We ask that you listen attentively to what our true humility, not any rashness, has striven to make known to you; that, out of reverence for those who, at the promise of the Lord himself, will come as judges of the whole world on the last day, you reverently receive it; and that you diligently strive to preserve it for the salvation of all of you.

We stated a little earlier that, after giving the reasoning and inserting the authority [Col. 1345A], we ought, for the sake of uniting the Church that you govern by the ordering of the Lord God, to offer you counsel—not of our own invention but by divine authority—by which that same holy Mother Church might be joined together in true peace, so that she might please him both in this age and in the age to come who, as he was about to ascend from the world, promised his followers, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

And since, as Paul attests among other things, it is true that “if someone hands over his body to be burned but does not have charity, he is nothing” (1 Cor. XIII), we desire with all our strength that the holy Church of God mentioned above be united in the concord of true peace, because we cannot understand in any way how she could possess mutual charity without it. It may happen that one person has with another a partial or feigned temporal peace; but no authority teaches that anyone can have true charity with another without possessing true mutual peace.

Therefore it must be considered very carefully [Col. 1345B] with what rashness or audacity anyone supposes that he can reach eternity if he does not care to restore with his neighbor the Lord’s present peace in this age whenever some occasion has torn it apart [Col. 1345C]. This is the first gift bestowed upon the human race, proclaimed by the angels immediately after the Lord was born into the world; and the same Lord, when departing from the world, finally left it to his faithful in his own place.

And although many, almost innumerable, things could be said about so great a matter subtly, sublimely, and with profound terror, everyone must beware of thinking that this concerns only the peace possessed in heaven. For the departing Lord said: “My peace I leave you” (John XIV). And the angels, announcing beforehand, say: “Glory to God in the highest,” and immediately add—not “in heaven,” but “on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

Consider this, therefore, O people and nation of God: if you wish to attain perpetual salvation, let us strive in this age to possess not a feigned but a true mutual peace.

[Col. 1345C]

But perhaps this may accomplish too little. It ought rightly to have been enough for so great and such an authority to suffice as the basis of counsel; nevertheless, it will be necessary to add other arguments, which would not justly be added if the wisdom given you by God from the beginning of the Catholic faith had, as it ought, striven to be concerned for you.

The Apostle says: “The Jews seek signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. I). Where, then, is your wisdom, when for any reason whatsoever you disdain to possess that without which you will in no way be able to reach the kingdoms of heaven?

We say this for the moment not by way of accusation or reproach, but by way of admonition, so that we may recall you to your inner person, in whom God is accustomed to dwell through faith, hope, and charity. If you wish to think about, love, or fear that inner person according to the wisdom given you by God, as stated above, it is astonishing that you do not fear having scandal and discord with one another, your brethren, for so long a time [Col. 1345D].

For behold, it is now a year, if not more, since we heard that this most wretched dissension had begun to sprout among you. It is well known that all my predecessors labored greatly, insofar as it was possible for them, to correct this discord, which is always hateful to God—as it deserves to be—and always beloved by the devil, as befits him.

We have taken care to set these few things before you in order to stir your hearts, which are beloved by God, so that what we have carefully prepared to say for the salvation of all our souls might make you more ready to listen and wholly solicitous in the Lord.

But just as we learn not only from sacred authority, but also observe through the daily practice of human experience, that a tree bearing bad fruit is never uprooted more effectively than when it is torn out by the roots, so, with the help of almighty God, we can more effectively correct your aforementioned discord together with you—who, though laid low by this most wretched and exceedingly unhappy condition, do not succumb, but rise above such great foulness on its lofty summit through the authority of the Lord God, pre-eminent over all good things—if we disclose and expose what the origin or kindling of this ruin may have been [Col. 1346A].

No one is permitted to doubt, among your sound and faithful brethren in the Lord, that there are many in this holy Church preserved by God who disdain to succumb to so great a misery, although a stronger human hand prevents them from being able to restore or complete what they do not doubt is just.

Therefore you must be lovingly admonished to strive with all your strength to entreat almighty God to command that such unhappiness be removed from this kingdom, and that in his immense mercy he grant you the peace that the world cannot give.

And since the order of so great an authority, or the reasoning of such sublimity, had not yet demanded that everything which deserved to be set forth first should be placed before those matters by which the state of the whole Church could have remained secure in faith, hope, and charity, we must nevertheless, for the satisfaction of those laboring in this work, consider that the principal cause of the discord mentioned above is said to have been the question of images.

[Col. 1346B]

The origin of that same cause is also reported to have arisen as follows. The emperor observed certain people among that same populace inflamed by indiscreet zeal, advancing further in the worship, veneration, or adoration of images than was proper or had ever previously been done. Wishing then, together with those who supported him, to remove that superstition—whatever it might be—from the Church altogether, he set aside in this matter the salutary discretion without which every virtue of human action is turned into vice. He chose to believe that the superstition could not be corrected in any other way than by completely destroying all images.

Yet if the matter was as has been said, illicit worship had to be restrained in the people or by the people, not through the destruction of images [Col. 1346C], which had committed no sin. Indeed, in the sense set forth above, images were useful to those who understood as a pious memorial and to those who did not understand as instruction. By breaking or dispersing them, he stretched out his left hand in place of his right [*infringendo*, “by breaking”; the printed reading *infrangendo* may be defective].

He who ought to have recalled the incautious in this matter—perhaps because the matter was recent, and therefore could very easily have done so—was led by the one who now plainly appears as the enemy of ecclesiastical peace and charity.

That enemy showed him, as though it were a brilliantly clear path—alas, proceeding by crooked turns far away from the one who said of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). What sweet and exceedingly religious—indeed, holy—paths do you suppose he strove to invent, so that by them he might drag the emperor toward these schisms that we all now lament?

Nor can it be judged that he could have carried this out in any other way unless he first touched the emperor’s heart, together with those who followed him, by soothing it with that impious sweetness; the devil himself, pierced by that poisonous dart, had deservedly fallen from heaven.

[Col. 1346D]

But what are we doing? What are we saying? In comparison with all the evils that could be spoken here, in a space fully adequate to them—not only concerning the devil but also concerning the emperor himself and his supporters—what we say amounts to nothing.

All the evils that, from that time until the present day, have been perpetrated among you through this kind of discord took their beginning from this. Although sobs and weeping do not permit us to remain silent, and although, because of the very brief time and the enormity of these miseries, innumerable grievous matters arise for discussion, as is customary among mourners, it pleases us to return briefly to the beginning of this unhappiness, so that we may behold the devil standing at the crossroads in the course of this life.

There the emperor is unavoidably compelled to choose one of two things: either to bend his neck to illicit worship by favoring images against ecclesiastical law, or else, by opposing or failing to favor such worshipers, to become ungrateful [Col. 1347A]. He could more easily have imitated the ancient princes and his fathers, recalled these people from illicit worship, and gently retained peace and charity with all the others who continued the ancient custom without offending God.

But the aforementioned enemy of peace and charity always persuaded him to take the path of destroying images, by which he would confuse and disturb all those who were sound in judgment and observant of proper discretion. He also persuaded those who, scorning that often-mentioned discretion or moderation—which is recognized as one of the cardinal ecclesiastical virtues—chose to devote themselves to the worship of images beyond anything that had ever pleased God or ought to please him, so that this choice might please those who had made it.

He did not consider what is written terribly: “Those who please human beings are put to shame, because God has rejected them” (Ps. LII).

Thus it happened that from that day onward [Col. 1347B] exiles did not cease among that ancient people, always pleasing to God; crosses and tortures did not rest; and, as is reported, the amputation of limbs and even homicides were perpetrated excessively on account of those same images.

These things continued for a long time, until that ancient enemy of the human race, as though satisfied in this area, turned to other instruments of destruction. He again stirred up against the worshipers of images Herena [Irene], together with her son, deceiving them with such a pestilential delusion that, without any mercy or fear of the majesty of almighty God looking down upon them, they issued a decree that every person subject to their rule must worship images or else be tormented by exile and various punishments; and, if he did not comply, he was to be severed and bound away from the universal Church by the bond of anathema.

But what he is now doing again in the opposite direction, returning once more to his former path and once again inciting the present emperor to permit anyone [Col. 1347C] who wishes to possess them to have painted or written images.

Who, then, is so eloquent beneath the heavens that he could enumerate this pestilential disaster? Who possesses a heart so iron-hard that, faced with it, he would not raise his voice—not only to write, but also, through the failure of tears, to wail?

[The remainder is missing.]

## Letter of Louis and Lothar to Pope Eugene

To the most holy and most reverend lord and father in Christ, Eugene, supreme pontiff and universal pope: Louis and Lothar, by the ordering of divine providence emperors and Augusti, your spiritual sons, send everlasting salvation in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Because we have rightly recognized that we are debtors, we ought in all matters pertaining to divine worship to offer assistance and support, according to the measure of our strength and the capacity of our understanding, to those to whom the governance of the churches and the care of the Lord’s sheep have been entrusted. Therefore we could not omit, when the envoys of the Greeks made known to us what embassy they were to convey to you, from considering with the greatest care and concern what assistance, with God’s help, we might be able to provide you in this matter. For this reason we ask your holiness to permit our priests to search out and collect from the books of the holy Fathers such opinions as might suitably contribute to defining truthfully the very matter on which those envoys were to consult you.

When they diligently sought these things, in accordance also with the permission granted by you, and, with divine grace assisting, had collected whatever they were able to find within so brief a period, they sent it to us for reading. Having read it, we have taken care to send it, for your holiness to read and examine, through these envoys of ours—namely, Jeremiah and Jonah, venerable bishops. If your fatherhood considers it worthwhile, you may hold with them a useful, indeed profitable, conference concerning the same embassy which is to be sent by you into Greece, since they are highly learned in sacred letters and also very well practiced in disputational arguments. We did not send them into the presence of your eminence with these collections of opinions so that they might perform here some kind of teaching office, or be thought to have been sent here for the purpose of instructing you; for, as we have already stated, we are debtors, obliged to offer assistance to this most sacred see in whatever affairs we can. For this reason we judged it appropriate to send both these men and the letters they carry, if they could contribute any assistance to you. We commend them to your holiness, so that they may find both a gracious reception with you and an opportunity to speak with you familiarly.

Your holiness knows, of course, how divided the Greek people are concerning this veneration of images. We therefore ask that your eminence deign to apply care and diligence [Col. 1348B] to the question of how, through your most salutary teaching and admonition, they may be recalled more to concord and unity than driven on this account to still greater discord and dissension. You must therefore consider most carefully that your embassy, which you intend to direct there, be supported by such prudence and moderation that it may rightly be reproached by no one, neither Greek nor Roman; rather, let it be of the kind that ought always to proceed from this most sacred see in every matter. And if it pleases your holiness that our envoys be sent together with yours to those regions for this very embassy, permit us to know this at a suitable time. And not only this, but also, if they are to go, where and when they ought to join your envoys. We do not, however, inquire about sending our envoys there as though it seemed necessary to us, or as though we doubted that your envoys could accomplish this embassy by themselves; rather, we offer them to you so that you may know that we are prepared in every matter which the need or will of this most sacred see may require. We wish that your holy, venerable, and pious fatherhood may always prosper in Christ, and remember us and all our people in your sacred and holy prayers, most holy and blessed Father.

To the venerable bishops Jeremiah and Jonah, greetings in the Lord.

Bishops Halitgar and Amalarius came into our presence on the eighth day before the Ides of December, bringing collections from the books of the holy Fathers, which you gathered together when assembled at the conference held at Paris; we also had them read aloud in our presence. Since they pleased us, and since we judge them necessary and useful for the purpose for which they were collected, we have decided that they should be sent with all haste. Therefore, by way of admonition, we command your diligence that, before you report anything concerning them to the apostolic lord, you carefully review them yourselves; and that whatever you find to agree better and more suitably with the present matter, you excerpt and transcribe, and diligently offer it to him for reading. For, as you know, we wished to ask him for permission to allow these collections to be made by our priests, and therefore it cannot be omitted that it be shown what was collected by his permission.

Nevertheless, take the greatest care to show him from these materials only those things which agree in every respect with the argument that must be maintained concerning images, and which neither he nor his people can in the least reject. You yourselves should also conduct your discussion with him on this matter so patiently and modestly that you take the greatest care not, by resisting him too strongly, to compel him to fall into some irrevocable obstinacy. Rather, by gradually accommodating yourselves to his words, as it were, instead of openly resisting him, you should be able to lead him toward the proper measure to be observed in the use of images. Therefore strive above all to bring about, with God’s help, that the matter under discussion be brought to a better rather than a worse condition.

But after you have completed this argument concerning the matter of those same images—if, indeed, Roman obstinacy permits the discussion held among you to be concluded with some good and suitable result—and if he informs you that he is willing to allow his envoys to go to Greece for the same reason, we wish you to ask him whether he is pleased that our envoys should go to Greece together with his. If he considers this preferable and replies that he entirely wishes it, [Col. 1350A] then we wish you, with all possible haste, to make us certain of the matter by letters sent from you to us, and at the same time to inform us of your coming to us, so that, when you come into our presence, you may find Halitgar and Amalarius with us. For your part, consider with the apostolic lord where and when he wishes his envoys and ours to join one another in order to board the ships; and when, God willing, you come, you can announce this to us yourselves.

[Col. 1349]

## WRITINGS OF THE BLESSED EMPEROR CHARLEMAGNE. SECTION THREE—POEMS.

[Note: [Col. 1349C] This poem was published by the celebrated Peter Lambecius, *Bibliotheca Vindobonensis*, vol. II, p. 262, from a manuscript codex of a Latin Psalter written in golden letters under the care and at the command of Charlemagne, which Charlemagne himself presented as a gift to Pope Adrian I, prefacing it with these dedicatory verses. Lambecius likewise judges that they were composed by Charlemagne himself. We do not oppose this opinion, for Einhard testifies that Charlemagne was not unskilled in the liberal arts and consequently also in the poetic art, or at least in versification. Nevertheless, Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, book III, p. 953, prefers to believe that these verses flowed from Alcuin’s vein, Charlemagne having entrusted him with expressing his thoughts in meter. Others consider it more probable that the author of these verses was that Dagulf who wrote the same golden codex and composed another poem, following immediately on the reverse page of the same leaf. For there he says to the king:

“Receive the labor of your humble servant Dagulf.”]

### POEM I. TO POPE ADRIAN.

*(From Frobenius, Works of Blessed Alcuin.)*

[Col. 1349B]

To Adrian, supreme and blessed pope:

King Charles sends you greetings and farewell, Father.

Receive this gift [L.: *isthoc*, “this very gift”] for the apostolic chair,

Poor in outward appearance, but inwardly bearing a crown.

It contains instruments sounding to David’s plectrum,

And holds lyric and sweet-sounding melodies.

This kindly lyre of yours sings of your miracles, Christ,

You who hold David’s key, scepters, and house [MS.: *donumque*, “and gift”].

These mystical poems had been enclosed by a sevenfold seal,

Had not Christ God disclosed them.

[Col. 1349C] For this reason, holy priest, I piously present this gift to you,

That, as a son, I may approach the mind of the Father.

And remember me in your prayers, holy and devout,

Often holding this little gift in your hand.

And although the little book shines with modest brilliance,

May David’s lofty song be pleasing to you.

May this little stream of mine be held within your river,

And may our little flowers seek your flower-bearing grove.

[Col. 1350B] May you flourish unharmed, ruler, through long ages,

And govern the Church of God by the art of doctrine.

### POEM II

[Note: [Col. 1349D] Quercetanus published this epitaph among other poems of Alcuin, nos. 217 and 218, and again in vol. II of *Scriptores Franciae*, p. 691. The author reveals himself in verse 17, where he says:

“After the Father, weeping, I, Charles, wrote these poems.”

Although some learned men have thought that Alcuin’s vein can be detected in these verses, we cannot, against the manifest wording, attribute any weight to an uncertain argument based on similarity of style—especially since Charles was not unskilled in poetry or versification, just as he was not unskilled in grammar and rhetoric [ [Col. 1350D] See *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. IV, p. 407.]. Moreover, all the ancient writers who mention this epitaph consistently attribute it to this most learned prince. In any case, some testify that this epitaph, engraved in marble at Rome, can still be seen today, with the following addition: “Adrian, pope of blessed memory, sat for twenty-three years, ten months, and seventeen days. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.” (Bouquet, vol. V, p. 412, note.)]

### EPITAPH OF POPE ADRIAN I, WITH WHICH CHARLEMAGNE ADORNED HIS TOMB

*(From the same source, in the same place.)*

Here the Father of the Church, Rome’s glory and renowned founder,

Blessed Pope Adrian rests in peace.

A man whose life was God, whose law was piety, whose glory was Christ,

An apostolic shepherd, ready for every good work.

Nobly born from a great line of parents,

But far nobler in his sacred merits.

As a shepherd, striving with devoted heart

Always and everywhere to adorn his consecrated temples for God,

He enriched churches with gifts and peoples with holy doctrine,

And opened to all the way to the stars.

Generous to the poor, surpassed by none in compassion,

And ever-watchful in sacred prayers for the people,

By teachings, resources, and walls he raised fortresses—

Your fortresses, Rome, city and head of the world, illustrious in honor.

Death harmed him not, for it was overcome by the death of Christ;

Rather, death was the gateway to a better life.

[Col. 1351A] Weeping after the Father [ed.: *lacrymis*, “with tears”], I, Charles, wrote these poems.

You were my sweet love; now I mourn you, Father.

Remember me; my mind always follows you.

May you hold the blessed kingdoms of heaven with Christ.

Clergy [ed.: *clarus*, “renowned”] and people loved you with great affection;

You were, excellent shepherd, the one love of all.

I join our names in the inscriptions, most illustrious [ed.: *charissime*, “dearest”]—

Adrian and Charles: I am the king, and you the Father.

Whoever reads these verses, humbly with devoted heart,

Say: “Gentle God, have mercy on both of them.”

[Note: [Col. 1351D] Beginning of poem 218 in Quercetanus.]

Now may this resting place hold your limbs, dearest one,

While your blessed soul rejoices with God’s saints.

[Col. 1351B] Until at last the trumpet sounds into your ears,

Rise with Peter the Prince to behold God.

You will hear, I know, the gracious voice of the Judge:

“Enter now into the great joys of your Lord.”

Then remember your son, excellent Father, I ask;

Say, “With the Father, let this son of mine also proceed.”

Seek, blessed Father, the heavenly kingdoms of Christ;

From there assist your flock with your prayers.

While the sun, fire-born, shines brightly from its radiant heaven,

Your praise, holy Father, remains forever in the world.

The following verses were appended to the epitaph of Pope Adrian from a very old manuscript codex preserved in the college at Regensburg. We have taken them from Frobenius, among the *Addenda et Supplenda* to the works of Blessed Alcuin, vol. II, p. 614. EDITOR.

[Col. 1351C] Although these things are not worthy of your tombs, Father,

Nor does your glorified faith need inscriptions,

Nevertheless accept the praises which, captivated by Peter’s love,

A stranger arriving from the farthest part of the world reads at your end.

You healed your country’s body, torn apart by schism,

Restoring to their proper places the limbs that had been torn away.

Greece, conquered by your pious authority, yielded to you,

Rejoicing that it had recovered its lost faith.

Africa rejoices, though captive for many years,

To have obtained pontiffs through your prayers.

I, Silverius, recorded these things, difficult though they were for me,

So that, fixed upon tombs, they might remain for a long time.

[Note: [Col. 1351D] Poem 185 in Quercetanus. Mabillon interprets this poem as concerning Alcuin’s chosen withdrawal and repose in the monastery at Tours, after his strength had been broken by age and labors. See *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 179.]

### POEM III. TO ALCUIN.

*(From the same source, in the same place.)*

[Col. 1351D]

King Charles, rejoicing in you, Father and teacher,

With these few verses asks eternal salvation [ed.: *in Christ*].

My mind, I confess, rejoices in love flowing like honey,

For you, beloved teacher; therefore I wished, in odes,

Revered one, to console your old age with the Muses.

And desiring that you too may know, with Christ ruling,

[Col. 1352A] that we and all our faithful are now well,

And that you may rejoice in perpetual triumphs,

Flourishing in holy virtues in the worship of God,

Holding fast to the footprints of a holy life toward better things,

Until you come to the heights of the heavenly kingdom,

Rejoicing forever with the saints, joined to Christ.

And carry me also with you in your prayers, I ask, teacher,

To the gracious heights of the compassionate King, toward which you are journeying;

There praise and honor, beauty, peace, glory, and light

Will remain forever and without end among the saints.

[Note: [Col. 1351D] No. 186 among Quercetanus’s Alcuinian poems. This is Paul the Deacon, celebrated in his own time and then a monk of Monte Cassino. Some hold that these verses were composed by Charles himself and sent to Paul around the year 787, when the king had returned to Francia from Monte Cassino. (Bouquet, *Scriptores Rerum Gallicarum*, vol. V, p. 411; Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 280, no. 67.)]

### POEM IV. TO PAUL, THEN A MONK OF MONTE CASSINO.

*(From the same source, in the same place.)*

[Col. 1352B]

King Charles sends these little poems to the elder Paul,

His beloved brother, with reverent honor.

The pen, suddenly seized by the love of one dictating,

Commands the page [ed.: *castae*, “the chaste woman”]: “Carry my words quickly.”

Go through cities to the venerable face of Paul;

Seek him through mountains, forests, rivers, and wastes.

Seek Monte Cassino, famous by the name of Benedict,

The great shepherd and distinguished Father.

There, amid the sacred heights, seek my Paul;

There, I believe, he dwells beneath God’s flock.

When you find the old man, greet him in a devoted voice,

And say: “King Charles sends you his greetings.”

And tell him, I think, of the great joys of our salvation,

Made fruitful through the help of merciful Christ.

[Col. 1352C] Then ask the Pious Father, always and everywhere,

To offer sacred prayers for us.

And ask him also to commend us to the prayers of the worthy brothers,

In whose prayers I am certain that God is present.

Therefore I have decided to send greetings through me

To all those companions of perpetual peace.

Behold, farewell together, young and old alike;

May Christ’s grace protect and govern you.

[Note: [Col. 1352D] Fabricius inserted this poem on the cited page 958 of his *Bibliotheca*, from Jean-Baptiste Maro’s notes on Peter the Deacon, *De Viris Illustribus Casinensibus*, chapter 8, p. 169.]

### POEM V. TO THE SAME PAUL THE DEACON.

*(From the same source, in the same place.)*

From here, departing swiftly, my page, with rapid flight,

Go through forests, hills, and valleys in an uninterrupted course.

[Col. 1352D] Seek the gracious dwelling of Benedict, beloved of God,

For there is sure rest for the weary who come there.

Here vegetables abound for guests; here fish and bread;

Holy peace, humble spirit, beautiful harmony among the brothers,

Praise, love, and worship of Christ together at every hour.

Say to the Father and all his companions: “Greetings and farewell.”

Embrace the neck of my Paul kindly, rejoicing.

Say many times: “Greetings, excellent Father; greetings.”

### POEM VI. TO THE SAME PAUL THE DEACON.

*(Bibliothèque de l’École des Chartes.)*

[Col. 1353A]

Christ, Father of the world, origin of the shining age,

Grant now my prayer, that I may be able to speak of your mystical gifts

Which your customary mercy [Note: [Col. 1353C] The verse would be more regular with *possim ut*; but the synaeresis in *queam* is intelligible and should remain.] may grant,

And convey saving greetings to the Fathers.

Rise, come, merry flute; make verses with me.

Begin at once to repay the deserved thanks,

And, with the plectrum of the heart, say farewell to the holy brothers,

Who supply us with the sweet honey of doctrine

And soothe our hearts with their songs.

Run through the fields of Ausonia, not sluggish letter, [Note: [Col. 1353D] This movement recurs in another epistle of Charlemagne to Paul the Deacon, printed in vol. V, p. 411, of *Scriptores Rerum Francicarum* (above, poem 4):

“Go through cities to the venerable face of Paul,

Seek him through mountains, forests, rivers, and wastes.”

The compound *gratificus*, used in our verse 12, is also found there:

“Made fruitful through the help of merciful Christ.”] and

Give greetings to my beloved Peter,

Speak grateful praises, and, for the joyful poem

Which he sent me long ago and which pleased me.

From there, bearing you onward, [Note: [Col. 1354D] A manuscript tear makes any reading of this passage impossible. There could scarcely have been anything other than *referens te*.] … to the dwelling

Of Bishop Adrian, finally, after visiting the holy places of Peter,

Leave them visited for me and for my people, [Note: [Col. 1354D] A quantitative error entirely consistent with the practices of this period, when Latin accentuation had been lost.] silently. [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Silentes* makes no sense; *silenter*, an adverb used as early as the fourth century by the poet Juvencus, should be read (*Historia Evangelica* III.462):

“… where the rich fields silently

Burst forth in the green procession of the Jordan.”]

From here, departing swiftly, my page, with easy flight,

Go through forests, hills, and valleys in a rapid course.

Seek the gracious dwelling of Benedict, beloved of God;

Embrace the neck of my Paul most often and kindly.

For there is sure rest for the weary who come there;

Here vegetables for guests, here abundant fish and bread,

Holy peace, humble spirit, beautiful harmony among the brothers,

Praise, love, and worship of Christ together at every hour.

Say to the Father and all his companions: “Greetings and farewell.”

### POEM VII. CHARLEMAGNE TO THE READER OF A MANUSCRIPT WHICH HE HIMSELF HAD PURGED OF ERRORS.

*(From Lambecius, vol. IV.)*

[Col. 1353C]

With a joyful pen I wished to shatter the thorns

[Note: [Col. 1354D] That is, errors.] which the scribe [Note: [Col. 1354D] Namely, Winidharius.] had heaped up through his idle mind.

And you who read, may you deign to strike the Thunderer with prayers for me,

That I may be able to live in Christ’s kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1354D] That is, *si* in place of *ut*.]

### POEM VIII. VERSES INSCRIBED IN A BOOK OF THE GOSPELS WHICH GODESCALC WROTE BY CHARLEMAGNE’S COMMAND IN THE YEAR 781 FOR THE CHURCH OF SAINT SATURNINUS OF TOULOUSE.

*(From Dom Bouquet, *Recueil des Historiens*.)*

A hero good and praised everywhere throughout the world,

Illustrious in the kingdom, relying on heavenly arms,

A triumphator renowned for praise, long known above the heavens,

Rightfully and happily installed as heir upon his fathers’ throne,

A peaceful ruler, powerful lord, and just,

Distinguished among many, proudly humble in piety,

Prudent and wise, devoted to the art of books,

An upright guardian of justice and true attendant,

Generous to the poor, bringing comfort to the afflicted,

Full of love for God and compelled by love of Christ,

While he happily opens the year in two sevenfold divisions,

King Charles, the pious, commanded this excellent work

To be written, together with Hildegard, his distinguished wife.

May the Lord, King of kings, Christ, glory of the heavens,

Guard their lives through the name that brings salvation.

Last of all, his servant Godescalc labored to complete this,

When, in the springtime, having crossed the Alps,

He wished to visit the city of Romulus,

So that he might behold Peter and Peter’s seat, and bring

Many gifts to Christ enthroned on high.

He granted many gifts to the poor pilgrims,

Celebrating there the annual solemnities of Easter.

At that time Adrian was fulfilling the office of bishop in the world

And governed the apostolic see in the city of Rome.

There the offspring of Prince Charles, increased by illustrious birth,

Karlmann, was raised up by the godfather in the sacred waters,

Renamed Pippin, reborn from the font, and washed

In holy baptism.

Seven times a hundred years had been completed,

And the sun had run eight times eleven years with its star,

Since Christ Jesus had blessed the ages by his birth

And stripped the whole world of its dreadful darkness.

### POEM IX. ON HIS DEAD ROLAND.

*(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)*

You return to your homeland, leaving us in a sorrowful world;

A shining palace holds you, while a tearful day holds us.

Having lived six lustrums and, in addition, eight good years,

You, righteous, snatched from earth, return to the stars.

With you, its citizen, restored to the banquets of paradise,

The world groans, while heaven rejoices in your honor.

[Col. 1355]

## APPENDIX TO THE WRITINGS OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE

### Address of the Emperor Charlemagne on the Foundation of the Marian Basilica at Aachen and Its Consecration by Pope Leo III.

[Note: [Col. 1355D] Although certain terms denoting titles or dignities make this address suspect to me, I nevertheless did not wish to omit this encomium of the most noble basilica among the Lower Germans. It still stands today in its round form, with a double row of columns of the finest marble, bronze screens, and other most precious ornament, which Einhard, in his *Life of Charlemagne*, and Peter Becanus, canon of Aachen, describe at length in his history of Aachen. Our Sigebert, in his chronicle under the year 795, says: “Charlemagne built at Aachen a basilica of exceeding beauty, for whose construction he had columns and marbles brought from Rome and Ravenna.”]

*(From Miraeus, *Opera Diplomatica*.)*

[Col. 1355A] I, Charles, who by God’s favor bear the care of the kingdom and am emperor of the Romans, after consultation with the princes of our kingdom—bishops, dukes, margraves, and counts—and at the request of both free persons and servants, in a very large general assembly held in various places of our realm, deliberated, as seemed more just and better to all, first concerning the law of the holy churches, the rendering of justice to bishops, and the life and law of priests and clerics. By our judgment and assent, in accordance with the ordinances of my fathers, I confirmed, strengthened, and enlarged all these things, diminishing nothing of those provisions which Catholic men wishing to live rightly and lawfully have contributed as good and useful for observance by spiritual and secular decree.

[Col. 1355B] Next, as seemed good to the more prudent men of our kingdom, I distinguished the law of the Saxons, Noricans, Swabians, Franks, Ripuarian Franks, and Salian Franks [Note: [Col. 1356D] Charlemagne says that the law of the Salian Franks is distinct from the law of the Franks.], as is the custom and authority of emperors and has always been that of all my predecessors. Having distinguished it, I established it under royal and imperial authority—not devised by me or brought forth from my own heart, but renewed by me, through the common counsel and general assembly of all Gaul, and improved, as my fathers and predecessors are reported to have done. For you know, and no one is unaware, that whatever has been commanded and decreed by emperors and kings must always be held valid and as law, lest what has been ordered and enacted by all sensible persons wishing to live with sufficient just discernment, and confirmed and made firm by our imperial and royal majesty, be violated.

Now, fathers, brothers, and friends, supporters and helpers of the glory of our kingdom: of all the ordinances of my father Pippin which you asked to be confirmed and renewed for the benefit and honor of the holy [Col. 1355C] Church, and which you sought to have established for the defense of secular affairs and laws, I have diminished or refused nothing, but have enlarged them for the better. I have acquiesced in the sound counsels of all and have been among you as one seeking and requesting the equity of the law, contradicting no one, nor any rightful petition. Therefore I willingly complied with your decree and request and listened to you as fathers and brothers. Now I ask that you be willing to become not merely hearers, but also willing doers, of my request and purpose. For I seek nothing improper or intolerable, but that which all Gaul and all its princes ought rather to grant than deny.

You know how, when I entered, according to custom, for the purpose of hunting, the place called Aachen, which derives its name from its supply of hot waters, I came there separated from my companions through the entanglement of forests and the error of the roads. There I found baths of hot springs and palaces which Granus [Note: [Col. 1356D] Granus. He is made the brother of the emperors Nero and Agrippa, but without support from any classical author. Certainly none of the ancient writers mentions him.], one of the Roman princes, brother of Nero and Agrippa, had originally built.
