[Col. 1355D] Deserted and demolished by long antiquity, and now overgrown with shrubs and briars, these I renewed after I had perceived and discovered the streams of hot water beneath the hoof of the horse on which I sat among the glades. There also I built, with every labor and expense within my power, a monastery for Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and adorned it with stones of precious marble. With the Lord’s help and cooperation it has taken such form that none can be compared with it.

Accordingly, when the magnificent work of this basilica had been completed in every particular, not only in accordance with my vow and desire, but through divine grace, I collected relics of apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins from diverse lands and kingdoms, especially those of the Greeks. I brought them into this holy place, that by their intercessions the kingdom might be strengthened and remission of sins granted. Moreover, because of the exceeding devotion which I had toward this work and the relics of the saints that are deposited there through my care and labor, I obtained from Lord Leo [Note: [Col. 1356D] Leo. Pope Leo III came twice from Italy into Gaul to Charlemagne, namely in 799 and 804. Unless I am mistaken, the consecration of the Aachen basilica must be referred to Leo’s earlier journey.], Roman pontiff, the consecration and dedication of this church. For it was fitting that this church, which seems to surpass all monastic buildings in our kingdom in form and construction, founded by us through royal zeal in honor of the holy Mother of God, should excel in the dignity of consecration, just as that Virgin, exalted above all the choirs of saints, herself excels. Therefore, from the sole consideration of my heart, I chose and summoned the apostolic lord, who surpasses all ecclesiastical ranks, to consecrate and dedicate it. With him I also summoned Roman cardinals, very many bishops of Italy and Gaul, together with abbots and a great number of clergy of every order, to be present at this sacred dedication. Many Roman nobles also were summoned to that solemnity—men advanced to the prefecture or to whatever rank—together with dukes, margraves, counts, and princes of our kingdom, of Italy and Saxony, Bavaria and Alemannia, and of both the eastern and western Francia [Note: [Col. 1356D] This declares that Francia is twofold, eastern and western.], all complying with my wish and desire.

There, when the apostolic lord and all the aforesaid noble and distinguished persons had assembled, I deserved to obtain from all, because of the divine devotion that I had toward that place and the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, that a royal seat be established in that church, and that it be regarded as a royal place and the head of Gaul beyond the Alps; that in that seat kings, successors, and heirs of the kingdom should be inaugurated; and that, thus inaugurated, they should thereafter more plainly attain the imperial majesty at Rome by right and without any contradiction. This was confirmed and sanctioned by Lord Leo, Roman pontiff, and by me, Charles, Augustus, emperor of the Romans and first founder of this church and place, so that this our ordinance and decree may remain valid and unshaken, and that here, beyond the Alps, the seat of the kingdom may be located and be the head of all the cities and provinces of Gaul.

We also decreed, with the assent and good will of all the princes of the kingdom who had gathered for this feast of dedication, that bishops, [Col. 1356D] dukes, margraves, counts, all the princes of Gaul, [Col. 1357A] and the faithful of the kingdom should protect this place and royal seat as a bulwark against every storm, always reverencing this place. We further decreed that, should any injury or trickery arise against the laws which we have established and attempt to harm a free person or a servant, he shall come to Aachen, to this royal seat which we have made the head of Gaul; the judges and defenders of the place shall come, and causes shall be decided with the equity of the law, the authority of the law restored, injury condemned, and justice re-established.

Now therefore, because we have exalted this place by the majesty of a royal seat, by decree of the apostolic lord, and by our imperial power and assent, and have made it magnificent through the splendor of this church and the veneration of very many saints, [Col. 1357B] it is fitting, and seems not inappropriate, [Col. 1358A] since our mind is fixed upon this most earnestly, that my request—which I have entreated you to become not only hearers but willing doers of—should obtain among you: namely, that not only clerics and laypeople native to this place, but all inhabitants and newcomers who wish to dwell here, present and future, may live under a safe and free law, without any servile condition; and that all alike who belong to this seat from grandfathers and great-grandfathers, though residing elsewhere, may not be deprived of the law which I shall now enact by any successor of ours or by any contriver, subverter of laws, and may never be handed over from the king’s hand to any noble [Col. 1358B] or ignoble person as a benefice.

[Col. 1357]

## CAROLINA, OR VARIOUS MATERIALS PERTAINING TO THE DEEDS, CULT, FAME, AND PRAISES OF CHARLEMAGNE. SECTION ONE—LITURGICAL MATERIAL.

### I. On the Public Veneration of Blessed Charlemagne

*(From the *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. II.)*

[Col. 1357C]

1. Charlemagne, king of the Franks and the first emperor of the Romans—after the imperial dignity, restored in the West only after four centuries, had been revived—is honored with the customary sacred honors paid to the saints and with annual solemnities. His name was entered into the sacred registers by Guido of Cremona, called Paschal III. Although, while Alexander III was legitimately administering the Catholic Church and the faction of the schismatics adhered to the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Guido was called pope contrary to law and right, Charlemagne nevertheless, on account of his illustrious benefactions, and perhaps even earlier, but certainly afterward, with the Roman pontiffs’ acquiescence, was regarded as a saint: churches were dedicated to him, and celebration was bestowed upon him in the ecclesiastical office.

2. Thus Henricus Spondanus, bishop of Apamea, explains the matter in the *Epitome of Baronius’s Annals*, under the year 814, no. 5:

“If you consider what has been written about him, you will behold a worthy example of virtues and, in every respect, a complete image of religion, one whom, in my judgment, neither the emperors who preceded nor those who succeeded him could altogether equal. Nor would he have had an equal in morals, unless he had stained conjugal chastity by introducing concubines. Yet afterward repentance wiped away these stains, when he continually wore out his aged flesh with a hair shirt fastened over his naked body. On account of the merit of these outstanding virtues, the Gallican Church celebrates his birthday; and under the emperor Frederick, Pope Paschal enrolled him among the saints. But since that man was not a legitimate pontiff, his canonization was not received by the Roman Church. Nevertheless, because no legitimate pontiffs are found to have opposed it, the matter continued through silent permission or tolerance, so that he might be venerated in the church where he was buried. Thus the principal interpreters of the canons have declared. His cult is subsequently known to have spread to other churches of Gaul, Belgium, and Germany, in which the same Charles is venerated with the title of sanctity; and the writings of many historians of Frankish affairs lend support to this.”

Such is Spondanus.

3. We have certainly seen the breviaries of several churches in which Saint Charles, emperor, is honored on 28 January, either with an office of nine lessons or with one of three. In the church of Minden, the following public prayer is recited on that day:

“God, who by the overflowing fruitfulness of your goodness exalted the blessed emperor Charles the Great, your confessor, after laying aside the garment of the flesh, to the glory of blessed immortality, graciously grant that we may always deserve to have in heaven as a merciful and favorable intercessor him whom you exalted on earth to the praise and glory of your name by the honor of empire. Through the Lord.”

An equal honor is paid to him in the old Parisian, Rheims, Rouen, Osnabrück, Tournai, and other breviaries. In the Rouen breviary the following prayer is read, which is also used for Saint Louis the King:

“God, who transferred your confessor, blessed Charles, from an earthly kingdom to the glory of the heavenly kingdom, grant, we ask, that through his merits and intercession we may become sharers in the King of kings, Jesus Christ, your Son. Through the same Lord.”

Source/review notes: Inherited source lacunae remain explicit; every supplied editorial note is retained.

### 4. The Name of Charles Is Also Recorded in Numerous Martyrologies

The oldest is believed to be that composed by Rabanus under Lothair, Charles’s grandson; in it there is only this: “Charles died.” The Bruges manuscript has: “On this day, the deposition of the lord Charles the Great, emperor.” The manuscript of Saint Lambert at Liège: “On the same day, of Charles the Great, emperor.” In the manuscript of the imperial monastery of Saint Maximin at Trier, which otherwise agrees in every respect with Rabanus’s Martyrology as published by Henricus Canisius, there is no mention of Charles. But in the Necrology and in the Catalogue of Anniversaries the following is found:

> “Charles the Great, emperor, who gave this church three estates, namely Stensele, Luniciacum, and Wimariskirca.” [Col. 1359A]

Wandelbertus writes for this day:

> Light, glory, love of the world, the homeland’s worship and grief,  
>   
> Charles, exalted as the head of empire by the highest honor,  
>   
> Then, departing, Charles leaves the scepters to Louis.

The Martyrology of Usuard printed at Paris in 1536: “Likewise, of Saint Charles the emperor.” Ferrarius: “At Aachen, of Saint Charles the Great.” Various Belgian manuscripts, both in Latin and in the German language: “At Aachen, the deposition of Saint Charles, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans.”

### 5.

The manuscript Florarium has:

> “At Aachen, the deposition of the blessed Charles, emperor of the Romans, king of the Franks, and light of the Brabantians, who on account of the greatness of his deeds was called the Great. From him the illustrious stock of the Carolingians takes its name; no stock more noble or more religious, except the genealogy of Christ, has arisen beneath the heavens. He died in the year of salvation 814, at the age of seventy-one.” [Col. 1359B]

From this extravagant praise of the Carolingians, or Carlingians, and from the designation “duke of the Brabantians,” it may be inferred that the author of that Florarium was a Brabantine. Yet Charles is nowhere said to have possessed or ruled, by any special right or title, the province called Brabant, foremost in dignity among the Belgian provinces, before he succeeded his father in the kingdom; nor was that region then called Brabant. This name was adopted much later by the counts of Leuven, who, because they possessed part of the territory that the ancients called Brabantum, called the other places under their jurisdiction Brabant and styled themselves dukes of Lower Lotharingia and Brabant. They themselves descended from the counts of Hainaut; from them descended the other very celebrated dukes of Brabant, who were succeeded by the Burgundians, and by the Austrians after them. Nevertheless, Pepin, Charles, and the other members of that family did possess private holdings throughout Belgium, especially in the region now called Brabant—what are commonly called allodial estates.

### 6.

Various manuscripts bearing the name of Usuard, though also frequently expanded in other copies, celebrate Charles’s feast in the following manner:

> “At Aachen, the deposition of Saint Charles, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, who, after pacifying and enlarging his kingdom and empire, and devoutly ordering the condition of the holy Church and zealously extending the faith, departed to the Lord in the year of the Lord 814, at the age of seventy-one, in the forty-seventh year of his reign and the fourteenth of his empire. On account of the greatness of his deeds he was called the Great.”

The Carthusians of Cologne have almost the same in their additions to Usuard. The Aachener Martyrology cited by Molanus in *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium* and in the additions to Usuard has:

> “On the same day, at Aachen, in the basilica, the feast of Saint Charles the Confessor, the first of the Frankish stock, by divine ordinance Augustus of the Romans. From the beginning of his life he despised the pomp of the world and, by the sword of imperial power, the word of holy preaching, and the example of a life that brings salvation, converted Gascony, Germany, and Gaul. He also converted Frisia and Alemannia to the Lord, and Saxony by a triple triumph. At his own expense he also built twenty-seven churches to the praise and honor of the holy and undivided Trinity; among them the church at Aachen possesses the distinction of excellence and now shines forth through glorious intercessions.” [Col. 1359C–D]

Galesinius:

> “At Aachen in Germany, of Saint Charles, king and confessor. After building many most august temples, converting nations to the Christian religion, and performing other illustrious deeds with the greatest devotion, he acquired the surname ‘the Great’; at last he rested in the Lord and was enrolled among the saints by Pope Paschal.”

Indeed, by a pseudo-pope.

### 7.

Others also honorably include Charles in their catalogues of the saints: Ghinius, Miraeus, Canisius, Felicius, Maurolycus, and, with the fullest encomium of all, Saussay. Some praise him for certain things that require correction, having accepted them from authors whose reliability is not established. Thus Maurolycus:

> “The commemoration of Charles, surnamed the Great, emperor, belongs here. His glorious deeds for Christ are celebrated at great length by Turpin, bishop of Reims. For, returning from the expedition to Jerusalem, he brought from Byzantium to Gaul a piece of the Cross, a nail, and the crown of thorns. He built twenty-four monasteries. He endowed the four bishops of Trier, Cologne, Mainz, and Salzburg with great wealth and honors. In the year of salvation 814, at the age of seventy-one, in the forty-seventh year of his reign and the fourteenth of his empire, he died at Aachen in Lotharingia.”

Felicius has much the same; the *German Martyrology* has more, but errs in stating that Charles recovered the Holy Land from Saracen servitude. The author of the book entitled *The Violet of the Saints* errs far more extensively.

## II. The Translation of Saint Charles the Emperor

*(From the Acts of the Saints, in the same place.)*

### 1.

The memory of Saint Charles is celebrated in the martyrologies on 27 July, the day on which his relics were raised and translated. The Cologne Martyrology has:

> “On the same day, the translation at Aachen of blessed Charles the Great, emperor and confessor.”

The Cologne Carthusians and Molanus in his additions to Usuard also mention it, as do Canisius and Saussay. The manuscript Florarium specifies the time:

> “At Aachen, the translation of Saint Charles the Great, emperor, carried out under the emperor Frederick, first of that name, and Pope Alexander, third of that name, in the year of salvation 1163.”

But Guido of Crema, called Paschal, the antipope under whose authority that translation is said to have been carried out, had not yet succeeded the antipope Octavian in that year; it took place in 1165.

### 2.

There exists a diploma of Frederick I, called Aenobarbus or Barbarossa, concerning that translation and canonization. We reproduce it from Peter Beka’s *Aachen* and from Aubertus Miraeus’s *Belgian Annals*. We append to it miracles from a Life written at that very time.

Since Frederick testifies that the body of Saint Charles was raised by the authority of the antipope Paschal, it is strange that Joannes Chapeaville, in volume II of *The Bishops of Liège*, apparently on the authority of the *Great Belgian Chronicle*—which we have not found making this statement—says that it was done “by the will and command of Pope Alexander,” unless perhaps Alexander later, after restoring Frederick to favor in 1177, confirmed the act. The account runs as follows:

> “In the second year of Alexander’s episcopate—that is, in the year of the Lord 1166—by the will and command of Pope Alexander and all the cardinals, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the presence of the emperor Frederick and many prelates, the bones of Charles the Great, emperor, were raised at Aachen from the place where they had rested for 352 years, with great reverence, and honorably placed in a silver coffin by Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, and Alexander, bishop of Liège, together with many offerings presented by the emperor, the empress, and others. There Charles was also canonized and called a holy confessor.”

### 3.

The head of Saint Charles was translated to Osnabrück. Concerning it Werner Rolewinck writes in book III, chapter 8, *On the Customs of Westphalia*:

> “After him came the glorious holy emperor Charles, our apostle, who completely converted this land to the faith. His head is honorably venerated at Osnabrück, together with Saints Crispin and Crispinian and many other relics.”

## III. Diploma of the Emperor Frederick I Concerning the Elevation and Canonization of Saint Charles

*(From the Acts of the Saints, in the same place.)*

### 1.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Frederick, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, ever-August emperor of the Romans.

Ever since, by the ordering of divine clemency, we first undertook the governance of the heights of the Roman Empire, the highest desire of our will and purpose has been to follow the kings and emperors who preceded us, especially the greatest and most glorious emperor Charles, as a model for living and for governing subjects, and, in following him, always to keep him before our eyes. In imitation of him, we would preserve throughout our entire empire the rights of the churches, the safety of the commonwealth, and the integrity of the laws.

[Note: [Col. 1361D] If he had done this, he would not have attacked for so many years what Charles had always fostered with the greatest fidelity: the Roman Church.]

### 2.

For he, longing with the whole intention of his heart for the rewards of eternal life, and seeking to extend the glory of the Christian name and propagate the worship of divine religion, established so many bishoprics and abbeys, raised so many churches from their foundations, enriched them with such extensive estates and benefactions, and shone forth through such generosity of almsgiving, not only in the regions on this side of the sea but also in those beyond it. His very works and the volumes of his deeds, numerous and great as they are, make these things more fully clear by the evidence of sight.

In extending the faith of Christ and converting barbarian peoples, he was a strong champion and a true apostle, as Saxony, Frisia, and Westphalia testify, and the Spaniards as well, as do the Vandals, whom he converted to the Catholic faith by word and by the sword. Although the sword did not pass through his own soul, the tribulation of various sufferings, perilous struggles, and the daily willingness to die for the conversion of unbelievers made him a martyr. Now we acknowledge and venerate on earth as an elect and most holy confessor him whom we believe to have lived in holy conduct, departed to the Lord through pure confession and true repentance, and been crowned in heaven among the holy confessors as a holy and true confessor.

[Note: [Col. 1361D] The schismatic emperor is hallucinating. Charles did not convert the Spaniards; he merely wrested some of their cities from the hands of the Saracens.]

### 3.

Therefore, confidently encouraged by the glorious deeds and merits of the most holy emperor Charles, and moved by the persistent petition of our dearest friend Henry, king of England, with the assent and authority of the lord Paschal, and on the advice of all the princes, both secular and ecclesiastical, we celebrated a solemn court at Aachen on the Nativity of the Lord, for the elevation and exaltation of his most holy body and for his canonization.

There his most holy body, carefully hidden away because of fear of an external enemy or a household foe, but revealed by divine revelation, was raised and exalted by us on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, to the praise and glory of Christ’s name, to strengthen the Roman Empire, and for the salvation of our beloved consort Beatrice, empress, and our sons Frederick and Henry. A great gathering of princes and a vast multitude of clergy and people were present, amid hymns and spiritual songs, with fear and reverence.

[Note: [Col. 1361D] Henry II, king of England, under whom Saint Thomas of Canterbury was killed, was crowned on 19 December, the Sunday before Christmas, in 1154; he died on 6 July 1189.]

### 4.

After all these things had been gloriously accomplished, while we were diligently investigating at the aforesaid place—of which Charles himself had been the founder—the liberties of that place and the institutions of law, peace, and justice by which he had ruled the whole world, behold, the brothers of that church brought before us a privilege of Saint Charles concerning the foundation and dedication of that most noble church, and concerning the institutions of human law and the civil law of that city. Lest antiquity erase it or forgetfulness destroy it, we renewed it by our imperial authority. The wording and institution of that privilege are as follows.

### Privileges Confirmed for the People of Aachen

Let Aachen therefore rejoice and exult with ineffable joy, Aachen, the head of cities; let the venerable clergy rejoice with their most devout people. Set upon the crown’s summit, as upon the diadem of the kingdom, distinguished by the most splendid ornament among other princely and glorious places, it shines with the brilliance of translucent gems and rejoices in that singular and bodily patron who adorns the Roman Empire through the illumination of the Christian faith and through the law by which each person ought to live.

For this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: in place of Grannus, Nero’s brother, it has Saint Charles the Most Holy as founder; in place of a pagan and criminal ruler, a Catholic emperor. Therefore, following, insofar as favorable Divinity has granted us the power, in the footsteps of his piety, we take under our imperial protection the venerable clergy of Aachen, together with the church of the Most Holy Mother of God, Mary, constructed with the most excellent workmanship and all its estates, and likewise the city of Aachen itself, which is the head and seat of the Teutonic kingdom, together with all its citizens, both lesser and greater.

We confirm to them every liberty and justice that Saint Charles and his successors granted them, establishing and confirming by a law of perpetual validity that all our citizens of Aachen may conduct their commerce throughout the Roman Empire freely and without impediment, exempt from every exaction of toll, road-tax, court-fee, or other levy. And just as the most holy emperor Charles decreed, no one shall attack the native inhabitants of this sacred and free city on account of servile status, nor presume to deprive them of their liberty.

Moreover, no king or emperor, wherever he may reside, shall have the power to grant in fief to any person anyone belonging to this see. Finally, so that all the most holy constitutions of the blessed Charles may possess the strength of perpetual validity, we have ordered this document to be written and sealed with a golden bull and the impression of our seal.

Seal of the lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans.

I, Henry, protonotary of the sacred palace, in place of Christian, archchancellor and elect of the see of Mainz, have examined and authenticated this document.

[Note: [Col. 1362D] Christian I, seventy-first bishop of Mainz, was expelled after Conrad because he favored Alexander III, although he had been elected before him; he was again appointed by Aenobarbus in 1164, more hostile to the pope, and died in 1180. Conrad, already created cardinal of Sabina, was restored. See Serarius’s *Moguntiaca*.]

Given at Aachen in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1166, in the fourteenth indiction, on 8 January, during the reign of the lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans, in the fourteenth year of his reign and the eleventh of his empire. Done happily in Christ. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1362D] After King Conrad, his uncle, died on 15 February 1152, Frederick succeeded him. He was crowned emperor by Pope Adrian IV on 17 June 1155.]

## IV. The Miracles of Blessed Charles the Great

*(From the Acts of the Saints, in the same place.)*

### 1.

Thus a faithful and wholly credible account of the life, conduct, and heavenly signs of the most holy emperor Charles the Great, produced only as a small portion of his deeds because the scarcity of books confines us, has continued down to events worthy of remembrance in our own time.

Although the opportunity afforded by the natural and appropriate order of narration urges us on through these events in the zeal of charity, we have heard—and have learned through the testimony of suitable and faithful men, in a report long and widely circulated among us—that in our own time a glorious miracle occurred at Aachen. We have not dared to suppress it in silence, for the praise of God and the most blessed memory of the orthodox Charles the Great, lest we rightly be accused of burying in the earth the Lord’s money.

### 2.

There was therefore in that royal city a certain young man, youthful in age, a cleric by profession, a subdeacon by rank, named Guibert. His life had for the most part been excessively devoted to reckless and intemperate lust.

One day it happened that this cleric entered the holy church at Aachen, not for the sake of prayer but merely out of habit. In his rash audacity, neglecting the offense he had committed during the night, he dared to break into the sacristy, contrary to the reverence due to the place and to the custom of the clergy. Then, with his head leaning before the venerable image of the venerable Charles, overcome by sleep after the vigils of the preceding night, irreverently and foolishly [that is, imprudently] he fell into the sleep of death.

For suddenly a certain hand—as those who reported this to us saw—hurled the young man, who was leaning upon a certain chest in the aforesaid venerable oratory, away with such force that it cast him far from the place where he had been reclining, to the opposite side.

Immediately struck there by a grave illness, he humbly confessed the error of his offense. After a few days had passed, condemned by the judgment of divine vengeance, he entered upon the way of all flesh, leaving the others an example of the reverence that was due.

Some scholars who happened to be present at the time saw the aforementioned hand of just vengeance, and, terrified, trembling, and fleeing, spread abroad what they had seen. Certain others, divinely admonished by such a vision, changed the habit of their secular life.

### 3.

After a short interval of time, it happened that a certain man came to Aachen, handsome in face, respectable in character, and worthy of esteem because of his courteous affability. He could rightly be judged distinguished by the nobility of his lineage and not insignificant in the possession of worldly goods.

He was a German, as he himself asserted, born in German Burgundy; a knight by occupation, named Thiethmar. Through the violent invasion of a powerful count of his land, he had been unjustly deprived of his possessions and mercilessly stripped of all his goods. Since he could obtain mercy nowhere from either the spiritual or the temporal sword, so as to receive fitting justice for his loss and injury, he hastened at last to Aachen with a devoted heart, firm hope, and unfeigned faith, having been admonished by divine revelation to seek the aid of the most just Charles.

Having placed before the venerable image of the emperor, out of the abundance of his heart rather than of his possessions, written breviaries, and having continued for many days in a multitude of most devout Masses and prayers, in unremitting affliction through fasts, and in the distribution of alms as far as was possible for an exile, he was admonished by a consoling oracle in a vision of the night.

Perhaps, bowed down amid a great outpouring of tears, he slept among the lights; strengthened by greater hope and better faith, he returned to his homeland. From his own report, when he returned after a year to the glorious memory of blessed Charles, we learned with complete certainty that through the prayers and merits of the most just emperor he obtained fuller satisfaction of justice than he had dared either to hope for or to request.

For he declared not only that he had received back all his own possessions fully and intact, with complete satisfaction, but also that the violent invader of his property and goods had paid, before the public testimony of the people, the penalties of a death most wretched and worthy of just vengeance for his deserved violence.

Moreover, after a short time he asserted that not one of the wrongdoer’s heirs remained anywhere in that land. Each year, for all the years he lived thereafter, he most devoutly observed the day commemorating the blessed Charles. In addition, in praise and glory of so great an avenger, he frequently scattered a large sum of Basel coins across the church floor through generous munificence.

### 4.

Amid so many glorious manifestations of God’s power, through which divine mercy has continually shone forth in its faithful champion, we rejoice in a glad and almost immortal joy, exulting in the Lord, who by his wondrous power judged the blessed translation of his most blessed Charles worthy of being wondrously and most wondrously canonized.

Since we desire, as far as lies within us, to transmit to posterity so celebrated and glorious an operation of divine majesty and to make it eternal in writing, we have recorded it in faithful testimony, so that the power of God, worthy of admiration everywhere and always, may be proclaimed more steadfastly and devoutly.

For, passing over in silence very many notable signs of the aforesaid canonization, we have recorded in faithful testimony that, by the nod of divine providence, something occurred that ought to be brought into the light and sounded forth far and wide to the ends of the earth.

On the third night after the exaltation of Charles the Great, most beloved of God, three candles, kindled by divine power, flashed with wondrous brilliance above the pinnacle of the church. Many peoples and nations saw them with joyful exultation.

Then those three lights of heavenly splendor, as though extinguished, circled three times around the cross of that same church’s tower. They illuminated places far and wide with the new brightness of a new light, to the astonishment of the darkness of night and to the joy of the new translation.

O admirable, O venerable threefold manifestation of the Holy Trinity! O truly blessed exultation of the canonization, confirmed by divine testimony from heaven, which was gloriously revealed by the threefold circuit of the three lights and strengthened in every respect from heaven by the oracle of the Holy Trinity!

### 5.

Let that true worshiper of Christ, the Augustus and emperor of the Romans, therefore know that he has good reason to exult and rejoice in the Lord. He was the author, in the Holy Spirit, of this translation, and God of the supreme Trinity is proclaimed its defender by such manifest signs.

The same emperor, therefore, rightly gladdened by so great and blessed a revelation and filled with immeasurable joy, in addition to the other ample and generous gifts of his imperial munificence, offered ten marks annually for the use of the refectory, both for the canons and for clerical guests. He established this gift as firm and perpetual, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his family.

### 6.

But since the continuous thread of this work has now flowed down to the events of our own time, as we bring the present undertaking to an end, we ask pardon—not for excessive length, but for our curtailed and interrupted brevity, since we have touched upon only a very few of the innumerable manifestations of the holiness of the most blessed Charles the Great.

We have scarcely tasted the sum of his imperial holiness, his praiseworthy character, and the heavenly signs written for his glory. In this matter we take comfort in the confidence that the faithful of Christ are more steadfastly and devoutly moved in the Lord to praise and honor this same prince, and that by our example we have stirred readers and writers to record these things and others like them, so that, without envy, we may permit them to fill the gaps that yawn in our account.

Let pious judges consider and approve not the weakness of human imperfection displayed in the formation of our discourse, but the ardent affection of our intention. Let those who hope for the same in similar matters taste and supplement our labor.

For we have heard and learned of many other things, both in the deeds of the Franks and from before our own time as well as in our own days, filled with divine praises and occurring everywhere and in various ways, as a sweet fragrance, through the merits of that same most just emperor. In all these things God, glorious and wondrous in his saint, has appeared, and every day does not cease to appear through the fruitful revelation of his goodness.

To him be glory, honor, and dominion for endless ages of ages. Amen.

## V. Office for the Feast of Saint Charles the Great, Emperor and Confessor

[Note: [Col. 1365D] This office is not celebrated today because the Supreme Pontiff, by his brief, ordered the Chapter not to celebrate it. Therefore it was decreed that the celebration should be suspended until the Apostolic See should order otherwise.]

*(From Florez, España Sagrada.)*

### At Vespers

[Col. 1365A]

Born of a royal stock and approved by God,  
Charles despised the contaminations of unlawful life.

Weekday psalms. Chapter: “There was not found.”  
Response: “You, O soldier, followed.”  
Hymn: “This Confessor.”

Verse: “He loved him.”

At the Magnificat. Antiphon:

> O hope for the afflicted, fear for enemies, sacrifice for the conquered, rule of virtue, path of justice, model of salvation, Charles, receive graciously the prayers of your servants.

Prayer:

> O God, who, through the superabundant fruitfulness of your goodness, raised blessed Charles the Great, your emperor and confessor, after laying aside the garment of the flesh, to the robe of blessed immortality, grant to us, your suppliants, that he whom you exalted on earth with imperial honor for the praise and glory of your name we may deserve always to have as a pious and perpetual intercessor in heaven. Through him.

Afterward there is a commemoration of blessed Agnes and of Saint Mary.

### At Matins

Invitatory: “The king of confessors.”  
Hymns: “Jesus, Redeemer.”  
At the nocturns: Psalm “Blessed is the man,” with the following; and the psalm and verse as in the Common of Confessors.

#### First Lesson

Saint Charles the Great, wishing to obey the admonitions of the blessed apostle James, resolved to go as far as Spain and subject it to the Catholic faith.

After capturing and fortifying the city of Narbonne, where Spain begins, he came to the land of Roussillon, which is the beginning of Catalonia, and humbly implored the aid of Christ and of the blessed Virgin Mary.

Response: “Well done, good servant.”

#### Second Lesson

When his prayer was completed, he looked toward heaven and saw the blessed Mary bearing Christ her Son. He also saw the blessed James and Andrew, one standing on the right and the other on the left.

As Saint Charles gazed at them, astonished by their splendor, he perceived the blessed Virgin speaking as follows:

> “Do not be afraid, Charles, soldier of Christ, arm and defender of the Church, for we shall be with you in battle, and we shall deliver you with victory.” [Col. 1365C]

Response: “He who confessed me.”

#### Third Lesson

> “But when you have crossed the Pyrenees Mountains, you will besiege the city of Girona and, although with difficulty, you will take it. In it you will build a cathedral church in my honor and reverence. I shall bless you and set you above all the soldiers of this world. You shall have Saint James, my nephew, as your guide and protector of all Spain.”

After these words the vision that had appeared vanished.

Response: “Saint Charles.”  
Response: “With the following,” IV and V, as in Saint Benedict.

#### Fourth Lesson

Then Saint Charles encouraged his army. When, in the fervor of his spirit, he had attacked the army of the unbelievers, they began to turn their backs and flee with all their strength, unable to resist the Christians.

After finally obtaining victory in the field called Milet, he built a church under the invocation of the blessed apostle Andrew. A monastery of religious men is now established there.

After capturing the fortresses and villages of the valleys of Piri and Roussillon, Saint Charles arrived at the place called Saclusa and learned that King Marsilius had again been enclosed there. For this reason it is called Saclusa, whereas previously it was called the Sharp Mountain.

Response: “Saint Charles.”

#### Fifth Lesson

After the unbelievers had finally been driven from there, he reached the summit of the mountain called Albarras. It was later called Malpartus, where he encountered resistance preventing his passage.

Then Saint Charles divided his battle line into sections. He sent one section through the pass of Panissars, where he built a church in honor of Saint Martin, and dispatched the other section through the precipitous mountain paths.

When the Saracens saw the divided battle line, they began to flee toward the city of Girona, fearing that they would remain trapped and enclosed in the middle.

Response: “Most holy confessor of Christ, Charles.”

#### Sixth Lesson

Hearing this, Saint Charles destroyed all the fortifications from which danger threatened Christians passing through. Pursuing the wicked as far as Girona, he set out on his way.

When he reached the place called De Ramis, he built a church in honor of Saint Julian. He also established a chapel of Saint Thecla the virgin at Rotulando, within the same boundaries.

The blessed Turpin, archbishop of Reims, likewise erected there an altar of Saint Vincent.

Response: “Behold the man.”

#### Seventh Lesson

Then Saint Charles rose devoutly and went toward the valley of Hostalets. Having left the place called Sen[lacuna]madir, he went out to meet the Saracens, over whom he gained victory and honor. For this reason he established there a monastery of monks, constructing a high altar under the invocation of the glorious Virgin.

But because that place was bitter to the Saracens, it was thereafter named Santa Maria de Amer by the inhabitants.

Response: “Blessed Charles,” as in Saint Nicholas.

#### Eighth Lesson

Departing from there, Saint Charles returned to the mountain of Barrufa, which lies beside the dark valley, and besieged the city of Girona. He was then unable to capture it, although he had attacked it many times.

Nevertheless, one Friday at the hour of Compline, when the face of heaven was shining, a great red cross adorned on every side with light appeared above the mosque of the city of Girona, where the cathedral church now stands. It remained there for four hours in the sight of everyone, and drops of blood also fell.

Response:

> This soldier followed you and was acceptable to you, O Christ.  
> Compared with Elisha, he performed a work worthy of God.

Verse:

> While he prays, sickness yields, death is driven away, life returns.

Verse: “Compared with Elisha.”  
Glory. Hymn: *Te Deum.*

Verse. Chapter: “There was not found.”

### At Lauds

Antiphon:

> Girded with strength and possessed of victory,  
> King Charles, girded with strength and having obtained victory, bestowed [gifts] gloriously through holiness.

Psalm: “The Lord reigns,” with the following antiphons.

A.

> Let us rejoice in the Most High, in the most holy champion,  
> when, sent by the Spirit, the hind led the army.

A.

## VI. Another Office

[Note: [Col. 1365D] It can scarcely be said when that Office of Charles the Great was composed. They report that Charles was canonized by Paschal, the antipope to Alexander III; but many will perhaps doubt the truth of the diplomas that the people of Aachen claim to preserve. It is still more astonishing that Baronius supports the testimony of Paschal.

For how could one who fostered schism, who had set up altar against altar, and who was utterly devoted to Frederick’s party and the cause of disturbances and wars have possessed such authority in heaven or in the Church that, by his declaration, Charles the Great should be enrolled among the heavenly saints?

Does the silence of subsequent pontiffs concerning the matter strengthen a diploma supported by no authority? Whether a judgment, even if it proceeded from a schismatic, becomes legitimate on the grounds that it was not revoked by others, let others decide.

Whatever the case may be, since Charles has been counted among the saints from the time of Paschal, according to Baronius, and since Paschal did not seize the papal see until 1164, as is reported by an unpublished chronicle of uncertain authorship, and held it for five years, we have believed that the Office can be assigned to the year 1166, until greater light should shine from elsewhere.

We indicated that year above all because, as the Annals of Steron report, in that year “the translation of Saint Charles the emperor took place on the Wednesday after the Nativity of the Lord.” JACOB BASNAGE.] Another office.

## VII

[Note: [Col. 1367C] On Charlemagne’s being numbered among the saints, see Baronius under the year 814: “On account of his exceptional virtues, the Gallican Church celebrates his natal day, and the records of the Church of Aachen have him listed among the saints. Under the Emperor Frederick, 166 years later, a pope called Paschal enrolled him among the number of the saints. They say that the document of his registration is preserved in the Church of Aachen. But because that Paschal was not a legitimate pontiff but a schismatic, this canonization was not accepted by the Roman Church; for that reason his name was not entered in the Martyrology of the Roman Church. Yet since no legitimate pontiffs are found to have abolished, challenged, or prohibited that document, the matter has continued through silent permission or tolerance: namely, so that he might be venerated in his own church, where he was buried, in Gaul. Thus, at any rate, the principal interpreters of the canons have declared it. Moreover, his cult is known to have subsequently spread to other churches of Belgium and Germany, in which the same Charles is celebrated under the title of holiness; numerous writings of Frankish historians support them.” The name of Saint Charles is indeed found in very many calendars of Gaul and Germany, especially those of the churches which he either founded or enriched and adorned with gifts and honors: Aachen, Hildesheim, Osnabrück, Minden, Halberstadt, Zurich (Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. VI, pp. 437 ff.), and others. His feast, 28 January (cf. *Acts of the Saints* under that day), was reckoned among the greater feasts, nor was the Feast of the Translation of Saint Charles, 27 July, lacking. J.-B. Rousseau, in the book entitled *Purple Violets of the Saints*, relates that in 1661 the University of Paris created Saint Charles its patron, asserting that the Germans had already venerated him from the year 1480. Aeneas Sylvius perhaps does not dissent from this view, *Germany*, chapter 10, when he reports that the head of Charlemagne is preserved among the relics at Aachen. The hymn written above is taken from the Halberstadt Breviary; it is not surprising that many miracles performed by the holy emperor are signified in it, for in these Church books Charlemagne appears to have passed wholly into the realm of fables. It is not irrelevant to add what the Breviary cited above relates about the Life of Saint Charles. (For the individual matters, see Pertz, *Monuments of German History*, vol. V, p. 708.):

“Lesson I. Blessed Charles the king, descended from royal ancestors, had coal-black hair, a ruddy face, a well-proportioned body, but a fierce appearance. He was eight feet tall, extremely broad in the shoulders, well formed in the loins, proportionate in the belly, thick in the arms and legs, and exceedingly strong in all his limbs. Swift in combat, a most vigorous soldier, with eyes sparkling like carbuncles. Everyone was immediately terrified whom blessed Charles, moved to anger, looked upon with open eyes. Most generous in gifts, upright in judgments, eloquent in speech, he acquired many different lands and subjected them in the name of Christ. Throughout the world he founded and solemnly endowed a great many cathedral churches and abbeys.

“Lesson II. One night, when blessed Charles was in ecstasy, Saint James the Apostle of Christ, the brother of John the Evangelist, appeared to him and said: ‘I am exceedingly amazed that you have not freed my land from the Saracens, although you have acquired so many lands and such great cities. Therefore I announce to you that, just as the Lord has made you more powerful than all earthly kings, so he has chosen you above all others to prepare my way and free my land from the hands of the Moabites.

“Lesson III. Thus blessed Charles, relying upon the apostolic promise, assembled many armies, entered Spain to conquer the faithless peoples, and besieged Pamplona. He could not capture it, because it was fortified with impregnable walls. Then blessed Charles made a vow to the Lord, saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, for whose faith I have come at this hour [*oris?*] to conquer this faithless people, grant me the power to capture this city to the honor of your name. O James, if it is true that you appeared to me, grant me the capture of the city.’

“Lesson IV. Then, by God’s gift and through the prayer of blessed Charles, the walls were utterly broken and fell. The cities acquired by him, upon which he pronounced a curse, have remained without inhabitants to the present day. He slaughtered with the sword the Saracens who were in the city and refused baptism, but spared the others for life. When the Saracens heard of these miracles, they all bowed before blessed Charles wherever he went, sent tribute to meet him, and surrendered themselves and their cities to him. Thus that entire land became subject to him through tribute.

“Lesson V. At that time also, when blessed Charles had undertaken war against Aygoland, the African king, for the faith of Christ, certain Christians, preparing their weapons for battle on the day before the engagement, planted their upright spears in the ground. At dawn they found them adorned with bark and leaves, and cut down the spears, attributing the miracle to divine grace. The roots that remained in the earth later produced a great forest, which is still visible in that place. On that same day a battle was fought in which forty thousand Christians received the palm of martyrdom.

“Lesson VI. Then blessed Charles, with nearly 134,000 fighting men, entered into battle against King Aygoland on the following terms: the law of whichever side won would be more pleasing to God, and would be a disgrace to the defeated, but a law and rejoicing to the victorious forever. After Aygoland was defeated and a truce had been made with blessed Charles, he acknowledged that the law of the Christians was better than that of the Saracens. He promised blessed Charles that on the following day he and his people would receive baptism, but he failed to fulfill this on a frivolous pretext. Therefore blessed Charles, with an army of 34,000, went to battle with Aygoland for the faith of Christ and killed so many Saracens, together with Aygoland, that the victors swam in blood up to their feet.”

Thus far the Halberstadt Breviary.] Hymn on Saint Charles.

# SECOND SECTION OF THE APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE—HISTORICAL

[Col. 1369]

## TWO BOOKS ON THE DEEDS OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE

Written by a certain monk of Saint Gall and first published by Canisius from a manuscript in the library of the Most Serene Prince of Bavaria.

*(From Canisius, Ancient Readings.)*

## CANISIUS TO THE READER

[Col. 1369C]

From that most illustrious Munich library of the Most Serene Prince of Bavaria I obtained a manuscript containing four books of the *Deeds of Charlemagne*, with no author’s name attached. The first is plainly and wholly Einhard. The second consists of annals, though not complete, which have been published elsewhere and by Justus Reuber under the title of a certain Astronomus, a member of King Louis’s household. The remaining two, so far as I know, have not yet seen the light; nor have I sufficiently determined whether they deserve publication. I incline to that opinion, as does the noble and distinguished Velserus, so that we may regard them as worthy.

The author is certainly ancient, a monk of Saint Gall, as he himself shows in several places, Book I, chapters 32 and 36. He wrote at the command of Charles himself, for Charles the Fat, Emperor, the son of Louis the German, grandson of Louis the Pious, and great-grandson of Charlemagne; this I gather from Book I, chapters 20 and 32, and Book II, chapters 14, 15, 25, 26, and 28. In that same fifteenth chapter he mentions Hartmut, formerly abbot and at that time a recluse. Stumpfius, Book V, chapter 5, writes that Hartmut was elected in 872 and resigned in 883 or the following year.

Although the style is humble and abject, and the history itself is sometimes sprinkled with fables, it nevertheless contains matters deserving the memory of all posterity. Pithaeus judged it worthy to insert a fragment from it among the omissions at the end of the Carolingian Laws. The most illustrious Baronius and the learned Jacobus Gretserus also cited it, the latter in volume I, Book II, *On the Cross*, chapter 52. In Book I, chapter 8, the author calls Gallus his master; in chapters 11 and 36 he shows himself to be German. In Book II, chapter 16, he promises to write more about Charlemagne, though whether he fulfilled that promise is unknown to us. In Book II, chapter 26, he testifies that he wrote these books when already weighed down by old age and toothless.

## J. BASNAGE’S OBSERVATION ON THESE DEEDS OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE

### 1. The time at which these books were written

The time at which these books were written can easily be inferred, since the author mentions Hartmut, who, after having served as provost during the abbacy of Grimald, abbot of Saint Gall, was later elected abbot and resigned his office in 883. The author calls him “the Recluse” (Book II, chapter 15). This work, therefore, was published after 883 and before 887, when all the nobles of the empire abandoned Charles the Fat, at whose command the author committed the deeds of his great-grandfather to writing. Within that three-year period anyone may prefer one year to another according to his pleasure. We assign the year 884; if anyone prefers 885, we will gladly yield the point.

### 2. The author

Goldast attempted to determine who the author was and chose, above all among the monks of Saint Gall, Notker the Stammerer, who was then alive. Quercetanus rejected rather than accepted the conjecture, observing that Goldast had asserted it after being led by “I know not what arguments.” Goldast relied chiefly on the observation that the author was a monk of Saint Gall at the end of the ninth century and had called himself “toothless and stammering.” The former description suits Notker, and so does the latter, for he was stammering:

> Sick, stammering, and full of faults,  
> With polluted mouth I sang  
> The triumphs of Stephen, unworthy Notker,  
> At the command of the holy bishop.

Notker could also have been toothless in 884, since he was then at least fifty-four years old and had often been ill, as the verses cited readily demonstrate. For this reason I would accept Goldast’s opinion, however much the learned man rejected it; for it can scarcely have happened that two contemporary monks in the same monastery of Saint Gall were toothless, stammering, and writers.

### 3. What should be observed in this work concerning the conduct of bishops

Although Notker here professes to describe the deeds of Charlemagne, you will scarcely observe anything about that emperor. In the first book there is a censor’s rod with which bishops are marked out, and their conduct is often sharply censured. He notes several things about episcopal arrogance and ambition: one bishop wished to use Charlemagne’s golden scepter; another received a marked loaf even before the emperor, and when he later wished to offer it to the emperor, he received the reply, “Keep that entire loaf for yourself.” Nor would Charles accept the blessing pronounced by him. One bishop procured a mouse, another a mule, at the highest possible price; another, while repeatedly indulging in wine and food, was unable to preach any sermon to the people and “pretended to celebrate the solemn rites”; another violated a beautiful woman brought to his bed; another adulterer was brought before the Bishop of bishops (Book I, chapter 27).

There can be no doubt who is meant: the emperor Charles is clearly indicated, although in our own day the Roman pontiff is best known by that title.

### 4. Fables and falsehoods

There are other matters that bear the mark of fables, indeed matters unworthy either of a religious man or of a historian. Among the former I include what he relates about the boys entrusted by the emperor to Clement so that they might compose letters and poems. He presents Charles as an imitator of the eternal Judge, who separates those who have worked well to his right hand and the others to his left, as will occur at the Last Judgment.

Among the latter you will readily notice what Notker says about Roman chant. It not only differs from the accounts of other writers, but the author errs in making Leo III the successor of Stephen; this cannot be reconciled in any way with historical truth. What he writes about the Greek envoys is also false, as we have noted.

### 5. On the military deeds of Charlemagne

The author had heard Charlemagne’s military deeds as a boy, “under compulsion, unwillingly, and often while trying to escape,” from an old man who had taken part in the Saxon war. Whether that old man narrated them faithfully, or whether they remained firmly fixed in the boy’s memory, who can say?

He gives a remarkable example of savagery, indeed cruelty, in Charlemagne, who “ordered the enemy’s boys and infants to be measured against swords, so that anyone who exceeded that measure would be punished by death.” Nor was Pippin more merciful, for he pointed out that the Franks should be exterminated, “pulling useless refuse from a garden”; this was the answer he gave to Charlemagne’s envoys, “so that the necessary vegetables might grow more freely.”

### 6. Various observations

According to Notker, Louis experienced that sacred things are polluted when peoples are compelled or forcibly driven to receive them. A Norman, for example, asserted that he had already bathed twenty times and had been dressed in white garments—that is, that he had been baptized—yet nevertheless declared that he would leave his clothing and Christ with the emperor, if only he were not ashamed of his nakedness. Let princes learn from this what torture and deception can accomplish in matters of religion.

There are still various things that might be observed, which we omit. The clothing of the ancient Gauls is described with sufficient accuracy in chapter 1 of the first book, as are the customs and camps of the Huns in chapter 2 of the second book. He not only sketches the virtues and natural character of Louis the German but extols them with many praises, which perhaps are not free from suspicion, since Charles the Fat, at whose command he wrote, was his son.

## THE MONK OF SAINT GALL ON THE DEEDS OF CHARLEMAGNE

[Note: [Col. 1371D] The preface to the first book is missing. It begins with “M.”]

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1371]

## CHAPTER ONE. Charlemagne’s care for the Church

[Col. 1371C]

[Col. 1371D] When the almighty disposer of kings [Note: [Col. 1371D] M. reads “of things” (*rerum*).] and ordainer of kingdoms and times had shattered the iron or clay feet of that wondrous statue among the Romans (Dan. II), he raised among the Franks, through the illustrious Charles, the golden head of another statue no less wondrous.

When he had begun to reign alone in the western regions of the world, and the study of letters was almost everywhere forgotten, it happened that two Scots from Ireland arrived on the coast of Gaul with British merchants. They were men incomparably learned both in secular matters and in the Holy Scriptures. Since they displayed nothing for sale, they would habitually call out to the crowds who gathered to buy:

> “If anyone desires wisdom, let him come to us and receive it; for with us it is for sale.”

They nevertheless professed to have wisdom for sale because they saw that the people purchased not free things but things for sale, so that they might thus encourage them to buy wisdom just as they bought other goods; or, as what follows confirms, so that by this proclamation they might turn them toward admiration and astonishment.

At last these cries continued until they reached the ears of King Charles, who had always been a lover and most eager seeker of wisdom, whether from those who admired them or from those who thought them mad. He summoned them to his presence with all speed and asked whether they truly possessed wisdom, as rumor had reported. They replied:

> “We possess it, and in the name of the Lord we are prepared to give it to those who seek it worthily.”

When he asked them what they requested in return for this wisdom [Note: [Col. 1371D] Read: “wisdom.”], they replied that they wanted only suitable places, ingenious minds [Note: [Col. 1372D] Perhaps *animos ingeniosos*. Canisius reads *animas ingeniosas*; Moiss.], and food and clothing, without which a journey cannot be completed.

When he heard this, the king was filled with great joy and at first kept both men with him for a short time. Later, when he was pressed by military campaigns, he ordered one of them, named Clement, to remain in Gaul [Note: [Col. 1373D] M. reads “made”], and entrusted to him many boys of the highest, middle, and lowest ranks. He ordered provisions to be supplied to them according to their needs and assigned suitable dwellings for habitation [Note: [Col. 1373D] M. reads “for meditation.”]. The other, named Albinus, he sent to Italy and assigned to him the monastery of Saint Augustine near the city of Pavia, so that those who wished to learn might gather there to him.

## CHAPTER II. Alcuin’s arrival in Gaul

When Albinus, an Englishman by nation, heard how gladly Charles, the most religious of kings, welcomed learned men, he boarded a ship and came to him. He was more thoroughly trained than other men of his time in the whole breadth of Scripture [Note: [Col. 1373D] M. reads “in all the Scriptures”], being, as it were, a disciple of the most learned Bede. At this point the text is corrupt: “who Saint Gregory * of the commentator” (*qui sanctum Gregorium * tractatoris*); it then continues, “whom he retained continually with him until the end of his life, except when he went forth to meet impending wars,” to such an extent that he wished himself to be called his disciple and Bede his teacher.

He gave him the abbey of Saint Martin near the city of Tours, so that whenever Charles was absent, Alcuin might rest there and teach those who flocked to him. His teaching bore fruit to such an extent that the modern Gauls, or Franks, became the equals of the ancient Romans and Athenians.

## CHAPTER III. Learning preferred to nobility

After the most victorious Charles had returned to Gaul following a long period away, he ordered the boys whom he had entrusted to Clement to come to him and present their letters and poems.

The boys of middle and lowest rank, contrary to expectation, presented works sweetened with every seasoning of wisdom, while the nobles, lukewarm in every kind of stupidity, presented their own efforts. Then the most wise Charles, imitating the justice of the eternal Judge, separated those who had worked well to his right hand and addressed them in these words:

> “Give many thanks, my sons, because you have applied yourselves, according to your ability, to carrying out my command and promoting your own advantage. Now strive to reach perfection, and I shall give you magnificent bishoprics and monasteries.”

Then, turning his face with great severity toward those on his left and shaking their consciences with a blazing gaze, he hurled these terrifying words at them in irony, thundering them forth rather than speaking:

> “You nobles, you sons of the foremost, you delicate and handsome boys, relying upon your birth and possessions, you have set aside my command and your own advancement and given yourselves to literary studies, luxury, games, idleness, and empty pursuits.”

After saying this, and turning his august head and unconquered right hand toward heaven with the oath customary to him [*with his customary oath*], he thundered:

> “By the King of heaven, I do not value your nobility and beauty highly, although others admire you. And know this beyond all doubt: unless you quickly recover your former negligence through vigilant study, you will never obtain anything good from Charles.”

## CHAPTER IV. A bishopric granted to a young man

From among the poor boys mentioned above, he took one excellent composer and writer into his chapel [Note: [Col. 1373D] It was called a *capella*, evidently from the cloak (*cappa*) with which the body of Saint Martin was covered. The sacred building in which that cloak was kept was called a *capella*, and hence came the term *chaplains*, who served the emperor in sacred matters and to whom the custody of that cloak was entrusted. Those emperors had many chapels, even in their military camps; but the one located in the palace, in which many relics were kept, was called the holy chapel in particular. On chaplains, see Walafrid Strabo, *On Church Matters*, chapter 31. BASN.], a term by which the kings of the Franks customarily called their sanctuary, because of Saint Martin’s cloak, which they continually carried with them to war for their own protection and the oppression of their enemies.

When word was brought to this boy that a certain bishop had died, and the most provident King Charles asked whether he had sent anything ahead of him from his possessions or labors for his journey, the messenger replied:

> “My lord, no more than two pounds of silver.”

The boy sighed and, unable to keep the thought within his breast, involuntarily burst out in the king’s hearing [Note: [Col. 1374D] M. reads “burst forth”]:

> “A small provision for a long and enduring journey!”

When Charles, the most temperate of men, had reflected for a little while, he said to him:

> “Do you think that if you receive that bishopric, you will take care to send more provisions ahead for that long journey?”

As the boy swallowed these suspended words, which fell into the mouth of one gaping like premature grapes, he fell at the king’s feet and said:

> “My lord, this lies in God’s will and in your power.”

The king said:

> “Stand behind the curtain hanging at my back, and listen to how many assistants you have for this dignity.”

When the courtiers heard of the bishop’s death, they—always lying in wait for the misfortunes, or at least the conduct, of others—each through persons close to the emperor, impatient of delay and envious of one another [Note: [Col. 1374D] M. reads “envious of another”], strove to acquire the office for himself.

But Charles remained firm in his resolve and refused them all, saying that he did not wish to deceive that young man. At last Queen Hildegard first sent the nobles of the kingdom and then approached the king herself to obtain the bishopric for her cleric. When he received her request most graciously, saying that he neither wished nor was able to refuse her anything, except that he disdained to deceive the young cleric—as is the custom of all women, who wish their counsel and desire to outweigh the decisions of men—she concealed the anger conceived in her mind, transformed her deep voice into a thin one, and attempted by languid gestures to soften the emperor’s unshaken resolve. She said:

> “My lord king, why give that bishopric to that boy, for his ruin? Rather, I beseech you, my sweetest lord, my glory and refuge, give it to your faithful servant, that cleric of mine.”

Then the young man, whom the king had ordered to stand behind the curtain so that he might hear how each person pleaded, said when the queen had spoken:

> “My lord king, hold fast to your strength, lest anyone wrest from your hands the power given to you by God.”

Then the strongest lover of truth summoned him into the open and said:

> “Have that bishopric, and take careful measures to send greater expenses and provisions for that long and irreversible journey ahead of both me and yourself.””

## CHAPTER V. A lowly and poor cleric becomes a bishop

There was a certain cleric in the king’s retinue who was lowly and despised and not sufficiently instructed in literary knowledge. The just and most pious Charles, moved by compassion for his poverty, could never be persuaded to cast him aside or remove him from his presence, although everyone hated him and tried to expel him.

It happened that, on the eve of Saint Martin, word was brought to the emperor that a certain bishop had died. He summoned one of his clerics, a man of considerable nobility and learning, and gave him the bishopric. Overcome with joy, the man summoned many courtiers to his residence, received the numerous people who came to him from that parish with great pomp, and had a magnificent banquet prepared for everyone.

Overburdened with food, gulping down unmixed wine and buried in drink, he neglected to attend the nocturnal vigils on that most holy night. It was customary for the master of the school to designate the responsory that each person was to sing during the night on the preceding day. To this man, who already held the bishopric almost in his hand, the responsory “Lord, if I am still necessary to your people” had been assigned.

When he failed to appear, and a long silence followed the reading, and they urged one another to take up the responsory, with one person after another saying that he ought to sing his own responsory, the emperor finally said:

> “Let someone sing.”

Then the despised man, strengthened by divine power and fortified by such authority, intoned the responsory. At once the most merciful king, not supposing that he knew how to sing the whole of it, ordered others to assist him. When the others sang, and the unfortunate man could learn no verse from anyone, after the responsory had been sung he began to chant the Lord’s Prayer in the most melodious manner.

Although everyone wished to interrupt him, the most wise Charles, wanting to test how far the man would proceed, ordered that no one disturb him. When he concluded the verse with the words, “Your kingdom come,” the others, whether they wished to or not, were compelled to respond, “Your will be done.”

When the morning praises were finished, and the king returned to the palace, or sleeping chamber, to warm and adorn himself for the honor of so great a festival [Note: [Col. 1375D] M. reads “because of the approaching festival”], he ordered the old servant but new singer to be summoned and said to him:

> “Who ordered you to sing that responsory?”

Terrified, the man replied:

> “My lord, you ordered me: ‘Let someone sing.’”

The king replied—“Good,” a word formerly customary in imperial usage—and added:

> “Who showed you that verse?”

Then, inspired, as is believed, by God, he framed his answer in the words by which superiors at that time were accustomed to be honored, flattered, or courted:

> “Joyful man, my lord, rejoicing king, since I could ask no one else for another verse, I considered in my mind that if I seized upon some unsuitable one, I would incur the condemnation of your displeasure. Therefore I decided to sing one whose ending would correspond, according to custom, with that of the preceding responsory.”

Then the most temperate emperor, smiling gently at him, pronounced before his nobles:

> “Let that proud man, who feared and honored neither God nor his chief friend enough to restrain himself from luxury even for a single night, so that he might at least have managed to begin the responsory which, as I hear, he ought to have sung, be deprived of the bishopric by divine and by my judgment. And you, by God’s gift and with my permission, take care to govern it according to canonical and apostolic authority.”

## CHAPTER VI. A bishop who mounts a horse too quickly

When another bishop had died, the emperor appointed a certain young man in his place. As the young man happily went out to depart, and his attendants, in accordance with episcopal dignity, brought a horse to the steps for mounting [Col. 1375D], he became indignant that they had treated him as though he were infirm. He mounted the horse from level ground so abruptly that he could scarcely keep himself from falling over the other side.

When the king saw this through the palace screens, he immediately ordered him to be summoned and addressed him as follows:

> “Good man, you are quick and agile, swift and fleet. As you yourself know, the serenity of the empire is disturbed on every side by many storms of war. For this reason I need such a cleric in my retinue. So remain for the time being as a companion of our labors, since you can mount your horse so quickly.”

## CHAPTER VII. On the readings

What I forgot to say about the arrangement of the readings when I was recounting the disposition of the responsories may be briefly completed here.

In the basilica of the most learned Charles, no one assigned readings to anyone for recitation; no one put a mark at the end, or on the wax, or at least impressed the slightest sign with a fingernail. Rather, everyone took care to make familiar to himself everything that had to be read, so that whenever he was ordered unexpectedly to read, he would be found irreproachable before the emperor [*they would be considered irreproachable*].

By extending a finger or staff, or by directing something from his side toward those seated at a distance, Charles indicated whom he wished to read. He marked the end of a reading by a sound of the throat. All were so intently attentive to this that, whether he indicated the end of a sentence, the middle of a division, or a point beneath a division, no one who followed, or who was lower down, dared to begin, however unsuitable the ending or beginning might seem.

Thus it came about that, even if not everyone understood, the readers in his palace were all excellent. No stranger, nor even any acquaintance, unless he knew how to read and sing, dared enter his choir.

## CHAPTER VIII. The cleric who did not know how to sing

When Charles, traveling, had come to a certain great basilica, a cleric from among the wandering religious, ignorant of Charles’s discipline, entered the choir of his own accord. He had never learned anything of this kind and stood mute and bewildered in the midst of the singers. The *paraphonista*, raising his little rod, threatened to strike him if he did not sing.

Not knowing what to do or where he could turn, and not daring to go outside, the man twisted his neck into a circle and, with his jaws hanging open [Note: [Col. 1375D] M. reads “jaws”], tried as best he could to imitate the manner of singing. When the others could no longer contain their laughter [Note: [Col. 1375D] M. reads “hold back”], the strongest emperor, who was not moved from his composure even by great matters, waited with perfect order for the end of the Mass, as though he had not noticed the man’s gesture of compulsion [reading: “singing” (*cantationis*)].

Afterward he summoned the poor man to him and, taking pity on his exertions and distress, consoled him in this way:

> “Give many thanks, good cleric, for your singing and your labors.”

To relieve his poverty, he ordered one pound of silver to be given to him.

Nor should I seem to forget or neglect this point: I learned from his diligence or merits that, of his disciples, none remained who did not become either a most holy abbot or a most holy bishop. Among them my master Gallus [Note: [Col. 1375D] Read “Grimald,” who was abbot of Saint Gall during Notker’s early years. In the manuscript there was only the first letter, G., and the copyists believed that Gallus was intended, since he was better known than Grimald, as Mabillon correctly observes. For in Ekerard’s *Life of Notker* we read that Notker’s parents “offered him to Father Gallus, under the archimandrite who at that time presided over this place, named Grimald, a canonical abbot.” BASN.] was first instructed in the liberal disciplines in Gaul and afterward in Italy.

But lest those knowledgeable about these matters accuse me of lying because I have excepted no one, there were two sons of millers in his school, from the household of Saint Columbanus. Since it was not fitting that they should be raised to the governance of bishoprics or monasteries, nevertheless, through the merits, as is believed, of their teacher, they successively governed the provostship of the monastery of Babbio with the greatest energy.

## CHAPTER IX. Charles desires clerics equal to Augustine

When the most glorious Charles saw literary studies flourishing throughout his kingdom, but mourned that they had not reached the maturity of the Fathers who had preceded them, and labored beyond human strength, he burst forth in weariness:

> “If only I had twelve clerics so learned and so perfectly instructed in every kind of wisdom as Jerome and Augustine were!”

At this, the most learned Albinus, rightly judging himself utterly unlearned by comparison with them, and since no mortal would dare presume to speak in the presence of the most terrible Charles, replied, conceiving the greatest indignation but displaying only a little of it:

> “The Creator of heaven and earth had no more men like them, and you wish to have twelve?”

## CHAPTER X. On Roman chant
It seems necessary to relate here something that people of our own time will nevertheless find difficult to believe. Even I myself, who am writing this, do not yet fully believe it, because of the great difference between our melody and that of the Romans—unless, indeed, greater credence ought to be given to the truth of the Fathers than to the feeble falsehood of modern times.

Therefore Charles, the indefatigable lover of divine service, rejoicing that he had achieved as much as possible of his desire in the science of letters, but still deeply distressed that all the provinces—or rather regions and cities—differed from one another in the praises of God, that is, in the modulations of the chant, obtained from Pope Stephen of blessed memory—who, after deposing and tonsuring Hilderic, the most sluggish king of the Franks, anointed himself for the governance of the kingdom according to the custom of the ancient Fathers—some clerics exceptionally skilled in divine matters. The pope, assenting to Charles’s good will and divinely inspired studies, sent twelve very learned clerics from the apostolic see to him in Francia, corresponding to the number of the twelve apostles.

Whenever I use the name “Francia,” I mean all the provinces on this side of the Alps. This was in accordance with what is written in Zechariah 8: “On that day ten men from every language of the nations shall seize the hem of a Jewish man.”

## CHAPTER XI. Roman Deceptions

At that time, on account of the excellence of the most glorious Charles, the Franks and Aquitanians, the Aedui and Spaniards, the Alamanni and Bavarians, took no little pride in their distinction. When the clerics mentioned above were departing from Rome—for, as always, all the Greeks and Romans were gnawed by envy at the glory of the Franks—they deliberated among themselves how they might alter the chant in such a way that its unity and concord would never be enjoyed throughout a kingdom or province not belonging to them.

When they came to Charles, they were honorably received and dispersed among the most prominent places. Each of them, in his own place, labored to devise the most different and most corrupt version he could, to sing it himself, and thus to teach it to others.

When the exceptionally intelligent Charles had celebrated the feasts of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord one year at Trier or Metz, and had most vigilantly—or rather, most keenly—detected, or better, penetrated, the force of the melodies, he celebrated the same solemnities the following year at Paris or Tours and heard none of the sound that he had experienced the previous year in the places mentioned above. He also discovered that those whom he had sent to other places were disagreeing among themselves as their locations diverged. He therefore reported the matter to Pope Stephen, successor to Pope Leo of holy memory.

[Note: [Col. 1377D] Should one read, “to Pope Leo, Stephen’s successor”? Yet Adrian, not Leo, succeeded Stephen IV. Or should one read, “to Pope Stephen, successor to Pope Leo”? Yet Stephen V succeeded Leo only after Charlemagne’s death and is said to have reigned for only seven months. I know what Walafrid Strabo says of Stephen III: “Pope Stephen,” he says, “brought a more perfect knowledge of chant—which nearly all Gaul has now learned—to Pippin, Charlemagne’s father, when he came (first into Francia) to seek justice for Saint Peter from the Lombards; at that same Pippin’s request, through his clerics. From this its use grew strong far and wide.” CAN. This is a lapse of memory on the author’s part, who doubtless did not remember Adrian, unless one attributes the error to the copyist and wishes to substitute “Adrian” for “Stephen.” BASN.]

Stephen summoned the men to Rome and condemned them either to exile or to perpetual imprisonment.

He said to the illustrious Charles: “If I provide you with others, they too, blinded by the same envy as their predecessors, will not fail to mock you.
