But I shall satisfy your studies in this way: give me two exceptionally talented clerics from your own household, so that those who are with me may not realize that they belong to you; and, God willing, they will attain perfect knowledge of the matter you seek.”

And so it was done. After a short time, he sent them back to Charles, excellently instructed. He retained one of them with himself, while, at the request of his son, he sent the other to Trogon, bishop of Metz, for service in that church.

Through the latter’s industry, this chant began to flourish not only in that place but to spread throughout Francia to such an extent that, even now, among those in these regions who use the Latin language, ecclesiastical chant is called “Metz chant.” Among us, however, who speak the German or Teutonic language, it is called in the vernacular Met or Mette, or, according to its Greek derivation, by the customary name Metisca.

[Note: Read “Trogon.” M.]

## CHAPTER XII. Charles’s Fast in Lent

The most religious and temperate Charles had this custom: during the days of Lent he took food at the eighth hour of the day, after the celebration of Mass had been completed together with the evening praises. Nevertheless, he did not thereby violate the fast, since, according to the Lord’s command, they ate from hour to hour.

A certain bishop, very strict against the prohibition of a wise man but excessively foolish, imprudently criticized this practice. The most wise Charles, however, pretending indignation, humbly accepted his admonition and said: “You have admonished me well, cheerful bishop. But I order you to taste nothing before the foreign officials who are in my court have been refreshed.”

While Charles was eating, dukes and tyrants—or kings—of various nations served him. After his meal, when they were eating, counts and prefects, or nobles of various ranks, served them. When those men had also finished eating, military men and scholars of the court were refreshed. After them came the masters of every sort of office, and then the servants, so that the last of them did not eat until midnight.

When Lent was nearly over and the bishop had continued in this discipline, the most merciful Charles said to him: “I think, bishop, you have learned that I dine during Lent before the evening hour not because of intemperance but for the sake of proper provision.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Blessed Bread

On another occasion, when Charles asked a bishop for a blessing, the bishop first made the sign of the cross over a loaf and took some for himself, then wished to offer it to the most honorable Charles. Charles said to him: “Keep that entire loaf for yourself.” And, having thus confused him, he refused to receive his blessing.

## CHAPTER XIV. One Benefice to Be Given to Each Person

The most provident Charles never granted any count more than one county, except those who were stationed on the frontier or boundary of the barbarians. He never entrusted any bishop with an abbey or churches belonging to royal jurisdiction except for the most compelling reasons.

When his counselors or household companions asked why he acted in this way, he replied: “With that estate or court, that little abbey or church, I make for myself a vassal as good as—or better than—that count or bishop, and one faithful to me.”

For certain reasons he did grant some men very great possessions, as, for example, to Udalric, the brother of the great Hildigard, mother of kings and emperors. After Hildigard’s death, Charles deprived Udalric of his honors on account of some offense. A certain jester then proclaimed in the ears of the most merciful Charles: “Now Udalric has his lost honors in east and west, since his sister is dead.”

At these words Charles shed tears and immediately had his former honors restored to him. To holy places as well, prompted by justice, he openly extended his most generous hands, as will become clear from what follows.

## CHAPTER XV. A Bishop’s Witty Remark

There was a certain bishopric that Charles encountered—or rather, could not avoid—when traveling. The bishop of that place, wishing to satisfy him, expended in his service everything he was able to possess.

## CHAPTER XVI

On one occasion the emperor arrived unexpectedly. The bishop was then thrown into confusion and, like a swallow, ran here and there, having not only the basilicas and houses but also the estates and the streets themselves swept and cleaned. Very weary and indignant, he went out to meet Charles.

When the most pious Charles noticed this, he cast his eyes in different directions and inspected everything, then said to the bishop: “Excellent host, you always have everything carefully cleaned for our arrival.”

The bishop, as though addressed by divine inspiration, came to a halt, embraced and kissed Charles’s right hand—“vengeful,” according to the received reading; alternatively, “coming to rest and [embracing] the invincible right hand”—and, concealing his indignation as best he could, replied: “It is right, lord, that wherever you come, everything should be cleansed down to the bottom.”

Then the wisest of kings, understanding one thing from another, said to him: “If I have learned how to empty, I have also learned how to fill.”

And he added: “You shall have that estate adjoining your bishopric, and so shall all your successors forever.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Charles the Great, Highly Skilled in Distinguishing Cheeses

During the same journey Charles unexpectedly came to a certain bishop stationed in an unavoidable location. That day he did not wish to eat the flesh of four-footed animals or birds, because it was Friday. The bishop, according to the resources of the place, was suddenly unable to find fish, and ordered an excellent cheese to be set before Charles, one rich in fat and mold.

The very temperate Charles, trained in all things and everywhere, sparing the bishop’s embarrassment, asked for nothing else. Taking up a knife, he discarded the disgusting mold, as it seemed to him, and ate the white part of the cheese.

The bishop, who was standing nearby in the manner of a servant, came closer and said: “Why are you doing that, emperor? What you are throwing away is the best part.”

Then Charles, who knew not how to deceive and thought that no one could deceive him, put a piece of that mold into his mouth at the bishop’s urging. Slowly chewing it, he swallowed it like butter. Approving the bishop’s advice, he said: “You have spoken truly, good host.”

He added: “Do not fail to send me every year two *karratae* filled with cheeses of this kind to Aachen.”

[Note: A kind of vessel. See Du Cange.]

Overwhelmed by the impossibility of the task, the bishop, as though his position and ministry were in danger, suggested to him: “Lord, I can acquire cheeses, but I do not know which ones are of this kind and which are otherwise; and I fear that I may be found blameworthy in your eyes.”

Then Charles, whom unfamiliar and unknown things could in no way escape or remain hidden from, said to the bishop, who had been raised amid such matters yet still knew nothing about them: “Cut them all in half. Those that you see to be of this kind, fasten together on a sharpened stick and send them to me in a *cuba*; reserve the others for yourself, your clergy, or your household.”

[Note: In Gallic usage, *une cuve*; thus Rather of Verona ordered that a *cuba* be loaded with grain. Yet one does not find this word used anywhere before the ninth century. Among the oldest writers, *cuba* meant a litter; here it has an entirely different sense.]

After this had been done for two years, and the king had ordered such gifts to be accepted without comment, in the third year the bishop himself took care, with great labor, to bring and present them from so far away. Then the most equitable Charles, taking pity on his cares and labors, gave to that same bishopric—or bishop—an excellent estate, from which he and his successors could obtain grain and wine for their own needs and those of their people.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Bishop Who Bought a Mouse

Since we have related how the most wise Charles exalted the humble, let us also relate how he humbled the proud.

There was a certain bishop very desirous of empty glory and worthless things. The extremely shrewd Charles perceived this and ordered a certain Jewish merchant—who was accustomed to visit the Promised Land frequently and to bring back from there many costly and unfamiliar objects to the provinces overseas—to deceive or mock that bishop in some way.

The merchant understood the order. He seasoned a domestic mouse with various spices and brought it for sale to the bishop, saying that he had brought from Judea this most precious animal, never before seen.

The bishop, filled with joy at so remarkable a thing, offered him three pounds of silver so that he might obtain the dearly prized gift.

Then the Jew said: “What a fitting price for so precious a gift! I would sooner throw it into the depths of the sea than allow any man to acquire it for so vile and disgraceful a price.”

The bishop, who possessed much but never gave anything to the poor, promised him ten pounds so that he might obtain the incomparable object.

Then the shrewd man, pretending indignation, declared: “God forbid, by Abraham, that I should lose my labor and the cost of transporting it in such a way!”

The avaricious cleric, longing for so precious a gift, offered him twenty pounds. The Jew, therefore, becoming agitated, wrapped the mouse in the most precious silk and began to leave. The bishop, seemingly deceived but in truth destined to be deceived, called him back and gave him a full *modius* of silver so that he might possess the most precious mouse.

At last the merchant, pressed by many entreaties, reluctantly consented. He took the silver to the emperor and recounted everything that had happened.

Not many days later the king summoned all the bishops and nobles of that province to his council. After many necessary matters had been discussed, he ordered all that silver to be brought in and placed in the middle of the palace.

Then he said: “You, our fathers and guardians, our bishops, ought to serve the poor—or rather, Christ in the poor—not yearn for empty things. Yet now, turning everything upside down, you pursue vainglory or avarice above all mortals.”

He added: “One of you gave this much silver to a Jew for a single domestic mouse seasoned with spices.”

The man who had been deceived in so shameful a matter fell at Charles’s feet and begged forgiveness for his offense. Charles rebuked him with an appropriate reprimand and allowed him to depart in confusion.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Bishop Who Carried a Golden Rod Instead of a Staff

When the warlike Charles was occupied in his war against the Huns, that same bishop was left in charge of the most glorious Hildigard. As he began to be encouraged by her familiarity, he proceeded to such insolence that, wickedly desiring the incomparable Charles’s golden rod—which Charles had ordered to be made according to his stature—to be carried on feast days in place of a staff, he sought to obtain it for episcopal use.

She cleverly mocked him, saying that she did not dare give it to any human being, but that she would nevertheless serve as a trustworthy ambassador for him before the king.

When she came to Charles, she jokingly reported what the foolish bishop had requested. The king most cheerfully assented to his petition and promised that he would do even more than the bishop had asked.

When nearly the whole of Europe had gathered around Charles, the conqueror of so great a people, he proclaimed the following in the ears of high and low:

“Bishops ought to be despisers of this world and, by their example, to summon others to seek heavenly things. Now, however, they are corrupted by such ambition above all other mortals that one of them, not content with the bishopric he holds in the chief see of Germany, wished, without our knowledge, to claim for himself our scepter, which we customarily carry in gold as a sign of our rule, in place of a pastoral staff.”

The guilty man recognized his guilt, received pardon, and withdrew.

## CHAPTER XX. The Bishop Who Could Not Preach a Sermon

I am exceedingly afraid, Lord Emperor Charles, that, while wishing to fulfill your command, I may incur the displeasure of every profession, and especially of the highest priests. Nevertheless, I care little about all of them, provided that I am not deprived of your protection.

The most religious Emperor Charles ordered that all the bishops throughout his vast kingdom should preach in the basilica of their ecclesiastical see before the appointed day that he had established. Whoever failed to do so was to lose the honor of his bishopric.

But why do I say “honor,” when the Apostle declares: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (1 Timothy 3)? Yet I confess frankly and secretly to you that there is great honor in it, while scarcely any good work is required.

The bishop mentioned above was terrified by this command. He knew nothing except how to luxuriate and be proud, and he feared that, if deprived of his bishopric, he would likewise be deprived of his luxury. He therefore summoned two of the leading palace officials on a feast day. After the reading of the Gospel, he ascended the steps as though he were about to address the people.

Everyone hurried forward in amazement at this unexpected event, except for a very poor little man, extremely red-haired, who had covered his head with his little Gallic garment—for he had no cap and was excessively ashamed of his color.

[Note: Read *alicula*. Scriverius, manuscript note. Indeed, *alicula* was a kind of garment, known from a fragment of Petronius, which says: “A huge barbarian, bound with leg-bands and dressed in a belted *alicula*.”]

[Note: M has “with his head.”]

The man who was called bishop, but was not truly one, said to his doorkeeper—or *scarion*:

[Note: “Aedituus,” Scriverius; he likewise emends the following word, *aedilitiorum*, and restores *aedituorum*. The *scariones* were not only doorkeepers but also servants of judges, and sometimes even judges. First, they were the men who swore in the name of monks and bishops. “Let no one dare to summon the abbots or monks of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Vulturno to swear, because we believe this contrary to divine law; but let them give proof through *scariones* at all times, as was the ancient custom.” Erchembert likewise says in his *History of the Lombards* that no oath was to be given personally to any man except through *scariones*.

“Second, they collected the dues of monks and bishops: ‘He shall have no collector, but the bishop’s and brothers’ stewards and *scheriones* shall collect what is owed to him.’ For *scheriones* are the same as *scariones*. Finally, they sat as judges, and disputes were settled through their intervention: ‘Let the *scheriones* judge the hearing . . . and if an outsider thief is caught in the village, let him be handed over to the count’s *scherio* outside the village.’ Thus it is clear that counts, like bishops and abbots, had their own *scheriones*.—Chronicle of Saint Vincent of Vulturno, book 2; *History of France*, vol. 3, p. 685; Rights of the Church of Bamberg in the *Metropolis of Salzburg*, vol. 3, p. 50.”]

“Call to me that capped man who is standing beside the church door.”

The doorkeeper, hastening to fulfill the Lord’s command, seized the poor man and began to drag him toward the bishop. Fearing that he would be punished severely for having dared to stand in God’s house with his head covered, he resisted with all his strength, lest he be led, as though before the tribunal of a severe judge.

The bishop, looking down from above, alternately shouted at his vassal and at the poor man, crying in a loud voice: “Drag him here! Be careful not to let him go! Whether he wishes it or not, he must come here.”

When the man had been overcome either by force or by fear and drew near, the bishop said: “Come closer, come nearer still.” Then he seized him, pulled the covering from his head, and proclaimed to the people: “Behold, people, you see that this sluggish fellow is red-haired!”

He then returned to the altar and celebrated the solemn rites—or pretended to have celebrated them.

[Note: M has “was dragged.”]

When these proceedings had thus been brought to an end, they entered a hall decorated with various tapestries and every sort of curtain. There the sumptuous banquet, served in vessels of gold, silver, and jewels, could have stimulated the appetite even of men suffering from disgust or nausea.

The bishop himself sat amid the softest cushions, covered with the most precious silk and dressed in imperial purple, so that nothing was lacking to him except that scepter and the royal title. He was surrounded by cohorts of the richest soldiers, in comparison with whom the palace officials—that is, the nobles of the unconquered Charles—seemed utterly contemptible even to themselves.

When, after that marvelous banquet, such as kings were unaccustomed to see, the men asked permission to depart, the bishop, wishing to display his magnificence and glory more clearly, ordered the most skilled masters of song to come forward with all the musical instruments.

[Note: M has “with the instruments of the musicians.”]

Their voices and sounds could soften the stoutest hearts and harden the clearest streams of the Rhine.

Meanwhile, the most varied kinds of drink, mixed with different spices or medicines, crowned with herbs and flowers that drew into themselves the splendor of gems or gold and infused their own redness into them, stood warm in their hands, their stomachs already brimming.

The bakers, butchers, cooks, and confectioners, while their bellies were full, prepared with exquisite skill every sort of stimulant to gluttony—such a feast as had never been prepared even for Charles the Great.

When morning came and the bishop had returned somewhat to sobriety, he began to shudder at the luxury he had displayed the previous day before the emperor’s attendants. He ordered them to be brought before him, honored them with royal gifts, and adjured them to report good and honorable things about him to the terrible Charles.

He also asked them to say publicly in the church, in their hearing, what they had heard him preach.

[Note: M has “modest” in place of “honorable.”]

When the emperor questioned them on their return about why the bishop had summoned them, they fell at his feet and said: “Lord, he summoned us so that, in your name, he might honor us above our modest station.”

They added: “He is faithful to you, and that bishop is the best of all your people; he is most worthy of the highest priesthood. If you deign to believe our humble testimony, we confess to your Highness that we heard him preach in the manner of a declaimer.”

The emperor, now better informed about his incompetence, asked about the manner of the preaching. Since they did not dare deceive him, they recounted everything in order.

Understanding that, because of fear, the bishop had attempted to say something rather than dare to neglect his command, Charles permitted him, though unworthy, to retain his bishopric.

## CHAPTER XXI. Charles Angry with a Bishop

Not long afterward, when a certain young relative of the king sang the Alleluia very well at a particular feast, the emperor said to that same bishop: “Our cleric has sung well just now.”

The bishop, accepting these words jokingly according to his own folly, and not knowing that the young man was a relative of the emperor, replied:

[Note: This passage is obscure and perhaps corrupt. Cangius thought that *pelliparii* should be read, understanding it as those who prepared hides; yet, while granting this alteration, he admits that he does not see the point of the reply. I would understand it as referring to the cries of plowmen used to urge on oxen while they work the fields, which the uncouth man compared with the cleric’s singing.]

“Thus, thus, all the *perriparii* can urge on oxen while they are ploughing.”

At this most outrageous reply the emperor directed lightning flashes of his eyes against him and struck him down to the ground in terror.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Bishop Who Wished to Be Worshiped

There was another bishop of a very small city who, while still living in the flesh, wished not to have the apostles and martyrs act as intercessors for him before God, but to be honored himself with divine worship. Yet he attempted to conceal this pride in the following way: he had himself called a saint of God, so that he would not be regarded by everyone as hateful, like the idols of the nations.

He had a vassal who was not insignificant among his fellow citizens, a very energetic and capable man. Yet the bishop had never granted him anything—not to say a benefice, but not even a single kindly word.

Not knowing what he could do to appease his harsh temper, the vassal devised a plan. If he could prove that he had performed some sign in the bishop’s name, he might perhaps win the bishop’s favor.

When he was preparing to travel from his house to the bishop, he took two little dogs in his hands, which in the Gallic language are called *veltes* [swift hounds].

[Note: Read *aviculas* (“little birds”); and likewise, in the following passage, read *aves* (“birds”) instead of “dogs.”] By their agility they easily caught foxes and other small animals, and they often deceived even deer and other birds by their rapid ascent.

When he saw a fox lying in wait for mice along the road, he suddenly and silently set the dogs upon it. They rushed after the fox with astonishing speed and caught it within an arrow’s cast. He himself followed at full speed, knocked the fox alive and unharmed from the dogs’ teeth or claws, and, hiding the dogs wherever he could, entered his lord’s presence in triumph with the gift.

He humbly said: “Behold, lord, what sort of gift I, a poor little man, have been able to obtain.”

The bishop smiled faintly and asked how he had caught it so unharmed.

The man came closer and, swearing by his lord’s safety that he would conceal nothing from him, continued: “Lord, as I was riding across this field and saw that fox not far away, I loosened the reins and began to pursue it. But when it fled so swiftly that I could scarcely see it any longer, I raised my hand and adjured it, saying: ‘In the name of my lord Rechon, stop and do not move any farther.’

“And behold, as though bound with chains, it stood fixed in the place until I picked it up like an abandoned sheep.”

Then the bishop, puffed up by this empty performance, said before everyone: “Now my holiness is apparent. Now I know who I am. Now I recognize what I shall become.”

From that day onward he honored the man, whom he had previously hated above all his attendants, with extraordinary affection.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Penance of a Bishop Who Violated the Fast

Since the occasion has presented itself, it seems not inappropriate to insert this account from elsewhere and to bind together in writing other events remembered from the same period.

There was a certain bishop in New Francia of remarkable holiness and abstinence, and also of incomparable generosity and mercy. The ancient enemy of all justice, envious of his goodness and greatly provoked by it, implanted in him such a desire to eat meat during the days of Lent that he thought he would die without delay unless he were refreshed by such food.

At last, strengthened by the counsel of many holy and venerable priests, he was advised to take meat for the recovery of his health and afterward to mortify himself in the customary manner throughout the year. Lest he be found disobedient to them and a traitor to his own life, he yielded to their authority and, compelled by the utmost necessity, put a little flesh of a four-footed animal into his mouth.

When he began to chew it and had barely perceived its taste upon his palate, he was seized by such weariness, disgust, or hatred—not only of meat and other foods but even of the light itself and of his present life—that, despairing of his salvation, he no longer wished to eat or drink or place his hope in the Savior of the lost.

Since these events took place during the first week of Lent, the Fathers mentioned above advised him that, recognizing himself to have been deceived by a diabolical illusion, he should strive to cover over, lessen, or wash away that momentary sin by harsher fasts, contrition of heart, and abundant almsgiving.

[Note: M reads *superducere* (“cover over”) for “lessen or wash away.”]

As he was excellently trained [or “instructed”], he obeyed their advice. To confound the devil’s malice and obtain forgiveness from the restorer of innocence, he afflicted himself with two- or three-day fasts, avoided the rest of sleep, personally served the poor and strangers every day, washed their feet, and offered them clothing and money according to his means, wishing to give still more.

On Holy Saturday he requested numerous vats from throughout the entire city and arranged for hot baths to be provided from morning until evening for all who needed them. With his own hand he shaved the necks of each person, drew out pus and scabies [alternatively, itching eruptions] with his fingernails through the bristles of their hairy bodies, anointed them with ointments, and clothed them in white garments as though they had just been reborn.

When the sun was approaching sunset and no one remained who needed such services, he himself entered the baths. When he came out, his conscience cleansed, he covered himself with the purest linen so that, according to the judgment of the holy bishops, he might celebrate the solemn rites for the people.

As he was already proceeding to the church, the cunning adversary, wishing to violate his purpose and to cause the bishop to dismiss some poor man unwashed against his vow, assumed the appearance of an extremely filthy leper, dripping with pus and wrapped in garments stiff with corruption. Staggering with trembling steps and pitiful with excessive hoarseness, the figure came to meet him before the church door.

Then the holy bishop, moved by divine inspiration, turned back so that he might recognize what sort of enemy had recently overcome him. He removed his white garments, ordered water to be heated without delay, and had the poor wretch placed in it. Taking up a razor, he began to shave the man’s most shameful neck.

When he had shaved from one ear to the middle of the throat, he began at the other in order to bring the shaving to the same place. When he reached that point, he found—wonderful to relate—that hairs longer than those he had cut had grown back.

When this happened repeatedly and he did not cease shaving, behold, between the bishop’s hands—I shudder to relate it—an eye of astonishing size began to appear in the middle of the throat.

[Note: M has “in the middle of the monster.”]

Terrified by such a monster, the bishop sprang back and marked himself with the sign of Christ’s name, crying out loudly. At the invocation of that name, the fraudulent enemy, no longer able to conceal his deception, vanished like smoke. As he departed, he said: “This eye watches attentively for the time when you ate meat during Lent.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Bishop Who Violated a Woman

In the same region there was another bishop of incomparable holiness who, through careless confidence, had become almost unaware of the female sex. He allowed young nuns to live with him for purposes of study no less than elderly priests.

During the very feast of Easter, after the divine office—which lasted beyond midnight—he had indulged too freely in that Alsatian *sigoltarium*.

[Note: M has “he indulged in food and wine.”]

Together with the stronger Falernian wine, he had, alas, drawn into himself far too feebly the face and meretricious gestures of a most beautiful woman. When the others had departed, he summoned her to his bed and lamentably violated her.

At dawn he rose quickly and, cleansing the night in a river according to pagan custom, came before the eyes of the true God with a stained conscience.

When, after the introductory melodies, he ought, according to his ministry, to have begun the angelic hymn, he was struck with terror and amazement and placed the sacred vestments upon the altar. Turning to the people, he confessed his guilt.

Then he fell at the steps of the altar and was washed by immeasurable streams of tears.

The people urged him to rise and bound themselves by the terrible sacraments, refusing to allow the Mass to be celebrated on that most solemn day by anyone other than the shepherd himself. He could not be moved from the spot, and this struggle continued for almost three hours.

At last the Creator’s mercy, looking with compassion [the text adds *respiciens*, “looking upon”] upon the prayers of the devout people and the bishop’s contrite heart, clothed him again as he lay on the pavement, assured [the text also has *certificatum*, “made certain”] him of his pardon, and mercifully encouraged him to handle the heavenly and fearsome mysteries as an example of true repentance and as a warning: no one in this world is ever or anywhere secure in vain confidence.

[Note: M has “the eyes of the divine majesty.”]

## CHAPTER XXV. The Avaricious Bishop

In what is called Old Francia there was another bishop bound by greed beyond all measure. When, in a certain year, an unusual failure of all the earth’s produce devastated the whole world, that avaricious merchant rejoiced in the final necessity of all mortals—or rather, of those already dying—and ordered his storehouses to be opened, with everything to be sold at an exorbitant price.

Then a demon or ghost, whose concern was to amuse itself with games and the deception of human beings, began regularly to visit the house of a certain blacksmith and to play there at night with hammers and anvils.

When the father of the household attempted to protect himself and his possessions with the sign of the saving cross, the hairy creature replied: “My fellow godparent, if you will not prevent me from playing in your workshop, place your little cup here, and every day you will find it full.”

The wretched man, fearing bodily poverty more than the eternal destruction of his soul, did as the adversary suggested.

The demon, taking up a very large flask, broke into the cellar of Bromius—or of the rich man—and, after carrying out the robbery, allowed the rest of the wine to flow across the floors.

When many vats had already been emptied in this manner, the bishop noticed that they had perished through demonic fraud. He sprinkled the cellar with blessed water and protected it with the sign of the unconquered cross.

When night came, the cunning servant of the ancient thief arrived with his little vessel. He did not dare touch the wine containers because of the impression of the holy cross, but he was also unable to leave. Found in human form, he was bound by the house’s guard, produced publicly as a thief, and beaten before everyone.

[Note: Read “led away for punishment.”]

While being beaten, he cried out only this: “Woe is me, woe is me, because I have lost my fellow godparent’s little cup!”

Although this story is true, I have related it so that people may know to whom things belong when they have been renounced and hidden away for times of necessity, and how powerful is the invocation of the divine name, even when employed by those who are not good.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Bishop Immersed in Water
When I turn my eyes toward the head of the Franks and survey its members, I leave the highest and lowest of the other nations behind me; but now we must come to our neighbors, the Italians, separated from us by only a single wall [maceria].

There was there a certain bishop exceedingly desirous of empty [Note: [Col. 1386D] Others: monstrous, which is wrong.] things. When the devil noticed this, he appeared in human form to a certain poor man who, although poor, had not been emptied of avarice. He promised to enrich him considerably if he chose to bind himself to him forever by a bond of companionship. When the wretch did not refuse to make such a profession, the cunning enemy said:

“I shall transform myself into an excellent mule. You mount upon me and go to the bishop. When he begins to desire that mule, pull me away, delay, refuse, inflate the price, and, pretending indignation, prepare to leave. Then he will necessarily send after you and promise a great deal. At last, having been overcome by entreaties and loaded with limitless money, concede the mule to him as though unwillingly and under compulsion, and flee at full speed, seeking a hiding place wherever you can.”

When this had been done, and the bishop—unable to endure waiting until the following day—mounted the swift-footed animal in the full heat of noon and rode proudly through the city, he proceeded toward the countryside as though he would fly across it, and hastened toward the river for the sake of refreshment. Everyone of every age followed, eager to witness the most rapidly rolling walk, the swiftest running, and swimming most like dolphins [Note: [Col. 1386D] M.: most noble.]. And behold, that ancient Belial, as though unable to bear bit or bridle and burning with the fires of true Gehenna, began to plunge himself into the depths of the whirlpool and drag the bishop down with him, so that he could scarcely be pulled out by the strength of soldiers and the skill of fishermen who were sailing nearby.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Fornicating Bishop

The adversary, skilled in ambushes and accustomed to hide snares for us along the road on which we walk, never ceases to trip one person by one vice and another by another. A certain priest was accused of the crime of fornication—the name “bishop” must indeed be suppressed in such a matter. When this had already become so widely known that it was also fully reported to the most religious bishop of bishops, Charles, by those who related it, that most prudent man for a time concealed the matter and refused to place faith in frivolous words.

But rumor, swifter than anything else, caused the evil to grow from the smallest fly to the size of an eagle, so that it could no longer be concealed. Therefore Charles, the most rigorous investigator of justice, sent two palace officials who, turning aside in the evening to a place near the city, were to come unexpectedly to the priest early in the morning and ask him to celebrate Mass for them. If he refused too strongly, they were to compel him in Charles’s name to celebrate the sacred mysteries himself.

Not knowing what he should do—for he had sinned that very night before the eyes of the heavenly Inspector and did not dare offend those men—yet fearing human beings more than God, he baptized his fevered limbs in an ice-cold spring and proceeded to offer the dreadful sacraments. And behold, whether because his heart was shaken by conscience or because the water penetrated his veins, he was seized by such cold that he could not be saved by any medical assistance. Overcome by the most savage illness of fever, he was brought to death and compelled, by the decree of the eternal Judge, to surrender his soul.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning Pope Leo

But while other mortals are mocked by the devil or his satellites through these and similar deceptions [Col. 1386D], it is pleasing to contemplate the Lord’s sentence by which, rewarding the most firm confession of Saint Peter, he says: “Because you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16). That Church remains unshaken and immovable even in these most dangerous and wicked days.

As envy always rages among rivals, it was customary and traditional among the Romans that all men of any importance who were appointed over time to the apostolic see should continually be hostile—or rather, actively inimical—to one another. Thus it happened that certain men, blinded by envy, laid a deadly charge against Pope Leo of blessed memory, whom we mentioned above, and attempted to blind him. But, terrified by divine prompting, they were restrained and drawn back: they did not gouge out his eyes, but cut through them with razors.

When he had secretly caused this to be reported through his attendants to Michael, emperor of Constantinople, Michael withdrew all assistance from him, saying: “That pope possesses a kingdom in his own right, and one more excellent than ours; let him defend himself against his adversaries.”

Then that holy man, following the divine constitution, wished that Charles, who already in reality ruled and was emperor of many nations, should also acquire, by apostolic authority, the name and glory of Emperor Caesar and Augustus. He therefore requested that the unconquered Charles come to Rome.

Since Charles was always engaged in an expedition and under arms, he immediately set out with his officers and the army of recruits, entirely unaware of the reason for which he had been summoned, and proceeded without delay to the once-capital of the world. When the most wicked people there learned of his unexpected arrival, they were concealed in various hiding places, crypts, and refuges, just as sparrows are accustomed to hide from the sight of their lord, so named [that is, under that name]. But since they could not evade his diligence and shrewdness beneath the sky, they were captured, chained, and brought to the basilica of Saint Peter.

There the blameless father Leo took up the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, placed it upon his head, and swore these words in the presence of Charles and his soldiers, with his persecutors also standing by:

“So may I be a participant in the Gospel on the day of the great judgment as I am innocent of the crime falsely brought against me by these men.”

Immediately the terrible Charles said to his men: “See that none of them escapes.”

Thus he condemned all those who had been seized either to various deaths or to irrevocable exiles. When he remained there for several days in order to restore his army, the apostolic bishop summoned as many bishops as he could from the surrounding regions. With them standing before him, and in the presence of the invincible counts of the glorious Charles, he proclaimed Charles—who suspected nothing of the kind—emperor and defender of the Church.

Charles did not, however, receive this gladly, because he thought that the Greeks, inflamed by even greater envy, would contrive some harm against the kingdom of the Franks—or would take still more effective precautions, as rumor then reported, to prevent Charles, arriving unexpectedly, from subjecting their kingdom to his rule.

This seemed especially likely because, some time earlier, when the ambassadors of the Byzantine king had come to the magnanimous Charles and suggested to him that their lord wished to be his faithful friend, and that, if they were nearer to one another, he had resolved to raise Charles as a son and relieve his poverty, Charles—unable to contain the fire within his breast—burst out with these words:

“If only that little channel were not between us! Perhaps we would either divide the riches of the East or, sharing them equally, possess them together.”

This is what people ignorant of African poverty are accustomed to tell about the king of the Africans.

But the donor and restorer of blessed Leo’s health so demonstrated Pope Leo’s innocence that, after that penal and most cruel incision, he restored to him eyes clearer than they had been before. Only a most beautiful scar, shaped like a very slender thread, adorned his snow-white, dove-like eyes as a sign of his virtue [Col. 1387D].

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the Buildings of Charlemagne

So that I may not be accused by the ignorant of ignorance, because I reported from the emperor’s own mouth that the sea—which he called a great little channel—lay between us and the Greeks, let those who wish know that even now the Huns, Bulgars, and many other most savage nations, still untouched and intact, deny a land route to Greece. Yet afterward the most warlike Charles either leveled them with the ground—as he did the entire race of the Slavs and Bulgars—or completely eradicated them, or completely eradicated the progeny of iron and adamant—not of Huns—about which I shall speak presently [the Latin construction is uncertain].

First, however, I shall briefly and modestly recall the buildings which Caesar Augustus Charles constructed at Aachen, following the example of the most wise Solomon, with marvelous magnificence for God, for himself, for all bishops, abbots, counts, and all guests coming from throughout the world [Col. 1388A].

## CHAPTER XXX. The Thieving Abbot

When the vigorous Emperor Charles might have taken some rest, he wished not to grow sluggish in idleness but to labor in divine service. Thus, by his own design, he undertook to construct on his native soil a basilica more splendid than the ancient works of the Romans, and in a short time rejoiced that his vow had been fulfilled.

For its construction he summoned from all the regions this side of the sea masters and craftsmen skilled in every kind of art. Over them he appointed an abbot, the most expert of all, to carry out the work, unaware of his frauds. As soon as Augustus withdrew elsewhere, the abbot accepted payment and sent away to their homes those whom he wished. Those who could not buy their freedom, or had not been released by their masters, he oppressed with immense labors, just as the Egyptians once afflicted the people of God with wicked works, never allowing them any rest.

By such fraud he accumulated an unspeakable weight of gold, silver, and silken garments. Suspending the cheaper things in his chamber and locking away the most valuable objects in chests and coffers, he was suddenly informed by messengers that his house had caught fire.

He hurried there and burst through the midst of the flames into the room where the chests full of gold were kept. Unwilling to leave with only one object, he placed each item upon a separate shoulder and began to make his way out. Meanwhile, a very large beam, overcome by the flames, fell upon him. It burned his body with material fire, but sent his soul to the fire [Note: [Col. 1387] M.: but his soul passed to the inextinguishable fire.] that is never quenched.

Thus divine judgment watched over the most religious Charles, where Charles himself, occupied with the affairs of the kingdom, paid less attention.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the Bell

[Col. 1388C]

There was also another craftsman, superior to everyone in every work of bronze and glass. When the monk Tancho of Saint Gall was casting an excellent bell and Caesar admired its sound considerably, that outstanding master of bronze said:

“Lord Emperor, order a great quantity of copper to be brought to me, so that I may refine it thoroughly; and, in place of tin, have as much silver as I need—at least one hundred pounds—given to me. I shall cast you such a bell that, in comparison with it, this one will be mute.”

Then the most generous of kings, who, although riches flowed to him, did not set his heart upon them, readily ordered everything requested to be supplied. The wretched man took these materials and went away happily. He melted and purified the bronze, but instead of the purest silver he substituted tin. In a short time he completed a bell from the adulterated metal, much better than that excellent one, and presented it to Caesar for approval.

Caesar, sufficiently amazed by the incomparable comparison, ordered it to be hung in the bell tower and struck with an iron clapper. When this had promptly been done, the church’s custodian, the other chaplains, and also the inexperienced novices tried one after another to make it sound, but could accomplish nothing.

At last the craftsman and contriver of this unheard-of fraud, angered, seized the rope and pulled the bronze. And behold, the iron slipped loose from its center, descended upon his head together with his iniquity, passed through his corpse as he was dying, and reached the ground with his virile intestines.

The just Charles ordered the aforementioned weight of silver to be distributed [distributed, according to the variant] among the poorer members of the palace.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Charles’s Law Concerning the Construction of Buildings

[Col. 1389A]

In those times it was customary that, wherever some work had to be done by imperial command—whether bridges, ships, ferries, clearing, laying down material, or filling muddy roads—the counts would carry it out through their deputies and officials, at least in the case of smaller labors. But no duke or count, no bishop or abbot, was excused in any way from the greater works, and especially from those newly to be constructed.

The bridge-piers of Mainz still bear witness to this. The whole of Europe completed that bridge through a common but carefully ordered contribution of labor; it also consumed the fraud of certain malicious men who wished to extort unjust wages for transporting materials by ship.

If there were churches properly belonging to the royal jurisdiction that needed to be furnished with painted ceilings or wall paintings, this was arranged by neighboring bishops or abbots. If new churches had to be founded, all bishops, dukes, and counts, as well as abbots and whoever presided over royal churches, together with all who had received public benefices, brought the work from its foundations to its summit with the most strenuous labor [Col. 1389B].

The still-existing proof is not only that divine and human basilica at Aachen, but also the dwellings of persons of every rank, which were constructed around the palace of the most skillful Charles according to his arrangement. He could see everything through the grilles of his upper chamber that was being done, as though secretly, by those entering or leaving.

The residences of the nobles were also raised so high above the ground that beneath them not only soldiers and their servants, but every kind of person, could be protected from the violence of rain, snow, or frost by fireplaces, and yet they could not be hidden from the sharpest eyes of Charles.

Leaving the description of this building to your completed chancellery, I, the Enclosed One, return to explain the judgment of God that occurred in connection with it [Col. 1389C].

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Leutfred’s Dream Foretelling His Death

The exceedingly foresighted Charles therefore ordered all the nobles stationed nearby to support with every effort the craftsmen sent by him and to provide everything necessary for the work. Those who had come from distant regions he commended to the steward of his household, a man named Leutfred, so that Leutfred might feed and clothe them from public resources and diligently continue to supply everything required for the construction.

While Charles was seated in the same place, Leutfred did this work to some extent; but whenever Charles departed, he ceased entirely. Thus the steward accumulated such great sums from the torments of those poor men that Mammon, Pluto, and Dis could have carried them to the underworld only with a camel as their vehicle [Col. 1389D].

The most glorious Charles used a long, hanging cloak for the nightly Lauds—a garment whose use and name have now disappeared. After completing the morning hymns, he returned to the heated chamber and put on the imperial garments appropriate to the occasion. All the clerics, likewise prepared, came to the early-morning offices and waited awake either in the church or in the portico, which was then called the courtyard, for the emperor to proceed to the solemn celebration of Mass; or, if anyone needed it, to rest his head briefly in the bosom of his godfather.

Now one of these poor men, a cleric who was accustomed to visit the house of the aforementioned Leutfred to have garments—or rather rags—washed or mended, as the poor palace servants required, fell asleep upon his companion’s knees. He saw a giant, taller than that Antonian adversary, coming from the royal court across the stream by the crossing toward Leutfred’s house and dragging with him an enormous camel weighed down by an immeasurable load.

Stunned in his sleep, he asked the giant from what region he was coming and where he wished to go. The giant replied:

“I am going from the king’s house to Leutfred’s house, to place him upon these bundles and plunge him with them into hell.”

The cleric awoke from this vision in even greater fear. Afraid that the terrible Charles might find him sleeping, he immediately raised his head and urged the others to keep watch. Then he burst out with these words:

“If you wish to hear my dream: I seemed to see that Polyphemus who, walking upon the earth, strikes the lofty stars and whose tall sides do not fit within the middle of the Ionian Sea, hastening from this court to Leutfred’s house with a laden camel. When I asked the reason for his journey, he said: ‘I am intent on placing Leutfred upon these loads and taking him down to the underworld.’”

Before he had finished recounting this, a girl from Leutfred’s house, well known to them all, arrived and fell at their feet, asking them to remember her master Leutfred kindly. When they asked what had happened, she said:

“My lords, he went out to the latrine in good health, and when he remained there for some time, we went out and found him dead” [Col. 1390B].

When the emperor learned of his sudden death, and the craftsmen and the rest of the household freely exposed his stubbornness and avarice, he ordered his treasures to be searched out. When they were found to be immeasurable, the most just judge after God, knowing by what iniquity they had been amassed, publicly declared:

“Nothing from what he fraudulently seized can contribute to the liberation of that wretched man. Let it therefore be divided among the laborers of this building and the poorer members of our palace.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. A Deacon’s Luxury Punished

Two further events that occurred in the same place must be related.

A certain deacon, accustomed, according to the practice of the people on this side of the Alps, to struggle against nature, had his head shaved very closely, against the grain, polished his skin, trimmed his nails, and cut his hair extremely short, as though with a compass. He put on the whitest linen garments [Col. 1390C], and, since he could not avoid appearing more splendid by these means, presumptuously undertook to read the Gospel before the highest God and the holy angels, and in the presence of the strictest king and his nobles, though—as what followed showed—his conscience was polluted.

While he was reading, a spider suddenly descended by its threads from the ceiling, struck his head, and swiftly withdrew upward. When the most rigorous Charles observed this a second and third time and allowed it to happen without intervening, the cleric, out of fear of Charles, did not dare defend himself—especially since he thought that it was not a spider attacking him, but merely flies troubling him. After completing the Gospel reading, he also finished the remainder of the service.

As soon as he left the basilica, he swelled up and wasted away within the space of one hour. The most religious Charles, because he had seen what happened and had not prevented it, punished himself publicly with penance as though guilty of homicide.

## CHAPTER XXXV. A Cleric’s Ingratitude Is Punished

[Col. 1390D]

The incomparable Charles had an incomparable cleric in every respect. It was said of him—something never said of any mortal—that in knowledge of secular and divine letters, in ecclesiastical or jocular song, in new composition and musical modulation, and, moreover, in the full sweetness of his voice and immeasurable delightfulness, he surpassed everyone.

Although the legislator himself—that is, Moses—was most wise through divine instruction, he complains of the thinness of his voice [variant: “talkativeness”] and the hindrance of a slow tongue (Exodus 4); and although he sends his disciple—that is, Joshua, who by the authority of the merciful God dwelling within him commands heavenly things, namely the sun at Gibeon (Joshua 10)—to Eleazar for counsel (that is, Moses; Numbers 27); and although Christ our Lord did not permit even the one of whom he testifies that no greater had arisen among those born of women to perform any bodily sign [Col. 1391A] (Matthew 11, 16); and although he wished Paul’s wisdom to be admired by the man whom he desired to know himself through paternal revelation and whom he had endowed with the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Galatians 2); and although he permitted the disciple whom he loved more than the others to fall into such great fear that he did not dare enter his tomb, even though weak women frequently visited it (John 20)—nevertheless, as it is written, “To everyone who has, more shall be given” (Matthew 25). Because they knew from whom they had received their gifts, they obtained even what they had lacked.

This man, however, not knowing from where he possessed his gifts—or knowing but failing to give worthy thanks to the author of those gifts—lost everything at once. For although he had stood beside the most glorious Caesar as his closest companion, suddenly he was nowhere to be seen.

When the unconquered Emperor Charles was astonished at this unheard-of and incredible event, he eventually came to himself and marked himself with the sign of the Lord’s cross. Then he found, in the place where the cleric had stood, something resembling a most vile and recently extinguished coal.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Garments of the Franks

[Col. 1391B]

The night-time, hanging cloak of Augustus still draws us back from the subject of military equipment.

The ancient adornment or costume of the Franks consisted of shoes gilded on the outside and distinguished by straps three cubits long; patterned bands for the legs; and beneath them linen stockings or coverings for the thighs [Others: and coverings for the thighs], though of the same color and varied with the most precious workmanship. Over these garments, and over the bands, those straps were stretched on the inside in the form of a cross, extending a very long distance in front and behind [Other reading: inside and outside, in front and behind, very long].

Next came a *cilizina* shirt [other readings: *glizina*, *glezina*]. After this there was a belt fastened to the sword, which was enclosed first in a scabbard [Other reading: a sagea scabbard], second in some kind of leather, and third in the whitest linen, strengthened with the brightest wax, so that it was hardened [*duraretur*] through its middle with projecting little crosses, for the destruction of the heathen [other reading: *auraretur*, “was gilded”].

The final part of their dress was a gray or sapphire-colored, square, double cloak, fashioned so that, when placed upon the shoulders, it touched the feet in front and behind, while at the sides it scarcely reached the knees. Then they carried in the right hand a staff of wild-apple wood, remarkable for its evenly spaced knots, rigid and terrible, fitted with a hand-sized point of gold or silver and distinguished engravings.

In this costume, I, who am slow and more sluggish than a tortoise and who never came to Francia, saw the head of the Franks shining in the monastery of Saint Gall, together with two golden-haired flowers emerging from his thighs. The foremost of these gradually grew and adorned the top of its own staff with the highest glory, surpassing and covering it.

But, as is the way of human nature, when the Frankish soldiers among the Gauls saw the Gauls shining in striped cloaks [Col. 1392B], they rejoiced in the novelty, abandoned their ancient custom, and began to imitate them.

For the time being the most severe emperor did not forbid this, because that clothing seemed more suitable for military affairs. But when he noticed that the Frisians were abusing this permission and discovered that they were selling those very short cloaks just as they had previously sold the largest ones, he ordered that no one should buy from them anything except those great, broad, very long cloaks at the customary price. He added:

“What use are those little scraps? I cannot cover myself with them in bed; when riding against winds and rains I cannot be protected; and when I withdraw for the necessities of nature, I waste away from the freezing of my legs.”

# BOOK TWO: CONCERNING THE MILITARY AFFAIRS OF CHARLEMAGNE

[Col. 1391]

## PREFACE BEGINS

[Col. 1391C]

In the preface to this little work I promised that I would follow only three authors. But since the foremost of them, Wernbert, departed this life on the seventh day, and since today—namely, the third day before the Kalends of June—we ought to celebrate his commemoration throughout the world as his sons and disciples, let this be the conclusion of this little book, which proceeded from the mouth of that same priest concerning the piety and ecclesiastical care of our lord Charles.

What follows, concerning the military affairs of the fierce Charles, is fashioned from the account of Adalbert, the father of that same Wernbert, who took part with his lord Kerard in the war against the Huns and in the Saxon and Slavic wars. When he was already very old and was raising me, a little child, he used to instruct me about these matters, although I resisted and often ran away, until at last I was compelled to listen.

## CHAPTER I. The Defection of the Gauls from the Roman Empire

Since we are about to speak from the report of a secular man who was less learned in the Scriptures, we believe it appropriate, in accordance with the testimony of writers, to recall a few matters from earlier times to memory.

When Julian, hateful to God, had been slain from heaven in the Persian war, and not only the provinces across the sea but also nearby Pannonia, Noricum, Raetia or Germany, and the Franks or Gauls had defected from the Roman kingdom; and when the kings of the Gauls or Franks themselves had begun to fall backward because of the killing of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, and the expulsion of the most holy foreigners, namely Columbanus and Gallus, the entire people of the Huns—which had previously been accustomed to plunder throughout Francia and Aquitaine, Gaul and Spain—departed all at once. Like a vast fire, it devastated everything and carried whatever remnants might survive into the safest hiding places [Other reading: safest refuges] [Col. 1392C].

These events were as follows, as Adalbert was accustomed to relate to me.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the Huns

“The land of the Huns,” he said, “was enclosed by nine circles.” Since I, unable to imagine more than six circles around them, asked—[Note: [Col. 1391] M.: And since I thought that he meant wicker circles, I said:] “What marvelous thing was that, lord?” he replied: “It was fortified by nine *hegin* [*haganis*].”

Since I did not know that these were of another kind, except insofar as such things are commonly stretched out before fields, I questioned him further about this. He said:

“One circle was so broad—that is, it enclosed as much space—as the distance from the fortress of Zurich to Constance. It was built with oak, beech, and fir trunks, so that from edge to edge it extended twenty feet in width and rose to the same height. The space within the entire town was filled either with extremely hard stones or with very tenacious clay; moreover, the surface of those ramparts was covered with perfectly intact sods [Col. 1392D].

“Between their boundaries they planted little trees which, as we often see, when cut off and thrown down, put forth crowns of branches and leaves. Villages and farms were arranged among these embankments in such a way that a human voice could be heard from one to another.

“Opposite these same buildings, gates not sufficiently wide were established within those impregnable walls. Through them, people used to go out not only from the outer areas but also from the inner ones, for the purpose of plundering.

“The second circle, likewise constructed like the first, extended for twenty German miles—which are eleven Italian miles—as far as the third. The same was true up to the ninth, although each circle was much narrower than the one before it.

“From circle to circle, estates and dwellings were arranged in every direction so that the blast of trumpets could be heard between each one and recognized as a signal for every matter [Col. 1393A].

“Thus, for two hundred years and more, they gathered to these fortifications whatever wealth there was among all the Western peoples. While the Goths and Vandals also disturbed the peace of mortals, they left the Western world almost empty.

“Nevertheless, the unconquered Charles subdued them within eight years, allowing only the smallest remnants of them to remain. He held back from the Bulgars because, with the Huns destroyed, they seemed unlikely to do anything harmful to the kingdom of the Franks.

“Moreover, he distributed the booty found in Pannonia among the bishoprics and monasteries with the utmost generosity.”

## CHAPTER III. The Destroyers of the Rampart Are Restrained

During the Saxon war, when Charles was once occupied in person, certain private men—whose names I would identify if I were not avoiding the appearance of arrogance—were vigorously destroying the walls or rampart of a very strong city by forming a tortoise [siege formation] [Col. 1393B].

When the most just Charles saw this, he first appointed one of them, with the consent of his lord Kerold, prefect between the Rhine and the Italian Alps.

## CHAPTER IV. Dukes Punished for Sleeping on Watch

In the same place, the sons of two dukes were required to keep watch at the king’s tent. But after gorging themselves with drink, they lay there as though dead.

Charles, according to his custom, repeatedly awoke and made the rounds of the camp. Then, quietly and almost without anyone noticing, he returned to his tent. When morning came, he summoned all the leading men of the kingdom and asked what punishment was deserved by a man who had delivered the head of the Franks into the hands of the enemy.

The aforementioned dukes, entirely ignorant of what had happened, condemned such a man to death. But Charles dismissed them unharmed after restraining them with the harshest words.

## CHAPTER V. Love of Freedom

[Col. 1393C]

There were also two illegitimate sons born of Columbrian lineage [*de genitio Columbrensi*]. Since they fought with great courage, the emperor asked them who they were and from where they had been born.

After learning this, he summoned them to his tent at noon and addressed them:

“Good young men, I want you to serve me and no one else.”

When they declared that they had come for this purpose, so that they might be in his service even in the lowest rank, he said:

“You must serve in my chamber.”

Although they pretended indignation while admitting that they would gladly do so, they seized the moment when the emperor had begun to rest [variant: “having taken counsel, when the emperor had begun to rest”], escaped to the enemy camp, and, having caused a disturbance, washed away the stigma of servitude in the blood of their own men or of the enemy.

## CHAPTER VI. The Saxons, an Unknown People to the Greeks

Even amid such occupations, the magnanimous emperor by no means failed to send, to the kings of the most distant regions, successive bearers of letters or gifts, by whom the honors of all the provinces were conveyed to those kings.

When he sent ambassadors from the seat [Note: [Col. 1393D] M.: slaughter.] of the Saxon war to the king of Constantinople, the king asked whether the kingdom of his son Charles was at peace or whether it was being attacked by neighboring peoples.

When the first of the envoys [Other reading: envoy] reported that everything else was peaceful except that a certain people called the Saxons disturbed the borders of the Franks with repeated raids, the man, dulled by leisure and of no use in the business of war, said:

“Alas, why does my son labor against a very few enemies, of no name and no valor? Take that people, with everything belonging to them.”

When the envoy returned and reported this to the most warlike Charles, Charles smiled and said:

“That king would have given you much better advice if he had given you a single linen loincloth for such a long journey.”

## CHAPTER VII. The Perjuries of the Greeks

The wisdom that the same envoy revealed in wise Greece does not seem worthy of concealment [Note: [Col. 1393D] Other reading: In Greece the same envoy became famous through the following incident.].

When he had come with his companions in autumn to a certain royal city, they were divided among different hosts. The envoy himself was entrusted to a certain bishop, who was constantly devoted to fasts and prayers and nearly killed the envoy by continuous starvation.

In spring, when the season had begun to smile somewhat, the bishop presented him to the king. The king asked him what he thought of that bishop. Drawing deep sighs from the bottom of his heart, the envoy replied:

“Your bishop is most holy, as far as it is possible to be without God.”

The astonished king said:

“How can anyone be holy without God?”

The envoy replied:

“It is written, ‘God is love’ (1 John 4), and this man is empty of love.”

Then the king summoned him to his banquet and seated him among the leading men. They had established the following law: no native or foreigner at the king’s table [Note: [Col. 1393D] These two words are absent from the manuscript and were added in another hand [Col. 1394D] to explain the word “native.” BASN.] might turn any animal, or any part of an animal, toward another side of the dish; instead, he had to eat only from the upper side as it had been placed.

A river fish was brought in and placed on a dish covered with spices. Since this guest was ignorant of the custom and turned the fish toward the other side, everyone rose and said to the king:

“Lord, you have been insulted as never before your predecessors were.”

Sighing, the king said to the envoy:

“I cannot prevent these men from handing you over to death immediately. Ask for anything else you wish, and I shall fulfill it.”

After deliberating briefly, the envoy burst out in these words before everyone:

“I beg you, lord emperor, to grant me, according to your promise, one small request.”

The king said:

“Ask whatever you wish, and you shall obtain it—except that I cannot grant you life contrary to the law of the Greeks.”

Then the envoy said:

“This one thing, as I am about to die, I ask: let everyone who saw me turn that fish be deprived of the light of his eyes.”

The king, astonished at such a condition, swore by Christ that he had not seen this himself but merely believed what others had told him. Then the queen also began to excuse herself, swearing by the joy-giving *Theotokos*—the Greek “God-bearer,” Saint Mary: “I did not notice it.”

Afterward the remaining nobles, each striving to free himself from such danger before the others, attempted by terrible oaths to absolve themselves from this offense: one by the heavenly key-bearer [Saint Peter], another by the teacher of the nations [Saint Paul], and the rest by the angelic powers and the hosts of all the saints.

Then that wise Frank, having overcome vain Hellas in its own house, returned to his homeland victorious and unharmed.

## CHAPTER VIII. Charles’s Envoy Is Badly Received by the Greeks

[Col. 1394D]

Some years later, indefatigable Charles sent there a certain bishop, a man outstanding in mind and body, together with a most noble count, who was also a duke. After being detained for a very long time, they were finally brought before the king, treated disgracefully, and separated into various places.

At last, after some time, they were released and returned at great cost in ships and possessions.

## CHAPTER IX. Charles’s Revenge
Not long afterward, that same king sent his envoys to the most glorious Charles. It happened that the same bishop and the aforementioned duke were then with the emperor. When the arrival of the envoys was announced, they advised the most wise Charles that the envoys should be led around through the Alps and trackless regions until, worn down and consumed by an immense scarcity, they were compelled to come into his presence. When they had arrived, the same bishop and his companion arranged for the count of the stable to sit in the midst of his subjects upon an elevated throne, so that he could in no way be believed to be anyone other than the emperor. When the envoys saw him, they wished to fall to the ground and adore him, but, driven back by the attendants, they were forced to proceed farther inside. When they came there, they saw the count of the palace addressing an assembly in the midst of the nobles. Suspecting him to be the emperor, they prostrated themselves flat upon the ground. When they were driven away from there as well with blows to the face, those present saying, “This is not the emperor,” they proceeded farther and, finding the master of the royal household with richly adorned attendants, believed him to be the emperor and fell upon the ground before him. Driven back from there, they found in the audience chamber the emperor’s chamberlains around their master. There seemed no doubt that he might be the ruler of mortals. Although he denied that he was what he was not, he nevertheless promised that he would confer with the palace dignitaries, so that, if possible, they might reach the presence of the August Emperor.

Then men were sent from the emperor’s side to escort them honorably. The most glorious of kings, Charles, stood beside a radiant window, shining like the sun at its rising, conspicuous with gems and gold, leaning upon Hetto [Note: [Col. 1395D] Hatto was bishop of Basel and was sent by Charlemagne to the emperor Nicephorus together with Hugh of Tours. He himself returned with the Greek envoys after peace had been confirmed and the boundaries of both empires had been defined; thus those two paired episodes of the narrative appear to be legendary. BASN.]. This was the name of the bishop who had once been sent to Constantinople.

All around him stood, like a heavenly army: his three sons, namely, already made partners in the kingdom; his daughters with their mother, adorned no less with wisdom and beauty than with necklaces; bishops incomparable in appearance and virtues; abbots outstanding alike in nobility and holiness; and dukes such as Joshua once appeared among the troops at Gilgal. His army was such as that which drove the Syrians, together with the Assyrians, from Samaria. If David had been standing in their midst, he might rightly have sung this beforehand:

[Col. 1395C] “Let the kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men together with the young, praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148).

Then the Greek envoys, terrified, their courage failing and their counsel lost, fell mute and lifeless upon the pavement. The most gracious emperor tried to revive them by lifting them up and addressing them with words of consolation. At last, when they saw Hetto—once hated and rejected by them—in such glory, they were again seized with fear and kept rolling upon the ground until the king swore to them by the King of Heaven that he would do them no harm whatsoever. Strengthened somewhat by this pledge, they began to conduct themselves with a little more confidence. They returned to their homeland and advanced no farther toward our territories.

## CHAPTER X. The Antiphons of the Greeks Rendered into Latin

Here it seems appropriate to repeat what supremely wise men the illustrious Charles had in every sphere. When the Greeks, after the Matins praises had been celebrated for the emperor, secretly sang in their own language on the eighth day of the Theophany, and he, concealed nearby, took pleasure in the sweetness of their songs, he ordered his clerics to taste nothing until they had presented those same antiphons to him translated into Latin.

This is why they are all in the same mode, and why in one of them *contervit* is found in place of *contrivit* (“he crushed”) [Note: [Col. 1396D] Another reading: *conteruit* is placed instead, to the contrary. BASN.].

Those same envoys also brought with them every kind of instrument and various other objects. All of these, after being viewed as though casually by the craftsmen of the most ingenious Charles, were most carefully reproduced in workmanship. In particular, there was that outstanding musical organ which, with bronze pipes marvelously blown through by bellows of cast bronze and bull hides, equaled the roar of thunder in its bellowing and the sweetness of a lyre or cymbal in its chattering. Where it was placed, how long it lasted, and how it perished among other losses is not for this place or time to relate.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the Envoys of the Persians

At the same time envoys of the Persians were also sent to him. Not knowing the location of France, they considered it a great achievement if they had been able to reach the coast of Italy, because of Rome’s fame, for they knew that Charles then ruled it [Note: [Col. 1396D] Without doubt read *si*, “if”; otherwise there is no sense. So also the manuscript. BASN.].

When they had announced the reason for their arrival to the bishops of Campania, Tuscany, Aemilia, Liguria, Burgundy, and Gaul, as well as to abbots and counts, they were received—or expelled—by those men with affected indifference. At last, after a year had come full circle, worn out and utterly exhausted, they reached the most famous Charles at Aachen, renowned for his virtues.

They arrived there during the greater week of the major Lent, and, after being announced to the emperor, were kept from his presence until the vigil of Easter. When that incomparable man had been dressed in incomparable splendor for the chief festival, he ordered the men of that nation, once terrifying to the whole world, to be brought in. To them the most excellent Charles appeared more terrifying than all others, as though they had never before seen a king or emperor.

He received them graciously and enriched them with this privilege: that, as though they were among his sons, they might walk wherever they wished, inspect everything individually, and have permission to ask or inquire about anything. Delighted by this privilege, they clung to him, gazed at him, and admired him, placing him above all the wealth of the East.

They climbed to the gallery surrounding the basilica and, looking down from there upon the clergy and army, repeatedly returned to the emperor. Unable to contain their laughter because of the magnitude of their joy, they clapped their hands and said: “Previously we had seen only earthly men; now we see golden ones.”

Then they approached each of the nobles, marveled at the novelty of their clothing and weapons, and returned again and again to the more marvelous Augustus. When they did this continually that night and on the following Sunday, on the very holy day they were invited to the sumptuous banquet of the most wealthy Charles together with the nobles of France and Europe. Yet, struck almost senseless by the marvel of what they saw, they nearly rose from the table still fasting.

> The next day Phoebus was scattering his lamp over the lands,  
> > Aurora leaving her saffron bed beside Tithonus,  
> > when, behold, Charles, utterly impatient of rest and leisure,  
> > prepared to go into the forest to hunt bison or aurochs,  
> > and to lead the Persian envoys out with him.

When they saw those enormous animals, they were struck by such great fear that they turned to flight. But the hero Charles was not terrified. Sitting upon his horse, he approached one of them most fiercely and, drawing his sword, tried to cut off its neck. His blow missed; the beast tore apart the king’s *gallicula* [Note: [Col. 1396D] French *galoches*, a type of footwear. BASN.] and little stocking, and, grazing his leg with the very tip of its horn, made him somewhat slower. Angered by the ineffectual wound, it fled into a very secure valley rough with trees and stones.

When all the attendants wished to draw out their *hossas* [Note: [Col. 1396D] The following words stood in the margin: “Theutzer mit den hosen” (“German with the trousers”).] in order to serve their lord, he prevented them, saying: “In this condition I must come to Hildegard.”

Isambard, son of Warinus, the persecutor of your patron Otmar, pursued the beast. Not daring to approach more closely, he poised his spear between its shoulder and throat, pierced its heart, and presented it to the emperor still quivering. Charles, as though he had not noticed what had happened, left the carcass with his companions and returned home. He summoned the queen, showed her his torn boots, and said to her: “What reward is worthy of the man who freed me from the enemy who inflicted this?”

When she replied, “Every good one,” the emperor narrated the whole affair to her in order. Bringing forward the enormous horns as evidence, he compelled the lady to tears, sighs, and beating of her breast. When she heard that Isambard—then hated and stripped of every honor—had rescued the emperor from such an adversary, she fell at his feet and obtained for him everything that had been taken from him; she herself also bestowed gifts upon him.

## CHAPTER XII. Charles’s Reputation among the Easterners

The Persians had brought an elephant, monkeys, opobalsam, nard, various perfumes, spices, fragrances, and very different medicines, so that they seemed to have emptied the East and filled the West. When many of them had begun to enjoy familiarity with the emperor, and one day had grown more cheerful and had become heated with a stronger *grecingarium* [Note: [Col. 1397D] Manuscript: *Mero.*], they addressed these words jokingly to Charles, who was always armed with seriousness and sobriety:

“Your power, O emperor, is indeed great, but it is far less than the reputation by which you are celebrated throughout the eastern kingdoms.”

When he heard this, concealing his deepest indignation, he asked them jokingly: “Why do you say this, my sons? Or from what does it appear?”

They began again from the beginning and recounted everything that had happened to them in the lands across the sea, saying:

“We Persians and Medes, Armenians and Indians, Elamites, and all the peoples of the East fear you much more than our ruler Aaron. But what shall we say of the Macedonians and Achaeans? They already fear that your greatness will soon overwhelm them more than the waves of the Ionian Sea.

“All the islanders through whose lands we traveled are so ready and attentive to serve you as though they had been raised in your palace and honored with immense benefits.

“But, as it seems to us, the leading men of these regions do not care sufficiently about you except when you are present. For when, as foreigners, we urged them to show us some favor out of love for you, since we were seeking you, they sent us away without help and empty-handed.”
