Then the emperor stripped of all honors the counts through whose territories those envoys had traveled. He fined or condemned the bishops to pay an immense sum of money, and ordered the envoys to be escorted with great care and honor all the way to their own borders.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Envoys of the Africans

Envoys of the king of Africa also came to him, bringing a Marmaric lion and a Numidian bear, together with Spanish-red iron, Tyrian purple, and the other insignia of those regions.

The most generous Charles, rewarding the Libyans also, who were worn down by continual poverty, with the wealth of Europe—namely, grain, wine, and oil—not only then but throughout the whole period of his life, and supporting them with a lavish hand, retained them forever as his subjects and loyal dependents, and received from them tribute of no mean value.

## CHAPTER XIV. Charles’s Gifts to the King of Persia

The emperor sent messengers to the king of Persia bearing Spanish horses and mules, and Frisian cloaks—white, gray, variegated, or sapphire-colored—which he discovered to be rare and very costly in those regions. He also sent dogs exceptional for agility and ferocity, such as he had previously requested for capturing or driving away lions and tigers.

The Persian king, having inspected the other gifts almost casually, asked the envoys what wild animals and beasts those dogs were accustomed to fight. When he received the answer that all creatures against which they were set were torn apart without delay, he said: “The outcome will prove this.”

And behold, on the following day there arose a tremendous uproar among the shepherds fleeing from a lion. When this was heard in the king’s court, he said to the envoys: “Come, Frankish companions, mount your horses and follow me.”

They immediately followed the king cheerfully, as though they had never experienced any labor or weariness. When they had come within sight of the lion, although still at some distance, one of the satraps said: “Set your dogs upon the lion.”

The dogs obeyed the command and rushed upon it with great ferocity. The Persian lion, seized by German dogs, was killed with swords hardened from Hyperborean ore for bloodshed [Col. 1398B].

When he saw this, Aaron, the powerful hero who bore the name of his people, recognized from such small things that Charles was the stronger man and burst forth in his favor with these words:

“Now I understand how true are the things I have heard about my brother Charles: through the continual practice of hunting and his tireless dedication to training body and mind, he has acquired the habit of mastering everything beneath the heavens.

“What, then, can I repay him that would be worthy of him, since he has taken such care to honor me? If I give him the promised land granted to Abraham and displayed to Joshua, he cannot defend it from the barbarians because of the distance of the regions. Or, if he begins to defend it according to his own greatness of spirit, I fear that the provinces bordering the Frankish kingdom may withdraw from his rule.

“Nevertheless, I shall try to show my gratitude for his generosity in this way. I shall indeed place that land under his authority, and I shall be his advocate over it. Whenever he wishes, or whenever it seems most convenient to him, let him send his envoys to me, and he will find me a most faithful administrator of the revenues of that province.”

Thus it came about that what the poet had declared impossible [Note: [Col. 1397D] Virgil, *Eclogue* 1]:

> “May the Parthian drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris,”

through the industry of the most victorious Charles, seemed entirely possible, indeed easy, to young men, children, and old men alike: the departure and return of his envoys, and the journey and return of Aaron’s legates from Parthia to Germany or from Germany to Parthia.

Let grammarians take either Arar as they wish: either the one that pours into the Rhine, or the one that pours into the Rhône; for men ignorant of these places have confused them [Note: [Col. 1397D] Read *praecipitat*, “casts headlong.” Lucan, Book VI:

> “The Arar cast headlong the delaying Rhône.”

CAN. Likewise the manuscript.].

As testimony to this matter, I shall summon all Germany, which in the time of your glorious father Louis was compelled to pay one denarius from each royal possession [the transmitted text reads *de singulis nobis*; the note prefers “from each ox or estate”] [Note: [Col. 1398D] Perhaps *huobis*. CAN., but better “from each ox or estate,” as the manuscript reads. BASN.], to be given for the redemption of the Christians inhabiting the Promised Land, who were pitiably imploring him for it on account of the ancient dominion of your great-grandfather Charles and your grandfather Louis [Col. 1398D].

## CHAPTER XV. A Prophecy Concerning Louis

Since the occasion has arisen for honorable mention of your incomparable father, I wish to recall the prophecy that the most wise Charles is known to have uttered concerning him.

When the boy had been born and had been most carefully raised for six years in his father’s house, he seemed, not without reason, wiser than men of sixty. His indulgent father, who had scarcely been able to wait until he could bring him into the presence of his grandfather, took the boy, tenderly cared for by his mother, and began to instruct him how seriously and reverently he should conduct himself before the emperor, or perhaps how he should answer if questioned, and how he should comport himself generally. Thus he brought him to the palace.

When Charles, on the first or second day, noticed him among the other attendants, with his eyes fixed intently upon him, he said to his son: “Whose little boy is that?”

When his son replied, “Mine and yours, if you are willing,” he asked for him, saying: “Give him to me.”

When this had been done, the serene Augustus kissed the child and sent him back to his former station. The boy immediately recognized his own dignity and, scorning to remain second to anyone after the emperor, collected his courage, arranged his limbs with perfect composure, and stood with an even step beside his father.

When the most provident Charles observed this, he called his son to him and ordered him to ask his namesake why he acted in that way and with what confidence he dared to make himself equal to his father.

He, however, gave a reasoned answer:

“When I was your vassal, I stood behind you among my fellow soldiers, as was proper. Now, however, I am your companion in arms, and not without reason I make myself equal to you.”

When Louis had reported this to the emperor, he pronounced this judgment:

“If this little boy lives, he will become something great” [Note: [Col. 1399] Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*: “The father said: ‘If this little child lives, he will become something great.’” CAN.].

We have altered these words from Ambrose because what Charles said cannot be translated exactly into Latin. Nor would it be inappropriate to apply to Louis the prophecy concerning Saint Ambrose the Great. Apart from those matters and duties without which earthly government cannot exist—namely, marriage and the use of arms—he was entirely like Ambrose. Indeed, to the extent that he possessed royal power, he was, if one may say so, in religious devotion even greater than Ambrose: Catholic in faith, an eminent worshiper of God, and the tireless companion, guardian, and defender of Christ’s servants.

This is so true that when his faithful servant, our abbot Hart[mann] [Hartmatus], now your recluse, reported to him that the little possessions of Saint Gall had been gathered not from royal gifts but from the small donations of private persons; that they possessed no privilege like the other monasteries, nor the common laws of all peoples; and that for this reason they had been unable to find anyone to defend or advocate for them, Louis did not hesitate to oppose all our adversaries and to declare before all his princes that he was the advocate of our humble estate.

At that same time he sent a letter to your noble character, so that through your authority we might be able to request freely, under compulsion of an oath [Perhaps *coacto*, “having been compelled.”], whatever we might need.

But alas, how foolish I am! Because of the special kindness he showed us, I have imprudently withdrawn from the account of his general, ineffable goodness, greatness, and magnanimity, being drawn away by private joy.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Character of Louis

He was therefore king or emperor of all Germany and the Rhaetian regions, of ancient France, as well as of Saxony, Thuringia, Noricum, Pannonia, and all the northern nations. He was excellent in stature, handsome in appearance, with eyes shining like the stars, a clear and thoroughly manly voice, and singular wisdom. Relying upon a most penetrating intellect, he never ceased to make that wisdom richer through constant study of the Scriptures.

Therefore, in anticipating or overcoming all the ambushes of enemies, settling the disputes of his subjects, and providing every advantage for his faithful people, he possessed incomparable alertness. To all the surrounding pagans he continually remained more and more terrifying than all his predecessors—and deservedly so, since he never stained his tongue with judgment or his hands with the shedding of Christian blood, except in the utmost necessity. I dare not relate that necessity before I see some little Louis or Charles standing before you.

Yet he could never in any way be compelled to yield so as to condemn anyone to death; nevertheless, he used this severity to restrain those accused of treachery or plotting: once deprived of their honors, he never allowed them, softened by any opportunity or length of time, to climb back to their former rank.

He was so devoted to prayer, fasting, and the care of divine service above all men that, following the example of Saint Martin, whatever else he did, he always seemed to be entreating the Lord as though present before him. On appointed days he abstained from meat and richer foods.

During the season of the litanies, he was accustomed to follow the cross barefoot from the palace to the pastoral church, or to Saint Emmeram, if it was at Regensburg [Another reading: Reganesbourg]. In other places he did not reject the customary practice of those who lived there.

He built new chapels at Frankfurt and Regensburg with marvelous workmanship. When there were not enough stones because of the size of the construction, he had the walls of the cities demolished. In those cities he found so much gold around the ancient bones that he not only adorned the basilica with it but also covered complete books written therefrom with cases made of the same material, nearly a finger’s breadth thick.

No cleric who was not trained to read and sing dared remain with him—or even come into his presence. But he despised monks who violated their vows so greatly that he loved those who observed them with all affection.

He was always so full of joy and sweetness that if anyone came to him sad, he departed made cheerful by the mere sight of him or by the slightest conversation with him. If anything unfortunate or inappropriate suddenly occurred in his presence, or if he happened to learn of it from elsewhere, he corrected everything merely by the warning of his eyes. Thus, what is written of the eternal inner judge was unmistakably begun in him, beyond what is ordinarily granted to mortal beings:

> “The king who sits upon the throne of his kingdom, by the look of his face dispels all evil” (Proverbs 20).

I have said these things briefly and by way of digression, intending, with life as my companion and the Divinity favorable, to write much more about him. We must now return to our subject.

## CHAPTER XVII. Charles Punishes the Children of His Enemies

Meanwhile, because of the frequent arrival or harassment of the unconquered Saxons, the robberies and piracy of the Nordmanns, or the attacks of the Moors, Emperor Charles had remained somewhat longer at Aachen. While his son Pippin was waging war against the Huns, barbarian nations coming from the north plundered Noricum and much of eastern France.

When Charles learned of this, he humbled them all personally to such an extent that he ordered even boys and children to be measured against swords, and anyone who exceeded that measure was to be punished with decapitation.

From this deed grew another work, far greater and more illustrious. When the most holy grandfather of your empire had died, certain giants—such as Scripture says were begotten, in God’s anger, by the sons of Seth from the daughters of Cain (Genesis 6)—inflated with the spirit of pride, and undoubtedly superior to those who said, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (1 Kings 12), despising his offspring because of their excellent stature, each attempted to seize the rule of the kingdom and wear the diadem.

Then, when certain men of middling rank, inspired by God, proclaimed that the renowned emperor Charles had once measured the enemies of the Christians against a sword, and that therefore, as long as someone of sword-length could be found among his descendants, he ought to rule the Franks—or rather Germany—that devilish faction was struck as though by a bolt of lightning and scattered in every direction.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Conspiracy against Charles

[Col. 1401A]

But Charles, victorious over foreigners, was surrounded by his own people through a remarkable yet fruitless deception. Returning from the Sclavs to his kingdoms, he was almost captured by a son born to him through a concubine, named the most glorious Pippin, a name ominously marked upon him by his mother; and, insofar as it lay within Pippin’s power, he was condemned to death.

This was discovered in the following way. A council concerning the emperor’s death had been held with the nobles assembled in the church of Saint Peter. When the council had ended, fearing every possible danger, Charles ordered a search to be made for anyone hidden in any corner or beneath the altars.

And behold, as they feared, they found a cleric concealed beneath the altar. They seized him and compelled him to swear that he would not betray their plot. In order not to lose his life, he did not refuse to swear as they directed. But when they had departed, he thought little of that sacrilegious oath and hurried to the palace.

With the greatest difficulty he finally penetrated through seven gates and doors to the emperor’s bedchamber. After he had knocked, he brought the ever-watchful Charles to great amazement: who would dare disturb him at that hour? Nevertheless, Charles ordered the women who were accustomed to attend the queen or the daughters to go out and see who was at the door and what he was seeking.

They went out and, recognizing a most contemptible person, closed the doors, and, with tremendous laughter and shrieking, tried to hide themselves in the corners, pressing their garments over their faces. But the shrewd emperor, from whom nothing beneath the heavens could escape, carefully asked the women what they had found and who was knocking at the door.

When he was told that some shaven *cocao* [variant: *coccio*], foolish and raving, dressed only in a linen garment and drawers, was urgently demanding to speak with him, he ordered the man to be admitted. The cleric immediately fell at his feet and disclosed everything to him in order.

The conspirators, suspecting nothing, were all transported before the third hour of the day, either to appropriate punishment or into exile, or were otherwise punished. Pippin himself, a dwarf and hunchback, was brutally beaten and tonsured, and was sent for a time to the cell of Saint Gall for correction—a place that seemed poorer and narrower than any other location in the vast empire.

## CHAPTER XIX. Pippin’s Answer Concerning the Cutting Down of the Franks

Not long afterward, certain leading Franks wished to lay hands upon the king. Although this did not escape him, he was nevertheless unwilling to destroy them, because, had they been well disposed, they could have been a great protection to the Christians. He sent his envoys to that same Pippin, asking him what ought to be done with them.

They found him in a garden with his older brothers, the younger ones being detained for more important tasks, removing nettles and every harmful plant with a three-pronged tool so that the useful plants might grow more vigorously. They informed him of the reason for their arrival.

But he drew sighs from the depths of his heart—as the weak are often more courageous than the healthy—and replied in these words:

“If Charles would deign to accept my counsel, he would not submit to such great insults. I give him no command. Tell him what you found me doing.”

Fearing that they would return to the formidable emperor without a definite answer, they asked him again and again what they should report to their lord.

Then, growing angry, he said: “I give him no other command than what I am doing. I am removing useless refuse so that the necessary vegetables may grow more freely.”

Thus they departed sadly, as though they were carrying back nothing reasonable. When they came to the emperor and were asked what they had to report, they complained that, despite so much labor and travel, they had been unable to obtain even a single clear statement:

“We found him,” they said, “sitting in a rustic *triecium* [uncertain term], weeding a vegetable bed with a three-pronged tool. When we went over the reason for our journey, we could extract from him, only after much pleading, this one answer: ‘I give him no other command than what I am doing. I am removing useless refuse so that the necessary vegetables may grow more freely.’”

After hearing this, the Augustus, not lacking in cunning and endowed with wisdom, rubbed his ears and flared his nostrils. Then he said to them:

“You have brought back a reasonable answer, excellent vassals.”

While they feared for their lives, he himself brought the force of those words into effect. He removed all those plotters from among the living and granted to his faithful men the places occupied by the unproductive, so that they might grow and expand.

One of the adversaries had chosen for himself the highest hill in France and everything that could be seen from it. Charles ordered him to be fastened to a very high beam on that same hill and raised up upon it.

As for the bastard Pippin, he ordered him to choose how he wished to spend his life. Given the choice, Pippin chose a place in a monastery that was then most renowned but is now destroyed—for a reason that is not uncertain. I shall not disclose that reason before I see your little Bernhard girded with a sword at the thigh.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the Giant

The magnanimous Charles was indignant that he himself had been provoked to go out against those barbarous nations, when any one of his dukes seemed suitable for the task [Note: [Col. 1401D] Manuscript: “It was believed.”]. I shall prove that this was indeed so by the deed of one of my countrymen.

There was a man from Durgonum [Note: [Col. 1401D] *Durgue*.], a great and terrifying member of the army, called *Cis Here* [Note: [Col. 1401D] Manuscript: “Cis Here.”]. His stature was such that he might have been believed to have arisen from the race of Anak, had there not been so great a difference in time and place.

Whenever he came to the river Dura, swollen and overflowing with Alpine torrents, where even the largest horse could not be driven into—not to say its waters—but even its flowing current, Seizing the reins, he dragged the horse floating behind him and said: “By Lord Gallus, whether you wish it or not, you must follow me.”

When, while in Caesar’s army, he mowed down the Bohemians, Wilzi, and Avars [Note: [Col. 1402D] Manuscript: “Bemanni, Winidi, and Avars.”] like a meadow and hung them from his spearshaft like little birds, he returned home victorious. When sluggish men asked him how he had enjoyed himself in the land of the Winidi, he despised them and, twice angered, replied:

“What were those little frogs to me? I used to pierce seven or eight, or certainly nine, of them upon my spear, and, while they muttered I know not what, carry them back and forth. Our lord the king and we wore ourselves out uselessly against such little worms.”

[Note: [Col. 1401D] The note identifies *Duranium*, a river of Gaul in Aquitaine flowing into the Garonne, as a possible referent. BASN. I understand the river Dura to be the one from which Durgovia received its name. Aventinus has the little history—or rather fable—on p. 353 of the Ingolstadt edition; I do not know where he obtained the giant’s name, Aenotherus. Certainly he had read our Saint Gall author, as is clear not only from this passage but also from pp. 322–323. CAN.]

## CHAPTER XXI. The War against the Normans

At that same time, when the emperor was putting the finishing touch to the war against the Huns and had received the peoples mentioned above into submission, the Nordmanns, coming forth, caused great trouble to the Gauls and Franks.

The unconquered Charles, returning by land—although the route was very narrow and trackless—attempted to attack them in their own territory [Note: [Col. 1402D] Others read “having been warned.”]. But whether divine providence prevented him, so that, according to Scripture, Israel might be tested through them (Judges 3), or whether our sins stood in the way, all his attempts were brought to nothing. Indeed, as proof of the hardships suffered by the entire army, fifty pairs of oxen belonging to one abbot were found to have perished by a sudden plague in a single night.

Therefore the most wise Charles, lest he disobey Scripture by striving against the river’s stroke [*ictum*] (Ecclesiasticus 4), abandoned his undertaking.

When he had traversed his vast empire for a considerable time, Godefrid, king of the Nordmanns, emboldened by his absence, invaded the borders of the Frankish kingdom and chose the Moselle district as his seat.

When he wished to remove his falcon from a duck, his son overtook him—the son whose mother he had very recently left and over whom he had taken another wife—and split him in two. After this deed, as once happened when Holofernes was killed (Judith 15), no one dared rely on courage of spirit or strength of arms, but only upon the refuge of flight.

Thus, lest France should boast against God after the example of ungrateful Israel, it was freed without any effort on its own part.

The unconquered and never-to-be-conquered Charles glorified God for such a judgment, but complained bitterly that, because of his absence, any one of them had escaped:

“Alas, what grief,” he said, “that I was not granted to see how my Christian hand played with those dog-headed men.”

## CHAPTER XXII. The Norman Pirates
It also happened that Charles, wandering about, unexpectedly came to a certain maritime city of Narbonese Gaul. While he was dining at its port, though this was unknown to him, the Nordmanns’ scouts were engaged in piracy [Note: [Col. 1403D] Some: “of pirates.”]. When the ships were seen, some said that they belonged to Jews, others to Africans, and others to British merchants. But the exceedingly wise Charles, recognizing from their equipment or speed that they were not merchants but enemies, said to his men:

“These ships are not packed with merchandise; [Col. 1403C] they are pregnant with the fiercest enemies.”

When they heard this, the men hurried eagerly toward the ships, each wishing to outstrip the others—but in vain. For when the Nordmanns learned that he was there—Charles the “Hammer,” as they themselves commonly called him—they escaped by a sufficiently incomparable flight, avoiding not only the swords but even the eyes of their pursuers, lest all their armor should be blunted against him or shattered into the tiniest fragments.

The deeply religious Charles, however, just and God-fearing, rose from the table and stood at the eastern window, weeping for a very long time with immeasurable tears. Since no one dared address him, at last the most warlike man gave his nobles an explanation of this gesture and weeping:

“Do you know, my faithful men,” he said, “why I have wept so bitterly? I am not afraid that these trifles can accomplish anything against me. Rather, I grieve that, while I am alive, they have dared to touch this shore; and I am tortured by the greatest sorrow because I foresee how many evils [Col. 1403D] they will inflict upon my descendants and upon their subjects.

“May the protection of Christ our Lord prevent this from happening, and may your sword, hardened in the blood of the Nordostuni, withstand them, joined by the blade of your brother Carloman, which has indeed been dipped in the blood of those same men, but which now has turned to rust—not through cowardice, but because of the scarcity of resources and the narrowness of the lands—belonging to your most faithful Ardnold, so that nevertheless, at the command and will of your power, it may readily be restored to sharpness and brilliance.

“For this single little branch, together with the thinnest splinter of *bennolinum* [Note: [Col. 1403D] In German, *bemlin*.], is sprouting from the most fruitful root of L. [Note: [Col. 1404D] Ludovicus.] beneath the singular summit of your protection. For we have learned something in your history concerning your great-great-grandfather Pipin; let something be inserted which, by the favor of divine clemency, may soon become your future Carloaster or Ludwiculus.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Lion Killed by Pipin

[Col. 1404A]

When the Lombards and other enemies were harassing the Romans, they sent their legates to the same Pipin, asking him, for love of Saint Peter, to come to their aid as quickly as he could. Without delay he subdued the enemies and entered Rome in triumph, solely for the sake of prayer; and the citizens welcomed him with this acclamation:

“Today the citizens of the apostles and the household of God have arrived, bringing peace and illuminating their homeland; giving peace to the nations and liberating the people of the Lord.”

Some, ignorant of the force and origin of this song [Note: [Col. 1404D] M., “Some, not knowing.”], became accustomed to sing it at the feasts of the apostles.

But he himself, avoiding the jealousy of the Romans—or, to speak more accurately, of the Constantinopolitans—soon returned to Francia. When he learned that the leading men of the army habitually despised and criticized him in secret, he ordered a bull, terrifying in size and untamable in spirit, to be brought before him, and a very savage lion to be released upon it. The lion attacked the bull with tremendous force, seized it by the neck, and threw it to the ground.

Then the king said to those standing around:

“Pull the lion away from the bull, or kill it while it is upon him.”

They looked at one another, their hearts frozen with fear, and could scarcely mutter these words through their sobs:

“Lord, there is no man beneath the heavens who would dare attempt this.”

Then he, growing more confident, rose from his throne, drew his sword, and with it severed the bull’s neck from its shoulders through the lion’s neck. Returning the sword to its sheath, he sat down on the throne and said:

“Does it seem to you that we may be your lord? Have you not heard what little David did to that enormous Goliath, or what the very short Alexander did to his extremely tall attendants?”

Then, struck as though by thunder, they fell to the ground, saying:

“Who but a madman would refuse to submit your dominion to mortal men?”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the Baths at Aachen

[Col. 1404C]

He displayed such extraordinary courage not only against beasts and men but also in an unheard-of struggle against spiritual wickedness. At Aachen, before the baths had yet been built, hot and very health-giving springs were bubbling up. He ordered his chamberlain to inspect whether the springs had been cleansed and to ensure that no stranger was allowed there.

When this had been done, the king took up his sword and hurried barefoot from his sandals to the bath. Suddenly the ancient enemy attacked him as though intending to kill him. But the king, fortified with the sign of the cross, saw a shadow in human form and, drawing his sword, drove it so deeply into the earth that he could scarcely withdraw it after a prolonged struggle.

That shadow, however, was of such great thickness that it polluted all those springs with filth, blood, and loathsome fat. Yet the unconquerable Pipin was not moved by this. He said to his chamberlain:

“Do not concern yourself with such things. Let that infected water flow out, so that I may bathe without delay in the water that runs pure.”

## CHAPTER XXV

I had proposed, Emperor Augustus, to weave for you a brief narrative solely about your great-grandfather Charles, recounting all that he did, matters of which you already know everything. But since the occasion has presented itself so that it is necessary to mention your glorious father Ludovicus, surnamed the Illustrious, and your deeply religious great-great-grandfather Pipin the Younger—men concerning whom the negligence of modern writers has produced a great silence—I judged it wicked to pass over everything without touching it.

For concerning the elder Pipin, the most learned Bede composed almost an entire book in his *Ecclesiastical History*. Having thus recalled these matters by way of digression, let your illustrious namesake Charles now return, like a swan, to his swimming. But if we fail to withhold something concerning the wars he waged, we shall never be brought back to consider his daily conduct. Therefore I shall recall, as briefly as I can, the matters that belong to the present subject.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Charles Goes to Rome

After the death of the most victorious Pipin, when the Lombards again began to disturb Rome, the unconquered Charles, although excessively occupied in the regions this side of the Alps, energetically undertook the journey into Italy. By a bloodless war—or by voluntary surrender—he received the humbled Lombards into service; and, to secure their loyalty, so that they might never separate themselves from the Frankish kingdom or inflict any injury upon the territories of Saint Peter, he married the daughter of Desiderius, prince of the Lombards.

After not much time had passed, because she was bedridden [Note: [Col. 1405D] This passage concerning the cause of the divorce between Charles the Great and the daughter of Desiderius deserves notice; as far as I know, it is reported by none of the ancient writers. Baronius, under the year 771, professes ignorance of it. I interpret *clinicam* as Baronius does in the letter which he himself attributes to Gregory II, while others attribute it to Gregory III, under the year 726: “If a woman, stricken by illness, has been unable to render the marital duty to her husband,” etc. CAN.], and incapable of producing offspring, she was abandoned by the judgment of the most holy priests as though dead. Her enraged father bound the provincials to himself by an oath, shut himself within the walls of Ticinum, and resolved to rebel against the invincible Charles. When Charles learned this with certainty, he hastened there.

Several years earlier, a certain man among the chief princes, named Ogger, had incurred the displeasure of the most terrible emperor and had therefore taken refuge with the same Desiderius. When they heard of the arrival of the dreaded Charles, they climbed a very high tower, from which they could see far and wide the approaching army.

When the baggage appeared, more expeditious than would have suited the expeditions of Darius or Julius,Desiderius said to Ogger:

“Is Charles coming with so large an army?”

He replied:

“Not yet.”

When he saw the army of common soldiers gathered from the vast empire, he declared emphatically to Ogger:

“Surely Charles is rejoicing in these forces.”

Ogger replied:

“Not yet—nor yet.”

Then Desiderius began to grow agitated and said:

“What shall we do if more men have come with him?”

Ogger said:

“You will see what sort of man he comes as. As for us, I do not know what will happen.”

And behold, as they were speaking, there appeared a company always ignorant of “calling” (*vocationis*) [Col. 1405C] [read *vacationis*, “leisure”]; when Desiderius saw it, he was astonished and said:

“This is Charles.”

Ogger replied:

“No, not yet.”

After this, bishops and abbots appeared, together with clerics and chaplains accompanied by their counts. When he saw them, Desiderius, already scarcely able to speak, the enemy of daylight and of death, stammered:

“Let us descend and hide ourselves in the earth from the face of the fury of so savage an adversary.”

To this Ogger, swelling with pride, replied. He had once experienced Charles’s incomparable power and had been accustomed to it in better days:

“When you see the fields bristling with grain, the iron Po and Ticino inundating the walls of the city with marine waves blackened by iron, then you may hope that Charles is coming.”

Before these things were completed, first, toward the west, by Circius or Boreas, there began to appear something like a dark cloud, which transformed the brightest day into dreadful shadows. But as the emperor drew nearer, the brilliance of the weapons deprived those within of daylight, making the day darker than every night.

Then the iron Charles himself appeared, crested with an iron helmet, wearing iron sleeves and bracelets, his iron chest and Platonic shoulders protected by an iron breastplate, his left hand filled with an iron spear raised high, while his right was always extended toward unconquered steel. His outer thighs, which in others are usually left unprotected by armor for easier mounting, were surrounded by little iron plates.

What should I say of his greaves? They, too, as was customary for the entire army, were always made of iron. Nothing appeared on his shield except iron. His horse also retained iron in its spirit and color. All those preceding him, surrounding him on either side, following him, and the entire common equipment imitated this appearance as far as possible.

Iron filled the fields and streets. The rays of the sun were reflected from the edge of iron. Honor was paid by cold iron to a people still colder. The most brilliant iron made the terror of the sewers grow pale.

“O iron—alas, iron!” the citizens’ confused cry rang out.

The strength of the walls trembled before iron, and the judgment of the young and the counsel of the old perished before iron.

These things, which I, a stammering and toothless man, tried to explain at greater length than I ought, by a slower circuit of words, the truthful observer Ogger perceived with the speediest glance and said to Desiderius:

“There is the man you have sought so earnestly.”

As he said this, he fell almost lifeless.

But because on that very day the citizens of the city, either through madness or from some hope of resisting, were unwilling to receive him, the highly resourceful Charles said to his men:

“Let us do something memorable today, lest we be blamed for passing the day in idleness. Let us hasten to build a small oratory, so that, if it is not opened to us quickly, we may devote ourselves to divine services.”

When he had spoken these words, the men scattered in different directions. Some gathered lime and stones, others timber and pigments, and brought them back; craftsmen always accompanied him.

From the fourth hour of the day until the twelfth, they built such a basilica—with walls and roofs, ceilings and paintings, assisted by the hands of recruits and soldiers—that anyone who had not yet seen it would have thought it impossible to complete in less than an entire year.

Afterward, on the fifth day, when some citizens wished to open the city to him and others, though unsuccessfully, wished to rebel—or, more accurately, to shut themselves in—I leave it to be written by those who accompany your Highness not out of affection but solely for gain how, without bloodshed and by skill alone, he overcame, captured, and possessed the city.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Charles’s Clothing

From there the deeply religious Charles proceeded farther and came to the city of Friuli, which those who think themselves learned now call the Forum of Julius.

It happened at that time that the bishop of that city—or, to use the terminology of modern times, its patriarch—was approaching the end of his life. When the deeply religious Charles hurried to visit him, so that the bishop might designate his successor by name, the bishop, drawing deep sighs from the bottom of his heart with great religious devotion, said:

“Lord, I leave this bishopric, which I have held for a long time without benefit or spiritual progress, to divine judgment and to your disposition, lest I be found before the inevitable and incorruptible Judge to have added something, even in death, to the heap of sins that I accumulated while alive.”

The most wise Charles took this so seriously that he judged the bishop not unworthy to be compared with the ancient Fathers.

Charles, the most active of the most inactive Franks, remained for some time in that region until, after the bishop’s death, he installed a worthy successor. On a certain feast day, after the celebration of Mass, he said to his men:

“Let us not be brought to idleness by becoming sluggish in leisure. Let us go hunting until we catch something, and let each of us go in the same clothing in which we are now dressed.”

It was a rainy and cold day. Charles himself had a sheepskin coat, worth little more than that *roccus* of Saint Martin with which the breast is encircled; divine testimony confirms that he had offered sacrifice to God with bare arms.

The others, however, since it was a holiday and they had just come from Pavia—where the Venetians had recently brought all the riches of the East from across the sea—were clothed in skins of Phoenician birds surrounded by silk, with peacocks’ necks, backs, and haunches beginning to bloom with colors, decorated with Tyrian purple or *diacedrina* lettering. Others proceeded wrapped in blankets; some in dormice skins.

Traversing the woods, they were torn by branches, thorns, and brambles, drenched by rain, and then returned stained with the blood of wild beasts and the mire of skins.

Then the most cunning Charles said:

“Let none of us remove his coat until we go to bed, so that the garments may dry more thoroughly upon us.”

At this command, each man, caring more for his body than for his clothing, sought out fires everywhere and tried to warm himself. When they returned, they remained in his service until deep into the night and were then sent back to their lodgings.

When they began to remove those very thin skins—or even thinner blankets—the tearing of their wrinkles and folds, like rods breaking in dryness, could be heard from a distance. They groaned and sighed, complaining that they had lost so much money in a single day.

They had received orders from the emperor to appear before him the next day in those same skins. When this had been done, and all of them appeared not splendid in finery but dreadful in rags and discolored squalor, Charles, full of practical wisdom, said to his chamberlain:

“Rub our coat between your hands and bring it before us.”

When it had been brought, perfectly intact and brilliantly white, he took it between his hands, displayed it to all who stood nearby, and declared:

“O most foolish of mortals, which coat is now more valuable and useful? This one of mine, bought for one solidus, or those of yours, purchased not only with pounds but with many talents?”

Then, with their faces turned toward the ground, they could scarcely endure his terrible rebuke.

Your most religious father imitated this example not once but throughout his entire life, so that no one who seemed worthy of his recognition and instruction dared to carry anything in the army against the enemy except military weapons and woolen garments with linen ones.

If someone ignorant of that lower discipline happened to encounter him while wearing silk, gold, or silver, he departed rebuked, improved, and indeed made wiser by these words:

“O you golden man, behold! O you silver man! O you entirely scarlet man! Wretched and unhappy creature, is it not enough for you alone to perish, whether by chance in war? Why, then, do you also hand over to the enemy the things by which your soul might be redeemed, so that they may adorn images of the nations with them?”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Strength of Ludovicus

How much the most unconquered Ludovicus delighted in iron from his earliest age until his seventieth year, and how he made iron a spectacle before the Nordmann legates, I shall recount more suitably for you, since you know it well.

When the kings of the Nordmanns, each according to his devotion, sent him gold and silver, and, as a sign of perpetual submission or surrender, their swords, the king ordered that the money be thrown onto the pavement and looked upon by no one except with disdain, but rather trampled by everyone like mud.

The swords, however, he ordered to be brought to him while he sat upon his lofty throne. The legates, fearing that some adverse suspicion might arise against them, offered the swords to the emperor at the risk of their lives in the manner in which servants usually present knives to their masters from the upper edge.

Taking one of them by the hilt, he attempted to bend it from its very tip all the way to the top. But the sword broke between his powerful hands.

Then one of the envoys drew his own sword from its sheath and extended it toward him in the manner of a servant offering something, saying:

“Lord, I believe that this sword will prove both flexible and rigid according to the wish of your most victorious right hand.”

The Caesar received it and, truly a Caesar, according to Isaiah’s prophecy—“Look to the rock from which you were hewn” (Isa. 51)—rose up by the devoted multitude of Germany, through the work of the unique divinity, into the ancient limbs and spirits of men. From the very tip to the hilt he bent it in the manner of a willow branch, then allowed it gradually to return to its former shape.

Then the legates looked at one another and stared in astonishment:

“O,” they said, “how contemptible gold must seem to our princes, and how precious iron!”

Since the Nordmanns have now been mentioned, I shall briefly set out how much faith and baptism meant to them in the days of your grandfather.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Nordmanns Despise Baptism

Just as, after the death of the warlike David, the neighboring nations, subdued for a long time by his mighty hand, paid tribute to his peaceful son Solomon under his authority, so the savage nation of the Nordmanns, because of their fear and the tribute they paid to the most august emperor Charles, used to honor his son Ludovicus with a similar reverence.

At last the deeply religious emperor took pity on their legates. He asked them whether they wished to accept the Christian religion. When they replied that they were always and everywhere, and in all things, prepared to obey, he ordered them to be baptized in the name of him concerning whom the most learned Augustine says:

“If there were no Trinity, the Truth would not have said: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’”

The principal men of the palace received them almost as adopted sons. From the emperor’s chamber they received a white baptismal garment; from their godfathers they received Frankish clothing of fine materials, weapons, and other ornaments.

When this practice had continued for some time, and each year many more men—motivated not by Christ but by earthly advantages—began to hurry to the emperor’s service on Holy Saturday of Easter, not as legates but as his most devoted vassals, it happened that on one occasion they came to Ludovicus.

The emperor asked them whether they wished to be baptized. When they confessed that they did, he ordered them to be sprinkled without delay with holy water. Since so many linen garments were not at hand, he ordered shirts to be cut up and sewn in the manner of hedges, or planted out like vines.

When one of these had suddenly been put upon one of the elders, and he had examined it for a moment with unusually inquisitive eyes, he conceived considerable indignation and said to the emperor:

“I have already been washed twenty times and clothed in rich, brilliant-white garments. And now, look: such a sack suits not soldiers but swineherds. Unless I were ashamed of my nakedness, I would leave your garment—and your Christ—with you, stripped of my own clothing and not covered by what you have given.”

Such is the value the enemies of Christ attach to what Christ’s Apostle says:

“All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3).

And:

“All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

And, most especially directed against those who despise the faith and violate the sacraments:

“Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. 6).

Would that this were found more often among the gentiles alone, and not also among those who are reckoned by the name of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXX. Ludovicus, a Lover of Justice

[Col. 1408D]

Something must still be said about the goodness of the earlier Ludovicus, after which we must return to Charles.

The very peaceful emperor Ludovicus, free from all incursions of enemies, devoted himself diligently to religious works alone: namely, prayers, almsgiving, and hearing and determining legal cases with the utmost justice.

In this business he was so well trained both by talent and practice that when a certain man, like an Achitophel (2 Sam. 15), regarded by everyone as an angel, tried to mock him, Ludovicus responded with a gracious expression and the gentlest voice, though his mind was somewhat disturbed:

“O most wise Anshelm, if permission allowed me to speak, I would dare say that you are not walking on the straight path.”

From that day the same jurist was considered worthless by everyone.

## CHAPTER XXXI. He Distributes Alms

The most compassionate Ludovicus was so devoted to almsgiving that he preferred alms to be given not only in his presence but also by his own hand.

Moreover, even when he was absent, he determined to regulate the affairs of the poor in such a way that he ordered one of them—weak in every respect but apparently more courageous than the others—to administer on their behalf the penalties for offenses, the restitution of thefts, retaliation for injuries or wrongs, and, in more serious crimes, the cutting off of limbs, beheading, and hanging.

After appointing their dukes, tribunes, centurions, and deputies, this man efficiently carried out the task entrusted to him.

The most merciful Augustus, however, honoring Christ the Lord in all these matters, never ceased to provide them with food and clothing; especially on the day when Christ, stripped of his mortal tunic, was preparing to put on the incorruptible one.

On that day he also distributed gifts to all who served in the palace and in the royal court, according to each person’s rank. He ordered that the nobles receive either belts, flasks, or the most precious garments brought from the vast empire. To those of lower rank, Frisian cloaks of every color were given. To the horse-guards, bakers, and cooks, linen and woolen garments, together with, perhaps, swords [Fort. *spatisque*], were thrown down according to their needs.

When no one lacked anything, and, according to the Acts and sayings of the apostles, “great grace was upon them all” (Acts 4), the ragged poor, now delightfully clothed in white, raised their voices to heaven, crying “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) to blessed Ludovicus throughout the broad court—or the little courts—of Aachen, which the Latins more commonly call porticoes.

Some of the soldiers could embrace the emperor’s feet; others worshiped him from a distance. As the Caesar was proceeding to the church, one of the jesters said playfully:

“O blessed Ludovicus, who have been able to clothe so many men in a single day! By Christ, no one in Europe has clothed more men today than you—except Atto.”

When the emperor asked him how Atto could have clothed them, the jester, almost delighted to have thrown the emperor into amazement, added with a loud laugh:

“Today, he gave many men new garments.”

The emperor, with his most gentle manner, accepted this playfully and, since his expression was simple, entered the church with humble devotion. There he conducted himself with such reverence that he seemed to have the Lord Jesus Christ himself before his bodily eyes.

At all times, moreover, not from necessity but for the sake of giving, he was accustomed to bathe every Saturday and to give his attendants everything he had removed except his sword and belt.

His generosity even reached the lowest ranks, so much so that he ordered his entire clothing to be given to Stracholto, a glassworker and servant of Saint Gall, who was then serving him.

When the wayward military vassals learned of this, they laid an ambush for him beside the road and attempted to rob him. When he said to them:

“What are you doing, inflicting violence upon Caesar’s glassworker?”

they replied:

“We permit you to retain your office, certainly …” [Note: [Col. 1409B] Some words appear to be missing.] [lacuna]

[Col. 1409]

# GENEALOGY OF CHARLES THE GREAT, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

Written in the year of the Lord 867 and first published by Canisius from a manuscript of Saint Gall.

## Canisius to the Reader

[Col. 1409C]

You may say that this genealogical note is of little importance because it is so brief and bears no author’s name. That is true. Nevertheless, it does not deserve to perish, since it commends itself by its antiquity, having been written in the year 867. I rescue it here from destruction. This is the sole purpose of this edition.

That Charles the Great is here said to have died in the year 815 is plainly contrary to the common opinion, which agrees on the year 814.

## Here Begins the Record of the Genealogy of the Emperor Charles

Anspertus, who was descended from the senatorial class, a distinguished and noble man, outstanding in many divine gifts, took as his wife Blichilt, daughter of Hlothar, king of the Franks. He had by her three sons and one daughter.

His firstborn was named Arnoldus; the second was Feriolus; the third was Modericus; and his daughter was Tarsicia.

Feriolus became a bishop and was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Uzes; there he rests in peace.

Modericus was ordained bishop at Harisium, and there, as a confessor of Christ, he rests in peace, where God performs many miracles on account of his merits.

Tarsicia, a virgin of Christ who persevered in her virginity, rests in the city of Rodinis. Through her merits the power of Christ is displayed there every day; she is also said to have raised the dead.

Arnoldus, his firstborn, begot Lord Arnulfus. Lord Arnulfus begot Flodulfus and Anskisus.

Flodulfus, by the favor of divine grace, was ordained bishop.

Anskisus begot Pipin.

Pipin begot Charles.

Charles begot Lord King Pipin.

Lord Pipin begot the glorious Caesar and most noble prince Charles.

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 815, Charles, the best of all the Augusti, departed from this world at Aachen on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, at the third hour of the day. He had reigned for forty-seven years. He died in the seventy-second year of his age.

His son Ludovicus succeeded him in the empire in the same year and reigned for twenty-six years, that is, until the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 840. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July on an island in the Rhine, near the palace at Ingelheim.

After him, his son and namesake Ludovicus assumed the empire in East Francia. In the present year—that is, in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 867—he appears to have been reigning for twenty-seven years.

[Col. 1409]

# OLD ANNALS OF THE FRANKS

*(From Martène, *Collectio amplissima*)*

## Preliminary Observation

[Col. 1409]

The ancient manuscript that once belonged to the monastery of Ripoll, and later to Étienne Baluze, from whom it passed into the royal library, furnished us with the old annals of the Franks presented here.

Their anonymous author proposed to describe, from the year 670 to 813, the distinguished deeds of Charles the Great and his ancestors. He wrote in a simple style, as was customary in those times, but one suited to persuasion, especially when he recounts matters that he had either received from highly trustworthy authors or seen with his own eyes.

He himself reveals his period when, intending to continue the account of Charles the Great’s glorious deeds, he excuses himself for saying nothing about Charles’s birth, infancy, or even childhood:

“For,” he says, “no one is now found to survive who claims to possess knowledge of these things.”

From these words two conclusions in particular may be drawn. First, the author began writing these Annals immediately after Charles the Great’s death, since none of those who had seen him as an infant or child remained alive, while many still lived who had seen him as an adolescent and an adult. Second, he judged it foolish to report matters of which he had not received reliable knowledge from eyewitnesses.

Furthermore, since these Annals have a close affinity with the Chronicle of the monastery of Moissac, published by André Duchesne in volume III of the *History of the Franks*, and often reproduce its words, we hesitated for some time over whether to commit them to print.

But after carefully examining the matter and comparing the two works with one another, we first discovered that several leaves are missing from the manuscript of the Moissac Chronicle—Duchesne himself admits this—which may constitute a third or fourth part of the present work.

Second, our manuscript contains several sections wholly different from those of the Moissac Chronicle. Finally, even the passages in which the two manuscripts agree often differ from one another, to such an extent that what is clear and open in ours is extremely obscure in the Moissac manuscript.

For these reasons, we judged this to be a new and not contemptible work, one that learned men should not be deprived of. The material that follows from the year 813 to 840, however, we believe was added by some monk of Aniane.

# Here Begins the Genealogy, Origin, Deeds, or Life of the Glorious and Most Devout Emperor Charles

[Col. 1411]

[Col. 1411A]

In those times, in the year 670 from the incarnation of the Lord, when the kings of Gaul were dying out, the most powerful dukes Pipin and Martin ruled in Austrasia.

These dukes, having turned against Ebroin, prefect of Gaul, drew up their battle line. Against them King Theoderic of the Franks and the prefect Ebroin advanced with an army to a place called Locustium [Note: [Col. 1411C] The Moissac Chronicle has *Lucofao*.]. They joined battle and struck one another down in a great slaughter; an innumerable multitude of people fell there.

The Austrasians were defeated and put to flight. Ebroin pursued them with the most savage slaughter, devastating most of that region. Martin escaped by flight, entered Laon, and shut himself up there; Pipin, however, escaped in another direction.

After accomplishing the victory, Ebroin returned. Coming with his army to the estate of Herciacum [Note: [Col. 1411C] The Moissac Chronicle has *Creiacum*, whereas the manuscript reads *Herciacum*.], he sent messengers to Martin and, after oaths had been given, promised that Martin should come confidently to King Theoderic. But he swore this deceitfully and falsely over empty chests [Note: [Col. 1411C] The Moissac Chronicle reads *se jurant*.].

Martin believed them, came to the estate of Herciacum [Note: [Col. 1411C] The Moissac Chronicle incorrectly has “from Herciacum,” instead of “to Herciacum.”], and was killed there with his companions.

Ebroin, meanwhile, continued to oppress the Franks more and more. While he was preparing an ambush for a Frank named Ermefredus, Ermefredus also secretly rose up against him and cruelly killed the aforementioned Ebroin. He escaped by fleeing to Pipin in Austrasia.

The Franks, after taking counsel, appointed the illustrious man Waratho as mayor of the palace in Ebroin’s place, with the king’s approval.

Waratho then received hostages from the aforementioned Pipin and made peace with him. Waratho had a son, vigorous and industrious, fierce in spirit and harsh in character, who plotted against his father and displaced him from his office. His name was Gislamaris.

Blessed Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, forbade Gislamaris to commit this wickedness against his father; but Gislamaris scorned listening to him.

There were wars and much discord between Gislamaris and Pipin. Struck by God because of the wrong done to his father and his other cruel sins, Gislamaris breathed out his wicked spirit, just as Saint Audoenus had foretold to him.

After Gislamaris’s death, Waratho regained his former office.

[Col. 1411C]

In those days blessed Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, full of days and distinguished by his virtues, departed to the Lord at the royal estate of Clichy, in the suburb of the city of Paris.

As time passed, the aforementioned Waratho died.

The Franks, wandering in different directions, appointed Berthcarius as mayor of the palace.

In those days Pipin rose from Austrasia with an army and drew up his battle line against Theoderic, king of the Franks, and Berthcarius. They came together for battle at a place called Textritium. When they had fought one another, Theoderic and Berthcarius turned their backs. Pipin emerged victorious.

As time passed [Note: [Col. 1411C] The Moissac Chronicle reads, “time having been allowed to pass.”], Berthcarius was killed by his flatterers.

After this, under King Theoderic, Pipin began to serve as mayor of the palace with supreme authority. After receiving the treasures, he left a certain Nordbertus, one of his own men, with the king and traveled to Austrasia.

Pipin had a most noble and wise wife named Plectrudis. By her he had two sons. The elder was named Drochus and the younger Grimaldus. Drochus received the duchy of Champagne.

At that time King Theoderic died, having reigned for 19 years [Note: [Col. 1411C] Moissiacensis: 16 years]. His son Chlodoveus, still a child, assumed the royal throne [Col. 1412B] and reigned for two years; after him [Note: [Col. 1412C] Moissiacensis: *postquam* (“after”), incorrectly] his brother Childebert was established as king. Grimald, the younger son of Pippin, became mayor of the palace of King Childebert. Grimald also fathered a son by a concubine, named Theodald. At that time Drochus, Pippin’s son, died. The aforementioned prince Pippin had a son by another wife, named Alpaigde [Note: [Col. 1412C] Moissiacensis: *Alpagede*], whom he named Charles, an attractive, outstanding, and useful man.

## THE ORIGIN OF CHARLES THE OLD.

Prince Pippin waged many wars against numerous peoples.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 710, Pippin died in Alemannia.

In the year 711 the waters rose greatly. For then the glorious Childebert, of good memory and a just man, departed to the Lord in the twelfth year [Note: [Col. 1412C] Perhaps the sixteenth year. Moissiacensis reads “in the eighteenth year.”] of his reign, and his son Dagobert reigned in his place in the year 713.

[Col. 1412C] Now Grimald had a wife named Thusinda, daughter of Rathbod, a pagan duke. When Prince Pippin was ill, Grimald went to visit him and was killed in the basilica of Saint Lambert at Liège [Col. 1413A] by the pagan Raganarius [Note: [Col. 1413D] Moissiacensis: *Ragngarius*]. His son Theodald, however, at the command of his grandfather, was elevated in the royal court to his father’s rank.

In the year 814 Pippin was seized by a severe fever and died. He had held the principate for 27 years. Plectrudis, Pippin’s widow, governed everything under prudent administration with her grandson Theodald, or with King Dagobert.

In the year 815 the Franks again attacked Theodald and the Austrasians in the Cotian Forest, and they struck one another down in an extremely harsh slaughter. Theodald, however, escaped by flight. After he had fled, they chose Raganfred as mayor of the palace. With King Dagobert’s army mobilized, he crossed the Carbonarian Forest as far as the River Meuse, ravaging and burning the land and forests, and made an alliance with the pagan duke Radhbod. [Note: [Col. 1413D] This passage is corrupt in the Chronicle of Moissac, where it reads: “Crossing the Carbonarian Forest with King Dagobert’s army.”] Charles, Pippin’s son, was held under guard by Plectrudis in those days; but, with the Lord’s help, he barely escaped.

At that time King Dagobert, being ill, died [Col. 1413B] in the sixth year of his reign. The Franks established as king a certain cleric named Daniel [Note: [Col. 1413D] Moissiacensis: *quemdam*, “a certain one”], whose hair had grown long, and called him Chilperic. Sema, king of the Saracens [Note: [Col. 1414D] Moissiacensis: *Soma*], in the ninth year after the Saracens had entered Spain, besieged Narbonne and captured it once it had been besieged; he ordered the city’s men to be killed by the sword. They led the women and little children away as captives to Spain, and in the third month of that same year set out to besiege Toulouse. While they were besieging it, Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, came out against them with an army of Aquitanians and Franks, and engaged them in battle. When they had begun to fight, the Saracen army turned its back, and a very large part of it fell by the sword. Five years later, Ambisa, king of the Saracens, invaded Gaul with a huge army, stormed and captured Carcassonne, and conquered as far as Nîmes under a treaty; he sent their hostages to Barcelona.

In the year 716 the Franks mobilized an army and directed it against Charles as far as the River Meuse, while on the other side the Frisians rose up with Duke Rathbod. Charles [Col. 1413C] also attacked the Frisians, suffered the greatest loss from his army, and departed in flight [Note: [Col. 1414D] Several leaves are missing from the Moissiacensis manuscript after these words; they can be restored with the aid of this manuscript, namely from the year 717 to 778].

In the year 717 Chilperic again, together with Raganfred and the Franks, having mobilized an army, entered the Ardennes Forest and reached the Rhine River and the city of Cologne, ravaging the lands. After receiving a large treasure from the matron Plectrudis, they returned. But at a place called Amblava, when Charles attacked them, they suffered a very great defeat.

At the same time the aforementioned Charles, having mobilized an army, rose again against Chilperic and Raganfred. They gathered an army against him and hurried to prepare for war; but Charles requested peace. When they rejected it, they went out to battle at a place called Vitiacum, as Sunday was dawning, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. When they had fought fiercely, Chilperic and Raganfred turned their backs. Charles was victorious, and those regions were ravaged and [Col. 1413D] their inhabitants taken captive. Then, returning to Austrasia with much booty, he came to the city of Cologne, where he caused a revolt, disputed with the matron Plectrudis, and shrewdly recovered his father’s treasures. There he established as king a man named Clotair.

Chilperic and Raganfred therefore sought the aid of Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, who mobilized an army and advanced against Charles. Charles met him steadfastly and without fear. But Eudo fled, returned to the city of Paris, and withdrew beyond the Loire, taking with him King Chilperic and the royal treasures. Charles pursued him but did not find him. The aforementioned King Clotair died that year. Meanwhile King Radbod died, and in the following year Charles sent an embassy [Col. 1414A] to Eudo and made an alliance with him. Eudo then returned King Chilperic with many gifts. Chilperic died in the city of Novicinum, having reigned for five years. The Franks then established over themselves as king Theodosius, the younger son of King Dagobert.

In the year 725 the Saracens destroyed the city of Augustodunum on Wednesday, the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. After seizing the city’s treasure, they returned to Spain with great booty.

In the year 731 Charles ravaged the lands beyond the Loire twice, and Raganfred died.

In the year 732 Abderaman, king of Spain, crossing through Pamplona and the Pyrenees Mountains with a large army of Saracens, besieged the city of Bordeaux. Then Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, gathered an army and went out to meet them in battle on the River Garonne. At the beginning of the battle, however, the Saracens were victorious, while Eudo fled and lost the greater part of his army [Col. 1414B]. Thus at last the Saracens began to plunder Aquitaine.

Eudo came to Charles, prince of the Franks, and asked him for help. Charles then gathered a large army and went out to meet them. When battle was joined in the suburb of Poitiers, the Saracens were defeated by the Franks. There King Abderaman fell in battle with his army, while those of them who survived returned to Spain in flight. Charles, having taken the spoils, returned to Francia in triumphant glory.

In the year 734 Charles entered Frisia with a large army, destroyed it utterly, and subjected it to his rule. At that time Phibin, son of Abderaman, was slain at Narbonne [Perhaps: *proficiscitur*, “set out”]. The following year he crossed the River Rhône. He entered the city of Arles under a treaty, seized the city’s treasures, and for four years devastated and plundered the entire province of Arles.

In those days Pope Gregory the Younger, bishop of the Roman Church, sent to Charles, prince of the Franks, the keys of the venerable tomb of the Apostle Peter and the chains of that same apostle, together with great gifts, in an embassy. No such gifts had previously been sent to any Frankish prince by any bishop of the city of Rome. The aforementioned Pope Gregory also sent, with the embassy and gifts, a letter and decrees of the Roman princes.

When this had been accomplished, the Roman people, wishing to abandon the Greek emperor and his rule and turn to the protection of the aforementioned prince and to his unconquered clemency, he, for all these things, joyfully giving thanks and praise to the Lord, sent the embassy back to Rome with great gifts. After this he chose from among his faithful Grimo, namely abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sigibert, a recluse of the basilica of Saint Denis the Martyr, and sent them with great gifts to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Through them he sent back in writing to the bishop everything that he and the Frankish people had been commanded [Perhaps: “had seen”] in the response.

After this the aforementioned prince [Col. 1414D], hearing that the Saracens were ravaging the province of Arles and the other surrounding cities, gathered a large army of Franks, Burgundians, and the other neighboring peoples who were under his authority. He stormed the city of Avignon by force, killed the Saracens whom he found there, crossed the Rhône, and hastened to besiege the city of Narbonne.

While he was besieging it, Ocupa, king of the Saracens, sent from Spain Amoribinailet with a large army of Saracens to relieve Narbonne. Charles then left part of his army to besiege the city, took the remainder, and went out to meet the Saracens in battle on the River Berre. When they had begun to fight [Col. 1415A], the Saracens were defeated by the Franks in a great slaughter, and the greater part of them fell by the sword. The Saracens experienced the battle of the Franks; those who had come out of Syria found Charles altogether the strongest.

As Charles was returning with the spoils he had gathered and abundant booty, he ordered Maguelonne to be destroyed. At Nîmes he ordered the city’s arena and gates to be burned. After taking hostages, he returned to Francia.

## THE ORIGIN OF PIPPIN.

In the year DCC [lacuna] Charles, the prince, died. He had reigned for 23 years and six months. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, and his sons Pippin and Carloman divided their father’s principate between them. Carloman received Austrasia, Alemannia, and Thuringia. Pippin received Burgundy and Provence.

Zacharias, a Greek by nationality, occupied the Roman See as pope. In his time Carloman, king of the Franks, son of the aforementioned prince Charles and brother of Pippin, moved by divine love and longing for the heavenly homeland, voluntarily abandoned the kingdom and entrusted his sons to his brother Pippin. He himself went to Rome and reached the threshold of the blessed Apostle Peter with many of his nobles and innumerable gifts. He laid them before the tomb of blessed Peter, cut off the hair of his head, and, when blessed Pope Zacharias ordained him, assumed clerical dress. He remained there for some time.

After receiving the counsel of that same pontiff, he went to Mount Cassino and the monastery of Saint Benedict. There he promised regular obedience to Abbot Optatus and pledged himself to the monastic profession.

Pippin, however, claimed his father’s entire kingdom for himself and, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, was made king from being prefect of the palace. After the death of Pope Zacharias, Stephen, a Greek by nationality, occupied the papal office.

Unable to endure the oppression of the Lombards and the arrogance of King Haistulfus, Stephen went to the regions of Francia to seek the defense of Pippin, king of the Franks. When this was announced to King Pippin, he was filled with great joy [Col. 1415C] and ordered his firstborn son Charles, who was to reign after him, to go out to meet the pope and bring him honorably into his presence at a villa called Pons Hugonis. When the aforementioned pope arrived there, King Pippin received him with honor.

On the following day, together with his clergy, the pope sprinkled himself with ashes, clothed himself in sackcloth, and prostrated himself on the ground. He begged King Pippin, through the mercy of almighty God and the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to free himself and the Roman people from the hand of the Lombards and from the servitude of the proud King Haistulfus. He refused to rise from the ground until the aforementioned King Pippin, together with his sons and the Frankish nobles, extended a hand to him and, as a sign of future assistance and liberation, lifted him from the ground.

King Pippin then fulfilled the pope’s entire wish, sent him to the monastery of Saint Denis the Martyr, and ordered him to winter there with the greatest honor and care. King Pippin also sent an embassy to Haistulfus [Col. 1415D], king of the Lombards, urging him, out of reverence for the apostles Peter and Paul, not to afflict the Roman cities and not superstitiously to undertake these impious presumptions against the bishop of the city of Rome.

But concerning all that Prince Pippin had commanded, those same envoys deserved to hear from that proud tyrant nothing but utterly arrogant replies and insolent words. Pope Stephen then anointed Pippin, that most pious prince, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, with the oil of anointing according to ancestral custom and sacred rite. He crowned Pippin’s two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same honor and in the hope of a happy succession.

King Pippin could not fail to fulfill what he had promised the Roman bishop; rather, with all his heart and with God’s help, he had to accomplish it. Crossing the Alps, Pippin sent his envoys to Haistulfus and asked him not to afflict the holy Roman Church, whose defender he had become by divine ordinance, but to render full justice for the possessions that had been taken away [Col. 1416A].

Haistulfus, however, puffed up with arrogance and also heaping insults upon the aforementioned pontiff in foolish words, promised to do nothing for him except provide him a road by which he could return to his own country. The envoys replied that Lord Pippin would not depart from the territories of Lombardy in any other way unless Haistulfus first rendered justice to Saint Peter.

Haistulfus asked what that justice was. The envoys replied: “That you return to him Pentapolis, Narnia, and Ceccano, and everything concerning which the Roman people complain of your injustice. Pippin also commands you this: if you wish to render justice to Saint Peter, he will give you twelve thousand solidi.”

Haistulfus rejected all these terms and dismissed the envoys without any words of peace. Pippin therefore continued the journey he had begun and reached the Lombard fortifications at the Clusae. After destroying them and driving Haistulfus and the Lombards into flight, he besieged the city of Pavia for one year and three months. Having shut Haistulfus inside it, he so constrained him, with God’s help, that he promised to render all the justice due to Saint Peter [Col. 1416B].

Terrified by these threats, the tyrant Haistulfus returned, through the hands of Lord King Pippin’s envoys, Pentapolis, Narnia, Ceccano, and the remaining debts that he owed Saint Peter as a pledge. He also gave King Pippin thirty thousand solidi and promised to pay an annual tribute to the Franks of five thousand solidi.

Haistulfus swore, together with his nobles and all the Lombard aristocracy, that he would fulfill all these terms. As a guarantee, he gave King Pippin forty hostages from among the Lombard nobles.

Pippin, having received the blessing of the lord apostolic, allowed him to depart in peace, handing over to him Ravenna, Pentapolis, Narnia, Ceccano, and whatever was contained in those regions. When all these matters had been completed, Pippin returned home victorious.

When he was returning to Francia, the treacherous King Haistulfus insolently set aside everything he had promised and drove Pope Stephen from his territory by force of arms [Col. 1416C].

That same year Carloman the monk departed to the Lord, and Archbishop Boniface, proclaiming the word of God in Frisia, was crowned. Then Haistulfus, king of the Lombards, broke the faith he had promised Pippin. He invaded Roman territory with an army and even besieged the City itself.

When King Pippin heard this, he gathered an army and, traveling through Burgundy, reached the city of Maurienne. When Haistulfus heard this, he ordered the Lombards to fortify the passes and to resist the Franks.

Meanwhile Pippin, having crossed the Alps with the strength of his army, destroyed the rampart and fortification that the Lombards had built, put their army to flight, and from there reached the city of Ticinum. Ravaging the entire region, he besieged that extremely well-fortified city.

When Haistulfus saw this and had no hope of escape, he asked the most excellent King Pippin for mercy through the supplications of priests [Col. 1416D], and promised, according to the judgment of the Frankish nobles, to correct with complete willingness the things he had done against law and oaths.

King Pippin, moved by mercy as was his custom, granted him his kingdom and his life. According to the judgment of the Franks, Haistulfus handed over to Pippin a third part of the treasure that was in Ticinum. Renewing his oaths and giving hostages, he promised that he would always remain faithful, that he would send every year through his envoys the annual tribute he had promised to the Franks, and that he would return everything he had promised in previous years to Saint Peter and Pope Stephen.

Pippin, victorious, returned home joyfully with his army unharmed, bringing the treasures and hostages with him. King Haistulfus, however, while hunting in a certain forest, was struck by divine vengeance: he was thrown from the horse on which he was sitting and died on the third day.

After this Pope Stephen died. At this time Jussiphibin, having seized tyrannical power over the Saracens in Spain, ruled there. A terrible famine then afflicted Spain. Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine, plundered Narbonne.

In the year 752 Ansemundus the Goth handed over the city of Nîmes, Maguelonne, Agde, and Béziers to Pippin, king of the Franks. From that day the Franks harassed Narbonne. Pippin pursued Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine, because he was unwilling to submit to Pippin’s authority as Eudo had submitted to Charles, Pippin’s father.

In the year 759 the Franks besieged Narbonne. They swore an oath to the Goths who were there that, if they handed the city over to the side of Pippin, king of the Franks, they would permit them to keep their own law. Once this had been done, the Goths killed the Saracens who were stationed there and handed the city itself over to the Frankish side.

In the year 762 a great frost afflicted Gaul, Illyricum, and Thrace. Many olive and fig trees were killed by the frost and withered; the grain shoots also withered. In the following year famine afflicted those regions [Col. 1417B] even more severely, so that many people died from lack of bread.

When King Pippin came to Narbonne, Toulouse, Albi, and Rodez were handed over to him. Not long afterward Prince Waifarius died in the month of June. King Pippin, having obtained his principate, died one hundred days later, in the month of September. He had reigned for 27 years, although he had ruled the Franks alone for 15 years or more. After the Aquitanian war, which he had waged continuously for nine years against Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, he died at Paris of dropsy.

## THE BEGINNING OF THE REIGN OF CHARLES THE GREAT.

His sons Charles and Carloman divided the kingdom between themselves, but Carloman, having possessed the kingdom for a short time, died, and Charles occupied the whole kingdom of his father.

In the third year of King Charles, Queen Berta, Charles’s mother, went to Italy to an assembly against King Desiderius. Many cities were restored to the side of Saint Peter. Berta brought Desiderius’s daughter to Francia, and in the following year Carloman died. After his brother’s death, Charles was established as king by the agreement of all the Franks.

Since nothing concerning the birth, infancy, or even childhood of Charles the Great has ever been set down in writing, and since no one is now found to survive who claims to have knowledge of these matters, I judge it foolish to write about them. I have therefore decided to pass over the unknown and explain and demonstrate his deeds, character, pursuits, and the other parts of his life. I shall narrate first his deeds at home and abroad, then his character and studies, and finally the administration and end of his kingdom, omitting nothing worthy or necessary to know concerning all the wars he waged.

First, he undertook the Aquitanian war begun by his father but not completed, since it seemed capable of being finished quickly; while his brother was still alive, he was also asked to provide assistance.
