For he forced Unaldus, after the death of Waifarius, to abandon Aquitaine and seek Wasconia. Yet he did not allow him to remain there. After crossing the River Garonne, he sent envoys to Lupus, duke of the Wascones, ordering him to return the fugitive and threatening that, if he did not do so quickly, he would demand it from him by war.

Lupus, however, adopting the sounder course, not only returned Unaldus but also surrendered himself and the province over which he presided to Charles’s authority.

Pope Adrian of the city of Rome sent his envoys to Charles, king of the Franks, for the defense of the Roman Church, because it was being severely oppressed by Desiderius, king of the Lombards, who had succeeded Haistulfus and held the Lombard kingdom through the donation of Pippin, king of the Franks.

At that time King Charles was in a place called Theodonisville. A messenger of the lord apostolic, named Peter, came there and, at the pope’s request, asked Charles to defend the holy Church and free the Roman people from the proud King Desiderius. He added that Charles was the legitimate guardian and defender of that people, since his predecessor, Pope Stephen of blessed memory, had anointed him with sacred oil and appointed him king and patrician of the Romans.

King Charles therefore promised with devoted mind, following the counsel of his nobles, that with God’s help he would fulfill the will of the lord apostolic.

That same year he held a synod at the city of Genoa. At that assembly he divided the army: he retained one part with himself so that he could cross by Mount Cenis, while he ordered the other part, placing it under the command of his uncle Bernard and the other faithful men, to enter Italy by Mount Jovis.

King Desiderius, forgetful of the benefits of King Pippin, through whose donation he had obtained the Lombard kingdom, ordered the fortifications to be strongly defended against Charles and his army.

King Charles therefore established his camp opposite the fortifications and rampart defended by the Lombards. He sent a legion of the most proven fighters up the mountain by a difficult ascent. They crossed the mountain and put the Lombards, together with their king Desiderius and Oggerius, to flight [Col. 1418B].

With his army, King Charles entered Italy through the opened fortifications, with the help of the Lord and Saint Peter, and reached the city of Pavia. After shutting Desiderius inside it, he besieged the city and surrounded it with a very strong rampart.

He celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in that same camp and Easter at Rome. When the glorious King Charles, with God’s help and through the intercession of the apostles Peter and Paul, returned from the Roman city to Pavia, Lombards came from every city of Italy and submitted themselves to his dominion and rule.

Adalgisus, son of Desiderius, fled, boarded a ship, and went to Constantinople. Charles besieged the city of Pavia for ten years, and in the month of June the city was captured by the Franks.

The glorious King Charles, having subjected or organized all Italy, left Frankish garrisons in the city of Pavia, drove King Desiderius, Oggerius, his wife, and his daughter into exile, and himself returned to Francia with a great triumph and with the Lord’s help [Col. 1418C]. Thus he brought the Lombard kingdom to an end. The Lombards had ruled for 214 years.

In the year 772, that is, in the fifth year of King Charles, King Charles entered Saxony in a hostile manner and destroyed their shrine called the Irminsul. He had begun the war against them, and scarcely a single year had passed without their committing some such act in return.

But the king’s greatness of spirit and his perpetual constancy of mind, in adversity as well as prosperity, could not be overcome by change or wearied by what he had begun to do. For he never allowed them to commit such acts with impunity, but either went against them himself or sent an army through his counts to avenge their treachery and exact fitting punishment from them.

At last, after all who were accustomed to resist had been defeated and reduced to his power, he removed ten thousand people from among those who inhabited both banks of the River Elbe, together with their wives and little children [Col. 1418D], and transported them, distributing them in many different settlements throughout Gaul and Germany.

The war, which had continued for so many years, is said to have ended on the condition proposed by the king and accepted by them: that they abandon the worship of demons and their ancestral rites, receive the sacraments of the Christian faith and religion, and, united with the Franks, become one people with them.

Although this war was drawn out over a very long period, Charles himself engaged the enemy in battle no more than twice: once near the mountain called Osneggi, at a place named Teotmelli; and again at the River Hase, in the same month, with only a few days between the battles. In these two engagements the enemy were so thoroughly routed and defeated that afterward they did not dare either to challenge the king or resist his advance unless protected by some fortified place.

Nevertheless, many men of both Frankish and Saxon nobility, including holders of the highest offices, perished in that war. At last it ended in the thirty-third year.

[Col. 1419A] In the year 771 [Note: [Col. 1419D] Some number seems to be missing here, since earlier events had been placed in the year 772. From the Metz Annals under the year 775: Charles “captured the fortress of Sigiburg and rebuilt Heresburg.”] King Charles went hostilely into Saxony, ravaged it, carried out a great slaughter of its people, and captured two fortresses there, Heresburg and Sigisburg. He placed garrisons in them.

In the following year King Charles went again to Italy and recovered the remaining fortresses. Rotgannus was killed. On his return he entered Saxony, took a very large part of the Saxons, and the Saxons were converted to the faith of Christ; many of them were baptized.

In another year King Charles held a great assembly of the Franks, namely the May Field, in Saxony at Paderborn. There a multitude of pagan Saxons was baptized.

In the year 778 King Charles gathered a large army, entered Spain, and conquered the city of Pamplona. There Taurus, king of the Saracens, came to him, surrendered to him the cities he possessed, and gave him hostages, his brother and his son. From there Charles proceeded as far as Zaragoza.

While he was staying in those regions [Col. 1419B], a very fierce battle took place on Sunday, and many thousands of Saracens fell. At the ninth hour the sun became as it had been at the second hour.

Again the Saxons, a treacherous people who broke their faith, came out from their territories and advanced as far as the River Rhine, burning and ravaging everything. When they were returning with great booty, a messenger reached King Charles, who was still staying in Spain.

[ [Note: [Col. 1420D] The material enclosed in brackets seems to have been taken from Einhard and inserted here by a monk of Aniane.] Since war was being waged against the Saxons with constant and almost uninterrupted conflict, Charles, after arranging garrisons at suitable points along the frontier, attacked Spain with the greatest military preparation he could muster. Having crossed the Pyrenean pass and accepted into submission all the towns and fortresses he approached, he returned with his army safe and unharmed, except that on the ridge of the Pyrenees, during the return journey, he happened briefly to experience the treachery of the Wascones.

For, as the army advanced in a long column, extended as the nature of the place and the narrowness of the passes permitted, the Wascones, having set an ambush on the summit of the mountain—for the place, because of the dense forests, of which there is a great abundance there, is well suited to ambushes—attacked from above the rear of the baggage train and those who, walking at the back of the column, were protecting those ahead. They threw them down into the valley below, joined battle with them, and killed every one of them. After plundering the baggage, they scattered rapidly in different directions under the protection of the approaching night.

The lightness of the Wascones’ arms and the terrain where the action took place assisted them in this deed. Conversely, the heaviness of their arms and the unfavorable ground made the Franks inferior to the Wascones in every respect. In that battle Eggihard, overseer of the royal table, Anselm, count of the palace, and several others were killed. Charles also returned with his army,]

But the Franks, gathered into one body, pursued the Saxons as far as the river called the Calerna. When the Saxons learned this, they turned against them in battle. Many of the Saxons fell; the rest fled, and the Franks took their spoils.

In another year King Charles again went with an army into Spain and reached the city of Medinaceli. The Saracens, making peace from across the river, gave hostages. In Spain there was a great famine and mortality, and the king stayed in the city of León.

In the following year, having gathered a large army, he entered Spain against the Navarri and reached the River Gállego. All the Navarri surrendered themselves to him. He took hostages, both free men and dependents, and divided that country among bishops, priests, and abbots so that they might baptize and preach there. A great multitude of Inmidorum [Perhaps: *Winidorum*], or Basques, or pagans, was also baptized.

Returning from there, he went to Italy and left his sons Pippin and Charles at Worms [Col. 1420A].

In the year 781, the thirteenth year of Charles’s reign, King Charles went with an army and entered Italy. He reached Rome, where his son, who was called Carloman, was baptized. Pope Adrian changed his name to Pippin and anointed him king over Italy; he anointed his brother Louis king over Aquitaine. There Ruotrud, King Charles’s daughter, was betrothed to the Emperor Constantine.

After this King Charles left Rome and, traveling onward, reached Capua, a city of Campania. Having established his camp there, he threatened war against the Beneventans unless they surrendered. Duke Aragisus of that people forestalled him by sending his sons Romald and Grimoald to meet the king with a large sum of money.

He asked the king to accept his sons as hostages and promised that he and his people would do whatever was commanded, except only that he himself should not be compelled to come into the king’s presence. The king, considering the advantage of the people rather than the duke’s stubbornness [Col. 1420B], accepted the hostages offered to him and granted Aragisus, as a great favor, that he would not be compelled to appear before him. Retaining the younger of the two sons as a pledge during the siege, he sent the elder back to his father. He then dismissed envoys together with Aragisus to demand and receive oaths of loyalty from the Beneventans, and returned to Rome.

After spending several days there venerating the holy places, he returned to Gaul. He held a conference with Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, and a great assembly of the Franks, namely the May Field, at the city of Worms.

In the year 782, the fourteenth year of King Charles, the abbot Benedict, called Vitiche, built a monastery at a place called Aniane by order of the aforementioned King Charles. Later he had three hundred monks under his direction, and through his example monasteries were built throughout Gothia and Aquitaine.

In the same year the king held a great assembly of his army in Saxony at Lippebrunn and appointed over it counts from the noblest Saxon lineage [Col. 1420C]. When he learned that they had again fallen away from the faith, had gathered to wage war, and that some of his own men had perished in this revolt, he went once more into Saxony, ravaged it, and stabbed a huge multitude of Saxons to death with a merciless sword.

In the year 783 King Charles went into Saxony with a large army. When the Saxons rebelled, battle was joined, and many thousands fell on the Saxon side. Battle was joined again, and the Franks fought with the Saxons; many thousands more fell on the Saxon side than before. Charles returned victorious to Francia.

That same year the heat was so intense that very many people expired from the heat itself. In the following year King Charles again went into Saxony twice.

In the year 785 King Charles stayed in Saxony at Heresburg [Note: [Col. 1420D] Chronicle of Moissac: *Hensburg*] from the Nativity of the Lord until the month of June. He rebuilt it from the foundations and also constructed the basilica itself. He held an assembly at Paderborn [Col. 1420D] with the Franks and Saxons, and then at last crossed the River Weser [Note: [Col. 1420D] Moissiacensis: “across the River Guisan”] and reached Bardowick.

When the Saxons had surrendered themselves to him, they again accepted the Christianity that they had earlier rejected. Since no one rebelled, the king afterward returned home.

Widukind, the author of so many evils and instigator of treachery, came with his companions to the palace at Attigny. There he was baptized, and the king received him from the font and honored him with magnificent gifts.

That same year the people of Girona handed over the city of Girona to King Charles.

In the year 787, certain counts attempted to rebel; some nobles also from the regions of Austria, conspiring together, compelled as many as they could to rise up against the king. This action terrified many. When they realized that they could not carry out their wicked undertaking and that the opportune time had not arrived, they became frightened and sought hiding places everywhere. When this was discovered, the king ordered them to come to him. Earlier, in the month of April, he had caused a synod of bishops and an assembly to be convened at Worms. There he decreed that those who had been chiefly overcome in this conspiracy should be deprived both of their rank and of access to the court; nevertheless, he mercifully absolved those who, though innocent, had been led astray in this conspiracy.  

[Note: Moissiacensis has *procedenti* (“ensuing”) rather than *praecedenti* (“preceding”).]

From this year, in the month of September, terrifying armies appeared in the sky, such as had never appeared in our time or earlier; signs of the cross also appeared on people’s garments, and some said that they saw blood raining down. Consequently, great panic and fear seized the people, and a great mortality followed.

In the year 787, an eclipse of the sun occurred at the second hour, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [Note: Moissiacensis: “the seventh day before the Kalends”], on a Sunday. In the same year King Charles came with an army as far as the borders of the Bavarians [Note: Moissiacensis: “as far as the borders of the Pannonians”] and entered that country. This war arose suddenly and was brought to a swift conclusion. It had been provoked by the pride and negligence of Duke Tassilo, who, at the urging of his wife—who was the daughter of King Desiderius and thought that through her husband she could avenge her father’s exile—attempted, after forming an alliance with the Huns, who border the Bavarians to the east, not only to refuse to do what was commanded but also to challenge the king to war.

Because his defiance seemed excessive, the king’s spirit could not endure it. Accordingly, after gathering forces from every direction, he intended to march against Bavaria and came himself to the River Lech with a very large army. This river divides the Bavarians from the Alamanni. Having placed his camp on its bank, before entering the province he decided to test the duke’s intentions through envoys. But Tassilo did not persist in his course; recognizing what was useful both to himself and to his people, he submitted himself humbly to the king, gave the hostages that were demanded—including his own son Theudo—and, in addition, gave his sworn pledge that, without anyone’s persuasion, he would agree to remain under the king’s authority for his protection. Thus the war, which had seemed likely to be extremely great, was brought to its swiftest possible end.

In another year Tassilo came to King Charles at Ingolheim, and an assembly of Franks and of the other nations subject to his rule was held there. The Franks recalled the very evil counsels and plots that Tassilo and his wife had been devising against the Franks with all the peoples living around them, both Christians and pagans. Tassilo’s counselors and envoys were also present and publicly recounted the plan before him, and he was entirely unable to deny it. Then they judged him worthy of death. But the king, moved by mercy, refused to kill him; instead, at Tassilo’s own request, he made him a cleric and confined him in a monastery.

The king proceeded into Bavaria to Regensburg [Note: Moissiacensis: “Ragansburg”]. There the Bavarians came to him, hostages were given to the king, and the country was organized and entrusted to him through counts [Note: Moissiacensis adds: “and, after the country had been organized, he returned to Francia. But our manuscript should be read as it stands”]. He then returned to Francia.

In the following year King Charles traveled through Saxony as far as the Slavs called the Wilzi, but properly—that is, in their own language—they are called the Veletabi [Note: Moissiacensis omits this entire line]. The kings of that land, with their king Tranuitus [Note: Moissiacensis: “Tranquitō”], came to meet him. They requested peace, surrendered all those lands under his rule, and gave themselves up as well. The king then returned to Francia.

In another year the king held an assembly at Worms, though not the May Field [Note: Moissiacensis: “the May Field”]. That year also passed without war.

In the year 791 the king went to Worms and celebrated Easter there. When the year was turning, at the season when kings customarily set out for war, he mobilized an innumerable army and marched against the exceedingly proud nation of the Avars. He divided the army into three parts. He himself entered through Bavaria into the territory of the Huns, on the southern side of the Danube. On the other side of the Danube another army entered, composed of men from the Ripuarians, Frisians, and Saxons, together with Thuringians. There was also a naval force on the Danube, so that the king might be able to exercise power with his army on both sides. Thus he entered that land, these forces from one direction and those from the other.

The naval force was in the middle; and the Lord terrified them before him, so that no one dared resist him. Wherever they had made either a ditch or some other fortification, whether in the mountains, along rivers, or in the forests, as soon as he or his army arrived, they immediately surrendered to him, were killed, or scattered in flight.

The other army, which his son Pippin had sent from Italy, also entered Illyricum and acted there in the same way, devastating and burning that land, just as the king did with the army where he himself was.

When King Charles saw that no one among the Avars dared resist either him or his men, he went around that land for fifty-two days, burning and devastating it. They also carried away booty beyond measure or number, as well as innumerable captives—men, women, and children. King Charles returned to Bavaria and wintered at Philopia [Note: Moissiacensis: “at Jupila.” But Jupila is not in Bavaria, but in the territory of Liège].

This war was the greatest of all the wars he conducted, except for the Saxon war—namely, the war undertaken against the Avars or Huns. He conducted it with greater determination than the others and with far greater preparations. He personally led only one expedition into Pannonia, for that nation then inhabited the province; the remaining operations he entrusted to his son Pippin, to the provincial prefects, to the counts, and to the envoys. Since these men conducted the war with the greatest vigor, it was finally completed in the eighth year.

How many battles were fought in it and how much blood was shed is shown by the fact that Pannonia was left entirely without inhabitants. The place where the khagan’s royal residence had stood was so deserted that not even a trace of human habitation appeared there. In this war the whole nobility of the Huns perished, their entire glory collapsed, and all their money and treasures accumulated over a long period were plundered. Human memory cannot recall any war that arose against the Franks by which they were more enriched and increased in wealth. For although they had seemed almost poor up to that time, so much gold and silver was found in the royal hall, and so many precious spoils were taken in battle, that one may rightly believe that the Franks justly took from the Huns what the Huns had previously unjustly taken from other peoples.

Only two of the Frankish nobles perished in that war: Erigus, duke of Friuli, who was intercepted by an ambush laid by the townspeople in Liburnia, near the coastal city of Tarsatica; and Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, who, while drawing up his line to fight the Huns in Pannonia, was killed—by whom it is uncertain—with only two companions who rode beside him as he went along encouraging each man in turn.

Otherwise, this war was almost bloodless for the Franks and had a successful outcome, although its great scale caused it to continue for a longer time. Afterward, the Saxon war also received an end proportionate to its length.

In the year 792 King Charles remained in Bavaria and celebrated Easter at Regensburg. But as summer approached, the Saxons, thinking that the nation of the Avars wished to avenge itself, most clearly displayed what had long been hidden in their hearts. Like a dog returning to its vomit, they returned to their paganism, which they had formerly rejected, abandoning Christianity once again and joining themselves to the pagans who lived around them.

They also sent envoys to the Avars and attempted to rebel, first against God and then against the king. They burned and devastated the churches that were in their territory, expelled the bishops and priests who remained among them [Perhaps: “who were over them”], and killed some whom they had captured. They turned completely back to the worship of idols.

In that same year a very wicked plot was formed. Pippin, the king’s son, born from the concubine named Himiltrude, wished to kill the king and his sons born of legitimate marriage, and to reign in his place like Abimelech in the days of the Judges of Israel. Abimelech killed his seventy brothers on one stone and reigned in place of his father Gideon, though with wickedness and hatred.

When the king learned of Pippin’s plot and of those who were involved with him, he convened an assembly of the Franks and of his other loyal men at Regensburg. There the entire people who were with the king judged that Pippin and those who had agreed with him should be deprived both of their inheritance and of their lives, and this sentence was carried out against some of them.

As for Pippin, his son, the king did not wish him to be killed; they therefore judged that he should be reduced to servitude. This was done: he was made a cleric and sent to a monastery, where he remained again.

In the year 793, during that same winter, King Charles again held an assembly at Regensburg. When he recognized his loyal bishops, abbots, and counts who were present with him there, together with the rest of the loyal people who had not participated with Pippin in that wicked plot, he honored them greatly with gold, silver, silk, and many gifts.

That winter King Charles sent his two sons, Pippin and Louis, with a large army into the land of Benevento. There a severe famine struck both the people and the army that had arrived, so that some were unable even during Lent to abstain from eating meat. A very severe famine also afflicted Italy and Burgundy, and certain regions of Francia; likewise in Gothia and Provence it was so severe that many died of hunger.

After King Charles had again celebrated Easter at Regensburg, and wished in the summer to return to Francia by ship, he ordered a large canal to be dug between two rivers, the Altmühl and the Rednitz [Note: Moissiacensis: “Alomonia and Rachantha”]. He remained there for a long time.

At this time Exam, son of Abderaman Abinmavia, ruled in Spain. This Abinmavia defeated Jussef ibn, killed him and his sons, and ruled in his place in Spain for thirty-three years and four months. He was more cruel than all the Saracen kings who had ruled in Spain before him. He killed innumerable Saracens and Moors by various tortures. He also ordered his father’s son—his own brother—to be burned alive after his hands and feet had been cut off.

By imposing such heavy tribute on the Christians in Spain and on the Jews, he oppressed them so severely that they sold their sons and daughters [Note: Moissiacensis: “they burned their sons and daughters and slaves”; our manuscript is better, reading “sold”], and the few who remained were afflicted by poverty. Through his oppression the whole of Spain was troubled and depopulated.

Abinmavia died, and his son Exam ruled in his place, doing evil as his father had done. When he heard that King Charles had marched against the Avars and supposed that the Avars had fought the king vigorously, so that for this reason he would be unable to return to Francia, he sent Abdelmelec [Note: Moissiacensis: “Aldelmelec”], one of his nobles, with a large army of Saracens to devastate Gaul.

They came to Narbonne and set its suburbs and many Christians on fire. After taking great booty, they wished to proceed to the city of Carcassonne, but William, formerly a count, came out against them with other Frankish counts. They joined battle on the River Orbieu. The battle became extremely fierce, and on that day the greater part of the Christian forces fell.

William fought bravely that day. But when he saw that he could not withstand them, because his companions had abandoned him in flight, he withdrew from them. The Saracens gathered their spoils and returned to Spain.

With Christ’s help, King Charles traveled by ship from the place where he had ordered the canal to be dug and reached Frankfurt, where he remained that winter.

In the year 794 King Charles celebrated Easter at the royal estate of Frankfurt. In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, the most devout and orthodox prince Charles learned that Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, together with another bishop of the see of Urgell, named Felix—or “unfortunate” in his teaching—were boldly asserting that our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he was ineffably begotten from the Father before the ages, was truly the Son of God, but that insofar as he deigned to assume flesh from Mary, ever-virgin, he was not the true son but an adopted son.

When he heard this, the aforesaid prince sent envoys to the apostolic see and to Hadrian, pope of the city of Rome, consulting him about the aforesaid heresy. Inflamed with zeal for the faith, he summoned with the greatest speed a multitude of bishops from his entire empire or kingdom and from the various provinces subject to his rule. In obedience to the sacred commands, they assembled in one college at the estate called Frankfurt.

There a universal synod was gathered, together with the envoys of the lord apostolic Pope Hadrian; Paul, patriarch and archbishop of Aquileia; Peter, archbishop of Milan; and bishops, abbots, monks, priests, deacons, and subdeacons from Italy, Gaul, Gothia, Aquitaine, and Galicia, as stated above. Among them was the venerable and most holy abbot Benedict, also called Vitiza, of the monastery of Aniane in the region of Gothia, together with the religious monks Bede and Ardo, also called Smaragdus, and all their brothers and disciples. These included Ingeila, Aimo, Rabanus, and Georgius, together with the other brothers and the entire clergy, as well as the devout people assembled with them. (At this time Ardo, also called Smaragdus, the teacher, flourished.)

One day, while everyone was sitting in the palace hall, with priests and deacons standing around them in the form of a circle, together with the entire clergy, a letter was brought into the presence of the aforesaid prince. It had been sent by Elipandus, the author of the affair in the city, bishop of the see of Toledo, *Spalensis finitimi* [uncertain reading], together with his associate Felix, bishop of the see of Urgell.

When the letter had been read aloud publicly at the king’s command, the venerable prince immediately rose from the royal seat and stood upon the step. He addressed them at length concerning the matter of faith and added:

“What do you think? From the whole of the past year, and from the time when this madness of the pestilence began, while perfidy swelled and the furrow boiled over, a not insignificant error has arisen in these regions, although they lie at the farthest boundaries of our kingdom. Faith’s judgment must cut it away from everyone.”

After a prolonged offering had been requested and granted for several days, it pleased his gentleness that each person should bring forward, through sacred words, whatever his understanding could grasp as the more correct view. On the appointed day, each was to carry upon the vessel of his mind the gift of faith held in his heart and present it to the prince.

After much prolonged discussion, and after reading through the New and Old Testaments and examining the teaching of the orthodox Fathers, all the most holy Fathers mentioned above and the universal synod rejected and opposed the impious heresy with one voice. They decreed that this heresy must be completely eradicated from the holy Church, declaring:

“The Son of God became the son of man. According to the truth of nature, the Son of God was born from God; according to the truth of nature, the son of man was born from man. Thus the truth of the one begotten should possess, by being born, the name of son—not adoption, not mere designation—in both births. He was true God and true man, one proper Son from both natures, not an adopted son. For it is impious and profane to say that the eternal Father’s coeternal and proper Son is adopted; rather, he must be believed and proclaimed to be true and proper, as stated above, from both natures.”

They also judged that the perverse doctrines of all heretics, together with their authors and followers, should be struck with eternal anathema. As for Elipandus and Felix, new enemies of the Church who polluted themselves with ancient dregs, unless they should recover from this folly and cleanse themselves through satisfaction in perfect faith and through the lamentations of repentance, they decreed that they, together with their followers, were unworthy and ungrateful and should, by perpetual punishment and [reading uncertain; perhaps *abjuratione*, “abjuration”], be excluded from the fellowship of Catholics; they judged them alien from the bosom of the orthodox Church.

In the same synod a question was also brought forward concerning the recent synod of the Greeks, which had been held at Constantinople concerning the veneration of the images of the saints. It contained the statement that anyone who did not render to the images of the saints the service or adoration offered to the divine Trinity should be judged anathema.

After this had been read at the aforesaid council, all the most holy Fathers mentioned above rejected and despised this service and unanimously condemned it.

The universal council also decided that, out of reverence for the holy apostolic Pope Hadrian of the city of Rome, a letter should be sent to him, with every legal privilege reserved to the supreme pontiff, just as the holy Fathers had once sent letters from the Council of Nicaea to blessed Pope Sylvester of the city of Rome after the condemnation of Arius and all the heretics.

The aforesaid pope, after again convening a council of bishops of the entire Roman Church, likewise condemned Elipandus and Felix, the chief authors of all this perfidy, and their followers, just as the holy council had done. He judged that this heresy must be completely eradicated from the holy Church.

He also sent a consoling letter to all the bishops and churches in the regions of Spain and Galicia. Whoever reads and believes it will find it fully furnished, from the New and Old Testaments, for following the path of faith.

King Charles then again proceeded into Saxony. The Saxons came to meet him at Heresburg, promising Christianity once more and swearing, as they had often done. He gave them priests and returned to Francia, settling at the royal palace of Aachen.

In the year 795 King Charles celebrated Easter at the royal palace of Aachen. Then the infidelity that had regularly arisen among the Saxons broke out again. The lord king wished to march against other peoples, but they neither came fully to him nor sent him the assistance he had commanded them to provide [Note: The Moissiacensis Chronicle corruptly reads: “because the lord king wished to come against them together with other peoples”].

When their infidelity had again become known, the king came with his army. Other Saxons, peaceful in their intentions, came out to meet him and accompanied him on his march as his support, completing the journey with him [Note: The same Chronicle incorrectly repeats *iterum expleverunt* (“completed again”), which makes no sense]. When he himself and his army reached the Elbe, however, others in the region of the Marshes and at Wacmoding did not come fully to him.

Nevertheless, when the lord king withdrew at Bardunuil [Note: Moissiacensis: “Bardanavil”], he took away so great a multitude of hostages that neither in his own days, nor in his father’s days, nor in the days of the Frankish kings had such a number ever been taken from there [Note: The column reference is printed as Col. 1425D]. At that time all the others came to him, except those whom we mentioned above and those who lived beyond the Elbe; they did not come fully to him because they had killed the king’s vassal, King Viudin of the Obodrites [Note: Moissiacensis: “Cahchita, king of the Abodrites”]. For this reason they did not believe that they could regain his favor.

All the rest came peacefully and promised to fulfill his command. Thus the lord king again trusted them and killed no one, keeping his word.

Then, from the land of the Avars, a certain prince named Thodanus [Note: Moissiacensis: “Sordarius”] came to the lord king at the royal palace of Aachen with his counts. The king received him honorably and ordered him and those who had come with him to be baptized. He sent him back to his own land with great honor and gifts.

In that year a great multitude of treasures also came from the Avars. The king gave thanks to Almighty God for them and distributed the treasure among the churches, bishops, abbots, and counts; he also magnificently honored all his faithful men from the same treasure.

That winter, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, the lord Adrian, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, died in blessed memory. On his account the most devout King Charles requested that prayers be offered throughout the Christian people within his territories, and he sent abundant alms for him.

He also ordered an epitaph to be composed in Francia in golden letters on marble, so that it could be sent to Rome and placed at the tomb of the supreme pontiff Hadrian.

In the year 796, during the summer, King Charles sent his son Pippin with the Franks, Lombards, and Bavarians whom he had in Italy, together with part of the Alamanni [Note: Moissiacensis: “Alemanni”], into the territory of the Avars.

Pippin came with his army and with all those whom his father had sent to him as auxiliaries. After crossing the Danube, he reached the place where the kings of the Avars customarily sat with their princes, called in our language the Ring [Note: Moissiacensis: “Kinn”]. From there he carried away the treasures of the Avars and reached Francia with many captives.

That summer King Charles remained in Saxony with his two sons Charles and Louis. He went around the land of the Saxons who had rebelled, burning and devastating everything, and brought innumerable booty—men, women, and children as captives—with him to Francia.

He also sent a third army during that summer, with his sons into Spain, into the territory of the Saracens, together with their princes. [Note: Moissiacensis reads “indeed, an army”; our manuscript’s reading, “a third army,” is better, since it had previously mentioned two armies that year: one led by Pippin against the Avars, the other led by Charles himself with his sons Charles and Louis into Saxony.] They acted in the same way, devastated that land, and returned safely to King Charles at the royal palace of Aachen.

For there he had established his residence and had built his church of extraordinary size in honor of holy Mary, perpetual virgin and Mother of God. He had its doors and grilles made of bronze [Note: Moissiacensis omits *et* (“and”) in “doors and grilles,” incorrectly], and with great care and honor, as was fitting, he adorned the basilica with its other ornaments; he decorated it with gold, silver, and lamps.

Since he could not obtain columns and marble for its construction from elsewhere, he arranged for them to be transported from Rome and Ravenna. He also built a palace there, which he called the Lateran, and ordered his treasures from each kingdom to be brought to Aachen. He also carried out many other great works in the same place.

In the year 797, the thirtieth year of King Charles, the aforesaid king entered Saxony with his army and reached the district called Vudmodi, where they had built a fortification. After breaking through the fortification, he entered that district with his army, devastated and burned it.

Then the Saxons came to him again from all the regions and corners where they lived, and he took from them whatever hostages he wished. He did the same with the Frisians, and so returned to Francia.

After several weeks he again entered Saxony, remained there during the winter, and established his residence near the place where Timella had been, in the forest called Saraca. He also called it Heristelli [Col. 1427A], because the dwellings in which his army lived had been constructed there.

He remained there during the winter and celebrated Easter there. In the summer he reached Bardunhuinc with his army, and all those people surrendered themselves into his hand. He took from them whatever hostages he wished.

Meanwhile our Slavs, called the Obodrites, assembled with the king’s envoys against those Saxons. They gathered together and joined battle. On that day 2,800 Saxons fell.

From there the king returned to Francia, to his residence at the royal palace of Aachen, and wintered there.

In the year 799 King Charles celebrated Easter at the royal palace of Aachen. After the death of Pope Hadrian, Leo succeeded him in the apostolate. He was born in Rome to a father named Asupius and a mother named Elisabeth [Note: From this passage we learn the name of Pope Leo’s mother; among the authors I have seen, there is deep silence concerning it]. He sat for twenty-two years and three months.

He was a lover of churches and a man of keen intelligence. The Romans wished to kill him. During the greater Litany, which is held on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, they suddenly attacked him, seized him, and cut out his tongue. They attempted to tear out his eyes [Note: It is commonly reported that Leo’s eyes were gouged out, although there are authors who seem to deny this] and sent him into custody.

From there he escaped by night and reached the envoys of the aforesaid glorious prince Charles, who were then at the basilica of blessed Peter—namely, the abbot Hunerondus and Hivinegisus, duke of Spoleto. They led him from there to Spoleto.

King Charles was then in Saxony, at a place called Partesburna. The aforesaid Pope Leo of the city of Rome was brought to him there. The king received him with the greatest honor and honored him with many gifts. He later sent the pope back to his own see in peace and with great honor. The king’s envoys escorted him honorably and sent to the king those who had plotted his death. The king sent them into exile.

In the year 800 King Charles gathered his nobles and held a synod at Mainz with an assembly of bishops and abbots. When he learned that peace prevailed throughout all his territories, he remembered the injury that the Romans had inflicted upon the apostolic Pope Leo and resolved to travel toward Rome. He did so.

When he was approaching Rome, Pope Leo and the Roman nobles came out to meet him at Nomentum, twelve miles from the city. The aforesaid king reached Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Eight days later, after holding a public meeting with the Romans, he made the purpose of his arrival known to everyone.

He then held a very great assembly of bishops and abbots, together with priests, deacons, counts, and the rest of the Christian people. Those who had wished to condemn the apostolic pope appeared there before him.

When no one was found to prove the charges, the aforesaid pope, without being judged by anyone but of his own free will, stood before all the people in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. Carrying the Gospel, he climbed the ambo, invoked the name of the holy Trinity, and cleared himself under oath of the crimes brought against him.

When these oaths had been completed, all the bishops, together with the entire clergy, the aforesaid king, and the devout Christian people, sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*.

When it had been completed, the king himself and the whole people offered praises to God, because they had been found worthy to possess the apostolic Pope Leo, sound in body and preserved in soul.

In the year 801, while King Charles was staying at Rome, the priest Zacharias—whom the king had previously sent to those regions with many gifts to the Lord’s tomb and to other holy places—came to Rome with two monks sent to the king by the patriarch from Jerusalem.

For the sake of blessing, they brought the keys of the Lord’s tomb and of the place of Calvary, as well as the keys of the city and of Mount Zion, together with a banner of the cross. After receiving them, the king blessed the Lord and sent the monks back to Jerusalem, rewarding them with many gifts.

On the most sacred day of the Nativity of the Lord, when the king rose from prayer before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle to attend Mass, Pope Leo, with the agreement of all the bishops and priests, the Frankish senate, and the Roman senate, placed a golden crown upon his head. The Roman people also joined in, acclaiming:

**“To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans, life and victory!”**

After the praises had been sung by the people and by the apostolic pope, he was adored by the apostolic pope according to the custom of the ancient rulers.

This too happened by God’s will. For while the aforesaid emperor was then staying at Rome, certain people were brought to him, saying that among the Greeks the name of emperor had ceased and that the imperial title had come to an end among them. A woman named Irene had seized the imperial title for herself after fraudulently capturing her son, who was emperor, and gouging out his eyes, just as Athaliah is said to have done in the Book of Kings.

When Pope Leo, the entire assembly of bishops, priests, and abbots, the Frankish senate, all the leading Romans, and the rest of the Christian people heard this, they took counsel together about whether they ought to name Charles, king of the Franks, emperor. He possessed Rome, the mother of the empire, where Caesars and emperors had always been accustomed to reside. They also wished to prevent the pagans from insulting the Christians if the title of emperor should cease among Christians.

It therefore seemed right to everyone that, with God’s help and at the request of the entire Christian people, the aforesaid king should possess the imperial title. King Charles did not wish to refuse their request. With complete humility, submitting himself to God and to the request of the priests and the universal Christian people, he accepted it on the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, through the consecration of Pope Leo, as stated above.

Immediately after he became emperor, he first of all devoted himself to restoring the Roman Church to peace and harmony, ending the discord that the Romans had had with the apostolic Pope Leo.

He then returned to Francia, to the royal residence at Aachen. Emperor Charles was exalted above all the Frankish kings who had preceded him in wealth and glory, honor and title. He was the first emperor of Frankish descent.

In the year 802 the most devout Emperor Charles remembered his mercy toward the poor who lived throughout the empire and were unable to obtain justice fully. He did not wish to send his vassals from the palace to administer justice to the poor in exchange for gifts. Instead, he chose archbishops, other bishops, and abbots, together with dukes and counts, who had no need to accept gifts from the innocent. He sent them throughout the kingdom to administer justice to churches, widows, orphans, the poor, and the entire people.

In October he convened a universal synod at Aachen. There he ordered the bishops, together with the priests and deacons, to reread all the canons prescribed by the holy synod and the decrees of the pontiffs, and he commanded that they be fully handed down before all the bishops, priests, and deacons.

Similarly, at the holy synod he gathered all the abbots and monks who were present. They held an assembly among themselves, read the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, and presented it, with its teachings, in the presence of the abbots and monks.

Then a general command was issued to all bishops, abbots, priests, deacons, and the entire choir of clerics: each person was to live in his own place according to the constitutions of the holy Fathers, whether in bishoprics, monasteries, or throughout the churches. The canons were to live according to the canons, and whatever faults or negligences appeared among the clergy or people were to be corrected according to the authority of the canons. Whatever had been done contrary to the Rule of Saint Benedict in monasteries or by monks was to be corrected according to that Rule.

He also ordered that every bishop throughout his kingdom or empire, together with his priests, should perform the office as the Roman Church chants it. He further ordered that schools for singers be established in suitable places. Likewise, in monasteries observing the Rule of Saint Benedict, the monks were to perform the office as the Rule teaches.

While this synod was being held [Note: read: *ut ipsa synodus facta est*, “while that synod was being held”], the emperor gathered the dukes, counts, and the rest of the Christian people together with the legislators. He caused all the laws of his kingdom to be handed down and corrected, and ordered that wherever the law needed amendment, it should be written down.

The judges were to judge according to written law and were not to accept gifts. Thus all people in his kingdom, poor and rich alike, were to have justice.

In the year 803, Emperor Charles celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen, held an assembly at Mainz, and that same year remained without warfare. In those days Abulaz, son of [Col. 1429B] Axam, ruled over the Saracens in Spain. For when Axa died, this Abulaz, his son, succeeded him in the kingdom, and did evil as his father and grandfather had done. While he was reigning in Spain, Emperor Charles sent his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, to besiege and capture the city of Barcelona. Having gathered an army from Aquitaine, Gascony, Burgundy, Provence, and Gothia, he sent them ahead of him to besiege the city. They departed, surrounded the city with the army, and besieged it for seven months; and they captured the king of that city, named Sathon. When bread had run out in the city and the city was already on the point of being captured, they sent to King Louis asking him to come to Barcelona, because the city was now about to fall, so that, once it had been captured, the victory might be credited to his name. The aforesaid Louis came to the city, and the city was handed over into his power. He established a garrison and military equipment there; but the king of that city, Sathon, bound in fetters, he sent to his father, Emperor Charles, in Francia. He himself returned to his own land in peace and triumph.

[Col. 1429C] In the year 805, Emperor Charles sent his son Charles, the king, with a large army against the Euhuvidines [Note: [Col. 1429D] Moiss., Windones.], and another army with Aulfo and Wuerinarius—that is, with the Bavarians. He sent a third force with the Saxons against Huvernofelda and Melchion [Note: [Col. 1429D] Moiss., Werinefelda and Dervelion.]; there they fought against their king, named Semela, and defeated him. He gave two sons as pledges of his loyalty. Then they proceeded against Fergunna and came to the river called Araga [Note: [Col. 1429D] Moiss., Agaru.], these three armies together. From there they came to Camburg, and laid waste that region around the Elbe. Afterwards King Charles returned victorious to his father in Francia. A fourth army, with a large fleet of ships, proceeded into the Elbe and reached Magdeburg; there they devastated the region of Genevara [Note: [Col. 1429D] Moiss., Gencuvanam.]. Afterwards they returned to their own country.

In the year 806, William, formerly a count, came to the monastery of Aniane, which had been built in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of his glorious [Col. 1429D] mother, the ever-virgin, with all his gifts of gold and silver and precious garments. He gave himself to Christ, intending to serve him for the whole of his life. Without delay he allowed his hair to be cut off; indeed, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, after laying aside his garments woven with gold, he assumed the habit of Christ’s worshipers, and rejoiced to be enrolled as quickly as possible among their number. In the same year Emperor Charles celebrated Easter at Neumagen, and sent his son Charles, the king, against the Thuringians [Note: [Col. 1429D] Moiss., Buringa.], to a place called Walada [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., Waladala.]. There he held a great assembly, and from there [Col. 1430A] sent his troops beyond the Elbe. He himself moved his army beyond the Saale, against Huverenaveldo [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., Guercaehveldo.]. There the proud king Melito [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., Nusito.], who ruled among the Siurbi, was killed. Afterwards he returned to the Elbe, ravaged those regions, and destroyed their cities. The other kings of that people came to him, promised that they would serve the lordly and pious emperor, and handed over hostages as he wished. King Charles ordered them to build two cities: one on the northern side of the Elbe, opposite Magdeburg; the other on the eastern side of the Saale, at a place called Balla [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., Halla.]. Then he returned to his father in Francia. In those days Albinus, also called Alcuin, the deacon, flourished in Francia.

In the year 807, Emperor Charles proceeded to the palace at Ingelheim. There he held an assembly with the bishops, counts, and other faithful men, and ordered them to administer justice in his kingdom. Afterwards he gave them permission to return to their own lands and sit in peace, and to give thanks to God for their peace and concord. That year he remained without warfare.

In the year 808, Emperor Charles sent his son Charles into Saxony beyond the Elbe, against those Slavs called the Linai, and devastated a very large part of their region; but some men from our side also fell there. Finally, war was undertaken against the Northmen, who are called Danes. At first they practiced piracy; later, with a larger fleet, they ravaged the coasts of Gaul and Germany. Their king, Godfrey, was so inflated with empty hope that he promised himself power over all Germany, and regarded Frisia and Saxony no differently from his own provinces. He had already brought his neighbors, the Abodrites, under his authority and had made them pay tribute to him. He even boasted that he would come to Aachen, where the king’s court was held, with the greatest forces; and his words, vain though they were, were not wholly disbelieved. Indeed, it was thought that he would undertake something of the kind, had he not been forestalled by a sudden death. For he was killed by one of his own retainers [Col. 1430C] and hastened the end both of his own life and of the war he had begun.

In the year 809, Emperor Charles held court at the palace of Aachen. That summer he sent his troops to the marches, and some of the Saxons among them came beyond the Elbe and, together with our Huninidi [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., Guinildinis.] called Semeldinc, destroyed a city, Connoburg.

In the year 810, during the summer, Emperor Charles proceeded with his son, King Charles, beyond the Rhine against Saxony, to a place called Ferdia. That same summer King Pepin of the Lombards, son of Emperor Charles, died. Charles appointed Bernard, Pepin’s son, king over Italy in his father’s place.

In the year 811, Emperor Charles sent an army of Franks and Saxons beyond the Elbe against those Slavs who are called the Linai and the Bethenzr [Note: [Col. 1430D] Moiss., and Bethelelereti.]. They devastated those regions and built a fortress called Abochi. There was also a great slaughter of the Normans. That same year King Charles, son of Emperor Charlemagne, died [Col. 1430D].

In the year 812, Emperor Charles sent three divisions against those Slavs called the Huvilti. One army came with them against the Abodrites, while two came to meet it at the march. Those Wilti also gave their right hands, offered hostages, and promised that they would give to Emperor Charles’s party. Afterwards the people returned to their own lands.

Up to this point the first author has written. What follows, however, appears to have been added by some monk of Aniane, who continued this work and first inserts a very extensive excerpt from Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne, which [Col. 1431A] was published by Chesnius in volume II, p. 99 [Note: [Col. 1431D] Patrologia, volume XCVII.], beginning with these words: “These are the wars which the most powerful king waged for forty-seven years,” and continuing through page 103. On page 100, line 17, after the words “By such an admonition he forbade,” the following is inserted:

“He did the same on the southern side, near the seashore, in the county of Maguelonne: he built a church in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Mary, the perpetual Virgin and Mother of God. He furnished its basilicas and adorned them with gold and silver. Since he could not obtain columns and marble for its construction, he ordered them to be brought with great care from the city of Nîmes. He also ordered his treasures, gathered from each of his kingdoms, to be brought to the monastery of Aniane. Likewise, he set up three wooden crosses of the Lord and constructed many great works in the same place.”

In the year 813 from the incarnation of the Lord, and the forty-sixth year of Emperor Charles, the most pious emperor held court at the palace of Aachen. There he held a great council with the Frankish bishops, abbots, and priests, and decreed that four synods should be held: one at the city of Mainz [Col. 1431B], another at Rheims, a third at Tours, and a fourth at the city of Arles [Note: [Col. 1431D] Some add a fifth, held at Chalon.]. He ordered that whatever they defined at each synod should be reported at the appointed assembly, and so it was done.

In that same year, in the month of February [Note: [Col. 1432D] Moiss., September.], the aforesaid Emperor Charles held a great assembly of the people at the palace of Aachen. From his whole kingdom and empire, bishops, abbots, counts, priests, deacons, and the senate of the Franks gathered before the emperor at Aachen. There they established forty-six chapters concerning matters necessary for the Church of God and the Christian people.

At the end of his life, when he was already weighed down by illness and old age, he summoned to himself his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, the only one of Hildegard’s sons who remained alive. After ceremonially assembling from the whole kingdom of the Franks and from his entire empire all the leading men—counts, princes, dukes, bishops, abbots, monks, priests, deacons [Col. 1431C], and the whole senate of the Franks—with the counsel of them all, he appointed Louis his associate in the whole kingdom and heir to his imperial title. He handed the empire over to him by means of a golden crown, while the people acclaimed: “LONG LIVE EMPEROR LOUIS!” After placing the diadem on his head, he ordered him to be called emperor and Augustus. This decision was received by those who were present with great approval and joy.

The emperor Charles himself blessed God, saying: “Blessed are you, Lord my God, who have today granted that a son from my own seed should sit upon my throne while my eyes behold it.” The father instructed him to keep the Lord’s commandment in all things. He handed over the kingdom to him and entrusted to him his sons Drogo, Theodoric, and Hugh. When he had completed everything, he dismissed each person to depart to his own place.

Emperor Charles himself returned to the palace at Aachen. For this act appeared to him to have been divinely inspired for the benefit of the kingdom; it increased his majesty and struck no small terror into foreign nations [Col. 1431D]. After sending his son to Aquitaine, he himself, according to his custom, although exhausted by old age, went hunting not far from the palace at Aachen.

In the year 814 from the incarnation of the Lord, the forty-seventh year of Emperor Charles, counting from the beginning of his reign, the Northmen came with ships into Frisia, wrought great harm there, and captured men, women, and much booty. In that same year, after this affair had been completed, during the remainder of the autumn, and so forth, as in Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne, p. 104, line 9, to the end.

But in the division made by Emperor Charles in the year 811, after the words “or judged its use necessary for himself,” our manuscript copy adds:

“He reserved one portion for himself, which he gave to Benedict, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Savior of Aniane, namely: [Col. 1432A] a cross of the Lord with jewels; gold cloths woven with jewels; golden belts similarly adorned with jewels; golden or silver chalices; and offertories with little patens and offering vessels decorated with gold and jewels. Among the other gifts he gave him a golden reliquary containing relics of all the apostles. Among these he gave him a royal scepter of ivory, exceedingly wondrous, and many other gifts, the enumeration of which would be lengthy. To Ardoni, also called Smaragdus, a religious monk, he gave a ringing stone tablet, like bronze.”

“After his death or voluntary …,” and so forth. Here it should be noted that, in place of the words on p. 106, “And the other, marked by a round form bearing the image of the city of Rome, should be given to the bishop of the church of Ravenna,” the manuscript codex reads: “The other, figured in a round form with the likeness of the city of Rome, should be given to the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ in the monastery of Aniane.”

Among the witnesses to this division, the first of the abbots named is Benedict; after him come Hirminon, George, Theobald, Adalelmus, and Lautfredus [Col. 1432B].

In the year 814, Louis, the most pious emperor, after the death of his father, the most glorious Emperor Charles, sat upon his throne at the palace of Aachen and celebrated Easter there. Having received his father’s treasures, he made a great almsgiving for his father and distributed them among churches, monasteries, and the poor, just as his father had ordered.

In the year mentioned above, the emperor Louis—that is, in the first year of his empire—removed Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, because of the fame of his life and holiness, and made him dwell near Aachen, the royal seat, in the forest of Ardennes. The aforesaid abbot, before departing for Francia, appointed in his place in the monastery of Aniane an abbot named Smaragdus.

In that same year bishops, abbots, counts, dukes, women, and widows came to the emperor, and he spoke with them about necessary matters and about the welfare of the holy Church. In that place he ordered that women who had been reduced to servitude should not remain so, but should receive their freedom [Col. 1432C]. Bernard, son of Pepin, king of the Lombards, also came to him. The lord Emperor Louis received him kindly, rewarded him, and sent him back to his own country. He also organized the marches everywhere, placing garrisons wherever necessary along the seacoast. That year he wintered at Aachen.

In the year 816, Emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen. That summer, having gathered a large army of Franks, Burgundians, Alamanni, and Bavarians, he entered Saxony and came to Paderborn. There King Bernard of the Lombards came to him with an army. The emperor held a great assembly there and sent his troops wherever necessary, to the marches, the garrisons, and the seacoasts. Afterwards he returned to Francia, to the palace at Aachen.

On the third day before the Kalends of August, he held a great council at Aachen and appointed two of his sons kings, Pepin and Lothar: Pepin over Aquitaine and Gascony, and Lothar over Bavaria. At that synod the lord Emperor Louis decreed that throughout his kingdom monks should live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, and that canons should live according to the authority of the canons. He also ordered his envoys and counts to administer justice in his kingdom. If any men had been unjustly deprived of their parents’ inheritance through the greed of counts or wealthy men, they were to compel its return. Likewise, if any men had been unjustly reduced to servitude in a city, they were to receive their freedom again. That same year the Gascons rebelled against the emperor.

In the year 818, the most pious Emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen. During the summer King Bernard of the Lombards came to him. In those days the apostolic lord Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, departed from this world, and the lord Stephen succeeded him in the priesthood [Col. 1433A].

That same year Pope Stephen came to Emperor Louis in Francia and found him at the city of Rheims. He brought him a golden crown. The emperor received him with great honor; Stephen blessed the emperor, placed the golden crown upon his head, and the lord emperor rewarded him with many gifts. Thus Stephen returned to Rome, to his own see.

The most pious Emperor Louis departed from Rheims for the palace of Compiègne and held counsel with his bishops, abbots, and counts. Then he returned to the palace of Aachen, the royal seat, and wintered there. The aforesaid Pope Stephen, after returning to Rome, departed from this world in that same year. The Gascons, however, chose Garcia Muci as their prince in rebellion; but in the second year he lost both his life and the principality which he held by fraud.

[Col. 1433B] In the year 821, Emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen. That same year Benedict, of blessed memory, Witiza, the religious abbot of the monastery of Aniane, died on the third day before the Ides of February, in the ninth year of Emperor Louis’s reign.

That summer he ordered a great assembly of peoples to be gathered at Aachen, the royal seat, from his entire kingdom and empire: bishops, abbots, counts, and the elders of the Franks. He revealed to them the plan of his counsel, which he had conceived: to appoint one of his sons emperor. He had three sons by Queen Ermengard: the first was named Lothar, the second Pepin, and the third Louis. Then all the people approved that, while he was still alive, he should appoint one of his sons emperor, just as his father Charles had appointed him.

For three days all the people fasted, and a litany was performed. Afterwards the aforesaid emperor chose Lothar, who was the elder, as emperor, and handed him a golden crown, while the people acclaimed and said: “LONG LIVE EMPEROR LOTHAR!” [Col. 1433C] Great joy arose among the people on that day, and the emperor himself blessed the Lord, saying: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who has today granted that one seated upon my throne should be seen by my eyes.”

He had a fourth son by a concubine, named Arnulf, to whom his father gave the city of Sens in the county. When Bernard, king of Italy, heard what had been done, he conceived a very evil plan and wished to rise up against the emperor and his son and usurp the empire by tyranny.

When this was discovered, the emperor immediately ordered [Perhaps: sent] messengers throughout his entire kingdom and empire, so that all might gather together and occupy all the passes into Italy. This was done. When Bernard heard this, the Lord struck him with fear, together with all who had agreed with him. They were captured by the army which the emperor had sent ahead of him, and the captives, together with the king, were brought to the emperor, who was at Chalon-sur-Saône, above the river Saône.

The aforesaid king was then placed under guard with Count Achiteus, who had been the author of the wicked plot, and with the others who had agreed with him, and they were taken to Aachen. Afterwards the emperor held a great assembly of the Franks and laid this case before them, to see what his faithful men would judge concerning him and those who had consented to rise up against the emperor.

They unanimously judged all of them worthy of death. But the most pious [Col. 1434B] emperor spared their lives and ordered King Bernard’s eyes to be put out. When this had been done, Bernard died on the third day. Achiteus likewise had his eyes put out, as did his other companions.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, who had also been the author of the wicked plot, was judged in a synod of bishops and abbots, together with other priests. Both he himself and all the bishops, abbots, and other clerics who had been partners in this wicked plan were judged by all to have fallen from their own rank. This was carried out; some were also sent into exile.

As for his brothers born of concubines—namely Drogo, Theodoric, and Hugh, whom their father had entrusted to him—the emperor ordered them to become clerics and sent each of them to a monastery. Then the kingdom was at peace, freed from anger.

In the year 838, Emperor Louis celebrated Easter at Aachen. During the summer he entered Britain with a large army. After the king of that land had been killed, the elders of the Britons came and surrendered themselves to him [Col. 1434C]. Having received hostages, he returned to his own country in triumphant victory. His army, which he had sent toward the East, likewise returned to the emperor in triumph.

In the year 840, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of the aforesaid emperor, the most pious Emperor Louis died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction. His sons reigned after him in great glory. Amen.

# Third Section of the Appendix to the Works of Blessed Charlemagne—Poetry

[Col. 1433]

[Note: [Col. 1433D] I do not dare to determine who the author of this poem is. The codex from which it was copied has, on its final page, the following signs preceding these verses: “fer helpere.” Hence a later writer conjectured and also attributed to it these words: “Ferius Helpericus, author of the following poem.” I remain uncertain, and incline more toward Alcuin—not because of those marks, which I do not think belong to this poem, but because it is established that Alcuin wrote about the deeds of Charlemagne. This is attested, among others, by the heretic Bale [Balaeus] in his catalogue of writers of Britain.

Perhaps, however, this poem is either a part or a fragment of that larger work; for I do not believe it to be the whole work. Its style and mode of expression do not differ from Alcuin’s vein, as those who know Alcuin’s poems will recognize. Moreover, why does it call Charles “David” several times? This title was so familiar to Alcuin that, when writing to Charles, he often omitted the name Charles and called him King David.

Nor does the chronology contradict this attribution. Pope Leo III came to Charles in the year 799, while Alcuin was still alive, since he did not die until 804. At the beginning the author himself indicates that he approaches writing already weary and that he has often tested fortune; nevertheless, on the occasion of so illustrious a subject, he had once more to undertake the risk of writing.

Certainly he describes the pope’s arrival to Charles and the Franks with such piety and devotion, and so fully recounts the honors paid to the pope, that even on this evidence the poem may reasonably be believed to have proceeded from the most religious workshop of Alcuin. Finally, the author of this poem seems to have personally witnessed everything he writes. Therefore no reason remains why anyone should perhaps refer it to that Helpericus of whom Trithemius writes in his book On the Illustrious Men of Germany:

“Helpericus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the Order of the blessed Father Benedict, was himself highly learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular literature. He was a very celebrated philosopher, astronomer, and poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, distinguished no less in life than in learning. He wrote many excellent little works in both verse and prose, but few of them have reached our hands. For I saw and read only a very distinguished book which he published On Ecclesiastical Computation, and another entitled On Music, as well as certain poems. He flourished at the same time as Hermannus Contractus, in the year of the Lord 1040.”

Canisius.—This poem is not by Helpericus, as Canisius observes, since its author must have been an eyewitness and must have personally seen what he narrates. But for the same reason it is not by Alcuin. For it is clear from his letters that, already worn out by old age, he did not wish to follow the emperor into Germany, and wrote letters excusing himself on that account.

Moreover, this poem cannot be identical with Alcuin’s book On the Deeds of Charlemagne, which Balaeus mentions. These verses contain nothing except a description of the hunt and the emperor’s meeting with Leo III. Yet the little work does not appear mutilated, but complete in its parts. Furthermore, Balaeus implies that Alcuin wrote the Deeds of Charlemagne not in verse but in prose.

Alcuin and the author of this poem agree only in being contemporaries, in being deeply devoted to Charlemagne, and in both having frequently violated prosody.

J. Basnagius.]

## Poem by an Unknown Author Concerning Charlemagne and the Arrival of Leo, Supreme Pontiff, to the Same Charles

(From Canisius, *Ancient Readings*)

[Col. 1433D]

Again the heavy anchor warns me onto uncertain paths:

to spread the sails, to entrust the fleet to uncertain winds—

he whose weary limbs have survived two storms—

and orders exhausted arms to prepare themselves for new wars,

and the victorious hand to rise again to the burdened oars,

where the light breeze calls us to cross the deep

by gentle blasts, testing the sea’s waves with fleets,

[Col. 1435A] to stretch across the waters toward unknown lands

with swift course, and to strike the precipitous reefs by swimming.

The gentle East Wind moves the sails with trembling breezes,

forcing me now to hasten rapidly toward the heights,

where Europe’s lofty beacon flashes with its light.

King Charles scatters his glorious name to the stars.

Look: the sun shines with its rays; thus at last David

illuminates the lands with the great power of his piety.

Yet one thing separates these two by variation,

and they are often distinguished by an altered succession:

clouds sometimes cover the one with a stormy course,

but no storms can ever alter the other.

The one lacks his own light for twelve hours;

the other preserves his light with an everlasting star.

He shines in joyful peace, overflowing with piety,

and knows no fall that could dim his pious light.

With cheerful countenance he shines; with ever-serene brow

he gleams, surpassing Phoebus by the eternal light of piety,

scattering his name from sunset to sunrise:

Charles, mighty in arms, victorious, pious, and triumphant.

The king surpasses all kings throughout the world in goodness;

he is more just than all and stands more powerful than all.

He ennobles commanders and counts with great affection;

he is gracious toward the just and shows himself cheerful to everyone.

A worshiper of justice, he loves all who practice it;

just, he offers himself as an example for all.

He himself goes first along the path where he wishes everyone to follow,

and attempts an easy road which all may rightly follow.

With good reason he restrains the unjust with harsh reins,

and places a heavy yoke upon the necks of the proud.

By divine deeds he urges them to learn justice;

he presses impious necks, bound in rigid chains,

and teaches them to fulfill the commands of the King enthroned on high.

What a light mind forbids and a perverse spirit persuades them to do,

that at least they may desire to fulfill when compelled by fear—

what the wretched rebels had earlier refused to do willingly.

Those who had long before resisted it in their savage fashion eagerly strive to practice it, urged on by fear;

the impious man, compelled by pious fear, becomes pious.

From here he raises the humble and lifts the lowly on high;

he honors the bowed necks, raising them to lofty summits.

The just king draws submissive faces toward lofty steps;

he crushes proud necks, subjecting those who seek exalted things.

And as much as the wretched strive to rise on high,

[Col. 1436A] by just deserts he makes them descend again to the depths.

Charles is vigorous in intellect, wise, and moderate;

distinguished in zeal, he shines with an astute mind,

and deservedly bears the name Charles throughout the world.

He is a dear light to peoples and wisdom to the lands;

at once the ornament of his servants and every honor,

he stands as the glory of the people and the supreme hope

of his name. His origin once promised him to the world,

as brilliant in intellect as he is renowned for his splendid merits.

Powerful, prudent, knowledgeable, and moderate, he shines throughout the world;

illustrious, approachable, learned, good, capable, honorable,

mild, outstanding, just, pious, renowned, a hero,

king, ruler, venerable summit, splendid Augustus,

distinguished arbiter, judge, merciful toward the needy,

peaceful, generous, diligent, cheerful, and gracious.

He stands forth as an exceedingly brilliant teacher of grammatical art.

Never in any age had there been so distinguished a reader;

he flourishes as an eminent teacher in the art of rhetoric,

the highest summit among kings, and likewise the greatest sophist in the world.

[Col. 1436B] He is also an orator, powerful in eloquent speech,

for his celebrated words surpass those of renowned Cato,

and in the sweetness of eloquence he conquers great Marcus;

even eloquent Homer yields before his words,

and in the art of dialectic he surpasses the ancient masters.

He also discerns the other four arts which rightly follow,

as their teacher, by a similar understanding of things.

Learned in these as well, the king flourishes in the same manner.

He alone has deserved to traverse the whole path of learning,

to penetrate hidden ways and know all mysteries,

with God revealing the sequence of things from their beginning.

For he has discovered every path of learning and every

Arosopacum [Note: [Col. 1436D] Read, probably: “the obscure path of art.”], every entrance, and all secret hidden words.

He alone, that pious man, has deserved to receive the talents,

and is preferred to all teachers in every art.

Clearly, just as he surpasses other kings in the height

of imperial power, so he is placed above all in learning.

Who could express the praises of so great a king?

Who, unskilled in speech, could think himself able to recount

the [Col. 1436C] deeds of the prince, when all aged poets are surpassed

and King Charles, head of the world, surpasses my intellect

by his most just deeds—Charles, head of the world, love and glory of the people,

venerable summit of Europe, best father, hero,

Augustus, powerful also in the city where a second Rome

[Col. 1437A] rises in fresh bloom to great heights

with immense mass, touching the stars with lofty walls and domes [Note: [Col. 1437D] This word should certainly be divided and read *Mole tholis*. A *tholus* is the summit of a temple or roof. Sedulius says in *Paschale*, book I:

“Where the royal palace shines forth

with golden domes.”

Alcuin himself says a little farther below:

“The foundations enclose the halls with lofty domes.”

There, lofty domes are always meant.]

The pious Charles stands far away upon the citadel, marking out each place

and arranging the lofty walls of the Rome to come.

Here he orders a forum to stand, and a sacred senate according to law,

where they may undertake the rights of the people and the sacred commands.

A laboring crowd presses on; one group, suited to columns,

cuts the hard stone and builds the citadel upward.

Others strive to roll the rocks upward with their hands;

they dig out harbors and establish the deep foundations

of the theater, and enclose halls with lofty domes.

Here others labor to discover hot springs;

they uncover, in a massive structure, baths boiling of their own accord,

construct beautiful seats with marble steps,

and a spring, with the heat of violently boiling water,

does not cease; it leads streams into every part

of the city. Here others strive to build

a pleasant temple for the eternal king with immense effort:

the sacred house rises to the stars with polished walls.

[Col. 1437B] Some, high above, ardently place stones upon the highest citadel,

firmly joining the marble with interlocking bonds;

another group stands upon the steps, receiving what the bearers bring.

Some supply burdens and very hard stones with eager hands;

others climb up and roll rocks toward the walls;

everywhere they carry enormous bundles, their necks bent backward,

and, exhausted beneath the heavy weight, lay them down from their shoulders.

Carts make a din; a vast crash strikes the air.

A noise arises; a great clamor grows in the city,

and the busy crowd, spread throughout the city,

comes and goes, zealously gathering building material

for lofty Rome.

Here others prepare tools, sharpening useful iron

with which marble can be sculpted and stone cut.

The work seethes, just as bees in summer, not forgetful

of the food supplies for the coming winter,
