[Note: [Col. 1437D] The passage is corrupt.] gather with their mouths, plucking little flowers,

and fly through the waters and thyme with buzzing wings.

Some settle upon flowers and strive to return

with their captured prey, revisiting their fragrant camps;

others strive to raise their offspring to maturity,

or arrange nectar-bearing honeycombs in orderly rows,

packing dewy honey into their curved legs.

In no other way does the broad crowd of Franks move about the city.

Not far away is a lofty grove and pleasant green land,

a wood verdant beside the city and fresh meadows crossed by streams,

occupying the center, surrounded by many walls.

Here every kind of bird flies around the river;

on the banks they sit, searching out pasture with their beaks.

Not far away, in the middle, they plunge into the river,

and now also hasten toward the banks with headlong speed.

Beside these swelling mounds a herd of deer feeds;

through the long and pleasant pasture of the banks

the doe runs here and there with timid step.

The open foliage leaves the place free; everywhere every kind of wild beast

lies hidden in these woods, among the shadowy groves.

Here the venerable father Charles, the hero,

is accustomed to practice pleasant games across the meadows,

to drive the wild beasts with dogs, and with trembling arrows

[Col. 1437D] to strike down the horned throng beneath the dark tree.

When Phoebus first rises with honorable rays [Note: [Col. 1437D] Here the *Maicampus* is being described, famous in the time of Charlemagne and in later centuries. For in the month of May the leading men of the kingdom were summoned not only for hunting but also to deliberate concerning the kingdom; this custom was common among many peoples. Among the Romans, too, there was a very celebrated *Maiuma*, perhaps so called from the month of May, although stricter critics object that it was named from the village of Maiuma near Gaza and from *Maiim*, that is, “waters.” The *Maiuma* of the pagans was dedicated to Venus; people indulged in dances, entertainments, feasts, and pleasure. Prostitutes and rites devised to arouse lust were especially present. Therefore Arcadius, who ordered the *Maiuma* to be celebrated again, wished people to abstain from sacrifices and the pleasures of Venus. BASN.],

and his fiery-haired radiance surveys the mountains,

touching the precipitous rocks and the highest peaks,

the beloved young men hurry from every part of the royal household,

and gather to wait upon the noblemen at the very threshold.

A din arises; a vast shout rises in the city.

From above, from the lofty roof, the bronze-covered buildings

answer; a distinctive [Note: [Col. 1438D] Perhaps: “settles.”] clamor rings into the air.

Horse neighs to horse; the foot-soldiers shout together,

and each servant in turn is summoned by his own token
to his lord and follows the one who calls him.

Here a horse adorned with trappings, destined to receive

the generous king upon its back, rejoices beneath heavy gold and metal.

Standing, it moves its eager head and longs to go through the high mountains.

At last he emerges, surrounded by a throng;

Europe’s venerable beacon reveals itself to the air;

he shines with an extraordinary countenance and flashes with his face.

For King Charles’ noble head is encircled with precious gold,

[Col. 1438B] and he rises above all others with his lofty shoulders.

The young men carry broad hunting spears with sharpened iron,

and nets joined by a fourfold line along the border.

They lead eager dogs, bound by their collars,

mastiffs ready for the prey and fierce in mouth.

Now Charles, the father of the exalted realm, has left

the sacred threshold of the temple; soon the leaders’ camps

and the foremost counts begin to move.

The trumpets of the lofty city’s gates are thrown open;

horns resound; a mighty crash fills the halls,
Source/review notes: Inherited poetic lacunae and corrupt readings remain explicit; every supplied editorial note is retained.

And the young men rush headlong at a gallop toward the shores.

From there the queen, long delayed in her proud chamber,

comes forth, with a great throng accompanying her:

Luitgardis, the most beautiful wife of Charles by name.  
[Note: [Col. 1438D] Whom Alcuin at one point calls his daughter. BASN.]

Her shining neck gleams, fashioned in rosy color,

and the rich purple garment yields to her hair bound with ribbons;

her white temples are encircled with purple bands,

golden threads fasten her cloak, and a beryl is inserted

into her headpiece, a diadem radiant with bright metal.

Her garment too shines with purple, double-dyed and fine,

[Col. 1438C] and her gleaming neck is adorned with various precious stones.

Surrounded by beautiful maidens, she divides the ranks.

Among the high-born men the queen rejoices on her splendid horse

and, burning brightly, shines forth amid the young men.

All the remaining royal children, most beautiful of youth,

await her at the doors, accompanied by splendid companies.

At last Charles too, resembling his father in bearing and face,

attempts to come forth, renowned by his father’s name,

and, as is customary, tires the back of a fierce horse.

Next follows Pepin, named after his grandfather;

he restores the public achievements of his own father,

the warlike, spirited hero, strongest in arms.

He bears himself as a splendid leader among his servants,

shining on high, surrounded by countless companies,

carried on an excellent horse, his face and features flashing,

his handsome temples encircled with gleaming metal.

A crowd of companions rushes around in whirling movement;

the senate strives to pour out through the wide-open gates,

[Col. 1438D] amid great murmuring and tumult.

The harsh horns sound; the dogs fill the air

with the eager barking of their mouths; a thunderous crash strikes the fiery stars.

[Col. 1439A] Then follows the glittering procession of maidens.

Rhodrud, before the others, borne upon a swift horse,
shines and first takes her place in the ordered procession.  
[Note: [Col. 1439D] A daughter of Charlemagne, betrothed to Constantine, emperor of the Greeks; deceived by Irene’s machinations, she died a virgin in 810. BASN.]

A purple amethyst-colored ribbon, flashing with the light

of gems arranged in various rows, is woven into her snowy hair.

A golden crown of precious gems encircles her head

and a clasp fastens her beautiful covering beneath her chin.

Next among the maidenly choirs and the following crowd

shines Berta, accompanied by many maidens.  
[Note: [Col. 1439D] Charlemagne’s second daughter, married to Angilbert. ID.]

With manly voice, spirit, bearing, and flashing countenance,

she bears her father’s mouth, character, eyes, and heart.

Her noble head is encircled by a golden diadem;

golden threads mingle with her snowy hair.

Indeed, they bear around her milk-white neck a precious marten-fur collar;

her garment is adorned beautifully with various gems

and flashes with a rich array of jewels.

The coverings are decorated with gold plates and chrysolites.

After these follows Gisala, flashing with radiant whiteness,  
[Note: [Col. 1439D] Charlemagne’s third daughter by Hildegard, who professed the monastic life. ID.]

[Col. 1439B] accompanied by a maidenly choir; the golden child gleams.

The woman shines beneath a melocine-colored covering;

soft veils glitter with purple threads.

Her voice, face, and hair flash with radiant light;

her splendid neck gleams, inflamed with rosy blush.

Her hand appears fashioned of silver; her golden forehead shines,

and the lights of her eyes surpass great Phoebus.

Joyfully the maiden mounts her swift horse.

The proud horse rolls foaming bits between its teeth.

On one side men accompany her, on the other she is surrounded by maidens;

an innumerable troop of horses resounds all around.

Loaded with these splendid adornments, leaving the lofty palace,

the modest maiden follows the footsteps of the pious king.

Next Rhodaid gleams, adorned with many metals.  
[Note: Counted among the illegitimate daughters of Charlemagne.]

The woman advances before the rejoicing procession with rapid steps.

Her breast, neck, and hair shine, varied with precious stones;

silken cloaks hang from her beautiful shoulders.

A jeweled crown is set upon her shining head;

a golden pin fastens her cloak with gem-studded bosses.

The beautiful maiden Rhodaidis is carried upon a splendid horse,

[Col. 1439C] in which stags usually lie hidden beneath shaggy hides.

Meanwhile Theodrada enters, her face flashing.  
[Note: Born from Charlemagne’s wife Fastrada.]

She shines with a beautiful brow, and gold yields to her hair.

Her beautiful necks gleam with foreign emeralds;

her feet, hands, mouth, cheeks, and neck shine radiantly.

Her clear eyes flash with flames beneath a tranquil brow.

Her hyacinth-colored cloaks gleam with mixed purple spots.

The maiden is splendidly adorned with a Sophoclean cothurnus.

A crowd of maidens resounds around her in a dense procession,

and a beautiful cohort of noblewomen shines in a long line.

The lovely maiden sits upon a snow-white horse

and, the pious daughter of King Charles, is borne on a swift horse.

Leaving the sacred palaces, she prepares to enter the grove.

Hildrud claims for herself the rear part of the procession.  
[Note: Another daughter of Charles, whom he had by Fastrada.]

By lot it is assigned to her; thereafter comes the final order of the senate.  
[Note: Perhaps “senate’s.”]

The maiden herself shines in the middle of the procession.

She regulates her exposed path with measured steps.

Beside the shore, the renowned company advances  
[Note: [Col. 1440D] The manuscript reads *plens*; perhaps *gens*, “people.”]
filled with the passion for hunting, and the whole army

[Col. 1439D] now joins it and is present. Soon, bound in iron,

all the packs of ravenous dogs fall loose; they seek

the deep lairs of beasts, properly tracking their prey by keen scent,

and the eager mastiffs scour the dense thickets.

All spread out and wandering through the shadowy woodland

strive to find their bloody prey among the trees.

A horseman surrounds the forest; against the fugitives

a crowd prepares itself. A tawny boar is discovered in the valley.

At once the mounted men rush into the grove and pursue it with shouts.

[Col. 1440A] The agile mastiffs strive to drive the fleeing prey,

and, scattered, run through the shadowy silences of the forest.

One silently flies swiftly after the properly tracked quarry;

another fills the empty air with barking.

One wanders deceived by scent among the shadowed thickets;

another circles here and there through the woodland.

[Note: So the manuscript.]

One has seen it; another senses by smell the fleeing prey.

A din arises; a shriek rises from the depths of the woods,

and a great trumpet inflames the mastiffs to battle

[Note: For *acria*, “harsh” or “rugged.”]

The dreadful boar, wherever it goes with threatening tusk,

shakes leaves from the tall trees all around.

It flees through the vast spaces and, with rapid course through pathless places,

makes its way, growling, and [reading uncertain: “wears down” or “holds”]

the lofty summits of the mountain.

Exhausted by running, panting, it comes to a halt on tired feet.

Now it prepares the weapons of death against the dogs and their pursuing crowd,

and with its terrible mouth whirls the swift mastiffs about.

Soon Father Charles himself flies into the midst of the pack

and, swifter than winged birds, pierces the beast’s breast

with his sword, dipping the cold iron into its vitals.

[Col. 1440B] It collapses, vomiting life mixed with blood,

and, dying, rolls itself about in the yellow sand.

From the high mountain the royal offspring watches this.

Soon Charles orders another quarry to be stirred up,

and thus addresses his companions in clear words:

“Fortune has granted us this joyful day

and supports our undertakings with favorable omens.

Therefore, all of you, encourage this labor,

practice the hunt, and apply yourselves to it willingly.”

Hardly had the hero spoken when the troop roared down from the high mountain.

The nobles rush here and there back into the grove,

swiftly striving to drive out the beasts.

The renowned father Charles himself flies ahead,

carrying in his hands a missile of iron;

he lays low innumerable companies of boars,

and many bodies of beasts fall prostrate everywhere.

Then Charles distributes the quarry among all the nobles

and burdens his companions and followers with the heavy spoils.

From there he turns back, returning to the former field,

the leafy grove with its broad openings,

its fresh springs shaded by branches and its cool, dark shade.

[Col. 1440C] Here golden tents stand fixed upon the ground everywhere,

the splendid camps of the commanders shine on every side.

Charles happily prepares a banquet for his companions;

joyful, he summons all the aged fathers in order,

the mature people born in better years,

the youthful commoners as well, and the chaste maidens.

He seats them and then orders Falernian wine to be served at the tables.

Meanwhile the sun sets and darkness soon takes possession of the light,

but their weary limbs long for peaceful sleep.

In his dreams the king sees a sad portent and dreadful apparition:

the supreme Leo of Rome standing before him  
[Note: Namely Leo III, who was persecuted in extraordinary ways by the family of Hadrian. He entered the papacy in the year 795.]

and the pontiff pouring forth mournful tears;

his eyes filthy, his face stained with blood,

his tongue cut out and bearing many horrible wounds.

A cold fear seizes the anxious limbs of Augustus.

He orders three men sent swiftly to the Roman walls

to investigate whether the excellent shepherd is safe

and what the sad dreams might signify.

He marvels and exercises pious, faithful care.

[Col. 1440D] The envoys hasten with rapid steps;

the hero himself returns to Saxony with many thousands.

Armies assemble from different parts of the world,

and allied forces hurry along the steep banks of the Rhine

to subdue the rebellious Saxon people

and cut down the savage nation with freezing iron.

Now from afar they see the lofty summits of the city of Rome,

and the envoys behold from the mountain the theater they desire.

A sadder report suddenly meets them and becomes known:

[Col. 1441A] the apostolic light has fallen in a cruel death,

struck by savage blows. For a fierce and dreadful serpent,

who is accustomed to set united brothers against one another in war

and to scatter the harmful seeds of poisonous venom,

persuaded everyone, their minds blinded, to rage

against the innocent and to slaughter the servants of their mighty lord.

A deadly plague entered their minds and clung to their senses;

their panting breasts conceived the pestilential poison.

They laid snares for the man and prepared his death.

The impious populace armed itself with weapons

against its innocent shepherd and against the mournful killing.

While kindly Pope Leo was passing along his customary route

and proceeding on foot to the sacred thresholds of Saint Lawrence,

the mad populace and senseless, wicked youth  
[Note: [Col. 1441D] Read *vecors* (“senseless”); the editor notes that the poet does not observe quantity very strictly.]
rushed as a whole crowd upon the supreme shepherd,

with clubs and drawn swords,

blindly raging, suddenly stirred by dreadful storms.

With scourges they tortured the sacred limbs of the priest.

In one man’s destruction the fury of many raged.

[Col. 1441B] The executioners pulled apart the two windows in his forehead,

and they cut out his swift-moving tongue from his lacerated body.

The pitiless crowd, infected with black poisons,

thought that it had utterly destroyed the pontiff.

But the father’s healing hand offered remedies to his eyes,

which had been deprived of sight, and restored his face

with a new light.

His pale features and foreign-looking eyes astonished them,

and he unfolded speech with his severed tongue.

The great priest then fled from there with a few companions.

Secretly he made for the city of Spoleto to seek aid.

There he was received with great honor by Duke Winigisus

and heaped with many gifts in due order.

He hears that faithful Franks have been sent into Italy
and that they had not wished to bring the Romans their customary aid,
because, without guilt, they had tortured their own mighty lord

with punishments. Soon he orders the men to come before him

and begins to speak as follows; his tongue, severed shortly below the palate,

[Col. 1441C] was producing calm speech with fluent voice:

“By the dear safety of Charles, I adjure you:
defend me in arms  
[Note: [Col. 1441D] Read *defendatis*, “defend.”]
and lead me, driven from my own territories

and deprived of the honor of my see,

to your mighty king.

Let me behold the face of that eminent prince,

who will examine our actions with just judgment,

avenge our most savage blows,

and, by adding comfort to my life,

lighten my distinguished grief and my groaning.

Come, then, and if your favor toward me is now certain,

rescue me from these lands, men;

present me to David with kindly eyes.

Let no delay now hold us back;

let us cross the frozen Alps with swift courses.”

When Pope Leo had spoken thus, the Frankish cohort mixed with Latins

stood astonished, returning thanks and praises to the Lord,

who had restored new sight to the supreme pontiff

and placed speech, thought lost, within his mouth.

But Germar, in reply, spoke briefly as follows:

[Col. 1441D] “Light, eminent glory of peoples, pleasant illumination,

venerable apostolic shepherd and priest throughout the world,

it is fitting that you command whatever you ponder in your heart;

it is right for us, excellent father, to obey your orders.”

Then they begin their journey joyfully and measure it with swift steps.

They are glad to go to the threshold of great Augustus.

They undertake difficult roads, overcome the harsh path,

and proceed eagerly through different towns.

Countless crowds meet them everywhere as a spectacle,

rejoicing to kiss the sacred feet of the pontiff.

They carry many gifts besides,

and, seeing new eyes in the old face,

they stand astonished  
[Note: Perhaps “they stand amazed”]

and marvel that the severed tongue speaks,

[Col. 1442A] restoring fluent speech after so long a time.

Meanwhile the pious king David crosses the cold river,

mastering the wandering blue waters of foaming Rhine.

Among the foremost he flashes, tall and armed,

holding weapons; at the summit of the entire cavalry

he rises above his companions.

Companies glittering with bronze hurry from every side

and join the ranks with varied roaring.
The earth itself, unaware, marvels and trembles  
[Note: [Col. 1441D] Read *tremit*, “trembles.”]
at so many corselets, swords, helmets, and shields of men,
and at the iron shaken beneath such weight.

A vast and crowded shout rises to the stars,

and the echo rebounds from the icy rocks

of the stony mountain.

There is a notable place where the Patra and Lippa flow.

It lies high in the open field, everywhere clothed

in a broad expanse.

From the lofty hill the whole legion can be seen,

and from here the entire army,

the commanders’ camps, and the radiant arms of the men.

Here the hero Charles arrives, surrounded by many thousands,

and at last is glad to enter the shelter there.

[Col. 1442B] A messenger proceeds to the royal palace of the apostolic man.

Meanwhile he announces that the supreme pontiff Leo has come,

expelled from the Roman see by his own citizens,

and recounts that he has endured so many blows,

mentioning his face deprived of sight

and telling of his tongue cut from his living throat,

now healed by God’s intervention, and free from all these evils.

The whole army itself is astonished.

Having recalled his earlier dreams

and recognizing in what had happened the signs of the past,

Charles does not doubt that this is the same pontiff

whom he had seen in his dreams long before,

pouring forth sad tears.

Then he immediately orders Pepin to go out

to meet the great shepherd and bring him peace

and tranquil greeting.

Pepin prepares to go out, carrying out his father’s orders,

and goes joyfully with a hundred thousand men.  
[Note: Read “went.”]

Charles himself, the just king, sits upon a lofty throne,
giving laws to his ancestral realm and confirming the bonds of the kingdom.

When he sees across the open field the apostolic shepherd

and Pepin, towering with a hundred thousand men,

advancing toward him,

[Col. 1442C] the shepherd extends both hands toward heaven,

pouring forth abundant prayers from his heart for the people.

Three times the entire army prostrates itself before the supreme priest,

and three times the suppliant multitude, fallen to the ground, adores.

Soon Pope Leo receives Pepin alone with kindly manner,

encircling his neck with sacred arms.

He clings to him in an embrace and for a long time freely gives peaceful kisses.  
[Note: Read “bestowing kisses.”]

He rises and towers above him with his whole height.

Pepin and he mingle various words in conversation,
and in turn relieve one another with differing [lacuna].  
[Note: [Col. 1442D] The manuscript has: *propteps innata umbo*; perhaps read *problemata verbo*, “problems by a word.”]

Meanwhile the pious king mounts his throne

and addresses all the people, the venerable hero Charles:

“Come, then, nobles,” he says, “you who are accustomed

to go to war armed and to test harsh Mars,
trusting yourselves to cruel combat.

Let us meet the excellent pontiff with swift course.”

Hardly had the hero spoken when the crowd roars with tumult on every side.

[Col. 1442D] It gathers weapons in its hands; soon corselets of triple links,

broad shields, helmets, and darts of bronze-shod bucklers resound.

Here and there lines of horsemen are seen advancing;

the clouds grow black with scattered dust.

The mournful trumpet sounds in the middle of the embankment;

the military standards ring out, and the open fields grow dense

with the procession.

The entire crested army flashes;

weapons glitter, and raised banners shine together.

The young men advance armed, and the vigorous youth

rejoices in its horses.

A dry ardor burns in their bones,
the desire to hear.

Charles shines joyfully in the middle of the procession.

A golden crest covers his forehead;

visible in his armor, he gleams,

the splendid leader borne upon an enormous horse.

[Col. 1443A] In front of the priests’ camp, the ranks stand divided

into three choirs, in long, dignified garments.

They raise the sacred banners of the cross,

and all the clergy and the radiant people await

the arrival of the bishop.

Now Father Charles sees the ranks in the open field,

and observes Pepin and the supreme shepherd advancing toward him.

He orders the people to await them in the form of a crown

and divides the line in the manner of a city.

He himself, blessed, stands in the middle of the circle,

awaiting the bishop’s arrival;

taller than all his companions, he rises above the whole people.

Now Pope Leo approaches and mingles with the foreign army.

He marvels at peoples of different regions of the world,

as varied in language as in dress and weapons.

At once Charles hastens forward and reverently adores him.

Embracing the great pontiff, he gives him peaceful kisses,

and they join their right hands together.

They proceed side by side, mingling words with much affection.

[Col. 1443B] Before the supreme priest the whole army  
[Note: [Col. 1443B] These lines are repeated a little above.]
prostrates itself three times,

and the suppliant people, fallen to the ground three times, adores.

The bishop pours forth prayers three times from his heart for the people.

The royal father of Europe and supreme shepherd Leo,

having met, converse with one another in varied speech.

Charles inquires and hears of the different circumstances of the sufferings.

He is astonished at the impious deeds of the people.

He marvels that the twin windows of sight,

long since extinguished,

[Col. 1444A] have now been restored to the face by light,

and they marvel that the tongue, cut with a knife,

speaks.

Each fixes his eyes upon the other’s face.

And with equal steps they proceed toward the heights.  
[Note: Perhaps “with matching steps.”]

Before the sacred priests the doors of the temple stand open.

In alternating turns they chant songs of praise

and repeatedly offer thanks and praise to the Creator,

who had restored new sight to the supreme pontiff

and placed speech thought lost within his mouth.

A shout rises; the lofty voice strikes Olympus.

The apostolic man enters, led by blessed Charles,

to celebrate the solemn rites of the Creator

in the customary manner, with the pious celebration of Mass.

When the divine offices have been duly completed,

Charles invites Leo inside the lofty palace.

Within, the bright hall gleams with painted garments.

The seats shine on every side with abundant gold and purple.

They sit happily at the tables and enjoy various delicacies;

in the middle of the hall they celebrate the banquet.

Golden vessels swell with Falernian wine upon the tables.

[Col. 1444B] King Charles and the supreme bishop Leo

eat and drink the foaming ancestral wines.

After the joyful feast and Bacchus’s sweet cups,

the pious Charles gives many gifts to Leo.

Then, joyful, the king returns to the private rooms of the palace,

and the apostolic man likewise returns to the camp of his people.

With such honor Leo is received by Charles,

having fled from Rome, expelled from his own shores.

[Col. 1443]

## VERSES ON CHARLEMAGNE

*(From Martène,* Amplissima Collectio*.)*

[Col. 1443C] O almighty God, creator of the vaulted citadel,

of lands and sea, and of all that so great a world contains,

receive the prayers of your people; hear our entreaty

and deign to secure the safety of the excellent Caesar Charles.

Prolong his life, ruler, through many years,

assigning the Ocean as the boundary of his empire.

With his enemies crushed, strengthen him with lasting peace,

so that, as the best prince, he may rightly govern what has been settled,

while your divine hand caresses him,

you alone who thunder on high and preside in the heavenly palace.

It is fitting that only he should rule upon earth beneath that One

who deservedly surpasses all mortal beings.

Let the various sects depart; let error also depart,

the ancient error once wickedly counseled by the malignant mouth.

Let holy faith shine, accompanying his lofty steps,

as it surveys the vast world together with Charlemagne,

with the proud subdued by both imperial command and strength,

and, after countless triumphs over captured enemies,

let faith herself rejoice victorious with her conqueror.

[Col. 1443D] After so much upon earth, after so many lofty deeds,

when at last the full span of time has been completed,

having reached a hundred years in a happy course,

let blessed faith, coming with a company of sister virtues

to meet him, raise Charles above the stars,

granting him, through Christ’s favor, an everlasting crown.

In unpolished verses, but with the highest love of mind,

I compose these offerings for you, Caesar;

deign, I ask, to receive them from your devoted servant.

By these little letters I ask lasting salvation

for Charles, the little servant of his own lord.

By these I greet you, illustrious Gundrada, maiden,

who shines with a beautiful mouth and is more beautiful in character.  
[Note: “A letter hastening to bring greetings to Lady Gundrada, excellent in character and appearance.”]

These verses for King Charles [are composed] by an Irish exile,

while the nobles of the world appear to honor the king,

bringing enormous gifts of massive weight:

an immeasurable quantity of shining silver and gold,

heaps of gems accompanied by sacred metal,

garments gleaming with purple beneath a golden covering,

[Col. 1444C] and foaming yellow horses held by their bridles,

their lofty necks bearing barbarian gold.

These annual gifts are owed to the exalted king.

“Tell me, prattling Muse, what shall we likewise return,

lest we seem to serve the king in vain?

What little gifts should we give to such a great and powerful father?

Let us also sing songs now in a full voice;

let us bring forth sweet-sounding praises to the king from our hearts,

and let the whole world echo with our cries.”

“O Muse, captivated above all others by the sweetness of song,

whose songs are equal to the riches of the world,

say this: what are the odes of our song now worth?

Alas, do you not know the names of your companion Muses?

Or perhaps, mocking us, do you despise our offerings?”

“Beloved companion, also a sweet foster-child of the Muses,

I certainly do not fail to recognize the Muses’ sweet gifts.

But now tell me, greatest nurse of ancient poets,

what will bring our praise to an end through the ages,

while the summit of the starry axis revolves,

and while dark night is driven away by bright stars,

while the radiant Morning Star rises from the remarkable shadows,

while the swift wind lashes the sea’s waves,

while rivers hasten into the sea in foaming courses,

while mountains touch the clouds with threatening summits

and humble valleys lie along muddy boundaries,

or while hills raise their precipitous peaks,

and while regal splendor flashes with refined gold—
the names of the Muses will remain eternal through the ages.

By these gifts the renowned deeds of ancient kings shine,

and their achievements are told to future generations.

By the gifts of the Muses the Creator of the world is praised,

shining in heavenly dwellings with benevolent powers,

and he rejoices in our constant and harmonious songs.

Therefore remember to honor the king with these gifts.”

“But I shall accompany him with my pipe’s preeminent song.”

“Then tell me, singing, greatest nurse of poets:

who attempted to break the excellent peace of the fathers?

Who vainly disturbed their noble repose for war?

What plague touched the servant who was faithful in all things,

so that he should deserve to see the face of his lord saddened?”

The slippery serpent poured this poison from his mouth,

the same serpent who once proclaimed to wretched spouses

mortal words of death from his breast,

who tore apart two brothers with a savage wound,

who stained brotherly hands with blood,

who turned the fraternal covenant of mortals into hatred,

and who persuaded them not to know their own affections and love.

Then the son, swearing falsely, mocked his father’s honor,

the one who once taught peoples to climb a tower

and ordered servants not to acknowledge the thundering Lord.

He alone tears apart the bonds of perfect peace

and rejoices in setting peoples against one another in savage wars,

so that no one may serve Christ worthily in the world.

With deadly words he urges quarrels to rise

and sows disputes where only the bonds of peace are commanded,

the bonds by which the rewards of the everlasting kingdom are granted.

This envious serpent attempted to break the peace

by which the excellent king Charles and the renowned leader Dasilo

were held together under one blessed and perpetual law.

He attacks through rumor and contaminates the entire world.

With these words the treacherous man struck pure ears.  
[Note: Perhaps “the ears of Hesperia.”]

[Col. 1445B] “Dasilo has sinned,” he says, “because he abandoned the royal commands

and did not fulfill the obligations of the service he had promised.”

These words revolved into the excellent Charles’s ears,

and rumor began to fly widely through the world.

The king’s presence was struck by these reports.

At first he lent pious ears to these words

and said to everyone: “This man is very faithful to me

and seeks prosperity for the Frankish kingdoms.”

But persistent rumor confirmed the accusation to the king,

and the whole earth cried out:

“That leader is not faithful.”

At last the most just hero, moved by these words,

joins his ranks and stations his fleet along the bank

of the Rhine, which encircles Germany among the lands of the Gauls.

With a fortunate course he crosses the river to the defeated side.

Illustrious Germany trembled beneath countless troops.

But the king of the Franks, surrounded by mighty thousands,

the greatest victor, rejoices in arms upon his ancestral soil.

He addresses his faithful nobles and says:

“O royal people descended from the lofty walls

of Troy—for our fathers brought them to these shores—

the ruler of the world allotted these fields to them

and subjected the peoples to the just laws of the Franks.

The creator of the stars forever sanctioned these borders for them,

gave them broad cities to possess utterly,

and entrusted to them all the maidservants, servants, and dependents.

But recently an enemy rose up in our fields,

perhaps this envious serpent, through a savage wound—  
[Note: [Col. 1445D] Much is missing here.]

[lacuna]

Armlets of great weight in gems and gold

are offered, and a gold-covered horse shines.

By these splendid gifts the boy is enriched by his lord.”

To him the king then spoke these words in a calm voice:

“Receive the pledges of our perpetual service.”

Then, kissing the king’s knees with the sweetest kisses,

the leader spoke these swift words from his heart:

“King, may the gift of salvation be granted to you forever.

But I shall render service to you through the ages.”

Having spoken thus, he withdrew to the camp with the king’s gift.

## Verses of the Emperor Charles

[Col. 1445D] This is the true faith of heaven that leads to the palace;

let whoever wishes to possess rest hold fast to it.

[Col. 1446A] For it is a great virtue for all who believe

to please God in the manner of the threefold faith in one nature.  
[Note: That is, “threefold in one nature.”]

Charles Caesar, highest summit, the rich peace of the world,

teaches the human companies to bow their necks to him.

As all, higher in honor, [recognize] the supreme king of the kingdom,

so Caesar, in the manner of faith and form, is like the former eighth.  
[Note: The wording is obscure.]

He who had granted himself the citadel of the present kingdom—

I ask that he grant himself the highest place in the citadel of heaven—

I, insignificant, now offer the king a little book,

collected from various flowers with flowering roses.

## Verses of the Emperor Charles

Paper, with Christ as your companion across the breadth of the earth,

go now to Caesar’s spacious palace.

Bring greetings to Caesar and his companies,

to the glorious boys and sacred virgins.

Proceed on a prosperous road through Christ’s assistance,

and, bending before Caesar, speak words such as these:

Say that Caesar Charles, through Peter’s proclamation,

[Col. 1446B] may be healthy, long-lived, and fortunate in victory.

Say that the ruler of all may grant him support,

strengthen him, guard him, and expand his empire.

Say that, as he was rightly a supporter of just kings,

so may Christ be [a supporter] of Charles and of his faithful.

Say that the royal boys, through extended years,

may be healthy and long-lived by the Savior’s grace;

say that they may be worthy of royal crowns and honors,

happy and victorious in their father’s character.

Say to the royal maidens: “Let exaltation be granted.”

May their virginity be holy, temperate, and true.

Christ loves virgins because of their chastity;

may he grant them the glory he promised for the future.

Say that the Lord protect the Frankish men-at-arms:

the king, clergy, counts, and warrior knights.

After this, paper, ask Caesar immediately

to remember me, his insignificant servant in Christ.

## Verses of the Emperor Charles

Ancient times are celebrated with extraordinary praises,

and everything past is accustomed to give pleasure.

While the present age moves famous tongues to speech,

and the troubling day weighs down the hearts of the people,

people willingly trust in uncertain outcomes

or even seize the future with excessive hope.

This commonly occurs among human beings everywhere:

new fame yields to the rumor of ancient things.

But for us the order and custom are reversed:
we prefer the present times that remain to ancient times.

In them the peaceful lord Charles

governs the Roman empire with supreme virtue.

The nobles yield to him, and the lofty glory of earlier men

is overshadowed as stars are by the sun’s rays;

rivers are overcome by the Nile,
hills are surpassed by Olympus,
and Arabian refined gold shines more brightly than silver.

So now, Augustus, greatest of kings, your fame yields to you:

your strength, virtue, glory, name, and honor.

For the gifts of virtue that are distributed individually among others

are all seen in you; everyone observes and acknowledges them.

[Col. 1446D] Some possess handsome form, others boastful speech,

noble blood, or strength in war.

[Col. 1445]

[Note: This epitaph is attributed to Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, and was published among his works. It is also found inserted in the Chronicle of Novalesa.]

## EPITAPH OF CHARLEMAGNE

*(In the year 814.)*

[Col. 1445D] After Christ, the golden one of heaven, had taken from the Virgin
members suited to himself for the world’s sin,
the fourteenth year after eight hundred was passing,
in which Charles, the glory of the Frankish people, deserved to cross
the waters of the fiery, wave-bearing ethereal heaven
and to reach the tranquil harbor.

He had happily held the scepters of the kingdom

for fourteen times six years,

and, as king, had joined kingdoms to his kingdom.

[Col. 1446D] He departed from the world on the fifth day before the Kalends of February,

having completed seventy-six years of life.

Therefore, reader, whoever you are, if you can be moved by any prayers,

whoever reads these verses of the inscription,

say that Charles’s spirit may possess the star-bearing citadel.

[Col. 1447]

## ADDENDA TO THE AUTHENTIC DIPLOMAS OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE RELATING TO ITALY

### I

[Note: In the Charter Collection of Maniago, from the book of the Treasury of the Church of Aquileia. Corrected from the diploma edited by Palladio, *History of the Church of Aquileia*, book II.]

## Diploma of Charlemagne to Patriarch Paulinus concerning the preservation of liberty for the clergy of Aquileia in the election of patriarchs

*(In the year 792.)*

[Col. 1447A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

If we willingly comply with the petitions of priests and servants of God that have been presented to our ears, and in God’s name bring them to fulfillment, we exercise royal custom; and we trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdoms.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable man Paulinus, patriarch of the holy Aquileian Church, [Col. 1447B] which was built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Mark, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom.

He asked that, when by divine calling he had departed from this light to the Lord, the holy congregation itself—which appears to govern its life there under holy discipline—should have permission, by our aforesaid indulgence and with our chief authority preserved, just as in other churches according to canonical authority, to choose from among itself for its own leadership whichever man it wished, the better and more worthy, entirely faithful, suitable, and appropriate to us, to our son King Pepin, and to all our people.

Moreover, he asked our Serenity that the men serving the aforesaid Church, both those residing there and those living elsewhere, should never at any time have to pay publicly any tithe from grain or from any livestock; nor, when they send their own ecclesiastical livestock to pasture in the regions of Istria, should they have to pay any grazing tax.

We did not wish to deny this venerable petition for three reasons.

The first is that those servants of God who appear to serve God there may more gladly and continually implore the Lord’s mercy on behalf of us, our wife, our sons and daughters, and the people entrusted to us by God.

The second is that they may devote themselves more fully to divine writings and spiritual teachings.

The third is that, compelled by his merits, we have granted this favor. Know that we have granted it in every respect.

Therefore, by this present authority of ours, we decree and order—and wish this to remain perpetual—that, as we stated above, the arrangement concerning that same sacred place shall remain permanently unshaken by virtue of our aforesaid indulgence.

In particular, as our alms to the aforementioned venerable man, we have granted that no one at any time dare provide or impose lodging-tax or billeting obligations upon the servants of the aforesaid Church, wherever they may be residing. [Col. 1448A]

The sole exception is if we ourselves, or our beloved son Pepin, or a royal force should come into the region of Friuli because of enemy disturbances, or should arrive at the border of the Trevisan territory.

Then, if necessity arises, our men may receive lodging there.

But otherwise, if they settle at Verona or Vicenza, or in more distant territories, as we have stated above, this privilege shall at all times be granted and confirmed for the increase of our reward.

And so that this authority may be held firmly and better preserved through long ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our own ring.

[Col. 1448B] Given on the day before the Nones of August, in the twenty-fourth and nineteenth year of our reign.

Issued at the public palace of Regensburg, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

### II

[Note: From the archive of the chapter of the Church of Udine.]

## Diploma of Charlemagne to Patriarch Paulinus

*(In the year 805.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and emperor of the Romans.

If we willingly accommodate the petitions of priests or servants of God that have been presented to our ears, and in God’s name bring them to fulfillment, we exercise royal custom and confidently believe that this contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Let it therefore be known to all the present and future faithful of the holy Church of God that Paulinus, patriarch of the holy Aquileian Church, made his complaint before our piety and the mercy of the pope at a certain synodal council in Rome: namely, that his church had been almost entirely laid waste by a vast invasion of pagans. When we heard such complaints from him, we feared that we would incur the guilt of a grave offense before the Giver of all good things if, with the obstacle of obstinacy standing in the way, his lament should seem unable to obtain any consolation from the mercy of our empire. Therefore, fearing to close our ears to just petitions, we began silently to inquire within ourselves how, according to the lament of the aforesaid Patriarch Paulinus, our piety ought to come to the aid of our Aquileian Church.

At last, having received the advice of the pope and the other bishops present, we judged it fitting and just to grant to the lord Paulinus, patriarch, and to his successors certain bishoprics belonging to the consecration of the Aquileian Church, for the exaltation of the aforesaid Aquileian Church [Col. 1449A], so that what is now seen cast down and trampled underfoot by the most savage fury of the pagans may be raised up and comforted by our imperial gift [the manuscript is lacunose; *consoletur* is conjectural].

Therefore, by these letters of command [the manuscript has lacunae; conjecturally *praeceptales*, “preceptual”], we have wholly transferred [lacuna; conjecturally *a nostro nunc jure*, “from our present right”] into the right and power [lacuna; conjecturally *et potestatem*] of the aforesaid lord Paulinus, patriarch, and of all his successors, six bishoprics [lacuna; conjecturally *omniumque illius successorum sex episcopatus*]. The first, namely, Concordia; the second, Udine; the third, that which is known to have been established at the New City in Istria; the fourth, Ruginum (*Ruginensem*); the fifth, Peneta (*Penetensem*); the sixth, Tarsatica [the manuscript is lacunose; *Tarsatiensem* is conjectural].

Finally, we decree and command by these letters of our magnificence that, in the aforesaid places [Col. 1449B], no one at any time presume to have or exercise the right or power of ordaining, governing, or appointing bishops, except the one who shall be found to govern the holy Aquileian Church. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for all time, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious emperor.

James wrote and subscribed in the place of Radovus.

Given on the day before the Nones of August, in the third year of our empire, in the first indiction.

Done at Rome, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### III. [Note: [Col. 1449D] From the charter collection of Maniaco, from the book of the Treasury of the Holy Aquileian Church.]

Diploma of Charlemagne to Patriarch Maxentius for the restoration of the Aquileian Church. (Year 812.)

[Col. 1449C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceable emperor, governing the empire of the Romans, who also, through the mercy of God, is king of the Franks and Lombards.

Whatever we grant and bestow out of love for almighty God and upon the holy places of His venerable ones, for the increase of the reward of our soul, we confidently believe will undoubtedly contribute to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore, let the greatness of all our faithful, both present and future, know how the venerable man Maxentius, patriarch, represented to Our Serenity that the see which in ancient times had been built in the city of Aquileia, but which, through fear of or treachery by the Goths and Avars, as well as by other nations, had remained abandoned and destroyed down to our own days, he desired, kindled by the torch of divine love and with Christ’s protection, to construct and restore to its former honor, together with our assistance. But because the place where he wished to do this was considered exceedingly confined and narrow, so that he could not carry out the work there suitably, he requested Our Highness that, as our alms, we should hand over or confirm to that same see some portion of the inheritance which the Lombard Rotgandus and his brother Felix had possessed within the city or outside it near the walls of that city. Because of their faithlessness, since they had been killed together with Rotgandus, formerly a faithless duke, this inheritance had passed into our public property according to Frankish or Lombard law. After the death of those two brothers, a certain faithful man of ours named Landola held it as our benefice, and after his departure his son Bonno appeared to hold it up to the present. He therefore asked that we hand it over or confirm it, so that he might more conveniently and suitably complete the buildings and other constructions pertaining to the honor of that place, according to the prudent plan he had devised [Col. 1450B].

We, rejoicing at the construction of so distinguished a work, grant and confirm to the church of God, holy Mary the Mother of God, or to that see of Aquileia, for the increase of the reward of our soul, the aforesaid portion of the two faithless brothers, namely Rotgandus and Felix, which was recognized as belonging to our right, so that it may contribute perpetually to the increase of that holy see. That is: houses, cultivated land with its dwelling-place, arable lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, and also that portion which they appeared to possess at the port of the river called the Natisone, as we have set out above. Whatever from that inheritance within the city or outside it near the city walls appears to belong to our authority, we hand over [Col. 1450C] and confirm, and we wish it to remain so forever.

Their third brother, named Landulphus, who did not persist in their faithlessness, still retains his own portion. In the remaining places, however, wherever anything from the inheritance of the aforesaid faithless men has come to us, we have reserved it for our imperial disposition.

Therefore, giving orders, we command that henceforth and in the future no one of our faithful, of whatever rank, office, authority, or dignity, obstruct the rectors of that holy Church of God from possessing peacefully and quietly, by perpetual right and free from anyone’s opposition, the aforesaid properties that we have assigned and confirmed forever to that holy place.

And so that this grant and confirmation of ours may be held firmly and better preserved throughout future [Col. 1450D] times, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth year of our empire, Christ being favorable, and the forty-fifth of our reign in France, the thirty-seventh in Italy, in the fifth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 1449D] An error has entered these chronological notices. From the years of the empire, the Frankish reign, and the indiction, we determine that the year in which the diploma was issued was 812; yet the thirty-seventh year of the Italian reign does not coincide with this, being short by two years. It should therefore be written, “the thirty-ninth in Italy.” At the end, moreover, the subscription of the scribe or notary is lacking.]

Done at Aachen, in the royal palace, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

Continuation of the first part of the complete works of the blessed Emperor Charles, surnamed the Great and Augustus.
