Admonition concerning the letters of Saint Gregory III to Charles, sub-king. 53

### I. Letter of Pope Gregory III to Charles Martel.—For the defense of the holy Church of God. 64

### II. Likewise, Gregory’s second letter sent to Charles.—Likewise for the defense of the holy Church.

Notice concerning Saint Zachary’s letter. 69

### III. Likewise, a letter of Pope Zachary sent to Lord Pippin.—

It is entitled under the name of the mayor of the palace because he had not yet been raised to royal dignity. Together with its chapters, after consultation also with the aforesaid Pippin—or with the priests in the regions of Francia—concerning how a response should be made, the aforesaid pontiff wrote it. 79

Notice concerning Stephen II’s letters. 91

### IV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope sent through Abbot Droctegand.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings. 100

### V. Likewise, a general letter of the same pope.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings. 101

### VI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord Pippin the king and to Charles and Carloman.—

For the defense of the holy Church of God, because Haistulfus [Aistulfus] had rendered void the pact that he had made with them and had not kept his oath, just as he had promised the same kings, and so forth. 103

### VII. Likewise, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to Lord Pippin, Charles, and beloved Carloman.—

It states that Haistolfus [Haistulfus] had rendered void the pact and oath that he had promised, with very solemn adjurations, to the same kings concerning the rights of Saint Peter; he again requests that he obtain assistance against that same man. 107

### VIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin, and to Charles or Carloman, or to the entire general body.—

Written in the name of that pope concerning the desolation and devastation of the holy Church of God and of the city of Rome, it was sent through George the bishop, Warneharius the abbot, and Thomaricus the count, emissaries of the apostolic pope, requesting, with very solemn adjurations, assistance against the Lombards. 111

### IX. Likewise, a letter of Pope Stephen to Lord Pippin the king.—

Sent specifically and individually for the defense of the holy Church of God, as is contained in the preceding letter of the same pope, desiring to obtain assistance against the Lombards; it was likewise sent through George and Warnebarius. 115

### X. Likewise, the third letter that Pope Stephen sent to Lord King Pippin and to Charles or Carloman, or to the entire general body of the Franks.—

Composed in the name of Saint Peter after the aforesaid pope himself had come to Francia, it sought assistance against the Lombards for a second time. 121

### XI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope sent to Lord King Pippin through Folradus the chaplain, George the bishop, and John the sacristan, after the death of Aistulfus.—

It contains [Col. 1452] thanksgivings and most abundant blessings for the victory and restoration of the holy Church of God, requesting that what was still lacking be restored. 126

Preliminary discussion of the thirty-one letters of Saint Paul I. 133

### XII. Copy of a letter.—

Paul, deacon and elect of the holy Roman Church, announces the death of Pope Stephen through Immo, who had been sent by Lord King Pippin. 147

### XIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin sent through Wulfardus.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant praises for the defense of the holy Church of God, requesting assistance against the Lombards, since those Lombards, persisting in great arrogance, were in no way restoring the rights of the holy Church of God. 148

### XIV. Likewise, a general copy of the same pope’s letter to the entire army protected by God of the Frankish kingdom.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings for their struggle, so that they might persevere more earnestly in contending in the service of almighty God and of the holy Church of God, and it encourages the mind of Lord King Pippin to carry this through. 151

### XV. Likewise, a copy of a general letter of the Roman people and Senate addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It contains thanksgivings and speaks of the letter that Lord King Pippin sent to that people concerning the faith to be preserved toward the holy Roman Church and toward Lord Paul the apostolic pope. 153

### XVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin sent through Langbard.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings for his life and safety, and for those of Lord Charles and Carloman, his most noble sons. He wishes to obtain assistance, with many solemn adjurations, against the Lombards. In an inserted section there is also a directive that he sent to the priest Marinus concerning the title of Chrysogonus and concerning the books that he transmitted to him. 156

### XVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope sent to Lord King Pippin through George the bishop, Stephen the priest, and Radpert, his emissaries.—

It contains thanksgivings for the defense of the holy Church of God. The aforesaid pope asks that Lord King Pippin restore to King Desiderius his hostages and confirm the treaties of peace with him. 159

### XVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope sent to Lord King Pippin for the defense of the holy Church of God.—

It announces that Desiderius plundered the Pentapolis and consumed all the people’s provisions with sword and fire; that he threw Albinus [Alboinus], duke of Spoleto, into chains; that the duke of Benevento, confined in the city of Osorotana [Otorontana, Otoritana], appointed another duke, Argisus, in Benevento; that he spoke with the imperial emissary George and invited the emperor’s army into Italy against Ravenna, as well as the army from Sicily against the city of Otorontana; and that he professed his intention to hand it over to the imperial party, along with several other articles. 161

### XIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

Concerning the priest Marinus, his wicked counsel, and his consecration. 168

### XX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin sent through the priest Peter.—

It contains the mission of Bishop Remedius and Count Audecarius [Andegarius], explaining how he received from the former King Desiderius, on behalf of the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, some of his rights, and how he promised to carry out the remaining rights. 169

### XXI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to the glorious Lord King Pippin, sent through Bishop George.—

It contains thanksgivings for the liberation of the holy Church of God; in an inserted section he asks to be deemed worthy to receive his son, then newly born, from the sacred baptismal font. 172

### XXII. A letter of the same pope addressed to Lords Charles and Carloman, kings.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings. 174

### XXIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It inquires about his health and safety, and likewise about his emissaries who had been sent to the royal [Col. 1453] city.

### XXIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin.—

It contains blessings. The aforesaid pope asks that Lord King Pippin send his emissaries to the regions of Rome and inform him of his health and well-being, and of how he had fared on the journey, and how the Lord had delivered his enemies into his hands and humbled them beneath his feet. 177

### XXV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It requests assistance against the Greeks. 178

### XXVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin, sent for the defense of the holy Church of God.—

It contains most abundant praises. In an inserted section it states that the aforesaid Lord King Pippin should send his directive to King Desiderius of the Lombards, so that, if necessity required it, he should provide assistance both to Ravenna and to the other maritime cities, to fight against the attack of the enemies. 180

### XXVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It contains thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and asks that he send his emissary to Rome. 182

### XXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lords Charles and Carloman, kings.—

It concerns the defense of the holy Church of God. 184

### XXIX. Likewise, a copy of a letter addressed to Lord King Pippin through the abbots Witmarus and Gerbertus and Hugbaldus.—

It contains grateful praises for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and asks that he should always strive in this cause. 186

### XXX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lords Charles and Carloman, kings.—

It contains thanksgivings and speaks of the letter sent by them, and asks that they should always strive with their lord father for the defense of the holy Church of God. 189

### XXXI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

Concerning a certain monk, Cosmas [a Cosma], sent by the patriarch of Alexandria. 190

### XXXII. Copy of a directive made by Paul, of holy memory, pontiff of the holy Roman Church and universal pope.—

He grants Pippin, by apostolic letters—what they call a bull—the monastery of Saint Sylvester on Mount Soracte, together with the three monasteries subject to it, namely those of Saints Stephen, Andrew, and Victor, annulling the earlier letters of Saint Zachary by which permission had been granted to Carloman, if they should be found anywhere. 192

### XXXIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope sent to Lord King Pippin for the defense of the holy Church of God.—

It contains thanksgivings and most abundant blessings for the preservation of the integrity of the orthodox faith. 194

### XXXIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord [Pippin] the king.—

For the defense of the holy Church of God, and concerning his conference with King Desiderius in the city of Ravenna. 196

### XXXV. Likewise, a letter addressed to Lord King Pippin through Abbot Haribertus and Count Dodo.—

It contains most abundant blessings and grateful praises for his firm and unchanging word of promise and his great perseverance in completing the apostolic affairs. 197

### XXXVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

Concerning Simeon or the monk [monks] of Bishop Remedius. 199

### XXXVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin.—

It contains thanksgivings; it speaks of his health, and of Charles [and Carloman], and of the priest Marinus, and of Ravenna—how evil schemes were being devised against it. 201

### XXXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin, sent through Flavinus the chaplain, John the subdeacon and abbot, and Pamphilus, regional defender of the holy Church.—

It contains thanksgivings for those emissaries, explaining how they had been honorably received together with the imperial emissaries, and so forth. 206

### XXXIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It states that six patricians with three hundred ships and a fleet from Sicily were hastening toward the regions of Rome or Francia; and it speaks of the rights of the holy Church of God that Desiderius promised, in the presence of his emissaries, to fulfill, because he had completed none of them, as he had promised. 210

### XL. Likewise, a letter of Paul, of holy memory, Roman bishop, sent through Andrew and Gundricus.—

It contains thanksgivings and requests, desiring to obtain assistance against the Lombards. 213

[Col. 1454] ### XLI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin sent through Wulfardus and his companions.—

It contains most abundant praises and speaks of the apostolic emissaries, or of the Greeks staying in Francia, and of George [Gregory the bishop] and Peter. 216

### XLII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

For the defense of the holy Church of God and for the monastery that he granted to it, situated near Mount Soracte; it returns great thanks. 221

### XLIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord King Pippin sent through Bishop Wilharius, Dodo, and Wichardus.—

It contains thanksgivings and speaks of the constancy of the same pope’s faith, so that no favor or fear might in any way separate him from the king’s love or charity. 225

Notice concerning the following letters of the antipope Constantine. 227

### XLIV. Letter of Constantine, a neophyte and pope, addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It contains thanksgivings, speaks of the death of Lord Pope Paul, and asks that he be allowed to remain in the favor of Lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had been. 233

### XLV. Letter of Constantine, a neophyte and pope, addressed to Lord King Pippin.—

It states that he was elected by the Roman people through violence and introduced into the apostolic see. He asks to be allowed to remain in the favor of Lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had been. It also speaks of a letter from Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, and of other letters from the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch; in an inserted section, it speaks of George, Marinus, and Peter. 235

Notice concerning the five letters of Stephen III. 239

### XLVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles and his exalted mother.—

Concerning Christopher and his son Sergius, who, together with Dodo and the other Franks, attempted to kill Pope Stephen. 245

### XLVII. Likewise, a letter of Pope Stephen to Lord King Charles and his exalted mother.—

It contains thanksgivings, praises Abbot Itherius [Ittherius], and asks that worthy recompense be made to him for his struggle. 248

### XLVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lords Charles and Carloman, kings.—

It contains most abundant blessings and thanksgivings for the concord of their brotherhood, and speaks of the rights of Saint Peter. 249

### XLIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Carloman.—

It contains thanksgivings and asks to be deemed worthy to receive his son from the sacred baptismal font. 252

### L. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lords Charles and Carloman, kings.—

It forbids them, binding them with very solemn adjurations, to take wives from the Lombard nation. 255

Preliminary discussion of Hadrian’s forty-nine letters. 261

### LI. Likewise, a letter of Pope Hadrian to Lord King Charles, sent through Abbot Gausfridus.—

It speaks of the victory of the aforesaid king and of the bishops of Pisa and Lucca, asking that, in his piety, he permit them to return to their own sees and churches. 280

### LII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the insolence of Leo, archbishop of the city of Ravenna. 283

### LIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles through Andrew and Anastasius.—

For the justice of the holy Church of God, and concerning Leo the archbishop, who had hastened to the aforesaid lord king. 286

### LIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains most abundant blessings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and speaks of a letter from John, patriarch of Grado. 288

### LV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and speaks of the lord king’s emissaries, who were to come to Rome in the autumn. 291

### LVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord [Charles] the king.—

It speaks of the death of Emperor Constantine and of Reginald, duke of Chiusi. The aforesaid pope asks that the lord king not permit him to retain or possess that office [the duchy], since he did not cease continually to commit many evils in the castle of Felicitas. 295

### LVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

For the exaltation of the holy Church of God, and concerning Possessor and Rabigaudus [Rabigandus], who, despising the apostolic pope, had gone to Duke Hildebrand at Spoleto and from there had reached Benevento. 297

### LVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It states that Hiltibrand and [Col. 1455] Aragis [Arogis], together with Rodgans and Regimbaldus [Raginaldus, Reginaldus], had taken counsel about how they might unite with the Greeks and Adalgisus, by land and sea, to fight against Rome and Italy; and it requests assistance against them with very solemn adjurations. 300

### LIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

The aforesaid pope asks that, when the lord king returned from Saxony, he should hasten to the threshold of Saint Peter, just as he had promised him. 302

### LX. Likewise, a letter of Pope Hadrian addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings for the life and health of Lord King Charles, his wife, and his son [sons], as well as for the exaltation of the holy Church of God; it asks to be deemed worthy to receive his son from the sacred baptismal font. 304

### LXI. Paul the priest and the entire Roman clergy.—

Shortly after the departure of the emissaries, hearing from the king’s letters that the territories of the Franks were about to be invaded by the Saracens, he turned day and night to continual prayers with the entire Roman clergy. He informs him of this as a consolation and foretells victory.

He reports that the Beneventans, joined by treaty with the Gaetans and Tarracinans, and also with the patrician of Sicily residing at Gaeta, had taken counsel to seize the cities of Campania belonging to the Roman see and subject them to that same patrician. He says that he had first acted through legates, but in vain, and had therefore resolved to send an army.

He asks that the king send an emissary to the Beneventans with rebukes, so that they may return to their duty. He says that he does not even admit them to the consecration of bishops, as enemies of the holy see and of Charles. Finally, he begs him to do what he requested through the emissaries. 308

### LXII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of his faith and constancy, and of Anastasius, the emissary of that apostolic pope, who had remained in Francia. 311

### LXIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

For the exaltation of the holy Church and concerning the prayers of that apostolic pope. 315

### LXIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the sale of slaves made to the pagan nation of the Saracens. The aforesaid pope excuses the Romans, saying that they had never perpetrated such a crime, but that they had been handed over by the Lombards and Greeks. 317

### LXV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of Bishop Maurice, whose eyes the Istrians had gouged out. 320

### LXVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It states that the Neapolitans, together with the Greeks, had invaded the city of Terracina. 321

### LXVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the beams, rafters, or timber necessary for constructing that church of Saint Peter, and of the holy body requested by Fulgatus [Fulradus]. 324

### LXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the territory of Sabina, which the aforesaid king had promised to Saint Peter and ordered to be restored in its entirety. 328

### LXIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the territory of Sabina: how Itherius and Maginarius, the lord king’s emissaries, wished to restore that territory in its entirety to the party of Saint Peter, but were entirely unable to do so because of wicked men. 331

### LXX. A letter of Pope Hadrian sent to Bishop Egila in the regions of Spain.—

For maintaining the orthodox faith and for observing the fast on Friday and the Sabbath. 333

### LXXI. Likewise, a letter of Pope Hadrian to Bishop Egila or to the priest John.—

It concerns preaching about their consecration or constancy in the regions of Spain; the paschal feast; the predestination of human beings, whether to good or to evil; their defilement both in food and drink; various errors; and their false priests, who take wives while those women’s husbands are alive. It also concerns free will and many other matters that had arisen in those regions against the Catholic faith. 336

### LXXII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the faith and constancy of that apostolic pope toward the aforesaid king. 340

### LXXIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the consecration of Bishop Peter and also of the territory of Sabina. 348

### LXXIV. Likewise, a letter addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the territory of Sabina. It explains how Machinarius [Maginarius], the most faithful servant of that exalted king, wished to restore that territory in its entirety to the party [Col. 1456] of Saint Peter, but could not do so because of wicked and perverse men. 352

### LXXV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings for the labors undertaken for blessed Peter and commends Bishop George to him. 354

### LXXVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the Persian plunder carried out in the territories of the Greeks and of the discord that existed among them. 355

### LXXVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It speaks of the faith and affection that he promised to have toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that it may remain firm and indissoluble and so that no crafty deception may separate his mind from love of the apostolic pope. 356

### LXXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent, who had been falsely accused before the lord king and removed from there. The pope asks that the king receive him most graciously, with a kindly expression and a most vigorous spirit, because false charges had been brought against him. 359

### LXXIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It indicates how he had settled the dispute of the monks sent to him. It also states that Abbot Potho wished to travel to King Charles with ten monks, so that there too he might clear himself of the charges brought against him. 360

### LXXX. Concerning bishops and priests.—

They should not put on military armor but spiritual armor—that is, they should devote themselves to fasts and prayers. It also concerns the selling or seizure of persons, and other unlawful matters perpetrated by wicked men, as well as the vision of the monk John, which appeared to be false or empty. 365

### LXXXI. Likewise, a letter addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the monastery of Saint Hilary the Confessor at Calligata. He asks that the monastery, or the hospices situated along the Alpine passes [roads] for receiving pilgrims, not be attacked by any person, great or small. 369

### LXXXII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns mosaic work [*molivo*, corrected *musivo*] and marble of the palace of the city of Ravenna. The aforesaid pope says that he willingly grants these to the lord king’s authority, or whatever he might wish to do with them. 371

### LXXXIII. A letter of Pope Hadrian addressed to the bishops residing throughout Spain, especially Elipandus and Ascaricus with their associates.—

It concerns the heresy or blasphemy of calling the Son of God adoptive; he rebukes them on many points with the authority of the holy Fathers. It also concerns the paschal feast, the blood of cattle and swine, and blood from strangled animals, which they preach in error, saying that anyone who does not eat such things is crude and uneducated; he declares them bound under the bond of anathema and excluded from the Church.

Likewise, it concerns the predestination of God: if someone had been predestined to good, it was not necessary for him to resist evil; but if he had been known [variant: born] for evil, exercising goodness would profit him nothing. For this article he chastises them with apostolic exhortations.

He also reproves them because they share a common life with Jews and unbaptized pagans, both in food and drink, and in various other matters, saying that they are not defiled; because they give their daughters to the pagan people; because of their consecrations; because women, while their husbands are alive, take another husband; and because of free will and many other matters too lengthy to enumerate. He rebukes them with the traditions of the holy Fathers. 374

### LXXXIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the Venetians [Venetics], so that they might be expelled from Ravenna and the Pentapolis; and it also concerns Duke Garamannus, who had violently invaded or stripped the possessions of the Church of Ravenna. 386

### LXXXV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the formerly faithless nation, namely the Saxons, and explains how the Lord and our Redeemer, through the aforesaid king’s arduous struggles, had brought them to the worship of God, to the uprightness of faith of his catholic and apostolic Church, and even to the sacred baptismal font. It also concerns litanies, fasts, and prayers for this matter. 387

### LXXXVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

He responds to an inquiry concerning certain Saxons who had fallen back into paganism, saying that after a long penance they could be received into fellowship with the Church. 390

### LXXXVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains [Col. 1457] thanksgivings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the honor of the priestly pallium granted to Bishop Ermenbertus. 392

### LXXXVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the large beams for restoring churches, which the lord king had ordered to be given to him. He says that the officials had negligently done nothing of what the aforesaid king had instructed them to do. It also concerns tin for reroofing that church of Saint Peter. 394

### LXXXIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings and blessings for the cross that he had sent him. It also concerns the territory of Populonia or Roselle, asking that the lord king send suitable emissaries who would be able to hand over to him the cities themselves, together with their suburbs, in their entirety. 396

### XC. Likewise, a letter of the same pope to Lord Charles.—

It concerns the arrival of Adalgisus in the regions of Calabria; asks that he not appoint Grimoald duke in Benevento; and concerns the cities of Benevento, Roselle, and Populonia. 398

### XCI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the emissaries of the Greeks, together with the *diucitin*, that is, the administrator of Sicily. After the return of the deacon Atto, the lord king’s emissary from Benevento, they took counsel with the widow of Duke Arichis [*conciliati*; variant *consiliati*], concerning how they might by treachery withdraw the duchy of Benevento from the power of the aforesaid king. 402

### XCII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns Arichis, duke of Benevento, who, after King Charles had returned from the city of Capua, sent his emissaries to the emperor—God opposing him—asking for assistance and the honor of the patriciate. He desired to invalidate the faith that he had promised and promised to adopt the practices of the Greeks both in tonsure and in clothing. 406

### XCIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings and concerns Roselle and Populonia, the cities of Benevento, and the treacheries of the Greeks. 411

### XCIV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

He accuses him of lying and rebukes him because he had sent his emissaries [legates] to Ravenna for the election of a new pontiff. 416

### XCV. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns Constantine and Paul, the apostolic pope’s dukes, who had been gratuitously accused before the aforesaid king by wicked men. He asks that the king deign to receive kindly one of them, namely Paul, whom he had sent to be presented before the king’s eyes. 418

### XCVI. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the emissaries of Offa, king of the English, who were hastening to Rome [*Roma properarent*; variant: *Romam properarunt*, “hastened to Rome”] together with the emissaries of the aforesaid King Charles, and explains how the aforesaid pope had honorably received the English emissaries, just as King Charles had instructed him through his legates; it also concerns other matters. 420

### XCVII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the dioceses or parishes of bishops in the regions of Italy and Tuscany, which they invaded against one another; and the monastic habit, which, contrary to the holy canons, they abandoned and then put on secular clothing again, joining themselves in unlawful marriages. 424

### XCVIII. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It concerns the parishes of bishops, their consecration, the honor of the lord king’s patriciate, and other matters. 427

### XCIX. Likewise, a letter of the same pope addressed to Lord King Charles.—

It contains thanksgivings and blessings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the Sacramentary, which had been transmitted by Saint Gregory and which the lord king had requested, and which he had sent through John, a monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna. 434

Index of matters and words contained in the first volume of the Carolingian Codex according to Cennio’s edition. 437

Preface prefixed to Volume II of Cajetan Cennio’s edition. 451

The ancient *Provinciale*, or register of the provinces of the universal Church. 457

The genuine *Book of Censuses*. 475

Treatise on the letters of Saint Leo III to Emperor Charles. 487

§ 1. Many more still remain hidden than those published by Conringius. Ibid.

§ 2. The Catholic faith and the Roman Church admirably defended by Charles the Great, patrician of the Romans, and pontifical dominion enlarged. 490

[Col. 1458] § 3. On the renewal of the empire carried out by Saint Leo III in the year 800. 498

§ 4. On the transfer of the empire to the Germans carried out by John XII in the year 962. 508

Here begin the letters sent by Pope Leo to Emperor Charles. 517

### FIRST LETTER.—How a certain bishop was found in exile. Ibid.

### LETTER II.—How emissaries sent to administer justice inflicted damage. 520

### LETTER III.—Concerning the accusers. 523

### LETTER IV.—Concerning benefits received. 527

### LETTER V.—Thanksgiving. 531

### LETTER VI.—Intercessions and other matters. 535

### LETTER VII.—Questions to be resolved. 538

### LETTER VIII.—Concerning the killing of the Moors against the Greeks [Latin reading uncertain: *De occisione Maurorum in Graecos*]. 540

### LETTER IX.—How the Sicilians made a pact with the Saracens and the captives were returned. 544

### LETTER X.—Concerning an evil counsel that was given. 548

Treatise on the diploma of Louis the Pious. 551

Privilege of the emperor Louis concerning the confirmation of the royal possessions granted to Pope Paschal. 579

## APPENDIX. 587

Treatise on the diploma of Otto I Augustus and Otto II, king. Ibid.

Copy of the privilege of Emperor Otto concerning the royal possessions granted to blessed Peter. 603

Treatise on the diploma of Henry I. 609

Copy of the privilege of Emperor Henry concerning the royal possessions granted to blessed Peter. 625

Treatise on the charter of Countess Matilda, or on the donation made once and again to the holy see. 631

### CHAPTER ONE.—On the name, condition, location, and changes of Matilda’s land. Ibid.

### CHAPTER II.—On the cities of Parma, Reggio, Modena, and Mantua, formerly belonging by right to Countess Matilda. 648

Charter of Countess Matilda. 659

Treatise on the Rudolphine codex, or on the three books of Rudolph’s letters. 661

§ 1. On the election of the Carolingian successors of Charles the Great. 663

§ 2. On the election of the three Ottos and their successors up to Frederick II. 664

§ 3. On the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire. 666

§ 4. The coronation rite of the August Carolingians. 670

§ 5. The coronation rite of the kings of Germany after the election of the Roman king had been established. 674

§ 6. On the three books of Rudolph’s letters. 685

Three books of the letters of Rudolph I, Caesar Augustus. 701

## BOOK ONE. Ibid.

### FIRST LETTER.—Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, asks a congregation of religious persons for the support of their prayers, in order to establish the auspices of his empire. Ibid.

### LETTER II.—Brother John, general abbot of the holy Cistercian order, responds to Rudolph’s preceding letter, commending his order to him. 704

### LETTER III.—Rudolph likewise asks the consecrated virgins for the support of their prayers for himself and his consort. 705

### LETTER IV.—On the same subject as the preceding letter, and written in nearly the same words. 707

### LETTER V.—Rudolph, elected king of the Romans, writes to all the estates of the empire concerning the restoration of peace, and that
they should render to him the obedience owed to him.

708 **LETTER VI.**—A certain city congratulates Rudolph on his election, gives thanks for the remission of an offense, and commends itself to him.

709 **LETTER VII.**—Another city likewise congratulates Rudolph on his election as king of the Romans, humbly commending itself to him.

710 **LETTER VIII.**—A certain person writes to Rudolph that, through the efforts of the supreme pontiff and by his own wondrous elevation, the previously collapsed condition of the Church and the empire will be restored.

711 **LETTER IX.**—A certain prince writes to the supreme pontiff concerning Rudolph’s election, commending him to the pontiff.

713 **LETTER X.**—A certain city rejoices at Rudolph’s advancement, wholly devoting itself to him.

714 **LETTER XI.**—He gratefully acknowledges the congratulation offered to him.

715 **LETTER XII.**—Rudolph thanks Gregory X, the supreme pontiff, because he had kindly received his dispatched chancellor, promising that he would always remain in every respect most obedient to the Roman Church.

**Ibid. LETTER XIII.**—Rudolph thanks a certain cardinal because he had supported his interests exclusively in the Roman Curia.

718 **LETTER XIV.**—He offers an abbot a first petition on behalf of conferring an ecclesiastical benefice upon someone.

719 **LETTER XV.**—A second petition, but with threats, he addresses to the abbot [Col. 1459] concerning the conferral of the ecclesiastical benefice for which he had previously interceded.

719 **LETTER XVI.**—On the same subject as the two preceding letters.

720 **LETTER XVII.**—He commends a certain man to a bishop, by a first petition, for appointment as a canon.

**Ibid. LETTER XVIII.**—He remits services not rendered during the vacancy of the empire.

721 **LETTER XIX.**—He gives thanks for the congratulation offered to him.

722 **LETTER XX.**—The Pisans invite Rudolph to quell the disturbances of Tuscany.

723 **LETTER XXI.**—The Emperor Rudolph replies to the Pisans.

**Ibid. LETTER XXII.**—Rudolph sends an envoy to the supreme pontiff.

724 **LETTER XXIII.**—Rudolph asks the Roman supreme pontiff to lend him three thousand marks, in addition to the previous loan.

725 **LETTER XXIV.**—He sends Count of Fürstenberg to Italy as governor.

726 **LETTER XXV.**—On the same subject as the preceding letter.

728 **LETTER XXVI.**—To a certain prince of Italy on the same matter.

729 **LETTER XXVII.**—He sends a certain religious man as envoy.

731 **LETTER XXVIII.**—To the pope, he promises that he will come to Milan for the coronation.

**Ibid. LETTER XXIX.**—Rudolph thanks Gregory X, the Roman pontiff, for the confirmation of his election.

732 **LETTER XXX.**—He asks a certain city for financial assistance toward holding the imperial assembly.

733 **LETTER XXXI.**—To a certain prince who had defected from him.

735 **LETTER XXXII.**—Rudolph writes to a certain prince who had joined the king of Bohemia.

**Ibid. LETTER XXXIII.**—He promises the pontiff that he will carry out his reform against the exorbitant bishops of Germany.

737 **LETTER XXXIV.**—Rudolph thanks a certain prince for the letters he sent, and indicates that he had held a familiar conversation with the pontiff at Lausanne.

**Ibid. LETTER XXXV.**—To a certain city on the same subject.

738 **LETTER XXXVI.**—He thanks a certain prince because the prince had preceded him into Italy in order to receive the imperial crown.

739 **LETTER XXXVII.**—He attempts to reconcile the same prince with his brother.

740 **LETTER XXXVIII.**—The archbishop of Salzburg promises that he will come to the coronation.

742 **LETTER XXXIX.**—The final letter of Gregory X, ill at Arezzo in Tuscany, to Rudolph.

743 **LETTER XL.**—He writes to someone in the Roman Curia and clears himself of an unfavorable suspicion.

745 **LETTER XLI.**—A reply to the preceding letter.

746 **LETTER XLII.**—To the cardinals after the death of Gregory X, urging them to choose a good pontiff.

748 **BOOK TWO.**

751 **LETTER I.**—Rudolph congratulates Pope Innocent V on his election as Roman pontiff.

**Ibid. LETTER II.**—Rudolph writes to a cardinal after the death of Gregory X, the supreme pontiff, and commends his envoy to him.

753 **LETTER III.**—He rejoices at the newly elected pontiff and appoints a representative in the Roman Curia.

754 **LETTER IV.**—Pope Innocent commends the Church of Cologne and its archbishop to Emperor Rudolph.

755 **LETTER V.**—He congratulates the new pontiff on his pontifical dignity, humbly commending himself to him.

**Ibid. LETTER VI.**—Rudolph writes back to the king of Hungary and excuses himself for not having granted his requests.

757 **LETTER VII.**—Rudolph promises that he will exact vengeance for a certain crime that had been committed.

758 **LETTER VIII.**—The archbishop of Salzburg accuses before Emperor Rudolph the Bishop of Seckau, his suffragan.

759 **LETTER IX.**—The most serious complaint of the archbishop of Salzburg against Ottokar, king of Bohemia, after the death of Gregory X, the supreme pontiff.

760 **LETTER X.**—Likewise, a more serious complaint of the Bishop of Salzburg to Rudolph against Ottokar, king of Bohemia, from whose tyranny he asks that he and his people be liberated.

761 **LETTER XI.**—The same bishop of Salzburg sends a notary to Emperor Rudolph and repeatedly urges him to prepare himself as soon as possible for the liberation of the bishop and his people. [Col. 1460]

762 **LETTER XII.**—Rudolph replies to the Bishop of Salzburg, thanking him for his exceptional care and vigilance toward Rudolph.

763 **LETTER XIII.**—The same bishop of Salzburg complains to Emperor Rudolph against a certain count concerning the violent occupation of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia.

765 **LETTER XIV.**—The Patriarch of Aquileia writes to Emperor Rudolph about many matters, especially the subjugation of the king of Bohemia.

767 **LETTER XV.**—Concerning the captain of Styria, who devastated all the property of the Church of Salzburg in the name of Ottokar, king of Bohemia; the same bishop of Salzburg writes to Rudolph, asking him for speedy assistance.

769 **LETTER XVI.**—Rudolph writes to the nobles of the kingdom of Hungary that he will soon take vengeance on their enemy, the king of Bohemia.

770 **LETTER XVII.**—Emperor Rudolph commends his firstborn son, whom he is sending ahead into Austria with military forces, to a certain prince, asking that he assist him in all things.

771 **LETTER XVIII.**—Emperor Rudolph informs a certain duke that he is going to march against the Bohemian, and asks him to occupy the nearer camps.

773 **LETTER XIX.**—Emperor Rudolph excuses himself to the Roman pontiff for not having come at the appointed time to receive the imperial crown.

**Ibid. LETTER XX.**—He summons Ladislaus, king of Hungary, and Andrew, duke of Slavonia, against the king of Bohemia.

774 **LETTER XXI.**—Rudolph invites the commander of an army to military service.

775 **LETTER XXII.**—Frederick, archbishop of Salzburg, absolves his diocesan subjects from the oath sworn to a certain prince.

776 **LETTER XXIII.**—Rudolph writes to the king of Hungary for assistance against the Bohemian.

777 **LETTER XXIV.**—Rudolph accepts someone’s excuse, but in such a way that he does not wish that person to serve as mediator of peace between himself and the king of Bohemia.

778 **LETTER XXV.**—Rudolph urges a kinsman to set out with him against the king of Bohemia.

779 **LETTER XXVI.**—Rudolph confers an office in the empire upon a certain prince and invites him to join the war, and, through him, others as well.

780 **LETTER XXVII.**—Rudolph congratulates a certain prince on the agreement that has been concluded and urges him against the Bohemian.

781 **LETTER XXVIII.**—Rudolph writes to a certain person about the defection of the Carinthians from Ottokar, king of Bohemia.

783 **LETTER XXIX.**—The archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans joyfully announce to the Roman supreme pontiff, through Emperor Rudolph, the liberation of Austria from the tyranny of Ottokar of Bohemia; they lavishly proclaim Rudolph’s virtues and praises.

**Ibid. LETTER XXX.**—Rudolph praises the king of Hungary for undertaking the war against the king of Bohemia together with him.

785 **LETTER XXXI.**—Rudolph informs a certain person of the terms of the alliance concluded between himself and the king of Hungary.

786 **LETTER XXXII.**—Rudolph informs a certain prince of the notable victory won over the king of Bohemia.

787 **LETTER XXXIII.**—The same Rudolph announces the same victory to the Roman supreme pontiff.

789 **LETTER XXXIV.**—Rudolph, victorious, shows mercy to the children of the defeated Ottokar.

791 **LETTER XXXV.**—Privilege of the city of Brno in Moravia.

**Ibid. LETTER XXXVI.**—Rudolph informs the king of Hungary about the condition of Bohemia and Moravia.

793 **LETTER XXXVII.**—Rudolph writes to the Roman supreme pontiff and most generously grants to the Roman Church everything that it had hitherto requested from him.

794 **BOOK THREE.**

797 **LETTER I.**—The electors of the Holy Roman Empire confirm the donation made by Emperor Rudolph to Empress Anna, his first wife.

**Ibid. LETTER II.**—A certain city congratulates Rudolph on his prosperous successes.

798 **LETTER III.**—On the same subject as the preceding letter.

799 **LETTER IV.**—He entrusts someone with the defense of a devastated monastery.

800 **LETTER V.**—Rudolph congratulates the king of France on the kinship contracted with him.

**Ibid. LETTER VI.**—Rudolph writes to a certain city, praising its loyalty.

801 **LETTER VII.**—Rudolph is distressed that someone had crossed his territory unrecognized. [Col. 1461]

802 **LETTER VIII.**—Rudolph forms a friendship with a certain cardinal.

**Ibid. LETTER IX.**—Rudolph writes to a cardinal, commending himself and the affairs of the empire to him.

803 **LETTER X.**—The citizens of Liège complain about certain clerics.

804 **LETTER XI.**—Rudolph urges the citizens of Mainz to harmony.

805 **LETTER XII.**—Rudolph writes to the clergy of Mainz about the same harmony.

806 **LETTER XIII.**—Rudolph provides for a certain religious house of the Order of Penitents.

**Ibid. LETTER XIV.**—A certain person from the Roman Curia commends someone to Emperor Rudolph.

807 **LETTER XV.**—A certain bishop lays before Rudolph the grievances of his diocese.

**Ibid. LETTER XVI.**—He commends to the counts and barons, and others, a newly elected bishop.

808 **LETTER XVII.**—Privilege of the city of Halle.

810 **LETTER XVIII.**—Rudolph commends the elected archbishop of Cologne to the Roman pontiff.

811 **LETTER XIX.**—Rudolph commends to Philip, king of the French, the monastery of Golden Valley of the Cistercian Order.

812 **LETTER XX.**—Rudolph revokes and invalidates all privileges contrary to the preceding letter, whether already granted or to be granted.

813 **LETTER XXI.**—Rudolph sends an envoy so that harmony may be established between a prince and the citizens.

814 **LETTER XXII.**—Rudolph commends a certain canon to the Church of Liège and asks that they send him back to the Curia as soon as possible.

**Ibid. LETTER XXIII.**—Rudolph confirms the judgment of the Bishop of Liège concerning the establishment of the boundaries of duels.

815 **LETTER XXIV.**—Rudolph again commends the monastery of Golden Valley to the king of the French.

816 **LETTER XXV.**—Rudolph takes the Hospitallers of the Teutonic House under his special protection.

817 **LETTER XXVI.**—Rudolph receives the brothers of the Hospital of Saint John in Jerusalem under his protection and confirms their privileges.

819 **LETTER XXVII.**—The Patriarch of Jerusalem urges Rudolph to undertake the passage overseas, setting out the dangers facing the Holy Land.

820 **LETTER XXVIII.**—Rudolph writes to the Bishop of Trent about arranging an amicable settlement with the count of Tyrol.

822 **LETTER XXIX.**—Rudolph writes to the queen of France about renewing the homage.

823 **LETTER XXX.**—Rudolph writes to an archbishop, urging him to judge justly.

825 **LETTER XXXI.**—Rudolph grants a certain person certain mountains to cultivate.

826 **LETTER XXXII.**—Rudolph commends a certain abbot to a bishop.

**Ibid. LETTER XXXIII.**—Rudolph sympathizes with a certain person and consoles him.

827 **LETTER XXXIV.**—Rudolph grants a certain prince the authority to mint money.

**Ibid. LETTER XXXV.**—Rudolph orders that the coinage which he had authorized a certain nobleman to mint be accepted without any impediment.

828 **LETTER XXXVI.**—Rudolph confirms the privilege of a certain monastery.

829 **LETTER XXXVII.**—Rudolph restores an infamous person to his former rank.

830 **LETTER XXXVIII.**—Upon the death of the representative, Rudolph appoints another in the Roman Curia.

831 **LETTER XXXIX.**—The king of Cyprus writes to Rudolph, asking him to write about his successes.

832 **LETTER XL.**—The Patriarch of Jerusalem writes to Rudolph concerning assistance for the Holy Land.

833 **LETTER XLI.**—Rudolph receives a five-year-old orphan under his protection.

836 **LETTER XLII.**—Rudolph remonstrates with a certain person.

837 **LETTER XLIII.**—Rudolph writes against those who improperly exact tolls.

838 **LETTER XLIV.**—Rudolph commends a certain person for an ecclesiastical benefice.

839 **LETTER XLV.**—Rudolph writes concerning someone’s rebellion.

840 **LETTER XLVI.**—Rudolph commends a certain learned man.

**Ibid. LETTER XLVII.**—Rudolph approves certain chapters against heresies issued by Emperor Frederick.

841 **Dissertation on the Diploma of Rudolph, King of the Romans, Confirmed by the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire.**

843 [Col. 1462] **§ 1. All the rights of the Holy See are confirmed.**

843 **§ 2. Concerning the kingdom of Sicily, both on this side of the Strait and beyond it.**

863 **II.**—Diploma of the princes of the empire concerning Emperor Rudolph’s donation and the confirmation of the privileges of the Apostolic See.

869 **III.**—Diploma by which Rudolph protects ecclesiastical rights through a strict edict.

**Ibid. LETTER II, or Decree Concerning the Schools of the Church of Osnabrück.**

895 **LETTER IV.**—To his subjects.—Concerning the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino.

896 **LETTER V.**—To Queen Fastrada.—Concerning the victory over the Avars and the litanies.

897 **LETTER VI.**—To Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain.—In it the three preceding little books are also mentioned.

899 **LETTER VII.**—To Pope Leo III.—Sent through Angilbert, abbot of Centula.

907 **LETTER VIII.**—To Angilbert, abbot.—A reminder to Angilbert, who was being sent to the pontiff with the preceding letter.

909 **LETTER IX.**—To Abbot Manasses.

**Ibid. LETTER X.**—A fragment of a letter to the bishops.

910 **LETTER XI.**—To Offa, king of the Mercians.—He sends an accused Scottish priest back to his homeland, to be judged there by his own bishop.

**Ibid. LETTER XII.**—To Abbot Albinus.

911 **LETTER XIII.**—To five bishops.—Concerning the sevenfold grace of the Spirit.

914 **LETTER XIV.**—To Garibald, bishop of Liège.—Concerning the care that pastors ought especially to devote to instructing the peoples entrusted to them before baptism.

917 **LETTER XV.**—To Garibald, bishop.—A fast is proclaimed for public needs, especially for famine, plague, and war.

918 **LETTER XVI.**—To Pippin, his son and king of Italy.—Concerning peace among the Churches of God and those who serve them.

920 **LETTER XVII.**—To Albinus, master, and the congregation of the monastery of Saint Martin.

921 **LETTER XVIII.**—To Pope Leo III.—Issued by Abbot Zmaragdus.

923 **LETTER XIX.**—To Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople.—He expresses his joy at the repeated embassy sent to establish peace between the two empires.

929 **LETTER XX.**—To Emperor Michael.—Concerning the strengthening of peace between the two empires.

931 **LETTER XXI.**—To Odilbert, archbishop.

933 **LETTER XXII.**—To Athilard (Aedilhard), archbishop, and Ceolwulf.—He commends certain exiles to them.

934 **LETTER XXIII.**—To Fulrad, abbot of Altaich.—He orders him to appear with well-armed men at the place called Starasfurt.

935 **Appendix to the Letters of Blessed Charlemagne.**

937 **III. Letter to Emperor Charlemagne.**—Concerning the rites of baptism.

938 **IV. Reply of an Anonymous Writer to the Chapters Sent by Charlemagne in the Year of Our Lord 811 to the Archbishops of the Kingdom of the Franks.**

939 **CHAPTER ONE.**—How and in what manner each priest of God should commend, preach to, and govern the people entrusted to him by God.

940 **CHAPTER II.**—Concerning the entire holy mystery of baptism, and the order in which we ought to celebrate it.

**Ibid. CHAPTER III.**—Why one becomes a catechumen, in what language, and what the term means.

**Ibid. CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning ecclesiastical scrutiny: why scrutiny is conducted, at what time, and what scrutiny is.

941 **SECTION TWO: THE CAROLINE BOOKS.**

**Ibid. PROLEGOMENA.**

**Ibid. Dissertation of Baronius on the Council of Frankfurt.**

**Ibid. Notice to the Reader by Francis Laurentius Surius Concerning the Synod of Frankfurt.** [Col. 1463]

965 **Mansi’s Note on the Same Synod.**

**Ibid. Extracts from the Dissertation of Natalis Alexander on Images.**
