**Ibid. § 2. The response of those who wrote that the Caroline Books were the work of some heretic is refuted, and it is shown that their author was Charlemagne.**

975 **§ 3. Replies are made to the objections drawn from the Caroline Books.**

979 **Capitulary of Blessed Charlemagne, King of the Franks and Lombards, Patrician of the Romans, Son and Defender of the Holy Church of God, Concerning Images, Against the Decree of Constantine VII, Emperor of Constantinople, and His Mother Irene, and Against the Second Council of Nicaea, the Pseudo-Seventh Ecumenical or Universal Council; Composed and Published at the Council of Frankfurt and Sent to Pope Hadrian in the Year of Our Lord 794.**

989 **Preface of Tile, Bishop of Meaux.**

**Ibid. Testimonies of Ancient Writers.**

995 **Preface of Charlemagne.**

999 **BOOK ONE.**

1005 **CHAPTER ONE.**—Concerning what Constantine and Irene say in their writings: “Through him, the God who reigns with us.”

**Ibid. CHAPTER II.**—Concerning what Constantine and Irene wrote in their letter addressed to the venerable Pope Hadrian of the Apostolic See: “God, who chooses us as we seek his glory in truth.”

1011 **CHAPTER III.**—Concerning the fact that Constantine and Irene call their acts or writings “imperial.”

1014 **CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning what Constantine and Irene wrote in their letter to the venerable Pope Hadrian of the city of Rome: “We ask your fatherhood—and above all, God asks it, who wishes no human being to perish.”

1016 **CHAPTER V.**—That it is no small sacrilege to understand the Holy Scriptures otherwise than they ought to be understood and to adapt them to meanings that they do not contain, as happened in the erroneous synod held in Bithynia under Constantine, with his mother Irene present and Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, presiding.

1018 **CHAPTER VI.**—That the holy Roman, Catholic, and Apostolic Church, placed above the other Churches, must be consulted entirely when a question concerning the faith arises.

1019 **CHAPTER VII.**—That the statement “God created man in his own image and likeness” (Genesis I) does not concern the worship of images.

1022 **CHAPTER VIII.**—What the difference is between image and likeness, or equality.

1025 **CHAPTER IX.**—How the statement “Abraham worshiped the people of the land, the sons of Heth” (Genesis XXIII), or the statement that Moses is read to have worshiped Jethro, is to be understood. By these examples those who hold synods on account of the worship of images seek to support their error; and yet neither Jacob is ever read to have worshiped Pharaoh, nor Daniel Nebuchadnezzar the king, as they claim.

1027 **CHAPTER X.**—Concerning the statement that John the presbyter and envoy of the Easterners, attempting rashly to establish the worship of images, is read to have said: “Jacob erected a pillar to God, and thus blessed him” (Genesis XXXV).

1029 **CHAPTER XI.**—Concerning the statement made by the aforementioned John: “He wrestled with him in human form, and called him Israel, which is interpreted as ‘a mind seeing God.’”

1031 **CHAPTER XII.**—That the statement which they make—“Jacob, receiving from his sons Joseph’s decayed long robe, kissed it with tears and placed it before his own eyes” (Genesis XXXVII)—does not concern the worship of images and is not found in our books translated from the Hebrew truth.

1032 **CHAPTER XIII.**—Concerning the ignorant and disorderly statement: “If you accuse me because I worship the wood of the cross as God, why do you not accuse Jacob, who worshiped the top of Joseph’s staff? But it is clear that he did not worship while looking at the wood; rather, through the wood he worshiped Joseph, just as we worship Christ through the cross.”

1034 **CHAPTER XIV.**—That the statement “Jacob blessed Pharaoh” (Genesis XLVII) does not concern the worship of images, as they claim.

1035 **CHAPTER XV.**—How absurdly those act who, to confirm images, produce the example of the divine law, saying: “At the Lord’s command Moses made the mercy seat, the two golden cherubim, and the ark of the covenant.”

1036 **CHAPTER XVI.**—That even from this the practice of worshiping images cannot be established, as they most foolishly and irrationally claim, on the basis of what is written in the law: “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, to complete the work from gold and silver; and I gave him Oholiab, son of Ahisamach” (Exodus XXXI). [Col. 1464]

1039 **CHAPTER XVII.**—That those who say the following do not think correctly: “If, according to the lawful tradition of Moses, the people are commanded to place purple and hyacinth-colored material on the fringes, at the edges of their garments, as a memorial and safeguard of the commandments, much more ought we, through a likeness depicted in painting, to see the outcome of the conduct of holy men and imitate their faith according to apostolic tradition.”

1042 **CHAPTER XVIII.**—That the hope of those who place their salvation in images is vain when they say: “Just as the Israelite people were saved by looking at the bronze serpent, so we shall be saved by looking at the likenesses of the saints.”

1046 **CHAPTER XIX.**—That it is greatly rash to say: “Just as tablets and two cherubim were given to the Jews, so the cross and images of the saints have been given to us Christians, for writing and worship.”

1047 **CHAPTER XX.**—That Tarasius is recognized as having raved no less than all the others, and almost more than them all, when he says: “Just as the ancients had cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat, so let us have images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God, and of all his saints overshadowing the altar.”

1049 **CHAPTER XXI.**—That the presbyter John did not think correctly when, in order to establish the worship of images, he said: “Joshua son of Nun also set up twelve stones in memory of God.”

1052 **CHAPTER XXII.**—That the worship offered by the prophet Nathan to King David is not equal to the worship of images, as they claim.

1053 **CHAPTER XXIII.**—That in the statements “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” and “Your countenance, O Lord, I shall seek,” nothing concerning a handmade image is to be understood, as they claim.

1056 **CHAPTER XXIV.**—That the statement “All the rich among the people will entreat your countenance,” as they assert, does not concern any handmade image.

1057 **CHAPTER XXV.**—The inappropriate and delirious statement of Leo, bishop of Phocaea, who, having turned to the worship of images, applies to himself a verse of the Psalmist, saying: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness.”

1058 **CHAPTER XXVI.**—That the Psalmist’s declaration—“Everyone has spoken vainly to his neighbor, with deceitful lips in his mouth, and so forth”—does not concern those who despise the worship of images.

1059 **CHAPTER XXVII.**—That the statement “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things” (Psalm XII) does not concern their forebears, as they claim.

1060 **CHAPTER XXVIII.**—That the statement “The swords of the enemies have failed completely, and you have destroyed their cities” (Psalm IX) was not fulfilled in their forebears, as they claim.

1061 **CHAPTER XXIX.**—How the statement “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” is to be understood; they interpret this beauty as images.

1062 **CHAPTER XXX.**—That the Psalmist did not speak concerning manufactured images, as they claim, when he said: “As we have heard, so also we have seen” (Psalm XLVIII).

1065 **BOOK TWO.**

**Ibid. Preface.**

**Ibid. CHAPTER ONE.**—That the statement “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places” was not written on account of those who refuse to worship images, as those who worship them claim.

1067 **CHAPTER II.**—That the statement “For there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us” does not concern this matter either, as they claim.

1068 **CHAPTER III.**—How the statement “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” is to be understood. As with the other passages, they understand this chapter differently from what was said.

**Ibid. CHAPTER IV.**—How the Psalmist’s statement “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have embraced one another” (Psalm LXXXV) is to be understood. John the presbyter and envoy of the Easterners rashly and flatteringly claims that this was fulfilled through the participation of the venerable Pope Hadrian and the patriarch Tarasius.

1070 **CHAPTER V.**—That the statement “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship his footstool, for he is holy” (Psalm XCIX) does not concern the worship of images, as they claim.

1071 **CHAPTER VI.**—That the worship of images cannot be established from the statement “Worship on his holy mountain,” as they think.

1072 **CHAPTER VII.**—That the statement “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Psalm CXXV) was not spoken, as they boast, on account of those who worship images. [Col. 1465]

1073 **CHAPTER VIII.**—That the prophet does not say, on account of those who despise the worship of images, as they deliriously claim: “He will lead those who turn aside to bondage along with those who practice iniquity” (Psalm CXXV).

1074 **CHAPTER IX.**—That the worship of images cannot be confirmed from the fact that Solomon is said to have made oxen and lions in the Temple, as those who yearn for their worship dream.

**Ibid. CHAPTER X.**—How the statement written in the Song of Songs is to be understood: “Show me your face, and make me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet to me and your face is beautiful” (Song of Songs II). They most shamelessly produced this passage as referring to the sight of images.

1075 **CHAPTER XI.**—How the statement written through the prophet Isaiah—“The altar of the Lord shall be in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Isaiah X)—is to be understood. They foolishly and with little learning attempt to refer this passage to the worship of images.

1076 **CHAPTER XII.**—The testimony of the Holy Gospel—“No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel” (Matthew V; Mark IV; Luke XI)—is brought forward most absurdly and rashly by those who worship images against those who refuse to worship them.

1077 **CHAPTER XIII.**—Concerning their claim, made to confirm their error, that blessed Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, brought images of the apostles to Emperor Constantine, although he is not read to have commanded that they be worshiped.

1078 **CHAPTER XIV.**—That the statement of blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, is not to be understood in the way those who attempt to adapt it to the worship of images think it should be understood.

**Ibid. CHAPTER XV.**—That those who wish to establish the worship of images improperly appropriate, in support of their error, a statement of blessed Ambrose, bishop of the city of Milan, which they falsely claim comes from Book Three, Chapter Nine.

1079 **CHAPTER XVI.**—That blessed Augustine did not speak of material images when he said: “What is the image of God except the face of God, in which the people of God have been marked?”

1080 **CHAPTER XVII.**—That the life and preaching of Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, from whom they draw testimonies to establish their error, are unknown to us.

1082 **CHAPTER XVIII.**—That the testimony they produced from the Sixth Synod does not concern the worship of images.

**Ibid. CHAPTER XIX.**—That the statement of John, bishop of Constantinople, which they invoke as testimony for the worship of images, is recognized not to concern what they think it concerns.

**Ibid. CHAPTER XX.**—That the statement of blessed Cyril in his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew does not concern the worship of images, as they assert.

1084 **CHAPTER XXI.**—That it is not contrary to the Christian religion, as they claim, not to honor and not to worship images.

1085 **CHAPTER XXII.**—That those who erect images so as not to forget the saints, or indeed the Lord himself, do not possess a good memory.

1086 **CHAPTER XXIII.**—That the practice of worshiping or destroying images was established contrary to the judgment of blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome.

1087 **CHAPTER XXIV.**—Since nothing other than God alone ought to be worshiped, worshiping a human being as an act of charity and greeting is one thing, and worshiping handmade images is another.

1089 **CHAPTER XXV.**—That nowhere, from apostolic examples or words, as they chatter, was the worship of images instituted.

1090 **CHAPTER XXVI.**—That it is no small error to attempt to equate handmade images with the ark of the Lord’s covenant, as they attempted to do in their synod.

1091 **CHAPTER XXVII.**—That it is greatly rash and immensely absurd to wish to equate the often-mentioned images with the Lord’s body and blood, as is read in the same vanity written on their behalf.

1093 **CHAPTER XXVIII.**—How greatly, and for what reasons, the mystery of the Lord’s cross differs from the images, which they nevertheless strive to equate with it.

1096 **CHAPTER XXIX.**—That Tarasius, with his followers, does not fear presumptuously and ignorantly to equate them with sacred vessels.

1098 **CHAPTER XXX.**—Against those who say: “Just as we have the books of divine Scripture, so we have images for the memory of veneration, observing the purity of our faith.”

1099 [Col. 1466] **CHAPTER XXXI.**—That those who anathematize their forebears act contrary to the command of the Lord’s voice; and if, according to their opinion, their predecessors were heretics, then these men were born, taught, and consecrated by heretics. The chapter also concerns the fact that those who have departed from this world are not to be judged, and how far the error of these men differs from the error of their forebears, since the former judged that images should be destroyed, whereas the latter judge that they should be worshiped.

1111 **BOOK THREE.**

**Ibid. Preface.**

**Ibid. CHAPTER ONE.**—The confession of the Catholic faith that we have received from the holy Fathers, hold, and believe with a pure heart.

1113 **CHAPTER II.**—That Tarasius attempted to heal one error with another and slipped from one sickness into another, since, having suddenly converted from the laity and been promoted to the episcopate, he tries to amend in the worship of images what he committed in his sudden acceptance of consecration.

1115 **CHAPTER III.**—Whether Tarasius thinks correctly when, contrary to the truest rule of the holy faith, he professes in his declaration of faith that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father and the Son but from the Father through the Son.

1117 **CHAPTER IV.**—Whether Theodore, bishop of Jerusalem, thinks correctly when, although he says that he believes the Father to be wholly without beginning and eternal, he nevertheless professes the Son, through some obscure entanglement of words, as acknowledging no other beginning than the Father and having his subsistence from him.

1121 **CHAPTER V.**—That Tarasius incorrectly called the Holy Spirit of the same tribe as the Father and the Son, when it would have been sufficient to call him coeternal, consubstantial, and of the same essence and nature.

1123 **CHAPTER VI.**—Concerning the fact that Basil, bishop of Ancyra, inserted into his profession of faith, after confessing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the kissing and worship of images and relics, saying that he possessed faith by participating in their sanctification; but he entirely omitted the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the life to come.

1124 **CHAPTER VII.**—Concerning the fact that Theodore, bishop of Amorium, negligently kept silent about the faith of the holy and unique Trinity, but spoke rashly and extraordinarily about images: “I confess and promise, and I receive, and I kiss, and I worship the images”; and shortly afterward: “Whoever does not diligently instruct every people beloved by Christ to worship and venerate the sacred and honored images of all the saints who have pleased God from the beginning of the world, let him be anathema.”

1127 **CHAPTER VIII.**—That there is almost doubt concerning everyone’s faith, since some have confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, while others have confessed that he proceeds neither from the Father nor from the Son.

1129 **CHAPTER IX.**—That if perhaps some error in the statements about the faith delivered by the aforementioned bishops has remained unexamined, it will remain so because of the difficulty and enormity of their language, which is often so covered with indolence that it is hardly clear what it wishes to signify or what sense is to be understood in it.

1129 **CHAPTER X.**—The statement in Bishop Theodore’s profession of faith is ridiculous and childish: “God is wondrous in his saints”; and immediately afterward: “He has made all my desires wondrous among them, the saints who are on earth,” as though this verse followed the preceding one.

1131 **CHAPTER XI.**—That the Greeks attempted uselessly and rashly to anathematize the Catholic Church in their synod because it does not worship images, although they ought first to have thoroughly investigated what the Church of each party thinks about this matter.

**Ibid. CHAPTER XII.**—That they largely cast aside gentleness and patience by not restraining their mouths and by speaking disorderly.

1133 **CHAPTER XIII.**—That a woman ought not to teach in a synod, as Irene is read to have done in their synod.

1136 **CHAPTER XIV.**—Against those who say: “As God’s co-workers, we directed ourselves to assemble you,” or “God assembled you, wishing to establish his own counsel.”

1138 **CHAPTER XV.**—Against those who say: “For if, when imperial likenesses and images are sent into cities and provinces, the peoples meet them with candles and incense—not honoring a board covered with wax, but the emperor—how much more ought images of our Savior God, of his undefiled mother, and of all the saints to be painted in the Churches of Christ?”

1142 **CHAPTER XVI.**—Against those who say that ...
the honor of the image passes over to the original form. 1146

**CHAPTER XVII.**—That Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, spoke disastrously and rashly, or foolishly: “I receive and honorably embrace the holy and venerable images according to the service of worship which I offer to the consubstantial and life-giving Trinity; and those who do not think or glorify in this manner I separate from the holy catholic and apostolic Church, subject them to an anathema, and consign them to the party that denied the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.” 1148

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—That Euthymius, bishop of Sardis, does not differ greatly from the error of the aforementioned Constantine, in that he says: “With my whole heart I receive the venerable images with fitting honor and embracing worship. For, judging those who think or teach otherwise or contrary to the holy images to be strangers to the catholic Church, I both designate and proclaim them heretics.” 1150

**CHAPTER XIX.**—The useless, foolish, and laughable statement of Agapius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is refuted, in that he said: “It is written in our divine Scriptures.” 1152

**CHAPTER XX.**—That when John the presbyter heard Theodosius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew, reciting the words of John Chrysostom and saying, “I saw an angel in an image pursuing a multitude of barbarians,” he said: “Who is this angel, unless he is the one of whom it is written: ‘For the angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians who were encamped around Jerusalem in a single night’?” 1153

**CHAPTER XXI.**—That there is no authority for, nor is it found in any authentic book, what they say: that by means of an image of a certain Polemon someone was restrained from committing adultery. They attempt to make this equal to the miracle effected through the fringe of the Lord’s garment, which the woman touched and thereby received the healing she desired. 1156

**CHAPTER XXII.**—That the judges who were present at the aforementioned synod insolently and incongruously attempted to extol the art of painting, saying: “For the painter’s art is pious, and certain foolish people wrongly disparage it; indeed, the Father himself commends the painter who acts piously.” 1159

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—The useless and lie-filled statement of John the presbyter and legate of the Easterners is refuted, when he says: “Painters do not contradict the Scriptures; rather, whatever Scripture says, they display, insofar as they agree with the Scriptures.” 1161

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—That images are not to be equated with the relics of holy martyrs and confessors, as they attempt to do in their erroneous synod, since relics are either from the body, or from things that were in the body, or from things that were around the body of a particular saint; whereas images neither were nor, according to them, are believed to be in the body or around the body of those to whom they are attributed. 1165

**CHAPTER XXV.**—That images are not therefore to be worshiped because they suppose that certain signs have been displayed through them, as they say, since not all things through which or in which miracles appear are worshiped. 1167

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—That Theodore, bishop of Myra, acted ridiculously and childishly when, in order to establish the worship of images, he related at the same synod the dreams of his archdeacon. 1170

**CHAPTER XXVII.**—That since God is not confined to a place, they spoke with insufficient learning when they said: “We venerate and worship as though it were the place of God.” 1173

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—The useless, foolish, and error-filled statement that they make: “Whoever fears God honors him entirely, worships and venerates him, as well as Christ our God, the Son of God, and the sign of his cross, and the image of his saints.” 1175

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—The utterly foolish and irrational statement of John the presbyter of the Easterners, in that he says that when the emperor is not present, his image is honored: “For it is not dishonored, just as even now Jesus Christ, the ruler of all, although he is not visibly apparent to us—for he is invisible to our bodily eyes—is honored. Just as God is everywhere present, so his image is to be honored, as the Father also understood concerning the emperor.” 1178

**CHAPTER XXX.**—That they inserted into their speeches apocryphal and laughable fables. 1179

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—A delirious statement full of error concerning a certain recluse, of whom it is reported that he swore to a demon and then invalidated that very oath. His abbot is recognized as having been not a little delirious when he said that it would be more advantageous for him to enter all the brothels in the city than to deny the worship of the image of the Lord or of his holy mother. 1180

# BOOK FOUR. 1181

**Preface.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER I.**—The utterly false and laughable statement of John the presbyter, who is recognized as having raved no less than the others in the worship of images. For he says: “Whoever worships an image and says, ‘This is Christ, the Son of God,’ does not sin.” 1183

**CHAPTER II.**—Concerning John’s incorrect statement: “Through the image that appears by means of colors, his power is worshiped and glorified, and we shall come to the remembrance of his presence on earth.” 1185

**CHAPTER III.**—Concerning what they say: “One should not give offense on account of the fact that lamps and fragrant incense are offered before images of the saints.” 1187

**CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning what they say: “The person who despises images is guilty of the same crime as Nebuchadnezzar, who brought out the bones of the kings of Judah from their tombs, tore out the eyes of the Jewish king after killing his sons, and removed the cherubim from the temple.” 1189

**CHAPTER V.**—That the letter which they foolishly call that of Saint Simeon, sent to the emperor Justinian, is very far from the divine Scriptures and from the teachings of the holy Fathers, both in what it says to the aforementioned emperor—“For these things we recall and report to your divine ears”—and in that it forbade the same emperor to show mercy. 1191

**CHAPTER VI.**—Concerning the fact that they call those who destroy images worse than all heretics, and worse than the Samaritans, although, according to their own opinion, their parents were worse than all heretics, since those parents certainly destroyed images. 1197

**CHAPTER VII.**—Concerning the fact that the more examples they draw from heretics who rejected or despised images, the more they dishonor their parents with greater insults and injuries, while unquestionably confessing that their parents were their followers in this respect. 1199

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Concerning the fact that, according to the statement of the deacon Demetrius, their parents acted carelessly and disorderly: they burned two books covered with silver because they contained something about images, and cut out two leaves of another book. 1200

**CHAPTER IX.**—Concerning the fact that in the same book, on silver tablets, Leontius the *a secretis*, seeing images, boasted that he had discovered the sharpest and most ingenious advantage of his error. 1201

**CHAPTER X.**—That no Gospel reading relates that Jesus sent an image to Abgar, as they say. 1202

**CHAPTER XI.**—That those books of the deeds of the Fathers, whose authors are unknown, are not entirely suitable for providing testimony or affirming the matters under dispute. 1203

**CHAPTER XII.**—Concerning the fact that Dionysius, presbyter of the church of Ascalon, is reported to have related at the same synod that a certain monk lit a lamp before an image of Saint Mary ever-virgin and, returning after the third, fifth, or even sixth month, found it still unextinguished. 1205

**CHAPTER XIII.**—That this synod can in no way be compared with the Council of Nicaea, although it was held in the same place, as the presbyter John is reported to have said flatteringly, since it is known to differ from it not only in other matters but also in the Creed. 1206

**CHAPTER XIV.**—Concerning what Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, says: “Let those rejoice and exult, and let those presume who, graciously making, loving, and venerating the true image of Christ, offer it for the salvation of soul and body—an image which he himself, the perfecter of the sacrifice and God, receiving from us our entire substance according to the time of his voluntary passion, manifested and delivered to his disciples as a sign and clear memorial.” 1213

**CHAPTER XV.**—Concerning what the deacon Epiphanius, wishing to establish the worship of images, said: “For here, having erected the Lord’s inscription and touching it itself at the fringes of the inscription, just as the holy Gospel indeed relates, she obtained salvation between it and the Lord’s image; a certain plant sprang up which, approaching the foot of the inscription, heals all illnesses.” [The Latin is corrupt; the precise relation among the woman, the inscription, and the image is uncertain.] 1215

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The useless statement of the deacon Epiphanius is refuted, in that he says: “Many things that are consecrated among us do not receive consecrated prayer”; and shortly afterward: “Nor do we venerate and magnify them in the highest degree as venerable things. For he says that the sign of the life-giving cross, without prayer, is to be venerated by us; and we shall be satisfied to receive his sign, sanctification through which certain people perform worship of him by the sanctification made by us on the forehead. We hope likewise that demons are driven away by the sign made in the air with the finger; similarly, by the image, through the name of the sign, we lead it back to the original form of honor, and by kissing it and honoring it honorably we shall receive sanctification. For we also kiss and embrace the various sacred vessels that we possess, and hope for a certain sanctification.” 1216

**CHAPTER XVII.**—The most ridiculous statement of Epiphanius is refuted, in that he says: “He spoke from his own belly.” 1220

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—Against those who say: “Those who called the image of idols similar to images of demons should accuse Abel and Noah and Abraham and Moses and Samuel and David, because they themselves offered foreign and pagan sacrifices to God.” 1221

**CHAPTER XIX.**—Against those who say: “If Saint Epiphanius was a destroyer and hater of images, how did his disciples paint images on the island of Cyprus in the church which they dedicated under the name of that same Father, when indeed many things are painted that are not worshiped, and bad disciples often arise from good teachers?” 1224

**CHAPTER XX.**—That they attempted flatteringly to compare their emperor or his mother with the apostles, saying: “Just as formerly Jesus, the ruler and perfecter of our salvation, sent forth his own apostles clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit, so now he has raised up our own faithful emperors, pleasing and like the apostles, made wise by the same Spirit and possessing power sufficient for our perfection.” 1226

**CHAPTER XXI.**—Concerning what they said: “For prophecy says: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son’ (Isaiah 7). Seeing this prophecy in an image—namely, a virgin carrying in her arms the one whom she bore—how shall we endure not to worship and kiss it? Who, undisciplined in mind, will dare to resist? Let us make ourselves worthy of such a kiss of worship, lest, approaching unworthily, we suffer the punishment of Uzzah.” 1229

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Concerning the fact that they do not even spare themselves when they inflict injury on their parents, saying: “Instead of true wheat they sowed weeds in the ecclesiastical fields; they mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a turbulent drink of destruction; being Arabian wolves, they mocked the wearing of sheep’s clothing; passing over the truth, they embraced falsehood; but they cast the eggs of vipers and, according to the prophet, wove spiders’ webs. Whoever hopes to eat their eggs will find, when he breaks the tail, a basilisk within, filled with poison and deadly breath.” 1231

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—The useless and unlearned interpretation of those who, wishing to assert that worship and kissing are one and the same, said: “Each of the holy leaders of our teaching and their successors [has] praised the distinguished [practice] of our Fathers, namely, that these should be worshiped—that is, kissed—for the same thing is meant by both. In the common usage of ancient Greek, ‘to kiss’ and ‘to embrace’ signify something, as do *fero* and *offero*, *firmo* and *confirmo*, *participo* and *adoro*; this demonstrates the kiss and the extension of friendship. For whatever someone loves, he worships; and whatever he worships, he certainly loves.” 1233

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—Concerning what they said arrogantly and without learning: “Likewise, we joined those who came from the East in the same metropolitan city of Nicaea, and, presiding over all, we made Christ the head.” 1239

**CHAPTER XXV.**—Against those who say that Epiphanius compiled eighty chapters concerning heresies, although, if he had known that worshiping images was a heresy, he would also have counted it among the heresies. 1241

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—Against those who call images holy and sacred, and command that they be placed on roads or in streets, which are for the most part polluted. 1243

**CHAPTER XXVII.**—That the worshipers of images can be deceived by poorly painted images; or rather, it should be asked of those who regard nearly the whole prerogative of the Christian faith as consisting in the worship or cult of images what the poor are to do, since they entirely lack artisans by whom images are made. 1244

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—That they call their synod universal in vain, since it is clear that it was not assembled by the universal Church. 1246

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—Conclusion. 1248

**Appendix to the Capitular of the Blessed Charles the Great on Images.**—Containing: 1. Pope Hadrian’s letter to the blessed King Charles concerning images, by which those who attacked the Second Council of Nicaea are refuted; 2. The Parisian assembly concerning images, held at Paris in the palace on the Kalends of November, in the year of Christ 824, in the first year of Pope Eugenius II and the eleventh year of Louis the Pious Augustus. 1247–1349
